en: We shall explain the sacrifice.
It is ordained by three Vedas:
by the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda; by all of them together, the Jyotiṣṭoma is performed.
The New and Full Moon sacrifices are [performed] by means of the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda;
the Agnihotra is [performed] by means of the Yajurveda; and the rites characterized by injunctions are likewise [performed by the Yajurveda].
The name "Veda" applies to both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas.
The Brāhmaṇas consist of the injunctions for ritual action;
the explanatory passages (arthavādas) are supplementary to them.
Censure and praise;
the deeds of others and ancient legends;
other than these are the mantras.
Worldly practices employed [in common parlance] are without mantras;
mantras are for the purpose of sacrificial rites.
Because of the exclusion of [Vedic] form, [mantras do not apply] to worldly matters.

"Just as I take your hand for the sake of good progeny, so do I dig this herb; carry the fat to the ancestors, O Jātavedas"—thus [he says]. Those who possess the Brāhmaṇa [text] act according to what is taught therein; others act according to the form [of the rite]. This is the disposal of the remainder.
The verses of the ten maṇḍalas have wandering meanings;
the Sāmans are for the repetition of the Stomas in the two subsequent Pavamānas;
and the Yajus is for the silent (tūṣṇīka) original [verses].
The Veda, when heard by means of the name of a ritual action, has that [action] as its meaning;
for example, the *vājapeya* sacrifice and the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses.
These are performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) according to the *Yajurveda*.
Except for the *pravara*, the *saṃvāda*, the *āśrāvaṇa*, and the *saṃpraiṣa*, [the formulas] are recited loudly; all others are recited in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, prior to the Agnīṣomīya offering,
whatever is performed for a specific purpose constitutes a single mantra;
the mantras are prescribed from the beginning.
One should know the end of the preceding [formula] by means of the beginning of the succeeding one (2).
One should bring the ritual act into conjunction with the end of the mantra.
While the act is being performed, the duties of the Hotṛ are recited.
Ritual acts have a single mantra;
the *hautra* formulas should be accumulated together,
except for the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses.
Where the purpose is accomplished in a single substance through a single performance, one should recite the mantra only once;
as, for example, in the case of sprinkling (*prokṣa*) and the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpacchedana*).
When there is a plurality of substances, [the mantra] is repeated.
As in the case of taking the clarified butter, cutting, and spreading;
because the purposes are distinct, the mantra for scratching is repeated.
Those acts performed for the sake of another may be done by a single person.
With that [formula] with which he scatters [the earth] using a skull, the Audumbarī post becomes one that is joined with the sacrificer.
The Adhvaryu performs his duties with the Yajurveda;
the Hotṛ with the Ṛgveda.
The Udgātṛ [sings] with the Sāmaveda;
the Brahman [priest acts] with all [the Vedas];
the others are characterized by their specific verbal functions.
Or because of impossibility,
as in the animal sacrifices of the Aśvamedha,
where oblations are offered with the *juhū* ladle into the Āhavanīya fire.
The monastery has its ritual services performed on the north side. || 2 ||
One who performs the ritual acts while facing east or north, keeping them to the right,
does not pass around himself or another with a limb of the sacrifice,
nor does he turn back from the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*).
The intermediate [rites] have the sacrificial implements as their constituent parts, while the external ones have the performers as their constituent parts.
One wears the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) when performing rites for the ancestors;
one wears it over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī) during the New and Full Moon sacrifices and the Agnihotra.
There is no fixed rule in other cases.

Because of their connection with the injunctions, the primary acts are simultaneous; for these, the auxiliary elements that are capable of being performed once apply by way of a common ritual procedure (*tantra*), while those that are not so capable must be repeated.
At various times, separately:
whatever is the time for the principal rite, that is the time for the subsidiaries; that is the place, that is the performer, and that is the fire.
From the time of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) onwards, the vessels are to be maintained for as long as one lives.
For them, the preparatory rite (saṃskāra) is repeated for each individual ritual system.
The New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa) fulfill all desires; they are governed by the same injunctions.
They are established by the specific instruction.
By means of these two, one sacrifices for as long as life lasts, or for thirty years.
In a single performance, one may desire all desires; or, in the case of separate performances, one may desire each [desire] individually.
The former is the full moon day (pūrṇamāsī) and the latter is the new moon day (amāvāsyā).

One sacrifices with the full moon oblation on the full moon day, and with the new moon oblation on the new moon day. At the full moon sacrifice, the principal offerings are: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, the low-voiced offering (upāṃśuyāja), and cakes on eleven potsherds for Agni-Soma, or for Viṣṇu, or for Prajāpati; and [the cake] for Agni-Soma is also [included]. These are the principal rites on the full moon day.

For some, the *āgnīṣomīya* sacrificial cake is not prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa who has not performed the *soma* sacrifice; rather, there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, and at the new moon, either an eleven-potsherd or a twelve-potsherd cake for Indra-Agni for one who does not offer the *saṃnāyya*, while for one who does offer the *saṃnāyya*, there is a cake for Agni and the *saṃnāyya* itself.
The other oblations are subordinate to these.
One should observe the fast on the first full moon day.
Or on the full moon day; or on the previous new moon day;
or on the day when [the moon] is not seen. || 3 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the first book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. || 1 ||

Having offered the morning *agnihotra*, having followed the *agnihotrika* fire [to its new place], or having removed it, once the sun has risen, he takes out the *āhavanīya* fire from the *gārhapatya*. He adds fuel with the verse "O Agni, may there be splendor for me" (*mām agne varcaḥ*), with the next verse the *gārhapatya*, and with the next the *dakṣiṇāgni*. Or he may add fuel to the *āhavanīya* with all the verses.
The remaining verses are for the purpose of providing options.
"According to some, he adds fuel with the *vyāhṛti*s;
according to others, with these [same verses].
He brings a branch of *palāśa* or a branch of *śamī*.
One should [cut] a branch facing east, north, or northeast, which is not deficient, has many leaves, and has undried tips.

For one whom he desires to be without cattle, he should take for him one that is leafless and has dried tips. For one whom he desires to be possessed of cattle, he should take for him one with many leaves, many branches, and undried tips.
With the words, "For sap thee," he cuts off a branch; with the words, "For strength thee," he bends it down, or he strokes it.
He brings it back with the mantra: "This branch, turned eastward and northward, prepared as sap and strength, with many leaves and unwithered tips—I, the protector of cattle, bring it.
With the words, "Ye winds," he drives away six calves with that branch.
According to some, [he does so] with *darbha* grasses or with those containing *darbha*.
He touches the driven-out [cows] with a single branch.
With the words "And the god," he sends the mothers toward the pasture.
One should recognize Indra in the invocations for those who sacrifice to Indra, and Mahendra for those who sacrifice to Mahendra;
according to some, [one should recognize him] as "with Darbha grass" or "together with Darbha.
He touches those that have been removed with a single branch.
And saying, "The god," he sends forth the mothers toward the grazing grounds.
He should designate Indra for those who sacrifice to Indra, and Mahendra for those who sacrifice to Mahendra.
Saying, "May they be firm in him," he turns back toward the house of the sacrificer.
"Protect the cattle of the sacrificer"—with these words, he hides a branch in front, facing westward, in the Agni-sthāna or in the fire-hall; according to some, facing eastward from behind.
With "By the impulse of the god," he takes up either a horse's rib or a flint-thrower.
With "Thou art the cry of the sacrifice," he stands worshipping the Gārhapatya fire.
He heats [the grass] on the Āhavanīya or Gārhapatya fire with the formula, "It has been heated.
With the formula, "May she go forth; go to the wide atmosphere," he walks forward either eastward or northward and brings from wherever it may be found sacrificial grass made of Darbha.
He leaves aside one bunch of the gathered grass with the formula, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s tuft," and he cuts another with the formula, "Thou art Indra’s cut portion," or "Of the gods."
He cuts all of that;
or else, saying, "I set aside for you the portion of the cattle," he leaves behind one or two stalks of *darbha* grass from what has been gathered.
He touches what has been bound up with the formula, "This is for the gods," and what has been released with, "This is for the cattle," or, "The portion of the cows is released.
[Then he takes it] with: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan..."
With the words, "With both hands I take up the sacrificial grass, the seat of the gods," he reaches for it at the *viśākha* (forked) part.
With the words, "For the gods, you who have upright sacrificial grass," he sweeps it upward.

With the words, "O divine sacrificial grass, do not let me [injure] you from behind, nor across," he places the knife down; or alternatively, with the words, "Neither below nor above may I fail in your layer."
"Of those herbs which were born for the gods three ages ago, may I attain the joint while bringing the sacrificial strew,"— having consecrated [the grass] with this,
he cuts it with the words, "May I, your cutter, not come to harm.
He cuts a handful together with the fingernails.
That is the prastara-bunch;
it should be as long as the handle of a sacrificial ladle, or as high as the knees or the thighs.
By this same procedure, he offers the other [bunches].
Whatever else there is, other than the cutting and the discarding,
having cut it all according to its purpose,
he touches the trimmed grass with the words: "O divine sacrificial grass, grow with a hundred shoots!"
He touches himself, saying, "May we grow with a thousand branches.
He cuts off either an odd or an even number of handfuls or knots.
He winds the cord clockwise, saying, "Thou art the girdle of Aditi."
He replaces it with the formula, "The womb has been inhabited. He repeats the mantra for each layer, whether there are three layers or five layers.
With the formula, "Protect me from the contact with the earth," he lays down a cord either directed toward the east or toward the north.

Having consecrated it with the formula, "Of the unlimited, I bind together the limited; for the sake of well-doing. May I not go to any sin whatsoever; rising again, may they become abundant," he then gathers the materials for the foundation upon the cord with the formula, "I gather thee, the well-prepared material."

With the words, "Unafraid, the source," he places the *prastara* on the last layer. With the words, "For Indrāṇī, the binding," he ties the girdle; having wound it clockwise with the words, "May Pūṣan [bind] thee," he pulls the knot toward himself from the front, or from behind toward the front, with the words, "So may he [bind] thee.
He takes hold of it with the words, "The waters have straightened thee, the Aśvins, the seven Ṛṣis; the *barhis*, with the rays of Sūrya, as the banner of the dawns, I take hold of."
"By the two arms of Indra, I lift you up"—with these words he lifts it up.
Having placed it upon the head with the words "Of Bṛhaspati," he carries it away.
Those which are the ways of going forth are the ways of returning.
With the formula, "Sit on the seat of Aditi," he places it within the altar (antarvedi) at the location of the enclosing sticks (paridhi), not on the ground.
With the formula, "Thou art going to the gods," he consecrates it once it has been placed.
He binds together the fuel (idhma) consisting of twenty-one pieces of wood, made either of Palāśa or Khadira.
There are fifteen verses for the purpose of the *sāmidhenī* offerings.
There are three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made from unspecified types of wood, provided with living organisms;
it is known that they should be fresh, for they are "juicy," and it is also known that they should be dry, for the sake of purity.
The largest is the middle one; the longest is the one on the southern side; the smallest is the shortest, being that on the northern side.
There are two *āghāra* fuel-sticks, and the *anūyāja* fuel-stick is the twenty-first.
Having made a cord (*śulba*) of an odd number of *darbha* blades—either with roots or without roots—he lays it down with its ends pointing either eastward or northward, saying:

"When you, having assumed the form of a black antelope, entered the trees, then I gather you together in twenty-one parts, well-gathered. I gather the three enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), the three fuel-sticks (*samidh*), the sacrificial grass (*yajñāyu*), the moving implements, the fire-brick (*upaveṣa*), the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), and the fire-tongs (*dhṛṣṭi*), well-gathered. With this, he gathers the fuel on the cord.
He binds it together, saying: "Black are you, dwelling in the pit; O God, go before us; may I attain you."
With the verse "pūṣā te," having wound the knot clockwise, he should release it according to that same procedure as when on the sacrificial grass (barhis), or having untied it;
with that same mantra.
He places it down together with the *barhis* grass.

He makes a *veda* (sweeper) of *darbha* grass with the formula: "Thou art the *veda*; by that [means] through which thou, O divine one, becamest a *veda* for the gods among the gods, by that mayest thou become a *veda* for me.
It is made with knees [shaped like those of] a calf, or with a handle of *mūta* grass, or with a handle of *paṅkti* grass, or threefold.

They prescribe a *vatsajñu* for one desiring cattle, a *mūtakārya* for one desiring food, a *paṅktikārya* for one desiring offspring, and a *trivṛt* with a triple-layered head for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
He cuts it at the distance of a span from the notch. He places the wood-chips used for cutting the fuel and the cuttings from the trimming of the *vedī* together.
Thus ends the second chapter in the first book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
1.3 Now begins the third chapter.
Having cut off the leaflets from the branch within the altar and having stripped all [the bark] from the base, he fashions that *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick) with the formula:

"Thou art the *upaveṣa*; they have held thee as a serving-vessel for the sacrifice. While preparing the oblation for Indra, mayest thou be auspicious and helpful to us. Thus he makes it the *upaveṣa*.
In that [water], he prepares a threefold filter made of Darbha grass, unsplit.

"Threefold, made of Palāśa and Darbha, of this size and measuring a span—may it act as the most excellent purifier in the sacrifice, making the milk an offering. He joins the root to the root and the tip to the tip; he does not tie a knot.
Or [he may recite]: "Thou art the filter of the Vasus, hundred-streamed."
When the evening *agnihotra* has been offered,
having washed the vessels for the *sāṃnāyya* sacrifice in pairs, he sets them down with their openings facing downward:

the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle, the *ukhā* pot, the *upaveṣa* fire-stirring stick, the *śākhāpavitra* branch-strainer, the *abhidhānī* rope, the two *nidāna* supports, the milking vessel, and either an iron vessel or a wooden vessel for covering [the milk].
He prepares two *pavitra* strainers from two *darbha* blades that are equal, with uncut tips, and measuring a span (*prādeśa*) in length.

Holding a blade of grass or a piece of wood between his fingers, he cuts them while reciting: "You two are *pavitras*, belonging to Viṣṇu; may Vāyu purify you with his mind. He does not cut them with his fingernails.

Having consecrated them with the mantra: "May these two, the *pavitras* that purify the oblation, move about, nourishing in every way the limbs of the sacrifice, Prāṇa and Apāna," [he places them in the water].
With the words, "You two are purified by the mind of Viṣṇu," he wipes [the ladle] with water.

Having poured water into the *agnihotra* ladle over which the strainers have been placed, he purifies it three times with the two northward-pointed strainers while reciting the *gāyatrī* verse, "The god for you... (RV 10.9.4), foot by foot.
He addresses the waters with the mantra, "āpo devīḥ. || 8 ||
"O divine waters, you are pure; purify the vessels for the sake of the gods' *upātaṅkyā* [offering], and purify the bark of the *parṇa* tree," or [he says] "purify.

With the formula "Be purified (*śundhadhvam*)," he sprinkles all the vessels while they are turned face upwards three times. Or [he says]: "May the all-working ones be purified for the sacrifice to the gods, for the divine rite; be purified! That which of you was impure when it went astray—that of yours, purify now with this."
"These cows, yielding honey, possessing offspring, glorious, and multiform, becoming many as they are born again—may Indra delight you here," with these words he awaits the cows as they approach.

Having taken up the fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*) with the formula, "Thou art bold," and having drawn out embers from the Gārhapatya fire toward the north with the formula, "The fear of the enemy is driven out; together with that [fear], drive away him whom we hate; rest for the sake of well-being," he proceeds.

With the words, "O Mātariśvan," he places the pot upon them so that the sacrifice may not slip away. Or [he says]: "I set down the two fire-pan lids; may they bear what is brought together with the cattle, cooked for Indra as curd.
With the words, "Be heated by the heat of the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases," he surrounds it with embers.
"Tell me when it has been approached," he commands.
With the formula, "Thou art the purifier of the Vasus, with a thousand streams," he places the branch-purifier with its tip pointing eastward into the pot.
Having taken hold of it from behind, he restrains his speech and remains seated, holding it.
With the words, "Thou art the girdle of Aditi," he takes up the halter.

"Thou art the thirty-third of the threads; come together with the strainer. May this auspicious rope, along with the fodder, attend upon the inviolable cow," or [he says]. "Thou art Pūṣan," [with these words] he lets the calf loose, or he addresses it as it runs away.
He issues the command: "Do not pass between the sacrificial hall and the cow that has been approached for milking. They do not pass between the sacrificial hall and the cow while she is being milked.
If they should pass through, he should say: "May the *sāṃnāyya* offering not be spoiled!
[He addresses] the cow that has been approached with the formula: "I unite you with health, with progeny, and with abundance of wealth; may you become prolific."
[He recites: "Swelling with strength, milk, and ghee, may I, living, sit near you who are living. [This is for] the cow that has been brought near.

"May Heaven and Earth, milking together this sacrifice, and Dhātṛ along with Soma—or Vāyu—bestow wealth upon the sacrificer. [This is for] the cow being milked. "They milk the fountain, the four-holed jar, the divine Iḍā, the wife-bearing, the finder of heaven; may Indra and Agni quicken that which is full of truth; may that establish the sacrificer in immortality. With these words, he consecrates the sound of the flowing stream. The milker carries [the milk].

He asks him: "O milker of desire, tell us for Indra the milk-offering that provides power—that [cow] in whom the milk of the gods and of men is contained. The milker replies, "This one," pointing her out.
He says, "She is Viśvāyuḥ (the Life of All). To this he responds: "So be it."
"May Savitṛ purify thee with the filter of Vasu, with a hundred streams, well-purified," [saying this] he pours [the milk] into the pot.
Whatever remains after the formal command (*saṃpraiṣa*), with that he causes [the cows] to be milked on the northern side.
"She who is all-encompassing"—with these words he milks the second [cow]; "She who is the maker of all"—with these words the third.

Having caused the three [cows] to be milked, he gives the command three times: "O you who yield much milk, having yielded for Indra and for the gods as an oblation, may you swell again; may you be fit for milking again for the cattle and for men. Having released his speech and not touching [the cows], he causes the others to be milked, either silently or with the same formula.
When all have been milked, he consecrates the drops with the words, "The drop has been offered," and the *sāṃnāyya* with, "May Heaven and Earth... and so forth.
Having washed the milking vessel, he pours [the milk] into the cooking pot with the formula, "Be united!

Having cooked it and having sprinkled it silently with clarified butter, he removes it from the fire while drawing [the vessel] toward the east, the north, or the northeast, as if pulling it away, with the formula: "Strengthen the cows, strengthen the lord of the cows; let not your sacrificer come to harm."

On the previous day, milk is curdled to produce curds for the *ātañcana* (curdling agent) of one, two, or three cows; this is done by continuously milking into it every day until the day of the fast (*aupavasatha*), using either rice grains, bark-shavings of the *parṇa* tree, *kvala* fruits, jujube fruits, or *pūtīka* leaves, while reciting:
"With Soma I curdle thee. Having thus made the bottom cool, he curdles it, or else with the formula: "I curdle thy own portion for Indra with Soma.
He curdles it with rice grains, *parṇa*-bark shavings, *kvalas*, jujubes, or *pūtīkas*.
"You are the continuity of the sacrifice; I continue you, the continuity of the sacrifice," [saying this] he brings the remains of the *agnihotra* offering, or silently.

"O Waters, be watchful among the oblations, as you are watchful among the gods; so be watchful for the sacrificer in this sacrifice"—[saying this] he pours water into the vessel for the purpose of covering it. "You are the unassailable; for Viṣṇu, for the sacrifice, I cover you with water from a non-empty vessel—those waters which remain pure"—[saying this] he covers it. If it should be made of clay, he should thrust a blade of grass or a piece of wood into it.

"O Viṣṇu, these two—the *parṇa* leaf and the *darbha* grass—which purify the oblation for the gods, protect them for the morning offering; for you guard the oblation. Having thus released the branch-strainer (*śākhāpavitra*), he sets it down in its known place.
With the formula, "O Viṣṇu, guard the oblation," he places the *sānnāyya* milk above the region of the *gārhapatya* fire. || 11 ||
Thus ends the third chapter in the first book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Thus ends the third chapter in the first book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin, composed by Mahādeva.
1.4 Now begins the fourth chapter.
Having brought another branch, he drives away the calves for the morning milking with that same procedure, or with that branch, or with *darbha* grass, just as he did for the evening milking.
Having placed the potsherds, he milks the morning milk; the procedure for this is explained by [the rules for] the evening milking.
"For the non-laxity of the sacrifice, I place the two fire-enclosures; brought together with cattle, carried apart, cooked for Indra"—with these words he completes the end of the mantra.
He places the branch-purifier (śākhāpavitra) with its tip pointing northward. He does not anoint it.
"One who has not performed the Soma sacrifice should not offer the *sāṃnāyya*"; regarding this, the Kāpeyas indeed say that one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice should certainly offer it.
Having sacrificed with Soma, one should offer the *sāṃnāyya* to Indra;
or rather, having sacrificed to Indra for a year or two, and having offered a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati, one may at will sacrifice to Mahendra.
Gautama says that Bhāradvāja, who has heard the sacred tradition, states that a village headman who is of royal descent may, in all cases, sacrifice to Mahendra at will.

He issues the command: "Strew around! Enclose the fire! May the enclosed fire protect the sacrificer. May these golden neck-ornaments, the essence of the waters and the plants, be for the sacrificer as wish-fulfilling cows in yonder world, in that other world.
He strews around the fires with *darbha* grass.

Having strewn grass around the Āhavanīya fire, he then [strews it] around the Gārhapatya and the Dakṣiṇāgni; or, having strewn grass around the Gārhapatya, he then [strews it] around the Dakṣiṇāgni and the Āhavanīya.
The blades point northward behind and in front.
Having performed this, he observes the fast on the new moon day.
On the full moon day, however,
on the preceding day he performs the adding of fuel to the fires and the strewing around of the fires; on the following day, he prepares the sacrificial wood, the grass, and the Veda-bundle.
Or it is done immediately;
everything is performed. || 12 ||
In the *sadyaskālā* rite, one strews grass around the fires after the performance of the Vedic ritual.
The summary: the word "tomorrow" (*śvas*) is omitted, as are both the mantra and the two fires in every respect;
there is no modification (*ūha*) either in the archetype (*prakṛti*) or in the ectype (*vikṛti*), because it is a modification of that [archetype].

Having offered the morning *agnihotra* when the sun has risen, he commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the full moon sacrifice before sunrise; for the new moon sacrifice, he does so before the sun rises. Having washed his hands with the formula, "For the two of you, for the sake of the rite," he spreads a continuous line of *ulapa* grass from the *gārhapatya* fire to the *āhavanīya* fire with the formula, "Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; I spread thee for the continuity of the sacrifice; for the continuity of the sacrifice, thee. He spreads it silently to the south and silently to the north.
To the south of the Āhavanīya fire, he prepares the seats for the Brahman and the sacrificer;
the eastern one for the Brahman and the western one for the sacrificer.
To the north of the Gārhapatya fire, having strewn Darbha grass, he washes the vessels and places them down in pairs, with their openings facing downwards.
The wooden sword, the potsherds; the Agnihotra-ladle, the winnowing basket; the black antelope skin, and the yoke-pin.
The mortar and pestle, the lower grinding stone and the upper grinding stone;
a dipping-spoon made of Khadira wood, a Juhū ladle made of Palāśa wood, an Upabhṛt ladle made of Aśvattha wood, and a Dhruvā ladle made of Vikaṅkata wood.

They are one *aratni* or one cubit (*bāhu*) in length, provided with spouts like a mouth; they have pouring-out spouts shaped like a swan’s beak, tapering from the base to the tip, with hollows for the skin [of the handle], and according to some, having tails like a crow’s; according to others, having lips like an elephant’s.
[One prepares] a vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), a *kuṭaru* ladle, a *pātrī* bowl, and a stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*).
The Veda, the *prāśitraharaṇa* vessel,
the *praṇītā* water-vessel, and the *iḍā* vessel;
and one *anvāhārya* cooking-pot.
Of those [vessels], whichever have no specified wood are made of *vikaṅkata*;
however, those intended for the *ahoma* (non-offering) are made of *vāraṇa*.
Here he prepares the vessels for the morning milking.
In this case, he prepares the two strainers for one who does not perform the *saṃnayya* offering;
for one who does perform the *saṃnayya*, they have been kept since the previous day.
Having taken up the cup for the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* waters with the formula, "For skill thee," he pours forth the *praṇītā* waters.
"You belong to the trees; be purified for the gods; be beautified for the gods; be cleansed for the gods"—with these words, he washes it three times.
He should lead it forward with a bronze vessel for one who desires spiritual luster, and with an earthenware vessel for one who desires food.
They should not be moved until the conclusion of the rite.
"May the divine subjects enter; the vessels for the sacrifice to the gods"—with these words, he touches the vessels with his hand holding the strainer. || 14 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra. || 4 ||
1.5 Now begins the fifth chapter.
With the formula, "Thou art made of wood for the sake of Dakṣa," he takes up the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle; with "For the sake of Viṣṇu, thee," the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*).
He heats them over the *āhavanīya* or the *gārhapatya* fire with the formula, "Burnt away is the evil! (*pratyuṣṭam*).
The sacrificer addresses [the priest], saying, "I shall pour out the oblation," while he is away on a journey. He should recite [the formula]: "O Agni, I shall pour out the oblation."
He goes along with the thought, "I follow the wide mid-region.
Behind the Āhavanīya fire, or behind the Gārhapatya fire, stands a cart with its yoke tied and its covering intact, filled with rice or barley, with the pole pointing either eastward or northward.
Having touched its southern pole with the formula, "Thou art the pole," he proceeds.
Touching the left [wheel] with the words, "Thou art of the gods," he mutters [the formula].
With the words, "Viṣṇu has stepped upon thee," he places his right foot on the left wheel.
With the words, "Unbending," he mounts [the chariot].
With the formula, "Thee for Mitra," he looks at the enclosing-fence (pariṇaha). With the formula, "Wide space for Vāta," he covers the door of the enclosing-fence.
With the formula, "Thee for Mitra," he looks at the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśya) and the enclosing-fence.
With the words, "Bestow vigor," he touches the sacrificial cakes;
with the words, "Place milk in me," he touches himself;
then, having cast away a blade of grass or a clod of earth with the words, "The Rakṣas is struck down," and having touched water.
Having explained the Daśahotṛ formula, having placed the two strainers in the winnowing basket, and having poured [the ghee] into the ladle.

With the formula "For thee, O god," he pours out four handfuls while the strainers are held between his fingers—three times with the sacrificial formula and the fourth time silently. Having poured them out, he pours the remaining grain over them.
By this same procedure, he pours out the subsequent sacrificial cake for each respective deity.

Or he pours [the grain] into a vessel; having drawn the wooden sword (sphya) toward the south and having recited all the cart-formulas, he touches the poured-out grain with the formula, "This for the gods," and with "This for us together" over that from which he has poured it out. With "For prosperity, thee," he touches those very grains that have been poured out.

Saying, "I am now released from the noose of Varuṇa," he takes the cake for Pūṣan and creeps out from under the binding cord, saying, "May I look upon the light of heaven. He gazes upon the entire sacrifice;
then, saying, "The light of Vaiśvānara," he looks toward the Āhavanīya fire.
"May the door-posts be firm," he says as he descends.

"Svāhā to Heaven and Earth," he says, consecrating the spilled portions. "Go through the wide atmosphere," he says as he proceeds. "I set thee down in the lap of Aditi," he says, placing [the vessel] to the west of the Āhavanīya fire or to the west of the Gārhapatya fire.
On whichever fire he cooks [the oblation],
he consigns it to the respective deity with the formula, "O Agni, protect the offering.
Having prepared the sprinkling waters in a ladle provided with a spout, as previously described.
He addresses [the materials], saying, "O Brahman, I shall sprinkle.

He sprinkles three times according to the respective deity, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni—for such-and-such, for such-and-such.
He should not sprinkle over the fire.
He sprinkles the vessels as before.
He takes up the black antelope skin with the formula, "Thou art the rush of the wind," or with "In the impulse of the god.
With the formula, "The Rakṣas is shaken off," he shakes it three times over the rubbish-heap (utkara) with its neck upwards and its hair-side outwards.
With the formula, "Thou art the skin of Aditi," he spreads [the hide] to the west of the rubbish-heap (utkara), with its neck toward the west and the hair upward.
With the formula, "May the earth recognize thee," he places the buttocks (bhasad) facing westward in front [of the hide].
With the formula, "Thou art the pressing-skin," he places the black antelope skin over the mortar without letting go of it.
With the formula, "Thou art the body of Agni," he pours the oblation into the mortar without letting go [of the pestle],
three times with a sacrificial verse and a fourth time silently. With the formula, "Thou art the stone, born of the tree," he takes up the pestle.

With the formula, "O tree, you are the upward-bearer," or "I shall bind the Rākṣasa, the rival from heaven," he threshes three times, or with the formula, "The sorcerers are struck down; the evil-plotters are struck down.
While threshing three times, or without threshing, he calls out to the preparer of the oblation: "O preparer of the oblation, come!"
"Come hither!"—this for a Kṣatriya; "Approach!"—this for a Vaiśya.
When the rice grains have appeared, he issues the command: "Gather them up loudly!
Then the Āgnīdhra takes up a stone with the formula: "Thou art a mountain, a maker of fame."
"Thou art the *kuṭaru*, honey-tongued," or "Thou art the cock, honey-tongued"—
with these words they do not strike together the lower and upper millstones with the formula, "Impel the food, impel the strength.
They strike twice on the lower stone and once on the upper stone.
Moving it three times, he completes it nine times. Or, silently, he takes up a wooden pin (śamyā).
With the formula, "Thou art increased by rain," he sweeps the winnowing basket (śūrpa) from the east or from the north.
With the formula, "O you who have grown through the rains," he touches the sacrificial cakes.
With the formula, "May that which has grown through the rains recognize you," he winnows them.
He winnows them three times over the heap [of refuse] with the formula, "The Rakṣas is blown away."
"Blown away are the enemies!"—with these words, he sweeps away the chaff from the winnowing basket.

Having filled the sacrificial cake's pan with the chaff, he throws it down toward the north-western intermediate direction, beneath the black antelope skin, saying, "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases.
He does not look at it.
With the words, "The Rakṣas is struck down," he strikes it down.
Having touched water and sprinkled the potsherd, he sets it down.
With the words, "Vāyu, indeed," he separates [the grains].
With the words "Devo vaḥ," he causes the rice grains to fall into the vessel. || 17 ||
Having given the command, "Pound [the grains] three times," he releases his speech at this point.
The sacrificer’s wife threshes them, or whoever among the servants might be the wife; she too threshes them a few times and hands them over to another, who then threshes them from that point onward.
The wife threshes them three times until they are well-purified, saying: "Be cleansed for the gods! Be beautified for the gods! Be purified for the gods!"
He sets aside the husks. Having washed the rice grains, he pours out the wash-water within the altar with the formula:
"That which remains as the refuse of the thrice-husked [grains], the portion of the Rakṣases—may the waters carry it away from here, svāhā!"
The ritual procedure for the black antelope skin has been explained.

With the formula, "Thou art the support of heaven," he places a yoke-pin with its knob pointing north upon the black antelope skin. With the formula, "Thou art Dhiṣaṇā, the mountain," he sets the grindstone upon it.
He places [the mortar] down with the latter half [of the verse]:
"Thou art Dhiṣaṇā, daughter of the mountain. He places the upper millstone upon the lower millstone. He gazes at the rice grains, saying: "Ye are stalks, full of honey."
With the formula "For thee, O god," he pours the rice grains onto the grinding stone;
three times with the Yajus formula and a fourth time silently.
With the formulas "For out-breathing thee, for in-breathing thee, for diffused-breathing thee," he grinds them.

Or rather, he ploughs the eastern furrow with "For out-breathing, thee!"; the western furrow with "For in-breathing, thee!"; and in the middle region he fixes [the furrows] apart with "For diffused breathing, thee!
Finally, he follows the long [furrow] towards the east;
from there upwards, he grinds [the grain] continuously according to the direction of his face.
With the words, "O God," he causes the flour to fall onto the black antelope skin.
With the words, "I look upon you with an undeceived eye," he looks at it.
He issues the command: "Grinding without spilling, make them fine."
The wife or a female servant grinds [the grain];
she performs all of this.
Here, she places the boiling water (*madantī*) on the fire. || 18 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the first book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the sixth chapter:
The sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi) are cooked either on the Āhavanīya fire or the Gārhapatya fire, behind the fire-altar.
As it has been stated, he takes up the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick) with the formula:
"The *rakṣas* is struck down; burn the hand of the *rakṣas*; you are a serpent of the depths. With it, he turns out two glowing coals toward the west.
Having cast one of them away toward the north-western intermediate direction with the formula "Away, O Agni," and having touched water, [he proceeds].

Having set aside the remainder with the words, "Bring [the gods] to the place of sacrifice," he places a potsherd upon it with the words, "Thou art firm. He then turns a glowing coal over it with the words, "Burnt up!"

"Thou art the supporter," he says; therefore [the first cake] is placed first. "Thou art the upholder," he says; therefore [the second cake] is placed first. Of the eight-potsherd cake, there are two in the middle, three to the south, and three to the north.
With the formula, "Thou art the law for these two," he places [the brick] in the southeast; with "The host of Maruts," in the southwest;
with "Make firm the barley-field, make firm wealth, make firm prosperity, encompass the kinsmen for this sacrificer," in the northwest;
and with "For all quarters, I place thee, unbroken, for the winning of kinsmen," in the northeast.
With the verse "cittis asi," he places the remaining one to the north.
Just as for the eight-potsherd cake, so for the eleven-potsherd cake he lays down three bricks;
of these, the largest is the middle one, and two are to the east of the middle one.
The first [layer] is with the verse "tayościdasī";
as stated regarding the intermediate directions;
and the remaining [bricks] are placed to the north with the formula "citaḥ stha."
The procedure for the twelve potsherds is the same as that for the eleven potsherds.

With the formula, "Of the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases, heat yourselves with austerity," he places embers upon the potsherds with the Veda-grass-bundle. Having heated the pan, he fans it while it is still hot.
With the formula "For thee, O god... he pours the flour through the strainer from the black antelope skin;
three times with the Yajus formula and the fourth time silently.
While pouring, he restrains his speech; while covering it, he releases it.

With the formula, "I purify you with the two strainers of the two bay horses," he purifies the flour three times with two strainers whose tips point north; or [he may do so] with the formula, "The god [Soma] for you.
Having taken water from the *praṇītā* vessel with the *sruva* spoon and supporting it with the *veda* grass-bundle, he pours it into the flour with the formula, "May the waters be united."

"If the *praṇītā* waters are not available, one should purify whatever other waters there may be with the *yajus* formula and mix them [with the flour]"—this is an explanatory statement for times of distress.
With the words "Born forth from the waters," he pours in the heated water. With the words "Be united with the waters," he causes it to flow around [the vessel] clockwise.
With "I unite you for Janayitrī," he unites [the flour]; or rather, with "I unite you for Janayitṛ.
With "You are the head of Makha," he forms the two lumps.
With "May you separate according to your respective portions," he divides them. || 19 ||

"May Savitṛ, the god, apportion for you both; may Savitṛ, Bhaga, apportion for you both; may Savitṛ, Pūṣan, apportion for you both; may Savitṛ, Vāyu, apportion for you both; I apportion you for procreation"—thus he says, or [simply], "I apportion you.
Having made two equal lumps, he touches the one intended for Agni with the formula, "This for Agni," and the other with "This for so-and-so," according to the respective deity.
With the formula, "Here I drive away the face of the attacking army," he drives away the embers from the southern junction of the potsherds with the *veda*-grass, and from the northern one as well.
In this manner, their ritual acts are performed in successive order;
each act is followed by one of the same kind, and each is completed in its entirety.
However, those acts that are joined together have a single completion, such as in the case of the cutting and offering of the portions.

The pouring out and the winnowing are performed everywhere at the primary conjunction. Having taken the southern lump with the formula, "Thou art the head of Makha," he places it upon the southern pair of potsherds with the formula, "Thou art Gharma, the life of all," or with "O Gharma, be heated."
The subsequent [action] is as follows:
he fashions it like a tortoise, not high, with the shape of a flat cake, and the size of a horse's hoof.
With the words "O wide one, spread yourself out," he spreads it.
He spreads out all the potsherds.
Having poured water into a vessel, he says, "Take the skin," and then, moving clockwise and without spilling, he smears around [the vessel] with the ointment.
Saying, "The Rakṣas is excluded," he carries fire around it three times with a firebrand.
Or [he recites] "The lord of wandering mendicants.
He causes it to blaze up with *darbha* grass, saying, "May the god Savitṛ cook you.
He heats it all around with firebrands, saying, "May Agni not burn your body."
With the formula, "Be united with the sacred word (brahman)," he covers the ashes along with the embers using the Veda-grass-bundle; or [he says], "Take up the sacred word.
He issues the command, "Cook without burning! and at this point, he releases his speech.

Having washed his fingers and rinsed the bowl, and having warmed it over a firebrand, he draws three lines toward the north with the wooden sword (sphya) either to the west of the Āhavanīya or to the west of the Gārhapatya. He pours water down behind each line three times without letting them touch one another, saying, "Svāhā to Ekata! After pouring the water, he warms the vessel over the fire.
To the west of the Āhavanīya fire, he prepares for the sacrificer an altar (vedi) of the proper size, extending across its full width.

"By means of the *veda*, they found the altar, the mistress of the earth; that earth spread out over the earthly realms. She bears the embryo within the worlds; from there the sacrifice is born at all times. With this [formula], before the *stambayajus* rite, he sweeps the altar three times with the *veda*. From the eastern third of the altar, he carries away the *stambayajus*.
Having taken up the wooden sword (*sphya*) with the words, "Thee, for the sake of the god... [he continues].
He consecrates it with the mantra, "Thou art the arm of Indra. With the words, "Thousand-spiked, hundred-edged," he sharpens its tip with a blade of *darbha* grass.
With the words, "Thou art the armor of the earth," he places a blade of *darbha* grass either pointing eastward or northward.
Saying, "O Earth, worthy of the sacrifice to the gods," he strikes it with the wooden sword (sphya).
Saying, "Araru is driven away from the earth," he removes the grass and the dust with the wooden sword, saying also, "May I strike down Araru."
He says, "Go to the cow-pen," as he carries [the fire];
"May the sky rain for you," as he looks at the altar; "May Parjanya rain for you," as he looks at the sacrificer.
Then, saying, "Homage to heaven! Homage to earth!", the Āgnīdhra priest sits down to the north with his hands turned palm-upward.
He says, "Come for the binding of the altar," and he pours [the earth] down for him;
that becomes the *utkara*.
With the words, "The wicked one is bound away," the *āgnīdhra* receives the *utkara* with his joined palms.
Having grasped it, he remains [there]. In this manner he carries away the second; in this manner the third.
He strikes the second [bundle] with the formula: "May I not harm the root of the auspicious plants for you."
"Struck is Araru from the earth, the place of sacrifice to the gods," with these words he takes up the second [clod].
"The sorcerers have been trampled down by the place of sacrifice to the gods," with these words he grasps the second [clod].
"May your drop not leap up to heaven," with these words he strikes the third [clod].

"Struck down is Araru from the earth, the non-sacrificer to the gods"—with these words he takes up the third [clod]. "Crushed is the evil-speaker"—with these words he seizes the third. The fourth is done silently.
He removes all the *darbha* grass.
He grasps the fourth [corner] with the formula, "May your *araru* not leap up to heaven!
He encloses the altar with the wooden sword (*sphya*).
With the words, "May the Vasus take hold of you," he draws a line to the south, directed eastward;
with "May the Rudras [take hold of you]," to the west, directed northward; and with "May the Ādityas [take hold of you]," to the north, directed eastward.
He raises the two shoulders of the altar facing east toward the Āhavanīya fire; the two hips face west toward the Gārhapatya fire; and it is depressed in the middle. ||2.1||

"O men, come and prepare this altar, which possesses wealth, possesses Rudras, and possesses Ādityas, upon the height of heaven, at the navel of the earth, so that this sacrificer may not come to harm. This [altar] is dear to the gods; in the lap of Aditi, O gods, all have taken pleasure in it. May the increase of wealth enter the sacrificer"—thus he gives the direction.

"Araru is driven away from the earth; bring hither the one who sacrifices to the gods. Having dug up the uppermost layer with the wooden sword (*sphya*), he throws it onto the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).
With the words, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he digs; or with the words, "Performing the work of the god Savitṛ in his presence, O men, may I not harm the roots of these auspicious plants.

He digs a furrow two finger-breadths deep, three finger-breadths deep, four finger-breadths deep, as wide as a ploughshare, as wide as a path, or as far as the white part of the heel; he does not dig deeper than these measures.
To the south, he makes a larger mound, containing loose soil, sloping toward the east and the north.
With the wooden sword (sphya), he cuts away whatever root extends beyond it;
whatever loose soil remains in excess, he causes that to go to the rubbish heap (utkara).
For one desiring cattle, [the altar] is to have its soil brought from elsewhere.
Having performed everything prior to the digging, he digs up the soil with a mantra and carries it away.
Here, on the full moon day, he prepares the altar (vedi).
On the day before the new moon,
prior to the bringing of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*),
he performs that which is before the second tracing around (*parigrāha*); or he performs it together with the second tracing around.
Having addressed [the Brahman] with the words, "O Brahman, I shall take up the subsequent enclosure," he takes it up.
Some transmit the opposite: first the enclosure with the *mantras*, then the subsequent one with the *yajus* formulas.

With the formula "Thou art Truth" (*ṛtam asi*) he encloses on the south; with "Thou art the seat of Truth" (*ṛtasadanam asi*) on the west; and with "Thou art the glory of Truth" (*ṛtaśrīr asi*) on the north.
With the formula, "Thou art *dhā*, thou art *svadhā*," he wipes [the *sphya*] toward the west with the *sphya*.
Having consecrated it with the mantra, "Before the cruel one...

and having fixed the *sphya* crosswise at the western third of the rear part of the *vedi*, he issues the summons: "Place the *prokṣaṇī* waters; set down the fuel and the sacrificial grass; wipe the *sruva* and the *sruk* spoons; gird the wife; bring the clarified butter."

Having poured water into the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle over which a strainer has been placed, and having drawn the wooden sword (*sphya*) toward the north and held it within the altar, he pours [the water] down along the track of the wooden sword and sets it down on the footprint of the wooden sword with the formula, "Thou art the seat of the Ṛbhus.
He should meditate upon whomsoever he hates.
With the formula, "Thou art hundred-edged, made of wood, the slayer of enemies," he throws the wooden sword onto the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).
He brings forward the large [wooden] vessel from the east.
Without having washed his hands, he should not strike the vessels; nor should he touch the altar until the spreading of the grass.
He washes his hands, cleanses the wooden sword (*sphya*), but does not touch its tip.
To the north, he places the consecrated fuel and sacrificial grass; the fuel to the south and the grass to the north. || 22 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the first book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
1.7 Now begins the seventh chapter.
He cleanses the *sruva* and the *sruks* together with the ends of the Veda-grass,
either dividing them or not dividing them.
Having consecrated them with the mantra, "You are unsharpened, destroyers of rivals," he takes them up with the mantra, "O ghee-dripping ones,
Agni calls you for the sacrifice to the gods," making two [spoons] face upward and the *upabhṛt* crosswise.
With the words, "It has been heated," he heats [the ladles] over either the Āhavanīya or the Gārhapatya fire.

With the formula, "May I not wipe out the cow-pen," he cleans the *sruva* spoon: with the tips [of the grass-blades] from the inside toward the opening, all around the bowl, and with the roots along the handle.

With the formula, "Speech, breath," he cleans the *juhū* ladle: with the tips from the inside toward the opening facing east, with the middle parts from the outside facing west, and with the roots along the handle.

With the words "The eye, the ear," he wipes the *upabhṛt* ladle from the front with the tips [of the grass blades], from the inside toward the outside; from the middle with the tips, and from the outside with the roots, [wiping] toward the east along the handle.
With the words "Offspring, the womb," he wipes the *dhruvā* ladle in the same manner as the *sruva*.
He does not combine that which has been wiped with that which has not been wiped.
He heats it as before.

With the formula, "O food-eater, may I not lose food, offspring, or prosperity; O vigorous one, I cleanse thee, the subduer of rivals," he cleanses the *prāśitra-haraṇa* vessel all around its cavity with the roots [of grass] and the handle with the tips.

With the formula, "The craft of heaven is spread out, resting upon the peaks of the earth; by that which has a thousand branches, we destroy the rival—svāhā! he sprinkles the cleansing-grass and places it into the fire on whichever side he has cleansed it.
With the formula, "Desiring goodwill," he girds the wife with a girdle of muñja grass having a loop on one side; she sits with her knees raised, or stands.
He should not gird her with a garment.
Having made a loose knot to the north of the navel with the formula, "May Pūṣan tie your knot," he draws it around to the south of the navel with the formula, "May it not stand against you."
"O Agni, lord of the house, summon me!"—with these words, standing, she worships the *gārhapatya* fire.

"O wives of the gods, summon me!"—with this, she worships the wives of the gods to the west of the *gārhapatya*. "O wife, this is your place; homage be to you; do not harm me"—with this, she gazes at that very spot.

"May I be like Indrāṇī, not a widow; may I be like Aditi, having good sons. O Gārhapatya, may you not have a single-stalked cart; through the secret doctrine (upaniṣad), may there be good offspring for me. Having spoken thus, she sits down to the north, behind and to the south of the Gārhapatya fire.
Thus, being properly bound, she remains seated until the release [of the ritual].
While sitting, she mutters: "May we, having good offspring, [attain] thee."

"My sons are slayers of enemies, and my daughter is Virāj; moreover, O Saṃjaya, I am the highest glory of my husband. [With these words] he uncovers the opening of the *gargara* vessel that holds the clarified butter, saying, "May Pūṣan open your opening," or "Thou art Pūṣan.
Having poured it into another vessel, he does so as long as there is still to be offered.

Having placed [the vessel] over the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with the verse, "Viṣṇu strode through this," and having taken the butter-pot with the formula, "Thou art Aditi, with an unbroken strainer," he pours abundant clarified butter into it while a strainer has been laid across it, with the formula, "Thou art the milk of the great ones. Then, with the formula, "For food thee," he places it over the embers in the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire.
Having taken it up with the words, "For strength, thee," and having supported it with the Veda-grass mat, he brings it near to the wife.
She, with the words, "Thou art the milk of the great ones," looks at it while closing her eyes and not breathing out.
With the words, "Thou art brilliance," he places it over the Gārhapatya fire.
Having taken it up with "For brilliance thee," he carries it forward with "Follow after the brilliance.
He places it upon the Āhavanīya fire with "May Agni’s brilliance not abandon thee," or rather, "I place the sacrifice within the sacrifice; the sacrifice is established in the sacrifice.
With "Thou art the tongue of Agni," he places it to the north of the *prokṣaṇī* waters along the track of the wooden sword (*sphya*).
He looks at the clarified butter with the formula, "Thou art ghee.

Or, after the upward purification (*utpavana*), he purifies the clarified butter three times by moving it back and forth with two strainers whose tips point northward, with the formulas, "Thou art the bright; thou art light; thou art splendor."
"Devo vaḥ" (The gods for you)—with these words, he sprinkles the Prokṣaṇī waters three times.
"O waters, dripping with sweetness, you have been anointed; sit down upon your station, not being ungracious toward food"— with these words, or simply [the first part],
he takes the portions of clarified butter within the altar using the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) which has not been turned over.
Having taken up the Veda, he draws four or five spoonfuls into the *juhū* ladle, or eight or ten into the *upabhṛt* ladle; as it is with the *juhū*, so it is with the *dhruvā*.
There is more in the *juhū*, less in the *upabhṛt*, and most in the *dhruvā*.
Holding the *juhū* ladle with its mouth upward, he takes sixteen portions of clarified butter (*ājya*)—
seventeen if desiring cattle, twenty-one if desiring stability— into the *upabhṛt*, which is held at waist-level, and into the *dhruvā*, which is placed on the ground.

He takes them into the *juhū* with the formulas beginning "Thee, the bright, into the bright," and into the *upabhṛt* and the *dhruvā* with the subsequent formulas beginning "Thee, for the five winds."

If there are fewer mantras, one should take [the portions] for the *upabhṛt* with half-verses, and for the other two with the remaining halves; if there are more, the surplus are for the purpose of optional choice (*vikalpa*).

Or, one completes the count with the formulas: "Thou art brilliance, thou art light, thou art the abode, the beloved of the gods, the inviolable place of sacrifice; I take thee for the enjoyment of the gods. Or, with the formula "Thou art the abode," one completes all of them. Having set down the clarified butter elsewhere than on the *utkara*, having removed the butter-pot, and having consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he addresses the *brahmán*.
Having placed the fuel with the words, "Thou art Kṛṣṇa," he sprinkles it three times;
[he sprinkles] the sacrificial grass (veda) with "Thou art the altar" (vedir asi), and the sacrificial grass (barhis) with "Thou art the sacrificial grass" (barhir asi).
Three times each.

Having placed the sacrificial grass with its knot toward the front inside the altar, he sprinkles the tips with "For heaven thee!", the middle parts with "For the intermediate space thee!", and the roots with "For earth thee!".
Having caused the tips to be poured over in the ladle, he causes the roots to be poured over.
Saying, "For nourishment, indeed," he unties the knot from the front toward the west with the *sruva* ladle.
Saying, "Svadhā to the ancestors," he pours out the remainder of the sprinkling water continuously from the southern hip to the northern hip.
Saying, "May Pūṣan untie your knot," he unties the knot of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
With the words, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s heap," he takes up the prastara-bunch from the front;
he does not pull it downward, nor does he lift it upward.
It does not shake it; it does not cause it to tremble;
it draws it away as if casting it off.

Having inserted the two strainers (*pavitra*) into the *prastara* bundle with the formula, "I place the out-breath and in-breath in the sacrificer," he hands it to the Brahman priest with the formula, "By means of the out-breath and in-breath, I make you one whose body is whole.
The Brahman priest then hands it to the sacrificer. (25)
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the first book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra. || 7 ||
1.8 Now begins the eighth chapter.
He strews the altar with sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Having placed blades of grass in between, he spreads the cord diagonally.
According to some, [he spreads it] to the southern edge of the altar.

With the mantra, "O divine sacrificial grass, soft as wool, I spread thee," he covers the roots with the tips, spreading it thickly so that it is not visible through, ending toward the east, either in three layers or five layers.
At each layer, he repeats the mantra.
Having drawn out two firebrands for the sake of the *anuyāja* offerings and having prepared the *āhavanīya* fire, he takes up the *prastara* and lays down the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).

With the formula, "Thou art Gandharva," he places the middle enclosing stick on the sacrificial grass behind the *āhavanīya* with its tip pointing north; with "Thou art the arm of Indra," he places the southern one so that it touches the middle one with its tip pointing north; and with "Mitra and Varuṇa, thee," he places the northern one so that its tip touches the middle one.
Then, having touched the *āhavanīya* with the formula, "May Sūrya protect thee from the east."

He places two supporting fuel-sticks upright: the southern one with the formula, "Thee, the enjoyer of the oblation, O sage," and the northern one silently, or with the formula, "Thou art a fuel-stick; for life, thee.
He makes two blades of *darbha* grass, equal in size and without internal shoots, into the *vidhṛti* (separators) of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
With the words, "May the people be in its support," he places it upon the sacrificial grass (barhis) in the middle of the altar with its tips pointing northward.
With the words, "Of the Vasus and the Rudras," he sets down the prastara-bunch between those two.
With the words, "Thou art the Juhū-ladle," he places the Juhū-ladle upon the prastara so that its handle is level with the roots [of the grass].
With the formula, "Thou art the Upabhṛt," he places the northern Upabhṛt below the two separating blades (vidhṛtis), drawing it closer together.
With the formula, "Thou art the Dhruvā," he places the northern Dhruvā above the two separating blades, drawing it closer and ensuring it does not touch [the others].

With the formula, "Thou art the Bull, belonging to the Śakvarī; I place thee in the measure of the Vaṣaṭ-call," he places the Sruva spoon to the south of the Juhū, or to the north of the Dhruvā. Or [he may place it] with the formula: "Thou art the Bull, belonging to the Śakvarī, the son of the butter-dripping ones; sit in thy dear seat by thy dear name. || 26 ||
He consecrates them with the mantra, "These have sat down.
Regarding the clarified butter (*ājya*): "You are Viṣṇu-portions, belonging to Viṣṇu, the abodes of Prajāpati.

With the *sruva*-ladle, he makes small portions of the clarified butter intended for the Gārhapatya and Dakṣiṇāgnis; with the *juhū*-ladle, he takes [portions] from the *dhruvā* for the Āhavanīya fire.
With the formula, "I drive away the face of this attacking army," he drives away the embers from the southern cake-offering with the wooden sword, and then he drives them away from the northern one.

He consecrates [the cake] with the mantra: "O Sun, shine forth as light for great sensory power. Having spread a base of clarified butter in the vessel with the mantra: "I prepare a pleasant seat for you; I fashion it well-favored with a stream of ghee," he pours over the cake dedicated to Agni with the mantra: "May Agni, whose source is ghee, swell; may he approve the oblations. Anoint the cavity, anoint the skin; I pour over you, who are well-formed and a finder of wealth, with the splendor of cattle, as one dear to Agni. He pours silently over the northern [cake].

"O Soma, you whose self has entered into the animals, who have spread throughout the abode of the gods—becoming possessed of self and rich in clarity (*ghṛta*), go to the gods; find the light for me, the sacrificer. With these words, he takes down the cooked offering.

"Moist, expanding, guardian of the world, the cooked one, the progenitor of thoughts, rises up. With this verse, he takes down the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), without breaking it and without turning it over. Having wiped away the ashes with the *veda* grass-bundle...

"In that immortal [substance], sit down; take your stand in the essence of the rice grains, being well-disposed"—with these words, he places [the cake] upon the vessel that has been spread with butter.
"May the nourishment, the prosperity, and the sap of the earth not depart"—saying this, he pours clarified butter over each of the potsherds one by one, counts them, and sets them aside.
"May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey"—with these words, he anoints the sacrificial cake.

Having anointed [the cakes] on top with clarified butter—leaving the surface unanointed, leaving the tortoise-pattern unanointed, and leaving the edge unanointed—he anoints them from below with his hand using the *sruva* spoon, saying, "May they sit upon their dear seat with their dear name. To the west of the offering-ladles, he places the two *puroḍāśa* cakes: the one for Agni to the south and the other to the north.
Having joined the two *sānnāyya* pots together in the middle of the altar, he separates them: the boiled milk on the southern hip of the altar and the curd on the northern hip.

"This Veda has found the earth, which was hidden in caves, in the depths, in the abysses; may it find a world for the sacrificer; may he of many deeds perform the flawless sacrifice"—having thus placed the Veda in front of the *dhruvā* [ladle], and having strewn grass around the edges of the altar, he prepares the seat of the Hotṛ. He prepares it. (27)
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the first book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra. || 8 ||
Thus ends the first book in the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. || 1 ||

Oṃ, salutation to the Brahman that is *tat-sat*. I bow to Nṛsiṃha, the Lord who is consciousness, bliss, and infinite; who is non-dual; who is the shatterer of the elephants of misfortune; and by whom, when offered, ritual action leads to its fruit, and when not offered, even to liberation from bondage. O you whose self is the three Vedas, whose self is the three fires, whose self is the three Lords, and whose self is the qualities of primordial nature!

May I, through my intellect, ever meditate with devotion upon the Lord—the reflection of the three states of living beings, whose nature consists of the three images; who is proclaimed by the syllable *Oṃ*, praised by the gods, and filled with compassion for his devotees; who bears the marks of the hand and the tooth, who has taken refuge in Hara, and who possesses a whiteness that pervades his body; who dispels the darkness covered by ignorance, who is the Seer (*kavi*), who is the "I" within the "I-consciousness," who is the goal of the earth, the object of meditation for embodied beings, and the destroyer of fear. *Oṃ*. I meditate with devotion upon the Infinite Lord, who is manifested by the syllable *Oṃ*, honored by the gods, endowed with compassion for his devotees, bearing the signs of the hand and the tooth, having resorted to Hara, possessing a whiteness extending over his body, removing the darkness veiled by ignorance, the Seer, the "I" within the "I"-intellect, the destination of the earth, the one to be meditated upon by all beings, and the cutter of fear.

By her, through the fortune of her body and her husband, Gaṅgādhara was made known as Hari, the Lord of Śrī; by her, who is named Mahālakṣmī, the Grandfather of the worlds became the Lord of Sarasvatī. Salutations to her, O Mother; salutations to you again; let there be further salutations to you from your compassionate glance. Protect me, a wretched man, from the cycle of rebirth, O storehouse of mercy! O Mother of my lineage, witness of the worlds, salutations to you. [The one] who has understood the meaning of the Yajurveda from his teacher Vyāsa...

Having received a branch from the Sage who set the Vedas in motion, that preeminent sage, assuming the form of a partridge bird, taught it to the lords of sages; thus he propagated the unbroken branch. (6) Wherein the excellent teacher Baudhāyana composed his Sūtra out of great reverence for the sake of preserving the meaning, and likewise the lord of sages Bharadvāja, as well as the teacher Āpastamba, clearly composed this supreme work. (7) Furthermore, having composed [the text] with reasonings not shown by others, which possess extremely hidden meanings, he again [established] the authoritative tradition. (8)

The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[which is] the *Hiraṇyakeśī*, whose name corresponds to its actual content, which has become the source of satisfaction for the eminent sages, and is approved by the lords of munis; || 8 || Furthermore, the excellent teacher Vādhūla composed a supreme *Sūtra* situated in the region of Yaskerala; and another, composed by the teacher Vaikhānasa, is joined with the *Pūrtasūtra*. Thus, there are six kinds of *Sūtras*. || 9 || I bow with devotion to Vyāsa and the other eminent sages, through whom this *Kalpataru* of the Yajurveda has attained renown in the world.

He has been brought [to this state] for the benefit of the world of dull-witted people by those with compassionate hearts through the various paths of the scriptures. I joyfully bow to the Lord of Sages, who is endowed with the power of discipline, whose speech is perfected, and who shines with the bliss of consciousness; I bow to my preceptor named Hiraṇyakeśin, an ocean of mercy, who is like a moon to me. He who is renowned as Brahmadatta in the first lineage, was given [the name] by his father Janaka, the son of Brahmā.

The son of Maitreyī, that best of sages, attained the supreme state of his true nature through the yoga, knowledge, and austerity bestowed by his father. (12) Appointed by his father to this world of action for the purpose of dividing the branches of the Veda and for its protection, he—this very one—is desirous of fully adorning my sinless lineage of Kuśika by means of his own incarnation. (13) Relying upon Truth, he received from his father the instruction regarding the feet of the primordial Truth, which had been known [only] as the source of untruth. (14)

He obtained the *Hiraṇyakeśīs* from the chief great seers (*maharṣi*), the authors of the Sūtras, who were filled with wonder at the composition of the Sūtra. (14) I bow to my Guru Gaṇapati, as well as to Maheśāna together with Gaurī, who bestow both birth and knowledge; and I bow to Viṣṇu together with Padmā. (15) The aphorisms (*sūtra*) were composed by the incarnation of the glorious Lord Viṣṇu; their commentary (*vyākhyā*) is being composed by Satyāpāda, [also known as] Mahādeva. (16) 1. Ka. Ga. read "°sidhyai so"; 2. Sa. reads "tmabhuvā pradattām"; Sk. Ga. reads "prado bhava".

He, for the sake of Somanātha, [composed] this [work]. Chapter 2, 150. This [text], along with the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva, has almost vanished; it was preserved only recently and in some places by Devadāsa on the banks of the Tānā in the south. Having examined the *Prayogaratna*, which contains a collection of the Sūtras and is established as the body of the sacrifice (*yajñatanu*), Viṣṇu shines within himself by his own self; and the one who has come together is considered an elder in learning.

Dharma and knowledge arise from the Vedas and the two Mīmāṃsās; likewise, from those two when conjoined with ritual action, the attainment of the fruit occurs. (19) Since Yājñavalkya and others have declared that [the goal] is to be attained through these fourteen branches of learning, both in regard to knowledge and in regard to the Lord, (20) I shall here expand upon what has been briefly indicated by the aphorisms and gathered from other sources as well, in order to examine my own intellect and to dispel the disease of dullness. (21)

Just as the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayanavidhi*) is the authority for the acquisition of the Veda along with its meaning (*sārtha*), so too is it for the *Kalpasūtra*. Why? Because the acquisition of that [Veda] must occur precisely through its essence (the meaning), and not otherwise. Therefore, the *Kalpasūtra* should be undertaken and studied together with its meaning. The Teacher himself will state regarding the religious duties (*dharma*) that the acquisition of the Veda includes the acquisition of the Veda with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*). In the *Gomadhuparkādi* [sections], the study of the Veda is taught; it is stated in the Sūtras that "the Veda consists of six parts."

Likewise, he will state elsewhere in that very work: "Grammar, phonetics, astronomy, etymology, and the prosody of meters constitute the *kalpa*. Because they are praised as limbs (*aṅga*), they are subordinate; this is due to their being auxiliary and because the Veda lacks the capacity [to function] independently of them. As it is said: "Grammar is its mouth, and astronomy is called its eye; Etymology is designated as its ear, and the investigation of meters is its feet; Phonetics is the voice of the Veda, while they declare the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) to be its hands."

Grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) and etymology (*nirukta*) provide instruction on the correctness of words and their meanings; astronomy (*jyotiṣa*) determines the proper time for rituals; the absence of initial *vṛddhi* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) anomaly; prosody (*chandas*) distinguishes between the meters such as the *gāyatrī*; phonetics (*śikṣā*) regulates the pronunciation of phonemes and so forth; and ritual manuals (*kalpa*) refers to the *Kalpasūtras*.

The *Kalpa* is that which, having stated the meaning of the Veda and indicated it through the principles of other branches (*śākhāntara*), arranges the three components—result (*phala*), instrument (*karaṇa*), and procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—into a ritual application (*prayoga*) according to the principles of specific mantras; it renders [the rite] capable and fit for performance in each branch. Āpastamba clearly states this as *chandokalpa*; the meaning is that it arranges the *chandas*, which is the Veda. Another Śruti passage clearly states the necessity of studying all six parts: "A Brāhmaṇa should study and know the sixfold Veda without motive" (*niṣkāraṇam*). "Without motive" means without aiming for a specific reward.

"Always" means for as long as time lasts. Now, one might object: surely the *Kalpasūtras* must be included within the Veda itself, because Vedic usage is observed therein. No; for they are remembered as being of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). The author of the Sūtras himself will state the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*uttara-pakṣa*) on this point. Therein, the prima facie view is that [the Vedas] consist of the collections of words (mantras), as they say: "But when the collection of rituals is completed, the word 'Veda' applies there; in that case, the number [of Vedas] is contradicted. [This refers to] the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[First Book]. The word "Veda" applies when the collection of rituals is finished; in that context, the traditional number [of four Vedas] is contradicted.

Those actions which are undertaken by means of verbal signification (*śabdārthatayā*)—and not as objects within the scope of perception or other means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣādipramāṇagocaratayā*)—are the Vedic rites such as the *agnihotra* and others that have verbal signification as their basis. The "collection" (*samāmnāya*) refers to their instruction (*upadeśa*). Upon the completion of that collection—that is, when it reaches its conclusion in terms of performance (*anuṣṭhāna*)—the word "Veda" (*veda*) applies there. It is called "Veda" because it makes known (*vedayati*) Dharma, or because one knows (*vidanti*) Dharma by means of it.

Furthermore, instruction does not extend merely to the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* portions up to the point of performance; rather, it includes the *kalpasūtras* as well. Consequently, since these too are included within the very nature of the Veda, there are only five auxiliary limbs (*aṅgas*). To the objection that the number six is thus contradicted here, he replies: "The convention of those who know the principles of logic is that the auxiliaries are not designated separately from their primary subjects. The *kalpasūtras* are indeed auxiliaries and not of the nature of the Veda, because they are remembered as being of human origin.

For among those [Vedic texts], there are only a few sentences belonging to the Brāhmaṇas, while the vast majority are their own sentences. Furthermore, it is the established conclusion of those learned in logic that it is not proper to designate those auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) by means of terms denoting the primary [text], such as "Chandas," "Veda," "Brāhmaṇa," and so forth. These two—the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)—should be seen more clearly in the section concerning the *Kalpasūtras*.

As for what was said—that the instruction is not complete by means of the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* alone—this is not the fault of the post that the blind man does not see; rather, it is the fault of the person, not the fault of the Veda. For the seers (*ṛṣis*), having conceived through their own intellects the Veda along with other Vedas and the principles indicated therein, perceive [the meaning] as fully established in every recensional branch (*śākhā*); they do not, however, introduce into it anything that is established merely by worldly means of knowledge (*laukika-pramāṇa*). You are incompetent.

The study of these [Kalpa-sūtras] is essential, as they serve as a refuge for people of the present day who wish to become capable of performing ritual applications (*prayoga*) after having studied other branches of scripture (*śāstra*). In this regard, the Kalpa-sūtra is distinct for each Vedic school (*śākhā*), though in some cases it is not. The distinction between schools arises either from a difference in recitation (*adhyayana*) or from a difference in the sūtras. Indeed, the Āśvalāyana and Kātyāyana Sūtras each belong to two different schools with distinct recensions.

In the *Taittirīyaka* recension (*samāmnāya*), which constitutes a common study (*samānādhyayana*), various *sūtras* are found. From this difference in *sūtras*, a difference in *śākhās* is also observed in the *Caraṇavyūha-śāstra*. Nor should it be argued that there is a circularity—namely, that a difference in *śākhās* results from a difference in *sūtras*, and a difference in *sūtras* results from a difference in *śākhās*—because, just as the difference in *śākhās* due to differences in study is beginningless, so too is the difference in *sūtras*. For the designation associated with the authors of the *sūtras* is not contemporary; rather, it pertains to their respective names belonging to various *kalpas*.

The genus (*jāti*) is eternal within individual instances (*vyakti*). It persists by depending upon the sūtras composed by him (Pāṇini), just as a name exists in branches marked with that name. Nor should it be argued that there is no principle of beginningless succession (*anādyānupūrvī*) in this case; for here too, the principle of succession is identical because it is beginningless. Although the sequence of words might possibly occur otherwise, nevertheless, the genus is not differentiated by the difference between individual instances. However, the order of performance belongs only to that which is non-human (*apauruṣeya*).

Even regarding study (*adhyayana*), the sequence is not eternal, because for each individual it is produced and thus non-eternal. In the *Āmnāya*, the study occurs through the recollection of the prior sequence; however, in the case of the *Sūtras*, they are manifested by a sequence that is merely human and even resides in the words themselves. Thus, the status of the *Sūtras* as *Smṛti* (recollection) was established in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa*, as seen in the acceptance of the Mīmāṃsā conclusion stated by the author of the *Sūtras* himself, namely that [the Vedas] are "devoid of logical reasoning" (*nyāyavirasa*).

Likewise, it has also been demonstrated that the authority of the Smṛtis likewise arises from the system of logic (nyāya). Scripture (Śruti) also declares that the Smṛtis have their root in the Veda: "Whatever Manu said is indeed medicine (bheṣaja).
