Just as medicine is beneficial, so too the word of Manu is beneficial in the sense of being authoritative. [End of Section 1] [This concludes] the first section, accompanied by the commentary Vaijayantī composed by Mahādeva.

Manu also says: "The sages perceive the Śruti and likewise remember the Smṛti. For this very reason, Marīci states: "Vedic words are difficult to understand, and because they are scattered, they are not entirely clear; therefore, by those who know them, their meanings have been established through the Smṛtis. In the *Smṛtitantra*, that is, in the scripture characterized as Smṛti, they are "established" by way of explaining the meaning.

Likewise, within a single *taittirīyaka* branch (*śākhā*) that possesses an identical recitation (*samānapāṭha*), a subdivision of the branch is shown in the *Caraṇavyūha* treatise due to a difference in the *sūtras*. Here, "branches" (*caraṇas*) means [Vedic] recensions (*śākhās*), and "arrangement" (*vyūha*) means the distinct classification of the *sūtras*. Moreover, there is no difference in the study (*adhyayana*) here; therefore, the division of the branches arises solely from the difference in the *sūtras*.

If it is argued that a single portion of one's own recitation (*svādhyāya*), consisting of both mantra and brāhmaṇa, is called a "branch" (*śākhā*), and that there would thus be internal divisions within the Veda based on the distinction between those two—mantra and brāhmaṇa—that is true. However, just as that *svādhyāya* is denoted by the term "Veda," so too does each branch, being a part of that [Veda], acquire the status of a distinct branch. In this regard, the study of one's own recitation is indeed differentiated according to the differences in the *aṅkas* (sections) and *sūtras*.

Let it be that the very difference in *caraṇa* (school) is the cause for the conventional usage of the difference in *śākhā* (branch). And thus, just as the study of a *śākhā* is strictly fixed, so too the study of the *sūtra* cannot be performed by transposition; furthermore, there is an injunction of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in the event of such transposition regarding the performance of ritual acts. He himself will also state: "The expiation for one who has fallen from his *caraṇa* is the *Trivṛt-stotra*"; and the state of having fallen from one's *caraṇa* results from the transposition of either the *śākhā* or the *sūtra* individually.

If it is asked: "Since the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*) is common [to all], how can there be a difference in ritual action (*karma-bheda*), how can there be a difference in the Sūtras, and if there is such a difference, how can there be a unity of fruit (*phala-ekya*)? It is replied: There is no difference in the ritual action.

Just as it is established in the Nyāyaśāstra that a single ritual action (*karman*) may have various branches (*śākhā*) as its conditions, so too, even though the ritual is one and the same for followers of different branches, they perform distinct applications (*prayoga-bheda*) by incorporating only those injunctions required by their own specific branch. Indeed, there is no difference in the ritual itself based on such means of knowledge as "difference of words" (*śabdāntara*); rather, just as within a single branch there is merely a difference in application due to the distinction between obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites, so too here there is merely a difference in application due to differences in sequence and subordinate qualities (*krama-guṇa*). As he will state: [text follows].

By the statement beginning with "those two have identical injunctions" (*tau samānavidhānau*), it is shown that even within the same study of the Veda, there is a difference in performance (*anuṣṭhānabheda*) in some cases due to the intention to express a single meaning for a word that has multiple meanings; and in other cases, when an option (*vaikalpika-prayoga*) arises because of the plurality of mantras and Brāhmaṇas from different recensions (*śākhāntara*) required by the injunction, there is a difference in performance through the adoption of one fixed alternative. Therefore, there is no disparity even in the result (*phala*) based on such differences in performance.

Just as the result obtained from offering oblations with *himī* on one branch is the same as that obtained with barley, and the result of an oblation offered after sunrise is the same as that of one offered before sunrise; and furthermore, these results apply only to those belonging to that specific branch and not to others, while a deviation even leads to undesirable consequences—therefore, it is established that since the performance of rites such as the *agnihotra* presents options for alternative practices through the combination of various branches, the *Kalpasūtras* serve to provide a systematic regulation (*vyavasthā*). Moreover, the incorporation of elements from other branches is necessarily required.

The performance of all Śrauta and Smārta rites, or the recitation of their mantras, is not prescribed in its entirety within a single branch (śākhā) of the Veda; rather, it is well known that one must depend on other Vedas for certain elements, such as those pertaining to the Adhvaryu or Hotṛ priests. Likewise, for the complete accomplishment of the duties of the Adhvaryu and others, there is a dependence on other branches of the Veda, such as the Ādhvaryava. Nor can the requirements of the scriptures be fulfilled by what is prescribed solely in one's own branch, for this would lead to the omission of sacraments such as initiation (upanayana), which are not prescribed in our particular branch.

And it is observed that there is a dependence on the injunctions regarding the *indrāmada* and other formulas found in other recensions (*śākhāntara*), because those specific mantras and *nigadas* are not recited in our own recension (*asmat-śākhā*). Furthermore, [the text] sometimes mentions something not already established in our recension and then prohibits it; sometimes, having censured one thing, it prescribes another—as in the passage: "He does not throw up the *uttaravedi*, for he went away like a thief," and so forth.

Therefore, it is understood that the prohibition and censure apply only to what has been obtained through the combination of all branches (*sarva-śākhā-upasaṃhāra*); thus, the accomplishment of the ritual action (*karma-siddhi*) occurs through the combination of all branches. If this were so, then for people of the present day who have not studied all branches, as well as even those who have studied them, it would be impossible to combine the nature of the duties (*dharma-svarūpa*) established in each individual branch. Consequently, it must be understood from the study of the Sūtras themselves that the duty is established [in its specific form].

Nor are other Ṛṣis of different names capable of declaring this established Dharma, because they lack those specific names that manifest such power. For even the Lord—who is one, omniscient, and omnipotent—is not able to accomplish the entire purpose through a single incarnation; thus, He descends in various forms. It is seen in the Purāṇas and Itihāsas that the Munis, too, are indeed incarnations.

Nevertheless, because they are incapable of transcending beginningless power (*śakti*), being bound by a chain of names that manifest through the continuous succession of preceding [traditions], they proceed—observed with the eye of yogic knowledge (*yogajñānacakṣus*)—and, without abandoning their own specific domain for another, they compose *sūtras* for the sake of those who know the rules of the *Prātiśākhyas*. For it is said: "When the third cycle of the ages had arrived, at the onset of the *Dvāpara*..."

The yogi Parāśara was born from Vāsavyā as a portion of Hari. Once, having performed his ablutions in the Sarasvatī and become pure, that sage sat alone in a secluded place when the solar disc had risen. That seer, who knew both the higher and the lower, perceived through time the decline of the unmanifested [dharma] on earth in age after age, the confusion of the duties of the Yugas, and the loss of power caused by that [confusion] among material beings. He saw them as lacking faith, devoid of strength, dull-witted, and short-lived.

Beholding people who were unfortunate, the sage, whose vision was unclouded, meditated upon what would be beneficial for all the social classes (*varṇas*) and stages of life (*āśramas*). Observing that the Vedic ritual of the four officiating priests (*cāturhotra*) was pure for the sake of progeny, he divided the single Veda into four parts for the continuity of sacrifice. The four Vedas known as Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan were extracted; and the *Itihāsa-Purāṇa* is called the fifth Veda. Among them, Paila was appointed to the Ṛgveda, and the wise Naimiṇi to the Sāmaveda.

Vaiśampāyana alone is considered proficient in the Yajurveda; Sumantu, the formidable sage, was [the authority] for the Atharvāṅgirasa; and my father Romaharṣaṇa was the father of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. Those very sages divided their respective Vedas in many ways; through disciples, grand-disciples, and their disciples, those Vedas became possessed of branches (śākhins). [End of Chapter 150] This concludes the section accompanied by the Vaijayantī commentary composed by Mahādeva.

"Just as those very Vedas are maintained by men of dull intellect, so did the Blessed Vyāsa, who is compassionate toward the miserable, act. The meaning is that Vyāsa is indeed Hari himself; by instilling power in his disciples and others, he performed everything through them. Since its purpose has thus been established, the Blessed Satyāṣāḍha, for the sake of consolidating the understanding of his students, presents in summary form the Sūtra he is about to compose:
"We shall explain the sacrifice (yajña)."

Sacrifice (*yajña*) is indeed the giving of a substance with mantras, directed toward a deity. Its nature is to be defined solely by means of the deity and the substance. Regarding this, the Mīmāṃsakas say: "The substance and the deity are the form of the ritual act. Therefore, its explanation consists in making known: "This substance belongs to this deity; one should give it in this manner with these mantras for the sake of this result. Likewise, the explanation of sacrifice includes [the distinction between] what is the archetype (*prakṛti*) and what is the modification (*vikṛti*).

In addition to that, the *davihoma* and other rites characterized by it, as well as the *upanayana* and other *sāmayācārika* (conventional) rites, are to be performed in this manner for the sake of this specific result; this too is the promise (*pratijñā*) of the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*), because it indicates the various ritual acts according to each *śākhā*. Although one could have simply said, "We shall explain the ritual acts," the word "sacrifice" is used specifically to indicate the abundance of such rites. Indeed, this is the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśī-Sūtra*, consisting of twenty-seven chapters (*praśnas*).

In that regard, following the introductory definitions, the two primary questions concerning the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices have been explained; likewise, the Unnetṛ, the Vāpyendra, the Ṛdhakāmya, the modifications of the Darśapūrṇamāsa performance, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, and the office of the Brahman priest have been expounded.

In the third book (*praśna*), there is the section on eligibility for all rites, the determination of substitutes, the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and its subsidiary offerings (*iṣṭis*), the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*), the *agnihotra*, the departure of one who maintains the household fires, the rules for *darvihoma* offerings, the method of extended application (*atideśa*), specific injunctions for modified sacrifices (*vikṛtis*), the performance of the *soma*, *āgrayaṇa-iṣṭi*, and *paśubandha* sacrifices, the times of the new and full moon (*amāvāsyā-paurṇamāsī*) for the *āgrayaṇa-iṣṭi*, and the *āgrayaṇa-iṣṭi* itself. In the fourth book, there is the independent animal sacrifice (*nirūḍhapaśubandha*) and specific injunctions regarding its variations. In the fifth book, there are the seasonal sacrifices (*cāturmāsyas*).

In the sixth [chapter], following the general rules for the measurement of the sacrificial ground (*yājamāna*), there is the treatment of the *yājamāna* duties for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices when the sacrificer is away on a journey, as well as the specific *ādhvaryava* duties; the extension (*atideśa*) of the *yājamāna* duties to the *iṣṭis*, animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*), and the direct and inferred hearing of the mantras for the offerings to Candra, Vaimṛdha, Sarasvatī, Pūṣan, Aditi, Dyāvāpṛthivī, Aryaman, Viśvedevas, Indra, Indriyavat, and Indratrātṛ; the *yājamāna* duties regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), beginning from the time of the installation and including the duties of one who has established the fires (*āhitāgni*); the specific sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) in the case of re-establishing the fires (*punarādheya*); and the *yājamāna* duties for the *agnihotra*.

The rules for attendance during the *homopasthāna*, attendance while away on a journey, and attendance upon returning from a journey; the *āmayaṇeṣṭi*, the *nirūḍhapaśubandha*, and the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices; the measurement of the sacrificial vehicle (*yānamāna*) and the intermediate vows within the *cāturmāsya*s. Then, in the seventh, eighth, and ninth [sections], the *jyotiṣṭoma* and its modifications—the *ukthya*, *ṣoḍaśin*, *atirātra*, and *aptoryāma*—as well as the eleven animals (*ekādaśinī*), the specific ritual duties to be performed through the application of the *tantra* method regarding those animals, and their particular characteristics.

In the tenth [book], there is the application of the *agniṣṭoma* for the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) and the *hotṛ*, as well as the office of the *brahmán* priest in the *jyotiṣṭoma*. In the eleventh and twelfth, the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*). In the thirteenth, the *vājapeya* and *rājasūya*, as well as the *caraka-sautrāmaṇī*. In the fourteenth, the *aśvamedha*, *puruṣamedha*, and *sarvamedha*. In the fifteenth, expiations (*prāyaścitta*) for errors in the ritual rules. In the sixteenth, the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) in its forms as an *ahīna* and a *sattra*, the *mahāvrata*, and the *gavāmayana*. In the seventeenth, the one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*) and the *ahīna*s.

In the eighteenth [chapter], the sacrificial sessions (*satra*) ending with the thousand-year sacrifice; in the nineteenth and twentieth, the Smārta rites beginning with the initiation (*upanayana*); in the twenty-first, the determination of the *Yājuṣa-hautra* and the *pravara*; in the twenty-second, the optional *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*); in the twenty-third, the Kaukilī, the Sautrāmaṇī, the *sava*s, and the *kāṭhaka-cayana*s; and in the twenty-fourth, the *pravargya*.

In the twenty-fifth *śulba*, the methods for constructing sacrificial altars (*vihāra-yoga*) have been explained; in the twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh, the duties (*dharma*) are treated. As for the *Pitṛmedha*, it consists of two sections (*praśna*) adopted by the sage Bhāradvāja. The word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) indicates what is set forth in this *sūtra* rather than denoting it directly; for the word "sacrifice," as in "the sacrifice" (*yajñam*), is conventionally established and well-known in the sense of a ritual offering (*yāga*) consisting of the presentation of the *vaṣaṭ*-call. [As it is said: "He who is Prajāpati, the seventeenfold..."

"Know that the sacrifice is dependent upon [the Self]"—thus, for the purpose of enjoining it as an auxiliary to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the body of Prajāpati, who is the Supreme Self whose body is the sacrifice, is described through such terms as "O, make the proclamation! (āśrāvaya).

Therefore, the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices are to be accomplished through such acts as the *āśrāvaṇa* (the call for the response), and likewise their subsidiaries such as the *prayāja*s are also sacrifices enjoined by specific injunctions that fall within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa and consist precisely of the *āśrāvaṇa* and other such limbs. Similarly, even in the case of Soma—which is denoted by the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) in the passage, "Prajāpati created the gods and the Asuras"—the text mentions the *āśrāvaṇa* and other limbs as being of the nature of vigor (*vīrya*) according to the metrical meters (*chandas*).

And thus, the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, other sacrifices such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and its modifications in the form of iṣṭis and paśubandhas, as well as the modifications of the qualities of the Jyotiṣṭoma—namely the Ekāha, Ahīna, and Satra sacrifices—are all designated by the terms *yajña* and *yāga*. No other meanings, such as "worship of the gods" (*devapūjā*) or "establishing a connection" (*saṃgatikaraṇa*), are taught by the grammarians (*śiṣṭa*) as the meaning of the verbal root *yaji*. The word *yajña* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for the act of offering with the *vaṣaṭ* call; when used elsewhere, it is employed either through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or through etymological derivation (*yoga*).

For this very reason, Kātyāyana says: "The *vaṣaṭ*-offerings are sacrifices (*yajati*s); the *svāhā*-offerings are oblations (*juhoti*s). Naimini also states: "There is a difference of action when there is a different word, because of the connection with a specific [verbal] suffix. And the author of the Vārttika also says: "In every case where there is a difference in the meaning of the verbal root, a different *bhāvanā* is to be understood."

Therefore, although the word *yana* here also denotes the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of merit in the form of sacrifice, it sets forth various rituals such as the Piṇḍapitṛyajña and the Agnihotra—beginning with those mentioned in the *Dharma-praśna* and ending with those mentioned in the *Pitṛmedha-praśna*—which have prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) as their fruits. Furthermore, he will state that the Pitṛmedha is a refinement of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*), and its fruit is infinite happiness, namely heaven. Likewise, the Self (*ātman*) is also intended to be explained among these duties; it has been proposed as a subject to be expounded.

How so? For it has been declared that "that which is denoted by the word *yajña* (sacrifice)—namely, *bhāvanā*—which was promised as the subject to be explained, is what is enjoined. Immediately thereafter, it is stated that the injunction has *bhāvanā* as its object: "one should bring about" (*bhāvayet*). Thus, [the injunction] must direct itself toward *bhāvanā*. And being possessed of the expectancy "what [should one bring about]?", it must effect [something]. In that regard, the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), whether expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) or implied, is understood as residing within the *bhāvanā*. And since that which is a means to a desired end is itself desired as the object to be brought about (*bhāvya*), it first grasps unqualified happiness (*sukha*) alone.

Therefore, if in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*) happiness is delimited by terms such as "heaven," it is apprehended in that very way; otherwise, in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), unsurpassed happiness itself is apprehended as the fruit to be accomplished. That [happiness] is apprehended as the fruit because the Self alone—being the object of supreme love—is to be attained through direct realization, which serves as its delimiting factor. As the Teacher will state: "Among duties, there is no fruit superior to the attainment of the Self, which occurs through the door of knowledge."

The "attainment of what has been obtained" consists in the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) that removes ignorance; this too he will state in the inquiry regarding the installation of the fires (*ādhāna*): "What is the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)? Direct realization and the realized nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*) constitute the meaning of the term "supreme good. Therefore, the Self is indeed presented as the fruit (*phala*). When there arises the expectation, "By what means should one cultivate [it]?", following the connection with the fruit, sacrifices and so forth are understood as the instruments (*karaṇa*) for that fruit. (Note: *ka*, *ga*, *ca*, *cha* read "hītī" twice).

[Chapter] 1.150, accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. The ritual actions (*kriyā*) are connected [to the principal act]. Subsequently, when there is an expectation as to "how" [it is to be done], the auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) are connected as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Thus, that very productive urge (*bhāvanā*) which was proposed is now explained in terms of its nature as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*) and so forth. Now, an objection: since the words "sacrifice" (*yajati*), "offers oblation" (*juhoti*), and "gives" (*dadāti*) are applied by taking up the common meaning of giving (*dāna*), how can they have different meanings?

True. Although the act of giving (*dāna*) is common to all three [Vedic sacrifices], it has nevertheless been established in the *Śabdāntarādhikaraṇa* that there is indeed a distinction in their meaning due to the difference in injunctions (*codanā*) such as "he sacrifices" (*yajati*). If you ask, "What is the specific difference in their essential nature (*svarūpa*), and how so?"—it is said: based on the well-known consensus of the ritualists (*yājñika*) beginning with the authors of the Sūtras. Therefore, my criticism is not directed against the system of Jaimini. For the ritualists, having understood the intention of the Sūtra-authors, themselves strengthen that position through reasonings indicated by those very [Sūtras], being free from any doubt.

Respecting established convention, these [scholars] are to be honored in matters of Vedic ritual (*śrautakarman*); let my impertinence in establishing their view not be taken into account. The term *yajati* (he sacrifices) refers to mere giving (*dāna*) without throwing-in (*prakṣepa*); the term *juhoti* (he offers) applies to that same act when accompanied by throwing-in; and the term *dadāti* (he gives) applies to the completion of the transfer of ownership to the recipient of the vessel. Since the completion of offering (*homa*) consists of throwing-in and the completion of giving (*dāna*) consists of the transfer of ownership to another, sacrifice (*yāga*) is merely giving; thus, there is no confusion among them. If it is argued that there is indeed throwing-in even in a sacrifice—

No, because that [pouring] lacks the nature of the meaning of *yajati* (sacrifices), whereas the pouring is merely a subordinate part of the meaning of *juhoti* (offers), as seen in the injunction "He offers the fourfold portion" (*caturavattaṃ juhoti*). Furthermore, in cases such as "He releases the *agniṣṭhā* animal after it has been consecrated with fire," the sacrifice is accomplished even without pouring. Therefore, sacrifice is simply the act of giving to the deity by means of the *vaṣaṭ*-call—consisting merely of mental and vocal activity—as in the formula "I offer this to you. For this very reason, the author will later state: "The other offerings are its subsidiaries. This is the opinion of the authors of the Sūtras, who characterize them as acts of disposal (*pratipatti*).

Now, it may be argued that in the triad beginning with *yaja* (sacrifice), the primary meaning is the relinquishment of one's own ownership (*svasvatyāga*). That very [relinquishment] is understood as the form of the sacrifice in *yāga*, and respectively as the meaning of *homa* ending in the act of throwing [into the fire] and *dāna* ending in the production of ownership in the recipient. In that case, the deity possesses merely the status of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatvamātra*), whereas the relinquishment of ownership is common to all three; it is not something to be conveyed by the *vaṣaṭkāra* or *svāhākāra*. Thus, [the relinquishment of ownership is the core].

Just as in the case of *dāna* (giving), where the act consists of the removal [of ownership], the production of another’s ownership, and the completion characterized by the dedication to a worthy recipient (*pātrasātkaraṇa*), so too in the acts of *tyāga* (renunciation) and *homa* (offering), the sacrificer alone is the agent. This is because it is the sacrificer—who possesses the property—by whom it is performed with the thought, "This is no longer mine. Kātyāyana also stated: "We shall explain the sacrifice: it consists of the material, the deity, and the renunciation (*tyāga*). Likewise: "The master is the primary [agent] because he enjoys the fruit. Jaimini, the knower of Nyāya, also said: "The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer, for that is its characteristic..."

This is because of the principles "the general rule [applies] when there is no specific exception" and "the general rule should prevail as it is primary," as established by the authors of the Bhāṣya, Vārttika, and others. Nor should it be argued that, since the deity expressed by the taddhita suffix is taught for the purpose of the offering, she must be a partaker of the oblation.

Furthermore, since even in the case of the *caturyuktā* (the fourfold yoke), the status of a deity is understood precisely through its being a recipient (*saṃpradāna-kāraka*), how can it be asserted—while abandoning the primary meaning of both the verbal root and the suffix—that either mere renunciation (*tyāga*) or mere being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*) is accepted as the secondary meaning for both? This is stated more fully elsewhere. It should be said: "This is the Vedic meter. Thus it should be stated. If the deity’s connection with the sacrifice were established through a physical body, only then could the acceptance of the primary meaning be possible; moreover, there is no abandonment of the meaning, because it is accepted that something additional enters into that very [deity] which already exists.

In the same way, it was established in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* (the section on deities) and in the ninth [book] that, by means of arguments such as "The deity would indeed be the prompter, for food belongs to the guest," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) asserting the corporeality of the deity was addressed; furthermore, by refuting corporeality through the statement "Or rather, the injunction regarding sacrificial acts would belong to the one who precedes the word [the deity], since deities are mentioned as subordinate elements," it was established that the sacrifice is not a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the deity. If it is then asked: "How can the sacrifice be the act of giving with the *vaṣaṭ*-call, and how can that [act] belong to the *hotṛ* priest who utters the *vaṣaṭ*-call?"—[the answer is: No.

By means of the nominal affix (*taddhita*) signifying "for the sake of giving" and the dative case, for the purpose of establishing the primary meaning—namely, to effect the status of being the recipient of the oblation (*havis*) and the status of being the giver—it necessarily results that [the deity] must be enjoined as possessing a physical form (*vigrahavattva*). Nor does this imply that the sacrifice would be a mere refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the deity. Furthermore, the objects such as Indra are not worldly (in the sense of being perceptible), such that the apprehension of the word-potency (*śakti*) for words like "Indra" could occur through common worldly usage; rather, they too are to be known solely from the scripture (*śāstra*).

Furthermore, the Śāstra speaks of [the deity] as possessing a body; the apprehension of its denotative power (*śaktigraha*) occurs precisely therein, and not in that which is devoid of a body, for there is no worldly usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding such a thing. Nor is the word itself the very nature of the deity as a referent (*padārtha*), because there is a lack of evidence and because it is not perceived as such. Therefore, whatever kind of object the apprehension of the denotative power concerns, that alone is what is expressed by the respective deity-word; it is in that very sense that the injunction (*vidhi*) prescribes [the deity] as a deity.

Furthermore, in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* of the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā*, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa established through the sūtra "And that [is] possible, according to Bādarāyaṇa" (*saṃbhavāt*)—on account of the possibility—that deities possess embodied forms for the sake of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*), thereby asserting their eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā-adhikāra*). Otherwise, there would result the invalidity of those Śrutis and Smṛtis which establish the fruit of liberation through the attainment of the respective forms of the deities by means of practices such as meditation (*upāsanā*). Thus it was established in the *Devatādhikaraṇa*.

There is no contradiction with the Blessed Bādarāyaṇa himself; for in the Sūtra, "If it be said that [the fruit] is action, no, because we see various attainments," he has stated that the deities possess embodied forms (*vigrahavattva*). One must understand that having accepted exactly what was stated there, the authors of the Sūtras teach in various places that the fruits of action consist of attaining similarity of form (*sārūpya*) with the deities and so forth. Nor should it be argued that the attainment of the very nature of a deity is impossible, on the grounds that things such as kingdoms are insentient and thus cannot be deities.

For even in those cases, it is accepted that divinity belongs only to the conscious being residing within each respective body. Indeed, the use of the second person pronoun *yuṣmad* (you) is observed in relation to deities; therefore, deities are not insentient. This has been established at length in the *Nirukta* and other works. Nor should it be argued that there is an inconsistency because the word *yuṣmad* is used in reference to branches and the like; for it has also been established in those very same works that even in such instances, a conscious presiding deity is accepted.

Furthermore, all systems of logic (nyāya) culminate in practical application (prayoga). Indeed, the arrangement of ritual performance cannot be understood from any source other than the Sūtras. Moreover, it is the authors of the Sūtras alone who must establish the rules regarding the specific performers of the rite and the rules concerning the procedure (itikartavyatā), such as the use of mantras and so forth.

In this regard, the established position is that linguistic usage depends upon the apprehension of word-potency through observation of usage, and not upon the apprehension of potency established by formal logic (*nyāya*); for such [logical] status does not exist in worldly usage, and thus the investigation of the potency of beginningless usage is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, the authors of the Sūtras, having determined and established the enjoyers of the fruit and the agents with respect to Vedic injunctions (*codanā*), do so for the sake of establishing worldly usage with brevity.

In the rites prescribed by the *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, and *Sāmaveda*, the *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, and *udgātṛ* are respectively the performers when no specific instruction is given; others become performers only when specifically instructed. Consequently, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) does not possess the default status of being a performer with respect to the Vedic ritual framework. Therefore, the sacrificer becomes a performer only in a specific rite when he is so instructed.

In the *Hotṛ-sūtra*, which proceeds based on the *Ṛgveda*, Āśvalāyana, following the rule "one should understand [the agent] from that very [Veda]," states: "In an injunction for ritual action (*karmacodanā*) such as 'he sacrifices' (*yajati*), [the agent is] the Hotṛ; in 'he steps forward' (*padāti*), [it is] the sacrificer (*yajamāna*); and in expiations (*prāyaścitta*) such as 'he offers oblations' (*juhoti*) or 'he mutters' (*japati*), [it is] the Brahman. The meaning is that the application [of the Hotṛ] is established by the designation "the Hotṛ acts with the *Ṛgveda*. Furthermore, because it is an injunction for sacrifice (*yajati-codanā*), and because the Hotṛ is appropriate [as the agent] even in other injunctions where no specific agent has been prescribed.

Why? Because the Adhvaryu says "yaj" (sacrifice) specifically to him; likewise, the Maitrāvaruṇa does so as well. He alone recites "ye yajāmahe. Therefore, according to the Śruti: "By means of the Yājyā ending with the Vaṣaṭ-call, he [the Hotṛ] sacrifices or causes [the Adhvaryu] to sacrifice; he offers with the Anuvākyā. Furthermore, the principal act is performed by that which ends with the Vaṣaṭ-call, according to the Śruti: "It is given to the gods either by the Vaṣaṭ-call or by the Svāhā-call. Thus, when prompted by the word "vāti," it should be understood as referring to the sacrificer (Yajamāna) as the agent.

In this regard, the intended meaning is as follows: what is called "giving" (*dāna*) consists in the transfer of ownership of a substance given by means of the solicitation of Brahmins and others; and that [transfer] is conventionally established in that very context as being limited to the renunciation of ownership (*svatvatyāga*). The renunciation of ownership must be performed by the owner himself and not by another. Furthermore, it is established in all treatises that the property belongs to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*); therefore, the sacrificer alone is the agent of the act of giving, according to the practice of saying, "I give this to you," and so forth. However, in the Vedic [context], there is the usage of "I give" (*dadāmi*), and so on.

The *mantras* beginning with "gavanto" are indeed recited by the *adhvaryu* in the *yajamāna-sūtra*, but there is no such scriptural injunction anywhere for the recitation of *mantras* for the purpose of the sacrifice itself. Furthermore, the consecration (*anumantraṇa*) of the oblation is a distinct ritual act, a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) of the nature of a disposal (*pratipatti*), which serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Even in the *Yājuṣa-hautra*, the instruction "having placed the firebrand at the heart-region, he should follow and sacrifice" establishes the *hotṛ* alone as the agent; likewise, in "he sacrifices with 'O Agni, the kindling-sticks of the clarified butter... there is not even a mention of the sacrificer being the agent in the sense of performing the act of sacrificing (*yanati*).

Likewise, in the *Adhvaryu-sūtra* as well, having begun with "He offers when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, or when the *vaṣaṭ* is being uttered; he offers with four portions in those [verses] possessing both *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā*," and concluding with "The *adhvaryu* offers with the *svāhā*-utterance"—just as in the case of the *davihoma*—there is a restrictive rule that the *adhvaryu* alone is the agent. This applies to all actions prescribed in the Yajurveda, as well as in cases where no specific agent is mentioned. Furthermore, having begun with "We shall explain the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*"), [it continues with] those which...

The actions enjoined are to be performed by the sacrificer; however, among them, the status of being performed by the sacrificer is not specifically taught for the acts of sacrificing (*yajati*) and offering oblations (*juhoti*). Therefore, the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇādāna*) alone is to be performed by the sacrificer.

Regarding the view that sacrifice (*yāga*) and oblation (*homa*) are performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) alone, and that in these acts the sacrificer performs a portion of the sacrifice and oblation with the thought "this is not mine"—thus establishing the sacrificer as the agent— we see no basis for such a logical position (*nyāya*). Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the performance [of the rite], nor is there any injunction for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in the event of its omission, such as "this is not mine. Moreover, if the mere renunciation (*utsarga*), which is synonymous with abandonment (*tyāga*), were the primary element, then, since sacrifice and oblation would be identical, it would contradict the *Śabdāntarādhikaraṇa* (the section on distinct verbal forms).

If it is argued that there is a distinction [between the two cases], we say no; for in both instances, the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is seen to be "this is not mine," and because there is an absence of any difference in external performance on the part of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). If it is argued that a distinction is established for the *hotṛ* and *adhvaryu* priests by means of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance and the *svāhā*-utterance, we say no; for regarding the effects produced by the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance and the *svāhā*-utterance, do they constitute a primary part (*pradhānāṃśa*) or a subsidiary part (*aṅga*)? Not the first.

Furthermore, the act of establishing a connection with the fruit is the *yāga* (sacrifice), which consists of the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) characterized by the renunciation of ownership over the substance, thinking "this is not mine. Now, in the case of the establishment of the *gārhapatya* and other fires, or in rites such as the *Mahārudra*, since the renunciation of the substance is impossible [for the sacrificer], the fruit of that establishment performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) would not accrue to the sacrificer.

Furthermore, even in the case of subsidiaries such as the *prayāja* offerings, the act of renunciation (*tyāga*) would have to be performed by the *hotṛ* priest and others, because it serves as the instrument for the fruit; for the meaning of the verbal root culminates in renunciation, and it is accepted that the verbal root’s meaning culminates [in that]. Therefore, your position ultimately results in the conclusion that "renunciation" is the primary meaning indicated by the word. That is not so. Are both parts to be performed simultaneously by both [the agent and the priest], or sequentially? Not the first.

When the giving is performed with the *vaṣaṭ* as its conclusion, dedicated to a deity, then the renunciation (*tyāga*) must be made of that which has been consecrated by the act of giving; for there can be no renunciation of what has not been given. If, on the other hand, the renunciation were made of the very thing being given, then one would not personally perform the *agnihotra* oblation; for when the oblation concludes with *svāhā*, there is no opportunity for renunciation in the middle. Furthermore, in the case of the *soma* sacrifice, when it is said, "O Householder, sacrifice," the sacrificer himself performs the sacrifice; even then, there is no opportunity [for a separate renunciation].

Now, if renunciation (tyāga) occurs immediately thereafter [of the offering], then when the casting [into the fire] takes place along with the *vaṣaṭ* call, since the casting constitutes a ritual of disposal (*pratipatti*) within the sacrifice, it would be impossible for a sacrifice to occur after that which has already been disposed of; thus, the primary sacrifice would not be accomplished. Alternatively, if the renunciation occurs at the very beginning, it would contradict the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). For if the sacrifice and the oblation were completed by means of the *vaṣaṭ* and *svāhā* calls respectively, they would result in being mere acts of disposal. However, we accept that renunciation itself is of the nature of a disposal.

The second practice consists of renunciation (*tyāga*), which is inferred from the conduct of ritualists who, with great care, reduce the offered oblation (*havis*) to ashes as if it were something cast away; however, there is no direct scriptural injunction (*sākṣād-apadeśa*) anywhere regarding either renunciation or the act of reducing [the offering] to ashes. In the event that this is not performed, the ritualists prescribe only a general expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). In your view, for a sacrificer who is traveling abroad, even the act of renunciation itself would not be accomplished.

If mere renunciation (*tyāga*) were the primary element, then what is accomplished by mantras ending in *vaṣaṭ* or *svāhā*—namely, the offering of the oblation toward a deity—would have to be described as merely a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the substance being abandoned, and not as "giving" (*dāna*). This is because it is impossible for both giving and renunciation to be primary with respect to the substance simultaneously; or, if both were primary, it would follow that both acts belong to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). Therefore, giving must necessarily be understood as [the means] for the purpose of [the act] having occurred or about to occur.

According to the principle that "a substance undergoes consecration for the sake of its future utility," it must be accepted that the consecration belongs to a substance whose utility is yet to be, while its disposal (pratipatti) occurs when the utility has already passed. In that case, for a sacrificer who is away on a journey, there can be no accomplishment of the rite due to ignorance of the state of the substance existing before or after its disposal. If [the disposal] occurred previously, how could there be a disposal by casting [it] into the sacrifice when it had not yet been relinquished by the sacrificer? Conversely, if it were disposed of first, how could there be a consecration of what has already been relinquished?

In my view, for one who is traveling, there is no performance at all of any purificatory rite other than that which pertains to the patron (*yajamāna*). Regarding mantras that do not perform an action, the patron performs only their recitation (*japa*); by means of mantras that do perform an action, the patron’s portion of the ritual is accomplished, while the wife should perform the renunciation of ownership (*svatvatyāga*).

Even if it is performed by the sacrificer, there is no fault; for when a *pratipatti* (disposal) that provides direct auxiliary benefit (*saṃnipatyopakārin*) has ceased, no further benefit is produced in its own form. Therefore, in order to establish its status as a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*), one must assume that the nature of the sacrifice remains in the form of the *apūrva* (unseen potency), and that it is either obstructed or not produced due to the absence of the *pratipatti*. 1. ga. 12 kha. 'miva | kṣi| 3 kha. ṇe ca sa | 4 kha. cha. homa | 5 ka. ga. va siṃ'| ka. ga.

The acquisition of grain and so forth; and that [acquisition] is not that ritual action itself. [End of] Chapter 150, together with the Vaijayantī commentary composed by Mahādeva. In that case, if there is a deficiency, there would be a remedy through expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the obstructing factor, which is the unseen demerit (*duritāpūrva*). In your view, however, since the primary rite does not arise, the unseen merit (*apūrva*) itself does not arise; therefore, even with a hundred expiations, no restoration is possible.

For there can be no renunciation or sacrifice of a substance that has been reduced to ashes or one that has not yet come into existence; and if [the sacrifice] were independent of a substance, it would either fail to accomplish the *apūrva* or, by failing to do so, would result in the action having an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*), just as in the prima facie view regarding the cooking of the barley-gruel (*yavāgū*). Furthermore, if the sacrificer is away on a journey and the performance of the *iṣṭi* and *darvihoma* offerings becomes impossible due to some cause, the destruction of the sacred fires (*agni*) would follow.

Likewise, since renunciation is impossible in the case of the *ādhāna* (the laying of the sacred fires), if it were performed by the *adhvaryu*, the resulting refinement (*saṃskāra*) would also necessarily accrue to him alone; however, enough of this over-elaboration. Like the system of the Nyāya school, the view of Kātyāyana is seen here and there to be inconsistent with the instructions of other Sūtras. For instance, while Jaimini and Kātyāyana state that in the event of a defect in the *avadāna* (the cutting of the sacrificial portion) there must be a new production [of the offering], they nevertheless maintain that the *avadāna* should be performed again out of a different underlying intention (*āśaya*).

For this very reason, commentators also demonstrate, in various places, by distinguishing between them, both the *Nyāya* (logical) view and the *Upadeśa* (instructional) view. It should not be said that the word *upadeśa* is never used for a matter devoid of logic; rather, a treatise primarily concerned with general principles of reasoning is designated by the term *nyāya*. Furthermore, it has been stated that *upadeśa* consists of the investigation of the instructions found in the *Prātiśākhyas*. Likewise, even the *Kalpasūtra*, which is primarily instructional, is indeed an *upadeśa* because it contains within it the principles that have been so instructed. The Veda is *upadeśa*, not an ordinary worldly sentence.

Therefore, if scripture were to declare that even the fruit of the principal rite—when performed by priests obtained through purchase—accrues to the sacrificer, what inconsistency would there be? It will be stated later that in all rituals, the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) "I shall sacrifice" made with the fruit as its object is itself scriptural (*śrauta*), and thus it appropriates the fruit for oneself. Consequently, by the mere resolve to perform the sacrifice along with its constituent parts (*sāṅga-yāga-saṃkalpa*), the entire sacrifice has the sacrificer alone as its agent.

For it is precisely for that purpose that seekers perform [these acts]; thus, there is no contradiction with the principle that "the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer," because one is a performer solely by virtue of the intention (*saṃkalpa*). Therefore, the word *yajña*—which is a synonym for *yāga* (sacrifice)—refers only to that action enjoined as such, consisting of the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call and so forth, and not elsewhere. Its application to other rites such as the *agnihotra* is not primary, because it is improper to assume multiple meanings when a single consistent interpretation is possible.

The author of the Sūtras will also state, regarding the five sacrifices: "The great sacrifices are the great sessions; this is a praise. By this, those [sacrifices] are explained in their practical application—those which have names and forms such as the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, the Pākayajñas, the Haviryajñas, and the Agnihotra sacrifice—and likewise those expressed through verbal suffixes (ākhyāta), such as "one should sacrifice with the Piṇḍapitṛyajña" and "he performs [the rite] with the Āgneya sthālīpāka," and so forth.

Expressions such as "those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods" are also to be understood—either through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on a portion of the act of giving, or through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the root *yaj* as meaning "to give," or in some cases as meaning "to offer oblations" (*homa*)—because the aforementioned grounds for its application are absent in mere oblations. Therefore, since sacrifice (*yajña*) is predominant in its nature as both primary and modified rites, the entire subject matter expounded in all the Sūtras is subsumed by the term "sacrifice. Furthermore, in the Śrutis and Smṛtis, there is the inclusion of all the duties (*dharma*) of the castes and stages of life under the term "sacrifice."

For instance: "By the great sacrifices and by the [regular] sacrifices, this body is made fit for Brahman"; "Through the three debts one is born: from the sages through celibacy, from the gods through sacrifice"; and "They desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice. In such passages, the word "sacrifice" (yajña) refers to the obligatory rites. For this very reason, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa stated: "There is a requirement for all [stages of life], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse."

In the Śruti, in the passages "by sacrifice to the gods" and "they desire to know through sacrifice," the singular number in the word *yajña* is not intended to be significant. What more need be said? It is the knowledge of the meaning of the entire Veda alone—whether with desire or without desire—that is the means. —14. The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the first section]: Because it is common to all, because it is eternal, and because its performance is necessary for the sake of attaining the fires; thereafter, if one is utterly dispassionate, one may perform rituals or not—let him do so, for the Veda does not forbid him, but rather demonstrates merely the relationship between the goal and the means. The knowledge thereof is mandatory, even in the case of the non-performance of optional (*kāmya*) rites, because that knowledge produced by such an explanation is certain even regarding one's own transgression.

"We shall explain" means that we shall analyze and describe the *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) as characterized by its three constituent parts: the result (*phala*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). An explanation of the sacrifice in its objective form is not possible; for explanation consists in stating the meaning of words through the analysis of sentences, words, roots, and suffixes, and such an analysis is not possible for an objective entity.

Therefore, it is understood in this way; as he will say, "by means of the Vedas," this very exposition of the Vedas, when being carried out through logical reasoning (*nyāya*), effectively becomes established in the form of ritual application (*prayoga*). The intention is that, setting aside the sequential order of the Vedic recitation, one follows the sequence of ritual performance; thus, while there is an instruction based on the primacy of meaning in the *Nyāyamīmāṃsā*, in the Sūtra there is a primacy of ritual application (*prayoga*).

By this explanation of the meaning, it is indicated that because of the predominance of the application of various elements such as substances and deities, these are known as the *Yājurveda*. It is made known that certain rites are produced by the mantra alone; thus, in the offices of the *Hotṛ* and *Udgātṛ*, the mantra is predominant. For this very reason, the teacher Āśvalāyana, having stated his thesis regarding the predominance of the word, declared: "We shall explain the application of this collection (*samāmnāya*) in its performance (*vitāna*)."

The explanation of the *brahmatva* (the duties of the Brahman priest), however, is for the purpose of demonstrating its existence within each Veda. The duties of the *āgnīdhra* have been explained; likewise, that which remains prescribed in the Yajurveda—the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*)—and the duties of all the priests at the end of the Adhvaryu Veda have been stated. As for the explanation of the *hautra* (duties of the Hotṛ priest) pertaining to the New and Full Moon sacrifices, although it is also prescribed in the Ṛgveda, it is intended merely to demonstrate the inclusion of Yajurvedic subsidiary elements and to show the alternatives available.

In this context, although an exposition of the general principles regarding rules not specifically initiated [in a particular section] has been provided as applicable to all the Vedas by way of incidental discussion, the intention here is that within this Sūtra, primacy belongs specifically to the production of the form of the sacrifice (*yajña*) in the Adhvaryu rites prescribed by the Yajurveda. For the "form" (*rūpa*) of an action consists of its material substance (*dravya*) and its deity (*devatā*). Thus it was stated by Kātyāyana: "We shall explain the sacrifice: [it consists of] the material, the deity, and the renunciation (*tyāga*). Furthermore, the deity prescribed for a particular rite is not any deity whatsoever merely by virtue of its genus (*jāti*).

The substance (*dravya*), however, is fixed. Regarding this, there are these verses: The substance produced from the animal (*paśu*) is declared to be ninefold: milk, curd, clarified butter (*ājya*), *āmikṣā*, omentum (*vapā*), meat, and whey (*vājina*). In the *Aśvamedha* sacrifice, when the omentum and the *iṣṭakṛt* offering have been performed, there are the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), gruel (*yavāgū*), cooked rice (*caru*), parched grains (*dhānā*), and *karambhaka*. Then there are the *parivāpa*, *surā*, and *mantha*; these eight are produced from plants. Soma is the creeper; others, such as *pūtīka* and so forth, are used in its absence. Water is used in the mixed oblation (*saṃsṛṣṭa-havis*); gold pieces (*kṛṣṇala*) and honey are at the beginning [of the offerings].

The oblations (*havīṃṣi*) are primarily characterized by the *vaṣaṭ* call and are used for sacrificial rites; those intended for the *homa* consist of milk, curd, clarified butter (*ājya*), meat, and vegetable substances, all of which are produced from animals or plants. Furthermore, there are rice, gruel (*yavāgū*), husked rice, parched grain with curd (*lāja-takta*), sesame cakes (*masūra*), flattened rice (*pṛthuka*), and various other items such as *bahir* and so forth. [Chapter 150, from the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva: There are also hard fruits, *karīra* shoots, fuel-sticks (*samidh*), and wood-shavings (*śakala*).

"Soma, honey, water," and other such items are worldly (*laukika*). Cakes, *kiṃśuka* flowers, sesame, *kaṅga* grain, and certain other things belong to the Śrauta [ritual]; therein, the performance of the Adhvaryu priest is enjoined as being primarily concerned with material substances (*dravyapradhāna*). Therefore, their detailed exposition is presented here: specifically, because the *Prātiśākhya* dharma is taught through application (*prayoga*) in the form of both direct instruction (*upadeśa*) and extension (*atideśa*), there is an exposition and demonstration of the sequence of performance according to the relationship between the primary and subsidiary elements (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).

The plural number is used for the purpose of including the speakers of other sūtras and other treatises. As they say: "Indeed, the authors of the sūtras, such as Kātyāyana and others, investigate certain matters themselves; yet they declare that this [investigation] is by means of Mīmāṃsā alone, for sciences become mutually contradictory [otherwise]."

Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā, along with various other sciences, are enumerated by the Lord Yājñavalkya, the master of yoga, as being mutually dependent and serving as the causes for both ritual action (*karman*) and knowledge (*jñāna*): "The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, and the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), together with the Vedas—these are the fourteen seats of learning and of dharma. The inclusion of the term "Purāṇa" is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the Itihāsas, the Rāmāyaṇa, epic poetry (*kāvya*), and so forth.

The purpose of the Purāṇas and Upākhyānas is the comprehension of the meaning of the Veda—along with its Arthavādas and Mantras—as well as the knowledge of the true nature of the deities and the knowledge of the nature of the fruits of heaven and liberation (apavarga). Nyāya refers to the systems of the Naiyāyika and Vaiśeṣika scriptures; therein lies the knowledge of the means of valid cognition such as perception, as well as substance, quality, action, genus, individuality, and so forth. Through the two Mīmāṃsās, knowledge regarding the subject matter of ritual action (karma) and Brahman is indeed explicit. The Devatākāṇḍa is also included within the Brahmamīmāṃsā.

Since the *Dharmaśāstra* prescribes conduct such as ritual sipping (*ācamana*) and purification—which are constituent parts of all rites prescribed by the *Smṛtis*—its utility has already been stated. Through the Vedas, however, the performance [of rites] occurs directly. These fourteen, including the Vedāntas, are the seats of the sciences of ritual action (*karma-vidyā*) and Brahman (*brahma-vidyā*), the uncommon causes for them, and the producers of Dharma. Among these, Mīmāṃsā is an internal auxiliary (*antaraṅga-aṅga*) for the composition of the application [of the Vedas] through its Sūtras. For instance: "Dharma is to be expounded by means of the twelve chapters (*lakṣaṇa*); therein, it is established by the chapters."

The topics designated as *pramāṇa* (means of knowledge), *bheda* (difference), *śeṣatva* (subsidiarity), *prayukti* (application), *krama* (order), *adhikāra* (qualification), *atideśa* (extension), both general and specific, *ūha* (modification), *bādha* (annulment), *tantra* (common performance), and *prasaṅga* (incidental application) have been set forth in their proper sequence. The definition [of the system] is as follows: the "Twelve-Lakṣaṇī" is the collection of the definitions of the twelve chapters; the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of such a treatise consisting of twelve chapters is Dharma. The twelve categories, beginning with *pramāṇa* and ending with *prasaṅga*, are the subjects of the twelve chapters respectively.

However, since the knowledge of the meaning is produced directly by the Sūtras through Mīmāṃsā—which functions as an intermediate operation—the knowledge of the formal application (prayoga) does not occur without that Mīmāṃsā. Therefore, these principles (nyāya), which serve as auxiliary components of the commentary, are also promised; some of them will be explained by [the author] himself, some are indicated merely by the formal application and must be learned from elsewhere, and some will be determined according to his own preference. This is indicated by the use of the plural verb "we shall explain" (vyākhyāsyāmaḥ).

— Thus, the sacrifice (*yajña*) is the subject matter to be explained, and the knowledge thereof is the purpose (*prayojana*) of this Sūtra, which is a technical treatise (*śāstra*). Furthermore, that knowledge is an auxiliary factor for the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). And so, since the entire range of ritual action (*karman*) has been proposed as the subject to be explained, as long as its fruit, nature, definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are not known, one does not proceed to the practical performance. Since the inquiry—"What is its fruit? What is its nature? What is its definition? What is its means of valid cognition?"—arises first, he says regarding that:
"It is enjoined by the three Vedas."

Sacrifice (yajña) must be explained because it possesses fruit; and its possession of fruit is known. Why? Because it is enjoined by the Vedas as a means to the highest good (śreyas). This too is the inherent capacity of the Vedas. Why? Precisely from the very form of the injunction for study (adhyayanavidhi). For it is not possible for anything else to be enjoined apart from a means to the highest good. Therefore, this [sacrifice] must be explained; the intention is that it cannot be performed unless it has been explained.

That [Dharma], established by the threefold means of knowledge and characterized by the term "sacrifice," is taught as something to be performed by means of the three kinds of Vedas—which, being non-human in origin, are free from all possibility of defect due to their status as Veda and are inherently authoritative. It is stated that it is "enjoined" (*vidhīyate*) for the purpose of ensuring that the entire body of scripture, consisting of Mantras and Brāhmaṇas along with their explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), results in a single syntactical unity with the injunction (*vidhi*). Otherwise, he would have simply said "it is made known" (*jñāpyate*).

If [the Veda] were intended merely as an instrument of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) like worldly means of knowledge, it could not be taught by the Veda as something to be performed that does not lead to the highest good (*aśreyas*). Therefore, the sense is that it is a means to the highest good (*śreyaḥ-sādhana*). By the injunction for study—"One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied"—which has a visible purpose, it is authorized that whatever can be accomplished by whatever means in whatever manner, that should be done by that means; however, the Veda, being of the nature of sound, possesses the capacity only for the production of knowledge.

This being the case, the injunction (*vidhi*), which expresses the impulsion (*pravartanā*), possesses authority as a sentence that makes known the required causal factors (*kāraka-artha*) for the scope of the injunctive operation, along with other words such as *bhāvanā*—which is synonymous with the effort consisting of activity—for they are part of the same syntactical unit. The name (*nāmadheya*) also forms a single syntactical unit by way of delimiting the instrument (*karaṇa*).

The explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) possess authority by way of characterizing the excellence (*prāśastya*) that constitutes the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) required by the injunction; thus, these words, having no other purpose, possess authority within the sacrifice.

Since mantras are employed in the sacrifice—either by reminding one of the sacrifice and its means, or by directly praising their own referents, or by providing remote assistance—they serve as instruments for the sacrifice only through the illumination of their own referents, and not merely by being uttered. Thus, even though they have attained the status of subsidiaries (*aṅga*) as word-meanings by implying restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*) regarding this purpose, they possess authoritative validity (*prāmāṇya*).

Just as in the case of ritual acts (*padārtha*), where the capacity of the act itself establishes the means for the cognition of the restrictive rule—as seen in the injunctions "he cuts with a bamboo splinter," "he cuts with his hand," and "he cuts with an axe"—so it is also with mantras. Thus, by the word "Veda," which is synonymous with the term "svādhyāya" (one's own recitation), the authority of the Veda is demonstrated through the injunction to study one's own recitation (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*). Otherwise, since this [authority] would already be established by the sūtra "rites are characterized by injunctions" (*vidhilakṣaṇāni karmāṇi*), this present sūtra would be rendered purposeless.

Since the definition of its own nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) and the means of its knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are established in that very [text], this aphorism is intended solely for the sake of establishing the authority of all the Vedas. Furthermore, it has been made known that even the fact that "one studies the Veda" is made known by the Veda itself through the injunction to study one's own portion (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*). The injunction to study finds its completion in the study of only one’s own branch (*śākhā*) of the Veda; otherwise, because it would enjoin an impossible task, the injunction to study would lack authority. Indeed, the fault of being unauthoritative (*dauṣṭulya*) attaches precisely to the non-study of one’s own branch.

This being so, the authority of the four Vedas is established. [End of section]. [Now, the objection: "If a ritual action is enjoined by three Vedas, it would certainly be subject to the defect of invalidity for one [of them]. [The reply: "Even that Veda which is not authoritative must be studied according to the injunctions; thus, even the fourth Veda, the Atharvaṇa, possesses authority. [End of] the first *paṭala* of the [second] chapter, together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

Even regarding non-worldly deviations from the Vedic rites of Brahman, such as those pertaining to the sacrificial fire (*vaitānika*), he himself will declare [the authority] by means of the Sūtra; and even in the case of worldly matters, he will declare it by means of the Sūtra itself. (3) Therefore, it is not proper to attempt an exhaustive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) of this [Sūtra] based on authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For there is no means of knowledge whatsoever for worldly matters other than the form of Mantra and Brāhmaṇa. (4) In that regard, establishing its status as a means of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) through the property of being "Veda" is also difficult to maintain. To this, it is replied: in the compound, three words are intended [to be understood]. (5) By virtue of their primary importance, all four [classes of texts] are included under the single term "Veda."

And for the sake of establishing the status of being a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) even among worldly things, there are two secondary [meanings] of the word "Veda. (6) Even if one [of these] could be possible as a secondary Veda by virtue of a single [criterion], nevertheless, both possess a secondary status due to two distinct intermediate conditions (*upādhi*). (7) A branch (*śākhā*) can be studied; that very [branch] is called "one's own Veda" (*svādhyāya*). One who is studying that very [branch] is designated as "a student of the Veda" (*vedādhyāyin*), just like a person who has completed his studies (*adhītakṛt*). (8) The word "Veda" applies either to the four [collections] as a whole or to each of the four individually; yet, even when used in the singular, it does not denote a single individual entity.

9–12. The Smṛti states: "Having studied the Vedas—either all four, two, or even one. For it is said in the *Kāṭhaka* as well: "The Vedas are indeed infinite. The definitive conclusion is that a single recensional branch (*śākhā*) is an individual instance (*vyakti*) of the universal genus (*jāti*) "Veda-ness" (*vedatva*). Furthermore, the status of being a "branch" and the status of being a "Veda" are both accepted for a portion of that [genus]. Moreover, when a Vedic rite is prescribed by only a portion of a branch, this is called "Vedic" only in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*), with the intention of referring to the Vedic sentence [from which it derives]. [Objection: But if this were so, would there not then be no Vedic rite whatsoever?

Or rather, it may be that all [this] is described in the Smṛtis and traditional practices as being rooted in the Veda (13). This is true; nevertheless, there exists a certain distinction that creates a division, [namely] the unity within one’s own Śākhā even with those belonging to other Śākhās (14). That which has been set forth by the Brāhmaṇas in a single section or in the same [textual] unit—whether it be a ritual act or Brahman-knowledge—is called Vedic (15). [Notes on variants: 1. ka, cha: *neṣyate*; ka, ga, cha: *laśrutyā*. 3. [End of fragment].

2.18–18. When the continuity of ritual action is made known by means of the Veda as a measure, that is the Vedic [tradition], and the rite contained therein is called Vedic. That which does not exist in its entirety within one's own *śākhā* [branch], nor is it completed by another *śākhā*, but is filled out through being part of a single context (*prakaraṇa*), is [called] *prakīrṇaka* [scattered]. Furthermore, that which is prescribed and brought together in one place by persons, using sentences found in various portions of *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* studied across different contexts, is [also so designated].

That which is called worldly action (*laukika-karma*) is understood from Manu and others; for it does not exist within the Veda with a direct sequential arrangement of its own recitation. (19) Even though that Veda is perceptible to seers (*ṛṣis*), it is held to be imperceptible [to ordinary people]. Another [portion] is not perceived as perceptible in a single continuous section (*praghaṭṭaka*). (20) Therefore, in that case too, its status as "Veda" is established only figuratively (*upacārāt*); for that [worldly action] is not grasped by the injunctions of the Veda as a scattered portion. (21)

Therefore, that [action] is non-Vedic; even though it was proclaimed by him (Manu), it is non-Vedic, being called "worldly" (*laukika*) or "based on tradition" (*smārta*) because of its instruction through Smṛti-mantras and the like. Even when that very same [action] is mentioned incidentally in some instances through mantras with different purposes or through explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) with different purposes, it is not established without an injunction (*vidhi*). For its establishment, an injunction must be inferred from those [mantras]; yet that too is said to be worldly or based on tradition, and not Vedic.

But surely, the *Ekāgnikāṇḍa* is regarded as directly perceived Veda; since it is grasped by some through recitation, its lack of perceptibility [as scripture] does not exist. (25) Therefore, how can a rite prescribed therein—whether Smārta or worldly—be [considered non-Vedic]? True; nevertheless, because it belongs to the *Prātiśākhya*, it is equal to Śrauta [Veda]. (26) For there are indeed mantras situated even in the Śrauta section to complete that [Ekāgnikāṇḍa]; yet they have departed from it, being not at all connected with the Śrauta rite itself. (27)

Whatever mantras here are devoid of an injunction (*vidhi*) but are directed toward that purpose, they attain the status of being subsidiary (*aṅga*) by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), even if they are unconnected to a specific context (*prakaraṇa*). Injunctions as well—whether they are unattached to a context or even those composed of the components of *mantra* and *arthavāda* as previously described—attain the status of being subsidiary to the ritual action. Furthermore, fire other than the sacrificial fires (*vaitānika*), whether it be the domestic fire (*gṛhya*), the traditional fire (*smārta*), or even one not commonly known, when it attains the status of being a subsidiary to a ritual action, is designated as "the single fire" (*ekāgni*).

[Paṭala 150] This section, together with the Vaijayantī commentary composed by Mahādeva, is established as follows: Since this section concerning the single fire (*ekāgni*) is spoken of as a distinct section (*kāṇḍa*), and since the *Upanayana* (initiation) therein belongs to the Śrauta rites found in another recension (*śākhā*), it is settled that the five sacrifices (*yajña*) proclaimed by Dharmaprabha are Śrauta. Therefore, the section on miscellaneous rites (*prakīrṇakāṇḍa*) is equal to the section on the single fire; and this [section] is similar to the Śrauta because it is set forth within a single context (*prakaraṇa*).

Therefore, the two sections concerning worldly matters—the *Gṛhya* and the *Smārta*—are secondary. The *Gṛhya-karma*, specifically that which begins with the domestic fire (*gṛha*), has been described; likewise, the *Smṛti-śāstra* consists of the established conventions (*samaya*) and the conduct (*ācāra*) followed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Rituals pertaining to conventions and conduct (*sāmayācārika*) are recorded as those performed by a person free from desire for gain through these two. That very section concerning the domestic fire (*gṛhya-kāṇḍa*) includes the initiatory rites (*upanayana*) and so forth. Furthermore, the *Smṛti-śāstra*, the *Dharma-praśna*, and the *Kāvya* proclaimed by the sages (*ṛṣi*), as well as the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*, constitute the teaching on conventions and conduct (*sāmayācāra-śāsana*).

The *Smṛti* also states: "The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the *Smṛti*, conduct (*śīla*), the practice of the virtuous (*sādhu*), and contentment with what is desired. Here, "conduct" refers to personal virtues such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and the like; "contentment" refers to the lack of desire for one alternative among optional rites. This was stated by Baudhāyana: "Only those [rites] that have been well-prepared are [valid]; therefore, in the case of modified forms (*vikṛti*), those same [rules apply] when there is no specific instruction."

In cases where there is no scriptural injunction regarding what ought to be done, and where in the Vedas—whether in mantras or explanatory passages (arthavādas)—the practice is merely restated as something already established by praise, and no visible purpose is perceived, that very practice is nevertheless performed by the learned (*śiṣṭas*). Therefore, [the rule] "one who is inferior should follow behind" is seen in such instances as: "having made light for the thirsty one, he surrounds him," "like a watering-trough in the desert," and "like boys with their hair-locks. Thus, following the teacher, giving food to a guest, establishing a watering-trough in a waterless region, and the *godāna* ceremony are all established.

Regarding the expression "the head with its top-knot shaven" (*saṃskāre saśikhaṃ muṇḍam*), where there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) by way of censure—as in the case of "given to a guest"—therein a prohibition (*niṣedha*) is also to be understood. This has indeed been demonstrated in the Purāṇas. Likewise, in the *Māghavata* (Mahābhārata): "The Itihāsas and Purāṇas are considered the fifth Veda. For all three [Vedas] are indeed authorities regarding matters not grasped by other means of knowledge (*māna*). These three types [of texts] mentioned above are equal; they have various meanings due to the principle of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a group). The number three is intended to indicate the mode [of their status] for those [texts] already grasped.

He now provides an enumeration of the other types [of Vedic texts]. Furthermore, since the threefold nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has been established, the Atharva Veda is not excluded from the category of "Veda" by this enumeration. Here, even a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is appropriate through both primary and secondary application (*mukhyāmukhyavṛtti*). That which consists of Mantra and Brāhmaṇa is designated as the "primary"; the *Ekāgni-kāṇḍa* is the "other," while the third is the "miscellaneous" (*prakīrṇaka*).

By them, this threefold Dharma has been proclaimed for each [of these sources]. With this very intention, Baudhāyana said: "The Dharma taught for each Veda we shall explain in detail; the Smārta is the second, and the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra) is the third. "Upadeśa" refers to the Veda; that which is enjoined as something to be performed by means of it is "vaitānika" (pertaining to the sacrificial fires), so to speak. "Prati-veda" means for each Śākhā. For it is not the case that in the Veda, taken as a whole, only a single performance is prescribed; rather, there are various performances.

Each [Veda] belongs to each individual person. Therefore, it has been explained by its own single branch (*śākhā*). Following that *prātiśākhya* rule, we shall explain the duty pertaining to that branch and the duty characterized by the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) belonging to that branch. The meaning is that both of these are restricted to their respective branches. Although both are based on tradition (*smārta*), the first is called "based on tradition" because it is inferred from conduct and is minor, whereas the second is so called because it is more extensive; thus, the first is the *prātiśākhya* and the second is the conduct of the learned.

Therefore, it has been well said that Dharma, characterized by sacrifice, is established as being threefold; it is recited by those who know the means of valid cognition such as the Vedas, who are endowed with the three methods of injunction. It produces a knowledge regarding its object that is uncontradicted in its status as something to be performed. Thus, the meaning is that it is a *pramāṇa* (valid means of knowledge) because it generates a clear, non-doubtful, and non-erroneous knowledge of its being a means to a desired end. In this way, it is enjoined—that is, it is taught as something to be performed—by the Veda, since no other agent than the performer is possible in the case of non-human (apauruṣeya) texts.

Because these [words] possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being instructions regarding what is to be done (*kartavyārtha*), their authority is established; however, there is no contradiction in their being agents (*kartṛtva*), since they serve as the locus for the operation of the injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, there is a purpose even in this figurative attribution (*āropa*): just as we observe the usage "the pupil has been impelled by the teacher" when one who has set out to act upon the command "bring the cow," it is understood that the operation expressed by the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) resides in the teacher.

Since the teacher is the composer of the verbal arrangement, and because there is no author of the Veda, he alone possesses the status of being its user; thus, his activity serves as the basis for [the Veda's] authority. Consequently, the purpose [of this discussion] is that the Veda—being authorless, free from the suspicion of any of the seven defects, and inherently self-evident—is possessed of unimpeded validity.

Now, an objection is raised: how can mantras—which lack suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) and so forth, and whose injunctive power is obstructed—possess injunctive force? Furthermore, this would contradict what will be stated later, namely, that "the Brāhmaṇa is the injunction of ritual action. It is replied: An injunction (*vidhi*) is the teaching of a matter as something to be performed (*kartavyatā*). As it is used in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra: "The knowledge of that [injunction] is the teaching, and its distinction [is the means]" (*tasya jñānam upadeśo vyatirekaśca*). In the treatises of that school, it is seen [that *vidhi*] occurs through the derivation from the root *kṛ* (to do), through the derivation from the verbal root *bhū* (to be), and as the operation of the word itself.

Sacrifice (*yajña*) is ordained; that is to say, it is taught as something to be performed. In this regard, for the Brāhmaṇa—which possesses the injunctive suffix—the authority [of the Veda] is clear. Furthermore, it will be explained that even the mantras, though they are auxiliary to the performance, possess authority by way of their literal meaning (*padārtha*). They do not function as injunctions merely by being associated with an injunction; for an injunction alone, without the mantra, is not capable of enjoining a productive effort (*bhāvanā*) qualified by the mantra through its mediation. Thus, the specific nature of each ritual act—whether Vedic (*śrauta*) or traditional (*smārta*)—has been stated.

Thus, having explained in general the fruit, nature, means of knowledge, and internal subdivisions of the threefold action thus proposed, [the author] now states the internal subdivisions according to the specific means of knowledge—namely, the four Vedas denoted by the primary term *veda*—in order to describe the specific duties of the agents within the Śrauta rites, because these are numerous due to their scriptural authority and because they require extensive explanation due to their nature as both archetypes (*prakṛti*) and modifications (*vikṛti*). 1. Kha, Cha: "layamarthama"; 2. Ka, Ga: "smārtata"; 3. Ka, Ga, Ca, Cha, Kṣa: "kṣaṇāvyā".
