Ra-ga. It has been explained. Chapter One. Accompanied by the Vaijayantī commentary composed by Mahādeva:
By means of the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda—by all of these, the Jyotiṣṭoma [is performed].

In this context, although the term *veda*—whether accompanied by a qualifying word (*sopapada*) or not—is a designator of a sub-class (*avāntarajāti*), only a single individual instance (*vyakti*) is intended. This is because there is a difference in application for each person according to their distinction as an individual. It is not the case that a difference in application is prescribed for the collection of branches (*śākhā-samudāya*) as a whole by means of the term *dṛgveda*; rather, it is for each branch and for each person. Therefore, by virtue of suitability, that specific difference in application is prescribed for each respective follower of a branch by that very branch. Otherwise, the other branches would be rendered useless.

The term "Jyotiṣṭoma" refers to the six forms (saṃsthās) beginning with the Agniṣṭoma; the word "is enjoined" (*vidhīyate*) is to be understood as carrying over from the previous context. In that regard, it is improper to enjoin multiple [details] for a single ritual action, because it would result in the invalidity of one or the other, lead to a confusion of agents and a confusion of properties, and render the injunctions that establish the lack of restriction purposeless. To avoid this, a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*) is indicated by the word "and" (*ca*). By the word "Jyotiṣṭoma," the primary constituent parts of the ritual action—along with its subsidiaries—are denoted.

Therefore, since each of the three portions was divided by the three gods, and all four [portions] were established as one portion through their respective combinations—namely, the *hautra*, *ādhvaryava*, *audgātra*, and *brahmatva*—it is well-known and stated in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* and other texts that these four portions, including the fourth, arose from the mouths of the Four-faced One (Brahmā) in the sequence of his eastern and other faces.

Although injunctions regarding qualification (*adhikāra*) are heard in multiple places across all four Vedas—resulting in an apparent intermixture (*saṃkara*)—nevertheless, the injunctions of origin (*utpatti*) and application (*viniyoga*) are strictly restricted: the origin and application of the *śastra* and other mantras are found only in the Ṛgveda; those of the *graha*, *brahmaṇa*, and other mantras only in the Yajurveda; and those of the *stotra* and other mantras only in the Sāmaveda. Even when such [injunctions] are heard in a transposed order, they do not derive their authority from that [transposition].

When there are specific actions prescribed by two different Vedas, even if only a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) is enjoined with reference to them, it is nonetheless enjoined by that Veda which prescribes the primary act (*guṇin*); thus, there is no confusion. Furthermore, regarding the origin of a mantra located in one Veda while its application (*viniyoga*) is determined by another Veda, the established conclusion of the *Nyāya* system is that its primacy belongs to the Veda by which it is applied; therefore, there is no confusion.

However, since the office of the *Brahman* priest is equally prescribed by all four Vedas, it is not known whether a particular injunction is for a subordinate quality or for the primary act, and thus an option (*vikalpa*) alone remains as the settled rule. This should be understood to apply likewise to modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).

The *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are [prescribed] by both the *Ṛgveda* and the *Yajurveda*. The term "in common" (*sādhāraṇa*) also applies here. By means of the *Ṛgveda*, the *sāmidhenī* verses and so forth [are performed]; by means of the *Yajurveda*, the *anvādhāna* and so forth; and the office of the *brahmán* priest belongs to both. Just as the office of the *brahmán* is prescribed for the *jyotiṣṭoma* by four [Vedas], so it is also for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. It is precisely for the purpose of prescribing the *brahmán*-priest's duties and expiations that the *Atharvaṇikas* compose their *sūtra*.

Just as each of these three authors of the Sūtras individually demonstrates the Brahman-hood [of their respective Vedas] in the Darśapūrṇamāsa and Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices, so too it is clearly perceived that the Ātharvaṇikas do the same. However, in the Jyotiṣṭoma, the duties of the Hotṛ and others are prescribed in much greater detail and with distinct clarity by the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas; therefore, there is no mention of them collectively [in the Atharvaveda]. In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, however, the Nigadas belong exclusively to the Yajurveda, and this remains the case even in their modifications (vikṛtis); thus, the Yajurveda is predominant in these rites.
Because they are designated by their own names, there is a collective inclusion of the two—the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda—which depend on the independent prescription of the office of the Hotṛ priest.
It appears that, according to this commentary, there should be "ca"s (and-s) in the Sūtra.
[The Agnihotra is performed] with the Yajurveda.

In other cases, the restatement of the principal [rite] is for the purpose of prescribing a subsidiary quality (*guṇa*). Since many subsidiaries are prescribed in the Yajurveda itself, this serves as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the placement of the fires (*ādhāna*), the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and the duties of the Hotṛ priest. Even though the office of the Brahman priest (*brahmatva*) exists here in the context of the fire-placement, it nevertheless belongs exclusively to the Yajurveda. Although the office of the Brahman priest at the fire-placement has been mentioned by others, that too is merely a prescription of a subsidiary quality regarding the Brahman priest of the fire-placement ordained by the Yajurveda; it does not exist as an alternative option (*samavikalpa*) like the office of the Brahman priest in other rites.

Since certain other specific rites prescribed in other Vedas are heard of here and there as being restricted [to those respective branches], the Teacher did not make an effort for their sake. The Agnihotra is heard of elsewhere for the purpose of enjoining accessory details; that very rite, characterized by the specific qualities of the Rigveda, is also shown in the Rigveda-sūtra. For this reason, it is restricted by the term "Yājurvedam" to mean the Agnihotra belonging to the Yajurveda, serving as an indicative mark for the Darvihomas.

Having made the formal promise, "We shall explain sacrifice," the presentation of the *agnihotra* as being performed with the *Yajurveda* is intended to demonstrate that the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) serves as an illustration for all such rites. Furthermore, the division of the Vedas into primary and secondary—namely, the *śrauta* rites prescribed by the Vedas and the *laukika* (worldly) rites prescribed by scattered [texts]—is stated for the purpose of distinguishing between the rituals ordained by them.

For it is not possible to say that, having first promised that ritual action—both Śrauta and Smārta—is to be understood by the word "sacrifice" (yajña), and then stating that the Veda prescribes it therein, one could then claim that only the Jyotiṣṭoma, Darśapūrṇamāsa, and Agnihotra are what the Veda prescribes.

Now, one might object: since all four Vedas are exhausted as authoritative sources only for the Jyotiṣṭoma, Darśapūrṇamāsa, and Agnihotra sacrifices, what portion remains? Furthermore, the two Vedas that are not primary have no authority regarding worldly matters; indeed, there is no other Veda that could serve as the source for those two non-primary ones. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that the status of being a primary Veda is a qualifying condition (*upādhi*) for their authority only in the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites. Through a portion of that [Veda], whether by direct perception or by an injunction inferred from it, [the scripture] functions as an injunction (*vidhi*) because its nature consists in impelling one toward what has not yet been undertaken.
To explain that validity is not established through all actions in common—just as one who has drunk three types of medicinal herbs [does not become healthy by mere ingestion]—he states:

"Actions characterized by injunction" (*vidhilakṣaṇāni karmāṇi*). Those for which the characteristic of injunction (*vidhilakṣaṇa*) is the unique means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are those actions adorned with sacrifice. Furthermore, although the word "injunction" (*vidhi*) denotes the general sense of instigation (*pravartanā*), he nevertheless says "characterized by injunction" after stating "enjoined by the Vedas. From this, it is understood that only a specific portion of the Veda constitutes an injunction.

And although that single part—the suffix alone—might be presented through the intention to express non-difference between the injunction and its suffix, even so, it possesses no authority regarding the ritual act in its form of the end (sādhya), the means (sādhana), and the procedure (itikartavyatā). Even if the suffix possesses the capacity to convey a blended productive urge (bhāvanā) by denoting several meanings connected within it, nevertheless, without specific words [denoting those elements], it is not able to impel a person toward action. Therefore, in this context, it is the sentence itself—consisting of words ending with the injunctive suffix—that is taken as the basis.

And the teacher Vārtikācārya says: "In the formulation of an injunction, the suffix is complete and capable [of conveying its meaning] when accompanied by those things required by the 'what' (kim) and so forth; therefore, in this treatise, a sentence that impels action is called *codanā*. Also: "'*Codanā*', 'instruction' (*upadeśa*), and 'injunction' (*vidhi*) are synonymous terms. And: "The meaning of the sentence is indeed the *bhāvanā* (productive activity), qualified by its own factors (*kārakas*). [End of section 10, Paṭala] [This concludes the section] together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

Therefore, it has been stated that the injunction (*vidhi*) is indeed the sentence that impels action. Consequently, by deriving the word from the agent (*kartṛ-vyutpatti*)—in the sense that "it enjoins"—the sentence itself is said to be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it possesses the operation of instigation and thus functions as the impeller; this is due to its being authorless (*apauruṣeya*). And by this, since all suspicion of human defects has been eliminated, and for that very reason it is inherently expressive, its status as an impeller is established through the communication of the means to achieve a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), which brings about one's own desired goal by way of the *apūrva*.

By the word "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), it is stated that [Dharma] is a unique means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By this, it is stated that it is not apprehended by means of valid cognition such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the like. For the nature of an action (*karman*), which is taught as something to be performed and consists merely of a single goal to be accomplished, cannot be known through other means of valid cognition. This has been established in the *Tarkapāda* (the section on reasoning) starting from the verse: "When there is contact of a person's sense organs with what exists... and so forth.

Therefore, it is stated that the form which is perceived through perception and other means does not belong to *dharma* as such; rather, its status as *dharma* consists in its being a means to the highest good (*śreyas*). And it has been said: "The fact that these [Vedic injunctions] are eternally understood from the Veda as being means to the highest good—that is their *dharmatva* therein; therefore, they are not within the range of the senses. Likewise: "The status of substances, actions, qualities, and so forth, as *dharma* will be established."

In this context, the word *dharma* is not employed to indicate that even protection (*pālana*) is characterized by injunction (*vidhi-lakṣaṇatva*). For the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that only that which is characterized by engagement (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*) possesses the nature of *dharma*. In our own system, however, even protection is indeed *dharma*, as seen in the usage: "We shall explain the conventional duties (*sāmayācārika-dharma*) regarding those actions in which protection predominates. Likewise, it is well-established that even the *apūrva* (unseen potency) possesses the nature of *dharma*.

To ensure that it does not fall under the definition of an injunction (*vidhi*), the term "action" (*karman*) is included there, based on the principle that what is not enjoined is not the subject matter of an injunction (*codanā*). Likewise, protection also possesses the quality of being a means to the highest good (*śreyas*) by virtue of the force of an injunction; furthermore, its nature as a protector against the occurrence of the undesirable is due to its prevention of prohibited actions. Thus, actions are defined solely by injunctions and do not have perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth as their object, because they are "dharma"—a synonym for action—by virtue of being exclusively a means to the highest good through the state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

And likewise, there is the capacity to be a means to the highest good (śreyas) in the future. Ritual actions alone are characterized by injunction (vidhi), not Brahman, because Brahman, being already established, is the fruit as that which is to be attained. Furthermore, the fruit itself is not something to be enjoined; as it has been said: "With respect to the fruit-component of the productive urge (bhāvanā), the suffix is not injunctive."

Since all three types of injunction (*vidhi*) share the same form by virtue of being common to both the *kalpita* (constructed) and *akalpita* (non-constructed), the action within their scope likewise shares the uniform nature of being a means to the highest good (*śreyas*). Nevertheless, the plural term "actions" (*karmāṇi*) is used to demonstrate the internal distinctions among Vedic (*śrauta*), Smārta, and conventional (*sāmayācārika*) rites. Among these, in the Vedic section (*kāṇḍa*), such as the passage, "At the Full Moon sacrifice, he offered a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma," those injunctions that are *kalpita* are included within the Vedic section itself.

In that regard, the rule that the status of being a means to the highest good (*śreyas-sādhanatā*) must be enjoined by an inferred injunction alone has been indicated by the injunction for Vedic study itself. There is no fault even in accepting such cases as instances where an eternally inferred injunction (*nityānumita-vidhi*) is admitted. Alternatively, one may infer only the injunctive passages belonging to other recensions (*śākhāntara*). This is because, in cases such as "one should immolate" (*ālabheta*) or "one should offer" (*nirvapet*), it is difficult to find corresponding direct injunctions in other recensions; thus, we simply infer the existence of an inferred injunction, and we do not infer a Veda consisting of Mantras and Brāhmaṇas as an eternal entity.

In this way, it should be understood that even in the two *prakīrṇaka* (miscellaneous) sections, any injunction established by the force of specific terms is to be included therein. To explain the primary nature of the Veda for the purpose of dividing the three Vedas, [the author] states: "The designation 'Veda' applies to both the *mantra* and the *brāhmaṇa*. (Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, 1st Praśna).

Although one should have stated "the characteristics of injunctions" (*vidhilakṣaṇāni*) after saying this, as it refers to the general category, nevertheless, because the Brāhmaṇa is to be described specifically as "injunction," it was stated first as "the characteristics of injunctions. Furthermore, in the compound *mantraśca brāhmaṇaṃ ca*, the dual number used in the *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) indicates that these two together constitute a single Veda; it does not mean that any random mantra and any random Brāhmaṇa constitute a single Veda. Here, the duality residing in the subject of the enumeration is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*).

It cannot be said that "mantra" refers to one thing and "brāhmaṇa" to another, such that the Veda consists of the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices along with the injunctions for the *hautra* portion, while the *brāhmaṇa* is something else; for there are many [such texts], and it is not well-known that the Veda is studied as a single unit in each individual case, nor that the study of two [portions] constitutes the Veda being "studied. Nor can it be argued that the justification for the dual number (*mantrau ca brāhmaṇam ca*) is that what is known as a *brāhmaṇa* work is the *brāhmaṇa*, and the other division is the *saṃhitā* (the mantras).

The term "Brāhmaṇas" refers to the injunctions (*vidhāyaka-vākya*) contained within the *Saṃhitās*, because even those are characterized as Brāhmaṇas by virtue of being injunctive. Furthermore, since it is accepted that the status of a Mantra belongs to those texts distinct from the *Saṃhitās*—namely, the other texts known as Brāhmaṇas—the dual number is used here with reference to these two classes of literature. As for the well-known designation "Brāhmaṇa" applied to the literary genre, that is intended to refer to the majority of such texts. For this very reason it has been said: "Where the three qualities of Mantra and Brāhmaṇa are recited together..."

"That is to be known as the Yajurveda. Even those [portions] contained within the *saṃhitā* that are recited with the three qualities (*triguṇa*) are well-known as *brāhmaṇa*. Therefore, that collection of *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* which is recited by the Vaidikas as a single work is one Veda for a single person. Likewise, for others as well, the entire mass of the Vedas—characterized generally as the collection of branches (*śākhā*)—is defined by this very mark. This has been established in the first aphorism (*sūtra*) by means of verses (*kārikā*).

Therefore, another [text] extracted from those very branches—whether it be a Brāhmaṇa or a Mantra—that does not enjoin the duties of the *hotṛ* priest and others in the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, and which is not employed by the *hotṛ* priests and others, does not possess the status of a Veda. Where there is formal study (*adhyayana*), there even those texts that are unconnected [to the core ritual] are included within the primary Veda; elsewhere, they are included within the secondary Veda. For this very reason, he will later state: "The apprehension of words belonging to the Veda through tradition (*smṛti*) constitutes the worldly [Vedic usage]."

Words that were previously recited as constituent parts of the Veda, even when extracted [from their context], do not lose their status as Vedic constituents; rather, they simply possess the nature of being Vedic words. Because these are considered non-primary Veda, they serve as injunctions for worldly (secular) rites; thus, Smārta rites are called "non-Vedic" (aśrauta) and "worldly" because they are not prescribed by the Veda. What was already stated has merely been reiterated here. Since it is said that "a mantra ends where the meaning ceases," the status of being a mantra is attributed to each individual sentence; the singular number used for them is a generic singular (*jātyekavacana*). Likewise, the status of being a *brāhmaṇa* pertains to the sentence itself.

Therefore, the intended meaning is that it is called "Veda" because it is prescriptive. Here, without stating the definitions of the *mantra* and the *brāhmaṇa*, he states the meaning of the word "Veda" as determined by them; he has thereby indicated that since the definitions of the Vedic texts must be understood through their very common usage, they cannot be properly defined by any other means. His intention is that even those definitions which will be stated later are either under-extensive (*avyāpaka*) or over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*).

Thus, by means of the first two sūtras, the formulation of the proposition (*pratijñā*) has been shown through the commonality of the three types of ritual action (*karman*). Thereafter, by distinguishing between the *vaitānika* (sacrificial) and *gṛhya* (domestic) rites, it was shown that they are primarily prescribed by the Veda; by implication, the others [were also indicated]. The authoritative source (*pramāṇa*) has been cited. Now, he states the definition of one part of the Veda: "The Brāhmaṇas are the injunctions of all ritual actions. [This concludes] Chapter 150, together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

That by which an action is enjoined is "vidhi" (an injunction); the meaning is that it is a sentence (*vākya*). In the expression "characterized by injunctions" (*vidhilakṣaṇāni*), agency (*kartṛtva*) is intended; for here, with the intention of referring to sentences possessing both non-conceptualized and conceptualized suffixes, there is no established status as a *brāhmaṇa* for that which is merely conceptualized. Therefore, that which is an enjoining [text]—by virtue of being common to both the conceptualized and the non-conceptualized—is a *brāhmaṇa* through the medium of the injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*). The point is that even that which lacks an injunctive suffix possesses the status of a *brāhmaṇa* because it functions as an enjoiner by implying an injunction (*vidhikalpaka*).

Therefore, it is "imagined" (kalpitā). The singular number is used to show that the capacity to incite action (*pravartakatva*) is indeed no different [in the case of injunctions] by virtue of possessing an imagined injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*). The plural number in the word *brāhmaṇāni* is used to show that not only those sentences possessing actual injunctive suffixes, but also those sentences possessing imagined injunctive suffixes—and even the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) which possess imagined injunctive suffixes—are indeed *Brāhmaṇas*. Furthermore, the plural number is for the purpose of indicating their manifold variety.

The nature of an injunction (*vidhitva*) resides only in that operation which culminates in the word, is conveyed by the word, is synonymous with *śabdabhāvanā*, or consists of knowledge; it does not reside elsewhere. Furthermore, this occurs only in the impersonal Veda. Moreover, its status as a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) arises from its having an unascertained object. [If one were to define a Brāhmaṇa simply as "that which is called a Brāhmaṇa"], there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the *paiṅgyopaniṣad* because it is well-known as a Brāhmaṇa, yet it is not an injunction of ritual action (*karmavidhāna*). Therefore, the general definition of a Brāhmaṇa as a means of valid cognition is: "A Brāhmaṇa is of two kinds: that which has an established fact as its object (*siddhārtha*), and that which is an injunction of ritual action (*karmavidhāna*)."

Likewise, in the mantra of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, there would be the status of being a Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, by the statement "other than these are the mantras," the status of being a mantra is not applicable to that [Upaniṣadic passage], because it lacks the quality of being distinct from a Brāhmaṇa. Consequently, that in which the established status of being a Brāhmaṇa exists is a Brāhmaṇa. Thus, the word "Brāhmaṇa" is not meaningless. In this context, this is the definition for that which is employed in the Karmakāṇḍa (the section on rituals). The same applies to the mantras as well.

In this regard, the nature of those mantras other than those employed in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) is that they are "other mantras"; their definition is that they are "mantras intended for sacrificial rites. However, in the Upaniṣads, the status of being a mantra or a Brāhmaṇa is to be defined by another criterion, and one must also accept the overlap between these two categories.

Alternatively, the Upaniṣadic passages characterized as Brāhmaṇas—which have entered into syntactic unity with injunctions such as "it should be heard" (śrotavya)—have Brahman as both the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*) and the fruit (*phala*). For the object to be refined and the fruit are the intended objects (*uddeśya*) in an injunction, since it is the three-factored productive urge (*bhāvanā*) that is enjoined. Brahman itself is not the object of the injunction, because the suffix does not enjoin the portions consisting of the object to be refined and the fruit. As it has been said: "Regarding the portion of the fruit, the suffix is not injunctive toward the productive urge."

Likewise, that which is to be refined (*saṃskārya*) is also not something to be enjoined, because it cannot be specified and is therefore not something to be undertaken as an object of action. Thus it has been said: "Place, time, cause, fruit, and that which is to be refined—those skilled in Mīmāṃsā declare these to be the pentad of non-objects to be undertaken (*anupādeya-pañcaka*). Now, one might ask: "In that case, how was the injunctive nature of the Vedāntas refuted? We reply: because they do not have knowledge as their object of injunction. Furthermore, an injunction regarding knowledge is not accepted; as the Teacher (Bhartṛhari) will state: "There is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self."

The attainment of what has already been attained occurs solely through knowledge produced by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, it is not an injunction (*vidhi*). This will be clarified in that very context. Therefore, it should be understood that even though the Vedāntas are primarily intent on describing the nature of that which is presented as the fruit, they constitute "sentences of injunction" (*vidhivākya*) because they provide the fruit to be refined, which is required by the injunction. In this regard, it should be known that the Vedānta-generated knowledge itself, when directed toward its object, removes improper mental cultivation (*abhāvanā*), impossible mental cultivation (*asaṃbhāvitabhāvanā*), and contrary mental cultivation (*viparītabhāvanā*).

The rites such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth are those that are to be enjoined. [Notes: 1. *ya* for *yaḥ*; 2. *ka*, *ga*: *kārya*; 3. *ka*, *ga*, *ca*, *cha*: *kāraṇa*; 4. *ra*, *ka*, *ga*: *kṣetra*; 5. *sa*: *nivartayanti*; *cha*: *nivartayati*]. [Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, First Praśna]: Now, if it is asked: "But if they are supplementary to the injunctions regarding hearing and so forth, how can the Vedāntas have established entities (*siddhārtha*) as their subject matter?"

It is replied: we do not assert that there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) by virtue of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) to an injunction; rather, it is by virtue of being a subordinate element required by the injunction. And thus, the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), which makes known Brahman—the fruit that is the principal object (*śeṣin*)—is indeed concerned with an already established fact (*siddhārtha*). [Objection: In that case, even a subordinate sentence (*avāntaravākya*) that presents fruits such as heaven would have to be concerned with an established fact. [Reply: Let it be so; what is the harm? [Objection: If this is so, how can the designation [of the Vedas] as "concerned with the means to an end" (*sādhana*) apply universally? *Note: The term *siddhārtha* refers to a statement whose primary referent is an existent or accomplished entity, as opposed to a *kāryārtha*, which has an action or duty as its primary referent.*

It is said: where there is no desire for the valid cognition (*pramā*) produced by a sentence that conveys an established fact (*siddhārtha*), in that case, that very knowledge—by virtue of being of the nature of the direct realization of bliss—is itself the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Such a sentence, because it does not produce knowledge of a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) of ritual action, is one whose meaning is established; and since it culminates in the supreme human goal by conveying only an established fact, it is all the more preeminently "one whose meaning is established" (*siddhārtha*), being the primary [subject].

However, that which prescribes hearing and so forth has entered into a single syntactical unity with that which conveys its own designated object; and even though it is characterized by the definition of being a "Brāhmaṇa" because it prescribes an action (*karma*), there is no fault. Although some among those [Brāhmaṇas] are well-known as *mantras*, the status of *mantra* for other *mantras* is established; and the status of that [Brāhmaṇa] as a *mantra* must also be demonstrated by another method—so enough of this excessive detail.

In the sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," although there would be the fault of *siddhārthatva* (describing an already established fact) if the word "heaven"—the object to be indicated (*uddeśya*)—were primary, nevertheless, because merely communicating an established fact does not have the person's welfare as its ultimate purpose, the knowledge produced is merely a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the subsequent performance of the ritual action. Therefore, since the primary aim is the generation of knowledge regarding what is to be performed, that [knowledge] is not for the sake of the established fact itself. For this very reason, having raised the objection that the *arthavādas* (explanatory passages) would lack authority due to their *siddhārthatva* and their failure to culminate in the person's welfare, [the author] states that they possess authority by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with injunctive sentences that do culminate in the person's welfare.
That is the *arthavāda* (explanatory passage).

The sense is that it is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to that injunctive [passage], and by entering into syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the injunction, it serves as a supplement to the Brāhmaṇa sentence that prompts the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) which is the object of the injunction. As it has been said: "But because they form a single syntactical unit with the injunction, they serve the purpose of praising the injunctions."

The meaning is this: when the injunctive sentences that enjoin the injunctions—which themselves consist of the efficient force (*śabdabhāvanā*)—impel a person toward action, then the *arthavādas* enter into syntactic unity with those injunctive sentences by serving as the providers of the "means" (*karaṇa*) and the "procedure" (*itikartavyatā*), namely the excellence (*prāśastya*) characterized within the objective efficient force (*arthabhāvanā*), which are required by the verbal efficient force contained in the injunctive sentences.

The use of the singular number in the term *arthavāda* is intended to indicate that all *arthavādas* possess the status of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) by virtue of having a single form. However, their specific function (*dvāra*) is understood from the words themselves. It is well known that those [statements] which do not speak of their own meaning with the intention of expressing that meaning, but rather for the sake of praising another, are called *arthavādas*.

Now, while those passages whose purpose is praise may indeed form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with an injunction by way of praising what is to be enjoined, how can those that perform censure of other things—such as "this [offering] remains as a stain attached to the slaying of a Brahmin" (*brahmahatyāyai dhēṣā varṇaṃ pratimucyā''ste*)—attain unity with an injunction? Nor should it be said that they do not form a single syntactical unit with a prohibition, for the prohibitions are accepted as distinct from the "Brāhmaṇas which are injunctions of ritual acts" (*karmavidhāna*). For this very reason, the Teacher employs the term "action" (*karman*) everywhere.

Even in prohibitions (*niṣedha*), there is the cultivation of cessation (*nivṛtti-bhāvanā*), because it is intended that the object is indeed the action (*karman*) in its alternative form (*paryāya*). Otherwise, dharma characterized by injunction (*vidhi*) would, by implication, result in adharma characterized by prohibition. And if that were so, the author would have composed the aphorism as: "Dharma and adharma are the means of valid knowledge" (*dharmādharmayoḥ pramāṇam brāhmaṇam iti sūtrayet*). Nor is it the case [that...]. [End of section] Accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva, First Paṭala. Likewise.

Therefore, in all cases, the Brāhmaṇa passage is indeed an injunction of cultivation (bhāvanā), and it is not the case that it is not required. Furthermore, in all instances concerning deprecatory explanatory passages (arthavāda), there is no prohibition that makes known the undesirability [of the act]; nor can such a prohibition be inferred from the deprecation itself. This is because, regarding enjoined acts, there exists no prohibition that makes known their status as a means to an undesirable result. For instance: "If one were to offer the morning oblation while the sun has risen, it would be as if one were to bring food for a guest who has already departed, leaving the dwelling empty."

Regarding such passages as "That is exactly like that," there exist prohibitions—imagined from the injunctive texts—that communicate [the action] to be a means to an undesirable end (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*). But how can those [prohibitions] communicate that something already enjoined is a means to an undesirable end, by virtue of which the injunctive texts and the deprecatory explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) would form a single syntactical unit? As the Bhaṭṭācāryas have stated: "Even if there were a prohibition concerning that which is touched by an injunction, such a prohibition does not exist; for [in such cases] the status of being an evil (*anarthatva*) is understood, as in the case of the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup and so forth."

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that such [statements] are understood to have the sense of prohibition (*anarthakatva*). Therefore, having raised the objection that "the explanatory passages of censure (*nindārthavāda*) are not included [within the category of *arthavāda*] because they lack the status of being a single syntactical unit with an injunction (*vidhi-ekavākyatvābhāvāt*)," he says:
"Censure and praise (*nindā-praśaṃsā*)."

That speech which is a censure of the censurer is indeed praise, being solely intent on conveying excellence. Whether in injunctions or prohibitions, whatever statement proceeds by way of censure—all that is ultimately intent on praising the duty to be enjoined, whether for engaging in it or desisting from it. Thus it has been said by Śabarasvāmin: "Censure does not function to censure the object censured; rather, it functions to praise the thing to be enjoined."

Therefore, it is established that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "Neither on earth nor in the intermediate space" form a single syntactical unit with injunctions (*brāhmaṇa*) such as "Having placed gold [underneath], one should perform the consecration. Now, raising the objection that certain passages treated as *arthavādas* might—by being restricted to their own literal meaning—serve to provide specific details regarding the agent of the enjoined act, and thus possess a more pervasive status as supplements to that injunction, he says:
"The account of another's performance (*parakṛti*) and the ancient narrative (*purākalpa*)."

It praises and conforms to [the injunction]. The *parakṛti* (deeds of others) and *purākalpa* (ancient narratives) are merely commendatory and not injunctive regarding a specific agent. For example: "Atri gave to Aurva," "Jamadagni, desiring prosperity," and so forth.

What action was performed by one person, another, or someone else born of that same lineage? That is "the work of another" (*parakṛti*). Regarding the specific statements that establish such works—namely, the *purākalpas* (ancient accounts) concerning multiple agents, such as "The Aṅgirases indeed performed a sacrificial session" (*aṅgiraso vai satram āsata*) and so forth—they do not have the function of establishing that those actions were performed by individuals born of those specific lineages; rather, they are merely praise, intended solely for the purpose of glorification. On this point, some maintain that "the work of another" refers simply to anything having an agent, citing: "In the beginning, this world was indeed water, a vast expanse."

Thus, they say that the *purākalpa* (ancient accounts) are merely narratives. In those cases where there are only *purākalpas* and no injunction (*vidhi*) is heard, the intention is that they cannot form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the *Brāhmaṇa* texts; therefore, the *purākalpa* is also a form of praise (*praśaṃsā*). Consequently, the resolution is that an injunction must be inferred in order to achieve syntactical unity with them, and thus they form a single syntactical unit through that very [injunction]. By the word "and" (*ca*), [the author] demonstrates that passages such as "Tvaṣṭṛ, whose son was slain, [slew] Vṛtra," which serve as the basis for the injunction regarding the Agniṣomīya sacrifice and others, are subordinate to that [injunction].

In this view, it is appropriate to mention *parakṛti* (the action performed by another) separately, as it constitutes a distinct category. Furthermore, the inclusion of *purākalpa* (ancient precedent) is intended so that various types of *arthavādas* which imply injunctions (*vidhi*) might be included by this very same term. Nevertheless, it should be explained that its purpose lies in removing the doubt regarding the distinctness of those [categories] that are designated by various different names. Some, however, define them as follows: *arthavāda*, *nindā* (censure), *praśaṃsā* (praise), and *parakṛti*.

28. Satpāṣāḍha’s *Śrautasūtra*—in the first book (*prathama-praśna*)—explains that the phrase "and the ancient tradition" (*purākalpaś ca*) is indeed the *sūtra*. The remainder is the division [of the text], such as the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and so forth. Now, how can there be a division of those explanatory passages and the rest, given that they are not mutually exclusive? In what way could the censure and praise be considered specific types of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)? Howsoever it may be.

Even so, the fact that the actions performed by others and those from former times do not result in blame or praise means that those two [types of action] are merely specific instances; this explanation states only the literal meaning of the words and does not establish their purposeful efficacy. Having reached the point in the sequence, he states the nature of *mantras* in order to describe their authority:
"Other than these are the *mantras*."

Other portions of the Veda, including the mantras, which are distinct from the injunctive (*vidhāyaka*), explanatory (*arthavāda*), and *brāhmaṇa* sections, are considered "subsidiaries" (*śeṣa*) to those; this previous principle must be maintained for the sake of their authority. A subsidiary of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is itself indeed a means of valid knowledge. There is no fault even if the statement "He sacrifices the *kapinjala* birds to Spring" is not a *brāhmaṇa* by virtue of being a mantra, nor if it is injunctive in its indicative sense (*vidhiśeṣatva*). This is because the Mīmāṃsakas accept two types of expressive power (*śakti*).

And those [mantras] are indeed diverse, being characterized by their inclusion within the *vaitānika* (sacrificial) and *avaitānika* (non-sacrificial) rites and their retention (*dharana*). As the Śruti says: "Guard my mantra; you shall lead forth the *ṛc*s and the *sāmans*. Furthermore, the inclusion of the *nigada* (proclamation) is also stated by Jaimini. Thus, since mantras are also subordinate to injunctions (*vidhi*), the statement that "the Veda is enjoined" is fully supported. Now, when the question arises as to how they are subordinate to injunctions—seeking the means (*dvāra*)—the means will be stated by the phrase "for the purpose of sacrificial acts" (*yajña-karmārthāḥ*).
Regarding the doubt that something might be considered a mantra simply because it is employed at the time of ritual performance, he says:
Worldly expressions employed [in common usage] are non-mantras;
they have not been taught according to the rules for the study of Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*),
such as the naming of a son or the sound of a drum.

There is no specific name [for it]; the sound of a drum (*dundubhi*) is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). The particle *ca* is used in the sense of *iva*. The meaning is: "He begins the hymn (*stotra*) with the sound of a drum. Just as that which has an indistinct sound, even if prescribed by its characteristic mark (*kaṅga*), does not possess the nature of a mantra, so too, for the reason stated previously, it does not have the nature of a mantra even when there is a purpose.

Having stated the authority of the Brāhmaṇa—which is one part of the Veda—with respect to ritual action, he explains that the portion of the Veda consisting of mantras possesses authority by showing that mantras are auxiliary factors (*aṅga*) to the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) of the parts prescribed in the Brāhmaṇas:
"Mantras are for the sake of sacrificial acts (*yajñakarman*)."

The actions to be performed are indicated by the word "sacrifice" (yajña), and these same actions are referred to by the phrase "actions characterized by injunction. Thus, there would be redundancy. Therefore, it should be explained as follows: by the word "sacrifice," all actions to be performed are included. "Karma" means the production of action; thus, those [injunctions] for whose sake that action exists are so described. For an action is not a means to the highest good merely by being known through an injunction like Brahman, but rather when it is actually performed.

Therefore, the purpose of these [mantras] is the performance of the sacrifice. Now, if it is argued that by the statement "it is enjoined by the Vedas," the authority of the Veda—consisting of both injunctions (vidhi) and mantras—is declared; and that therefore those for whom the performance is to be established are "thus" [defined], and their authority will arise from the communication of meaning, we say: no. For even the performance is made known by the injunctions through the revelation of the necessity of performing the action, since they possess authority. Therefore, [this is] established. [End of] Chapter 10, with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

In this case, it is logical that only the production [of the mantra] is required for its own sake; that [production], by virtue of being a means of purification (*saṃskāratva*), serves as the purpose. This is because mantras are producers only insofar as they restate what has been enjoined. Thus, its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is stated through its being a direct auxiliary (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) by way of producing the sacrifice. Likewise, it does not have the status of an auxiliary merely through its utterance. By the force of the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), which has a visible purpose, it is understood that mantras culminate in the comprehension of their meaning.

For the mantras, having been taught by the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*) which has a visible purpose, do not inquire, "What visible result is produced by us, who are concentrated upon by the person? Rather, being authorized by the injunction for study with the understanding that "that which can be produced as a visible result by whatever means is produced by that," they conclude: "The mere manifestation of our own meaning is what can be produced by us; and that, through a visible medium, shall become a means for the person's concentrated purpose. Thus they remain, awaiting [the fulfillment of this].

In that context, rites consisting of recitation (*japa*), praise (*stotra*), and invocation (*śastra*) are prescribed as forms of presentation (*pratipādana*). Among these, those who are capable of recitation, praise, and invocation reach fulfillment merely by producing them; being thus purposeful, they become free from further expectation (*nirākāṅkṣā*). Other mantras, however, do not become free from expectation merely by making their own meaning known, because the making of their own meaning known is not enjoined by the injunction as a means for achieving the desired end.

And thus, they remain full of expectation, wondering, "How can we be seen by us to provide assistance to the *ajina*? In that regard, the constituent parts (*aṅga*) depend upon a recollection for their own production; for indeed, they cannot be performed by a person unless they have been brought to mind.

Although that connection [of the ritual] might indeed be established by means of injunctive sentences (*vidhi-vākya*), nevertheless, because those sentences are exhausted in their function as the means of valid cognition for the duty to be performed (*kartavyatā-pramāṇa*), and because it would otherwise result in the mantras being purposeless or having only visible purposes (*dṛṣṭārtha*), the [injunctive sentences] become free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣā*) only after they have themselves recalled their own subsidiaries through the mantras which are enjoined as such. The mantras, too, having attained the status of subsidiaries by way of recollection, likewise become free of expectancy.

Even those for whom there is no injunction (*vidhi*) indicating ownership, by assuming an injunction through the optative suffix (*liṅ*), come to understand that [the mantra] is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) for the performance of their own purpose, in order to achieve uniformity through similarity with mantras enjoined by an injunction. For this very reason, there would be uniformity because the injunction for study has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). Otherwise, there would be a discrepancy: a visible purpose in some cases, such as with worldly mantras, and an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) in others.

If it is argued that the verbal root *japati* denotes merely utterance, and that its status as a means of perceiving its own object does not follow from its being a manifestation of that object—since the manifestation of the object's meaning is not enjoined—and furthermore, since even the recollection of that meaning is not required as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the ritual action, then the following is said in reply: For the sake of securing a visible purpose for the injunction of study (*adhyayanavidhi*), the manifestation of the meaning must be understood as implicitly enjoined by the very injunction "one mutters" (*japati*). This is just as, in the case of the rule "this should be done with a mantra," the utterance of the mantra is implicitly enjoined.

The recitation [of mantras] with a view toward their own meaning is not the primary purpose; rather, through the recitation of mantras characterized as *japa*, one should cultivate the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) by means of the manifestation of their meaning. Since the injunction thus culminates in this, the cultivation of the manifestation of meaning is itself what is enjoined. Therefore, the purpose of the sacrificial act lies solely in the visible door [of meaning-manifestation], and not in the production of an unseen potency (*apūrva*) by mere recitation. Rather, because the recitation common to all [mantras] serves only the visible purpose of manifesting their respective meanings, an unseen result is postulated [only when that visible purpose is absent]; thus, it is for the sake of the unseen.

The verbal designation [of the drum] is figurative (*gauṇa*), and not primary (*mukhya*) like the designation of the sound of a drum and so forth as the commencement of a hymn (*stotra*). Likewise, even for the mantras of the *stotra* and *śastra*, because they serve as the means of expressing the glorification of the deity’s qualities through the roots *stu* and *śaṃs*—which denote the acts of praising and reciting—they constitute the performance of the ritual acts consisting of the *stotra* and *śastra* as enjoined; thus, these too have the purpose of the sacrificial rite (*yajña-karma*).

In this same manner, it should be understood that this applies to the mantras for the *upasthāna* (standing near), *abhimantraṇa* (addressing), *anumantraṇa* (reciting after), and *abhimarśana* (touching) performed by the *pratyagāśīḥ* (those containing blessings directed toward oneself). This will be clarified in the section on the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), where he should mutter them. [Notes: 1. ka, ga, ca read *dhakasya*; 2. ka, ga, gha read *janyatve'ne*; 3. kha reads *kyāda*; 4. ka, ga, ca, cha read *labpā*; 5. kha reads *laihiṣeṣu*; 6. ka, ga, gha, ṅa read *vā*; 7. Composed by Satyāṣāḍha, the Śrautasūtra—First Book—its applicability.]

However, regarding mantras such as those for *upasthāna* (reverential attendance) which do not have a visible purpose (*pratyakṣārthin*), where the mere presentation [of the deity] produced by the primary act is predominant, there too they are equal to *japa*. For in that case, the mantra—by means of presenting its own expressed meaning—effects a refinement of the object through the form of revealing the purpose, namely the reverential attendance and so forth; thus, when the person to be refined is the intended object, the refinement perceived in oneself arises through the mantra’s presentation of the meaning.

The visible purpose of the *yājyā* and other mantras, whether by means of the utterance *vaṣaṭ* or *svadhā*, is simply the recollection (*smṛti*) of the deity and the sacrificial substance. Since the substances, deities, and so forth—which serve the purpose of the sacrifice—are themselves to be accomplished as *dharma* by virtue of being means to the highest good (*śreyas*), they too possess the status of being sacrificial acts (*yajña-karma*). Thus, it is established that all [mantras] are subsidiary to the sacrifice (*yajñāṅga*) and are for the purpose of the sacrificial act. But why was it said that their status as subsidiaries (*aṅgatva*) is not the door to their authoritative validity (*prāmāṇya*)? For even if the *bohas* (the *yājyā* and *anu-vākyā*) are subsidiaries, they do not possess authoritative validity. True.

For the authority of mantras does not consist in their being verbal statements [of meaning]; nevertheless, this is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) stating that "only mantras are for the purpose of sacrificial acts. For this very reason, the teacher Baudhāyana says: "That which is remembered and performed through the mantra alone is the means to the highest good (*śreyas*). And for those for whom there are no mantras at all, the *smṛti* (tradition) itself serves as the injunction. Indeed, a Vedic rite cannot be carried out by any other means. Therefore, since there is no other recourse, the character of a reminder (*smārakatva*) must be attributed to the injunction itself.

Just as in such mantras as "He offers the *kapicalā* to Vasantā," the Mīmāṃsakas, out of necessity, postulate an injunctive force; thus they have attributed the power of injunction to such mantras. Nor should it be said that these too are [purely] mantras, because in cases such as "the fourth [offering] silently" (*tūṣṇīṃ caturtham*), since an action is enjoined apart from a mantra, it is understood that what is enjoined by an injunction is not something already recalled by a mantra. Otherwise, there would be no such thing as a silent (*tūṣṇīka*) rite at all.

Thus, in the case of actions characterized by maintenance (*pālana*), the injunction (*vidhi*) itself serves as the reminder (*smāraka*). This is likewise true for those Smārta rites that are performed silently (*tūṣṇīka*). On this point, there are summary verses: "The effort toward action, colored by the meanings of verbal roots (*dhātvartha*), is enjoined by suffixes (*pratyaya*) which are injunctive and derived from the verbal roots themselves. (1) That very action, consisting of three parts—the deity, the substance, and the sacrifice—which is entered into by the ritual act, is called 'sacrifice' (*yajña*) by the wise. (2)

There is no denotation of effort (*prayatna*) anywhere by its own nature; rather, it is understood through the coloring (*anurajaka*) of the verbal root (*dhātu*). Even when the verbal root is identical, there is indeed a distinction due to the five factors, beginning with repetition (*abhyāsa*). That action (*karma*) is said to be of two kinds: that which pertains to the meaning (*artha-jñāna*) and the other. The one pertaining to the meaning is of two types: that which is a quality (*guṇa*) of either the deity or the purpose, and that which is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāraka*). Those mantras which serve as purificatory rites are called *saṃskārārtha*. Those seen as purificatory are the *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses and those belonging to the *hautraka* (the duties of the Hotṛ priest).

When being recited, they become auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) to the unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*). Since a second cognition of the meaning is not produced by which an impression (*saṃskṛti*) would arise, that [cognition] is the primary element for it; and the mantras are the means for the *apūrva*. Water, the hymn (*stotra*), and likewise the *śastra* are declared to be for the sake of the *apūrva*. [Note: This passage is extracted from the *Vaijayantī* commentary on the *Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra*, attributed to Mahādeva.]

And by that very means, those mantras, even though they have perceptible purposes, lead to the *apūrva* (the unseen potency). (8) But those mantras which are the producers of the action consisting of knowledge—which is subordinate to the primary [action]—are traditionally known as "non-performers of action" (*akarmakaraṇa*). (9) For the operation of all mantras is indeed knowledge; they produce the enjoined knowledge while being devoid of any other operation. (10) Indeed, an instrument (*karaṇa*) possesses an operation; therefore, they are "non-performers of action. As for the various types of action, distinct from the knowledge of the object, they are twofold. (11)

Its definition is as before, distinguished by the predominance or subordination of its qualities; likewise, those mantras are instruments of action and possess the operation of knowledge. (12) Thus, the author of the Sūtras has established these designations for the sake of their own technical usage; one must employ these very terms when dealing with both the ritual actions and their corresponding mantras. (13) Now, since it is said that "the Vedas, consisting of Mantra and Brāhmaṇa, enjoin [the rites]," the authority of the mantras—based on their being syntactically unified with the injunctive passages—is proposed, and that must now be substantiated.

For this very reason, the teacher Āpastamba states: "The Mantra and the Brāhmaṇa are the authorities for the sacrifice. Even though the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is established through a visible means, the authority of the *Tuhīṇas* (the *Tuhīṇa-mantras*) is not thereby established. And it has been said: "The injunction of performance attains authority together with the mantras. The meaning is that the injunction of performance—the ritual rule—obtains its authority in conjunction with the mantras.

If it is asked, "Since the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) has been established in this way, what follows regarding their authority (*prāmāṇya*)?", it is replied as follows: When the status of being an auxiliary is established through a visible means (*dṛṣṭadvārā*), the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) is manifested by the mantra through the production of memory (*smṛtyutpādena*). Even though the mantras have been enjoined, they attain the status of being auxiliaries precisely through that memory, and not merely through their utterance; thus, they are restrictors of the purpose (*arthaniyāmakāḥ*). Therefore, they also obtain authority by way of being word-meanings (*padārthavidhayā*). Their status as auxiliaries is established by the injunction (*vidhi*), while the performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*) takes on their form.

Because they consist of elements already enjoined, mantras do not exercise a restrictive function; thus, the knowledge of the restriction is obtained from another source. For mantras, even though they take the form of sentences, are capable only of generating a recollection of the enjoined matter, and are not an authority regarding their own literal meaning by virtue of being words.

Nevertheless, in cases such as "he offers with the *srava*," "he cuts with the hand," and "he cuts with the *svadhiti*," although these [instruments] are prescribed without qualification, they produce a restrictive cognition (*niyamapramā*) by their own inherent capacity—that is, "only liquid substances are to be offered with the *srava*, hard substances like the *puroḍāśa* cake with the hand, and meat with the *svadhiti*. Thus, the *srava* and other instruments are themselves auxiliaries to the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*). [Note: The textual variants indicated in the footnotes (ka, ga, ca, cha) regarding the specific words used do not alter the core meaning of this sentence.]

— 2.32. It is stated that even those [texts] which do not take the form of sentences (vākya) serve as authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being constituent parts [of the ritual]. Thus, because they constitute the elements of the rite as enjoined by the application-injunction (*viniyoga*), they produce a restrictive authority (*niyamapramā*) for generating recollection through the capacity of their meaning, rather than through mere utterance. Indeed, by enjoining the elements of the rite as prescribed by the performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*), they certainly become authoritative as auxiliaries to that performance-injunction.

If it is asked, "Surely let word-meanings also be means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); in which [category] of pramāṇa will they be included? we reply: "In the sentence (vākya) itself. The masters have stated: "But even if they are auxiliary elements (aṅga), only the purpose (prayojana) is obtained, not validity (prāmāṇya). [To this it is replied: "This is not a fault, because the validity of word-meanings with respect to the sentence-meaning is admitted. Having said this, Pārthasārathi Miśra confirms it by the words of the Vārtikācārya: "For it has been said: 'Either the word-meanings [are the means], or the cognition of them.'"

Having thus stated the agreement with the Vārtika, they conclude: "Therefore, since mantras make known a specific meaning, they are authoritative regarding the primary meaning of the sentence. Thus, it is established that because mantras also serve a purpose, they possess authority. However, in the Vārtika, after stating that a collection of words has authority regarding its own meaning, it is said: "The meaning of the individual words, the cognition thereof, or even the comprehension of the sentence-meaning [is the result]. That is to say, sentences or words, by making known a specific relation, are authoritative.

The meaning of the *Vārttika* is that either the cognition of the word-meanings (*padārtha*) or the cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) produced by that [cognition of the word] possesses validity (*prāmāṇya*). Alternatively, the cognition of the sentence-meaning is itself a means of valid knowledge because it prompts action or causes cessation. The sense is that since their validity is rooted in verbal testimony (*śabda*), they are included within verbal testimony itself. It has been stated that mantras, while being subservient to ritual acts (*karmāṅga*), are a means of valid knowledge by virtue of regulating the connection with transcendental results (*apūrva*).

In that regard, those [mantras] which do not produce their prescribed effect while remaining in their own place due to the absence of a ritual injunction, nor do they reach what is enjoined by a characteristic mark (*liṅga*), might lack authority because they would then have no status as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*). Therefore, he says:
"Because of the contradiction of form, [they apply] to worldly [actions]."

Where a form (*rūpa*) is recited, that constitutes its status as a subsidiary (*aṅgatva*), and through that, the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the mantras arises. "Contradiction of that form" means its abandonment; because it would be purposeless and lack authority, it would result in not being included within the Veda—that is to say, it would incur the status of being non-Vedic (*avedatva*). Therefore, having departed from the primary Veda, they must be transferred (*utkṛṣya*) to worldly, Smṛti-specific rites for the sake of ritual action; thus the word [from the sūtra] should be understood to follow. In that case, by inclusion within the secondary Veda, they obtain purposefulness and authority because they serve the purpose of prescribed rites—this is the meaning. He provides an example:
"Just as I take your hand for the sake of good offspring, so do I dig up this herb; carry the fat offering to the ancestors, O Jātavedas! Thus [he says].

Three mantras are cited by their opening words (*pratīka*). Among these, due to their inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), the first is employed for the grasping of the bride's hand in the *vapaitānika* rite; the first is also used in her marriage (*vivāha*); and the third is employed in the *govapā-homa* (offering of the cow's omentum) during the *aṣṭakā* rites. This is established by [Baudhāyana] himself. In the manuscripts of the Sūtra alone, the word *yathā* is found. 1. "gavidhivi" | 2. "vāḍrenoṃ" | 3. "kha. cha, bhavantaḥ" | 1. "ka, kha. ga. ca. ti, bhaṅga" | 51. "bhāvādanā" | cha. "bhāvo'prā" | 6. "ka. ga, gha. padhi ba" |

Chapter 150: Accompanied by the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva. It is explained as follows: Regarding the middle [rite], Vāstamba states: "I dig up this herb, the most powerful of plants, by which a co-wife is overcome and by which one finds a husband. This mantra is enjoined for the digging up on the previous day of that plant called *pāṭhā*, after having tied it in the hand of the wife—when there is affection for only one husband among the wives and it is absent for the other—so that affection may arise.

But surely, if some action prescribed in its own proper place is indicated by secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then since *lakṣaṇā* is easily available everywhere, it would follow that [the action] becomes a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to everything. Furthermore, there are certain silent actions (*tūṣṇīka-karmāṇi*) which are dependent [on other factors]. Moreover, when direct denotation (*abhidhā*) is possible, it is not proper to resort to *lakṣaṇā*, even in the case of worldly actions. Indeed, even through *lakṣaṇā*, the placement [of an action] in its own proper place is observed.

For instance, having begun with the statement, "They worship the Gārhapatya fire," the text enjoins the mantra "niveśanaḥ saṃgamano vasūnām" (the dwelling-place, the gatherer of riches), which reveals Indra, for the purpose of worshipping the Gārhapatya fire. Nor is this mantra one that seeks a blessing for oneself, whereby it might be thought that one is seeking a blessing directed toward the Gārhapatya fire itself; rather, it indeed reveals Indra.

Even though the Gārhapatya fire is not something to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*), once it is understood that "one should produce the *apūrva* by means of the worship of the Gārhapatya in the form of manifesting the Gārhapatya," then the manifestation of the Gārhapatya is indeed performed through etymological derivation (*yoga*) and secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, let some silent rite (*tūṣṇīka-karma*) manifest [the deity] by whatever mode of operation; however, its displacement (*utkarṣa*) is not logical. Therefore, he says:
"Those who possess the Brāhmaṇas [should perform it] as prescribed; others [should do so] according to the form [of the mantra]."

The Brāhmaṇa consists of the injunctions that assign the mantras, accompanied by the Śruti that characterizes the assignment. Those mantras which possess such [Brāhmaṇas] are "possessors of Brāhmaṇas" (brāhmaṇavantaḥ). Not obtaining their primary denotation, they serve the purpose of sacrificial acts through some secondary function, strictly following the meaning as it was taught by the Śruti according to its specific purpose. For a secondary (gauṇī) function is not equal in strength to the primary (abhidhā) denotation, precisely because it is secondary.

Therefore, wherever an expression is sublated by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there the secondary sense (*gauṇī*) is resorted to for the sake of attaining its own perceived meaning, and not otherwise. And it has been said by Pārthasārathi Miśra: "Even though the capacity exists in the secondary sense, it does not manifest without another means of valid cognition; but in the primary sense, that [capacity] manifests from the word itself. Furthermore, while the primary sense is inherently meaningful, the fact that the secondary sense is directed toward an object is to be known through another means of valid cognition; in its absence, it is not established."

Now, since there is no sublation, he states that [the words] are for the purpose of the primary ritual action: "The others according to their form. The others are those whose denotative capacities have not been sublated by an injunction; they serve the purpose of the sacrificial ritual according to their denotative capacity, but not all sacrificial rituals through a secondary or figurative application. The meaning is that because there is no other function besides denotation (*abhidhā*), they do not serve the purpose of all rituals. If it is asked, "From what [source] is the attainment of serving all rituals? [it is answered as follows:]

It is said: it has been stated that mantras serve the purpose of sacrificial acts (*yajña-karma*). In that context, through the methods of syntactical connection (*vākya*), contextual indication (*prakaraṇa*), and position (*sthāna*), their purpose is understood to be the performance of the ritual along with its constituent parts (*sāṅga-karma*). In this regard, their form consists of denotation (*abhidhā-rūpa*)—[as found in the various recensions] *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *pāda*. [The text continues: ...*tamam*; as in *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *yathā*; [the definition is] characterized by beneficial action (*hitakarma-lakṣaṇā*); or [the reading is] *vā*.

If it were not a regulator (*niyāmaka*), then by some means of subsistence (*vṛtti*), there might even be a sense that the sentence pertains to all rites. Therefore, since the primary status among those things whose purpose is understood through sentences and other means is established precisely through direct denotation (*abhidhā*), the weaker means of proof—such as syntactical connection (*vākya*) and so forth—are restricted; thus, the Sūtra serves a specific purpose.

Thus, the conclusion is that those [subsidiaries] are assigned by other means of knowledge (pramāṇa), whether they be sublaters or non-sublaters. Now, one might object: "In cases where there is no general injunction from a scriptural statement (vākya) or other such means of knowledge, even by means of indicative mark (liṅga), those [subsidiaries] would belong to various different rites. To this he says: "The determination of the subsidiary."

The remaining [mantras] have not been restricted by any other means of proof (*pramāṇa*) besides *liṅga* (indicative power) to serve the purpose of specific ritual acts (*karma-viśeṣa*). And at that time, since the performance of multiple rituals is involved, the ritual acts are already confined within the end of the respective mantras. In that case, there is no combination (*samuccaya*), because those mantras applied by *liṅga* assisted by another means of proof lack the same status as those applied by *liṅga* alone. For this very reason, there is also no option (*vikalpa*). "Viniyoga" (application) is the specific placement of a mantra that has a requirement for a specific ritual act; "is stated" (*ucyate*) is the ellipsis to be supplied.

This is established by the mere statement for the purpose of demonstrating its fitness. Fearing that the remaining *sāmans* might lack application because they do not illuminate a unified meaning, he says:
"The verses from the ten maṇḍalas have a miscellaneous purpose (*pāriplava*)."

That which consists of ten *maṇḍalas* is the *Daśataya*; the hymns (*ṛc*) contained therein are the *Dāśatayyas*. When the *pāriplava* litany—which consists of praising the qualities of the deities—is to be recited, those [hymns] are intended to fulfill it. Because they are designated as "Hautra" (pertaining to the Hotṛ priest) and because they are designated as "Pāriplava," they are for that purpose alone; they "float around" (*pariplavante*) elsewhere, as there is no other application for them. Furthermore, since the recitation in the *pāriplava* is performed without a fixed sequence, it likewise depends upon other mantras.
The term *bhakta* means "desiring both," that is, seeking the sacrifice. Now, he states that those *sāmans* which were not previously assigned go toward the *vikṛti* (modified sacrifices):
"In the repetition of the *stomas* in the two subsequent *pavamānas*, the *sāmans* [are used].

When there is an increase (*vivṛddhi*) through the repetition of the *stomas*—which are collections serving as the substratum for the *sāmans*—the repetition of the *sāmans* already assigned should not be performed; rather, those which are not assigned elsewhere and are thus in need (*sākāṅkṣāṇi*), by them alone the increase should be effected. For example, it is heard regarding the *kratūs* with increased *stomas*: "One desiring offspring should cause him to sacrifice with the *ekaviṃśatirātra*."

In that context, the *trivṛt* stomas, the *pañcadaśa* stomas, the *saptadaśa* stomas, and the *ekaviṃśa* stomas are to be performed as *ekaviṃśa* stomas alone. Regarding this, when it was stated that "in the case of the two *pavamāna* [laudations], [the rule applies] upon the arrival [of new Sāmans] for the purpose of filling those Sāmans not already assigned to all the other laudations," the intention is as follows: in the laudations other than the *pavamānas*, there is no arrival of previously unknown Sāmans. [End of Paṭala 10].

This is accompanied by the commentary titled *Mahādevakṛtavaijayantī*. It is logical that there is indeed an addition (*āgama*) [of verses] during the *sarga* (the *prastāva*). Why? Because it is stated: "There are three bellies of the sacrifice—the *gāyatrī*, the *bṛhatī*, and the *anuṣṭubh*"; likewise, it is understood that they insert [verses] into these very [metres] and extend them from these very [metres], as these are the foundational supports for the metres. Since the triad of metres does not exist in the *pavamāna* chants, there is no addition of metres there, but rather only of *sāmans*. For what purpose is the phrase "in the latter two" used? It is said: because of the prohibition against adding *sāmans* in the *bahiṣpavamāna*.

For it is heard thus: "There is indeed one *sāman* there," because the *gāyatrī* is sung with the *svarasāman* itself; therefore, in this case as well, there is only the addition of the *ṛc*, and it is not stated that [the *sāman*] belongs to the two following [verses]. Here too, the application is by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the glorification of the deity's qualities, the designation (*samākhyā*) as belonging to the *audgātra* [priesthood], and the state of being expectant (*sākāṅkṣatvena*). Having thus stated the application of the *ṛcs* and *sāmans*, he states the application of the remaining [elements]:
"In the silent [rites], the *yajus* is archetypal."

Having stated the application (*viniyoga*) of the remainder (*śeṣa*) in the *Ṛgveda* and *Sāmaveda*, the application of the remainder in the *Yajurveda* and *Atharvaveda* must now be stated; therefore, the mention of the *Yajus* is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of both the *Yajurveda* and the *Atharvaveda*. By this, all those [formulas] which constitute the remainder in those two—whether they be *yajus* or *ṛc* verses—are applied. Where? In the silent (*tūṣṇīka*) rites, and in the archetypal (*prakṛtibhūta*) *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, *Jyotiṣṭoma*, and *Agnihotra* sacrifices. The *Agnihotra* mentioned in the rule "One performs the *Agnihotra* for a month" is also an archetype.

Prākṛta (archetypal) actions are those connected with the original nature (*prakṛti*). Those in which mantras are not prescribed even though they are performed silently are called *tūṣṇīka* (silent); these require mantras due to their expectancy. However, even a *vikṛti* (modified rite), though silent, does not have an expectancy for mantras in the mind, because it does not require other mantras in the absence of an explicit instruction. Among those archetypal rites, the *yajus* (prose formula) applies. All mantras apply according to their specific form, not everywhere indiscriminately; rather, even among the archetypal rites, they remain restricted to their respective actions. Now, [an objection]:

If it is argued that this is already understood by the phrase "as is the other," [the reply is: True; however, this is the case for these [mantras] because their status as subsidiary elements (*śeṣatva*) arises through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), and because there is an absence of application (*viniyoga*) through the lack of auxiliary support from syntactical connection (*vākya*) and so forth. Therefore, they are to be recited during the *pāriplava* [narration].

Although there is no remainder of any mantra because all Ṛks, all Yajus, and all Sāmans are prescribed for recitation as the *pāriplava* (the revolving narrative) according to the Śruti—"He recites the *pāriplava*,"—nevertheless, since the application [of mantras] therein occurs independently of their indicative power (*liṅga*), the principle "the other [mantra] is according to its form" (*yathārūpam itaraḥ*) would be sublated. To avoid that, just as specific applications were demonstrated by means of the deity, substance, quality, and indicative power (*devatā-dravya-guṇa-liṅga*) of the *yathā-rūpa* rule, so too is there a specific application here by means of the capacity characterized by the manifestation of the meaning residing in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

This Sūtra is for the purpose of determining application (*viniyoga*). In that regard, although there is an application to all [mantras] in common simply by virtue of their being unseen in purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), because the quality of manifesting a meaning inherent in the ritual action (*karman*) results in them having a seen purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), and because the *sāmans* do not manifest a meaning inherent in the action, they do not attain [this status]; thus, the *stotras* and *śastras* have an unseen purpose.

17... Or on the *śyāmā* [day]. 2.100. According to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: having milked in the evening on the thirteenth or the twelfth day, he milks continuously in the evening and morning for the sake of the curds (*dadhi*). Likewise, on the following day—the fourteenth, the thirteenth, or the twelfth—he milks the curds in the morning and again milks them continuously. This applies to all three [days]. This second alternative is observed in the *Āpastamba-sūtra*.
With the formula, "I anoint thee with Soma," he makes the bottom cool and anoints it; or [he says], "I anoint thy own portion with Soma for Indra."

The mantra ends with *indrāya dadhi* (for Indra, curds). In both cases, for one who sacrifices to Mahendra, the word *mahendra* is used; by means of that previously prepared curd, he causes the milk to coagulate—that is, he brings about the modification characterized by the state of curds. Having made the bottom cool, he pours it into the vessel; as long as the bottom of the vessel is not cool, the milk, undergoing transformation, would not become curds—this is why "cool" (*śītam*) is specified. In the absence of curds for the purpose of coagulation, he states five optional substances: with rice-grains, with bark-shavings, with *kvala*-berries, with *badara*-berries, or with *pūtīka* leaves.

The mantra, however, is the one previously mentioned. With *parṇavalkas*—that is, parts of the bark of the *parṇa* tree—namely wild *avadara*, *iṅgudāra*, and *pūtīka* (fragments of herbs used as substitutes for *soma*), he pours the remnants of the *agnihotra* [into the water], either with the formula: "Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; I continue thee, the continuity of the sacrifice," or silently.

Regarding the *agnihotroccheṣaṇa* (the remnant of the *agnihotra*): some say it is what remains in the pot after the *agnihotra* has been offered; however, it is more logical that it refers to what remains in the ladle (*srug*), as supported by the *Vājasaneyi-śruti*. He pours it—that is, brings it—into that *kumbhī* (pot) either with a mantra or silently. The rule "he anoints another [cow] with the remnant of the *agnihotra*" indicates that this is a *pratipatti* (disposal) rite for the existing remnant, serving as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the milk-offering. Therefore, in the event of the loss of the remnant, there is no need to perform the *agnihotra* again, as Baudhāyana suggests.

Āpastamba states the favor to be granted in the absence of remnants: "In the absence of remnants, one should curdle [milk] with rice; in the absence of rice, with herbs. These two [substitutes] are to be used silently. In the Soma sacrifice, fresh milk serves as the substitute for the curdling agent (*ātañcana*). From this it is understood that the *agnihotra* need not be performed again when the remnants are lost.

The offering of the *yavāgū* (barley-gruel) as an *agnihotra* at night on the new moon day is a contingent (*naimittika*) rite for the sacrificer who performs the *saṃnayana* (the milking of the cows). It is not prompted by the remnant (*uccheṣaṇa*), nor is the remnant a by-product (*anuniṣpādi*). This [offering] is the disposal (*pratipatti*) of that [remnant], because of the accusative case in the statement, "he pours down the remnant of the *agnihotra*" (*agnihotroccheṣaṇam abhyātanakti*). Furthermore, this is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the milk-offering (*doha*), because of the verbal root *ā-nī* (to bring/pour down) which takes an object, and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating "for the continuity of the sacrifice" (*yajñasya saṃtatyai*), and because of the Brāhmaṇa passage which praises the continuity of this sacrifice through the *agnihotra*.

For the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the remnants of the *agnihotra* does not become something to be performed by means of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* brāhmaṇa.
