Therefore, so that there may be no loss of the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), a substitute (*pratinidhi*) was resorted to by the teacher Āpastamba. However, our own teacher has not stated a substitute; rather, it follows that ordinary barley-gruel (*yavāgū*), the rice grains which are its source-material (*tat-prakṛti*), or other similar herbs are indeed obtained. Thus [ends] the fourth section of the *ka*, *va*, *ga*, *paṃ*, *cha*, *a*, *meṭa*, *i*. [End of] the sixth chapter, accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

"O Waters, be watchful among the oblations, just as you are watchful among the gods; even so, be watchful for the sacrificer at this sacrifice. With these words, he pours water into the vessel for the purpose of covering it, using either an iron or a wooden vessel, according to the Śruti: "With an iron [vessel] or a wooden vessel. Regarding the specific rule for when those two are unavailable, he says:
"If it should be made of clay, one should pierce it with a blade of grass or a piece of wood."

He should place [the two blades] into an earthen vessel. Having untied the branch-strainer (*śākhāpavitra*) with the mantra: "These two—the leaf and the *darbha* grass—are the purifiers of the oblation for the gods; O Viṣṇu, guard it for the morning offering, for you protect the oblation," he deposits it in its known place. This mantra applies specifically to the *palāśa* branch-strainer, as its applicability is obscured when used with a *śamī* branch-strainer. In that case, the depositing is done silently. Furthermore, in the previous instance as well, the depositing was done with the mantra, not the untying.
With the words, "O Viṣṇu, protect the oblation," he places the *sānnāyya* offering above the location of the *gārhapatya* fire.
Thus ends the third chapter in the first book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.

He places [the vessel] upon a sling or similar support. Regarding this similarity, Baudhāyana states that for one who is measuring out the milk, he should recite the mantras beginning with the extraction of the fat (*vasāpākaraṇa*); Śālīki says they should begin from the pouring (*āsecanaprabhṛti*). In the absence of cows or if milking is impossible, only milk should be taken; in that case, the aforementioned purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) must be performed.

However, for the Teacher (Ācārya), since the application of the milking-mantras (*dohanamantra*) is undesired when there is no [cow] to be milked, the opinion of Śālīki is preferred: the pouring, the milking, the washing, and the pouring out [of the water] must be performed from that point onward with the mantras. But when a substitute (*pratinidhi*) is used for the cow, there is no performance of the *yajus* at all; this should be understood as being according to the view of Baudhāyana, and not otherwise, nor according to the view of the Teacher.
Thus ends the third chapter in the first book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* composed by Mahādeva.
1.4 Now begins the fourth chapter.
Having brought another branch, he drives away the calves for the morning milking with that same procedure—either with that branch or with *darbha* grass—just as he did for the evening milking.

By that very same [procedure], he brings a branch of the *palāśa* or a branch of the *śamī*; by means of that bringing, [the action] is connected to the purpose. [The text] "He removes the calves from their mothers" is connected with the phrase "as for the evening milking. By saying "for the milking," it is stated that all the rules prior to the milking are the same.

In the midst of that, there is no *prasthāpana* with the mantra "devo vaḥ," no touching of a single [branch], and no following after (*anumantraṇa*) once they have set out; these are not found here. Everything else is performed up to the end of the *upagṛhana*, and the disposal (*pratipatti*) of that branch is together with the *prastara*. However, when the alternative view of "driving away the calves" (*vatsāpākaraṇa*) is adopted, there is no further fetching of the branch because it serves no purpose. And the previous *śākhāpavitra* remains for the sake of the subsequent milking, due to the injunction based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra.

Although the spreading of the grass and the placing of the forest-food (āraṇyāśana) are to be enjoined at this point, they are nevertheless presented here not through an intervening separation but as belonging to the same context, in order to demonstrate that the procedure for the evening milking and the morning milking is indeed based on direct instruction (aupadeśika). Likewise, these two milkings—the evening and the morning—should also be explained without intervention as pertaining to the Sānnāyya sacrifice. To state the specific sequence therein, he says:
"Having placed the potsherds, he milks the morning milk; its ritual procedure is explained by that of the evening milking.
This is clear. He states the distinction:
"I place the two sacrificial hearths (ukhā) for the non-lapse of the sacrifice; brought together with the animals, well-prepared, for Indra. With these words, he concludes the mantra.
This means that he recites it according to this specific reading. He states another particular detail:
"He places the branch-purifier (śākhāpavitra) with its tip pointing northward."

In the evening milking, the distinction is that the blades [of the grass] are pointed toward the north-east, whereas previously they were pointed toward the north. The procedure up to the pouring out of the washing water is the same; however, the action performed silently does not exist here, because the sprinkling with the butter contained in the vessel will be described later. He states another distinction:
"He does not anoint."

This is a restatement of what has already been established for the purpose of excluding subsequent items. Consequently, the bringing of the remnants of the *agnihotra*, the covering [of the vessel], the placing of the *śākhāpavitra*, and the setting aside of the *sāṃnāyya* are all excluded. Thus, when both milkings have been performed, it is said with reference to the *darśa* sacrifice alone: "The *sāṃnāyya* belongs to one who performs the *saṃnayana*. Now he states the distinction between those who perform the *saṃnayana* and those who do not:

"One who does not sacrifice with *soma* should not perform the *saṃnayana*; however, regarding this, the Kāpeyas say that even one who does not sacrifice with *soma* should indeed perform the *saṃnayana*."

"One who has not sacrificed with Soma should not perform the *sāṃnāyya* offering"—this is found in our own recension (*śākhā*). "Indeed, they say [otherwise]"—this is found in another recension. Indeed, the followers of the Kāpeya recension have cited another ritual manual (*kalpāntara*). What then? That it should indeed be performed, and so forth. Thus, even for one who has mentally resolved upon both the enjoined and the prohibited Soma sacrifices, there is an option. [End of Chapter 4, Section 6] Accompanied by the commentary *Baijayantī* composed by Mahādeva: Regarding the deity for the *sāṃnāyya* of one who has not sacrificed with Soma, he states:
"Having sacrificed with Soma, one should offer the *sāṃnāyya* to Indra; thereafter, one should sacrifice to Mahendra."

When the two deities are established, one should sacrifice to Mahendra immediately after the Soma sacrifice, or at the New Moon (Darśa). Prior to the Soma sacrifice, whether the *sāṃnāyya* has been prepared or not, one should sacrifice to Indra alone immediately before it. Now, he states another alternative for the Soma-sacrificer according to his own school:
"Or rather, having sacrificed to Indra for a year or for two years, and having offered an eight-potherd cake to Agni Vratapati, one may sacrifice to Mahendra as one pleases."

Whether one has previously performed the *sāṃnāyya* sacrifice or not, after having sacrificed with the *sāṃnāyya* at the *Soma* sacrifices for one year or two years, one should perform an offering of eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapālāmiṣṭi*) to Agni Ṛtapatī; then, if there is a desire, one should sacrifice to Mahendra. This indicates that when such a desire exists, there is first the offering to Agni and so forth, followed by the sacrifice to Mahendra; however, when no such desire exists, there is neither the offering to Agni nor the sacrifice to Mahendra, but rather only the sacrifice to Indra.

How so? By using the gerund *nirūpya*, which indicates the completion of a prerequisite action, the speaker demonstrates a sequence of priority (*paurvāparya*); thus, it follows from this interpretation that this *naimittika-iṣṭi* (occasional sacrifice) is not prescribed for when a year has elapsed, but rather is prescribed precisely upon the expectation of [the sacrifice to] Mahendra. He states another ritual alternative:
Gautama, Bhāradvāja, Śuśruvān, Grāmaṇī, and Rājanya—these may all at will sacrifice to Mahendra.

The word *iti* is used here in the sense of "thus" or as a particle of emphasis (*vā*). The three beginning with Aurva are his lineage-holders (*gotra*), mentioned in other recensions (*śākhāntara*), while others are mentioned in one's own recension by the term *gataśrī*, as in the passage beginning, "There are indeed three who have attained prosperity (*gataśrī*): the learned (*śuśruvān*)," and so forth. The *śuśruvān* is one who has heard all the Vedas; for the Brāhmaṇa states: "Whom the seers know through the threefold knowledge—the Ṛks, the Sāmans, and the Yajus—that is indeed the immortal prosperity (*śrī*) of the virtuous. One by whom prosperity has been reached or attained is *gataśrī*. [Such a person is] the *śuśruvān*.

There is also this etymological explanation: "The Kṣatriya is indeed one who wears bright garments, a seer (kavi), and one of lovely appearance. The word *śrī* is clearly used for the supreme prosperity of Vaiśyas who have reached the pinnacle of wealth. A *rājanya* is the son of an anointed king; he too has attained *śrī* through the possession of great sovereignty. All these six [classes]—the meaning is that everywhere, both before and after the Soma sacrifice, they may worship Indra alone or Mahendra alone at their own will with the *sāṃnāyya*. Here, in the ritual of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), there is the eating of forest food. Having thus explained what is obtained, he states what must be performed after the evening milking:

"Strew around! Enclose the fire! May the fire, being enclosed, protect the sacrificer. May these gold neck-ornaments, the essence of the waters, the essence of the plants, be for the sacrificer as wish-fulfilling cows in that world, in yonder world," he thus commands.

The act of strewing (paristaraṇa) has an indefinite agent, as it is expressed by the plural verb "strew" (*paristṛṇīta*). Therefore, a priest other than the Āgnīdhra performs the strewing. The author of the Bhāṣya states that when a visible result is possible, one should not assume an invisible (transcendental) one. This interpretation is not accepted by others; for since there is no specification of the agent of the action in the *preṣa* (direction), and since the title "Adhvaryu" is established [by convention], by what could it be sublated?

Nor should it be said that [the injunction] is useless because of the capacity of the medicine, for we observe that the *preṣa* (direction) applies even to oneself; since in the case of the *agnihotra* oblation, one sees it apply to the self in the rule, "One should offer the *agnihotra* oneself or have another do it. Nor is the medicine redundant; for a *smṛti* (recollection), when produced in oneself just as it is produced in another by verbal recitation, would indeed result in a visible refinement (*saṃskāra*). Thus it has been stated by Kātyāyana: "Just as another performs what he is directed to do because of the authority of another, so too do we perform it [ourselves]."

"Because of contradiction," [it is said]. Bhāradvāja also states: "One view is that the Āgnīdhra should perform these rites; another is that the Adhvaryu [should]. Furthermore, there are injunctive formulas (*praiṣa-vacanāni*) even in the absence of one who is to be addressed, as has already been indicated by the Blessed One in the *Pariśiṣṭa-paribhāṣā*: "Since a *praiṣa* is intended for communicating with another, and although it is prescribed in the Yajurveda, its loud recitation would normally follow the rule for Sāman chants, this [text] declares that—except for the *pravara*, the *saṃvāda*, and the *āśrāvaṇa-praiṣas*—it is to be recited in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), as prescribed in the Yajurveda."

By this, he indicates that even when there is an injunction for high-pitched recitation directed toward oneself, it is distinct from the case where the purpose is explicitly specified. Furthermore, because of the formulation of this *paribhāṣā* (technical rule), it is the opinion of the author of the Sūtra that in the Yajurvedic rites where no agent is specified, the Adhvaryu alone is the performer. He states the manner of strewing: "He strews around the fires with *darbha* grass.

The plural number is intended to express a specific requirement regarding the materials to be used; thus, although there are four *darbha* blades in each section according to established custom and logic, the plurality ultimately results in a group of three. He states the sequence:

Having strewn grass around the Āhavanīya fire, [one should do so] for the Gārhapatya and then the Dakṣiṇāgni; or else, having strewn grass around the Gārhapatya, [one should do so] for the Dakṣiṇāgni and then the Āhavanīya.

The first is the primary sequence, while the second is the sequence of installation (*ādhāna*); this option exists because of specific [scriptural] injunctions. As for what is heard in the scripture, "They say that the fire is surrounded by the sacrificial grass on the north, on the west, and on the rear," even there, the word "first" (*pūrva*) cannot be explained as meaning "in the eastern quarter" or "installed first. However, it should be understood that the sequence for the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires is exactly as stated here. He describes the specific arrangement of the strewing: the tips of the grass blades point toward the north at the back and at the front.

The *ca* (and) in the middle of the word *pacyāc ca* is for the purpose of preventing the misconception that *paścāt* and *purastāt* form a single compound. It follows as a matter of course that the [lines] are on the south and the north; however, there is no vertical relationship (upper and lower) here, because it has not been so prescribed. Regarding this, Bharadvāja stated: "The southern wing is above, and the northern is below. Since the author of the Sūtra prescribes a rule for the Smārta (tradition-based) ritual, it is understood that there is no fixed rule for the Śrauta (Vedic) ritual.
The word *yat* is redundant.

Ka. Sa. Ga. Ca. Cha... i, 'pākāra| i—Chapter 105, together with the Vaijayantī commentary composed by Mahādeva. Now, one might object: "He will state that the construction of the altar (vedi) takes place on the previous day, the new-moon day; why then was this not mentioned while demonstrating the procedure (tantra) for the Darśa sacrifice? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Having performed this, he observes the fast on the new-moon day."

It is true that what is stated there belongs to another *śākhā* (branch of the Veda), and thus it is an option (*vikalpa*) with this [rule]. Why? Because it is stated in our own *śākhā*: "Having performed this very [rite], one should fast. This is the intention: this injunction for fasting does not apply during the sacrifice itself, because the vow (*vrata*) is a duty belonging to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Therefore, when the sacrifice has ceased, either fasting or dwelling near [the place of sacrifice] is enjoined. And that [fasting] follows the previously mentioned textual sequence.

At the conclusion of the *parisaraṇa* (sprinkling), one reaches [the point where] "therein this [is performed]"; that being redundant, it is understood that the statement "this very [act]" is common [to all], and serves the purpose of a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*) regarding the ritual rules of other schools. Nor should it be said that there is no restriction of the oral tradition (*śruti*) by the written text (*pāṭha*). By not employing the word "or" (*vā*), the author has shown that this is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of such a *śruti*: "Having performed this, he fasts on the new moon day."

Furthermore, that [other Vedic text] prohibits the preparation of the altar on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) which was obtained from another Śruti; there is no need for the word "or" (*vā*) in that case. Since it is both enjoined and prohibited, an option (*vikalpa*) arises within our own recension (*śākhā*). Thus, neither is the word "or" used here, nor is it used at the time of preparing the altar; rather, the option is shown by the Śrutis themselves. It will also be stated later that the preparation of the altar may take place on the preceding day, either before the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) or immediately after the altar.

The author of the Bhāṣya has demonstrated only one application [of the rule], namely that which precedes the bringing of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), because of its priority. It should not be argued that, on the strength of the restatement (*anuvāda*)—"he places it within the altar" (*antavedi*) and "the branch within the altar" (*antarvedi śākhāyāḥ*)—the construction of the altar must necessarily take place on the previous day, specifically on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). For, by virtue of being a first-time restatement, this would also apply to the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*). Therefore, this is not a primary restatement; rather, by the word "altar" (*vedi*), the region of the altar is intended.

Just as in the case of a transgression in the Agnihotra, the injunction "one should pour [the water] within the enclosing sticks" (*antaḥparidhi*) indicates a location, so too here there is no inconsistency whatsoever. On the previous day, there is the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) and the strewing around the fires (*agniparistaraṇa*). This much alone constitutes the "previous day's duty" (*pūrvaguru*); as for where the other ritual items belong, he says:
on the following day, one prepares the fuel-sticks (*idhma*), the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and the *veda*.

The indeclinable *śvas* indicates the basis of the immediately following day; in the subsequent context, it means "on the next unseparated day. This is because of the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) stating that *bhū-prāptau* [is used] when something has occurred or is attained. The meaning is that one prepares the fuel (*idhma*) and so forth by virtue of the injunctions found in another recension (*śākhā*). Now, although the sequence of ritual items established by the reading of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas is indeed set aside by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) of another recension, nevertheless, one prepares the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) on the previous day.

How can there be a sublation of that which is prescribed by the Śruti text, "Having commenced the sacrifice, he takes it up and sits near it" (Satyāṣāḍha Śrautasūtra 1.14.106)? Nor should it be argued that this applies only to one who does not perform the *sānnāyya* offering because of its association with that term; for if that were so, it would not apply even to one who does not perform the *sānnāyya* on the tenth day, and thus the summary statement "on the new moon day" (*amāvāsyā*) without qualification would also be untenable. Furthermore, it is established by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "those two are subject to the same injunction."

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "On the full moon day one undertakes the vow with sacrificial grass (*barhis*); on the new moon day, with calves; this is the abode of these two; having spread [the grass], the first [day] is the prior," since the proximity (*saṃnidhi*) of the *sāṃnāyya* offering is weakened by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) supported by the very order of sequence, how could the unrestricted direct scriptural statement (*śruti*)—"on the previous day"—be sublated? To that, he says: "Or rather, immediately" (*sadyo vā*).

The word "he performs" (karoti) is understood [from the previous context]. The meaning is that there is an option (*vikalpa*) because the two scriptural injunctions (*śruti*) possess equal authority. For when [the ritual] is performed on the same day, on the day of the fuel-piling (*anvādhāna*), one should act exactly as prescribed in our own *śākhā*, and not otherwise; this is the intention. [Objection: But would not everything then apply even on a Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) performed on the same day (*sadyaskālā*)? To this he says: "Everything is performed. On a *sadyaskālā* [Full Moon sacrifice], after the rite of the *veda*, he strews grass around the fires.

Because the two days—the day of fasting (*upavasatha*) and the day of sacrifice (*yajana*)—are identical as a single day by virtue of being performed on the same day (*sadyaskālatva*), the designation "immediate" (*sadyas*) is applied based on this occasion of performance. Consequently, "everything" is performed immediately; that is to say, by the force of other scriptural authorities, one performs everything within a single lunar date (*tithi*) characterized by the immediate time, rather than across two separate days. This is the intention according to Bhāradvāja.

It was not stated that "the full moon day is of immediate time" (*sadyaskālā*); however, if that too is to be considered, then the preceding sūtra should be explained as follows: the sūtra "or immediately" (*sadyo vā*) refers to what was said regarding the previous day and the following day; on the same day, one performs [the rite] either with the preceding [set of actions] or with the subsequent. When it is with the preceding, then it is exactly as previously stated: the second [set] consists of the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*), the fetching of the *idhma* wood, the preparation of the *veda*, the strewing [of grass], the fasting (*upavāsa*), and so forth, beginning with "on the following day for the sake of the ritual" (*śvo bhūte karmaṇe vām*), according to the recited text. This option is indeed alternative.

When it says, "If [the fire-laying] is performed on the following day," then the third alternative is stated as "on the same day" (*sadyaskālā*) or "on the next day" (*paradvā*). This means that on that very day one performs the setting up of the fires (*agnyādheya*), the fuel and sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*), and the strewing of the altar (*vediparistaraṇa*). In another Sūtra, this alternative is explained as being an equal option (*samavikalpa*) to the two preceding ones, and is prescribed as restricted specifically to the Full Moon day (*paurṇamāsīmātra*) by way of a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*). The alternative "he does everything on the same day" is explained as applying to the *sadyaskālā* [rite].

In this context, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakṛt), by refuting the second alternative—"or immediately"—which had been treated as a prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), has explained [the sūtra] with "or immediately. Consequently, only one single position is established; however, that explanation is to be disregarded because it fails to render the author of the Sūtras' excessive effort meaningful. This is because in other sūtras, various alternatives are accepted according to this very same method.

To demonstrate that on the *sadyaskāla* day—following the evening *agnihotra*—the ritual strewing (*paristaraṇa*) which would normally occur at its appointed time must nevertheless be performed according to the sequence of the constituent elements (*padārtha-krama*) by the force of logic, it is shown in the *Sadyaskālā* [section] that "one strews over the fire after the subsequent rite. This is so that, even in the absence of the specific time, there may be no violation of either the sequence or the constituent element. Here, regarding the *sadyaskāla* full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), there is this further distinction:
the summary verse states—"The word 'tomorrow' (*śvas*) is omitted, as are both the mantra and the two fires in every respect."

It exists neither in the primary form nor in the modified form, due to its being a modification thereof. [Note: In the manuscript commentaries, the word "karoti" (he does) occurs in place of "kriyate" (it is done). Chapter 10, accompanied by the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva.
Thus ends the procedure for the previous day. Now follows the procedure for the following day:
having performed the morning *Agnihotra* sacrifice, one commences the ritual framework (*tantra*) of the Full Moon sacrifice after the sun has risen, or that of the New Moon sacrifice before sunrise.

Because there is no distinction regarding the time, and based on the scriptural injunction that "having offered the morning *agnihotra* when the sun has risen," the rule for the offering must apply before sunrise on both *parvan* days. Thus, it is appropriate that the *sūtra* establishes a fixed rule regarding the commencement [of the rite]. As for the explanation that "having offered the morning *agnihotra* when the sun has risen, [one performs] the *tantra* of the Full Moon sacrifice," that is not very convincing. The suffix *ṇic* in the word *prakramayati* is used in its own sense (causative), meaning he urges the attendants (*parikarmiṇaḥ*) toward the commencement.
Or, having washed his hands with the formula "for the sake of the ritual" (*karmaṇe vām*).

The phrase ends with "may I be capable. *Anis* refers to the unseen refinement (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*), characterized by the capacity for ritual action, as established by the indicative power of the mantra (*mantra-liṅga*) and the supplementary portion of the text (*vākya-śeṣa*). For this very reason, it is established by logic that [the grass] is not merely for the purpose of spreading the *ulaparājī*, nor even for that much alone; rather, it is for the sake of the entire sacrifice. [The priest recites: "Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; I spread thee for the continuity of the sacrifice; for continuity, I spread thee for the sacrifice. He spreads the *ulaparājī* in a continuous line from the *Gārhapatya* fire to the *Āhavanīya* fire. He spreads the southern one silently, and the northern one silently.

Starting from the site of the *gārhapatya* fire and extending as far as the site of the *āhavanīya* fire, he spreads a continuous line of dry *darbha* grass. The word "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*) is intended to demonstrate the reading found in another recension (*śākhāntara*), which states it for each [line] individually. What is the purpose of demonstrating this reading? It is so that, by the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) "silently," the repetition of the mantra—which would otherwise be required by logical necessity—may be prevented.

For since the *rājya* and *bhūtamāvī* are not things that can be utilized [as objects], their status as things to be consecrated (*saṃskāryatva*) is not understood through the accusative case; nor is there a status as things to be consecrated for the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires when they are indicated by the ablative case, because the end of the mantra is not perceived [to signify such]. Furthermore, from the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), "for the non-interruption of the sacrifice," it is understood that the function of the sacrifice is merely to effect continuity. Therefore, it is a primary act (*pradhānakarma*) that provides assistance from a distance (*ārādupakāraka*).

Although in our own recension (*śākhā*) only this much is prescribed as a primary ritual act—namely, "he does not interrupt the *āhavanīya* fire"—nevertheless, in another recension two other lines, southern and northern, are prescribed with distinct qualities (*guṇabheda*). Thus, these three are indeed primary acts.

Consequently, since the rule "where there is one [act]" does not apply to prevent the repetition of the mantra, and because the principle of "repetition for each primary act" would otherwise lead to the repetition of the mantra, it is established that the reading of the word "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*) serves to prevent such repetition.
To the south of the Āhavanīya fire, he prepares the two seats for the Brahman and the sacrificer.

On the southern side, not far from the Āhavanīya, he prepares seats with sacrificial grass (yājñika-tṛṇa) for the purpose of sitting. Since it is observed in the scripture that "he throws away a blade of grass from the seat" (*namasadanāt tṛṇaṃ nirasyati*), the seats consist of grass. There, to the south of the Āhavanīya hearth which measures one aratni, because it is impossible for both [the Brahman and the sacrificer] to sit directly adjacent to each other, the two seats are placed at a distance from one another; according to the Sūtra, the former is for the Brahman and the latter for the sacrificer.

Because it has been restricted for the sake of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and since it is impossible for both [the Brahman and the sacrificer] to simultaneously occupy the primary position on the south side, even though one or the other would naturally be expected there, the primary place belongs to the Brahman alone. Consequently, if the sacrificer occupies a slightly different spot in accordance with that [primary placement], it is not defective. Thus it is said: "The Brahman indeed has his seat to the south," and likewise, "He lies to the south; this indeed belongs to the sacrificer."

Regarding the term "yatanam," even though there are two identical scriptural statements (*samānaśrutī*), a resolution of the contradiction is also seen from another scriptural passage: "The sacrificer sits upon the southern part of the altar. Here, the fourth case ending is used in the sense of location (*sadarthe*). This has been explained as: "In this context, he prepares the eastern and western seats for the Brahman and the sacrificer, respectively."
Having strewn *darbha* grass to the north of the *gārhapatya* fire, he washes the vessels in pairs and places them face down.

Having spread *darbha* grass for the subsidiary portions—either with the tips pointing eastward or northward—he places the vessels upon them. The word "to the north" (*uttareṇa*) is connected with "not far from" (*adūre*) or with "places" (*prayunakti*). The term "in pairs" (*dvaṃdvam*) is also connected specifically with "places" (*prayunakti*). Likewise, "face down" (*nyañci*) and "having washed" (*prakṣālya*) are primarily connected with the act of placing itself; their mutual relationship follows subsequently by implication.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having washed the vessels with water, she arranges them all in pairs, face down and turned toward the earth. This is because of the Vedic text stating, "She brings them in pairs, two by two. He specifies those very vessels—from "the wooden sword" (*sphya*) up to "the *iḍā*-vessel. Then, the word "and" (*ca*) that is heard [in the text] is connected either with both or with one, for the purpose of explaining the Vedic "and" which is heard in each instance. Indeed, it is heard: "The wooden sword and the potsherds."

In this context, when two words are embraced by a single cognition (*ekadhi*), two "ends" (*pāra*) are intended. The state of being a pair (*dvitva*) is brought about by the term *dvaṃdva*, which results in the formation of two [words] in some cases and in others it culminates in [a compound]. Therefore, the completion of the *dvaṃdva* must be effected by a single meaning as the referent of a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*). For example:
*sphyaṃ kapālāni* (the wooden sword and the potsherds).

"All the *kapālas* (potsherds) constitute a single vessel; its form is that of a sword (*sphyas*)," says Āpastamba. *Sphya* means a sword. Because it is not used for making oblations, it is made from the *vāraṇa* tree. Āpastamba, however, states that the *sphya*, the *śamyā*, and the *prāśitra* [vessel] are made of *khadira* wood. Bhāradvāja says that the *sphya* and the *śamyā* are one cubit (*bāhumātra*) long. Baudhāyana says they are thirty-two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long; others say thirty-six. The *kapālas* are the fragments of a new, broken earthen vessel, suitable for placing the *puroḍāśa* cakes upon.

Regarding the *rauhiṇaka-pātras*, since their form is prescribed, one should make them out of clay, draw some lines for division, bake them, and then break them [into pieces] to be used; however, the word *kapāla* (potsherd) is not appropriately applied to each individual piece once it has been separately made and baked. This is because of the scriptural observation: "He places [the oblation] upon the potsherds turned face-upward. Thus, the term denotes the whole [composite object]. But regarding the *rauhiṇas*...
