It is possible to perform each [act] individually according to the injunction. In that case, the word *kapāla* (potsherd) will be used figuratively (*gauṇa*) for the purpose of obtaining the properties of a potsherd; its status as having the accusative ending is for the purpose of connecting it with the verb "to employ" (*prayuñjati*).
[The same applies to] the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle and the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*).

The *agnihotra-havaṇī* is the ladle by which the *agnihotra* is offered; it is characterized by the proper marks of a sacrificial ladle. It is made of *vikaṅkata* wood because it is used for oblations; as he will state later, "Those trees not specifically prescribed [for sacrificial implements] belong to the *vikaṅkata*. The winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) is well known in the world; Baudhāyana states that it should be made of bamboo or reed (*nalama*). Some say it is made of *iṣīkā* grass, based on the mantra-text "Thou art grown by rain" (*varṣavṛddham asi*) applied to the basket and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that "the *iṣīkā*s are grown by rain"; *iṣīkā*s are grasses resembling *iṣīkā*. The black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) and the wooden pin (*śamyā*).

The neck [of the post] is covered with the skin of a black antelope; this has already been explained by means of the *śamyā* and the wooden sword (*sphya*). As for its shape, it is according to the purpose. The *śamyā*, however, is a piece of wood inserted into the hole of the yoke.
The mortar and pestle are of that same size, which is established by the requirements of the task. These belong specifically to the *varaṇa* tree.
A lower millstone and an upper millstone;
two artificial stones made for the purpose of grinding, which are well-known in the world and denote a species;
a *sruva* ladle made of *khadira* wood, a *juhū* ladle made of *pālāśa* wood, an *upabhṛt* ladle made of *aśvattha* wood, and a *dhruvā* ladle made of *vaikaṅkata* wood.

Because it has been stated thus in the *anuvāka*: "The *vaṣaṭ*-call is indeed the *gāyatrī*. He states the measurement according to another recension: "They are one cubit (*aratni*) long or one forearm (*bāhu*) long; they have mouths like [the *gāyatrī*], with pouring-out [nostrils] like the beak of a swan, and their tips are sharp. Some say they have ear-holes like bark and tails like crows; others say they have lips like elephants."

This is the measurement for the *agnihotrahavaṇī* and the *sruva*, because no other measurement for those two has been prescribed. Although the phrase "measuring with the span of the forearm" (*aratnimātryā*) and so forth uses the feminine gender, nevertheless, since the *sruva* is included by virtue of the predominance of the term "ladle" (*sruk*) in passages such as "he cleanses the ladles, beginning with the *sruva*," the measurement alone is connected with the *sruva*. The specific shape, however, belongs only to the four types of *sruc* ladles; the shape of the *sruva*, on the other hand, is incompatible with the form of a ladle, since its praise is solely for the purpose of taking portions (*avadāna*).

This is because of the supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa): "He for whom the *sruva* ladle is made of *khadira* wood cuts with the very essence of the meters," and because other scriptures prescribe it as having a hole the size of an axle (*akṣa*) or a hole the size of a thumb-joint (*aṅguṣṭhaparva*). Furthermore, the qualities of being pointed at the tip and being smooth are also connected here due to lack of contradiction. An *aratni* consists of twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Some maintain that the "arm" (*bāhu*), measured from the tip of the fingers to the bone joined at the elbow, consists of forty-two finger-breadths.

According to the views of Baudhāyana and Māradvāja, the length of the *sruva* ladles is thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Baudhāyana has also stated that the *sruk* spoons are one span (*prādeśa*) long. "Having mouths" means that their mouth—the cavity—is at the upper end, and not that the cavity extends all the way to the bottom like a *sruva*. Those whose pouring-out is like the beak of a swan are called *prasaghaṇa*; by means of this, the liquid is poured out (*prasicyate*). Thus it is said in the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha.

The "mouth of the swan" refers to the lower nozzle of a five-chambered vessel; the meaning is that it has a nozzle resembling that [of a swan]. The substance situated in the *khum* (ladle) falls into the fire by means of the nozzle; that portion through which it passes and undergoes division is the limit of the wooden vessel for pouring (*prasecanakāṣṭhānamani*). Those [streams] which have that very [limit] are [described as such]. By the word "flowing" (*bhavanti*), it is stated that this is established through the force of various scriptural authorities.

According to the scriptural statement, "Trees indeed have excellent bark," the suffix *tasil* is used here in the sense of the locative case (*svataḥ*). Thus, they are those [trees] which have a cavity (*bilam*)—a hollowed-out space for the collection of substances such as clarified butter—in their bark portion. A cavity should not be made in the interior of a piece of wood split in two; rather, having leveled the surface, the cavity should be made right there on the bark side. However, in the case of unsplit wood, the meaning is that the cavity should be made such that it extends further than the middle portion and is narrower toward the end, so that the cavity remains close to the bark.

"Those whose handles are like the tail of a crow" means that they are thick at the base of the handle, curved in circumference, and from there upwards, toward the edge of the bowl, they are very slightly tapered. Here, the phrase "according to some" (*ekeṣām*) is for the purpose of indicating a specific view, not for the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*), because there is no contradiction between the two usages in the compound *haṃsamukhyo vāyasapucchayaḥ*. The statement "according to some" is intended to demonstrate an option by way of combining contradictory attributes, as in the case of "those whose lips are like the trunk of an elephant."

By the term *haṃsamukhya* ("having the tip like a swan"), there is an alternative to *hastyoṣṭhya* ("having a tip like an elephant's trunk"). For example, Baudhāyana says: "The *sruva* ladle should have [a cavity] the size of a *śyena* (hawk). Maradvāja says: "The *sruva* has a cavity the size of a thumb-joint; the *sruks* have cavities the size of half a span. According to another scripture, the vessels for the *sruks* are shaped like a *majjala*. The *ājyasthālī* is a *kuṭaru*. The earthen vessel for the purpose of pouring out the clarified butter (*ājya-nirvāpa*) is a *kuṭaru*; a *kuṭaru* is a stone used as a means of crushing.
The *pātrī* and the *mekṣaṇa*.
The *mekṣaṇa* for the purpose of pouring in the flour is made of clay alone. The *mekṣaṇa* is a wooden spoon, shaped like a ladle, used for mixing the flour.
The *veda* is the *prāśitraharaṇa*.

The Veda has been explained. The *prāśitra-haraṇa* is the vessel by which the portion for the Brahman (*brahmaṇe 'vadāna*) that has been tasted is removed; Bharadvāja says it is shaped like a cow's ear or like a cup (*camasa*), while Kātyāyana says it is shaped like a mirror. [It also includes] the *praṇītā-praṇayana* and the *iḍā-pātra*. The *praṇītā* waters are those by which the water is brought forth; that vessel is a cup made of *vāraṇa* wood. Likewise, there is also a cup for the purpose of holding the portions of the *iḍā*, made of wood, bronze, clay, or metal. The word "and" (*ca*) is to be connected with both [the *praṇītā-praṇayana* and the *iḍā-pātra*].

"One *anvāhārya* pot"—the word "one" is established by the sense [of the context]. Furthermore, in the case of a human vessel, there is no formation of a *dvandva* (pairing). Because the *anvāhārya* is carried away for the purpose of purchase (*parikrayaṇa*) from its origin, it is therefore human. According to the scriptural statement, "all human [vessels] together," since there is no mention of others, the Teacher [says] that only one is to be employed; thus, by making it one with the preceding divine [vessel], the formation of a *dvandva* must be effected. This is the meaning.

By this, it is indicated that even in other modifications (*vikṛti*), one should somehow effect the accomplishment of these [requirements] by unifying the two categories of objects. Having thus explained, according to one's own branch (*svaśākhā*), the fact that the ladles (*sruva*) are made from wood specifically prescribed for them, [the author] now explains, according to other branches (*śākhāntara*), that they may be made from a single tree, such as the *vikaṅkata*—namely: "Of those [ladles], whichever have not been specified as to their wood, they are of *vikaṅkata*. [This concludes] Chapter 150, together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

In this case, even though the word "or" (*vā*) is absent, an option (*vikalpa*) is to be understood, because it is impossible to combine two scriptural injunctions that prescribe contradictory qualities into a single instance. By this Sūtra, [the author] has explained by implication—without explicitly showing a non-contradictory example—that one does not adopt a second branch from another Śākhā which prescribes contradictory qualities.

Among those various vessels made of various trees mentioned in our own *śākhā*, those which are made of *vikaṅkata* wood, as well as those for which other trees are specified in other *śākhās* but which in our own *śākhā* are not specified [as being of any particular tree], these too are indeed of *vikaṅkata*. Regarding the two *agnihotra-havaṇī* spoons, just as in other *śākhās*, in our own *śākhā* as well, only *vikaṅkata* is prescribed; in that case, there is no option. However, for the others, the meaning is that there is an option regarding the use of the *vikaṅkata* tree.

In that regard, it will be stated later that for those items not intended for oblation, the *vāraṇa* wood is prescribed as a fixed rule. By process of elimination, there is an option between *vaikaṅkata* and *vāraṇa* only for those items intended for oblation;
however, for those not intended for oblation, they must be made of *vāraṇa*.

All [the implements] beginning with the *śamyā* are also included. This explains the two statements recited in another branch (*śākhā*) regarding the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*): "Therefore, the sacrificial implement (*yajñāvaicara*) should indeed be made of *vāraṇa* wood, but one should not offer oblations with it; rather, the sacrificial implement should indeed be made of *vikaṅkata* wood, for one offers with that. This is cited by the followers of Jaimini. "Sacrificial implement" (*yajñāvaicara*) refers to the sacrificial vessels (*yajñapātra*). The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, in the context of the fire-consecration, these vessels are subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the consecration itself by virtue of their status as sacrificial implements. Thus, there is an injunction regarding the vessels therein.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: because of the statement, "When they offer in the *āhavanīya* fire, by that he has sacrificed for him," and so forth, it is understood that these sacrifices (*iṣṭis*) are indeed consecrations (*saṃskāra*) of the fire. Since they are of the nature of consecrations, they are not [independent] sacrifices; therefore, the sentence is displaced from its context (*prakaraṇa*), and thus it is a rule (*vidhi*) not connected to any specific context (*anārabhyavidhi*). In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the Veda goes to the *agniṣṭoma*; this is the case in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Even there, one meaning of the sentence is: "Those [wooden spoons] which are for oblations are made of *vikaṅkata* wood."

The second [view], however, holds that those [spoons] which are not for the purpose of *āhuti* offerings belong to the *varaṇa*. Bharadvāja has stated exactly the same: "The ritualists teach the characteristics of the *sruks*: having divided the length into five parts or four, the penultimate [portion] among the two front [parts] is called the 'vessel' (*pātra*), because it serves as the receptacle for the oblation. The width in the penultimate section should be equal to its own length; it is described as being shaped like a hollowed palm (*añjali*), and the cavity (*bila*) therein is circular. (1–2)

The depth from both sides of the arm-length (six finger-breadths) and half of that (three finger-breadths) is prescribed; the measurement of the cavity for the hand-palm at the distance of one *aratni* is thus recorded. At the final part, the depth should be half the width; this is the determination.

The two paths at the end should be joined and not extended. Its opening should be like the beak of a swan or like the trunk of an elephant; the channel from the aperture should extend as far as is appropriate for the purpose. Two hollow ears are likewise said to be on the sides of the neck. At the base of the aperture there should be a lotus; now follows the description of the staff (daṇḍa). These two paths, being indistinguishable, are called the staff. At its root, the circumference should be nine finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and thick.

"Venerable sir, the handle (*daṇḍa*) should be five fingers wide, smooth, and round, produced by a lathe; thus the state of being like a crow’s tail for the *sruva* ladles has been proclaimed. (8) "The *sruk* ladles should be made according to what is aesthetically pleasing," so Baudhāyana said. However, whatever further distinction exists here should be understood from other scriptures. (9) According to the opinion of Baudhāyana and others, there may also be the measure of a span (*prādeśa*). The handle should consist of two parts, and the bowl (*pātra*) should likewise consist of two parts. (10)"

The neck [of the *sruk*] is one part above, according to the true measurement; the *sruva* together with the *sruk* should be made from the aforementioned trees, or alternatively, they may be made of *vikaṅkata*. All other vessels are made of *vāraṇa* wood. Māṣṭamba has also stated: "One should have the *sruks* made from one of these trees. This means that one should have the *sruks* made from any one of these trees—*khadira*, *palāśa*, *aśvattha*, or *vikaṅkata*.
Here, he employs the vessels for the morning milking.

Here too, "the two" and so forth are as before. In this regard, the distinction is that there are only six items: the *upaveṣa*, the *śākhāpavitram*, the *idhānī*, the *nidāne*, and the milking vessel (*dohana*), [excluding] the milk-pails (*sāyadohapātra*). This is because the *agnihotrahavaṇī* has already been employed for all purposes. However, there is no covering (*pidhāna*) at the morning pressing. At this time—prior to this—the procedure involving the carrying away (*sanayata*) has already been demonstrated in accordance with the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas.

In this regard, what is deficient should be supplemented by another branch; the preparation of the altar (*vedikaraṇa*) on the previous day will be mentioned later, following the maxim of the "lion's glance" at the time of preparing the altar. Similarly, here too, he explains two particulars established by implication:
"In this case, for one who does not maintain the *saṃnaya*, he prepares the two strainers (*pavitra*)."

Because there is no milking in the evening, he performs this at a time when it would otherwise not have been done for that purpose; this is the meaning. This *saṃnayana* (the mixing of curds and milk) takes place on the new moon day for one performing the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña*, and also on the full moon day. For even regarding the new moon, the text will state: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña*; he should perform the *saṃnayana* on the full moon day and sacrifice with the *āmikṣā* for Mitra and Varuṇa on the new moon day. Thus, on both lunar phases, [this applies]. [End of] Paṭala 410, accompanied by the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva.

The doubt as to how the Sūtrakāra could have shown the performance of the Darśa sacrifice alone, bypassing the Paurṇamāsī—despite the two performances being accompanied by the *sāṃnāyya*—is also dispelled. For these two specific features, prompted by particular lunar days (*parvan*), are stated in such passages as "having performed this, he fasts" (*etatkṛtvopavasati*). Although the meaning that for one who performs the *saṃnayana*, the two strainers (*pavitra*) are already prepared beforehand is not explicitly established, it is understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*) that even the two strainers made at the time of the evening milking serve all purposes.
Thus he says: "For one who performs the *saṃnayana*, they are kept [prepared] on the previous day;
for others, they are kept [prepared] on the day before. But if they are not kept, there is an expiation. This is the meaning.
With the words, "For Dakṣa thee," he takes up the cup for the carrying forward of the Praṇītā waters.

Because of the inclusion of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), the mantra for it is also silent (*tūṣṇīm*). Āpastamba has stated the same. If one asks, "Why is this so?"—it is because the substance of bell-metal is not for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*); therefore, it is not grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*). Consequently, the mantra, which is grasped by the context, does not require the bell-metal, nor does the bell-metal connect with that mantra, since it is not part of the context. And thus, in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there is no extension (*atideśa*) of that which is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
[The mantra is: "Thou art born of the forest; be purified for the gods; be cleansed for the gods; be made pure for the gods"—with these words, he washes it three times.

[The word] "with water" is understood by implication. Here, because distinct actions are observed for each [mantra], and since the act of washing is manifested by the action [of reciting the mantra], there is no authority to establish that the three mantras—"Thou art for the gods," "Be pure," and "Be purified"—form a single mantra, as there is no evidence indicating a combination of these three ritual acts. Furthermore, the purpose is accomplished through the distinctness of the performance, because the instruction "he washes three times" prescribes repetition.

Because the conceptualization of mantras is marred by eight defects, it is understood that the mantras themselves are merely auxiliary to the performance; thus, the Commentator [Śabara] maintains that all three washings are accompanied by mantras. Others do not accept this. Why? Because the triad beginning with "To the gods" is a restatement of the Brāhmaṇa passage from another recension (śākhā) by means of the particle *iti*, and not an application of mantras obtained through indicative power (*liṅga*), since their indicative power is not manifest.

Therefore, since it is taught that "one who possesses the Brāhmaṇas" is indeed [the one who acts], there is a combination [of mantras]; thus, they established the very position that the entire thing is a single mantra, which, having been recited, first performs the washing and then twice silently. [In cases where the author of the Sūtra intends a plurality of mantras, he indeed makes an effort for greater precision; for example, in the case of "śukraṃ tvā śukrāyām," he employs this word in the plural form.]

It is understood that every mantra is enjoined for the washing of the *sara* by means of the *Vaikhānasa* [Brāhmaṇa]; thus, it is known that the Brāhmaṇa alone is the enjoining authority. And so, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it prescribes two vessels for the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) for the sake of the person; this is connected with what was shown previously by the word "not" (*na*). [Note: The text fragments provided appear to be marginalia or variant readings from manuscripts (ka, kha, ga, ca, cha) regarding the specific wording of the sūtra. This concludes the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [First Praśna].
One desiring *brahmavarcasa* (spiritual luster) should have the water carried forth in a bronze vessel (*kāṃsya*), and one desiring food (*annādya*) in an earthen vessel.

A sacrificer who desires for himself *brahmavarcasa*—that splendor consisting of the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas and their practical application—and *varcas*, which is beauty, should have the Adhvaryu priest carry forth the water in a bronze vessel (*kāṃsya*). For one desiring *annādya*—the state of being an eater of excellent food (*annāda*)—the Adhvaryu should carry forth the water in an earthen vessel, as previously described. In another recensional tradition (*śākhāntara*), it is stated within the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices that "one should carry forth the water with a *camasa* (wooden cup)."

That statement makes known the subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*) of the cup (*camasa*) with respect to the act of carrying forward (*praṇayana*). By means of the accusative case in the word "water" (*apaḥ*), it is understood that the water is the object to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*), according to the sense: "One should consecrate the water by means of the carrying forward. And the application (*viniyoga*) of the consecrated water is stated as: "One mixes the sacrificial oblations (*haviṣ*) with the *praṇītā* waters. Having cited this in the Nyāya-darśana, it was established that [the act] has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) alone. Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras also stated: "Taking the *praṇītā* waters, one pours them over the flour."

When they are not employed for the purpose of mixing, then one should not provide a substitute. If no *praṇītā* waters are available, [the text says] that one should purify whatever waters there may be with a *yajus* formula and mix [the flour] with them; from this it is understood that the authors of the Sūtras do not disagree regarding the visible (practical) purpose [of the action]. Likewise, where *ājya* and *payas* are mentioned for the purpose of cooking a sacrificial cake (*caru*), he will state there that "one brings those two forth" (*te praṇayati*).

Therefore, in the sūtra "he causes [the fire] to blaze" (*jvālayati*), it is the meaning alone that is expressed, whereas the sentence "he mixes the sacrificial offerings with the *praṇītā* waters" has already been shown in the Nyāyaśāstra. Otherwise, what occasion would there be for the *praṇītā* waters in the case of a cooked rice offering (*caru*)? Therefore, the *praṇītā* waters are for the purpose of mixing the sacrificial offerings. Furthermore, their purposefulness is understood because the texts prescribe the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* waters even in rites such as the initiation (*upanayana*). And Bharadvāja says: "The *praṇītā* waters are present in all ritual forms."

And thus, if the act of carrying forward (praṇayana) has an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), then the status of that carrying forward—established through the context (prakaraṇa) of all sacrifices recited within the section on the New and Full Moon sacrifices—is proven to be an auxiliary to all of them. However, if it had only a visible purpose, it would be an auxiliary to the cake-offering (puroḍāśa) alone, and its status as an auxiliary to the Upāṃśuyāja and the Sāṃnāyya sacrifice, which is established by the context, would be sublated. Therefore, because of the author of the Sūtras' statement that "those two [sacrifices] share the same injunction," it has an invisible purpose; likewise, it is logical that it is an auxiliary to all sacrifices.

Likewise, in the *Praṇītā-brāhmaṇa*, the praise of the *praṇayana* (carrying forward of water) is observed to be for the sake of the fruit of the entire *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice; thus, it is appropriate that its purpose be transcendental (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Or rather, even though the water is employed for the visible purpose of the *praṇayana*, according to the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), one portion of it is for the purpose of mixing with the sacrificial oblation (*haviḥ-saṃyavana*) and thus has a visible purpose. Even so, there is no fault in the fact that another portion has a transcendental purpose on the strength of other scriptural injunctions.

Nor should it be said that because of the accusative case in the phrase "he brings water" (*apaḥ praṇayati*), there is a purificatory consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the water; for apart from the act of bringing, no other action can possibly exist for the sake of all sacrifices that would have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Nor should it be said that this is a consecration intended for the mixing of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*); as has already been stated, such a view would be contradicted by the context (*prakaraṇa*), which establishes that [the bringing] is for the sake of all sacrifices. Therefore, in the passage "he offers groats" (*saktūñ juhoti*), the accusative case must be explained differently.

Consequently, since the *praṇayana* (the carrying forward of the fire) is an auxiliary to both the *upāṃśuyāja* and the *sāṃnāyya* sacrifice, it follows that it must also be performed in their modifications (*vikṛti*), such as sacrifices consisting solely of clarified butter (*ājya*) or the *āmikṣā* offering, even for the sake of an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). If it is objected: "If the *praṇayana* were to occur in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), then the fixed order of sequence—namely, 'having prepared the *pavitra*, he gives the command, "O sacrificer, restrain your speech"; while restraining his speech, he touches the vessels; and having sprinkled them, he releases his speech"—would be contradicted," we reply: No.

This sūtra is not intended to establish a fixed order of sequence for the animal sacrifice (*paśu*); rather, it is for the purpose of prescribing the *pavitra* (strainer) which has not been previously established for the animal sacrifice, as well as for the purpose of prescribing the time for its removal. He will state that the animal sacrifice is a modification of the morning milk-offering (*prātahsavana*). And at the morning pressing, the *pavitra* prepared during the evening milking is taken up.

Since that [specific action] is impossible in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), when it is inquired whether [the *pavitra*] should be performed, it is shown that once the function of the *pavitra*—which has been brought forward by the rule of extension (*codaka*)—is present, it must be performed at that very time. Although one might have said, "Having prepared the *pavitra*, while the Brahman priest remains in his own place, he issues the command: 'O Brahman, I shall lead forth the waters; O sacrificer, restrain your speech,'" the text instead says, "He issues the command: 'O Brahman... just as the ritual action obtained through the rule of extension was stated with the words "For your work" (*karmaṇe vām*) and so on; thus, because it is already established, the statement beginning with "O Brahman" occurs at the appropriate time.

Therefore, it is stated that the purification itself has not been attained. Since the injunction "he restrains his speech until the *haviṣkṛt* [call]" is found in the *Yājamāna* section, and the injunction "he releases his speech at the *haviṣkṛt*" is found in the *Ādhvaryava* section, the rule for restraining speech also ceases to apply in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), because the time for releasing speech is impossible there. Why? Because the completion of the restriction is impossible; the restriction of speech would have to persist until the conclusion of the ritual action, and that is not desired.

Therefore, as long as there is the possibility of the ritual action being governed by the previously established rule up until the invocation of the *havīṣkṛt* in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), it is logical that the rule applies and then follows its release; however, it is not correct to say that there is an absence of the rule due to the absence of the time for its release mentioned in the archetype (*prakṛti*). By the passage beginning with "O sacrificer, [restrain] your speech," the rule and its subsequent release are demonstrated for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). His [officiating] priest (*adhvaryu*)...

In both cases, one restrains speech until the call for the *haviskṛt* (the preparer of the oblation), after which one releases it; thus, even though the actual release [of speech] is impossible [for the Adhvaryu], the possibility of the time of release is established just as it is for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). This shows that the procedure of the Adhvaryu is directly demonstrated, just like that of the sacrificer. How so? By stating, "Having made the two strainers (*pavitra*), he gives the command; having touched [the vessels], and once they have been sprinkled, he releases [speech]," the action of the Adhvaryu alone is shown. By saying, "The sacrificer should restrain his speech," the time for the command is indicated for the sacrificer by implication.

If the injunction "while carrying forward [the fire], he restrains his speech" were not accepted as being obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of extension), then what occasion would there be for prescribing the time of its release? Nor should it be argued that the prescription of the time for release follows from the force of the restatement "he restrains his speech over the vessels," because since the injunction "he restrains his speech" is absent here and there is no extended application (*atideśa*), how could such a thing be obtained? Therefore, the phrase "while carrying forward, he restrains his speech" is indeed obtained through the *codaka*.

Demonstrating, by means of the previously stated reasoning, that the object pervaded by this restrictive rule (*niyama*) is the very time of the *visarga* (the pouring out), it is established that the statement "having made the *pavitra*" and so forth is merely an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the permission to carry forward the water (*praṇayana-anujñā*), and not for the purpose of excluding (*parisaṃkhyā*) the carrying forward of water. Nor should it be argued that when there is an animal sacrifice, since the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* water has already occurred, it would be improper to place the vessel for the *praṇītā* water at the time of the animal-cake offering (*paśu-puroḍāśa*).

In the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the carrying forward of the fire (*praṇayana*) serves only an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Therefore, it cannot provide assistance to the cake-offering (*puroḍāśa*) through a visible medium by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*). Consequently, for the sake of the cake-offering, a separate act of carrying forward the fire must be performed, which has its own distinct visible purpose; for even if there were assistance through an invisible medium by way of incidental application, the visible purpose would not be accomplished through that incidental application.

Nor should it be argued that because water assists through an unseen means (adṛṣṭa) by way of incidental application (prasaṅga), it must also assist through a seen means (dṛṣṭa) in part by way of incidental application; for it is logical that while the act of carrying forward (praṇayana) assists incidentally through an unseen means, the status of other ritual acts as means [for the water]—which are themselves enjoined as means—is not established merely by incidental application.

Just as, even when there is an application [of the water], the grains mixed with the portions cut for the animal sacrifice do not—because they are intended for that specific purpose—attain the status of being for the sake of the *puroḍāśa* or the *iḍā* by way of incidental benefit (*prasaṅga*), so too, when something is a benefactor through one type of assistance, it cannot be considered a benefactor through another form of assistance by way of incidental benefit; thus, a separate act of carrying forward (*praṇayana*) is indeed enjoined. Furthermore, the prescription of the *praṇītā* waters in the case of the established animal sacrifice by Kātyāyana, Āpastamba, and others serves to prohibit the carrying forward [of those waters] for the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice according to their own other scriptural tradition.

According to his view, even though the prohibition has become established regarding its modification, the injunction for bringing [the fires] forward (*praṇayana*) is prescribed again for the purpose of reviving that which was prohibited. In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: on the spot strewn with Darbha grass, there is the covering of the vessel-mouth with a lid (*maṇḍapa*). Since it is defined that "the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) is to be approached from the north," the bringing forward is indeed by the northern path. However, some ritualists perform it by the southern path; the basis for this should be investigated. They do not move them until the conclusion of the rite.
And he does not move them; they remain excellent until the point near the *saṃsthāna* and *asaṃsthāna*, from which the excellent liberation (*praṇītāvimokā*) is performed—meaning, prior to that.
With the words, "May the divine clans enter; the vessels for the sacrifice to the gods," he touches the vessels with his hand holding the strainer (*sapavitra*). || 14 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra. || 4 ||

[The actions beginning with] "smayādīni": Having fixed the *pavitra* (strainer) with the thumb on the palm of the hand, either facing east or north, he touches [the vessels] with that hand. Just as in the world one touches [an object] properly for the sake of fondling a child and so forth, so he touches the vessels with his hand. Since the substance is one, the mantra is recited once for the touching of all of them. The summary (*saṃgraha*): In one's own *śākhā*, there is no preparation of the altar (*vedi*) on the previous day for the *darśa* sacrifice; likewise, on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), there is no spreading of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) according to another *śākhā*.

On the previous day, however, there is a fixed rule for one’s own Vedic branch regarding the immediate performance; the spreading of *darbha* grass; the use of vessels for subsidiary rites and oblations; the use of *vaikaṅkata* wood in one alternative; the dual nature of the *praṇītā* waters; that in optional rites there is no mantra, whereas in obligatory rites there is the inclusion of the *manas* mantra. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Sūtras* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin, composed by Mahādeva.

1.5 Now begins the fifth chapter. With the formula, "For dexterity, thou art made of wood," he takes up the *agnihotrahavaṇī* (ladle); with "For impulsion, thee," the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*). The mantra for the *agnihotrahavaṇī* is used only at the time of taking it up for the purpose of pouring out the grain (*nirvāpa*), not for the purpose of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) during the animal sacrifice (*paśu*). The word "takes up" (*ādatte*) is connected to both [the ladle and the basket]. Because it can be grasped, it is taken with the right hand alone. There is no relinquishing of the two until the grain has been poured out. [End of] Chapter One. Accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.
He heats [the grains] on either the Āhavanīya or the Gārhapatya fire with the mantra beginning "pratyuṣṭam" (burnt away).
The end of the mantra is "arātayaḥ" (enemies). The meaning is already explained.
He addresses the sacrificer, saying, "O Sacrificer, I shall pour out the oblation."
He asks the sacrificer for permission while the sacrificer is away on a journey.

One should recite: "O Agni, I shall pour out the oblation. This is for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), as it has been stated that there is no recipient of the response. It might be argued that its status as having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) can be maintained by considering it a refinement of the self (*ātmasaṃskāra*). [The sacrificer] says "Om" and pours out the oblation. Here, there is no lapse in the rule regarding speech (*vāniyama*), because of the force of the injunction. It was previously defined that when the *praṇava* is uttered, one performs the action. Regarding the oblation, whether it be rice or barley—according to the scripture, "one should sacrifice with rice" or "one should sacrifice with barley"—there is no conjunction (*samuccaya*) even in the absence of the word "or" (*vā*), because the understanding is that they are independent means, and conjunction is not established where there is mutual independence.

Since it would not be an offering with rice (*vrīhi*) nor with barley (*yava*) if they were considered distinct substances, an option (*vikalpa*)—though flawed by the eight defects—is appropriate out of fear of subverting two injunctions. Even in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there is no modification (*ūha*) even when the oblation is of a different kind, because all [the grains] possess the status of being an oblation (*haviṣṭva*).
One proceeds [with the mantra] "I follow the wide mid-region" (*urv antarikṣam anvemi*);
one proceeds facing toward where the cart containing the oblation stands.

To the west of the Āhavanīya fire, or to the west of the Gārhapatya fire, there stands a cart with its yoke fastened and its side-boards attached, filled with rice or barley, with its pole pointing either eastward or northward.

The word "exists" (*bhavati*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding the option that it may be to the west of the Gārhapatya, the author will later state, "The oblations are cooked on the Āhavanīya or on the Gārhapatya"; according to that, the choice is determined as "or on the Gārhapatya. Why? Because, even though the word "west" (*apara*) is already present in the phrase "to the west of the Āhavanīya," the word "or" (*vā*) is used again in the phrase "or to the west [of the Gārhapatya]."

"Yoked" (*naddha*) means that whose yoke (*yuga*) is so; "with its yoke bound by means of the two poles" (*īṣābhyām bandhanaprakāreṇa baddhaṃ yugaṃ yasya*). "With its side-boards" (*sapariṇatkaṃ*): it is provided with side-boards (*pariṇaddha*), such as mats or the like, which are bound all around the cart for the purpose of stability; thus it is "with its side-boards. Since the word denotes the genus (*jāti*) and not a specific refinement (*saṃskāra*), the worldly usage is accepted as established. The syntactical connection is: "it stands positioned behind [the other]."

The option "with rice or with barley" is established by the scriptural injunction: "Having sacrificed with rice, one should sacrifice again with rice; having sacrificed with the *āgrayaṇa* [grains], one should sacrifice again with barley. For one who has not yet commenced the *āgrayaṇa*, there is an optional choice between the two. The term *vrīhimat* means "that cart (*śakaṭa*) in which rice (*vrīhi*) exists. According to the rule *mānupadhāyāśca* (Pāṇini 8.2.9), the *makāra* is not changed to *vakāra*; this is because of the restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyāna*) of the *yavādi* group in the rule *yavādibhyaḥ*. That whose poles (*īṣā*) are directed eastward is thus described; likewise for "having northward poles" (*udagīṣam*).

*Īṣe* refers to the specially fashioned wooden yoke-pins that connect the two poles of the cart. Regarding the mantra *dhūr asi*, having touched its southern pole—this is an injunction because it is not previously established—the place where the ox is bound is the location of the yoke. *Ālambha* means touching. *Pūrvām* is the end of the mantra. *Satyāṣāḍhaviracitaṃ Śrautasūtram* (The Śrauta Sūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha), First Book, Chapter 120.1. (Note: The textual variants provided in the footnotes regarding the specific readings of the manuscript traditions are noted here for philological accuracy.)

Having touched the left [wheel] with the mantra "tvaṃ devānām," he mutters it. He does not touch it; rather, he mutters the mantra immediately after touching it. "devahūtamam" is the end of the mantra. Having muttered "svaryam," he places his right foot upon the left wheel with the mantra "viṣṇustvā'kraṃsta."

He causes [the sacrificer] to mount the cart because it has been seen as something noble; having merely touched it with his foot, he should not withdraw his foot. He mounts it with the formula: "Thou art unswerving, the vessel of the oblation; stand firm! Do not waver! May the lord of the sacrifice not waver! May Viṣṇu step upon thee! Wide space for the wind! Struck away is the Rakṣas! Let the five [fingers] restrain [thee]. He mounts.
He mounts the cart with his left foot. He does not let go of the edge of the garment.
With the mantra "Of Mitra thee," he looks at the yoke-tie.
With "May I not harm thee," he concludes.
With the verse, "Wide open for the wind," he covers the door with the enclosing-stalk mat (*pariṇaha*).
When the sacrificial oblation has been placed upon it, he uncovers the opening of that enclosing-stalk mat. The mantra is the same [as before].
With the formula, "Thee for Mitra," he gazes at the sacrificial cakes and the enclosing-stalk mat.

[He offers] the sacrificial cakes made of *puroḍāśa* grains; there is a separate mantra for each because the substances are distinct. The singular number in the mantra is intended to refer to the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) in general. The end of the mantra is as before. He touches the *puroḍāśa*-grains with the words, "Bestow strength. The mantra is in the singular because it intends to refer to the *puroḍāśa* as a means [of sacrifice] in general; thus it is explained everywhere.
With the words, "Place milk in me," he touches himself.

Having contemplated his own self as residing in the region of the heart through the realization of its inwardness—thinking "I am"—he touches the region of the heart. This is followed by the traditional ritual touching of water.
Then, with the words, "The Rakṣas is struck down," he throws away a blade of grass or a clod of earth and touches water.

The mantra for the removal [of the ashes] is as follows. The ritual touching (*upasparśana*) is prescribed by the Śruti. In their absence, however, Kātyāyana states: "If they are not present, one should touch [the body] with this mantra. This is because of the Śruti text: "One should touch it with that which is called *nāman*. Having explained the *Daśahotṛ*, one should recite it word by word; since it is of the nature of a muttered prayer (*japa*), it is performed with the *yātuḥsvarya* intonation. The portion beginning with "The mind is the clarified butter" (*cittam ājyam*) and ending with "the Adhvaryu" constitutes the *Daśahotṛ*. It should be understood that the name *Daśahotṛ*—that is, the mantra designated as such—is the basis for its application in the duties of the Hotṛ priest. [End of Paṭala 15, Section Kha-ga-ca-damabada, from the Vaijayantī commentary by Mahādeva. 121.
Having placed the two strainers in the winnowing basket,
silently filling it with a handful [of grain] while reciting, "May the five [fingers] yield for your protection, not for hostility," and having taken a full handful of sacrificial cake material,
he pours it into the offering ladle.

According to the statement of Vaikhānasa, "Having taken [the grain] with the left hand, or having placed the *śūrpa* on the *āhavanīya* fire," one pours a handful into that *agnihotra-havaṇī*, and after emptying it, the handful already grasped is poured silently; for the injunction regarding the filling applies only to what is written in proximity to the mantra.
Then, with the mantra "devasya tvā," while the two strainers (*pavitra*) are held between, he pours out four handfuls: three times with the Yajus formula and the fourth time silently.

When the strainer has been placed inside the winnowing basket, one pours out the offering with the formula "I pour out what is pleasing to Agni," ending at that very point where the strainers are located, taking only a handful. For that [offering], there is no pouring in of four [handfuls]; indeed, the pouring in of four is prescribed for other [offerings]. However, in this case, the pouring in would serve no visible purpose; furthermore, according to the statement of Āpastamba, "One pours out four handfuls using the *agnihotra-havaṇī*," it is possible to pour out all four at once, as it is impossible to hold them in the ladle (*sruc*) simultaneously.

Although the number "four" refers to the substance, nevertheless, because the injunction "three times with the Yajus formula, and the fourth time silently" prescribes only the repetition of the action, one cannot argue that there is a single offering of a quantity measured by four handfuls, followed by a repetition of such offerings three times with the Yajus and once silently. This is because no distributive repetition (vīpsā) such as "four [handfuls] each time" is heard; rather, by the word "four," it is understood that the entire offering consists of exactly four handfuls.

Regarding the term "handfuls" (*muṣṭīn*): because they are intended as the object of the action by way of being "handfuls," and because there is a distinctness of substance for each handful, it is understood that one offers them by repetition. Thus, although a single ritual act consists of four handfuls, the clarified butter (*ājya*) taken with the *juhu* ladle and consecrated by the mantra becomes unconsecrated again when it is taken up once more.

Just as, even though the substance is one, the mantra is repeated because the individual part is delimited by the measure of a handful, so too here, even though the object is one, the mantra for the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) is repeated in each of the four handfuls according to the principle that "it is repeated when there is a distinction between intermediate substances despite the non-separation [of the whole]. Furthermore, the filling of the handful and the placing [into the vessel] are subsidiaries of the pouring out for a visible purpose; yet, since these are joined and terminate with a single unit, the filling, the placing, and the pouring out of one handful are likewise performed in that same manner for each.

For others as well, the mantra likewise extends over each individual handful. Thus, the meaning is this: with the mantra "devasya tvā," one pours out four handfuls of grain placed in the *sruc* ladle, one by one. The insertion (*āvāpa*), however, is established by the force of the context; since the mantra is repeated for each individual handful, the filling [of the vessel] occurs in the same manner due to the distinctness of the substances.

Thus, since by means of this specific injunction the rule "while restraining [the breath]" and so forth would generally apply to all four mantras, the Brāhmaṇa text presents an exception, beginning with "thrice," and so on. The purpose of the prescription "silently" (tūṣṇīm) is to preclude the application of the rule "thrice with a Yajus formula" (trir yajuṣā). By using the word "Yajus" to refer to the two Yajus formulas—namely "yacchantām" and "devasya tvā"—the singular number inherent in that reference is not intended to be significant.

Alternatively, although the first *yajus* formula is not recited in our own *śākhā*, nor is the corresponding *brāhmaṇa* passage, nevertheless, because the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) pertains to the sacrifice with all its auxiliary parts (*sāṅga*), every fourth handful that is poured out is prescribed to be done silently (*tūṣṇīm*). Consequently, there is also an omission of the formula "yacchantām" in the case of the fourth handful. Here, the phrase "having filled the handful" means having taken it up once it has been made full by the fist.

Therefore, the designation "with a handful" (*muṣṭinā*) should be understood as applying specifically to the Adhvaryu priest. If it were taken to mean "measured by a handful," then it would also apply to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*); in that case, the designation "belonging to the Adhvaryu" (*ādhvaryava*) would be contradicted. If you argue that it may be contradicted because of the specific instruction, we say no. For if [the term] "having approached" (*opya*) implies a common agent, it would become disconnected from the phrase "four handfuls.

Therefore, the "handful" (*muṣṭi*) is simply the grain grasped by the hand; the measurement by a full grasp is established by the sense of the matter, but there is no explicit injunction for it. That very thing is designated by the word "handful" through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). He pours [the grains] after having measured them out.

Why is it stated "having poured out" (*nirupya*)? [Is it not] established by the mere recitation [of the text]? It is for the purpose of ensuring the continuity (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "three times with the *yajus*, the fourth time silently"; therefore, one pours out [the grain] while [the vessel] still contains what has been poured out. For the pouring out [of the oblation] is connected only to the phrase "he pours out with the *āgnihotra-havaṇī*," and since that [connection] has ceased [to apply], the subsequent pouring (*anvāvāpa*) is performed with that [same vessel].

And thus, even at the conclusion of each individual handful being poured out, it is established that "the portions [of the grain] remaining in the vessel are not auxiliary parts," because of the connection in the text: "Having cut with three *yajus*-verses, he pours out the fourth and pours after. Otherwise, if one were to look only at the sequence, it would not be known whether the pouring out consists of merely a handful or the whole; this is the purpose. This has been clearly stated by Āpastamba: "Having poured out four handfuls, he pours after them once they have been poured out."

And thus, having set aside one handful for each individual deity, it is stated that one should not do so a second time for each. For the act of offering (*nirvāpa*) consists of four handfuls; these handfuls are merely its constituent parts. By this, the meaning is that, in order to avoid subverting the *padārthānusamaya* (sequential performance by item), the *kāṇḍānusamaya* (sequential performance by section) is adopted, such that "one [handful] for each" refers to the whole. Since it is established by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "those two are governed by the same injunction," he states that this same ritual procedure applies to others as well:
"By this very method, he offers the subsequent sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) according to the respective deity."

This is not an extended application (*atideśa*); rather, the meaning is that by this very method and procedure, beginning with "they should give," and so forth. The answer is: if there is the mention of the *puroḍāśa*, let there be no pouring out of clarified butter (*ājya*) for the deity of the *upāṃśuyāja*. For it is recited as "I pour out what is pleasing to Agni" and "to Agni and Soma," but not for the deity of the *upāṃśu* [sacrifice]; this is the sense. In the case of the *āgnīṣomīya* [pakṣa] on the full moon day, having recited "Of the god thee," etc., the pouring out occurs only when it has been poured out with the words "I pour out what is pleasing to Agni and Soma."

Immediately after the mantra addressed to Agni, the mantra from another recension (śākhā), "I offer what is pleasing to Indra and Agni," should be seen as supplied in the Brāhmaṇa. The fourth [offering] is performed silently. By the statement, "He wins an unlimited amount; he offers the oblations in this very sequence," the triad of sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) is understood from the plural number. This purpose is not accomplished by modification (ūha), because modification is prohibited on the grounds that "there is no modification in the archetype" (prakṛti). The Brāhmaṇa passage refers to the two [full-moon and new-moon] parvans. The same should be understood regarding other mantras as well. Without a cart, he states another ritual procedure (kalpa) from another recension:
Or he pours [the grain] into a vessel, having dragged the wooden sword (sphya) to the south and having recited all the cart-formulas.

Since it is stated that one mutters all the cart-formulas over that earthen vessel which has been placed in the position of the cart—and not in the position of the winnowing basket—there is no application of the cart-formulas when [the vessel] is placed in the position of the winnowing basket. This substitution based on explicit scriptural statement occurs in the *Manana-ṭīkā* manuscripts, where "mutters" (*japati*) is used in place of "recites" (*uktvā*).

[Section 1, Chapter 8, Part ḍa] Siddheḥ | [Variant readings: ka, kha, ga, ca, śa, ṭa, ṭha, ha: *ceti*] [End of Paṭala 9, Section 150]. Together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva: 123. Because it is not accepted that the *paśu* (animal victim) is the agent of the performance of its own *yajus* (sacrificial formula). In the statement "He pours out [the oblation] upon that vessel," the vessel serves as the substratum (*ādhāra*) because it is the substratum for the sacrificial material (*havis*) alone; however, the vessel does not become the substratum for the agent and the object, which are the locus of the action.

Alternatively, the locative case here denotes proximity; standing near the vessel (*pātrī*), he pours out the grain. As before, the muttering (*japa*) is performed over the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) itself, because—as in the case of the cart-mantras—it is impossible for them to function as *karaṇa*-mantras (instrumental mantras). The mantras beginning with "Of the god... (*devasya tvā...*) are used exactly as previously prescribed. Having drawn the wooden sword (*sphya*) beneath the southern part of the vessel and placed it there—according to the Vaikhānasa, "Having placed the *sphya* behind the Gārhapatya fire, [he places] the vessel upon it"—he returns to the subject at hand:
with the mantra "This belongs to the gods" (*idaṃ devānām*), he touches the poured-out grains; and with "This is ours together" (*idamu naḥ saha*), he touches that from which he has poured them out.

One should offer those from which the portion was taken, or whatever remains in the winnowing basket (*pātryā*). Because of the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "from whatever," there is no abandonment of the previous [grains]; thus, by means of the second mantra, one offers together both those already poured out and the remaining ones. Confirming this very point, he says: "For prosperity, thee!"—this refers specifically to those already poured out.
The end of the mantra is "not for misfortune. The particle "only" (*eva*), however, serves to exclude the remainder.
Saying, "I release myself from the noose of Varuṇa," he takes the sacrificial cakes and steps out from the enclosure (pariṇaha).

It should be understood that he does so with the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*). Having taken them silently, he stands near the enclosure with the mantra, or having gone forth from the vicinity of the vessel. Since there is no mantra in our own recension at this stage, the entire [mantra] is recited here because it belongs to another branch (*śākhāntarīyatvāt*): "May I behold the light of heaven. He gazes upon the entire sacrifice.

Having observed each individually—the fires distributed for the sacrifice, the oblation-offering persons (*puruṣas*), and the other vessels and implements that are the means of sacrifice—the meaning is "having distinguished them. The mantra "yajñam" is recited only once; thus, there is no separate treatment of the substances as distinct entities.

He gazes at the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra "vaiśvānaraṃ jyotiḥ. The meaning of the word "paretya" (having gone forth) is "standing right there," as seen in the injunction: "He should gaze at [the fire] in the southern half."
"May the difficult paths be firm," he says as he descends from the cart; this is the meaning. He mutters over the path [the mantra] ending with "of heaven and earth.
With "Svāhā to heaven and earth," he consecrates the spilled [grains]. With "Enter the wide atmosphere," he proceeds.

"Anvīhi" (Follow after) is the end of the mantra. He goes near that fire upon which he cooks the oblation. [Note: *na* is not present in manuscripts ka, kha, ga, ca; *yataḥ* is also not present. [Note: *kṣam* is not present in manuscript ka, kha, ga. He consecrates what has been spilled. With the words, "I set thee down in the lap of Aditi," he places it either to the west of the Āhavanīya fire or to the west of the Gārhapatya fire.
He places the oblation-spoon (*haviḥśūpa*) near one of the two fires. He states the settled rule:

"In whichever fire he cooks [the oblation], he places [the vessel] right near it"—this is the meaning. By this, it is stated that the previously mentioned option between the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires is optional according to one's preference; for it is precisely here that a fixed option is prescribed by the rule: "wherever the cooking takes place, there the placing [of the vessel] occurs. He hands it over to the respective deity with the formula: "O Agni, protect the offering."

For the sake of protecting each respective deity, he offers [the oblation] with the corresponding mantra. "O Agni, protect the offering"—this is for the [oblation] belonging to Agni; "O Agni and Soma, protect the offering"—and for the *darśa* sacrifice, "O Indra and Agni, protect the offering"—these two mantras from another recension (*śākhā*) are indicated by their characteristics.
Having prepared the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*) in the ladle (*sruk*) provided with a handle, as previously described.

It is not the state of having awns (*saśūkatva*) that is enjoined, but rather the removal of the awns (*śūkaprakṣālana*) that is prohibited. "Awns" (*śūkāḥ*) are the fine, filament-like parts adhering to substances such as rice (*vrīhi*) when they are placed in the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle. By this, it should be understood that only those grains which possess awns are true *vrīhi*; others, such as *śāli*, though resembling *vrīhi*, are distinct. Therefore, due to the similarity of possessing awns, in the absence of *vrīhi*, only *nīvāra* (wild rice) is substituted, and not *śāli*, because the latter lacks awns.

Barley (*yava*) is indeed possessed of awns (*saśūka*); that only those with awns possess the nature of rice (*vrīhitva*) has been stated even by those learned in logic (*nyāyavid*). Since there is the instruction, "having consecrated those which are *prokṣaṇī*s," it follows that the status of being *prokṣaṇī* exists even prior to the consecration (*saṃskāra*); therefore, the term is not merely a designation for the consecrated substance. Consequently, in such cases as "bring the *prokṣaṇī*s" and likewise "the clarified butter (*ājya*) is for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*)," the status of being *prokṣaṇī* is established even without the consecration.
He addresses [the Brahman] with the formula, "O Brahman, I shall sprinkle. The meaning is already explained.

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni—for such-and-such [deity], for such-and-such"—thus he sprinkles three times according to the respective deities. This is done by a single ritual procedure (*tantra*) because there is no division [of the act]. The end of the mantra is "to Agni and Soma," as it is recited in the text. There is no *anuṣaṅga* (supplying of a word from a previous sentence) such as "I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni and Soma," because *anuṣaṅga* applies to different sentences, whereas in this case the sprinkling is performed by a single ritual procedure; thus there is no employment of a separate sentence. This has been clearly stated in another ritual manual (*kalpa*).

Just as [in the case of the *darśa* sacrifice] one sprinkles [the oblation] saying, "I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni," and "to Agni-Soma, to such-and-such, to such-and-such," so too in the *darśa*, another mantra—namely, "I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni" and "to Indra-Agni"—is to be understood as before. [End of Paṭala 550. [Included here is: Accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

One should not sprinkle over the fire. Sprinkling should not be performed directly over the fire; rather, while sprinkling the sacrificial offering (*havis*), it should be done in such a way that drops do not fall into the fire. Otherwise, due to the damage caused, there would be a need for an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). This is the meaning.
He sprinkles the vessels as previously described.
Having turned them face upwards, he sprinkles them three times with the mantra "śundhadhvam" (be purified), meaning that it is to be done exactly as stated before.
He takes up the black antelope skin with the mantra "vātasya dhrājirasi" (you are the speed of the wind) or with "devasya tvā" (of the god).

The second [mantra] ends with "ādada. The black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina) has been placed down. With the mantra "avadhūtaṃ rakṣaḥ," he shakes it three times over the rubbish-heap (utkara), turning its neck upward and shaking it outwardly.

The section ends with *arātayaḥ*. Having made the place where the flesh is cut—the spot where meat adheres—the "place of slaughter" (*viśasana*); that which is slaughtered, separated from the flesh, and cut—that is the meaning. The suffix is applied according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. The sense is that this portion should not be assigned to oneself. Having repeatedly pulled it out, he shakes it; that is, he causes it to tremble or winnows it. Regarding the rubbish heap (*utkara*) where it will be placed, although it will be explained later, it will also be reminded of here and there.
With the formula *adityās tvag asi*, he spreads [the hide] behind the rubbish heap, with the neck facing west and the hair facing north.
On the western side of the *utkara*, he strews [the grass] with its tips pointing westward and its hairs facing upward—meaning he spreads it out.
He then places the buttocks [of the skin] facing westward in front, with the words: "May the earth recognize you."

The phrase "in front of the skin at the region of the buttocks" (*bhasadaṃ gudapradeśe tvacaḥ purastāt*) is merely an imitation of the *Brāhmaṇa* text, since its meaning is already conveyed by the word "buttocks" (*bhasadam*). One should join that buttock [skin] downward from below; that is, one should effect a joining of the flesh with a portion of flesh. Furthermore, it is not appropriate to connect [the words] as "the buttock in front, above, and facing westward. If that were the case, the expression "one joins" (*upasamasyati*) would be untenable; otherwise, he would simply have said, "one should double it," had the joining been intended for the fleshy part itself.

Regarding the Brāhmaṇa passage, "The earth has received you," he says this for the sake of stability (*pratiṣṭhiti*). Stability must be established by means of this [formula]. How could it remain stable when being leveled on top? It would be unstable; therefore, the previous explanation alone is correct. With the formula, "Thou art the pressing-surface," he places the mortar upon the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) without letting go of it. He causes the mortar to be placed upon the black antelope skin so that it rests directly on it; thus he "turns" or "places" it. "Let the skin know" is the end of the mantra.

With the formula, "Thou art the body of Agni," he pours the oblation into the mortar without releasing his grip on it; he does so three times with a sacrificial verse (*ṛc*) and a fourth time silently.

The word "I take" marks the end [of the formula]. "Without releasing the mortar" is understood from the context. He pours the oblation—that is, he deposits it—into the cavity. With the hand holding the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), three times, etc., is clear. *Note: This is from the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha.*

The word "of Agni" (*agner*) does not denote a deity; rather, it refers either to the fire under discussion (*prakṛta-agni*) or to the *āhavanīya* fire. This is because, in the Brāhmaṇa, it is praised as the nourisher of Agni: "Plants are indeed this body of Agni. Furthermore, [the text says]: "I take thee for the gods" (*devavītaye tvā gṛhṇāmi*), and "he thus perfects this very remnant with the deities. Since this establishes that [the substance] is for the sake of the deities, one need not assume another mantra such as "Thou art the body of Agni and Soma. For this very reason, the phrase "according to the deity" (*yathādevatam*) was not stated. [He takes up the pestle: "Thou art the stone, belonging to the trees" (*adri-rasi vānaspatya*). || 16 || [Thus he] takes up the pestle.

The end of the mantra is "muśami śamiṣva. He states another mantra from a different recensional branch: "ūrdhvasūrasi vanaspate" (O tree, you are one whose fruit is upward-turned), or "avarakṣo divaḥ sapatnaṃ badhyāsam" (May I bind down the Rakṣas, the rival from heaven); he threshes [the grain] three times with either of these, or with "apahatā yātudhānā apahato'ghaśaṃsaḥ" (Struck away are the sorcerers; struck away is the evil-planner).

The mantra is recited once; the threshing is three times. Now, if it is argued that since the threshing is enjoined according to its purpose, the triple repetition is improper, and therefore this must be an injunction for the threefold recitation of the mantra—this is true. Nevertheless, it is for the sake of indicating the time for the *preṣa* (direction), namely, "O preparer of the oblation, come! and for the sake of establishing the connection: "Having threshed three times, he then calls the preparer of the oblation. Thus, it is so that the calling of the preparer of the oblation does not occur immediately after threshing only once. He calls the preparer of the oblation while threshing three times with the words, "O preparer of the oblation, come!"

The connection is as follows: "Having threshed three times, he threshes again above [the grain], and thus he causes the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation) to separate the husks. The singular number in the term *haviṣkṛtam* is used because it refers to the office (*upādhi*) of preparing the oblation, though the individuals performing it are many. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "He calls those who are the *haviṣkṛts* of the gods. Baudhāyana, however, explains this as follows: "In the call 'O *haviṣkṛt*, come!', it is Parjanya himself [who is addressed]."

It has been stated; furthermore, they cite this as an example: "This [formula] refers specifically to the preparer of the oblation (*havis-saṃskārin*). Even though Parjanya is reached through his being the preparer of the divine oblation (*deva-havis*), that invocation would serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) if a visible purpose were possible; therefore, it is improper [to assume an invisible purpose]. Furthermore, they cite this: the ritualists (*yājñika*) say thus: the word of direction (*praiṣa-vacana*), "Hearken! (*ehi*), is addressed precisely to him who is the preparer of the oblation in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Why? Because this statement, by means of the comparison with Parjanya, has expressed the meaning that it refers specifically to the preparation itself.

And so it is in the present case. Following the injunction "triṣphalīkartavai" (you must husk three times), after the command, the wife is the agent for the threshing, another person or a female slave for the husking, and the Āgnīdhra priest for the threshing; he addresses them with a singular form. "Avaghnat" means performing the act of threshing, or "anavaghnat" means not performing it.

Having summoned [the *haviṣkṛt*] even before the threshing, one should subsequently say "Drive away the Rakṣas" once; there is no separate ritual act for the threshing itself until the appearance of the rice grains. This has been stated by Bharadvāja: "Taking up the pestle, he summons the *haviṣkṛt*, saying, 'O *haviṣkṛt*, come! Then they say, 'Strike! Drive away the Rakṣas from heaven! while they thresh. Since the invocation was stated to occur even before the threshing, in this alternative view there is no "three times" [repetition]; rather, one merely threshes with the mantra, "The Rakṣas from below, from heaven... This much alone suffices. Alternatively, the explanation is that there is a pause (*viramya*). Because the threshing was introduced with the statement, "Or, without threshing, he invokes the preparer of the oblation," the injunction here is for a pause in the middle of the threshing. The construction is: "Having threshed three times, without threshing—that is, not performing the act of threshing—he extends [the mantra] three times.
For a Kṣatriya, [he says] "Come hither! (*ādrava*); for a Vaiśya, "Come hither! (*āgahi*).

For two sacrificers distinguished by caste, the two [mantras] belonging to other recensions (*śākhā*) are optional alternatives; however, for those of the three [higher] castes as well as for the *rathakāra* and the *niṣāda*, the one belonging to their own recension mentioned previously is mandatory. This is because the specific rule "for a Brāhmaṇa" is not stated in either the Sūtra or the Brāhmaṇa. Āpastamba also says: "Or rather, [the first mantra] is for all. Since it will be stated later that for the *niṣāda* and the *rathakāra* as well, the *ādhāna*, *agnihotra*, and *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are restricted [to their own recension], [the procedure is as follows]:
when the rice grains have appeared, he issues the command: "Recite loudly! (*uccaiḥ samājahīti*).

Regarding the statement "one should strike loudly," which is mentioned in the Brāhmaṇa, it should be understood that this applies everywhere to those [actions] mentioned in the Brāhmaṇa that lack a specific application, so that there may be no pointlessness of what has been studied as an alternative.
The Āgnīdhra priest takes up a stone with the mantra, "Thou art a mountain, a maker of verses.

Although the stone is already placed there by the word *kuṭaru*, the explicit mention of "the stone" (*aśmānam*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the mantra does not apply to the *śamyā* (wooden pin), even though the *śamyā* might be obtained from another scriptural source through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of "thou art a mountain" (*adri*), which refers to the stone as a constituent part.
"Thou art the *kuṭaru*, honey-tongued," or "Thou art the cock, honey-tongued"—
this is an alternative to the former [formula], because here too there is a clear indicative mark [in the word *kukkuṭa*].
With the formula, "Bring hither food, bring hither vigor," he strikes the two millstones together.

The mantra ending with "jeṣma" is indeed one and the same, according to the *Uttarādi* [text]. Likewise, Bodhāyana has also recited it as a single mantra. It has already been stated that where a plurality of mantras is intended, a separate effort is certainly made. Furthermore, because of the use of the accusative case in the expressions "dṛṣadupale" (the mortar and pestle) and "dṛṣadau samāhanti" (he strikes the two grinding stones), this constitutes a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the mortar and pestle. This was stated by Bharadvāja: "In the absence of a substance, there is the cessation of the ritual; however, in the case of the *caru*, there is the striking, the sprinkling of water, and the pouring out."

If it is argued that the mention of "by him" (*tena*) is for the sake of the meaning [of the action], it is replied: [The mention] is so that the grasping of the *kuṭaru* (wooden mallet) may not be for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), and so that there may not be a mutual striking of the *dṛṣad* (lower millstone) and *upala* (upper millstone). For in the Brāhmaṇa, the destruction of rivals is said to result from the production of sound by the vessels themselves striking one another. Thus, since no other means is heard of among the vessels—other than the *dṛṣad* and *upala* striking each other—the phrase "by him" is intended to mean that this is according to another Vedic branch (*śākhāntara*).

Thus, since it would have been established by the statement "twice on the stone, once on the muller" alone, the use of the accusative case in the separate words *pṛthak* (separately), *upa* (muller), and *upale* (on the muller) indicates that the consecration (*saṃskāra*) applies to those two alone; this is what has been stated. Furthermore, the Brāhmaṇa passage has been explained as being merely laudatory (*stāvaka*) of those two, on the strength of the direct hearing of the accusative case. The phrase "twice on the stone, once on the muller" follows from the verb *samāhanti* (he strikes). Although one could have simply said "twice on the stone, once on the muller," the use of the locative case (*saptamī*) is for the sake of what follows. [From the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, First Book]
Moving [the pestle] three times, he completes [the action] nine times.

By the mention of the locative case in "on the grinding stones" (*dṛṣad-upalayoḥ*), it is indicated that no other action need be supplied here; rather, the meaning of the sentence ends with "he strikes together" (*samāhanti*). Thus, "striking together once on the lower stone (*dṛṣad*) and once on the upper stone (*upalā*)," he completes this by repeating it nine times. He completes it nine times by moving [the pestle] through repetition, performing only the act of "striking together."

"Moving it about" means that the movement is performed by shifting from one location to another, ending either toward the east or toward the north. In this regard, on the lower grinding stone (*dṛṣad*), the first [stroke] is with the mantra and the second is silently because of its unity; on the upper grinding stone (*upalā*), it is done once with the mantra alone because of the distinctness of the substance. Thus, "three times" refers to the mantra being recited six times and the striking nine times. Or, he takes up the wooden wedge (*śamyā*) silently.

He strikes with the *śamyā* while reciting the mantra, "The impulse has reached. Here, because the mantra is not otherwise required due to a conflict with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, the instruction to perform it "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*) is given; this is so that the taking up [of the *śamyā*] mentioned in another ritual manual with the mantra "Of the god... (*devasya tvā*) shall not take place. Regarding this, Āpastamba says: "Or, having taken the *śamyā* with the *Sāvitra* mantra.
With the mantra, "Thou art increased by rain," he pushes the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) from the front or from the north.
He brings the mortar (*ulūkhala*) near—that is, he brings it close to the front part, or rather, he places the mortar facing toward him.
With the formula, "O you who have grown through the rains," he touches the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*). The meaning is already explained.
With the formula, "May that which has grown through the rains recognize you," he scoops [the flour] out.

Having raised [the grain] upwards, O Sage, he pours out the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) into the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) with his hand. He winnows it three times over the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), saying, "The Rakṣas is blown away. This means holding the winnowing basket above the location of the rubbish-heap. He purifies—that is, cleanses—by winnowing three times in the winnowing basket; he causes the husks to emerge from the rice grains, doing so in the winnowing basket itself. The mantra is recited once, ending with the words "O kinsmen" (*bhrātaraḥ*).

"Blown away are the enemies," with these words he winnows the chaff from the winnowing basket. He causes it to fall onto the rubbish heap (*utkara*) by means of the winnowing basket; this process of removing the chaff is repeated until all the chaff has been expelled.

Having filled the sacrificial cake-pans (*puroḍāśakapāla*) with the chaff, he scatters them below the black antelope skin in the northwestern intermediate direction, saying, "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases."

Having identified the northwestern intermediate direction as the lower portion of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), he scatters the husks (*tuṣa*) using the very potsherd (*kapāla*). Having taken by hand from the rubbish heap (*utkara*) exactly as many husks as can be held by that potsherd, he fills the potsherd with them; the meaning is that he fills it with the husks already gathered by hand. The *Baudhāyana-Śrautasūtra* specifies "by hand" for the sake of the sacrificial pap (*caru*). On this point, the Mīmāṃsakas have cited the sentence: "He scatters the husks with the cake-potsherd" (*puroḍāśakapālena tuṣān upavapati*). Here, the disposal of all husks is stated without distinction.

Accordingly, it should be understood that the mantra is recited once for each repetition of "having filled," repeated until the completion of the husks (*tuṣa*), and so on, up to the time of the *upavāpa* (the scattering of the grains) and as far as the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) is brought out. [End of] Paṭala 50, together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 129.
He does not look back.
And [he acts] up to the point where he brings out the black antelope skin.

"Driven away is the Rakṣas," with these words he drives it away; pressing down with his hand according to the instruction, he drives it away, meaning he should effect the warding off of the Rakṣases by means of the mental state alone.
Having touched water.
The ritual touching of water is prescribed by the Śruti.
Having sprinkled the potsherd with water, he sets it down;
having sprinkled it with water, he places it in its proper position.
"May Vāyu separate you"—with these words he separates them; "may [Vāyu] separate [you]" is the end of the mantra. He winnows the unhusked rice and the husked grains.
"O gods, [separate you]"—with these words he causes the grains to fall into the vessel. || 17 ||

"He throws [them] in" means for the purpose of pouring them into the *pātrī* (winnowing basket). The formula ends with "may he accept. Here, by implication, even the rice that has not been threshed is threshed, and he silently removes the husks (*tuṣa*). Having poured the grains of rice into the *pātrī*, while they are there, he issues the direction: "Thresh them three times! At this point, he releases his speech.

In this context, what is enjoined is not three separate acts of threshing; rather, the entire collection of threshings serves a single purpose, which is the husking (*phalīkaraṇa*). Thus, there are three such huskings. Although these three are each addressed individually and separately by the formula "O preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), come!"—with the intention of expressing merely the role of the preparer as a single entity—they are nevertheless invoked as one. This should be explained in this sense: "He performs [the act] so that he may act. Consequently, the invocation would serve a visible (empirical) purpose.

*Phalana* means the splitting apart; *visarga* refers to the removal of the husks, which are the characteristic covering of the grains. The meaning of the command is: "One should perform that action which results in [the husks being removed].
