The vowel lengthening (*cira-dīrgha*) occurs in the sense of the transformation of something into its opposite state (*abhūtatadbhāve*). *Triṣphalīkaraṇa* is the act of making the rice pure by separating it from the husks and kernels three times. It is precisely at this point that one releases speech; the meaning of what was stated previously—that "one releases speech with the call to the preparer of the oblation" (*haviṣkṛtā vācaṃ visṛjata*)—is fulfilled here by the release of speech.

The word "jātā" (born) [is used] and not before the invocation of the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation). Kātyāyana stated that it occurs immediately after; however, to ensure that this does not also apply to the followers of Vaikhānasa and others who have stated it to be so, the word "atra" (here) was used. This is the intention: [the term] "haviṣkṛtā" refers to the preparer of the oblation.

In the expression "kṛṇu" (make), there is no indication of the word-meaning (*śabdapadārtha*), but rather of the object-meaning (*arthapadārtha*). In that context, the word must be indicated by secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*); therefore, it refers to its own utterance, and through that utterance, time [is indicated]. Consequently, the designation "haviṣkṛt" (the preparer of the oblation) is applied to one who is engaged in performing the preparation of the oblation for the sake of the ritual purpose; specifically, it is one who, by means of the three-fold threshing (*triṣphalīkaraṇa*), brings about the state of being an oblation (*havirbhavati*). Thus, he is called "haviṣkṛt."

In this context, even the action (*kriyā*) must be stated as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and time is indicated by that; thus, there is no infinite regress of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, it is appropriate to release speech only when that [action] has occurred. [The commentary continues: "The wife of the sacrificer threshes, or whoever else may be her servant—if she is his wife, she too threshes a few times and hands it over to another, who then threshes from that point onward. *Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa* (or *Śrauta-sūtra* attributed to Satyāṣāḍha), First Part. (Note: Variants noted in the manuscript sources: 1. *ka*, *ga*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṭe*, *ṭha*, *ṅa* read *kartavyāniha*; 2. *ka*, *ga*, *ca* read *phalīkaraṇaṃ*.)

Here, two attendants (*preṣya*) are indicated; one is shown in the subsequent sūtra. Regarding the first two, he states the restriction of the specific individuals by means of the method of *sphalīkaraṇa* (threshing). In that context, there is one agent who may be either the wife or anyone else present there—these three being optional alternatives. The second is the one mentioned by the phrase "to another" (*anyasmai*). Since the sacrificer’s wife alone is the subject under discussion, the mention of the "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is for the purpose of showing that even the female servant (*dāsī*) who will be mentioned later for the sake of the sacrificer’s threshing belongs specifically to the sacrificer who is the current subject.

The word "api" (also/even) has the sense of modification. A "dāsī" (female slave) is well-known. Of what sort is she? She is one who is not a wife (*patnī*); that is to say, she is not one born of the three [higher] castes who was accepted as a wife in the presence of witnesses according to the *Smṛti*, but later attained the state of slavery, or she is one unfit for the status of a wife because she is born of the Śūdra caste. According to Pāṇini’s rule, "A wife is so called because of her connection with the sacrifice (*yajña-saṃyoga*"), there is no connection with the sacrifice for a Śūdra woman. Therefore, she is merely a Śūdra offspring, incapable of being a wife.

Since those [grains] are optionally subject to threshing at the first threshing, the threshing is restricted to being performed only a few times—not excessively—so that they do not become completely pulverized by the second threshing. Among them, one or another [of the two options] is combined with the *agnīdh*’s threshing as the second; however, it must be performed until they have become well-dehusked (*suphalīkṛta*). To express this, it is said: "He threshes from that point onwards."

The term *adhvaryu* is used here to include the *āmīdha*, because it will be stated later that even he is designated by the word *adhvaryu* in the context of the Soma sacrifice. Thus, when two instances of threshing have occurred, the text prescribes the third threshing with the words, "Thresh three times" (*triṣphalī kartavai*). Here, the wife is summoned by the call, "O preparer of the oblation, come! (*haviṣkṛdehi*). She alone is the one to be summoned, because she is the one who will be enjoined to "thresh three times. "Thresh" (*kartavai*) means perform the threshing—the separation of the husks from the grains.
"Be purified for the gods! Be beautified for the gods! Be cleansed for the gods!"—with these words, the wife threshes the grains three times until they are well-threshed.

Thus, having thoroughly winnowed the rice grains by means of the two types of threshing characterized by the removal of the husks; [regarding] the wife’s role in the winnowing: since the purpose of the command (*praiṣa*) is already established there, the statement "again, the fire-god... is for the sake of the ritual rule (*dharma*) alone. The winnowing is to be accomplished three times with the entire mantra, once with the mantra and twice silently. These three acts of threshing constitute a single act of winnowing; together with the two preceding ones, there are thus three acts of winnowing—this is the conclusion.
However, if the wife is in her menstrual period (*anālambhukā*), the Adhvaryu himself performs the third threshing with the mantra.

He sets aside the *phalīkaraṇas* (the husks). The term *phalīkaraṇa* refers to those things separated (*viviktīkṛta*) from the rice grains. The suffix *-lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. The Brāhmaṇa states: "The *phalīkaraṇas* are the leftovers. This means they are the remnants set apart from the rice grains; he places them in another vessel, meaning they are kept for future use. [Note:
The commentary by Mahādeva, the *Vaijayantī*, contains various readings regarding the placement of these husks.]

Having washed the rice grains—meaning having made the grains in the winnowing basket free from impurities by means of water—he pours out the wash-water within the altar (vedī) with the formula: "That husk which remains when the grains are being thrice-husked, that is the portion of the Rakṣases; may the waters carry it away from here, svāhā!"

He pours out that water with which they were washed; he pours it out upon the site of the altar, having taken the water used for washing the winnowing basket into another vessel. "This for the Rākṣasas. The touching of water by both [the sacrificer and the Adhvaryu] is established here by Smṛti and is not based on Śruti, because its application is prescribed specifically for the husks in the Brāhmaṇa: "He touches water for the sake of purity. The ritual procedure for the black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina) has been explained.

The meaning is that because the procedure for taking up the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) and so forth was stated for the purpose of threshing, one should perform it again up to the end of the spreading [of the skin]. The point is that even though there is no difference in time or place, there is a repetition due to the difference in purpose.
With the mantra "Thou art the pillar of heaven," he places the *śamyā* pin with its knob facing north upon the black antelope skin.

"Without laying aside the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), [the mantra] ends with *ādityās tvag vettu*. Therein, having placed the thick end of the *śamyā*—which has its bowl facing north and its upper part directed upwards—into the hole of the yoke so that it does not fall below the opening, [one places it] with the words *dhiṣaṇāsi parvatī*.
Upon that *śamyā*, one sets down the grinding stone (*dṛṣad*). [The mantra] ends with *prati tvā divaḥ skambhanīr asi*."
He places it down with the rear half.
With the rear half of the lower millstone, he covers the yoke-pin.
He places the upper millstone upon the lower millstone with the formula: "Thou art Dhiṣaṇā, daughter of the mountain."
The term "he assents" (*adhivartayati*) is understood to carry over. Up to the word "having scattered" (*parvattitvā*).
He looks at the rice grains with the formula, "Ye are rays, full of sweetness.
He looks at those situated in the winnowing basket from a respectful distance.
With the mantra "devasya tvā," he pours the rice grains onto the lower grinding stone;
the end of the mantra is "adhivapāmi.
He does this three times with the sacrificial formula (yajuṣ) and a fourth time silently.
The meaning has been explained.
He grinds [the grain] with the formula: "For out-breath thee, for in-breath thee, for diffused breath thee.
The recitation of the entire mantra is intended to preclude any optionality; thereafter, he grinds it as required, having recited the mantra only once.

133. According to the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha: Alternatively, he pushes forward the eastern stone with the formula, "For out-breathing (prāṇa) thee"; he pushes back the western stone with "For in-breathing (apāna) thee"; and he places it in the middle region with "For diffused breathing (vyāna) thee. He presses down the eastern stone; likewise, he makes the western stone remain in the middle region of the mortar (dṛṣad) using the third mantra.
With the words "dīrghāmanu" (along the long one), he [draws] toward the east from the end;

with "dhām" (the abode), [he draws] from the middle. Because of its suitability, the phrase "he pushes up the clod toward the east from the middle region" is drawn back [into the context], even though it is distant.
From that point upward, he grinds continuously according to the face [of the altar].

Therefore, from this point on, without observing the previously mentioned restrictions and ceasing [the grinding] midway, he causes the flour to fall onto the black antelope skin with the mantra, "The gods... The word "praskandayati" (he causes to fall) is used to indicate that he causes it to fall from the lower millstone by means of the upper millstone alone. "Gṛhṇātu" (may he take) is the end of the mantra.
"Behold with an unimpaired eye," he says, and thus he looks.
Bending down, he looks at the flour-powders placed upon the black antelope skin that have spilled out.
"Grinding without scattering, make them fine," he issues the command.
By the phrase "not covering," the mind is deliberated upon. She says to the servant:
"The wife or a female slave grinds [the grain] for this purpose. Thus is the meaning.

He performs all of this. That which was stated in the *praisha* (directive), beginning with "not mixing the distinct [flours]," was sent for a visible purpose. He should do everything that was said: not mixing the flours so as not to scatter them from the wooden board or from the black antelope skin, nor causing them to be displaced outside, and likewise making the flours fine. It is ruled that even in the absence of those two [the board and the skin] due to their being unavailable, or even in the absence of the *praisha*, he must certainly perform it; for at that time, the Adhvaryu is occupied with the placing of the potsherds (*kapāla-upadhāna*). The absence of the *praisha* is due to a contradiction with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and because there is no modification (*ūha*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Here he places the boiling water on the fire. || 18 ||

Thus ends the fifth paṭala in the first praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. He places the *madantī* water over the Gārhapatya fire; according to Vairavānasa, the *madantī* waters are placed over the Āhavanīya fire. This term is based on a preparatory refinement (*saṃskāra*). Thus, once the refinement has been effected by the act of placing [the vessel] over the fire, one subsequently employs the designation that will apply to it. [End of Paṭala 150] :: Together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

The statement that "one mixes with the *praṇītā* waters" is seen in the *Āpastamba* [Kalpasūtra]; therefore, what is said—namely, "having brought water from those [waters], he places the *madantī* waters on the fire"—will become clear in our own Sūtra itself. The word "here" (*atra*) is used so that it may not be the case that, as seen in another ritual manual (*kalpāntara*), the placing on the fire occurs after the setting down of the potsherds (*kapāla-upadhāna*). Regarding this, some say that the placing on the fire must be at that very same place where the cooking of the oblation (*havir-śrapaṇa*) takes place.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the first book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin, composed by Mahādeva. ||5||

1.6 Now begins the sixth chapter. The sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) are cooked either in the Āhavanīya or the Gārhapatya fire, behind the fire; there is an option according to one's preference for the *sattra* sacrifice. In that regard, the placement of the potsherds (*kapāla-upadhāna*), which will be described later, must be performed. Regarding the statement "the oblations are cooked," the plural number is used in accordance with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), referring to the two *puroḍāśa* cakes of the two ritual sections (*parvan*). However, the *sānnāyya* (milk offering) is cooked in the Gārhapatya alone, because of a specific scriptural injunction. The phrase "behind the fire" connects with the preceding [statement], meaning they are cooked in the western half-portion of the fire's location.
As it has been stated, he takes up the *upaveṣa* with the formula "Thou art the bold one" (*dhṛṣṭir asi*).

By saying "as," he causes [the sacrificer] to remember what was previously mentioned. He has shown that because of the difference in time, there is a repetition of the action and the mantra even though the substance is the same. For one who is performing the *saṃnayana*, he states another mantra for the optional taking up in the morning:

"The demon is struck down; burn the hand of the demon! Thou art the serpent of the depths" (*abhihataṃ rakṣo rakṣasaḥ pāṇiṃ daha, ahirasi budhniyaḥ*). With this, he turns out two embers toward the west.

With that *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick), he separates two embers from the fire right at the hearth itself. By the phrase "with that" (*tena*), it is established that the function of the embers is performed with that very stick and not with the left finger as stated by Kātyāyana.

Having cast one ember toward the north-western intermediate direction with the mantra ending in "apāgne" ("O Agni, go away"), and having touched water, [he recites] the portion ending in "kravyādam sedha" ("drive away the flesh-eater"). According to Vaikhānasa, he casts the southern ember outside the hearth in the north-western direction; this is the Vedic method of touching water.

Having set aside the remainder [of the mantra] with the words "Bring [the gods] to the place of sacrifice" (*ā devayajam vaha*), one should place it exactly where one intends to lay down the potsherd (*kapāla*). By the inclusion of multiple words in the mantra, the completion of the mantra is indicated. Otherwise, there might be the misconception that the application belongs to the word *nirdagdham* from another recensional branch—which is not recited immediately after *dhruvam asi*—and consequently, following the sequence of the text, the mantra would end with *arātayaḥ*. To prevent this from occurring with *dhruvam asi* and the subsequent portion, the sequence of the text is interrupted according to the sequence of meaning; such is the meaning.
With the mantra, "Thou art the firm," he places a potsherd upon it.
Once the charcoal has been settled, he places a single potsherd; "pahā" is the end of the mantra.
Thinking "it is burnt," he places a charcoal ember upon it;
when another potsherd has been placed, he places another ember upon that first one with the formula,
"Thou art the supporter."

In this case, because the word "thus" (*evam*) is not mentioned, only the verb "he places" (*upadadhāti*) is drawn forward [from the preceding rule], and not even the other properties of the preceding [rule]. This is the intention: since the scriptural injunction states, "He places one [potsherd] having many potsherds," in that sūtra—namely, "he places a potsherd"—the singular number is used for "potsherd."

The singular number used in reference to the locus is intended to be significant; therefore, in the rule "he places only one potsherd first upon that very [locus]," as well as in "he constructs the house upon that," the singular "upon that" (tasmin) is intended to be significant. Thus, he places the second [potsherd] before that first one, and the third before that second one, with the formula "thou art the support. Before that [second], [he places the third].
Before the second.
Of the cake on eight potsherds, there are two [bricks] from the middle; three are to the south and three to the north.
This is clear. With the formula "Thou art the law" (tayordharmāsi), he places one in the southeast; with "The host of the Maruts" (marutāṃ śardhaḥ), he places one in the southwest.
To the south of those two, in the south-eastern direction (the Āgneya quarter), [he says]; in the south-western direction (the Nairṛti quarter), [he says]:
"O Yavamatī, strengthen the region, strengthen wealth, strengthen prosperity; for this sacrificer, exclude his rivals!
In the north-western direction (the Vāyavya quarter), [he says].
With the formula, "From all quarters I lay thee down, unbroken, for the acquisition of kinsmen," he lays it down in the northeast—that is, in the Īśāna direction.
These two [formulas] are intended to establish the order for the three subsequent [bricks]. For the middle one, the third, he says, "Thou art consciousness"; the remainder is placed to the north.

From the middle [of the text]: these eight potsherds (*kapāla*) are prescribed as constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the *āgneya* sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Thus, this number is for the sake of the *āgneya*, and the potsherds are likewise; it is not that the potsherds are for the sake of the number. This is according to the principle: "But there is no mutual connection between subordinate elements (*guṇa*), because they exist for the sake of another. Therefore, in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) where there are eleven or twelve potsherds belonging to a modification of the *āgneya*, the potsherds are to be placed [on the fire] by means of the very same ritual procedure (*dharma*) for placing them, and not by virtue of a similarity in number—such as in the case of the eleven potsherds for the *āgnīṣomīya* or the twelve potsherds for the *aindrāgna*.
In the north-western [corner], [ends] the first ninth section, together with the Vaijayantī commentary composed by Mahādeva:
one lays down three [bricks] for the cake on eleven potsherds in the same manner as for the cake on eight potsherds.

Because of its connection with the eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*), it is indeed on the north side; this he will clarify later. The taking up of the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick) is performed for all purposes. Since there was no separate substance or separate purpose in the previous mantra, and because the purpose of placing all the potsherds was already present in the mind, when that which was set aside in the middle is taken up again, there is no repetition of the mantra. However, the action beginning with the removal of the firebrand (*anāra*) is repeated, because it does not assist in the subsequent joining of the potsherds.

Regarding the phrase "on eleven potsherds" or "on twelve potsherds," because of the extension (*atideśa*) from the preceding [model sacrifice], the first [element] acquires its primary characteristics by virtue of being the first. Nor should it be said that the removal of the embers (*aṅgāra-nirasana*) is a subsidiary act (*tantra*) for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). For two embers, having been joined together and consecrated (*saṃskṛta*) by the placing [of the cake], the abandonment of one occurs through the act of separation; since that which is separated produces a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the other, its abandonment is therefore an act of disposal (*pratipatti*), as indicated by the use of the second case ending.

The principle that when a visible result is possible, the postulation of an invisible one is not logical, applies here as well. Indeed, it is seen in the Brāhmaṇa: "He says, 'O Agni, drive away the raw-flesh-eating Āma; expel him from this place; carry [the offering] to the sacrifice for the gods. Having thus struck down that very Āma who devours the *kavyas*, he places the potsherd upon the pure fire. He says, 'The *rakṣas* is burnt up; the enemies are burnt up. Thus, he burns away the *rakṣases* and the enemies."

The purification of the charcoal that has been placed [on the fire] is prescribed by the ritual act of removing other coals; likewise, through the disposal of that very purification, the burning away of the Rakṣas-demons occurs, as demonstrated by the phrase "of the eight-pot-sherd. Here, the portion ending with "in this way" constitutes a single sentence, while "he lays down three" is another; in that regard, the word "which" (*yāni*) must be supplied, as seen in the subsequent sūtra "of those" (*teṣām*).

And the phrase "in this way and that way" (*evaṃ caivam*) is not connected with the word "three" (*trīṇi*), but rather with the phrase "of the eleven potsherds" (*ekādaśakapālasya*). It is indeed so. Here, the preceding term "he places" (*upadadhāti*) must be understood as carrying over. Regarding that, he states the specific detail:
"Of those, the largest is the middle; two are before the middle.

Among the three, that which is the middle is the largest—that is, somewhat more extensive—and the eight-potsherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) is placed before that middle one; however, only one is offered here. In this regard, he states the final mantra:
"tayościdasīti" is the first [verse].
"He places" is the elliptical reference (anukarṣa).
As stated, [he places them] in the intermediate directions.
In the directions of Agni, Nairṛta, Vāyu, and Īśāna, as before;
the remaining [bricks] are piled up to the north with the formula "Citaḥ stha."

They are laid down. To the north, one should lay them out from the middle one toward the east. Although there is a plural number in the mantra, the laying down of the three is not performed with only a single mantra. Because of the distinctness of the substances according to the intermediate number "of the eleven potsherds" (*ekādaśakapālasya*), there is a repetition of the mantra. The plural number is used in mutual dependence, just as in the dual form "I lay you two down on the face. [Note: Variants noted: 1ka.ba.ga.cha.ṭa.ṭa.ḍa. read *nivarta*; 2ka.kha.ga.ca.cha.ṭa.ṭha. read *stheti sarvāgyava*; 3ka.ga.].

Ca, cha, ṭa, ṭha, ḍa; the rest is as stated above. Regarding the placing of the cake for Indra and Agni, Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra states: "The procedure for the twelve-potherd cake is exactly like that for the eleven-potherd cake.
Even the twelfth potsherd is touched with the same formula."

With the formula, "O Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases, heat yourselves with austerity," he places the embers upon the potsherds. The phrase "all [this] is not to be turned back" (*sarvam anapācī*) is for the purpose of concluding the mantra; therefore, the mantra "temayāni dharmā" is extracted separately from the recitation, because it is intended to be applied at the time of removing the potsherds. Otherwise, it would constitute a single mantra together with the preceding one. The plural form in "tapyadhvam" is clearly shown for that reason; thus it is stated that all the potsherds, even when joined in multiple groups, should be consecrated by this single mantra.

Having taken [the clay] with some vessel capable of holding the heated material, he spreads it out—that is, extends it—over the potsherds (kapāla) in such a way that they do not burn, according to the specific requirement. This refers to the state of not burning. Therefore, from this point forward, the repetition of the mantra for each individual application (pratiyoga) should be performed when joined with the yoga; however, prior to this, there is no repetition, because there is no distinctness of substance (dravyapṛthaktva) based on the limiting condition (upādhi) of being a potsherd.

The Teacher also, intending exactly the same thing, employed the term *kapāla* in the passage ending with "he places upon the potsherds" (*kapāleṣvadhyūhati*). He further employed the term *yoga* in the passage "from the southern [potsherd] up to the connection with the [other] potsherds he pours out, and from the northern [one] he pours away. Beyond this, it is observed that because these [potsherds], characterized by their mutual conjunction, constitute the locus, there is no repetition of the mantra according to the principle that "there is no separation from the primary [action]," which is the view of the author of the Sūtras; however, even that is in accordance with the Brāhmaṇa.

Beginning with the statement, "He places three potsherds," and so forth, up to the limit of eight potsherds, and then again stating [the numbers] eight, nine, ten, eleven, and twelve, the total of twenty is completed by means of the numerical count alone. Since no internal distinction is perceived there, even in the concluding summary, he will immediately thereafter state, "In this sequence he performs the rites," using the plural forms "these" (*enāni*) and "these deities" (*devatānām enāḥ*) to show the absence of internal differentiation, saying, "he heats these by means of austerity. If it is asked, "Whence does this rule arise?"—

It is said: as long as the two *puroḍāśas* are mixed together, because there is no separate distinctness between the two *puroḍāśas*, even when they have been placed upon the potsherds (*kapāla*), the action should be performed in conjunction [with them] and not by division. Since there is no division of the mass, for each individual mass there is only one [action]; therefore, the repetition of the mantra is prompted by that [single action]. This is the intention of the Teacher. Here, it is clarified: because it is stated that "the morning milking is on the potsherds that have been placed," the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) refers to that very [place]. Having heated the vessel (*pātrī*) and having blown upon it...

Regarding the phrase "in the portion of the pit for heating" (*niṣṭapana-bilabhāge*), it is explained that this refers to the act of heating itself, since there is no actual cooking vessel; thus, when the pit has been heated and cooled down, one should perform the action of making it thoroughly red-hot. This [explanation] is to be considered, because the word *upavāta* is conventionally established in the sense of "cooling. In this context, the practitioners place the pot on the *gārhapatya* fire, pour the contents into it, and then carry it away. This is the other method, as there is no other injunction, and by this means the cooking is accomplished.

Or, according to the rule of Kātyāyana—"when [the mortar] is standing on the Gārhapatya fire with the *antarvedha* [crossing] behind it"—our own established practice (*vyavasthā*) allows for it to be poured in that manner. With the formula "Of the god... (*devasya tvā*), he pours the flour from the black antelope skin across the strainer (*tiraḥpavitra*).

The pouring ends with the words "...I pour together" (*saṃvapāmi*); there is no mention of a deity because there is no injunction to do so "according to the respective deities" (*yathādevatam*). Having placed the strainer crosswise, he deposits the flour from the black antelope skin into that [mortar].

Three times with the *yajus* formula, and silently a fourth time. The mantra "Of the god... ending in "...I pour upon" (*adhivapāmi*) is recited in the *Saṃhitā*. That very same [mantra] is supplied (*anuṣakta*) here as a supplement to "I pour together" (*saṃvapāmi*), as explained in the *Brāhmaṇa*. Considering that this supplied portion is indeed included in the *Saṃhitā*, it is presented here by its opening words (*pratīka*). Since there is no mention of a deity in either case, the reading is simply as it stands; therefore, the phrase "according to the deity" (*yathādevatam*) was not stated. Āpastamba, however, having seen the version from another *śākhā*, stated "according to the deity," which we do not accept.

Although it is seen in the Brāhmaṇa that "according to the deity," this is a praise and not an injunction. Why? Because there is no specific instruction in the Mantra or Brāhmaṇa regarding the first fire. Just as there is an instruction in the case of "pleasing for Agni" (*agnaye juṣṭam*), when such an instruction exists, that very sequence is the injunction. "He restrains his speech while pouring [the rice], and releases it while covering [it with ashes]. While he is covering the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) with ashes—though he will later state "he covers it with ashes"—nevertheless, because the usage in both the *Saṃhitā* and the Brāhmaṇa is "he covers it with the Veda," the term "while covering" (*abhivāsayan*) is used here.
With the mantra, "I purify you with the two strainers of the two bay horses," he purifies the flour three times with two strainers whose tips point north;
this is the mantra.
Or alternatively, [he uses] "The god for you... (devo vaḥ).
In the manner previously described,

beginning with "This behind," he takes some of the *praṇītā* waters with the *sruva* spoon, supports them with the *veda* grass-bundle, and pours them onto the ground flour, saying, "May the waters be united."

Regarding this, after Bharadvāja has stated, "One mixes the oblations with the *praṇītā* waters," he further says, "He brings the water. From this, it is understood that the cooking of the oblation is performed with the *praṇītā* waters. Even the Mīmāṃsakas cite this very sentence as a scriptural authority (*śruti*) to assert the visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) of the *praṇītās*. In the phrase "of the *praṇītās*," the word "water" (*apaḥ*) is connected with the genitive case indicating relationship—meaning "the waters belonging to the *praṇītās*"—and this is merely a rule (*dharma*) as prescribed for the water obtained for its ritual function. The mantra concludes with the words "be released" (*sṛjyadhvam*).

"If the *praṇītā* waters were not available, one should purify whatever other waters there may be with the *yajus* and mix [the offering] with them"—this is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) for times of distress (*āpad*). With the *yajus*, "O gods... and so forth, it is an explanatory statement for times of distress. When an option regarding the *praṇītā* waters has arisen, even if only the primary rite is performed using whatever waters are at hand during distress—whether they be *praṇītā* or non-*praṇītā*—therein lies the explanatory statement regarding the purpose; that is to say, the attainment of the purpose occurs through the rule of option regarding the *praṇītā* waters.
With the mantra, "Born from the waters," he brings in the heated [milk].
When they have been ground, he pours in the heated *madantī* waters; with the mantra, "Be united with the waters," he causes them to flow around [the flour] from left to right.

The term *pradakṣiṇam* is stated as a technical (paribhāṣika) term. To explain its meaning as "on all sides," [the author] says "anuvyāpya" (pervading), for otherwise "paritas," "samantāt," or "paritaḥ" would mean only "around" or "outside. He causes them to be moistened on all sides, just as flour-dusts float [in water]. From the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, the word "taptāḥ" (heated) is modified to the instrumental case, "taptābhiḥ" (by the heated ones). Thus, by implication, the flour-dusts are the objects of the action [moistened] by the heated waters. This has been stated by Bharadvāja: "By the heated ones, the flour-dusts."

In the Sūtra, regarding the word *saṃnayēt*, because it functions as a transitive verb, the locative ending is transformed into an accusative; thus, through its connection with the double-object construction—as in "he brings the heated flour"—those very [substances] are intended in the present context.
With the formula, "I unite thee for Janayati," he unites [the flour and water]; or rather, with "For Janayī," he unites them.

He unites means he mixes the flour and the waters, stirring them with a stirring-stick (*mekṣaṇa*) so that the cooking of the flour may occur, according to the Śruti: "He unites the oblations with the *praṇītā* waters. For this very reason, he places the boiling waters (*madantī*) on the fire; these are indeed the *praṇītā* waters, as will be made clear in the Sūtra where it is stated that the *praṇītā* waters are for the purpose of cooking when the cooking of milk is prescribed. Therefore, having brought them forth, he brings the heated *madantī* waters.
With the formula, "Thou art the head of Makha," he forms a ball of dough (*piṇḍa*).
This is clear.
He distributes them with the words, "May you two separate according to your respective portions. || 19 ||
The term "piṇḍam" (the lump) is carried over [from the previous rule]. He divides it into two parts. Regarding the division, he states another mantra:

"May Savitṛ the god divide you two; may Bhaga the Savitṛ divide you two; may Pūṣan the Savitṛ divide you two; may Vāyu the Savitṛ divide you two; I divide you for procreation," or [simply], "I divide you for procreation.

Here, according to the Nyāya school, these five mantras are understood to belong to the Teacher (Ācārya), because of the use of the particle *iti* at the very end. When there is only one sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), the division is omitted by implication of the purpose.
Having made two equal balls, he touches the one for Agni with the formula, "This for Agni," and the other according to its respective deity with, "This for so-and-so.

Having first made two balls of equal size and having cut them into two equal portions, he subsequently forms them into the shape of balls in that same manner; this is stated by means of the suffix *-tvā*. He touches [the second ball] only where there is a division, because since there is no division in the case of the first, there is no mention of touching it due to the absence of such a distinction. The conclusion of the mantra is indicated by the plural reading: "I unite thee for generation."

Therefore, "to Agni, thee" and "to Agni and Soma, thee" are not remnants of the preceding mantra, but rather two separate mantras; this [latter] is an alternative to the one having the same meaning as "to Agni. Baudhāyana has stated: "To Agni, svāhā; to Agni and Soma, [svāhā]. There too, a similar mantra is shown: "to such-and-such, to such-and-such. By that [principle], "to the Moon and Agni, thee" should not be understood here. [End of] Paṭala 10. [From the Vaijayantī commentary by Mahādeva. 139
With the words, "I drive away the face of this attacking army," he drives away the embers from the southern junction of the potsherds with the *veda*, and then drives them away from the northern one.

The term *yoga* refers to the collection of the joined potsherds which, being united for a single purpose, constitute a composite whole; having first driven [the embers] away from the southern one, he then removes and extracts them from the northern one with a separate mantra.

Up to this point, having described the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) under the single condition of being merely a skull according to the general rule (*tantra*), that which was separately specified as the task to be performed under the conditions of the conjunction of the south and north—beginning with the removal of ashes—is here supported by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra as well. Since an army is observed to be a collection of various individuals directed toward a single purpose, and since that collection is manifested by the very wording of the mantra, it is understood that the distinction between south and north must exist, for without such a division, that [army] could not be established;
thinking thus, he said, "from the southern," and so forth.

In this way, their ritual acts are performed in successive order. Just as it is said that "having removed [the oblation] from the southern pot-fragment, one removes it from the northern pot-fragment," a sequence of succession is described through the repetition of the same ritual act despite the difference in location; likewise, for the sacrificial offerings (*havis*) distinguished by the difference between the southern and northern locations, the ritual acts are performed in sequence through the repetition of the mantra-accompanied rite, and not according to one's own whim. By the use of the present tense, it is stated that this is not a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), but rather something established by logical necessity (*nyāyaprāpta*).

Although it appears that this [procedure] applies only to the aforementioned *puroḍāśa* cakes connected with the two sacrificial sessions (*parvan*), nevertheless, lest one fear that the ritual action prompted by the distinct nature of the substances—the boiled milk (*śṛta*) and the curd (*dadhi*)—which have attained the status of being south and north respectively during the *sāṃnāyya* offering from the time of their placement onwards, should not occur, there must be a "cutting" (*avadyati*) and "cuttings" (*avadānāni*). Likewise, other subsequent rites should also be performed for those two by repetition and in the order of south and north; otherwise, how could the possibility of a single performance (*tantra*) or the order of origin (*utpatti-krama*) be precluded?

Therefore, there is the taking of all the oblations. Thus, it has been stated that the constituent elements (*padārtha*) are to be consecrated in their proper sequence; now, regarding the actions—both of the same class and of different classes—that are performed upon them, a doubt arises: must all [actions] be completed with respect to one element before moving to another element, or should each individual action be completed across all the elements? To show the settled rule for both cases, [the author] first states the general rule according to the sequence of elements, that each single action follows its own sequence: "One follows each [action] with its counterpart of the same class; one completes each [action] in its entirety."

An action prescribed by a single rule is of one kind; that is, a single instance of an action is of the same genus as other instances because it is performed in an identical manner and is connected to the same purpose. Indeed, it is not the case that the very same individual instance—which was performed and then perished in the first object—is what can be connected to a subsequent object. Therefore, since there is a difference between individual instances (*vyakti*), the universal (*jāti*) must necessarily be denoted; and that which manifests this universal is each specific prescription (*vidhi*).

*Tattvamātra* (mere identity): by this [principle], among the objects to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*), one follows each individual object in sequence with a single action of the same class (*sanātīya*), and immediately thereafter likewise with one of a different class (*vijātīya*). "Follows" (*sameti*) means he connects (*saṃbadhnāti*). This specific order is designated as *padārthānusamaya* (consecutive performance according to the objects).

An action first performed is undertaken by way of enjoining all the constituent elements at once; until that is completed, the meaning of the sentence is not complete. Consequently, there is no application of another, similar sentence that has been enjoined elsewhere. Even if singularity were heard in relation to the object to be designated (*uddeśya*), it would still not be intended as significant; for if the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of all the constituent elements were not performed within a single sentence, the meaning of that sentence would remain incomplete.

The sense is that if a heterogeneous element were inserted in the middle, the procedure would have to be repeated again and again. In that regard, concerning a word-meaning that consists of a collection of items, there arises the same doubt as before: does one proceed by taking each individual instance within the collection and performing the action for the second one in that same manner, following this sequence; or rather, having completed the entire collection as a single unit, does one then proceed with another collection in the same way? Regarding this, he says: "One completes each [instance] in its entirety. Here, there is no [interruption] by those of the same class (*sajātīya*).

Regarding the rule stated for the pouring out (*nirvāpa*), one handful is poured out for the first oblation, and likewise one for the second; similarly, this same principle applies to the placing of the potsherds (*kapālopadhāna*). It is said here that one completes and finishes each individual ritual act (*padārtha*) in its entirety. Why? Because as long as a ritual act is not completed, the action enjoined with reference to that act is not finished—such as "he pours out four handfuls" or "he places eight potsherds. In that context, a single handful or a single potsherd does not constitute a complete ritual act (*padārtha*).

That constituent part of an action is enjoined for the sake of that [result]; that which is delimited by a single property and has attained the status of being either a subordinate element (*aṅga*) or an objective (*uddeśya*) is called "one," but this oneness does not consist merely in the oneness of the individual instance (*vyakti*). Thus, the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) measured by exactly four handfuls is delimited by the verbal root *nirvap-*; it is therefore a single action. Since the activity undertaken with reference to that term is completed within that [single instance] without extending beyond it, it does not reach out to another external action. Likewise, in a single conjunction (*yoga*), [the same principle applies].

The meaning of "an eight-potherd [oblation] for Agni" is that one completes the entire single constituent element (*padārtha*) within that which consists of various constituent elements. The sequential performance of similar and dissimilar actions with respect to a single constituent element, followed by the same for the second constituent element, is called *kāṇḍānusamaya* (section-by-section sequence); however, this is not the case here. By way of an exception to that, he states the *kāṇḍānusamaya*: "But those [actions] connected [to one another] have a single completion, as in the case of the cutting and the offering."

Those [acts] which are conjoined, possess a fixed sequence of priority and posteriority, and consist of both similar and dissimilar elements, are capable of reaching completion within a single ritual act (*padārtha*). In this context, if there were a performance according to each individual *padārtha* (*padārthānusamaya*), it would result in a contradiction of the authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) regarding the *paupīyava* offering. Consequently, at the end, even for the *kṛcchra* [penance], a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by repetition must be accepted in accordance with the authority of the texts; this is the intended meaning. Why? Because the taking of portions (*avadāna*) and the offering (*pradāna*) are conjoined. Regarding that, some say that the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) is conjoined with its own subordinate acts (*svāpakarman*), as in the injunction "he offers the fourfold portion."

In this context, the status of being an illustrative example (*udāharaṇatva*) applies to the acts of cutting (*avadāna*) and offering (*pradāna*) because they are conjoined, but not to the acts of cutting and pouring (*homa*) themselves. Kātyāyana, however, states: "But [the sequence is determined] by the scriptural statement regarding the taking up (*grahaṇa*), placing down (*sādana*), and cutting. And in his commentary on that sūtra, it is explained: "The taking up ends with the placing down, and the cutting ends with the offering," based on a scriptural statement from another recension (*śākhāntara*). Furthermore, such a scriptural statement is not universal; since the conjunction is seen even through functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), the teacher [Kumārila] stated this reason—namely, "by the scriptural statement"—considering it non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*). Rather, by the word *tu* ("but"), he indicates precisely the impossibility of the previous logical principle (*nyāya*) applying here.

And the reason for this is that they are "conjoined" (*saṃyuktāni*). By whatever means of proof (*pramāṇa*) they are conjoined, all of them have a single final purpose (*ekāpavarga*); however, in the present context, the state of being conjoined is established by the verbal statement, whereas elsewhere it occurs according to possibility. For indeed, without performing the double-cutting (*dviravadāna*), a single cutting would not be possible; rather, [the rule] applies to the entire sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), as in: "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni. [Note: The text contains fragmentary citations from the *Mahādevakṛta-vaijayantī* commentary, including references to specific sections such as the sixth *paṭala*.]

141. Because the connection with the deity is heard through this method of application (*yoga*), and because the offering of what has been cooked and placed on the altar is possible by means of the *vaṣaṭ* call—it should be explained that here the procedure follows the sequence of the sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) precisely by way of non-statement (*avacana*). This was indicated by the author of the Sūtras when he showed that the capacity for the connection between the taking of portions (*avadāna*) and the offering (*pradāna*) is established by implication, as seen in the subsequent example beginning with "proximity to the principal act" (*pradhānasannikarṣa*). Regarding the connection established by the sense (*arthasiddha*), he gives an example:
"The pouring out (*udvapanam*) and the winnowing (*niṣpavanam*) are performed everywhere at the time of the contact with the principal act."

By the word "and" (*ca*), threshing, scattering, and so forth are included; because of the plural number in the phrase "they are performed with reference to that," it follows that in all modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) involving various seeds, when there is proximity to the primary acts—that is, when there is proximity to each of the seeds which are the objects to be consecrated by the primary acts—the procedure is by sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*). The meaning is that only when that [proximity] exists are the acts such as sowing (*udvapa*) and so forth performed.

The refinement of grains to be prepared—such as threshing—is for the purpose of producing visible rice-grains; since that purpose is not accomplished by mere threshing alone, each preceding step serves as the means for each subsequent one, thereby achieving the purpose of producing rice-grains. In this case, there is a fixed sequence of groups (*kāṇḍānusamaya*), and not a single homogeneous act of threshing performed upon all the seeds at once. Therefore, the meaning is that for the act of pouring out (*udvapanādi*), it is likewise one by one.
Thus, it is established that while sequential performance by individual items (*padārthānusamaya*) is the general rule, other forms may serve as exceptions to it.

Having taken the southern *piṇḍa* with the mantra, "Thou art the head of Makha," he places it upon the southern pair of potsherds with the mantra, "Thou art Gharma, the life of all. It is called "southern" because it is fit to be placed on the southern pair of potsherds; it is not called "belonging to Agni" (*āgneya*) because that term does not indicate a difference in location. Therefore, by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) which indicates a difference in location, the doubt is resolved: since the actions are capable of being performed separately due to the difference in location, the mantras—being distinct in substance—are repeated. Thus, the reason for the previously stated principle, "of these... and so forth, has been explained.

And likewise, although the ritual action is enjoined by encompassing it through the terms *piṇḍa* and *puroḍāśa*, there is indeed a distinctness of substance (*dravyapṛthaktva*), just as there is a distinctness of parts (*avayavapṛthaktva*) in that which is encompassed by the nature of being clarified butter (*ājyatva*) and so forth. Regarding the placing on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*), he states an alternative mantra: "O Gharma, be heated," or [he places it on the fire] with this [mantra]. He extends the previously stated remainder of the injunction (*vidhyanta*) to another oblation (*havirantara*).
The same applies to the subsequent [offerings]. The term "lump" (piṇḍa) is carried over [from the previous rule]. The remainder is as before, accompanied by the mantra.
One fashions a shape like a tortoise, not raised high, not in the form of a cake, and the size of a horse's hoof.

The word *piṇḍam* (the lump) is drawn over from the previous context. One makes an image that is a slight imitation of a tortoise (*kamaṭha*). In this regard, some tortoises are high, while others are shaped like a cake (*apūpa*), being low like a cake; [the image] is distinct from both of these, meaning it is neither too high nor too low. The *Vaikhānasa* says it should be "neither high nor too low. However, the measurement all around is "the size of a horse's hoof. (Note: The various manuscript readings cited—ka, kha, ga, ca, etc.—indicate textual variants for the surrounding portions of the commentary.)

The meaning is: "No. 11.142. In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāṭha, it is stated that the spreading [of the dough] is done from half [the size] by means of measurement; in that very context, another recension (*śākhāntara*) states the mantra:
"Spread wide" (*uru prathasva*), with which he spreads it. He expands the ball itself into its former form. The mantra ends with "may it spread" (*prathatām*).

He spreads out all the potsherds. The statement "he spreads" is a restatement of what has already been said; it is accomplished simply by making them the size of a horse's hoof-print. In this case, the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is not made from grain measured by a handful with the addition of filler material (anvāvāpa). Here, however, the size of a horse's hoof-print must be achieved by filling in the gaps. The arrangement of the potsherds should also be done in such a way that they form a certain shape; thus, the spreading itself should be performed in a manner that is not raised or otherwise irregular, rather than being a separate, independent action. For this very reason, Āpastamba has recited two sūtras in reverse order.
Having poured water into the vessel, [the teacher] says, "Take the skin," and [the student] wipes around it with the smear, moving clockwise and without spilling any of it.

In the case of "he brings water for the mixing-vessel" (*saṃyavanapātryām apa ānīti*), there is no intention to express either the subordinate quality (*guṇa*) or the primary result (*pradhāna*) of the cooking process, as seen in the statement "he pours curds into heated milk. If that were not so, the bringing of water—which is not itself something to be processed—would serve only an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Therefore, the meaning established is that one should prepare the vessel with water for the sake of taking up [the mixture]. Thus, the phrase "having taken the smear" (*tam ādāya lepaṃ*) is also intended here; otherwise, even the expression "with the smear" (*lepena*) would not be accepted. By means of that smear—that is, by the act of smearing—one brings the dough-ball (*piṇḍa*) to completion.

"Pradakṣiṇam" means "all around. "Without letting it flow over" (*anatikṣārayan*) is said for the purpose of rubbing [the vessel] so that no dripping occurs due to the application of the paste to the parts [of the body]. This is done by taking up the paste again with each portion while reciting the mantra. In this context, the washing of the *pātrī* (offering bowl) is to be performed.

The washing of the cooking vessel (*pātrī*) is for the purpose of the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the residual smear (*lepa*), and for the sake of its consecration (*saṃskāra*) for subsequent use; likewise, the washing of the smeared fingers must also be performed for both purposes, since both the smearing and the washing are seen to have the purpose of disposal in the *Āgnihotra*. In that case, having washed the fingers, the pouring out (*ninayana*) would serve only an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Therefore, because of its association with the washing of the vessel, it too serves only a visible purpose. "He performs the circumambulation with fire (*paryagni-karaṇa*) three times with a fire-brand (*ulmuka*), [saying] 'The Rakṣas is excluded.'"

The mantra ends with *arātayaḥ*. According to the previously stated rule, the mantra is to be repeated for each individual *piṇḍa*. The term *agnim parito nirdhamati* refers to that ritual action in which one blows around the fire; the meaning is that one should extinguish the flames of the fire around the *piṇḍa* with a burning piece of wood (*ulmuka*). This refinement (*saṃskāra*) also serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Furthermore, because there is no mention of "all the oblations" (*sarvāṇi havīṃṣi*)—as in the statement of Āpastamba and Vaikhānasa—and because of the lack of excessive effort and the continued application of the word *piṇḍam*, this is not the view of our own Sūtrakāra nor of our own Śākhā.

"Or rather, this ritual act is not peaceful; it is performed every half-month, namely the *puroḍāśa*. Having begun thus and praised it with explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), [the text] concludes by referring back to the *puroḍāśa* itself. Because of this contradiction with the Brāhmaṇa, the version from another recensional branch (*śākhā*) is not accepted. He states another mantra: "The lord of the bards (*parivājapati*)," etc. Even though the full text is not present, it is taken as a partial citation (*pratīka*). [End of] the sixth section (*paṭala*). This is accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 143.

With the words, "May Savitṛ roast you," he ignites [the fire] with *darbha* grass; the mantra ends with "above the firmament. He encircles the fire above with the blazing *darbha* blades, creating a flame for the purpose of cooking. Although, as in the previous case, only a ritual duty (*dharma*) is understood from the remainder of the sentence—"for the warding off of obstacles"—nevertheless, because of the indicative power of the mantra "may he roast" and the remainder of the sentence "he roasts," there is a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*). Therefore, he ignites it in such a way that the roasting may take place.
With the words, "May Agni not burn your body," he heats it all around with firebrands (*ulmuka*).

The mantra ends with "rakṣasva" (protect). He heats it with many firebrands (*ulmuka*), causing them to heat it; this is either a transitive verb with the causative sense included within it, or it takes an object. The mantra is recited for each individual lump (*piṇḍa*). "On all sides" means with [firebrands] that are not touching [the lump] but are directed toward it, as is also indicated by the mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra: "O oblation, do not burn excessively; protect yourself. With the mantra "Be united with the *brahman*," he covers the ashes together with the embers using the *veda* grass-bundle.

Having taken [the ashes] with the *pātra* vessel and having covered [the fire] with the *veda* grass-bundle, he spreads out the *piṇḍa* (the mass of embers). The meaning is that he covers it with the charcoal-bearing ashes in such a way that the afterglow (*pratitāpa*) does not burn; thus, there is a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*). Or, [he says] "Grasp the Brahman.
This is an alternative to the former [formula].
He issues the command, "Cook without burning," and at this point he releases his speech.

Since the *Brāhmaṇa* states, "In the case of the *Brāhmaṇa*, 'Cook without burning,' [he] releases his speech," it appears that this release of speech occurs at every performance; however, that is not possible. For a release is the absence of restraint, and it is impossible to enjoin such an absence as a positive act. Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra. Therefore, some action must be supplied here, and from the indicative power of the mantra, its purpose is understood to be that of a formal direction (*praiṣa*).

Furthermore, the attendants (*preṣyāḥ*) are not understood [to be the agents], nor is any action conducive to the baking of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) enjoined for others immediately thereafter, nor for oneself; therefore, by the word "he sends forth" (*preṣyati*), only the high-pitched utterance is expressed. Consequently, it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), like the injunction: "He issues the command: 'Milk the cow,' 'Cleanse the strainers,' 'The rope,' 'All the vessels.'"

Since Āpastamba states, "He makes the oblations well-cooked for the Āgnīdhra," a directive addressed to him is conceivable according to his view; however, that is not the case here because the plural number would otherwise be untenable. It is better, therefore, to assume an invisible (transcendental) purpose; for this very reason, Vaikhānasa prescribes this according to the Brāhmaṇa, and its meaning is generally understood to be that one releases speech after reciting this Yajus formula.

Even the Brāhmaṇa passage, along with its explanatory praise (*sārthavāda*), does not state any visible result; rather, having uttered the *yajus* concerning the oblation (*havī*), it extends [the ritual] by means of the *puroruc*, saying, "He makes [it] for the sake of non-burning and for the sake of cooking. Therefore, the pronunciation is for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) alone, since there was the possibility of the restriction being abandoned. Consequently, what was stated—that "he releases his speech while covering [the fire]"—is also not contradicted. By that, it follows that immediately after the covering, they do not burn [the offering].

Because the *cāraṇa* (the act of moving) is observed as being accompanied by the *praisha* (the call), the act of throwing the coals (*aṅgāra*) onto the self is indeed a constituent part (*aṅga*) of that very rite; thus, since the term "ablution" (*abhivāsana*) previously included the rite together with its parts, it does not constitute an interruption—this has been stated at length to demonstrate everything. The meaning is that this very *visarga* (release/conclusion) which was mentioned as occurring after the ablution reaches its finality at this time. Regarding this, the author of the *Bhāṣya* stated, "It is said 'here' for the sake of non-forgetfulness"; however, because that merely serves to display the ingenuity of the author of the *Sūtra*, it should be disregarded. [The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—First Praśna]—144.

The washing of the fingers and the rinsing of the vessel [are performed] after heating them with a firebrand (*ulmuka*). "The rinsing of the vessel" means that which is used for the purpose of cleaning the vessel; likewise, the washing of the fingers. Having heated the two vessels separately and having rinsed the vessel-rinsing water, the vessel remains placed in another vessel. This is because of Baudhāyana’s statement "having heated separately," because of the separate mention of the firebrand, and because of the word "and" (*ca*), the meaning is that one should heat them separately and then mix [the contents]. As for the firebrand, it is from the very fire used for cooking (*śrapaṇīya*).

To the west of the Āhavanīya fire, or to the west of the Gārhapatya fire, having drawn three lines directed northward with the wooden sword (sphya), he pours water down behind each line three times without letting them touch one another, saying: "Svāhā to Ekata! "Svāhā to Dvita! "Svāhā to Trita!"

Since it serves no other purpose, even though the option (*vikalpa*) exists, the phrase "with the other" (*apareṇa*) should simply be stated as "to the west" (*amim*). However, for the sake of establishing a specific rule (*vyavasthā*), it is said "with the other" in cases such as the animal sacrifice (*paśu-puroḍāśa*) where the *Āhavanīya* fire has been spread outside; otherwise, it would not apply. Three lines are drawn facing north and extending eastward; this is done so that the lines do not become merely for an unseen spiritual result (*adṛṣṭārtha*). By using the suffix *-tyap*, its status as a subsidiary part of the subsequent action (*uttarāṅga*) is expressed. One pours [the water] onto the spot consecrated by those lines, as is clearly stated in another Sūtra.

In this manner, it occurs only once for each [line]. How so? He says "afterwards, afterwards" (*paścāt-paścāt*) by way of repetition (*vīpsā*); thus, there should be the practice of drawing three lines. The meaning is that one should not join each preceding [line] with each succeeding one—that is, from west to west, one does not merge the eastward [line]. Here, the subsequent movement is not prohibited; rather, the joining of the preceding [line] by means of the subsequent drawing is what is prohibited.

And thus, what was stated by way of illustration becomes established: the performance of every smearing is once with the mantra and twice silently, because the purpose is fulfilled by that triad. By the phrase "without shaking," it is established that the pouring from west to east—ending toward the east—is as stated by Āpastamba; for "without shaking" means not letting them touch each other as they pour from one to the other. It is expressed as "without shaking" due to its proximity [to the preceding context].

In the *Kātyāyanīya*, it says "not moving toward the west" (*pratyagasaṃspandamānam*); and this was refuted by the teacher Karka, who stated that because of the prefix *prati* in "toward the west" (*pratyak*), it does not mean "not moving east, north, or upward," since the mention of the prefix indicates that the prohibition applies to movement [in general] rather than being restricted to the west. Vaikhānasa also states: "He pours it out so that it does not touch [anything] behind. Furthermore, the entire mantra is indicated as a single unit by the single particle *iti*.

Nor can it be argued that because there is no other distinct effort [for each pouring], Āpastamba prescribes a separate effort for that very act, and thus it is intended to be so; for the mantra is an auxiliary to the act of pouring (*ninayana*), not an auxiliary to its repetition, and therefore it should be used only once. Furthermore, one cannot say that "only as much as has been poured is consecrated by the mantra," and that for subsequent pourings the mantra must necessarily be used again, such that even though the substances are distinct, the mantra would repeat—implying that all three pourings are accomplished by the complete mantra [as a single unit].

Just as in the case of measuring sacrificial grass (*barhis*) by the handful or filling the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter (*ājya*), there is no factor here that establishes separate purposes; therefore, the substance itself is the single defining characteristic. Now, if it is argued that because of the difference in deities and the difference in the utterance of *svāhā*, where a ritual action is enjoined by a collection of mantras, one should offer oblations for each individual mantra—and thus there is a division of the ritual—it is not so. Since these are acts of disposal (*pratipattikarma*), they do not possess the characteristics of a *darvihoma*.

Nor do these [waters] possess the status of being recipients of the oblation (*havirbhāktva*), for the gods do not consume them in this manner; according to the Śruti, they do not have the status of a deity (*devatātva*). The term "offering" (*vidhikaraṇa*) is merely a designation. Furthermore, because the root *ninayati* (to pour out) does not signify "giving," the word *svāhā* in the mantra is used by Satyāṣāḍha merely for the purpose of casting [the offering], and not for the purpose of giving. In this context, the Commentator has explained the phrase "afterwards, afterwards" (*paścātpaścāt*) as meaning "ending at the rear. [End of] Chapter 110, together with the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva. [Page] 145. The author states that the act is for the purpose of mere casting and not even for the purpose of giving. Here, the Commentator has explained "afterwards, afterwards" (*paścātpaścāt*) as having the sense of "concluding at the rear" (*paścādapavargatvena*).

The word *pratīcīna*, which denotes "liberation" (*apavarga*), has not been employed; however, how could the word *paścāt* (meaning "afterwards") express liberation when it is repeated? For liberation is one among the three [stages], so repetition (*vīpsā*) would be entirely irrelevant there. Nor can the explanation be "the part after and after," because of its lack of connection with the first [stage]; in relation to what would the first be "after"?

The orientation toward the east (prācīnāpavargatā) has been explicitly stated by Āpastamba and others; other Sūtras with the same meaning should be explained precisely in the manner I have described. How the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) has explained it by overriding the Paribhāṣā must be carefully examined. Regarding the Mantra, Baudhāyana accepts it as a single unit and has stated the deities; Kātyāyana also [accepts this] for the purpose of the deities. However, if the pouring out (ninayana) is intended for the deities, then in the event of the loss of the remnant (śeṣa), the pouring out should be performed with any water whatsoever, and the designation of the deity [remains]. But if it is merely a ritual disposal (pratipatti), it should be understood that there is no substitute, and the pouring out itself is omitted.
Or, having poured [the water] together, he heats it.

Having brought the two together in one place and poured them together, he subsequently heats what has gone onto the ground with a firebrand. As for the deities beginning with Ekata, they have been explained by Baudhāyana; even though they are distinct, because of the plural form in the phrase "those gods purified themselves in the Āpyas," their status as deities is mutually dependent through the formation of a *dvandva* compound. Thus, there is only a single mantra. Even in the view that there are three—namely, the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—the *prācīnāvīta* position does not apply; this has already been demonstrated in the *paribhāṣā*. Now follows the preparation of the altar (*vedi*).
To the west of the Āhavanīya fire, he prepares an altar (vedi) measuring the height of the sacrificer.

Starting from the western line of the Āhavanīya, he prepares the altar on the western side. The word *vedi* is a term denoting a consecrated space; therefore, the meaning is that one should consecrate a plot of ground measuring the height of the sacrificer by means of the consecrations to be described hereafter, and that [ground] becomes the *vedi*. It measures four *ara* lengths, which is to say ninety-six *aṅgulas*. [He should prepare it] according to the method stated in the Śulba-sūtra, extending transversely as far as required. 20.

The word "karoti" (he makes) is carried over [from the previous rule]. "Yāvarthā" means whatever the purpose or requirement may be; "tiraścī" means extended. To whatever extent of width is required for a space sufficient to place the oblations (*havis*), to that extent the width should be made. However, the amount to be given must indeed be the measure of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). This [formula], "idaṃ tasmai," belongs to the sacrificer. Since this is a ritual instrument mantra (*karaṇa-mantra*) and not a benedictory mantra (*āśīr-mantra*), it does not possess the property of being recited as a *japa*; rather, the performance of the rite occurs precisely at the conclusion of the mantra.

"By means of the *veda*, they found the altar, the mistress of the earth; that earth spread out over the earthly realms. She bears the embryo within the worlds; from that, the sacrifice is born every day. With this mantra, before the *stambayajus* rite, he sweeps the altar three times with the *veda*. He sweeps it once with the mantra, sweeping the whole [altar]; then, silently, during the second and third rounds, he sweeps as much space as is required for the altar to be formed, because at this point the altar has not yet been fully produced. Before the *stambayajus*, behind the [cut-off] grass-bundle... [text fragment]. Having taken hold... [text fragment]. [Note: The provided source text contains fragments of commentary regarding the ritual procedure (the *stambayajus* and the sweeping of the altar) and the state of the altar prior to its completion.]

19.146. The term *stambayajuḥ* is used here to imitate the *Brāhmaṇa* in order to exclude the possibility of an option (*vikalpa*), for an option is indeed seen in other Sūtras regarding the phrases "in front" (*purastāt*) and "behind" (*upariṣṭāt*). The *stambayajuḥ* is the carrying away of the clump of grass (*stamba*) with a sacrificial formula (*yajus*). Alternatively, this is the name for the portion of the clump being carried away.

And in this case, no etymological derivation based on its constituent parts is required, as is the case with the conventional term *aśvavāla*. Here, by the phrase "before the *stambayajus*," the act of carrying away is indicated through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), just as in the statement "at the full moon sacrifice, one undertakes the vow with *barhis*," the bringing of the *barhis* grass is indicated. The phrase "with four tufts" refers to the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).
He carries away the *stambayajus* from the eastern third part of the altar.

The dust, being joined with the *stambha* and the *yajus*, is thus described as being carried away. This is a rule regarding the location. He states that location with the words beginning "pūrva" (eastern half), etc. The altar (*vedi*) which is to be constructed is measured by the *śulba* according to its dimensions; in the middle of that, one measures thirty-two *aṅgulas* from the eastern half of the third part of the altar-ground—that is, from the third division of the altar situated in the eastern half—and [the place] where that measurement ends is thus described.

The word *vedi* (altar), although requiring a complement, is always compounded with the word *deśa* (place) as part of the third [syllabic] unit (*tritīya-pada*), because it is an obligatory term. This *vedi* word is connected both before and after [the *deśa* word]. Therefore, the place for the pouring of the *prokṣaṇī* water will be described as being to the east—not to the west—of the eastern abandoned third-part of the altar, but not to the west of the western abandoned third-part. The meaning is that one should remove the sacrificial post (*stambayajuḥ*) measuring thirty-two *aṅgulas*.

This "carrying away of the *stambayajus* grass" is not a primary act (*pradhānakarma*), but rather a subsidiary act (*guṇakarma*), because it is understood from the Brāhmaṇa text to be a purification (*saṃskāra*) of the altar (*vedi*). By carrying away the grass and dust from the vicinity of the altar, a visible purification is effected through the removal of its harshness; thus, the meaning of the sentence is that "the altar is purified by the carrying away of the *stambayajus*. Having taken up the wooden sword (*sphya*) with the formula, "Of the god thee... [and so forth].

The phrase "ādada" (I take), which is recited in the *Saṃhitā* as the remainder of a mantra, is employed here together with the preceding portion of the *adhivapana* (pouring) that is supplied by *anuvṛtti* (supply from a previous context). This is stated to indicate its application (*viniyoga*) as it is read in the *Brāhmaṇa* commentary. One should understand that the same applies to the earlier [mantras] such as "saṃ vapāmi" (I pour together).
He consecrates [the vessel] with the mantra, "Indrasya bāhur asi" (Thou art the arm of Indra); this is clear.

With the mantra, "Thou hast a thousand spikes and a hundred-fold brilliance," he sharpens its tip with a blade of *darbha* grass; with the words, "of keen brilliance," he sharpens the end—that is, he makes the tip of the *sphya* properly sharp, meaning he whets it. This is merely a ritual act (*dharma-mātra*) and not that the *sphya* actually becomes sharp through the sharpening. According to the *Mantra-Brāhmaṇa*, it is stated only that he wipes the upper edge all around with it.
With the mantra, "Thou art the armor of the earth," he places a blade of *darbha* grass either pointing eastward or northward.

In the case of Baudhāyana, it is the previously mentioned [measurement], because it has been observed [in his text]. The meaning is: at the eastern third part of the *vedi*. [Regarding the word] *yajuṣo*: [various readings exist]. [The text continues: "Having consecrated [the spot] with the formula, 'O Earth, thou art the place for sacrifice to the gods,' he strikes it with the wooden sword (*sphya*) upon that [spot]. [This concludes] the sixteenth section, accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. Page 147. 3. ka. kha. ga. ca.
