In that [spot], it is cut as if by the tip of a wooden sword (sphya), because of its very nature of being compacted. "Mā hiṃsiṣam" is the end of the mantra. "Yo mā hr̥dā" is for the sacrificer.
With the words "apahato 'raruḥ pṛthivyāḥ," he takes up the grass and the dust with the wooden sword, and also [recites] "apāraruṃ vadhyāsam."

The mantra is only this much: "Struck down is Araru from the earth. While cutting the grass, he takes the clod of earth from the edge of the dug-out pit with the wooden shovel (*spaya*), not with his hand—his hand providing assistance only where necessary—and carries it to the cow-pen (*vraja*) using the shovel alone, saying, "Go to the cow-stall.
The remainder [of the ritual] is that he carries the sacrificial refuse (*utkara*) from the altar (*vedi*) using the shovel alone.
"May the sky rain for you"—with these words he looks at the altar; "may Parjanya rain for you"—with these words he looks at the sacrificer.
The word "he looks" carries over from the preceding [sūtra].
Having placed his hands with the palms upward to the north, saying "Homage to the sky! Homage to the earth!", the Āgnīdhra sits down.
"To take hold of the mound" means to place both hands palm-upward with the fingers joined and extended;
at this point, he pours [the grain] for him upon the altar.

The mantra ends with *māmaug*. The Adhvaryu pours [the dust] down. Because of the subsequent mention of "again" (*punar*) and the reference to "this one" (*asmai*), there is no further qualification [of the agent]. What is poured down? By virtue of the context, the previously mentioned dust together with the clod of earth taken up by the wooden sword (*sphya*) is drawn back into the procedure. To the question "Where?", it is said: "at a *prakrama* from the altar. The word "altar" (*vedeḥ*) is in the ablative case; it is drawn back as "to the north of it. The meaning is that after a distance of two steps (*padadvaya*) has been traversed, measured by a *prakrama*.

What is meant by this? This is what is being said: having performed the taking up of the *stambayajus* from the eastern third part of the *vedi*, one then pours it out upon a spot situated to the north of the *vedi*, after stepping two steps outside the *vedi*. This very meaning has been made explicit by Āpastamba: "With the mantra 'Bind, O God Savitṛ,' he pours [the earth] out to the north-east, in the third part, on two footprints or on a measured space of the *vedi*."

The meaning demonstrated by the commentators through the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having turned northward on a spot near the altar, at a distance of one-third from the front part of the altar, he scatters [the earth]. To that *Āgnīdhra*, while instructing him on the meaning of the mantra—[variants: *tṛṇaṃ pāṃsum upī*]—[variants: *kārtham*]—[variants: *pratīkṣaka*]—[variants: *karau*]—[variant: *padapa*].

If it is asked why this is so, it is said: because in the mantra "Bind him, O God Savitṛ," the agent who is being instructed speaks in the second person (*madhyama-puruṣa*), while the respondent, addressing himself as the agent, says, "He who is bound away is the enemy. Therefore, instructing him in the act of binding, he pours [the earth] into the rubbish heap (*utkara*). Otherwise, the word "to him" (*asmai*) would be meaningless, and the word "away" (*apa*) as well. That [place] becomes the rubbish heap.

That spot where he pours [the earth] is designated by the word *utkara*. Although the term *utkara*—derived from the etymological analysis of the action as "that in which one scatters (utkirati) the dust along with the grass"—is based on its constituent parts (*avayava-anusaṃdhāna*), it is shown to be a conventional term (*rūḍha*) by the use of the pronoun "that" (*saḥ*), meaning "that very same [spot]. This location of the *utkara* becomes established.
With the formula, "Subdued is the evil-doer," the *Āgnīdhra* priest takes hold of the *utkara* with his joined palms.

One takes hold of the *utkara* (the heap of rubbish) and covers it, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra: "May he not release me from this. And Vāmana has explained this with the words, "Thus he says by way of non-release. The established meaning is that one takes [the earth] with a hollowed palm (*añjali*) that is deficient, so that the rival (*bhrātṛvya*), once placed in the *utkara*, is not released. Regarding this, the author of the *Bhāṣya* stated, "He pours [earth] into the hollowed palms of the *āgnīdhra*"; however, that is according to the intention of another *sūtra*, since it is so stated in the *Vaikhānasa-sūtra*. But since such a meaning is not perceived from our own *sūtra*, it is inconsistent with our *sūtra*.

Others consider that [this view] should be disregarded, because it has been stated even more clearly by Svāmin Āpastamba, whose commentary conveys the same meaning: for in the *Āpastamba* [Śrautasūtra], the qualification for the office of the *āgnīdhra* is not shown until the point of the scattering [of the grains], as it says, "The *āgnīdhra* receives [the grain] with his joined palms once it has been scattered. Such is indeed the intention of our own teacher.

Furthermore, as for the fact that the Āgnīdhra sits down after first placing his hands palm-upward, although the forming of the *añjali* (joined palms) is not explicitly mentioned there, it is intended to prevent an adversary from performing an *añjali* [to obstruct him]. One must remain equipped with armor; the purpose of the mantra and Brāhmaṇa is shown to be that, so that no delay occurs in the performance of the *añjali*, once one is armored, the adversary is seized immediately upon the scattering [of the earth] with the *stambayajus* formula for the sake of non-release.

It is well known and supported by reasoning that whoever wishes to restrain a wicked person unobserved stands first at a distance with his hands extended, and only afterwards seizes someone standing nearby;
having seized him, he remains there.
For it is only by means of an *añjali* joined from below that one can grasp someone on all sides, and not otherwise.
In this manner he strikes a second time; in this manner a third time.

Here, by the term "he strikes," the primary act of preparing the altar is indicated, which, being the principal element, extends by analogy (atideśa) from the initial subsidiary acts such as taking up [the grass] to the end of the formula "he sits down. The repetition "in this manner, in this manner" is for the purpose of indicating the application of the mantra to each other [of the three rounds]; therefore, the mantra is not used only in the first round, but in all three, according to the scriptural injunction: "three times with the Yajus-formula. He states the specific detail:
"May I not harm the roots of the auspicious plants"—with these words he strikes the second time.

In this context, in place of the formula "O Earth, thou art the sacrificial ground for the gods," this mantra is used: "Thou art the armor of the earth. This is the *tantra* (the underlying ritual framework), because of its pervasive application. He takes up the second [shovel] with the formula: "The enemy has been struck down from the earth, the sacrificial ground for the gods."

The three [formulas] beginning with "Come to mind" (*manaṃ gaccha*) are as before. However, there is no longer the sitting down of the Āgnīdhra nor the raising of the hands, because those two are occupied with the enclosing of the altar. "Bind them" (*badhāna*) is as before. Then the Āgnīdhra takes hold of the second [layer] with the formula, "The sorcerers have been struck down from the sacrificial ground. The word "second" is an adverbial modifier; however, the subsequent action—taking hold again with the joined palms and remaining seated—is the same up until the fourth layer. The Adhvaryu:
He strikes the third [time] with the formula, "May your drop not leap up to heaven.
This is clear.
He takes back the third [piece] with the formula, "Araru, the non-sacrificer to the gods, is driven away from the earth."
"Go to Vraja; may it rain for you"—these two [verses] are as before, ending with "vadhāna. The Āgnīdhra recites the third [verse], "avabāḍho 'ghaśaṃsaḥ," while he takes hold [of the vessel].
This has been explained. The Adhvaryu:
The fourth [act] is performed silently.
The taking away from the source, the carrying, the two lookings, and the two pourings are likewise performed silently. Regarding the throwing [of the grass], he says:
"He carries away all the darbha grass."
The rest is all as before. The Āgnīdhra takes up the fourth [portion] with the formula: "May your wealth not leap up to heaven.
There is no enclosing [of the fire] here. The term "he sits" (āste) is excluded, because there is no taking up [of the vessel] beforehand.
He encloses the altar with the wooden sword (*sphyá*).

This is the Adhvaryu’s prerogative. The enclosure is merely a declaration of what is about to be performed; it is for the purpose of demonstrating the meaning of the term "enclosure. By the subsequent ritual action, the site of the altar is enclosed—that is to say, it is surrounded, delimited, and established as a constituent part of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
With the formula, "May the Vasus enclose you," he draws a line toward the east on the south side.

"With the wooden sword," as before. To the south, starting from the southern shoulder and proceeding toward the southern hip, he draws a line eastward reaching as far as the southern shoulder. Although "eastward" is already established by the sense of the context, the explicit statement is made because it was previously stated that "he encloses from the front"; otherwise, due to the proximity of the rule regarding circumambulation, one might assume the movement is clockwise (pradakṣiṇa), and this is for the purpose of precluding that. "With the Gāyatrī metre" is the end of the mantra.
"The Rudras thee... [is used] to the west, directed northward.

"He writes the lines," as before; it ends with "with the *triṣṭubh* metre. In all cases, the explicit statement "towards the north" follows the wording of the mantra, for the purpose of precluding the completion [of the lines] toward the south when performing the joining.
With "O Ādityas, you... he draws [the line] from the north towards the east;
this is to be understood as before. While the act is being performed with "O Rudras, you...", the *yājamāna* formula is: "O Bṛhaspati, enclose [it]."
He raises the two shoulders of the altar facing east toward the Āhavanīya fire; the two hips face west toward the Gārhapatya fire; and it is depressed in the middle. ||2.1||

All of this is to be seen in the *Śulba* [Sūtra] commentary. Regarding the statement "he encloses the altar" (*vediṃ parigṛhṇāti*), which is established as a general rule, the sentence "he draws two lines toward the east on both sides of the Āhavanīya fire" makes it perfectly clear that these two [lines] terminate toward the east; the meaning is that for that purpose he draws an eastern line, by which the two edges of the altar become oriented toward the east. Similarly, the phrase "toward the west the two furrows" (*pratīcī gāṇī*) is stated as "toward the north behind" (*paścād udīcīm*) in order to accomplish its fulfillment—this is the intended sense.

Since the raising of the two shoulders (*aṃsau*) is observed here, the Bhāṣyakāra’s opinion is that the raising of the middle part should be performed; thus, the commencement is from the middle of the southern and northern enclosures. How can that [opinion] be consistent with the prohibition against grasping around [the middle]? [The Adhvaryu] says: "Bending down in the middle, crowded together—O men, come and prepare this altar, which is rich in wealth, rich in Rudras, and rich in Ādityas, upon the height of heaven, at the navel of the earth, so that this sacrificer may not suffer harm. This [altar], beloved by the gods, is in the lap of Aditi; O gods, all of you have delighted in it. May the increase of wealth enter the sacrificer. Having thus given the command, he proceeds.

In this context, although he says "he sends" (*preṣyati*) but does not specify what is to be sent, nevertheless, according to the manner already stated and based on the statements of Kātyāyana and Āraḍāma, it can be said that either the *āmantraṇa* (invitation) or the sending of oneself (*ātmapreṣa*) is intended; yet, even so, what is to be done by means of what has been sent?

Regarding the phrase "O men, prepare this altar," only this much is understood as being within the scope of human capability; everything else is mere praise, for it cannot be performed by men. Thus, since the function of a *praiṣa* (an injunction to act) is untenable here, it is proper that one should merely recite the mantra according to the rule for mantras used for transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*) purposes, just as in the case of the formula "O cow, [be] the purifier for milking. Baudhāyana says exactly the same: "O men, drive away... and so forth.

Having removed the uppermost layer with the wooden sword (*sphya*), he throws it onto the rubbish heap (*utkara*) with the words: "Araru is driven away from the earth; bring [the gods] to the sacrifice to the gods."
The Veda-maker himself [says]:

"With the mantra *devasya savituḥ sava* (at the impulse of the god Savitṛ), he digs. Or [he digs with]: "*devasya savituḥ save karma kṛṇvanto mānuṣā mā vaḥ śivā oṣadhayo mūlaṃ hiṃsiṣam*" (At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, we humans performing the rite—may I not harm the root of you, the auspicious plants).
The word *vedhasaḥ* (of the ordainers) marks the end of the preceding [mantra]. It should be performed ending toward the east, using the very same [spade] as before.

[One should dig] two finger-breadths, three finger-breadths, four finger-breadths, as much as a furrow (*sītā*), or as much as the path [of a wheel]; or as far as the white part of the heel. Regarding the measurement of the depth: it begins with three finger-breadths and so on. A *sītā* is a furrow made by a plow; a *varman* is a hole for a chariot. "As far as the heel" refers to the fourth case-ending used in the sense of the sixth year. The heel (*pārṣṇi*) is the back part of the foot; "as much as" refers to its extent. "White" (*śveta*)—because it is an adjective, it is neuter; "or as much as that" means up to the white part near the heel. The verb "one should dig" (*khanet*) is connected to every instance. One does not dig deeper than these measurements.

The measure of the *dhyāla* and so forth is the *mātrā*; having exceeded these measures, one should not dig—that is to say, one should not dig more than that. [Objection: But how could there be any possibility of excess when the rules are clearly prescribed? [Reply: True; this is stated for the purpose of permitting even a deficiency. Precisely because of this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), the meaning is: "Let there be either a deficiency or equality compared to these measures, but let there never be an excess.
To the south, he makes it higher, filled with loose soil (*purīṣavatī*), and sloping toward the east and the north.

This is an imitation of the Brāhmaṇas for the purpose of recalling the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). In that context, the statement "sloping toward the west and the south" is intended to demonstrate a censure regarding the inclination toward two directions; its practical application will be stated later. [The ground] on the southern side should be slightly elevated; this is an instruction for an elder. "Containing loose soil" (*purīṣavatī*) means it is dug up and possesses such soil; one should dig with such [earth] so that the soil comes up from above by digging, but one should not dig merely by piercing the surface of the dry ground.

[The ground should be] sloping toward the east, or toward the north, or toward the northeast; [that is,] low-lying. Although it would have been sufficient to say "sloping toward the east and north" (*prāgudak-pravaṇām*), the heavy formulation is used so that there may be a connection with each term individually. Thus, there are three alternatives: sloping toward the east, sloping toward the north, or sloping toward both the east and the north. The word "or" (*vā*) is not stated to exclude the third option, but rather to show that the alternative will arise naturally due to the contradiction [of the requirements]. For this very reason, Āpastamba says: "Sloping toward the east, or sloping toward the east and north. He cuts away with the wooden sword (*sphya*) that part which exceeds the root [of the grass].
That which remains over from the root-plants, he cuts off with the wooden sword (*sphya*).
As for the loose soil (*purīṣa*) that remains over, he causes it to go to the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).
The meaning is that when making the slope or leveling [the ground], whatever loose soil remains over should not be led to another location; rather, it is to be discarded right there on the outside.

[The altar] with imported soil is for one desiring cattle. For that sacrificer who desires cattle, the Adhvaryu should prepare an altar for the New and Full Moon sacrifices with soil brought from elsewhere. Having brought earth from another place, he pours it into the middle of the altar; this is called "imported soil" (*āhāryapurīṣā*). Satyāṣāḍha, in his *Śrautasūtra*, states the procedure for that as follows:
Having performed that which was done prior to the digging, one digs up the loose earth (*purīṣa*) with the mantra and carries it away.

The meaning is that, having dug at another spot with the mantra "Of the god whose father is the sun," one should bring that loose earth to the altar (*vedi*) which has not yet been dug. When the intention has been formed, "Desiring cattle, I shall prepare an altar with brought-in loose earth" (*āhāryapurīṣāṃ vedim*), one should bring the loose earth by digging and thus make it an altar with brought-in loose earth.
In this case, one prepares the altar on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*).

According to the maxim that "an undertaking is for the sake of restriction once [the general rule] is established," it follows that one constructs the altar (*vedi*) right here on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), whereas on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), one does so on the preceding day. It is precisely to indicate this that it was not stated previously; otherwise, by mentioning the *sattra* either after the construction of the altar or before the fetching of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the altar would have been located only there on the new moon day, and not here as well. For that very purpose, it is stated there that having performed this, one should observe the fast, and that on the new moon day, one should perform exactly what has been prescribed as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Thus, in that context...

Since the construction of the *vedi* (altar) is not explicitly mentioned [in the preceding rule], it should be understood that its performance is explained in that very context. Regarding the phrase "having performed only that much," this [subsequent section] is commenced on the basis of two alternative views. [The first view: On the previous day, on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), [the word] "he performs" (*karoti*) is understood to carry over. In that case, because the scripture states "having made the *veda*, he makes the *vedi*," and since it is impossible to construct the *vedi* without the *veda*, one performs it immediately after the *veda* situated at its proper place; for this reason, no specific location is mentioned in this view, as it is established by implication alone—this is the sense. He states another alternative view:

[This occurs] prior to the bringing of the *barhis* grass. In this alternative (*pakṣa*), having moved the *veda* from its place and placed it to the east by implication, one subsequently prepares the *vedi*. Then follows the taking of the *bahirgha*, the cutting of the tips of the branches, the making of the *śākhāpavitra*, and so forth, as before. Although there is no word such as "or" (*vā*) to distinguish between the two alternatives, the authoritative source has been cited and should not be forgotten. Regarding the preparation of the *vedi* on the previous day, he asks: "If there is the option of addressing and obtaining permission from the *Brahman* during the subsequent tracing (*parigraha*), how would the *vedi* be prepared?
To this he replies: "Whatever [is done] prior to the second tracing, that he performs on the previous day; or [he may do it] together with the second tracing."

The alternative view is that after the sprinkling of water following the second tracing (*uttara-parigrāha*), when there is a specific modification at the *sadyaska* (immediate) time, the ritual action regarding the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) and so forth is performed with the Brahman priest as previously described, or "together" with him. Alternatively, the second tracing is preceded by an invitation and a permission;
he says, "O Brahman, I shall perform the second tracing," and having invited him, he performs it.
It has already been stated that once the *praṇava* is uttered, [the Brahman] performs [his part].

Some authorities prescribe the opposite order: that the first tracing (parigraha) is performed with *mantras*, and the subsequent one with *yajus* formulas. In our own recension (*śākhā*), the first tracing is taught with the *mantras* beginning with "O Vasus, you [protect] this," and they prescribe those same for the subsequent tracing. However, other recensions will describe a different first tracing with the *yajus* formulas beginning with "Thou art the earth" (*pṛthivyasi*). Thus, the order is reversed. [End of] Chapter 10: [From] the *Mahādevakṛtavaijayantī* commentary. 153. Iti viparītam. (Thus, it is reversed. (Note: The various manuscript variants regarding the specific mantras and the sequence are indicated by the abbreviations ka, ga, ca, cha, sa, ha, ḍa, etc., as per the critical apparatus.)

Although both are *mantras*, nevertheless, in the Brāhmaṇa there is a conventional usage of the term *yajuṣ* for those [formulas] that follow the *pāṅkta-śaṃsan* (the fivefold recitation), as in the expression "like a *yajus*. While the word *mantra* is applied to those *yajus*s expressed by that very term in its general sense, it is used in a specific sense with reference to the *ṛc*s because they are composed in two-footed meters, as seen in cases such as "vasavas tvā... and so forth. In this Āraṇyaka, regarding the *vikṛtis* (modified sacrifices), wherever the *pūrva-parigraha* (the first enclosure) is performed using only the *ṛks*, the sequence (*krama*) and the *mālā* (garland/arrangement) are determined by that very *ṛk*-tradition.

Otherwise, the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the *Bāma-gava* mantra, which prescribes the application of the mantra beginning with "vasavas tvā," would be contradicted. To explain: the passage—"They led [the horse] eastward by means of Agni, southward by the Vasus, westward by the Rudras, and northward by the Ādityas"—is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended to establish the connection of the mantras with the directions. Since it has been stated that "one wins by means of Agni alone in the front," if this were not restricted to the ritual layout (*vihāra*), it would contradict the *Paśu* and *Varuṇapraghāsa* sacrifices. Therefore, it is said to be "contrary," because of the contradiction between the Yajus-mantras and the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the Brāhmaṇa in the previously mentioned determination.

The meaning is that the sequence belonging to another recension (*śākhā*) should be adopted. By this, the purpose of the term *mantra*—as that which possesses the nature of protecting through reflection—is also stated, since the *Brāhmaṇa* describes the protection from the enemy by means of the mantras themselves: "With the words 'Those Vasus [protect you],' they enclosed him on the south. Thus, for those belonging to other recensions, the mantras are for the purpose of the northern enclosure. This, however, is inconsistent.

For the prior appropriation of the earth was intended for the sake of obtaining it from one's rivals; since it was impossible for the sacrificers to perform the mere act of delimitation with mantras when that [earth] had not been obtained, there is no contradiction regarding the purpose of that [appropriation]. Therefore, the contradiction with the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) need not be resolved. Consequently, it is proper that the original form (*prakṛti*) remains unchanged in modifications (*vikṛti*); thus it is also in the case of the modifications:
"Thou art Truth" on the south, "Thou art the seat of Truth" on the west, and "Thou art the glory of Truth" on the north.
The word "he takes hold" (*parigṛhṇāti*) is understood [from the preceding context]. This is the sequence for one's own *śākhā*. The term *parigrāha* is used here in its etymological sense.
With the mantra, "Thou art *svadhā*, thou art *svadhā*," he sweeps [the line] westward with the wooden sword (*sphya*).
The word "thou art" (*asi*) is at the end; the word "earth" (*bhūmi*) is the remainder. He levels it up to the western leaf. Here, the earth is called "become" (*bhūtā*).

Having consecrated [the earth] with the mantra "purā krūrasya" (with the word "bailim" understood as the remainder), and having concluded the mantra with "yajante," he fixes the wooden sword (sphya) crosswise at the rear third of the altar's back half. Then he issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the dipping-spoon (sruva) and the offering-ladles (sruc); gird the wife; bring the clarified butter."

The latter half has been explained by the former half. The third part of the rear [section] is also deficient; thus, the rear portion (paścārdharaṅga) should be made in the very back, due to the force of the word "rear-half" (paścārdha). Immediately after the first third-part, or in the middle part, he—standing with his hands facing north on the ground, having made it firm—issues the formal command (saṃpreṣyati). Since the Adhvaryu is defined by the Yajurveda, all duties pertaining to the Adhvaryus, such as the sounding of the *tisrasāraṇa* and so forth, belong to him.

Regarding the term "he himself" (*svayaṃ*), there is no statement here [in the text] by which one might conclude that the other [the *adhvaryu*] is characterized by the verbal command, as in the case of the rule: "By means of this verbal characteristic, the other [should eat]" (*vacanalakṣaṇa itaraḥ*). Nor is there an explicit direction through an indicative mark (*liṅga*) or a Brāhmaṇa passage, such as "Distribute the fires" (*agnīn vihara*) or "He gives the command for the fires" (*agnīn saṃpreṣyati*). Furthermore, it is not possible [for the *adhvaryu* to act], because this [act of eating] produces a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) directed toward oneself when the time has arrived.

The observations regarding the injunctions directed toward oneself and the supporting indicative marks (*liṅga*) have already been established; these must not be forgotten. [Objection: "It is not the teacher's desire that the work be performed by another," as stated in another Sūtra. Having observed this, those skilled in ritual practice say that the action is performed by the one who maintains the fire (*agnihotrin*) due to his proficiency. [Response: This view is to be disregarded because of the previously mentioned principles and because of contradictions in other Sūtras. Thus, the determination regarding the injunction (*praiṣa*) should be understood elsewhere in the same way.

In the phrase *idhmābarhiḥ*, the mention of *idhma* first is for the purpose of fixing the sequence according to the rule "the feminine [noun] ending in a short vowel comes first" (*ajādyadantam*), because the sequence is prescribed as "the fuel (*idhma*) to the south and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) to the north. Even for one who has multiple wives, the formula *patnīṃ saṃ nahyati* (he girds the wife) remains unchanged; for the Teacher will state that there is no modification (*ūha*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Since the mantra applies universally to all primary materials (*prakṛti*) without distinction, there is no contradiction even when the word "wife" (*patnī*)—by virtue of its generic sense—is capable of signifying multiple wives. Furthermore, the singular number attached to the noun stem (*prātipadika*), being part of the objective case (*uddeśya*), is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). Regarding that, he describes the method for placing the *prokṣaṇī* water: having poured water into the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle upon which a strainer (*pavitra*) has been laid, and having drawn the wooden sword (*sphya*) toward the north, while holding it within the altar, he pours [the water] onto the track of the wooden sword and places it on the footprint of the wooden sword with the formula, "O you who sit together."

Wherever the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle stands, right there, having brought water in that vessel and set aside the wooden sword (*sphya*) at its fixed place for the sake of proceeding, he should draw the water toward the north with the sword held crosswise; then, as if making a path by slightly moving it away to the north, holding it with his left hand and taking the *agnihotra-havaṇī* with his right, he should pour some of the water contained therein onto the previously prepared mark made by the sword, without spilling it, pouring it down so that it does not touch [the ground].

According to the statement of Āpastamba, having poured [the water] so that it does not touch the wooden sword (*sphya*), at the moment of the formal command (*praiṣa*), he places the wooden sword upon its footprint— the place where it was fixed horizontally— with the mantra,
while meditating upon whomsoever he may hate.

Whomever the sacrificer hates, that person the Adhvaryu priest should meditate upon in his own form or by means of his name; this is an act of remote assistance (*ārādupakāraka*). Although there is a supplementary statement in the Brāhmaṇa, "He whom he should hate, him he should meditate upon; thus he strikes him with impurity," nevertheless, that is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) and does not prescribe malevolent magic (*abhicāra*); this is shown by the fact that such an explanatory passage is not recited [in the ritual context].

Just as in the absence of the word *kāma* (desire) [the statement] is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) regarding the result, so too in the absence of the word *abhicaran* (performing malevolent magic), the phrase that conveys the sense of being contrary to the enemy is also merely an explanatory praise; it is not, however, an injunction for the performance of enmity. The term *svāhā* is to be understood everywhere. Even in the absence of an actual enemy, the enemy is indeed evil (*pāpman*), because of his hostility; this is also evident from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the text: "He strikes down evil itself, his adversary.
