"You are the hundred-edged, made of wood, the slayer of enemies"—with these words, he throws the wooden sword (sphya) onto the rubbish heap (utkara). He places the wooden sword on the spot of the rubbish heap; he throws it from a slight distance so that, once released, it falls upon the rubbish heap.
From the front, he pushes back toward himself the thicker end.

Having taken up the *sphya* from the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) facing the east, he holds it at the thick end over the area where the *mucī* is located; then, without washing his hands, he strikes the vessels but does not touch the altar until the spreading of the grass.

One should not touch the vessels without having washed one's hands; and even though the hands must be washed after the spreading [of the grass], one should not touch the altar before that spreading—this is understood by implication. Otherwise, if washing were prescribed only prior to the spreading, and many other ritual acts were likewise enjoined, what occasion would there be for touching the altar with unwashed hands before the spreading?
One washes both hands, washes the wooden sword (sphya), but does not touch its tip.

Although the first two elements have the same meaning, they are distinct for the sake of following the traditional recitation (*śruti*). At the time of washing the wooden sword (*sphya*), one touches its name-part with the hand; this is a prohibition against washing the tip, but rather a prohibition against touching it at all. Otherwise, for the sake of brevity, one would simply say, "He washes the wooden sword. By this, it is meant that the washing of the other parts should not be done merely with a stream of water, but rather with the hand, such that even the removal of dirt must be performed.
To the north, he places the consecrated fuel and sacrificial grass; the fuel to the south and the grass to the north. || 22 ||
Thus ends the sixth paṭala in the first praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. || 6 ||

First, taking hold of the *samit* (fuel-stick) and the *idhma* (faggot) together as a whole, he places them with both hands, one on the right and one on the left, along with the oblation (*sahoma*), as it is understood that they are to be placed together. Thus ends the sixth chapter in the first book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*, composed by Mahādeva.
Now begins the seventh chapter:
With the fringes of the *veda* grass, he cleanses the *sruva* and the *sruk* ladles together.

The "remnants" (*parivāsitā*) of the Veda are its terminal portions; by this, the rejection of the position stated by Baudhāyana is expressed. In that regard, some maintain that there is no sequential performance (*kāṇḍānupūrvya*) of a single ritual act (*padārtha*), such as wiping (*saṃmārga*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and heating (*niṣṭapana*). We, however, say "together" (*saha*) in order to demonstrate the simultaneous performance of the acts. Furthermore, the coexistence of the *prāśitra* portion has been refuted; for a collective wiping of these [portions] is not possible, because each possesses its own specific, fixed property.

This is the proposition regarding what is about to be stated: by making it known that in the context of the *saṃmārjana* (cleansing), whatever is mentioned constitutes its constituent part (*aṅga*), a restriction is established that these ritual properties (*dharma*) apply wherever the *saṃmārjana* occurs—whether [the cleansing] is performed by dividing [the vessels] individually or not.

The term *vedaprāntān* (the ends of the Veda) should be understood as being modified into the accusative plural case (*vedaprāntān*) and carried over [from the previous rule]. Having divided as many vessels as there are to be cleansed, one performs the cleansing with each individual part and then casts each one into the fire; this same procedure applies at the end for all [vessels] in the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), with the distinction that the casting is performed multiple times. Alternatively, "without dividing" means the cleansing is done with them all together.
They may be placed face upwards, or sideways; or else two are placed face upwards and the *upabhṛt* ladle is placed sideways.

This very rite involves the *sruva*-ladles; at the time of the ritual with the path, he offers three *pārthavila* oblations turned upward. The word "api vā" (or) is used in the sense of an alternative.

Having consecrated them with the mantra, "You are unsharpened, destroyers of rivals," [he offers] the four beginning with the *sruc*. Because there are many *sruc* ladles, they are referred to in the feminine gender. The mantra is recited once.

Having taken them with both hands simultaneously for the sake of efficiency, using the formula, "Ghṛtācī, Retas, Agni calls you for the sacrifice to the gods," he heats them over the Āhavanīya or the Gārhapatya fire with the formula,

"Pratyuṣṭam" (Burnt away!). This arrangement— wherein the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* are held in the right hand and the *dhruvā* in the left— is not contradicted by the rules stated by Baudhāyana and Vaikhānasa.

The passage ends with *niṣṭapāmi*. Therein, by means of the *tṛṇa* grass, he heats [the ladle] while it is joined [to the fire]; this is a form of a transitive verb, meaning "he makes something slightly heated. With the words *goṣṭhaṃ mā nirmṛkṣam*, he cleanses the *sruva* ladle on all sides: from the front toward the interior, he cleanses the bowl on all sides, and with the roots [of the grass], the handle.

The mantra ends with *saṃmārṣṭi*. The injunction is *yuvaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*. Here, the parts to be wiped from the inside are the tip, middle, and root of the enclosing sticks (*parivāsana-darya*). However, for the *sruva* ladle, the application is to the middle part. The suffix *-tas* in *antaratas* has the sense of the locative case. *Bilāvakāśe* means "in the hollowed-out space. How is it "repeatedly" (*abhyākāram*)? It is formed with the suffix *ṇamul* in the sense of frequency; the meaning is "again and again. Again, where? Everywhere within the hollow.

On all the outer sides of the opening, starting from the front of the hole with the syllables *ka, ka, ca, ṭa, ṭha, i*, and so forth—this is the meaning: beginning with a single wiping on each side, the completion of the wiping should be performed precisely within the space of the hole itself. Thus, one repeatedly wipes only within the space of the hole, whereas elsewhere the wiping is done only once.

If repetition were intended in every case, then one would read "snūvam abhyākāram" without distinction for the sake of connecting it [to all]. Therefore, the connection is only with "antarataḥ," and not with "abhyākāram. In this way, the repetition would have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*), because the wiping away of dust from within occurs only through repetition and not otherwise; in that context, even a restrictive rule regarding the number [of repetitions] is not intended. However, if it had an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*), then there would be an intention to specify the number three.

One should say "three times" precisely for the sake of brevity; thus it is established that this practice of wiping the space has a visible purpose. Furthermore, because it serves a visible purpose, the repetition must indeed be performed so as to encompass all parts, and not just once—this is proven. Having wiped the base of the staff with the roots of the *parivāsana* grass, ending toward the east, starting from the base up to the neck, he wipes it once; however, for the middle part, he does not wipe both inside and out, because that was already accomplished previously.

In this context, regarding the single ladle (*khuvam*) which is prescribed as the substance for the established procedure, the mantra is performed only once at the beginning; for it has been defined that "the mantra is uttered only once when there is a single substance, because the action is not distinct. Nor can it be argued that this rule is set aside and the mantra must be repeated when there is a plurality of substances, because the ladle is not a composite substance (*saṃsargidravya*).

For substances that come into contact, such as the clarified butter (*ājya*) and others, are designated as a single substance by virtue of being subsumed under a common genus; this has been explained there and is further elaborated here for the sake of avoiding forgetfulness. Furthermore, the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) of the ladles (*srucaḥ*) must be performed starting from their bases up to the ends of their handles, ending toward the east, because no other method is observed in any of the ritual manuals (*sūtras*).

Furthermore, although some commentators, by pointing to an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the Brāhmaṇa, explain that one should wipe the staff downward from top to bottom and upward from bottom to top, others do not accept this at all, because there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to override the rules for moving eastward (*prāṅnyāya*) and northward (*udaṅnyāya*).

As for the Brāhmaṇa passage which they cite as an indicative mark (*liṅga*), stating, "Therefore, the hairs on the upper side are directed forward (*prāñci*) and those on the lower side are directed backward (*pratyañci*)," that too is not [conclusive]. For this [passage] is an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) intended to justify the two methods of cleaning the *juhū* ladle—namely, that one cleans it from the top downwards in a forward direction (*prācīm*) and likewise from the bottom upwards in a backward direction (*pratīcīm*)—as these two methods of terminating toward the east (*prāgapavarga*) and terminating toward the west (*pratyagapavarga*) have been prescribed. It does not, however, establish the state of terminating toward the west or the east in the case of the shaving of the head (*muṇḍana*).

An explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) does not constitute an injunction because it does not prescribe an action; furthermore, there is no evidence for assuming an injunction elsewhere based on an explanatory passage intended for another purpose, and this would contradict the context—so let us leave that matter aside. Nor is it the case that the [staff] is obtained through the analogy of the *araṇi*, because the ladles (*sruk* and *sruva*) are arm-length and the fire-drill wood (*araṇi*) occupies the place of the vessel. Even if it were of the measure of an *araṇi*, the vessel could still be only half the length of an *araṇi*. As for the claim that the vessel’s length is equal to the *araṇi* from its front hair to its back hair, enough with such excessive effort. Moreover, even according to the *Bhāṣya*, the orientation ending toward the east (*prāgapavargatā*) is not contradicted.
One offers speech and breath as the *juhū* ladle: with the tips facing eastward, with the middle parts inwardly curved toward the west, and with the bases outwardly on the handle.

In this mantra-sentence, due to the absence of a verb, either the action must be indicated through the word *iṣe* and so forth, or an ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) must be supplied. Between these two options, the ellipsis is more appropriate because it is based on direct scriptural statement (*śrauta*). Since the preceding [mantra] is unsuitable, the subsequent one—characterized by the feminine gender—is supplied. That [mantra] is: *mā nirmṛkṣaṃ vājinīṃ tvā sapatnasāhīṃ saṃmārjmi*. This same principle should be understood for the passage *cakṣuḥ śrotram* as well. By the word *saṃmārṣṭi* (he cleanses), which is carried over from the preceding [mantra], the connection is made with the word *juhūm* (the offering-ladle).

158. According to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: "Internally, facing east, with the tips [of the blades], ending towards the east, starting from the opening up to the tip—this has been explained elsewhere. Externally, facing west, with the middle parts; 'the vessel itself externally' and 'internally of that very same thing' is understood from the context. The middle portion of the *darbha* used for cleansing, facing west, starting from the tip up to the joint of the handle of the vessel, and the root-handle—as before, ending towards the east."
"Eye and ear"—with these words, he places the *upabhṛt* ladle with its tips facing westward, its middle parts inward, and its bases outward; the handle [is placed] facing eastward.
Starting from the base, it faces westward; starting from the joint, it extends to the tip facing eastward. The rest has been explained.
"Offspring and the womb"—with these words, he places the *dhruvā* ladle as one does the *sruva*.

From the tip of the sweeping-brush (*saṃmārga*) toward the interior of the hole, and likewise from the exterior starting at the joint of the handle (*daṇḍa-saṃdhi*), one brings [the brush] back along the back to the limit of the base, leading it through the channel (*praṇālī*) so that the completion (*apavarga*) occurs right in the hole. In this same manner for the southern and northern sides as well, the completion occurs in the hole; the bases [of the brushes] are handled as before. There is no application of the *darbha* grass to the middle here. Thus, the rule is that repetition (*abhyāsa*) is mandatory everywhere in the hole, whereas elsewhere it is merely a ritual duty (*dharma-mātra*); the mantra is recited once for each vessel—this is the summary. One does not mix together what has been swept and what has not been swept.

In this context, although there is a prohibition against contact between cleaned and unclean vessels, since Āpastamba has stated that this applies to all vessels by prescribing, "the cleaned ones [should be used] with the unclean," the same should be understood for us as well. Furthermore, regarding contact, the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) prescribed in other ritual manuals (*kalpa*) is "heating and wiping" (*niṣṭapana-sammārjana*); in our own *sūtra*, it is simply "heating. He heats it as previously described.
Since heating is preceded by taking up the vessel, he takes it up with the mantra "O Agni, protect me from the heat" (*vatācīrata*) and heats it while reciting "it is burnt away" (*pratyuṣṭam*).

"O food-eater, do not destroy my food, offspring, and prosperity; I cleanse thee, O vigorous one, the subduer of rivals," with these words he cleanses the *prāśitra-haraṇa* vessel all around its cavity and the handle with its base.

In the silent rites (*tūṣṇīka*), the taking up and the final pouring out (*ādāna-niṣpana*) [are performed] because of the contradiction with the plural number found in the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra. Wherever there is the cleaning of the vessels (*pātra-saṃmārjana*), it has been shown that the preliminary and subsequent subsidiary acts (*pūrva-paścima-aṅgāni*)—which consist solely of consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) accomplished by the mantra—are excluded, due to the contradiction with the indicative mark, as they are to be avoided. As for the rule "with the *agra* blades inwardly," since it was not stated previously, it simply does not exist [in this context]. If it were so, one would have stated it more concisely as "like the *sruc*."

Therefore, having brought [the grass] from behind with the tips [of the blades] facing forward, there is a release [of the grass] into the hole; likewise on both sides, it should be described as being directed inwardly toward the *dhruvā* vessel. The handle is [prepared] with the roots as before. Here, the specific detail mentioned by Āpastamba should be adopted, as it is not stated in our own sūtra: "Having sprinkled [it], he places it on the *darbha* grass to the north of the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), or behind it."

Baudhāyana has also stated that one should place [the ladles] on the grass at the *utkara* with this formula; Vaikhānasa has stated that having heated the *sruva* and *sruk* ladles and the *prāśitra-haraṇa* vessel, one places them to the north of the edge of the altar (*vedi-śroṇi*). After that, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) may be performed or not, but the placing (*āsādana*) must certainly take place. Thus ends the section. [End of] Paṭala 70, from the *Vejayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva. 159.

"The craft of heaven is spread out, resting upon the heights of the earth; by means of that which has a thousand branches, we destroy our rival—Svāhā! Having sprinkled the broom-brushes with water, he places them in the fire on whichever side he has swept.

Although the specific term "cleansing" (*saṃmārjanāni*) has been employed, nevertheless, having unified the separate cleansings of the *anuvāka*, the *prāśitra*, and the *saṃmārga*, he places them together. However, in the absence of such division, he sprinkles all those things indicated by that word and places them where the cleansing takes place. The locative case in "in whichever [place]" (*yatarasmin*) denotes proximity, for there is no cleansing of vessels within the fire itself. He sprinkles silently and places [the items] with a mantra, because the mantra serves the purpose of the primary ritual act.

Regarding the statement that "the Veda belongs to Prajāpati" according to the injunction of the *prājāpatya* ascetic and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), as well as the sacrificer’s formula "This is for Prajāpati," that is not so; for here there is no designation of a deity because Prajāpati is not perceived through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, and because [the offering] is a duty of disposal (*pratipatti-dharma*). On this point, Baudhāyana says: "Then, having led the wife past the space between the fires..."—thus the wife has entered. Āpastamba says: "To the west of the Gārhapatya fire, facing upwards," and so forth.
Baudhāyana says that she should sit down to the south behind the Gārhapatya fire. Therefore, that [view] is contrary to the sequence for me.
With the formula "Seeking favor," he binds the wife with a triple-stranded cord of Muñja grass having a loop on one side; she remains either sitting with her knees raised or standing.

The mantra ends with *sukṛtāyakam*. *Mauja* means made of *muñja* grass; it refers to that particular kind of rope by which one is bound at the feet or the neck with a noose when captured. She whose thighs (*ūrū*) and knees (*jānunī*) are [thus bound] is seated; this is one specific view, while the second view holds that she remains standing and not seated.

In this context, if the word *patnī* is in the nominative case (*prathamā*) and [the verb] is used in the active sense (*kartari*), then the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the form *saṃnayate* would have to denote the agent; however, since the object must be supplied as "himself" (*ātmānam*), then the use of the active voice (*parasmaipada*) in *saṃnahyati* and the accusative case (*dvitīyāvibhakti*) in *patnīm* would be contradictory. On the other hand, if the suffix in *saṃnahyate* denotes the passive/objective sense (*karmaṇi*), then the first person singular (*uttamapuruṣa*) in grammatical agreement (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with "desiring" (*āśāsāna*) and so forth would be contradictory. The [text] is supported by the Adhvaryu priest, while the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is: "She says, 'Desiring goodwill... (*āśāsānā saumanasam ity āha*).

Having made [the sacrifice] complete by means of the Madhyama-tantra, he fulfills it with a benediction (*āśis*). Thus, the Brāhmaṇa portion conveys that the accomplishment of the fruit which constitutes the meaning of the mantra is the primary purpose (*mukhya-kārya*). For that purpose, the employment of the mantra is for the sake of conformity with the *uttama-puruṣa* (first person), while the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) acts as the instigator (*prayojaka*) for the sake of the wife’s successful execution. Considering that this is established by such reasoning, the Teacher composed the Sūtra following the model of the Brāhmaṇa.

Āpastamba, however, has stated: "According to some, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite. But the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that the recitation of the mantra is the path; yet, [his claim] that it accomplishes the binding of the girdle even at that time is not consistent. Nor is it consistent to say that one person causes another to utter the instrument-mantra (*karaṇamantra*). Therefore, what Āpastamba has stated is simply a specific injunction from another Vedic branch (śākhā) which says, "He causes someone to recite."

He binds [the sacrificer] by means of reciting the *ṛtvij-mantra*. By means of the mantra being recited, which serves as the instrument, there arises mindfulness; through that mindfulness, the binding is effectively accomplished. Without this, the binding would not be properly performed. Thus, the wife also binds [the sacrificer] with that same effort and recitation; therefore, neither the Sūtra nor the Brāhmaṇa is contradicted, but rather they are both supplemented. Enough with these alternative views.

One should not gird the garment; that is, one does not gird it over the cloth by making it the target. Although the girding of a woman is indeed not applicable over a garment already worn, nevertheless, because there is a prohibition against what is obtained through a specific injunction from another *śākhā*, there is an option (*vikalpa*). Āpastamba, however, has shown this very option. The middle voice (*parasmaipada*) in the word "girds" (*saṃnahyet*) depends upon an instigating agent. Having made a knot on the right side of the navel—one that is not loose—with the formula, "May Pūṣan tie your knot," he draws it around to the left side of the navel with the formula, "May it not stand against you."

Having formed a knot on the northern side of the navel, it is explained that the making of the *śikhā-granthi* (topknot-knot) is performed with the words "niṣṭāya. This must not be forgotten. He brings that knot toward himself by drawing it across from the right side. Since this is considered a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the wife, it is repeated for each wife of one who maintains the three sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), because the singular number is not intended to be significant; it is repeated for each principal act (*pradhāna*). [She says: "O Agni Gṛhapati, call upon me. Standing, she worships the *Gārhapatya* fire.

One who was sitting on his feet and was armored then rises and stands near [the fire]. It should not be argued that the rising is already established by the very fact that one "stands near" (*upatiṣṭhate*). For, according to the rule *upa-mantra-karaṇe* (Pāṇini 1.3.25), the ātmanepada suffix is prescribed; thus, in this context, the meaning of the verbal root and its suffix is not "rising," but rather "requesting a blessing with humility, preceded by the joining of the palms (*añjali*) while employing a mantra. As it has been said: "He stands near this [fire] for the sake of requesting a blessing for the one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). Therefore, the text prescribes the rising as something distinct from the act of standing near.

Just as there is an act of worship (*upasthiti*) performed while seated—such as when one approaches the *Āhavanīya* fire after rising for each subsequent oblation—the same applies here. Although this is a ritual action that assists from a distance (*ārādupakāraka*), it repeats with each performance (*pratipad*). The principle that "actions for the sake of another may be performed by a single person" does not apply here, because that rule pertains only to actions for the sake of another. Furthermore, if one were to argue that there is no repetition of the performance because the purpose is to produce the new transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the archetype (*prakṛti*), even so, it is established that since the worship consists of a prayerful petition based on desire, the prayers of the performer repeat with each performance, as they constitute a refinement of that [desire].

"O wives of the gods, call upon me!"—with these words, he worships the wives of the gods behind the Gārhapatya fire. The phrase "he worships" carries over from the previous context. The meaning is that, standing in the region behind the Gārhapatya, he worships while keeping in mind that the wives of the gods reside there; for the Brāhmaṇa states that this is the place of the wives of the gods. He also performs a counter-worship: "O wife, this is your world; homage be to you; do not harm me," as he gazes at that very same spot.

He gazes only at the western part of the *gārhapatya* fire, and not at the eastern part; this remainder of the mantra is a primary action (*pradhānakarma*), as it were, even though it appears otherwise. However, the accusative case ending (*dvitīyāvibhakti*) that is heard is prescribed by the rule "and [the object] which is not desired but is connected with the action" (*tathāyuktaṃ cānīpsitam*); therefore, it indicates that [the object] is to be consecrated (*saṃskāryatva*), because it lacks the status of being the most desired (*iṣṭatama*) by the agent through his action. Thus, in all cases, the *upasthāna* (reverential standing) [is established]. [End of] Chapter 1, Section 710, together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

The mere fact of being second does not establish its status as a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*). Because she seeks for herself the avoidance of what is undesirable through the inspection of the site, it is therefore a rite of acquisition (*pratipatti*).

"May I be like Indrāṇī, never widowed; may I be like Aditi, possessed of good sons. O Gārhapatya fire, may I not be childless; may I have good offspring"—saying this, she sits down to the south-west of the Gārhapatya fire, facing north.

He sits facing north in the intermediate direction between the south and west of the *gārhapatya* fire. The principal wife sits according to her assigned place. The others sit nearby, leaning toward that same direction with some interval; this is because this rite is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) intended for the husband. Thus, she remains seated, bound [in ritual silence] until the unbinding; the meaning is that she remains in this manner, contemplating the unbinding until the moment of its release.
Seated, she mutters, "May we be rich in offspring for you";
"adāmpam" is the end of the mantra; and also: "My sons are slayers of enemies, and my daughter is a sovereign lady; and I am victorious; may my fame as a wife be supreme."

The term *apapat* (she goes away) is connected [to the previous context]. The particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Although the act of sitting down is already established by the word *āste* (she sits), he says "sitting down" (*padāsīna*) so that it may be understood: she sits after having gone behind the cart and having become silent. This is not a rule regarding sitting; rather, the meaning of *āste* is merely a continuous state resulting from the rule of becoming silent while following. By this, it is also understood that even if she has risen from her seat, she remains at ease during the ritual performance (*vihāra*), even if she is restrained from moving about.

The act of seating (*upaveśana*) is a subsidiary part of the *jarā* rite and must necessarily be performed preceded by the *japa*. Here, *saṃskāra*, *naya*, and the recitation of the *āśī-mantra* constitute the *japa*; these three also recur as indirect auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*). These mantras are to be learned from the father or husband prior to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) and employed [therein].
With the mantra "May Pūṣan open your opening" (*pūṣā te bilaṃ viṣyatv*), he opens the opening of the *gargara* vessel containing clarified butter, or with "Thou art Pūṣan" (*pūṣā'si*).

The section concerning the wife has concluded. By the principle that [the term] "another" (*anya*) is used because of its mention alongside a feminine gender, the general rule regarding the *adhvaryu* as the performer is set aside; however, since there is no such word here, it is not excluded. The *sapiḥ*—that vessel called by the word *gargara* in which the clarified butter (*sarpis*) is placed—is distinguished: having first covered its mouth with wood or the like, he carries it to the *vihāra* (the sacrificial ground) and sets it down. At that very moment, the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *sapiḥ* must be performed by means of this covering; otherwise, it would spill out.
Because it would follow that there is the impossibility of the formation of an unfavorable characteristic (*alakṣaṇasaṃskāra*). "He pours out" means he opens the mouth of the vessel;
having poured [the contents] into another vessel, he remains until he is about to pour them out.

In this context, even though the word *sarpiḥ* (clarified butter) is contained within a compound, it must be extracted and supplied (*adhyāhāra*), because supplying a word is less objectionable than resorting to a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇikatva*). Since it will be stated later regarding the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) that one should take "as much as is sufficient for the sacrifice," the meaning is: when one intends to take by pouring out from the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) an abundance sufficient for the sacrifice, one first takes [some] into the vessel silently (*tūṣṇīm*). This is because it will be explained during the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) that one should take "as much as is sufficient for the sacrifice" from the vessel for clarified butter; therefore, the meaning is that one takes [it] at the very beginning into the vessel silently.
Having placed [the vessel] over the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with the verse, "Viṣṇu strode across this," which is clear;
then, having taken the ghee-pot with the formula, "Thou art Aditi, with an unbroken strainer," he pours abundant ghee into it while a strainer has been laid inside.

Having taken [the vessel] from a trustworthy person and accepted it, once that has been received, one silently places a purifier inside it. Immediately thereafter, one pours abundant clarified butter (*ājya*) into it, establishing it for the purpose of sacrifice through the act of pouring (*nirvāpa*). The use of the word *ājya* in place of the previously introduced term *sarpis* is intended to indicate that it is a generic class-term (*jātiśabda*). Thus, it is stated that the etymological derivation of the word—such as "that which flowed forth became *sarpis*" (*yad atarpat tat sarpir abhavat*)—is not for the sake of demonstrating its derivative nature (*yaugikatva*), but rather for the purpose of praise (*stuti*).

*Prabhūta* means "excessive. In the *saṃhitā* version of the phrase *mahīnām*, the word *nipāta* occurs; however, in the *brāhmaṇa*, the word *devayajyāyai* is additionally recited. Therefore, these two mantras should be understood as optional alternatives (*vikalpa*). Due to the force of the two readings, there is a break in the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) [of the mantra]. Because they share the same purpose, the application (*viniyoga*) of the *saṃhitā* mantra occurs in the *brāhmaṇa* even without the [usual] indicators of context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), or name (*saṃjñā*). Nor is this an improper assumption due to a lack of equal strength; rather, their equal strength is to be understood through their functional necessity (*ānarthakya*).

Alternatively, their equal strength is established because they are enjoined for that very same purpose in another Brāhmaṇa passage. From the address "O milk of the earth" (*mahīnāṃ payo 'si*), it is understood that the clarified butter (*ājya*) must indeed be derived from a cow; the word *mahi* is used as a synonym for *go*. Just as in the mantra, "In the ear of the cow, O great one, these are thy names for Agni," [the term refers to the cow]. If, as a substitute for that, one takes clarified butter from a buffalo, a goat, or something else, it will be stated later that there is no modification of the formula (*noha*).
With the words "For food, thee" (*iṣe tvā*), he places [the butter] upon the embers in the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire.

The term *ājyam* (clarified butter) is understood to carry over from the previous context. He places it upon the embers on its southern side—not on the ashes, nor on the flames—for the purpose of melting it by setting it above them.
Having taken it with the formula "For strength, thee! and supported it with the *veda*-grass-bundle, he hands it to his wife.

Having supported the *ājyasthālī* (clarified butter vessel) with the *veda* (sacrificial broom), and having held it with the hand assisted by the *veda*, he places the *ājyasthālī* together with that [broom] into the hands of the wife. As for the mantra, because it reveals the ritual vessels through the accusative case ending in the word *tvā*, and because it does not reveal the *veda* or the wife, the mantra is connected as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the act of supporting, not to the primary act of bringing [the vessel], due to its unsuitability for the latter.
Supporting with the *veda* is a subordinate part of the bringing; however, when the wife is not eligible [to perform the bringing], there is no bringing, and thus no supporting.
With the mantra, "Thou art the milk of the earth," she looks at it while closing her eyes and not breathing out.

The mantra ends with *suprajāstvāya*. The inspection is performed with the mantra because it possesses its characteristic mark; other [acts] are done silently. That which has been offered belongs to her alone; thus, when he offers again to another woman, she likewise does so in the same manner. He spreads it with the words *na tat* (not that). The mantra ends with *nivapāmi*. The mantra ends with *mitim*. [The variants include: *svādhi*, *āyatanasya*. (Paippalāda recension, Ja.)

[The commentary states: Regarding the point that the clarified butter (*ājya*) specified [in the text] is the object to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*), and that things intended for another purpose should be performed by a single person—how then can another [person] look at it? It is said in reply: The accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*) is common to both what is desired (*īpsita*) and what is not desired (*anīpsita*); thus, it is not a decisive factor [for determining the status of the action]. However, as with the clarified butter, the "utility for what has occurred or what is to occur" (*bhūtabhāvyupayoga*) applies equally to the wife (*patnī*) as well.

Therefore, this characteristic mark—the act of looking—is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) belonging specifically to the wife. For it is so understood from the mantra itself, where the praise of the fruit in the words "May you be well-blessed" indicates a rite for the wife; likewise, from the supplementary statement "for the sake of forming a couple. Furthermore, in the supplementary statement, "Indeed, she makes this impure when the wife looks [at the clarified butter]; she places it on the Gārhapatya fire for the sake of purity," how could there be such a censure if the looking at the *ājya* were a purificatory rite for the *ājya* itself? Therefore, because it is a rite for the wife, the looking must be performed by all the wives.

Baudhāyana has also stated that one causes [the sacrificer] to look at the clarified butter for the sake of its purpose. Regarding the instruction "having closed his eyes," this refers specifically to the consecration of the wife; having closed them, he opens them again and looks. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction. This has been clearly stated by Vaikhānasa: "Having closed [his eyes], having looked, and without exhaling, he looks. In the phrase "having looked," the opening of the eyes is not intended to be emphasized. Since it is a consecration of the wife, it is repeated for each wife.

This *saṃskāra* (consecration) belongs not to the agent, but rather to the enjoyer; therefore, such *saṃskāras* also result in being merely indirect auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*) to the principal rite, just like the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice. For this very reason, even in the Mahāpitṛyajña, he will state: "The wife, sitting in her own house, looks at the clarified butter (*ājya*). This is because of the prohibition of agency in the words "she does not sit near [the fire]" and "they do not perform the *saṃyāja* offerings. And because it is an indirect auxiliary, in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, she looks at the clarified butter in both sacrificial enclosures (*vihāra*) according to the entire ritual procedure (*tantra*).
She places it over the Gārhapatya fire with the mantra, "Thou art splendor" (*tejo 'si*).

On this point, some say: when the wife does not look on because she is unable to do so, then there is no placing [the vessel] over the *gārhapatya* fire; for since that which is looked upon by the wife becomes impure (*amedhya*), the placing over the *gārhapatya* is prescribed for the sake of purity.
Having taken it up with the words "For brilliance," he carries it forward with the words "Go after the brilliance."

He carries [the vessel] over to the Āhavanīya fire for the purpose of placing it upon it, having taken it from the Gārhapatya. Regarding this, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) has stated that he carries it after leading the Brahman and the Sacrificer to the south. The intention there is as follows: because of the observation of the directive "O [priest], pour out the clarified butter," the ritual action begins with the pouring out of the clarified butter and concludes with the sprinkling of water and so forth.

Regarding this, if it is argued that "the ritual procedure is from the north" (*uttarataupacāraḥ*), then if one were to carry [the vessel] from the north, there would be a placement ending toward the west (*pratyagapavargatā*) starting from the *āhavanīya* fire; let this not occur. Therefore, it is stated [that the movement is] in such a way that both the circumambulation (*prādakṣiṇya*) and the placement ending toward the east (*prāgapavargatā*), which are established by the general rules (*paribhāṣā*), remain uncontradicted.

He places [the vessel] upon the *āhavanīya* fire with the mantra: "May Agni not take away your brilliance," or alternatively: "May Agni not take away your brilliance; I place the sacrifice within the sacrifice; the sacrifice is established in the sacrifice. This is for the sake of clarity.
With the mantra, "Thou art the tongue of Agni," he places the *prokṣaṇī* (sprinkling) waters to the north along the track of the wooden sword (*sphya*).

The end of the mantra is "mavā. Having returned from the Āhavanīya fire, he places them; the word "varman" is used in the sense of "varmani" with the elision of the case-ending according to the rule *supāṃ suluk...* [Pāṇini 7.1.39]. He places them to the north of the *prokṣaṇī* vessel. [Reference: Baudhāyana Śrauta Sūtra 15.6.3].
With the mantra, "Thou art clarified butter (*ājya*)," he gazes at the clarified butter.
The Adhvaryu alone [performs it]; the sacrificer also [performs it] according to the *Yājamāna-sūtra* and other texts. "Bhakṣīya" is the end of the mantra.
Or [it occurs] after the purifying (*utpavana*).

The word "he looks" (*avekṣate*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Or, it may be performed after purifying [the butter]. In this *Brāhmaṇa*, it is stated as a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*) that "having closed his eyes, he should look"; likewise, it has been stated by Āpastamba and others as well. However, the Teacher [Baudhāyana] explained it as "the wife looks," and since that will also apply here, he did not state it explicitly. In that case, however, because it belongs to another recension (*śākhā*), it was explained; therefore, wherever it says "he looks at the clarified butter (*ājya*)," those two rules—"having closed his eyes" and "without speaking"—are to be known as belonging to other recensions.

Therefore, even when [the action] is performed for its own sake (*māna*), the accomplishment (*siddhi*) [of the purpose] is established. This consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya-saṃskāra*) is understood through the accusative case ending and from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). For the *arthavāda* states: "Verily, he is liable to become blind who gazes at the clarified butter. Having thus censured [gazing], it prescribes: "He should gaze with eyes closed; thereby he preserves his sight for himself. Thus, since there would be a loss of the eye's function for the sake of the consecration of the clarified butter, the closing of the eyes is mentioned as the means of restoring that normal state.

For where there is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), one should not cause impurity (*vaiguṇya*); therefore, since the ghee (*ājya*)—which serves as the object when the purificatory rite of the wife (*patnī-saṃskāra*) is to be produced—has itself become non-purified (*amedhya*), it has thereby brought about the purification of the other [substances]. Consequently, even when the sacrificer is away on a journey, the Adhvaryu must indeed perform the inspection of the ghee once again.
With the formula, "Thou art bright, thou art light, thou art splendor," he purifies the ghee three times by moving it back and forth through two strainers (*pavitra*) whose tips point northward.

The recitation of all [mantras] together has a cumulative (samuccaya) purpose; for this is likewise shown by the cumulative reading in the Brāhmaṇa, and by following that reading, other opinions are also refuted. As Āpastamba says: "He recites 'Thou art the bright' first, 'Thou art light' second, and 'Thou art splendor' third"—this is not desired [by us]. However, the cumulative position is clearly stated by Vaikhānasa: "With the three [mantras], 'Thou art the bright,' etc."; it is not said that they are used individually.

For here, it is intended that the purification (*utpavana*) be performed three times with the mantra, because the Brāhmaṇa prescribes "three times with the Yajus. If it is argued: "But surely, where an action is performed upon a single substance and its accomplishment occurs through separate acts, the mantra should be recited only once," we say no; for that principle applies only to cases where there is no intervening repetition.

But here, however, because the food is separated by a different class [of substances], the mantra previously recited does not apply to the *anitā* (the act of leading forward). According to the principle that "when there is an interruption of what has been remembered, one must perform it again with the mantra," the previous rule will be set aside. As for the Brāhmaṇa passage, it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that same principle; therefore, that too has not been mentioned [as a new point]. In the Brāhmaṇa, however, there is a combination (*samuccaya*): "He says, 'Thou art bright, thou art light, thou art splendor. He thereby declares its form and its greatness. Three times with the *yajus* formula; these worlds are three."

"For the attainment of these worlds. "Three times. "The sacrifice is for distinction; moreover, it is for the sake of purity. Thus, they establish the combination [of the formulas] by means of the singular number in the phrase "by this *yajus*," and the restatement as "three *yajus*s" is for the sake of connecting with the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, because the purpose is an unseen refinement (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*), there is no apprehension [of a visible result]; otherwise, since a visible result—namely, the mere removal of impurities from the clarified butter—is possible, it would follow that postulating an unseen result is not logical. Let this not be so. Ka.Ga...

[The text continues: "Thine" (tava). Although [the word] *ya* occurs in Ga. Ha. Do, and because the purpose has been shown by the two [verses] beginning with "for the sake of the purity of the worlds" (*lokānām āpya-medhyatvāya*), it is clear that the purpose of the restatement is to indicate an invisible refinement (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*). Thus everything is clarified; the commentary (*bhāṣya*) should also be construed in this manner. With these mantras taken together—each mantra being threefold—one pours out [the water] again and again.

Thus, here in sequence, in another vessel, having started from the western part of the *pavitras* and led them to the eastern part, and then having brought them back to the western part, one purifies [them] with the mantra. One should purify them again in exactly this same manner. Nor should it be said that the rule of "ending toward the west" (*pratyag-apavargatva*) must be avoided; for the direct Vedic injunction (*śruti*) itself, which prescribes ending toward the west, would override the general rule. In the Brāhmaṇa it says: "Bringing them back again."

"For in this very way the prāṇa and apāna circulate"—thus it is stated that the circulation of the two *pavitra*s, which take the form of prāṇa and apāna, occurs. For the prāṇa circulates ending at the front (*prāgapavarga*); its cessation occurs through the closing of the mouth and nostrils. The apāna, however, ends at the rear (*pratyaṃgapavarga*); its cessation is observed through the closing of the genitals, which is the gateway of the apāna. Therefore, because the movements of prāṇa and apāna are successive, the fact that [the *pavitra*s] end at the rear during the subsequent re-introduction of food is not to be prevented. The word "punarāhāram" ends in the suffix *ṇamul*.

Replenishing [the water] is a constituent part of the purification (*utpavana*); therefore, there is no connection with a mantra during the replenishing. Having performed the replenishing silently, the purification is done with a mantra. The purification of both [the *ājya* and the *prokṣaṇī* waters] is connected to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), as in "The *ājya* with waters," and so forth.
With the mantra "O gods... (*devo vaḥ*), he sprinkles the *prokṣaṇī* waters three times.

The word "purifies" (*utpunāti*) is understood as the governing verb. It should be known that this is clearly stated in the Brāhmaṇa: "verse by verse with the Gāyatrī. The term "repeatedly" (*punarāhāram*) does not apply; although it could have been understood from the preceding "thrice" (*tris*), because the word "thrice again" (*punastris*) is explicitly mentioned, the meaning is that it is only "thrice," and not "repeatedly.
Or alternatively, [the mantra may be]: "O Waters, you who are gladdened by the *repha*, mixed with honey, anointed, seated upon the seat, and not being hostile toward food.
This is an optional alternative for the purification of the sprinkling-water (*prokṣaṇyutpavana*).

He takes the clarified butter within the altar (*antarvedi*). The meaning is that he takes it while holding the ladle (*sruk*) over the middle of the altar. This is merely a formal declaration in order to state the ritual rules (*dharma*):
[he takes it] with the *sruva*-ladle, which has not been taken out.

The word "takes" (*gṛhṇāti*) is understood as a carry-over from the previous rule. "Niṣkāsī" means that which has a residue remaining as a *niṣkāsa*; he is not such, meaning [he acts] without a *niṣkāsa*. "Having supported with the *veda*"—the word "ladle" (*srucaṃ*) is understood as the object. The sense is that he holds the ladle together with the *veda* in his left hand and the *sruva* spoon in his right hand; this is established by implication. Baudhāyana has stated it thus: "Having placed it on the *veda*, he takes [it]."

He takes four or five portions into the *juhū* ladle, and eight or ten into the *upabhṛt* ladle; as it is with the *juhū*, so it is with the *dhruvā*. According to this fixed rule, both alternatives apply: all [portions] are either taken four at a time or five at a time. Regarding the sixteen-fold or ten-fold [portions], he himself speaks of the "sixteen-fold" in accordance with his own name [in the *Śulba-sūtra*]. Āpastamba states that some authorities record that there should be ten portions in the *upabhṛt* and five portions in the other two [ladles].
"One takes more into the *juhū*, less into the *upabhṛt*, and most into the *dhruvā*.

The word "takes" (*gṛhṇāti*) carries over from the previous context. "More" (*bhūyaḥ*) and "most" (*bhūyiṣṭham*) have the same meaning, signifying a greater quantity; "less" (*alpiṣṭham*) signifies a smaller quantity. Although the intended sense is established merely by saying "less into the *upabhṛt*" and "most into the other two," the use of the cumbersome designations "more" and "most" is for the purpose of indicating an extreme degree of gradation.
Holding the *juhū* over the opening of the vessel, he takes sixteen portions of clarified butter into the *upabhṛt* at its middle point, and into the *dhruvā* which is resting on the ground.

Holding the *juhū* spoon level with the opening of the *ājyasthālī* by means of its spout, he takes [the butter]. The word "from the *juhū*" (*juhvāḥ*) is to be supplied by modification. The connection is that he holds it over the middle part of the vessel; here, "the *upabhṛt*" is the term subject to modification. When [the vessel] is resting on the ground, there is no need for such modification.

The two optional alternatives were stated as "sixteen" and "twenty-one. If that were not so, then even in the case of twenty, because of the reduction [of the number], the optional state of being seventeen would not apply; therefore, it was stated by implication that in the case of sixteen there is a combination with the optional twenty-one, and even in the case of twenty, there is a combination of the optional one-and-twenty with the obligatory one-and-twenty.
[The texts state: "One desiring cattle should perform seventeen; one desiring stability should perform twenty-one."

At the time of taking the clarified butter (ājya), the sacrificer makes a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) according to the verbal root and its suffixes, saying: "Desiring cattle, I shall perform seventeen [oblations] with clarified butter," or likewise, "Desiring stability, I shall perform eleven [oblations]. Once the sacrificer has made this resolve, the Adhvaryu priest takes the butter. Having thus provided this general instruction, he states the sequence of the ritual performance:

he takes [the butter] into the *juhū* ladle with the formulas beginning "Thee, the bright, for the bright," and into the *upabhṛt* and the *dhruvā* ladles with the subsequent formulas beginning "Thee, for the five winds."

In the three [verses] beginning with *śukram tvā*, the phrase *dhāmne dhāmne* is to be supplied as an *anuṣaṅga*. These three are recited by the teacher in the *saṃhitā*; there are thirteen in the *yājamāna*. Their application in the *ādhvaryava* rite is the same based on their indicative marks (*liṅga*). In the *yājamāna*, the first [verse] is repeated; this is the division of the mantra for the sixteen-fold oblation (*ṣoḍaśapala*).

In the rule "it recurs when there is a plurality of substances," the *ājya* offerings were cited as examples; since it has been established that all acts of taking up [the substance] are accompanied by mantras, when the taking up in the *juhū* ladle is performed with the mantra "O bright one (*śukra*)," the particle "iti" indicates that the entire mantra is intended. If, however, only a single [mantra] were used, then its repetition three times would follow as a consequence. To prevent this, the word "etair" (by these) is stated to indicate plurality. [Objection: Even so, due to the grammatical principle of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a group of identical items), there would still be only singularity. [Reply: No, for if that were the case, the word "etair" would be redundant.

Furthermore, having defined that "rites consist of single mantras," how could the Teacher use the plural form "by these"? Where a collection of mantras is intended to be treated as a single mantra, its unity has already been established; moreover, because it requires greater effort and contradicts the plural number, there is no multiplicity of mantras. For this very reason, in the previous instance, the absence of a reason was explained as being simply a single mantra. In some cases, there is even the repetition of that same mantra. In various places, the commentary has been made consistent in some way, while in others it has been set aside.

This *sūtra* is not found in the commentaries (*vyākhyā*) on the books. [End of] Chapter 710. Together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva, [page] 167. Regarding the formula "Of the five winds thee... and those following it—"Of the five self-ruling ones... and so forth—there are eight [drawings] in the *upabhṛt* ladle and four more in the *dhruvā* ladle; thus, seventeen [drawings] should be understood for that very [ladle], because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the passage "For desire thee," which pertains to the optional rite (*kāmya*). Āpastamba also stated: "For one desiring cattle, there are five drawings in the *dhruvā*. Now, he states the division of the mantras for the two sides of the *viśvekaśī* [offering]: [The text continues with the mantras: "Of the five winds thee... "Of the five self-ruling ones thee... "For the all-uncontained thee... "For the all

If there are fewer mantras, one should take [the offerings] for the upabhṛt with half-verses, and for the other two with the remaining halves; if there are more, the surplus are for the purpose of providing options.

Whether the mantras are specifically distinguished or undistinguished, they are few; of these, when divided into four parts, the middle two portions are taken with the *upabhṛt* ladle by those [mantras] belonging to the latter half, while the first portion is taken with the *juhū* and the fourth portion with the *dhruvā*. The completion of the count is achieved through the first repetition of each. Thus, according to the view that there are sixteen [verses], those which are assigned to a particular [ladle] must be taken from that very place.

He will state that the fulfillment of the number is by means of the mantras to be mentioned later; thus, there are one hundred mantras. As for how the application [of the mantras] occurs in the case of the sixteen portions of clarified butter (*ājya*), he says: "The four remaining [mantras] are to be taken as alternatives with the preceding ones"—this is the sense.
Or, one completes the number with the mantra: *śukram asi jyotir asi dhāmāsi priyaṃ devānām anādhṛṣṭaṃ devayajanam devavītaye tvā gṛhṇāmi*; or else, one uses *dhāmāsi* in all cases.

The mantras beginning with "śukram asi" (Thou art the bright) are three in number. The phrase "priyaṃ devānām" (The beloved of the gods) is to be supplied as an *anuṣaṅga* (an appended word). They end with "gṛhṇāmi trayāṇām" (I take [thee] for the three). In the case of the sixteen-fold division (*ṣoḍaśapakṣa*), the *vikarṇā* mantras are used elsewhere to complete the count. The mantra beginning with "dhāmāsi" and ending with "gṛhṇāmi" is likewise intended to complete the count. The meaning is as follows: when four portions have been drawn into the *juhū* ladle—three times by the mantra "śukraṃ vā" and once by the mantra "pañcānām"—[it is the *śukra*].

"One takes five times [the oblation] with the formula, 'Thou art dear; I take thee for the five peoples, for the five [fingers], for the five [seasons],' and 'Thou art the five-fold porridge; I take thee, thou art light, I take thee as the dear one'—this is the fifth. With 'For the splendor of the Brahman, for the power of the Kṣatriya, I take thee for great heroism,' he again approaches and takes four times [the oblation] with 'Thou art the abode; I take thee as the dear one'—this is the sixth. It is the established conclusion of the Nyāya that two four-times-taken portions are taken in the *upabhṛt* ladle."

When the taking up of the *caturgṛhīta* (fourfold portion) is being performed, it fulfills the required number; however, this does not apply to the *aṣṭagṛhīta* (eightfold portion). As for the statement "eight or ten," that refers to the measure of the ladle (*prastha*) by way of its result, but it is not an integral part of the oblation (*homāṅga*). This has been established by them on the grounds that one must conform to the primary number, namely "he offers with four portions" (*caturavattaṃ juhoti*); thus, this is not a restrictive injunction (*vidhi*) regarding the specific portion. Likewise, regarding the *dhruvā* [ladle], there is the mention of the *upayaj* offerings.

In the case of the four-fold portions (*caturgrahītāni*) such as "brāhmaṇa," "bhūḥ," and "gṛhṇāmi," the fifth portion is taken with the formula "dhāmāsi" alone. In the case of the single-fold portions (*ekaviśeṣu*) dedicated to specific desires, the fifth is taken with "kāmāya svā" and "dhāmāsi," etc. Or, according to the alternative view where "dhāmāsi" is used, for the first two [formulas] it serves as an option; then, by means of "gṛhṇāmi," he takes four portions, and with the fifth [formula], he takes the fifth portion. In the case of the single-fold portions, the twentieth is taken with "kāmāya svā," etc., and the twenty-first with "dhāmāsi. This is the established rule for all of them. And this is the arrangement.

In accordance with the sūtra "sthā'dhairupabhṛti" and the phrase "sarvāsu" (in all) from this same sūtra, the completion of the number must occur in all *sruks*; otherwise, how could it be so? As for the *yājamāna* (the sacrificer's portion), the formula "pañcānāṃ tvā vātānām" (of the five winds, thee) is to be repeated four times in the seven [verses]. In the specific [verses], there is a repetition of "dhāmāvṛttiḥ," "carostvā" twice, "suvīryāya" twice, and "bhūrasmākam" twice. It should be understood that in the twenty-one [verses], there is a double repetition only of "kāmāya svā," and not of "bhūrasmākam."

Having set down the clarified butter elsewhere than on the mound (*utkara*), having removed the butter-pot (*ājyasthālī*), and having consecrated the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*), he addresses the Brahman priest.

Having moved the butter-pot together with its ladle away from its place on the altar and set it down elsewhere, and having consecrated the sprinkling waters with the formula "O divine waters" (*āpo devīḥ*), he addresses the Brahman priest, saying, "O Brahman, I shall sprinkle. When [the Brahman] has given permission, he places the fuel (*idhma*) down with the formula "Thou art black" (*kṛṣṇo 'si*) and sprinkles it three times.
It ends with "To Agni, svāhā! He sprinkles [the materials] while releasing the horse with the mantra; he sprinkles the *veda* grass-bundle with "Thou art the altar," and he sprinkles it three times.
With the formula "Thou art the sacrificial grass" (*barhir asi*), he spreads the grass;
with "Svāhā," he concludes the two [offerings] as before,
three times for each.
The repetition [of the rule] is so that, although it was previously established that "three times each," this might not continue to apply to what follows.

Having placed the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with its knot toward the east within the altar (*vedī*), he sprinkles the tips with "To Heaven thee!"; the middle parts with "To the Atmosphere thee!"; and the roots with "To the Earth thee!

Thus, having placed the tied grass—whose knot is in the eastern part—with its tops pointing upward in the middle of the altar, he sprinkles its middle, tips, and roots in sequence, once each, with those same respective formulas.

Having caused the tips [of the grass blades] to drink [water] from the *sruc* ladle, he causes the roots to drink. This refers to the *barhis* grass by implication. From the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle, he brings the portions of water remaining at the front—the tips and the roots—successively near [the roots] in silence, thereby making them appear as if they are drinking the water. Since this is a preparatory rite for the roots (*mūla-masaṃskāraḥ*), the accusative case is used; furthermore, because of the verb "he causes to drink" (*pāyayati*), the water must be present in the ladle. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states: "He sprinkles that water-remnant from the front onto the roots. If that [water] is lost, he uses other water.
With the formula "For nourishment, thee," he unties the knot from the east toward the west, using the *sruc* ladle.

The *sruva* and *agnihotra-havanyā* ladles are accompanied by water; with those two held together in the hand, one sprinkles [the grass] from the front—that is, from the eastern part—with the other hand already present, so that the knot is at the western end (*pratyag-apavarga*). The meaning is that one sprinkles for the purpose of purification with the hand situated nearby. The realized sense is that one pours water over the knot from above with the hand holding the ladle. [Note: This concludes the section on the seventh chapter, first section, sixty-ninth section (paṭala), according to the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva.]
With the words, "Svadhā to the ancestors," he pours out the remainder of the sprinkling water continuously from the southern hip to the northern hip.

"Go!"—this is the end of the mantra. Starting from the southern corner of the altar (*vedi-śroṇi*), he pours out the remaining water of the *prokṣaṇī* vessels toward the northern corner. "This for the fathers who are outside"—thus he recites while pouring. According to the Smṛti, there is a touching of water by both [the sacrificer and the priest]. Regarding the word "remaining," the experts in logic (*nyāyavidaḥ*) maintain that if the remainder spills, the act of pouring it out (*ninayana*) is not omitted. The opinion of the authors of the Sūtras is that one should take other water as a substitute (*pratinidhi*) and pour it out for the deities. "May Pūṣan untie your knot"—with these words, he unties the knot of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). "Untie" means "release."
With the formula, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s heap," he takes up the *prastara* from the front.
Leading the *prastara* forward from the vicinity of the *barhis*, he takes it up with his hand. This very point has been clearly stated by Āpastamba: "He moves toward the Āhavanīya fire;
he does not draw it back."
He does not cause it to emerge from the vicinity of the Bārhaspatya toward the downward direction or toward the rear; he does not lift it upward;
nor does he hold it up.
He does not shake it;
he does not shake it together with his hand; he does not cause it to tremble.
While the *kampana* remains in his hand, he proceeds in this manner; drawing it as if pulling it, he causes it to descend.
From the vicinity of the *barhis*, he gently places it upon the altar (*vedi*), touching it lightly.
Having inserted the two strainers into the *prastara* grass-bundle while reciting, "I place the out-breath and in-breath in the sacrificer," and having set it down,
he hands it over to the Brahman priest with the formula, "By means of the out-breath and in-breath, I make you one whose body is whole."
He hands the Āhavanīya fire to the sacrificer with the *apreṇa* formula;
the Brahman priest [hands it] to the sacrificer. || 25 ||
Thus ends the seventh paṭala in the first praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

The phrase "he hands over" is understood as a carry-over. It will be stated in the section on the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) that "the sacrificer remains holding [it]. Thus ends the seventh chapter in the first book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha and Mahādeva.
1.8 Now begins the eighth chapter.

He strews the sacrificial altar (*vedi*) with sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Since the Veda declares the altar to be the substratum for the oblation, and since the sacrificial grass is taken up for the purpose of consecrating that [altar], the mantra consequently results in having the sacrificial grass as its object. Therefore, this sūtra is intended to state that whatever is subsequently mentioned as being "performed" (*aṅgīkṛtam*), when it is executed, results only in the strewing of the altar, and that indeed must be done silently (*tūṣṇīm*). Although the word *barhis* is not itself a term denoting a consecration, nevertheless, because there is no application of the consecrated grass elsewhere, and due to indicative marks such as "beginning the settling," the sacrificial grass is indeed the one under discussion (*prakṛtam*) and not something new (*apūrvam*).
With that, he covers the altar. When it is asked how [he does so], he states the preliminary parts:
having covered [the altar] with grass, he spreads the cord diagonally.

Having concealed [the cord] with grass-blades, he spreads—that is, extends—the *śulva* (cord) used for binding the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) upon that [altar], because it is to be presented by the second [verse] of that very [hymn], and thus does not constitute a new act. On the southern side of the altar, he lays it down diagonally, with the root toward the northeast and the tip toward the southwest. Since the verb *stṛṇāti* (he spreads) has the sense of covering as its established meaning, one might suspect a lack of connection with the word *śulvam* (cord); therefore, the author employs a different verbal root, namely *punar stṛṇāti* (he spreads again).

According to some teachers, [he spreads it] reaching to the southern edge of the altar. The syntactical connection is: having interposed grass-blades, he spreads the cord there, with its tip facing either east or north.

"With the words 'O divine sacrificial grass, soft as wool, I spread thee,' he spreads it with the tips covering the roots, thickly, so that it is not seen through, ending toward the east, either in three layers or five layers. The word "he spreads" is understood from the preceding context. It should be understood that "barhis" (sacrificial grass) is the object qualified by these adjectives, both through grammatical modification (*vipariṇāma*) and by supplying the word (*adhyāhāra*), as is seen in the mantra "O divine sacrificial grass" (*devabarhiḥ*). Furthermore, in the Brāhmaṇa, the accusative form of the word *barhis* is clearly seen: "He spreads the sacrificial grass; [the sacrificial grass] is indeed offspring. "Three layers" refers to that sacrificial grass (*barhis*) which consists of three divisions or parts.

Likewise, the five *dhātus* are combined with the form of the external *nidhanas*. The *nidhanas* are either odd numbers beginning with three, or even numbers beginning with four. When one spreads them out externally, if there are three or five, they themselves constitute the *dhātus*. If there are four, then by merging the fourth into the [first] three, one makes them three *dhātus*. When there are six or more *nidhanas*, [the procedure is as follows: [Note: The text fragment provided contains technical details regarding the arrangement of *nidhanas* (concluding phrases) and *dhātus* (musical sections) in Vedic chant (*stotra*). The specific instructions concern how to adjust the number of *nidhanas* to correspond to the required number of *dhātus* when performing the ritual.]

[This refers to] the desire for other [materials]. [In the eighth section, chapter on the altar (aṣṭama-paṭala), in the Vaijayantī commentary composed by Mahādeva: If there are more [straw layers] than those [three], then having combined them into three or five, one makes [the altar] three-layered or five-layered. In that case, one spreads each layer individually on the outside. The syntactical connection is as follows: starting from the western part of the altar and extending to the eastern part—or conversely—in both cases, one spreads [the straw] such that the roots of those situated in front cover the ends of the layers situated behind.

He spreads [the grass] so that it is neither too visible nor too hidden, just as it should be. That same act is further specified by the word *bahulam* (abundantly): he spreads it most densely so that the sacrificial altar (*vedi*) is not visible at all. By the term *prāgapavargam* (ending toward the east), only the ending toward the north (*udagapavargam*) is excluded; however, the ending toward the west (*pratyagapavargatā*), which was not previously established, is here prescribed as an optional alternative.
He inserts a mantra for each layer (*dhātu*).

Regarding the statement "He spreads the altar with *barhis*," since there is only one *devata*, the repetition [of the action] would not otherwise be established; thus, he says this. In that context, although the *barhis* is being spread, it is stated that its consecration (*saṃskāra*) is not performed by that very [single] thread. Likewise, although the *barhis* to be joined together is a single entity and the distinctness of the substance (*dravyapṛthaktva*) does not otherwise apply, let there be no distinctness of substance merely through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the *nidhana*; rather, it is stated for the sake of restriction that it is "because of being spread by way of the limiting adjunct of the root" (*dhātūpādhinā*). This is the intended meaning.

Likewise, with the mantra "tathā corṇām radaṃ," he spreads [the grass] only on the exterior, because of the Vedic injunction: "he spreads the *barhis* on the arms. Thus, even though the altar is being covered by the *barhis*, it is already covered; therefore, there is no mantra for that part. This very point is stated in another Vedic text: "He spreads the *vedi* with the *barhis*. The two meanings of the root *stṛ* (to spread) will be made clear in the section concerning the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).

One consecrates with the mantras beginning with *ūrṇāmṛdu* (soft as wool), which are applied according to their indicative marks (*liṅga*), by means of the directions: "the sacrificial grass being strewn," "the altar being strewn," and "having been strewn. For if there were no difference in meaning between those two [terms], it would not be possible [to speak of] "the sacrificial grass being strewn"; therefore, he shows that this [phrase] "he strews the sacrificial grass" has the sense of spreading it out. Likewise, we conclude that the phrases "the altar being strewn" and "having been strewn" show that this [phrase] "he strews with sacrificial grass" has the sense of covering it. The portion beginning with *ūrṇāmṛdu* pertains to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).

Having drawn out two firebrands for the sake of the after-offerings (anuyāja), having prepared the Āhavanīya fire, and having taken back the prastara-bunch, he lays down the enclosing sticks (paridhi).

From the statement, "Holding the *prastara*," and by means of the suffix *-tva*, its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the enclosing (*paridhāna*) is established. The meaning is that one should separate the two flaming firebrands (*ulmuka*) in the eastern direction, having resolved that they are for the sake of another purpose in their very place; this is because of the injunction in the *Vājasaneyaka*: "The two firebrands are directed eastward. With the formula "Thou art a Gandharva," he places the middle blade, with its tip pointing north, upon the sacrificial grass to the west of the Āhavanīya fire; with "Thou art the arm of Indra," the southern one, touching the middle blade at its tip; and with "Mitra and Varuṇa thee," the northern one, touching the middle blade at its tip.

The word "īḍita" (praised) applies everywhere at the end of the mantra. The phrase "he places it around on the sacrificial grass already spread behind near the site of the Āhavanīya fire" is carried over from the previous [section]. The tip of the *am̐śu* [grass-bundle] extends beyond the site of the Āhavanīya fire; the Āhavanīya fire faces toward this [tip]. [Notes: 1. Not in Pṛ; 2. In Cha., it says "bhūditi"; 3. In Kha., it says "terā"].

In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [in the first praśna]: Only contact with the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) is required for the tips; there is no rule regarding their being upper or lower. However, it is held that the uppermost [stick] must have its tip facing downward. That which stands lower than the site of the Āhavanīya fire due to its diminished length is "downward-tipped" (*avāgra*); he lays it down in such a way that its base touches the middle enclosing-stick. Having made it extend further to the west beyond the site, this one, however, remains according to the site.
The eighth [section] should be performed in that manner; the rest is clear. "Thou art the earth," etc., is the portion for the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).

Having touched the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra beginning "May Sūrya protect thee from the east," the mantra ends with "from calumny" (*abhiśastyai*). This procedure, which involves the use of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), does not apply to those modified rites (*vikṛti*) where the enclosing sticks are absent, as indicated by the remainder of the sentence and because Baudhāyana has stated: "He does not enclose [the fire] with the sun in the east."

He places two supporting fuel-sticks (*ādhāra-samit*) above [the fire]: the southern one with the mantra "Thee, the enjoyer of oblations, O wise one," and the northern one silently, or with the mantra "This fuel-stick for life.

The word "sacrifice" (*adhvara*) is the end [of the formula]. Regarding the northern stick, there is an option: either "for life" or silently. Likewise, Āpastamba also states that the two supporting fuel-sticks are placed above, at the front of the hearth, serving as supports for the two *āghāra* libations; they should be positioned such that they correspond to the two *āghāra* libations being performed—namely, the southern and northern ones, relative to each other.

In this context, there is a variety of options regarding the two supporting blades (*ādhāra*), and according to those, the two fuel-sticks (*samidh*) are placed anywhere, either to the south or the north.
He makes two *darbha* blades with internal cores from the *barhis* grass into the two separating blades (*vidhṛti*).

The word "from the *barhis*" (*barhiṣaḥ*) is in the ablative case; he makes the two *darbha* blades named *vidhṛti* from the *barhis*, but not by cutting them beforehand. There is no internal core; those two are needles that have become the internal core. This is the view of Baudhāyana and the principle of Jaimini regarding the middle blade.
He places [the two spoons] on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) in the middle of the altar with their tips pointing north, [reciting] "In the support of the people.

Although it was said "in the middle of the altar," the phrase "on the sacrificial grass" is stated in order to prevent the impression that there is a direct connection with the altar itself. The rest is clear. [The priest] recites the *yājamāna* formula, "O you who are separated.
He deposits the *prastara* (grass-bundle) upon those two [spoons], [reciting] "Of the Vasus, of the Rudras..."

The mantra ends with "sit in the assembly" (*sadasī sīda*). This ritual action for the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), beginning with "This is the *prastara* [grass-bundle] of those two *paridhi* sticks," is to be understood as applying even to the *sruva*-offerings.
With the mantra "Thou art the *juhū*," he places the *juhū* spoon level with the base of the *prastara*, its handle aligned with it.

The subsequent connection is shown in the *Brāhmaṇa* because it is certain; likewise, it is also shown in the *Sūtra*. The end of the mantra is "sodeti" (he sits in the assembly). The meaning is that he causes [the ladle] to be moistened so that the handle of the *juhū* becomes level with the roots of the *prastara*. In the manuscript copies of the *Sūtra*, the reading is "abhimantrya. [End of] 18th [Section]. [End of] 80th Paṭala. [From] the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva:
"Upabhṛd asi" (Thou art the supporting ladle)—[this refers to] the northern *upabhṛt*, which is drawn closer below the two *vidhṛtis*.
The connection is as before. She sets down [the *juhū*] such that its root extends further back than the root of the *juhū*, being drawn westward from the base of the *juhū*. The rest is clear.
With the formula "Thou art firm," she sets down the northern *dhruvā* above the two *vidhṛtis*, drawn even further back and not touching them;
it is free from contact with the *upabhṛt*. This is clear.

"Thou art the bull, belonging to the Śakvarī verses; I set thee down in the measure of the Vaṣaṭ-call," with these words he places the *sruva* spoon to the south of the *juhū* ladle, or the *dhruvā* ladle to the north. Or [he may say]: "Thou art the bull, belonging to the Śakvarī verses, the son of the ghee-sprinkling ones; by thy dear name, sit in thy dear seat. Thus [he sets it down]. 26.

The meaning is clear. He places the *sthālī* (pot) as well, according to the available space. He consecrates them with the mantra, "These have sat down. Because the ladles (*sruva*) are the subject under discussion and because of the feminine gender in the mantra, the consecration refers to the *sruc* ladles, excluding the *sruva*. This has been clearly stated by Āpastamba: "And in the case of the *nuvanas-pati*, [it applies] to the *sruc* ladles."

"Ye are Viṣṇu’s portions, belonging to Viṣṇu, the abodes of Prajāpati"—with these words he consecrates the clarified butter (ājya), as understood from the preceding [text]. He formulates this technical definition for the sake of the subsequent rule:

with the *sruva* spoon, he makes small portions of the clarified butter intended for the Gārhapatya and Dakṣiṇā fires; with the *juhū* ladle, he takes portions from the *dhruvā* vessel into the Āhavanīya fire.

The word "performs" (*karoti*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Regarding the purposes served by the clarified butter (*ājya*) in connection with the Gārhapatya and Dakṣiṇā fires, it is restricted that these are to be performed with clarified butter from the *ājyasthālī* (the butter-pot) itself; likewise, regarding those purposes served by the *sruva* ladle, they are also to be performed with that very butter contained in the *ājyasthālī*. This is a restatement of the specific rule already established by the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) "one offers into the Āhavanīya fire. It is further restricted that whatever is required for the purpose of the clarified butter must be taken specifically from the *dhruvā* vessel.

The intention is as follows: because of the supplementary statement, "Indeed, this clarified butter which is taken in the *dhruvā* is for the sake of the entire sacrifice," once the [butter] has been set aside, the *śruti* cited by Āpastamba—"he carries it westward from what was taken within the altar"—applies. However, since it is impossible to carry the *dhruvā* to both the *dakṣiṇāgni* and the *gārhapatya*, it is stated that it remains in its place (*sthānāt*). Thus, the rule regarding the *khūṇā* (the pit) is distinct.

Therefore, although two [offerings] are performed with the *juhū* ladle, the clarified butter for the subsequent sprinkling (*pratyabhighāraṇa*) of the oblation, the spreading of the *prastara* grass-bundle, the anointing of the *parṇa*-twig, the portions for the sacrificer and the *iḍā*, the anointing of the joints of the *iḍā*, and the *ājyabhāga* and *pārvaṇa-homa* offerings, all belong to the *ājyasthālī* (the vessel for clarified butter). In that regard, it is established by the very general rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "oblations are offered into the *āhavanīya* fire with the *juhū*"; thus, everything for that purpose is stated once and for all (*tantra*). [End of section] 1.15. [Variant readings: ṅa. ja. sa. na. ṭa. read *spṛdhāḥsā*.]

174.
