In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, within this section on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the clarified butter in the *dhruvā* vessel is prescribed for that purpose; furthermore, by the word "purpose" (*artha*), the acts of under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and so forth are also prescribed from the *dhruvā*. However, Kātyāyana and others will state (or say) that the under-spreading and the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) are to be done with clarified butter from the *ājyasthālī* itself; it has been stated that this is not the view of our Teacher (*ācārya*).

Why? Because it will be stated later that the spreading [of the grass] and the pouring [of the butter] serve a purpose for the *juhū* and the *āhavanīya* fire respectively, both before and after the offering of the cut portions (*avadāna*). As for the first libation (*prathamāghāra*), although there is no application of this rule, it shall nevertheless occur by virtue of a specific scriptural injunction. Other cases should be understood in the same way. However, regarding the occasional expiation (*naimittika-prāyaścitta*), it should be understood that for those who hold the view that "the two fires are to be consigned [into the kindling wood] by means of the *sruva* ladle," it is done specifically with the *gārhapatya* and *dakṣiṇāgni* fires.
On this point, Baudhāyana says: He takes up the clarified butter vessel with his right hand, the *sruva* spoon with his left, and the *vedā* grass-bundle with the *pātrī* dish.
With the formula, "Here I drive away the face of the attacking army," he drives away the embers from the southern *puroḍāśa* cake with the *vedā*, and then from the northern one.

The suffix *-lyap* indicates that the procedure is stated; thus, the sprinkling of water and the under-spreading of butter are also performed on the two cakes, as is the recitation of the mantra over them.

He consecrates [the cake] with the mantra: "O Sun, shine forth as light for great power. Having spread a base layer in the vessel with the mantra: "I prepare a pleasant seat for thee; I fashion it well-favored with a stream of ghee," he pours ghee over the cake dedicated to Agni with the mantra: "May Agni, whose source is ghee, swell; may he approve the oblations. Anoint the cavity, anoint the skin; I pour ghee over thee, who art well-formed and a finder of wealth, with the splendor of cattle, as one dear to Agni. He pours ghee silently over the subsequent [cake].

In the word *pācyām*, the locative case expresses merely the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*), not that it is something to be consecrated (*saṃskāryatva*). Therefore, although the singular number in *syonaṃ te* refers to only one sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), the spreading (*upastaraṇa*) is performed for each cake, as indicated by the gerund *upastīrya*. Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in *agnaye juṣṭam*, it is stated to be for the cake dedicated to Agni (*āgneya*). Furthermore, because there is no modification (*ūha*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), and because the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) is heard in scripture as being for the purpose of all the oblations (*havir*), and because of the direction "silently the latter," it refers specifically to the sacrificial cake.

In this mantra, although it should have been stated that "the southern [portion] with the mantra and the northern silently," the term "āgneyam" (belonging to Agni) is used for the purpose of indicating the characteristic mark (*liṅga*). By this, the distinction between the southern and northern locations is recalled. Regarding the second case, if it is *sāṃnāyya* (curdled milk offering), he says:

"O Soma, you whose self has entered into the animals, who have spread yourself according to the stations of the gods; having become possessed of self and rich in ghee, go to the gods, find the light of heaven for me, the sacrificer. [This is said over] the cooked [milk]. He recites the formula for obtaining [the portion], because it is prescribed among the rules for the *sāṃnāyya*. The word "he pours over" (*abhidhārayati*) is understood to carry over from the previous context.

"Moist, spreading, the guardian of the world, cooked, he rises up, the progenitor of thoughts"—with these words, he removes the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) from the fire, without breaking it and without turning it over.

Because the term "cooked in the middle" (*madhye śṛtam*) cannot be understood as applying [to the sacrificial cake] due to the lack of continuity across the intervening steps, the word *puroḍāśam* (sacrificial cake) is explicitly stated. Having been drawn out from its connection with the potsherds, he places it elsewhere in some vessel; then, with his right hand, the wiping of the sacrificial cake with ashes is performed. [End of Section] (from the *Mahādevakṛtavaijayantīvyākhyā*). When that occurs, placing [the cake] there is not possible; therefore, the word *ādatta* (he takes up) was not used, for the procedure without the left hand is even more impossible.
He sets it aside while performing it in such a way that it neither breaks nor turns over;
having wiped away the ashes with the Veda— that is,
having wiped away and removed the ashes clinging to the sacrificial cake from all sides.

"In that [seat], sit; be established in the nectar; O essence of rice, be well-disposed"—with these words, he places [the sacrificial cake] into the vessel over which the ghee has been spread. Because of the context, this refers specifically to the *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake). The word "spread" (*upastīrṇe*) is used in the phrase "in the vessel over which the ghee has been spread" to preclude the view that the spreading serves no visible purpose. Since the indicative power of the mantra—"I make a pleasant seat for you"—and the masculine gender reference in "sit in that" (*tasmin sīda*), the vessel itself cannot be the locus [of the action]. Therefore, the spreading of the ghee is not for the sake of consecrating the vessel; rather, he places or establishes it upon the ghee that has been spread within the vessel.

The ritual procedure beginning with the removal [of the oblation] should be performed according to the *anusamaya* (sequential) method; likewise, Kātyāyana has stated that the second drawing [of the soma] should be done up to the placing [on the altar], because of the scriptural injunction. When the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is made of barley, then because of the contradiction in the gender of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) regarding "of rice" (*vrīhīṇām*), there is no mantra; the placing is done silently. This has been clearly stated by Vaikhānasa. However, when barley is used as a substitute for rice, the mantra is indeed present. The same should be understood regarding the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*). If it is the second hundred [of verses], then there is no under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*); having sprinkled the second [portion] over it, he removes it [from the fire]. This has been explained together with the evening milking (*sāyaṃdoha*).
"May prosperity, the essence of the earth, not depart"—having thus anointed each of the potsherds one by one and counted them, he sets them aside.
It has been stated that this is done "joint by joint, one by one. The sequence of priority and posteriority is specified in the Śruti text by the phrase "having counted, he sets them aside."

By means of the suffix *lyap*, which has the sense of its own reflexive pronoun (*sva-pratyaya*), [the action] is indicated; for in that very context, what belongs to another recensional branch (*śākhāntarīya*) is subsumed by that very *lyap*. Having sprinkled [the butter] once, one sets it aside after counting that very number—thus is the other case. By the hearing of the word "you" (*tvā*), the non-substitution of the sections (*kāṇḍa-anupamaya*) is shown. Otherwise, the plural number would be meaningless; rather, from that single nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the singularity of the substance (*ekadravyatā*) is understood.

Nevertheless, it is stated that the removal [of the potsherds] is by means of counting, in the phrase "he removes them after counting the potsherds. This "counting" is the means for their separation, beginning from the placing [of the earth]. It is said "after counting" for the purpose of prescribing the mantra for the removal; by the word "counting," the mantra is intended, and that mantra is recited by the Vaikhānasa as "one, two, three," and so forth.

In that case, however, the mantra would be divided for each individual number, and the *udvāsana* (removal) would likewise be performed individually; yet, if one were to count all [the items] together at once and then perform the *udvāsana*, the suffix *-lyap* would become meaningless. Furthermore, the phrase "one by one" (*ekaikaśaḥ*) connects with the act of counting before the removal, and not with the singular "one" (*ekam*), because otherwise the counting would serve no visible purpose. By contrast, through the suffix *-lyap*, the sense of "counting one by one" is established as having a visible purpose, since it serves as the means (*sādhana*) for the removal.

Although the mantra would be recited only once because the "potsherds" (*kapālāni*) constitute a single substance, nevertheless, by virtue of the scriptural statement, even the act of sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) is an auxiliary to the removal (*udvāsana*). Having stated this, it is shown that the connection [of the mantra] is with each individual potsherd as it is being removed, according to the rule "one by one" (*ekaikaśaḥ*); thus, since the second sprinkling is separated from the removal of the first [potsherd], the second sprinkling must be performed with the mantra itself. (Kha, Ra, Ja, Jha, Sa, Ha)

[The text] has been shown: *dasta pra* | 2. *va* | *udastaraṇasrā* | 3. *ka. ga. ca, cha. ṭha. ḍa. śitaṃ* | *ka. ga ca, chaṭha, ḍa, canam* | *tena* | 176. The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the first praśna]—has thus demonstrated that both the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) and the lifting (*udvāsana*) are performed for each potsherd (*kapāla*) according to the method of section-by-section performance (*kāṇḍānusamaya*).

Regarding this, some commentators say that numbers such as "one," "two," or "three" do not reside in each individual potsherd, but rather that the number is uttered in the manner of "the first," "the second," "the third," and so forth. That is not correct; for just as in the case of the formula "May Viṣṇu follow thee for the sake of one [share]" (*ekam iṣe viṣṇus tvā 'nv etu*), primacy is maintained even when there is duality in the second and subsequent portions, so it is here as well.
[The priest] anoints the sacrificial cake with the words: "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey."

The mention of the *puroḍāśa* is for the purpose of excluding the *sānnāyya*; the singular number is for the purpose of repeating the mantra. He anoints it—that is, he makes it smooth. Thus, this act of anointing will later be referred to by the word "ornament" (*alaṃkāra*). How does he anoint it? Right here he specifies: having anointed it well—without leaving spots like a tortoise’s back, without leaving any part out, and without rubbing against the vessel—he anoints it from above with the *sruva* spoon and from below with his hand.

The term *puroḍāśam* (the sacrificial cake) is carried over [from the previous rule]. Although it is established by the force of the context that [the action] is performed with the *sruva* ladle, the phrase "with the *sruva*" is stated again in order to preclude its connection with the subsequent word *abhyajya* (having anointed). "Upariṣṭāt" (above) means having anointed the entire [cake], excluding only the bottom layer which has been smeared [with ghee], using the *sruva* ladle and the clarified butter (*ājya*) contained therein; thus it is made well-anointed (*svakta*), meaning thoroughly smeared with abundant ghee. The word *abhyajya* is to be construed with each [of the following items].

In this context, the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), because the act of anointing is already established by the suffixes *-aṇ*, *-ika*, and *-ap*. This is for the sake of favoring the verbal root, just as in the expression "he cooks the cooking" (*pākaṃ pacati*). Therefore, the word *abhyajya* expresses the sense of "having performed" (*kṛtvā*); the meaning "having smeared with oil" (*svaktaṃ kṛtvā*) is thus accomplished. Since this was not previously established, it is an injunction (*vidhi*) that must be understood. If this were not stated, words such as *svakta* would merely be restatements of what is already obtained. Furthermore, by the mere statement "previously he anoints" (*pūrvam anakti*), all of this [the specific manner of anointing] is not obtained; therefore, because it was not previously established, [it is an injunction].

In such a way that the verbal root (*svakta*) may be connected with an effort characterized by mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), an inference of a mere injunction will subsequently arise. Furthermore, this root *añj*—being occupied by another verbal root—is not capable of being construed with words denoting substances subordinate to an action, such as *svakta*. Therefore, it is established that the root *añj* is a reference to what has been previously stated.

Alternatively, *svaktam* is an adverbial modifier that should be connected with the word *anakti*; thus, having performed a thorough anointing by means of a stream of clarified butter, one subsequently performs the rubbing (*mrakṣaṇa*) or friction with the *sruva* ladle, in which regard [the rule] states "not spotted like a tortoise," and so forth.

Furthermore, in response to the expectation of how the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) should be prepared, the three words beginning with *apṛṣantam* are connected. It means: having made it "spotless," that is, such that there are no spots (*pṛṣantaḥ*) like those on a tortoise; just as there are spots on a tortoise, one should prepare it so that drops of clarified butter do not remain in the places where it has been smeared with the ladle (*sruva*). Also, it should be "unfragmented" (*aparivargam*); "fragmentation" (*parivarga*) means abandonment, so the meaning is that it should not be [abandoned] part by part, nor should it be incomplete.

Alternatively, "not abandoning" (aparityajya) means not letting go. In the middle of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), no separation from the vessel should be made until the point of being fit for anointing is reached. Likewise, "without friction" (*anikāyam*): where there is no *nikāya*, that is, no rubbing or scraping with the ladle (*sruva*). Even though the suffix is *ṇamul*, the meaning remains the same; the absence of the nasal (*ṇatva*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). Such is the manner. [End of Section] — This is accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

"Having performed the anointing from above with the *snuṣā* [ladle], he subsequently brings the hand near the *ājya* from behind. Because of the statement "the hand is brought near," as found in the *Paingī* text, one takes the *ājya* in the hand and anoints the lower part [of the cake]. When it is said "he anoints (*anakti*)," it might be thought that this refers merely to the falling of the *ājya*; however, that is not possible while the *puroḍāśa* is not turned over. Therefore, the word "having approached" (*upetya*) is stated to mean that he brings the hand near to the bottom of the *puroḍāśa*, in the sense of "without turning it over."

Since the statement "he anoints from above and spreads [ghee] below" is heard in proximity to the injunction "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni," and since this is supplemented by another recensional text (śākhā) stating that "these two have the same procedure," it would follow that this applies even to other sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa). To show that there is no application to the *sāṃnāyya* offering because it belongs to the *puroḍāśa-brāhmaṇa*, the term "the cake" (*puroḍāśam*) is mentioned and carried forward. Henceforth, only the placing (*āsādana*) of the cake and so forth is being described.

However, it is not known whether one should place [the oblations] after having carried them in the *pātrī*, or whether one should carry and place the oblation itself after having taken it up; for that purpose, Baudhāyana and Vaikhānasa have stated, "One should cover all the oblations with the *pātrī*. This is not contradictory even for us.
With the formula, "May they sit upon the dear seat with their dear name," he places the two *puroḍāśas* behind the ladles—the one for Agni on the south and the other on the north.

He places the *suc* spoons behind the *barhis* grass; because the mantra is joined with the verb "let them sit" (*āsīdatām*) in the second person dual, the mantra is recited only once, and the placing is done simultaneously with both hands. One might think that this implies taking hold of them in the right and left portions [of the grass], but that is not so, because of the established rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "the actions for these [implements] are performed in successive order."

Furthermore, although it would have been more concise to state simply that "one places the two sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) in the south and north," the teacher has given a cumbersome instruction—first placing the southern cake dedicated to Agni and subsequently placing the other, the northern one—in order to demonstrate the repetition of the mantra when there is a distinction between substances. This repetition is shown by making clear the difference in location. As for the dual number, however, it refers to the two cakes in mutual relation to each other, just as in the mantra for the placement of the bricks.

In the case of a single *puroḍāśa*, there is no mantra; the placing is done silently (*tūṣṇīm*). This applies neither in the archetype (*prakṛti*) nor in the ectype (*vikṛti*) where there is only a single *puroḍāśa*. Although the purpose is accomplished by merely saying "the southern and the northern," the use of the specific designation "Agni’s" and "the other" is for the sake of indicating the deity; thus, even where there are multiple modifications of the *Āgneya* sacrifice, there is no mantra because of the absence of the other—the modification of the *Upāṃśuyāja* or the *Aindrāgna*.

And thus, it is the intention of the author of the Sūtra that the mantra applies even to the Āgnīṣomīya or Aindrāgna cakes when they are not combined with other deities, despite the absence of a connection with various deities. Consequently, in modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) where the sacrificial cakes have various deities, there is a modification (*ūha*) using the plural form, as in "sīdantu" (let them sit). In subsequent modifications, however, whether there is one or two [cakes], the modification is made according to the actual number. As for the practice of placing them together with the cooking vessel (*pātrī*), that is to be disregarded because it lacks a scriptural injunction, contradicts logical reasoning, and contradicts the indicative mark (*liṅga*).

For instance, in the injunction "he places the two *puroḍāśa* cakes," it is heard directly that the status of being the object of the act of placing belongs to the two *puroḍāśas* themselves; since there is no evidence for resorting to an indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in this case, the prescription of the southern and northern positions as well as their anterior-posterior sequence would be impossible, because the placement of those [cakes] previously deposited in the vessel together with her [the Adhvaryu] could not take place—given that it is established by the principles of the system (*nyāyasamaya*) that the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), once strewn, alone serves as the substratum for the oblation (*havis*). Furthermore, if the vessel were the substratum, the status of being the substratum for the oblation would not be possible.

In the case of the *sānnāyya* and other such offerings, although there is an intervention [of other elements], since there is no intervention for those [specific acts], it occurs even when [the mantra] is separated by that [intervention]; thus, there is no fault. [The phrase] "devasadanam āram" [is used], and likewise "ūrṇāmṛdu prathamāna syona... [is used]. [Note: Variants noted in the manuscript notes: kha. shows *darśitam*; kha, ga, cha, ṭa, u. show *mānāmī*; ka, ga, ca, ṭa, ḍa. show *iti do*.]

In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—“O grass, agreeable for the gods, for a seat”—declares that the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) itself is the seat. As for its softness, where would it be useful? It would be useful as a supporting base for the vessel (*pātrī*). Nor should it be argued that the phrase “a pleasant seat for thee” implies that even what is spread out in the vessel is a seat; for that status of being a seat belongs only to the act of placing [the offering] upon it, occurring incidentally (*prasaṅgena*) in relation to the vessel which was produced for the purpose of pouring the grains.
However, since the sacrificial grass is produced specifically as the support for the oblation, it serves as the direct substratum; thus, there is no over-extension of the principle.

Having joined the two *sāṃnāyya* pots together in the middle of the altar, he separates them: the boiled milk on the southern hip of the altar and the curd on the northern. Having caused the two pots to press against each other at the rear of the altar, he places them separately one after the other; this very act of setting them down is expressed by another term. This has been stated clearly by Āpastamba. Otherwise, the reference in the *Yājamāna* section stating "they have been set down" would not be appropriate. The passage beginning with "Thou art the sacrifice" (*yajño 'si*) and so forth belongs to the *Yājamāna*.

"This Veda has found the earth, which was hidden in secret, in the depths, in the caverns. Having placed the Veda in front of the *dhruvā* with [the mantra], "May he find a world for the sacrificer; may he of many deeds perform the flawless sacrifice," he strews around the edges of the altar [with the formula]: "The *dhruvā* by means of the *anaḥ* (cart), or by means of one or the other, not far away—provided it is not in the ablative case; 'not far' (*adūre*) [is used] when preceded by *ena*; 'in front' (*agreṇa*) [is used] when preceded by *ena*, and the second case ending is employed. Having strewn around the edges of the altar...
Having covered the edges of the altar with darbha grass to be strewn around its perimeter, he prepares the Hotṛ’s seat, moving from left to right and ending toward the north. || 27 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the first book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra. || 8 ||
Thus ends the first book in the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. 1.

The Hotṛ sits down upon this; that is the *hotṛṣadana*, the seat made of *darbha* grass. He prepares it—that is, he makes it fit and suitable for sitting. The place of the Hotṛ is to the north of the northern corner (*uttaraśroṇi*) of the altar (*vedi*); the meaning is that he prepares it there, with the blades of grass pointing either eastward or northward. The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of concluding the question, and according to the established usage of the ritualists (*yājñika*), it is for the purpose of establishing the conventional terminology of the section on questions (*prabhapaṭala*).

Because it is seen in the *Bāḍhaca* [text] that the Hotṛ is addressed as "Hotṛ, Hotṛ," and because it is stated in the *Vaikhānasa* [text] that "he addresses the Hotṛ with 'Hotṛ, Hotṛ,'" this must be done. And if he (the Adhvaryu) should ask: "O Adhvaryu, declare the deities, their sequence, and whether they are to be recited loudly or in a whisper," the response to him is as follows: "At the Full Moon sacrifice, the deities are Agni and Agni-Soma; or the deities are Agni-Viṣṇu and Agni-Soma; or the deities are Agni, Prajāpati, and Agni-Soma."

The first two offerings are for Agni and Soma in a low voice (*upāṃśu*); Viṣṇu and Prajāpati [are also offered] in a low voice. For one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice, the rest is explicit. In the case of a Brāhmaṇa, there is the omission of the third oblation; the sequence and the loudness or low-voiced nature of the recitation correspond accordingly. On the new moon day, the deities are either Agni and Indra, or Agni and Mahendra. Or, for one who does not offer the *saṃnayya* (curd-mixture), the deities are Agni and Indra-Agni.

Thus ends the eighth chapter in the first book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin composed by Mahādeva. Now, the first book of the commentary on the *Sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha is completed; it contains the hidden meanings and is endowed with the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*). Thus ends the first book in the commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra*.
2.1 Now begins the first chapter of the second book.
He issues the command: "Recite for Agni as he is being kindled," or "Recite for him as he is being kindled," or "O Hotṛ, recite for Agni, the god, as he is being kindled."

He gives the command to the Hotṛ by means of one of the three *praiṣa* mantras. In this case, the command is not for the purpose of purifying oneself, because the recitation (*anuvacana*) is performed by the Hotṛ. The time for the command is when the Hotṛ has entered and is standing upon the edge of the altar (*vedīroṇi*). The author of the Commentary (Mādhavācārya) stated that it is shown in another Sūtra: "Having taken up a single fuel-stick (*samidh*), he gives the command. And Kātyāyana has also said: "Having taken up this fuel-stick, he gives the command."

In every respect, this is appropriate only in that way; otherwise, how could there be a designation of "present tense" for that which is being kindled? Here, the formulas beginning with *cittiḥ sug* pertain to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). Seated, he places a fuel-stick upon each utterance of the *praṇava*.

From the mention of "seated" (*āsīna*) here, it is established that there is no fixed rule for other rites, such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. At the end of the *sāmidhenī* verses, while the *praṇava* is being uttered by the Hotṛ, he places one fuel-stick (*samidh*) at a time. Regarding the phrase "in the Āhavanīya fire," the reference to the Āhavanīya fire is made in the injunction "for Agni being kindled" (*agnaye samidhyamānāya*) because of its primary status; this is also indicated by the scriptural mark (*liṅga*) in the passage, "having brought down [the sticks] along the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) and the central post (*pradhiman*)," which implies that he causes all the fuel-wood pieces to touch [the fire]. And thus, when the eleven fuel-sticks have been placed—

At the verse "samiddho agna āhuta" (O Agni, kindled with oblations), either at this final [verse] or having set aside one *anūyāja* fuel-stick, he places the entire *idhma* (sacrificial fuel) on the fire. Here, having set aside one fuel-stick for the purpose of kindling another, while the verse "samiddho agna" is being recited, everything remaining is placed on the fire—not at the *praṇava* (the syllable Om). For this very reason, Āpastamba has stated: "He places the entire remainder of the *idhma* on the fire. "The entire *idhma*" refers to the four sets of fuel-sticks. Alternatively, even here at the final [verse], there are four sets of fuel-sticks as before; thus there are two options. Now begins the first chapter of the second book (*praśna*).
He issues the command: "Recite for the fire being kindled," or "Recite for the fire being kindled," or "O Hotṛ, recite for Agni, the god, being kindled.
Sitting down, he places a fuel-stick on the fire at each *praṇava*.

At the final *praṇava* of the verse "Kindled, O Agni, with an oblation" (*samiddho agna āhuta*), or alternatively, having set aside the *anūyāja* fuel-stick, he places the entire fuel-wood (*idhma*) on the fire; or he does so after each *sāmidhenī* verse.

He fans the Āhavanīya fire three times with the *veda*-grass whisk. Taking clarified butter from the *dhruvā* vessel with the *sruva* ladle and supporting it with the *veda*, he draws it along the northern joint of the enclosing sticks. Mentally reciting "To Prajāpati, to Manu, svāhā!", he pours the oblation straight, long, continuous, and radiant, directed toward the south-east; or alternatively, he pours it transversely so as to touch all the fuel-sticks of the firewood.
Taking clarified butter from the butter-pot with the *sruva* ladle, he replenishes the *dhruvā* vessel with the formula, "May the *dhruvā* be filled with ghee."

It is the same everywhere. Having given the command, "O Āgnīdh, cleanse the enclosing sticks and the fire three times each," the Āgnīdhra, holding the faggot-binders on the wooden sword (sphyá), moves around by the right and cleanses the enclosing sticks— the middle one pointing northward and the other two pointing eastward.

"O Agni, winner of booty, I cleanse thee, the winner of booty, who art about to run for booty, who art about to win booty, the winner of booty, for the sake of winning booty; [I cleanse] Agni, the eater of food, for the sake of eating food"—thus he cleanses the fire three times.

At all offerings, he places the *juhū* spoon upon the *upabhṛt* spoon. Having brought it forward from the front, he places the *juhū* into the *upabhṛt*. When he is about to offer, he withdraws it by that same path.
He does not let them clink together, nor does he hold the two spoons over his navel. According to some teachers, they should be held level with the breaths.

To the west of the Āhavanīya fire he passes to the south with his right hand and to the north with his left; or alternatively, he passes to the south with his left hand and to the north with his right.

Intending to pour the Āghāra libation, he makes a reverential salutation (añjali) toward the east for the gods with the formula, "Thou art the world," while placing it in front of the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles; or he says, "Homage to the gods.
With "Svadhā to the fathers," he makes the salutation toward the south.
"Bring the *juhū*," he says, and takes the *juhū*. "Bring the *upabhṛt*," he says, and takes the *upabhṛt*.
"May you two be well-guided for me today, O butter-dripping ones; may you be well-enclosed, well-encircled," with these words he places the *juhū* upon the *upabhṛt*.
Saying, "O Agni and Viṣṇu," he steps across to the south without letting the *prastara* fall.
He stands with the formula, "Thou art the station of Viṣṇu.
[He stands] where Indra, standing, performed his heroic deed; thinking, "Standing, may I perform a heroic deed," he places his right foot inside the altar while keeping the left one outside.

Having moved the offering-spoon along the southern junction of the enclosing sticks, he pours the libation while maintaining contact with them, reciting either "O Agni, you whose heat is intense... or the other [formula].
He pours the libation straight forward, upward, straight, long, and continuous, with the *jyotiṣmatī* verse; or he does so crosswise.
He causes all the fuel-sticks to touch one another.
Having offered, he breathes over it.
One who desires heaven should pour the Āghāra-libation upwards; one who desires rain should pour it downwards.
For one whom he hates, he pours it downwards or cuts it off.

If he should desire of someone, "May he be short-lived," he should pour the oblation for him crookedly. He lifts the ladle with the words, "O Great Splendor! Without touching the ladle, he steps across with the words, "Protect me, O Agni!"

He anoints the *dhruvā* three times with the *juhū* using the formula, "Anointed with fire is the ghee; anointed with oblation is the oblation; may the mid-region be anointed with radiance," or with the formula, "Thou art the head of Makha.

Having taken the clarified butter from the *dhruvā* with the *sruva* ladle using the formula, "Uplifted for wealth," he pours it over the *juhū* with the formula, "Svāhā to the one possessing brave heroes!"
With the formula, "By sacrifice, sacrifice is continued," having set down the *dhruvā* ladle with the *juhū* ladle,
he chooses the *pravara*.
Having taken hold of the faggot-binders, the wooden sword (sphya), and a blade of grass from the Veda that is not at the end, the Adhvaryu stands ready for the Pravara invocation.

"Who shall be the Adhvaryu here? He indeed shall be the Adhvaryu here. "The sacrifice stands in the place of the sacrifice, of Viṣṇu; let Speech perform the office of the priest, let Mind perform the office of the priest; I take refuge in Speech—Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ! Thus the Adhvaryu murmurs. The Āgnīdhra, having taken hold of those [vessels], stands behind him.
He modifies the mantra: "Who shall be the Agnīdh here? He indeed shall be the Agnīdh here."
He addresses [the Āgnīdhra], saying, "I shall cause the announcement to be made for the Brahman-pravara.
He causes the announcement to be made by saying either "Āśrāvaya" or "Ośrāvaya.
The Āgnīdhra responds with "Astu śrauṣaṭ."
In this manner, the *āśrāvaṇa* and *pratyāśrāvaṇa* are performed.
On the *utkara*, the Āgnīdhra stands facing south, holding the wooden sword (*sphya*), and responds with the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* at all other calls for *āśrāvaṇa* until the *pravara*.
Once the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* has been made, he pronounces the *pravara*.

"Agni, the divine Hotṛ, shall sacrifice to the gods, he who is wise and discerning, like Manu, like Bharata, like so-and-so, like so-and-so"—thus [the Hotṛ recites] according to the ancestral lineage (*ārṣeya*) of the sacrificer, including the one beyond him and three preceding ones.

From this point upward, the Adhvaryu chooses the composers of the mantras; for it is known: "He chooses the composers of the mantras according to the ṛṣis. It is also known: "The Hotṛ [chooses] those descending from that point downward."
The king chooses his *pravara* by means of the family lineage (*pravara*) of the domestic priest;

it is known from the royal tradition that he should announce [the lineage] by means of the priest’s ancestral seers (*ārṣeya*). As for the Niṣādas and Rathakāras, he chooses their *pravara* by means of whichever ṛṣi they recite.
Likewise, this applies to Brāhmaṇas who have been placed under the king, or to kings who have been placed under a Brāhmaṇa.
In the case of one belonging to two *gotras*, one should indicate three *pravaras* from each respective *gotra*.
Likewise, for one whose ancestral lineage (*bandhu*) is unknown, [the *pravara*] should be determined by that of the family priest (*purohita*) or the teacher (*ācārya*).
Some, having prohibited the entire *pravara* [of the teacher], prescribe it as being simply "Manu-like" (*manuvad*).
"May he speak with sacred knowledge; may the Brahmins be the protectors of this sacrifice"—this is the remainder of the *pravara* invocation.
He pronounces the name of the Hotṛ in a whisper as "So-and-so," and loudly as "the human one."
The Hotṛ sits down;
he throws a blade of grass onto the sacrificial altar.
2.2 Now begins the second chapter.

Regarding the insertion of verses for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and the *patnīsaṃyāja*s, there are both the *puronuvākyā*s and the *yājyā*s; however, for the *prayāja*s and *anūyāja*s, there is only the *yājyā*.
For both types of offerings, there are the *āśruta* and *pratyāśruta* calls, as well as the *yājyā-saṃpraiṣa*.

They proceed without speaking out of turn. That Adhvaryu should not speak out of turn before the *āśrāvaṇa*; once the *āśrāvaṇa* has been made, he should not speak out of turn before the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*; once the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* has been made, the Adhvaryu should not speak out of turn before the call "yaj" (sacrifice); once "yaj" has been uttered, the Hotṛ should not speak out of turn before the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
To the north, intending to cut the *puronuvākyā* portion, or while cutting it, or having already cut it, he gives the command.
"Recite for such-and-such [deity]"—thus according to the respective deity.
Having stepped across to the south, having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, and once the response has been given, he issues the direction "Sacrifice to such-and-such" according to the respective deity.

At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* or when it has been uttered, he makes the offering; in the case of those [verses] possessing both *puronuvākyā* and *yājyā*, the portion consists of either four or five cuttings.
The five-fold cutting belongs to the Jamadagnis; the four-fold cutting belongs to other lineages.
Even one who is not a Jamadagni, having addressed a Jamadagni, should perform the five-fold cutting.
The portions for the deities are the size of a thumb-joint.
The subsequent portions are larger than the preceding ones.
From the portions for the deities, [he takes] those for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt; from those for Sviṣṭakṛt, those for the Iḍā; likewise [those] belonging to the fourfold division.

He cuts the sacrificial cake with the thumb and two fingers joined together; he cuts the clarified butter and the *sāṃnāyya* with the *sruva* ladle, and the *caru* offerings with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*).

Having taken a portion from the middle of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), he takes a second portion from the eastern half and a third from the western half for one who performs the five-fold cutting. For one who desires to overcome his enemies, the final portion is the first to be taken.
Having taken it, he should place the ladle (sruk) in the eastern half; the first [portion] in the eastern half and the final [portion] in the western half.

One should cut portions from the front parts for the eldest son born of the first wife; or [for one] desiring the office of domestic priest (*purodhā*). One should cut portions from the rear parts for the youngest son born of the first wife, or for one who is slow to prosper (*ānujāvara*).

For the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and the *sāṃnāyya* offering, having spread a base of clarified butter (*ājya*) for the under-layering and sprinkled clarified butter over it for the over-layering, one should cut portions of the oblation and then sprinkle them with clarified butter.

Having spread a base of ghee in the *sruc* [ladle], he touches the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) while about to take a portion, saying: "Do not fear; do not tremble; may I not harm you; may your brilliance not depart. Support him! Raise him up! O Manu’s daughter, I shall take portions from your offerings in return. Homage be to you; do not harm me.

Having taken the portions and having sprinkled them with ghee, he re-sprinkles the oblation, saying: "Whatever I have done contrary to the natural order (*viloma*) regarding your portions while taking them from myself, I now anoint that back with ghee;
let it swell again for you. It is known from tradition: "Having taken each portion, he anoints the *prastara* and the *barhis* together."
As if closing [the mouth] and as if not letting it flow out, he offers the cake-oblation; having offered ghee, he offers the portion (avadāna); finally, he pours out the remainder with ghee.
He causes the others to flow out by means of the mouth.
He offers each preceding insertion-oblation (āvāpāhuti) in its proper sequence.
He offers the *āghāra* libation with the *sruc*.

Having chosen the *pravara*, when it is said, "O Adhvaryu, place the butter-filled *sruc* upon [the altar]," he takes up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, steps across once, and performs the five *prayāja* offerings, either stepping forward for each or standing in one place.
He steps away from his enemy.

He gives the first *prayāja* command, "Sacrifice the *samidhs*," and for the subsequent ones, "Sacrifice, sacrifice. He sacrifices to the *samidhs* in the east, to *tanūnapāt* in the south, to *iḍ* in the west; having taken half of the butter from the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*, he sacrifices to *barhis* in the north. He makes the *svāhā* utterance in the middle, or behind the junction of the two *āghāra* lines, sacrificing each one joined with the preceding one, or all together in one place.
Having stepped back, he sprinkles the sacrificial oblations with the remainder of the *prayāja*.
In that they are offered in successive order:
having sprinkled the *dhruvā* ladle, he sprinkles the *āgneya* [offering], and finally the *upabhṛt*.
He proceeds with the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), which have clarified butter as their oblation-material.
Simultaneously, he offers two oblations with light in the northern half for Agni and in the southern half for Soma;
he offers the others between those two.
He takes up the two offering-spoons for the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) and does not set them down until the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
Having performed the ritual with the cake for Agni, he proceeds with the *upāṃśuyāja*, which has clarified butter as its oblation.
For that [offering], the calls for the *āśruta* and *pratyāśruta*, the *puronuvākyā* and *yājyā* verses, and the *vaṣaṭkāra* are pronounced aloud.
The announcement of the deity is performed in a whisper.
He proceeds with the northern cake according to its respective deity.
Having taken portions from both the *sāṃnāyya* offerings, he proceeds twice.
He cuts from the boiled [milk] twice; from the curd, three times for one who offers five-fold portions.
Having made equal portions, he proceeds with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
When the portions are offered in sequence, he cuts once each time from all the northern halves.
For one who offers five cuttings twice, he pours clarified butter over them twice; he does not pour butter over the remnants of the oblation.
He offers it in the eastern part of the northern half of the fire, so that it does not touch the other offerings.

Having stepped back and filled the offering-ladle with water, he sprinkles it around the middle enclosing-stick from left to right, saying: "In Vaiśvānara I offer this oblation; this is a thousandfold spring with a hundred streams. In it, may he support my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, swelling [with abundance] in the heavenly world. ||6||
2.3 Now begins the third chapter of the second book.

Having set down the two offering-ladles (*srucau*) and having split the cake for Agni toward the east, he touches it with his thumb and ring finger, saying: "May this [portion] be cut from the oblation by a measure of a barley-corn; may we not tear the sacrifice; may this oblation be pure and well-sacrificed. Having touched it thus, he cuts off the *prāśitra* (the portion for the Brahman) measuring a barley-corn or a *pippala*-berry.
He does not split [the cake] from the northern part.
Having spread an underlayer [of ghee] upon the *prāśitraharaṇa* vessel, he cuts off a portion and pours ghee over it;
according to some, he should spread an underlayer and pour ghee over it.
According to some, he cuts off the *prāśitra* from the cake for Agni.

Having placed that [portion] down, he spreads an underlayer of ghee in the *iḍā*-vessel and cuts off the *iḍā* portion, whether it be fourfold or fivefold; the sequence for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering has already been explained.

With the mantra, "I cut off the *ghṛtapadī*, seen by Manu and impelled by Mitra and Varuṇa, the single-faced one from the southern half without piercing through," he first cuts off the *iḍā* portion from the southern half of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
From the eastern half, he takes a portion as long as an atom; from the northern half, likewise.
Having gratified it with clarified butter and brought it near the *dhruvā* ladle, he makes the cutting from the junction.
The third part from the rear half belongs to the five-fold cutting.
Having sprinkled it with clarified butter, he places the *iḍā* for the *hotṛ*,
or he pushes it forward.
Without letting go of the ladle, he encompasses the Adhvaryu; if it has been handed over to the Hotṛ,
he passes to the south of the Hotṛ in front of him and, sitting behind him facing east, anoints the two finger-joints of the Hotṛ—
the first one first, then the other.
Having smelled that, he touches water.
Having returned by the same way he came, sitting in front facing west, he cuts off the intermediate *iḍā* from the *iḍā* into the right hand of the Hotṛ;
he makes an under-layer from the smearings.
The Hotṛ himself, or the Adhvaryu, takes [the portion] twice from the middle; the other [portion] [is taken by] the other.
He sprinkles it with the smearings.
The Hotṛ invokes [the gods].
While the *iḍā* is being invoked, the Adhvaryu, the Āgnīdhra, and the sacrificer touch it from behind.
When the words "The divine Adhvaryus are invoked" are being uttered, he mutters: "May I be invoked and possessed of cattle.
Once the *iḍā* has been invoked, he carries the *prāśitra* portion for the Brahman around the front of the Āhavanīya fire.

When that has been consumed, the officiating priests, with the sacrificer as the fifth, eat the *iḍā* while it is being invoked, reciting: "Thou art the *iḍā*; thou art pleasant; thou art the maker of pleasantness; do thou bestow upon us abundance of wealth and excellent offspring. I eat thee for the glory of my mouth, and for the fragrance of my mouth.
They remain silent until the ritual cleansing (*āmārjana*).
With the mantra, "May the mind, the light, be gratified," they perform the purification rite within the sacrificial altar (vedī) over the strainers (pavitra).
Having divided the cake for Agni into four parts, he places it upon the sacrificial grass (barhis).
While that portion is being assigned, he assigns the sacrificer's share with the words, "This for the sacrificer."

For the portion assigned to the Āgnīdhra, he prepares a sixfold cutting (ṣaḍavatta) from the largest piece. Having spread a base of ghee and having taken a cutting, he pours ghee over it; in this same manner, he takes another cutting. "Thou art the portion of heaven; thou art Agni’s Āgnīdhra; thou art Agni’s Śāmitra; I eat thee with the mouth of Agni; homage be unto thee; do not harm me"—with these words, the Āgnīdhra eats it.
With the *veda* he distributes the portions for the Brahman and the Sacrificer;
with one vessel [he gives] to the Hotṛ, and with another to the Adhvaryu.
"Thou art the portion of the Earth," says the Hotṛ as he eats; "Thou art the portion of the Atmosphere," says the Adhvaryu; "Thou art the portion of Heaven," says the Brahman.
A large and unlimited *anvāhārya* mess of cooked rice is prepared on the *dakṣiṇāgni*; having either sprinkled it with clarified butter or left it unsprinkled, he places it within the *antarvedi*.
He issues the command: "Let it be brought to those who sit in the south.
When the sacrificer says, "Come hither from the south," they act according to the command.
Having received the *anvāhārya* rice, they return;
having removed the remnants of the oblation;
and having reinserted the two firebrands (*ulmuka*) for the sake of the after-offerings (*anūyāja*).
"O Brahman, we shall set forth; O Āgnīdh, having placed the fuel-stick, cleanse the enclosing-sticks and the fire once each," thus he gives the command.

"This is your fuel-stick, O Agni; through it may you grow and swell; may the lord of the sacrifice grow and may he swell, Svāhā! Having thus placed the fuel-stick, the Āgnīdhra, without stepping across, cleanses the enclosing-sticks with the wooden sword and the cord used for binding the fuel-wood—the middle one facing northward and the other two facing eastward.

He modifies the mantra: "O Agni, winner of booty, thee who hast run for the booty... He sprinkles the cleansing-grass with water and throws it into the Āhavanīya fire, saying: "He who is the lord of beings, Rudra, the youth who moves along the threads—do not harm our cattle; let this be an oblation for thee, Svāhā!
He should cast it out either on the rubbish-heap (utkara), in the hall, or in the stable.
Or he may carry [the fire] to another's cow-pen or to another's pasture-land.
Thus ends the third chapter in the second book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Now begins the fourth chapter in the second book.
Having poured the clarified butter from the *upabhṛt* into the *juhū*, he crosses over once with it and performs three *anūyāja* offerings.
He issues the call for the first *anūyāja*: "Sacrifice to the gods! and for the two subsequent ones: "Sacrifice! Sacrifice!
He offers them behind each of the kindling-sticks (*samidh*), in front of the junction of the *āghāra* streams.
He extends the final [strand] eastward, long and continuous, and with it he joins the others.
Having stepped back and placed them in the ladles according to their respective places,
he spreads them apart with two verses containing the word "vāja."

With the formula, "By the impulse of strength," he lifts up the *juhū* ladle together with the *prastara* grass-bundle with his right hand, palm upwards; then, with the formula, "May Indra [drive] my rivals away," he presses down on the *upabhṛt* ladle with his left hand, palm downwards. With the words, "The uplifting," he lifts up the *juhū*; with the words, "And the pressing down," he presses down on the *upabhṛt*. With the formula, "The gods have increased the sacred power (*brahman*)," he pushes forward the *juhū* eastward with his right hand, palm upwards; then, with the formula, "May Indra and Agni [drive] my rivals away," he throws the *upabhṛt* westward outside the altar with his left hand, palm downwards.

"May the god Savitṛ drive away him who hates us and whom we hate"—with these words, or [simply] having sprinkled [the butter], he takes the *upabhṛt* and anoints the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the *juhū*:

"For the Vasus, thee!"—thus the middle one; "For the Rudras, thee!"—thus the southern one; "For the Ādityas, thee!"—thus the northern one; or [alternatively]: "Thou art the winner of wealth; thou art the bestower of wealth."

Having placed the *juhū* ladle on the *prastara* bundle [except for this case], and having smoothed the *prastara* with the two *vidhṛti* blades while reciting, "May Heaven and Earth agree; may Mitra and Varuṇa protect you with rain," and having cast the two *vidhṛtis* back onto the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he anoints the *prastara* in the ladles:
the tips in the *juhū* with the verse, "Licking what is anointed"; the middle parts in the *upabhṛt* with, "May the birds fly apart"; and the roots in the *dhruvā* with, "Offspring, the womb.
He anoints them again in the same manner.
On the third occasion, he marks the roots at the beginning on the *dhruvā* ladle, the middle parts in the *upabhṛt*, and the tips at the end in the *juhū*;
or alternatively, he says, "Mark it in heaven, mark it in the intermediate space, mark it on earth.
Having wiped the [ladle] with the formula "For life, thee," he removes a blade of grass and sets it aside in a known place.
Having taken up the prastara-bundle and the branch,
and having moved them along the upper junction of the enclosing-sticks (paridhi), and having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* and received the response (*pratyāśrāvita*), [he performs the offering]. || 9 ||

The divine Hotṛ-priests have been impelled for the utterance of auspicious speech; the human [Hotṛ] has been dispatched for the Sūktavāka. He issues the command: "Recite the Sūktas! Thereupon the Hotṛ begins the Sūktavāka.
The Adhvaryu throws the prastara-bundle and the branch after [the fire], saying:
"May the waters swell; may the plants swell," or: "May the licking ones lick what is anointed; may the birds eat; having become the dappled cow, may she go to heaven."
Holding his hand neither too high nor too low, not leaning back, and as if not bent, he turns it around from below as if drawing it.
When it is said, "This sacrificer, so-and-so, hopes [for success]," he releases the *prastara* and issues the command: "O Agnīdh, bring [the fire]!"

The Āgnīdhra raises the *prastara* upward with three handfuls of water. He issues the command: "Throw it after [the fire]! saying, "Svāhā! Go to your own bodies! The Āgnīdhra throws a blade of grass from the *prastara* into the fire.
With the words, "This is that," he points to it three times with his finger.
With the formula, "O Agni, protector of life, protect my life," he touches the seats of the vital breaths according to their respective forms. With the formula, "Be firm," he touches this [earth].
"Converse!"—thus the Āgnīdhra gives the command.
"Has he come, O Āgnīdh? the Adhvaryu asks. "He has come," replies the Āgnīdhra.
"Make it heard," says the Adhvaryu. "Śrauṣaṭ," replies the Āgnīdhra.
Having touched the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*), he issues the command: "May there be success for the divine *hotṛ*s; may there be well-being for the human ones; pronounce the *śaṃyu* formula!
The *hotṛ* begins the *śaṃyuvāka*, and the *adhvaryu* throws the enclosing-sticks into the fire.
With the words "That which is the enclosing-stick," he places the middle one;
with the words "To the path of the sacrifice, you have been brought together," he places the other two.
He pushes the tip of the northern one downward into the embers.
He addresses all [the priests] with the formula, "May he extend the sacrificer.
Placing the tip of the *upabhṛt* ladle into the hollow of the *juhū*, he causes both ladles to drip with the formula, "Those who have a share in the drippings.
When the *śaṃyuvāka* has been recited, they consume the remnants of the oblations.
Having washed away the remnants of the clarified butter, || 10 ||
2.5 Now begins the fifth chapter of the second book.

The Adhvaryu takes up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles; the Hotṛ takes up the *veda*; and the Āgnīdhra takes up the *sruva* and the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*). Intending to perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, they proceed westward. The Adhvaryu passes to the south of the Gārhapatya fire, while the other two pass to its north.
With the formula, "I set you down in the seat of Agni, whose house is secure from the left," he places the two offering-spoons on the *kaṣṭambhī* pillar.
With the formula, "O two draft-horses, protect the yoke-pole," he wipes them along the yoke-poles; some authorities prescribe that the wiping (*prohaṇa*) be performed first.
Or he pours out the grain on the wooden sword (*sphya*), or having released them [the spoons] onto the wooden sword.
Having sat down at the Gārhapatya fire with the two ladles already released, they perform the *saṃyājana* for the wives with the ladles in silence alone.

Having placed the *veda* on the *upabhṛt* ladle while the wife holds on to it, he sacrifices to Soma in the northern half and to Tvaṣṭṛ in the southern half; between these two, he performs the other sacrifices.
He sacrifices to the wives of the gods either in an enclosed space or in an unenclosed one.
One desiring a son should sacrifice to Rākā in an unenclosed place; one desiring cattle, to Sinīvālī; and one desiring prosperity, to Kuhū.
Some authorities prescribe that Rākā and Sinīvālī should be recited before the wives of the gods.

Having sacrificed to Agni Gṛhapati, he offers the *saṃpatnīya* oblation with the *sruva* ladle while the wife holds on to him from behind, with the mantra: "May the wife go together with her husband through their good deed; may they become the two yoke-horses harnessed to the sacrifice; being in harmony, may they cast away their enemies; may they grasp the undecaying light in heaven. He offers this while the wife maintains contact with him.
He anoints the two finger-joints of the Hotṛ; having anointed the rear one, he then anoints the front one, or otherwise.
Having smelled that, he touches water. He cuts four drops of clarified butter from the *iḍā* into the right hand of the Hotṛ.
There are six Āgnīdhra priests.
The Hotṛ priest invokes;
the Adhvaryu and the Āgnīdhra invoke the *iḍā*; and the wife touches them from behind.
When it is said, "This sacrificer is invited," he murmurs, "May I be invited, possessing cattle.
The Hotṛ eats [the portion] when it has been invited.

The Āgnīdhra eats, saying: "Father Heaven is invited; may Father Heaven invite me from the Āgnīdhra-fire for long life, for splendor, for living, and for merit"—or alternatively: "Mother Earth is invited; may Mother Earth invite me from the Āgnīdhra-fire for long life, for splendor, for living, and for merit."
Having consumed [the portion], he performs the *mārjana* (sprinkling) silently;
[this concludes] either with the *iḍā* or with the *śaṃyu*.

At the conclusion of the *śaṃyu*, having taken a blade of grass from the *vedī*, he should smear its tip in the *juhū* ladle, its middle in the *sruva* ladle, and its base in the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*).
The ritual procedure for that is the same as that for the *prastara* [grass-bundle].
Having placed the wood-chips from the faggot onto the *dakṣiṇāgni*, he offers the oblations of the flour-smear and the husks.
Having poured the husks into four ladlefuls of clarified butter, he offers them with the mantra: "O Agni, of unassailable life-force... (RV 10.87.22).

Furthermore, having taken four portions of butter, he offers the flour-smear (piṣṭalepa) with the mantra: "What clung to the mortar and the pestle, and what stuck to the winnowing basket, the grinding stone, and the potsherd;

the drops and the scattered sprays—I sacrifice them together. May all the gods enjoy this oblation. Whatever many drops there are in the sacrifice, I offer them all well-sacrificed and well-poured into Agni. Thus he offers the flour-smear. Some authorities prescribe offering the flour-smear first. Then the Hotṛ gives the Veda-bundle to the wife with the mantra: "Thou art the Veda; thou art the means of finding."
"You are the Veda; for the sake of the Veda I take you; may the Veda find me for me"—saying this, or "the ghee-filled, nest-like one," he places it upon his lap and throws it.
The Hotṛ throws [the grass];
according to some, he pauses three times. "Drive away the hater, drive away the enemy"—with these words, the Veda is thrown out by the wife.
Thinking, "I shall loosen this," she loosens the noose of the yoke-cord.
As it is being brought, he pours the full vessel into her cupped hands, which still hold the yoke-cord, while she mutters: "May we be united in life."
Having led that [water] and wiped his mouth as was appropriate, he departs.
While spreading the Veda-grass from the Gārhapatya fire continuously up to the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra "The butter-rich, nest-like," the Hotṛ priest goes forward.
Having returned in this manner, the Adhvaryu, having offered two oblations to Sarasvatī with the formulas:
"To that Sarasvatī who is the bringer of glory, svāhā! To that Sarasvatī who is the bringer of dwellings, svāhā!", [recites]:
"O Indra, make the dwellings of my breath and mind here; make my kinsmen well-disposed, svāhā!"

"We sacrifice to the bull, the vigorous one, the Full Moon; may it yield for us excellent heroic power and thousandfold abundance of wealth. Svāhā to the Full Moon, for out-breathing and for the bountiful giver!"—thus he offers on the full moon day. "The New Moon is fortunate and very gracious, swelling again like a milch-cow; may she yield for us excellent heroic power and thousandfold abundance of wealth. Svāhā to the New Moon, for in-breathing and for the bountiful giver!"—thus he offers on the new moon day with the *sruva* ladle, performing the two *pārvaṇa* oblations.
Some authorities prescribe that these be recited before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.

Ten are your bodies, O Sacrifice, worthy of worship; may the sacrificer gratify them with clarified butter. Praising the command of the two *Nāriṣṭhas*, the sacrificer has become immortal within the divine domain of the gods. O you two of a hundred powers, that portion of strength which the gods ordained for you both—I gratify you with this; be satisfied with it here. I am in the world of the gods who perform good deeds; let this sacrifice of mine not be in vain.

I, the wise one, follow and sacrifice with the *nāriṣṭha* oblations, since Indra bestowed a share upon them that cannot be assailed. O divine Soma, you who do not cause the house to leak, be present at this sacrifice; O Maruts, be gracious to us! Let not the overwhelming curse find us, nor let the hateful host of enemies find us. Brahman is the foundation of the mind, Brahman of speech, and Brahman of sacrifices, oblations, and clarified butter. Whatever is redundant in the rite and whatever is deficient, may the sacrifice go forth, smoothing over its joints and restoring them, as the offering consecrated by *svāhā* reaches the gods.

"I unite your mind with my mind; I place your breath within my breath. I unite your diffused breath with my diffused breath; I place your downward breath within my downward breath. Having taken hold [of you], the sacrificer has become immortal. Be auspicious to us—be auspicious to our bipeds, be auspicious to our quadrupeds! Svāhā! With these words, he offers the *nāriṣṭha* oblations. 1.3.
2.6 Now begins the sixth chapter of the second book:

*Svāhā* to the desired; *vaṣaṭ* to the undesired; *svāhā* to healing from ill-sacrificed offerings; *svāhā* to expiation; *svāhā* to misfortune; *svāhā* to failure; *svāhā* to the divine bodies; *svāhā* to prosperity; *svāhā* to success.

O Agni, with that which is straight (*ayās*), drive away curses; you indeed are truth, you are straight. Held by a straight mind, carry the oblation straight; bestow healing upon us, *svāhā*! "O Varuṇa, this [is mine]... (*imaṃ me varuṇa*); "Whatever [we have done] against you... (*tat tvā yāmi*); "You, O Agni, for us... (*tvaṃ no agne*); "So you, O Agni, for us... (*sa tvaṃ no agne*); "You, O Agni, are straight... (*tvamagne ayāsi*). With the *vyāhṛtis*—"Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ"—he offers oblations, both individually and collectively.

Whatever in the sacrifice has been called for (*āśrāvitam*), over-called (*atyāśrāvitam*), accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ* call (*vaṣaṭkṛtam*), or recited excessively (*atyanūktam*), whatever is redundant in the rite or whatever is deficient—may the sacrifice, mending its joints and making them fit, go as an offering consecrated by *svāhā* to the gods.

Whatever is performed erroneously in the sacrifice—whether it was not recognized as such or was recognized—O Agni, make that right for him, for you know the truth exactly as it is; may the offering consecrated with *svāhā* go to the gods.

I offer what is in excess into what is deficient, and I offer what is deficient into what is in excess; I offer what is equal into what is equal; may the offering consecrated with *svāhā* go to the gods.

Whatever we have done, whatever we have not done, whatever we have overstepped, whatever we have not overstepped, whatever we have left in excess, whatever we have not left in excess—O Viṣṇu, establish that sacrifice within the sacrifice; may the offering consecrated with *svāhā* go to the gods.

Whatever in this sacrifice has gone amiss within me through negligence—whether by mantra or by ritual act—I pacify all that with this oblation. May the gods be satisfied; may this offering, consecrated with *svāhā*, go to the gods. "The Veda is the foundation of the mind"—this is the verse. "That which was woven by me, the waters weave it again; the sweetest prayer is recited for the hymn. This is the ocean and the universal healer; may it satisfy the one to whom the *svāhā* has been offered. *Bhuvaḥ*.

Up from the darkness we have risen; up that [sun], the bright one. O Gods, whatever offense against the gods I may have committed through my speech, even though it was offered with devotion—O Maruts, cast that away from us to another, to the enemy who seeks to harm us with ill fortune.
O Indra, from whatever we fear, grant us freedom from fear therefrom. O Maghavan, be gracious for our protection; slay those who hate us and those who oppose us.
Bestower of well-being, Lord of the people, slayer of Vṛtra, dispeller of enemies, the Controller; may Indra, the Bull, go before us, the giver of well-being and the creator of fearlessness.

O Lord of the bay horses, increasing in strength, fill up with these songs whatever in us is deficient; when you burst open the great cow-pens for your praisers, may we then be those who receive the greatest portion. Away with your wrath! Raise up the highest [of our bonds]!

The sacrifice is commensurate with the Person; the sacrifice is commensurate with the Person. O Agni, fashion that for him, for you indeed know it as it truly is. Let the oblation, consecrated by *svāhā*, go to the gods.

Whatever mortals, with simple minds and feeble resolve, do not properly conceive of the sacrifice—may Agni, the Hotṛ who knows the ritual, being the most skilled in worship, sacrifice to the gods according to the seasons.
"Svāhā!"—thus the Adhvaryu offers with the ladle into the Āhavanīya fire. 14.
He offers all the expiatory oblations.

Having replenished the *dhruvā* ladle, standing upright within the altar, he offers three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations into the *āhavanīya* fire with the *dhruvā* ladle, reciting the mantra: "O gods, you who know the way..."
One, two, or three times continuously, or intermittently;
he cuts off [the flow] of one who is hateful, either downward or by breaking it off.
If he should desire, "May he be short-lived," he should offer while standing crookedly.
At the middle *svāhā*-utterance, he throws the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) after [the oblation],
or a handful of sacrificial grass.
Either he offers the oblation after the sacrifice has been completed,
or having offered it, he should subsequently pour the libation.

If the sacrificer should go abroad, he should place the sacrificer’s portion into the *dhruvā* ladle with the formula, "The world of Prajāpati named Vibhān," and offer it together with the *saṃiṣṭayajus*.

"Strew [the grass] over it; enclose the altar; do not harm your kin lying there. "These golden, bright ornaments of the sacrificer are the Hotṛ’s seats, O Bradhna! With these words, he strews the Hotṛ’s seats upon the altar.

Having carried the *praṇītā* waters around the front of the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "For prosperity for you," he releases them within the altar with the formula, "He who has sprinkled you, let him release you."

"The implement which the gods placed among men—those who are ill-disposed toward us, bring them here for us! O implement, settle upon us: progeny, prosperity, and wealth; make our bipeds and quadrupeds firm and never-departing.
Having taken up the fire-brick (upaveṣa), he should bury it or cast it away on the rubbish-heap (utkara) with the words: "O implement, let the heat reach so-and-so whom we hate!"

Drive him away from our dwelling, O friend—the rival who attacks us. With this oblation that drives away the foe, Indra has cast him out. Go to the three distant realms; go beyond the five peoples. Go to the three luminous spheres as far as the sun dwells in heaven. May Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, lead you to the furthest distance, from which you shall not return for eternal years.

"He is slain! We have struck so-and-so!"—thus he meditates in his mind upon the death of him whom he hates. Or, having touched water, he recites: "Fly away, O arrow, released and sharpened by sacred power (brahman)!"
"Who yokes you? Let him release you," with these words he releases the sacrifice. He looks over everything, [saying] "Those potsherds which were on the cauldron," referring to the potsherds.
When the full moon has arrived. || 15 ||
He commences the ritual procedure for the Vaimṛdha offering.
Its ritual arrangement is explained by that of the Aindrāgna offering.
There are either fifteen or seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.
At the time of the offering, he pours out abundant rice for Indra Vaimṛdha.
At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives a fee according to his ability.
In this matter, one may proceed according to one's desire.
However, it is restricted by the context:
"We shall explain the optional rites of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
By means of these Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one who desires prosperity should sacrifice.
One should sacrifice on two full-moon days and two new-moon days.
According to some, he who desires "May I overcome" should sacrifice only on the full-moon day;
he who has rivals should not sacrifice on the new-moon day. He should sacrifice at intervals of two or three [days]. At every transition, he hurls the thunderbolt at his rival.
The Agniṣomīya offerings should be the principal rites for one who has rivals, or who practices sorcery, or who desires to cross over difficulties.
One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Sākaṃprasthāyīya.
There are many evening milkings and many morning milkings; with these, he sacrifices immediately following the milking.

Alternatively, just as they milk the oblation on the new moon day, having thus milked it and heated it, he should set it aside; whatever is to be used in the morning, that he should prepare as cooked. At the time of arranging the vessels, he sets out the vessels according to their purpose, including large ladles made of Udumbara wood and large cups (camasa); the ritual procedure for these is explained by the same rules as those for the Juhū ladle.

Having performed the ritual with the cake for Agni (āgneya-puroḍāśa) and having placed the two offering-ladles (sruc) in the Āgnīdhra fire-shed, he steps across together with the water-jars (kumbhīs) while the Hotṛ recites the invitatory prayer for Mahendra; he causes the announcement to be made, saying, "Recite the offering-prayer for Indra! As many as there are jars, so many Brāhmaṇas, wearing their sacred threads over the left shoulder (upavītins), should stand up on the south side, taking wooden vessels and bringing the jars into them; they all sacrifice simultaneously, pouring their libations after the libation of the Adhvaryu.
One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Dākṣāyaṇayajña. There are two full-moon sacrifices and two new-moon sacrifices.

On the first full moon day, there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Soma; on the subsequent full moon day, there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and curds for Indra. On the first new moon day, there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and clotted curds (āmikṣā) for Mitra-Varuṇa; on the subsequent new moon day, there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra-Agni.

For this sacrifice, the following is the vow: one must not speak untruth, nor eat meat, nor approach a woman; they must not wash his garment with lye (palpūlana), nor anoint themselves, nor rub themselves with oil; however, he may approach his wife during her season.

Thus, this option regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices from the very beginning is stated: "One may either sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, or, having sacrificed for fifteen years with them, one discontinues the New and Full Moon sacrifices. This concludes the sixth chapter of the second book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
2.7 Now, the seventh chapter in the second book.
On the afternoon of the new moon day, he performs the Piṇḍapitṛyajña sacrifice;
or when the sun is over the treetops.

On the day when they do not see the moon in the east—if it is still visible, however, one should fast and sacrifice on the following day—he cuts the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) once, including its roots, with the formula:
"May that which is pure, worthy of sacrifice, divine, and auspicious among the waters be mine; may I, your cutter, not suffer harm; may I live for a hundred autumns."
Having strewn darbha grass with its tips pointing south and east around the Dakṣiṇā fire,
and having spread darbha grass to the north of the fire,
he sets out the vessels for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña one by one.

Having placed the wooden sword (*sphya*), the pot (*sthālī*), the stirring-ladle (*mekṣaṇa*), the winnowing-basket (*śūrpa*), the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), the mortar (*ulūkhala*), and the pestle (*musala*) to the west of the fire, and having stationed a cart laden with rice to the west of the fire, he fills the pot—which has been covered with a single strainer—with rice, wipes it, and pours [the grain] into the winnowing-basket all at once, saying: "I pour thee out, acceptable to the ancestors.

To the south of the southern fire, he spreads the black antelope skin with its neck pointing westward and its hairy side upward, either to the southeast or southwest of the fire, and places the mortar upon it.

The wife stands facing southeast and husks [the grain]. She threshes it once, separating the chaff from the grain. Having cooked the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) in the southern fire so that the grains remain intact, she bastes it with clarified butter—either fresh butter that has been strained or unstrained ghee—and then removes it from the fire.
The Adhvaryu, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*), bends his right knee.

Having taken a portion of the *sthālīpāka* with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), he offers the first oblation with the formula: "To Soma, drunk by the fathers, svadhā! Adoration! The second [he offers] with: "To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the fathers, svadhā! Adoration! The third [he offers] with: "To Agni Kavyavāhana, the maker of good offerings, svadhā! Adoration! He then offers those rice grains which remain in the stirring-spoon. 17.

He silently places the stirring-stick (mekṣaṇa) [on the altar]. With the mantra: "The Asuras who, assuming various forms, wander about with their own power (svadhā); those who carry off the outer forts and the inner forts—may Agni drive them away from this world," he takes a single glowing ember from the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, carries it toward the south, and places it to the south of the spot for the single wooden sword (sphyā).

Having drawn a line with the wooden sword on the southern part of the single-sphyā altar at the place of threshing, with the mantra: "The Asuras and Rakṣasas who sit upon the altar are struck down," he draws the line toward the south or southeast.
With the verse, "May those who are below rise up," he sprinkles [the ground] with water.

With the *sakṛdācchinna* grass—soft like wool, pleasant—he says: "I bring you, O Barhis, for the ancestors; may my ancestors, the Soma-loving ones, along with their grandfathers and great-grandfathers and their followers, sit upon this. With this *sakṛdācchinna* grass, he spreads a single line [of grass] using the wooden sword (*sphya*).
Upon that, he places the *sthālīpāka* (cooked sacrificial rice).
To the south, he establishes collyrium, ointment, a head-rest, a pillow, and a water-pot.

The sacrificer, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), bending his left knee, and with his hands turned downwards, pours out three handfuls of water ending toward the south, using the formula:

"May the Soma-loving fathers purify themselves; may the Soma-loving grandfathers purify themselves; may the Soma-loving great-grandfathers purify themselves," or alternatively, "O [Name], pour down; O [Name], pour down."
With his hands turned downward, he offers three rice-balls (piṇḍas) ending toward the south.
He gives a rice-ball to the father with the words, "This for you, O Father, [Name]!
To the grandfather with the words, "This for you, O Grandfather, [Name]! And to the great-grandfather with the words, "This for you, O Great-grandfather, [Name]!"
The fourth [offering] is made silently;
that is considered both performed and unperformed.

Now, if he should not know their names, he should give a rice-ball to the father with the words, "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling on earth"; to the grandfather with the words, "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling in the intermediate space"; and to the great-grandfather with the words, "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling in heaven."
If he perceives two fathers in each single ball of rice,
he should offer [the balls] saying, "To the living father," "To the grandfather," and "To the great-grandfather.
According to some, one does not offer beyond a living person.
One should perform only up to the end of the oblation (*homānta*).
For one whose father is living, everything from the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) onwards is omitted.
Having deposited the rice-balls...

"O divine waters, being honored with the *svadhā* offering—may they, who are pleasant, go to you, O fathers! Carrying strength, possessing inexhaustible water, milk, water, clarified butter, honey, milk, *kīlāla*, and flowing nectar—you are the *svadhā*; satisfy my fathers. With these words, he pours out three handfuls of water.
Having said, "O fathers, rejoice according to your portions; satisfy yourselves according to the *svadhā*," he turns away.
Once the heat has subsided, he waits and consecrates the rising steam with the mantra: "Svāhā! May the heat not distress me."
Having said, "Whether the heat has subsided or not, the ancestors have rejoiced; they have attained their own portion according to their nature," he turns around toward the fire.
He either smells the remnant that remains in the pot or touches it.

One who is ill, or one who desires food, or one who, though capable of obtaining food, does not eat it—any such person may consume [the rice]. Having consumed it, he gives collyrium, ointment, and a garment along with each rice-ball. He says, "Anoint yourself, so-and-so! Anoint yourself, so-and-so! three times for the collyrium; "Oint yourself, so-and-so! Oint yourself, so-and-so! three times for the ointment.
"O fathers, these are your garments; therefore, O fathers, do not take anything else from us"—having thus cut off a fringe or a tuft of wool, he places it down during the earlier stage of life;
having cut his own hair, he does so during the later stage. He pays homage with the words, "Homage to you, O fathers, to the essence."

"Full of vigor, honoring you with the *svadhā* call—may they, being pleasant, go to you, O ancestors! Carrying vigor, providing inexhaustible water—milk, water, clarified butter, honey, milk, nectar, and flowing liquor—you are the *svadhā*; satisfy my ancestors! With these words, he pours out three handfuls of water as before. (19)

"Arise, O ancestors who have passed away before us, you who have followed the ancient path of Yama! Bestow upon us wealth and that which is auspicious; speak for us in favor among the deities who grant their portions. With these words, he causes the ancestors to rise.
"Depart, O ancestors," with this he dismisses them.
"May the ancestors go with the speed of thought," with this he sends the ancestors forth.
He worships with the three verses containing the word "mind," beginning with *mano nvā huvāmahe*.
He returns with the two verses dedicated to Prajāpati, which are in the *paṅkti* meter, beginning with *akṣann amīmadanta prajāpate*.
He worships the Gārhapatya fire with the *paṅkti* verse beginning with *yad antarikṣam*.

"Jātavedas was our messenger for the oblation; having made the offerings fragrant, he has carried them away. He has given them to the ancestors, and they have eaten them with the *svadhā* call. O Agni, knowing [this], go back again to the gods. Having thus thrown back a single firebrand [into the hearth], and having sprinkled [the area], he brings back the vessels in pairs.
He places the rice balls (*piṇḍa*) back into the cooking pot.
"I cause you to consume the essence of the waters and the plants; conceive a fetus created by the beings," with these words he gives the middle ball of food to his wife.
