"O Fathers, bestow a fetus, a boy wearing a lotus-wreath, so that there may be a man here," with these words the wife consumes it;
she gives birth to a male child.

"Those ancestors who are equal and of one mind in the realm of Yama—for them let there be a world, *svadhā*, reverence, and may the sacrifice be prepared among the gods. Those kinsmen who are equal and of one mind, living among the living and belonging to me—for them let prosperity be prepared in me in this world for a hundred years. Having sprinkled the once-cut blades of grass with water, he places them on the fire.
He causes the funeral cakes to be cast into the water, or he feeds a Brāhmaṇa.
This very procedure is prescribed even for one who has not maintained the sacred fires.
In that regard, those [rites] connected with cooking are performed on the *aupāsana* fire;
he offers oblations on the *atipraṇīta* fire;
and he pays reverence to whichever [fire] he makes the offering.
In this case, the designation "gārhapatya" is sublated. || 20 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the second book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

2.8 Now, the eighth chapter in the second book. "I am the lord of the earth; I am the lord of the world; I am the lord of the great being. Impelled by the god Savitṛ, I shall perform the office of the *ṛtvij*. O god Savitṛ, they choose you here as Bṛhaspati, the divine *brahman*. That I announce to the mind; the mind to the *gāyatrī*; the *gāyatrī* to the *triṣṭubh*; the *triṣṭubh* to the *jagatī*; the *jagatī* to the *anuṣṭubh*; the *anuṣṭubh* to the *bṛhatī*; the *bṛhatī* to the *paṅkti*; the *paṅkti* to Prajāpati; Prajāpati to the All-gods (*viśve devāḥ*)."
"Bṛhaspati for Bṛhaspati; Bṛhaspati is the Brahman of the gods, I am the Brahman of men; Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ. Having been chosen as the Brahman, he murmurs this.
Saying, "O Lord of Speech, protect the sacrifice," he passes to the south of the Āhavanīya fire by its western side.
Having cast away a blade of grass from the Brahman's seat with the formula, "O serpent of the sonless woman," and having touched water, [he sits down].
He sits down with the formula: "May we go over the heights and the hollows.

Facing the Āhavanīya fire, he sits down with the formula: "Here I sit in the seat of Arvāgvasu, impelled by the god Savitṛ; I sit in the seat of Bṛhaspati. I announce this to Agni, this to Vāyu, this to Sūrya, and this to Pṛthivī.
He remains seated until the conclusion of the rite.
At every ritual action, he restrains his speech;
however, regarding mantra-accompanied rites as well as those performed silently, he may act according to his desire.
Alternatively, he restrains his speech during the *sāmidhenī* verses, the *prayāja* offerings, and the *anūyāja* offerings.
If he should speak out of negligence, having muttered a verse dedicated to Viṣṇu and the *vyāhṛtis*, he restrains his speech again.
When it is said, "O Brahman, I shall lead forward the waters," he gives the impulse: "Lead forward the sacrifice; cause the deities to prosper; let the sacrificer be upon the back of the firmament;
where the world of the seven seers who have performed good deeds is, there place this sacrifice and the sacrificer—*oṃ*, lead forward! Thus he impels.
In all instances of addressing [the officiants], he gives the impulse with the syllable *oṃ*.
With whichever specific ritual act he addresses them, he gives the impulse for each of those.
When it is said, "O Brahman, I shall sprinkle," he says, "Sprinkle the sacrifice," at the sprinkling of the oblation, the fuel, and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

When it is said, "O Brahman, I shall perform the northern tracing-out," [the Brahman responds]: "O Bṛhaspati, trace out the altar; may the gods with their own cattle have their seats. Upon it let the sacrificial grass be spread well within; O divine Earth, be free from injury! This is for the northern tracing-out. When it is said, "O Brahman, I shall recite the *sāmidhenī* verses," [the Brahman responds]: "Recite the sacrifice for Prajāpati! This is for the *sāmidhenī* verses.

When it is said, "I shall cause [the name] of the Brahman-pravara to be proclaimed," [he says]: "O Vācaspati, cause this speech to be proclaimed; proclaim this sacrifice among the gods, and me among men. At the *pravara*, he appends everywhere the words, "Make the deities prosper," and he gives the impulse with, "Om, cause [the name] to be proclaimed.
He gazes at the *prāśitra* being cut off with the formula, "I gaze upon you with the eye of Mitra."
"Go along the path of Truth," [he says] as it is being carried around. "I gaze upon you with the eye of the Sun," he says as it is being brought forward, and he gazes at it.
Having taken it up with the formula, "Of the god... [he continues].

Having spread out grass-blades to the west of the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "I set thee on the navel of the earth, on the place of Iḍā," he places [the vessel] with its handle pointing eastward.
Having looked at it with the formula, "I gaze upon thee with the eye of Suparṇa Garutman," and having taken it up with his thumb and ring finger with the formula, "Of the god... [he proceeds].
He eats it with the words, "I eat you with the mouth of Agni.
With the words, "With the belly of a Brāhmaṇa," he swallows it without chewing and without letting it touch his teeth.
"May those deities who are within the waters pacify this; may it, consecrated by *svāhā*, go to the belly of Indra"—with these words, he pours water over [the food] while immersing it.
Having sipped water, he touches the region of his navel with the formula: "Do not be united with my eater; sit above my navel; I place you in the belly of Indra."
"Speech has entered my mouth, breath into my nostrils"—with these words, he touches the seats of the vital breaths according to their respective forms.
"May all my limbs be uninjured"—with this, he touches all his limbs.
Having washed the vessel and filled it, he pours out the water toward the outside with the formula, "Quicken the quarters."
Having filled another vessel, he pours it toward himself, saying, "May you refresh me.

He does not consume the portion belonging to the Brahman before the conclusion of the rite. When the *anvāhārya* rice has been placed within the altar (*antarvedi*), he touches it, saying: "O Brahman, you are the Brahman; for the sake of the Brahman, may you be offered today; do not harm me; being unoffered, be auspicious to me," and also, "You are the portion of Prajāpati."

When it is said, "O Brahman, we shall set forth," [the Brahman] recites: "O God Savitṛ, you have declared this; impel it and sacrifice it. Bṛhaspati is the Brahman; may he protect the sacrifice, may he protect the lord of the sacrifice, may he protect me. Om! To a firm foundation! This is for the *anūyāja* oblations and the kindling-stick (*samidh*). "Earth has gone to earth; mother has gone to mother. May we prosper with sons and cattle; may he who hates us be split asunder. With this, one should consecrate whatever earthen object might break during the sacrifice. Some authorities prescribe this as a universal rule (*sārvatrika*) for all such cases.

Having consumed the portion belonging to Brahmā, and having either placed a fuel-stick on the fire, offered an oblation, or performed a reverential salutation [with the mantra]: "Agni Jātavedas, the undeceived, has sacrificed; sitting first within this [fire], may he release the boon for the one who presses [the Soma]. O Jātavedas, bestow upon us wealth and whatever is auspicious; grant us prosperity; unite us with your favor, O possessor of strength," he then goes out by the same way he came.
Thus is prescribed the office of the Brahman priest for the Iṣṭis and the Animal Sacrifices; this is the Brahman's duty. || 22 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the second book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Thus ends the second book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.

For a Brāhmaṇa, there is the omission of the third oblation. The sequence and the loudness or low-voiced nature [of the recitation] correspond to that. At the New Moon sacrifice, the deities are Agni and Indra, or alternatively Agni and Mahendra; or, for one who does not offer the *saṃnayya* (curd-mixture), the deities are Agni and Indrāgnī. Thus ends the eighth paṭala in the first praśna of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* composed by Mahādeva, authored by Satyāṣāḍha.

8. Now, the first book (praśna), containing the hidden meaning and accompanied by the technical definitions (paribhāṣā), has been fully explained in this commentary on the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha. Thus ends the first book in the commentary on the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. 1.
2.1 Now begins the first chapter of the second book.
He issues the command: "Recite for the fire being kindled," or "Recite for the fire being kindled," or alternatively, "O Hotṛ, recite for Agni, the god, being kindled."

He issues the command to the Hotṛ with one of the three *praiṣa* mantras. In this case, the command is not for the purpose of self-purification (*ātmasaṃskāra*), because the recitation (*anuvacana*) is performed by the Hotṛ. The time for the command is when the Hotṛ has entered and is standing at the edge of the altar (*vedīṣāṇi*). The author of the Commentary (*Mādhyakṛt*) stated that another Sūtra shows: "Having taken a single fuel-stick (*samidh*), he issues the command. And it was said by Kātyāyana: "Having taken this fuel-stick, he issues the command."

In every respect, this is appropriate only in that manner; otherwise, how could there be a designation of "present tense" for that which is being kindled? Here, the formulas beginning with *cittiḥ sug* pertain to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). Sitting down, he places a fuel-stick upon each utterance of the *praṇava*.

It is established that because of the mention of "seated" (*āsīna*) here, there is no such restriction regarding other rites, such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. At the end of the *sāmidhenī* verses, while the *praṇava* is being uttered by the Hotṛ, he places one fuel-stick (*samidh*) at a time. Regarding the phrase "in the Āhavanīya fire," the mention of the Āhavanīya fire in the injunction "to Agni being kindled" is due to its primary importance; furthermore, this is supported by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the passage "having brought down [the sticks] along the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he makes all the fuel-wood touch [the fire]. And thus, when the eleven fuel-sticks have been placed—
At the verse "samiddho agna āhuta," he places the entire fuel-stick (idhma) on the fire, leaving aside only the final *anūyāja* fuel-stick.

In this case, having set aside one fuel-stick (*samidh*) for the purpose of another, while the verse beginning with *samiddho agne* is being recited, nothing remains except for that very verse; there is no *praṇava*. For this very reason, Āpastamba has stated: "He places the entire remainder of the fuel-wood (*idhmaśeṣa*) [into the fire]. This means the entire fuel-wood, consisting of four fuel-sticks. Alternatively, even here at the final [verse], there may be four fuel-sticks as before. Thus, there are two positions. (Note: The manuscript variants indicated are as follows: 1. Kha, Cha, Da read 'darśanami'; 2. Kha, Ṭa read 'yetyādi'; 3. Ka, Ga, Ca, Cha, Ṭa, Cha.)
Thus [ends] the section on the *liṅga*. 4. Gha, Ṅa, Ja, Śa, Ma, Da. Regarding the third alternative (*pakṣa*), he says:
"Or, for each *sāmidhenī*.

This means that one does not place all the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) at the twelfth or the fifteenth [verse], but rather places only one at each of the four *praṇavas*. To express this, it was stated "for each *sāmidhenī*" (*prati sāmidhenīm*)—just as was previously stated regarding each *praṇava*—with the intention that there will be an increase in the number of verses (*kāṇḍavṛddhi*). There too, the procedure is exactly the same.

The formula "To Agni being kindled" (*agnaye samidhyamānāya*) is a consecratory act (*saṃskāra*); therefore, the kindling is not for the sake of the deity. Consequently, there is neither a dedication nor a relinquishment [of the offering] to the deity, and because the *svāhā*-utterance and *vaṣaṭ*-utterance are absent, the deity is not perceived as the recipient. Furthermore, the formulas "Agni is kindled and offered to" and "O gods! belong to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). With the Veda-bundle, he fans the Āhavanīya fire three times.

"He fans it" means he blows upon it. This is merely a ritual rule (*dharma-mātra*), for the kindling of fire does not occur by means of three blowings. Therefore, it occurs even at the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath). Regarding the phrase "when the deities have been led away," this will be restated in the context of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) as "when the deities have been led away. From that, it is understood that it is applicable here [in the archetype] at this time as well. Furthermore, since the author will state it regarding the water at the *avabhṛtha*, it is known from this that it is merely a ritual rule intended for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

Having taken clarified butter from the *dhruvā* vessel with the *sruva* spoon and held it over the *veda* grass-bundle, he brings the *sruva* down along the northern joint of the enclosing sticks; then, while mentally reciting "To Prajāpati Manu, svāhā!", he pours the oblation straight, long, continuous, and radiant, directed toward the south-east, or else transversely so as to touch all the fuel-sticks of the fire-wood.

The word "seated" (āsīnaḥ) is to be understood as carrying over [from the previous rule], based on the Vedic scripture stating, "one who is seated [offers] another vessel. Since it is defined in the *paribhāṣā* that "one offers into the Āhavanīya fire," the phrase "with the *sruva*" is stated for that purpose. Regarding the phrase "of the *dhruvā*": although the *paribhāṣā* establishes that an offering with the *sruva* is made from the *ājyasthālī*, the specific mention of "the *dhruvā*" is made here. "Having taken" means having grasped [it]; "having wiped with the *veda*" means using the *veda* as a substitute for the *upabhṛt*.

Having caused the northern [line], situated in the north-western corner, to enter the sacrificial ground (*āyatana*) by means of the junction with the western line, he—being pleased with you two—utters the mantra and, meditating upon its meaning, maintains the stream; he releases the stream into the sacrificial ground. How? Toward the south-east (*dakṣiṇāprāñcam*), that is, into the intermediate space between the south and the east, directed toward the south-eastern corner (*āgneyī*), straight and not crooked, like a lamp-flame; the meaning is that he releases the stream not only at the place of the fuel-stick (*samit*) but immediately thereafter as well.

This [fire] is continuous and uninterrupted, possessing light—that is, endowed with flames. Or, having caused it to enter slightly into a horizontal space, starting from the northern direction, one reaches the southern direction within that horizontal space; such is the name "āghāra" (libation), which should be understood as a masculine noun to agree with its substantive, as seen in the Brāhmaṇa: "He pours the āghāra with a reed. The remainder of the sentence is: "He brings all the wooden sticks into contact with the āghāra. [Alternative readings: *dhanī* or *yā*.]
2kha. For the purpose of replenishing the clarified butter in the *ājyasthālī* [butter-pot]. [Chapter 150] Together with the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva:
Having taken clarified butter from the *ājyasthālī* with the *sruva*-ladle, he replenishes the *dhruvā* [constant spoon] with the mantra, "May the *dhruvā* be replenished with clarified butter.
By means of the clarified butter deposited in the *sruva*-ladle—which was previously taken and had become deficient—he again makes it complete with the mantra, "May [the *dhruvā*] be replenished."
It is thus everywhere:

wherever the clarified butter (ājya) is taken from the *dhruvā* vessel, there at each taking, the replenishing (*āpyāyana*) must be performed immediately with the mantra. The meaning is that it should be done in this very manner until [the vessel] has been replenished; as long as it has not been replenished, it must not be drawn elsewhere. He issues the command: "O Agnīdh, cleanse the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) and the fire three times each."

"O Āgnīdhra, cleanse the fire thrice"—this option is stated in the Brāhmaṇa. By the word "fire" (*agni*), the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) are understood through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on proximity; and by *ajahallakṣaṇā* (retaining-indication), the fire itself is also included. The repetition (*vīpsā*) is appropriate for the fire alone. Therefore, since the remainder of the Brāhmaṇa shows that one cleanses [them] after the enclosing has been performed, the meaning should be explained just as in other Vedic branches. Taking the cord used for binding the fuel-wood (*idhma-saṃnahana*) in his hand along with the wooden sword (*sphya*), the Āgnīdhra, moving clockwise around [the altar], cleanses the enclosing-sticks: the middle one facing north, and the other two facing east.

The "bindings of the fuel" (*idhmasya saṃnahana*) refer to the ropes used for tying; the plural number indicates that there are many strands of it. Having gathered them together in one place along with the wooden sword (*sphya*), they should be used collectively for the sweeping. Moving around from left to right (*pradakṣiṇam anuparikrāman*), he remains standing in the north facing east. The phrase "the middle enclosing-stick" (*madhyamam iṣkam*) is intended to exclude those directed toward the east. Having swept [the middle stick], he then goes to the Āhavanīya fire and, standing to the south facing north, sweeps the southern enclosing-stick. Returning by the same way he came, he sweeps the northern enclosing-stick and returns as he went.

"O Agni, winner of booty; thee who art about to run for booty, who art about to win booty, the winner of booty, I cleanse for the winning of booty—Agni, the eater of food, for the sake of eating food," [he says] three times to Agni.

Since the repetition regarding the *paridhi* is established by the very force of the distributive term (*vīpsā*) in the injunction, the author of the Sūtra did not explicitly state it for the purpose of the *paridhi*. Anticipating the objection that the word "fire" (*agni*) is unfit to be connected with a distributive term, [the commentator] explains that just as in one's own Brāhmaṇa the distributive term "three times each" (*tristriḥ*) is connected to the collective set of items indicated by the word "libation" (*āghāra*), so too here, in the collection consisting of the *paridhis* and the fire from another recensional branch (*śākhā*), a connection with the distributive term can be explained; it is with this intention that he stated "three times" (*triḥ*) specifically in reference to the wiping of the fire.
"With the mantra once, silently twice; the enclosing sticks (paridhis) silently three times. He formulates this technical rule for the sake of the subsequent injunctions:

"In all oblations, he places the *juhū* spoon upon the *upabhṛt*; having brought it forward from the front, he places the *juhū* into the *upabhṛt*; when about to offer, he does so with that very [spoon]."

In all oblations—whether pertaining to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), consisting of *darvī*-offerings, or other such offerings—that are to be performed, one places the *upabhṛt* ladle, which has been taken up as an instrument, so as to cover the *juhū*. Because it is used for the purpose of covering (*saṃvaraṇa*) near (*upa*) the *juhū*, the etymological meaning of "upabhṛt" is also demonstrated. Regarding that, he states a specific detail: one covers the *juhū* with the front part of the *upabhṛt*, not from the side.

Having brought [the ladle] to the level of the ground, he places it down—that is, he sets it—in the *upabhṛt* during the performance of the rite, until it is lifted up for the casting of the oblation, meaning prior to its being carried over to the sacrificial site. Then, intending to offer—that is, intending to carry it over to the sacrificial site for the sake of the oblation—he withdraws it by means of that very same front portion; he moves it back toward the place of the offering, but does not detach the *juhū* from the *upabhṛt* by means of any part other than the front portion. This is the meaning.

"Śijati" means it makes a sound; "śiñjayati" means it causes a sound to be made. Thus, the meaning is that one should not produce a sound by mutual pulling. As long as the two [the *mud* and the *upabhṛt*] are joined together, the *prāṇa* (breath) remains concentrated upon them, or rather, it is concentrated on the *adhvaryu*'s breath alone. To the west of the *āhavanīya* fire, he passes southward with his right hand, or alternatively, he passes southward with his left hand, or northward with his right hand.

When the crossing to the south for the sake of the *dakṣiṇā* presents itself, he should cross with one foot and turn northward with the other; this is restricted as a rule regarding the crossing in the region behind the *āhavanīya*. Having thus provided this general instruction, he states the current subject, the *āghāra*: "Intending to pour the *āghāra*, [the priest] makes a gesture of reverence (*añjali*) toward the east for the gods, either with the formula *bhuvanam asi* in front of the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, or with *namo devebhyaḥ saprathāḥ*."

The word *namaḥ* (homage) marks the end of the preceding [formula]. Regarding the mantra *devebhyaḥ* (to the gods), the meaning is that its reference to the gods is to be explained through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because it reveals Agni; for since Agni is the self of all the gods, the figurative indication is as taught, owing to his being the essence of the sacrifice (*parimāktitvāt*). This is clear. *Svadhā pitṛbhyaḥ* (svadhā to the ancestors) is the southern [direction].

"Añjali" refers to the previous [position]. "Touching water" is prescribed by the Smṛti. From the statement, "Intending to pour the Āghāra," it is stated that forming the two hollowed palms (añjali) is an auxiliary part of the Āghāra. That "Āghāra" is the name of the ritual act; this has been established by those learned in logic as referring to the two pourings. Because there is no Āghāra during the Upasad days, there is no forming of the añjali.
He takes the *juhū* ladle with the words, "O *juhū*, come! and the *upabhṛt* ladle with the words, "O *upabhṛt*, come!"

“Ādasa” is as before. “Devayajyāyāḥ” marks the end of the two mantras. Saying, "O Agni and Viṣṇu," he steps across to the south without letting the *prastara* grass touch his foot.
At the time of stepping across, he must not let the *prastara* be touched by his heel nor crush it; there is no fault if there is merely contact.
He stands still, saying, "Thou art the station of Viṣṇu."
Facing the Āhavanīya fire, he should perform the standing to the south with the mantra. "Vīryāṇi" is the end of the mantra;
or, "Where Indra stood and performed valor, there standing, may valor be performed. This is an alternative to the previous [formula].

Having placed the left foot inside the altar (antarvedi) and having smelled the right foot, he places it down; he then smells—that is, touches—the left (vāma) foot. Having firmly established the right foot, he touches the right hand with the forepart of the left foot; this is what is meant. Thus it has been stated by Vaikhānasa:
"Having brought the ladle (sruk) along the joint of the southern enclosing-stick (paridhi)."

Having introduced the *juhū* ladle here as before, [he takes hold of] the two junctions of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). Of these two, starting from the southern one—which is situated at the southern end of the sacrificial ground—he pours the libation, beginning [from that point]. By this, the simultaneous performance [of the two acts] prescribed by the mantra is precluded.

Or [one may use] "ucchuṣmo agne" (O Agni, the drying one). The first mantra ends with *svāhā*; the latter, however, ends with "suvīryāya" (for the sake of heroic vigor). Here, because it is performed as a *homa* (oblation), it also ends in *svāhā*. For the first pouring (*pūrvāghāra*), Prajāpati is the deity; the formula for the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) is "thou art mind" (*mano 'si*). Regarding the second [pouring], Vaikhānasa says that Indra is the deity and the first mantra belongs to Indra, calling it the "Indra-pouring" (*aindram āghāram*). As for the second, Agni is the deity. The subsequent recitation (*anumantraṇa*) is "speech has arrived" (*vāg atīt*). This first pouring is mental, whereas this [second] is vocal; thus it is a praise of speech, for "Indra is indeed speech," and not a praise of a deity.

He pours the libation straight forward, upward, straight, long, and continuous, with the *jyotiṣmatī* [verse]. "Straight forward" means toward the north-east (*īśānī*). Although the repetition of "straight" and so forth is established by the previous rule alone, the Teacher makes it here to indicate that in another school the pouring (*āghāra*) is not desired, but rather the oblation (*homa*) itself is desired; lest that view prevail, he ensures that one should perform even this pouring characterized by qualities such as being straight and so on. Thus it was stated by Āpastamba: "Or rather, in all manuscripts [the reading] 'he smells' (*avajighrati*) exists, but it appears that 'he strikes down' (*avahanti*) is required. (Note: *ka*, *ga*, and *ca* manuscripts).

It is said: "Having commenced along with the support and that which is supported, at this time the gods went to the heavenly world; the sacrificer himself goes directly to the heavenly world"—this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) in the Brāhmaṇa is an interpretation of the word *samārabhya* found in the mantra, and it does not mean that the sacrificer must perform the act of taking hold (*anvārambha*). Therefore, the author of the Commentary has explained in detail that the teacher does not accept an injunction for the sacrificer to take hold here.
Or, "across" (*tiryañcam*);
this too is to be explained as before, meaning one should proceed from the south to the north.
He touches all the fuel-sticks.
The meaning is understood.
Having offered the oblation, he breathes upon it.

Although the phrase "having offered" (*hutvā*) here is a restatement (*anuvāda*), this is not a *darvihoma* because it is a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*); for it will be established that a *darvihoma* is indeed a primary act (*pradhānakarma*). Nevertheless, since there is also the form of giving by means of the utterance *svāhā*, the meaning is that while this is a *homa* for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*), it is also a preparatory act. As for the rule regarding the preparation of the vessel from which the *prayāja* offerings are taken—namely, that which is understood to be for the purpose of the *prayājas* and serves as the source (*apādāna*) when pouring into the *juhū* ladle—that preparation is for the sake of the *prayājas*; such is the principle.

The first *āghāra* (libation) should be understood as the primary action itself. Therefore, it is established that where there are no *prayājas*, there is no second *āghāra*. "He breathes after" (*anuprāṇiti*) means that at the time of the *homa*, having offered while following his own breath, he should release it.
One should perform the *āghāra* upward for one who desires heaven, and downward for one who desires rain.

For a sacrificer desiring heaven (*svarga-kāma*), one should perform the *āghāra* oblation by holding the *juhū* ladle upward at the beginning and increasingly higher until the completion; this has been stated for one desiring heaven. For one desiring rain (*vṛṣṭi-kāma*), it should be understood that at the beginning it is held downward and at the conclusion it is brought lower. Since there is no specific distinction otherwise, this applies to both types of *āghāra*.

Regarding an enemy (*dveṣya*), one should hold it downward or interrupt it. This is a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended as a prohibition; the meaning is that one should never perform the *āghāra* downward without a specific desire, nor should one ever effect an interruption.
If one should desire, "May he be short-lived," one should pour the oblation for him crookedly.
This too is a deprecatory explanatory passage (arthavāda), intended as a prohibition just like the previous one.
He lifts up the ladle with the words, "O Great One! (bṛhadbhāḥ).

He takes up the *juhū* ladle; immediately after the completion of the stream [of oblations], he leads it upward. [As it is said: "Whatever [portion] remains in the sacrificer. Without touching the *sruva* with the *sruk*, he steps across [the altar]. Ensuring that there is no mutual contact between the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt*, he passes to the north. "O you of good conduct, protect me"—this is the end of the mantra. [This concludes] the 150th Patala, together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

He anoints the *dhruvā* ladle three times with the *juhū* using the formula: "The ghee is anointed by Agni; the oblation is anointed by the oblation; the atmosphere is anointed by the flame. He anoints the *dhruvā* with the same [ladle] in the reverse order: once with the mantra and twice silently. In this context, the *dhruvā* serves as the instrument for the consecration of that clarified butter (*ājya*).
Or [he may do so] with the formula: "Thou art the head of Makha."
The modification is by means of the preceding mantra. It ends with "jyotir asi.
Having taken clarified butter from the *dhruvā* vessel with the *sruva* ladle using [the mantra] "unnītaṃ rāyaḥ," he pours it over the *juhū* with [the mantra] "suvīrāya svāhā.
The preparation of the *juhū* is performed by pouring the clarified butter in a continuous stream.

"The sacrifice is connected by means of the sacrifice"—thus [the rule] "he supports the *dhruvā* with the *juhū*" follows from the preceding [text]. This is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *dhruvā*. There is a distinction between the two verbal roots: "smearing" (*samañjana*) is performed by the sprinkling of a mere drop, whereas "supporting" (*pratyabhighāraṇa*) is performed by creating a small stream. Having set down the two ladles (*srucau*).
The place for the path.
He chooses the *pravara*.

This is merely a formal declaration for the sake of the ritual authority. A *pravara* is the recitation of the common ancestry established through the lineage of the Ṛṣis by name; that procedure is now stated:
Having taken hold of the faggot-binders, the wooden sword (sphyá), and a blade of grass from the Veda that does not reach beyond it, the Adhvaryu stands ready for the Pravara invocation.

Having untied the cord used for binding the fuel (idhma-saṃnahana), he should attach those prepared grasses to the wooden sword (sphya) and also attach a blade of grass from the altar (vedi). Of what nature is that? It is "not separated" (avyantam); that is to say, it is not detached from the edge or the middle of the altar. Such being the case, he should attach one blade of that sacrificial grass (barhis) to the altar at its root-end; this is what is meant by "attaching. The mention of the Adhvaryu is intended to indicate his specific role as the performer of the commencement.

The meaning is that the *adhvaryu* alone should not be embraced by the *āgnīdhra*. Alternatively, it will be stated later that these ritual duties (*dharmas*) do not apply even to the *hotṛ*. For the *pravara*—that is, to utter the *pravara*—he stands; the meaning is that he remains standing and does not sit. According to Bhāradvāja and Baudhāyana, this is near the altar or to the north of the *utkara*. By this, it is understood that they stand either in the northern part of the *utkara* or at the altar, facing southward. [The others] face eastward and westward respectively. 1. ka. ga. ca. cha. [End of manuscript fragment]

4.3. Regarding the *pravara* (the choosing of the priests): [The text] "satyāpāḍhaviracitaṃ śrautasūtram" [is the title]. If the simultaneous commencement (*sahānvārambhaṇa*) by the Adhvaryu and the Āgnīdhra—while they stand facing each other as the primary agents (*mukhabhāvena*)—were to be performed as prescribed for the Hotṛ, it would contradict [the rule]. Having turned toward the south, having joined the *sphya* with the upper part [of the hand], and having grasped it together—it is said that while grasping it, the Adhvaryu faces south. He states the *japa* (muttering) for the *pravara*: [Note: The provided text contains various manuscript variants indicated by abbreviations such as vi'12, ka, pa, pa, cha, ṭa, 8, etc., which are typical in Vedic textual criticism.]

"Who shall be the Adhvaryu here? He indeed shall be the Adhvaryu here. "I stand in the place of the sacrifice, of Viṣṇu, the sacrifice. "May speech perform the office of the priest; may mind perform the office of the priest. I take refuge in speech: Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! Thus the Adhvaryu mutters. This is well-known. Having taken hold of them from behind, the Āgnīdhra stands there.

"Those" refers to the sacrificial grass (barhis), the skin, the garment, and the reeds. The neuter gender is used because of the rule "the neuter [remains] when combined with a non-neuter. Afterward, it belongs to the Adhvaryu. Vaikhānasa says: "The Āgnīdhra stands behind.

He modifies the mantra as: "Who will be the Āgnīdhra here? He shall be the Āgnīdhra here. This modification does not apply even to the mantra; rather, for the sake of brevity, it is shown that the same mantra is recited, containing the word *asi* (you are) in place of the word *adhvaryu*. Regarding the simultaneous recitation during the choosing (*pravaraṇa*) of both, he says:

He addresses the Brahman priest with the words, "I shall cause [the announcement] to be heard by the Brahman-pravara. This means he addresses the Brahman priest. He says this either to state the *pravara* (ancestral lineage) of the sacrificer, or for the sake of the *pravaraṇa-kriyā*—the act of choosing [the Hotṛ]; that is to say, "I shall cause [the announcement] to be heard" in order to perform that act of choosing, meaning "I shall impel or urge the Āgnīdhra to respond. When the Brahman priest gives the command, "O [Hotṛ], cause [the announcement] to be heard," he then says, "Āśrāvaya" or "Ucchrāvaya," and thus causes the announcement to be made.

The word division is *o śrāvaya*; the vowel *o* results from the rule of *pararūpa*. He urges one of the two [the Āgnīdhra] to express approval; the meaning is that he addresses the Āgnīdhra. That very act of self-purification he describes as follows: the Āgnīdhra responds with "astu śrauṣaṭ.
The meaning is that he causes [the Hotṛ] to hear in response to the approval. How so? [With the words] "may there be the consent, śrauṣaṭ. In this matter, according to the Smṛti of Pāṇini...

1kha, "having performed [the rite], [there is] no [fault]. 2 ka. ga. ca. cha. ṭha. *caraṇaki*. 3 ka. ga. ca. cha. ṭha. *modina*. 4 gha. i. ja. śa. ma. da. *vayomāśrāvaya*. 5 va. *iti*. By one of the three [methods]. 6 ka. ca. ṭha. *nātra saṃ* [is not here]. [End of] Paṭala 150. [This is] accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 187. *plutaḥ* (protracted). [The rule] "of *vahipreṣya*, *śrauṣaṭ*, *voṣaṭ*, and *āvaha*, [the first syllable is] protracted" (*ādeḥ*) follows from the word *plutaḥ*.

The protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs for an initial syllable that has the form *bū*, *pre*, *śrī*, *vau*, or *ā*. Likewise, according to the rule "and in the case of the *agnītpreṣaṇa* (the call to the *agnīdh*), as well as for the subsequent [syllable]," the *agnītpreṣaṇa* consists of the words *āśrāvaya*; therein, there is protraction of both the initial syllable and the subsequent syllable. Thus, it should be understood that there is protraction of the vowel *ā* and of the syllable *śrā*. Because of the mention of *agnīdh*, the protraction would not occur in the case of *om āśrāvaya* when the impulsion (*prasava*) is performed by the *brahman*.
In this way, the *āśruta* and *pratyāśruta* occur.

The word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) is to be understood as an ellipsis. Wherever the *āśrāvaṇa* (calling) and *pratyāśrāvaṇa* (response) are prescribed for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), in all those instances—even though they are mentioned in the section on the *pravara* (ancestral invocation) within the context of the archetype (*prakṛti*)—those [formulas] which are prescribed in the section on the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) as being for the sake of the entire Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice, are to be understood as serving that same universal purpose even when spoken for the sake of the *pravara*. He states a specific rule:
"On the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), standing facing south and holding the wooden sword (*sphya*), the Āgnīdhra priest responds to the call; in other cases of calling, [he does so] after the *pravara*."

The connection is as follows: when the *āśrāvaṇas* other than those from the *pravara* section have been performed by the *adhvaryu*, the *āgnīdhra* responds with the call (*pratyāśrāvayati*), characterized by the specific qualifications such as "on the rubbish heap" (*sattu utkare*) and so forth. Here, only the *sphya* together with the *idhma-sannahana* (faggot-binders) is to be understood. For this very reason, Āpastamba has stated: "and holding the faggots. The *idhma-sannahanas* are mentioned for the purpose of anointing the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the fire. He states the subject at hand: "When the response has been given, he chooses the *pravara*. This has been explained. How does he do so there? He says:

"Agni, the divine Hotṛ, shall sacrifice to the gods—he who is wise and observant—like Manu, like Bharata, like so-and-so, like so-and-so," thus [he says], according to the *ārṣeya* (lineage) of the sacrificer, together with those beyond him, three immediate [ancestors].

The phrase "he chooses" (*pravṛṇīte*) is understood to carry over here. In this *pravara*, by means of the repetition in "like so-and-so" (*amuvat*), he declares the names of the ancestral sages (*ṛṣi*). By specifying "three," it is stated that exactly three are to be taken. And since it will later be said, "and let him speak like a Brahmin," he chooses only three immediate, uninterrupted [ancestors] along with those beyond. To provide confidence in this matter, the Śruti provides the authority:

From this point forward, the Adhvaryu chooses the composers of the mantras according to the *ṛṣis*, for it is known from the tradition: "He chooses the composers of the mantras according to the *ṛṣis*.

Regarding the ancestors (*pitaras*) who are heard of as composers of mantras in the enumeration of the sacrificer’s lineage, one should begin with the *ṛṣi* who was first born among them; that is the meaning. For instance, when the Kauśika is the sacrificer, after saying "like Manu, like Bharata," they say "like Kuśika" (and so on). [Note: The manuscript variants cited in the brackets refer to specific readings found in various versions of the text.]

One should recite "as at the *marṣaṇa* of Viśvāmitra" (i.e., *satyāpāḍhaviracitaṃ śrautasūtram*, second section). Then, one should recite "brahmaṇvad ā ca vakṣat," and so forth. The mention of the *adhvaryu* is for the purpose of excluding the *agnīdh*.
Regarding the *pravara* of the *hotṛ*, it is traditionally known (*vijñāyate*) that "the *hotṛ*s are from there downwards.

"From there" means from the third ancestor; "downwards" (*arvāñcaḥ*) means those who go downward. These "downward ones" (*arvāñcaḥ*) are the reverse order, beginning from the most recently born and proceeding to the ancestors in successive order.
The king chooses [his lineage] by means of the *pravara* (ancestral seers) of his domestic priest (*purohita*).
For the king, there is no *adhvaryu* or *hotṛ* of his own due to the absence of such a lineage. Regarding this, scripture provides the authority:

"One should announce [the lineage] by means of the *ārṣeya* (lineage of seers) of the domestic priest"—so it is known concerning the king. As for the *niṣāda* and the *rathakāra*, one chooses their *pravara* by means of that seer whom they recite.

The Teacher will later describe the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), the *agnihotra*, and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices for the others as well; this was stated for that purpose. For them, there is not even a family priest (*purohita*) whom they might invoke as their ancestral *ṛṣi* by virtue of being the progenitor of their lineage.
This applies likewise to Brāhmaṇas who have been surrendered to a king, or to kings who have been surrendered to Brāhmaṇas.
The meaning is: "by means of the *pravara* of the one who surrendered them."

For one who belongs to two lineages (*dvigotra*), one should indicate three [names] from each lineage; "indicate" (*upalakṣayet*) here means one should recite them. Likewise, for one whose ancestral connection (*bandhu*) is unknown, one should use the *pravara* (ancestral sages) of the family priest (*purohita*) or the *pravara* of the teacher (*ācārya*).
The meaning is: "of him for whom the kinsmen are not born [and] are submissive.
Having prohibited the entire *pravara* (ancestral lineage) of some, Manu enjoins exactly this:

having prohibited the entire *brāhmaṇa* (textual authority) regarding the *pravara* of certain reciters (*śākhins*), he enjoins that one should simply say "Manu" without distinction. He will state in the *Pravarādhyāya*: "For all creatures are descended from Manu."
"May he speak with the sacred word; may the Brahmins be the protectors of this sacrifice"—this is the remainder of the *pravara* (invocation).
This remainder is to be understood everywhere in the previously mentioned [formulas].
He pronounces the name of the Hotṛ in a whisper, saying "Asau" (so-and-so).
Because the section on *pravara* deals with high status (*uccaistva*), he utters the name of the *hotṛ* in the nominative singular;
"mānuṣa" [is uttered] loudly.
This is clear.
The Hotṛ sits down.

(In the manuscripts designated gha, ja, śa, a, and da, the reading is *athāsaṃprajñātā*). [Variant: *thā'jñā*]. [Variant: *tyetadvida*]. This, however, has been stated for the purpose of releasing the previous undertakings once the Adhvaryu has released them. This concludes the tenth Paṭala of the second section, accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 109.
He places even a blade of grass upon the altar.
The Adhvaryu and the Āgnīdhra take a blade of grass for the purpose of starting [the rite] and, together with the wooden sword (sphyá), place it exactly as it was.
Thus ends the first paṭala in the second praśna of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* composed by Mahādeva. || 1 ||
2.2 Now begins the second chapter.

Regarding the insertion of verses for the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga), the sviṣṭakṛt offering, and the patnīsaṃyāja offerings, there are both invitatory (puronuvākyā) and offering (yājyā) verses; however, for the fore-offerings (prayāja) and after-offerings (anūyāja), there is only the offering verse.

The word *ca* (and) is connected separately. The phrase "the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā*" is intended to mean that there are two [verses] for each sacrifice. Regarding the term *āvāpa*: it refers to the principal acts performed through repetition (*āvṛtti*), which are like a ritual framework (*tantra*). It is designated by the word *āvāpa* because they are inserted individually, and thus it is used as an antonym to *tantra*. In that context, the expression "therein the *āvāpas*" is used. For what purpose is this? It is for the purpose of establishing the specific arrangement of the conjunctions of the sacrifices. By the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakṛt*), it has been explained as being well-established, referring specifically to the principal sacrifices themselves.

The rest is clear. In the *anūyāja* offerings, it is precisely the *yājyā* that serves to exclude the *puronuvākyā*. Regarding both types [of offerings], namely those accompanied by both *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* as well as those consisting of the *yājyā* alone, it is established as a general rule (*paribhāṣā*) that there is the *āśrāvaṇa*, the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*, and the *yājyā-saṃpraisha*.

They proceed without speaking out of turn; they remain as they are, not speaking. He elaborates on this very point: that Adhvaryu priest should not speak out of turn before the *āśrāvaṇa*; once the *āśrāvaṇa* has been made, he should not speak until the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*; once the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* has been made, the Adhvaryu should not speak until the command "yajā" (sacrifice); once "yajā" has been uttered, the Hotṛ should not speak until the *vaṣaṭkāra*.

That is the first [case]. If they should speak at these points, then one should perform the *āśrāvaṇa* and so forth again and mutter the *āhutis*; this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is to be understood as stated by Āpastamba.
To the north, while about to recite the *puronuvākyā*, or while cutting the portions, or having cut them, he issues the command.

Standing to the north of the *vaide* vessel, intending to perform the cutting (*avadāna*), he issues the call either before the beginning or together with the beginning; for once the portion has been cut and taken, it is also counted as having been cut because it is accompanied by the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*). The meaning is that he calls for the recitation of the *puronuvākyā*. As to how he issues the call, he says:
"Recite for such-and-such," according to the respective deity.
He issues the *saṃpraisha* (direction) with the name of the deity in the dative case, such as "amuṣmai" (*to so-and-so*), according to the specific deity involved.

Having stepped across to the south [of the fire], and after the *āśrāvaṇa* has been made and the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* responded, he issues the direction "Sacrifice to so-and-so" (*amuṃ yaja*) according to the respective deity.

The syntactical connection is as follows: having stepped across and stood to the south, and once the *āśrāvaṇa* and *pratyāśrāvaṇa* have occurred, he issues the direction for the *yājyā* (offering verse), "Sacrifice," according to the respective deity. Taking the name of the deity in the accusative case, such as "amum," he then issues the direction "Sacrifice to Agni" (*agnim yaja*).

At the *vaṣaṭ*-call, or when the *vaṣaṭ*-call has been made, one offers [the oblation] in those [verses] accompanied by both the *puronuvākyā* and the *yājyā*, whether in four portions (*caturavatta*) or five portions (*pañcāvatta*).

According to the scriptural statement, "at the *vaṣaṭ*-call" or "together with the *vaṣaṭ*-call," the meaning is that one offers—that is, pours into—the *āhavanīya* fire with the *juhū* ladle either while the *vaṣaṭ*-call, which serves the purpose of offering, is being performed, or together with it, or once the *vaṣaṭ*-call has been made. Here, the act of giving is not what is enjoined by the term "offers" (*juhoti*), because it is impossible to give again what is already being given or has already been given by means of the *vaṣaṭ*-call; rather, the denotation of the root *hu* (to offer) is merely the act of pouring.

In this context, since there is no separate division for each of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings, it is not possible to have the fourfold or fivefold portions that will be described later; therefore, this sūtra has been composed as a general rule, whereas that [other sūtra] was composed specifically for the particular case—this is the distinction.
For the Jamadagnis, the portion is fivefold (*pañcāvatta*); for other lineages (*gotra*), it is fourfold (*caturavatta*).

The word "juhoti" (he offers) is carried over from the preceding sūtra. In the phrase "possessing both *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā*," the word "in the *ṛc*s" (*ṛkṣu*) is understood as a supplement because it is appropriate. "Offerings" (*āhutayaḥ*) refers to the acts of oblation; for it is seen that there are three offerings, or rather, the measure of an offering is the act of pouring. Because they are performed with a *yājyā* verse ending in the *vaṣaṭ*-call accompanied by a *puronuvākyā*, these offerings come to possess both *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā*. When those [verses] are being performed, that which he offers, characterized by the *vaṣaṭ*-call, is what he offers as either a fourfold or a fivefold portion (*caturavattaṃ* or *pañcāvattam*); such is the syntactical connection.

It is understood that one offers only that which has already been prepared as fourfold or fivefold portions (*caturavatta* or *pañcāvatta*), and not otherwise. There are two oblations to be offered, for substances, because of the scriptural observation: "The oblations go forth from the *juhū* into the *āhavanīya* fire. Furthermore, it should be known that these [oblations] possess the quality of having an invitatory verse (*yājyā*) and a concluding verse (*anuvākyā*). When those [verses] are applied, whatever one offers, one offers it after having made it either fourfold or fivefold; it is thus restricted that one offers it only as it was previously prepared in that manner.

Alternatively, when the oblations (*āhutis*)—which consist of substances—are to be offered, what are their specific characteristics? [They are] accompanied by *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses. (Note: Here, the letter *kā* serves as an indicator for the *yājyā*; this is found in manuscripts kha, ga, ca, and gha. In manuscript cha and ṭa, it is indicated by the word *yājyā*. Manuscript ca reads *pāca*. Manuscript kha reads *yadā'hu*. Manuscript kha reads *su pūrvavadyājyāpuronu*. Manuscript ca reads *dravyeṣu*. And the sacrifice is... [End of] the second section (*paṭala*), together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

The meaning is that, because they are being offered by those two [the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ], in those sacrifices characterized by deities and accompanied by *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses, the *yājyā* comes first; and since the *yājyā* and the deity are prescribed for the sacrifices by the passage beginning with "of the two *ājyabhāgas*," when those [verses] have been employed, one offers the portion belonging to the deity as either fourfold or fivefold; that is, having made it fourfold or fivefold while it is being offered, one subsequently performs the oblation.

He will indeed state the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that the *avadāna* portions are intended for the deities: "The *devatāvadānas* are the size of a vertebra. This is because those *avadānas* belonging to the deity—connected to the sacrifice for the deity—are intended to be specified as being "the size of a vertebra" while they are being cut off. And it is not the case that the sacrifice has the mere *avadāna* as its purpose. Thus, the performance with the two *ājyabhāgas* has been stated, and [the rule] "he sprinkles [the clarified butter] over the oblation" (*bījamidhārayati*) follows accordingly.

Since it will be stated that "they are offered in succession," the status of being the object of offering belongs only to the oblations (*havir*); thus, even in the case of Indra, [the rule] applies as "he pours over each oblation. For the sacrifice (*yāga*) is accomplished by means of the entire *puroḍāśa* cake and the *sānnāyya* offering, because it is heard [in scripture] as such in the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*).

Of every substance produced by the sight of the deity, one portion is the *avadāna* (cutting-off) from the *sruk* (ladle), while the other portion remains on the *vedī* (altar). Both portions are offered with the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses ending in the *vaṣaṭkāra*. Among these, the disposal (*pratipatti*) of one portion—consisting precisely of the *avadāna*—is by means of the *homa* (offering); its form is either the fourfold (*caturavatta*) or fivefold (*pañcāvatta*) cut. The disposal of the other portion remaining on the *vedī* is by means of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and so forth. Furthermore, in another Vedic text (*śruti*), it is stated that [the offering] is either fourfold or fivefold.

This is established for the other Jamadagnis and for those performing the sacrifice as Adhvaryus and Hotṛs; this is the meaning. Furthermore, this collection of rules already mentioned and those yet to be stated applies equally to the three types of oblations: the *puroḍāśa*, the clarified butter (*ājya*), and the *sāṃnāyya*. Regarding the forms *jāmadagnyaḥ*, *jāmadagnyau*, and *jamadagnayaḥ*, the suffix is elided in the plural. Because there is no distinction between the lineage (*gotra*) and its descendant (*gotrin*), the term "of the lineages" (*gotrāṇām*) was used. Even one who is not a Jamadagni, having addressed a Jamadagni, should perform the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvatta*).

The son of Jamadagni, having asked the son of Jamadagni, said, "O son of Jamadagni, I shall perform the five-fold cutting (pañcāvatta) afterwards"; the meaning is that he should subsequently perform the five-fold cutting.
The portions for the deities (daivata-avadāna) are the size of a thumb-joint (aṅguṣṭha-parva).

A thumb-joint is the section of the middle joint of the hand's thumb; they are of that measure, being "as much as a joint. This same dimension applies to as many portions as there are deities, even in the case of the clarified butter (ājya) and the Sāṃnāyya offering.
The subsequent ones are increasingly larger.
This is a general rule from the Śrauta tradition; he explains it as follows:
[the portions] for the deities follow those for Sviṣṭakṛt, those for the Iḍā follow those for Sviṣṭakṛt, and likewise those for the fourfold division.

The phrase "more substantial than the portions for the deities" (*daivatebhyo'vadānebhyaḥ sthavīyāṃsi*) is to be connected with what precedes it as well. Likewise in the subsequent cases regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. These are the portions corresponding to the *anurūpa* offerings; they are related in that same manner. Here, the form is established by the rule *na vāmyām*, which excludes the augment *āṭ*. And the portions for *iḍā* and those pertaining to the fourfold division (*cāturdhākaraṇika*) are exactly the same.

He cuts portions from the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) with two fingers joined by the thumb; from the clarified butter (ājya) and the milk-offering (sāṃnāyya) with the dipping-spoon (sruva); and from the cooked rice dishes (caru) with the stirring-ladle (mekṣaṇa).

The term "he cuts" (*avadyati*) is understood to carry over [from the preceding rule]. Regarding the *caru* (rice-porridge), although the use of the hand for cutting is obtained through the general injunction (*codaka*), it is stated that [the cutting] is done with a stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) because of its functional suitability (*tatsāmarthyāt*). For the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) states without distinction: "He cuts with the *sruc*," "he cuts with the hand," "he cuts with the *mekṣaṇa*," and "he cuts with the *svadhiti*. That [general rule] is restricted by functional suitability; specifically, on the basis of another scriptural authority, the rule taught is that [the cutting] is performed with the hand in such a way that it results in a specific application: with the two fingers joined for a month, and with the thumb and finger.

In this context, since the capacity [of the instrument] determines the procedure, it is shown that although the omentum (*vapā*) is a modification of the *sānnāyya*, its cutting is performed with the hand alone; whereas for the *caru* and *yavāgū*, which are modifications of the *oṣadhi*, the cutting is done with a stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) or a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*). When [the meat] is attached to the flesh, because all the fingers are likewise so joined, the meaning "joined on both sides by flesh" results in there being two middle fingers. For this very reason, Vaikhānasa stated: "with the ring finger and the middle finger. Having cut from the center of the *puroḍāśa*, one cuts from the eastern half; for one who performs the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvattin*), a third portion is taken from the western half.

In this context, only the rule regarding the location for the *puroḍāśa* will be stated; however, the rules to be mentioned later apply to the clarified butter (*ājya*) and the *sāṃnāyya*, which are [to be taken] from the middle and so forth. Even when there is a division [of the cake], that [specific location] is absent. Having first made an offering from the upper-middle portion of the *puroḍāśa* and placed it in the *sruva* ladle, one then takes an offering from the "fore-part" (*pūrvārdha*)—that is, from whichever part constitutes the front half of the *puroḍāśa*—and having placed that too in the *sruva* without deviating from the fore-part, [this applies] to the son of Jamadagni or to one permitted by him.

The third portioning for the Pañcāyattina is explained as being from the rear half [of the animal] toward the front half. Regarding this, Āpastamba states the distinction: "He portions out a middle portion the size of a thumb-joint crosswise; the second [portion] from the front half he portions lengthwise. Vaikhānasa has stated that the third is from the rear half; thus, the third is like the second.

Having moved the hand to the southern region and made the tips of the fingers and the thumb face upward, the portion cut off by the southern and northern [fingers] is *tiraścīna* (transverse); that which is cut off by the fingers facing eastward is *anūcīna* (longitudinal). Āpastamba has stated another distinction: "Do not let it burn. According to the view of Kātyāyana, the junction between the two [cuts] in the middle is for the purpose of establishing a boundary; however, that is not desired here, and thus "non-junction" (*asaṃbheda*) is said to mean non-adherence (*asaṃśleṣa*).

The meaning is that, due to the joining [of the portions], one should perform the subsequent cutting at the spot where the previous cutting location joins with the place of the new cutting. However, our teacher has stated that the restriction applies only where it is said, "not breaking, do not move," and not elsewhere. Regarding what was stated previously—that the third [cutting] is from behind—he states an exception to that:
for one who desires offspring, the last cutting is to be performed first.

Since the mere act of offering (*avadāna*) is already established, it cannot be the object of a restrictive injunction (*niyamya*) merely by its being first. Furthermore, if both qualities—being "inferior" (*jaghanya*) and "first" (*prāthamya*)—were enjoined independently and without mutual connection, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, the offering, which is already established as "inferior"—meaning it is subsequent in relation to the "first" because it is performed after what was done previously—is the locus where "firstness" is restricted.

The word *ānujāvara*, however, is seen in such passages as "Prajāpati created Indra as the *ānujāvara*," where it refers to the most excellent among equals. Regarding this, some derive it as: "He who is the follower (*anumantṛ*) of his equals is the *ānujāvara*. Alternatively, those born with him in equal status are *anujāḥ*; the best among them is *ānujāvara*. Or else, it refers to the most excellent among those who follow behind (*paścādgāminaḥ*), that is to say, among the twins (*yamyāḥ*). It should be understood according to these various etymological explanations.

Some say that this is an optional (kāmya) ritual procedure, because such is seen in the explanatory passages (arthavāda), such as "if a Rājanya should be one who is inferior in birth" and so forth; however, that is not the intention of the Teacher. Having restated [the portion] as "inferior" (jaghanya), "firstness" (prathamatva) is enjoined. If it were a new injunction for the sake of a specific desire (kāmārtha), then a qualified injunction would have to be made, namely, "the first cutting-off (avadāna) from the rear. Furthermore, the subsequent sūtra does not serve this purpose; for this very reason, there is a restrictive rule by Vaikhānasa.

The injunction beginning with "having made the portion" (*avadāya*) and so forth, as well as the word "desire" (*kāma*), is thus [explained]. Therefore, for a sacrificer who is younger than his brother (*ānujāvara*), this specific injunction is indeed obligatory.
Having made the portion, he should place the *sruk* ladle on the eastern half first, and the latter one on the western half afterwards.

The first *avadāna* (portion) which has been cut from the middle, one should place that in the front half of the *sruva*—that is, in the very first half-portion. The subsequent [portion], the second or third that was cut immediately after, one should place in the rear half of the *sruva*; thus the connection is made with both. This has been clearly stated by Vaikhānasa: "Having placed the first [portion] in the front half of the *sruva*, [one places] the subsequent [portion] in the rear half. By that, [the rule for] the *ānujāva*...

The inferior portion alone has been designated by the term "jaghanya" (inferior), so that there might be no suspicion that the scope [of the rule] applies to the *ānujāvara* as well. For even in the case of the *ānujāvara*, it is possible that the first portion was cut from the front half in the same manner, while the "jaghanya" portion was cut later from the rear half. [Objection: But how can the sequence of the second and third cuttings for the *ānujāvara*—which is cut from the rear half—be established? [Response: It is said: when cutting from the rear half, the first [cutting] is from there, the second from the front half, and the third from the middle.

For this very reason, Āpastamba has stated regarding one who is younger in birth and offers four portions: "Having first taken a portion from the eastern half for the one younger in birth, he should place the *sruva* in the eastern half; having then taken the second portion from the middle, he should place it in the western half of the *sruk*. Thus it is said.

And thus it can be explained in our own Sūtra as follows: for one who offers four portions (*caturavattin*), that which is the "lowest" portion—that is, the second—is to be made the first. For one who offers four portions and is desirous of offspring (*ānujāvara*), and likewise for one who offers five portions (*pañcāvattin*) and is desirous of offspring, whatever portion was previously offered from whichever [animal] should be offered from that same animal in the reverse order. Therefore, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), that which was the lowest [portion] from the middle-cutting should be offered before it. One should offer the portions in reverse order for the eldest son of the eldest wife (*jyeṣṭhasya jyaiṣṭhineyasya*), or for one who desires the office of the domestic priest (*purodhākāma*).

Regarding those sacrificial portions (*avadāna*) which have the "prior-prior" (*pūrvapūrva*)—meaning those whose first part is from the front—for such a sacrificer who offers five cuttings (*pañcāvattin*) and is the eldest son born of the eldest wife (*jyeṣṭhasya jyaiṣṭhineyasya*), the first [portion] is taken from the front part, the second from the middle, and the third from the rear; however, for one who offers four cuttings (*caturavattin*), there is no third portion for the eldest son born of the eldest wife.

In relation to the third, the second indeed becomes the middle one; and it is possible to establish that which stands in the first position as being the first in relation to the third. Thus, this is a mandatory rule (*nityavidhi*). The office of the domestic priest (*purodhā*) and the duties thereof (*purohitya*) are for one who desires them (as an optional rite).
The rites for those whose sisters have not been previously married are for the youngest son, the son of a younger sister (*kāniṣṭhineya*), or for one who is slow to attain prosperity (*ānujāvara*).

*Kha* and *ṭha* are for the southern quarter. 2. *Kha* and *ṭa*: "Always" (*nitya*). 25. 194. Composed by Sāyaṇa Mādhava (Salyāṣāḍha), the Śrautasūtra—[Second Book]. "That which is posterior" means situated in the western part; "those of whom that is the first" refers to the eastern part. Everything else is just as before. There is an option for one who is "inferior in lineage" (*ānujāvara*). Regarding the four-fold portioner (*caturavattin*), there is no "third [portion] from the eastern half"; thus the arrangement remains exactly as before.

For the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and the milk-offering (*sāṃnāyya*), one should perform the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) with clarified butter: having spread [butter] underneath, having cut off a portion of the oblation, one should sprinkle it over with clarified butter.

In this context, it has been stated that there is a fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) regarding the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses; however, since only two portions have been mentioned for the sacrificial cutting (*avadāna*), how then does the fourfold portion come about? By this [passage], he demonstrates that there is also a fivefold portion (*pañcāvatta*). Because of the mention of the *puroḍāśa* and the *sāṃnāyya*, the fourfold portion is achieved through the fourfold cutting of the clarified butter (*ājya*). For those two, the fourfold portion must be performed by means of the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the over-pouring (*abhighāraṇa*) alone. Indeed, it is heard in the *Vājasaneyaka*: "Having spread under [the butter] with clarified butter, having cut off two portions of the oblation, he then pours clarified butter over the top."

"This very oblation, mixed with clarified butter (ājya), is offered. Although the Sūtra mentions only the mere cutting (avadāna) of sacrificial material in general, nevertheless, because it specifies "of the *puroḍāśa* and *sānnāyya*," for a sacrifice where clarified butter is the offering material, there is no under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) or over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) when the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) are present. In that case, it is established by the very sense of the text that one offers after having prepared either a fourfold or fivefold portion (*caturavatta* or *pañcāvatta*) using clarified butter alone; and here, the clarified butter comes from the *dhruvā* vessel itself, as it serves as the clarified butter for the *āhavanīya* fire.

Nor should it be argued that [the clarified butter] should not be poured from the *sruc* because it is already exhausted by its function as a consecration for the *ājyasthālī* itself; for even though it is a substance to be offered (*pradeyadravya*), its destination to the *āhavanīya* fire has been stated in such passages as: "He offers the cake-oblation," "Having offered the clarified butter, he offers the portion (*avadāna*)," and "Finally, he pours the remainder of the clarified butter over it. Furthermore: "Having spread a base of butter in the *sruc*, [he says]: 'Do not fear, do not tremble; may I not harm you; may your brilliance not depart. Bring it forward, lift it up, sprinkle it; I shall offer your portions in return. Homage be to you; do not harm me. Thus he touches the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) while about to take the portions."

The term *upastīrya* is prescribed as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), while *upastīrya* itself is a restatement (*anuvāda*). The connection with both [the spreading and the touching] is established by the phrase "he touches the oblation after having spread [the ghee]. This is an instrumental mantra; it says "the oblation" here so that there might not be a re-touching in the case of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.

Having cut the portions and sprinkled [ghee] over them, he sprinkles the oblation again with the mantra: "Whatever of my own I have made crooked while cutting the portions for you, I straighten that back with clarified butter; may that swell again."

In this context, the preceding restatement is for the sake of establishing the proper sequence. The re-sprinkling (*pratyabhighāraṇa*) is for the purpose of replenishing; since the clarified butter from the *ājyasthālī* is intended for the *ājya-offerings*, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) is performed only upon the two oblations—the *puroḍāśa* and the *sāṃnāyya*—which are situated on the altar, and not for the sake of the subsequent offering by way of being conveyed to the *āhavanīya* fire. Now, one might object: "This is not an oblation (*havis*)," [but rather] it is taken as being for the purpose of the sacrifice through the act of cutting (*avadāna*). However, in the case of the *puroḍāśa* and the *sāṃnāyya*, there are four [cuttings]. [Note: The text fragments provided appear to be footnotes or marginalia indicating variant readings in different manuscript versions (kha, ka, ga, ca, cha, ṭha).]

"But what [is the reason] that it must be of a different kind? This is because of the scriptural statement, "This is the oblation for Mitra with clarified butter (ājya)"; therefore, the mixing of clarified butter [must indeed take place]. [End of section 195]. This concludes the second section of the sixth chapter, together with the Vaijayantī commentary composed by Mahādeva. It should be so.

Thus, the Teacher indicates that the sacrifice is not performed by means of a mere portion for purification, but rather with the entire *puroḍāśa* cake. Consequently, when the substance has been offered into the fire with the *yājyā* verse and into the vessel with the *vaṣaṭkāra*, everything remaining thereafter is indeed the remnant (*śeṣa*). Therefore, both the touching (*pratyabhimarśana*) and the re-sprinkling (*pratyabhighāraṇa*) do not pertain to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.

If it is argued that, since it is heard in the Vājasaneyaka—"Therefore, whatever oblation one cuts off, he pours butter over it again; thus he causes the Sviṣṭakṛt to swell"—it follows from this hearing of its being for the sake of the Sviṣṭakṛt that [the pouring] is for the sake of the clarified butter in the Āhavanīya fire, we say: no.

That is a praise of the re-sprinkling (*pratyabhighāraṇa*). Regarding the injunction "he sprinkles it again," even though the oblation being offered is situated on the altar, it has been consecrated by that [sprinkling] and thus does not go to the *āhavanīya* fire; for once it is exhausted, how could it be cut off for the *sviṣṭakṛt*? Therefore, since the exhaustion is replenished by the re-sprinkling, this praise—by producing the fitness for the offering to the *sviṣṭakṛt*—is indeed for the sake of the injunction regarding the re-sprinkling itself.

This has been explained by the Vārtikācāryas, who have mastered the Mīmāṃsā, that the entire sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is an auxiliary to the sacrifice, not merely the portion sliced off. By the suffix *-ktvā* in the word *upastīrya*, it is stated that the touching (*abhimarśana*) with the formula "May I not [be harmed]" occurs after that time; therefore, because there is no spreading of butter (*upastaraṇa*) in the Upāṃśuyāja, there is no touching of the *dhruvā* vessel.
It is known from scripture: "Having sliced off each portion, he anoints the *prastara* and the *barhis* grass."

Having cut the four-fold portion (caturavatta), because that very substance constitutes the offering-material, one should not begin another portion until that is completed. However, regarding the repetition (vīpsā), Vaikhānasa says: "It should be with clarified butter in the *sruva*-ladle so that the four-fold cutting is performed once at the end for all the sacrificial oblations (*havir*). It is stated that this is understood as being merely a ritual rule (*dharmamātra*). As if covering it without scraping it off, he offers the cake-oblation; having offered the clarified butter, he offers the cut portion; finally, he pours the remainder of the clarified butter over it.

He offers the oblation of the *puroḍāśa* cake; by doing so, he covers it, making it covered as if by a lid with the bowl of the *sruva* ladle, thereby not letting it spill. Regarding this specific detail, [the text] says: having first offered clarified butter (*ājya*) for the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*), and having poured [butter] from the mouth into the place of the offering, one offers the two portions (*avadāna*) upon that from the side on the north. By the force of the word "covering," it is understood that this is done with the side [of the ladle]; for there is a specific rule stating, "the others [are offered] with the mouth. Thus, having offered the *puroḍāśa* oblations with the side alone, immediately thereafter—[one offers] one...

He causes the remainder of the oblation to flow out through the mouth with the remaining clarified butter (*ājya*), making it overflow with dripping ghee. It is stated in the *Bhāgavata*: "He ate [the offering] as it overflowed with dripping ghee through the mouth of the fire-eater (*hutabhuj*). This is not possible in a sacrifice where the offerings are *ājya* and *āmnāyya*, because one offers the *avadāna* after having offered the *ājya*. Since that [offering] is distinct, the general rule is simply: "One offers either a fourfold or a fivefold portion.
He causes the other [offerings] to flow out through the mouth.

The other oblations consist of clarified butter (ājya), the Sānnāyya, and the Darvihoma offerings; they say that the offering of salt, meat, and the like is also made with the mouth, as is the offering of barley and other grains. For this very reason, Āpastamba says in his ritual manual (kalpa-sūtra): "One offers all substances with the mouth. This is indicated by the plural number in the word *itarāḥ* ("the others"). [Notes on variants: gha, cha, ja, śa, ja, da read *hutīrjuho*; ka, ga, ca, cha, da read *thagabhāvā*; ka, ga, ca, cha, ṭa, dha read *suveṇa*. This concludes the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Second Praśna.]
He offers each preceding *saṃhitā* and *āvāpa* oblation.

"Each preceding" means in the eastern part, in the successive eastern portions; that is to say, arranged from east to west. He offers the *saṃhitā*, which is mutually connected [to the previous], and the subsequent *āvāpa* oblation—that is, the principal *āvāpa* oblation.
He subsequently offers the *āghāra* poured into the ladle.

One offers the oblation without disregarding the second supporting line (*ādhāra-rekhā*). The Brāhmaṇa passage, "The deities [are] between Agni and Soma," is clear and thus understood; it was therefore overlooked by Āpastamba, yet he has stated exactly that. Likewise, it has been stated that one establishes the deities by means of the distinction between the two supporting lines, and that one enters [the fire]. This is not contradictory for us. Furthermore, it should be understood that when the two supporting lines are transverse, they should be made between the two *ājyabhāga* offerings in order to favor the principal oblations (*pradhāna-āhuti*).
Having thus provided this technical definition (*paribhāṣā*), he states the subject at hand:

Having performed the *pravara*, when it is said, "O Adhvaryu, place the butter-filled ladle upon the mouth [of the fire]," he takes up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, steps across once, and offers five *prayāja* oblations, either stepping forward with each or standing in one place.

He offers (*yanati*) and he sacrifices (*juhoti*), because this is so designated by Āpastamba and others. If that is the case, then the term *yajati* (he sacrifices) is indeed seen in the originative injunctions such as "he sacrifices the *samidhs*" (*samidho yajati*), yet the designation *hautra* (pertaining to the Hotṛ priest) does not apply here; for it is observed there that the act of sacrificing belongs to the *adhvaryu* alone. Since the duties of calling for the *āśrāvaṇa* and the *praṇayana* are prescribed for the *adhvaryu*, the term *yajati* is employed in the sense of the *adhvaryu* himself. Thus, by virtue of being the instigator of the one who performs the sacrifice, it is the *adhvaryu* alone who sacrifices through him.

In all the various recensions (*āṭavarya*) of the *Yajurveda*, numerous *yajati* (sacrificial acts) are heard. Among these, there are injunctions for the performance of the ritual along with its auxiliary parts (*sāṅgakarma*). Just as the office of the *Brahman* priest (*brahmatva*) is performed by the *Brahman* according to his own designation, so too is the office of the *Hotṛ* (*hotra*) performed by the *Hotṛ*. Since the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses are designated as belonging to the *Hotṛ*, the remaining sacrificial acts are performed by the *Adhvaryu* alone; he, too, is said to "sacrifice" (*yajati*) by means of indirect indication (*jahallakṣaṇā*).

If it is argued: "When there is an injunction for specific subsidiary rites (*viśeṣakarma*), then the injunction is indeed by means of those respective verbal roots; yet, since the Śruti text already exists in the form 'He offers the Āmikṣā,' for what purpose is the use of the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) employed here through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)? [The answer is: No. By the number "five," a distinction is restated, and that [distinction] is produced by the repetition of the root *yaji*. Furthermore, that [repetition] does not apply to the *homa*s (pouring oblations), but only to the *yāga*s (sacrifices).

It has been shown that even the name *prayāja* belongs to sacrifices (*yāga*) alone; that in the originative injunctions (*utpattividhi*), the sacrifices are each designated by names such as "he offers the *samidh*" and so forth; and that the deities to be propitiated, who are the basis for those names, belong to the sacrifices themselves and not to the *homa*. If it were said "he offers" (*juhoti*), all of this would be entirely inconsistent.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "He offers while stepping forward" (*abhi-krāman juhoti*), which is heard within the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-prakaraṇa*): since it is connected with all the offerings occurring within that context, how could it be restricted to the *prayāja* offerings alone? Indeed, there is no such sentence as "He offers the *prayājas* while stepping forward," for the use of the term "stepping forward" is intended to exclude [other actions]. This is because the sentences concerning the *prayājas*, which are connected with the verb "to sacrifice" (*yajati*), occur both before and after [this statement].

The oblation falling at the time of the *daṃśa* (the biting) is taken as a subsidiary part of the *prayājas* by virtue of the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*). Thus, "five *prayājas* are offered" [is stated]. [It is performed] either while stepping forward or standing in one place, as grasped by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice). Subsequently, due to the designation of its constituent parts, it is to be performed by the Adhvaryu priest.
