It has been shown that, by the force of the intermediate sentences (*avāntaravākya*) in the *baṅga* [sections] and by the logic of the "ten descents" (*daśāvatāranyāya*), [the rule] applies specifically to the *homāḥ* (oblations). Thus, the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) found even in other recensions—namely, "from where, having stepped forward repeatedly, does one offer? or "standing in what common place does one offer?"—is fulfilled by the words "from their place," referring to those subsidiaries of the *prayāja* that are not separately enjoined; and by the phrase "in that same place" (*samānatra*), [it is explained that] "having stepped forward repeatedly" (*abhikramyābhikramya*) is expressed by the suffix *ṇamul* due to the proximity (*sthāna*) of the two: the call for the announcement (*āśrāvaṇa*) and the command "sacrifice! (*yajeti*). Thus, "having stepped forward repeatedly."

Likewise, by the phrase "standing in the same place as he [the Adhvaryu] stands," the fact that the Adhvaryu is the performer of the action is established; in this very way, the meaning of the word is shown in the context of the Soma sacrifice, both as something to be prohibited and as something to be enjoined.

"Since it is said that one should cause the announcement (*āśrāvayet*) while standing at the spot where one thinks, 'I shall offer without stepping forward,' therefore the offering must be made by one standing in the same place for the sake of stability; likewise, it is stated as a prohibition that 'if one were to offer after stepping forward, one would fall away from stability. Therefore, because they share the same purpose, the explanation here is also exactly the same. Now, there is no other injunction such that both stepping forward and not stepping forward could be enjoined by way of a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*), since one or the other is already established as a constant requirement."

It is said: having stepped forward (*abhikramya*), one is restricted to either [of the two options]; thus it becomes meaningful. Whether by stepping forward five times or by standing in the same place, the meaning is simply "five. This is indicated by the number "five"; otherwise, the accomplishment of all requirements would have been established merely by the plural number. And likewise, in all *sa-vaṣaṭkāra* oblations, except for those involving Soma, it is also established as a matter of course that there is no restriction regarding stepping forward or not stepping forward.

The phrase "having proceeded with the *pravara*" is stated for the purpose of recalling what was not present [in the mind]. Since he has already stepped forward at the very beginning, there is no intervening *puronuvākyā-praiṣa* (the call for the invitatory verse). Furthermore, the phrase "sad" is used to indicate that there is likewise no returning [to the original place] from that point. The construction is: "stepping toward the one who hates. This is a deprecatory statement intended as a prohibition. For it is not the case that the sacrificer becomes hateful to the *adhvaryu*; rather, having stepped toward him—that is, having gone behind the place of the *āśrāvaṇa*—he does not offer the oblation. "Pṛthivī hotā" is the portion belonging to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

He issues the first *prayāja* command with "Sacrifice the fuel-sticks (*samidhaḥ*)"; he issues the subsequent ones with "Sacrifice, sacrifice. The word "first *prayāja*" is used in the accusative case with the sense of the locative. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says: "He sacrifices the five *prayājas*, [beginning] with 'the fuel-sticks,' because the first is most kindled (*samiddhatama*). The first *prayāja* is the one most thoroughly kindled; thus the Śruti states: "It is offered as one that has been made prosperous by the act of kindling. This state of being most kindled belongs to the first, and thus the *saṃpraisha* would be intended for all five. Furthermore, Bharadvāja has stated that it is the first.

This is a simultaneous direction (*praiṣa*) for all five [verses] by means of the word *samit*, just as in the case of the *prāṇabhṛts* [where the direction applies to all] due to the connection with the gender. Here, because of the specific statement, the direction is by the name itself. In other cases, the direction is directed toward the deity to whom the offering is made, such as "Sacrifice to Agni," "Sacrifice to Soma. Therefore, in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), even though there is no hearing of the deity in the *yājyā* verse for the animal sacrifice, it is appropriate to say "Direct the call to the *samidhs*" (*samidbhyaḥ preṣya*), since the original name (*nāmadheya*) has been applied to the modification.

The mention of the *prayājas* need not be made, as it is already established by the context (*adhikāra*). It should be made so that the designation applies to each individual one. From the context, the meaning is "the offerer. The repetition "O sacrifice, sacrifice! is used for all of them; he issues the command "Sacrifice! with respect to each *prayāja*.

Now, in this context, the word *samidhaḥ* (the fuel-sticks) is heard in the originative injunction (*utpattivihita*) as "He offers the *samidhs*" (*samidho yajati*), where it is a name for the ritual action (*karmānāmadheya*). It is not connected with the *saṃpreṣa* (the call for assistance), because these are deities; for deities are established as those to be worshipped, as is seen elsewhere in the *praiṣa*. If these are understood from the *yājyā* (offering verse) to be deities, then that which is stated—namely, "The *prayājas* are indeed the seasons; he thus gratifies the seasons"—and so forth, which establishes them as deities, would be contradicted.

Even that which was stated by Baudhāyana—that "the *prayāja*s belong to Tvaṣṭṛ"—would be contradicted. Likewise, the statement made by the author of the *Nirukta*—beginning with "The *prayāja*s indeed belong to Agni, the *anuyāja*s belong to Agni; such is the *Brāhmaṇa*"—which, after raising the doubt regarding various deities based on various *Brāhmaṇa* passages, concludes by determining that "they belong to Agni" is the settled rule while the others are merely figurative expressions—that too would be contradicted. To this it is replied: the word *samit* denotes the ritual action itself, because of its syntactic connection (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "subsequent ones" (*uttarān*).

For the word "subsequent" (*uttara*) does not bring about the presence of a deity; rather, the word "subsequent" is a qualifier. Since it is dependent [on something else], no qualificand is perceived for it, and thus it connects with the phrase "the subsequent *prayāja*s," meaning "the *prayāja*s that follow. Here too, the sense is "in the subsequent *prayāja*s. The word "kindling-sticks" (*samidhaḥ*), ending in the accusative case, is connected with the verb "sacrifice" (*yajeti*); as in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice, one sacrifices to the kindling-sticks, just as one says "he sacrifices."

Regarding the determination of the deity (*devatā-nirṇaya*): here, there is no cognition of the deity through the *saddhiti* formula or by means of the dative case; rather, the determination of the deity arises solely from the wording of the mantra (*mantra-varṇa*). In that regard, the *yājyā* is internal (*antaraṅga*), whereas the *yājamāna* [formula], such as "I gratify the Vasanta among the seasons," is external (*bahiraṅga*). Even names such as *samit* and so forth, which serve as the basis for the deity, follow the deity of the *yājyā* itself. Furthermore, in those cases, the deities are precisely those denoted by the words *samit* and the rest.

For even the Mīmāṃsakas maintain in the section on repetition (*abhyāsādhikaraṇa*) and elsewhere, up until the second quarter of the ninth book, that a name which restates a deity established by the wording of a mantra is [a *nāmadheya*]. Furthermore, in all *yājyā* verses, Agni is also heard, as in "O Agni, may the kindling-sticks (*samidhaḥ*) of the clarified butter (*ājya*) go forth," and so on; nevertheless, the word "Agni" is not connected with each individual term such as "may they go forth" (*vyantu*). Rather, the words "kindling-sticks" (*samid-*) and so forth are used in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) [with the word "Agni"].

In the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), the very words *samit* and so forth are heard as names based on the deities; even where the word *agni* is not present, the name is still based on the deity Agni, and even when there is a discrepancy, the word *samit* itself remains. Therefore, the intention of the author of the Sūtras is that the dedication (*uddeśa*) is performed by means of the words *samit* and so forth. Why? Because in the *yājyā* verses, the plural number and the first person do not connect with the word *agni*; rather, the connection is: "O Agni, these bodies of yours are the *samits*."

Even the *Nirukta*, while stating that [the deities] possess the nature of Agni, does not alter the verbal expression; rather, it maintains that the deities signified by the words *samid* and so forth are indeed Agni. This was stated by that very same author through the verse beginning with "my *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s," and by the verse "those portions were sought by Agni for me—those portions are your *prayāja*s. Thus, it is established that the deities of the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s are to be meditated upon in the form of Agni, as they were given to him as his portions by the gods. Regarding this, it is asked: "For what purpose is this stated? and so on.

The purposefulness [of the rule] is stated by way of a rebuttal to the following doubt: "When one is about to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call, one should mentally meditate upon that deity for whom the oblation has been taken. Here, the intention of the doubt is this: the deity is represented by the *yājyā* verses; whichever word brings that deity forward, by that very word the deity attains its status as such, and not by another word.

Furthermore, the various examples cited by the Brāhmaṇas regarding the attainment of the status of multiple deities and their subsequent refutation—such as the conclusion that "the *prayāja*s belong to Agni" and "the *anuyāja*s belong to Agni"—are also useless, because there is no difference between the word [indicating the deity] and the actual performance. However, the intention of the subsequent [text] is that the word [itself] is the authority. [End of] Second Paṭala. [This concludes] the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva.

Furthermore, regarding the *yājyā* verses, since meditation on the deities is established by scripture, as long as it is not known which deity is to be represented by each respective word, meditation cannot be performed; thus, there is a purpose in determining the deities. Consequently, even in the view of Baudhāyana, the determination is simply that the seasons are denoted by words such as "samidh" and so forth, but it does not mean that the mention must be made using words such as "spring" (*vasanta*) and so on.

Now, an objection is raised: in the fifth *prayāja*, however, [the mantra] is an auxiliary that assists by direct contact (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*), serving as a consecration (*saṃskāraka*) for the deity about to be sacrificed to; in that case, how can the term *svāhākāra* be a name (*nāmadheya*)? Furthermore, if it is a name, how can there be a basis for a deity (*devatānimittatā*)? Or, if it refers to Agni, how can those words be expressive of him? It is replied: The *svāhākāra* is the word "svāhā" which constitutes the form of the mantra. Its etymological derivation (*nirukta*) is as follows: it is "svāhā" because it is "well-said" (*su-āha*); or "svāhā" because "speech says well" (*svā vāk āha*); or "svāhā" because "it says together" (*sam-āha*); or "svāhā" because "it offers the oblation that has been well-offered" (*svāhṛtaṃ haviḥ nuhoti*).

And its purport has been well explained in the commentary [on the *Taittirīya-Brāhmaṇa*] in such passages as "he says... and so forth. "That is the birth of the *svāhākāra*," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Those to whom the *svāhā* is performed are the *svāhākāras*, namely the deities; for instance, in the formulas "Agni, svāhā! Soma, svāhā! and so on, the accusative case is employed. These very deities are the "clarified-butter drinkers" (*ājyapāḥ*); therefore, even the fifth *prayāja* is called *svāhākāra* by means of the word *svāhākāra*, which denotes deities in general. Herein is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the animal sacrifice: "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the *svāhākṛtis*. From that, however, it is modified...

In the three [sacrifices], the renunciation is indicated by the words of the *yājyā* verses themselves; this has been clearly demonstrated in the *Mānī-sūkta* of the *Nirukta*, and it should be understood accordingly in each case. Just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is a recitation of consecration (*anumantraṇa*) using the words "spring" (*vasanta*) and so forth—which serve as indirect indicators (*lakṣaka*) of the deities—in the same way, in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), there is also a recitation of consecration using those very same words as indicators; thus, there is no modification (*ūha*).

In the *anuyājas*, however, the dedication (*uddeśa*) and the subsequent recitation (*anumantraṇa*)—such as "I am the *barhis*" and so forth—are performed using the very words found in the *yājyās*, such as *barhiḥ* and others, which reveal the meaning inherent in the ritual action. Since this is observed in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is determined that by means of *ūha* (modification) in the same manner, the deity of the *yājyā* is to be conveyed in the *anumantraṇa*. As for those who dedicate [the offering] with the word "fire" (*agni*), in their view, the *anumantraṇa* performed in the *anuyājas* would be authoritative only for themselves. Why? Because [it contradicts the established rule].

The accompanying mantra, "Not outside am I through the sacrifice to the gods," expresses a relevant meaning either through primary denotation (*abhidhā*) or through indication (*lakṣaṇā*); however, the same resolution applies to the *prayāja* offerings themselves. Enough of this over-elaboration; let those learned in logic understand this.

One sacrifices to the *samidhs* in the east, to *tanūnapāt* in the south, to *iḍ* in the west—having brought half of the *aupabhṛta* butter into the *juhū*—one sacrifices to *barhis* in the north, and to the *svāhākāra* in the middle, or behind the junction of the *āghāra* libations, joining each preceding one with the next, or performing all of them at the same place.

In the *samid-yāga*, one should understand the sequence as "from the front of the middle" (*madhyāt purastāt*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "to the west of the junction of the *āghāra*," the arrangement of options has been stated as follows: it is joined to each preceding [point] toward the east, and joined to each succeeding [point] toward the west, proceeding generally from west to east. Thus it has been stated by Vaikhānasa: "To the west of the junction of the *āghāra*, or toward the east."

Where the two bases meet, that is the middle region; behind it (to the west), near the edge of that [middle] region, at the very same spot, there is the option of placement. Regarding each direction, there are three positions: always facing east, or facing the same way [as the previous]. In all these cases, one brings half of the *aupabhṛta* [ghee] into the *juhū* and performs the sacrifice outside.

Regarding the statement "having brought it outside," it is said that one sacrifices with what has been brought outside; therefore, he sacrifices with the clarified butter (ājya) from the *juhū* after the three *āghāras*, and with the clarified butter from the *upabhṛt* during the fifth [offering]. Thus, the Brāhmaṇa states: "He brings together [the butter] from the *upabhṛt*; clarified butter is indeed splendor (*tejas*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is offspring; verily, he bestows splendor upon the offspring. This praise is given precisely because the butter brought together is for the purpose of the *barhis*.

Some say that this statement is merely a prescription for the time [of the action]; that is refuted by the Brāhmaṇa passage already shown. With this very intention, the author of the Bhāṣya has also explained it. The practical purpose (prayojana), however, is as follows: when one offers the *prayājas* elsewhere than at the *aparihoma*, there is no first *caturgṛhīta* in the *upabhṛt*; rather, there is only one *caturgṛhīta* for the *brahman* and so forth. Likewise, in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) as well, one should take [the butter] in the *upabhṛt* with the very same initial mantras. Having stepped back, one sprinkles the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) with the remnant of the *prayāja*.

[The act of] sprinkling [clarified butter] occurs when there is a remnant; in its absence, there is no sprinkling, because that [sprinkling] is of the nature of a disposal (*pratipatti*) for the remnant. If it is argued: "Since the accusative case is heard in the injunction 'they sprinkle the oblations' (*havīṃṣyabhighārayanti*), the oblations are the objects to be refined (*saṃskārya*); therefore, having made them a remnant, one must perform the sprinkling of the oblation. In the event of its loss, the sprinkling should be performed with a substitute, namely another clarified butter," we say: No. This has been established by those learned in the principles of logic (*nyāya*) that this is indeed a disposal of the remnant.

That very point has been shown by the Teacher as well through the word *śeṣa* (remnant) as a statement of an established fact, in that he does not say, "one should make this [offering] with the remnant of the *prayāja*. By this, it is established by those [authorities] themselves that at the *paśu* sacrifice and elsewhere, as soon as the *āgneya* offering arises, the remnant of the *prayāja* must not be placed in another vessel; and thus, because it is purely of the nature of a disposal (*pratipatti*), there can be no substitute even in the opinion of the authors of the Sūtras. This will be supported by the rule: "The second [accusative case] is likewise applied to that which is not intended [as a goal]. As for the sequence in which they are offered:

Because they are given in that specific sequence, being distinguished by their respective order; for in this case, if [the remains] were for another purpose, how could they be performed by a single [act]? Otherwise, the disposal of the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings would occur with respect to only one oblation, and the disposal of the husks would occur with only a single potsherd—this is the concern expressed by the phrase "because they are in sequence. Since the plural form is heard in the scriptural injunction, "He sprinkles the oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja*," and since it says, "One should dispose of the remnant upon the oblations (*haviḥṣu*)," the plural number is intended to be significant.

By the word "oblation" (*havis*) in this context, both the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and primary (*pradhāna*) offerings, as well as the *vaṣaṭ*-utterances and the acts of presentation (*pradāna*), are included. Therefore, it is not established that the act of disposal (*pratipatti*) must be performed at a later time even for an oblation that is yet to arise; rather, it must be performed at the very time of disposal using those [substances] that have already been established. It does not tolerate a delay until the time of the arising of that which is to be disposed of, because it is already accomplished by the established primary oblations. He states their sequence accordingly: "Having sprinkled the *dhruvā* [ladle], he sprinkles the *āgneya* [offering]; finally, the *upabhṛt*."

Based on the principle that when both the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*) are mentioned, only the principal is to be understood, one might fear that there would be no inclusion of those [offerings] that do not consist of sacrificial oblations (*havis*). To address this, it is stated: "the *dhruvā*," and so forth. Since the sacrificial oblations are constituent parts of the sacrifice, they all possess the status of being subsidiaries (*aṅga*) without distinction. The point is that these are not the objects to be referred to (*uddeśya*) here, but rather the things to be enjoined (*vidheya*). In modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) where there are no *ājyabhāgas*, there is no pouring over the *dhruvā*. [The offerings to be known] in the middle, as far as possible, are: the *dhruvā*, the *āgneya*, the *āgnīṣomīya*, the *dhruvā*, the *āgneya*, the *aindrāgna*, the boiled milk (*śṛta*), and the curd (*dadhi*).

1kha. With the clarified butter that has been heated. [Ravi’s Paṭala, with the commentary Vaijayantī by Mahādeva: Even though the *dhruva* vessel serves the purpose of the *upāṃśuyāja*, there is no further pouring (*abhighāraṇa*) over it. This is because it was drawn individually before [the *upāṃśuyāja*], because it is a single unit at that time, and because it is not something to be consecrated again. There is no repetition [of the action] because it is a disposal (*pratipatti*). By the word "finally" (*antataḥ*), it is shown that as many [offerings] as are possible in the middle should be performed. He proceeds with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, which have clarified butter as their sacrificial material.

The term *ājyabhāgau* is the name for two rites; it refers to those two for which clarified butter (*ājya*) is the portion (*bhāga*). Nevertheless, it should be understood that while this is a conventional designation (*rūḍhi*), the etymological derivation (*yoga*) is "the two portions belonging to Sarasvatī. As for the rule regarding the production of the substance of clarified butter, it was stated as "the oblations of clarified butter" (*ājyahaviṣām*) in order to show that "this clarified butter in the *dhruvā* vessel is indeed taken for the sake of the entire sacrifice. Thus, "those two for which clarified butter is the oblation" (*ājyaṃ havir yayostau*)—with them, one proceeds (*pracarati*), that is, one performs the ritual.

Where it should have been said "he sacrifices" (*yajati*), the term *pracarati* ("he proceeds with") is employed in the sense of the root *yaj*. Here, clarified butter (*ājya*) is prescribed as either fourfold or fivefold portions, accompanied by the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses; this is because of the specific injunction that these two [verses] apply to the cake-offering (*puroḍāśa*) and the curd-mixture (*sāṃnāyya*), and not to the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*). Therefore, the sequence ending with "having spread [butter] underneath, having touched it with 'May it not be harmed,' having thus cut the portion, and having sprinkled [butter] over it, he sprinkles the oblation back over it" applies specifically to the cake-offering and the curd-mixture. These two [offerings] are made together: he offers to Agni on the northern half of the radiant [fire], and to Soma on the southern half.

The two arms [of the fire-pit] are equal in length and flaming. It should be understood that the northern part of the site is the northern half, and likewise the southern part is the southern half. Baudhāyana and Āpastamba have stated that the eastern part of the northern half is the eastern part of the southern half. In the Gṛhya-sūtra, he himself will state the same. The Śruti, however, is quite explicit: beginning with "He offers in the eastern half," it says, "He offers to Agni in the northern half; to Soma in the southern half."

Nevertheless, since the two *āghāra* libations are performed transversely, whenever they serve as the substratum for the principal *ājyāhutis*, and since the *āghāras* are offered at the middle and at the two ends—specifically at the southeastern quarter—then the expression "between those two" (*tāvantareṇa*) which will be mentioned later becomes appropriate. Therefore, it is stated that "in the southeastern quarter" and so forth, in order to declare that the position of the two *ājyabhāgas* is fixed precisely according to the requirement of the *āghāras*.
Between those two, he offers the other oblations. (5)

The term "jyotiṣmatī" is carried over [from the previous rule]. The phrase "the others are brought" is the ellipsis. These [offerings] are [placed] between the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, because the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* oblations have fixed positions; therefore, the *darvihoma* oblations are regulated here. Regarding this, there is a specific statement from the Atharvaṇikas: "When the flame flickers in the kindled fire that carries the oblation, then one should present the oblations between the two *ājyabhāga* offerings. Āpastamba has stated the same: "He takes up the two offering-spoons for the two *ājyabhāgas* and does not set them down until the *sviṣṭakṛt*."

Having aimed at [the previous time], when it was previously said, "O Adhvaryu, place the ladle containing clarified butter," even though the placing of the two [ladles] already held was not explicitly mentioned, the statement "he takes them up again" is a restatement for the purpose of prohibiting their placement in the middle. There is no fault in placing those two which were previously taken up, as it is implied by the sense; however, there is an expiation for placing those taken up now in the middle, since the sipping of water and other such rites would otherwise be required. [Notes on variants: 1. ca. ṭa. "sya pu| 2. gha. u ja. a. na. ḍha. 'pmatī juhotyu | 3. ka. kha. [omitted] The meaning is that although the act of placing the two ladles—which had already been grasped—was established by the context, the explicit mention serves to preclude their being set down in the interim. While there is no transgression in setting them down after they were first taken up (as this is naturally understood), a penance is prescribed for setting them down in the middle after they have been taken up at this later stage, because the standard ritual requirements such as sipping water (*ācamana*) would then apply.

[The syllables] *ga*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṭha*, *naṃ*, *na*, *ni*, *ra*, *gha*, *u*, *ja*, *śa*, *tra*, *da* [are used]. One should sacrifice (*yajati*). 55. From *ṅa*, *ja*, *śa*, *ma*, *da* onwards. 202. Having placed [the vessel] in his hand, one should proceed; this is to be understood as continuing until the conclusion of the *iṣṭakṛt* (Sviṣṭakṛt) offering. By Māradvāja, in the *prayāṇa* (procession).

Immediately after those [offerings], the placing [of the ladles] and the taking back of the *ājyabhāga* portions were mentioned; however, that is not accepted by the Teacher (*ācārya*), because it would result in the placing in the middle serving no visible purpose, which contradicts logic—so they say. That is not so; for it is stated that "having taken up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt*, he performs the *prayāja*s," thus the *prayāja*s are declared to be performed with both ladles. Then, from the statement "he takes up the two ladles toward the *ājyabhāga*s," the taking back for the sake of the *ājyabhāga*s is established. The Teacher accepts only the initial placing. Having performed [the *prayāja*s], he proceeds with the *āgneya* cake and the *upāṃśuyāja* which has clarified butter as its oblation.

Whether by means of four portions or five portions, the mere fact that the offering of clarified butter (*ājya*) precedes the cake-offering (*puroḍāśa*) to Agni has been stated. In that regard, the sequence is as follows: having commenced with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, and taking the *juhū* ladle with the right hand and the *upabhṛt* with the left, [one offers] to Agni...

Having given the command, "Recite the invitatory verse," he takes a portion from the *dhruvā* ladle according to its own channel, replenishes it, and having placed the *prastara* and *barhis* back into the vessel, he returns with the ladle, causes the announcement to be made, and when the response has been given, he commands, "Sacrifice to Agni. With the *vaṣaṭ*-call, or when the *vaṣaṭ*-call has been uttered, he offers the oblation outside the *āghāra* lines, in the north-eastern part, across the two *āghāra* lines, on the northern side.

Having returned by the same way he came, he gives the direction: "Recite the invitatory verse for Soma. Having taken four portions and stepped across, he performs the *āśrāvaṇa* and so forth, and sacrifices to Soma as before. He offers it in the eastern part of the southern half, across the two supports of the *āghāra* libations. Agni and Soma are the deities. With the formula, "By the sacrifice to the gods, Agni and Soma, may I become possessed of sight," he makes the offering. And likewise with the *agnitṛpti*. Having returned by the same way he came, he [proceeds] with the *guhyu*...

Having spread [the sacrificial grass] and having caused it to swell with the formula "Mā me," he touches the cake for Agni with "For Agni, announce! He makes two oblations; having taken the first portion from the fixed place, he places it in the ladle in the eastern half, and having placed the second portion in the western half, he pours clarified butter over it. Having re-poured over the portions with "That which belongs to the portions," and having caused the *prastara* to swell and having stepped across the outer edge, he causes the announcement to be made. When the response has been given, he commands, "Sacrifice to Agni! Having caused the clarified butter to flow forward at the place of the offering with his face turned toward the north, he offers it either simultaneously with the *vaṣaṭ*-call or when the *vaṣaṭ*-call has been uttered.

He offers the oblation. Having inserted the *juhū* ladle in front of the junction of the *āghāra* lines, he offers the portion from the front part of the *āghāra* line, covering it with the bowl of the *sruva* ladle so as not to let it scatter. Having offered the *avadāna* (cutting-off portion), he causes the remaining portion to flow through the mouth of the *sruk* using the *ājya-sthālī*. "To Agni, svāhā"—this is the formula for the offering. Having returned by the same way he came, he proceeds with the sacrifice called the *upāṃśuyāja* using clarified butter as the sacrificial material; here, there is no "to Prajāpati" formula, but rather according to the respective deity.

Having cut off four or five portions, having sprinkled [the oblation] and set aside the *prastara* grass-bundle, having stepped across [the altar], and having performed the calls for the announcement (*āśrāvaṇa*) and so forth, he offers it by pouring it together with the [oblation] for Agni—either at the utterance of "vaṣaṭ" or when the "vaṣaṭ" has been pronounced—into the northern part of the eastern section, or in the north-eastern direction, along the line of the *cyāpāra*, using the mouth of the *juhū* ladle. Here, there is no rule that after offering the *ājya*, one should pour the remainder over the edge; nor is there the rule of "not covering as it were," and so forth. Prajāpati, Agni-Soma, and Viṣṇu are the deities.
"Thou art a piercer" (*dabdhir asi*) is the formula for the sacrificer in all cases.

For that [Upāṃśuyāja], the loud *āśrāvaṇa* and *pratyāśrāvaṇa*, the *yājyā-puronuvākyā* summons, and the *vaṣaṭkāra* are performed loudly. Since the designation "Upāṃśuyāja" (the silent sacrifice) would otherwise result in all its elements being performed in a whisper, it is stated that these are "loud" by virtue of their purpose; the meaning is that because the *āśrāvaṇa* and so forth are intended for making oneself understood to another, they must be loud. "To Prajāpati, we sacrifice to Prajāpati"—this [formula] he recites in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). Even for those [formulas] intended to inform another, there is a restriction of low-voiced recitation by the Śāstra. Since the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* consist in the designation of the deity, they too are recited in a low voice. Alternatively, because the place for low-voiced recitation belongs to those two, the sacrifice itself possesses low-voiced recitation by way of connection; this is because they are not subordinate in the sense of having a visible purpose, since they directly produce the sacrifice. Having returned from that [spot], he proceeds with the subsequent cake according to the respective deity.

If it exists, then it is practiced; for one who sacrifices to Agni and Soma, there is the *puroḍāśa* offering, while in the alternative case of one who does not sacrifice to Agni and Soma, there is the *aindrāgna* [offering] on the full moon day, but not on the new moon day.

When the offering belongs to Agni and Soma, having spread the base-butter (*upastīrya*), having replenished the butter, and having taken a portion from the front part of the animal, he places the first portion on the *muc* (the front part), the second and subsequent portions on the *puṣkara* (the rear part). Having sprinkled it with clarified butter and replenished it, and having laid down the *prastara* (grass-bundle) and the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, and having performed the call for the *āśrāvaṇa* and so forth, he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Agni and Soma. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the oblation by means of the procedure of the *upāṃśuyāja*, as if covering the connected [portions] while moving forward. He offers in the eastern part, in the northeast, and in the rear part. Agni and Soma are the deities; the drinking of the remnants belongs to Agni and Soma.

On the new moon day (amāvāsyā), there is no Upāṃśuyāja; for one who does not offer the *saṃnāyya*, the Aindrāgna offering follows immediately after the Āgneya. Having performed the rite with the Āgneya, having returned by the same way he came, and having spread a base of clarified butter (*upastīrya*) in the *ājyasthālī* [saying] "Do not spill," he takes the first portion for Indra and Agni. Having placed the second and subsequent portions in the front half of the ladle, having moved it back, having sprinkled it, having taken the *prastara* and *barhis* grass, having stepped across, and having caused the announcement (*āśrāvaṇa*) and so forth to be made, [he pronounces] "Vaṣaṭ."

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers the oblation pertaining to Agni, as if covering it with the ladle joined [to the spoon] on the eastern part, in the northeast, or in the northern part, while moving it forward. Indra and Agni are the deities; "of Indra and Agni" is the formula for the measurement.

For one who prepares the *saṃnayya*, having taken portions from both, he proceeds with the two *saṃnayya* offerings: he cuts twice from the cooked milk and twice from the curds; for one who follows the five-fold cutting, he cuts three times.

"Samavadāya" means taking a single portion from each of the two dancing [flesh-portions]. Although the two are primary individually—as indicated by the dual number—their performance is simultaneous; this is what is stated. Furthermore, by the word "puniḥ" (again), it is made known that there is a repetition of the two portions, whereas the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) are performed with a mantra.

Due to the re-enactment (*punarvidhāna*), the procedure is performed for both the *puroḍāśa* and the *sāṃnāyya* in that same manner. Following the injunction beginning with "the spreading of the base-layer" (*upastaraṇa*) and so forth, one spreads the base-layer, pours clarified butter, and says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra or Mahendra. The phrase "Do not let [it] fall" (*mā mer*) is repeated because of the difference in location. Having cut off two portions (*dvir-avadāya*), sprinkled them with clarified butter, and replenished [the vessel], one places the *prastara* and *barhis* aside. Then, having performed this twice according to the principle of sequential performance of constituent parts (*padārthānusamaya*), one proceeds to the subsequent ritual sequence, such as the call for the *āśrāvaṇa*, while maintaining the common framework (*tantra*).

Having sent out the call as "Indra" or "Mahendra" according to the respective authority, and having caused the mixture to enter the *cucū* vessel without, as it were, covering it, he offers the *sānnāyya* oblation at the place of the *upāṃśuyāja* with only the opening of the *buṅ* vessel, using the formula "Indra" or "Mahendra" for the deity; the *yājamāna* formula is either "of Indra" or "of Mahendra. Having returned by the same way he came and having taken portions together, he proceeds with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.

In one case, the *avadāna* (cutting off) and *samavadāna* (collecting together) constitute a sacrifice known as the *sviṣṭakṛt*. It is threefold in nature: it has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) by way of being a disposal (*pratipatti*) of the primary oblation, and it has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) by way of being an act of giving (*dāna*) directed toward a deity. The *puroḍāśa* and *sāṃnāyya* sacrifices consist of the *upastaraṇa* (under-spreading) and other such acts. [The rule] "Do not fear for me" applies because it concerns the remnants of the oblation (*haviḥśeṣa*). As for the sequence in which they are offered: from all the northern portions, he cuts off [the portion] once each.

In whatever order they exist, without overstepping that sequence, in that same order they are offered. To the principal deities, one cuts portions from all the remaining oblations (*haviḥśeṣa*) in their respective order, taking them once each from the northern halves; "are offered" means they have been presented. Having cut once, [the portion] is taken with the thumb as the primary [finger], as appropriate, using either the hand or the *sruva* spoon.
For those who follow the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvattin*), it is done twice.
The word "simultaneously" (*saddhiḥ*) is stated for the purpose of setting aside the previous rule.

He pours the clarified butter over [the offering] twice; he does not pour it over the remnants of the oblation (*haviḥśeṣa*). Since the previous [rule] established that the specific injunction regarding the single pouring of butter applies to what has already been reached, the prohibition—expressed by the mention of "remnants of the oblation"—is shown to demonstrate that very principle. The intended meaning is this: this is not the oblation itself, but rather the remnant of that which was offered with the *vaṣaṭ* call; therefore, the application of the pouring of butter upon the oblation does not occur here.

It was argued that because the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance occurs at the time of offering, there is also an offering for the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice, and thus it possesses the nature of an oblation (*haviṣvatva*). This is denied; for although the substance is taken by virtue of the injunction even after it has been offered, it is merely the disposal of the remnant (*śeṣapratipatti*). Furthermore, it has been stated regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* that there is no taking of a portion from the *dhruva* vessel for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt*. This is due to the restrictive rule: "Of those which are offered in successive order. Therefore, the *dhruva* vessel does not yet possess the status of being a remnant of the oblation.

Since that [clarified butter] serves the purpose of all sacrifices, it is for that purpose only as much as has been taken; however, at the time of the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) or at the time of taking from the *dhruvā* vessel, there is no separate mention of individual deities by which each would have a distinct purpose according to its originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*). Therefore, only as much as has been taken is offered with the *vaṣaṭ*-call, and not even that which remains in the *dhruvā*—just as the sacrificial oblations (*havis*) consisting of the *puroḍāśa* cake and the *sāṃnāyya* milk, though situated on the altar, are offered with the *vaṣaṭ*-call.

Why? Because that which is fixed (*dhrauva*) serves the purpose of all sacrifices and thus cannot be offered at a single sacrifice; furthermore, this has been established by those learned in logic that the *viṣṭakṛt* portion is not for the sake of the *upāṃśuyāja*.
One offers it in the eastern half of the northern half, unmingled with the other oblations.

Previously, the locations for the *ājyabhāga* oblations were stated by the terms "northern half" (*uttarārdha*) and "southern half" (*dakṣiṇārdha*). To ensure that this [central] location does not become the place for those two, it was stated as "the eastern part of the northern half" (*uttarārdhapūrvārdha*). Consequently, because it was stated that "one offers the others between those two," the *ājyabhāga* for Agni is slightly to the north; from there, one offers the *āghāra*, the principal oblations, and the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering slightly to the south, without allowing them to touch one another.

For one performing the *saṃnayata* sacrifice, there are ten portions of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). First, the portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt* is taken; then, since the primary [portion] is to be offered from the right side of the heart (*bukkā-pārśva*), and because multiplicity (*bhūyastva*)—in this case the two-fold nature of the *śatadānu*—is more powerful than primacy (*mukhyatva*), the offering is made from the mouth. The formula for the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) is: "This is for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, not mine; I belong to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Now, how is it that Agni is indeed Sviṣṭakṛt? [Note: Variants *ka*, *ga*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṭa*, *ṭha* read *pratiśeṣo*; variants *ka*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṭha* read *vaikā*.]

10th Paṭala: Accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. If it is asked: "Just as in the fifth fore-offering (*prayāja*), although it is a consecration of the deities who are about to be sacrificed to, those same deities [are the recipients]; likewise, in the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, which is a consecration of the deities already sacrificed to, why are they not also the deities? [The answer is: No, because in the fifth fore-offering, the mantra...

The rule regarding the deity is based on the [Vedic] syllable (*varṇa*). However, in this case, because there is an originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhāna*) such as, "They gave him this portion, which they cut off for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the deity. There is a consecration of the deity by means of the mantra, the disposal of the substance (*dravya-pratipatti*), and the offering by means of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance; thus, the offering is for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt alone, resulting in a threefold nature. As they say: "By the mantra, there is the consecration of the deity; by the casting [into the fire], the consecration of the oblation (*avyasaṃskṛti*); and by the renunciation (*tyāga*), the *apūrva* (transcendental merit) is produced, which goes toward the primary *apūrva*."

Having stepped back and filled the offering-ladle with water, he sprinkles it around the middle enclosing-stick from left to right, saying: "In Vaiśvānara I offer this oblation; this is a thousandfold spring with a hundred streams. In it, may he support my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, swelling [with abundance] in the heavenly world. ||6||

The author of the Bhāṣya [Śabara] states that the filling of the *juhū* ladle is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*). Others, however, maintain it is merely a ritual duty (*dharma-mātra*). "To the father, to the grandfather, to the great-grandfather—this [is for them]. The touching of water according to the *Smṛti* is because of their state as ancestors (*pitryatva*). Or rather, it is merely a duty of disposal (*pratipatti-dharma*) following the washing. Even in the absence of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), it must be performed along the enclosing sticks (*anu paridhim*), meaning along the location of the enclosing sticks; the accusative case is used due to its connection with a term governing direction (*karmapravacanīya*). Therefore, it is not a purificatory rite for the enclosing stick itself. For this very reason, Āpastamba says, "He pours [the remains] inside the enclosing sticks," and Baudhāyana says, "The washing is inside the enclosing sticks. (6)
Thus ends the second chapter in the second book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* composed by Mahādeva.
2.3 Now begins the third chapter of the second book.

Having set down the two offering-ladles and having split the cake dedicated to Agni toward the east, he touches it with his thumb and ring finger, saying: "Let this [portion] be cut from the oblation by the measure of a barley-corn; let us not tear the sacrifice; may this oblation be pure and well-offered. Having thus touched it, he cuts off the *prāśitra* (the portion for the Brahman) by the measure of a barley-corn or a *pippala* fruit.

He restates what has reached its proper occasion with the words "having set aside" (*sādayitvā*). Having broken off the *āgneya* cake and moved it slightly from the place where one will cut the portions, how so? "Eastward" (*prāñcam*). Although the masculine gender indicates that this is not an adverbial modifier of the action but rather an adjective qualifying the cake, it nevertheless functions effectively as an adverbial modifier of the action. The meaning is that the setting aside should be performed toward the east.

Having touched the portion torn off with the thumb and the ring finger, and having moved the thumb and finger inside toward the belly, he cuts the portion with the mantra. Āpastamba says, "From the middle. Regarding the measure: some explain that "yava" (barley) is a grain and its size is the *pippala* fruit; that is the size for the *aśvattha* leaf. On this they say: "Some assert that it is the size of a barley grain," but in that case, because of the contradiction with the gender of the indicative marks (*liṅga*), the cutting should be done silently (*tūṣṇīm*). This concludes the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [the second book]. Some recite thus; therein, due to the contradiction with the gender of the indicative marks such as "of the size of a barley grain," the cutting is indeed silent.

According to the statement of Bhāradvāja, however, others explain that it is the size of a grain of rice or, according to some, the size of a *pippala* fruit; in this regard, there is indeed a mantra. "Prāśitra" is the name for the portioning of the sacrificial cake.
One should not separate [the portion] from the northern part.

Some say "from the subsequent oblation" (*uttarasmāddhaviṣaḥ*), and thus they desire the *prāśitra* even from the *sānnāyya*. And it has been stated: "The bringing [of the portion] for the others is by way of another. The word "subsequent" (*uttara*) also denotes an oblation that is offered at a later time; therefore, they desire the *prāśitra* from both the *āmikṣā* and the animal sacrifice. It has already been stated that the logical conclusion is that all the remaining ritual acts (*śeṣakāryāṇi*) do not proceed from the mouth [of the sacrificer], but rather from the *dhruva* vessel. Others, however, explain that the oblation situated in the "subsequent place" is specifically the *puroḍāśa*.

Furthermore, since there is recognition [of the deity] by means of the word *bhāneya* as the indicator of the deity, it is logical that there is recognition by means of the deity-word from the subsequent [offering]; yet, there is no usage of the deity-word in relation to the *sānnāyya*. Therefore, either the *āgneya* or the *aindra* is taken. Vaikhānasas have stated that it is from the subsequent *puroḍāśa*. Moreover, because there is an absence of the use of the *prāśitra* vessel in the animal sacrifice, and because it is seen in the case of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), there is no *prāśitra* in the *sānnāyya*.

In the case of the second [portion], because it is a separate substance, there is no rule regarding the repetition of the mantra, nor is there any authoritative evidence for it; some say that because it is "separated" (*virujya*), there is no "touching" (*anumṛśya*).
One spreads an under-layer of ghee (*upastīrya*) in the *prāśitraharaṇa* vessel, takes the portion, and then pours ghee over it (*abhighārayati*).
Since it is carried by means of this, it is called a "carrier" (*haraṇa*), meaning a vessel; thus, the sequence of first spreading the under-layer has been shown.

"One should spread [the butter] underneath and pour over it," so say some; the word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of indicating an option. Thus, there is an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) that one should either spread it underneath or pour over it. This has been stated by Āpastamba: "Having spread [the butter] underneath, he does not pour over it, or vice versa. The clarified butter for the spreading is taken from the pot itself, because it is distinct from the butter intended for the Āhavanīya fire. The same should be understood regarding the portions (*avadāna*) at the *iḍā* and other rites.
According to some, one cuts off the *prāśitra* portion from the cake dedicated to Agni.
This is an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) meaning "only from the Āgneya [offering] and not from any other.

Having placed that—that is, having placed the *prāśitra-haraṇa* vessel—the question arises as to where. In response to this expectation, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakṛt) states: "Having led it between the Bhr̥gu and the Āhavanīya fire, and having led it between the Brahman and the Āhavanīya fire, he places it behind the Āhavanīya; for if it were otherwise, there would be an intervention (*vyavāya*)," as found in another Sūtra.

When the sacrificer comes for the purpose of touching the *iḍā* (the sacrificial portion), then, because the portion cut out (*avatta*) and the *prāśitra* would be situated near the *sūktavāka*, there would be an intervention (*vyavāya*) between the Brahman and the *prāśitra* by the sacrificer; therefore, Baudhāyana stated "having placed the *praṇītā* waters with the *dhanaḥ*" in order to prevent such intervention.
Having spread [clarified butter] under the *iḍā*-vessel, he cuts off the *iḍā*, whether it be fourfold or fivefold; the sequence following the *sviṣṭakṛt* has been explained.

Since it is stated that for those [offerings] accompanied by *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras there is a fourfold or fivefold cutting (*caturavatta* / *pañcāvatta*), this applies by extension to the *iḍā* offering as well. Regarding that *iḍā*, the injunction "fourfold" or "fivefold" constitutes a new prescription (*apūrva-vidhāna*). Thus, there is a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*) concerning the *sviṣṭakṛt*. Likewise, because the *iḍā*-cutting is of the nature of a disposal (*pratipatti*) of the sacrificial remnants, one cuts from all the primary substances in the same sequence of portions as the *sviṣṭakṛt* itself, which takes portions from all the remaining oblations (*haviḥśeṣa*).

The entire *iḍā* is a single substance, because it is designated by the singular term "iḍā. Therefore, even though there is a first collective portion (*samavadāna*) from among the oblations, the mantra is recited only once for that; for from the mantra beginning with "manunā," the singularity of the substance called *iḍā* is understood. And thus, the second [portion] is also a single [substance] taken from all [the parts]; there, however, the mantra is again recited only once. Because of the intervention of the ritual act of the *āgāva-dāna* (the cutting for the sacrificer), the second cutting, although belonging to the deity, does not receive the mantra due to its being a mere speckling (*pṛṣad-dravyatayā*).

Then follows the sprinkling (*abhidhāraṇa*). In the case of the fourfold or fivefold portioning, the third [portion] is done silently; because there is no intervention, there is an absence of a mantra. Regarding how one cuts this *iḍā*—the text states the mantra: "I cut from the southern half the single-faced [portion], seen by Manu, having ghee as its foot, and impelled by Mitra and Varuṇa," while not breaking through [the cake]. Thus, he first cuts the *iḍā*-portion from the southern half of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

Next is the mantra for the portioning of the *iḍā* from all the sacrificial oblations (*havir-iḍā-avadāna*). In this mantra, qualifiers such as "having been seen" (*dṛṣṭām*) and so forth are connected only with the act of portioning (*avadyati*). Here, the repetition of the word "he portions" (*avadyati*) is intended so that, by omitting the prefix *sam*, the connection may be made with the single act of portioning the *iḍā* through the qualifiers such as "from the southern half" (*dakṣiṇārdhāt*) and so on. In reality, however, it is connected only with that [act of] portioning; because the *iḍā* is obtained through the portioning, it is that very act which is primary. Since the injunction of the mantra occurs only once, it culminates precisely in that first portioning of the *iḍā*.

[Objection: But then, since this mantra is employed for a single [act], would it not constitute a single sentence? [Response: No; for if that second portion, beginning with the *puroḍāśa*, were being offered, the mantra would not apply, because of its connection specifically with the first [portion]. Furthermore, regarding the combined offering (*samavadāna*) which is enjoined by the rule "he cuts off from both together," one who desires a single [result] [would have to rely on] extension (*atideśa*). Moreover, it has been stated that all the qualifiers contained in the mantra—whether indicated as neuter in the first cutting or otherwise—are [applicable to] the whole.

It has been clearly stated by Vaikhānasa: "Having spread a base [of ghee] in the *iḍā*-vessel, thinking 'I shall look upon it with Manu,' one cuts off the *iḍā*—whether fourfold or fivefold—from all the sacrificial oblations (*haviryaḥ*) like the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; from the southern half of the *puroḍāśa*, first from the front part so as not to cause a breach, and second likewise from the remainder of the entire oblation. This was also stated by Āpastamba in the same manner. Bharadvāja says: "The mantra is for the sake of all; thus the *iḍā* is cut off from all the oblations."

Therefore, it must be admitted that the sentence "from the southern foot of the *puroḍāśa*, first" (*dakṣiṇāpātpuroḍāśasya pūrvam*) is indeed a distinct [independent] statement. "First" (*pūrva*) means initially. The inclusion of the word "first" is intended to prevent [the portion] from being a second [offering] from the southern half. Since the location for its division is fixed, and because the first portion is to serve as the substance for the *iḍā* by being cut from the southern half, it is logical that it comes "from the south. [Notes on variants: 1. *na*. *cha*. *ṭa*. [*yāla*] 2. *ka*, *ga*, *ca*, *cha*, *u*. [*ṣaṇairyayā syāgniramāyā*] 3. *ṭa*. [End of fragment]
[The portion] from the eastern half is as fine as a hair and long.

"He cuts off equally" is an elliptical reference (anukarṣa). "Of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa)" is also [to be supplied]. From the eastern half, he cuts a small, thin, and long portion for the sacrificer, which is indeed devoid of the requirements of the fourfold cutting (caturavatta) and other such rules; however, for the two sacrificial cakes, he cuts them together. This has been explained in the commentary according to another Sūtra, but it is not seen in our own Sūtra.

For a technical definition does not apply everywhere; otherwise, the fourfold and fivefold portions would not obtain, whereby the spreading under and the pouring over would be precluded. This is because of the force of the elliptical extension (*anukarṣa*) of the word "of the sacrificial cake" (*puroḍāśasya*).
Having satiated it with clarified butter and having drawn [the portion] from the *dhruvā* vessel—

Having satisfied [the fire] with the clarified butter contained in the *sthālī*—the root *tṛp* being used here as transitive; otherwise, it would be *saṃtarpaye*—he should move it near the *dhruvā* and pour it out. According to Vaikhānasa, "he should place it in front of the *dhruvā*"; according to Baudhāyana, "in front of the *dhruvā*. This means in some vessel upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). He takes the portion from the junction.

The word "second" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. He cuts from that very junction (*saṃbheda*), which is the intervening space between the portions to be cut off. He cuts from the eastern part of the southern half—that is, the portion of the *iḍā* offering—and from the front part of the northern half; he cuts from that very space which is the junction or interval between those two. The qualification of the mantra, "without joining together" (*asaṃminnan*), is thus appropriate, because the other portions are being cut off while remaining in contact with one another. The third portion is from the rear half, for the sake of making five cuttings (*pañcāvattā*).

"Subsequently" means in the southern portion [of the sacrificial ground]; "of the *iḍā*" is the ellipsis. Regarding "the five-fold cutting": the author of the Bhāṣya stated that one cuts off the sacrificer’s portion from both sacrificial cakes together; however, that should be explained as follows: when the first cutting of one cake is completed, the first cutting of the second cake is performed in the very same place.
Having sprinkled [the *iḍā*] with clarified butter, he places the *iḍā* before the Hotṛ.

Having sprinkled the *iḍā* with a large quantity of clarified butter from the vessel, he hands it over into the hand of the Hotṛ. The formula beginning with "Of beautiful form, of rain-like color," etc., belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).
Or he pushes it forward to the east;

there is an option regarding its offering. He pushes the *iḍā* forward on the altar, which means he causes it to flow forward. When it has been handed over to the Hotṛ—on that alternative—without releasing it, he encompasses the Adhvaryu with the *iḍā*, provided it has been handed over to the Hotṛ.

If modification (*ūha*) is intended, then the Hotṛ, without abandoning that [original form], takes hold of it from all sides by means of the modification; thus, it is logical that in the Yājuṣa [tradition], one should effect the modification at the place where "ūya" occurs.

Having passed the *dakṣiṇā* by the front of the *hotṛ*, sitting behind him facing east, he anoints the two finger-joints of the *hotṛ*. Taking clarified butter with the *sruva* spoon, having gone south along the side of the *hotṛ*, having performed a circumambulation to the right, and having turned back to the right, sitting behind him facing east, he anoints those two joints of the *hotṛ*'s fingers first because of their priority. "He anoints them with the *sruva*"—so says Āpastamba. "He anoints the joints on the forefinger (*pradeśinī*)"—so says Vaikhānasa. The anointing is a consecration of the *hotṛ*. Regarding the order, he says: first the front one, then the rear one.

Having first anointed the tip of the lower root-joint (*mūlaparva*), he then anoints the other, which is the lower root-joint. Here, by the word *parva*, the joints (*saṃdhi*) are meant; for the word *kāṇḍa*—as in the expression *kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt*—is a synonym for *parva* and can also denote a joint. The distinction here is that only two of those [joints] are joined together, measuring the size of a thumb-joint (*aṅguṣṭhaparvamātra*), as is seen from the statement "as far as this [uppermost] finger-joint. Having anointed it, he smells it and touches water. He is the Hotṛ priest; that is the anointed clarified butter (*ājya*). This touching of water is according to the Śrauta ritual; the prescription for the Hotṛ is based on its belonging to the Yajurveda.
Having returned as he came, sitting facing west in front [of the Hotṛ], he cuts off the *avāntareḍā* from the *iḍā* into the right hand of the Hotṛ.

If the *iḍā* has not yet been handed over, then having returned, he places it into the hand of the Hotṛ. Then, sitting facing west in front of the Hotṛ, [he takes] from the *iḍā* into the right hand of the Hotṛ. The rest is clear. He states the procedure:
"He spreads [the butter] from the smearings."
The Hotṛ makes an under-layer of clarified butter using the butter-residue remaining in the *iḍā* vessel, which has been taken up with the *sruva* ladle.
The Hotṛ himself takes two portions from the middle, or the Adhvaryu takes one and the other.

Then, the Hotṛ himself takes two portions from the middle of the *iḍā* vessel; or alternatively, the Adhvaryu takes one portion and the Hotṛ takes the other, or vice versa. [This is done] from the middle of the *iḍā* vessel.
He anoints and pours over [the offering];
this is clear.
The Hotṛ invokes.

[The section on] the duties of the Hotṛ priest is appropriate here because the *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ) will be explained by way of its being performed according to the *Yajurveda*; however, in the case of the *Bahvṛca* (Ṛgveda), those duties have already been stated there. The meaning is that he makes the deity Iḍā present before him by means of an invitation. Here, the formulas beginning with "O Iḍā, come" (*iḍa ehi*) pertain to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). The Adhvaryu, the Āgnīdhra, and the sacrificer touch the Iḍā while she is being invited. 7. [End of section] 210. Composed by Satyāṣāḍha, the Śrautasūtra—[Second Praśna]. The sense is that he turns the deity Iḍā toward himself by means of an invocation. In this context, the formulas beginning with "O Iḍā, come" (*iḍa ehi*) belong to the sacrificer. The Adhvaryu, the Āgnīdhra, and the sacrificer take hold of the Iḍā as she is being invoked. 7. [End of section] 210. Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra—[Second Praśna].
