The word *iḍām* is connected with both [the preceding and following phrases]. Having touched the vessel with his hand, he remains seated until the conclusion of the invitation (*upahava*). The sacrificer, having approached from the north behind the Āhavanīya fire and turned clockwise, takes hold of [the Adhvaryu] from behind. The enumeration [of the priests] is for the purpose of excluding the Brahman, since in another Sūtra his taking hold is also prescribed.
When the words "The divine Adhvaryus are invited" are being uttered, he mutters: "I am invited; may I possess cattle.

The Adhvaryu causes him to recite this because it falls within his jurisdiction; as for the sacrificer's own muttering, the author will describe that in the section concerning the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).
When [the portion] has been invited, he carries the *prāśitra* (the portion for the Brahman) around in front of the *āhavanīya* fire.

Together with the vessel, the *adhvaryu* brings the *prāśitra*, which is the portion cut for the *prāśitra*. That previous carrying-around mentioned by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) for the sake of non-interruption is to be explained as referring to another *sūtra*, because here the time is directly prescribed by the words "when it has been invited.
When that has been consumed:

When the *prāśitra* portion has been consumed by the Brahman priest according to the procedure beginning with "devasya tvā," the officiating priests—along with the sacrificer as the fifth—consume the *iḍā*, which has been invited with the formula: "Thou art *iḍā*; thou art pleasant; thou art the maker of pleasure; do thou bestow upon us abundance of wealth and excellent offspring. I eat thee for the glory of my mouth, that my mouth may be fragrant.
Thus, all four priests and the sacrificer as the fifth consume the *iḍā* after it has been invited. The Brahman priest also consumes his portion by approaching from behind.
From the time of the cleansing until the consumption [of the remnants], everyone remains restrained in speech;
they perform the purification within the sacrificial altar (vedī) provided with the strainers, reciting: "May the mind, as light, be pleased."

*Mādayantām* is the end of the mantra. *Antarvedi* means within the middle of the altar; having stood there—that is, having stood near the *prastara* (grass-bundle) upon which the *pavitra* (strainer) has been placed—the meaning is that he stands close to it. The phrase *antarvedi* is used because standing nearby is possible even for one situated outside [the altar]; therefore, it is specified as "within the altar. At the conclusion of the *mārjana* (sprinkling) mantra, he sprinkles water on his head. Then, he may depart as he pleases. The *brahman* priest, having returned by the same way he came and performed the *mārjana*, sits in his own seat. Having divided the *āgneya* cake into four parts, he places it upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

[The cake] for Agni is not [the same as] that for Agni-Soma, nor that for Indra-Agni, nor the *sāṃnāyya*. Having divided it into four parts—that is, having split the whole into four portions—he sits upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). In this way, the elision of the letter *ṣ* in the word *barhiḥ* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). [In some recensions, such as Gha, Ḍa, Ja, Sa, Ja,] the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is the fifth. Having made the fourth part, they place the sacrificial grass; the final portion is thick. Therein, the ritual duty of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) begins with "O Bṛhaspati, swell... and so forth. [End of] the Fourth Patala, from the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva. Page 211. The fourth part having been made, they set aside the sacrificial grass; the last portion is thick. Therein, the sacrificer's duty is "O Bṛhaspati, cause [the milk] to swell," etc.
When that [portion] is being assigned with the words "this for the sacrificer," he assigns the sacrificer’s portion.

Regarding the phrase "in that": when the *āgneya* [oblation] has been prepared in the dative case, and while it is being assigned with the formula beginning "this for the Brahman," the *adhvaryu*, having first cut off the sacrificer’s portion, assigns it—while it remains near the *dhruvā*—with the words "this for the sacrificer."

Regarding the statement "in that [case] being assigned," if it is intended to indicate time, then even in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) where there is neither the *Āgneya* cake nor its modification, and where the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*) is absent, the assignment (*vyādeśana*) of the sacrificer’s portion alone serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). This is because, when there is a multiplicity of items to be assigned, it is impossible to know the time; therefore, in that case, the assignment applies to the portion alone.

Regarding the sacrificer’s portion in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there is no instruction at all because its purpose is visible; since that [visible purpose] is possible, there is no assumption of an invisible purpose—this is the opinion of the author of the *Bhāṣya*. However, others argue that since the portion had already been cut out by the Adhvaryu as the sacrificer’s share, how could there be any doubt? Therefore, it is logical that its purpose is indeed invisible. One prepares the six-fold portion for the Āgnīdhra from the coarsest part of what has been instructed. The sacrificer must instruct the Āgnīdhra that the very last portion is coarse; he then prepares the six-fold portion from that very same [portion]. Thus it is said:
Having spread a base [of clarified butter] and having taken a portion, he pours clarified butter over it; in this same manner he takes a second portion.

In a certain vessel used for dividing into four parts, having spread a base with clarified butter from the pot, having taken a single portion along the path to the Āgnīdhra fire, and having poured clarified butter over it, he then takes the second part—beginning with the spreading of the base and ending with the pouring of clarified butter—in its entirety. Thus, the six-fold portion (*ṣaḍavatta*) is accomplished; this is the meaning. "Thou art the portion of heaven; thou art the Āgnīdhra of Agni; thou art the *śāmitra* of Agni; I eat thee with the mouth of Agni; homage be unto thee; do not harm me"—with these words, the Āgnīdhra eats it.
[He gives] the *svabhāma*.

According to the *Vaikhānasa* [sūtra], he distributes the portions for the Brahman and the sacrificer along with the vessels, or having taken the two portions together with their respective vessels, and so forth. He "carries around" (*pari harati*) means he brings them all the way around; because the root *hṛ* takes two objects, the meaning is that he should place them near the Brahman and the sacrificer.
With one vessel he offers to the Hotṛ, with another to the Adhvaryu;
with those vessels which were passed to the Brahman, the Yajamāna, and the Āgnīdhra, [he offers] with two others. The Adhvaryu alone carries [the portion] to the Adhvaryu.

"Thou art the portion of the Earth," with these words the Hotṛ eats; "Thou art the portion of the Atmosphere," with these words the Adhvaryu; "Thou art the portion of Heaven," with these words the Brahman.

1 gha. i. ja. sa. ma. da. smin vyādi | 2 gha. ṅa. ja, jha, ña, ḍha, vyādiṣṭasya | 3 ca. pātrāhi | — 212 Śatapatha Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[Book 2, Chapter 8]: A large, unlimited *anvāhārya* mess of cooked rice is prepared on the *dakṣiṇāgni*; having sprinkled it with clarified butter, or not sprinkling it, he places it within the altar (*antarvedi*).

He places [the vessel] to the north from the vicinity of the *dakṣiṇāgni*. "Great" means more than sufficient for all the sacrificial priests. "Immeasurable" means that he should not count the rice grains with handfuls (*prasṛti*) and so forth when placing them in the pot. The *anvāhārya*—so named because it was cooked on the *dakṣiṇāgni*—has already been placed on the fire and is now cooked. The rest is clear. There is no consumption of this [rice] here; since it was given as a fee (*parikraya*), its disposal (*pratipatti*) is not a constituent part of the sacrifice. Here, in the *brahma* and *yajamāna* sections, [the formulas begin with] "O Brahman," etc. He issues the command: "Let it be served to the *dakṣiṇāsads*."

The sacrificer issues the command, "Bring them to the right for those ṛtviks," and it is for him alone that the bringing [of the gifts] takes place, because he is the one who performs the act of giving the characteristic marks.
When the sacrificer says, "Go to the south," they act according to the command.

"Come from the south," he thus directs the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). While being addressed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the priests should come from the south and pass in front of the *āhavanīya* fire. To the priests standing to the south, the sacrificer points out the divided rice (*odana*) with the words, "O Brāhmaṇas, this rice is for you. Then, the *āgnīdhra*, intending to receive the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), says, "Of the god... and so forth, ending with "...I receive; King Va... [offers] the rice to the Brahman. (1:1)

"Please accept," [he says], and [the recipient] accepts. Then, in the same manner, the Brahman and the Hotṛ [proceed] according to their own manuals. Now, because of the observation that "the Adhvaryu follows this very procedure," the sequence for the fourfold division and the offering should be understood here as being the same.
Having accepted the *anvāhārya* rice, they return.

The rule regarding the acceptance of the *dakṣiṇā*—one’s own share of what is to be taken away—is as follows: having accepted it with the individual formulas for acceptance, such as "Who [gives] this? To whom? they return again from the north. The *brahmā*, having come from the north by the same way he came, having gone to the south and accepted [the gift] according to the rule, returns by the same way and sits upon his own seat.
Then, having removed the remnants of the oblation (*havir-śeṣa*).

Having placed the remaining items outside the altar to the north according to their respective order— the plural number being intended to refer to the specific sacrificial offerings of both sessions— if the *udghāsana* (the lifting of the fire) has not been performed, then at the commencement of the subsequent rite, one offers into the *āhavanīya* fire with the mantra "tataṃ me āpaḥ" (according to another *sūtra*). Having cast the two firebrands (*ulmuka*) used for the *anūyāja* offerings back into the fire— that is, having merged them with the fire— one [proceeds].

"O Brahman, we shall set forth; having placed the fuel-stick, O Āgnīdhra, cleanse the enclosing sticks and the fire once each," thus he issues the command. The option regarding the recitation by the Brāhmaṇa is already covered by the formula "O Āgnīdhra, the fire once each. [The formula is: "This is your fuel-stick, O Agni; through it, may you grow and swell; and may the lord of the sacrifice grow and swell. [End of] Chapter 4, together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 213.

"May [the waters] quench themselves, svāhā!"—having said this, the Āgnīdhra places a fuel-stick on the fire and, without stepping away, cleanses the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) with the wooden sword (*asphya*) and the cord used for binding the fuel-wood: the middle one facing north, and the other two facing east. This is not a *darvihoma* performed on the sacrificial seat; since there is no mantra ending in *svāhā*, this is a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for Agni, being neither a primary nor a secondary act. "Without stepping away" means remaining in that very place while moving clockwise. The rest is self-evident. "This is your food"—this is the portion for the sacrificer.
He modifies the mantra to: "O Agni, winner of booty, thee who hast run for booty."

He recites: "To Dyau..."—this is the end of the mantra. The mantra previously employed for the cleansing of the fire (*agni-samārge*) is here used for the cleansing of the *amita* (unmeasured) fire with the reading "sasacāsam.

[The mantra is: "O Rudra, lord of beings, who moves along the threads, the youthful one; do not harm our cattle. May this oblation be yours, Svāhā! Having sprinkled the cleansing materials, he throws them into the *āhavanīya* fire.

The mention of the *āhavanīya* fire is intended so that these previously swept [brushes] are not thrown into the *gārhapatya*, and also so that the mantra does not apply to the *utkara* (the rubbish heap) and other such places. Because the mantra ends with "svāhā," it has the nature of an offering; however, it is a disposal (*pratipatti*) because it is no longer useful [for its original purpose]. Rudra, the Lord of Beings (*bhūtānām adhipatiḥ*), is the deity. Regarding the phrase "on the altar" (*vedihari*), some say it is a specific instruction for the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) and not for Rudra; they maintain that there is no touching of water (*udakopasparśana*) in that case. He states another form of disposal: one should throw them on the *utkara*, in the hall, or in a haystack.

*Utkara* is well known. *Śālā* means in the fire-hall; some say "in that very hall" or "on the fire-altar within it. *Valam* is a heap of grain; however, the Commentator says that here *śālā* refers to a house entered by a person, and *valanā* refers to the rafters (*pṛṣṭhavaṃśa*) there—some say these are the wooden beams tied on top of the grain, others say it is the binding rope for those beams.
"Or he may carry it to another cow-pen, or beyond the range of a cow's pasture" (8).
Thus ends the third chapter in the second book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.

"Paragoṣṭha" means a place beyond the cow-pen; the meaning is that it is a region beyond the cow-pen, or a region beyond a *gavyūti*. Thus ends the third chapter in the second book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* composed by Mahādeva. 3.
2.4 Now, the fourth chapter in the second book.
Regarding the "Great Oblation" (*mahāhavis*) in the section on the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*):

1. According to some, [the formula] is *ye'nuṣa*. 2. According to others, it is *ni yāni kā*. 3. According to others, it is *nyūtimilekaṣām*. 4. According to some, it is *kā veti*. — End of the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Second Book, Fourth Chapter —
Having brought the clarified butter from the *upabhṛt* into the *juhū*, he crosses over once and performs three *anūyāja* offerings with it.
This has been explained.
He issues the call for the first *anūyāja*: "Sacrifice to the gods," and for the two subsequent ones: "Sacrifice, sacrifice."

Regarding the *saṃpreṣa* (direction) for the *anūyāja* offerings: "O Hotṛ, sacrifice to the gods!"—the meaning is that he directs the Hotṛ at the first *anūyāja* using the plural form. This is an indication of time (*kālalakṣaṇā*) for the purpose of all *anūyājas*, intended here to demonstrate the *saṃpreṣa*. How so? Because of the mention of "gods" (*devān*) as a common qualification for the deities of the three [offerings], the subsequent direction applies only to these two.
He makes the offering behind each fuel-stick (*samidh*), in front of the junction of the *āghāra* libations.

He offers the first oblation at the front part, just like the *anūyāja* and the *samidh* offerings. Then he offers the second behind that. The formula for the sacrificer is "O Aṅgiras! Then, behind that, he offers the third, just like the *samidh* offerings; all three are indeed at the front part, starting from the *āghāra*. Regarding this, he states the specific rule:
"The last [offering] is directed eastward, long, continuous, and with it he connects the others.
This means he connects the other two—the second and the first—with that third one; he should join them together in the middle at the place of the third offering. The rest is clear.
Having stepped back and placed the two offering-spoons in their respective places—
this is for the sake of clarity—
he separates them with the two *vājavatī* verses.
The meaning is that he performs the rite up to the *vyūhana* (spreading apart) with the two verses beginning with *vājavatī*. He explains this very point:

with the verse "By the impulse of strength" (*vājasya mā prasavena*), he lifts up the *juhū* ladle together with the *prastara* grass-bundle using his right hand, palm upward; then, with the verse "Indra [has struck down] my rivals" (*asapatnāṃ indro me*), he presses down on the *upabhṛt* ladle with his left hand, palm downward. With the words "the uplifting" (*udgrābham ca*), he lifts up the *juhū*; with the words "the pressing down" (*nigrābham ca*), he presses down on the *upabhṛt*. With the verse "The gods have increased the sacred power" (*brahma devā avīvṛdhan*), he pushes forward the *juhū* eastward with his right hand, palm upward; then, with the verse "Indra and Agni [have struck down] my rivals" (*asapatnān indrāgnī me*), he throws the *upabhṛt* westward outside the altar with his left hand, palm downward.

In the first half-verse there is one mantra; then there are three mantras of that same length; then follows the half-mantra beginning with "atha sapatnān. With his right hand, palm turned upward and placed on top, he lifts the *juhū* ladle—which had been placed upon the *prastara* grass-bundle—upward together with the *prastara*.

Holding the *upabhṛt* with his left hand low, he places his hand over it and grasps it; he presses it down, joining it slightly with the *barhis*. Again, in the same sequence, he performs the *udgrābha* and *nigrābha* with those two. He pushes the *juhū* forward toward the eastern direction, moving it across the altar itself. He throws away the *upabhṛt* outside the altar, discarding it. [Chapter 4, Paṭala] With reference to the *upabhṛt*, he states another mantra: *Mahādevakṛtavaijayantīvyākhyāsametam* (Accompanied by the commentary Vaijayantī composed by Mahādeva). 215. In the *upabhṛt*, he recites another mantra:
"May the god Savitṛ drive away him who hates us and whom we hate"—
with these two [verses], he performs the ritual for the sacrificer.
Having sprinkled [the butter] and taken up the *upabhṛt* ladle, he anoints the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the *juhū*.
Having taken [the portions] with the right hand using the *juhū* ladle smeared with clarified butter—saying "For the Vasus, thee!

over the middle portion; "For the Rudras, thee! over the southern half-portion; and "For the Ādityas, thee! over the northern half-portion—or else saying "Thou art the winner of wealth, thou art the bestower of wealth"—these three [formulas] are optional alternatives for the preceding three [mantras], even though they are applied by means of a single concluding particle (*iti*).

The mantras are as follows. The rest is clear. "To the Vasu gods," and so forth, pertains to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). Regarding the phrase "to the Rudras," they say that both [the priest and the sacrificer] must touch water because there is no distinction in their being associated with Rudra, and because no other ritual action prescribed for synonyms of the word "Rudra" is mentioned here. That is not correct. Such [water-sprinkling] occurs only in a ritual where Rudra is the presiding deity (*devatā*). However, this is merely a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*); therefore, it should be understood that there is no requirement to touch water.

Having placed the *juhū* ladle on the *prastara* bundle, [he says]: "May Heaven and Earth agree; may Mitra and Varuṇa protect you with rain. Having smoothed the *prastara* over the two *vidhṛtis*, he inserts the two *vidhṛtis* into the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
Having smoothed the *prastara* together with the two *vidhṛtis*, having lifted it up, having pulled it out, and having placed the two *vidhṛtis* down, he anoints the *prastara* in the ladles:

the tips in the *juhū* with the verse, "Licking what has been anointed"; the middle parts in the *upabhṛt* with the verse, "May the birds disperse"; and the roots in the *dhruvā* with the verse, "Offspring, the womb."
"May I not be released"—this is the end of the third [verse].
In this way, he anoints again;
the word "he anoints" is also connected with what precedes.

In the third [offering], the roots are first in the *dhruvā*, the middle parts in the *upabhṛt*, and the tips last in the *juhū*. Although it would have been sufficient simply to say that the third option is the reverse, by using this elaborate description it is shown that the reversal applies only to what has been specifically indicated; however, those mantras which are stated for a particular place remain exactly as they were in the first case. The tips, middle parts, and roots belong to the *prastara* (grass-bundle). "O you who are well-anointed" (*samaktām*) is the portion for the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). Or else: "Mark me in heaven, mark me in the intermediate space, mark me on earth."
These [mantras] are optional for these [acts].

Having removed a blade of grass from that which has been smeared with the formula "For life" (*āyuṣe tvā*) and having set it aside in its known place, he takes a single stalk of *darbha* grass from the smeared *prastara* bundle with the mantra and sets it aside silently in its known place. The term "in its known place" means that he places it so as not to be displaced later.
Having taken the prastara-bunch and the branch,
and having smeared them as required—
[this concludes] the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [in the] second praśna, [section] 216.

Regarding the *darśa* sacrifice for one who performs the *saṃnayya* offering, it is stated that "the branch" [is used], but no entirely new branch is being enjoined; rather, it is the very same milking-branch (*dohaśākhā*) that is recognized here for the purpose of disposal (*pratipatti*) along with the *prastara*. As for the *śākhāpavitra*, there is no other disposal for that strainer.

"Having brought it under the upper junction of the enclosing-sticks" means having caused it to enter; the meaning is: "if the branch exists, together with it. He then states the ritual action to be performed:
Having called for the response, when the response has been given. || 9 ||

In this case, there is no bypassing of the *dakṣiṇā* (the sacrificial fee), because such a rule is prescribed only for the *yājyā* verses. Having sat down and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, since it is stated by Vaikhānasa that "he who is seated," the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* is performed by the *agnīdh* standing on the *utkara* (mound); it is further stated that his *pratyāśrāvaṇa* occurs on the *utkara* itself, except in the case of the *pravara*.
Having issued the command, "The divine Hotṛs are impelled for the auspicious recitation; the human [Hotṛ] is impelled for the *sūktavāka*; recite the *sūkta*," the Hotṛ begins the *sūktavāka*.

He proceeds; he begins. In that context, the word "hotṛ" is used for the purpose of connecting [the action] with the duties of the Adhvaryu during the middle course. "Āpiḍi" refers to the duty of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).
With the words "May the waters and the plants swell," the Adhvaryu throws the *prastara* and the branch after [the fire].

Having performed the *sūktavāka* as a secondary characteristic (*anulakṣākṛtya*), and that [branch] when a branch is present. The mention of the *adhvaryu* is for the purpose of showing that there should be no recurrence of the term "hotṛ. "Meraya" is the end of the mantra. Here, according to the view of Jaimini, the deities associated with the *ājyabhāga* offerings and so forth are [invoked] in the *sūktavāka* according to their textual order; likewise, in the statement "he throws the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*," the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) indicates that the *sūktavāka* is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the throwing of the *prastara*.

Since it has been established that mantras serve as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) by way of visible utility (*dṛṣṭadvārā*), the *sūktavāka* must manifest the throwing of the grass-bundle (*prastarapraharaṇa*). Furthermore, for the sake of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), the relationship between the deity and the throwing of the grass-bundle must also be manifested. However, that [relationship] cannot exist without a sacrifice (*yāga*). Since neither of those two exists in the present context, the act of "throwing" (*praharati*) itself must indicate a sacrifice, without abandoning its own primary meaning, just as the root *nirvap-* (to offer) does.

Next, the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) that has been employed [in the sacrifice] is the subsidiary sacrifice (*aṅgayāga*) belonging to the *animita-yāga*, which is accomplished by means of the *sūktavāka*. Here, the term "throwing" (*praharati*)—by way of *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-exclusive indication)—is also a subsidiary of the sacrifice, just like the act of "offering" (*nirvapati*). It expresses the placing of the *prastara*, the substance to be given away, into the fire, just as one speaks of "offering."

In that context, regarding the disposal (*praharaṇa*) characterized by ritual performance, there is co-occurrence (*sahabhāva*) with the branch, as expressed in the injunction: "He disposes of the *prastara* together with the branch. This disposal of the branch—just like the disposal of the *prastara* which was used—is a disposal of what has been utilized; thus, the branch must be taken even by one who performs the *saṃnaya*. This subject matter (*prameya*), established through the third, fourth, and sixth chapters, has been demonstrated with focused intent. Regarding this, Āpastamba says: "There is no utterance of *svāhā*."

The commentators became adorned by raising the objection that this is a negation of something not applicable; they said that he stated this having assumed its applicability according to the opinion of Jaimini. That is extremely weak. It is precisely Jaimini’s own view that has been presented by him. How so? Because it is not a disposal (*pratipatti*) of this [offering] which is subsidiary to a sacrifice already accomplished by means of the *sūkta*; rather, it is a preliminary limb (*pūrvabhāvyaṅga*) of the sacrifice, [as described in] the fourth chapter of the *Mahādevakṛtavaijayantī* commentary. 217.

Regarding the phrase "like the offering of that substance," there is no *svāhākāra* [exclamation] with it; however, according to that view, the *svāhākāra* is established in the mantra "O Jātavedas, with the omentum... In our own teacher’s view, the *svāhākāra* occurs only in *davihoma* offerings and not elsewhere. As for the wording of the mantra, it is a praise because of its dual nature as a sacrifice: "Go to heaven, send down rain, and thereby may the plants flourish. The venerable Hiraṇyakeśin neither raised this doubt nor provided a refutation.

Since the term *spaprāharati*—derived from the root *prahṛ*—denotes its own primary meaning alone in the manner described, the throwing of the grass-bundle (*prastara*) is not a *homa*; therefore, it is established that the mantra consists solely of the utterance *svāhā*. Although the author of the Bhāṣya, relying on the view of Jaimini, stated that the mantra ends with *svāhā*, even that [position] is to be reconsidered.

How, even in this view of Jaimini, does the utterance of *svāhā* in this mantra serve the purpose of the throwing (*praharaṇa*) in the *sūktavāka*? For the sacrifice is not of the nature of giving to the deities; nor is it a disposal (*pratipatti*) of the grass-bundle (*prastara*) previously performed, otherwise the throwing of the branch (*śākhā*) would also be a sacrifice, since it is already accomplished by that very mantra accompanied by the utterance of *svāhā*. Furthermore, a connection between the branch and the sacrifice is not desired by Jaimini, as such a possibility has been directly refuted.

Therefore, it is not within the scope of our understanding why the author of the Bhāṣya stated that "the mantra ends with *svāhākāra*. Consequently, it is established that the *sūktavāka*—which reminds one of the deities who have been sacrificed to, from the *ājyabhāga* deities up to *Sviṣṭakṛt*—serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) by generating a refinement (*saṃskāra*), while it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) as part of the sacrifice itself. However, the *śaṃyuvāka* has exclusively an invisible purpose; because it does not illuminate a matter inherent in the ritual action, it is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), like a *stotra* or *śastra*. Regarding the *praharaṇa*, he states another mantra:
"May the licking ones lick what has been anointed; may the birds lick it; having become the speckled cow, may she go to heaven"—thus [it is said].
Regarding the specific manner of striking there, he says:
"Neither too far forward nor too far back, not pressing against the tip, holding the hand as if it were not crooked."

The connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: "holding his hand straight, as it were, he strikes. That *prastara* (grass-bundle) whose tip does not extend excessively beyond the fire is "not over-tipped" (*nātyagra*); one should strike such a bundle. Thus, it results that he strikes it toward the east, with its tips directed toward the north. Likewise, "without roasting the tip" means not roasting it; the root *śṛ* means "to cook. He should not roast—that is, he should not parch—the tip, which is the foremost part, upon the embers.
And thus it is said that one should strike as if [the opponent] were not there. But by Vaikhānasa it is stated: "He raises [the hand] upwards as if pulling, and finally he turns it downwards.
He finally turns it downwards as if pulling.

Having raised it upward, he then brings it downward; having placed it in the position of lower and upper parts, he finally turns it around in the place of offering, meaning he causes it to revolve like a water-wheel (*ghaṭīyantra*). "emā agman" is the formula for the sacrificer. "agniridam" and so forth: he mutters the *japa* while bowing to the honored one, beginning with "agneraham ujjitiman. It has already been stated that the mention of the deities is "agnaya idam" and so forth, referring to the deities of the sacrifice. [Note: The text includes manuscript variants such as "vṛṣṭinarayeti" and references to Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, 2nd Praśna.]
When it is said, "This sacrificer, so-and-so, desires [this]," the Adhvaryu, having cast aside the *prastara*, issues the call: "O Agnīdh, bring [the *prastara*]!
While the Hotṛ recites "He desires," he issues the command to the Agnīdh.
With his cupped hands, the Agnīdh thrice raises the *prastara* upward.

Having thrice offered the *prastara* with his joined palms (*añjali*) into its very place, he performs the ritual duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) beginning with "O Rohita," and so forth. Then the Āgnīdhra releases the *prastara* into its place. He issues the command, "Throw [it] after [the fire]," saying, "To your own bodies, svāhā! The Āgnīdhra then throws a blade of grass taken from the *prastara* after [the fire].

Having removed that which was taken, it is set aside in a known place. The ritual duty of the sacrificer is: "To your own bodies; this for the vault of heaven. Taking aim at the *prastara*, he throws it and subsequently offers it into the fire.

"This is that," he points out three times with his finger. Having cast away that blade of grass, the Adhvaryu points it out—that is, speaks—aiming toward the Āgnīdhra; it is logical that the mantra is recited only once.
He touches the seats of the vital breaths according to their respective forms, saying: "O Agni, you are the protector of life; protect my life."

The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are the senses; their abodes (*āyatana*) are their locations. With the mantra "Protector of life" (*āyuṣpā*), he touches the nostrils once. With the mantra "Protector of sight" (*cakṣuṣpā*), he touches the two eyes once. This very point has been stated as "according to form" (*yathārūpa*) and "according to gender" (*yathāliṅga*).
With the mantra "Be firm" (*dhruvāsi*), he touches this [earth], that is, the earth. According to Āpastamba, he touches the interior of the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*).
"Converse," thus the Āgnīdhra gives the command;
he commands the Adhvaryu, "Engage in conversation with me. "Has he come, O Āgnīdh? the Adhvaryu says.
He replies to the Āgnīdhra: "The *prastara* has gone; it has reached the fire. When the Adhvaryu has asked thus, the Āgnīdhra says: "It has gone. This means that the *prastara* has reached the fire.
"Śrāvaya" [says] the Adhvaryu; "Śrauṣaṭ" [responds] the Āgnīdhra. This is the sixth [section]. 1 ka, gva. ga. ca. cha. ṭa. 3.

"māna itya" | 2 ka, kha, ga, ca. cha. sa. u. ne'mī' | 3 ke. kha, ga. cha, na.ṭa,, tadi | 4ca0 paṭalaḥ] [This concludes] the fourth section, together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 219.

Having taken hold of the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*), he issues the command: "May there be success for the divine Hotṛs; may there be well-being for the human ones; pronounce the *śaṃyu* formula.
This refers to the Hotṛ.
The Hotṛ then begins the *śaṃyuvāka*.
He begins with the formula for the sacrificer: "O Viṣṇu, [grant] auspiciousness. This is clear.
The Adhvaryu throws the enclosing sticks (paridhis) into the fire.
Regarding that, he says:
The verse beginning with "yaṃ paridhim" is the middle one; "cetayātāḥ" is the end of the mantra and does not include the word *svāhā*;
and "yajñasya pātha upasamitam" are the other two.
The two [fires] are the southern and the northern. Since the dual number is seen in the mantra, he fans them both simultaneously. He states the distinction between the two:
he pushes the tip of the northern [fire] downward onto the embers.

Thinking that the word *agram* (the tip) is masculine and that *avāñcam* is a qualifier [of it], this was said. He pushes the tip of the northern enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) down into the embers beneath the middle one; by implication, he moves it around the southern one. Thus it has been stated by Vaikhānasa: "Simultaneously striking the southern and northern enclosing-sticks with both hands, he pushes the tip of the northern one down into the embers beneath the middle one, and the tip of the southern one above. The formula *vi te muñcāmi* belongs to the sacrificer. He addresses all [the priests] with the words *yajamānaṃ prathaya*.

The word "paridhīn" (the enclosing sticks) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Here too, since a visible purpose is possible, it is not logical to assume an invisible one (*adṛṣṭa*). As for the *śaṃyuvāka*, its nature as a sacrifice is to be known from such indicative marks (*liṅga*) as "the counting of twenty-one oblations," "Viṣṇoḥ śaṃyor ahaṃ devayajyayā," "tathā śaṃyumeva bārhaspatyaṃ bhāgadheyena samardhayati," "tathā jūrṣa bharāmi," and "yajñasya pāthaḥ. The *sūtra* should also be applied here in the same manner as the *sūktavāka*.

Some say that the *śaṃyuvāka* has Viṣṇu as its form and Śaṃyu as its deity; that is not correct. Because there is no application (viniyoga) of it in the throwing of the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), as there is in the case of the rule "he throws the grass-bundle with the *sūktavāka*," there is no sacrificial character (*yāgatā*) in the throwing of the enclosing-sticks. Since it serves merely as a commendation (*liṅgāstāvakatva*) based on indicative marks, it does not have the power to imply a direct Vedic injunction (*śruti*). Therefore, even if the *śaṃyuvāka* is displaced, the throwing of the enclosing-sticks must be performed right here at its proper place.
Having placed the tip of the *upabhṛt* ladle into the hollow of the *juhū*, he causes the two ladles to drip, saying: "O portions of the drippings! (*saṃsrāvabhāgāḥ stha*).
The meaning is that one should drop the remaining ointments into the fire. Thus says Vaikhānasa: "The remainder of the clarified butter (ājya) from the *caru* [is to be poured] into the fire...

[Note: The manuscript variants for this portion are indicated as follows: 1. ka, kha, ga, ca, cha, ṭa, ṭha read *rādhyasyā*; 2. gha, ja read *lamupa*; 3. gha, i, ja, jha, ña, da read *bhāgā iti*. This concludes the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Second Praśna, Section 5.1].

"He causes [them] to flow," thus [it is said]. "Mādayadhvam" (rejoice) is the end of the mantra. Here, a connection between the substance and the deity is perceived; and since that [connection] is not possible otherwise than through giving, it follows that either the root *yam* (to give) or *hu* (to sacrifice) must be employed in the sense of giving. This being the position reached, however, since the act of pouring is understood by means of the word *saṃsrāva* (residue/flowing), the root *hu* is to be inferred. And so it is stated in the Brāhmaṇa: "He says, 'You are sharers of the residue.'"

Furthermore, the inference of the act of *juhuyāt* (he offers) follows from the injunction of the connection between the substance and the deity in such passages as, "The Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas are the sharers in the *satra*. For this very reason, Āpastamba says, "He offers with the *sanāveṇa* [formula]," and Baudhāyana, having stated the same, recites the mantra ending with *svāhā*. Therefore, even though it takes the form of a disposal of remnants (*śeṣapratipatti*), since the offering (*homa*) consists of giving directed toward a deity, the substance remains a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*); thus, because it is a *darvihoma*, it must be offered with the utterance of *svāhā*.
"The sacrifice is completed" refers to the portion for the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). When the *śaṃyuvāka* has been recited, they consume the remnants of the oblation.

They consume the remnants of the sacrificial oblations (*havis*) consisting of *puroḍāśa* cakes and other offerings that remain after what has been employed [in the ritual]. Since these serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), do they not all partake? Indeed, the principle that "some things, being for the sake of another, should not be performed" (like the scattering of husks) does not apply here. For the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) also has the right to consume the remnants, as it serves as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, it is stated that this is not restricted to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) alone, as is the case in other Sūtras. Having washed off the traces of clarified butter (*ājyalepa*). 10.

The *dhruvā* group [of ladles] does not receive the remnants of the clarified butter (*ājya-lepa*) that have fallen away; for the *lepa* is a small residue remaining in the vessel of what was taken for a specific purpose, and since such a residue is not possible in the *dhruvā*, there is no washing of it.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the second book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin composed by Mahādeva. 4.
2.5 Now, the fifth chapter in the second book.

The Adhvaryu takes up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles; the Hotṛ takes up the *veda*; and the Āgnīdhra takes up the *sruva* and the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*). They proceed westward, intending to perform the offerings for the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*).

By means of a portion of the name or through the association of the gender with the word *patnī*, it is the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings alone that are understood here, not merely the wives of the gods. The name "the four *patnīsaṃyājas*" is clearly expressive of four [offerings]. The mention of "the Adhvaryu" and so forth is for the purpose of precluding others. "Vedo 'si" is the formula for measuring the path. "They go westward, having turned to the right," means they turn clockwise in order to join with the wives. Thus he states the formal proposition: "The Adhvaryu passes to the south of the Gārhapatya fire, while the other two pass to the north."

Having gone in front of the *gārhapatya* fire and turned clockwise, the *adhvaryu* passes by the *gārhapatya* on its southern side; the meaning is that he steps out behind it. The other two, the *hotṛ* and the *agnīdh*, pass by it on the northern side. [End of] Paṭala 6, Section 550. Accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva: "I place you in the seat of Agni, whose house is unassailable," with these words, he places the two *sruk* ladles upon the *kaṭambhī* (the wooden post).

The *kaṣṭambhī* of the cart is that part where the two yoke-pins (*yuga-neṣa*) are bound; that region is the middle of the yoke. It is called *kaṣṭambhī* because the cart is supported by it; by means of that region, the cart is propped up from the two ends of the yoke. Vaikhānasa says: "If one offers with the *pātrī*, having released [the cart] with this very *sphya*. "Dhattam" is the end of the mantra.
"Dhuri dhuryau pātam" (Support the two draft-animals at the yoke)—some prescribe this as the *prohaṇa* (lifting), and they recite it first.

The meaning is that he pushes forward the two yoke-pins (*dhura*)—which are being placed upon the shoulders of the oxen—as they enter the yoke, with their tips pointing eastward; that is, he causes them to flow forward. Regarding this pushing forward (*prohaṇa*), some teachers recite it before the fixing of the post (*kaṣṭambhi*), while others recite it after; thus there is an option regarding the sequence. Āpastamba has expressed approval for performing it in the afternoon, stating: "If one should throw [the pins] in the afternoon, [he does so] with these two *yajus* formulas: 'O Sphya, be pure! etc.

With the two verses beginning "agnervāṃ" and "dhuri dhuryau pātam," there is only the placing [of the two oxen], not the driving forward (*prohaṇa*); the meaning is that there is no difference [in the ritual action]. Since the wooden sword (*sphya*) for the cart is a scripturally prescribed substitute (*pratinidhi*), the mantra "dhuri dhuryau pātam" is omitted due to the contradiction in gender; it is established by logical principle (*nyāya*) that there is neither modification (*ūha*) nor substitution of words in the case of a substitute. Thus he says: "Or he offers on the wooden sword, having unyoked them on the wooden sword. This meaning—that [the action] is performed with the two mantras—is understood. That very point was stated and demonstrated by Āpastamba.

Having sat down at the *gārhapatya* fire with the two spoons released, they perform the *saṃyājana* of the wives by means of the noise alone from the two spoons. The connection is "with the two released spoons. If it is asked: "Since the two [original] spoons are already the subject under discussion, and since it has been stated that 'first he takes up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* before [the others],' for what purpose is it said 'with the two released'? It is replied: In another *sūtra*, after stating, "They go westward together with the two [original] spoons, intending to perform the *saṃyājana* of the wives," and having described the consecration of those very two spoons with the formula "O Agni's arms" (*agnervām*), it is further stated, "they go with the two spoons. Thus, the mention here is to distinguish them from those two.

"One should set down the two *sruva* spoons; [it is] said that 'one causes the wives to sacrifice with the two *sruc* spoons or the two *sruva* spoons. In that regard, it has been explained that 'the two *sruc* spoons' refers to those not previously used, and likewise that 'the two *sruva* spoons' refers to those not previously used. It has also been explained therein that the bringing [of them] is solely for the purpose of setting them down at the outset. Thus it is also stated by Vaikhānasa: "Sitting behind the *gārhapatya* fire, they cause the wives to sacrifice with the two *sruc* spoons, either in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) or aloud (*uccaiḥ*)."

In that case as well, since it was not desired by him that the two [fires] themselves be "unprecedented" (*apūrva*), he said "by the two liberated ones" (*vimuktābhyām*). And by specifying "by the two paths" (*sugbhyām*), he intended—just as Āpastamba stated—that there should be no doubt again, lest it be thought they were "not-yoked" (*anāmyām*). The word "having sat down" (*upaviśya*) is for the purpose of excluding the *tiṣṭhad-dhoma* (offering while standing); furthermore, the *āśrāvaṇa* (calling for the response) of the Adhvaryu and the Āgnīdhra should not take place while they are standing on the *utkara*, as would be the case according to the opinion of Vaikhānasa, [but rather] on the south...

1. ka. ga. ca. cha. ṭa. ṭha. read *pratyāmrāyatvena*. 2. ka. ga. ca. cha. ṭa. ṭha. read *bhya*; gārhapatye pa. 6 222: In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāṭha—[in the second praśna]—it has been stated that the Adhvaryu sits at the *utkara*, the Āgnīdhra in the middle, and the Hotṛ at the Gārhapatya fire. To express that all three sit behind the Gārhapatya for the purpose of officiating at the sacrifice, the plural form "they cause the sacrifice to be performed" (*yājayanti*) is employed.

Regarding the term *patnīḥ*, in accordance with the name of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, the word *patnī* (spouse) includes all deities because of their association with the spouses of the gods. For this very reason, he will later say "the spouses of the gods" (*devānāṃ patnīḥ*) in order to refer to them alone. As for the three *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, they are understood by the Adhvaryu through the resonant sound (*dhvāna*) of the Hotṛ’s call, such as "Recite for so-and-so," and the Adhvaryu’s response "Śrauṣaṭ. Among these, the Hotṛ’s recitation is in the loud (*uccaiḥ*) tone, since it is prescribed by the Ṛgveda.

Because the other two [the *ājyabhāgas*] are prescribed by the *Yajurveda*, they would otherwise be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). However, since there is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) stating that for those two, "except for the *āśruta* and *pratyāśruta*," the loud voice (*uccais*) is again obtained; this [rule] serves to prevent that. Although it is impossible for the loud voice to apply to the *bahis* and other formulas ending in *vaṣaṭ*—since their capacity implies they are intended to inform another person—nevertheless, thinking that even by means of these [formulas] another might be informed, the loud voice is indeed employed there as well.

For *dhvāna* is defined as the non-perception of the harsh consonants (*khara-vyañjana*) separately; by the word "only" (*eva*), it is stated that this applies even to those [recitations] intended for communicating with others. Alternatively, by the plural number itself, that has been expressed; the word "only" is used so that there may be no option between the low-voiced (*upāṃśu*) and the loud (*uccaiḥ*) tones mentioned in other sūtras. Regarding this, Vaikhānasa says "low-voiced or loud," while Āpastamba says "by *dhvāna* or low-voiced. In this regard, the substance is indeed clarified butter (*ājya*), for Baudhāyana has stated: "In the absence of a specific instruction, clarified butter [is the substance]."

Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "Thou art the milk of the earth; I pour thee out for the sacrifice to the gods," and because of the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) for the sake of all [the deities], even though it is also heard in scripture that "the clarified butter (*ājya*) which is taken in the *dhruvā* ladle is indeed for the sake of this entire sacrifice," nevertheless, with the intention of prohibiting [the practice] that "what is taken on the altar-ground is not brought forward later," it is stated: "with the clarified butter from the vessel intended for the *gārhapatya* fire. All of those [portions] are indeed fourfold-sprinkled (*caturhotṛ*), because they are for the purpose of sacrifice.

Since it has been established by the general rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "in offerings accompanied by *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses, there is a fourfold or fivefold cutting for the Jamadagnis," these sacrificial details apply here as well. It has also been stated that the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses exist in the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. Likewise, one should keep in mind all the following: the *āśruta* and *pratyāśruta* calls, the *saṃpraiṣa* (direction) regarding the *yājyā*, and the direction "Recite for such-and-such" given when about to cut the portion or after having cut it. However, it is stated that they perform the sacrifice here silently (*tūṣṇīm*).
Having taken up the *veda*, while the wife holds on to him, he sacrifices to Soma in the northern half and to Tvaṣṭṛ in the southern half; between these two, he sacrifices to the others.

The term "he sacrifices" has been explained in the context of the *anūyāja* offerings. In the phrase "and the *veda*," the particle *ca* indicates a conjunction with the *upabhṛt* vessel; the rest is clear.
He sacrifices to the wives of the gods either in an enclosed space or in one that is not enclosed.

The term "no fixed rule" (*aniyama*) is stated in order to exclude the restriction mentioned in other *sūtras*. According to Āpastamba, it is "enclosed" (*pariśritam*), meaning covered or screened from the *Āhavanīya* fire; otherwise, it is "unenclosed" (*aparicitam*). By using the term with its qualifying suffix, "of the wives of the gods" (*devānāṃ patnīḥ*), there is an exclusion of all deities associated with the *Patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. However, this is not a name for all [deities] simply because they possess the gender (feminine) in common. Thus, [the term is] "the *Patnīsaṃyājas*. 1. Ga, Ca, Cha, Ṭa, Ṭa... is understood. 3. Kha, Ṭa... *athagupa*; Kha, Ra... *vinirvā*; Pa, Ka, Ja, Ma... [End of fragment]

Ma. Ka. 55. Paṭala. [This section is] accompanied by the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva. The name for all sacrifices is "Patnīsaṃyājas" (those offered together with the wives), because they are performed together with the wives (*patnībhiḥ*). Since there is a specific re-mention of them in that context, it is not a mere figurative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). Nor is this a partial name, because of the addition of the word "devānām" (of the gods). Because of the re-mention as "devānāṃ patnīḥ" (the wives of the gods), the single entity denoted by that term is expressed by the plural number.
One desiring sons should sacrifice to Rākā in an unenclosed place; one desiring cattle, to Sinīvālī; and one desiring nourishment, to Kuhū.

The term *apariśrita* applies everywhere. It has been stated that this is said by the sacrificer when he has made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) "I shall sacrifice desiring this. In the archetype, the Adhvaryu performs the optional rites.
Some authorities record that before the offerings to the wives of the gods, Rākā and Sinīvālī are mentioned.

In this view, these two [formulas] remain constant even in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*): "Recite for Soma" (*somāyānubrūhi*), "Make the announcement" (*āśrāvaya*), "Let it be heard" (*astu śrauṣaṭ*), "Sacrifice to Soma" (*somaṃ yaja*), and at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* or when the *vaṣaṭ* has been pronounced, he offers at the stated place; and the formula for the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) is "For Soma, may I be the portion of Soma. In the same way, the sacrificial formulas for Tvaṣṭṛ and the others are to be understood. When the wives of the gods (*devānāṃ patnīḥ*) and Agni Gṛhapati follow immediately after, then the sacrificial formula is "The wives of the gods, Agni Gṛhapati."

Having sacrificed to Agni Gṛhapati, he offers the *saṃpatnīya* oblation with the *sruva* ladle into the Gārhapatya fire while the wife holds on to him from behind, with the mantra: "May husband and wife go together through their good deed; may they become the two yoke-bearers joined in the sacrifice; being in harmony, may they cast away their enemies and attain undecaying light in heaven."

Because it is enjoined by the root *hu* (to sacrifice), the mantra ends with *svāhā*. It was previously stated that "he sacrifices while she maintains contact," which refers specifically to that sacrifice; therefore, this rule is prescribed again for that purpose. The mention of "with the two thumbs" (*mugbhyām*) is intended solely for the sake of the sacrifice. Since the *juhū* ladle would be obtained through its technical name (*samākhyā*), the word "with the *sruva* spoon" is used. The mention of the *gārhapatya* fire is for the purpose of excluding the *āhavanīya*, which would otherwise be obtained by the technical name. Consequently, the status of being a "standing oblation" (*tiṣṭhaddhoma*)—which is inherent to the rule "he sacrifices in the *āhavanīya*"—is also excluded. This is the oblation named *saṃpatnīya*.

Because it has a different name, because it exceeds four [in number], and because it is not an *iṣṭi*, it is distinct from the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings; nor is it a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of them, as there is no evidence for that and because the *gārhapatya* fire is prescribed separately. Since the rule "by one for the sake of another" applies, and the *anvārambha* (taking hold) of the wife is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *adhvaryu*, the *anvārambha* is performed by a single woman even in the case of one who has many wives. If she is unfit for taking hold due to being barren or similar reasons, the *anvārambha* certainly takes place by means of another—either by the sacrificer or by the *agnīdh*—since it is a general rule that only the refinements pertaining to the wife are to be omitted. For this very reason, there is no omission of the *saṃpatnīya* offering. Its deity is Jyotis (Light).

He anoints the two finger-joints of the Hotṛ; having anointed the rear one, he then anoints the front one, or otherwise. Having anointed the second, he then anoints the first; or otherwise. (The name "patnī" is also withdrawn. ... and from the interval. Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra—[Second Praśna, Second Chapter].
Having anointed the second, he then anoints the first; or otherwise.
Having smelled that,
the Hotṛ priest touches water.
The ritual touching [of water] is performed according to the Śruti.

He cuts four drops of clarified butter into the right hand of the Hotṛ for the iḍā-portion; the cutting of the viḍā-portion is done into the left. It is specified as "in the right" so that there may not be a simultaneous grasping from behind with the right hand.
There are six portions for the Āgnīdhra. He cuts off the drops of the iḍā from the right hand;
the Hotṛ pronounces the invitation.
Having marked both *iḍā*-portions, they place their hands together with the *seḍā* formula. [This is done] so that the Adhvaryu should not be the one authorized to say "Hotar!
while the *iḍā* is being invoked. The Adhvaryu, the Āgnīdhra, and the wife touch [the *iḍā*] from behind;
this is clear.
When it is said, "This sacrificer is invited," he murmurs, "May I be invited and possessed of cattle.

By virtue of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), this refers specifically to the wife. This reading follows the *Yājuṣa-hautra* tradition; however, according to Bābū [the other tradition], when it is simply said, "This sacrificer is invited," the sacrificer himself always murmurs as before. When it is said, "The divine Adhvaryus," the Adhvaryu murmurs as before, "I am invited and possessed of cattle. In both versions of the *hautra*, he indeed murmurs; by this enumeration, the sacrificer's participation in the *anvārambha* (taking hold) is excluded.

Because there is no touching (*anvārambha*) by the sacrificer, his recitation (*japa*) also does not take place; furthermore, the phrase "the *iḍā* being brought" (*iḍām āhriyamāṇām*) is also absent because there is no actual bringing of it. The sacrificer’s portion, "O *iḍā*, favor us" (*iḍā asmān avatu*), serves as an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of others. The Hotṛ eats the *iḍā* once it has been invoked. Regarding the statement by the Vaikhānasa that "they eat while standing," the word "Hotṛ" was used so that this might not apply to him. [He eats] silently (*tūṣṇīm*).

"Invoked is Heaven, the Father; may Heaven, the Father, invoke me from the Āgnīdhra fire for long life, for luster, for living, and for merit"—thus says the Āgnīdhra as he eats. Or: "Invoked is Earth, the Mother; may Earth, the Mother, invoke me from the Āgnīdhra fire for long life, for luster, for living, and for merit. These two [formulas] for the Āgnīdhra are optional.
Having consumed [the portion] silently, he performs the *mārjana* (sprinkling) rite;
this is understood to apply to the Āgnīdhra because of the continued application [of the term]. The procedure for the Hotṛ alone is to be known [as follows]:
it ends with the *iḍā* or with the *śaṃyu*.

The *patnīsaṃyājas*, performed near the *gārhapatya* fire, including the *sapatnīya-homa* and the consumption of the *iḍā*—this very sequence is being referred to here. Having restated that it ends with the *iḍā*, the option "or ending with the *śaṃyu*" is presented. The ritual concludes precisely at the *iḍā*; "ending with the *iḍā*" means ending with the consumption of the *iḍā*. Regarding the specific detail for when it ends with the *śaṃyu*, he says: "At the end of the *śaṃyu*, having taken a blade of grass from the *vedī*, one should smear its tip in the *juhū* ladle, its middle in the *sruva* ladle, and its base in the *ājyasthālī*. The meaning is that one should smear [the grass] in this manner.
The rule for that [grass] is the same as the rule for the *prastara* (the grass-bundle).

That is to say, the rule for that blade of grass is the same as the rule for the *prastara*-grass; this is the meaning. According to the view of some, when that ritual procedure ending with the *śaṃyu-formula* is to be performed, the throwing of the *prastara* is accomplished by means of the *sūktavāka*; therefore, there is no displacement (*utkarṣa*) of it, but rather only a repetition (*āvṛtti*), because of the difference in time between the two primary acts: the throwing of the *prastara* and the throwing of the *vedatṛṇa*.

Nor can the throwing of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) be drawn [into the context], because as an independent act, it is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the throwing of the grass, whereas the *sūktavāka* is indeed an auxiliary; therefore, its repetition alone is logical. Nor should it be argued that there must be a repetition of the *śaṃyuvāka* because of the injunction "the Hotṛ priest begins with the *śaṃyuvāka* over which [he places] the enclosing-stick" (*yaṃ paridhim*), since the *śaṃyuvāka* is also an auxiliary to the throwing of the enclosing-stick.

Based on the force of the Vedic revelation stating, "The *sūktavāka* is the *yājyā*; the *prastara* is the oblation," Jaimini established that the *sūktavāka* alone possesses the status of a means (*sādhana*). However, there is no direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) regarding a relationship of means and end between the *śaṃyuvāka* and the throwing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhipraharaṇa*). Furthermore, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "He satisfies Śaṃyu Bārhaspatya with his share" do not establish this, because they serve a different purpose.

Furthermore, although the Śruti text "the *śaṃyuvāka*" mentions its status as an oblation (*āhuti*) among the twenty-one oblations, that is not intended as an authority for its being an actual oblation; rather, it is an authority for the principle that in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices there is only one *śaṃyuvāka*, [to be performed] by way of a single ritual application (*tantra*) for all subsidiaries. Just as the *iḍā-oblation*, though enumerated as an oblation, is not actually an oblation, so too the *śaṃyuvāka* does not have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), but is merely an indirectly contributing factor (*ārādupakāraka*). Therefore, its displacement (*utkarṣa*) alone is logical.

The throwing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the pouring out of the remnants (*saṃsrāva*) should be understood as occurring only in their respective places there, preceded by the *sūktavāka*, *yuvākā*, and *praisha*; this distinction is to be known. This [practice] is not established in our Sūtra; rather, the meaning of the Sūtra is that the one who has been prompted for the sake of the *śaṃyuvāka* throws [the grass] into the *gārhapatya* fire during the *śaṃyuvāka*, like the grass already mentioned and the grass of the *prastara*.

It has been well said by Kātyāyana: "At the end of the *śaṃyu* formula, having taken a blade of grass from the Veda, he anoints it like the *prastara*; having said 'O Āgnīdh, throw it into the fire,' he throws the grass and so forth as before; at the end of the *śaṃyu*, he holds up the *sruva* ladle. In this same way, for us too, [the procedure regarding] the *prastara* [is established]. By means of the prescribed mantras, the application of collyrium (*añjana*) is performed in this manner for the *suṇa* as well; likewise, Kātyāyana has shown that the grass belonging to the sacrificial stone (*prastara*) is to be disposed of in the same way by means of casting it away. Similarly, Āśvalāyana also stated here that there is an option regarding the *śaṃyu* formula. He states the subject at hand:
having placed the wood-chips from the faggot (*idhma-pravraścana*) into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, he performs the two oblations of the flour-smear (*piṣṭalepa*) and the husks (*phalīkaraṇa*).

Having turned counter-clockwise to prevent the *stru* ladle from falling into the *yava* grains, he sits behind the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire. At the time of arranging the fuel (*idhma*), he throws into the *dakṣiṇāgni* those roots and tips that remained and were set aside as markers; then he performs the two oblations known as *piṣṭalepa* (the flour-smear) and *phalīkaraṇa* (the husks). These are technical designations for these two.
Having poured the husks into the clarified butter taken four times, he offers them with the mantra: "O Agni, of unimpaired life... (RV 3.29.10).

When the particle *iti* follows a non-Vedic word, there is optionally a preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for the vowel *o*, as in the case of *anedadhyāyo iti*. [The mantra] ends with *svāhā*. The Brāhmaṇa also states this very same thing. Its supplementary portion, however, is: "The fuel-sticks for the broom (*idhmasaṃvṛścana*) are redundant; the husks (*phalīkaraṇa*) are redundant; the remnant of the clarified butter (*ājyoccheṣaṇa*) is redundant. This explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) serves to praise the oblation by means of the redundancy of these three. Its technical name (*saṃjñā*), however, is *phalīkaraṇahoma*. Baudhāyana and others have also stated this very same thing.

The *Vaikhānasa*, however, does not prescribe this by name; rather, it merely says, "having sown the *phalīkaraṇas*, he offers. Nevertheless, since the *phalīkaraṇas* are the very substratum (*ādhāra*) for this fourfold-drawn portion (*caturgṛhīta*)—and not the substance of the oblation itself—the consecration (*saṃskāra*) occurs through the careful placement therein, because the *phalīkaraṇa*-oblation is indeed the remnant (*śeṣa*), as expressed in the rule: "he places the remnant upon the remnant."

The placing of the wood-shavings (*idhmasaṃvṛścana*) has been praised as occurring prior [to the offering]. Likewise, in a sacrifice where there are no medicinal herbs (*anauṣadha-yāga*), there is no offering of husks (*phalīkaraṇa-homa*) because they are absent. Nor can it be said that the offering is performed by taking other [materials] instead; for since they are praised as being "excessive" (*atiriktatvena*), their disposal (*pratipatti*) applies only to those that actually exist. Even in their absence, the placing of the wood-shavings must certainly be performed, because that act is not a subordinate part (*anaṅga*) of the offering itself. This is because the suffix *-lyap* denotes merely the state of occurring prior [to another action].

In the Vaiśvānarī rite, which involves the threshing of grain, the *phalīkaraṇa* oblation must be performed even in the absence of those [threshed grains]. Even when there is no vegetable substance (*oṣadhi*)—as in the case of a sacrifice involving *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) and the like—the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *saṃvraścana* (cuttings) still takes place. Nor is there an oblation with clarified butter (*ājya*) alone, because that is not prescribed even in the Brāhmaṇa. Regarding the *phalīkaraṇa* oblation itself, it is stated that "the remaining clarified butter is an excess" (*atiriktaṃ ājyocchiṣaṇam*); this praise is based merely on its status as a consecratory act (*saṃskāraka*). Furthermore, in reality, there is no "remnant" (*ucchiṣaṇa*) residing in the pan (*sthālī*), since designations such as *māriṣṭha* and others are already present.

Furthermore, having taken four portions of clarified butter, he offers the flour-smear (piṣṭalepa) with the mantra: "Whatever clung to the mortar, the pestle, and what adhered to the winnowing basket, the grinding stone, and the potsherd; the droplets and the scattered drops—I sacrifice them together. May all the gods enjoy this oblation. Whatever numerous droplets exist in the sacrifice, I offer them all, well-sacrificed and well-poured, into the fire. Thus he offers the flour-smear.

Because it is enjoined by the root *hu* (to sacrifice), the mantra ends with *svāhā*. Here, the repetition of the term "piṣṭalepa" (flour-smear) is for the purpose of showing that, according to other sūtras, the oblation is intended to be caused by the spilling of the flour-smear, but not the offering of the flour itself; whereas in our own view, the offering of that flour is also desired. This is likewise the consensus of other authors of sūtras. Baudhāyana, for instance, says: "Having taken four portions in the ladle," and having thus introduced the topic, he states, "One offers the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) on the *anyāhāryapacana* fire."

Bhāradvāja also states: "One offers the flour-smear with clarified butter alone. The intention of these two [texts] is the same: this mantra, by its very indicative power (*liṅga*), is enjoined for the mortar; and by the force of that, this offering belongs specifically to the flour-smears. However, it is not merely that; rather, by its indicative power, it is an offering caused by the spilling of the flour-smears adhering here and there. Thus, even the designation [of this rite] as found in other recensions (*śākhāntara*) is justified. But the Teacher does not accept that.

However, although the *ājya* oblation is an incidental (*naimittika*) rite, once the flour-residue (*lepa*) has appeared, the oblation must indeed be performed as a combination of both. For this very reason, it is stated: "Having poured four portions of *ājya* into the ladle, he throws in the husks (*phalīkaraṇa*). In the present case, however, only "having taken four portions" is mentioned as the primary act; whereas the phrase "throwing in the flour-residues" is also stated independently of the former. Therefore, both are equally primary substances for the oblation, and not as in the previous case. Just as:

The *phalīkaraṇahoma* is performed for the purpose of disposal (*pratipatti*); furthermore, although it is for the purpose of disposal, it also serves as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), just as the *soma* [libation] is [performed] on account of vomiting. Therefore, even in the absence of a smear of flour, the oblation is to be made with clarified butter (*ājya*) alone; that too [is performed] upon the ground of flour.

The phrase "the one characterized by that [residue] as its cause" (panimittastathāsaṃjñaka) refers to the very fact that the Teacher intends the application of the designation [only] where he says, "He offers the flour-residue and the husks," and does not say, "He offers from the husks. For if their status as things to be offered were already established by the designation itself, then the same would apply to the flour-residues; yet he does not say "he offers in the flour-residues," but rather says it again [specifically for them]. Therefore, there is no attainment [of the offering] through the designation, because that designation applies only to the flour-residues remaining after the smearing.

The repetition [of the rule] is intended so that there might not be an offering (*ahoma*) for those [portions] already taken; the sense is that when they have arrived, an offering should be made even of them. It should be understood that even in the case of the flour (*piṣṭa*), although it is not physically grasped, an offering with the mantra is indeed desired by omitting the two words "on the grinding stone" (*dṛṣadi*) and "the potsherd" (*kapāla*).

Some authorities prescribe the *piṣṭalepa* (flour-smear) first: "Thou art the Veda, thou art wealth" (*vedo 'si vittir asi*); with this, the Hotṛ gives the Veda to the wife. The end of the mantra is "may I obtain" (*saneyam*).

"Thou art the Veda; for the sake of the Veda I take thee; may the Veda be found by me"—this mantra is optional at the time of giving. Having placed it upon his lap with the words, "The ghee-filled, nest-like one."

15.7.j.a. "I am he, svāhā! [End of section]. 2. [The variants] kha, ca, cha, ṭa, ṭha read *some*. 3. [The variants] ka, kha, ga, ca, cha, ṭa, ṭha read *m*. 3... 228. From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha:
[In the second praśna—] ending with "the swift one" (*vājinam*). By this [formula], the sacrificer's portion is also [performed]. That wife [takes] that Veda-bundle; it is thrown.

The mantra is not connected with this [action], because it lacks conformity with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and because the mantra is prescribed for another purpose. Here, a mere promise is made to state an alternative; however, the mantra is for the purpose of establishing the lap (*upastha*). "Lap" means the lap. This is a rule from another recensional branch (*śākhā*); for the sake of the origin of the Veda, it states the giving of one's own branch. The Hotṛ priest pours [the water].

According to some, "he throws" (*asyati*) means he draws toward himself, gives, or casts; this is because it is seen thus in the *Āpastamba* [Śrautasūtra] regarding the lap (*upastha*). "He throws" (*asyati*) means he casts; there, he throws with the two verses, "Thou art the Veda" (*vedo 'si*) and "Held by the hand" (*dhṛtavantaḥ*). It has been stated by Āpastamba in that very way. Or, in the absence of an actual offering, there is no performance even on the lap for the wife. According to some, he throws three times.

The mantra is recited once; it is silent twice. The phrase "the Hotṛ throws [it]" also connects with the view of some teachers. *Avasyati* means he brings about a cessation. This is a different verbal root from *asyati*. Cessation (*avasāna*) means bringing to a standstill; that is performed only after having grasped it again, and not otherwise. With the words "Drive away the hater, drive away the enemy," the Veda is cast out by the wife.

If [the fire] has been taken up and placed on the lap, or if it has been set down in the *aṅka*, or if it has been kept for three nights, then having taken it up again and again with the mantra, it is cast away; as Āpastamba states, "it is cast away against each instance of its being set down. By the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the word *niras-yate*, it is indicated that the fruit produced by the action ending in the casting away accrues to oneself. From this, it is understood that the taking of the Veda and so forth is performed by each wife individually. Furthermore, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, characterized by benedictions such as "full of clarified butter" (*ghṛtavat*), is quite clear.

The act of "setting down" (*niṣinta*) is also intended as the removal of what is unfavorable; thus, because it serves a human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), there is repetition. Since the acts of taking up and setting down are purificatory rites for the wife (*patnī-saṃskāra*), the mantra addressed to the Adhvaryu priest, "Thou art the Veda" (*vedo 'si*), is also merely a prayer for a blessing (*āśīḥ*). Furthermore, according to the logical conclusion, that blessing accrues to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). The Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "These are indeed the beard-hairs of Prajāpati" also states the fruit [of the rite]; therefore, it must serve multiple functions. With the words "I loosen this" (*imaṃ viṣyāmi*), the knot of the cord (*yoktra-pāśa*) is loosened.

The use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) refers to the wife, precisely because it is merely a benediction (*āśīrmatra*). And thus, it contradicts the Brāhmaṇa: "He who performs a sacrifice not according to its deity is cut off from the deities and becomes worse off; he who performs it according to its deity is not cut off from the deities and becomes better off. The noose belongs to Varuṇa; 'I untie this noose of Varuṇa,' he says; thus he releases himself from Varuṇa’s noose."

In all instances, because the masculine gender is used, the Adhvaryu is not the agent; rather, the wife is designated as the object distinct from the agent. Therefore, the unyoking is not performed by the wife. This is also evident from the use of the *parasmaipada* ending in the word "viṣyāmi" (I shall unyoke). Having this very point in mind, Vaikhānasa stated: "He causes the wife to recite, 'I unyoke this [cord]'"; and then she says, "May I make it pleasant for myself along with my husband, for our well-being."

The instruction of the result, "My body [is purified] by the mantra," is also appropriate; likewise, the designation "adhvaryava" (pertaining to the Adhvaryu) is not [applicable here]. [End of] Paṭala 1.2.550, accompanied by the commentary Vaijayantī composed by Mahādeva. 229.

This is also contradicted by the Sūtra. In that case, although more has been introduced, there is no loss of what was previously established; indeed, the introduction of the additional element is accepted by the use of the plural number in the statement, "We shall explain the sacrifice. To dispel the doubt that the word *patnī* (wife) would not recur when the Hotṛ’s office precedes and follows [the wife's], the Ātmanepada is shown in the injunction despite the use of the Parasmaipada in the mantra.
He pours the full vessel into her joined palms while she holds the yoktra.

He pours out—that is, empties—the *pūrṇapātra*, a vessel filled with water, into the joined palms (*añjali*) of the wife which are provided with the *yoktra* cord. Here, it is understood that this is the duty of the Adhvaryu. There is no mention of the Hotṛ in the phrase "he brings the *pūrṇapātra* to the joined palms. Furthermore, in the Sūtra, the word "wife" (*patnī*) is carried over from the preceding context; thus, the distant mention of the "Hotṛ" later on will apply to him. Therefore, the Commentator considers this to be the duty of the Adhvaryu.

And since he did not say [the mantra] himself for the *hotṛ*, it follows that it belongs to the *adhvaryu* alone. This is the settled rule here: according to the *Bāḍhaca* Sūtra, when the rule for the pouring of water (*ninayana*) is prescribed for the *hotṛ*, it must be performed by him; otherwise, in the *hautra* ritual, it is done by the *adhvaryu* who knows the Yajurveda.
He mutters [the mantra] while the water is being brought with the words "O long-lived one" (*samāyuṣā*).

Regarding the phrase "when the full vessel (pūrṇapātra) is being brought," although the previously mentioned Adhvaryu would [otherwise] be understood as the one who mutters [the mantra] here, the wife (patnī) is understood through the indicative power (liṅga) of the mantra, because the power of the immediate context (saṃnidhi) is stronger. Even though the word "wife" (patnī) is carried over from the previous section, the fact that she is specifically designated by the pronoun "her" (sā) in the subsequent sūtra indicates that this [designation] is for the purpose of restriction—that it refers specifically to her.

Therefore, although the wife is the agent for both the tying of the cord (*yoktra*) and the recitation of the mantra in the preceding sūtra, since the agent of the pouring out (*ninayana*) has not been specified, the former possesses the status of the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) by virtue of being the one who provides the mantra, while the other possesses the status of the prompted agent (*prayojya-kartṛ*). Thus, the very meaning explained previously is indicated by the sūtra and further confirmed by us through another sūtra. The mantra ends with the word "mine" (*mama*).
Having poured that [water] out and wiped her face, she goes about her business as usual.

That wife, having poured the water held in her joined palms onto the ground with her right hand alone—since that very [hand] is the means when no specific direction is given—performs the wiping of the face. Because it is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the wife, it is repeated for each wife. Pouring from the joined palms is likewise [repeated], because the indicative mark of the mantra conveys a blessing (*āśis*). The wiping of the face is also clearly a consecration of oneself, and from the remainder of the sentence: "Having wiped his face, he rises, having made it the very form of the final bath (*avabhṛtha*)."

The meaning is that the Brāhmaṇa goes according to his purpose; he attains whatever purpose has been stated word by word [in the text]. The remainder of the sentence is: "He rises having assumed the very form of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath). This was stated by Baudhāyana: "The Brāhmaṇa says, 'He rises having assumed the very form of the *avabhṛtha*. In the explanation of this term *avabhṛtha*, it was stated by Vaikhānasa: "Having wiped his face and risen, he goes according to his purpose, being prosperous and possessing cattle."

"Having wiped his face, he rises with the thought: 'May I be well-nourished, possessed of cattle, possessed of offspring, and a householder,'" according to Āpastamba. These various purposes are understood solely from the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*) of different recensions (*śākhā*).
"Rich in ghee, providing a nest"—with these words, the Hotṛ priest goes from the Gārhapatya fire to the Āhavanīya fire, spreading the Veda-grass continuously. || 12 ||

The phrase ends with *vājinam*. Since the ritual action (*karman*) is observed at the front of the *veda*, this is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *veda* consisting of a portion of it sufficient for the continuity [of the grass], as indicated by the use of the accusative case; furthermore, its purpose is purely transcendental (*adṛṣṭārtha*), because no visible result is perceived and because the mantra contains a praise of the fruit. In the expression *ā gārhapatyāt*, the ablative case is used in place of the gerund (*lyap*), meaning "starting from the Gārhapatya fire. Here, the limit should be understood as extending up to the Āhavanīya fire. While spreading—that is, extending—the sacrificial grasses of the *veda*, one does so continuously, without interruption; that is the meaning. It is done in the form of a line.

Since the *hotṛ*’s duties have been prescribed in the *brāhmaṇa* for the *ādhvaryava* ritual, they have already been explained by me there according to that recension; setting that aside for now, they will be explained here according to the *hotṛ-sūtra*.
