Therefore, this [explanation] does not stand as an alternative to the *bāhvṛcya* (Ṛgvedic) *hautra*, but rather its placement is within the *yājuṣa* (Yajurvedic) *hautra* alone; however, what is stated in the *bāhvṛcya* must certainly be adopted in the performance, because it has been stated by the author himself that "the *hotṛ* performs his duties with the Ṛgveda. Having returned by the same way he came, the *adhvaryu* takes two portions of ghee for the *hotṛ*; the mention of "middle" (*madhya*) is for the purpose of excluding the *hotṛ*. Having taken two portions...
Having offered two oblations to Sarasvatī with the formulas: "To that Sarasvatī who is the bringer of glory, svāhā! To that Sarasvatī who is the bringer of a dwelling, svāhā!"

The two [fires] have Sarasvatī as their deity; thus they are true to their names, namely the *juhu* and the *āhavanīya*. For this very reason, it has already been stated that [the oblations] are for the sake of clarified butter (*ājya*). Although this and what follows apply specifically to *darvihomas*, it indicates that there is no fixed rule regarding the characteristics of *darvihomas* when they are included within the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. Regarding this very point, he says "twice," which implies that by that [statement], other characteristics are excluded (*parisaṃkhyā*). The general rule is that the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) is prepared toward the north. [He offers with the mantra: "O Indra, make the dwellings of my breath, speech, and mind auspicious; make my kinsmen well-disposed, svāhā! The word "he offers" (*juhoti*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

"We sacrifice to the bull, the swift one, the Full Moon; may it yield for us excellent heroic power and thousandfold abundance of wealth. Svāhā to the Full Moon, for the out-breath and for the bountiful giver!"—thus at the full moon. "The New Moon is fortunate and very gracious, swelling again like a milch-cow; may she yield for us excellent heroic power and thousandfold abundance of wealth. Svāhā to the New Moon, for the in-breath and for the bountiful giver!"—thus at the new moon, he performs the two *pārvaṇa* oblations with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*).

By the phrase "with the *sruva*," there is an exclusion of the *darvihoma* characteristics that had been operative through the connection between the tongue (*jihvā*) and the *āhavanīya* fire. The *pārvaṇī* [offerings] belong specifically to each of the two *parvan*s—the ritual complex known as the Full Moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and that called the New Moon (*amāvāsyā*)—just as the *vaimṛdha* belongs to the Full Moon complex. Since the two complexes are indicated by the locative case, they are performed with their constituent parts; because the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices together with their subsidiaries are prescribed for the *parvan*s themselves, this is the prescription of a specific name for each individual *parvan*.
[Ca. Ṭa. Ṭha. Dhaṇahaḥ | 550 Paṭala: Together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

For the purpose of establishing the essential nature of the constituent parts of the aggregate of rites (*kartavyasamudāya*), there is no application [of these rules] in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), because the modified sacrifice lacks the form of an aggregate; this is the sense. This has been established by those learned in the Nyāya.
Some authorities record [the following] before the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
The two *pārvaṇī* [oblations] are offered with a specific sequence:

"O Sacrifice, these ten bodies of yours are worthy of sacrifice; may the sacrificer gratify them with clarified butter. Praising the instruction of the two *nāriṣṭhas*, the sacrificer has become immortal even in the divine realm of the gods. "O you two of a hundred powers, that portion of strength which the gods have ordained for you—by this I gratify you both; by this, be satisfied here. "I am in the world of the gods who perform good deeds; let this sacrifice of mine not be in vain."

I, the wise one, follow and worship the *nāriṣṭhas*, since Indra bestowed their portion upon them when they were invincible. O divine Soma, you who do not leak through the vessel, be present at this sacrifice; O Maruts, be gracious to us! Let no overwhelming curse find us, nor let any hateful host find us. The *brahman* is the foundation of the mind, the *brahman* of speech, the *brahman* of sacrifices, oblations, and clarified butter. Whatever in the ritual is excessive and whatever is deficient—may the sacrifice go forth, smoothing out its joints and making them fit, with the offering consecrated by *svāhā* reaching the gods.

"I unite your mind with my mind; I place your breath within my breath; I unite your diffused breath with my diffused breath and your downward breath with my downward breath. Having taken hold [of you], the sacrificer has become immortal. Be auspicious to us—be auspicious to our bipeds and auspicious to our quadrupeds, svāhā! With these words, he offers the *nāriṣṭha* oblations. || 1.3 ||

Having taken them up, he performs the *nāriṣṭha* oblations. Because it is enjoined by the word "he offers" (*juhoti*), and according to the general rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "one offers with the utterance of *svāhā*," the oblation in the first five [verses] is performed ending with *svāhā*. In the sixth, however, the *svāhā* is stated by the very wording [of the mantra]; the word *svāhā* is the cause for the application of the deity there. Although among those three mantras the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the *nāriṣṭha* is present, while in the others there are various marks, nevertheless all [the mantras] associated with the preceding three are indeed *nāriṣṭha*. Some [hold that] even here the deity is qualified by the term *nāriṣṭha*.

They desire the *nāriṣṭha* offerings for my vital breaths—the *brahman*, *yajña*, *vāmanas*, *prāṇa*, and *vyāna*. Even at the end, when the *svāhā* call occurs, they are performed because of the plural number in the word *nāriṣṭhān*. Furthermore, since it will be stated later that "where a rite is enjoined by a group of mantras, one should offer oblations with each mantra," there is an oblation with each individual mantra. Thus ends the fifth chapter in the second book of the *Mayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* composed by Mahādeva. Now begins the sixth chapter in the second book of the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha.

Having taken [the portions] thirty-eight times: "Svāhā to the beloved ones! Vaṣaṭ to the unbeloved! Svāhā to the remedy for ill-sacrificed offerings! Svāhā to the expiation! Svāhā to Nirṛti! Svāhā to misfortune! Svāhā to the divine bodies! Svāhā to prosperity! Svāhā to success!
These nine mantras ending in *svāhā* belong to other Vedic branches. In that context, one must touch water after the [mantras for] *nirṛti* and *niṣkṛti*.

"O Agni, with *ayās* (the unswerving) and without reproach; you indeed are *ayās*, the Truth itself. Held by a mind that is *ayās*, you carry the oblation with *ayās*; grant us healing medicine, *svāhā*!—this for me, O Varuṇa; that for you; do you come to us, O Agni; you, O Agni, are *ayās*. With these [mantras], he offers oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*—*bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, *suvaḥ*—both individually and collectively.

This [section] ends with the utterance of *svāhā*. In the section beginning with "yatpākatre," the last two [verses] are recited ending in *svāhā*. In the tenth [section], the deities of the *iṣṭi* and others are clear; [in the first], Agni is the deity. The mantra "imaṃ me varuṇa" has Varuṇa as its deity, and likewise for "tattvā yāmi. The two mantras "tvaṃ no agne" and "sa tvaṃ no agne" have Agni-Varuṇa as their deity. "tvamagne ayāsi" has Agni as its deity. "prajāpate na tvat" has Prajāpati as its deity. These six mantras are presented by their opening words (*pratīka*).

In this [section], those [mantras] recited elsewhere in that same branch (*śākhā*) are likewise recited by way of citation (*pratīka*) for the purpose of demonstrating their reading here as well. In the same manner, the author of the Sūtra has shown only the readings from other branches. In that regard, the inclusion of the word *svāhā* at the beginning and end of the mantras is for the purpose of supplying the missing portion (*anuṣaṅga*) in the middle; just as in the case of the mantras beginning with *ṛtāṣāṛtadhāma* and ending with *sa idam*, the word *sa idam* is recited [at the end].

Having recited "bhūr" and so forth, it was stated [in the preceding verse] that one seeking the removal of doubt should do so "one by one and with all [the vyāhṛtis together]. In that context, because of the plural number in the word "vyāhṛtibhiḥ," the status of each as a separate mantra is established; yet, according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "rites consist of single mantras," even so, the individual application within the collective would not be obtained—thus both [modes] were mentioned. [The mantras for] the other deities: "Whatever in the sacrifice has been *āśrāvita*, *atyāśrāvita*, *vaṣaṭkṛta*, or *atyanūkta*; whatever is redundant in the rite and whatever is deficient—the sacrifice, mending its joints, let the offering consecrated by *svāhā* go to the gods.
"The sacrifice is the gods."

Whatever is performed erroneously in the sacrifice—whether it was not known or was known—O Agni, make that right for him, for you know the truth exactly as it is; let the offering consecrated with *svāhā* go to the gods.
This line is disconnected [from the context].
[End of] Chapter 40. [Section] 233. [Chapter] 650. [This concludes the section] accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.
The fires are the gods.
I offer what is excessive into the deficient; I offer what is deficient into the excessive. I offer what is equal into the equal. May this oblation, consecrated with Svāhā, go to the gods.
O gods!

That which was not done, that which was not left undone, that which we have overstepped, that which we have not overstepped, that which we have exceeded, that which we have not exceeded—O Viṣṇu, establish that very sacrifice within the sacrifice; let the offering consecrated by *svāhā* go to the gods.

O Viṣṇu, O gods! Whatever we, being heedless, have omitted in this sacrifice, whether in respect of the mantra or the ritual act—all that I pacify with this oblation. May the gods be satisfied by the clarified butter offering; let the offering consecrated by *svāhā* go to the gods.
"O gods, Brahman is the foundation of the mind"—this is the [verse].
"The two Brahmans, O gods"—the meaning is that it should be taken as recited elsewhere. It is stated thus because it is indeed recited elsewhere in that same Śākhā.

The waters have been stretched out for me, and they are stretched out again; the sweetest prayer is recited for the hymn. This ocean is indeed the all-healing medicine; may you both be thoroughly satiated by the *svāhā*-offering.
Bhava! We have risen up above the darkness; we have risen up toward that bright one.
Thus, by way of a representative citation, there are two [verses] concerning Sūrya in two [sections].
"O Gods, whatever transgression I may commit, or even through speech an offense against the gods; O Maruts, let that misfortune which the enemy seeks to bring upon us be cast away from us elsewhere.
[The deities are] the Gods, the Maruts.
From whatever we fear, O Indra, from that grant us freedom from fear. O Maghavan, be gracious; let that be for our protection. Slay our enemies and those who attack us.
Maghavan is Indra.
The giver of well-being, lord of the people, slayer of Vṛtra, subduer of attackers, the controller—may the bull-like Indra go before us, the giver of well-being and the creator of fearlessness.
Indra is the slayer of Vṛtra.

(Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.7.3.1) "O Lord of the bay horses, with these songs, make full whatever of ours is deficient, increasing in strength. When you burst open the great cow-pens for your praisers, may we then be those who receive the greatest share of your bounty. (Ṛgveda 8.91.6)
Indra, possessor of bay horses; "Avert your wrath," and "Up from the highest";
two [hymns] with two faces, the first of two.

The sacrifice is commensurate with the person; the sacrifice is commensurate with the person. O Agni, ordain that for him, for you indeed know it as it truly is. Let the oblation, consecrated by *svāhā*, go to the gods.
Agni is the god.

When mortals, with simple minds and feeble resolve, do not comprehend the sacrifice, may Agni—the Hotṛ who knows the ritual, the most skilled sacrificer—sacrifice to the gods according to the seasons.
The Adhvaryu offers oblations into the Āhavanīya fire with the *juhū* ladle, saying, "Agni, O gods! Svāhā! He then performs all the expiatory offerings (*sarvaprāyaścitta*).

[He performs] the oblations known as the *sarvaprāyaścitta* (all-expiation). Alternatively, he offers the *sarvaprāyaścitta* sacrificial acts, which consist of the reconnection of what has been interrupted. Here, the reference to those [oblations] obtained through the general rules (*paribhāṣā*) is for the purpose of excluding the ritual characteristics (*dharma*) of other oblations prescribed by different rules. For instance, Āpastamba has stated that "one offers all the *sarvaprāyaścitta*s with the *juhū* or the *sruva*. To exclude that, [the text says] "with the *juhū*," meaning specifically with the *juhū* ladle. The mention of the *āhavanīya* fire is for the purpose of restricting [the application] to other ritual characteristics.

The mention of the *adhvaryu* is for the purpose of excluding the *brahmán*. When Āśvalāyana prescribes, "One offers oblations during the expiations (*prāyaścitta*s)," it is understood that this refers to the *brahmán*. Because the *davihoma* (oblation with a ladle) status applies to all implements other than the *juhū* spoon, the *āhavanīya* fire, and the *adhvaryu*, they would otherwise be required for the expiations; their exclusion is therefore specified. For which [implements] is there exclusion? The placing of fuel (*samid-ādhāna*), the passing to the south in front of the *āhavanīya*, and the requirement of standing—all these are excluded.

In this regard, all the expiations (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) recited in one's own *śākhā* are optional alternatives. However, the section beginning with "Brahman is the foundation" (*brahma pratiṣṭhā*) is an uninterrupted liturgical passage (*ācchidrika-anuvāka*). This has been adopted by the Vaikhānasa school as the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). Having gone to the Āhavanīya fire, one offers the oblations for the universal expiation with either the *juhū* or the *sruva* ladle, using this liturgical passage beginning with "Brahman is the foundation" and "Whatever [was] not performed," as stated in the relevant section. Therefore, this entire liturgical passage serves the purpose of the universal expiation; otherwise, there would be no application [of it]. After having replenished the *dhruvā* ladle...

There is no depletion of what has been taken four times, five times, or six times; nevertheless, by virtue of the scriptural injunction, it is to be replenished for the sake of the *samiṣṭayajus* offering.

Standing upright within the *antarvedi* (the space between the altars), he offers three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations into the *āhavanīya* fire with the *dhruvā* ladle, using the mantra: "O gods, you who know the way... [The mantra ends with] "yā te dhāḥ svāhā. The specification "standing upright" is for the purpose of avoiding the state of being prone (*āvṛt*), as might otherwise happen. The rest is clear. He performs the sacrificial acts known by the name *samiṣṭayajus*. [Paṭala 150: Accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. The specific restrictions are made for the purpose of setting aside the ritual rules that would otherwise apply because this is treated as a *davihoma* (a sacrifice performed with a ladle). The end of the mantra is "yā te dhāḥ svāhā. The mention of "upright" is so that he does not remain in a prone position. Everything else is explicit. He offers the sacrificial rites designated as *samiṣṭayajus*.

In this context, since it has been established by the general rule (*paribhāṣita*) that "one should offer oblations for each mantra," three oblations are obtained using the three mantras; likewise, Maradvāja has also shown this through the division of a single mantra. Thus, although a triad [of oblations] was already established, the statement is made again so that one offers three oblations by repeating the entire mantra.

Why? Because the wind itself is seen to be the foundation of the sacrifice (*yajñapratiṣṭhā*), it is understood that from "vāte dhāḥ" up to the end of "svāhā" there is a single mantra; therefore, there is no repetition. Furthermore, because these [words] do not denote [separate acts], and because of the rule, "At the middle *svāhā*-utterance, he throws [the grass] outside," which applies without distinction to all three *svāhā*-utterances at the end of the mantra, and likewise because Āpastamba has prescribed the oblation with the entire mantra only once—therefore, "vāte dhāḥ svāhā" is indeed a single mantra.

The Brāhmaṇa also establishes the entire mantra as ending with "vāte dhā" (in the wind, place it): "From the wind, indeed, the Adhvaryu impels the sacrifice. 'O gods who know the way, having found the way, go on the way,' he says; for it is from this that he impels the sacrifice. Thus, he establishes it. Indeed, the word "vāta" (wind) is employed at the end of "vāte dhā. Therefore, the mantra is not divided into one part [only]. This should be understood to apply likewise to the two-part division as well.
If it is asked, "Even so, how is there the cessation of repetition? we reply: from the subsequent sūtra, namely, "continuously" (*satatam*) or "alternately" (*vimāham*).
Either one, two, or three [oblations] continuously;

that is, at the commencement of the mantra, "The gods who know the way," he offers with a continuous stream of clarified butter (*ājya-dhārā*) up to the *svāhā* utterance as a single unit. Or likewise, two or three [units] in the same manner.
Or [it may be] separately.

Lest the previous sūtra be rendered meaningless, this option is stated right there for the purpose of including what was mentioned by Maradvāja. One should offer exactly three oblations with the mantra, each accompanied by its own *svāhā* utterance. If "or [it may be] separately" were explained as meaning "with an interruption of the stream," then since the optional sense would already be established by the word "three" in this very [sūtra], the word "three" in the previous sūtra would be redundant.

If, however, this were explained as "in these three *svāhākāras*," then there would be no connection between the words "one" and "two. Therefore, the connection is indeed with the preceding sūtra; it is connected specifically with the word "three. In that which is continuous (*saṃtata*)—where the flow of *svāhākāras* is uninterrupted—the repetition and the analysis of the compound are naturally permitted in this alternative view.

If "three" were not stated here, then the rule of continuity would apply only to "one" and "two"; therefore, so that it may be connected specifically with "three," this term is mentioned again. [Objection: In that case, let the first sūtra "three" be omitted. [Response: No; otherwise, it would be connected with the triad beginning with "one," due to the force of the repetition.
He cuts the hated one downward or severs him.
The word "even so" (*tathāpi*) is redundant.

10. Second [section], ṇa, ttiri; ṇa, "maḥ"; e; ṇa, "tataṃ viprāī vā". [Variants: 5 ka. ga. ca. cha. u. u. pa. read 'pūrvasū'; 6 ṇa. reads 'te. svā'; 7 ga. reads 'ptāvativi'; 8 ga. 2. 8. reads 'naivam']. In the passage "satyāṣāḍhaviracitaṃ śrautasūtra" (The Śrauta Sūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha), in the second praśna, [the word] "nyañcam" is in the masculine gender; therefore, the substantive to be understood is "homa" (oblation). Starting the oblation from a high place and completing it at a low place [is prescribed]. If there is an interruption in the middle of the oblation, that fault belongs to the officiating priest (adhvaryu) and not to the sacrificer (yajamāna); such is the meaning.

If one should desire of someone, "May he be short-lived," one should offer while standing crookedly. This means that for whichever sacrificer one desires to be short-lived—that is, subject to death—one should not offer in this case as was done previously; "crookedly" means obliquely. At the middle *svāhā*-utterance, one throws the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) after [the oblation].

When there is one [verse], then it is at the middle; when there are two, then it is at the first repetition of the mantra and at the middle *svāhākāra*. Thus, it should be understood that in this case there are three [offerings] at the very first repetition. Regarding the term *barhis*, if intended as a genus (*jāti*), it refers to all [the grass]; if intended as an individual (*vyakti*), it refers to a single stalk of *darbha* grass. Or, "a handful of *barhis*" means merely a handful.
Or he offers it as an after-offering;
when the final *svāhā* has been offered, he offers it as an after-offering— or, having offered it, he may make a further oblation.
Having first struck [the fire], he should afterwards offer oblations over it according to the sequence.

If the sacrificer should be away on a journey, he should place the sacrificer’s portion into the *dhruvā* ladle with the formula, "The world of Prajāpati named Vibhān," and offer it together with the *samiṣṭayajus*.

The section ends with "by the sacrificer. The mantra is intended for the act of attention (*avadhāna*) because of its indicative mark (*liṅga*). For the *sam̐iṣṭayajus* offering is performed with that mantra, and two mantras cannot be used simultaneously. [The formula] "To Vāta, this! belongs to the sacrificer; as do "O Agni, of unassailable life! and "The vault of heaven! It is not connected with the *bahiḥ* offering, since there is no bringing forward [of the material]; it is merely a disposal (*pratipatti*). "Strew [the grass], enclose the altar, do not harm the kin lying there; these golden, bright Hotṛ-seats are the gold neck-ornaments of the sacrificer, O radiant one"—with these words, he strews the altar with the Hotṛ-seats.

He covers [the altar] starting from the Hotṛ’s seat. Because the Darbha grass and the Veda have been established as primary in the mantra and are thus employed, and because both are indicated by the accusative case, there is a mutual consecration of both.

Having carried the *praṇītā* waters around the front of the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "For your nourishment," he releases them within the altar with the formula, "May he who has sprinkled you release you. This refers to the *praṇītā* waters. The rest is clear. From "In the assembly, may I be in the assembly" up to the end of the sacrificer’s concluding recitation (*saṃsthājapa*) is for the sacrificer. And the Brahman priest, having consumed his own portion, sipped water, and placed a fuel-stick on the fire, goes back by the same way he came.
[The phrase] "he throws it outside" does not exist in the manuscript designated *gha*.
[In the manuscript] *ka* and *u*, there is *kāra-huti-nu*. [Folio 650] [This is] the *Mahādevakṛta-vaijayantī* commentary.

"O gods, that which you have established as the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick) among men—those who are ill-disposed toward us, bring them here for our sake. O *upaveṣa*, settle upon us: progeny, nourishment, and also wealth; make our bipeds and quadrupeds stable and never-departing. Having thus taken up the *upaveṣa*.
The taking up is with two [mantras].
With the mantra, "O Upaveṣa, let heat reach him whom we hate," he should either bury it in the utkara or cast it away;
or, having dug [the hole], he should place it there or abandon it.

Drive him away from our dwelling, O Indra, that rival who attacks us; with this oblation that drives out the foe, Indra has cast him away. Go beyond the three distant realms; go beyond the five peoples; go beyond the three luminous spheres, as far as the sun is in the sky. May Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, lead you to the furthest distance, from which you shall not return for eternal years.

"He is slain! We have struck down so-and-so!"—thus one should meditate in his mind upon the destruction of him whom he hates. Or, having touched water, he recites: "O arrow, sharpened by prayer, fly forth released!"

The ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is indeed constant, because it is not designated as being for the purpose of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). The name "this evil" (*asau pāpmā*) refers first to the one who is hated. If such a person exists, then one should meditate upon him—the object of hatred or the evil—ending with the accusative case at the conclusion of the mantra. Some declare that meditation is to be enjoined in the case of malevolent magic, because it is seen in the *Āpastamba* [Sūtra]. With the words, "Who yokes you? May he release you," one releases the sacrifice.
He states the explanation of this very point:
He gazes upon everything; he gazes upon the sacrifice in its form as the entire course of movement. This indeed is the meaning of "liberation.
"The potsherds which [were used] in the Gharma" refers to the potsherds.
"Let them be released"—this is the end of the mantra. There is the release of the potsherds at the beginning and at the end. Thus the New and Full Moon sacrifices are concluded.
When the Full Moon sacrifice has been completed, [the following takes place]. 15.
When the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice is concluded with the satiation of the Brāhmaṇas,
he commences the ritual procedure (tantra) for the Vaimṛdha offering.

The Vaimṛdha is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) as a collective whole, but it does not have the status of an auxiliary for each individual constituent. Therefore, because its properties are not extended (*atideśa*) to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) as a collective, the intention is that the Vaimṛdha does not serve the purpose of the *vikṛti*. This has been elaborated by those learned in the Nyāya. Thus, regarding the Vaimṛdha sacrifice: Indra is the deity (*devatā*) of that rite; "Vaimṛdha" is the name of the rite whose deity is Vaimṛdha. It is a name formed with a secondary suffix (*taddhita*), according to the rule *sā'sya devatā* ("that is its deity"). — [From] the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Second Book, [Section 238].

Or rather, this [designation] may apply without distinction to the deity and the oblation in those rites characterized by a qualified deity; however, the designation is made by means of the quality alone, not by the qualified [compound], because a *taddhita* suffix does not arise from a qualified [compound]. If a case-ending were applied to each member of the qualified [compound], it would result in two deities for two separate rites—as in the case of "Indra-vaimṛdha. A suffix does not arise from a *karmadhāraya* [compound] in such a way. Furthermore, in a compound, the substantive is traditionally stated first and the qualifier immediately after; therefore, if one were to follow that sequence in a compound, it would be grammatically incorrect.

According to Pāṇini’s rule that "the qualifier comes first," if the qualifier were to precede, the nominal stem *vaimṛdhendra* would denote a different deity, because the sequence is intended to be significant when denoting a deity, as the deity is connected [to the sacrifice] by means of the word. As stated by the Vārttikācāryas: "The deity is connected to the sacrifice by means of the word, not by its form. For this very reason, in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*), they offer an option between Agni-Soma and Indra-Agni based on the difference in deities.

Therefore, in cases such as "vaiśvānaram," there is no usage of the compound or the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) of the deity by means of a secondary quality (*guṇa*), nor is there usage by means of a *taddhita* suffix—as seen in expressions such as "related to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa," "to Agni Vaiśvānara," or "to Indra Vaimṛdha. In the present case, however, it is stated: "The Vaimṛdha is to be offered subsequently at the Full Moon sacrifice; therefore, the Full Moon sacrifice is accompanied by Indra. Thus, this is not an original injunction (*utpattividhi*), but rather a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already established by another scriptural authority.

By means of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the author will show the injunction for the purpose of accomplishing the state of being "sentient. Regarding the subject at hand, the author of the Sūtra employs the name of a quality as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already established. The suffix *ṇin* [is used] in the sense of "one who initiates" (*prakramayati*) a ritual action together with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*). The root *pra-* preceded by *ā-* is either intransitive or has the meaning of "manifestation" (*prādurbhāva*). Therefore, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied to express the causal agent; thus, the meaning is "he causes to manifest" (*prādurbhāvayati*). Its ritual procedure (*kalpa*) has been explained by that of the offering to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*).

The *kalpa*—meaning the procedure or performance—is explained and demonstrated. How so? To this he says: "by means of the Aindrāgna. This does not mean by direct instruction (*upadeśa*), but rather by extension (*atideśa*). The meaning is that its performance is identical to that of the Aindrāgna rite belonging to the New Moon sacrifice (*dārśika*). He will later explain the relationship between the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*), stating that "in that case, for each deity, there is a single portion"; thus, the intention is that this is a modification of the Aindrāgna, not a modification of the Āgneya. There are fifteen or seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.

Having raised the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the modification (*vikṛti*) and the option (*vikalpa*), it was stated [in the sūtra] "or rather, there is no option" (*avikalpo vā*); this statement here is intended so that what is about to be said may not apply.
At the time of the offering (*nirvapaṇa*), one offers abundant *vrīhi* rice to Indra Vaimṛdha.

Having performed the rites beginning with the placing of the firewood (*anvādhāna*), such as the spreading of grass around the altar (*vediparistaraṇa*) for the sake of the ritual—the seat of the sacrifice—and having arranged the vessels and so forth, when the time for the pouring out of the oblation (*nirvāpa*) arrives—that is, at the point established in the performance of the archetype (*prakṛti*)—he pours it out with the mantra beginning "Of the god... and ending "...I pour out what is pleasing to Indra Vaimṛdha. Furthermore, one must ensure abundance by using full handfuls (*muṣṭi*) and by adding more through supplementary pouring (*anvāvāpa*).

At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives a fee according to his ability. There is no *anvāhārya* rice-offering. [The fee] is gold measured by *guñjā* and other units. There is no *pārvaṇa-homa*. [Notes on variants: 1. *ka*, *ga*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *śiṣṭhā deṃ*. 2. *ka*, *ga*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṭa*, ... "*tā yasya ka". 3. *kā*, *ga*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṭa*, *u*, *pa*, "*tāstu ni*". 4. *ga*, *ca*, *cha*, *u*, *pa*, "*vatāṃ bhe*". 5. *ka*, *ga*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṭa*, *u*, *pa*, "*darthe yatra*". 6. [End of section] Paṭala 10; accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 229. [Translation of the final sentence: At the time for the sacrificial fee, he gives a fee according to his capacity. There is no *anvāhārya* (rice-offering). [The fee is] gold measured by weight such as *guñjā* and so forth. There is no *pārvaṇa-homa* (offering at the new or full moon).

In this regard, there is freedom of choice at the outset; it is optional, and its non-performance does not constitute a deficiency. This is because the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsa-yāga*) possesses superior merit precisely through its performance. However, once begun, there can be no abandonment. Thus, at the first commencement, if one intends—out of a desire for superior merit—that "this must be performed by me," then it must indeed be carried out as long as the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) continues. Why? Because an option is not heard of in a single recensional branch (*śākhā*); rather, in our own branch, it is strictly obligatory (*nitya*). Therefore, there is no abandonment for one who has commenced in accordance with that [obligation].

[The action] has already begun. Because of the contradiction [otherwise]. If, however, a prohibition exists in another branch of the Veda (*śākhāntara*) and one does not act in accordance with it, then the subsequent undertaking (*uttarārambha*) would not be "begun" (*anārabdha*). This is because it would entail the abandonment of the accepted authority of the scripture (*śāstraprāmāṇya*). Therefore, the sense is that once a single scripture has been accepted as authoritative from the very beginning, one must not bring about its lack of authority.
However, the rule is restricted by the initial commencement (*prakrama*).

The restriction is stated according to the aforementioned intention. Having thus explained the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices together with their constituent parts, the author makes a formal declaration (*pratijñā*) in order to explain the specific forms (*saṃsthā*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, which are distinct applications based on differences in secondary qualities (*guṇabheda*):
"We shall explain the optional rites (*kalpa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
This declaration is intended to dispel the doubt that these might be separate ritual acts (*karmāntara*).

"One desiring prosperity should sacrifice with these Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa [rites]. This means one who desires the attainment of prosperity characterized by these Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa rites as modified by the qualities (guṇa) about to be mentioned. The point is that, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words "Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa," this is not a distinct ritual modification (*vikṛti*), but rather a modification of the qualities; for there is no difference in the ritual action (*karman*) due to the absence of other factors such as a different name (*śabdāntara*). He states the performance: "One should sacrifice on two full-moon days; [one should sacrifice] on two new-moon days."

The injunction "one should sacrifice" applies to both occasions. Since [the sacrifice] is already established, the repetition is enjoined as a restatement (*anuvāda*). In the case of the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña*, it is clearly stated: "Sacrificing on the previous day, he thereby prepares the altar; in that he drives away the calves, he constructs the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds; and when he sacrifices... Just so here, two [performances] are repeated. One sacrifice, having commenced on the fifteenth day, is to be completed according to the original model (*prakṛti*) on the first day of the next month (*pratipad*). Then, having been commenced again on the *pratipad*, it is to be completed on the second day; thus, the incidental element (*āgantuka*) is placed at the end.

[The word] *śāt* [is used]. Thereafter, the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) must be performed as obligatory rites (*nitya*), because the optional quality characterized by repetition has been accomplished. In that regard, the procedure is as follows: "Desiring prosperity, I shall sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices performed through repetition. [This would be restricted. [End of section from] Satyāṣāḍha’s *Śrautasūtra*.

[In the second chapter—The first step is the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). Having performed the rites on the same day as the Full Moon sacrifice, at the conclusion of feeding the Brahmins, one performs the re-kindling of the fires (*anvādhāna*) and so forth; then, on the first or second lunar day, the sacrifice is completed. If the *Vaimṛdha* offering exists, one should perform that as well. This is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) belonging to the repeated performance, because it lacks the designation of the term "Full Moon sacrifice" (*paurṇamāsa*) when performed only once. For one who does not offer the *Sāṃnāyya*, it is the same on the New Moon day; and for one who does offer the *Sāṃnāyya*, it is likewise. The entire ritual, including the *Pārvaṇa-homas*, remains unchanged, beginning with the verse "imām ūrjaṃ pañcadaśīm. Here, he shows another method of performance:
"One who desires, 'May I overcome [my enemies],' should sacrifice only at the full moon (paurṇamāsī)," according to some;

the statement in another *śākhā* means that he who desires "whichever" [should sacrifice] should sacrifice only at the full moon. This was stated by Āpastamba: "Having said, 'One who desires, "May I overcome,"' some say one should sacrifice only at the full moon. The meaning is that he should repeat the full moon sacrifice as it has been commenced, but he should perform the new moon (amāvāsyā) sacrifice in its regular, obligatory form. One who has rivals should not sacrifice at the new moon for less than two or three years; at every transition [of the sacrifice], he hurls a thunderbolt at his rival.

This statement, which is recited along with its explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), is an imitation of a Brāhmaṇa passage. It is intended to dispel the doubt as to how the result can be understood here in the absence of words such as "desire" (*kāma*). Even in the absence of the word "desire," a result is accepted for a primary rite that has not yet been established by other means, through the explanatory praise; for it is understood from the statement, "This sacrifice should be performed by that sacrificer who has enemies facing him," that the removal of those enemies constitutes the result.

In response to the question "How so?", the meaning is that whenever there is a *saṃkrāma* (transit) toward an enemy (*bhrātṛvya*) and whenever the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is transgressed, that very form of the thunderbolt (*vajra*) becomes struck. Therefore, one should not perform [the sacrifice] on the new moon day. Here too, the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) involves repetition. The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is: "Desiring to slay my enemy, I shall sacrifice with the full moon sacrifice accompanied by transit and repetition. The term *vyavarāya* is an adverbial modifier of the action, meaning "in which two or more [transits] are inferior" (*dve avare yasmin*).

The word *avara* means "inferior" or "less. The word *artha* means "place. The meaning is: in whichever place two [verses] with a transition (*saṃkrāma*) have been practiced as inferior, there the work should be exceeded rather than diminished. Likewise, it should be understood that it must be exceeded, but not be less than three.
These *agnīṣomīya* principal offerings are for one who has rivals, one who practices sorcery, or one who desires to cross over [difficulties].

The meaning is that on both fortnights (parvan), whatever principal offerings there are—consisting of the *puroḍāśa*, clarified butter (*ājya*), and the *sāṃnāyya*—and however many of them there are for whichever [deity] at whichever fortnight, all of those belong exclusively to the deities Agni and Soma. This was stated by Āpastamba regarding both the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*).

Having set aside the quality pertaining to Agni as the deity, one should understand that the formulas beginning with "I sprinkle what is pleasing to Agni and Soma" and ending with "the eater of food, the pervader," refer specifically to the *prāśitra* and the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*). On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), the formula beginning with "Through the sacrifice to the gods, Agni and Soma, may I become possessed of power and an eater of food" is to be understood. The placing of the potsherds (*kapālopadhāna*) is exactly as in the archetype (*prakṛti*). The phrase "for the destruction of the enemy" is as before. Following "of him who hates us," [the mantra] "may he strike two new moons together."

[Chapter 6, Section 6] Accompanied by the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva. The desire [is expressed as follows]: regarding the form *titīriṣataḥ*, the vowel *i* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) shortening. The meaning is: "of one who desires to cross over," that is, one who wishes to overcome calamities such as disease and the like. By the very force of the word *abhicāra* (malevolent magic), the desire for the death of another is established. In the case of *titīriṣataḥ*, the desire itself is expressed by the desiderative suffix (*san*) denoting the sense of wishing. "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *Sākaṃprasthāyīya*."

By means of the ritual of the *darśa-sāṃstheta* (the completion of the new-moon sacrifice), which possesses the qualities and characteristics of the *sāka-prasthāyīya*, [the following is established]. Here, lest it be suspected—due to the lack of prior establishment of this quality—that this is a name for the ritual itself (and thus a distinct ritual, as in the cases of "This is the Jyotis" and "This is the Viśvajyotis"), the followers of Jaimini demonstrate the well-known nature of the quality to refute that suspicion of a difference in rituals based on a difference in names. The sacrifice is enjoined here together with the *kuṃbhīs* (pots) by means of the *prasthāna* (setting forth). Therefore, one might argue that because of the different name, it is a separate ritual.
He states the performance: there are many evening milkings and many morning milkings; with those, he subsequently performs the sacrifice.

It is precisely because [the Dākṣāyaṇayajña] is a modification (*vikāra*) of the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*). In that regard, by virtue of the commonality of the constant observation of the *sānnāyya* offering, it is not a modification of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*). If it were a modification of the Full Moon sacrifice, then—according to the maxim "one does not beg from a mendicant"—it would not be a modification of the modified *mānavī* quality; with this intention, it was stated. Āpastamba makes this clear: "The New Moon sacrifice is modified."

Although plurality culminates in three, if it is so intended, then one should simply state, "there are three milkings. Therefore, milkings from four onwards are also permitted, as long as the oblation can be performed. For the sake of each individual milking, having driven away six cows with their calves, one prepares a single *śākhāpavitra* with a single branch; having suspended it and divided it, one places the pots upon them. Thus, those parts that are capable of being performed once are done once; those that cannot be so performed are repeated.

He performs the milking of each cow up to the stage of washing and pouring out the milk. Thereafter, having completed the evening milking by performing the ritual acts up to the driving away of the goats in the same order as before, he should sacrifice in the evening immediately after the completion of those milking rites.

In this case, the preliminary subsidiaries (*pūrvāṅga*) of the principal rite (*pradhāna*) are postponed—those which are performed collectively (*tantra*), such as the *ājyabhāga* offerings, those which are indirect auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*), and those which are direct auxiliaries (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) that must also be performed collectively, such as the strewing of grass (*staraṇa*) and so forth. However, there is no postponement for those [subsidiaries] that serve exclusively the purpose of the *prātardoha* (morning milking); for them, there is merely a displacement from their sequence, or they are to be performed in the vicinity of the principal rite. And thus is the performance: following the pouring of the remnants of the *agnihotra*, the strewing of grass is performed.

At the conclusion of the ritual action, or at the seat of the sacrifice, he arranges the vessels: the vessel for the *auṣadha* (herb-offering), the *prātahsavanīya* vessel, the *anvāhāryasthālī* group, and after the placing of the *juhū*, he arranges as many large *audumbara* cups as there are milkings; their procedure regarding the *juhū* is modified by the formula "O Vājina, thee" during the cleansing. Following the selection of the Brahman and so forth, the leading forward of the *praṇītā* waters, and having consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he sprinkles the vessels while they are turned face-upward; being impelled, he sprinkles them, and there is the release of speech by the sacrificer.

The rites beginning with the *uttaraparigraha* (the northern tracing) and ending with "having placed another vessel" are performed; then, having placed the pots on the southern shoulder, up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, at the invocation (*āvāhana*), however, one says: "Bring Agni hither; bring Soma hither; bring Indra or Mahendra hither; bring Agni hither; bring Indra or Mahendra hither. The rest, beginning from that point, remains unchanged.

The principle is that there is an intervention by another deity in the midst of Indra’s [portion], hence it is called "re-drinking" (*punarāpyāyana*). At the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, while passing to the south with the *kumbhīs*, he issues the command: "Recite for Indra or Mahendra! The attendants bring the vessels (*camasas*) around the front of the *āhavanīya* fire. As many *kumbhīs* as there may be, so many Brahmins wearing the sacred thread (*upavītin*) take up the *camasas*. The Adhvaryu takes one, brings the *kumbhīs* into them, and performs the *āśrāvaṇa* and subsequent rites for the *camasa*.

Regarding this, because of the statement of Āpastamba: "In that [rite], they offer the oblation following the two [main] offerings as a *sarvahuta*; furthermore, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *śakala* offerings do not exist," [the procedure is as follows]. Then, having ceased [the previous day's work], on the next morning, having set out the vessels for the morning milk along with the vessels for the vegetable offerings, having performed the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) and so forth and sprinkled [them], and having milked the cows at the time of the morning milking as before, having poured the residue into the *barhis* grass, and having performed the offering to Agni, they proceed with the offerings as before. Then, from the *āgneya* [offering] onwards, including the *sviṣṭakṛt*, the *iḍā*, and so forth, up to the feeding of the Brahmins, it remains unchanged.
He states another method for the performance of this very [rite]:

Alternatively, just as they milk the oblation on the new moon day, having thus milked it and heated it, he should set it aside; whatever is for the morning, he should prepare that as cooked. At the time of arranging the vessels, he sets out the vessels according to their purpose, including the large ladles made of Udumbara wood and the large cups (camasa); the procedure for these is explained by the rule for the *juhū*.

In this view, there is no reduction of the sacrifice. One should milk many cows at dawn; having prepared curds from each of those separately, one likewise prepares the morning milk-offerings. At the time of milking, one sets out the cups for both the evening and morning offerings separately, having set out the *juhū* ladle as prescribed. The rest has already been explained.

Having performed the rite with the cake for Agni (āgneya-puroḍāśa) and having placed the two ladles (srucau) in the Āgnīdhra fire-shed, he steps across together with the jars (kumbhīs), saying, "Recite the invitatory verse for Mahendra! and "O Śrauṣaṭ! Pronounce the offering-verse for Indra! As many as there may be jars, so many Brāhmaṇas, wearing their sacred threads over the left shoulder (upavītinaḥ), should stand up from the south, taking wooden vessels; having poured the jars into them, they all offer simultaneously, pouring their libations after the oblation of the Adhvaryu.

The meaning of this has already been explained. Thereafter, the rites for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the oblation to Agni follow in their unmodified form, ending with the feeding of the Brahmins. A sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given to the Brahmins according to one's ability. Thus concludes the *Sākaṃprasthāyīya*. Now follows the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña*:
one who desires heaven should sacrifice with the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña*.

This is not a mere designation (*saṃjñā*), but rather an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*). This was stated by Kātyāyana through the positions of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "The subsequent injunction of an accessory [is determined] through the connection with a name, a result, or an accessory, by means of proximity (*saṃnidhi*) and the statement of completion (*saṃpadvacana*). Proximity refers to the context (*prakaraṇa*). The statement of completion refers to such expressions as "By performing this, the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice is completed," and "He sacrifices on the previous day," and so forth. Therefore, this is an injunction of an accessory for the sake of a result; this very point has been clearly formulated in the sūtra: *guṇavikārācca* (and because of the modification of the accessory). Ga.Pa.Ja.Ma.I.

The meaning is that the excellence [of this sacrifice] is evident upon demonstrating its subsequent performance. How so? "Dakṣa" means skillful, that is to say, energetic; "dākṣāḥ" refers to those performances which are fit to be carried out by such a person; "ayanam" of those performances means their repetition; and the analysis of the compound is: "that which is both a monthly repetition (*ayana*) and a sacrifice (*yajña*). This very point has been established by the followers of Jaimini as well.
Some followers of Āpastamba maintain that it is a separate ritual (*karmāntara*), but that contradicts both the logic and the Sūtra. He states the performance:

There are two full-moon sacrifices (*paurṇamāsī*) and two new-moon sacrifices (*amāvāsyā*). Thus, in place of the two original performances (*prayoga*), there come to be four performances; the meaning is that these recur every month, rather than being performed repeatedly because they are optional rites (*kāmya*). There are two performances called "full-moon": one should sacrifice according to the original model on the first day (*pratipad*) following the full moon; then, on the second day, one should perform the sacrifice characterized by the repetition [of the ritual], beginning with the *anvādhāna* (the adding of fuel) and so forth. This is the meaning.
The meaning of the statement "he sacrifices on the previous [day]" is that the same two offerings take place on the new moon day as well.

He states the distinction: on the first full moon, there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Soma; on the latter [full moon], there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and curd for Indra. On the first new moon, there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and clotted curd (āmikṣā) for Mitra-Varuṇa; on the latter [new moon], there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra-Agni.

In this context, just as on the previous day one prepares the *aindra* curd for the place of the *āgnīṣomīya* on the following day according to the natural order, so too should it be stated regarding the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*). By means of this specific mention of the heavy [curd], it follows that there is no *upāṃśuyāja* even for one who does not perform the Soma sacrifice; likewise, there is no *āgnīṣomīya* for one who does not perform the *saṃnaya* (the mixing of milk), and there is no *aindrāgna* even for one who performs the *saṃnaya*. Such is the meaning of this statement. Others, however, say that the mention of the *āgnīṣomīya* is solely for the purpose of restriction and not for the purpose of excluding the *upāṃśuyāja*, because restricting both would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*); thus, the *upāṃśuyāja* does indeed take place.

The ritual application here is as follows: having made the formal resolve, "Desiring heaven, I shall sacrifice with the Dākṣāyaṇayajña for fifteen years," the performance of these [offerings] is to be understood as being like the performance of the Carvikā offerings on the full moon day and the first day of the lunar fortnight, and likewise on the new moon day and the second day of the lunar fortnight.

In this case, there is no reduction of the primary substance alone; rather, there is a repetition of the entire ritual procedure, beginning with the *sākamprasthāyīya* offering and the *anvādhāna*, and ending with the feeding of the Brahmins. When the repeated performance is concluded, the *vaimṛdha* sacrifice is performed, but they should not proceed on both days simultaneously. Although the *āmikṣā* for Mitra and Varuṇa belongs to the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, it is nonetheless a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *vaiśvadevī-āmikṣā*.

In this regard, since our own Śākhā does not describe the performance of the subsidiary rites up to the end of the Vājina sacrifice, and because the Sūtra treats this as a modification (*vikṛti*) due to the presence of specific qualities (*guṇa*), this [Vaiśvadeva] is indeed a modification; however, its extension of application (*atideśa*) proceeds precisely from the Vaiśvadeva Āmikṣā sacrifice as enjoined with all its subsidiaries. Here, for the Vājasaneyins, there exists the injunction for the production of the Maitrāvaruṇī Āmikṣā in the form "When the morning milk has been heated... and so forth. And that [injunction], according to the principle of the cognition of all Śākhās (*sarvaśākhāpratyayanyāya*), should be explained right here by the author of the Sūtra; nevertheless, [the procedure] begins with the drawing out of the Āmikṣā... [end of fragment].

[The rites] are completed with the *āmikṣā* for the goddesses. — 244. In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, many [details] regarding the *vaiśvadevyāmikṣā* itself will be explained according to the sequence of the ritual procedure (*krama*). Therefore, even the original injunction (*utpattividhi*) for that [offering], though belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*), will be explained there for the sake of brevity; hence, he will state its extension (*atideśa*) to all *āmikṣā* offerings. Consequently, even here, we shall not prevent the application of the nine fore-offerings (*prayāja*) and other elements which are obtained through that [extension]. Regarding this, he states a specific distinction:

His vow is this: he shall not speak untruth; he shall not eat meat; he shall not approach a woman; they shall not wash his garment with lye; he shall not apply collyrium nor anoint himself; he may approach his wife only during her season.

The purpose is that lying, eating meat, and sexual intercourse with women are prohibited even during the interval because, otherwise, there would be a deficiency in the ritual action (*karma*). The triad [of prohibitions] is clear. Regarding *palpūlana*: disciples, attendants, and others should not have the garment or cloth of this performer of the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice washed by means of stones or other well-known implements used for scrubbing and washing clothes; rather, they should do so only with their hands and the like. Likewise, it should not be washed by a washerman either.

In another way, the washing of clothes should not be performed. Since no specific exception is mentioned here, the observances (*vrata*) should apply at all times. *Añjana* (anointing) and *abhyañjana* (oil-massage) are well-known; these two occur because they are prescribed for the *Gṛhyamanthi* sacrifice. Regarding the statement "one should not approach a woman," he states a restriction: "One should approach—that is, go to—one's wife according to the rule. When one approaches her in accordance with the scriptural injunction (*vidhi*), there is no deficiency in the sacrifice. On this point, Bharadvāja has said: "The internal observances are as in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices."

When there is a desire for other modifications of qualities (*guṇavikāra*), one performs them at that time, but otherwise, the two sacrifices remain unmodified. Why is this not the case in the systems of the Yāvanas and others? He says: because of the application of the archetype (*prakṛti*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa from the very beginning, there is an option;
thus, this option regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa from the outset is expressed by the statement: "Or one should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa."

Thus, this Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice—whether performed as a compulsory (nitya) rite or as an optional (kāmya) rite—is fulfilled. The alternative (vikalpa) for this Dakṣāyaṇa sacrifice is to be understood as starting from the very beginning, that is, immediately after the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna). It is not by way of interruption; rather, when those two have been commenced, this [Dakṣāyaṇa] is performed, or when this has been commenced, those two are performed. If one asks, "How is it so?", he says in response: "Having sacrificed with it for fifteen years, he discontinues the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. (16)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the second book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

Since this fifteen-year-long performance is prescribed, even though the desire [for the specific result] has passed away, it cannot be abandoned as long as life—the occasion—remains; therefore, like the optional *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it has attained the status of a compulsory (*nitya*) rite. Regarding the phrase "that which is prohibited here," it is found in the manuscripts *ka*, *ga*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṭa*, and *ṇa*; thus, it appears that [the reading] is "tasmāt mādikaṃ" (therefore, beginning with that), and the word "na" (not) is redundant.
[End of] Chapter 70, from the *Mahādevakṛtavaijayantīvyākhyā*. 245.

Thus it has been stated by Āpastamba; the meaning is "for as long as one lives. In either case, it is established that a renewed commencement of the original *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is prohibited. The relinquishment (*utsarga*) of these two is also [prohibited]. Alternatively, the meaning is that one should relinquish the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices characterized as the *dākṣāyaṇayajña*. Here too, it is established by implication that there is no renewed commencement of the original sacrifices; this will be made clear in the subsequent question.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the second book of the *Prayogavṛtti*, the commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* composed by Mahādeva.

2.7 Now begins the seventh chapter of the second book. The New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are concluded. Having thus explained the two sacrifices known as the New and Full Moon—along with their modifications, their subsidiary offerings (*anunirvāpya*), and their various options—it is now necessary to explain the *brahmasva* (the priest’s fee). However, even though it is to be explained, one must state that although it is to be performed by the Adhvaryu priest during the New Moon sacrifice due to its similarity [in ritual procedure], it is nevertheless not an integral part (*aṅga*) of the New Moon sacrifice itself. To this end, he explains the rite called the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, which consists of the combination of the *darvihoma* and the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*), based on the scriptural injunction: "He offers three oblations; he places three [balls]; they amount to six. He explains as follows:

On the new moon day (amāvāsyā), in the afternoon, one performs the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. Because of its distinct name, because of the prescription of its own specific ritual procedure and time, and because it is mentioned separately from the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) by such statements as "having purchased [the Soma], he performs [the sacrifice]," it is rightly understood as a permanent (nitya) rite, not an optional (kāmya) one, nor a separate ritual act (karmāntara). Although the verbal root *yan* is heard in the text, nevertheless, it is not a *yāga* (sacrifice); for by the technical name *iṣṭi*, it is shown to have a different purpose. It is a *yajña*—a *homa* (offering)—to the Pitṛs and the Devas, accompanied by *piṇḍas* (rice-balls); thus it is called *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. It is well known that the *piṇḍas* are offered to the human ancestors.

This *piṇḍadāna* (offering of the rice-ball) is indicated by the word *piṇḍa*; by that, the coexistence of the *piṇḍadāna* and the *pitṛhoma* (oblation to the ancestors) as having the nature of a sacrifice (*deva*) has been stated. Thus, the primacy of both the *piṇḍadāna* and the *homa* is declared, and by that, this rite possesses the character of being both for the gods (*daivata*) and for the ancestors (*paitrya*). Consequently, even when the *piṇḍadāna* is omitted for one whose father is living, its accomplishment is achieved through the *homa* alone—just as the accomplishment of the *Paurṇamāsa* sacrifice is achieved for one who does not perform the *Soma* sacrifice by means of the *Āgneya* and *Upāṃśuyāja* offerings. In this rite, which consists of both giving and offering, there is no use of the root *dā* (to give), nor of the root *hu* (to offer).

For this very reason, in another Sūtra and in another Śruti, there is the general usage: "They perform with the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. Therefore, the author of the Sūtra employed the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) belonging to a different Vedic branch along with the word *yajña*, because here too, like a complete sacrifice (*sāṅgayajña*), there is an injunction for the performance of the rite together with its constituent parts (*sāṅgakarma*). [In contrast,] the roots *hu* (to offer oblations) and *dā* (to give) denote only the commonality of "offering" (*pradāna*) as a subordinate element. In that case, if both [the principal and the subsidiary] were primary, would the ancestral (*pitrya*) subsidiaries—characterized by the wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītitva*)—[apply]? Regarding that:

When there is doubt as to whether the divine rites (*devāni*) are limited or not, and an absence of restriction would otherwise result, the Teacher states the rule based on practice; his intention is now set forth. In that regard, because the ancestral ritual (*pitṛtantra*) proceeds from the very beginning, it possesses greater force. How so? Since the fetching of water for the purpose of purification (*medhya*) is for the sake of the ancestors alone, the strewings (*paristaraṇa*), however, are indeed separate, using the *paribhojanīya* grasses, provided there is no offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*). [Note: The manuscript variants cited (kha, ga, ca, cha, ṭha, ṇa) regarding the reading *vapituḥ* and the reference to Sāyaṇa’s commentary on the Śrautasūtra are included for fidelity to the source text.]

In that case, there is no need to bring [the materials] from outside because there is no purpose for it. However, the bringing of the *paribhojanīya* (food for consumption) for the sake of strewing (*paristaraṇa*) must indeed be performed. Therefore, everything prior to the *homa* should be done according to the rules of the *pitṛs* for both purposes. Even the strewings (*paristaraṇa*) serve both purposes, because they are praised as being for the dwelling of both classes of deities.

Therefore, having become one wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), the Adhvaryu should perform all the ritual acts. Because the primary and the subsidiary acts share a common agent, and since he will specify the Adhvaryu as the performer for the first primary act—the oblation—it follows that the Adhvaryu alone is the performer of the subsidiaries there. It should be understood that this is shown by such rules as "ending toward the south" and "not proceeding clockwise. For this very reason, it is said: "Facing south and east," and "the Adhvaryu, seated for the purpose of the oblation, wears the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*)," and so forth.

Since the word *aparāhṇa* (afternoon) denotes time, the word *amāvāsyā* (new moon day), when used in conjunction with it, must also refer to time; this is because its primary meaning is temporal. Thus, the sense is "one performs [the sacrifice] at the afternoon. Āpastamba also states, "they perform [the rite]. Here, the afternoon refers to the eighth part of the day divided into nine parts, as defined by the phrase "the impulsion of the Sun. When one is entitled to perform the monthly *śrāddha*, the afternoon should be understood according to a two-fold division; otherwise, there would be a lapse in the timing for that which is performed immediately after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. For others, however, there is a three-fold division.
Or "when the sun is behind the trees":

where the sun is above the trees, that is the place for the sacrifice. He states the rule regarding the application of the term *amāvāsyā* (the new moon day) to both the fifteenth and the first days [of the lunar fortnight]: "on whichever day they do not see the moon in the east."
The meaning is that [the sacrifice] is performed there when there is no beginningless obscuration by either perception or scripture. If it is seen, then he says:
"When it is seen, having fasted, he sacrifices on the following day.

Having fasted—whether the junction of the lunar phases (*parvan*) is present or not—he sacrifices on the next day during the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), or when the sun is behind a tree. Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*)—

"May that which is pure, worthy of sacrifice, divine, and auspicious among the waters be mine. May I, the one who cuts you, not come to harm; may I live for a hundred autumns. With this, he cuts the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) once, together with its roots, in a single effort along with the roots, because of the Śruti text, "That which has roots belongs to the ancestors," and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra for spreading it, namely "cut once" (*sakṛdācchinnam*). He touches water. Having strewn darbha grass around the Dakṣiṇā fire with the tips pointing south and east.

"Those whose tips are directed toward the south and the east" means that they are in front and behind with their tips facing south, while to the south and north they have tips facing east; the meaning is that one should spread them around clockwise starting from the east. Having spread the *darbha* grass to the north of the fire—[as stated in] Taṇḍulamañjarī 8.2.1]. Having spread the *darbha* grass to the north of the fire.

For both the strewing and the spreading [of the grass], only those intended for consumption (*paribhojanīya*) are used; however, in the case of spreading, they are not directed toward the south, as there is no specific injunction to that effect. One arranges the vessels for the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* one by one.

Furthermore, the mention of "the vessels for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña" within the section on the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is for the purpose of indicating that they are distinct from those used in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. At the commencement of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, the vessels intended for that rite must be prepared. However, if one is not an Āhitāgni (one who has maintained the sacred fires), then it need not even be mentioned, as the use of different vessels is already established by default. The meaning is "one by one. All [vessels] are not brought together at once, nor two by two; rather, they are brought one by one, because of the Śruti text: "The vessels dedicated to the Pitṛs are brought one by one. [The vessels are:
the wooden sword (sphya), the cooking pot (sthālī), the stirring-spoon (mekṣaṇa), the winnowing-basket (śūrpa), the black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina), the mortar (ulūkhala), and the pestle (musala).
They should end toward the east or toward the north, because that is prescribed by the Śruti.

Having placed a cart filled with rice to the west of the fire, and having filled a pot covered with a single strainer with rice and wiped it clean, he pours [the grain] into the winnowing basket all at once, saying: "I pour thee out, acceptable to the Pitṛs.

Having wiped it and removed the excess grains that have formed a heap on top with his hand—the rest is clear. In the absence of a cart, [he may do so] on a wooden sword (sphya) or in a cooking vessel.

To the south of the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire, having spread out a black antelope skin with its neck pointing westward or northward—either to the southeast or southwest of it—and having placed the mortar upon it; [the direction] "to the south" means either by the southeast or the southwest. [The skin is] with its neck toward the northwest. The rest is clear and its meaning understood.
Standing to the south-east, the wife threshes [the grain].

Facing the Āhavanīya fire, she performs the *parāpāva* (winnowing) and *aviveka* (separation) once. Having cooked the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) in the Dakṣiṇāgni with rice grains still containing their husks (*jīvataṇḍula*), she bastes it with either clarified butter that has been strained or unstrained fresh butter, and then removes it from the fire.

The suffix *ṇamul* occurs after the root *pū* with the prefix *parā*. The meaning is "having performed the winnowing (*parāpavana*) of the husks—that is, having repeatedly removed the chaff. The suffix *ṇamul* is also used here in the sense of non-separation (*aviveka*). The meaning is "without separating"—that is, without separating the grain from the husk, but merely removing the husk itself. He threshes it only once (*sakṛt*), in a single action, for the sake of easily releasing the kernel. It refers to a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) in which the grains are still alive—that is, unbroken rice-grains—and thus not overcooked. [He does this] with butter that has been strained through a single filter.

Ka. Va. Ga. Ca. Cha. Ṭa., "dhivṛtla ||3ga, ca. u. gyāmi | 3 gha... ja. jha.pa.ṭa. 'thena cā sapiṃṣāmi'| X 248 Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra—[In the second book]: The Adhvaryu, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (upavītī), having bent his right knee, takes a portion from the *sthālīpāka* with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*). The specific mention of the Adhvaryu is for the purpose of establishing his agency in the primary portion; it is intended so that in other portions the sacrificer may be the one characterized by his own specific duties.

How so? This Piṇḍapitṛyajña is a collection of ritual acts; in it there are three oblations, as it is said, "he offers three āhutis. Because these are enjoined by the verb *juhoti*, they possess the character of a *davihoma*. Although some of the *davihoma* characteristics are set aside by specific injunctions located within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, the statement "the Adhvaryu" is made in order to remind us that the agent is not set aside.

It has been stated that "the Agnihotra is performed with the Yajurveda"; this is an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa) for all *darvihoma* offerings. Thus, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is also a *darvihoma*, and consequently, it is to be performed by the Adhvaryu priest. Furthermore, a separate Adhvaryu is not enjoined as something unprecedented; rather, it is stated that the Adhvaryu is already chosen for the sake of the *Dārśa* sacrifice. Since no other sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed for this, its accomplishment follows by extension from the rites included within that time-period. Indeed, the Smṛti rule regarding the non-performance of the fee is optional; therefore, this [injunction] is solely for the purpose of establishing a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

Because the *homa* has deities as its recipients, it is stated that one is "purified" (*pavītī*). For this very reason, "having bent the right knee" means having brought it down to the ground; this is a form derived from the root *añc*, meaning "to go," with the prefix *ā* and the suffix *lyap*. The statement "having taken [it] with the stirring-spoon" (*mekṣaṇena*) is for the purpose of precluding the ritual rules (*dharma*) pertaining to the formal *avadāna* (cutting-off). "Having taken with the stirring-spoon from the *sthālīpāka*" means having taken a portion of that [very thing]. The intention is that since the *sthālīpāka* serves both purposes, there is no status of "remnant" (*śeṣa*) for what remains.

He offers the first oblation with the words: "To Soma, drunk by the ancestors, Svadhā! Adoration! The second with: "To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors, Svadhā! Adoration! And the third with: "To Agni Kavyavāhana, the maker of good offerings, Svadhā! Adoration! He then offers those rice grains which remain in the stirring-spoon. || 17 ||

The phrase "the third oblation" is established by implication. Here, although the utterance of *svāhā* would normally apply because this is a *davihoma* (oblation from a ladle), the *svāhā* is not used because the purpose [of the offering] is expressed by the word *namas*, according to the maxim that "what has already been stated need not be employed again. For instance, both *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ* have the meaning of "giving," as the Vedic scripture states: "It is given to the gods either with *svāhā* or with *vaṣaṭ*. Furthermore, the word *svadhā namaḥ* serves the function of *vaṣaṭ* according to the scripture: "He makes the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance with 'svadhā namaḥ'. Therefore, since this word (*svadhā namaḥ*) fulfills the purpose of giving, it supersedes the word *svāhā*.

For this very reason, even in the *dadhi-homa*, the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) applies because it possesses the specific characteristic of being offered with the *vaṣaṭ* call. Regarding the verses beginning with "the first," only one is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa—namely, "To Soma, drunk by the ancestors, *svadhā*! Homage!"—while a second is not prescribed. Therefore, so that there may be no confusion with the two [verses] belonging to other recensions (*śākhā*), the third is also prescribed in one's own recension: "To Agni, the bearer of the oblation. That [verse], which is mentioned alone as the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, is taken from another recension; this is shown for the purpose of establishing the proper arrangement. As for those grains of rice adhering to the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*):

They say the second [offering] consists of the characteristic of the rice grains; the meaning is that one offers those very same remnants left over from the two previous offerings as the third oblation.
One silently places the stirring-spoon [into the fire]. This is clear.

"Those Asuras who, assuming forms, move about by means of their own nature (svadhā), who carry away the *parāpur* and *nipura*—may Agni drive them away from this world. Having taken a single glowing ember from the Dakṣiṇāgni while it is still smoking and carrying it away toward the west, he places it to the south of the spot where the single wooden sword (*ekasphya*) lies.

When [the earth] has been brought with its face turned downwards, he places it at the edge of that place where a single-stone altar (ekaraphyā) was intended to be constructed; "he places it at the end of the marked-out area," so says Āpastamba. The connection is: "having carried it to the south from the vicinity of the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇāḥ). This rite is enjoined either for an invisible purpose as a remote auxiliary (ārādupakāraka), or as a purificatory rite (saṃskāra) for the altar. That too is an ancillary part of the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍadāna); in its absence, [the rite] would not take place. After the throwing of the stirring-spoon (mekṣaṇa), the Adhvaryu priest wears the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī).

Having drawn a single furrow on the altar-ground with the wooden sword (sphya) in the place of threshing—either towards the south or towards the southeast—with the mantra "Struck down are the Asuras, the Rakṣas who sit upon the altar" (*apahatā asurā rakṣāṃsi vediṣadaḥ*), [he prepares] the altar to the south of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. The analysis of the compound *ekasphyā* is: "that which has one wooden sword as its instrument. The meaning is that it is marked with a single line. Āpastamba has stated: "having once drawn [the line] with the wooden sword.
He sprinkles [the ground] with water with the mantra "May the lower ones rise up" (*udīratām avare*).
Sprinkling and sprinkling downward are performed with the hand not turned downwards. The word "with water" is stated for the purpose of excluding the consecration of the *prokṣaṇī* waters.

With the *sakṛdācchinna* grass, he strews it along the single wooden sword (*ekasphyā*), saying: "I bring you, the wool-soft and pleasant, as a seat for the fathers; may my Soma-loving fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers sit upon this together with their followers.
This is clear.
Upon it he places the cooked mess of rice (sthālīpāka).
He places half of it on a single-ribbed stool and sets it down.
To the south, he establishes collyrium, ointment, a head-rest, a mattress, and a water-pot.

*Āñjana* is collyrium; *abhyañjana* is oil. According to the Śruti, "the whey (*mastu*) belongs to the ancestors," it refers either to the curd-whey or the upper layer of fat. *Kaśipu* is a couch; some say it is a mattress with a pillow. *Upabarhaṇa* is a pillow for the head. A full pitcher joined with water—by this much the Adhvaryu ceases. The sacrificer, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), bending his left knee, and with his hands turned downward, pours out three handfuls of water toward the south on the *sakṛdācchinna* grass.

The meaning is that the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) has been spread once and cut. "With hands turned downward" means the hands are turned sideways and joined in the *añjali* gesture; the meaning is that at the time of pouring out the water, the sprinkling with the *añjali* must be performed by means of the *pitrya* (ancestral) *tīrtha*. Alternatively, "downward" refers to... [Note: The text fragment indicates a variant reading or commentary regarding the specific term used]. This is from the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Second Praśna.

The meaning is that at the time of pouring out [the water], the right hand of the one who has formed the *añjali* (cupped hands) must be turned downward—that is, made lower. He pours out, or lets flow, the *añjali*s filled with water. The rest is clear. Regarding this, he states two mantras as alternatives:

"May the Soma-loving ancestors purify themselves; may the Soma-loving grandfathers purify themselves; may the Soma-loving great-grandfathers purify themselves," or "O [Name], pour down! O [Name], pour down! (with the specific names inserted).

In this case, by virtue of a single introductory formula (*itikaraṇa*), there would be a single mantra; thus, it would be "once with the mantra, twice silently. Since there is no reason for a division in the middle, nevertheless the Teacher, having demonstrated the application (*viniyoga*), demonstrates the mantra; he thereby makes known that the three *añjali*s are for the purpose of consecrating separate locations. Thus, there should be a mantra for each, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, and they [the mantras] apply only through division. He points out the places of pouring separately.
