And these [offerings] belong to the triad beginning with the father in sequence; thus, by the division of the mantra, there is a threefold nature for each because of the presence of the respective actions. In place of the word "asau" (that one), he takes the worldly names of the father and the others in sequence, ending in the vocative case, because of the use of the second person; however, he does not say "O father, O dear one" (*pitastāta*), nor both [names], because there is no injunction for that, nor does he say "the Adhvaryu priest," for the offering of the *piṇḍas* is performed by those who are close [to the deceased]. In this regard, it is understood that there are three [offerings] for each one. [The formula] "O Kṛṣṇa, descend into the earth" (*kṛṣṇāvaneniṅkṣva*) or "O Kṛṣṇa Śarman, descend into the earth" (*kṛṣṇaśarmannavaneniṅkṣva*), and so forth.
With his hands turned downwards, he offers three balls of sacrificial food (*piṇḍa*) ending toward the south.

He places them down, because here the act of "giving" (*dāna*), which consists in the transfer of ownership to another, is impossible. For this very reason, the Śruti says simply, "he places [them] down three times. Although there is a single ritual action defined by the three deities, the Śruti specifies "three times" for the purpose of indicating repetition (*abhyāsa*) for each deity; thus, this is a portion of the oblation (*homabhakti*). He offers the three balls of cooked rice (*caru*), prepared in sequence, precisely in those locations consecrated by the pouring out of water.

"Downward-turned" (*avācīna*) refers to that hand whose thumb-side portion is directed downwards; such is the downward-turned [hand]. He gives them in sequence, ending with the right [hand]. Although the hand cannot function as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the act of giving—since that act, like a sacrifice (*yāga*), is mental in nature—nevertheless, because it ends in the act of casting [the gift] through the aspect of transferring ownership to another, just like a *homa* offering, it is called a "locus. Previously, we stated that giving culminates in the transfer of ownership to another with respect to the act of casting; however, that [is the case here].

It follows all forms of giving (*sarvadāna*). For in the case of gifts such as land and the like, the act of "throwing in" (*prakṣepa*) is not possible; however, in the present context, this is not the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), but rather "throwing in" is the meaning of another root, *ni-dhā* (to place down), as it is heard in the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*) that "he places it down three times. Thus, the gift characterized by that [act] culminates here in that manner, and so there is no contradiction. He states the mantra: "This for you, O father, [Name]," with which he gives the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to the father.

"Etatte tata ye ca tvāmanu" is the opening of the mantra. The word "asau" (so-and-so), obtained from another *śākhā*, is supplied in the middle. For this very reason, Āpastamba stated: "With these [words]: 'Etatte tata asau ye ca tvāmanu'. And in the *Pitryeṣṭi* sacrifice, it is likewise recited as: "Etatte tata ye ca tvāmanu. Thus, having taken the *piṇḍa*: "Etatte tata amukaśarman... [End of the section] from the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva.

And thinking, "I consider you [to be such]," he places a drop [of water]. Here, there is no utterance of words such as *gotra*, *vasu*, or *rūpa*, because it is not prescribed; likewise, it is not performed in the Smṛti. Some perform it even here, but that should be disregarded by ritualists (*yājñika*) as it contradicts the Sūtra, its Bhāṣya, other Sūtras, and other commentaries.
"This for you, O grandfather, [named] so-and-so"—this is for the grandfather. "This for you, O great-grandfather, [named] so-and-so"—this is for the great-grandfather. The explanation is as before.
The fourth [offering] is made silently.
"The rice-ball" (piṇḍa) is as before;
it is both prepared and unprepared.
The meaning is that [an action] is prescribed in one branch, prohibited in another, and optional in yet another. While that [rite] is to be performed, [one should do so] silently.

Now, if he should not find the [specific] names, he should give the rice-ball (piṇḍa) to the father with the words, "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling on earth"; to the grandfather with the words, "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling in the intermediate space"; and to the great-grandfather with the words, "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling in heaven."

If, however, the names of the father and others are unknown, one should offer with these very same mantras as before. This refers to the case where a child died while his parents were still living, after which he was later consecrated by another through the *upanayana* and other rites; in that situation, the names of the father and others were not known. It also applies when the sacrificer is away on a journey and concerns the *adhvaryu*. In the phrase "to those dwelling on earth" (*pṛthiviṣadbhyaḥ*), the shortening of the vowel in the word *pṛthivī* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). If there are two fathers, one should designate both for each individual *piṇḍa*.

The meaning is that one who has adopted a son (dattaka) and so forth should mention two fathers in the single *piṇḍa* for the father; two grandfathers in the *piṇḍa* for the grandfather; and two great-grandfathers in the *piṇḍa* for the great-grandfather. Or else, [he may say]: "To Viṣṇu and Kṛṣṇa Śarmā, and to those who come after them. The same applies in subsequent cases as well. Here too, if the names are unknown, the offering is made with the words "Svadhā to the ancestors" (*svadhā pitṛbhyaḥ*) and so forth.
One whose father is living should offer to the grandfather and the great-grandfather.

"One whose father is living" (*jīvapitṛ*) is thus described; he should offer two *piṇḍas*. The particle *iti* expresses a manner. By this, one whose paternal grandfather is living offers to his father and to his great-grandfather; one whose great-grandfather is living offers to the other two; while for one whose [other ancestors] are living, he offers to someone other than those. Regarding the purpose of the particle *iti*: in the manuscript of the Sūtra, the phrase "if one knows" (*veda yadi*) is found. [In the versions] gha, ja, ma, and na, it says "he gives *svadhā*. [Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra—2nd Praśna, 252]

"According to some, one does not give beyond [the living]. The meaning is that one does not give by bypassing whichever of the two is alive. When the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) is alive, the offering must indeed be given to the father, even though both ancestors are living; for the prohibition applies only to the act of bypassing. When the one to whom it was previously to be given is alive, it is given to the next; the prohibition therein applies only to what was established by the preceding sūtra. In that case, only so much of the rite should be abandoned as one lacks authority to perform, but not the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* itself. With the intention that the prohibition applies only to the act of giving—as indicated by the phrase 'one does not give'—he says:"
One should perform [the rite] only up to the end of the oblation;
that is to say, up to the throwing away of the stirring-spoon (mekṣaṇa).
For one whose father is still living, everything subsequent to the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) is omitted.

Why is this stated? Because its meaning is already understood. It is replied: we say that this is stated for the purpose of showing that as long as one of two fathers lives, from that point forward, only those two [offerings] headed by him are omitted, and no others. He recalls the subject at hand with the restatement:
"having placed the rice-balls" (*nidhāya piṇḍān*).

"O divine waters, being honored with the *svadhā* call—may they, who are pleasant, go to you, O ancestors! Carrying strength, possessing inexhaustible water—milk, water, clarified butter, honey, milk, *kīlāla*, and flowing liquor—you are the *svadhā*; satisfy my ancestors! With these words, he pours out three handfuls of water.

Regarding the pouring [of water] over the *piṇḍas*, although this consecration (*saṃskāra*) is obtained for each one individually, nevertheless, by means of the plural number, it is stated "three" so that there might not be a single simultaneous discharge over all of them as a continuous stream. Taking a single vessel full of water from the water-jar (*udakumbha*), he should pour it over each of the *piṇḍas* according to the principle that "an action is repeated when the substances are distinct. Having said here, "O Fathers, enjoy according to your respective portions; flow forth according to your own nature," he turns away.

He turns around clockwise. The meaning is that the mantra should have been recited previously, and he should remain with his back turned toward the *piṇḍas*. Once the heat has subsided, he waits and consecrates the rising steam with the mantra: "Svāhā! May the heat depart.
With his back still turned, he consecrates the rising steam from the *piṇḍas* as it issues forth.

In the Sūtra manuscripts, the form *ninīya* is found where [the text says] *ninayati*. Having said, "The ancestors have rejoiced according to their own nature; they have attained vigor," he turns around toward the fire, whether the *ūṣman* (hissing sound) has ceased or not.

The term "having turned away" (*vyāvṛtta*) refers to the injunction of our own *śākhā*, because there exists another injunction prescribed in other *śākhās*. The phrase "he worships until the heat has turned away" means that he worships while remaining turned away as long as the heat has not emerged from the rice-balls; however, the rule of another *śākhā* is the opposite of this, and for that reason there is an option (*vikalpa*). Having recited the mantra "They have rejoiced," the meaning is that he should face the rice-balls again in the same manner he came.
He smells the remnant that remains in the vessel; the act of smelling is to be performed with the intention of eating. Then there is the touching of water.
Or he touches [it] with water;

having brought it outside, he touches it with his hand. There is no touching with water. One who is ill, or one who desires food, or one who, though capable of eating, does not eat food—such a person may consume it.

A sick person desires or eats suitable food for the sake of recovery from illness. A man who is capable of eating food but does not eat it due to the defect of lack of appetite—by him, following the Vedic injunction, these two actions are performed. Here, he gives collyrium, ointment, and clothing along with the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*). The mention of "here" is so that there may be no option regarding what was stated in another Sūtra as occurring after the pouring [of water] with joined palms; this is the intended meaning. He states the rule:
"Anoint him, O so-and-so! Anoint him, O so-and-so!"—thus three times for the collyrium. "Anoint him, O so-and-so! Anoint him, O so-and-so!"—thus three times for the ointment.

Regarding each [rite], the Commentator says that one should perform it three times with the mantra and twice silently; thus for each. Others hold that the mention of "three times" is intended to exclude a fourth application; in that case, one performs it only once. Having cut off a fringe or a tuft of wool, he places it down, saying: "These are your garments, O fathers; therefore, O fathers, do not take anything else from us," provided he is in the earlier stage of life.

Having cut a loose end of one’s own garment that is not knotted or gathered, but which has not fallen [to the ground], he places it upon all the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) once with the mantra; it is said that he "places" it for the purpose of ensuring that the mantra occurs only once during the entire deposition. "Earlier age" refers to the first half of the hundred years of a man's lifespan, namely fifty years. Āśvalāyana states that from the age of fifty onwards, it is "one's own hair. Therefore, "earlier age" means prior to that.

Alternatively, when life is divided into three parts, the first two parts constitute the earlier stage of life. Regarding this, Baudhāyana states: "After sixty-six years and eight months. [This refers to] the *vajina* [offering]. Having shaved his own hair on the northern side—since it is stated in the Śruti that "the upper part of a man's body is indeed above the navel"—this point is established.
He worships with prostrations, saying, "Obeisance to you, O Pitṛs, the essence" (*namo vaḥ pitaro rasāya*).

These seven mantras are preceded by the word *namaḥ*; with these seven, seven separate acts of worship (*upasthāna*) should be performed. In matters concerning visible results, there may be an option; however, because this concerns invisible results (*adṛṣṭārtha*), it is stated that "with prostrations" (*namaskāraiḥ*) to indicate that there is no fault even in repeating the ritual action through the repetition of the mantras.

"Full of vigor, honoring with the *svadhā* call—may those pleasant ones of yours come, O Fathers! Carrying vigor, possessing inexhaustible waters—milk, water, clarified butter, honey, milk, *kīlāla*, and flowing *parisrut*—you are the *svadhā*; satisfy my fathers! With these words, he pours out three handfuls of water as before. (19)

The meaning has already been explained. The statement "as before" is intended to prevent the application of the pouring of the ointment (*lepaninayana*) mentioned in another sūtra from being applied here.

"Arise, O ancestors who preceded those who have passed away; follow the ancient path of Yama. Bestow upon us wealth that is auspicious, and announce us as partakers among the gods"—with these words, he causes the ancestors to rise.

The meaning is that, having performed the ritual raising of the ancestors, he mutters the prayer. Or, he causes the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) to rise. He dismisses them with the verse, "Depart, O ancestors."

*Pravāhaṇaṃ* is the leading toward the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*) by means of appropriate vehicles. The mantra is as before; it ends with the word *madanti*. With the mantra, "May the ancestors go with speed of mind," he prepares the ancestors and causes them to reach the world of the ancestors, as before.

He worships with three verses containing the word "mind" (*manas*), beginning with *mano nvā huvāmahe*. The second verse contains the word "mind," and the third ṛc is *punarnaḥ*. He worships the ancestors who abide in their own world.
He returns with the two verses addressed to Prajāpati, which are in the *paṅkti* meter, beginning with *akṣannamīmadanta prajāpate*.

Knowledge of [the verse] as a *paṅkti* is an auxiliary element of the ritual; otherwise, there would be an expiation for a sacrificial defect (*yajñabhreṣa*) due to a violation of the *Yajus* formula, performed in the *Dakṣiṇāgni* fire. "Harī" is the first [word]; "rayīṇām" is the second. Having become one who wears the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*), he approaches the *Gārhapatya* fire for the purpose of worship.
With the *paṅkti* verse beginning "yad antarikṣam," he worships the *Gārhapatya*.
"Manenasam" is the end of the mantra. By counting the syllables, it is a *śakvarī*; the intention is that the meditation upon it as a *paṅkti* should be performed.

"Jātavedas has been our messenger for the oblation; having made the offerings fragrant, he has carried them away. He has given them to the ancestors, who have eaten them with the *svadhā* call. Knowing [the way], O Agni, he returns again to the gods"—having thus thrown back a single firebrand (*ekolmuka*) into the established fire, and having reunited that placed firebrand once more with the Dakṣiṇāgni. [Note: This passage is from the *Mahādevakṛtavaijayantī* commentary on the seventh chapter (paṭala) of the *Vaikhānasa-smārtasūtra*, verses 1–2.]
Having sprinkled them with water, he brings back the vessels in pairs.
Having sprinkled the vessels used for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña with water, he carries them away two by two from the place where they were set down;
he pours them out and places the rice-balls (piṇḍas) back into the cooking pot.
He places the rice-balls upon the vessel containing water.
He gives the middle rice-ball to his wife with the formula: "I cause you to consume the essence of the waters and the plants; conceive a fetus created by the beings.
This is clear.

"O Fathers, bestow the embryo, a boy wearing a lotus-wreath, so that there may be a man here"—with these words the wife eats [the rice]. Since it is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the man, and because its purpose for the man is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, it should be given separately to each wife; the settled rule is that it is to be consumed by all of them with the mantra. For that very reason, he recites the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*):
"He produces a male."
The word "son" (*putram*) is to be supplied as the object. There is no desire [expressed here], because the word "desire" (*kāma*) is absent.

"Those ancestors who are equal and of one mind in the realm of Yama—may their world, their *svadhā*, their homage, and their sacrifice be prepared among the gods. Those kinsmen who are of one mind, living among the living and belonging to me—may their prosperity be prepared for me in this world for a hundred years. Having sprinkled the once-cut blades of grass with water, he places them on the fire.
Having sprinkled them, he places them on the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern fire) with the two mantras.
He causes the rice-balls to be cast into water, or he feeds a Brāhmaṇa.
That is, he deposits them with water as the target; this is clear. This very rite, thus prescribed, is for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni).

This very Piṇḍapitṛyajña, as described in this manner, is performed even by one who has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni). In that case, those acts connected with cooking are performed on the Āvasathya fire; however, the oblation (homa) may be performed even on the Atipraṇītā fire, but the cooking itself does not take place there. Those vessels used for the preparation of that [oblation] are restricted to being placed upon the Āvasathya fire.
He offers very refined oblations.
Once the firebrand has been carried forward, the offering is made right there; thus, the carrying forward of the fire occurs at the very time of the offering.
He stands in worship over that fire into which he offers.

The meaning is that one should attend only to the most excellent [fire]. This has been explained by the author of the Bhāṣya: because of the teacher's instruction, "in which one offers," there is an option; for the teacher's instruction has a specific purpose—to ensure that, even when the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is performed in the Dakṣiṇāgni, the attendance upon the Āvasathya (Aupāsana) fire does not cease, just as there is attendance upon the Gārhapatya. To this end, the words "in which" and so forth were stated.
In this context, the designation "Gārhapatya" is set aside. || 20 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the second book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.

The term *gārhapatya* is omitted and there is no modification (*ūha*), because this *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is also a primary archetype (*prakṛti*). Nor can it be explained through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For while in the primary rite there is an injunction stating "he worships the *gārhapatya*," and thus an interpretation based on the force of the accusative case in "he worships the *gārhapatya*" is possible; in the present case, where the injunction is simply "he worships that [fire] into which he offers," there is no basis for such an application. Therefore, it is logical that the word *gārhapatya* is simply omitted.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the second book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin, composed by Mahādeva.

2.8 Now begins the eighth chapter in the second book. "I am the lord of the earth; I am the lord of the world; I am the lord of the great being. Impelled by the divine Savitṛ, I shall perform the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*). O divine Savitṛ, they choose you here as Bṛhaspati, the divine Brahman. That I announce to the mind; the mind to the Gāyatrī; the Gāyatrī to the Triṣṭubh; the Triṣṭubh to the Jagatī; the Jagatī to the Anuṣṭubh; the Anuṣṭubh to the Bṛhatī; the Bṛhatī to the Paṅkti; the Paṅkti to Prajāpati; Prajāpati to the Viśvedevas; and the Viśvedevas [to the All]."
"O Bṛhaspati, Bṛhaspati is the Brahman of the gods; I am the Brahman of men; Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ"—thus the chosen Brahman mutters.

When chosen by the sacrificer with the words "O Lord of the Earth," he mutters [the same]. At this point, rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) is prescribed for the Brahman by Vaikhānasa. Having stepped around the southern side of the Āhavanīya fire, [he says]: "O Vācaspati, protect the sacrifice. [End of Section 257] [This concludes the section from the *Mahādevakṛta-vaijayantī* commentary. [Note: The manuscript variants cited in the source text regarding specific readings (gha, cha, ja, etc. have been omitted as per the instruction to provide only the translation.]
Here, there is an option with the formula recited by the Brahman priest, "O Vācaspati, protect the sacrifice. It has been stated by Vaikhānasa that the sacrificer steps across [the altar] beforehand.
Having cast out a blade of grass from the seat of the Brahman with the words, "O son of a remarried woman," and having touched water, he [proceeds].
The term *pākatara* is used when the *mashra* has ended. The touching of water is prescribed in the Śrauta ritual.
He sits down with the mantra, "May I go over the heights and the hollows.

This sitting is performed facing eastward, because another form of sitting is subsequently prescribed as being toward the Āhavanīya fire. "Ayā" marks the end of the mantra. He sits facing the Āhavanīya fire with the words: "Here I sit in the seat of Arvāgvasu, impelled by the god Savitṛ; I sit in the seat of Bṛhaspati. I announce this to Agni, this to Vāyu, this to Sūrya, and this to Pṛthivī."
Having previously sat facing the east, he now sits down facing the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra. He remains seated until the conclusion of the rite; the meaning is that he does not move away.
He restrains his speech at every ritual act.
Once a ritual act has begun, he should not speak until its completion.
In the case of rites accompanied by mantras as well as those performed silently, he may act according to his desire.
This is the eighth [section]. Alternatively, one restrains speech during the *sāmidhenī* verses, the *prayāja* offerings, and the *anūyāja* offerings;
from the commencement until the conclusion of the *sāmidhenīs*, and likewise in other cases as well.

If one should speak while distracted, having muttered a verse addressed to Viṣṇu (*vaiṣṇavī ṛc*) and the *vyāhṛtis*, he restrains his speech again. Regarding the specific rule that has been undertaken, if there is an abandonment of that rule through negligence, one should mutter "iha viṣṇuḥ" and the three *vyāhṛtis*. When it is said, "O Brahman, I shall lead forward the water," [one should say]: "Lead forward the sacrifice; cause the deities to prosper; on the back of the firmament, may the sacrificer..."

"Ka sa. na. ca. cha. ṭa, ṭha 'pū yā' | 33. May it be so! Place this sacrifice and the sacrificer in that world where the Seven Seers of good deeds dwell; Om, lead forward! Thus he gives the impulse (*prasauti*). When asked, "Lead forward?", the response of approval is the impulse (*prasava*). This is clear.
At all invocations, he gives permission with the syllable *oṃ*.

Even for future invocations, he gives permission preceded by the syllable *oṃ*; that is, having uttered the syllable *oṃ* before the verb of the appropriate act of approval, he utters the verb, such as "Oṃ, sprinkle" (*oṃ prokṣa*), and so forth.
With whichever specific ritual action he invokes, at each instance he gives permission with that very same [formula].

The word *yena* is used here in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) in the sense of a characteristic (*itthaṃbhāva-lakṣaṇe*). The meaning is this: by whatever action he characterizes [the rite] when addressing [the Brahman priest], saying "O Brahman, I shall sprinkle," and so forth—that very action of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) by which he addresses the Brahman, by that same action he gives the impulse (*prasauti*), saying "Sprinkle!

When it is said, "O Brahman, I shall sprinkle," he [the Brahman] says, "Sprinkle the sacrifice," and thus he impels the sprinkling of the oblation (*havis*) as well as the fuel (*idhma*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

Regarding the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), this refers to the ritual act of sprinkling. The invocation mentioned for the sprinkling of the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is to be understood as being addressed to the Adhvaryu; he gives the impulse (*prasauti*) only in that case, not according to our own Sūtra. The phrase "May the deity prosper," etc., is stated to be supplied everywhere. When it is said, "O Brahman, I shall perform the second enclosure (*parigrāha*)," [the Brahman recites]: "O Bṛhaspati, enclose the altar; may the gods go their own way to their seats. Upon it, let the sacrificial grass spread out well; O Earth, Goddess, be free from injury. This is for the second enclosure.
In this case as well, the word "deity" is to be supplied by ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*).
When it is said, "O Brahman, I shall recite the *sāmidhenī* verses," [the response] regarding the *sāmidhenīs* is, "Recite for Prajāpati the sacrifice.
This is the response of the Hotṛ, provided that he addresses him. In this instance too, the word "deity" is to be supplied by ellipsis.

When it is said, "I shall cause the announcement for the Brahman-pravara," [the response is]: "O Vācaspati, cause this speech to be announced; announce it! [Announce] me among the gods at the sacrifice, and among men. The connection is as before. He appends "Make the deity prosper" everywhere, and he gives the impulse with "Om, announce! (oṃ āśrāvaya).

He performs the *anuṣaṅga* (addition) for those [formulas] mentioned previously. It has already been stated that he impels [the sacrifice] with the syllable *Oṃ* at the end of each respective ritual act, following the word "place" (*dhehi*).
He gazes at the *prāśitra* (portion for consumption) while it is being cut off with the formula, "I gaze upon you with the eye of Mitra.
As soon as the Adhvaryu has begun the cutting of the *prāśitra*, he consumes it; thus, he looks intently at the *prāśitra*.

1 gha. 'psa kampīṇā5 | 2 ka. kha. ga. ca. cha. ṭa. ṭha. 'jati || 80paṭala, together with the Vaijayantī commentary composed by Mahādeva | 259. "Go along the path of Truth"—this is said as [the fire] is being carried around. "With unerring guidance, having begun to bring [it] around the Āhavanīya fire, he waits for it" when it has reached the north-eastern direction; "waits" is to be supplied [as the verb].

With the words, "I gaze upon you with the eye of the Sun," he looks toward [the *praśitra*] as it is being brought. He looks while facing it, that is, facing the direction from which it is being brought—toward the southeast. Previously, having been seated in the *parṣan* arrangement, he looked while standing facing the *āhavanīya*; here, however, the distinction is that he looks while having turned to face the *praśitra*. Having received it with the words, "Of the god... (*devasya tvā*).
The word "prāśitra" is to be supplied [to the preceding]. "I accept" is the end of the mantra.
Having spread out grass-blades to the west of the Āhavanīya fire with the words, "I set thee on the navel of the earth, in the place of Iḍā," he places [the vessel] with its handle pointing eastward.

Having spread out and removed the grass-blades, he places it with its handle pointing eastward upon the *barhis* that has been strewn. The phrase "with its handle pointing eastward" is stated because there is no intended distinction between the *prāśitraharaṇa* vessel and the *prāśitra* [portion of food].

Having looked down with the words, "I gaze upon you with the eye of Suparṇa Garutman," he gazes upward while bending down and becoming inclined; this is the distinction. Because of the qualification "of Garutman," the word "having looked down" (*avekṣya*) is used to indicate that the gaze is directed downward.
Then, with the words "Of the god... (*devasya tvā...*), he takes [the substance] with the thumb and the ring finger.
The sixth [section]. He consumes it with the words, "I consume you with the mouth of Agni.
He places it in his mouth; Vaikhānasa has stated that one should place it on the tip of the tongue.

With the words "By the belly of the Brāhmaṇa," he swallows it without chewing; he swallows it with the mantra and leads it downward. "Without chewing" means without causing it to wither or become exhausted, and without mixing it with saliva—having previously placed it on the tip of the tongue—he introduces it into the lower part exactly as it was, without breaking it apart. Having taken the *prāśitra* portion, he eats it within the sacrificial hall (*antarvihāra*). He does not let it pass his teeth.

He brings the teeth [into contact] at the time of depositing and at the time of the *prasana* (swallowing). With the formula, "May those deities who are within the waters pacify this; let that which is consecrated by *svāhā* go to the belly of Indra," he pours it down with water.
Having taken water, he causes it to reach the stomach from below through the esophagus by means of those [waters] and the mantra; it is understood that he holds it in the throat for that long.
Having sipped water (ācamya).

The ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) is of two types: that pertaining to the Smṛti and that pertaining to the Śruti. Having first performed the Smārta rite, one should perform the Śrauta rite for the sake of the ritual action. Alternatively, the accomplishment of both may be achieved through the Śrauta rite alone. Regarding the Smārta rules, it is stated: "Having sipped water three times, having wiped the mouth twice with the base of the thumb, having touched [the lips] once with the tips of the fingers, having sprinkled the left hand and the feet, and having sprinkled the head. However, in the Śrauta rite, the specific distinction is that one touches [the face]. Having touched the eyes, the nostrils, and the ears once each with the thumb and forefinger along with water, in the Śrauta rite, however, one touches the heart with the hand.
The word *talenā* is an addition. It should be understood that sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the head is prescribed in the Smārta ritual, whereas in the Śrauta ritual, it is merely touching (*ālambha*).
He touches the region of the navel with the formula: "Do not be joined with my stomach; sit above my navel; I place you in the belly of Indra.
Having touched it, he steps away.
"Speech in my mouth, breath in my nostrils"—with these words, he touches the seats of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) according to their respective forms.

He touches them thoroughly, meaning he touches them with his fingers moistened with water. With whichever mantra possesses a particular form or characteristic mark (*liṅga*), that mantra is used for the seat of that specific vital breath or sense organ (*indriya*). "Strength in my two arms"—with both hands together, he first touches both arms at once. "Speech in my mouth"—he touches the face along with its hair.
"May all my limbs be uninjured"—he touches all the limbs.
With the mantra ending in *mā mā hiṃsīḥ*, he [anoints] with both hands from the head down to the feet.
Having washed the vessel and filled it with water, he pours it out away from himself with the formula *diśo jinveti*.

Having washed the *prāśitra-haraṇa* vessel and filled it with water, he pours out the water; that is, he lets it fall away from himself. At the time of pouring, when the pouring is done through the vessel which has an upward handle and many apertures, the sacrificer's body remains behind the vessel. If this were an adverbial modifier, the form would have been *parāṅ ninayati*; thus, the masculine accusative *parāñcam* would be untenable.
Having filled it again, he pours it toward himself with the words, "May you gladden me.
The term *abhyātmam* is an adverbial modifier meaning "toward oneself," its vowel-final form (*-am*) being derived through a secondary suffix (*samāsāntapratyaya*).
He does not consume the portion for Brahman that has been set aside before the ritual is concluded.

The prohibition "he does not eat before the previous arrangement" is intended so that the other officiating priests (ṛtvij) do not consume their respective portions immediately after setting them aside;
He touches the *hārya* (the portion to be carried) when it is near with the formula, "Thou art the portion of Prajāpati.

There is a conjunction of both [formulas], for the recitation does not apply to each individually, as their purpose is transcendental (*adṛṣṭārtha*). When it is said, "O Brahman, we shall set forth," he [recites] over the *anūyāja* fuel-stick: "O God Savitṛ, this has been declared to thee; impel it and sacrifice it. Bṛhaspati is the Brahman; may he protect the sacrifice, may he protect the lord of the sacrifice, may he protect me. Om! May there be stability."
"Prasauti" (he impels) refers to what is drawn from a distance.

"The earth has gone to the earth; the mother has gone even to the mother. May we prosper with sons and cattle; may he who hates us be split asunder"—with this, whatever earthen vessel should break during the sacrifice, one should consecrate it with this mantra.
This is for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). It is to be performed at the time of the ritual application in the sacrifice.

Some authorities prescribe this as a universal rule, applicable not only at the time of the ritual performance but also at other times. Even on another occasion, when a different earthen vessel has been used, the Brahman priest, having been chosen for the upcoming performance, should consecrate it; for its substitute must indeed be prepared at the very beginning.
Having consumed his portion of the *brahmabhāga*, [he performs the consecration].

With the mantra previously shown, "Thou art the portion of heaven," having placed a fuel-stick and offered it, or having merely stood in worship, [he recites]: "Agni Jātavedas has sacrificed—he who is undeceivable, the inner one, who sat down first in this [sacrifice]. O Jātavedas, while sacrificing, grant us gain; being released, release for us wealth and that which is auspicious. Bestow upon us prosperity; unite us with thy favor, O thou rich in booty."

However, at the *ādhāna* (the laying of the fires), there is no utterance of *svāhā*. In the *homa*, the *svāhā* is indeed present because it follows the rules of the *darvihoma*. Then, having gone before the *āhavanīya* fire and having taken the clarified butter (*ājya*) from the vessel once into the *sruva*-ladle, three options arise. From this, it is understood that where there is no injunction for a *juhoti* offering, the *svāhā* is not used anywhere. Where the *svāhā* occurs by way of explicit recitation, that too is specifically in the case of a *darvihoma*; otherwise, the dullness of faith regarding the use of *svāhā* elsewhere is refuted by this.

In another Sūtra, having observed some underlying basis, they provide an explanation; for example, in the Āpastamba [Sūtra], it is stated that there is no *svāhākāra* in the *sūktavāka*. But according to the position of our own Sūtrakāra, there is neither such a doubt nor such a response.
He goes out by the way he came. This has been explained.
1 ga, gha, cha. 3. "The *laṃ* has been omitted. 262. Thus is prescribed the office of the Brahman for the *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices (*paśubandhas*). This concludes the office of the Brahman. 22.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the second book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Thus ends the second book in the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. 2.

The extension (*atideśa*) to the *Ādhvaryava* [section] will be explained. He indicates that there is no such explanation required here. The repetition is for the purpose of concluding the inquiry. Thus ends the eighth chapter in the second book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* composed by Mahādeva. The wise, who delight in the nectar of truth, have not reached satiety by repeatedly drinking in, through their investigation, the vast words of Satyāṣāḍha.

Those of noble intellect, being satisfied with these instructions in the Sūtra, remain established for the protection of the Lord—who is like a reed—to rescue people from the dense darkness of delusion. || 1 || By repeatedly calling to mind the best of sages for the sake of a clear exposition, this most lucid commentary on the Sūtra has indeed been attained by me, though my intellect is small. It is now offered to Viṣṇu, the Sacrificial Body, the Ancient Person; it should not be joined with sin, but rather be seen again by the virtuous, whose minds are purified by grace through their immeasurable insights. || 2 ||

Thus, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, and the office of the Brahman priest for those two have been completed. Thus ends the second book in the commentary on the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.

3.1 Now begins the first chapter of the third inquiry. I bow to Viṣṇu, the Lord, who is infinite consciousness, bliss, and infinity; who, when his action is offered [to him], leads to fruit, and when offered, also leads to liberation from bondage; and who is the destroyer of misfortune. O You whose self is the three Vedas, whose self is the three fires, whose self is the three Lords, whose self is the qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti), and whose self is the three archetypes that correspond to the three states of the individual soul—protect me from calamity!

I, with a mind full of pride, meditate upon the unborn Lord, who is praised by the gods, endowed with compassion for his devotees, and who holds the son of Hara (Ganesha) and the gift-bestowing goddess (Lakshmi) upon the lotus of his arm; who possesses a body of pure whiteness, dispels the darkness covered by ignorance, is a seer, is the goal of the earth, and is the master of Lakshmi who cuts through the fear of embodied beings. 3. Oṃ. I worship the unborn Lord, who is praised by the gods, who is compassionate toward his devotees, who holds the son of Hara and the bestower [of boons] upon the lotus of his arm, whose body possesses whiteness, who destroys the darkness covered by ignorance, who is the Seer, who is the goal of the earth, and who is the Master of Lakṣmī, the remover of the fear of embodied beings.
3.1 Now begins the first chapter of the third book.
The apprehension of Vedic words occurs through worldly memory.
Prosperity results from performing ritual acts, while no transgression occurs from their non-performance; however, this applies only to those [Vedic acts] that are not mandatory.
In this world, for those for whom there is fault in inaction and censure for being inactive, these duties are mandatory: the intent for the highest good, concern for the continuity of progeny,
honoring guests, honoring elders, and salutation when meeting.
Because they are the ones who perform it, the study of the Veda is restricted to the Brāhmaṇa, the Rājanya, and the Vaiśya.
For them alone are the sacrifices prescribed by the Brāhmaṇas, in which the completeness of the sacrifice is not prohibited—
just as [the requirements of] possessing wealth and bodily integrity [are required].

And for those whose natural characteristics and sacrificial rites are heard in the scriptures—such as it is known [from the texts]: "He chooses three; he chooses the composers of the mantras; he chooses the composers of the mantras according to the ṛṣis";

and "One should conclude the Brāhmaṇa's [sacrifice] with a Gāyatrī, the Rājanya's with a Triṣṭubh, and the Vaiśya's with a Jagatī"—for them, the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are obligatory.
Soma-sacrifices are for the Brāhmaṇa.
From the time of the *ādhāna* (the establishment of the sacred fires), the *agnihotra* and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are obligatory.
For the Niṣāda and the Rathakāra as well, from the time of the *ādhāna*, the *agnihotra* and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are likewise made mandatory.
Likewise in the case of one whose father is living.
The other [subsidiary elements] should be restricted by the opening statement and so forth.
In that regard, when the prescribed substance is absent, a substitute is used on account of similarity.
In the attainment of the purpose, there is a similarity of substance;
however, in the case of a contradiction regarding the purpose, there is a similarity of purpose.
For example, when ghee is unavailable for the anointing of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), oil is used.
The substitute is that which has desisted from prohibited acts;
for the prohibition is heard without qualification. In the case of an option, it is characterized by engagement.
In the absence of the whole, there is a substitute;
in the case of a deficiency in the measure, it should be completed with that [substitute].
In the absence of the substance, there is a substitute; in the case of a transgression of the rule, there is an expiation.
There is no substitute for ownership, a wife, a son, a country, time, fire, a deity, a ritual action, or a word. || 1 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the third book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
3.2 Now begins the second chapter of the third book.

For one who is about to establish the sacred fires, he takes out the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) from a *śamī*-enclosed *aśvattha* tree with the mantra: "That *aśvattha* which has grown upon thee, O *śamī*, together with thee—I bring that to thee by means of the sacred word (*brahman*) along with the sacrificial signs.
Alternatively, he may take them from a *aśvattha* tree itself, for it is known: "This earth is indeed the *śamī*; this *aśvattha* is its embryo."

"I gather together the sacrificial body born from the *aśvattha* tree, the bearer of oblations, the body of Agni, whose womb is peaceful and which is the heart of the *śamī* tree, for the sake of generating Agni. With these words he gathers [the wood]. Once it has been gathered, he consecrates it with the mantra: "May they bestow life upon me; may they bestow life upon the sacrificer. The lunar mansions (nakṣatras) suitable for the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) are Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, the two Punarvasūs, the two Phalgunīs, Hasta, Citrā, Viśākhā, Anūrādhā, Śroṇā, and the two Uttarā-Proṣṭhapadas. Kṛttikā is for a Brāhmaṇa; the two Uttarā-Phalgunīs and Citrā are for a Rājanya; the remaining ones are for others.
However, all of them are optional for everyone according to their specific desires.
One who desires, "May I be preeminent and endowed with spiritual luster," should establish the sacred fires under the Kṛttikās;
[but] let it be his wish that "my fire may burn down my house.
One who desires, "May I cause all growth to grow," should [establish the fires] under Rohiṇī.

One who, under the asterism Mṛgaśiras, should desire, "May I be possessed of splendor," [should sacrifice]; one who, having previously been fortunate, should desire, "May I become more wretched," [should sacrifice] under the two Punarvasus;
one who should desire, "May my offspring be desirous of giving," [should sacrifice] under the two former Phalgunīs.
He who desires, "May I be fortunate," [should perform] the two subsequent [offerings].
Some recite them in reverse order.
He who desires, "May it be given to me," [should place the offering] in his hand.
One who has rivals [should sacrifice] under Citrā;
one desiring offspring, under Viśākhā; one desiring prosperity, under Anurādhā.
One who desires prosperity [should establish the fires] under Śroṇā;
one who desires spiritual luster under the Proṣṭhapadas; or under the constellation of the Sun.
Moreover, indeed, one should establish them at whatever time faith approaches him.
Spring is the time for the Brāhmaṇa’s establishment of the sacred fires;
summer and winter are for the Rājanya;
and the rainy season is for the Rathakāra.
For a Vaiśya, it is autumn;
for all [castes], it is the cool season (śiśira).
It may be on the new moon day, the full moon day, or during the waxing fortnight.
On an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*),
where the three— the season (*ṛtu*), the lunar mansion, and the festival day (*parvan*)— concur, that is fully successful.
In case of conflict between the season and the lunar mansion, the season is more powerful.
"One who is about to sacrifice with the Soma or one who is establishing the sacred fires need not observe either the season or the lunar mansion," say some.
Having moved his residence to the east or the north, a householder should establish his fires on a sacrificial ground sloping toward the east;
a traveler should establish them in his own home.
The hall has its rafters pointing northward.
To the east of that hall, at the middle rafter, he establishes the *brāhmaudana* fire from the *aupāsana* fire while the sun is still above the trees.
At night, he offers four *śarāva* measures of *brahmaudana*.
On a red hide or a *pājaka* skin, he offers the oblation with the formula:

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I offer what is pleasing to Brahmaṇaspati for out-breath (*prāṇa*); to Brahmaṇaspati for in-breath (*apāna*); to Brahmaṇaspati for diffused breath (*vyāna*); [to] Brahmaṇaspati [for] the fourth.
Having poured it out, he cooks the *caru* in milk.
He does not rinse [the vessel] in four water-pots, nor does he pour out [the remainder].
Having cooked [the oblation], sprinkled it with clarified butter, and removed it from the fire, he offers it while reciting:

"To the impelling one, the sage, the pure, the word of praise to the bull, the vigorous; may that from which there is fear become for us free from fear; I worship the gods who are to be adored. Or he consecrates it with this mantra.
Having divided that into four parts and basted it with abundant clarified butter, he pours the remainder of the clarified butter into the pot; then,
as if not cutting off [the portions], he places them before the four officiating priests who belong to the same ancestral lineage (ārṣeya).
When they have consumed [the offerings], those who remain moist and with their leaves [are placed] in that which is left in the vessel. || 3 ||

He anoints three sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) from a marked *aśvattha* tree, each a span (*prādeśa*) in length, with butter from a vessel containing sediment or with sediment itself, [reciting]:

"You are gathered from a distinguished *aśvattha*, great ones, fashioned for the body; joined by Prajāpati, the mouth of the sacrifice, you are thrice-threefold pairs for procreation. Having consecrated them thus, he places them on the *brāhmaudanika* fire.

"May the king who dwells in heaven, accompanied by oblations and the ladle dripping with ghee, go forth toward the gods seeking their favor. "O beloved Agni, may my ladles dripping with ghee approach you; graciously accept our offerings. "O Agni, that flame of yours shines forth from the ghee when it is offered, kissing the mouths of the ladles. With these three *gāyatrī* verses, [the offering is made] for a Brāhmaṇa.

"Serve Agni with fuel"—this is the verse. "O beloved Agni, let the ladles full of ghee and bearing oblations approach you; accept my fuel-sticks. Or: "O Angiras, we strengthen you with fuel and ghee; shine brightly, O youngest one!"

Being kindled, he is now the first sacred law; he who possesses all boons is anointed with unguents. With flames for hair, purified by ghee, the purifier, the excellent sacrificer—Agni is fit to sacrifice to the gods. Ghee-faced, ghee-born is Agni; kindled by ghees, ghee is his food. The rivers carry you, dripping with ghee; drinking the ghee, perform the sacrifice well and worship the gods. "O Agni, giver of life"—with these *triṣṭubh* verses [one worships] for a kṣatriya.

O Agni, most youthful one, when you were kindled, the gods made you their messenger, the bearer of oblations; they established you as their brilliant eye, impelling it toward the swift-moving one—broad-striding, having ghee for his womb, and being invoked with offerings. O Agni, from of old, they have kindled you with ghee and excellent fuel for your favor; growing strong through the offerings and nourished by them, you spread abroad over the wide expanses of the earth. With ghee upon your face, they strive to enkindle Agni—who sits at the pole of the *ṛta*—like a friend.
"Kindling [the fire], the ruddy one, shining in the assemblies, shall lift up our thought toward the bright color"— with these *jagatī* verses, [this is] for the Vaiśya.
He maintains the *brāhmaudana* [oblation] for a year,
a season, twelve days, four days, three days, two days, or one day.

When [the disciple] has thus followed him as he departs, [the teacher], having prepared the *brahmaudana* (sacrificial rice-mess for Brahman), should anoint these fuel-sticks and place them on the fire.

If the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) does not occur for him within a year, he should cook this *brahmaudana* as prescribed, anoint these fuel-sticks (*samidh*), and having placed them [on the fire], he establishes the fires whenever he is able.
On the day before he is to establish the fires, he cooks the *brahmaudana*.
On the day before the establishment, the Adhvaryu observes the vow (*vrata*) during that night.

"He speaks no falsehood, he eats no meat, and he approaches no woman. O Agni, cause the progeny to dwell together with the quarters and with cattle. Bestow upon her those kingdoms which were Savitṛ’s at his impulsion. With these words, he binds a spotted goat at the site of the Gārhapatya fire. On this night, they keep the sacrificer awake with artistic performances.
Thus ends the second chapter of the third book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the third chapter.
Thereafter, he brings together the ritual materials according to their respective forms with the formulas beginning, "The form of Vaiśvānara."

"O Jātavedas, pour here the seed of the world, which shall be born from austerity. Having generated Agni, the bearer of oblations, from the *aśvattha* tree and [Agni] who brings bliss from the womb of the *śamī* tree—'This is your seasonal womb,' with these two verses, he heats the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) at dawn for the *brāhmaudana* rite.
'The milch-cow and the udder-bearing one, O Earth, I offer to you as your portion; through them I enkindle you,' with this verse he hands the two kindling woods to the sacrificer.
Then, having taken the fire into himself with the two verses, 'I take into myself that Agni who is ours...'"
"The immortal Agni with bright radiance drives away the demons; he is pure, purifying, and worthy of praise"—having consecrated [the site] with this, he follows after the *brāhmaudana* fire.
To the east of the site of the *brāhmaudana* fire, he digs up the ground for the *gārhapatya* hearth, saying:

"May what is being dug out remove from this earth the impure and the evil of the sacrificer. May the four quarters be auspicious to us; may Mother Earth be propitious to us for the sake of offspring."
To the south-east, at a distance of one-third [of the space] closer to the Gārhapatya fire, is the site for the Dakṣiṇāgni.
One digs out the site for the Āhavanīya fire to the east of the Gārhapatya site, outside of the other two.
It is heard in the scripture without qualification that "one should establish the fire at twelve paces."
In eight [steps] for a Brāhmaṇa, in eleven for a Rājanya, and in twelve for a Vaiśya;
twenty-four or an unlimited number in the case of a common [sacrifice].
It is known from tradition that one measures the steps with the eye.

To the east of the Āhavanīya fire is the assembly hall (*sabhā*); there is the *Sabhya* fire. To the east of the assembly hall is the dwelling (*āvasatha*); there is the *Āvasathya* fire. Thus their rites are performed in this successive order.
He sprinkles with water, saying: "May the divine waters be for our aid; may they be for our drinking; may they flow toward us for our well-being and prosperity."
Regarding the verses "ud vayaṃ tamasaḥ parastāt" and "ud u tyaṃ citram," some authorities prescribe the performance of the *khara-homa* (oblation on the mound).
The materials have been prepared: five or seven belonging to the earth, and likewise those belonging to the trees;
having divided each of these into two parts.
He pours out [the earth] for the Gārhapatya and Dakṣiṇāgni fires.
Having divided half into three parts, he places them in the eastern [fires].
He pours out sand with the formula: "Thou art the ash of Agni."
"Thou art consciousness, the upholder of desire"—with these words [he takes] the saline earth (*ūṣān*).
As he scatters them, he meditates with his mind: "Whatever is black in the moon, may that be here.

"Arise, O Agni, from the mother earth; enter the people from the great assembly-place. Thee, the swift one, the carrier of oblations, the guardian of the world, have the seekers of the gods established"—with these words [he takes] the mound of soil (*āradūtkaram*).

"That immortal essence of the earth which has come into being together with thee—that Agni gave to Agni; in that may this [sacrificer] be established"—with these words, he places a termite mound in the site of the Gārhapatya fire.
"That immortal essence of the intermediate space," [he says] for the Dakṣiṇāgni; "that immortal essence of heaven," [he says] for the Āhavanīya. For the other two fires, [he does so] silently.

"From the ocean a honeyed wave has come, bestowing wide sovereignty; may these wealthy patrons and we ourselves gather together food, strength, honey, and nourishment. With this verse he scatters earth dug up by a boar. "So great wast thou, O Agni," [he says].

"When thou, O Goddess, first expanding, didst spread abroad with thy greatness as thou wert scattered separately by the gods; thou didst make firm thyself with pebbles, and having three-fold support, didst conquer the worlds and the four quarters"—with these verses he scatters pebbles, and while scattering them, he meditates in his mind upon the destruction of him whom he hates.
Iron and Udumbara pieces serve as alternatives for those made of clay.

"O Jātavedas, those auspicious bodies of yours which are in the atmosphere and those which are on earth—with those, having united with your troop and being well-disposed, O Agni whose source is gold, carry the oblation. With these words, he places a piece of gold among the ritual materials from the north.
He hands over silver to one whom he hates; if he finds no one to hate, he should cast it away. He should not place it down and then pick it up again. 6.

"The gods have established here the moon-like Agni, who has the moon as his chariot, whose vow is to the bay steeds, Vaiśvānara, who dwells in the waters, who finds the light of heaven, the one who plunges forward, the swift, who is encompassed by powers, the impetuous, and the highly glorious"—with these words he consecrates the fire at sunset.

The lotus leaf, the *udumbara*, the *śamī*, the *vikaṅkata*, the *aśvattha*, the tree struck by lightning, and the *palāśa*—or else whatever other trees there are besides the lotus leaf and the *vikaṅkata*—these are the "wood-born" (*vānaspatya*) ones. With the verse, "From this [earth] Agni was first born," he scatters [the wood] once upon each [of the fires].
With the verse, "O you whose bodies are dear," he mixes the saline earth and the sand.
With the verses, "I mix your hearts together; may your minds be united; may your breath be united," he mixes all the ritual materials.

With the formula, "I spread the *ṛta* as the soil upon the earth; upon the *ṛta* I place the fire; upon the truth I place the fire; with the vigor of heaven, with the greatness of the earth, with the nourishment of the intermediate space, I place you, possessing all cattle," he arranges the mixed materials.

While the rays are rising, having removed the ashes of the *brāhmaudana* [sacrificial rice] vessel and having placed the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) with the *daśahotṛ* formula, he churns the fire while standing near it with the mantra:

"O Agni, be born together with Agni, together with progeny, together with wealth, together with nourishment, together with cattle, together with Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*). He then stands by the horse.
While the fire is being churned, he causes the sacrificer to recite the *Caturhotṛ* formulas.
He consecrates the fire as soon as it has been produced with the mantra: "Agni, the Hotṛ, has gone forth, the first for the ancients; the purifying, the bright, worthy of praise.

He takes hold of the fire once it has been produced with the mantra: "Mortals have generated the immortal one, the tireless, the swift, the strong-jawed; may the ten sisters, the maidens moving together, grasp the male newborn. Thus ends the third Paṭala in the third Praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
3.4 Now begins the fourth chapter.

Having taken that [fire], with the first two *vyāhṛtis* according to the ritual for establishing the seers (*ṛṣi*), with the first two *sārparājñī* verses, and with the first *gharmaśiras*, [he establishes it] with the formula: "In breath I establish you, the immortal, as a consumer of food for the sake of eating food; as a protector for the sake of protection."

"O Agni, lord of the house, seated in the assembly, find a world for the sacrificer from heaven, from earth, and from the intermediate space. Sit upon the head of the earth, in the world worthy of sacrifice. "O Agni, whoever is an enemy to us, whoever is an outsider who seeks to harm us—here I place him down by means of you. With these words, he establishes [the fire] upon the ritual materials at the site of the Gārhapatya fire.
He does not lift himself up so high as to be above [the fire], nor beyond ear-level; he holds himself [at that height]. He lifts up the fuel and places the supporting ladles beneath it.
While the *upayamana* is being held,
the *Āgnīdhra*, having brought a common fire or having produced it by friction, establishes the *Dakṣiṇāgni*.

With the second *vyāhṛti*, according to the *ṛṣi*-based installation; with the second and third *sārparājñī* verses; and with the second *gharmaśiras*: "O Agni, source of food, bringer of bliss, most auspicious one, from heaven, from earth, and from the atmosphere, find a world for the sacrificer! Sit upon the head of the earth, in the world worthy of sacrifice!"—while the *yajñāyajñiya* is being sung—he establishes [the fire] on the materials in the site of the *dakṣiṇāgni* with the formula: "O Agni, whoever is hostile to us, whoever is hostile and seeks to harm us—this one I place under you."
If there be a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra who is as well-nourished as a god, one should fetch [fuel] from his house and establish the fires.
From that time forward, one should not eat his food.
For one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), [one should fetch fuel] from the top of a tree that is burning.
[The offering] for one desiring food is from the frying pan.

With the verses, "O powerful Agni, bring hither that dear body of yours which is purifying among cattle; O powerful Agni, bring hither that dear body of yours which is purifying in the waters; O powerful Agni, bring hither that dear body of yours which is bright in the sun," he causes the sacrificer to recite these forms of Agni into the right ear of the horse. With the verses, "Stride forth, you are great, the knower of the altar for the sake of men; be watchful in the three worlds with offspring and wealth," and "Stride forward toward the eastern direction, led by Agni," they proceed eastward with the horse in front, accompanied by these three [verses].
First he carries it at knee-height, then at navel-height, and then at mouth-height;
thus he does not separate from the fire and the sun.

He carries the fire first and follows behind it, or he carries it while as if enclosing it from the south. Having placed gold in the middle of the path with the mantra, "Thou art the vault of heaven, the firmament, the foundation, the stepping-stone," and having given a boon, he steps across.

"O Bṛhaspati, drive around with your chariot"—with these words, the Brahman priest turns the chariot from the south, or [he turns] the chariot-wheel. As long as it takes for the wheel to revolve three times—six times for one who is an enemy—he causes the horse to step upon the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*) with its right forefoot, while facing eastward; or he does so from the side, or from the north of the materials, so that the embers of the fire once established will fall upon the footprint.
Having led the horse around clockwise with the verse, "When you first neighed at being born," he causes it to step upon that same footprint while facing westward.

In the absence of a horse, one should place the footprint of an ox; however, it should be one that pulls from the left side, for its significance is the same as before. While the ox is being held facing westward, he should recite over it: "That which is of heaven and that which is of earth—when the two worlds, in mutual agreement, came together, may Jātavedas sit upon their back, bringing welfare to offspring and comfort to the body. Thus he consecrates it.

With all the *vyāhṛtis*, according to the ritual installation of the seers, with the first and last verses of the *Sārparājñī* hymns, and with the final *gharmaśiras* verse: "I establish you, O Prāṇa, in the immortal, as an eater of food for the sake of food, as a protector for the sake of protection. O Agni, sovereign, one-footed Aja, Āhavanīya fire, find a world from heaven, from earth, and from the intermediate space for the sacrificer. Sit upon the head of the earth, in the world worthy of sacrifice. O Agni, whoever is our adversary, whoever is our enemy who seeks to harm us—here I place him down by means of you."

He establishes [the fire] upon the materials at the site of the Āhavanīya while the *yajñāyajñiya*, the *bṛhat*, and the *śyaita* are being sung; once it has been established, he sings the *vāravantīya*. According to some, the Sāmans are prohibited at the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*). He pays homage to the established Āhavanīya with the formula: "It has attained, it has pervaded; it has pervaded the full span of life."
He does not touch [the vessel] unless it has been offered into the fire.

It must be appeased with clarified butter and herbs. Having placed the herbs into the clarified butter, [he recites]: "O Agni, that body of yours which is purifying (*pavamānā*), which is dear among cattle, which is on the earth, which is in the fire, which is in the *Rathantara* [Sāman], and which is in the *Gāyatrī* metre—this I secure for you; to that body of yours, *svāhā*! O Agni, that body of yours which is purifying (*pāvakā*), which is dear in the waters, which is in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), which is in the wind (*vāyu*), which is in the *Vāmadevya* [Sāman], and which is in the *Triṣṭubh* metre—this I secure for you; to that body of yours, *svāhā*!"

"O Agni, that pure and beloved body of yours which is in the sun, which is in the sky, which is in the Āditya, which is in the *bṛhat* [sāman], which is in the thunder, and which is in the *jagatī* metre—this [body] of yours I now secure; to that body of yours, svāhā! Having offered these three *pavamāna* oblations, he brings a common fire, or kindles one by friction, or takes it from the *āhavanīya*, and establishes the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires.
According to some, the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires are prohibited.
With the three verses beginning "O Agni, you purify the lifespans," he places three fuel-sticks of *aśvattha* wood, one in each [fire]. 10.
"Agni is the seer, the purifying one, the domestic priest of the five peoples; we seek him, the possessor of great wealth"—thus some recite the third [verse].

"From the ocean a wave rich in sweetness has arisen; it attained immortality together with the *upāṃśu* [cup]. That which is the secret name of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is the tongue of the gods, the navel of immortality. Let us proclaim that name with clarified butter at this sacrifice; let us maintain it with our homages. May the Brahman hear the hymn being recited; the four-horned bull has bellowed this. "Four are his horns, three are his feet, two are his heads, and seven are his hands."

"Bound in three ways, the bull bellows; the great god has entered mortals"—with this verse, he places a fuel-stick of *śamī* wood, anointed with ghee, on each of the three hearths. "O Agni, kindled, shine before us"—with this verse, he places a fuel-stick of *udumbara* wood. "We would worship thee in thy highest birth, O Agni"—with this verse, a fuel-stick of *vikaṅkata* wood. "That wonderful [splendor] of Savitṛ, the most excellent"—with this verse, a fuel-stick of *śamī* wood. Some teachers prescribe placing the *śamī* stick first and the *vikaṅkata* stick afterwards.
Following the procedure for the morning *agnihotra*, he silently offers the morning *agnihotra*.

Having cleansed the *juhū* and the *sruva* spoons, and having filled the *sruk* with either four, eight, or twelve ladlings of clarified butter, he offers the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verse, "Seven are thy... (RV 3.27.5).
For some, however, he prescribes that the *agnihotra* be performed silently. [The mantra:

"Those fires which are in heaven, those which are on earth, coming together and yielding nourishment and vigor—may those fires, having been offered to, being pleased, and having become partakers of the oblation, bestow wealth upon us and go back again to their own world, *svāhā*. This is the second [mantra]. 11.
Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the third praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the fifth paṭala in the third praśna:
At that very time, one commences the rites beginning with the anvādhāna for the cake on eight potsherds (aṣṭākapāla) dedicated to Agni.

Having performed that which was previously prescribed prior to the sprinkling, he digs up the ground for the gaming board in the middle of the assembly hall, sprinkles it, places the dice upon it, arranges them, spreads them out, and having placed gold among the dice, he offers an oblation with the verse: "He who sits down, firm in his vows.

Having placed gold in the middle of the assembly hall within the dwelling, he offers an oblation with the verse: "Now indeed Brahmaṇaspati utters the hymn worthy of praise, in which Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, and the gods have made their dwellings."
"May Ahi Budhnya hear us, as well as Aja Ekapād, Pṛthivī, and Samudra;

may all the gods who increase the *ṛta*, being invoked, and the hymns recited by the sages, carry these [offerings]. O King, rejoice in the oblation! Having thus consecrated the dwelling, he gives a hundred nuts to the sacrificer.
Having won the game among them, he plays for victory.
While the rice grains are being offered to the members of the assembly, he issues the command: "Strike the joints of the cow being gambled for!
He worships the fires with the two *klṛptisāmanasī* verses appropriate to the season, beginning with "May heaven and earth be prepared" and "Those which are the fires.
He proceeds with the rites of the offering to Agni beginning with the sprinkling; it concludes in the established manner.
One sacrifices with the Pavamāna offerings at the end of a year, a season, a month, a half-month,

on the twelfth day, the fourth day, the third day, the second day, on the next day, or immediately. For one who is about to sacrifice with Soma or is about to establish the sacred fires, the ritual procedure for the Pavamāna offerings lasts for a year.
One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna, to Agni Pāvaka, and to Agni Śuci.
This may be performed on a single sacrificial grass mat or on separate mats.
Alternatively, having first offered the oblation for the first deity, one may combine the subsequent two.
One should perform the rites with a common *tantra* using an eight-potherd cake for Agni.

One subsequently offers an eleven-potherd cake for Agni-Soma, an eleven-potherd cake for Agni-Viṣṇu, an eleven-potherd cake for Indra-Agni, a pap cooked in ghee for Aditi, and a pap cooked in ghee for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa at the threefold increase. There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses for Aditi. Having set aside the portion of the *iḍā* for Aditi for the Brahman priest, everyone consumes it, as do the portions resulting from the fourfold division.

One who is about to begin the Agnihotra, having mentally recited the Daśahotṛ formula and offered the oblation with the cup (graha), performs the evening Agnihotra according to the procedure for the evening Agnihotra with the [appropriate] mantra; he places the first Agnihotra vessel down with the Vyāhṛtis, and likewise at the end of the year.
Now begins the commencement of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

One who is commencing the New and Full Moon sacrifices, on the day of fasting (*aupavasathya*) of the preceding lunar phase, having mentally recited the *caturhotṛ* formula and offered it along with its *graha*, and having offered the two *sārasvata* oblations with the verses "Full behind" (*pūrṇā paścāt*) and "That which the gods placed" (*yad te devā adadhuḥ*),
he performs the *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice.

One who desires, "May I be fortunate and an eater of food," should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu, a pap to Sarasvatī, a cake on twelve potsherds to Sarasvant, and a cake on eight potsherds to Bhagin. Some authorities prescribe the offering to Bhagin as a regular (obligatory) rite.
Before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, he performs twelve Jaya oblations with ghee taken in twelve ladlings, saying: "Citta svāhā! Cittis svāhā! and so forth.
The thirteenth oblation is offered with the formula: "Prajāpati [gave] the Jayas to Indra."

"O Agni, giver of strength, bestow power and vigor upon me as I advance; for one who has been cursed, grant immunity from being cursed; for this community, grant preeminence. With these words, he performs the fourteenth [offering]. "May that splendor belong to whichever community I hate"—thus it becomes as if variegated within his own self.
Alternatively, one need not perform the Anvārambhaṇīyā; he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni.
This is the unmodified rule for one establishing the fires at the New Moon sacrifice.

On the day of the fast preceding the full moon of the first *parvan*, having established the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) and concluded with the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, he performs at that very time the *caturhotṛ* formulas, the two *sārasvata* oblations, and the *anvārambhaṇīyā* offering. On the following day, he sacrifices with the *paurṇamāsa* [sacrifice]; he places the sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) down with the *vyāhṛti*s; and likewise [he does so] after a year.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the third book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

Now begins the sixth chapter. We shall now explain the re-establishment of the sacred fires (punarādheya); its ritual procedure has been explained by that of the initial establishment of the fires (agnyādheya).

Having established the sacred fires, if within this year he suffers a loss of wealth or the death of a son, or if he comes into conflict with his own body, or if he does not prosper, he should perform the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*).

Having sacrificed at the full moon, on the new moon day he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara, if he intends to extinguish the fires—so say some.
He should subsequently offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Soma, a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Apsumat, and a pap to Mitra.

Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering: "O Agni, that dear form of yours which dwells in the cattle as the purifying one (*pavamānā*), enter the earth together with it; by means of the *rathantara* chant and the *gāyatrī* metre, bring us great prosperity from there. O Agni, that purifying form of yours which is dearer to the mind—your dear form—enter the intermediate space together with it; by means of the *vāmadevya* chant and the *triṣṭubh* metre, provide us with strength from there and increase the domestic sacrifice. O Agni, that bright form of yours which is in the sun—together with that [form]..."

Enter the sky with the *Bṛhat* Sāman, with the *Jagatī* metre; from there, protect us with rain. O Agni, those portions (*vibhakti*) of yours which Indra and Sukra brought hither—sit upon them, within those flames, as the ash of Vaiśvānara. O Agni, those wish-fulfilling portions of yours that have been gathered together—with those, milk for us here our desires: offspring, prosperity, and wealth. O Agni, those wooden materials of yours that have been gathered together—go with them to the trees, to your own womb, in due order.

Having offered seven oblations with the verses: "Agni has come as he entered the world in his own abode," "I have approached the gods, free from the sin of violence, together with my mind," he releases the blazing fires. He remains with the fires released for as long as it takes to perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices, or for a year, or for twelve days.
Rohiṇī, the two Punarvasūs, and Anurādhā are the lunar mansions for re-establishing the fires.
One establishes the fires during the rainy season or in autumn.
At midday, all the ritual materials, both prepared and unprepared, are brought forward. He establishes the Gārhapatya fire with all the Sārparājñī verses.
With *darbha* grass, including the roots, that have been blown about for a year, he draws out the blazing *āhavanīya* fire from the *gārhapatya*.
He establishes the *dakṣiṇāgni* with the verse, "When thou, being angry, didst scatter [the seed] beyond," and the *āhavanīya* with the verse, "That which was scattered by thy wrath.
With the mantra, "May the mind, the light, enjoy [it]," he pays homage to the established *āhavanīya*.

"May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus kindle you again"—with these words he adds fuel. "May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus kindle you again"—with these words he adds fuel. "May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus kindle you again; may the Brahmans, O leader of wealth, [kindle you] with sacrifices. Those offerings which were made at dawn and at sunset, those sacrificial portions I unite with the oblation of ghee, Svāhā!"—with this he offers the first oblation. "May the mind, as light, enjoy [the offering]"—with this he offers the second.

Having cleansed the *juhū* and the *sruva* ladles, and having filled the *sruk* with either four, eight, or twelve portions of clarified butter, he offers the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verse, "Seven are thy...
He offers a cake on eight potsherds or five potsherds to Agni in place of the cake on eight potsherds belonging to the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* sacrifice.
For this offering, everything is performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) up to the final *anūyāja*.
In the four *prayāja* offerings, he inserts four case-forms of the word "Agni"—namely, *agnāgne*, *agnāvagne*, *agnināgne*, and *agnimagna*—before the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
He offers an oblation with the formula *punarūrjā* before the *prayājas*; some authorities state it should be offered after them.
In the invocations (*nigama*) for the *ājyabhāga* offering to Agni, one should employ the form containing the word *vṛdhanvat*.
[He recites] "Pavamāna" for the Soma cup.
He offers an oblation with the verse "Together with wealth" before the after-offerings (*anūyāja*); some authorities state it should be offered after them.
For two of the after-offerings, he places two case-endings [in the formulas]: "The god in Agni, the god in Agni."

He gives the loud command for the final after-offering (*anūyāja*). One who has established the sacred fires again after having let them go out should offer a cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni and Varuṇa as a subsequent oblation (*anunirvāpa*). He should offer these oblations: "Leka, Saleka, Suleka; Keta, Saketa, Suketa; Vivasvat, Aditi, Devajūti."

From the time of the fire-laying (ādhāna) until the end of one's life, the Gārhapatya and Dakṣiṇāgni fires are maintained, as are the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires. Regarding the Dakṣiṇāgni, if it has gone out, there is the procedure for churning; if it is produced by churning, it is established; if it is brought from elsewhere, it is brought for each specific purpose. One who has attained prosperity (gataśrī) maintains the Āhavanīya fire constantly, or so does one who desires long life.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the third book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the seventh chapter:
We shall now explain the Agnihotra.
For him, he draws the *āhavanīya* fire from the blazing *gārhapatya* fire every evening and morning:
at sunset for the evening *agnihotra*, and at dawn for the morning *agnihotra*.
Or they may maintain it throughout the night.

When the command "Lift him up" has been given, [he says]: "With speech as the Hotṛ, with breath as the Udgātṛ, with sight as the Adhvaryu, with mind as the Brahman, and with hearing as the Agnīdh—by these five divine officiating priests (ṛtvij), I lift you up. I abandon death; I establish you with immortality. Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! Being lifted up, lift me up from whatever evil I have done unknowingly or knowingly. Whatever sin or evil has been committed by day—being lifted up, release me from all that. Thus at evening. "Whatever sin or evil has been committed by night—being lifted up, release me from all that. Thus in the morning.

"I offer the oblation of nectar into the nectar; I offer Agni upon the earth for the conquest of nectar. Through that, I conquer the infinite desire which Prajāpati first conquered. Saying "Svāhā! To Agni in Agni," he establishes [the offering] in its place in the evening. Saying "Svāhā! To Sūrya in Agni," he does so in the morning.

He performs the evening *agnihotra* when the sun has just set after seeing the stars, or at nightfall. He performs the morning *agnihotra* at dawn, before sunrise, or once it has risen; according to some, it should be offered at the moment speech begins to flow.

At this time, all the ritual actions are performed, except for the removal [of the embers]. He makes the fires ready by sweeping around them: with "O Agni Gṛhapati, be pure," he prepares the Gārhapatya; with "O Agni Vahni, be pure," the Dakṣiṇāgni; and with "O Agni Samrāj, be pure," the Āhavanīya. The decorations are performed first in the evening, and the decorations are performed afterwards in the morning.
They prescribe various ornaments for both [the sacrificer and his wife].
He strews grass around the fires as in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

He sets out the implements for the *agnihotra*: a *sruva* ladle made of *khadira* wood, an *agnihotra-havaṇī* spoon made of *vikaṅkata* wood that is without wheels, not turned over, not made by a *śūdra*, and with its bowl facing upwards; and the *agnihotra-sthālī* pot.
To the south of the dwelling, she stands with dignity.
