Having called her—"O Ida, come! O Aditi, come! O Sarasvatī, come! O Gauḥ, come!"—he lets the calf loose with the formula, "Thou art Pūṣan," or he addresses it as it runs.
Turning toward the east or the north, someone other than a Śūdra milks her; he does not touch her, or he follows her movements as they occur.

One should milk the two front [teats] for the eldest son of the eldest wife, or for one who has attained prosperity; one should milk the two rear [teats] for the youngest son of the youngest wife, or for one who desires to thrive.
Having milked into a vessel, he pours it into a pot, or he milks directly into the pot.
For one desiring cattle, he should offer the milk of both [teats], having first placed the front [milk] on the fire and then pouring the rear [milk] into it. 16.
"May I sprinkle you with *ṛta* through *satya*," he says while sprinkling in the evening; "may I sprinkle you with *satya* through *ṛta*," he says in the morning.

Having sprinkled the Āhavanīya fire, he sprinkles the Gārhapatya, and then the Dakṣiṇāgni; or having sprinkled the Gārhapatya, he sprinkles the Dakṣiṇāgni, and then the Āhavanīya. With the formula, "Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; I lead thee for the continuity of the sacrifice; for the continuity of the sacrifice, thee," he causes a continuous stream of water to flow from the Gārhapatya to the Āhavanīya.

Taking up the *upaveṣa* with the formula, "Thou art bold," he pushes out the embers from the *gārhapatya* fire toward the north with the formula, "The common danger that has arisen, together with that [danger] which we hate, do you resort to prosperity," or alternatively, "O makers of beings, you are; the common danger that has arisen, together with that [danger] which we hate.
He makes them separate.

"O Jātavedas, enjoy this oblation, the footprint of Iḍā, rich in ghee, moving and unmoving. May there be delight here for those seven domestic animals of all forms, and may there be nourishment. With these words, he places the Agnihotra milk upon them.
It should be offered when it has reached the surface.
Or, immediately after placing it on the fire, he kindles a blade of grass and looks at it, saying: "You are the source; may I abound with offspring and cattle."
With the formula, "May I not lead thee away from thy own," he sprinkles it with water using the *sruva* ladle, or with the formula, "Thou art immortality.
He may sprinkle it with the rinsing-water from the *godohana* vessel; he should sprinkle it with a single drop for one who desires cattle.
It should remain unsprinkled for one who desires splendor, or for one practicing sorcery, or for one wishing to cross over [difficulties].
If he should desire, "May a hero be born to me in my kingdom," he looks at it again just as before.
He carries fire around it three times with a firebrand, saying, "The Rakṣas is excluded," or with the verse, "The Lord of Prayer has gone around.
Saying, "Thou art the Gharma, the bestower of increase of wealth; bestow vigor here," he carries it out toward the north while making a path.

He holds [the embers] with the formula: "Grant me offspring. He pushes back the embers on the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "The danger from people has been driven away; together with that [danger], may we drive away him whom we hate; may it be well-made," thinking, "O makers of beings, stay here," or "for the crop of the sacrificer.
Having taken up the *sruva* ladle and the *agnihotrahavaṇī* spoon with the formula, "At the impulse of the god... (devasya tvā...).
He heats [the ladle] over the Āhavanīya or the Gārhapatya fire with the formula, "It has been heated.

He cleanses the *agnihotra-havaṇī* (the Agnihotra-offering ladle) with the formula, "Thee, the well-winged one, made of well-winged [wood]; thou art a golden shaft, with immortal leaves, the stream of sacrifices. He cleanses both, saying, "May the sacrificer and his wife be unharmed."

"I shall carry up the oblation for the gods; [I shall rescue] the sacrificer from evil," with these words he addresses [the fire] in the evening. While traveling, he should say to himself, "Carry it up. He draws four ladlefuls [of ghee], saying: "I carry thee up for Agni and for the Earth; I carry thee up for Vāta and for the Atmosphere; I carry thee up for Sūrya and for the Sky; I carry thee up for the Waters and for the Plants"; with the last formula, he draws twice for one who offers five portions.
"Bhūriḍā, bhuva iḍā, suvariḍā, karadiḍā," or "jvaladiḍā"—thus [the mantras] for those who perform the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvattin*).
For whichever of his sons he might desire, "May I prosper through this one," for him he should draw up the full [portion].
If he should desire, "May they all be equal," he should draw up equal portions for all.
He touches the [milk] drawn out by the *daśahotṛ* formula, or he does not touch it.

At evening, he touches the vessel from which the [milk] has been drawn out with the formula: "In harmony with the gods who go at evening; may the gods who go at evening bring me well-being; may I be united with cattle. At dawn, he touches it with the formula: "In harmony with the gods who go at dawn; may the gods who go at dawn bring me well-being; may I be united with cattle.
When he draws out the barley-grains for the cattle, saying "Grant me cattle," he sets that down.
Having brought it from the east or the north, he places it to the west of the Gārhapatya fire; so say some.
Having taken hold of one, two, or three fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood, each a span (*prādeśa*) in length, at the top of the ladle-handle,
he carries them across the flame of the *gārhapatya* fire with the formula, "Go through the wide atmosphere. Running forward to the east, he recites the *daśahotṛ* formula.
He holds it steady at the middle with the formula, "For Agni Vaiśvānara, thee!
He lifts it up with "For Vāta, thee! He places it down among the plants to the west of the Āhavanīya fire with "Grant me life! He lays on a fuel-stick with "This is thy fuel, O Agni."

"Thou art golden, the beam of the heavenly world, the bridge for crossing over; thus I place thee"—or "Thou art the Sūdadohas of this [world]"; "Thou art silver, with gold within, Agni by light, full of light, leading to heaven, the wish-fulfilling cow, imperishable for the sake of imperishability, for attainment, pervasion, complete attainment, for the fulfillment of desire, for the heavenly world, for immortality—thus I place thee, the brick of night," he says at evening. "Thou art tawny, with silver within, Sūrya by light, full of light, leading to heaven..."

"In order to milk the wish-granting cow, for the imperishable, for the attainment of the imperishable, for pervasion, for completion, for the fulfillment of desire, for heaven, for the world, and for immortality, I place thee, O brick, as a bringer of prosperity"—thus [he says] in the morning.

"Thou art lightning; drive away my evil. I approach the immortal truth. May faith be in me"—having touched water with this, when it has become dark-grey, he then offers the oblation into the blazing fire.
Or when the flame has subsided and it seems to flicker as it smokes, for one desiring a village,
he should offer a fuel-stick two finger-breadths from its base, letting the butter flow down along it.

At evening, [he offers] with the *hotrā* formula: "Bhūḥ bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā! At dawn, [he offers] with the *hotrā* formula: "Bhūḥ bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā!
Some prescribe a combined offering (*saṃsṛṣṭahoma*):
at evening, "Agni is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā! and at dawn, "Sūrya is light, light is Agni, svāhā!"
With the words, "May it bestow radiance upon me," he places [the spoon] back among the plants.
Taking the smearings, with the words, "For the plants, thee; invigorate the plants," he wipes the smearings onto the sacrificial grass to the north.
With the words, "O Agni Gṛhapati, do not consume me; place immortality within me; may I attain offspring and light," he gazes at the Gārhapatya fire.
Having passed over [the first] silently, he offers a further oblation on the northern kindling-stick with the mantra:
"In harmony, O Jātavedas, from heaven and from earth, enjoying this oblation of ghee, partake of it, Svāhā! He should offer with clarified butter wherever Paśupati might cause harm to the cattle.
If he should strike that [offering] too much, he should offer with: "O Agni of ill-formed body, of ghee, Svāhā!"

If he should omit [the offering] for twelve nights, he should offer every evening with milk. If he should omit that as well, he should first place two [pots of milk] on the fire and then pour the later one [into the other]. If he should omit even that, it is not to be heeded.
With the words "For food, thee," he wipes off the smearings in the evening;
with the words "For strength, thee," he wipes them off in the morning.
If he should desire of someone, "May he become more wretched," he should offer the later portion in greater quantity and the earlier portion in lesser quantity.
If one should desire of someone, "May he become neither worse nor better," one should offer for him equally.
If one should desire of someone, "May he become more prosperous," having offered the first [oblation] in a smaller measure, one should offer the subsequent one in a greater measure.
He leaves over more for eating.
Having offered the oblation, he should gaze at the great [fire] with the mantra:
"O Rudra, be gracious; O Arbha, be gracious; O Dhūrta, be gracious; homage be unto you, O Paśupati; do not harm me. With the offering-ladle, he thrice moves the fire upward in a winding motion.
Having set down the *sruva* ladle and taken the residue, he smears the residue on a mound to the south, saying: "For the fathers, thee; gladden the fathers! Having touched water, [he continues].
Pūṣan shall obtain it; having eaten twice with two fingers and having sipped water, he eats again.
Taking the offering-ladle and the *darbha* grass, he steps out toward the north, saying:

"May there be for me generative seed, Agni-like, possessing ten heroes and a full retinue, for my well-being. May it win for me the self, win offspring, win cattle, win safety, win the world, and win rain. May Agni make my progeny abundant; may you bestow upon us food, milk, and seed. May he maintain for us the increase of wealth, nourishment, and vigor. (18)
With a ladle whose handle points either eastward or northward, he sips water twice and licks his lips twice, saying either, "For the embryos, thee!
Delight the embryos! or, "May there be for me solar seed and procreation," at the morning [libation].
Having filled the *sruk* with water, he pours it out [on the ground] with the words, "For the serpents, thee! Refresh the serpents!
Having sipped water and having washed the *sruk* with *darbha* grass, [he sets it aside].
Having filled [the ladle], he pours out water with the formula: "Satisfy the serpents; satisfy the ants.
He pours out a second time with "Satisfy the serpent-deities"; a third time with "To the beings, svāhā!"; and a fourth time with "To the great gods, svāhā!
Having filled the ladle with water, he pours it out behind the Āhavanīya fire or behind the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "I offer nectar upon the earth, svāhā!"
"From the houses, may you bring joy to the houses"—with these words, he places a portion of it into the joined palms of his wife.
If the wife is not present, he places the whole upon the ground. Having warmed his hand, he pours it into the ladle; or, having heated the ladle, he pours it into his hand.
With the formula, "I place you for the Seven Seers; gladden the Seven Seers," he points the ladle toward the north.
Having set down the ladle and returned, he offers oblations with the *sruva* spoon into the Gārhapatya and Dakṣiṇāgni fires, placing a fuel-stick after each offering.

He offers two oblations into the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "May the Lord of Prosperity bestow prosperity upon me; may he maintain for us wealth, nourishment, food, and strength. To Agni Gṛhapati, Lord of Wealth, Lord of Cattle, Lord of Prosperity, [to him] who is desire, [and] who is the eater of food, svāhā!"
"O Lord of Food, give us food"—with these two verses, he should offer oblations in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire;
or alternatively, he may offer four oblations in the Gārhapatya fire and four in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire; or indeed, he need not offer them at all.
"Agni has glowed; he has offered his own body. O Heaven and Earth, bestow vigor upon us! Having smeared a blade of grass with the butter in the pot, he throws it into the Āhavanīya fire, or not.
He pours out the rinsing water within the altar with the formula, "For Heaven and Earth, thee! May Heaven and Earth quicken thee! He sprinkles around as before.
"Shine! May you shine! You have shone for us!"—with these words he kindles [the fire].

One desiring splendor should offer with clarified butter; one desiring cattle, with milk; one desiring sensory power, with curds; one desiring vigor, with rice grains; one desiring a village, with barley-gruel; one desiring the enjoyment of food, with cooked rice; one desiring heroism, with meat; and one desiring spiritual luster, with Soma.
Whatever else is done after the placing on the fire and before the pouring out [of the remnants] is performed with curds, rice grains, and Soma.
At the time of pouring water [into the fire], one should pour clarified butter using two *darbha* blades; he cooks the gruel for the sprinkling. As it is with the gruel, so it is with the meat.
On the festival day (*parvan*), a Kṣatriya should offer his *agnihotra*; not in the intervals between.

Whatever food is prepared in his house, from that they bring [a portion] to a Brāhmaṇa first; that becomes his offered *agnihotra*. He who, speaking like the truth and the sacred law (*ṛta-satya*), would be as if performing the *soma* sacrifice, for him one should always offer the *agnihotra*. Thus ends the seventh chapter in the third book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
3.8 Now begins the eighth chapter.
We shall explain the departure from home when it is without one's house.

However, if one is departing with his household and stays elsewhere for five, nine, or ten nights, or wherever he stays for nine nights, he should, upon returning to that dwelling, dwell there for one night and offer the oblation to Vāstoṣpati.
He places all the utensils in the vehicles; whatever else they intend to carry, that they load first,
or they remove it from that place before the offering has been made.

When all [the oxen] have been yoked, the one on the right is yoked to the Agniṣṭha post; the thong of the left one has been passed around and is still attached. Then, having recited the verse addressed to Vāstoṣpati, he offers with the following verse. He does not add fuel after the offering has been made.
Without having washed away the embers, he departs.
"‘This is your seasonal womb’—having thus consigned the fires into the two separate fire-drills (*araṇī*), he departs.

Now they say: ‘If one who has consigned the fires into the two fire-drills should perish, his fire would be extinguished; it would have to be re-established. [Therefore, he says: ‘O Agni, with that body of yours which is worthy of sacrifice, come and ascend to yourself, bestowing upon us many human riches. Having become the sacrifice, sit upon the sacrifice, O Jātavedas, in your own womb; being born from the earth, come to this dwelling! Having thus consigned the fires into himself, he departs. Wherever he dwells, there he churns the fire before sunset.”

"Descend, O Jātavedas, you who know the way, so that you may carry the oblation to the gods; bestow upon us long life, progeny, and wealth; shine for us unceasingly within our home"—having thus caused him who was mounted upon himself to descend into the two kindling woods (*araṇis*), he churns [the fire].
Or, having brought a common worldly fire, he causes him to descend into that.

"This is the better dwelling-place which you have come to; may heaven and earth be gracious to me; may the quarters be free from disease for me—rich in cattle, rich in wealth, rich in horses, rich in gold, rich in men, and rich in heroic sons, Svāhā!"—he offers this oblation when [the descent] has been completed.
We shall explain the *darvihoma* offerings.
Where it is enjoined that "one offers" (*juhoti*), and where there is the utterance of *svāhā*, that is a *darvihoma*.

Having gone around the front of the *āhavanīya* fire with clarified butter taken once silently, the *adhvaryu*, standing to the south, offers into the *āhavanīya* with the *juhū* ladle while pronouncing *svāhā*.

In the case of groups of oblations numbering two or more, having taken [the fuel-sticks] for each oblation and having placed the fuel-sticks upon the fire for each oblation, one offers them separately.
Where one should enjoin a rite by means of a group of mantras, there one should offer the oblation for each individual mantra.
We shall explain the specific applications regarding the word "juhoti" (he offers).
In a place made by oneself, in a barren spot, in a cleft, in a clump of darbha grass, or at the base of a tree stump—thus [it is said]. || 20 ||
If the Āhavanīya fire is removed because there is no fire, one offers the oblation in that very same place.
The principal offerings of the New and Full Moon sacrifices are prescribed for the subsequent sequence, with the exception of those pertaining to the Soma sacrifice and the Darvihomas;
these [offerings] possess their own specific ritual characteristics.
Modification occurs due to similarity; it would be understood through an indicative mark (*liṅga*),
whether by the commonality of the deity or the commonality of the oblation, wherever the oblation is offered.
In case of conflict, the similarity of the oblation is more powerful.
For example, the *puroḍāśa* dedicated to Viṣṇu.

However, those [oblations] with a single deity that are modifications (*vikāra*) of the *āgneya* sacrifice follow the original deity (*prakṛtidevatā*), except for those [specifically] assigned; as in the case of the *saumya* porridge (*caru*) and the *aindra* *puroḍāśa*.
Now, as for the others, [the rules apply] to the Agniṣomīya or the Aindrāgna.
When there is a conflict of subsidiaries regarding specific properties that are integrated into the subsequent performance (uttarā tantra), the status of being primary (mukhyatva) is more powerful.
Due to the status of being primary, the greater number (bhūyastva) prevails.
From abundance comes the locus;
from the locus comes the rule;
from the rule comes the subordinate member.
The primary act is stronger than the subsidiary.
When there is a conflict between the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) and a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the New and Full Moon sacrifices are more powerful.
However, those [procedures] of the *iṣṭi* and animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*) which are directly perceived [in the texts] apply specifically to them.

The *iṣṭis* and *paśubandhas*, which have the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as their archetype (*prakṛti*), possess their own specific characteristics (*svadharma*) and constitute the general modification (*sāmānyavikāra*).

Substances connected with a ritual action in the archetype acquire their properties through that connection; when the action is absent, the substance along with its properties ceases to apply. For example, the threshing of grains does not apply to *kṛṣṇala* berries.
Furthermore, when another substance is joined with that purpose, there would be an intrusion of properties:
the property of being a pot-sherd would apply to the cooking vessel, and the property of rice would apply to the *śyāmāka* grains.
If the origin of the sacrifice were prohibited, everything would be prohibited.

They do not set up a sacrificial post, nor do they prepare the northern altar (uttaravedi). When another substance is employed for that same purpose, these ritual duties are applied: they place the whey (vājina) on the rubbish-heap (utkara), they tether the sacrificial animals to a horse, and they tether the sacrificial animals to the enclosing-stick (paridhi).
When the *sāmidhenī* verses are being increased. ||21||
The wooden pieces increase when they are being withdrawn, according to their original nature.
There is modification (ūha) according to the purpose.
No modification exists in the archetype (prakṛti).
Having girded his wife, [the Adhvaryu] says, "This sacrificer has been invited.
Likewise in the subsequent performance, as it is recited in the sacred texts.

In the case of substitutes, those [rites] whose purpose is lost should not be performed; just as when [grain] is already harvested, the mantra for harvesting is not used, and when [wood] is already cut, the mantra for cutting is not used.

Where milk is boiled for the purpose of cooking, the purification with the formula "May the god Savitṛ purify thee" is adapted; the consecration with the formula "Milk is foremost among the gods, foremost... is likewise applied to the clarified butter (*ājya*). We shall now explain the ritual procedures for the *caru* (boiled rice).
One employs a cooking pot (*sthālī*) in place of the sacrificial potsherds (*kapāla*).
Having prepared the grains by husking them until they are completely dehusked, he places the cooking pot upon the hearth with the first *kapāla* mantra.

Having poured the rice from the winnowing basket into it, purified it, and placed it on the fire with the *adhiśrayaṇa* mantra, he carries a firebrand around it, cooks it, pours clarified butter over it, and removes it from the fire using the very same pot.

With the formula, "O you two cakes, separate yourselves according to your respective shares," he cuts off each cake one by one from the group of cakes. With the formula, "Separate yourselves according to your respective shares," he cuts off the two remaining ones.
For those two alone, there is the assignment of the deity.

The *caru* and the *puroḍāśa* grains should be divided before the pouring [of the grain]. There, he murmurs the mantra for division; he divides the equal portions into two, and the unequal portions according to their respective shares.
On each heap, he should designate one deity, saying, "This for so-and-so and for so-and-so.
Having set aside the portion for Pūṣan, he grinds it together with the *puroḍāśa* grains.
At the time of placing [the grains] on the fire, they should divide among themselves.
There, he mutters the mantra for the division.
When various seeds have been brought together, there is a single mortar, pestle, winnowing basket, and black antelope skin.

At the first seed-syllable he calls for the preparer of the oblation; at the last, he releases his speech. One should sacrifice with Soma, or with the Āgrayaṇa-iṣṭi, or with the Paśubandha, on either the new-moon day or the full-moon day.
For the iṣṭi or the Paśubandha, one should recite seventeen [verses]; or there may be an option of fifteen, or there may be no option at all.
We shall explain the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice.
Without having performed it, one does not eat the fruits of new herbs, whether cultivated or wild.
One sacrifices of the first ripening of rice, and likewise one sacrifices of the first ripening of *śyāmāka* millet and barley.
Likewise, at the time of offering the grains, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni from the old rice, and the others from the new rice:
a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni-Indra or Indra-Agni, a pap cooked in milk to the Viśvedevas, a pap of *śyāmāka* millet to Soma, and a cake on one potsherd to Heaven and Earth.
Some authorities prescribe that the ritual for the *śyāmāka* millet is performed separately.
When the oblation has been brought near and sprinkled with water, he offers five *ājyānī* oblations with the verse beginning "To him of a hundred weapons.
Some authorities prescribe that these should be recited before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
The ritual procedure for the cakes baked on a single potsherd (*ekakapāla*) is explained by the procedure for the single-potsherd cake belonging to the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice.
He does not turn the back upward. He does not offer oblations with the names of the months.
Having sacrificed with rice, he should sacrifice again with rice until barley is available; having sacrificed with barley, he should sacrifice again with barley until rice is available.

Some prescribe *śyāmāka* millet for those who possess bamboo. Alternatively, one need not perform the *Āgrayaṇeṣṭi*; one may instead sacrifice with the new grain on either the new-moon or full-moon day. Or, one may offer the *Agnihotra* with the new grain; or, having fed the *agnihotrī* cow with the new grain, one may offer the oblation in her milk; or, having cooked four-śarāva-measures of rice, one offers it to the deities of the *Āgrayaṇa*, with the *Sviṣṭakṛt* as the fourth, and then causes [the sacrificer] to eat that as a side dish—[he causes him to eat]. 23.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the third book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
Thus ends the third book in the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. 3.
Thus is prescribed the office of the Brahman priest for the *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices. This concludes the section on the Brahman’s duties. 262.22.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the second book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra. || 8 ||
Thus ends the second book (praśna) in the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. 2.

The extension [of rules] to the office of the Adhvaryu will be explained. He indicates that there is no such explanation required here. The repetition is for the purpose of concluding the inquiry. Thus ends the eighth chapter in the second book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśisūtra* composed by Mahādeva. The wise, who delight in the nectar of truth, have not reached satiety by repeatedly drinking in vast words through their investigation, even as they honor Satyāṣāḍha.

Those of noble intellect, who are satisfied with these instructions in the Sūtra, remain established for the protection of the Lord—who is like a god—to uplift people from the dense darkness of the reed-like ascetics. || 1 || By repeatedly calling to mind the best of sages many times over for the sake of the clarity of the exposition, this very lucid commentary on this Sūtra has indeed been attained by me, though my intellect is small. It is now offered to Viṣṇu, the ancient Person whose body is sacrifice; it should not be joined with faults by those of limited understanding, but rather let it be viewed again by the virtuous, whose minds are purified by grace through their insights. || 2 ||

Thus, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, and the office of the Brahman priest for those two have been completed. Thus ends the second book in the commentary on the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. 2.

3.1 Now begins the first chapter of the third inquiry. I bow to Viṣṇu, the Lord, who is infinite consciousness, bliss, and infinity; who, when his action is offered [to him], leads to fruit, and when offered, also leads to liberation from bondage; and who is the destroyer of evil. (1) O You whose self is the three Vedas, whose self is the three fires, whose self is the three Lords, whose self is the qualities of Prakṛti, and whose self is the triad of reflections and the original source corresponding to the three states of the individual soul—protect me from misfortune! (2)

I, with a mind full of *soham* (I am He), meditate upon the unborn Lord, the object of meditation for embodied beings, who destroys their fear; who is established by the syllable *Oṃ*, praised by the gods, endowed with compassion for his devotees; who holds the son of Hara (Ganesha) and the tusk in his lotus-like arms; who possesses whiteness in his body; who dispels the darkness covered by ignorance; who is the Seer (*kavi*); who goes to the earth (*ga*) with the intellect (*manas*) of "I am He" (*sohaṃ*); and who is the master of Lakṣmī. [Chapter 150] Accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

By her, who is the fortune of the body of Gaṅgādhara, Hari was made known by the name Śrīpati; and by her, who is named Mahālakṣmī, even this Grandfather of the world became the Lord of Sarasvatī. (4) Salutations to her, O Mother; salutations to you again; salutations to you once more through your compassionate glance. Protect me, a wretched man, from dullness, O treasure-house of mercy! O Mother of my lineage, O Witness, protect me who have come to you. (5) [This is] the common procedure for all sacrifices and their constituent parts, preceded by the general rules...

Likewise, through Mīmāṃsā, the specific exposition of the performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices is now set forth in detail. Following the sequence of performance for rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) and others that are mandatory, the necessary result which is common to all and established through the investigation of Mīmāṃsā is first addressed. This is determined in the third section (praśna) by means of the sixth chapter (paṭala), which provides a classification of the fixed [elements] and instructions regarding substitutes (pratinidhi).

Those characteristics of words are maintained for the sake of the ultimate excellence (*niḥśreyasa*) resulting from actions. Since there is an engagement even for the purpose of avoiding the undesirable through the hearing of the portions of prescribed rites (*niyata-karman*), a doubt arises as to whether these [rites] have a result to be accomplished or not. In this regard: "But those rites which are indeed necessarily to be performed—for these rites, no result to be accomplished is ever obtained. (Verse 1) Because no result is heard in the scriptural statement (*vākya*), because of the split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), and because there is no requirement for a result to be accomplished.

When it is argued that there is an absence of fruit (*phalābhāva*), the answer is stated by means of the Sūtra: || 2 || "Whether desire exists or does not exist, those acts which are declared by injunction (*vidhi*) to be 'to be performed'—for this very reason, it is understood from them that there is indeed an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭa*) in their non-performance. Since no fruit to be accomplished (*sādhya-phala*) is heard [stated] in those [injunctions], there is none. Nor should it be said that [a fruit] must be supplied according to the *Viśvajit* principle. For even if one were so supplied, activity would depend upon the existence of desire; otherwise, such activity would contradict the nature of obligatory (*nitya*) rites."

Now, if it is held that the result is exclusively the superior happiness intended for all men, then there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because both the motive (*nimitta*) and the result (*phala*) would be intended as objects of the injunction. Nor should it be argued that syntactical split is not a defect here because the injunction remains incomplete due to its expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*). For even if the mere meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) were the goal to be accomplished, activity would still be established by observing the fault incurred when the rite is not performed; thus, there is no incompleteness.

Activity is not caused solely by [the cognition] that something is a means to a desired end, because activity is observed even in the case of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) for the avoidance of the undesired. Nor should it be argued that there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) here due to the presence of two intended objects (*uddeśya*), because even if the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is not the intended object, it is nevertheless to be accomplished as an inseparable concomitant (*nāntarīyakatayā*), since otherwise the injunctive force would remain unfulfilled. [Objection: "Indeed, it is by action alone that people have attained perfection..."

If it is argued that since the fruit of the action is seen to be the attainment of perfection (*saṃsiddhi*) for those beginning with *kāda* and so forth, how can there be a non-hearing of the fruit [in these cases], we say: no. For fear of splitting the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), let the fruit belong only to those [acts] which are not restricted by conditions; for in those sentences, no specific occasion (*nimitta*) is heard. Furthermore, even for those acts that are not restricted, the fruit of supreme bliss (*niḥśreyasa*) is seen to be conveyed by the word "heaven" (*svarga*). Nor should it be said that heaven is merely a specific place; rather, the word is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of preeminent happiness itself.

Likewise, rites such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Paśu, and Soma sacrifices—which have all desired objects as their aims—will also serve one's own purpose characterized by the highest good (niḥśreyasa). Similarly, numerous rites heard of in the scriptures, beginning with the Vājapeya and Dvādaśāha and ending with those lasting for thousands of years, which have fruits such as procreation, preeminence, universal victory, and union with Brahman (brahmasāyujya), are means to liberation; thus, it is not the case that there is a hearing of results only in connection with obligatory (nitya) rites.

Although it is established by another scriptural statement—namely, "having discarded the three debts"—that even obligatory rites (*niyata-karmāṇi*) have liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) as their fruit, nevertheless, that result would arise only from a separate performance; for it is impossible for two distinct purposes to be connected within a single performance (*ekaprayoga*). Alternatively, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that when obligatory rites are not performed, demerit (*durita*) arises which acts as an obstacle to liberation; therefore, liberation is presented as the result through the performance of those rites.

This being the case, it is replied: "Supreme good is determined by actions; they are maintained by the Vedic words. An injunction is that which impels those desiring a desired fruit toward that very means of the desired [fruit]; otherwise, its essential nature would be undermined. Therefore, even in the case of obligatory rites (*niyata*), the desired fruit to be accomplished is always [the avoidance of evil], whereas the avoidance of sin is not something to be accomplished [as a primary goal] but is an inseparable consequence. The remainder of the sense is: "Since that supreme good, which is desired and established by actions, is attained through them."

Although the previous explanation was made with a focus on sacrifice (*yajña*), the word "action" (*karman*) is employed here to capture the intended meaning—that regarding the result, the status of action as a means is identical, and there is no gradation of intensity based on the greater or lesser frequency of sacrificial performance. If it is argued that since the word "action" can also apply to what is not prescribed (prohibited), one should have used the word "duties" (*dharma*) for the sake of brevity, we say: no.

In the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, the term *dharma* is used exclusively for that which is enjoined solely by a positive injunction (*vidhi*), and not for the preservation of the prior non-existence of what is prohibited; for there is no usage of the term "righteous" (*dhārmika*) for one who merely avoids what is forbidden. Furthermore, the employment of the word "action" (*karman*) is intended to state that even such [injunctions] are means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). From the context, from the inherent capacity [of the words], and because it is not restricted to those defined by verbal testimony alone (but includes those inferred from the Veda), it follows that there is no application [of the term] to the prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*); thus, it will be understood as referring to "those that are enjoined."

If it is asked: "But how can there be an injunction regarding observance (*pālana*) in this science of prohibition (*niṣedhaśāstra*), given that there is a lack of authority for both [prohibition and injunction]? The answer is: No, because in all instances such as "one should not drink" (*na pibet*) or "one should not kill" (*na hanyāt*), an injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*) is observed. Furthermore, the negative particle (*nañ*) does not connect with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) which serves as its base (*prakṛti*), nor with the suffix alone; rather, it connects with the word (*pada*) as a whole. Since the word contains the meaning of the root as a qualifier, the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is: "One should bring about the desired end by means of the absence of killing."

In that context, since a non-existence (abhāva) cannot directly serve as a delimitor of a positive injunction (*bhāvanā*), it is the action itself—consisting in the preservation of the prior absence of killing and so forth—that is indicated. Thus, the meaning of the word is: "One should bring about the desired end by means of the preservation of the prior absence of killing and so forth. Furthermore, from this, it follows by implication that killing and the like are means to suffering.

And since it will be stated that "that which one censures is unrighteousness (adharma)," it is understood that killing and the like are of the nature of unrighteousness. Furthermore, according to the principle that "that which is a purpose [derived] from a purpose is not [directly] enjoined," such [unrighteous acts] do not fall within the scope of the term *codanā* (injunction), because they fall within the scope of presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*). In our own view, however, even protection is indeed *dharma*; according to the view of others, it is also [included]. The employment of the word *karman* (action) is for the sake of pervasion [of the definition]. [End of] Paṭala 150, accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 265.

In his own view, however, the word *dharma* is seen to be used even for "protection," as in the phrase *sāmāyācārikān dharmān*. It is the teacher’s intention that those practices (*ācāra*) which consist primarily of protection are what is denoted by the word *dharma*; other usages should likewise be understood. Usages such as those of Yājñavalkya are to be known from such passages as: "Tell us, in their entirety, the *dharmas* of the castes (*varṇa*), the stages of life (*āśrama*), and others."

Now, it is indeed said that obligatory rites (*niyata-karman*) are the means for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). If it is asked how the obligation (*niyatatva*) of protection (*pālana*) is established, it is as follows: because even in the case of failing to protect, one is seen to incur sin—just as in the case of killing and the like—even one who, though intent on killing, is prevented by fate and does not actually commit the act, yet makes no effort toward protection, is called a sinner. Therefore, it is understood that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) even in the absence of protection, just as there is in the case of killing.

And it has been stated by the venerable Vidyāraṇya, the commentator on the Vedas: "Even in the case of prohibitions such as 'one should not kill' or 'one should not drink,' the preservation of the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) is what is enjoined. This constitutes the qualification (*adhikāra*). Upon its transgression, there is expiation (*prāyaścitta*), just as in the case of the omission of the *saṃdhyā* prayers. Furthermore, they have stated that the avoidance [of prohibited acts] possesses the nature of dharma: "A Brāhmaṇa who is constantly endowed with the eight qualities attains the Brāhma state from which he does not fall again. The eight qualities are non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and the rest.

"The avoidance of the wicked, association with the blameless, and steadfastness in one's own duty—this is proclaimed as purity. Therefore, the observance of what is prohibited is strictly necessary; for even if it does not itself produce demerit (*pratyavāya*), demerit arises through another action that is invariably concomitant with it, because demerit is produced by an action. In this regard, an action such as killing, which is prohibited in one context, is pervaded by the absence of actions such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice, whose prohibition is inferred elsewhere.

Thus, while it is heard in scripture that certain acts are simply "to be performed," they are said to be "obligatory" (niyata) when it is stated that they must be performed as a rule. Where a fruit is mentioned, the duty to perform the act is stated provided there is a desire for that fruit. In that regard, although injunctions such as "one should offer an oblation when [the vessel] is broken" are indeed prescriptive of obligatory rites, they are cited here because their status as examples is justified by the fact that they yield results merely through the removal of defects in the sacrifice (*kratuviguṇya*). By means of these obligatory rites, one attains the certain welfare (*śreyas*) known as *niḥśreyasa*.

By the rule *acatura*, the word *dhruvam* becomes *dhravam* when forming a *karmadhāraya* compound ending in *a*. The Self alone is certainly eternal (*dhruva*), supreme, and of the nature of infinite bliss. For this very reason, in the *Dharmapraśna*, it will be stated that there is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self. Therefore, the Self, whose nature is bliss, is to be attained through direct realization; and the means to its attainment is either the "effected Brahman" (*kārya-brahman*) or the Supreme Brahman itself. He will later state that those who attain the effected Brahman by the path of light (*arcirādi-mārga*) do not return, saying: "Having gone by the northern path, they do not return."

In this regard, since there is no state superior to both [pleasure and pain], that which is denoted by the term "immortality" (*amṛta*)—namely, the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) consisting of the seven stages—is in fact the Self itself manifested through a *sāttvika* modification, because no other happiness exists. Indeed, no discerning person is found who does not desire one or another of these three. Therefore, following the inclination of the qualified agent regarding the obligatory action that must necessarily be performed, there is likewise the non-existence (negation) consisting in its non-performance. (Note: This refers to the reading *ka.ga.cha.u.ṇa.*, even though...)

266. According to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the third book]—the fruit that exists, being determined by the relative degree of excellence among the auxiliary factors (*sahakāri-guṇa*), is certainly not abandoned by anyone. Why? Because of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For those rituals are maintained as being characterized by verbal testimony (*śabda-lakṣaṇa*). "Word" (*śabda*) refers here to the hearing of the injunction (*vidhi-pratyaya-śruti*), which is independent. The sense is that an injunction does not reach its full completion without the status of being a means to a fruit (*phala-sādhanatā*) in the ritual action to be enjoined.

If "injunction" (*vidhi*) is stated, then the sentence (*vākya*) would also be included there, because the word "injunction" is seen therein; thus, that which consists of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) [of words] is not merely the word itself. Those actions for which that word is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), being a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) through the exclusion of other meanings, are "defined by injunction" (*vidhilakṣaṇāni*). Even when "actions" (*karmāṇi*) has already been stated, the repetition is for the sake of the sentence in order to prevent their connection with a fruit. How so? It is as follows: the fruit to be accomplished by action is determined as the highest good (*śreyaḥ*); however, the actions are indeed enjoined by the scriptural injunction (*vidhiśruti*) independently and invariably.

In the same way, because the result is obtained [from the same source], a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) does not occur. Everywhere, it is understood through the injunctive hearing (*vidhiśruti*) alone that the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) itself is the means to the desired end. In other cases, however, it is understood through the sentence (*vākya*); thus, that very [activity] is qualified by the desired end. But a split in the sentence occurs only where there are two objects of reference (*uddeśya*) to be understood from the sentence; this [split] does not occur when a single object of reference is understood through the hearing. The knowledge of being a means to the desired end is the sole province of the injunctive hearing. Furthermore, the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), which requires an object to be accomplished that is desired, [requires] that which has the nature of the undesired [to be excluded].

How could [the sacrifice] become free from expectancy while still grasping the meaning of the verbal root? That verbal root, as the instrument (*karaṇa*), cannot by itself grasp the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). This [requirement], being observed in the case of established [rites], would be contradicted [if applied here]. For let it proceed toward the destruction of sin produced by expiation (*prāyaścitta*); but it does not apply to that which is not produced, since the absence of the undesirable result [of sin] already existed even previously. Since the desired object is limited to what is intended and is not delimited by other words, once it has been understood through a single hearing of the text, it is contradicted by repetitions.

Just as in Vedic ritual an action performed with indifference yields fruit through repeated practice by virtue of its inherent capacity, so it is here. That action which is enjoined by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*)—and not merely enjoined by repetition due to the influence of other words—is the supreme means for attaining the highest good when performed in that very manner. You too must necessarily accept the obligation to perform these prescribed duties for those seeking liberation; otherwise, how could liberation occur? For one who is obstructed by sins cannot [attain it] even by hundreds of ritual acts.

Therefore, let it be maintained that the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) arises from those [obligatory acts] alone. Even if it were to arise from other acts as well, they would not be prohibited; for by their non-performance, there is no evil that could destroy the fruit [of the sacrifice]. [End of Paṭala] In the case of the obligatory acts (*niyata*), however, let there be benefit in both ways (both through performance and non-performance) without confusion. As for the mention of the fruit previously stated by means of words such as "becomes perfected" (*saṃsidhyet*), that is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of this fruit already obtained from the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). It is intended [only] as a desired [result]. *Mahādevakṛtavaijayantīvyākhyāsametam* (Accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva).

The fruit of ritual actions, which is established as the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), has been declared by the Śruti. Having thus understood those very things expressed by the words, the determination of the study [of the Veda] is for the sake of the successful performance [of rites] by all students at the end [of their study]. Furthermore, that which is made known by the Śruti itself requires no other word, such that there would be a split in the sentence once it has reached the status of a single syntactical unit (*vākya*). As it was said by Pārthasārathi Miśra: "But surely, the connection between the occasion (*nimitta*) and the fruit is joined by a single sentence."

"Otherwise, if there were a connection with two objects of reference (uddeśya), a syntactical split (vākya-bheda) would result. Having raised this objection stated by the Prābhākaras, it is said in reply: "It is argued: A syntactical split results from the connection of two [factors] with that which is to be enjoined (vidheya); there is no connection between the object of reference (the occasioning cause, *nimitta*) and that which is to be enjoined. This has been explained by that same author: "A syntactical split occurs when that which is to be enjoined is connected with two [factors]; but here it is not so, for the action—which is what is to be enjoined—is connected with the fruit (*phala*), while the state of being something to be performed (*kartavyatā*) is connected with the occasioning cause (*nimitta*)."

And this being so, there is no split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Because of mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*), for when it is said, "When this exists, one should do that," there arises the expectancy, "For what purpose? In that context, the result (*phala*) being connected as "for this purpose" does not split the sentence. It is a sentence of the same class [of injunctions] that splits a sentence, such as the two conditions in "He whose father or grandfather has not drunk Soma," or the two results in "He who desires offspring or desires cattle. Therefore, it has been explained that there is no split in the sentence.

If it is argued that a *kāmya* (optional) rite, being enjoined with reference to a specific result as its motive, should not—due to the principle of syntactical unity (*vākya-bheda*)—result in a difference in performance, we say no. When desire exists, one engages through that longing; when it does not exist, one does not. However, in the case of a mandatory (*nitya*) rite, there is a fixed rule of obligation. Therefore, even if there is a contradiction, syntactical unity is not forcibly imposed. Thus, because the distinct meanings of the various words heard in the scripture exist as separate sentences, there is indeed a difference in performance.

In the present case, however, since the injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*) functions as the motivator (*viniyojaka*), it conveys through *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of a word in relation to others) the *bhāvanā*, the result, and the connection between them; these are understood precisely from the word itself. Subsequently, the connection with the occasion (*nimitta*) is established by means of the sentence (*vākya*). Thus, this occurs through a single sentence alone, and there is no abandonment of the former [meaning]. For this very reason, even if the avoidance of sin (*pratyavāyaparihāra*) were intended by the sentence, it would not sublate the directly stated (*śrauta*) status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), because there is no contradiction.

Now, as for what was said—that [the means of knowledge] is independent of a probandum (sādhya)—that too has been refuted. For expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) is not a factor in the connection of the cognition being expressed through syntactic relation (anvitābhidhāna), but rather in the sentence itself. And since there is indeed expectancy regarding the prior occurrence of a relationship, it has already been stated that this [expectancy] is sublated by this very part of the Sūtra. [Objection: Is it not reasonable that liberation occurs through the cessation of bondage caused by ignorance, and not through actions which are instruments of valid cognition? To dispel this doubt, this very Sūtra is appropriate.

These means for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) are maintained and determined. Why? Because words such as "those who desire to know" (*vividiṣanti*) establish their status as means for attaining the supreme good by way of generating the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). (Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram, Third Praśna, 268).

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The sense is this: although ritual actions themselves are not [directly] authoritative, they are determined to be "means for attaining the supreme good" (*niḥśreyasa*) because they assist the means of valid cognition that achieve the supreme good. Now, one might object: "Why is it not stated in the Veda or in the Sūtra in such a form as 'one desiring liberation should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]'? It is precisely by this [explanation] that such a doubt must be dispelled.

By whatever words those [means] are characterized, by those very words they are maintained; having understood that those alone are the means for attaining the highest good (*śreyas*), it is performed for the sake of the fruit, and not otherwise. And so says the Śruti: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, that alone becomes more powerful."

In some cases [the texts] are injunctive sentences, in some they are names, in some they are mere restatements, in some they express only the relationship between a substance and a deity, in some there is the verb "to sacrifice" (*ālabhati*), and in some the verb "to offer" (*nirvapati*); those [acts] established by such words have been recorded by us exactly as they are, characterized precisely by those respective terms.

For this very reason, even the Veda is not to be censured in this manner; for it has been made known that the apprehension of the meaning of the Veda exactly as it was seen through the injunction of study, or as it was taught as a means to the highest good (*śreyas*), leads to the desired result. Thus, we are here to provide an exposition of the Veda, not to censure it.

However, regarding the phrase "not by the three [Vedas]," it has been stated that there is no authority for those actions characterized by the conduct of the Smṛtis within the Veda—which consists of Brāhmaṇas and Mantras that enjoin them. Consequently, since they are not enjoined by Śruti, they do not possess the nature of action defined by injunction (*vidhi-lakṣaṇa-karmatva*), nor do they have the status of obligatory action (*āvaśyaka-karmatva*); thus, [the previous definition] is too narrow (*avyāpaka*). To this, he says:
"The grasping of Smṛtis by Vedic words is worldly."

The phrase "those characterized by verbal testimony (śabdalakṣaṇāni) are to be upheld" is carried over from the preceding [verse]. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: even those worldly actions which are such means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) are to be upheld as being characterized by verbal testimony. Now, it was previously stated that there is an absence of direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*) regarding such worldly matters; to this, he replies with the words beginning "of the Vedic... (*vaidikānām*).

The Veda, consisting of Mantra and Brāhmaṇa, is composed of certain parts that are exclusively Mantras, certain parts that are exclusively injunctions (vidhi), and certain parts where neither is present; rather, they are merely portions of explanatory passages (arthavāda) or Mantras occurring within the context of sacrificial rites (*vaitānika-karma*), which incidentally restate established facts. Those are the Vedic words, and the Smṛtis of Manu and others—who have seen the meaning of all the Vedas—which arise from those [Vedic words] along with their meanings, are themselves the "graspings" (*grahaṇa*), meaning the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for those [Smṛtis]. Thus it is said.

Since these [texts] are scattered across various sections and lack a single continuous recitation, they are incapable of conveying a single unified ritual act; therefore, the collection of these words in one place is not perceived by people such as ourselves through mere recitation, and thus [the author] says "Manu."

Even by these [means], they are not apprehended in their entirety; therefore, even for them, when scattered here and there, only memories arise. By means of those [memories], having mentally synthesized them in one place, it is not those very same verbal forms that are held together, because by their own nature they do not convey the meaning of a sentence. That knowledge in the form of a definitive conclusion which arises when the *karmas* are investigated according to logic by Manu and others—that alone is the authority (*pramāṇa*) in those cases where they are subsequently set in motion by Smṛti or custom (*ācāra*), following the deliberation of the world by Manu and others.

Those who investigate and reflect upon Vedic matters through reasoning (*kāra*) are likewise [called] *kāriṇaḥ*. For they alone, possessing knowledge refined by logic (*nyāya*) which is rooted in the Vedas, are the determiners of the meaning of all the Vedas, and no others. Therefore, it is said that "the *smṛtis* themselves are the graspings" (*grahaṇāni*), because the *smṛtis* alone are the causes for the grasping that consists of determination. [Objection: That is not so; for here [in the context of the *smṛtis*], there are neither errors (*apramoṭṭāḥ*) nor reflections (*vimarśāḥ*). It appears that "errors" (*apramoṭṭāḥ*) is what is required here. [End of] Chapter 1, Section [X]. With the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

The meaning is that these [scriptures] are the indicators of what is to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment. If, in this context, the word "śabda" were intended to mean the revealed scripture (*śruti*), then since this matter would already be established by the previous [sūtra], there would be no need to commence another sūtra for this purpose. Nor should it be argued that another sūtra is commenced because of a doubt arising from the fact that the revealed scriptures have been lost; for if the revealed scriptures were seen [to be lost], there would be no distinction between the Vedic and worldly actions for those [who hold such a view]. Nor should it be argued that the commencement is for the sake of establishing a scripture that is eternally inferable.

Furthermore, this would contradict [the view that] "of Vedic words. Nor should it be said that the teacher's (Guru) position is that there are certain Vedas that are eternally inferable; for the teacher's teacher did not hold such a view, and thus the earlier position of the Guru must be disregarded—this is the intention of the Ācārya. And it has been stated by Pārthasārathi Miśra: "Even if the Veda were inferred, it would still be non-worldly (alaukika); however, because of the absence of a perceptible Veda, it is not considered equal [to the actual Veda]."

[Objection: But surely that Veda too is indeed directly perceived by some, since the theory of an eternally inferred source has been refuted. [Reply: True; nevertheless, it is indeed dissimilar. How so? The three Vedas (*trayī*) function in connection with the sacrificial rites (*vaitānika-karma*). Within that context, however, certain non-sacrificial matters are mentioned incidentally (*prasaṅgāt*). Thus, because there is a constant dependence [on the Vedas], the compound is formed as *smṛtigrahaṇāni* (the "graspings of tradition"), following the analogy of the expression *devadattasya gurukulam* ("Devadatta’s teacher's house").

By this, it is stated by implication that Vedic rites (*śrauta-karmāṇi*) are not maintained by means of worldly words, but rather they are maintained by the difficult [Vedic] texts exactly as they are recited; thus, that very point was explained in the preceding sūtra. Relying on this very principle, the threefold injunction (*vidhāna-traya*) mentioned by us should be understood as having been explained. Now, an objection: "In every case, the desired fruit is indeed obtained through the Veda itself. That which is expressed in the sentence is its [fruit], but that qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣya*)."

Furthermore, if the qualifiers "yat" and "tat" were intended to qualify the subject—which has already been rendered syntactically complete by the preceding [word]—there would be a splitting of the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Nor is the status of being something-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatva*) ever produced by those words such as "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), since all of them serve as qualifiers for that which is already established by the Vedic text (*śrauta-sādhya*). Indeed, that word [the subject] does not express a qualified object; rather, ending in the nominative case, it functions as a qualifier of the agent and is connected with the fruit. An expression such as "O one desiring a village, come and eat" would be merely a secondary indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Alternatively, since there is a connection even in a single instance between the past and the future, the injunction is established by the maxim that "the past is taught for the sake of the future. For sacrifice is indeed the means to achieve heaven, which consists of happiness, through such instruments as sandalwood paste and the like; therefore, it is established that the fruit of all ritual acts is [heaven]. Furthermore, the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) alone is the goal, for no other fruit is logically consistent. This being the position reached, it is replied: "Through action there is prosperity, and through non-action there is no transgression; but this applies to those [acts] whose time is not fixed. *Note: The text provided contains fragments from Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra (3rd Praśna) and a commentary on the nature of ritual fruits.*

This does not exclude the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). The performance of optional rites (*aniyata-karman*) yields a fruit; yet it is heard in scripture that there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*) from their non-performance. One understands the desired end merely through the cognition that it is a means to achieve what is desired. A discerning person (*prekṣā-kārī*), however, does not engage in an action based on that alone when it is something to be accomplished. Nor does one engage in it because of a specific occasion (*nimitta*), for no such occasion is mentioned in scripture. Therefore, because they are optional, these [rites] do not produce any fault [from non-performance]. But since engagement is necessary, [the rite] is a means to one's own desired end.

For indeed, it would proceed as if it were a number, or perhaps by some other means. Thus, for the sake of establishing the operation [of the injunction], the qualifying factor of the sentence-meaning, when accepted, should not anywhere cause a division of the sentence. Therefore, from the performance of those [acts], prosperity arises as the fruit. From the worldly statement, "One desiring a wife should choose a spouse," it is understood that the acquisition of a wife occurs through the act of choosing alone; otherwise, there would be no syntactic connection between the two words according to the previous method.

And it is said: "If the two words 'one desiring heaven' (*svargakāma*) and 'should sacrifice' (*yajeta*) are both injunctive, then a mutual relationship between them is not possible even in a restatement (*anuvāda*). Therefore, having restated [the sacrifice] with one word, the other is enjoined; if the relationship occurs therein, then [the injunction] arises, and not otherwise. If, however, after restating the sacrifice, the person desiring heaven is enjoined, then an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) would have to be postulated from the sacrifice for the sake of that desire. But if, on the other hand, after restating the person desiring heaven, the sacrifice is enjoined..."

Because it serves as an auxiliary to that [effort], heaven is the intermediate goal (*mādhyatā*). This sacrifice, which consists of effort, is not desired to be fruitless; for even that which is to be enjoined arises as a means to an end that is to be accomplished. Heaven is the goal to be accomplished, and nothing else whatsoever is accepted as the goal. Therefore, the sacrifice, consisting of effort, becomes its means. However, when the desire for heaven is aimed at and the connection with the sacrifice is clear, heaven—being situated within the same sentence—is accomplished here by that very [sacrifice]. [This concludes] the first section (paṭala) from the *Mahādevakṛtavaijayantī* commentary. 271.

"For there is nothing else to be accomplished by sacrifice, nor is there any other means for attaining heaven; therefore, the relationship between the goal and the means is intended to exist between heaven and sacrifice. Thus, those actions which are prompted by the performance of what has not been [explicitly] enjoined are "non-obligatory" (aniyata), in that their performance depends on one's desire—performance occurs when there is a desire, and does not occur when there is none—and no transgression (pratyavāya) arises from the non-performance of such actions.

Therefore, the meaning of the sūtra is that it must necessarily be communicated by means of the sentence itself: "Whatever characterized by prosperity (*abhyudaya*) is prescribed here, that shall come to pass through the performance of that ritual action. By implication, it is stated that even in the non-performance of obligatory duties (*niyata-karman*), demerit (*pratyavāya*) arises. That is incorrect; for from [the scriptural injunction] one understands only that the act must be performed when the conditions (*nimitta*) are present, but not that the non-performance produces demerit, nor that the performance of a prohibited act produces demerit.

Furthermore, non-performance (*ananuṣṭhāna*) is not an action (*kriyā*), because it consists of the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of that action. Nor can there be a prohibition of it, because since the prior absence of a prescribed action is beginningless, its production is impossible; thus, even regarding the maintenance of that prior absence, there is no prohibition, as no such prohibition is heard in scripture. Nor should it be argued that the state of non-performance of what is prescribed also generates sin, on the grounds of the following verse: "By the non-performance of what is prescribed, by the performance of what is prohibited, and by the lack of restraint over the senses, a man incurs downfall. For this would imply that the mere absence of performing a prescribed act produces demerit.

It has been stated that this is not a command of kings, and therefore it is improper; consequently, neither the incurrence of sin from non-performance nor the status of these acts as obligatory duties is established. To this, the following is said:
Those actions for which there is blame in the world for their non-performance involve a fault [in such non-performance]; they are the obligatory ones.

Just as those actions which consist in the preservation of certain absences—their opposites being non-performance in the form of prohibited acts—result in fault (*doṣa*) and the unseen merit of transgression (*pratyavāyāpūrva*), and are therefore fixed (*niyata*) actions to be performed by rule (*niyamena*) with fixed results; likewise, those prescribed actions for which there is censure (*upālambha*) or blame (*nindā*) in the world, in the form of Smṛti and the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), when one fails to perform them (which failure consists in the preservation of the prior absence of that action contrary to its performance)—those too must be performed by rule and have rule-bound results. This is the meaning.

This is what is meant: just as there is a fault in performing a prohibited action and a fruit in maintaining its prior non-existence, so too, because of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding a prescribed action, there is necessarily a prohibition by way of excluding non-restriction; when that [non-restriction] is warded off, a fault is inferred through censure (*garhā*) with respect to the very act consisting in the maintenance of prior non-existence.

There is no time whatsoever that is not pervaded by the activity of the mind, because even deep sleep (suṣupti) is pervaded by the activity of the vital breath (prāṇavṛtti). Therefore, for one who does not perform external actions through mental or vital activities, there is always indeed an action. Since that [action] which is pervaded by what is preceded by a scriptural injunction produces a transgression (pratyavāya), another [action] is all the more so. Now, it may be argued: "For someone who does not desire a specific result, there is no rule regarding the performance of an act; rather, it is performed without a rule. Thus, for one who does not desire a result, there is no necessity. To this, it is replied: "They are indeed necessary."

If it were not so formulated, an undesirable consequence would follow; out of fear of that, even if one intends to perform the sacrifice only when the specific conditions (nimitta) are present, it must be understood as "one should perform the sacrifice," and thus there would be no requirement for the procedure (itikartavyatā). Consequently, it would follow that the rite could be performed even if deficient in its constituent parts. Furthermore, the word "as long as life lasts" (yāvajjīva) does not occur everywhere, nor can it be inferred through censure (garhā). Moreover, the general rule (utsarga) extends beyond thirty years.
