And since [the results] are seen after old age, it is not known how or for whom there is certainty, nor how the performance is to be carried out. It is said in reply: Certainty belongs to those rites for which no specific fruit is enjoined in the Sūtra; their certainty is accumulated starting from the *ādhāna* (consecration of the fires). Regarding the phrase "every spring," even in the case of the *soma* sacrifice, because all desires are attained through different modes of application, there is certainty for that which is obligatory (*nitya*).

Since a substitute will be described even for those [rites] that have been omitted, and since the performance of auxiliary rites is prescribed even for the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) and other such fixed duties, it is understood that the fulfillment of obligatory (*nitya*) rites is intended to be achieved through whatever materials are available, by means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) which is stated to remove defects. This is made explicit by the term "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. Furthermore, because the *ādhāna* is enumerated first among those things that lead to the fruit of supreme bliss (*niḥśreyasa*) for anyone who undertakes them, it follows that nothing can be commenced without it.

It will be stated that for a Brāhmaṇa, the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna), the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, and the Soma sacrifice are obligatory. In that regard, the non-performance of the fire-establishment is declared a secondary sin (upapātaka) in the Smṛtis; likewise, regarding the Agnihotra and other rites, there are Smṛti texts such as "He whose Veda and sacrificial altar... and so forth. Furthermore, even in Śruti texts such as "He who does not drink Soma until the third generation," the prescription of expiations (prāyaścitta) is found everywhere, which indicates their obligatoriness. The specific occasions for these rites, such as "as long as one lives" and so on, are also to be understood from other scriptural sources.

All of this has been correctly explained by Kātyāyana. For it is said: "At the commencement of rites intended for specific results, one may act according to one's desire (*yāthākāmī*), because of the desire for results; for it is the seeker of results who is impelled toward ritual action. Therefore, acting according to one's desire would seem to follow. [Response: No, because engagement occurs in the case of the obligatory *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *dākṣāyaṇāgrayaṇa*, and animal sacrifices, which have restrictive causes. In these restrictive rites, there is no acting according to one's desire, because the scripture enjoins engagement therein by way of a mandate (*niyoga*), as in: "One should be a speaker of truth," and "One should sleep on the ground."

This restrictive rule (*niyama-śāstra*) operates within a specific context. For if the optionality (*yāthākāmya*) were already established prior to this, then the injunction to speak the truth would be entirely purposeless if it were not to be performed as a mandatory obligation. Therefore, there is no optionality regarding restrictive rules. Furthermore, even in the case of that which is enjoined upon the occurrence of a specific occasion (*nimitta*), there is no optionality, because the injunction is made contingent upon the teaching of that occasion—as in the rule: "When the house is burning, one should offer an oblation to Agni Kṣāmavat. If there were optionality regarding the *Sāmavati* and other such rites, then the mention of the "burning of the house" would be utterly meaningless.

For even prior to the taking up of the house-burning [as a cause], acting according to one's own desire (*yāthākāmya*) was already established. Therefore, even in the case of an occasional rite (*naimittika*), there is no acting according to one's own desire. Nor is there acting according to one's own desire in the Agnihotra; for it is heard in scripture: "One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives. [Objection: But surely there is the injunction, "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra. In that case, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), this must be a property (*dharma*) of this very ritual action, and consequently, acting according to one's own desire applies. [Reply: No, it is said in response. By virtue of the context, this would be a property of the ritual action only so long as life lasts.

In that case as well, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the repetition of the action is indicated. However, when it is a property of the agent—as in the injunction "one should offer the oblation"—the word functions in its primary sense alone and does not indicate repetition. Since the oblation is enjoined with living as the occasion (*nimitta*), it is therefore a duty of the agent (*kartṛdharma*) for as long as one lives. Consequently, by virtue of that [lifelong obligation], there is freedom of choice (*yāthākāmya*). As for what was further stated—that "one desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra"—that is a separate performance undertaken for a specific desire (*kāmyaprayoga*).

"This is another occasion for living" means that in this case, even when a rite is performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*), it necessarily becomes one performed as a lifelong obligation (*naiyamika*). That too is indeed a performance of the *Agnihotra*. The same should be understood regarding the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices; for there too, there is both an injunction for a specific desire and an injunction for as long as one lives. The mention of the *Dākṣāyaṇa* sacrifice is due to the suspicion of its connection with a specific desire. Furthermore, regarding the *Āgrayaṇeṣṭi*, according to another Vedic branch (*śākhāntara*), there is no optionality (*yāthākāmya*).

Even in one’s own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā*), they prescribe the *nava* (new grain) sacrifice with reference to the *prakṛti* (archetype), stating: "This is the essence (*rasa*) of these two, heaven and earth; having offered this essence to the gods, one then eats the new grain. Furthermore, there is the obligatory nature (*nityakartavyatā*) of eating [the new grain]. Nor is that obligatory duty performed merely by offering it to the gods; therefore, its obligatory character is understood. Moreover, there is the prescription of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in this regard: "If one has not sacrificed the *āgrayaṇa* of the new grain... [End of Section 130]. This is from the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva.

"One should eat. Therefore, even in the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, there is no optionality (*yāthākāmya*). It is the same regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśu*). With reference to the *Nirūḍha* sacrifice, they state: "The year should not pass for one who has not performed that [sacrifice]. For some, the *Jyotiṣṭoma* is the occasion (*nimitta*) for the *Soma* sacrifice, just as lifelong performance is the occasion for the *Agnihotra*. Others, however, say otherwise: the injunction is stated in terms of a result, namely, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. Therefore, in this case, optionality is mentioned; [however,] it is said that this is indeed a separate performance (*pṛthakprayoga*).

One application is for one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*), while the other is the obligatory (*naiyamika*) duty of the agent. And having established this, there is the scriptural statement regarding the *Gavāmayana*: "How does their Soma sacrifice become uninterrupted? [The answer is] "By means of the *savana*s. He should say, "By means of the *savana*s. When that which must necessarily be performed is interrupted by some other cause, it is stated [in the scripture] that there is no interruption [of the primary rite]. Therefore, even in this case, there is no optionality (*yāthākāmya*). And thus says the traditional law (*smaraṇa*): "When the performance of animal sacrifices and Soma sacrifices is impossible, [this is done] for the sake of expiation (*niṣkṛti*)."

One should regularly perform the Vaiśvānara-iṣṭi at the end of each year, because of the scriptural statement regarding the "mouths of the four-month periods" (*cāturmāsya*) in the *Caturmukha-śruti*. Furthermore, there is no optionality (*yāthākāmya*) regarding the Cāturmāsyas. Why is this so? Because of the mention of the "mouths of the seasons" (*ṛtumukha*). It is heard in scripture: "One should sacrifice with the Cāturmāsyas at the mouths of the seasons. Moreover, because they are recited as fixed [obligatory rites]. Indeed, the Cāturmāsyas are recited together with the obligatory rites; for it is said: "They performed these sacrifices: the Agnihotra, the Darśa... and so forth.

"The Full Moon sacrifice, the Cāturmāsyas, the animal sacrifice, and the Soma sacrifice"—from this fixed recitation together, their equality is understood. Furthermore, it is seen from scriptural evidence (*darśana*). This meaning is observed: that the Cāturmāsyas are obligatory (*nitya*). With reference to one performing the Gavāmayana, it is said: "How do these Cāturmāsyas become uninterrupted for him? Since they are initiated, there is a prohibition [against performing them]; however, by the statement "One should say 'by means of the *payasyā*'," it shows the favoring of the Cāturmāsyas through another cause.

Furthermore, regarding that which must necessarily be performed, there is an accommodation for it by means of another cause. Others, however, maintain that this refers to the performance of all ritual acts; for instance, how is it that their *agnihotra* remains uninterrupted? How is it that their *paurṇamāsa* oblation remains uninterrupted? In such cases everywhere, an accommodation is seen through another cause. It is not because of the connection with abandonment (*utsarga*), nor are the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices obligatory. For those are connected with abandonment.

How can there be a relinquishment (*utsarga*) of that which is called "obligatory" (*nitya*)? It may be like the *triṃśacchandas* [verse]; or rather, even if it is obligatory, there may be a relinquishment, as in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, where it is said: "Therefore, one should sacrifice for exactly thirty years. Furthermore, that which must necessarily be performed is called "obligatory. Ritual action (*karman*) is of two kinds: obligatory and optional (*kāmya*). Regarding these, concerning the obligatory, it is deliberated: "Should it be performed only with its constituent qualities (*saguṇa*), or even without them (*viguṇa*)?"

Since there is a scriptural enumeration of qualities, it might be concluded that [the rite] must possess those qualities; to this, he says: "In the case of a deficient [rite], there is the non-attainment of the result, because of the distinction between the subsidiary and the primary. Even when a compulsory (*nitya*) rite is deficient in its subsidiaries, the attainment of the result still occurs. Why is this so? Because the subsidiaries and the primary acts are distinct. Here, in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices as long as one lives," it is the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices themselves that is enjoined, not their subsidiaries. Therefore, once the primary act is performed, whatever result belongs to it is indeed accomplished. Only the basic meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) needs to be performed.
By that, there is no duty to be performed for another. [End of section] 274. The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[Third Book].

Furthermore, when the sacrifice is heard of as a means (*sādhana*), there arises an expectation of an end (*sādhya*) or an expectation of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). However, in this case, it is not a means [to another action]. Therefore, the fruit arises even from a deficient performance. [Objection: What then is the purpose of the scriptural injunction of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*)? [Reply: There is no fault, for they pertain to the performance of optional rites (*kāmyaprayoga*). Moreover, because expiations (*prāyaścitta*) are prescribed; for even when the obligatory rite (*nitya*) is deficient, expiations are enjoined, such as "one offers an oblation when [the vessel] is broken" and "one offers an oblation when [the grain] is spilled," and so forth.

For if a defective rite were not to produce its fruit, there would follow the absurdity of the injunctions for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) being purposeless. Moreover, it is observed that even a compulsory (*nitya*) rite, though defective, must be completed in some way or another. Otherwise, there would be no provision for substitution, such as when it is asked, "With what should one offer? and the answer is, "With rice or barley. Or when it is asked, "If rice and barley were not available, with what should one offer? and the answer is given, "Whatever other herbs [are available]," and so forth—having thus stated this, [the text] concludes again.

"Was there then nothing at all here? Then this was breathed forth: 'Truth in Faith. This shows the completion [of the ritual] in some way or another. Furthermore, these are not injunctions, because of the absence of injunctive suffixes. Therefore, even when deficient in its constituent parts, the obligatory rite certainly accomplishes its fruit. Others explain it differently: since the mention of the auxiliary elements occurs in proximity to the obligatory rite, it must be performed with those auxiliaries. And the explanation of the Sūtra is that even in the case of an obligatory rite that is deficient, the production of the fruit indeed occurs.

Even if, due to divine or human obstacles, it is impossible to perform the inclusion of all constituent parts (*padārtha*), the rite must certainly be performed even with the inclusion of only a few parts. Here, the meaning of the phrase "as far as one is able" (*yathā śaknuyāt*) is thus determined. It is impossible that a rite should always be performed with all its qualities intact, for deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) caused by divine or human obstacles is inevitable. Having established this, the persistence of archetypal constituent parts (*prākṛta-padārtha-anuvṛtti*) is observed in modified rites (*vikṛti*) and obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*).

For example, in the Varuṇapraghāsa rites, the text "Then the Adhvaryu says, 'Wipe the fire,' and it remains unwiped" shows the instruction for wiping the fire within a sentence primarily devoted to the injunction for bringing the wife (as in "Then the Pratiprasthātṛ returns, leading the wife"). Similarly, in the Mahāpitṛyajña, the text "Having become one wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, he takes the clarified butter" restates ritual elements such as drawing lines, carrying [the fire], and the subsequent tracing of the altar, within a sentence primarily devoted to that injunction.

For if there were no connection with the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) for that which is eternal, there would have been no restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the drawing [of the ladle], the taking [of the oblation], and so forth. Yet such [restatement] does exist; therefore, even eternal rites possess a connection with the subsidiaries. Furthermore, it shows this in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*): "Having performed the second *āghāra* libation, moving around without letting the two ladles touch, he anoints the animal with the *juhū*. This sentence, while intent on enjoining the anointing of the animal, mentions the second *āghāra*. As for what was said—that nothing else is accomplished by means of the sacrifice—[that is refuted].

Either the destruction of previously accumulated demerit (*durita*) or the non-connection with future demerit certainly occurs by the force of the scriptural tradition (*āmnāna*). Therefore, it should be understood that even in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), there is a connection with the constituent parts (*aṅga*), as stated by the teacher Kātyāyana. It has been stated that the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is the goal to be attained through ritual action (*karman*). Likewise, it was stated in the middle [of the work] that the means characterized by the desire for knowledge (*jijñāsā*) is the gateway; it was said that ritual action produces that very knowledge which brings about the attainment of the supreme good. In this regard, one might raise the doubt: "Even if the desire for knowledge (*jijñāsā*) were to be accomplished by ritual action, the establishment of knowledge itself would not follow from that alone. Anticipating this, he says: "The cognition of the supreme good depends upon the connection with its production."

The intellect, which is the means for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), as well as that eminent person—the teacher (*ācārya*) who knows Brahman best—require a relationship [with the disciple]. This is because of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*): "A man who has a teacher knows [Brahman]. It is not through the mere performance of ritual acts (*karmānuṣṭhāna*), but rather through the attainment of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and other qualities. [End of section 15, Ja, Sa, Du, Pra-paṭala, accompanied by the commentary *Baijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 275.

"By the radiance of Dharma" (dharmaprabhā) refers to that which will be described hereafter. The sense is that when there is a thorough study of the Upaniṣads as revealed through inquiries into Dharma from the mouth of a teacher, a cognition in the form of direct realization arises at all times through the purification of the senses and so forth. Having thus stated that obligatory duties have liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) as their fruit, [the author] now demonstrates—by way of illustration—that all duties pertaining to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*) possess that same nature, using the word "karma" (action), which was employed to exclude the notion that only Śrauta rites are denoted by the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*). He expresses this as follows:

"Hospitality toward guests, worship of the guru, and salutation upon meeting"—these are "constant," as is the connection with the subsequent term. Since these will be explained among the *sāmayācārika* (customary) duties, they are considered worldly (*laukika*). Saluting the guru upon meeting the guru is clear; the rest is self-evident. He provides an example of that which is accomplished through the *śruti* and *smṛti*:
because it is caused by those [scriptures], the study of the Veda is constant for the Brāhmaṇa, the Rājanya, and the Vaiśya.

The meaning is as follows: "by the teachers" (*adhyāpakaiḥ*) means those who have been caused to perform—that is, caused to undergo refinement for the purpose of study—the aforementioned study; their state of being so refined is "their being caused to perform it. For that reason, study belongs exclusively to the triad beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, and that [study] is mandatory. Since only the Brāhmaṇas and the others are refined by the teachers during the seasons such as spring for the purpose of study, therefore study belongs to them alone.

And he will say: "For those who are not impure, whose actions are not defective, and who are seekers of knowledge, there is refinement through sacred learning (*śruti*). This is the intended meaning: although study might be accessible to all who seek the fruits of Vedic rites for the sake of knowing the means to those fruits, nevertheless, it is prescribed only for those who have undergone initiation (*upanīta*). Since initiation is restricted to the three higher castes during specific seasons such as spring, study—which is invariably concomitant with it—belongs to them alone.

The inclusion of the Vaiśya for a period of up to one month, together with the Brāhmaṇa, is for the purpose of excluding [certain] ritual acts in rites such as the *dvādaśāha*. Thus it has been stated that study is mandatory for the three castes. In connection with that, he states the restriction on eligibility in order to show that even for those of the three castes who seek results other than liberation, there is no performance of all ritual acts: "For them alone are the sacrifices prescribed for Brāhmaṇas, in which the completeness of the sacrifice is not prohibited."

Among those of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) in whom there exists complete knowledge of the sacrifice along with its auxiliary parts (*sāṅga*), as well as its purposefulness, the marriage to a wife of the same caste, and the full attainment of the status of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and so forth—it is for them alone that sacrifices are intended; they do not become performers of sacrifices by asking another for permission, nor by thinking, "I shall accomplish it later. For this very reason, it is said: "He who possesses grain sufficient for three years may indeed drink the Soma," and so forth.

Likewise, a woman who does not belong to the same caste (*asavarṇī*) is not authorized for the recitation of mantras among those of the three higher castes. By the formation of a *ekaśeṣa* compound from the two sūtras "strī-puṃ-ca" and "pumān striyā," the women of those three castes are also included. The particle "eva" (only) is intended to exclude any indicative marks (*liṅga*) that might lead even Śūdras—who desire the fruits of ritual action—to perform the laying of the fires (*anyādhāna*) and other such rites.
