This is for the purpose of precluding the possibility that Śūdras might perform the duties prescribed by the Smṛtis. To clarify this very point—that the Śrauta rites are ordained only for Brāhmaṇas—it is stated "sacrifices" (*yajñāḥ*). By the word "sacrifice," the *Ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) and other rites characterized as Śrauta are indicated. This matter is heard in scripture: "A Brāhmaṇa should consecrate the fires in spring, a Rājanya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn. Therefore, due to the absence of the *Ādhāna*, the Śūdra is without fire; how then could he engage in rituals that must be accomplished through fire?

These fires are established for one's own sake and not for the sake of others; that is why the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) occurs in the form "āvadhīta" (he should establish). Therefore, only Brāhmaṇas and the other [twice-born] classes are capable of producing fire through the rite of establishment (*ādhāna*), whereas Śūdras are not, because they lack the right to perform the establishment. Consequently, the Śūdra has no entitlement [to Vedic rites]. Now, there are indeed other scriptural indications from which the entitlement of the Śūdra is understood. Regarding the specific offering of the *haviskṛt* oblation, it is stated: "He should run [to fetch water], O Śūdra. Likewise, there is a specific vow for the Śūdra.

Likewise, regarding the statement in the *Pitṛmedha* ritual, "the *aṣṭhīvaghna* [is for] the Śūdra," it is replied: it has already been stated that there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*) for a Śūdra. As for those scriptural indications (*darśana*) that have been mentioned, they refer to the *rathakāra* (chariot-maker). For the *rathakāra* is called a "Śūdra" because of his connection with the Śūdra; indeed, he was born of a *kariṇī*, and a *kariṇī* is the daughter of a Śūdra woman. Similarly, those [indications] concerning the *niṣāda* also pertain to him, since he too is a Śūdra.

Alternatively, it is heard in scripture that study is prescribed only for Brāhmaṇas, Rājanyas, and Vaiśyas—beginning with the injunction, "In spring, one should initiate a Brāhmaṇa," and so forth. And initiation is for the purpose of study. Therefore, due to the absence of that [initiation] and because he is not entitled to the sacred rites (*avaidha*), the Śūdra lacks the qualification [for Vedic study]. Moreover, there is a prohibition against the Śūdra's study: "For listening, filling both ears with lac; for reciting, cutting out the tongue; for memorizing, splitting the body. Therefore, because he is not entitled to the sacred rites, the Śūdra does not possess the qualification.

This very point has been stated by Ekkāra: that [the Veda] is not established otherwise for women, and there is an absence of formal study. Nor should it be argued that because women possess only the status of being auxiliary (aṅga), they have only as much Vedic study as is required [for the ritual], but no entitlement to perform the rites themselves. For it is taught: "As long as the separation of husband and wife does not occur, there is joint participation in rituals beginning with the taking of the hand; likewise in meritorious acts and the acquisition of property. Indeed, when the husband is away on a journey, giving for a specific occasion by a woman is not theft."

The Teacher will also declare the eligibility of women for religious duties (dharma). Kātyāyana states: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires; one desiring heaven should sacrifice. Since a specific gender is heard [in the text], it follows that women have no eligibility; to this he replies: "And the woman, because there is no distinction, is also eligible. Why is this? Because even though a gender is mentioned, it does not serve as a restrictive qualifier; therefore, eligibility belongs to men alone. This [phrase] "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" is merely a qualification of the person being addressed (the subject).

Where there is no contact with an injunction (*vidhi*), both gender (*liṅga*) and number (*saṃkhyā*) are not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). However, where there is contact with an injunction, both gender and number are intended to be significant. For example, in the case of "one should sacrifice an animal" (*paśumālabheta*), both its qualifiers—masculinity and singularity—are enjoined; otherwise, the sacrifice of a qualified animal would not take place. Therefore, women also have the right [to perform sacrifices]. Furthermore, because it is observed (*darśanāt*): this fact—that women also have the right—is indeed seen.

"By means of the girdle he consecrates the sacrificer, by means of the cord the wife. This statement, which concerns the rules for the cord, demonstrates the wife's entitlement to perform the sacrifice. She is entitled to act together with the man, not separately; and the entire fruit belongs to each one [jointly]. Just as the sacrificer is designated by the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," so too is the wife. Just as the sacrificer accomplishes the fruit through the sacrifice, so too does the wife.

The action [is performed] together with another sentence, and thus they are heard [together]; this is shown in manuscripts Ka, Ga, and Tha. 2. Kha: "That; because there is no distinction; since... [End of section]. 3. Praśna Paṭala: Accompanied by the commentary named Vaijayantī composed by Mahādeva. 277.

"There is no separate sacrifice for women, nor a vow, nor even a fast; by serving her husband, she is exalted in heaven. Therefore, it is established that women of the same caste as the three *varṇas* who have been initiated and educated possess the entitlement to perform the rites prescribed by the Brāhmaṇas, such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), the *Agnihotra*, the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, and so forth. Now, one might object: "By the logic already stated, initiation and study would also apply to women, since the gender is not intended to be significant in passages such as [the injunction] beginning with 'a Brāhmaṇa'. True.

In the case of women, marriage alone is recorded in the Smṛtis as the sacrament (saṃskāra) in place of the initiation ceremony (upanayana). Since study [of the Veda] follows marriage and its purpose is thereby already achieved, she is prohibited from pronouncing other mantras just like a Śūdra; the same applies to the Niṣāda and the Rathakāra. As it has been said: "The three Vedas are not within the range of hearing for women, Śūdras, and those who have lost their caste."

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "A Brāhmaṇa of eight years should marry; he should study," because the grammatical marker of the agent (*kartṛliṅga*) indicates that which is to be enjoined, there is an absence of initiation (*upanayana*) and study for those [who lack it]. This also excludes certain individuals among the three higher castes—namely, those who lack wealth and bodily integrity. "Wealth" refers to inheritance (*dāya*); that which is not prohibited for one is what is meant here. Possession of wealth arises through the receipt of inheritance, yet such inheritance does not exist for eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍa*) and others, as will be stated later. Therefore, since they are ineligible due to impurity, the prohibition of inheritance for them is recorded in the Smṛti precisely on account of their impurity.

Likewise, the performance of all the bodily limbs [of the sacrifice] is neither prohibited nor contradictory for them alone; those sacrifices belong to them and not to others—such as the blind, the lame, the mute, the deaf, those who have not studied the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), or those who possess nothing. There would be a contradiction regarding the sacrificial limbs such as the inspection of the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*), the Viṣṇu-steps (*viṣṇukramaṇa*), the recitation of mantras, the formal address, the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), and the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

Even for one who has not studied [the Vedas], the *Trivṛt-Agniṣṭut* sacrifice is prescribed as a penance; since it is intended to ensure the excellence of rites such as the *Ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) for one of virtuous conduct, he too possesses the entitlement to perform the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites. Furthermore, even for one who possesses nothing, there is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) because the *Anvāhārya* fee alone will be prescribed as the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) for the obligatory *Iṣṭi*, *Paśu*, *Cāturmāsya*, and *Soma* sacrifices. Likewise, for one whose wife has died or who is incapable of taking a wife, the *Kalpasūtra* will state that the *Ādhāna* may be performed for his own sake even without a wife.

In the *Kalpasūtra* itself, it is stated that "the wife burns [the body] with the *nirmanthya* fire"; even there, the *āmaya* (fire) must be established for its own sake, and it must be maintained constantly even in the absence [of the sacrificer]. This confirms that the eligibility (*adhikāra*) belongs to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*):

"For whom the sacrifices are heard to have natural gender marks (*prakṛtiliṅga*)," such as "he chooses three," "he chooses the mantra-composers (*mantrakṛt*)," and "he chooses the mantra-composers according to the *ṛṣis*. Thus it is understood.

It is understood from the *Mānava* school that this is for the purpose of the *pravara*. The *liṅgas* (indicative marks) that determine its nature are the sacrifices and the implements of sacrifice; for there is no *pravara* for others besides the three classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. In that regard, the *pravara* of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya is clearly through the *pravara* of their domestic priest (*purohita*), while the *pravara* of the Brāhmaṇa is by his own right. [Gha... Ja.Sa.Ma.Ka. in the sacrifice. 278. In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Āpastamba, in the third book, he states the *liṅgas* of the three [classes]:

"One should conclude with the Gāyatrī for a Brāhmaṇa, with the Triṣṭubh for a Rājanya, and with the Jagatī for a Vaiśya. The word "iti" (thus) indicates a manner; the meaning is that other such [rules] are also to be understood. Having thus established the scope, he now states those [rites] which are obligatory: "Of these, the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are obligatory."

Because it occurs simultaneously with the *ādhāna* (consecration of the fires) and because it is recorded as a minor offense (*upapātaka*) for failing to perform it beforehand; therefore, it is recited among the obligatory rites (*niyata*). Among those sacrifices prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa, there is the hearing of the rule regarding their obligatory nature: "One should offer the *agnihotra* as long as one lives, and one should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as long as one lives. Regarding the Brāhmaṇa specifically, [the text] states: "Soma-sacrifice is for the Brāhmaṇa."

Regarding the injunctions "one should sacrifice a bull let loose again to Indra and Agni" and "one should sacrifice a smoke-colored, forehead-marked [bull] to the Aśvins," since these are prescribed as the sole expiation for a Brāhmaṇa, his performance of Soma sacrifices is thereby restricted. The meaning is that the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are even more strictly obligatory for him to avoid the state of being a non-Brāhmaṇa and the loss of his own [caste]. He states the specific rule regarding the commencement [of these rites]:
from the time of the *ādhāna* (consecration of the fires), the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa are mandatory.

Once the *ādhāna* (the laying of the sacred fires) has been performed, the commencement of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is restricted by the rule of non-interruption. Although the *soma* sacrifice is mandatory for a Brāhmaṇa, there is no such rule regarding its non-interruption from the *ādhāna*. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to show that the restriction applies not to only one of the two, but to both. This need not be stated, because it is heard in scripture that if there is an interruption between them, there is an expiation for the loss of the fire. It must indeed be stated; for the purpose is to ensure that the commencement occurs when there is a desire for the optional rites, and does not occur when there is no such desire.

And how could there be an undertaking for that purpose when [the result] exists? But when it does not exist, [the performance] will certainly occur for those who are restricted [to obligatory duties]. This is for that reason. However, since it has been stated that when [the result] exists, even the sin (pratyavāya) caused by non-performance is avoided by means of the optional rite (kāmya) alone, therefore, the distinction is merely this: [the optional rite] does not lead to the supreme good (niḥśreyasa). Even so, since this is accomplished from another source, there is the fault of being restricted to that alone. In that case, whether the desire exists or not, when there is an undertaking of the optional rite, this [obligatory performance] will serve the purpose of preventing its abandonment.

Just as there is no abandonment of [rites] undertaken as obligatory (*niyata*) for as long as one lives, so too in the case of rites undertaken for a specific desire (*kāmya*), when the desire ceases, their abandonment precludes the performance of the obligatory rites. For there is no time for the commencement [of the obligatory] other than the period immediately following the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration). Thus, once the desire has ceased, if the optional rite is completed by performing it only at dawn and sunset for as long as desired, then the subsequent performances will serve the purpose of ultimate liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) for as long as one lives; therefore, there is no need for a separate occasion for commencement.

The intended meaning is that the *saptahotṛ-homa* and other rites, as well as the *anvārambhaṇīyā* and others, must be performed. [End of] Paṭala 150, from the *Mahādevakṛtavaijayantī* commentary. Regarding those other than the three *varṇas*, he says:
for the *niṣāda* and the *rathakāra*, the *ādhāna* (consecration of the fires), the *agnihotra*, and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are prescribed as obligatory.

Regarding the injunction, "A chariot-maker (rathakāra) should establish the sacred fires during the rainy season," and because we see such mantras as, "I establish thee, the path for the heat of the abundant gods," and "for the chariot-maker," the establishment of the fires belongs to the chariot-maker. Since the fires produced by that establishment are for the sake of others, there is no obligation regarding the Agnihotra or the New and Full Moon sacrifices for him. Furthermore, in the case of the statement, "One should cause a Niṣāda-sthapati to sacrifice with this [offering]," it is stated that he is a "Niṣāda" based on the intention of a *karmadhāraya* compound, meaning he is both a Niṣāda and a sthapati.

Therefore, in the *Āpastamba-sūtra*, the view that the *sthapati* (architect) among the *niṣādas* is indeed a member of the three higher castes (*trairvārṇika*) has been refuted; for the teacher [Āpastamba] considers that, since the performance of the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) is prescribed for him, the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) must also be performed. According to the principle of logic (*nyāya*), the establishment of the fires is mandatory for one [the *niṣāda*], while for the other [the *sthapati*], it is introduced as part of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛteṣṭi*). For both, however, the *agnihotra* and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are enjoined. By the standard of logic, the *niṣāda*’s establishment of the fires consists merely of a modified sacrifice performed with common (non-consecrated) fires—just as the donkey used by a student who has broken his vow (*avakīrṇin*) is for a modified rite. The same applies to one whose father is still living.

"It is restricted" means it is specified. That restriction which has been stated for a member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) or others applies only to one whose father is living among them, and not to anyone else. Likewise, "one whose parents are living while performing the obligatory *Agnihotra*, *Darśa*, and *Pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices": if both parents are alive, the son's entitlement [to perform these rites] exists only when those two have already performed the triad beginning with the *Ādhāna* (the establishment of the sacred fires), and not otherwise.

The meaning is that even when one of the two has died before the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) has been performed, the entitlement (*adhikāra*) certainly remains. Likewise, although Baudhāyana prohibited the *ādhāna* and other rites for one whose father was still living, there is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to that rule.

"By the initial statement, the others should be restricted. If there is a desire, then having commenced [the rite], it is restricted; however, its commencement itself is not obstructed, as in the case of the *Agnihotra* or the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. Or, like the Brāhmaṇa’s single performance of the *Soma* sacrifice. In the absence of such a desire, there is no fault even if one does not commence the rite.

The intended meaning is this: just as in the case of the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, because they are enjoined by the term "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) with reference to a specific occasion, they must necessarily be performed whenever that occasion—namely, life—is present; it is not so in the case of the animal sacrifice, the Cāturmāsya, and the Soma sacrifices, where the term "as long as one lives" does not establish such an occasion. Rather, what is stated is the necessity of repetition (*abhyāsa*), meaning that once these have been commenced through repetition, they must not be abandoned.

The other rites, beginning with the Cāturmāsya and ending with the Soma sacrifices—whether they be optional (*kāmya*) or obligatory (*nitya*)—exist as established entities; therefore, the rule is that, like the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa, there is no abandonment of the optional rite even at its commencement. However, when the commencement of an obligatory rite occurs, the non-abandonment of those rites for which there is no rule of relinquishment is what is enjoined, but this does not apply to the commencement of an optional rite.

Why? Because the term "as long as life lasts" (*yāvajjīva*) is absent, even the abandonment of what has been commenced is appropriate when the desire [to continue] ceases; however, for another [act], there is no commencement. Regarding the commencement of what is obligatory (*niyata*), the sense is that there can be no abandonment because of the lack of a limit to prior practice, whereas in the case of a fixed limit, there is relinquishment. Even for one whose parents have died, provided there is capability, this same rule applies to the commencement of the *Cāturmāsya* and other such rites, since they are obligatory.

Since it was not stated that "all other rites" (itarāṇi) were commenced there without distinction, the use of the masculine gender (*puṃliṅga*)—in reference to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices which are separated in context—is intended to include only other sacrifices of the same class. By this, it is stated that the rule of commencement applies only to those other sacrifices, and not to other means of attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), even if they are prescribed as obligatory. Regarding their commencement, however, [the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Third Book... [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.]

This is because that [obligation] is also fixed. Thus, there is no exclusion of non-sacrifices such as honoring guests, offering hospitality, and Vedic study. Other sacrifices—the Āgrayaṇa, the Iṣṭi, the animal sacrifice, the Cāturmāsya, and the Soma—are both obligatory and optional. In the case of the Satras, the Iṣṭis, animal sacrifices, and Somas, their performance must continue for as long as one lives, like the Agnihotra. For a Brāhmaṇa, the Soma sacrifice is obligatory even if performed only once. Why? Because of the indicative mark (liṅga) stating, "He becomes one whose Soma-drinking is not to be repeated. Furthermore, the two modes of performance regarding the Soma are not contradictory.

In the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi, from its very commencement, a restrictive rule for the teacher is intended; that which is prescribed in its place is indeed mandatory, even for optional rites (*kāmya*). For there is an injunction of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for one who, having said "I shall sacrifice," does not complete it, stating: "One should sacrifice with the Traidhātavīyā [offering]. In that case, if the required substance for the obligatory rite (*nitya*) is absent, a substitute (*pratinidhi*) is permitted by virtue of general principle.

In that regard, if among those prescribed items the fixed substance—such as *vrīhi* rice or *soma*—is not obtained, this applies to its absence (*abhāva*), but not to its destruction (*nāśa*). In the case of destruction, however, just as in the case of a separate [substance], the fixed ritual act must indeed be performed by some other substance acting as a substitute (*pratinidhi*) that takes its place. Even if it is not obtained prior to the commencement [of the rite], the rite must be commenced using a fixed substitute. [This is] the method.

In the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), when there is non-availability or destruction of the prescribed substance that serves as the means (*sādhana*) for the obligatory rite (*nitya*), a substitute (*pratinidhi*) is employed in its place; it is taken in its own form, being a different entity from the original. This [substitution] excludes lack of restriction (*aniyama*) on the basis of generality—that is, by way of the generality of genus (*jātisāmānya*), the generality of quality (*dharmasāmānya*), or similarity (*sādṛśya*).

Regarding this very point, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and final (siddhānta) positions are stated in the *Kātyāyanīya*: "In the absence of that which has been enjoined, there is no undertaking [of the rite], because that enjoined substance is already established. When the substance enjoined is absent, that ritual action should not be commenced. Why is this so? Because that very [specific] substance is heard in scripture as the means for that ritual action; another substance is not heard. Therefore, by means of another substance, the action becomes something else, for the form of a ritual action consists of its substance and deity. This applies thus to optional (kāmya) rites. By implication, it applies to obligatory (nitya) rites as well. How so?

And even in the case of a compulsory (*nitya*) rite, when the prescribed substance is absent, it might follow that the rite should not be commenced at all because one perceives it as a different act; to this he says: "In the case of a compulsory rite, there should generally be a substitute. In a compulsory rite, that rite must be commenced with a substitute that is equivalent to the prescribed substance. Why is this so? Because in the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice," the mention of rice is merely a restriction (*niyama*). Furthermore, it is not possible to override the scriptural injunction regarding lifelong performance (*yāvajjīva*) for the sake of adhering to the restriction.

When an obligatory rite must necessarily be performed, it is more appropriate not to employ even a mere restrictive rule [regarding the specific material]. Therefore, that rite should be completed by means of a substitute. Why is this so? It is said: because of the commonality of what is heard in scripture. By the injunction "one should sacrifice with *vrīhi* grains," the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is prescribed for specific individual instances characterized by the genus *vrīhi*, and not by the genus *vrīhi* itself, because the genus lacks physical form (*amūrtatva*). Nor can the production of the eight-pot-sherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) be accomplished [by the genus alone].

Furthermore, there is no other denoter for specific individuals apart from the genus-word (*jātiśabda*). Therefore, it is these very specific individuals that are [intended] here by the term "existent" (*abhūta*). Thus, when substitutes are being taken up, the inclusion of some specific individuals is thereby accomplished. For this reason, it is rightly said that the substitute is based on the commonality (*sāmānyāt*). A substitute occurs in the case of an obligatory rite (*nitya*); and even in the case of an optional rite (*kāmya*), a substitute is indeed desired once the rite has been commenced. To that end, he says: "From the commencement, there is a restriction. For that ritual act has already been begun.

And the commencement has the completion as its purpose. Furthermore, the completion of that [rite] does not occur without a substitute substance. Therefore, even in this case, there is indeed a substitute. Moreover, because of this, there is also the performance of the commenced optional rite. [End of] Paṭala 150, accompanied by the commentary Vaijayantī composed by Mahādeva.

In the case of non-completion, there is a fault; for that [non-completion] is equal to the case of permanent rites (*nitya*). Just as there is censure by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) for the non-performance of a permanent rite, so too is there censure by the learned for the non-completion of a rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*). Now, one might ask: what is the fault in being censured by the learned? There is indeed a fault because of which the learned censure [one]. Or, even if there were no other fault, the censure itself would be the fault. And this is also known from scriptural observation.

It demonstrates completion by means of another substance, as in the statement: "If one does not find Soma, one should press Pūtīka plants. It has been stated that Kātyāyana’s rule regarding the commonality of substances (*dravyasāmānya*) is applicable everywhere. To the question of whether this applies without distinction, he says:
"The commonality of substances [applies] when the purpose is achieved."

The word "upalakṣaṇam" (indication) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. If a purpose is accomplished by means of a substitute belonging to the same class (*sajātīya*), then that very thing—belonging to the same class even if it possesses fewer prescribed qualities—is to be accepted provided some purpose is somehow attained; however, a thing of a different class (*vijātīya*), even if it possesses all the prescribed qualities, is not to be accepted if it is not indicated by that term. He shows the contrast: "But when there is a conflict between the literal meaning and the purpose, the commonality of purpose prevails."

If, in any way whatsoever, there is no need for something of the same class (*sajātīya*), then one should take that which is not characterized by a specific purpose, which resides in the prescribed substance, which is other [than it], immediate, directly expressive, and not excessive; such a thing is to be understood as "of the same class," but not as being of the same class merely through a general property such as being pervasive or non-pervasive. That too is indeed to be taken when each preceding one is unavailable, continuing up to the limit of what is of the same class. This very point is shown by the phrase "this is the generality of purpose" (*arthasāmānyam*).
To demonstrate that this is precisely what is intended, he provides an example:

Just as in the case of anointing the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), oil is used in the absence of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*). Here, although the Brāhmaṇa prescribes it with the word "clarified butter" in the passage, "He anoints the sacrificial post; clarified butter is indeed splendor; [he anoints] it for the sacrificer with fire," it is shown that the word *ājya*—derived from the root *as* (to flow) in the sense of "that which flowed out" (*asarpat*) and thus became *sarpiḥ*—denotes the general class of oily substances, and not specifically a consecrated preparation. For this very reason, he will later state: "with ordinary clarified butter," etc., and "the sacrificer anoints the sacrificial post. When clarified butter is in any way unavailable, even an oil of a different species is accepted as a substitute because it possesses the quality of unctuousness (*sneha*).

An objection was raised that when a substitute (*pratinidhi*) is prescribed, there must be a restriction (*saṃkoca*) of the prohibition; to this, the answer is given: A substitute is that which has desisted from those things prohibited. Indeed, what is prohibited as being fit for sacrifice (*yāgīyatva*) should not be taken as a substitute, because the purpose can be accomplished by something else of a different class. Therefore, the substitute obtained through logic is one that has desisted from those things prohibited as being fit for sacrifice; such is the substitute. Now, an objection is raised: "The prohibition read within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*) would apply only there, not elsewhere"; anticipating this, he says:

For a prohibition is heard without qualification. Since a prohibition is heard without qualification in the Śruti, Smṛti, and so forth, it must not be restricted; for although its capacity through a visible means is established by a rule obtained through logic, the absence of power through an invisible means is understood from that very prohibition. — 282 [Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa] Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, Third Praśna.

The meaning is that in the case of an *aktapaṇa* (an offering mixed with clarified butter), there would likewise be an omission arising from [the application of] the ritual action (*karmaja*). When *śyāmāka* grain is prescribed for the *caru* (cooked sacrificial rice) and a substitute is sought, it is heard in the scripture: "Kodrava grains are unfit for sacrifice; varaḍaka beans are unfit for sacrifice. Likewise, regarding the *maudga* (mudga-bean) *caru*, it is said: "Māṣa beans are unfit for sacrifice. The meaning is that here, that which is related to the sacrifice is prohibited without distinction, not merely these two types of *caru*. This same prohibition should also be understood to apply to such statements as "that which is not fit to be eaten by the Āryas," and so forth.

Now, in a case where an optional substance has been taken up and subsequently lost—such as when the *vrīhi* rice is lost—is a substitute to be taken on the basis of the general category (*sāmānya*) of *vrīhi*, or should the *yava* barley, which is the scripturally prescribed substance (*śrutadravya*), be taken? Since a substitute is desired only in the absence of the scripturally prescribed substance and not while the scripturally prescribed substance is still available, it follows that the *yava* should be taken. To this, he says: "In the case of an option, the characteristic is the commencement [of the performance]."

In this alternative, whatever substance has been prescribed is to be taken as a substitute in its general capacity. Even a substance that is explicitly mentioned in the scripture (*śruta*) should not be adopted [as a substitute]. Why? Because in all optional substances, the sacrificer himself chooses one to serve as the means of accomplishment; and in that case, only that [chosen] substance is the means, not another, for it is equal to what was not mentioned in the scripture. If that other substance were adopted, there would arise the notion of a different ritual action (*karmāntara*), and that is not desired.

Therefore, a substitute is taken on the basis of similarity to the substance under discussion. Even when there is an absence of a substance of the same genus (sajātīya), there is no omission of the mantra "medhasumanasyamāna" for rice, even if a substance of a different genus (vijātīya) is used. Regarding this, he states an exception: "A substitute [is used] when there is a total absence.

This means that a substitute is used when everything prescribed and prepared has been destroyed, but not when only a part is destroyed. Now, one might ask: "Is not everything destroyed even when only a small portion remains? To this, he replies:

In the case of an improper measure (*mātrāpacāra*), the ritual action (*karman*)—this is the understood remainder—is completed by that [remaining portion]. When the primary oblation and so forth are possible and the material already acquired is present, there is an omission of the subsidiary acts (*śeṣakārya*); however, the primary act itself must be performed with that very [material]. Thus, when the prescribed material is available in a quantity sufficient for the primary act, that alone should be taken. Even in that case, it is better to omit the subsidiary acts than to take a substitute (*pratinidhi*) capable of performing those subsidiary acts. Furthermore, even regarding a substitute, he states that an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed because of the abandonment of the prescribed genus (*jāti*) and other such factors:
"In the absence of the material, there is a substitute; in the transgression of the injunction, there is expiation."

In the case of an improper measure (*mātrāpacāra*), there is no substitute (*pratinidhi*), yet an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) certainly does occur. Regarding the phrase "in the absence of the substance," the repetition of the word "absence" is for the purpose of demonstrating that a substitute is to be employed only when there is an absence of a substance sufficient for the primary rite. Even if a substitute has not been taken due to the fear that the prescribed substance already procured might be destroyed, once the performance of the primary rite is accomplished by means of that substitute, if the originally procured substance should be recovered, then the rite must indeed be performed again with that [original substance].

Even though the substance has been appropriated and is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), if there is a fear of its destruction, the purpose is fulfilled by taking a substitute. Thus, even when the original substance—such as a sacrificial post (*yūpa*)—is already obtained, acts such as tying the animal (*niyojana*) are not to be performed again. These specific details are to be understood through the principle that "that which serves another purpose is guided by a single [rule]" (*parārthānyeka-neti nyāya*) and from other sūtras. 1ka. sa. ga. ca, cha, ṭa, ṇa, *lakṣaṇam*. 1praḥ *paṭalaḥ*. [This is accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 283. Not [to be performed] again; the work of the priests and others is [as previously stated]. These specific points are to be known from the aforementioned logic and other sūtras.
There is no substitute for an owner, a wife, a son, a country, time, fire, a deity, an action, or a word. || 1 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the third book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

When the master has perished, by whom could a substitute be taken? For one who has already undertaken the role of agent, the fruit of the action would belong to him alone; thus, there can be no substitute in his absence or incapacity, and that ritual action must simply be omitted. While it might have been stated "of the sacrificer," [it is specified as] those duties and purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) occasioned by the status of ownership, for they are for the sake of enjoying the fruit; there is indeed no substitute for these, whereas there is for other purposes. On this point, Kātyāyana states the distinction: "There is a substitute for secondary qualities (*guṇa*), because they exist for the sake of another."

Even the master is substituted in the case of subordinate items (guṇapadārtha) such as the placing of the sacrificial vessels (pātrāsādana) and the inspection of the clarified butter (ājyāvekṣaṇa). Why is this so? Because they are for the sake of another. For he [the master] exists for the sake of another; he does not accomplish his own purpose like the primary [sacrifice]. Therefore, even the master is substituted for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the sacrifice. Thus it is said.

For this very reason, the Teacher will state: "Thus, even for one who has gone on a journey, the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) are performed; facing whichever direction his fears lie, the Adhvaryu mutters the mantras while performing the rites, such as the touching of the other [sacrificer], until the conclusion of the assignment of the mantras. In this way, although a substitute for the wife is likewise impossible, she is mentioned again to state that the same applies to her for another reason as well.

In that regard, no substitute is possible for a wife, a son, or the sacred fires. Regarding the statement "of a permanent substance," it is meant that there can be no substitution for a fixed substance that has been perfected through ritual consecration (*saṃskāra*). Among these, the category of "birth" (*jāti*) is not applicable to a wife and so forth; for these entities are not established anywhere by birth alone, but rather, they receive their respective designations only when they have been consecrated by specific rites such as the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*), the sowing of seed (*vījāvāpa*), and the placing [of the fire] (*ādhāna*).

That [fire], however, cannot exist anywhere else. Although *māyā* may be possible for another as well, if it has been consecrated by the *ādhāna* rite, then it is obtained through its own specific authority and does not serve as a substitute for another. Furthermore, that which has not been consecrated by the *ādhāna* is ineligible as a substitute in Vedic rituals precisely because of the prohibition. The same should be understood regarding a son in the performance of paternal rites. There is no such thing as a "second fire" that is consecrated; indeed, no one is established according to the rule of the *āhavanīya*, *gārhapatya*, and other sacrificial fires.

Since place and time are intended as objects of reference (*uddeśya*) and are not themselves things to be prescribed (*anupādeya*), how could there be a specific substance to be prescribed? For when a place is characterized by that property, it is the [place] that must be enjoined by the word; an object that is not to be prescribed cannot serve as a substitute. [Objection: But how can time be a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the ritual action, since it is not itself enjoined? [Reply: This is not so, because we accept that the ritual action itself is enjoined in connection with a specific time; thus, the status of being "not to be prescribed" belongs only to that which is not an auxiliary. Therefore, the ritual action must be enjoined precisely where [the time] occurs.

Furthermore, since the quality of sloping toward the east can be accomplished in another location, there is no substitute for the deity either. There is no such thing as a "deity-genus" (jāti), nor does it possess a common universal (sāmānya), because its nature is understood solely through the injunction. Deityhood is established by a secondary derivative suffix (taddhita), the dative case, or the wording of a mantra; it is not apprehended through any other means of knowledge or through functional capacity (sāmarthya) such that a substitute could exist.

For even in the case of an action with a visible purpose, such as threshing, pounding is indeed capable [of performing that function]; however, in the case of an action with an invisible purpose, there is no such capacity. (Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram—Third Praśna)

Another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) must be sought by which [the word] could be substituted when it is capable [of performing its function]. In the case of a word whose substitute has been forgotten, if that [original word] is not remembered, the meaning to be conveyed would remain unknown; therefore, what kind of meaning could the substituted word convey? If any [random] thing were taken up as a substitute, it would serve a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*), and thus it would not fulfill its own specific purpose. The particle "ca" (and) is intended to include such things whose capacity is not understood without the authority of the sacred scripture (*śāstra*).

3.2 Now begins the second chapter of the third book. I have composed this detailed commentary on the first chapter of the third book, following the path of the two-fold Mīmāṃsā according to my understanding. This explanation, which follows the Sūtras, should be regarded as a garland offered to Viṣṇu, whose body is the sacrifice, by one desiring great fruit. In the first chapter of the third book, the fruit of the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*)—namely, supreme liberation (*niḥśreyasa*)—and the qualification for those obligatory rites have been defined. [The topics include] the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), the re-establishment (*punarādhāna*), the Agnihotra, and the journey (*prayāṇaka*).

The extension of rules from the *Davihoma* and other matters, as well as the ritual manuals (*tantra*), are proclaimed here. In this third book (*praśna*), the *Navānneṣṭi* sacrifice and the *Tṛṣṭi* are fully described. The first book (*praśna*) sets forth the *Ādhāna*, which is the initial rite for the Śrauta sacrifices. However, in this [third book], the *Ādhāna* is treated in five chapters beginning with the second. Therein, the *Ādhāna* is threefold: preceded by the *Soma* sacrifice, preceded by an *Iṣṭi*, or preceded by a *Homa*. In all these cases, there is an option according to one's preference; however, the *Ādhāna* preceded by the *Soma* sacrifice is only for one who does not possess the expiatory (*prāyaścitta*) and animal (*paśu*) sacrifices.

However, some, asserting that the expiatory animal sacrifice (*prāyaścitta-paśu*) shares the same ritual framework (*samānatantra*) as the *āmīṣomīya* or the *savanīya* animal sacrifices, maintain that the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) must be preceded by the Soma sacrifice, based on the statement of the Kalpakāras. Prior to the *ādhāna*, the wife also studies the mantras required for the rituals from her father, her husband, or from the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). The *ādhāna*—characterized as the consecration (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the installation of the fires in their respective hearths (*āyatana*) according to the prescribed rule—is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to any specific rite, because it is enjoined as a general rule (*anārabhyādhīta*).

Nor does the sentence establish these as auxiliary parts of the ritual (*karmāṅgatā*) by means of the injunction "one should kindle the fires" (*agnīn ādadhīta*); rather, their status as auxiliaries is understood only with respect to the fires themselves. Consequently, because they produce those fires, they are to be performed entirely outside of the ritual acts. This is also the case for the *patramāneṣṭis*, which are purificatory rites (*saṃskārakarma*). [End of] Paṭala 6. [From the work] *Mahādevakṛtavaijayantīvyākhyāsameta*. 285.

This has already been shown. By such statements as "when one offers in the Āhavanīya fire," and by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating that "thus all his desired objects are accomplished," it is demonstrated that the status of these acts as *saṃskārakarma* (preparatory rites) is accepted. Through that consecration, the fires, once purified, are subsequently enjoined by other sentences as constituent parts (*aṅga*) of various respective rituals. For there are two kinds of substances that serve as ritual constituents (*karmāṅga*): one is established through worldly means and enjoined as a constituent, while the other is established through Vedic action and enjoined as a constituent.

The action that accomplishes that [result] is also of two kinds: that which is included within the *prayoga* (the ritual procedure) and that which is not included therein. The first, being a primary subsidiary (*pradhānāṅga*), is indeed productive of the substance, such as threshing and so forth, which produces the *puroḍāśa* cake. The other, without having attained the status of a subsidiary to the primary action, is productive of the substance while serving as a subsidiary to a subsidiary; for example, Vedic study (*adhyayana*) produces the *svādhyāya* (one's own portion of the Veda), and the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is likewise. The qualified performers (*adhikārin*) of these have already been determined.

Furthermore, in the first chapter, he will state that for those who are not Śūdras and whose actions are not defective, there is the initiation (*upanayana*), the study of the Vedas (*vedādhyayana*), and the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) even among the *dharṣas*. Because it is recited among the obligatory rites (*nitya*) by virtue of its being obligatory, it is included among the purificatory acts (*saṃskāras*) even when performed alone, provided it is devoid of sacrificial oblations (*havirvarja*). Since it is a cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) through the mediation of the transcendental result of the rule (*niyamāpūrva*), it must therefore also be understood here as having a distinct ritual procedure (*kalpa*).

With this very intention, Baudhāyana stated: "One should not desire the fruit of the *ṛtu* at the beginning of the *ṛtu*, nor the fruit of the *yajñāṅga* at the beginning of the *yajñāṅga*"; having begun thus, he says: "The fire-installation (*ādhāna*) is for one who desires all fruits. Vaikhānasa, however, having stated that the fire-installation is for the sake of all rites, concludes that the installation must be preceded by a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). In this regard, if there is a deficiency in the constituent parts of the installation, the entire rite must be performed again, but not merely the deficient part alone.

Why? Because after performing the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), the subsidiary rite (*aṅga*) must be performed. However, there is no *āhavanīya* fire when the *ādheya* (the act of establishing the fires) has not been accomplished; yet, in the case of the *pavamāna-havis* offerings, the procedure proceeds by means of future designations. Regarding this, Baudhāyana states that it is beneficial: "One who intends to establish the fires for the first time should make himself pure (*prājya*); by whatever means he may achieve well-being, by that he should bring about well-being," as well as the aforementioned preliminary purification (*puraścaraṇa*) of oneself. *Prājya* means pure; by whichever ritual act his well-being—that is, the expiation—is achieved.

Likewise, it has been stated by Vaikhānasa as well: "The sacrificer, disciplined and endowed with faith, having been authorized and having shaved his hair, beard, body hair, and nails according to the rule, shall study the Veda beginning with 'For food thee,' 'For strength thee,' and so forth; he shall perform a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while meditating on Nārāyaṇa; having fasted together with his wife and consuming an oblation mixed with ghee with milk, he shall observe the vows prescribed in the Smṛtis for the sake of purification; and he shall offer the *amātya-homas* and the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* oblations."

"Disciplined" means free from the fickleness of the senses. "Permitted by the Brāhmaṇas," he should have his hair and so forth shaved. "Reciting the Veda" means the complete study (*pārāyaṇa*) of the Vedas; "meditating on Nārāyaṇa"; and "having restrained the self" means subsisting by the abandonment of food. Regarding the complete study of the Vedas, breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and other such vows prescribed in the Smṛtis—such as the *āmātyahoma* and others—the rule for eating applies to one together with his wife, consisting of food mixed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and so forth.

In this manner, having performed other acts mentioned in the Smṛtis—such as recitations (*japa*), oblations (*tilahoma*), and so forth, as well as penances like the *Kṛcchra* and *Cāndrāyaṇa*—according to one’s capacity and for as long as one considers one’s own purification to be achieved, one should cut the *araṇi* wood before the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). Whether the period is twelve days or another, if the resolve is for a year, the wood must be brought [prepared] beforehand. Regarding the measurement of the *bharaṇī*, the opinion of the Teachers (*Ācāryas*) is that it is defined by its purpose; that is, it should be of such a size as is sufficient for the task. Baudhāyana, however, says: [text fragment].

2kha cha. "Thā ta"|—286. Satyāṣāḍha’s *Śrautasūtra* [Third Praśna]: "It has four corners, twelve *aṅgulas* in width, and sixteen *aṅgulas* in length. Kātyāyana says it is twenty-four *aṅgulas*. It is also stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "By the number of syllables of the Gāyatrī," and so forth. Bhāradvāja, however, says: "That *aśvattha* tree which is 'born from within the *śamī*' (*śamīgarbha*) and is joined with the earth by its root. The meaning is that it is that *aśvattha* whose root has actually reached the ground, not one that has merely begun to grow even within a *śamī* tree. Both [criteria] are accepted by our teacher.

Likewise, one should construct the hall (śālā) that will be described hereafter, as well as the sanctuaries (āyatanas), even beforehand. This has been stated with specific detail by Vaikhānasa: "If [the tree] is an Aśvattha growing from within a Śamī, or if it is not a Śamī..."

Having gone to a place that is white, like a sprout, uninjured by lightning or thunderbolts, belonging to another, not too dry, not decayed, and not defiled by low-born people; having circumambulated it clockwise while reciting the Vaiśvānara-sūkta and bowing down; and having cut a branch facing east or north in a clockwise direction starting from the east—with its tip pointing eastward, its base toward the south, with the lower part serving as the support, stripped of bark from the sides, the bark removed, dried, twenty-four finger-breadths in length, eight finger-breadths in width, and four finger-breadths in height.

Likewise, with the upper portion, he makes the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇī*) by means of the *gāyatrī* [meter]. In this regard, the first four finger-breadths are the head, the eyes, the ears, and the mouth; the second are the neck, the shoulders, the heart, and the breast; the third are the abdomen and so forth; the fourth are the hips; the fifth are the thighs; and the sixth are the shanks and the feet—so say some. In this way, the two fire-drills become complete with all their limbs. If he churns [the fire] when they are deficient in limbs, the sacrificer becomes deficient in limbs; if they are deficient in joints, he becomes jointless.

If one were to churn at the top, his sacrifice would remain uncommenced; [churning] the thighs would provide a womb for the *rakṣases*, and the feet a womb for the *piśācas*; the buttocks (*śroṇī*) are the womb of the gods. Therefore, one should churn first at the buttocks. Leaving eight finger-breadths from the base and twelve finger-breadths from the top, and three finger-breadths on each side, one should thus effect procreation during the first churning. Having fashioned the upper fire-stick (*uttarāraṇi*) to be eight finger-breadths long and having measured the circumference of the churning-stick (*pramantha*), he joins it to the base of the churning-stick (*manthamūla*); together with that, it is complete.

"It is said that the pit (*chidra*) is twenty-six finger-breadths deep and long; the *prācīrā* is the fire-drill (*araṇi*), and likewise the altar (*vedi*). In the house, O gentle one, having constructed a large hall extending from west to east and with its longitudinal beam (*anuvaṃśa*) toward the south-east, and having removed bones, hair, nails, husks, wood, stones, clods of earth, ants, and so forth, and having purified it with clay—the construction of the sites for the *gārhapatya* and other fires is thus described. The meaning of this *Vaikhānasa-sūtra* is clear.

Regarding the phrase "tvak-pārśva-vibhāgāt," the meaning is that one should not perform excessive carving on its own sides or on its upper portion; rather, only that much of the shaft (*śākhā*) should be taken as is necessary so that the width becomes eight *aṅgulas*. On the lower portion, however, the carving should be done up to the interior cavity (*garbha*). Then, in the middle portion, it should be made twenty-four *aṅgulas* long, eight *aṅgulas* wide, and four *aṅgulas* high.

It is not stated here that one should produce two pieces by splitting the branch and then make the lower and upper fire-drills (*araṇī*) from those two; rather, some maintain that by the very act of splitting—that is, according to the ritual procedure beginning with the head—one should take the lower section of that branch as the lower fire-drill (*adharāraṇi*) and the portion above it as the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇi*).

These are not merely explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) beginning from the top; rather, they are injunctions (*vidhi*). Leaving aside eight finger-breadths (*aṣṭāṅgula*) from the base, one should leave twelve finger-breadths on each side; in the middle, there is a space three finger-breadths wide and four finger-breadths long, which is the place for the first churning. This applies to the lower fire-drill (*adharāraṇi*); likewise, it applies to the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇi*) as well. However, regarding the upper fire-drill, the circumference is eight finger-breadths, equal to the wrapping of a cord eight finger-breadths long all around; and the piece called the "churner" (*pramantha*) should also be placed within the belly [of the wood]. This too is based solely upon tradition.

At the base of the churning-stick (manthamūla), [the mantra is recited]. [End of] the second section (dvi-paṭala) of the twenty-eighth chapter, accompanied by the Vaijayantī commentary composed by Mahādeva.

The *mantha* is a device made from the heartwood of a sacrificial tree, around which a rope is wound for rotating. Having carved away the root-end of this *mantha*, one joins the root-end of the *pramantha*, which is in the form of a splinter; the length of both once joined is twenty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). By this, the single-hall structure is described. However, the teacher Prācīnavaṃśa will state regarding the measurement of the space that it may be in either the *āhavanīya* hall or the *gārhapatya* hall. From this, it is understood that two halls with beams running northward must be constructed.

Āpastamba, however, has explicitly stated two distinct halls (*śālā*). Regarding these, first, on the day prior to the establishment of the *brāhmaudanika* fire, one should perform the *nāndīśrāddha*, the *mṛd-akaśānti*, and the binding of the *pratisara*; prior even to that, one should perform the offering to the *ṛtvij*s. As for the characteristics of the vessels, they have been described specifically in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. The author of the Sūtra did not explicitly state the measurements for the sacrificial altars (*āyatana*); therefore, the measurement of the *gārhapatya* and other fires, as well as the *dhiṣṇya* hearths, is determined by their respective proportions.

They are grasped by all the ritualists (*yājñika*), for they are those fires belonging to the *dhiṣṇya* hearths. Regarding their measurement, it is known from the tradition of the *dhiṣṇyas* that "they are the size of a *piśīla*"; some say they are square, while others say they are circular—this is the rule (*sūtra*). Among these, there is an option regarding the circular shape. It is the consensus of many teachers who composed the *sūtras* that all sacrificial seats (*āyatana*) may be either square or circular. In this regard, they describe the measurement of a *piśīla* in five ways: one is the distance between the two arms.

"Arani" for the second; "aranis" for the third; "thirty-two finger-breadths" for the fourth; and "thirty-six finger-breadths" for the fifth. One should draw a circle using half the measurement of these [fingers]; this applies to all fires. Alternatively, the conclusion is that all [the hearths] may be square using either one of these measurements. Or else, the specific rule stated by Vaikhānasa should be adopted.

Having drawn a circle eighteen finger-breadths in diameter for the site of the *gārhapatya* fire, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) eight finger-breadths high; leaving a margin of four finger-breadths in width all around, one makes a depression in the center six finger-breadths wide. What remains above that shall be the upper girdle (*mekhalā*), and all around it, one makes a lower girdle four finger-breadths wide and high.

Likewise, having prepared the site for the Āhavanīya fire as a square altar with four corners, measuring thirty-two finger-breadths on each side and eight finger-breadths in height, and having left a space around it as before, he constructs a middle girdle and a lower girdle that is depressed in the center. (Anvā.)

Having drawn a circle with a radius of twenty-five *aṅgulas* for the *āhavanīya* fire, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the shape of a half-moon in the southern half, as previously described. Its center should be elevated, while the edges are depressed; it should have upper and lower ridges (*mekhalā*), with the altar (*vedi*) situated on the northern side. It is stated that at a distance of one *prakrama* from the eastern edge of the altar, one should make the raised mound (*utkara*). As for the altar itself, its dimensions are already shown in its own specific manual, so it need not be described here; however, it should be understood that its height is four *aṅgulas*, and the same applies to the *utkara*.

This too must be accepted because it is based on the Śruti. According to the view of the Bhāṣya, there is equality of area. Following this, the ritualists say: "The Gārhapatya is circular, the Āhavanīya is square, and the Dakṣiṇāgni is semicircular; these have equal areas."

Thinking this to be more pleasing, our own ritualists (*yājñika*) also follow the measurement of the *piśīla* prescribed in their own *sūtras*—namely, one *aratni*—and, adhering to the squareness or roundness prescribed in their own *sūtras*, they lay out the sacrificial hearths (*āyatana*), making all the hearths equal in size. [From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Third Praśna] 1. Ka, Ga, U, Pa: *chāṅgu*; 2. Ka, Ga, Ca, Cha, Ṭa, Ṭha, Ṇa: *tulaṃ vā*. 288.
