Having established the primary house as having the *araṇi* (the fire-drill) as its width and that as its fundamental form (*prakṛti*), they construct other [houses] equal to that field, either by themselves inferring them according to the method stated by Śukra, or by taking the *araṇi*-measure as a square (*caturaśra*) as the fundamental form, or as a circle equal to that field; and whatever is on the other side of the fire-altar is done as before. Regarding this, the following *kārikās* have been uttered: "Having first determined the east, one should then design the monastery (*vihāra*). As for the method of determining the east, the Teacher has declared it in the ritual manual (*kalpa*)."

I shall explain this very matter after consulting the commentary: one who is discerning should know that the direction of the East lies between the constellations Citrā and Svāti; or, for those dwelling in the southern regions, it is the constellation Śroṇā (Jyeṣṭhā); however, for those situated in the northern quarter, the Kṛttikās should be known as the East. This common rule for all lands will now be stated by me: on a desired level site measuring two cubits, [one should prepare a board] six finger-breadths in circumference and twelve finger-breadths in length.

A peg made of *khadira* wood, smooth, unblemished, straight, one *akṣṇu* (or *kṣṇukra*) in length, and with a level head, should be fashioned; one should place it in a level spot. One should lay down a line extending eastward from the peg, using a cord equal in length to the peg and provided with two loops. Having released the two loops at the center, one should mark the *ciḍa* (the center). One should then draw a circle around that peg on all sides using the *ciḍa* as the radius. At the intersection of the previously drawn line and the circle—

Two stakes (śaṅku) should be fixed at the east and west; the east and west directions are determined by means of a cord (tāntra). One should know the desired [extent] as far as it reaches. Then, having fastened a loop (pāśa) on the eastern [stake], one should draw a circle with another loop; likewise, having released the loop on the western [stake], one should draw another circle. At the intersection of the two circles, starting from the stake, the south and north directions are established. In this way, one should then determine the intermediate directions (vidiś). Likewise, having fastened loops in the directions starting from the east, [one proceeds] according to the mark.

One should thus draw four mandalas in their proper sequence. The junctions of these mandalas are proclaimed to be the intermediate directions (vidiś). This is the method taught by the Teacher for determining the east, characterized by the knowledge of the eastern direction. There is another way of knowing the east according to the system of the Sūryasiddhānta; that same meaning is here also explained by me according to my understanding. [End of] the *Sadviṃśati-ṭala* [section], together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

When the sun has entered the sign of Capricorn (*maunakanyā*) and sixteen days have passed, the wise man should understand that the east has been determined by the sun. In other months, however, it should be known that [the direction] is indeed covered by the seasonal winds (*vṛta*), as will be described. On level ground, one should draw a circle with a cord (*rajju*) twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long. In the center of that, one should fix a gnomon (*śaṅku*) twelve finger-breadths in length. Wherever the tip of its shadow touches the lines running from east to west, there one should drive two more gnomons and slightly extend the cord on both sides.

Having fixed those two pins at the western end, one should draw a line across [from east to west]. Likewise, having fixed them at the eastern pin, one should fashion a line in that same manner. When this is done, there will be a fish-shaped figure extending from south to north. Having fixed pins at the head and tail of that fish in the southern and northern directions, one should fashion another fish extending from east to west using a cord. Following the head and tail of that [east-west] fish, one should determine the eastern direction.

Having thus subdued the intermediate directions (vidiśas), one should then prepare the sacrificial ground (vihāra). Regarding the measurement in finger-breadths (aṅgula) and so forth, the Preceptor has already spoken; however, because it is useful for determining the size of the altar (vedi), I shall now state that measurement. From fourteen atoms (aṇus) up to that same number, it constitutes a finger-breadth (aṅgula). Alternatively, thirty-three sesame seeds placed within a sheath (kośa) constitute a finger-breadth here. Ten finger-breadths make a small step (kṣudrapada); a span (prādeśa) is twelve finger-breadths; a cubit (pṛtha) is thirteen finger-breadths; and a yoke (yuga) is likewise [fourteen].

A *pada* (step) is fifteen or twelve *aṅgulas*; two *padas* constitute a *prakrama*. A *prādeśa* is two *aranis*. The knee (*jānu*) is thirty-two or thirty-six *aṅgulas*. The axle (*akṣa*) is four hundred *aṅgulas*, and the yoke (*yuga*) is eighty-six *aṅgulas*. The measure of the pole (*īṣā*) is one hundred and eighty-eight *aṅgulas*. Four *aranis* is the measure of a *vyāyāma*. Five *aranis* is a *puruṣa* and also a *vyāma*.

In this context, one should determine the dimensions for both the sacrificer and the Adhvaryu priest. In sacrificial enclosures (vihāras) involving the sacred fires, the measurement is indeed that of the Yati. First, the sequence of measurements for the altar of the Ādhāna is declared. [Note: The text fragment provided appears to be a portion of a commentary on Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, specifically concerning the measurements of the sacrificial ground.]

The house for the *agnihotra* should measure four cubits (*hasta*). In its center, one should fashion a straight line extending westward along the *pṛṣṭhyā*. After leaving two paces behind that, there shall be the site for the secondary fire (*parāgni*). Having fixed a peg (*śaṅku*) in the middle of that site, measured by a span (*arali*), one should draw a circle from the peg using a cord measured by a span (*prādeśa*). Leaving three paces in front of that, the pit for the eastern fire (*pūrvāgni*) shall be located; it measures twenty-one finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) together with nine sesame seeds (*tila*).

The altar should be made square and level; its enclosure is now described. A cord equal in measure to the [intended] length of the altar should be taken as an addition. A mark should be made at the midpoint of this added portion, and that mark should serve for the two hips (the western corners). Furthermore, a mark should be made at the midpoint of the distance between those two, which will be used for the drawing (the eastern corners). One should fix a loop situated on the long side to the front peg. From the mark, one should pull a loop extending along the short side to the rear peg. Then, from the established marks, one should determine the two hips to the south and north.

Having reversed the noose from the gnomon (śaṅku), one should fix it upon its shoulders in front. Between the eastern and western [lines], there shall be a fivefold *pṛṣṭhyā* line. Then, one should apply the sixth part as an additional [section] equally there. Having again folded that rope—which has nooses at both ends—into five parts, one should then mark the middle between the second and third parts. Thus, there shall be three parts in front and two parts behind.

One should fix the two loops of the cord upon the central stake situated between the eastern and western marks. Having drawn the cord toward the southern mark, one should direct a stake at that mark. Here, the central stake of the southern altar-site shall be established. Then, having drawn the cord toward the northern mark, a stake is set for the purpose of the *ānavakṛpti* (the measurement of the space). Having drawn that same cord with the loops reversed toward the northern mark, a stake is placed at the mark; there shall be the *ulmuka* (embers) and the path of movement (*saṃcara*) between them. And the southern altar-ground shall be thirty-four *amulyas* in extent.

To the south of the central gnomon (śaṅku), at a distance of eight and a half finger-breadths, one should drive in a gnomon. Having drawn a circle with a radius equal to half the length of that very gnomon, one should place a cord (spandhā) extending eastward in the middle of that circle. The southern arc would belong to the fire-altar (agni), while one should leave the northern arc free; or else, the outer circumference may be [measured] by twenty-seven finger-breadths. [End of] Second Paṭala. [This text is accompanied by the commentary Vaijayantī composed by Mahādeva.]

The mandala should be drawn with a cord measuring thirteen and a half *aratnis*. Alternatively, the hearth for the eastern fire (*pūrvāgni*) should measure one *aratni*. One should make it square and even, according to the procedure described therein. Leaving a space of one *aratni* between the *bhaṇī* and the *āhavanīya*, there should be the chamber for the *sabhya* fire; the intervening space should be the same as before. Leaving the site for the *āvasathya* fire, one should construct it like the *āhavanīya*. From the central peg of the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*), [one proceeds] twelve *tilas* [to the east].

When two fingers have passed [the mark], one should then indicate the *maṇḍala*. The diameter of the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire-altar is thirty *aṅgulas* along with four *tilas*, and its *maṇḍala* is half of that. Another *maṇḍala* is to be drawn from the *śaṅku* situated on the northern line of the [first] *maṇḍala*. At the junction of the two *maṇḍalas*, one should cast two markers (*spandhā*) to the east and west. There should be two winnowing baskets (*śūrpa*), the southern one for the *dakṣiṇāgni* and the northern one for the *āhavanīya*. The altar (*vedi*) is ninety-six *aṅgulas* [in width] to the west of the *āhavanīya* fire.

Subsequently, the transverse line should be known to measure sixty-four *aṅgulas*. That [line] joined with the *bharata* is said to be the front transverse line. The two ends of the cord measuring seven *aratnis* should have loops. From the final loop, at a distance of one *aratni*, there should be a mark for the purpose of the shoulder (*aṃsa*). At thirty-two *aṅgulas* from the loop, there should be a mark for the purpose of the neck (*śroṇi*). For the purpose of pulling the loop across three *aratnis*, there is a non-marking [space]. Having fastened the loops to the two stakes at the corners, [one proceeds] from the mark.

Having drawn [the cord] from the southeast corner peg, the architect should fashion the hip-line according to the established marks. It should be long and square; in this same manner, he should do the other side. Having doubled the side-measure, he should fix the two ends of the cord with loops. Then, having stretched the two loops over the peg situated at the southeast corner, and having made a mark in the middle, he should pull the mark toward the south. When the peg is established at the mark, and having fixed the two loops on the peg, he should draw the side-line using the mark, reaching as far as the southeast corner.

In the same way, one should draw the northern line reaching the northwestern and northeastern corners. By doubling the cord, one should draw the lines for the east and west. That which remains in front of the western fire-altar is the space for the Ārya, measured by the distance between the two thumbs (ratni). If the ground there consists of atoms, how could one prepare the sacrificial altar (vedi)? —Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Third Book.

From the two pegs (śaṅku) situated at the outer corners, one should direct four pegs on the southern and northern sides at a distance of eight finger-breadths (aṅgula). One should extend the side-measuring cord (pārśvamānī) by eight finger-breadths; having cast the loop outside the peg, one should gradually bend that cord with the rope. The wise one should draw the line on the outside and fashion the lower girdle (adhomekhalā) with clay, four finger-breadths wide and six finger-breadths in height. This is shown to be the sacrificial ground (vihāra) for the establishment of the fire and the ritual acts.

Thus says the Vṛddha-kārikā of the Baudhāyanīyas; that very same view is desired by us as well. However, two measurements have been mentioned for the sacrificial sites (āyatanas), and those are to be applied according to a specific rule. The author of the Sūtra stated that the site for the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths follows the *piśīla* measurement. That *piśīla*, however, is said by him to be equal to an *arani*. Then he stated that the *viṣṇiya* hearths are either circular or square. The western fire-altar (*paścimāgni*) has a diameter of one *arani*; the area shown by that measurement is equal to the previous one [the *piśīla*]. The eastern direction is likewise indicated.

With twenty-one finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and nine sesame seeds, the square altar for the Dakṣiṇāgni is likewise declared. If the square altar situated at the hearth (dhiṣṇya) is measured by the span of an aratni, then that field is circular, measuring twenty-seven aṅgulas. By that measure of the aratni, the square is declared; however, a specific distinction regarding our Dakṣiṇāgni hearth is now stated: the intermediate space is divided either fivefold or sixfold.

One should bring a sixth or even a seventh part to be added. Having tripled that cord, the drawing [of the line] occurs at the first part. Alternatively, having placed the loops on the stakes situated between the eastern and western fires, and having also placed the loops on the initial and final stakes between the two mounds (khara), one should pull it toward the south. In that drawing, one should plant a stake; that is the middle [stake]. Or, to the south of that, there is the site for the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni). That method shall be twofold.
One should place a śaṅku eight and a half aṅgulas to the north; or else, one should rotate it in a circle with a radius of seventeen aṅgulas.
1 ka. ga. 8. u. kṛptare | 3 ka. ga. caṃ, cha, ṭa, ṭha. śīlaṃ mata' | — [Second Paṭala] Together with the Vaijayantī commentary composed by Mahādeva: 293.

To the south, or indeed in the southern half, the other portion is said to be located. At that time, the eastern fire-altar (pūrvāgni) should have a base measuring one *aratni* in extent; however, in this case, one should mark it out using a cord nineteen finger-breadths long plus a third part of a finger. There, one should prepare the southern fire-altar (*dakṣiṇāgni*) within a circle as before, by means of making four corners of the circle according to the scriptural injunctions. Therefore, the cord is connected [to the center], and thus it has been explained by the commentators.

However, for those [altars] whose diameter is slightly greater than circular, there will inevitably be a contradiction with the mathematical calculation; of this there is no doubt. Thus, prior to the *brāhmaudana* (the rice-offering for the Brahman), one should prepare for the *ādhāna* (the establishment of the sacred fires). Having thus completed the preliminary requirements, with his soul purified and accompanied by his wife, he should perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). Preceded by the recollection of Gaṇeśa and other chosen deities, while the husband and wife are seated upon *darbha* grass with *darbha* blades in their hands and their mouths restrained, the procedure for the acquisition of the fires as described in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices should be observed.

In this regard, the specific detail is as follows: having remembered, "On this day, in this year, in this season, on this lunar day (*parvan*), or under this asterism (*nakṣatra*); or else, twelve days, four days, three days, two days, or one day from today; or under this asterism or lunar day," the husband and wife both recite three times in a whisper and three times aloud: "I shall establish the sacred fires for the sake of accomplishing all rites—whatever rites I am capable of performing and in which I have the authority—and through that rite, may I please the Lord of Sacrifice."

Some say that [the rites] may be preceded by the Soma sacrifice, the Homa, or the Iṣṭi, and that this should always be remembered; however, there is no difference [in the result] thereby. Prior to the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should perform the offering to Ārā, the water-purification (*udakaśānti*), and the binding of the *pratisara* cord. On the previous day or on that very day, one should perform the *nāndīśrāddha*. Then, one should select officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) possessing the prescribed characteristics: the Brahman, the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Agnīdhra. For the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), one should choose the Brahman with the formula: "I choose you as the Brahman. They should respond: "So shall it be."

[He should choose] those who have the Adhvaryu as their primary [Vedic branch], who are clear in speech, and who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*). Here, according to the *Vaikhānasa*: having tied the protective cord (*pratisara*) on that day, the sacrificer chooses the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who possess the aforementioned characteristics and honors them; the sacrificer and his wife give the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and they both become adorned with new lower garments, upper shawls, ornaments, flowers, and so forth. According to the Śruti, "one should offer oblations with these [mantras]," one should offer the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* oblations in the domestic fire (*aupāsana*). Having cut [the wood] according to the procedure involving the supporting [fire], the two fire-drills (*araṇī*)—which were previously dried—are established.

The word *araṇī* is well-known to refer to the wood used for churning fire; it is not a term denoting a ritual consecration (*saṃskāra*). Both [the Aśvattha tree and the Araṇī] are brought at one time with a single mantra, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra "I carry" (*harāmi*). Since the Aśvattha has been uprooted or dug up, he carries the Araṇī [from it], because they are substances that have become joined together. From the understanding of the meaning of the mantra—"that [Aśvattha] of yours, I carry in the form of the Araṇī"—having taken them together, he leads them away with the mantra. For this very reason, Āpastamba says, "He brings [them]. Likewise, Bharadvāja also says, "He should bring [them] in this manner."

Alternatively, one may extract it from the *aśvattha* alone; for it is known from scripture: "This *śamī* is indeed [the earth], and this *aśvattha* is its embryo. Or rather, one may extract it from the *aśvattha* alone. To establish the validity of the mantra, he cites the scriptural passage beginning with "This, indeed... This well-known earth itself is the *śamī*, and the *aśvattha* is its embryo—such is the explanation of the scripture. Therefore, the mantra is not contradicted even when used with a fire-drill made solely of *aśvattha*.

"I gather together the sacrificial body of Agni, born from the Aśvattha tree and the fire that carries the oblation, whose womb is the Śamī tree, for the purpose of generating Agni. With these words he gathers it; once gathered, he consecrates it with the formula, "May [the two fires] bestow life upon me, may they bestow life upon the sacrificer. He gathers it and places it in the domestic fire-hall. As before, he consecrates it by means of the ritual procedure (*tantra*); therein is one [view].

Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, the two Punarvasūs, Phalgunyau, Hasta, Citrā, Viśākhe, Anūrādhā, Śroṇā, and the two Uttara-proṣṭhapadās are the lunar mansions for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya). Kṛttikā belongs to a Brāhmaṇa; the two Uttara-phalgunyau and Citrā belong to a Rājanya; the remaining ones belong to others.

*Kṛttikā* is a single asterism expressed by a feminine plural ending; *Anurādhā*, *Proṣṭhapadāḥ*, and *Punarvasū* are masculine; *Phalgunyau* and *Viśākhe* are feminine; the others are clear. *Kṛttikā* alone belongs to the Brāhmaṇa. For the consecrated Kṣatriya, that is, the Rājanya, [the asterism is] "Pūrva-phalgunyau"; here, although both the former and latter Phalgunīs are included, the term is in the dual ending (*phalgunyau*) because the intention is to express the general category alone.

And thus, these very same lunar mansions (nakṣatras) are both permanent and optional; this is the meaning regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya). As for the remaining ones—those other than the three [previously mentioned] lunar mansions for the establishment of the fires—they are the lunar mansions for the establishment of the fires specifically for those [classes], namely the Vaiśyas, Niṣādas, and Rathakāras, without distinction. Although the specification of particular lunar mansions as times should have been preceded by the mention of the seasons, months, and times, it has nevertheless been done in this manner according to the order of the text.

In this context, although specific castes such as Brāhmaṇas and others are mentioned, there is no subsequent application of that restriction to those rites prescribed for other purposes. Since no specific distinction is heard regarding optional (kāmya) rites, it applies to all who have performed the *ādhāna* (consecration of the fires); thus [the text] says:
"But the optional rites are for all.
The optional rites are indeed the same for everyone from Brāhmaṇas down to Niṣādas. [End of Section] [This concludes] the chapter composed by Mahādeva, together with the commentary *Vaijayantī*.
He states those very [details]:
"One who desires, 'May I be preeminent and possessed of Brahman-splendor,' should establish the sacred fires under the Kṛttikās.

The desire is: "May I be preeminent; may I possess *brahmavarcasa*—that is, splendor (*varcas*) consisting of brilliance (*tejas*) resulting from study, teaching, and so forth. Regarding that, he states the fault:

"Let fire indeed be a burner of my house"—this is the meaning: "If the fault seen in the Brāhmaṇa passage, namely the burning of the house, should occur, let it be; however, let there be for me the supreme fruit. Thus, he who desires such a fruit should perform the rite (*ādadhīta*). But in the case of the obligatory (*nitya*) rite, there is no fault. Why? Because in our own recension (*śākhā*), the fault is heard only in connection with the statement regarding the fruit. However, in other recensions, the fault is not heard in the context of the obligatory injunction for a Brāhmaṇa; thus, to demonstrate this, the fault was stated in that manner specifically within the statement regarding the fruit.

Nor is it the case that because the word "desire" (*kāma*) is not heard in the *Brāhmaṇa* text, [the rite] is not optional; for in other recensions (*śākhāntara*), the word "desire" is seen among similar passages. Thus, when a fruit is postulated here by means of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it is effectively mentioned as if it were already present—as in:

"He who, under the asterism Rohiṇī, should desire, 'May I cause all prosperities (*roha*) to flourish'"; where "prosperities" (*rohān*) refers to growths such as offspring, cattle, wealth, and so forth.
If one should desire under the asterism Mṛgaśiras, "May I be possessed of fortune," [he should sacrifice];
this is clear.
He who was formerly auspicious but would become more wicked should [sacrifice] under the two Punarvasus.
The meaning is: for one who previously possessed many virtues, but subsequently fell into decline, this is for the sake of avoiding that decline.
"He who should desire, 'May my subjects be desirous of giving to me,' he [should sacrifice] during the two former Phalgunīs.
This refers to one who desires: "May my subjects—those who are givers of worlds—have the intention, 'We shall give gifts to him. He is the one who so desires.
He who desires, "May I be fortunate," should perform [the sacrifice] during the latter two Phalgunīs; for Bhaga is excessive fortune. Some authorities record the opposite.
The meaning is that whatever fruit belongs to the two former [nakṣatras] belongs to the two latter, and whatever belongs to the two latter belongs to the two former.
Regarding the *hasta* nakṣatra: "He who should desire, 'May it be given to me'—that is, 'May it be bestowed upon me'—his desire is as before."
Under Citrā, one who has rivals [should sacrifice];
this has been explained.
Under Viśākhā, one desiring offspring [should sacrifice].

[This has been explained. Ka, Kha, Ga, Cha, Da, Ṭha, Ṇa, [and others read]: "I shall be. [In the third section—296: According to the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—] one who desires prosperity under the Anūrādhā asterisms [should perform the rite];
prosperity (*ṛddhi*) is complete success (*samṛddhi*).
One desiring prosperity should [perform rites] under Śroṇā;
prosperity consists of good fortune such as having sons and so forth.
One desiring spiritual splendor should [perform rites] under the Proṣṭhapadas.
It has gone; or [it is] under the constellation of the Sun;
the meaning is that this fruit is in the *hasta* [constellation].
Moreover, indeed, one should establish this fire at the very moment faith arises.

This has been recited specifically for the Brāhmaṇa. There is no restriction regarding a specific caste or a specific desire; rather, the meaning is that one should establish the fires on any of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) mentioned, provided there is faith. This was stated by Āpastamba: "Some transmit all [the rites] as if they were obligatory (*nitya*). This refers to all the optional (*kāmya*) ones. On this point, Bharadvāja says: "Now, therefore, for one who possesses faith, there is no restriction regarding the lunar mansion. Baudhāyana, however, states that it applies to the case of one who is ill. Spring is the time for the Brāhmaṇa’s establishment of the fires.

The months of Caitra and Vaiśākha, when the sun resides in Pisces and Aries, constitute spring (*vasanta*). For it is said, "Spring is indeed the mouth of the seasons. And that which is the full moon of Phalgunī is the mouth of the year.

Summer (*grīṣma*) and winter (*hemanta*) belong to the Rājanya. Following spring, the two months [of Jyeṣṭha and Āṣāḍha] are summer; winter consists of Mārgaśīrṣa and Pauṣa, or alternatively, when the sun is in Scorpio and Sagittarius.
The rainy season belongs to the chariot-maker;
it consists of the months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada, or when the sun is in Gemini or Cancer. Autumn belongs to the Vaiśya.

The months of Āśvina and Kārtika occur when the sun is in Virgo (Kanyā) or Libra (Tulā); or else, all the seasons are to be understood according to the Jyotiḥśāstra by the commencement of spring in Aries (Meṣa) and so forth. For all [classes], including Brāhmaṇas and others, as well as for the Rathakāra and the Niṣāda, Śiśira is [the season].

On the new moon day, on the full moon day, or during the waxing fortnight—the waxing fortnight being the first (or bright) fortnight—on these very seasons mentioned previously, as well as on the full moon days, the new moon days, and the waxing fortnights; [these are] optional alternatives. By the mention of "the waxing fortnight," there is a reiteration of the full moon day for the sake of emphasis and to indicate its specific commencement. Chapter 10, together with the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva:
under an auspicious constellation.

By the phrase "in the waxing fortnight" (*āpūryamāṇapakṣe*), [the condition] "under an auspicious lunar mansion" (*puṇye nakṣatre*) is conjoined; for the word *vā* ("or") has no connection here. In that regard, the five auspicious lunar mansions mentioned for the same day are not to be connected here. Since the installation of the *gārhapatya* fire occurs precisely before sunrise, and the installation of the *āhavanīya* fire occurs after sunrise, there is no purpose for this [conjunction]. Therefore, by the term "auspicious lunar mansion," the twelve previously mentioned lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā are understood. These are to be taken without distinction in all cases.

Regarding the castes: in this view, there is an exclusive restriction (*parisaṃkhyā*) for the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). However, in the view that "the Kṛttikās are for the Brāhmaṇa," even during the dark fortnight, there would be no obstacle [to the performance]; yet, because a lunar conjunction (*parvan*) is impossible in the spring among the Kṛttikās, the possibility of the Vaiśākha new moon being reached is rare, and thus the time for the Brāhmaṇa’s fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) would be difficult to obtain.
That [time] is "perfect" (*samṛddha*) where the three—the season (*ṛtu*), the asterism (*nakṣatra*), and the lunar conjunction (*parvan*)—concur.

This very Śruti is recited by the Vājasaneyins: "If those [materials] gathered—that is, brought together at the time of establishing the Gārhapatya fire—are obtained, then it is 'prosperous,' meaning highly meritorious.
Regarding the conflict [between the season and the lunar mansion], the season and the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) are stronger.

When the combination of all three is not possible, one should not pay heed to the lunar day (*parvan*), but rather, during the aforementioned seasons such as spring, one should adopt the lunar mansion alone. Here, the phrase "the waxing fortnight" (*āpūryamāṇapakṣa*) is combined; the commencement of this [treatise] is for that very purpose.
"One who is about to sacrifice with the Soma or one who is establishing the sacred fires need not observe either the season or the lunar mansion," so say some.

That Brāhmaṇa for whom there is no occasion for the *Ātyāśvina* sacrifice should perform the *Soma*-preceded establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*). For another, however, that is not possible. Even one who has not performed the *Sāṃnāyya* offering has no entitlement to its modification, the animal sacrifice; therefore, having performed either the oblation-preceded or the *Iṣṭi*-preceded [form], and having performed both the New and Full Moon sacrifices as well as the expiatory animal sacrifice, he should sacrifice with *Soma*. Some, based on the words of the ritual manual (*kalpaka*), desire the simultaneous immolation of those two animals together with the *savanīya*; one should neither follow nor disregard this.

The term *sūrtadhātu* is used for the sake of respect. Having established the fires on that particular lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) or during a festival (*parvan*), one may perform the rite after completing the sacrifice and concluding it, provided one adopts the procedure of consecration (*dīkṣā*) until the next festival arrives. One may likewise perform it starting from the eleventh or the twelfth [lunar day]. Thus it has been stated: "One should establish the fires in the spring alone; one need not wait for a specific season. This applies to those other than Brāhmaṇas. For them, spring is not the time for establishing the fires; however, the Soma sacrifice is for all in the spring alone. Therefore, one may establish the fires in accordance with the requirements of the Soma sacrifice.
Having moved to a site either to the east or to the north, a *śālīna* should establish the sacred fires on a sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) that slopes toward the east.

The term *śālīna* refers to one who dwells in a house (*śālā*) or a home (*gṛha*); this is the etymological derivation. According to the *Dharmaśāstra*, his livelihood is by means of the *śālīna* mode of life; he is one who possesses that mode of subsistence. Having gone to a region suitable for a sacrificial ground—either to the north or to the east of his home—together with the *aupāsana* fire, he should establish the fires there. The sacrificial ground will be explained in the section on the *Soma* sacrifice; there, he should naturally establish the fires on a spot sloping toward the east, meaning within that hall (*śālā*).

38. In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the third book]: A *yāyāvara* is one who is habitually itinerant; having gone from place to place, he maintains his livelihood and lives. He too is to be understood as characterized by the *Dharmaśāstra*. Wherever he stays, in those very houses he should prepare a shed and establish the fires. Now, regarding the shaving of the sacrificer: he cleanses his teeth and puts on a new, unwashed garment; the shaving is also for the wife. Eating is also seen for both of them in another *śāstra*.

"A hall with its rafters pointing north" is to be constructed; this is the ellipsis. Regarding this, Āpastamba has stated that the chamber for the Āhavanīya fire is one thing and the chamber for the Gārhapatya fire is another. Although our teacher has not specified a distinction here, he has nevertheless mentioned two separate chambers in the section on measurement. He will state later: "The site for the Śamyāvasathya fire is separated from the chamber, whereas the sites for the other two are within the chamber. One should construct a single hall such that, at the front portion of the hall, there are the sites for the Brāhmaudanika, the Gārhapatya, and the Dakṣiṇā fires.

It is understood that in the western half of the hall, all the materials and implements are to be placed for the purpose of storing them for everyone. Thus it is stated by Baudhāyana: "Furthermore, there is no house of unlimited size at the *devayajana* (sacrificial ground); they make two doors for it, one facing east and one facing south. They prepare the site for the *gārhapatya* fire in the middle, and the site for the *āhavanīya* fire ten steps to the east of that. To the east of that, over the central beam, at the point where the sun is visible above the trees, he establishes the *brāhmaudanika* fire from the *aupāsana* fire.

The connection is as follows: "In the space to the east of the lower part of that central beam of that hall, he establishes the *bāhyaudana* fire. Although that [hall] is already understood from the context, the qualification "of that" is used so that it might not refer to another. By this, the second hall is also indicated by virtue of being the *āhavanīya* chamber. And that [second hall] is either with its beams facing east or north; Kātyāyana has stated that the second hall has its beams facing east.

With reference to the trees, the time when the sun stands neither below nor above them is called *adhivṛkṣasūrya*; this is the meaning. Having taken a portion from the *aupāsana* fire, he places it silently in that spot. It is given its future name because "the *bāhyaudana* (outer rice-offering) is cooked in it. Having drawn out a portion from the *aupāsana* fire, he establishes—that is, places—that fire in the previously mentioned spot. Āpastamba says: "The entire *aupāsana* [is to be used]."

In the view that all [fires] must be established, the evening and morning *aupāsana* oblations and the *parvaṇa-sthālīpāka* are omitted; these are not to be performed with a substitute fire, such as a common (*laukika*) fire. A substitute is employed only when the substance required by a mandatory (*nitya*) rule is absent. However, the *aupāsana* fire does not exist [as a substitute], because when it reaches another state such as the *gārhapatya*, its previous form is absolutely non-existent. Furthermore, he will later state that there can be no substitute for fire.

When, however, there is a re-establishment (punarādheya), one should establish the fire by churning alone for the *brāhmaudana* rite, but not the *aupāsana* fire; for the *āhavanīya* is established for the purpose of its own production and does not come from the *gārhapatya*. It is held as the *gārhapatya* only when it has gone out (*anugata*); it does not return to its former source because that source no longer exists. This same principle applies even in the case of the *ardhādhāna* (half-establishment). Even then, the production is from churning alone; thus, the establishment by churning has also been stated by Āpastamba.

Let us return to the subject at hand. Some maintain that in the *ardhādhāna* (partial establishment of the sacred fires), there is a *pārvaṇa* (monthly śrāddha) and a *prātarāhnika* (morning rite) performed in the *aupāsana* fire. Why? Because through that *aupāsana* fire, one attains the status of an *āhitāgni* (one who has established the fires); and by means of that *pārvaṇa* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*), [the rites of] the New and Full Moon sacrifices are accomplished. [End of] Second Paṭala; together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. Page 229.

If someone were to say, "And [the rule] 'not sacrificing for a month' applies," then, since the status of having formally established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) has been directly attained, there would be no performance of the alternative rite (*anukalpa*) which consists of devotion to that [fire]. In this regard, Satyāṣāḍha’s opinion is that the mention of "permanently" (*nityam*) in the passage "from now on permanently" and "every evening and morning permanently" serves to exclude the application of the term "permanently" to other rites. However, as for other *smārta* (traditionally taught) rituals, they are to be performed at that very same time.

Regarding the *sarvādhāna* (the rite of establishing all fires), they say that for those rites performed for specific results which have fixed auxiliary requirements, if the sacred fire (*agni*) is absent, one must employ only worldly fires (*laukikāgni*). For example, in the case of the donkey-sacrifice (*gardabhapaśubandha*) performed by a student who has broken his vow (*avakīrṇin*), only worldly fires are taken. As in the case of the widower (*vidhura*), the procedure is to be performed using only worldly fires; there is no omission [of the rite]. This differs from the previous case because of the scriptural injunction; for Manu prescribes the *agnaukaraṇa-homa* even in the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*), and thus it must be performed accordingly in the monthly rites (*māsika*) and so forth. However, the *aṣṭakā-homa* is performed in a worldly fire alone, because it does not fall under the designation of the term *agnaukaraṇa*.

As long as the fire-drill (araṇī) has not been exhausted, the *aupāsana* and *pārvaṇa* fires remain in the *bāhyaudānika* [external] state. However, in the case of following [the deceased], one must again produce the *aupāsana* fire and deposit that [deceased's fire] into it; since that [fire] has already attained the status of the *gārhapatya* and other hearths, its entry into the *aupāsana* is indeed established—this is to be understood from all principles of logic. Even in the case of the *ardhādhāna* (half-consecration), although the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* was commenced previously in the *aupāsana*, it takes place only in the *dakṣiṇāgni* after the consecration (*ādhāna*) along with the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*). But if there is an omission prior to the completion of the consecration, there is only an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

Let us follow the subject at hand. Thereafter, he prepares the vessels for the *brāhmaudana* oblation. First, having strewn sacrificial grass (*darbha*) around the fire and having spread it to the south for the seats of the Brahman and the Sacrificer, and to the north of the *brāhmaudana* fire, he arranges the vessels: two *darvī* ladles, a fuel-stick (*samidh*), a vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the *agnihotra* offering-ladle, a pot for the rice-oblation (*carusthālī*), a stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), a winnowing-basket (*śūrpa*), a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇajina*), a mortar and pestle, a red bull-hide, a drinking-vessel made of *citriya-aśvattha* wood, and three [spoons].

Having prepared the sacrificial fuel (samidh), the shallow bowls (śarāva) for the purpose of pouring out the oblation, as well as four [bowls] for the purpose of drawing it out, and a piece of wood for the under-layer (upaveṣa);
he pours out at night the Brahma-rice (brahmaudana) in four bowls.

At night, during the first part of the night, he offers the *brahmaudana*—the rice-gruel belonging to the deity Brahmā—with that in mind. Regarding its quantity, it is said to be "four *śarāvas*"; although a *śarāva* is a specific type of vessel, it is impossible for it to be the material substance (*prakṛtidravya*) of the rice-gruel itself; therefore, by implication, the grain measured by it is what is intended, as that is what is appropriate. Likewise, in the statement "he offers four handfuls," the word "handful" (*muṣṭi*) refers to grain measured by a handful.

Nevertheless, since the capacity of the vessel (*pātra*) is not known, the quantity of grain would remain undetermined. Therefore, by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the word *śarāva* here should be understood as referring to the amount of grain that serves as the raw material for a single meal of boiled rice (*odana*). He will state that this [grain] is to be taken four times in the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*). However, it is not possible to take a handful (*muṣṭi*) of grain using the well-known *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle, because of the large quantity of the substance.

Therefore, a shallow bowl (*śarāva-pātra*) capable of holding the quantity of grain required for a full meal—the very substance from which the rice is made—should be taken in place of the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle. For it is the settled conclusion that when four such measures of grain have been sown, the resulting rice is called "four-bowl rice" (*catur-śarāva*). Furthermore, because Kātyāyana states, "the rice is to be eaten by four," it is understood that the four portions are sufficient for a meal. Since it is understood that this rice is to be consumed by the Brahmin deities denoted by the word "Brahman" (*brahma*), the act of consumption (*prāśana*) is the primary element.

Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement accompanied by its explanatory purpose (*sārthavāda*), which says, "The four *ārṣeya* priests eat," the oblation (*homa*) is merely a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of that [food]. Therefore, if it is forgotten, there is no re-performance. In this context, one does not infer a sacrifice (*yāga*) from the term "offers" (*nirvapati*), because here the injunction is for mere eating (*prāśana*) through direct perception; moreover, since the unprecedented (*apūrva*) act is the connection with the four-measure vessel (*catuḥśarāva*), one offers the substance measured by the four-measure vessel. For the offering (*nirvāpa*) does not belong to the vessel itself.

Although the number is heard as pertaining to the vessel, nevertheless, since the measurement of the substance is not established by any other means, it serves the purpose of measuring that very substance. In such cases as "He offers the cake on eight potsherds" (*āgneyam aṣṭākapālam nirvapati*), because the limiting factor—"he offers four handfuls" (*caturaḥ muṣṭīn nirvapati*)—is explicitly stated, there is a connection between the potsherds and the baking. This is not the case for the *dadhi* (curd) offering, as it is a liquid oblation (*homa*). That rice which is prepared by means of four *śarāva* measures through the act of pouring out is called "four-śarāva" (*catur-śarāva*). This means that it has been poured out four times using one *śarāva* measure.

Now, if the cooking is done in four shallow bowls (*śarāva*), then it is consistent with the rule *saṃskṛtā bhakṣāḥ* (the prepared portions are for consumption), just as in the case of the eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*). However, in that case, the statement "clarified butter in a pot" (*sthālyāṃ sarpiḥ*) would not be appropriate. Therefore, one should set aside four vessels filled with water and perform the cooking therein; this refers to the method of cooking with water. For this very reason, Vaikhānasa stated, beginning with "he offers four *śarāvas*," "he pours the rice grains into the four *śarāvas*. It has been explained that the occasion for the application [of the term] is established at the time of pouring; however, according to the teacher’s view, it should be understood to apply either at the time of the offering (*nirvapaṇa*) or during the cooking in water.

On a red hide or a *pājaka* [mat]. "Red" (*rohita*) means crimson; according to another *sūtra*, it refers specifically to the hide of a bull, meaning the hide of an ox that draws a cart. A *paunaka* is a vessel used in the kitchen, a specific type of bamboo container denoted by the word *paṭachaka*. Having taken [the grain] with a shallow bowl (*śarāva*), he pours it out. He states the procedure for that:

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour thee out, acceptable to Brahmán, for Prāṇa; to Brahmán, for Apāna; to Brahmán, for Vyāna; to Brahmán—for the fourth."
"He offers" means that on the fourth day, he offers exclusively for the Brahman priest without any prefix. The formula "I offer what is pleasing" (*juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*) is to be supplied everywhere.
Having husked [the grain], he cooks the *caru* in milk.
Having husked it according to the requirements, he cooks the *caru* in milk in a single pot.

[The milk is cooked] in four water-pots. There is an option between the milk and the four water-pots, but not with the pot itself as prescribed by the text. Therefore, when the pot has been placed upon the four water-filled vessels, he pours water from the vessel into the pot four times and cooks it therein. He does not wipe [the vessel].
The meaning is that it does not wash away;
it does not pour out.
That water which has been poured onto the grains, it does not let flow away—that is to say, it does not abandon it.
The word *cam* does not appear in the manuscript copies of the Sūtra. [Variant readings:
5ka, sva. *ca... syāt*; 1 kha. *pācake*; 3 ka, kha, ṭa. *pāca*; 2 dvi-paṭanaḥ. [This concludes] the section accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.
Having cooked it, having sprinkled clarified butter over it, and having removed it from the fire.

The statement "having cooked again" is for the purpose of refuting the position of other Sūtras. Vaikhānasa has stated that it is a secondary cooking (*aupacchrapaṇa*), and likewise Āpastamba says, "he cooks it like rice grains that are still alive. However, in our own system, the cooking is indeed as prescribed [once]. Having sprinkled it with ordinary clarified butter (*ājya*), he offers the oblation with the verse: "To the all-pervading, the seer, the pure, the word-honoring, the bull, the vigorous one—may there be freedom from fear for us from whatever causes fear; I worship the gods who are to be praised. Because this is enjoined by the term *juhoti* ("he offers"), the utterance *svāhā* is required.

Or he consecrates [the food] with a mantra. There is no utterance of *svāhā* here. The consecration is performed while the food remains in the cooking pot. According to this view, however, there is neither an offering to the sage (*kavi*) nor a gift to the Brahman; therefore, it results in the term *brahmaudana* meaning "rice for the Brahmans. The consecration, however, is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*). In the case of the offering-view, it is a purificatory rite for the substance and the deity. By the word *kavi*, both the *brahmā* priest and the Brahmanas are included.

In both cases, those same deities are intended; here, the preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is subordinate, and they are mentioned using a singular form to denote their genus. For it is stated in the Śruti: "They have heard for the sake of the wise seer (*kavi*)," and "Indeed, the seers [are many]. To demonstrate this very point, it is said: "He brings [the offering] to the *ṛtvij*s who are *āyus*. In that context, the term "*āyu*" is used because of the Śruti: "This Brāhmaṇa is indeed the seer *Āyu*"; if it were not so, the qualification would be redundant.

Now, the qualification "expanding" (*pravedhate*) is either because he alone is the ordainer of the sacrifice, or it is for the sake of praise by attributing the status of ordainer [to him]. In any case, Brahmā, described in the form of Parameṣṭhin, is the deity for the oblation (*homa*); all this is consistent with that. Regarding the phrase "having struck out the faults," Āpastamba and Vaikhānasa prescribe two oblations, since no other is ordained and thus not otherwise obtained. Having divided that [oblation] into four parts and having sprinkled it abundantly with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*).

Having removed the rice for the dark-colored [deities] from the pot individually into four separate bowls, he sets them down. Having poured over each portion a copious amount of worldly ghee and prepared it accordingly,
he brings the remaining ghee back into the pot and pours the leftover liquid for basting back into it.

He brings [the portion] near to the four *ārṣeya* priests as if not cutting it off; that is, without depriving the priests of their share of the earth, he brings it individually into their presence. This is not a formal gift (*dāna*), because it is performed by the *adhvaryu*. Since the fourth case ending is used in the word "to the priests" (*ṛtvigbhyaḥ*), what is enjoined here by the verb "he brings near" (*upo-hati*) is an announcement directed toward them. Although this is indeed a gift, it is not designated by the root *dā* (to give); therefore, it is explained as being preceded by the *adhvaryu*, [the formula being] "to the *ārṣeyas*. [This occurs] when they have already consumed [their portions].

The granting of the boon is the act of the sacrificer. 1. Ka, Ga, Ca, Cha, Ṭa, U, Pa, Ri-kāre pra; Yaḥ 302. In the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the third book]: He anoints three sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) from a marked *aśvattha* tree, each a span (*prādeśa*) long, which are either provided with clusters (*stibhika*) or without clusters, and which have fresh leaves and twigs remaining on them, using the remnant that is in the pot. 3. He anoints the fuel-sticks with the remainder of the *brahmaudana* rice placed in a vessel containing beeswax; by this, he makes them greasy. "With palāśa leaves" means with their petals; "stibhikas" are fruits or buds—so some say. The purpose of the commencement of this sūtra is to indicate whether they possess such [leaves] or not, and whether all of them are indeed uniform in that same manner. The space between the extended thumb and forefinger is a *prādeśa*, or twelve finger-breadths (*dvādaśāṅgula*); it is a "measuring-mark" (*lakṣaṇya*) useful for measurement, by which villages, sacred bathing places, boundaries, and so forth, are marked. The rest is clear.

"From the variegated *aśvattha* tree you have been gathered; you are the *bṛhatī* verses, fashioned for the body. Joined by Prajāpati, the mouth of the sacrifice, you are threefold, consisting of triplets, forming a pair for procreation. Having consecrated them thus, he places the fuel-sticks on the *brāhmaudanika* fire.

With each of the mantras to be recited hereafter, he places one kindling-stick at a time into the *brāhmaudana* fire; there is no utterance of *svāhā*. He recites only the *śrī-mantras*: "Forward toward you, O kings who dwell in heaven, the offerers of oblations go with the butter-spoon, seeking favor from the gods. "O beloved Agni, may my butter-dripping ladles approach you; graciously accept our offerings. "O Agni, that flame of yours shines forth when the oblation is poured, dripping with ghee, kissing the mouths of the ladles"—with these three *gāyatrī* verses, for a Brāhmaṇa. The word "he places" (*ādadhāti*) is to be supplied as a refrain. He mentions three other [verses] among these for the purpose of providing an option:

"Serve Agni with fuel"—this is [the first verse]. "O Agni, let the ladles full of ghee, bearing oblations, approach you, O beloved one; graciously accept my fuel-sticks. Or: "O Angiras, we strengthen you with fuel and ghee; shine brightly, O youngest one! These two [verses] belong to the Aṇiman.

Being kindled, he is the first law, adorned with all-desirable offerings. With hair of flame and cleansed by clarified butter, Agni the Purifier is a perfect sacrificer for the worship of the gods. Having clarified butter as his face and clarified butter as his source, Agni is kindled by clarified butter; clarified butter is his food. The rivers carry you, dripping with clarified butter; drinking the clarified butter, perform the sacrifice well and worship the gods. "O Agni, giver of life"—with these *triṣṭubh* verses, [the offering] of the Kṣatriya is completed.
Thus ends the second chapter, accompanied by the commentary named Vaijayantī composed by Mahādeva.

O Agni, most youthful one, when you were kindled, the gods made you their messenger, the bearer of oblations; they established you as their brilliant eye that impels the swift, you who have wide-reaching power, whose source is clarified butter, and who are invoked with offerings. O Agni, from of old, they have kindled you with excellent fuel for the sake of your favor, you who are invoked with clarified butter; thus, increasing through your nourishments and strengthened, you spread abroad your wide-reaching domains upon the earth. They strive to kindle Agni—who has clarified butter as his face and sits at the pole of the cosmic order—just as one strives to win a friend.

"Kindling [the fire], shining in the assemblies, may he raise up our thought of bright color"—with these *jagatī* verses, [this is] for the Vaiśya. This has been explained. For the Niṣāda and the Sthapati, he establishes the fires silently, because it is prescribed as such.
He maintains the *brāhmaudana* fire.

A couple whose semen has been emitted bestows [the fruit] upon the sacrificer; he neither departs nor travels abroad for a year, a season, twelve days, four days, three days, two days, or one day. Retention is prescribed according to the prior resolution made.
And when [the fire] has thus departed while following [the sacrificer], one should cook the *brahmaudana* as prescribed, anoint these fuel-sticks (*samidh*), and place them [on the fire].
This is a contingent rite (*naimittika*).

If the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) does not come to him within a year, then having cooked the *brahmaudana* as prescribed, anointed these fuel-sticks, and placed them [on the fire], he establishes the fires whenever he is able.

If, within a year, either from the gods or from men, this *agnyādheya* (the laying of the sacred fires) which was intended for the sacrificer does not come to pass—that is, if it does not arrive or fail to take place—then that which has been prescribed must be performed. The mention of "a year" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) because the rite had been intended [for that specific time]. When he is able, he should then establish the fires at a suitable season and under an auspicious constellation, during the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*) and in the waxing fortnight (*āpūryamāṇapakṣa*), according to the previously stated method.
On the day before he is to establish the fires, he cooks the *brahmaudana* (the sacrificial rice for the Brahman).

In this case, there is no placing of fuel as before, because it has not been so prescribed; nor is this an auxiliary part of the *brahmaudana* (the sacrificial porridge). This is a separate consecration of the fire (*agni-saṃskāra*), since it is not enjoined [as part of the porridge]; therefore, it does not apply to the second *brahmaudana*. On the night before the fire is to be established (*ādhāna*), the Adhvaryu observes the vow (*vrata*). Or rather, the suffix [expressing the future sense] refers to the action performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) when the fire is to be established.

"He speaks no untruth, he eats no meat, and he approaches no woman. O Agni, cause the subjects to dwell together, along with the quarters and the cattle. Bestow upon her those kingdoms which were Savitṛ’s at his impulsion. With these words, he ties a spotted goat at the site of the Gārhapatya fire.
On this night, they keep the sacrificer awake with various arts and crafts.
3.3 Now begins the third chapter.

Thereafter, he brings the *saṃbhāras* (materials) with the verses beginning "vaiśvānarasya rūpam" according to their respective forms. "According to their forms" means according to the indicative marks (*liṅga*); that is, as many *saṃbhāras*—meaning those items named *saṃbhāra* in which fires are contained—as there are of these mantras beginning with "vaiśvānarasya," and whatever form is to be established by them, so many *saṃbhāras* are prepared. Although elsewhere the application of mantras recited in the Brāhmaṇa is made through their recitation, here the application is made solely by way of indicative mark (*liṅga*) in order to demonstrate that this Brāhmaṇa belongs to one's own Vedic branch (*sva-śākhā*).

Previously, the mantras were applied solely by means of their recitation; therefore, to dispel the doubt that this [Brāhmaṇa] does not belong to our own Śākhā, the applications are indicated here by means of mere indicative marks (liṅga) using initial pratīkas. The non-inclusion of pratīkas previously was for the purpose of demonstrating the alternative versions of this Brāhmaṇa. By means of these alternatives, it is shown that there exist various Brāhmaṇas belonging to this Saṃhitā, and that this Brāhmaṇa is situated among them.

Therefore, in some instances, having set aside these Brāhmaṇa-mantras, he shows other Brāhmaṇa-mantras; by this it is made known that even in those cases, they are optional. Although the word "sikatā" (sand) does not appear in the mantra, "The form of Vaiśvānara... [is] not," nevertheless, in the Brāhmaṇa it says, "He scatters sand in due order; this indeed is the form of Agni Vaiśvānara"—this serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*). In the case of other mantras, there is a clear indicative mark.

Therefore, since this [first mantra] is the illuminator of the first *saṃbhāra*, its application to the sand (*liṅgāsikatāsu*) should be understood according to the *Brāhmaṇa*. The bringing [of the materials] takes place near the site; for this very reason, each mantra is distinct. Thus, although two sets of mantras are shown by the *Brāhmaṇa*, it should also be understood that there is only one mantra for each pair, as the two mantras manifest a single form. "Of Vaiśvānara" refers to the sand. "That which is from heaven" refers to the saline earth (*ūṣān*). "Fashioning upward" refers to the gravel (*āravatkaram*).

With "unai pṛthivyā" he takes the mound of an anthill; with "prajāpatisṛṣṭānām," the soil; with "yasya rūpam," the earth dug up by a boar; with "yatparyapaśyat," a lotus leaf; with "yābhirahat," pebbles; with "agne retaḥ," silver; silently, pieces of gold; with "aśvo rūpam," the wood of the *aśvattha* tree; with "ṭharnaḥ pṛthivyāḥ," the wood of the *udumbara* tree; with the two verses "gāyatriyā" and "devānām," the wood of the *palāśa* tree; and with "yayā te," the *śamī* tree.

With the verse, "That which was created by thee," [he takes] a piece of *vaikaṅkata* wood; with the verse, "That which was exhausted by thee," [he takes] a piece struck by lightning; and with the verse, "Thee whom they have gathered together," having collected them, he places them together. Then, having prepared them, [he proceeds]. From this section: With the two verses, "O Jātavedas, pour here the seed of the world" and "From the *aśvattha* tree, the bearer of oblations, from the womb of the *śamī*, generating Agni who is the source of bliss," he heats the two fire-sticks (*araṇī*) at dawn over the *brāhmaudana* fire.

The time of dawn (*uṣaḥkāla*) is that which precedes the break of day (*upavyuṣam*) by four *ghaṭikās*. "At dawn" (*vyuṣi*) means it shines intensely; it heats, so to speak. This is the usage of a transitive verb. [The priest says: "And may these two be milch-cows for you, and may the earth be full of milk for you; I bestow upon you their portion; with them I place you [the fire]. With this, he hands the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) to the sacrificer. This is clear. The sacrificer awaits the gift with the verse, "Great, the two lords of the people. He receives them with the words, "Ascend [the fire]. Having received them, he consecrates them with the formula, "You two are possessed of the proper season."

Having taken the fire into himself with the two verses, "I take the fire which is ours... and "May he who is our fire...", and having established it within himself, both practitioners recite the mantra; however, the distinction lies in the visualization (*bhāvanā*) for the installation of the fire.
Having consecrated the fire with the mantra, "The immortal, bright-shining fire wards off the demons; pure, purifying, and worthy of praise," he follows after the *brāhmaudana* fire.

The connection is that he consecrates the *brāhmaudanika* fire; subsequently, he brings about peace. Having murmured the mantra, "This I [place] from the end," the sacrificer restrains his speech. He digs out the site for the *gārhapatya* fire to the east of the *brāhmaudanika*. This promise is made within the very house at the eastern part. "Digging out" means excavating. Since the phrase "the site for the *gārhapatya*" is a restatement of what is already established, it was previously prepared according to the *śulba* rules.

"May the impurity being dug up destroy the sin of the sacrificer; may the four quarters be auspicious to us; may Mother Earth be propitious to us for the sake of offspring"—this is said with the mantra beginning "He digs. The meaning is that [he digs] with this [mantra]. To the south-east, at a distance of one-third [of the space], closer to the Gārhapatya fire, is the location for the Dakṣiṇāgni.

In that region of the space between the east and the north where the third part of the third [measure] has passed; that is, in the area situated between the east and the west, very close to the *gārhapatya* fire. This very procedure has been shown by means of the measuring-cord (*śulba*) and is found recorded in the books of the Sūtras.
(Note: In manuscripts *ka*, *ga*, and *ṇa*, there is the reading "atyāgārhapatyāpa"; this is the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [Third Book]).
One digs out the site for the Āhavanīya fire from the east of the site for the Gārhapatya fire, and on the outside of the other two.

The term "uddhanti" (he digs up) is intended to connect with both the preceding and the following iron nails (*āyasī nābhi*). Since the Āhavanīya fire is seen as distinct from the two [other fires] by means of the iron nails, a separate hall (*śālā*) with its rafters pointing north (*udagvaṃśā*) must be constructed for the purpose of the Āhavanīya. Outside that hall, there are the two halls for the Gārhapatya and the Āvasathya; these two are indeed independent halls employed for other purposes. The *sabhā* is a hall for gambling, while the *āvasatha* is a guest-hall; the two [fires] belonging to those are the *sabhya* and the *āvasathya*. Their altars (*āyatana*) are not, however, within the hall whose rafters point north.
Regarding the question of how far east from the *gārhapatya* fire the site for the *āhavanīya* fire should be, it is stated:

"One should establish the fire at twelve steps (*vikrāma*). This is heard in the *Brāhmaṇa* without qualification. Since the measurement of "twelve steps" is prescribed in the *Brāhmaṇa* for all castes (*varṇa*) without distinction, the meaning is that this applies not only to the three *traivarṇika* classes but also to the *niṣāda* and the *rathakāra*. A "step" (*vikrāma*) is explained by the term "stride" (*prakrama*); the stride has been explained as being optional.
For a Brāhmaṇa there are eight [days], for a Rājanya eleven, and for a Vaiśya twelve.
There is an option between the former and the preceding [number] for the first two classes. Twenty-four or an unlimited number [of days] apply to both [classes] in common.
The meaning is "of all castes. Regarding the phrase "one should establish [the fires] with an unlimited [number]," he states its meaning:
"It is known that one measures the steps with the eye.

With the intention of explaining that the word "unlimited" is already explained by the Brāhmaṇa passage, "One should establish [the fires] measured by the eye," he says, "it is known"—that is, the specific detail is known from the Śruti itself. Another view is that one should perform the measurement with the eye, thinking, "There will be this many strides," and thus measure them, but not with a staff or other such means. This first method of measurement is optional. Both of these two positions apply to everyone.

To the east of the Āhavanīya fire is the assembly hall (*sabhā*); there is the location for the *Sabhya* fire. To the east of the assembly hall is the dwelling (*āvasatha*); there is the location for the *Āvasathya* fire. The word "location" (*āyatana*) is to be supplied everywhere. Thus, their ritual acts are performed in this successive order.

The ritual acts of preparation for these *āyatanas* and *agnis* are performed in the same sequence in which the *āyatanas* were shown, and not by proceeding clockwise (*prādakṣiṇya*). The phrase "being dug up" (*uddhanyamānam*) is repeated for each *āyatana*; he digs them up in sequence. He sprinkles them with water, reciting: "May the divine waters be auspicious for our aid; may they be for our drinking; may they flow toward us for our well-being and prosperity. (ŚB 2.1.4.9) [End of] Paṭala 307, from the *Mahādevakṛta-vaijayantī* commentary. *Note: The manuscript variants noted in the source (gha, i, ja, sa, a, da) refer to specific textual readings.*
With the *bhavācīna* fist, he covers each sacrificial post with the mantra;
here, some prescribe the *kharahoma* oblations for the verses "ud vayaṃ tamasas pari" and "ud u tyam citram."

The oblations offered on the mounds (*khara*) in their respective locations are called *kharahoma*s; because they serve as the consecration of the locations, the Vaikhānasa priest offers them separately on each individual mound, stating, "Having placed gold," and so forth. The materials (*saṃbhāra*) are prepared: either five or seven earthen ones.
However, for the purpose of the application of the fire, all seven are indeed collected.
Thus [are] the wooden vessels (*vānaspatya*);
the meaning is that there are five equal ones. They have been previously collected and are already prepared.
Having divided each one of them into two parts.

Of those five or seven [portions], one part each is measured out until it is again divided into two. This has been stated by Vaikhānasa and Āpastamba: "Having divided the sand into two parts," he pours them down upon the Gārhapatya and Dakṣiṇāgni fires.
Then, that which has been divided into two is [deposited] in the two fire-places (āyatana) which are charmingly referred to by the word "fire" (agni), though they are not yet consecrated (anuṣakta).

Having divided half into three parts among the first three—the Āhavanīya and the others—if there is only one [fire], then there is no division of the half; the entire half belongs to the Āhavanīya alone. Having thus stated the method of division, he describes the ritual application accompanied by the mantra:
"Thou art the ash of Agni," with which he scatters the sand.

According to the principle that "the mantra is repeated when there is a difference in purpose," the mantra is to be repeated for each location (*pratyāyatana*). This means it follows the method of logical division. It ends with *purīṣam asi*.
With *saṃjñānam asi kāmadharaṇam*, one addresses the saline earth (*ūṣān*).
*Bhūmāt* is the end of the mantra. This has been explained.
While pouring them out, he meditates in his mind: "Whatever black [form] was placed in the moon, may that be here.

As he pours those sands (*ūṣān*) into their respective locations, at the time of pronouncing each mantra, he intends: "May that black form which is seen here in the moon be here on this earth. Such a supposition, though its purpose is unseen, arises from the force of the Vedic text. These two mantras are established by their indicative mark (*liṅga*), because in the *Āpāna-brāhmaṇa* they are praised as being of the same nature as the sand and the saline soil (*purīṣa*).

"Go forth, O Agni, from the mother earth; enter the subjects from the great assembly-place. The god-seeking ones have established you, the swift bearer of oblations, the guardian of the world"—with these words he throws up the mound (utkara).

"That immortal essence of the earth which came into being together with you—that Agni gave to Agni; in that let this one be established. With this, he places a termite-mound (valmīkavapā) in the site of the Gārhapatya fire.
It is stated that one pours [the offering] into the middle for the purpose of showing each one separately:
"That which is the immortal essence of the intermediate space" for the Dakṣiṇāgni, and "that which is the immortal essence of heaven" for the Āhavanīya.
The phrase "it has come into being" (*saṃbabhūva*) from the first verse is to be supplied as an *anuṣaṅga* (elliptical extension) to both.
For the other two fires, [the pouring] is silent.

Here, because the purpose is distinct, the principle that "it is repeated" applies, which would result in the repetition of the final mantra; nevertheless, since the triad beginning with the Gārhapatya fire has been praised in the form of the earth and so forth for the purpose of prescribing the Sāmans, and such praise does not exist for the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires, the Teacher [Baudhāyana] intends silence for them, as this avoids contradiction with the mantra "of heaven. According to Vaikhānasa, however, as in the case of Āpastamba, the mantra is used everywhere.

"From the ocean a honeyed wave has come, bestowing imperial sovereignty for further advancement. May these wealthy patrons and we ourselves gather together food, strength, honey, and sweet broth. Thus [he places] the *sūda*.
"So much, O Agni, wast thou," thus [he places] the earth dug up by a boar.

The mantra is exactly as follows: "O Goddess, spreading out first, when you were scattered separately by the gods, you flowed forth with your greatness; you made yourself firm with pebbles, you conquered the triple heaven and the four quarters. While scattering those pebbles, he meditates in his mind upon the destruction of him whom he hates. Because it is constant, he meditates upon evil itself in the absence of a specific object of hatred. Thus there are seven mantras for the earthen [pebbles], but not for the lotus-leaf or the earth. In the five-pebble version, whichever five mantras there may be, they possess the same indicative marks (*liṅga*). In the absence of all these, he states an alternative:

The iron and udumbara [wooden] vessels serve as alternatives to the earthen ones. By the word "or" (vā), it should be understood that there is an option between "iron" and "udumbara"; however, this was not explicitly stated because it was considered that for items serving the same purpose, an option would be established by itself. By this, the disciples were instructed so that an option might occur even in the absence of the word "or. This has already been demonstrated previously in the context of preparing the altar regarding the new moon sacrifice. "Iron" refers to pieces of iron; likewise, [pieces of] udumbara wood refer to pieces of copper.
"O Jātavedas, those auspicious forms of yours which are in the intermediate space and those which are on earth— with them, united and accompanied by your hosts, O Agni, you who are of golden origin,
carry the oblation," [with this verse] he throws a piece of gold into the materials from the north.
He places it— that is, establishes it— in the very locations where the materials were gathered.
If he gives silver to one who is hateful, and if he does not find something else hateful [to give], he should discard it; he should not offer it up and then take it back again. || 6 ||
The giving [of the horse] and the dismissal are for the sake of the unseen; the dismissal is not performed at the sacred sites (*āyatanas*). The rest is clear.

"The gods have established here the one who is bright as the moon, whose chariot is the moon, whose law is golden, Vaiśvānara, who dwells in the waters, who finds the light of heaven, the diver, the swift, surrounded by powers, the impetuous, the highly glorious"—with these words he consecrates the setting sun.
There is no consecration in the case of the gift [of the horse].

The lotus leaf (*puṣkaraparṇa*), the *udumbara*, the *śamī*, the *vikaṅkata*, the *aśvattha* struck by lightning, and the *palāśa*—these are the "wood-born" (*vānaspatya*) [bricks]. He scatters them with the mantra: "From this [earth], Agni was first born. Because of their suitability, the word "scatters" (*nivapati*) is not to be supplied [from the previous rule] here; rather, it is for the purpose of providing an alternative to the second option. Thus, the meaning is as follows: just as the preceding earthen bricks were scattered after being divided, so too these should be scattered in that same manner; however, the mantra for all of them is one and the same.

Alternatively, by [the rule] "or the bringing [of the materials]," there is a repetition of those [terms], or rather, the subsequent phrase "those belonging to the trees" (*vānaspatyāstān*) is drawn forward from that point, while the earlier distant term "he pours down" (*nivapati*) is drawn back. This has been stated by Vaikhānasa: "Some say there is a repetition of the mantra for the collection.
Or else, those which are other than the *puṣkaraparṇa* and the *vikaṅkata*—namely, the "tree-born" ones—he pours down with the verse "From here Agni was first born," only once in each case.

Having divided the *puṣkara-parṇa* and the *vikaṅkata* wood as before, and having placed the other materials together, he pours them out over all the foundations (*āyatanas*) one by one with the repetition of the mantra; however, to dispel the misconception that "once" means "all at once," it is stated "in each one. He mixes the saline earth (*ūṣas*) and the sand (*sikatās*) together with the mantra, "O your dear bodies, come together," while they are still in their respective locations. Thus it is understood that he should place each of those previously gathered piles separately in its own foundation.

"I unite your hearts; may your minds be united; may your breath be united"—with this [formula], he unites all the materials. With the preceding mantra, he mixes those already joined and those not yet joined together in one place, repeating the mantra for each respective receptacle:
"I spread the *ṛta* as soil upon the earth; upon the *ṛta*, I establish the fire; upon the *satya*..."

He arranges the combined materials with the mantra: "I place you, who possess all cattle, with the virility of heaven, with the majesty of the earth, and with the prosperity of the intermediate region."

The word *kalpate* means "he makes all equal"; it refers to the preparation (*kalpana*) and the empowering (*samarthīkaraṇa*) of each of the sacrificial sites (*āyatana*) through the repetition of the mantra for the purpose of strewing (*staraṇa*) across all the sites during the maintenance of the fire. This is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra. Having removed the ashes of the *brāhmaudanika* fire while the rays are rising—where "rising" is used in the sense of proximity to the present, meaning before sunrise, since the rule for establishing the *gārhapatya* fire is prescribed prior to sunrise—one should clear away everything located at the sacrificial sites without remainder.

Having placed the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) with the *daśahotr* formula, he joins the two drills together with the *cittiḥ* verse and places them there in the position of the *vāmaudanika* fire. Regarding the orientation of the opening, Vaikhānasa states that it should face westward; Āpastamba states that after removing the ashes, one churns the fire from that spot using the *śamyā* and *garmā*. Here, Vaikhānasa says that while meditating on the lower drill as half of himself and Viṣṇu, and the upper drill as half of Agni, he churns it with the mantra "O Agni, come hither."

"O Agni, be born together with fire, together with progeny, together with wealth, together with nourishment, together with cattle, and together with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). At this point, he churns the fire and stands near it while facing the horse.

The mantra is recited only once, even though the actions are distinct, because the substance (the fire) is one. He stands near (*upa*) the horse (*aśva*). Here, at the place where the *bāsaudanika* fire was previously located; while the fire is being churned, he causes the sacrificer to recite the *Caturhotṛ* formulas.

The exponents of Brahman ask: "What constitutes the fourfold nature of the *caturhotṛ*s? In this context, by the word *caturhotṛ*, it is the [five] *hotṛ* priests who are intended and designated by the plural number; it does not refer solely to the formula "Pṛthivī is the *hotṛ*," for that would result in an inconsistency regarding the plural. He causes the five [formulas], beginning with "Thought is the *suk*," "Pṛthivī is the *hotṛ*," "Agni is the *tā*," "Sūrya is your eye," and "The great *āhuti*," to be recited word by word as a continuous text. He consecrates the fire that has been produced with the mantra: "Agni, the *hotṛ*, has gone before the former ones; he is the purifying, the bright, the one worthy of praise."

Having made [the fire] the secondary object of focus, he should manifest it with the mantra. Here, the ritual duty of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) is: "By my breath, O Lord of Life" (*prāṇapate tvā prāṇena*). He breathes upon the fire that has been kindled; the meaning is that he breathes toward it and breathes down upon it. Having consecrated the fire that has arisen with the words "I am you" (*ahaṃ tvad asmi*), he grants a boon and releases his speech. At this point, the sacrificer and his wife put on two linen garments (*kṣauma-vāsasī*). Regarding the statement "these are given to the Adhvaryu when the subsequent establishment of the fires (*anyādheya*) has concluded," this refers to the sacrificer's duty. The Adhvaryu:

"Men have generated the immortal one, the tireless, the swift, with firm jaws; may the ten sisters, the maidens, moving together, embrace the male as soon as he is born"—with this verse, he takes hold of the newborn child. (1.11.4) [End of Paṭala].
