Thus ends the third paṭala in the third praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. Regarding the "encircling" (*parigrahaṇa*) with the hollowed palms (*añjali*): Vaikhānasa says, "He receives the newborn with the hollowed palms," while Āpastamba says, "He encircles [the child] with the hollowed palms. The meaning is that he encircles [the child] with both hands turned upward, making the thumbs slightly extended; the mental visualization (*bhāvanā*) is: "You are encircled. Thus ends the third paṭala in the third praśna of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra composed by Mahādeva.
3.4 Now begins the fourth chapter.

Having taken that [fire], with the first two *vyāhṛtis* according to the rite of establishing the seers, with the first two *sārparājñī* verses, and with the first *gharmaśiras*, [he says]: "In my breath I establish you, the immortal, as a consumer of food for the sake of obtaining food; as a protector for the sake of protection."

"O Agni, lord of the household, seated in the assembly, find a world for the sacrificer from heaven, from earth, and from the intermediate space; sit upon the head of the earth in the world worthy of sacrifice. "O Agni, whoever is our enemy, whoever is our adversary who seeks to harm us—here I place him down by means of you," with these words he establishes [the fire] upon the ritual materials at the site of the Gārhapatya.

Having taken that fire and nourished it with cotton, dry cow-dung powder, and so forth, one should take it up in a vessel and carry it toward the east while seated; thus state Vaikhānasa and Āpastamba. Regarding the phrase "by means of the two *vyāhṛtis* according to the *ādhāna*": this is a name for the mantra. "According to the seers" (*yatharṣi*) means not bypassing whichever seer is the patron's own; that mantra which is the instrument for the *ādhāna* (fire-laying) is designated as "according to the *ādhāna*" (*yathādhāna*). That [mantra] will be explained further on. He himself will explain everything in due order.

When the *rathantara* Sāman has begun at the end of all the mantras during the *saṃmāra* (sprinkling) rites, even though the mantras of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) function as *karaṇa*-mantras (instrumental mantras), there can be no coincidence of the ritual action with the end of the mantra because it is interrupted by the commencement of the Sāman; since this is impossible, someone else sings the Sāman until that point. For this very reason, Āpastamba says: "The Brahman priest sings the *āgnyādheya* mantras."

Baudhāyana, however, states that regarding the meaning of the Sāmans, it is the Udgātṛ alone whom one addresses with "Recite the Rathantara," and then he places it upon him. This is appropriate only for the Chāndogas. Although, because it is prescribed in the Yajurveda, the rule of whispering (*upāṃśutva*) was shown in the general definition (*paribhāṣā*), nevertheless, in the Sāmaveda—according to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—one does not raise oneself above the level of the chest, nor does one hold oneself higher than the level of the ears.

One should hold oneself as if above, as if over the head; likewise, one should measure it at the level of the ear. One does not hold oneself too high beyond the measure of the ear. Regarding this, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "While taking out [the fire], one should take it out as if above the fire. This has been explained by this Sūtra. How so? When taking the Āhavanīya fire from the Gārhapatya, one should hold oneself as if above; here, when "above" is mentioned, it is stated by the word "as if" that it is neither on the head nor even at the level of the ear.

By way of contrast, the Veda itself has stated: "If one were to carry [the fire] higher and higher over the head, he would cut off the vital breaths; if he carries it lower and lower from the head, he preserves the vital breaths. The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is expressed as "he carries himself from below upwards to the ears. "He carries it lower and lower from the head" is an explanatory elaboration of this very point. He lifts up the fuel and places the supporting ladles (*upayamanī*) down.

He takes hold of this vessel. It was previously stated that [the term] refers to the carrying forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*); now, when he says "fuel" (*idhma*), the Teacher indicates that the word *nema* does not denote a ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*), but rather an action—namely, that by which the fire is kindled (*idhyate*). Thus, his intention is that it brings about the greatness of the refinement. He "takes hold of" (*upayacchati*) means that the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) is shown to be the very support-vessel (*upayamanī*); according to the statement of the Vaikhānasa, he should cover this vessel with another vessel filled with sand, so that the heated vessel does not burn the hand as he takes hold of it. "While being taken hold of" (*upayate*) means while it is being held.
Because he is taken home (*upayamyate*), the fire is "taken" (*upayata*);
while that [fire] is being maintained, the *Āgnīdhra* priest brings a common fire or produces one by friction and establishes the *Dakṣiṇāgni*.

One may kindle the kitchen fire from another [source], or by means of pure worldly fire produced by friction in the forest; however, some say that the *vaikhānasa* (hermit) brings the fire from the *gārhapatya*. Baudhāyana, moreover, states that one may establish the *ānyāhāryapacana* fire from the *gārhapatya* itself. The Brāhmaṇa text has also been cited: "Prajāpati emitted the fire. Some say they have a single origin; Āśvalāyana says this because there are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) similar to injunctions stating, "Where the fire is established in three ways," which indicates that the *gārhapatya* is indeed their source. Thus, having brought the fire from the *gārhapatya*, he establishes it in the *āgnīdhra*.

With the second *vyāhṛti*, according to the *ṛṣi*-assignment, with the second and third *sārparājñī* verses, and with the second *gharmaśiras* verse—"O Agni, source of food, bringer of joy, most auspicious one; from heaven, from earth, and from the intermediate space, find a world for the sacrificer"—he establishes [the fire] upon the materials in the site of the *dakṣiṇāgni* while the *yajñāyajñiya* is being sung, with the words: "Sit upon the head of the earth, in the world worthy of sacrifice; O Agni, whoever is our adversary, whoever is our adversary who assails us—here I place him down by means of you."

If there be a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra who is as well-nourished as a god, one should fetch [the fuel] from his house and prepare the fire.

Some explain that the phrase "like a *sura*" (god) is used to indicate that he is nourished and flourishing with wealth, grain, cattle, sons, and so forth in many ways. Others, however, take the word as *asura*, explaining it as one whose *asu*—meaning wealth (*rāyaḥ*)—is like his own life-breath (*asu*). The shortening of the vowel is a Vedic archaism; the meaning is that he is unable to spend his wealth, which is as dear to him as his own life. Alternatively, *asura* means one who transcends the *asus* (life-breaths); from the root *rā* (to take), the meaning is that he nourishes only his life-breaths.

They explain that he is extremely miserly and cruel, having attained nourishment and growth solely by taking from others. According to another ritual procedure (*kalpa*), one brings fire from his house and establishes it as the *dakṣiṇāgni*.
From this point forward, one should not eat his food. This prohibition is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*); from the moment the fire is brought, the sacrificer must not consume his food.

For one desiring *brahmavarcasa* (spiritual luster), [fire] from the top of a tree that is burning of its own accord by some fire; having taken fire from the upper part of a tree that is being consumed by some fire spontaneously, one should establish it for the sacrificer who desires *brahmavarcasa*. The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) therein is: "Desiring *brahmavarcasa*, having taken fire from the top of a tree, I shall establish the *dakṣiṇāgni*. For one desiring food, [fire] from a frying pan.

From the ocean a honeyed wave has arisen; it attained immortality together with the *upāṃśu* [cup]. That which is the secret name of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is the tongue of the gods and the navel of immortality. Let us proclaim that name with clarified butter at this sacrifice, and let us sustain it with our homages. May the Brahman priest hear the hymn being recited. The four-horned bull has uttered this. Four are his horns, three are his feet, two are his heads, and seven are his hands. Bound in three ways, the bull bellows loudly; the great god has entered into mortals. Having wiped clean the *juhū* and the *sruva* ladles.

Having gone forward to the Āhavanīya fire, he stands to the south and offers an oblation. That which is established in the *prakṛti* (archetype) remains established and is completed [therein]. The sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), however, will be explained in the section concerning the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).

He performs the sacrifice with the *pavamāna-havis* offerings after a year, a season, a month, a half-month, twelve days, four days, three days, two days, on the next day, or immediately. By stating "three days" and then again saying "on the next day," it is indicated that three days have elapsed. Similarly, it should be understood that this refers to when a year has elapsed. Baudhāyana says, "after twelve nights have dawned. This refers to those [offerings] known as the *pavamāna*. This is clear.
For one who is about to sacrifice with the Soma or who is establishing the sacred fires, the ritual procedure for the Pavamāna oblations lasts for one year.

However, in the case of the *somapūrvādhāna* (the establishment of the sacred fires preceded by the Soma sacrifice), the previously mentioned alternatives do not apply at all; rather, having performed the Soma sacrifice, one performs the Pavamāna offerings at the end of the year. Regarding this, there is an alternative according to the view of Āpastamba: "Some say one should offer [the oblations]; if one offers, one should offer three oblations of clarified butter to Agni Pavamāna, Agni Pāvaka, and Agni Śuci, or having offered to the deities of the Soma sacrifice, one should then offer [the Pavamāna oblations]. According to the logicians (*nyāyavidaḥ*), it is the opinion of the Sūtra-authors that the evening and morning *agnihotra* should not be performed prior to the Pavamāna oblations.
One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna, [a cake] to Agni Pāvaka, and [a cake] to Agni Śuci.
The phrase "one should offer a cake on eight potsherds" carries over from the previous context.
This may be performed using either the same sacrificial grass or different sacrificial grass.

By being common to the outside, a single ritual procedure (*ekatantratā*) is indicated; that is to say, whether they are of the same ritual procedure (*samānatantra*) or of different ritual procedures (*nānātantra*). Alternatively, having first prepared [the offerings] separately, one should subsequently combine them. The meaning is that for Agni Pavamāna, one should prepare [the offering] separately, and then for Agni Pāvaka and Agni Śuci, one should combine them—that is, one should offer them by means of a single ritual procedure (*samānatantreṇa*).
One should perform these rites as having a common ritual procedure (*samānatantra*) with the cake-offering to Agni (*āgneya-aṣṭākapāla*).

These three, together with the previously mentioned [rite], all four should indeed be performed with a common ritual procedure. However, the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇās*) will be explained in the section on the measurement of the chariot (Paṭala 650), in the *Vaijayantī* commentary by Mahādeva. When the Pavamāna oblations are performed on the same day (*sadyas*), then they share the common ritual procedure with the offering to Agni; it is not otherwise, because there is no other time for the offering to Agni. Thus, the sacrifice is concluded.

He subsequently offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma, a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni, a pap cooked in ghee to Aditi, and for the sake of triple success, a pap cooked in ghee to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses for the offering to Aditi. Having set aside for the Brahman the portion of the *iḍā* belonging to Aditi, they all consume it; likewise with the portions resulting from the fourfold division.

The five oblations have a common ritual procedure (*tantra*) as subsequent offerings (*anunirvāpya*) following the *pavamāna* oblations. In the case of a division [of the sacrifice], there are three elevations (*ṛddhi*); these elevations refer to the height around whichever vessel contains the clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses are fixed. The full-moon (*paurṇamāsa*) ritual procedure applies because of its primary status and because of the word "first" (*mukhya*). It is prescribed that for the rice-pap (*caru*) of Aditi, the consumption of the *iḍā* portion is performed separately for the Brahman priest.

There is no eating by anyone else for that purpose; having set it aside and placed it separately in the *iḍā* vessel, the division into four parts is likewise performed separately for the Brahman priest. At the time of that fourfold division, one should place the entire portion belonging to Āditya in the very first share intended for the Brahman. Regarding the consumption of the *iḍā*, there is a scriptural injunction stating: "At that time, everyone consumes all of it together. Here, the duties pertaining to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) are explained for the sake of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the Āgneya [offering], one gives food, a full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*), a horse with its entire harness, a chariot, a garment, six cows, twelve, twenty-four, or an unlimited number, or an increasing number. Regarding the "full vessel": it is a conventional term for a quantity of rice or other grains measuring four or eight *puṣkala*s. Eight handfuls (*muṣṭi*) make one *kiṃcit*; eight *kiṃcit* make one *puṣkala*; and eight *puṣkala*s are declared to be one *pūrṇapātra*.

The *upavarhaṇa* (pillow) and the *upadhāna* (cushion) are called *sārvasūtra*; that is, the *upavarhaṇa* is fixed as having threads of many colors. The others are clear. Among those [animals], the cow, the ox, and the pair [of animals] are of prescribed forms. The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the *Āgneya* [offering] is the *Anvāhārya* rice; since it occurs at that time, it follows by implication that this refers to the sacrificial fees of the *Agnyādheya*. Therefore, the sequence is as stated by Baudhāyana and Vaikhānasa: "Having placed the *Anvāhārya* for the *Āgneya*, he gives the sacrificial fees for the *Agnyādheya* up to twelve."

It has been stated that one gives [the cow] immediately after the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) for the *anyādheya* (the initial establishment of the sacred fires). The *anvāhāryapacana* fire must necessarily be maintained; otherwise, the success of the *ādhāna* (the formal installation of the fires) would not be achieved. This is because of the scriptural declaration: "Inasmuch as they cook the *anvāhārya* rice-offering on the *anvāhāryapacana*, by that means his desired [deity] becomes pleased. Among those cows numbering six or more, it is said that the milch-cow (*dhenū*), while suckling her calf, draws him toward herself as she grows.

Since it has been stated that "those which serve for successive purposes are to be given," and because there is no increase without a calf, he says that ten items result by prescribing nine substances for the purchase, including the *liṅga* (the sign). In that context, by the rule "he purchases with a cow (*dhenu*)," the calf is also understood to be included. The *anaḥ* is a cart; the draft animal for it is a bull; and the two cattle, male and female, are a pair (*mithuna*). [Note: The commentary mentions variants such as *tryaddhau* and refers to Satyāṣāḍha’s *Śrautasūtra*, Book 3.]

However, among those verses which were mentioned merely by their own forms and numbered six and so forth, four are specifically indicated here. But in the Brāhmaṇa, other items whose forms are specified in the Brāhmaṇa itself are mentioned. This is the intention: for in the Brāhmaṇa it is heard, "He gives twelve; he may give as much as he desires. Therein, the items ending with the *anadvān* (ox) have their forms not previously specified [in the verses], while the cow and the ox are specified by the passage beginning with "the cow is for the *Āhavanīya* fire," and likewise, by the statement "he gives a pair," four objects are established.

And thus there are ten perfected [offerings]. Regarding this, it is heard that "six are prescribed" (*ṣaḍ-nadātī*); therein, although there are more than ten, only four have their forms specifically prescribed (*ādiṣṭa-rūpa*), while among the six, two have forms not specifically prescribed (*anādiṣṭa-rūpa*). Therefore, in the Brāhmaṇa, for the purpose of completing the twelve, the statement "at will" (*kāma-sūtra*) should be understood as follows: when there is the capacity [to perform more], the additional [offerings] are merely an elaboration of that very same rule; in another recensional branch (*śākhāntara*), it says "twelve," and so forth. According to Karka, those four are indeed obligatory (*nitya*), while the others are optional (*vaikalpika*).

He gives a full vessel of water and a cushion to the *āgnīdh*; a horse to the *brahmā*; a milch cow (*dhenu*) at the site of the *gārhapatya* fire; and an ox (*anaḍvān*) at the site of the *āhavanīya* fire to the *adhvaryu*. Whatever remains is common [to all]. For the first two *pavamāna* offerings, he gives gold as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) weighing thirty *mānas*; for the last, weighing forty *mānas*. Among the subsequent offerings (*anunirvāpyas*), there is an abundance; for the offering to Āditya, he gives a cow to be brought from elsewhere (*āhārya*). He gives these as the sacrificial fees.

Regarding this, Āpastamba states: "One who has not previously maintained the sacred fires may establish them; he may give one cow at his pleasure, for that serves as the substitute for all the cows [required]. Vaikhānasa, however, says that it is the substitute for all sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). It should be understood that the *anvāhārya* rice is prescribed specifically for the fees of the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*), for the *pavamāna-havis* offerings, and for the *āditya* offering; whereas for others, the *anvāhārya* is different.

The measure of thirty is determined by the thirtyfold [units] beginning with the *mita*, *suvarṇa*, *pavamāna*, and *havis*; in another treatise (*śāstrāntara*), a single measure of one hundred is observed there. Thus ends the section on the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*). Now begins the Agnihotra. The sacrificer, together with his wife, having restrained his breaths (*prāṇāyāma*) and intending to commence the Agnihotra, should perform the mental recitation of the *daśahotṛ* formula along with the *graha* formulas, thinking "I shall offer," because [the rite] is employed for a different transcendental result (*apūrva*) than the primary result of the Agnihotra itself.

Regarding the phrase "about to perform" (*ālapsyamāna*), since this refers to the future time of the *agnihotra*, it should be understood that the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the *agnihotra* occurs immediately after the *vaiśvadeva-homa*. The resolve is: "Having performed the *agnihotra*, I shall offer it morning and evening as long as I live."

If there is a desire [to perform sacrifices], one who desires heaven [should do so] as "the wife desiring heaven"; there is no additional requirement here such as the rule of being thirty years of age or more, as in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. However, even for one living in the forest (*vanastha*), there is cessation [of duties] upon renunciation (*pravrajita*) due to lack of qualification—just as in the case of a husband who has become impotent (*vidhura*). And when the husband has renounced, the wife should maintain all the ritual vessels and the two churning sticks (*araṇī*) for as long as she lives. Because of the Vedic text stating, "One should offer oblations in these at the beginning of rituals," and according to the words of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), the *kūṣmāṇḍa* oblation is to be offered in the *āhavanīya* fire.

One who is about to begin the Agnihotra, having mentally recited the Daśahotṛ formula and offered the oblation with the Sagraha, performs the evening Agnihotra according to the procedure for the evening Agnihotra with the [prescribed] mantra. He sets down the first Agnihotra oblation with the Vyāhṛtis; likewise at the end of the year.

This should be stated; although it will be explained later in the section on the *yajamāna* (the sacrificer's duties), nevertheless, in order to enjoin two things—the commencement of the *agnihotra* with a mantra immediately after the completion of the *pāvamāneṣṭi*s along with their subsidiary offerings (*anunirvāpya*s)—and because it will be stated that "another may indeed offer at the first commencement," the recitation is placed here for the *adhvaryu*. Even in the case of the option of carrying [the fires] forth (*uddharaṇa*), the offering into these fires occurs during the twelve nights; thus ends the fifth hundredth section, accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

Because it will be explained later that there is neither following [the fire] nor lifting [it up], even in the view where there is an interruption by the Pavamāna oblations, one must maintain the fires in an unbent position until the commencement of the Agnihotra; and since the twelve-night period for the *oma* is prescribed immediately after the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) and is not yet completed, the maintenance of the fire in the interim means that if the fire goes out in the middle of the sacrifice, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) certainly applies, as has already been stated.

Therefore, the conclusion is that the maintenance [of the fires] for twelve nights, both morning and evening, begins with the *āśvapadika* [first] *agnihotra*, because its commencement is prescribed specifically there; thus, in the case of *somādhāna* (fire-consecration accompanied by Soma), the *agnihotra* begins in that very fire immediately after the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath). Likewise, in the case of *iṣṭipūrvādhāna* (fire-consecration preceded by a sacrifice), the commencement occurs on the first day (*pratipad*) at night, immediately following the sacrifice.

One who is about to begin the *agnihotra*—immediately after the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*)—offers an oblation at night, having first uttered "Citti" and so forth mentally, and then with the formula beginning with "Vācaspati," ending in "svāhā," according to the procedure of a *dravyahoma*, following the method of the evening *agnihotra* which will be described hereafter.

The statement "with a mantra" refers to the fact that, having begun with the injunction regarding the Pavamāna oblations—"the Agnihotra should be offered silently; [alternatively] the Agnihotra should not be offered"—the Śruti declares, "it should be offered only silently. Likewise, Kātyāyana states: "The Agnihotra is silent because of the Śruti. Furthermore, by the inclusion of the word "mantra," it is indicated that this should not occur immediately after the initial commencement; the meaning is that the first Agnihotra is commenced in the evening, not at the morning commencement.

In the evening, the Agnihotra substance is placed behind the Āhavanīya fire with three *vyāhṛtis*. In place of the formula "Give me life," one should place it with the *vyāhṛtis*. At the end of the year, on whichever lunar day the night of the commencement of the Agnihotra falls, on that same lunar day at the morning Agnihotra as well, the placing [of the oblation] is to be done with the *vyāhṛtis* alone.

"When the year has come around, he should set them down with these [verses]; thus, by means of the Brahman, he encompasses the year on both sides. The word "around" (*pari*) is used to state that the setting down is prescribed at the beginning and end of the year; thus, the meaning is that it occurs at the final Agnihotra at the conclusion of the year.

Since the Agnihotra, which is to be performed in the evening and morning, constitutes a single ritual application (*ekaprayoga*), it should be understood that on whichever lunar day the evening rite was commenced, the annual cycle of applications is completed on that very same morning; thereafter, the commencement of the second year begins from the evening. The specific details regarding the sacrificer’s duties will be explained in the *Yājamāna* section.
Now follows the commencement of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

In this case as well, if there is a desire [to perform the sacrifice], the *saṃkalpa* (formal resolve) is exactly as before; otherwise, however, the accepted *saṃkalpa* is: "I shall sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa for thirty years," or "until old age," or "for as long as I live. It should also be understood that if one intends to sacrifice for fifteen years, it is by means of the Dākṣāyaṇayajña.

One who is about to commence the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, on the day of fasting (*aupavasathya*) of the preceding lunar phase (*parvan*), should mentally recite the Caturhotṛ formula and offer it along with its *graha*; then, having offered the two Sārasvata oblations with the verses beginning "Full is the earth... and "That which the gods bestowed...", [he proceeds].

The commencement here is intended to take place on the fifteenth day; however, because of the statement "commencing on the previous day," it should be understood that the commencement occurs through the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). Thus, first there is the ritual of the resolve and oblation for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), and for that purpose, there is another resolve such as "I shall sacrifice" when beginning. Since every preceding day—including the fifteenth and the first of the lunar fortnight—is considered a "sacrificial day" (*parvan*), it is said to be "of the preceding [day]. The meaning is: "on that [fourteenth day] which is the fasting day (*aupavasathya*) of the preceding *parvan*."

Although the *aupavasathya* day is the day of the *anvādhāna*, it is nevertheless used here as a designation for the preceding day. While it would have been sufficient to say "on the day prior to the fifteenth," the inclusion of the term *parvan* (the junction) is intended to indicate the time of the sacrifice. As for the exclusion of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), since the commencement is established on the full moon itself—according to the rule that "the former is the full moon and the latter is the new moon"—the *caturhotṛ* formula and so forth are performed as before, being auxiliary to the commencement.

Having taken two portions from those two [ladles] with the formulas "The full one behind" and "And these two," he offers them; these are the two *pārvaṇa* oblations because they are performed by means of mantras dedicated to the deities of the *parvan*.
He performs the *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice.

Because of the statement, "having offered, he pours out," it appears that the *anvārambhaṇīyā* is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to both the *hotṛ-homa* and the *pārvaṇa-homa*. In this regard, the phrase "one who is about to begin the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsāvārambhamāṇaḥ*) is connected to everything [in the context]; otherwise, there would be a mutual relationship of principal and auxiliary (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) between the two *homas* themselves. Furthermore, the *iṣṭi* of the *homas* and the *anvārambhaṇīyā* are intended to be auxiliaries to the commencement (*ārambha*) itself. This is expressed in the rule: "One who is about to begin the New and Full Moon sacrifices should offer the *caturhotṛ* oblations and the *sārasvata* *homas* beforehand."

Likewise, because it is understood from the rule "one should first offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu" that this applies to each [performance] prior to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), there is a separate re-establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyuddharaṇa*) for each; provided that, according to the *Āśvalāyana-śrautasūtra*, the sacrifice is completed within twelve nights, with the fire-installation (*adhāna*) preceded by the oblation.

Likewise, when the *soma*-preceded *ādhāna* and the *pavamāna* oblations have been performed, if the *ajas* (goats) are offered for twelve nights thereafter, the extraction (*uddharaṇa*) is to be done for each [offering] provided there is no completion of the *homas*. Furthermore, it should be understood that even if a full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) occurs in the interim, the *anvārambhaṇīyā* and other rites are to be performed only upon the birth of the *ajas*. Although some commentators have explained this differently, I shall desist from refuting them for fear of prolixity.

One should perform the *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice; that by which the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are commenced and praised for the sacrificer is the *anvārambhaṇīyā*. One should offer it. [The offerings are]:

a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Viṣṇu, a pap for Sarasvatī, a cake on twelve potsherds for Sarasvant, and a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Bhagin. Some prescribe the offering to Agni Bhagin as a constant rule for one who desires, "May I be fortunate and an eater of food. This [offering to Bhagin] is to be performed when such a desire exists; otherwise, there is an option. The rest is clear.

Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he performs twelve *jaya* oblations with ghee taken in twelve ladlings, using the formulas: "Consciousness, svāhā! Perception, svāhā! and so forth. Although it would follow from the rule regarding the taking of oblation-materials that they should be as many as there are offerings, this repetition is for the purpose of restriction (*parisaṃkhyā*), so that there may not be thirteen ladlings. He performs these supplementary offerings (*anupahoma*) called *nayana* according to the rules of the *davihoma*. There is no fuel-stick, strewing, or sprinkling, because those have already been concluded therein. The thirteenth [offering] is with the formula: "Prajāpati to Indra, the *jayas*, svāhā!"

This undertaking is for the purpose of establishing that the oblation (*homa*) is performed with [the ladle] held by the *pṛśni* [finger]. The Commentator has stated that this clarified butter (*ājya*) is "contained in the vessel" (*sthālīgata*). Since it is a *darvihoma* preceded by a mantra, it would have been expected to be performed silently (*tūṣṇīka*); the statement regarding it is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). The intention is that the offering is made with what is contained in the vessel as it happens to be present in the context. Furthermore, although it is a general rule (*paribhāṣita*) that the clarified butter is taken from the *dhruvā* vessel at the *āhavanīya* fire, that rule applies only within the ritual framework (*tantra*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). And because it is an auxiliary offering (*upahoma*), the equality of the portions should be taken from the *dhruvā* itself.

"O Agni, giver of strength, grant power and vigor to me as I advance; for one who has been cursed, grant immunity from being cursed; for this community, grant preeminence. Regarding the fourteenth [verse]:
"May there be prosperity in that community which I shall overcome"—as if variegated, such a mark appears upon his body.

The syntactical connection is as follows: having made the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), "May the people—the multitude of men—be afflicted with *śvitra* (leucoderma) or *kuṣṭha* (leprosy) through this oblation on the fourteenth day," he offers the oblation on the fourteenth day. Its fruit arises as a variegated whiteness, like a leprous spot, upon his own self—that is, upon the self of the one he hates.
Alternatively, one need not perform the *Anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice; one should instead offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni.

There is an option regarding the place of the *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice. Here too, [the phrase] "one who is about to begin the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsāv ārapsyamānaḥ*) applies exactly as before. But one might object: "Since this [Āgneyī offering] is also an *ārambha-prayuktā* (occasioned by the commencement) just like the *anvārambhaṇīyā*, why should one not perform the *anvārambhaṇīyā*? True. However, the Āgneyī, though distinct from the *anvārambhaṇīyā*, is indeed an *ārambhaṇīyā* when performed by one who is about to begin the New and Full Moon sacrifices. But what is the distinction? There is a distinction.

The *anvārambhaṇīyā* is that which is performed immediately after the *ādhāna* for the purpose of commencing [the sacrifice]. That which is commenced after performing a *homa* in the midst of the *viṣṭi* does not follow the *ādhāna*, and therefore it is not the *anvārambhaṇīyā*. Why is this so? We say: because of the consideration of the subsequent sūtra.

In this case as well, it should not have been stated in the sūtra that "one should perform the Anvārambhaṇīyā," but rather, after stating "they prescribe [it] for one who has a sister," it should simply have said, "one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni"; for in that case there would be brevity. And if that were so, the subsidiary offerings (upahoma) such as "cittam" and so forth would apply to the offering to Agni as well. Even though that is the case, [the author], by means of a cumbersome instruction, says "or else one should not perform the Anvārambhaṇīyā," thereby preventing those subsidiary offerings from being designated by that specific name in the case of the offering to Agni.

If it is asked: "But why should the *āgneyī* verse, occurring in the context of the Āgneya [offering], connect with the distant, unrelated, and interrupted [phrase] 'performing the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices'?"—this is true. However, since this *āgneyī* verse would otherwise remain without a specific application (*niradhikārā*), one must determine with what it connects; for the Darśapūrṇamāsa [procedure] is not yet concluded.

Therefore, the section concerning *sārambha* (the commencement) is connected with the phrase "one who is about to commence the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. By that very same sūtra, it is stated: "One should offer the cake on eight potsherds to Agni for one who is establishing the fires on the new moon day"; this is the modification (*vikṛta*) of that [general rule]. In the case of the establishment of the fires on the new moon day, this offering to Agni applies; however, the *anvārambhaṇīyā* (introductory sacrifice), which is obtained without distinction, is prohibited by the sūtra "or even on the new moon day," precisely by warding off its application.

And thus, in order to state the option regarding the establishment of the fires (ādhāna) on the full moon day, it was said "or else" (*api vā*); that option might otherwise apply even to the new moon day, and for that purpose it was stated that "this [fire] remains unmodified. When the establishment of the fires is performed specifically on the new moon day, the Pavamāna-iṣṭis are completed on the fifteenth itself; and on the fourteenth—the day preceding the upcoming full moon—only the Āgneyī [offering] takes place, not the Anvārambhaṇīyā.

Alternatively, in the subsequent sūtra, after concluding that [Iṣṭi], one performs the two Sārasvata oblations and the Anvārambhaṇīyā at that very time; this re-enactment of the Anvārambhaṇīyā establishes that for the Full Moon fire-laying, it is mandatory and not optional. Consequently, it is established that the Anvārambhaṇīyā occurs on the Full Moon day, while on the New Moon day, only the Āgneyī [offering] takes place. Nor should this be disregarded as a mere fabrication.

For it is stated likewise by Vaikhānasa: "For one who establishes the sacred fires on the new moon day, there is no Ārambhaṇīyā; he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni. This also is considered: do these two offerings reach the modified sacrifices (vikṛti) by extension (atideśa) as being constituent parts? [Note: The manuscript variants are noted as ka, ga, ca, da, ṇa, dadhikṛ. This is the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[3rd Praśna].

Or rather [it is not]. Having deliberated on that purpose, one must consider what kind of subsidiary (*aṅga*) it is. Some say: "This [subsidiary] is a subsidiary of that which is performed throughout one's life and so forth; since it occurs within the time-period of the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), it assists them by falling within that interval, but it is not to be performed for their sake. In that regard, according to the view that lifelongness (*yāvajjīvatā*) is a property of the agent (*kartṛdharma*), there is no injunction of the time characterized by lifelongness as a subsidiary.

For it is the time known as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) that is enjoined as the occasion [for the performance]; however, since that [time] is completed at every lunar phase (*parvan*), there is no establishment of *prasaṅga* (incidental performance). [Objection: Then let them not apply; why do these two sacrifices apply through the sentence taught outside of any specific context (*anāramyādhīta*), namely, "one who is beginning the New and Full Moon sacrifices"? [Reply: Because, according to the Sūtra, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the aggregate, like the *vaimṛdha* sacrifice. Furthermore, there is nowhere an extension (*atideśa*) of the subsidiaries of an aggregate. For the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) applies [the subsidiaries] to each individual [component].

Among the two types of archetypes (*prakṛti*), one adopts that very archetype for which the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) prescribes the *aikādaśina* [set of eleven animals]; otherwise, even the *vaimṛdha* sacrifice would obtain among the modifications (*vikāra*) of the Full Moon sacrifice. Therefore, the constituent parts of the composite whole are not extended by transfer. And it will be stated later that the discussion regarding the extension of application (*atideśa*) concerns each individual [part], because a composite form as an archetype is impossible.

Furthermore, if these two were auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the performance (*prayoga*), they would have to be repeated at every performance; yet this is not the case. For what reason? Because they are obtained as auxiliaries to the entire performance merely by the first performance being previously consecrated (*pūrvapāvita*). How so? We say: by virtue of their names (*saṃjñā*). For the names *anvārambhaṇīyā* and *ārambhaṇīyā* [apply] from the very beginning.

Nor would it be so even in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*); for in that regard, whether the *pāviṣṭi* occurs at both times or at either one, the Sūtra merely mentions its connection with the animal, and the author himself will later state that there is no *paśviṣṭi*. Since this [substitution] pertains only to the animal and exists prior to the commencement [of the rite], it is an auxiliary to the entire performance; bearing this very point in mind, the Sūtrakāra made no effort to refute it, considering that it would obtain in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) by default.

Furthermore, there is also an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*). In a case where [the application] was already established, it has been stated as follows: "Among animals that have not yet become parts of the sacrifice (*aṅgabhūta*), the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* and the animal-sacrifice (*paśviṣṭi*) do not exist. In that context, in order to show that [the application] is established, it is said "animal-sacrifice" (*paśviṣṭi*). Therefore, if [the application] were already established even for the *iṣṭi*, he would have simply said, "not among those *iṣṭis* that have become parts of the sacrifice, nor at the *vārambhaṇīyā*.
This [rule] applies without modification to one who establishes the sacred fires on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).

As for what was stated regarding the *ādhāna* (the laying of the fires), that which is prescribed for the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) remains unchanged; it is exactly as described. The meaning is that having performed the *ādhāna* on the new moon day, the completion of the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) occurs on that very same day. This is also an indicative rule (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *nakṣatra-ādhāna* (the laying of fires under a specific lunar mansion); there too, in whichever lunar mansion one performs the morning *ādhāna*, the completion of the *ādhāna* along with the *iṣṭi* occurs on that very day. Regarding this, the view is that if the *pavamāna-havis* (oblations to the Pavamānas) are to be offered, one should offer them at that very time; otherwise, one may conclude after performing only the oblation to Agni (*āgneya*). This applies specifically to the *nakṣatra-ādhāna* and the *amāvāsyā-ādhāna*.

On the fourteenth day— the fast-day (*aupavasathya*) of the preceding full-moon (*paurṇamāsī*) parvan— one establishes the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), performs the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), and concludes it. Having brought the establishment of the fires and the sacrifice to completion on that very same day— the morning of the fourteenth, the fast-day of the preceding full-moon parvan— one then performs the *caturhotṛ* formulas, the two *sārasvata* oblations, and the *anvārambhaṇīyā* offering.

On the fourteenth day itself, he performs everything: the Caturhotṛ and the Catuhhotṛ homas. On the following day, he sacrifices with the Paurṇamāsa [offering]; he places the oblations with the Vyāhṛtis, and likewise at the end of the year.

Thus ends the fifth chapter in the third book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. On the following day, beginning with the *anvādhāna* (the adding of fuel), one performs the sacrifice on the first lunar day (*pratipad*). Therein, one should perform the placing of the sacrificial oblations (*havis*) upon the altar (*vedi*). Likewise, on whichever new moon day the year concludes, the placing [of the oblations] is performed with the *vyāhṛtis*. Beyond this, there is no repetition for the subsequent year, as such a repetition is not heard in the text. Thus ends the fifth chapter in the third book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra composed by Mahādeva. 5.

3.6 Now begins the sixth chapter. The establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), which was taught in four chapters, is now described; the re-establishment (*punarādhāna*) in one, and the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*) in two.

We shall now explain the *punarādheya* (re-establishment of the fires). Its ritual procedure (*kalpa*) has been explained by [the rules for] the *agnyādheya* (initial establishment of the fires). That ritual action by which the fires are established again is the *punarādheya*; however, the *agnyādheya* was mentioned previously, and this is a modification (*vikāra*) thereof. For it will be stated: "Having given the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) pertaining to the *agnyādheya*, he gives the sacrificial fees pertaining to the *punarādheya*. Thus, while the status of being an *agnyādheya* remains the same, the *punarādheya* is modified by certain specific qualities; therefore, the meaning is that its ritual procedure—the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*)—has been explained by that [previous description].

If, after having established the sacred fires, within this year he suffers a loss of his son or his wife, or if he comes into conflict with a limb of his own body, or if he does not prosper, he should perform the re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya).

If there is loss of wealth and so forth, or the death of a son, or if one is contradicted by one's own limb—meaning one encounters such opposition that one becomes deficient in a limb—or if one does not attain prosperity or even more, then upon the occurrence of any one of these causes within the first year, one should perform the *punarādheya* (re-establishment of the sacred fires). Āpastamba has stated that this applies whenever there is a desire for progeny or cattle;
however, Bharadvāja maintains that the time for *punarādheya* does not expire as long as one lives, while Āśmarathya says it is within a year, and Ālekhana says it may be at any time.

Having performed the Full Moon sacrifice, one who intends to extinguish the sacred fire (agnyudvāsan) should, on the New Moon day, offer an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni and an oblation on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara; so say some teachers.
In this case, the deity is Agni as characterized by the attribute of Vaiśvānara.

[Notes on variants: 1. gha, ṅa, ja, śa, va, da: māsī ya°; 2. gha, ha, ja, jha, ya: 3. vā’nveti; ka, ga, ṭa: tarasmi; 4. ke, kha, ga, cha, ṭa, 8: vāsyayā vāḍa:me; 330: Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra—Third Book.]
One should subsequently offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Soma, a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Apsumat, and a pap to Mitra.

When one intends to extinguish the sacred fires, one should offer [these]; the statement regarding Vaiśvānara read in one's own recensional branch (śākhā) specifies that there are only two oblations there. According to some, in one recension there are only these two, while in another recension all five are prescribed.

Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering: "O Agni, that form of yours which dwells in the cattle as the purifying one (*pavamānā*) and is dear—enter the earth together with it, with the *rathantara* chant and the *gāyatrī* metre; from there, bring us great prosperity. O Agni, that form of yours which is purifying (*pāvakā*) and most beloved by the mind—enter the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) together with it, with the *vāmadevya* chant and the *triṣṭubh* metre; from there, bestow strength upon us and increase our domestic sacrifice. O Agni, that bright form of yours which is in the sun—together with it..."

Enter the sky with the *Bṛhat* Sāman, with the *Jagatī* metre; from there, protect us with rain. O Agni, those portions (*vibhakti*) of yours which Indra and Sukra brought—sit upon those flames, [taking] the ash of Vaiśvānara. O Agni, those wish-fulfilling portions (*kāmadughā vibhakti*) of yours that have been gathered together—with those, milk for us here our desires: offspring, prosperity, and wealth. O Agni, those wooden materials (*vānaspatya saṃbhāra*) of yours that were gathered together—go with them to the trees, to your own womb, in due order.

Having offered seven oblations with the mantra, "Agni has entered the world as he did his own dwelling; I have approached the gods for the removal of sin, accompanied by the mind," he releases the blazing fires. He keeps them released for as long as it takes to perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices, or for a year, or for twelve days.

Immediately after the *nimitta-parvan*, having performed the *utsargeṣṭi* on the first day (*pratipad*), one offers seven oblations prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* of that sacrifice and then concludes the rite. By "concluding" (*saṃsthāpya*), the meaning is that one extinguishes the kindled fires; this is understood from the scriptural injunctions, "having extinguished [them], one should re-establish them" and "being about to extinguish. The term *avasnati* means "he releases.

The sense to be understood is that he effects a release by severing the connection with the purpose for which the fires were established, and causes them to reach their own natural state—the place from which they came—which is observed as the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*) in the worship of the gods and similar rites.

It should have been stated that "the time for re-establishing the fires (*punarādheya*) lasts until the end of the rainy season or autumn, during which period the fire remains neglected"; however, it is instead said, "as long as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) [are not performed]. This is so that the re-establishment of the fires does not occur at any festival day during the rains, nor merely under the influence of any one of the three lunar mansions such as Rohiṇī according to one's own whim; rather, it is so that there may be no omission of the obligatory sacrifice (*nityeṣṭi*) on whichever the first festival day occurs according to either the solar or the lunar measure within the rainy season.

In that case, if the asterism for the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) should coincide with the onset of the rainy season, then the re-establishment must be performed at that very time; otherwise, it should be done on the first *parvan* (lunar festival) or on the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*). Prior to that, having adopted whichever option is possible according to one’s capacity, one should first cook the *brahmaudana* (sacrificial rice for the Brahmins). Then, [the rites follow]. [Note: The text fragment includes manuscript variants and commentary references.

The meaning is that on the day prior to the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) on which the fire is to be established, one should perform the second [re-establishment], then the *punarādheya* on that very mansion, and thereafter the obligatory *iṣṭi*. Regarding this, the limit has been stated as "one year. In this context, it is not prescribed that "the fires are to be left unattended for a period up to one year"; rather, the meaning is that one should not leave them unattended for more than a year. To this effect, Āpastamba says: "He becomes one whose fires have been left unattended for a year at most. Here, "most" (*para*) means the ultimate limit.

Then, after the autumn [season], when the cause [for the suspension] has occurred and the *utsarga* (formal release) has been performed, as long as the year does not elapse, they remain released; beyond that, it is as before. If, by fate or through human agency, the first *parvan* (lunar festival) passes away, then after the *utsargeṣṭi*, as long as the thirteenth month has not yet commenced, one must perform the *punarādheya* (re-consecration) even before that time. The meaning is that if this is exceeded, there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the occasion of abandoning the sacred fires (*agnityāga*).

If, due to a cause—whether divine or human—the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*) must be performed during the rainy season or autumn, one should not allow a lapse of twelve months even if the *tyotvā* fire is unavailable; it should be understood that in such a case, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is required once the rite has been performed.

By the phrase "or for twelve days," it should be understood that this demonstrates another view: that the *utsargeṣṭi* (the sacrifice of relinquishment) does not necessarily occur only on the *parvan* immediately following the [auspicious] sign; rather, when the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) suitable for re-establishing the fires (*punarādheya*) arrives prior to the first *parvan* of the year, one should—before that time and within the twelve-day period—relinquish the fires as before on a *parvan*, perform the *punarādheya* at the [new] lunar mansion, and only thereafter perform the obligatory sacrifices (*nityeṣṭi*) and so forth. This is how the alternative opinion is shown.

And thus, when the occasion for re-establishment arises due to a sign occurring in autumn, one should perform the *utsarga-iṣṭi* preceded by the obligatory *iṣṭi* on the final festival day (*parvan*) of autumn; then, having prepared two portions of *brahmaudana* on that very first day (*pratipad*) at night, the re-establishment (*punar-ādhāna*) takes place on the second day, and that too, following the sequence beginning with the *pratipad*, is indeed an establishment on a festival day (*parva-ādhāna*).

This has been clearly stated by Baudhāyana, Kātyāyana, and Vaikhānasa: "Or, having sprinkled the fires with water at that very moment and having cooked the *brahmaudana*, he observes the fast. The meaning is that the *ādhāna* (the formal establishment of the sacred fires) takes place on the following day. In their view, there is only one *brahmaudana* to be performed at the time of the immediate rite (*sadyaskāla*). This option among all the alternatives has been stated by them, yet it is explained here as being restricted. As for the statement "immediately after the occasion [for the rite]... and so forth—

If, immediately after performing the obligatory *iṣṭi* and other rites, no constellation is found prior to the *parvan* at the onset of the rainy season, then one should perform the obligatory *iṣṭi*, the *utsarga-iṣṭi*, and so forth, right at that first *parvan*. In this case, the preparation of the *brahmaudana* and subsequent rites are to be understood as before. This alternative view is indeed authorized by the Sūtra-author himself when he says, "or for twelve days. Thus it should be explained. [The following] verses state: "By the loss of the forest and so forth, the destruction of the fires is recognized."

Therefore, when the cause for re-establishment (*punarādheya*) arises and occurs, one should first produce the fires through the rite of expiation (*prāyaścitta-ādhāna*); immediately thereafter, one should perform the re-establishment according to its prescribed procedure, preceded by the ritual of renunciation (*utsarga*). And thus, when the cause for re-establishment exists and the fires are destroyed by some cause, the rite of expiation and re-establishment is desired. Following that, one should perform the re-establishment preceded by renunciation. But if there is destruction of the *vaidika* fires, where would the *Utsargeṣṭi* (the sacrifice of renunciation) take place?

When that [rite] has been performed, however, a re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya) is desired; it is prescribed by the Śruti text: "Having removed [the fires], they are to be re-established. Here, the term "removal" (udvāsana) indicates the Udvāsaneṣṭi sacrifice. Both the removal and the sacrifice are constituent parts (aṅga) of the re-establishment of the fires. [Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, Third Praśna, Section 332]

The *iṣṭi* sacrifice is understood from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) to be a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person; and thus, one who has been so refined should perform the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādhāna*). (7) But the *udvāsana* (setting aside) of the fires is a refinement, not their destruction; for since it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) for the sake of the *iṣṭi*, it is an act of disposal (*pratipatti*) according to the injunction. (8) The term "one should set aside" (*udvāsayet*) implies a removal (*udvāsa*), which indeed refers to the re-establishment itself. Therefore, the refinement of the fires is proclaimed as a subordinate element. (9) When the fires have been destroyed by the setting aside, there is no refinement whatsoever [other than re-establishment].

It is said: "Indeed, this is not destruction; let it be declared as 'evacuation' (udvāsana). Rather, having relinquished their status as auxiliary parts of ritual action within their respective sources, they remain here on earth and other elements in the form of power (śakti). That [power] which is perceived through the aforementioned homa-mantras, such as 'yā te agne', is for the purpose of re-establishing those [deities] that have been installed in their former state. Indeed, re-installation (punarādheya) is desired when [the fire] is present in its own manifest form; and such re-installation is not intended for the sake of expiation. (10–13)

When the fire is destroyed, the sacrifice performed there ceases, for its performance depends on that [fire] as its means; therefore, this [new fire] is extended [to it] as appropriate. (14) It is to be concluded by the fires alone, and not together with the constellations or seasons. This is an extension of the *ādhāna* (initial consecration), just as [the fires are established] not together with the constellations or seasons. (15) Therefore, the *anyādheya* (re-consecration) is primarily the *ādhāna* itself; otherwise, it is secondary. Likewise, the *punarādhāna* (re-establishment) is distinct from the occasional (*naimittika*) rite, since it is prescribed as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and thus acquires those specific characteristics. (16)

Now, regarding expiations (*prāyaścitta*), where the name "re-establishment" (*punarādheya*) is heard, there the establishment for expiation possesses the characteristics of the re-establishment; whereas where the injunction is given by the name of the rite "establishment of the fires" (*agnyādheya*), the establishment for expiation possesses the characteristics of the establishment of the fires. Thus, the distinction between the two injunctions is established by their respective names.

Where there is no specific name, such as "one should perform the re-establishment [of the fires]," and even where there is only a verb, the re-establishment of the fires is characterized by the same ritual rules as the original establishment, provided the word "again" (punar) is present due to the recognition [of the act]. However, when the word "again" is absent, it is understood from the statement "one should establish [the fires]" that it refers simply to an unmodified establishment; thus, the rule is that the re-establishment of the fires possesses those specific characteristics. Let us return to the subject at hand: Rohiṇī, Punarvasū, and Anūrādhā are the lunar mansions for the re-establishment of the fires.

The re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*) occurs only under these lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and not otherwise. However, there is no such restriction for the establishment of the fires as an expiation (*prāyaścittādheya*), because it is performed immediately after the occasion (*nimitta*) arises. [This concludes] the sixth section. According to the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva: "One establishes the fires in the rainy season or in autumn; this sets aside spring and the other seasons. As stated by Baudhāyana: 'That new moon which occurs before the full moon of Āṣāḍha coincides with the Punarvasu asterism once every year.'"

"At midday" applies to all [the fires]. The previously mentioned time, beginning with "at sunrise" (*āditaḥ*), is set aside. The inclusion of the word "all" is so that what was stated by Āpastamba—namely, that the time may be according to one's convenience regarding the *gārhapatya* fire—should not apply to all [fires]; rather, the *ādhāna* (consecration) must take place at midday specifically, during the eighth *muhūrta*. This is either the middle of the fifteen-fold division, or the fifth, or the ninth.
The preparatory materials (*saṃbhāra*) may be either prepared or unprepared.

The meaning is that they are both prepared (*kṛta*) and unprepared (*akṛta*), and thus optional (*vikalpita*). In this regard, [the text states]: "The materials (*saṃbhāra*) are to be prepared by the Brāhmaṇa; no *yajus* formula is to be performed," and then again, "Indeed, the materials are to be prepared, and the *yajus* is to be performed. From this, the optionality of the *yajus* formulas is understood. This has been stated by Āpastamba: "The materials are both prepared and unprepared; the *yajus* formulas come into being [as options]. The *yajus* formulas are those such as "with fuel" (*yathāpūdhānena*) and so forth. In that context, when the position of the materials is adopted, the *yajus* formulas must indeed be performed.

When the materials (*saṃbhāra*) are not present, then the [ritual acts] enjoined by conjunction (*saṃniyogaśiṣṭa*) should not be performed; for according to the logical principle that there is either simultaneous engagement or simultaneous cessation, it has been explained by the followers of Āpastamba that the sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) begin with the fire-consecration (*adhāna*). However, the Vaikhānasa school holds: "The materials are not to be collected, or rather, the mantras for the materials do not exist"—thus, according to one view. The meaning is that in either case, there is an option regarding the mere sacrificial formula (*yajurmātra*).

The Teacher, however, did not state whether the *yajus* formulas are performed or not performed; by this, the Teacher indicates that the *yajus* formulas are the "preparatory materials" (*saṃbhāra*) which may be performed or not performed—the meaning being that they are for the sake of the *Brāhmaṇa*. Therefore, the established rule is accepted: they are to be performed when the preparatory materials are present, and not when they are absent. One should not ask: "Why was no effort made by the Teacher to prevent the performance of the *yajus* formulas when the preparatory materials are absent? [Because such a contingency does not arise.]

However, regarding the omission of the *dvāra*, it has already been stated in the *Parimāṣā* that there is no application of the *yajus*; thus, since the previously mentioned rule is established by itself, the Teacher has said nothing further concerning the subject of the *yajus*.

Regarding the Brāhmaṇa as well, he says that there is no performance of the *yajus* in the case where the preparatory materials (*saṃbhāra*) are absent; however, in another recensional branch (*śākhā*), it is stated that the materials need not be prepared and the *yajus* need not be performed. He states that even though the performance of the *yajus* is mentioned in that [other branch] despite the absence of materials, it does not exist there either due to the lack of materials. He asserts that [the rite] occurs only when the materials are present. The statement "the *yajus* must be performed" is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). Thus, the position of performing the *yajus* alone does not exist at all in either the Brāhmaṇa or the Sūtra.

Just as the *ādhāna* mantras and others are indeed combined even with the *sārparājñī* verses, so too, although the *ādhāna* mantras function as performance-mantras (*karaṇamantra*), their combination is established by the scriptural statement itself.
"He establishes the *gārhapatya* fire with all the *sārparājñī* verses.
This is an exception to what was stated regarding the first verse.
"Not so," is the addition. With *darbha* grasses that have been trimmed at the base and have been exposed to the wind for a year, he draws out the flaming *āhavanīya* fire from the *gārhapatya*.

In place of the *praṇayanīya* fuel, one should take darbha grass cut near the roots (*upamūla-lūna*), which has grown from the roots of previously cut darbha grass; these are dried for a year and exposed to the wind for a year. Having tied them into a handful, one should remove [the ashes] with that. For the sake of the ritual, the taking of other materials afterwards is not prohibited.
With the mantra, "What another, being angry, has scattered," he establishes the *dakṣiṇāgni*; with the mantra, "What of thee has been scattered by anger," he establishes the *āhavanīya*.

The purpose [of specifying] the second and third [verses] is solely as an exception (*apavāda*) to the first and last ones; it has already been stated that other mantras are indeed to be combined (*samuccīyante*). Regarding the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires, however, [the rule applies] according to their respective places, even in the duties of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
He worships the *āhavanīya* fire that has been established with the mantra "May the mind, like light, enjoy [the oblation]" (*mano jyotir juṣatām*).

According to Āpastamba, the Adhvaryu [worships] with the verse containing the word Bṛhaspati (*bṛhaspativatī*). Since, by the order of the recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), the attainment of the verse "May Bṛhaspati extend [the sacrifice]" (*bṛhaspatistanutām*) alone would follow, he did not specify [any other].
He kindles [the fire] again with the formula: "May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus kindle you again.

It ends with the word "desires" (*kāmāḥ*). He kindles it again with: "May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus kindle you again; may the Brahmins, O leader of wealth, [kindle you] again with sacrifices. Those offerings which were made at the dawns and at the sunsets—those *yājyā* verses I unite with the oblation of ghee, *svāhā*! With this he offers the first oblation. With "May the mind, the light, enjoy [the offering]" (*mano jyotirjuṣatām*), he offers the second.
This is the sixth [section].

Having cleansed the *juhū* and the *sruva*, and having filled the ladle with either four, eight, or twelve portions of clarified butter, he offers the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verse, "Seven are thy... (RV 10.53.6).

Fearing that the *pūrṇāhuti* might be redundant because of the two previous oblations, it is enjoined again by the Brāhmaṇa passage: "Seven are yours," namely, "Seven, O Agni, are your fuel-sticks; seven your tongues. Thus, one performs the *agnihotra*. Furthermore, while an option regarding the silent morning *agnihotra* is mentioned there for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*), here, however, there is indeed a repetition even of the morning *agnihotra*. All other duties pertaining to the sacrificer and the officiating priest (*ādhvaryava*) must be performed exactly as in the *agnyādheya*.
He offers a cake on eight potsherds or five potsherds dedicated to Agni in place of the eight-potsherd cake used in the *agnyādheya*.

But this [offering] belonging to the re-establishment of the sacred fires (paunarādheyika) is dedicated to Agni and has a distinct ritual procedure (atantra) from the Pavamāna offerings, because of its many differences and because the position that it constitutes a separate ritual procedure is also accepted. Everything for it is performed in a low voice (upāṃśu), up to the final after-offering (anūyāja).

As for those *nigadas* whose purpose is to direct others, by their very nature, everything else—both the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*)—is to be recited in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). The phrase "until the last" (*ā uttamāt*) indicates a limit. Now he states the specific rule regarding the *yājuṣa* *hautra*:

One should observe the *vṛdhanvat* formula in the recitations (*nigama*) of the *ājyabhāga* belonging to Agni:

[The offering] for the *pavamāna* [laud] of the *saumya* [cup].

He who establishes the fire after the time for the *punarādheya* has passed should offer these oblations: "Leka, Saleka, Suleka, Keta, Saketa, Suketa, Vivasvant, Aditi, Devajūti."

The phrase "parācīm" (once for all) is stated in order to indicate that one who establishes the sacred fires due to a cause such as the destruction of the forest [or the fire] does not do so because of a cause for re-establishment (*punarādheya*). The term "third" does not refer to the third *parvan* (section) of the ritual; rather, there are two primary types of fire-laying: the *agnyādhāna* and the *purādhāna*. Any other non-primary form of fire-laying, which is a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*) with prescribed characteristics (*atidiṣṭadharma*) performed as an expiatory fire-laying (*prāyaścittādhāna*) according to some specific rule, is called the "third."

The result is that these oblations are to be performed during its first, second, third, and subsequent applications. That is not so; for in the *Punarādheya-paribhāṣā*, he himself said: "Now, regarding this third establishment [of the fires], which of these two is appropriate: the initial establishment (*agnyādheya*) or the re-establishment (*punarādheya*)? Thus, both are accepted.

These oblations are to be understood as occurring before the *iṣṭakṛt* offering of the eight-pot-sherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) for each respective animal sacrifice. Āpastamba has also stated: "It is a re-establishment (*punarādheya*), according to Āśmarathya; it is an original establishment (*agnyādheya*), according to Ālekhana. These oblations should take place not only at the primary re-establishment, but also at the re-establishment by way of expiation (*prāyaścitta-punarādheya*). This is precisely what our teacher intends, because he prescribes [the rite] generally with the words, "one should establish the fires elsewhere than at the primary re-establishment."

"Are these *homās* also to be performed at the re-establishment (*punarādheya*) of the fires? No, this is not an injunction regarding an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) for the re-establishment, because it is stated [elsewhere] that "it is subsequent to the re-establishment. Well then, would this apply only to the original establishment (*ādhāna*) performed immediately after a re-establishment that was preceded by a formal abandonment (*utsarga*)? No; if the intended meaning of the phrase "subsequent to the re-establishment" were that, then it would simply be what was already stated by Baudhāyana. How so?

How is it that the third [fire], which is to be performed immediately after the *punarādheya* (re-establishment), is described as being distinct by way of a difference in its preceding cause (*pūrvanimitta*) when there is a second *punarādheya*, or likewise when there is a second *anyādheya* (initial establishment) following a *punarādheya*? Therefore, it is stated that the third is distinct from both the *agnyādheya* and the *punarādheya*. However, Baudhāyana, Āpastamba, and Vaikhānasa have stated right here—without any distinction in the ritual action—that it concludes as the third, merely to indicate a difference in the performance (*prayoga*).

Having said "yamā yam," it was stated by me that one proceeds with the *brahmaudana* for the seeker of fire (*āhitāgni*) alone. Thus [it is] in Kha. 'pratya| 2 kha. ca. chaṭavāditi | ta| - 7sa0 paṭalaḥ], accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 337.

"If one who has mounted the two fires should perish, or if both [fires] of someone should follow [him], or if they should set or rise again, there is either a re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya) or a new establishment of the fires (agnyādheya). Here, having prescribed a third [type of] fire-establishment as the mere act of *agnyādheya* independent of any specific cause or result, when the requirement arises as to what object this distinct rite (*karmāntara*) is to be performed for, the causes are stated by the passage beginning with "if the fire has been carried away," and by those very [causes], the distinction between the rites is made known.

However, since the Teacher has stated that in the event of a transgression of the rule, there must simply be a re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*), it appears that he does not consider this [rekindling] to be an alternative to the former in these circumstances. Nevertheless, according to another scripture, the mere establishment of the fires (*agnyādhāna*) is prescribed as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) by those causes alone, even without the specific name [of *punarādheya*]. In that case, either one of the two should be adopted; and that too is certainly acceptable to the Teacher. How so?

Thus, since the author [of the Sūtra] formulates the Brāhmaṇa rule by following the general restatement found in the section on expiatory re-consecration—namely, "one should consecrate the fire in the third way"—it is understood that the third re-consecration (*punarādheya*) is either a ritual similar to the original consecration (*agnyādheya*) or a distinct ritual altogether; in both cases, the oblations (*homāḥ*) are to be known as occurring in both instances. Otherwise, this third prescription for the consecration of fire would be rendered meaningless.

Therefore, this term "Punarādheya" (re-consecration) primarily denotes a re-establishment, and not [a mere rite] for a transgression of an injunction regarding the causes that will be mentioned later; for if it did not apply there, it would be entirely meaningless. Regarding the transgression of an injunction, this word is not a name [of a sacrifice], but rather the intended meaning of the term "Punarādheya" is that when these causes—namely, the destruction of the fires—occur, the fire must be produced again by means of this ritual act.

Furthermore, this cannot be a name for a separate ritual action in the third *ādhāna*; rather, it must be stated that it is like a re-installation (*punarādheya*). It is not the case that it is meaningful only through the previously mentioned sense; thus, there is nothing inconsistent.

From the time of the formal establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) until the end of one's life, the *gārhapatya* and *dakṣiṇāgni* are maintained, as are the *sabhya* and *āvasathya*. Regarding the *dakṣiṇāgni*, if it has gone out, there is the rule for churning; if it is produced by churning, it is established. If it is brought from elsewhere, it is brought for each specific purpose. One draws the *āhavanīya* fire from the *gārhapatya* for each respective purpose. It is maintained permanently by one who has attained prosperity, or by one desiring long life.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the third book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

Thus ends the third fire-installation (ādhāna). The section on the installation of the sacred fires (agnyādheya-prakaraṇa) is completed. [Thus ends the sixth chapter in the third book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra composed by Mahādeva.]

We shall explain the *agnihotra*.

That the term *agnihotra* is the name of a ritual action was determined by Jaimini in the rule: "And there is another scriptural passage that makes known that [action]" (*tatprakhyaṃ cānyaśāstram*). This is the promise to provide an exposition of it. Since many mantras are not found here in our own recension (*śākhā*), [there will be an exposition] of many ritual actions.
