This is a formal declaration (*pratijñā*) intended to demonstrate the sequence for the application of mantras according to the rule stated in the *paribhāṣā*: "In the case of silent (*tūṣṇīka*) rites, [the mantra] is that of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) rite. It has already been stated that immediately after the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), the *agnihotra* and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are obligatory.

In this context, the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices were explained previously as an introductory topic (*upoddhāta*), and the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires) has been explained; therefore, the *agnihotra*, whose turn has now arrived, is explained next. Considering that the attainment of the fruit of supreme bliss (*niḥśreyasa*) in the injunction for lifelong performance, and the attainment of heaven as the fruit in the injunction for those desiring heaven, have already been explained through the exposition of the two *darśapūrṇamāsa* injunctions, [the author] demonstrates only the practical application (*prayoga*). The specific distinction here is that the time for cessation is thirty days and so forth; [the performance occurs] at the evening and morning times.

The single performance (*prayoga*) for the *nivayaṃ* [offering] has already been shown as a type of commencement. Although Agni alone is the deity in the evening, nevertheless, since it is a single performance to be accomplished at both times, the morning *agnihotra* is also indeed the *agnaye hotram*—the offering of oblation to Agni; such is the nature of the rite because Agni is the primary deity. Even though Prajāpati is also a primary deity, there is no division of the ritual here due to the repetition of the oblations (*homābhyāsa*) in accordance with the two deities; nevertheless, because of his primacy, it belongs to Agni alone.

The *Nyāyadarśanasaṃgraha* states that [the name] is based on the occasion for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*). However, the teaching of one's own school (*svaśākhopadeśa*) proceeds by way of another method. For example, beginning with "Prajāpati created Agni," it provides an etymological derivation (*nirvacana*): "He gave this as his portion (*bhāgadheya*), namely the *agnihotra*; therefore it is called *agnihotra*. Thus, even though it was offered in the morning to Sūrya by means of that fire, it is not a non-*agnihotra*. Likewise, although Prajāpati is the second deity, it is still so named.

The term *agnihotra*—meaning "the offering (*hotra*) to Agni"—is applied here to the ritual as a whole, which is accomplished over two time-periods; or rather, because of its connection with that [offering], the specific term *darvihoma* is used figuratively even for the substance that serves as the means of accomplishment. This is because it is enjoined by the root *juhoti* (to sacrifice). Thus, the formal proposition is made to demonstrate that the complete rite, including its subsidiaries, is being defined here; therefore, those characteristics (*dharma*) belonging to the *darvihomas* do not apply to this case.

Therefore, those rites for which the specific details (*aṅga*) are not established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and other means are called *apūrva* (novel); their own ritual properties (*dharma*) will be explained first. They are termed *apūrva* because they lack a "prior" (*pūrva*) archetype (*prakṛti*) that would provide them with details through extended application (*atideśa*). This [rite] likewise does not require extended application, as its own properties are established by means of direct scriptural statement and other authorities; nor does it depend on the collection of ritual properties that are to be enjoined for the *apūrva* *dravyahoma* (substance-oblation) sacrifices through logical principles (*nyāya*) and detached injunctions (*anāramya-vidhi*).

Furthermore, the *prakṛti* (archetype) of this [Agnihotra] is the single Agnihotra; therefore, it is not a previously unknown (*apūrva*) ladle-offering (*darvihoma*). Since the word "offering" (*homa*) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for that which is prescribed by an injunction lacking specific subsidiary details (*aṅga*), it should be understood that the application of the term "ladle-offering" (*darvihoma*) to the Agnihotra is figurative (*gauṇa*). Here too, the formulation of the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is as before: having resolved, "Desiring heaven, I shall perform the Agnihotra in the evening and in the morning," it is heard in scripture that there is "one officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) for the sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*) of the Agnihotra"; because it is prescribed in the Yajurveda, the Adhvaryu alone is the priest.
Since another Sūtra states that "one may offer the oblation oneself," the self-offering is not merely for times of distress, but is indeed the primary rule.
For that purpose, he draws the Āhavanīya fire from the Gārhapatya every evening and morning while it is blazing.

Therefore, although the drawing out [of the fire] for the purpose of the *agnihotra* rite has already been established, it is restated here for the sake of prescribing a specific quality (*guṇavidhi*). The quality prescribed is that one should draw out the fire while it is indeed blazing at both times. Even by others, having kindled the *gārhapatya* with fuel-sticks, one should separate a portion while it is still blazing into a vessel; this is stated as the *āhavanīya* because of the rule for its constant maintenance as the *dakṣiṇāgni*.

Since it is a general rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "the time of the principal [rite] is the time of its subsidiaries," he states an exception to that: [This concludes] the sixth section (*paṭala*) of the *Mahādevakṛtavaijayantī* commentary.

"At the time when the sun is above the trees" means for the evening *agnihotra*, and "at dawn" means for the morning *agnihotra*. The term "he takes out [the fire]" (*uddharati*) is carried over [from the previous rule]. Because of its connection with two times, there are two names. The meaning is that the taking out of the fires for the primary rite along with its subsidiaries must occur at a time prior to the [specific] time [of the sun's rising or setting], namely, when the sun has neither risen nor set. "Above the trees" (*adhivṛkṣa*) refers to the time when the sun stands over the trees; at that time, one takes out the fire for the sake of the evening *agnihotra*, and likewise at dawn for the sake of the morning *agnihotra*. Even though the offering might take place immediately after sunrise, the taking out of the fire should be understood as occurring at dawn; the same should be understood for the evening.

The Vaikhānasa, however, says that one should kindle the fire in the evening when the sun is behind the trees, or when it has half-set, and in the morning before sunrise. Kātyāyana, on the other hand, says it should be done when the sun has neither set nor risen. Even that [time] should be accepted if the others are not possible. Regarding the statement "one should kindle in the morning for the sake of the Agnihotra," the word *uṣas* is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the Agnihotra that is heard to be performed at dawn.
Or, they may maintain the fire at night.

The sacrificer, his wife, or another may draw out the fire in the evening for the sake of the morning *agnihotra*; the plural number used at the outset is intended to express this possibility. This drawing out of the fire does not apply to the permanently maintained fire (*dhārya*), nor to that drawn out for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; furthermore, it should be understood that this applies even when the *darśapūrṇamāsa* have not been completed, as well as in the *paśubandha* and modified *iṣṭi* sacrifices. This has already been explained previously.

When the command "Lift him up! has been issued, [he says]: "With speech as the Hotṛ, with breath as the Udgātṛ, with the eye as the Adhvaryu, with the mind as the Brahman, and with the ear as the Āgnīdhra—with these five divine officiating priests (ṛtvij) I lift you up. I abandon death; I establish you with immortality. Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! Being lifted up, lift me out from evil—whatever I have done unknowingly and whatever I have done knowingly; from whatever sin has been committed by day, being lifted up, release me from all of that. Thus at evening.

The word "extracts" (*uddharati*) is to be supplied [from the previous context]. In the *Yājamāna* section, it is stated that one should recite the mantra "extract" (*uddhara*) while the fire is being extracted; this is because of the scriptural statement that the mantra is for the fire "being extracted" (*udbhriyamāṇa*) once the act of extraction has commenced. Furthermore, in this [other] passage, it is stated that the priest who has been directed extracts the fire, and there the mantra contains the word "extract" (*uddhara*). Since the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra suggests a prior time, it is appropriate—by means of the rule *vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavat* ("when there is proximity to the present, the present tense may be used")—to accept the meaning as "about to be extracted. The sense is: "having aimed at such [a fire]."

It has been stated that [the priest] is dispatched by means of the words of the *anumantraṇa* (consecratory formula). In that regard, the purpose is that even in the case of an oblation (*homa*), there may be a dispatch by means of the *anumantraṇa*, so that even when [the sacrificer] is not present, he should perform the act only after it has been consecrated by another [priest] through the dispatch. Alternatively, the meaning is that he addresses [the fire] with a mantra while looking toward the sacrificial butter (*ājya*) which has begun to flow by the throwing of wood and other materials; thus he "dispatches" (*preṣati*). This very term *anumantrayati* is seen in the revealed scripture (*śruti*), and it is that same term which is here restated. In the morning, [he says]: "Whatever sin or evil has been committed during the night, release us from all of that."

The ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) extends from "with speech" (*vācā tu*) up to "he has done" (*cakāra*), and also includes the phrase "he draws out" (*uddharati*). [Sūtra 340: "I offer the immortal oblation into the immortal; I offer Agni upon the earth for the winning of immortality. Through that, I win the infinite desire which Prajāpati first won—Agni in Agni, Svāhā! With these words, he establishes [the fire] in its western place of rest (*āyatana*) in the evening.
At the site of the Āhavanīya fire: "To Sūrya in Agni, svāhā!"—this is for the morning.

The phrase beginning with "an oblation of immortality" and ending with "he has conquered" is to be supplied as an *anuṣaṅga* (elliptical extension). And there is also the statement, "he establishes [the fire]. Other sūtras also state that one faces east in the morning and west in the evening. Regarding the option of maintaining the fire at night, the mantras for the lifting of the fire apply only to the evening, because the lifting is an ancillary (*aṅga*) solely to the evening oblation; therefore, what was lifted for that purpose is maintained at night according to the rule, since the time for lifting is superseded here by the morning [maintenance], just like one's own obligatory daily maintenance.

When the sun has first set, he performs the evening *agnihotra*; or when the stars have appeared, at the beginning of night; or at dawn for the morning *agnihotra*, either before sunrise or after sunrise. According to some, it should be offered at the moment when speech begins to sound.

The time for extraction (*uddharaṇa*) was stated previously; by this [verse], another time for the fire-oblation (*homakāla*) is shown. From this it is understood that there is no fault even if a pause occurs in the interim during the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsti*). Regarding "the first setting" (*prathamāstamaya*), one performs the evening *agnihotra* either immediately after the sun has disappeared, or upon the appearance of the stars, or at nightfall (*pradoṣa*) consisting of two *ghaṭikās*, or at the beginning of the night; all three types of time refer specifically to the evening.

Likewise, the morning time (*prātaḥkāla*) is threefold: two *ghaṭikās* before sunrise, or immediately before sunrise, or after sunrise. Regarding that, some followers of particular *śākhās* maintain that the morning *agnihotra* should be offered when birds begin to call or when they become visible. Vaikhānasa, Āśvalāyana, and others hold that the evening [sacrifice] ends at *pradoṣa* and the morning [sacrifice] ends at *saṃgava*. In this regard, if the commencement occurs before sunrise and the sunrise happens during the middle of the offering, then because an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is observed, two distinct times have been stated; however, there is no fault even if there is an overlap in other alternative views.

Although the word *prātaḥ* (morning) is conventionally established as referring to the first division of the day, and thus applies as a causal factor in the expression *prātar agnihotram* (the morning Agnihotra), nevertheless, because it is conventionally established in scriptural injunctions prescribing specific times—such as *upasi purodayam* (before sunrise)—other times distinct from the conventional morning are also prescribed; these too are indicated by the word *prātaḥ* through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) due to their proximity. The same should be understood regarding the word *sāyam* (evening), which denotes the final portion of the day. There is no fault here, as the prescription of various distinct times follows the authority of the revealed scripture (*śruti*). During this time, all rites are performed, except for the act of lifting [the fire].

It has been stated that for each of these [subsidiaries], the time of the primary rite is their own time; nevertheless, because an expiation is prescribed for its rising and setting even when it has not been extracted, one must observe only one specific time among the various times mentioned for the subsidiaries of the Agnihotra. Those [subsidiaries] should be performed at that very same time, rather than having a separation such as some subsidiaries being performed at one time among the times for the oblation and the primary rite at another; thus, this demonstrates the various times established by various scriptural injunctions.

The extraction established by this sūtra, based on the aforementioned principle, is restricted to the preceding times alone. Here, the sacrificer enters the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) with the mantra "viśvadānīm. With the mantra "yad anna," he places a large fuel-stick (*idhma*) on the Āhavanīya fire, and with the following [mantra], on the Gārhapatya; likewise elsewhere. On the Śālāmukhīya and Āvasathya fires, it is done silently. Having touched water with the mantra "vidyud asi," and having passed to the south behind the Āhavanīya, he sits down in his own place, as does the wife in her own place. Then the Adhvaryu:

He makes the fires pure by sweeping them around: "O Agni, lord of the house, be purified," for the Gārhapatya; "O Agni, bearer, be purified," for the Dakṣiṇāgni; "O Agni, sovereign, be purified," for the Āhavanīya.

Having sprinkled [water] all around with the hand, *parisamūhana* consists of removing grass and the like and making [the ground] smooth; one then adorns the fires thus characterized with flowers and other offerings. As stated by Vaikhānasa: "One adorns the fires by means of sprinkling around (*paryukṣaṇa*), sweeping around (*parisamūhana*), and providing flowers (*paripuṣpakaraṇa*). The acts of sprinkling around and so forth should be completed once for each fire with the mantra.

The entire process, beginning with the sweeping (*parisamūhana*) and so forth, is indeed an act of adornment (*alaṃkaraṇa*). Thus, the mantra is connected with the primary act of adornment; or else, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the word "be purified" (*śundhasva*), the mantra applies to the sweeping immediately following the sprinkling (*paryukṣaṇa*), while the adornment—the removal of impurity—is performed silently. This shows that the two acts constitute a single unit (*ekāpavargatā*), as indicated by the instrumental case ending. "Adornments before" refers to the evening rite; "adornments after" refers to the morning rite. The phrase "they occur" is to be supplied. "After" means at the conclusion of the oblation (*homa*) ritual.
Some authorities enumerate ornaments for both [the bride and the groom].
In this view, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of what was previously stated according to their respective positions.
For example: "He strews grass around the fires with *darbha* blades, as in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices."
The meaning is clear.

He sets out the implements for the Agnihotra: a sruva-spoon made of khadira wood, an agnihotra-havani ladle made of vikaṅkata wood, which is without wheels or spiral markings, not fashioned by a śūdra, and with its bowl turned upwards; and the agnihotra-sthālī pot.

The phrase "the vessels for the *agnihotra*" is stated in order to indicate that these are distinct from the vessels used for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. The *sruva* and *agnihotra-havaṇī* have already been explained. "Not having a whorl" means that there is no circular turning (*bhramaṇa*) produced by a potter's wheel; thus, the meaning is that it must be made by someone other than a *śūdra*, namely by one of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). "Having broad rims" means that its potsherds (*kapāla*) are wide at their edges. Such is the earthenware vessel (*sthālī*) which serves as the receptacle for the *agnihotra* materials. These three [items] are mentioned; there is no rule regarding their pairing (*dvandva*), as that is determined by the specific ritual context (*vaiṣṭika*).

In this case as well, the phrase "as in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices" is to be understood as applying here. Thus, there is a *dvaṃdva* (copulative) compound consisting of the *sruva* spoon, the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle, and one [other] vessel. However, the Vaikhānasa says that he places a grass-bunch (*kūrca*) to the north of the *gārhapatya* fire. To the south of the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), the cow stands ready; she has been brought there even before the commencement of the *homa*. *Vihāra* refers to the place where the fires have been spread out. By the use of the suffix *enap*, it is stated that she is not far from the *vihāra*. Kātyāyana says she should be with a male calf. [This concludes] the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [Book] 3, [Chapter] 1.342.
"O Iḍā, come! O Aditi, come! O Sarasvatī, come! O Gauḥ, come! Having thus called her, he brings the calf near with the formula, "Thou art Pūṣan," or he addresses it as it runs.

The statement that he calls her when she has stood still is merely for the sake of the ritual rule (*dharmamātra*). He brings it near, meaning he joins it with the cow. Whether the calf is released [to the cow] or running, he addresses it with "Thou art Pūṣan.
Turning toward the east or the north, someone other than a Śūdra milks her; he does not touch her, or he follows her as she is perceived.

Having separated the calf from a Śūdra [cow], a member of any of the other three castes (trivarṇika), standing facing a cardinal direction, turns to the right and places [the cow] facing either east or north, and then milks her. He does not touch [the udder] with his hand for the sake of causing the milk to flow, nor does he touch it below. A total prohibition against touching is not appropriate because it is impossible; therefore, having touched the teats according to the rule so that the milk may be obtained, he milks. In this regard, it is restricted: if he touches for the purpose of making the milk flow, then he touches only the teats, from the base of the teat down to its edge.

One should milk the two front teats for the eldest son of the eldest wife (*jyaiṣṭhineya*), or for one who has already attained prosperity; one should milk the two rear teats for the youngest son of the youngest wife (*kāniṣṭhineya*), or for one who desires to prosper. This rule is occasional (*naimittika*). The rest has been explained. This [alternative] is optional (*kāmya*) for one who might desire prosperity. Having milked into a vessel, he pours it into a pot, or he milks directly into the pot.
Regarding the milking, [the milk] may be in the milking vessel or in the *agnihotra-sthālī*. Kātyāyana and others maintain that one should bring that milk to the east of the Āhavanīya fire.
For one desiring cattle, one should offer with the milk of two cows: having placed the first on the fire, one should bring the second. 16.
For a sacrificer who desires cattle, one should place the milk previously milked upon the embers and then bring the *payasyā* (curd-mixture) after another [cow] has been milked.
He sprinkles it in the evening with the formula, "I sprinkle thee, the Ṛta, with the Satya," and in the morning with, "I sprinkle thee, the Satya, with the Ṛta.
He sprinkles it with water while moving clockwise.

Having sprinkled water around the Āhavanīya fire, [he sprinkles] the Gārhapatya; then the Dakṣiṇāgni. Or, having sprinkled water around the Gārhapatya, [he sprinkles] the Dakṣiṇāgni; then the Āhavanīya. Because the scriptural injunction is identical, there is an option; the word "or" (*vā*) occurring in the scripture has been restated here. At the end, [he sprinkles] the two fires, the Āvasathya and the Gārhapatya. With the formula, "Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; for the continuity of the sacrifice I lead thee; for the continuity of the sacrifice thee," he causes a continuous stream of water to flow from the Gārhapatya to the Āhavanīya.

Having established the boundary at the *āhavanīya* fire and starting from the *gārhapatya*, he pours an unbroken stream of water. This serves as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*). Taking the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick) with the formula, "Thou art the bold one," he removes the embers from the *gārhapatya* toward the north with the formula, "The conquered fear of the people, together with that which we hate—be ye established for well-being. The *upaveṣa* is a wooden tool for removing embers; by means of it, he causes them to exit from the northern hearth.
"O you who are made by the elements, O abode, the sixfold danger arising from men—along with that, [drive away] whomsoever we hate," or so it is said.
At the time of removal, the mantra is used optionally.
He makes them end in *vyant*.

"From the end of the hearth, therefore, he removes the embers"—the meaning is that he causes them to go out from the location of the *gārhapatya* fire. "The footprint of *iḍā*, rich in ghee, moving and unmoving; O Jātavedas, enjoy this oblation! May there be delight here for those seven domestic animals of all forms, and may there be nourishment!"—with these words, he places the *agnihotra* material upon them.
By implication, he places the substance related to the *agnihotra* which is contained in the *agnihotra-sthālī* (the *agnihotra* pot) upon those embers.
It should be offered while still bubbling.

"While still bubbling" means that immediately after milking, having brought it over as if with foam, and just as soon as it has been placed on the fire, it should be offered by means of pouring out [the butter] and so forth.
Alternatively, immediately after placing it on the fire, he lights a blade of grass and gazes at it, saying: "May I rise up with offspring and cattle."

Alternatively, the term *saṃskāra* (preparation) refers specifically to the act of placing [the vessel] on the fire. Therefore, having bent down, one observes the substance contained in the pot by means of the light of the blazing grass. However, in the case of the rule "it should be offered after it has been ignited from the *Āhavanīya* fire and immediately thereafter abandoned," there is no such observation and so forth.
One sprinkles water with the *sruva* ladle, saying either "May I not lose your heat" or "You are immortality.
The word *sruveṇa* is used for the purpose of excluding the hand or other vessels, while the word *adbhiḥ* (with water) is stated for the purpose of excluding even a mere drop.
It is to be sprinkled with the water used for washing the *godohana* vessel; it is to be sprinkled with a single drop.

For one desiring cattle—that is, for a sacrificer desiring cattle—it is to be sprinkled with that very water by which the *godohana* vessel was washed (*saṃnijyate*). It is to be sprinkled with that single drop; thus it is "sprinkled" for one desiring cattle, and not with [ordinary] water. The meaning is that even a single drop is sufficient, and this alone is what is required. As for the mantra, it is either one of the two previously mentioned.
It is not to be sprinkled for one desiring splendor, nor for one practicing sorcery, nor for one wishing to cross over [a difficulty].

Even for one who desires to extinguish the fire by means of water, weapons, or other such methods; likewise for one desiring *abhicāra* (sorcery); and likewise for a sacrificer who, having crossed over, desires to transcend evil and other undesirable things while still embodied—for all such persons, it remains as before, unextinguished. Regarding the one who might desire, "May a hero be born in my kingdom," he looks at it again just as he did previously. *Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa*, Satyāṣāḍha’s *Śrautasūtra*, Third Praśna—Section 344.

"This is the king's desire: 'May a hero, a Kṣatriya alone, be born in my kingdom. Because this desire has arisen, he looks again, meaning he constantly observes with the light of the grass-blade. These desirable rites are to be performed by the sacrificer once the resolve (saṃkalpa) has been made.
He carries fire around [the victim] three times with a firebrand, [reciting] either "antaritaṃ rakṣaḥ" or "parivājapatiḥ.

First, that very Yajus-mantra is recited as found in the Agnihotra section; secondly, there is the taking from all the Gārhapatya fires and the offering into the Gārhapatya—these are the purificatory acts (saṃskāra). The meaning is already explained."
"Thou art heat, bestowing increase of wealth; grant vigor here," saying this, he moves the vessel toward the north while making a path.
Drawing [the fire] slightly toward the north among the *bhakāra* syllables, he brings the pot forward.
"Grant me progeny," saying this at the end, he holds it steady.

He stabilizes [the embers] in front of the edge of the fire-wood; then, the establishment of the embers from the outside is performed silently. He pushes back the embers at the *gārhapatya* with the formula, "The danger from kinsmen has been warded off along with him whom we hate; may he make it well-being. [This is done] for the sake of the creator of beings, or for the sake of the grain of the sacrificer.
"Pushes back" means he brings them together.

Having taken up the *sruva* ladle and the *agnihotrahavaṇī* spoon with the mantra "devasya tvā" (VS 1.6), ending with "ādade" (I take you). There is a repetition [of the action] when there is a plurality of substances, because of the singular number [in the mantra].
He heats them over the *āhavanīya* or the *gārhapatya* fire with the mantra "pratyuṣṭam" (VS 1.7).
The statement is completed, ending with the word "rakṣa.
[He cleanses] the *agnihotrahavaṇī* with the formula: "Thee, the well-winged one, made of good wings; thou art a golden staff, with branches of immortality; thou art the stream of sacrifices.
The cleansing of the cavity with the hand serves a visible purpose; likewise, the repetition continues as long as the dust within the cavity has not fallen away.

Both the sacrificer and his wife are *ariṣṭa* (unharmed). Thus, taking both together with the right hand, placing one by one in the left, and holding them with the right until the pouring out (*unnayana*), there is no relinquishing. "Both" refers to a single entity consisting of two parts; therefore, even though the actions are distinct, there is no repetition of the mantra. [End of section]. [This concludes] the sixth chapter of the *Mahādevakṛtavaijayantī* commentary. 345.
"In the evening, he addresses [the sacrificer], saying: 'Om, I shall draw up the oblation for the gods; [may I] draw the sacrificer away from evil.

Since the term 'impulse' (prasava) refers to the sacrificer, the meaning is that he addresses the sacrificer, saying: 'O Sacrificer, do you draw it up. In the morning, he says: 'Om, I draw up the oblation for the gods; [may I] draw the sacrificer away from evil.'"

The word "addresses" (āmantrayate) is drawn in [from the previous context]. When about to depart, one should say "Oṃ, lift up! to oneself alone; that is, the Adhvaryu himself should speak to himself while the sacrificer is departing. Likewise, by that same logic, it is established that even in the case of a self-offering (*svayaṃ-homa*), one speaks to oneself. Thus, when the performer of the action intended by the command is not otherwise specified, this very principle applies, as has been shown by us previously in various instances. Furthermore, the formula beginning with "the oblation of the gods" (*havir devānām*) impels the sacrificer.

"I draw you up for Agni and for the Earth; I draw you up for Vāta and for the Atmosphere; I draw you up for Sūrya and for Heaven; I draw you up for the Waters and for the Plants"—with these words he draws up four ladlefuls; for one who offers five portions, he does so twice with the last formula.

Since there is a single application (*viniyoga*) by means of a single formula (*ekena itikaraṇena*), it would follow that there is only one mantra; however, because of the statement "with the last one" (*uttamena*), there is a plurality of mantras. The substances are measured out with the *sruva* spoon; for each of those, one should draw up [the butter] with each individual mantra—thus making four in number. "Drawing up" (*unnayana*) means bringing upwards from what has been filled, until it reaches the end of the transfer. Thus, because it has two objects, one draws up—that is, transfers—the *sruva*; the mantra is used at the commencement of the action. This is done with the last mantra: "And from the fire, and from the plants, I draw thee up. For those who perform the five-fold division (*pañcāvattin*), there are the options: "Abundant food (*iḍā*), earthly food, heavenly food, sacrificial food," or "blazing food."

The first four [drawings] are for the purpose of distributing among the four; the fifth, which follows later, is for the purpose of distribution among those who have turned back. With regard to whichever son the sacrificer should desire, "May I prosper through this one," he should draw it full for that son.
Among his sons, whichever son the sacrificer intends, thinking, "Through this one may I attain prosperity," for that son he should draw one ladle full and the others not full.
If he should desire, "May they all be equal," he should draw up all [the portions] equally;
that is to say, if he should desire, "May they all be similar. "Equally" means in equal, full measures.
He touches what has been drawn up with the *daśahotṛ* formula, or he does not touch it.
The formula *unnītaṃ jughutaṃ daśahotrā cittiḥ* is an option because its wording is identical to the other.

At evening, he touches the vessel from which the offering has been poured out with the formula: *sajūr devaiḥ sāyamyāvabhiḥ sāyamyāvāno mā devāḥ svasti saṃpādayantu paśubhiḥ saṃpṛcīya*; at morning, he does so with: *sajūr devaiḥ prātaryāvabhiḥ prātaryāvāṇo mā devāḥ svasti saṃpādayantu paśubhiḥ saṃpṛcīya*. (Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Third Praśna).
The phrase "and touching the vessel that has been filled" (*unnīta-sthālīm abhimṛśati*) is connected to both instances.
Wherever he pours out [the oblation] with the words "May you grant me cattle" (*paśūn me yaccha*), there he places it down;

wherever he has poured it out, right there he places it down. This was stated in this way to indicate that it is not placed in another location, but rather in the vicinity of the place where the pouring took place.
Having brought it from the east or the north, he places it to the west of the Gārhapatya fire; so say some.

Having brought the *sruva* ladle from the place of pouring toward the eastern direction—meaning having led it there—and likewise [having brought] the *sruc* toward the north; behind the *gārhapatya* fire, near it (*upa*), there is an option. According to the *Vaikhānasa* and others, the placement is on a *kūrca* grass mat. Furthermore, since the *pitṛmedha* prescribes the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *upasādanīya* and *upāvaharaṇīya* *kūrca*s, these two should be understood as *kūrca*s.

It is understood from the two designations that for those two [kūrca-grass bundles], the first serves the purpose of placing [the ladle] in both cases, while the second is for the purpose of supporting the ladle-handle during its movement forward; or else, the first is for placing on the ground, while the second is for placing among the plants, as indicated by the specific injunction: "He places it among the plants. Thus, the Teacher provides two kūrca bundles.
Having taken a single fuel-stick of Palāśa wood, a span in length, or two or three, and having grasped them above the handle of the ladle—

The length of the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) is restricted to being one span (*prādeśa*) long. Consequently, in other cases, the measure of one cubit (*aratni*) or one span is subject to option. Holding [the ladle] above the handle, one or more [strokes] are made optionally.
With the formula, "Purify the atmosphere," he carries it level with the flame of the *gārhapatya* fire;
that is, he brings the ladle near to, or level with, the flame of the *gārhapatya* fire—this is the remainder of the sense.

First, while moving forward, he recites the *Daśahotṛ* formula; he should recite it word by word. Having stood up and moving eastward—meaning while proceeding toward the eastern direction—he takes the *kūrca* grass-bundle and, having brought it near the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), he should then utter the *Daśahotṛ*. By the use of the present participle (*śatṛ*), the simultaneity of the mantra-recitation and the movement is indicated. He carries [the fire] from the *Gārhapatya* to the *Āhavanīya*. According to Kātyāyana, he holds it at the level of his mouth.
At the middle point, he stops it with the formula: "For Agni Vaiśvānara, thee."

The *madhyadeśa* (middle region) refers to the space between the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires; in that very region of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), he "holds it down," meaning he makes it low, restrained, and firm.
With the words "For the wind, thee! (*vātāya tvā*), he lifts it up, performing a slight upward movement from the point where it was held down.
[The mantras] *pa. u. ja. jha. na.* [read as *prācīṃ vā pāhaty apa*]. [The mantras] *pa. i. ja. ma. ma. da.* [read as *prāhuḥ*]. [End of] Chapter 7.
[With the mantra] *āyur me yaccha*, he places [the Agnihotra vessel] to the west of the Āhavanīya fire upon the plants.

The plants are Darbha grass; they are arranged in the form of a *kūrca* (a bundle of grass), and he places it upon them. This is clear. He places the first Agnihotra with the *Vyāhṛtis*. And at the end of the year, the morning Agnihotra is also [performed] with the *Vyāhṛtis*.

With the words, "This is your fuel-stick, O Agni," he places a fuel-stick [on the fire], ending with the word "pyāyatām" (may it swell). Baudhāyana says it should be placed in the middle of the Āhavanīya fire. However, two fuel-sticks are for the purpose of consecrating the *nūkt* (the verse); no other purpose for them has been stated.

"Golden indeed is your beam, the bridge for ascending to the heavenly world," he says; or, "These are his Sūdadohas verses. Or, "Silver indeed are you, with gold within, Agni by means of light, luminous, leading to heaven, a cow of plenty, imperishable for the sake of imperishability, for attainment, pervasion, complete attainment, for the fulfillment of desires, for the heavenly world, for immortality—place me this brick, the Night. Thus at evening. "Tawny indeed are you, with silver within, Sūrya by means of light, luminous, leading to heaven..."

"In the morning, he places the brick with the formula: 'The wish-granting, inexhaustible one—for the sake of non-exhaustion, for attainment, for pervasion, for completion, for desire, for the heavenly world, and for immortality—I place thee.

With the mantra 'This is thine,' these two [bricks] are subject to the same option; with 'These are thine,' two others are established separately. Some authors of Sūtras say that these two are optional (kāmya). Having touched water with the formula, 'Thou art lightning; drive away my evil; I approach the immortal truth; may faith be in me.'"
Having touched the water consecrated by the mantra, ending with the word "pāpmānam" (evil), which is recited in one's own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā*), there is an option.
When [the fire] is smoky (*śyāva*), then he offers into it when it is blazing;
"smoky" means dark-grey, at which time it is endowed with flames.

Or, when the flame has subsided and it seems to flicker, then one offers; this is an alternative to the previous [rule]. One view is that it refers to when it is burning properly, dark-colored, and has not yet reached the state of being extinguished. The second view, however, is that it refers to the state when it is properly ignited and the flames have subsided, and afterwards the fire-tongue flickers slightly, emitting broken, intermittent sparks.
For one desiring a village, [the offering is made] when it is smoking.

For a sacrificer desiring a village, when the fire is smoking—that is, when it is pervaded by smoke—he offers an oblation into it; this is the syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*). He does so at dawn, placing the fuel-stick two finger-breadths from the root, without letting the drops run down over it.

The base is the lower end; from that point, starting from the base, for a distance of two finger-breadths in the middle, it causes the stream to flow. "He offers facing each [corner]," says Baudhāyana. The word "offers" (juhoti) connects with what precedes. Because of the expression "causing to flow," it is understood that this is done "with the mouth. Since pouring is generally accomplished by means of the mouth—as seen in the rule "pouring with the beak of a swan"—the statement "the others with the mouth" is also simply a general injunction. Having thus defined the procedure, he explains the two principal oblations accompanied by mantras:

*Hotrā bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā*—thus in the evening; *hotrā bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ sūryo jyotir jyotir sūryaḥ svāhā*—thus in the morning. The word "he offers" (*juhoti*) is understood [to apply here]. In this regard, the established rule is that the first oblation consists of four measured portions of food drawn out, the second is offered with the ladle (*sruva*) just as it is poured out, and the third is offered after having licked the residue from the ladle. Some authorities prescribe a combined offering (*saṃsṛṣṭahoma*).

The *saṃsṛṣṭahoma* (combined oblation) is an oblation offered to a combined deity by means of a mantra that designates both Agni and Sūrya as deities; some followers of other Vedic branches [perform] this. Although both [the combined and the separate oblations] are recited in our own branch, the word "some" is used for the sake of showing respect, as other followers of different branches prescribe only the *saṃsṛṣṭahoma*. Consequently, the *asaṃsṛṣṭahoma* (separate oblation) mentioned in our branch is cited merely for the purpose of censuring the practice of other branches, and not because there is an injunction for it [in our tradition]. Why?

For while there is an injunction for the *saṃsṛṣṭahoma* (mixed oblation) preceded by its praise and followed by the censure of the other, such is not the case with the *asaṃsṛṣṭahoma* (unmixed oblation); rather, only its injunction is restated from another recensional branch (*śākhā*). How is this known? It is known because [the text] does not praise that [unmixed oblation], nor does it enjoin the rule for the unmixed while censuring both the rule for the mixed and the unmixed; it certainly does not censure the mixed for the sake of enjoining it.

Thus, the intention of the author of the Sūtras is that the purpose in our own branch [of the Veda] lies solely in the prescription of the combined [offering]. Consequently, because both the prescribed offerings made at sunrise and those made before sunrise are seen to be enjoined—preceded by the praise of both through the mutual deprecation of each—there is no option; rather, there is an intent for both. He shows the combined deity-mantra: "Agni is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā" in the evening, and "Sūrya is light, light is Agni, svāhā" in the morning.

"He offers" (*juhoti*) is as explained previously. Here, according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, Agni alone is the deity, even in both types of mantras. They demonstrate that the sentences "He offers in the evening to this [Agni] and to Prajāpati" and "In the morning to Sūrya and to Prajāpati" constitute the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*). However, in the instruction of one's own school (*svaśākhopadeśa*), it is stated: "In the evening he offers to both; in the morning to both. Because this prescribes the deities in combination, the offerings are made with the formulas: "To Agni and Sūrya, this! and "To Sūrya and Agni, this!"

The ritualists, however, state that at dawn this is reversed for Agni Jyotis and Sūrya; this must be considered, since the Mīmāṃsakas have refuted the view that the deity is determined by the wording of the mantra.
He places [the vessel] among the plants with the words, "May it bestow luster upon me.
This is clear. [End of Section 15, Ja, Jha, Aṭha, Ḍha. [This concludes] the 790th Paṭala, together with the Vaijayantī commentary composed by Mahādeva.

Taking the smear from the medicinal herbs with the mantra, "From the herbs, [I take] the herbs; may you prosper," he wipes the smear onto the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) on the northern side. For the smear does not remain on the hand; therefore, having taken with his fingers that which has been smeared and which adheres to the fire-pans (*praṇālī*), he wipes that smear onto the sacrificial grass—the tuft (*kūrca*)—and as far as the northern part, thinking "upon the herbs. He wipes it low with his hand; he smears it. [The formula is: "To the herbs, this.
He gazes at the Gārhapatya fire with the mantra: "O Agni, Lord of the House, do not burn me; place immortality within me; may I attain offspring and light."
Vaikhānasa, Kātyāyana, and others maintain that "dakṣiṇāvṛt" means moving to the right; thus it is established that for us, this refers to the circumambulation to the right during sacrificial rites.
Having passed over [the first] silently, he offers a greater quantity of fuel-sticks on the northern one.

The word "oblation" (*āhuti*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Since it is enjoined by the root *hu* (to sacrifice), the formula *prajāpataye svāhā* would [otherwise] apply; however, since the *vyāhṛtis* are obtained from another recensional branch (*śākhā*), it is stated that this [second oblation] is "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*). And the deity is indeed Prajāpati alone, by virtue of the force of the injunction—this has already been demonstrated. Having passed over the location of the first oblation, some say that the second, which is greater—that is, more than—the first, is the "later" one, meaning it is in the later part; for that purpose, it is said to be "on the fuel-stick" (*samidhi*). According to another recensional branch, it is "on the northern half" (*uttarārdhe*) of the fuel-stick.

The fact that the fuel-sticks (*samidhaḥ*) have their tips pointing eastward and are placed in the middle is established by custom alone. Here, the ritual attendance (*upasthānam*) belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamānam*). Now, when a specific occasion arises, he shows the modification of the *Agnihotra* based on a particular quality:

"In harmony with Jātavedas, from heaven and from earth, enjoying this oblation of clarified butter, partake of it, Svāhā!"—with this [formula], one should offer with clarified butter (*ājyena*) at a place where Paśupati might afflict the cattle.

In whatever place—whether in the house, village, or kingdom of that sacrificer where Paśupati Rudra resides; or, alternatively, in the sense of the genitive case, "where" meaning "in whose [ownership]"—if he should afflict or cause pain to those animals such as cows, horses, and so forth, one should offer oblations of clarified butter for that sacrificer with this mantra at evening and morning. Even though it is a modified form of a ritual, because it is an Agnihotra, by that very act there is also the avoidance of the transgression incurred by not performing the obligatory daily rites. One should offer the oblation with the mantra: "O Agni, you of ill-disposed body, svāhā to the clarified butter," if he should neglect that [offering].

If, even after the *homa* has been performed, that [affliction] should cause excessive suffering, then one should offer oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) both morning and evening with this mantra; this is the specific rule.

One should offer oblations every evening for twelve nights if it should still strike him down. This means that if there is no pacification even by this much, one should perform the evening *homa* every single day using the aforementioned clarified butter with the mantra beginning "O Agni... (agnaye). However, the morning *homa* is to be performed with the original ritual substance (*dravya*).

1. Gha, ṅa, ja, jha, ña, ḍha: *patyam* for *pratyave*. 2. Gha, ṅa, ja, jha, ña, ḍha: *'heti ghṛtasya ju* (omission). 3. Gha, ru, ja, jha, ña: *'śañchamāyata*; ḍha: *'śūmachamayet*. 4. One should offer two oblations with milk; having first placed [the vessel] over the fire, one should pour in the latter. If that [milk] should overflow, [one should perform the following]. This concludes the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [Book] 3, [Third Praśna], section 350.

One should first bring the milk from the eastern [cow] and then subsequently bring the milk from the northern [cow], the second one, once it has been placed on the fire. The cause [for this] is as before; it is not to be disregarded.

Even beyond this, one should strike that [milk], and this disregard is not to be ignored; it is not to be done again, but rather according to the fixed rule alone. For a Kṣatriya, the Agnihotra is only on the Parvan days; it should be understood that for him, the occasional (naimittika) rite occurs on non-Parvan days. Thus, having completed the occasional rite as recorded in another Śākhā within the Agnihotra section, he states the original (prakṛta) procedure:

With the words "For food, thee," he wipes away the smear in the evening; without taking it up, he causes the smear that has reached the water-channel to flow out. With the words "For strength, thee," he wipes upwards in the morning.
Starting from the nest, it is as before.
If one should desire of someone, "May he become more wretched," one should first offer a larger portion for him and then offer a smaller portion later.
This is a deprecatory explanatory passage (arthavāda) for the purpose of indicating that one should not offer the second oblation in a smaller measure than the first oblation.
If one should desire of someone, "May he be neither worse nor better," one should offer for him equally.
This has indeed been stated as a censure; for there is no officiating priest (*adhvaryu*) who does not desire the welfare of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Therefore, it is indeed a censure.
If one should desire of someone, "May he become wealthier," one should first offer a smaller portion for him and then offer a larger portion subsequently.

This is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the sake of commendation, as there is no other way to perform the obligatory rite (*nityakalpa*). These explanatory praises are taught for the purpose of understanding the ritual action and the knowledge [required]. The terms "less" (*kanīyaḥ*) and "more" (*bhūyaḥ*) are qualifiers of the substance or qualifiers of the action, since the [specific] offering under discussion (*prakṛta*) is impossible [in that context]. Alternatively, even if it is the third [type], the optional rite (*kāmyakalpa*) may apply when there is a desire.
He leaves over more for eating.

Because the second oblation is the subject under discussion, the additional [text] is intended only to exclude that. Indeed, two oblations are the motivators for the fourfold lifting; therefore, when they are destroyed by spilling or other causes at the completion of the rite, new material must certainly be produced. However, in the case of the destruction of the portion intended for consumption, there is no production [of new material]; rather, it has already been explained that there is merely the omission of the subsequent rites for the remnant. This very point is made known by the statement "he leaves a remainder. The meaning is not that one should produce a remnant for the sake of consumption, as an injunction; since the remnant is not yet fully accomplished, it is not something to be produced anew. If it exists... [the text continues].
This Sūtra exists prior to the *dvādaśarātri* Sūtra among the manuscript collections of Sūtras.

[Variants follow: 15. cha, ja, jha, na, ḍha: "She [performs] the evening *agnihotra*... 2. kha, ca, cha, da, na: [omission]. 6. na, ḍha: "'yārupāntyā'. 1. ka, ca, ṭa: 3. ṇa: "reṇāni. 3. pa, ja: 7th Paṭala, accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 351.

Only the disposal (*pratipatti*) is to be performed. As it was stated by Kātyāyana: "That which remains in the cooking pot (*sthālī*), a Brāhmaṇa should drink; a non-Brāhmaṇa should not drink that, according to the Śruti. Therefore, the disposal is prescribed for what remains in the ladle (*sruca*) alone, and not for what is in the pot. Thus, the setting aside of the remnant (*uccheṣaṇa-nidhāna*)—which is enjoined in the rule, "He sets aside the remnant of the Agnihotra for the purpose of curdling"—applies specifically to what is in the ladle, because that alone is the remnant of what was drawn up for the primary Agnihotra.
And thus says the Śruti of the Vājasaneyins: "That which he leaves over in the ladle is the remnant of the Agnihotra. Regarding that, there is an omission of the consumption when it is curdled.
Having offered the oblation, he should gaze at the Great One (Mahat).

The word "having offered" (*hutvā*) is stated for the purpose of ensuring there is no interval; it is intended so that [the wiping] occurs precisely before the wiping of the smearings, and not after the wiping from the place. If that were the case, why was it not stated right there? There is no fault here, as it is stated according to the sequence of the Vedic recitation (*śruti-pāṭha-krama*). Some say that "great" (*mahat*) refers to space (*ākāśa*) because of its pervasiveness; however, this would result in a merely visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) by observing an object not inherent to the ritual action (*karma-asamaveta-artha-avekṣaṇa*). Therefore, others say that "great" refers to what remains in abundance.

Furthermore, since there is no usage of the word *bhūyas* (more/abundant) remaining [after its application], how could it be designated by the word *mahat* (great)? The word *bhūyas* is a modification of the word *bahu* (much) and denotes a number of multiple mixed substances; the word *mahat*, however, denotes the dimension (*parimāṇa*) of a substance. Indeed, the word *bhūyas* is not appropriately applied to that which is denoted by the word *mahat*. Therefore, Brahman alone is what is expressed by the word *mahat*; it is to be meditated upon through the vision of pervasiveness, and for that very reason, it possesses neuter gender. This is because of its greatness (*bṛhattva*) and its capacity for expansion (*bṛṃhaṇatva*).

Indeed, the Self alone is Brahman. Thus, regarding the purification of the Self, since it serves as a purification of the agent, its purpose is seen in this world; furthermore, numerous purposes are accomplished—such as the offering to Brahman, expiation, and so forth—by virtue of the Self’s nature as Brahman and its status as the agent. This is the most excellent position. Accordingly, it has been stated by Vaikhānasa: "For the sake of consumption, one should perform [the rite] again; having consumed, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, the Infinite. According to the Śruti, "He who is indeed the Infinite," one should meditate upon the Self as Viṣṇu, the all-pervading.

"O Rudra, be gracious; O Arbha, be gracious; O Dhūrta, be gracious; homage be unto you, O Paśupati; do not harm me. With this mantra, he thrice moves the fire upward with the *sruk* ladle, causing it to sway.
The mantra is recited once, and twice silently. He causes the flame of the fire to move upward—that is, he impels or makes it tremble. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says, "He causes it to tremble twice.
Having set down the *sruk*, he takes up the residue (*lepa*).

Taking the smearings from the channel with his fingers, he wipes the smearings onto a mound to the south, saying: "For the ancestors, thee; gladden the ancestors. This place for the mound is on the southern part of the *sruk* ladle. The mention of a "mound" (*sthaṇḍila*) is so that it may not be understood as being on the grass-bundle (*kūrca*) as in the previous case. According to Vaikhānasa, [the wiping is done] with the hand held downward; according to Kātyāyana, with the hand turned upward.

Having touched water—this refers to the Vedic (śrauta) touching of water—he offers the oblation with the formula, "Thou art rain; rain away my evil," and touches water; for the Brāhmaṇa says, "Having offered, he touches. As for the additional formula from another recension (śākhā), "May I know my evil," it does not apply here because that which is additional has not been recited. Since it is recited in the section on the duties of the sacrificer (yājamāna), it is an option only there, not here, because that [additional part] has not yet been recited and is therefore not present to the mind. Having twice tasted [the remnant] with his finger while reciting, "Thou art Pūṣan," and having sipped water, he tastes again.

The substance remaining from the consumption [of the sacrificial food] is to be taken with any finger whatsoever, because the singularity of the qualifying attribute "one" is intended to be significant; however, Vaikhānasa and Kātyāyana specify it as the ring finger (*anāmikā*), which is also not contradictory. Having consumed [it]... 5.

Since the phrase "again at dawn" (*punaḥ prābhāti*) already establishes that there are two instances of eating, the explicit mention of "twice" (*dvis*) is for the purpose of indicating the repetition of the mantra. Regarding the two instances of eating, this same mantra is used for each; however, the mantra *garbhebhyas tvā* (as shown by Bhāradvāja) is not used for the second eating. Having taken [the food] with his finger and eaten right there, he sips water once (*ācamya*) to drink water, then goes outside and sips water again for the sake of purification. Then, having taken [the food] again and eaten it with the mantra, he goes outside and sips water for the sake of purification.

Since sipping water (*ācamana*) for the sake of purification is already established by *smṛti*, the sipping of water prescribed in the middle [of the rite] is not enjoined for the purpose of purification, as it is already obtained through *smṛti*. Therefore, only the drinking of water is enjoined as a constituent part of the ritual action. Furthermore, between the first eating and the drinking, the sipping of water for purification according to *smṛti* does not apply; however, this is because of the traditional rule that there is no impurity caused by food remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*) during the interval of the *prāṇāhuti* offerings. Nor should it be argued that even between the drinking of water and the second eating, the sipping of water for purification is not required.

Furthermore, since the water for drinking has risen up and cannot be touched with the remains [of food], one performs *ācamana* (sipping water) for the sake of purification; thereafter comes the second consumption. That which was taken with the finger and consumed with a mantra is indeed consecrated by that mantra; thus, there is a further mantra for the purpose of consuming that [finger-portion]. In this practice, making a sound and touching the teeth are prohibited by Āpastamba, Vaikhānasa, and Kātyāyana, and they are likewise not contradictory for us.
Having taken the *sruk* ladle and the *darbha* grass, he steps out toward the north.

They say that the *darbha* bundle (*kūrca*) serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*); therefore, one should obtain it, for [the ritual] will prescribe its washing with the tips (*daśaiḥ*). This implies that there are indeed *darbha* blades. However, according to Bāharadvāja, after stating "having taken hold with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)," he says, "he wipes the smearings on the *barhis*," and then states, "he throws the *barhis* after [the oblation] into the Āhavanīya fire. Since this mentions no throwing of the *kūrca* into the fire, [the *kūrca* must be distinct]. Furthermore, the placement of the medicinal herbs (*oṣadhīnām upasādana*) has been mentioned. From the word "then" (*atha*), it is understood that the *darbha* blades used for washing are indeed different [from those used as the *kūrca*].

Taking the *truca* (wooden spoon), he goes toward the northern direction, having placed the *vihāra* (fire-altar) behind him outside the monastery; however, turning back and placing the *vihāra* behind oneself is forbidden in the technical terminology (*paribhāṣā*), yet it is performed here because of this specific injunction.

[He recites: "May there be for me fiery seed, procreative, with ten heroes and a complete host, for my well-being. May it gain for me self, progeny, cattle, fearlessness, worlds, and rain. May Agni make my progeny abundant; may you bestow upon us food, milk, and seed. May he maintain for us the increase of wealth, nourishment, and vigor. (18)
With the *sruc* held either towards the east or towards the north, he sips water twice and licks [the vessel] twice.

Having drunk a little from the stream of the *sruc* once, when that has gone inside, he drinks again; then he tastes the *sruc* completely with his tongue. That too is done twice. As for the word "and" (*ca*), some teachers of the Sūtras say it is for the purpose of refuting various opinions—such as eating once and licking twice, or the reverse, or even once for both—and thus [the author] employs the word "twice" (*dvis*) to indicate that he sips exactly twice.

"He licks twice" means that the mantra is used for the first sipping of water, while the second is done silently. Since the substance already mixed [with the mouth] and subsequently removed is what is to be purified, there is no injunction for its separate removal by the fingers alone. According to the principle that "where there is one [act], [the mantra is used once]," the mantra is employed only once; the second licking is done silently. The mantra, having fulfilled its purpose by being connected with the primary meaning of the verbal root in the first instance, is not connected with another distinct act.

In this regard, since the *Smṛti* prohibits licking with the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle during the Kali age, the author of the Bhāṣya states that rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) with it is likewise prohibited; therefore, he specifies "with the hand. Consequently, if the entire quantity of *guggulu* cannot be taken up by the hand at once, then one should take it in another vessel, move away, and consume it—or lick it—by means of a stream [from that vessel]. The vessel must be made of a metal other than copper, because any other [copper] vessel is unfit for being used again after it has been defiled by remnants.

Alternatively, having taken [the offering] with the *sruva* ladle just enough to fill the hollow of his hand, and having sipped water twice, he licks his hand twice; here, having taken it with another vessel and moved away, he eats and licks it with his hand.
Or [he may offer it] with the formula, "For the embryos, thee! Make the embryos rejoice!
This is an alternative to the previous [method].

"In the morning, [the formula is]: 'May there be for me solar semen and procreation. This and the previous [formula] are optional; even in the morning, by this [statement], the reading 'solar' (saurya) is shown, and the reading 'Sūrya progeny' (sūryaḥ prajām) is also indicated. Bharadvāja, however, says that the *svāhā*-utterance exists in offerings and in the consumption [of the oblation], and thus it is another [view]; but that is not desired by the Teacher, because the injunction is prescribed only when prompted by the word *juhoti* (he offers). Thus, regarding substances other than milk, the mantra is simply 'for the embryos' (*garbhebhyaḥ*), as it does not require modification; therefore, there is an option between the two mantras for both the evening and the morning milk."

Having filled the *sruva* ladle with water, he pours it out [into the fire] with the formula, "For the serpents, thee; gladden the serpents. He discards the poured-out water on the ground to the north of the *Āhavanīya* fire. Because of the statement of Vaikhānasa, "He should release the water to the north of the *Āhavanīya* with the formula, 'Gladden those who partake of the remains,'" the filling and the discarding are performed from the *sruva* itself even when the consumption is done by hand. Furthermore, among the followers of Kātyāyana, the release of water from the *sruva* is observed even when the consumption is done using another vessel. Accordingly, following that *sūtra*, one should fill the *sruva* with water even when the consumption is done with another vessel or by hand. Then, having sipped water (*ācamya*).

Even though it is obtained through recollection (*smṛti*), lest it should occur prior to the filling [of the ladle], there is therefore a restrictive rule (*niyama*) that one should pour out the *sruva* ladle while still not having sipped water, and then sip water immediately after the consumption. Alternatively, just as there is a prohibition against licking, so too, if one were to assume a prohibition against touching the *sruva* with the remains of food (*ucchiṣṭa*), this very position [that one should sip water first] would be superior. Since the sipping of water prescribed by the author of the Sūtra occurs only after the initial pouring has taken place, it is not to be performed again because it has already occurred. However, if that [sipping] were based on Śruti, then it should be performed once more. Having washed the *sruva* with *darbha* grass...
The washing is done with water alone, but the removal of smears is done with *darbha* grass.
This sūtra begins from the sūtra "from the wombs" (*garbhebhyaḥ*) in the Sūtra-manuscripts.
45. Composed by Satyāṣāḍha, the Śrautasūtra—[in the third book].
Having filled [the vessel], he pours out water with the formula, "Quench the serpents, quench the ants.

The word *anu* (after) is drawn forward from the previous [formula]. He pours upwards and discards [the excess]; the word "water" (*apaḥ*) is used in order to express the pouring out of a portion already filled.
With the formula, "Quench the serpent-deities," he pours the second [portion]; with "To the beings thee," the third; and with "To the great gods," the fourth.

One should understand that "the second" (*dvitīyām*) and so forth refer to what one pours out; the water poured out is the object of the action. Furthermore, even the suffixes of completion (*pūraṇapratyaya*) function as qualifiers; thus, one should understand that first [one pours] what was previously poured out, then the second, and so on. For this very reason, Bharadvāja stated that "the first," "the second," and so forth, are indeed qualifiers of the action itself. Nor does [the word] connect with the phrase "having completed the second," even though that is being supplied by ellipsis (*anuṣajyamāna*).

If this were so, then one should not say "having again filled the ladle" (*srucam punaḥ pūrayitvā*) at the beginning; rather, one should simply say "the fifth time" (*pañcamīm eva*). Therefore, it is established that it is indeed the "filled one" (*pūritakā*) that is offered four times.

Having filled the ladle with water, he pours it out behind the Āhavanīya fire or behind the Gārhapatya fire, saying: "I offer nectar upon the earth, svāhā! He pours it out; he empties it; that is indeed half [of the offering].
"From the houses, may you satisfy the houses"—with this [formula], he pours a portion of it into the joined palms of his wife.
The phrase "he pours" is drawn forward [from later in the text]. A portion.
If the wife is not sitting beside him, he pours the whole onto the ground.

"He leads it away" is as explained previously. When she is not present because she is unable to touch [the fire] or because she does not believe in [the efficacy of] the ritual, another person says: "Lead this either to the *gārhapatya* fire or entirely from the houses to a second place; let it flow onto the earth itself. It is led away dedicated to the wives of the gods; in that case, the wife of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is the locus for the *añjali* (handful offering). However, when she has departed, there is no loss of the primary element [of the rite].

Nor is this a purificatory rite for the sacrificer’s wife, because there is no scriptural mention of her being second [to the sacrificer] or similar; for this very reason, there is no pouring out [of the water] by dividing it between the two. The connection is as follows: "If she does not stand by his side, he pours a portion into her joined palms (*añjali*); if she does not stand by his side, then [he pours] upon the earth"—meaning a portion of that [water] into the *añjali* of the wife, and if she does not stand by his side, then [the remainder] upon the earth.

The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of excluding the recurrence [of the act] through each individual wife, based on the principle that "other purposes may be accomplished by one. Lest it be thought that the application [of the rule] is restricted only to those acts performed for the sake of others (*parārtha*), and not to those performed for one's own sake (*svārtha*)—such as this rite which has an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*)—it is stated "all," so that the pouring out (*ninayana*) may be accomplished by even a single wife. Furthermore, the phrase "on the earth" (*pṛthivyām*) does not refer back to what was previously mentioned; rather, it is prescribed as a substitute for the water-offering made by the wife.

The meaning is that when the wife makes the añjali gesture, it is upon that earth which is below; Āpastamba, however, calls it the "station of the wife. This is also shown there, because the possibility of an option exists between the sacrificer and the gods. For us as well, even the station of the wife—which is established by the implication of the mantra-text—is presented by means of the word "earth. For this very reason, Bharadvāja says "twice upon the earth. From the use of the word "twice," it is understood that [the action] is performed in two places.

The ground is the subject under discussion; by another [text], it is the Gārhapatya fire; therefore, there is an option regarding the ground. Having heated the hand, he places the *sruk* [ladle] into it; or, having heated the *sruk*, he places it in his hand. With the formula, "For the Seven Seers, thee! Refresh the Seven Seers!", he points the *sruk* toward the north.

Because it will be stated later, "having returned to the *āhavanīya* for heating," Kātyāyana says: "Having heated the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles over the *āhavanīya*, he sets them down. He points toward the northern direction with his hand joined [to the ladle] and indicates it mentally.
Having set down the *sruk* and returned, he offers oblations with the *sruva* ladle into the *gārhapatya* and *dakṣiṇāgni* fires, adding fuel sticks after each oblation.

It has been stated that the phrase "with the *nuveṇa* ladle" serves to set aside the *jūḥ* obtained through its designation (*samākhyā*). Furthermore, the substance under discussion is that contained in the *sthālī* (cauldron), because as a remnant (*śeṣa*), it requires a final disposal (*pratipatti*). Regarding this, Bharadvāja says: "He offers from the remnant. Since the injunction regarding the substance is for the sake of the primary act, the two offerings in the *āhavanīya* fire constitute the primary rite; therefore, if the substance in the *sthālī* is destroyed, there is no re-production of it, but rather simply the absence of the offering in the other two fires—the *sabhya* and *āvasathya*. Indeed, there is no offering at all in those two fires in the absence of [the primary substance].

It is shown that if one should drink what remains from the *homa*, then he is indeed a *brāhmaṇa*. Although it is a *darvihoma* because it is enjoined by the root *hu* (to sacrifice), the phrase "for each oblation" (*pratyāhuti*) is stated for the purpose of excluding other ritual properties.

He offers two [oblations] into the *gārhapatya* fire with the mantra: "May the Lord of Nourishment bestow nourishment upon me; may he maintain for us wealth, prosperity, food, and vigor. To Agni Gṛhapati, Lord of Wealth, Lord of Cattle, Lord of Nourishment, [Lord] of Desire, [and Lord] of Edible Food—*svāhā*!";
the word "oblations" (*āhutī*) is understood as the remainder.
"O Lord of Food, give us food"—with these two verses, one should offer oblations into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.
Since this *ṛc* is enjoined by the term "juhoti," the offering is performed with the word "svāhā" at the end.
Alternatively, one may offer four oblations into the Gārhapatya fire and four into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.
The instruction regarding the teacher is intended to exclude [the performance of the rite] in a formal assembly hall or a private residence.
Or rather, one should not offer the oblation at all;
the absence of the original *juhoti* sacrifice is itself one alternative view.

"Agni has glowed; he has offered his own body. O Heaven and Earth, bestow vigor upon us! Having smeared a blade of grass with the *sthālī* (pot), he throws it into the *āhavanīya* fire, or he does not.

According to the Śruti, "He does not throw the *barhis* (sacrificial grass) into the fire. The throwing of the grass occurs only when the Agnihotra is performed at the conclusion of the sacrificer's life, and not otherwise, because of the statement: "This sacrifice is indeed uncompleted [if interrupted]. Furthermore, there is an option based on the Vājasaneyi Śruti: "He throws the *barhis* into the *āhavanīya*."
