In the middle of this place it is clear.
He sprinkles around as before; the meaning has already been explained.

He kindles [the fire] with the mantra: *dīdihi dīdyāsaṃ dīdidāmesi*. According to the Śruti, "Having offered, he kindles," when the oblation has been performed in one place, the kindling occurs right there; when the oblation is performed everywhere, the kindling occurs everywhere as well, just like the placing of the fuel-sticks (*idhmādhāna*). Furthermore, the removal of the surrounding grass (*paristaraṇa*) is observed in the case of a subsequent performance. The consecration (*alaṃkaraṇa*) has been explained previously. Regarding the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), there are the mantras *vṛṣṭirasi*, the recollection of Viṣṇu for unknown omissions, and the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the unknown, after which the sacrificer proceeds as he came.

One should offer oblations with clarified butter for one desiring splendor; with milk for one desiring cattle; with curd for one desiring sensory power; with rice grains for one desiring vigor; with barley-gruel for one desiring a village; with cooked rice for one desiring food; with meat for one desiring heroism; and with Soma for one desiring Vedic luster.

The phrase "he should sacrifice" (*juhuyāt*) is to be supplied everywhere. Regarding the place for a permanent substance, one who has expressed a specific desire should sacrifice in the evening and morning, preceded by the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) expressing that desire once. On this point, Kātyāyana says: "Having first performed [the rite] according to the view of a year-long period, [one may then perform it] in the evening and morning. Therefore, the optional (*kāmya*) performance is to be done only once. "Splendor" (*tejaḥ*) refers to bodily luster or invincibility against others. The phrase "for one desiring cattle" (*paśukāmasya*) is clear.

*Indriya* refers to the sharpness of the senses and the sharpness of the mind; *grāma* refers to preeminence among one's kinsmen and community; *annādya* refers to the abundance of food and the prosperity of people; *vīrya* refers to strength or an abundance of semen; and *brahmavarcasa*—attained through teaching and other such means—is for the Brāhmaṇa alone. These are the optional [results]. However, Paiṅgya says that the ten substances are both obligatory and optional, citing the Paiṅgi-śruti: "Oil and water—for one desiring rain from the waters, and with oil for one practicing sorcery."

Whatever is done for the curd other than placing it on the fire and pouring it out is performed for the rice-grains and the Soma. Because heating is prohibited, there is no placing [the curd] on the embers, and consequently, the pouring out [of the boiled milk] for that purpose does not exist either. The curd is of a worldly nature, as are the rice-grains; likewise, rice is well-known in that context. For Soma, however, it is the juice itself and not the creeper; but the *pūtīka* plant is a scripturally enjoined substitute for the sake of the sacrifice, and this applies only in specific cases, not universally.

1. Gha, Jha, Va: *anvati*; Ja, Ṭha: *anvati* [variant: *sthālīra saṃkṣālyāntarvedi ni*]; Gha, Ja, Śa, Ma: *u*, *mesi svāhetyu*. 3. Ka, Kha, Ga, Ca, Cha, Ṭa, Ṇa, Ṇātsarikāca. [End of Paṭala] Together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva: 357.

At the time of pouring water [into the vessel], one should pour clarified butter using two blades of *darbha* grass; one cooks the groat-mash (*yavāgū*) for sprinkling. As it is with the groat-mash, so it is with the meat.

One should cast clarified butter onto the grass with the mantra, "May thy heat not carry me away"; there is no sprinkling of water [at this point]. Having first performed the sprinkling, the subsequent emergence (udbhava) should be performed later; there is no further sprinkling. The same applies to barley-gruel and meat. Regarding meat, it is pure when obtained through purchase and so forth, but not by way of killing, because that [act of killing] is not prescribed. Furthermore, the instruction of the Guru is given to specify that only such meat as is fit to be cooked in water [is permitted].
Just as rice gruel (*yavāgū*) is cooked by means of water, so too is meat cooked by means of water; in that very same way, the other preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are identical for all substances.

One should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice of a *rājanya* on the festival day (*parvan*) and not in the interval. A *rājanya* is one born of the royal caste; for him, [the sacrifice is to be performed] only on the festival day and not at other times.

But whatever food is prepared in his house, from that they take for the Brāhmaṇa; that becomes his *agnihotra* offering, poured from the mouth. He who, speaking as if of truth and reality, would be like Soma while sacrificing, for him one should always perform the *agnihotra*. || 19 ||

Thus ends the seventh chapter in the third book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. The word *tu* (but/then) indicates a special rule: when the Agnihotra is not performed, whatever food is cooked in the house of a Rājanya, they first bring that to a Brāhmaṇa; the wife and others should give it to him. By that gift, his Agnihotra rite becomes as if offered and completed in the place of the regular Agnihotra—this is the meaning. Thus ends the seventh chapter in the third book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra composed by Mahādeva. 7.
The Agnihotra is completed.
3.8 Now begins the eighth chapter.

In this eighth chapter, there is an exposition of various rites. Among them, those that are fixed (*niyata*) and whose commencement is invariably immediate following the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) are explained as being the archetypal forms (*prakṛti*). Following that, those fixed rites whose commencement is not invariably immediate following the *ādhāna* are explained as being the modified forms (*vikṛti*).

Desiring to explain the forms (rūpa), and because even the indicative mark (naimittika) is necessarily fixed, the sacrificer’s departure to another place—which is established as a necessity—is qualified by the author, wishing to explain the rule therein and to state two specific rules according to the two-fold nature of the departure: [The text continues with the sūtra: "He offers... [omitted portion] ...he offers. (Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram—Third Praśna)

We shall now explain "residence abroad" (*pravāsa*) as distinct from [residence] at home. Residence abroad is the dwelling of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) beyond the boundary of the village in the absence of his wife. The meaning is that we shall explain the inquiry regarding the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) because the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) therein pertains to the sacrificer. The word *ṛte* means "without" or "in the absence of"; here the genitive case (*gṛhasya*) is used in the sense of the instrumental or the ablative. Because there is no separate mention of "he does not reside abroad" or "he does not depart," the term *pravāsa* is conventionally established as residing away from one's wife upon crossing the boundary.

Regarding the departure together with his wife, the sound of departure occurs right there; however, the rule occasioned by departure—namely, "if one should depart without having offered the *vāstoṣpatīya* [oblation]"—does not apply to a journey abroad (*pravāsa*), because that constitutes a separate ritual act. With this intention, he demonstrates the distinction of the scope and explains the rule for departure here as pertaining to the *adhvaryu*’s duty:

"But one who is departing from home, whether he stays at another place for five, nine, or ten nights, or wherever he stays for nine nights, upon returning again to that original site, he should stay for one night and there offer the *vāstoṣpatīya*."

"One who is about to depart with his household performs the oblation. The word "tu" (but/however) serves to distinguish this from the case of temporary absence (*pravāsa*). By the phrase "about to depart," it is stated that he shall go accompanied by his wife after crossing the boundary; for it is not ordained that one may go with his wife while abandoning the fires. If that were the case, then at the time of the *agnihotra* sacrifice, if the husband and wife were situated on opposite sides of the boundary, the fire would surely be extinguished; thus, this rule for the departure of both does not apply to leaving the fires behind. Even in the case of a man with many wives, there is no fault if he departs with only one of them.

When the sacrificer is away on a journey, this same rule applies even when his wife, who maintains the sacred fires, departs by means of a *māyā* (magical illusion) or other such means. "Departure" refers to going from one village to another, not merely moving from one room to another within the house. Regarding the phrase "about to depart," meaning intending to go to another village, he says "where... and so forth, to clarify that it is not without qualification.

Regarding the passage, "where [one stays] five or nine [nights]," this shows a view from another recensional school (*śākhāntara*). According to one's own recension, there is the scriptural injunction: "Therefore, having stayed ten nights, one departs. Thus, when the stay is less than ten nights, there is no oblation upon departing from that residence. However, as for a stay of fewer than ten nights—such as where one resolves, "I shall dwell five [nights]"—if one departs after five nights during which the *saṃhitās* have been studied without interruption by other times, there is no oblation if the duration is less than that. In this way, the settled option (*vikalpa*) based on the resolution regarding nine [nights] has been shown.

Even in the absence of an initial formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), it should be understood that the fire-oblation (*homa*) must be performed according to one of the five alternative options (*pakṣa*) at the time of departure. For a householder does not make a formal resolve for the purpose of residing in his own home; therefore, among the stages of the journey, the adoption of one of the options occurs only where a residence is established after a resolve has been made, and not elsewhere. For instance, having resolved upon ten nights, if he dwells for nine nights and then, by divine necessity, goes to his own home or another location and subsequently returns to the place where he had stayed for the nine nights, stays there for one night, and then departs from there—[in such a case, the ritual requirements apply].

The word "he offers" (*juhoti*) is a specific injunction (*viśeṣavidhi*). Some hold that even in the case of a resolve for nine nights (*pañcanava-saṃkalpa*), one should understand that after staying for some of the resolved nights and returning, he stays for the remaining ones and then offers; thus, [the rule] is not futile. Furthermore, the mention of "one" (*ekām*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of both the deficiency in the resolved number and the specific completion thereof. This matter is accessible only through an injunction; in the absence of an injunction, it would not be established. Having explained the occasion for the *homa*, he states what must be done prior to the *homa* as part of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) regarding departure: "He places all the utensils (*bhāṇḍa*) upon the vehicles."

The meaning is that he causes the collection of goods to be conveyed from Māṇḍana—whether by chariots, carts, oxen, or whatever means of transport are available among the men—and brings those goods to their destination, placing them in those various vehicles and conveyances.

[Chapter 1, Section 1] Accompanied by the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva. Whatever else they intend to carry away, that they first carry forward. Whatever else besides the vessels belongs to the sacrificer and is intended to be taken, the men carry it out from the house before the oblation; they take hold of it on the head and so forth to lead it away.
Or, before the offering is made, they remove it from that place.

When men are unable to carry what they intended to carry, they then lift it up from that place and set it outside. However, in the case of the *homa*, even before it has been offered, once it has been offered, they should lead it out; they should not keep it in the houses at the time of the *homa*. When all are yoked, the right ox of the one standing by the fire is yoked, while the thong of the left one is loosened but not yet detached. Then, having recited the verse addressed to Vāstoṣpati, he offers the oblation with the following verse.

Regarding vehicles and conveyances—such as oxen, horses, mules, and so forth—which have been procured and harnessed with yokes; when oxen are thus yoked, those upon whom fire has been placed are called *agniṣṭha* (standing near the fire) by the term "fire," referring to the firewood in the forest. Having halted these at that place, they are led away; that cart or chariot is the *agniṣṭha*, and its right-hand draft animal is yoked.

The thong of the left [pole] has already been passed through and drawn out from the hole of the *śamyā* (wooden pin), and it remains fastened and attached there at that *śamyā*-hole. Then, having kindled the fire and prepared the clarified butter (*ājya*), the Adhvaryu, following the procedure for a *darvihoma*, recites the formula "O Vāstoṣpati, lead us back" and offers the oblation with the words "O Vāstoṣpati, with your auspicious [favor]. Rudra is indeed the deity Vāstoṣpati, according to the scriptural statement: "Rudra is truly Vāstoṣpati."

Regarding his *vāstoṣpatīya* rite, it is stated: "Having recited the *puronuvākyā*, he offers with the *yājyā*. Although it is established that the *oṃ* should be uttered at the end of the *puronuvākyā* and the *vaṣaṭ* at the end of the *yājyā*, nevertheless, because it is enjoined by the root *hu* (to sacrifice/offer) and is thus a *davihoma*, it does not possess the nature of a *yāga* (sacrifice).

Having recited the *puronuvākyā*, [he offers] "with the *yājyā*"—by means of this third case ending, the mantra is established as the instrument (*karaṇa*). To indicate that the mantra ends with *svāhā* and that even the ending with *praṇava* is not desired in the *puronuvākyā* because it is a *darvihoma*, it is stated: "he offers with the subsequent one" (*anuvākyottarayā juhoti*). Here, it results in the conclusion that a single oblation (*homa*) is to be accomplished by two verses (*ṛc*). Just as when it is said "he offers with two," where there is an oblation with a group of mantras, there would otherwise be a separate oblation for each individual mantra; therefore, the word "having recited" (*anudrutya*) is used. This same principle regarding "having recited" (*anudrutya*) is to be understood everywhere.
He does not add fuel to the fire after it has been offered into.
While the fire is burning, he does not throw anything into it—neither wood, grass, leaves, nor clarified butter. Nor does he depart without having extinguished the embers.

Immediately after the re-establishment (*samāropa*), while the fires are still present in the kindling woods (*araṇi*)—such as the wood being burnt—he does not depart without having extinguished them or without having burnt them; rather, he departs only after they have been burnt. This being the case:
having re-established the fires in the separate kindling woods with the mantra, "This is your seasonal womb," he proceeds on his journey.

The mantra ends with *rayim*. Two or four [fires] are to be maintained permanently; or, according to the view that the Āhavanīya fire is to be maintained, three or five [fires]. Having performed the *samāropaṇa* (consignment) of each pair of kindling woods (*araṇī*) with its respective mantra, one should take the other fires—those consecrated by the *ādhāna* rite as well as the ordinary worldly ones—from the Gārhapatya fire. If there is a Gṛhya fire, having consigned that as well, the heating of the two kindling woods and the consignment are stated to be repeated for each fire. With the mantra "This is thy womb, O Viś" (*ayaṃ te yonirviyaḥ*), he heats the two kindling woods; "separately" means that for each fire, he consigns [the fire] into the two kindling woods in the order of their installation (*ādhāna*).

Now, moreover, they say: "If one who has mounted the two kindling woods should perish, or if his fire should go out, it would have to be re-established. [To this he replies: "O Agni, that body of yours which is worthy of sacrifice, ascend with it; enter your own self, bringing many human riches to us. Having become the sacrifice, sit upon the sacrifice as your own womb, O Jātavedas; being born from the earth, come to your dwelling! Having thus consigned the fire into himself, he departs.

Now, "atho" (then) indeed signifies an alternative view. This explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) is presented for the sake of the preceding option; it serves as an illustration of a subsequent *arthavāda*. Although the designation "belonging to the sacrificer" (*yājamāna*) does not apply because [this passage] is recited in the *Ādhvaryava-kāṇḍa*, the mention [of the sacrificer] is intended to make known that the sacrificer is the agent, by demonstrating the logical principle that "it is another [than the officiating priest] because of the specific instruction."

For instance, another indication is seen in the case of a different sacrificer: "The sacrificer is the womb of Agni; he causes him to ascend into his own very womb. This use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) expresses that the action has the sacrificer as its agent. Furthermore, this [middle voice] overrides the *samākhyā* (name/designation), the seventh-case *śruti* in the phrase "into his own womb" (*svāyām eva yonau*), and the indicative power (*liṅga*) in the mantra "sit down on your own seat" (*sīda tvam sādanam svam*), because the *śruti* of the middle voice and the seventh-case *śruti* possess greater authority than the *samākhyā* and the *liṅga*.

Regarding the *ātmasamāropaṇa* (the internalizing of the fire within oneself): some say it is the heating of the hands; others say it is the heating of both hands; others say that after heating them, one takes the heat with the mouth; others say there is a mantra for taking the heat after heating [the hands] silently; Vaikhānasa says the sacrificer heats his hand and brings it to his mouth. They also maintain that the *samāropaṇa* should be performed even when there is fear of thieves and the like, though no *homa* (offering) is performed there, because that [offering] is occasioned by the [sacrificer's] departure. They record in their tradition that it should be performed when he is ill or away on a journey.

Since it has been established that even when the *adhvaryu* is absent, or when the wife acts as a substitute for the sacrificer (*yanamāna*), a substitute may indeed be used for rites other than those constituting one's own personal consecration (*saṃskāra*), it follows by logical principle that the internal mental transfer (*ātmasamāropa*) must also be performed by the wife; and if she is incapable of doing so, it must be performed by the *adhvaryu* as well. Thus, the departure (*prayāṇa*) belongs to both. This is so provided that the occasion for departure has arisen.

When the sacrificer is present, it should be understood that the kindling woods (*araṇī*) are to be consigned into the fire by the Adhvaryu, or the self-consignment (*ātmasamāropa*) is performed by the wife, and so forth. Upon crossing the boundary of the village, the husband and wife perform the "taking hold of the forest" (*araṇyanvārambha*); if this is not done, there is the destruction of the fires. Some say this applies even when they are in different villages, provided they are at the beginning or the end [of the journey]. In times of distress, or when the sacrificer is absent, the wife performs the taking hold. However, when the sacrificer is away on a journey, if the wife goes to another village or crosses a river during the time for the *homa*, the fires become merely worldly (*laukika*).
Wherever he resides, he churns the fire before sunset.

"Descend, O Jātavedas, knowing again how to carry the oblation to the gods; bestow upon us long life, progeny, and wealth; shine for us unceasingly in our home"—having thus caused him who was mounted upon himself to descend into the two kindling woods, he churns [the fire].
The word "churns" serves both prescriptive purposes: in the case where he has mounted [the fire] upon himself, [he descends into the woods];
or else, having brought a common (laukika) fire, he causes it to descend into that [fire].

Having brought forth the pure fire mounted upon the *ātman*, one causes it to descend with the previously mentioned mantra. Regarding this, the Commentator says: "In the event of extreme distress, [this is done]. The Commentator also states that "descending" (*upāvarohaṇa*) means "breathing upon" (*anuprāṇana*). However, in the case of warming the hands, "descending" consists of touching the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) with the mantra; if taking hold with the mouth, it consists of the contact with the breath from the mouth. Having churned the *gārhapatya* fire and placed it in its hearth, one does the same for the *dakṣiṇāgni*. Then, having spread out the *āhavanīya* fire—either by carrying it from there or by churning it—one places it in its hearths.

Even in the case where the fires are consigned into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), the practice of chanting the *upāvarohaṇa* mantra after the fire has been churned is not contradictory; therefore, that too is authoritative. Then he offers the *agnihotra*:

"This is the most excellent conclusion which has come to me; may Heaven and Earth be gracious to me. May the quarters be free from disease for me—rich in cattle, rich in wealth, rich in horses, rich in gold, rich in men, and rich in heroic sons, svāhā! He offers this at the conclusion [of the recitation].

When the journey has ended—that is, when it has concluded and is finished, such that one has stayed for five or seventeen nights and there is no further travel remaining—even then one offers the oblation according to the rules of the *darvihoma*. Thus, even if one stops at intervals along the way, there is no offering; rather, the *vāstoṣpati-homa* is performed only when the designated place has been reached. Since neither extended application (*atideśa*) nor direct instruction (*upadeśa*) provides for the accessories such as clarified butter (*ājya*), and because of the expectancy "how does one offer?", the author, wishing to explain the *darvihoma* which is established by its very purpose, introduces [the topic] with:
"We shall explain the *darvihomas*."

The formulation of a formal proposition (*pratijñā*) is intended to demonstrate the gravity of the matter, on the grounds that the performance [of these rites] is impossible without an explanation, as they would otherwise lack authority. This designation is established by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). For indeed, a *darvi*-oblation (*darvihoma*) could not consist of a continuous stream, nor of separate portions, nor of four-fold ladlings (*caturgṛhīta*), etc.; nor could it be performed with a serving-spoon (*pariveṣaṇakāṣṭha*), because that would contradict the requirement of implements such as the *juhū* ladle. If one asks, "How then are *darvihomas* to be identified?", he says: "A *darvihoma* is that which is enjoined by the word 'he offers' (*juhoti*), and where there is the utterance of *svāhā*."

When an action is enjoined by means of the root *hu* (to sacrifice) ending in an injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*), it should be understood as having the name "oblation" (*homa*)—specifically, in the case of a *dadhi-homa* (curd-oblation). Regarding this, in the passage "He offers with four portions" (*caturavattaṃ juhoti*), the status of being a *dadhi-homa* might be suspected; therefore, the text says "where... and so forth. The form *juhoti* is derived from the verbal root *hu*; the action enjoined by that term is a gift (*dāna*) ending in the act of throwing into the fire (*prakṣepānta*). In that context, the word *homa* is used for such a gift by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) through a derivation based on the abstract state (*bhāvavyutpatti*), and not for a gift enjoined by the root *hu* or for a gift enjoined by the root *dā*.

1. Gha, Ḍa, Ja, Ḍha: *svāhākārāḥ*. 46. 262. In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, in the third book: Or rather, in that very context, the *svāhākāra* is employed for the purpose of giving at the end of the pouring, by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). For although the Śruti states without distinction—"The oblation is given to the deity with the *svāhākāra* or with the *vaṣaṭkāra*," thus expressing its purpose as being for both—nevertheless, in the case of the offering of Soma, the *vaṣaṭkāra* alone is recognized as prescribed as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) by both conventional usage and Śruti, through the section beginning "Just as those who had prepared the Soma... and by the passage "Prajāpati created the gods and the Asuras... In the same way, the word *svāhā* is employed in the sense of giving (*dāna*) when prompted by the injunction to offer (*juhoti*), either through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or through scriptural authority (*śruti*), as in the passage beginning "Speech offered praise" (*vāg abhyavadat*). This very point was explained during the discussion on the *prayājas*.

And likewise, in such cases as "he offers the four-fold portion" (*caturavattaṃ juhoti*), since it is impossible for that which has been enjoined by the root *hu* (to sacrifice) to be a gift (*dāna*) performed again by the *vaṣaṭ*-call after having already been performed by the *svāhā*-call, the abandonment (*jahāti*) mentioned there consists merely in the act of throwing [the offering] into the fire. Thus, because it is impossible [otherwise], it cannot be designated by the term *sadavihoma*, as it lacks the *svāhā*-call; this is the conclusion (*pāvaḥ*). Now, what is to be explained here? Is it that by the general procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the oblations (*homāḥ*) are performed together with all their constituent parts (*sāṅgāḥ*)? Indeed, there exists even a constituent part of that [procedure].

By the statement, "If one should eat [food] containing an insect," and so forth, the pouring out [of the remains] within the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) in the *agnihotra* is seen to be for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). If there were no extension (*atideśa*) of that rule, the state of being within the enclosing sticks would not occur; thus, this serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) [for the existence of such an extension]. To refute this [objection], it is specifically stated that these are *darvihomas*. In the Śruti, those acts which, by virtue of being *darvihomas*, are neither archetypes (*prakṛti*) nor modifications (*vikṛti*), and are denoted by the term *darvihoma* through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), are what we shall explain. Furthermore, it is implied that their specific nature—such as the *juhū* ladle and other details—is to be understood from the *Juhūgī* and other sources, as it was not explicitly stated here.

Now, if it is asked: "How is it that, despite similarity and the fact that it is neither a primary nor a modified form, there is no contradiction with the gender?"—it is replied: It should be understood from the *Jaiminīya* [school] that the gender is established otherwise, as being characterized by the location of the *paridhi* (enclosing sticks).

In the case of the injunction for the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara," since the sacrifice is inferred through the term *nirvapati*, and because the procedure is obtained from the rules of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the statement "He performs a *darvihoma*" serves to prohibit the subsidiaries such as the *prayāja*s; thus, by virtue of its similarity to a *darvihoma*, the prohibition becomes meaningful.

Having deprecated the state of possessing *prayāja* offerings and other elements—on the grounds that "whatever distress one might cause through such exertion belongs to the sacrifice"—and having concluded that one should instead perform only the *darvihoma* as prescribed, it is understood from this that the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *darśa* and other sacrifices does not apply to these *homas*. Likewise, after praising the *darvihoma* with the words "If one were to offer with a single [ladle]," and then deprecating the status of being a *darvihoma*, it is stated that even in a *homa* accomplished by two [elements], there is a gift (*dāna*), following the praise of its equality with the two-fold [sacrifice] and the injunction beginning with "having recited the *anu-vākyā*."

Therefore, the *homāḥ* (oblations) are neither *vikṛti*s (modifications) nor *prakṛti*s (archetypes), because they lack their own specific properties (*svadharma*). For it will be stated that being an archetype consists in possessing its own specific properties. Even if there were possession of specific properties—as in the case of the *agnihotra*, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, and so forth—that too would not be the cause for extension (*atideśa*). Furthermore, since there are many specific properties present among those oblations that lack specific properties, which one would be extended? Moreover, it is impossible to combine all of them, and because an option (*vikalpa*) is vitiated by eight defects.

Furthermore, extension (*atideśa*) does not occur merely through similarity of inherent properties (*svadharma*), but rather through extension inferred by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). Once extension has been inferred, a mere restriction is established on the basis of similarity for the purpose of excluding other possible alternatives. Otherwise, if the relationship of archetype and ectype (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*) were to exist between all ritual actions characterized by injunctions simply through a general similarity, that would be undesirable; therefore, when an indicative mark exists, extension is sought.

Furthermore, there is no observation here of the performance of one's own specific duty (*svadharmaśīla*) within the *akhadharmas* or the *homās*. Therefore, they are not the *prakṛtis* (archetypes) for those [other rites], and for that very reason, others are not the *vikṛtis* (variants) of other [rites]. In this context, it is stated that the term *davihoma* is a conventional designation (*rūḍha*). Consequently, the intention is that the authority (*pramāṇa*) which indicates the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) must be set aside. As for the statement from the *vacana* regarding the rite belonging to the *kauṇḍapāyināmayana*: "For a month, the *agnihotra*... [End of section]. This is accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 363.

From the statement "he offers" (*juhoti*), the Agnihotra is established as the archetype (*prakṛti*) and that [other rite] as the ectype (*vikṛti*). In this regard, the *darvihoma* does not subvert its own injunctions, but rather establishes them. If the extended application (*atideśa*) were based solely on similarity, then there would be no extended application by way of name (*saṃjñā*). Thus, one should understand the extended application as being stated in the Smṛti: "Having offered into the fire, like the Pitṛyajña. Now, regarding the *darvihoma* to be described hereafter...

Even though the characteristics (*dharma*) of the *agnihotra* might apply to the two oblations here, and the characteristics of the *samit* (fuel-stick) might apply to the two fuel-sticks, their re-enunciation is for the purpose of excluding other characteristics; therefore, the characteristics of the *darvihoma* do not apply there. Similarly, in the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, because of the injunction "bending the right knee" (*dakṣiṇaṃ jānvācya*), which is a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*), it should be understood that by implication this results in the exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of other characteristics. Regarding the subsidiary oblations (*aṅgahoma*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the indicators (*jñāpaka*) have already been stated to prevent the application of the *darvihoma* rules; so enough of this digression.

Having gone around the front of the Āhavanīya fire with that clarified butter (ājya) taken once silently, the Adhvaryu, standing to the south, offers it into the Āhavanīya with the *svāhā* exclamation using the *juhū* ladle. Although there is the rule that "this [offering] is to be performed when there is no specific instruction (*anādeśa*)," nevertheless, since a specific injunction (*viśeṣavidhi*) must set aside the general rule (*utsarga*), the term "when there is no instruction" remains as the final conclusion. In that case, clarified butter is the substance when there is no instruction; for even from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—"This indeed is Agni's dear body"—Baudhāyana states that clarified butter is mentioned because it undergoes purification quickly, and thus the word *ājya* denotes a genus (*jāti*).

Even though there is no explicit statement, the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) consisting of speech certainly exists; that which is based on direct audition (*śrauta*) belongs to the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Therefore, there is no application [of this rule] to the silent (*tūṣṇīka*) offerings or to the new and full moon sacrifices performed for the first time (*apūrva*). Hence it is said, "by the silent one" (*tūṣṇīkena*); the meaning is that the silent offering is that which becomes devoid of mantras. When no specific distinction is mentioned, the term "original" (*prakṛti*) is understood. From the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the meaning is: "You have poured out four times, you have offered twice. Since pouring out twice is enjoined in the original sacrifice, it is stated that in the case of pouring out four times, pouring out twice is redundant. Thus, [it is performed] once.

"Once only"—this is stated here because [the offering] is made with a single scoop from the *ājyasthālī* (clarified butter vessel). "In front"—this is said for the purpose of establishing a rule, since there is otherwise no fixed rule regarding the direction of the Adhvaryu’s actions due to the requirement of circumambulation (*prādakṣiṇya*). "Standing"—this is also stated for the same reason. He offers with the *juhū* ladle; it is called the *āhavanīya* fire because one offers into it. And likewise, when one offers into the *āhavanīya*...

And because of the scriptural statement, "The Āhavanīya fire is for all oblations," that which is already established is restated so that there may be no restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of those two; the mention of the Adhvaryu is for the purpose of pervasiveness even in the minor expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta-vihoma*), lest one follow the view in another *sūtra*—the *Āśvalāyana*—which states that when an expiation is enjoined with the word "one offers," one should understand the Brahman priest to be the performer. Otherwise, since the Adhvaryu’s agency would be established simply by the fact that the rite is prescribed in the Yajurveda, [the specific mention would be redundant]. As for the phrase "with the *svāhā*-utterance," it means that the sacrificial offering (*havis*) is given with the *svāhā*-utterance.

Thus is the application of the *svāhākāra* for the purpose of giving (*dāna*). And so, ritual practitioners apply the *svāhākāra* at the end of the mantra even in cases such as "he pours out," "he causes to flow," "he offers," or "he places [the fire]," and so forth. This is incorrect, because the *svāhākāra* is prescribed only in connection with the injunction of *juhoti* (offering). Furthermore, even in the injunction of *juhoti* such as "he offers the fourfold portion" (*caturavattaṃ juhoti*), there is no attainment of the *svāhākāra*, because of the maxim that between the secondary and the primary, the function belongs to the primary; thus, it is understood as a constituent part of the sacrifice (*yāga*).

Since the oblation to the beings (*bhūta-homa*) is accomplished by the *vaṣaṭ* call itself, the term *juhoti* indicates merely the act of pouring; thus, it appears that the word "not" (*na*) is redundant, as there would otherwise be a figurative usage.
(Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Third Praśna, Sūtra 364).

Thus, it is established that there is no *svāhākāra* even in cases such as the *caturavatta-homa* (the fourfold-cutting oblation) or "O Jātavedas, with the omentum... (*jātavedo vapayā*). Although one might expect the expression "those oblations by means of oblations" (*tān homān homaiḥ*), in instances such as "he performs the *agnihotra*" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*), the accusative case is heard; since the injunction of origin (*utpatti-vidhi*) is understood simply as "one should perform the oblation" (*homaṃ kuryāt*), the use of the verb *juhoti* is for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). In cases such as "he sacrifices with the *jyotiṣṭoma*" (*jyotiṣṭomena yajate*), the instrumental case is used for sacrifices; however, in the case of oblations, the accusative is generally used, which should be interpreted according to the method previously stated.

If it is argued that because the mantra ends with "svāhā," there is no actual conjunction of the ritual action (*karma*) with the act of giving (*dāna*), which constitutes the rite—this is replied: since the intended meaning of the mantra ending in "svāhā" is "he casts [the oblation] into the fire" (*davaprakṣipati*), and because the root *juhoti* signifies a gift that culminates in casting [into the fire].

Since the *svāhākāra* (the utterance "svāhā") is also of the nature of being recited (*vācita*), it follows by implication that the act of giving is accomplished there by means of the word ending in *svāhā*. Consequently, because it is impossible for it to coincide with [the mantra] ending in *m*, one must—whether one likes it or not—accept that the coincidence with the end of the mantra occurs precisely through the offering of that single part. Thus, where the coincidence of the commencement of the rite and so forth is possible, it occurs accordingly; elsewhere, even by means of a single part, and where even that is impossible, there is no coincidence, as in the case where the sacrifice is accomplished by a *yājyā* verse ending in *vaṣaṭ*, since there is no remainder [of the verse to be offered].

There is no conjunction even by way of a single part. Since the *vaṣaṭ* call is conventionally established as the act of giving and offering, the same applies to the root *yajati* (to sacrifice). Therefore, the pouring [of the oblation] does not occur at the end of the *yājyā* verse ending with *vaṣaṭ*; rather, because the pouring is a distinct action, the portion consisting of the pouring is enjoined at the time indicated by the *vaṣaṭ* call. However, it has been explained in the *Paribhāṣā* itself that the *yājyā* ending with *vaṣaṭ* is not the instrument (*sādhana*) for that [pouring]. In the case of groups of offerings numbering two or more, having taken [the portions] for each offering and having placed fuel-sticks (*samidh*) for each offering, one offers them separately (*vigrāham*).

There are two groups of offerings; in that collection, for each individual offering, as many [portions] as there are offerings, one should take them up. However, the attainment [of the specific number] is indeed from the explanatory passage (arthavāda) itself: "He offers twice, O singer of the triple-verse."

Regarding the statement, "At every oblation, he should place fuel-sticks," even in the case of the *agnihotra*, one should not place two barley fuel-sticks, for that would produce a rival for him; thus, there is a censure regarding the placing of fuel-sticks. Since this censure applies when the rule "at every oblation, he should place fuel-sticks" is followed, [the author] says: having placed [fuel] only once, and having separated [the portions], he offers the oblations in distinct portions, each sufficient for an offering, according to the previously stated rule. Although the spreading of grass (*paristaraṇa*) and the sprinkling of water (*paripeka*) are included within the ritual procedure (*tantra*), they were not mentioned here because they are among those rules established by custom (*sāmayācārika*). They are indeed included within the *tantra*.

Regarding the statement, "The oblations are offered into the Āhavanīya fire for those [rites] involving *pāhomā*s," one should understand that there are groups of oblations such as "he offers two oblations," "three," "four," and so forth, even in the case of fuel-sticks (*samidh*).
Where one enjoins a rite by means of a group of mantras, one should offer the oblation with each individual mantra.

However, where the agent prescribes a rite called *homa* by means of a collection of mantras—such as "he offers with two verses addressed to Viṣṇu" or "with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* [verses]"—there, according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "in that rite, the actions are indeed without mantras," it is stated that there is only a single mantra, even though various mantras accompanied by specific numbers are mentioned.

In this context, because it is a quality-action (*guṇakarman*), the number residing in that quality-action does not differentiate the action; since it serves as a refinement (*saṃskāraka*) and does not produce a new transcendental result (*apūrva*), the differentiation of actions is not prompted by a difference in *apūrva*. Thus, there would be a single action repeated, and a single mantra [would apply]. 15. cha. ja, ma. ma. da. bhūtiyāī | 2 ka, kha, ga, ca. cha. da. sohaiṃ ni | sa (Fifth Paṭala) [This is] accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 365.

It might be so in other cases, but why not in the case of *homās* (oblations)? Since *homās* are enjoined as being primary in themselves, they produce a unique transcendental result (*apūrva*); and because that [result] is understood to be one, there is no differentiation of the action based on the number of the subordinate factors (*guṇa*). Therefore, for each individual action accomplished by a mantra, there is only one mantra. Just as in the injunction, "One should sacrifice seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati," the number residing in the animals serves to differentiate the sacrifices, that [argument] is incorrect.

With respect to a single substance, only one refinement (*saṃskāra*) is required, and that occurs through a single action, either by virtue of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*) or by number; thus, there is repetition (*abhyāsa*) of that very same action, not a difference in the actions themselves. Therefore, another mantra must necessarily be employed for the purpose of conjunction (*saṃnipāta*). Consequently, even when there are various parts, there is only a single mantra [for each], because it has been stated that mantras do not constitute subordinate members (*anaṅga*) with respect to one another—this is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, because the combination [of mantras] has been rejected through the censure that "if one were to offer with only one [mantra], one would perform a *darvihoma*," the first [mantra] is not praised as having a connection with another function [other than the *puronuvākyā*]. Therefore, it is established that there is no combination of mantras in *darvihomas*.
We shall explain the applications of the word *juhoti* later on.

The word *juhoti* (he offers) is the scriptural injunction for that ritual action characterized by oblation (*homa*). In that ritual, where the general rule of offering in the *āhavanīya* fire would otherwise apply, certain specific locations are prescribed by the mention of particular places as the substrates, setting aside the *āhavanīya*. These are not substitutes for the *āhavanīya*; rather, even when the *āhavanīya* is available, these locations are enjoined as exceptions. Thus it is shown that these places are indeed "locations" (*sthāna*) which serve as independent substrates (*adhikaraṇa*), namely:
"in a depression made by oneself," "in a cleft," "on a clump of darbha grass," and "at the base of a tree trunk. (20)

The particle *iti* expresses a manner or type. One offers [the oblation] in a naturally formed saline soil (*irikṇa*) or in a fissure (*pradara*). At the *avamṛtha* bath of the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice, one offers in a clump of *darbha* grass with the mantra "O Son of Waters," and on a stump with "O Son of the Lord. A naturally formed saline soil is ground that is naturally salty; a fissure is a crack in the earth. Because of the use of the particle *iti*, it should be understood that one offers in a hollow or similar places. Regarding the substitutes for the *āhavanīya* fire, he states the specific rule: when the *āhavanīya* has been removed and there is no fire, one offers in that very same place.

Where there is the removal, denial, or non-attainment of the Āhavanīya fire, in that very place—the location of the Āhavanīya’s hearth—one should bring a single piece of wood, such as a fuel-stick or the like, and offer it into the fire at the edge of the sacrificial ground.

However, one should not offer the oblation wherever one happens to be standing; for while the *āhavanīya* fire may have a substitute in the form of a goat and so forth, there can be no substitute for the specific location of its hearth, as that is directly available. The commencement of this *sūtra*, however, is intended to prevent the following: [the misconception] that if the fire produced by friction does not arise, one should fetch another fire from wherever it is seen and offer the oblation there—since such an act is not prescribed for other fires, it would not be valid in this case. Therefore, he says this so that such a thing may not occur.

Having thus explained the *darvihomas*, which do not consist of either the original form (*prakṛti*) or its modification (*vikṛti*), he now explains the means of knowledge called *atideśa* (extended application), for the purpose of obtaining the ritual properties (*dharmas*) in those modifications of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices—both those already explained and those yet to be explained.
The principal rites belonging to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* are enjoined in the subsequent performance, with the exception of the *soma* sacrifice, the [other] *dharma*s, and the *darvihomas*.

Those belonging to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* are so called because they arise from the two collections of rites (*karmasamudāya*) known as the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* by virtue of being members of those collections. The principal rites...

A, Gha, Ṅa, Ja, Jha, Ma, Ḍha, °bde de. The Āgneya and other sacrifices are explained by the Darśapūrṇamāsa section in the third book; for in the Saṃhitā, within the first *prapāṭhaka* beginning with "iṣe tvā," the mantras have been explained through the two sections on the *puroḍāśa*. Likewise, they are explained by the six initial *anuvākas* beginning with "saṃ tvā siñcāmi" regarding the *pākayajña*, as well as by the two sections beginning with "viśvarūpa" and "samidhaḥ," and by the *yājyākāṇḍa*.

Of these two, the first section (*kāṇḍa*) is designated as "prior" because it begins with the words *iṣe tvā*; those [rites] which are prescribed subsequently in the branch are the "successive" ones. All of these have been explained by the author of the Sūtra in their distinct forms through a continuous sequence, beginning with the Vaimṛdha and ending with the Pavamāna. These are enjoined and elaborated upon in that subsequent section. [The sacrifices include] the Soma sacrifice, the Jyotiṣṭoma, the Ekāhas, the Ahīnas, and the Satras.

The *dharma*s to be extended are the *pravargya*, the *davihomāḥ*, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the *agnihotra*, and so forth; these [are extended] to another series (*tati*). Now, an objection may be raised: "Since the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices consist of a collection of various distinct *dharma*s that differ from one another, how can they serve as the restrictors of the *dharma*s? To address this, the meaning is that by grasping the members of the collection for the sake of that [collection], each individual member—possessing both general *dharma*s and specific, restricted *dharma*s—is extended to each respective ritual action. Now, the collection...

For the *dāya* (the primary sacrifice) is the means of accomplishing the fruit, while the *itikartavyatā* (the procedure) is the auxiliary that brings about the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the fruit. How could this [procedure] apply to each [primary sacrifice] individually? To this he says: "The primaries. For the originative injunctions (*utpattividhi*) are specific; since the adoption of the procedure occurs only with respect to those [sacrifices] enjoined by them, each possesses both its own constituent parts (*aṅga*) and its status as a primary (*pradhānatā*). Indeed, it is the collection of primaries that is enjoined for the sake of the fruit; therefore, the meaning is that each primary is extended (*atidiśyate*) one by one to each respective subsequent action.

Now, one might ask: why are there these two restrictive rules—that only the elements of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsika) are extended [by analogy], and that they are extended only to those other than the Soma sacrifice and so forth? Furthermore, when the primary rites (pradhāna) are thus extended, how is the attainment of the subsidiary parts (aṅga) achieved, for the primary rites themselves do not become the subsidiaries? To this, he says:
"They possess their own inherent properties" (tāni svadharmāṇi).

Those [rites] whose constituent parts (*aṅga*) are their own specific duties (*svadharma*) as prescribed by their respective relationships are thus; for those various [rites] are complete in their own duties. Indeed, that which possesses complete duties is extended (*atidiśyate*) to that which possesses incomplete duties. The *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, having been taught with complete duties, are to be extended to the *Vaimṛdha* and other rites which have incomplete duties and are thus dependent, but not to the *Soma* sacrifices, even though they possess complete taught duties and are independent.

Furthermore, where it is stated that "it should be performed like the Āgneya," it is understood through the suffix *-vat* that it should be performed in that manner; however, it is not the case that "this very thing" is being extended by way of analogy (*atideśa*), because that would involve a contradiction. For when there is a ritual action that requires auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), the word "like that" (*tadvat*) is used for the purpose of removing that requirement [of auxiliaries]. If this very [Āgneya] were to take its place, the use of the suffix *-vat* would be contradicted. Therefore, even though the primary rites (*pradhāna*) are being extended, they are extended along with their own properties (*svadharma*), being endowed with those properties by implication.

And thus, the meaning is that this [object] must be understood as being endowed with those properties; for in the world, when a child is being educated to grasp phonemes, one says, "Having joined vowels such as 'a' to the consonant 'ka', the letter 'kha' is also like that," and then the child, though they do not exist in 'kha', joins the vowels 'a' and so forth which were seen in 'ka'—and it is the same here as well.

Furthermore, that which has already been performed cannot be performed again; however, although such [actions] and their constituent parts (*aṅga*) have already been performed, it is not the case that those very same ones cannot be performed here again, but rather that others of the same class (*tajjātīya*) may be performed. It should be understood that since the ritual action (*karman*) is recognized as belonging to a distinct class through means such as different verbal roots (*śabdāntara*), one is able to perform an action of that same class within that context. [End of Adhyāya 1, Paṭala 8] — accompanied by the *Vejayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva. 367.

Now, one might object: even if the Jyotiṣṭoma alone possesses its own specific characteristics (*svadharma*), since the *Ekāha* sacrifices and others do not, why would there not be an extension (*atideśa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa rules to them? Likewise, if here there were no transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa ritual into the subsequent rite (*uttaratati*), how could there be the relationship of archetype and ectype (*prakṛti-vikṛti*), given that such a relationship is observed only between things like clay and a jar? Furthermore, if all subsequent rites were thus extended, there would still be either a contradiction or an option regarding the ritual characteristics (*dharma*). To this, he says: "The modification [occurs] due to similarity."

Although the *Ahīna* sacrifices and others possess mutual expectancy, they are modifications (*vikāra*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* alone because of their similarity as having unmanifest injunctions (*avyakta-codanā*), and not of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices which have manifest injunctions (*vyakta-codanā*). Therefore, it is also established that only the *Iṣṭi* and animal sacrifices—which arise through the connection of substance and deity—are modifications by virtue of their similarity as having manifest injunctions, whereas this does not apply to the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, which arises without such a connection of substance and deity.

Thus, the modification (*vikāra*) occurs precisely because of the similarity to the primary rites of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), and not because actions—which by their very nature exist for only three moments—could undergo transformation into another form; therefore, the relationship between the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*) is figurative rather than primary, as it is in the case of clay and a jar. However, in the sense that the constituent parts—the subsidiaries (*aṅga*)—which are like the limbs of the Darśapūrṇamāsa with all its subsidiaries, exist in the subsequent rite, it is indeed a modification.

Furthermore, not all [elements] are extended everywhere; rather, by virtue of mutual intermediate similarity, the extension applies only one [element] to one [other]. Thus, the Sūtra should be construed through a threefold repetition. To that extent, this entire textual section of the Sūtra has stated that an "extension" (atideśa) is a statement to the effect that "this work is to be performed here as well" on account of such similarity. As it has been said by those learned in the *Abhiyukta*: "The extension (*atideśa*) is defined as the attainment, by way of functional necessity, of the entire series of properties perceived in one place within another place."

"Because, from the archetypal rite (*prakṛti-karman*), there is that by which a portion of its dharma occurs in rites similar to it; that is remembered as *atideśa* (extended application). Now, one might object: "A Vedic rite is effective for its fruit exactly as it is enjoined; there is no injunction stating that it must be performed in that same manner [in other rites], nor can such an injunction be inferred, due to a lack of authoritative evidence. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It is to be understood through an indicative mark (*liṅga*)."

A modification is to be understood through similarity by means of a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) or the observation of such a mark. When a specific characteristic mark exists, the presence of extended application (*atideśa*) to that specific case is all the more established; this is the meaning. For instance, there is a restatement of the *prayāja* offerings in the injunction "At each *prayāja*, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* grain," as well as a restatement of the *āghāra* libation in the injunction regarding the animal sacrifice, "Having poured the *āghāra*, he anoints the animal"; however, such [restatements] do not exist in the case of one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*) and the like.

Therefore, it is known—both by the maxim of the "grains in the cooking pot" (*sthālīpulaka*) and because the extended application (*atideśa*) is seen to include all auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) even in those cases where the extension is based on explicit scriptural statement—that the primary characteristics of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices apply to the *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices. Likewise, the characteristics of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, such as the *stotras* and *śastras*, are prescribed as subordinate qualities (*guṇa*) in certain one-day (*ekāha*), multi-day (*ahīna*), and other sacrifices; from this it is known that these are modifications (*vikāra*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
[Note: Ra, Ja, Jha... read *sāmānyādi*; 3. This is the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [Book] 2, Third Section.]

Now, it was argued that modification (*vikāra*) occurs due to similarity (*sādṛśya*), and that similarity consists in the commonality of many constituent parts; however, such [similarity] is not possible in the case of a ritual action. If by "similarity" one intends the similarity with the root (*dhātu*) serving as the instrument, then since that inferred root *yaj* would be identical everywhere, how could there be a specific relationship of original form (*prakṛti*) and modification (*vikṛti*)? Furthermore, if the cause of similarity were the commonality of the deity or the commonality of the oblation (*havis*), that too is not the case. For there is no oblation or deity whatsoever defined by a universal genus (*jāti*), nor is there similarity through a commonality of procedure (*itikartavyatā*), because that is also unestablished. Anticipating this objection, he says:

Where an oblation is offered by virtue of a common deity or a common oblation, the term "modification" (*vikāra*)—though separated in the text—is appropriately supplied due to similarity. The meaning is that because of the similarity in the ritual action, whether through a common deity or a common oblation, there is a fixed rule regarding the modification. Now, [one might object] that there is no deity by way of genus (*jāti*), nor is there an oblation; therefore, it is said: "wherein"—that is, in whichever ritual, for whichever [deity], whatever is given, that is the deity and that is the oblation. Because of the similarity between those two, either through both types of similarity or through one or the other, it is stated that there is a specific rule regarding the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*).

In this context, that which is designated by a generic term for the oblation—such as the *puroḍāśa* cake and so forth—is prescribed precisely as it is well-known in the world as being fit to be offered; however, the deity is not so known in the world. That [deity] is cognizable solely through the word [itself], nor is it established even in the Veda by way of a genus (*jāti*). Therefore, it should be understood that what is intended here as the "generic nature of the deity" is the generality residing in the specific word by which that [particular deity] is enjoined.

That alone which is offered is the oblation (*havir*), and not merely that which has been taken up by that word; for example, the curd taken up for the sake of the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) is not offered. Therefore, it is stated by way of contrast that it does not obtain the properties of curd.

Now, one might object: "Surely, the similarity [of a substitute] would exist with respect to *puroḍāśas* (sacrificial cakes) for that which is enjoined by the word *puroḍāśa*, but not with respect to *caru*, *yavāgū*, *dhānā*, *karambha*, and so forth; likewise, how could there be a similarity based on the mere commonality of the deity's name, such as 'Agni' and so on, between substances like clarified butter (*ājya*), milk, and curd, and their respective types—namely oil, honey, animals, *āmikṣā*, and *vājina*—and how could there be a similarity with the sun (*sūrya*) and other such entities? [This objection is addressed as follows:]...

It is said: here, by the word "general" (*sāmānya*), not merely the genus (*jāti*) is intended, but rather any property (*dharma*) residing therein; and since it is easy to conceive a similarity based on whatever [property] is possible there through the distinction between internal and external [factors], once the extension of the general rule (*sāmānyātideśa*) is established, that [extension] is indeed accomplished by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) which makes known the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) required. The author of the Sūtras himself will clarify this. Even though the nature of a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśatva*) is absent in the *caru* and other such offerings, [the similarity is established].

He himself will state that the similarity of the *kṛṣṇala* seeds to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is by virtue of their being vegetable substances; and that when they do not originate from an animal, their similarity to the cake is by virtue of their hardness, as in the rule: "In the case of *kṛṣṇalas*, the procedure for vegetable substances applies. Likewise, regarding the *prājāpatya* sacrifice involving mixed substances, there is a modification of the *yājyā* verse stating that honey and water are mixed; this is because honey and water, while being non-white, are liquid substances.

The similarity of the animal sacrifice to clarified butter (*ājya*) is direct due to its origin from the animal; the similarity of *āmikṣā* to milk is due to its origin from the animal, its whiteness, and its sweetness; and the similarity of *vājina* to curds is due to its acidity—all of this is to be understood from the *Mīmāṃsā*. As for the deity, however, the grounds for similarity—such as identity of deity, multiplicity, or similarity of color—will be demonstrated in the sūtras themselves. Now, one might ask: what is this "extended application" (*atideśa*) that serves as the means of knowledge?

It is said: *Atideśa* (extended application) is the supply of a sentence from a previous ritual action into the context of a modified (*vaikṛta*) action, necessitated by that modified action’s requirement for assistance. It should be understood that the injunction (*vidhi*) itself, aided by this [supply], is the authority; for indeed, in the Sūtras and manuscripts, one does not see the opposite—that [the modification applies] by way of the generality of the oblation (*havis*) or the generality of the deity (*devatā*). [End of Paṭala] — together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

In the case of an action characterized by an injunction (*vidhi*), there exists another means of knowledge [for its requirements]. For an action enjoined by an injunction gives rise to an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as to how the desired result is to be brought about. In that regard, not seeing any auxiliary (*upakāraka*) in close proximity, and observing that it can be obtained from something similar to what preceded, one avoids the excessive burden (*atigaurava*) that would arise if all the numerous auxiliaries (*aṅga*)—which are connected to the principal act (*aṅgin*) and provide various types of assistance—were each individually brought into proximity; therefore, the principal action (*pradhānakarma*) itself, which is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), is brought into proximity.

This has also been stated: the principal rites of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, having been previously enjoined, are subsequently attached [to other rites]. In that context, while only the auxiliaries (aṅga) are grasped as the factors providing assistance, the principal (pradhāna) is also grasped by virtue of being the counter-correlate of similarity; it is not grasped as an assistant itself, because the principal is already established as the recipient of assistance from the auxiliaries.

Furthermore, it has been stated that modification (*vikṛti*) occurs by way of similarity alone, and not by way of identity (*tādrūpya*). Having taken up other limbs similar to those [of the archetype], that which was previously established as the relationship between limb and principal becomes a modification. For when there is no direct scriptural injunction (*pratyakṣanirdeśa*), the sentence is seen exactly in this manner. For instance, from the understanding of the meaning of the sentence "The other is the same as the Śyena,"—which refers to the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) known as the *Veṣu*—it follows that a procedure similar to the procedure of the Śyena sacrifice is appropriate and must be performed. Therefore, it is said that "the Saurya [sacrifice] is like the Āgneya" and so forth, implying that a similar sentence is inferred here as well.

And thus, these very five Brāhmaṇa passages—"There are these oblations," "This is the Brāhmaṇa for the Aindrāgna," "This is the Brāhmaṇa for the Ekakapāla"—are direct statements (*pratyakṣavākya*). The expression "the Agnihotra for a month" concludes through figurative application (*gauṇavṛtti*) and serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) without an explicit example. From the previously mentioned statement of extended application (*atideśavākya*), when [the word] is supplied, it is stated by way of the generality of the deity and the generality of the oblation that this pertains to the *iṣṭi* and the animal sacrifice; however, in the case of the Soma sacrifice, it will be explained that the injunction is unmanifest (*avyaktacodanā*).

Now, it might be argued: "Has it not been stated regarding the *iṣṭis* and *paśubandhas* occurring in the latter part [of the year] that the primary elements (*prakṛti*) are indeed those of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśapaurṇamāsika*), and that their *brāhmaṇa* texts are the same? Here, the oblations of the *vaiśvadeva*, the *varuṇapraghāsas*, and so forth, are heard as being the archetypes (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, in the case of the *māsāgnihotra* and the *darvihoma*, the status of being a modification (*vikṛti*) of the original *agnihotra* is observed. True. However, while the rule that "those of the New and Full Moon sacrifices" and so forth applies to the extension of ritual details (*atideśa*) by way of logical principle (*nyāya*), there is another [rule] established by direct scriptural statement (*vacana*).

Even in that case, there is no fault. For while it is true that [the animal sacrifice] has the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as its archetype (*prakṛti*), it also possesses other archetypes; furthermore, based on the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*), even among animals other than the five sacrificial animals (*pañcapaśu*), it has the five sacrificial animals as its archetype. Therefore, the injunction of the ritual action—consisting of the aforementioned definition together with the necessary ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*)—is precisely what constitutes the means of knowledge known as "extended application" (*atideśa*). The meaning of the two authoritative statements cited by the learned is exactly the same. To explain further: ...

The meaning is this: elsewhere—in rites such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and the Jyotiṣṭoma—the entire sequence of ritual elements (*dharmasaṃtati*) is established and prescribed; the extension (*atideśa*) refers to that scriptural statement which brings about the application of that sequence to other rites devoid of such a sequence, by means of the functional assistance (*upakāra*) to be performed.

The meaning is as follows: from that which is archetypal (*prākṛta*)—that is, from the archetype endowed with a property—to those things that are similar (i.e., endowed with the same property), or to those devoid of the property, or to those that require it, that provision of the property—that is, the attainment of the property—which occurs through a sentence accompanied by an injunction, namely a sentence of *adhyāhāra* (supplementation), exists in the form of *atideśa* (extended application).
Having thus stated the nature of *atideśa*, the consideration of its relative strength and weakness is now undertaken:
"In case of conflict, the commonality of the oblation (*havir-sāmānya*) is stronger."

When there is a conflict between a commonality of deity and a commonality of oblation (*havis*), that which possesses similarity by way of the oblation is stronger. This is because the oblation is "internal" (*antaraṅga*) as it is the substratum for the act of offering, whereas the deity is "external" (*bahiraṅga*) as it is the recipient; furthermore, the deity always functions as a qualifier of the oblation. The sense is that in a *taddhita* derivative or in a word ending in the dative case, the deity is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), while the established conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) becomes fixed in the intellect as the thing to be qualified. 4. He provides an example from the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: "For instance, a *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to Viṣṇu (*vaiṣṇavaḥ puroḍāśaḥ*)."

The properties of clarified butter (*ājya*) pertaining to Viṣṇu as the deity of the *uṣāsūyaja* sacrifice are obtained [by extension], but they are set aside by the properties of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Similarly, in the case of the offering "to Agni and Viṣṇu on eleven potsherds," Viṣṇu's status as a deity is established here even though he is distinct from the deities of the archetype (*prakṛti*), because it will be stated later that deity-status applies even to a single portion.
Offerings with a single deity are modifications of the *āgneya* [cake], provided they are other than the deities of the archetype; for example, the *saumya* pap and the *aindra* sacrificial cake.

A specific ritual action (*karmaviśeṣa*) that has as its deity a divinity expressed by a word ending in the singular number is called "having a single deity" (*ekadevata*). Through the grammatical rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining one of two identical words), the form *ekadevataśca ekadevataśca* subsequently becomes plural, i.e., "those having a single deity. Regarding the medicinal substances such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), the oblation (*caru*), and the barley-gruel (*yavāgū*), their commonality is shared among the offerings to Agni, Indra-Agni, and Prajāpati; therein, [the author] prevents the contingency of an option (*vikalpa*) in the case of an offering to two deities (*dvidevatya*).

By the word "myastu," it is intended to state that those specific modified forms (*vikṛti*) which have a single deity are indeed modifications of the *Āgneya* sacrifice alone, and not of the other two sacrifices with dual deities; furthermore, even in the case of those with dual deities, the commonality residing in their constituent parts serves as an obstacle to [the application of] the status of having a single deity. This is what is meant by the phrase "elsewhere."

Although Soma and Indra are constituent parts of a dual-deity (dvidevatya), where they function as the direct deities themselves, the similarity based on the number one is set aside by the deity-similarity—which, though arising from the constituent parts of a dual-deity, is more rapidly presented due to its being external and involving a greater number of common elements. Therefore, the sacrificial cake for Soma-Indra is a modification of the dual-deity offerings; the term *saumyaśvaścaundraḥ* refers to the deity belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*), and the compound is formed by the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member).

Although those two deities do not form a dual compound (*dvandva*) nor is a dual suffix (*taddhita*) used—since through such means only the status of a single deity for the two would be understood—nevertheless, because the status of having two deities is well-established by the dual number, the nature of being a deity is stated even for each individual part. The examples are clear. The particle *iti* is for the purpose of including specific deities such as Indra-Vimṛdha and others. Showing that the determination of *Somen-dra* and *Indrā-soma* occurs precisely through their non-distinctness (*avyatvena*), he says: "Now, the others belong to the *Agnīṣomīya* or the *Aindrāgna*."

"Modifications (vikārāḥ)," as stated previously. Now, other than those with a single deity (*ekadevatā*) from the original archetype (*prakṛti*), the [offerings] to Agni-Soma and Indra-Agni—possessing the commonality of having multiple deities—are modifications. The word "vā" (or) has the sense of a restrictive option (*vyavasthāpikalpa*), because an absence of restriction is not tenable when there is a restriction. In that case, even if the corporeal form of the deity is accepted, the status of the word as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*) is not abandoned.

Since a deity is designated by a specific word in a particular context, she is associated with that very same word; therefore, even the commonality residing in the number of syllables within the word is accepted as a basis for determination, just as the quality of gentleness and so forth resides in the components of the word. And it has been shown that this commonality of the deity is produced solely by the word.

Therefore, here too, there is a commonality based on the number of syllables contained in the words, just as a word [is considered one] despite having unity or plurality; for the deity is not perceptible such that its unity or plurality could be understood through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For this very reason, Kātyāyana says: "Those of Agnīṣomīya have two syllables, those of Aindrāgna have three syllables. There is also an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the word "below" (*adhas*) as the counterpart to the word "above" (*ūrdhva*). Those below the two-syllable [words] are three-syllable [words]. [End of] Chapter 80, together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

The meaning is that, by virtue of the commonality of being deficient by four syllables, they are modifications (*vikāra*) of the *aindrāgna* [offering]. However, in the case of the *somendra*, although it is deficient by three syllables, because *soma* comes first and thus resides more quickly in the mind, and because there is no contradiction with what has not yet been established, it should be known as a modification of the *agnīṣoma*. Likewise, in the *indrāptomīya*, even though there is an excess of two syllables, it should also be known as a modification of the *aindrāgna*. Thus, even regarding the modification of the *āgneya*, a fixed rule based on the commonality of time is accepted; for he will state later, in the section on the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), "on account of the commonality of time."

When that [modification] occurs in the essential nature (*tattva*) or in a modification (*vikāra*) of the Full Moon sacrifice, performed either on the full moon day or in its vicinity, the *tantra* (ritual framework) belongs to the Full Moon sacrifice; the same applies to the New Moon sacrifice as well. The deities such as Sarpas, Pitṛs, and Svāti are equal to Indra and Agni by virtue of their qualifying adjectives alone, because the nouns to be qualified—which possess different genders and numbers—are extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). Having described the modifications, he states the relative strength and weakness among their constituent parts:

when there is a conflict between subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) whose specific properties are integrated into the subsequent performance (*uttarā tantra*), the status of the primary element (*mukhyatva*) is more powerful.

In the *prakṛti* (archetype), namely the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, as well as in the *vikṛti* (ectypes) consisting of *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*) which likewise possess their own specific properties—those primary rites characterized by specific, mutually distinct properties, and those subsidiaries (*aṅga*) belonging to them, such being "those possessing specific properties" (*viśiṣṭadharma*)—the suffix *aniC* is not applied because the word *viśiṣṭa* is preceded by the prefix *vi-*; for according to the rule *dharmād anic kevalāt*, the suffix *aniC* is not used when the word *dharma* is preceded by anything other than a single [non-compounded] term.

In the latter extension (*uttaratantra*), which consists of modified forms such as *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices (*paśubandhas*), when there is a conflict among the subsidiary elements (*aṅgas*) brought forward by the extended injunction (*codaka*) that are inherent in each modified primary (*vaikṛta-pradhāna*), then for each modified primary, the respective archetypal (*prākṛta*) element is inherent.

When these are performed through a single performance (*tantra*), if there is mutual contradiction, whether in a case of incidental application (*prasaṅga*) or independent performance, and since a combination (*samuccaya*) is impossible due to the conflict between the primary and its subsidiaries, an option (*vikalpa*) arises. To ensure the successful execution in that situation, the author states "priority" (*mukhyatvam*) as the authoritative means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) for determining one of the two alternatives.

In the context of the archetype (*prakṛti*), "primacy" (*mukhyatva*) means being primary; that is, the first performance by the principal elements. When an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is not in conflict with the archetype and is performed first in the original model, it is "primary" (*mukhya*) because it has entered the "mouth" (*mukha*) [of the ritual] through the medium of the principal act. Its state is "primacy" (*mukhyatva*); its property is "the mark of primacy" (*talliṅga*). This is stronger than other auxiliaries that would obstruct its performance there; the meaning is that it sublates those other auxiliaries.

In the Vaiśvadeva section of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, eight principal offerings are to be performed by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). Among these, the principal offerings belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are extended there by analogy. Of those, four are modifications of the Āgneya offering; they do not conflict [with the model sacrifice] because they share commonalities with the Full Moon sacrifice. For the Saumya and Dyāvāpṛthivya offerings, the Agnīṣomīya is the archetype; for the Māruta, the Aindrāgna; and for the Āmikṣā, the morning milk-offering (*prātardoha*). For the first [offering], the ritual procedure of the Full Moon sacrifice applies.

The *tantra* (common ritual framework) for the morning offerings to Indra-Agni and the New Moon sacrifice is such that it cannot be performed as a single *tantra*. In this regard, the first *anvādhāna* (placing of fuel on the fire) for the offering to Agni-Soma is common to both; however, the subsequent carrying away of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is not common. For the offering to Indra-Agni, there is the preparation of the altar (*vedi*), and for the Sānnāyya offering, there is the fetching of the branch.

In that regard, regarding the *Dākṣāyaṇa* sacrifice on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), both [the requirements] apply: that which is connected to the full moon sacrifice and that which is connected to the bringing together of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
