When there is a conflict between the two, the status of the primary (*mukhyatva*) is more powerful. How so? Because of the recitation of the mantra and Brāhmaṇa text beginning with "For food, thee! (*iṣe tvā*), the fetching of the branch (*śākhā*) occurs first; subsequently, the fetching of the grass is stated in the passage beginning with "The roar of the sacrifice... (*yajñasya ghoṣad asīti*).

In that regard, since the sequence in the Vaiśvadeva parvan consists of fetching the branch and fetching the sacrificial grass (barhis) one after another, the statement found in all manuscripts— that "the specific properties [apply] because of their primacy, characterized by being present in the prior cognition due to the absence of any specific desire for [other] distinctions such as the *bhyaḥ* [suffix]"— is merely a result of negligence (*prāmādika*). [From the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Third Book.]

It provides the *tantra* (common procedure) only for the *darśa* sacrifice, as well as for the *aindrāgna* and the *sāṃnāyya*. Even though there are two offerings of *sāṃnāyya*, because the evening milking is intended solely for the sake of the *āmikṣā*, it does not possess the status of a primary substance; thus, it does not have the requirement for subsidiaries (*aṅgākāṅkṣitva*). Therefore, one should not suspect that there is a greater number [of subsidiaries] on its account. The modified (*vaikṛta*) primary sacrifices require subsidiaries simultaneously, and in them, the archetypal (*prākṛta*) primaries are connected all at once. In that case, a single [deity], whether Āgneya or Agnīṣomīya, cannot enter into a simultaneous connection with multiple [subsidiaries].

And thus, since the state of being contrary to the modification (*prativaikṛtatva*) belongs to the primary [elements], and the *aindrāgna* occurs in the repetition while the *aindra* does not, one should not suspect a greater number for the latter two. In this way, it should be understood that primacy or plurality resides only in what pertains to the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the primary [elements], but not in what pertains to the modification (*vikṛti*) and the secondary elements; for plurality follows from primacy.

From this point forward, the previous sūtra is to be supplied everywhere except for the word *mukhyatva* (primacy). "Abundance" (*bhūyastva*) means a greater number among the primary elements of the same class. A category in which the primary elements of a similar nature are fewer is sublated by a category in which the primary elements are more numerous.

The intention is as follows: At the outset, the collection of modified elements is understood in its mere essential form through the rules of original production (*utpattividhi*). Once that essential form is determined, at the very time of its ascertainment, its deficiency or excess is perceived for the sake of obtaining the extended application (*atideśa*). In that situation, it is logical to favor the majority; thus, when a determination is made regarding the sublation of the few by the many at the stage when the conflict first arises, the sequence of performance—which is established subsequently in the mind—cannot later invalidate the primacy (*mukhyatva*) existing therein, nor can that primacy again prevail to sublate the excess (itself).

Just as in the case where curd, honey, clarified butter, water, and parched grain are mixed together to form an oblation for Prajāpati, the predominance of the curd is known through its being the primary element brought in by the fetching of the branch; by that much alone, it is understood beforehand that the triad beginning with honey is a modification of clarified butter (*ājya*). Because of this abundance, it sublates the predominance that was understood immediately [afterward]. [This is an example of] position (*sthāna*) being sublated by abundance (*bhūyastva*).

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because the *savanīya* oblations—such as the parched grains (*dhānāḥ*) and the groats (*karambhaḥ*) prescribed within the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) at the *agniṣṭoma* and other rites; and the eight sacrifices beginning with "He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Gṛhapati," which are to be performed following the *agnīṣomīya* animal-cake offering at the *vājapeya* and other rites—are more numerous than the *darśapūrṇamāsa* procedures, the animal-sacrifice procedure—including its eleven *prayāja* offerings and so forth—should be set aside. However, it has been stated that "position" (*sthāna*) is stronger [than sequence].

Position (*sthāna*) is twofold: proximity by recitation (*pāṭhasādeśya*) and proximity by performance (*anuṣṭhānasādeśya*). In the present case, it is proximity by performance that constitutes the position. In that context, at the time of performance, the *savanīya* and the *agnīṣomīya* are performed together because they have been commenced in that place. This is because, at the commencement of that [commencement], the *anuniṣvāpya* offerings of the *savanīya* are not yet present to the mind.

In that case, for one who has performed only a few of the contradictory constituent parts of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) according to its ritual manual (*tantra*), the animal sacrifice does not serve as the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the subsequent sublation of many [details] belonging to the *tantra* already commenced. Therefore, the animal sacrifice assists the cake offerings (*puroḍāśa*) by way of extension (*prasanga*). Regarding "position" (*sthāna*): a rule inferred from position is sublated by an explicit (*pratyakṣa*) rule. The position of the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice] is [the day before the Soma-pressing], namely the day of fasting (*aupavasathya*).

1kha. ca. cha. ṭa. Authorship. [This is the first section. Together with the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva: 373. Regarding the *Sādyaska* sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "One should immolate the animals together. Therein, since the simultaneous immolation of the *agnīṣomīya*, the *āgneya*, and the *anūbandhya* animals is understood through the scriptural mention of "together" (*saha*), the precedence of the *agnīṣomīya*—which is obtained by virtue of its proximity due to the commonality of position before the *savanīya*—is established as immediate. However, in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), this is overridden by what is heard there: "Having taken the *āśvina* cup, one should encircle the sacrificial post with a triple-twisted cord (*trivṛt*)."...

The injunction "one who dedicates the Savanīya animal to Agni" prescribes immediate succession to the Āśvina cup by means of an injunction supported by the suffix -tvā; this [succession] is obtained in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) by the rule of extension (codaka) in exactly that same way, and by this, the position of the Agnīṣomīya [animal] is set aside. For the injunction—being a direct (pratyakṣa) injunction—prescribes only the mere immediate succession between the taking of the cup and the dedication of the animal to Agni, both of which are already established.

Although the injunction inferred from the position (*sthāna*) of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice is indeed the authority, it is nevertheless inferred by depending upon that position which has been extended (*atidiṣṭa*). Since that [injunction] is also sublated when the position is sublated, it is said that "the injunction [is derived] from the position. Nor can an injunction accompanied by a simultaneous recitation (*sahaśruti*)—being directly taught (*aupadeśika*)—sublate what is extended; for what is simultaneously recited must be understood as mere proximity (*saṃnikarṣamātra*), not priority (*paurvāparya*).

Furthermore, the injunction regarding simultaneous performance (*sahālambha*) is not directly taught (*aupadeśika*) as being assisted by position (*sthāna*), such that it would become more powerful. Moreover, once the act of touching (*ālambha*) has been established, it is impossible to enjoin two qualities—namely, simultaneity (*sāhitya*) and priority (*pūrvabhāvitva*). Therefore, the injunction inferred from position is indeed sublated; it is merely a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the injunction.

The sequence following the Āśvina cup is understood through the injunction to apply to the entire Savanīya animal sacrifice along with its subsidiaries; just as there is no room for the Āgnīṣomīya sacrifice in the interval, so too there is none for its subsidiaries. This being the prima facie view, it is replied: since the injunction establishes the sequence of the sacrifices, and because the injunction of simultaneity (*sāhitya*) makes known the proximity of the various immolations, it is impossible to perform the immolation without first performing the subsidiaries characterized by those respective immolations (such as the ritual slaughter). Therefore, the injunction of simultaneity overrides the injunction regarding the subsidiaries.

Furthermore, it is not logical that for all of those [animals], the performance [of the subsidiaries] should occur prior to each respective primary act (*ālambha*), because this would be sublated by the general rule of *padārthānusamaya* (sequential performance of individual constituent acts). When it is stated that "those which are conjoined terminate with one [act]," there is no authority for *kāṇḍānusamaya* (sequential performance of groups of acts). Therefore, since the subsidiaries are understood to be performed together, the immediate succession of the group of subsidiaries of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice—established by *padārthānusamaya*—sublates the extended application (*atideśa*) regarding the subsidiary *savaniya* sacrifice.
The primary act follows after the subsidiary.

Regarding one afflicted by *pāpayakṣma* (consumption), it is heard in scripture that there is a *puroḍāśa* cake for Indra and Varuṇa and a *āmikṣā* curd-mixture for Indra and Varuṇa. Furthermore, it is heard: "Having completed the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsau*) with the optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭibhiḥ*), one should sacrifice.

Consequently, on the first day (*pratipad*), since the *sāṃnāyya* offerings are performed either on the same day (*sadyaskālā*) or on the following day (*yahakālā*), and because the modification of the *sāṃnāyya* follows the time of the [following] day, it would follow—given that one has sacrificed with the obligatory oblation and performed the evening milking—that the sacrifice takes place on the second day. However, it has been stated that "the principal [act] prevails over the subsidiary"; thus, the time of the subsidiary is sublated by the time of the principal, which is the *parvan* (the junction day).

Having raised the objection that "the milking occurs on the fourteenth day and the sacrifice on the fifteenth day in the Vaiśvadeva parvan, because it is seen so," [the author] states—on the authority of the Śruti—that the performance of optional (kāmya) iṣṭis and animal sacrifices follows immediately after the obligatory (nitya) iṣṭi, saying: 11. In the case of a conflict between the Darśapūrṇamāsa and a modified sacrifice (vikṛti), the Darśapūrṇamāsa are stronger. *Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram*, Third Book. 374.
[In the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and the vikṛtis occurring together, the Darśapūrṇamāsa are more powerful.]

When there is a conjunction of the New Moon (darśa) or Full Moon (paurṇamāsa) sacrifice with a modified sacrifice (vikṛti)—whether in the form of an *iṣṭi* or an animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*)—the simultaneous performance would result in a conflict of auxiliary elements (*aṅga-vipratiṣedha*) due to the identity of time. Whether the New Moon or Full Moon sacrifice is the model (*prakṛti*) and the modified sacrifice is the opposite, or vice versa, when there is a conflict regarding the modified sacrifice, its auxiliaries—which are obtained through inferred extension (*atideśa*)—are set aside by those of the model sacrifice, because the latter's auxiliaries are directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*). The directly enjoined auxiliaries are stronger and thus sublate the others.

And thus, it is understood that sometimes even a great *tantra* exists separately from a modification (*vikṛti*). For instance, when the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) belonging to the new-moon rite is performed on the full moon day by means of a *tantra*, it takes on the *tantra* of the full-moon rite. It should not be argued that this [sūtra] does not enjoin a *tantra* but rather enjoins the sequence (*paurvāparya*); for such an interpretation would contradict the subsequent sūtra, since the alternative method—consisting of sequence and so forth—is determined in various places.

This has been stated quite clearly by Bharadvāja: "The modified sacrifice (vikṛti) may have the same ritual procedure as the New and Full Moon sacrifices. And thus, among the modified sacrifices, a modified sacrifice with the same ritual procedure is performed on the same day [as its archetype] only when it is a Full Moon sacrifice performed on the same day; it is not otherwise.

The *sadyaskālā* [rite] performed on the fourteenth day is not similar to the *cāturmāsya* festivals which begin on the first day (*dyahakāla*) according to their original form (*prakṛti*). In that case, since the original form is not identical, it is impossible for there to be similarity with the *vikṛti* (modified rite) that was commenced on the previous day. Thus, the established rule is that the *vikṛti* must be performed even before the principal sacrifice (*pradhānayāga*), and so forth. This is how the procedure is to be understood.

And thus, because the *iṣṭi*s and animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*)—along with their modifications such as the *sāṃnāyya* and *avatsāṃnāyya*—are prescribed to be performed at the time of the cup-offerings (*graha*), and because they are prescribed to be performed immediately after the obligatory *iṣṭi*, it is impossible for the two [the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa*] together with their subsidiaries to be performed simultaneously. Therefore, when there is a common performance (*tantra-anuṣṭhāna*), since the simultaneity of the principal acts alone would be lost, their performance must necessarily follow the sequence [of the original]. In this regard, the strength [of the sequence] has also been stated by the rule of "reading in order" (*krama-pāṭha*) regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and its modifications; this is the intended meaning. As for those [elements] of the *iṣṭi*s and animal sacrifices that are directly perceived, they apply there [in that specific context].

The phrase "the stronger ones" refers back to the discussion on conflict (*vipratipatti*). "Those which are directly perceived" means those things brought forward by the means of knowledge such as direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and so forth for the sake of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*); that is to say, those brought forward by a source of authority other than the injunction for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-codaka*). For it is not the case that in every instance only those things enjoined by direct Vedic statement are possible. By the word "but" (*tu*), the sublation of the previous principle is stated. How so? Even though both are based on direct instruction (*aupadeśika*), that injunction which is commenced when something has not [otherwise] been established becomes the sublater of that [previously established thing].

Thus, when the extension (*atideśa*) has already been established, certain directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) subsidiaries in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) which are incompatible with the extended subsidiaries arise precisely through the sublation (*bādha*) of that extension, and not otherwise. As it has been stated: "Because it is not yet born, the later [element] arises without having sublated the earlier; since there is no other way for the later to arise, sublation is indeed possible."

Therefore, even though both [the archetypal and the modified] are directly taught (*aupadeśika*), the modified subsidiaries (*vaikṛtāṅgāni*) are stronger; thus, when there is a common ritual procedure (*samānatantre*) involving a modified *aindrāgna* or *āśvina* sacrifice, there is no direct scriptural injunction (*pratyakṣāṅgatā*) for them. Nevertheless, because they were already obtained through the general extension (*atideśa*) from the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices prior to this, this animal-sacrifice extension (*pāśukātideśa*) proceeds as the more powerful one according to the previously stated principle. Furthermore, the modified animal sacrifice does not become devoid of its requirements (*nirākāṅkṣa*) merely by the extension from the Darśapūrṇamāsa.

Because there is an expectation of the *māyāvatī* [verse] based on the previously mentioned *aṅganāta* (the sequence of ritual acts), and because the extension (*atideśa*) from the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices—which functions by subverting that previous extension—would itself be subverted; for it is impossible for what has already been applied to be applied again. Furthermore, the state of having five *prayāja* offerings is not subverted by the eleven *prayāja* offerings and so forth, because the number of five *prayājas* does not disappear even when they are repeated. [End of] Chapter [X], together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 375.

Having explained the extension (*atideśa*) by means of the passage beginning with "those belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*dārśapaurṇamāsikāni*), as well as its strength and weakness, [the author now argues: in certain cases—namely, the *āmikṣā*, the *avabhṛtha*, and the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*)—there is no status of being a modification (*vikṛti*) because the cause for extension, namely the lack of intrinsic properties (*asvadharmatva*), is absent. However, other *āmikṣā* offerings and animal sacrifices are modifications of those [sacrifices] alone due to the commonality of the name "oblation" (*havis*). Thus, the subsequent section—which was stated without distinction as a modification of the New and Full Moon sacrifices—must be restricted. Why? Because the distinction between them is based on the principle that "that which possesses its own properties is the archetype (*prakṛti*), while that which lacks its own properties is the modification (*vikṛti*)."

Having raised the objection that [the modified sacrifices] possess their own specific properties (*svadharma*) because of the scriptural fragment stating "those [are] their own properties," and because they exist as actualized results, he says:
the *iṣṭi*s and *paśubandha*s, which have the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as their archetype, possess their own properties; the modification [of the archetype] occurs through commonality.

Those very sacrifices which possess their own specific characteristics (*svadharma*) by virtue of their commonality with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*—namely, the *iṣṭis* and the *paśubandhas*, which are modifications (*vikāra*) of it—are also stated without distinction to have the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as their archetype (*prakṛti*). The analysis of the compound is: "those for which the *darśapūrṇamāsa* is the archetype. The *iṣṭis* are enjoined by the verb *nirvapati* (he offers), and the *paśubandhas* are enjoined by the verb *ālabhati* (he immolates). In this regard, it is established merely that there is an extension (*atideśa*) [of details] on the basis of indicative marks (*liṅga*); however, the similarity that prompts the application [of the archetype] consists in the commonality of the deity or the commonality of the oblation (*havis*) in a ritual action (*karman*) that is otherwise new (*apūrva*).

Therefore, although the similarity of the deity (*devatāsāmya*) is not all-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), the similarity of the oblation (*havis-sāmānya*) is indeed all-pervasive. Furthermore, although the universals (*jāti*) such as "being medicinal herbs" (*auṣadhatva*), "being clarified butter" (*ājyatva*), "being curd" (*dadhitva*), and "being milk" (*payastva*) are not all-pervasive, nevertheless, even in their absence, a similarity in the form of an adjunct (*upādhi*) is certainly possible everywhere. And that [adjunct] has already been shown previously: as "solidity" (*kaṭhinadravyatva*) in the case of black-gram seeds (*kṛṣṇala*), and as "liquidity" (*dravadravyatva*) in the case of honey and water.

And thus, for all *iṣṭis*, there exists a pervasive similarity based on the commonality of each being a *darśapūrṇamāsa* primary sacrifice, which indeed serves as the basis for extension (*atideśa*). Furthermore, when the extension to the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) is established by means of indicative marks (*liṅga*), there too exists a similarity based on the commonality of "originating from an animal," which is shared by all animal sacrifices and serves as the basis for extension. Moreover, the basis for being the archetype (*prakṛti*) is the possession of all enjoined constituent parts; and that [possession] applies precisely to all the primary sacrifices of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

The determining factor for being a modification (*vikṛti*) is the deficiency of constituent parts (*aṅga*) in all *iṣṭis* compared to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Therefore, all *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*), as shown by their specific injunctions, have the New and Full Moon sacrifices as their archetype (*prakṛti*). These [archetypes] possess their own inherent properties (*svadharma*), yet they do not possess the properties of the New and Full Moon sacrifices; thus, while being modifications of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, they also come to possess their own inherent properties. Those which [possess] their own inherent properties...

The *prakṛtis* (archetypes) belong only to those [rites] that possess their own specific characteristics (*svadharma*) and are devoid of those [characteristics] belonging to others; and those [rites] which are devoid of such characteristics acquire [the details of another] through extension (*atideśa*), and by that much they are its *vikṛtis* (modifications), but not exclusively its *vikṛtis*. This is because there is no extension of the subsidiaries of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśapaurṇamāsa*) to them. Nor can those very rites possessing their own characteristics, when accompanied by extended subsidiaries, be the instigators of a complete extension.

If that were the case, then a *vikṛti* (modified sacrifice) performed immediately after the performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* would be complete with all its auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), while the *prakṛti* (archetype) performed immediately after it would [be incomplete], and that [in turn] would apply to the one performed immediately after it, and so on. Furthermore, there is no fixed commonality that serves as the basis for *atideśa* (extended application) in those cases. Nor is there a universal sequence of performance for the *iṣṭis* and *paśubandhas* common to all persons.

Furthermore, there would be a lack of systematic order (*avyavasthā*). Moreover, the application of extended injunctions (*atideśa*) to rites performed in a specific sequence, as well as a commonality (*sāmānya*), would be difficult to establish. Therefore, the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) alone are the archetype (*prakṛti*) for all at the outset. Since everything other than those shares that commonality, it is simpler to regard all others as modifications (*vikṛti*). Furthermore, it must be stated that even though a modification possesses its own inherent properties, it acquires its subsidiary parts through the extension from the New and Full Moon sacrifices and then transmits them to another.

Even in the case of a qualified extension (*viśiṣṭātideśa*), when the extension from the *darśapūrṇamāsa* is present in the mind, and subsequently the qualification by its own specific properties (*svadharma*) is present in the mind, then the qualified extension applies to the modifications (*vikṛti*) of those modifications. It is simpler, however, to have one universal extension and a second [extension] for the modification of its own specific properties; for in the case of a qualified extension, there would be two extensions even in the modifications of those modifications. (Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, Third Book—376)

Furthermore, the sequence between the two types of extended application (*atideśa*) is indeed established, and that is what is intended. How so? In the case of modifications (*vikṛti*) of the primary ritual (*prakṛti*), there is first a requirement for the "how" (*kathambhāva*), followed by the connection with the elements already extended; subsequently, there is the connection with the enjoined (*aupadeśika*) subsidiaries. For the "how" is a requirement for assistance (*upakāra*). This [requirement] first seizes those very subsidiaries that have been extended, by way of the assistance already provided. However, in the case of the enjoined subsidiaries, no assistance has yet been rendered. And because the injunction would otherwise be inexplicable, there is a requirement for those elements whose purpose is perceptible (*dṛṣṭārtha*).

In the case of a primary rite (*aṅgin*), the expectation of assistance (*upakāra*) arises; therefore, once the connection with the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) is understood through the mutual expectation (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*), the assistance must be postulated from them. Even in the case of those [subsidiaries] whose purpose is visible (*dṛṣṭārtha*), the postulation of a visible assistance occurs appropriately after the connection with the primary has been established. Therefore, for the subsequent subsidiaries, their application (*anvaya*) occurs only after they have been extended (*atidiṣṭa*). By this very sequence, the order of the two types of extension is established even in the case of modifications of modifications (*vikṛti-vikṛti*). And at the beginning, the universal extension remains present in the mind.

[The transfer] would follow from itself. Subsequently, through the general principle of specific [elements], there is a transfer of specific details that were previously unobserved but are now to be inferred;

thus, the transfer of sequence is also established. For this very reason, the elders have said: "A beggar does not beg from another beggar. For a modification (*vikṛti*) is like a beggar because its constituent parts (*aṅga*) are obtained from elsewhere. It obtains food solely for its own nourishment, and not to give to another—this is the meaning of the maxim. Thus, when the fixed relationship between archetype (*prakṛti*) and modification is established...

The sequence of priority and posteriority is established even among the modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *āmikṣā* sacrifice, as is the determination of its constituent parts (*aṅga*). For instance, all *āmikṣā* offerings are modifications of the morning milking and are thus modifications of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*). Subsequently, the *vaiśvadeva-āmikṣā* possesses its own specific characteristics (*svadharma*), because the extraction of the curds (*dhyuddharaṇa*) and other such constituent parts, as well as the *hautra* (priestly recitation), are prescribed for it in our own Vedic branch (*śākhā*). Likewise, in the *Dākṣāyaṇa-yajña*, the *āmikṣā* also possesses its own specific characteristics. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says with reference to it: "In that very case, the milking is performed, or one adds curds to the heated milk."

Having poured out the *vājina* (curdled milk) onto the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), or having offered a blade of grass smeared with clarified butter (*ājya*), he proceeds with that; or, having released the two *khuda* vessels, he takes [the *vājina*] while pouring it outside. "He thus places the seed in the *darbha* grasses," so says the Śruti—thus [it was stated] by our own Sūtra-author.

"Furthermore, according to one's own *śākhā*, even the instruction regarding the duties of alms-gathering for the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña* is explained within the context of the *Vaiśvadevī* [offering] itself. Just as the instruction regarding the duties of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) such as the *Agnīṣomīya* applies specifically to the *Nirūḍha* [animal sacrifice], so it is here as well. And thus, although the nine *prayāja*s and other elements are obtained in the *āmikṣā* of the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña* by extension (*atideśa*) from the *Vaiśvadevī*, they are sublated in that [offering] denoted by the term 'Darśa' by the five *prayāja*s and other elements belonging to the *aupabhṛta* [portion]."

Similarly, the five *prayāja*s and so forth obtained for the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice by means of extended application (*atideśa*) are set aside by the nine *prayāja*s and so forth obtained through direct injunction (*upadeśa*). The same applies to the *varuṇapraghāsa* and the *āmikṣā* offerings as well. In that case too, because of the statement, "These very *brāhmaṇa*-texts prescribe five oblations," the nine *prayāja*s and so forth are obtained for the five [oblations] by means of a scriptural extension; since these are more numerous, the five *prayāja*s and so forth belonging to the *āmikṣā* are set aside by them.

In the case of the other *āmikṣā* offerings, by the extended application (*atideśa*) from the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, nine *prayāja* oblations and so forth are obtained; and by the extended application from the *dākṣāyaṇayajña* *āmikṣā*, five *prayāja* oblations and so forth are obtained. Thus, since the five *prayāja* oblations and so forth are already obtained first through the modification (*vikāra*) of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*), the extended application from the *dākṣāyaṇayajña* *āmikṣā* is more powerful, and consequently, the five *prayāja* oblations and so forth are established.

However, it should be understood that in the case of the *savanīyāmikṣā* offerings, the *tantra* of the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*)—which consists of the eleven *prayāja* offerings and so forth—is not at all sublated. This is because the *savanīya-puroḍāśas*, as the established procedure (*sthānin*), provide assistance by being present [at the time]. Thus, having explained the relative strength and weakness of the extended applications (*atideśa*) regarding the primary rites of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) and so forth, he now states the exceptions (*apavāda*) to those extended applications: [End of Section] [From the Vaijayantī commentary composed by Mahādeva] 377

Substances connected with a ritual action acquire their specific properties through that connection in the archetype (*prakṛti*). When the action no longer exists, the substance together with its properties ceases. Regarding the sublation of prescribed subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) due to the absence of a means (*dvārābhāva*), the purposefulness of this is established in this sūtra by the prescription of other subsidiary elements in its place. This is stated sequentially by the two following sūtras on account of prohibition. In the case of the *kṛṣṇala* oblation, where the substances are bones rather than plants, it is considered whether the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅgatā*) and their properties apply to items such as the wooden sword (*sphya*) and so forth without distinction, or only specifically to those actually employed in the ritual action.

In that context, because items such as the *sphya* (wooden sword) are praised as sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*), those for which no visible benefit is perceived are considered subsidiary (*aṅga*) by virtue of having an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Consequently, since the properties of those [implements] are likewise [invisible], the principle "the modification (*vikṛti*) should be performed like the archetype (*prakṛti*)" applies through extension (*atideśa*) without distinction. Thus, setting aside the *kapāla* (potsherds), *śūrpa* (winnowing basket), and so forth, how could the *Aṅgahīneṣṭi* sacrifice accomplish its fruit? Therefore, when it is argued that these too are subsidiary, the following reply is stated, beginning with the words "connected with the ritual action" (*karmasaṃyuktāni*).

Substances connected with ritual actions are prescribed as subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) within the archetype (*prakṛti*), not in their own right; this is the remainder [of the argument]. The meaning is this: when the sacrifice together with its subsidiaries is being enjoined by the threefold means of injunction, there is nothing—neither a primary element (*pradhāna*) nor a subsidiary (*aṅga*)—that is not encompassed by the injunction. Furthermore, an injunction is not possible regarding a mere substance. For an injunction, while making known that something is to be done (*kartavyatā*), makes known that what is to be done is a means to achieve a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*). And a substance, being already established (*siddha*), cannot be made known as something "to be done."

Otherwise, by virtue of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), [the action] would be indeterminate, and it could only become a means to a desired end through the mediation of generating an *apūrva*. Furthermore, there is no other authority (*pramāṇa*) for the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) apart from the injunction (*vidhi*). For this very reason it has been said: "Ritual acts are characterized by injunction. Nor should it be argued that, this being the case, substances (*dravya*)—being non-injunctional and thus not auxiliary members (*aṅga*)—would consequently lack the status of being part of the ritual; for even substances are indeed enjoined when they are connected with a ritual act, even though they are not themselves to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in their own nature.

Nevertheless, when conjoined with an action, those [factors] become subservient to the action precisely because they serve as its means; thus, they are indeed things to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Therefore, in all cases, even an action is something to be enjoined by virtue of being a means to the *apūrva*, and its status as a means to the highest good (*śreyas*) does not exist in its own form alone. For it has already been stated that since the mere form [of an action] is cognizable through other means of knowledge, the form of the ritual act itself cannot be the object of an injunction, which has as its domain only that which is not already known.

For this very reason, Jaimini stated that "words denoting action have the sacrifice as their purpose; from them, the action is to be understood," thereby asserting that action alone is the means to the *apūrva*. By stating that "those [words] which denote existing things are connected with words denoting action" (*tadbhūtānāṃ kriyārthena samanvayaḥ*), and further declaring that "if the *apūrva* arises from one [action], then the other is for its sake," Jaimini taught that the *apūrva* results from action itself, and that it also results from substances through their connection with that action. It has been stated more than once that being a subordinate (*aṅga*) or a primary (*pradhāna*) element depends on the capacity to generate the *apūrva*, and not upon the intrinsic nature of the thing itself.

Therefore, he says that when an action—which produces its own unique result (*apūrva*) either directly or through a series—is no longer present, even a substance that serves as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) ceases to be a subsidiary merely by virtue of being a means to that [action]. Thus: "When the action is absent, the substance is withdrawn. And in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* berries, there is no action to be accomplished by means of the potsherds, the winnowing basket, and so forth.

Furthermore, in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*), items such as the potsherds (*kapāla*) and the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) are not established as means for performing rites for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*); rather, the potsherds, the winnowing basket, and so forth are established as means for performing rites for the sake of a visible result (*dṛṣṭārtha*). For that [visible purpose] is the means for producing the *niyamāpūrva* (the transcendental result of the restrictive rule), and thus it is what should be enjoined. If it is objected: "In that case, since the potsherds, the winnowing basket, and so forth are subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) by virtue of being the means for washing, wiping, and sprinkling, their employment [in the modified sacrifice] should still occur," the author replies to that: "In the archetype, they acquire their properties through connection with those [subsidiaries]; when the rite [to which they belong] no longer exists, the substance together with its properties ceases."
1. Kha. cha. *samānāya* | 2. cha. *rasada* | 48 | 378. The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[Book 3, Chapter 1]—the third section.

In the passage "one shall wash the vessels" (*pātrāṇi prakṣālyet*), the substance is not enjoined as a means for the acts of washing and so forth by virtue of its being the object of the accusative case; for, through the direct denotation of the accusative, it is understood as the primary objective (*uddeśyatva*). Thus, the vessels do not possess the status of an instrument (*sādhanatā*) with respect to the action of washing, but rather they are the objective (*karmatva*) as that which is intended to be reached. This is because of Pāṇini’s rule: "That which is most desired to be reached is the *karman* (object); the second case ending is used for the *karman*. Consequently, the state of being "most desired to be reached" must be stated as the instrument for those actions whose purpose is the *apūrva* (the unseen spiritual merit).

Their status as instruments (*sādhanatā*) is understood from such injunctions as "one places [the grain] upon the potsherd" (*kapāle 'dhiśrayati*), which prescribe placing, pouring out, and so forth, in relation to the potsherds, the winnowing basket, and other implements. Because they are intended as the most desired means (*īpsitatama*) for achieving those results, they possess the status of the object (*karmatva*) with respect to actions such as washing. Therefore, substances do not have washing and the like as their own inherent goals (*sādhya*); rather, through their connection with various actions that have those acts as their goals, the substances acquire properties in the form of washing and so forth.

By the term *dharma*, it is stated that the substance (*dravya*) possesses the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) by virtue of being an action of refinement (*saṃskārakarma*). However, that substance deserves refinement only if it is to be employed elsewhere, and not otherwise; for according to the maxim, "only a substance whose utility is either past or future deserves refinement. Actions of refinement do not directly produce the *apūrva* (transcendental result), such that they would be enjoined as auxiliaries [by virtue of producing it].

However, according to the principle stated by Jaimini—that "wherever a substance is intended [by an action], a quality is understood therein"—the capacity to produce the *apūrva* (unseen merit) belongs to those things that serve as the means for actions which directly or indirectly produce the *apūrva*. Thus, while they produce a visible benefit (*dṛṣṭopakāra*) in the substances used as the instruments of such actions, they also produce an unseen benefit (*adṛṣṭa*), characterized as an inherent potentiality (*ādheyaśakti*), in those substances by way of restrictive rules (*niyama*).

From acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), only the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) is produced; and a substance possessing an unseen power directly accomplishes the action that serves as the means to the *apūrva*. For example, the substance [of the sacrifice] belonging to the minor rites (*aṅga*) such as the *prayāja* [accomplishes the action], whereas a certain substance [of the main rite] accomplishes, through its constituent parts or by way of its existence, the action that is the means to the *apūrva*, being an action that possesses a visible power and serves as the means to the *apūrva*; just as a substance consecrated by acts such as washing serves as the primary means to the *apūrva*.

That which accomplishes threshing and other such acts, serving as the means for the ritual action, accomplishes the action that is the means for the *apūrva* (the unseen transcendental result). Now, no one would seek an invisible benefit (*adṛṣṭopakāra*) from threshing and the like in the case of [substitutes] such as the *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces, because an invisible benefit has not been established for them through the rule of extension (*atideśa*). Therefore, since the rituals whose benefits have not been produced are excluded, the substances that serve as their means are also excluded; consequently, even the purificatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*) upon those substances are excluded due to the absence of their own substrates. For this is the nature of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).

It does not take up the subsidiaries by means of the extension of the original nature (*prakṛtyatideśa*) and then acquire the visible and invisible assistance as appropriate; rather, desiring visible and invisible assistance, it takes up other subsidiaries. In that regard, while being a general attractor (*grāhikā*) of those subsidiaries that produce invisible assistance—namely the *ārādupakāraka* (indirectly assisting) ones—it takes up only those *saṃnipatyopakāraka* (directly assisting) elements that provide the required visible assistance, and not even those that would be purposeless.

Therefore, just as materials that serve no purpose are excluded, so too are ritual preparations (saṃskāra) that serve no purpose excluded; such is the meaning of the Sūtra. He provides an illustration:
"as, for example, the threshing of black rice-grains (kṛṣṇala)."

"One who fears death should offer this *prāṇāpatya* [oblation] consisting of a hundred *kṛṣṇalas*. Since *kṛṣṇalas* are made of gold, they do not require visible processing—such as the removal of husks—which is characteristic of vegetable products; therefore, threshing (*avahanana*) is excluded. This is the implied meaning. The phrase "when the ritual action is absent, the properties and the substance are excluded" follows from the previous sūtra. [End of Section] [This is] accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

But surely, when the taking [of the offering] has ceased even in the case of the *kapāla* vessels during the *iṣṭi*, those *kapālas* which possess those properties (*sadharmaka*) are excluded; likewise, in the *iṣṭi* of *śyāmāka* grains, when the pouring out of *vrīhi* rice has ceased and the *vrīhis* possessing those properties are excluded, would not those properties fail to exist in the cooking-pot (*sthālī*) and in the *śyāmākas*? To this he says:
"And when another substance is joined with that purpose, there is an entry of the properties."

When that archetypal [element] is connected with another substance—being enjoined as a subsidiary (aṅga) by means of that same archetypal purpose which is to be accomplished by the archetypal substance, yet possessing a new purpose—in that case as well, there is the entry of the ritual properties (dharmas), that is, their manifestation through extended application (atideśa). This is the underlying intention: here, the cessation of the cooking does not entail the cessation of the potsherds; rather, the cooking of the sacrificial porridge (caru) is obtained through a vessel established by functional capacity (sāmarthya) which has taken the place of the potsherds. In that context, the action that serves as the means for the transcendental result (apūrva) has not ceased.

And its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), even though qualified by a different class (*jātyantara*), is obtained; that which takes its place and subverts it is indeed that very thing, as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) by virtue of being the means for producing the new transcendental result (*apūrva*) born of cooking. In that very auxiliary prompted by the *apūrva*, the ritual properties (*dharma*) also certainly occur. Thus Pāṇini says: "The substitute (*ādeśa*) has the same properties as the original element (*sthānin*). Otherwise, that *apūrva* would not arise from it at all. He provides an illustration:
the property of the potsherds [belongs] to the pan, and the property of the rice-grains [belongs] to the *śyāmāka* millet.

The word "is extended" (atidiśyate) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. By this, the determination of extension (atideśa) even with respect to a non-original substance (aprākṛta-dravya) is made clear. Fearing an over-extension (atiprasaṅga)—namely, that when an action to be accomplished by a substance fails, its properties would be extended even to another substance substituted in its place—he says:
"If [the sacrifice] were prohibited at its origin, everything would be prohibited."

It arises from the sacrificial act—that is, from the action which is a constituent part of the sacrifice—or else it arises for the sake of the sacrifice, that is, for its purpose. The word "substance" (*dravya*) is understood to follow here. By "arising," one indicates the attainment of fitness for the purpose. Since the substance, when consecrated by ritual action, becomes fit for its purpose, when a substance qualified by such action is prohibited, the action intended for that purpose—which serves as a means to the *apūrva* (the unseen spiritual merit)—is thereby prohibited. Furthermore, other categories of dharma would also be prohibited.

For the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is produced by the act characterized by digging and measuring; it is to be obtained as something fit for the purpose of the sacrifice and for the tethering of the animal. When that [post] is specifically excluded from being obtained, its consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*) would also be excluded.

It should not be argued that, just as in the case of "he does not place the curd on the fire," only the measuring (*māna*) is prohibited while other consecrations (*saṃskāra*) qualified by it are not, and therefore tying (*niyojana*) is also not prohibited; thus, even without measuring, the animal might be tied to another object such as a *paridhi*, a fire-brand (*ulmuka*), or sacrificial grass (*barhis*) that has been consecrated by other rites. For if that were so, one would have to say merely "they do not measure" in reference to the *paridhi* and others which have taken the place of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); the mention of the "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) would then be redundant.

Nor should it be argued that the meaning is "they do not erect [it] like a sacrificial post" (*yūpa*); for in the case of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and so forth, even their very nature—namely, their suitability for the purpose of the animal sacrifice—would be sublated. Therefore, since the injunction regarding them prescribes the tethering of the animal precisely without subverting the form inherent to their own nature, the act of measuring (*māna*) ceases of its own accord; what, then, would be the purpose of a prohibition? Consequently, the prohibition applies only to the substitute (*sthānin*) which serves as the functional equivalent of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) as an object of action. Thus, a different substance must be enjoined as something entirely new (*apūrva*). Nor can there be an instruction (*upadeśa*) for that [new substance].

Other consecrations (*saṃskāra*) would exist by means of both direct injunction and extension. When the original substance (*prākṛtadravya*) is obtained, however, those consecrations belong to its substitute. Thus says the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the third book].

They do not obtain [the properties] otherwise. By the prohibition of that [sacrificial post], the extended application (*atideśa*) itself is prohibited; there is no longer any direct instruction (*upadeśa*). Even if the tying (*niyojana*) were archetypal (*prākṛta*), and even if it were thus [obtained] through extended application, those [properties] would not be employed merely for the sake of the means of tying; otherwise, they would undesirably apply even to the sacrificial ladle (*aśvaśapha*), which is also a means of tying. Therefore, when the sacrificial post is prohibited, the properties of the post are indeed prohibited. For the *uttaravedi* (high altar) is prescribed in place of the archetypal *āhavanīya* fire.

And upon its prohibition, the *prākṛta* (archetypal) *āhavanīya* fire itself is established as the locus for the oblation. Just as it is obtained by virtue of being the archetypal requirement through the technical name "āhavanīya" and the scriptural injunction "one offers in the āhavanīya," so too is it obtained by virtue of being the modified (*vikṛti*) requirement, even when the injunction is formulated by a rule not studied apart from the context (*anārabhyādhīta*). Consequently, since there is no extension (*atideśa*) to that [modified fire], the performance of the ritual duties of the *uttaravedi*—which is enjoined as distinguished by a different, unprecedented substance—is not subject to extension.

In this context, although the location for the *āhavanīya* fire has not been specifically prescribed, it is nevertheless obtained by implication (*paryāptyā*) through its very designation as something new (*apūrva*). For the location of the *āhavanīya* has not been established as the substratum for the *homa* in the case of Soma-offerings; thus, the same principle applies here. This is heard in the first Vaiśvadeva section of the Soma and Cāturmāsya sacrifices: "The Vaiśvadeva is a *trivṛt* *abhiṣṭoma*; there is an animal sacrifice for Savanīya and an *anūbandhyā* for Bṛhaspati.
They do not set up a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), nor do they prepare the northern altar (*uttaravedi*)."

"They bind the animal to the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*), to the fire-brand (*ulmuka*), or to the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Regarding the *Vaiśvadeva* section of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, it has already been explained that there is no *uttaravedi*. Now, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that where there is no prohibition, the ritual properties (*dharma*) prompted by both [the primary act and the subsidiary] would be optional alternatives; to this, he says: "And when another substance is employed for that same purpose, these properties [apply]. For example: "They place the whey (*vājina*) on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*)," "They bind the animals to the horse," and "They bind the animals to the enclosing-stick."

Although the meaning is already established by the intervening sūtra beginning with "anyasmin," both types of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) indeed occur as prompted by the *apūrva* of both [the primary and the subsidiary]. For ritual duties (*dharma*) are not connected to the essential nature [of the act] alone, but rather are prompted by the *apūrva*; and since the *apūrva* differs according to the difference in the acts, this sūtra is commenced again to state that the *apūrva* of both acts does not arise if either one of them is left unperformed.

Even when another substance—though already consecrated by a consecration enjoined for a different *apūrva*—is being employed for that purpose [the original one] along with a different purpose, the ritual duties (*dharma*) are indeed prompted by the *apūrva* of that other purpose. This is seen in the first section of the *Parva*, where the statement "He spreads the sacrificial grass on the *utkara* heap" applies; likewise, in the *Aśvamedha*, the statement "They bind the horse as the victim" has its meaning established. Having thus explained the determination of *atideśa* (extended application), he demonstrates the principles for specific performance within the domain of the *vikṛti* (modified sacrifice) itself, ending with the phrase "they may be optional or non-optional."

When the *sāmidhenī* verses are being increased, the fuel-sticks increase; when they are being reduced, they are restored to their original state. Being kindled by the fires, it is illuminated; those *ṛc* verses are the *sāmidhenīs*. In them, according to one's desire and with specific modifications of the syllables—[the text here refers to various textual variants and ritual details regarding the horse sacrifice and the binding of the animal]. [End of Section] This is accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 381.

Or rather, when the number [of verses] increases due to specific injunctions such as "one should recite seventeen *sāmidhenīs*," and when more than fifteen [verses] are prescribed, the pieces of wood (*kāṣṭha*) placed upon each of those [recited verses] as fuel-sticks (*samidh*) must be made according to that same number. Although it is not the case that the pieces of wood increase as parts of the *sāmidhenīs* themselves—since they increase in accordance with the primary act—they nevertheless serve to assist the *sāmidhenīs*. How so? It is said: having taken a fuel-stick, one throws it into the fire.

It has already been stated that at the *praṇava* (the syllable *om*), the fire is said to be "being kindled" (*samidhyamāna*). For if that [first] *sāmidhenī* verse were employed, the fire would not be "being kindled" as long as the kindling process had not yet begun. According to the view that each *sāmidhenī* verse corresponds to one [kindling], in the case of the two other views where fuel-sticks have already been placed previously, the fire is manifested as being kindled by each individual *sāmidhenī* verse, and not by many fuel-sticks being piled up together.

Because it is enjoined by such passages as "He kindles with one [verse]" and "He places fifteen pieces of fuel-wood," there is an application of each of the twenty-one verses to a single act. Likewise, when kindled by one [verse], it is not illuminated by another. Even in the *hautra* (the portion recited by the Hotṛ), there is a combination of mantras only when multiple objects of reference are possible, but not everywhere. Therefore, since each individual *samidhenī* verse serves as an auxiliary to a single piece of fuel-wood, the fuel-wood is increased for the sake of that assistance.

In the cases where it is said, "one should recite these very *sāmidhenī* verses," and "he recites one [verse]," there would be a reduction of the *samidh*s; therefore, it is stated, "while they are being withdrawn. The number observed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) is not sublated when there is an increase, but it would be sublated in the case of a reduction. To prevent such sublation, one adds fuel exactly as fifteen according to the archetype.

The restriction that "it is kindled with one [verse] and made manifest with one" is set aside by the scriptural statement; for in the case of the Mahāpitṛyajña, the text itself will show the statement: "having divided the fuel-wood (idhma) into three parts. Likewise, regarding the Upasad rites, it will indicate: "having recited exactly three Sāmidhenī verses, one should divide the fuel-wood into nine parts.

Although this is read in the very words of the Sūtra, nevertheless, the sublation of the heard number fifteen cannot be effected by mere logical capacity; thus, there is no sublation of the number fifteen. The modification (ūha) is according to the purpose.

The word "in the modification" (*vikṛtau*) is to be supplied [to complete the sense of the sentence]. When there is an increase in the number of logs, the mantra must be modified (*ūhanīya*). This is explained as follows, given that the modification (*ūha*)—namely, "twenty-one times"—is present in the mind: just as the meaning exists as inherent in the ritual act, so too must the application of words expressive of that meaning be performed in the mantra according to worldly usage. If it is asked: "How can it be a *mantra* if worldly words are employed, since there is no traditional recitation (*āmnāna*) of such words? Is it not possible for the manifestation of the meaning to occur through the etymological derivation (*yoga*) of the word 'mantra' or through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)? [The answer follows:]...

It is said: In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the mantra is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) by means of inference, not through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), because it has been established in the rule "those which possess a Brāhmaṇa [explanation] are as taught" (*brāhmaṇavantaḥ*). However, when the mantra is not obtained through direct scriptural statement, if the expression of meaning is not possible, then the word—being purposeless—is to be displaced and a capable worldly term should be used in its place. In that case, the visible purpose (*dṛṣṭaprayojana*), which is the manifestation of the meaning, is accomplished; there merely results the absence of the restriction that the manifestation must be by the mantra alone.

If the mantra-word were ineffective, both [the following] would be sublated: neither its manifestation nor the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that protects it. Furthermore, because of the prohibition of modification (*ūha*) in the *Mīmāṃsā*—based on the *Hautra* mantra "May the mother think of him, may the father," where it says "therefore one should not modify it thus"—it should be understood in detail from the *Mīmāṃsā* that modification occurs elsewhere;
for there is no modification in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

If a mantra is indeed incapable in the archetype (*prakṛti*), then it must be justified through some intended meaning in accordance with its Vedic application (*śrautaviniyoga*). One should understand that in certain cases there may be the elision of a word within the archetype, or that the mantra belongs exclusively to the modified form (*vikṛti*), and so forth. In every case where it is incapable, whether a word is capable through its primary denotative function (*abhidhā*) or through another mode of signification (*vṛttyantara*), if the mantra is incapable of expressing the meaning of the archetype, then since it would be incapable anywhere, there is no modification (*ūha*) in the archetype.

Regarding the formula "Having girded the wife, this sacrificer is invited," in the case of a sacrificer who has many wives, there is no modification (*ūha*) of the mantra to the plural form "the wives" (*patnīḥ*). This is because the status of being a "wife" (*patnītva*) must be established as the referent of the word. Furthermore, regarding the formula "this sacrificer is invited" used during the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, some teachers maintain that there is no modification; the intention is that this can be justified by disregarding the gender (*liṅga*) and intending only the office (*adhikāra*) of the sacrificer. It should be understood that in the formula "may he rest for the sacrifice tomorrow" (*śvo yajñāya ramatām*), even though there is a sublation (*bādha*) in the *sadyaskāla-pūrṇamāsa* (immediate New Moon sacrifice), the word "tomorrow" (*śvas*) and so forth remain [as they are].

Likewise, regarding the subsequent extension (*uttaratati*), as it has been traditionally handed down: whatever mantra is not modified in the archetype (*prakṛti*) remains unmodified in the ectype (*vikṛti*) and must be applied in that very same manner; it is not to be modified (*ūhya*). Thus, just as it is traditionally handed down in the archetype—according to the reading of the archetype—in an ectype involving a time-shift such as the *paurṇamāsī*, the word "tomorrow" (*śvas*) must be replaced by the word "today" (*adya*), and according to the archetype's reading, the formula should be supplied with the elided word, because the underlying principle (*nyāya*) is the same.

In the case of substitutes, those [rites] whose purpose is lost should not be performed; for example, the mantra for cutting when [the grain] has already been cut, or the mantra for reaping when it has already been reaped.

It was stated at the end of the first chapter of the second book that there is no taking of a substitute; this was not stated here because it was mentioned incidentally in the context of the mantras. However, here the sublation (*bādha*) is also discussed in order to refute the position of Maradvāja and others regarding the performance of *yajus* mantras.

"Arthaluptāni" means those whose purpose has been seen; therefore, actions, materials, or sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) that have lost their purpose should not be performed or employed, as they are already accomplished. For example, when a substitute for the *barhis* grass has already been taken, [the original] is not used; likewise, when the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) has already been cut, there is no employment of the two mantras that reveal the cutting and the lopping. Similarly, since acts such as lopping and cutting are established as having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), they should not be performed in their absence.

Where milk is boiled for the purpose of cooking, the purification with the formula "May the god Savitṛ purify you" is applied; the consecration with "The milk was foremost among the gods at the beginning" is likewise applied to the clarified butter (ājya).

In that sacrifice where milk is prescribed for the purpose of cooking the *dadhi*, the purification (*utpavana*) is performed there with the modification (*ūha*) "O God, thee... by means of this mantra; he transforms it [the milk] with that. Having stated the case-ending (*vibhakti*), the meaning of the word-modification (*pada-ūha*) is expressed as "O Gods, the milk," and so forth. That by which one consecrates is "consecration" (*abhimantraṇa*); with this mantra—"Lead this sacrifice, place the lord of the sacrifice, thee Indra has chosen as his own Indra, it is sprinkled"—the remainder is to be modified (*ūhya*).

Regarding the butter, the text says "the gods [take] the butter. It is heard that it is brought by means of the *āpaṇārya* vessel; thus, the remaining details are like those of water. This has been stated because the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are obtained through the ritual status of the *praṇītā* water. In this regard, the following is considered: how is the application of the *praṇītā* rites obtained? It is not the case that one hears "he brings water" or "he brings butter," nor is there a scriptural statement to the effect that it is for the purpose of mixing (*saṃyavana*), such that—because water intended for mixing is connected to a specific purpose—the application of those rites would occur when that purpose is joined to another substance.

[This concludes] the Bha-paṭala, accompanied by the Vaijayantī commentary composed by Mahādeva. [Page 383] He obtains [the result]. "Mixing" (saṃyavana) means cooking; for it is stated that one pours [water] into the flour, and since it is explicitly heard in the scripture that the *madantī* waters serve the purpose of mixing with the flour, there is no injunction for taking up the *praṇītā* water for the sake of the *madantīs*. Therefore, being for the purpose of cooking is not the motive.

In this regard, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the author of the Sūtras, by stating "where milk is for the purpose of cooking," has accepted that the injunction "he cooks the sacrificial oblations with the *praṇītā* waters" is rooted in Śruti; furthermore, it is made known that the *praṇītā* waters themselves are prescribed for the purpose of kneading the flour. It is stated accordingly that in the archetype sacrifice (*prakṛti*), only the flour is to be cooked. This has been clearly stated by Āpastamba: "He kneads [the flour] with the *praṇītā* waters.
Through kneading, a lump (*piṇḍa*) is formed, and its cooking follows; thus, kneading is indeed for the sake of cooking. We shall now explain the ritual procedures for the *caru*.

Having explained that *ūha* (modification) is not obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), he now makes a formal promise (*pratijñā*) to explain other characteristics (*dharma*) likewise not obtained from the archetype, in order to demonstrate that [the treatise] is rooted in logic (*nyāyamūla*); for if they were not explained, their application would be established by its own force. What are these characteristics?
He employs a cooking pot (*sthālī*) in place of the sacrificial potsherds (*kapāla*).

The *sthālī* (pot) is well-known in the world; it is employed at the time of using the vessels in place of the *kapālas* (pans), which are obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) and are incapable of holding the cooked offering—this being for the sake of that specific purpose. It also performs the subsequent refinements equally, just like the *kapālas*. This meaning has already been illustrated in that sūtra by the phrase "in another [vessel]" (*anyasmin*). Its well-known measure is from the husked grains (*aphalīkṛtebhyaḥ*).

The reference "of that" (*tasya*) applies even to the *caru* that has been completed and set down, as it is drawn back [to the mind] by the intellect. The remainder of the sentence is: "the ritual action—which is established and obtained from the very nature of the substance—is to be performed for the sake of those husked rice grains related to it which have been extended [by analogy]. This includes everything up to the pouring out of the washing water, as indicated by the act of husking three times. Having placed the cooking pot upon the fire with the first *kapāla* mantra.

By the first [verse], namely *dhruvāsī* modified as *dhruvamati*, the placing [of the potsherds] is performed with the first one alone, because multiple options would otherwise result from the plurality of the mantras for the potsherds (*kapāla*). The first vessel (*sthālī*) is to be placed according to the characteristics of the first potsherd; the others, having fulfilled their purpose, are excluded. By the word "having placed" (*upadhāya*), it is shown—as in the archetype—that there is a conjunction with the preceding consecrations, including the preliminary subsidiaries such as the production of embers, the removal, and the setting down (*avasthāpana*).

The use of the gerund *upadhāya* (having placed) indicates that there is no placing of coals on top immediately after the placement [of the pot], because such an action serves the purpose of heating from above and has no utility for the *caru*.

One should pour the rice grains from the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) into it, cleanse them, place them while reciting the mantra for setting down [the vessel], carry fire around it, cook it, sprinkle clarified butter over it, and then remove it from the fire using the very same cooking pot.

The statement of the sequence of ritual items (padārthānupūrvī) is for the purpose of demonstrating specific details and for the purpose of precluding certain items from the middle of the procedure. The phrase "from the winnowing basket" (*śūrpādeḥ*) is intended to preclude any interruption by the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). The commentator has indeed accepted that it extends as far as the flaming edge. Beyond that, it should not be placed directly on top, but rather all around, by virtue of the logical necessity (*sāmarthyāt*). With the formula ending in "I pour out" (*saṃvapāmi*), having purified [the grain] through the strainer (*pavitra*) across the vessel, one should offer with the formula "May he sacrifice" (*juṣasva*). Having placed it upon the *praṇītā* water-line... [End of Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Third Praśna].

The bringing of those [grains] and the mixing with the *madantī* waters are performed after pouring them together. The mantra "Thou art the Dharma, O Agni" is for the purpose of placing [the grains] upon the potsherds (*kapāla*) for the sake of cooking—that is, for the purpose of establishing them there—and it implies the act of setting them down. When the word *dharma* is used as a qualifier for that [Agni], even though the word *viśvāyuḥ* occurs, there is no modification [of the mantra], because the oblation itself is established as being the *dharma*. There is neither spreading nor wiping.

Having performed the *paryagni* rite, the act of igniting [the fire] above so as to produce flames—expressed by the phrase "having enclosed" (*antaritam*)—is explained according to what is actually observed. However, in this case, such [igniting] would not occur because cooking from above is impossible. Furthermore, [the formula] "O Brahman, unite! (*saṃ brahmaṇā*) would also be inappropriate due to contradiction. [The text says: "He does not ignite [it]; there is fire here. There is no [formula] "O Brahman, unite! [but rather] "they do not burn it. [The text says: "having cooked" (*śrapayitvā*); [this means] having heated it with firebrands, saying "there is fire here"—that is the meaning of "having cooked."

The Prāyaugikas, however, bring forward the *praṇītā* waters silently immediately after the placing [of the vessel], and this is the view accepted by the author of the *Mādhyaka*. Even if that were the case, here the bringing forward must indeed be performed with the mantra after mixing and straining; it cannot be said that the mantra belongs to the bringing forward performed previously. This is because it would contradict the scriptural injunction: "Mix yourselves, unite yourselves. Furthermore, regarding the instruction "Cook without burning," there is indeed the rule: "Relax the speech [at this point]."

Because of the absence of the finger-washing vessel (*aṅguliprakṣālanapātrī*) and the pouring out (*nirṇejana*), there is no pouring out for the sake of unification. The rites beginning with the preparation of the altar (*vedikaraṇa*) up to the end of *viṣṇūni* proceed according to the archetype (*prakṛti*). The formula "idamaham" is absent; the formula "sūryaṃ jyotiḥ" is present. The formula "syonaṃ te" is absent. He causes [the rice] to swell either according to the archetype with the formula "āpyāyatām" or silently. He causes it to be removed from the place, either by standing or by sitting.

Because it is stated in the context of the removal (*udvāsana*) that one should remove [the cake] while moistening it with the mantra "āīḥ prathasva" and not turning it over, and because one desires to avoid the loss of the distinction between the central and other parts, it is said "sthāsyā" (you shall stand). The particle *eva* (only), however, is for the purpose of prohibiting the removal from the *pātryā* (the vessel) with the mantra "tasmin sīda.
Regarding "by means of a *puroḍāśa* in a group of *puroḍāśas*":
when there is a collection or group consisting of three or more, where the *puroḍāśa* is alone—meaning it is of the *puroḍāśa* type and not separated by another [type of offering].

He cuts off each lump individually with the formula, "Separate yourselves according to your respective portions," and the two remaining ones with, "Separate yourselves according to your respective portions. In the case of three [lumps], he does so all at once; in other cases, he does so one by one until only two remain, for the purpose of obtaining the mantra in the plural form. He separates each lump according to its portion. When two remain, he separates the two with, "Separate yourselves according to your respective portions.
For those two alone, there is the assignment of the deities.

For those two, there is no [assignment] even for the previous [portions], such as "this for so-and-so, this for so-and-so," or "I take thee for so-and-so, for so-and-so" regarding those belonging to one's own *śākhā*. Since the order is understood through the sequence of the disconnections (*apaccheda*) among the previous [priests]—as being for the purpose of the first deity and so forth—and since there is no sequence of disconnection between the final two simultaneously, the assignment must be performed according to that sequence.

The *caru* and *puroḍāśa* portions should be divided before the pouring of water; therein, he mutters the mantra of division: he divides the equal ones into two, and the unequal ones according to their respective shares.

The pouring out [of grains] for the sake of the *caru* and *puroḍāśa* offerings is performed with the formula beginning with "Of the god" (*devasya te*) and ending with "I pour upon" (*adhivapāmi*). Prior to that, however, is the division. Regarding how it is done there, he says: in that case, for the purpose of division, one uses a mantra in the dual number when dividing two, and in the plural number when dividing many *puroḍāśas*.
[End of section 1.23]. This is accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 385.

It has been stated that one should recite the mantra only once; it is not said that one should recite it for each individual deity. Since no separate procedure is performed for each deity such that there would be a repetition of the instrument (the mantra) for each Manava, but rather [the division is made] by two groups, the recitation of the mantra is done only once. If there are as many *caru* offerings as there are *puroḍāśas*, then one divides them into two equal portions by means of two groups. If some are in excess, then one makes the two divisions unequal by that same measure.
One should designate a single deity for each group, saying, "This is for so-and-so and for so-and-so."

If the first deity is for the sake of the *caru* (mixture) and is located in one of the two heaps, then, having first identified the *caru*-deity within the *caru*-heap, he should subsequently identify the *puroḍāśa*-deity [in the other heap]. If the order is reversed, it should be stated in the reverse manner; thus, it is said "in each heap" so that one may know which deity belongs where.
Having set aside the portion for Pūṣan (*pauṣṇa*), he grinds it together with the portions for the *puroḍāśas*.

That is to say, having separated the portion for Pūṣan from the heap and joined it with those for the *puroḍāśas*, he grinds them all together. This means he performs the rites beginning with the pouring of the grain (*adhi-vapana*) and ending with the forming of the balls (*piṇḍa-karaṇa*).

At the time of placing [the vessel] on the fire, they should divide [the materials] among themselves. When the time for cooking has arrived, they mutually, that is, one another, divide the lumps and the rice grains.
Therein, he mutters the mantra of division.

...In both groups, the aforementioned matter is stated only once; it is not repeated because the assignment of deities has already occurred. When various seeds are brought together, there is only one mortar, pestle, winnowing basket, and black antelope skin. This is for the purpose of setting aside the views of Bādarāyaṇa and others regarding different lineages and different properties—such as in the case of *śyāmāka* and *vrīhi* grains, or when *kṛṣṇavrīhi*, *mahāvrīhi*, and *āśuvrīhi* are brought together within a single ritual procedure (*samānatantreṣu*). By logical principle, these are treated as one among the seeds used for the *caru* and *puroḍāśa* offerings, whether they be cultivated or wild plants.
At the first seed he calls for the preparer of the oblation; at the last, he releases his speech.

Since the arrival of the *haviṣkṛt* is already established by the mere non-abandonment of the first grain, there is no purpose for summoning her again. When the final grain is reached and the command for the three-fold husking (*triṣphalīkaraṇa*) has been given, one releases speech; since the release occurs at the very first [grain], the threshing of the others would otherwise become irregular and non-scriptural. Furthermore, threshing is for the purpose of producing the visible state of rice-grains (*taṇḍulībhāva*); as long as the three-fold husking continues, the state of rice-grains is being produced. Therefore, according to the principle that "those things which have a single completion are performed together," the *kāṇḍānusamaya* (sequential performance by groups) is to be observed here.

One should sacrifice with the Soma, the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi, or the Paśubandha on either the new-moon day or the full-moon day. Regarding this, it is said: "The Soma is a previously unestablished injunction (apūrva-vidhi), while for the other two it is a restatement of what is already established (prāptānuvāda). This is indeed a direct scriptural statement (śruti). For what purpose is it a restatement? It is replied: [The text continues with various manuscript variants regarding the specific details of the ritual]. [This concludes] the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [Third Book].

It has been stated that when the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa) and a modified sacrifice (vikṛti) coincide, the Darśapūrṇamāsa are stronger. In that case, the fifteenth day (the full moon) and the first day (the new moon) would be occupied by the primary sacrifice (prakṛti) during the morning time; thus, the times for the modified sacrifice obtained through extension (atideśa) would be sublated by the primary sacrifice. Nor can it be argued that the prescription of time for Soma and the modified iṣṭis in the primary sacrifice is independent, such that after performing the preparatory rite (anvādhāna) for the animal sacrifice, the preparatory rite for the modified sacrifice could be performed, resulting in one sacrifice immediately following another.

There is no omission of the ritual action in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), because it follows the principle of justice; therefore, it should occur immediately after the primary sacrifice (prakṛti-yāga). For that purpose, there is a restatement by direct scriptural hearing (pratyakṣa-śruti) of what was already obtained through extended application (atideśa); consequently, those [details] of the Viṣṭi, Paśu, and Jyotiṣṭoma which are directly perceived—

Among those various [elements], the stronger ones proceed by setting aside the morning time of the archetype (*prakṛti*) on the fifteenth day through an improper method; or rather, the time for the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) to be joined with the archetype occurs after the archetype sacrifice, and that inferred two-day duration is set aside by the archetype because there is no other recourse. Thus, whether the performance of the modification (*vikṛti*) is established as preceding or following [the archetype], it is settled. In this regard, he will state that the optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) have an immediate (*sadyas*) time, and the animal sacrifices (*paśu*) have the *upāṃśu* ritual procedure (*tantra*).

Thus, as he will state that one should perform the sacrifice with the *āmāvāsya* or *paurṇamāsa* oblation, or with optional animal sacrifices (*paśu*) or *iṣṭi*s, but not so in the case of other animal sacrifices; and as he will state the option for the sacrifice to take place on the same day or the following day (*yahakālatā*) regarding the animal sacrifice when "tomorrow's time" applies—therein, it follows by implication that the *anvādhāna* (preparatory rite) takes place on the preceding day. And he says: "On the *aupavasathya* day of the preceding *parvan*"; thus, for a sacrifice being performed on the fifteenth day of the preceding *parvan*, the *aupavasathya* day is the fourteenth.

In this [tithi] as well, the rule regarding the deficient day (*vaikaliṣaka*) should be understood.
