And there exists the status of both the fifteenth and the first [lunar day] as being full; just as the fifteenth has the nature of the new moon (*darśa*), so too does the first have the nature of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*). This was explained in detail in the first chapter, and here it is stated in brief.

The term *amāvāsyā* (new moon) is based on the cause of the maximum proximity between the sun and the moon, while the term *paurṇamāsī* (full moon) is based on the cause of their maximum distance; therefore, that moment of conjunction or midpoint consisting of the transition from the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*) to the first day (*pratipad*) is identical for both. Consequently, both of these [periods] are included by the terms *amāvāsyā* and *paurṇamāsī*, as they are formulated in the Sūtras for the purpose of prescribing the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).

Regarding this, some say that the reversed designation "on the new moon day and on the full moon day" is intended to indicate that the time situated between the new moon and the full moon is an auxiliary element (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice. Furthermore, the scriptural injunctions regarding prescriptions and prohibitions—such as "one who desires [prosperity] should sacrifice in the first fortnight" and "one who desires to become worse off should sacrifice in the latter fortnight"—would likewise be supported. Similarly, the *Chāndogya-sūtra* states: "In the absence of a specific instruction, [the rite should be performed] during the northern course of the sun and in the waxing fortnight."

Similarly, since a single *phalāpūrva* (resultant transcendental potency) is produced by both the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), there is a single performance (*ekaprayogatā*) for the two; thus, the principle that "there is no separate commencement for each ritual act" (*na karmaṇi karmārambhaḥ*) is also upheld. This, however, is not accepted. Because the optional sacrifices (*kāmyayāga*) are prescribed to be performed after one has sacrificed with either the New Moon or Full Moon oblation (*havir-iṣṭi*), and because in the Soma sacrifice one must sacrifice on the day of the New Moon or the Full Moon when it is the day of sacrifice (*yajanīya*).

Because there is an authoritative basis for the prescription of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the soma-pressing (*sutyā*) on the same day, and because there is also a scriptural text stating, "Having sacrificed with the New Moon or Full Moon oblation, one has finished," the direct scriptural injunction regarding the Soma sacrifice necessarily sublates the scriptural rule restricting the sacrifice to the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*); likewise, there is no interval between them. As for the *Chāndogya-sūtra*, since it says "in the absence of an instruction" (*anādeśe*), it does not apply here because there is indeed an instruction; thus the *Chāndogya-sūtra* applies to cases where one might desire something specific, and even that scriptural text remains applicable only in the absence of such an instruction. Therefore, it is not without scope.

And he will state in the Gṛhya-sūtra: "In the *pākayajñas* during the waxing fortnight... This does not mean that the commencement of the rite is prohibited; rather, it is a prohibition against merely beginning [the rite at that time]. Furthermore, in the case of the performance following the feeding of Brahmins, another performance is prohibited; otherwise, in the midst of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, there would be the omission of the *Āgrayaṇeṣṭi*. Enough of this digression. [Now begins] the sixth chapter, accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva:
"One should recite seventeen [verses] for the *iṣṭi* or the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*); one may optionally choose fifteen, or there may be no option [at all]. (22)

The statement "seventeen [sāmidhenīs] without taking up [fuel-sticks]" is heard as an unattached injunction (*anārabhya-śruti*). However, that does not sublate the number fifteen already established by the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), nor is it an optional alternative. Therefore, the statement heard in another recensional branch (*śākhāntara*)—"one should recite seventeen sāmidhenīs at the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) or at the animal sacrifice (*paśu*)"—is subsumed for the purpose of providing an option to the number fifteen of sāmidhenīs obtained through extended application (*atideśa*); this is the view of others. One's own view is that the number seventeen is constant; it applies to the animal sacrifice and to those modified sacrifices where it is specifically prescribed.
In that regard, there is the removal of the fifteen [sacrificial cups] inferred from general rules, because direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) is more powerful.
"We shall explain the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice":
the meaning is that the performance is accomplished through various methods of extended application (*nyāyātideśa*), and it would not be accomplished if it were not explained.
Without having performed that sacrifice, he does not eat the fruits of the nine kinds of plants, whether they be cultivated or wild.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Without having sacrificed with that [offering], one does not eat. When there is no ripening of grain, the *prāyaṇīya* rite is performed for the sake of the deities by means of this [offering]; here, the lengthening of the vowel at the beginning is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). And because the sacrifice has not yet taken place, the fruits of cultivated and wild plants do not appear first; therefore, it must be repeated. Since it is prescribed as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for eating new grain before each ripening—prior to the *Pārthiva* sacrifice—this [rite] is indeed obligatory (*nitya*), being occasioned by eating when there is no ripening. And thus Maradvāja says: "By this [rite], as long as..."

It should be understood that the injunction "one should sacrifice" implies a fixed commencement either immediately after the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), since Kātyāyana prescribes the *āgrayaṇa* as a substitute for the *pavamāna-havis* offerings in the *ādhāna*. Regarding the term "new grains" (*navānām*), their status as "new" is well-established as that which is produced by rain starting from the rainy season until the autumn; there is no prohibition against the fruits of trees, nor is there a prohibition against the roots, tubers, leaves, flowers, and so forth of plants, provided they are distinct from [the aforementioned] fruits.

This has been clearly stated by Āpastamba, Bharadvāja, and others. They themselves have declared the favor [to be shown] toward green barley, leguminous grains, and those that have not yet yielded fruit. For the gods generally favor the first-fruits of rice and barley; indeed, their production occurs primarily in autumn and spring. The Śruti also speaks of these two: "The Āgrayaṇa sacrifice is performed in autumn and spring. Thus, according to Vaikhānasa, Āpastamba, and Bharadvāja, one sacrifices with rice in autumn and with barley in spring, while in the rainy season—

If [the text] said "with *śyāmāka*," then since it is observed that other grains ripen at other times as well, they would possess "newness" (*navatva*) at all times; consequently, the mention of autumn and spring would be purposeless. Furthermore, the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice for rice and *śyāmāka* would be mandatory, whereas the *Āgrayaṇa* for barley would be optional—namely, one sacrifices with the first-ripened rice, and likewise one sacrifices with the first-ripened *śyāmāka* or barley.

The sacrifice is to be performed either then [in the spring] or in autumn, provided that one does not let the autumn pass; the meaning is that one should perform it right there at that time. When the first-fruits of the *śyāmāka* grain are ripened, the sacrifice is performed either in the rainy season or in autumn with a common ritual procedure (*samānatantreṇa*), provided there is no other [conflicting] ripening. This is according to Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, composed by Satyāṣāḍha. The ripening (*prapāka*) of the barley is indeed distinct from that of the rice, due to the difference in their respective stages of growth. By the term "first ripening" (*agrapāka*), the ripening at that specific time is intended. Furthermore, it is not possible for both the old and new grains to ripen simultaneously.
Thus, at the time of the offering (*nirvapaṇa*), one offers the eight-pot-sherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Agni with the old rice, while the other offerings are made with the new rice.

And likewise, when there is a state of non-distinction between the same ritual procedure (*samānatantra*), at the time of the offering of rice (*vrīhi*), specifically during the *āgrayaṇa* of rice, there is a specific injunction for the *Āgneya* sacrifice; however, this does not apply to the *āgrayaṇa* of *śyāmāka* or barley (*yava*) within a different ritual procedure (*bhinnatantra*), because in those cases there is no old *Āgneya* rice. As for the other [offerings] to be mentioned later, they belong only to the new grains. In that regard, although there may be a difference regarding the deities specified for the *śyāmāka*, the triad of deities remains the same.

In the *Yavāgrayaṇa*, there is no offering of old rice (*vrīhi*) or barley (*yava*), nor is there an offering of new [grains] for the deity Agni. Likewise, in the *Śyāmāka* sacrifice, although it has a different ritual procedure (*tantra*), the deities are not the same. This was stated by Vaikhānasa: "In the spring, when one performs the *Yavāgrayaṇa*, the procedure for those [grains] is like that of the *Vrīhyāgrayaṇa*; however, the *Śyāmāka* is prescribed [with a different rule]. And thus it was said by Āpastamba: "One offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni-Indra or Indra-Agni, a pap (*caru*) cooked in milk to the Viśvedevas, a *Śyāmāka* pap to Soma, and a cake on one potsherd to Dyāvāpṛthivī.
The phrase "one offers" (*nirvapati*) is to be supplied from the preceding context.

Some authorities prescribe the Śyāmāka sacrifice as having separate ritual procedures (*nānātantra*). This means that, whereas the previously mentioned [rites] are said to share the same ritual procedure (*samānatantra*), the Śyāmāka alone is a distinct ritual procedure; there is no difference in the deities involved therein. When the oblation has been presented but not yet sprinkled with water, he offers five *ājyānī* oblations with the mantra beginning "śatāyudhāya."

Having sat down with the formula, "In the lap of Aditi I settle," and once the vessel has been sprinkled with water by means of the formula, "By the impulse of the god... he takes five portions with the five verses beginning, "Hundred-armed for me," "Spring," "Winter," "The calf," and "May the auspicious food... and offers them, because of the Śruti text: "Having poured out the *āpaṇa*, he offers the oblations.
Some authorities prescribe this before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.

Some followers of other recensions maintain that one should offer with the verses beginning, "Hundred-armed for me," prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt*; since the scriptural authority is equal, there is an option between the two, and in both cases it is performed according to the rules of a *darvihoma*.

The ritual procedure for the single-pitcher offerings (*ekakapāla*) has been explained by means of the single-pitcher offering belonging to the Vaiśvadeva [parvan]. This applies to all single-pitcher offerings for which no specific ritual properties (*dharma*) have been taught; it does not, however, apply to those for which specific properties have been taught, such as the Varuṇa offering at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). The Vaiśvadeva is the first parvan of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; therein, the ritual rule (*kalpa*) exists by means of the single-pitcher offering. Therefore, it should be understood that there is an inclusion of the mantras and other elements whose subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) have been extended [by analogy], but this does not apply to the single-pitcher offering of the *avabhṛtha*.

But how can there be an extension (*atideśa*) of those [details] here, since it has been stated that the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti-iṣṭis*) have the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) as their archetype (*prakṛti*)? And according to the maxim, "A beggar does not beg from another beggar," there is no modified sacrifice for a modified sacrifice except by specific scriptural statement. Therefore, the one-pot-sherd offering (*ekakapāla*) has the Agniṣomīya alone as its archetype because of the commonality of the oblation (*havis*). Furthermore, modified sacrifices possessing their own specific characteristics (*svadharma*) do not serve as archetypes for other modified sacrifices that lack such characteristics. [This concludes the section from] the *Mānava-Śrautasūtra*, accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva, [Chapter] 1.6.1.

It should not be said that there is similarity here; for it is accepted that the commonality of the deity, the commonality of the sacrificial vessel, and the commonality of the oblation are distinct. Since the state of having a single potsherd (*ekakapālatva*) is a qualification of the oblation rather than the oblation itself, when there is a conflict between the primary oblation and its qualifying attribute, the primary element is stronger, not the subordinate one.

If there were a similarity based on the fact of having a single potsherd (*ekakapālatva*), then in the case of the Varuṇapraghāsa and other rites, the injunction and its Brāhmaṇa stating "the single-potsherd [cake]" would be subject to modification. Nor should it be argued that there is a commonality of deity in the form of being dedicated to Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivya*); for it has already been stated that this is not present in all single-potsherd offerings and is moreover weak. Furthermore, this is not a name (*nāmadheya*) such as "Single-Potsherd," by which an extension (*atideśa*) of rules—similar to the monthly *Agnihotra*—might apply here. Therefore, if it is argued that no extension of rules applies here, [we reply: [The response follows: This is not so. Just as in the case of the *Sākamprasthāyīya*, where the term "single-potsherd" is used as a name despite the absence of a common deity, so too here the term "single-potsherd" functions as a name. Consequently, through the force of that name, the details of the archetype (*prakṛti*) are extended to this modified rite (*vikṛti*). Thus, the extension of the ritual procedure is established.

It is said: it was stated in the section on extended application (*atideśa-prakaraṇa*) that [an element] is understood through an indicative mark (*liṅga*). In the case of an extended application of specific details, the indicative mark is the regulator; that same mark exists here as well. Kātyāyana says: "Because of the observation of an indicative mark. And the indicative mark has been explained. For there is a statement found in the Vājasaneyi Śākhā which is heard thus: "Whichever single deity's oblation is taken, in every case the Sviṣṭakṛt [portion] is included; he offers all of it, not [only a part]."

He cuts a portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; that is one point of reproach. When it has been offered and offered, it turns back; that is the second point of reproach. Since both of these are undesirable, there is a scriptural injunction stating that the sacrifice should be performed with clarified butter (*ājya*) alone; thus, in the *Āgrayaṇa*, eight [portions] are mentioned. For the purpose of praising the *ājya* sacrifice, the characteristics of the single-pot-sherd cake (*ekakapāla*) dedicated to the Viśvedevas—namely, its being a complete oblation (*sāhuti*) and its turning back—are heard in the text. And since there can be no censure of what is not established, it is said in that very context: "He offers it as a complete oblation (*sarvahuta*), without turning it back."

The two dharmas mentioned in the Śruti—"He offers all" and "he does not turn back"—are restated in the *āgrayaṇeṣṭi* for the purpose of censure with respect to the single-pot offering (*ekakapāla*). Therefore, since there is an extension (*atideśa*) of those [dharmas] here as well, and thus "offering everything" and "not turning back" are extended precisely by way of that [extension], those other dharmas which are not contradicted by the other oblations are also extended. Regarding the statement, "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is tied in three parts," some say that this additional quality regarding the original sacrificial grass (*prākṛta-barhis*) is not contradicted by the other oblations; but that is not correct.

The single-fold binding by means of the *sainahanena* is indeed contradictory to the three-fold binding. Likewise, the state of having nine *prayāja* offerings also contradicts that [standard form] when repeated for Indra and others, due to the abandonment of the original qualities (*prākṛtaguṇa*). Like the *vaiśvadeva*, the leading forward of the fire (*praṇayana*), the performance with the *nirmanthya* fire, and the offering of the whole oblation (*sarvahuta*) or its being established (*pratiṣṭhitatva*) are performed; however, in the event of a transgression of the rule, there is an expiation for that transgression. Therefore, it is also established that there is no extension of rules (*atideśa*) from that [model] into the *avabhṛtha* or the one-potsherd rite (*ekakapāla*) which possesses its own specific characteristics, and thus it is not a modification (*vikāra*) of that.
One does not make the back exposed (*āviḥpṛṣṭhaṃ karoti*).

In that [other context], the practice of making the back visible was prescribed; here, it is prohibited on the basis of another branch of the tradition (*śākhāntara*). Nor does this prohibition follow from logical necessity (*nyāya*), because as a property belonging solely to the single-pot offering (*ekakapāla*) dedicated to Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivīya*), there is no contradiction with other [rules]. Therefore, since a prohibition of what has not been obtained would be illogical, its acquisition must necessarily occur through extension (*atideśa*); thus, by this [prohibition], the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is also stated.

"He does not perform the supplementary oblation (*abhihoma*) with the names of the months"—here, the performance of the supplementary oblation with the four names of the months is obtained [by extension]. And since that [oblation] is not employed for those [offerings] occurring in the interval prior to the *āgāmi*, it is therefore prohibited by that very scriptural authority (*śāstra*).

Having sacrificed with rice, one should sacrifice again with rice until barley becomes available; having sacrificed with barley, one should sacrifice again with barley until rice becomes available. Regarding the original model (prakṛti), it is taught that one should sacrifice with rice after having stationed a cart containing either rice or barley; thus the scripture prescribes [the use of] rice without fixed restriction. Having relied upon the general procedure (*pravṛtta*), the option based on personal preference (*icchā-vikalpa*) was stated; now, it is stated by relying upon the established rule (*vyavasthita-śāstra*). The established rule is as follows: having performed the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, until one performs the *Vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, for that entire interval the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices must be performed with rice alone. Regarding the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), there is no fixed rule, because Bādarāyaṇa and others have stated that they are simply "the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*. This applies similarly to the *Prāyaṇīya* sacrifice as well, up to the limit before the *Āgrayaṇa* from the ripened grains.

When the *yavāgrayaṇa* rite is performed, this alternative (*pakṣa*) is prescribed; however, when it is not performed, there is one alternative based on personal choice. Even when the *yavāgrayaṇa* has been performed, the *Śruti*—as seen in the *Āpastamba-śrautasūtra*—indicates that the sacrifice may be performed according to one's own preference: "Or rather, [one may sacrifice] with rice alone at both [times]; for they (the rice grains) are indeed the most enduring," so says the *Nadīka-brāhmaṇa*. This means that [rice] is easily managed, being simple to prepare through processes such as dehusking and cooking. Some authorities prescribe *śyāmāka* millet for those living in bamboo thickets.

Regarding the phrase "when the grain is similar [in ripeness] to bamboo," the word *veṇugava* implies that the bamboo has not yet ripened; at that time, some followers of a particular Vedic school recite the *Śyāmākeṣṭi* (the Śyāmāka sacrifice). Having set aside the ripened *śyāmāka* grains, when the bamboo-barley (*veṇuyava*) ripens, it is precisely then that the *Śyāmākeṣṭi* is performed for the purpose of authorizing the eating of forest-grown food. As stated by Kātyāyana: "And the *śyāmāka* [is used] when the forest-grown [grain] has not ripened."

These *śyāmāka* grains are for the *bhāraka* [sacrifice]; "the *āgrayaṇa* of bamboo-grains" is the ellipsis to be supplied—just as in the cases of "the *āgrayaṇa* of *śyāmāka*" and "the *śyāmāka* month-long *agnihotra*. This has been stated by Vaikhānasa: "Because of the *priyaṅgu*, bamboo, and barley, it is like the *śyāmāka*. Likewise, there is a restrictive rule that Soma alone is the deity for the sacrificial pap (*caru*). However, Āpastamba has stated an option with various deities such as Prajāpati and others. Alternatively, some hold that the *caru* consists only of those bamboo-grains denoted by the word *śyāmāka*.

For in the case of the *yava* (barley) usage, where the supplementary statement says, "While other plants wither, these remain rejoicing," it is specifically the long-awned barley (*dīrghaśūka*) that is understood by the word *yava*, and not the *śyāmāka* (millet), even though the latter is also sometimes designated by the word *yava*. However, that principle of similarity does not apply here in the case of the *guṇavrata* (subsidiary vows) of the Āraṇyaka. Therefore, those [millet grains] alone are denoted by the word *śyāmāka*, and the sacrificial pap (*caru*) made from them yields the same result as the immediately preceding position.
Furthermore, one should not perform the *Āgrayaṇeṣṭi*; indeed, one who is wealthy should not sacrifice on either the new-moon or the full-moon day.

Alternatively, on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) or the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), when it ought to be stated that one should perform [the sacrifice] with ease, the phrase "one should not do so" serves as a prohibition intended to establish an option (*vikalpa*). As for the subsequent passage to be mentioned—"The options are equal even to the established sacrifice; one should offer the *agnihotra* with new [grain]," etc.—some say that this is a prescription for one who has not yet commenced the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; however, that is refuted. The meaning is that one should indeed perform the obligatory sacrifice (*nityeṣṭi*) with new grain on either of the two parvan days, and by that alone the *āgrayaṇa* is accomplished.

The equality [of the new and old grains] has also been stated by Āpastamba; that too has been explained in the very passage concerning the conjunction of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices with the *aupavasathika* offerings. In that case, the first [offering] is not performed separately. Rather, one should perform the obligatory (*nitya*) offering of the *āgneya* cake using only new grains. Likewise, having offered the four [cakes] for Indra and others using only new grains—whether of rice or millet—one should offer the obligatory oblation. Or, one may offer it with old grains. However, in the case of millet (*śyāmāka*) when the ritual procedures are distinct (*nānātantra*), having offered that [millet], one should then perform the obligatory sacrifice.

[Regarding] *śyāmāka* (millet): at another time, whether it belongs to a different ritual manual (*tantra*) or the same manual, or with a constant oblation (*nitya-havis*), then having offered that one alone as the constant [offering], [the procedure follows]. In the *Mahādevakṛtavaijayantī* commentary, it is stated: "The *Āgneya* cake for the *Āgrayaṇa* is performed whether it has been prepared or not; this has been accepted by Āpastamba, Bharadvāja, and others. Our own Teacher also approves of this, for he will say: 'Having offered to the deities of the *Āgrayaṇa*, with the *Sviṣṭakṛt* as the fourth,' thus there are exactly four *Āgrayaṇa* deities along with Soma."

Or he may offer the Agnihotra with new grain; or, having caused the Agnihotra cow to eat new grain, he may offer it with her milk; or, having cooked four śarāva-measures of boiled rice, he may offer it to the deities of the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, with Sviṣṭakṛt as the fourth, and then feed his guests that as a side-dish—yes, he feeds them. 23.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the third book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
Thus ends the third book in the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. || 3 ||

These [rites] are prescribed as obligatory for one who has not yet commenced the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices when the time for the Āgrayaṇa has arrived, provided there is no other possibility [of obtaining the required materials]. It has been stated by Āpastamba and others that this is accomplished with new rice-particles (*taṇḍula*)—whether of *vrīhi* or *yava*—in the same manner [as the regular offerings] both morning and evening; however, the Teacher (Baudhāyana) did not state that it is accomplished in exactly that way. Regarding the milk-offerer (*kṣīrahomin*), he is a performer of the Agnihotra who, after having eaten rice, *śyāmāka*, or barley, gives them to his cow for her consumption; then, once they have been digested, he performs the evening and morning [offerings] with her milk.

One should offer the morning *agnihotra*. These two [offerings] are the wings when the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices have not been commenced; they are indeed obligatory when the time for the *āgrayaṇa* has arrived. It has already been stated that even for another [sacrificer], there is a prohibition against eating [the remnants] due to the force of the rule. As for the four-śarāva [offering], it was explained during the *ādhāna*; its cooking is on the *gārhapatya* fire according to Āpastamba, or even on the *aupāsana* fire according to Vaikhānasa. Regarding the alternative of either an oblation or a silent recitation (*japa*), it was stated by another [teacher]; however, the Teacher [Āśvalāyana] says that having offered [the oblation], one should make the remaining rice into a ball (*odana*).

One should feed Brāhmaṇas with various side-dishes according to one's ability. This option, however, is fixed for the displacement of the Pavamāna oblations when one is unable to perform the other. Regarding the two options for the Agnihotra oblation, there is a restriction to the Parvan days; and for the four-śarāva offering, which is a substitute for the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi, there is a restriction to the Parvan days for the deities of the Āgrayaṇa. The repetition is for the purpose of concluding the inquiry.

In this regard, Kātyāyana has stated specific details: having declared that "the Agnihotra is performed with milk from a cow that has not yet calved," he further mentions the vows of the initiated, the *rauhiṇa* offerings during the *upasads*, and the *savanīya* offerings at the Soma-pressing. In that context, it is said that one who has established the sacred fires but has not yet performed the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice should wait until spring; however, when the time for the *āgrayaṇa* has passed, this is stated: "Or, if one has not sacrificed with the *āgrayaṇa* in autumn, one may be initiated for the *vājapeya*; even then, the *āgrayaṇa* must be completed in this manner."

Thus ends the eighth chapter in the third section on the *Ādhāna* (establishment of the sacred fires) in the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* composed by Mahādeva. And the section is completed. Thus ends the third section in the commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra*.
