4.1 Now begins the fourth book (*praśna*). Therein is the first chapter (*paṭala*).
One should sacrifice with an animal dedicated to Indra and Agni every six months, at each turn of the year, or every year.
It belongs to Sūrya or Prajāpati;
we shall explain it.
Having mentally recited the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula, "Sūryaṃ te cakṣuḥ," and having offered the oblation together with the cup, he performs the Anvārambhaṇīyā sacrifice.
An offering on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu is prepared;
it concludes in the established manner.
Alternatively, one offers four spoonfuls of clarified butter into the Āhavanīya fire with a verse addressed to Agni and Viṣṇu.
He performs the remaining rites with clarified butter and maintains the Āhavanīya fire.
With the formula, "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely," he offers the oblation for the sacrificial post (yūpāhuti) into the Āhavanīya fire using the dipping-spoon (sruva).
He takes up the remainder of the clarified butter and the *sruva* ladle; he hands over the axe to the *vakṣaṇa*; they go to where they are about to cut the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
The trees suitable for the sacrificial post are the *pālāśa*, the *khadira*, the *bilva*, and the *rauhītaka*.

For one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) or food, it should be made of *pālāśa*; for one desiring heaven, of *khadira*; for one desiring spiritual luster, of *bilva*; and for one desiring progeny, of *rauhītaka*.
Having passed beyond trees that are not fit for sacrifice and are less than three years old:

one that is straight, upright, with upward-cuttings and upward-branches, grown upon level ground from its own natural source—[he should cut] such for one whom he desires [should be] unestablished; for one whom he desires [should be] without cattle, he should cut one that is leafless and has a dried tip; for one whom he desires [should be] possessed of cattle, he should cut one that has many leaves, many branches, and a non-dried tip.
It is established for one who desires establishment.
One should cut [the wood] that leans westward; or that which leans eastward or northward;
or that whose tip, while being straight, is slightly bent.
"He goes beyond others" (atyanyānagāmi). He stands near that which he chooses.
With the formula, "May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey," he anoints it all around with the *sruva* ladle, [measuring] up to the ankle or up to the knee.

With the formula, "O herb, protect him," he places an herb with its tip pointing upwards between [the tree and the axe]. With the formula, "O axe, do not harm him," he strikes with the axe. He catches the first chip that falls away.
Leaving behind a stump that is free from contact with the axles, he cuts [the tree] to a height reaching the ankles.
He causes it to be felled toward the east or the north with the words, "Go to heaven with your top.
He offers an oblation on the stump with the words, "O Lord of the Forest, grow with a hundred branches! and touches himself with the words, "May we grow with a thousand branches!"
With the verse, "Thou whom this axe [prepares]," he fashions the limbs [of the sacrificial post] with an axe in the natural direction;
with the verse, "Unbroken is wealth, rich in heroes," he trims the top.
The optional measurements of the sacrificial post, beginning at one *aratni*, have been explained in the Brāhmaṇa; regarding these, one may act according to one's desire.
The number [of sacrificial posts] may be up to thirty-three;
or there may be three or four *pālāśa* posts for the *nirūḍhapaśubandha*. For other Soma sacrifices, the post is made of other wood.
He has it fashioned with eight corners, neither too thick nor too thin, and well-planed at the top.
It should be progressively thicker toward the front, or shaped like a cow's tail.
He places the *caṣāla* (the wooden ring) at the top of that very tree;
it has eight corners, is as wide as a span, and is curved in the middle.
He extends the sacrificial post above the *caṣāla* by as much as this first finger-joint,
or by just a finger’s breadth, or even less than a finger;
he makes the *svaru* from these same shavings, measuring two, three, or four finger-breadths.
If he should desire, "May another ascend to his world," he should make the *svaru* and the *caṣāla* from the wood of an *armya* tree.
Having prepared the *veda*, [he places it] in front of the *āhavanīya*. He makes the altar the size of a chariot:

as long as the pole of a chariot extending eastward, as long as the axle of a chariot across at the back, and as long as the distance between the two side-poles of a carriage extending northward in front.

Alternatively, it is six *aratnis* long from east to west, four *aratnis* wide at the back, and three *aratnis* wide at the front; it is not curved. Having performed that which precedes the northern *parigraha*, and having left space in the eastern half of the altar for the sacrificial post-hole, he measures out the *uttaravedi* with a *śamyā*.
Having placed the *śamyā* in front with its knob pointing north, he draws a line toward the north with the wooden sword (*sphya*), saying: "Thou art my path to prosperity."

Having placed a jar with its opening facing east to the south, [he says] "Thou art the one who leads me across," and places it to the south facing east. Having placed a jar with its opening facing north behind [the southern jar], [he says] "Protect me from distress," and places it to the west facing north. Having placed a jar with its opening facing east to the north, [he says] "Protect me from agitation," and places it to the north facing east. He traces a line around the interior.
To the north of the northern shoulder of the altar, at a distance of one *prakrama*, he traces the *catvāla* pit according to this same procedure for everything other than the mantras.
Taking the spade with the formula "Thee, belonging to the god... (*devasya tvā*), he digs with the formula "May Agni find thee; thy name is Nabhas."
Having dug a pit knee-deep or three spans deep,
he strikes the spade with the formula, "O Agni Aṅgiras.
With the formula, "He who is on this earth," he takes up the loose soil.
"Come with life and with name," he says, as he carries [the earth].
"That which is unassailable for thee," he says, as he pours it out upon the high altar (uttaravedi).
In this same manner he carries a second time, and in this same manner a third time.
With the words, "That which is on the second [layer]," he takes the second; with "that which is on the third," the third; and the fourth silently.
With the words, "Thou art a lioness, thou art a buffalo-cow," he prepares the high altar (uttaravedi).
With the words, "Spread out widely," he spreads it.
With the words, "Thou art firm," he strikes it down with the *śamyā* pin;
with the words, "Be prepared for the gods," he prepares it;
with the words, "Be purified for the gods," he sprinkles it with water.
With the words, "Be purified for the gods," he scatters sand over it.
With the words, "That which is cruel in thee, that which is fixed," he sprinkles it again with water.
Having drawn out a single furrow to the north or to the south with the wooden sword (sphya), saying, "Carry away the impurity," he pours out the remainder of the water.

"May the radiant, great one drink the Soma-mead; may he bestow unimpaired life upon the lord of the sacrifice. Impelled by the wind, he who protects by his own self, nourishes all creatures and shines forth in many ways"—with these words, he fashions the borders of the high altar (*uttaravedi*).

"O four-tufted, youthful, maiden-like ones, with faces of ghee, in the midst of the world! May the gods dwell upon them and rejoice here in the highest firmament (*nāka*)"—with these words, he touches both the altar and the high altar.
In the middle of the high altar, he makes the *uttaranābhi* (the northern navel), measuring either the size of a cow's footprint, the size of a horse's hoof, or the size of a span (*prādeśa*).
"May Indraghoṣa with the Vasus protect you from the east," saying this, he sprinkles the northern altar while walking around it clockwise, direction by direction;
"May Tvaṣṭṛ with the forms protect you from above," saying this, he sprinkles from above.
He pours out the remainder as before.
If it is to be performed tomorrow, he causes [the sacrificial ground] to be covered with branches of the *Audumbara* tree and enclosed.
Thus ends the first chapter in the fourth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra. || 1 ||
4.2 Now begins the second chapter of the fourth book.
He kindles the fires to be carried forward at the Āhavanīya fire-altar.
He also prepares the sand and the under-layer (upayamanī).

He lifts the firewood; he brings the supporting-sticks (*upayamanī*) and places them [on the fire] while it is being held. With the verse, "Whatever sin we have committed against you, O Purifier—whether you were previously and now become distant—make our bodies grow with clarified butter; do not harm me who have approached you from the front," he offers the remainder.
He gives the command, "Recite for the fire as it is being led forward," or "Recite for the fire as it is being led forward."

When [the verse] has been recited three times, he carries [the fire] to the *uttaravedi*. Having reached it and taken five portions of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle, placing a piece of gold between [the ladle and the fire], he sprinkles [the butter] transversely across the *uttaravedi*:
"Thou art a lioness, overcoming rivals, svāhā! on the southern shoulder;
"Thou art a lioness, winning good progeny, svāhā! on the northern hip.

"Thou art a lioness, winning increase of wealth; svāhā!"—thus on the southern hip. "Thou art a lioness, winning the Ādityas; svāhā!"—thus on the northern shoulder. "Thou art a lioness; bring the gods for the god-seeking sacrificer; svāhā!"—thus in the middle.
Having lifted up the *sruk* ladle and the gold with the formula, "To the beings thee," he encloses [the altar] with enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *pūtudru* wood:
with the formula, "Thou art all-living," the middle one; with "Thou art firmly seated," the southern one; and with "Thou art immovably seated," the northern one.
The ritual materials have been prepared: bdellium, fragrant resin, and a tuft of white wool from between the horns of a ram.

With the formula, "Thou art the ash of Agni," he pours them all at once upon the northern navel [of the altar]. When the verse, "O Yajña, sit down first upon the womb rich in wool," is being recited, he establishes the fire upon the materials with the formula: "O Yajña, be established in our good-will, most auspicious; may riches enter thee in many ways. Granting long life to the sacrificer, then refresh the singer with immortality. Thus, "The Yajña has been established," he causes it to stand firm upon the materials.
With the formula, "Thou art the nest of Agni," he pours down the supporting coals from the south.

He kindles [the fire] with the verse: "As men [did], we set thee down; as men [did], we enkindle thee. O Agni Aṅgiras, like a man, sacrifice to the gods for the one who seeks the gods. Having offered the four *atimukti* oblations with the formulas: "May Agni, knowing, lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find it. Proclaim the sacrifice to the gods; further the lord of the sacrifice, Svāhā! May Vāyu, Āditya, and the Sacrifice, knowing, lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find it. Proclaim the sacrifice to the gods; further the lord of the sacrifice, Svāhā!"

Having cleansed the *juhū* and the *sruva* ladles, and having filled the *sruk* with four, eight, or twelve portions of clarified butter, he offers the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verse, "Seven are thy... (RV 10.53.6).
This is the Āhavanīya fire; that from which it is carried forward is the Gārhapatya.
Having added fuel to the Āhavanīya, the Gārhapatya, and the Dakṣiṇāgni, he brings the sacrificial wood (idhma) and the grass-bundle (barhis).
There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; he does not bind the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) to the fuel-wood.
Having strewn around the fires, washed his hands, and spread out a layer of *ulapa* grass,
he arranges the vessels used for the animal sacrifice according to their respective purposes.

The wooden sword (*sphya*), the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle, the *sruva* spoon, two axes, two *juhū* ladles, a second *vasāhomahavanī* ladle, two *upabhṛt* ladles, a second *pṛṣadājyadhānī* (curd-butter vessel), the *dhruvā* ladle, two *ājyasthālī* (ghee-pots), a second *dadhidhānī* (curd-vessel), the *veda* broom, a second *samavattadhānī* (vessel for collected portions), two ropes— one double-stranded and two cubits long, and one triple-stranded and three cubits long— two *vapāśrapaṇī* (omentum-roasting spits) made of *kārṣmarya* wood, one with two prongs and one with a single prong, a cooking pot (*kumbhī*), the heart-spit (*hṛdayaśūla*), a branch of the *plakṣa* tree, the *svaru* chip, the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa, the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the splinter of the post (*yūpaśakala*), the *paraṇī* (water-vessel), and whatever else is required.
Having prepared the strainers, he issues the command, "Let the sacrificer restrain his speech. Restraining his speech, he touches the vessels.
Once they have been sprinkled, he releases his speech.
Having performed the second tracing around, he proceeds with the formal call, ending the call with the words, "Bring the clarified butter and the curds!"

Having performed whatever [rites] were to be done prior to the pouring out of the clarified butter (*ājya*), and having poured out the *ājya*, he pours out the curd for the sake of the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*).
Upon that [curd], the ritual procedures (*dharmāḥ*) pertaining to the *ājya* are performed, except for those [procedures] concerning the placing on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*).
At the time of taking the portions of *ājya*, having taken four portions each into the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, he pours a third part of the *ājya* into the curd.

"Thou art light, multiform; thou art the kindling-stick of all the gods"—with these words he takes fivefold-drawn speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*); or [he may take it] with "Thou art the milk of the great ones.
He pours it into the *dhruvā* ladle according to the standard procedure.
Once the clarified butters have been set down, he proceeds with the wiping of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

Having taken up the spade with the formula, "By the impulse of the god... (TS 1.3.1.a), he traces around the sacrificial post-hole three times clockwise with the formula, "It has been traced around" (TS 1.3.1.b), half of it within the altar and half outside the altar.

Having traced it around, he commands the Āgnīdhra, "Dig the sacrificial post-hole as deep as the bottom [of the post], leaving two, three, or four finger-breadths above the bottom; dig! Having dug it to that depth... (6)
"Whatever craft the carpenter has fashioned with his hand for the axe—may those pure, sacrificial waters purify that, O pure one! With these words, he washes the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

Having prepared the sprinkling waters containing barley, he sprinkles the base with "For the earth, thee!"; the middle with "For the atmosphere, thee!"; and the top with "For the sky, thee! He pours water into the post-hole with "May the world, the seat of the fathers, be purified.
He throws a grain of barley into it with "Thou art barley," and spreads eastward-pointed sacrificial grass over it with "Thou art the seat of the fathers."

With the formula, "Thou art well-penetrating," he places the first chip that fell behind, with its bark facing downwards, into the pit. Having placed a piece of gold in between, he makes an offering over it with the *sruva* ladle, saying, "O Heaven and Earth, be filled with ghee, svāhā!

Then, having given the command, "Recite for the sacrificial post as it is being anointed," or "Recite for it as it is being anointed," he stands to the east of the *Āhavanīya* fire facing westward and anoints the sacrificial post with the chip using ordinary clarified butter (*laukikājya*). Regarding the term "with ordinary [butter]": it refers to butter not prepared for a sacrifice.
"May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey," [he says]; "Thou art for Indra," [he says] regarding the top-ring;
"For the plants with good fruit, thee," [he says] as he fastens on the top-ring.
"May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey," [he says] up to the end, as he anoints the edge facing the fire.

He strokes [the sacrificial post] three times clockwise at the level of the girdle, or at its middle. He stops once it has been anointed. From the time of the anointing until the encircling with the cord, the sacrificer does not release his hold on the sacrificial post.
Having issued the command, "Recite for the sacrificial post being erected," or "Recite for the one being erected," he raises it with the words,
"Support the sky, fill the mid-region.
He places it into the pit with the verse, "These are thy stations."
With the two verses beginning "Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu," he prepares [the post] by means of fire and fixes the one standing near the fire (agniṣṭhā) together with its direction.

If he should desire of someone, "May I deprive him of brilliance, of the deities, and of sensory power," he should measure the corner facing the Āhavanīya fire of that [post] beyond the sun or in such a way as to overshoot it; thus he deprives him of brilliance, of the deities, and of sensory power. If he should desire of someone, "May I endow him with brilliance, with the deities, and with sensory power," he should align the corner facing the Āhavanīya fire of that [post] with the Āhavanīya.
He aligns it so that it leans toward the fire, is pushed outward at the base, and the upper part is not visible.
With the words, "O winner of the Brahman," he piles up earth around it, moving clockwise.
With the formula "O firm one of Brahman," he steadies it with the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa. With the formula "Make the earth swell," he sprinkles water around it clockwise.
Taking a triple-stranded cord made of wood, three fathoms long, with the formula "Thee, belonging to the god... [he girds the post].
With the verse "Viṣṇu strode across this," he wipes the sacrificial post three times with his hand while holding the girdle.
With the verse "That highest step of Viṣṇu," he gazes at the top of the sacrificial post.
He issues the command, "Recite for the post being girt," or simply, "Recite for the one being girt."
With the words, "Thou art the surrounding hero," he winds it three times clockwise around the region of the navel, or at the middle.
He makes each subsequent strand higher than the preceding one.
If he should desire of someone, "May I deprive him of vigor," he should wind it upwards for that person, or downwards.
If he should desire, "May Parjanya be rainy," he should lay it down facing downward. If he should desire, "May it be rainless," he should lift it up facing upward.

For him for whom he desires, "May a female be born to him," he should intertwine the ends near the edge but not wind them through. For him for whom he desires, "May a male be born to him," he should wind them through to the very end; having wound them through, he winds the thicker part around the thinner part.

With the formula, "Thou art the ridge of heaven," he takes up the sacrificial stake (svaru); or with "Thou art the son of heaven," or "Thou art upon the ridge of heaven. With the formula, "I conceal thee on the ridge of the intermediate space," he hides the sacrificial stake in the middle ring-hole to the north of the post fixed to the fire (agniṣṭha), or in the uppermost one.
Thus ends the second chapter in the fourth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
4.3 Now begins the third chapter of the fourth book.

A sacrificial animal has been prepared: one that is not hornless, not earless, not blind, not lame, not mutilated, not neuter, not scarred, not crippled, not having seven hooves, possessing teeth, a goat, belonging to either of the two [classes], born of a herd, having a mother, having a father, having brothers, and having friends; him he bathes.
With the words "For food, thee," he takes two blades of *barhis* grass. With the words "Thou art the protector," he takes a branch of the *plakṣa* tree.

"I dedicate you, acceptable to Indra and Agni; I dedicate [you] to the gods, the divine clans, the offspring of Prajāpati. Having dedicated the animal with these two *barhis* blades and a branch of the *plakṣa* tree, he offers five oblations after the dedication with the verse beginning "Knowing...

He offers the fifth oblation in the middle with the verse: "The animals of Paśupati are of diverse forms as well as similar; may the self-ruling Lord approve that one among them which the gods have chosen."
Taking the lower friction-piece with the formula, "Thou art the birthplace of Agni," he places it upon the sacrificial grass (barhis) to the west of the Āhavanīya fire.
With the formula, "Ye two are the testicles," he places two darbha-blades pointing eastward upon the friction-pieces.
With the formula, "Thou art Urvaśī," he takes the lower fire-drill (adharāraṇi), and with "Thou art Purūravas," the upper fire-drill (uttarāraṇi).
With the words, "Anointed with ghee," he anoints [the two churning sticks] in the cavity of the butter-pot.
He places them together with the formula, "Thou art life," or "Support the bull.
He issues the command, "Recite for the fire being churned," or "Recite for the fire being churned."
When [the verse] has been recited three times, [he says], "Be born after the Gāyatrī metre," and having begun by turning three times clockwise, he churns from that point upward as he pleases.
When [the fire] is born, [he says], "Recite for the one who is born. || 9 ||
When [the fire] has been produced, he gives the command: "Recite for the one being hurled! while it is being hurled.
Having hurled it with the words, "Agni in Agni," he makes an offering over it with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*).
Taking a double-folded, two-span-long rope made of *darbha* grass with the formula, "Thee, of the god... (*devasya tvā*), he wipes the right arm of the horse with the end of that rope.
With the words, "O divine oblation, I bind you with the noose of *ṛta*," he fastens [the animal] to the southern foreleg and half the head.
With the words, "Be bold against the non-human ones," he binds it to the sacrificial post from the front, facing westward or northward.
With the words, "I sprinkle you for the waters and the plants," he sprinkles it.
With the words, "Thou art the drinker of waters," he causes [the sacrificer] to drink. With the words, "Truly well-tasted, O divine one," he sprinkles [the butter] from below.
He then proceeds with the ritual acts beginning with the *sāmidhenī* verses.

Having poured the libation, he anoints the animal with the formula, "May your breaths unite," on the right half of the head; with "May your limbs unite with the sacrificial objects," on the two shoulders; and with "May [the sacrifice] not abandon the lord of the sacrifice," on the buttocks. He then proceeds with the rites beginning with the anointing of the *dhruvā* ladle.
Having performed the *pravara* invocation, he hands the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa priest. "May I not be one who stumbles; may I become one who does not stumble," [the priest] says as he receives it.
In the *prayāja* and *anūyāja* offerings, in the *paśupuroḍāśa-sviṣṭakṛt*, in the *vanaspati*, and in the *paśu-sviṣṭakṛt*, there are the *preṣas* (directions) for the *yājyā* and the *saṃpraiṣa*.

Therein, the *adhvaryu*, having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* and the response (*pratyāśrāvita*) having been given, directs the *maitrāvaruṇa* with the words "Direct [the Hotṛ] for such-and-such," and he [the maitrāvaruṇa] urges the *hotṛ*.
He issues the first *prayāja* call with "Prompt for the fuel-sticks! (*samidbhyaḥ preṣya*), and he issues the subsequent calls with "Prompt! Prompt! (*preṣya preṣya*).
Having poured together [the butter] at the fourth [offering], he pours all of it together at the eighth.
Having performed ten offerings, he leaves a remnant of clarified butter for the eleventh.
With the formula, "Anointed with ghee," he anoints the *juhū* ladle, the *svaru* chip, and the *svadhiti* axe;
he anoints the *svaru* twice and one edge of the *svadhiti* once.
With the words, "O slaughterer, may this sharp edge of yours be well-known," he points out the anointed edge to the slaughterer and hands over the *svadhiti* axe to him.
Having inserted the *svaru* at its proper place.

Taking a firebrand from the Āhavanīya fire, the Āgnīdhra performs the carrying of fire around [the victim] five times with the verse, "The Lord of the Path" (*parivājapati*). He runs three times around the animal, the place of the *śāmitra* fire, the *catvāla* pit, the sacrificial post, and the Āhavanīya fire.
According to some, he also carries it around the clarified butter offerings.
While the fire is being carried around, he offers three *apāvya* oblations with the formula, "Those who follow the one being bound, those who are being bound... etc.
Having placed the firebrand on the Āhavanīya fire, he goes around it three times again from right to left.
Having released the animal and called for the announcement, and once the response has been given, he issues the direction: "O Hotṛ, give the impulse for the oblations to the gods.
The Hotṛ then proceeds with the *adhrigu* formula.

With the words, "O Revatīs, enter the lord of the sacrifice with a fond dwelling," the sacrificer and the Adhvaryu both touch the animal from behind with two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the two omentum-roasting spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*), and a branch of the *plakṣa* tree.
With the formula, "May our breaths be separate," the Adhvaryu addresses the sacrificer.
When the words, "Bring Agni for him," are being uttered, the Āgnīdhra takes that very firebrand and goes forward first.
"O chest, O atmosphere!"—saying this, they go out northward between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara* heap.
To the north of the *cātvāla* is the place for the *śāmitra* fire; having placed a firebrand (*ulmuka*) there, he steps past the *śāmitra* to the north.

When it is said, "Lay down his two feet pointing northward," he lays down either one of the two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) used for the dedication, with its tip pointing east or north, saying, "May you be united with his body. Upon that [grass], they kill him, with his head toward the west and his feet toward the north, while reciting, "Make him lifeless; cause him to be quieted; announce when he is ready. Having spoken thus, he proceeds.
The sacrificer and the *adhvaryu* turn away from each other; [thinking] "our breaths are separate," the *adhvaryu* addresses the sacrificer with the mantra:

"May cattle of every form delight here, dwelling together around Agni as their nest. May they favor us with milk and ghee—those whose udder has four openings, full of honey and ghee; may they, rich in milk, increase our truth (*ṛta*) in this cow-pen. While gazing at the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), both the sacrificer and the *adhvaryu* remain silent.

"Bestow Indra's portion upon prosperity; protect this sacrifice and the sacrificer in the sun. Whoever hates us, seize him! May the sons of the sacrificer be sinless"—with these words, the Adhvaryu addresses the animal if it cries out. (11)
Thus ends the third paṭala in the fourth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
4.4 Now, the fourth chapter in the fourth section.
He offers an oblation with the verse, "When the victim has uttered its cry," once it has been immolated.
With the words, "O immolators, come hither," they approach the immolated animal.
Having loosened the animal's tether with the words, "O Aditi, loosen this bond," and having attached it to a single-pronged fork, he places it in the *cātvāla* pit.
For one practicing exorcism, he fixes it upon a dry stump or a clump of *darbha* grass with the words, "I make him who acts as an enemy subject to my power.
With the words, "Homage to you, O Ātāna," the wife worships the sun.
With the words, "Go, O unassailable one," the Pratiprasthātṛ leads the wife forward while she holds the full vessel.
With the words, "O divine waters," he pours the water into the Cātvāla pit;
according to some teachers, this is prohibited.
By this very [formula], they all step out and sprinkle themselves at the *cātvāla* pit.
According to some, the Adhvaryu sprinkles [the sacrificer] and the wife causes him to swell; the wife sprinkles [the sacrificer] and the Adhvaryu causes her to swell.
They do so with the formulas, "May speech swell for thee," and so forth, according to their respective forms.

"May your navel swell," [he says] over the navel; "may your penis swell," over the penis; "may your anus swell," over the anus; "pure are your movements," having placed [the water] near the feet; "with the two great ones," he pours out the remainder along the spine.

Having turned the animal onto its back, he places the remnant of the two sacrificial grass-blades used for the preliminary offering at the site of the omentum—three finger-breadths, three finger-breadths, or four finger-breadths to the right of the navel—with the mantra, "O herb, protect him.
He cuts across with the knife, saying, "O axe, do not harm him."

Having taken the tip of a severed blade of grass in his hand, having smeared it with blood from the stump, he throws it toward the north-western intermediate direction, saying, "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣasas," and touches water.
With the words, "Be purified for the gods," he sprinkles it with water; with the words, "Be cleansed for the gods," he wipes the omentum with the knife.
With the words, "O Heaven and Earth, cover yourselves with ghee," he covers both the two-pronged and the single-pronged forks.
With the formula, "I cut you out, acceptable to Indra and Agni," he cuts it out; or [he says], "May wealth with good heroes be uncut.
Holding the grasping of the omentum with his fist, the *śamitṛ* stands by until the offering of the omentum.
With the formula, "Blazed up," he heats the omentum over the *śāmitra* fire.
He worships the Āditya with the mantra: "Homage to the sight of the Sun; may he keep us apart [from evil].
Having left behind the fire for the purpose of cooking, the Āgnīdhra takes that very same firebrand and proceeds first, saying:
"The wide atmosphere! as he goes.
The sacrificer and the Adhvaryu priest again take hold of the two omentum-spits.
With the three verses beginning "Upa tvāgne dive dive," they approach the Āhavanīya fire.
Once the firebrand has been brought near, he holds the omentum over the final ember of the Āhavanīya with the formula "Pratyuṣṭam.
He throws the tip of the sacrificial grass (barhis) into the fire with the formula "Vāyo vīhi stokānām"; according to some, he throws it beneath the omentum.
Between the sacrificial post and the Āhavanīya fire, he hands the omentum to the Pratiprasthātṛ.
Sitting to the south facing north, the Pratiprasthātṛ cooks the omentum.
With the verse, "Thee they have established as the bearer of oblations," he makes an offering over the omentum.
When the drops have appeared, he issues the command: "Recite after [the offering] from the drops.

Having made the *śyenī* well-cooked, he places it upon a branch of a *plakṣa* tree at the southern corner of the altar with the formula: "Make the plants full of fruit. He pushes forward the two *vapāśrapaṇī* spits with the formula: "May enmities be driven away."

The Hotṛ causes the two *sruva*-ladles to be taken up with the words, "O Adhvaryu, take up the ladle full of ghee. When this is said, having taken up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, having stepped forward and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, and when the response has been given, he issues the direction: "Prompt for the *svāhākṛtis*! Having offered the oblation at the *vaṣaṭ*-call and having stepped back, he sprinkles the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) with the remainder of the *prayāja* offerings, and then sprinkles the omentum (*vapā*). [He sprinkles the omentum twice and the speckled butter once. Or, if he is about to offer the two *ājyabhāga* portions, he first sprinkles the *dhruvā* ladle; the two *ājyabhāgas* may be either performed or not performed.

Having spread a base of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle and placed a piece of gold within it, he cuts off the entire omentum (*vapā*). Having placed another piece of gold on top and poured clarified butter over it, he issues the command: "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra and Agni for the fat of the omentum of the goat.
After calling for the formal announcement (*āśrāvaṇa*), he does not issue the call for the offering; instead, the Maitrāvaruṇa priest urges the Hotṛ.
Prior to the offering of the omentum, he first offers the *parivapya* with the formula: "Svāhā to the gods!"
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, [he offers] with "O Jātavedas, go to the gods with the omentum! and subsequently with "To the gods, svāhā!

Having stepped back, he throws the two omentum-spits apart—the double-pronged one eastward and the single-pronged one westward—with the formula "Svāhā! Go ye to the Maruts of the upward sky! He then makes an offering with the remnants of the clarified butter.
They perform the purificatory sprinkling at the *cātvāla*. || 13 ||

With the three verses beginning "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss," [he says]: "O Waters, carry away this defilement and impurity today—whatever treachery I have committed and whatever falsehood I have sworn;
may Agni release me from that sin and from all distress. I release myself from curses, and I release myself from Varuna."

Having cleansed [him] from the fetter of Yama, from all divine offense, and from human offense; he then proceeds with the rites beginning with the setting out of the vessels for the *paśupuroḍāśa* sacrifice. He arranges the vessels for the vegetable offering as required: eleven or twelve potsherds, along with them a winnowing basket, a black antelope skin, a wooden pin, a mortar, a pestle, a lower grinding stone, an upper grinding stone, a *kuṭaru* (small wooden scraper), a pot, a stirring spoon, a *veda* (broom), a *prāśitraharaṇa* (vessel for the portion to be consumed), the *praṇītā* water-vessel, and the *iḍā* vessel.
At the time of the offering, he prepares an animal-cake made of rice, having the same deity as the animal.
Having released his speech with the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he dissects the animal:
[first] the heart.
The tongue, the chest, and the breasts.
In the Matasne [tīrtha],
on the side,
the left arm.
The right hip belongs to the deities;
the right arm and the left hip belong to Sviṣṭakṛt.
The rectum is common [to both].
He issues the command: "Do not strip off the rectum; do not tear apart the *kloman*, the spleen, the mesentery, and the fat.
He does not strip off the rectum, nor does he pull out the *vaniṣṭhu*.
He places the omentum, the tail, and the rectum [on the spit], as well as whatever else he considers fit for sacrifice. Having placed the animal in a pot, he cooks it.
With the *śūla* (spit), he pierces the heart from the side.
Having dug a pit in the earth at the place where the undigested contents (*ūvadhyagoha*) are kept, he throws the excrement into it.
When the animal has been cooked, he proceeds with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) belonging to the animal sacrifice.

Having spread an underlayer of butter in the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, having taken the portions, and having sprinkled them with butter, he issues the direction: "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra and Agni regarding the sacrificial cake.
Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he does not issue the *pra-vaṣaṭ*; rather, the Maitrāvaruṇa urges the Hotṛ.
Having poured the contents of the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*, he issues the directions: "Recite for Agni" and "Prompt for Agni.

The *prāśitra* and the *iḍā* are prepared; after the *prāśitra* has been consumed, the purification (*mārjana*), the offerings of the flour-smear (*piṣṭalepa*) and the husks (*phalīkaraṇa*), the purification with the *praṇītā* waters, the removal of the *upaveṣa*, and the release of the potsherds (*kapāla*) are performed.
When that is done, having taken five portions into the *juhū*—

Taking the *pṛṣadājya* and the *sruva* spoon, he approaches the slaughterer again and again and asks three times, "Is the oblation cooked? The slaughterer replies three times, "It is cooked. Having walked around to the north and seized the heart from the spit, he places it into the cooking pot.
With the formula, "May your mind unite with my mind," he sprinkles the heart with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*).
With the formula, "Svāhā! May the steam not cause distress," he consecrates the rising steam.
Having sprinkled the animal with clarified butter (*ājya*) with the formula, "That self of yours which has entered into the animals."
Having carried it by the same path as the omentum, he places it with the Pañcahotṛ formula where the omentum is;
he deposits the heart-spike in its known place. || 14 ||
Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the fourth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
4.5 Now begins the fifth chapter of the fourth book.
He spreads an under-layer [of ghee] in the *juhū*, the *upabhṛt*, the vessel for the fat-oblation (*vasāhomahavanī*), and the vessel for the portions (*samavattadhānī*).
Having placed two chips of gold into the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt*, he issues the command: "Recite for the Manotā as the oblation is being portioned out."
With an unbroken stream from the branch of a Plakṣa tree, he cuts portions for the deities twice each;
first he cuts from the heart, then from the tongue, then from the chest— having cut these in their proper sequence—
he cuts the remaining parts as desired.
He cuts off the portion from the rectum either from the front or from above.
He divides the rectum into two parts; he sets aside the thicker part for the *upayaj* offerings.
Having divided the thinner part into three, he cuts off the middle section of that rectum in two portions and offers them to the deities.
From the *upabhṛt* ladle, he cuts portions from the two large tri-angled [pieces of meat] and from one of the two remaining rectum-sections.
Having divided the fat into three parts and placed it in the broth, he covers the *juhū* with one third and the *upabhṛt* with another third.
Into the *samavattadhānī* vessel, he places the heart, the tongue, the breast, the nipple, and the kidneys.

He adds the remaining rectum, the third part of the fat, and the seventh part, the large intestine (*vaniṣṭhu*), to the *iḍā* if it has been cooked; if it is uncooked, he increases the *iḍā* with boneless parts.
Having placed both the cooked and the uncooked portions of the animal together, he touches them while reciting, "The breath belongs to Indra.
He takes the fat-oblation into the fat-offering ladle (*vasāhomahavanī*).
With the formula, "Thou art glory," he cuts across the flowing stream with the knife;
once for one who offers four cuttings, twice for one who offers five.

With the formula, "The waters have flowed together," he stirs the fat-oblation (vasāhoma) with the side [of the knife]; according to some, he stirs it with the knife, while according to others, he covers it with the side [of the knife].
In this regard, some authorities prescribe the consecration of the hot vapors.
Having sprinkled it with broth, placed two pieces of gold on top, and poured clarified butter over it, he issues the direction:
"Recite the invitatory prayer for the goat-offering to Indra and Agni."
Having caused [the Hotṛ] to hear, the Maitrāvaruṇa does not send [him]; he urges the Hotṛ at the half-verse beginning with "ghṛtaṃ ghṛtapāvānaḥ. || 15 ||
The Pratiprasthātṛ offers the *vasā* oblation after the *yājyā*.
He sacrifices toward the quarters with the remainder of the *vasā* oblation:

"To the quarters! in the east; "To the intermediate quarters! in the south; "To the directed quarters! in the west; "To the intermediate directions! in the north; and "To the upward quarters! in the center. To each of these he appends "Svāhā! everywhere.
With the words "Svāhā to the quarters," he sprinkles water around [the fire] from left to right.
Having offered with the words "Homage to the quarters," he stands in worship.

Remaining in that very spot, having taken the *pṛṣadājya* in the *sruva*-ladle and poured it into the *juhū*-ladle, he issues the command: "Recite the invitatory verse for Vanaspati; give the call to Vanaspati."

Having poured the contents of the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*, he issues the summons for the animal *sviṣṭakṛt*: "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt; give the command for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt!
At this very point, some authorities prescribe the touching of the animal and the sacrifice to the quarters (*diśām pratījyā*).
He cuts off the intermediate *iḍā* portion mixed with fat.

If he should desire of someone, "May he be without cattle," he should offer that [portion] to him without fat; if he should desire of someone, "May he be rich in cattle," he should offer that to him with fat.
Having been invited, they eat with the Maitrāvaruṇa as the sixth.
He brings the adhyuddhi to the Hotṛ and the vaniṣṭhu to the Āgnīdhra, thus completing the sixfold portion.
When the *prāśitra* has been consumed, having performed the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), he issues the summons:

"O Āgnīdhra, bring the embers for the *aupayaja* offerings; O Upayaṣṭṛ, sit down; O Brahman, we shall set forth; O Āgnīdhra, having placed a fuel-stick, cleanse the enclosing sticks and the fire once each.
The Āgnīdhra, having taken embers from the *śāmitra* fire and having spread out the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) on the northern corner of the altar, scatters them and adds them as fuel.

"O Pratiprasthātṛ, having divided this rectum into eleven parts without piercing it crosswise, perform the secondary offerings (upayaja) with the fat-offering ladle (vasāhomahavanī) or with your hand," he thus commands.
Having poured the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) into the *juhū* and making the *upabhṛt* the vessel for the speckled butter, he performs the eleven after-offerings (*anūyāja*) with the speckled butter.
He issues the call for the first after-offering: "Prompt for the gods! and for the subsequent ones, "Prompt! Prompt!"

From the fourth [offering] onwards, when the Maitrāvaruṇa says "Sacrifice!", the Adhvaryu says "Sacrifice! Sacrifice! except for the tenth; [at the tenth, he says] "Go to the ocean, svāhā! (samudraṃ gaccha svāhā).
With these [formulas], the Pratiprasthātṛ performs the secondary offerings (upayajas) after each oblation of the after-offerings (anuyājas) has been made.
Having performed the secondary offerings with "To the waters thee! To the plants thee!", he wipes the smear on the grass-bundle to the north.
He touches the region of his heart with "May you grant me mind and heart."

Having anointed the *svaru* three times with the *juhū* ladle, the Adhvaryu offers the *svaru* into the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "May your smoke go to heaven, your flame to the intermediate space; fill the earth with ashes, Svāhā!
He then proceeds with the rites beginning with the *vājavatī* verses.
At the *sūktavāka*, he issues the direction: "Recite the *sūkta*! and "Prompt [the Hotṛ]!"
Having returned, he performs the *saṃyāja* offerings for the wives of the gods.
He sacrifices with the tail-flesh (*jāghanī*) to the wives of the gods and to Agni Gṛhapati; the other two [offerings] he makes with clarified butter.
From the upturned tail-flesh he cuts a portion for the wives of the gods, and from the downward-turned part for Agni Gṛhapati.
He places the *iḍā* portion upon the upward-turned tail for the *hotṛ*; he prepares a sixfold portion from the downward-turned [tail] for the *agnīdh*.
When the [portion] has been consumed, the wife gives the remainder of the tail to the *adhvaryu*, and the arm to the *śamitr*.
He gives that [arm] to a Brāhmaṇa, if he is not a Brāhmaṇa himself.

With the formula, "O sacrifice, go to the sacrifice; go to the lord of the sacrifice," the Adhvaryu offers three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations into the Āhavanīya fire using the *juhū* ladle. They proceed with the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*).
Having carried it away without letting it touch anything else, he extinguishes it at the junction of the dry and the moist with the formula, "Thou art heat; burn him [the enemy]."
Where the moist earth has been followed by that which is strewn over it,
they worship with the verse, "From every abode... They purify themselves with the verse, "May we have good friends..."
With the words, "Thou art fuel; may we prosper," they place fuel-sticks on the Āhavanīya fire.
With the words, "I have moved along the waters," they worship the Āhavanīya; in the same way, the wife, having placed a stick on the Gārhapatya fire, worships it.
This is the ritual procedure for all sacrificial animals.
The animal victim is a modification of the morning milk-offering because of the similarity of time;
likewise is the *āmikṣā*.
This remains unchanged in the case of the offerings to Agni and Indra-Agni, as well as in their modifications.

In the Agniṣomīya sacrifice and its modifications, the *prastara* is made of *aśvavāla* grass, the crosswise-stick (*tiraścī*) is made of sugarcane, and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are made of *kārṣmarya* wood, in addition to those made of *pūtudāru*. He issues the summons for the animal deity with the words: "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the omentum and fat of so-and-so; prompt [the Hotṛ] for the cake of so-and-so; prompt [the Hotṛ] for the oblation of so-and-so.
In the sacrifice to Indra and Sarasvatī, and in their modifications, the procedure for choosing the *pravara* and the procedure for the performance are those of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fourth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Thus ends the fourth book in the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Brahman that is *tat-sat*.
The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyaṣāḍha, together with the commentary Vaijayantī composed by Mahādeva.
Now begins the fourth book (praśna).

Therein is the first chapter (paṭala):— The sacrifices involving oblations (haviryajña), beginning with the fixed commencement [of the daily rites] and ending with the Darśa and other iṣṭis, have been described; now four others are being described. The animal sacrifice (paśu) follows the constant practice (nityābhyāsa) and precedes the non-constant ritual acts; likewise, it precedes the Cāturmāsya sacrifices and the Sautrāmaṇī. In this fourth book, the independent (nirūḍha) Aindrāgna sacrifice is treated together with its modified forms (vikṛti).

Even the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), though prescribed for all who desire [results], has been shown by Baudhāyana as being merely explanatory (*arthavādaka*); and by Āpastamba, the determination of eligibility regarding the various options was already dealt with in the first chapter of the first book, just like that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Therefore, it is not explained here. Furthermore, regarding the injunction for repetition, the discussion concerning its common eligibility with the injunction for lifelong performance was already concluded in the first chapter of the third book; hence, he explains only the actual performance (*prayoga*).
One should sacrifice with an animal dedicated to Indra and Agni every six months, at the beginning of each cycle, or every year.

That sacrifice whose deities are Indra and Agni is so designated. By the word *paśu* (animal), a goat is meant, according to the indicative mark in the text, "The goat's [offering] is for Vāyu. Baudhāyana states that when no specific animal is prescribed, it is a goat. This is both an originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*) and a temporal injunction (*kāla-vidhi*). In effect, this refers either to the entire life or to the ritual after the period of option; the term *paśu* denotes the sacrifice characterized by the animal, as it is called the "animal-binding" (*paśubandha*) rite—that in which the animal is bound.

*Ṣāṇmāsyaṃ* (the six-month rite) refers to a period of exactly six months; the word is used for the aggregate. When six months have passed, on whichever full-moon day (*parvan*) the first animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) occurs, that is the starting point. Here, because no specific [direction] is mentioned, the *udagayana* (northern solstice) is understood as the default, according to the statement "the *udagayana* is the instruction. Because there is no limit on time due to the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), it is understood to last "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*). Regarding the "return" (*āvṛtti*) at the solstices (*ayana*), some say it is at the "beginning" (*mukha*) of the two solstices—that is, on the full-moon day immediately following the transit (*saṃkrānti*)—while others say it is on the day immediately following the transit.

In this case as well, the commencement is only during the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*); it is the same even according to the view that the rite may last for a year. [The manuscripts] ka, kha, ca, cha, ṭa, da, ka, pha [read *dakapha*]. [This is from] the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha (Fourth Book): "It is either dedicated to Sūrya or to Prajāpati;

the animal sacrifice is to be performed at these times"—this is the remainder [of the rule]. That which has Sūrya as its deity or Prajāpati as its deity is the option between these two; the restriction regarding the commencement of these two [options] belonging to other recensions was stated by Kātyāyana. That is also desired by us. There are three types of animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*):...

We shall explain that. The meaning is as follows: although the five constituent parts (*pañcāṅga*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma are intermingled, they are extracted and explained together specifically in the *Nirūḍha* sacrifice. Even though the general duties of the Adhvaryu (*ādhvaryava-sāmānya*) pertaining to the animal sacrifices of the Soma ritual, such as the Agniṣomīya, are already obtained here in the *Nirūḍha* by means of extended application (*atideśa*), nevertheless, because the duties of the Hotṛ (*hautra*)—such as "Oṃ śoṃsāvoṃ" and so forth—are taught specifically for the Aindrāgna animal sacrifice in our own Śākhā within the *Nirūḍha*, that [Aindrāgna] also serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*). Thus, all the Adhvaryu duties, even those extended from elsewhere, are explained right here. These [five parts] apply to the three types of animal sacrifices.

The sacrificial post, the altar, and so forth are common [to all sacrifices] as they are directly taught; those that are specific [to particular rites] must be inferred. For example, in the *saurya* and *dhānā-pātnīvata* offerings, one says: "I dedicate you, acceptable to Sūrya," or "I dedicate you, acceptable to Indra and Agni," and so on. Such is the explanation of the triad [of deities]. Because no rule for moving the fire is prescribed here, the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) takes place in the house itself. Kātyāyana states it is "in the house. Since the *darśapūrṇamāsa* is its archetype, it may be performed in the house provided that, when possible, the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) is prepared elsewhere and the ritual is completed there.

Having mentally recited the *Ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula, "The sun is your eye," and having offered the oblation along with the *graha*, he performs the *Anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice. The *Ṣaḍḍhotṛ* mantra, which ends with the words "by the bodies" (*śarīraiḥ*), is recited mentally; the *graha* mantra begins with "O Lord of Speech" (*vācaspati*). According to the Śruti, it is called a *graha* because it "becomes a *graha*" (is held). Having recited that [mantra] in a whisper (*upāṃśu*), the final offering is made with silent (*tūṣṇīka*) clarified butter. The *Ṣaḍḍhotṛ* is the offering-mantra accompanied by the *graha*. The sequence expressed by the suffix *-tvā* refers to the priority of one act over another, not in relation to the subsequent *iṣṭi* sacrifice.

"One who is about to perform the animal sacrifice (paśubandha), having mentally recited the six Hotṛ-formulas, shall offer oblations in the Āhavanīya fire"—this statement "one who is about to perform" refers to the period prior to the commencement of the sacrifice. Therefore, having led forward another [fire], he performs the Anvārambhaṇīyā sacrifice. This very leading forward of the fire is for the sake of the primary rite; for it has been stated that whatever is led forward for the sake of the primary rite, the subsidiary rites belong to that very [fire] which was led forward for the sake of the primary rite. Thus, when the fire is led forward for its own sake, the primary sacrifice must be performed in the fire led forward for the sake of the primary rite alone.

The *Anvārambhaṇīyā* [is so called] because by means of it there is the subsequent undertaking (*anvārambha*) of the fire for the sake of the principal rite; thus, what will be stated later—that "by means of it he shall establish the *Āhavanīya*"—is logically consistent. And this alone is the purpose of the name *Anvārambhaṇīyā*, and not that it is obtained through the extension (*atideśa*) of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa-anvārambhaṇīyā*; rather, this [rite] is prescribed as a substitute (*bādha*) for that [extended rite], and therefore it is called *Anvārambhaṇīyā* because it serves the same function as the *Anvārambhaṇīyā*. If it is argued that it is so called because its occasion is the "commencement" (*ārambha*), we say no.

If that were the case, it would not be appropriate to say, "he maintains the fire" (*dhārayati*); therefore, this [act] is for the purpose of consecrating the fire (*agni-saṃskāra*). For this very reason, Āpastamba states that this is a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) for the *anvādhāna*. In his view, since the *anvādhāna* is for the purpose of consecrating the fire, it is omitted in our view; however, for the sake of encompassing the deities (*devatā-parigraha*), the *iṣṭi* is performed, and the *anvādhāna* is also performed.

Therefore, in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is a new *anvārambhaṇīyā* [offering]; for while the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are indeed occasioned by the commencement (*ārambha*), the commencement itself is not the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. Alternatively, it pertains to the first performance (*prathamaprayoga*); and while the extension (*atideśa*) does not apply to the first performance of a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it does apply to a performance that is common to both the first and subsequent instances. Nor should it be argued that because of the similarity in being "first," the first performance of the modified sacrifice would likewise possess the *anvārambhaṇīyā*.

In that case, if the performance of the *vikṛtis* (modified sacrifices) were necessarily continuous, it would apply only to those *vikṛtis* that follow the *cāturmāsyas*, and not to all *vikṛtis*; for there is no continuous performance of all *vikṛtis*, as they consist of occasional (*naimittika*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites. And in the absence of such continuity, the status of being a "first performance" (*prathamaprayogatā*) is not established. When there is a single resolution (*saṃkalpa*) regarding many [rites], then the distinction between first, second, and so forth, arises.

If it is argued that even when a rite is performed only once, the term "commencement" (*ārambha*) is observed in the sense of the undertaking of the fruit and its cause, and thus it does not refer exclusively to the very first commencement—this is true. Nevertheless, such a view is not consistent with the logic of the Sūtra author either. To explain: there exists the rule, "And there is the *anvārambhaṇīyā* for the commencement of the animal sacrifice," which implies that the *anvārambhaṇīyā* is not performed in the case of animals belonging to the *soma* sacrifice. Since the *iṣṭi* (the *anvārambhaṇīyā*) is extended by injunction to both types of sacrifices, it would follow [that it must be performed in both], which contradicts the stated exception. Thus, the Sūtra author’s position remains unrefuted.

But that which is prohibited has been observed in the case of the *nirūḍha* (independent sacrifice). As he will state regarding the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya*): "The ritual procedure is explained by [the rules for] the *nirūḍha-paśubandha*. Therefore, having raised the doubt that [the procedure] might apply here as it does in the *nirūḍha*, he prohibits it with the words "not in the *anīkavati*" and so forth, referring to the *agnīṣomīya* and other such sacrifices. In that regard, concerning the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices, it is stated: "Having commenced the slaughter of those [animals], having mentally recited the *pañcahotṛ* formula and offered the *sāṃhitī* oblation, one performs the *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice."

In that case, because it serves as the cause for the commencement [of the sacrifice], the *anvārambhaṇīyā* is indeed the primary one; however, the word *anvārambhaṇīyā* does not signify the extension (*atideśa*) of the *anvārambhaṇīyā* belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśapaurṇamāsika*). This is because when the primary sense is possible, it is improper to accept a secondary one.

And likewise, just as in the case of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, if even in the primary form another deity were enjoined in place of those [deities] on the full moon day of Phālguna or Caitra, then—considering the brevity of the injunction "he sacrifices with the Vaiśvadeva; there he should offer the Anvārambhaṇīyā, a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara, and a pap for Pānnya"—there would be no explicit instruction [for these], since they would already be obtained from the archetype (prakṛti) itself.

Therefore, since the *Anvārambhaṇīyā* has already been obtained [by extension], and its cause and time have been indicated by the *pṛṣat* [verse], the text prescribes a previously unestablished sacrifice (*iṣṭi*). Thus, it is not stated [explicitly] regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśu*); by that, it makes known that its function is distinct from that of the animal sacrifice. In this regard, the intention of the Sūtra is that another sacrifice is not [required] there through extension (*atideśa*), as is the case with the *Cāturmāsya* and the *Vaiśvadeva*, and likewise in the *Āgrayaṇeṣṭi*.

Here, the justification is as follows: the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) indeed precede the Animal Sacrifice, the Four-Monthly Sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), and the *Iṣṭis*. In that context, the *Ārambhaṇīyā* (Introductory Rite) has already been performed; it is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person. It must be stated whether this [refinement] belongs to the agent who is about to act, or whether the status of being an agent is established for the enjoyer even without such a refinement. By this, it is established that it pertains to all primary rites (*pradhāna*). And the primary rite is to be performed as long as one lives (*yāvajjīvam*).

One desiring to perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices should perform the Anvārambhāṇīyā-iṣṭi at the first performance, and that [performance] must indeed be outside of the actual ritual procedure. When performed there, it purifies the sacrificer for the sake of the *phalāpūrva* (the transcendental result) arising throughout his lifetime, and not merely for the sake of the *phalāpūrva* of the first performance alone. For the *phalāpūrva* is not produced by the Pūrṇamāsa sacrifice alone, but rather by both the Darśa and the Pūrṇamāsa; nor does the [Anvārambhāṇīyā], when performed during the Pūrṇamāsa, become an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Darśa for the first time.

Therefore, the *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifice is performed immediately outside of that ritual application (*prayoga*), being carried out for the first time. Just as with the *darśa*, it is performed throughout one's life once its obligation has been established; there is no interval of time. In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, regarding the lack of interruption therein, one should be satisfied with the fact that, because of the mention of the *viṣṭakṛt* offering, it is just as with the *darśa* for the subsequent sacrifices as well.

And thus, according to the *tantra* (single performance) principle, it is established that for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices themselves—and by extension for others—the *anvārambhaṇīyā* apūrva is not completed throughout one's lifetime; rather, when the master has been consecrated by it, the *phalāpūrva* (resultant apūrva) of the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) may also arise. Furthermore, regarding the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices, even if there were a need for another *anvārambhaṇīyā* due to the requirement of a distinct *apūrva* for their result, there would be no inconsistency whatsoever; for what could a scriptural injunction (*vacana*) not accomplish? Other arguments have already been demonstrated in the analysis of the *anvārambhaṇīyā* of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

Furthermore, even in the first performance, the *anvārambhaṇīyā* does not fall at the end of that performance. How so? The *anvārambhaṇīyā* and the *vaimṛdha* belong to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*). In that context, the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, having subsumed all their requirements, do not extend [the *anvārambhaṇīyā*] to the modified sacrifices by means of extended application (*atideśa*) until their own completion.

If the *anvārambhaṇīyā* and the *iṣṭi* have been performed, then the performance would be complete with its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*). Likewise, since the *anvārambhaṇīyā* and the *iṣṭi* require assistance, they obtain their subsidiary status through the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices which are extended [to them]. However, because the assistance provided by the subsidiaries of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* is not yet established at this point, it is not logical that the subsidiaries should be grasped in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) by way of such assistance. The word *anvārambhaṇīyā* is derived here as "that by means of which the fire for the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) is touched. It means one performs or offers the *iṣṭi*. Regarding that, he says: "An eleven-potherd cake for Agni-Viṣṇu."

The term "he offers" (nirvapati) is drawn forward [from the previous context]. The meaning is that one should perform an *iṣṭi* sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Viṣṇu, which has the *anvārambhaṇīyā* deity as its recipient and an eleven-potherd sacrificial cake (*ekādaśakapāla-puroḍāśa*) as its substance. It is completed successfully; that is to say, it is completed in the same manner as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, by virtue of being a modification (*vikāra*) of the *agnīṣomīya*. It is concluded—that is, brought to an end. There is no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), because the purchase of services is accomplished by the principal fee itself, and because there is no specific injunction to the contrary. It should be understood that the phrase "and the sacrifice is successful" (*yajñaśaṃ ca*) does not apply here either.

Alternatively, one offers the four-spoonfuls of clarified butter (*ājya*) into the *āhavanīya* fire with a verse addressed to Agni and Viṣṇu. At the place of the *iṣṭi*, however, one offers with clarified butter prepared silently in four spoonfuls. Although the rule "into the *āhavanīya*" would already apply because of the presence of the *davihoma* (oblation with a ladle), this specific statement is for the purpose of ensuring that the fire has been specifically drawn out for the sake of the primary rite; thus, there should be no drawing out of another fire by abandoning the one already drawn out. This oblation, being a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the fire for the sake of the primary rite, shares the same function as the *iṣṭi*; therefore, it is stated that the fire is the object of consecration, just as in the case of the morning milk (*prātardoha*) when it is heated. Furthermore, both the *iṣṭi* and the oblation possess the character of a consecration and the nature of a ritual act (*karman*), just like the *dīkṣaṇīyā-iṣṭi*.
He prepares the remainder of the clarified butter (ājya) and maintains the Āhavanīya fire.

He prepares the remainder of the clarified butter for either of the two *iṣṭihoma* offerings for the purpose of the *yūpāhuti* (sacrificial post oblation). And because of the statement, "In the *iyāṃ* offering, he prepares the remainder of the Āhavanīya which has been brought back for the sake of the primary rite," even if the remainder is lost, it is not necessary to produce it again; rather, the task must be performed with a substitute. However, the term "remainder" does not apply when the *homa* itself is omitted. [End of Paṭala 5, Section 150] With the mantra, "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely," he offers the *yūpāhuti* into the Āhavanīya fire using the *sruva* ladle.

Here, the mention of the *āhavanīya* fire is intended to prevent [the fire] from being produced by friction near the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), because in the ritual for the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, it is prescribed that the fire is produced by friction even in Kātyāyana’s tradition. The phrase "he offers with the *sruva*" is stated to preclude the use of the *juhū* ladle, which would otherwise be obtained due to the nature of this being a *darvihoma*. It refers to the oblation known as the *yūpāhuti*. In the Soma sacrifice, if the consecrated person (*dīkṣita*) cuts the sacrificial post, the offering is made with fresh clarified butter (*ājya*), because there is no remainder of the butter due to the absence of both the *anvārambhaṇīyā* and the *iṣṭi* offerings. He takes up the remainder of the clarified butter and the *sruva*, hands over an axe to the wood-cutter, and they go to where they are about to cut the sacrificial post.

Then the Brahman, the sacrificer, and the Adhvaryu go to that forest where the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) have been prepared; there the attendants and the carpenter stand ready to cut them down. The rest is as before. He hands over the axe; this [axe] was not previously accepted outside the *ārṣeya* [section] in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. The sacrificial posts are made of *Palāśa*, *Khadira*, *Bilva*, or *Rohītaka* wood.
They are called *yūpya* because they are fit for a *yūpa* (sacrificial post).

One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) or food should make a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of *pālāśa* wood; one desiring heaven, of *khadira*; one desiring spiritual luster, of *bilva*; and one desiring progeny, of *rohītaka*. The phrase "one should make a sacrificial post" is to be supplied to complete the sense. These [posts] should be made after forming such a resolution when there is a specific desire; otherwise, they are obligatory and serve both purposes. The *rohītaka* is similar to the *vaṭa* (banyan) tree, though its leaves are somewhat smaller. One should select trees for the sacrificial posts that are at least three years old.

Having passed by trees suitable for sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), that is, having passed by those trees which have at least three branches (meaning those with three or more branches), and even beyond those;
[he should take one] which is straight, upright, with upward-pointing sections and upward-pointing branches, grown upon level ground from its own natural source.

The phrase "he should cut that" is to be connected with what follows. *Avakaḥ* means not crooked, not thick, not having its bark peeled away, and not having branches—this is the sequence of meanings. It must grow from the earth itself (*bhūmyai bhūmeḥ sakāśāt*), and not from a stone or similar substrate. It must grow from its own source (*svādyoneḥ*), meaning from its own material cause, and not from a branch. Therefore, Āpastamba uses the term *upaśākhaja* ("born from a branch") specifically in the first book (*prathamakāṇḍa*) for such [a tree].

If one should desire, "May he be without a firm foundation," one should cut a branch from the top of a tree for him. If one should desire, "May he be without cattle," one should cut a leafless branch for him with a dried tip. If one should desire, "May he possess cattle," one should cut a branch with many leaves, many twigs, and an undried tip. The statement beginning with "If one should desire" is a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the third optional alternative. "A climber" (*ārohaḥ*) means one who has climbed up a tree to its branches; the rest is clear. For one desiring a firm foundation, [the wood] should be firmly established. [Note: *Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram*, Chapter 4, Section on the Optional Branches.]
The meaning of the passage beginning with "same mūmyām" is whether the *maṇika* is obligatory (*nitya*) or optional (*kāmya*).
One should dig [the pit] where it slopes toward the west; or where it slopes toward the east or the north.

The word "or" (*vā*) is connected to each of the three positions for the purpose of providing an option regarding the phrase "facing the east" (*prāṅmukha*). "Slopes toward" (*upanata*) means inclined.

For one who possesses such vigor (*vīrya*), even though its tip has only slightly approached [the goal], the previously mentioned alternative—that it is "not primary"—is set aside; for it is by the statement "he who is proximate" that the excellence of those very two is expressed. To explain this, the Sūtra says: "This [vigor] has slightly approached. Thus, the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) is not contradicted. Having stated that one should cut down a tree of such a form, he describes the manner of doing so:
"It does not go beyond others. (1) Whomever one chooses, to him one approaches.
The officiants, being eager, approach the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), which they consider a source of pleasure because of its nature as a pillar.
[He addresses it: "O tree, may the divine Savitṛ anoint you with honey. With the *sruva* ladle, he anoints it all around at the height of the ankle or the knee.

The ankle is the joint of the foot. Having avoided the space between the two joints of the thighs, he anoints it all around on the adjacent surface. It is said that the word "wide" (*uru*) is used for the purpose of distinguishing the hand.

With the words, "O herb, protect him," he places an herb with its tip pointing upward between [the tree and the axe]. With the words, "O axe, do not harm him," he strikes with the axe. He catches the first chip that falls away.
He sets it down on a stone. The rest is clear.
He cuts [the tree] leaving a stump that does not obstruct the axle, or one reaching to the height of the ankles.

He said, "One should cut [the wood] leaving a stump," for the sake of the Brāhmaṇa's purpose, stating that there should be a stump remaining so that it does not get stuck in the axle of the cart as it would if it were small; thus, "gulphadāna" (leaving a stump) is an alternative to what was previously mentioned. The place for the cutting is specified by the sūtra "devas tvā... as the location for the *añjana* (anointing). It is understood that the splinter (*śakala*) is produced there by the blow, and that the place for the *añjana* is for the sake of the splinter, because the place for cutting the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) has already been stated. With the formula "divam agreṇa...", he causes it to be struck either toward the east or toward the north.

The end of the mantra is *pṛṣicyā saṃbhava*. He causes [the tree] to fall by letting it go. With the mantra, *O Lord of the Forest, grow with a hundred shoots*, he offers an oblation upon the stump (*āvraścana*). With the mantra, *May we grow with a thousand shoots*, he touches himself. The stump is the *āvraścana*. He offers the oblation according to the rules of a *dravahoma* (liquid oblation), using only the remainder of the clarified butter (*ājya*). The rest has already been explained. [End of section]. With the mantra, "Thou whom this axe... ending with "...for good fortune," he fashions the limbs [of the sacrificial post] with the axe in the natural direction. With the mantra, "Unbroken be the wealth... he trims the tip. He fashions and cuts the large side-branches in the natural direction, beginning from below and moving upwards by means of cutting.
With the mantra, "Unbroken be the wealth... he trims the top.

One cuts the tip of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with a measuring device at the very place where the post is to be; this is a consecratory act (*saṃskāra*). For this very reason, Kātyāyana [states] "having trimmed it, one should cut again," because of the prohibition against cutting again.
The sacrificial post measurements beginning with one *aratni*, which are explained in the Brāhmaṇa as being for optional rites (*kāmya*), are to be used according to one's desire.

"Looking at it with the foot, he makes a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of twenty-one cubits; by that, he conquers this very world. Then a post of twenty cubits; by that, he conquers the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*)," and so forth, according to the *Vājasaneyaka Brāhmaṇa*. Those [posts] beginning with "for one desiring splendor" up to the limit of twenty-one cubits have been explained in their respective *Brāhmaṇas*; they are indeed for optional purposes (*kāmya*) and should be employed according to the specific desire.
Together with the latter, the number extends up to thirty-three cubits.

The portion above ground, the part dug into the earth, and the *ātala*—the base section that enters into the middle of the sacrificial ground—all together constitute the measurement of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), up to a maximum of thirty-three units.
Alternatively, for the *nirūḍhapaśubandha* sacrifice, the post is made of *pālāśa* wood and measures three or four *aratnis*; other types of posts belong to the *saumya-adhvara*.

Regarding those sacrificial post trees (*yūpavṛkṣa*) that were previously mentioned without distinction, and among those materials for the sacrificial posts, the *nyagrodha* (fig tree) is eight or four *aratnis* in height; it is prescribed as the standard for the animal sacrifice dedicated to Indra-Agni, to Sūrya, or to Prajāpati. For other [sacrifices], other trees are joined with it, such as the *śamyā* tree for the Soma sacrifice, the *audumbara* for the *agniṣṭoma* and subsequent rites. For thus it is heard in the Vājasaneyaka: "This sacrificial post for the animal sacrifice is either six *aratnis* or four *aratnis* in height. Likewise, in that very same context, there is the rule: "One should make it of *palāśa* wood alone."

He fashions it with eight facets, neither too thick nor too thin, and he fashions the edge until it is finished. That is, he fashions it so that its edge has eight facets; such would be the bringing of the fashioner observed. He does not fashion the upper part. The rest is clear.
[He makes] either progressively thicker or like a cow’s tail.
From the top downwards, it is somewhat narrow; from the bottom upwards, it is somewhat wider; then it is somewhat broad, and then again somewhat narrow—just like a cow’s tail.
Therefore, [the claim that it is] "not connected" (asaṃgata) is incorrect.
Ga., Ṭha., Ṇa.: "sthāmīṣoma. [This is from] the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [Book 4, Chapter 1].
He makes the *caṣāla* from that very tree [from which] the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) was made;
it is not from another tree. It is made from the remaining portion of the part above the trimmed section of that specific tree from which the post was taken. As for how it should be made, he says:
"It should have eight corners, be as thick as the palm of the hand, and be curved in the middle."

That which has eight bases (or supports) is [the post] by virtue of that [number]. It is broad from the wrist of a hand whose fingers are slightly contracted, extending as far as the tips of the fingers. Baudhāyana says it is ten finger-breadths broad at the base. It is ten finger-breadths long in the middle, measured in relation to the front and back parts.
As long as this first section of the finger is, so long does one extend the *caṣāla* and other parts above the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

The first joint of the forefinger is its measure; the top of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) should extend beyond the *caṣāla* by that length. One inserts it into the mouth of the *caṣāla* once a hole has been made.
It should be the size of a finger, or even slightly less than a finger.
The part to be inserted into the base of the post is thick enough to be the measure of a finger; or even finer than that, as he will explain regarding the fastening.
One makes the *svaru* from one of these very shavings, measuring two, three, or four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
From among these very shavings, one makes a chip named *svaru*, measuring one finger-breadth or more, using any one of the shavings produced by the carving.
If one should desire, "May another ascend to his world," he should make both the *svaru* and the *caṣāla* from the wood of the *armya* tree.

This is a deprecatory explanatory statement (*nindārthavāda*). The meaning is that another rival (*bhrātṛvya*) might ascend to the world or place of this sacrificer; therefore, one should make [the altar] from that very tree. (चित्त):** Mind, the faculty of thought and perception. * **Vasana (वासना):** Latent impressions, subconscious tendencies. * **Prarabdha Karma (प्रारब्ध कर्म):** Karma that has already begun to bear "The materials have already been prepared; the fire is being kindled. This is the recitation regarding *guggulu* incense—known in the vernacular as *guggu*. *Sugandhitejana* is a specific type of grass which, because of its bitterness, is not eaten by cattle. It is white and full; "full" refers to the woolly tuft (*stukā*) that grows between the horns of a castrated ram (*petva*). Kātyāyana states that a *petva* is simply a castrated bull (*vṛṣṇi*).
Regarding the phrase "of him whose woolly tuft is cut," Bharadvāja says that according to some, it means "of one whose woolly tuft has been severed."

He pours those materials onto the northern navel [of the altar] only once with the mantra, "Thou art the ash of Agni. Regarding these materials (*saṃbhārān*): although the singular form is heard in the mantra—"Thou art the ash of Agni," "Thou art the soil (*purīṣa*) of Agni"—and because each substance is distinct like a cow or a horse, and because a separate mantra is seen for each individual act of placing them, such [a repetition] would logically follow; yet it is stated that it is "once" (*sakṛt*). This is because they are enjoined by the single term *saṃbhāra*, and because they constitute a single composite substance. Since the plural number in the word *saṃbhārāḥ* stands in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the singular [referent], there is no repetition. This is the meaning.

When the verse "Sit down first upon the woolly womb" is being recited, he establishes the sacrifice upon the sacrificial materials with the mantra: "O Sacrifice, be established in the benevolent and most gracious favor; may riches enter thee in many ways; creating long life for the sacrificer, then anoint the singer with immortality. With the words "The sacrifice has been established," he establishes it upon the materials. While the Hotṛ recites, he establishes that kindled fuel upon the scattered materials with the mantra.
