To the south, he pours out the supporting earth with the formula: "Thou art the nest of Agni."
He pours out the supporting sand near the fire, saying:
"As for men, we set thee down; as for men, we kindle thee. O Agni Aṅgiras, like a man, sacrifice to the gods for the one who desires the gods. He kindles the fire with a piece of wood.

"May Agni, knowing [the way], lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find it. May he announce the sacrifice to the gods; further, further extend the lord of the sacrifice—*svāhā*! May Vāyu, the Āditya, the sacrifice, knowing [the way], lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find it. May he announce the sacrifice to the gods; further, further extend the lord of the sacrifice—*svāhā*! Having offered these four *atimukti* oblations—namely, the two mantras beginning with "Vāyu, the sacrifice... and "Āditya, the sacrifice... respectively, with the word *svāhā* appended to both through ellipsis—he offers them according to the ritual rules of the *dravahoma*.

Having cleansed the *juhū* and the *sruva* ladles, and having filled the *sruk* with four, eight, or twelve portions of clarified butter, he offers the *pūrṇāhuti* (full-offering) with the verse, "Seven... thee" (*sapta ta iti*). || 5 ||

Because the oblation is unprecedented (*apūrva*), there is an injunction for an unprecedented cleansing (*saṃmārga*). Regarding the statement "having filled," it is said that one takes [the liquid] in such a way that it becomes full—whether by twelve portions, eight portions, or four portions—as indicated by the word. Furthermore, the name *pūrṇāhuti* (full-oblation) is derived from the etymological explanation: "an oblation made with what is full. That fire from which this is carried forth is the *āhavanīya*; that [from which it was originally taken] is the *gārhapatya*.

Having carried forward [the fire] onto the *uttaravedi* and consecrated it up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), that fire here serves the purpose of the *āhavanīya* specifically for the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), and not for the *agnihotra* homa; for the fire which is carried forward here is the *gārhapatya*, not the one used in the *agnihotra*. Accordingly, the *agnihotra* must be performed at its proper time even during the middle of that [sacrifice], and that [performance] occurs only in the original fires, not in the one situated on the *uttaravedi*. As for the option stated by Bharadvāja—"either when the animal sacrifice has concluded or at the proper time"—that has been refuted.
Having added fuel to the *āhavanīya*, *gārhapatya*, and *dakṣiṇāgni*, he brings the sacrificial wood (*idhma*) and the grass-bundle (*barhis*).

This is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), intended for the purpose of establishing the sequence and for the purpose of setting aside the opinion of others. Regarding the *anvādhāna* (the adding of fuel), it has been stated that its purpose is the formal acceptance (*parigraha*) of the deities; since the acceptance of the deities is accomplished by the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, there is no scriptural statement [regarding such acceptance] here. Therefore, there is no accomplishment of the *anvādhāna*. Thus says Bharadvāja: "One should not take up the fire in the animal sacrifice or the *iṣṭi*—this is another view. For in the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, the purpose of accepting the deities is established by a direct scriptural statement (*vacana*). However, the mention of each individual [sacrifice] is for the purpose of demonstrating the absence of *anvādhāna* in the case of the *prājihita* fire.

The accomplishment of the *anvādhāna* (the adding of fuel) is achieved through the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), because it is a modification of the *sānnāyya*. The fetching of the branch, which is mentioned in another Sūtra, should not occur here; therefore, he brings in the fuel for the *anvādhāna* from outside. For it is a liquid substance that must be purified by the branch, not meat; since it has been stated that when that [meat] is absent, the substance associated with its ritual properties (*dharma-dravya*) is likewise excluded.

Since the Veda was already studied previously, preceded by the taking of vows (*vratagrahaṇa*), there is no fetching of a *plakṣa* branch here either. Its purpose is not for the sake of the primary (*prakṛta*) ritual branch, but rather for the sake of instruction and memorization regarding the modified (*vikṛti*) ritual. Furthermore, immediately after the fetching from outside, one brings it in; however, there is no specific injunction for its bringing in, because there is an absence of injunctions for items intended for external purposes. The ritual specialists (*prāyaugika*), however, bring it in silently. Or, since the act of bringing it in is already established, why "silently"? Because [it is] grass (*barhis*). It is indeed the primary (*prākṛta*) [grass], but not the two stalks of sugarcane (*ikṣuśalāka*), because it is a modification of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice.
There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses, and one does not bind the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) to the fuel-wood (*idhma*).

Regarding the number seventeen, one view stated here is that it is prescribed by direct injunction (*vācanika*) for the *nirūḍha-paśubandha*, whereas in other modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), there is an option; however, in this case, it is said that the *samidh*s are invariably increased. As for the function of the enclosing sticks, since they are praised in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) as being "brothers of Agni," this preparation of the northern altar-ground (*uttara-vedi*) serves a visible purpose; nevertheless, by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*), a non-visible preparatory effect characterized by the warding off of *rakṣas* demons can also be accomplished by these [sticks]. Furthermore, because they are enjoined by the word "enclosing stick" (*paridhi*), the other original [enclosing sticks] are set aside.

Then follows the modification: "you [enter] twentyfold. The term *trī paridhīn* ("the three enclosing sticks") is elided. Regarding *yajñāyuranusaṃcarān*, the masculine gender is used with the intention of referring to the *upaveṣa* and the *dṛṣṭi*; this has already been demonstrated previously. Having strewn around the fires, having washed his hands, and having spread out a layer of *ulapa* grass, [he proceeds].

This is a restatement (anuvāda) of what is already established by the general injunction (codaka), intended for the purpose of enumerating the ritual items (padārthakrama). Since the preparation of the altar (vedikaraṇa) occurs after the bringing of the grass (bahirāharaṇa), it has already taken place. Where there is the spreading of grass (paristaraṇa) and fasting (upavāsa), even in the absence of the ritual action at night, there is no loss of the purificatory refinement (saṃskāra); this is stated for the purpose of demonstrating that principle. Following the spreading of grass, one simply washes the hands. One employs the vessels used for animal sacrifice (pāśukāni pātrāṇi) according to their respective purposes (yathārtham). The word "yathārtham" is used to indicate that, although the vessels for medicinal herbs (auṣadha-pātrāṇi) are obtained through extended application (atideśa), they have no further use here. Thus, the meaning is: "one employs the vessels used for animal sacrifice according to their respective purposes."

The wooden sword (*sphya*), the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle, the *sruva* spoon, two axes, two *juhū* offering-ladles, a second *vasāhomahavanī* ladle, two *upabhṛt* supporting-ladles, a second *pṛṣadājyadhānī* vessel for the speckled butter, a *dhruvā* ladle, two vessels for clarified butter, a second vessel for curds, the *veda* broom, a vessel for collecting the cuttings, two ropes— one double-stranded and two spans long, and one triple-stranded and three spans long— two *vapāśrapaṇī* omentum-roasting spits made of *kārṣmarya* wood, one with two prongs and one with a single prong, a cooking-pot, the heart-spit, a branch of the *plakṣa* tree, the *svaru* chip, the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa priest, the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), a splinter from the post, a *paraṇī* vessel, and whatever else is required.

The ordinary items—the skull-bowl (*kapāla*), winnowing-basket (*śūrpa*), hide (*ajina*), wooden pin (*śamyā*), and so forth—are excluded due to the absence of vegetable substances as the offering material. *Khādhiti* is the weapon for cutting up the animal; *juhū*—although this is not a change of name for the *juhū* vessel, the designation *juhū* here is Vedic (chāndasa), for in the common language (*bhāṣā*) it ought to be *juhvau*. *Dadhidhānī* means "the second one," referring to that vessel in which curd is first poured; thus, it is called *dadhidhānī*. And that in which the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) is prepared is indeed the *pṛṣadājyasthālī*.

The *samavattadhānī* is the *iḍā*-vessel used for the animal sacrifice; the *yūpaśakala* is a chip from the sacrificial post intended for anointing. The rest is clear. "With whatever there is need"—that is, with whatever [implement], such as a piece of gold and so forth. Other items are to be understood in the same way.
Having prepared the two strainers (*pavitre*), he issues the command, "Restrain the speech of the sacrificer," and while remaining silent, he touches the vessels.

Immediately after the purification (*pavitrakaraṇa*), there is indeed the statement: "O Brahman, I shall lead forward [the water]. The leading forward of the *praṇītā* water is to be performed preceded by this address, as explained in the *Vājasaneyaka Brāhmaṇa*: "The leading forward of the *praṇītā* for the New and Full Moon sacrifices has been explained. This has already been explained in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices themselves. The rest is clear. He releases his speech once the [grains] have been sprinkled (*prokṣita*).

Having reflected upon the speech uttered by the *havikṛt*, O Hotṛ, because of the absence of time while the vessels have been sprinkled—since among the items to be performed even in a simple sacrifice that are subject to the *prakṛti* and obtained through *codaka*, there are no others [remaining] once they have been sprinkled—it is said, "while they have been sprinkled.
Having performed the second tracing (*parigrāha*), he proceeds with the call, "Bring the clarified butter and the curds," and he concludes at the end of this call.

Immediately after the *sphya* and the *sruva*, the formula beginning with "Bring the *mokṣaṇī* waters" and so forth, along with the drinking, is recited; the specific modification for the *abhyātāna* formulas follows immediately after this. The word "and the binding" (*bandhā ca*) is to be supplied [from the previous context], as it refers to the day of preparation (*saṃnāma ahaḥ*). Although it has already been stated that the modification is according to the purpose, the phrase "the end of the *śreṣa*" is mentioned here specifically to ensure that the *sruva* and the *svadhiti* are not included in the middle.

The intended meaning is as follows: just as in the rule *sūtraṃ samāṣṭi* (he smooths the thread), the word *sūtra* itself is understood [to include its specific type], so here, by the mention of *avagraha* (the wooden sword), the mention of the *svadhiti* (axe) is established. Because there is no substance to be offered (*pradeya*) in the case of curd (*dadhi*), it does not share the same status as clarified butter (*ājya*). Therefore, when another substance is joined with that purpose, the application of the ritual properties (*dharmāveśa*) would not occur; for that reason, it is stated and shown that "he measures out" (*samunatti*). Having performed that which precedes the pouring of the clarified butter, and having poured out the clarified butter, he pours out the curd for the sake of the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*).

Following the primary (prakṛta) items, for the purpose of introducing the modified (vaikṛta) ones, there is the instruction: "Having performed that which precedes the pouring of the clarified butter (ājya), according to the sequence of the directions. In that context, the wiping of the *svadhiti* knife is like [the wiping] of the *bhūvana* vessel, because it is a means for the portioning (*avadāna*). Thus, having taken the curd-pot with the formula "Aditi is yours," he pours out the curd with the formula "Of the great ones. Its purpose is for the sake of the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*); the meaning is that this is for the refinement of that which possesses the speckled quality.

Therefore, this is not the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) itself, but rather that which consecrates the oblation; consequently, the properties of curd (*dadhi-dharma*), such as the evening milking and so forth, do not apply. Although there is no mention of the generic category "oblation" here—unlike the statement "where the oblation is offered"—and although *āmikṣā* (the specific curd-mixture) is what is intended, nevertheless, the properties of clarified butter (*ājya-dharma*) apply to the stated object. However, it is not the case that there are no consecrations for that [curd], for it is not prescribed in the place of the clarified butter used for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), such that the properties of clarified butter would necessarily apply. To this, he says: "The properties of clarified butter are performed for that [curd] insofar as it is other than the act of placing it on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*)."

For in the *Vājasaneyibrāhma�aṇa* it is stated: "This [offering] is indeed twofold: clarified butter (*sarpis*) and consecrated ghee (*ājya*)," which establishes the ritual properties (*dharma*) as belonging to a substance that is independent. Therefore, it is said that the properties of *ājya* are performed upon it. If it is argued that both [substances] together constitute the sacrificial offering (*havis*), we say no; for the scripture (*śruti*) declares their unity in the term *pṛṣadājya* (speckled ghee). Moreover, Kātyāyana explicitly states regarding the animal sacrifice: "From the wording of the mantra and from the scripture," and further: "In the animal sacrifice, [the formula is] 'Svāhā to the gods who drink ghee, Svāhā!'"

Likewise, because of the hearing of the singular number in the injunction "he takes the *pṛṣadājya*," there are not two substances; thus, the word *ājya* refers to something else that is mixed with curd. Therefore, this is indeed *ājya*. If it is argued: "But since the mention of duality is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), how can there be an attainment of the [ritual] refinements (*saṃskāra*)?"—we say no. For another scriptural text of the Vājasaneyins, "he places the curd on the fire," prohibits the placing on the fire. Indeed, that which is not already established is not prohibited; therefore, the attainment of the ritual properties (*dharma*) is necessary.

Furthermore, that with which the oblation (*havis*) is mixed is also consecrated by the properties of the oblation, such as the evening milking (*sāyaṃdoha*) and so forth; for it is only through the consecrated [milk] that *āmikṣā* is produced. Therefore, because the substance would be destroyed during the placing upon the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*), there is no [consecration]. For this very reason, there is a modification (*ūha*) at the end of the *nigada* formula: "With curd, O churner! According to the Nyāya view, however, there is no consecration.
At the time of taking the clarified butter (*ājya*), having taken four portions each in the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, one brings the third portion of the clarified butter into the curd.

He takes four portions each of clarified butter (*ājya*) and of the curdled milk (*nirupta*). Because of the mention of "the third part," the clarified butter is not to be consecrated; likewise, it is the third [portion] of the curd. This is because of the division of the qualities. Having taken [these], he takes five portions of speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) with the mantra: "Thou art light, multiformed, the kindling-stick of all the gods," or with "Thou art the milk of the great ones.
Or, according to the injunction of both mantras, the repetition of the mantra for either one is performed here.
As in the original model, it is performed in the *dhruvā* vessel.
This is a restatement for the sake of establishing the sequence.
Once the clarified butters have been poured out, he proceeds with the measuring of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

After the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the spreading of *plakṣa* branches is performed on the southern shoulder. Thus it is stated in the *Kātyāyana-Śulba-Sūtra*: "He spreads *plakṣa* branches upon the sacrificial grass"; the meaning is that he performs the rite characterized by the measuring of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and that which precedes it. Regarding this, [the text] says: "Having taken the spade with the formula *devasya tvā*... and so on; he traces around the hole for the sacrificial post three times clockwise, half within the altar (*antarvedi*) and half outside the altar (*bahirvedi*).

The mantra ends with "I cut. Since there is only one pit (*avaṭa*), the mantra is recited once; it is recited twice silently. This is said in order to express "on all sides. Regarding "clockwise": he draws a line around the sacrificial post-pit—which is dug for the sake of the post—to the extent required for the digging, starting from the middle. He traces the outline so that the great [altar] is on one half of the excavation and the small [altar] is on the other half outside the *vedi*. Here, although the *vedi* is prescribed as a subordinate element (*aṅga*), it is rather the location of the *vedi* that is indicated.

And thus, [the phrase] "dug in a place of such a nature" [is used]; otherwise, if there were an injunction regarding the location or an injunction regarding the altar as a subordinate element (*aṅga*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the location. Consequently, the result is that in the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpa-ekādaśinī*), [the post] is not on the altar (*vedi*).

Having traced around [the site], he gives the command: "Dig the pit for the sacrificial post (*yūpāvaṭa*) up to the base; dig until it is level with the top, or two finger-breadths, or three finger-breadths, or four finger-breadths [below the surface]."

The part being measured is denoted by the word *upara*; therefore, when a pit is dug to that measure, it is deeper than even that, being further lowered by the measure of a *yaśas* or a *śalā*. He performs the duties according to the direction (*praisha*).
Having dug only as much as the *upara*, [he proceeds]. || 6 ||

Having dug [a hole] for the Agnīdh’s post, he washes the sacrificial post with the formula: "Whatever craft of thine the carpenter has injured with his hand or with the adze—may the pure, sacrificial waters purify that of thine!
This is clear.

Having prepared as many sprinkling waters (prokṣaṇī) as there are [required], he sprinkles the base with "For the earth, thee!"; the middle with "For the atmosphere, thee!"; and the top with "For the sky, thee! With "May the world, the seat of the ancestors, be purified," he pours water into the hole for the sacrificial post (yūpāvaṭa).

Having prepared the sprinkling waters mixed with barley, there is no further refinement [of the water]. This is clear. Baudhāyana says that the water used as a remnant is [poured] into the hole. With "Thou art barley (yava)," he throws a grain of barley; with "Thou art the seat of the ancestors," he spreads eastward-pointed sacrificial grass (barhis).

The scattering of barley and the strewing with grass are performed only in the pit. The word "eastward" (*prāc*) is used to exclude the quality of being "northward-pointed" (*udagagra*). The mantra "Thou art barley" (*yavo 'si*) ends with the words "the enemies" (*arātīḥ*). With the mantra "Thou art easy of access" (*svāveśo 'si*), he places the first chip that fell away, with its bark facing downward, into the pit. Having placed a piece of gold between [the chip and the ladle], he makes an offering over it with the *sruva* spoon, saying: "O Heaven and Earth, may you be filled with clarified butter, svāhā!"

A mantra belonging to another Śākhā that ends with *svāhā* is not used here in our own Śākhā because it is not heard [prescribed] here. When the application of the *juhū* ladle would otherwise be obtained for the *davihoma* offerings, the specific injunction "with the *sruva*" results in the exclusion of other ritual implements. Having placed gold as an interposition upon the splinter (*śakala*), the offering is made there; the two deities are Heaven and Earth, and the oblation is clarified butter from the *ājyasthālī*. The mantra ends with "be favorable" (*vittāt*) and "easy of access" (*svāveśa*).

Having given the command, "Recite for the sacrificial post being anointed," or "Recite for the one being anointed," he stands facing west in front of the *Āhavanīya* fire and, while reciting the *yajyā*, anoints the post with a splinter using ordinary clarified butter.

The injunction for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) within the *ādhvaryava* section is stated by both Kātyāyana and Bharadvāja as being for the purpose of providing an option. [The sacrificer], standing to the east of the existing sacrificial post (*yūpa*) facing westward, [should perform the act] with the sacrificial chip (*yūpa-śakala*) as the instrument, using his hand—meaning, with a common (worldly) hand.

When a word denoting a genus refers to both [the generic and the specific], it is stated here that "by means of the worldly [ladle]" so that the clarified butter (*ājya*) contained in the vessel (*sthālī*) might not be used. Because the act of anointing lacks the character of a primary rite (*prakṛta*) and because it is not a *homa* (oblation), it is understood to be performed with the worldly [ladle]. Although this *homa* is indeed non-primary (*aprākṛta*), nevertheless, by virtue of being a *homa* and having the *āhavanīya* fire as its locus, it would otherwise involve the butter in the vessel; however, the specific object to be anointed is not indicated. That [object] is the *caṣāla* (the top-ring of the sacrificial post), as seen from the context: "He anoints the *caṣāla*; he fixes the *caṣāla*. [The formulas are: "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey," and for the tip, "Thou art Indra's. The *caṣāla* [is thus anointed].

The word "anakti" (he anoints) carries over [from the previous rule]. He fastens the *caṣāla* (top-ring) onto the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) on all sides with the formula: "For the plants that bear good fruit."

He releases [the cord] at the front and places it upon the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). This is the food for the sacrificer; or rather, the releasing belongs to the Adhvaryu, because of the injunction that "the sacrificer does not pass beyond. From this point upward, the anointing (*añjana*) belongs to the Adhvaryu alone, because the supplementary statement regarding the excess of the sacrificer's portion specifies his role as the agent: "He anoints the sacrificer himself with that essence. With the formula, "May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey," he anoints the corner facing the fire (*agniṣṭhā-aśri*).
He anoints that part of the sacrificial post which faces the Āhavanīya fire, starting from the end and reaching up to the end. He does not stop merely at the base.
He strokes it three times clockwise at the place where the cord is fastened, or at the middle;
that is, either where it is encircled by the cord or at the middle of the post.

"He anoints it up to the top"—the word "he makes" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. This repetition was stated by Kātyāyana so that [the rule] "having offered the iṣṭi, he should mark it with a number including the top" should not apply here. From the anointing onwards, the sacrificer does not release his hold on the sacrificial post until the encircling with the rope.
This is clear. He issues the command, "Recite for the sacrificial post being raised," or "Recite for that which is being raised. This is clear.
"Supporting the sky, supporting the mid-region," with these words he raises [the post];
"Thou art the foundation of the world, thou art the support of the world," with these words he establishes the post in the hole by means of the lower ring; "Be firm," is the end [of the formula].
"These are thy abodes," with these words he places [the upper ring] into the hole.
"The sacrificial post," ending with "of the abundant one";
with the two verses beginning "Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu," he prepares it; with the fire, he fixes the post that stands toward the fire in its proper direction. || 7 ||

With the two [verses] ending with "of the virtuous" (satām), he establishes [the posts] according to their respective positions. With the verse beginning "with the Āhavanīya fire," which was previously mentioned, he plants that [post] in the same direction as the Āhavanīya, facing toward the Āhavanīya.

If he should desire of someone, "May I deprive him of brilliance, of the deities, and of sensory power," he should measure out the corner of that [post] standing nearest the Āhavanīya fire toward the sun or beyond it; thus he deprives him of brilliance, of the deities, and of sensory power. If he should desire of someone, "May I endow him with brilliance, with the deities, and with sensory power," he should join the corner of that [post] standing nearest the Āhavanīya fire together with the Āhavanīya fire itself.

The first is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) for the injunction that one should always make [the fire] facing the *āhavanīya* while it is established in the fire-chamber (*agniṣṭhāmaśri*). The second, "he desires," is for the purpose of prescribing the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) when there is a desire for such [a result]. [It means that] one should not turn away from the *āhavanīya* toward the east, the west, or toward another person; having stated the fault of speaking untruth, it says one should not act in that way. (Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, Book 4).
He piles up [the earth] such that it is directed toward the Āhavanīya fire, sloping outward at the edge, not protruding, and with its upper surface not visible;

he thus properly establishes it so that it inclines toward the Āhavanīya fire, slopes down at the outermost part, is not elevated, and has its upper surface unexposed. With the mantra "brahmavaniṃ tvā," he covers it all around with loose soil, moving clockwise.
He digs a pit with loose earth (*puroṣa*) and fills it around with soil. It ends with the words "I release" (*prahāmi*).
He makes it firm with the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa, saying "O Brahman, make it firm" (*brahmadṛṃha*).
He causes the loose earth to descend beneath the base of the staff with the formula ending in "make it firm as much as there is nourishment" (*yati poṣaṃ dṛṃha*).
With the verse, "Unbind the earth," he sprinkles water around [the pit] clockwise;
the word "leather bag" (dṛti) marks the end [of the formula]. He sprinkles water around the dug-out area of the sacrificial post clockwise.
Having taken a triple-stranded rope made of wood, three fathoms long, with the formula, "Of the god... (devasya tvā...).
The mantra ends with *ādada*. [The sacrificial post] is measured by three *guṇas*—that is, its width is equal to the distance between two extended *darbha* blades.
With the mantra "This Viṣṇu strode forth," he wipes the sacrificial post three times with his hand holding the rope.
Holding the rope with his hand, he wipes it once upward with the mantra and twice silently. The mantra ends with *sura*.

He gazes at the top of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with the mantra, "That highest step of Viṣṇu," which is situated higher than the *capāla* (the wooden ring). He issues the command, "Recite for the post being girt," or "Recite for that which is being girt."
This is clear.

With the mantra "Thou art the encircler" (*parivīr asi*), he wraps [the cord] three times clockwise around the middle of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) at the level of the navel, or [he wraps it] in the middle.
The word "men" (*manuṣyāḥ*) marks the end [of the mantra]. He binds [it] around the portion of the post measured by the navel, or in the middle of the post.
He makes each subsequent turn a superior quality;
wrapping [the cord], he places the second turn above the first, and the third turn above that, for the wrapping of the girdle.
If he should desire of someone, "May I deprive him of vigor," he should wrap it upward for him or downward.

"If the Adhvaryu should desire, 'May I bring about the separation of the sacrificer from strength,' he should place the two [ropes] wrapped around the middle or the navel-region of that sacrificer's sacrificial post; or he should place them below for the purpose of obstructing [the flow of strength]. The meaning is that the invocation (āvāhana) has multiple purposes. [Notes on variants: 1. ka, ja, etc.: *diṣṭhāṃ ni*; sa: *hiṃṣṭau ni*; ga, ma, ṭha, ṇa: *hiṃcho ni*; i, ṭa: *hiṣṭānni*; ca, cha, da: *viṣṭāni*; jha: *hiṣṭāṃ ni*. 2. ra, ja, etc., u, da, mi, ma. The sense is that the Adhvaryu who desires to cause the sacrificer to be deprived of vigor (*ūrj*) should wrap the two ropes around the middle or the navel-section of the sacrificer’s sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Alternatively, they may be placed below for the sake of obstruction. The point is that the ritual invocation (*āvāhana*) serves various functions.
[The word] *ba* [is used]; not *abhidanne*. 4 *pra.ṭha*, *ṇa*, ‘amarthavā’. 5 *ga*, 8. *ṇa*, *kārthaḥ*. [End of the eighth paṭala: Together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.
If one should desire, "May Parjanya be rainy," one should throw [the grass] downwards.
Only when such a desire exists should one form that intention and place it below, and not otherwise. "Rainy" means having the nature of bestowing rain.
If he should desire, "May it be without rain," he should draw [the cord] upward;
when there is no rain, it is just as before.

For whomsoever he should desire, "May a female be born to him," he should interlace [the strands] near the ends but not twist them inward. For whomsoever he should desire, "May a male be born to him," he should twist them inward to the very end and then wind the thicker part around the thinner.

The meaning is that one should not act in such a manner out of a desire for the sake of someone else, as expressed by the phrase "May you become the offspring of his form" (which is used as a reproach). Regarding the phrase "near the end": when a threefold rope has been wound around the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and a knot is tied, two portions remain—the base and the tip. The meaning is that one should not perform the "untying" (*vyaniṣaṅga*), which consists of failing to wind the rope twice near those two ends and instead joining them together with one another.

This praise of one [rite] by means of the censure of another is for the purpose of praising the latter; this is both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*). Then, having entered each one individually, he weaves the remaining ends through the thicker and the thinner parts: he causes the thickest, the coarse part—the root-end—to enter into the thinnest, the fine end.

With the formula, "Thou art the ridge of heaven," or "Thou art the son of heaven," or "Thou art the summit of heaven," he takes up the *svaru*. With the formula, "I hide thee on the ridge of the atmosphere," he hides the *svaru* in the middle loop of the northern post, or in the uppermost one. (8)
Thus ends the second chapter in the fourth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.

He causes [the animal] to enter between the two pillars to the north of the *amiṣṭhā* pillar. The rest is clear. Thus ends the second chapter in the fourth section on animals, in the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin composed by Mahādeva.
4.3 Now begins the third chapter of the fourth book.

A sacrificial animal has been prepared—one that is not hornless, not earless, not one-eyed, not lame, not mutilated, not castrated, not scarred, not crippled, not seven-hoofed, possessing teeth, a goat, belonging to either of the two [classes], born in a herd, having a mother, having a father, having brothers, and having friends; him he bathes.

It was already prepared there prior to the commencement [of the rite]. Although there is a general indication by the term "animal" (*paśu*), [the specific detail] such as "of the goat's omentum" (*chāgasya vapāyāḥ*) follows. [Variant readings: ka. sa. ga. ca. cha. ṭa. read *bajedī*; ṣa. ja. ma. ma. da. read *ti śakalamā*; 3. ka. ja. i. sa. i. read *rumavara*; 4 ka, read *tara vā*; 5 ṣa duḥ, ja, jha, ja. sa. read *nāpayitvā*.

In the *Baudhāyana-Brāhmaṇa* (4.16), in the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, the connection with the subsequent [sūtra] is "a goat (*chāga*) because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*). A "broken-horned" (*kaṭa*) animal is one with crooked horns; therefore, it is something other than that. In the same way, the exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) should be understood for the following cases as well: one who is "deficient in ear" (*karṇavikala*)—by conventional usage this refers to one called "earless" (*akarṇa*)—he is not [to be used]. One who is "one-eyed" (*kāṇa*) is one with only one eye; he is not [to be used]. One who is "lame" (*khañja*) is one with weak legs; he is not [to be used]. One who is "mutilated" (*khaṇḍa*) is one deprived of teeth; he is not [to be used]. One who is "impotent" (*ṣaṇḍa*) is a eunuch (*klība*); he is not [to be used].

One that has been rubbed [with salt] is not [acceptable]; one that is lame or deaf is not [acceptable]. One with seven hooves—that is, one lacking two hooves on a single foot—is not [acceptable]. One whose teeth have fallen out (*pannadanta*) is to be accepted; the meaning is that they fell out first and then grew back again. And so it is said: "When the teeth of an animal grow back again, then it becomes fit for sacrifice. Thus, there should be understood to be no contradiction between the terms *akhaṇḍa* (unbroken) and *pannadant* (one whose teeth have fallen out). A goat (*chāga*) is an animal. One born as the middle one between twins.

"Leading the herd" (*prayūthya*) means being born within a herd or a group, not alone. The fourfold set beginning with "possessing a mother" (*mātṛmān*) is to be understood as referring to a mother, father, brother, and sister who are present at that time. He bathes him; that is, he washes him. Regarding this, Bharadvāja states the favor [to be granted]: "If he is deficient in limbs, or if it is night, or if the purpose cannot be accomplished, one should offer oblations to Viṣṇu, to Agni-Viṣṇu, to Sarasvatī, and to Bṛhaspati, and then perform all the expiatory rites (*sarvaprāyaścitta*)."

Having offered oblations with the verses, "The Vādhūla [is dedicated] to Agni," "The Mānava-Vaiṣṇavī to Prajāpati," and "The Aindravāyavī," one should perform the *upākaraṇa* (commencement). Furthermore, whatever expiations (*prāyaścitta*) have been prescribed in the Sūtra for transgressions of the rules are to be combined with the three beginning with "unrecognized" (*anājñāta*) and the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*), even in the Vādhūla tradition. It should be understood everywhere that all *homa* offerings follow the procedure of the *davihoma*; those not previously mentioned are performed with clarified butter from the *ājyasthālī*, while any rite accomplished by means other than a *homa* offering is performed with ordinary (*laukika*) clarified butter.
With the mantra "For food, thee! (*iṣe tvā*), he takes two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Two [blades].
"The Upavīra you are"—with these words he takes hold of a Plakṣa branch; "he takes" is to be supplied from the previous context.

"I dedicate you, who are pleasing to Indra and Agni, to the gods, to the divine subjects, to the offspring of Prajāpati being born; O Lord of Cattle, this animal [for you]"—with these words, using two blades of *barhis* grass and the Plakṣa branch, he dedicates the animal.

With the mantras beginning with "The twenty goddesses first... and ending with "...O Revatīs, rejoice," and with the mantras "Of Prajāpati" and "This animal," he touches the animal while holding the outer branches of the *plāśa* tree, thereby consecrating it for the sake of the deity. Having performed the introductory rite (*upākaraṇa*) with the mantra "Those who know," he offers five oblations.

Because the *juhū* ladle is occupied and because this is an unprecedented (*apūrva*) rite, one takes five portions of clarified butter from the vessel into the *vasāhomahavanī* ladle and performs a *darvihoma* according to the ritual rules. One offers with the five mantras: "Those whose lord is...", "Those that are being bound...", "Those that are wild...", and "Being released...". The statement "having consecrated" (*upākṛtya*), which follows in sequence, is intended to show that it is an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the consecration; by this, the modification (*ūha*) for the consecrated animal is established. [Note: The variants *kha*, *ga*, *cha*, *ṭha*, *ṇa* read *gatadanta*; *ga*, *ṭha*, *ṇa* read *maindra vā*.]

"O Paśupati, the animals are both diverse and similar; may Svarāj grant his approval to whichever among them the gods have chosen"—with this verse, or alternatively, he offers the fifth oblation in the center. These are the variations for the verse beginning with "pramucyamānāḥ."
Taking the lower friction-wood with the formula, "Thou art the birthplace of Agni," he places it upon the sacrificial grass (barhis) to the west of the Āhavanīya fire.

Having taken hold of it, he places that specific wood-piece thus. Upon the sacrificial grass, he lays two blades of Darbha grass pointing eastward upon the wood-piece with the formula, "Ye two are the testicles."

When the two pieces for friction have been placed down, someone establishes two fires; this preparation of the pieces is because they are intended to be employed elsewhere in the *upākaraṇa* and *bahiṣpavamāna* rites.
He takes up the lower fire-drill with the mantra "Thou art Urvaśī" and the upper fire-drill with "Thou art Purūravas," because those two alone are present in the mind during the consecration.
With the formula, "Anointed with ghee," he anoints [the two kindling woods] in the cavity of the *ājyasthālī* (ghee-pot).

The phrase "of the *ājyasthālī*" is stated to exclude the use of previously prepared ghee. The word "in the cavity" (*bile*) is stated to exclude the taking up of the *sruva* and other implements. The locative case in "in the cavity" is employed to indicate that he anoints them in the very cavity of the *ājyasthālī* while it is still together with the *araṇis*, and not by holding them separately.
He places them together with the formula, "Thou art life," or "Support the male."
He places the two kindling woods together in one spot; "having placed the two kindling woods together," says Bhāradvāja.
He issues the command, "Recite for the fire being churned," or "Recite for the fire being churned. This has been explained.

When the mantra has been recited three times with the words, "O Gāyatrī meter, be born after me," he begins by turning three times clockwise and then churns as he pleases from that point upward. With the word "eta" (come), having likewise begun each time by turning clockwise for each mantra in succession, he then churns as he pleases, both clockwise and counter-clockwise. Following the repetition of the triple recitation of the mantra, when the first [mantra] has been recited three times, he says, "O Triṣṭubh meter, be born after me."

"Recite for the one born," [he says]. When [the child] is born, he issues the command: "Recite for the one being cast [into the fire]," as it is being cast. This has been explained. [The mantras are: *viśva...* (RV 7.38.5), *bhava...* (RV 7.38.6), and *sa...* (RV 7.38.7). From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [in the fourth praśna]:
With the mantra, "May you two be of one mind toward us," he casts [the fire] in front of the junction of the northern enclosing stick (*paridhi*).
The mantra ends with *mayā na*. He pours the remainder into the *uttara-veṇu*.

Having offered it into the fire with the words *agnāvagniḥ*, he makes an additional offering (*abhijuhoti*) with the *sruva* ladle; the mantra ends with *ghreyam*. With the fat (*vasā*), he reaches the *vasāhomahavanī* vessel which is common to both [fires]. This concludes the cessation of the other duties. Having aimed at the *āhavanīya* fire, the *amara* has entered. Thus it is said. Regarding this, Mādhava states the concession: "If the fire is not produced while being churned, one should offer a piece of gold (*hiraṇya-śakala*) in its place as a substitute offering."
Taking a double-stranded rope made of darbha grass, two spans in length, with the words "For the sake of the god" (*devasya tvā*), he strokes the animal's right foreleg with the end of that rope.
[The mantra] "Dara iṣitaḥ" is for the measuring; the measuring is done silently. The connection is: "of that animal, the right foreleg.
With the words "For the sake of Truth, O divine oblation, with the bond" (*ṛtasya tvā devahaviḥ pāśena*), he binds it to the right front foot and the middle of the head.

With the mantra "pārśanā," he fastens the noose made from a portion of the cord onto the right foreleg of the animal, which has its head turned toward the south and is still provided with horns; he thus loops the noose around it.
With the mantra "dharṣā mānuṣān," he binds the animal to the sacrificial post (yūpa) from the front, facing westward or northward.
He binds the animal to the front part of the sacrificial post, either facing west or facing north.
He sprinkles [the animal] with the formula, "From the waters, from the plants, I sprinkle thee"; the word "the animal" is to be supplied as the object.
He makes it drink with the formula, "Thou art the drinker of water."
He gives water to drink to the animal itself, if it is conscious. With the words, "May the gods taste [it]," he sprinkles from below;
with "May they taste [it]," he sprinkles within. He sprinkles along the hair on the lower part of the animal's belly.

He undertakes the rites beginning with the *sāmidhenī* verses. The phrase "having deposited the Veda," and so forth, is intended to indicate the sequence of the archetypal (*prakṛta*) ritual. Having poured the *āghāra* libation, he anoints the animal victim.

Having poured the second Āghāra libation, he anoints the animal, for the Śruti says: "Having poured the Āghāra, he anoints the animal. How does he do so? [The various readings are: *paraja.ma.ḍha* read *ṛdhisandhinā vā'nupra*; *śa* reads *ṛdhisandhimapra*; *ka.ca.ra* reads *kaṭeda*. [End of] the sixth Paṭala. [This is] accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

With the mantra "saṃ te prāṇaḥ" (May your breath be united), he anoints it on the right half of the head; with "saṃ yajatrairaṅgāni" (May your limbs be united with the worshipful ones), he anoints the two shoulders; and with "sa yajñapatirāśiṣā" (May the lord of the sacrifice be united with his blessing), he anoints the buttock.

He anoints the two shoulders with *jalā* and *śiras*, [respectively] for the southern and northern shoulders, with the mantra beginning "dakṣa" and "nadīśeraśca," ending with the word "gacchatām. For the first [mantra], this is the end; for the other two, however, by changing the plural number to "gacchantām," it applies to the middle and the last [shoulders]. From the remainder of the sentence, "yajñapatiṃ dīrghāyuṣam āśiṣaṃ gamayāti," it is understood that he causes the patron of the sacrifice to attain long life and blessings. Regarding the practice of the shoulders, they consider that because the two ends are distinct, there is a doubling [of the action]. In that context, since the word "aṃsa" (shoulder) refers to the location of the rubbing, there is a single substance.

In this regard, according to the principle that "where there is one [action], [the mantra applies]," the entire mantra is [employed]. By the use of the singular number in the phrase "Amoghāra," it is indicated that [the action] pertains to a single deity. It is further indicated that the sequence of actions—beginning with the smearing of the *dhruvā* vessel—is such that the archetypal (*prakṛta*) rites, starting from the smearing of the *dhruvā*, follow immediately after the modified (*vaikṛta*) ones; this rule of sequence applies everywhere.
Having recited the *pravara* invocation;

here, in this *nirūḍha* sacrifice, since it is stated without modification that "the *pravara* of the Maitrāvaruṇa is also to be recited just as the ordinary *pravara*," he hands the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa.
The Adhvaryu hands over the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa; however, in the Sāman [tradition], the giver of the staff does not recite the formula.

The Maitrāvaruṇa receives it with the mantra: "May I not be one who stumbles, but become one who does not stumble. In the Yājuṣa [tradition], the prescription for the Hotṛ-mantras is according to Bāḍava; in that case, the Maitrāvaruṇa indeed possesses the duties of the Hotṛ.
In the *prayāja* and *anūyāja* offerings, in the *paśupuroḍāśa-sviṣṭakṛt*, in the *vanaspati*, and in the *paśu-sviṣṭakṛt*, there are the *praiṣas* (directions) for the *yājyā-sampraiṣa*.

The word "which have been obtained" (*ye prāptāḥ*) is the understood remainder. By way of enumeration, these are the *pragāna-piñca*s. These are the *praiṣas* for the *yājyā-sampraiṣa* which have been obtained.

Therein, the *adhvaryu*, having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* and once the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* has been made, issues the direction to the *maitrāvaruṇa*, saying, "Direct [the Hotṛ] to such-and-such," and he thus impels the *hotṛ*.

By calculation, [the rule] applies to the *puroḍāśa*, the *pāyasa*, the animal sacrifices, and the principal offerings; the *preṣa* (direction) addressed to the Maitrāvaruṇa, "He sends [the offering] to such-and-such," is excluded from these cases. The meaning is that it should be performed in the five [cases] beginning with the *praiṣa*. The singular form "to such-and-such" (*amuṣmai*) is not intended to be restrictive; rather, wherever a dual or plural form is applicable, such as in the case of "the Sāmans," that should be understood there. According to this teaching, that [portion] is to be known as the division of the southern half of the head.
"Oṃ, let us bow! 1. kha. ga. ṭa... "namo"; 2. kha. maṭha, ṇa, because of the absence of *nā*; 3... ya. 'aśe vi'. || 420 || From the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[In the fourth praśna]:
He issues the call for the first fore-offering (*prayāja*) with "Prompt for the fuel-sticks (*samidh*)," and for the subsequent ones with "Prompt! Prompt! (*preṣya preṣya*).

The word "prayāṇān" (the fore-offerings) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The deities [of these offerings] are those mentioned in the mantras, such as Vasanta and the others, with the mantras remaining unmodified. Objection: Since the deities are not understood from the wording of the mantras themselves, how can the term "samidbhyaḥ" (to the Samidhs) be based upon them? Response: It is said that in the Āprī-sūktas, the word *samiddha* (kindled) appears in some places, while the word *samit* (fuel-stick) appears in others; by this much, the designation [of the offering] is established. Alternatively, since this is a modification of the first fore-offering (*prayāja*) which has "Samidhs" as its deity, it receives that name; thus, the deities are expressed in the plural form.

The place [of recitation] is indicated by the words "samit-samid" (fuel-stick—fuel-stick). In the *Sūkta*, it is used with the singular ending as "samit," and in the *Samiddha* [Sūkta], it is used with the masculine word "samiddha. This should be understood similarly for other *Sūktas*. As for the plural form "samidbhyaḥ," it arises from the formation of a collective compound (*ekaśeṣa*) with other dissimilar names. Although the fuel-sticks are fixed in number in the archetype (*prakṛti*), nevertheless, in that context, the formation of a collective compound with dissimilar names such as Tanūnapāt and others is intended.

For this reason, the first [text], considering that to be an extended application (*atideśa*), prescribes the *ājya* offering by means of the word "yan" alone, without the names *tanūnapāt* and so forth, saying "he sacrifices to the gods. Since the word "deva" (god) is uniform across all [the verses], and since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) one sacrifices with the *samidh* verses, when those same calls (*preṣas*) are obtained for the subsequent [sacrifices], these [verses] are prescribed accordingly; because they perform the same function, they sublate those [original ones]. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says: "He says 'yaj' in the place of 'preṣya'.
Having brought [the butter] together at the fourth [offering], he brings it all together at the eighth.

That which was prescribed in the archetype regarding the fourth [offering] as the "bringing together" (*samānayana*) of the *aupabhṛta* butter, that here remains as half of the fourth; the remainder is all [of it] in the eighth. Regarding the number that is heard in the original injunction itself—namely, "he offers five fore-offerings" (*pañca prayājān yajati*)—this does not apply to the archetypal [offerings] when they are joined with a different number, such as when a different number is prescribed in a modification (*vikṛti*), as in "nine fore-offerings" or "eleven fore-offerings. In those cases, it is by way of sublation (*bādha*) of the archetypal [number], and not... [of the archetypal form].

The statement "by repetition alone" was made in the eighth [chapter] to demonstrate the view of the Nyāya school; the sense is that everything belonging to the modified (*vaikṛta*) repeated eighth [offering] also possesses the status of being the fourth. The word "everything" is used to exclude others, because there is no remainder. However, the Teacher considers the repetition of the fourth, which is penultimate, to extend up to the eighth, and the repetition of the last [offering] to include the ninth, tenth, and eleventh. This will become clear in the *Yājamāna* section. And thus, having sacrificed four times according to the original model (*prakṛti*), he sacrifices another four to the north, and then sacrifices three in the middle.
Having sacrificed ten times and leaving the ghee for the eleventh [offering],
it is clear.
He anoints the *svaru* and the *svadhiti* with the *juhū* ladle using the clarified butter, saying, "Anointed with ghee."

In this context, the dual number must be explained as being equivalent to the plural used for the *uparava* holes, since its application to each individual [hole] is untenable; nor can it refer to two [holes] together, because of the distinctness of the substances and because we observe repetition due to specific ritual characteristics, such as "twice the *svaru* [is struck], once the edge of the *svadhiti*."

The mantra is recited once, and it is understood that the silent action is performed once; "he anoints a single edge of the axe" is drawn in [as a corollary]. Even there, the mantra is explained in detail as previously stated—"the *svaru* and the axe anoint themselves"—and not as a separate injunction, because it constitutes a single sentence and involves a single action. With the words, "Anointed with ghee, may you two protect the animal," he anoints the animal with those two [the *svaru* and the axe].

The recitation of the entire mantra for the former [the *svaru*] is intended to indicate that it consists of only that much; otherwise, since both [mantras] would be cited as mere fragments (*pratīka*), the mantra would be complete in both cases. However, the former [mantra] belongs to another Vedic branch (*śākhā*) and is of that same extent as those two—the *svaru* and the *svadhiti* under discussion. Having said, "O slaughterer, let this edge of yours be well-known," he hands the *svadhiti* to the slaughterer, pointing out the sharpened edge. "Let the edge be sharpened by your own mind"—this is for the purpose of calming [the animal]; one should know that there is no other [purpose] than this.
Having inserted the *svaru* at its proper place.

The *praśas* mantra, having been previously recited for that specific purpose, is not used elsewhere; when the *pariyāga* (circumambulation) is being performed, he shall direct him, saying either "recite after me" (*anubrūhi*) or "recite the *pariyāga*" (*pariyāge 'nubrūhi*). This is clear. Taking a firebrand from the *āhavanīya*, the *āgnīdhra* performs the *pariyāga* around the animal five times with the mantra "The Lord of Prayer... (*parivājapatiḥ*), and he runs three times around the *śāmitra* site, the *cātvāla* pit, the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and the *āhavanīya* fire.

The *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulatory fire-purification) has been explained; here the specific detail is as follows: moving around that [substance] on all sides with the ladle (*dānusmukena*), he performs the purification by carrying it around. He does this five times for each substance, such as the goat and so forth—once with the mantra and twice silently. Because the substance is the primary factor, there is a repetition for each one. Here, the *paryagnikaraṇa* consists simply in moving around together with the ladle; therefore, the movement is also three times for each individual substance.

It has been stated likewise by Kātyāyana: "Taking the firebrand, he carries it around on all sides. It should not be said that there is a single circumambulation for all [the substances] at once; rather, because they are distinct substances, there must be repetition, as the sequence beginning with the animal would otherwise be untenable. Regarding the clarified butter (*ājya*), some say the same applies.

According to some followers of our own Vedic branch, one performs the *paryagni* (carrying fire around) in the same manner even for the sixth *ājya*; this constitutes an alternative option (*vikalpa*).
Regarding the statement "those who follow the one being bound," while the fire is being carried around [the victim], he offers three *apāvya* oblations.

While the rite characterized by the circumambulation of the fire is being performed, at the *Āgnīdhra* altar, he offers the oblations named *apāvya*—as previously described—with clarified butter taken three times from the *ājyasthālī*. In this case, there is no placing of fuel-sticks (*samid*), as the *sāmidhenī* verses have already served their purpose; however, the specific characteristics of a *darvihoma* (ladle-oblation) certainly apply here.
Having placed a fire-brand (*ulmuka*) on the *Āhavanīya* altar, he circumambulates it again three times in the reverse direction.

Without the *usmuka*, he goes around each [of the fires] three times in reverse order and non-pradakṣiṇa fashion respectively. Having released the animal and called for the announcement (*āśrāvya*), once the response (*pratyāśrāvita*) has been given, he issues the direction: "O Hotṛ, announce the oblations to the gods.
The word "Hotṛ" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. He states this in order to establish that very person as the agent for the purpose of the direction.
The Hotṛ priest begins with the *adhrigu* formula, that is, the section known as the *adhrigu-nigada*.

Then, the sacrificer and the Adhvaryu both touch the animal from behind with the two *barhis* grass-blades, the two omentum-roasting spits, and a branch of the *plakṣa* tree, while reciting: "O wealthy ones, enter the lord of the sacrifice with what is dear."
When both have grasped the three [stalks] together, they touch them while following along.
The Adhvaryu addresses the sacrificer with the mantra beginning "Nānāprāṇa" and ending with "Kāmā. This is clear.
When it is said, "Bring Agni for him," the Āgnīdhra takes up that very firebrand and goes first;
he precedes the animal, taking up that same firebrand which was previously set aside for the purpose of the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite.
Saying, "The wide atmosphere," they go out toward the north between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).

Regarding the plural form "they go out," it includes both the *āmīdhra* and the *yujamāna*. He who goes together with the sacrificial animals; or, according to the *Vāmaneyīśrotra*, he leads them by tying them to his neck with a rope. Likewise, they emerge from the middle of the *cālāla* pit.
Having placed a firebrand (*ulmuka*) in the *śāmitra* area to the north of the *cātvāla* pit, he passes to the north of the *śāmitra*;
he remains seated.

When it is said, "Place his foot toward the north," he places either one of the two *barhis* blades used for the introductory rites with its tip pointing eastward or northward, saying, "Be united with his body. Upon that [blade], they lay him down with his head toward the west and his feet toward the north, while saying, "Make him lifeless; cause him to be quieted; announce when he is ready. Having said this, [he proceeds].

The mantra ends with *pāhi*. According to Kātyāyana, the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) takes place behind the *śāmitra* fire. Having laid the animal upon that grass, the slaughterers (*śamitṛs*) seize its head and bend it downward; according to Kātyāyana, they do so until it reaches the ground. They cause it to "die" by means of the suppression of breath, making it utter the sound *mā mā haṃsi* (do not kill me), while it is being made to low and bleat. Having said, "Do not speak," the sacrificer and the Adhvaryu turn away. With the mantra *nānā prāṇaḥ*, the Adhvaryu consecrates the sacrificer.

Having turned away from the enemy's back, they return by the same way they went out. The rest has already been explained. 12... [Ja. A. A. 4] ... "He takes the omentum-spreader (vapāśrapaṇī) from the entrails. 2 Ka. Kha. Ca. Cha. Ta. Tāśakya; 1. Ka. 'tānyaṃ pra'; 3 Ka. Kha. Ca. Cha. 8. Pa. Śakya; Kha. Kha. Ca. Cha. 8, Paśuṃ; 4 Sapaṭalaḥ; accompanied by the commentary Vaijayantī composed by Mahādeva; 423.

"Here let the cattle of every form rejoice, dwelling together around Agni as their nest; may they favor us with milk and ghee. May those whose udder has four openings, filled with honey and ghee, be full of milk for us in this stall, O increasers of Truth. While reciting this, the sacrificer and the Adhvaryu priest remain silent, looking at the *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter) contained in the vessel. Here, the movement [of the butter] is performed with the mantra "svadisi svatva," etc. The rest is clear.

"Bestow Indra’s portion for the sake of prosperity upon this sacrifice and the sacrificer at the rising of the sun. Seize him who hates us! May the heroes of the blameless sacrificer [be safe]. With these words, the Adhvaryu consecrates the animal with a mantra if it cries out.
Thus ends the third paṭala in the fourth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

"He bellows" means he makes a sound while being addressed with the *saṃjñapti* formula. This is the mantra for the specific occasion (*naimittika*). Thus ends the third chapter in the fourth book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* composed by Mahādeva. 3.

4.4 Now, the fourth chapter in the fourth book. He offers an oblation when the animal has been immolated with the verse: "That lowing which the beast has uttered... [The formula continues: "When the beast was immolated, its consciousness departed; that [consciousness] is here. [He then recites: "Tahasa. [This is the formula for the cart.]

"O pacifiers, approach!"—with these words, they approach the animal that has been immolated. Because of the plural number, all the *ulūkhalas* (mortars) as well as the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) come near the animal.
They go around it. Having released the animal's tether with the formula, "May Aditi release this bond," and having attached it to a single-pronged pin, he deposits it in the *cātvāla* pit.

The section ends with "karogi. With the cord (*raśanā*) by which the animal was bound at the neck, having extracted that cord, and having strengthened it with the *vapāśrapaṇī* (the omentum-roasting fork), he takes hold of it and places it in the *cātvāla* pit; he sets it down silently, for the mantra for its release is indicated by the indicative mark (*liṅga*). For one practicing sorcery (*abhicār*), he places it upon a dry stump or a clump of *darbha* grass with the mantra: "I make the one who acts as an enemy lower."
The word "pāśam" (the noose) marks the end [of the mantra]. He deposits it with the mantra upon a clump of *darbha* grass that is indeed dry, for a sacrificer who desires the death of his enemy.
With the mantra, "Homage to you, O Ātāna," the wife worships the sun.

It has been stated that "this [line] which was behind is now brought forward," thus describing the bringing forward from the west. Since its place is originally in the west, it is called *prācī* ("eastward"); that is, facing east toward the sun. How is it brought forward? By the understanding derived from the scriptural statement, "One should worship the rays of the sun with the verse *anodhā yopayastamanā*," it is recognized that the act of bringing forward (*udānayana*) is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the ritual worship (*upasthāna*). Because it is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the wife, it is to be repeated for each wife. With the mantra "Unconquered, go forward" (*anarvā prehi*), the Pratiprasthātṛ leads the wife while she holds the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*).

Taking a vessel filled with water, he raises the seated wife and leads her toward the *cātvāla* pit by the shoulder-blade [of the altar]. This concludes with the word "poṣaṇā. This consecration of the wife, indicated by the second case ending, is repeated at each subsequent turn. The holding of the full vessel is for the sake of refreshing (*āpyāyana*) only one [wife] at a time.
With the mantra "O divine waters" (*āpo devīḥ*), he pours the water into the *cātvāla*.

He pours a small amount of water from the *pūrṇapātra* with the mantra ending in "bhūyāsma. The second water, which has not been specifically designated, is indeed subject to the consecration (*saṃskāra*). Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra—"We have become pure"—which is clearly understood as a consecratory formula, it is to be repeated for each person.
According to some, this is prohibited.
Since the pouring out of the water is both enjoined and prohibited, it constitutes an option (*vikalpa*).

By this very [formula], having all stepped out, they purify themselves at the *cātvāla*. Standing in the region of the *cātvāla*, they perform the purification with this mantra. By the use of the particle *eva* (only/very), the entire mantra is enjoined for the acts of purification (*mārjana*), refreshing (*āpyāyana*), and stepping out (*samutkramaṇa*). If it were otherwise—as Bharadvāja stated, where the formula ending in "Oṃ" is used for stepping out, and the formula beginning with "We are purified" (*śuddhā vayam*) is used for the others—then that would not be the case; thus it was stated in this way. Otherwise, the significance of the particle *eva* would be lost. When the connection is made such that "having stepped out with this very [formula], they purify themselves with this very [formula]," then the particle *eva* is meaningful.
Having come together and stepped out from the side of the consecrated animal, they go to the *cātvāla* pit and are consecrated along with their wives; so says Bharadvāja.

According to some, the Adhvaryu consecrates [the sacrificer] while the wife causes him to swell [with strength], and the wife consecrates [the sacrificer] while the Adhvaryu causes her to swell. Then, one should perform the sprinkling of water from that very place. The touching of the water at its location is the act of swelling [strengthening]. One should perform that by means of the secondary [subordinate] action; thus, he performs the primary consecration and the swelling [strengthening].
With these [mantras], "May speech swell," and so forth, [the sprinkling] is performed according to their respective forms.

The sprinkling (*abhiṣecana*) is done silently, while the swelling (*āpyāyana*) is done with a mantra. A mantra should be employed for the swelling of that specific object which corresponds to the form and meaning of that mantra. Among those, four [parts] are clear: "That which is yours... [is for] the region of the heart, according to Āpastamba; "the neck," according to Bharadvāja; "that which is harsh of yours..."—with this distinct mantra, [it is for] the limbs, according to Bharadvāja and Kātyāyana. The word "him" (*tam*) appears in all manuscripts, but because it is incoherent, it should be rejected as a scribal error.

18. ga. *lanmanā*; 1 ka, ṇa, ṭa, ‘*kyārya*’; 3 gha, cha, ja, jha, ña, ḍha, ‘*māṇāma*’. [Chapter 188, Section 6]: Accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva: Regarding the mantra “yā śrotram,” in the view that it is a *pṛṣadmantra*, scholars learned in logic have stated that the phrase beginning with “tatt āpyāyatām” is to be supplied (*anuṣaṅga*) from the preceding [mantra] and also from the subsequent one.

"May your navel swell," [he says] over the navel; "may your penis swell," over the penis; "may your anus swell," over the anus; "pure be your ways," having placed [the water] near the feet; "with the two great ones," he pours out the remainder along the spine.

The phrase "may [they] swell" (*āpyāyatām*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. Because the mantra from another recensional branch, *medas*, is inserted in the middle, the terms "navel" (*nābhi*) and "anus" (*pāyu*) are shown in their respective preceding and succeeding positions. "Meḍhra" means the organ of urination, that is to say, the generative organ or the penis. "Pāyu" means the anus. Having placed [the mantras] together with the section ending in "pure are the paths" (*śuddhāścaritrāḥ*) and "peace to the earth" (*śaṃ pṛthivyai*), he causes the feet to swell repeatedly.

Following the back with the back [of the hand], he pours out the remainder of the waters used for the consecrations (*abhiṣecanīya*) exactly until the conclusion of the ritual, provided there is a remainder; otherwise, it is omitted. The Adhvaryu, the Abhiṣektṛ, or the Patnī pours it out. The pouring out of the remainder takes place on the earth itself, because of the supplementary statement: "For the sake of the earth, he pacifies the dog.

Having turned the animal over with its belly upward, he places the remaining portion of the two *barhis* blades used for the dedication (*upākaraṇa*) at the site of the omentum (*vapādeśa*), three finger-breadths, four finger-breadths, or five finger-breadths to the right of the navel, while reciting: "O herb, protect him! (*oṣadhe trāyasvainam*).

This is clear. Of the two *barhis* (grass mats) taken for the purpose of the *upākaraṇa* (dedication), one has been placed at the site of the animal dedication; the other remains here clearly [unused]. With the words, "O *svadhiti* (axe), do not harm him," he cuts across with the *svadhiti*. Having placed the [blade] of the *svadhiti* upon that which was previously laid out facing east, he draws it across from south to north while making a downward stroke, cutting at the location of the omentum (*vapā*). He makes a long incision, cutting as much as is required so that the omentum is obtained at its designated place.

Having taken the tip of the cut grass in his hand and having smeared its thick root with blood at the place of cutting, he throws it toward the north-western intermediate direction (the Vāyavya corner) with the mantra, "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣasas," and then touches water. Kātyāyana and others hold that one should take the tip of the cut *barhis* grass in the left hand; having placed it there, one smears the thick root with blood at the place of cutting. Kātyāyana says one should smear it on both sides. He throws it away toward the north-west—the Vāyavya corner—using the mantra ending with "we lead [him] to the darkness of unrighteousness. This refers merely to the direction as the locus.

The phrase "in the intermediate space" (*avāntaradeśam*) is stated so that it may not be understood as referring to the *mā* (the sacrificial grass), but rather to the ground; the meaning is that it is thrown away on the ground itself, not in the intermediate space of the air. Because he is a Rākṣasa, he touches water. With the formula "For food (*iṣe*) thee," he digs up the clod of earth; with "For strength (*ūrje*) thee," he loosens it at its base. "Digs up" (*ukhidati*) means he separates what is attached, but he does not entirely remove it from the outside. *Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram*—[4th Praśna]—426. By that, having dug it up... [text fragment]. With "For food thee," he digs up the clod; with "For strength thee," he loosens it at its root. He digs up—that is, he separates what is stuck—but he does not completely take it out.
With a single-pronged spit fixed upon it, he carves [the omentum], joining together only a portion of the omentum itself.
He sprinkles it with water, saying, "Be pure for the gods. He wipes the omentum with the knife, saying, "Be bright for the gods.
He wipes it downward. This is clear.
"O Heaven and Earth, cover yourselves with ghee," he says, as he covers the two-pronged and the single-pronged omentum-spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*). He also covers them [with ghee].
"I cut you out, acceptable to Indra and Agni," he says as he cuts it out, or "uninterrupted wealth, accompanied by brave sons."
He separates [the omentum] from the animal.

Having grasped the taking up of the omentum with his fist, the *śamitṛ* remains seated until the offering of the omentum (*vapa-homa*). Regarding the "taking up of the omentum": he remains seated, covering with his fist that torn spot from which the omentum was taken up—that is, removed—from its location, until the offering of the omentum takes place.
With the words "It has been heated," he heats the omentum over the *śāmitra* fire—that is, over the *śāmitra* fire. The mantra ends with "the enemies.
With the words "Homage! May you ward off the gaze of the sun," he worships the sun.
[The Adhvaryu] has departed.

Having left behind the fire for the purpose of cooking [the oblation], the Āgnīdhra takes that very same firebrand (*ulmuka*) and proceeds first. Having placed the remainder of the fire at the *śāmitradeśa* (the place for the slaughterer) for the purpose of kindling the firebrand, he takes up that very firebrand which was previously brought and returns toward the *āhavanīya*; he goes ahead of the Adhvaryu, preceding him.
"O wide atmosphere!"—with these words he proceeds. "Follow after!"—this is the end of the mantra. He goes toward the Āhavanīya fire.
The sacrificer and the Adhvaryu both again take hold of the two omentum-spits. || 12 ||

The mention of the *yajamāna* (sacrificer) is for the purpose of excluding the *prakṛta* (the subject under discussion). However, because of the word "again" (*punar*), the application would belong only to the *ālambhaka* (the one who touches/holds); therefore, the mention of both should not be made. True. It was stated by Bharadvāja: "The sacrificer follows along... [and so on]. [Notes on variants: 1. ka. kha. ca. cha. ṭa. read *vapayā śra*. 2. gha. cha. ja. sa. pa. u. da. read *pauddharaṇa*. 3. ga. u. ga. read *yoddharaṇaṃ*. 4. ra. ya. i. ja. sa. a. ṭha. da. read *dṛśa*. [End of excerpt]

[Chapter 1, Section 4] Together with the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva: 427. [The text says: "Thus, let that not be"—therefore, both are mentioned. One might argue: "Having taken [the portions] from the Adhvaryu’s hands, as he goes, he simply performs the touching (*anvārambha*) of the two omentum-roasting spits; thus, it should have been stated only as 'and the sacrificer'. No; [it is not so], lest there be merely the touching of the omentum by the Adhvaryu, but rather the touching of both the omentum and the roasting spit.
With the three verses beginning "O Agni, day by day," they approach the Āhavanīya fire.

"Rājantam adhvarāṇām" (He who shines over the sacrifices) and "sa naḥ pitā iva" (May he be like a father to us)—these two other verses [are recited]. With these three verses, they approach the vicinity of the Āhavanīya fire. The performers of the sacrifice—the Adhvaryu, the Agnīdhra, and others—are the subjects under discussion. When the firebrand (*ulmuka*) has been brought near, the Adhvaryu holds the omentum (*vapā*) over the final ember of the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra beginning "pratyuṣṭam" (It is burnt away). Once the Agnīdhra has brought the firebrand near and merged it with that [fire], the Adhvaryu, using the entire mantra "pratyuṣṭam," holds the omentum over that final ember—where no other ember exists outside of it—and having hidden it within that ember, he secures it specifically from the north.
With the formula, "O Vāyu, come to the drops," he throws the tip of the *barhis* grass; according to some, he throws it beneath the omentum (*vapā*).

As for the tip of the severed *barhis* that remains in his left hand, that is [thrown] into the Āhavanīya fire itself. If the Āhavanīya is not currently situated beneath the omentum, then once the grasping has been performed, he does not place the omentum back on top again, but rather [places it] in the Āhavanīya.

"For some of us who belong to this very *śākhā*, it is said: 'O Vāyu, come to the drops (*stoka*)'; therefore, the drops fall separately. This [omentum] is indeed the essence of the animals, and the *barhis* is that of the plants; by means of the tip [of the *barhis*], he unites the tip [of the omentum]. Moreover, he establishes the animals in the plants," so says the *Brāhmaṇa*. Therefore, we consider it appropriate that the *anudūta* (the assistant) should [place the drops] beneath the omentum while it is being cooked.
This very point is clearly stated by Bharadvāja: "The *pratiprasthātṛ* cooks the omentum on the *āhavanīya* fire; he throws the *barhis* beneath the omentum."
He hands the omentum to the Pratiprasthātṛ between the sacrificial post and the Āhavanīya fire;
having positioned it between the post and the Āhavanīya, he gives it to the Pratiprasthātṛ standing to the south.
Seated to the south facing north, the Pratiprasthātṛ roasts the omentum.
Facing north, seated to the south of the *uttaravedi*, he cooks the omentum (*vapā*). At this point, there is the discarding of the tip of the outer [grass-blade] beneath the omentum.

He makes an offering over the omentum with the verse, "Thee they have established as the bearer of oblations. Because the *juhū* ladle is occupied, the Adhvaryu offers it with the clarified butter from the *ājyasthālī* using a reed (*veṇa*) or a spoon (*sruc*). The mantra ends with "be pleased" (*juṣasva*). [Notes on variants: 1. *na. ḍha.* reads *apisṛṣṭaḥ*. 2. *ga ṭha.* reads *nadbhuta*. 3. *ṇa.* reads *ti prasthātre vapāṃ*. 4. This concludes the section from the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, in the fourth book.
When the *stokas* have appeared, he issues the command: "Recite after the *stokas*.
When the omentum (*vapā*) is being cooked, as soon as those parts of it that are elevated like bubbles become visible in the midst of it, he issues the command to the Maitrāvaruṇa.
Having made it well-cooked and golden-colored, he places it on a branch of a *plakṣa* tree at the southern corner of the altar with the words: "Make the plants well-fruited."

In this context, because it is understood that "having made [the ladle] well-heated, he deposits it" implies a single agent, and since the Pratiprasthātṛ is the agent for the heating, it might appear that he alone is also the agent for the depositing; nevertheless, due to the designation (*samākhyā*) beginning with the *abhihoma*, the Adhvaryu alone is the agent, and thus it is understood that the suffix *-sva* merely expresses anteriority in time. Alternatively, it should be understood that the Adhvaryu himself makes the ladle well-heated.

The *śyenī* is white; having first made it thoroughly cooked while its whiteness remains unchanged, one pours clarified butter over it as with the *sāṃnāyya*, carries it out to the north, and leads it between the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the *āhavanīya* fire. Saying "well-peeled," he places it upon a branch of a *plakṣa* tree that has been spread out on the southern corner of the great altar (*mahāvedi*). Thus it was stated by Bharadvāja: "Having poured butter over it like the *sāṃnāyya* and having carried it out in that manner, he establishes it upon a *plakṣa* branch outside. [End of] *Sāṃnā*.
Having separated [the omentum], he carries it out together with the pot; having carried it out together with the two omentum-roasting spits, he sets them down together.
He pushes aside the two omentum-roasting spits with the formula: "May we drive away our enemies."

Immediately after the placing [of the omentum], he pulls out the two omentum-spits which have been covered by the omentum; he causes it to emerge from the pit. Regarding the mantra "That which is your self, this is the sense-organ; with this for Indra, O gods, [cook] the omentum," some hold that there is an *ūha* (modification) [substituting *indrāya* for *indrāya*], while others do not accept this. Since the neuter gender and singular number are appropriate either through the nature of being an oblation (*havis*) or the nature of being the mind (*manas*), the mantra remains unmodified as "May the omentum be cooked in me" (*vapā mayi śrayatām*); only this much is modified. The *yajus* belonging to the sacrificer is the Pañcahotṛ formula.

The Hotṛ causes the two *sruva*-ladles to be taken up with the words, "O Adhvaryu, take up the ladle full of ghee. When this is said, having taken up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, having stepped forward and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, and the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* having been made, he issues the direction, "Prompt for the *svāhākṛtis*! Having offered the oblation at the *vaṣaṭ*-call, having stepped back, and having sprinkled the clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*) with the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings, he sprinkles the omentum (*vapā*); [he sprinkles the omentum twice and the clotted butter once].

The items obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) that are to be performed before the *prayājas* must be remembered here as being displaced to this point, for the purpose of prescribing the rule "one issues the call for the *svāhākṛtis*" (*svāhākṛtībhyaḥ preṣya*). Furthermore, it is for the purpose of prescribing the rule "having sprinkled the *pṛṣadājya* with the remainder of the *prayājas*, he sprinkles the omentum" (*prakṛtaprayānaśeṣeṇa pṛṣadājyam abhighārya vapām abhighārayati*), [Bharadvāja states]: "The *pṛṣadājya* contained in the vessel, intended for use in the *vanaspati* sacrifice, is not in the *sruva* ladle, nor in the *upabhṛt* ladle; [it is taken] at the end," so says Bharadvāja.
