Therefore, based on the Vedic injunction, "Having sprinkled the *pṛṣadājya* [spotted butter], he sprinkles the omentum (*vapā*) alone," the sequence is determined by this scriptural statement, not by the order of practical application. 10. This is the [section]. [Chapter] 45, Paṭala: [From] the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva. 429.

Or first the *dhruvā* [ladle], if he is about to offer the two *ājyabhāga* [butter-portions]; the two *ājyabhāgas* are both performed and not performed; they are optional. If he intends to offer them, then at that very time the *dhruvā* is also [offered] first, and not otherwise. The sacrifice of those two occurs right here. The *pañcahotṛ* [formula] has been explained.

Having spread a base of clarified butter in the *juhu* ladle and placed a piece of gold within it, he cuts off the entire omentum; having placed another piece of gold on top and poured clarified butter over it, he issues the command: "Recite the invitatory verse for the fat of the omentum of the goat for Indra and Agni."

This is a restatement of the items prescribed by extended application (*atideśika*) for the purpose of performing the rites of the middle *iṣṭakā* and so forth. The phrase "the whole" (*kṛtsnām*) is stated in order to set aside the practice of cutting [the portion] twice or thrice; having said "Do not fear," he cuts it once as if it were already cut. The rest is clear. Standing to the north, he should perform all this. Having entered for the purpose of cutting the omentum (*vapā*), and standing to the north of the *pāyī*, he should proceed with the omentum, go toward the *āhavanīya* fire, and stand to the south. This same procedure should be understood to apply to the cutting of the sacrificial oblations (*havis*) as well.
Having stepped across and called for the announcement (*āśrāvya*), the Maitrāvaruṇa does not give the command (*preṣyati*), but rather urges the Hotṛ.

This recalls exactly what was previously enumerated by way of exclusion. "He does not give a *preṣa*"—the remainder of the sentence is "to the Maitrāvaruṇa. The meaning is that he gives no *preṣa* (directive) here. Even without being prompted by a *preṣa*, the Maitrāvaruṇa urges and impels the Hotṛ with a *nigada*.
Prior to the offering of the omentum (*vapā*), he first offers the *parivapya* with the formula, "Svāhā to the gods!"

The statement "before the offering of the omentum" (*purastād vapāyā homāt*) is intended to indicate that there is no interval [between these acts]. Having performed the *āśrāvaṇa* and other rites for the sake of the omentum-sacrifice, one first offers the oblation known as *pūrvavapya* with the clarified butter in the pot (*sthālīājya*) using the *juhū* ladle, not the *sruva*. According to the view of Āpastamba, however, the *pūrvavapya-homa* is performed with the *juhū* even before the cutting of the omentum (*vapāvadāna*). To the effect that "it should not be so," the statement beginning with "before" (*purastād*) is given. Having placed the *juhū* in the hand of another and having gone toward the *āhavanīya* fire, [one places] the clarified butter in the *vasāhomahavani* ladle.

Having taken [the ladle] and returned by the same way he came, having offered according to the rules for a *davihoma*, and having taken up the two *sruca* spoons, there is a *svāhā*-utterance at the beginning for those other deities mentioned in the *Śruti* as "the other gods," and again at the end with *svāhā*. This is because we see in the *hautra* liturgy that there is no intervention between the deity and the *svāhā*—as in "svāhā to Speech, svāhā to the Lord of Speech" (*svāhā vāce svāhā vācaspataye*)—whereas when there is an intervention by another word, the *svāhā* would indeed be at the end, as in "svāhā to Tyā, svāhā to Subhava, svāhā to Sūrya. Even in that case, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) such as "svāhā to Ādhi, to Ādhīta," and so forth.
The author of the *Sūtra* himself will clarify this point regarding the *vasāhoma* offering.
"O Jātavedas, go to the gods with the omentum (vapā)," he says when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered; "To the gods, Svāhā!"—this is the subsequent [formula].

The word "jahoti" (he offers) is understood to carry over. When the *vaṣaṭ* has been made at the end of the mantra "devāḥ" (O gods), he casts the omentum [into the fire]. Here, the *svāhākāra* does not have the sense of giving, as that [giving] belongs only to Indra and Agni.

Because it has been offered with the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, there is no further offering with the *svāhā*-utterance to other deities. Therefore, even though this is enjoined by the root *hu* (to sacrifice), it is not a *darvihoma* in the sense that one would otherwise have to offer "in a single [manner]. However, when the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses have been performed, it lacks the character of a *darvihoma*. Likewise, regarding the statement "whatever modification (*vikasti*) one makes in the *prayāja*s and *anūyāja*s, that is the [character] of the sacrifice," and the rule "one performs the *darvihoma*," the status of being a *darvihoma* is stated for a sacrifice devoid of the *prayāja*s and so forth; that [status] does not apply to a sacrifice accompanied by the *prayāja*s and others, and thus there is no occasion for the *svāhā*-utterance.

In this context, the statement "he offers when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered" is a restatement of what is already established by extension (*atideśa*); therefore, the casting [of the oblation] at the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is fixed, as is the conjunction with another mantra. However, both of these occur generally (*prāyika*) and not necessarily. In that regard, since an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed for failing to cast [the oblation] at the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, the casting must certainly take place. As for the mantra, however, if it was already completed previously, it must be begun again; even if the casting has already occurred, it must be brought to completion.

Nevertheless—even if there should be no actual conjunction (*saṃnipāta*) with the end of the mantra, nevertheless the mere conjunction with the mantra must by all means be accomplished; it is not possible for that which is enjoined by the injunction to be omitted. Therefore, it is understood that even the mere conjunction with the mantra here has been stated and authorized by other authorities. This was stated by Kātyāyana: "Or rather, there is no fixed rule, according to Vātsya. And the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) should be performed. However, in the case of a non-conjunction of mantras, there is no expiation.
[The phrase] "he offers after having enclosed [the fire] on the north side" is drawn back [as a reference]. It is poured from the *juhū* ladle with clarified butter (*ājya*), as previously described.
Having stepped back, he says, "Svāhā! Go to the upward-moving Marut of the sky," and throws the two omentum-spits apart—the two-pronged one toward the east and the single-pronged one toward the west.
This is done for the sake of a restrictive rule regarding the direction of the two prongs, which are otherwise scattered in various directions.
Having offered the residue of the clarified butter over them:
Having taken up the two omentum-spits from the Āhavanīya fire, he offers an oblation with the *abhimatra* verse.
They perform the purification at the *cātvāla* pit. || 13 ||

The meaning is that all [the participants] together with their wives [should perform this]. He states the mantras for the purification (*mārjana*): with the three verses beginning "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss," and with the verse, "O Waters, carry away this defilement and whatever impurity there is; whatever treachery or falsehood I have committed, and whatever harsh word I have uttered—may Agni release me from that sin, from all distress. Having performed the purification with the mantra, "I release myself from curses, and from Varuṇa as well; I release myself from the fetters of Yama, from every offense against the gods and from every offense against men"—the purification is performed with the final syllable of each mantra.

He commences the rites of the *paśupuroḍāśa* (animal-cake offering), beginning with the setting out of the vessels; he employs the vessels for the vegetable offerings (*auṣadha*) as required, eleven [in number].

[End of Section] 1. Kha, Ga, Gha, Ṅa, Ca, Ja, Sa, Sa, 8, Da, Ṇa, 'm | Āpomā.ta' | 2. Gha. Ka, Ja, Ma, Ma, Ṭha... mauṣadhipā | ... 4. Ca, Paṭala: Accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 431.

There are twelve potsherds; along with these, there is a winnowing basket, a black antelope skin, a yoke-pin, a mortar, a pestle, a lower grinding stone, an upper grinding stone, a *kuṭaru* (small wooden scraper), a vessel, a stirring-spoon, a *veda* (sacrificial grass-broom), the *prāśitra-haraṇa* (offering-ladle for the portion), the *praṇītā-praṇayana* (water-vessel for consecrated water), and the *iḍā-pātra* (portion-vessel). The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is an ancillary part of the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*). For this cake-offering—which has not yet occurred—the procedure begins with the arranging of the vessels and so forth, but it does not include the kindling of the fires (*agnyādheya*) and other such rites. This is because the benefit provided by those rites performed during the half of the day dedicated to the animal sacrifice extends here as well through the principle of *prasaṅga* (incidental application). He undertakes; that is, he performs.

Since the sacrificial vessels for the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) have already been employed, and since the common implements such as the wooden sword (*sphya*), the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle, and so forth, have also been employed, it follows by implication that only the uncommon vessels for the vegetable offerings (*auṣadha*) should be employed. However, because of the scriptural statement "in this manner" (*yathā-yam*), the *barhis* grass, the *madantī* water, and the *vedaparivāmana* (the sweeping of the altar) are also included. Furthermore, although the *veda* grass-bundle has already been placed [on the altar] for the animal sacrifice, its placement is specifically enjoined again; whereas for the *sphya* and *agnihotra-havaṇī*, which have already been placed there, a re-placement is not enjoined. Thus, even though those items which assist the animal sacrifice [are already present], [they are not used].

Nevertheless, for those for whom a specific connection to the sacrifice has been prescribed individually, it is proper to employ other [portions] because there is an absence of anything remaining from the *puroḍāśa* that could be used again in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*). Since the release of the *praṇītā* waters and the removal of the *upaveṣa* are about to be performed, and since the abandonment by the *hotṛ* priest is also seen in the Veda, even though there is no difference in the nature of the act, the dismissal is permitted after releasing [the fire] silently.

Furthermore, because of the rule for placing the Veda, even though there is a cake (puroḍāśa) for Indra and Agni, and although the number eleven or twelve is obtained through the extended application (codaka), the restriction is stated so that it may not be said that the eight-pot-sherd [cake] applies even to the animal sacrifice for Sūrya or Prajāpati. This restriction should be understood to apply to other animal sacrifices as well. Having set aside the wooden sword (sphya) and the Agnihotra-ladle (agnihotrahavaṇī), even if the carrying forward of the Praṇītā waters occurs subsequently for the sake of the animal sacrifice, that [act] which was performed merely with the intent for that specific purpose—being of an unseen nature—is not to be employed elsewhere where it has been seen [in the archetype].

Furthermore, because the rule for disposal (*vimoka*) is prescribed for that which has already been employed, and because it is impossible to move [the vessel] again once its function is complete, it is stated that "the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) together with the other implements" constitutes a pair. Since the *iḍā*—which was employed for the sake of the animal sacrifice and whose benefit has not yet been realized—cannot be employed elsewhere, the original *iḍā* is what is taken here. On the other hand, a new [portion of the *iḍā*] is taken for the sake of the animal sacrifice, as indicated by the term "the portions of the shared offering" (*samavattadhāna*). Only one *iḍā*-vessel has been mentioned.

The *anvāhārya* rice mess is not the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), because the priests have already been remunerated by the primary fee. Regarding the "vessels for the vegetable offerings" (*auṣadhapātrāṇi*): in the archetype ritual (*prakṛti*), these were taken for the purpose of the *puroḍāśa*; however, in this case, there is no *puroḍāśa*, as the vegetable offering consists of the grinding stones (*dṛṣadupalau*) and the winnowing baskets (*śūrpa*). He issues the command: "O Brahman, I shall lead forward the waters; restrain your speech. Restraining his speech, he touches the vessels.
At the time of pouring out the grains, he pours out the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) made of rice, which shares the same deity as the animal sacrifice.

While it would have been sufficient to say merely "of the *puroḍāśa*," the inclusion of the word "animal" (*paśu*) is for the purpose of demonstrating that the deity of the animal sacrifice is the same as the deity of the *puroḍāśa*. Consequently, like the fifth *prayāja*, it serves as a rite of consecration for the principal deity; furthermore, regarding the portion of the offering, it functions as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*). [Notes on variants: 1. Ga. 8. *sauryaprā* | 2. Ga. u. *'śvayeṃ sa* | 3. Ka. *yuktam*; Kha. Ga. Ṭhaṇa. *dhamāna* | 4. Ka. *śunā pra* |

And there is unity. Since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) there is an option between rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*), this statement "made of rice" (*vīhimaya*) is for the purpose of restriction. Likewise, some say that in every modification (*vikṛti*), rice alone is invariably required; however, that is not the intention of the Teacher (*ācārya*), because he establishes a restriction here. It is shown that the deity is the same as that of the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*): in the case of the solar rite (*saurya*), a solar offering; in the case of the one dedicated to Prajāpati (*prājāpatya*), an offering to Prajāpati; and the same applies elsewhere as well.

In every case, the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) for the animal sacrifice is invariably made of rice. This is stated thus because it serves as a consecration for the principal deity, according to the Vedic injunction: "The sacrificial cake belongs to whichever deity the animal belongs. Having released his speech with the call to the preparer of the oblation (haviṣkṛt), he dissects the animal.

The statement, "having released his speech with the *triṣphalīkaraṇa* injunction regarding that sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)," is a restatement intended for the purpose of prescribing what follows. He dissects the consecrated animal. By the rule, "having released his speech, he dissects," it is stated that the Adhvaryu alone is the agent in the act of cutting, not the *śamitṛ*. In that regard, because the Adhvaryu is seen to be the one who issues the injunctions such as, "Do not let joy stain you," he is distinct from the one who is enjoined, and he is not a priest (*ṛtvij*). Regarding the act of dissection, the *śamitṛ* is drawn forward [with the words], "O *śamitṛ*, may this shoulder-blade be known to you. [This applies] to the Adhvaryu.

Because he is the instigator, his status as the agent of the slaughter is not contradictory; Kātyāyana maintains that the *adhvaryu* alone is the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) in this case. Regarding how the dismemberment of the animal and the portioning of its parts are performed, when this is questioned, there follows the specification of their utility beginning with "the heart" and so forth:
the heart is like the interior of a lotus bud.
The tongue;
well-known; the chest.
The *kroḍaśyenākṛti* (the part shaped like a hawk's breast) consists of the bones and flesh situated below the heart and above the *stanima*.
*Yakṛt* is a synonym for *kāla-ja*; it is located on the right side of the heart and is somewhat dark in color.
The kidneys are the two masses situated at the sides, shaped like mango fruits;
they are located at the flanks.

The two collections of ribs (*vatisaṃhatī*) are on the right and left; thirteen bones are joined together in each, which constitute the side and the left arm. [The word *pārśva*] ends in the letter *ṣ*, is neuter in gender, and is used in the plural; it refers to the left arm and thigh.
The right hip is the *dakṣiṇā*.

The right thigh is the sacrificial plank (*phalaka*) located on the southern side of the hind leg; that is to say, [the deities]. [End of] Chapter 410, accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 433.
The deities.
The *avadānas* are the portions for the principal deities; at the proper time, the portions are the meats.
The right foreleg and the left hip are for the *Sviṣṭakṛt*.
For the deity Sviṣṭakṛt, there are two large portions.

The rectum (*guda*) is common [to all]. It is used for the portions for the *Sviṣṭakṛt* deity and for the *upayaḍ-ḥoma*. By the word "rectum" (*guda*), that which is cooked within the *purītat* (omentum) is meant; having drawn it out from there, that rectum is called the "rectal section" (*gudakāṇḍa*).
He issues the command: "Do not tear the rectum; preserve the *kloman*, the spleen, the *purītat*, and the fat together."

The *kloma* is the duct of the throat (*galanāḍikā*). The *plīhā* (spleen) is similar to the *yakṛt* (liver) and is situated on the left side of the body. This flesh is not enclosed by any duct and remains unattached. The *purītat* is that which covers the heart; it is called *purītat* because of the Vedic statement: "The *purī* (heart) is covered by the *tat* (that). *Medas* (fat) is the solid casing that envelops the stomach and the intestines. Regarding the phrase "do not pierce these internal parts," the meaning is: "Do not cut the inner regions of the rectum. As for the *śamitṛ*— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]
One does not extract the rectum, nor does one pull out the large intestine (*vaniṣṭhu*).

The thick part that serves as the support is the rectum; the *vaniṣṭhu* is the thick [portion]. One should not invert these—that which is external should not be made internal. This has been explained.
He places the *adhyuddhi*, the *jāghanī*, and the *vaniṣṭhu* upon it.
The *adhyuddhi* is the meat located above the *ūṣas*. The *jāghanī* is that which belongs to the hindquarters; having identified each of these—the tail and the *vaniṣṭhu*—he sets them down with care.
He also places whatever else he considers fit for sacrifice.

The word "meat" (*māṃsa*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the animal], and the phrase "he places it together" (*anvavadadhāti*) is supplied from the context. Having placed the animal in the cooking pot (*kumbhī*), he cooks it. Those portions of the animal that are to be cut out are placed by the *adhvaryu* into the animal-pot situated on the *śāmitra* fire according to the rule for the *sānnāyya*. Having performed the act with the *mānasya* mantra, the *śamitr* (the slaughterer) cooks it. Since it is stated, "leaving aside the fire for cooking," the cooking takes place on the *śāmitra* fire itself. Because of the indicative mark in the question, "O *śamitr*, is the oblation cooked? (*śṛtaṃ haviḥ śamitar*), the *śamitr* is the one who cooks. By the simple statement "he will cook that," it follows that he "cooks" (*apayati*).
"With the spit, [he cooks] the heart from the side.

The word "he cooks" is carried over [from the previous rule]. Just as before, according to the possibility and following the procedure for the cooking-pot (*kumbhī*), he cooks the enlarged heart on the spit near the *śāmitra* fire. Having dug a pit in the earth for the receptacle of the entrails (*ūvadhyagoha*), he throws the dung into it.
The Adhvaryu alone carries away the entrails and the dung; having dug a pit in the earth with the same trench used for the entrails, he throws all the refuse into that hollow.
When the animal has been cooked, he proceeds with the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) belonging to the animal sacrifice.

This [procedure] shown is from another recension (śākhā). It is stated that after the offering of the omentum (vapā), having caused the announcement (mānayitvā), one proceeds with the rites of the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa), beginning from the placing of the vessels; then, it concludes with the rule: "Having released the speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (haviṣkṛt), when the animal has been cooked, he proceeds with the animal-cake. However, according to our own recension, it is heard: "Having immolated the animal, he offers the cake; he immolates it together with its fat-tissue (medhas); having proceeded with the omentum, he proceeds with the cake. Therefore, there is an option (vikalpa) between the two.

In this regard, the noble procedure is as follows: once the animal has been designated, having restrained speech and commenced the rites beginning with the setting out of the vessels for the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), when the washing of the rice grains is completed, they approach the animal; then, following the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) up to the sprinkling (*mārjana*), and having performed the offering of the animal-cake beginning with the taking of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) up to the release of the potsherds, they immolate the animal.

By the passage beginning with "stītyādinā," our school's ritual sequence (*śākhākrama*) is as follows: once the animal has been cooked, one performs the animal ritual procedure (*paśutantra*)—to be described later starting with "fivefold ladling into the *juhū* spoon"—without any interruption. Regarding the statement that "when the animal has been carried forward, one proceeds with the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*)," it is explained that once the rites from the taking of the black antelope skin up to the placing of the oblation have been performed, and since the assistance for the animal-cake offering is already provided by the incidental application (*prasaṅga*) of the animal sacrifice itself, he demonstrates only the specific ritual procedure for that [cake] as follows:
"having spread a base [of butter] in the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* spoons, having taken the portions, and having sprinkled [them with butter]."

With the *juhū* spoon, he performs the portioning of the oblation for the deities; with the *upabhṛt* spoon, he performs the portioning for the *viṣṭakṛt*. Then, having performed it in both cases according to the rule, he issues the command: "Recite the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for Indra and Agni regarding the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
This has been explained. Having stepped across—

Having caused [the announcement] to be heard, the Maitrāvaruṇa does not send [the call]; he urges the Hotṛ. This has already been explained. When the cutting of the omentum (*vapā*) is completed and the offering is made, having poured the contents of the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*, he issues the command: "Recite for Agni; give the call for Agni! (*agnaye 'nubrūhi agnaye preṣya*).

Standing on the right side, he pours the scrapings from the *āpabhṛt* vessel into the *juhū*; saying "To Agni," and so forth, he issues the call, "O Agnīdh, give the command for the *āśrāvaṇa*. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers according to the procedure for the *sviṣṭakṛt*. When the act ending with "having turned back" has been performed, and the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is completed, the *prāśitra* and the *iḍā* are prepared; once the *prāśitra* has been consumed, the purification (*mārjana*), the offerings of the flour-smears (*piṣṭalepa*) and the husks (*phalīkaraṇa*), the pouring out of the *praṇītā* waters, the removal of the *upaveṣa*, and the release of the potsherds (*kapāla*) are performed.

The words beginning with "prāśitāyām" (when it has been tasted) are connected with the plural number, as they refer to multiple actions. This serves to exclude other specific subsidiary elements that might otherwise be implied, and to exclude those subsidiary elements that are relevant and about to be employed. It also serves to exclude the sacrificer’s portion (*yajamāna-bhāga*), even though it is a specific element. When that [portion] has been offered, one takes five spoonfuls (*pañca-gṛhīta*) into the *juhū* ladle. Since the act of unyoking has been performed, there is an anointing (*abhighāraṇa*) with the clarified butter in the *sthālī* vessel, just as in the *Sānnāyya* offering; thus, it is said to be "with the clarified butter in the *sthālī*" and "five spoonfuls. The word "*juhū*" is used to ensure the cessation of the anointing with the *vṛṣa* [ladle].
Taking the *sruva* ladle for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*),
and likewise taking the vessel full of speckled butter along with the pot of speckled butter by means of the *snuṣā* ladle,
he approaches step by step and asks three times, "Is the oblation cooked? The *śamitṛ* replies three times, "It is cooked."

Having taken five portions of the omentum and having gone a short distance toward the front, he causes [the Adhvaryu] to announce, "The oblation is cooked. Having stepped forward again, he asks the same question; having stepped forward a third time as well, he receives the same response. Thus there are three questions and three answers.
Having circumambulated from the north, he takes the heart from the spit and places it in the pot.
Having circumambulated and gone clockwise to the north of the pot, he removes the heart pierced on the spit and, having placed the heart in its known position, deposits it in the pot.

With the formula, "May [your] mind unite with [my] mind," he bastes the heart with the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*). Having taken some of the speckled butter held in a reed, he bastes it after it has been placed into the cooking pot. The word "svāhā" concludes the mantra for the mind.
With the formula, "Svāhā! May the steam not cause distress," he consecrates the rising steam.

The pot is raised; the rest is clear. Having sprinkled the animal with clarified butter, [reciting] "He who has entered into the animals as its self," he [sprinkles] the animal situated in the pot with five-fold taken clarified butter from the *juhū* ladle. The phrase ending with "for me" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already obtained through the general rule (*codaka*), intended to specify the pouring of the meat with the five-fold taken butter. The citation of the mantra is for the purpose of excluding the continuation of the mantra "saṃ te manasā."
Having carried it by the same path as the omentum, he places it with the Pañcahotṛ formula at the place where the omentum is.

Having carried the omentum (vapā) along the same path between the Āhavanīya fire and the sacrificial post by which it was taken, one places it upon that very branch of the Bārhaspatya tree on the sacrificial grass (bahiḥ). In this very [branch], he sets down the Agnihotra [milk]; there is an exclusion of the original (prakṛta) mantras. 1. Pa., Sa., Sa., Da.: *sviṣṭakṛt-prāśitra* 2. Pa., Sa., Sa., Da.: *kriyante* 3. Gha., Jajha., Ga., Ra.: *kriyate* 4. Pa., Ru., Ja., Sa., Ma., Da.: *khurva cāyā* 5. Ga., Ga.: *sutaṃ* —The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha— [Book 4, Fourth Section] In that very [branch], he sets down the Agnihotra; there is an exclusion of the original mantras.

"That which is the self" refers to the vehicle (the sacrificial cart). "One's own sense-organ" refers to the unmodified [portion], because the oblation (*havis*) has been consumed therein. Regarding the oblation being portioned out, the injunction "Recite for the oblation" (*anubrūhi*), as well as "of the *chāgasya* oblation" and so forth—even in the phrase "the cooked oblation" (*śṛtasya haviḥ*)—it has been established by those learned in logic through the principle that it is the oblation itself that is being portioned out, not the various [animal parts].
He deposits the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*) in its known place. || 14 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the fourth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.

The meaning is that it is for the purpose of prescribing the performance at the outset. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the section on animal sacrifice within the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* composed by Mahādeva. 4.
4.5 Now begins the fifth chapter in the fourth book.
When the *pañcahotṛ* formula has been recited by the sacrificer, he spreads an underlayer [of ghee] in the *juhū*, the *upabhṛt*, the *vasāhomahavanī*, and the *samavattadhānī*.
The *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles contain clarified butter (*ājya*), while the other two vessels contain the collected butter for the *iḍā* portion;
he places a piece of gold in each of the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* and issues the command: "Recite for the *manotā* as the oblation is being cut.
Having placed pieces of gold in the *juhū* and *upabhṛt*, he then issues the command.

He cuts off the portions for the deities twice each with a continuous stream from the Plakṣa branch. Because of the scriptural statement, "In that the Plakṣa branch serves as the northern under-layer (*uttarabarhis*), he cuts off from the very sacrificial animal provided with consciousness," the meaning is that [the cutting occurs] upon the Plakṣa branch already spread out. Like the *sānnāyya* offerings, the portions for the *sviṣṭakṛt* are the size of a thumb-joint; those for the *anuyājās* are even larger than those. Regarding the cutting with the *sruva* ladle, it has already been stated previously that the term "with a stream" (*dhārayā*) is used here by implication to mean "in a continuous flow. These sacrificial portions for the deities have already been mentioned as being cut with a well-known, sharpened knife (*svadhiti*). Of these—

"Two, two, one, one. In this context, since the rule for cutting twice applies when the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) is extended, the prescription "again two" is intended so that it may apply to each individual limb; otherwise, by virtue of the *codaka*, there would result a single cutting of the whole. It has been stated that the injunction regarding the cuttings is novel (*apūrva*), based on the scriptural statement: "He cuts eleven portions. Having cut these in their proper sequence—first the heart, then the tongue, then the chest—as indicated by the order of the scriptural recitation.
He cuts off portions for the subsequent [deities] according to his desire;
this is indeed the revealed scripture (śruti). It is for the sake of the eightfold purpose.
[End of] Paṭala 610, from the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva.

One cuts off the portion from the rectum (*guda*) either from the front or from above. Regarding the rule that one may cut from the front or from behind the hip-portion (*śroṇi*), there is no restriction; it is according to one's preference. Here, although because the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is a single unit, it might seem sufficient to offer once with the thought "let me not injure it," nevertheless, due to the difference in intermediate locations and the difference in names, there is a separate mantra for each. Furthermore, since the items beginning with the heart and ending with the hip have been mentioned individually, two portions are to be cut from each without distinction. It has already been stated that the rectum is common to all. In this regard, he states the method of division:
He divides the rectum into two parts; he sets aside the thicker portion for the *upayaḍ* offerings.
Having divided the remaining part of the rectum—which has been separated from the thick section—into three parts, he sets aside the middle section for the *upayaḍ* offerings.
Having made the thinner part into three, he divides its middle rectal section into two and cuts portions from it for the deities.

Of the rectum (*gudakāṇḍa*) not cut for hatred, that portion which belongs to it is divided into three; its middle portion is divided into two, and he makes a double cutting (*dviravadāna*) from it, offering it to the deities and setting it aside. Here, regarding the recitation of the mantra and the subsequent sprinkling (*pratyabhighāraṇa*) of the cuttings, since the word "he cuts" (*avadyati*) is heard right here, the division performed by the phrase "he divides into two" (*dvidhā karoti*) and so forth is merely a partitioning of the substances to be cut, and does not constitute a formal cutting (*avadāna*). Thus, there are eleven cuttings, each made twice. In the *upabhṛt* ladle, he cuts portions of the large [pieces] of the three-limbed [offering], and one of the remaining two rectums.

Of the great thigh-section divided into three parts, that which remains as the larger and more massive [portion] is so [designated]. By convention, the term *vyaṅga* refers to the right arm and the left thigh; and the term *guda* refers to the first half of the pelvic region (*doṣapūrvārdha*), while the middle part is the *śroṇi*, and from there [comes] the half-thigh (*jaghanārdha*). Then the gods and the Asuras were present. According to the Śruti, "He cuts portions for the sacrifice," he cuts only three portions. Having divided the fat (*medas*) into three parts and placed it in the broth, he covers the *juhū* ladle with one third and the *upabhṛt* ladle with another third.

"He covers" [means this] in both cases, because of the third part of the fat (*medas*) that has been cut out, [which is placed] in the broth (*yūṣa*), that is, in the animal juice; for there is a scriptural statement (*śruti*): "This is indeed the essence of animals, namely the broth. Fat (*medas*) has already been explained. For here, since the animal itself is being given to the deity—as in the passage beginning with "The animal for Indra and Agni"—there is the offering of the oblation (*havis*). Consequently, there is a rule that from each of the eleven portions (*avadāna*) individually, an offering is taken from the middle and the front half, while the *sviṣṭakṛt* portion is taken from the rear half, as in the case of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). In the sacrificial cake, the deity...

It should be understood that, by virtue of their connection, even in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), although the portions for the deity (*daivata*), for *Sviṣṭakṛt*, and for *Iḍā* are offered from distinct locations due to the separation of the sacrificial substance itself, these portions—namely the *Sviṣṭakṛt* and others—are nonetheless of the nature of the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the remnants of the oblation (*haviḥśeṣa*).

This is because they are taken from different places, such as the heart, the tongue, the breast, the two flanks, the kidneys, and the perinephric fat, which are all deposited together in the *Samavattadhānī* vessel.
The remaining portion of the rectum,
the third part of the fat, and the seventh, the large intestine (*vaniṣṭhu*), if it has become cooked, he increases the *iḍā* with these boneless parts.

If the *vaniṣṭhu* (rectum) is cooked, one should cut off its many portions; if it has not been cooked along with the animal, then one does not cut from it, but cuts from what is cooked. These six offerings end with the *matasna*. If the *vaniṣṭhu* is cooked, having first cut the seventh portion from the *vaniṣṭhu*, then the section of the rectum (*gudakāṇḍa*), and then the fat (*medas*)—it is stated that the *vaniṣṭhu* is the seventh for the purpose of showing this sequence. One increases the *iḍā* with boneless meats such as the *kloman* and so forth, making it abundant; one does not cut these [specific organs] for the *iḍā*.

In the Vānapeya sacrifice, it will be stated in various places that "he gives what is not to be cut off (anavadānīya) to the Vājasṛts," and this is appropriate [only if the aforementioned restriction applies]. Furthermore, as for other sacrificial meats (medhya-māṃsa), their application is precisely here; otherwise, their separate extraction would be purposeless. In this context, the portion to be cut off (avadāna) from the sacrificial animal is for the ten deities alone, because the rectum (guda) is distributed and assigned separately.

Because the *aupabhṛta* and *iḍā* portions are presented separately by means of a distinct division, the ritual action for the remnant—characterized as the sacrificer’s portion (*yajamānabhāga*)—does not come from the other remnant materials, but rather from the primary cuttings themselves. Thus, the sequence is as follows: having taken one portion each from the eight organs beginning with the heart and ending with the intestines (*guda*) and placing them into the *iḍā*, the sacrificer’s portion is then taken from the ten organs beginning with the heart; thereafter, another cutting is made from the eight organs, and finally, he increases the *iḍā* with boneless parts.
Having placed both the cooked and uncooked portions of the animal together, he touches it while reciting, "The breath belongs to Indra."
He touches the boiled and the unboiled [fat] with the mantra, ending with "May the mother and father rejoice.
He takes the *vasā-homa* (the fat-oblation) in the *vasā-homa-havanī* (the vessel for the fat-oblation).

*Vasā* means essence or juice; it is called *vasā-homa* because it is both the *vasā* and the *homa*—that is, the oblation which is taken up (*grahaṇa*). Although one should simply say "he takes the *vasā*," it is stated as "he offers the *vasā-homa* from the side" because of the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) so heard.
With the mantra "Thou art glory," he cuts across the flowing stream with the knife.

Only the method for taking the portion of fat (*vasā*) is stated here. With the mantra ending in "let it be mixed," he cuts the stream made by the right hand across with the left hand using the knife. It is flowing, that is, continuous.
This is done once for one who offers four cuttings, and twice for one who offers five cuttings.

For one who offers four portions (*catur-avadānavat*), there are two cuttings made at once, resulting in four portions through the addition of the under-layer (*upastaraṇa*) and the over-pouring (*abhighāraṇa*). However, for one who offers five portions (*pañcāvadāvin*), there are three cuttings made twice; this is the meaning.

With the words "The waters have flowed together," he mixes the fat-oblation (*vasāhoma*) with the rib-bone; according to some, he mixes it with the knife (*svadhiti*), while according to others, he covers it with the rib-bone.

He stirs the fat that has entered the *vasāhomahavanī* ladle with the *prayot*. Regarding the *prayavaṇa* (the act of pouring out) and the *svadhiti* (the knife), there is an option. There is also an option between the *prayavaṇa* and the covering (*apidhāna*). The mantra ending with *rohiṣyāḥ* applies to all three.

Here, some authorities prescribe the consecration (*anumantraṇa*) of the steam (*ūṣman*). That consecration which was prescribed for the pot (*kumbhī*) with the words *svāhoṣmaṇo 'vyathiṣyāḥ* is [prescribed] here for those belonging to certain recensional schools (*śākhins*). [Notes on variants: 16. °niṣṭu sa; 2. gha, a, ja, jha, gha, da read "gācchapati"; having crossed over—650th Paṭala; accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 439.
Having sprinkled [the portions] with broth, placed two gold chips on top, and poured clarified butter over them;

having taken those [portions] with the *juhū* ladle, sprinkled them with broth, brought them back by the same way they were brought, and placed two gold chips in the *upabhṛt* ladle; then, having poured clarified butter over all [the portions] according to the rule, he issues the command:
"Recite the invitatory verse for the oblation of the goat for Indra and Agni."
This is also for the purpose of illustrating the Saurya and Prājāpatya offerings; the rest is clear.
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he does not issue a *praisha*; rather, the Maitrāvaruṇa urges the Hotṛ.
The explanation of the *kṛsara* has been provided.
"O drinkers of clarified butter, [drink] the clarified butter"—this is for the half-verse. || 15 ||
The Pratiprasthātṛ offers the *vasā-homa* (fat-oblation) following the *yājyā*.

Having gone to the front of the Āhavanīya fire, the Pratiprasthātṛ begins with the mantra "ghṛtam" together with the *yājyā*, and offers it at its conclusion with the formula ending in "antarikṣāya svāhā. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, the Adhvaryu offers the oblation of the omentum (*vapā*). The formula for consecrating the omenta of all the animals is either "indriyāvī bhūyāsam" or "nemānam.
He sacrifices toward the quarters with the remainder of the *vasā-homa*.

He sacrifices with the formula *yamati juhoti*. With the remainder of the water, he performs the oblation by means of a continuous stream (*dhārā*), sacrificing even the subsequent oblations without making an interruption in the middle.

He appends the word *svāhā* everywhere: to "the quarters" (*diśaḥ*) in the east, "the intermediate quarters" (*pradiśaḥ*) in the south, "the directed quarters" (*ādiśaḥ*) in the west, "the sub-quarters" (*vidiśaḥ*) in the north, and "the upward quarters" (*uddiśaḥ*) in the center.

In "sarvaprēti svāhā" and "antarikṣāya," the suffix "iti" is also attached at the end. Although [the *svāhā*] would normally occur at the end because this is a *darvihoma*, the *tīkāra* (the *i* sound) of the *svāhā* is placed in the middle according to the tradition of Bharadvāja and others; furthermore, it must be performed at the end for the purpose of excluding the act of throwing [the oblation] at the very end. [The formula continues with] "diśaḥ" and so on.

One might suspect that because [the act] is enjoined as a *pratiyajati* (offering for each), it is not a *darvihoma* (ladle-oblation). Anticipating this, [the author] states: since the mere sense of "sacrificing" (*yajati*) is not employed here, and because there is no *yājyā* verse, there is no *vaṣaṭ*-utterance. Rather, the offering is indicated here by the term *pratiyajati* through the very addition of *svāhā*. This is precisely what is intended by the scriptural injunction, "He offers to the quarters," which establishes its status as a *darvihoma*. Now, the mantra "The *svāhā*-utterance was placed before" does not constitute a "pre-*svāhā*" (*purastāt-svāhākāra*) by means of a *svāhā*-utterance preceding the word for the deity.

Because of the intervention by the word *svati*, it is already indicated by the phrase "to the intermediate space" (*antarikṣāya*) that the words for the deities are modified in the *vayah-homa*. Here, the word *svāhā* is to be supplied after *antarikṣāya*, or else the word *svāhā* is to be supplied before "to the quarters" (*digbhyaḥ*). He states that "svāhā to the quarters" is not a *darvihoma*:
"With 'svāhā to the quarters,' he sprinkles water around [the fire] while moving clockwise."

It is not considered a *darvihoma* because of the application of the term "anupariṣiñcati" (he sprinkles around), nor is it so considered by the rule "where there is the utterance of *svāhā*," since that intends to refer to another view. Why? Even if it were an oblation (*avadāna*), if it were a *darvihoma*, one would have said simply "pradakṣiṇam" (to the right) after "svāhā digbhyaḥ. Furthermore, because the root *yajati* (he sacrifices), which has the sense of giving, is not employed, there is no requirement for the utterance of *svāhā*.

Therefore, this subsequent ritual procedure (*śeṣapratipatti*) is shown by the application [of the rule]: "he circumambulates while pouring water around [the fire] from left to right" (*pradakṞṣimanupariṣiñcati*). Consequently, because the *svāhā*-utterance occurs at the beginning, it is a *darvihoma*; thus, the *Māruta* mantra is accompanied by *svāhā*, and it is not a *darvihoma*. Enough of this digression. Having offered with the words "Homage to the quarters" (*namo digbhyaḥ*), he stands in attendance (*upatiṣṭhate*).
The explicit mention of "having offered" (*hutvā*) is for the purpose of indicating that the standing in attendance belongs specifically to the *pratiprasthātṛ*.
Standing right here, having taken the *sruva*-ladle of speckled butter into the *juhū* ladle, he issues the directions: "Recite for Vanaspati" and "Prompt for Vanaspati."

In this very context, the particle *eva* (only) following "to the south" is intended to exclude staying to the north, as stated by Bharadvāja. [The oblation is made] with the *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter), which is full and contained in the *sruva* ladle, because that which is in the *upabhṛt* ladle is for the sake of the *anūyāja* offerings. The ellipsis is "he offers when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered. Here, by the general nature of the sacrificial offering (*havis*), the rules of the *upāṃśuyāja*—namely, the single cutting (*sakṛdavadāna*) and the consecration of the deity for the *sviṣṭakṛt*—are set aside by the rules of the *sviṣṭakṛt*. Why? Because the general nature of the offering is more powerful in the primary sacrifice, whereas it is not so in the subordinate *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice.

Having poured the contents of the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*, he issues the two calls for the animal *sviṣṭakṛt*: "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt" and "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.

"Having poured out," means having caused it to flow out. The rest is clear. The phrase "he offers when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The phrase "standing right here" also continues to apply here.
Regarding this very point, some authorities prescribe the touching of the animal and the offering to the quarters (*diśām pratījyā*).

[This applies] to the animal that has been cooked and the one that has not been cooked; the meaning is already explained. The ritual duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) proceed according to the archetype (*prakṛti*).
He cuts off the intermediate *iḍā* portion mixed with fat (*medas*).
The specific mention is "the intermediate *iḍā* mixed with fat."

If one should desire, "May he be without cattle," one should cut for him a portion without fat (*amedaska*); if one should desire, "May he be possessed of cattle," one should cut for him a portion with fat (*medasvat*).

The first [statement] is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) consisting of a censure of the intermediate *iḍā*-portion as being without fat; the second is an injunction. The meaning is that when there is such a desire—even if it does not exist—the intermediate *iḍā* must indeed be provided with fat. The Maitrāvaruṇa and the others, with the Maitrāvaruṇa as the sixth, consume the *iḍā* once it has been invoked.

In the case of the *iḍā* of the preceding animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), only those with the Maitrāvaruṇa as the fifth had consumed it; here, however, it is not the same. Because the Pratiprasthātṛ has a use for the omentum (*vapā*) offering, it is stated that the animal’s *iḍā* belongs to him as well, and thus it is said "with the Maitrāvaruṇa as the sixth," not for the purpose of excluding the sacrificer. He says "no" [to the question] whether this applies without distinction:
he brings the *adhyuddhi* (the upper part) to the Hotṛ, and prepares the sixfold portion (*ṣaḍavatta*) for the Agnīdh, including the *vaniṣṭhu* (rectum).

They carry [the portions] away; having given [the portions] from those two to both [the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu], they eat what remains. The Hotṛ eats his portion together with the *iḍā*. The Adhvaryu, having prepared the *vaniṣṭhu* (rectum) as a sixfold portion according to the procedure for the fourfold division, hands it over. When the *iḍā* has been eaten according to the rule, he says, "They purify themselves after the *iḍā* has been eaten.
Having purified themselves after the *iḍā* has been eaten, the sacrificer also performs the eating and the purification according to the original model (*prakṛti*).

"O Āgnīdhra, bring the embers for the *upayaj* offerings; O *Upayaṣṭṛ*, sit down; O Brahman, we shall set forth; having placed the fuel-stick, O Āgnīdhra, cleanse the enclosing sticks and the fire once each," thus he gives the command.
The embers intended for the *upayaj* are the *aupayanāḥ*; the *upayaṣṭṛ* is the Pratiprasthātṛ. "Stand near the embers. The rest is clear.

Having brought the embers from the *śāmitra* fire, the Āgnīdhra spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) on the northern shoulder of the altar, scatters [the embers], and places them as a supplementary layer.
"O Śāmitra, come here! Having placed grass and other materials there, he adds fuel sticks and fans the fire; then he spreads the sacrificial grass around it. He issues the command:

"O Pratiprasthātṛ, having cut this rectum into eleven pieces crosswise—without breaking them, without splitting them, and without turning them over—perform the secondary offerings (upayaja) with your hand or with the vessel for the fat-oblation. He cuts it crosswise into eleven pieces, without breaking, without tearing, and without turning it over. The cutting is strictly crosswise, not lengthwise. It is cut into eleven pieces once, for the subsequent offering; there is no further cutting for each individual oblation.

Having taken the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) into the juhū-ladle and having made the vessel containing the speckled butter (pṛṣadājyadhānī) the upabhṛt-ladle, he performs the eleven after-offerings (anūyāja) with the speckled butter.
The speckled butter is that which is contained in the vessel for the speckled butter. The rest is clear.
He issues the first call for the after-offering with "Prompt for the gods! (devebhyaḥ preṣya), and for the subsequent ones with "Prompt! Prompt! (preṣya preṣya).

Having gone to the right of all [the fires] as well—this is clear. Here, the word "to the gods" (*devebhyaḥ*) is in the plural by means of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining only one of identical forms) for the sake of Virūpas and Sarūpas alike. And thus, since the command "sacrifice" (*yaj*) would apply without distinction to both the *prayājas* and the *anuyājas* by virtue of the term "having sent forth" (*preṣya*), this statement provides a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding the second and third *anuyāja* offerings. In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, from the fourth [offering] onwards, when the Maitrāvaruṇa says "sacrifice" (*yaj*), the Adhvaryu says "sacrifice, sacrifice" (*yaja yaja*), except in the case of the tenth [offering].

When the *hotṛ* is addressed with "O *maitrāvaruṇa*, come to the *anuyāja*s," the *adhvaryu* says "Come! Sacrifice! along with that word "come. Having offered the tenth [anuyāja], there are three primary modifications (*prathamavikāra*) among the seven [anuyāja*s] beginning with the fourth, because the tenth is the first modification. These are, in order: of the middle [set], then two of the last, the eighth of the middle, the ninth of the last, the tenth of the first, and the last of the last; such also is the sacrifice (*ijyā*). [The formula is: "Go to the ocean, svāhā! (16). With these, the *pratiprasthātṛ* performs the secondary offerings (*upayaja*) after each *anuyāja* has been offered.

And because of the statement "where there is the utterance of *svāhā*," even in the *davihoma* (oblation with a ladle), there is the cessation of other [ritual] properties due to the prescription of independent properties. "He offers" (*juhoti*) means he sacrifices (*yajati*) near the offerings that have already been offered (*huta-hutam*), specifically near the *anūyāja* oblations. With these eleven mantras beginning with "Go to the ocean" (*samudram gaccha*), he performs the eleven *upayāja* offerings.
Regarding the *upayāja*—from the waters for you, from the plants for you—he wipes the residue on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) to the north.

Regarding the secondary offering (*upayaj*) of that which has reached its turn, the statement "having offered" (*upejya*) is intended to prescribe the Pratiprasthātṛ’s own procedure for the disposal of the portions and the drops; it is stated that this occurs when the *barhis* grass has been spread upon the altar.
He touches the region of his heart with the formula, "May [the sacrifice] grant my mind and my heart," ending with the word "may I eat. This is the same [as before].

Having anointed the *svaru* three times with the *juhū* ladle, the Adhvaryu offers it into the Āhavanīya fire with the *juhū* while reciting: "May your smoke go to heaven, your flame to the mid-region, fill the earth with ashes, Svāhā!

The mention of the "Adhvaryu" is for the purpose of excluding the Pratiprasthātṛ from this office, and the inclusion of the term "Yajus" (sacrificial formula) is to exclude the characteristics of a *dravyahoma* (material oblation) prompted by the verb "to sacrifice. This is clear.
He then proceeds to the rites beginning with the *Vājavatī*.

This is for the purpose of indicating the occasion for the *prākṛta* (archetypal) items; that rite from which the *vājavatī* [offering] is performed is indeed called "the *vājavatī*. Because both [ladles], the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt*, are connected, she separates them all. She anoints the *prastara* (grass-bundle) upon all of them. Thus Bharadvāja says: "She separates all [the ladles] from the *juhū* and *upabhṛt*; she anoints the *prastara* upon all of them"; and "she places all of them on the *kaṭambhī*. With the words "sūktā preṣya," he issues the call for the *sūktavāka*. This is for the sake of the modified (*vikṛti*) rite; in place of the words "sūktā brūhi," it is as in the archetype until the end of the *śaṃyuvāka*.
Having gone around [the fire] in the opposite direction, he performs the *saṃyāja* offerings for the wives.

This restatement is intended to state a specific detail; that very point he expresses as follows: 1. "The two middle ones are the middle. 2. [In the versions] ga, u, pa, nīye ju. 3. [In the versions] kha, ga, gha, cha, ja, śa, ma, u... ga, they perform the *saṃyāja* offerings. 15. [This concludes] the section following the *paracaḥ*, accompanied by the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva.
With the tail-portion (jāghanī), he sacrifices to the wives of the gods and Agni Gṛhapati; the other two [portions] are with clarified butter.
The other two [deities] are Soma and Tvaṣṭṛ.
From the tail-portion held upward, he cuts off for the wives of the gods; from the downward-turned portion, for Agni Gṛhapati.

Regarding the phrase "he cuts" (*avadyati*), in both cases, when the portion connected to the tail is made on top, then the dative case is used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe caturthī*). This is clear.

For the *hotṛ*, he places the *iḍā* from the tail-end (*jāghanī*) turned upward; for the *agnīdh*, he prepares the six-fold portion (*ṣaḍavatta*) from the downward-turned [portion]. He prepares the six-fold portion in place of the *ājya-iḍā*. The meaning is that for the *agnīdh*, there is a four-fold portion through the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*), and likewise for the *hotṛ*, there is a four-fold portion.
When she has eaten, the wife gives the remainder of the tail to the Adhvaryu and the foreleg to the Śamitr;
this is done only once. This is clear. He gives it to a Brāhmaṇa, if he is not a non-Brāhmaṇa.

If that *śamitṛ* (the immolator) is not a Brāhmaṇa, then he should give that arm to a Brāhmaṇa; otherwise, he himself cooks it. By this, it is shown that the *śamitṛ* may be either a Brāhmaṇa or another [twice-born], since in the Kali age, the office of *śamitṛ* is prohibited for a Brāhmaṇa. He will himself state in the *Dharma* texts that in the absence of such a person, the duty of preparing the cooking belongs to another twice-born man, or even to that [Brāhmaṇa] when presided over by an Ārya.
With the ladle (*juhū*), the Adhvaryu offers three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations into the Āhavanīya fire, [reciting]: "O sacrifice, go to the sacrifice; go to the Lord of Sacrifice."

All three of these mantras end with *svāhā*. In the third [mantra], although there are two instances of *svāhā* in the middle, it should be understood that because of the form "ghāḥ svāhā," it constitutes a *dravahoma* (liquid oblation). The mention of the *juhū* ladle is for the purpose of excluding the *dhruvā* ladle. The mention of "the other two" is for the purpose of excluding other properties; and the word "three" is for the purpose of excluding the optionality found in the original models (*prakṛti*). They proceed with the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*).
Because of the plural number, all [the priests] together with their wives go for the sake of the performance. Thus he says:
"Having taken it without touching it, you are heat; burn that!"—with these words, he extinguishes the fire at the junction of the dry and the moist.

The section ends with *dviṣmaḥ*. He throws the *hṛdayaśūla* (heart-spike) into the junction of the dry [ground] and so forth, which is established there. Where moist earth has followed [the dry], that is called *upopta* (scattered).
"Attained" means reached; "covered" means shielded from the influence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
They worship [the sun] with the words "from station to station" (*dhāmno dhāmnaḥ*).
"Upatiṣṭhante" means they stand near [in worship]. All [of them] perform this worship.
They cleanse themselves with the formula, "We do not [hate]," ending with "we hate. According to Āpastamba, they do so at that *cātvāla* pit.
They place fuel-sticks on the *āhavanīya* fire with the formula, "O fuel, may we prosper through thee."

In this case, because the mantra is singular, they offer only a single fuel-stick (*samidh*). Although there is a plural number in the *Baudhāyana Sūtra*—namely, "Offering [the sticks], bowing, they approach"—this is based on the Vedic text: "Offering [them], bowing, they approach. Thus, having taken them one by one, they come and offer each one individually. With the words, "I have followed the waters," they worship the *Āhavanīya* fire; likewise, the wife, having placed [her stick] in the *Gārhapatya* fire, worships it.

In this context, there is no modification (*ūha*) [of the word] into the masculine form as in "payasvān annabhāgama"; for this mantra is recited and applied in the *saumika-avabhṛtha* (the purificatory bath at the Soma sacrifice), which is the archetype (*prakṛti*) of the animal sacrifice. Since modification is prohibited there, it has already been stated that there is no modification even in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*).
This is the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for all animals.

This very procedure applies to all animal sacrifices (paśubandha); it is not merely an extended application (atideśa), but rather the procedure for the Soma sacrifices—namely the mixed, the Agniṣomīya, and the Savanīya—which has been extracted and explained here as it applies to the Nirūḍha sacrifice where it is obtained through extended application. This [procedure] is common to all, including the Aupaveśika, the Agniṣomīya, and others that are obtained through extended application.

And thus, those specific mantras belonging to other recensions (*śākhā*) which are heard in the *nirūḍha* sacrifice as "I offer what is acceptable to Indra and Agni" (*indrāgnibhyāṃ svā juṣṭam nirvapāmi*), must also be applied by extension (*atideśa*) to the *saurya* and *prājāpatya* sacrifices, just as they are to the *agnīṣomīya* and others. In this regard, the *agnīṣomīya* and so forth are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *nirūḍha* in certain respects; furthermore, these [latter] are the archetypes (*prakṛti*) for the duties of the Adhvaryu priest, while the *nirūḍha* is the modification.

This has been stated: the *iṣṭi*s and *paśubandha*s have the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as their archetype; they possess their own specific characteristics because they are modifications (*vikāra*) by virtue of commonality. Among these, those whose subsidiaries (*aṅga*) are directly perceived are the modifications of others, whereas those whose subsidiaries are not directly perceived [are modified differently]. The animal sacrifice (*paśu*) is a modification of the morning milk-offering (*prātardoha*), due to the commonality of time.

Although there is a similarity in sweetness, that alone is not the deciding factor according to the Nyāya system; even if the status of being a modification of curd (*sāya-doha-vikāratva*) is inferred based on the similarity of non-liquidity, it is set aside by the greater similarity of time. For at the morning time, the production of the *prātaḥsavana* and the animal sacrifice is equal, and thus, by virtue of being its modification, it is a modification of the *darśa*.
[The text] extends this principle elsewhere by way of analogy: "The same applies to the *āmikṣā*."

Even though there is a mixture of both milk products in that [offering], it is designated by the singular number because the two together constitute a single oblation; furthermore, since only a single modification of milk is observed, and because in the mantra-text the word "milk" (*payaḥ*) is used in the singular—as in the phrase "may they enjoy the appropriate milk"—the *āmikṣā* is a modification of milk. Moreover, since the *āmikṣā* is prepared in the morning, its identity of time with the other [morning offering] has also been stated.
This remains unchanged for the offerings to Agni and Indra-Agni, as well as for their modifications.

These two *savanīya* animals belong to the *agniṣṭoma* and *ukthya* terminuses; for them, this procedure (*tantra*) has been stated as neither deficient nor redundant by six [elements]. Whatever their modifications (*vikṛti*) may be, even in those cases it is likewise so, because these two possess direct (*pratyakṣa*) ritual characteristics. Other similar [animals] are modifications of these two, as their animal-characteristics have not entered directly into them. However, for those who perform the ritual duties, there is no modification of these two on the basis of the commonality of being a subsidiary animal (*aṅga-paśu*).

In the Agniṣomīya sacrifice and its modifications, the *prastara* is made of *āśvavāla* grass, the crosswise bar (*tiraścī*) is made of sugarcane, and there are additional enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made of *kārṣmarya* wood besides those of *pūtudāru*. He issues the summons for the animal deity with the words: "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the omentum and fat of so-and-so; prompt [the Hotṛ] for the cake of so-and-so; prompt [the Hotṛ] for the oblation of so-and-so."

The animal sacrifice for Agni and Soma (Agnīṣomīya) is the Upavasatha animal; in its modifications, there are additional elements such as the *āśvavāla* grass and so forth within the *vipravaṇa* sections. However, that which was performed previously at the *Ātithyā* sacrifice—namely, "that which is the *barhis* of the *Ātithyā* is for the Agni-Soma [animal]" and so on—was stated specifically for the sake of the Agni-Soma sacrifice. Therefore, in its modifications, there is no carrying forward (*praṇayana*) of the fire, nor are there *pautudravas* enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) in its modifications, because the carrying forward is already established by a scriptural statement for the Agni-Soma sacrifice itself. As for the *kāmayamāna* [elements], they are not present here.

It has been stated right here that those specific sheep which are established by another branch (śākhā) do not exist in the Nirūḍha [animal sacrifice]; likewise, it is stated by the phrase "this is unmodified" that they do not exist in the Savanīya [animal sacrifice] either, on account of another scripture. In the [sacrifices] dedicated to Indra and Sarasvatī, as well as in their modifications, the procedure for the selection of priests (pravaraṇakalpa) is that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices. || 17 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fourth book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
Thus ends the fourth book in the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. 4.

The meaning is that the function of Maitrāvaruṇa does not apply to these two. Thus, it is stated that the Agniṣomīya, the four Savanīyas, and the Nirūḍha as the sixth constitute the archetype (*prakṛti*) for all animal sacrifices (*paśu*). [Objection: But the Mīmāṃsakas have stated that the Agniṣomīya alone is the archetype for all animal sacrifices, because the ritual duties pertaining to the animal (*paśudharma*) are explicitly prescribed (*pratyakṣa-āmnāna*) only there. [Response: In our own Vedic branch (*hotra*), however, [the duties are found] in the *Śa. Ma. Ṭha.* [text], namely in the *Śepauṇe*.

In the *Baudhāyana Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the *nirūḍha-paśubandha* has been explained according to its original form (*prakṛti*) through the question, "They lead it forward" (*añjanti tvā*). By that means, it is obtained through the rule of extension (*codaka*) for other animal sacrifices. Furthermore, there is no direct injunction (*pratyakṣa-vidhāna*) for those others. Therefore, because it is a directly prescribed subsidiary (*pratyakṣāṅgatva*), the *nirūḍha* serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*) for other occasional (*naimittika*) and optional (*kāmya*) independent animal sacrifices, providing them with the *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ priest). And thus, the *ādhvara*...

Thus, having obtained the specific [Vedic] injunctions such as the *vaidimāna* (measuring of the altar) and others which are directly taught (*aupadeśika*), one applies them to other instances; likewise, having obtained the *ādhvaryava* duties such as the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice which are extended by analogy (*atideśa*), they apply even to its modifications (*vikṛti*), according to the maxim: "A beggar does not beg from another beggar."

And thus, among the animals included therein, because of similarity, the Agniṣomīya and others are determined to be the archetype (*prakṛti*). Even there, a distinction is made: for those performed during the intermediate period, the Agniṣomīya is the archetype; for those performed during the *savana*s (pressings), the Āgneya and others are the archetypes. Although the Āgneya and Aindrāgna are equal in that regard, a distinction is established based on the difference in the ritual details (*dharma*) of the animal-cake offerings (*paśupuroḍāśa*): for those whose animal-cake offerings are modifications of the Āgneya cake, the Savanīya Āgneya is the archetype; but for those belonging to the dual-deity (*dvidevatya*) or multi-deity (*bahudevatya*) classes, [the Aindrāgna is the archetype].

Alternatively, those animal-cake offerings (*paśupuroḍāśa*) that are modifications of the cake offering for Indra-Agni (*aindrāgna-puroḍāśa*) have that Aindrāgna as their archetype (*prakṛti*). As for those multi-deity offerings where the Agni-Soma cake is the archetype of the animal-cake, they too are modifications of the Savanīya cake dedicated to Agni, because of the similarity in the ritual properties of the potsherds (*kapāla*). For those single-deity offerings whose animal-cakes possess the properties of the cake for Indra-Agni, the Savanīya cake for Indra-Agni is the archetype; it has already been stated that the commonality of the oblation (*havis-sāmānya*) is more powerful [than other factors].

The established rule is that those [animals] dedicated to Sarasvatī as a male deity (*sarasvad-devatāka*) are modifications (*vikāra*) of the ewe (*meṇī*) dedicated to Sarasvatī because of the similarity of their nominal stems (*prātipadika-sāmya*), and those dedicated to a female deity (*strī-devatāka*) are modifications of the ewe because of the similarity of their female deities. Furthermore, it is not the opinion of the Mīmāṃsakas that the four *savanīya* animals are modifications of the *agnīṣomīya* animal, since they possess the same ritual properties (*dharma*) as prescribed for the *agnīṣomīya*. Why? Because their ritual properties are taught directly from the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Because for those [subsidiaries] included within the *jyotiṣṭoma* structure, the instruction regarding their status as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) is identical to that found in the *jyotiṣṭoma* context itself. Indeed, no specific deities have been prescribed there for the *āgnīṣomīya* and other [sacrifices], so there could be no restrictive rule based on a separate intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*). Rather, from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—"He immolates the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma"—which serves as an introduction providing the reason for the injunction "The food of the initiated one is to be eaten," an injunction is inferred; however, that injunction does not exist explicitly in our own recension (*śākhā*).

Similarly, even for the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices, injunctions are inferred solely from restatements (*anuvāda*). For it is heard in the context of the *Vājapeya*: "He immolates an *Āgneya* animal; by that he obtains the *Agniṣṭoma*. By the *Aindrāgna*, the *Ukthya*; by the *Aindra*, the *Ṣoḍaśin* chant; by the *Sārasvata*, the *Atirātra*."

By the explanatory passage (arthavāda), "The hymn for the great Māruti," the injunction regarding the deity of the animal sacrifice in the Vājapeya is established; by this, the injunctions for the Agneya and other animals in the subsequent sacrificial terminuses (saṃsthās) such as the Agniṣṭoma are inferred. Therefore, all those animals, having entered the Jyotiṣṭoma without distinction, share the same intermediate context (avāntara-prakaraṇa). Consequently, the mantras beginning with "atyanyān agām" and ending with "dhāmno dhāmno rājan," being recited within that context, do not specifically designate any particular animal deity.

They do not designate [it as such]. Likewise, even in the case of the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "Having offered with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, [he should address] the sacrificial post" and ending with "He who hates him, let him meditate upon him; verily he pierces him with grief," the procedure from the injunction regarding the sacrificial post up to the removal of the heart-spike is entirely the same; it does not adopt a specific deity. Therefore, as many animal sacrifices (paśus) as there are in the Jyotiṣṭoma, all of them [are included] without distinction. (Note: The textual variants indicated by the footnotes—*yādiḥ*, *yostu*, and *śasya vi*—refer to manuscript readings for the specific words or phrases within the quoted Sanskrit text.)

[Paṭala 2, Section 550: Together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 447. Since these belong to the primary context (*prakaraṇin*), the Adhvaryu’s duties for all [the offerings] are indeed based on direct instruction (*aupadeśika*). However, the formulas for the *upākaraṇa* (dedication) and so forth are extended (*atideśita*) from the *Nirūḍha-paśubandha*. Likewise, the specific *praiṣas* (directions) for the [offerings to] Indra, Sarasvatī, and Mitrā-Varuṇa, as well as their absence, are known from another scripture (*śāstrāntara*). Similarly, it has been stated that the restriction regarding specific *praiṣas* and the rule concerning the use of the *bahirvidhṛti*, the *prastara*, and the *paridhi* made of *mayu*-wood are also established solely by the authority of another scripture through explicit injunction (*vacana*).

Therefore, among the five animal sacrifices, the Agniṣomīya and the others are established as the archetypes (*prakṛti*) for those included within the *tantra* of the Soma sacrifice; however, for those excluded from the *tantra* of the Soma sacrifice, the Nirūḍhāgnīṣomīya alone is the archetype. Thus, all five animal sacrifices possess direct ritual characteristics (*pratyakṣadharma*) in their *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ priest), being modifications (*vikṛti*) of the Nirūḍha in that regard, while the other duties—pertaining to the *ādhvaryava* (the duties of the Adhvaryu) and the specific *hautra*—are extended by rule (*atideśa*).

Although the same [application] would have been obtained from other treatises (*śāstrāntara*), it has been established in the case of the sacrifice to Indra and Sarasvatī precisely by way of precluding the function of the Maitrāvaruṇa priest; thus, enough of this digression. As for Jaimini, having raised the objection that the five animals constitute the archetype (*prakṛti*), he refuted it through reasoning; in our commentary on the reasoning indicated by the teaching of our own branch, the purport of the Sūtra has been shown. Therefore, this very method is to be understood in our Sūtra. Some assert an option (*vikalpa*) between reasoning and scriptural teaching, but that is not so.

"How can reasoning (nyāya), which is inference (anumāna), be equal to Śruti? Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fourth [book], the section on Animal Sacrifices (Paśubandha), in the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* composed by Mahādeva, the son of Satyāpāda. Thus ends the fourth book (praśna) in the commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra*.
5.1 Now begins the first chapter of the fifth book.

Although the Cāturmāsya sacrifices are indeed recited within the Rājasūya, for their mention is found even among the obligatory (nitya) rites—such as in the Smṛti where it says, "The Darśapūrṇamāsa and the Cāturmāsyas," and so forth—the meaning here is that because those [sacrifices] recited in the Rājasūya possess both obligatory and fruit-bearing results, they are also obligatory.
"Indeed, the merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is inexhaustible."

"He performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. Because his well-performed merit yields inexhaustible fruit, the two words *akṣamya* and *ha* are indeed read as they appear in the Śruti. The word *ha* signifies "well-known," and the word *vai* has the sense of "for" (*hi*). Therefore, the meaning is that one must necessarily sacrifice with the Cāturmāsya rites. Nor should it be argued that the result is merely imagined from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because in this context, their repeated performance (*abhyāsa*) is what will be enjoined; and there is no such repeated performance in the case of optional (*kāmya*) rites.

This is the application for the obligatory rites alone, since the performance of the optional rites will be explained by the author himself later on. The term "in each four-month period" (*caturṣu caturṣu māsyāni*) is the name for the sacrifices together with the Gṛhamedhīya, Traiyambaka, Paricaryā, and two Darvihomas; it refers to the collection of sacrifices because they are enjoined by the verb *yajati*. The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is: "I shall sacrifice with the Cāturmāsya rites; may I gratify Yajñanārāyaṇa through them. This concludes the commentary on the Anvārambhaṇīyā [rite]. 5.1 Now begins the first chapter in the fifth book.
The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is indeed inexhaustible.

One who is about to undertake them, on the fast-day of the preceding Parvan—either on the full moon of Phālguna or Caitra—having mentally recited the Pañcahotṛ formula and offered it along with the Grahas, performs the Anvārambhaṇīyā sacrifice: a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara and a pap for Pārjanya.
He performs the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice on ground sloping toward the east.
Whether having moved out from the sacrificial ground or not,
having led forward the fire according to the ritual procedure for the fire,
and having placed a tuft of wool in the fire-pit and established the fire therein.
Having added fuel to the fires for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva offering characterized by the *abhijñā* formula, he drives away the calves for the evening milking.
There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.
Having tied together three bundles of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with their tips intact, he ties them together again as one.
In this same manner [is performed] the fuel-wood rite. The rule applies again at the re-binding [of the girdle].

At the time of arranging the vessels, he sets out the vessels according to their purpose: the *juhū*, two *upabhṛt*s, a second *pṛṣadājya* vessel, the *dhruvā*, two *ājyasthālī*s, a second *dadhi* vessel, a *pālāśa* vessel for the *vājina*, a *sruk* or a *camasa*.

At the time of the offering, he prepares these five *saṃcara* oblations: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Sarasvatī, and a pap for Pūṣan.

There is a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts, clotted curd (*āmikṣā*) for the Viśvedevas, and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth. Regarding the subsequent seasonal sacrifices (*parvan*), some authorities prescribe a cake on eight potsherds for Savitṛ.
When the rice has been thrice-pounded, he sets aside the portion for Pūṣan with the *vibhāga* formula and grinds it together with the grains intended for the sacrificial cakes.
Following the procedure for the morning milking, he causes the morning milk to be milked. When the morning milk has been heated, he pours the evening milk into it and prepares the *āmikṣā*.

Having drawn out the thickened curds into another vessel, he pours the *vājina* (whey) over them, sets it aside in a known place, and places the remainder of the *vājina* on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*). || 1 ||
Having separated the mixed and ground portions with the *vibhāga* formula, he cooks them according to the procedure for *caru*.
Having performed the second tracing (*parigrāha*), he proceeds with the call: "Bring the clarified butter and the curds! He modifies the end of this call [to include the mixture].
On the full moon day of Phālguna, he takes the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) just as he does for the animal sacrifice.
On the full moon day of Caitra, having spread a layer of clarified butter twice and taken up curds twice, he sprinkles it once with clarified butter.
He proceeds with the rites beginning from the removal [of the oblation from the fire].
Having removed the cake on one potsherd into another vessel and having brought it forward with abundant clarified butter, he makes it visible on its back.

He places the oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*, as [he does] at the end of the year. He proceeds with the fire produced by friction (*nirmanthya*) according to the procedure for the fire produced by friction. Having laid down the *veda* grass-bundle, he issues the call for the *sāmidhenī* verses.
He performs nine fore-offerings (*prayāja*); having poured together [the butter] at the fourth, he pours it all together at the eighth.
At all [these offerings], he sacrifices to the deities of the *sāvitra* and the one-potsherd (*ekakapāla*) oblations in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
Having taken the entire cake on the single potsherd, having spread it out over the supporting vessel, he offers it straight, well-established, and without turning it over.

If the oblation, once offered, should turn back while the boon has been granted, he should arrange it with the tip of the *sruva* ladle; or, having taken it back, he should offer it again, but not with his hand—so say some.
He makes an offering over the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) with the four names of the months: "Madhu and Mādhava," or alternatively, "To Madhu, svāhā! To Mādhava, svāhā!
He performs nine after-offerings (*anūyāja*) with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*).
