The Hotṛ recites the concluding formulas of the *sūktavāka*, including the blessings: "He invokes the prosperity of the year-long [sacrifice]; he invokes the divine abode.
After the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) have been cast into the fire, he makes an oblation with the residual drops (*saṃsrāva*) and proceeds with the *vājina* (curd-mixture).
Having spread a base of butter in the *vājina* vessel, he takes the *vājina* while pouring it out upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); having filled it, he does not pour clarified butter over it.
"Recite for the Vājins; sacrifice to the Vājins," he issues the command.
Sitting with his knees raised, the Hotṛ recites without taking breath.
At the utterance of "vaṣaṭ," he offers the oblation with the ladle being tilted.
He performs the after-offering with the formula, "O Agni, enjoy the whey.
He offers the whey toward the quarters with the remnants of the whey, just as one does with the remnants of the fat-oblation.
Having invited one another, they all consume the whey, seeking mutual invitation; the summons is "Invite me! and the response is "I am invited!"

"May the portion of the swift ones protect us; may the vigor, the poured seed, the nectar, be for our strength. May Indra bestow upon us that power and wealth. May we not come to harm while consuming the swift one. "O swift one, of thee who hast been made into a portion by the swift ones, who art full of sweetness and invited, being myself invited, I consume thee"—with these words they consume it.
Either the sacrificer is first or last.
On the following day, having sacrificed with the Full Moon sacrifice, he either departs from the sacrificial ground or does not depart.
"May the divine waters, impelled by the god Savitṛ, moisten [the head] for long life and luster"—with these words, he moistens the head.

"Truth indeed is the Supreme Lord; nothing whatsoever transcends Truth. In Truth the ocean is placed; in Truth this earth is supported. Agni with his sharp flame has overcome the heat; the head is placed within the *uṣṇih* (heat). By the power of Truth I turn it back; by Reality I turn it around; by austerity I follow it after; by the auspicious I turn it toward; by the helpful I turn it hither. With these words, using a three-pronged porcupine quill or a stalk of sugarcane, he parts the hair.
With a razor made of iron or of udumbara wood, he trims the hair;
he shaves the beard, or he has his entire head shaved. || 3 ||
Thus ends the first paṭala in the fifth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. || 1 ||
5.2 Now begins the second chapter of the fifth book.
Then, after four months, on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha or Śrāvaṇa, he performs the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices.
Their ritual procedure is explained by that of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.

There are two Āhavanīya fires; the insertion (āvāpa) occurs in both places. The entire ritual procedure (tantra) is performed in the northern sacrificial area, and likewise in the southern one. The Adhvaryu performs those rites connected with the Gārhapatya fire as well as those that are common to both.
In that regard, the Adhvaryu issues the calls for the duties of the Hotṛ concerning the ritual limbs;
these are treated as a single unit when connected with the fire—
namely, during the Sāmidhenī verses, the leading forward of the fire, and the sweeping of the fire.
Both address the Brahman priest; the Brahman grants permission for both.

At the place where they are about to carry forward the two fires, they construct two altars on level ground facing east, separated by two, three, four, or a span's measure, such that their hips and shoulders do not overlap.
Whatever the Adhvaryu does, the Pratiprasthātṛ does.
In the northern shed, the Adhvaryu performs the rites; in the southern, the Pratiprasthātṛ.

From the northern corner (śroṇi) of the southern altar to the southern shoulder (aṃsa) of the northern altar, he cleaves a single furrow with the wooden sword (sphyá). The rubbish-heap (utkara) is common to both. The Brahman, the Hotṛ, and the Āgnīdhra [are likewise common].

Having performed that which precedes the northern enclosure-line, the Pratiprasthātṛ proceeds toward the *utkara* heap for the sake of the northern *vihāra*. According to the ritual procedure for the *uttaravedi*, he prepares the *uttaravedi* on the north side.
In both cases, the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*) and the leading forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) are as prescribed for animal sacrifices.
Having established the fires (*agnīnvādhāya*), [the rites proceed].

They drive away the calves for the two *āmikṣās*: the Pratiprasthātṛ for the one dedicated to Maruts, and the Adhvaryu for the one dedicated to Varuṇa. They prepare the curds according to the procedure for the evening milking.
At the time of arranging the vessels, they employ the vessels as required; the offering-spoons (*sruva*) are made of *śamī* wood, or else they are made of gold.
At the time of the pouring out of the oblations, the Adhvaryu, having poured out the five common offerings, pours out the cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and Agni.
The Pratiprasthātṛ pours out barley for the ewe dedicated to Māruta.
Having poured out a ram for Varuṇa, the Adhvaryu pours out a cake on one potsherd for Ka;
or indeed, all [the offerings] contain barley.
Having mixed barley grains with the excess water from the sprinkling-vessel, they thresh them.
When the hearth-stones have been placed up to those for the offering to Indra and Agni, the Pratiprasthātṛ places eleven or twelve potsherds on the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire.
Having placed eight for the ram, the Adhvaryu places those for the goat.
The procedure for the morning milking is as follows: they perform the two morning milkings and prepare the *āmikṣā* curds as previously described.
When the offerings have been placed on the fire up to the one for Indra and Agni, they fashion two effigies of rams.
The Pratiprasthātṛ fashions a ewe for the Maruts, while the Adhvaryu fashions a ram for Varuṇa. He fashions the female characteristics of the ewe and the male characteristics of the ram.

The Pratiprasthātṛ places the ewe on eleven or twelve potsherds; having placed the ram on eight potsherds, the Adhvaryu places the cake for Ka on a single potsherd. Alternatively, the two animals may be cooked in pots (*kumbhī*).
For other [animals], there is the grinding of raw [grain].
The sacrificer and his wife prepare bowls of *karambha* (barley-meal) from slightly parched barley grains;
there is one more bowl than the number of the sacrificer’s servants and kinsmen who are accompanied by their wives.
Having performed the subsequent tracing of the altar, he proceeds with the formal command: "Bring the clarified butter and the curds! At this point, they both conclude the ritual procedure.

As on the full moon of Āṣāḍha and likewise on that of Phālguna, they take the *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter). But on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, having spread a base of clarified butter once, they take the curds twice and then pour clarified butter over it once. They proceed with the rites beginning from the removal of the oblations. When the offerings ending with those for Indra and Agni have been adorned, they make two woolly effigies of rams out of the wool of sheep that are not black-necked; if such wool is unavailable, they bind together *kuśa*-grass wool.
He places a ram upon the offering for the Maruts and a ewe upon that for Varuṇa.

He places the other oblations on the northern altar, and the offering to the Maruts and the *karambha* vessels on the southern altar. Having placed them, they exchange the two ram effigies: he places the ewe upon the offering for the Maruts and the ram upon the offering for Varuṇa.
While scattering more than a hundred or more than a thousand *śamī* leaves and *karīra* fruits over those two, he also pours them into the *karambha* vessels.

The procedure for the *nirmanthya* fire is as follows: they proceed with the *nirmanthya* fire according to its prescribed ritual. Having laid down the Veda-grass-bundle, he issues the call for the *sāmidhenī* verses. When the northern fire has been swept and the southern fire has not yet been swept, the Pratiprasthātṛ asks the wife: "Wife, how many lovers do you have? He points them out, saying, "May Varuṇa seize as many as she declares. If she does not declare him who is her lover, she would obstruct a beloved kinsman.
With the verse, "We invoke those who are to be slain," the Pratiprasthātṛ leads the wife forward.

Having placed the bowls of *karambha*—which have been poured into a winnowing-basket of *aiṣīka* reeds—upon her head, the wife goes between the two altars. Then the sacrificer and the wife stand facing west in front of the southern fire.

With the invitatory verse, "Do not indeed [slay] us," the sacrificer recites; and with the offering verse, "That which belongs to the village," they both, having spoken together, offer with the winnowing-basket into the southern fire.
The Adhvaryu offers the oblation while the other two hold on to him from behind. Reciting "The doers of the rite have performed the rite," they both mutter the verse as they turn away.
He then cleanses the southern fire.
When the offerings have been performed up to those for Indra and Agni,
the Pratiprasthātṛ cuts off the entire ewe from the offering for the Maruts together with the first portion, and the Śamī leaves and Karīra fruits with the second;
the Adhvaryu cuts off the entire ram from the offering for Varuṇa together with the first portion, and the Śamī leaves and Karīra fruits with the second.
"O Kāyānubūhi, sacrifice to Ka! Thus he gives the direction for the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*).
He offers the cake on one potsherd with the four names of the months: "To Nabhas, svāhā! To Nabhasya, svāhā! or alternatively, "To Nabhas, svāhā! To Nabhasya, svāhā!
At the benedictions of the *sūktavāka*, the Hotṛ recites, "May he pray for well-being throughout the year."
When the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) have been removed, having offered the remnants of the oblation (*saṃsrāva*), they proceed with the *vājina* offering as before.

"Whatever semen of mine is shed, whatever is born from me again, or whatever remains established within me—with that, make me vigorous; with that, make me well-progeny. "Of thee, O *vājina*, who art made ready with the *vājins*, who art full of sweetness, and who art invited—I, being invited, partake," saying this, they consume it in the southern sacrificial area (*vihāra*).

"May the drops enter me; may the veins flow toward me. Fill my essence with your essence. O winner of prizes, of that which is mixed with prizes, prepared, and offered—being invited, I partake. Thus [he says] over the northern [portion].

Having concluded [the sacrifice], they go down for the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with the scrapings of the offering to Varuṇa and with the husks. The ritual procedure for this is explained by the purificatory bath of the Soma sacrifice.
No Sāman chant is sung.
Having gone away silently,
he offers the scrapings according to the ritual rule for Varuṇa;
he then offers the husks according to the ritual rule for the *ṛjīṣa*.
Having emerged from the *avabhṛtha* bath, two garments are given to whomever he desires.

On the following day, having performed the *paurṇamāsa* sacrifice, whether they have moved away from the sacrificial ground or not, he moistens himself with water while reciting: "Impelled by the god Savitṛ...
and "When Gharma turned around the boundaries of the earth and the sky, Agni [did so] as the lord through his might."
"May Varuṇa with his prayers, Indra with his friends the Maruts, and Agni with his flame come hither"—this is the returning and the shaving, as before. (7)
Thus ends the second paṭala in the fifth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
5.3 Now, the third chapter of the fifth book.

Then, after four months, on the full moon of Kārttika or Mārgaśīrṣa, he sacrifices with the Sākamedha offerings for two days. He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Anīkavat; according to some, [he does so] "rising together with the sun, proceeding together with the rays. At midday, he offers a pap to the Maruts Sāṃtapana; according to some, he does not throw the sacrificial grass (barhis) into the fire. In the afternoon, he drives away the calves for the Gṛhamedhīya offering; according to some, he drives away as many calves as the sacrificer has, without reciting a formula.
When the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, he commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *gṛhamedhīya*.
We shall now explain everything that is performed therein.
Having added fuel to the fires, prepared the *veda*, strewn grass around the fires, washed his hands, and spread out the *ulaparājī*, he arranges the vessels according to their purpose.
There is one *kumbhī* and three *pātrīs*.
At the time of the *nirvāpa*, he pours out abundant *vrīhi* rice for the Maruts Gṛhamedhins, as much as he considers sufficient for the milk.
He causes the cow to be milked with a strainer.
According to some, one does not winnow the rice grains; rather, one cooks them with milk that has already been purified by the *yajus* formula.
One cooks the *prativeśa* porridge on the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire.
Having taken up the wooden sword (*sphya*), he performs the *stambayajus* rite over the hair of the strewn altar.
Having taken up the northern enclosing stick, he proceeds with the formal command (*saṃpraīṣa*).
He issues the command for everything other than the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*) and the binding of the wife (*patnīsaṃnahana*).
Having performed that which precedes the taking of the clarified butter (*ājyagrahaṇa*), he takes [the butter] from the *dhruvā* vessel itself.

Having consecrated the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*), having addressed the Brahman priest, and having sprinkled the altar (*vedi*), he pours out the remainder of the sprinkling water. Having cast back the two strainers (*pavitra*) [into the vessel], he sets down the *dhruvā* ladle and the *sruva* spoon. He modifies the mantra to "This one has sat down" (*eṣā'sadat*). He consecrates the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the mantra: "Thou art Viṣṇu; thou art the abode of Viṣṇu; thou art the domain of Prajāpati."
The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) used for the Ānīkavata offering is the same as that for the Sāṃtapanīya and the Gṛhamedhīya; according to some, it remains already spread.
He proceeds with the ritual acts beginning from the removal [of the oblation from the fire].
Having drawn out a portion of the cooked oblation and set it aside in a known place...
Having spread an underlayer of ghee in the vessels, he draws up three portions of boiled rice.
He sets down the pot from which the rice has been drawn out. Having placed the stirring-spoon, without wiping it, upside down [upon it].
Having sprinkled [the oblation] over it, purified it, and adorned it, he places the portions of cooked rice (odana) down.

When the deities have been invoked, having fanned the fire and performed the ritual with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, he makes an under-layering of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle, takes portions from all the portions of cooked rice, sprinkles them over, and issues the direction: "Recite the invitatory verse for the Maruts, the householders; recite the offering verse for the Maruts, the householders."

The *sviṣṭakṛt*, the *prāśitra*, and the *iḍā* are performed; once the *iḍā* has been consumed, they offer portions of the cooked rice to the attendants who are entitled to eat the sacrificial oblation (*havirbhojana*).
The wife eats of what has been cooked by a neighbor.
The *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice concludes with the *iḍā*.
They anoint themselves and oil their bodies; they let the calves stay with the cows;
neighbors cook for one another; and they slaughter cows.
Well-fed, contented, and free from the fear of death, they pass this night.
In the latter part of the night, he binds two calves—one belonging to a cow that has been suckled by another and the other being the *agnihotrī* cow—together.
Before the morning *agnihotra*, they proceed with the *pūrṇadarvya* offering.

Having spread an underlayer of ghee in the ladle (*darvī*), having filled the ladle with the scrapings from the winnowing basket (*śara-niṣkāsa*), having wiped it, having taken a portion for the stirring-stick (*udāyuvana*), and having sprinkled it with ghee;
Having recited "Full is the ladle," he calls out to a bull, "Give me! and while it bellows, he makes an offering in the *gārhapatya* fire.

If the bull does not bellow, he should address the *brahmán* priest; being permitted by him, he should offer. He prepares a cake on seven potsherds for the sporting Maruts. According to some, [he offers] at the time when the sun rises together with its rays, saying, "Moving forth together with the rays. || 10 ||
At that very time, he performs the sacrifice with great oblations (*mahāhavir*).
Their ritual procedure is explained by that of the *Vāruṇapraghāsa* sacrifice in the northern sacrificial area (*uttara-vihāra*).

Having offered the five common oblations (*pañca saṃcarāṇi*), he offers a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*), a pap (*caru*) for Indra, and a cake on one potsherd for Viśvakarman.
Having brought forward the unmixed *aindrāgna* [oblation], he sets aside its well-known husks.

As at the *kārttikī*, so at the *āṣāḍhī*; as at the *mārgaśīrṣī*, so at the *śrāvaṇī*, he takes the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*). He pours the oblation from the ladle with the formula: "O Agni, fulfill the office of the Hotṛ; fulfill the office of the messenger. Standing erect at the sacrifices, may Heaven and Earth protect you; protect Heaven and Earth; be the *Sviṣṭakṛt* for Indra and for the gods. Accepting this oblation, of the clarified butter, enjoy it, Svāhā! Thus he pours the *āghāra* libation.
He offers an oblation on a single potsherd (*ekakapāla*) with the four names of the months: "Saha," "Sahasya," and so forth, or [alternatively] with the formula, "Hail to Saha! Hail to Sahasya!
The Hotṛ priest continues with the blessings of the *sūktavāka*, saying, "He invokes well-being for the year-round [cattle]; he invokes the divine abode.
They proceed to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) with the husks of rice dedicated to Indra and Agni; thus, the disposal of the husks is performed in connection with the journey.
Thus ends the third paṭala in the fifth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
5.4 Now, the fourth chapter in the fifth book:
At that very time, he performs the Mahāpitṛyajña.
To the south-east of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, he prepares a square altar (vedi) measuring one fathom in length.
Its corners face every direction;
they are slender in the intermediate directions.
Everywhere, one adapts the mantra containing the invocation of the gods to accord with both the gods and the ancestors.

"Just as the earth is the place for the sacrifice to the gods and the ancestors, you are strewn for the gods and the ancestors; O *barhis* of the gods and ancestors, let me not harm you lengthwise nor crosswise; may I be able to perform the rite for the gods and the ancestors.

Having performed everything up to the sweeping, having enclosed it on all sides and made a door in the northern corner, he brings embers from the southern fire, places them in the middle of the altar, and adds fuel to them.
This is the Āhavanīya fire here.

Having added fuel to the Āhavanīya, Gārhapatya, and Dakṣiṇāgni fires, he brings the sacrificial wood (idhma) and the sacrificial grass (barhis). He takes the sacrificial grass longer than the usual measure, cutting it with the roots or cutting it near the roots.
He binds all two enclosing-sticks (paridhis) together. At the time of arranging the vessels, he sets out the vessels according to their purpose:
six potsherds for Soma Pitṛmat, a potsherd for the roasted grains (dhāna) for the Barhiṣad Pitṛs.
For the sake of the *mantha* offering to the Agniṣvātta ancestors, there is a vessel made of *vāraṇa* wood or a shallow cup (*śarāva*).
At the time of the *nirvapaṇa*, the Adhvaryu, having mounted the cart from the south, wears his sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) and pours out the barley;
or, from the north, he does so wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*).

He offers a cake on six potsherds to Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs, or clarified butter. For the Pitṛs seated on the sacrificial grass (barhiṣad), he offers parched grains; for the Pitṛs consumed by fire (agniṣvātta), he offers a stirred drink (mantha); according to some, a stirred drink for Yama.
Having mixed barley with the water remaining from the sprinkling-vessel, he threshes it.
When the grains have been husked three times, he divides them with the *vibhāga* mantra and pounds them.
Having placed six potsherds in the southern half of the *gārhapatya* fire, he places a potsherd on the *dakṣiṇāgni* for the purpose of roasting with the first *kapāla* mantra.
Having placed the six potsherds on the fire and poured [the grain] onto them with the *adhiśrayaṇa* mantra, he roasts the parched grains (*dhānā*).
They lie down unburning. || 11 ||

The altar is not dug out; having performed the northern tracing-out, he proceeds with the formal command (*saṃpraiṣa*). He issues the command for everything except the girding of the wife. He does not gird the wife, nor does he sit near her; sitting right there in the house, she gazes at the clarified butter (*ājya*).
Having performed that which precedes the taking of the clarified butter (*ājya*) and having turned back, he takes the *ājya* portions at the Gārhapatya fire.
He takes all of them in four ladlings, or twice in the *upabhṛt* spoon.

Having consecrated the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*), having addressed the Brahman priest, and having sprinkled the fuel, the altar, and the sacrificial grass, he pours out the remainder of the sprinkling waters, inserts the two strainers (*pavitra*) [into the water], and takes hold of the tips of the sacrificial grass.
Moving three times around the fire from right to left while shaking [the grass-bundle], he stands upright; holding it, he moves back three times without shaking it.

He lays down two enclosing sticks, or all of them. Since the two separating blades are prohibited, he silently deposits the *prastara* and proceeds with the rites beginning with the removal [of the ashes].
Having performed those rites which precede the decoration [of the fire-altar].

Having divided the parched grains with the *vibhāga* mantra and having made half of the flour into groats according to the procedure for flour, he—sitting to the south and not touching [the vessel]—three times stirs the mash counter-clockwise with a cane-stick into the milk of a cow whose calf has been taken away, using a vessel that wards off [evil], namely a half-śarāva. He makes the stick, the stalk, and the mash into a single mass. Having brought a glowing ember from the *dakṣiṇa* fire towards the west, having carried it past the rear of the *gārhapatya*, having carried it around the front of the *āhavanīya*, he places it within the altar to the south of the *āhavanīya*.
Having adorned each [offering] individually, he places the clarified butter and the sacrificial oblations down.
To the south, he establishes the collyrium, the ointment, the cushion, the mattress, and the water-pot.
He puts on the sacred thread if he has been wearing it over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī).

He issues the command: "Recite for Agni, for the gods, and for the ancestors, as he is being kindled. He recites this *sāmidhenī* verse, "Desiring you, we invoke you," three times. Having divided the fuel-wood into three parts, he places the whole of it upon the fire.

When the deities have been invoked, having fanned the fire and poured the *sruva*-libation, he issues the command: "O Āgnīdh, cleanse the enclosing sticks and the fire three times each. Once they have been cleansed, he chooses the *pravara*.
"Sīda hotar" (Sit down, O Hotṛ)—this much is the *pravara*.
He performs the *prayāja* offerings excluding the one for the *barhis* grass; he does not pour the butter from the *upabhṛt* ladle.
The two *ājyabhāga* portions contain the word "life" (*jīvātu*).

Having performed the offerings with those two, they loosen their sacrificial cords and convert them from the *upavīta* position to the *prācīnāvīta* position; they then transpose the clarified butter and the oblations.
The officiating priests move around.
To the south, he places the *upabhṛt* ladle upon the *juhū*;
to the south of the *upabhṛt*, he places the *dhruvā*.
To the south, he places the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) and the parched grains (dhānāḥ); to the south of the grains, he places the stirred drink (mantha).
The Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Āgnīdhra walk around to the south;
the Brahmā and the Sacrificer [walk] to the north.
The *juhū* ladle and the six-pot-sherd offering are placed together;
according to some, the Brahman and the sacrificer [are also placed together].
Having taken portions from all the oblations, he sacrifices to each deity one by one.

Having spread a base of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle, he takes a portion from the *puroḍāśa* cake and adds to it some roasted grains (*dhānās*), and then some from the stirred drink (*mantha*).
He pours clarified butter over it twice if the portion consists of four cuttings, and thrice if it consists of five cuttings.

He issues the call: "Recite for Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs, Svadhā! He recites two invitatory verses (*puronuvākyā*), and there should be one offering verse (*yājyā*) each, both accompanied by the *praṇava*.
When the command "Open the enclosing sticks" (*paridhīn aporṇu*) is uttered, he joins the southern, the northern, and the middle enclosing sticks together.
Having stepped across toward the north, he causes the announcement to be made with "Svadhā! (*ā svadhā*).

"Let there be *svadhā*," he responds; "Soma accompanied by the ancestors, *svadhā*! he issues the direction; "Those who [deserve] the *svadhā*," he utters as the *āgūr*; "Svadhā! Homage! he utters as the *vaṣaṭ*.
He proceeds with the two subsequent [oblations] according to this same ritual procedure.

Having stepped across to the south and spread an underlayer of ghee in the *juhū* ladle, he takes a portion of the parched grains (*dhānā*) and adds a portion from the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Then, having stepped across to the north, he gives the command: "Recite the *anuvāda* for the *mantha* for the Pitṛs seated on the *barhis*: 'Svadhā! He causes the announcement to be made with "Svadhā! and the response is given with "Let there be *svadhā*! He gives the command: "For the Pitṛs seated on the *barhis*, *svadhā*! The *āgūḥ* formula is "Those who [desire] *svadhā*... He utters the *vaṣaṭ* as "Svadhā! Homage! Having stepped across to the south and spread an underlayer of ghee in the *juhū*, he takes a portion from the *mantha* and [from the cake]...

He takes a portion from the cake; then, having announced, "For the fathers, Agniṣvātta-s, *anusvadha*," he steps across to the north and causes the announcement to be made with "Let there be *āśrāvaṇa*"; the response is "Let there be *svadhā*. He issues the command, "To the fathers, Agniṣvātta-s, *svadhā*! The *āgūr* formula is "Those who [enjoy] the *svadhā*... He utters the *vaṣaṭ* as "*svadhā namaḥ*. By this same procedure, he sacrifices to Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt. Having stepped across to the south, having spread an underlayer of ghee in the *juhū* ladle, and having taken a cutting from the cake...

He takes up portions of the parched grains; then, for the Mantha, he issues the direction: "To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, *anusvadha*! Having stepped across toward the north, he causes the announcement to be made with "*āsvadha*"; the response is "*astu svadha*. He issues the direction: "To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, *svadha*! The *āgūr* formula is "Those who [deserve] *svadhā*, ah! He utters the *vaṣaṭ* call as "*svadhā namaḥ*. || 13 ||
Some prescribe the *mantha* as the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering;
one does not cut off the *prāśitra*,
and in this very same manner one cuts off the *iḍā*.
Some teachers say that one cuts off the *iḍā* from the stirred drink (*mantha*) and cuts off the *iḍā* from the stirred drink;
having set aside a portion of the stirred drink for the purpose of smelling it,
and having mixed the remnants of the oblation into the *iḍā*.
With the words "This is for thee, father," he places three balls upon three corners—
on the eastern, the southern, and the western corners.
He wipes the residue on the northern corner.
Having said, "O fathers, enjoy [the offerings] according to your respective portions," they go out toward the north.
Then they approach the Āhavanīya fire. They worship the Āhavanīya with the verse: "We [worship] you, who are beautiful to behold."
They remain standing [in worship].
With the words, "They have eaten, they have rejoiced," they pay homage to the Gārhapatya fire.
They proceed with the words, "The fathers have eaten, the fathers have rejoiced."
The Hotṛ smells the stirred drink (mantha).
Then the Adhvaryu, then the Brahman, then the Āgnīdhra, and then the sacrificer.
According to some, having smelled the stirred drink, the Hotṛ pours it out within the altar (antarvedi).
Taking a water-pot, he goes around three times clockwise, sprinkling while reciting, "Arising, generating heroic deeds...
Having set down the pot, he goes back around three times without sprinkling.

At this point, they prescribe the application of collyrium and ointment, the gift of a garment, the salutations, the *anutthāpanīyā*, the *pravāhaṇī*, the *saṃsādhanī*, the *manasvatī*, and the *paṅkti* and *prājāpatyā* verses.
Just as in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña:
they cover the enclosure and they spread out the enclosing sticks.

Having loosened their *prācīnāvītas* and put on their *yajñopavītas*, they transpose the clarified butter and the sacrificial oblations. Moving around, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) perform two after-offerings (*anūyāja*) without the *barhis* grass. He issues the call for the first after-offering, "Sacrifice to the two gods! Sacrifice!", and for the second, "Sacrifice! At the *sūktavāka*, the Hotṛ puts on the *nivīta*. They do not perform the sacrifices for the wives, nor do they offer the *samiṣṭayajus*;
everything else is performed as usual.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the fifth book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
5.5 Now, the fifth chapter in the fifth book.
He prepares *raudra* cakes on single potsherds for Tryambaka,
one for each male member of the sacrificer’s household, plus one additional cake for all the female members, including the wives.
They are treated silently.
They are cooked on the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire. Having sprinkled them with clarified butter, or without sprinkling them.

Having removed [the fire] from the bags, or from two bags, or from among the living beings, or from the covering of a chest, they carry a single burning coal from the *dakṣiṇāgni* smoke-smelling toward the west; having brought it across the rear of the *gārhapatya*, they carry it in front.
With the words, "As many as we are who belong to the household," he pays homage to the *gārhapatya*; they go to the intermediate space between the north and the east.

Saying, "The mouse is your animal, O Rudra," he leads [the victim] along the path; then, having thrown one cake (*puroḍāśa*) onto a molehill, and having kindled a firebrand at a crossroads and strewn grass around it, he takes portions from all the cakes with either the middle leaf of a *palāśa* branch or the last one, sprinkles them with clarified butter, and offers them with the formula: "This is your portion, O Rudra."
They stand in worship with the two verses beginning, "The medicine for the cows."
Having taken up the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) for each person, they circumambulate the crossroads three times to the right, reciting: "We worship Tryambaka.
Having thrown them upward, saying, "O blessed ones, you belong to Bhaga; may I obtain a share of Bhaga," they take them back, walk around, and pour them together for the sacrificer.

If the sacrificer’s daughter should desire a husband, she should walk around [the fire] and mutter: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, who finds a husband; like a cucumber from its stem, may I be released from death, not from [my] life. Having walked around, she mutters. 15.
During the first two circumambulations, they pour [the grains] together for the sacrificer; during the last one, for a woman desiring a husband.
If such a woman is not present, they do so for the sacrificer in all cases.
Having tied them in a bag and gone beyond the distance of a *gavyūti*, he hangs them upon a tree.
"This is your portion, O Rudra; accept it. With that favor, go beyond the Mūjavat mountains, with your bow unstrung, the Pināka in hand, and clad in a skin"—thus they descend three times.
Having sprinkled water around, they return without looking back.
They perform the purificatory rite (mārjana) outside the cow-pen.

With the words, "Fuel art thou; may we prosper," he places fuel-sticks upon the Āhavanīya fire. With the words, "I have moved along the waters," they perform the ritual worship (upasthāna). In the same manner, the wife, having placed fuel on the Gārhapatya fire, performs the worship.
Having returned, he offers a sacrificial pap of rice cooked in ghee to Āditya.
On the following day, having performed the Full Moon sacrifice, whether they have moved their sacrificial fires or not, they moisten [the hair] with the formula: "Impelled by the god Savitṛ...

[and] "He who upon the skin of this earth causes the plants to grow—Agni, ruling by his might, Varuṇa with his thoughts, Indra with his friends the Maruts, and Agni with his sharp flame. The turning back and the shaving are as described previously. 16.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fifth book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
5.6 Now, the sixth chapter in the fifth book:

Then, on the second day, third day, fourth day, half-month, month, or season, or after four months, he performs the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice. Its ritual procedure is explained by that of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. Having offered the five *saṃcara* oblations, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni; a pap for the Viśve Devas; a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra Śunāsīra; milk for Vāyu; a cake on one potsherd for Sūrya; barley-gruel for Vāyu; and curdled milk for Indra Śunāsīra; and a cake for Indra Śunāsīra.

Some prescribe a cake on twelve potsherds as the final offering. In the benedictions of the *sūktavāka*, the Hotṛ recites, "He invokes well-being for the year-long [cattle]; he invokes the divine abode," or alternatively, "He invokes well-being for the annual [cattle]."

In the dark fortnight, having performed the *Samasya* sacrifice at its proper time, and having offered the *Paurṇamāsa* sacrifice, they either depart from the sacrificial ground (*udavasāya*) or do not depart (*anudavasāya*). When the cows have calved, they moisten them with water while reciting: "By the god Savitṛ... "One month Parameṣṭhin released for the sake of creatures; thereby he brought great fortune to them, bringing immortality to mortals. You are born after the offspring; that indeed is your immortal [portion], by which months, half-months, seasons, and years [are formed]. By that which you caused to turn back for me, O Prajāpati, as I sacrificed—by that sacred formula (*brahman*), I cause it to turn back for the sake of life, O Agni."
With the verse "stigmena śociṣā," there is the turning back and the shaving, as previously described. ||17||
The Cāturmāsya sacrifices are concluded;
the Phālgunī full moon shall not arrive while he has not yet performed the Soma sacrifice.
In the absence of Soma, [he should sacrifice] with an animal.
In the absence of cattle, however, there is a repetition of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva at whatever time in spring the milk is most abundant.
One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva until he obtains a thousand cattle.
When the thousand [cows] have been obtained, he sacrifices with the others in their own places.

One desiring a village, desiring offspring, desiring cattle, desiring rain, or desiring food, should sacrifice with the Śunāsīrīya [offering]. Having settled near "rainy" water—that is, having gone to a place where there is water that occurs in the rainy season—and performing his water-related needs from that very water, he sacrifices. From that very water, he fulfills his requirement for water.

We shall explain the five-year cycle. Having performed the Pañcahotṛ, Vaiśvānara, and Pārjanya sacrifices on the full moon of Phālguna, one should sacrifice for two seasons and two years, but not perform the sacrifice during the third month. However, having performed them on the full moon of Caitra, one should sacrifice for three seasons and three years, but likewise not perform the sacrifice during the fourth month.
Thus prescribed, one should repeat [the cycle] for at least two or three [years]; indeed, one should repeat it. 18.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the fifth book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
Thus ends the fifth book in the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. 5.

[Paṭala 2, Section 550] This is accompanied by the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva. [Page 447] Only those [procedures] belonging to the primary context [apply]; thus, for all [the deities], the *ādhvaryava* (duties of the Adhvaryu) is indeed based on direct instruction (*upadeśika*). However, the mantras for the *upākaraṇa* (dedication) and so forth are extended (*atidiṣṭa*) from the *nirūḍha-paśubandha*. Likewise, the specific *praiṣas* (directions) are also [extended] from that same source; furthermore, the absence of the Maitrāvaruṇa’s *praiṣas* in the offerings to Indra and Sarasvatī is known only from another scripture (*śāstrāntara*). Similarly, it has been stated that the restriction regarding specific *praiṣas* and the restriction regarding the use of the *paridhis* made of *mayu* (wild goat) skin—instead of the usual *vidhṛti* and *prastara*—are also due solely to the authority of another scripture.

Therefore, among the five animal sacrifices, those beginning with the Agniṣomīya are established as the archetypes (*prakṛti*) for those included within the *tantra* of the Soma sacrifice; however, for those outside the *tantra* of the Soma sacrifice, the Nirūḍha-Aindrāgna alone is the archetype. All five animals possess direct ritual characteristics (*pratyakṣadharma*); they are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the Nirūḍha in respect to the *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ priest), while the others are modifications in respect to the *ādhvaryava* (the duties of the Adhvaryu) and the specific *hautra* extended by injunction.

Although the same [application] would have followed from other treatises (*śāstrāntara*), it has been established—both in the case of the offering to Indra (*aindra*) and that of Sarasvatī (*sārasvatī*)—solely by way of precluding the function of the Maitrāvaruṇa priest; thus, enough of this digression. As for Jaimini, having raised the objection regarding the five animals being the archetype (*prakṛti*), he refuted it through reasoning (*nyāya*). In our commentary on the reasoning indicated by the instruction of our own branch (*śākhā*), we have demonstrated the intended meaning of the Sūtra; therefore, this very method is to be understood in our Sūtra. Some assert an option (*vikalpa*) between reasoning and scriptural instruction (*nyāyopadeśa*), but that is not so.

"How can reasoning (*nyāya*), which is inference (*anumāna*), be equal to Śruti? Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fourth [book], the section on Animal Sacrifices (*paśubandha*), in the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha composed by Mahādeva. Thus ends the fourth book in the commentary on the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
5.1 Now begins the first chapter of the fifth book.

Although the Cāturmāsya sacrifices are indeed recited in the context of the Rājasūya, for their mention is found even among the obligatory (nitya) rites—such as in the passage "the New and Full Moon sacrifices and the Cāturmāsyas"—and they are also mentioned in the Smṛti, beginning with "one should perform the Cāturmāsyas. Therefore, the meaning is that since those [sacrifices] recited in the Rājasūya possess an obligatory fruit here as well, they are also obligatory.
"Indeed, the merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is inexhaustible."

"He performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. Because his well-performed merit has inexhaustible fruit, the two words *akṣamya* and *ha* are indeed read as they appear in the Śruti. The word *ha* means "well-known," and the word *vai* means "indeed" (*hi*). Therefore, the meaning is that one must necessarily sacrifice with the Cāturmāsya rites. Nor should it be argued that the result is merely imagined from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because in this context, their repeated performance (*abhyāsa*) will be enjoined; and there is no such repeated performance in the case of optional (*kāmya*) rites.

This is the application for the obligatory rites alone, since the performance of the optional rites will be explained by the author himself later on. The term "cāturmāsyāni" (the four-monthly sacrifices) is the name for the collection of sacrifices—consisting of four sets of four sacrifices each—when combined with the Gṛhamedhīya, Traiyambaka, Paricaryā, and two Dārvihomas, because they are enjoined by the verb *yajati* (he sacrifices). The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is: "I shall sacrifice with the Cāturmāsya rites; may I gratify Yajñanārāyaṇa through them. This concludes the introductory explanation for the Ārambhaṇīyā rite. — 448. Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Fifth Book.

Sacrificing those [animals] on the full moon day of Phālguna or Caitra, on the Upavasatha day of the preceding Parvan, having mentally recited the Pañcahotṛ formula and offered it along with the Grahas, he performs the Anvārambhaṇīyā sacrifice, offering a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara and a pap for Pārjanya.

The plural form “tāni” (those) refers to [the offerings] being performed on various festival days (*parvan*). [The phrase] “one who is sacrificing on the full moon of Phālguna or on the full moon of Chaitra” connects with the words “of the preceding festival day. The mention of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) is for the purpose of excluding the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), and for the purpose of establishing the identity of the ritual procedure (*samānavidhi*) by stating “having offered, he pours out [the oblation]” (*hutvā nirvapati*). Vaiśvānara, characterized by the quality of fire (*agni-guṇaka*), is to be understood [as the deity], because of the specific designation in the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses.

Therefore, [he offers] the *gharma* dedicated to Parjanya with the formula beginning "acceptable to Agni Vaiśvānara," and so forth. Because it is performed near the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and because its duration is that of a single day (*sadyaskāla*), the *tantra* of the Full Moon sacrifice is followed, and there is a separate carrying forward of the fires for each. The rest is clear. Gold is given as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the Vaiśvānara offering, and a cow for the Parjanya offering; this is also stated by the rule regarding the Bharageśī. Having made the formal resolve, "I shall sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva," he performs the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice on ground sloping toward the east.

The requirement for the ground to slope toward the east is restricted even though slopes toward the north, toward both the north and the east, or level ground are also possible. In such a location, the *āmikṣā* dedicated to the Viśvedevas is primary because its procedure was initiated first by the fetching of the branch; thus, "Vaiśvadeva" is the name of the entire collection of rites characterized by that [offering].

Because the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) of the Saumya and the Dyāvāpṛthivya offerings is identical and thus non-differentiating, it does not serve as a factor for establishing a common ritual procedure (*tantra*); therefore, the primary [designation] alone is stronger. As for the Brāhmaṇa passage, "That which the Viśvedevas sacrificed together—that is the Vaiśvadeva-nature of the Vaiśvadeva," this is an etymological derivation (*nirvacana*). Since the name of the collective group is primary, the common procedure belongs specifically to the Āmāvāsya. It has already been stated that this is because the *āmikṣā* is a modification of milk (*payovikāra*).
[The performance may be] either after departing from the sacrificial ground (*udavasāya*) or without departing (*anudavasāya*).

Having gone elsewhere from the dwellings, or having prepared the slope toward the east in those very places, one should proceed. However, the *Anvārambhaṇīyā* [introductory offering] takes place in the original sacrificial enclosure (*vihāra*) alone. The slope toward the east is for the sake of the *Vaiśvadeva* [offering] specifically, because it is prescribed in that very manner.
Having carried forward the fire according to the procedure for the fire (*agny-āvṛt*).

When the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) of another fire is required, the possession of its specific ritual properties (*dharmavat-tva*) is enjoined therein. This means that when the carrying forward of the fire for the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) has been performed according to the established procedure (*āvṛt*), the properties of that carrying forward are applied by rule to the subsequent carrying forward. This is because Vaikhānasa and Āpastamba state: "The carrying forward of the fire from the *gārhapatya* is like that of the animal sacrifice," and also: "There is no offering of the lifted oblation (*udyata-homa*). In this case, the distinction is as follows: the carrying forward of the fires takes place at the *gārhapatya*, and so forth.
The oblation [performed] with the mantra "yatte pāvaka" is not the first one, because it would contradict the indicative mark (liṅga) in the phrase "that which was before has become after.
Having placed a tuft of wool (*ūrṇāstukā*) in the fire-pit (*agnyāyatana*) and having established the fire there...

The phrase "having established [the fire] according to the procedure for Agni" is supplied as a supplement. Vaikhānasa has stated: "In the same way, having established it on the Āyavana hearth. Regarding the statement "he scatters the earth up to the Uttaravedi," the opponent argued that since the origin of the sacrifice is prohibited, everything else would be prohibited. However, because of the specific prohibition regarding the Uttaravedi, those elements such as the *śikya*-cord and others intended for its consecration—namely the *gulgulu*, *sugandhitejana*, and *pautudrava* wood—are excluded. By explicit scriptural injunction (*vacana*), the tuft of wool (*ūrṇāstukā*) is prescribed. In this case, there is no ritual depositing (*samāropa*) of the fire, as there is during a journey.

According to the statement of Kātyāyana, there may be a formal installation (*samāropa*) even when going to another place or to one's own house; for he has stated that they should churn [the fire] by means of that [installation], because of the restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyāna*). It was previously stated that "falling into another" (*anyapatana*) and so forth [is the case]. In the very original (*prākṛta*) location, the establishment with a mantra is performed because it is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the ritual fire (*prayogāgni*); everything else from this point forward, which consists of the consecration of the fire accompanied by mantras, must be performed. This is stated by Māradvāja: "Everything else is performed except for the scattering of earth upon the *uttaravedi*."

For this very reason, it is not stated that "it is like the animal sacrifice" (*paśubandhavat*), because there is an absence of the previously mentioned reasoning. Regarding the *praṇayana* (carrying forward of the fire), the mention of the "repetition" (*anāvṛtti*) is intended to express the lack of repetition for the establishment (*pratiṣṭhāpana*) and so forth. Even though it is stainless (*amala*), the eastern slope (*prācīnapravaṇatā*) must be performed as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice; however, even in the case of the fire to be maintained perpetually (*nityadhārya*), once the eastern slope has been prepared at the site (*āyatana*), the fire is simply placed there silently (*sūṣṇīm*), and nothing further follows. Having added fuel to the fires (*agnīnanvādhāya*), he separates the calves for the sake of the evening milking dedicated to the Viśvedevas (*vaiśvadevī sāyaṃdoha*).

This is a restatement of what has already been established for the purpose of explaining the form of the *māmāvāsyatantra*. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the *āmikṣā*," although the milking of the *māyā* cow is not itself the primary oblation (*havis*), but rather serves to prepare it, nevertheless, it has been stated that the ritual rules (*dharmas*) pertaining to milking do indeed apply there. This is intended to exclude the option of using ordinary curds (*dadhi*) and the option of silent evening milking mentioned by Baudhāyana.

And since "Viśvedevāḥ" is derived from the sense that "all those gods are her deities," it is a *taddhita* formation; thus, when it is a *karmadhāraya* compound, the suffix is applied [to the whole], and not from two separate words. This is the grammatical conclusion, and it is logical that one drives away the calves for the sake of the Viśvedevas. As for what was said—that one drives away the calves according to the injunctions for fetching branches and so forth—the meaning is that there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses;
this statement regarding the fuel (*indhma*) is for the purpose of increasing the quantity of wood.

Having bound together three bundles of *barhis* grass that have flowers—meaning those possessed of blossoms, or according to some, those that have grown back after being cut—he binds them once again into a single unit. Regarding "three bundles": there should likewise be only three *nidhana*s. Or, he binds each individual *nidhana* separately at first and then binds them all together as one.
The same applies to the fuel (*idhma*).

Some also extend the term *prasūna* [to this case]. He cites the measure of the aforementioned *prasūna*-tree: "twenty-threefold" is the modification (*ūha*). He clarifies what was stated previously: "the potsherds (*kapāla*)... [The meaning is: the ritual rules (*dharma*), such as the mantras and so forth, which are the constituent parts (*aṅga*), apply only to the re-fastening (*punaḥ-saṃnahanam*).

At the time of arranging the vessels, he sets out the vessels according to their purpose: the *juhū*, two *upabhṛt*s, a second *pṛṣadājya* vessel, the *dhruvā*, two *ājyasthālī*s, a second *dadhi* vessel, a *pālāśa* vessel for the *vājina*, a *sruk*, and a *camasa*.

Having performed the rites ending with the evening milking according to the procedure for the evening milking, [he recites] "For the rite of tomorrow... and so forth. Then, when the time for the setting out of the vessels has arrived—this is the meaning—the cleansing of the *camasa* ladles and the *stotra* cups is done silently. This is because of the use of the word *juhū* and because the *vaiśvadeva* offering is prescribed only for the full moon day. Thus, the preliminary rites such as the *anvādhāna* on the previous day have been explained.

That very point was stated by Āpastamba and Vaikhānasa: "He causes the evening milk to be milked as for the *sāṃnāyya*, and [the procedure] beginning with 'on the following day' and so forth. The rest is clear. Regarding the evening *agnihotra*, they add barley-grains; that remnant is for the purpose of curdling (*ātañcana*), and such details will be explained in the section on the sacrificer's duties (*yājamāna*) under the *sāṃnāyya*.

At the time of the pouring out (*nirvapaṇa*), he offers these five *saṃcara* oblations: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Sarasvatī, and a pap for Pūṣan.

These oblations, which move across the Varuṇapraghāsa, Sākamedha, and Śunāsīrīya festivals, proceed as they are prescribed by the extension of the injunction (*vākyātideśa*), and thus they possess this very procedure (*itikartavyatā*). For it is heard in the *Brāhmaṇa*: "There are five oblations.

At the subsequent festivals, there is an offering on seven potsherds for the Maruts, a curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) for the Viśvedevas, and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth; some authorities prescribe an eight-potsherd offering for Savitṛ at these later festivals.

The phrase "he should offer curdled milk" (*āmikṣāṃ nirvapet*) is also connected [to the previous injunction], because of the statement "he should offer the *payasyā*. If it is argued that there is no actual act of offering (*nirvāpa*), that is true; however, just as elsewhere the term "offering" (*nirvapati*) is understood to mean a sacrifice, here the meaning is that "he performs the sacrifice of *āmikṣā*. In this same way, the phrases "the sacrifice to Agni" (*āgneyayāgam*) and so forth should also be understood. At the end of all the oblations, such as the *sāvitra* and the *varuṇapraghāsa*, once the grains have been husked three times, he sets aside the portion for Pūṣan using the division-mantra and grinds it together with the portions intended for the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*).

The procedure for the offering to Pūṣan (pauṣṇa) has been shown here according to another recension (śākhāntara). That was previously mentioned for the purpose of making its nature as a *caru* known; however, since it is now being presented as it stands in the Śruti text, it is not a redundant repetition.
He causes the morning milk (*prātardoha*) to be milked according to the procedure for the morning milk. When the morning milk is heated, he pours the evening milk into it and prepares the *āmikṣā*.
[End of] the commentary on the explanation of the ritual procedure. [End of] the first section (*paṭala*). [This concludes] the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva. 451.

Having drawn the curdled milk (āmikṣā) from one vessel into another, having sprinkled it with whey (vājina), and having set it down in a known place, he places the remainder of the whey on the rubbish-heap (utkara). || 1 ||

Having placed the potsherds ending with those for the Maruts, he milks the cows in the morning according to the procedure for the morning milking, beginning with the driving away of the calves. When that morning milk has been heated, he pours into it the evening milk prepared as curd. By that act, he prepares the *āmikṣā*. Having drawn out the thickened, solidified portion into another vessel—that which is thickened is the *āmikṣā*—it is said to be "the whey together with the barley. This has been stated likewise by Āpastamba, Vaikhānasa, Bhāradvāja, and others.

Having taken that [curd] from the pot into another vessel, one pours the whey (*vājina*) into yet another; thus, by implication, the Vaikhānasa school holds that the whey is placed in a different vessel. Bhāradvāja and Āpastamba maintain that it is done in two vessels. Having moistened the *āmikṣā* with a portion of the whey and set it aside in a known place, he also places a portion of the whey on the rubbish heap (*utkara*). Regarding this very point, Bhāradvāja has stated the procedure for taking out and pouring down [the whey]. Having done so, he lays down the single-pot-sherd cake (*ekakapāla*); or rather, because of the scriptural injunction that "he places the remainder of the whey on the rubbish heap."

At the very time of removal (udvāsana), one should prepare this curd-mixture (āmikṣā) and place the cake on a single potsherd (ekakapāla); then, at the time of removal, [the mixture is placed] in another vessel, and so forth. This is because Āpastamba and Vaikhānasa have stated it in that very manner. There is no fault in this, for while the sequence of subsidiary elements (aṅga) has been stated following the order of the Vedic recitation (śruti-pāṭha), the actual order of performance is to be understood through functional capacity (sāmarthya). Furthermore, elsewhere it is observed that even the tying of the animal to the sacrificial post (yūpa) is prescribed at the very time of making the wooden ring (caṣāla). Having separated the portion for Pūṣan from the mixed flour by means of the division-mantra (vibhāga-mantra), he cooks it according to the procedure for a rice-oblation (caru).
The explanation has already been provided. Since the *madantī* waters have already served their purpose, other water must be taken for the sake of cooking.
Having performed the second tracing (*parigrāha*), he proceeds with the call, "Bring the clarified butter and the curds," and he concludes the ritual procedure at the end of that call.
Regarding the animal sacrifice, the explanation has already been provided. It has been stated here that the characteristics of the altar (*vedi*) apply to the *utkara*.

On the Phālgunī day, one takes the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) just as in the case of the animal sacrifice. Although it should have been stated simply as "as in the animal sacrifice," the use of the elaborate expression "just as in the animal sacrifice" indicates that what is prescribed by the direct scriptural statement (śruti) for the animal sacrifice is likewise prescribed for the Phālgunī sacrifice; thus, there is no extended application (atideśa). However, on the Caitrī day, having spread the clarified butter twice and having taken the curds twice, one sprinkles it once with the clarified butter.

In that context, the mixed [offering] was described as "consisting of five portions," whereas here, by the statement beginning with "having spread twice with ghee" (*dvirājyenopastīrya*), it is indicated that curd alone is the sacrificial material (*havis*) and that the ghee serves only for the purpose of spreading and sprinkling (*upastaraṇābhighāraṇa*). However, this contradicts what was stated previously, because the Vedic scripture stating "he sacrifices the after-offerings (*anūyāja*) with speckled ghee" (*pṛṣadājyena anūyājān yajati*) is without distinction, and because the after-offerings are explicitly designated as being performed with curd. Therefore, the terms "spreading" and "sprinkling" must be explained [otherwise]. In the word *ājyasya*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*).

Therefore, the meaning of the phrase "having spread the clarified butter" (*tenā'jyamupastīrya*) is as follows: the clarified butter in the vessel for speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) serves as the base-spread (*upastaraṇa*), and it is not a purificatory agent because it is itself the object to be purified; thus, it takes on the status of a substrate (*adhikaraṇa*) by virtue of the injunction "the morning milk [is poured] into the heated [butter]. In this way, the clarified butter that has been spread is [further processed] by the double taking of curds.

Having prepared [the offering], there is a single consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the clarified butter (*ājya*) which has been consecrated by the sprinkling (*abhidhāraṇa*) designated as the third [in the sequence]. Having kept this in mind, the Śruti itself declares: "He makes an under-layer (*upastīrya*) of clarified butter" and likewise, "he sprinkles with clarified butter. Thereafter, he takes it up with five [verses].
He proceeds with the rites beginning from the removal from the fire (*udvāsana*).
Having removed the portion for the Maruts (*māruta*), he removes the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture).

Having removed the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) into another vessel, he pours over it abundant clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) and makes its back visible (*āviṣpṛṣṭham*). Just as when a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is filled with butter in a vessel at a time other than the first [offering], its back becomes manifest and clearly visible, so it is here. "At the time of the decoration," says Āpastamba.
He places the oblations (*havīṃṣi*) down with the *vyāhṛti* formulas, just as he does in the case of the year-long sacrifice.

Because it is associated with the *havīṃṣi* offerings, one should deposit the *vājina* silently on the *utkara* mound; likewise, when a year has passed, one should deposit the *havīṃṣi* at the Cāturmāsya sacrifices using only the *vyāhṛti* formulas. This is the rule concerning the Cāturmāsyas. One proceeds with the fire churned by friction (*nirmanthya*) according to the procedure for the *nirmanthya*. The meaning is already explained.
Having set down the Veda, he issues the call for the *sāmidhenī* verses.
This restatement of the sequence is for the sake of the subsequent injunction:
"He performs nine *prayāja* offerings; having poured together [the butter] at the fourth, he pours it all together at the eighth."

The ninth [section] concerning the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), which is a modification of the final [portion], has been explained. He offers the *samidh* verses; he sacrifices first to the first [deity] and then to the subsequent ones.
In all cases, he sacrifices to the deities of the *sāvitra* and the one-pot-sherd (*ekakapāla*) offerings in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
This applies both here and elsewhere wherever the word "iti" occurs. The rest is clear.
Having cut off the entire offering from the single-pan cake (*ekakapāla*), he pours it back into the receptacle (*āśaya*), places it straight and steady, and offers it without turning it over.

With the contents of the receptacle itself serving as the under-layer (*upastaraṇa*), having cut off the whole, and having poured clarified butter (*ājya*) over it, he places it with its surface straight toward the east; after the act of throwing it into the fire, he offers it so that it remains exactly as it was offered, without turning it over—that is, without making it face upward. He pours [butter] into the receptacle itself both before and after the offering.

If the offered cake should turn over, he should arrange it with the front of the *sruva* ladle after giving a choice (*vara*) to the officiant, or he may take it up again and offer it once more; according to some, however, not with the hand.

When the choice has been given to the Adhvaryu, he should make it level with the front of the *nuc* (the wooden ladle) or, having cut [the portion] with his hand, he should offer it again with the *nuc*, according to some; for others, however, this is not so because of the subsequent call for the announcement (*āśrāvaṇa*) and so forth. With the four names of the months—“Madhu and Mādhava”—he makes an offering over the one-pot-sherd cake, saying either “To Madhu, svāhā! To Mādhava, svāhā! or simply “To Madhava, svāhā! and “To Mādhava, svāhā! respectively.

At the end of the mantra, there is the utterance of *svāhā*. In other Vedic branches (*śākhā*), the mantras are indeed recited ending with *svāhā*. Regarding the statement, "They should undergo initiation on the full moon of Phālgunī, for this is the mouth of the year," and "They should undergo initiation on the full moon of Citrā, for this is the mouth of the year"—since the commencement of the year is observed in both cases, the names beginning with Māgha and so forth should be understood as starting from either Phālguna or Caitra.
He performs nine after-offerings (*anūyāja*) with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*). || 2 ||

The explanation regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) has already been provided. "To the gods" (*devānyaneti*) is the first [formula]. "Whither whither" (*yana yaneti*) is for the subsequent ones. He will state in the *Yājamāna* section that the three *prayāja*s are modifications (*vikāra*) of each one [of the original three]. Because the first, eighth, and ninth [original *prayāja*s] are archetypal (*prākṛta*), the second and following [formulas] are respectively the modifications of those three; two [formulas] belong to each one, and the deities are those associated with the *mātrāṇikya*. At the end of the deity-formulas, which number six, the Hotṛ should recite "By the sacrifice to the gods," etc., according to the modification of the archetype. In the blessings of the *Sūktavāka*, the Hotṛ follows with "He invokes the well-being of the year-long [sacrifice]" and "He invokes the divine abode."
"May he attain this divine, preeminent abode"—before this [formula], the Hotṛ continues with "may he attain the prosperity of a year," and thus makes "divine" the recurring element.
After the enclosing sticks have been cast into the fire, having offered the remnants of the oblations, he proceeds with the *vājina* (curd-mixture).

It has been stated that where there is the casting away of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), there the oblation is performed with the *saṃkhāva* formula; thus, [the text] says "pratevi" and so forth. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the *Vājasaneyibrāhmaṇa*, which states, "Having cast away the enclosing sticks, he offers the oblation. The meaning is that the *samidh* oblation does not involve the act of casting away. The meaning is that this is the time for the *vājina* sacrifice.
Having spread a base of clarified butter in the *vājina* vessel, he takes the *vājina* while pouring it out upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); having filled it, he does not pour *ājya* over it.

Having brought the *utkara* (heap of rubbish), he takes [the grain] from that vessel, pouring it out while scattering it outside, according to the *Deśaka*. According to Āpastamba, he does so "until the end. Thus, by the rule "he fills [the vessel] while the pouring-vessel remains within the altar," this is not merely a rule for the disposal of remnants; rather, he takes as much as is required to fill the vessel. At this point, the *pañcahotṛ* formula belongs to the sacrificer. He issues the directions: "Recite for the *vājins*," and "Sacrifice to the *vājins*," in due order.
Sitting with his knees raised, the Hotṛ performs the sacrifice without taking breath.

"With knees raised" means that he does not let his knees fall; the word "sitting" is stated so that there may not be straightness (rigidity) while standing. It should not be forgotten that it has been stated that the description of the duties of the Hotṛ everywhere is intended for the Yājuṣa-hotṛ, because they are recited in the *Āvayava-kāṇḍa*, and thus the explanation here is based on the Śruti. "He joins together" means that he does not make a pause between the *puronuvākyā* and the *yājyā*. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers with the ladle being poured out.

The *camasa* (cup) also serves as an indicator for the *sruva* (ladle). The Kaikhānasas state: "Pour out [the remnant] with the *camasa* or the *sruva*, saying 'O Hotṛ, pour it out'. [The formula is: "This for the *vājins*; through the sacrifice to the gods, the *vājins*, may I become possessed of power and victorious," or [simply] "victory," because it is a modification of the *vadhi*. However, at the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the *yājyā* do not take place; for there is the Śruti cited by Āpastamba: "Of three oblations, they do not cut portions for the *sviṣṭakṛt*: of Soma, of the *dharma*, and of the *vājina*. He performs the *anuyāja* with the formula: "O Agni, consume the *vājina*."
The ritual for the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) is exactly as before. "To Agni, this! "May I be among the Vājins, O God...
With the remainder of the *vājina*, he performs sacrifices toward the quarters, just as one does with the remainder of the *vasā-homa*.
It has been stated by the Teacher that this is not an extension (*atideśa*), as it is shown to be based on identical scriptural authority (*samāna-śruti*).
Having invited one another, they all consume the *vājina* while desiring an invitation from each other; "invite me" (*upahvayasva*) is the address, and "invited" (*upahūta*) is the response.

By means of these addresses and responses, desiring an invitation from one another and performing them, they consume the *vājina* after having invited—that is, having obtained permission—regarding the *vājina*. Baudhāyana and Āpastamba say "the remnant" (*śeṣam*). That is not desired here, because of the specific designation "the *vājina*"; it refers specifically to that which is in the *utkara*, with the word "mantra" being understood as the remainder. Āpastamba says [it is consumed] by means of the name of the ritual action itself.

Therefore, after the *hotṛ* has invoked with "Upahūta-sva" (Be invited), the addressing of the others—such as "O Brahman," "O Adhvaryu," "O Agnīdh," "O Neṣṭṛ," and so forth—is to be understood as being distinct from himself. This very sequence was also stated by Bhāradvāja. The response is simply "Upahūtaḥ" (I am invited); the meaning is "I am authorized."

"May the portion of the swift ones protect us; may the strength, the poured seed, the nectar, be for our power. May Indra bestow upon us that sensory vigor and wealth. May we not come to harm while consuming the swift one. "O swift one, of you who have been made into a portion by the swift ones, who are full of sweetness and invited, being invited myself, I consume.
Thus they consume, each with his own mantra. The sacrificer is either the first or the last.
The word "devours" (*bhakṣayati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Regarding the phrase "the first," the invitation (*upahava*) for the others begins with him.
On the following day, having performed the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsa*), they may either depart from the sacrificial ground (*udavasāya*) or not depart (*anudavasāya*).

Having sacrificed with the Full Moon rite on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), then—either elsewhere than their homes or in those very same places—the following [rites] should be performed.
"May the divine waters, impelled by the god Savitṛ, moisten [her] for long life and splendor"—with these words, he moistens her head.

From the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, it is understood that "they moisten" means they cause to become wet. Therefore, this is the form of the root *ud* with the prefix *abhi*, belonging to the *bhvādi* class, as in the expression *abhyunatti*. [End of section] Ja. Sa. Bha. Dha. [End of second paṭala]. [This concludes the work] accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

"Truth alone is the Supreme; nothing whatsoever transcends Truth. In Truth the ocean is placed; upon Truth this earth rests. Agni with his sharp flame has overcome the heat; the head is placed within the *uṣṇih* meter by means of austerity. By Truth I turn its [the hair] back; by Truth I turn it around; by austerity I follow after it; by the auspicious I turn it toward; by the helpful I turn it forward. With these words, he parts the hair using a three-pronged porcupine quill or a stalk of sugarcane.

That [needle] which has three white parts is a *śalalī*. A *śalalī* is a specific type of animal with which living beings are pierced by means of arrows released from its own body that are shaped like spikes (*śūla*) and provided with feathers; thus, even a part shaped like a spike is called a *śalalī*, such as the tip of a sugarcane leaf. Alternatively, by means of a rod (*śalākā*), he makes the hairs on the head well-arranged and humble—that is, lowly—by removing them.
He trims the hair with a metal razor made of *udumbara* wood.

He causes [the hair] to be turned back with the previously mentioned mantra characterized by the word "nivartana" (turning back), or silently; for it is seen that there is an option regarding the shaving—whether the turning back applies only to a few hairs at the front, or whether all [hair] is shaved. He causes it to be turned back with *lohita*, which is an iron product (*vikāra*) of black iron (*kāla-ayas*), namely with copper-joined red iron, according to the Śruti. The meaning of the Śruti is: "red" means copper, and "joined with that" refers to iron. That [mantra] belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). He shaves his beard, or he has all [his hair] shaved. || 3 ||
Thus ends the first paṭala in the fifth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. || 1 ||

In the two scriptural passages stating "he shaves" (*vapati*) and "he causes to shave" (*vāpayati*), no distinct meaning is restated; nor is a different meaning expressed by the *parasmaipada*, *ātmanepada*, or the causative suffix (*ṇic*). When the Adhvaryu is capable, he himself shaves; in his incapacity, the barber shaves. Thus ends the first section in the fifth book on the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, in the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* composed by Mahādeva. This concludes the Vaiśvadeva Parvan (5.2). Now begins the second section of the fifth book:
Then, after four months, on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha or Śrāvaṇa, he performs the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices.

The option is determined by the sequence of commencement and the established rule. When four months have passed, Varuṇa is the deity for the *āmikṣā* in the northern sacrificial area (*vihāra*), and the Maruts are the deities in the southern one; they are designated by the term *praghāsa* because they possess excellent fodder (*pra-kṛṣṭa ghasa*) due to their partaking in the *karambha* (flour-offering), as indicated by the mantra-marking (*mantra-liṅga*) "We invoke the *praghāsya*s. By these two deities, the entire collection of rites performed in both sacrificial areas is indicated; that alone should be understood as the name [of the sacrifice]. [From the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Fifth Book]
For these [rites], the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) has been explained by the [procedure] of the *vaiśvadeva*.

Just as in the *vaiśvadeva* there is the rule beginning with the kindling of the fires (*anvādhāna*), so too here, up to the evening milking (*sāyaṃdoha*), it is explained by the extension (*atideśa) from the *vaiśvadeva* rite—that "there are five oblations, including the *etavāma*. This means that whatever procedure belongs to the *vaiśvadeva* rite is extended to these rites characterized as the *varuṇapraghāsas*. Regarding those rites, previously only the collective whole was to be mentioned; this is one view.

The seven constituent parts (*samudāyin*) whose members are raised up by the act of cooking are indicated by the deity-pot as having a plural ending; hence the plural number. [The formulas] *udāsāya*, *apānudat*, and *avasāya* are according to the preceding rule regarding the syllables.

There are two Āhavanīya fires; the insertion (*āvāpa*) is performed in both places. The entire ritual procedure (*tantra*) is carried out in the northern sacrificial area (*vihāra*), and likewise in the southern one.

Since the Āhavanīya fire is established by the single act of *ādhāna* (consecration), its duality is stated here because it exists in two locations. The *praṇayana* (carrying forward) consists of dividing and establishing it at those two places. There would be no *uttaravedi* (high altar) nor its purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). It should not be said that there are nine Āhavanīyas; for the primacy of both is understood from a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*). At the time of *praṇayana*, the word "he carries forward" is the understood supplement. However, in the case of carrying it forward from the [original] Āhavanīya, these two future Āhavanīyas are indeed primary by virtue of their designations.

In this context, the demonstration is for the purpose of making known that [the northern] sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) is the cause for performing the two-fold ritual action. "With the insertion in both" means: in that rite where there is the insertion (*āvāpa*) of the two Āhavanīya fires, such a complete sacrifice (*kṛtsna-sāman*) is performed; the meaning is that one performs the ritual procedure (*tantra*) in the northern *vihāra*. There are two types of *vihāras*: the *pretānya-āyatana* (the site of the deceased) and the *śālā-vihāra* (the hall-site). Neither of these two exists in its entirety here.

Therefore, relying on the primary Gārhapatya fire, two sacrificial enclosures (*vihāra*) must be described by means of the northern and southern halves of that single enclosure; for when the Gārhapatya is not divided, it does not appear as a single [separate] northern one. Why? Because it would be impossible to know which is "northern," because there is no specification of a location for the southern enclosure either, and because they would fall into mutual confusion. Therefore, the two enclosures are the two paths of the enclosure; the same applies here to the phrase "in the southern enclosure. That which is the principal...

Since both [the fire] and that place—that *karka*—are being performed as two primary elements, there is a distinction between the fires, the places, and the agents; thus, the meaning is that the fires must be established in both locations. While it could have been stated simply that "in both cases, the steps are taken southward and northward," the specific designation "thus southward" is made to indicate that where success is achieved through a single common procedure (*tantra*) such as the *praiṣa* (direction) performed by the Ārya alone, let there not be [such a procedure] in both cases; therefore, similarity is extended [to the other case]. The Adhvaryu performs those rites connected with the Gārhapatya fire.

The word "rites" (*karmāṇi*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Since both *āhavanīya* fires are one and the same, even though there is a difference in the agents (the *adhvaryu* and the *patnīsaṃyāja*), the meaning is that they belong to both. According to the principle that "that which is for another's sake is performed by one," and because it will be stated later that these are common (*sādhāraṇa*), it follows that the *anvādhāna* and *paristaraṇa* should be performed only once, since they pertain primarily to the *adhvaryu*. If it is argued that the rule should simply be "the *adhvaryu* [performs] at the *gārhapatya* fire," with the term "therein" (*tatra*) being supplied from the context, we say no. This is because of the purpose of the commencement of this specific *sūtra*, which establishes the *patnīsaṃyājās* and the *saṃpatnīyahoma*. If that were the case, the rule would simply be "the *adhvaryu* [performs] at the *gārhapatya*"; thus, the term "therein" (*tatram*) must be understood as continuing from the previous context. However, this is not so.

One might think that everything, including the placing of the skull-cup (*kapāla*) as a support and so forth, should be obtained [by the Adhvaryu]; let that not be the case. If it is asked, "In that case, since the *Patnīsaṃyājas* and the *Saṃpatnīya* [are already included] in this way, why is there such an emphasis on knowledge?"—it is replied: By the statement regarding "those connected" (*saṃyukta*), even though those [rites] are connected, Jaimini holds that because the explicit scriptural statement (*vacana*) is stronger despite any conflict with logic (*nyāya*), the Adhvaryu alone should perform the *Patnīsaṃyājas* and others. Thus ends the sixth section, accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.
