It has been stated by the Vājasaneyins that the Adhvaryu alone should respond to the call "O Pratiprasthātṛ, come! and attend to the wives with the *saṃyāna* formula. By the inclusion of the term "wives" (*patnī*), the *saṃpatnīya* offering is also included. Bharadvāja also states: "The Adhvaryu alone attends to the wives. However, Āpastamba, relying on the principle of logical reasoning, has stated:
"The *patnīsaṃyāja* belongs to both [the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ]," referring to those rites which are common to both.

Those [acts] which are common, uniform, and related to common ritual objects belong to the *adhvaryu* alone. These have been enumerated by Kātyāyana: the *praṇītā* water, the girding of the wife (*patnīsaṃnahana*), the churning of the fire (*agnimanthana*), the *āśruta* and *pratyāśruta*, the sixfold recitation (*ṣaḍvācana*), the choosing of the seat for the *hotṛ* (*hotṛpadanavaraṇa*), the *prāśitra* portion, the *aṅgulipañji*, the intermediate *iḍā* portion (*avāntareḍābhāga*), and the final bath (*avabhṛtha*). Regarding these, it has been explained by the learned that the churning of the fire, the fire-offering (*agnihotra*), and the final bath are performed according to specific injunctions, while the others are performed because they are possible [to do so]. The *hautra* (the duties of the *hotṛ*) is a common subsidiary; the *adhvaryu* gives the directions (*saṃpreṣya*) for it.

The additional [rite] is created because it is to be grasped as something distinct; other [elements] are common to both you and the *Hautramaya*. The assistance regarding the meaning of the words is the *tantra* (the common procedure). The ritual act of the *hotṛ* priest is the *tantra*, because it manifests only once. The word "limbs" (*aṅga*) is used for the purpose of excluding the primary *hautra* (the main priestly function), since the *tantra* is impossible there due to the difference between the *yājyā* and other [verses]. Only the *adhvaryu* gives the summons (*saṃpraishya*), not the *pratiprasthātṛ*. The *pratiprasthātṛ* also [performs] the primary [act].

For that one [offering] whose consecration is performed by means of the *preṣa* (command), its result is likewise one; therefore, since that single act has been accomplished, there is no dependence upon what has been done by another. It was stated that the *ājyabhāga* is mentioned for the purpose of establishing the primary *āmikṣā*; in that regard, the *puronuvākyā* and *yājyā* verses, which separately manifest the deities, belong to the *pratiprasthātṛ*.
Those connected with Agni are treated as a single unit.

The *āhavanīya* fire is [the subject]. The remaining point is that one should employ single-word designators (*vācaka*) connected to it when they are being recited by the officiant. That ritual action in which a single meaning exists as the object to be conveyed is described thus; it is a neuter compound formed with the suffix *kṛt*. In a *honā* sacrifice where a simultaneous injunction (*praiṣa*) is applicable—such as "Recite for Agni being led forward" (*agnaye praṇīyamānāyānubrūhi*)—since it concerns two fires, one might expect the dual form "for the two fires" (*agnibhyām*). However, it has been stated that it should be in the singular.

The meaning is that even though it exists in two places, it remains a single entity. He states the *praiṣas* (directions) which, although consisting of various synonyms, are everywhere joined with the notion of oneness, regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses, the leading forth of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*), and the cleansing of the fire (*agnisaṃmārjana*).

In the first example, by way of incidental discussion, the third [case] applies to the *āgnīdh* alone in the *Autratantra*. Regarding the phrase "as a single unit," this is common to all three. Although the example concerning the *praṇayana* (carrying forward) was mentioned first, the example cited by Bharadvāja—namely, "Recite for the two fires being kindled" (*agnibhyāṃ samidhyamānābhyām anubrūhi*)—was presented first as a refutation of that which had been held in mind at the outset regarding the cleansing of the fires (*agni-saṃmārjana*). This is a Nyāya-sūtra. By virtue of that statement, "like the *sāmidhenī* verses," it applies everywhere in the context of the *sāmidhenīs*.

In that regard, even the prohibition regarding *namuhedi* is upheld. Furthermore, in passages such as *pra vo vājāḥ*, the word *amī* should not be substituted with a dual ending. And in the *Yājamāna* section, examples such as *samiddho agniḥ* and so forth serve as illustrations. In the second example, there is the addition of *sa-ga-u-i-pa-ca* for *agnaye praṇīyamānāya*. It should also be understood that this applies to passages such as *pra devaṃ devyā* and so forth, according to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha.

Nor is there an application [of the mantra] here in the phrase "O Agni, do not [be] weary," because it is impossible to perform the ritual action only once for both [offerings]; furthermore, due to the difference in location, there is a repetition of the mantra.
Both [the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ] address the Brahman priest, and the Brahman priest gives his permission using the dual form.

"O Brahman, I shall sprinkle both [the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ]"—in this manner [he addresses the Brahman]. Herein lies the intention: although the Brahman, having been addressed by the Adhvaryu, impels both [officiants] with the *prasava* (authorization), nevertheless, how could the Adhvaryu, as the agent of the future action, present only one person—the one who is to be addressed (*aṅgāśrāvaṇa*)—as the object of his direction using the singular number? In that case, the *prasava* would be "sprinkle! (*prokṣa*), and it would not apply to both.

Now, when they address one another saying, "We two shall rejoice," it should be expressed as "he and I—we two shall rejoice. In that case, when the word *asmad* (I/We) is used as a coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) adjunct, even though the first person is present, the rule for the first person (*uttama-puruṣa*) is prescribed. Therein, although both [the speaker and the other] are denoted by the dual number—since among words beginning with *sarva*, that which follows remains—the latter is designated as "other" (*parāñc*). Nevertheless, by superimposing "selfhood" (*pratyaktva*) upon that which is other, one should employ the dual form of the first person.

And as for what they say—that otherwise it would be impossible to express [the deity] as the "inner self" (pratyak)—therefore, by means of the singular number, he denotes his own self primarily as the inner self. Consequently, there is no contradiction; even the invocation of the name "Ām" is accomplished through the Vedic word itself, so that both together address Brahmā. He does not disregard the dual number. By means of the very same formula—"Lead the sacrifice forward, prosper the deities, establish these"—he simultaneously grants permission for both actions.
This is an illustration of those cases that follow the same principle. "I shall offer," [he says]; "you two offer. It has not been reached.

At that place where the two are about to carry forward the fires, they construct two altars on level ground facing east; they are separated by two finger-breadths, three finger-breadths, four finger-breadths, or by the measure of a span, and their hips and shoulders remain unjoined.

Having thus explained [the general rule], he states a specific exception regarding the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. Although the carrying forward of the fires (*agnipraṇayana*) would normally follow the procedure of the Gārhapatya fire, this is an exception (*apavāda*). At the time of the carrying forward, in whatever place and by whatever measurement they have previously made a resolve, thinking, "In the midst of these eight or more *prakramas*, we shall carry forward the fire by this measurement," they should construct the two altars (*vedi*) in that place, encompassing that very space. For it is not possible to construct two altars in a single location.

Likewise, the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) is obtained through extension (*atideśa*) as being only in the eastern direction; however, that is not possible in its primary sense when there are two *āhavanīya* fires in one place. Therefore, having performed the division in a single location to the east of the primary *gārhapatya*, they construct the altars (*vedi*) as far as possible. Nor can it be the case that one is primary and the other is secondary, because it is impossible to regard the primary and secondary locations as one and the same.

For in the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, the altar (*vedi*) and the sacrificial ground (*āyatana*) are established; here, however, the northern sacrificial hall (*uttara-vihāra*) and the ground to the south of the northern altar (*uttara-vedi*) are both necessarily situated within the space between the two altars. Therefore, since those [two halls] would not be possible without constructing the altars, the construction of the altars is logically required first. Although one might simply say "therein" (*tatra*)—meaning it should be performed in proximity to that place—it is stated as "in that [place]" (*tasmin*) for the purpose of establishing the conventional usage of the two sacrificial halls as "southern" and "northern."

Regarding the location of the two Āhavanīya fires: although in the archetype (prakṛti) it is prescribed to be in front of the altar (veda), nevertheless, here, because the leading forward of the animal sacrifice (pāśuka-praṇayana) involves the fire that has been carried forth (praṇītāgni), its establishment is obtained on the northern altar (uttara-vedi) itself; therefore [it is placed there]. [End of] the second section (paṭala). [This is] accompanied by the commentary (vaijayantī) composed by Mahādeva.

In the Śruti text, "He scatters the sacrificial grass on the northern altar (uttaravedi)," there is an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) regarding the southern [altar]. By the logic already stated—that the northern altar is prohibited at the origin of the sacrifice—just as the duties of the northern altar such as the *vitti* and so forth are excluded, the preparation of the altar-ground (*vedi*) itself is also precluded. To address this, it is said: "On level ground, facing east."

Furthermore, if the altar were made equal on both sides, and if its site were established in front [of the Gārhapatya], then while the distance for the Gārhapatya would remain the same, the distance for the Āhavanīya would be greater to the north, and consequently, the southern Āhavanīya would be further away; thus, the symmetrical east-west and north-south alignment of the two Āhavanīyas would not be achieved. Therefore, [the altar must be measured] from the Vedi.

One should construct the fire-altar (āyatana) such that its western transverse line is equal to the western transverse line of the Uttaravedi. For this very reason, to achieve equal intervals, it is appropriate to perform the construction by relying on a position slightly to the south or north of the two shoulders of the Āhavanīya fire. In this way, the praise of the "carrier" (vāhas) also becomes consistent. Therefore, the carrying forward of the two fires (praṇayana) also occurs slightly upward and horizontally by means of the eightfold and other sequences.

Nor can it be said that the performance of the primary rite cannot be accomplished even after [the altar] has been moved from its southern location; for the altar is not distinct from the mere *prstha* (the back-line). Following the rule that "the *prstha* is one *vitasti* wide," the intervening space between the two corners (*śroṇi*) and the two shoulders (*aṃsa*) is stated to be five *aṅgulas*. This is taught in order to show that the level ground in that region—wherein the lines are not separated or joined by a measure such as five *aṅgulas*—should be oriented toward the east. Thus, it is said: "In that place, on level ground, [the lines are] directed eastward. They must be made so that they do not overlap or touch one another by a measure of five *aṅgulas* and so forth.

Pṛthu, however, has been explained as being thirteen *akulas* in measure. Regarding the two *pāśukī* [stakes] for the purpose of joining the sacrificial post (*śrīyaṃsā śleṣaṇa*), the southern one is *pāśukī* and the northern one is *dauśikī*; this is taught according to the Naudhasa and Vaikhānasa schools, though it is not favored by others. It has been stated that there are two *āhavanīya* fires; in that case, while the *gārhapatya* remains in its place, the *āhavanīya* must be divided into two. Even regarding the bringing forward of the *āhavanīya*, although the performance of the duties of one *āhavanīya* is obtained as in the *paśubandha* sacrifice, the procedure for making it twofold is here prescribed.

And it has been stated regarding the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices that there is the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) of two *prastha* measures [of water] from the Gārhapatya and the Āhavanīya fires, as seen likewise in other Sūtras. That both [fires] are intended by the Teacher is certain; however, the expression "it is done" (*kṛtam*) is not a reference to the past, but rather a present-tense indication. Thus, because of the statement "where the fires are to be carried forward," the preparation of the altar is mentioned as the basis for the carrying forward. Since there is no carrying forward of the fire in the Anvāhāryapacana, the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) is indeed precluded.

Just as in the case of the *Paśubandha* sacrifice, the bringing forward (*praṇayana*) of the fire is enjoined as something new (*apūrva*); in its absence, the ritual act would not be counted [as complete]. Even if there is no door [of access], there is no fault; thus, like the *Paśubandha*, the bringing forward from the *Āhavanīya* fire is established, and in that system, there is no loss of the door. The masters Bhaṭṭācārya, who are experts in logic (*nyāyaviśārada*), cite such a statement: "If the bringing forward from the *Gārhapatya* fire was not mentioned by Āpastamba, it was not accepted by Śabarasvāmin; however, that too follows from the very nature of the ritual procedure (*sāmarthyāt*). Therefore, both [options] are desired by us. Whatever the *Adhvaryu* performs, the *Pratiprasthātṛ* performs that.

Regarding the statement "the Pratiprasthātṛ follows what has been performed [by the Adhvaryu]," Kātyāyana and Baudhāyana have stated that since the duties are shared, both should address the Brahman priest and so forth; however, this would be incorrect. Therefore, the mention of the Pratiprasthātṛ following what has been performed is intended to define his role as a performer who acts at a time prior [to the Adhvaryu]. The meaning is: whatever rite the Adhvaryu performs, that very same one the Pratiprasthātṛ also performs; he should not act on his own initiative, either before or after [the Adhvaryu].
The sublation of this rule will be stated by the author himself in various places through specific injunctions.
In the northern sacrificial area (*vihāra*), the Adhvaryu performs the rites; in the southern, the Pratiprasthātṛ.
Since no such restriction was previously mentioned, it is now being prescribed here. This is clear.
With the wooden sword (*sphya*), he joins the northern shoulder of the southern altar to the southern shoulder of the northern altar, following a single line (*ekasphyā*).

Starting from the northern hip of the southern sacrificial shed (*dakṣiṇavihāra*) up to the southern shoulder of the northern altar, he draws a single line with the wooden sword. The particle *anu* has the sense of "along. By means of this line, the Adhvaryu effects the separation of the two altars. Here, the construction of the altars is described only up to the point of their joining (*saṃnāma*) according to the measurement; the sweeping and other such acts are not mentioned, because they will be stated immediately thereafter in the words, "The rubbish heap (*utkara*) is common [to both]."

Therefore, once the name has been assigned [to the altar], having smoothed it along with the wooden sword (*sphyá*) and having made two rear corners, the meaning is that "make two altars. He demonstrates this very point: the *utkara* (the heap of earth) is common [to both]; the Brahman, the Hotṛ, and the Āgnīdhra [are common].

Because of the statement, "There are five officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) for the sacrifice of the Cāturmāsya rites," the Brahman and the others are not different on both sides; rather, the fifth is simply the Pratiprasthātṛ. Due to the lack of space at the *utkara*, there is only one [officiant] to the north. Even by another measurement, such as "measured by two feet," it has already been stated that those things which are common belong to both, performed by the Adhvaryu alone.
The Pratiprasthātṛ proceeds toward the *utkara* mound by way of the northern *vihāra* (having performed whatever was to be done prior to the northern tracing-out).
This is clear.
According to the ritual procedure for the *uttaravedi*, he prepares the *uttaravedi* on the northern [altar].

The meaning is that, according to the prescribed procedure for the *uttaravedi*, it is established that one performs [the rites] only on the *uttaravihāra-vedi* and not on the *dakṣiṇavihāra-vedi*. The ritual application (*prayoga*) therein is as follows: while the sacrificer stands to the south of the *dakṣiṇavihāra*, both perform their respective duties. When the two are being swept with the *veda*-grass-broom, the sacrificer performs the formula "The *vedi* is large" (*bṛhatī*) and so forth only once; there is no modification (*ūha*), because the substance being swept together is a single unit.

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that even though there is a difference in location, because the instruction in the *yajamāna* section is simply "the Veda," and because the object among related things possesses an unstable dimension, when the singularity is justified by referring to the genus (*jāti*), there should be no sublation of the scriptural reading through modification (*ūha*). And the ritual specialists (*prāyaugika*) perform it thus; for instance, in other cases as well, people do not experience confusion merely by the utterance of "bring the *prokṣaṇī* waters, the cow, the milking vessel, and the straining cloth."

In both cases, there are the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*) and the leading forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*). It has been stated that the materials are to be placed even in the southern sacrificial pit (*dakṣiṇāyatana*); thus it is said "in both. The phrase "the leading forward of the fire pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*)" is also connected to both. As for the method of leading forward: one leads the fires from the *gārhapatya* [to the other hearths] and so forth; having divided the fuel-stick (*idhma*), both lead the fires forward. There is no offering of the *novatahoma*; and even for the purpose of the constant maintenance (*nityadhārtha*), the leading forward is from the *āhavanīya* itself. Having added fuel to the fires (*anvādhāya*).
Both the Gārhapatya and the Dakṣiṇāgnis are used; the Adhvaryu alone performs everything pertaining to the sacrificer without modification.
They drive away the calves for the two Āmikṣās: the Pratiprasthātṛ for the Mārutī and the Adhvaryu for the Vāruṇī. They prepare the curds according to the procedure for the evening milking.

It has been stated that because the sacrifice to the Maruts precedes [the Vaiśvadeva] according to the procedure for fetching the branches and so forth, the Pratiprasthātṛ drives away the calves first. Although it was already stated that "the ritual procedure is according to the Vaiśvadeva," the rule is restated as "of the evening milking" and so forth, in order to ensure that the opinion of certain Sūtra-authors—that the Āmikṣā is to be prepared on the same day—does not apply here; thus it is said, "he prepares the curds. In this case, one pours pure water [with the formulas]: "A hundred for the Maruts; a hundred for Varuṇa," and so on elsewhere. "Thou art the fire-stirring stick (upaveṣa)."

These [priests] perform [the rites], being free from fear. [The formulas are: *kāmadhuk*, *bahudhuk*, *somena tvā*, *indrasya tvā*. Thus there are eight mantras ending with those respective case-terminations, addressed to the Maruts and Tvaṣṭṛ. Having divided the remnants of the gruel (*yavāgū*) and curdled it, he places it on top; the strewn grass belongs to the Gārhapatya and Dakṣiṇā fires. On the following day, for the sake of the ritual, [he recites] "for the sacrifice" and so forth. Both [the Brahman and Adhvaryu] sit down facing each other; the Adhvaryu alone [performs] to the south of the southern sacrificial area (*dakṣiṇavihāra*).
At the time of arranging the vessels, he employs the vessels according to their purpose; the *sruva*-ladles are made of *śamī* wood, or they may be made of gold.

The meaning is that the vessels for the sacrificial path, the medicinal herbs, and the *sāṃnāyya* [milk offering] are intended. The *śamyā* is a yoke-pin made of wood, silver, or gold, with its ends joined. According to Bharadvāja, it belongs to the southern sacrificial area (*dakṣiṇavihāra*). Baudhāyana says it belongs to both. Since there is no distinction, the meaning of the Sūtra is simply that it belongs to both. Because the *sruks* are mentioned, their inclusion is already implied. According to Bharadvāja, one should place the *praṇītā* waters on the northern fire alone; however, Kātyāyana has stated that because it is common to both, the Adhvaryu [should place them] on both.

In this matter, the position of commonality (*sādhāraṇatā*) alone must be adopted. It has been stated that the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* waters is performed as a single act (*tantra*) because its purpose is transcendental (*adṛṣṭārthatā*). For where the primary rite is accomplished by means of fire, there is no commonality due to the restrictive rule that one must go to the fire-altar. However, these [waters] are not accomplished by fire; rather, being consecrated by the Adhvaryu for a transcendental purpose, they are employed at both locations. Therefore, the Adhvaryu alone [recites] "O Brahman, the waters... The Brahman also recites [the formula] without modification. The invocation ending with "Who art thou? (*kastvam asi*) is likewise unmodified.

Because of the statement "the vessels are according to their purpose," the medicinal vessels (*auṣadhapātra*) are also distinct. The vessels for the clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth are indeed different from those used for ordinary purposes, as they are specified for each respective rite. At the time of the pouring out (*nirvapaṇa*), the Adhvaryu, having poured out the five common oblations (*saṃcarāṇi*), pours out the cake for Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*) on eleven potsherds. Having poured out the previously mentioned oblations for Agni and the others—which have been circulated—he pours out the specific oblation for Indra and Agni. *Note: Ga, Ca, Ṭa, Ṭha, Ra, La: among the ritual materials.* *Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram—[Fifth Praśna]* *At the time of the pouring out, the Adhvaryu, having poured out the five common oblations, pours out the cake for Indra and Agni on eleven potsherds. Having poured out the previously mentioned oblations for Agni and the others—which have been circulated—he pours out the specific oblation for Indra and Agni.*
The Pratiprasthātṛ pours out barley for the ewe dedicated to Māruta;
the pouring out of barley is prescribed as a substitute for the ewe. [He does so] with the formula "To the Maruts, agreeable," and so forth, using his own winnowing basket.
Having poured out the ram for Varuṇa, the Adhvaryu pours out the cake on one potsherd for Ka.

Regarding the barley for the ram: Bharadvāja states that the Adhvaryu pours out barley for both the ram and the ewe, as they are the primary materials (*prakṛti*). Vairūpānasa, however, says it is for the ram alone. But Kātyāyana maintains it is for the rice alone, because of the force of the separate commencement in the text "having poured out, he scatters. The Adhvaryu acts according to the ritual rules for various seeds (*nānābīja-dharma*). By restricting the barley specifically to the two images of the ram and ewe, he shows that there should be no restriction of rice for the others;
the meaning is that all may be barley, or there is no restriction of rice for the others, but rather a choice according to what has been prescribed.
Having mixed barley grains with the surplus of the *prokṣaṇī* water, they thresh them;
for there is no threshing of those [grains] that are already dry. When any surplus whatsoever might occur, the rule is that it must be done with the remainder of the *prokṣaṇī* water.
Once the cakes have been placed upon the fires up to the one for Indra and Agni, the Pratiprasthātṛ arranges eleven or twelve potsherds on the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire.
In the southern half, in the southern part, according to the procedure for the Indra-Agni [bricks],
the Adhvaryu, having laid down eight bricks of the ram, lays down those of the goat.
It has been stated that he lays them down by moving toward the south.
The procedure for the morning milking (*prātardoha*) is as follows: they perform two milkings for the sake of the *āmikṣā*, just as previously described.

Although the application [of this rule] is established by extension (*atideśa*), there are several statements that serve as the basis for its application; in another Sūtra, it is stated that the *āmikṣā* is prepared at once (*sadyas*) and is not obtained through the ordinary method of milking. It is just like the *vaiśvadevī-āmikṣā* mentioned before.
When the offerings have been placed on the fire up to those for Indra and Agni, they fashion two figures of rams.

The Pratiprasthātṛ and the Adhvaryu prepare a ram-shaped image from a mixture of ground barley grains that have been husked and shaped like ewes; however, in the case of a single seed, there is a division [of the task].
The Pratiprasthātṛ prepares a ewe for the Maruts, or the Adhvaryu prepares a ram for Varuṇa; he forms the female characteristics of the ewe and the male characteristics of the ram.

These [details] have been explained previously in the Sūtra. The female characteristics are the vulva and the breasts; the male characteristics are the penis, the testicles, and the prepuce. [End of] Chapter [Number]: Together with the Vaijayantī commentary composed by Mahādeva.
Upon eleven or twelve potsherds, the Pratiprasthātṛ places the ewe on the fire; having placed the ram on eight potsherds, the Adhvaryu places the single-potsherd cake for Ka on the fire.

Having analyzed this repeatedly, some authorities state that the procedure for making *āmikṣā* consists of milking immediately after placing the potsherds on the fire, while others say it consists of milking immediately after placing the vessel on the fire; this is intended to exclude the various sequences observed in other traditions.
Alternatively, there may be two sheep cooked in a single pot.

The two *kumbhī* vessels are for cooking (*pākya*), meaning they are to be used for boiling; these are the ewe and the ram. Here, it appears that the phrase "the two *kumbhī*s are to be cooked" was stated so that the covering of the *kumbhī*s might not take the place of the potsherds (*kapāla*), lest the ritual duties of the potsherds—such as those mentioned at the time of laying down the potsherds—not apply to the *sthālī* (small cooking pots). Furthermore, it is understood that this was said to ensure that even though the *sthālī*s are used, the specific characteristics of the potsherds do not erroneously extend to them.

In that case, the ritual requirements (*dharma*) must necessarily apply because the act of cooling (*nirvāpa*) and so forth has been performed with the specific quantity to be given; therefore, when another substance is joined for that same purpose, it is stated that "the *dharmas* are extended" (*dharmātideśa*). Just as a pot is well-known to be obtained for the *caru* offering, so too is the *kumbhī* (large jar) obtained here by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*); it is precisely to demonstrate this that the scripture itself has been shown.

Likewise, the flour-cakes (*piṣṭeṣu*) which have been exhausted [in the previous rites], spread out, brought forward, prepared, and employed here for the sake of cooking, obtain [the water] again; therefore, the boiling must be performed with other waters by means of placing them [on the fire] and so forth, just as in the case of the *parvan* offerings. This is stated for the purpose of demonstrating that, since no option with the potsherds (*kapāla*) is mentioned in the *dhṛti* formula, and because only the cake itself is enjoined, the properties of the latter should be extended to the former. The sacrificer and his wife prepare the *karambha-pātra* vessels from ordinary, raw, slightly heated barley grains.

The *śamī* and *karīra* fruits, as well as the *karambha*, require vessels as their support; these are made of barley alone, as stated by Āpastamba and Bhāradvāja. Having silently ground the barley, they are subsequently heated over the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*). Thus, according to the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa, the husband and wife prepare those vessels. By the term "worldly" (*laukika*), it is understood that those already prepared are to be taken.
There should be one more vessel than the number of the sacrificer's servants and relatives, including their wives.

And those who are to be sent forth—his servants, sons, grandsons, and disciples, together with their wives and their sons and grandsons—are the "burden-bearers" (bhāradvānaḥ). The meaning is that there are as many of them as exceed that number by one. In every respect, Kātyāyana has stated that there are exactly three [of these].
Having performed the subsequent tracing of the altar, he proceeds with the formal command: "Bring the clarified butter and the curd! He concludes at the end of this command.

Nor should it be said that because the vessels are common [to both], he issues the *saṃpraiṣa* (direction) for them as a single unit; for it has been stated that the self alone is to be consecrated here, and therefore it applies to each individually. The rest is clear. 1. Sva. Ga. I. I. ṇa, 'myau no; Kha. Ga. I. Da. Ga. "nā ka; Ra. 'dupataptā. 464. According to Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra—[In the fifth book]—as at the Phālgunī festival, so at the Āṣāḍhī festival they take the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*). The meaning is already explained.

On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, having spread a layer of clarified butter once, and having taken up curds twice, they sprinkle it over with clarified butter once; this is as previously explained. He then proceeds with the ritual acts beginning from the removal of the oblation from the fire.
The meaning is clear.

When [the cakes] ending with those for Indra and Agni have been adorned, they make two hairy effigies of rams out of wool from sheep other than ewes; if that is unavailable, they join them with *kuśa*-grass wool. Or rather, it is stated in the Vājasaneyi-Brāhmaṇa: "He fills the single-potsherd [cake]."
He places a ram upon the Mārutī [cart] and a ewe upon the Vāruṇī.
He places the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) in the middle [of the northern altar] in reverse order.
On the northern altar he deposits the other oblations; on the southern altar, the *mārutī* *āmikṣā* and the *karambha* vessels.

All other oblations containing speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), even those used in the southern sacrificial area, the Adhvaryu deposits only on the northern altar, because of the singular number [in the injunction]. The Pratiprasthātṛ deposits one *mārutī* *āmikṣā* and the *karambha* vessels on the other [the southern altar], or both may deposit them on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).
Having set down two effigies of rams, he places a ewe upon the offering for Māruta and a ram upon that for Varuṇa.

Although their placement follows the natural order, the text specifies "having set down" again; thus, whoever sets them down takes them from there and places them crosswise upon the other *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture). The rest is clear. While scattering more than a hundred or more than a thousand leaves of the *śamī* tree and *karīra* fruits, he pours them into the *karambha* vessels.

In front of the two rams, both [officiants] proceed with those same [oblations] for the sake of the axle. They proceed with the fire produced by friction according to the procedure for the fire produced by friction.

The sense is that there is only one fire produced by friction (*nirmanthya*), because of the singular endings in the phrases *paśubandhoktena nirmanthyavidhinā* ("by the procedure for the fire produced by friction as stated in the Paśubandha") and *nirmanthyena* ("by the fire produced by friction"). This is not so because it is common to all [rites], but rather due to the statement of another Śākhā. That has been stated by Kātyāyana: "The mere act of churning belongs to the Adhvaryu"; later, it is shown that "having divided [the fire], both proceed," because of the dual ending; and Bhāradvāja says, "They proceed with two fires produced by friction.
Furthermore, Āpastamba has stated in the sixth Paṭala of the Mahādeva-kṛta-Vaijayantī commentary: "The two fires produced by friction [are used] against the enemy."
Having set down the Veda, he gives the direction for the *sāmidhenī* verses.
It has been stated that the Adhvaryu himself performs the *anūha*; it has also been stated that because of its commonality, the *saṃpraiṣa* (direction) belongs to Āgnīdhra.

When the northern fire has been swept and the southern one has not yet been swept, the Pratiprasthātṛ asks the wife: "Wife, how many lovers do you have? He points them out with the formula, "May Varuṇa seize as many as she declares. If she does not declare him who is her lover, she would obstruct a dear kinsman.

Having gone near his wife, the Pratiprasthātṛ asks her: "How many lovers do you have? [referring to those other than her husband]. [The Adhvaryu says: "May Varuṇa seize them who are united with her through sexual intercourse. Thus the Adhvaryu alone speaks again after the Pratiprasthātṛ's proclamation. Regarding the number of lovers being one or two, she is told to say "so many" (*tāvat*). If there is a lover and she does not speak, then Varuṇa shall inflict restraint upon her beloved kinsman or relative by means of a curse, a disease, and so forth.

If they are not present, there are no Māras; therefore, the phrase "then he approaches them" does not apply. Some say that in the case of the *jāraka* (the one who causes impurity), the expiation is performed by him alone. Others say it should be done at the end of the ritual action.
The Pratiprasthātṛ leads the wife forward with the verse, "We invoke those who are to be slain.
This is clear. It ends with the word *sajoṣasaḥ*.

The sacrificial flour-pots (*karambhapātra*) have been poured into a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) made of *aiṣīka* grass. The wife, having placed them upon her head, goes between the two altars; the sacrificer and the wife then stand facing west in front of the southern fire.

Having gone to the north of the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), passing between the northern *Āhavanīya* fire and the two altars, and having set down those previously prepared flour-pots—which were poured into the *aiṣīka* winnowing basket—along with the basket itself upon the ground, the couple goes between the two altars in front of the southern *Āhavanīya* and stands there facing west.

The sacrificer recites the *puronuvākyā* with "mo ṣū ṇaḥ" (RV 7.1.20). Having both spoken together [the *yājyā*] with "yad grāve" (RV 10.94.1), they both offer the oblation with the winnowing basket into the southern fire.

Standing, he recites the *puronuvākyā* according to the rule with "mo ghū ṇaḥ"; it ends with "gīḥ". He recites the *puronuvākyā*, and then both the husband and wife, having uttered the words beginning with "yāma" and ending with "svāhā", both offer the oblation at the end. The *praghāsya* deities are the great ones. The rest is clear.
Either the *adhvaryu* offers the oblation while the other two hold on to him from behind.

Having recited the mantras, the sacrificer alone offers the oblations; the husband and wife both touch him from behind. Reciting "They have performed the rite, O performers of the rite," they go back and forth. Reciting up to the end of the verse "The bounteous ones," they return by the same way they came and go.
