He cleanses the southern fire.
The Āgnīdhra now cleanses the fire that was previously uncleansed. This is done after the ritual has proceeded with the offerings ending with those for Indra and Agni.

According to Kātyāyana, from the *Ādhāra* libation up to the portion of the *Tantra* for both [the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ], beginning with the Āgneya and so forth, belongs to the Adhvaryu; meanwhile, the Pratiprasthātṛ remains with his hands washed until the end of the spreading out of the cake for Indra-Agni.
Then, the Pratiprasthātṛ cuts the entire ewe together with the first portion (*sahāvadāna*) to the east of the offering for the Maruts, and the Śamī leaves and Karīra fruits to the north.
The meaning is that having cut the previously mentioned items together with the subsequent portion (*uttarāvadāna*), he proceeds with the ritual. The rest is clear.
The Adhvaryu cuts off the entire ram from the offering of the female sheep dedicated to Varuṇa with the first portion, and the Śamī leaves and Karīra fruits with the second.

The meaning is that one proceeds after having cut [the portion]. The rest is clear. Since the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) and the *anna* (food) are modifications of the *sāṃnāyya*, the sacrificer’s formula should be the same as that for the *sāṃnāyya*. However, the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that because it is a modification of the *vaiśvadevī-āmikṣā*, the formula "May I go to union with the Maruts through the path of the gods and by means of the vital breaths" should be used even for the wild-food (*vāraṇyā*). This should be disregarded as it contradicts the Bhāṣya; for when the formula is already obtained from the archetype (*darśa*), it is not possible to adopt a formula belonging to a modification (*vikṛti*). Nor can its specific property (*dharma*) be [extended] to the *āmikṣā*.

Regarding the *vaiśvadevī* [offering] in the section on the *kṣāya*, because the mantra "of the Viśvedevas" has not been recited there, that mantra—being taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*)—would apply by its indicative power (*liṅga*) wherever the Viśvedevas are the deity, whether in the *āmikṣā*, the *caru*, or the *ājya-havis*. Consequently, the address to Agni and Soma mentioned in the context of the *vaiśvadeva-caru* is also improper, because the indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger than a statement based on inference (*ānumānika-vākya*).

Thus, the mantra belongs to the Vaiśvadeva oblation in general, and is not the specific property of the Vaiśvadeva Āmikṣā alone; therefore, it is not extended [by analogy] to other types of Āmikṣā. Furthermore, Bhāradvāja has stated regarding the Vaiśvadeva caru in the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi: "For the Viśvedevas with the breaths," and so forth; and regarding that single-kapāla offering: "For Heaven and Earth," and so forth. Then he says again: "Moreover, from this point forward, one should recite the mantras for the Vaiśvadeva offerings."

And thus, these mantras are employed for specific deities alone and do not apply to oblations intended for other deities. Therefore, it is established that there is no *anupraharaṇa* (throwing into the fire) for [the remnants] of the *dyāvāpṛthivī* and other such offerings. And that [belongs] to which deity? To this very one. Kātyāyana also has the same rule in his Sūtra. Let us return to the subject at hand: "Recite the invitatory verse (*anuvācya*) for whom; sacrifice (*yajya*) to whom? || 6 || He issues the command regarding the cake on a single potsherd (*ekakapāla*).

This scriptural passage from another recension (*śākhāntarīyā śruti*) has been cited primarily for the purpose of determining the deity; however, it may also be interpreted otherwise as referring to the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*). Furthermore, the word *sarva* (all), being a pronoun, can denote a deity, as seen in such expressions as *kasmai svāhā* ("Hail to whom!"). Therefore, it is shown that its meaning should be understood as "to whom [the deity] is dear" (*kāya juṣṭam*). The formula *kasyāhaṃ devānādaḥ* ("Of whom am I the eater of the gods? is the consecration (*anumantraṇa*). [End of Section] 2.6.1. [From the Vaijayantī commentary by Mahādeva. 467.
He offers the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) with the four names of the months, saying: "To Nabhas, Svāhā! To Nabhasya, Svāhā! and so forth.

By the rule "with the names of the months," it should be understood that in all cases the months themselves are taken as the deities, not the *āstāra-likapanas*. Therefore, it should be known that while the previously mentioned monthly offerings (*māsa-homas*) occur only at the optional *Vaiśvadeva* parvan, they do not occur here in this case of the single-potsherd offering.
At the conclusion of the *sūktavāka*, the Hotṛ recites the benedictions, including: "May he grant us prosperity for the coming year."
The explanation has been provided.
When the enclosing-sticks have been removed, having offered with the residue, they proceed with the whey;
this is for the sake of what has already been stated.

As before. The word "as" (*yathā*) is used because the *kānina* [portion] lacks the status of being a name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*). This is the underlying intention: that the view of the *Nyāya* school is that this is an extension (*atideśa*) of the injunction together with its explanatory passage (*sārthavāda*), namely, "There are indeed five [portions] for the Brāhmaṇas.

"In whatever semen of mine is emitted, in whatever is born again from me, or in whatever remains established within me—with that, make me vigorous (*vājina*); with that, make me possessed of good offspring. O vigorous one, of that [portion] of yours, which is made ready with the vigorous [grains], which is honeyed, and which has been invited, I, being invited, partake. With these words, they partake in the southern sacrificial hall (*vihāra*).
Since all [the priests] perform the function of sending the call for the horse-sacrifice, even the *adhvaryu* has a portion to consume.

[The formula is: "May the drops enter me; may they flow into my veins. Fill my essence with essence. O Vājin, of that which is made ready by the Vājins, of the honeyed, invited portion, being invited myself, I partake.

This applies to the latter [formula]. The word "they consume" (*makṣayanti*) carries over [from the previous rule]. The *pratiprasthātṛ* does not participate here, as he has no further use [for the substance].
Having performed the final bath (avabhṛtha) with the Vāruṇī offering, with the residue of the milk, and with the husks, its ritual procedure is explained by that of the Soma-related avabhṛtha.

The *niṣkāsa* (residue) is that which has gone into the *kumbhī*. For this very reason, Bharadvāja stated: "One should deposit the *niṣkāsa* from the *sthālī* in a known place. The author of the Sūtra also says: "The *niṣkāsa* of the *prāyaṇīya* [is the] *udayanīya*," and likewise: "The *niṣkāsa* is not a remnant of the portioning (*avadāna*). In passages such as "This indeed is the *avabhṛtha* of the Darśapūrṇamāsa," the word *avabhṛtha* is used figuratively; in the case of the *ekāha* sacrifices, it is used in its primary sense, referring specifically to the *avabhṛtha* of the Soma sacrifice, because that alone possesses its own inherent characteristics (*svadharma*). By that [primary usage], this *avabhṛtha* is explained. No *sāman* is chanted.

The meaning is "because of the prohibition. [In the variants] gha, ja, sa, ma, da, it says: "He prays for the divine abode. 1. In ga, ṭha, ḍha, ṇa, pyā—there is *āmikṣā*. From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [in the fifth book]:
"Having gone away silently," the word "water" (*udakam*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

Having offered the scrapings (*niṣkāsa*) according to the rule of the Vāruṇa [oblation]. Regarding the question of where the one-potsherd (*ekakapāla*) cake for Varuṇa is prescribed, it is stated in the scripture that "in its place they mix the scrapings and the husks together. This refers to the scrapings of the *puroḍāśa* for Varuṇa; it is said to be "quickly" (*dhak*) because it is joined with another substance for that purpose. Now, an objection might be raised: "The scrapings are a remnant (*śeṣa*); how can they be given as an oblation (*havis*) to Varuṇa? With this concern in mind, it is said "having offered" (*pratipādya*). The intention is that even though it is a disposal (*pratipatti*), by virtue of the scriptural injunction, it also functions as an offering to Sviṣṭakṛt. And thus, everything that is prescribed for the *avabhṛtha*, such as the *prayāja*s and so forth, occurs there as well.
He offers [the remnants] according to the nature of husks and the *ṛjīṣa*.

Since it is stated that "the *avabhṛtha* [concluding bath] is with the husks," the term "husks" (*tuṣān*) is used. Therefore, in the mantras such as "that which they cut from thee, O Soma, with the *prāva*"—whereby they cut the barley, wheat, or grains with the pestle—one should apply the appropriate modifications (*ūha*), such as "the limbs through fear" or "the joints with the pestle.
Having emerged from the *avabhṛtha*, two garments are given to whomever one desires.
The two garments have been put on; this is clear.

On the following day, having performed the Full Moon sacrifice, whether he has moved out from the sacrificial ground or not, he moistens himself with water while reciting: "Impelled by the god Savitṛ...
The meaning is understood.

"That which Gharma has turned around—the teeth of the earth and the sky—Agni as the lord by his might, Varuṇa with his prayers, Indra with his friends the Maruts, and Agni with his sharp flame"—with these words, the turning back and the shaving are performed as before.
Thus ends the second chapter in the fifth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.

In this case as well, it has been stated that [the rite] is performed because of the absence of a specific designation (*saṃjñā*). Thus ends the second chapter in the fifth book, the Varuṇapraghāsa section, of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* composed by Mahādeva. 3.

5.3 Now begins the third chapter of the fifth book. Then, after four months, on the full moon day of Kārttika or Mārgaśīrṣa, he performs the Sākamedha sacrifices for two days. The Sākamedhas are sacrifices (*medhā*) performed according to a common ritual framework (*tantra*); they are called "Sāka" because they are performed together (*sākam*, meaning "together"). In the compound, the word *sākam* [undergoes a specific grammatical modification] according to the rule of Gha, Ja, Ma, Da, etc. [The text here contains various manuscript variants regarding the formation]. [The term] *āmāveṣṭyaḥ* [is used]; [the text continues with citations from various sources such as] Sa, Ga, Pa, U, 3, Ra, Ṇa, Sūta, etc., and Gaja, ending in *ndanti*. The elision of the letter *m* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). [This concludes the section] accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

The *Mahāhavis* sacrifices performed on the fifth full moon day have their simultaneous performance (*yahakālatā*) with the subsidiary offerings (*iṣṭis*) occurring after four months have passed. The *Sākamedhas* are prescribed by the text beginning with "Together with the sun" (*sākara sūryeṇa*). Therefore, the meaning is that the principal rites of the *Sākamedhas* are to be accomplished simultaneously with those [subsidiaries]. Consequently, the commencement takes place on the fourteenth day before sunrise.

He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Anīkavat at the time when the sun rises together with its rays; so say some. At midday, he offers a pap to the Maruts Sāṃtapana; according to some, he does not throw the sacrificial grass (barhis) into the fire. In the afternoon, he drives away the calves for the Gṛhamedhīya offering; according to some, he drives away as many calves as belong to the sacrificer without reciting a formula.

"By one who has come with rising [light]," or rather, "the extinguishing [of the fire] or the primary performance. This means by those rays that are rising—that is, the first rays. As many calves as belong to the sacrificer, all of them are included; here, the masculine gender is not intended to be significant, as established by the rule of *ekaśeṣa*. The sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) is performed in the afternoon for the sake of the *Gṛhamedhīya* rite, or for the *caru* (oblation) whose deity is the *Gṛhamedhin*. Although the deity is qualified [by the term *gṛhamedhin*], its name is derived from the substantive alone, just as in the case of the *Vaimṛdha* sacrifice.

Therefore, the separation of the calf from its mother is not for the sake of milk for a deity; rather, it is said that wherever the separation is performed for the purpose of cooking the meat, there it is a worldly (laukika) separation of the calf. According to some, one separates the calves with a *yajus* formula. Where a *yajus* such as "For food (*iṣe*) thee," etc., is not employed in the ritual act, the mere separation of the calf should be performed silently (*tūṣṇīka*), provided that such an act serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).

In this case, the branch is not permanent as previously [stated]; rather, having silently brought the branch without the *sāṃnāyya* sacrificial formulas, one silently removes it. From this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), some say that there is a mantra optionally; however, because this is a *dravahoma* (liquid oblation), it is already stated [that there is no mantra], for there is no inference of extension (*atideśa*) by way of similarity in the case of a *dravahoma*. When the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, he commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice.
This is clear.
In this regard, we shall explain whatever is performed.

Since its status as a *darvihoma* has been determined in the *Nyāya-śāstra*, there is no acquisition of auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) through extended application (*atideśa*); therefore, those which are obtained from the instructions of other branches are explained here. And for this purpose it has been stated: "The principal rites of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśapaurṇamāsika*) are enjoined in the subsequent procedure (*tati*), except for the Soma sacrifice and the *dharmādharmahoma*s"; these possess their own inherent characteristics (*svadharma*). Therefore, there is no extended application; rather, only those with their own inherent characteristics as they have been stated should be adopted.

Having added fuel to the fires, having prepared the *veda*, having strewn grass around the fires, having washed his hands, and having spread out a layer of *ulapa* grass, he arranges the vessels according to their purpose:

the vessels for the vegetable offerings; and, if there is to be milking, the *pavitras*, the pot for the cooked rice (*caru*), the *kumbhī*, and also the milking vessel—or, in place of the potsherds, the *kumbhī* and three *pātrīs*. [This concludes] the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Āpastamba, in the fifth book, [section on] the *Ahīnas*.

Having cooked the *kumbhī*, he lifts up the *uddharaṇapātrī* vessels. Regarding the number of *praṇītā* waters, Bādarāyaṇa says that one does not bring the *praṇītā* waters [again] once they have been brought; Bādarāyaṇa also prescribes the selection of the Brahman priest at this point. It should be understood from the instruction that the act ends with the pouring out (*stīttyanta*) and that the other [rites] are performed during the *sāmayana*. At the time of the offering (*nirvapaṇa*), he pours out abundant rice for the Maruts Gṛhamedhins, as much as he deems necessary for the milk.

The offering of many [portions] is according to the sequence of the verses. Having taken four handfuls, one pours in a large quantity; thus say Bharadvāja and Āpastamba. The mantra is also permitted with the word for the deity in the dative case, as in "of the god... and so forth. One causes the cow to be milked using a strainer.

Furthermore, because of the restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyāna*), the other ritual duties are excluded by the *śākhāpavitra* brought for the purpose of driving away the calves. Having stated this, Āpastamba mentions an alternative view: "As in the case of the *manāyya*. That view holds that there is [no *pavitra*] here. The driving away of the calves is performed without a vessel; the milking is done without a vessel. The meaning is that it is performed with a *pavitra* over the *kumbhī* placed upon the *gārhapatya* fire.
According to some, one does not purify the rice grains; rather, one cooks them with milk already purified by the *yajus*-formula.

Because it has been obtained as a desirable quality (*caru-dharmatva*), there is no prohibition against purifying it. However, regarding the alternative of fetching a branch while remaining silent, this [rule] "with a strainer" (*pavitreṇa*) is the injunction for some reciters (*śākhin*); when there is no fetching of a branch, then for some [others] the injunction is "purified with a Yajus formula. The particle *eva* (only) is for the purpose of excluding the *praṇītā* water. Even though milk is mentioned here for the purpose of cooking the sacrificial porridge (*payas-śrapaṇa*), because of the prohibition, the meaning is that one does not bring forth the *praṇītā* water. It is purified with the Yajus formula, namely, "The god Savitṛ... and so forth.

For here it is heard: "In the evening, [he milks] all [the cows] for the sake of the *āmikṣā*. Since the milk is heard of there as being for the purpose of cooking (*śrapaṇa*), it is not a substance to be offered (*pradeyadravya*). Therefore, the driving away of the calf is worldly (*laukika*), as is the milking itself. In that regard, the position that [the milk is prepared] with water purified by the *yajus*-formula is established by logic, in order to exclude the *praṇītā* water. However, in another recension (*śākhāntara*), it is stated: "Having driven away the calves with a branch and having milked with a filter (*pavitra*), he cooks that *caru*."

Likewise, with reference to that very [offering], it is heard: "Its [name] is Dākṣāyaṇa. The meaning of the scriptural statement is that the action is of two kinds, like the *sāṃnāyya* and the *auṣadha*. In that case, since this is a new (*apūrva*) rite, only what is explicitly stated should be adopted. However, the properties (*dharma*) of the *auṣadha* are appropriately shown in this way. As for the properties of the *sāṃnāyya*, they are to be adopted according to the explicit statement only optionally; indeed, even their *gaṇas* (collections) are not included because there is no extended application (*atideśa*) of the mantras, due to the absence of being a modification of the milking (*doha*). Therefore, this milking is also without mantras.

As for what is heard—that "one prepares the sacrificial food with the Yajus"—that too is for the purpose of obtaining [the rite], not for the purpose of prohibiting what has already been obtained; for that Yajus is not obtained through either extended application (*atideśa*) or direct instruction (*upadeśa*), nor is there any scriptural extended application here. The status of having an extended application is based on grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); thus the Śruti is "the evening Agnihotra," and likewise the sentence "these are its Brāhmaṇas. Nor is there an injunction that "this must be performed like the obligatory [Agnihotra]"; rather, how much of the character of the medicinal herb (*auṣadha*) and how much of the character of the cooked oblation (*śrta*) is seen here? (Note: *kha* indicates a variant reading).

This is the meaning. By such [an action] as the driving away of the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*) and so forth, however, because of its being a *dahoma* (a burnt offering), the extension of its own specific properties (*svadharma*) has already been rejected by [the author] himself. Herein is the sequence of the ritual procedure: having said, "O sacrificer, restrain your speech," he remains silent, [and proceeds with] "the vessels," and so on. [Notes on variants: 1. ga. ca. 1, ṭha. i. . m | ma | 2. ca. ṭa ma | tuṣadha | 3. ca. ṭa. kṣeṇa | 4. ca. ṭa. vācyam | 5. va da. tu prāptaḥ ki | 471. Third Paṭala: [From] the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva. The meaning is as follows. By such [an action] as the driving away of the calves and so forth, however, because of its being a *dahoma*, the extension of its own specific properties has already been rejected by [the author] himself. Herein is the sequence of the ritual procedure: having said, "O sacrificer, restrain your speech," he remains silent, [and proceeds with] "the vessels," and so on.

Then, having performed the pouring out of water and so forth according to the purpose, having thrice husked [the rice] and washed it, and having poured out the wash-water, he places the cooking pot with the formula "Thou art a support" (*dhruvāsi*) and sets it on the fire at the proper time. However, he does not purify the rice grains; rather, having caused the milk to be milked silently into the pot which contains the branch-strainer (*śākhāpavitra*), he adds the unpurified rice grains and cooks them.

In the alternative case of cooking [milk], there is no fetching of the branch nor the making of the branch-strainer; having placed the pot on the fire and milked the cow by common practice, he purifies that milk with two *darbha* strainers using the *yajus* formula, pours it into the pot, adds the unpurified rice grains, and cooks them.

The third option, that of performing the milking with mantras, belongs exclusively to Āpastamba; it is not mentioned by other sūtra-authors such as Bharadvāja, nor even by our own teacher. Some say that the first option—beginning with the fetching of the branch—is entirely accompanied by mantras, but this is to be considered further. He cooks the *prativeśa* rice in the *dakṣiṇāgni*. It has been stated by Vaikhānasa that "he cooks the *prativeśa* rice for the husband, the wife, and the children" in the *dakṣiṇāgni* by means of a worldly rite (*laukikena karmaṇā*).
Taking the wooden sword (*sphya*), he performs the *stambayajus* rite over the hair of the strewn altar.

It has been stated that in the *Sāṃtapanīyeṣṭi*, one does not carry away the grass-bundle; therefore, while the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is still strewn, he performs the *stambayajus* over the hair—that is, from the parts—upon it.
Having performed the second tracing of the altar, he proceeds with the formal command (*saṃpraiṣa*).

The construction of the altar has been described by means of the carrying away of the *stambayajus*. It is clear that he issues the command for whatever else remains apart from the *idhma* (sacrificial fuel), the *barhis* (sacrificial grass), and the binding of the wife (*patnīsaṃnaha*). The meaning is that, according to the injunction "he does not bind the wife, nor does he recite the *sāmidhenī* verses," this is because the *barhis* has already been spread and the *idhma* is absent.

Having performed that which precedes the taking of the clarified butter (*ājya*), he takes it in the *dhruvā* vessel itself. It is stated that "it is in the *dhruvā* alone" because of the scriptural injunction: "Neither the *prayāja*s are offered, nor the *anuyāja*s, nor the two *āghāra* libations. Having consecrated the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*), having addressed the Brahman priest, having sprinkled the altar, having poured out the remainder of the sprinkling water, and having inserted the two strainers (*pavitra*) back [into the vessel], he sets down the *dhruvā* and the *sruva* ladle.

Because it is a *dahoma* (an oblation poured out), this is stated for the purpose of enjoining another new action (*apūrva-karma*): "On the very altar that has been strewn, the remainder of the *prokṣaṇī* water," and so forth. He modifies the mantra "This has sat down" (*eṣā'sadat*) to the mantra "These have sat down" (*etā asadan*). This is understood. [End of section] Kha. Ga. Pa. Ca. Ṭa. Gā. Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra—[Fifth Praśna].
He consecrates the clarified butter with the mantra: "Thou art Viṣṇu's; thou art the abode of Viṣṇu; thou belongest to Prajāpati.

This is the name of the [offering] belonging to Viṣṇu. Whatever sacrificial grass belongs to the Ānīkavata [offering], that belongs to the Sāṃtapanīya and that to the Gṛhamedhīya; according to some, it remains already spread out.

The meaning is that even at the Sātapana [rite], one should not offer the *barhis* grass beforehand, even for one who has brought it outside. However, the throwing of the *prastara* bundle exists in both cases.
One commences the rites beginning with the removal [of the fire].
This is clear.
Having extracted the scum from the boiled oblation and set it aside in a known place,
he takes the scum— the froth that has risen from the oblation of the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice which stands nearby—
into the vessels after spreading a base of butter, and scoops out three portions of cooked rice.
Having spread the sacrificial ladle (*pātrī*) with clarified butter, he draws out from the cooking pot (*kumbhī*) as many portions as there are [deities] into those very vessels.
He sets aside the emptied cooking pot. Having placed a greater amount of the remaining rice inside, he leaves it there.
Having placed the *udāyuvana*— the broad,

unpolished part of the ladle (*darvī*) by which the rice being cooked is stirred upward from below and mixed on all sides— into the pot while it still contains its residue and has not been wiped clean;
and having poured clarified butter over it, purified it, and adorned it, he sets down the portions of rice.
On the sacrificial altar, once the deities have been invoked, he should offer the *upavāja* oblation and proceed with the two *ājyabhāga* portions.

There is an omission of the *sāmidhenī* verses, the *pravara*, the *āghāra*, and the *prayāja* offerings. After the invocation of the deities, having said to the *agnīdh* "Gather [the fire] three times," he should proceed only with the *upavāja* and the two *ājyabhāga* portions.

Having spread a base of clarified butter in the *juhu* ladle, having taken portions from all the rice-offerings (*odana*) and having sprinkled them with clarified butter, he issues the direction: "Recite the invitatory verse for the Maruts Gṛhamedhins; recite the offering verse for the Maruts Gṛhamedhins.

Having taken a single portion from each of the three rice-offerings and having sprinkled them with clarified butter, he offers them at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*; this is the remainder [of the instruction]. [End of section] Paṭala, Kāṇḍa, Adhyāya, Anuvāka. With the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 473.

The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the *prāśitra*, and the *iḍā* are performed. Once the *prāśitra* has been consumed, they offer portions of rice to the attendants (*amātya*) who are entitled to eat the sacrificial oblation (*havirbhojana*).
He gives the rice remaining in the vessel to those attendants who are entitled to eat the oblation—that is, those other than women and the uninitiated (*anupanīta*).
The wife eats the rice cooked by the neighbor.

According to the Vaikhānasa, [the ritual includes] the wife, the woman, and the son. The Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice concludes with the *iḍā* portion. However, the *pūrṇādarvi-homa* (the offering from the full ladle) is not an auxiliary of this [Gṛhamedhīya], but rather of the Kraiḍinīṣṭi. Bharadvāja states that one initiates the procedure for the Kraiḍina before the morning Agnihotra, performing the rite with the *pūrṇādarvi*; thus it is said that it "concludes" (*saṃtiṣṭhate*) when [the Agnihotra] has been performed.

They apply collyrium, they anoint themselves, and they allow the calves to stay with their mothers. Collyrium is applied to the eyes of all the attendants, as well as of the husband and wife and the unmarried girls. After that, the anointing is performed; this refers to the anointing of the feet. The calves are made to stay together with their mother-cows; these acts are to be performed. And the neighbors cook [the food].
They kill other animals as well; they slaughter cows and cook them for seasoning.

They dwell this night well-satisfied, contented, and with faces free from distress. "Well-satisfied" means satiated; "contented" means affectionate. That which has no *avarti*—meaning distress or weariness—is "anavarti"; that which is on the face is "anavarti-mukha. Those who possess such [faces] are so described; that is to say, they have faces that are untired and pleasing.
In the latter part of the night, he binds the two calves of the cow intended for the *agnihotra* sacrifice, whose calf has been led away (*abhivānyavatsā*).

The calf is to be one that has been milked. That cow whose calf has died and which has been made to flow with milk by means of another calf is [the one to be used]. According to their statement, for those two purposes—the purpose of churning and the purpose of the Agnihotra—there are no two milks. "The other portion of the night is turned away" means the night is spent with the face turned away.
Before the morning Agnihotra, they proceed with the *pūrṇadarvyā* offering.
The oblation performed with the mantra beginning with "Full" (*pūrṇā*) is the *pūrṇādarvihoma*.

Having spread a base of clarified butter in the ladle, having filled the ladle with the residue of the *śara* (barley-gruel), and having taken a portion from the wiped-off scrapings (*nimṛṣṭa*) for the purpose of pouring over it;

then, having filled the ladle with the mixture contained in the pot along with the *śara*, and having wiped it clean, having taken a portion from the wiped-off scrapings as if for the purpose of pouring over it, and having poured clarified butter over it. 1. Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṭa, Ṭha, I, Ṇa: *kriyate*. 2. Pa, I: *trātpīrṇada*. 3. Ca, Ta: *pūrṇāda*. 4. Gha, I, Ja, Ma, Ma, Da, Ṇa: *ca*. 5. Ga, 4, Cha, Ṇa: *pracarati*. 6. Jha, Na: *kāsena da*.
Having recited the verse, "Full is the ladle" (*pūrṇā darvī*), and having summoned the bull with the words, "Give me," he offers an oblation into the *gārhapatya* fire while the bull is bellowing.

Having uttered the mantra ending with "O Śatakratu," he then summons—that is, calls—the bull, the draft-ox. It is well known in this world that when a cow is called by its wife, the bull bellows; while that sound is being made, he offers the oblation into the *gārhapatya* fire with the mantra ending in "svāhā" and concluding with "I lead you out" (*niharāmi ta*). Indra is the deity, according to the scriptural authority: "The *śara* belongs to Indra."
When the bull has bellowed, he should address the Brahman priest and, being permitted by him, offer the oblation.

Having addressed him with "O Brahman, I shall sacrifice," he prepares a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts Krīḍins. According to some teachers, he should perform the offering at the same time as the sun rises, saying, "They move together with the rays."
The meaning is clear. The *tantra* (ritual procedure) of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsa*) is concluded.

At that very time, one sacrifices with the Mahāhavis offerings. When the sacrifice is completed, one sacrifices with the offerings known as the Mahāhavis. In that context, those offerings are also to be designated as belonging to the Sākamedha. Thus, in all five sacrifices beginning with the Ānīkavat, they are simply called "the Sākamedha offering."
Their ritual procedure is explained by that of the northern sacrificial enclosure (*uttara-vihāra*) used for the *Vāruṇapraghāsa* sacrifice.

The purpose of the assembly (*gaṇārthatā*) is explained by the ritual actions of the northern enclosure; in this case, the option of not departing from the sacrificial ground (*anudavasāna-pakṣa*) is more beneficial for many.
Having offered the five common oblations (*saṃcara*), he offers a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and Agni, a pap (*caru*) for Indra, and a cake on one potsherd for Viśvakarman.
The meaning is clear.
Having threshed the unmixed *aindrāgna* [grain], he sets aside its well-known husks.

Like the sowing of various seeds, there is a separate threshing; for that very *aindrāgna* portion, he sets aside the husks for the purpose of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath). The sowing of the other [grains] is done with their own respective husks.

As on the full moon day of Kārttika and likewise on that of Āṣāḍha, he takes the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya); but on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, it is as on that of Śrāvaṇī. [The meaning is] explained. He pours the oblation from the ladle with the formula: "O Agni, fulfill the office of the Hotṛ; fulfill the office of the messenger; standing erect at the sacrifices, may Heaven and Earth protect thee; do thou protect Heaven and Earth. O Sviṣṭakṛt, be for Indra and for the gods. Accepting this oblation of clarified butter, enjoy it—Svāhā! Thus he pours the āghāra-libation.
In the second *āghāra* offering, the specific mantra has its meaning already explained. Indra, or the gods (*devāḥ*), are the deity.

With the four names of the months—*sahaḥ* and *sahasyaḥ*, etc.—he makes an oblation upon the single-pot-sherd cake (*ekakapāla*) with the formula: "To *sahaḥ*, svāhā! To *sahasya*, svāhā! The meaning is understood. [End of] Chapter 1, Section 550, from the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva. 475.
"In the hope for the well-being of those who dwell through the years, he prays for the divine abode"—with these words of blessing from the *sūktavāka*, the Hotṛ priest follows along.
This is for the sake of the journey.
They perform the *avabhṛtha* (concluding purificatory bath) with the husks of the rice offered to Indra and Agni; thus, both the act of going and the disposal of the husks are carried out. || 10 ||
Thus ends the third paṭala in the fifth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

[This is] for the sake of going. Here, the word *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) is used figuratively, as it does not denote the actual [bath] as before; therefore, it is stated [in this way] to show that there is an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of other rites. The meaning is: having performed only as much as is connected with the departure, and having gone to the *avabhṛtha*, one should dispose of the husks silently. Thus ends the third section on the Sākamedha in the fifth book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* composed by Mahādeva. || 3 ||
5.4 Now, the fourth chapter in the fifth book:

At that very time, he performs the Mahāpitṛyajña. Since the sacrifice dedicated to the Great Ancestors (*mahāpitṛdevatāka*) follows the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, it possesses equal status as a primary rite alongside the Sākamedha offerings and the Tryambaka offerings; for they are mentioned separately in the sequence: "the Sākamedhas, the Pitṛyajña, and the Tryambakas."

To the south and slightly to the east of the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire, he prepares a square altar (*vedi*) measuring one *yajamāna* (the height of the sacrificer). The specification "to the south and slightly to the east of the *dakṣiṇāgni*" indicates that it faces the *āhavanīya* fire; it is square and not elongated, following the measure of the standard altar. Its corners (*sraktayaḥ*) are directed toward each of the cardinal directions.

The corners of the altar are red; they are located in the cardinal directions. There, having fixed a peg in the middle of the *ūrdhvajyu* (the north-south line) and the *dakṣiṇāgni*, and having made it square, one places the loop of the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord upon the peg in the center, and that cord [extends] to the four corners of the southeast...

Having led [the cord] along the corner and stretched it out, one should then fix a *śaṅku* (peg) at the junction of the line for the southern sacrificial shed (*dakṣiṇānyāyatanaśramagāra*) and the cord. There, having placed a loop on both ends of a cord the length of which is equal to the sacrificer, and having stretched it across the second side, one fixes it upon the *pṛṣṭhyā* line where the peg was previously set; that is the eastern line. Having laid out a square measuring the width of the sacrificer by means of this cord, one should make the sides equal. That altar of the *Pitṛmedha*, bent at the intermediate corners and straight at the cardinal points, has its center thinned out from the intermediate directions.

The intermediate directions (vidiśaḥ) are narrow and contracted in their middles; the middle sections are four times as long. Regarding the intermediate directions... [Note: Variants noted in the manuscripts: kha, ga, ca, ṭa, ṭha, u, pa read "naṃ kiṃ"; ca, da read "samāna"; 1.1, da read "śānanu"; ja, sa, pa read "śātanu"; ca, ṭa read "viśānprati"]. It should be understood that in rites beginning with the *āmecya*, the directions such as east and so forth are established by their very nature.

The southern corner is to the south of the positions of the Brahman and the sacrificer; the *utkara* is to the north; the eastern corner is toward the east in the middle of the site. In the third part, at a distance of two steps near the western corner to the north, is the position of the *hotṛ*; the positions of the sacrificer and the *hotṛ* are established accordingly.
In all cases, one adapts the mantra addressed to the gods to include both the gods and the ancestors (*devapitṛvat*).

The inclusion of the term "all" (*sarva*) in all [categories] is for the purpose of excluding the opinion of Āpastamba; this will be explained later. A mantra is that which speaks of the gods (*deva-pravāda*), meaning it refers to them as being preeminent, as being the means of performance, or—in other words—as being inherent in the primary ritual acts. Thus, whatever speaks in such a manner is a mantra addressed to the gods.

The singular number is used for the purpose of indicating a genus (*jāti*). "Those [deities] possessing the mantra" (*mantravat*) refers to that naming-act (*abhidhānakarman*) in which the gods and the ancestors exist as the objects to be addressed; "sanati" means he honors them, and "tathohati" is an adverbial neuter expression. Alternatively, "he honors those beginning with the gods and ancestors like a mantra," performing it with both case-endings. Demonstrating the inclusion of the modified (*vikṛta*) rite immediately after the archetypal (*prākṛta*), he cites an example:

"Just as the earth is the place where offerings are made for the gods and ancestors, so you, O divine ancestral *barhis*, are strewn for the gods and ancestors; do not let me cut you from below nor across; may I be able to perform the rite for the gods and ancestors."

The mantras were recited as two [pairs] so that there might be no abandonment of the status of a deity through the act of donning armor. For it is stated here: "Both the gods and the ancestors are indeed honored. In that context, regarding the injunction, "He offers a six-potherd cake to Soma accompanied by the ancestors," Soma is worshipped as a god; he is called a "parent" (*pitṛ*) because he is the king of the ancestors. Regarding the offering, "To the ancestors seated on the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣat*)," it is said, "The months are indeed the ancestors seated on the grass"; thus, the deities who preside over the months possess that same nature.

In the same way, their status as ancestors (*pitṛtva*) is also heard of in subsequent passages: "Those who are indeed performers of sacrifice, they are the ancestors known as the Agniṣvātta-s. Since all possess both the state of being gods (*devatva*) and the state of being ancestors, the plural designation "the gods" (*devāḥ*) occurs; therefore, the intention is that both terms are to be included. Here, he has omitted the first mantra, *devasya tvā*.

In this regard, the intention is as follows: the word *deva* (god) denotes the deity being worshipped (*ijyamāna*), whereas the word *pitṛ* (father/ancestor) denotes one who is to be honored (*mahanīya*). Thus, it has been stated that the modification (*ūha*) is according to the actual meaning. However, since in this context only those ancestors who are being worshipped are applicable, the word *pitṛ* should be modified only in a mantra where the word *deva* refers to deities who are being worshipped. But in the mantra "of the god [his] own" (*devasya sva*), the word *deva* does not denote a deity being worshipped; rather, it signifies the nature of luminosity (*dyotana*) which is not inherent to the ritual act. Therefore, there is no modification of that word.

Regarding the worship (*upāsana*), Āpastamba states: "Those mantras which are connected with the gods, [beginning] with 'To the gods, to the ancestors' (*ye ke ca devasaṃyuktā mantrā devebhyaḥ pitṛbhyaḥ*)," he bows to them. As for the mantra "O Earth, you who are the place of sacrifice for gods and ancestors" (*pṛthivi devapitṛyajanī*), there is no modification (*avikāraḥ*) because of the hearing of the subsequent sentence. The sense is that, just as in the case of "to the gods" (*devebhyaḥ*), where the manifestation of the gods is directly present, so it is here as well; thus, when it is said "O Earth, you who are the place of sacrifice for gods and ancestors," the manifestation of the gods is inherently included. Regarding the bringing of the *barhis* grass, this is the first example.

The second *upasthāna* (worship) of the gods is that which establishes them; therefore, in the midst of that, there is a modification (*ūha*) of the *anvādhāna* mantras [for those ending in] *-ga*, *-ja*, *-śa*, *-ma*, *-da*, *-i*, *-ṇa*, and *-piṇ*. [Variants: 2. *ca*, *da*, *vaya*; 477; 4. *paṭalaḥ*. This is accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. It has not been stated there because the *vihavya* verses do not illuminate a meaning connected to the specific ritual context; thus, there is no conformity to the gender (*liṅga*), while the application to various rites is by means of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). In the worship during the *agnihotra*, it is performed by means of a certain part of the fire itself.

Therefore, these [formulas] do not serve to designate the deities of the New and Full Moon sacrifices; consequently, there is no modification (*ūha*) [of the words]. Furthermore, in phrases such as "I take Agni," there is no modification in the words denoting the deity, because that term is common to both gods and ancestors who receive a share of the oblation. For the word *deva* (god) here refers to the genus (*jāti*) as used in the archetype (*prakṛti*), and not to the specific term for a sacrificial deity (*devatā*), since the latter denotes the recipient of an offering (*saṃpradāna*). Thus, after stating, "He who first appropriates the deities," and following with "This indeed belongs to the gods," etc., the text concludes by including gods, ancestors, and humans in the summary, saying, "He takes Agni."

"He encompasses the deities in their own abode"—by this, all gods, humans, and ancestors are included under the term "deities" (*devatā*). The author of the Sūtra also uses the expression "the word *deva*" precisely to clarify the meaning that they are indeed called by the word *deva*. Thus, the phrase "those gods who are ancestors" (*tān devān pitṝn*) occurs; and it will be stated later: "O beloved one, come hither for the gods and the ancestors" (*devebhyaḥ pitṛbhyo juṣṭām ehi*). Furthermore, in the passage "The sacrificial grass of the gods and ancestors, with a hundred shoots," it is said: "Thou art the resort of the gods and ancestors."

In that regard as well, [the substitution] does not occur in the case of "yajā devān" (sacrifice to the gods). Where the word *deva* refers to the deities common to both the primary and subsidiary rites, or where it is intended for the primary rite alone, that is the single *ūha* (modification), and not any other; this is the first point. This will become clear in the ritual application (*prayoga*). In the Veda, one should recite "deva veda" without modification, and "devebhyo veda" is also not to be modified, because these function through the praise of an existing state of affairs (*bhūtārtha-stuti*).

In the passage, "Thou art the Veda, thou art acquisition, may I acquire," the actual state of affairs is understood through the deities' nature as the knowers of acquisition; here too, it is so because of the past-participial suffix (*bhūta-pratyaya*) in the word *abhava*. "Whatever the gods and the ancestors perform"—this refers to the three types of rites: those involving the primary oblation (*pradhāna-havis*), those involving the sacrificial formulas (*mantra*), and those involving the purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*). Just as there are the subsidiary acts such as the pouring out of the offering, the inspection, the threshing, and so forth, ending with the placing of the vessels (*āsādana*), so too are those [rites].

Certain things are to be known as belonging to the primary act (*pradhāna*), while others are subordinate (*aṅga*) and have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). The first category consists of those [acts] that are subordinate and have an unseen purpose, such as the taking up of the *āsya* vessel for the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles. The second category consists of those acts which are subordinate and consist of the preparation of substances (*dravyasaṃskāra*), such as the *anvādhāna*, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the washing of the hands, the preparation of the altar (*vedikaraṇa*), and the pouring out of the clarified butter (*ājyanirvāpa*). The third category consists of those acts which prepare substances for the sake of both the subordinate and the primary acts, such as the *anvādhāna*, the sacrificial grass, the washing of the hands, the preparation of the altar, the pouring out of the clarified butter, and so forth. Among these, there is no modification (*ūha*) in the case of those with an unseen purpose, nor in the case of those that manifest what is already present (*samavetaprakāśaka*), such as "O gods, come hither" (*devān yakṣi*) or "Of the god... (*devasya tvā*), and so on.

In the other [rites], the substitution of the word "pitṛ" (father/ancestor) for the words denoting the deities associated [with the rite] must be performed. On this point, some say: "In the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) involving the principal substance, the word 'pitṛ' takes the place of the word 'deva' (deity). Their intention is that Soma and the others are indeed of the nature of *pitṛ*s. As for the statement in the Śruti, "For both the gods and the *pitṛ*s are worshipped," that refers to those who are not the primary [deities]. That [view] is extremely weak; for the Śruti declares that each one of Soma and the others possesses a dual nature.

Why? Because both sets of characteristics are observed through the alternative injunctions: "He offers from the south, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī)," and likewise, "Having brought it from the north, he should set it down. Furthermore, by such statements as "Soma is indeed the year, possessed of the ancestors," the dual nature of the principal deities themselves is expressed; therefore, even in mantras such as "Thou art for the gods," although the word "gods" (deva) is present, the word "ancestors" (pitṛ) must also be inserted as a second term—this is the summary. Here, first having prepared the *veda* grass-bundle, he says that he prepares the altar (*vedi*) itself: having performed everything up to the sweeping, having enclosed it on all sides, and having made a door in the northern corner.

According to the Śruti text, "The altar is indeed that which ends at the *uddhana* (the dug-out portion) and is not excavated," the mantra beginning with "imāṃ narāḥ" (*imāṃ narā upa sīdata*) and so forth is not omitted, as it serves an invisible (transcendental) purpose. In the absence of the *svādanapraiṣa* (the call for tasting), there is the *pūrvaparigrāha* (the first tracing out). The enclosure of the altar on all sides with mats and the like constitutes its covering. Having made the northern corner the entrance, one brings embers from the *dakṣiṇāgni*, places them in the middle of the altar, and adds fuel to them.
"Fire is established in the middle," according to the Śruti;
this [fire] here is the Āhavanīya. This has been explained.

Having added fuel to the Āhavanīya, Gārhapatya, and Dakṣiṇāgnis—this sequence is stated in order to declare that there is no adding of fuel (*anvādhāna*) to this very Āhavanīya, even though it has been carried forward (*praṇīta*) from the archetype (*prakṛta*). Otherwise, if one were to say simply "having added fuel," it would follow that the adding of fuel applies to all three fires; thus, to prevent this from applying to the Āhavanīya of the archetype which is not a constituent part (*anaṅga*) here, only the three specific fires are mentioned. With the formula, "I encompass the gods and the ancestors," he takes the sacrificial oblation for the Mahāpitṛyajña.

He brings the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); the sacrificial grass is longer than that used in the archetype, and he lays it down with its roots, or having cut it near the roots.

The fuel (idhma) and the sacrificial grass (bahir) are longer than those prescribed in the archetype; for the Śruti states, "The fuel becomes longer than the [archetypal] fuel. As for the sacrificial grass, it is torn out together with its roots, or cut near the root, as was done previously; there is no separate cutting, nor is there a mantra for that. He binds all the enclosing sticks (paridhi), or two of them. He brings together two or three pieces of fuel. When there are two, then the modification (ūha) is "twentyfold"; if not, then it is not. This is because it has been stated that when the *sāmidhenī* verses are the same, it should be according to the archetype.
At the time of arranging the vessels, he sets out the vessels according to their purpose. [This has been explained.
For Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs, there are six potsherds; for the Pitṛs seated on the sacrificial grass (barhiṣad), there is a potsherd for the parched grains (dhānā).
"Sthalam" means a place. For the ancestors known as the Agniṣvātta-pitṛs, there is a vessel for the sake of the *mantha*—either a vessel made of *varaṇa* wood or an earthen *śarāva*.
A vessel made of *varaṇa* wood or an earthen *śarāva*.

At the time of the pouring out [of the grains], the Adhvaryu, having mounted the cart from the south, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), pours out the barley. It is the Adhvaryu alone who wears the sacred thread over the right shoulder, because the rule for all [participants] to wear it that way has been prescribed. [This applies] even to him. Having mounted the cart from the north and wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), he pours out the oblation.
He offers a cake on six potsherds to Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs, or else clarified butter (ājya).
However, the clarified butter is [offered] only at the time of the watch (yāmaka), not now; the meaning is that he proceeds with the sacrifice using clarified butter.
He offers parched grains (*dhānā*) to the *barhiṣad* ancestors and a stirred drink (*mantha*) to the *agniṣvātta* ancestors; according to some, a stirred drink for Yama as well.
One may optionally consider these two deities as alternatives.
Having mixed barley with the surplus of the sprinkling water, they thresh it.
[The procedure] has been explained. When [the grains] have been husked three times, he divides them with the *vibhāga* mantra and grinds six potsherds' worth;
he grinds that very portion. At the time of placing [the cakes]—

Having placed six potsherds on the southern half of the *gārhapatya* fire, he places a potsherd in the *dakṣiṇāgni* for the purpose of roasting the parched grains (*dhānā*) using the first *kapāla-mantra*.
The potsherd is one suitable for roasting the *dhānās*; the mention of "first" is for the purpose of excluding the *mūha* (the second mantra).
Having placed the set of six potsherds over the fire and poured [the grain] onto them with the *adhiśrayaṇa-mantra*, he roasts the *dhānās*.
Seeking other things for the sake of drink, they lie around without being burned. 11.
The meaning is that he acts in such a way that the grains, while still in the pan, do not get burnt. The altar is not dug out; having performed the second tracing around, it is as explained before.
He proceeds with the formal command (*saṃpraisha*); he issues the command for everything other than the binding of the wife’s girdle. This has been explained.
He does not bind the wife, nor does he sit beside her; remaining seated in the house itself, she gazes at the clarified butter (*ājya*).
This is clear.

Having performed that which was previously done prior to taking the clarified butter (ājya), and having brought it back, he takes the clarified butter at the Gārhapatya fire. He takes the clarified butter after bringing it toward the Gārhapatya; there is a taking [of the butter] after bringing it back again.
In the marginal notes (pustakaṭippaṇyā) of the manuscripts Gā., Ca., Ṭa., and Ṭha., the reading is "ṇamanyapra".

16. I. reads "ṇadhānā"; I. reads "madhānādhaiṃ da". 2. Ca., Da., and others read "maupānā". 3. Kha., Ga., Ha., and Tha read "braṇathā". The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Book Five, Chapter Fifteen:
All [portions] are taken four times, or twice in the Upabhṛt ladle.
Having performed the *prayāja* offerings excluding the *apabahiṣaḥ*, he takes four portions twice each for the *upabhṛt*.

Having consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* waters and addressed the *brahmán*, and having sprinkled the fuel, the altar, and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he pours out the remainder of the *prokṣaṇī* waters, inserts the two strainers (*pavitra*) [into the vessel], and takes up the tips of the sacrificial grass.
This very procedure was previously stated in order to prescribe it.
Shaking the fire three times from left to right, he goes around it; holding the *prastara* upright, he goes back around three times without shaking it.

Having grasped the entire *barhis* grass, he goes around the fire counter-clockwise, scattering the blades of grass as he shakes them, until he has gone all the way around. He leaves behind that portion which was originally grasped by the fist, and while still holding that very *prastara*, he goes back around in the same manner, spreading [the grass] clockwise. This indeed is the spreading of the altar; the *prastara* becomes possessed of its calf, as in the archetype.
He lays down two enclosing sticks, or all of them; the meaning is already explained.
Since the two separating blades are prohibited, he silently places the *prastara* [grass-bundle] down and proceeds with the ritual acts beginning with the removal [of the fires].

According to the Śruti, "In place of the *prastara* [grass-bundle], one should silently deposit the *upam̐śu* [grass] even without the *vidhṛti*s," he therefore deposits a handful as the *prastara*. Having performed that which was previously done prior to the decoration, it is concluded.

Having divided the grains with the *vibhāga-mantra* and having prepared half of the flour into groats (*saktu*) according to the procedure for flour (*piṣṭānām āvṛtā*), one separates them according to their respective portions, thinking, "May I distinguish them part by part. Having thus separated them, one grinds the flour according to the procedure for flour—namely, by the method beginning with placing [the vessel] upon the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*). The Vārttikakāra has established that the phrase "according to the procedure for flour" is intended to indicate the underlying principle (*nyāya*), or rather, to ensure that the original ritual properties (*prākṛta-dharma*) are obtained even when the cooking and grinding are performed out of their normal sequence.

Sitting to the south and not touching [the vessel], he churns three times counter-clockwise with a stalk of sugarcane the *mantha* stirred from the milk of a cow whose calf has been led away, in a vessel made of *vāraṇa* wood or in a half-śarāva measure; he forms the *mantha* as a mass around the stalk.

Facing south, he churns three times counter-clockwise the flour for the *ābhivānya* oblation—which has been mixed with curds and placed in a vessel used for warding off evil—without touching it directly. How then does he churn? Regarding this, it says: [he uses] sugarcane stalks. [Note: This passage is from the *Vaikhānasa-smārtasūtra*, with commentary by Mahādeva known as the *Vaijayantī*. The flour for the *ābhivānya* sacrifice consists of half-measures of parched grain.]

481. With a stirring-stick (*mantha*) made of *chāka-pā* wood, or with a bundle of small sticks (*śalākā-samudāya*), he stirs the milk in the *vāraṇa* vessel using a *śarāva* cup; the specific cord is the *taracharāva*, which is half-filled with milk. The rest is as before. Having taken a single fire-brand (*ekolmuka*) from the *dakṣiṇāgni* while it is smoking, having carried it westward past the *gārhapatya*, having carried it around the front of the *āhavanīya*, he places it to the south of the *āhavanīya* within the altar (*antarvedi*).

Having brought [the fire] from the west and led it back toward the east, having passed behind the Gārhapatya, and having brought it to the north of the sacrificial ground (vihāra), he carries it around the Āhavanīya fire and leads it along the front of the Dakṣiṇāgnī fire; then, to the south of that very fire, he places the embers.
Having adorned them, he sets down the clarified butter and the oblations one by one.

Taking each portion of clarified butter and each oblation individually, he places them one by one on the southern side of the Āhavanīya fire upon the bundles of sacrificial grass (barhis), according to the original model.
To the south, he places collyrium, ointment, a mattress, a pillow, and a water-pot.
On the southern side of the sacrificial oblation, he sets down soot for collyrium, whey or oil for ointment, a mattress, a bolster, a head-pillow, and a water-filled pot.
He puts on the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) if he has been wearing it over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*).

At the time of placing the oblation (*havir-nipaṇa*), if he is wearing the sacrificial thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), then that state indeed exists. If, however, he were wearing it over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) at that time, he should likewise maintain the *yajñopavīta* position for this duration.
He issues the command: "Recite for Agni, for the gods, and for the ancestors, as he is being kindled.
This command is based on the explicit scriptural injunction (*vācanika*), and not by means of modification (*ūha*), because there is no occasion for modification here.

He recites this *sāmidhenī* verse, "Desiring you, we invoke you," three times. He recites one [verse] once and another three times; thus, this *yājuṣa-hautra* (the sacrificial priest's recitation according to the Yajurveda), as read in the *Ādhvaryava-kāṇḍa*, has been explained. Herein, regarding the *yājuṣa-hautra*, he himself will state later: "With the first [verse] there is no interruption of the sacrifice, nor with the subsequent one. For those two verses seen by Viśvāmitra, there is no recitation (*anuvacana*) that interrupts the gods. Having divided the fuel-stick (*idhma*) into three parts, he places the whole of it on the fire.
In each of the five [verses], he places one *praṇava* at the end of each; in all [the verses] he places them thus.

When the deities have been brought near (*oḍhāsu*), having offered the *upavāja* and poured the *sruva*-oblation, he issues the command: "O Āgnīdhra, cleanse the enclosing-sticks and the fire three times each. Once they have been cleansed, he chooses the *pravara*. 12.

Whether there are two enclosing-sticks (paridhi) or three, it is according to the original model (prakṛti). That which follows immediately after the first pouring (āghāra) is the modification (vikṛti); the rest remains as in the original model. When the two [fires] have been cleansed and the fire has been led forward, the *pravara* (invocation of ancestors) is performed with only this much: "Sit down, O Hotṛ."

Impelled by Brahmā and having caused the announcement, he says, "O Hotṛ! Bhāradvāja and Āpastamba state this very thing; it has been said that this is all there is to say. The rest is clear. Having released the *mucya* [ladle] and supported the *āghārya* [ladle], he performs the *prayāja* offerings excluding the *barhis*; he does not pour from the *upabhṛt*. The meaning is already explained.

The two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) contain the word "jīvātu. These are the optional portions characterized by specific qualities. Having performed the offering with these two, [he proceeds].
[The section] on going is finished. Having loosened their sacrificial threads (*yajñopavīta*), they make them into *prācīnāvīta* [threads].
Together with the sacrificer, all loosen their sacrificial threads, having made them slack, and all make them into *prācīnāvīta*.
They exchange the clarified butter offerings and the sacrificial oblations;
they arrange them out of their regular order;
and the officiating priests move about in a reversed direction.
They stand in reverse order.
He places the *upabhṛt* ladle to the south of the *juhū* ladle;
the *juhū* has returned to its proper place, and the *upabhṛt* is in its southern part.
To the south [he places] the *upabhṛt* ladle and the *dhruvā* ladle;
to the north of those, the vessel together with the *sruva* spoon. This has been explained.
To the south [of that], he sets down the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and the parched grains (*dhānāḥ*); to the south of the grains, the stirred drink (*mantha*).
[The section] is concluded. The Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Āgnīdhra move around by way of the south.
Standing at the northern pit, they come to the southern corner and stand there.

To the north stand Brahmā and the sacrificer. They both remain with their right shoulders turned toward [the fire] and their faces turned to the north. All [priests] face the Āhavanīya fire. The *juhū* ladle and the six-pot-sherd offering are common to all.

There is no transposition of these two; rather, they both remain in their respective original positions. [The syllables] *gha*, *i*, *ja*, *ma*, *ma* are possessed of life (*jīvavant*). Regarding the two *anuvākyās*, their displacement was mentioned previously; in that regard, there is an option. According to the statement of Āpastamba and Bharadvāja—"Some maintain they remain as before;

having taken portions from all the oblations, he sacrifices to each deity individually, taking a single portion from each of the three [sets] at once"—he sacrifices to each deity one by one. He says this very thing:

Having spread a base of clarified butter in the *juhu* ladle and having taken a portion from the *puroḍāśa*, he takes up some of the parched grains (*dhānās*), and then [some] of the stirred drink (*mantha*).

The taking of the portion from the *mantha* is done only once; this is because the scriptural injunction regarding "taking up" (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of consecration (*saṃskāra*). Otherwise, how could there be an offering of another [substance] after it has been poured out? Therefore, it is said, "he takes up.
He pours clarified butter over it twice—four times for one who offers four portions, and three times for one who offers five portions.

According to the instruction of the sacrificer who has performed the four-fold cutting (*caturavadāna*), there is a sixfold portion (*ṣaḍavatta*) here by means of two sprinklings (*dvirabhighāraṇa*), while for the other [portion] there is a sevenfold portion (*saptāvatta*) by means of three sprinklings.

He issues the command: "Recite the invitatory verse (*anuṣvadhā*) for Soma accompanied by the ancestors (*pitṛmat*). He recites two invitatory verses; each one of these should be accompanied by the *praṇava*.

There should be two invitatory verses ending with the *praṇava*. As exceptions to [the usual sequence of calls], namely *bahiḥ*, *śrāvaya*, *śrauṣaṭ*, *ye yajāmahe*, and *vaṣaṭ*, the word *svadhā* is prescribed in place of these five, and at the place of the *vaṣaṭ*-call, the words *svadhā namaḥ* are used.
When it is said, "Open the enclosing sticks," he joins the southern and northern enclosing sticks together with the middle one;
he sets them down together. When the three words of the *pādhyā* verse—"For by you indeed our fathers [offered] preceded by Soma... winning the forest-dwelling...
the enclosing sticks..."—are being heard, he steps across toward the north and calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* with "Oṃ svadhā!"

Standing to the south, having approached with a reddish face, he causes the announcement to be made with "Let there be *svadhā*," facing toward the south; so too in other Sūtras. He responds with "Let there be *svadhā*";
he issues the command, "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, *svadhā*!"; the response is "Those who [desire] *svadhā*, *Om*!"; and he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call as "Svadhā! Homage! (*svadhā namaḥ*).

The *pluta* (protracted) vowel is to be understood as it occurs in the original form even when applied to the modified forms (*vikāra*). For example: *vṛtrahaṃ pūyāsam*. Likewise, the *pitaro bārhaṣadaḥ* and *pitaro'gnisvāttāḥ* are modifications of the *āgneya* and *saumya* offerings, due to their being distinguished by specific qualifiers. The rest has already been explained. It must be deliberated whether or not the *anānāvat* is required. 1. [Variants: cha. ja. sa. ma. da. read *mānau cale*; 2. kha. ga. gha. ca. ja. sa. ma. ṭa. ka. ṇa. read *ma upa*] 484. According to Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra—[Fifth Praśna]:
By this very procedure, he proceeds with the subsequent two [offerings].

The grains (*dhānā*) are for the other two oblations. Regarding the phrase "this much" (*etāvat*), it refers to what has been stated concerning the portions to be cut off for those who offer four cuttings and those who offer five cuttings; as for whatever else remains beyond that, he himself demonstrates it directly.

Having stepped across to the south and spread an underlayer of ghee in the *juhū* ladle, he takes a portion of the parched grains (*dhānā*) and adds a portion from the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Then, having stepped across to the north, he issues the call: "For the fathers seated on the sacrificial grass (*pitṛbhyo barhiṣadbhyaḥ*), [an offering] with *svadhā*! He causes the announcement to be made: "Let there be *svadhā*! The response is: "Let there be *svadhā*! He issues the call: "To the fathers seated on the sacrificial grass, *svadhā*! The *āgūḥ* formula is: "Those who have come for the *svadhā*... He utters the *vaṣaṭ* as "Svadhā! Adoration! Having stepped across to the south and spread an underlayer of ghee in the *juhū*, he takes a portion from the stirred drink (*mantha*) and [from the cake]...

He takes a portion from the rice-cake; then, having called out, "For the fathers, Agniṣvātta-s, *anusvadha*," he steps across toward the north, causes the announcement to be made with "Let there be *āśrāvaṇa*," and the response is given with "Let there be *svadhā*. He issues the direction, "To the fathers, Agniṣvātta-s, *svadhā*! The *āgūr* formula is "Those who [deserve] the *svadhā*," and he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call as "*svadhā namaḥ*. By this same ritual procedure, he sacrifices to Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt. Having stepped across to the south, he spreads a base of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle and cuts a portion from the rice-cake.

He takes up portions of the parched grains; then, for the Mantha, he issues the direction: "To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, svadhā! Having stepped across toward the north, he causes the announcement to be made with "Svadhā! The response is "Astu svadhā! He issues the direction: "To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, svadhā! The *āgūḥ* formula is "Ye svadhāmaha," and he utters the *vaṣaṭ* as "Svadhā namaḥ. || 13 ||
In this context, within the discussion of repetition, it should be understood that this is for the purpose of refuting the Vaikṛtika position seen in another Sūtra.
Some authorities prescribe the Sviṣṭakṛt offering at the end.

Having set aside the *mandha* for Sviṣṭakṛt itself, that very deity belongs to the ancestors who have entered the fire (*agniṣvātta*) by way of modification; however, Yama is [the deity] by way of modification, as has already been shown previously. Thus, these three deities are to be understood in the expansion of the *mandha*. For this very reason, Āpastamba says: "As prescribed: to Yama Agni Kavyavāhana, or to Yama, the *mandha*. And likewise, for the sacrifice to Sviṣṭakṛt, one again offers that same *mandha* to Sviṣṭakṛt;
since it is not enjoined in the place characterized by Sviṣṭakṛt which was previously established, there is indeed the Sviṣṭakṛt offering with the formula "May he not neglect us."

He does not cut off the *prāśitra* portion because of the prohibition. [15. ja. ma.u. As for the subsequent [portion], it is according to the respective deity. ... ja. a. na. da. [Regarding] the *sauṣiṣ*: "He does not offer that at all," and "ṭa, only the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) belongs to him. [410 pahā] This is accompanied by the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva.
In this very manner, he cuts off the *iḍā* portion.

From all the remnants of the oblations, those who take four portions or five portions do so according to the prescribed rule for cutting the portions (*avadāna*). Regarding the *manthin* and the *iḍā*, some say he cuts the *iḍā* from the *manthin*; others say he cuts the *manthin* and the *iḍā* together; still others say he cuts only the *manthin-iḍā* and nothing else; or there is an alternative view that he cuts only from the *manthin*.
Having set aside the *mantha* for the purpose of smelling it,
one should set down the known remainder of the *mantha* separately after having extracted it from the vicinity of all the remnants of the oblation (*havis*).
Then, one should join the remnants of the oblation to the *iḍā*.
Those remnants of the oblation (*havis*) that remain after the offerings have been made, he should not cause them distress;
rather, having gathered them together by crushing them, he places three balls (*piṇḍas*) in the three corners [of the fire-altar] with the three formulas:

"This for you, O Father, and for those who follow you"; "This for you, O Grandfather, and for those who follow you"; "This for you, O Great-grandfather, and for those who follow you. Regarding this, the teacher Āpastamba has also stated the same in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* ritual, and thus the word "this" (*asau*) is not used here. Consequently, some maintain that the mantras should be understood as being exactly like those of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. He now states the locations for the balls:
[He offers] in the eastern half, the southern half, and the western half.
The eastern half is that which is full in the east; while it exists, he successively pours the drops of the rice-ball upon it. This is indeed the Adhvaryu's duty.
He wipes the smearings on the northern [half].
He wipes the handle of the ladle on the northern corner.

Having said, "O Fathers, partake according to your portions," they go out toward the north—all the priests together with the sacrificer, standing to the south. If the Brahman and the sacrificer were both to the north, then the others [always] remain [to the south].

Then they approach the Āhavanīya fire. The officiating priests, moving toward the south, come near the Āhavanīya; from there, they stand to the north and worship the Āhavanīya with the verse: "Thee, who art so fair to behold, we [approach]."
Up to the word "harī" [the mantra is recited].
They remain until the breath is exhausted; having restrained the breath, they remain for as long as there might be an immersion in sin.
They worship the Gārhapatya fire with the verse beginning, "They have eaten,
they have rejoiced," ending with the word "harī.
They proceed with the verse beginning, "The fathers have eaten, the fathers have rejoiced."
They come from the north up to the end of the *madantī* (hot water) passage.
The Hotṛ smells the stirred offering (*mantha*).
The Hotṛ smells the portion of the stirred offering that has been set apart from the remainder of the oblation.
Then the Adhvaryu, then the Brahman, then the Āgnīdhra, and then the sacrificer—
these also smell that very *mantha* in succession.
According to some, the Hotṛ, having smelled the *mantha*, pours it out within the altar.
No others enter.
Taking a water-pot, he goes around three times clockwise, sprinkling [water] while reciting, "Coming hither, generating heroic deeds. He goes around the sacrificial altar. This is clear.
Having set down the water-pot, he goes around three times sprinkling [water] behind him; the meaning of this has already been explained.

Here they prescribe the application of collyrium and ointment, the gift of clothing, the salutation without rising, the *pravāhaṇī*, the *saṃsādhanī*, the *manasvatī*, and the verses addressed to the *Paṅkti* and *Prājāpatya* meters.

He says: "He sprinkles water," "O you who dwell in the new moon," "These indeed," "Homage to you, O fathers," "Rise up, O fathers, having gone before," "Go forth, O fathers," "Let them go, O fathers," "We invoke the mind hither," "They have eaten, they have rejoiced," "O Prajāpati"—with these [verses], he states that the rite should be performed according to the injunctions, just as in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. This has been explained.
They uncover the enclosure;
they remove the covering;
they spread out the enclosing sticks.
They arrange them in their proper places.
Having loosened their *prācīnāvīta* [sacred threads], this is a restatement (*anuvāda*). He prescribes [the following]:

While they are putting on the sacrificial threads (*yajñopavīta*), they transpose the clarified butter offerings and the oblations. Moving around, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) perform two after-offerings (*anūyāja*) without the *barhis* grass. [The Adhvaryu] gives the call: "O gods... [and so forth]. He issues the direction for the first after-offering as "Sacrifice! and for the second as "Sacrifice! The Hotṛ puts on the *nivīta* (the sacred thread over the right shoulder) at the *sūktavāka*. They do not perform the joint sacrifice of the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*), nor do they offer the *samiṣṭayajus*. Everything else is performed. 14. [End of] Chapter 550, with the commentary *Baijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.
Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the fifth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

These have been explained by the [preceding] statements. He performs everything from the offering of the flour-paste (piṣṭalepa) and the husks (phalīkaraṇa), the Sārasvata offerings, and so forth, up to the end of all expiations (sarvaprāyaścitta). Thus ends the fourth chapter on the Mahāpitṛyajña in the fifth book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* composed by Mahādeva.
Now begins the fifth chapter in the fifth book:
He offers the cakes for Rudra (raudra) and Tryambaka, one cake on a single potsherd (ekakapāla) for each person.

The Rudras are the deities for the offering; they are indeed those named "Ayaṃbaka. [One should offer] one more than the number of the sacrificer’s attendants, including his wives. The meaning has already been explained.
They are performed silently.

Because these are *davihoma* offerings, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) from other rites; thus it is said they are "silent. Except for the mere act of pouring out the oblation, everything else is silent. They are cooked on the southern half of the *gārhapatya* fire.

The *puroḍāśas* (sacrificial cakes) are the subject remaining [in the context]. One should sprinkle them with clarified butter or not sprinkle them; there is an option because the scriptural statement is identical.
Having removed the sacrificial cakes from either a container, two containers, or among the vessels and covers, [the cakes] are placed [therein].

A "container" (*mūrta*) is explained as a grass-made vessel for the purpose of binding grain; there is an option regarding their number. A "box" (*kośa*) is a basket or a chest, and its "cover" (*apidhāna*) is a lid. Having removed the cakes from some of these, they carry them forward. From the *dakṣiṇāgni*, a single burning coal, emitting smoke, is brought across behind the *gārhapatya* fire toward the west and carried in front [of the cakes].

[The sacrificers], with their faces turned away, looking downwards, and going outside while emitting smoke, together with their wives and ministers, [proceed] until they reach the place where the fire is being carried. This is clear. (In the versions *kha*, *ga*, *ṭha*, *ra*, and *pā*, there is the reading *nasya preṣyāmā*; in *i*, there is *madharmamā*; in *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṭa*, and *ṇa*, there is *pegā*). From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [Fifth Book]:

"As many as we are, householders," with these words he worships the *Gārhapatya* fire; they go to the north-eastern intermediate direction. It is the Adhvaryu alone [who recites]. The mantra ends with the words "for the second time, for completion."
They go toward the intermediate region between the north and the east.
All of them go outside the monastery toward the north-eastern direction, the corner of Īśāna. Then they go to where there is a crossroads.
Reciting, "O Rudra, the mouse is your sacrificial animal," he throws one *puroḍāśa* cake upon a molehill as he walks along.

The mantra ends with "enjoy that" (*taṃ juṣasva*). He places [the earth] dug up by a rat (*ākhu*) upon it, saying "go, O Kha. In such a way he should go to a crossroads so that the middle becomes a mole-hill (*ākholkara*).
Having kindled a single firebrand (*ekolmuka*) at the crossroads and having strewn [grass] around it—the crossroads being the junction of armor (*varma*)—this is clear.

Having taken portions from all the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) with a middle-sized *palāśa* leaf or the last one, and having sprinkled them with clarified butter, he offers it with the formula: "This, O Rudra, is thy portion.

Having taken a portion once from each of all the sacrificial cakes, he offers it upon the firebrand (*ulmuka*) with a *palāśa* leaf. The mantra ends with "taṃ juṣasva" (Be pleased with that). With the two verses beginning "bheṣajaṃ gavām" (The remedy for cattle), they pay reverence.

All of them stand by that fire with the section beginning with "vyavasāyaya" and ending with "āditya. Having taken the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas), one for each person— that is, for every individual.
With the mantra "We worship Tryambaka," they circumambulate the crossroads three times to the right.
The mantra is repeated for each individual circumambulation. Having stated the general rule, he states the specific procedure:
"Throwing them upwards, saying 'O blessed ones, you belong to Bhaga; may I obtain a share of Bhaga,' they take hold of them, circumambulate, and pour them together for the sacrificer."

First, having silently taken the *puroḍāśa* cake, he then hurls it upward into the air. Then, with the mantra "O Bhaga, stay! (*bhagavaḥ stha*), he catches the falling *puroḍāśa* as it descends. With the mantra "Tryambaka" (*tryambakam*), having gone around and returned [to the spot], he places it at a crossroads.
