Then, having placed it in the hollowed palms of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and taking it back again, he hurls it upward and catches it. Having gone around and placed it in the sacrificer’s palms once more—he does exactly the same in the third round as well.
In the Sūtra manuscripts, the word "they stand near" (*upatiṣṭhante*) is understood to follow.

[The various manuscript variants are noted as follows: Sa. Ga. Ha. Da. read "nti"; Bhā. 2 Gha. Ja. Sa. Ma. Da. read "hāśānām u"; Pa. Ka. read "nāntane"; Kha. Ma. Ca.... read "bhyaḥ"; Apra.... Da. read "paryeti"; Ga. Ka. Ca. Ja. Sa. Me. Ṭaṇaḥ read "sa parītya ya". [End of section 550]. [This concludes the] *Paṭala* accompanied by the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva.
If the sacrificer’s daughter should desire a husband, she should walk around [the fire] in reverse.
She [performs] that specific rite for Indra which is about to be described. He states that mantra:

"We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the bringer of a husband. May I be released from death, as a cucumber from its stem; may I not fall [into it]. Having circumambulated, he mutters this. (15) During the first two circumambulations, they pour [the grains] together for the sacrificer; during the last, for one who desires a husband. The mantra is the same for each circumambulation. Thus, during the circumambulation and the recitation, they pour together for the sacrificer; at the last [circumambulation], they pour for one who desires a husband. In the third round, they pour for one who desires a husband; in the first two rounds, they pour for the sacrificer, not in the third. If such a woman is not present, they pour for the sacrificer in all cases.
If she is unwilling even at the third stage, he binds those [portions] in a skin-bag, goes beyond two *gavyūtis*, and hangs them on a tree.

A *gavyūti* is two *krośas*; having gone even further than that, they tie the remains of the sacrificial cakes together with the skin-bag to a tree. "They hang them beyond the cow-pen," says Bharadvāja.

"This is your portion, O Rudra; accept it with favor. With that protection, go beyond the Mūjavat mountains, having unstrung your bow and holding the Pināka in your hand, clad in a skin-garment. Having thus recited the mantra ending with the syllable *Oṃ*, they stand without breathing until they can no longer hold their breath. This repetition is performed three times.
Then, having sprinkled water around, they return without looking back.
They pour water into the skin-bag. They return without looking back. Turning back, they do so without looking at the suspended skin-bag.
They purify themselves beyond the cow-pen (*goṣṭha*).
A *goṣṭha* is a place where cows rest; they purify themselves beyond that. Regarding this, Bhāradvāja says: "With the verse, 'May we be well-friends to one another... (RV 10.191.3).

With the formula, "Fuel art thou; may we prosper," he places fuel-sticks upon the Āhavanīya fire—either the Adhvaryu or the sacrificer, according to the singular number. With the formula, "I have followed the waters," they pay reverence [to the water].
All likewise.

In this manner, having placed [fuel] on the Gārhapatya fire, the wife stands in worship. This has been explained. [Notes: 1. kha. *mantrāva*; 2. ca.ṭa. *baṇa vi*; 3. kha. ga. dha. ha. ca. ṭa. 8. ṇa. *nādito mukṣī*; 4. gha. ja. sa. va. i. *patikāmā*; 5. va. ga. ba. u. u. ha. ṇa. *ti | pūrvo*; 6. ca, u. *samayatāni*. 62 [5 Fifth Praśna—The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—]]

Having returned, he offers a *caru* oblation of clarified butter to Āditya. Bhāradvāja maintains that this is not an independent ritual procedure (*ananyāyika-kalpa*). In that regard, it is stated that the *caru* is for Āditya alone; therefore, Aditi is the deity. Likewise, there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses. The entire portion of the *idā* belongs to the Brahman priest alone. Regarding the fourfold division of the portions: "This for the Brahman"—thus it is said. Āpastamba holds that all the portions belong to the Brahman alone, as in the previous case. Because of the explicit statement "having returned," this sacrifice is an ancillary part of the Tryambaka offerings. Thus, the Tryambaka rites are concluded.

On the following day, having performed the Full Moon sacrifice, whether they have moved out from the sacrificial ground or not, they moisten [the hair] with the mantra: "Impelled by the god Savitṛ... With the mantra: "He who upon the skin of this earth causes the plants to grow—Agni, ruling by his might, Varuṇa with his thoughts, Indra with his friends the Maruts, and Agni with his sharp flame"—they perform the shaving, which is the ritual of cutting, just as described previously.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fifth book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
5.6 Now begins the sixth chapter of the fifth book.

Then, on the second day, the third day, the fourth day, half a month, a month, a season, or after four months, he performs the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice. Its ritual procedure is explained by that of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. Having offered the five *saṃcara* oblations, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni, a pap for the Viśvedevas, a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra Śunāsīra, milk for Vāyu, a cake on one potsherd for Sūrya, barley-gruel for Vāyu, and curdled milk (*pratidhuk*) for Indra Śunāsīra; [then] a cake for Indra Śunāsīra.

Some authorities prescribe a cake on twelve potsherds as the final offering. Since it was performed on the previous full-moon day, it is called the *Śunāsīrīya* rite by virtue of the scriptural injunction and because it is characterized by Śunāsīra (Vāyu and Āditya). It has been stated that because there is no northern altar (*uttaravedi*), it is performed with the *Vaiśvadeva* [offering]. The meaning is already explained. In place of the milk-offering to Vāyu, there is a barley-gruel (*yavāgū*) for Vāyu. [End of] Paṭala 650, accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

On the previous day, having performed the fetching of the branch and other preliminary rites for the sake of the milk, he drives away the calves in the evening, along with the *upaveṣa* and the *śākhāpavitra*. In the morning, at the proper time, he causes the cow to be milked according to the procedure for the morning milking. This has been stated likewise by Āpastamba and Bharadvāja. The consecration (*anumantraṇa*) for the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) is the same as that for the *sāṃnāyya*. The gruel (*yavāgū*) is prepared according to the ritual rules for cooked grain. The milk is heated until it forms a skin (*pratidhuk*). In this very context, there is a traditional indicative mark (*rūdiliṅga*): it is well known [in common usage] that "the milk of a cow that has formed a skin is boiled."

The meaning of the scriptural statement (*śruti*) is that it is "cooked" (*śṛtam*) in that very [milk]. The indicative mark (*liṅga*) is found in the passage for the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*): "Prepare this cooked offering for him. Likewise, Bharadvāja also states: "The *pratidhuk* is milk that has been freshly drawn. Regarding the *pratidhuk* as gruel (*yāvaka*), that too belongs to Vāyu; having milked it according to the rules for milking, there is no washing of the vessel. That the sacrifice is performed by taking a portion only from what has been obtained (*āpta*) is to be understood as established by Kātyāyana through both the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Likewise, in the case of the Saurya sacrifice, the *puroḍāśa* cake prescribed for Indra in the highest position is from another recension (*śākhā*). Thus, in all these alternatives, there are ten oblations (*havīṃṣi*).
With the formula "The gliding one, to Aṃhaspatya thee," he makes an offering with the single-potsherd cake (*ekakapāla*) using the name of the final month.
According to Āpastamba as well, only one [name] is intended; it is exactly the same for him.

"He invokes the blessing of the annual [seasons]; he invokes the divine abode"—thus the Hotṛ repeats these blessings in the Sūktavāka, or he says "of the yearly" (*vatsarīṇām*). The meaning is already explained.

In the dark fortnight, having performed the *Samasya* sacrifice at its proper time, and having offered the *Paurṇamāsī* sacrifice, they either depart from the sacrificial ground (*udavasāya*) or do not depart (*anudavasāya*). When [the cows] have calved, they moisten them with water while reciting: "By the god Savitṛ... "One month Parameṣṭhin released for the sake of creatures; thereby he brought great bounty to them, bringing immortality to mortals. You are born again following the creatures; that indeed is your immortal part by which months, half-months, seasons, and years [are formed]. By which, O Prajāpati, you turned back for yourself as you were sacrificing—by that sacred word (*brahman*), I turn it back for this [person] so that he may live. [Then they touch] the fire...
With the verse "stigmena śociṣā," there is the turning back and the shaving, as previously described.

On the other fortnight—the dark fortnight—one should pile the *śunāsīrīya* sacrificial grass-bundles and sacrifice with them at their proper time. Having sacrificed with the *āmāvāsya* oblation at its proper time, and having sacrificed with the *paurṇamāsa* oblation at its proper time, then follows the injunction beginning with "departing from there" (*udavasāya*). This has already been explained. The Cāturmāsya sacrifices are completed;
the completion of the Cāturmāsyas ends with the *śunāsīrīya*, as they are followed by the Soma sacrifice and others.
"Phālgunī shall not reach this one who has not sacrificed with Soma.

This means that the full moon day of Phālguna (Phālgunī) shall not reach this sacrificer who has not yet performed the Soma sacrifice; that is to say, one must necessarily sacrifice with Soma on the full moon day of Phālguna. As for the alternative view that "one should sacrifice with the Śunāsīrīya [offering] during the four months," this is only possible when one intends to perform the sacrifice again, and not at other times; even in that case, it is on the day before the Phālgunī [full moon].

[6 Pañcamapraśna—Lic—492] According to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: One should proceed with the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice on the fourteenth day itself; thereafter, there is a renewed performance (*punaḥprayoga*) of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices on the full moon of Phālguna. Regarding the first commencement on the full moon of Caitra, the mention of Phālguna is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all such cases; all this has been clarified by Kātyāyana. The Soma sacrifice is the Agniṣṭoma. In the absence of Soma, one performs it with an animal sacrifice.
If unable to perform even that, one performs it with an animal sacrifice according to the *Nirūḍha-kalpa* on the immediately following Parvan day.

In the absence of an animal sacrifice, there is a repetition of the Cāturmāsya offerings. A sacrificial oblation (iṣṭi) has also been prescribed by Kātyāyana, Baudhāyana, and Āśvalāyana; if that is not performed, there is a repetition. This means that even without performing those [Cāturmāsyas], there is a repetition, which is to say a re-performance. Following that, completion is achieved through either a Soma sacrifice or an animal sacrifice. According to the followers of Kātyāyana, the oblation is dedicated to Agni (Āgneyī). Others have stated it is the Savaneṣṭi. The offering to Agni consists of a cake on eight potsherds (aṣṭākapāla), that to Indra-Agni on eleven potsherds (ekādaśakapāla), and that to the Viśvedevas on twelve potsherds (dvādaśakapāla); or else there is a Vaiśvadeva oblation of cooked rice (caru). These may share the same ritual framework (samānatantra) or have distinct frameworks (bhinna-tantra).
Having described the other Nitya Cāturmāsya sacrifices, he speaks of others:
"One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva at that spring in which there is most milk for him.
That is, one should commence it in that spring in which the yield of milk from the sacrificer's cows is abundant.

One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva [offering] until he obtains a thousand cattle. Until the attainment of a thousand cattle, there is a repetition of the Vaiśvadeva rite itself within the Vaiśvadeva section.
Once the thousand have been attained, he sacrifices with the other [deities] in their respective places.
When the time for the Varuṇapraghāsa has arrived, one should perform the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices; likewise, at the conclusion, there is either the Soma sacrifice or an animal sacrifice.

One who desires a village, offspring, cattle, rain, or food should sacrifice with the Śunāsīrīya [Iṣṭi]. Having settled near "varṇya" water—that is, having gone to where there is water existing in the rainy season—and performing his water-related needs from that very water, he sacrifices. From that very water, he fulfills the purpose of water.

We shall explain the five-year cycle of the Tantra. Having performed the Pañcahotṛ, Vaiśvānara, and Pārjanya sacrifices on the full moon of Phālguna, one should sacrifice for two seasons and two years, and then not sacrifice for the month of the third year. However, having performed them on the full moon of Caitra, one should sacrifice for three seasons and three years, and then not sacrifice for the month of the fourth year. Thus prescribed, one should repeat [the cycle] for a minimum of two or three [years]; one should indeed repeat it. 18.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the fifth book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
Thus ends the fifth book in the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. || 5 ||

The *pañcasaṃvatsarāṇi* refers to those Cāturmāsya sacrifices for which five years constitute the duration. This performance may be undertaken for both the obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites with the desire for an abundance of results, because it constitutes a single commencement. At the very first performance, the *pañcahotṛ* and other offerings take place. When the commencement occurs on the full moon day of Phālguna, then by repetition, two cycles of the year are completed. [End of] Paṭala 650, accompanied by the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva.
There is a double repetition of all the Cāturmāsya sacrifices within two years; furthermore, within that period, there occurs once more only the Vaiśvadeva parvan among the Cāturmāsyas.

After that, the month of Āṣāḍha occurs; when it has arrived, one should sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings. Having passed over that month, one should sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa. After practicing this for three years at Caitra, and having sacrificed again with the Vaiśvadeva at Caitra, one should sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa. Thus, beginning from Caitra, after three seasons, it falls in Bhādrapada. Then, having passed over that month, one should sacrifice with the Sākamedha offerings in Kārttika.

In this manner, he sacrifices for five years. Thereafter, having obtained the fruit [of the sacrifice], he should perform the Cāturmāsya sacrifices two or three times for five years. Thus, there are three applications—either five, ten, or fifteen—in alternation. The repetition is for the purpose of concluding the inquiry. Thus ends the sixth chapter concerning the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice in the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin composed by Mahādeva, in the fifth book.
Thus ends the fifth chapter on the Cāturmāsya sacrifices in the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* composed by Mahādeva.

6.1 Now begins the sixth question. (Therein, the first chapter: The duties of the Hotṛ and other priests have been defined with respect to the Sāman-based rituals performed by those seated according to the Ṛgveda and other Vedas; likewise, the duties of the Adhvaryu have been defined regarding the Yajurvedic rituals. Furthermore, in those Havis-sacrifices, the duties of the Brahmā priest have also been set forth. In these [sections], while warding off the non-attainment of the fruit for the primary agents—the husband and wife—he declares that their primary agency arises from mere *saṃkalpa* (volition/intention). Moreover, he establishes that the fruit of all ritual acts resides in this very [volition] alone, and other matters follow as incidental corollaries.

Having briefly explained the performance of the *haviryajña* sacrifices in detail, [the author] now proceeds to define the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) even regarding those rites prescribed by the designations of the *Hotṛ* and other priests' Vedas (4). This is done by setting aside the restrictive rules concerning the performers, such as the *Hotṛ* and others, through the sublation [of general rules] by means of indicative marks (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), specific designation (*viśeṣābhidhāna*), and direct statement (*śruti*) (5). In the sixth book (*praśna*), there is a formal declaration regarding general designations concerning the non-Vedic (*avaitānika*) rites, including those performed with the *Brahman* priest (6). Among these, it is established that the fruit belongs to the performer;
this is to be understood through proficiency in logic, and is stated as "the duty of the sacrificer" (*yājamāna*) (7). 2.
6.1 Now begins the sixth question. (Therein is the first chapter:
We shall explain the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).
Whatever purpose is heard of in the entire sacrifice, the sacrificer desires it.
Likewise, among the permanent constituent parts of the sacrifice, those which the *kāmayati* (injunctive statement expressing desire) causes to be heard—
such as the upwardness or downwardness of the *āghāra* libation—
are injunctions; the others are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

Likewise, regarding other constituent parts of the sacrifice, he makes [the altar] possessed of *purīṣa* (filling soil); verily, by means of progeny and cattle, he makes him possessed of *purīṣa*. If he plants the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), it is for the sake of discerning the world of heaven. With the words, "For food thee! For strength thee! he cuts off a branch; verily, he bestows food and strength upon the sacrificer.
The preparation of materials, the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) by the sacrificer, celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and the recitations (*japa*) [are prescribed].
He recites the mantras containing blessings directed toward himself (*pratyagāśis*) which do not pertain to the performance of the ritual action.
He attends to her as she is being instructed; he addresses her, consecrates her, touches her, and mutters prayers.
He performs all the rites exactly as they have been prescribed.
He likewise performs all the duties of the wife, as well as the observances of celibacy and the recitation of prayers, exactly as they have been prescribed.
We shall now explain the duties of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) at the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
On the day of the festival (*parvan*), the sacrificer has his hair and beard shaved.
At the full moon, in the morning meal, the husband and wife eat food mixed with clarified butter (*sarpis*).
Anything other than meat and beans. They should not eat their fill. Before the driving away of the calf on the new moon day, they may eat their fill at will.

While the fires are being kindled, he mutters: "I take Agni, the good chariot. When they have been kindled, he says: "Here I announce the sacrifice to the Vasus, with Agni as their chief; here I announce the sacrifice to the Rudras, with Indra as their chief; here I announce the sacrifice to the Ādityas, with Varuṇa as their chief. At the full moon, he undertakes the vow with sacrificial grass (*barhis*); at the new moon, with the calves.
Some authorities prescribe these in this sequence: the adding of fuel to the fire (*agnyanvādhāna*), the eating (*aśana*), and the undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*).
Others prescribe them as: the adding of fuel to the fire, the eating, and the undertaking of the vow.
These two times—the time when the *praṇītā* waters are being poured forth and the time when the sacrificial oblations (*havis*) are set down—are common to both.

Having touched water with the formula, "Thou art lightning," he steps around the south of the Āhavanīya fire and sips water with the formula, "The plants are full of sap. He worships the deities with the formula: "O gods, exert yourselves among the gods; may the first [beings] aid me in the second [stages], the second in the third; O you three times eleven, protect me here! May I be able to do this which I am doing; the self does this for the sake of the self; I shall do this as a remedy; this is my all-healing medicine. O Aśvins, protect me both of you! Thus he worships the deities.

Meditating on the ocean with his mind, he worships the sun, saying: "Thou art the sovereign; thou art the guardian of vows; thou art the lord of vows. I undertake the vow; I declare this to thee. May I be capable of this; may I be successful through this.

The Brāhmaṇa worships Agni, saying: "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall perform the vow. He worships Vāyu, saying: "O Vāyu, lord of vows. He worships Āditya, saying: "O Āditya, lord of vows. He worships the Lord of Vows, saying: "O Lord of vows, lord of vows."
These [rites] are common [to all], with the exception of the Agnihotra.
On the Parvan day, the sacrificer himself performs the Agnihotra. 1.
At the new moon, he prepares the *yavāgū* (gruel).
He sets aside the residue of it for the purpose of curdling [the milk].
He speaks no untruth, he does not eat meat, he does not approach a woman, and he does not eat during that night.
He eats forest food in the evening.
According to some, this includes everything up to raw grain, honey, and food obtained by begging.
While fasting for forest food, he should eat water, or nothing at all.
While the fires are being strewn around, he mutters: "May both fires spread out; may the deities dwell near me.
May I also dwell near the domestic animals for my own possession of cattle.
He lies down either in the chamber of the Āhavanīya fire or in the chamber of the Gārhapatya fire.
He keeps watch during the night of the new moon;
or rather, he may do as he is able.
However, he must certainly not sleep on top [of the fire].
Or he may sleep on top;
however, he should remain one who observes the vow. When the next day has dawned:
"O lord of the earth, O lord of the world, O lord of the great being, we choose you as our Brahman"— having thus chosen the most learned Brahman priest,
he passes behind the Āhavanīya fire to the south and sits down behind the Brahman’s seat.
He remains seated until the conclusion of the rite.
When it is said, "O sacrificer, restrain your speech," he restrains his speech until the call for the *haviskṛt* (the preparer of the oblation).

He addresses the *praṇītā* waters as they are being brought forward with the mantra: "Bhū, ka, vāk, car, go, vaṭ, kha, dhū, nū, pū—these ten monosyllabic *virāj* verses which have pervaded this entire world; may those goddesses, acting in unison through their power, lead the sacrifice to well-being, O wise ones. As they are being set down, he addresses them with: "You are purified by the Brahman; who yokes you? May he yoke you.
As the sacrifice is being yoked, he says: "Who yokes you? May he yoke you. Thus he yokes the sacrifice.
He gazes at everything.

When the sacrificer says, "I shall pour out the oblation," he replies, "Om, pour it out. He recites the mantra, "Invoke Agni, the Hotṛ, here," over the sacrificial food as it is being poured out, or over the vessel intended for the pouring. 2.
Thus ends the first chapter in the sixth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. || 1 ||

6.2 Now, the second chapter in the sixth section. He touches the site of the altar with the words: "O gods, I build this mansion for him among you who practices the life of a student; wise, ascetic, and a messenger within, he moves through the quarters and among human beings with his mind."

The four-tufted young woman, well-formed, with ghee as her face, in the midst of the world—being cleansed for great good fortune, milk for me, for the sacrificer, according to my desire! With the *veda* they found the high altar; she was extended upon the earth among earthly things. Upon her let the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) be spread out effectively; may the goddess Earth be non-injurious toward us. "With the *veda*, the altar"—he addresses the altar being swept with the *veda*.
The mantra recited as "with the *veda*" belongs to the *ādhvaryava* ritual.

"O gods, whoever hates me with his heart, his mind, or his speech; whoever hates me with sacred knowledge, with ritual action, with learning, or with his inner feeling—his head I cut off with Indra’s thunderbolt," [so it is said] when the *stambayajus* is being carried away. "When we, digging up [the earth], have harmed the earth, the plants, or the waters, O Adhvaryus who have made the wooden sword (*sphya*), protect us from that through the wooden sword in the intermediate space. "When we, digging up [the earth], have harmed its living [beings], and we, longing for the gods, have fashioned the altar-ground with our minds..."
"Do not come near it with anger from the earth; may she be auspicious to us through all the worlds," [he says] as the uppermost skin is being dug up with the wooden sword (*sphya*).
"O Bṛhaspati, encompass the altar," [he says] during the two enclosures.

"Becoming the earth, she nourished her greatness; then the goddess increases her waters. Holy ones, they go forth to the sacrifice for the sake of peace; may the plants, the waters, and the *śakvarī* verses be here," [he says] when it has been prepared.
"I praise the others, whose will is different; I address the divine Waters who have flowed through day and night, the active ones," [he says] as the *prokṣaṇī* waters are being set down.

"Thou art ghee," [with these words] he gazes at the ghee, just as the Adhvaryu [does]. "With the Waters purify the ghee, and with the ghee the Waters, thoroughly by the purifiers of Savitṛ. O divine Śakvarīs, protect this sacrifice with the Śakvara [chant], being in agreement. [Thus he says] as the ghee and the waters are being purified.

With the verses beginning "Of the five winds," while the clarified butter is being taken, they have refreshed themselves; they have caused the sacrificial grass to sprout within the earth, making the severed plants grow again. May those plants whose roots you have struck with the wooden sword (sphyá) become auspicious and easy for us to invoke—so saying, as the sacrificial grass is being placed within the altar (vedí). May the plants and the waters here be well-disposed toward the sacrificer, O powerful ones.

"May Parjanya, who rains upon the heavens, cause these to sprout—golden-hued, hundred-branched, and inviolable," he says over the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) being sprinkled with water. "Soft as wool, spreading out, pleasant for the gods to sit upon—place me, the sacrificer, upon this sacrificial grass, which is dear to the gods for their dwelling, in the world of heaven, on the back of the firmament, in the highest sky," he says over the sacrificial grass being spread.

"The four-tufted maiden, well-formed, with ghee for her face, clothes herself in sacred ordinances; being spread, may she lead to great fortune; grant my desires to the sacrificer," he says over the altar being strewn with sacrificial grass.

"Be auspicious and gracious to me; be pleasant and comfortable to me; be full of vigor and full of milk for me; be easy of access and good of resort to me; swell me with food and vigor; swell me with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmatejas*); swell me with the power of the ruling class (*kṣattra*); swell me with the prosperity of the common people (*viś*); swell me with long life and the eating of food; swell me with offspring and cattle"—thus [he addresses] the strewn [grass].
"In this sacrifice, indeed, for my support, I now set up the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) against agitation. Agni, the supporter, the sustainer, the most steadfast, [drives away] our enemies."

With the two verses, "Is it not the giver? while the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are being laid around, and with "Thou art firm; may I be firm among my kinsmen," as well as the two verses, "I yoke thee" and "Whatever [debt] I have, O Agni," while the fire is being enclosed by the enclosing sticks.

"Most brilliant are your burnings and your lights; O Agni, with those bodies of yours that are glowing, clothe yourself all around in armor so that the *ātudhāna* demons and *piśāca*s do not harm you"—thus [is] the enclosing.

With the two separating-spacers (*vidhṛti*), I cut asunder my rivals, the kinsmen already born and those yet to be born. With the two separators (*yantra*), I drive them away; may I be the highest among my own people, O Gods. As the two separators drive away the enemy, all evil, lack of thought, and the short-lived, they sit as goddesses in the world of the well-performed deed. "You two are the separators, the sustainers, the self-sustainers; sustain the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in me, sustain offspring in me, sustain cattle in me"—thus [he says] when the two separating-spacers are being set down.

"This sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara) is the supporter of both; it is the supporter of the fore-offerings (prayāja) as well as the after-offerings (anūyāja). It has supported the fuel-sticks (samidh) of every form; upon it I place the offering-spoons (sruk)," [he says] as the prastara is being placed within the two separating-blades (vidhṛti).

Ascend the path, O *juhū*, that leads to the gods, where the first-born seers of old abide. With golden wings and well-formed limbs, carry me to the worlds of the righteous. You are the *juhū* ladle, dripping with ghee; cherished by the wise poets, you are the singer of the *gāyatrī*. Without wavering, attend to the sacrifice; lead the sacrifice forward with good guidance toward the gods through the divine protection of Agni. With the *upabhṛt* ladle, I drive away my rivals—those born enemies and those yet to be born.

With the *dohā* (two-line verse): "As one who milks a cow that yields well, may I be the superior one; let my rivals be beneath me. O *sruva* and *upabhṛt*, full of ghee, O all-knowing one, with the *triṣṭubh* meter, being unshakable, attend to the sacrifice. Lead the sacrifice with good guidance; bring it to the gods with divine protection, O Indra. [He says this] regarding the *upabhṛt*. "O Agni, whoever, difficult to overcome, should from afar attack me with word or mind, seeking to harm me from the heart—"
This mind of mine is lower; may I be higher than Dhruvā; may my rivals be lower than I. You are Dhruvā, the supporter, full of wealth; [I invoke you] with the Jāgata metre, O All-Knowing One.

"Unwavering, oversee the sacrifice; lead the sacrifice with good guidance toward the gods by means of the Vaiśvadeva protection, divine and secure. [With these words, he places] the *dhruvā* [ladle]. "Be gracious to me; sit on the earth, which is easy to sit upon. Spread out with progeny and cattle in the world of heaven. Sit in the sky, on the earth, and in the intermediate space. May I become superior, and may my rivals be inferior. This *sruva* ladle offers the oblations with the hundred-syllabled *anuṣṭubh* metre."

"May all the parts of the sacrifice be anointed with the divine protection of Bṛhaspati," [with these words] he takes the dipping-spoon (*sruva*). "This vessel is full of ghee; it is a fountain with a hundred streams whose milk has been cut off—with the divine protection of the Maruts," [with these words] he takes the butter-vessel (*ājyasthālī*). (5)

"You are the sacrifice, resting on all sides; may the past and the future rest upon me from every side. May there be for me a hundred blessings; may there be for me a thousand pleasant and nourishing truths. This is the formula for the offering to Agni. "You are Prajāpati, resting on all sides; may the past and the future rest upon me from every side. May there be for me a hundred blessings; may there be for me a thousand pleasant and nourishing truths. This is the formula for the offering to Agni-Soma. "Whoever here desires what is less for us than this sacrifice, for me, the sacrificer..."
"O Indra and Agni, drive away those worlds; may I obtain that offspring rich in heroes"—with these words [he offers] to Indra and Agni.
"That self of yours which has entered into the cattle"—[this is said] when the *sāṃnāyya* is being set down.

"This faculty is immortal; this is vigor. By means of it, the animals provided healing for Indra. Through that, O gods, protect me here! May I win nourishment, strength, glory, power, and force. May the cooked [milk] rest within me! Thus he says regarding the cooked [milk]. That which moved upon the earth entered it; with that by which Prajāpati sprinkled strength into Indra—this is that bright, honeyed, vigorous [substance]. "May the curd above, rich in power, strengthen me, O Great Indra! Thus he says regarding the curd.

"This sacrifice, rich in oblations, has been completed with the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus verses, and with the deities; through it may we conquer the worlds possessed of the sun, and may we attain the friendship of Indra and immortality"—with these words he touches the parts that have collapsed.
Thus ends the second chapter in the sixth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
6.3 Now begins the third chapter of the sixth book.

With eight verses of the *vihavya* hymn, he touches the oblations placed on the altar at the full moon sacrifice, and with the *caturhotṛ* formula as well. At the new moon sacrifice, he does so with the *pañcahotṛ* formula. While the *sāmidhenī* verses are being recited, he mutters: "O Aṅgirases, protect this sacrificer from the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*). He should recite the *daśahotṛ* formula either before or after the *sāmidhenī* verses: "May Agni, kindled, offered with oblations, and consecrated by the *svāhā* call, fulfill our desires."

"Welcome! To the gods, this homage!"—with these words he addresses the kindled fire. With "The heat is yours, O Agni," and "Thou art the mind, belonging to Prajāpati," he consecrates the stream from the *sruva* ladle. With "Thou art speech," he consecrates that in the *sruc* ladle. "O gods, fathers, and deities, I sacrifice with that which I am; I do not neglect him to whom I belong. Mine is the sacrifice, mine the gift, mine the fulfillment, mine the toil, and mine the oblation. Over this mine, Agni is the witness, Vāyu the listener, Āditya the announcer, Heaven the father, and Earth the mother."

"Prajāpati is my kinsman; being who I am, I sacrifice; him to whom I belong, I do not neglect"—with these words he mutters during both the *hotṛ-pravara* and the *adhvaryu-pravara*. During the *adhvaryu-pravara*, he says, "Make me heard among the gods for long life and splendor. He should recite the specific *caturhotṛ* formula either before or after the *prayāja* offerings. With the formulas beginning, "I gratify Vāsanta of the seasons," he consecrates each *prayāja* offering as it is made. [He also recites: "Agni is possessed of sight; through his worship of the gods, may I [attain]..."

"May I become possessed of sight," [he says] for the *ājyabhāga* of Agni; "Soma is possessed of sight; through the sacrifice to that god, may I become possessed of sight," for the one belonging to Soma; "Of Agni and Soma, I..."—thus some prescribe the combined consecration (*anumantraṇa*). He should recite the *pañcahotṛ* formula either before or after the portions of the oblations. For the portion of Agni, [he says]: "Through the sacrifice to the god Agni, may I become an eater of food."

With the formula "Thou art the piercer," he [performs] for the Upāṃśuyāja; with "May I [be] of Agni-Soma," for the Agniṣomīya; with "May I [be] of Indra-Agni," for the Aindrāgna; with "May I [be] of Indra," for the Aindra; with "May I [be] of Mahendra," for the Māhendra; and with "May I [be] of Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," for the Sviṣṭakṛt. And with the formula "May Agni protect me from ill-sacrificed offerings" and "O thou of beautiful form and rain-like color, come hither! he awaits the iḍā being brought forward. || 7 ||

"O Iḍā, come! O Aditi, come! Come for greater prosperity, come for better fortune, come for greater wealth; O Citta, come! O Dadhiṣa, come!"—with these words he mutters the seven divine cows in a low voice during the silent invitation (*upāṃśūpahava*). "You are consciousness, you are thought, you are the wealthy one, the delighter, the joyous one, the noble one, the true joy"—with these words he recites the seven human cows aloud during the loud invitation (*uccairupahava*). "Do you breathe after all beings; let all beings breathe after you. You are *bhūḥ*, you are life-force, you are sacrifice. O you of beautiful form and excellent color, come! Come toward these auspicious dwellings. Be gracious to my devoted followers and to my heads."

May she be our dear one; may she be our victorious advance, our dear one, our good friend, our dear one, our wealthy patroness. Come as one who is well-pleased; come as one who delights us; come, O joyous one; come, O you who are easy to invoke! Come with the increase of wealth! O goddesses, together with the gods, turn back toward me! With your pleasantness, sprinkle me with pleasant ghee! This is the homage which the physician, the seer, and the priest have bestowed. As if rising upward from the ocean, the Speech stands at the head of the sage with two ladles, pointing with its ten horns—thus [it speaks] loudly at the invocation: "O Vāyu, I know you!"

Looking at the Hotṛ while saying "O Mother," he should meditate on Vāyu with his mind. When the words "This sacrificer is invited" are being spoken, he mutters: "May I be invited and possessed of cattle. And [he says]: "May Indra bestow power upon us. Regarding the *iḍā*: "Through the sacrifice to the gods, may I become prosperous and possessed of cattle. O *iḍā*, enjoy our portion; quicken our cows, quicken our horses. May we, with our whole selves and all our kinsmen, be partakers of thee. The *iḍā* has come to us like a cow with her calf, yielding strength, swelling with milk."

"May that Iḍā, invoked with the words, 'May she quicken us with food, with oblation, with cattle, and with milk,' quicken us. Thus is explained the Iḍā, which is the subject of the ritual sprinkling (mārjanī).

"O radiant one, swell; may what I give not diminish, may what I do not fail. You are the ordainer of the quarters; may the quarters be favorable to me; may the quarters be favorable to me—the divine and the human. May day and night be favorable to me; may the half-months be favorable to me; may the months be favorable to me; may the seasons be favorable to me; may the year be favorable to me. You are the ordainer; may my hopes be favorable. To you, the guardians of the quarters, the four immortal overseers of all that has come to be, we offer this oblation."

"He distributes [the portions] toward each direction: 'May he who is entitled to a share receive his share; may we not be without a share; let us honor the one who has no share among those who have shares. You, O Apaspinvat, quicken the plants; protect the two-footed; protect the four-footed; send down rain from heaven. This oblation belongs to the Brāhmaṇas, to the Somyas, to the Soma-drinkers. The Brāhmaṇa has been excluded; here there is no place for the non-Brāhmaṇa. (8) He assigns [the portions] in four parts: "This for the Brahman; this for the Hotṛ; this for the Adhvaryu; this for the Agnīdh. Some authorities record that the assignments begin with the Agnīdh.

"This vessel is full of nectar; it is a thousand-streamed, inexhaustible spring. It has supported the earth, the mid-region, and the sky. By means of this food, may I overcome death. With these words, he touches the *anvāhārya* rice placed within the *vedi*. He also says, "Thou art the portion of Prajāpati.
When it is announced, "It is to be offered to those who sit on the south," he gives the command to the priests, "Come hither from the south!"

"O Brāhmaṇas, this rice is for you," he says as they walk around from the south; having divided it into four portions, he gives it to them. "This is your fuel-stick, O Agni; through it may you grow and swell, and may we grow and swell. That which I cut off from you, O Agni, while you were moving about with swift speed—his offspring and his root, O gods, cut down low. O Agni, whoever seeks to harm us, whether he be one of our own kin or a stranger."

"May nothing remain of him who hates me, O Jātavedas, nor of him whom I hate, nor of him who hates me—burn them all, O Agni, and those whom I hate and those who hate me," [he says] as the *anūyāja* fuel-stick is being placed upon the fire.

"The altar, the sacrificial grass, the cooked oblation, the fuel, the enclosing sticks, the offering spoons, the clarified butter, the splendors of the sacrifice, the Yajus-formulas, the Yājyās, and the Vaṣaṭ-calls—may my prostrations bow down together! Thus he says when the fuel-bunch has been offered during the binding of the fuel. "O Aṅgirases, you have sacrificed for me at this sacrifice with the morning recitations," he mutters during the after-offerings (anūyājas).

One should recite the Saptahotṛ formula either before or after the after-offerings (*anūyāja*s). With the formulas beginning, "By the sacrifice to the gods, may I become possessed of offspring," he consecrates each after-offering as it is being offered. When the two ladles are being separated, he uses the two verses beginning, "At the impulse of strength (*vāja*)."

"I have gladdened the Vasu gods with the sacrifice; I have gladdened the Rudra gods with the sacrifice; I have gladdened the Āditya gods with the sacrifice"—with these words he anoints the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). "May the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) be anointed with the oblation and with clarified butter; may it be anointed with the Ādityas, with the Vasus, and with the Maruts; may it be anointed with Indra and with all the gods; may it go to the celestial sky, svāhā!"—with this he anoints the *prastara* bundle in the offering-spoons. "The sacrifice has gladdened the sacrifice; the gods have been duly honored; Soma [has been honored]. "May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, and Uṣas enter the sacrificer with wealth"—with this he removes a blade of grass from the *prastara*.
With the words, "May I win the victory of Agni," the Hotṛ recites the *sūktavāka*; whatever deity he pronounces, the sacrificer consecrates each one with a mantra.

When the Hotṛ utters the name of the sacrificer, then [the sacrificer] should say: "These blessings have come, desiring to yield milk. He mutters the blessings: "May this my blessing be true among the gods; from that which is thought, may it be most highly thought; from that which is beloved, may it be most beloved; through a mind full of *ṛddhi*, may I accomplish that. May the sacrifice ascend to heaven; may the sacrifice go to heaven. By that path which leads to the gods, may the sacrifice reach the gods. Thus he mutters over the blessings.
He takes the name of whomever he desires, thinking, "May [the fire] not come near him.
With the formulas, "May Agni cause you to go to the deity by means of the ruddy one," he releases the *prastara* [grass-bundle].

"The post of heaven is stretched out; it has risen up from the earth. By means of that thousand-jointed [post], we cause our enemy to suffer; let the hater be tormented, let the many-harming [enemy] be scorched, O plants!"—with these words, he throws a blade of grass from the *prastara* into the fire.
At the *śaṃyu-vāka*, he recites: "Of Viṣṇu, of Śaṃyu, I...
When the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are being thrown into the fire, he recites the two verses beginning with "I loosen thy cords.

He recites: "The sacrifice has been offered by the Bhṛgus; may the giver of wealth come to me through the Yatis; may the giver of blessings come through the Vasus; may the one possessing blessings come through the Atharvans. Of that sacrifice of mine, which has been offered and enjoyed, may wealth come; may the sacrifice be wealthy; may the wealth of that wealthy sacrifice come here to me; may that [wealth] come to me. Regarding those portions of the residue (*saṃsrāva*), he pronounces the name of whomever he desires.
"Thou art the Veda, the giver of wealth"—with these words he touches the *antarvedi* (the space within the altar).

"May I obtain [it]"—before or after this [formula], whatever he might covet from his rival, he should utter that person's name; it is known [from tradition] that by doing so, he seizes all of that from him. 10.
Thus ends the third chapter in the sixth *praśna* on the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) in the *Sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin. 3.

6.4 Now, the fourth chapter in the sixth book. At the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings: for Soma, [he says] "By the sacrifice to the god Soma, may I, possessing good seed, deposit seed"; for Tvaṣṭṛ, "By the sacrifice to the god Tvaṣṭṛ, may I nourish the form of cattle"; for the wives of the gods, "By the sacrifice to the wives of the gods, may I procreate through offspring and cattle"; for Rākā, the wife of the gods, "By the sacrifice to the goddess Rākā, may I become possessed of offspring"; for Sinīvālī, "By the sacrifice to the goddess Sinīvālī, may I become possessed of cattle"; for Kuhū, "By the sacrifice to the goddess Kuhū..."

"May I be prosperous," [he says] regarding *Kuhū*; "Agni Gṛhapati is the foundation of the sacrifice; through the sacrifice to this deity, may I become possessed of a foundation," [he says] regarding Agni Gṛhapati; "The wives of the gods, Agni Gṛhapati..."—some prescribe this as a collective consecration (*anumantraṇa*).

"May *Iḍā* favor us with clarified butter, she in whose place those seeking the gods purify themselves; the *Śakvarī* verse belonging to Vaiśvānara has increased and has approached the sacrifice, [she] belonging to the Viśvedevas"—[this is] the *Īḍā* for the clarified butter.

When the offering of husks (*phalīkaraṇa-homa*) is being poured with the formula, "To that Sarasvatī who possesses glory, svāhā to thee," he wipes his mouth. When it has been offered with the formula, "To that Sarasvatī who possesses dwellings, svāhā to thee," he wipes his mouth.
As the *veda* grass-bundle is being handed over to the wife by the Hotṛ, [he recites]: "Thou art the *veda*;
thou art the acquisition" (*vedo 'si vittir asi*), or alternatively, "Thou art the *veda*; for the sake of the *veda* thee; may the *veda* find me."
[He recites] "Rich in ghee, nest-like" over the *veda* grass being placed on his lap;
or [he recites], "Thou art the *veda*, bring me the *veda*; may I, satisfied by thee, be satisfied with offspring and cattle.

[He recites] "By thee they found the altar, the earth; by thee the sacrifice is born, all-bestowing; thou, the wise one, followest the flawless sacrifice; by thee the Hotṛ completes the half-months," over the *veda* grass as it is being strewn.
"O Agni of unerring life-force," [is the formula] for the *saṃiṣṭayajus* offering.

"A pillar of heaven, stretched out, risen up from the earth—with that thousand-branched [pillar], we cause our enemy to burn; let my enemy burn much, O herb, and may I not burn. Thus he throws the *barhis* grass after [the fire].

"May the lord of the sacrifice attain his blessings," [with this] he eats the sacrificer's portion of boiled milk and curds. A Brāhmaṇa eats it, but neither a Vaiśya nor a Rājanya. "May this oblation be productive for me," [with this] he eats of the boiled milk; "I have performed the praise of Dadhikrāvan," [with this] he eats of the curds.

He performs the *mārjana* (sprinkling) within the altar (*antarvedi*) while the waters have been led forward. The Adhvaryu causes a continuous stream to flow for him. He mutters the formula, "May it be abundant for me in the assembly," as the waters are being brought in. He pours out the water in each direction with the formula, "May the gods and the officiating priests purify me in the eastern direction. He pours out the remainder with the formula, "I send you forth to the ocean; O imperishable ones, go back to your own source. May I be unimpaired in my offspring; may this [water] not be spilled away from me. He wipes his mouth with the formula, "O Sarasvatī, whatever sweetness is in your waters, in your cows, and in your horses—with that, O spirited one, cleanse my mouth, O Sarasvatī."
In this regard, some authorities prescribe the consumption of the sacrificer’s portion.

Thereupon, having risen, he takes four steps of Viṣṇu with the formula, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu. Having stepped forward with the right foot, he follows with the left; he does not cross over with the left foot, nor does he step beyond the Āhavanīya fire. Standing still, he mutters the fourth formula, each subsequent step being larger than the preceding one.

Rising today, O thou of friendly luster, destroy my rivals. Strike them down with lightning by day; as thou settest, cast them beneath thy feet. Rising today, do thou bestow upon us our share, as a father bestows upon his sons. Thou art the lord of long life; grant us that, O Sūrya. Rising today, O thou of friendly luster, ascending the highest heaven, O Sūrya, destroy my heart-disease and my jaundice. We transfer my jaundice to the parrots and to the thrushes; moreover, we deposit my jaundice among the yellow wagtails.

"Risen is this sun together with all-pervading power, subduing him who hates me; may I not be subdued by those who hate me. He who curses us when we do not curse, and he who curses us when we do curse—may both Dawn and Night sweep away all that evil from him. O Gods, whatever rival or mortal enemy seeks to harm us, let nothing of him remain, as if of a log being consumed by fire. (12)
He worships the Sun with the mantra: "We have gone to heaven; may we go to heaven.

He meditates in his mind on the destruction of that enemy whom he hates, saying: "Here I [drive] such-and-such an adversary away from these directions and from this sky. If he should perform an act of exorcism, he says: "Here I suppress the breath of such-and-such a person, the son of such-and-such a lineage," and turns clockwise with the words: "I turn following the turning of Indra. Then, turning toward the right shoulder, he says: "May those fortunes be auspicious; may those that are evil perish."
Saying, "Thou art splendor," he turns around the Āhavanīya fire.
Saying, "May I be united with offspring," he pays homage to it. Saying, "O Agni, well-kindled," he kindles it.

He worships with the mantra: "May the sacrifice be rich in wealth. He worships the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern fire) with: "O Agni, O carrier, cook for us food that is savory for our offspring; may it be abundant, auspicious for our children, and pleasant for our bodies. He worships the *gārhapatya* (householder's fire) with the two *āgnipāvamānī* verses beginning with "O Agni, [grant] long lives" and "O Agni, purify yourself," and also with the verse "O Agni, lord of the house. One who has not yet fathered a son should say regarding that blessing: "I pray for this blessing, which is full of light, for my lineage. One who has already fathered a son should say: "I pray for this blessing, which is full of light, for so-and-so."

Having recited the names of all his sons, the father of many sons says at the end, "Jyotiṣmatīm" (The Radiant One). Saying, "For light, for offspring, thee! May so-and-so [the son] follow me with light and offspring," he sits down between the two fires. Having placed blades of grass from the *veda* in his lap, sitting within the *vedi*, he mutters the *atīmokṣa* formulas, beginning with, "Those gods who are destroyers of the sacrifice..."

"Who yokes you? May he release you," with these words he releases the sacrifice; he looks all around. "O Agni, lord of vows, I have performed the vow," and so on—with these [formulas] he releases the vow. "The sacrifice has come into being, it has fully come into being"—with this he mutters the re-attainment of the sacrifice. "O Agni, the sacrifice is rich in cattle, rich in sheep, rich in horses"—having stepped forward toward the east, he mutters this. || 13 ||

"O Sacrifice, hail to you! O Sacrifice, obeisance, obeisance to you! O Sacrifice, may you be established for me with auspiciousness; may you be established for me with comfort; may you be established for me with prosperity; may you be established for me with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). May you be established following the success of the sacrifice! O Sacrifice, homage to you! Homage to you! Homage to you!"—thus he mutters. "You are rain; cut off my evil! From the Untrue I have gone to the True. Having touched water with this formula, he steps out by the same way he came. He issues the command: "Satisfy the Brāhmaṇas!"
Thus is prescribed the duty of the sacrificer even while he is away on a journey.
Facing the direction in which his fires are located, he mutters the mantras;
the Adhvaryu performs the ritual acts.
Because of the mutual touching of one another.
The sacrificer mutters other mantras than those of the formal assignment (*vyādeśana*).

Thus is prescribed the ritual duty of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) for the *iṣṭi* and animal sacrifices. The follow-up recitations (*anumantraṇas*) are according to the specific modification of each rite.

Through the sacrifice to Indra Vaimṛdha, may I be free from rivals. Through the sacrifice to Sarasvatī, may I nourish speech and the food I eat. Through the sacrifice to Pūṣan, may I become prosperous and possessed of cattle. Through the sacrifice to Aditi, may I procreate with offspring and cattle. Through the sacrifice to Heaven and Earth, may I prosper in both worlds and attain abundance and firm standing. Through the sacrifice to Aryaman, may I nourish the heavenly world. [Of] all...

"Through the sacrifice to the gods, may I attain union with the vital breaths of the gods; through the sacrifice to the god Indra, the possessor of power, may I become powerful and rich in cattle; through the sacrifice to the god Indra, the protector, may I become protected"—these are the consecratory formulas (anumantraṇas) as directly recited in the Vedic texts. 14.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the sixth *praśna* on the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) in the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra*.
6.5 Now begins the fifth chapter of the sixth book.
We shall explain the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*).
Prior to the *brāhmaudana* [rice-pot] rite, he has his hair and beard shaved, trims his nails, cleanses his teeth, bathes, and puts on a new, unwashed garment.
He grants a boon to those who have consumed the *brahmaudana* rice-porridge.
When the kindling-sticks have been laid, he gives a pair whose seed has been infused.
He does not go forth on a journey, nor does he travel abroad.
They do not carry his fire from the house,
nor do they fetch it from elsewhere.
He keeps watch during this night with artistic performances.

"Kindling the fire with wood-shavings, may I win both worlds; having prospered in both worlds, may I cross beyond death"—with these words he kindles the fire with wood-shavings for that night. "When the two great queens of the people sit in the seat of Order, you two, the supporters of riches, come hither; pregnant with the kinsman, O Jātavedas, you two generate him as the leader of the sacrifices"—with these words he looks toward the two kindling-sticks (*araṇī*) as they are being handed over. "Ascend, O Agni, my ten fingers, together with the *ṛta*, with long life, and with splendor."

"Living long, may I see each succeeding year; may I perform the sacrifice according to the New Moon and Full Moon rites"—with these words he accepts [the gift]. "You two possess the proper season and have Agni as your seed; receive the embryo. I take that from you both. It is true that you shall bear a hero and shall bring forth a hero. You two shall procreate me in the morning; once procreated, you shall cause me to procreate through offspring, cattle, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and the heavenly world. Having accepted it, he consecrates it with this mantra.

He takes the fire into himself, just as the Adhvaryu does: "Here I go from untruth to truth; from truth I go to the human state; from the human I go to the divine; I restrain my speech. Thus he restrains his speech. He breathes over the newborn [fire] with the formula: "With the breath of Prajāpati I breathe upon you; with the nourishment of Pūṣan for me, for long life of a hundred autumns, for a hundred autumns of life, for vitality, for splendor, for living, and for merit. "I am yours, you are mine; this is mine, you are its source; I am your source."
"O Agni Jātavedas, carry my oblations as a son carries them for his father, creating a world [for me]"—having thus consecrated the newborn [fire], he gives a boon.
At this point, he releases his speech; the sacrificer and his wife put on two garments of linen.

When that establishment of the fires (agnyādheya) is completed, whatever two *vyāhṛtis*, whatever specific *ṛṣi*-based installation, whatever two *sārparājñī* verses, and whatever *gharmaśiras* formula he employs, with each of those he worships [the fire] in every instance. || 15 ||

"May the Gārhapatya fire, burning away the enemies and making each dawn more auspicious than the last, O Agni, driving away our rivals, bestow upon us abundance of wealth, food, and vigor"—with these words he worships the established Gārhapatya fire. "May these riches come to me; may I dwell here with these offspring; may the multiform Iḍā abide here; shine in the midst of wealth, O Jātavedas!"—with this he addresses the fire as it is being carried to the middle space. At the halfway point, he gives a boon. "I have attained, I have pervaded; I have pervaded the full span of life"—with this he worships the established Āhavanīya fire.

O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Virāj and the Svarāj—may they enter me; may they quicken me. O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Samrāj and the Abhibhū—may they enter me; may they quicken me. O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Vibhū and the Paribhū—may they enter me; may they quicken me. O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Prabhvī and the Mahimānī—may they enter me; may they quicken me. With those auspicious bodies of yours, O Agni, I establish you.

He worships the Āhavanīya fire with the auspicious forms: "Snik, Snīhiti, Snihiti, Sadāmni, Āmati, Anāhuti, and Nirṛti—these, O Agni, are your terrible forms; let the immortal [Agni] go to those [forms] of you which are mortal, [namely] him who hates us and whom we hate. Thus he worships with the terrible forms prior to the Pūrṇāhuti. At the Pūrṇāhuti, he gives a boon. Having worshipped with the auspicious forms after the Pūrṇāhuti, [the ritual concludes].

He worships with the *virāj* meters: "O Atharvan, protect my food, my sustenance measured by the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Protected by you, rejoicing in nourishment and vigor, may we live for a hundred autumns with our heroes"—with these words he approaches the *dakṣiṇāgni*. "O Narya, protect my offspring, the continuity of the world's root; I entrust to you that which was fashioned from my own heart"—with these words he approaches the *gārhapatya*. "O Śaṃsya, protect my cattle, the wealth of all forms."

"May I bestow upon you the prosperity and joy of houses; protect that for me, O Āhavanīya fire! Protect my assembly hall, which increases sensory power and prosperity; may it be a shelter for all people; may I bestow that upon you. "Protect my assembly hall, O Saṃprathas; make those who are members of the assembly and the councilors endowed with sensory power; may they abide in full life-span. "Protect my mantra, O Ahabudhnya fire, along with fortune and glory."

"To the serpent of the deep, for the sake of prosperity and glory, I entrust this mantra"—with these words, the Virāj, created by Prajāpati, stepped forth fivefold as the fires of the household (*āvasathya*).

"The Rohiṇī has ascended upwards; it is the womb of Agni, his foundation"—with these words, she stepped over all [the fires]. Where they offer him a hundred dice, having won at them, he presents the winnings to the members of the assembly (*sabhāsadaḥ*). Whatever they win, that is both kinds of food; having prepared it, he feeds the Brāhmaṇas.

At the time of the sacrificial fee for the Āgneya offering, he gives a goat, a full vessel, a pillow, a garment made of all kinds of threads, a horse, a chariot, a cloth, six cows, twelve, twenty-four, or an unlimited number of increasing [cows]; among these, a milch cow and a draft ox, as well as pairs of animals of specified forms, a goat, a full vessel, and a pillow, he gives to the Āgnīdhra; a horse to the Brahman; a milch cow to the Hotṛ; a draft ox at the site of the Gārhapatya fire; and at the site of the Āhavanīya fire, to the Adhvaryu; the remainder is common to all. There are thirty measures in the first two Pavamāna chants.
He gives gold as the sacrificial fee for the two oblations; a cow weighing forty [mānas] is the fee for the final [offering] to Aditi.
From the time of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) until the end of his life, he shall not speak untruth.
No Brāhmaṇa shall dwell in his house without food.
One should not turn away a guest who has arrived at sunset for the sake of lodging.
One should not give anything else at night except food. When giving food at night, one should eat as well.
One should not eat food cooked with human excrement.
One should not eat of those waters that flow within ships.
One should not place silver or gold upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
One should not add wet wood to the fire, or one may so add it.
He should not stay overnight in a place made by himself, such as a salt-flat or a cleft in the ground.
Having uttered the syllable *hiṃ*, he may engage in sexual intercourse with a woman while remaining silent,
or he may speak.

During this year, one who has not sacrificed with an animal should not eat meat unless it is specifically prescribed. If he should eat it, he says: "I send this food to the fires with my mind; let them consume it together with my speech. Being heedful and vigilant, I move about; let them consume it together with a gracious mind. Having said this, he eats when it is prescribed. For twelve nights, he himself performs the Agnihotra with clarified butter while the fires are kept continuously burning. He wears an unwashed garment.
One should offer the Kāmamanyu oblation;
however, one must remain a practitioner of the vow.
He himself offers the Trayodaśī oblation.

The cow which they first milk for the Agnihotra is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the Agnihotra. At the Anvārambhaṇīyā offering, he gives a pair of cattle. Having given both the fees belonging to the original establishment of the fires (agnyādheya) at the re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya), he then gives the specific fees of the re-establishment: a chariot repaired again, a garment sewn together again, a bull set free again, and gold weighing a hundred mānas; these are the sacrificial fees for the re-establishment of the fires. Or rather, he may give only those fees pertaining to the re-establishment; such is the Paiṅgya Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the sixth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra. ||5||

6.6 Now begins the sixth chapter of the sixth book. Reciting, "Bringing [offerings] at all times with an unailing mind; O Agni, may we, your neighbors, not come to harm," he approaches the sacrificial enclosure (*vihāra*). With each mantra, beginning with "Whatever, O Agni, [be thy fires]," he places the largest piece of fuel (*varṣiṣṭha idhma*) upon the Āhavanīya fire.

He consecrates the ghee being taken up with the formula, "Lift it up. From the time of lifting until the oblation is offered, he shall not eat. Having touched water with the formula, "Lightning art thou," and having stepped around the south of the Āhavanīya fire, he sits down to the south. The wife sits to the south of the wife’s place. [The sacrificer says: "Thou art Iḍā, the bearer of vows; I shall observe the vow for both of us. O Āditya, bearer of vows; I shall observe the vow for both of us. O Surūpa, I shall observe the vow for both of us. With the formula, "O Iḍā, come; rest in me," he places within himself whatever vow was observed by the Agnihotrī cow.

"O Faith, come! By truth I call you," he says as she is being summoned. "You are this [cow]; Agni is her calf; may she yield for me both the heavenly world and [this] world," he says as she is being milked. When it is said, "I shall draw up [the ghee]" or "I am drawing it up," he says in a low voice, "You are the oblation of the gods; may there be safety from death for me; may there be well-being for me; may there be freedom from fear for me," and then aloud, "Draw it up. While it is being drawn up, he stands still and does not walk about; he restrains his speech until the offering is made. Once the ghee has been drawn up, he sits down. Rising for the subsequent oblation, he stands somewhat sideways.
He worships the Āhavanīya fire with all the worship-formulas (*upasthāna*).

With the six [verses] beginning "Going forward to the sacrifice" (*upaprayanto adhvaram*), he should worship it with the verse addressed to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīyā*) during the first half of the month, and with the verse addressed to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgnī*) during the second half.

Of those two, the verse addressed to Agni and Soma is "O Agni and Soma, this [sacrifice] well... (*agnīṣomāv imaṃ sume*), and the verse addressed to Indra and Agni is "Both of you, O Indra and Agni... (*ubhā vāmindrāgnī*).
After the *vihavya* hymn, he worships with the first four verses;
after those, he worships with the six *āgnipāvamānī* verses beginning with "O Agni, you purify the lives" (*agna āyūṃṣi pavase*).

At the end of the year, he worships the *gārhapatya* fire with the four verses beginning with "O Agni, giver of life, give me life. He repeats twice the verse "O Citrāvasu, may I reach your end in safety," and pronounces the names of all his sons, saying for each one twice: "May there be safety for [Name]! May there be safety for [Name]!"

With these [mantras]—"O Agni, you are the fuel-stick; protect me from imprecation! O Soma, you are the fuel-stick; come to me from the highest [place]! O Yama, you are the fuel-stick; protect me from death!"—he should place three fuel-sticks [on the fire]. With the fourth [verse], "Kindling you for a hundred winters," he places the fourth. Then, having wiped his mouth with the [mantra], "O Soma, we, bearing our minds within our bodies, may we, possessing offspring, attain [prosperity]," and also with, "O Agni, you have united with the splendor of the Sun."

"I behold the creatures," [he says]. He approaches the humans with the words, "O waters, may I partake of you as water. With the words, "O wealthy ones, rejoice," he approaches the cattle. Standing between the two fires, he mutters, "Thou art united, possessing all forms. He touches the cow with the words, "Or rather, the calf. With the six Gāyatrī verses in two-footed meter beginning with "Upa tvāgne dive dive" (Come to thee, O Agni, day by day), he worships the Gārhapatya fire. [He says], "With vigor I look upon you; may you look upon me with vigor. [He says regarding the cowpen], "Thou art the world, possessing thousandfold prosperity; thou rulest over thousandfold prosperity."

"May we be among those who receive the greatest portion of it"—with these words, he again touches the cow or the calf. "May there be the great protection of the three—of Mitra, of Aryaman, and of Varuṇa—which is heavenly, invincible, and unassailable. For neither in their presence nor on the difficult paths does an evil-speaking enemy have power over them. May those sons of Aditi grant us eternal shelter."

With the triplet of Māhitra, "To him who bestows desirable things," he worships; with the Sāvitrī verse, "That excellent glory of Savitṛ"; and with this [verse]: "O Brahmaṇaspati, make us a bringer of fame like Kakṣīvat, the son of Uśij. May he who is the other, the friend, the healer of disease, the finder of wealth, the increaser of prosperity—he who is swift—be with us. Let not the curse of the stingy man, nor the malice of a mortal, reach us."

He worships with the verses addressed to Brahmaṇaspati, beginning with "Protect us, O Brahmaṇaspati," and "Never indeed art thou barren, never indeed dost thou fail. With two verses, "Around thee, O Agni, we [place] a fortress," and "May thy hard-to-overcome chariot reach us from every side, wherewith thou protectest the worshippers"—having turned around, he finally worships with this last verse.

Some recite the *Dūḍhabhavatī* as the *Uttamā*: "Thou art the crusher; may I crush him who hates us and whom we hate"—with this, if he should vie with one who is superior, he should press down with his forefoot from the front. "Thou art the overcomer; may I overcome him who hates us and whom we hate"—with this, if he should vie with an equal, he should press down with his foot from the south. "Thou art the subduer; may I subdue him who hates us and whom we hate"—[with this, he should press down from the west].

If he should compete with one who is more wicked, he should press down on his heel from behind. Having murmured: "May Pūṣan, the protector of cattle, protect me; may Pūṣan, the protector of paths, protect me; may Pūṣan, the guardian, protect me; may Pūṣan, the overlord, protect me," [he continues]: "The eastern direction has Agni as its deity; whoever would do me harm from this direction, may he encounter Agni; may Agni guard me from that direction. The southern direction has Indra as its deity; whoever would do me harm from this direction, may he encounter Indra; may Indra guard me from that direction. The western direction..."

The Maruts are the deities of the northern quarter; whoever would do me harm from this quarter, let him fall upon the Maruts; may the Maruts protect me from that quarter. Mitra and Varuṇa are the deities of the upward quarter; whoever would do me harm from this quarter, let him fall upon Mitra and Varuṇa; may Mitra and Varuṇa protect me from that quarter. Bṛhaspati is the deity of the zenith; whoever would do me harm from this quarter, let him fall upon Bṛhaspati; may Bṛhaspati protect me from that quarter.
This Aditi is the deity of this quarter; whoever would seek to harm me from this quarter, may he encounter Aditi; O Aditi, protect me from that quarter.

Having thus worshipped the quarters with the formula, he murmurs while standing between the two fires: "May Dharma protect me, the righteous; may Adharma protect me, the unrighteous. May life and further life, sight and wide-sight, out-breath and in-breath, the forward breath and the downward breath, the broad one and the wide-striding one—may we go to thee, O Arka, with speech that is shared. May the divine thread not be cut; may the human not cut it. May I not be severed from the divine abode. [I have not been severed] from life, for the sake of light and the thread, thee! So-and-so, may I be followed by the light through the body. He murmurs "O Agni, thou art life-giving" and "O Agni... [and so forth].

With the two verses beginning with "Flow on" (*pavasva*) dedicated to Agni-Pavamāna, and with the verse "O Agni, lord of the house" (*agne gṛhapate*), he worships the Gārhapatya fire. One who has not yet fathered a son should say: "I invoke this blessing for my progeny, may it be full of light. One who has fathered a son should say: "I invoke this blessing for [name], may it be full of light. One who has many sons should recite the names of all his sons and finally say: "may it be full of light. He performs this worship every evening. 20.
Or rather, this [is for] the day:

"Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! May I be rich in offspring through my offspring, rich in heroes through my heroes, rich in splendor through my splendor, and rich in nourishment through my nourishments. Or, according to his desire: "May Indra know [this]."
Whether it be [the thought], "May my faith not depart," or "May I be able to support you"—
all that, whether performed or left undone,
must be attended to by the morning libation; one should approach [the fire] in the morning.
There, while the oblation has been placed on the fire or is being ladled out,
one should worship with the first four verses of the Vihavya hymn.

With the verse, "O Lord of Waters," he pours out three handfuls of water; with the formula, "The enemies are driven away," he sprinkles around [the fire] three times. With the formula, "For Time, for you two, for victory," he washes his hands. Having sipped water with the formula, "Here I cause the evil-eaters to float away," he spits out. Again he washes his hands with the formula, "Of my rivals and co-wives. With the formula, "May I today utter speech endowed with power," he cleans the seats of the vital breaths according to their respective forms. He then worships with the subsequent Anuvāka, up to the verse beginning with "arvāg vasoḥ."

He repeats three times, "May there be well-being for you at the further shore," [and says] "May there be well-being for you, so-and-so; may there be well-being for you, so-and-so. He pronounces the names of all his sons, three times for each one.
Having performed the worship with the four subsequent verses after the two oblations of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, he worships with the remainder of the Anuvāka.
Therefore, according to some, one should not descend [the fire-sticks] before the morning Agnihotra.
"He sweeps away the grass from around the fire; he becomes radiant and endowed with spiritual luster"—so it is known. || 21 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the sixth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
6.7 Now begins the seventh chapter of the sixth book.
We shall explain the rules for living abroad away from one's home.

"Prepare the fires," he commands. When about to depart on a journey, he worships the radiant fires with the four verses beginning, "My name was first [known], O Jātavedas. Having worshipped the Āhavanīya fire with the verse, "O Śaṃsya, protect my cattle; guard them for me until my return," he breathes toward it and then worships it with, "O Agni, thousand-eyed one... Having worshipped the Gārhapatya fire with, "O Agni, lord of the house, protect my offspring; guard them for me until my return," he breathes toward it and then worships it with, "O food for me..."

"O thou dwelling in the depths, protect that for me; guard us until our return," with these words he worships the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire. Having breathed over it and worshipped with "O Agni, O bearer," he worships with the *virājakrama* verses as performed previously. Standing between the two fires, he recites: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, do you two guard these houses of mine, unimpaired and undisturbed; may they prosper and protect them until our return. Standing between the two fires, he mutters: "May we not stray from the path, nor from the sacrifice, O Indra, we who possess the *soma*; may no enemies stand against us."

"Lead us upward, O Agni, when offered with clarified butter; unite us with the increase of wealth and with progeny, and make us many"—with these words he steps forward. He restrains his speech in the presence of the fires and releases it when out of their presence. He observes the vow at the times prescribed for the vow.
He pays homage to each season as it arrives.
If he is forced to travel while the fire has not been paid homage to, he may go into exile.

"Right here, even while you are there, O Agnis, I support you with breath, speech, and mind. May life not abandon me while I am away; I worship you with the Vaiśvānara light. Having thus worshipped, he departs.

Upon returning, while carrying the fuel-sticks, he approaches the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) with the verse: "Bringing [the sticks] at all times with an unafflicted mind, O Agni, may we, as your neighbors, not come to harm. In the presence of the fires, he restrains his speech; he releases it in their presence. He issues the command: "Prepare the fires! He worships the blazing fires with the verses: "Homage be to thee, the bountiful one; homage to thee, O thou who art fanned by the *upasad*."

"O Agni, beautify thy body; unite me with wealth"—with these words he kindles the fire. With the three [verses] beginning "Thou art the fuel of Agni; protect me from imprecation," he should place three pieces of wood on the fire. With the fourth verse, "Kindling thee for a hundred winters," the Adhvaryu offers an oblation with the mantra, "May the mind delight in the light. If he departs on a journey on the tenth day, he should worship the Āhavanīya fire with the four verses beginning, "My name and thine, O Jātavedas... and "Thou hast protected my cattle, which are worthy of praise; give them back to me. Having worshipped the Āhavanīya, he should blow upon it.

He worships with the verse, "O thousand-eyed one," [saying], "The offspring that you have protected for me, O hero, give that back to me. Having worshipped the *gārhapatya* fire, he fans it and worships it with, "O Agni, lord of the house. Having worshipped the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire, he fans it and worships it with, "The food that you have protected for me, O Budhnya, give that back to me. Having worshipped [the *āhavanīya*] with, "O Agni, bearer," he worships with the *virājakrama* verses as performed previously: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two have protected these houses for me."
Standing between the two fires, he mutters: "O Pūṣan, do not look upon these [cows] as lost or strayed until our return"; he appends "protect them" or "you have protected them" to every [verse].

Now, according to some, it is known: "Who will awaken one who is sleeping in bliss? Therefore, the worship [of the fires] should be performed while they are still unkindled. When about to depart on a journey, [he says]: "O Giver of Fearlessness, grant me fearlessness; may it be well with me as I go forth. Having departed, when he returns, [he says]: "O Giver of Fearlessness, you have granted me fearlessness; may it be well with me as I have returned. "O houses, do not be afraid, do not tremble; bearing strength, we come to you. Bearing strength, a winner of wealth and wise, I come to the houses, rejoicing in my mind."

To those whose goodwill becomes manifest when they go abroad, to those houses we offer our invitation; may they recognize us as we recognize them. Invited here are the cows; invited are the goats and sheep. And the sweet essence of food is invited into our homes. Invited are our many friends, companions in pleasant revelry; may our houses always be uninjured, with all their men intact. May they be full of vigor, full of milk, full of refreshment, and full of joy.

"Free from hunger, free from thirst, O house, do not fear us"—with these words he approaches the house for security and peace. "I enter what is auspicious, what is beneficial, for well-being and for peace"—with these words he enters. On that day, having returned, he does not engage in quarreling.
