"I enter the houses which are well-disposed, which slay the enemy, most heroic, and very kind; carrying nourishment and being well-intentioned, among them I lie down with a well-disposed mind"—with these words he lies down. "May we, by means of you, cross over all enemies, as one crosses streams of water"—with these words he gazes upon his wife. 24.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the sixth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.

6.8 Now begins the eighth chapter of the sixth book. At the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, one gives a first-born calf. In the case of a separate ritual procedure involving *śyāmāka* grain, [one gives] a brownish-tawny [calf]. There is a honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), a honey-paste (*madhumantha*), and a curd-paste (*dadhimantha*). Or there is a vessel of milk-rice, a linen garment, and a cloak worn during the rains. With the mantra, "May the gods lead us from good to better," he eats of the rice; [he says], "May Agni eat first, for he knows how the oblation is."

"May Śivā make the plants auspicious for us, she who dwells among all people"—this [verse] is for *śyāmāka* grains. "They have plowed this barley, mixed with honey, along the Sarasvatī; Indra, the lord of the hundredfold rite, was the master of the plow, and the Maruts, the bounteous givers, were the plowmen"—this is for *yava* (barley). According to the specific modification, he recites eleven *prayāja* formulas over the animal sacrifice. He recites four [formulas] with the first four [verses], the fourth with the formula for the fourth [offering], four [verses] beginning with *duraḥ*, and the remaining ones with the last [formula].

"You are the winner of light; having won the light, go to the light for me, [win] the light for the cattle. You are the winner of space; having won the space, go to the space for me, [win] the space for the cattle. You are the winner of the path; having won the path, go to the path for me, [win] the path for the cattle. You are the winner of refuge; having won the refuge, go to the refuge for me, [win] the refuge for the cattle. When the animal is being slaughtered, he mutters, "Verily, you do not die here; you are all the quarters of the quarters. When the omentum has been offered, he gives away the supreme [gift], or he should lead away three sacrificial fees.

He recites the formulas for the eleven after-offerings (anūyāja) according to the specific animal sacrifice: three with each of the first [formulas], the tenth with the first, and the last with the last. "Like the horns of horned animals, the sacrificial posts with their cross-pieces appear clearly upon the earth. These divine sacrificial posts have stood firm; homage to my friends! May I not fall away from those who are seated. (25) When the rite is completed, he stands by the burnt sacrificial post, reciting: "May I obtain great heroic power. He likewise stands by the sacrificial post when the rite has concluded.

In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, he gives a bull to Vaiśvānara, or gold for the bull; a cow to Pārjanya. He consecrates nine fore-offerings (*prayāja*) according to their respective modifications: four with the first four formulas, and four beginning from the *duraḥ* with the formula used for the fourth [fore-offering]; the last one with the last formula. He gives the first-born calf to the Viśvedevas. He consecrates nine after-offerings (*anūyāja*) according to their respective modifications: three with each of the [first] three formulas.

"That is the *ṛta*, that is the truth, that is the vow; may I be capable of that, may I be empowered by it, may I succeed through it"—with these words he mutters while his hair is being shaved everywhere. For four months he does not speak untruth, he does not eat meat, he does not approach a woman, and he does not sit upon anything elevated. He should feel aversion toward untruth; he sleeps facing the east, he does not eat honey, he does not apply collyrium to his eyes, and he does not anoint himself with oil. During the fertile season he may approach his wife. These are the intermediate vows for all the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. At the Varuṇapraghāsa rites, he gives away a cow; at the Sākamedha rites, a bull that has reached its full age.

In the Sākamedha rites, he offers to whichever deity the horse neighs; at the Paurṇadarvya sacrifice, [he gives] a white horse to Āditya; a white ox, a six-oxen team, or a twelve-oxen team of ploughs; or a pair of plough-oxen, or a single plough-ox, or either one at the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice; a white horse to Sūrya; or a white ox; and in the absence of that, there should be a white non-ox; it should be white. It should be white. 26.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the sixth book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
Thus ends the sixth book in the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. ||6||
There is a double performance of all the Cāturmāsya sacrifices within two years; furthermore, within the interval of the Cāturmāsya cycle, there occurs only the Vaiśvadeva parvan once again.

After that, the month of Āṣāḍha occurs; when it has arrived, one should sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings. Having passed over that month, one should sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa. After practicing this for three years at Caitra, and having again sacrificed with the Vaiśvadeva at Caitra, one should sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa. Thus, beginning from Caitra, after three seasons have passed, it falls in Bhādrapada; then, having passed over that month, one should sacrifice with the Sākamedha offerings in Kārtika.

In this manner, he sacrifices for five years. Even after that, one who desires the fruit may perform the Cāturmāsya sacrifices two or three times for five years. Thus, there are three applications—five, ten, or fifteen years—which occur as optional alternatives. The repetition is for the purpose of concluding the inquiry. Thus ends the sixth chapter concerning the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice in the fifth book of the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin composed by Mahādeva.
Thus ends the fifth section on the Cāturmāsya sacrifices in the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* composed by Mahādeva.

6.1 Now begins the sixth question. (Therein, the first chapter: The duties of the Hotṛ and others have been defined for the Sāman-chanting rites performed by those seated according to the Ṛgveda and other Vedas; likewise, the duties of the Adhvaryu have been defined for the Yajurvedic rites. Furthermore, the duties of the Brahmā priest have been established for those Havis-sacrifices. In these [rites], the author—precluding the attainment of the fruit [of action] for the primary agents, namely the husband and wife—declares that their primary agency arises from mere intention (*saṃkalpa*) alone. Moreover, he explains the fruit of all actions here, as well as other matters incidentally.

Having briefly explained the performance of the *haviryajña* sacrifices and the duties of the sacrificer in detail, [the author] now proceeds to determine—by setting aside the restrictive rules regarding the performers such as the *hotṛ* priests—even with respect to those rites prescribed by the names of the Vedas (*hotrādi-veda-saṃjñābhiḥ*). This determination occurs through the sublation of general designations by means of indicative marks (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), specific mention (*viśeṣābhidhāna*), and direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). In the sixth book (*praśna*), there is a formal declaration (*pratijñā*) concerning those rites belonging to the *vaitānika* (sacrificial) category, including those performed with the *brahmán* priest and even those without a name. Among these, it is established that the fruit of the action accrues to the performer who accomplishes it.

In order to declare that the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) are to be understood through proficiency in logic, [the author] first extends this declaration for the whole work; it is now being defined in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices, such as the *haviyajña*. (7–8)
We shall now explain the *yājamāna* (the duties of the sacrificer).

Although, by the grammatical rule for the verbal root *yaj*—namely, that it signifies "worship" and so forth—and by the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacau*, which prescribes the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* as substitutes for the present tense (*laṭ*), the word *yajamāna* is etymologically derived as denoting one who performs acts such as worship; and although due to its *ātmanepada* ending it is understood to be the enjoyer of the fruit [of the action], nevertheless, by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the word refers specifically to that person who is the enjoyer of the fruit in a ritual (*karman*) to be accomplished through sacrifice.

Because the term *yajamāna* (sacrificer) is applied even to those who perform acts of public utility (*pūrta*) and acts intended for sacrifice (*yajaty-artha*), and because it is not observed to be used for one who merely performs the worship of a deity, therefore, in a rite performed by priests for whom a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has been set in motion, the person who is the enjoyer of the fruit is alone denoted by the word *yajamāna*. Nor is its usage seen for one who enjoys the fruit of mere ritual action; for there is an absence of its application even in the case of the enjoyment of fruits in rites prescribed by custom (*sāmayācārika*), such as the initiation (*upanayana*). The action of those two—the performer and the enjoyer of the fruit—is that which leads to [the respective result].

Since the wife’s status as an enjoyer of the fruit has already been established in the inquiry concerning the *ādhāna* (the laying of the sacred fires), although it has been settled that the various *vaitānika* (sacrificial) rites—such as the *agnihotra* and others—are restricted to specific performers designated by terms like "Hotṛ" and "Veda," nevertheless, because there exists specific authoritative evidence (*viśeṣapramāṇa*) that overrides that restriction, the possibility of the husband and wife acting as joint performers in certain cases arises; this is what is now being determined. In that regard, he states the authority for the fact that the means of attaining the fruit is to be performed by the sacrificer alone:
"In an entire sacrifice, whatever purpose is heard [in the scripture], the sacrificer desires it."

In the entire prescribed and unprescribed ritual with its constituent parts—a rite enjoined by injunctions through the employment of the word *kratu* and performed by officiating priests—the term *kratu* is applied here to include the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), as well as the Agnihotra, the Cāturmāsya, the Animal sacrifice, and the Agnihotra itself. This is established by the passage beginning with "In the New and Full Moon sacrifices there are four priests" and ending with "of the sacrificial rite of the Agnihotra," whereby even those rites not primarily of the nature of a *kratu* are included under the word *kratu* in a figurative sense. However, the Jyotiṣṭoma is included in its primary sense as a specific type of sacrifice involving the Soma juice and the animal offering.

The word *ṛtu* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) through common usage as referring to the Vājapeya sacrifice, as seen in such Vedic passages as "In the Vājapeya, all sacrificial seasons (*sarve yajñakratavaḥ*) are included. However, elsewhere—in the context of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*)—it is used figuratively (*gauṇa*), just like the terms *yajña* and *sattra*. In the present case, if only the primary meaning were accepted, the injunction regarding the performance of the *haviḥ-yajña* and the duties of the sacrificer would be contradicted; therefore, both the figurative and the primary meanings are to be understood.

In the statement "We shall explain sacrifice (*yajña*)," and in passages such as "rites characterized by injunctions" and "the highest good through ritual action," the Teacher—by employing the word *ṛtu* instead of the words *yajña* and *karman* used therein—indicates that he intends by the term *ṛtu* only those rites accomplished through sacrificial sessions (*sattra*). The "purpose" (*artha*) is that which is aimed at with the thought, "May this be mine"; that is to say, it is the fruit. In the context of a *ṛtu*, the purpose is the motivating factor by virtue of being the goal to be accomplished.

The agent desires that which is to be accomplished through ritual action—namely, heaven in the case of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice and so forth; stability and the like in the case of the *Rātrisatra* and so forth; or prosperity and the like in the case of such injunctions as "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu"—all of which are communicated as the purpose by the verbal suffixes (*liṅ*) indicating the means for achieving a desired end, assisted by the word for desire (*kāma*) and, where appropriate, by the indicative mark of ultimate liberation (*niḥśreyasa*). Nor should it be argued that because these are expressed in the present tense, they are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) of a desire; for if they were, the statement would be purposeless and thus redundant.

Therefore, the use of the form *kāmayeta* (he should desire) is an injunction (*vidhi*) because [the object] has not been previously established by other means. Furthermore, there is no injunction regarding the desire for a result itself; desire is simply a wish. It arises solely from the knowledge of the excellence of an object, and not through an injunction. For an injunction does not impel one toward the result itself. For this very reason, it has been stated that the suffix in the case of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is not injunctive with respect to the element of the result. Therefore, it must be said that the injunction pertains to the means of attaining the result.

In that regard, the verbal performance of desire (*kāmābhinaya*) which was previously unattained is precisely what is prescribed for one who desires; therefore, this restriction—that "one must indeed exert oneself"—is also appropriate. Furthermore, although the fruit resides in various Vedas, it should nevertheless not be mentally resolved (*saṃkalpanīya*) by the *adhvaryu* priests, because that would contradict the uniformity of the name (*samākhyā*). For this very reason, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is heard in the passage: "having said, 'I shall sacrifice' (*yo yakṣye*)."

By the phrase "having spoken," the verbal nature of the *saṃkalpa* (formal resolve) is stated; that very [resolve] is the first act of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), as declared by the Śruti itself. Having attained the form of a person, he becomes a "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) by virtue of engaging in the sacrifice—not one who has not yet commenced the sacrifice, but rather one who is about to sacrifice (*yakṣyamāṇa*). Therefore, having made the verbal resolve, "I shall sacrifice with this sacrifice," and while still in the state of being a preparatory member [of the rite], he makes the resolve, "I shall sacrifice with such-and-such a seasonal sacrifice" (*ṛtu*).

In that context, even the result being heard [in the scripture] is restated as having the object of desire as its domain by means of the phrase "desiring such-and-such" (*amuka-kāmaḥ*), because otherwise, if the result were not established as part of the remainder of that sentence, the sentence of intention (*saṃkalpa-vākya*) would be ineffective. The meaning is this: when one says, "I shall bring about [the result] through sacrifice," an expectancy arises as to "what? and to fulfill that, one must state "desiring such-and-such. For this very reason, in the case of an action whose result is other [than heaven], the use of the *parasmaipada* ending in the word "sacrifices" (*yajati*) is for the purpose of enjoining the agent's volition; for [the result] is not merely the locus of effort and physical motion.

Primary agency cannot belong to the *mātra* (the "mere" one). According to Pāṇini’s rule, "the independent one is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*), independence belongs primarily to the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). However, since independence exists only figuratively in those [factors] impelled by him, the author uses the *parasmaipada* (active voice) to show that this [figurative] independence is intended to be expressed. The author of the Sūtras also demonstrated this state of being impelled by another through the use of the *parasmaipada* in such passages as "the Hotṛ priest acts with the Ṛgveda," for one does not engage in an action whose fruit is for another's sake unless prompted by another.

But how can he be the enjoyer of the fruit if he is not the agent of the primary action? For agency in Vedic ritual does not consist in mere independence. Thus Jaimini states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the sūtra: "The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer, because that is its characteristic. Having first asserted that every ritual must be performed by the very one who enjoys its fruit, he concludes: "Or rather, in the case of a general rule, it should belong to the principal [agent]."

For even though this entire ritual action is impossible to accomplish [by oneself alone], the wife must perform that which has sacrifice as its sole primary element; by this much, the attainment of its fruit occurs. Therefore, Kātyāyana says: "The owner of the primary [act] is the partaker of the fruit. By him also, it was stated that sacrifice (*yāga*) is the relinquishment of substance and deity. Consequently, it is logical that the fruit of the action belongs to her because she is the performer of the primary act alone. However, in your position, the primacy of relinquishment (*tyāga*) was refuted in the first chapter. The primary sacrifice is one whose agent is the *hotṛ*, while the *homa* is...

If it is argued that the status of being performed by the *adhvaryu* or the *hotṛ* is established merely on the basis of independence—that the fruit of the action should belong to the agent—then it is replied: since it is a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "he who is the agent of the principal [act] is the agent of its subsidiaries," if the principal act of pressing were to have the sacrificer as its agent, then the subsidiaries would also have the sacrificer as their agent; thus, by virtue of these designations, there would also be self-agency for him. Therefore, the author of the Sūtras does not intend for the sacrificer to be the agent of the principal act.

Therefore, the purport of the Sūtra is that one who does not act for the sake of a result through volition (*saṃkalpa*) is not an independent agent; it is only he who acts through volition who is the independent agent, and no other. Nor should it be argued that one person cannot be the enjoyer of the fruit of what was done by another, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For instance, when the sacrifice has been performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the fruit belongs to the sacrificer’s wife as well. If it is asked by what cause this occurs, the answer is "by volition" (*saṃkalpena*). In this regard, there is the resolution provided by Āpastamba; such is the uniform method of resolution.

Just as the *apūrva* (unseen potency) arises even when the sacrificer is other than the one who performs the subsidiary acts (*aṅga*), so too the primary *apūrva* and its fruit must belong only to the agent of the resolve (*saṃkalpa*). Thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the result. As stated in the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: "Just as in the world a king and others enjoy sovereignty through mere resolve, even though the actual undertaking of the kingdom is performed by ministers and others who have been impelled [by him]."

Even in the case of "taking hold" (grahaṇa) during established acts such as the installation of deities (*devatā-pratiṣṭhā*) and other works of public utility (*pūrta*), which primarily consist of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), since renunciation (*tyāga*) is impossible, it likewise applies to the planting of trees and so forth; thus, because the modified primary rite occurs through mere intention (*saṃkalpa-mātra*), the sacrificer alone obtains the *apūrva* and its fruit—therefore, nothing is untenable.

Or rather, the construction of the Sūtra is as follows: In the entire performance of ritual action (*karmakratu*), although there is a fruit in the declaration (*saṃkalpa*) "I shall sacrifice"—which is expressed by the restatement (*anuvāda*) "he who will sacrifice" and by the indicative gesture of speech—nevertheless, the fruit heard in the injunctive sentence regarding the ritual is desired by the sacrificer himself. In the sentence "He shall sacrifice with this," the ellipsis (*vākyaśeṣa*) is "he desires this fruit through this [means]. Thus, he desires it.

Therefore, having stated at the very commencement of the sacrifice—as far as possible—"I shall sacrifice with this rite for as long as I live," and so forth, he should say, "I desire the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) by means of this," and so on, according to his specific desires. As Āpastamba has also stated: "At the beginning of a *kratu* (sacrificial session) and the like, one should desire the fruit of the *kratu*; at the beginning of a *yajña* (sacrifice), one should desire the fruit of the sacrificial limbs. It is taught that one should cause [the sacrificer] to hear what is desired as the goal even when the *kratu* is complete along with its limbs; and that, as it has been explained, refers to the primary fruit at the start of the *yajña*, and the fruit of the limbs when there is no commencement [of the main rite].

Now, when the constituent parts are fixed, one should not assume the fruit to be *niḥśreyasa* (the highest good) based merely on the scriptural injunction (*vidhi-śruti*), nor according to the logic of the *Rātrisatra*, nor even the fruit of heaven (*svarga*) according to the logic of the *Viśvajit*. Nor can it be [assumed] from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

However, the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*), being required by the principal act (*pradhāna*) for the sake of its own fruit and being grasped through the requirement for auxiliary status, do not themselves possess a desire for separate fruits. Nevertheless, because of this [Vedic] statement containing the word "desire" (*kāma*), which has no other purpose, even where a fruit exists—whether in the subsidiaries or in non-subsidies—a desire is heard in some cases as being directed toward the agent. In that case, is the fruit for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) or for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) alone? Even regarding the fruit of the sacrificer, there is a doubt as to whether it belongs to the priests or to the sacrificer. To reach a conclusion on this point, [the author] says:
"Likewise, among the obligatory sacrificial subsidiaries, those which the text declares as being connected with 'desire'..."

The sublation of the *utsarga* (general rule) by the *tuṣa* (exception) does not apply everywhere; nor is it the case that in all instances the mention of a fruit (*phalaśruti*) in explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is merely an *arthavāda*. Rather, in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), because of the scriptural injunction (*vidhiśruti*) which is independent of a fruit, they possess a fruit as parts of the principal rite. Likewise, even though there is no separate fruit mentioned, those limbs of the sacrifice (*yajñāṅga*) which are to be performed invariably are fruitful by virtue of possessing the fruit of the sacrifice itself.

Now, one might object: "What is the point of saying 'in the case of the eternal [rites]'? For since the performance of the constituent parts of a sacrifice (*yajñāṅga*) is mandatory, this is already established by the mention of 'sacrifices' alone. This is not so. In cases where a constituent part is optional—such as "one takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice" and "one does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice"—activity toward the optional *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice occurs solely for the sake of the fruit, and not otherwise, because the sacrifice lacks no deficiency (*avaiguṇya*) without it. Therefore, the meaning is that what is performed for the purpose of avoiding a deficiency is "eternal" (*nitya*).

Even among those other established locations, regarding those forms which are objects (*artha*), the word *artha* is derived in the [Pāṇinian] sūtra as "that which is sought" (*aryate*), and thus the result is stated there; therein, by means of the neuter indication, there is a reference—by the neuter plural form *yāni*, which denotes individuals—to that which was taught by the term denoting the genus (*jāti*).

Those objects of honor (*artha-māna*) which are to be constantly accomplished by a person—the root *kāmayati* (to desire) causes them to be heard and makes them known through direct denotation (*abhidhā*)—these alone are the fruits of the subsidiaries (*aṅga-phala*), and no others; these alone he desires while performing the sacrifice (*yanamāna*). This applies as a universal connection (*sarvānuṣaṅga*). This is the intended meaning: even regarding the subsidiaries of the sacrifice, [the result follows] because of the scriptural statement (*śruti*) that has no other purpose. [Note: The text fragment containing "ca. ṭa, ṭha, "sti yā| ha pra.paṭala: mahādevakṛtavaijayantīvyākhyāsametam" appears to be a colophon or commentary marker indicating the end of a section in the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva.]

The fruits [of action] have indeed been explained; that [textual passage] is not a mere *arthavāda*, for it is certainly not a negation (*apavāda*) even with respect to those [actions] which, though lacking a fruit, must nevertheless be performed. What more need be said regarding those [actions] without a fruit that cannot be undertaken? In such cases, there would be non-authoritativeness characterized by non-performance on the part of the injunction itself. Therefore, in both instances, there is no status as a *arthavāda*, but rather the status of being for the sake of a fruit. Here, the root *kāmayati* (to desire) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for words that convey an object through its being the content of a desire. This is because the two roots *bubhūṣati* (desires to be) and *titīrṣati* (desires to cross over) directly possess the same meaning.

The other [term] is *arthanam*. This is because the suffix (*pratyaya*) also has the same meaning. Even in the case of injunctions (*vidhi*) involving words such as *abhicarant* (performing sorcery) or *āmayāvī* (afflicted with disease), which denote undesirable objects, since the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—which is the unseen potency (*apūrva*) and is desirable—is made known by the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), it is impossible for it to be something to be accomplished without being an object of desire. Therefore, these [words] necessarily imply that the object is an object of desire; thus, they serve as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). These fruits, whether belonging to the primary or secondary parts of the rite, belong only to the independent agent of those actions.

Even though a desire for [the status of] an *adhvaryu* priest and so forth is heard in the scriptures, nevertheless, these [desires] cannot be established as having their own independent purpose, according to the principle that "the fruit of ritual actions belongs only to the independent agent. For the fruit of an action performed by one person cannot belong to another. Although there is also satisfaction as a result for others in certain actions such as providing water-stations (*prapā*), even so, that is not the fruit of the injunction itself; rather, it is merely a secondary (*ānuṣaṅgika*) result of the injunction. Thus, there is no deviation [from the rule].

And likewise, in the passage "whichever sacrificers he may desire," as well as "whomsoever he may desire, that he should attain a full lifespan," the fruit is indeed intended for the desire of the sacrificer; the fruit would not belong to the Adhvaryu priest if the sacrificer did not desire it. Similarly, in some cases, the fruit of the officiating priests is seen to be their own by virtue of being the object of their own desire. Even there, it occurs only when the sacrificer himself desires, "May the fruit of this rite accrue to the priests," and not otherwise. This very point is demonstrated by the phrase "sa yān."

Likewise, even in such passages as "He who desires that [the sacrificer] should be short-lived," there is no status as a statement of a result (*phala*), because they lack the character of authoritative means of knowledge (*māna*). It has been stated that even though something undesirable is desired by the *adhvaryu*, it does not come about through a rite performed by the instigating sacrificer (*yajamāna*); for example, "just as he desires what is undesirable for the sacrificer, so indeed [it happens]. Similarly, the phrase "it should not be done" is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, by the word "desires" (*kāmayati*), it is also stated that where a desire is not conveyed by words whose meaning is identical to the desire itself, even that which is desired is not a subsidiary result (*aṅgaphala*).

By the word "śrāvayati" (he causes to hear), [the result] such as desire (*kāma*) and so forth—though it is indicated by the words—is not presented through direct denotation (*abhidhā*), but rather is merely praised, because its denotation is obstructed by other words. Even in that case, there is no status as a fruit (*phala*); rather, it is simply an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Just as in the passage: "One should conclude with a *triṣṭubh*; the *triṣṭubh* is indeed power; the *rājanya* is indeed desirous of power," and likewise regarding the *jagatī*, here the words do not function as a cause for denotation, but are like an explanatory praise by way of restatement (*anuvāda*).

"If one should desire, 'May there be spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*),' he should conclude with a *gāyatrī* verse"—here, because it is directed toward a fruit, it is not a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). In this context, actions, substances, and qualities possess fruits. Regarding action first: at the *āghāna* (fire-consecration), there is the offering of a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla-iṣṭi*) to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. That [offering] is both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*). Likewise, the *sinīvālī* and *rākā* verses are portions for the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. As for genus: "One desiring spiritual luster should make the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of *pālāśa* wood. Regarding substance as well: milk is the substance for the *agnihotra* oblation.

*Guna* (quality): the state of being three *aratnis* or five *aratnis* in length for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). By the principle of "separateness through conjunction" (*saṃyogapṛthaktvanyāya*), these possess the status of being auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice. Similarly, even those things that are not [direct] auxiliaries but are dependent upon the ritual (*kratu*) are fourfold: the wall-offering (*kuḍyāga*) in the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings; *jāti* (genus)—for example, if one should desire, "May there be spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*)," then one should conclude with a *gāyatrī* verse, whereby the *gāyatrī*-ness [of the verse] is an auxiliary in the concluding rite (*paridhānīyā*); *dravya* (substance)—bronze or earthenware vessels used as beds; and *guṇa* (quality)—[as noted in the commentary]... *Ca. Ṭa. tayā'pi* (And by that also).

62. Regarding the height and depth of the *āghāra* oblation: there is no authoritative means of proof (*pramāṇa*) that establishes these as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice. If their status as auxiliaries were established by context (*prakaraṇa*), then there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) of the sentence, since it is heard only once. He provides an example:
as in the case of the upward and downward directions of the *āghāra*.

"One should pour upwards for one desiring heaven; downwards for one desiring rain. Just as the sacrificer desires, so he should act, thinking, "I shall make them equal. In the injunction regarding the *vyāhṛtis*, the specific quality characterized by the particular position—being prescribed as a fruit for the sacrificer—is to be desired by the sacrificer himself through mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*); this is the meaning. By means of this restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) in the sūtra, it demonstrates the exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) that results:
"The others are explanatory passages (*arthavādas*)."

The term "of the substrate" (ādhārasya) is carried over [from the preceding]. The other explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)—which enjoin qualities pertaining to conduct (*ācāra*)—are those that convey their meaning through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) alone, as they cannot be established otherwise; these are included within the injunctive core (*vidhyuddeśa*). Other explanatory passages, however, which are not included within the injunctive core, convey the meaning of the sentence even when standing apart, and by entering into a syntactic unity with the entire sentence (*vākyaikavākyatā*), they function as glorifications (*stāvaka*); the meaning is that they do not directly bestow the fruit [of the action].

For the authors of the Sūtras, as for the Mīmāṃsakas of Brahman, the unity of meaning (*vākyaikavākyatā*) of the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) is desired, because they accept the authority of these passages even with respect to the meaning of intermediate sentences; however, this is not like the unity of words (*padaikavākyatā*) held by the followers of Jaimini. Just as in the case of the injunction "he pours the oblation continuously" (*saṃtatamāghārayati*), where explanatory passages such as "for the continuity of the vital breaths and of food" serve the purpose of the *āghāra* libation, so too in other fixed sacrificial limbs, the explanatory passages established through other means are indeed [authoritative]. Thus he says:

Likewise, regarding other auxiliary elements of the sacrifice, [the text says]: "He makes it possessed of *purīṣa*; verily, by means of progeny and cattle, he makes him possessed of *purīṣa*"; "If he fixes the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), it is for the sake of discerning the world of heaven"; "With the words 'For food thee! For strength thee! he cuts off a branch; verily, he bestows food and strength upon the sacrificer. This is a statement from another recension (*śākhā*). The word "iti" is used for the purpose of including the various types of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) previously shown.
The preparation of materials includes the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) by the sacrificer, celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and the silent recitations (*japa*).

The substance that constitutes a constituent part of the sacrifice is established by [the rules concerning] materials such as *nīvāra* and so forth; even though it is enjoined in various specific Vedas, it should not be confused [with other substances]. For in those respective Vedas, the act of procuring the substance is not what is enjoined, but rather the status of the already established substance as a constituent part (*aṅga*). Therefore, the preliminary preparation of the substance is established by the sense of the text itself; however, for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) alone should perform this. Indeed, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), having been engaged out of desire for their sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), are not capable of incurring expenditure on their own initiative.

Therefore, while intending to procure the clarified butter, rice, animal victim, grains, cow, bull, and so forth, one should acquire them either through the exchange of one's own property or by other means. In this context, the mention of the "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is intended to ensure that the act of procuring the materials belongs to the one who is about to sacrifice (*yakṣyamāṇa*) even prior to the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and not to someone who might subsequently engage in the resolve. Thus, the term "sacrificer" is not connected with the phrase regarding the procurement of materials; rather, its connection is established only through the subsequent arrivals [of the materials]. This applies to the obligatory (*nitya*) rites.

[Chapter] 15, with the commentary *Baijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. The phrase "so that it may be" (*yathā syāt*) is connected with the triad beginning with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for a specific purpose, and it also carries over into the subsequent section. Giving a sacrificial fee consists of the renunciation of one's own ownership; this is not possible for one who is not the owner. Furthermore, its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*) is set aside by direct scriptural injunctions (*śruti*), such as "the Hotṛ priest should be given a horseless chariot," and so forth. Celibacy (*brahmacarya*)—defined as the renunciation of the eightfold sexual union—is indeed a mental refinement (*mānasa-saṃskāra*), because its application is restricted by the specific context of the ritual procedure (*samaya*).

For since the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) can function as agents even in the absence of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) belongs to the owner of the wealth—that is, it is a consecration for the sacrificer alone, serving an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). For this very reason, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the designation (*samākhyāna*), there is an injunction regarding celibacy: "He who is to be seated [as the sacrificer] shall observe celibacy for this night. Furthermore, there is the recitation (*japa*) of the mantras read anywhere in the Veda by the wife as well.

And he will state later that "the sacrificer does not depart while the ritual acts (*yajña*) among the Naimiṣeya people are being performed; they do not teach theft regarding gifts. Thus, she too certainly possesses ownership; therefore, when the sacrificer has departed, the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) must be performed by the wife as well, and the *vara* (gift) must be given. By the rule beginning with "he should give the severed parts," even the gift prescribed for occasions such as a spill is included under the term *dakṣiṇā*, since it refers to anything that is to be given. He shows that the recitation of mantras is established by the injunction: "He mutters the mantras which contain blessings directed toward himself and which are not instruments of the ritual act (*karmakaraṇa*)."

The term "the sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is understood to carry over [from the previous context]. Those [mantras] which, being directed toward the speaker, result in the attainment of what is desired for oneself—those mantras for which such blessings (*āśis*) are the objects to be conveyed are thus characterized. The phrase "may it be manifest to me" indicates that they are directed toward oneself (*ātmagāmitva*). The term "blessings" (*āśis*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) consisting of prayers for the attainment of what is desired. The sacrificer alone recites them; both [the restriction of the agent and the nature of the act] are thus enjoined.

Therefore, by the principle of Pāṇini’s *smṛti* regarding the unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) and the fourfold nature [of injunctions], it is established that what is unestablished must be understood as being enjoined for the sake of a specific purpose; thus, the meaning results in the fact that the act is directly performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) as its agent. Furthermore, he will state later that "the application (*viniyoga*) of those not enjoined by direct perception is not established"; from this it is known that an injunction (*vidhi*) must be inferred here.

This is the underlying intention: it has been stated by the *paribhāṣā-sūtra* that "mantras are for the purpose of sacrificial rites," meaning that mantras produced by the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) serve as means for fruitful rituals through the medium of understanding their own meanings. In that context, by what authority could those mantras for which there is no specific injunction of application (*viniyojaka-vidhi*) be considered for the purpose of sacrificial rites? Therefore, they are generally applied by the very injunction to study itself.

For those who desire specialized knowledge, the *dhātu* (the root/essence) alone—characterized by the mark of its own unique, incomparable, and singular nature as the object of injunction—should be the goal to be accomplished, and no other would be suitable. Now, one might object: since the *Daśatayī* (the ten books of the Ṛgveda), which was not previously enjoined by such rules as "the placement of the remainder," has been enjoined for the *sūṣṇīka* and *prākṛta* rites by the rule stating that "for those [verses] other than the Sāmans, it is a Yajus," there are no mantras other than these.

Regarding those for whom an application (*viniyoga*) is said to be inferred, he says here: "from the instruments of action" (*karmakaraṇāt*). Action (*karman*) is activity (*ceṣṭā*); those which are perceived as instruments (*karaṇa*) in that [activity] are the "instruments of action. For indeed, even when the archetypal silent rites (*tūṣṇīkakriyā*) have been enjoined, the mantras—even those containing self-benedictions (*pratyagāśis*)—possessing expectancy, proceed there by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) characterized by the capacity to convey that specific action.

Furthermore, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the internal benediction (*pratyagāśīḥ*), having set aside the injunction-generating capacity [of the mantra], does not proceed with full authority, because it gains its purpose through the indicative mark of the action itself, which is the very rite to be enjoined by the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). As for those mantras that do not perform an action, they lack the capacity to lead toward an action performed silently; even if there is a requirement for their absence, they cannot—being solely intent on internal benediction and not expressive of an action—attain an action through direct denotation (*abhidhā*).

Furthermore, there is no status here as "prescribed by a Brāhmaṇa" (brāhmaṇavihitatva) by virtue of which they could be understood as signifying ritual action—even through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā)—according to the rule *yathopadiṣṭaṃ brāhmaṇavantaḥ*. Therefore, it is more appropriate that these [mantras], by the force of the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*), serve only to generate an injunction for their own recitation (*japa*) as their specific result. It is not the case that the status of being an auxiliary to a rite (*karmāṅgatva*) of what has not been recited is made known by the injunction for study; rather, it is only that which has arisen through or is manifested by recitation that is now seen to be an authoritative means.

By the utterance of that [mantra], which is the object to be performed, the *apūrva* (unseen potency) itself must be directly expressed, because the object to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*) is not perceived. Nor can it be argued that there is a second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) indicating an object to be consecrated in the phrase "he mutters the mantra" (*mantraṃ japati*), since the mantra is intended to be employed elsewhere. By the second case-ending, one does not understand the status of being the most desired (*īpsitatamatva*), but rather merely the status of being a grammatical factor (*kārakatvamātra*), according to Pāṇini’s rule: "The [object] is that which is least desired [by the agent] when the action is directed toward it."

Therefore, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), which is synonymous with the "deposited" (*ādheya*) or "mental" (*mānasa*), is not produced through the substance alone; rather, the *apūrva* is directly generated by the act of reciting the mantra in the sacrificer himself—the master who is the enjoyer of the fruit—by way of the general rule (*autsargika*). For ritual acts, the primary fruit is the attainment of the desired result, and it is the master alone, and not the officiant (*ṛtvij*), who is capable of desiring, "May this desired thing be mine."

In the case of the instruction regarding other fruits, although it is true that whatever benediction (*āśis*) a priest pronounces belongs to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), nevertheless, when the fruit of the sacrificer is to be expressed by the mantra, the phrase "may this be for me" is merely figurative (*gauṇa*). Furthermore, there is no authority (*pramāṇa*) for assigning [the mantra] to another when its primary denotation (*abhidhā*) is contradicted. Since the name (*samākhyā*) is set aside by the indicative power (*liṅga*), the agent who utters [the mantra] in its primary sense is the sacrificer, who has set out to accomplish the fruit through the sacrifice, because he is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the fruit and the unseen potency (*apūrva*).

Just as one makes oneself consecrated (*dīkṣita*) by means of the *dīkṣā* rite, thereby rendered refined by an unseen potency (*apūrva*), so too, like the *Dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi*, although the recitation (*japa*) is an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), its character as a refinement of the sacrificer (*yajamāna-saṃskāraka*) is established. While a substitute for a sacrificer who is traveling will be mentioned for rites other than those that refine oneself, because this [recitation] is a refinement of oneself, there is no substitute for it; thus, it will be stated that the recitation belongs to the sacrificer himself even when he is away on a journey.

Thus, we consider it logical that the status of *japa* (muttering) as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) is established only when this [interpretation] is accepted. Therefore, since the name [of the ritual] is obtained from the *Ṛgveda* and other sources, and because there is no sublation of the primary [status], wherever there is the recitation of a mantra, there *japa* must be performed in proximity to the ritual act. Wherever in the mantras there is a manifestation of the sacrificial material or a prayer for personal blessing, there it should be performed as an integral part of those respective acts at the time characterized by the specific action produced by each of them.

In that regard, even the displacement [of a mantra] from its place of recitation is permitted by an internal indicative mark (*liṅga*), because that mark is stronger than the order of recitation. Furthermore, those mantras which, through the performance of an action, are intent upon bestowing blessings upon the individual self (*pratyag-āśīḥ-parāḥ*), cannot achieve their purpose of bestowing blessings without an action; therefore, the indicative mark of the action alone is stronger. Consequently, in the case of silent (*tūṣṇīka*) archetypal (*prākṛta*) rites, they apply themselves even by means of a figurative function (*gauṇī vṛtti*), superimposing the status of the individual self upon each respective ritual act.

Those [mantras] which have internal indications (*pratyagāśis*) and are enjoined by direct statement (*śruti*) for use in a ritual action—since their indicative power (*liṅga*) is all the more set aside by that direct statement—they possess a purpose directed toward the ritual action through figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*). Thus, in the section on the *anapanyūṅkha* Sāmans (1st Paṭala), Pāṇini, relying on the principle that will be stated here, has declared that even the rule of monosyllabic pronunciation (*ekaśrutya*) is set aside; consequently, its fourfold intonation (*cātuḥsvarya*) is established by the recitation of the Adhvaryu priest.

And when this rule has been thus stated regarding the muttering (*japa*) performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), then—by the principle of such a general rule—it extends the duty of being performed by the sacrificer to certain other acts enjoined by their respective injunctions, even though they are distinct actions indicated by different words, such as: "he worships," "he consecrates with a mantra," "he addresses with a mantra," "he touches," and "he mutters."

Even though the mantras directed toward the inner self (*pratyagāśis*) are taught by that very injunction ending with "he recites" (*mapati*), and even though they are assigned to other specific rites by their respective specific [indications], the sacrificer himself does not employ them as such. For he does not employ them as the means for those actions, even though they appear as such through the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā śruti*) prescribed in each Veda, which indicates their instrumental role in the *ṛtvik-japa* (the silent recitation of the officiating priests).

In this context, by virtue of being directed toward a blessing for oneself (*pratyagāśīḥ-paratva*), the status of the sacrificer as the agent is extended [to the recitation]; that is to say, when the *japa* (recitation) is prescribed, the sacrificer is the agent. This is the underlying point: although there is a difference in ritual acts (*karma-bheda*) [between the original rite] and [the recitation] expressed by such phrases as "he stands near" (*upatiṣṭhate*), and while there is a difference in the mode of performance (*prayoga-bheda*) in the case of the *japa*, nevertheless, the mantras—being understood as the means of accomplishing that [original] act—do not thereby abandon their character of being directed toward a blessing for oneself.

With respect to the action (*kriyā*) which constitutes a constituent part, instrumentality (*sādhanatva*) is not expressed by the instrumental case; rather, because they are primary only with respect to the injunction of self-benediction (*pratyagāśīḥśāsana*), they are [regarded as instruments] through that [injunction], since they are non-different from it. Even though there is a denotation of a qualified entity by the verb "he approaches" (*upatiṣṭhate*) and so forth, the constituent parts of the qualification—which, although of the nature of actions, occur simultaneously with the recitation of the mantra—cannot be accomplished by the mantra, due to their lack of suitability [for such accomplishment].

For joining the palms in *añjali* is not performed at the conclusion of the recitation during attendance (*upasthāna*), nor is facing [the deity] during invocation (*abhimantrya*), nor is touching with the hand during consecration (*abhimantraṇa*), nor is stroking with the hand during anointing (*mārjana*). Rather, that which was commenced beforehand continues through the utterance of the mantra; how then could it be accomplished by the mantra? Furthermore, because they are not conveyed by the mantras—indeed, those actions are not seen in the words of the mantras. Therefore, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is appropriate only insofar as they are the means for conveying the benediction (*āśis*) conveyed by the mantra.

The praise of the object is the meaning of the subordinate sentences (*avāntara-vākyārtha*), while the pronouncement of blessings after having praised is the meaning of the principal sentence (*mahāvākya*). That [blessing] alone is the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) as that which is to be conveyed by the mantra; the praise is merely its ancillary part (*aṅga*), and thus there is no contradiction with that [principle]. Furthermore, it should not be argued that because they are the objects of refinement (*saṃskārya*) here, they are indicated by the accusative case. For instance, in the case of the *upasthāna* (approaching), even though the objects such as the door-panels are indicated by the accusative, they are not inherent to the ritual action (*karma-asamaveta*). Moreover, although the *bhānya* and other items are inherent to the action, they do not possess the status of being objects of refinement, as that would result in a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*).

Furthermore, for the sake of obtaining the expectation of results from those [deities], the "approaching" (*upasthāna*) of those objects is indeed a form of praise (*stuti*); thus, it is designated by the accusative case as being the object of praise. Moreover, praise is the proclamation of qualities (*guṇakīrtana*), just like the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns. In the act of approaching, the nature of praise is clearly seen in such passages as: "They praised the Abhīvarta; he, being praised, [bestowed] nights upon them," and "He praised Agni; he, being praised, [bestowed] this [world] upon him. This is because approaching is itself praised by virtue of its being of the nature of praise.

Within these very *āryavāda* (laudatory statements), he also demonstrates the attainment of results through praise, as in: "The gods, having purified the animal sacrifice, fulfilled their desires," and "He, being thus praised, led [them] to the heavenly world. Furthermore, regarding the rule "one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should stand in worship (*upatiṣṭhate*) before the fire-altar," this standing in worship is likewise solely for the sake of a benediction (*āśis*). In that case, there is a praise of the purpose; however, by means of the accusative case, the subordinate element (*guṇin*) is not presented as the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*), nor is that which is to be expressed [the fire] presented as the substratum of the quality (*guṇāśraya*), but rather [the fire is understood] in its primary sense.

Thus, even in the case of consecrations (*anumantraṇa*) and the like, the accusative case is used because of their status as objects of praise (*stutya*), and not because they are the most desired (*īpsitatama*) as things to be refined (*saṃskārya*). Furthermore, by the rule *akathitaṃ ca*, it expresses merely the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*) or a means (*sādhana*). *Śrautasūtra* composed by Sāyaṇa Mādhava, Sixth Book, Section 502.

Or rather, the substance offered during the consecration (anumantraṇa) is indicated by the second [word]; however, praise (stuti) is seen to consist of the names of the deities and benedictions (āśīrathī), because the teaching of the fruit is directed toward them alone—as in: "With the divine ordinance, may I become an eater of food," he says; "Agni is the eater of food among the gods; by that very means he takes food into himself," and so also for the Brahman priest.

Although it may be possible that in the case of food and the like, the substance itself is what is to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*), nevertheless, even as something revealed by the mantra, it is [the object] only with respect to the *apūrva* (transcendental result) which constitutes a part of the action, and not with respect to the communication of the mantra itself; for the mantra has the purpose of expressing a benediction (*āśīḥ*). Since the consecration of the object is established precisely through that [benediction], it is not [the object] in its primary sense. For this very reason, when one is traveling, [the recitation] is just like the muttering (*japa*) performed while departing.

He will state that because the acts of standing and so forth are themselves the ritual acts (*karma*) that effect their own consecration (*saṃskāra*), their respective mantras are recited by [the agent] himself. If the object to be consecrated were a material substance (*dravya*), then, since such acts are for the sake of another (*parārtha*) and are performed by the Adhvaryu priest, a substitute would be permissible. However, those acts—standing and so forth—are not merely auxiliary acts (*ārādupakāraka*); they do not have action as their primary purpose, but consist essentially of praise and recitation. [Objection: But how can a specific form of recitation be enjoined here, given that in expressions such as "he stands in worship" (*upatiṣṭhate*), the nature of recitation (*japa*) is not perceived?

And if [the mantra] were understood [as the instrument], there would be no connection with the third case ending (*tṛtīyā-nirdiṣṭa*). It is said in reply: By Pāṇini’s sūtra *upānmantrakaraṇe* (1.3.25), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the word *upatiṣṭhate* is prescribed; thus, that action for which the mantra is the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the object (*karman*) [of the verb]. The root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *upa* signifies "standing near" (*paridhāna*), and the utterance of the mantra is what is enjoined. The communication of meaning, however, follows from its inherent capacity (*sāmarthyāt*). Or else, the meaning...

Regarding the rule that "the injunction [of an action] must be expressed, while its performance follows from the capacity [of the words]," when it is established by this principle that one or the other of the two must be enjoined, the author of the Sūtra enjoin[s] the *naptṛ* suffix alone. This is because of its primacy and because it is directly accomplished through human effort. As for the communication [of meaning], it is not directly accomplished by human activity, since it is an operation of the word; rather, only when the act of utterance—which is directly accomplished by human effort—is enjoined as the object of the injunction, the communication subsequently arises as a result produced by the person through a series of intermediate steps.

For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras has employed the accusative case for the mantras being taught solely for the purpose of indicating their relationship [to the ritual action]. In that context, regarding the statement "one worships with a mantra" (*mantreṇopatiṣṭhate*), one should consider that the instrumental case merely restates the status of being a means of accomplishment (*sādhanatā*) which is already established by the sense of the matter; thus, even though the accusative case is implied—since the mantra is the object (*viṣaya*) rather than the instrument (*sādhana*)—it is shown in the instruction by the very rule *akathitaṃ ca*. It is indeed prescribed by that rule.

And likewise, having risen and joined his palms in *añjali*, one should offer [the oblation] while reciting the mantra; here, "one who recites the mantra" refers to one who praises the deities of the limbs (*aṅga*) of the ritual. Even in the case of the expression "he consecrates with the mantra," it is the same: having focused on the substance, one praises the deities of the substance by means of the sequence of the mantra, and so forth. The verbal root *mantr* is well-known to denote speech that expresses one's own intention, and it functions in specific ways according to the variation of prefixes (*upasarga*).

In this case as well, "he consecrates" (*abhimantrayate*) means facing [the object], looking at the substance while reciting the mantra, praising the substance itself with the mantra, and so forth; the rest is the same. In the case of "he touches" (*abhimṛśati*), it also means touching the substance while uttering the mantra, praising the meaning of the mantra with the mantra, and so forth; the rest is the same. In all instances, although terms such as *pratyagāśīḥ* ("blessings directed toward oneself"), *mukhyayā vṛttyā* ("by the primary function"), and *yajamānasya naṣṭer upatiṣṭhate* ("he stands near for the sake of the sacrificer's loss") denote the act of recitation (*japa*), one should understand that there is a distinction between the rites due to the difference in meaning conveyed by these different words.

Just as in the *Dhātuanuśāsana-sūtras*—where, despite the prescription of identical meanings through roots such as *yaja* (in sacrifice), *hu* (in giving), and *ḍudā* (in giving)—there is a distinction of action (*karmabheda*) due to differences in conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) and thus they are not synonyms; so too here, there is a distinction of action through different words. Regarding those beginning with *yajati*, the explanation has already been provided in the first chapter on technical definitions (*paribhāṣāpaṭala*). It is more appropriate that this same principle applies to [roots] such as *upatiṣṭhati* and others; thus, the rule is entirely consistent with the sacred revelation (*śruti*). As for the word "and" (*ca*): [it serves to include other cases].
The purpose of the instrumental case is to indicate a connection with each [item]. [Chapter 1, Section 150] This concludes the section accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.
He performs the rites exactly as they have been prescribed.

The sacrificer alone performs even those actions that are subsidiary to the recitations such as the *upasthāna*, not exceeding what has been prescribed. By means of the mantras containing prayers for personal benefit (*pratyagāśī*), he performs only those rites that are specifically enjoined for him through the general rule of recitation, and not wherever they might otherwise occur. Likewise, since the bringing forward of the *praṇītā* water and other such acts are heard of in the section pertaining to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), and thus their performance by the sacrificer would follow as a matter of course, this sūtra is applied once again to clarify the point.

Whatever is to be done by us for the sake of the sacrificer is to be performed by him alone; it is not everything prescribed in the section concerning the sacrificer. This is the intended meaning: although acts such as the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* water are prescribed in the *Adhvaryava* (the duties of the Adhvaryu), two persons cannot perform a single ritual act together. Therefore, when the Adhvaryu performs [the act], it becomes as if performed by the sacrificer; thus, there is no absolute subordination of the sacrificer. However, if it were performed by the sacrificer, it would not be performed by the Adhvaryu, and thus there would be a total subordination of the *Adhvaryava* duties.

Even in the case of the recitation of mantras that illuminate the *praṇītā* water and other such items during their being brought forward (*praṇayana*), it is logically established that these acts belong to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). Furthermore, the fact that purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the inspection of the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*) are to be performed by both [the sacrificer and the officiating priest] is established because of the specific injunction. Now, one might ask: "In that case, why was it stated—as opposed to simply saying 'wherever one stands near or recites a consecratory mantra (*anumantrayate'), the sacrificer alone should do so,' as stated by Bhāradvāja—that one should do so 'when not possessed of power' (*apatau'), by supplying the word *apatau*? It is said in reply: It is thus...

If it were being recited, it would necessarily be a *karaṇa-mantra* (an instrument mantra). If it is argued, "Let it be so; what is the harm?", we say no. In that case, it would belong exclusively to the Adhvaryu. If it is objected, "But surely it belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) because of a direct scriptural statement (*vacana*)," we reply: no. Because that [assignment] is rooted in logical principle (*nyāya*), when such a principle is absent, it cannot belong to the sacrificer. And the principle is as follows: if the purpose is solely to invoke the fruit, then the capacity to produce the *apūrva* of the fruit resides in the sacrificer through the *japa-apūrva* (the transcendental result of the silent recitation), or perhaps in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice. However, if it were a *karaṇa-mantra*, it would not be so; consequently, it would also belong to the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*).

Furthermore, when the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is away on a journey, the duties should belong to the officiating priest (*adhvaryu*) alone, because it is accepted that he acts as his representative (*pratinidhi*) in rites performed for others. Regarding the personal consecrations (*svasaṃskāra*), however, these are indeed the duties of the sacrificer. In that regard, if there is a mere omission of a subsidiary act, the deficiency may be remedied by the recitation of the *anājñāta* hymns or by the remembrance of Viṣṇu and so forth. But the primary act of recitation (*japa*) must be performed even by one who is traveling. As for the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) and similar acts, we consider it logical that the mental action which constitutes their constituent part can only be performed by the sacrificer himself.

Furthermore, when [the mantra] is enjoined as a *japa* (muttering), its quality of being recited with the accentuation of Vedic study (*adhyayanadharmatā*) is also established. This is because Pāṇini records in his Sūtra that "there is a single accent (*ekaśruti*) in the case of a vocative address, in the performance of a sacrifice, and in *japa*, *nyūṅkha*, and *sāman*. However, the author of the Sūtras establishes the quality of being recited with the accentuation of Vedic study through reasoning alone. How so? Because, just like the verbs *adhīte* (he studies) and *paṭhati* (he recites), the verb *japati* has utterance as its primary sense. Whatever manner of utterance occurs in Vedic study, that very same manner is intended by *japati*; it is not something [merely] indicated [by the root].

If, however, it is merely an instrument (*karaṇa*), then only as much as is required for the recollection of the meaning is expected as an instrument; but since the single accent (*ekaśruti*) suffices for conveying the sense, the various accents (*svaras*) are not prescribed. Although it is stated in rules such as "the first member [of a compound] has its original accent" (*bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam*) that accent also plays a role in the cognition of meaning, even that is merely a means for determining the meaning at the time of recitation and is not an essential factor (*aṅga*). Therefore, the ritual action must be accomplished by a mantra whose meaning has already been determined. For this very reason, it is said: "in the sacrificial rite" (*yajñakarmaṇi*).

Even though there is an absence of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) in the case of the *śastras*, they possess the status of a primary act (*kaśrutya*) because of the scriptural statement. The injunction "he recites" (*śaṃsati*) culminates merely in the manifestation of the qualities of the deity. And it has been stated that they are not instruments. Furthermore, in the rule "or rather, he praises (*stauti*) and recites (*śaṃsati*)" (ŚB 1.8), it is exactly so. According to Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, these two would not be subordinate acts; rather, they constitute primary acts because the emphasis is on the manifestation [of the deity] itself, and not on the mere utterance.

In the case of the *śāstra*s (recitations), the act of recitation itself is the instrument (*karaṇa*), just as it is in the case of the *mantra*s used for performance. Regarding the *stotra*s, since it is stated by Jaimini that "one should praise with the *sāman*" (*sāmnā stuvīta*) and that "the *sāman* is the essence of the chant" (*gītir eva sāma*), and because the *āna* (the *udātta* accent) is indeed the essence of the tone, one should manifest the qualities of the deity Agni through the *sāman*—that is, through the chant (*gīti*)—as the final purpose of the act of praising (*stuti*). Thus, while in the case of the *mantra*s used for performance, the production of the *apūrva* (transcendental result) occurs through the manifestation of the meaning by means of the action accomplished by the *mantra*, it is understood from the force of the injunction, supported by the direct Vedic statement (*prakṛti-śruti*) regarding the base [of the *sāman*], that in the case of the *stotra*s and *śastra*s, the *apūrva* is produced by the mere utterance. This is well-established.

In cases such as *saparyopasthāna* (attending with reverence), although the act of recitation (*japa*) is common to both, designations occur based on what is unique [to one]; and according to the principle that "the cognition of the qualified object arises when its qualifier has been apprehended," it is [the root] as distinguished by the prefix (*upasarga*) [that is intended].

Since that which is qualified by [specific] words must indeed be expressed as qualified, the designation, the presentation, the consecration with mantras (*anumantraṇa*), the invitation (*āmantraṇa*), and the touching (*abhimarśana*) apply only to those [acts] characterized by such qualifications. However, when there is merely the utterance of a mantra that has previously arisen, the designation "recitation" (*japa*) applies; when for the purpose of memorization, it is "study" (*adhyayana*); and when the recitation of mantras is distinct from these two, it is simply "reading. Since the primacy of the act of utterance does not deviate in any case, this Sūtra is more appropriate.
As far as is stated: "The duties of the wife are celibacy and recitations."

The sacrificial duties that apply without distinction to both husband and wife are restricted to the wife alone. Why? If every action were to belong to her as well, then the rule "the wife looks [at the clarified butter]" would be redundant; therefore, it is understood that she must perform only what is explicitly stated for her. In this context, the restriction is that "only those actions which are stated" apply to her, and not that "only those actions which are stated" are permitted (thereby excluding others). To express that this does not constitute an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and silent recitation (*japa*), it is stated: "celibacy and silent recitations."

Regarding the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*): although it is already established by implication that she [the wife] must observe celibacy for the sake of her husband’s, this statement is repeated in order to say that she should also restrain even mental fluctuations. Furthermore, since there is no application of the mantras containing responses directed toward herself (*pratyagāśis*) within the *Yājamāna* section, this undertaking is made so that they may be used according to their indicative power (*liṅga*). By the word "recitation" (*japa*), acts such as worship (*upasthāna*) and others are also restricted to her own responses directed toward herself.
We shall now explain the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

The *haviḥ-yajñas*, such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and others, have already been described; it is precisely within them that the *yājamāna* (the duties of the sacrificer) was intended to be explained. Nevertheless, the term "of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*" was stated in order to declare that the preceding *yājamāna* is common to all rites. The meaning is that the preceding [section] applies to everything by way of context (*prasaṅga*). Although the purpose would have been accomplished merely by saying "we shall explain [it] for the *darśapūrṇamāsa*," the inclusion of the word *yājamāna* is so that the word *darśapūrṇamāsa* should not be taken as denoting time (*kāla*).

The shaving being prescribed by him is not enjoined merely for the sake of time; rather, because it is designated as occurring prior to all other constituent parts of the sacrificer’s resolve, it must be performed as an auxiliary to one who has already set out for the sacrifice. It is not to be performed by one who, due to fate, is unable to perform the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, nor even by one whose sacred fires have been extinguished. In the subsequent sūtra, the mention of the "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is for the purpose of excluding the wife.
On the day of the full moon or new moon, the sacrificer shaves his hair and beard.

The word "parvaṇi" is used in the singular again for the purpose that it should apply to the very first *parvan*. Since the qualification applies to both [the full moon and the new moon], the new ritual result (*apūrva*) is to be accomplished through the performance of both; therefore, Vaikhānasa says: "Having declared, 'I shall sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsa,' he shaves his hair and beard and observes the fast; having declared, 'I shall sacrifice with the Darśa,' he observes the fast."

Immediately after the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), the shaving of the hair is intended to take place on the full-moon day itself as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of that rite. However, some say that the mention of the "parvan" (the lunar phase) is intended to indicate that the time for shaving extends until the completion of the ritual performance. He has his barber shave the hair on his head and the beard on his face. Here, the word "hair" (*keśa*) is mentioned first because it ends in the vowel *a*, and not for the sake of the sequence. As for the actual order: first he shaves the beard, then the armpits, then the hair, then the nails—starting from the little finger of the left hand, then the right, and likewise for the feet.
On the full moon day, at breakfast, the husband and wife eat food mixed with clarified butter (*sarpis*).

In the previous sūtra, the wife was excluded; here she is taken up again. "Breakfast" (*prātarāśaḥ*) means eating in the morning; this word *prātarāśa* is conventionally established as referring to the first meal, and not merely to that which occurs specifically in the morning. Therefore, the morning time for the *anvādhāna* (the preliminary rite) mentioned in the section for the Adhvaryu priest—beginning with "when the sun has risen, [he brings] the *āhavanīya* fire from the *gārhapatya*"—is not contradicted, since performing the *anvādhāna* in the morning is desired. As for the specific time, it is unrestricted; however, when there is sufficient food, the rule regarding eating applies.

In this context, the mixing with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) is prescribed as an integral part of the ritual act, whereas the eating itself occurs solely by desire. Therefore, even when the [usual] time for eating is bypassed due to a lack of hunger, the requirement of mixing with clarified butter is not set aside, because of the scriptural injunction; thus, there is a restriction (*niyama*) regarding both. When the possibility of eating other things arises, it is excluded by the statement: "whatever else besides meat and beans.
Because of this dual exclusion (*parisaṃkhyāna*), that which is not prohibited may be eaten.
They should not be well-fed; let them not be satiated. Prior to the driving away of the calf on the new moon day, they may, at their pleasure, be well-fed.

"At the Full Moon sacrifice (Pūrṇamāsa), there is no fixed rule regarding the time for eating; this [time] is restricted here. Having completed the rite at the end of the fortnight, one who maintains the sacred fires (Sāgnika) should perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. Then the wise man should perform the Piṇḍayajña, and after that, the Anvāhāryaka. Thus, in sequence, there follows the feeding, the driving away of the calves (Vatsāpākaraṇa), and the observance of the vow. Here too, the inclusion of meat (sapiṃśmitatā) continues, as it is said: "whatever else [is offered]. In this context, for one performing the Piṇḍapitṛyajña and the monthly rites (Māsika), Kātyāyana states that the driving away of the calves occurs after the meal in the afternoon.
In this case as well, it is exactly as before. According to Āpastamba and Vaikhānasa, [one may use] curds or milk in the absence of clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*).
When the fires are being replenished (*anvādhīyamāneṣu*), he mutters the formula "I take Agni, the good chariot" (*agniṃ gṛhṇāmi suratham*).

The remainder [of the procedure] pertains to the forms of the deities according to their respective characteristics (*yathāliṅga*). He mutters those formulas prescribed for the replenishing of the fires, ending with "Ahibudhnya restrains [him]," according to their respective characteristics. Having entered by the eastern door and gone around the Āhavanīya fire to its north, he sits down in his own place.
In this context, the word "paryanta" (limit/end) is superfluous.
506. Regarding the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, in the sixth book:

"I announce this sacrifice to the Vasus, with Agni as their chief; I announce this sacrifice to the Rudras, with Indra as their chief; I announce this sacrifice to the Ādityas, with Varuṇa as their chief"—[these formulas are recited] when the fires have been placed upon the hearths (*anvāhita*).
The word "he recites" (japati) is to be supplied [to each clause].
He undertakes the vow with sacrificial grass (*barhis*) at the Full Moon sacrifice, and with the calves at the New Moon sacrifice.
It should be understood that this means "along with the fetching of the sacrificial grass" and "along with the driving away of the calves."
Some authorities prescribe these steps in this specific sequence: eating, the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*), and the undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*).

Regarding the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*), eating occurs at an unrestricted time when hunger arises; it is stated that one should eat when hungry at the proper time, and only then perform the *anvādhāna*, not necessarily in the morning. Following that comes the vow; for it is said, "One undertakes the vow with the *bahiḥ* grass on the full moon day," implying an interval between them. The alternative view is that for some, the undertaking of the vow follows immediately after the *anvādhāna*. However, on the following day, if the option of bringing the *bahiḥ* grass is chosen, this same sequence applies.
Some say that the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*), the eating, and the undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*) [are performed at these times];
the meaning is that they should indeed follow the sequence. This is exactly the same even for one who does not offer the *saṃnāya* oblation.
These two are common times for both [the *praṇītā* water] while it is being poured out and the sacrificial offerings (*havis*) when they have been placed near.

The meaning is that for both of these [observances], the undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*) is optional (*vikalpate*) at the two *parvan* (junction) times. Here, because they are common to both sides, it is understood that the option is fixed sequentially for each of the two *parvan*s. He demonstrates the very undertaking of the vow:
"Having touched water with [the mantra] 'Lightning art thou' (*vidyud asi*)," and here [he recites] the *agnihotra-offering* formula ending with "Faith in me" (*mayi śraddhā*).

Having passed to the south of the Āhavanīya fire by another way, he sips water with the formula, "The plants are full of sap," ending with *sarasvant*. He sips and then eats [the food]. Then follows the sipping for the sake of external purification.

He worships the deities with the formula: "O gods, exert yourselves among the gods; as the first among the second, the second among the third—ye who are the three times eleven, protect me here! May I be able to do this which I do; the Self does this for the Self; 'I shall do this,' 'this is my remedy,' 'this is the all-healing for me. O Aśvins, protect us both! Thus he worships the deities.

He worships the thirty-three deities while still remaining on the south side. [End of] Paṭala 15.
