[From] the *Vaijayantī* commentary composed by Mahādeva: Meditating upon the ocean in his mind, he worships the sun with the mantra: "Thou art the sovereign (*samrāj*), thou art the guardian of vows; thou art the lord of vows. I undertake a vow; I declare it unto thee. May I be able to perform it; may I be capable through it; may I succeed through it. He should indeed perform the meditation upon the ocean. This is stated in another Sūtra: "One who is about to undertake a vow meditates upon the ocean in his mind," and then worships the sun with the words, "Thou art the sovereign."
"O Agni, lord of vows, I shall perform the vow," with these words the Brāhmaṇa stands before Agni;
ending with "sadhyaṅ mā.
"O Vāyu, lord of vows," [he addresses] Vāyu; "O Āditya, lord of vows," [he addresses] Āditya; "O lord of vows, lord of vows," [he addresses] the Lord of Vows.
He worships Agni with the words, "Agni is the lord of the vows of the gods," according to the Vedic revelation; the phrase "I shall fulfill my vow" is to be supplied to all three [verses].
These [verses] are common, with the exception of the one addressed to Agni.

The meaning is that, except for the mantra for the attendance upon the Sun (*ādityopasthāna*), other mantras may be used by Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and even Brāhmaṇas. If the sun should have set, he attends upon the Āhavanīya fire itself with the mantra for the attendance upon the Sun. If, due to divine or human causes, the commencement of the vow (*vrata-upāyana*) should occur at sunset during the performance of a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), then he should attend upon the Āhavanīya fire itself with the mantra for the attendance upon the Sun, because the Sun has entered into it.
On the full-moon and new-moon days, the sacrificer performs the Agnihotra himself. || 1 ||

"By himself" means the sacrificer; this refers to one who has already commenced the performance. The mention of "on the parvan day" is a reiteration to show that this entitlement applies specifically to the parvan day, and that there is a rule for both morning and evening [offerings]. The inclusion of the term "parvan" is intended to demonstrate that the Agnihotra, which is already established as occurring on the parvan day, is here restricted to that time, and not that the sacrificer's duty is being prescribed as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). [The rule is: "On the new moon day, he should offer gruel (*yavāgū*)."

The phrase "the sacrificer himself" is understood to carry over. The optional substance is restricted by the rule "only with gruel (yavāgvā). Although one could simply say "performing the *saṃnayana*," the specific mention of the *amāvāsyā* (new moon) is intended so that this does not apply on the first day (*pratipad*) when the ritual is known as the morning [offering]. Regarding this, Bharadvāja states: "On this very new moon night, the children do not drink milk; having offered the Agnihotra for him with gruel on this night... Here, the prohibition of milk for the children is caused by the injunction to milk all the cows for the *sānnāyya* offering.

Therefore, on the night of the new moon, only one who performs the *saṃnayya* offering does not have his children drink milk; instead, there is an offering of barley-gruel (*yavāgū*). Even in that case, at the time of the full moon (*parvan*), the offering of gruel is performed by oneself; it is not for one who does not perform the *saṃnayya*. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says: "The Agnihotra offering with gruel is for the *saṃnayya*-performer on that night. Now, one might object: "For the *saṃnayya*-performer on the full moon day, would there not be an offering of gruel at night? This is not so. The rule is that where there is an offering of barley-gruel for the Agnihotra, it occurs where the cows are milked for the sake of the *sāṃnāyya* (the curd-mixture).

And it should not be so even in the morning. Because they do not drink milk at night, the Agnihotra cow must be kept away from other animals in the morning. [Variant readings: 1. *cha*, *ṭa*: *yām* for *yāṃ*; 3, 4: *cha*: *yamityeva*]; according to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Āpastamba, he places the scrapings of that [milk] aside for the purpose of curdling.

Regarding that *yavāgū* (gruel) with which the *agnihotra* was performed—that is, the *yavāgū* by means of four ladlings of which the *agnihotra* was offered—its remnant remaining in the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle is intended for the purpose of curdling (*ātañcana*), as indicated by the statement regarding its utility. This implies that this remnant is not a mere ritual disposal (*pratipatti*). Therefore, it has already been stated that in the event of the loss of the remnant, one should perform the curdling with a substitute. Furthermore, it is not appropriate to offer the *yavāgū* again for the sake of curdling, because there is no injunction stating, "One should offer [the gruel] for the purpose of curdling."

And that [offering] is indeed obtained through its own specific injunction; it is prescribed for the sacrificer on the new moon day with barley-gruel (*yavāgū*). For this very reason, it is stated that the remnant (*uccheṣaṇa*) of that [gruel] is produced as a byproduct for the purpose of curdling. Therefore, what was said by Baudhāyana—that "one should offer again for the sake of the remnant"—is refuted, as it contradicts the principles of the *Nyāya* system. [The sacrificer] does not speak untruth, does not eat meat, does not approach a woman, and does not eat during that night.

Since the prohibition of speaking untruth has already been established, its restatement specifically regarding one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) is for the purpose of making it known as an integral part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*). By this, it is shown that if one speaks untruth through negligence, one must perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) at that very moment and then proceed with the subsequent rite. The phrase "not meat" (*na māṃsam*) prohibits meat even apart from eating; whereas the previous prohibition was of meat obtained as a side-dish (*vyañjana*) during the morning meal, this present one is another prohibition of meat that might otherwise be obtained, such as fruit and the like.

Alternatively, for one who performs the monthly *śrāddha* and other rites, the consumption of the remaining portions [of the food] would otherwise be required; even in that case, the prohibition is established by the rule that one should consume only the remainder excluding meat.
He eats the forest-grown [food] in the evening.

If he eats in the evening, then he eats forest-grown food. This is for the purpose of excluding village-grown food. Although eating in the evening was already established by the sequence [of the rules], the mention of "evening" (*sāyam*) is for the sake of indicating the second meal; thus, these options—eating forest-grown food, fasting, or not fasting—apply only to the second meal. Even if, by chance, the morning meal is postponed until the evening, these options do not apply; rather, the morning meal remains as it was before. This is the purpose [of the specification]. According to some, [the forest food may be] from the *āma-mārga* (raw grain), honey, or the *prāśātika* (food fit for consumption).

Having avoided deer meat and honey, he eats other forest-grown food. Regarding the slaughter: according to some, having offered the *prāśātika* (wild grain) as a religious duty, he eats other forest-grown food. According to the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya, *prāśātika* grain consists of the seeds of *apāmārga* and *śyāmāka*. Others say it refers to *kośīdhānya* (sheaf-grain). Regarding the fast for the sake of the forest-food: he may eat water, or nothing at all. For one fasting for the sake of forest-food—meaning avoiding [all food]—even that water he should not eat; this is the third position.
The *bhagārama-pavāraka* is a chamber; there he "enters," which means he lies down. He remains awake during the night of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*).
This is clear.
Or rather, he should do as he is able. This is clear. However, he must certainly not sleep on top [of anything].
"On top" means on a bed or similar furniture;
or he may sleep on top [of the ground]. Here too, there is an option as before.
He should indeed be one who observes a vow. Therefore, he should not speak an untruth, nor should he eat meat while studying, nor should he approach a woman; thus he should observe these vows.
On the following day:
[The section on] the *gata* is concluded.
Having chosen as the *brahmā* one most proficient in the Veda (*brahmiṣṭha*), [with the words]: "O Lord of the earth, O Lord of the world, O Lord of the great Being, we choose you as the *brahmā*.
According to another *sūtra*, [the place for the *utkara* is specified]. "Brahman" means the Veda; one who is established in that, and intent upon its teaching and investigation, is [the *brahmā*].

Having passed to the south of the Āhavanīya fire by the western side, he sits down to the west of the Brahman’s seat, on his own seat. The meaning of this is already explained. According to Bharadvāja and others, [the Brahman] faces the Āhavanīya. Seated here, he performs these ritual acts;
he remains seated until the conclusion of the rite.

The meaning is that he does not go from the *vihāra*. This extends up to the end of the *saṃsthāna*. According to Āpastamba and others, the path of movement (*saṃcara*) is exclusively made of earth; thus, in the case of ordinary movement, it is in front of the *āhavanīya* fire. When it is said, "O Sacrificer, restrain your speech," he restrains his speech until the call for the *haviṣkṛt*.
At the *viṣphalī-praiṣa*, he releases his speech. This has been explained in the *Ādhvaryava* section.

"Bhūśca, kaśca, vākca, rkaśca, gauśca, baṭca, khaṃ ca, dhūśca, nūśca, pūśca—these ten monosyllabic Virāṭ verses which have pervaded this entire world, those goddesses, being in agreement through their power, lead the sacrifice to well-being, they who are wise. Thus [are the] Praṇītās [addressed]. While they are being led forward, he recites over them: "Purified by the Brahman, you are; who yokes you? May He yoke you. While they are being set down, [he says] himself: "Brahmapūtā stha" (You are purified by the Brahman). "Ko vaḥ" (Who you...), "sa vaḥ" (He you...). "Yunakti" (yokes), "yunaktu" (may He yoke). Thus while they are being set down. Himself.
"Who yokes you? May he yoke you"—with these words he yokes the sacrifice. He explains this as follows:
he gazes upon everything.
"Every dwelling," so say Āpastamba and others.

When it is said, "I shall pour out the sacrificial oblation for the sacrificer," he replies, "Om, pour it out! He then consecrates with the mantra, "Agni, the invoker, him I summon here," either the oblation while it is being poured out, or the vessel intended for the pouring out, once it has been poured out. || 2 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the sixth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra. || 1 ||

6.2 Now, the second chapter in the sixth section. He touches the site of the altar with the verse: "O gods, I build this mansion for him among you who practices the life of sacred study (brahmacarya); wise, ascetic, and a messenger within, he moves through the quarters and among human beings with his mind."

Touching the site of the altar with his hand, he mutters [the mantra]. This principle—that where there is the phrase "he touches" (*abhimṛśati*), it should be understood as applying everywhere—is to be known. From this point forward, whenever an action is indicated by the accusative case, the term "he consecrates" (*abhimantryate*) is to be supplied, even if it is separated [by other words], because it is appropriate. Why? Because in the passage "this for him" (*idaṃ tasmai*), that which is directly present before one is indicated; and it has been stated that "he touches right here" (*atraiva abhimṛśati*) in cases such as "four-tufted" (*catuḥśikhaṇḍā*) and so on, whereas such an indication does not exist there. Therefore, the word "he touches" (*abhimṛśati*) must be supplied.

Bharadvāja and others read simply, "he recites the consecratory formulas (*anumantrayate*) over these. However, the term "recites" (*anumantrayate*) is generally employed only when [the substance] has already been cast into the fire; therefore, one must supply the word "consecrates" (*abhimantrayate*) from the preceding context. But in the case of the phrase "while they are being carried around" (*paristoryamāṇeṣu*), it should not be supplied. When indicated by the locative case, however, one merely "murmurs" (*japati*). [End of] the Second Paṭala, accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

The four-tufted young woman, well-formed, with a face of clarified butter, in the midst of the world; being cleansed for great good fortune, yield milk for me, the sacrificer, according to my desire. With the *veda* (sweeper), they found the lofty altar; it was extended upon the earth among earthly things. Upon it let the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) be spread out effectively; may the goddess Earth be non-injurious to us. "With the *veda*, the altar"—he addresses the altar as it is being swept with the *veda*. The mantra recited as "with the *veda*" belongs to the *Ādhvaryava* ritual.

"O gods, whoever hates me with the heart, with the mind, or with speech; whoever hates me with sacred knowledge, with ritual action, with learning, or with the intellect—his head I cut off with Indra’s thunderbolt. With these words, he addresses the sacrificial post as it is being carried away.

"When we, digging up [the earth], have harmed the earth with our thoughtless minds, O Adhvaryus who have fashioned the wooden sword (*sphya*), protect us from that [injury] to the atmosphere! When we, digging up [the earth], have harmed the living [beings] of this [earth] while preparing the altar (*vedi*) with our minds, seeking the gods—may we not incur its displeasure through that; may it be auspicious to us along with all the worlds! Thus he intends [this] as the wooden sword digs up the uppermost skin.
"O Bṛhaspati, encompass the altar! [he says] regarding the two enclosures.

He mutters [the formula] beginning with "Brahmanhood has been recited" and ending with "O Goddesses," for such is the propriety. He touches the prepared altar with the verse: "The Earth, having become the brow, nourished greatness; thence the Goddess increases her waters. The holy ones go forth to the sacrifice, and may the plants, the waters, and the Śakvarī verses here bring us peace.
He takes refuge in the prepared altar.

"I praise the others, whose will is different; I address the divine Waters who have flowed through day and night, the active ones. With these words, he consecrates the *prokṣaṇī* waters as they are being set down.

"Thou art ghee," with this he looks at the ghee, just as the Adhvaryu does. "With the Waters and with Ghee, purify thoroughly the Waters by means of Savitṛ’s purifiers. O divine Śakvarīs, being in harmony, protect this sacrifice with the Śakvara [chant]. With these words, he consecrates the ghee and the waters while they are being purified.

Only once. Three mantras other than those of the Adhvaryu are prescribed as being added at the beginning. Thereafter, however, they are common to both; therefore, the phrase "of five" (*pañcānām*) recurs in the section concerning the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). Otherwise, there would be a discrepancy between the two at the final repetition. It should be understood that among the *viśveṣu*, the fourth mantra is used in the optional rite (*kāmya*) with the words "having desired seventeen" (*saptadaśa kāmayitvā*). (Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, Sixth Praśna, 512).

With the verses beginning "Of the five winds," while the clarified butter is being taken, [the sacrificer] recites: "We have refreshed the sacrificial grass within the earth; may they cause the severed plants to sprout again. May those whose roots you have struck with the wooden sword (sphya) become auspicious and well-invoking for us. Thus he recites as the sacrificial grass is being placed within the altar (vedī). "May the plants and the waters here be well-disposed toward the sacrificer, and may the *śakvarī* verses be present."

"O Parjanya, who rains upon the heavens, may he cause these to sprout—golden-colored, hundred-branched, and inviolable," [with these words] the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) being sprinkled; "soft as wool, spreading out, pleasant for the gods, the sacrificial grass favored for their seat—place me, the sacrificer, in the world of heaven, on the back of the firmament, in the highest sky," [with these words] the sacrificial grass being strewn.
There is a repetition of the mantra for each placement.

"The four-tufted young woman, well-formed, with a face of ghee, clothes herself in sacred ordinances; being strewn for great good fortune, may she milk desires for me, the sacrificer"—thus [he recites] over the sacrificial grass as it is being strewn upon the altar, with the middle layer of the altar.

"Be auspicious and gracious to me; be pleasant and easy for me to sit upon; be full of vigor and full of milk; be easy of access and good to dwell in for me. Make me swell with food and vigor; make me swell with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmatejas*); make me swell with the power of the ruling class (*kṣattra-ojas*); make me swell with the common people and prosperity; make me swell with long life and the eating of food; make me swell with offspring and cattle"—with these words he consecrates the strewn altar. On the previous occasions, he consecrated the altar; here too, he consecrates it in this very manner.

"In this sacrifice, having partaken, I now set up the enclosing-sticks for my protection against disturbance: Agni, the sustainer, the support, the most enduring, is the giver who drives away hatred from here"—thus [he speaks] while the enclosing-sticks are being laid around.

With the plural form "I place the enclosing-sticks" (*paridhīn dadhāmi*) and because the substances are combined, there is a single recitation for all of them. Likewise, it has been stated by Māraṇḍa that [the mantra applies] to all. Vaikhānasa, however, has stated a repetition according to the principle of *yaṃ* (?). Therefore, the author of the Sūtra, having first declared the application, subsequently stated "Thou art firm" (*dhruvo 'si*). Consequently, the statement regarding repetition for each individual stick is dependent on the others, since they are being encircled one by one. This is also seen in the formulas: "Thou art firm; may I be firm among my kinsmen," and so forth. Thus, it is for each one individually. This has been stated in the same way by Āpastamba and Māraṇḍa.
He addresses the fire as it is being encircled by the two verses, "I yoke thee" (*yunajmi tvām*) and "That which is mine, O Agni" (*yan me agne*).

Since the act of encircling is to be performed even before the third enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) with the verse "Sūryas tvā" (*sūryas tvā*), that [use of the first two verses] is therefore appropriate. [With the verse: "Thy most brilliant heats and thy luminous realms, those bodies of thine, O Agni, which are glowing—clothe thyself in armor on all sides with them; let not the *ātudhānas* or *piśācas* harm thee," he addresses the fire once it has been encircled. *Note: The commentary by Mahādeva, the Vaijayantī, notes variants such as *tvā brahmaṇāya* (ka, ga, ca, ṭa, ka, ṇa) and refers to the *ravi-paṭala*.*

Regarding the reading "parihitam": it is derived from the root *dhā* with the prefix *pari*, meaning "donned," and is established by grammatical rules (*vyākaraṇa*). "Paridhitam" is a Vedic form (*chāndasa*).

With the two separators (*vidhṛtī*), I cut asunder my rivals—those born, those who are my kinsmen, and those yet to be born. With the two supports (*yantra*), I drive them away; may I be the highest among my own people, O Gods. As the two supports drive away the enemy, all evil, lack of thought, and the short-lived, may you two Goddesses sit in the world of the well-done. You two are the separators, the sustainers, the self-sustainers; sustain the vital breaths in me, sustain offspring in me, sustain cattle in me—thus [he says] when the two separators are being set down.

"This *prastara* is the supporter of both; it is the supporter of the *prayājas* as well as the *anūyājas*. It has supported the *samidhs* of all forms; upon it I place the offering-spoons"—with these words, the *prastara* is placed upon the two separating blades (*vidhṛtī*).
From "here upwards" until the end of "the vessel being placed," the phrase "being placed" (*sādyamānam*) should be understood as appropriate to each case.

Ascend the path; offer oblations upon the paths leading to the gods, where the first-born seers of old dwell. O you of golden wings, whose limbs are swift and well-formed, carry me to the worlds of those who have performed good deeds. You are the *juhū* ladle, dripping with clarified butter, praised by the wise poets through the *gāyatrī* meters. Without wavering, attend to the sacrifice; lead the sacrifice forward with skillful guidance toward the gods, through the divine protection of Agni. With the *upabhṛt* ladle, I drive away my rivals—those born enemies and those yet to be born.

With the *yajñāyajñīya* chant, [I perform] the sacrifice like a cow that yields well; may I be superior, and may my rivals be inferior. O *subhṛt*, *upabhṛt*, and *ghṛtācī*, you who possess all knowledge, with the *triṣṭubh* meter, being unshakable, attend to the sacrifice. With good guidance, lead the sacrifice toward the gods through divine protection belonging to Indra. O Agni, whoever, difficult to overcome in spirit, should approach me with malicious speech or mind from afar, [may he be struck down].
This mind of mine is lower; may I be higher than Dhruvā; let my rivals be lower than I. You are Dhruvā, the supporter, full of wealth; [I invoke you] with the Jāgata metre, O all-knowing one.

"Unwavering, oversee the sacrifice; lead the sacrifice with good guidance toward the gods, by means of the Vaiśvadeva protection, divine. [With these words,] he places the *dhruvā* ladle [with the formula]: "Be pleasant to me, sit on the earth as a comfortable seat. Spread out with offspring and cattle in the heavenly world. Sit in heaven, on the earth, in the mid-air. May I be superior, and may my rivals be inferior. This *sruva* ladle offers the oblations with the hundred-syllabled *anuṣṭubh* metre."
"May all the parts of the sacrifice be anointed with the divine protection of Bṛhaspati," [with these words] he [takes up] the *sruva* ladle. (Śatapatha Śrauta Sūtra, Book 6, Chapter 5, Section 14)

"A vessel full of ghee, a fountain with a hundred streams whose waters flow unceasingly—by means of the divine protection of the Maruts," [he says] regarding the vessel of clarified butter (ājyasthālī). "You are the sacrifice, resting on all sides; may the past and the future rest upon me from every side. May there be for me a hundred blessings; may there be for me a thousand pleasant truths, rich in nourishment and abounding in cattle"—[he says] regarding the oblation for Agni (āgneyam). "Prajāpati you are, resting on all sides; may the past and the future rest upon me from every side. May there be for me a hundred blessings; may there be for me a thousand pleasant truths."

With the mantra, "Rich in food, rich in cattle," [he offers] to Agni and Soma. With the mantra, "O Indra and Agni, whoever here desires what is less for me, the sacrificer at this sacrifice—drive him away from these worlds; may I obtain that offspring which is rich in heroes," [he offers] to Indra and Agni.
It should be understood that [the mantra] "The radiant ones" applies to three [offerings], because a specific rule will be stated later regarding the *sāṃnāyya* being set down:
"He whose self has entered into the cattle," [is used] when the *sāṃnāyya* is being set down.

He mutters: "This is the sense-power, the immortal vigor; by this the cattle healed Indra. With that, O gods, protect us here! May I win for myself refreshment, nourishment, glory, force, and strength. May the cooked [milk] take its place within me!"—this refers to the cooked [milk] which moved upon the earth and entered it, with which Prajāpati sprinkled strength into Indra. "This is that bright honey, full of vigor; with it, may the curds placed above on high strengthen Mahendra; may the curds satisfy me!"—this refers to the curds. He recites these mantras up to this point.

"This sacrifice, rich in oblations, has been completed with the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus verses, and with the deities. Through it, may we conquer the worlds possessed of the sun; may we attain the friendship of Indra and immortality"—with these words he touches the sacrificial implements that have been set down.
Thus ends the second chapter in the sixth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.

By the plural form "sasannāni" (those which have been set down), all [the offerings] are included. This has likewise been stated by Āpastamba and Bharadvāja: "all the oblations. What is meant are the primary and subsidiary parts. The inclusion of the prefix *sam-* in the term *sasannāni* is in accordance with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). It is not, however, according to the injunction "he sets them down together" (*saṃsādayati*), as if some were already set down; rather, it refers to the sequence "he sets them down" (*sādayati*) and "he brings them near" (*āsādayati*). Alternatively, since they constitute a collective whole, the commonality of being "set down" (*sannāni*) exists in both cases, which is therefore appropriate.

Thus, since there is one collection of clarified butter (*ājya*) and another collection [of grains], the mantra is repeated for each. He touches them once; then, in the same manner, he touches the other [collection], because of the force of the ritual application (*prayoga*). Thus ends the second section (*paṭala*) in the sixth book concerning the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), in the *Mayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* composed by Mahādeva.
[Section 6.3] Now begins the third section of the sixth book.
With eight [verses] of the *vihavya* hymn and with the *caturhotṛ* formula, he touches the oblations placed on the altar at the full moon sacrifice.

With the first eight verses of the section beginning "O Agni, may there be splendor for me" (*māgne varcaḥ*), ending with "do not harm us, do not abandon us" (*mā no rīriṣo mā parādāḥ*), he performs this.

At the new moon sacrifice, while the *sāmidhenī* verses are being recited, he mutters the *pañcahotṛ* formula, saying: "May the Aṅgirases protect me through the morning litany of this sacrifice. He should recite the *daśahotṛ* formula either before or after the *sāmidhenī* verses: "May the kindled Agni, invoked and consecrated by *svāhā*, fulfill our needs."

"Go to your own [abode], O gods; this homage to the gods"—with these words, he addresses the kindled fire with the verse "The swelling strength, O Agni," and he consecrates the stream from the *sruva* ladle with "Thou art the mind, belonging to Prajāpati," and the stream from the *sruc* ladle with "Thou art speech. Then he recites: "O gods, fathers, and gods, I sacrifice as who I am; I do not neglect him to whom I belong. My own is the sacrifice, my own the gift, my own the fulfillment, my own the toil, my own the oblation. Of that which is mine, Agni is the witness, Vāyu is the hearer, Āditya is the proclaimer, Heaven is the father, and Earth is the mother."

"Prajāpati is my kinsman; being who I am, I sacrifice; him to whom I belong, I do not neglect"—with these words he mutters during both the *hotṛ-pravara* and the *adhvaryu-pravara*. During the *adhvaryu-pravara*, he says, "Make me heard among the gods for long life and luster. He should recite the specific *caturhotṛ* formula either before or after the *prayāja* offerings. With the formulas beginning, "I gratify the spring among the seasons," he consecrates each *prayāja* offering as it is made. [He further recites: "Agni is possessed of sight; through the sacrifice to that god, may I [attain]..."

"May I become possessed of sight," [he says] for the butter-portion (ājyabhāga) of Agni; "Soma is possessed of sight; through the sacrifice to that god, may I become possessed of sight," [he says] for the portion of Soma; "Of Agni and Soma, I..."—thus some prescribe the collective consecration (anumantraṇa). One should recite the Pañcahotṛ formula either before or after the portions of the oblations. "Through the sacrifice to the god Agni, may I become an eater of food," [he says] for the portion of Agni; "Thou art the unerring one," [he says] for the Upāṃśuyāja.

"May I be of Agni and Soma"—[this is for] the offering to Agni and Soma; "May I be of Indra and Agni"—[this is for] the offering to Indra and Agni; "May I be of Indra"—[this is for] the offering to Indra; "May I be of Mahendra"—[this is for] the offering to Mahendra; "Of Agni..."—here, in all the manuscript copies of the commentary (*ṭīkā*), it is found that the leaf containing this portion is torn. The portion enclosed within the brackets does not exist in the manuscript copies of the commentary. 2. *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[Sixth Book].

He looks toward the *iḍā* as it is being brought forward, saying: "Of the *sviṣṭakṛt* am I," "May Agni *sviṣṭakṛt* protect me from ill-sacrificed [acts]," and "O thou of beautiful form, of rain-like color, come! During the silent invitation (*upāṃśūpahava*), he mutters the seven divine cows: "Thou art consciousness (*cit*), thou art mind (*manas*), thou art wealth (*vasvī*), thou art delight (*rantī*), thou art pleasure (*ramati*), thou art noble (*sūnarī*), thou art truthfulness (*sūnṛtā*). During the loud invitation (*uccairupahava*), he mutters the seven human cows: "Do thou breathe after all beings; may all [beings] breathe after thee."

May the elements breathe after you; *bhūḥ* are you, *āyuḥ* are you, *iṣṭiḥ* are you. O you of beautiful form and excellent color, come hither; come toward these auspicious dwellings. Make my heads favorable to me; be gracious to us. You who are dear, come with swift onset; you who are dear, come as a friend to us; you who possess what is dear, come, O wealthy one! Come as one who is well-pleased; come, O delight; come, O joy; come, O you who are easy to invoke! Come together with the increase of wealth! O divine ones, turn back toward me with the gods! Sprinkle me with pleasant ghee! This is the homage for the footprint.

When the Brahman, the seer-physician, gives [the portion] as if rising from the ocean with two ladles, [the word] *vāk* (speech) stands at the tip of the wise man, indicating [it] with ten horns. While saying "O Vāyu, I invite you" (*upa-hūve*) loudly, he should, while looking at the *hotṛ*, meditate on Vāyu in his mind. When it is said, "This sacrificer is invited," he mutters, "May I be invited and possessed of cattle. And [he says], "May Indra bestow sensory power upon us. With the words, "Through the sacrifice to the gods, may I become prosperous and possessed of cattle; O *iḍā*, enjoy our portion; quicken our cows," [he concludes].

"May we, with our whole selves and all our groups, be those who enjoy the food of that swift steed. May the cow Iḍā come to us together with her calf, milking out strength, swelling with milk. May she, Iḍā, quicken us with food, with oblation, and with cattle; may she quicken us with milk. Thus is the invocation of Iḍā explained. The sprinkling [of water] is explained by the verse beginning "Mind is light" (*mano jyotiḥ*). The recitation of the *Mānava-gā* [is prescribed].

"O radiant one, swell; may that which I give not diminish; may that which I do not fall away from me. You are the ordainment of the quarters; may the quarters be ordained for me; may the quarters be ordained for me—the divine and the human. May day and night be ordained for me; may the half-months be ordained for me; may the months be ordained for me; may the seasons be ordained for me; may the year be ordained for me. You are the ordainment; may it be ordained for me. To you, the guardians of the quarters, the four immortal overseers of what has come to be, we offer worship with this oblation."

He distributes [the portions] in every direction: "O portion, belong to those who share; do not be a non-portion for the sharer. O you who have no portion, be shared. Quicken us; cause the plants to swell; quicken [us]; protect the bipeds; protect the quadrupeds; send down rain from heaven. This oblation belongs to the Brāhmaṇas, to the Soma-drinkers, to those who drink Soma. The Brāhmaṇa has been excluded here; there is no portion here for the non-Brāhmaṇa. And [he recites]: "May the waters swell... and so forth. 8.

In this case as well, it should be understood that one mutters [the mantra] while spreading [the material]. Alternatively, having divided [it], one spreads it and then touches it. Otherwise, how could there be a separate application for each of the two mantras? For there is no re-expansion of what has already been expanded. Therefore, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the muttering (*japa*) accomplished by each individual mantra is not anything else. If it is argued that it was the same previously, then in all cases, one does not spread it; rather, one performs the fourfold division with those [mantras] ending in *anta*, spreading it toward each direction in the order of the cardinal points starting from the East.
However, the meaning is that while touching the expanded [material], one mutters the single mantra.

"This for the Brahman, this for the Hotṛ, this for the Adhvaryu, this for the Agnīdh"—thus he assigns [the portions] in four parts. According to the Śruti: "Having touched the fourfold-divided portions that have been set aside in the directions beginning with the east, he assigns them. The meaning is that the Adhvaryu, having touched those portions divided into four which were set aside by the sacrificer, and having first performed the touching, recites the mantras. Having touched them with his hand, he assigns them—that is, he points them out and announces them as belonging to each respective officiating priest.

Therefore, since there is a visible purpose produced by the knowledge of the relationship—namely, the fourfold distribution of the objects of knowledge—a visible refinement (*saṃskāra*) occurs; for it is not possible for those who are ignorant of the specific relationship with each respective *ṛtvij* to take up items that have not been specified.
Some recite the "assignment beginning with the Āgnīdhra" (*āgnīdhraprathamānvādeśān*);
that is, those assignments in which the Āgnīdhra is first. The meaning is that they proceed in order: "This for the Āgnīdhra, this for the Brahman," and so forth.

"This vessel is full of nectar; it is a thousand-streamed, inexhaustible spring. It has supported the earth, the intermediate region, and the sky. By means of this food, may I overcome death. With these words, he touches the *anvāhārya* rice that has been set down within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*), saying, "Thou art the portion of Prajāpati.

In the first instance, this is for the sake of the modified forms (*vikṛti*) of the sacrifice; however, there is no modification (*ūha*) in the second case, because the designation "Prajāpati" is applicable everywhere as a mere generic reference.
When the call is made, "Let it be brought to the priests sitting on the south," he gives the direction to the priests, "Come from the south!"
While the Adhvaryu is speaking, because of the mention of the *ṛtvij* (priest), the *śamitṛ* (slaughterer) does not receive the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) nor the share of the sin.

To the Brahmins who have circumambulated from the south, saying, "This rice-porridge (*odana*) is for you," he gives it to them after having divided it into four parts. "O Agni, this is thy fuel-stick (*samidh*); through it mayest thou increase and swell, and may we also increase and swell. "O Agni, that which thou hast covered... [End of section] [From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Sixth Praśna.]

"May I, moving about, consume him who reviles me, along with his offspring and his root; may the gods strike him down low. O Agni, whoever seeks to harm us—whether he be one of our own kin or a stranger—may nothing of him remain, as if he were wood consumed by fire. O Jātavedas, whoever hates me and whomsoever I hate, and whoever hates me—burn them all together, O Agni, and those whom I hate and those who hate me. This is the mantra with which one consecrates the *anūyāja* fuel-stick as it is being placed [on the fire];
"he consecrates" is the understood remainder of the sentence.

"The altar, the sacrificial grass, the cooked oblation, the fuel, the enclosing sticks, the offering-ladles, the clarified butter, the splendors of the sacrifice, the Yajus-formulas, the Yājyās, and the Vaṣaṭ-calls—may my prostrations bow down to me. Having offered the fuel-bunch (idhmasaṃnahana), he mutters this when the fuel-bunch has been offered.

"The Aṅgirases have offered for me with the morning recitations of this sacrifice," he mutters during the after-offerings (*anūyāja*s). He should recite the *Saptahotṛ* formula either before or after the after-offerings. With the formulas, "Through the sacrifice to the gods, may I become possessed of offspring," he consecrates each after-offering as it is being offered. With the two verses beginning, "By the impulse of strength (*vāja*)," he [consecrates] the two ladles as they are being separated.

He consecrates [the offerings] with: "May I satisfy the Vasu gods with the sacrifice; may I satisfy the Rudra gods with the sacrifice; may I satisfy the Āditya gods with the sacrifice. As the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are being anointed, he says: "May the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) be anointed with the oblation, with clarified butter; may it be anointed with the Ādityas, with the Vasus, with the Maruts; may it be anointed with Indra and with all the gods; let that which goes to the celestial sky, Svāhā! As the *prastara* (handful of grass) is being anointed in the offering-spoons, [he recites]: "The sacrifice has satisfied the sacrifice; the gods have been honored; Soma has been made ready."
"May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, and Uṣas enter the sacrificer with wealth"—with these words, he removes a blade of grass from the *prastara* bundle.
He consecrates it, saying:
"May I win the victory of Agni. With each deity that the Hotṛ pronounces in the *sūktavāka*, the sacrificer consecrates that very deity in turn.

The sacrificer, being present, consecrates each [deity] with the respective mantra. Thus, he consecrates all those deities who have been worshipped, according to the recitation found in other Vedic branches (śākhā). As the Commentator has said: "By the words *agner aham*... Although it would have been more concise to say that one consecrates the deities "according to their indicative marks" (*yathā-liṅgam*), he instead says "whichever deity he pronounces, that very one," [repeating] "that, that. [Notes on variants: 1. ka. sva. ga. ca. ṭa, ṭhaṇa. read *tiyām*. 2. ḍha. reads *ke hoṃ*. 3. ka. sa. ga, gha, ṭa. ṭha. read *vato hotāmi*.

[The section on] the *tapas* chapter, accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva: [verse 519]. The statement is intended so that for whichever [offering] there is an utterance by the *hotṛ*, there may be a corresponding consecration (*anumantraṇa*) for that very one. By this rule, the consecration must be performed for the *upāṃśuyāja* and the *ājyabhāgas*, even though they are not present in the Taittirīya recension; the reading from another *śākhā* (branch) must be inferred. Some, however, do not perform it for the *upāṃśuyāja*, the *ājyabhāgas*, their modifications, or the deities of the *savana*s, on the grounds of the absence of a textual recitation.

The efforts of those teachers would otherwise be rendered useless. The venerable Satyāṣāḍha’s intention is that the *aindrāgna* [offering] has the same *nipavana* as the *agnīṣomīya*, and that their recitation exists in other recensional branches (*śākhā*) just like the *paridāna*.
When the Hotṛ pronounces the name of the sacrificer, then he should say: "These blessings have come, desiring to yield milk.
When [he says] "when," then [the formula] ends with: "May spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) come to me."

"May that blessing of mine among the gods be true—most honored from among those honored, most beloved from among those beloved; may I attain that with a devoted mind: 'May the sacrifice ascend to heaven; may the sacrifice go to heaven; by that path which leads to the gods, may the sacrifice reach the gods'.

He mutters this over the blessings while the Hotṛ is reciting the blessings, beginning with "He prays for long life," and so forth. He pronounces the name of whatever he desires, saying, "May that come to me."

With the formula beginning "May heaven come to me," he should take the name of whatever he desires—such as "May fame come to me," "May devotion to Viṣṇu come to me," or "May knowledge of Brahman come to me"—in this manner, according to what pleases him.
With the formulas beginning "May Agni cause you to go to the deity Rohita," he releases the *prastara* (grass-bundle).

He consecrates with three [verses] that which has been cast into the Āhavanīya fire. From here onwards, whenever something is indicated in the accusative case and is thrown into the fire, the phrase "he consecrates there" (*tatrānumantrayate*) is to be supplied; elsewhere, where the accusative ends, "he consecrates" (*abhimantryate*) is to be supplied in the same way, according to the instruction of Bharadvāja.

"The peg of heaven is stretched out, risen up from the earth. With that thousand-jointed one, we cause our enemy to suffer; let the hater suffer, let the many-harming ones suffer, O plants! [With this verse], he throws a blade of grass from the *prastara* bundle into the Āhavanīya fire.

He mutters "viṣṇoḥ śaṃyor aham" during the *śaṃyu-vāk* formula, ending with "gameyam. He recites the two verses beginning with "vi te muñcāmi raśanā" while the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are being thrown into the fire.
He addresses the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra:

"The sacrifice has been offered by the Bhṛgus as the giver of wealth; it is the giver of blessings by the Yatis; it is full of blessings by the Vasus; it is full of blessings by the Atharvans. May the wealth of that sacrifice of mine, which has been offered and consumed, come to me—the sacrifice, the possessor of wealth, O possessor of wealth! (Note: Variants in the manuscripts regarding the specific wording are recorded here). [End of the sixth Praśna, Section 520, from the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha.]

"May this sacrifice of his, rich in wealth, come here as a possessor of wealth; may that [wealth] come to me. He utters the name of whatever he desires for which the portions of the *saṃsrāva* are intended.
He consecrates the *saṃsthāvān* with a formula. The rest is as before.
"Thou art the Veda, thou art the acquisition"—with these words he touches the *veda* grass placed within the altar.
Having brought it near, he touches it with the formula "May I know.
It is known from tradition that whatever one might covet from an enemy, whether before or after this [formula], one should utter that person's name; thus one seizes all of that from him. 10.
Thus ends the third paṭala in the sixth Yājamāna-praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. ||3||

Regarding the word *videya*, whether before or after it, whatever one might covet from a rival, thinking "May it be mine," one should utter its name [with the formula] *videya* for the purpose of excluding that evil. This is to be understood as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended to inspire confidence. Thus ends the third section in the sixth chapter on the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) in the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* by Mahādeva, composed by Satyāṣāḍha. ||3||

6.4 Now begins the fourth chapter of the sixth book. In the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, [he recites]: "By the sacrifice to Soma, may I, possessing good seed, impregnate seed"—this is for Soma; "by the sacrifice to Tvaṣṭṛ, may I nourish the form of cattle"—this is for Tvaṣṭṛ; "by the sacrifice to the wives of the gods, may I procreate through offspring and cattle"—this is for the wives of the gods; "by the sacrifice to Rākā, may I become possessed of offspring"—this is for Rākā; "by the sacrifice to Sinīvālī, may I become possessed of cattle"—this is for Sinīvālī; "by the sacrifice to Kuhū, may I..."—this is for Kuhū.

"May I be possessed of nourishment"—thus [he addresses] Kuhū; "Agni Gṛhapati is the foundation of the sacrifice; through the sacrifice to that deity, may I become possessed of a foundation"—thus [he addresses] Agni Gṛhapati; "The wives of the gods, Agni Gṛhapati"—thus some prescribe a single combined consecration formula for all [the deities].

Where there are exactly four *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, then there is a collective invocation (*āmantraṇa*). It should be understood that the phrase "the offering of Soma has been made" applies to both cases. In other instances, although the deities differ, it is still said "the offering has been made.

[The Adhvaryu] addresses the *iḍā* with clarified butter (*ājyeḍā*) using the formula: "May the *iḍā* favor us with ghee, she whose foot the seekers of the gods purify; the *vaiśvānarī* and *śakvarī*, increasing in power, has approached the sacrifice, she who belongs to all the gods (*vaiśvadevī*). He recites this over the *iḍā*.

When the offering of husks (*phalīkaraṇa-homa*) is being made with the formula, "To that Sarasvatī who is possessed of glory, svāhā to thee," he wipes his mouth. When it has been offered with the formula, "To that Sarasvatī who is possessed of dwellings, svāhā to thee," he wipes his mouth. He rubs [his face] with his hand in the direction of the hair. [He offers with the formulas: "To Agni, the one who does not burn, the one whose body is not cold, this [offering]; to the Viśvedevas, this [offering].
[The Hotṛ recites over] the *veda* grass-bundle being handed over to the wife by the Hotṛ: "Thou art the *veda*, thou art acquisition."
He consecrates [the grass-bundle] as it is being handed over to the wife by the Hotṛ, ending with the word "saneyam.
Or he says, "Thou art the Veda; for the sake of the Veda, I take thee; may the Veda find me.
The former [formula] is intended as an alternative.

With the mantra beginning "The ghee-filled, nest-like... he consecrates the Veda as it is being placed upon the wife's lap. He recites this until the end of the word "vājinam. Alternatively, he may recite: "Thou art the Veda; bring the Veda to me. Satisfied thou art; may I be satisfied with progeny and cattle."
It has gone.

Through you they have found the altar and the earth; through you the sacrifice is born, all-bestowing. As the wise one, you seek out the flawless sacrifice; through you the Hotṛ priest extends the half-months—thus [he says] while the Veda is being strewn.
From the Gārhapatya fire, the Hotṛ’s portion [is taken].
"O Agni of unimpaired life-force," [with these words] he consecrates the *samiṣṭayajus* offering.

The mantra ends with "svāhā" and is recited only once, even though there is a plurality of *samiṣṭayajus* offerings. At the end, [the formula is]: "To Vāta, this! Although various deity-terms are heard here, it should nevertheless be understood as stated by Āryava:

"The pillar of heaven is stretched out; it has risen up from the earth. With that thousand-fold [pillar], we cause our enemy to burn. May my enemy burn greatly; O herb, may I not suffer the pain. Thus the *barhis* grass is thrown into the fire.
He approves [the portion] with the mantra:

"May the lord of the sacrifice [attain] his blessings" (TS 3.2.8.4). He consumes the sacrificer’s portion consisting of boiled milk and curds. A Brāhmaṇa eats it, but neither a Vaiśya nor a Rājanya does so. He consumes the boiled milk with the mantra: "May this oblation be productive for me" (TS 3.2.8.4), and the curds with the mantra: "I have performed the praise of Dadhikrāvan" (RV 4.39.6). This is clear.
He performs the *mārjana* (sprinkling) within the altar (*antarvedi*) once the waters have been led forward.
This is for the sake of what follows.
And the Adhvaryu causes a continuous stream to flow for him. He mutters the formula, "May it be abundant for me," as the waters are being brought into the *sadas*.
While the *praṇītā* waters are being poured out by the *adhvaryu*, he sprinkles them out toward each of the directions, saying:

"May the gods, the officiating priests, purify themselves in the eastern direction. He pours out the remainder, saying: "I send you to the ocean; O imperishable ones, go back to your own source. May I be unbroken in my progeny; may I not spill this [water]. He pours the remainder of the *praṇītā* waters onto the sacrificial altar (*vedi*).

"O Sarasvatī, that sweetness of yours which is in the waters, in the cows, and in the horses—with that, O winner of prizes, cleanse my mouth, O Sarasvatī. With these words, he wipes his mouth with his hand. Regarding this, some authorities prescribe the consumption of the sacrificer's portion at this point.
The rest is clear.

Therefore, having risen, he takes four steps of Viṣṇu with the formula, "Thou art the step of Viṣṇu. Having stepped forward with the right foot, he follows with the left; he does not cross over with the left foot, nor does he cross over the Āhavanīya fire. Standing, he mutters the fourth [formula], each subsequent step being greater than the preceding one.

Therefore, having risen from the place where he was standing for the sake of the sacrificer, and not remaining elsewhere, he first steps forward with his right foot, followed by the left; each subsequent step is longer than the preceding one. There are exactly three such steps, and there is no fourth step. While standing during the third step, he mutters at the fourth: "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu, O thou who art hostile to the enemy. "Rising today, O thou of sun-like splendor, drive away my rivals. By day, strike them down with lightning; as thou settest, cast them below. "Rising today... [550] ...[end of] the commentary on the *Vijayantī* composed by Mahādeva. [526]

Do you apportion to us as a father does to his sons; for you, O Sūrya, are the master of long life—grant that to us! Rising today, O Mitra-glorious one, ascending the highest heaven, destroy my heart-disease and my jaundice, O Sūrya! We transfer my jaundice onto the parrots and onto the thrushes; then we deposit my jaundice upon the yellow wagtails. This Āditya has risen with all his power, bringing my enemy under my control; may I not fall under the control of my enemies!

"May Dawn and Sunset sweep away all the evil of him who curses us though we do not curse, and of him who curses us though we do curse. O Gods, whatever mortal enemy or adversary seeks to harm us, let nothing of him remain, as if of a log that has been consumed by fire. (12) He worships the Sun with the formula: "We have gone to the light; we have gone to the light," ending with "Bestow [it].
He meditates in his mind on the destruction of him whom he hates, saying: "Here I [drive] that rival from these quarters, from this heaven."

It ends with the word *dviṣmaḥ*. If he should practice sorcery, he says, "I now entwine the breath of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so," and entwines it with the heel of his right foot. He pronounces the name of the enemy in the genitive case as *amuṣya*, and the patronymic as *amuṣyāyaṇasya*, which is formed by adding a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) to the name of whose offspring he is speaking. This rite is not connected with a sacrifice; it is not a constituent part of the sacrifice.

"Turning along the turning of Indra," he says, and turns clockwise; "May those fortunes be auspicious, may those that are evil perish," he says, and turns around toward his right shoulder—he turns having aimed at his right shoulder. "Thou art splendor," he says, and turns around toward the Āhavanīya fire.
He turns around toward the Āhavanīya fire keeping his left side toward it.
He worships the Āhavanīya with the mantra "May I be united with offspring," ending with the word "prosperity" (poṣa).
With the verse, "O Agni, being kindled," he adds fuel, ending with the words, "May I shine.
With the formula,
"The sacrifice is wealthy," he stands in worship.

The mantra ends with *bhūyāsam*. He worships the Dakṣiṇāgni with the mantra: "O Agni, O bearer, cook for us food that is savory for our offspring; grant it abundantly as a blessing for our children and ourselves, providing comfort. He worships the Gārhapatya fire with the two *āgnipāvamānī* verses beginning with *agne āyūṃṣi* and *agne pavasva*, and with the verse *agne gṛhapate*. One who has not yet fathered a son should say: "I invoke this blessing for the sake of progeny, full of light.
One who has no son at all should say it aloud.
"I desire for this [son] that luminous blessing"— thus says one who has a son born. One who has sons living,
or many sons, recites the names of all his sons and finally says, "the luminous one."
"I desire this blessing for [Name], [Name], may it be luminous," he says.

Having said, "For light, for continuity, thee! he sits down between the two fires, saying, "May [Name] follow me with light and continuity. Having said, "For light, for continuity, thee!", he utters the name of the eldest son in the vocative case: "O [Name]! (or "O [Name]-śarman!").
Having placed the "grass of the Vedas" upon his lap, sitting within the *vedi*, he mutters the *atimokṣa* formulas, beginning with "Those gods who are slayers of the sacrifice.

Regarding the *atimokṣa* mantras: having placed his right knee upon his left thigh (the "lap"), he should bring his two hands, palms upward, across one another near his knees; this is the "lap" (*upastha*), well known in the Yogaśāstra as the "cow-mouthed posture" (*gomukhāsana*).

"Who yokes you? May he release you," with these words he releases the sacrifice; he looks all around. "O Agni, lord of vows, I have performed the vow," with these [verses] he releases the vow. "The sacrifice has come into being, it has become manifest," with this he mutters the re-attainment of the sacrifice. "O Agni, the sacrifice is rich in cattle, rich in sheep, rich in horses," with this he mutters while stepping forward toward the east. || 13 ||

Having stepped out toward the eastern direction, he mutters: "O Sacrifice, hail to you; O Sacrifice, obeisance, obeisance to you. O Sacrifice, may you be established for me with auspiciousness; may you be established for me with comfort; may you be established for me with prosperity; may you be established for me with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). May you be established following the success of the sacrifice. O Sacrifice, homage to you; homage to you; homage to you. [This is clear. [This is clear. [Note: The text provided contains references to manuscript variants (ka, kha, ga, etc. and citations from the *Mahādevakṛta-vaijayantī* commentary, which have been omitted as per instructions to provide only the translation of the main text.]
"You are rain; cut off my evil. From the Unreal I have come to the Real. Having touched water with this formula, "Faith in the waters," he goes back out by the same way he came.
This is clear.
He issues the command: "Satisfy the Brahmins!"

By virtue of the plural number, one gratifies more [guests] by serving various kinds of food, both solid and soft; Vaikhānasa says there are eight or ten. Likewise, regarding the sacrificial animal, there are a hundred. The injunction "gratify them" (tarpayata) is addressed either to another person, such as the Adhvaryu, or to the preparer of the cooked food. However, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that it refers to oneself alone.
Thus, even for one who is away on a journey, the duties of the sacrificer (yājamāna) are prescribed. Even for him while traveling, the duties of the sacrificer indeed still apply.
Facing the direction in which his fires are located, he mutters the mantras; [he recites] the mantras pertaining to the sacrificer. This is clear.
The Adhvaryu performs the ritual acts.

Although there is no substitute for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), nevertheless, a substitute certainly exists for the sake of others; therefore, the Adhvaryu should perform those acts intended for others precisely with the mantras. It has been established that there is no substitute in the case of consecrations (*saṃskāra*) prompted by ownership (*svāmitva*). The sense is that, however, there is indeed a substitute in the case of agency (*kartṛtva*).
This is because [the acts] are other than the touching (*abhimarśana*).

The touching (*abhimarśana*) of the *vedehavi* offerings is performed without other [mantras]; it has been shown that this touching is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the recitation (*japa*). If this were an instrument-mantra (*karaṇamantra*), then the ritual act would have to be performed with the mantra by the *adhvaryu* alone. A mantra is not an ancillary that must precede the recitation. For this very reason, it is explained on the strength of the statement: "having touched, he recites."

Since the *japa* (muttering) is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the altar, the touching (*abhimarśana*) is therefore an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to it; as a consecration, it serves the purpose of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) with respect to the *japa*. Thus, the touching is not for the sake of another, but rather an auxiliary that precedes the *japa*; even though it exists for that purpose, it is indeed a consecration of the sacrificer. He states that even if this auxiliary is omitted, one should still mutter the mantras intended for the primary rite:
"The sacrificer mutters the other mantras because of the instruction."

The assignment (*vyādeśana*) consists of saying "this is for the Brahman," and so forth, regarding the fourfold division of the portions. It has already been stated that this [assignment] follows immediately after touching [the portions] with the words "this is... and so on. In that case, although touching does exist, its status as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the assignment is established; furthermore, since the assignment is for the sake of another, the Adhvaryu himself performs the assignment—saying "this is for... and so on—even after having performed the touching. Even though it lacks the character of an *injunction-mantra* (*karaṇamantra*), it is just like an *injunction-mantra* because even mantras that perform a consecration of the substance (*dravyasaṃskāramantra*) serve the purpose of another; thus, there is indeed the status of being a substitute for the Adhvaryu.

Therefore, the meaning is that the sacrificer does not mutter those [mantras]. Even the muttering of "O Aditi, swell... and so forth is a part of the *vyādeśana* (assignment), because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the Brāhmaṇa: "This is the oblation for the Brahmins. Consequently, by the word *vyādeśana*, the muttering of the mantras that constitute its constituent parts is indicated. One should not suspect that even this must be performed by the Adhvaryu alone; rather, since the muttering is a direct refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificer, it must be performed by him alone. [In place of "Oṃ, pour out," the formula is] "O Agni, [pour out] the oblation... [End of fragment].

*Ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ṇa*. In whichever direction this [is], "we shall look for it there"—this has already been stated [at 5.26]. The substitution for the word *yuṣmad* (you) is *etad* (this), as in: "O Brahmins, this rice-porridge is for you," and so forth. The selection of the Brahman priest (*brahmavaraṇa*) must be performed by the Adhvaryu with the mantra "O Lord of the Earth, O Lord of the World," and not merely as a silent recitation (*japa*). This also applies to the formula "Om, enter. The meaning is that the mantras other than those previously mentioned are to be used for the instruction (*ādeśana*).

The author of the Bhāṣya has clarified that these are the duties to be performed by the Adhvaryu; we shall now describe them. [These include]: the selection of the Brahman priest (*brahmavaraṇa*); the offering of the oblation (*haviḥ*) with the formula "This is for the Brahman" (*idaṃ brahmaṇaḥ*), which constitutes the formal assignment (*vyādeśana*); the gift-giving mantra to the south: "Come, O Brāhmaṇas! This food is yours" (*ayaṃ vo bhojanaḥ*); and the exhortation: "O Brāhmaṇas, satisfy yourselves," since even in relation to himself, his action is for the sake of others. Next are the duties of the Adhvaryu to be performed without mantras: the holding of the *prastara* grass-bundle, the commencement of the *iḍā* portion, and the consumption of the *iḍā*.

There is the spreading out [of the grass] in each direction; and in the case of the *praṇītā* waters, there is the sprinkling and the kindling. Now, by the sacrificer who is away on a journey, all the mantras are to be recited according to the sequence of performance, with the exception of those ritual acts pertaining to the *adhvaryu* which are performed by the sacrificer himself—such as the choosing of the *brahman* priest (*brahmavaraṇa*), beginning with "Oṃ, come hither" (*o nipeti*) and so forth. Those belonging to the *adhvaryu* are: "Sacrificer, restrain your speech" (*yajamāna vācaṃ yaccha*), "Sacrificer, I shall pour out the oblation-materials" (*yajamāna havinirvasyāmi*), and "May Parjanya rain for you" (*varṣatu te parjanya*). Regarding these two as well, it is only logical that the sacrificer should perform a silent recitation (*japa*) while keeping them in mind.

Because of the statement "other than the instruction," the Adhvaryu performs the distribution [of the offerings] in every direction. The recitation (*japa*), the mounting, and the measuring are likewise accompanied by mantras; this [procedure], beginning with "this belongs to the Brahman," pertains to the Adhvaryu. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Sūtra.
Thus is prescribed the duty of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) for the *iṣṭi* and animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*).
Likewise, in the case of modified *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices such as the *nirūḍha*, these very same specific rules are stated in their respective places.

The consecratory formulas (*anumantraṇa*) follow the modification [of the offering]. Although only the deity is heard in the formula, "By the sacrifice to Agni, may I [attain]... and so forth, it has nevertheless been stated that this is the consecration for that which has been offered. It should be understood that the consecratory mantras are modified according to the specific oblation; they are not fixed such that a mantra for two deities remains for two deities and one for one deity remains for one, as in the case of Indra and the phrase *indriyāvī*. Rather, it is due to the commonality of the oblation itself. Whichever modification occurs for whichever oblation, the consecratory mantra applies to that very oblation, either in its unmodified form or with the appropriate substitution (*ūha*). He states an exception:

Through the sacrifice to Indra Vaimṛdha, may I be without rivals. Through the sacrifice to Sarasvatī, may I nourish speech and the food of the eater. Through the sacrifice to Pūṣan, may I become possessed of prosperity and cattle. Through the sacrifice to Aditi, may I procreate with offspring and cattle. Through the sacrifice to Heaven and Earth, may I prosper in both worlds and attain abundance and a firm foundation. Through the sacrifice to Aryaman, may I nourish the heavenly world. Of all...

"Through the sacrifice to the gods, may I attain union with the vital breaths of the gods; through the sacrifice to the god Indra, the possessor of power, may I become powerful and possessed of cattle; through the sacrifice to the god Indra, the protector, may I become protected"—these are the consecratory formulas (anumantraṇas) as directly recited in the scripture. || 14 ||
Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the sixth Yājamāna-praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the sixth Yājamāna-praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

Regarding these oblations, the formulas for recitation (*anumantraṇa-mantras*) which are obtained through extension (*atideśa*) from the archetype (*prakṛti*) are set aside by those formulas obtained through direct statements (*pratyakṣa-vacana*) that are not connected to a specific context (*anārabhya*). These mantras, by virtue of their indicative power (*liṅga*), apply to whichever oblation—whether a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), a pap (*caru*), or curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*)—has as its deity the one they are intended to express. However, they do not apply to modified sacrifices (*vikāra*) where the deity is different, because in those cases extension applies only from the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). This has been established.

Thus ends the fourth chapter in the sixth section on the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna-praśna*) in the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* composed by Mahādeva.
6.5 Now begins the fifth chapter of the sixth book.
We shall explain the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*).
This is clear.

Before the *brahmaudana* [offering], he has his hair and beard shaved, trims his nails, cleans his teeth, bathes, and puts on a new garment. Everything else is clear. To those who have consumed the *brahmaudana*, he gives a gift.
For one who is not wealthy, two *guñjā* seeds of gold are the fee for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
When the sacrificial fires have been kindled, he gives a pair of animals whose semen has not yet been discharged.

Having anointed them, when the fires have been kindled, he gives to those same priests a male and female animal, such that the semen of both has not previously been discharged and has not yet reached [the womb].

He does not go forth, nor does he travel abroad. He does not go forth from his home, nor does he live abroad without his home; even that [abroad] he does not do. They do not carry his sacred fire away from his home.
No others lead the fire away from this sacrificer's house;
nor do they bring it from elsewhere.

His own people do not fetch it from any other source either. This is a prohibition against using a common (laukika) fire, whereas bringing it from another source would not have been applicable anyway.
He keeps awake this night with artistic performances.

On this night, when the sun has risen and he is about to settle the Āhavanīya fire, he passes the time without sleep through artistic performances such as playing the lute (*vīṇā*), the flute (*veṇu*), and the drum (*mṛdaṅga*). With the verse, "Kindling the fire with wood-shavings, may I win both worlds; having prospered in both worlds, may I cross beyond death," he kindles the fire that night with wood-shavings.

He prepares the fire for the *mālodanika* (the rice-porridge offering) by churning wood with splinters. The mantra is recited once, followed by silence; it is continuous because of the statement, "The night," which indicates an uninterrupted connection of time.

While the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) are being handed over, he looks on [with the verse]: "O Earth, mistress of the world, in the seat of Order, come hither, you two who support the treasures. You two, pregnant, give birth to the kinsman, the Jātavedas, the leader of the sacrifices. [Then he recites: "Ascend my ten fingers, O powerful ones! With the mortal life, O Agni, together with vigor."

"Living long, may I see each succeeding year; may I perform the sacrifice according to the New Moon and Full Moon rites"—with these words he accepts [the gift]. "You two possess the proper season, you two have Agni as your seed; receive the embryo. I take that from you two. That is the truth: that you two bear a hero and shall procreate a hero. You two shall procreate me in the morning; you two, having been procreated, shall procreate me. Through offspring, cattle, and spiritual luster, [may I attain] the heavenly world. Having accepted it, he consecrates it with this mantra. The preceding mantras are recited only once.

He takes the fire into himself, just as the Adhvaryu does, saying: "Here I go from untruth to truth; from truth I go to the human; from the human I go to the divine; I restrain my speech. Thus he restrains his speech. He breathes over the newborn [fire] with the formula: "By the breath of Prajāpati I breathe upon you; by the nourishment of Pūṣan, for me, for long life of a hundred autumns, for a hundred autumns of life, for vitality, for splendor, for living, for merit. "I am yours, you are mine; this is mine, you are mine; you are my womb, I am your womb."
Having consecrated the newborn with the mantra, "O Agni Jātavedas, carrying my oblations like a son for his father, you are the maker of worlds," he grants a boon.
He breathes upon the glowing fire through his nostrils.
At this point, the sacrificer and his wife release their speech and put on two linen garments.

By the use of the dual verb *paridadhāte* (they two put on), although the sacrificer and his wife alone are understood from the context of the sacrificer’s ritual (*yājamāna*), this specific mention is intended to dispel any doubt regarding the presence of two sacrificers.

When the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) has been completed, those two [the *yajñāyajñīya* verses] are given to the Adhvaryu priest. With whichever *vyāhṛtis*, with whichever specific *ṛṣi*-based installation, with whichever *madādevakṛta* [verses], with whichever *sārparājñī* verses, and with whichever *gharmaśiras* [formula] he establishes [the fires], he worships [the fire] with each and every one of them in all cases. 15.

This is clear. [The sacrificer] worships the established Gārhapatya fire with the mantra: "O Gārhapatya, burning away the enemies, making each dawn better than the last, O Agni, driving away our rivals, bestow upon us abundance of wealth, food, and strength. He addresses the fire being carried to the middle space with the mantra: "May these riches attend me; may I dwell here with these offspring; may the multiform nourishment (iḍā) stand here; shine in the midst of wealth, O Jātavedas! At the halfway point, he gives a choice gift. He worships the established Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "I have attained; I have pervaded; I have pervaded a full lifespan."

When the sun has risen at the appointed time, he gives the gift. "O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Virāj and the Svarāj—may they enter me; may they quicken me. O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Samrāj and the Abhibhū—may they enter me; may they quicken me. O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Vibhū and the Paribhū—may they enter me; may they quicken me. O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Prabhvī and the Prabhu-ti—may they enter me; may they quicken me. O Agni, with those bodies of yours which are auspicious, I establish you."

He worships the Āhavanīya fire with the auspicious forms: "Snik, snīhiti, snihiti, sadāmnī, āmatī, anāhuti, and Nirṛti—these, O Agni, are your terrible forms; let the mortal go to them, not the immortal—him who hates us and whom we hate. Thus he worships with the terrible forms prior to the *pūrṇāhuti*. At the *pūrṇāhuti*, he gives a boon. Having worshipped with the auspicious forms subsequent to the *pūrṇāhuti*—namely, those beginning with "O Agni, those two auspicious forms of yours"—he repeats the rite.

He worships with the *virāj* meters: "O Atharvan, protect my food, the food measured by the breath; guarded by you, rejoicing in nourishment and vigor, may we live a hundred autumns with our heroes. He worships the *dakṣiṇāgni*: "O Hero, protect my offspring, the continuity of the world's root; from yourself...
[End of section 60, Chapter 6, composed by Satvāṣāḍha in the Śrautasūtra].

"From my heart I fashion you; I entrust you to you," [he says] regarding the Gārhapatya fire. "O Śaṃsya, protect my cattle, my manifold wealth, and my treasure. Protect the prosperity and the joy of my houses; I entrust them to you. [He says] regarding the Āhavanīya fire: "Protect my assembly hall, which is wide-extending, which increases my sensory power and prosperity, and which is the shade for all people. I entrust it to you. "O Sa-pratha, protect my assembly hall, and those who are members of the assembly and the court."

"Make them possessed of sense-faculties; let them enjoy a full lifespan. "O Lord of the Assembly, protect my mantra at the base; protect my prosperity along with glory. "To the serpent at the base I entrust the mantra; for prosperity I entrust glory. Thus he stepped across the fires fivefold. The Virāj, created by Prajāpati, ascended upwards as the Rohiṇī, the womb and foundation of Agni. He thus established all the fires. There is an option regarding these steps according to the sequence of the Virāj in one's own Vedic branch.

At which point he gives him a hundred dice; having won at them, he gives [the winnings] to the members of the assembly (*sabhāsadaḥ*). Whatever they win, that and both kinds of food he prepares and serves to the Brāhmaṇas.
This has already been explained in the section on the *Ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires).

At the time of the sacrificial fee for the Āgneya offering, he gives a goat, a full vessel, a pillow, a garment made of all kinds of threads, a horse, a chariot, clothing, six cows, twelve, twenty-four, or an unlimited number of increasing cows; among these, there is a milch cow and a bull as a pair, and those of specified forms. He gives the goat, the full vessel, and the pillow to the Āgnīdhra; the horse to the Brahman; the milch cow to the Hotṛ; the bull at the Gārhapatya site to the Adhvaryu; and the remainder is common to all. In the case of the two preceding Pavamāna chants, the measure is thirty.
He gives the sacrificial fee consisting of two oblations and gold; at the highest [level], forty measures [of gold], and at the Āditya [rite], a cow.
This has already been explained up to the conclusion of the fire-installation (ādhāna).
From the time of the installation until the end of his life, he shall not speak untruth.

Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya [states]: "The venerable Patañjali, the author of the *Sārasvata-aṣṭādhyāyī*, has not mentioned [the following] at the end of the section on words. They are to be understood here by implication. Rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), the *vyāhṛtis*, and the remembrance of Viṣṇu are to be combined in all cases. [As stated in the *Paippalāda-śākhā*: "Of these two... (1.150)].
[In the *Mahādeva-kṛta-vaijayantī* commentary: "No Brāhmaṇa who has not eaten should dwell in his house."]

"A Brāhmaṇa who has not eaten should not stay overnight in the house of this Āhitāgni"—the Āhitāgni should act in such a way that this occurs; his vow alone continues for as long as he lives, not that of the Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, while this Brāhmaṇa stays in his house, if there is a desire to eat, one should certainly give him food; in its absence, one should give something else to ward off hunger; but if even that is unavailable, Bādhūla, citing Māṇḍavya, says: "The recitation of the *vyāhṛtis* and the feeding of a Brāhmaṇa. One should not turn away a guest who arrives at sunset from staying overnight.

A guest is one for whom the sun has set before and who has no other place to stay. Even if such a person arrives at one’s residence, there must be no obstruction; rather, a suitable place for lodging must certainly be provided. Regarding this matter as well, the penance for failing to do so is exactly that stated by Bādūla:
"One should not give [food] at night, except for food."

One should not give anything other than food at night. One should not, during the night, perform the transfer of ownership (*svatvāpādana*) regarding gold, grain, cattle, and so forth. It is understood that on auspicious occasions such as an eclipse, one may make a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) at night and bestow the gift upon a worthy recipient the following day. Some, however, explain this as a prohibition against giving even in general. Regarding this, it is stated: "If one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should act as if he were without them, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Agni Vratapati; this alone is declared to be the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in times of distress.
