this manner]. *na pakvānnam anyatra hiraṇyadhānyāder dadāti |* "One does not give cooked food [at night], except for gold, grain, and the like. *ahorātram adhaḥśāyī brahmacārī tryahaṃ kṣapet ||* "Sleeping on the ground and observing celibacy for a day and a night, he should spend three days [in this manner]. *na pakvānn

Giving food, one should eat it at night; even while being given, one should eat the food right there in the house, that is, one should have it consumed there. One should not give it away to take outside. I have explained the reading *adayīta* as occurring in several sūtras; however, the commentator has explained the reading *na dayīta*. He explains that *day*, in the sense of "giving," refers to the act of transferring ownership to another, which is characterized here as taking [the food] out of the house; thus he interprets it with the intention that one should not do that. This is the same meaning as what is stated in the reading *adayīta*.
One should not eat food cooked on a fire fueled by cow-dung (*narmūṣa*).

Some explain that one should not eat fruit and the like placed in a pit or similar location which has been cooked by fire immediately above it; this is what they call *ṛbbīṣa*. Others, however, explain it according to the *Nirukta*. For in the *Nirukta*, this word is read by the authors of the Taittirīya Sūtras as having the vowel *ṛ* followed by the letter *b* (*ṛbbīṣa*), as a synonym for "earth. Kātyāyana, however, reads it there with the letter *s* (*ṛṣbīṣa*). Thus, both forms are accepted.

Furthermore, "earth" (*pṛthivī*) itself is what is to be expressed; by that [earth], it means "cooked by the heat of the fire residing therein. And thus, this which is the "fire of the earth" (*pārthivo 'gniḥ*)—the reading *ṛjīṣapakvasya*, however, was found and explained by the author of the Bhāṣya as meaning "one should not eat *ṛjīṣa*," such as buttermilk, oil-cake, and so forth, from which the essence has been extracted. This reading *oṣam* is seen everywhere in the Taittirīya Sūtras and in our own Sūtra; moreover, it is the appropriate one.

For nothing is cooked without fire; therefore, this would also be a *karmadhāraya* compound, and by the rule for the word *anīṣa*, the word *paśu* would have to be placed first. Consequently, the reading should be *ṛbīṣam* alone. Regarding the word *paśu*:
one should not eat those waters that are navigable within the river (*antarnāvya*).

One should not consume water that is contained within a boat, or placed inside it, or has fallen into it, or has entered through a hole. There is no fault, however, in the case of water situated separated by another vessel. Āpastamba says, "One should not drink from within," and the meaning "having stood upon a boat" is also possible. Therefore, regarding the waters of a boat, one should not eat [of them]; and since it says "one should not drink from within," the sense is that one should not consume even a little water from within the boat.
One should not give silver or gold upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

The meaning is that where gold is prescribed as the object to be given, or where it is obtained as a substitute for cows and other such items, silver must not be given there; rather, it should be given as gold (*suvaya*). Regarding the phrase "on the sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣi*), this refers to the Vedic ritual (*śrauta-karma*). One should not place wet wood into the fire, or one may place it [if necessary]. The word "in the fire" (*agnau*) is to be supplied. It means "wet with water. And one may place it [the wood] if nothing else is available—this is how it should be explained, otherwise these two sūtras would be entirely purposeless.
One should not dwell in a place made by oneself, such as a salt-flat or a cleft;

one should not make a dwelling—that is, establish a residence—in a region that is naturally stony. One should also not dwell in a cleft, which is a fissure in the earth. Having uttered the sound "hiṃ," one should approach a woman while remaining silent.
Thinking "him," he may subsequently approach a woman;
or he may utter [the word]; the meaning is that he should not utter it.

In this year, one should not eat meat unless it has been prescribed [for a specific purpose], without having first performed the Nirūḍhapaśu sacrifice or the Aṅgapaśu sacrifice. Even if the eating of meat occurs due to illness, one should not eat meat in this year without having performed the Nirūḍhapaśu or the Aṅgapaśu sacrifice. However, if it has been prescribed, he may eat it. If he should eat it, he does so having prescribed it with the words: "I send this food to the fires with my mind; let them consume it together with my speech. Being vigilant and heedful, I move about; let me consume it together with an auspicious mind. Thus, having spoken, he eats it when it has been prescribed.
Instructed by the Brahmins, he may consume [the meat] even without having sacrificed with an animal victim.
For twelve nights, he himself performs the Agnihotra with clarified butter (ājya) while the fires are kept continuously burning.

The term *satra* is applied here to a period of a day and night. Regarding this, the rule for the commencement has been stated specifically for the Adhvaryu priest; having performed it thus, from the beginning until the end, he himself performs the Agnihotra with clarified butter, offering twenty-four oblations twice daily—both evening and morning—for twelve nights. However, for one who is not a *sattrin*, the twelve days must be observed as a rule. He states the vow: [Chapter 15, Section 150, accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva].
He wears an unwashed garment.
For twelve nights, it is an unwashed garment—washed by a washerman who has not cut or torn it, and which has not been washed before.
Another may certainly offer the oblation.
"By himself" is an alternative [to the previous rule].
It means that he should indeed be one who observes the vow; he should not eat meat, nor should he approach a woman.

He himself offers on the thirteenth [night]. "Himself" means by his own hand. That is to say, he performs the offering on the night of the thirteenth. The first cow they milk for the Agnihotra—that is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the Agnihotra.

On the thirteenth day, one should give the cow that they milk for the *agnihotra* to another person who might have performed the *homā* beforehand; or else, at the commencement of the *agnihotra*, [one should give it] to the *adhvaryu*. However, according to Baudhāyana and Āśvalāyana, as stated in the *Māṣya*, the carrying of the fire on horseback (*āśvapadika-dhāraṇa*) is prescribed for twelve days after the *ādhāna*. This is because of the Vedic injunction: "One should carry [the fire] on horseback for twelve days. Some explain that this period of twelve days begins after the *pavamāneṣṭi*, since the establishment of the fires (*agni-siddhi*) is completed at the conclusion of that sacrifice.

In the *Śāṭyāyanaka*, the maintenance of the fires (*dhāraṇa*), as well as the *svayaṃ-homa* and *ājya-homa*, are prescribed for the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*). Therefore, the teacher Satyāṣāḍha has taught that the oblation (*homa*) alone is the primary element. Consequently, after the commencement of the *agnihotra*, if the *anvārambhaṇīyā* is required in the interim, it should be performed in those very same fires, as should the *paurṇamāsī*. However, some maintain that where there is scope for the twelve-day sacrifice, there is only the maintenance of the fires; whereas where there is scope for water, such as in the case of the *nakṣatra-adhāna* and so forth, there is no maintenance of the fires during the *ārambhaṇīyā*.

Regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), some describe it as not requiring the maintenance of the firewood (*anvārambha*). That is incorrect, because there is no reason for such a restriction. It might be argued that the statement "having performed the *iṣṭi* and the *apavarga*" serves as a restrictive rule. But that is not so, because that statement is intended to exclude other alternatives, such as the annual (*sāṃvatsara*) and other rites. According to Bhāradvāja, [the maintenance is] by means of the *soma*-fire-establishment. For us, since the maintenance of the firewood is primarily for the sake of the oblation (*homa*), the maintenance of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) occurs after the *udavasānīyā* offering.

The *homās* are indeed *āśvapadika* (performed every day until a dog's footprint appears). Since the others are not *amlāna* (extinguished), one should say "they are *ajasra* (continuous)"; however, the purpose of specifying the plural number is to prohibit the *pakṣahoma* (fortnightly offering) and the *samāropaṇa* (formal consigning of the fires), precisely because the *homa* is the primary element. At a second *ādhāna* (establishment of the fires), the duties such as the *ajasra* do not apply. When the sacrificer has gone abroad, having performed the *sarvaprāyaścitta* (general expiation), the *ājyahoma* (ghee-offering) should be performed in the *ajasra* fires themselves, and the *praṇayana* (leading forth of the fire) after twelve days. Some, however, desire [the *praṇayana*] upon his return.

For them, on that day, having performed the expiation on the thirteenth day at dawn, there is the abandonment of the fires (*agnityāga*). [The formula: "O gods... and so forth; "Vāmam hoti. Here too, there is non-existence [of the fire] and the offering of clarified butter (*ājyahoma*). [The verse: "He who has perished... Because of the statement, "It should first be given to the Adhvaryu," the first oblation is with milk (*payas*); thereafter, with clarified butter. Alternatively, after the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), the evening oblation is with milk, because priority is required for that. [The verse: "He gives together..."

Regarding the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, Vādhūla states that the Pavamāneṣṭis should be performed at the time of their commencement. According to another view, the commencement should take place at the primary time itself. The Dakṣiṇā (sacrificial fee) for both is a cow; however, there is another Śruti text stating that the fee is an ox, as noted in the Bhāṣya commentary. [Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram—Sixth Praśna] ...iti vādhūlaḥ | anantare mukhyakāla evā''rambhaḥ | ubhā0dakṣiṇā | parivā brāhmaṇam | anaḍvāndakṣiṇeti śrutyantaramitimāṣyagranthaḥ | [End of Section] **Note on Diacritics:** The Sanskrit terms have been transliterated using standard IAST conventions. At the Anvārambhaṇīyā offering, he gives a pair of cattle; having given both those belonging to the original establishment of the fires (Agnyādheya) and those belonging to the re-establishment (Punarādheya), he gives a repaired chariot, a mended garment, a released ox, and gold weighing a hundred mānas as the sacrificial fee for the Punarādheya—this is the Paiṅgya Brāhmaṇa, or alternatively, he may give only those belonging to the Punarādheya.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the sixth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra. ||5||

The passage beginning with "punar" and so forth has been explained by Baudhāyana: "A chariot that has been renewed is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)," meaning it must be one that has been restored; "a garment that has been resewn"—that too is simply something that has been restored; "an ox that has been released again"—by this, it is said to be one that was previously worn out. Regarding this, Āpastamba states an exception: "If the other [prescribed items] are not available, one should give even just an ox; for these desires reside in the ox, and they become even greater than that," according to the Paiṅgāyani Brāhmaṇa.

Thus ends the fifth chapter of the sixth book, the section on the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna-paṭala*), in the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha, composed by Mahādeva.
6.6 Now begins the sixth chapter of the sixth book.

The *agnyādheya* (the establishment of the sacred fires) is completed. We shall now explain the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) regarding the *agnihotra*. Carrying the fuel-wood himself, he brings it to the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*); even if it has been brought by another, he brings it back himself.
"Bringing [offerings] at all times with an unailing mind, O Agni, may we, your neighbors, not come to harm"—with these words he approaches the sacrificial ground.
This is clear.
With the mantra "O Agni, whatever [fires] there be," he places the largest fuel-stick upon the Āhavanīya fire for each respective verse.
In the Āhavanīya fire, he places the largest kindling-stick; in the others, he places them one by one, each successively smaller, reciting a verse for each stick as it is placed.
He consecrates the fire being taken out with the mantra "Take it out" (*uddhara*).

In the case of a self-offering, this is a consecration (*anumantraṇa*), whereas in other cases it is a direction (*praiṣa*), because it has been stated in the section on the Adhvaryu's duties that "having been directed, he takes it out. Here, take it out... [end of fragment]. This is from the *Mahādevakṛtavaijayantī* commentary, Paṭala 15. [End of manuscript variants noted].

Although the fuel-wood offering (*idhmādhāna*) ought to be discussed immediately after this, the injunction "for twelve nights he offers the *agnihotra* without water" was stated first; this demonstrates that the fuel-wood offering, which is performed after the fire has been drawn out, cannot take place starting from the thirteenth day.

From the time of the lifting [of the spoon] until the pouring into the fire, he should not eat. Having touched water with the formula, "Thou art lightning," he crosses to the south of the Āhavanīya fire and sits down to the south. The wife [sits] in the place of the wife. [The sacrificer says: "Thou art the sacrificial food (iḍā), the bearer of the vow; I shall observe the vow for both of us. O Āditya, bearer of the vow; I shall observe the vow for both of us. O Surūpa, I shall observe the vow for both of us. O Iḍā, come; rest within me. Whatever vow belongs to the Agnihotra cow, he places that within himself.
He should contemplate within himself that vow which was relinquished from the Agnihotra cow, such as grass, leaves, and so forth.

"O Faith, come! By this truth I call you," he says as she is being summoned. "You are this [cow]; Agni is her calf; may she milk for me both the heavenly world and [this] world. As she is being milked, when it is said, "I shall draw it up," or "I draw it up," he says in a low voice, "You are the oblation of the gods; may there be safety from death for me; may there be well-being for me; may there be freedom from fear for me," and then aloud, "Draw it up! While it is being drawn up, he stands still and does not walk about; he restrains his speech until the drawing is finished, then he sits down once it has been drawn.
[He offers the portions saying: "To Agni, svāhā! To the plants, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! In the morning, [he offers] "To Sūrya, this! svāhā.
Having approached the northern oblation, standing somewhat crosswise—
facing slightly eastward and facing the Āhavanīya fire, being somewhat crosswise—
he worships the Āhavanīya with all the worship-formulas.

As many optional attendances (*upasthāna*) as there may be, they should be performed at the *saraṇa* [of the fire] toward the *āhavanīya* alone. Because of the general injunction regarding the "subsequent oblation" (*uttarām āhutim*), this applies to both times when no specific instruction is given.

With the six verses beginning with "Approaching the sacrifice" (*upaprayanto adhvaram*), one should perform the attendance for them: with the verse addressed to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīyā*) during the first half of the month, and with the verse addressed to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgnī*) during the second half of the month.
Among those, the verse "This is your womb" (*ayaṃ te yoniḥ*) should precede the *agnīṣomīyā*, while the *aindrāgnī* follows according to the recited order.
With the verses beginning with *agnīṣomāvimam su me* he worships the two deities Agni and Soma; with *ubhā vāmindrāgnī* he worships Indra and Agni.
Between these two—referring to the two previously mentioned—he approaches with the verse *anāpyāyaya indra*, meaning he stands near them with the six verses beginning with *eṣa te yoniḥ*.
He stands beyond the *vihavya* hymn, beginning from the first four verses.

With the verses beginning with "māmāna" and ending with "adhivocatā me," and following those with the six Agni-Pāvamānī verses beginning with "agna āyūṃṣi pavase," he offers into the Āhavanīya fire itself. With these same verses, he does so again after a year.

At the end of the year, he worships the Gārhapatya fire with four [verses], beginning with: "O Agni, giver of life, give me life. He worships the Āhavanīya fire twice with the verse: "O Citrāvasu, may I reach your end in safety," repeating for each son: "May there be safety for so-and-so; may there be safety for so-and-so," pronouncing the name of each son twice.
For Yajñaśarman, he says: "May there be safety for you" twice.

With the verses, "Thou art the fuel of Agni; protect me from imprecation," "Thou art the fuel of Soma; come to me from the highest [place]," and "Thou art the fuel of Yama; protect me from death," he should place three pieces of fuel. With the verse, "Kindling thee for a hundred winters," he places the fourth.

He wipes his mouth with the verse, "O Soma, we abide in thy service, bearing our minds within our bodies; may we, possessing offspring, attain prosperity," and also with the verse, "O Agni, mayest thou unite with the splendor of the Sun."

"Furthermore: 'I behold the creatures,' [he says]. He approaches the humans with the formula, 'May I enjoy you as water in the water'; he approaches the cattle with 'O wealthy ones, rejoice! Standing between the two fires, he mutters, 'You are united, possessing all forms. He touches the cow with [the verse], 'The calf or [the cow]—O Agni, day by day... He worships the Gārhapatya fire with six Gāyatrī verses in two-footed meter: 'With strength I look upon you; may you look upon me with strength. [He addresses] the cow-pen: 'You are the world, possessing thousandfold prosperity; you rule over thousandfold prosperity.'"

"May we be among those who receive the greatest portion of her," [he says], and he again touches the cow or the calf with the verse: "May there be the great protection of Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa—the heavenly, the invincible. For neither at home nor on the paths that ward off enemies does a malicious foe have power over them. May those sons of Aditi grant eternal refuge and desirable boons to the giver. With this triplet addressed to the Great Gods (*mahitrīṇām*), he worships them, and so forth. [End of Section] 1. 4. 610. Paṭala. Accompanied by the commentary *Vejayantī* composed by Mahādeva. 537.

"Of that Savitṛ, the most excellent... with this *Sāvitrī* verse; and "Make us hear the Soma-presser..."—this [verse] is: "O Brahmaṇaspati, make us hear the Soma-presser, Kakṣīvat, the son of Uśij. He who is the other, the friend, the remover of disease, the finder of wealth, the increaser of prosperity—he, the swift one, may he attend to us. Let not the curse of the stingy man, nor the malice of a mortal, reach us."

He worships with the verses addressed to Brahmaṇaspati, beginning with "rakṣā ṇo brahmaṇaspate. He recites two verses, "kadācana starīrasi" and "kadācana prayucchasī," and the verse "pari tvā'gne puraṃ vayam. Then, having turned around, he worships at the end with the verse, "pari te dūḍabho ratho'smān aśnotu viśvato | yena rakṣasi dāśuṣaḥ. Having turned around, he worships with the verse "pari tvā'gne," which was previously recited, immediately after the verse "viparīta," because of its reading in another Śākhā. Even regarding the reading as it has been shown, he states the authoritative source:

Some recite the *dūḍabha* verse as the final one: "Thou art the crusher; may I crush him who hates us and whom we hate. If he should compete with one who is superior, he should press down with his forefoot from the front, saying: "Thou art the overcomer; may I overcome him who hates us and whom we hate. If he should compete with an equal, he should press down with his foot from the south, saying: "Thou art the subduer; may I subdue him who hates us and whom we hate."

If he should contend with one who is more wicked, he should seize him from behind with his heels. Having murmured, "May Pūṣan, the protector of cattle, protect me; may Pūṣan, the protector of the path, protect me; may Pūṣan, the overseer, protect me; may Pūṣan, the lord, protect me," [he continues]: "The eastern direction has Agni as its deity; whoever would do me harm from this direction, let him fall upon Agni; may Agni guard me from that direction. The southern direction has Indra as its deity; whoever would do me harm from this direction, let him fall upon Indra; may Indra guard me from that direction. The western direction..."

The Maruts are the deities of the northern direction; whoever would seek to harm me from this direction, let him fall to the Maruts. May the Maruts protect me from that direction. The north is the direction; Mitra and Varuṇa are its deities. Whoever would seek to harm me from this direction, let him fall to Mitra and Varuṇa. May Mitra and Varuṇa protect me from that direction. The upward direction is the zenith; Bṛhaspati is its deity. Whoever would seek to harm me from this direction, let him fall to Bṛhaspati. May Bṛhaspati protect me from that direction.

This quarter has Aditi as its deity; whoever seeks to harm this quarter, may he encounter Aditi; protect that quarter for me. — 2.538 — Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra), Sixth Praśna.

Having thus worshipped the quarters with the formula, he mutters while standing between the two fires: "May Dharma protect me, the observer of dharma; may Adharma protect me, the non-observer of dharma. May life and further life, sight and wide-sight, out-breath and in-breath, the forward breath and the downward breath, the broad one and the wide-striding one—may we go through the shared enjoyment of your speech, O Arka. May the divine thread not be cut by the human; may I not be severed from the divine abode. For life, for light, for the thread, [I take] you. So-and-so, may I be followed by light, by the body. He mutters this while standing between the two fires: "O Agni, grant long life; O Agni..."

With the two verses addressed to Agni Pavamāna, beginning with "Flow on" (*pavasva*), he worships the Gārhapatya fire; and with the verse "O Agni, lord of the house" (*agne gṛhapate*), he says, "I pray for that blessing, full of light, for my progeny. One who has no son born should say, "I pray for that blessing, full of light, for so-and-so. One who has a son born should say, "I pray for that blessing, full of light, for so-and-so. One who has many sons should recite the names of all his sons and finally say, "full of light. He performs this worship every evening. 20.

Having risen, immediately after rising near the *uttarāhuti*, he himself performs the oblation before the first tasting (*prāśana*). The six verses beginning with "upaprayanta" are recited in the Taittirīyaka. In the Paiṅgaka tradition, having made that verse addressed to Agni and Soma the fifth, one worships during the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*) with six verses. Having made the verse addressed to Indra and Agni the fifth, one worships during the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) with six verses according to the textual order. Before the verse "yaṃ te," [one recites] the *vihavya* hymn; then, with the verses beginning with "mama agne," one worships with four verses.

After those [offerings] have been performed, having worshipped the Gārhapatya fire with the first six verses beginning with "O Agni, you purify yourself in the waters" (*agne bhāyūṣi pavaḥ*), he worships it with those same verses once every year, but not in the intervals between years. Some say that because of the scriptural statement "with the next six," the worship is obligatory with all twelve, and that there is a repetition at the end of the year; however, the former view should be accepted as correct in this case.

Since the worship with the *āmipāvamānī* verses is fixed for every year, and because that [worship] is connected with the preceding ones, the "Great Worship" (*mahopasthāna*) must be performed regularly every year according to all versions of the ritual. Thereafter, he worships the Āhavanīya fire with four verses beginning, "O giver of life... and "...O Agni, protector of our bodies. In the fourth mantra, he repeats the phrase, "O thou whose wealth is manifold, may I attain thy well-being at the end," twice.

Immediately thereafter, he addresses each person by name individually, saying: "Devadattaśarman, may it be well with you; Yajñadattaśarman, may it be well with you. Having placed fuel-sticks upon all the fires with the verses, "Of Agni, of Soma, of Yama, of Indra," he pays reverence to them. With the verse, "Ambhasvatī," he likewise honors humans and animals. Standing between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires, he mutters the verse, "Revatīḥ. He touches the Agnihotra cow, or a bull from which the milk-offering is drawn, with the formula, "Saṃhitāsi."

With the three *gāyatrī* verses beginning with "idam pitu" and the three two-footed verses beginning with "ase tvam naḥ," he worships the *gārhapatya* fire with these six verses. With the verse "ūrjā vaḥ," he worships the cattle standing in the pen. With "bhuknam asi," it is as before. With the triplet beginning with "mahitrīṇām ako astu," he worships the *āhavanīya* fire. And with the verses addressed to Savitṛ—"tatsaviturvareṇyam," "somānaṃ svaraṇam," and "evā hyasi vīrayuḥ"—and with those addressed to Brahmanaspati—"mā naḥ śaṃsaḥ," he worships the *āhavanīya* fire.

Having worshipped the Āhavanīya fire in this sequence with the verses, "Never art thou barren, never dost thou fail; O Agni, [protect] thee from the evil-minded," standing right there, having murmured "May Pūṣan protect me," and having worshipped the directions according to their respective characteristics with "The eastern direction," etc., standing between the two fires, he mutters, "May Dharma protect me. Here, the name of the eldest son is mentioned: "O Agni... [End of Paṭala 150, with the commentary *Vaijayantī* by Mahādeva].

With the three verses, "O Agni, leader of life," "O Agni, purify," and "O Agni, lord of the house," he worships the Gārhapatya fire. He pronounces this blessing: "I invoke this blessing for [Name], who has many sons—for Devadattaśarman, Brahmadattaśarman, and Yajñadattaśarman—may it be full of light. Regarding the passage beginning with "They approach" and ending with "full of light," there is an option when both times [of worship] have arrived.

Regarding the phrase "he worships every evening" (*sāyaṃ sāyamupatiṣṭhate*), the rule *sāyaṃ sāyam* establishes a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) meaning "only in the evening"; thus it is stated that the worship is only in the evening and not in the morning. Here, the absence of the word *vā* (or) is due to conformity with the revealed scripture (*śruti*). Although the injunction "he offers the Agnihotra" is without qualification, after prescribing the worship, there is again the rule "he worships at night, not in the morning. Because of this being both prescribed and prohibited, there is an option (*vikalpa*).

Thus, although [the time] is applicable to both [morning and evening] in the Sūtra, because of the repeated mention of "in the evening" (*sāyam*), it is established that it is only in the evening and not in the morning; therefore, the evening is fixed, while the morning is optional. Regarding this very point, he states the morning attendance (*upasthāna*) as an alternative: "Or rather, this [is done] during the day. By the phrase "or rather," an option for the daytime is stated regarding the attendances to be performed when [the sun] is about to set.

"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! May I be rich in offspring through my progeny, rich in heroes through my men, rich in splendor through my luster, and rich in nourishment through my possessions"—or [he may say], "May Indra grant me what I desire," or "May my faith not depart from me," or "May I be able to support you.
This is clear.
All that is both performed and unperformed.

The meaning is whether the two-fold attendance (*upasthāna*) should be performed or not. Thus, the Śruti, having begun with "Agni is to be attended upon," and having stated "therefore he is not to be attended upon," further says, "therefore he is to be attended upon. Because it is both enjoined and prohibited, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the attendance. Even in the case of performing the attendance, the scriptural authorities (*śruti*)—"by the Great Attendance (*mahopasthāna*) at night," "of the four [verses] beginning with *bhūḥ* [one at] night," "not [at] day," "he attends at night, not in the morning," and "he attends during the day"—are the evidence.
He states another alternative along with the [option of using] all four [verses]:

One should attend upon [the fire] in the morning with the *prātaravaneka* rite. "Morning attendance" (*prātaravaneka*) is the name of a ritual act; one should attend upon it using only those mantras belonging to that rite. In the absence of a specific instruction, the *āhavanīya* fire is used.
This applies when the oblation has been placed on the fire or while it is being poured out.
The meaning is that when the *āghāra* oblation for the *agnihotra* has been placed on the fire, or while it is being poured out, one should first perform the rite to be described hereafter.
Having performed the worship (*upasthāna*) with the first four verses of the *vihavya* hymn,
and having worshipped the *āhavanīya* fire with the verses beginning with "O Agni, [grant] me luster" (*mama agne varcaḥ*).

With the formula, "O Lord of Waters," he pours out three handfuls of water; with the formula, "The enemies are driven away," he sprinkles around three times. For Kāla, for you two, for the victorious one... [the text continues]. That which is true, that which is real... [the text continues]. Day by day... [the text continues]. Composed by Satyāṣāḍha, the Śrautasūtra—[Book Six].

With the words "With which [you wash] you two," he washes their hands; with the words "Here I wash away misfortune," he sips water and spits it out, saying "of my rivals and enemies. Again they wash their hands; with the words "May I today utter speech endowed with power," he cleans the seats of the vital breaths according to their respective forms. He worships with the following section of the Anuvāka, repeating three times the verse beginning with "O Arvāgvasu, may there be well-being for you" and ending with "may you reach the further shore," substituting the name of each of his sons, saying, "May there be well-being for so-and-so; may there be well-being for so-and-so."

He recites the names three times before each [deity], and after performing the worship with the four verses following the Vihavya hymn dedicated to Agni and Soma, he worships with the remainder of the Anuvāka.

For each sprinkling, there is a repetition of the mantra with the hands joined in the *añjali* gesture, preceded by the four verses beginning with "purastād devīḥ paḍuḥ. The rest is clear. The recitation of the mantras belonging to other Vedic branches has been shown by Āpastamba: "O Lord of Waters, those whose portion you are... [he says as he pours water into the joined palms]. Having sprinkled around on the ground three times with the words "Repelled are the enemies! Repelled are the enemies!", [he continues] "To Kāla for you, to Maitriya for you, to Audbhatriya for you, to Anāyāya for you..."

"O left hand, protect the well-performed act"—with these words he washes his hands. "Here I cast out misfortune"—this is the mantra for spitting after rinsing the mouth. "May I be the highest among my rivals and enemies; [I take] water as the friend of the waters"—having washed his hands with this, he says, "May there be no fire against us. This [mantra] was not employed by our own Sūtrakāra, but it was employed by Āpastamba: "Bestow prosperity upon me, place prosperity within me; make me the sovereign lord of prosperity."

Having muttered, "I enter as the lord; O bountiful Indu, may he lead me with glory," one should recite the two additional mantras belonging to Āpastamba: "O Agni, speak to the god at dawn" and "The waters have made me free from the curse born of a false oath; [they have] placed auspicious oaths within me"; then one should sip water (ācamya).

"Today I shall utter speech endowed with the senses; may I speak speech that is long-reaching, unbroken, and undeceived. O Guardian, [place] the divine light, free from weapons, and the eye of the Suparṇa bird once within my nostrils. The two eyes are joined together, the two ears are heard by the gods. *Kauṃ*—the hair on the outside, the tuft on the sacrificial grass-strew. The tuft [is placed] in its proper place. *Kaspaṣam*—from the heart and all other limbs. Do not abandon me!"—thus he touches all the limbs according to their respective marks. From this point forward is the worship (*upasthāna*) of all the fires; that has not been stated by our own Sūtra-author.

"Ye are the rains; may they be with me, O Gṛhamedhins, O lords of life, svadhā! Ye who are fond of cattle, protect me, guard me, dwell within me! May no one strike us down, nor may we perish! Come near, come near! Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Grant me long life! Thus says Āpastamba regarding the worship of all [the fires]. With the *anuvāka* beginning "uttaraṇa," he worships the Āhavanīya fire. With the *anuvāka* beginning "upaprayanta," the branch-holding [priest] becomes the superior; in that *anuvāka* [is found]: "O Citrāvasu... (Ka., Kha., Nā. 2).

*ṭha*, *ṇa*: the sphere of Yayā. 2. *gha*, *ra*, *ca*, *da*: "touching" (*mṛśata*) is added at the end. 3. *jha*, *bha*, *ḍha*: "trivira". 4. *ba*: "mīya yā vii". 5. *gha*: "'yā viha". 6. *ca*, *ṭa*: "vajūtā". *ca*: "'miva prā". *ca*: "suśrutau". 7. *Saṃhitā-paṭalaḥ*, together with the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva: 541. Before the word "svasti," one should repeat the names of the sons one by one three times each, as before. There too, [the formula] is "viśe viśa iti."

Immediately after that, in the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*), one worships with "O Agni and Soma, you are rich in food" (*agnīṣomāvimaṃ su ma*), and in the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) with "O Indra and Agni, you two are rich" (*umā vāmindrāgnī*). Then, having worshipped with the remainder of the section beginning "This is your womb" (*ayaṃ te yoniḥ*), he recites: "May we be eaters of food from the belly, possessing cattle and horses among this people; may he who hates us be without food. According to some, one should not descend [the fire] before the morning *agnihotra*.

According to the opinion of some followers of other *śākhās*, one should not worship [the fire] in front of the *agnihotra* fire in the afternoon. Some explain that the entire ritual pertaining to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) is thus suspended.
"He sweeps away the grass from around the fire; he becomes radiant and endowed with spiritual luster"—so it is known. || 21 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the sixth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.

The meaning is that he brings out and places the grass for the strewn covering from the Āhavanīya fire. This is known in the Śruti. Thus ends the sixth chapter in the sixth section concerning the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna-praśna*) in the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* composed by Mahādeva. 6.6.6.
6.7 Now begins the seventh chapter of the sixth book.
We shall explain departure on a journey apart from one's home;
we shall also explain departure on a journey without the sacred fires.

"Prepare the fires," he commands as he is about to depart on a journey. He pays homage to the *bhāsvat* fire with the four verses beginning, "O Jātavedas, my name was first... Having paid homage to the Āhavanīya fire with [the verse], "Protect my cattle, O Śaṃsya; guard them for me until my return," he breathes toward it and pays homage to the Gārhapatya fire with, "O Agni, thousand-eyed one... Having paid homage to the Gārhapatya fire with, "Protect my progeny, O Narya; guard it for me until my return," he pays homage to the [Gārhapatya] with, "O Agni, lord of the house... [The verse continues: "...protect my food for me."

"O thou dwelling in the depths, protect that for me; guard it until our return," with these words he worships the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern fire). Having breathed over it and worshipped it with "O Agni, O bearer," he worships it with the *virājakrama* verses as previously described. "O Mitra and Varuṇa, do you two guard these houses for me... [The rest follows]. [Note: Variants from manuscripts are noted:

1. *ca.* has *śeṣaḥ*; 2. *vi*; 3. *ka.*, *ga.*, *ca.*, *ṭa.*, *da.* have *smi jane*; in the *ṭīkā* manuscripts the reading is *°sya paśūnme pā°*; 5. *ca.*, *ḍha.* have *°ruṇau*. This is from the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Sixth Book.]

"May he protect these [fires] which have been lost or carried away until our return; stay between the two fires," he murmurs while standing between them. "May we not stray from the path, nor from the sacrifice, O Indra, we who possess Soma; may no enemies stand against us. Lead us upward, O Agni, you who are invoked with ghee; unite us with abundance of wealth and with progeny, and make us many. He steps forward; he restrains his speech in the presence of the fires and releases it when out of their sight; he observes the vow at the prescribed times for the vow.

From the lifting [of the vessel] until the oblation is offered, one should not eat; this and other such observances (*vrata*)—such as "thou art lightning" (*vidyud asi*) and so forth—are purificatory rites for the sacrificer (*yajamāna-saṃskāra*). Furthermore, the recitations (*japa*), the attendances (*upasthāna*) with the formulas "thou art *iḍā*" (*iḍā asi*) and "the oblation of the gods" (*havir devānām*), and everything else should be understood to be performed just as in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). At the attendance, the Adhvaryu alone performs the placing of the fuel-stick (*samid-ādhāna*). However, the immolation of the cow (*gavālambha*) is omitted because it serves the purpose of another. There is another Sūtra stating: "Facing the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), he mutters the mantras."

Thus Bharadvāja said: "Even for one who has gone on a journey, this very rite prescribed for the *upasthāna* (homage) must be performed; the Adhvaryu priest shall perform those ritual acts, while the sacrificer shall mutter the mantras.
He pays homage at each season (*ṛtu*).
If there is a delay in returning from the journey, he should perform the *pravāsopasthāna* at each season; that is to say, every two months.

If one who has not performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) of the fires finds himself in a state of travel—whether by divine or human necessity—and thus departs without having attended to the fires, then he performs the attendance that will be described hereafter:
"Right here, O Agnis, I maintain you who are there with my breath, speech, and mind; may life not abandon me while I am away; I attend upon you with the Vaiśvānara light. Thus he attends.
Wherever he stays, there he is intent upon the monastery; having returned at once, he attends with a gesture of fearlessness;
having gone abroad, he returns from his journey.

"Always holding the fuel-sticks and bringing them with an unailing mind, O Agni, may we, your neighbors, not come to harm. Having approached the sacrificial area (*vihāra*) in the presence of the fires, he restrains his speech; he releases it in their presence [after the rite]. He issues the command: "Tend the fires! While they are burning, he pays homage: "Homage be to you, the bountiful one; homage to you, O forest-consumer."

"O Agni, beautify thy body; unite me with wealth"—with these words he kindles the fire. With the three mantras beginning "Thou art the fuel of Agni; protect me from imprecation," he should place three pieces of fuel on the fire. With the fourth mantra, "Kindling thee for a hundred winters," the Adhvaryu offers an oblation with the verse, "May the mind, the light, enjoy [the offering]. If he departs on a journey on the tenth day, he should offer to the Āhavanīya fire with the four verses beginning, "My name and thine, O Jātavedas... and "Thou hast protected my cattle, which are to be praised; them [protect] for me. [End of Paṭala 70] [This concludes the section] accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

Having again approached the Āhavanīya fire with the words, "Give [it] back," and having fanned it, he worships it with, "O Agni, thousand-eyed, you have protected my offspring; give that back to me. Having approached the Gārhapatya fire with the words, "O Agni, lord of the house, you have protected my food; give that back to me," and having fanned it, he worships it with, "O Agni, bearer, you have protected my foundation; give that back to me. Having approached the Dakṣiṇāgni fire and fanned it, he worships it with the Virāj-krama formulas as before: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two have protected these houses of mine."

"O Pūṣan, look after these [cows] which are neither lost nor strayed until our return," he mutters while standing between the two fires; "protect them, you have protected them," he adds to every [verse], or simply "protect them.
This is clear.

Now, according to some, it is known: "Who will awaken one who is sleeping soundly? Therefore, the worship should be performed while the fires are still unkindled. When about to depart on a journey, [he should say]: "O Giver of Fearlessness, grant me fearlessness; may it be well with me as I go forth. Having departed, when he returns, [he should say]: "O Giver of Fearlessness, you have granted me fearlessness; may it be well with me as I have returned. "O houses, do not be afraid, do not tremble; bringing strength, we come to you. Bringing strength, a winner of wealth and wise, I come to the house, rejoicing in my mind."

To those whose goodwill shines forth when they go abroad to others—to them we call our homes; may they recognize us as we recognize them. Invoked here are the cows; invoked are the goats and sheep. And the sweet essence of food is invoked within our homes. Invoked are the friends with many companions, who share in pleasant gatherings. May our homes always be free from harm and full of all men. May they be rich in vigor, rich in milk, refreshing, and full of joy.

"May you not perish, may you not thirst; do not be afraid of us," with these words he approaches the house. "For your security, for your peace, I enter; may there be auspiciousness, prosperity, and well-being—well-being, well-being! with these words he enters. On that day, having arrived, he does not engage in quarreling. "I enter the houses which are well-disposed, which slay the enemy, most heroic, and very kind; bringing nourishment and being well-intentioned, among them I lie down, well-disposed. With this he lies down. "And may we all, by means of thee, cross over our enemies like streams of water. With this he looks at his wife. (24)
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the sixth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśī Sūtra.

*Sāma-darśana*: "In the *ruṇī-gṛ* [text], 2. *ca-da-pāyari-vati*. 3. *ka-ga-ka-8, ṇa, bāravataḥ*. [1. Sixth Chapter—The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: Regarding the alternative view of not performing the worship (*upasthāna*) while the fire is not yet made manifest, that which was stated starting with "Now for some" (*athaikeṣām*) concerns the worship performed by one who has returned after traveling while the fire was unattended. However, the passage beginning with "having traveled abroad" (*proṣya*) and so forth applies equally to one who has returned from a journey. The phrase "he lies down" (*saṃviśati*) refers merely to a ritual duty (*dharma-mātra*). The rest is clear.

The *manasvatī* [offering], however, is to be offered with the *āyus* [formula]; it is recited in the section concerning the sacrificer (*yājamānakāṇḍa*). And since that [section] falls within the concluding part of the "approaching" (*upasthāna*) of the kindled fires, the author of the Bhāṣya states that it does not exclude the "fearless" (*abhayaṅkara*) approaching. Others, however, desire the *manasvatī* for the purpose of the oblation when the Āhavanīya fire has been carried forth; likewise [they say this applies] when one is away from home without water. When one is away from home for a season, neither the *ātithī* nor the *vrātabhṛtī* [offerings] are performed. When one is away from home for a year, the *pavitreṣṭi* is prescribed by both Āśvalāyana and Bharadvāja.

According to Baudhāyana, there is a combination of the Vaiśvānarī and the Manasvatī offerings. Regarding the re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya), it is traditionally taught that this applies when both husband and wife have left the sacred fires and are traveling abroad: "If one who has established the fires goes beyond the boundary while accompanied by his wife, yet the time for the fire-oblation (homa) has passed, a re-establishment of the fires is required for him. However, there is no fault if even one of them is present, even if there are many wives. Likewise: "The oblation must be offered in the absence of the couple by means of a representative; if it occurs in the absence of both, it would be useless."

When the sacrificer is away on a journey and his wife is in her menstrual period, the author of the *Bhāṣya* states that she should be excluded and the oblation offered. However, he says that the *Tapeṣṭi* sacrifice should be performed when she is pure. Others, however, desire that even while she is excluded, the *Vaṣaṭ* call should be made. Since the performance of the obligatory (*nitya*) sacrifice has been declared by the *Smṛtis*, they maintain that one must offer it even after excluding her. Regarding this, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has stated that likewise [the rule applies] to the two twilights and the river.

In the event of crossing a river or overstepping the boundary, one should consign the fires into her and then set out on the journey; upon crossing the boundary or a river, she takes hold of the lower fire-drill (*araṇī*). However, in times of distress, Bharadvāja has stated that even a combined offering (*samasya*) may be performed. On the day of the full moon or new moon, every evening—starting from the first evening and including the evening offering of the upcoming fourteenth day—one performs the offering by means of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*) using only one fuel-stick (*samit*) for which four portions have been ladled out. In the morning as well, one again ladles out four portions for that many offerings and completes the remainder as before.

In the event of an extreme emergency, or in the evening or morning, having counted the omitted *abhihomas*, he draws out [the oblation] for both with the formulas "I shall draw out" and "I will draw out," drawing four times in each case. If it is the morning, he offers the first [portion] to Sūrya and the second to Agni; if it is the evening, he does the reverse. Having offered, he consecrates the remainder of the *saurya* and *āgneya* oblations by means of the common ritual procedure (*tantra*). Or, having offered in the reverse order, he completes the remainder and departs. Then, having churned the fire in the morning of the *parvan* day, he performs the morning and evening rites.

If the *Homo* (Soma sacrifice), the *Iṣṭi*, or the *Paśu* sacrifice is not performed on the prescribed lunar day (*parvan*), then from that point forward, up until the second lunar day, one must perform the *Tantumatī-iṣṭi* and the expiation for the transgression of the *Iṣṭi*. If even that is impossible, or if the churning [of the fire-drill] fails, then the re-establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) itself must be performed. Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Absence from Home," in the sixth section concerning the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) within the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* composed by Mahādeva. || 7 ||
6.8 Now begins the eighth chapter of the sixth book.

In the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, one gives a first-born calf; in the case of a separate ritual procedure (*nānātantra*), [one gives] a brownish-pink animal for the Śyāmāka grain, as well as honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), honey-gruel (*madhumantha*), curd-gruel (*dadhimantha*), or rice cooked in milk (*kṣīraudana*). [End of section]. [End of chapter]. [This is] accompanied by the commentary *Vaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva.

"A vessel, linen clothing, a rain-garment—may the gods lead us from prosperity to greater prosperity. With this verse he eats rice (*vrīhi*). "May Agni eat first; for he knows how the oblation is. May he make the plants auspicious for us, he who dwells among all people. With this verse he eats millet (*śyāmāka*). "That barley, mixed with honey, which they ploughed out by the Sarasvatī—Indra was the lord of the plough, the hundred-willed one; the Maruts, the bounteous givers, were the ploughmen. With this verse he eats barley (*yava*).

The connection is that [the sacrifice] takes place at dawn. The "first-born calf" is the one born first within the year; the commencement of the year may be from the Ekāṣṭakā, or from Phālgunī, or from Caitrī. When the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is the same, there is only one sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). A "brown" (*babhru*) cow is either tawny (*kapila*) or reddish-brown (*piṅgala*), or indeed reddish-eyed; thus the cow is of two forms. The *madhuparka* consists of curd, honey, ghee, water, or barley meal (*saktu*). *Madhumaṇḍa* is barley meal mixed with honey; *dadhimanda* is barley meal mixed with curd.
A full vessel of rice mixed with lye, Soma, a garment, and ghee used during the rainy season are prescribed. The rest is clear.

According to the specific modification, one recites eleven *prayāja* formulas for the animal sacrifice; whichever formula is the modification for a particular *prayāja*, that is used for its consecration (*anumantraṇa*). To clarify this very point, he says:

One offers four oblations with four [verses] from the beginning; the fourth is performed by means of the consecration formula (*anumantraṇa*). For the first four, beginning with *duraḥ*, one uses the highest [verse] for the others. In modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) where the number of *prayāja* offerings and so forth must be completed by repetition when the count exceeds the original, the modifications (*vikāra*) are heard of as occurring between the fourth and fifth [offerings]. With the intention that these modifications belong specifically to the fourth and fifth because of their proximity, it is said: "four with four from the beginning. As in the archetype, there are four; the modifications of the fourth consist of nine additional [offerings], and for the last [offering], the deity-invoking *yājyā* verses ending with the word "Agni" are prescribed.

"You are the winner of light; having won the light, come to the light; light for me, light for the cattle! You are the winner of space; having won the space, come to the space; space for me, space for the cattle! You are the winner of the way; having won the way, come to the way; the way for me, the way for the cattle! You are the winner of refuge; having won the refuge, come to the refuge; the refuge for me, the refuge for the cattle!"—he mutters this while the animal is being slaughtered with the words "Not indeed, you do not die here; you are all the quarters of the quarters. When the omentum has been offered, he gives away the supreme [gift], or he should lead away three sacrificial fees.

A choice cow, or whatever cows are available from this [herd]—some say that the rule for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā-dharma*) does not apply to the choice; however, the consensus of all authorities is that the rule for the sacrificial fee certainly applies in both cases, because it is so enjoined. According to the modification, one consecrates eleven after-offerings (*anūyāja*) at the animal sacrifice:
three with each of the first [verses], and the tenth and the last with the last [verse].

The first [offering] is the original (prākṛta) and is clear. Its repetition is the tenth. The Sviṣṭakṛt, however, like the original, is the eleventh; thus, according to Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, two [offerings] are understood as fixed. Consequently, nine remain. Among those, three by three [groups] follow the original first consecration formula (anumantraṇa). Since the first is original, the two situated near it are the modifications (vaikṛta) of the first.

And so, he consecrates the first three with the *prathamānumantraṇa* formula. Then, when it would follow that the remaining [verses] are to be applied in their respective order, it is improper to state that the eighth, which is clearly the *narāśaṃsa*, serves as the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; for the sequence is set aside by the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Therefore, the four modified verses beginning with the fourth are applied in order: two belong to the *narāśaṃsa* and the other two to the *sviṣṭakṛt*. And thus, the *narāśaṃsa*...

With the third consecration formula (*anumantraṇa*), there is a ninth [offering] together with the *sena* [portion]; because it follows immediately after the *narāśaṃsa*, there is no displacement (*nikāra*) of the *iṣṭakṛt*. And thus, since it is established that the sixth, seventh, and ninth—these three—are [consecrated] by the third formula, and likewise the first, second, fourth, fifth, eighth, tenth, and eleventh by each of the [other] formulas respectively, even though the eleven *anuyāja* offerings are thus settled, the example "the tenth by the first" is presented once again for illustrative purposes. By this, the determination regarding the first and eighth [offerings] is also established.

The meaning is that, thereafter, for the seven remaining [sacrificial posts], there is an application according to their respective modifications, following the principle of immediate sequence from what was previously stated. "Like the horns of horned animals, the sacrificial stakes (svaru) with their top-rings (caṣāla) are seen upon the earth; those divine stakes stand firm—homage to my friends! May I not fall away from those who have sat down. (25) Having sacrificed the stake, he worships it with the mantra, "May I obtain good heroic power," and when the rite is completed, he worships the sacrificial post.

At the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, he gives a bull to Vaiśvānara, or gold for the ox; a milch-cow to Pārjanya. He consecrates nine fore-offerings (*prayāja*) according to their respective modifications: four with the first four formulas, and four beginning with *duraḥ* with the formula used for the fourth [fore-offering]; the last one with the last formula. At the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, he gives the first-born calf; he consecrates nine after-offerings (*anūyāja*) according to their respective modifications, three with each of the formulas. The procedure for the Adhvaryu has already been explained.

"That is the Ṛta, that is the Satya, that is the Vrata; may I be able to perform it, may I be capable through it, may I succeed through it"—with these words he mutters while the hair is being shaved on all occasions. For four months he speaks no untruth, he does not eat meat, he does not approach a woman, and he does not sit upon anything elevated. He should feel aversion toward untruth; he sleeps facing the east, he does not eat honey, he does not apply collyrium to his eyes, and he does not anoint himself with oil. He may approach his wife only during her season. These are the intermediate vows for all the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. At the Varuṇapraghāsa rites, he gives away a cow, and at the Śunāsīrya, a bull that has reached its full age.
1. t. 'ga. 'mānu| 8 paṭa] Together with the Vaijayantī commentary composed by Mahādeva:

In the Sākamedha sacrifices, he offers [the oblation] for whichever [deity] the sound resounds; at the Paurṇadarvya [offering], a white horse for Āditya, or a white cow, or a plough drawn by six oxen or twelve oxen, or two oxen, or one ox, or either [of these] at the Śunāsīrīya [offering]; a white horse for Sūrya, or a white cow; in the absence of that, it should be a white goat; it should be white. || 26 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the sixth book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
Thus ends the sixth book in the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. ||6||

He does not sit on a high seat or similar elevated place. He sleeps with his head toward the east. An old man (*pravayasam*) means one who is aged. To him whose *śamya* (mortar-post) is broken, he offers an oblation of clarified butter; he gives that very bull as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). A plough (*halas*) yoked with oxen—either two or twelve—is the fee. An *uṣṭāra* is a large ox. In its absence, a white ox; in the absence of a white ox, another white animal, such as a goat or a sheep. There is mutual substitution between the ox, the goat, and the sheep.

The term *vibhāva* will be explained in the section concerning inquiries regarding ritual transgressions (*vidhyaparādha*). The repetition (*abhyāsa*) is for the purpose of concluding the book. Thus ends the eighth chapter (*paṭala*) on the *āgrayaṇa* animal sacrifice and the *cāturmāsya* animal sacrifices within the sixth *praśna* on the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), in the *Prayogavaijayantī*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* composed by Mahādeva. Thus ends the sixth *praśna* of the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* commentary. This commentary on the *Prayogavaijayantī* composed by Mahādeva is completed. [Endorsed by] M.B.A., Na. Paṃ. Rāma Betāba... The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, together with the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.
Therein,
this first volume consists of the first two questions, namely the seventh and eighth.

Edited by Ve. Śā. Saṃ. Rā. Rā. Kāśīnātha Śāstrī Āgāśe.

Oṃ, obeisance to the True, the Existent, and Brahman. The Śrauta Sūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha,
together with the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.
Now begins the seventh book;
therein is the first chapter:
The Agniṣṭoma sacrifice fulfills all desires.
He may desire [them] simultaneously,
or in separate meals;
with that [procedure], he should sacrifice every spring.
There is no eating for him until the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices have been commenced;
that is the first of the Soma sacrifices.
Some authorities teach that the Atirātra is the first sacrifice.
On the day of the new moon, which is the day of sacrifice, he undergoes initiation;
on the day of the full moon, which is the day of sacrifice, is the day of the Soma-pressing.
This occurs either on the new moon or on the full moon.
If there is one initiation, two, three, four, or an unlimited number, then on a non-parvan day, he performs either the pressing-day rite or the initiation.

Having been chosen, each time he is chosen, he mutters: "Greatness you have spoken for me; glory you have spoken for me; splendor you have spoken for me; enjoyment you have spoken for me; the *stoma* you have spoken for me; everything you have spoken for me—may that protect me, may that enter me, through that may I enjoy.
He proceeds forward, saying: "May the god go to the god; may Soma go to Soma by the path of Truth, leaving behind all evil-doing."
Or he stands upon the path with the formula, "Thou art the path named Śruti, the channel for Soma; may I go to the Soma.
He addresses the ancestors three times with the formula, "The fathers are Bhūḥ.
For one who is about to be initiated, he offers twelve *saṃbhāra-yajus* oblations with the formula, "Agni with the *yajus*-verses."
Having mentally recited the Saptahotṛ formula and offered it along with the cup (graha), he performs the Dīkṣaṇīyā sacrifice:
a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu, or a caru oblation of clarified butter for Agni and Viṣṇu.
There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.
In all the Soma-related *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices (*paśubandhas*), he does not cut off a portion for the sacrificer;
he does not give the *anvāhārya* rice;
and he leaves a remnant of the *dhruvā* ladle.
The Dīkṣaṇīyā offering concludes with the Patnīsaṃyāja; having consumed the Ājyeḍā portion, they cease.
He maintains the Āhavanīya fire.
They construct the Prācīnavaṃśa shed.
Enclosing [the structure], they leave openings at the corners;
the fifth [opening] is toward the intermediate direction between the north and east. The doors are in the cardinal directions.

The optional ritual procedures have one door each: for one desiring heaven, a door to the east; for one desiring the world of the ancestors, a door to the south; for one desiring the world of men, a door to the west; and for one desiring offspring, a door to the north. One who desires, "May I prosper in both worlds," should have a door to the northeast. One who desires, "May I prosper in all directions," should have doors on all sides.
And they construct vestibule-like structures for the image in the various directions.
To the north of the *prāgvamśa* hall, within an enclosed space, the sacrificer has his hair and beard shaved.
He has the beard shaved first, then the armpits, and then the hair on the head.
"May the waters moisten you for life," with these words he moistens the hair at the back of the right side of the head.
"O herb, protect him," with these words he places an herb with its tip pointing upward between [the hair and the razor].
"O razor, do not harm him," with these words he applies the razor.
"O divine Śrī, may these grow," he says as he sows them. || 1 ||
He trims his nails, starting from the inner ones on the hands, then those of the feet; first those of the left hand, beginning with the little finger, and then those of the right.

When his eyes have been anointed, he purifies him with twenty-one bunches of *darbha* grass, divided into three groups of seven each, with the mantras beginning "May the Lord of Thought purify you. He wipes upwards above the navel twice and downwards once; the phrase "with the flawless strainer" is appended to every [mantra].
Having led him into the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, some authorities prescribe the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering at this point.
With the *dhruvā* spoon, he offers four initiation oblations (*dīkṣāhuti*) with the formulas: "To Dhruva, to Aśeṣa, to Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, svāhā!
With the *sruc* ladle, he offers the fifth with the formula, "O divine Waters...
Having filled the *sruc* with twelve portions of clarified butter—or having made an opening at its bowl—he pours it into the uppermost *sruva* spoon, or into the one next to the last.
He sews around the right front foot of the black antelope skin, including the flesh;
or he makes two [seams] diverging from each other and joined by flesh.

With the formula, "O Indra Śākvara, I resort to the Gāyatrī; I yoke it for you; O Indra Śākvara, I resort to the Triṣṭubh; I yoke it for you; O Indra Śākvara, I resort to the Jagatī; I yoke it for you; O Indra Śākvara, I resort to the Anuṣṭubh; I yoke it for you; O Indra Śākvara, I resort to the Paṅkti; I yoke it for you," he spreads the black antelope skin within the altar, with its neck toward the east and the hair upward.
When the sacrificer has ascended [the chariot], he fastens a net upon the head of the wife.
He consecrates her with an upper garment of unspun linen cloth.
A girdle made of *śara* reeds and *muñja* grass should be fashioned as a triple braid.

With the formula, "Thou art strength," he winds it three times clockwise around the waist of the sacrificer at the level of the navel—some say twice. Having made a loose knot to the north of the navel with the formula, "May Pūṣan tie the knot for thee," he draws it down to the south of the navel with the formula, "May it not come loose for thee. He should meditate upon whomsoever he hates.
With the formula, "I bind thee together," he girds the wife as in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
With the formula, "Thou art the womb of Indra," he hands over to the sacrificer a black antelope horn with three or five ridges, or he fastens it on him.
He arranges the net upon his wife's head as perfectly as possible. || 2 ||

The consecration staff (*dīkṣitadaṇḍa*) is made of *udumbara* wood, or from whatever tree bears fruit. It should be the size of a fist, measured by the mouth, or reaching down to the chin. With the formula, "O upright one, belonging to the trees, well-shining; bestow splendor upon the sacrificer," he hands it to the sacrificer and causes him to recite the *saṃbhārayajus* formulas while he offers oblations with these mantras.

While he is restrained from speech, the Adhvaryu announces him three times in a whisper and three times aloud: "This Brāhmaṇa, so-and-so, the son of such-a-one, the grandson of such-a-one, the great-grandson of such-a-one; the son of such-a woman, the granddaughter of such-a woman, the great-granddaughter of such-a woman, has been initiated.
He pronounces the name [with] "so-and-so," and "the son of such-a-one" by means of the father's name.
Whosoever is being initiated, one should announce him simply as "Brāhmaṇa."

"May the sacrifice, having gone to the gods, come back to me with the blessing of the sacrifice; may the sacrifice, having gone to the Gandharvas, come back to me with the blessing of the sacrifice; may the sacrifice, having gone to the ancestors, come back to me with the blessing of the sacrifice; may the sacrifice, having gone to the waters, the plants, and the trees, come back to me with the blessing of the sacrifice; may the sacrifice, having gone to the five peoples, come back to me with the blessing of the sacrifice. May prosperity increase through curd and ghee; may the sacrifice release the lord of the sacrifice from distress. Svāhā to the Lord of Beings!"—with these words he consecrates [the offering].

If he should sit elsewhere than on a black antelope skin during the regular course of the ritual from this point forward, [the Adhvaryu] issues the summons before the sun has risen above the treetops: "Make the fires radiant; O consecrated one, restrain your speech; O wife, restrain your speech. After sunrise and at sunset, he causes the milk for the fast-food (*vrata*) to be milked, leaving one teat of the calf untouched.
He cooks the vow-food (*vrata*) for the initiated sacrificer on the *gārhapatya* fire, and for the wife on the *dakṣiṇāgni*.
Having brought the vow-food across behind the *āhavanīya*, he hands it to the initiated sacrificer.
He consecrates the departing initiated sacrificer with the mantra: "Go from good to better."
Having been initiated, he cuts the sacrificial post (yūpa) as in the Nirūḍhapaśubandha sacrifice.
He does not offer the oblation for the post; instead, having murmured the verse intended for the offering, he proceeds forward.
Alternatively, taking clarified butter and the two kindling woods (araṇī), he churns fire near the post, offers the oblation for the post, and then cuts the post.
Or, when the Āhavanīya fire has been purchased, having offered the oblation for the sacrificial post (yūpāhuti), he cuts the post;
[this applies] to the Agniṣomīya, the Savanīya, and the Anūbandhyā [sacrifices].

The sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the wooden chip (*svaru*), the *āhavanīya* fire, and the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*) are common [to all]. When the period for the initiation (*dīkṣā*) has elapsed, one spreads a red bull-hide with its neck to the east and its hair upwards upon the site of the *uttaravedi* or over the *uparava* holes; having scattered King Soma upon its southern side and placed a water-pot to the north, and having enclosed it on all sides and made a door facing north, he causes the Soma-seller—either a member of the Kautsa clan or a Śūdra—to enter.
He gives the command, "O Soma-seller, purify the Soma! or "Purify the Soma; cast out what has entered it," or "Purify the Soma; what has entered, is cast out.
He removes whatever is other than the stalks (*aṃśu*).
The Adhvaryu must not sift the Soma; neither his servant, nor the sacrificer, nor the sacrificer’s kinsmen, nor anyone who witnesses the sifting may be present.

In the *iṣṭis* and *paśubandhas* beginning with the *prāyaṇīyā* and ending with the *avabhṛtha*, there is no taking up of the vow (*vratopāyana*), no keeping of the vigil (*jāgaraṇa*), no binding of the wife (*patnīsaṃnahanam*), and no eating of forest-food (*āraṇyāśanam*).
All these [rites] are performed in the subsequent [sacrifices].
In the *savanīya* animal sacrifice and in the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśas*), the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhānam*) does not take place.
7.2 Now begins the second chapter of the seventh book. He commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *prāyaṇīyā* offering.
Having added fuel to the fires, he brings the sacrificial wood (*idhma*) and the grass-bundle (*barhis*).
There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; he does not tie on an additional fuel-stick for the *anūyāja* offerings if there are no *anūyāja*s.

Having prepared the *veda* grass-bundle, strewn around the fires, washed his hands, and spread out a layer of *ulapa* grass, he arranges the vessels as required; he places a cooking-pot (*sthālī*) in the place of the potsherds.
At the time of the pouring out [of the grain], he pours out the *prāyaṇīya* oblation of boiled rice for Aditi and cooks it in milk.
If there are no after-offerings (anūyāja), he takes four portions of clarified butter for each;
he places the Prāyaṇīya offering with the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula;
and if there are no after-offerings, he puts on the entire fuel-wood and pours out the entire butter remaining in the Upabhṛt ladle.

He offers four portions of clarified butter: Pathyā Svasti in the east, Agni in the south, Soma in the west, and Savitṛ in the north; Aditi is in the middle. He places the vessel of oblation, the scrapings, and the stirring-spoon [in their respective places]. He makes the remnant for the *dhruvā* ladle, or he completes the entire ritual up to the *śaṃyu-formula*.
He does not cut off a portion for the sacrificer if [the sacrifice] ends with the *śaṃyu*-formula. At this point, some authorities prescribe the pouring out of the King [Soma].

Having taken four or five spoonfuls from the remnant of the *dhruva* vessel, and having tied a piece of gold with a *niṣṭarkya* knot using a blade of *darbha* grass while reciting "This is thy bright body," he places it into the clarified butter.
One should carefully avoid anything inauspicious in the performance of rites for the gods.

The cow intended for the purchase of Soma (*somakrayaṇī*) should be well-proportioned, possessed of auspicious marks, and accompanied by her calf—just as the animal for Agni-Soma is brown, ruddy, or red; or it may be dappled, full-bodied, or even red with yellowish-brown eyes, brown hair, and white appearance, having variegated tail-hair, variegated hooves, and being either one-year-old, two-year-old, or three-year-old; [he addresses it] with "Thou art swift" (*jūrasi*), and while looking at it, he offers this fourfold-drawn oblation (*caturgṛhīta*).
Having taken another fourfold-drawn portion, he draws out the gold from the clarified butter, saying, "Thou art light (*śukra*), thou art immortality (*amṛta*)."
He consecrates it with the mantra, "The oblation for the Viśvedevas.
He gazes at it with the mantra, "Thou art the oblation for the Viśvedevas.
With his hand holding gold, he worships the sun with the mantra, "I have mounted the eye of Sūrya. || 5 ||
One should make the hand not empty by holding gold, silver, and *kuśa* grass.
With the mantra "Thou art consciousness," he addresses the cow for the purchase of Soma.
With the mantra "May Mitra bind thee by the foot," he binds her by the right forefoot.
With the words, "May Pūṣan protect the paths," he leads [the cow] to where the Soma is—whether it be unbound and not held by the ear, or bound and held by the ear.
With the mantras beginning with "Thou art a Vasu," he steps out six paces following her with his right forefoot.
With the words, "May Bṛhaspati gladden thee for happiness," he takes hold of the seventh step.
Having placed gold upon it, he offers this fourfold-drawn portion with the mantra, "I sprinkle thee on the head of the earth.

Taking away the gold, he traces around the footprint with the wooden sword (sphya) using the mantra, "It has been traced around," as far as the clarified butter has spread. Having silently traced around it with the horn, he pours the footprint-clay into the vessel with the mantra, "In us be wealth.
Having washed his hands together with the gold at the place of the footprint, he gives the footprint-clay to the sacrificer with the mantra, "In thee be wealth."
"May all wealth come [to me]," says the sacrificer for the sake of the wife;
"May I not be separated from the increase of wealth," says the wife as she gazes at what is being given.
"O Goddess, look together with the goddess Urvaśī," he makes the wife gaze together with the Soma-purchasing cow.

Having poured out a vessel of water with the verse, "Unfold the earth," and having divided the footprint into three parts, he scatters one third upon the cool ashes of the Gārhapatya fire and one third in the Āhavanīya fire.
According to some, scattering in the Āhavanīya is prohibited.
He gives the third part to his wife, and she places it in her house.
Regarding the verse, "I have mounted the eye of the sun," some prescribe the worship of the Āditya [the Sun].
With the verse, "We have gone upon the path," he proceeds toward the King [Soma] in a wagon that is enclosed, covered with a roof, and from which the front plank has been removed.
Having stationed the wagon facing the north with its front toward the King, he consecrates it with the formula, "Thou art a companion," or "Thou art ours."
With the formula, "May your stalk be joined with my stalk," he pours out the stalks.

To the north of the King (Soma), having spread upon a skin a large, new linen garment— either double or quadruple— with its fringe toward the east and its border facing upward, he measures the King with the *aticchandas* verse, "Abhi tyam devam," using his hand together with gold,
measuring with each finger as it is extended, while pressing the thumb against all the fingers.
With that [formula] by which he measures the first [soma-plant], he does not measure the fifth with it, nor the tenth;
five times he measures with the *yajus* formula, and five times silently. With the words, "For the sake of offspring thee," he gathers together the remaining stalks.

Having gathered up the ends of the garment, he binds [the head] with a linen turban, saying, "For the out-breath (prāṇa) thee! He ties the knot, saying, "For the diffused breath (vyāna) thee! Having looked at it, saying, "Breathe after the offspring; let the offspring breathe after thee," he consecrates it with these mantras: "This is thy Gāyatra portion. || 6 ||

"O Lord Sūrya, we shall buy the Soma; we announce it to you. Do you, for all the gods, arrange the seasons and arrange the sacrificial fees according to the season and according to the deity. With this, he worships the Sun with his hand containing gold.
Having handed over the King (Soma) to the Soma-seller, he asks him: "O Soma-seller, is your Soma for sale?
"It is for sale," he replies.
He purchases [the Soma] for ten:
seven cows, gold, a garment, and a goat—these are the three;
or, according to some, there are ten cows and then these three.
Or rather, it is with four [cows] alone:
with this cow and these three.
This applies to one for whom the sacrificial fee consists of twenty-one cows.
In the sacrifice where thirty thousand is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*),
there are twenty-seven cows, gold, a garment, and a goat— these three; or, according to some, there are thirty cows and these same three items.
He purchases [Soma] for a hundred at the Vājapeya, for two at the Rājasūya, and for a thousand at the Aśvamedha.
Saying, "I purchase Soma from you," he purchases it.
Having said, "Soma, great, of many benefits, and beautiful," he assigns each one individually.

"I will buy it from you for a sixteenth part; I will buy it from you for a kuṣṭhā; I will buy it from you for a hoof; I will buy it from you for a foot"—having thus enumerated four feet of the cow, [the seller says] "I will buy it from you for a cow.
The Soma-seller replies with a counter-offer: "King Soma is worth more than that.
The Adhvaryu says: "He is indeed worth even more."
"I buy your semen with semen," [with these words] he buys gold; "Thou art the body of austerity," [with these words] he buys a goat; "I buy thee with a cow," [with these words] he buys a cow.
"I buy it from you for a bull," [saying this] he takes a bull; "for a young bull with testicles," according to some.
"I buy it from you for an ox," [saying this] he takes an ox. "I buy it for a pair of cattle," [saying this] he takes a pair of cattle.
"I buy from you a garment," [he says] regarding the garment.
He prepares it with ten [cows]; some authorities prescribe more than ten for the purchase of Soma.
He purchases with fifteen [cows], he purchases with seventeen, he purchases with twenty-four, he purchases with an unlimited number; finally he says, "I purchase.
Having completed it, he takes back the gold with the verse, "O well-protecting one, may the bright ones be with us."
With the words, "Thou art our kinship," he gives a white tuft of wool to the sacrificer.
At the time of spreading [the filter], he makes it the center of the *daśāpavitra*.
There are two *daśāpavitra* filters made of white sheep's wool; one of them is without fringes.

Having moistened a black tuft of wool with water and tied it around the necks of the biting snakes, saying, "I tie this upon the necks of the biting snakes," he then strikes the forehead of the Soma-seller with it, saying, "O Soma-seller, [I strike] thee with darkness. With the formula, "Thou art self-born, thou art self-existent; born for this rite, I take thee by the *ṛta*; protect us by the *ṛta*," he takes the King (Soma) from the Soma-seller.
If the seller should be distressed, he should simply carry him away.
With the words, "Enter the right thigh of Indra," he places the King (Soma) upon the thigh of the sacrificer.
He holds it as if grasping it firmly.

The sacrificer asks, "O Adhvaryu, have you been able? The Adhvaryu replies, "I was able. The sacrificer asks, "How did you manage? [The Adhvaryu recites: "We have remembered Viṣṇu, the Stoma, and the Maruts; Bṛhaspati, the meters, and the Yajus-formulas have risen up. The mountains have opened wide; I have crossed over the waters that were easy to cross. Thus says the Adhvaryu.
With the verse "svānabhrāja," he points toward the Soma-purchasing cows.
With the formula "May Rudra turn you back," having turned the Soma-purchasing cow back and having redeemed her with another cow, he releases her among the sacrificer's own cattle.
With a spotted leather thong, he causes the Soma-seller to lose his eye.
