Some strike them with clods of earth, others strike them with clubs. || 8 ||
Thus ends the second paṭala in the seventh praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the third paṭala in the seventh praśna.

With the formula, "Thou art the seat of Aditi," he spreads a black antelope skin in the interior of the cart with its neck toward the east and the hair upward. He places the King (Soma), who has been handed over, upon it with the formula, "Sit on the seat of Aditi."
He consecrates the nearby [fire] with the mantra, "He has propped up the sky.
According to some, he places it down.
He wraps it around with a cloth, saying, "In the forests he has stretched out the atmosphere."
With the verse, "That light, Jātavedas," he covers [the cart] with a black antelope skin, its neck pointing upward and the hair on the outside; or with the verse, "The traverser, visible to all.
With the formula, "Come hither, you two oxen, bearers of the yoke," he yokes the two oxen.
With the formula, "Thou art the yoke," he touches the two yoke-poles.
With the formula, "Thou art Varuṇa's," he lifts up the cart.
Having stationed it with the pole facing east, he props it up with the formula, "May Varuṇa prop thee.
He yokes the right ox that has no companion.
With the formula, "Thou art Varuṇa's," he draws the cord around.
With the formula, "Thou art Varuṇa's prop," he drives in the peg.
With the formula, "Varuṇa's noose is cast off," he casts off the noose of the cord.
And he fastens a bull;
in the same way, he yokes the subsequent ox.
Holding two tawny branches—either branches of the *palāśa* or branches of the *śamī*—the *subrahmaṇya* priest approaches between them.
Having taken hold of the cart, he issues the command: "Recite for King Soma as he is being carried away after purchase; O Brahman, restrain your speech; O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā!
When the verse has been recited three times, they move forward with the words, "O Lord of the Earth," and having gone eastward, they turn to the right.
With the verse, "We have indeed reached the path," the sacrificer and the Adhvaryu pass by the north of the King [Soma] as before.
They kindle the fires; he places the largest [fire-stick] in the Āhavanīya.
The animal for Agni and Soma is prepared: it has all its limbs intact, is well-proportioned, and—just as in the Nirūḍhapaśubandha—is reddish-brown, hornless, bearded, large, and fat. 9.
"Whether it be black-and-white or red-and-white, the sacrificer, having grasped it by the ear, awaits the king.
A general rule that is unclear may be restricted by a specific one; however, such a restriction is not desired for a rule that is already clear.

Thus, the Adhvaryu priests lift up the Audumbara throne-seat, which has a head-rest of one cubit, a back-strap reaching to the waist, and legs reaching to the navel, and which is bound with girdles of Muñja grass.

Having drawn the cart forward along the front of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall with the formula, "Thou art Varuṇa's," and having stationed it with its pole facing north, he props it up with the formula, "May Varuṇa support thee. He then unyokes the southern ox.
With the formula, "Thou art Varuṇa's," he draws the yoke-thong around.
With the formula, "Thou art Varuṇa's unloosening of the pillar," he pulls out the pin.
With the formula, "Varuṇa's bond is loosened," he unties the knot of the yoke-thong.

Saying, "The noose of Varuṇa is released," he unfastens the halter; in this same manner, he unyokes the northern ox. Without unyoking the northern ox, he proceeds with the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the *ātithyā* offering.
Or, having released both [the fires],
he adds fuel to the fires and brings the sacrificial wood and grass;
there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.
The two *vidhṛti*-strainers are made of sugarcane.
He binds the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made of *kārṣmarya* wood and the fuel (*idhma*) together; the *prastara* bundle is made of *aśvavāla* grass and placed upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
At the time of the pouring of the oblation, he pours out the offering for Viṣṇu on nine potsherds with the hand of his wife.

Or from the hand of his wife; or while she holds on to him with a ladle. With these five [formulas] beginning with "Thou art the guest-offering for Agni," he joins the *sāvitra* formula and the word *juṣṭam* to each of the three [verses].

One should recognize Viṣṇu alone in the subsequent Vedic citations. Having performed that which was prior to the removal [of the ox], he unyokes the northern ox according to that same ritual procedure, provided it has not already been unyoked from the front.
With the formula, "Thou art belonging to Varuṇa," he takes away the garment of the King (Soma).
"Thou art Varuṇa, whose vows are firm," [he says] regarding the King (Soma). || 10 ||
With the verse, "O tree with unsevered leaves, descend for the sake of offspring, bringing food and prosperity; be soft, for they are soft," he brings it down.
At this point, some prescribe the lifting up of the *āsandī* seat.
With the verse, "Wide is the intermediate space," he proceeds.
With the verse addressed to Soma, "Those which are thy abodes," he causes the King [Soma] to enter through the eastern door of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall.

With the words, "Go through the wide atmosphere," he carries him across behind the *āhavanīya* fire. With the formula, "Thou art the seat of Varuṇa’s truth," he establishes the throne-seat to the south of the *āhavanīya*.
With the formula, "Thou art the seat of Aditi," he spreads upon it a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and the hairy side upward.
He places the offered King Soma upon it with the formula, "Sit upon the seat of Aditi," or alternatively, "Sit upon the seat of Varuna’s Law."
With the words, "He has stretched the atmosphere across the worlds," he encloses it with a cloth.
He addresses the King Soma with the mantra, "Thou art Varuṇa," or with "For Varuṇa, thee."

"Thus, worship Varuṇa, the lofty one; pay homage to the wise guardian of immortality. May he grant us a triple-layered shelter; may Heaven and Earth protect us in their lap. With this verse addressed to Varuṇa, she attends upon the king.
Wherever she may sit, let her sit with this very verse.
He issues the command: "Do not pass between Agni and the king."
He undertakes the ritual acts beginning with the pouring out [of the grain].
He places nine potsherds on the Gārhapatya fire. He takes portions of clarified butter by four ladlings each.

He presents the guest-offering (ātithya) with the Caturhotṛ formula. Having laid down the Veda-grass-bundle, he issues the call for the Sāmidhenī verses. He places the entire fuel-stick (idhma) on the fire and pours the entire butter from the Upabhṛt ladle into the Juhū.
Having performed the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, he sacrifices to Viṣṇu with the oblation. He makes the remnant of the *dhruvā* vessel.
The *ātithyā* ceremony concludes with the *iḍā*.
With the formula, "I take you for Dhruva, the lord of the remainder," he scoops the *tānūnaptra* into a bronze vessel (*kaṃsa*) or a wooden cup (*camasa*), either in four portions or five portions.
The remaining option is for the case of four portions.
Then all the officiating priests touch it together with the formula, "Thou art unassailable."
Having smelled it three times with the formula, "I offer you in Prajāpati, in the mind," he pours it out within the altar;
according to some, this is prohibited, while according to others, he pours it out in a place where there is no passage.
"Do the waters rejoice in the fires? he asks.
"The divine waters rejoice, immortal, increasing the cosmic order (ṛta)," the Āgnīdhra replies.
"Come hither with them," he issues the command.
They wash their hands with the *madantī* waters; the Brahman priest unties the King Soma.
Saying "Ray, ray," they all cause him to swell with their hands containing gold.
Having touched water after the [Soma] has been re-bound, they conceal it on the *prastara* grass, saying "Desired riches," while keeping their left hands downward and their right hands turned upward.
Thus ends the third paṭala in the seventh praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the fourth paṭala in the seventh praśna:
Having performed the *pravargya* rite, he performs the *upasad*; or, having performed the *upasad*, he performs the *pravargya*.
That which is the sacrificial grass for the *ātithyā* is also that of the *upasad*s and the *agnīṣomīya*; it serves as both the *prastara* and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
In the *upasad*s, the *prastara* and the sacrificial grass have already been spread, and the enclosing sticks remain lying there.
We shall now explain the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the *upasad*s.
In that [offering], clarified butter is the oblation;
Agni, Soma, and Viṣṇu are the deities;
the ritual procedure is explained by [the rules for] the Upāṃśuyāja.
Having added fuel to the fires, he binds together the sacrificial fuel (idhma) consisting of sixteen pieces of wood.

Having prepared the Veda-grass mat and strewn grass around the fires, having washed his hands and spread out a layer of *ulapa* grass, he sets out the vessels for the clarified butter as required: the wooden sword (*sphya*), the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), the offering-ladles (*sruc*), the pot for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), and whatever else is needed.

Having prepared the two strainers (*pavitra*), he issues the command: "O sacrificer, restrain your speech. While remaining silent, he touches the vessels; once they have been sprinkled with water, he releases his speech.
Taking the wooden sword (sphya), he removes the *stambayajus* from the hair of the strewn altar; having performed the second tracing of the altar, he proceeds with the formal command (*saṃpraīṣa*).
He issues the command for everything other than the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and the binding of the wife.
Having performed that which precedes the taking of the clarified butter (*ājya*), he takes [the butter] from the *dhruvā* ladle itself.

Having consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* waters, having addressed the *brahmán*, and having sprinkled the fuel and the altar, he pours out the remainder of the *prokṣaṇī* water, inserts the two strainers (*pavitra*), consecrates the fire, and places the first *āghāra*-fuel stick upon it. He sets down the *dhruvā* ladle and the *sruva* spoon, modifying the mantra to "This one has sat down. He consecrates the clarified butter with the mantra: "Thou art Viṣṇu; thou art the abode of Viṣṇu; thou art that of Prajāpati. Having laid down the *veda* grass-bundle, he issues the call for the *sāmidhenī* verses. Having divided the fuel into nine parts, he places the entire fuel upon the fire.

Having offered the *upavāja* oblation to the eight deities and having poured the *sruva-āghāra* libation, he issues the direction: "O Āgnīdh, cleanse the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the fire three times each. Once they have been cleansed, he chooses the *pravara*, saying "Sit down, O Hotṛ," as in the Mahāpitṛyajña.
He takes eight portions for the *dhruvā* into the *juhū* ladle and four into the *upabhṛt*.
He sets down the two ladles, and the *hotṛ* causes them to be taken up.
When it is said, "O Adhvaryu, take up the ladle full of ghee," he takes up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt*, crosses over once, and performs the sacrifice to the three deities.

He gives the call for the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*) for the first [offering] from the north, and for the other two from the south. With half of the clarified butter that is in the *juhū* ladle he sacrifices to Agni, and with the other half to Soma. Having poured the butter that is in the *upabhṛt* ladle into the *juhū*, he sacrifices with that to Viṣṇu.
Having stepped back, he offers the *upasat* oblation with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), saying: "O Agni, that body of yours which is the *ayāśayā*."

They wash their hands with the *madantī* waters; the Brahman priest causes the King [Soma] to relax, they cause him to swell, and they conceal him as previously described—with the right hands turned upward in the forenoon and the left hands turned upward in the afternoon.

Having issued the command, "O Āgnīdhra, announce the wives of the gods; O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā," the Āgnīdhra sits down to the west of the Gārhapatya fire and announces the wives of the gods, saying, "Speech is the wife of Vāyu," or "The cow is Indra’s."

The Subrahmaṇya priest invokes the Subrahmaṇyā formula. These rites are performed following each Upasad. In this manner, for three nights, he proceeds with the Pravargya and Upasad rites in the evening and the morning.
In the early forenoon, he offers with the two [formulas] belonging to the forenoon; in the afternoon, with the two belonging to the afternoon.

On the first day, at evening and morning, he offers the *sruva*-ladle oblations with the formula: "O Agni, that body of yours which dwells in the earth"; on the second day, with the formula: "O Agni, that body of yours which dwells in the mid-region."
With the verse, "O Agni, those flames of thine that lie within," [he offers] on the third day.
If they should fight in front, he should place iron in the first [ladle] and offer;
silver and gold in the middle [ladle].
[The ritual] is green in the *uttamā* [night].
According to some, if they should fight a battle, this is the procedure not connected with a sacrifice. 13.
Having performed the two midday *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, he strides three steps eastward in front of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall and drives in a peg; that is in the western half of the altar.
With the mantra, "I measure thee, the milk-rich, the well-milking cow of the gods, who does not fail; may Indra drink the Soma;
may there be peace for us," he strides thirty-six steps eastward and drives in a peg; that is in the eastern half.

From the western peg, having stepped fifteen paces to the south and fifteen to the north, he drives in two pegs; these are the two hips. From the eastern peg, having stepped twelve paces to the south and twelve to the north, he drives in two pegs; these are the two shoulders. Having adjusted them by a diagonal measurement, he stretches a cord around them from left to right. He then stretches the *pṛṣṭhyā* line along it.
He performs that which is other than the *saṃnāma* in the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices:
with the wooden sword (*sphya*), the *vighana*, the rib-bone (*parśu*), and the axe (*paraśu*).
Having performed that which precedes the second tracing of the altar, he constructs the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) measuring ten steps according to the ritual procedure for the *uttaravedi*.
According to some teachers, it should be shorter in front;
the northern shoulder of the altar is further north, and the *cātvāla* pit is twelve steps behind it, or it may be of unlimited size, with the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) located behind it.
In the space between them is the path for movement around the altar (vedi).
According to some, it extends eastward from the Āgnīdhra shed and westward from the Cātvāla pit.
He causes it to be covered with branches of the Udumbara tree.
On the following day. || 14 ||
Having performed the two excellent morning *pravargya* and *upasad* rites and having given the half-vow (*ardhavratam*), he then performs the two afternoon *pravargya* and *upasad* rites.
If he is the first [to perform them], he dismisses the *pravargya* and enters the *upasad*.

Having given the half-vow, he leads forward the fire according to the procedure for the fire, places a tuft of wool in the fire-place, establishes the fire, and drives away the calves for the evening milking intended for the *āmikṣā* offering to Mitra and Varuṇa.
He gives the calf to the one who milks the *gharma* for Indra and Dadhigharma;
according to some, all [the verses] belong to Indra.
He performs the subsequent tracing of the altar with a verse addressed to Agni.
He does not step upon [the wood] that has not been taken up or sprinkled until the spreading [of the altar].

The wood intended for the Soma-pressing and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the great altar (*māhāvedī*) have been prepared. He silently sprinkles the wood, the altar, and the sacrificial grass three times each with water.
He silently spreads the sacrificial grass over the altar in the same manner as at the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
"Those who kindle Agni and spread the sacrificial grass in succession—those for whom Indra is a youthful friend"—some recite this as the *staraṇī* verses. (15)
Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the seventh praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the fifth paṭala in the seventh praśna.

When the two carts with circular wheels, which have been previously employed, are prepared, they untie the old knots of those two, wash them, and make them new. Having made them provided with covers and fitted with yokes, and having stationed them in front of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, he offers an oblation on the northern altar (*auttaravedika*) with the verse, "They yoke the mind."

With the words "O you who are heard by the gods," using the third part of the word *devaśrutau*, he anoints three times with his right hand the southern wheel-axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, from front to back, with the palm turned upward; likewise for the northern one.
According to some, he anoints all [the axles];
according to others, [he anoints them] with clarified butter as well.
He issues the command: "Recite for the two *havirdhāna* carts as they are being moved forward," or "Recite for them as they are being moved forward.
When the verse has been recited three times, they move the carts forward while lifting them up with the words, "Go forward, O ye two, toward the east.
If the axle should creak, he consecrates it with the mantra: "O divine one, fair-voiced, enter the dwellings."

Where he steps onto the altar, having placed gold at the edge of the altar on the northern track of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, he offers with the mantra, "This [is] Viṣṇu... The Pratiprasthātṛ performs the same for the northern cart with the mantra, "Abounding in food, abounding in cows... The Adhvaryu performs the rites for the southern *havirdhāna*, and the Pratiprasthātṛ for the northern one.

"Drive away the fear of enemies; turn the wheels; go to the house of Soma, to the assembly of Indra"—with these words, at the western half of the altar, at one-third of its length from the back, the Hotṛ mentally drives away the fear of enemies with his foot, whether he be the Adhvaryu, the Sacrificer, or the Brahman.
Having stepped three steps westward from behind the Uttaravedi, they both place the two Havirdhāna carts on either side of the Pṛṣṭhyā line so that their naves are aligned, saying, "Rest here.
They arrange the two Havirdhānas according to the requirements, leaving an interval between them.
"Thou art Vaiṣṇava; may Viṣṇu support thee!"—with these words they prop up [the two Havirdhāna carts].
They become elevated in front.

With the verse containing the word "blessing," "Whether from heaven, O Viṣṇu, or from earth," the Gāyatrī-singer strikes down the southern corner-joint of the southern Havirdhāna cart from behind. With the verse, "Of Viṣṇu indeed... the Pratiprasthātṛ strikes down the northern corner-joint of the northern [Havirdhāna cart] from behind.
With the formula, "Thou art the fixed point of Viṣṇu," they two fasten [the yoke-pins] there;
with the formula, "Thou art the fixed point of Viṣṇu," they two make knots, which become well-known.
Having drawn the pins upward, they wrap them around from above so that it is well-fastened.
The boundary-posts are set up so that there is a passage in front of the *khara* mound.
Having driven two posts in front of the two *havirdhāna* sheds and having placed a bamboo beam upon them with its tip pointing northward, he lays down the bamboo beams running eastward.
With the formula, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s back," he places the middle roof-covering on top. With the formula, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s forehead," he encloses the front with a forehead-strap.
This forehead-strap is made of *tejana* grass, consisting of a stalk of reed (*eṣīkā*) pointing eastward and slender in the middle; he fastens it to the bamboo beam.
With the formula, "O Viṣṇu, you are the two corners of the nose," he fastens the two ends of the forehead-strap. They lay down mats and reed-bundles in the intervals between the roof-coverings;
these they call the *antarvartas*.
"O lover of songs, let our songs encompass you"—with these words, they enclose [the shed] on both sides.
They make the eastern and the western doors.
The Adhvaryu fastens the southern door-panel; the Pratiprasthātṛ fastens the northern one.
With the formula, "Thou art the needle of Viṣṇu," they sew;
with the formula, "Thou art the fixed point of Viṣṇu," they make two knots, which are well-known;
with the formula, "Thou belongest to Viṣṇu, for Viṣṇu thee," they touch the joined part.

"Viṣṇu is praised for that heroic deed, like a fearsome beast, roaming and dwelling in the mountains; in whose three wide strides all the worlds abide. [This mantra is recited] by one who steps forward from the measured *havirdhāna* shed;
or, having stepped out, he recites it;
or, according to some, he recites it after taking three steps toward the east. (17)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the seventh book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Now begins the sixth chapter in the seventh book:

In front of the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, there are four *uparava* holes in the intermediate directions; they are a span wide at the mouth, separated by a span, one cubit deep, perforated at the bottom, and separated from one another at the top.
The taking up of the mallet and the tracing around have been explained in the context of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

Having traced around the southern [corner] of the two eastern [stakes], he traces around the northern [corner] of the two western [stakes]; then the southern [corner] of the two western [stakes] and the northern [corner] of the two eastern [stakes].
In this manner, their ritual actions are performed in successive order.
"Destroyers of demons, destroyers of secret spells, belonging to Viṣṇu, I dig," with these words he digs.
"Destroyers of demons, destroyers of secret spells, belonging to Viṣṇu, I extract," with these words he extracts.
"Thou art great," with these words he strikes the spade.
With the words, "Thou art Virāj," he lowers his arm or both arms.
With the words, "Here I dig out that hidden worm," he scatters the dust. With the words, "Here I make him lower," he presses it down into the cavity of the *uparava*.
With the words, "The spell is repelled," he takes [the earth].
With the words, "The malicious one is struck down," he pours it out in that place where he intends to prepare the *khara* mound.
With the words, "By the Gāyatrī metre the spell is struck down," he presses down with the wooden mace into the hole of the *uparava*.
In the same way for the others.
With each successive mantra he brings down the arm, and with each successive meter he secures it.
The meters as they are traditionally recited are the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, and the Anuṣṭubh.

"Thou art a sovereign ruler (*virāj*)," with these words the sacrificer touches the southern one of the two front [stones]; "Thou art a universal ruler (*samrāj*)," with these words the Adhvaryu touches the northern one of the two rear [stones].

They both touch them together from below, saying: "Touch these for long life and splendor! Thou art the treasure-store of the gods; drive away hatred, O Yavanas! Mayest thou ward off all those hostilities which we have committed. This which belongs to the gods is deposited here; now shine forth toward the four quarters, making our other rivals low!
The Adhvaryu asks, "What is here? The sacrificer replies, "Auspiciousness. The Adhvaryu says, "May that be ours in common."

The sacrificer touches the southern one of the two rear [stones] with the formula, "Thou art self-ruling" (svarāḍ asi); the Adhvaryu touches the northern one of the two front [stones] with the formula, "Thou art all-ruling" (viśvārāḍ asi). They touch them together as before.
"What is here? the sacrificer asks; "Blessing" (bhadram), the Adhvaryu replies; "May that be mine" (tan me), the sacrificer says.

"O slayers of demons, O destroyers of secret spells, I sprinkle you, who belong to Viṣṇu," [with these words] he sprinkles the *uparava* holes three times with water containing barley. "O slayers of demons, O destroyers of secret spells, I pour down [the water], who belong to Viṣṇu"—with this he pours down the water containing barley.
"Thou art barley," [with this] he throws a grain of barley [into each hole].

With the formula, "I strew the slayers of Rakṣases, the slayers of Valagas, belonging to Viṣṇu," he strews the sacrificial grass (barhis) facing eastward. With the formula, "I offer oblations over the slayers of Rakṣases, the slayers of Valagas, belonging to Viṣṇu," he makes an offering with the dipping-spoon (sruva), having placed a piece of gold in between.

With the formula, "I sprinkle the two slayers of Rakṣases, the slayers of Valagas, belonging to Viṣṇu," he sprinkles the two pressing-boards (adhiṣavaṇaphalaka). These boards are made of Udumbara, Kārṣmarya, or Palāśa wood; they are planed, joined at the front, and have their edges smoothed together at the back. They are either joined or unjoined at the back, and are separated by two, three, or four finger-breadths at the rear.

With the formula, "I place the two Rakṣas-slayers, the Valaga-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu," he covers the *uparava* holes with the two pressing-boards—one with two on the south side and two on the north side. With the formula, "I heap around the two Rakṣas-slayers, the Valaga-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu," he heaps earth around the *uparava* holes. With the formula, "I strew around the two Rakṣas-slayers, the Valaga-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu," he strews around with *darbha* grass.
He consecrates [the hide] with the mantra: "The two slayers of Rakṣas, the destroyers of Valagas, belonging to Viṣṇu.
He sprinkles the pressing-skin with the formula: "I sprinkle you, the slayer of Rakṣas, the destroyer of Valagas, belonging to Viṣṇu.
It is the red skin of an ox, with the hair on the upper side, provided with a spout so that it is suitable for the pressing.
Saying, "I spread what destroys the Rakṣases, what destroys the Valagas, the Vaiṣṇava," he spreads [the skin] over the two pressing-boards.
Upon it, he places four pressing-stones with their upper surfaces upward, arranged so as not to strike one another; the fifth is placed in the middle, being the broadest.
He addresses each one individually with the formula, "Thou art great."

"Destroying the Rākṣasas, destroying the secret spells, I sprinkle you, who belong to Viṣṇu"—with these words, having turned the pressing-stones so that they face each other, he sprinkles them upon the lower stone.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the seventh book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the seventh chapter in the seventh book.
He erects the Āgnīdhrīya shed to the north, half within the altar and half outside the altar. They construct a measured hall with its ridge-pole facing east, with the ritual approach from the south.

From the front edge to the rear limit of the *vedī*, at a distance of three steps or an indefinite measure toward the north, the *sadas* is constructed with its beam facing north. It is situated further south, as far as one deems sufficient for the sacrificial fires (*dhiṣṇiyas*), the officiating priests, and those who move forward.
To the south of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, at the midpoint of the *sadas*, is the pit for the *audumbarī* post.
The taking up of the wooden mallet (*abhri*) and the tracing of the outline have been explained in the section on the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
With the words, "For the day," he sprinkles [the post] from the top downwards.
The pouring out of water, the scattering of barley, and the spreading of sacrificial grass (barhis) around the sacrificial post have been explained.

With the mantra, "Rise up, O Lord of the Forest, in harmony with the divine sacrificial grass," he raises the post—whose top-ring is turned toward the east—along with the Udgātṛ priest; or alternatively, with the mantra, "Support the sky."
With the formula, "May Dyutāna Māruta set thee up," he places [the post] into the pit.
The procedures for filling around it, protecting it, and sprinkling water around it have been explained in the section on the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Having placed gold in its ear or at the forked branch, he makes an oblation with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) while reciting: "O Heaven and Earth, fill yourselves with clarified butter; svāhā!"
He pours [the water] down from the very root.
The tallest posts are measured to the height of the sacrificer; they are measured so that they stand well.
The surrounding ones are measured to the height of the navel; he measures the Udumbara post so that it reaches the fire.
One desiring rain should have the sacrificial hall (sadas) built low; one not desiring rain should have it built high. Some authorities record the opposite.
Nine roof-coverings are prepared.
Having laid down the northward-pointing rafters, he lays down the eastward-pointing rafters.
With the formula "Thou art Aindra's," he places three middle roof-panels facing northward;
with "Thou art Indra’s seat," three southern ones; and with "Thou art the shelter of all people," three northern ones.
He arranges the northern panels so that they face south toward the Audumbara post.

"One should measure nine coverings for one desiring splendor"—thus the optional coverings have been explained in the Brāhmaṇa; regarding these, one may act according to his desire. They place mats of reeds (*kaṭān*) and *tejanī* grasses between the coverings; these they call the "inner partitions" (*antarvartāḥ*). Two men enclose [the shed] on both sides with the verse, "O lover of songs, the songs surround thee," and they make two doors, a front one and a back one. The Adhvaryu sews up the southern door-panel, and the Pratiprasthātṛ the northern one, with the formula, "Thou art Indra’s seam. With the formula, "Thou art Indra’s fastener," they make knots; these two remain well-known.
They touch the *saṃmita* [post] with the formula, "Thou art Aindra; for Indra thee!
[and likewise] the *prāgvaṃśa*, the *sadas*, and the two *havirdhāna* sheds. The *sāṃkāśina* [formula] is the same [for all].

As long as the *soma* sacrifice has not been concluded, the *adhvaryu* should not enter the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door and exit by the western one; if he should so exit, he should mutter, "This Viṣṇu strode forth."
One should not enter the assembly hall (*sadas*) by the western door and exit by the eastern one; if he should so exit, he must recite the formula: "Rising with vigor.
Regarding this, some authorities prescribe the ritual of the *uparava* holes.
Having brought earth from the *cātvāla* pit, he scatters it upon the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths, making them either square or circular.

With the formula "Thou art all-pervading," he places [the fire] at the Āgnīdhrīya in the Āgnīdhra shed so that there is a path of passage to the north of the inner altar. He places the other fires within the Sadas.
With the formula "Thou art the bearer," he places the Hotrīya fire on the Pṛṣṭhyā line at a distance of one step behind the opening of the Sadas.
With the formula "Thou art auspicious" (*śvātra*), he places the post for the Maitrāvaruṇa to the south of the *hotrīya* shed;
to the north of the *hotrīya*, he places the others oriented toward the north.

With "Thou art Tutha," [he places the post] for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; with "Thou art Uśij," for the Potṛ; with "Thou art Andhāri," for the Neṣṭṛ; and with "Thou art Avasyu," for the Acchāvāka, at a distance closer [to the shed].

With the formula, "Thou art pure," he prepares the *mārjālīya* mound outside the *sadas*, in the southern half of the altar, level with the *āgnīdhrīya*, so that there is a passage to the south within the altar. He appends the verse "The fierce face... everywhere.
Here, some prescribe the strewing of the altar.
He does not spread grass over the *uttaravedi*, the *khara*, the *uparavas*, and the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths. || 21 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the seventh book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Now begins the eighth chapter in the seventh book:
He commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma.
The ritual procedure for this [animal sacrifice] has been explained by that of the Nirūḍhapaśubandha.
The Ṣaḍḍhotṛ offering and the animal-offering (paśviṣṭi) do not exist as constituent parts here.
Having added fuel to the fires, he binds the enclosing-sticks of the Ātithyeṣṭi together with the fuel-bundle.
Having strewn grass around the fires, washed his hands, and spread out a layer of *ulapa* grass, he arranges the vessels used for the animal sacrifice according to their purpose.
Having performed those rites prior to the taking of the clarified butter (*ājya*) and having returned, he takes the portions of clarified butter for the animal sacrifice over the *gārhapatya* fire.
With the verse "Thus, O Aditya, do thou praise," the *brahman* priest places the King Soma upon his lap.

They take up the pressing-stones, the Vāyavya cups, the *droṇakalaśa* vessel, the *camasa* ladles, the sacrificial grass for the guest-offering (*ātithyā*), the fuel-wood, the clarified butter, and they lead forward the animal victim for Agni and Soma.
They lead the wife forward; they cause the carts to move along.
"Let the wife of the Brahman proceed," says the Neṣṭṛ as he leads the wife out.
Then, being led forward while saying "I am following," she mutters:
"May we have good offspring through you. Having sat down to the west of the *śālāmukhīya* fire, she mutters the mantras belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
They assign the *śālāmukhīya* for the duties of the *gārhapatya*; in it, the *gārhapatya* rites are performed.
"Call those who share the same vows," he commands.
The members of the sacrificer's household call him.
The sacrificer takes hold of the Adhvaryu from behind; the wife takes hold of the sacrificer; and the members of the sacrificer's household take hold of the wife.

Having covered them with an unwashed cloth and having taken four spoonfuls of clarified butter into the *pracaraṇī* ladle, he ties a piece of gold to the fringe of that cloth intended for covering, places it into the clarified butter, and having fastened the end of the cloth to the handle of the ladle, he offers the two *vaisarjana* oblations on the *śālāmukhīya* fire. He offers the first oblation with the verse, "O Soma, you [protect us] from those who harm our bodies," and the second with, "May the swift one, enjoying the clarified butter, partake of it, svāhā!
He then prepares the remainder of the clarified butter.

He kindles the fires for the carrying forward at the Śālāmukhīya fire; he prepares the sand for the supporting-wood (upayamanī); he lifts up the fuel (idhma); he takes hold of the supporting-wood; and while it is being held, he takes his seat upon the supporting-wood.
He issues the command: "Recite for Agni and Soma as they are being led forward," or "Recite for the two as they are being led forward.
When the verse has been recited three times, they proceed toward the east with Agni first or with Soma first, saying, "This Agni is ours.
They lead them along according to the purpose.
The ministers follow after;
they lead forward the victim for Agni and Soma.
Having established this fire on the Āgnīdhrīya altar, he offers an oblation in the Āgnīdhra shed with the verse containing the word "lead," beginning with "Agni, lead us."
He performs the remaining rites with clarified butter.
They set down the pressing-stones, the Vāyavya vessels, the *droṇakalaśa*, and the cups;
they carry away the other items.
Having gone around the Āgnīdhrīya hearth on the north, he offers an oblation on the Uttaravedi with the formula, "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely.
The attendants return by the same way they came.
With the verse addressed to Soma, "Soma goes forth, the knower of the way," the Brahman causes the King [Soma] to enter the Havirdhāna shed by the western door.
[The Adhvaryu] has already gone [to the Sadas] by the eastern door.

[The sacrificer] says, "I follow the wide mid-region. Having entered by the eastern door, the Adhvaryu spreads a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and its hairy side upward in the interior of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, saying, "Thou art the seat of Aditi.
He places the offered King Soma upon it, saying, "Sit on the seat of Aditi."

Having consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* waters with a mantra, having addressed the *brahmán*, and having sprinkled the fuel and the altar, he pours out the remainder of the *prokṣaṇī* water. Having cast back the two strainers (*pavitra*), he spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) behind the northern altar with the mantra used at the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Once the clarified butter has been placed, he proceeds with the ritual of preparing the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). He dedicates the animal for Agni and Soma; its form has already been explained.

Having performed the *pravara* (the choosing of priests) according to the prescribed procedure, he chooses the Soma-priests (*saumika-ṛtvij*) by means of the *āśrāvaṇa*, the *ṛtupraiṣa*, and so forth.
He chooses the *hotṛ* with the formula: "Indra from the office of the *hotṛ*; may he be in harmony with Heaven and Earth.
Having released the *sphya* from the grass-blade, he chooses the subsequent priests.
From Agni [he takes] the Āgnīdhra from the office of the Āgnīdhra;
from the Aśvins [he takes] the two Adhvaryus, himself as an Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ from the office of the Adhvaryu;

from Mitra and Varuṇa [he takes] the two Praśāstṛs, the Maitrāvaruṇa from the office of the Praśāstṛ; from Indra [he takes] the Brahman, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin from the office of the Brahman; from the Maruts [he takes] the Potṛ, the Potṛ from the office of the Potṛ; from the Gnas [he takes] the Neṣṭṛ, the Neṣṭṛ from the office of the Neṣṭṛ.

"Agni is the leader of the divine clans; this sacrificer, pressing the Soma, is [the leader] of men. For these two, the Gārhapatya fire has shone forth as an unswerving [bond]. Go ye both! Let not Vāyu seize you! Being united, yet not mingling your bodies"—with these [words], he addresses the sacrificer.
"May I be beloved of speech"—with these two [verses], each time he is chosen, after the choosing has been made.
Having offered the oblation, the Adhvaryu chooses the subsequent [priests].
Some prescribe the *pravara* formulas at the *savanīya* [offering].
When the omentum has been offered, he issues the command: "O Subrahmaṇyā priest, summon the Subrahmaṇyā! The Subrahmaṇyā formula is that which belongs to the father and son.
In the afternoon, he takes up the *vasatīvarī* waters from flowing streams.
One should not cross rivers that flow toward the end [of the world],
nor the shadow of a sandbank,
nor the shadow of a tree on a bank, nor one's own shadow.
Standing against the current, he fills the jar or the pot with the water while reciting, "These waters are rich in oblation.
If the sun should set before the water has been taken, he should take water from the pot of a Brahmin who performs many sacrifices.
If they cannot find such a person, he should take fire and gold and go to where there is water; holding the light above and placing the gold between, he takes the water when a boon has been granted.

With the formula, "I set thee down in the seat of Agni Vaipānagraha," he places [the vessel] to the west of the *śālāmukhīya* fire. At sunset, he proceeds with the animal sacrifice ritual beginning from the *saṃvāda* (dialogue). He carries the *samavatta* (the collected portions) either to the south or to the north of the *havirdhāna* shed.
The sacrificer does not consume the portions; some prescribe the consumption [of them].
[The ritual] concludes with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings. The Agniṣomīya sacrifice is completed. At night, he carries around the Vasatīvarī waters on all sides, but not from the front.
Having said, "Come forth," the sacrificer and his wife stand within the altar-ground (*antarvedi*).
He does not carry [the fire] around one who has not been initiated.

Taking the pitcher and placing it on his left shoulder, having passed behind the *prājahita* fire and brought it out through the southern door, and having carried it along the southern edge of the altar, he sets it down on the northern corner of the southern *uttaravedi* with the formula: "O you who belong to the portion of Indra and Agni."

Having taken the pitcher and placed it on his right shoulder, he returns by the same way he came, carries it out through the north-eastern door, and having carried it around along the northern edge of the altar, he sets it down on the northern hip of the northern altar with the formula: "You are the portions of Mitra and Varuṇa.

Having taken the pitcher and placed it on his left shoulder, he brings it in by the ritual passage (tīrtha) and sets it down in the Āgnīdhra fire-hall with the formula: "You are the portions of the Viśve Devas."

They dwell here. He issues the command: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; let the Subrahmaṇyā be that which belongs to father and son. He issues the command: "Let her who is the cow providing the *vratadhuk* milk for the sacrificer be milked for the *āśira*; let her who is the cow providing the *vratadhuk* milk for the wife be milked for the *dadhighraha*; let her who is the cow providing the *gharmadhuk* milk be milked for the *dadhigharma*; let the warm milk, not yet coagulated, be prepared for the Maitrāvaruṇa cup; and let the curd, already coagulated, be prepared for the Āditya cup."
The Āgnīdhra priests, having adorned themselves, remain [in their places]. In the *prāgvamśa* hall, they keep the wife awake.
In the *havirdhāna* shed, the sacrificer guards the King (Soma); he guards him. || 25 || Thus ends the eighth paṭala in the seventh praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
This seventh book is complete.
Oṃ, that is the True; salutation to Brahman. This is the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha.
Accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.
Now begins the seventh book;
therein, the first chapter.

Seeing his parents, who had come out of affection to kiss the pair of his cheeks, he quickly closed his stainless lotus-face with a gentle smile; then, as those two fair-faced ones of Śiva and Pārvatī joined together, may that Lord, the elephant-faced child who thus entertained them, protect us. (1) [I bow to] the god Vidyā-Mahāgaṇapati, as well as Vyāḍīśvara, Yogeśvarī, the goddess of speech (Sarasvatī), Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, and the Sun. (2)

Having bowed to Satyāṣāṭha, the best of sages, whose hair is like gold, and to my teachers—my mother and father—I shall now, according to my intellect, explain the Sūtra composed by the wise Gopīnātha Satyāpāḍha out of a desire to benefit [students]. This crossing over by means of the boat of the Sūtra has been undertaken by me, who am of feeble power; in this endeavor, my support for reaching the further shore is the remembrance of my teacher.

The Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is for all desires (*sarvakāma*). Those things desired are called *kāmāḥ*; that by which all such desired objects are to be accomplished is the Agniṣṭoma for all desires. And those desires include heaven, progeny, cattle, gold, and so forth. Likewise, other things to be accomplished through different actions—such as knowledge of the worlds immediately following the placement of the worlds (*lokanyāsa*), and the knowledge of the worlds attained through the practice of yogic concentration (*dhāraṇā*) as taught in the Pātañjala Sūtras beginning with "By constraint upon the sun, [there is] knowledge of the worlds" (Yoga Sūtra 3.26)—are also to be understood by the word "all."

The word *stoma* denotes the number that serves as the basis for chanting (*pragīti*). In this context, it should be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as referring to the specific praise performed by means of the particular chant named *yajñāyajñiya*. That in which the *stoma*—that is, the praise—is directed toward Agni is the *agniṣṭoma*; this is a term formed through both etymological derivation and conventional usage (*yogarūḍha*). Thus, the term *agniṣṭoma* is analyzed as meaning "that whose conclusion (*saṃsthā*), i.e., completion, is achieved by means of the chant named *yajñāyajñiya*, which effects the praise of Agni. 5.

1.550. Regarding the meaning of the term *agniṣṭoma*: it is heard in another recension (*śākhāntara*) that the *agniṣṭoma* possesses all desires as its object: "Other sacrifices are undertaken for a single desire, but the *agniṣṭoma* is for all. The word "are undertaken" (*āhiyante*) means "are performed. Jaimini has established that fruitfulness consists precisely in being subject to desire (*kāmya*). Furthermore, no fruit for the *agniṣṭoma* is heard in our own recension.

Furthermore, in the absence of that [result], how could the discussion concerning the nature of the injunction arise? Thus, it would not be appropriate to explain such passages as, "One should sacrifice every spring," or "There is no taking up of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* for one who has not commenced them," and so forth; rather, it is proper to state at the outset that a person engages in action only after having understood the result.

If it is argued that the sentence "The *agniṣṭoma* is for one desiring all desires" enjoins the *agniṣṭoma* as a means to a result, and since the result resides in the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), this sentence ought to be read in the *Yājamāna-sūtra*—we say no.

Since the expectancy for the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*) has been satisfied, there arises an expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*); therefore, it is logical that the statement "the *agniṣṭoma* [is performed] for one who desires all objects" (*sarvakāmaḥ agniṣṭomaḥ*) should be recited precisely before the injunction of the procedure—consisting of the performance by the *adhvaryu* and others—which serves to satisfy that expectancy for the goal and the means. Now, it is also heard in scripture: "Sacrifices are undertaken for a single desire, but the *jyotiṣṭoma* is for all [desires]. Furthermore: "The *trivṛt*, the *pañcadaśa*, the *saptadaśa*, and the *ekaviṃśa*..."

If it is asked: "Since the capacity [of these acts] is understood through the scriptural statement, 'These indeed are those very lights, which are its Stomas,' regarding the four excellent rites characterized by the Stomas, why has the indication of the subordinate attribute (vyāpyadharma) been made while abandoning the pervading attribute (vyāpakadharma)?"—it is not so.

"One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Ukthya; one desiring virility should sacrifice with the Ṣoḍaśin; one desiring progeny should sacrifice with the Atirātra"—by such scriptural injunctions, since the hearing of fixed results in the rites beginning with the Ukthya—which possess the fourfold Stomas and are modifications of the Agniṣṭoma quality—is not sublated, the term *jyotiṣṭoma* refers exclusively to the Agniṣṭoma. Nor should it be argued that even though there is the scriptural statement, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma," the Agniṣṭoma should be understood by the name-word *jyotis*.

Nor can it be said that "other sacrifices belong to one [of these]," for such a statement is impossible due to the contradiction with the scriptural injunctions (*śruti*) that prescribe all [the rites] as optional (*kāmya*). Furthermore, it is impossible to claim that they refer to the *ukthya* and other such sacrifices, because even in those cases, independent fruits are heard in the texts. Nor can it be argued that there is no scope for the scriptural injunction, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," since its application is possible in the *agniṣṭoma*, *atyagniṣṭoma*, and other forms of the sacrifice.

However, regarding the word *viśvajit*, since no specific fruit is heard [in the scripture], and because the hearing of an injunction is untenable without a fruit, a fruit must necessarily be postulated. Since it is desired by all, Jaimini postulated heaven itself as that fruit, according to the sūtra: "That heaven would be [the fruit], because it is not distinguished for anyone" (*sa svargaḥ syātsarvānpratyaviśiṣṭatvāt*). The meaning of the sūtra is: that which is the single fruit shall be heaven, because it is not distinguished for all—that is, for all persons. [Heaven is defined as: "That which is not mixed with pain, nor seized by it immediately thereafter..."

"And that happiness, brought about by desire, has heaven as its locus. This means that because heaven—defined as the nature of unsurpassed excellence of happiness as propounded by the Yavanas—is desired, it is distinguished [as superior] due to its equality [with other forms of happiness]. The meaning of the previous sūtra is this: since heavenly happiness is not accompanied by suffering, it is desired by all; whereas the happiness of animals and the like, being accompanied by suffering and lacking such a form, is sought by only a few. However, many people seek heavenly happiness. This is the meaning of the first sūtra. The second sūtra begins with "pratyayācca" (and because of conviction).

Its meaning is as follows: it is understood (*pratyayate*) by all as being unsurpassed happiness, and thus it is "pratyaya"; and for that reason is the sense [of the term]. And so, this is the established meaning: because heaven—which consists of unsurpassed happiness whose locus is not subject to the destruction of moments associated with suffering—is desired by all persons and longed for by all, it is postulated as the fruit [of action].

The avoidance of transgression (*pratyavāya*), though desired by all, reaches the heart only after some delay relative to the transgression itself. There is no distinction here as to whether heaven is desired by one person or not desired by another; rather, it is desired by every person. Therefore, by the sūtra [Jaimini 4.3.15], "That which is not distinguished for all persons shall be heaven. The sūtra states: "That which is a single fruit should be heaven, because it is undistinguished for all, with respect to all persons."

"That which is not intermingled with suffering, nor followed immediately by its seizure, and which is brought about by desire—that is happiness, the locus of the state of heaven (*svarga*). Because heaven, characterized by such specific types of happiness as set forth in this statement, is desired by many, is agreeable to all, and is free from distress, it alone is postulated as the fruit [of ritual action]. Although the avoidance of transgression (*pratyavāya*) is also desired by everyone, it is not postulated as a fruit because it is difficult to achieve.

The meaning of the second sūtra is as follows: it is called *pratyaya* because it is realized through conviction (*pratyayān*) and experienced as unsurpassed bliss; and for that reason, heaven alone is designated as the fruit. Therefore, that [cessation of suffering] is not the fruit. Nor is the cessation of this suffering the fruit, because it is difficult to achieve. Consequently, easily attainable knowledge and happiness alone are the supreme fruit, and it should be understood that this takes the form of heaven due to its unsurpassed nature.

This method occurs in the third pāda of the fourth adhyāya. As for the fact that [the sacrifice] has *niḥśreyasa* (supreme beatitude) as its fruit, it was demonstrated by the Teacher through the statement, "by means of rites common to the Agniṣṭoma, Ukthya, and so forth, there is *niḥśreyasa*. Alternatively, this may refer specifically to obligatory (*niyata*) rites alone; whether [the attainment of the fruit] occurs through knowledge or directly is another matter. Furthermore, even the postulation of a fruit based on an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), such as "he who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Agniṣṭoma procreates offspring" and "as one who procreates, he grasps [them]," is [set aside] when a fruit is directly heard in the Vedic text (*śruti*).

[The result] is not logical when [the ritual] already possesses a fruit. However, in the case of the *rātrisatra*, which is an independent rite, it is said in the injunctive statement: "Those who undertake these nights certainly find firm standing. Since no fruit is heard in this injunction, and because an injunction cannot be valid without a fruit, a fruit must necessarily be postulated; thus, the fruit called "firm standing" (*pratiṣṭhā*) mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) has been stated.

By the principle of the *Viśvajit* section, rather than postulating a heaven that is not present and then postulating its connection with the context—which would involve the burden of complexity—it is simpler to postulate that what is already present is indeed the fruit of the context. This was stated by Jaimini: "Kāśyapa [held] that the statement of the fruit in the ritual context is like a subsidiary (*aṅga*); Ātreya [held] that the fruit [is primary] because of the explicit direction, for there would be no fruit where none is heard; [and] regarding the subsidiaries, there is a scriptural statement because they exist for the sake of another."

The first sūtra means as follows: "Those who undertake these nights (the *rātrisatra*) certainly attain firm standing"—this is a statement of fruit (*phalaśruti*). Regarding the injunction concerning the use of *parṇa* wood, such as "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood does not hear an evil report," the teacher Kāmājini considers it to be an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the purpose of the fruit, just as in the case of the injunction regarding the *āraṇi*. However, the teacher Bhāradvāja maintains that because the scripture states, "Those who undertake these sacrificial sessions (*satra*) certainly attain firm standing," and because "firm standing" (*pratiṣṭhā*) is explicitly mentioned, firm standing itself is the fruit.

In cases where no fruit is heard of even in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), one must indeed assume a fruit such as heaven through inference. However, in the present case, there is actually the hearing of a fruit in the form of "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*). Therefore, it is considered that heaven should not be assumed here as the fruit. By the word "night" (*rātri*), the sacrificial rites (*sautya-karmāṇi*) produced by sentences such as "The Jyotiṣṭoma is the first night" are denoted. [Note: This is a portion of the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, specifically concerning the results of specific ritual acts.]

The meaning of the second sūtra is that the collection of actions (*karmasamudāya*) is of such a nature [as to constitute a single ritual]. The meaning of the third sūtra is as follows: regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), there is a scriptural mention of results (*phalaśruti*); because these are for the sake of others—namely, for the sake of the primary rites (*pradhāna*)—the scriptural mention of results concerning the subsidiaries is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). This is equal in the views of both the followers of the *kāmya* (optional) and *nitya* (obligatory) rules. This topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) occurs in the third pāda of the fourth adhyāya.

In the case of the *Rātrisatra*, because the proximity (*sannidhi*) of the fruit is directly heard, there is no assumption of a fruit based on an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). In the case of the *Bhaṅgas*, the hearing of a fruit occurs without the hearing of a verbal root denoting action (*karman*); thus, it is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). And so says the Sūtra: "When a fruit is heard in connection with an entire ritual act..."

In the same way, regarding the permanent sacrifices (*nitya-yajña*), those [passages] which the verb *kāmayati* (he causes to desire) makes heard are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*) concerning the elevation and depression of the *āhavanīya* fire; so too are others in other sacrifices. For instance: "He makes it possessed of loose soil (*purīṣavat*); by means of the *praṇayana* water, he makes it possessed of loose soil through the animals"; "If he plants the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), it is for the sake of making known the world of heaven"; "With the words 'For food, thee! he cuts the branch; verily, he bestows food upon the sacrificer."

Jaimini also, in the third pāda of the fourth adhyāya, states: "In the case of substances, purificatory acts, and subordinate rites, the mention of a fruit for one's own sake should be considered an arthavāda (explanatory praise), because the origin [of the rite] does not have that as its primary purpose. Here, the mention of a fruit regarding a substance is, for example: "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood hears no evil report"; and the mention of a fruit regarding a purificatory act is, for example: "When he anoints [his eyes], he surely blinds his enemy."

The scriptural declarations regarding the fruits of ritual action—such as, "Other sacrifices are performed for the sake of the sacrifice, while this [sacrifice] is performed for the sake of the sacrificer," and so forth—here, the term *karman* should be understood as referring to the *arthakarman* (the primary action), because the *saṃskārakarman* (the preparatory action) is mentioned separately. Thus, those actions alone in which a verbal root of the first class (*kam*) is seen are the objects of desire (*kāmayitavya*), and no others.

The meaning of the previous sūtra is that the mention of a fruit in connection with a substance (*dravya*), a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), or a ritual act for a purpose (*arthakarma*) must be an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), because these are subservient to something else—that is, they are subservient to the sacrifice. "From the origin" (*utpatteḥ*): this refers to the origin of properties such as being made of *parṇa*-wood, which is enjoined by specific sentences such as, "He whose sacrificial ladle (*juhū*) is made of *parṇa*-wood... and so forth. Because the person is subordinate to that [sacrifice], the person is mentioned by means of that [subordinate element].

That very [Prakṛti] is the primary factor in something; that is "having that as its primary factor" (*tatpradhāna*). "Not having that as its primary factor" (*atatpradhānī*) means it does not have that as its primary factor. The state of being so is "thatness" (*tattvam*); therefore, the meaning is "due to the absence of having the Puruṣa as its primary factor. By this, the fact that Prakṛti is not the primary factor is established. The literal meaning is "because of the absence of having that as its purpose" (*tadarthatvam*), which constitutes the meaning of the second Sūtra.

In the sūtra *sthānaḥ kratvarthapuruṣārthayonijñāseti*, the application (*prayukti*) of the sacrifice, indicated by the first-mentioned term *kratvartha* (for the sake of the sacrifice), was examined in two sections (*pāda*). Now, the application indicated by the last-mentioned term *puruṣārtha* (for the sake of the person) is being examined; thus, one should understand the difference between the sections and their immediate succession. Regarding a ritual involving Soma, the Teacher uses three terms: "The Agniṣṭoma is for all desires," "He whose rival exists should sacrifice with the Soma," and "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, before the Āgnīṣomīya [offering]."

In the passage "prior to the Āgnīṣomīya [animal sacrifice] in the Jyotiṣṭoma," the word *jyotiṣṭoma* is indeed common to all [the forms], as there is no contradiction. Or rather, I think it refers to the Anapeya sacrifice, for these very ones—the Trivṛt, Pañcadaśa, Saptadaśa, and Ekaviṃśa—are indeed those *jyotis*.

If it is argued that because this [sacrifice] lacks the four stomas established by the Śruti, it does not possess the nature of the Jyotiṣṭoma, and therefore—just as with the mantras of the Ṛgveda—the mantras of the Ārcika Sāmaveda would also necessarily be recited in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) prior to the *anīṣomīya* offering, we say: no. Since the rule for low-voiced recitation is already established for the archetype (*prakṛti*) by this very statement, it applies to the Vājapeya as well, following the principle of the archetype. (From the *Jyotsnā* commentary on the *Sūtra* by Gopīnātha). [Note: The text provided contains a mix of Sanskrit commentary and what appears to be page/section metadata from a printed edition.]

Since that [result] can be obtained through the very principle of what is to be performed (*kartavyatā*), there is no need for it. Nor should it be argued that the word *agniṣṭoma* alone should be employed here, while in the *ukthya* and other [sacrifices], a restriction on the low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśu*) would apply just as it does in the *vājapeya*. This is because the term *jyotiṣṭoma* is introduced to indicate that all four—beginning with the *ukthya*—serve as archetypes (*prakṛti*) for their respective specific sacrifices; thus, by using the word *jyotiṣṭoma*, the necessity of performing the *āghāra* oblation is established even for those [four].

Furthermore, this is for the purpose of making known that the Ukthya and other sacrifices possess the same obligatory character as the Agniṣṭoma. It has already been stated that the word *jyotiṣṭoma* refers to the ritual action characterized by four *stomas*. The word *agniṣṭoma* refers to a specific form (*saṃsthā*) of the sacrifice. Here, the word *soma* refers to a specific plant and not to the moon or other meanings, because those would be irrelevant to the present context; otherwise, the requirement for a substance (*dravya*) would remain unfulfilled. By means of a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), the specific substance denoted by the word *soma* functions as a qualifier of the particular sacrifice.

And thus, the meaning [of the injunction] becomes: "One should effect the desired result by means of a sacrifice possessed of *soma*. By this, it should be understood that its status as a name for the sacrifice—like the word *udbhid* and others—is refuted. In that regard, the nature of *soma* is to be understood from the *Āyurveda*: "That which is dark, sour, produced on the bark, exuding sap, fleshy, phlegmatic, and creeping—that creeper called *soma* is the food of goats. And that [soma] is primarily the one born on the mountain, because of the indicative mark: "The drinking of *soma*, like that of Maunavata."

According to Baudhāyana, [the term] *mūjavat* is used in the questions and answers between the Adhvaryu and the Soma-seller because he has stated it so; the other [teacher] maintains that [the term] does not apply. The word *mūjavat* denotes a mountain. In the absence of Soma, one should press *pūtīka* plants and so forth; this is the rule for a substitute (*pratinidhi*). Even in the case of a substitute, the primary term itself is employed, because Āśvalāyana states: "The words of the original mantras are indeed used even for the substitutes. Since the [substitute] is prescribed [in the ritual], the lack of the specific term would result in a deficiency of expression.

Therefore, it would be of that same nature, because it is not distinguished from the original by its *saṃskāras*. And it has been stated that the mantra "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) must be employed even in the case of a substitute, relying solely on the unchanging [essence]; this is the meaning of the first sūtra. Because of the scriptural injunction regarding substitutes, as in: "In the absence of Soma, one should press the *pūtīka* plants. This refers to the other, namely the substitute, as opposed to the primary [substance]. Even when a substitute is taken up, there is no difference [in essence].

The state of being "non-verbal" (aśabdatva) does not exist in a substitute; for where there is a word, that word denotes the primary substance. The word *soma* belongs to that [primary substance]; its essence would thus reside in the substituted substance. However, the application of the word denoting the primary substance does not occur in the case of a substitute—this is the meaning of the second sūtra. This is a sūtra presenting the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the meaning of the preceding sūtra. That alone is the true meaning of the primary.

That which has the Ṛṣi as its source is "tadārṣa"; the state of being such is "tadārṣatva," and it is from that [state] [that the name is derived]. Because it is a substitute, the substance having the form of the substitute is "tadārūpa"; that which has this as its designation is "tadākhyam"—it would indeed have that very name. Because it is not distinguished by the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), and because the purificatory rites are identical—meaning the purificatory rites belonging to the primary substance are the very same as those of this [substitute]—there is thus equality of purificatory rites. The secret [teaching] is that even when the rite is performed with a substitute, it is as if it were performed with the primary substance itself.

The word "vā" (or) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). This is the meaning of the third sūtra. It was stated in the third quarter of the sixth chapter that the reality [of the substitute] is not distinct from the original consecrations (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, in the third quarter of the ninth chapter, it is stated by Jaimini: "Because there is no modification even when this substance used as a substitute is itself substituted. And: "One may desire [the results] simultaneously."

In the preceding sūtra, it was stated that the *agniṣṭoma* fulfills all desires. Regarding the inquiry as to whether all desires should be sought within a single performance (*prayoga*) or through a distinction of performances, it is said: in a single performance, one should desire all the desired objects together—such as heaven, cattle, gold, and so forth—as mentioned in the word "all. [From the seventh book, section 554 of the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha.]

Just as one desiring cattle might desire many cattle in a single performance [of a sacrifice], so too one may desire all desires; or, just as from the planting of a single tree, fruits, flowers, and fragrance arise, so too multiple fruits arise from a single performance—this is the meaning of the sūtra.
Or, [it refers to] the distinctness of the nourishment.

The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). That [view]—that one may desire them simultaneously—is not so; rather, it is only the distinctness of the performance (*āhāra-pṛthaktvam*). "Performance" (*āhāra*) means the ritual application (*prayoga*). One should desire each desire in each individual performance. For the rituals, which have those desires as their purpose, are the primary elements; and a subsidiary (*guṇa*) enjoined in proximity to the primary is divided according to each primary. Indeed, in the illustration of the animal sacrifice, even though many animals are embraced by a single act, they possess only a single result.

It is not the case here that [the fruit is grasped] as such; rather, each respective fruit possesses the status of being a fruit precisely by its own specific nature, and not by being subsumed under the general category of "fruit-ness. For indeed, everything is not desired simply because it is desirable. Thus, since that which is apprehended by the cognition "this is this" cannot be grasped by a single [cognition], non-repetition with respect to each primary object is indeed logical. Furthermore, the observation that a single action has multiple fruits is likewise inconclusive.

In general, since all fruits are independent, it is impossible to take an incidental fruit as an illustrative example. In the third section (pāda) of the fourth chapter, Jaimini likewise established this very conclusion through the two sūtras: *tatra sarve 'viśeṣāt* and *yogasiddhirvā'rthasaṃyogāt*. The meaning of the sūtras is as follows: regarding the action for the sake of all desires (*sarvakāma-karma*), because there is no distinction—since the nature of being a desire is non-distinct—all desires would indeed be realized simultaneously; such is the meaning of the first sūtra.

The meaning of the subsequent Sūtra, however, is as follows: for one who has a desire for a particular object, success comes through the application, practice, and performance of that very object or desire, and not simultaneously for all objects. This is because it is impossible for everything to arise at once, and because the word "all" (sarva) does not function here to define the intended subject (*uddeśya*), as it would require a correlative reference; rather, it is the word "desire" (*kāma*) alone that defines the intended subject by virtue of its independence.

Therefore, since the status of being "all" (*sarvatva*)—unlike the status of being a "cup" (*grahatva*)—does not serve to complete the cognition of the object to be enjoined (*uddeśya*), it is merely a qualification of that object. Consequently, like the singularity of the cup, it is not intended to be significant; thus, the result does not accrue through their combination, but rather to each one individually. Since the agent is primary and the action is subordinate, it is logical that the subordinate factor should repeat for each primary factor.
Therefore, [the injunction is]: "One should sacrifice every spring."

[The phrase] "by means of the Agniṣṭoma" [is explained as follows]: Since the pronoun *tat* (that) generally refers back to what has been previously mentioned, and since the desire for results (*kāmya*) is not restricted by a fixed time, the pronoun *tat* refers only to the proximate qualificand, the Agniṣṭoma, and not to the qualifier "desire for all results" (*sarvakāma*). For there is no rule that desire is produced only in the spring. Therefore, it concludes that [the sacrifice] is permanent (*nitya*). The mention of "spring" implies that only the spring is to be taken [as the time]. If [the word] were connected with "year" (*saṃvatsara*), [then it would be permanent].

If it were said that [the initiation] occurs at the *mṛgaśīrṣa* [nakṣatra], then the practice would have to be performed on that very lunar day (*tithi*) upon which the first application occurs; thus, let it not be so. Rather, it should be performed during the spring on any unprohibited lunar day. Furthermore, although this is obligatory, its connection with a fruit should be understood as being like that of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other rites. Its obligatory nature is also established by the praise of the *sarpaṇa* (creeping). For it is stated: "When one is initiated, he indeed becomes a Brahmin; he is born from the Ṛṣis of the Brahman, from the gods... [555].

Chapter 150: Accompanied by the *Jyālā* commentary composed by Gopīnātha. Regarding the verse, "With this [verse], [one offers] to the ancestors" (*anayā pitṛbhyaḥ*), Vasiṣṭha’s statement—"Having enumerated the sacrifices ending with the Soma sacrifice, this obligatory [rite] is indeed praised"—and the scriptural injunction regarding expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in the event of the interruption of Soma-drinking, as well as the hearing of the sin incurred by non-performance, are proofs for its obligatory nature (*nityatva*). Furthermore, the scriptural hearing of the transgression (*pratyavāya*) in the case of non-performance—namely, "Without having studied the Vedas, without having procreated sons, and without having offered sacrifices according to one's ability, one who desires liberation falls downward"—is also a proof for its obligatory nature.

In this context, although it was stated without qualification that "it is *yajuḥ*," nevertheless, the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, when performed with the *agniṣṭoma* as its concluding form (*saṃsthā*), is indeed the *Soma* sacrifice. This is because of the statement: "Since this [Soma] is fivefold—namely the *Agnihotra*, the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *Cāturmāsya*, the animal sacrifice, and the *Soma*—it is the most perfect (*saṃpannatama*) among sacrifices. In this scriptural passage, which indicates the necessity of the *agniṣṭoma* as the concluding form, the term "most perfect" explicitly designates the *Soma* sacrifice alone as the primary sacrifice.

This Jyotiṣṭoma is indeed the first among sacrifices, namely that which is the Agniṣṭoma. Regarding the statement, "Having not sacrificed with this, if one should sacrifice with another," the Jyotiṣṭoma is understood here as the Agniṣṭoma-saṃsthā (the Agniṣṭoma form) by virtue of its being the first sacrifice; this is according to the principle stated in the third pāda of the fifth adhyāya in the sūtra *prakaraṇāl liṅgāc ca*. Because it is the first sacrifice, the Jyotiṣṭoma in the Agniṣṭoma form is obligatory (*nitya*), since it is connected to all desires (*sarvakāma*), and it is also optional (*kāmya*). As for the meaning of the sūtra: by the word "this" (*etena*), the Agniṣṭoma form is determined.

"Because that [term] refers specifically to its own context," such is the meaning of the first sūtra. "Even though it is mentioned after the *chin* sacrifice, the reference is specifically to the *agniṣṭoma* form as the 'first sacrifice,'" such is the meaning of the second sūtra. The *jyotiṣṭoma* in the *agniṣṭoma* form is obligatory (*nitya*), while in its connection with all desires (*sarvakāma*) it is optional (*kāmya*).

This very point was established by the Mīmāṃsakas in the second quarter (pāda) of the sixth chapter, where, under the sūtra *tadetadbrāhmaṇasya somavidyāprajāsamanvākhyānena saṃyogāt*, the view that these [rites] are optional (*kāmyatva*) was presented as the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), and it was subsequently proven that they are indeed obligatory (*nityatva*) because of the praise of the three castes therein. As for the sūtra: *somaśca vidyā ca prajā ca*; the compound *somavidyāpraja* is a collective (*samāhāra*) of these [three].

Regarding the statement, "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born with a debt," you might think that because of this connection with the word for debt (*ṛṇa*), the acquisition of knowledge is mandatory for the Brāhmaṇa alone. However, this is not correct, because there is no specific qualification [restricting it] within the injunctive sentence itself. Thus, it is established that the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" serves as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya as well. Another method may be seen in the original treatise (*ākara*). As for the four forms of the Soma sacrifice, however, they are purely optional (*kāmya*).

"One desiring cattle should perform the Ukthya; one desiring vigor should praise with the Ṣoḍaśin; one desiring progeny should sacrifice with the Atirātra; one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Āptoryāma"—since this is the connection of results to the four terminuses (*saṃsthā*) based on the previously mentioned Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, just as curd is connected to the previously mentioned Agnihotra oblation. Even though the four terminuses are performed solely for the sake of specific desires (*kāmyatva*), they also possess the character of being obligatory (*nityatva*) by virtue of the force of the context. And that has already been stated.

On this point, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the Agniṣṭoma alone is to be performed first, based on the Vedic injunction: "He who, having not sacrificed with this [Agniṣṭoma], [sacrifices with another]. Even in the view that the Atirātra is the first sacrifice, there is no commencement of another sacrifice without the Agniṣṭoma. They declare that in the case of the *somapūrvādhāna* (the establishment of the sacred fires preceded by Soma-sacrifice), the Agniṣṭoma is prior for everyone, and not the Atirātra.

From the forthcoming sūtra stating, "The Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśin, the Atirātra, and the Āptoryāma are modifications (guṇavikāra) of the Agniṣṭoma," it is understood that this is the opinion of the Teacher (Ācārya) that the nature of the Agniṣṭoma applies to all four—the Ukthya and the others—and thus the Ukthya and the rest are indeed primary forms (prakṛti). Consequently, apart from the Jyotirukthya and so forth, there are no Ukthya and other sacrifices that are mere modifications (vikṛti). [Satyāṣāḍhaviracitaṃ Śrautasūtram—Seventh Praśna] (Note: The text mentions variants *kha* and *ga*, and the phrase *mādhi* appears to be a scribal or typographical error.)

The status of being the first sacrifice (*prathamayajyatva*), however, belongs primarily to the *agniṣṭoma* alone; by virtue of a specific scriptural statement, it also applies to the *atirātra*. It does not, however, mean that the *ukthya* and other sacrifices must precede the *agniṣṭoma* and *atirātra*. Rather, it should be understood that the status of occurring later belongs specifically to the *agniṣṭoma* and not to the *atirātra*. [The sequence is: *agniṣṭoma*, *atyagniṣṭoma*, *ukthya*, *ṣoḍaśī*, *vājapeya*.

Some maintain that all seven forms of the Soma sacrifice are obligatory (nitya), because they are enumerated among the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) by Gautama in the passage, "The Tirātra and the Atirātra—these are the seven forms of the Soma sacrifice"; because of the statement, "One who is consecrated by the forty-eight purificatory rites attains union with Brahman" (brahmaṇaḥ sāyujyam āpnoti); and because of the scriptural declaration of sin (pratyavāya) incurred through their non-performance. In this sūtra, a division of the rule (yogavibhāga) must be made: "In spring" (vasante) constitutes one sūtra; the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice) is drawn from the subsequent [sūtra] and applied here.

The meaning of that [text] is: "One should sacrifice with that obligatory *agniṣṭoma* in the spring. "One should sacrifice in the spring" is a separate sūtra. In this sūtra, the preceding entire sūtra is drawn in. Thus, the meaning becomes: "By means of that obligatory *agniṣṭoma*, one sacrifices in the spring, in the spring. By the preceding sūtra, the single performance of the obligatory [rite] is enjoined as something to be performed in the spring. By the subsequent sūtra, repetition (*abhyāsa*) is enjoined. Since there is no limit to the repetition, it follows by implication that it lasts for as long as one lives (*yāvajjīvatvam*).

There is also an indicative mark for the non-permanence of the repetition: "He who drinks the Soma becomes one who is not to be eaten again. Alternatively, by the word "thereby" (tena), the permanent Agniṣṭoma is obtained; and in that case, the spring season along with the repetition is prescribed as the time. But elsewhere, it consists of the entire northern course of the sun. As it has been stated by the Chandoga: "The time for sacrifice, when no specific rule is given, is during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, on an auspicious day. This very [time] is also the time for those rites for which no time has been specified.
