Regarding the rule "In the *somapūrvādhāna* (the establishment of the sacred fires preceded by the Soma sacrifice), one who is about to establish the fires while intending to perform the Soma sacrifice should not specify either the season (*ṛtu*) or the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*)," according to some teachers—this being the injunction established by the Sūtra—there are various conflicting interpretations. Among these, some say that only the time for the *ādhāna* itself is set aside by the context, whereas the fact that the Soma sacrifice belongs to the spring season is not set aside at all. Others, however, say that even the specific season of the Soma sacrifice is not specified; thus, they maintain that there is a setting aside of both times.

Others, however, maintain that for the *somapūrvādhāna* (the establishment of the sacred fires preceded by the Soma sacrifice), the time is prescribed as the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*), the waxing fortnight (*āpūryamāṇapakṣa*), and an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), according to the rule in the *Candoga-sūtra* stating "the time for sacrifice is undefined when not specified. They hold that while the Soma sacrifice itself does not depend on the northern course of the sun, this specific timing applies to the fire-establishment preceding it. Others, however, argue that since the *Bhāradvāja-sūtra* states, "Whenever the sacrifice may come upon him," there is no regard for any specific time; thus, they conclude that the fire-establishment may take place at any time in both cases.

One intending to perform the Soma sacrifice should resolve upon the *soma-pūrvādhāna* (the establishment of the fires preceded by Soma), thinking: "I shall establish the fires, performing those rites which I am capable of performing and for which I am authorized. Once the *pavamāneṣṭis* have been completed, if the commencement of the Soma sacrifice does not take place due to some obstacle, then until the commencement of the Soma, one should perform silent (*tūṣṇī*) oblations for the sake of protection, devoid of the formal rite of commencement (*ārambha-dharma*). Even the commencement of the *iṣṭi* does not occur [at that time]. After the Soma sacrifice, having performed the *anvārambhaṇīyā* on the subsequent full moon day, one should perform the *paurṇamāseṣṭi* and other rites.
For him, there is no resumption of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices unless they had already been commenced previously.

The meaning is that there is no performance—that is, no undertaking—of that Agniṣṭoma sacrifice while the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices remain unentered upon and uncommenced. Thus says Bharadvāja: "One should not perform the Soma sacrifice without having completed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. Vaikhānasa and Bādhūla also state: "Having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, one should sacrifice with the Soma."

In the *Brāhmaṇa*: "He who, having performed the New and Full Moon sacrifices, sacrifices with Soma, at the very end of his life, attains the favor of the gods"—this introduces precisely the fact that the Soma sacrifice occurs subsequent to the New and Full Moon sacrifices. In another recension (*śākhā*), within the very context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is the scriptural statement (*śruti*): "Having sacrificed with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, one should sacrifice with Soma. [End of] the first section (*paṭala*) of the first chapter, accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa.

It should be understood that this [passage] merely prescribes the time subsequent to the *darśa* sacrifice, and does not enjoin the *anuyāja* offerings as its constituent parts (*aṅga*). Accordingly, Jaimini, in the third pāda of the fourth adhyāya, expresses this very point in the sūtra: "The time [of the *anuyāja*s] should be [prescribed], because the sentence has that [time] as its primary object" (*kālaḥ syādvākyasya tatpradhānatvāt*).

The meaning of this Sūtra, however, is as follows: when there is doubt regarding whether the time is an injunction for the production of a separate ritual act, it must be a time-injunction, because in the sentence "by means of the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa," the time is the predominant factor. Furthermore, since there is a prohibition—namely, "one who is about to sacrifice with Soma and is establishing the fires [should not do so]; nor [should he wait for] a lunar mansion, according to some"—this indicates an option (vikalpa) between the commencement of the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa and the establishment of the fires (agnyādhāna).

Āśvalāyana also states the option itself: "One may perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, or the Iṣṭi, Paśu, Cāturmāsya, or Soma sacrifice; or one may perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa according to usage, or even before that, one may perform the Soma sacrifice. Jaimini also stated the option through two sūtras: "The performance of the Soma sacrifice after the Vadhana-iṣṭi and others is for some," and "For others, because of the statement regarding the passing over of the seasons and constellations for the Ādhāna, it would otherwise be purposeless at the end of that [period]."

The meaning of the *sūtra* is as follows: based on the injunction "Having performed the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, one should sacrifice with *soma*," it follows that for *soma*, the *iṣṭi* must necessarily precede it; this is the meaning of the preceding *sūtra*. The meaning of the subsequent *sūtra* is as follows: according to the view of some teachers, even for one who intends to perform the *soma* sacrifice and is establishing the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), there is no requirement to inquire about the season or the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), because of the scriptural statement regarding the "transgression" of the season and the lunar mansion. Thus, there is a position that the *soma* sacrifice may occur even before the *iṣṭi*. Furthermore, the expression "ending with that" (*tadanta*) is a designation emphasizing the state of concluding with that; by this, the meaning is "by virtue of ending with that."

Because it is desired that [the sacrifice] ends with the *iṣṭi*, occurs after the *iṣṭi* has been performed, and follows the *iṣṭi* in sequence, this statement is not purposeless; for there is a rule that since the *iṣṭi* has already occurred, it cannot end with anything other than the *iṣṭi*. By the phrase "not by one not commenced," it is demonstrated that a modification (*vikṛti*) must not be performed without its archetype (*prakṛti*). That which is the *jyeṣṭhayajña* (the first sacrifice), namely the *agniṣṭoma*, does not occur without the commencement of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*; what need is there to mention that the *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices (*paśu*) do not occur?

For one who does not possess the Aindrāgna and Āśvina animal sacrifices, three types of fire-installations (*ādhāna*) are optional. However, for one who does possess them, some maintain that the *soma-pūrvatva* (the state of being preceded by the Soma sacrifice) is impossible; the intention of this view is that because they are separated by the intermediate expiatory and animal sacrifices, and because those two cannot occur without the commencement of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the condition of being preceded by Soma is unattainable. Others, however, assert that since these two [sacrifices] are conducive to the commencement of the Soma sacrifice, they do not act as an interruption at all.

Immediately after the Pavamāneṣṭi, on the fourteenth day, one should perform the two animal sacrifices (paśu) by way of a single ritual framework (tantra), completing them up to the preparation of the northern altar (uttaravedi); then, having performed the animal sacrifices by way of a single ritual framework on the full-moon day (parvan), one should commence the Soma sacrifice on the day of the actual offering. Alternatively, immediately after the Pavamāneṣṭi, on the fourteenth day itself, one should perform the animal sacrifices by way of a single ritual framework, and then commence the Soma sacrifice on the full-moon day.

Alternatively, on the fourteenth day, having performed the rites for the animal sacrifice to Indra-Agni up to the preparation of the high altar (*uttaravedi*), and having sacrificed with the Indra-Agni offering on the full-moon day, one should, on the day of the fast (*upavasatha*) of the subsequent full moon, perform the rites for the animal sacrifice to the Aśvins up to the preparation of the high altar, and having sacrificed with the Aśvin offering on that full-moon day, one should commence the Soma sacrifice on the third full-moon day.

The assertion of certain authorities—who, relying on the *Kāpeya* school's position, maintain that first comes the *sāṃnāyya*, followed by the expiatory animal sacrifice—is refuted. In any case, it is established that for one whose Soma-drinking has been interrupted and who has not performed the *vrātyapaśu* sacrifice, there is no [right to] Soma. The meaning of the term "one whose Soma-drinking has been interrupted" (*vicchinnasomapītha*) is stated in the Brāhmaṇa: "One whose Soma-drinking has been interrupted should offer the *punarutsṛṣṭa* animal dedicated to Indra and Agni, if he has not drunk Soma up to the third generation."

In that context, regarding the phrase "three to the east" and "three to the west," the three ancestors beginning with the father—who are referred to as being "to the east" in the *Dīkṣā*, *Vedana*, *Nāman*, and *Subrahmaṇyā* rites—are to be invoked by name. Among these three generations, the third intended is the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*), and not one's own third ancestor, the grandfather. Why? Because for oneself, who is intent on drinking the Soma, there is no severance of that [lineage]. This is expressed in the mantra: "This is for you, O Father, and for those who follow you."

He places [the oblation] upon three potsherds; therefore, they do not utter the name [of the child] beyond the third generation, because the meaning is clear from the beginning. Thus, its status as an injunction (vidhi) should also be understood from this very illustration. They further state that if there is an absence of the drinking of Soma for three generations in immediate succession beginning with the father, one should sacrifice an Aśvina bull that is smoke-colored with a mark on its forehead after performing the Aindrāgna sacrifices.

The *aindrāgna* sacrifice mentioned for one who lacks the drinking of *soma* is not appropriate; for the *Agastya-sūtra* states, "He whose two subsequent ancestors were non-drinkers of *soma* should sacrifice with the *aindrāgna* and then proceed with *soma*," thus specifying that it applies only when two generations lack the right to drink *soma*. Thus, in the *Smṛti*, some—considering that one loses the status of a *brāhmaṇa* upon the interruption of both sacrifice and Vedic study—do not desire the *āśvina* cup when there is an interruption of the *soma* alone. This is the first of the Soma sacrifices.

Among the Soma sacrifices, that Agniṣṭoma is the first because it is the archetype (*prakṛti*); this is the implied meaning. Before all other Soma sacrifices, the Soma sacrifice called Agniṣṭoma must be performed, and not the Trivṛt and others which are modifications of its qualities, nor any others such as the Ukthya and so forth—the one-day sacrifices (*ekāhas*), the two-night sacrifices (*dvirātras*), and the multi-night sacrifices (*ahīnas*). Thus, concerning the Agniṣṭoma, the Brāhmaṇa states: "Therefore they say, 'The Agniṣṭoma is the foremost sacrifice,' for Prajāpati is the eldest; he indeed sacrificed with this first."

The primacy (*jyeṣṭhatva*) of Prajāpati arises from his being the first-born. Likewise, the Agniṣṭoma possesses primacy because it was performed prior to all other Soma sacrifices. Just as Prajāpati is the eldest because he is the creator of all, so too the Agniṣṭoma is the eldest among all Soma sacrifices because it is the locus where the ritual duties (*dharmāḥ*) are entrusted. The fact that Prajāpati is the creator of all is established in such mantras as "Hiraṇyagarbha came into being in the beginning," and so forth. Hiraṇyagarbha is indeed Prajāpati himself.

According to the Vedic revelation, "Prajāpati is Hiraṇyagarbha. Thus, in the Agniṣṭoma, what is called "primacy" (jyeṣṭhatva) is simply its status as the archetype (prakṛtitva). The Chandogya Brāhmaṇa also states the primacy of the Agniṣṭoma: "This indeed is the first of sacrifices; he who, having not sacrificed with this, sacrifices with another, is born as one who has lost his offspring, or he perishes. Furthermore, there is the complete recitation of all ritual properties (dharma) within the Agniṣṭoma itself. Therefore, the Agniṣṭoma alone is the archetype; for this very reason, it is the first.

Bharadvāja also states very clearly: "One should not perform other sacrifices without having first performed the *agniṣṭoma*. The word "should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. If it is argued that this sūtra is redundant—since the principle that "a modification cannot exist when the archetype has not been performed" is already established by a rule well-known in other scriptures—the answer is no. This sūtra was composed precisely for the purpose of establishing such a principle within one's own school (*svaśāstra*).
Some teachers maintain that the *atirātra* sacrifice is to be studied as the first sacrifice.

Although the *atirātra* lacks the status of a primary archetype (*prakṛti*), some teachers state that it occurs even prior to the *agniṣṭoma*, which is the archetype, on the basis of a specific scriptural injunction (*vacana*). And that [mention], which consists of the recollection of the Teacher—who is the substantive (viśeṣya) evoked by the single word serving as the qualifier—is for the sake of the unobstructed completion of the treatise; its inclusion in the middle of the work, however, is for the purpose of instructing the disciples. In the present case, the purpose is also to perform auspicious rites (maṅgala) at intervals during the ritual action itself. For the learned (śiṣṭas) do not practice [the mention] only at the beginning of a work, but rather perform the auspicious rite at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end of the work out of apprehension of obstacles.

At the beginning of the work, the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) was performed by employing the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) in the statement, "We shall explain the sacrifice. For the sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu himself, according to the Vedic revelation: "The sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu. Regarding ritual action as well, Baudhāyana has stated that the performance of an auspicious rite consists in meditating upon Viṣṇu, the presiding deity of the sacrifice. As for the fact that an auspicious rite is a means to completion, it is established by the *pariśeṣa* (residual) inference propounded by the logicians: "An auspicious rite has completion as its fruit, because, while not having any other fruit than completion, it is nonetheless fruitful."

Regarding this, the modern logicians (*navīna-tārkikas*) maintain that the fruit of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is simply the destruction of obstacles (*vighnadhvaṃsa*). The ancient logicians (*prācīna-tārkikas*), however, hold that the fruit is the completion [of the work] preceded by the destruction of obstacles. Let this digression suffice. It should be understood that in cases where an alternative is indicated by the word "or" (*vā*), there is merely the presentation of an equal alternative, and not necessarily the status of being for the sake of auspiciousness as well. If it is argued: "In cases where it is read as 'one' (*ekaḥ*) or 'some' (*ekeṣām*), let it be intended solely to show that that particular position is to be rejected," we say no.

Since the matter could be resolved simply by not stating that position, it would follow that demonstrating that position is useless. Therefore, one should understand that the guiding principle here is simply this: in some instances, an alternative is presented after first showing that [the former] serves the purpose of *maṅgala*, while in others, only the alternative is shown; for a sage who acts according to his own independent will (*svatantra*) is beyond the reach of injunctions or challenges.

In both cases—on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*)—the locative case denotes proximity (*samīpa-saptamī*). On whichever day near the new moon is the day of the *dīkṣā* (initiation), and on whichever day near the full moon is the day of the *sutyā* (the pressing of Soma)—the word *sutyam* being derived from *sutyā* with the suffix *yat* according to the *arśa-ādi* group—the [sacrifice] takes place. The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. In the term *sutyam*, by the word *sutyā*, the ritual action consisting of the crushing of the Soma is expressed; the meaning is "like that [action]."

Although the word *amāvāsyā* (new moon) is based on the extreme conjunction (*saṃnikarṣa*) of the sun and the moon, and the word *paurṇamāsī* (full moon) is based on their extreme separation (*viprakarṣa*), and since this conjunction and separation last for only the duration of the junction (*saṃdhi*), which is common to both the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*) and the first day (*pratipad*), it follows that both of these days are established as being denoted by the terms *amāvāsyā* and *paurṇamāsī*; nevertheless, in this context, when the initiation (*dīkṣā*) takes place on the day of sacrifice near the new moon, [the full moon is intended].

This is for the purpose of demonstrating that the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing) occurs on the very day of the sacrifice (*yajana*) that is proximate [to the new moon], and not even on the *parvan* (the full moon day). Furthermore, it is intended to exclude the opposite view—that the initiation (*dīkṣā*) takes place on the day of sacrifice proximate to the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), while the *sutyā* takes place on the day of sacrifice proximate to the new moon (*amāvāsyā*).

If it is objected: "Is it not the case that *paurṇamāsītva* (the state of being the full moon) is caused by proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*), while *amāvāsyātva* (the state of being the new moon) is caused by remoteness (*viprakarṣa*), and since this is the same for the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*) as it is for the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*), the terms *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* should accordingly apply to the *pratipad* as well? How then is this explained? It is replied: The sacrifice enjoined by the two sentences, "One sacrifices with the *paurṇamāsī* on the *paurṇamāsī*" and "One sacrifices with the *amāvāsyā* on the *amāvāsyā*," is established by the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) "one sacrifices at the conjunction" (*saṃdhau yajeta*) as occurring at the junction of the *parvan* (the fourteenth day) and the *pratipad*.

In that context, because the time consisting of the junction (*saṃdhi*) between the fourteenth and the first lunar day—which serves as the locus for the sacrifice—is difficult to perceive and thus unfit [for the rite], the Vedic injunction "one should sacrifice at the junction" (*saṃdhim abhito yajeta*) indicates some coarser period situated on both sides of the junction. Since even that is unfit, Gobhila states, "The days ending with the new moon (*lakṣāntāḥ*) should be observed as fasts; the beginnings of the fortnights (*pakṣādayaḥ*) are for sacrificing. Because he accepts the first lunar day (*pratipad*) as the locus of the sacrifice just like the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*), the status of being a "new moon day" (*parvatva*) must necessarily be accepted there as well.

Otherwise, the sacrifices on the full moon and new moon days, which are enjoined by the two sentences, "He sacrifices with the Paurṇamāsī [offering] on the full moon day" and "He sacrifices with the Amāvāsyā [offering] on the new moon day," would be contradicted if they were performed on the first lunar days (pratipad). Therefore, for the sake of logical consistency, one must necessarily accept that even on those respective *pratipad* days, they possess the status of *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā*, as they are characterized by the occasion of the moon's filling (*candrapūraṇa*) and the occasion of the moon's lying down (*candraśaya*).

Likewise, the first day (pratipad) following that [lunar day] which is characterized by the fullness of the moon is called *paurṇamāsī*, and the first day following that which is characterized by the waning of the moon is called *amāvāsyā*; thus it is implied that one should sacrifice on those days. In the statement of Gobhila, "The *paurṇamāsī* is the maximum separation of the sun and the moon; the *amāvāsyā* is their maximum conjunction," the terms "maximum separation" and "maximum conjunction" refer to a duration of only a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).

In both cases, regarding the two days—the full moon day (*parvan*) and the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*)—that very conjunction (*saṃdhāna*) is identical for both lunar dates; thus, that time consisting of two lunar dates is indeed a single *kṣaṇa*. Furthermore, the subsequent moments characterized by the moon's filling (as the cause of the full moon) and its waning (as the cause of the new moon) constitute that duration of time denoted by the term "conjunction" (*saṃdhi*).

Since it is connected to both lunar dates, it is entirely appropriate to designate both the fourteenth day (*pañcadaśī*) and the first day (*pratipad*) by the terms "new moon" (*amāvāsyā*) and "full moon" (*paurṇamāsī*) respectively; thus, [the definition] is well-established.
[This applies] on either the new moon day or the full moon day.

The phrase "he undergoes initiation" (*dīkṣate*) should be understood as carrying over [from the previous rule] by means of a "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*). Consequently, the meaning becomes: "He undergoes initiation on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) or he undergoes initiation on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*). As for the *sutyā* (the soma-pressing), it occurs either on the new moon day or the full moon day, based on the general sūtra stating that one should sacrifice with the Soma sacrifice or the Animal Sacrifice (*paśubandha*). In this sūtra, however, the word "sacrifice" (*yāga*) refers primarily to the *sutyā* itself.

In this way, here too, the performance of the sacrifice in the latter fortnight (aparapakṣa) is established as having sixteen concluding rites. If it is objected: "How can this be so? For the sacrifice in the former fortnight (pūrvapakṣa) has been introduced with the statement, 'If one should desire that he might become more prosperous, one should cause him to sacrifice in the former fortnight; he indeed becomes more prosperous'; and the sacrifice in the latter fortnight has been censured with the statement, 'If one should desire that he might become worse off, one should cause him to sacrifice in the latter fortnight; he indeed becomes worse off,'" we reply: no.

Because the direct Vedic injunction, "Having performed the New Moon or Full Moon sacrifice, one should undergo initiation," sublates the rule regarding the performance of the preceding sacrifice at the Soma ritual; for in this injunction, the hearing of the suffix *ktvā* (having done) establishes that there is no interval between the commencement of the Soma sacrifice and the completion of the primary sacrifice. The hearing of the two words *vā* ("or") is for the purpose of indicating that the two options possess equal force. Nor is there a contradiction with the *Chandoga-sūtra*, which states: "The time for sacrifice, when no specific instruction is given, is during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, on an auspicious day."

Since this very sūtra mentions "in the absence of an injunction" (*anādeśe*), this time-period applies only to cases other than those where an injunction exists. Because there is no contradiction with the sūtra—given that an injunction is indeed present in the current context—and because of its association with the term *puṇyāha*, it is understood that the Chāndogya-sūtra refers specifically to *pākayajña* sacrifices. Furthermore, the Vedic text which introduces the preliminary sacrifice, stating "one who desires that he should possess cattle," also finds its scope only in the absence of an injunction.

And it will be stated in the Gṛhya-sūtra regarding the *pākayajñas*: "In the waxing fortnight," [and] "at the two junctions (*parvan*). When the junctions are divided, the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the pressing (*sutyā*) take place on the day and night of the conjunction (*saṃdhi*). In accordance with this, there is an increase or decrease of the initiations. Since the commencement and conclusion of the rite are the primary factors, he says—with the intention that when there is a single initiation or other options such as two, three, four, or an unlimited number, and the principal time for both is not possible, the rite must be performed at whichever of the two prescribed times is available:
"But if there is one initiation, or two, three, four, or an unlimited number, then in that case, even if it is not a *parvan*, the day of the pressing or the initiation may take place."

The word *dīkṣā* (initiation) is construed with "two," "three," and so forth, by changing its grammatical number. The word *aparimita* (unlimited) denotes a measure exceeding the stated measurements; as Kātyāyana has stated: "Unlimited means beyond the [stated] measure. In this context, the limit of the unlimited period is either a month or a year, according to one's capacity. Alternatively, it lasts as long as there is emaciation.

Likewise, Āpastamba says: "The initiated one should fast for twelve days at least, or for a month, or for a year; or when he becomes emaciated"—this is another [view]. Regarding this, Āśvalāyana states the settled rule: "The initiations (dīkṣās) are unlimited by the number of nights starting from the initiation; they range from one day up to a year, or even a year for the Tāpaścita sacrifices. Or as follows: in the case of the Ekāhas, there is one initiation and three Upasad days; the Soma-pressing day (sutyamahar) is the last. At the end of the initiation, there is the purchase of the Soma (soma-kraya); on that same day is the Prāyaṇīyeṣṭi."

Regarding the two sūtras stating that "the twelve-day [sacrifice] should be [determined] from the indicative mark," it follows that in those *satras* (sacrificial sessions) characterized by the twelve-day period, just as the *upasad* days are twelve, so too are the *dīkṣā*s (initiation days). Since no other number has been prescribed elsewhere, the rule is inferred right here: the *sutyā*s (pressing days) and the *upasad*s are of that same number. What is meant is this: in those *satras* characterized by the twelve-day period, whatever the number of *sutyā*s, that same number applies to the *upasad*s and the *dīkṣā*s as well.

"Ācāra" is that in which something is practiced; thus, it refers to time. "Karmācāra" means the practice of ritual action, specifically the time of performance for the *ekāhas*. This is the meaning: by the word *ekāha*, the *ekāha* sacrifices belonging to the *vikṛti* (modified) rites are intended, due to the connection with the plural number. Since initiation (*dīkṣā*) is prescribed in the *prakṛti* (archetypal rite), the word "four" is for the purpose of a specific injunction; the rest is clear. These ritual options (*kalpas*) are optional within the *prakṛti* itself, because there is no distinction among all the contexts (*prakaraṇas*).

As stated by Jaimini in the sixth chapter, fifth section (*pāda*), regarding the duration of initiation (*dīkṣā-parimāṇa*): "There is no restriction [on the number of days] because there is no distinction" (*yāthākāmyam aviśeṣāt*). This means that since there is no distinction among all the alternative positions (*pakṣa*), there is an absence of a specific rule. However, the second sutra states: "But it should be twelve days on account of an indicative mark" (*dvādaśāhas tu liṅgāt syāt*). The meaning of this second sutra is that the position of twelve initiations is also established by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the text: "For twelve days, the initiated one seeks wages" (*dvādaśāhaṃ dīkṣito bhṛtiṃ vanvīta*). Thus, the mention of seeking wages will apply to the twelve-day option. Alternatively, only this much is enjoined: "The initiated one should seek wages."

The mention of "twelve" is for the sake of illustration; this is the explanation following the intention of the Pātikakāra. However, if one adopts a view where initiation (*dīkṣā*) occurs on any one of the [lunar] days, then by the principle of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇa-mukhya-nyāya*), the meaning is that the initiation or the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*) may take place on a non-parvan day. In that regard, when the Soma-pressing occurs on a parvan day, this very [latter] position is stronger, according to the *paribhāṣā* rule concerning the Soma-sacrifice (*somaiṣṭi*). How then, among the ritual options for initiation lasting at least one day, could there be initiation on a non-parvan day? [This is not so.]

According to the *Bhāradvāja-sūtra*, "The initiation (*dīkṣā*) may take place on a non-parvan day, but one should ensure that the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*) occurs only on a parvan day"; and because Jaimini states in the second pāda of the twelfth adhyāya, "In case of a conflict between a subsidiary (*aṅga*) and its quality (*guṇa*), [the quality prevails] due to its being for the sake of that [subsidiary]. Here, the subsidiaries are the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and others; their quality consists in the requirement that they be performed on the first day and so forth. Among these, everything from the *Saṃkalpa* up to the *Śākhāpavitra* must be performed on the first day; if the *Pravargya* is to be performed, the preparation of the *Pravargya* materials must also be done.

The Prāyaṇīyā, the purchase of Soma (Soma-kraya), the Ātithyā, the Pravargya, the Upasads, and the Pravargya-Upasad—these are to be performed on the second day. The Pravargya-Upasad, the preparation of the altar (Vedi-karaṇa), the Vārya, and the Upasad—these are to be performed on the third day.

The Pravargya, Upasad, and Pravargya-upasad; the fetching of water (udvāsana), the leading forward of the fire (agnipraṇayana), the bringing of the branch (śākhāharaṇa), the sprinkling of the wooden altar (kāṣṭhavedi), the spreading of the sacrificial grass (vedistaraṇa), the leading forward of the Havirdhāna carts, the preparation of the Uparava holes, the placing of the Āgnīdhra hearth, the erecting of the Audumbarī post, the preparation of the Sadas, the pouring out of the Dhiṣṇiya mounds, the adding of fuel (anvādhāna) and so forth, the leading forward of Agni and Soma, the fetching of the Vasatīvarī waters, and the common procedure (pamutantra) including the carrying around of the Vasatīvarī waters—these are to be performed on the fourth day.

The primary Soma sacrifice, including the Savanīya offerings and so forth, is to be performed on the fifth day; in that case, when there is a conflict with the time for the *parvan* (junction) prescribed by the rule "on which [day]... (*yaḥ*), the favoring of the qualities (*dharma*) belongs to the primary sacrifice alone. This is because the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) exist for the sake of ensuring the excellence (*sāguṇya*) of the primary, and thus, in the event of a conflict, the excellence of the subsidiaries is of no consequence. This is stated in the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha.

Furthermore, it is observed in the world that when a place has first been occupied by many people, even a single king who arrives later is seen to take possession of it. Therefore, in this case, although the Soma sacrifice is junior—both in terms of textual sequence (*pāṭha*) and performance (*anuṣṭhāna*)—it possesses the status of being the primary element regarding the time of the lunar festival (*parva-kālatva*). As for the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, although they are presented first both in textual sequence and in performance, there is no compliance with the festival time in the case of one or more days of initiation (*ekādi-dīkṣā-pakṣa*). However, in the case of twelve days of initiation (*dvādaśa-dīkṣā-pakṣa*), since there is no conflict, that [compliance with the festival time] applies to the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* as well.

"Contradiction with the quality of the subsidiary" (*aṅgaguṇavirodha*) means contradiction together with the quality of the subsidiary. Regarding that "contradiction with the quality of the subsidiary," the word "of the quality of the principal" (*pradhānaguṇasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Thus, the meaning becomes: "when there is a contradiction between a quality and the quality of the principal. Because the pronoun *tat* refers back to the principal, the meaning is: "because of that, for the sake of the principal"; "of the subsidiaries" (*aṅgānām*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

The meaning of the sūtra is that since the subsidiary parts exist for the sake of the primary, it is logical that they should indeed assist the primary. Regarding the singularity and other details of the initiation (*dīkṣā*), the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* records: "Having been initiated for one night, he purchases the King (Soma); [or] for two nights, three nights, four nights, or an unlimited time. This has also been restated by the Teacher in the *Yājamāna-sūtra*. As for the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*), it occurs on the new moon day, or on the day of sacrifice, or on the fourth, fifth, or subsequent days from the initiation, as circumstances permit.

On the full moon day, or on the day of the sacrifice at the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing), one should follow that [lunar date]; there is no requirement for a single day of initiation (*dīkṣā*) or other such calculations. In the absence of these, it may be performed during the bright fortnight or under an auspicious lunar mansion (*devanakṣatra*). For those who are "doers of what [is right]" (*yatkārī*), they should perform [the rite] under those very auspicious lunar mansions, because of the Vedic text: "One should perform [it] on an auspicious day. And because of Baudhāyana’s statement regarding the Soma sacrifice: "Having sacrificed with the new moon oblation, or under a lunar mansion. One whose nature it is to perform whatever action [is prescribed] is a "doer of what [is right]."

The divine lunar mansions (*devanakṣatras*) are indicated in the *Śruti*: "The Kṛttikās are the first, and the Viśākhās are the last; these are the divine lunar mansions. In the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), it is stated that an undertaking under a lunar mansion presided over by Soma is highly auspicious. An undertaking under Soma is especially auspicious in the spring. "Presided over by Soma" refers to the mansion Mṛgaśiras, or perhaps exclusively during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). And it has been said by the Kauṣītakins: "On the new moon day or the full moon day, or on the day of the Soma sacrifice, one may undergo initiation, or indeed only during the bright fortnight."

The meaning is that both [the initiation and the conclusion] may take place during the bright fortnight alone. Śāṅkhāyana states: "The initiation occurs in the bright fortnight, and the conclusion on an auspicious lunar mansion. The author of the Sūtra also makes this known by stating the opposite—that one should sacrifice with the Soma or the Animal Sacrifice on either the new moon or the full moon day—thereby indicating that even a time occurring exclusively between the new moon and the full moon possesses the status of being an integral part of the entire sacrifice. By this, it is established as a matter of course that there is no such [exclusive] time in the dark fortnight.

It should also be understood that when the initiation (*dīkṣā*) takes place on the full moon day, the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*) occurs on the fourth day and subsequent days; likewise, when the initiation takes place on the new moon day, the pressing occurs on the fifth day and subsequent days. Regarding this matter, the Śruti of the Taittirīyas is heard: "Having sacrificed with either the New Moon oblation or the Full Moon oblation, one should undergo initiation upon that very oblation and upon that very sacrificial grass (*barhis*); this is the single initiation. [The term] *amāvāsyā*...

The oblation (*havis*) that is to be performed at the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is the *Amāvāsya* sacrifice; the oblation to be performed on the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) is the *Paurṇamāsa* sacrifice. Here, the word "oblation" (*havis*) indicates the sacrifice. The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of conjunction. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having sacrificed with the sacrifice associated with the new moon, or with the sacrifice associated with the full moon, one should undergo initiation (*dīkṣeta*). The word "on that [sacrificial grass]" (*tasmin barhiṣi*) is also connected with the word "only" (*eva*). Here too, the word "oblation" (*havis*) indicates the sacrifice; likewise, the word "sacrificial grass" (*barhis*) does as well.

The meaning is that one should undergo initiation (dīkṣā) only after that sacrifice known as the New Moon (Amāvāsyā) oblation has been performed, or after that sacrifice known as the Full Moon (Paurṇamāsī) sacrifice on the sacrificial grass (barhis) has been completed. "In that very oblation, in that very [sacrifice on] the sacrificial grass, one should undergo initiation" is an elaboration of what was already stated. The word division is *eṣā u* (this also). The particle *u* signifies the sense of "also. This is one initiation; even though it has been stated thus, there is also some other initiation.

Thus it is indicated. For this very reason, the author of the Sūtra has presented both alternatives: that the Soma sacrifice is preceded by an Iṣṭi, and that it is preceded by the Soma sacrifice. Lāṭyāyana and Drāhyāyaṇa have stated: "On the first day of the bright fortnight they undergo initiation; this is one form of initiation, or having observed the conjunction with a lunar mansion. The meaning of "having observed the conjunction with a lunar mansion" is as follows: having observed the conjunction with a lunar mansion such as Citrā on the full moon day of Caitra and so forth, one undergoes initiation.

However, according to another scripture (*śāstrāntara*), twelve initiations (*dīkṣā*) are fixed for the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*) on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). It has already been shown previously that the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) prescribing the sacrifice on the first half of the month applies only to cases other than those specifically ordained. In this alternative (*kalpa*) where the initiation is on the new moon day and the pressing is on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-iṣṭi*) would have lapsed; therefore, after the completion of the season (*ṛtu*) for their sake, there are the *pathikṛt*, *vaiśvānara*, and *kāya* offerings. This applies if the second or subsequent performance of these two [sacrifices] is intended.

Upon the omission of one [of these], there is either the *pāthikṛtī* or the *vaiśvānarī* [offering]. Regarding the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*), some hold that when the initiation occurs on the full moon day, or on the new moon day, or during the *saṃdhi-mālya* (the twilight period) prior to the sun's turning back (*āvartana*), there is no fault in the omission of the full moon or new moon sacrifices. However, when it occurs after the sun's turning back...

When the initiation (*dīkṣā*) occurs on an amāvāsyā that possesses a *saṃdhi* (conjunction with the previous day), and the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*) occurs on a pūrṇamāsī that likewise possesses a *saṃdhi* prior to the *āvartana*, then—because it is otherwise impossible to account for the production of a single unique transcendental result (*apūrva*) for the Full Moon sacrifice—the performance of a rite of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for its omission must certainly be accepted as mandatory. However, when first the Full Moon sacrifice is omitted and subsequently the New Moon sacrifice, the wise should understand that there is no expiation in that case. The mention of *juhoti* (the root *hu*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *yajati* (the root *yaj*).

It is well known from the *Yājñika* tradition that the commencement of the *Soma* sacrifice must be performed during the spring (*vasanta*) in the first year following the *ādhāna*. In this context, spring is of two kinds, distinguished as lunar (*cāndra*) and solar (*saura*). The lunar spring consists of two months, namely Caitra and Vaiśākha. Even if an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) occurs in between, it does not contradict its being composed of two months, for the *Smṛti* states: "The sixty days [of the intercalary period] have been declared by Bādarāyaṇa to constitute one month. Thus, it remains composed of two months.

By this Vedic text, "Karttika, Vasanta, and Mādhava—these two are the spring seasons (vāsantika-ṛtu)," the solar spring consists of the signs of Pisces and Aries, or alternatively, Aries and Taurus, because the *Vasantapāyana* states that spring belongs to either Pisces and Aries, or Aries and Taurus. Regarding their application, there is a Smṛti rule: "One should perform all Śrauta and Smārta rites during the lunar months; in the absence of those, one may do so during the solar months"—such is the opinion of the astronomers (*jyotirvid*).

Among the various festivals occurring within such two-fold spring seasons, a determination is made for those occasions that do not fall during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), because it is precisely there that the performance of the *Soma* sacrifice is required. Regarding this, the *Smṛti* in the *Kālādarśa* states: "Optional acts without a specific cause, great gifts and the like, the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*), sacrifices (*adhvara*), unprecedented rites (*apūrva*), pilgrimage to holy places (*tīrthayātrā*), protection of living beings, the consecration of deities, groves, tanks, and so forth, the investiture of the sacred thread (*maujibandhana*), the formal entry into a stage of life (*āśramasvīkṛti*), the optional release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*), and the departure [from the householder's life]."

7—566. One should avoid the following during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*): the consecration of a king; the first tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākarma*); the sacred observances (*vratas*); the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*); the commencement of building houses and their entry; the naming ceremony (*nāma*); marriage; the naming of a child after it has passed the ten-day period; divine festivals; the commencement and completion of optional vows; and expiation for all sins. *Adhvara* refers to a sacrifice (*yajña*).

In the *Kāṭhakagṛhya*: "Whatever rule regarding the observance of vows (*vratavidhi*) is prescribed for when the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*) is deficient, that very same is declared for a month with two transits (*dvisaṃkrānta*) and also for an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). Bṛhaspati: "Whether Venus is in its infancy (*bāla*) or its old age (*vṛddha*), or when it has set, one should avoid visiting deities during these times, just as one would in an intercalary month. Lalla: "When Venus is in its sign of debilitation (*nīca*), in retrogression (*vakrasaṃstha*), or even when it has moved beyond its fourth quarter (*caraṇagate*), or when it is in its infancy, old age, or has set—then renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), pilgrimages to deities (*devayātrā*), the rules for vows and observances (*vrata-niyama-vidhi*), ear-piercing (*karṇavedha*), and initiation (*dīkṣā*) [are forbidden]."

"The tying of the *mauñjī* (sacred grass girdle) for women, the rite of marriage, or the consecration of a deity for the household—these should be diligently performed by the virtuous when Jupiter is situated in the sign of Leo. Thus [it is said]. *Dīkṣā* refers to both initiation for sacrifice (*yāgadīkṣā*) and initiation for mantras (*mantradīkṣā*). Prohibitions regarding the intercalary month (*kṣayamāsa*) and their corresponding exceptions are to be understood from my work, the *Smārta-saṃskāra-ratnamālā*. Although one should avoid both the commencement and completion of optional rites (*kāmya*) during an intercalary month, [the following applies]:

Although there is no prohibition against the commencement and completion of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites by the prohibition of the commencement and completion of *Diti* [the period of impurity], nevertheless, because of the statement, "In the case of *mala*, one should perform obligatory and occasional rites only when there is no other way," there is indeed a prohibition of these two as well when it is possible [to avoid them]. In the first performance, if no other alternative exists and the time has not yet passed, the commencement must certainly be made. As for those [texts] stating: "If an eclipse or an intercalary month occurs during the first *parvan*..."

"Likewise, when Pauṣa is an intercalary month (malimluca), the Anvārambhaṇīya [Iṣṭi] is not desired; nor during the retrogression of Jupiter or Venus, nor during an eclipse of the moon or sun. Such statements refer to cases where the commencement of the pure time has been bypassed due to negligence and the like. Regarding this, the authors of the Dharmaśāstra digests cite Garga’s statement in the *Aparārka*: "One should perform the naming ceremony (nāmakarma) and the Darśa-iṣṭi according to their proper time; if there is a lapse, they should be performed in a praiseworthy month under an auspicious asterism. The underlying sense is that there is no fault in performing what has reached its [proper] time.

In this way, the conceptual construction (vikalpa) afflicted by eight defects is avoided, provided it is possible [to avoid them]. The mention of the *darśeṣṭi* is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites. The mention of the *ārambhaṇīyā* is an elliptical indication for the commencement of ritual acts. The prohibition of initiation (*dīkṣā*) mentioned previously refers to optional initiation (*kāmyadīkṣā*), or else it refers to the prohibition of initiation when there is the possibility of another time. Now, however, the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭas*) is as follows: [the text continues with] the non-returning of those who have not [received initiation], etc. [End of] Chapter 10.

Accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. It is indeed the *chāna* [the specific time]. However, although it might follow that if the final [period] in spring is specifically prescribed and yet afflicted by defects such as *vyatīpāta*, one must nevertheless commence the rite because of the superior authority (*prābalya*) of the Śruti, nevertheless—since the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) is without exception and possesses equal weight as a limb (*aṅga*) of the Veda—the defects mentioned therein must also be accepted. Let this digression suffice.

If, however, one were to say merely "one initiation and so forth" or "initiation on a non-parvan day" or "initiation on a festival day," the separate mention of the four [numbers] is intended to ensure that the specific resolution (*saṃkalpa*) must be made regarding whichever option is to be adopted at the commencement; thus, in the case of the option of an "unlimited initiation" consisting of any number from five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, or eleven, [the specific number such as] five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, or eleven [must be determined].

This is intended to demonstrate the distinction in purpose: that when adopting the alternative of an unlimited number of initiations (*dīkṣā*), one must resolve upon the recitation in the form "having uttered the word for number in its uninflected state"; and when adopting the alternative of a limited number of initiations—consisting of one, two, three, or four—one must resolve upon the recitation in the very same form: "having uttered the word for number in its uninflected state as one, two, three, or four, having adopted the alternative of that specific number of initiations."

The investigation initiated by the first sūtra—"one may desire [the two] simultaneously, or in separate meals"—is examined immediately thereafter. Following that, the rule regarding time is established, as time is the most fundamental among all requirements. Next, by way of incidental connection (*prasaṅga*), the prohibition against performing the *darśapūrṇamāsa* at the commencement of the *prakṛti* and *vikṛti* sacrifices is discussed as the regulator of their relationship. Subsequently, again through incidental connection, it is demonstrated that the *agniṣṭoma* is the archetype (*prakṛti*) for all *soma* sacrifices.

By way of incidental connection (*prasaṅga-saṃgatyā*), the fact that the *atirātra* sacrifice precedes the *agniṣṭoma* is demonstrated. It should be understood that because it was required, the demonstration of the number and other details of the consecrations (*dīkṣā*) intended for the sacrifice has also been made right here. The section beginning with "on the day of the new moon sacrifice" (*amāvāsyāyāṃ yajanīye 'hani*) and ending with "or the consecration" (*dīkṣā vā*) is common to all sacrifices (*sarvakratu-sādhāraṇam*). However, the author of the Sūtras will state the specific details in their respective places.

Where there is no explicit mention of the performer, the rule is universal that the Adhvaryu alone is the performer, according to the technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) that "wherever [the agent] is not specified, it is the Adhvaryu."

"You have spoken greatness for me; you have spoken glory for me; you have spoken splendor for me; you have spoken enjoyment for me; you have spoken praise for me; you have spoken everything for me—may that protect me, may that enter me, through that may I enjoy. Thus he murmurs each time he is chosen.

Having placed the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder and having sipped water, Bharadvāja states that one should mutter [the mantra] while standing facing east or while sitting. The meaning is that each priest who has been chosen by the sacrificer mutters this mantra. The repetition "each and every one" (vṛto vṛtaḥ) is for the purpose of ensuring that it applies to all priests; otherwise, according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "whenever [it says] 'the Adhvaryu'," it would apply to the Adhvaryu alone. Rather, it is intended so that it applies to everyone. "Chosen" means one who has been requested by the sacrificer and has undertaken the performance of the priestly duties (*ārtvijya*) in the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice which is his own duty.

Thus, it is understood that this recitation of the mantra occurs only upon the commencement of the *āśvin* sacrifice. To this effect, Āpastamba and Baudhāyana state: "One who is about to appoint a *somapravāka* should say, 'Homage to King Soma,' and then dismiss him; one who is about to perform [the sacrifice] should recite [the mantra], 'A great thing you have spoken to me.'"

By this [formula], even for one who intends to cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice, [the priest] says: "O Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ! You have proclaimed long life for me; you have proclaimed vigor for me; you have proclaimed glory for me; you have proclaimed prosperity for me. May I become possessed of long life, possessed of vigor, possessed of glory, possessed of prosperity, and possessed of honor. Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ! May I become everything. Having said this, he either announces [his acceptance] or acknowledges [the invitation]. This is what is stated by Bhāradvāja, and it is here set aside. *Pratyākhyānam* means rejection or refusal. [End of] Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Seventh Praśna. 568. [Section on] Rejection.

The resolve, "I shall perform the office of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)," constitutes the formal acceptance (*pratijñāna*). By this, it is also established that because there is no formal selection (*varaṇa*) in a *sattra* sacrifice, there is likewise an absence of the *japa*. *Japa* is merely the utterance [of the mantra]. According to the rules of grammar, if the accents (*svara*) are clearly discerned, it is *cātuḥsvarya* (fourfold accentuation) due to its being a *japa*; if they are not discerned, it is *ekaśrutya* (monotone). This should be understood to apply everywhere regarding the *japa* of Vedic mantras (*sautramantra*).

In rites other than *japa*, regarding both Sautra and Vaidika mantras used in sacrificial acts—specifically those that are not *japa*, *nyūṅkha*, or *sāman*—there is only *ekaśrutya* (monotone), according to Pāṇini’s rule: "In sacrificial acts, [the monotone applies] to those [mantras] other than *japa*, *nyūṅkha*, and *sāmans*. Alternatively, based on Kātyāyana’s *Prātiśākhya-sūtra*—"either *tāna* or *prāvacana*"—there is also the possibility of *cātuḥsvarya* (four accents). *Tāna* means monotone. Āśvalāyana describes its nature: "The closest proximity of the acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita*) accents is *ekaśrutya*. *Prāvacana* refers to what has come from the recitation (*pravacana*) of the Veda; thus, it is the accentuation found in the Vedic text itself.

The meaning is that the accent should be exactly as it is recited in the Veda. It is understood from the absence of any specific statement that both [the high and low pitch] are intended by the Teacher. However, in the silent recitation (*japa*) of Vedic mantras, there is indeed the fourfold accent (*cātuḥsvarya*). Furthermore, regarding consecration (*abhimantraṇa*), authorization (*anumantraṇa*), touching (*abhimarśana*), and standing near (*upasthāna*), their accent is likewise *upāṃśu* (inaudible), because they are subordinate to the *japa*; according to the maxim "a cognition does not grasp a qualified object unless it has grasped the qualifier," these share the same accent as the *japa*. This is established by the Yajurvedic paribhāṣā rule: "That which belongs to the Yajurveda is to be performed inaudibly" (*yājuṣaṃ tūpāṃśu*).

In the *Sāmpāśu Jyotiṣṭoma*, beginning from the Sūtra stating "prior to the Āgnīṣomīya" up until the point where it says "he commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the Āgnīṣomīya animal sacrifice," whatever mantras belong to the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda must be employed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). Beyond that, they should be understood as being recited in the prescribed accentuation. Regarding the Śrauta rites, there is an option (*vikalpa*) concerning the recollection of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other details for both the Sūtra mantras and the Vedic mantras. In this regard, the seers are to be found in the *Kāṇḍānukramaṇikā*.

The meter (*chandas*) of these verses composed in metrical feet is derived from the *Piṅgala* and other treatises; the deities (*devatā*), however, are determined from the indicative marks within the mantras themselves. Since they are not accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) nowadays, the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other such details are not presented here. At the time of ritual application (*prayoga*), the recitation of the mantras should always be at a medium pace (*madhyamā vṛtti*), and not at a rapid (*drutā*) or slow (*vilambitā*) pace. Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "One should employ the rapid pace for the purpose of practice, the medium pace for the purpose of ritual application, and the slow pace for the purpose of instructing disciples."

"May the god go to the god; may Soma go to Soma by the path of *ṛta*, leaving behind all evil deeds"—with this mantra, he sets out, departing from his house to go to the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering. Or else, [he mounts] the path with the mantra: "Thou art the name 'Path', the track that leads to Soma; may I reach Soma. Thus he takes his stand upon the road.
He proceeds along the path leading to the sacrificial hall for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering with the mantra beginning with "paveti.

He consecrates the ancestors three times with the mantra "pitaro bhūḥ," and he consecrates his own fathers, or alternatively, the divine ones. *Abhimantraṇa* (consecration) consists of reciting a mantra while meditating upon the object denoted by that mantra, facing toward that object, and praising it. In this context, the objects denoted by the mantra are the ancestors; [of them...]
The term "īkṣan" (looking) is due to negligence.

Since [the object] is perceptible, the meaning of the prefix *abhi-* as "facing towards" does not apply; rather, it signifies only "meditating upon. Thus, the prefix *abhi-* is used in the sense of the inseparable preposition (*anv-*) *anu*. Consequently, the meaning of "abhimanyate" (he meditates upon) is simply "he thinks of" (*āmantraṇa*).

Alternatively, since the Śruti declares, "This indeed is the direction of the ancestors," thereby showing that the southern direction is related to the ancestors, even though the ancestors themselves are imperceptible, the direction associated with them is perceptible; thus, facing that direction is equivalent to facing the ancestors. By the word "direction" (dik), it is simply a location (deśa) that is intended here; otherwise, the aforementioned defect would remain unavoidable. By this, the objection—"How can the direction, which is accessible only through inference based on the signs of 'farness' and 'nearness' resulting in 'priority' and 'posteriority,' be perceptible?"—is refuted.

In this context, there is a facing toward the south, based on the observation that "this is the direction of the ancestors. Āpastamba also refers to it by the term *dakṣiṇāvṛtta* (turned toward the south), stating, "turned toward the south, he worships the ancestors. Bharadvāja, however, explicitly states the facing toward the south, saying, "facing south, he worships the ancestors. Regarding this, there is an option (*vikalpa*) for the *prācīnāvīta* mode of wearing the sacred thread, according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā-sūtra*) stating, "there is no fixed rule in other cases."

It must necessarily be stated that the prescription of wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīti*) applies only where it is specifically enjoined and not elsewhere; otherwise, it would result in its being purposeless. And thus, since there is no such prescription in the present case, the rule of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*)—"there is no restriction elsewhere"—comes into operation.

Regarding the rule that "where the action is performed upon a single substance, one should recite the mantra only once," this technical definition (paribhāṣā) does not mean that there is one recitation with the mantra and two silently; rather, there is a repetition of the mantra here because the consecration (abhimantraṇa) consists primarily in the utterance [of the words]. For one whose father is living, there is an option regarding the consecration for the side of his paternal ancestors. Thus say Lāṭyāyana and Dvaidhāyana: "In the case of an interruption in the Yajus, Dhānañjayya [prescribes] a supplementary recitation (anvāhāra), while Śāṇḍilya [prescribes] neglect (upekṣaṇa)."

Regarding this: "In the *yajurantaraya*—that is, in the interval (*antaraya*) between the *yajus* formulas; for *antaraya* means omission (*utsarga*). For one whose father is living, there is a deliberation (*vicāra*) concerning the omission of these mantras: should the omission be performed or should it not be performed? In this regard, Dhānañjayya maintains that it is an *anvāhāra*, meaning non-omission. Śāṇḍilya, however, maintains that it is *upekṣaṇa*, meaning avoidance."

The intention of Dhānañjaya is that the recitation (*japa*) must indeed be performed by addressing either the *pitṛs* of the sacrificer, such as the *Agnivāttas* and others, or the *pitṛs* beginning with *Avama*. The intention of Śāṇḍilya is that the recitation should be addressed to one's own *pitṛs* only, and it is to be omitted when one's own *pitṛs* are living. Thus, this is established: in the case of one's own *pitṛs*, it is omitted when one's own father is living; in the case of the sacrificer’s *pitṛs*, it is omitted when the sacrificer’s father is living. However, in the case of the celestial (*divya*) *pitṛs*, the worship of the *Agnivāttas* and others must certainly be performed even by one whose father is living.

Or rather, it refers to the "lowest ones" (avamāḥ) and others mentioned in the *Chandoga-śruti* as "the three indeed are the Pitṛs: the Aurvas and the Kāvyas. Because of the singular number [in the mantra], this applies only to the Adhvaryu priest in the phrase "devo devam," etc., and not to all the ṛtvij priests. Alternatively, the word "each" (*vṛtaḥ*) should be understood as recurring [with each priest]. In this way, the ritual entry with the mantra, the standing upon the path (*panthya*), and the non-invitation (*animantraṇa*) apply to all of them as well.

In this view, even in the *saṃsāra-yajña*, the statement to be uttered in the subsequent sūtra is intended solely to preclude the status of being the creator of all; for here, the *kūśmāṇḍa-homa* is performed at the beginning of the rites, according to the Vedic injunction (*śruti*). And that [homa] is performed either according to the method stated in the *śruti* or according to the method stated by Baudhāyana. When performed according to the method stated in the *śruti*, the worship (*upasthāna*) is done with the *ṣaṇṇava* [mantras] of the section beginning with "vaiśvānarāya," and not with the final verse; likewise, there is no offering of fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*) nor the bestowing of boons (*vara-dāna*).

When performed according to the method prescribed by Baudhāyana, the placing of the final fuel-stick (*samit*) and the granting of the boon (*varadāna*) take place. However, in this *Kuśmāṇḍahoma*, even when performed according to the method prescribed by Baudhāyana, these two do not occur. In the case of the option of "drawing out" (*uddharaṇa*), one should abandon the Āhavanīya fire drawn out for the purpose of the *Kuśmāṇḍahoma*, smear the hearth (*āyatana*) with cow-dung, re-establish that fire, and then perform the preparation of the Pravargya materials.
In this preparation of the Pravargya, because the sacrificer has not yet undergone initiation (dīkṣita), the oblation indeed takes place.
For one about to be initiated, he offers the twelve Saṃbhāra-yajus oblations with the formula "Agni with the Yajus-verses."

The meaning is that one offers oblations with twelve *yajus* mantras known as the *saṃbhāra-yajus*. Alternatively, it means one performs twelve oblations named *saṃbhāra-yajus*. The deities are Agni and the others, appearing in the nominative case, and the *yajus* and the others, appearing in the instrumental case. For the last [oblation], the formula is "to me, from Śraddhā. Alternatively, the indeclinable word "I" (*aham*) is the designator for the specific deity called Ahaṃkāra. In this view, the formula for the dedication of the offering is simply: "This is mine, from Śraddhā."

The sacrificial formulas (*tyāga-vākya*) are appropriately joined as follows: "To Agni, accompanied by the *yajus* formulas, this [offering]"; "To Savitṛ, accompanied by the *stomas*, this [offering]," and so forth. However, it should be understood that the final formula is either: "To me, accompanied by faith, this [offering]" or "I, accompanied by faith, this [offering]. The mention of one who is about to be initiated (*dīkṣiṣyamāṇa*) is intended to indicate that this oblation serves the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*) itself, and not the purpose of formal selection (*varaṇa*).

The partial purpose previously mentioned is precisely that the exclusion of all other options (*vikalpa*) follows from the absence of any application of a restrictive rule (*varaṇa*). Furthermore, there is another purpose: by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating "that which is the time of the principal is the time, place, agent, and fire for the subsidiaries," since the initiation (*dīkṣā*) is performed in the afternoon, its performance must likewise be carried out only in the afternoon.

In this regard, the procedure is as follows: when the ritual actions beginning with the *saṃkalpa* and ending with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa-homa* have been performed in the morning, one should pause in order to await the afternoon; then, in the afternoon itself, one begins with the twelve *saṃbhāra-yajus* offerings. According to the ritual manual (*kalpa*) which states that the gathering of materials (*saṃbharaṇa*) for the *pravargya* ceremony occurs immediately after the *Kūṣmāṇḍa-homa*, one should pause when the ritual actions at the end of that [homa] have been completed in the morning, and then begin with the twelve *saṃbhāra-yajus* offerings in the afternoon.

Here, "afternoon" (*aparāhna*) refers either to the second part of a day divided into two, or to the third part of a day divided into three; indeed, the basis for the division here into five parts will be demonstrated in the *Yājamāna-sūtra*. The mention of "twelve" is intended either to exclude other mantras or to exclude other oblations (*homa*).

The statement "Agni is the Yami" refers to the *saṃbhārayajus* formulas; he causes [the sacrificer] to recite them and offers oblations with these mantras. Having explained the *saṃbhārayajus* formulas, [the text says] "he proceeds with the fire churned by friction (*nirmanthya*) according to the procedure for churning. In order to remove the expectation as to what these *saṃbhārayajus* formulas are, it is stated that there are twelve from the very beginning because they are present [in the context]. This is because the formulas beginning with "Agni is the Yami" are dependent [on others] and thus incapable of manifesting [the meaning] independently, whereas independence is seen in the formula "May these protect this sacrifice."

It should be understood that Āpastamba used the term "as recited" (*āmnāta*) in order to ensure that the connection [of the mantra] does not apply to all sentences. The re-spread of the fires (*punarviharaṇa*) is for the purpose of the *saṃmāra* (rubbing) *yajus*. The abandonment [of the offering] occurs at the end of the *homa*. According to the general rule (*paribhāṣā*)—"where one enjoins a rite with a group of mantras, there one should offer for each mantra"—the *homa* is performed for each individual mantra. Because these are enjoined by the root *hu* (to sacrifice), the utterance of *svāhā* is required in them.

According to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "offerings are made with the *juhū* ladle into the *āhavanīya* fire," the *āhavanīya* is the locus and the *juhū* is the instrument. However, regarding the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*), the *Bhāradvājīya-paribhāṣā-sūtra* states that one may offer the oblation after strewing grass around whichever fire is available. Furthermore, the acts of wiping (*parimārjana*) and sprinkling water (*pariṣeka*) are established by the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) found in the *Agnikārya-sūtra*, which says, "having wiped it, he sprinkles it as before. We shall now explain the *darvihoma* offerings; when the injunction "he offers" (*juhoti*) is issued, it refers to a *darvihoma* wherever it occurs. In the case of the *śrāddha* rite, [the offering is made] in the *kha*. [Note: *kha* likely refers to a specific vessel or location].

And where there is a *svāhākāra*, that [offering] is with clarified butter taken once silently; having gone around the front of the Āhavanīya fire and standing to the south, the Adhvaryu offers it into the Āhavanīya with the *svāhākāra*. In the case of groups of offerings consisting of two or more, having taken [butter] for each offering and having placed fuel-sticks for each offering, he offers them separately.
This is the rule for *davihoma* (libations from a ladle) everywhere, based on the Paribhāṣā-sūtra: "Where one enjoins an action by means of a group of mantras, one should offer for each mantra."
Having mentally recited the *Saptahotṛ* formula and offered the oblation along with the *graha*, he performs the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice.

Regarding the *Saptahotṛ* oblation, Baudhāyana has stated that the sacrificer must perform the act of following-touch (*anvārambha*) upon the Adhvaryu, according to the sūtra: "Having mentally recited the *Saptahotṛ*, he offers [the oblation] into the Āhavanīya fire while the sacrificer maintains the touch, saying 'khāhā'. The deity of this [oblation] is Vācaspati, as indicated by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra. On this point, some say that because of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating "The Brahman is indeed the *Catuhhotṛ*," the word "Brahmaṇaḥ" (of the Brahman) should also be uttered; thus they maintain that the formula of relinquishment (*tyāga-vākya*) is: "This is for Vācaspati, the Brahman."

The term "dīkṣiṣyamāṇa" (one about to be initiated) from the preceding sūtra is understood here as well. Furthermore, there is scriptural authority (*śruti*) for both cases: "One about to be initiated, having mentally recited the *saptahotṛ* formula, should offer [oblations] in the *āhavanīya* fire," and "One about to be initiated offers a cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni-Viṣṇu. By the use of the suffix *-luṭ* in the word "dīkṣiṣyamāṇaḥ"—which is prescribed when another action is the purpose of the action denoted by the verbal root—the fact that it effects a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agent of initiation is understood.

Initiation (*dīkṣā*) consists of the state of fitness conducive to the adoption of the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*); it is called *dīkṣaṇīyā* because its purpose is the purification of the one who performs it. However, since the items to be described later—such as the black antelope skin, the girdle, and the staff—are not themselves ritual acts, they merely manifest initiation; they do not have "initiation" as their purpose in the same way that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice does. Therefore, immediately after the sacrifice, the duties of the initiated one (*dīkṣita*), such as "he does not offer oblations" and "he does not give gifts," apply.

This was stated by Jaimini in the third pāda of the fifth adhyāya: "One becomes initiated after the announcement, because of the connection with the initiation and its implements; or rather, at the end of the sacrifice, because it is for that purpose and connected to specific objects; and the designation is likewise. Because of the connection with the initiation and its implements, such as the sacrificial post (samiṣṭi) and the staff (daṇḍa), one becomes initiated after the announcement—meaning immediately following the "announcement" (āvedana) prescribed in the injunction "he announces the initiated one"—as expressed by the words "one should become initiated."

Regarding the phrase "enapā dvitīyā," the *Tattvaratna* states that one must justify the usage "pareṇāvedanāt" by postulating the grammatical rule *pañcamy api dṛśyate*. Thus, the meaning of the first sūtra is that the duties (*dharma*) of initiation (*dīkṣā*) commence at this very point. As for the meaning of the second sūtra: the word "or" (*vā*) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The duties of initiation commence only at the conclusion of the sacrifice (*iṣṭyanta*).

For this reason—because there is no distinction in the connection with the purpose, and because that purpose belongs to it—the *iṣṭi* (sacrifice) itself is primary; therefore, immediately after its conclusion, the duties of initiation (*dīkṣā*) commence. "No distinction exists" means that there is no dependence on specific supplementary statements (*viśeṣavākya*); in other words, it is independent. Such is the meaning of the *dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi*.

The meaning of this is as follows: the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice is designated as an "offering" (*iṣṭi*), and consequently, the duties of the initiated (*dīkṣita*) apply after that offering; thus, it serves as a supporting factor for the preceding [sūtra], just as in the previous case. This is the meaning of the third sūtra. If it is argued that, in this way, the author of the Sūtras’ statement regarding the undertaking of the duties of the initiated after the restraint of speech (*vāgyamana*) would be without a reason, the answer is: true. Even though the rites beginning with the giving of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), the girdle (*mekhalā*), and the staff (*daṇḍa*) do not themselves constitute the form of initiation (*dīkṣā*), they certainly possess the status of being for the sake of initiation (*dīkṣārthatva*).

And thus, since this action also must be performed only in the afternoon—by obtaining a reason in the form of making this known—the fallacy of being causeless (*nirhetukatva*) does not arise. Furthermore, even when the *dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi* sacrifice is performed after the completion of the *prapādana* (leading forward) of the eastern portion, it occurs immediately thereafter. Because the *dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi* is for the purpose of purifying the agent of the consecration (*dīkṣā*), its repetition in every performance is established.

The *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice also serves the purpose of securing the deities, based on the scriptural statement: "Having secured the deities on both sides, the sacrificer attains [the goal]. Therefore, in the *sarvatomukha* sacrifice, that [rite] occurs for each separate sacrificial arrangement (*vihāra*). The *saptahotṛ* formula is not a part of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, but rather a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) itself. Consequently, when the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is postponed, the postponement of the *saptahotṛ* and the separation of the *āhavanīya* fire from the *saptahotṛ* and the *dīkṣaṇīyā*—these two points—are established. However, by the suffix *-ktvā*, only priority in time (*pūrvakālatā*) is expressed.

Then, having carried forth the Āhavanīya fire from the Gārhapatya for the sake of the Saptahotr and offered the Saptahotra oblation, one should carry forth the Āhavanīya for the sake of the Soma sacrifice and perform the Dīkṣaṇīyā. Due to the displacement of the Dīkṣaṇīyā caused by the obstacle, the Saptahotra oblation must indeed be performed even if it falls between the Saptahotra and the Dīkṣaṇīyā-iṣṭi; the Saptahotra is [to be recited] mentally.

The rule "Having performed the *sagraha* oblation in sequence, one offers the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice" is overridden by the principle of "the non-conflict with what is established" (*śiṣṭākopanyāya*) regarding the immediate succession following the *saptahotṛ* oblation as indicated by the gerund suffix (*ktvā*). That principle is as follows: when it is argued that the sequence prescribed by Vedic injunctions—such as "having prepared the altar (*vedi*), one prepares the sacrificial site (*vedī*)"—overrides the rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and other acts enjoined by Smṛti (e.g., "one should perform [acts] after rinsing the mouth") because the latter are merely subsidiary details, we reply that since sequence is a property of the ritual action (*padārtha-dharma*), the rinsing of the mouth and such acts possess greater authority (*prābalya*) than the sequence itself, owing to their status as primary ritual elements (*padārtha*).

In consideration of the relative strength or weakness of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is the strength or weakness of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) alone that is stronger, because it presents itself first. Since the contradiction between the means of knowledge is rooted in the contradiction between the objects of knowledge, one must first examine the strength of the object of knowledge based on that prior contradiction; therefore, the final determination is made by that [object] alone. Thus, there is no sublation of acts such as rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), but rather only of the sequence. In the present case as well, having set aside the obligatory (*nitya*) rite which has arrived at its time and lacks any other occasion (*niravakāśa*), the optional (*sāvakāśa*) rite must then be performed; thus, the performance of the *homa* enjoined by general Smṛti remains mandatory.

By this [rule], the immediate succession [of the *saptahotṛ-homa*] must be understood as being set aside. Thus, the *agnihotra-homa* must indeed be performed in the middle. Jaimini states this very point in the third pāda of the first adhyāya through three sūtras: "If it is argued that there is no contradiction because the learned [tradition] does not object; [we reply] no, because the scripture has a fixed measure; or rather, when no specific cause for exclusion is perceived, those [acts] employed [in the sequence] should be recognized [as valid]."

In this context, the first sūtra is intended to raise an objection regarding the commencement of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*); the second sūtra refutes that objection; and the third is the sūtra stating the established conclusion itself. The meaning of the first sūtra is that when there is no contradiction or subversion of the Vedic sequence and so forth belonging to the remainder [of the ritual], the Smṛti injunction for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) and other such acts is not inconsistent. By the word "if" (*cet*), the commencement of the established conclusion is raised as a possibility. In the second sūtra, by the word "no" (*na*), that [objection] is rejected. It is not non-contradictory, but rather it is indeed contradictory. He states the reason for this: "because of the fixed measure of the scripture" (*śāstraparimāṇatvāt*).

The meaning of the phrase "because they are limited by scripture" (*śāstraparimitatvāt*) is that since the sequence, time, and quantity of the constituent acts—such as sipping water (*ācamana*) and so forth—are already determined by the perceptible scripture (*pratyakṣa-śāstra*) prior to their performance; [the acts] are thus limited by scripture. The meaning of the third sūtra is that when there is no apprehension—that is, no perception—of a cause for sublation, the acts such as sipping water performed by the learned (*śiṣṭas*) should be recognized as authoritative. By the word *api vā* ("or rather"), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is set aside.

The *aupāsana-homa* should likewise be performed in the middle [of the ritual]. Regarding the separate carrying forward (*praṇayana*) of the *āhavanīya* fire for the sake of the *kūṣmāṇḍa-homa* and other rites, this should be understood to apply under the option of "carrying forth" (*uddharaṇa-pakṣa*), based on the sūtra: "For each purpose, he carries forth the *āhavanīya*. However, under the "uninterrupted" (*ajasra*) option, there is no carrying forth because the *āhavanīya* is to be maintained perpetually. Even under the option of "carrying forth," the *dakṣiṇāgni* is indeed to be maintained perpetually; the *gārhapatya* and *dakṣiṇāgni* are maintained perpetually.

According to the sūtra: "vācaspate hṛdvidhe" is the mantra known as the *graha*. Reciting the mantra known as the *saptahotṛ*, namely "mahāhaviḥ," mentally along with that [first mantra] in such a way that they occur together, one offers the oblation between the two *upayāma*s without breathing in.
