Since it is so enjoined, having uttered the word *svāhā*, one offers it according to the rules for a *darvihoma* (ladle-oblation).

In the Sūtra, the qualification "I" (*sāham*) is for the purpose of reciting even the *maha* formulas mentally, but not for the purpose of including them in the *graha*-offerings. As for that [qualification], its establishment is achieved by the very Sūtra to be stated later: "Those which are heard in the texts as being for the purpose of the *homa*, they should be employed together with the *grahas* and the *svāhā*-utterance. The term "mentally" (*manasā*) is intended to exclude the state of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*), which would otherwise be obtained through the general rule (*paribhāṣā*). "Dīkṣaṇīyā" means that by which one is consecrated (*dīkṣate*); the meaning is that he performs—that is, prepares—the *iṣṭi*.

It is impossible to state that the word *nirvapati* has the meaning of "offering" (*nirvāpa*), because the term *iṣṭi* refers to a specific ritual action, and thus [the act of] offering is not possible [within its scope]. The inclusion of the word *iṣṭi* is for the purpose of securing the use of the term *aiṣṭa* in the *anvādhāna* mantra: "*deikṣaṇīyameṣṭara haviridameṣāṃ mayī*" (This is the sacrificial oblation of the *deikṣaṇīyā* sacrifice; may it be among these for me). Otherwise, it would have been merely "*deikṣaṇīya haviridameṣāṃ mayī*. Therefore, the word *iṣṭi* is included.

The statement, "He offers the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice," is a general proposition intended to demonstrate that this is the name of this particular sacrifice. By this, it is established that for sacrifices possessing names, there is a designation by the name even in the *anvādhāna* mantra, and not merely as "sacrifice" (*iṣṭi*). Thus, the term "dīkṣaṇīyam" should also be uttered.

By the rule stating that "in the iṣṭis and paśubandhas beginning with the Prāyaṇīyā and ending with the Avabhṛtha, the undertaking of the vow (vratopāyana), the keeping of vigil (jāgaraṇa), the girding of the wife (patnīsanahana), and the forest-food (āraṇyāśana) do not exist," the prohibition of the undertaking of the vow and other such rites from the Prāyaṇīyā onwards implies that the Dīkṣaṇīyā sacrifice is to be performed immediately after the Satahotṛ-homa. Thus, the Soma [sacrifices]...

Because it is not yet established [as a sacrifice], there is the undertaking of the vow; after the strewing of grass, there is the absence of keeping watch (jāgaraṇa), which consists in not closing the eyes for even a moment in place of sleep; there is the girding of the wife; and if hunger exists, there is indeed the eating of forest food. Regarding the requirement for the substance and deity in the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* [initiation] sacrifice, he says:
"An offering on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni and Viṣṇu, or a caru-oblation of clarified butter dedicated to Agni and Viṣṇu."

In this context, the word "from the *havirbhāna*" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Alternatively, the accusative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "He performs the *dakṣiṇīyā* sacrifice with an *āgnāvaiṣṇava* offering consisting of eleven potsherds, or with an *āgnāvaiṣṇava* oblation (*caru*) of clarified butter placed in a vessel made from a corpse. Thus, the meaning is: "One should perform a sacrifice characterized by either eleven potsherds or an oblation. By the suffix *-aṇ*, which denotes the deity, the deity is established in the term *āgnāvaiṣṇavam*.

The term *ekādaśakapāla* (eleven-potsherd) denotes a substance: a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) prepared upon eleven potsherds is called *ekādaśakapāla*. By the phrase *ghṛte carum* (the rice-mess in ghee), another substance is prescribed in place of the eleven-potsherd cake. The meaning of *ghṛte carum* is that the rice-mess (*caru*) which is prepared when it has been placed in ghee while in the state of being boiled is the *ghṛte-caru*; it does not mean "a rice-mess boiled in ghee. This is because pure ghee lacks the inherent capacity to provide the heat necessary for the cooking process suitable for preparing a rice-mess. In the case of [boiling] in ghee...

Baudhāyana also says, "When the cooking of the oblation is near. This means that one should pour the clarified butter (ghṛta) when the cooking of the sacrificial porridge (caru) is imminent. Although this is established by the mention of the Āgnāvaiṣṇava [offering] alone, the repetition is for the sake of restriction: the porridge in clarified butter belongs specifically to the Āgnāvaiṣṇava, and not to the Āditya, as stated by Āpastamba, that the porridge in clarified butter becomes [the offering] for the Āgnāvaiṣṇava.

By this it is known that the statement of Āpastamba—that the *puroḍāśa* is for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), while the *caru* cooked in clarified butter is for one desiring progeny or cattle—should also be understood as prescribing the optional nature (*kāmyatva*) of both the *puroḍāśa* and the *caru*. Regarding the specific characteristics of the *caru*, the *Sārasaṃgraha* states: "A *caru* is well-cooked when its steam has not yet escaped, when it is thoroughly steamed, neither burnt nor hard; it should not be excessively soft, nor should it be cooked until its essence is lost."

— 43.7 — Regarding the definition of *caru*, the Mīmāṃsakas also state in the third chapter of their treatises that it is "rice cooked with internal heat (*antarūṣmapakva*) without being drained, independent of clarity (*vaiśadya*). The portioning (*avadāna*) of the *caru* is performed with a stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), according to the sūtra: "Of the *carus*, with a stirring-spoon. After the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice, there is the disposal (*praharaṇa*) of that stirring-spoon; for this is established elsewhere by the explicit injunction regarding the *Prāyaṇīyā* offering, as has been largely demonstrated.

This is because it has been clearly stated by Baudhāyana. In this context, the natural (prākṛta) accent applies to the *prayāja*s, *ājyabhāga*s, *sviṣṭakṛt*, *anūyāja*s, *sūktavāka*, *śaṃyuvāka*, and the *patnīsaṃyāja*s. Regarding the accent for the principal offerings (*pradhāna*), there is a specific rule from another recensional branch (*śākhā*): "In the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, one should recite with as much loudness as one desires. By this, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is to be performed with as much loudness as is appropriate. Similarly, it is said that it should be "low" (*mandra*) in the *prāyaṇīyā* and "lower still" (*mandratara*) in the *ātithyā*; thus, [the accents] for the *prāyaṇīyā* and *ātithyā* are established.

This should also be observed regarding the specific accents of the *ṣayaka* (the concluding formula). In that regard, Āpastamba has stated several alternative views concerning the primary accent: "They proceed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) for everything prior to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice; then, according to some, he recites at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* with as much voice as he possesses, then lower at the *prāyaṇīyā*, and still lower at the *ātithyā*; [he proceeds] in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) during the *upasads*, and [finally] with a soft tone (*mandra*) at the *agnīṣomīya*. Or, [another view is: with a soft tone at the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, with a softer tone at the *prāyaṇīyā*, and with an even softer tone at the *ātithyā*."

Regarding the rule: "The *śūpasat* [formulas] are loud; the *agnīṣomīya* [offering] is whispered; in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* it is more whispered; in the *prāyaṇīyā* it is even more whispered; in the *ātithyā* it is whispered; the *śūpasat* [formulas] are loud; the *agnīṣomīya* [offering] is whispered. Because of the statement "they proceed" (*caranti*), according to the principle that "whispering applies only to the principal part," whispering belongs only to the principal offerings of the *iṣṭi*. However, the commentators maintain that for the subsidiaries, such as the *prayāja*s and so forth, it is "as in the archetype" (*yathāprakṛti*).

However, Jaimini, in the first section of the ninth chapter, states through the sūtra *deśasaṃbaddham upāṃśutvaṃ teṣāṃ syāc chrutinirdeśāt tasya ca tatra bhāvāt* that the low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) belongs specifically to the subordinate elements such as the *prayāja*s. He maintains that the low-voiced recitation connected with the spatial region consisting of the eastern part should be a property of those ritual items situated within that portion. This is because of the scriptural injunction (*śruti-nirdeśāt*), that is, because of the connection with the scriptural word "whatever" (*yatkiṃcit*).

The meaning is this: because the preceding word is expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*), it must necessarily be rendered non-expectant (*nirākāṅkṣa*). In that regard, its expectation cannot be satisfied by the word *yajña* which is heard [in the context], because that [word *yajña*] is connected with the word *sarva*. Consequently, another unmentioned word *yajña* would have to be postulated. Therefore, it is rendered non-expectant by the word *agnīṣomīya* which is actually heard.

Consequently, since the Agniṣomīya sacrifice is not composed of parts, it is impossible for the word *prācīna* (eastern/preceding) to refer to a part characterized as a constituent member; therefore, it must necessarily refer to the ritual items (*padārtha*) situated within those parts. Thus, the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is prompted by that *apūrva* (transcendental result), because that *apūrva* exists in its entirety (*tantra*) within those ritual items related to the parts. On this point, a great deal of detail should be consulted in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*).

In this Sūtra, the term *tsarā* is employed in the scriptural passage: "This [voice] is indeed the *tsarā* of the sacrifice; therefore, whatever is prior to the Agniṣomīya [offering], one performs that in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). This performance in a low voice is what is meant by *tsarā*. *Tsarā* signifies a stealthy or deceptive movement. However, Āśvalāyana, in the section prescribing the quality of being in a low voice (*upāṃśutva*), stated that for the principal rites within the Saumika offerings, the low voice applies specifically by using the expression "those belonging to the Saumika."

Śāṅkhāyana also has clearly stated that for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other offerings, the oblation for Upāṃśu is to be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśutva*) for each one individually. In this regard, regarding the position that accepts the restrictive application (*upasaṃhāra*), the view consistent with the *Hautra-śāstra* should be accepted. However, in the position that does not accept the restrictive application, the natural middle pitch (*madhyama-svara*) alone applies. It should be understood that the low-voiced nature (*upāṃśutva*) in the *Upasad* is indeed mandatory because it is prescribed by one's own branch of the Veda in the text: "We shall proceed with the Upāṃśu. [End of] Chapter 150, with the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.

The meaning is clear. If the *Yājuṣa* tradition of the *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ priest) is followed, there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses according to the *Yājuṣa* method; if the *Āśvalāyana* tradition of the *hautra* is followed, they are according to the method stated by Āśvalāyana. In that regard, "Agni is the mouth, the first of the deities" and "O Agni and Viṣṇu, heat is your highest greatness" are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses according to the *Āśvalāyana* school. "Agni, O Amsa, is the first of the deities" and "O Agni and Viṣṇu, heat is your highest greatness" are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses according to the *Yājuṣa* school. In all Soma-related *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices (*paśubandhas*), one does not cut off a portion for the sacrificer.

Even under the view that the *prāyaṇīyā* [offering] is performed in its entirety, the phrase "he does not cut off a portion for the sacrificer's share" (*na yajamānabhāgam avadyati*) is intended precisely to preclude such a prohibition; for it is from this very statement regarding the *prāyaṇīyā*—if one performs the *śamyu*-formula—that it follows [by extension] that the same applies to all *saumika*, *iṣṭi*, and *paśubandha* sacrifices. Consequently, the prohibition against cutting off a portion for the sacrificer's share is established for the unbroken *iṣṭi* and *paśubandha* sacrifices other than the *prāyaṇīyā*. The carrying forward of the *praṇītā* waters, however, certainly takes place.

Because there exists a visible purpose in the form of kneading, because there is no prohibition as in the case of the *avabhṛtha* bath, and because there is no scriptural injunction such as "he kneads with [water] consecrated by *yajus*-verses," one does not give the *anvāhārya* rice-offering.

In all *saumika* rites—whether *iṣṭi*, *paśubandha*, or *soma* sacrifices—the same applies. The giver is indeed the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). This is because the *Yajamānasūtra* states: "The preparation of materials, the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and the recitations (*japa*) belong to the sacrificer. Furthermore, the *Āśvalāyanasūtra* states: "He gives; [this refers to] the sacrificer. And the *Kātyāyanasūtra* states: "In the acts of giving, the formal declaration (*vācana*), the touching of the materials (*anvārambha*), the choosing of the officiants (*vara-varaṇa*), the vows (*vrata*), and the measurements (*pramāṇa*), one should understand the sacrificer as the agent."

The term *iṣṭipaśubandhāḥ* refers to the *iṣṭis* (sacrifices) and the *paśubandhas* (animal sacrifices). The term *saumikāḥ* refers to those [rites] belonging to the Soma sacrifice; they are both feminine (*saumikyaḥ*) and masculine (*saumikāḥ*), and thus "all" (*sarvāḥ* and *sarve*). By the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one of two identical words), as applied here according to the gender of the qualifying term (*iṣṭipaśubandheṣu*), the meaning is established as follows: "In all the *iṣṭis* belonging to the Soma sacrifice and in all the *paśubandhas* belonging to the Soma sacrifice, he does not give the *anyāhārya* (the guest-offering). The underlying intention is that the purpose is accomplished through the principal sacrificial fee (*pradhānadakṣiṇā*) itself by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*).

In the first pāda of the twelfth chapter, Jaimini also stated this principle in the sūtra: "And because they have already been engaged, there is no separate hiring" (*bhṛtatvācca parikrayaḥ*). From the sūtra, "Because of the injunction of another [fee], there should be no forest-food meal, for both are for the purpose of livelihood," the word "not" (*na*) is understood by *maṇḍūkapluti* (frog-leap) as carrying over from the previous context. The meaning of the sūtra is that since the officiating priests have already been engaged and remunerated by the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) belonging to the Soma sacrifice itself, there is no separate hiring in the form of the *anvāhārya* fee.

Since the *anvāhārya* rice is entirely absent in animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*), its non-giving is established by implication; therefore, the explicit prohibition serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that even in animal sacrifices, where it is absolutely non-existent, the *anvāhārya* alone constitutes the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and through that alone the fruit of giving the fee mentioned for animal sacrifices is accomplished. The mention of *anvāhārya* is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the sacrificial fee of the animal sacrifice; thus, there is also a prohibition of that [fee].

By the use of the plural number alone, since all the *iṣṭis* and *paśubandhas* included within the Soma ritual system are obtained, the inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of excluding the *drāghna* and *āśvina* expiatory animal sacrifices that fall outside the Soma system, indicating that even for those two, there is no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). It has been stated by this [textual] method that these two are to be seized as victims either at the *pātnīṣomīya* or the *savanīya* stage. Likewise, when the *pāthikṛt* and other such sacrifices are included within the Soma system, there is likewise no sacrificial fee.

If the sun does not appear while the *Āśvina* Śastra is being recited, one should offer the *Bahurūpa* animal sacrifice dedicated to Sūrya. Even though the performance of that sacrifice must be carried out immediately after the animal has been led forward (*upanīya*), no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is required. Since this is the case, and because it is expected within the *Baudhāyana-sūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha (in the seventh book, section 576), the procedure is shown here in connection with the present context. In that rite, there are the same implements as before—the sacrificial knife (*svadhiti*), the wooden splinter (*svaru*), the staff for the Maitrāvaruṇa priest, the heart-spit (*hṛdayaśūla*), the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and the wooden sword (*sphya*), among others.

For the sake of lightness in handling the materials, the shoots, branches, and *kumbhī* vessels containing the equal portions of grain should be washed and used as they are. The fat for the animal’s tethering-rope and the two omentum-spits is obtained by implication. The *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* offering and the animal sacrifice (*paśviṣṭi*) do not exist here because they fall within the scope of other ritual procedures (*tantra*). There is no cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), no preparation of the altar (*vedi*), and no preparation of the *uttaravedi* and *cātvāla*. There is no carrying forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*), no adding of fuel (*anvādhāna*), no bringing of the *barhis* grass, no making of the altar, no strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*), and no washing of the hands.

There is an option regarding the spreading of the grass mat (*ulaparājī*). There is no seating for the Brahman and the Sacrificer. Only these items are set down: the vessel for the portions of the offering (*samavattadhānī*), the animal’s tethering-rope (*paśuraśanā*), the omentum (*vapā*), the cauldron (*kumbhī*), and the branch of the *plakṣa* tree. There is no choosing of the Brahman priest (*brahmavaraṇa*) nor his taking of his seat (*upaveśana*). At the time of the preparation of the strainers (*pavitra*) and the wiping of the vessels, he touches with the formula "May they settle" (*saṃviśantām*) only those vessels already set down, such as the vessel for the portions, the animal’s tethering-rope, and so forth.

Following the sequence of procedures prescribed for the *Paśubandha* sacrifice, beginning with "For Dakṣa, you are made of wood" (*dakṣāya tvā vānaspatyā asi*) and ending with the sprinkling of the vessels (*pātraprokṣa*), the rites from the northern tracing (*uttaraparigraha*) up to the taking up of the *Svaru* are omitted. Thereafter, there is the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścittahoma*), the dedication of the animal (*paśūpākaraṇa*), and the five oblations that are ancillary to the dedication (*upākaraṇāṅga*). This animal is multiform (*bahurūpa*). There is no churning of fire. The rites beginning with the taking of the ropes (*raśanādāna*) and ending with the sprinkling beneath [the animal] take place. The rites beginning with the *Sāmidhenī* verses and ending with the *Cyāvāra* are excluded.

In the absence of *pṛṣadājya*, the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the principal deity should be performed here by the Hotṛ as previously described, while remaining in that very spot. Regarding the prohibition of invocation mentioned by Āśvalāyana—"not for others [deities] already invoked"—it should be understood that this prohibition concerns the invocation of fixed deities, and not the invocation of incidental deities who fall within the end of the sequence. As for Vanaspati, since he has already been invoked, there is no further invocation. There is no smearing of the *dhruvā* vessel and so forth, nor are there *prayāja* offerings.

Having taken clarified butter from the *ājyasthālī* into the *juhū* with the *sruva*, and having anointed the *svaru* and the *svadhiti* with it, he performs the smearing of the animal with them. Having handed over the *svadhiti* to the *śamitṛ* with the words "This is your share," and having directed the stream [of blood] toward the east, he places the *svaru* in its proper place; this concludes the sequence beginning with the [handing over of the] *svadhiti* up to the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the entrails (*vaipāyā*). Both [the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ] look at the production of the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) in the middle [of the vessel].

There is no final *prayāja* offering. According to the Śruti, "The omenta of the animals dedicated to Sarasvatī and Prajāpati are indeed raw, for that which is not sprinkled [with ghee] is raw," and according to the Vājapeya-sūtra, "They proceed with omenta that have not been sprinkled," it should be understood that just as they are used in the sacrifice, here too they are used in the sacrifice in their unsprinkled state. There are no *ājyabhāga* offerings. The *pañcahotṛ* formula is recited by the sacrificer; the offering of the omentum is performed like the *nirūḍha-paśubandha*.

The specific modification in the *puronuvākyā-praiṣa* is: "Recite for Sūrya the omentum and fat of the goat. There is no *yājyā-praiṣa* when the sacrifice has the Agni animal-sacrifice as its archetype; however, when it has the Agni-Soma animal-sacrifice as its archetype, there is indeed a *yājyā-praiṣa*: "Prompt [the recitation] for Sūrya of the omentum and fat of the goat. The *anumantraṇa* is: "Through the sacrifice to the god Sūrya, may I become possessed of sensory power (*indriyāvī*). For one who sacrifices to Mahendra, the formula is: "May I attain victory. Regarding the throwing into the *cātvāla* pit and the granting of the boon, it has already been stated previously that there is no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

[The procedure] begins with the placing of the vessels for the *paśupuroḍāśa* and ends with the eating [of the portions]. In the case of it being a modification (*vikāra*) of the *āgneya* [offering], the formula is: "Thou art the sacrifice; this is the sacrifice, the Pañcahotṛ. In the case of it being a modification of the *āgnīṣomīya*, the formula is: "Thou art Prajāpati; this is the sacrifice, the Vihavya, the Caturhotṛ. Then, having performed the spreading of the base [butter] in the *juhū* and so forth, ending with the release of the potsherds (*kapāla-vimocana*), there is the specific modification: "For Sūrya, of the *puroḍāśa*... The determination of the calls (*bhaiṣa-nirṇaya*) is as before. Then, having taken five-fold drawn butter (*pañcagṛhīta*) into the *juhū* and having taken the *pṛṣadājya* ladle, [he says]: "O Śṛta... [Kha. 1, Ba. sāyā].

[Chapter 150] Together with the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa: From "O Śamitṛ, the oblation! and so forth, up to the disposal of the remnants of the oblation (*haviḥśeṣodvāsana*). The specific modification in the *praisha* (direction) is: "For Sūrya, of the goat-oblation. The determination of the *praisha* is as before. There is the existence of the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice and the existence of the *vanaspati* sacrifice. This is because, since the *vanaspati* sacrifice is a modification of the *sviṣṭakṛt*, its properties are taught as being necessarily connected (*saṃniyogaśiṣṭa*) due to their belonging to the same class. All this constitutes the animal ritual (*pāśuka karma*).

After the consumption of the cup-oblation (camasa-homa) related to the Aśvins, one should perform the rites beginning with the oblation of the flour-smear (piṣṭalepa-homa) and ending with the removal of the Aśvin vessel (kapāla). Then, the rites beginning with "O Agni, fetch the embers for the Upayaj offerings" are performed according to the common procedure (samānatantreṇa). However, in the Atirātra sacrifice, there are four Sandhi-stotras and Śastras after that; the specific difference is that the rites beginning with "O Agni, fetch the embers for the Upayaj offerings" follow. The six verses beginning with "Sūrya [has sent forth] the goddess Uṣas" are the Yājyās and Puronuvākyās. The remainder is for the purpose of providing options.

Immediately after the *vanaspatipreṣa* (the call regarding the Lord of the Forest), [the formula begins]: "Where the dear abodes of the oblation of clarified butter are, where the dear abodes of the oblation of Soma and clarified butter are, where the dear abodes of the oblation of the goat for Sūrya are, where the dear portions of Vanaspati are," and so forth. [This concludes] the *sviṣṭakṛt*.

"Let the Hotṛ sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Agni has sacrificed to the dear abodes of the oblation of the kingdom; he has sacrificed to the dear abodes of the oblation of Soma and the clarified butter; he has sacrificed to the dear abodes of the oblation of the goat for Sūrya; he has sacrificed to the dear paths of Vanaspati," and so forth. If the two Ājyabhāga offerings have not been performed in the Savanīya animal sacrifice, then the mention of the Ājyabhāgas should not be made in the *preṣas* (directions) for Vanaspati and Sviṣṭakṛt pertaining to that animal sacrifice.

Thus, by way of digression, the application of the Saura-Paśu sacrifice has been stated therein. Now, the subject at hand is discussed: since the connection with the Soma sacrifice is already established by the very context (*prakaraṇa*), the statement "in the Saumika [rites]" is for the purpose of excluding the Vāyavya-Paśu and others, and also to indicate that those [rites] which are established as being part of the Soma sacrifice do not occur here either. Consequently, in these sacrifices, the choosing of the Brahman priest (*brahmavaraṇa*), the concluding of the sacrifice (*yajñavimoka*), and the gratification of the Brāhmaṇas (*brāhmaṇatarpaṇa*) do not take place.

It is understood from the association with the prohibition of the *anvāhārya* rice that these ritual items (*padārtha*) must be performed even after the *avabhṛtha* bath. Although the commencement of the vow (*vratopāyana*) and other such acts have their purpose fulfilled by the subsidiaries of the Soma sacrifice, they must be understood as distinct because their fulfillment occurs only prior to the *avabhṛtha* and not thereafter; thus, there is a difference in injunctions (*vidhibheda*). Some say that the preparation of a seat for the sacrificer should also not be performed, since the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) serves the purpose of a seat; however, that is not logical.

Because of the observation of the dismissal [of the guest] with the words, "O you who have a brother-in-law," and because of the statement, "In the *iṣṭis* and *paśubandhas*,"—this latter statement, in accordance with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the word "in the *saumika* [rites]," would apply only to the *paśubandhas* and not to the *iṣṭis*; therefore, it is for the purpose of excluding those. From the scriptural text of another branch, "One should offer the *anvāhārya* at the Soma sacrifice, but one should certainly not be without a Soma sacrifice," this prohibition of the *anvāhārya* applies to one who is wealthy, not to one who is not wealthy. For such a person, at all *saumika-iṣṭis* and at all *saumika-paśubandhas*, only the *anvāhārya* is to be given.

At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), gold is to be given to the *Āgnīdhra* and the *Ātreya*; the *mantha* and other items are for the others. By this much alone, the Soma sacrifice is accomplished. This entire passage is intended to establish that [these acts] must necessarily be performed. However, this scriptural statement from another recension (*śākhāntara*) is intended to demonstrate the absence of fault when there is a reduction in the sacrificial fee for one who is extremely indigent. But for one who is not indigent, giving a small sacrificial fee results in both the absence of fruit and a fault. Thus says the Smṛti: "He who performs the *Agniṣṭoma* and other sacrifices with small sacrificial fees..."

"He does not obtain the fruit when the primary substance is available, and he incurs a fault. Thus says Śatātapa. Manu also says: "He who is capable of following the primary rule (*prathamakalpa*) but acts according to a secondary rule (*anukalpa*) finds neither the fruit pertaining to the hereafter nor any good result. Also in another Smṛti: "He who is capable of following the primary rule but acts according to a secondary rule does not obtain its fruit and indeed incurs a fault."

For that prohibition against officiating at a sacrifice where the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is insufficient should be understood as referring to a sacrifice where the fee is capable of being provided. Although this Sūtra is appropriately recited in the *Yājamāna-sūtra*, it should nevertheless be seen as placed here because of its connection with the Adhvaryu through the intermediary of the *abhighāraṇa* (sprinkling), the *vedyāsādana* (placing on the altar), and the *saṃpraiṣa* (direction). In the word "dadāti" (he gives), the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is to be understood as elided.
He makes the remainder of the *dhruvā* [vessel].

By the word *bhū* (floor), that which is situated upon it (*tadgata*) is grasped through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), just as in the expression "the platforms cry out" (*mañcāḥ krośanti*), the word "platforms" indicates the persons standing upon them. The failure of the intended meaning (*tātparyānupapatti*) is the basis for this figurative indication here. The meaning is that one makes a remnant (*śe�ṣa*) of the clarified butter (*ājya*) located in the *dhruvā* vessel—that is, one sets it aside. Alternatively, the word "of the clarified butter" (*ājyasya*) may be understood as an ellipsis following the word "of the *dhruvā*" (*dhruvāyāḥ*). Its sense would then be: "one makes a remnant of the clarified butter belonging to the *dhruvā*. Or, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) may be used in the sense of the locative (*saptamī*).

Based on the statement "he performs the remainder," there is no replenishing (*āpyāyana*) of the *dhruvā* vessel during the two libations for the *sviṣṭakṛt*; this is for the purpose of establishing the status of the *dhruvājya* as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*). For replenishment is intended for the sake of filling, and that which has been filled cannot logically function as a "remainder. Therefore, the final conclusion of this injunction is precisely the prohibition of replenishment. Since the two libations for the *sviṣṭakṛt* are the very last acts, it is only in those instances that there is an absence of replenishing the *dhruvā*.

He sets aside even the remainder of the clarified butter (*ājya*) from the *ājyasthālī* because there is a future requirement for it. From the remainder in the *dhruvā*, he offers four *dīkṣā*-oblations with the *sruva* spoon, saying "To Ākūti, to Agni, Svāhā! and so on; and with the *sruk* ladle, he offers the fifth oblation with the words "The Waters are divine. Since the setting aside of the remainder is already established by the force of its subsequent application, this specific statement is intended to clarify a particular point: that in the event of the loss of the remainder, the status of the remainder is still maintained, and the offering must be performed using the *dhruvā* itself after taking [butter] from it with the final three mantras beginning with "Dyauḥ" (Heaven).

If, through confusion, the swelling (āpyāyana) of the two *iṣe tvā* formulas has ever been performed for the *sviṣṭakṛt*, then one should nevertheless offer the oblation with those [formulas]. In both cases, there is the offering for all expiations (*sarvaprāyaścitta-homa*) and the recitation of the *anājñāta* verses, etc.
The *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice concludes with the *Patnīsaṃyāja* offerings; having consumed the *Ājyeḍā*, they cease.

That which has its conclusion within the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings is called "ending with the *patnīsaṃyājas*" (*patnīsaṃyājāntā*). Although the completion of the ritual action is already established by the mere statement that "the *vīkṣaṇīyā* [offering] ends with the *patnīsaṃyājas*," the repeated mention of "it concludes" (*saṃtiṣṭhate*) as an indicator of completion serves to show that even during the conclusion, it is brought to a final end by means of the concluding rites (*pratipattikarma*) following the *patnīsaṃyājas*. [Note: The commentary portion regarding the manuscript variants and the name Gopīnāthabhaṭṭa is omitted as per instructions.]

579. *Pam*. Therefore, the ritual acts of performance (*pratipatti-karmāṇi*) are accompanied by mantras. The performance of the Veda (*veda-pratipatti*) is also accompanied by mantras. The untying of the girth-rope (*yoktra-mocana*) and the vow (*vrata*) are also held to be with mantras. Since it is established by the rule "In the rites following the *avabhṛtha*, such as the *udayanīyā* sacrifice, all [acts] are performed with the subsequent [mantras]" that the binding (*saṃnahana*) and the taking up of the vow (*vatopāyana*) must be performed, it is understood that their accomplishment through the *ṛṣi*-mantras occurs in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice.

Otherwise, if the untying and discarding [of the cord] were performed at the *udayanīyā* sacrifice while the binding and taking up [of the cord] had been performed at the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, then the rule stating that "all [acts] are to be done in the subsequent [sacrifices]"—and specifically the injunction for the *pratipatti* (disposal) at the *udayanīyā* sacrifice—would be inconsistent. Since the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is already obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*), the repetition here is for the purpose of ensuring that these acts of disposal are mandatory only in this [specific] case, and not in the *prāyaṇīyā* which is incomplete (*khaṇḍā*).

If it is argued that this contradicts the scriptural statement, "Therefore, these sacrifices conclude with this [the Ājyeḍā]," we say no; for there is no contradiction when one assumes that the sacrifices are completed within this interval by means of the *apratipatti-karmāṇi* (rites of non-disposal). This is because of the scriptural injunction: "Having consumed the Ājyeḍā, they cease."

Since that much alone would suffice for the accomplishment [of the purpose], the statement "the Dīkṣaṇīyā sacrifice concludes with the Patnīsaṃyājas" is intended to establish that it ends with the Patnīsaṃyājas; this is to show that the meaning of the injunction regarding the *dakṣiṇā* is precisely that it concludes with the consumption of the *ājyeḍā*. Consequently, wherever the conclusion with the Patnīsaṃyājas is heard—such as in "the Agniṣomīya sacrifice concludes with the Patnīsaṃyājas," or "the day concludes with the Patnīsaṃyājas"—in each of those instances, its conclusion with the consumption of the *ājyeḍā* becomes established.

Regarding the phrase "having consumed the *iḍā*," the mention of *ājya* (clarified butter) is for the purpose of demonstrating that where there is a mention of *iḍā* without a qualifying prefix, it refers specifically to the *iḍā* connected with the primary oblation (*pradhānahavis*). For example, in the case of the *ātithyā* [rite], in the statement "the *ātithyā* ends with the *iḍā*," the remainder of the rule is "they cease" from the acts of disposal (*apratipattikarma*). To this extent, the status of ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings indeed remains. *Patnī*...

The meaning of this very sentence, "The *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering] arises from the *saṃyāja*," is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "having consumed" (*bhakṣayitvā*) and ending with "they cease. In the word *bhakṣayitvā*, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is included. Therefore, because the consumption of the *ājyeḍā* is performed by both [the sacrificer and the priests], even though there is no plurality of agents, the causative status is assumed; thus, the coreferentiality and the identity of agent indicated by the plural verb form in "they cease" (*viramanti*) becomes logically consistent.

And thus the meaning is as follows: having caused the Hotṛ to consume the Ājyeḍā, the Adhvaryu, Brahman, and Yajamāna emerge from the rites of disposal (*apratipatti-karma*). Since the status of the Hotṛ belongs to the Yajurveda, after the consumption of the Ājyeḍā, only the disposal of the *medas* remains; that indeed takes place. For the Āgnīdhra, there is no ritual action of his own at this point. In the previous case, under the alternative of performing the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*, the unloosening of the girth-rope (*yoktra*) must certainly be performed.

Even when the sacrificer belongs to a Yajurvedic school (Yajuḥśākhin), although the presence of the *yājuṣahautra* exists, the *mārjana* does not take place; for the prohibition of measurement (*māna*) stated by Āśvalāyana—"this measuring and so forth [do not occur] prior to the *udayanīyā*"—applies here as well, since it is a specific (*vaiśeṣika*) rule.
He maintains the *āhavanīya* fire.

By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "whatever is the time of the principal [rite] is the time of its subsidiaries; whatever is the place is the place; whatever is the performer is the performer; and whatever is the fire is the fire," there is a maintenance [of the fire] until the completion of the sacrifice, and not a repeated leading forward (*praṇayana*). The underlying idea is that since the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering] is for the purpose of securing the principal deity alone, it is impossible to abandon the fire—which has already been secured as the form of the deity. The proof for the fact that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is for the purpose of securing the principal deity alone will be stated later.

Regarding a specific detail concerning the *dīkṣaṇīyā* (initiation offering), Baudhāyana states in the *Dvaidhasūtra*: "Bhāradvāja says that one should enter the sacrificial hall (*śālā*) either in the forenoon or in the afternoon; however, Śālīki says that one should cause the *dīkṣaṇīyā* to be concluded before sunset. The sacrificer is initiated in the afternoon"—in order to fulfill this injunction, the Adhvaryu priest should cause the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice to be completed prior to sunset.

The meaning is that he should cause it to be completed or brought to its conclusion. Before sunset, the Adhvaryu priest should employ [the sacrificer] to complete the *dakṣiṇīyā* (the sacrificial fee-offering); the sense is that the completion depends upon the authority of the Adhvaryu. The reading "saṃtiṣṭhāpayet" is straightforward. By the rule, "The initiated one does not offer any oblation other than those connected with the sacrifice," from tomorrow morning onwards—

The sense is that since all *homa* offerings are prohibited for those who have received the initiation (*dīkṣita*), if they were omitted, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice must necessarily be completed before sunset; this is because the evening and morning *homas* share a single result, and thus the evening *homa* of the first day must also be omitted [if the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is not finished].

If, at any time, the initiation (*dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi*) should cease before its completion, then—having postponed the evening *agnihotra* from the middle of the day and having offered both the evening and morning *agnihotra* together in a combined manner—one should complete the sacrifice begun, pause, and on the following day, after offering all the expiations (*prāyaścitta*), undergo the initiation in the afternoon; for by the force of the injunction "on the following day he is initiated," the shaving of the head and other rites occur only on that subsequent day. However, since there is no time available then, the original model sacrifice (*prakṛtīṣṭi*) is simply omitted.

In this matter, in order to accomplish the production of a single *apūrva*, the expiation for omission (*lopa-prāyaścitta*) must indeed be performed immediately after the attainment of consecration (*dīkṣā*). Alternatively, having offered the universal expiation (*sarva-prāyaścitta*), the consecration itself may take place at that very moment; or the offering of the universal expiation may occur either immediately after the consecration or before it. However, if the sun sets even before the commencement of the *dakṣiṇīyā* sacrifice, then the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice and subsequent rites shall take place on the following day. The morning *agnihotra* offering, however, occurs precisely at its own prescribed time.

If the time for the *sattva* [offering] has passed, even the *prākṛtīṣṭi* (archetypal sacrifice) is not performed; rather, only the *lopa-prāyaścitta* (expiation for omission) is performed, or at that very time the *dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi* and subsequent rites. In this view, the morning oblation (*prātaḥ-homa*) and the sequence of the *prākṛtīṣṭi* are as before. However, if the completion is hindered by an obstacle during the *ārāgrā* initiation, then after offering the *sarvaprāyaścitta*, the remaining ritual must be concluded at that very time. It should be understood, however, that if the sun sets before the *saṃbhārayajur-homa*, then the *saṃbhārayajur-homa* and following rites must take place on the next day, and not at that very moment.

They construct the measured *prācīnavaṃśa* shed, which is elevated in the front. The suffix *-kta* in the word *vimitam* has the sense of a completed action (*bhūtārthe*). By the force of the prefix in the verb *minvanti*, the meaning is that they cover it from above. Consequently, the measurement takes place even before the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering; here, the covering from above and so forth occurs [subsequently]. By this, the doubt as to how the measurement of the *prāgvaṃśa* can take place after the *dīkṣaṇīyā*—since the site would be occupied—is resolved.

He makes the *prācīnavaśa* [the sacrificial seat facing east]. According to the Śruti, "The gods and humans divided the quarters: the gods [took] the east, the ancestors the south, humans the west, and the Rudras the north. However, this division of directions is merely an *arthavāda* (an explanatory or commendatory statement). Thus, in the third chapter, fourth pāda, Jaimini states: "And the division of directions is like that, because the connection is for the sake of the purpose [of the ritual]. The division of directions—the assignment of the western direction to humans—is also for the sake of the *arthavāda*, just like the *nivīta* (the manner of wearing the sacred thread).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: since it is generally the case that when men are occupied during the forenoon, they naturally turn their backs toward the sun, an injunction [regarding this] would be redundant because the connection is already established by the very nature of things. Everything here is exactly like the section concerning the *nivīta* (the sacred thread worn around the neck). Thus, even though the matter has already been resolved by that [preceding discussion], in the case of the statement "the *nivīta* is for men," since no direct injunction (*pratyakṣavidhi*) is heard, an injunction must be inferred from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) alone. [Question: How so? [Answer: Because... (Note: The text fragment provided ends abruptly with "ka. yadi | 2 kha, ga, 'karṣaprā".)

150th Paṭala: Together with the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. Furthermore, since the meaning of the *nivīta* formula itself is not directly perceived there, the postulation of an injunction for *nivīta* based on an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is ruled out from afar; thus, because an independent injunction is impossible, let it be that [the passage] serves as a praise for the *upavyāna*.

In the present case, however, because of the statement "formerly men divided toward the west," one understands the excellence of the division toward the west due to its being practiced by ancient persons; thus, the injunction that "the division of the quarters should be performed toward the west" is easily established. This section is intended to ward off the specific doubt [that such an injunction might not exist].

The explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—"In the injunction 'he makes the *prācīnavaśa* [post] auspicious,' the gods, humans, and the quarters divided [the directions]: the gods [took] the east, the ancestors the south, humans the west, and the Rudras the north"—is the subject matter of this section. Here, the term "gods" (*deva*) is intended to include the ancestors (*pitṛ*). Although the Rudras are also deities, they are mentioned separately according to the maxim of "the cow and the ox" (*govālīvardanyāya*). Thus, it should be understood that in the phrase "the gods [took] the east, the south... the word "gods" refers to those other than the Rudras.

The sacrificial shed (*vimita*) whose ridge-pole (*vaṃśa*) is oriented toward the east is designated as the "shed of the consecrated" (*dīkṣitavimita*). This very quality of being "eastward" (*prācīna*) belongs specifically to the ridge-pole, according to the Vājasaneyi-śruti: "One should make the ridge-pole extended toward the east. The word *prācīna* denotes "eastward" and not "upward," based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating that "the gods and humans divided the quarters [starting] from the east. Furthermore, this is confirmed by the fact that in another ritual context—the *udīcīnavaṃśā śālā* (the hall with the ridge-pole pointing north)—the quality of being "northward" serves as a substitute for it.

And that backbone (the central ridge) should be as long as is necessary so that the vihāra, together with its sacrificial altars (āgnīdhriya), its wives’ quarters (sapatnīśālā), and its walkways (saṃcara), may be completed. Although there is the specific qualification "the eastern ridge of the vimita," it is understood that the eastern orientation must be established only after the measurement of the vimita. All pillars, too, are required as far as they are useful for supporting it. It should be slightly elevated in front—that is, somewhat higher in the eastern part. This also must be done prior to the construction of the āgnīdhra altar.

Because the purpose is to cover a measured space (*vimita*) characterized by such attributes as having a "front-gabled roof" (*prācīnavaṃśa*) that is elevated in the front, the erection of the bamboo posts and their elevation must be performed first; for the subsequent acts—such as covering, enclosing, and making the door—are prescribed after the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*). Since the elevation is prescribed for the front portion, there is no [elevation] at the back. This has been clearly stated by Āpastamba: "He makes it front-gabled, elevated in the front and sloping down at the back."

Baudhāyana states: "The hall is constructed on a site consecrated for the gods. Since no specific measurement for this is mentioned, its length and width are determined by the requirements of the ritual purpose (*arthalakṣaṇa*), according to Kātyāyana’s statement that "the dimension follows from the purpose. However, Baudhāyana says in his Śulvasūtra: "The eastern part is sixteen steps long and twelve steps wide; in its center is the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) measuring twelve [steps]."

And in the *Prayogasūtra*: "The hall has its beams facing east and is open on all sides; it is higher toward the south. For it, they construct four doors: one facing east, one south, one west, and one north. To the south, they construct the fire-hall for the sacrificial observances (*vrataśrapaṇāgāra*); behind that, the wife’s chamber (*patnīśālā*). The sacrificial sites (*āyatanāni*) consist of five kinds of bricks, having the maximum prescribed dimensions, equal in area, according to the available space.

In the case of the *sampāvatathya* ritual, the two hearths (*āyatana*) for those [fires] are also located in the *prāgvaṃśa* hall itself, in front of the *āhavanīya*, arranged in sequence facing east, just like the site of the *āhavanīya*. However, the site for the *aupāsana* fire is in a secluded area near the *prāgvaṃśa*, enclosed by a screen (*pariśrita*). Regarding the measurement of a *prakrama*, it is that of either the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) or the officiating priest (*adhvaryu*), for the *Śulbasūtra* states: "The sacrificer and the officiating priest are indeed the performers of the ritual movements. According to the *Śulbasūtra*, a *prakrama* consists of either two or three *padas*.

By the etymological derivation *padyate gamyate* ("that which is stepped upon" or "that which is traversed"), even a single word [can denote various measures]. Regarding the manifold nature of the *pada*, it is stated in the *Kātyāyana-Śulba-Sūtra*: "In the *piśālā*, the *satyāpāḍha*, the *yuga*, the *aratni*, the *iyati*, and the *śamyā*—among these measures, one may proceed according to one's desire, because the meaning of the word is subject to uncertainty (*viśayitvāt*). The term "because of uncertainty" means "because of its being of many kinds. According to Baudhāyana, a *pada* is fifteen *aṅgulas*; he also states that a small *pada* (*kṣudrapada*) is ten *aṅgulas*.

"Ten finger-breadths is a *pada*," says Kātyāyana; these measurements are universal. The east is to be determined everywhere by common worldly usage. Regarding this, Baudhāyana states: "The Kṛttikās do not indeed leave this [direction] as the east; one may infer it by the sight of them—this is one view. One may infer it by the sight of Śroṇā—this is another view. One may infer it by the interval between Citrā and Svāti—this is yet another view. These indicators are restricted to specific regions.

Kātyāyana stated a definition common to all regions: "Having driven a peg into level ground and having drawn a circle with a cord equal in length to the *śara* (the distance between the two outermost pegs), that direction in which the shadow of the peg falls upon the two lines is the east. From the subsequent injunction regarding the making of the corners (*srakti*) at the front, it is understood that the measured area is square. Furthermore, from the injunction that "the corners are in the cardinal directions" during the *piñjya* sacrifice, it follows that in the rites involving squares, the corners are indeed in the intermediate directions (*vidiś*).
Āpastamba has stated this matter quite explicitly: "The corners are in the intermediate directions."
While encircling [the structure], they create *atīroka*s in the corners.

Encircling—that is, covering on all sides with mats and such—the *prāgvaṃśa* shed which is covered above, the attendants create *atīroka*s in the corners (*srakti*). The word *āroka* denotes an interval, meaning "lattices" (*gavākṣa*). This is because it is heard in the *Aśvamedha*: "In the *āroka*s they hold wild animals. The lengthening of the *l* and the substitution of *r* for *l* are Vedic (*chāndasa*). The meaning is that they make lattices in the corners.

Because of the use of the present participle (*śatṛ*) in the expression "pariśrayantaḥ" (while enclosing), the making of the *atīroka* occurs at the very same time as the enclosing. "Toward the intermediate region between the north and the east" means toward the fifth [space] facing the intermediate region between the north and the east; this meaning is obtained from the word "prati. If it were merely stated, "the fifth toward the northeast," the term "northeast" would refer only to the window (*gavākṣa*).

Furthermore, the mention of "intermediate direction" (*avāntaradeśa*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the fifth window does not occur in the immediate vicinity itself, but rather in a portion adjacent to that vicinity—either in the eastern or northern part—as distinct from the intermediate direction. There are four parts situated in the cardinal directions (*dik*) and four situated in the intermediate directions (*vidik*); it should be understood that the fifth window is to be placed in either the eastern or northern part. The specific mention of "northeastern" (*uttarapūrva*) is intended to exclude the other intermediate directions.
The doors are located in the cardinal directions.

The word "they do" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. In the Śruti text, "he makes openings (atīkāśān) in the quarters," the word *atīkāśa* indeed signifies a door. These [openings] are one cubit (*aratni*) in measure. From the point where the western sūtra of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line intersects with the northern sūtra, one should place a door-post at a distance of one span (*prādeśa*) to the south; likewise, a door-post to the north. In this way, the western door is completed. From the point where the eastern sūtra of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line intersects with the northern sūtra, one should place a post each to the south and to the north, just as before.

In this manner, the eastern door is completed. From the intersection of the northern cord and the southern boundary cord, one should place a pillar each to the east and to the west as before; thus the southern door is completed. From the intersection of the northern cord and the northern boundary cord, one should place two pillars to the east and to the west as before; thus the northern door is completed.

The measurement of an *ara* is stated in the *Śulbasūtra*: "Twenty-four *aṅgulas* are an *ara*, and half of that is a *prādeśa*; such is the established rule (*kḷpti*). It should be understood that this established rule is universal.

Regarding the phrase "rites with a single door are for optional purposes" (*ekadvārāḥ kāmyāḥ kalpāḥ*): the remainder of the meaning is that those ritual procedures (*kalpa*) or methods which have only one door are intended for optional desires (*kāmya*). This is not, however, a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) of the doors belonging to the archetypal model (*prakṛta*), as in the case of [the statement] "When there is an eight-potsherd cake, he purifies him with the *Gāyatrī* through spiritual luster," and so forth; for there is a specific injunction [beginning with] "He who should desire... (*yaḥ kāmayeta*).

Having gone out by whichever [door], one performs everything that ought to be done through any door; however, regarding such passages as "having approached by the southern door," if there were only a western door, then the prohibition stated in another scripture—"one does not go out by the western door"—would apply. Likewise, the rule "having entered the *prāgvaṃśa* by the eastern door" would not exist. Similarly, for tethering cows and other animals, and for stakes, there is no fixed rule regarding the doors and so forth.

In the case of the Hotṛ’s inspection, it is merely a mental visualization (*abhidhyāna*). Prior to the *Śālāmukhīya* fire, the *Sokāśin* must always be performed. Even after exiting through another door, the preparation of the *ucchiṣṭakhara* (the mound for food scraps) must take place in the north-eastern region alone. If it is argued that this sūtra is redundant because the requirement is already established by the rule beginning with "for one desiring heaven [should exit] from the eastern door," that is true.

Even if the eastern door is constructed with the aim of desiring heaven (*svarga-kāmanā*), there would be no cessation of the other doors because they are obligatory (*nitya*); let that not be the case. Rather, since there is no lack of purpose in making this known for the sake of understanding such a meaning—namely, that when one [door] is for a specific desire (*kāmya*), there should be a cessation of all [doors] even though they are otherwise obligatory—the desires are stated as follows:

"The eastern door for one desiring heaven; the southern door for one desiring the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*); the western door for one desiring the world of men (*manuṣyaloka*); the northern door for one desiring offspring; and to the north-east for one who should desire, 'May I prosper in both worlds.'"

Regarding the phrase "to the north" (*uttarataḥ*): although two doors might be understood from the reading joined with that suffix (*tas-pratyaya*), nevertheless, because of the introductory statement that "the optional rites (*kāmyāḥ kalpāḥ*) have a single door," and because of the observation that "one enters by the north-eastern door," there is only one door; the north-eastern intermediate direction is intended, and the reading joined with that suffix is indeed a corrupt reading (*apapāṭha*). The rest is clear. By stating "doors in all directions," he also indicates that the rite of having doors on all sides is optional: "He who desires, 'May I prosper in all directions,' [should make] a [shrine] with doors on all sides."

This is clear. Now, one might object: "Since it is stated as an established fact that 'one enters by the north-eastern door,' that [door] must also be permanent. This is not so, because it would contradict the scriptural injunction regarding desire (*kāma-śruti*), and because the purpose of the designation is accomplished even by an occasional [door].
Furthermore, they construct structures in the form of porticos (*praghāṇa*) around the images in the various directions.

The word *pratimā* signifies similarity. A hall (*śālā*) having the form of the *prāgvaṃśa*; "its counterpart" (*tatpratimā*) means similar to it. Having reserved a space for the *sadas* and *havirdhāna* pavilions in its vicinity, another hall is constructed outside over as much area as desired; the meaning is that one should place doors at the ends of that hall as well, in the various directions. Here, the similarity consists in [the two halls] having dense shade and height. Kha. Ga. states the specific desires.

584. The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the seventh book, regarding the specific details at the doors—it says: "They are of the form of *praghāṇas*. This means that they make the doors of the outer hall (*bāhyaśālā*) like *praghāṇas*. The mention of the word *didivi* is for the purpose of excluding the intermediate directions (*vidik*). That which is struck (*prahaṇyate*) with the feet during going and coming is a *praghāṇa*. "Striking" (*hana*) means injury. Here, by the word "striking," the fitness for striking is indicated. It is a word formed through both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

The words *praghaṇa* and *praghāṇa* are correct by virtue of their being technical nipātanas (irregular formations) for "a portion of a house" (*agāraikadeśe*). This term refers to a specific part of the door known as the *alinda*. The rule stating that "the *sāṃkāśina* [altar] is common to the *prāgvaṃśa*, the *sadas*, and the *havirdhāna*" does not apply to the eastern and western doors of the outer hall (*bāhyaśālā*), because such a prescription is not provided for them and because it would be conducive to exposing them to the sight of impure persons and the like. All the doors of the outer hall must be provided with panels (*kapāṭa*) in order to prevent dogs and other animals from entering. There should be a complete enclosure (*pariśrayaṇa*) on all sides of the assembly of doors.
To the north of the *prāgvaṃśa* (the eastern hall), in an enclosed space, the sacrificer has his hair and beard shaved.

The word "to the north" (*uttareṇa*) ends in the suffix *-ena*. It means immediately to the north, outside the *prāgvaṃśa*. The use of the suffix *-ena* is for the purpose of excluding directions such as east; the use of the prefix *enap-* is for the purpose of excluding a distant location. By the mention of the *prāgvaṃśa*, there is an exclusion of the fire-altar site, the outer hall, and the hall with its beams facing north intended for the *gārhapatya* fire. Consequently, there is only one hall, not two. The term *prāgvaṃśa* denotes a specific type of hall.

And so says the *Kośa*: "The *prāgvaṃśa* is that which is before the *havirdhāna* house. The meaning is that the pavilion situated in front of, or to the east of, the *havirdhāna*—the house where the sacrificial oblations (*havis*) are placed—is called the *prāgvaṃśa*. By this very [statement], it is understood that the collection of items used for the sacrifice, such as the sacrificial oblations and so forth, should be placed behind the *prāgvaṃśa*. This point is also clearly stated in another scripture: "To the west is the *patnīśālā*; near it, one places the cleansing materials (*saṃmāra*). In this regard, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) faces the east.

If the monastery were facing north, [the student] would have his back turned toward it; and that is utterly improper. Intending this very point, Baudhāyana prescribes facing eastward here: "Then, while facing east, he moistens the hair on the right side of the head with water, saying: 'May the waters moisten you for life, for long life, and for splendor.'"

To the north of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, in an enclosed space, the sacrificer first has his beard shaved, then his armpits, and then his hair. Although this much alone would suffice, the separate general statement is made so that even in other cases where it is heard in the scripture, "wherever one shaves the hair and beard," this same sequence applies, and not a sequence following the specific wording of the sentence "one shaves the hair and beard. In the term *prāgvaṃśam*, the accusative case ending is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe*), according to the rule *anaupā dvitīyā*.

One should construct a door to the east for the purpose of entering the *pariśris*—the area for sowing seeds and so forth—with mats and other materials. This is done to the north of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall in the case of initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the forest, because it is only in this case that the *prāgvaṃśa* is possible. However, in the case of initiation at home, since the *prāgvaṃśa* is not present, this [door] is constructed to the north of the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) intended for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering; but if the *prāgvaṃśa* is present, it is constructed to the north of that very hall. Alternatively, even in the case of initiation at home, the *prāgvaṃśa* is mandatory.

Because of the statement "the *prāgvaṃśa* for the crossing over" (*uttaraṇa-prāgvaṃśa*) and because of the sūtra to be stated later, "having led him to that *prāgvaṃśa*," the *prāgvaṃśa* intended for the *prāyaṇīyā* and other rites is indeed distinct [from the one used for shaving]. The mention of the "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is for the purpose of excluding the wife. Āpastamba states clearly: "In this same way, the shaving of the wife's hair [is performed]. The *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti* also says: "For women, there is no shaving of the hair during vows or sacrifices; however, in cases such as the killing of a cow, one should have two finger-breadths cut off. (Paṭala 10)

The exclusion of the *ṛtvij* (priest) is even more certain, because they lack primacy. Jaimini also states this in the third chapter, seventh section (*pāda*), by means of the sūtra: "But on account of the connection with the fruit, that which is joined with the master belongs to the principal [act]. The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: shaving, fasting, and so forth, when joined with the master, are the duties of the principal [sacrificer]. Why? Because of the connection with the fruit—that is, because of the status of being an enjoyer characterized by the possession of the fruit.

Because it is connected [to the main rite], and because it serves the purpose of producing the primary result by way of generating fitness (*yogyatā*). Regarding the term *keśaśmaśrūṇi* (hair and beard): since the word *keśa* ends in a vowel, it is placed first according to the Vedic rule, "The form of Tatpuruṣa compounds beginning with *śmaśru* [is such]," or because the beard is mentioned first as it contributes to the beauty of the person. Since the ritual action (*karman*) is prescribed later, this [phrase] does not prescribe the action itself. The mention of hair and beard is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for body hair (*loman*) in general.

If not, then because a fixed sequence for the two armpits would be impossible; furthermore, in the word *vāpayate*, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used in its own sense (reflexive). Therefore, the Adhvaryu priest himself should shave, and he should not cause [the sacrificer] to be shaved by another. The *Yājamāna* sūtra stating "the barber's work is done" (*kṛte nāpita-kṛtye*) is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this view. Because it is loathed by the world and because there is an absence of instruction, one should perform a small amount of shaving with a mantra and then have the barber complete the remainder of the entire shaving. By this, the assumption of a recitation of mantras—similar to that of the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*)—is also refuted. [The sequence is: first he shaves the beard, then the armpits, and then the hair.

Furthermore, the statement "he has [the hair] shaved here" is for the purpose of making it known that the shaving of the deity occurs on this occasion. This has been clearly stated by Āpastamba: "To the north of the *bahis* and enclosed, the sacrificer has his hair and beard shaved—the armpits first, then the beard, then the hair; or else, the beard and armpits first, then the hair."

In this context, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) has the sense of "instigating" (*prayojaka*) alone, and not its own inherent meaning; this is for the purpose of making known such a restrictive rule. Furthermore, the shaving of the beard (*godānondana*) is performed exclusively by the Adhvaryu priest. This performance by the Adhvaryu is logical because the act is accompanied by mantras and because there is no causative suffix (*ṇij*). The clipping of the nails (*nakhanikṛntana*) is likewise performed by the Adhvaryu alone, as evidenced by the previously cited statement: "When the *ṇij* is absent, it is the work of the barber (*nāpita*)."

Since the recitation of the mantras for shaving (*vapana*) serves as an instrument for their performance (*yajanakaraṇatva*), it should be understood that there is no fault in reciting the mantras in the middle [of the ritual], in accordance with the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭasamācāra*). There is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*) here: "He mutters while the hair is being shaved. The hairs on the face are the *śmaśru* (beard). The *upapakṣa* is the root of the arm. This is because the etymological usage (*rūḍhi*) of the term *upapakṣa* is seen right here in the injunction (*praiṣa*) stated by Baudhāyana: "With my *upapakṣas* shaven by the barber, with my nails clipped, may I prosper. Some, however, say it refers to the region of the cheek.

The hairs located on the head are simply "hair" (*keśa*), as there is no other designation for them. The inclusion of the word "end" (*agra*) is for the purpose of restriction; the meaning is that one should have the hair shaved at the very beginning or at the front. By this, the shaving of the beard in the middle—which belongs to the *āsura* rite—is excluded. Although the exclusion of that [beard-shaving] is already established by the fact that it involves shaving the beard in the middle, nevertheless, due to the force of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) mentioned immediately above, its exclusion does not occur. In the phrase "having shaved the armpits and then the hair," both instances of the word "then" (*atha*) are for the purpose of imitating the Brāhmaṇa text.

Alternatively, in the phrase "athopapakṣau," the word *atha* is intended to indicate the application of both [the husband and the wife]. By this, the shaving of the armpits (*upapakṣa*) for the wife is also established. This is stated by Baudhāyana in the injunction beginning with "one whose armpits have been shaved by the barber," and so forth. In the phrase "atha keśān" (then the hair), the word *atha* is for the purpose of excluding the application of both; therefore, the shaving of the hair applies to the sacrificer alone, not to the wife. Thus Āpastamba also says, "In this way, the wife [undergoes] the shaving of the hair. Regarding this, [the author] states the rule for the shaving: "Not [the wife's]," etc. [Note: The text provided contains a fragmentary corruption at the end: "ka. 'na ke| - MER satyāpāḍhaviracitaṃ śrautasūtraṃ- [7 saptamapra- apa vapana vidhimāha-". This has been interpreted as a reference to Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, where he states the rule for shaving.]
"May the waters moisten for life"—with these words, he moistens the right *godāna*.

That which is given (*dīyate*) upon the cow (*gavi*), that is, upon the earth (*pṛthivyām*), for the sake of digging (*khāpanārtham*), is the *godāna*, the region situated near the ear. He moistens—that is, he wets or makes it damp—the right one. The mixing with warm water is optional. By metonymy, the hair located in the region called *godāna* is understood.

Although there is a requirement for the anointing of the hair (*keśondana*), nevertheless, because the roots of the hair are connected to the region of the *godāna*, it should be understood that this is the injunction for the anointing of the *godāna*, since the anointing of the roots is impossible without that [anointing]. The word "cow" (*go*) signifies the earth, as the *Nighaṇṭu* lists "earth" among its synonyms in the passage: *gauḥ gr̥ṣṭiḥ*.
He places a herb with upward-pointing tips between [the hair and the ground], reciting: "O herb, protect him! (*oṣadhe trāyasvainam*).

One places the *darbha* grass upon the region where the *godāna* [hair-cutting] was performed, using the word "herb" (*oṣadhi*) for the *darbha*. The application of the word "herb" to *darbha* is seen in the mantra for the consecration of the sacrificial grass: "O herbs born in the three ages for the gods... (RV 10.97.1). Āpastamba says, "They trim [the hair] with [the word] *damanta*.

A bundle of *darbha* grass is to be understood by the word "herb. Likewise, at the end of the ritual, Baudhāyana states: "With the formula 'The bundle of *darbha* grass is the womb of the sacrifice,' he places the bundle of *darbha* grass upon the footprint."
With the formula, "O Svadhiti, do not harm him," he applies the razor.

[The commentator] says that the word *svadhiti*—which elsewhere refers to the act of slaughtering an animal—is not intended here because it is not applicable to the present context; thus he says, "with the razor. The instrumental case in *kṣureṇa* is used in the sense of the accusative; therefore, the usage becomes *kṣuram*. "Applying" (*abhinidhāna*) means placing it upon the *darbha* grass.
With the formula, "O God, hear this; I shave these," he shaves. || 1 ||

The word "right" (*dakṣiṇa*) refers to the *godāna* [hair-lock], which is the meaning of the phrase "the hair at the site of the right *godāna*. This is a case of metaphorical usage (*lakṣaṇā*), as in the expression "the sheaths are swelling. This is indicated by the gender of the word *vapana* (shaving) in the compound *sadarbhāṇāṃ keśānāṃ vapanam*. The neuter gender is used because it denotes a general category (*sāmānye napuṃsakam*). Thus, the established meaning is that starting from the right *godāna*, one shaves all the hair in a clockwise direction. It is precisely with this intention that the [specific mention of] the left *godāna* is not stated.

The mention of "shaving the hair on the right side" (*dakṣiṇagodāna*) is intended to show that the ritual acts beginning with the *undana* (sprinkling of water) are to be performed specifically in that region; by this, the removal of the remaining hair is effected. For this very reason, the shaving of the hair was previously promised in general terms: "First he shaves the beard, then the armpits, and then the hair. Furthermore, it is stated in the Śruti: "This skin is indeed dead and impure where there is hair and body hair; having struck away that dead and impure skin, one becomes fit for sacrifice and speaks thus."

The subsequent gift of a cow (*godāna*) is performed silently, by way of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*). However, there is no shaving of the *śikhā* (topknot) at all. But in the case of all [sacrifices], there is shaving of the *śikhā* because of the statement in the *Dharmasūtra*: "One must always wear the sacred thread (*upavīta*) and always have the *śikhā* tied; whatever one does while being without the sacred thread or without the *śikhā* is as if not done. And from the *Smṛti*: "Whatever one does while being without the sacred thread or without the *śikhā*, that is not considered performed. [10th Paṭala] Accompanied by the *Jyotsnā* commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa: Having shaved the eyebrows, the forearms, and the private parts, the remaining hair is shaved.

"An excellent twice-born man should always have his sideburns, beard, and hair shaved in due order, having first shaved the top-knot (*śikhā*), the forearms, and the ground of the private parts," because of this prohibition in the *Smṛti*. Here, the mention of the "private parts" (*upastha*) is an elliptical indication for the anus as well. This shaving applies even to one whose father is living, according to the statement in the *Nigama*: "Shaving is prescribed in seven cases: at the Gaṅgā, in the field of the Sun (*Bhāskarakṣetra*), upon the death of mother and father, at the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), and at the drinking of Soma. [This applies] except at a holy ford (*tīrtha*), except at a sacrifice, and except upon the death of mother and father.

"He who causes the hair to be shaved is a son who has killed his father"—thus it is stated in the *Pracetas-smṛti*. Even in that case, the son's entitlement to perform the shaving occurs only when the father has already undergone the initiation (*dīkṣā*). Otherwise, the fault of being a "supplanter" (*parivettṛ*) and so forth would arise. The details should be understood from my work, the *Smārta-saṃskāra-ratnamālā*. If the initiation takes place on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), there is no shaving if the *kṛtapana* rite has been performed, due to the purpose [of the rite]. Likewise, some say this applies to the establishment of the *Soma* sacrifice (*somādhāna*).

Others hold that even when the hair and beard have grown, shaving is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) like the purchase of the Soma; therefore, there is no recitation of mantras at that time, because of the statement of Bhāradvāja: "When it is cut, it is 'lūna' (shorn). According to this view, the shaving is performed by dividing [the hair] into southern and northern sections. From the very absence of a specific injunction, it is understood that what was stated by Āpastamba—that this is the "Godāna" (hair-cutting ceremony) for the north—is not accepted. Thus says Baudhāyana: "With this same [rite], he moistens the northern Godāna with water, either with a Yajus formula or silently."
He trims the inner nails, first those of the forefeet, then those of the hindfeet; for the left foot, starting from the little toe, and then for the right.

Just as one finger is inside another, so he trims—that is, cuts—the nails; indeed, he does not cut them off [entirely]. Because of the absence of formal instruction (*śikṣā*) and because they have been previously prepared, the barber does not perform this. In the word *nikṛntate*, the prefix *ni-* has the sense of cutting thoroughly. Since the Adhvaryu priest is also the one performing the shaving, his bathing is done silently for the sake of purification. He trims—that is, cuts—the "hand-related" (*hastya*) nails, beginning with the tips; and immediately after that, the "foot-related" (*padya*) nails.

The suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *pācāryāmyām ca*. By the rule *padyatyatadarthe*, the word *pāda* undergoes the substitution *pad*. Since the forms *hastyañjali* and so forth are already established immediately after [the mention of] *padya-nikṛntana*, the specific statement *atha padyāni* is for the purpose of indicating an absence of temporal interval. Regarding the left (savya) hand, the remainder of the sense is that one begins first from the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*). Then, immediately thereafter, [one proceeds] with the right hand.

By the phrase "starting from the little finger of the left hand," although the subsequent clipping of the nails of the right hand is already established, this specific statement is intended to show that for the right hand as well, the nail-clipping must begin precisely from the inner side of the little finger and not in any other manner commonly practiced by people. Likewise, for the left foot, it should be done immediately after [the right], beginning precisely from the little toe.

In the preceding passage, because both [hands] are introduced with the words "first those for the hands" (*hastyāni*) and then "those for the feet" (*padyāni*), the terms *savya* (left) and *dak�paringa* (right) in the subsequent phrase "from the little finger of the left, then of the right" refer respectively to the left hand and foot and the right hand and foot. Since the reference "of the left" and "of the right" is made in general terms, this same procedure applies to the clipping of the toenails just as it does to the clipping of the fingernails. One clips the nails from the inside; first those of the left hand, starting with the little finger...

In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, although the sequence "from the little finger" (*aniṣṭhikātaḥ*) and then "the right ones" (*dakṣiṇāni*)—and subsequently "the toes" (*padyāni*)—is established through a single continuous connection, the author's separate formulation of the sūtra indicates that the order of the rule "from the little finger" and then "the right ones" is not fixed. Furthermore, the clipping of the nails (*nakhanikṛntana*) pertains to the wife, as the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is not heard in this context;
for Āpastamba makes it known that the clipping of the wife's hair (*patnīkeśavapana*) entails the performance of nail-clipping, and Baudhāyana states this explicitly.

When his eyes have been anointed, he then purifies him with twenty-one bunches of *darbha* grass, divided into three groups of seven each, using the mantras beginning with "May the Lord of Thought purify you. He wipes upwards above the navel twice and wipes downwards once; the phrase "with the flawless strainer" is appended to every [mantra].

When he has taken out the eyes, then [the ritual proceeds]; this indicates the lack of temporal interval between the taking out of the eyes and the purification. It is not for the purpose of knowing the sequence of the performance; rather, immediately after the threshing which is to be prescribed by the sūtra situated in the section on the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna-prakaraṇa*), beginning with "The pupil of Vṛtra... and ending with "...he does not pour it out again," there follows [the mantra] beginning with "O Lord of the Purifier, that [grain] of yours... and ending with "Pavamāna, the well-born."

This is because the teacher, while about to prescribe the purificatory rite (*pāvana*) by means of the sūtra ending with "with the *anuvāka* beginning with *naina*" (ĀśGS 1.15.2), will indicate that very rite by means of a sūtra situated within the section on the *yāma* [rite]. That [sūtra] follows immediately after. Furthermore, the employment of the word *tat* here, and the employment of the word *enam* in reference to the object of purification, are for the purpose of establishing the connection between the purificatory rites of smearing (*abhyañjana*), anointing (*añjana*), and purification (*pāvana*).
