However, explaining that those [rites] connected with him (the sacrificer) have a single final goal (*ekāpavarga*), one should perform this triad for the sacrificer first, and subsequently for his wife—not by performing each one individually. By this, it is understood even from our own sūtra that this triad belongs to the wife as well.

When—at which time—he becomes such that his two lips are joined, then immediately thereafter he purifies him three times with twenty-one bunches of *darbha* grass, meaning with seven bunches each divided into three parts. (The singular number in "twenty-one" is used because the word for "twenty" and its multiples are always singular, according to the lexicon. Now, one might ask: why say "with seven" when it would suffice simply to say "he purifies him in three ways"? It is not so.

By the phrase "predhā vibhaktaiḥ" (separated threefold), the mere separation is indicated; however, it should be understood as meaning that all [the blades], having been separated and then mixed together again, are purified three times. This is either for the purpose of excluding such [a simple separation] or to indicate the application of the maxim "it should be combined because it is not explicitly heard. Regarding "darbhapuñjīla," some say it means a stalk of *darbha* grass consisting of seven blades. In the *Bahvṛcabrāhmaṇa*, however, it is stated as "piñjulaiḥ. Some say that *piccha* refers to a branched *darbha*. Others hold that the words *piñjūla* and *puñjīla* are synonyms. When that...

In the statement "Time becomes the sacrificer" (*kālo bhavaty auṇam*), the masculine gender should be understood as unintended because it resides in the subject (*uddeśya*), just as in the case of "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires" (*brāhmaṇo 'gnīn ādadhīta*). One should not raise the objection: "Since the Vedic text 'Wearing the *sauma* garment, the husband and wife should establish the fires' (*jāyāpatī agnīn ādadhīyātām*) prescribes joint entitlement (*sahādhikāra*), the masculine gender in the [preceding] 'Brāhmaṇa' is unintended; however, in the present case, since there is no Vedic text indicating joint entitlement, how can the masculine gender be considered unintended? This doubt is to be set aside.

In the passage "The husband and wife, being purified, undergo initiation" (*pūtau jāyāpatī dīkṣete*), because the scriptural statement regarding the great qualification (*mahādhikāra-śruti*) is heard here as well, there is no loss of the intention to express masculinity (*puṃstva*). The reading "citpatistvā punātu vākpatirityetaiḥ" follows the commentary; the text according to the *Ṭīkā* is "citpatistvā punātu vākpatiravatu".

[Chapter 1, Section 1] Accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. With one of these three mantras—“May Vākpati purify you,” “May the god Savitṛ purify you,” or “May [Savitṛ] purify you”—the *tūṣṇīm* (silently) should be performed twice; otherwise, the other two would merely serve as optional alternatives. To prevent that from occurring, so that all of them may function as means of purification, this is stated.

The expression "with the mantras" is used to indicate that the status of being the instrument (*karaṇatā*) for each individual action belongs equally to each individual mantra, as established by the maxim *aśvatvāt* (because of the nature of the horse). By this, the view that "the purifying [act] is accompanied by mantras, while the others are silent" is refuted. Previously it was stated that "the priest purifies"; this [passage] is a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*) concerning that, beginning with "on the hair-tuft" (*sa-mi*) and so forth. "Above the navel" means upward from the navel. Because of the word "upward" (*ud*), one must measure upwards. "Once" means a single time. For this very reason, the purification is performed without interruption.

Otherwise, one might think it is done only once. "Avāk" means that which goes downward or reaches down; thus it is *avāk*. The word "from the navel" (*nābheḥ*) is understood to follow. The meaning is that one should wipe from the navel down to the feet. There is also a reading *avāc*. Even though there is no explicit scriptural statement regarding the purification of those parts covered by the end of the garment, because loosening the knot is also censured, the learned (*śiṣṭas*) perform the purification only of those parts covered by the end of the garment. This is because otherwise there would be the consequence of [the garment] becoming bent and the consequence of censure.

One appends the phrase "with the flawless purifier, with the rays of the Vasu Sūrya" to all the mantras. Regarding the statement "one appends 'with the flawless [purifier]' as an addition," although this very [phrase] is established as an addition for the other two [mantras], the expression "in all" is used to ensure its addition even to the three *yājamāna* mantras: "May the Lord of Wisdom purify me; may the Lord of Cooking purify me; may the divine Savitṛ purify me. However, in the case of the final mantra of the *ādhvaryava* section, it is already recited in the Śruti itself.

Therefore, there is no further connection here. Regarding the specific procedure for the removal (*nirasana*) of these bundles of *arbha* grass, Baudhāyana states in the *Dvaidha*: "Then, having sprinkled them with water, one should remove them toward the north. The opinion of Śālīki is: "Then, having sprinkled them with water, one should remove them toward the north. The distinction between these two is as follows: *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) is to be performed with the hand palm upwards; *abhyukṣaṇa* (pouring over/sprinkling from above) is to be performed with the hand closed into a fist. *Khedana* means removal. Because of the prefix *ava*, it should be done downward; because of the prefix *ud*, it should be done upward—this is the distinction to be observed regarding the removal.
Having led him to that *prāgvaṃśa* hall, some authorities prescribe the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering here.

Since the *dīkṣaṇīyā* cannot be accomplished for a sacrificer who has gone outside without his entry into the *prāgvaṃśa*, this statement is established by implication; however, it is intended to establish the Adhvaryu’s status as the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*). Therefore, having held the sacrificer’s hand until he is seated, the action must be performed by him [the Adhvaryu]. But the ritual act accompanied by mantras belongs to the sacrificer alone.

And this status as an instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛtva*) has also been stated by Baudhāyana with specific detail: "Then, having laid [the animal] down upon his left hand, he leads it to the hall, [saying]: 'O gods, we approach you at the sacrifice, you whose laws are true; O gods, worthy of sacrifice, since we invoke you for your consent (*āgura*),' so it is said. Regarding the difference of opinion (*dvaidha*): "Having laid it down upon his left hand"—this is the first ritual procedure (*kalpa*), according to Baudhāyana; "upon the right," according to Śālīki.

Then, having laid him down on his left hand—this is the specific distinction here—and "some recite the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering] at this point"; such is the syntactical connection. The meaning is that at this time, the *dīkḹṣaṇīyā* which was previously mentioned should be performed here, and not before. In the absence of this explicit statement, the optional second *dīkṣaṇīyā* would be understood as occurring after the presentation of the *prāyaśas*; therefore, this explicit statement is necessary to preclude that.

In this context, because of the employment of the word *iṣṭi*, it is observed that "this oblation belongs to them in me. [Note: This refers to the specific ritual application. The use of the suffix *-ya* in the word *prapādya* is for the purpose of ensuring there is no interval between the *prapadana* and the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice. By this, it is established that the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the Āhavanīya fire occurs only after the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, and not prior to it.

In this context, "leading forward" (*prapādana*) means simply seating [the sacrificer]. When the *dīkṣā* takes place in the house (*gṛha*), if the *prāgvaṃśa* hall is unavailable, he leads him forward to the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) intended for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering. Here, in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, the rites such as the taking of the vow (*vratopāyana*), the girding of the wife (*patnīsanahana*), and so forth, do not take place, because their purpose has already been fulfilled. Since the rule for leading him forward to the *prāgvaṃśa* is prescribed here, it follows by implication that everything up to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) takes place within the *prāgvaṃśa* itself. From the remainder of the *dhruvā* vessel, he offers four *dīkṣā* oblations with the *sruva* ladle, saying: "To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, svāhā! and so on.

The acceptance [of the oblation] is performed with a mantra, while the swelling of the *dhruvā* vessel is as prescribed in the archetype (*prakṛta*). Some maintain that the swelling for those other than the *iṣṭi* sacrifices is not accompanied by a mantra. Initiation (*dīkṣā*) consists of a fitness conducive to the undertaking of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*); the *bhakṣa*-offerings made for its sake are the initiation-oblations (*dīkṣā-āhutayaḥ*). These initiation-oblations serve to purify the mind through restraint; therefore, in a *sattra*, these offerings are performed for each individual sacrificer. Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement "for the lifting up of the sacrifice," they also serve the purpose of elevating the sacrifice.

Therefore, these mantras are prescribed for every direction at each dwelling. Likewise, in the *asthi-yajña* (bone-sacrifice) and when the sacrificer is absent, one oblation is offered with each individual mantra. The mantras end with "to Agni, svāhā! (*agnaye svāhā*). In these cases, the *svāhākāra* is already recited [within the mantra]; by that alone the offering is made, and no other *svāhākāra* should be employed.

Since it has been determined that the *svāhākāra* which immediately follows a word denoting a deity (*devatāpada*) alone possesses the purpose of giving (*dānārthatva*), in the present case, the act of giving is accomplished by that very *svāhākāra* which exists in such a form. The employment of a second *svāhākāra* when one already exists is for the sake of those who are proud (*mānikāṇām*) alone, not for Vaidikas; for among Vedic rites, that which is declared in the Veda is more authoritative.
With the mantra "The divine waters" (*āpo devīḥ*), [he offers] with the ladle (*sruca*) the fifth [oblation].

The word "he offers" (*jahoti*) is understood from the preceding context. The mention of the *khava* (ladle) is for the purpose of excluding the *dhruvā* (the perpetual vessel), or rather, to ensure that the non-technical *sruk* (ladle) is obtained. The use of the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is intended to establish that this [offering] also possesses the nature of a *dīkṣā-huti* (consecration oblation). By this, it is established that the offering is made from the remainder of the *dhruvā* itself, and that the performance of the ritual is to be carried out facing all directions at each sacrificial arrangement (*vihāra*). The mantra ends with "May he prosper, Svāhā!

Having filled the *sruk* with twelve scoops (*dvādaśa-gṛhīta*) for the sixth oblation, using the formula "Of the All-Gods, the Leader," one either makes an opening in the bowl or fills the uppermost *sruc* or the one next to the last.

The syntactical connection is as follows: having filled the *sruva* ladle with twelve scoops, one offers the sixth oblation with the verse beginning "viśve devasya netuḥ. The word "juhoti" (he offers) is understood to carry over from the previous context. Here too, the *svāhā*-utterance is recited exactly as it stands; the offering is made with that very *svāhā*, and no other *svāhā* is to be employed. In this case, there are ten repetitions of the replenishing (*āpyāyana*). At the end, the *dhauva* [offering] is completed. The purpose of mentioning the sixth oblation is the same as for the fifth. The mantra ends with "puṣpase svāhā."

Having made the *sruk* such that there is space for a cavity (*bila*) within it, or by means of it, he offers. By this, the position that one offers with a vessel that is deficient [in capacity] is demonstrated. If the filling of the *dhruvā* with clarified butter taken in twelve ladlings does not occur, then the alternative is to make it such that there is space for a cavity. He states the means for accomplishing the position of fullness: "In the last *sruk*, etc. When the last *sruk* has been taken, he fills it with clarified butter, [thinking], "I shall fill [it]."

[Chapter 150] With clarified butter from the *sthālī* (pot) using the *sruva* (ladle) or the *sruc* (spoon). When the spoon has been taken in the penultimate position—that is, the one preceding the last—the meaning is that one should take clarified butter sufficient to fill the *sruva*, leaving behind a space equal to the measure of the *sruva*. Some say that because this is a remnant of a previous *iṣṭi*, the placing of the fuel-sticks (*samidādhāna*) and the circumambulation (*parikramaṇa*) do not take place. This very [act] is designated as *audgrahaṇa* (taking up).

And thus says the Śruti: "Prajāpati created the sacrifice; once created, it fled away from him. He [the sacrifice] swallowed the Yajus, he swallowed the Sāman; the Ṛk rescued it. Because the Ṛk rescued it, that is the nature of the Audgrahaṇa. The meaning of this is as follows: among the three classes of persons presiding over the mantras, who were dispatched by Prajāpati to seize the fleeing Person of Sacrifice (Yajñapuruṣa), that sacrifice thoroughly swallowed—that is, concealed—the person presiding over the Yajus and the person presiding over the Sāman.

The man who was free from pride seized the *ṛc*. Because he (*yad*) seized it (*udagṛhṇāt*), therefore this [verse] bears the name *audgrahaṇa*; this indeed is the reason for the *audgrahaṇa* being called *audgrahaṇa*.
He sews around the right forefoot of the black antelope skin, including the flesh.

*Kṛṣṇa* means a black deer; its skin is *kṛṣṇājina*. The inclusion of the word "black" is for the purpose of excluding [the skins of] tigers and other animals; therefore, there is no stitching (*pariṣīvana*) of a tiger skin. It will be stated later in this very section that the use of a tiger skin is found in the context of malevolent rites (*abhicārakarman*), and it is also seen in another Sūtra. By the phrase "the right foreleg," it is understood here that the skin is complete with its limbs. *Antarmāsam* means cutting within the flesh. He sews it together with a needle, a thong, or a cord. Or he makes two pieces joined by flesh, placed in opposite directions.

He joins two black antelope skins, which have their heads and tails reversed and are thick with flesh, by sewing them together at the fleshy parts with a needle, a thorn, or thread; the meaning is that he does this so they do not come apart.

"O Indra-Śākvara, I take refuge in the Gāyatrī; I yoke it for you. O Indra-Śākvara, I take refuge in the Triṣṭubh; I yoke it for you. O Indra-Śākvara, I take refuge in the Jagatī; I yoke it for you. O Indra-Śākvara, I take refuge in the Anuṣṭubh; I yoke it for you. O Indra-Śākvara, I take refuge in the Paṅkti; I yoke it for you. With these words, he spreads a black antelope skin within the altar, with its neck pointing eastward and the hair side up.

Regarding the statement "he spreads the black antelope skin within the altar" (*antarvedi kṛṣṇājinam āstṛṇāti*), because of the repeated mention of the "black antelope skin" (*kṛṣṇājina*), it should be understood that in cases such as malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) where there is a substitute for the black antelope skin—such as a goat skin—or whenever the black antelope skin itself is a substitute, it is not spread within the altar; rather, it is to be placed only in the sacrificer’s station (*yajamānāyatana*). "Within the altar" (*antarvedi*) means in the middle of the altar; "with the hair upwards" (*uttaraloma*) means with the hair on top. By this, the necessity of the presence of hair is indicated. Some maintain that these five formulas are intended for the purpose of distribution and optional alternatives (*vibhāga-pravada-vikalpa*).

Others maintain that because the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), denoted by the terms *indraśāvaram*, is associated with specific meters such as the *gāyatrī* and others, it possesses multiple purposes and thus there is a combination (*samuccaya*) [of the skins]. This alone is appropriate because of the complete recitation [of the formulas]. When the sacrificer has mounted [the chariot], he fastens a net (*jāla*) upon the head of the wife.

"When he has ascended" means when the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) has mounted—that is, when he has performed the act of ascending—upon that black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). "He releases" means he casts [the cord] off. Since it will be stated later that the muttering of the mantra "May I attain consecration" (*ā'haṃ dīkṣām*) is an ancillary part of the act of ascending, the releasing of the garland and so forth occurs immediately after this muttering. The mention of the "sacrificer" is for the purpose of excluding the wife; by this, it is established that the black antelope skin belongs to the sacrificer alone and not to the wife, and likewise, the act of ascending belongs to him alone.

The mention of the "wife" (*patnī*) is for the purpose of excluding the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). By this, it is established that the fastening of the net (*jāla*) is to be done only on the head of the wife, not on the head of the sacrificer. The *jāla* is made of thin strips of silk thread (*paṭṭasūtra*). It is called a *māṣayā jālī*. According to another text, it is the wool (*ūrṇā*) of a living ram; according to yet another scripture, in its absence, it may be made of *darbha* grass. And that is tied to a split bamboo ring (*vedalevalaya*). As Baudhāyana says: "The *vidala* is a bowl, the *nāla* is a *kurīra*. He initiates her with an unwashed linen garment (*kṣauma*) as an upper covering (*ūrdhvavāsya*).

Regarding that *paṭṭī* (cloth): "That which is slightly washed, new, white, unworn, and not yet used—one should know that as *ahata* (unwashed/unworn), purifying for all rites. Thus, it refers to an *ahata* cloth characterized by these qualities. Baudhāyana states: "Washed, unwrinkled, with their fringes intact, and unused—these are *ahata* garments. Since the quality of whiteness is not included in the definition of *ahata* in the *Dharmasūtra*, it is not mandatory. Therefore, even cloth that is red, yellow, or other colors may be considered *ahata*.

Since blue is prohibited in every respect according to the Smṛti, it is not to be worn at all. "Worn-out" means old; "not worn-out" means new. "With linen" (kṣomeṇa) means made from the bark of the *atasī* plant; that is, sufficient for a wrap. By this, cotton and other materials are excluded. If even this is unavailable in any way, then that [other material] may be used. "Upper garment" (ūrdhvavāsyaṃ) means it should be worn with fringes pointing eastward, or rather, it should be worn with fringes pointing upward.

And thus Āpastamba says: "The wife consecrates [the sacrificer] with a fringe [mātrā], saying, 'Wearing the fringe, he shall speak. Here, the word *mātrā* denotes a part consisting of ten finger-breadths (*daśā*). "With a fringe" means "with a fringe measuring ten finger-breadths. Alternatively, *avāsya* refers to the upper garment (*uttarīya*); this is because it has been prepared specifically for the wife's station.

Regarding the items pertaining to the consecration (*dīkṣā*), some—following the *Āpastamba-sūtra* which states, "The wife should be consecrated with as many insignia as are prescribed," and based on the sūtra, "He consecrates her with an unwashed linen garment as an upper cloth"—assume the exclusion of all other items related to the consecration from the wife. This is incorrect, because of the rule: "This very same procedure applies to her until the Soma-pressing."

In the *Yājamāna-sūtra*, because it is intended that the items connected with the initiation (*dīkṣā*) apply to the wife as well through the use of the word "that" (*tat*), and because this would contradict logic and because Baudhāyana has stated it explicitly; [it says] in the *Mānava-sūtra*: "One should not fasten a cord with loops on both ends upon the head of the wife.
A girdle (*mekhalā*) made of *śara* or *muñja* grass should be made of three strands (*trivṛt*).

"Śaramuñjas" means that the *muñja* grasses are indeed reeds (*śara*). That girdle which is made is made of reeds alone. In the expression "of the śaramuñjas," the mention of *śara* (reeds) indicates that the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) of being reeds should be applied to the *muñja* grasses. Alternatively, it is a compound meaning "those whose roots (*mūla*) are like reeds (*śara*)," i.e., *śaramuñjas*. According to another Vedic text stating "the *muñja* grasses are the *ūrgarda*," the girdle becomes one made of reeds (*śaramayī*). [End of] Paṭala 150, accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

The meaning is that, because the fruit of prosperity (*ūrṛddhi*) is obtained only through what has been previously heard (*śrutāpūrṇam*), the word *śara* must be understood as referring specifically to *muñja* grass. "Śaramuñja" is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) of *śara* and *muñja*. Some maintain that there is no singular form (*ekavadbhāva*) here—either due to the rule beginning with *dadhipayas* (Pāṇini 2.4.14) or because of its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*). Others hold that it is an option between *śara* and *muñja*; since the girdle (*mekhalā*) made of *muñja* is seen elsewhere, the sense is that this [girdle] consists exclusively of *śara*. Or, it may be a copulative compound (*samuccaya*). In this case too, others say it is because of the displacement of the status of being made of *śara*.

In the alternative view that it is a choice (*vikalpa*), the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), as in the rule "the girdle is made of *śara*-grass. In the alternative view that it is a combination (*samuccaya*), the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of accumulation (*prācurya*). Both these positions are untenable; for the state of being made of *śara*-grass has the result of shattering the enemy—as seen in the statement "the *śara*-grass [altar] indeed shatters him"—and thus its application is restricted solely to rites of sorcery (*ābhicārika-karman*). Consequently, it is inappropriate for the state of being made of *śara*-grass, which has the result of shattering enemies, to be employed in any rite other than those.

Therefore, it should be understood that by the word *śara*, only *muñja* grass is intended, and not other grasses of the *śara* species. "Trivṛdveṇī" means threefold (*trivṛt*) and braided (*veṇī*); that is, a braid consisting of three strands, having the form of a braid. The meaning is that the girdle made of *muñja* grass should be prepared in this manner. Alternatively, it may be analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "that which has three braids" (*trivṛd-veṇīkā*). This [girdle] should also be made broad, according to the Vedic text: "It becomes wide. Or else, there is a division of words as *trivṛd-veṇīkā āryā*; in the term *trivṛdveṇīkā*, the suffix *kap* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).

The word *ārya* denotes excellence (*śreṣṭhatva*). Here, excellence takes the form of extensiveness (*vistīrṇatva*). Thus, the meaning of the Vedic text is established by the sūtra itself: "it becomes broad" (*pṛthvī bhavati*). After the word *āryā*, the word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. In this way, it is understood that the girdle (*mekhalā*) is similar to a rope (*rajju*), whereas the sacrificial cord (*yoktra*) is similar to matted hair (*jaṭā*).

With the formula, "Thou art strength," he winds it three times around the waist of the sacrificer from left to right; according to some, twice. Having made a loose knot to the north of the navel with the formula, "May Pūṣan tie the knot for thee," he draws it down to the south of the navel with the formula, "May it not come loose for thee. While doing so, he should meditate upon whomsoever he hates.

Regarding the phrase *trivṛdveṇyā śaramuñjānā mekhalayā yajamānaṃ nābhideśe triḥ pradakṣiṇaṃ parivyayati*: although the injunction would be established by this alone—that one should wrap the sacrificer three times clockwise around the waist with a triple-braided girdle made of *śara* and *muñja* grass—the separate formulation of the sūtra stating "the girdle should be made of *śara* and *muñja* grass, triple-braided" is not redundant. This is because the subsequent reference by means of the word *tat* (it) would otherwise be purposeless; however, since that word serves to indicate that the preparation of the girdle must be performed prior [to the act of wrapping], there is no redundancy. By the word *tayā*, it refers to that which has been prepared.

The mention of the "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is for the purpose of excluding the wife. "In the region of the navel" means in the middle of the navel. If it were simply said "in the navel" (*nābhau*), there might be a suspicion that the locative case has the sense of proximity; let this not be so, but rather, by taking its sense as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), it is intended that it should be precisely in the middle of the navel. For this reason, the word "region" (*deśa*) is employed; it also indicates that the encircling is to be performed in that region which has the navel as its point of reference, even though it is separated by a cloth.

By this [passage], the Vedic revelation is explained: "In this way, indeed, for a person, that which is below the navel is impure and that which is above is pure; in that he ties it at the middle, he separates his pure part from his impure part. *Nāmyai* means "from the navel" (*nābhyāḥ*). The word "of a person" (*puruṣasya*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); therefore, even with the yoke-thong, the fastening must be done exactly at the navel. According to the technical rule, [the mantra is recited] once with the mantra and twice silently.

In this context, the word *pradakṣiṇa* does not denote "circumambulation from left to right," as that meaning is already established by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating, "one performs the *pradakṣiṇa* at sacrificial rites. Rather, it denotes "favorable" or "conducive. As stated in the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: "While King Candrasena was ruling the kingdom, the wind blew favorably (*pradakṣiṇa*), and the subjects were favorable (*pradakṣiṇāḥ*). All his neighboring vassals were also always favorable (*pradakṣiṇāḥ*) toward him."

In this context, because the word *pradakṣiṇa* is seen to signify "favorability," it is established that the winding [of the cord]—whether tight or loose—is performed in accordance with the favorability of the sacrificer. The first mantra ends with "mā mā hiṃsīḥ" (do not harm me). It is like the binding of a topknot (*śikhābandhana*). He draws it around from the right side of the navel; having brought it from the northern region, he places the knot on the right side of the navel so that it does not go to any other place. This is the meaning.

While the girding with the girdle (*mekhalā*) is being performed, the sacrificer should meditate upon the person whom he hates. "He should meditate upon the one hated by the sacrificer" is the explicit meaning. Through such meditation, misfortune befalls the one who is hated. Alternatively, the meditation on the hated one occurs at the time of drawing [the girdle] around. The "hated one" refers to both an enemy and evil (*pāpman*).

In the context of the *pradhikaraṇaparikarṣaṇa*, since the matter is already established by the statement "as in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa," the re-enactment of both ritual actions is redundant; it serves, however, to inform us that the recitation of those two mantras and the performance of those two actions exists here as well as in other branches of the Veda. The purpose, moreover, is to establish the necessity of knowing [the procedure]. In the absence of such knowledge, the expiation for a Yajus-error is performed in the Dakṣiṇāgni with the mantra "bhuvaḥ svāhā. He girds the wife with the mantra "saṃ tvā nahyāmi," just as in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

The mantra "āśāsānaḥ" is set aside, and in its place this mantra "saṃ tvā nahyāmi" is prescribed; the mantra ends with "vānam asme. The mention of the *patnī* (the wife) is for the purpose of excluding the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). The binding itself is performed by the *adhvaryu* priest alone, because of the indicative mark "sva" [in the mantra]. He binds, that is, he ties it together.

Just as by the rule "as in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," there is the application of the *yoktra* (girdle) as the instrument for binding—with the formulas "The *yajus* is seated" or "Standing" [for the wife], "Pūṣan is your [guardian]" for the making of the knot, and "May it not stand against you" for the drawing [of the knot]—so too for Soma, the *yoktra* is to be bound. Its detailed procedure will be explained later. With the formula "Thou art the womb of Indra," he gives or ties to the sacrificer a black antelope horn with three or five ridges.

That which has three folds is *trivalī*; that which has five folds is *pañcavalī*. The "folds" (*valayaḥ*) are elevated regions located on the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*). According to the *Dvaidhasūtra*, "O Aupamanyava, this [horn] should be entirely [used]," it follows that the whole is primary. In its absence, a cut [horn] may be used. When a horn with more than five folds is obtained, one must cut away the fold exceeding the five and then take it, because it is stated that only such [a horn] is to be taken.

Even there, only the tip (the *agrabhāga*) is to be taken, because that alone serves as the means for removing the itching. The mention of the *yajamāna* is for the purpose of excluding the wife (*patnī*). He either gives it or ties it. In the case of giving, it is given into the hand. The mention of "towards" (*ā*) indicates a specific manner of tying. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says: "One should tie it to the fringe (*daśā*) of the garment. Baudhāyana says: "Having tied it to the fringe at the edge of the garment, one digs up a clod of earth with it within the altar-ground (*antarvedi*)."

Regarding the black antelope horn (kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā), Āpastamba states the distinction: "It has three ridges or five ridges; it turns to the right, or according to some, it turns to the left. Maradvāja also says: "Then he hands him the black antelope horn, which has either three ridges or five ridges and which turns to the right. Baudhāyana says: "It is bound all around with a hempen cord. The mantra ends with "mā mā hiṃsīḥ" (do not harm me).

This is because of the force of the subsequent mantra seen in the sequence of initiation mantras (*dīkṣā-mantra*) recited in the *Yājamāna-sūtra*: "Having drawn [the earth] with 'Come, O Sleep,'... Furthermore, this handing over of the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*) occurs only after the wrapping of the sacrificer's head. This is because the author of the Sūtra will demonstrate the lack of interruption between the two acts—the handing over of the black antelope horn and the act of digging up clods of earth using the black antelope horn as an instrument—which stand in a relationship of cause and effect, by stating in the *Yājamāna-sūtra*: "with the black antelope horn that has been handed over."

There are pegs for the purpose of scratching the wife's body, because it has been stated by Baudhāyana. Regarding the nature of those pegs, Kātyāyana says: "They are made from sacrificial wood and have broad heads," so that they may properly arrange the net over the wife's head. || 2 ||

He arranges the net that has been placed upon the head of the wife so that it is well-fitted and secure; that is to say, he fastens it to her head with cords so that it does not fall from her head, joining it with the *vidala* (wickerwork). By this, it is established that in the previous case, merely placing [the net] was required. The staff for the initiated is made of *udumbara* wood, or it may be from any fruit-bearing tree.

The staff (*daṇḍa*) of one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*) should be made from *udumbara* wood. Alternatively, it may be from any tree whatsoever that bears fruit. According to Āpastamba’s statement, "one that is fit for sacrifice" (*yajñiya*), when such a sacrificial tree is available, that alone is primary; in its absence, however, even a tree other than those fit for sacrifice may be used, since the Teacher has stated generally, "any tree whatsoever. Regarding the term "fruit-bearing" (*phalāhaka*): it means either that which bears fruit but is not to be broken (or destroyed), or else that which bears only fruit—like the *udumbara* and others—and does not bear flowers. Of such a fruit-bearing tree, he states its measurement: it should be the size of a fist, or equal to the mouth, or reaching down to the chin.

The term "staff of the initiated" (*dīkṣitadaṇḍa*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. "The size of a fist" (*muṣṭimātra*) means having the measure of a fist. The suffix *mātrac* is applied here by the rule *pramāṇe dvayasacdadhnamātracaḥ*. By this, the circumference of the staff of the initiated is stated. "Equal to the mouth" (*mukhena samita*) means equal to the mouth up to the edge of the lips; its measure is that [of the mouth]. The expression "equal to the mouth" (*mukhena samita*) is used instead of "reaching to the mouth" (*mukhadaghna*) in order to imitate the wording of the Vedic scripture (*śruti*). "The size of the jaw" (*cacukadaghna*) means having the measure of the jaw (*cacuka*, i.e., *hanu*).

Regarding the suffixes *mātraC* and *danac*: when both horizontal (*tiryak*) and vertical (*ūrdhva*) measurements, which have a single object as their referent, are presented simultaneously, the suffix *mātraC* is applied to the horizontal measurement and *danac* to the vertical measurement; this is generally the style of the Teacher (Pāṇini).

[The ritual proceeds as follows: Having given that [wood] to the sacrificer with the mantra, "O tree-dweller, you who are high-standing and well-glorious, bestow glory upon the sacrificer," he causes him to recite the *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas and offers oblations with these mantras.

That staff. The word "that" (tat) indicates that the preparation of the staff has already been performed previously. The mention of the "sacrificer" (yajamāna) is for the purpose of excluding the wife. Furthermore, the word "sacrificer" occurring within the mantra cannot serve to exclude the wife; for even in the view that the rite is accompanied by a mantra, it is possible for the wife also to receive the staff—either by modifying the mantra to "give it to the sacrificer" (*yajamānāya dhehi*) or by omitting the word "sacrificer. [From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Seventh Book]

Therefore, the mention of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is indeed necessary for the purpose of excluding [others]. Nor should it be argued that since the taking of the staff (*daṇḍapratigraha*), which is recited in the *Yājamāna-sūtra*, is understood to have the sacrificer as its agent, it follows that the giving of the staff (*daṇḍapradāna*) must also have the sacrificer as its recipient; thus, what is the purpose of mentioning the sacrificer?

In this context, just as the performance of the purificatory rites (*dīkṣā-saṃskāra*) prescribed for the sacrificer—such as bathing and so forth—is obtained through the force of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) by means of the wife, so too, since the taking of the staff (*daṇḍa-pratigraha*) would likewise be obtained through the force of the indicative mark, the mention of the "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is necessary to exclude that [application to the wife]. This is because an indicative mark depends upon its own class (*sajāti*). And indeed, the taking of the staff possesses the quality of being a purificatory rite, which constitutes its membership in that same class.

Nor can it be argued that, simply because the singular number is heard in reference to the staff (*daṇḍa*), the taking up of the staff must belong to the sacrificer alone, and the giving of it also must be for the sacrificer alone and not for the wife (*patnī*). This is because the singular number may be understood as intending plurality; thus, when two staves are obtained, the mention of the "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) in the injunction for the handing over of the staff is absolutely necessary for the purpose of excluding the wife. Furthermore, the word *pradāya* (having given) serves to indicate the lack of interruption between the handing over of the staff and the recitation of the *saṃbhāra-yajus*.

Nor should it be argued that this [sequence] is untenable because the giving of the staff and the recitation of the *saṃbhāra-yajus* are separated by the acceptance performed by the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). For there is no actual separation, since the giving of the staff and the acceptance occur simultaneously. We shall demonstrate this simultaneity in the *Yājamāna-sūtra*, where it states: "He accepts the staff with [the mantra]: 'The divine Vanaspati has stood well; may the protector guard me.'"

In this way, the immediate succession between the giving of the staff and the recitation of the *saṃbhāra-yajus* becomes easily established. Therefore, immediately after the *saṃbhāra-yajus*, the rites beginning with the *keśinī-dīkṣā* and ending with the restraint of speech (*vāgyamana*) take place. He causes her to recite those [verses] which have already been shown previously in the *saṃbhāra* section as well, for the sake of their subsequent application. By this, the exclusion of the wife from the recitation of the *saṃbhāra-yajus* is established.

The *paribhāṣā-sūtra* stated by Kātyāyana—"One should understand the sacrificer [to be the agent] in the cases of giving, reciting, beginning, choosing the bridegroom, vows, and measurements"—is also an authority here. Now, one might object: "It should have been stated simply as 'and he offers' (*juhoti ca*). For the rule that 'where a ritual action is enjoined by a group of mantras, there one should offer for each mantra' is established by that very *paribhāṣā*. What is the purpose of the statement 'with these mantras'? This is true.

Reciting each preceding *saṃbhārayajus* formula after the preceding one, he offers with each succeeding formula, and likewise with the *vyāhṛtis*. The mention of "Vāsiṣṭha" is for the purpose of excluding others. The use of the word "with these" (*etaiḥ*) is for the purpose of excluding the *vyāhṛtis*. The explicit statement "with the mantras" is for the sake of restriction, meaning that the offering is made with the mantras alone, and not with mantras qualified by the [specific] substances. The particle "ca" (and) in the phrase "juhoti ca" (and he offers) is for the purpose of including the recitation. Because it is enjoined that he "offers," the exclamation *svāhā* is used in these cases. Here, the clarified butter (*ājya*) is simply that which is contained in the *ājyasthālī* vessel.

In the absence of that [sacrificial substance], one should consecrate clarified butter (*ājya*) according to the method prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtra* and perform the oblation (*homa*) with it. Here, because there is no statement such as "as before" (*pūrvavat*) or "twelve" (*dvādaśa*), all the *saṃbhārayajus* formulas are to be employed for both the recitation and the oblation. In this context, beginning from "The earth is the initiation; by that initiation of Agni he is initiated" up to "May they initiate you who are being initiated," the *ācchidrika* mantra—because it bears the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of initiation and the word "long-lived" (*āyuṣmat*)—is to be recited by the Adhvaryu priest immediately prior to the muttering (*japa*) of the *Keśinī-dīkṣā*.

By the phrase "as is the case with the other," the author of the Sūtra has also stated the application of the injunction; however, because it was not explicitly mentioned, it is considered both performed and unperformed. [A.

1, Section kha, ga] He announces him while he is restrained from speech, three times in a whisper and three times aloud: "This Brāhmaṇa, so-and-so, the son of such-a-one, the grandson of such-a-one, the great-grandson of such-a-one, the son of such-a woman, the granddaughter of such-a woman, the great-granddaughter of such-a woman, has been initiated. This concludes the first Paṭala, together with the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

By the phrase "him, being restrained from speech," it is understood that the rites beginning with the *keśinī-dīkṣā* and the *japa*, and ending with the restraint of speech, are to be performed immediately after the *saṃbhārayajus*. Since the sequence is already established by the mere expression "restrained from speech," the reference by means of the pronoun *tam* (him) serves the purpose of restriction. Thus, the restraint of speech applies to him alone and not to the wife; consequently, due to the absence of the restraint of speech, there is an absence of the *āvedana* (announcement). Furthermore, the *āvedana* of the wife is not seen even in other *sūtras*.

The *keśinī-dīkṣā*, the silent recitation (*japa*), the making of fists (*muṣṭikaraṇa*), and the releasing of the fingers (*aṅgulyutsarga*) do not belong to the wife either. This is because, due to the mutual connection between the restraint of speech (*vāgyamana*) and the *keśinī-dīkṣā* and so forth, the cessation of one does not entail the cessation of the other. Their mutual connection is indicated by the particle "and" (*ca*) in the *Yajamāna-sūtra*, which is about to be cited: "He moves at his pleasure with those [fingers] and restrains his speech. The word "restrained in speech" (*vāgyata*) connects with the verb "he informs" (*āvedayati*). "Informing" (*āvedana*) means speaking.

In the phrase "he makes known [the victim] as possessing three forms," the words "to the gods" (*devebhyaḥ*) are to be supplied. In the phrase "three times loudly" (*tris uccaiḥ*), the verb "he makes known" (*āvedayati*) is to be supplied. Here, the words "to the gods and to men" (*devebhyo manuṣyebhyaś ca*) are to be supplied. Thus says the Śruti: "When he says 'this Brāhmaṇa has been initiated' three times in a low voice, he announces him to the gods; when he says it three times loudly, he announces him to both—the gods and the men. In the expression "to the gods and men," the term *devamanuṣyebhyaḥ* is a *dvandva* compound, since the word "both" (*ubhayebhyaḥ*) is used.

The definition of *upāṃśu* (whispered) in the *Prātiśākhya* is: "That which is performed mentally, without sound, like the [internal] articulatory organs (*karaṇa*), is called *upāṃśu*. Regarding the mention of two lineages, it follows the principle of Āyanī having two fathers. Likewise, some say that one mentions the co-wives, such as the mother and others.
One takes the name by saying "So-and-so," using the father's name in the form "the descendant of So-and-so" (*āmuṣyāyaṇa*).

The word *asau* (this one) refers to the first-case nominative form of the sacrificer’s conventional name, such as "Amuka. It must end in *śarman*, because Baudhāyana states, "The name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in *śarman*," and the Vāsiṣṭha-sūtra says, "That by which a Brāhmaṇa is commonly addressed [should be his name]. The phrase "by which he is commonly addressed" is intended to exclude names derived from lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and the like from being required to end in *śarman*. Furthermore, this conventional name used here is not secret; rather, it should be understood as that which was created for the purpose of well-known worldly usage.

In this manner, the names of the father and others also end in *śarman*. However, the names of women end in *dānta*, according to the Smṛti which states: "The name of women ends in *dānta*. In another Smṛti, however, it is stated that the name of women ends in the word *devī*; there is an option (*vikalpa*) between these two. Some say they should be combined (*samuccaya*). This should be understood as universally applicable: wherever the word *asau* occurs, there the conventional name (*vyāvahārika-nāman*) ending in the nominative case is to be taken. In the expression *āmuṣyāyaṇaḥ*, the term refers to the name derived from the *gotra* of the father.

The meaning is that he announces him by name; that is, he announces the initiated person who has restrained his speech by means of a common name derived from his *gotra* (clan), using the nominative case-ending. For example: "This Brāhmaṇa Gopīnātha Śarmā, of the Vasiṣṭha lineage, has been initiated—the son of Gaṇeśa Śarmā, the grandson of Keśava Śarmā, the great-grandson of Kṛṣṇa Śarmā, the son of Yamunādā, the grandson of Lakṣmīdā, and the great-grandson of Rukmiṇīdā."

In the view that the word ends in "devī" (goddess), the usage is as follows: "the son of the goddess Yamunā," "the grandson of the goddess Lakṣmī," and "the great-grandson of the goddess Sakmiṇī. The name is that which is derived from the father's gotra; by that name is what is meant by "nāma" (name). In the term *nāmadheya*, the suffix *dheya* is used in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), according to the rule *mārgarūpanāmabhyo dheyaḥ*.

In the *Mānavasūtra*, it is stated: "He utters the name [of the deceased] as 'the shoulders' (*aṃsau*) and the lineage (*gotra*) as 'the descendant of so-and-so' (*āmuṣyāyaṇa*). Wherever the term *āmuṣyāyaṇa* occurs, it should be understood that the specific name of the lineage (*sadgotranāma*) is to be employed; this is a universal rule. Regarding the names of the father and others, some maintain that when the names are unknown, one should proceed using the names of deities. Likewise, even when the names of the mother and others are unknown, one should invoke them by the names of deities, because a *smṛti* text concerning *śrāddha* and other rites states: "When the name is unknown, one should recite [the names] by means of the names of deities. The meaning is that one uses the names of other deities [in place of the unknown names].

Regarding the knowledge of lineage, the Kāśyapa lineage is [the one]; for it is stated in the Smṛti: "But when the lineage is not discerned, it is called the Kāśyapa lineage. And from the Śruti: "All progeny are Kāśyapīs.
Whoever undergoes initiation should announce himself simply as a Brāhmaṇa.

If any Kṣatriya or Vaiśya undergoes initiation—that is, takes the *dīkṣā*—one announces him simply as a "Brāhmaṇa," saying: "A Brāhmaṇa has been initiated. The meaning here is that the word "Brāhmaṇa" should not be modified (*ūha*). [The rule] "one should announce him according to his caste" is intended to refute the opinion of Baudhāyana; this is indicated by the emphatic particle *eva*. Āpastamba states the reason for this: "He who undergoes initiation is indeed born as a Brāhmaṇa; therefore, one announces even a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya simply as a 'Brāhmaṇa'."

Since he is indeed initiated from the Veda, which is Brahman, one might ask: "Who is this? In response to this doubt, it is he who is initiated; as Manu has said: "The first birth is from the mother, the second at the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass, and the third at the initiation for sacrifice."

Therefore, even for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, one announces [the name] as "Brāhmaṇa" alone, and not as "Uha. Kātyāyana also states: "The word 'Brāhmaṇa' alone is heard in the case of both the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya. Although the announcement is made using the word "Brāhmaṇa" itself, nevertheless, the suffix "-śarman" does not apply; rather, for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya respectively, the suffixes are "-varman" and "-gupta. This is because, regarding the suffix "-śarman," only the word "Brāhmaṇa" denoting the specific caste is intended. This [ceremony] takes place during the afternoon itself.

This is because of the forthcoming sūtra stating, "The initiate [is seated] in the afternoon. Regarding this, some hold that only the initiation with the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) takes place within the altar (*antarvedi*), while the bestowing of the girdle (*mekhalā*) and so forth may be either within the altar or elsewhere. Others maintain that everything from the initiation with the black antelope skin up to the formal announcement (*āvedana*) occurs strictly within the altar. The intention of the former view is that only the act of spreading [the skin] is prescribed as being within the altar; therefore, only that much is restricted to the interior of the altar.

The intention of the latter view is that since it is observed that the sequence beginning with the black antelope skin initiation (*kṛṣṇājinadīkṣā*) and ending with the announcement (*āvedana*) occurs at the same time in the afternoon (*aparāhne*), and because no separate location is prescribed, the place is also the same. The purificatory rites for the wife (*patnīsaṃskāra*) intended for the initiation are established by implication and are accompanied by mantras. In this view, there is a modification of the formula to "puṃsī" (in the masculine), or alternatively, they may be performed silently. Baudhāyana states that everything should be done silently. If the preparation of the *pravargya* vessels was not performed previously, one should perform it here. Since the sacrificer is already initiated, there is no oblation; rather, there is only the rinsing (*napanam*).
1kha, ga: *ṇam iti*. 2kha, ga: *...ṣṇīkam iti*. [Chapter 10] Together with the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa. 599.

The sacrifice has gone to the gods; may the blessing of the sacrifice come to me from there. The sacrifice has gone to the Gandharvas; may the blessing of the sacrifice come to me from there. The sacrifice has gone to the ancestors; may the blessing of the sacrifice come to me from there. The sacrifice has gone to the waters, the plants, and the trees; may the blessing of the sacrifice come to me from there. The sacrifice has gone to the five peoples; may the blessing of the sacrifice come to me from there. May prosperity increase with curds and ghee; may the sacrifice release the lord of the sacrifice from distress.

He consecrates it with the mantra, "To the Lord of the Earth, Svāhā! if he should sit elsewhere than on a black antelope skin, provided this is not his constant practice from that point onward. These five mantras constitute the consecration; any one of them may be used. The remaining ones are for the purpose of option (*vikalpa*). Alternatively, there may be a combination (*samuccaya*), as in the case of the spreading of the black antelope skin accompanied by its mantra. In the case of the option, the phrase "May prosperity increase" and so forth must be appended to all of them; in the case of combination, it is not. The mantra "The waters, the plants, the trees... is a single mantra, and not two mantras with appended sections.

Otherwise, since the reading "devān aganyajñe" occurs in one place alone, the connection (*anuṣaṅga*) with "gandharvān" and so forth would be established even there; thus, the repeated reading in these [verses]—"gandharvān," "pitṝn," and "pañcajanān"—would be redundant. Therefore, it should be understood that the reading of "devān" in these three [verses], excluding the mantra containing "devān," serves solely to prevent the connection from applying individually to each of the others—namely, "gandharvān," "pitṝn," and "pañcajanān. This consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the sacrificer is to be performed by the *adhvaryu*.

Nor should it be argued that the mantra, due to the absence of contradiction with its indicative power (*liṅga*), impels the self for its own consecration (*saṃskāra*) alone; for there is no contradiction whatsoever with the mantra’s indicative power. To explain: "O Agni, go to the gods from here" (*devān yaja gaccha tataḥ*); here, by the word *jana*, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) himself is understood. The meaning is: "May the sacrifice come toward the sacrificer from the presence of the gods"; and regarding the "desire of the sacrifice that has arrived," the sense is: "may it not go even slightly (*ā īṣad*) elsewhere than to the sacrificer."

The intended meaning is: "May my sacrifice not be fruitless. Alternatively, the meaning is: "O gods, let the sacrifice come to me; let the sacrifice initiated by me return to me from the gods. It means that the blessing associated with the sacrifice should return to the sacrificer. The same applies to the others as well.

May my prosperity and sovereignty increase through this sacrifice which has returned to me from the presence of the gods and others; and may that sacrifice increase by means of curd and clarified butter. May the sacrifice, thus augmented by curd and clarified butter, release the lord of the sacrifice—the sacrificer—from great sins. *Bhūpataye* (to the Lord of Beings): to the deity named Bhūpati, *svāhā*—the meaning is "I offer all this well."

The author of the *Nirukta* has assigned four meanings to the word *svāhā*: "this is mine," "well-spoken," "O Speech, come! "it proclaims 'vaṃ'," or "he offers the oblation that has been well-offered. The intention here is that, because particles (*nipāta*) have multiple meanings, these interpretations are possible. Among them, according to the first meaning, the sense described is: "I declare all this well. By this, the doubt as to how the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the sacrificer can be performed by the Adhvaryu priest—given the contradiction with the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra—is dispelled.

He consecrates [the seat] with the mantra *yan-mānam* (or *yan-mānam*), for this is the remainder [of the mantra] according to the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra, and not [the word] *kṛṣṇājinam*. The syntactical connection is: "If he should sit elsewhere than on the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), then he should consecrate it with the mantra *devāñ janam aganma*. By the word "if" (*yadi*), the conditional nature (*naimittikatva*) of the consecration is demonstrated. "Elsewhere than on the black antelope skin" means he should sit having abandoned the black antelope skin. Sitting (*āsana*) is indicative of lying down (*śayana*) as well, based on the Sūtra: "He does not sit or lie down anywhere other than on the black antelope skin."

In this regard, there is a specific rule in the *Mānava-sūtra*: "From the hairy side—meaning on the portion possessing hair—the use of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) for a bed, a seat, or a covering is prohibited. This constant practice will become clear in the *Yājamāna-sūtra* with the passage beginning, "This practice begins from the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* [initiatory offering]," and so forth.

Therefore, the statement "the wide one" (urvam) indicates that the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) caused by the cutting of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) occurs only after the announcement (*āvedana*), not before; for in the case of a prior cutting, there is only the recitation of the three *anājñāta* verses. The expression "in the constant performance" (*nityavṛttau*) is intended to show that even when the intermediate initiation (*avāntaradīkṣā*) has been completed, this [procedure] continues until the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). Prior to this, while the sun is over the tree, the giver of the vow (*vrataprada*) issues the command: "Make the fires luminous! O initiated one, restrain your speech! O wife, restrain your speech!"

Standing to the north of the Āhavanīya fire, Baudhāyana says that one should issue the *praisha* (direction): "Make [the fires] luminous; O initiated one, restrain your speech; O wife, restrain your speech. Because of the plural form "fires" (*agnīn*), this refers to all the fires. This includes both the *Gārhapatya* and *Dakṣiṇāgni* when they are present, as well as the *Āvasathya*, though not the *Aupāsana* because of the absence of a connection with the Śrauta rites. By this, the doubt that the kindling is for the purpose of the vow-reception (*vrata-upanayana*)—which exists only for the Gārhapatya and Dakṣiṇāgni—is refuted.

The meaning is: "Make them luminous and blazing. One for whom *dīkṣā* has occurred is a *dīkṣita*. The meaning of the word *dīkṣā* has already been stated previously. Furthermore, based on the Dhātupāṭha rule *dīkṣa mauṇḍayejyopanayananiyamavatādeśeṣu*, the word *dīkṣā* refers specifically to a particular kind of observance (*niyama*). "Before sunrise" means prior to the rising [of the sun]. The word *purā* signifies "before"; thus, the meaning is "prior to sunrise. The sun that moves over the trees is *adhivṛkṣasūrya*.

By the word "sūrya" (sun), its rays are expressed through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The plural form in the command "auṣe kuruta" (make it hot) is for the purpose of including any one of the various officiating priests (*parikarmin*). By the general statement "the giver of the vow" (*vrataprada*), it is understood that whoever among the *adhvaryus* is the giver of the vow; he who is the giver of the vow is himself the performer of the formal direction (*saṃpreṣakartā*). Because of the scriptural injunction regarding the time "before sunrise" or "when the sun is above the trees," there is no formal direction on the first day.

The *Yājamānasūtra* will also state: "On that day, the initiated one does not sleep at night, nor does he eat; having seen the stars, he releases his speech silently. At the time when the one who bestows the vow issues the command, he restrains his speech. Since the absence of the vow is stated in this sūtra, the absence of the formal command (*praiṣa*) is also established as a matter of course.

The instruction "Make the fires radiant" applies to the Āhavanīya fire; since the act of making it radiant serves an invisible (transcendental) purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), the same applies to the other two fires as well. Consequently, the fulfillment of the purpose consisting of the "bargaining for the vow" (*vratapaṇa*) occurs by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*). Thus, although it might follow that the formal command (*praipa*) regarding the making of the fires radiant should indeed occur, nevertheless—because the sequence is heard in the texts as "before sunrise" and "when the sun is above the trees"—the intention is that even the mere command "O Agni, make them radiant" does not take place.

When [the sun] has risen or set, he milks the *vrata* [milk], leaving one teat for the calf. The grammatical connection is: "leaving it, he milks. The singular word *vratam* functions in the sense of both the singular and the dual. It should not be argued that because of the singular number, the milk produced from the milking of only one cow constitutes the *vrata* for both; for in the passage, "Of those cows which are the *vrata*-milkers for the sacrificer, he milks them for the *āśira*; of those for the wife, he milks them for the *dadhi-graha*," since a separate cow is prescribed for the wife’s *vrata*, such an assumption is impossible. The words "of the sacrificer" and "of the wife" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.

"For the calf" (*vatsasya*) means leaving one teat for each respective calf of each respective cow; the genitive case in *vatsasya* is used in the sense of the dative, meaning "for the sake of the calf. "When the sun has risen" (*udite*) means when it has reached its rising, and "when it has set" (*astamite*) means when it has reached its disappearance; the meaning is that he causes [the cows] to be milked while observing this vow. The word *dogdhi* is a remainder [from the previous context]; *dohayati* is a form derived from the causative suffix (*ṇic*). [End of] Paṭala 15357–150, accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 601. The genitive in *vatsasya* is used in the sense of the dative, meaning "for the sake of the calf. "When the sun has risen" (*udite*) means when it has attained its rising, and "when it has set" (*astamite*) means when it has attained its setting; the meaning is that he performs the milking while observing the vow. The word *dogdhi* is a remainder; *dohayati* is a form ending in the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

Regarding the rule, "A Śūdra shall not milk for the Agnihotra," because this prohibits a Śūdra from performing the milking associated with the Agnihotra, there is no restriction regarding other forms of milking. Furthermore, that Śūdra is specifically a cowherd (*gopa*), both because his livelihood is such and because the Smṛti states, "The cowherd and the barber are considered twice-born (*dvija*)," thereby affirming his suitability for that task. If a Brāhmaṇa is the one who performs the milking, however, it is even better.
He cooks the vow-food (*vrata*) of the initiated sacrificer on the Gārhapatya fire, while the wife's food is cooked on the Dakṣiṇāgni.

It is called *vrata* because one undertakes it (*vratayati*). The meaning is that milk is for the purpose of the *vrata*. Even in the statement "milk is the *vrata* of the Brāhmaṇa," this is precisely the meaning of the word *vrata*. Regarding this, Baudhāyana states the specific detail: "Having performed the ritual procedure for the Agnihotra, having heated [the milk], having moved it toward the north, having cooled it, and having either curdled it or not curdled it, he suspends it on a sling in the northern part of the hall. As for the wife's *vrata*, the specific detail is: "He suspends it on a sling in the southern part of the hall. Everything else is the same.

The natural sense of the word *ceṣṭet* (one should perform) indicates that only the mere action is to be performed, and not an action accompanied by mantras. Whatever expiation (*prāyaścitti*) there is for the spilling of the *agnihotra*, the same applies to its spilling in this case as well. Accordingly, Āpastamba states: "That which is the expiation for the spilling of the *agnihotra* is [the expiation] for the *vrata*. Here, because the expiation for the *agnihotra* is extended by analogy (*atideśa*), its specific rules regarding cooking (*śrapaṇadharma*) are also indicated by Āpastamba.

The expiation (prāyaścitta), however, must indeed be accompanied by mantras, because it possesses the efficacy to effect the rejoining of that which has been destroyed exactly as prescribed. Regarding the specific procedure for the bestowal of the vow (vrata), he says:
having brought the vow around behind the Āhavanīya fire, he hands it to the consecrated one (dīkṣita).

The word *vrataprada* is understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. *Aparṇā* ends in the suffix *-ena*. According to the rule *enapā dvitīyā*, the second case ending is used. *Ati* has the meaning of "transgressing" or "passing beyond. By that very [route], he returns by the same way he came. Since the wife was already seated near the *dakṣiṇāgni*, there is no carrying [the food] to the *āhavanīya* fire and offering it to her; rather, the offering is made right there. Because this is established by the very sense [of the context], no specific injunction for that purpose has been formulated.

This Sūtra is to be given as a vow (*vrata*) to one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*) while seated in his own place, not to one who has merely come into the vicinity; this is the meaning. Kātyāyana has stated quite clearly that [the offering] is made with the verse "ye devā" while [the priest] is in his own seat. The mention of the *āhavanīya* fire is for the purpose of excluding the *dakṣiṇāgni*. The word "other" (*apara*) is for the purpose of excluding the front portion. It is for the sake of its being a single oblation (*enavad*). Āpastamba says, "One should pour out silently, as in the Agnihotra. According to the distinction between those who offer four portions (*caturavattin*) and those who offer five portions (*pañcāvattin*), there are four or five pourings of ghee. In the final [pouring], it is just enough [to fill the ladle].

He recites the mantra, "Go forth from the auspicious to the more auspicious," over the initiated person as he departs. He recites this over him as he sets out toward the place of sacrifice along with his wife, the two kindling-sticks (*araṇī*), and the ritual vessels, according to the rules for departure. By definition, *anumantraṇa* (recitation following) consists of reciting a mantra while contemplating the object to be accomplished through the Adhvaryu’s mantra, directing one's attention toward that object, and praising it. In *abhimantraṇa* (recitation facing), everything is the same as in *anumantraṇa*, except for the addition of looking directly at the object. If the reading is *prayāntam* (as he is departing), the recitation occurs precisely at the time of departure.

Because it is subordinate to the subject matter (*uddeśya*), the masculine gender is not intended to be significant, as in the case of "A Brāhmaṇa kindles the fires. Therefore, the consecration formula (*anumantraṇa*) applies to the wife as well. Likewise, the singular number is not intended to be significant, as in the case of "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*). Consequently, in a *sattra* sacrifice, the Adhvaryu must perform the consecration formula for all the initiated sacrificers; it should be understood that he does so for himself as well. [From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Seventh Book:
The initiated sacrificer cuts the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) as in the *Nirūḍhapaśubandha* sacrifice.

Since the status of being initiated (*dīkṣita*) is already established by implication, the explicit mention of "of the initiated" is for the purpose of indicating that when there are multiple initiations, the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpacchedana*) may be performed on any day of the initiation period, and not necessarily on the very first day. It is precisely for this reason that the plural form is heard in another recensional text: "He cuts the sacrificial post during the initiations" (*dīkṣāsu yūpaṃ chinatti*).

Although this is already established by the statement "this is the ritual procedure for all animals," the specific mention of "as in the Nirūḍhapaśubandha" is intended either to exclude [the measurement] that would otherwise be obtained from the rule "the sacrificial post for the Nirūḍhapaśubandha is four aratnis or five aratnis, made of Palāśa wood, while others belong to the Soma-sacrifice"—thereby restricting that measurement to the cutting of the post during the *dīkṣā* initiations—or to indicate an option among all the ritual procedures.

And likewise, Āpastamba [states]: "The sacrificial post for the Nirūḍhapaśubandha is made of Palāśa wood and is either four aratnis or five aratnis in height; other than this is that of the Soma sacrifice—so says the Vājasaneyaka. The mention of the *Vājasaneyaka* is intended to indicate an option. He does not offer the oblation to the sacrificial post; rather, having muttered the verse intended for the offering, he proceeds forward.

Since it is already established by the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) that this oblation has the post as its cause, the mention of the "post" indicates that this oblation is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the mere act of cutting the post; it is not an oblation caused merely by the existence of the post. Consequently, it is proven that this "post-oblation" does not occur in cases such as the *khava* sacrifice, where there is no cutting. Furthermore, although the post-oblation is connected to the ritual (*kratu*), this [text] establishes its prohibition: "not [in the case of] the post..."

This statement is necessary so that, in the event that the injunction "he offers" (*juhoti*) is not applicable, there might otherwise be a combination of both the oblation (*homa*) and the recitation (*japa*); it is intended to prevent this. For this is the alternative of no oblation found in another recensional branch (*śākhā*), which states: "They do not offer into the fire for the initiated; having recited the verse dedicated to Viṣṇu, he goes toward [the sacrificial post]. The meaning of the word *acchaiti* as it occurs in the Śruti is: "he goes toward," meaning he proceeds facing the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

If the phrase "the verse intended for the *homa*" (*homārthām ṛcam*) and so forth were not stated, there would also be an absence of the *japa* (muttering), as it has not been prescribed; therefore, to ensure that this does not happen, the statement "having muttered, he proceeds toward the fires" (*japitvāgnīn abhipravrajati*) is given. The mention of "intended for the *homa*" is for the purpose of obtaining the status of the original location (*sthānāpatti*). By this, it is established that having muttered [the verse] in the vicinity of the *Āhavanīya* fire itself, he proceeds toward the fires. The mention of "the verse" (*ṛcam*) is for the purpose of making the knowledge of its being a *ṛc* mandatory. Consequently, in the event of the loss of that knowledge, the rite toward the fires must be performed only after performing the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for a breach.
And since that [expiation] pertains to the *Adhvaryu*, it is specifically occasioned by a breach of a *yajus*.

Alternatively, having taken the clarified butter (*ājya*) and the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), and having churned fire near the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and offered the oblation for the post (*yūpāhuti*), he cuts the post. This is another method belonging to a different recension (*śākhāntarīya*). Since the taking of the clarified butter is established by implication through the existence of the oblation, the explicit mention here is for the purpose of ensuring its concomitance with the two kindling woods. By this, it is understood that one should go near the base of the post having taken both the two kindling woods and the clarified butter together. The mention of "taking" (*ādāna*) is intended to exclude the possibility of the assistant (*parikarmika*) being the agent; thus, it is known that in other cases where there is no such mention of "taking," the agency of the assistant may also apply as an alternative.

The term *araṇī* serves to exclude any wood that lacks the characteristics of an *araṇī*. Regarding the word *antike* (near): here, the meaning of "proximity" (*antikapadārtha*) is not the state of being in direct physical contact with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), as that would entail the consequence of burning [the person]. Rather, the proximity intended by the word *antika* is precisely that degree of nearness by which one may conventionally say, "I have reached the vicinity of the sacrificial post."

And since that [fire] is one, it is indeed a *tantra* (common procedure) in the case of eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*); however, in the case of its division, the division of the churning must be understood to apply. The application of the term "of the post" (*yūpasya*) takes up a future designation, just as the application of the word "Āhavanīya" occurs in the phrase "he offers in the Āhavanīya. The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of including the *sruva*-ladle and other implements not explicitly mentioned. The mention of "of the post" is for the purpose of excluding the Āhavanīya fire, the Prācīnavaṃśa hall, and the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*).

The word *antike* ("nearby") is for the purpose of excluding a distant location. The expression "near the fire" (*agniṃ samīpe*) is intended so that the oblation might not sometimes be performed upon the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) themselves while they are near the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), as would be the case with the *sthāṇvāhuti* (the offering to the sacrificial post). Even if it were merely stated "having taken the two kindling woods and having churned," this mention of "fire" (*agni*) serves to indicate that when fire is obtained [in this manner], this churning is a primary (*apūrva*) act distinct from ordinary fire-production. By this, it is established that the two kindling woods are of a common (*laukika*) nature and that the churning is to be done silently (*tūṣṇīm*).

Having made another spot the sacrificial ground, having leveled it, having sprinkled it with water, and having placed the fire, the oblation (*homa*) is performed. Although it has been stated that by the use of the gerund suffix (*ktvā*) in the word "having churned" (*mathitvā*), immediate succession is expressed [between the churning and the oblation], this does not contradict the immediate succession [of the churning] even when the preparation of the *prokṣaṇī* water, the cleansing of the *sruva* spoon, and the preparation of the clarified butter (*ājya*) intervene; for since these are subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of the main action, they are compatible with it, and that which causes no actual separation does not invalidate the state of non-separation even when there is an intervention.

The statement "the *yūpāhuti* [is] *iṣve*" is for this purpose: in the absence of this statement, the prohibition from the preceding sūtra—"he does not offer the *yūpāhuti*"—would apply; and if that were to apply, it would result in the act having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*). To prevent this, [the rule is stated]. The *yūpāhuti* is an offering consisting merely of the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). The mention of the word "post" (*yūpa*) is for the sake of clarity. By using the expression "having offered" (*hutvā*) instead of "he offers" (*juhoti*), the intention is to arouse the expectancy of the meaningful statement "he cuts the post."

He cuts the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with its natural splendor and *caṣāla* [top-ring], meaning by way of the ritual procedure ending with the *araṇi*. The statement "he cuts the sacrificial post" is intended to demonstrate that even when there is a combination of expiatory offerings and animals, there is only one sacrificial post. The scriptural injunction, "He immolates at a single sacrificial post," is also an authority for this point. As for the alternative involving eleven sacrificial posts mentioned in the *Pālika*, that is based on a specific textual rule (*vācanika*) regarding the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice.
Or, once the King Soma has been purchased, he offers the oblation for the sacrificial post into the *Āhavanīya* fire and then cuts the sacrificial post.

Some say [the ritual ends] immediately after the presentation of the staff (*daṇḍapradāna*). Others say it ends with the verse *svajā asi*. Still others say it is completed with the verse *udu saṃ jātavedasam*. Yet others say it follows the verse *agnir rājānam*. In reality, however, [it is as stated] in the *Śrīsoma*.

Regarding the injunction "he gives the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa," which prescribes the handing over of the staff immediately after the purchase [of Soma], and the injunction "or [the staff goes] to the King," which prescribes the oblation for the sacrificial post (*yūpāhuti*) and so forth immediately after the purchase—since there is a difference in the agents for both and simultaneity is possible, it is logical that while the sacrificer performs the handing over of the staff, at that very same time the Adhvaryu must offer the oblation for the sacrificial post.

One should strive so that the completion of the act of striking the sacrificial post with the staff and the offering of the oblation occur simultaneously, in accordance with the relinquishment of the substance; however, the relinquishment must be performed by one who is seated at the place of purchase. Furthermore, the mention of the *āhavanīya* fire is intended to exclude this procedure [of producing fire] by taking clarified butter and the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) and churning fire near the sacrificial post.

The statement "having offered the *yūpāhuti* (sacrificial oblation to the post)" is for the purpose of excluding the ritual procedure [stated in the rule]: "having muttered the verse intended for the *homa*, he bends toward [the post]"; for this would otherwise be established by the very force of the injunction that prescribes the *āhavanīya* fire as the locus. If it is argued that the phrase "having offered the *yūpāhuti*" is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended only to fulfill the syntactic expectancy, we say no; for if it were merely stated, "Or, the *āhavanīya* is in the *koṭi*," the locative case [of *āhavanīye*] would [otherwise remain unaccounted for].

If one were to take the word as having the sense of proximity (*sāmīpya*), two such meanings might be possible: either "having performed the *apām* [offering] near the *āhavanīya*, he proceeds toward it," or "having brought it near the *āhavanīya*, he cuts it right there near it. To prevent such an interpretation, since a restatement (*anuvāda*) serves as a purpose, it is improper to assume that its function is merely to fulfill a syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā-pūraṇa*), which would be a resort of last resort (*agatika*).
This applies to the *agnīṣomīya*, the *savanīya*, and the *anūbandhyā* [offerings]. (7.3)
The sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the wooden splinter (*svaru*), the *āhavanīya* fire, and the heart-spit (*hṛdayaśūla*) are common [to all].

That animal sacrifice for which Agni and Soma are the deities is called *agnīṣomīya*. An animal that exists at the *savana*, that is, at the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing), is *savanīya*. There is a sacrifice to Vāyu in the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), a sacrifice to the *puroḍāśa* cakes that cover the gaps in the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), and a sacrifice in the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*); thus it possesses the quality of being *savanīya*. These are the principal oblations (*pradhāna-havīṃṣi*). According to Āśvalāyana, the omentum (*vapā*) and the *puroḍāśa* are the subsidiary oblations (*aṅga-havīṃṣi*). The term "Agni-Soma and Savanīya" is a copulative compound (*dvandva*). The *anubandhyā* is the animal known as the *anūbandhya*.

The term *anūbandhyā* means that which is bound after the principal [sacrifice]; thus, the meaning is that the rites for the animal designated by that name are similar to those of the others. Since the Vedic text (*śruti*) shows the form ending in a long vowel—as in "vaśā anūbandhyā so" (the barren cow is the *anūbandhyā*)—the author of the Sūtra has also made his reference in that very same way. The mention of the *agnīṣomīya* and *savanīya* sacrifices together by compound indicates that there is a specific distinction between these two and the *anūbandhyā*.

Therefore, regarding the *anūbandhyā* cow, just as there is no restriction on the animal for the *gopashu*, there is likewise no restriction on these two [the *savanīya* and *anūbandhyā*]; rather, even a goat may optionally serve for these two. For these animals, four elements—such as the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and so forth—are common to all.
