This is because they are prescribed in the context of the Soma sacrifice, because all three are not yet performed at that time, and because there is no definitive determination of "this one's" [specific animal] due to their performance later during the rites known as the *āgnīṣomīya*, *savanīya*, and *anūbandhyā*. This was stated by Jaimini in the third pāda of the eleventh chapter in the sūtra: "And the sacrificial post, because it does not share the same time of performance."

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: because the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) prescribed as the substratum for the act of cutting—by the injunction "on the days of initiation, one cuts the post"—are employed by the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, they are common to all [the animal sacrifices]; thus, the post is common to all the animals. After the word "and the post" (*yūpaśca*), the word "common" (*tatram*) is to be supplied as the remainder. "The state of having the time of the ritual" means that its time is precisely the time of the ritual pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka-karma*). "Not the state of having the time of the ritual" (*na karmakālatvam*) means the absence of the state of having the time of the ritual; the sense is: "because of that [absence]."

For at the time consisting of the day of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth, there is indeed an absence of connection with the time for the *pāśuka* ritual, because that [time] is connected with the time for the *jyotiṣṭoma* ritual; and since the initiation is common [to all], it is logical that the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), which is to be performed on that day, is common to all the animals. Indeed, the status of being at the time of initiation is not prompted by the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the initiation itself, because there is no proximity of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-sādeśya*) to bring that [apūrva] to mind.

However, because it is prompted by the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the Jyotiṣṭoma through the context (*prakaraṇa*), and because it cannot be directly applied to that [result], it is applied to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) belonging to the animal sacrifice which is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to it. Since being a subsidiary to that is common to all [the animals], its application to all is established. In reality, even though there is a direct instruction (*upadeśa*) regarding the time, since its application to the *Savanīya* and other sacrifices is possible through the occasional extension (*atideśa*) of the *Āgnīṣomīya*, the unity of the ritual procedure (*tantratva*) regarding the post follows precisely from the unity of the time (*kālatantratva*).

By this, the contingency of three sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) occurring even at a single time is avoided. Since there is a single ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the post, the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*)—such as selecting (*joṣaṇa*) and carving (*takṣaṇa*) it—are also performed once as a common procedure. It should not be argued that because the injunction "he cuts the post during the initiations" (*dīkṣāsu yūpaṃ chinatti*) prescribes only the act of cutting, and since the selection and carving are performed only at the time of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, they would be restricted to that specific occasion; and thus, since they appear to serve only that purpose, they would have to be repeated upon the completion of that rite (*apavarga*). [This is because the cutting is merely a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta-viśeṣa*), and therefore its completion does not necessitate the repetition of the entire procedure.]

If the reference were to the cutting of the sacrificial post (yūpa), it would result in the application of a specific location; if the reference were to cutting alone, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Therefore, the injunction regarding time is made precisely with reference to the sacrificial post itself. The word "cuts" (chinatti) is merely an indicator (upalakṣaṇa) for the entire series of consecratory acts (saṃskāra) that produce it. And those consecratory acts which produce it are only those beginning with the oblation for the post (yūpāhuti) and ending with the making of the eight-sided shape (aṣṭāśrikaraṇa), just as in the case of the fire-altar (agni) they are the laying down (ādhāna) and so forth, but not even the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and other such acts.

But those [mantras] that arise at the time of the six rites, such as the sweeping (*saṃmārga*), are bestowers of refinement (*saṃskārādhāyaka*) upon the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) once it has been produced. Thus, even within this established distinction, those which are producers [of the object] possess the character of *mantras*—just like the [mantras for the] sacrificial post—precisely because no distinction can be perceived between them due to their occurring at a time different from the time of the ritual action (*karmakāla*).

As for those acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) which are purificatory rites for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) once it has been produced, since there is no statement to the effect that they should be displaced [to an earlier time], they must be performed at the very time of the ritual action. Even though they possess a specific character in this regard, because the individual sacrificial post is one—as established by the principle of the "sprinkling outside at the *ātithyā* sacrifice"—the sprinkling and other rites performed upon it can validly serve as a contributory factor (*upakāraka*). Therefore, there is no repetition (*āvṛtti*) of them either.

Some, however, accept the insertion of two words—“he cuts the *khadira* tree” and “to make a sacrificial post (*yūpa*)”*—in order to include the preparatory rites such as carving and so forth. That is not correct; for compared to that, the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is simpler. Furthermore, in the third quarter of the eleventh chapter, even in the foundational sūtra for that principle, it is stated by Jaimini: “But the preparatory rites should recur, because they have both a purpose and a specific time. The preparatory rites are the rites of the sacrificial post, such as carving and so forth. The word “but” (*tu*) [indicates] that the sacrificial post is not of the same time as the ritual action.

The word "svāditi" (as before) is used to indicate that this is not a repetition of the previous section. The meaning is that the purpose or utility of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)—namely, the primary act of animal sacrifice (*paśubandhana*)—must be repeated because it occurs at that specific time. This is the meaning of the preceding sūtra.

That time is the time for the consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*); however, the primary time—which serves as the purpose for the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*)—is connected to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Because that action connected to the post is a duty prescribed within the ritual (*kratu*), the rule "he cuts the post during the initiations" (*dīkṣāsu yūpaṃ chinatti*) establishes that the duty is prompted by the ritual at the time of the initiations and so forth. By this, the performance of the consecratory rites at the time of the animal sacrifice is excluded.

The meaning of the second sūtra is as follows: [The opponent argues that] the preparatory rites (saṃskāras) such as carving (takṣaṇa) pertain to all sacrificial posts (yūpa) equally; the word "or" (vā) is used for emphasis to indicate that because of the scriptural statement, these rites belong to a different time [than the sacrifice], whereas the time for the post itself belongs to the sacrifice because it is an act of the post and its properties are prescribed as part of the ritual (ṛtudharma). Alternatively, because of the scriptural statement, the rites pertain to all [posts] and thus belong to a different time, and the text shows that the measuring is done only once. This is the meaning of the second sūtra.

The meaning of the third sūtra is as follows: regarding the scriptural injunction, "At the time of initiation, one sets up the sacrificial post" (*dīkṣāsū yūpaṃ minoti*), this shows that the measurements and consecrations (*saṃskāra*) are also to be performed at the same time as the initiation and other rites. However, because it is a rite pertaining to the sacrificial post (*yūpakarma*), its timing is determined by the injunction of the ritual duties (*ṛtudharma*); or, because there is a specific statement that it serves all purposes, it may have a different time. Furthermore, the scripture shows that the measurement is to be done only once.

The meaning is as follows: the purpose (*artha*) is the binding of the animal, which constitutes the form of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). If the sacrificial post were to exist at the time of the animal-binding, there would be a repetition of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*); however, that is not the case, because its time is that of the initiation (*dīkṣā*). This is the meaning of the Sūtra (1). At the very time of cutting the sacrificial post, the *svaru* must be taken up for the purpose of removing confusion and for the purpose of preventing loss or theft; since no specific distinction [regarding its timing] is perceived, the *svaru* is common to the whole ritual (*tantra*).

For this very reason, even the injunction for the disposal (*pratipatti*) at the end—stating that "when the *soma* has been concluded, one carries forward the *prastara* and offers the *svaru*"—is consistent. In the Vedic text, "In the *soma* sacrifice, one carries forward the *prastara*," the grammatical connection is "one throws the *prastara*. Because it is a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), the insertion of another word between the prefix and the verb is not contradictory. Nor is this an injunction regarding the time for that which is a subsidiary of the *anūbandhyā* sacrifice; for since its independence is understood through reasoning, there is no authority for such a restriction.

For this very reason, where the distinction is understood through logic alone—as in the case of the *prastara* (grass-bundle)—contraction is indeed accepted. This was also stated by Jaimini in the third pāda of the eleventh adhyāya by the sūtra: *svarūpottatrāpavargaḥ syādasvakālatvāt* ("The completion [of the rite] would occur there because of its own form, due to the absence of its own time"). Because of the "absence of its own time" (*asvakālatvāt*): that which has no time belonging to itself is "without its own time" (*asvakāla*); the state of being such is its "nature" (*tattvam*). Therefore, unlike the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), for which a specific time consisting of the sprinkling and so forth is prescribed for its own sake, here there is no such time. Thus, there is an "absence of its own time. (Note: *kha* and *ma* manuscripts read *vālāḥ saṃ*.)

2 kha. ga. 'kālāḥ esa. ga, gha | 73 Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[Seventh Book]: Regarding the two sacrificial posts (*svaru*). For this reason, within the very midst of the animal sacrifice (*pāśukakarma*), the two *svarus* are produced as a secondary result (*anuniṣpādana*). Their completion (*apavarga*) occurs through the common procedure (*tantra*). Indeed, their completion is caused by the *tantra*; if there were completion [of the *svaru*] independently, that completion of the *svaru* would result in its becoming a worldly object (*laukikatva*). Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that for the sake of the *savanīya* and other offerings, there must be separate and distinct *svarus*.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: it must be stated that the principle of "concluding with the main ritual" (*tantrāpavarga*) applies only when the reason—that [the *svaru*] does not have its own specific time—is established; yet that very reason is not applicable here. Since the *svaru* is produced as a by-product (*anuniṣpanna*) of the sacrificial post, its production is established immediately upon the production of the post itself. Consequently, like the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), it also serves its own purpose through the acts of cutting and so forth performed at that same time. Therefore, there is no "concluding with the main ritual" in this case either. Thus, the meaning of Jaimini’s Sūtra is that because the sacrificial post has its own specific time for its work, the *svaru* is also part of that same procedure (*tantra*). The *āhavanīya* fire is the one situated on the northern altar (*auttaravedika*).

Because that [Agnīdhra fire] serves as the locus for the sacrifice, it is mentioned in the middle [of the section]. The mention of the *āhavanīya* is for the purpose of prohibiting the practice of bringing the fire from the *uttaravedi* for each individual animal sacrifice (*pratipaśu*), which would otherwise be required. Since the *uttaravedi*, which serves as the locus for the fire brought from the *uttaravedi*, is established as serving all purposes by being prompted by the *apūrva* of the Jyotiṣṭoma, it follows that the fire placed upon it—the *auttaravedika*—must also serve all purposes. Thus, its restriction is negated.

By the rule establishing the singularity of the *hṛdayaśūla* (heart-spit), it is understood that the *hṛdayaśūla* also belongs to the time when there is no ritual action (*akarmakālatva*). Consequently, it is established that the *hṛdayaśūla* must be produced from the very same tree as the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and it must be prepared at the very time of bringing the post. In the case of the *ekādaśinī* (eleven posts) arrangement, because the *agniṣṭha* (central post) is encountered first, it alone serves as the *āgnīṣomīya* and *anūbandhya* [posts].

Although it is prohibited by the statement, "If one were to tie [the animal] to three sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), one would place the senses and vigor outside of him; one would produce a rival for him," thereby establishing that there should be a post for each animal, nevertheless, it should be understood that by the force of the specific injunction, this will occur in the case of the *ekādaśinī* (the set of eleven animals).

"When the duration of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) has concluded" means when the determined duration of initiation—whether two days, three days, or otherwise—has been completed and finished. By this, it is indicated that the performance of the rite regarding the location of the *uttaravedi* and so forth takes place on the day of the *prāyaṇīya* sacrifice.

On the site of the *uttaravedi* or near the *uparava* holes, having spread out a red bull-hide with its neck to the east and the hair side up, he scatters the King (Soma) upon its southern wing; having placed a water-pot to the north and having enclosed the area on all sides, leaving a door to the north, he causes the Soma-seller to enter—either a member of the Kautsa clan or a Śūdra.

The two [terms] *uttaravedi* and *paradeśa* are to be understood by means of measurement. In the phrase "of the *uparavas*," there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the word *deśa*, which is a constituent part of the compound. Furthermore, Pāṇini himself has accepted the connection of a single part of a compound [with another word], as in the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.4.58), where the word *savarṇa*—which is a constituent of the compound *parasavarṇa*—is connected with the word *pūrva* found in the rule *udasthāstambhoḥ pūrvasya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.139). The word *lohita* means red in color; even that which is slightly red is [called] *lohita*.

Regarding this point of dispute, Baudhāyana states in the Sūtra that there should be two skins of the *rohita* (red deer), while Śālīki maintains that they may even be non-*rohita*. "Anaḥ" means a cart; "tadvāhī" refers to the ox that pulls it; "ānaḍuha" is its skin. It should have its neck toward the east, its hair at the top toward the north, and its hair on the upper side. Having performed the purification prescribed for a skin by means of oil, it should be used. Indeed, if the prescribed skin is unavailable, a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) should be accepted as a substitute for all of them.

5.1 [Chapter 10] Accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* by Gopīnātha Mahākūṭa. 607. "In the absence of a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), there should be the skin of other animals; in its absence, however, there should be the skin of another sacrificial animal (*medhya-paśu*)," as stated in the section on substitutes (*pratinidhi-prakaraṇa*) in the *Saṃgraha*. At the entry into the house, the spreading of a bull's hide (*anaduha-dharma*) is prescribed; in its absence, however, the spreading of a grass mat (*tārṇa-talpasya*) should take place.

Thus, since the *Āśvalāyanasmṛti* prescribes a grass mat as a substitute for the hide of a bull (*ānaḍuha-carma*), a grass mat must be taken in every case where such a hide is unavailable. In the absence of a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), however, the substitute is the skin of any other animal that lacks the black color. In its absence as well, skins such as those of the Ruru deer may be used, or else a grass mat according to the method just described. It should be understood that the mention of the "bull's hide" in the *Āśvalāyanasmṛti* is intended to indicate the category of "hide" in general.

On the right wing—that is, on the right side—of that skin which has been spread out, the northern part of the skin is left over for the sake of the king’s discernment; this is the established rule (*āpikam*). Regarding the word "uttarataḥ" (to the north), the word "tasya" (of that) is understood to carry over. To dispel the doubt that the placement of the water-pot might refer to the northern part of the skin, the author abandons the previous synonymous term "uttara" and employs a different word, "uttarataḥ. A water-pot (*udakumbha*) is a pot filled with water.

In the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), the word *udaka* undergoes the substitution of *ud* according to the rule *udakasyodaḥ saṃjñāyām*. Having enclosed it on all sides—that is, having covered it all around with mats and the like—in every direction; [facing] the north, that is, directed toward the northern quarter. The word *dvār* ends in the letter *r*; its second case dual form is used here. This word is feminine. The form *devīdvārau* is derived by adding the suffix *ki* [to *dvār*]. Because of the prescription of doors, there is an enclosure with materials corresponding to them.

He causes the Soma-seller—the one who sells Soma—to enter the enclosed space for the purpose of separating the Soma. That Brāhmaṇa is Kautsa, belonging to the Kutsa lineage, whose actions are censurable. Regarding this, Āpastamba, having stated that "one should purchase [Soma] from a Kautsa or from another Brāhmaṇa," further says, "or even from a non-Brāhmaṇa. A Śūdra here is a "good Śūdra"—either a cowherd or a barber—according to the Smṛti rule: "Cowherds and barbers are good Śūdras."

In another Vedic branch (*śākhā*), because the *kulāla* (potter) is traditionally taught alongside the *śamitṛ* (slaughterer) and the *somavikrayin* (seller of Soma)—as in the passage "the *kulāga* [is like] the *kulāla*"—the potter is also included as an alternative. Furthermore, if the study of these [professions] is intended to be exhaustive, then the *śūdra* should be understood as a candidate only in the absence of a Brāhmaṇa. From this very point, it is understood that they are indeed distinct [from the officiating priests]. The sense is that if any ordinary priest were to act as the Soma-seller, he would be disqualified from his own ritual duties due to being tainted by the fault arising from the sale; therefore, someone else [of a different class] is more appropriate.

In the third chapter, seventh section, Jaimini also says: "The seller is another person, because the act of selling is not enjoined. The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: the seller of Soma is indeed another person. Why? Because the act of selling—that is, the act of selling—is not enjoined (*acoditatvāt*), meaning it is not prescribed (*avihitatvāt*), nor is it for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatvāt*), and is even censured (*ninditatvāt*). His engagement [in the act] should be understood as being due to the power of greed for wealth, since there is an absence of formal appointment (*varaṇa*).

The word "su-" (well-) is used to indicate a distinction, showing that this is not like the sale [of Soma] by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who have approached the *śamitṛ* (the slaughterer). Kātyāyana also says the same: "A seller of Soma is one guilty of a minor offense (*upapātaka*). Since there is a rule that 'Soma is to be purchased,' for the sale of raw meat, liquor, wool, salt, or sesame oil, as well as for the sale of all other commodities, a twice-born man (*dvija*) shall perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance."

Since Śātātapa has stated in the section on minor offenses (*upapātaka*) that "one should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa*," there is a fault in the sale of Soma. As for what is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "Having sold liquor, one should perform four *Saumya* penances; for lac, salt, and meat, one should perform three *Cāndrāyaṇas*; for honey, clarified butter, oil, and Soma, one should perform two *Cāndrāyaṇas*."

Thus, as for the statement of Viṣṇu: "One who sells dyed cloth or sweet wool should fast for three nights; one who sells living beings or Soma should perform the Taptakṛcchra penance and undergo initiation again"; and as for the statement of Śaṅkha and Likhita, beginning with: "One should not sell items that must not be sold—sesame, oil, curd, honey, salt, lac, liquor, meat, cooked food, women, men, elephants, horses, perfumes, liquids, linen, black iron, Soma, water, and indigo—for by selling these, a Brāhmaṇa falls immediately."

"One should perform seven *kṛcchra* penances for one year"—and as for the statement of Paiṭhīnasi: "In the case of selling a garden, a pond, a well, a lotus-pool, or Soma, one becomes purified after one year by bathing at the three periods of the day, sleeping on the ground, eating only at the fourth meal-time, and reciting the *Gāyatrī* ten thousand times"—these two [texts] are to be applied according to whether the person is capable of repeated performance or incapable thereof. *Sukṛtam* means merit; *kṛtānnam* means cooked food.

Regarding the touch of a seller of *soma*, a penance has been stated by Parāśara: "A Brāhmaṇa, having touched a sacred tree (*caityavṛkṣa*), a funeral pyre (*citi*), a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), a Caṇḍāla, or a seller of *soma*—having touched these, he should enter the water with his clothes on. "He should enter the water" means he should perform a bath. Although the action is prohibited, one engages in it due to the force of greed. In the term *somavikrayī*, the suffix *ini* is applied after the root *kri* preceded by *vi* in the sense of the object, according to the rule *karmaṇy-ani-vikrīṇāteḥ*. Furthermore, by the Vārttika stating that the suffix should be added when there is a sense of contempt, it occurs here in the sense of something despicable.

He issues the command: "O Soma-seller, purify the Soma!"—or "Purify the Soma; cast out what has been reached [as impure]!"—or "Purify the Soma; what has been reached is cast out! Here, "cast out" (*nirasta*) is used in the locative case. O Soma-seller, purify—that is, separate—the Soma, which consists of well-formed stalks, from the heap and from the grass and other debris; the meaning is that you should set it apart on the upper part of the hide. The two formulas, "Purify the Soma; cast out what has been reached" and "Purify the Soma; what has been reached is cast out," are alternatives belonging to different recensional branches (*śākhā*) and are to be used in conjunction with the preceding one.

"Having cast away—that is, having removed to a distance—the grass and other debris that have fallen into the *soma*, 'purify all the *soma*'; the meaning is: separate it so that it becomes a proper stalk. When the grass and other debris have been cast away, having been thrown outside, 'purify that *soma* which has been obtained'; the meaning is: again separate even that so that it becomes a proper stalk, i.e., distinguish it. The two occurrences of the word *vā* are intended to indicate that these two *preṣas* belong to a single recensional branch (*śākhā*) and not to different branches. He states the method of purification: 'whatever else there is besides the rays (*aṃśu*), that he removes.'"

From among the stalks (*aṃśu*), whatever else there is—such as grass and so forth—he removes it, meaning he takes it out. This is now explained in accordance with the subsequent injunction: from among the excellent stalks (*aṃśu*), whatever else is not excellent—namely, the mass of stalks and grass and so forth—he removes it, meaning he takes it out. Just as when it is said, "Bring a pot," a pot capable of performing its function is brought, so it is here.
The Adhvaryu shall not sort the Soma; neither his attendant, nor the sacrificer, nor the sacrificer’s kinsmen, nor anyone who witnesses it being sorted shall do so.

He is called an *adhvaryu* because he "yokes" (*yunakti*) the sacrifice (*adhvara*), or because he "leads" (*nayati*) the sacrifice, or because he "desires" (*kāmayate*) the sacrifice. Thus, the *Nirukta* states: "An *adhvaryu* is one who desires the sacrifice (*adhvarayu*), or he yokes the sacrifice, or he is the leader of the sacrifice, or he desires the sacrifice. Because of the scriptural warning that "the *adhvaryu* might become hungry," the *adhvaryu* should perform the separation of the *soma*; even the person of this *adhvaryu* should not perform the separation.

The sense is that even for the subordinates (*tatpuruṣas*) of the *adhvaryu*, there exists the same fault mentioned in the scripture—that the *adhvaryu* would become "crushing" (*akṣodhuka*). Now, one might object: "In that case, it should simply have been stated, 'The *adhvaryu*-subordinates shall not select the *soma*'; since the prohibition of the *adhvaryu*-subordinates is thus established by this much alone, the separate formulation of the *sūtra* is redundant. This is true.

The prohibition "nāsya puruṣaḥ" (he has no man) found in another recension is independent; it does not, however, imply that the singular number in the word *adhvaryu* occurring in one's own recension should be interpreted as intending all *adhvaryus*, for such an interpretation is impossible because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) everywhere. Thus, there is no absence [of the rule] in this sense.

Therefore, it is established that in such passages as "the Adhvaryu priest should not pass by [the Soma] while it stands on the nose," the prohibition applies only to the Adhvaryu and not to his male descendants (*tatpuruṣas*). Furthermore, because of the scriptural mention of a fault—that "the sacrificer becomes hungry"—the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) also should not perform the separation. Another Śākhā states a prohibition regarding the separation for others as well: "The sacrificer’s attendants (*amātyas*) [should not separate the Soma]. Here, "attendants" refers to sons, grandsons, and so forth.

When a person is being sifted, even those who stand nearby—whether they have been mentioned or not—do not even look on; what need is there to say that they should not perform the sifting? By this, the prohibition against performing the sifting applies not only to priests other than the Adhvaryu and his assistants, but also to others, excluding the sacrificer’s kinsmen.

[Objection: But if this is so, there would be no observers of one who is separating [the Soma]; what then need be said regarding the fact that separation should not be performed? By the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so"), the prohibition of separation for the *adhvaryu* and others is established as a matter of course; thus, the separate prohibition for the *adhvaryu* and others in the passage beginning with "they should not separate the Soma" (*nāvayuḥ somaṃ vicinuyāt*) is redundant. [Reply: This is not so. Since that [separate prohibition] serves to demonstrate an excess of fault [in the case of the *adhvaryu*], it is not redundant.

The phrase "not his man" (*nāsya puruṣaḥ*) is intended to show that just as there is a fault for the [Soma-seller], so too there is a fault for the man belonging to him (the sacrificer). Similarly, the phrase "not the sacrificer's ministers" (*na yajamānasyāmātyāḥ*) is intended to show that just as there is a fault for the sacrificer, so too there is a fault for his ministers. Since the prohibition of the act of separating [the Soma] is already established by the very prohibition [of the sale] at the time when the separation is performed by the Soma-seller, the separate prohibition of the separation is for the purpose of indicating an excess of fault. Due to this excess of fault, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of both Vedic (*śrauta*) and traditional (*smārta*) expiations.

In the case of a *drapsa* (a drop of soma), since there is no excess of fault, only the Vedic (*śrauta*) expiation applies. In that regard, the Vedic expiation is indeed the "universal expiation" (*sarvaprāyaścitta*), as no specific rule has been stated. Furthermore, there is the recitation of the *anājñāta* verses and the recitation of the *vaiṣṇavya* ṛks. The Smārta expiation is likewise the general one. [From the *Baudhāyana Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—Section on the Sacrificial Ground]: "The gift of sesame, the gift of gold, the gift of a cow, and likewise the gift of land, quickly destroys all sins, even those equal to the great crimes (*mahāpātaka*). Thus says Saṃvarta.

"Prāṇāyāma destroys the defects born of speech, mind, and body; or else, the recitation of the *praṇava* or even the waters [consecrated by] the Mother of the Vedas [achieves this]. Thus it was stated by Aṅgiras. "But for an unordained minor defect, one should perform a *prājāpatya* penance. Or rather, the expiation should be understood according to the degree of the defect, as stated in the Caturviṃśatimata. The meaning is that while the Soma is being measured, there are not even observers nearby. Because of the inclusion of the word "nearby" (*upa*), there is no fault in seeing it from a distance.

Regarding the contingency that there may be no seller of Soma, Baudhāyana states in the *Karmānta*: "Now, if there should be no seller of Soma, having driven in a Palāśa branch at the time for the sacrificial post-hole (*yūpāvaṭa*) and having placed the King (Soma) upon it, one should wait. Then, if someone should utter a word connected with impelling—such as 'Look!', 'Hurry!', or 'Do it!'—one should cause him to announce the King; the calls for conversation should not be repeated until there is a seller of Soma."

In the iṣṭis and animal sacrifices beginning with the Prāyaṇīyā and ending with the Avabhṛtha, there is no taking up of the vow, no keeping of vigil, no binding of the wife, and no eating of forest food.

The sense is that [the sacrifice] is successful because its purpose has been accomplished. The word *anta* (end) is used in the sense of a limit (*avadhi*). The term *avabhṛthāntāḥ* is a *ekaśeṣa* compound meaning "those ending with the *avabhṛtha* bath. The meaning is: in whatever sacrifices have the *avamṛṣā* as their limit, and in those animal sacrifices (*paśu*) which have the *avabhṛtha* as their limit. Although there are only two types of animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*), the plural number is used by including the two expiatory animal sacrifices (*prāyaścitta-paśu*). By the phrase "beginning with the *prāyaṇīyā*," the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is excluded; by the phrase "ending with the *avabhṛtha*," the *udayanīyā* and others are excluded.

The purpose for including the terms *iṣṭi* and *paśubandha* in the sūtra—"In all *saumika* (Soma-related) *iṣṭis* and *paśubandhas*"—should be understood here as it was demonstrated there. This very reason is implied by the phrase "ending with the *avabhṛtha*. Since the performance of rites such as the assumption of vows (*vratopāyana*) serves a completed purpose only within the fixed sequence beginning from the *prāyaṇīyā* and ending with the *avabhṛtha*, it is for this reason that the state of beginning with that and ending with that is stated. By the phrase "beginning with the *prāyaṇīyā*," the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is excluded.

If it is objected: "Is this [sleeping] being prohibited when, according to the *Yājamāna-sūtra*, it is stated that 'one consecrated on that day keeps watch during the night,' since the act of keeping watch at the time of consecration is about to be enjoined and there is no possibility of its occurrence through any other means such as the *sadyaskāla* [immediate] rite?"—this is true; however, [the prohibition applies] to that which is obstructed by purposelessness (*ānarthakya*).

According to the maxim that "the strength and weakness [of a rule] are reversed" (*viparītabalābala*), and by means of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the word "waking" (*jāgaraṇa*) denotes the non-performance of the momentary closing of the eyes—which occupies the place of sleep and brings about the absence of waking. It is this [non-performance] that is prohibited here. Thus, it implies that there exists a specific ritual act consisting of the closing of the eyes at a time subsequent to the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*). The underlying sense is that [the requirement is met] precisely through the "waking" defined as the non-performance of eye-closing.

The primary *jāgaraṇa* (keeping awake) occurs on the night when one has become one who has fasted for the *savanīya* [offering]. Since this [act] falls within the scope of the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), its absence must be understood as merely momentary, as no other duration is possible. Furthermore, that specific ritual act (*padārtha*) occurs only after the *paristaraṇa* (strewing of grass), because the time following the *paristaraṇa* is established by the archetype (*prakṛti*) as the locus for it. Alternatively, the meaning is this: the prohibition here does not apply to the *jāgaraṇa* performed for the purpose of vigilance by means of protecting the implements of the sacrifice.

[First Paṭala] Accompanied by the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. Because there is no possibility of preserving the ritual acts belonging to the iṣṭis and animal sacrifices that have different timings [from the Soma sacrifice]. Indeed, there is no iṣṭi, animal sacrifice, initiation (dīkṣā), or night belonging to the Soma sacrifice. Since the Dakṣiṇīyā, being of the same day (saghaskālā), occurs on the very same day [as the Soma sacrifice], and in the case of the Prāyaṇīyā and others, their distinct timing is quite evident.

However, since the explanatory passage (arthavāda) states, "But then the initiated one keeps watch this night; thus sleep is averted," it is understood that the act of staying awake—which has the result of averting sleep—is for the sake of an unseen merit (adṛṣṭa). Therefore, its prohibition is made here. The sense is that because the final transcendental result (paramāpūrva) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice persists until the conclusion, the [sleep] that would otherwise occur is precluded by that very fact.

Jaimini also established the incidental accomplishment (*prasaṅgasiddhi*) of the undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*) in the first section of the twelfth chapter by means of the sūtra: "Likewise, the vow [is not performed] because it has already been undertaken" (*tathā vratamupetatvāt*). The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: since its purpose is for the sake of maintenance (*dhāraṇārthatvāt*), the placing of fuel on the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) does not exist in the Soma sacrifice. Just as in the preceding sūtra it was stated that the placing of fuel does not exist because it is accomplished incidentally, so too the vow—the formal acceptance of the vow—does not exist, because it has already been undertaken; that is, because the vow for the sake of the Soma has already been undertaken.

And because that [act] is not completed and is not forgotten, its application (*prasaṅga*) is established. However, in the view of the Naiminis, there is no such application for the *jāgaraṇa* (vigil). Thus, in the first section (*pāda*) of the twelfth chapter, that sūtra and its commentary state: "Because of the difference in time. The meaning of the sūtra is this: the vigil associated with that—that is, associated with the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and associated with the time of initiation—would not apply [to the other sacrifice] due to the difference in time. The underlying intention is that there is no evidence for the production of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) arising from the *naiṣṭika-jāgaraṇa* by means of the *saumika-jāgaraṇa*.

The binding of the wife's girdle (*patnīsanahana*) is also not required, because it is already accomplished by the very binding for the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*). In the first section of the twelfth chapter, Jaimini also states: "And the binding [is not to be performed], because it has already been undertaken. The meaning of the sūtra is that the binding need not be performed at the Soma sacrifice, since it has already been undertaken; the binding is for the purpose of performing the rites while already bound, and not for some unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*), as is the case with the binding for the sake of the Soma.

The sense is that there is no separate act of girding because its purpose is already accomplished and it lacks an unseen (transcendental) result (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Furthermore, the fact that the consumption of forest-herbs (*āraṇyāśana*) is also established by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*) has been accepted even by Mīmāṃsā; for [it is said]: "Because of the injunction of another, there would be no eating of forest-herbs, for the milk-drink (*payovrata*) is for the sake of subsistence. Since another specific rule, the milk-drink, is enjoined, there is the cessation of the original practice of eating forest-herbs.

Why? Because both the milk-vow (*payovrata*) and eating forest-food (*āraṇyāśana*) serve the purpose of subsistence—that is, for the sake of satisfaction (*tṛpti*). Thus, since the satisfaction produced by the vow itself establishes the satisfaction produced by eating forest-food, there is no need for the latter. Nor should it be argued that "how can there be establishment through incidental application (*prasaṅga*) given that the milk-vow and eating forest-food have distinct effects in the form of different types of satisfaction? [This is because] they are... [anu-]śāsana.

The sense is that, because satisfaction is subordinate as it occurs through the state of being crippled, while the sustenance of life is primary as it serves the purpose of the *ṛtu*, this is established by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*). Furthermore, since the absence of eating forest-food (*āraṇyāśana*) is already established by the fact that [the sacrifice] takes place on the same day (*sadyaskālatva*), this prohibition indicates that even in independent *tapas* sacrifices performed on the same day, there is eating of forest-food in its own place.

Based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "The initiation from semen and so forth is a release from austerity," the prohibition of [offering] the *pratopāyana* and other items applies up until that point, because the *avabhṛtha* bath has the purpose of releasing the initiation. After the *avabhṛtha*, these [items] indeed occur, because at that stage they have been released. The binding of the wife (*patnīsanahana*) also certainly takes place, since the girdle (*yoktra*) has been discarded. In the *Yājamāna-sūtra*, he will state the discarding of the girdle. By this, it is established that the girdle is to be worn from the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice until the *avabhṛtha*.
And Baudhāyana says: "The wife, having girded herself, sits down facing west.
All these [rites] are performed in the *uttarā* [verses].

The meaning is that all these are to be performed in the *uttarā* verses. [Regarding the compound *uttarāśca*]: *uttarā* (feminine), *uttara* (masculine), and *uttarā* (feminine)—this is the remainder [of the compound]. By the rule *paravalliṅgam* (the gender of the last member prevails), it ends in the feminine gender, because there is no specific characteristic [to indicate otherwise].

This sūtra is intended to convey the meaning that just as there is an exclusion of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* in the context of prohibition by the phrase "starting from the *prāyaṇīyā*," there is likewise an exclusion in the context of performance. For this very reason, instead of saying "the others are performed," the word "subsequent" (*uttara*) is employed in the expression "they are performed in the subsequent [rites]. Thus, since the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is excluded in both cases, an option (*vikalpa*) is established.

And it should be understood that since [the purpose] was not accomplished in the earlier *dīkṣaṇīyā*, all these [rites] take place; whereas since the purpose was accomplished in the later *dīkṣaṇīyā*, these do not take place. Furthermore, it has already been stated previously that the selection of the *brahmán* does not occur either, because it is accomplished by the very selection of the *brahmán* for the sake of the Soma sacrifice. Nor should it be argued that, in this same way, the original selection of the *hotṛ* priest would also be accomplished by the mantra-accompanied selection of the *hotṛ* for the sake of the Soma sacrifice.

Since the ordinary (*prākṛta*) selection (*varaṇa*), which has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), cannot be established through incidental application (*prasaṅga*) by means of the Soma-related (*saumika*) selection—which has a visible purpose—[the former must remain]. For, while certain ritual acts have already commenced, the selection of the Hotṛ is prescribed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) with the mantra, "Agni, the god, the Hotṛ, shall sacrifice to the gods, he who is wise and discerning," and so forth; because that [selection] has already occurred, it is impossible for it to have a visible purpose, and thus it possesses an unseen purpose. However, since the Soma-related selection consists of an invitation to one who has not yet been engaged, it indeed possesses only an unseen purpose.

And likewise, Jaimini states in the first pāda of the twelfth adhyāya: "Because the choosing has already taken place, the choosing of the Hotṛ should be performed for each ritual cycle (*tantra*). The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: because the choosing of the Hotṛ who is already engaged in the rite—that is, because of the choosing pertaining to the Hotṛ who is engaged—the choosing pertaining to the Hotṛ who is engaged [is required]; this refers to the choosing [expressed by] "Agni is the divine Hotṛ. By this, its having a visible purpose consisting of propitiation (*ānati*) is excluded. Thus, it is stated that this choosing has an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose.

And thus, because the undesirable consequence of the omission of the unseen purpose would follow from the omission of the seen purpose, the selection (*varaṇa*) of the Hotṛ must indeed be performed in every instance; for the term "tantra" refers to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites pertaining to the sacrificial cake and the animal sacrifice. In that regard, the selection of the Hotṛ is to be performed everywhere.
However, in the case of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice and the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes, the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) does not take place. || 4 ||

The prohibition is intended precisely to indicate that through the *dīkṣaṇīyā*—which serves the primary purpose, acts as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāriṇī*), and effects the refinement of the sacrificer (*yajamāna-saṃskāriṇī*)—one must also perform the formal acceptance (*parigraha*) of the Soma-deity, by virtue of both the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the *yājyā*. For if the acceptance of the Soma-deity were not established by the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, then the acceptance of the deities of the *āgnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice and the *savanīya* animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) occurring at that time would also remain unestablished; consequently, the prohibition would become incoherent, as it would fail to attach itself to those [deities] following the sequence of the "needle and thread" (*sūcīsūtra-nyāya*).

Therefore, by the force of this prohibition, one must accept that the acceptance of the deity Soma is performed through the *īkṣaṇīyā* (the rite of looking). There are two kinds of *anvādhāna*: the first limb consists of the grasping of the physical fire, and that is accomplished by means of the *vihavyā* verses. The second consists of the grasping of the fire in its form as a deity. For thus is the intention of the author of the Sūtra: the acceptance of the deity occurs through the acceptance of the fire in its form as a deity, and not through the maintenance of the physical fire; this very point is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the statement that the *anvādhāna* is performed with the *vihavyā* verses.

Having begun with "He offers an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu," [the text] says: "Agni is the lowest of the deities, Viṣṇu is the highest; when he offers an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu, the sacrificer, having encompassed the deities on both sides, secures them. By this, the encompassing of the principal deity is stated through the encompassing of the two deities, Agni and Viṣṇu. The Soma-pressing (sutyā) is the principal rite; initiation (dīkṣā) is for its sake. And it has been stated in the third [section], Chapter 150, by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary Jyotsnā.

In the seventh pāda of the sixth adhyāya, it is stated in the sūtra *aumnimā dīkṣādakṣiṇa tu vacanāt pradhānasya* that the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) belong to the primary sacrifice. It should not be argued that, although the initiation belongs to the Soma sacrifice according to the scriptural statement *dīkṣā somasya*, and thus the initiation serves only the primary sacrifice, there is nevertheless no evidence that the deity of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*—which is the generator of that initiation—is restricted solely to the deity of the primary sacrifice; rather, since there is no proof for such restriction, the deity must be understood as belonging to both the primary and the subsidiary sacrifices alike. This is because there is an absence of any authority (proof) for the claim that the deity of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* refers exclusively to the deity of the primary sacrifice.

Since the scriptural statement "The initiation [is for] Soma" establishes that initiation serves solely the purpose of the primary sacrifice, it follows by implication that the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*—which brings about that initiation—also has as its sole aim the primary sacrifice. Just as this is established, so too is the fact that [the initiation] pertains solely to the deity of the primary sacrifice established by this very scripture. Consequently, since the acceptance of deities of the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) is not established, it is entirely appropriate to enjoin the *anvādhāna* (placing of the firewood) for the sake of those various *iṣṭi*s and animal sacrifices.

The meaning of the *Naimini-sūtra*, however, is as follows: *dīkṣā* (initiation) and *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee); the combination of these two is *dīkṣādakṣiṇam*. This is a collective *dvandva* compound according to the rule *gavāśvaprabhṛtīni ca*. Because of the statement, "Initiation and sacrificial fee [belong] to the Soma; the sacrificial fee [belongs] to the Soma," both initiation and the sacrificial fee would pertain to the principal [rite]. This is the purpose regarding whether there is extension (*atideśa*) or non-extension of that [rule] to the modification (*vikāra*) of the *āmīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice]. The details should be seen in the original treatises (*ākara*). Furthermore, the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses also express the very appropriation of the deities of the principal [rite].

In that [mantra], it is recited: "O Agni and Viṣṇu, through austerity, being in harmony as the Viśvedevas, bestow initiation upon this sacrificer. In that context, regarding the word *viśvedeva*, [the following is said]: "The Ādityas, Viśvas, Vasus, Tuṣitas, Āmās, Apsarases, Anilas, Mahārājikas, Sādhyas, and Rudras are the deities of the *gaṇas*."

When the specific nature of the *itika* group is understood through its established status as a class, then—since the Vasus are the deities of the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*), the Rudras are the deities of the midday libation (*mādhyaṃdinasavana*), and the Ādityas and Viśvedevas are the deities of the third libation—it is understood that these very deities, who are already established as a group (*gaṇadevatā*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), serve as the principal deities in this instance as well. It is precisely such deities that the *yājyā* verse refers to. By the term "guardian of initiation" (*dīkṣāpāla*), all deities of the Soma sacrifice, including Indra and others, are also included.

Just as one who protects his own favorable servant is himself the protector, so too, because he is the master of the deities themselves, he is the protector of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) that is favorable to him. [The mantra says: "O you two joined with all the gods, bestow initiation upon this sacrificer. And initiation has the primary purpose [of the sacrifice] as its goal; therefore, the deities alone, having the primary purpose as their goal, are the accomplishers of the initiation.

Likewise, even the word "deity" (*devatā*) occurring in the *puronuvākyā* mantra, "Agni is the first of the deities," refers only to the principal deity, in accordance with the corresponding *yājyā* mantra. By this same logic, just as the word "lower" (*avama*) signifies that which is inferior, so too it signifies that which is first; and similarly, the word "highest" (*uttama*), which is synonymous with "supreme" (*parama*), signifies that which is excellent as well as that which is last.

Thus, in the passage "Agni was the first of the deities, and Viṣṇu was the last of those who have come together," since Agni and Viṣṇu—the first and last among all the deities—are mentioned, the doubt that this might also include the subordinate deities (aṅgadevatā) situated between them—just as the primary deities (pradhānadevatā) are included by the principle of elliptical extension (pratyāhāranyāya)—is thereby dispelled. Consequently, it is logical that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, which serves the purpose of the primary rite, effects the selection of the primary deities alone through the sacrifices to Agni and Viṣṇu, and not the selection of the primary rite along with its subsidiaries (*sāṅgapradhāna*).

For he will state that in the *prāyaṇīya* and other rites, although the *anvādhāna* (the adding of fuel) is already obtained by extension (*codaka*) for the purpose of again taking possession of the deities, that very *anvādhāna* which was prohibited by others is here enjoined once more. If it is objected: "But even here, since 'Agni is all the deities,' the taking possession of the deities of both the primary and subsidiary rites is accomplished by the commencement of Agni—who is the very form of the deities—for the sake of the primary and subsidiary rites along with their subsidiaries; so how can the *agnyanvādhāna* be enjoined?"—this is true.

Since the mere taking hold (*anvārambha*) of the deity is established by the taking hold of the deity’s form, there is no prohibition of the *anvādhāna* (the piling of the fires), because that is a separate act due to being a different verbal root. Thus, in the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Āpastamba, he prohibits the *anvārambhaṇīyā* in the case of the animals which are subsidiary parts, and because of the prohibition of the *anvādhāna* in the case of the *savanīya* animal alone, he permits it in the *prāyaṇīya* and other offerings, as well as in the *agnīṣomīya* and *anūbandhya* sacrifices.

For this very reason, even though [the fire] has already been established (*nirūḍha*), after stating "he maintains the Āhavanīya," [the text] says immediately following the *Anvārambhaṇīyā* rite, "he does not add fuel. From this it is understood that even though the commencement [of the sacrifice] is already accomplished, the adding of fuel (*anvādhāna*) is not thereby accomplished. Therefore, it is established that by means of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, there is the formal inclusion (*parigraha*) of the deities of the principal sacrifice alone. Now, an objection: since the adding of fuel is not prescribed for the Savanīya animal sacrifice nor for the Savanīya cakes, [one might argue] that by virtue of this very prohibition, [the rule] applies to other cases.

If it is argued: "Since the *anvādhāna* has already been established [by the previous rule], why was a re-performance (*punaḥsiddhi*) not performed for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice—just as it was for the *prāyaṇīyā*—in order to restore the *anvādhāna* that had been prohibited by another school's view? The answer is: No. For even in the absence of that [re-performance] at the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, its accomplishment is achieved. If one asks how, it is said: It is only when the *dīkṣaṇīyā* has actually taken place that it possesses the capacity to encompass the deities (*devatā-parigraha*).

And for the sake of its inclusion [in the Soma sacrifice], because the *iṣṭi* was previously intended for that purpose—according to the view of Jaimini—in the Soma sacrifice, which has the Darśapūrṇamāsa as its archetype, there is the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*), the undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*), the eating of forest-food (*āraṇyāśana*), and the keeping of vigil (*jāgaraṇa*).

According to the view of Āpastamba, the giving of the anvāhārya rice and the binding and unbinding of the wife’s girdle do not exist; he initiates the *tantra* for the Prāyaṇīya sacrifice, and therein these [acts] are not performed—the anvādhāna, the taking up of the vows (*vrata-upāyana*), the binding of the wife, and the anvāhārya. According to the view of Bhāradvāja as well, in all Soma sacrifices, Iṣṭis, and animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*), these are not performed at all. Furthermore, in that context, [the author] seeks to refute the claim—made by some—that these acts serve the purpose of formally accepting the deities of the primary rites along with their subsidiaries.

In that regard, there is the rule for the *anvādhāna* (the adding of fuel). Otherwise, since it would already be established by the statement, "In the case of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice and the *savanīya* cakes, no other *anvādhāna* exists," the specific prescription for each instance would be redundant. This is because the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering], being unaccomplished, lacks the capacity to appropriate its own deity; for this reason, Āpastamba states that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is for the purpose of appropriating even the deities of the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*).

Furthermore, the *anvādhāna* (the adding of fuel) for the purpose of formally accepting the deities of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice must necessarily be performed even by the opponent. Thus, since that view has already been effectively refuted by the venerable Teacher through demonstrating its equivalence to his own position, he did not take the trouble to provide a formal injunction for the *anvādhāna* specifically for the purpose of dismantling that view. It should be understood that this remains well-established, as the injunction for *anvādhāna* would also be considered a new (*apūrva*) prescription in the case where the *prāyaṇīyā* is regarded as a unique rite.

Regarding the meaning of the *Jaimini-sūtra* cited as "And because the previous [rite] is for the purpose of the *grahaṇa*, since that is its purpose": the previous *anvādhāna* would also be dispensed with even if it were for the purpose of the *grahaṇa*, because the *dakṣiṇīyā* sacrifice is also for that purpose—that is, for the purpose of the *anvādhāna*. Thus [ends the work] by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was a performer of the *Agniṣṭoma*, *Sāhasra-Agnicayana*, *Vājapeya*, *Sarvatomukha*, *Dviṣāhasra-Agnicayana*, and *Pauṇḍarīka* sacrifices, and who belonged to the lineage of the venerable Okopāha.

Thus ends the first Paṭala of the seventh Praśna in the commentary named Jyotsnā, composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa, which allays the distress of learned men caused by the failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the ocean of the Śrīmad-Bhagavat-Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Now begins the second Paṭala of the seventh Praśna:
He commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the Prāyaṇīyā [Iṣṭi].

"One who is initiated enters the sacrifice by means of this [rite]"—thus, the *prāyaṇīyā* initiates, that is, begins, the *tantra*, which is the collection of ritual acts related to it. The suffix *ṇic* is used here either in its own sense (reflexive) or for the sake of another; in the latter case, the instigator (*prayojaka*) is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and the one being instigated (*prayojya*) is the Adhvaryu priest. By this, it is made known that the injunction "begin the *tantra* of the *prāyaṇīyā*" must be uttered as a command. Furthermore, it should be understood that this [injunction] is not explicitly seen in the *prāyaṇīyā* itself. Whatever is performed therein, we shall explain.

In this regard, we shall explain the ritual procedure (*tantra*) connected with the *prāyaṇīyā* offering as far as it must be performed; that is to say, we shall describe it by synthesizing it from various scriptural injunctions (*śruti*). This sūtra is intended precisely to indicate the novelty (*apūrvatva*) of this sacrifice.

Now, regarding the *prāyaṇīyā* [offering], we shall explain what is performed therein. Although it would have been sufficient to state simply "we shall explain this" for the sake of brevity, the author composed a cumbersome sūtra stating "he commences the procedure (*tantra*) of the *prāyaṇīyā*" in order to indicate that the novelty (*apūrvatva*) applies only to the procedure of the Adhvaryu, and not to the procedures of the Hotṛ and others. Consequently, everything such as "O gods who... and "O Lord of Speech... occurs here exactly as in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

In this context, the word *yāvat* refers to that [action] by whose attainment other actions connected to it are also attained. Therefore, when it is said, "he brings the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) from outside," it does not mean merely the act of bringing; rather, it includes the entire procedure for the sacrificial grass, such as its taking from the *āsida* vessel, its sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and so forth. This should be understood similarly in other cases as well. Because such actions do not cause the displacement of the *codaka* (the general rule), they constitute a new, independent injunction (*apūrva*). And that [new injunction] consists of the *codaka*-derived portions, such as the offering of the *ājyabhāga* and the taking of the *prāśitra*.

It should be understood that although there is no direct Vedic revelation (śruti) serving as the root for this unprecedented matter, it is nonetheless inferred through the authority of the words of the venerable teacher.
"Having added fuel to the fires, he brings the sacrificial wood and grass."

The *anvādhāna* (the placing of fuel on the fires) is enjoined as something not previously established (*apūrva*). However, according to the view that the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) is complete [in itself], even though there is no *apūrva* status, the injunction is necessary because it has been prohibited by others. If it is objected: "It should be stated only as 'having placed fuel on the fires, he brings the sacrificial grass (*barhis*),' for the bringing of the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) is already established by the injunctions such as 'there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses,'" we say: No. Because that [text] serves the purpose of prescribing the bringing of the fuel-sticks together with the *āghāra* oblations and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). By this, the preparation of the *āghāra* and the enclosing sticks is also accomplished.

This is a restatement following the sequence [of topics], intended to demonstrate that the *paurṇamāsī* sacrifice possesses a single ritual procedure (*tantra*) according to the view that the *iṣṭi* is a complete whole.
There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; one does not tie on a fuel-stick for the after-offerings (*anūyāja*) if there are no after-offerings.

If it were stated merely that "one does not prepare the *anūyāja* fuel-stick," then even though other *anūyājas* might exist, there would be an absence of the *anūyāja* fuel-stick due to its being something previously unestablished (*apūrva*). To prevent this, it says, "if the *anūyājas* do not take place. Since the absence of the *anūyāja* fuel-stick is established simply by the injunction of the non-existence of the *anūyājas*—on the grounds that the fuel-stick is connected to them—the specific statement, "one does not prepare the *anūyāja* fuel-stick if the *anūyājas* do not take place," serves to exclude the option of [performing] the *anūyājas* in the case where they are performed in their entirety. Thus, there is no option regarding the *anūyājas*.

This is done, however, for the purpose of making it known that they are indeed fixed. Even though there is no *anuyāja* (after-offering) in the *ātithyā* sacrifice, the *anūyāja* formula exists here. And that [formula] is for the purpose of causing the dropping [of the offering] together with the pieces of wood to be thrown into the fire, according to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Hiraṇyakeśin-Satyāṣāḍha: "The *samidhs*, O Agni, at the oblation... The Sūtra itself is quite clear.

Having prepared the *veda* grass-bundle, having strewn around the fires, having washed his hands, and having spread out a layer of *ulapa* grass, he arranges the vessels as required; he arranges the cooking pot (*sthālī*) in place of the *kapālas* (potsherds).

By the expression "having made the *veda*," the existence of rituals connected with the *veda* is indicated; otherwise, the act of making the *veda* would result in being purposeless. Rituals connected with the *veda* include: "having wiped the altar with the *veda*," "having taken [the fire] up with the *veda*," "holding the vessel with the *veda*," and "having purified with the *veda*. Since the *barhis* (sacrificial grass) serves as a covering for the *veda*, and since the *veda* cannot exist without the construction of the altar, the injunction for bringing the *barhis* also implies the construction of the altar.

The expression "having made the Veda" (*vedaṃ kṛtvā*) ends in the suffix *ktvā* and is a restatement (*anuvāda*). It signifies that the Adhvaryu, who is the maker of the Veda, is the very same person who performs the strewing of the fire (*agniparistaraṇa*), for the purpose of establishing a single agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). By this, the duties of the Āgnīdhra and others are excluded here. The expression "having strewn around the fire" (*agnī paristīrya*) ends in the suffix *tyap* and is likewise a restatement for the purpose of establishing a single agent. Consequently, the one who is the performer of the hand-washing is the very same person who is the performer of the strewing of the fire. By this, the possibility of different agents is precluded.

Because the purpose of the *śreya* (the better) also exists, there is no cessation [of the action]. In the original model (*prakṛti*), precisely because of the use of the suffix *-lyap*, it is expected that "he shall wash his hands" (*pāṇī prakṣālya*). Otherwise, if it were stated as "having strewn around the fire, he shall strew the *ulapa* grass" (*agnī paristīrya ulaparājīṃ stīrṣyati*), there would indeed be a cessation of the hand-washing. Therefore, this statement is for the purpose of ensuring that the hand-washing does not cease. The phrase "he shall wash his hands" (*pāṇī prakṣāsyati*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) ending in the suffix *-syap*, on the grounds that it exists in the original model in this very way.

In the case of the *samyāva* sacrifice, there is also the spreading (*paristaraṇa*) of those two. *Ulapāḥ* are dry *darbha* grasses; some say they are *ballana* grasses, others say they are *uśīra* grasses, and still others say they are *urdha* grasses. Having spread them out—that is, having scattered them—over the altar, one arranges the vessels according to their purpose, meaning according to the requirements of the ritual.

The statement "according to the purpose" (*yathārtham*) is intended to demonstrate the exclusion of the *śamyā*, the *dṛṣad* and *upala* stones, the mortar and pestle, the flour, the frying pan, the stirring spoon, the *bāharya* vessel, the *sthālī*, the *madantī* vessel, and the *yoktra* for those who lack a specific purpose. Furthermore, according to the view that these are *apūrva* (novel) acts, there is also the exclusion of the *prāśitra-haraṇa*. As for the *kapālas* (potsherds), their exclusion follows from the sūtra yet to be cited: "He employs the *sthālī* in place of the *kapālas*."

Nor should it be argued that, in the case where the mortar and pestle are struck with the wooden mace (kuṭara) or the yoke-pin (śamyā), there should be the placing of the yoke-pin for the purpose of striking; for, since the striking in the case of the cooked rice (caru) is intended as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the mortar and pestle, and since the mortar and pestle are absent here, their refinement—the striking—also ceases to exist. And because of the absence of the striking itself, there is likewise the cessation of its instruments, namely the wooden mace or the yoke-pin.

Bharadvāja has clearly stated all of this: "If the substance is absent, there is an omission of the ritual action, as in the case of the threshing of the *caru* or the pouring out for the Āpyas. In that regard, the formation of a *dvaṃdva* (copulative compound) is as follows: "the wooden sword (*sphya*) together with the *mekṣaṇa* and the pot" is a *dvaṃdva*; "the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) and the grass" is a *dvaṃdva*, because in another *sūtra* the use of grass is prescribed for the purpose of forming a *dvaṃdva*; "the butter-pot (*ājyasthālī*) and the grass" is a *dvaṃdva*; and "the vessel (*pātrī*) and the grass" is a *dvaṃdva*.

In the absence of the *prāśitraharaṇa* vessel, the term "the *veda* and the grass" (*vedaṃ tṛṇaṃ ca*) forms a *dvandva* compound. By the use of the suffix *-kyap* in the word *stīrṇa*, the silent preparation of the seats for the Brahman and the sacrificer—as expressed in the phrases "silently to the south" and "silently to the north"—is excluded. Alternatively, the word *rājīm* may be understood as a singular form used for a collective sense (*bhāta-ekavacana*). In that case, the instructions "silently to the south" and "silently to the north" certainly apply. However, since the preparation of the seats for the Brahman and the sacrificer has been excluded here, it must be performed by the Adhvaryu at the very time of their sitting down.

[Second Paṭala] Accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa. However, the spreading of the *darbha* grass and the washing of the vessels indeed take place. This is because, as subordinate elements (*aṅga*) of those two acts, they do not constitute an interruption. The *sthālī* (pot) is well-known in common usage; it is to be used in place of the *kapālas* (potsherds). At the time of employing the vessels, one employs that pot—which has been extended by analogy (*atideśa*) from the *kapālas*, which are capable of cooking the *caru*—in place of the *kapālas*, for their purpose and with them as the intended object.

The meaning—that even the subsequent consecratory rites (*uttara-saṃskāra*) are equal [to those of the *kapāla*]—has already been illustrated in the Sūtra: "And in another substance... We shall explain the *caru*: "He employs a cooking-pot (*sthālī*) in place of the *kapālas*," and so forth; this is established here by that very [Sūtra]. This repetition, however, is for the sake of establishing it as a new rule (*apūrva*), lest the properties of the *kapāla* fail to apply. The statement "He employs a cooking-pot in place of the *kapālas*" is intended to demonstrate the properties of other *carus*.
At the time of the offering (*nirvapaṇa*), he offers the introductory *caru* (*prāyaṇīya*) to Aditi and cooks it in milk.

*Prakṛṣṭam ayanam* means a pre-eminent going toward the sacrifice—that is to say, a connection with the sacrifice. That which is capable of that [going] is *prāyaṇīya*. Although the primary sacrifice is distant, the "pre-eminence" (*prakarpa*) here consists simply in its existence from this point until the time of the primary sacrifice. In that context, its existence until the time of the primary sacrifice occurs by way of the *niṣkāsa* (the scrapings). Although the root *i* signifies "going," it is taken here in the sense of "connection," for it is observed elsewhere that verbal roots possess multiple meanings.

The statement "at the time of offering" (*nirvapaṇakāle*) is for the purpose of indicating the *pavitrakaraṇa* (purification) and other such rites; otherwise, because it would be a novel (*apūrva*) injunction, these would not be obtained. It should be understood that the term "Prāyaṇīya" is used according to the explanatory interpretation (*vyākhyāna*) of the Brāhmaṇa. He pours [the milk] when the water has been carried forward (*praṇīta*), as in the case of the *praṇītā* water, but not when the milk has been produced through the ritual acts such as driving away the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*). Thus, in the fourth pāda of the ninth adhyāya, Jaimini states: "The observation of the act of offering occurs during the cooking; therefore, those ritual properties [of the *praṇītā* water] apply, because [the cooking] is for the purpose of consumption and because of the contact, like honey and water."

[The opponent argues: "Because of the granting of unrighteousness (*adharma*), because of the excellence of the injunction, and because of inequality, there is no connection. In the passage, "The *āditya* [offering] is the introductory; [he offers] a milk-porridge," since prescribing the connection with the deity for the milk and the connection with the porridge would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) in the injunction, the injunction must be one that prescribes the connection with the deity as qualified by two substances.

The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the milk’s status as the substrate (*ādhāra*) is established by the fact that it is cooked together [with the rice]; thus, since there is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) in the injunction of a relationship with a deity qualified by both the substrate-substance and the [rice]—namely, "the milk for Āditya is the horse"—the milk does not possess the status of being the substance to be offered (*pradeya*). Therefore, the milk is not connected with the acts such as driving away the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*), but rather only with the *praṇītā* water; this is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). As for the meaning of the Sūtra: in the case of cooking—that is, cooking together—an offering is also seen to be made together, because of the observed experience that the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) is abandoned along with the milk.

Therefore, "its properties" (*taddharma*) means the properties of that substance to be offered; it is "of such a nature" because, being for the purpose of eating [in the case of honey and water] or for the purpose of sacrifice [in the case of meat], it acquires a variegated character through contact, as explained in the previous sūtra. The meaning of the subsequent sūtra is as follows: "without its properties" (*adharma*) refers to that which lacks the properties of the substance to be offered. The word *tu* (but) serves to highlight the distinction from the analogy of honey and water. This is because of "non-offering," that is, the absence of offering.

Just as in the case of "curd, honey, ghee, water, and parched grain—these mixed together," there is no simultaneous cooking here because both [the milk and the rice] lack equal status as primary substances (*samapradhānatva*). If it is asked, "In that case, for what purpose is the prescription of milk? he says: "Because of the prescription as *praṇītā* water. Therefore, there is no mention of the *caru* being the object of measurement; rather, there is a mention in the locative case. By the locative case, the status of being a substratum (*ādhāratva*) is indicated. For this very reason, it is said, "because it is oily" (*snigdhatvāt*). Consequently, these are not the properties of a sacrificial offering (*pradeyadharma*).

Non-contact; there is no contact like that of a mother cow with her calf. There is no contact with those of equal status, but rather a contact with one who is superior. Or, he cooks [the oblation] after the butter has been purified by the *yajus* formula. — [In the case] where there are no *anūyāja* offerings, he takes four portions of clarified butter (*ājya*). — *Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra*, Book 7, Chapter 1.4: If there are no *anūyāja* offerings, he takes four spoonfuls of clarified butter.

Because the first group [of offerings] is for the purpose of the *prayāja*s, one takes that very [portion]; however, because the second group is for other purposes, one does not take it in the case where there are no *anūyāja*s. But when the *anūyāja*s are present, one takes that as well—this is the meaning. It should have been stated simply that "one takes four portions in the *upabhṛt* if the *anūyāja*s do not exist," since that alone would exclude the eight portions; the statement "one takes the four portions suitable [for the *upabhṛt*]" is intended to exclude the optional five portions prescribed in the archetypal (*prakṛta*) rite.

If the statement "if there are no other [substances]" were not present, then even when other substances exist, the *ājya* would still be taken four times (*caturgṛhīta*) and not eight times (*aṣṭagṛhīta*); it is to exclude this possibility that the word is used. By the inclusion of the term *ājya*, it is made known that the specific modification occurs solely due to the absence of the [other] items, and not because of a modification produced by an *apūrva* (transcendental result). Therefore, following this, the entire original (*prākṛta*) ritual procedure (*tantra*) takes place.
With the *Ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula, he places the *Prāyaṇīya* offering.

The word "case" (*casa*) is understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Regarding that [Udayanīyā], the ritual procedure has been explained by the *Prāyaṇīyā*; thus, the mention of "Prāyaṇīya" is intended to prevent the application of the *Ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula at the setting down of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) for the Udayanīyā, which would otherwise follow from the upcoming sūtra. Because it is not for the purpose of an oblation (*ahomārthatvāt*), the *Ṣaḍḍhotṛ* is without the *svāhā*-utterance. Here, the *Ṣaḍḍhotṛ* consists only of "Sūrya te cakṣuḥ" and not of "Vāg ota," because in the Śruti and in the Sūtra we find the term "prāyaścittī" (expiatory), and because that [formula] serves exclusively for expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
He places the entire fuel-stick (*idhma*) on the fire and pours out the entire butter from the *aupabhṛta* ladle, provided that there are no after-offerings (*anūyāja*).

He pours out the entire *aupabhṛta* butter in the case where there is an absence of other [after-offerings]. However, when the after-offerings exist, because the second portion has been taken for their sake, there is no pouring out of the entire *aupabhṛta* butter. Furthermore, he does not leave behind the after-offering fuel-stick nor the *aupabhṛta* butter; the reason is the absence of after-offerings. The statement "he places the entire fuel-stick" is intended to exclude the alternative archetypal rule (*prākṛta-pakṣāntara*) that one may place it with each *sāmidhenī* verse.

The statement, "Bring all the clarified butter (ājya) together," is intended to prescribe a single act of bringing for the purpose of the *prayāja* offerings; it does not merely enjoin the act of bringing itself. By this it is understood that in the *paśubandha*, the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices, and the *soma* sacrifice, the bringing is performed by drawing [the butter] from each vessel separately.

He performs four *ājyabhāga* offerings: Pathyā Svasti in the east, Agni in the south, Soma in the west, and Savitṛ in the north; Aditi is offered in the middle. He places the vessel of oblation (*havisthālī*), the scrapings (*niṣkāsa*), and the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) [in their respective places].

Those for whom there is an *ājyabhāga* (portion of clarified butter) are called *ājyabhāgās*; the meaning is that they have clarified butter as their oblation (*havis*). He performs those four. When there is an expectation of how this is done, [the text says] "with the view of well-being," and so forth; the meaning is "with the oblation, namely the *caru*. "He sacrifices the four *ājyabhāgas*" is the general proposition.

Since the number four is already established by the mention of "four" in the subsequent passage, the inclusion of the word "four" in the formula *caturo yajati* ("he sacrifices to four") is for the purpose of making it known that there is a single group (*gaṇa*) of four, and because of its status as a group, the final consecration (*anumantraṇa*) of the four occurs at the very end with the formula: *caturṇām anta evānumantraṇaṃ bhavati*: "I am the ocean; may I become the ocean; may I overcome evil. The section beginning with *pathyā svasti* and ending with *savitāram uttaraḥ* is for the purpose of prescribing the deities and the directions. [End of] the second Paṭala, accompanied by the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

Now, one might object: since the sacrifice toward each direction is accomplished by the mere recitation of "pathyā svastimāni," "soma," and "savitāram" as each [deity] goes toward its respective direction, what is the purpose of specifying the directions with "purastāt" (in front) and so forth? It is for the purpose of indicating the necessity of knowing the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as, "Going toward *pathyā svasti*, they recognized that very eastern direction through it. The clarified butter (*ājya*) from the *dhruvā* vessel is used for *pathyā svasti* and the others, because that [butter] serves all purposes.

[Objection: Should it not be sufficient to say simply "nanvadi" (indeed, [the word] *aditi*) and "madhye" (in the middle)? The desire for *caru* (cooked rice offering) is established by the mere continuation of the previous context; and thus, if that is so, the mention of "haviṣā" (with the oblation) in the cooking instruction is redundant. [Reply: This is not so, because its purpose is to demonstrate the equal status of all five [offerings]. The primacy of the five is also stated in the Śruti: "He sacrifices to five deities. Consequently, since offerings such as *pathyā svasti* and others, which have clarified butter (*ājya*) as their oblation, possess the status of primary oblations, it is established that they are modifications (*vikāra*) of the *upāṃśuyāja*.
