One might object: "If it is for the purpose of demonstrating the equality of the five [offerings], then one should simply say 'of the ghee' (ghṛtasya); why is the expression 'of the oblation' (haviṣaḥ) employed? This is not so; for it is employed to indicate the attainment of those properties related to the oblation—beginning after the cooking and ending with the removal from the fire—which, being *apūrva* (unprecedented), would otherwise not be obtained. Furthermore, the term *ājyabhāga* is the name of the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*) in this context, as indicated by the statement: "He proceeds with the two *ājyabhāgas*, which have ghee as their oblation" (*ājyabhāgābhyām ājyahaviṣā pracarati*).

And since clarified butter (ājya) has been specified for all purposes, it constitutes the *dhauva* oblation. Thus, these [offerings] do not have the function of the original *ājyabhāga* (butter-portions); rather, they are themselves the principal oblations (*pradhānahavīṃṣi*). Furthermore, because the term *ājyabhāga* is etymological (*yaugika*), it indicates that these consist of clarified butter as their oblation, just as in the expressions "the *sarasvatyājyabhāga*" and "the *vāyavya ājyabhāga*. Moreover, from the scriptural statement, "At the *udayanīya* [offering], one sacrifices to Pathyā Svasti last with clarified butter," their status as principal offerings is understood.

Where there is a dual-number designation—as in "the two *ājyabhāga*s are offered in succession," "the two living *ājyabhāga*s," and so forth—it is precisely in those instances that the archetypal (*prākṛta*) *ājyabhāgas* are understood, and not elsewhere. Therefore, even though the *ājyabhāgas* are obtained through the extended application (*codaka*), they must be performed separately. Regarding the *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ priest) according to Āśvalāyana, the Sūtra states: "The *iṣṭi*, animal sacrifice, and Soma sacrifices are taught by means of the Full Moon sacrifice. This applies to both the Yajurvedic *hautra* and the Sāmavedic *hautra*, since they both follow the procedure (*tantra*) of the Full Moon sacrifice. However, the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the principal deities are exactly as stated by Āśvalāyana.

Nor can it be argued that because the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses bearing the marks (*liṅga*) of the deities Agni, Soma, Savitṛ, and Aditi exist within one's own *śākhā*, only those found in one's own *śākhā* should be selected; for since the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses bearing the marks of the deity Pathyā-Svastidevatā are absent from one's own *śākhā*, one must accept those very verses prescribed by Āśvalāyana.

Since the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses employed for the *prāyaṇīyā* [offering] are not prescribed in one’s own *sūtra*, while they are prescribed by Āśvalāyana, it is logical to select only those that are prescribed from among the "unprescribed" and "prescribed" categories. Furthermore, regarding the subject matter of the *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ priest), in the absence of a statement in one’s own *sūtra*, that which is stated by Āśvalāyana alone is more authoritative. Nor should it be argued: "Let there be no inclusion of those [verses] mentioned by Āśvalāyana; even if some are not included, let their recitation still occur according to the tradition of one’s own branch (*svaśākhā*)."

Because there is scope for this mantra-text here, and because it must be adopted in accordance with the injunction, it is proper to accept that very text. Since there is no *yājyā* verse concerning the deity Savitṛ in one's own *śākhā*, one does not adopt the *yājyā* mentioned elsewhere; rather, in accordance with that requirement, it is proper to accept only those *yājyā*s found in the recension of Āśvalāyana. Without such a means of resolution, this [mantra] would not be accepted, and other [mantras] belonging to that same *śākhā* would likewise be accepted, as they are restricted by the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Because it is impossible to carry out the mantras recited in the specific *śākhā* (branch of the Veda), only those [mantras] belonging to the *Āmnāya* (the traditional collection) are taken here. By means of these two, the four deities are to be sacrificed according to the rules of the *iṣṭi* and the *upāṃśuyāja*. Furthermore, by stating that "the butter-maker, with the sacrificial ladle, pours clarified butter over [the oblation] five times," he demonstrates the existence of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings. In this regard, one pouring is observed for the purpose of the original (*prākṛta*) *ājyabhāgas*, and four pourings for the purpose of the four *upāṃśuyāja* offerings. This statement is only logical if the two *ājyabhāgas* exist, and not otherwise. Therefore, the two *ājyabhāgas* certainly exist. However, there is another opinion: let it be that these [other offerings] serve as the primary oblations (*pradhānahavis*), since the two *ājyabhāgas* are not explicitly taught here.

Because of the instruction regarding the *ātithyā* [offering]—namely, "These two are indeed the eyes of the sacrifice"—and because of the observation of Agni and Soma in the statement, "These two are indeed the eyes of the sacrifice, namely Agni and Soma," and because the term *ājyabhāga* (butter-portion) found in the Sūtra is intended to exclude [the standard] butter-portions, the two original (*prākṛta*) butter-portions do not occur. Regarding this, Āśmarathya says, "Having performed the two butter-portions, they recite [the verses]," while Ālekhana says, "These two do not occur," and Bharadvāja says, "They are performed at the end of the *śaṃyu* formula, without the butter-portions. Thus says Āśvalāyana.

The portioning [of the oblations] from the *caru* vessels is done with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating "with the stirring-spoon for the *carus*. After the sacrifice to Aditi, one should recite the verse addressed to the Maruts. This is based on the Vedic injunction: "Having sacrificed to Aditi, he recites the verse to the Maruts. Regarding this, some hold that it should be done immediately after the casting [of the oblation] into the fire; others say it should be at the end of the consecration formula (*anumantraṇa*); and others maintain it should be after the ritual re-stepping back (*pratyākramaṇa*). However, because of the suffix *-ktvā* in the word "having sacrificed" (*iṣṭvā*), it is logical that it occurs immediately after the casting. Since it is not mentioned in the collection of mantras (*mantrasamāmnāya*) nor in the *sūtra*, the recitation of the verse to the Maruts is considered optional (*kṛtākṛtam*).

Regarding the phrase *sā pa maruto yaddhava*, it has been stated by Baudhāyana that the recitation of the *mārutī* (verse to the Maruts) is to be performed by the Adhvaryu priest due to the force of the *samārūpa* (the act of mounting the fire). Here, the ritual properties (*dharma*) pertaining to the *āditya-varuṇa* (the vessel for the Ādityas and Varuṇa) do not apply, because there is no scriptural authority (*prāpaka*) for them. The term *sthālī* refers to the sacrificial cooking-pot (*carusthālī*). *Niṣkāsa* is the residue adhering to the pot and the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*). The *mekṣaṇa* is a ladle used for stirring. Because the *niṣkāsa* is mentioned as a distinct entity, one sets it aside in a known place, such as a sling (*śikya*), having separated it from the pot.

In this manner, both the pot and the stirring-spoon are to be set down in their designated places. From the very mention of "setting down" (nidhāna), it is understood that the stirring-spoon is not to be cast into the fire; rather, by the force of the term "setting down," it is understood that there is a complete disposal (*pratipatti*) for the entire remainder of the oblation—from the *viṣṭakṛt* offering up to the fourfold division—rather than just for one part. Otherwise, the text would have simply stated: "He sets down the pot and the stirring-spoon containing the remainder of the *caru*."

Therefore, only a mere smear (lepa) should be set aside; for everything other than that, all the *sviṣṭakṛt* offerings and so forth must be performed as their respective disposal rites (*pratipatti*). According to the view of some, there is an exclusion of the *praśitra* because it is not a new offering (*apūrva*); they hold that the *praśitra* is itself a disposal rite. On this view, the *praśitra* indeed remains. The Brahman priest also consumes the portion belonging to the Brahman from the fourfold division (*cāturdhākaraṇika*) together with him [the Adhvaryu]. Or rather, since the sacrifice ends with the *śaṃyuvāka*, it may be at the conclusion of the *śaṃyuvāka*.

This [procedure] applies to the case where the remaining acts of disposal (*pratipatti-karman*) are not performed. However, in the case where they are performed, the placing [of the remnants] occurs either at the point in the sequence where they would naturally fall, or at the time of the final dismissal (*utsarga*). By this, the act of abandonment (*tyāga*) is excluded. The word "and" (*ca*) signifies simultaneity; therefore, the placing of the three [remnants] occurs in one single location.
He performs the disposal of the remnant of the *dhruvā* vessel.
This is to be explained as before, and the purpose is also as before.
"Ending with the Śamyu-formula, or complete.

The word "becomes" (bhavati) is understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. It becomes complete; it does not cause the sacrificer to incur sin. If, by the mere mention of "ending with the Śamyu," the optional nature of the rite were already established, then the explicit statement "ending with the Śamyu" is for the purpose of indicating that this particular method is a novel (apūrva) procedure specifically for the Śamyu-ending option, and not for the other option. Therefore, from the time of the Anvādhāna (the adding of fuel) onwards, the entire ritual action is performed, and there is no cessation at the mere point of ending with the Śamyu.

If the *śaṅkha* and *iḍā* were the limits [of the *anuyāja*s], there would be an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the subsequent ones; furthermore, the prohibition of the wife’s *anuyāja* would be rendered meaningless. Alternatively, it might be a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) because the ritual action is not explicitly stated in the text (*aśābdatvāt*). Since this conforms to the logic of Jaimini and is consistent with one's own *śākhā*, the former position is primary, while the latter is weak. That principle is established in the seventh section (*pāda*) of the tenth chapter (*adhyāya*).

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: since the prohibition of the subsequent rites is already established by the very injunction of the Śāṇḍilī-antah-svavidhi, the further prohibition of both [the Patnīsaṃyāja and the Anuyājas]—which would have been established by that alone—would be redundant and purposeless. Therefore, one must necessarily say that the prohibition of both is intended to prescribe the performance of other auxiliary parts (aṅgas) by way of negating their non-performance; that is, "one should not perform only the Patnīsaṃyājas, but one should certainly perform the others."

One should not perform only the *anūyāja* offerings, but rather one must certainly perform the others as well. Therefore, because the injunction for the complete conclusion (*saṃsthā*) is established by the non-prohibition of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, and because that same conclusion is established by the statement ending with the *śaṃyu-ṛk* and the *iḍā*, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) between these two conclusions due to their mutual contradiction; such is the meaning of the preceding sūtra. The meaning of the subsequent sūtra, however, is that it is a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*) for the sake of establishing the permanence of the injunction ending with the *śaṃyu-ṛk* and the *iḍā*; this very injunction is permanent, not the entire conclusion.

Therefore, since this very procedure is praised, this restatement for the sake of praise is a *nityānuvāda* (an obligatory restatement). The word "or" (*vā*) serves to exclude the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). A *nityānuvāda* is a prohibition; it does not, however, enjoin the entire ritual action other than the *patnīsaṃyāja* and the *anūyāja*. Why? Because the ritual action—namely, the action other than the *patnīsaṃyāja* and *anūyāja*—is non-verbal (*aśābda*), as it is not conveyed by a verbal injunction (*vidhi*); being non-verbal, its state of being so is its "non-verbal-ness," and it is on that account [that it is not enjoined].

In the case of the view that the sacrifice is completed as a whole (*kṛtsnasaṃsthā*), there is no explicit injunction by which an option could be stated. Since it is logically appropriate to regard [the statement] as a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*), it is improper to assume that it culminates in an injunction. Thus, according to the position that the sacrifice is concluded [early], there is no option regarding the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. Accordingly, Āpastamba states: "The sacrifice should be concluded with the *śaṃyu* formula, or one should not perform the *patnīsaṃyājas*; however, one should perform them at the *udayanīya* [concluding] offering, or both should be performed together. The meaning of "both together" is that both [the main sacrifice and the *udayanīya*] should include the *patnīsaṃyājas*.

[Objection: But surely, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there are two *śaṃyu*-formulas: one before the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings and another after them. In that case, the injunction regarding the conclusion [of the ritual] by means of the latter *śaṃyu*-formula alone would suffice. Furthermore, in this way, the prohibition of the *patnīsaṃyāja* found in another recension (*śākhāntara*) becomes meaningful; otherwise, it would result in being a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Therefore, the entire procedure involving the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings must be performed ending with the latter *śaṃyu*-formula. [Response: This is not so.

Since the cessation of the performance is prescribed specifically upon the occurrence of the *śaṃyu* as the cause, and since that cause has already arisen even when the preceding *śaṃyu* has been performed, it is logical that the cessation should take place right there. As for the prohibition of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, it is not contradictory; being a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*), it serves merely as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) intended, by its very propriety, to extol another instance of the *śaṃyu*.

And thus, Jaimini states in the tenth chapter, sixth section: "Because the prohibition is purposeful, the prohibition of the latter [should occur] after [the *śamyu*]; or rather, because of the attainment [of the former], there should be a transgression [of the rule] due to the statement regarding the former. The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: since the prohibition of the *patnīsaṃyāja* and *anūyāja* offerings is purposeful, the performance of the subsequent *śamyu* and *iḍā* offerings should take place after that; thus, there would be a prohibition of those [latter offerings]. Consequently, this is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the prohibition, but rather it serves to indicate the necessity of performing the other [remaining rites].

Thus, this section (adhikaraṇa) is an objection raised against the conclusion (siddhānta) of the preceding section; such is the meaning of the previous sūtra. The meaning of the subsequent sūtra, however, is that there would be a clear deviation from the previously established rule because of an explicit statement. Since there is no statement authorizing the abandonment of what is already present, one should conclude at the previous point. — 622. According to the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha:
"If the ritual ends with the *śaṃyu* formula, one does not cut off a portion for the sacrificer (*yajamāna-bhāga*)."

That which has *śaṃyu* as its end is called *śaṃyvantā*. The reading *śaṃyuvantā* is simply a corruption. Since the prohibition [of the sacrificer’s portion] is already established by the rule, "In all Soma-related *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices, one does not consume the sacrificer’s portion," this statement is intended to indicate that the prohibition of the entire sacrificer’s portion does not apply here. By this, it is understood that the sacrificer’s portion exists in its entirety. Because another duty is prescribed for the remainder of the *dhruvā* vessel immediately thereafter, there is no *samiṣṭayajus* even in the case where the sacrifice is concluded (*saṃsthāpya*).

And there is no release of the sacrifice (*yajñavimoka*). In the case of the *saṃsthāpana* (concluding) option, there is no swelling (*āpyāyana*) of the vessels for the final expiation and the drawing of the *amṛta* portion; however, the swelling does indeed take place during the two libations for the *sviṣṭakṛt*. With the exception of the giving of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), everything else up to the feeding of the Brahmins takes place.
Regarding this, some teachers prescribe the pouring out of the King Soma (*rājño nivapana*).

The meaning is that the ritual actions previously mentioned—beginning from "the pouring out of the King Soma in the region of the northern altar" (*uttaravedideśa*) up to the end of the *praiṣas*—should not be performed there [at the original time], but rather should be performed at this present time; so say some teachers.

Having taken four or five spoonfuls from the *dhruva* vessel, he ties a piece of gold with a *niṣṭarkya* knot using a blade of *darbha* grass and places it into the clarified butter, reciting: "This is your bright body."

Some maintain that this is a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*), such that for one who performs the four-fold cutting (*catur-avattin*) there is a fourfold taking (*catur-gṛhīta*), and for one who performs the five-fold cutting (*pañca-avattin*) there is a fivefold taking (*pañca-gṛhīta*). The replenishing of the *dhruvā* vessel is as in the original ritual. Regarding the *niṣṭakya*: having tied gold in the shape of a ring with a blade of *darbha* grass—just like the tying of a topknot—one places it into the clarified butter (*ājya*) held in the *juhū* ladle. The meaning is that one holds that *darbha* blade by which the gold was tied, and thus causes the gold, bound by the *darbha*, to fall into the clarified butter held in the *juhū*.

The word *niṣṭakrya* is grammatically correct due to its technical derivation (*nipātana*) by the rule *niṣṭakryadevayajyāvijāmi* in the Vedic language (*chandas*). The mantra ends with the word "go" (*gaccha*). A long blade of grass devoid of flowers is called a *dī*. However, *kuśa* blades are short and possessed of flowers. According to the Vedic scripture (*śruti*), "That which is cut at a joint belongs to the gods," these *darbha* blades used in rites for the gods must be cut precisely at a joint. According to the scripture, "That which is with roots belongs to the ancestors," since the presence of roots is prescribed for rites for the ancestors, it follows that the absence of roots is required for *darbha* blades used in rites for the gods.

Regarding grass, however, it is a universal rule that one should say, "I am cutting *darbha* grass. Although there is no distinction between silver and gold as forms of *hiraṇya* (precious metal), since it is stated in passages such as "therefore, gold should be worn" that only *hiraṇya* in the form of gold is to be worn at all times, and because its purity is thus affirmed while silver is considered inauspicious due to its dull color, one should diligently avoid that which is inauspicious in rites for the gods.

Thus, because the *Smṛti* prohibits the use of silver in rites for the gods and because it is censured as being "born of tears," in all rites for the gods, only gold—which is of a beautiful color (*suvarṇa*)—is to be taken, and not silver, which is of a bad color (*durvarṇa*). In that regard, the measure of the gold is optional; this is established by the rule alone that "he places [the vessel] with it. The mention of *ājya* (clarified butter) in the *Śruti* indicates that the word *ghṛta* denotes *ājya* in general, yet it shows that it refers specifically to that *ājya* which has become solidified, as established by the *Śruti* passage: "That which was poured out became *ghṛta*. Therefore, there is no restriction regarding the state of solidity at the time of pouring.

The Soma-purchasing cow (*somakrayaṇī*) has been prepared; she is well-limbed (*samaṅgā*), auspicious (*bandhumatī*), like the one for Agni-Soma—either brown (*babhru*), reddish-brown (*aruṇā*), or ruddy (*rohiṇī*), or dappled (*upadhvastā*), or full-bodied (*prapīnā*). Alternatively, she is ruddy (*rohiṇī*), with reddish-brown eyes (*piṅgākṣī*), with brown hair (*babhru-lomnī*), appearing white-spotted (*śvitra-upakāśā*), with variegated tail-hair (*pṛśni-vālā*), and having variegated hooves (*pṛśni-śaphā*); she is either one-year-old (*ekahāyanī*), two-year-old (*dvihāyanī*), or three-year-old (*trihāyaṇī*). Looking at her while reciting "Thou art swift" (*jūrasi*), he offers this fourfold-drawn oblation (*caturgṛhīta*).

Baudhāyana says that [the ritual act] is performed when the sacrificer has taken hold [of the cow]. That cow by which Soma is purchased is the *somakrayaṇī* (Soma-purchasing cow); she is prepared (*upaklptā*). From the use of the past participle (*upakṛtā*), it is understood that the preparation must be carried out even before the commencement of the performance on that very day. She is "complete" (*samajhā*), meaning having all her limbs intact. She is "possessing kin" (*bandhumatī*); here, by the word *bandhu*, one's own mother, father, brothers, and friends are meant. Thus, the meaning is that she is accompanied by [the presence of] mother, father, brothers, and friends.

The meaning is understood through the *mantra* "May the mother approve, may the father approve, may the brother of the same womb approve, may the friend of the same herd approve," just as by the term "related to Agni and Soma" (*āgneyīya*) the qualities of stoutness and fatness are extended [to what follows], and just as by the statement "the animal is bound for Agni and Soma," the characteristics mentioned in the *Paśusūtra*—such as "the animal is not mutilated" (*akūṭa*) and so forth—are also extended [by way of *atideśa*].

The Soma-purchase cow has been prepared just as [the animal] for Agni-Soma; by this much alone, since the possession of auspicious marks (*samaṅgatva*) and the possession of kinship (*bandhumattva*) are established, the repetition is intended to show that these two—possessing auspicious marks and possessing kinship—are strictly necessary, and not merely one or the other, nor [specific qualities like] stoutness or fatness. As for the black-and-white color, it is excluded precisely because of the specific injunctions regarding colors such as tawny (*babhru*) and so forth. *Babhru* means reddish-brown; *aruṇā* means tawny-colored.

*Rohiṇī satyupadhvastā* means "being *rohiṇī*, she is *upadhvastā*"; *upadhvastā* refers to a class (*varṇa*) that is overwhelmed by another color. Thus, it means she possesses such a pair of colors: in some parts she is purely *rohiṇī*, while in other parts she is of mixed color; the meaning is that she is characterized by these two colors. *Babhru-varṇā* (tawny-colored) and *aruṇa-varṇā* (reddish-colored)—meaning she possesses a pair of colors consisting of a mixture of red—any one of these three is the *somakrayaṇī* (the cow for purchasing Soma).

If *rohiṇī* and *upadhvastā* were two separate entities, it would result in the redundancy of the word *rohiṇī*; therefore, the referent is indeed a qualified entity. Nor should one suspect that this fault remains even so; for since that [word] refers to the color red alone, that fault does not apply. *Aprapīnā* means fleshy or plump. Some, however, making the word division *a-prapīnā*, explain it as "one whose lips are not swollen, having a color like flesh, and different from that [other]. The word *atha* in the middle serves to mark a change in the sequence of the sentence.

The subsequent [text] enumerates all [the options] as alternatives (*vikalpa*). Regarding this, Āpastamba states a specific rule: "For a Kṣatriya, [the cow] is of two forms. A cow of two forms is one that is both white and black. [This is because] it was stated previously regarding those very two colors: "If one were to purchase [the Soma] with a white [cow], the sacrificer would become leprous; if with a black [cow], the sacrificer would die. The specific details for the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice and others will be stated later. A *rohiṇī* is one of exclusively red color. A *piṅgākṣī* is one with tawny eyes.

"Babhru-lomnī" means one whose hair has grown tawny-colored, or one who is possessed here and there of body-hair of various types. "Śvitropakāśā" means having a color similar to *śvitra*—*śvitra* being a variegated skin disease (leucoderma). "Pṛśnivālā" refers to one whose eyelashes are white-spotted. "Pṛśniśaphā" means one whose hooves are white-spotted. "Ekahāyanī" is one that is one year old; likewise for "dvihāyanī" and "trihāyaṇī"—here the word *hāyana* denotes a year, meaning one-year-old, two-year-old, or three-year-old respectively.

By the rule *dāmahāyanāntāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.27), the suffix *kīp* is applied. Regarding the form *trihāyaṇī*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* in the word *hāyana* after the words *tri* and *catur* must be stated; thus, there is the substitution of *ṇ*. Since this denotes age (*vayovācakatvāt*), the presence of *ṇ* is indeed appropriate here. Furthermore, this [application of the suffix], such as in *ekahāyanī* and so forth, should be understood as common to all [such cases]. Now, it should not be argued that in the passage "He purchases Soma with a ruddy, one-year-old cow" (*aruṇayā ekahāyanyā somam krīṇāti*), because the quality of redness (*aruṇaguṇa*) is incorporeal (*amūrta*), it cannot serve as a means for the purchase; therefore, it must reside in all the substances used for the purchase, such as the cloth (*vāsaḥ*) and others. This is not to be said.

For even that which is formless can function as a means by way of delimiting a substance; and since there is a requirement for such a medium, the Mīmāṃsakas accept that it must be applied to the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) itself, by postulating its connection with the *ekahāyanī* mentioned in its own sentence. Thus, Jaimini states in the first pāda of the third adhyāya: "In the case of a single purpose, there would be a restriction of substance and quality to one [action]. The meaning of the sūtra is that when there is a single purpose, [the application] is prompted by that.

Since there is syntactic unity (*kavākyatva*) between the substance and the quality, because they both serve the purpose of a single action—namely, the purchase of Soma—there must be a mutual connection (*parasparānvaya*) as a rule. While looking at that cow used for the purchase of Soma, he offers the previously drawn fourfold oblation (*caturgṛhīta*) with the mantra "Behold [her], O cow. By the use of the present participle "looking" (*īkṣamāṇaḥ*), the simultaneity of the looking and the offering is established. The cow used for the purchase of Soma should stand facing eastward inside the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, in front of the *āhavanīya* fire.

Because it would be impossible for one standing outside to see [the fire] if it were enclosed on all sides with only one or two doors, it must be placed within the *prāgvaṃśa* hall. Since both [the fire and the fuel] are enjoined by the specific singular expression "this is the fourfold-drawn [offering]," it is understood that wherever there is an injunction for the application of the fourfold-drawn [offering] preceded by this word, the rule for the fivefold-drawn [offering] is an option.

According to the maxim that "fifty is contained within a hundred," since the number four is included within the number five, that [offering] is indeed a *caturgṛhīta-homa* (an offering of four ladlings). One should not argue that there is no loss of the number four even when a higher number is included, based on the maxim that "what has entered as an addition is not a subtraction"; for it must be said that there is no over-extension of this principle to cases such as six ladlings, because the number four is still present within them as well.

This is because, by virtue of the equality between the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) connected to the *caturgṛhīta* offering—namely, "Animals have four feet; he wins animals; there are four quarters; he finds firm footing in the quarters"—and the explanatory passage connected to the number five found in both sentences—namely, "There is a fivefold [offering]; for animals are fivefold; he sacrifices to five deities; he finds firm footing in the five quarters"—the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of the rule] to numbers such as six is prevented due to the absence of that [fivefold connection].

The exclusion of a lower number, however, is established simply by the absence of the inclusion of the number four. Therefore, this is proven: in the injunction regarding the application of the "four-drawn" (*caturgṛhīta*) preceded by the word *etat* (this), the "five-drawn" (*pañcagṛhīta*) is indeed an option; thus, the injunction for the oblation with the "four-drawn" is also established by that [option]. Nor should it be argued that the mention of the "four-drawn" is intended solely for the purpose of excluding gold.

However, since that [exclusion of gold] is already established by the injunction itself—namely, "he draws [the butter] from the ghee"—it is impossible for this [text] to serve the purpose of excluding it; furthermore, it would follow that the mention of "five-fold drawing" (pañcagṛhīta) would have to be performed just like the mention of "four-fold drawing" (caturgṛhīta).
Having taken another four-fold portion, he draws the gold out from the ghee with the mantra: "Thou art light, thou art immortality."

The word *apām* (they took) is for the purpose of connecting with what precedes; therefore, this [offering] must also be offered from the remainder of the *dhruvā* vessel alone. If only the word *aparam* (the other) were stated, there would be the possibility of taking five portions (*pañca-gṛhīta*) even in certain cases; to prevent that, the term *catur-gr̥hītaka* (four-portioned) is used. The first two [actions] are the replenishing of the *dhruvā* and the completion of the *dhruvā*. The mention of *ghr̥ta* (clarified butter) is intended to indicate the state of being liquid in the other [substances]. The word *ghr̥ta* is derived from the root *ghr̥*, meaning "to flow" or "to shine," with the suffix *kta* according to the *uṇādi-sūtra* rule *ani-vṛṣi-bhyaḥ ktaḥ*.
By this, it is also possible to establish that clarified butter (ghṛta) possesses the status of an ablative (apādāna).
He consecrates it with the mantra, "The oblation for the Viśvedevas.

The remainder [of the mantra] refers only to the clarified butter (ājya), and not to gold, because of the hearing of the word "oblation" (havis) in the mantra; this is made explicit by Āpastamba, and because it is designated as such—[End of Second Paṭala]. [This is] accompanied by the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.
With the mantra, "Thou art the oblation for the Viśvedevas," he gazes [at the clarified butter].

The meaning is that he gazes while remaining bowed down. Here too, "the clarified butter" (*ājyam*) is the understood object, because of the mention of "oblation" (*haviḥ*) in the mantra. Up to this point, he remains seated.
With the mantra, "I have ascended the eye of Sūrya," he worships the sun with his hand holding gold. || 5 ||

"With gold" (*sahiraṇyena*) is an adjective qualifying the hand (*pāṇi*). The instrumental case in "with the hand" (*pāṇinā*) is used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, gold must necessarily already be in the hand beforehand.
One should keep the hand not empty, [filling it] with gold, silver, or *kuśa* grass.

Thus, by means of this Smṛti, the wearing of gold on the fingers is enjoined as a purificatory act at all times; therefore, the wearing of gold on the palm of the hand—which is distinct from that—is enjoined by this [text] as something previously unestablished (*apūrva*). Alternatively, it may be that the very wearing of gold on the fingers already established by Smṛti is here enjoined as being for the sake of a specific ritual action (*karma*). Consequently, even the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed in the Śruti must be performed. Furthermore, by the wearing of gold on the fingers, there is indeed the wearing of gold on the hand, because the fingers are also part of the hand.

Otherwise, one would have to make the hand non-empty with gold, silver, and *kuśa* grass; for by enjoining the connection of the hand with gold, silver, and *kuśa*, it would follow—contrary to the *Smṛti*—that wearing them on the fingers is prohibited, since the fingers are distinct from the hand. Indeed, the words "hand" (*kara*) and "palm" (*pāṇi*) are synonyms. Furthermore, regarding the rite of *upasthāna*, there may be either standing or sitting. Nor should it be argued that the state of standing is established solely from the word "he stands near" (*upatiṣṭhate*).

Because the Ātmanepada ending is prescribed by the rule *upānmantrakaraṇe* (Pāṇini 1.3.25), the meaning of the root *sthā* and its suffix here is not merely "standing," but rather a request for a blessing with humility, preceded by the joining of the palms (*añjali*) and the employment of a mantra. As it has been said: "One who has established the sacred fires approaches the fire for a blessing. Therefore, the state of "standing" (*tiṣṭhattā*) is indeed distinct from the act of approaching (*upasthāna*).

If the state of standing were inherent within the act of *upasthāna* (worship) itself, then in such injunctions as "standing, she worships the *gārhapatya* fire" and "having risen after the subsequent oblation, she worships the *āhavanīya* fire by way of the *kavātiryañcī*," the specific prescriptions of standing and rising would not have been formulated. Therefore, it is established that these apply only where they are specifically prescribed; elsewhere, however, there is no fixed rule.

Thus, the meaning of the term *upasthāna* (worship/approach) is this: while meditating upon the object denoted by the mantra, joined with the *atimudrā* gesture, one should recite the mantra while praying for blessings (*āśīḥ*). Here, because of the mention of "with the hand" (*pāṇinā*), the worship is not performed with the *añjali* (joined palms), but rather with the hand alone. Furthermore, wherever the term "right" (*dakṣiṇa*) is employed, it indicates that the right limb is to be used there, whereas in other cases there is no fixed rule; this is made known by the repeated use of the word "right" in those respective instances.

In the present case, since there is no mention of the right hand, there is indeed no fixed rule. This is likewise elsewhere. And this applies to cases where a specific limb is specified; however, in cases where no limb is specified, the use of the right hand alone is mandatory. The proof for this is found in the *Yājuṣa-darśapūrṇamāsa-hautra-sūtra*: because of the subsequent sūtra, "He breathes in silently with the left hand," the right hand is obtained in the preceding [sūtra]; thus, the mention of the right hand indicates that in an unspecified location, the right hand alone must be used. The mantra ends with *vipaścita*. With the words *cidasī*, he instructs the *somakrayaṇī* (the cow for purchasing Soma).

Remaining seated. The word "sam" (together) indicates the clear pronunciation of the mantra; by this, the state of being whispered (*upāṃśutā*) is excluded. *Saṃśāsana* is the recitation of the mantra characterized by looking [at the object]. Since instruction, which is what is expressed by *saṃśāsana*, is possible only for the wife, she alone would be understood [as the recipient]; therefore, the expression "the Soma-purchasing cow" (*somakrayaṇīm*) is used in order to exclude her.

[Objection: "In that case, since it is possible to refer to her by the word *tām* (her) when instructing her, what is the purpose of the explicit statement 'the Soma-purchasing cow' (*somakrayaṇīm*)? [Response: True; however, because one must necessarily accept that the word *tad* denotes only what is already well-known (*prasiddha*), the aforementioned defect remains unavoidable.

He binds her by the right front foot with the mantra, "May Mitra bind you by the foot. He remains seated throughout. The term "Soma-purchasing cow" (*somakrayaṇīm*) is carried over from the preceding [sūtra]. The mention of "foot" (*pāda*) is for the purpose of excluding the head (*proh*). The mantra consists of this much alone.
With the words, "May Pūṣan protect the paths," he leads her to where the Soma is—whether it be unbound and not held by the ear, or bound and held by the ear.

With the mantra "Pūṣan, protect from injury," he leads [the cow]—either unbound and not held by the ear, or bound and held by the ear—to where the Soma is; this is the syntactical connection. Here too, the term "Soma-purchasing cow" (somakrayaṇī) is understood to carry over. The words "unbound," etc., are qualifiers of the Soma-purchasing cow. In the phrase "where the Soma is," the ellipsis is "he becomes deposited. The option of "unbound and not held by the ear" belongs to one's own Śākhā; the option of "bound and held by the ear" belongs to another Śākhā.

"If it were not bound at the foot, it would be uncontrolled; if it were bound at the foot, it would be controlled. If it were not bound at the foot, it would be uncontrolled; if it were bound at the foot, the *anustaraṇī* cow would be subject to death, and the sacrificer would be short-lived. If it were held by the ear, one [animal] would overcome the other, or the other would overcome it. 'I bind you with the non-mantric [formula],' he says. Mitra is indeed the auspicious one among the gods; by him alone he binds her at the foot. In the Śruti, by the statement "if it were not bound at the foot, it would be uncontrolled," the binding is established. And that [binding] is the binding at the foot.

It concludes with the matter of binding the neck. "Unrestrained" (ayatā) means uncontrolled in movement. "Like a sacrificial cow" (anustaraṇī) refers to the cow associated with the deceased. "Prone to die soon" (pramāyukaḥ) means one who dies quickly. "Vārcana" means a slayer of enemies; alternatively, it refers to a rope bound even around the neck. This lack of restraint, however, must be ensured by holding [the head] firmly with both hands. "Bound" (baddhāṃ) means tied around the neck. As for binding at the feet, it is forbidden in both cases.

By the mere recitation of the mantra, the binding of the foot by a friend (*mitra*) occurs; thus, there is no lack of auspiciousness for the friend, nor does the sacrificer incur the shortness of life resulting from that [binding]. For that defect exists only when the binding is performed by oneself. To clearly demonstrate this meaning, the entire reading is given as "May Mitra bind thy foot. The subsequent mantra ends with "To Indra, the Soma.
With the mantras beginning "Thou art Vasvi," she steps forward six steps with her right forefoot.

Here too, since the cow for the purchase of Soma (*somakrayaṇī*) is already obtained through the recurrence of that very term, the purpose of the word "she" (*sā*)—which refers to her being instructed, bound, or led—is not fulfilled by the expiation when the *anunikramaṇa* (following) is performed out of forgetfulness after one of those acts has been omitted; rather, its purpose is to indicate that after what was omitted has been performed, the *anunikramaṇa* must be performed again for a distance of six steps. Nor is its purpose the exclusion of the Adhvaryu, since that is already established by the feminine gender and the word "she" (*sā*). Nor is its purpose the exclusion of the wife (*patnī*), because she follows [the sacrificer] immediately after.

Since [the act] is already established by its very presence, the absence of [any other] requirement is self-evident. For her, as she is being led northward, there are six mantras beginning with "vasyasī" and ending with "asthāt. The expression "with these" (etaiḥ) is intended to exclude the possibility that only a single mantra, taken as a mere pratīka (opening phrase), should be used. The expression "with each" (mauḥ) is intended to indicate that the stepping is performed one by one with each mantra.

*Anukrāmati* means he steps along in sequence; it means he restrains himself and moves, or he desires [to move]. Here, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is understood internally. Alternatively, the essential meaning is that the Adhvaryu follows closely behind those six steps which are stepped by her right forefoot; he "steps after" or "steps upon" them, placing his foot directly over each one. Because of the context, it is the right foot alone that is intended here. In this interpretation, the causative suffix (*ṇi*) is to be heard [as implied]. In this case, both the sacrificer and the wife also proceed.

The sacrificer follows the *adhvaryu*, and the wife follows him. Thus says Baudhāyana: "The sacrificer follows behind, and the wife follows behind, taking the vessel and the *paddharaṇī*"; the word "goes" is to be supplied in both cases. For the *paddharaṇī* is that by which the footprint (*pada*) is carried; the meaning is that she goes while taking that vessel. Furthermore, he says: "Then they cause this Soma-purchase cow to pass northward beyond the sacrificial hall. He takes hold of the seventh footprint with [the mantra]: "May Bṛhaspati make you rejoice in happiness."

The taking of the seventh step is performed silently, as no mantra is prescribed for it. "He covers" means he conceals [the earth]; the words "with his joined palms" (*añjalinā*) are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence], because this is seen in the archetype (*prakṛti*) and because Āpastamba has stated it explicitly. By this, covering with a cloth is excluded. "In the three worlds" (*cikevi*) is the end of the mantra. Having placed gold upon that [spot], he offers the fourfold-drawn ghee (*caturgṛhīta*) with the mantra: "I sprinkle thee on the head of the Earth."

Here too, as before, there is an option regarding the "five-fold ladling" (*pañcagṛhīta*). Having placed gold upon that footprint, he offers four-fold ladled butter over the gold with the mantra, "Of the earth... Some say there is no circumambulation because it is a remnant of the *iṣṭi* materials. The mantra ends with "To the one possessing ghee, svāhā! Regarding this, Baudhāyana says at the end of the ritual: "What deity indeed belongs to the offering of the footprint? Starting from that point, some say it belongs to Agni, some to Viṣṇu, some to Prajāpati, but one should simply say it belongs to Vāk (Speech).

Therefore, some hold that because of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "The Soma-purchasing cow is indeed the goddess of speech (*vāgdevatā*)," the ritual relinquishment (*tyāga*) is made with the formula, "This [belongs] to Vāk, the Soma-purchasing cow. The oblation (*homa*) is to be offered directly upon the gold, according to the scriptural injunction (*śruti*): "In that the Adhvaryu [offers] where there is no fire... In the event of the loss of the remainder of the *dhruvā*-ladle, one should take it up again with the *dhruva*-mantras as before, and perform the oblation with the mantra, "Thou art refreshing (*nūrasī*)."

If, through error, the *āpyāyana* (invigoration) is performed twice—either at the two instances of the *abhighāraṇa* for the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering, or at the two instances of taking portions for the final expiatory oblation (*prāyaścittāhuti*)—then one should offer with that very [portion]. In both cases, there is also the *sarvaprāyaścitta* oblation and the recitation (*japa*) of the *anājñāta* verses and so forth. If, while a cow characterized by qualities such as being one-year-old is being led away for the purpose of purchase, by chance her seventh step falls on a barren spot (*āvani*), then because the oblation is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), it should be performed even on the barren spot itself.

The anointing of the dice, however, must be performed by anyone with whatever dust is available; for when a secondary quality (*guṇa*) is omitted, it is impossible for the primary act (*mukhya*) to be omitted. Nor should it be argued that there should simply be an omission, as in the case of the pouring-out sacrifice (*vājinayāga*); because this [act of anointing] does not depend on materials provided by another, an omission cannot be asserted. The pouring-out sacrifice, by contrast, depends on materials provided by another.

In this case, however, it is not the substance itself that is prompted by another; rather, it is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the substance in the form of dust—consisting of the placing of the one-year-old cow at the seventh step—that is thus prompted by another. Because of this disparity, its omission here is indeed appropriate. And so Jaimini states in the first quarter of the fourth chapter: "The act of stepping is not the motive for the leading [of the cow], because it serves another purpose."

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: "The act regarding the foot [is] 'he takes up the seventh foot,' and so forth. This act of leading does not serve as the motivator for the leading of the *soma-krayaṇī* (the cow used for purchasing Soma), because it is for another purpose—that is, because its purpose is something else. Since its purpose is different, it is "for another purpose. Nor can it be argued that, because in another recensional text (*śākhā*) there is the hearing of the words "her seventh foot," and because there the word "her" refers back to the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), the leading must be for the sake of taking up the seventh foot of the *ekahāyanī*; for in that case, there would be a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*). Thus, the leading [is not for that purpose].

It should not be argued that even the *syona* (the sacrificial bed) is merely a motivator (*prayojaka*). For even in that case, the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) is not introduced by its own form, but rather as being for the purpose of purchase—specifically through the statement "he purchases [it] with a one-year-old cow"—and thus it is employed only when its use has already been determined by another factor. Therefore, the lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) remains unestablished.

Thus, this is the distilled meaning: regarding that one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) which is led for the sake of accomplishing the purchase (*kraya*), [the text] says, "He takes her seventh step. Although there is a connection with the taking of dust merely by way of being an incidental benefit (*prasaṅga*) to the cow—one who is present in the mind as the object of the purchase—the sentence concerning the seventh step is self-sufficient (*nirākāṅkṣa*). Consequently, because there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to indicate that it has that [dust-taking] as its purpose, the one-year-old cow belongs to the purchase; she does not belong to the taking of dust from the footprint.

Having taken up gold, he traces around the footprint with the wooden sword (*sphya*) while reciting, "Traced around is the gold," as far as the ghee has spread; then, having silently traced it around with the horn, he pours the footprint [dust] into the pot while reciting, "In us be wealth."

"Having taken up" means having grasped. The *sphya* is either made of *iṣṭakā* (brick) or common (worldly). He draws around the footprint—that is, the area connected with the foot. The meaning is that he draws around it, taking as his mark a footprint exactly as large as may sometimes have been spread or extended with clarified butter either outside or inside the area of the footprint; by this, drawing around an area merely the size of the footprint itself is excluded. Moving clockwise is established by the general rule (*paribhāṣā*).

The commencement is from the east, and likewise the completion. "He traces around three times," so says Āpastamba. In this view, it should be understood that the mantra is used once and [the action] is performed twice silently. The taking up of the wooden sword (*sphya*) for the purpose of tracing is done silently, because no mantra is prescribed. However, Āpastamba states that the taking up is with the *Sāvitra* mantra; its full extent is the mantra beginning with "May his neck-cords cut the waters. [The tracing is done] with the horn belonging to the sacrificer—that is, with the black antelope horn—because that alone is present at hand.

The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of drawing forward [the phrase] "until it has been extended along the cord"; thus, it is established that here too the tracing is neither less nor more than that. Alternatively, it serves to indicate the conjunction of the black antelope horn with the wooden sword (*sphya*); by this, it is established that the tracing is performed with both joined together. Since the mantra would also be obtained from the preceding rule, the expression "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*) is stated to exclude it.

The word *sthālī* denotes a vessel made either of metal or clay, characterized by a specific shape. By this, other vessels as well as the act of pouring onto the ground are excluded. *Pada* means the foot-dust. Since the context has already begun with "he pours into the *sthālī*," the mention of *pada* (foot-dust) serves to obtain that specific substance; it is for the purpose of excluding the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*). [Objection: But surely this is accomplished by the pronoun *etat* (this) alone; for what purpose is the mention of *pada*? [Response: It is not so. *Note on the Sanskrit:* The text provided contains a fragmentary discussion regarding the ritual procedure involving the *sthālī* (pot) and the *pada* (foot-dust). The commentary clarifies the specific meaning of these terms within the ritual context and addresses a potential objection concerning redundancy. The phrase "sa. ma. 'taccha|" appears to be a scribal or editorial marker indicating the end of a section or a reference to a specific rule or commentary. I have translated the core explanatory portion. The final fragment is left as is, as its full meaning is unclear without further context.

If it is asked [why this is so], then it should be understood that the mention of that [the foot] is for the purpose of excluding its association with the black antelope horn (kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā). According to the scriptural statement "as much as is held" (yāvad dhṛtam), the meaning should be understood as "as much as is grasped.
Having washed his hands along with the gold at the place of the footprint, he gives the footprint to the sacrificer with the mantra, "Thine be wealth" (tve rāyaḥ).

"At the foot-print" means at the place of the foot-print. The inclusion of the term "foot-print" (*āyatana*) is intended to exclude the washing of hands when the foot-print has been placed in the cooking pot. "Together with gold" means accompanied by gold; by this, it is understood that the gold itself is also washed. By this [rule] regarding the washing of the hands, it is known that the foot-print dust must be poured directly from the hand into the vessel, and not brought into another vessel using a *sphya* (sacrificial wooden sword) and then poured from that.

And thus, this gold has a visible purpose because it is smeared with clarified butter; the washing of the gold is performed only by means of the hands, as indicated by the statement "the two together with the gold.

The phrase "to thee, O wealth" (*tote rāya*) is for the sake of the sacrificer’s wife—the word "gives" (*prayacchati*) is to be supplied. However, if there are multiple wives, he gives it to the principal wife (*mahiṣī*) alone, because it is intended for depositing and because it is not a purificatory rite (*asaṃskārakarma*). The mention in the *Ādhvaryava-pūtra* is for the purpose of indicating the proper occasion.
"May I not be separated from the increase of wealth," with these words the wife awaits the cow being given;
she awaits the step as it is being given, meaning she looks at it while facing it. All [the priests] must perform the looking, because it is a preparatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*).
He causes the wife to look together with the Soma-purchasing cow, saying: "O Goddess, look together with the goddess Urvaśī."

The meaning is that he performs an action conducive to counting. This mantra serves as the instrument for that act; therefore, the mantra belongs to the Adhvaryu alone. Counting (*saṃkhyāpana*) means pointing out [the items]. In this case, even though there are many [items], counting is possible through a single performance (*tantra*). As for the singular number found in the mantra, it should not be justified as being intended to denote a single individual, because—as in the case of the *patnī-saṃyāja*—it is prohibited from modification (*ūha*) since it does not belong to the archetype (*prakṛti*). The mantra ends with the word *saṃghaśas*.

Having poured out a vessel of water with the verse "Unbend the earth," and having divided the footprint into three parts, he scatters one third into the cool ashes of the Gārhapatya fire and one third into the Āhavanīya fire.

He scatters the third portion on the ashes and the third on the Āhavanīya fire. Regarding the phrase *pade sthālyāṃ nikṣipteṣu padapāṃsuṣu*: it refers to the dust of the footprint deposited in the vessel; *udapātra* means water belonging to the vessel—that is, water contained within the vessel—or alternatively, "the water in the vessel" (*pātre udakam udapātram*). The intended meaning is exactly as before. This is a compound of the *rājadantādi* type. The substitution of *uda-* for *udaka-* occurs by the rule *udakasyodaḥ saṃjñāyām*. [The word *ninayet* is used] because of its connection with the word *pada*.

The compound *udapātram* here means a vessel filled with water and earth; this is because it is impossible to pour out (ninayana) a vessel [of water] itself. By implication (*sāmayāt*), it refers to a quantity of water sufficient for mixing with the dust of the footprints, measured by as much as will fit in such a vessel. The mantra "visṛjāhatim" is to be understood here because its indicative mark (*liṅga*) accords with the meaning of pouring out water, just as it is seen in other instances such as "unnambhaya pṛthivīm bhindhi. Thus, the mantra composed by Satyāṣāḍha in the Śrautasūtra is to be employed here.

By the rule *traidha saṃkhyāyā vidhārthe dhā*, the suffix *dhā* is applied after a numeral word when expressing a mode of action (*kriyāprakāra*). According to the rule *dviyośca dhamuñ*, the suffix *dhā* is replaced by *dhamuñ*. In the grammatical instruction (*upadeśa*), the letter *m* is designated as an *it* by the rule *anunāsika idit*; the letter *n* is designated as an *it* by the rule *halantyam*; and that *it* is elided by the rule *tasya lopaḥ*. Then, by the rule *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ*, the first vowel is subject to *vṛddhi* substitution, resulting in the form *traidham*. [The phrase] *padaṃ padapāsūn* means "a footstep, footprints."

The prefix *prati-* is used to indicate that the distribution (*vibhajana*) must be performed directly toward each recipient. The word *vi-* serves to convey the sense of division. The inclusion of the term "cold" (*śīta*) is for the purpose of excluding "hot" (*uṣṇa*); the point being that since the presence of fire is impossible in hot ashes, if the term "containing water" (*sodaka*) were not added there, the penance for destroying fire (*agnyupaghāta-prāyaścitta*) would undesirably apply. In relation to one another, all [the fires] constitute the third [in the sequence]. For some, it is prohibited in the *āhavanīya* fire;
this is a prohibition found in another Vedic school (*śākhā*). According to this view, the division is twofold.

He gives the third footprint to his wife, and she deposits it in the house. That third footprint—that is, in the "houses," meaning the dwellings; the plural number is used to demonstrate that the deposit may be made within any one of these three types of halls—the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, the *patnīśālā*, or the outer hall—and not that there is a rule restricting the deposit to the *patnīśālā* alone. Alternatively, the plural is used due to the inherent nature of the word itself. This is observed in the mantra: "O houses, do not be afraid of us—you who are unanxious and unthirsting."

In this view, the placing [of the cup] occurs in the *patnīśālā* (the wife’s hall) alone, because that hall is primary due to its connection with the wife. After the third [offering] is given to the wife, the sacrificer takes it back from her and gives it to the wife again, saying either "Thine be wealth" (*tote rāyaḥ*) or "Thine be thy wealth" (*tava te rāyaḥ*). Regarding this giving, this mantra from the Sūtra is optional.

And the *Yājamāna-sūtra* will state: "He hands over the offered foot to the wife with the words *tote rāyaḥ*, or with *tava te rāyaḥ*. It should not be said that this [second formula] is merely a supplement to the first offering; for otherwise, the inclusion of both would be rendered purposeless. The sense is simply: "The foot offered by the Adhvaryu [is given] to the wife. Furthermore, the word *api* (also/even) is to be supplied after *prattam*, and the word *punaḥ* (again) is to be supplied immediately after *patnyai*.

It should be understood that the consistency with the Sūtra occurs only in this manner and not otherwise. Here, the demonstration is given according to the sequence of performance (*prayoga-saṃgati*). In the seventh chapter, everything from the tracing of the footprint up to the wife’s waiting is omitted because it pertains to the footprint; likewise, everything from the pouring out of the water-jar at the footprint up to the placing of the footprint in the house is omitted for the same reason. However, the washing of the hands with gold in the footprint-site does indeed take place, as it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).

"O lady, look at the two goddesses!"—with these words, he causes the wife to look at the *somakrayaṇī* cow; since this too lacks a connection to the [specific] foot-step, the performance indeed takes place. As for the occasion of omission, there is the offering of the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta-homa*) and the recollection of Viṣṇu with the *anājñāta* formula. When there are many wives, the offering is made only to the principal wife, because it is a consecration of the foot-step. From this point onward, there is no longer association with the wife, as there is no further purpose. For this very reason, Baudhāyana says, "They lead the wife.
Regarding the verse "I have mounted the eye of Sūrya," some authorities prescribe the worship of the Sun (*ādityopasthāna*).

The meaning is that some teachers say that the worship of the Sun (ādityopasthāna) which was prescribed previously should not be performed there, but rather it should be performed at this time. The recitation of the mantra "sūryasya cakṣurāruham" is for the purpose of excluding the performance of the subsequent worship here. [End of Second Paṭala] With the verse "api panthām agasmahi," he proceeds toward the King (Soma) by means of a cart that is enclosed, covered with a roof, and from which the front plank has been removed.

With a cart that is well-strewn with fragrant grass mats and the like, provided with a roof—meaning it is covered with a covering made of such grass—and from which old, worn-out, or previously situated wooden planks have been removed (which indicates the installation of new planks), he goes toward King Soma; that is to say, he goes facing him.

The use of the word *rājā* (king) instead of the word *soma*, by way of metaphorical identification (*rājamāvanā*), is for the purpose of approaching [the Soma] directly. Regarding the purchase of the Soma on the mountain, there is a specific scriptural statement: "Therefore, life is carried on the head from the mountain. Āpastamba also states: "They carry the purchased Soma on the head from the mountain. In this view, all actions such as the spreading of the bull's hide (*ānabūhacarma*) and so forth take place on the mountain itself, as the cart is absent. Some maintain, however, that the mantra "api panthām agasmahi" (We have entered upon the path) does indeed apply, because it denotes the act of going.

Regarding the mantra, "With which he drives away all enemies," some say there is an elision of the word *śakaṭa* (cart) from the mantra. Having gone there, one should perform worship with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Having established the cart facing north with its front toward the king, he consecrates it with the mantra, "Thou art a companion" (*amātyo 'si*), or "Thou art ours" (*āsmāko 'si*).

"By the north" (uttareṇa) means in the vicinity of the king, by means of the suffix -ena. Therefore, having enclosed it on all sides, one should make its door facing north; in this regard, it should be understood that the enclosure with mats and so forth, as well as the door, must be constructed in such a way that the cart can pass through the door once enclosed. The cart approaches the vicinity of the king specifically from the west, in accordance with its orientation toward the east. "With the front" (mukhena) refers to the forepart. By this, the act of propping [the cart] is excluded.

Regarding the phrase "having established it to the north by means of its front": since the reference to both [the king and the cart] is already established by the respective words ending in their specific case-suffixes and denoting their respective genders, the repetition of the word "the king" (*rājānam*) is for the purpose of indicating that in every instance, the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) must be performed preceded by the mental identification (*bhāvanā*) with the king. The repetition of the word "cart" (*śakaṭasya*) is for the purpose of indicating the restriction that the establishment is to be done only by means of the front of the cart and not that of a chariot (*stha*). By this, it is understood that there was also a position regarding the chariot.

The chariot has four wheels. The consecration (*abhimantryana*) belongs to the king alone and not to the cart, because the masculine gender is heard in the mantra and because Āpastamba has stated this explicitly. By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "the first word of the subsequent [mantra]," the word *graha* marks the end of the mantra. The phrase *āsmāko 'si*, which is a portion of a mantra from another recensional branch (*śākhā*), is an alternative to *amātyo 'si*; however, it is not an alternative for the entire mantra *amātyo 'si śukraste grahaḥ*, but rather only the portion *āsmāko 'si* serves as the optional substitute.

And thus, in the case of "Thy cup is bright" (*śukras te grahaḥ*), this [formula] must likewise be supplied. Alternatively, the mantra consists of only "Thou art a minister" (*amātyo 'si*), because it is complete in itself. In this view, "Thou art ours" (*āsmāko 'si*) is even more clearly limited to that much alone. According to such an interpretation, the mantra "With stalk thy stalk is joined" (*aṃśunā te aṃśuḥ pṛcyatām*) should be understood as ending with "the cup" (*grahaḥ*). Regarding the setting down of the cart, Āpastamba states the specific rule: "The cart, with its yoke harnessed, is placed facing east or north, with its front part resting on the ground.
He pours out the stalks with the formula: "With stalk thy stalk is joined."

He makes them into a single heap. "Parts" refers to the stalks; the words "on the pure ground" are to be supplied as the ellipsis, because leather is mentioned later on. If the piling together were intended to take place on the leather, he would have stated that here as well. "O Acyuta" is the end of the mantra; or "O Graha" is the end of the mantra. (Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, Seventh Praśna).

To the north of the king, having spread upon a skin a large, new linen garment—either double or quadruple in thickness—with its fringe toward the east and its border above, he measures the king with the *Aticchandas* verse, "Abhityaṃ devam," using his hand together with gold, with each finger extended one by one.

In this *Brāhmaṇa*, there is a specific rule: "If one should desire of someone, 'May he be without cattle,' one should measure [the Soma] for him from the boneless part; that indeed is unfavorable to cattle, and he becomes one without cattle. But if one should desire, 'May he be rich in cattle,' one should measure for him from the hairy part. This is indeed the form of cattle; by means of its very form, one secures cattle for him, and he becomes rich in cattle. The meaning is: on that part of the skin which is boneless, one measures the King (Soma). "From the hairy" (*lomataḥ*) means on the hairy region. The suffix *ac* is added after the word *loman* in the sense of possession, according to the rule beginning with *adarśa-ādi*.

In both cases, the locative case ending (*saptamī*) is used with the suffix *tasi*. According to the maxim that "censure does not function to censure, but rather to praise that which is to be praised," this censure of the former position is intended to proclaim the excellence of the latter position. The term *enapāt* (from the suffix *enap*) indicates proximity; thus, it means "near" or "upon. The phrase *carmaṇy āstṛte* means "on a spread skin. Here, by the general mention of "skin" (*carmaṇi*), the hide of any sacrificially pure animal may be understood. *Kṣumā* is the bark of the *atasī* plant; that which is manufactured from it is *kṣauma* (linen).

In the absence of this, a substitute such as silk (*kauśeya*) may be used, characterized by the previously mentioned features of being washed and so forth. This [substitute] must be large enough to serve as a binding for the *soma* stalks, for the purpose of obtaining the scriptural expiation (*śrauta-prāyaścitta*). There is an optional choice (*vikalpa*) between it being double or quadruple [the size], according to one's preference. Alternatively, there is a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*): it is double in the *Atirātra* and *Aptoryāma* sacrifices and in multi-day sessions (*ahargaṇa*), because of the abundance of *soma*; it is quadruple in the one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*) such as the *Agniṣṭoma*, because of the scarcity of *soma*.

In the phrase "prācīnopariṣṭādaśam," when forming a single compound, "prācīna" (eastward) is an adjective qualifying "upariṣṭādaśānām" (the upper fringes). Thus, only the upper fringes are eastward, not the lower ones; otherwise, it might be understood that the fringes facing westward (pratīcīnāḥ) are intended, and to prevent this, two words are used. On that cloth which has been spread out, the phrase "sahiraṇyena" (with gold) is to be explained as before. The term "aticchandasa" (exceeding the meter) is for the purpose of providing knowledge; in the absence of such knowledge, the expiation for a breach of the Yajus formula is the offering of "bhuvaḥ" into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.

Here, the measure by means of *ṛc* verses has been stated. As an ancillary (*aṅga*) to that, the prescription of the number "five" is to be explained. The mention of the *ṛc* verse—specifically the phrase "that which one has studied of the *ṛc*"—is for the purpose of accomplishing an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Wherever else the word "measure" (*mimīte*) is used, this same purpose should be understood. "With each one": the meaning is that he measures as much as can be grasped with each single finger extended. The word "throwing up" (*utsarga*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence], because of the Vedic text: "He measures with each one."
The meaning is that one should measure by repeatedly setting aside each preceding finger in succession, using each subsequent finger one by one. The mantra ends with "suvaḥ";
at all [fingers], one should press the thumb down. The meaning is that one should join the thumb to all the fingers at the time of measuring.

The meaning of the statement "not with that same [finger] the fifth" is as follows: if, after measuring in sequence with the four fingers beginning with the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*), one were again to adopt the sequence beginning with the little finger, there would be the abandonment of both the middle and ring fingers (*madhyamā* and *anāmikā*). In that case, a contradiction would arise with this Vedic injunction: "He measures with each [finger], omitting one."

Having measured four times in sequence with the four fingers beginning with the little finger (kaniṣṭhikā), having measured three times in sequence with the middle, ring, and little fingers, and again measuring three times in sequence with the middle, ring, and little fingers—this alone is the proper order of measurement. To adopt any other sequence, such as beginning with the thumb (tarjanī) and so forth, would result in a contradiction of the Vedic injunction: "He measures with each [finger] separately, omitting one [at a time]."

Thus, by the scriptural statement, "He measures it with that which is not exhausted (ayātayāmnī), indeed with that which is not exhausted," when the measuring is performed with each [verse] separately as it is released, the measuring is accomplished with that which is truly not exhausted; for there is no further application immediately after what has already been applied once. The intended meaning is that there will be no loss of essence (*yātayāma*)—that is, no depletion of its potency.

Alternatively, it may be in this order: the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*), the middle finger (*madhyamā*), the ring finger (*upakaniṣṭhikā*), the index finger (*tarjanī*), the ring finger (*upakaniṣṭhikā*), the index finger (*tarjanī*), the ring finger (*upakaniṣṭhikā*), and the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*). By this, it means: by the four fingers beginning with the little finger in regular order, and by the [fingers] beginning with the index finger in reverse order, [using] the ring finger and the little finger; or alternatively, by the four fingers beginning with the little finger in regular order, and by [the fingers] beginning with the index finger in reverse order, [using] the index finger and the little finger.

Alternatively, [the following sequences] are excluded: measuring with the four fingers starting from the little finger in order; again, with the four fingers starting from the little finger in order, but beginning with the index finger; and measuring with only the little finger. The meaning is that the measurement must be performed with the same finger by which the first measurement was made, so as to achieve uniformity between the first and last measurements. One measures five times with the *yajus* formula and five times silently.

If it is argued that the mention of "by means of a *yajus*" is inappropriate because the verse beginning with *abhityam* is composed in metrical feet (*pādabaddha*), that is true; however, this is not a fault. Why? Because the extension (*atideśa*) follows the *Brāhmaṇa*. Even for those *ṛks* recited in the *Yajurveda* that are employed by the *Adhvaryu*, there is the status of being a *yajus* according to the *Maitrāyaṇīya* school. Therefore, for their omission, only the expiation prescribed for a *yajus* should be performed. As for the purpose of the mention of "*ṛk*," it has already been stated previously that it is for the sake of attaining the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the study of the *ṛks*.

By this very same principle, for the *yajus* mantras located in the *Ṛgveda* that are employed in the *hautra* ritual, the expiation for an error in the *ṛc* is indeed the same. However, regarding the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) merit, according to the application of the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇānugati*), even though it is prescribed in one's own specific Veda (*svavedokta*) within the jurisdiction of that Veda, it belongs to this [same] person. But if it is a great rite such as the *Atirātra*, then bundles (*jūṭikā*) consisting of a collection of stalks characterized by three long joints must be measured out.
With the formula "To the offspring" (*prajābhyaḥ tvā*), he gathers the remaining stalks together.

Measuring ten times from the remainder, one should measure half [of that] for the King (Soma). Thus Baudhāyana says: "Measuring ten times, he measures half the limit (*velā*) for the two Kings. *Velā* means a boundary. The prefix *pari-* indicates that only those situated on all sides [of the center] remain; it signifies that only they are to be taken here. By this, it is established that when measuring ten times, only those situated in the middle are to be taken.

One gathers [the Soma] right on top; one pours in as much as is required for the King (Soma), for there is no fixed measure for these. And it is heard in scripture: "If the Soma were only as much as one measures out, it would belong to the sacrificer alone and not to the members of the assembly (*sadasyas*); saying 'May there be offspring,' he gathers it together, thereby favoring the members of the assembly. Therefore, there is an increase in the quantity to be offered in the *asaṃstha* sacrifices. Kātyāyana has stated this by means of the sūtra: "The measure is according to the purpose," which indicates an increased measure.

If the Soma were limited to exactly ten handfuls (*muṣṭi*), then it would belong only to the sacrificer and not to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) present in the assembly (*sadas*). Therefore, with the mantra "May the offspring be yours" (*prajāsyastvā*), he gathers together the remaining Soma shoots—that is to say, he unites them with the Soma measured by ten handfuls. This being so, it should be understood from the Śruti that the Adhvaryu priest has thereby shown favor to those in the assembly.

Having gathered the ends of the garment, he binds [the Soma stalks] with a linen turban (*uṣṇīṣa*) while reciting, "For the out-breath (*prāṇa*). Having gathered the ends of the garment—having properly collected them upward for the purpose of unifying the Soma shoots—he silently binds the ends of the garment, the fringes of the cloth, firmly with a linen turban, that is, with a long strip of cloth. And this is a garment suitable for wearing; for it will be stated later, at the *avabhṛtha* rite, that "the sacrificer puts on the garment worn by the Soma. Moving from left to right (*pradakṣiṇam*) is established by the general rule.
He sews [the ends] together while reciting, "For the diffused breath (*vyāna*)."

*Anuśṛnthati* means he loosens it. The meaning is that for the sake of a slight inspection, he unties it in a certain place while remaining silent; this is because no mantra is prescribed for it. Furthermore, this [loosening] is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the inspection. Nor should it be argued that since the inspection would be impossible without loosening, the matter is established by implication alone and thus the explicit statement is redundant; for there is no lack of purpose in that statement, as its function is to specifically preclude the inspection of the King while he is still bound.

Or [the text] beginning with "having given the king to the seller of Soma, he asks him" is intended to indicate that [the king] has been requested. Regarding this, Baudhāyana states the rule: "Then, having made a space above with his finger...

Having looked at [the Soma] with the formulas, "O progeny, breathe after me; O progeny, may they breathe after you," he consecrates it with these mantras: "This is your Gāyatra portion," and so forth. || 6 ||

One might raise the objection that there are two separate mantras because of this difference in meaning—wherein in the former instance the act of breathing after (*anuprāṇana*) has the people as its object, while in the latter the act of breathing after has the breaths as its agent. However, just as Jaimini established in the first pāda of the second chapter by the sūtra, "Because of the unity of meaning, it is a single sentence, provided that upon division there remains mutual expectancy" (*arthekatvādekaṃ vākyaṃ sākāṅkṣaṃ cedvibhāge syāt*), that in the mantra "bhago vām... there are multiple mantras despite the unity of meaning due to the absence of mutual expectancy; so too, in this case of the act of breathing after, [there is no such expectancy].

The entire recitation is provided here in order to dispel the doubt that there might be two separate mantras due to the presence of the word *amāvān*. As for the meaning of the sūtra—"That which has a single purpose is a single sentence, provided that it remains expectant when divided"—the word *artha* here does not denote "meaning" (*abhidheya*), but rather signifies "purpose" (*prayojana*). Thus, the sense is: "because it serves a single purpose."

One might object that since it should simply have been stated, "In some cases, it is indeed a *yajus*," the investigation into the measure of a *yajus* and the definition of a single sentence (*ekavākyalakṣaṇa*) are irrelevant. Anticipating this, [the author] maintains that the definition of a single sentence is not being stated here as something common to worldly sentences; rather, with the intention that "as much as that is one *yajus*," the word *vākya* in the Sūtra refers specifically to the *yajus*. If it is asked, "How can the words *vākya* and *yajus* have the same meaning?"—it is replied: A *yajus* is so called because it is a means for the sacrifice (*yāgasādhana*), and it is a *vākya* because it is to be spoken during the performance of the sacrifice (*yāgaprayoga*).

And thus, the fact that the word "yajus" and the word "sentence" (vākya) have the same meaning is established. Consequently, the sense is that this [definition] also culminates in being a means for the sacrifice. By the very phrase "because it must be spoken," the practical purpose is also indicated: as long as there is one *yajus*, it must be employed at the time of performance in its entirety, and not merely a portion of it. And so, for the sake of indicating that very purpose, the word "yajus" is used in the Sūtra. [End of Second Paṭala]. [This is] accompanied by the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

It should be understood that there is no lack of skill on the part of the author of the Sūtras in employing the word *vākya* when *prayoga* (usage) should have been used. Since [formulas] such as "O two of you, divide the sacrificial cake" (*mago vāṃ vibhajastha*) possess a single purpose—namely, the manifestation of the manner of dividing the sacrificial cake—they would otherwise be considered a single *yajus*; it is for the sake of excluding this that [the definition specifies] "when there is a division, there is expectancy."
