In that case, the entire mantra beginning with "I prepare a pleasant seat for thee" (*syonaṃ te sadanaṃ karomi*) would constitute a single injunction; however, because of the force of the word "in it" (*tasmin sīda*), there is a mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) when separated, and thus they share a single purpose. In this regard, the purpose of the preceding portion is the manifestation of the preparation of the seat, while the purpose of the subsequent portion is the cognition of the act of placing [the oblation]; therefore, there is no over-extension of the principle. In the phrase "having looked down" (*avekṣya*), the word "Soma" is to be supplied as the object. The meaning of "having looked down" (*avekṣya*) is "having bent down and inspected from above."

The word "with these" (*etair*) is intended to exclude the optionality of the remaining formulas, such as "this is yours, [O brick], belonging to the *triṣṭubh*," and so forth. The word "with mantras" (*mantraiḥ*) is used so that the phrase "belonging to the *triṣṭubh*" may be understood as an elided continuation (*anuṣaṅga*) for what follows, and the phrase "belonging to the *jagatī*" may be understood as an elided continuation for what precedes. The preceding elision consists of two words; the subsequent elision consists of five words.

And thus the recitation of the mantras occurs as follows: "This is your Gāyatrī portion; speak this for my sake to Soma," "This is your Triṣṭubh portion; speak this for my sake to Soma," "This is your Jagatī portion; speak this for my sake to Soma," and "Go to the sovereignty of the Chandomas; speak this for my sake to Soma. Baudhāyana also says likewise in his Kalpasūtra: "This is your Triṣṭubh [and] Jagatī portion; speak this for my sake to Soma"—or else there is only one mantra.

Because there is no statement regarding *anuṣaṅga* (the supplying of an ellipsis). It should not be argued that—just as in the case of the mantra "O Gāyatrī metre, be born after me," where even though there is no explicit statement of *anuṣaṅga* in the passage "from here upwards he churns as he pleases turning to the right"—there is nevertheless an *anuṣaṅga*, so it should be here as well; for this illustration is inconsistent and therefore irrelevant. To explain: in the case of the churning, in the mantra "O Triṣṭubh [metre]," the *anuṣaṅga* is established because, without it, a plurality of mantras would be impossible, which would result in the plural number being inapplicable.

In the present context, regarding the term *triṣṭubham*, the plural number is indeed appropriate even without an ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*). In this ritual procedure (*kalpa*), the mention of the mantras (*mantragrahaṇa*) should be understood as intended to effect a separation between each mantra. Since the act of consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) lacks the character of an external physical action, there would be no contradiction whatsoever in reciting the mantras without interruption; thus, the mention of the mantras here is precisely appropriate to prevent such uninterrupted recitation. Bodhāyana also states this triad of mantras in the *Dvaidhasūtra*.

"O Lord Sūrya, we shall buy the Soma; we announce it to you. Do you, for all the gods, arrange the seasons and arrange the sacrificial fees according to the season and according to the deity. With these words, he worships the Sun with his hand containing gold. This is to be explained as before. Having handed over the King (Soma) to the Soma-seller, he asks him: "O Soma-seller, is your Soma for sale? 3.

Having given the king, who is bound, to the Soma-seller, he asks that Soma-seller: "Soma-seller, is your Soma for sale? Baudhāyana says that he asks this while standing near. "O Soma-seller, is it yours?"—the meaning of the sentence is: "Is this Soma, which has been spread out in this place with the certainty that it must indeed be sold, for sale to whom? There is a protracted vowel (*pluti*) at the end of the question.
Baudhāyana says that after sprinkling it with water, he drives it onto the hide. He replies, "It is for sale."
That seller of Soma should reply, "It is for sale.
He purchases it with ten [items].

Regarding the phrase "with ten," the remainder [of the meaning] is specifically "with individual entities" (*vyaktibhiḥ*), and not "with substances" (*dravyaiḥ*). Even though there are seventy cows—consisting of a cow, a milch-cow, a heifer, a bull, a draft-ox, and a pair—the number "ten" in the expression "he purchases with ten" would be untenable if the referent were the single entity delimited by the universal *gotva* (cowness). Nor should it be argued that the referents here are indeed substances, by taking the differences among the properties consisting of the universals *dhenutva* (milch-cowness), *tadvatsatva* (heiferhood), *ṛṣabhatva* (bullhood), *anaḍutva* (draft-oxhood), *mithunagotva* (pairhood), and *gotvajāti* (the universal cowness). This is because, due to the commingling (*sāṃkarya*) caused by *gotva* and the other [universals], *dhenutva* and the rest cannot be established as true universals (*jāti*).

Furthermore, it would be untenable for the author of the Sūtra to refer to them as "seven cows" (*sapta gāvaḥ*) if they were intended merely as members of the genus cow. [Objection: One might argue that the word *krayaṇāni* ("means of purchase") should be supplied immediately after the word *etāni* ("these") found in the forthcoming Sūtra; by doing so alone, the number ten will be obtained. [Response: This will not be the case. Why? Because even the possibility of option (*vikalpa*) remains. Therefore, this Sūtra is indeed necessary to establish their conjunction (*samuccaya*).

This point was stated by Jaimini in the fourth quarter of the twelfth chapter through two sūtras: "But there shall be an option regarding the means of purchase, because they serve a single purpose; or rather, there is a combination in the performance, because of the connection with the substance. The meaning of the sūtras is as follows: "krayaṇeṣu" refers to those substances which are the means of purchasing the Soma. The word "tu" (but) is used to highlight the distinction that, unlike the combination of the mantras belonging to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), there is no combination here; rather, there is an option. Thus, it indicates the difference [between the two cases].

"Because they serve a single purpose and because the effect of the *ānati* (bowing) is identical, there should be an option. Although the *ānati* produced by the purchase of the respective substances is indeed distinct, and thus an option would not be possible due to the difference in the mediated effects (*dvārakārya*), nevertheless, the sense is that because the commonality of the *ānati* is one, the mediated effect is also one. This is the meaning of the preceding sūtra. The phrase "due to the inherence in the substance" refers to what is established by the statement "he purchases with eight [cows]," and so forth; the rest is clear. [This is] the meaning of the subsequent sūtra. He states those specific instances: "Seven cows, gold, clothing, and a goat—these are three."

Among the seven cows, the first—the referent of the word "cow" (*go*)—is characterized by the definition beginning with "the Soma-purchasing cow, the well-born, the prolific," and so forth. The second is of the form of a milch-cow (*dhenu*); a milch-cow is one that has recently calved. The third is of the form of a milch-cow and its calf. The fourth is of the form of a draught-ox. The fifth is of the form of an ox capable of pulling a cart. The sixth and seventh are of the form of a pair of cattle. These are the seven cows. Together with these three substances consisting of gold and clothing, the meaning is that there are ten individual entities.

The word *ca* (and) serves the purpose of mutual conjunction (*parasparasamuccaya*). The expression "seven cows" (*vīṇī*) intends the simultaneous placing together of the seven cows in the region of the sacrificial post (*kaṭapradeśa*). This is for the sake of making it known that the placing together of all three [substances] must be performed simultaneously. Although the matter would have been established by the word "three" (*trīṇi*) alone, the inclusion of the word "these" (*etāni*) is for the purpose of making it known that there is no restrictive rule (*niyama*) stating that only the individual instances (*vyakti*) of gold, clothing, and grain constitute the required number, but rather that even their respective classes (*jāti*) may sometimes fulfill the numerical requirement.

Therefore, two or three pieces of gold in the form of leaf-ornaments (tarṇa), consisting of sixteen māṣas each, or even more than that according to one's capacity, should be given. Likewise, two or three garments, or even more; and similarly, two or three goats, or even more. However, as for the mantras, because of the prohibition "there is no modification (ūha) in the archetype," they should be recited in the singular number only, just as in the case of the formula *patnīḥ saṃ nahya*.

Likewise, regarding the phrase "on the northern skin," because of the sūtra prohibiting modification (*ūha*), this [singular] number must be justified as referring to the genus (*jāti*) even in the modified form (*vikṛti*). He will prescribe the offering of the three substances in the sequence: gold, a goat, and cloth. Since the mention of the goat has been made here out of order—after the mention of the cloth, instead of following its own sequence—that deviation indicates that this sequence also exists as an alternative option concerning the order of offering the three substances. As it is said: "There are ten cows; then these three, according to some."

"Ten cows"—the meaning is that these three [items] together constitute thirteen individual entities. According to this view, there are four cows (gāvaḥ): a milch cow (*dhenu*), her calf, a bull (*ṛṣabha*), and an ox (*anaḍvān*); and two more cows (*miyunau gāvau*). These ten cows, along with these three substances—gold (*hiraṇya*), a garment (*vāsaḥ*), and a wagon (*anā*)—make thirteen; such is the opinion of certain teachers. This position belongs to another Vedic school (*śākhāntarīya*). Furthermore, the word "atha" (then) indicates that the gift of gold, the garment, and the wagon occurs immediately after the giving of the ten individual cows.

The word "nam" (or "na") is used to indicate an alternative sequence. By this, it is also understood that, according to the view of some, the gift of these three occurs even before the gift of the ten cows.
Or rather, [the purchase] may be by four alone.
For one who is not wealthy and lacks the ten individual items, the purchase is made with four substances. He states those [substances]:
And with a cow, and with these three [previously mentioned items].

"With these" refers to the items consisting of gold, clothing, and a goat just mentioned. In the phrase "and with a cow," the word *ca* (and) serves to include other alternative views. Thus, the purchase is established even according to the view that there are seven items—four cows, gold, a cloth, and a goat. These various options are to be applied according to whether one is capable or incapable [of providing the full set].
[This applies] to one whose sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of twenty-one cows.

This sūtra is for the purpose of restriction; its meaning is that for a sacrifice with twenty-one dakṣiṇās, the purchase [of Soma] is to be made with only one cow. Furthermore, there is no recurrence (anuvṛtti) of the phrase "and with these three. If the recurrence of the phrase "and with these three" were intended, then he would have said, "and of that which has twenty-one dakṣiṇās. Since he did not say so, there is no recurrence. In this view, the taking back of the gold is omitted.

By the statement "with a cow for the one whose sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of twenty-one," it is understood that a higher number applies to the one whose fee consists of sixty. Āpastamba states this explicitly: "With three [verses] for the one whose fee consists of sixty. Regarding the alternative of an unlimited fee, he says the same: "With an unlimited [number of verses] for the one whose fee is unlimited.
For the one whose fee consists of thirty thousand, [the rule is as follows].

This is clear. In a sacrifice where the entire property is given as the sacrificial fee (*sarvasvadakṣiṇa*), the sequence is by twenty-four. Thus Āpastamba says: "With twenty-four at a thousand [cows], or at the *sarvavedasa* [sacrifice]. Satyāṣāḍha, having composed the Śrautasūtra, states those specific items: "Twenty-seven cows, gold, a garment, and a goat—these are the three."

There are twenty-one cows: a milch cow, its calf, a young bull, a draft ox, and a pair of cattle; thus there are twenty-seven cows. Gold, a garment, and a goat—these are the three articles. The meaning is that all these together amount to thirty units. The purpose for stating "these are three" is to be understood here as it was previously.
According to some, there are thirty cows and then these three.

The phrase "of one whose sacrificial fee is a thousand" (*sahasradakṣiṇasya*) carries over from the previous context. The purpose of the word "atha" (now/then) is as before. The rest is to be explained as previously.
[He gives] a hundred at the Vājapeya, two at the Rājasūya, and a thousand at the Aśvamedha.

Because of the initial introduction with "a hundred," the word "hundred" is to be supplied by changing its number (to the dual) in the phrase "with two"; thus, the meaning becomes "with two hundreds. This term "a hundred" should be understood as being elliptically supplied from the preceding [phrase] "of individual objects" (*vyaktīnām*) according to context. The same applies to the subsequent cases. In all three [sacrifices], two alternatives are to be understood: either ninety-seven cows plus the triad of gold and so forth, or one hundred cows plus these three. He purchases the Soma with the formula, "I purchase your Soma."

The meaning is that, having recited the mantra beginning with "Soma te krīṇāmi" and ending with "abhimātiṣāham," he points out each respective substance with the specific mantras to be mentioned hereafter and offers it.
Or, having said "Soma, the great, the many-valued, the shining one," he assigns each one individually.

In place of the mantra "I purchase Soma from you" (*somaṃ te krīṇāmi*), having uttered this [other] mantra, he points out each substance one by one; the meaning is that having pointed it out, he hands it over. Alternatively, the syntactical connection follows exactly as heard in the text: "Soma, the great, the shining one. In the former alternative, there is an option between these two: "I purchase Soma from you" and "Soma, the great, the much-shining one."

It should be understood that in the *Uttarakalpa*, immediately after the mantra "I purchase Soma from you," the reading of this [other mantra] is also optional. Just as one says both mantras—"I purchase Soma from you, full of vigor, full of milk, full of strength, the overcomer of enemies"—and "The great Soma, being purified by many," and then offers [the substance] while pointing out each respective article of purchase with its corresponding mantra to be mentioned hereafter; such is the meaning.

"I will buy it from you for a sixteenth part; I will buy it from you for a drop of soma; I will buy it from you for a hoof; I will buy it from you for a foot"—having thus enumerated the four feet of the cow, he says, "I will buy it from you for a cow," and [offers] a cow.

*Kalā* is the lower part of the hoof; *kuṣṭhā* is the lower portion of the hoof; *śapha* is the hoof; *pad* is the foot. By means of these mantras, reciting them for each foot while touching the cow's feet in their respective places—one by one, as the meaning is that they are pointed out—the sequence is: first the two hind feet, then the right [fore] foot, and then the front [fore] foot. While touching the fourth foot anywhere, one points out the cow with the words, "O cow, these are your corners. This is the meaning.

Having enumerated three-quarters of that [cow] by means of the word "tat" (that) in the mantra "gavā te krīṇāni" (I buy from you with a cow), the explicit mention of "goḥ" (of the cow) is for the purpose of indicating that this purchase by parts is not mandatory. [End of] Chapter 2, with the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

Having criticized the purchase of parts by saying, "I will buy it from you for a sixteenth part (kalā) of yours" or "for a hoof (śapha) of yours," [the text] states, "One should say, 'I will buy it from you for a cow,'" thus introducing the purchase of the whole in the Brāhmaṇa. The purchase of parts, however, is mentioned in another recensional branch (śākhā). In the Brāhmaṇa, the mention of the *kalā* and the *śapha* is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *kuṣṭha* and the *pāda*.
[The seller] replies to the excellence of the Soma-seller with the words, "King Soma is indeed worth more than this."

In the mantra, the word *vā* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). The phrase *bhūyo vā ataḥ* constitutes a formulaic statement regarding the purchase. Facing the Soma-seller, the Adhvaryu speaks until the completion of the purchase (*ā krayasaṃpadaḥ*). The term *saṃpadaḥ* is the singular ablative case. Because of the expression *ā saṃpadaḥ*, this [formula] does not apply to the tenth individual in the view that one purchases with ten; nor does it apply to the thirteenth in the view of thirteen. The same should be understood for other numbers as well. The Adhvaryu says, "He deserves even more. The words "he should respond" (*pratibrūyāt*) are to be supplied.

The meaning is that he gives gold while reciting the mantra: "I buy your brilliance with brilliance," ending with "Soma I buy from you, the overcomer of enemies," and then saying, "I buy your brilliance with brilliance, the bright with the bright, the immortal with the immortal. Some, however, append "I buy [you] with gold" at the end of the word "immortal.
He gives a goat with the formula, "Thou art the body of austerity."

At the end [of the verse], "abhimātiṣāham," he gives the goat with the formula: "The body of austerity, the color of Prajāpati; of thee, who art nourished by a thousandfold prosperity, I purchase with the last animal. Some recite here the additions: "I purchase with an animal, I purchase thee with a goat. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says in the *Dvaidha* that one should bargain with the goat with its neck turned toward the west. As for the seizing of the goat, the *sūtra* is that of Baudhāyana: "One should mutter the mantra even without seizing it," while Śālīki says, "One should not seize it at all."

*Upanigrahaṇa* is the act of holding [the cow] firmly by clasping her with one's own armpit region near the soma-seller for the purpose of obstructing her movement; it is characterized by a close contact. Even in the absence of *upanigrahaṇa*, mere restraint (*niyamana*) certainly occurs.
[The formula is: "I buy you with a cow. Thus, [one buys] the cow.

At the end of the mantra "abhimātiṣāham," he gives a cow with the formula "vanasena te krīṇāmi. At the end of "abhimātiṣāham," he gives a calf with the formula "vatsena te krīṇāmi. Although the calf is not mentioned by the author of the Sūtra, it is nevertheless obtained through implication, even though it serves as a subordinate element.

Otherwise, it would be impossible for the suckling calf of the cow to survive; it would contradict the Vedic scripture stating, "they amount to ten"; and it would contradict both the statement "he buys with ten" and the enumeration of the number of cows as seven. Now, one might argue that after the prescribed gift of the cow has been made, another cow must be given as the means of purchase to complete the number ten, and that this [additional] cow's possession of a calf is merely incidental.

And if it is argued that, even though the calf is present together with the cow, the fulfillment of the required number does not occur by means of that calf—since it is more logical to assume that another cow alone is the means of purchase than to assume that the subsidiary calf is the means of purchase—that is not so.

Even so, in the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Āpastamba (Satyāṣāḍha), it is stated: "I purchase thee with a milch cow," and "I purchase thee with the choice of a milch cow"; furthermore, according to another *Sūtra*, immediately after the gift of the milch cow, its calf itself is employed as the means of purchase. Therefore, in accordance with that other *Sūtra*, it is more appropriate to employ the calf as the means of purchase for the sake of completing the number ten.

Therefore, in accordance with other sūtras, the calf alone should be counted among the cows. This meaning is also obtained from the scriptural statement, "They become ten. If it is asked how so, it is said: having mentioned nine substances in the section beginning with "yat kalayā te," the statement "they become ten" makes it known that there is indeed a tenth substance in addition to the nine substances.

And that [cow] consists precisely of the cow and her calf, because the calf’s life is otherwise inexplicable given that the cow has recently calved, and because it is the one immediately present; for the calf belonging to the pair of cattle, however, its being suckled at the udder and its gift must occur only in association with its mother, not independently. Therefore, the fulfillment of the number ten should be understood as being accomplished by the cow and her calf alone.
Regarding the phrase "I buy you with a bull," some say it is with a young bull that has testicles.

At the end of the mantra "abhimātiṣāham," one buys the bull with the words "ṛṣabheṇa te krīṇāmi" (I buy you for a bull). According to the opinion of some teachers, in place of the bull, the purchase is made with a castrated yearling (*sāṇḍa-vatsatara*). A *vatsatara* is a calf that has ceased sucking milk. By the word *sāṇḍa*, its robustness is indicated. The suffix *-ṣṭarac* is applied according to the rule "after *vatsa*, *akṣa*, and *ṛṣabha*, [the suffix] denotes smallness. At the end of "abhimātiṣāhana," the mantra is "sāṇḍena vatsatareṇa te krīṇāmi" (I buy you for a castrated yearling). For the ox, one uses "anaḍuhā te krīṇāmi" (I buy you for an ox).

An *anaḍvān* is a draft ox capable of pulling a cart; at the end [of the formula], with the words "I buy the subduer of enemies," he buys an *anaḍvāh*. With the words "I buy a pair," he buys a pair of cattle consisting of two cows.

A bull and a cow constitute a pair (*mithuna*), and not two bulls or two cows; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement "seven cows. The same applies to the expression "he gives a pair of cows" (*mithunau gāvau dadāti*). Likewise, in the Brāhmaṇa passage "he buys [the Soma] with a pair" (*mithunābhyāṃ krīṇāti*), this is precisely the intended meaning of the word *mithuna*: the sense is that he buys it simultaneously with those two. Some read at the end of the verse "abhimātiṣāham" the words "with a pair of cows I buy from you" (*mithunābhyāṃ gābhyāṃ te krīṇāmi*).

The intention is that this is because the word "that" (tat) is seen everywhere [in the formulas]. Among these substances, the phrase "more than that, or even more than that" (bhūyo vā'to bhūya eva) is repeated. In the formula "I buy you with a garment" (vāsasā te krīṇāmi), it is a garment; at the end of the formula "the subduer of adversaries" (abhimātiṣāham), there is "I buy you with a garment," which is a garment. Here, the phrase "more than that, or even more than that" does not apply. In this context, the "garment" is sufficient for wearing. This injunction regarding ten specific items, due to the general command and in the absence of a specific rule, applies everywhere.
He accomplishes it with ten; some prescribe even more *somakrayaṇī* cows.

The meaning is that some teachers say that by these ten items, one should merely accomplish the required number for the sake of pleasing the Soma-vendor; furthermore, one should give many other things such as cows, goats, sheep, horses, and so forth. [End of] the second section of the second chapter, together with the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. "With two [items] you have bought it. Alternatively, some authorities maintain that one should procure more Soma-purchases than the prescribed number by means of exactly ten manifestations, for the sake of satisfying the Soma injunction; this is the meaning of the statement, "Some recite [the rule] thus. In the cases where it is said, "by a hundred at the Vājapeya, by two at the Rājasūya, and by a thousand at the Aśvamedha," there is no giving of additional Soma-purchases beyond the prescribed number, because satisfaction is achieved through that very number itself due to its multiplicity. If, however, there were dissatisfaction with that in every respect, then the remedy to be mentioned later—namely, "one should simply take it away"—would apply. In that regard, he states the restriction concerning the plurality [of purchases]:
He buys with fifteen, he buys with seventeen, he buys with twenty-four, he buys with an unlimited number; finally, he says, "I buy."

The intermediate numbers beginning with sixteen and eighteen, up to the number twenty-four, are enumerated by means of words expressing the numbers fifteen, seventeen, and twenty-four. Even when satisfaction is achieved through these intermediate numbers, the gift must be made according to one of the two specific numbers [fifteen or seventeen]; this restriction is for the sake of an unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*). If there is no satisfaction with fifteen, satisfaction is achieved with seventeen; if there is no satisfaction with seventeen, satisfaction is achieved with twenty-four.

If there is still dissatisfaction even after twenty-four [pieces], satisfaction is achieved by giving three, four, or more than that according to the prescribed measure (*pramāṇa*). If there is no satisfaction whatsoever, then the following method applies: when giving further gifts for the sake of satisfying the Soma-seller, finally—at the very end—after uttering one of the numerical words denoted by the term "more" (*bhūyas*), namely fifteen, seventeen, twenty-four, or "unlimited" (*aparimita*), he says "I buy" (*krīṇāmi*) even while silently handing over the specific coins. This is the meaning.

Just as when one possesses cloth, [one says], "I buy with fifteen," "I buy with seventeen," "I buy with twenty-four," or "I buy with an unlimited amount. The word *aparimita* (unlimited) denotes a quantity exceeding that which has been specified; as Kātyāyana stated: "*Aparimitaṃ pramāṇāya*" ("Unlimited refers to a measure"). Alternatively, regarding those items that are to be given for the sake of satisfaction, one utters the word "I buy" only once at the end after pronouncing them, rather than repeating it for each individual item.

It should not be argued that, just as one says "I purchase with cows, gold, goats, and clothes," or "I purchase with cows, gold, goats, and clothes," this act of begging for materials enjoined by the scripture—"one who has been initiated for twelve nights shall win prosperity"—and this purchase of Soma enjoined by such scriptural texts as "he purchases with a reddish-brown animal" and "he purchases with gold," apply only to one who lacks the materials and Soma, because for one who already possesses them, they would be purposeless.

Because, in the absence of that [apūrva], it would follow that [the sacrifice] does not arise, it is absolutely necessary to accept the eternality of these two. And thus, in the sixth chapter, eighth section (pāda), Jaimini states: "Begging and purchasing [are required] when [the substance] is not available, as in the world; or rather, they are obligatory because of their purposefulness. The meaning of the preceding sūtra is this: begging—that is, requesting—and purchasing—that is, buying—occur only when the substance, namely the *soma*, is not already available, and not otherwise. This is well-known, and it is expressed by the phrase "as in the world."

Because it possesses purpose, and because it serves a function through the *apūrva* (unseen potency), both of these two are necessarily present even when [the action] exists. Having completed the purchase, he takes back the gold with the mantra, "O cow, may you be well-disposed toward us; O moon-like one... The word "having completed" (*saṃpādya*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Even though many cows might be given as payment for Soma out of satisfaction, the taking back of the gold must be performed immediately after the completion of the transaction. This is intended to convey that the subsequent giving of the cows for the sake of satisfaction follows immediately thereafter. Thus, he takes from the hand of the Soma-seller the gold that was previously offered.

With that gold with which one would purchase Soma, he takes it back again—this is from the *Brāhmaṇa* statement, "He places splendor within himself," and from the explanatory passage (*pratiśabda*). When the purchase is made with a single cow, the taking back of the gold is omitted.
He gives a tuft of white wool to the sacrificer with the formula, "In us is thy kinship."

The *ūrṇāstukā* is a tuft of wool that has been cut and regrown; it is of such a kind. And that is white; he gives that white tuft of wool to the sacrificer so that it may be kept well-guarded. The giving to the sacrificer is for an invisible (transcendental) purpose. "Jyotiḥ" is the end of the mantra.
At the time of spreading [the filter], he makes it the center of the *daśāpavitra*.

The time for spreading out the *daśāpavitra*—when it has been given to the sacrificer and the Udgātṛ priests hold it stretched out with its fringes pointing north—is the time for spreading the *daśāpavitra*. At that time, having taken [the vessel] from there, the Adhvaryu alone makes a "navel" (*nābhi*) in the middle of the *daśāpavitra* which is about to be spread; this is a tube-like form hanging downward, conducive to the flow of the stream. This is because it is recited in the *Adhvaryu-sūtra*. Its recitation here is due to the connection of context. Alternatively, in the expression "he makes the navel" (*nābhiṃ karoti*), the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is inherent.

By that [interpretation], the injunction for making the *nābhi* (navel) becomes *atyanta* (absolute); thus, the injunction "make the *nābhi* of the *daśāpavitra*" is established as a direct command (*preṣa*). This is because, in the *Yājamāna-sūtra*, it will be stated regarding the making of the *nābhi* that the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is the agent; therefore, the injunction is directed toward the sacrificer. Alternatively, in the passage "the sacrificer makes its *nābhi*," the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is included within the word itself. Thus, as before, the injunction is established.

It should be understood that this must be given by the sacrificer to the *adhvaryu*. Regarding the dimensions of the *pavitra* and the *daśā*, the *Mānava-sūtra* states: "The *pavitra* is one *aratni* in measure; the *daśā* is one *prādeśa* in measure.
Two *daśā-pavitra*s are made from white sheep's wool; one of them may be without a fringe (*adaśāka*).

Kātyāyana says they are made of white wool—that is, wool that is white in color. They are made of sheep’s wool, not of wool unrelated to sheep. "Amā" means together; they are woven together with a thread. There are two fringes (*daśā*) at their ends; these are called *daśāpavitra* because they serve as the means for purifying the Soma juice, and thus receive the name *pavitra*. By the word "together" (*amā*), it is understood that the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ act in unison here. Therefore, one is woven by the Adhvaryu and one by the Pratiprasthātṛ.

Alternatively, the word *amā* signifies the equality of the fringe (*daśā*) and the strainer (*pavitra*). The mention of "two" is intended to indicate that both are woven: one fringed-strainer is thus made, and likewise a second; thus there are two. The meaning is that between those two woven [strainers], one of them—the other—becomes devoid of a fringe (*adaśāka*), being without a fringe. By this, it is understood that the second of the two woven [strainers] possesses a fringe. And in this way, the quality of being a strainer endowed with fringes on both sides also becomes consistent.

Having moistened a black tuft of wool with water and having tied it on with the formula, "I tie this upon the necks of the biting serpents," he pierces the forehead of the Soma-seller with that [tuft] using the formula, "O Soma-seller, pierce him. [End of] Second Paṭala; accompanied by the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 643.

The grammatical connection is: "having moistened black wool-fibers with water. *Upaprathana* means making them into small balls (*golikā*). With that [wool] in the form of a ball, on the forehead—since *ra* and *la* are interchangeable, the meaning is "on the *lalāṭa*"—he pierces or strikes. The absence of the word "with that" (referring to the wool) is for this purpose: so that there may not be merely the spreading out of the wool-fiber, while the piercing is done by something else, or even by a wool-fiber that has not been spread out.
He takes the King [Soma] from the Soma-seller with the mantra: "Thou art self-born; thou art born for this rite; I take thee by the Truth; protect us by the Truth."

The meaning is that he takes or seizes the *ājya* from the soma-seller. The prefix *apa-* indicates that the gift should be made in such a way that it does not fall from his hands; alternatively, it may indicate binding with a cloth in this context. If the soma-seller should hesitate (*kṛcchrāyeta*) while giving, then one should indeed take it away by force (*upaiva haret*). However, if the soma-seller should hesitate or feel distressed (*duḥkhāyeta*) while giving, then one should simply take it away. In the reading *upaiva hotā*, the prefix *upa-* has the sense of "quickly."
With the words, "Enter the right thigh of Indra," he places the King [Soma] upon the right thigh of the sacrificer;
on the right hand, according to the indicative power of the mantra.
He holds it as if grasping a garment.

The causative suffix (*ṇic*) is understood here by implication. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is Vedic, according to the rule *sup-tiṅ-upagraha-* from the sūtra *vyatyayo bahulam*. By the term *upagraha*, the middle voice is intended; thus, the meaning is "as if he causes [him] to be seized. *Nigrahaṇa* means embracing. This connects with what precedes the word *āsādayati*. Therefore, this [action] belongs to the Adhvaryu alone.

"O Adhvaryu, have you been able? asks the sacrificer. "I have been able," replies the Adhvaryu. "How were you able? [asks the sacrificer]. [The Adhvaryu replies: "We have celebrated Viṣṇu with a hymn, Maruts, Bṛhaspati, and the meters; having risen, we have mastered the sacrificial formulas; the mountains have opened wide; I have crossed over the waters that are easy to traverse. Thus says the Adhvaryu.

The suffix *tava* is used in the sense of a *kṛtya* (gerundive) after the root *śak* (*śaktavai*), meaning "to be able. The sacrificer asks the *adhvaryu*: "O *adhvaryu*, are you able to come from the mountain to fetch the *soma*? The form *āśakāma* is the *luṅ* (aorist) tense. The word division is *ā aśakāma*. From the root *śak*, the *ch* is substituted by the rule *icchāluṅośca*. Then, by the rule *puṣādidyutādladitaḥ parasmaipadeṣu*, the *cli* is replaced by *aṅ*. Finally, by the rule *luṅlaṅlaṅvaḍudāttaḥ*, the augment *aṭ* is added.

Therefore, *yajī* is long; it is a long vowel. In *ā aśakāma*, there is a single substitution (*ekādeśa*) of the two vowels *ā* and *a*, which is a *savarṇadīrgha*. Its meaning is: "We were able" (*atyantam aśakāma śaktāḥ sma*). The Adhvaryu priest replies with *āśakāma*. [The question] *katham āśakava* is the second person plural of the *luṅ* (aorist) tense. According to the rule *tasthasthamipām*, the *th* is replaced by *ta*; furthermore, because it is plural, the suffix is *va*.

Although there is no explicit mention of the agent here, nevertheless, because it falls within the context of the *saṃdaṃśa* (the "tongs" of the ritual sequence), it is Yama himself who acts as the questioner, asking: "In what way, by what means, are you capable? To provide the answer to this, he recites the mantra beginning with "Viṣṇu. [The meaning is: "O Viṣṇu, we have celebrated (*asmahi*)—that is, we have accomplished and fashioned—the form of the *stoma*, which is a collection of people. This concludes the seventh section of the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha.

In both instances, the phrase "stomam marutsmahi" (we celebrate the hymn for the Maruts) follows "bṛhaspati chandāsī" (Bṛhaspati and the meters). Viṣṇu, whose nature is all-pervasive, is favorable to us by virtue of bestowing capability. Bṛhaspati is favorable to us by virtue of being the giver of intelligence. The meters are favorable to us by virtue of providing protection. When these are favorable, what wonder is there in our possessing power?

O sacrificers, rising quickly from this place, go forth, scattered, to the *yajus*-mountains—to those mountains that consist of *yajus* formulas. A transposition of the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) must be understood; thus, the sense of the optative (*liṅ*) expressing a prayerful injunction, "go," is established here. The mountains possess the nature of *yajus* formulas due to their similarity in being dispersed. Just as there is a dispersal in the *yajus* because they lack connection between their parts, so too there is a dispersal among the mountains because they consist of rugged, difficult terrain.

And thus, the state of being like a mountain (*parvata*) on the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) is established through some similarity. The word *parvatāḥ* is in the nominative case used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*). Although the waters are difficult to cross (*dustaraṇāḥ*), they have become easily crossable (*sutaraṇāḥ*), meaning "I have crossed over" (*atāriṣam*)—that is, "I have emerged. Alternatively, by changing the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) of the word *atāriṣam*, the meaning should be taken as "I shall cross" (*tariṣyāmi*), in accordance with the context. The Adhvaryu priest responds with the words "Viṣṇu-stomam. These questions and answers serve an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

Because of the indicative mark "the mountains are unassailable," these [rites] take place on a mountain; by this, the purchase on a mountain is authorized. With the mantra "svānabhrāja," he designates the *somakrayaṇas*;

the meaning is that he intends—that is, he mentally resolves upon—the seven Gandharvas beginning with Svānabhrāja as the objects for which the *somakrayaṇas*, the footprints serving as the means for purchasing Soma, are intended.

Regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa states: "He says, 'Khānabhrāja. These [deities] indeed guarded the Soma in yonder world; they carried it away from them. If he were not to assign the purchase-offerings to these [deities], his Soma would be lost, and they would guard the Soma for him in yonder world. In that he assigns the purchase-offerings to these [deities], his Soma becomes secure; [he does so thinking,] 'These [deities] will guard the Soma for him in yonder world. The mantra ends with the word *damana*."

Regarding this, some say that even when there is only one cow for purchase, one should modify the formula as: "O Tārkṣya, protect her who is your Soma-purchaser. However, in reality, since modification (*ūha*) is prohibited in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the plural number must be used for the sake of honor.
Having turned the Soma-purchasing cow around with the words, "May Rudra turn you back," and having redeemed her with another cow, he releases her among the sacrificer's own cows.

Turning to the right is established by the general rule (*paribhāṣā*). Having turned the Soma-purchase cow (*somakrayaṇī*) around—that is, having made her face away—and having redeemed her with another cow distinct from the Soma-purchase cow, and having given that cow to the Soma-seller, he "merges" (*apisnāti*) that Soma-purchase cow into the cows belonging to the sacrificer; this is the meaning.
With a spotted leather thong (*varatrākāṇḍa*), he causes the Soma-seller to perish out of sight.
That is, with a spotted (*pṛṣata*) leather thong—a piece of a rope made of hide—he causes him to perish or vanish "out of sight" (*apakṣāmaṃ*), meaning secretly.
Some strike them with clods of earth; others strike them with sticks. || 8 ||

Thus ends the second paṭala in the seventh praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. [Paṭala 3] With the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. "With clods of earth" (loṣṭapiṇḍaiḥ). "With sticks" (lakuḍaiḥ) means with pieces of wood. "They strike with clods" (loṣṭairhanti) means they first drive them away from that place with clods; "they strike with sticks" (lakuḍairhanti) means they drive them away from that place as well with sticks—this is the opinion of certain teachers (ācāryas). In this very manner, the two verbs become meaningful.

Regarding this, Āpastamba states: "If the seller of Soma should dispute, they should destroy him with a spotted leather thong, making him unable to move; some say 'they should strike him with sticks,' while others prescribe death as a constant rule. "As a constant rule" (nityavat) means even in the case of one who does not dispute. "Death" (vadha) means a blow; and that [blow] should be such as to cause pain to the body. In all instances, the reading "loṣṭam" (a clod of earth) alone is appropriate, because in the *Uṇādi-sūtra* on the word "loṣṭapalita," the formation is established specifically through the suffix -ka.

In the Śruti text, "tasyai diśo loṣṭam āharet," the reading ending in the *kta* suffix (*loṣṭam*) is indeed explicit. Therefore, it should be understood that "loṣṭham" is simply a corrupt reading. Thus ends [the section] from the *Śrīmad-Bhagavat-Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśī-...*, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was the grandson of the venerable Agniṣṭomayājin, Sāhasrāgniyukta, Vājapeyayājin, Sarvatomukhayājin, Dviṣāṣṭrāgniyukta, and Pauṇḍarīkayājin, the illustrious Okopāha.

In the commentary named *Jyotsnā*, which pacifies the mental anguish of learned persons caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the ocean of the Sūtras, this is the second chapter of the seventh question. ||2||
7.3 Now begins the third chapter of the seventh book.

With the formula, "Thou art the seat of Aditi," he spreads a black antelope skin in the interior of the wagon with its neck toward the east and the hair upward. He places the offered King Soma upon it with the formula, "Sit on the seat of Aditi."

This is the king’s place for sitting down. The term "prattavacana" (the mention of what has been given) is intended to indicate that the offering occurs after the spreading [of the grass], whereas the rising and moving away occur beforehand; or else, it is for the purpose of showing that he places [the vessel] having taken it only as it was already given by the sacrificer, and not taking it from the sacrificer himself. Upon that [grass] being spread, over the black antelope skin, he consecrates the placed [king Soma] with the mantra beginning, "He has propped up the sky," ending with "vratāni. "The placed [king Soma]" refers to the king Soma who has been set down. The mantra ends with the word "vratāni."

"According to some, he sets it down," because of the scriptural statement: "He sets it down with a verse addressed to Varuṇa. The meaning is that some teachers maintain that the setting down itself must be performed with this mantra, *astanādyām*. In this view, the mantra *adityāḥ sada āsīda* should be understood as a supplement to the mantra *adityāḥ sada atīhi*, which serves as the instrument for the spreading of the black antelope skin.
He wraps it around with a cloth [reciting]: *vaneṣu vyantarikṣaṃ tatāna*.

"Vāsaptā" means that it is surrounded by another great thing; the meaning is that it completely encircles it. Because Soma arises within the joints of the tree, there is an enclosure. Furthermore, by this encirclement by the wind, it is as if not even the boat is encircled. From such explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) as "The pressing-stones (*grāvan*) are indeed the mountains (*adri*); upon them he places this Soma," this meaning is obtained. The word "cart" (*śakaṭa*) is to be supplied [as the object], because it is present in the context. The mantra ends with the word "adrāu" (on the mountain).

With the verse, "That light, Jātavedas... (RV 7.49.1), he covers [the fire] with a black antelope skin, its neck pointing upward and the hair on the outside; or alternatively, with the verse, "The crossing one, visible to all... (RV 1.50.1).

In the phrase "he covers," the word "door" (*dvāram*) is to be supplied as the object. The mantra ends with the word *sūryam*. Or it may be the alternative mantra beginning with "The crossing one, visible to all... and ending with *rocanam* (RV 1.50.2).
He yokes the two oxen with the formula, "O you two oxen, harnessed to the pole... (RV 10.101.3).

With the mantra beginning with "ulāvetam" and ending with "brahmacodanau," he drives the two oxen toward the cart. The mantra is recited only once, because of the dual number in the indicative mark and because of the abundance [of the object].
With the mantra "dhūr asi," he touches the two yokes; the mantra is repeated for each of the two yokes.
With the formula, "Thou art Varuṇa's," he lifts up the cart;
"lifting up" means raising it.
Having placed it so that the pole is toward the east, he props it up with the formula, "May Varuṇa prop thee up."
"Having established" means having fixed. "Supporting" (upastambhana) refers to the fixing of wood. The formula "Thou art the support of Varuṇa" is optional according to one's own Vedic branch.
He yokes the southern ox that has not yet been harnessed.
This is to be understood as a general rule.
With the formula, "Thou art Varuṇa’s," he draws the yoktra—
the rope for binding the oxen— around the two holes of the śamyā.
With the formula, "Thou art Varuṇa’s support," he thrusts the śamyā downward.

"Avagṛhana" means the placing of the mentioned noose of the yoke-cord into the hole of the yoke; this applies to the second [cord] as well. The "untying of Varuṇa’s pillar" (varuṇasya skambhasarjana) is an alternative to what is stated in one's own recension.
With the words "The noose of Varuṇa is cast off," he casts off the noose of the yoke-cord. He casts it onto the *śamyā* and fixes it there.
And he fastens a bull;
with this same mantra, he binds a rope to the horns of the bull as well. In the same way, he yokes the second ox.

Holding branches of the *hariṇī* tree—characterized by the ploughshare, the pin for the yoke-halter, the sling, the throw-stick, and the horn-fastenings—he approaches among them as the *subrahmaṇya*; or he holds branches of the *palāśa* or *śamī* trees.

Between the two shafts of the cart—the southern and northern—one places one's feet within the space between whichever shaft it may be, and holding the two poles, one creeps or moves along in accordance with the movement of the cart; or alternatively, holding the two poles, one moves toward that intermediate region which lies between whichever shaft it may be.

As for the "cart-vehicle" (śakaṭavāhana), it is indeed well-known in the world. *Hariṇī* means green or of a greenish-yellow color; according to the *Amarakośa*, "hariṇī" may refer to a doe, a golden image, or something that is green. By this much, its softness is established.

In the case of the first two [cases], when the substitution of the homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*) would apply, that is set aside; and since the *n* from the rule *nādici* is carried over by the *ca* in the rule *dīrghāj jasi ca*, the prohibition of the homogeneous preceding vowel would result. However, by the rule *vā chandasi*, the long homogeneous preceding vowel is re-established as an option. Thus, the form *hariṇī* is more appropriately supported by the sūtra. *Hariṇī* is the dual number. And this is a qualifier of the branch (*śākhā*).

The word *śākhā* (branch) which follows the word *hariṇī* (deer-marked) refers—by way of the maxim of the ox and the bullock (*vobalīvardanyāya*)—to the branches of sacrificial trees other than the *palāśa* and *śamī*. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of this word *śākhā* being syntactically unconnected (*ananvaya*). If it is objected: "In that case, the mention of the *palāśa* branch and the *śamī* branch is redundant; for they are already included by the single general term 'branch' (*sāmānya-śākhāśabda*)," we reply: No, because their inclusion serves the purpose of indicating their primary importance (*mukhyatva*). Regarding the word *īṣām* (the pole), the accusative case ending is used according to the rule: "When joined with *antarā* or *antareṇa*, the second case is employed."
Having taken hold of the cart, he issues the command: "Recite for King Soma as he is being carried away after purchase; O Brahman, restrain your speech; O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā."

Baudhāyana says that [the Adhvaryu] should proceed while holding onto the southern pole. The command "Recite! (anubrūhi) is directed toward the Hotṛ; for such a command is seen to be addressed specifically to the primary Hotṛ unless there is a sublation [of that rule]. Furthermore, Āśvalāyana, in his injunction regarding the ritual action, establishes the general agency of the Hotṛ himself by using the term "Hotṛ. This should be understood in other instances as well. Here, the meaning is that he issues the summons to the Hotṛ, the Brahman, and the Subrahmaṇya by means of these three commands.

Therefore, the three *śreṣas* must be stated separately and individually; the same should be understood for other cases as well. Regarding the word *brūhi*, the form *brū* [is used] because of Pāṇini’s sūtra: "In the case of *hi*, *preṣya*, *śrauṣaṭ*, *vaṣaṭ*, *āvaḥ*, and *āvaḥ*, there is elision of the initial [vowel]" (*hipreṣyaśrauṣaḍyaupaḍāvahānāmādeḥ*). Alternatively, it may be recited without elision, because of the single *iti*-particle. According to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "the Adhvaryu [recites] with the Yajurveda," the Adhvaryu—and not the Hotṛ, Brahman, or Subrahmaṇya—is the one [who performs this].

Because it is impossible for one to issue a *praiṣa* (directive) to oneself by name, and because it is impossible for the Hotṛ, the Brahman, and the Subrahmaṇya to be mutually related as the one who issues the directive (*preṣya*) and the one to whom it is issued (*preṣya*), [the Subrahmaṇya must act]. Regarding the duty of the Subrahmaṇya, Lāṭyāyana and Āśvalāyana state: "When the King (Soma) has been purchased, the Subrahmaṇya goes to the north of the Soma-cart and stands between the two poles, holding a Śamī branch or a Palāśa branch with leaves in his hand. While the Adhvaryu looks toward him everywhere during the Subrahmaṇyā litany, he holds the reins and, with the branch, [drives] the two oxen forward to the south-east."

One should cause the *subrahmaṇyā* formula to be recited three times while the cart is turning; six times when it is facing west; and once with the first [recitation] when the roof-covering has been removed and the branch has been fixed in front of the wife’s hall (*patnīśālā*), following that very branch as they proceed according to their purpose. In this matter, everything that is not in contradiction with one's own *sūtra* should be performed. This is because of the rule "the Jyotiṣṭoma is [performed] by all [branches]" and because of the principle that a single ritual action is understood through all its branches. When there is a conflict between one's own *sūtra* and another *sūtra*, one should rely solely on one's own *sūtra*.

This is because the fault of abandoning one's own *śākhā* (branch of the Veda) is heard of in the scriptures. Furthermore, the status of the *Sūtra* as a *śākhā* is demonstrated in the *Caraṇavyūha-śāstra*. The *Caraṇavyūha* is the name of that treatise which provides a detailed classification (*vyūha*)—that is, a systematic exposition—of the *caraṇas*, *śākhās*, and *sūtras*. The various divisions of the *śākhās* are shown therein; they should be consulted from that source. From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: [In the seventh Praśna:
When the verse has been recited three times, having stepped forward with the words "pracyavasva bhuvaspate," they turn back toward the east, moving clockwise.

In the phrase "in the *trisnūkta*," because the first [verse] is present there, it is recited three times. For this very reason, Āpastamba clearly stated: "there is no recitation of the first [verse]. Here, the *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ priest) follows the Āśvalāyana school alone, as there is an absence of the Yajurvedic (*yājuṣa*) tradition. In all cases, there is no recitation of the first and last [verses]; the *śastras* (recitations) follow exclusively the Yajurvedic *hautra* method, because, being a specific rule regarding the *śastras*, it possesses greater force than general injunctions.

"Facing east," "they turn back"—because of the plural number, this refers to the Adhvaryu, the Brahman, and the Yajamāna, as these alone are connected to the ritual under discussion. As for the Subrahmaṇya priest, there is no mantra for him because it is not mentioned in the *Chandoga-sūtra*. "Facing east" means with their faces turned toward the east. The meaning is that they go along both sides together with the cart. The word *ami* (together) indicates "on both sides. Even regarding the turning back, the Adhvaryu is on the northern side, while the Brahman and the Yajamāna are on the southern side.

In the word *prayāhi*, the prefix *pra-* indicates the specific characteristic of the cart's movement. Here, the word *pradakṣiṇa* denotes conformity; that is, it means in accordance with the turning of the cart. Otherwise, since the sense would already be established by the conventional rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating "one performs ritual acts in a clockwise direction (*pradakṣiṇa*) at a sacrifice," the explicit mention of *pradakṣiṇa* would be redundant. The mantra ends with *svastyāpanīya*. This mantra belongs specifically to the act of setting out, as indicated by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the word *pracyavasva*. *Pracyavana* means moving away from one's current place.

From this very indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is understood that the departure takes place together with the king who is seated in the chariot. The mantra belongs to the Brahman and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). By means of the plural form "forward" (*prāñcaḥ*), the accomplishment of the sacrificer’s agency—just as there is the agency of the Brahman and the *adhvaryu*—in the act of departing and in the recitation of the mantra which serves as its instrument, is established. However, the application of the term "sacrificer" to himself [by the Brahman] should be seen as being like [the usage] in the mantra "O Agni, be strong for the sacrificer" (*ucchuṣmo agne yajamānāya edhi*), namely, as a metaphorical designation. With the subsequent mantra, "We have gone upon the path" (*api panthām agasmahi*), both the sacrificer and the *adhvaryu* pass by the king, as was done previously.

To the north of the king, and not far to the north of the king. Both are mentioned for the sake of distinguishing them from the *brahman*. Moving eastward from the cart and westward from the [other] direction, they go past the king. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that both [actions] occur together. The mind of both [is directed toward] "Vasu," which is its end.
They kindle the fires; he places the largest [fuel-stick] on the *āhavanīya* fire.

The plural form "they kindle" (*prajvalayanti*) is used to include any one of the various types of attendants (*parikarmi*). "Varṣiṣṭham" means the largest or thickest; the word "fuel" (*idhmam*) is to be supplied as the object, due to its association with the verb "he places" (*ādadhāti*). They kindle it, meaning they make it possessed of flames by means of fine fuel-sticks. In the case of the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires, they kindle those two as well. The meaning is that at the *pratipad* [day], he places the largest ordinary fuel-stick into the *āhavanīya* fire.

This distinction regarding the Āhavanīya fire is to be understood in comparison with the other fires. This state of being kindled [is required] for the fires until the point when the King (Soma) has been seated upon his throne; if this is exceeded, the *sarvaprāyaścitta* expiation must be offered. Beyond that point, however, it depends on the requirements of the ritual. And this [kindling] is to be performed by the Adhvaryu or by the Āgnīdhra. [End of] Paṭala 3, accompanied by the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 649.

The animal dedicated to Agni and Soma has been prepared—possessing all its limbs, accompanied by its kin, according to the procedure of the Nirūḍhapaśubandha sacrifice: a reddish-brown, hornless, bearded, large, and fat animal, either black-and-white or red-and-white; with this animal, held by the ear, the sacrificer awaits the King (Soma).

The animal victim (paśu) dedicated to the deities Agni and Soma is "prepared" (upaklṛpta). By the use of the past participle "prepared," it is established that this preparation must be performed even prior to the commencement of the performance on the day [of the sacrifice]. He describes its nature with the words beginning "having all its limbs" (samaṅga): "having all its limbs" means having complete limbs; "possessing kin" (bandhumat) means having a mother, father, brothers, and friends, as indicated by the wording of the mantra beginning with "after him, the mother... (anvenaṃ mātā).

Just as in the case of the *nirūḍhapaśubandha* sacrifice, where characteristics such as "the animal is uncastrated, without horns, not one-eyed," and so forth, are stated by the sūtra, so too is the meaning that the animal for the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice must be of this kind. From this very sūtra, it is established that only a goat (*chāga*) is intended here. Furthermore, Jaimini, in the sixth chapter, eighth section, of his work, raised the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of uncertainty regarding the injunction for the animal with the sūtra "There is no restriction because there is no specific distinction," and then established the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that only a goat is required with the sūtra "Or rather, a goat, because of the indicative mark in the mantra."

In the statement "Or the goat [is the victim], because of the indicative power of the mantra," the word *vā* ("or") serves to set aside the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). The meaning of the two sūtras is quite clear: the intention is that a general rule must be restricted to a specific case. And this restriction has been stated in the Smṛti:
"An unclear general injunction should be restricted by means of a specific one; however, such a restriction is not desired for a clear injunction."

Restriction (*upasaṃhāra*) occurs only where there is a requirement for a specific detail in order to carry out a general statement. For instance, in the case of the general injunction, "One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni-Soma," there is a requirement for a specific detail provided by the mantra section, namely, "of the omentum and fat of the goat. However, a general statement is not restricted merely by the presence of a specific statement.

If that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of subsuming even the general statement, "One should not kill a Brāhmaṇa," under the specific statement, "One should not kill an Ātreya. Therefore, subsumption occurs only in the manner previously described. It should be understood that when it is said that a general rule is "unclear" (aspaṣṭa), this "unclearness" refers precisely to its requirement of a specific detail for its practical application. Regarding this, he states another specific detail with the words beginning with "loha": *loha* means red; *tūpara* means hornless; *śmaśrula* means one endowed with a beard.

Even if the reading is *śmaśruṇaḥ*, this same meaning is to be understood. This reading is consistent with the Brāhmaṇa. *Sthūlaḥ* means fleshy; *pīvā* means having smooth limbs. *Kṛṣṇaśvetaḥ* means black-and-white in color; *lohitaśvetaḥ* means red-and-white in color. Even one that is not hornless (*atūpara*) is permitted by Āpastamba: "A horned one becomes [acceptable] as a non-horned one if it is black-spotted or red-spotted. With such an animal, holding it by the ear—that is, grasping it by the ear—one goes toward the King and gazes upon him.

Rather, one waits with the animal held either by its ear or at a spot other than the ear from the beginning of the churning until the striking; for since the scripture states that "by the very act of producing fire by churning and striking it, the hospitality (ātithya) is offered to Agni," it is proper to wait precisely during that interval, as the entire ritual action from the churning to the striking is declared to have the nature of hospitality.

Since the animal sacrifice dedicated to the deities Agni and Soma is prepared here, just as it serves the purpose of the *vājapeya* and the *ātithya*, its purpose for the *araṇya-ātithya* must also necessarily be assumed. The injunction regarding the vehicle for the Adhvaryu is for the sake of ensuring his presence. In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satvāṣāḍha, [in the seventh book]:

"The Adhvaryus lift up that Udumbara throne, which has a head-rest (*śīrṣaṇyā*) measuring one cubit (*aratni*), side-rails (*anūcyā*), and feet reaching to the navel, and which is bound with a girdle of Muñja grass."

*Audumbarī* means made from the *udumbara* tree. *Āsandī* is a specific type of couch. Its definition is stated as follows: "That which has head-boards and side-boards measuring one *aratni*, with crosswise planks [and] longitudinal planks. This means that the couch whose head-boards (*śīrṣaṇya*) and side-boards (*anūcya*) are each one *aratni* in measure is called *aratnimātra-śīrṣaṇyānūcyā*. That whose legs (*pāda*) are navel-high is called *nābhivaghnā* (or *nābhimātrā*). That whose weaving (*vivāna*) is done with *muñja* grass is called *mauñjavivānā*; the meaning is that it is sewn together with *mauñja* ropes.

They lift up that very throne-seat (āsandī). The parts [of the ritual] are performed by the Adhvaryu, Pratiprasthātṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Unnetṛ; these [priests] lift it up. The word "tat" (that) is for the purpose of preparation. This must be done even before the commencement of the performance of that day's rites. According to the *Yājamāna-sūtra*—which states, "The Adhvaryu, Pratiprasthātṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Unnetṛ are the Adhvaryus"—the Pratiprasthātṛ and the others also possess the status of Adhvaryu. Some maintain that three [priests], excluding the Adhvaryu, lift it up. Having drawn forward the cart from the front of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall with the mantra "Thou art belonging to Varuṇa," he stops it with its pole facing north.
In front of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, not far from it, he supports [the post] slightly upward with the formula, "May Varuṇa support thee from above.
The meaning is clear. This mantra is an alternative to the mantra, "Thou art the pillar of Varuṇa."
He unyokes the southern ox.
This is a general declaration.
He drags the yoke-halter with the formula, "Thou art belonging to Varuṇa."
One should pull out the yoktra for the purpose of its release.
With the formula, "Thou art the loosener of Varuṇa’s bond," he pulls out the śamyā;
"pulling out" means uprooting. This [formula] is deficient in the words "Varuṇasya skambhasarjanir asi."
"Loosened is the noose of Varuṇa"—with these words, he unties the noose of the yoke-cord;
"loosening" means making it slack. "Released is the noose of Varuṇa"—with these words, he unfastens the head-stall.
The *āmikṣā* is the rope for binding the horns;
in this manner, he releases the northern ox.

The meaning is that the ritual procedure for the unyoking of the southern ox is thus. Regarding this, Lāṭyāyana and Drāhmāyaṇa state a specific rule: "One should give the southern ox to the Subrahmaṇya priest; both [oxen] should be given," so it is known from the Śāṭyāyana [Brāhmaṇa], because of their connection with the ritual act (*karmasaṃyogāt*). By implication, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is the giver. Both oxen are to be given, as the Śāṭyāyana Brāhmaṇa is understood to teach, because of their connection with the ritual act. For the work was performed by both. The reason is provided: "because of their connection with the ritual act."

The meaning is that whatever one has a connection with through a particular action, one obtains the opposite of that. [End of] the eighth paṭala. With the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa: He begins the procedure for the Ātithyā offering without unyoking the northern fire.

"One ox is released, while the other remains unreleased; then he performs the *ātithya* (hospitality rite)"—this is the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) belonging to one's own Vedic branch (*svaśākhīya*). This is what is being demonstrated by this [text]. *Ātithya* is the name of a ritual action. If it is asked what the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is here, it should be understood that it is simply the mention of Agni and the other deities as guests (*ātithya*) in the mantras for the pouring out of the oblation (*nirvāpamantra*), such as: "Thou art the guest-offering of Agni; thou art the guest-offering of Soma; thou art the guest-offering of the Guest."

The *Ātithyeṣṭi* is so called because its purpose is hospitality (*ātithya*). Its *tantra* is the collection of its constituent parts; he "commences" (*prakramayati*) it, which means he begins it. In the word *prakramayati*, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used in its own sense (without changing the meaning). Since it has not been stated here that "whatever is performed therein shall be explained," everything indeed occurs according to the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Or, having unyoked both [oxen].

The syntactical connection is: "Having unyoked both [the fires], he proceeds with the ritual framework (*tantra*) of the *ātithyā*. This is the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) belonging to another recension (*śākhā*). The combined meaning of the two sūtras is: "Without unyoking the northern [fire], or having unyoked that as well, he proceeds with the ritual framework of the *ātithyā*.
Having added fuel to the fires, he brings the sacrificial wood and grass (*idhmā-barhis*).
This restatement is for the purpose of indicating that the framework of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsa-tantra*) is being applied; therefore, the framework is not extended here by way of time.
There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses;
this is clear.
The two stalks of sugarcane serve as the *vidhṛti*.

Regarding *ikṣuśalāke*, some say it refers to the skin of sugarcane (*ikṣutvagāmike*), while others say it refers to the essence of sugarcane (*ikṣuvatrātmike*). The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that it refers to the root of *kāśa* grass (*kāśamūlake*). The intention of the first view is that since there is no supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) here, and thus no evidence for it referring to the root of *kāśa*, only the common worldly meaning should be accepted. The intention of the second view is that although there is no such clear supplementary statement as there is for *āśvavāla* when it refers to *kāśa*, one should nevertheless search for such a statement to support its reference to the root of *kāśa*.

From the recitation here, this is understood: for these two [the *vidhṛtī*], there are external rites such as fetching; like the external *barhis*, there is the holding [of the *vidhṛtīs*] for the purpose of the *upasads*, and they are also placed down when the *barhis* is spread.
He binds the enclosing sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood to the fuel, and the *prastara* of *aśvavāla* grass upon the *barhis*.

It has been stated that "one brings the fuel and the sacrificial grass"; regarding this, one binds together the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made of *śrīparṇī* wood and consisting of *kārmārya* material. According to the maxim that "a substance deserves refinement because it is intended for a future purpose," since the enclosing sticks are intended for a future purpose, their collection within the fuel-wood must be performed with a mantra for the sake of their refinement, followed by the binding. The phrase "made of *kārmārya*" is used to exclude the possibility of using wood from other unspecified trees for the enclosing sticks.

The prefix *upa-* in the word *upasamnahana* is intended to indicate the restriction that the binding of the fuel-sticks (*idhma-samidh*) must be performed in this very manner. The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is made of *āśvavāla*, and the *prastara* is made of *kāśa* grass. The term *āśvavāla* means "the tail-hair (*vāla*) of a horse" (*aśva*), as it is well known in common usage that the *prastara* is made from that material. Indeed, the sacrifice, having become a horse, departed from the gods; it entered the waters. As stated in the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: "It was seized by its tail; having released those hairs, it indeed entered."

"Those hairs have attained the state of *kāśa* grass; therefore, the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) should be made from them. From this remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), and with regard to worldly convention, only that meaning indicated by the remainder of the sentence is accepted—namely, that *kāśa* grass itself is to be taken, and not the horse's hair. Thus, in the first chapter, fourth quarter, under the sūtra "In cases of doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the sentence," Jaimini stated this very point. The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: [in cases where the primary sense is] doubtful...

The construction [of the sentence] should be understood by supplying the word *kalpanā* (postulation) from the subsequent sūtra, as follows: "From the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), which consists of respect shown toward the injunction, there is the postulation of that [specific substance] as its object. Although there is no primary doubt because the injunction is already determined in a general sense, the commentators have explained this term as referring to a secondary doubt, based on the perception of an indeterminate meaning—namely, that any one of ghee, oil, or fat might be the means for the ointment.

In the view of the ritualists (*yājñika*), the word *aiśavī* refers to either the leaf or the bark of the sugarcane; in the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, it refers to the root of the *kāśa* grass. Since no contradiction is observed among these views, there would be an equal disagreement (*samā vipratipattiḥ*). Furthermore, the principle that "the rule established in the scripture prevails because it is based on that [scripture]" can also be applied here. The word "having taken" (*upasaṃnahya*) is to be supplied after the phrase "the sacrificial grass-bundle made of horse-hair" (*āśvatrālaṃ prastaram*). The bringing of the two separating blades (*vidhṛtī*) occurs simultaneously with the horse-hair sacrificial grass-bundle.

These horse-hair [grass] (*aśvavāla*) are indeed the eyelashes of Prajāpati, and the *aikṣavī* grass is the transverse [eyelash]. Since the Śruti states, "When the *prastara* is made of horse-hair and the transverse [grass] is *aikṣavī*, one thereby gathers the eye of Prajāpati himself," this establishes the identity of form between the two. The statement regarding their reversed order is intended to refer to the sequence mentioned in the sentence, "On the previous day, he brings the fuel and the sacrificial grass. However, the actual order of performance remains exactly as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), and there is no sublation of the sequence obtained through the general rule (*codaka*).

In this case, because there is a substitution (*pratyāmnāna*) of the quality alone—namely, the mere circumference consisting of the fear of the effect—the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is made of *khadira* wood and specifically of *pālāśa* wood; and it consists of exactly twenty-two pieces of wood, due to the absence of the *anuyāja* fuel-sticks (*samidh*). However, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is made of *darbha* grass alone, because the *āśvavāla* grass is prescribed only for the *prastara* bundle. If *darbha* and *kāśa* grasses are present in the same location, then the ritual action ending with the touching (*abhimarśana*) is performed only once. If they are in different locations, then [the action] is repeated.

The mantra beginning with *kṣam* and ending with *devānām* is repeated. The repetition of the touching (*abhimarśana*) of the *ālābū* gourd occurs because of the difference in location. Since the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is also designated by the word *barhis*, there is no exclusion of this [mantra] in the case of *kāśa* grass. However, the touching of oneself (*ātmābhimarśana*) occurs only once at the end. In the *śulba* [ritual], it is performed using *darbha* grass alone.
At the time of the pouring out (*nirvapaṇa*), he pours out the oblation for Viṣṇu on nine potsherds with the hand of his wife.

Since there are many specific details regarding this *nirvāpa* that will be described hereafter, the statement "at the time of the *nirvāpa*" is made for the sake of ensuring attentiveness. "At the time of the *nirvāpa*" means at the place of the *nirvāpa*. That the word *kāla* (time) refers to the location is seen in the *Baudhāyanīya*, where it says, "that is the *kāla* of the *uparavas*. From the phrase "at the time of the *nirvāpa*," the word "previously enclosed" (*parigṛhīta*) is to be supplied. The meaning is: at that place which was previously enclosed during the first performance of the Full Moon sacrifice (*Paurṇamāsa*). Since the matter is already established, this commencement is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*).

Thus, it becomes a restrictive statement meaning "only at the time of the *nirvāpa*. Consequently, the meaning is this: this *nirvāpa* is to be performed precisely at the place where the *nirvāpa* was established during the first performance of the *Paurṇamāsa*. By this, it is intended to indicate a specific meaning, namely that there is no fixed rule regarding all other *vikṛti* sacrifices. Nor should it be said that this is for the purpose of indicating the acts such as the preparation of the altar (*vedakaraṇa*), because those are already established by the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself; however, in the case of the *Prāyaṇīyā*, the statement is made because it is not otherwise obtained.

The hand is the substitute for the *agnihotrahavaṇī* (the fire-offering ladle). In this case, the properties of the *agnihotrahavaṇī* must be applied to the hand. At the time of the employment of the vessels, the hand is employed together with the *agnihotrahavaṇī*. And that [hand] is the right one. This is because of the statement of Āśvalāyana: "When only one limb is mentioned, one should understand it to be the right one, unless there is a specific instruction to the contrary."

Furthermore, regarding the hand, even when no specific location is indicated, it is understood that only the right hand is to be taken; this meaning is established by the mention of the "right hand" (*dakṣiṇagrahaṇa*) in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa-yājuṣahautra-sūtra*, which prescribes the *anvārambha* (touching) of the Hotṛ priest. The touching of the hand [is performed] with the mantra: *saṃviśantām* ("may they settle together"). [He recites: *dakṣāya mānuṣyāpti* ("for dexterity, may the human [power] reach me"). There is no [recitation of] *pratyuṣṭam*. The emptying of the left fist into the right hand [is done]. As many as are the duties pertaining to the *agnihotra-havīṃṣi* (the oblations for the Agnihotra), those should be performed with the hand alone.
This applies to the view that the hand is a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) for the *agnihotra-havaṇī* (the offering spoon). Or [it may be taken] from the wife's hand.
This is a substitute for the *śakalahoma*. According to this view, the recitation (*japa*) of all mantras is performed with the hand alone.

Or, while the wife is holding on (*anvārabdhāyām*), the pouring (*nirvāpa*) is done with the *sruk* ladle; that is, when the wife is holding on, the pouring is performed with the *sruk* itself. In this case, the preparation of the *prokṣaṇī* water and so forth takes place directly at the *agnihotra-havanī*. The first two views belong to other *śākhās*, while the final one belongs to one's own *śākhā*.

With these five [mantras], beginning with *agnerātithyam asi*, one appends the Sāvitra [formula] and the word *juṣṭam* to the first three. The five mantras end with *viṣṇave tvā*; the remainder [of the ritual action] is that "he pours out" (*nirvapati*) with those five. This same meaning is also established in the Śruti text: "He takes [the portion] five times. Regarding this, there is a specific rule: according to the Āpastamba-sūtra, "some say it is not [appended] to the last two because they are already present. The Sāvitra portion begins with *devasya tvā* and ends with *hastābhyām*; the meaning is that one appends the word *juṣṭam* after the pouring-out mantras and before these [Sāvitra formulas].

From the statement "three," it is understood that there is no *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation) for the final two mantras, namely those beginning with *sāvitra*. For example: *devasya tvā savituḥ prasave'śvinorbāhubhyāṃ pūṣṇo hastābhyām agnerātithyam asi viṣṇave tvā juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*; and *devasya tvā savituḥ prasave'śvinorbāhubhyāṃ pūṣṇo hastābhyāṃ somasyātithyam asi viṣṇave tvā juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*.

"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I offer you as a welcome guest for the guest-offering to Viṣṇu, acceptable to him. For Agni, the giver of increase of wealth, I offer you; for Viṣṇu, I offer you. For Śyena, who has become Soma, for Viṣṇu, I offer you"—such is the formula. The mention of "with these" (etair) is for the purpose of establishing the offering for each individual mantra.

The expression "with five" is for the purpose of making known the meaning that these five mantras exist, and by means of those five, there are five offerings (*nirvāpa*). The word "and" (*ca*) is for the sake of obtaining the connection (*anuṣaṅga*) with the two [phrases]: "that which is called Sāvitra" and "the word *juṣṭa*. It is not the case that, because the latter part of the mantra "juṣṭam" is only "juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi," it refers only to that [latter part] and not to the word *juṣṭa* alone; rather, it is thus [connected] as "I offer (*nirvapāmi*)."

It must be stated that its application also occurs only in three [verses], not in the remaining two.
