For if the word *juṣṭa* were intended to refer to the subsequent part [of the mantra], then one could simply state with brevity: "He joins the three archetypal [mantras] with these five, beginning with *agner ātithyam asi*"; thus, the employment of the cumbersome word *sāvitrajuṣṭa* would result in meaninglessness. Therefore, it must be stated that the word *juṣṭa* does not refer to the part [of the mantra], but rather refers to the word itself.

By this, the doubt that the word *ca* (and) has the sense of conjunction with the unspoken formula *nirvapāmi* is dispelled. Nor should it be argued that, just as the word *juṣṭa* is supplied to the three mantras, the word *sāvitra* alone should be supplied; for if that were the case, the sequence would be *sāvitraṃ juṣṭam*, and since these would form a single syntactical unit (*ekapadārtha*) due to being thus supplied, there would be no other distinct element (*padārthāntara*), resulting in the redundancy of the word *ca*.

Nor should it be argued that the word *sāvitra* is to be appended to the beginning of the mantra and the word *juṣṭa* to the end, thereby obtaining another item to be combined and thus avoiding redundancy; for the word *sāvitra*, if it were intended merely as a sound, would be utterly useless in the ritual action well-known to the practitioners of sacrifice (*yājñika*). Thus, the particle *ca* serves solely to indicate mutual conjunction. And so, the phrase "I offer" (*nirvapāmi*) indeed exists in all the mantras.

Alternatively, one must accept that the word *juṣṭa* refers specifically to the *bhāga* (portion). It serves as a substitute for the assignment of the deity performed with each mantra, namely, "Thou art the guest-offering of Agni" (*agner ātithyam asi*). Regarding the rule, "In five [verses] he recites the *sāvitra* and the *juṣṭa*," and "Not in the last two," according to the *Āpastamba Sūtra*, the word *juṣṭa* is naturally understood to refer to the *bhāga*. Furthermore, the phrase "may they yield" (*yacchantām*) indeed occurs everywhere.

According to the principle that "only that which is of the same class occupies the place of that which is of the same class," these five offerings accompanied by mantras take the place of the three original offerings accompanied by mantras. The original silent offering (*tūṣṇīm*), however, remains distinct and constitutes the sixth. The seventh is the *anyāvāpa* (the subsequent insertion), beginning with the words "This for the gods" (*idaṃ devānām*).
In the subsequent recitations (*nigamas*), one should specifically refer to Viṣṇu alone.

From here onwards, the term *nigama* refers to those [Vedic] verses (*mantras*) in which the name of a deity occurs; in these specific *mantras*, one should characterize Viṣṇu alone as the deity—that is, one should employ Viṣṇu alone [as the deity]. The use of the particle *eva* (only) is for the purpose of ensuring that words ending in the dative case, such as *agnaye*, *rāyaspoṣadāne*, and *śyenāya somabhṛte*, do not appear in the *mantras*. By the sūtra, "He offers a cake on nine potsherds to Viṣṇu" (*vaiṣṇavaṃ navakapālaṃ nirvapati*), however, the status of Agni and other deities as the recipient is merely excluded.

Having performed that which precedes the unyoking, he unyokes the northern ox according to that same procedure, provided it has not already been unyoked previously. Having recited up to "You are increased by rain" (*varṣavṛddhāḥ stha*), he unyokes the northern ox according to that very procedure—the procedure previously indicated—silently. The phrase "provided it has not already been unyoked previously" is intended to exclude the alternative procedure mentioned in other *sūtras*. The rest is clear.
He takes away the garment of the King (Soma) with the formula, "Thou art belonging to Varuṇa" (*vāruṇam asi*).

The word "paryānahanīyam" (to be wrapped around) is understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Chitsma" is the end of the mantra. "Varuṇo 'si dhṛtavrata" (You are Varuṇa, whose vow is firm)—[with these words, he addresses] the King [Soma]. || 10 ||
The word "he takes down" (apādatta) is understood to carry over. This much alone is the mantra:
"O uncut-leaved one, descend among the subjects, providing food, being auspicious for hundreds; be pleasant, O pleasant one. He thus lowers [the Soma].
The meaning is that he brings the King (Soma) outside through the door of the cart. [End of] the third section, with the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 655.
Regarding this, some teachers prescribe the lifting of the *āsandi* [seat] at this point.

The meaning is that some teachers say that what was previously mentioned as the lifting of the *āsandi*—namely, "the Adhvaryus lift it"—should not be performed there, but rather should be performed at this time.
He proceeds with the formula, "Wide is the mid-region."

The word "prāgvaṃśam" (to the hall) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Because it is seen in one's own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā*), the end of the mantra is simply "anvihī" (come hither).
With the verse addressed to Soma, "yā te dhāmāni," he causes the King [Soma] to enter the *prāgvaṃśa* hall by means of the eastern door.

That which has Soma as its deity is *saumī*; [the offering] is *saumyā* because it is for Soma. The suffix *ḍo* [is applied] because it is offered to Soma; *saumī* is the remainder [of the compound]. This word *saumyā* ends in the third case (*tṛtīyā*). It should be understood that in the absence of a compound, it would be *saumyā uc* (with the vowel *u*); the mention of *saumyā* is for the sake of knowledge. In the absence of such knowledge, the expiation for the breaking of the *yajus* formula is "bhuvaḥ" in the *dakṣiṇāgni*. The purpose of the statement "if there is no consciousness" (*acetita-vacana*) is to be understood here just as it was stated regarding the *aticchandas* verse. He causes to enter = he causes to lead in.

Since entry is impossible at any time without a door, the mention of the "door" (*dvāra*)—which is already obtained by implication as the locus of the action—is intended to indicate that there is another substance involved in the act of entry, namely a window (*vātāyana*), because it is necessary for the members of the assembly to observe the proceedings. Furthermore, in accordance with the need to accommodate two or more members of the assembly, it is large; in that [hall], there are two windows in every direction.

In that regard, because it is possible for someone to enter even through a window due to its large size, the word "door" (*dvāra*) is used to exclude that possibility. By this, the eight windows should also be arranged in such a way that two, three, or four people sitting at each window are able to observe the ritual activity.

Thus, there should be eight lower openings corresponding to the doors, four windows (dvāra) designated by the term *atīroka*, five small latticed windows (*gavākṣa*), and five upper openings; this enclosure (*pariśrayaṇa*) should be constructed excluding that [central part]. This should be understood to apply wherever the word "door" (*dvāra*) occurs hereafter as well. The mantra ends with the words "duryān. With the mantra "urvantarikṣaṃ vīhi," he carries it across to the south behind the Āhavanīya fire.

The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is on the right; he carries [the Soma] by passing beyond it, but not by going in front of the Āhavanīya fire himself, nor does he carry the King [Soma] behind the Āhavanīya. With the formula, "Thou art the seat of Varuṇa’s truth," he establishes the throne-seat to the south of the Āhavanīya.

Having returned by the same way he came, he leads the throne-seat (āsandī) past the front of the Āhavanīya fire and places it to the south near the Āhavanīya with the mantra: "The seat of Varuṇa art thou. Even if the throne-seat is carried by another person, it must be placed back exactly as it was brought. By means of the prefix *prati*, he establishes it so that it does not move.
In this context, the phrase "O Soma-loving one" (*saumyūcaye*) is required in the compound.
[End of] Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Seventh Book. 1kha, ga, tyevaṃ mā 1 656.

With the formula, "Thou art the seat of Aditi," he spreads upon it a black antelope skin with the neck toward the east and the hairy side upward. When that seat has been established, he places the King [Soma], who has been handed over, upon it with the formula, "Sit on the seat of Aditi."

The giving [of the animal] to another after it has been given away is established; and that must take place before the placement of the stool, because it is impossible to perform that [giving] without it. When the black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina) has been spread upon that [stool], the placing [of the animal] upon the black antelope skin is performed with this mantra: "Sit on the seat of Varuṇa's Law. Or [it may be done] with this mantra.
With the words, "He has spread the intermediate space within the forests," he encloses [the altar] with a cloth;
he encloses it with a large cloth, beginning from the east. Moving clockwise is established by the general rule (*paribhāṣā*).
With the formula, "Thou art Varuṇa," or "For Varuṇa thee," he addresses the King (Soma).

[The sixth [chapter] is concluded. "Thus indeed, worship the lofty Varuṇa; pay homage to the wise guardian of immortality. May he grant us a threefold protection; may Heaven and Earth protect us in their lap. With this verse addressed to Varuṇa, she attends upon the king.

The statement regarding the *vāruṇī* (belonging to Varuṇa) here is intended to demonstrate that the meaning established by Śruti is that the Soma itself—which has been purchased and bound—is denoted by the word "Varuṇa," and not that it refers to the deity Varuṇa. That Śruti passage is: "The Soma that has been purchased and bound is indeed *vāruṇa*. In this Śruti, the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix in the word *vāruṇa* should be understood in its own primary sense (svārthe). This is because of another Śruti passage which states: "This [Soma] that has been purchased and bound is indeed Varuṇa; he approaches the sacrificer."

In the word *vāruṇī*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120), and because it ends in that suffix, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. The purpose of stating "not [ending in] *it*" is to be understood here in the same way as it was explained for the rule *aticchandasa ṛc* (Pāṇini 5.2.123). She attends upon him with services such as perfumes and flowers—she worships him and pays homage to him.
Wherever one may sit, one should sit with this very [attitude].

In whatever situation—whether prescribed by rule or occurring by chance—one should approach the king with this very Vāruṇī verse. If one sits down near the king, then one should sit down near him with this very same verse. Likewise, another Sūtra states: "One should honor the king with the Vāruṇī ṛc; with this very verse one should curse the king and sit down. In this context, the sacrificer honors the king with the madhuparka offering.

According to the *Dharmasūtra*, "one who has studied the Vedas, a teacher (*ācārya*), an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a father-in-law, or a righteous king [are entitled to] the cow and honey-mixture (*gomadhuparka*)," because the honoring with the honey-mixture is prescribed for the king; and since Soma is also a king, as well as from Baudhāyana’s *Sūtra* stating, "Then he offers him the honey-mixture," there is the honoring with the honey-mixture. In that case, there is an omission of the responses. Or the Adhvaryu may recite them, because Baudhāyana’s *Sūtra* shows the Adhvaryu’s agency in the act of cutting, stating, "He instructs the Adhvaryu regarding that."

Since this [practice] is prohibited in the Kali age, its relinquishment alone is prescribed now. He issues the command: "Do not pass between the fire and the king. [This concludes] the third section (tṛtīya-paṭala), together with the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. Page 657.

They all perform [the rites] as if following a formal summons (*saṃpreṣavat*). Because of the singular number in the word "Agni," there is only one fire; and that is specifically the *Āhavanīya* fire, because of its proximity, its primacy, and because of Baudhāyana’s statement: "Let no one pass between the King (Soma) and the *Āhavanīya*. By this, it is implied by the sense that there is no fault in passing between the Soma and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). This summons (*praiṣa*) serves both for one's own sake and for the sake of others.

Therefore, the Adhvaryu, all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the cup-bearers (*camasādhvaryu*), the assistants (*parikarmin*), and others—all of them are protectors of the prohibitions prescribed by Prajāpati. Because it is intended for the purpose of communicating with another, there is both loudness (*uccais*) and monotony (*ekaśrutyam*). Whether it be the King or another Kṣatriya who approaches the vicinity of the Soma, he too must indeed recite this mantra. In that case, one must not approach the vicinity of the Soma while bearing weapons or similar items.

Regarding this matter, Baudhāyana has stated it in the form of a formal injunction (*praiṣa*): "Let no one whatsoever pass between the King and the Āhavanīya fire—neither one bearing a weapon in his mind, nor one with a staff, nor one with a parasol, nor one with a turban, nor one with shoes. Here, the particle *mā* serves the purpose of prohibition. "Any person whatsoever" refers to anyone, such as the King and others. "Him" refers to the King. "Weapon" (*āyudha*) refers to arms and missiles. Regarding these two, it is said in the *Dhanurveda*: "That which is held for striking is called a *śastra*, while that which is released for striking is called a *śastra* [missile]. "Shoes" (*adhaspādi*) refers to sandals.
He undertakes the ritual acts beginning with the pouring out [of the grain].

Having returned by the same way he came, or having returned, he undertakes the ritual acts such as "I know thee, increased by rain," or "Thou art increased by rain. This is because [the acts] prior to the spreading of the grass and the touching of the sacrificial cake are auxiliary to the pouring out.
He places nine potsherds on the Gārhapatya fire.

This [injunction] is for the purpose of setting aside the *āhavanīya* fire which would otherwise be obtained as an option. Therefore, it should be understood that even for one who accepts the alternative of placing the oblation on the *āhavanīya*, the placing must indeed take place on the *gārhapatya*. At the time of placing the sacrificial materials (*havir*) for the *ātithyeṣṭi*, one should also place the *madantī* waters; this is because of the upcoming statement, "O fires, the *madantī* waters," and because of Baudhāyana’s statement: "Cook this *vaiṣṇava* cake on nine potsherds for the *ātithya*; together with it, he places the *madantī* waters."

The word *madantī* denotes the state of water being heated; therefore, this placing on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) is for the purpose of heating it. Because the placing on the fire is prescribed together with the *ātithya* offering, the placing must take place at the *gārhapatya* fire alone. Some say it may be done in a common (worldly) fire. Since it is impossible to place mere water on the fire, it is placed on the fire together with a vessel; and that [vessel] is either made of tin, of lead, or of clay. The same applies elsewhere as well. However, in the case of milk intended for transport, there is no tin vessel whatsoever for its milking or cooking.

Because the Smṛti prohibits placing *gavya* (cow-products) in *tānna* (food cooked for a funeral rite). As for the Smṛti statement: "In the case of an oblation (*homa*), likewise in milking, cooking, serving, and even in the consumption of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), *gavya* does not cause impurity in *tānna*," that refers only to ordinary milking, being a permission granted solely for times of extreme distress (*saṃkaṭa*). The same applies to cooking and serving. Here, the "oblation" (*homa*) refers specifically to the offering of *pañcagavya*. Alternatively, even in this case, it must be understood as referring only to situations of distress.

By the phrase "eating the five products of the cow" (*pañcagavyāśana*), a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) is made regarding the vessel used for taking the five products of the cow. He takes four spoonfuls of clarified butter (*ājya*).

Even for one who performs five cuttings, this statement is intended to establish the rule of four cuttings. Since the purpose of performing the after-offerings (*anūyāja*) is already established by implication through the cessation of taking [the portions], its specific purpose is not stated.
One offers the guest-offering (*ātithya*) with the *Caturhotṛ* formula.

The guest-offering (*ātithya*) is an oblation (*havis*). Because it is not for the purpose of a *homa*, this is not a drawing of soma (*agraha*) and lacks the *svāhā* call. Having explained the *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas, he proceeds with the fire-drilled wood (*nirmanthya*) according to its ritual procedure (*āvṛt*). Having explained—that is, recited word by word—the *saṃbhāra-yajus* beginning with "Agni is the *yajus*" and ending with "I [offer] with faith," he proceeds with the fire-drilled wood according to the procedure for the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) stated as "O Agni, you are the bit (*nitram*)," etc., up to the throwing-in (*praharaṇa*) with the formula "The fire is in the fire.
Having laid down the *veda*-grass bundle, he issues the call for the *sāmidhenī* verses.

This is a restatement intended to exclude the spreading of grass around the altar (*vedyanta-paristaraṇa*). As for the preparation of the Hotṛ’s seat, it must be prepared by the Hotṛ himself for his own purpose. Since the Adhvaryu [prepares] the altar with the mantra "O Hotṛ, carry the Veda with the seventeenfold thunderbolt," the seat must be prepared first; however, because of the natural force of this being a restatement, no such preparation is to be made here. In the *Āśvalāyana* version of the Hotṛ ritual, since the mantra "O Hotṛ, carry the Veda with the seventeenfold thunderbolt" is absent from the *japa*, the seat must be prepared when the Hotṛ has arrived at the spot near the northern corner of the altar (*uttaraśroṇi*).
And this [phrase] "etacca hovarehi" is meaningful under the view that one accepts the injunctions (*praiṣa*) mentioned in other scriptures; otherwise, it should be understood as not being so.
One offers the entire fuel-stick (*idhma*) and pours out the entire contents of the *aupabhṛta* ladle.

The sense is that because the *anūyāja* offerings are absent, there is also an absence of the *samidh* (sacrificial fuel stick) intended for them and the fourfold-drawn clarified butter (*caturgrahīta-ājya*) intended for them. Since the absence of the *anūyāja* offerings is already established by the fact that the rite ends with the *iḍā*, the statement showing the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that indicates the absence of other [offerings] is merely a reiteration (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of praising the prohibition of other offerings mentioned in another recensional branch (*śākhā*), and not an injunction; this is for the purpose of demonstrating the *Mīmāṃsā* principle. That principle will be demonstrated immediately hereafter. Having performed the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, one sacrifices to Viṣṇu with the oblation (*havis*).

The mention of the *ājyāga* (the offering of clarified butter) is for the purpose of identifying its specific characteristics. That specific characteristic has been stated by Āśvalāyana: "With the two verses containing the word *atithi*, [one worships] Agni with fuel: 'Do thou swell; let [the offerings] come together unto thee'. Even in the case of the *Yājuṣahautra* method, these two [verses] alone are used. In that context, however, the recitation of the verse beginning with *āpyāyasva* may be performed either according to the rules of the Yajurvedic (*yājuṣa*) tradition or otherwise.

If it were merely stated that "one sacrifices to Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇuṃ yajati*), there might arise the following concern: by changing the case-ending or by grammatical transformation, the word *ājyabhāga* (the butter-portion) from the preceding context might be understood as applying here, such that the meaning would become "one sacrifices to Viṣṇu as the *ājyabhāga*. If that were the case, one might suspect—based on the injunction "having sacrificed to Viṣṇu with the *ājyabhāga*, he offers a cake on nine potsherds to Viṣṇu"—that the sacrifice immediately follows the offering of that specific oblation (*havis*). To prevent such a confusion, the term *haviḥ* (oblation) is specifically mentioned.
This is for the purpose [of ensuring] that it may be so. The statement "he sacrifices to Viṣṇu" is a subsequent restatement intended to prescribe a specific portion of the clarified butter (ājya).
He makes an offering from the remnant of the Dhruvā vessel.
This is to be explained as being like the Dīkṣaṇīyā sacrifice; and the application is likewise. [End of] the third Paṭala, with the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 659.

The *ātithyā* [offering] concludes with the *iḍā*. That which has its end (*anta*) in the *iḍā* is "concluding with the *iḍā*" (*iḍāntā*). Although the sense is already established by the statement alone that "the *ātithyā* concludes with the *iḍā*," the explicit mention of "it concludes" (*saṃtiṣṭhate*) as a term indicating the completion of the rite serves this purpose: even though it ends with the *iḍā*, it must be brought to a formal conclusion (*saṃsthāpanīyā*) by means of the disposal rites (*pratipatti-karma*) of the materials previously employed. Therefore, in this case, the disposal rites are performed with their respective mantras; the disposal of the *veda* [grass-bundle] is also performed with its mantra.

Since the [status of the] *iḍā* is already established by the context (*prakaraṇa*), its re-statement is for the purpose of indicating that the rites of disposal (*pratipattikarman*) are not mandatory during the *upasad*. Furthermore, the *mārjana* (sprinkling) also takes place because it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *iḍā*. Nor should it be argued that, due to the inconsistency of the prohibition in another recension—"they do not sacrifice the *anūyāja*s"—the state of being "complete" (*kṛtsnatva*) must also be assumed, and thus there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the ending with the *iḍā*.

If there were an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the end of the *śakhiḍā*, then the prohibition of other wives in subsequent rites would be meaningless; or else, it would become a mere reiterative statement (*nityānuvāda*) of the ritual act because it lacks scriptural authority (*aśabdatvāt*). This would result in a contradiction with the logic stated by Jaimini in the sixth section of the tenth chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]: "It is a mere reiterative statement because of the lack of scriptural authority. Therefore, the prohibition is merely an reiterative statement. This is the logic established in the preceding proposition. These two sūtras have been explained in the context of the *Prāyaṇīyā* sacrifice.

[Objection: "But surely, in the present context, there are two *iḍā*s for the *anuyāja* offerings: one before them and another after them. In that case, the injunction regarding the end of the rite applies only to the latter *iḍā*. Thus, the prohibition of the *anuyāja*s found in another recension (*śākhā*) also becomes meaningful; otherwise, it would result in being a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Therefore, all other [ritual] actions should be performed ending with the latter *iḍā*. [Reply: This is not so.

Since the cessation of the performance is prescribed on the condition that the *iḍā* [offering] is the limit, it is logical that the cessation should occur at that very point once the preceding *iḍā*-free state has been brought about, as the condition has then been fulfilled. As for the prohibition of the *anuyāja* offerings, it is merely an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) in the form of a constant restatement; thus, it does not contradict the principle that the *iḍā* constitutes the limit of the rite.

And likewise, Jaimini states in the sixth pāda of the tenth adhyāya: "Because of the prohibition and because it serves a purpose, the prohibition should apply after the latter; or, because of the attainment [of the former], there should be a transgression of the former due to the specific statement. These two sūtras were explained in the context of the *prāyaṇīyā* sacrifice.
From the remnant of the *dhruvā*, one takes the *tānūnaptra* into a bronze vessel (*kaṃsa*) or a cup (*camasa*) with the formula, "I take thee for Āpataya," as either a fourfold or fivefold portion.

In this case, it is an ordinary wooden cup (*camasa*) and not a *camasa* for the *praṇītā* water, because the latter serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*). Furthermore, the taking up of the *tānūnaptra* vessel has a function that is not part of the original archetype (*aprākṛta-kārya*). Since this cup is not intended for an oblation (*ahoma*), it is made from the *vāraṇa* tree; its specific form is like that of the *soma-camasa*, as will be described later. If it is argued that this cup also serves the purpose of an oblation on account of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) "I offer" (*juhomīti*), then it must be made of *vaikaṅkata* wood. Even so, since smelling (*avaghrāṇa*) is a form of eating (*adana*), the cup remains a means for that act, and thus the meaning of the word *camasa* is not sublated.

The fact that smelling (*avaghāṇa*) is of the nature of eating (*adanarūpa*) is indeed self-evident; that it is "eaten" (*prāśita*) and yet "not eaten" (*aprāśita*) is to be known from the Vedic scripture (*śruti*). For the verbal root *aś* (to eat) is indeed synonymous with *camu-dhāra-varṣa* (drinking from a vessel). The designation *tānūnaptra* for the clarified butter (*ājya*) is due to its connection with the deity Tanūnapāt. By means of this, those who are purified enter into friendship. Some maintain that this is an option restricted by specific conditions (*vyavasthitavikalpa*). There are five mantras ending with the word *gṛhṇāmi*. From among these mantras, he takes a portion (*samavadyati*) with each individual mantra one after another.

In the case of the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvatta*), one cuts five times; in the case of the four-fold cutting (*caturavatta*), one cuts four times. "Cutting" (*samavadāna*) means taking [a portion]. Although there is no explicit statement to this effect here, this meaning is obtained from the subsequent sūtras. The remaining portion [of the text] serves as an alternative (*vikalpa*) in the event that it is a four-fold cutting.

The mantra, "What remains, for the sake of most powerful power, I take you," is intended as an alternative if there is a fourfold portioning (*caturavatta*). According to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, if it is a case of the *tānūnaptra* rite, then the application belongs exclusively to the fivefold portioning (*pañcāvatta*) option; however, the refined meaning is that even in the case of the fourfold portioning, it becomes an alternative to the last of the four mantras. Then, with the formula, "Thou art unassailable," all the officiating priests touch it together.

Then they all—the *tanūnaptra* [officiants] and all the priests (*ṛtvij*)—touch it together; that is, being bowed down, they touch it simultaneously. If the *sadasya* is present, he too touches the *tanūnaptra* together with them. The inclusion of the word "all" is for the purpose of ensuring that everyone touches it themselves and not through a representative of another. The mention of "all" is intended to exclude the *camasādhvaryus*.

If the Yājuṣa *hautra* is present, the duties of the *hotṛ* and others should be performed according to that very method; if the Āśvalāyana *hautra* is present, they should be performed according to that method or by way of the Yājuṣa method. The mantra ends with the words "anabhiśastenyam. Regarding this, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "Therefore, he who first acts treacherously toward those who have partaken of the *anūbandhya* [victim] meets with misfortune. Having smelled [the substance] three times with the formula, "I offer you in Prajāpati, in the mind," he pours it out within the altar (*vedī*).

"Samavamṛṣṭam" (touched together) refers to the act of touching by all [the priests]. Regarding the smelling (*avaghrāṇa*) of that *tānūnaptra* [mixture] after it has been touched together: if, due to some obstacle for a particular person, the touching together does not occur, then for the sake of that person's touching, one should set aside a known portion and perform the smelling immediately after that [portion] has been touched. However, the ritual action itself must certainly be performed.

In every case, if a deliberation (*samavamarśa*) does not occur due to some great obstacle, then because the person is unfit to perform the office of the *adhvaryu*, another should be chosen; once that other has performed the deliberation, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be carried out. Regarding this, the Kauśika-sūtra states that while the *ātānūnaptrīya* rite is being performed by the sacrificer or the *adhvaryu*, one must fast for as many days as it appears will be required to complete the sacrifice, and at the conclusion of the ritual, an oblation should be offered with the mantra "mano jyotiḥ."

Some say that one should consume [the clarified butter] three times—once with the mantra and twice silently. Others, however, do not consume it nor offer it as a libation; for they argue that since the smelling (*avaghrāṇa*) is prescribed after introducing both the offering and the consumption as the means by which the *tānūnaptra* rite becomes established, and because of the verbal suffix indicating non-offering (*anu-homa*), the smelling is performed with the mantra alone. According to them, there is smelling of the entire clarified butter, though some maintain that this is prohibited.

According to the opinion of some teachers, the pouring [of the *tānūnaptra*] within the altar (*antarvedi*) is prohibited. Because of this prohibition against pouring within the altar, pouring outside the altar (*ahirvedi*) certainly takes place; however, it is not the act of pouring itself that is prohibited by this rule. Nor should it be argued that the smelling (*avaghrāṇa*) is also prohibited, for in the Śruti, the smelling of the *tānūnaptra* is described as being of the nature of the firm establishment (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the *tānūnaptra*, and thus it is unfit to be prohibited. Furthermore, it is more appropriate to assume that the prohibition applies specifically to the pouring within the altar, based on its being a practice rooted in a corrupted tradition (*vigītatva*). According to some, one should pour it in a place where there is no passage (*asaṃcara*).

According to the opinion of some teachers, one pours water where there is no path for people to travel; therefore, it should be understood that while in the previous view the pouring out occurs only where there is no passage, in this view there is no overflowing—this is the distinction. [1 Kha, Ga, Manasā] 661 3 Tṛpaṭalaḥ] With the commentary Jyotsnā by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa:
"O Agnīdh, are the waters rejoicing?"—thus he asks.

"What are these boiling waters? Have the waters become hot?"—this is the question directed at the Āgnīdhra. The word *madantī* denotes the state of being heated in the waters. When "the boiling waters" (*madantya āpaḥ*) is expected, the sandhi *madantyā āpaḥ* is an archaic (ārṣa) usage. In the question, however, there is praise. From this very fact, it is understood that previously the waters were placed over the fire by the Āgnīdhra; the time for that has already been shown. The loudness [of the voice] is for the purpose of making oneself understood to another. The Āgnīdhra replies: "The divine, immortal waters, increasers of cosmic order (*ṛta*)."

The divine waters are pure, immortal, and equal to nectar; they are the *ṛtāvṛdhaḥ* (increasers of cosmic order). They are called *ṛtāvṛdhaḥ* because they cause that mental truth (*mānasika satyam*) to rain down. Such are these waters, whose very touch purifies the mind; "they are heated" (*taptāḥ*) is the meaning of the response. Here too, as before, there is the quality of loftiness. One who kindles the fire is the *āgnīdhra*. His house is the *āgnīdhra*; and because it is a place of rest (*śaraṇam*) for the *āgnīdhra*, it is called *āgnīdhram*. A "place of rest" (*śaraṇam*) means a house; and by virtue of being located therein, the person is also designated as *āgnīdhra*.

Since the *aiṣṭika* (sacrificial) and *pāśuka* (animal sacrifice) rites do not involve the *ṭahāsa* [specific movement] as in the *saumika* (Soma) ritual, only the location must be indicated; he becomes the *āgnīdhra* by virtue of being situated there. The *āgnīdhra*’s place in the *aiṣṭika* and *pāśuka* rites is that spot where, standing, he issues the call (*āśrāvayati*). In the *saumika* rite, however, the *āgnīdhra* pavilion itself is prescribed; that indeed is his place.

This word [āgnīdhra] denotes a specific officiating priest (*ṛtvij-viśeṣa*), since the author of the Sūtras uses the term *āgnīdhra* even for a specific type of priest. Accordingly, the particle *ca* in the Sūtra (or Vārttika) "In the shelter of the *āgnīdhra*, the sound *raṇam*" must be stated as having the sense of an "inclusion of what is not mentioned" (*anukta-samuccayārtha*). By this, the inclusion of the meaning in the form of that specific priest not otherwise mentioned is established.
[The ritual master] issues the command: "Come hither with those [ladles]."

"Come together with those waters; 'drava' means 'come near'—this is the meaning of the *saṃpreṣa* (directive). Here too, as before, there is loudness [of voice]; however, because the question implies proximity, and since there is no summoning from a distance, there is no protracted vowel (*pluti*). It should be understood that a question is possible only when there is proximity, not when there is non-proximity.
They wash their hands with the *madantī* waters; the Brahman priest unties the King [Soma]."

With the *madantī* waters—that is, with heated water. Because of the plural number, all those [priests] wash their hands; the plural "hands" (*pāṇīn*) is used in view of the multiple officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Once the washing of the hands has been performed, the *brahmā* priest subsequently causes the King to mount [the chariot]. He is called *brahmā* because he discerns the good and the bad (*sat-asat-vivecana*) during the sacrificial rites. According to the *Nirukta*: "The *brahmā* is one who possesses all knowledge; he is worthy of knowing everything. Possessing all knowledge means the capacity to discern the good and the bad. The meaning of the *Nirukta* is: "He who knows all becomes the *brahmā*."

The explanation of the term *sarvavit* (all-knowing) is provided by the phrase "one who is worthy of knowing everything. *Vistrapsanam* means liberation from bondage. This statement is made here for the purpose of indicating the occasion for the injunction regarding the status of Brahman.
Saying "A ray, a ray," they all cause him to swell with their hands holding gold.

All of them are *tānūnaptriṇaḥ*. "Satisfying" (*āpyāyana*) consists simply in touching [the clarified butter] with a mantra characterized by the word "to satisfy"; others say it is sprinkling with water. They satisfy [the butter] either according to the order of their selection or all together. By the phrase "with hands containing gold," the holding of gold in the hands is prescribed as an ancillary part of the act of satisfying. When the [butter] has been bound back, they touch water and then assign [the butter] to the *prastara* grass-bundle with the mantra, "O beloved wealth... while keeping their left hands lowered and their right hands turned upward.

Thus ends the third paṭala in the seventh praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. The syntactical connection is: "Having performed [the rites], they recite the *nihnavas*. When the swelling (*āpyāyana*) has been performed by all and the King [Soma] has been re-bound—that is, tied again—some say that the binding is done by the Brahman priest and the attendant (*parikarmin*). However, it is more appropriate that it be done by the Brahman alone, on the principle that the same person who performed the loosening should perform the binding. Because the Soma, having been swollen, has the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*) as its deity, the covering is performed with a gesture of salutation consisting of joining the palms in the form of a *añjali*, with the left hands turned downward and the right hands turned upward; this is the *nirvahaṇa*.

Beginning with the statement, "Verily, these fall away from this world," the Śruti declares, "By bowing to Heaven and Earth, they become established in this world. Furthermore, the Ṛgveda Śruti states, "They indeed bow to Heaven and Earth; moreover, they cause them to prosper. And because of the scriptural injunction and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "Obeisance to Heaven, obeisance to Earth," one places [the grass] upon the *prastara* (grass-bundle). The word *nyak* is the accusative plural form of *nīca*.

Regarding this, some Udgātṛ priests perform the invocation of the Subrahmaṇyā, while others do not; it should be performed according to the authority of one's own Udgātṛ. Thus ends [the section] from the *Śrīmad-Bhagavat-Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra-Ambudhi*, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—the son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was himself the son of Śrīmad-Agnihotri Agniṣṭomayājin Sāhasrādhvaryu Vājapeyayājin Sarvatomukhayājin Dvipāhisāgniyukta Pauṇḍarīkayājin—written to alleviate the distress of learned people caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within that ocean.
In the commentary known as Jyotsnā, the third chapter of the seventh question [ends]. || 3 ||
7.4 Now begins the fourth chapter of the seventh book.
Having performed the *pravargya* rite, one performs the *upasad* rite; or, having performed the *upasad* rite, one performs the *pravargya* rite.

In this regard, since the *pravargya* is taught as an independent (*anārabhyādhīta*) rite in both the *Mantra* and *Brāhmaṇa* texts, it is likewise explained by the author of the Sūtras as being self-contained. Regarding that, "having performed the *pravargya*, one performs the *upasad*" is one alternative concerning the order of performance; "having performed the *upasad*, one performs the *pravargya*" is the other.

In this regard, although it could have been stated more briefly as "this is the reverse," the purpose of the elaborate instruction is as follows: "The *upasads* are the neck; he chooses the *pravargya* before the *upasads*. Because the *pravargya* is chosen before the *upasads*, therefore the sun moves away from here toward those worlds while heating them. Because the *pravargya* is chosen after the *upasads*, therefore the sun moves toward these worlds from above while heating them. One should not suspect that this [instruction] contradicts direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) because it employs censure and praise; rather, it should be understood that even this is indeed a form of direct revelation.

For the Mādhyandinas indeed recite: "The Pravargya is the head of this sacrifice, the Upasads are the neck; one should perform the Pravargya after the Upasads, therefore the head is above the neck. [End of] Chapter 4, with the commentary Jyotsnā by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.
That which is the sacrificial grass (barhis) of the Ātithyā is for the Upasads and that for the Agniṣomīya; it serves as the Prastara and the Paridhis.

When that which is external to the *ātithyā* is also external to the *upasad*s, it is likewise so for the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice as well. By this, it is established that there is a single common *barhis*, *prastara*, and *paridhi* for the *ātithyā*, *upasad*s, and *agnīṣomīya*. Nor should it be argued that what is meant here is that the *barhis* and other materials—such as the *āśvavāla* grass used in the *ātithyā*—are exactly the same for the *upasad*s and the *agnīṣomīya*, rather than their commonality.

If that were the case, since the injunction would have described the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) as belonging to the ritual act, there would be an injunction for it in a different context; or else, the connection with the original production (*utpatti-sambandha*) of those things not distinguished [by specific marks] would be the cause for their single application, which would result in a contradiction with the *Naimittika* principle. This principle is found in the second quarter of the fourth chapter. And thus, there is only one [set of materials]: the sacrificial grass, the *prastara*, and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). As for the meaning of the Sūtra: regarding the sacrificial grass whose connection with the *Atithyā* is understood through the injunction, [the question is whether it serves] the ritual act...

The meaning of the previous sūtra is as follows: "In the case of that which has such a form, at its *apavarga*—that is, its completion—the extension of properties (*dharmātideśa*) would be an injunction for a different object (*arthāntara*) in a modified sacrifice (*upasaṃhāri*), because it is devoid of the original description (*apavarṇitva*) due to being excluded (*apavṛkta*). The phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The meaning of the subsequent Sūtra is as follows: since the production of the *barhis* (sacrificial grass) occurs for all three—the *Ātithyā*, the *Upasads*, and the *Agniṣomīya*—which are not distinct from one another, and because of its connection with them, it is demonstrated by the statement "the *barhis* is outside for that [Ātithyā], for those Upasads, and for that Agniṣomīya" that there is a single performance consisting of the preparatory rites (*upādāna-saṃskāra*) for that *barhis*. Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) should be understood as: for the sake of all three, one and the same *barhis* is to be procured and consecrated.

In the sūtra *yadātithyāyā bahiḥ*, the term *bahiḥ* (the sacrificial grass) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the two separating blades (*vidhṛtī*). The evidence for this is precisely stated in the sūtra *ātithyeṣṭāvikṣuśalāke vidhṛtī*. Here, the mention of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is for the purpose of indicating that elsewhere, the mention of *barhis* (sacrificial grass) does not include the *prastara*. Consequently, in rites such as the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, in passages like *prasūnaṃ barhiḥ trīn kapālān saṃnahyaikabhyaṃ punaḥ saṃnahyati*, there is no inclusion of the *prastara*.

In passages such as "the *barhis* outside is made of *śara* grass," the *barhis* and other materials for the *ātithyā* and subsequent rites are produced for the sake of the triad beginning with the *ātithyā*; therefore, having taken those, one should silently bind them together and employ them again and again. The phrase "that [barhis] which has the *prastara* and *paridhis*" is a qualification of the *barhis*. *Prastara* and *paridhis* constitute "the *prastara-paridhis*"; that *barhis* upon which these very *prastara-paridhis* are placed is "that which has the *prastara-paridhis*."

By this [statement], the binding of the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) also occurs with the cord itself, and not with the *vidhman* (the middle part of the cord). Therefore, its nature consists of exactly sixteen pieces of wood. Alternatively, the term *tat-prastara-paridhi* is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). That action is of the nature of binding. "Prastara" and "paridhis" form the compound *prastara-paridhayaḥ*.

That very *prastara* and those very *paridhis* are such that, through the action of binding which consists in the binding on the outside, they become respectively as they are; thus, by being combined through the commonality of the act of binding both, there occurs the binding of that *prastara* and the *paridhis*.

The meaning is that the binding of the *barhis* (sacrificial grass) is the *prastara*, the binding of the *idhma* (fuel wood) is the *paridhi* (enclosing sticks), and by means of that very *prastara*, the binding of the *vāhaḥ* (the horse) occurs; likewise, by means of those very *paridhis*, the binding of the *idhma* occurs. Alternatively, it is an adverbial modifier for the specific ritual actions consisting of the *upasada* and the *īṣomīya*. Here, the word *ātithyā*, ending in the genitive case and accompanied by a relative pronoun (*yat*) characterized by the masculine gender, nominative case, and plural number, is to be supplied from the preceding context.

And thus the meaning is as follows: that which is the *prastara* (grass-bundle) of the *ātithyā* sacrifice, and those which are the *paridhi* (enclosing sticks), these very same items become part of the ritual consisting of the *upasads* and the *agnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice]. The compound, however, is to be understood as before. The gathering (*saṃbharaṇa*) of the *paridhis*, moreover, is indeed separate and without a mantra. If they were gathered together, there would be a contradiction with the mantra. Nor can it be argued that there should be a modification (*ūha*) such as "twenty-one times," for in that case, there would still be no contradiction in gathering them together.

As for the Sūtra statement, "He binds sixteen wooden sticks," it should be understood as intending the view that the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are already encircled. This must be accepted because it is improper to perform the gathering again with a mantra for those items already gathered with a mantra during the *ātithyā* offering; otherwise, one would incur the undesirable consequence of having to gather the *barhis* grass of the *ātithyā* again with a mantra. If such an unintended result were accepted, it would contradict the Mīmāṃsā principle.
Therefore, it is logical that the gathering (*saṃbharaṇa*) is indeed without a mantra; likewise, the binding (*saṃnahana*) is also silent in this very manner.
The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) has been spread for the *upasad* rites, as have the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).

This sūtra should be applied with the intention of presenting an alternative view (*pakṣāntara*). The preceding sūtra, however, is intended to convey the sense that those same materials are to be employed by taking them up again and again. The grass spread for the sake of the guest-offering (*ātithyā*) should be kept in the same state, and it should be kept in conjunction with the sacrificial grass-bunch (*prastara*).

In this context, the meaning of the sūtra "the *barhis* with the *prastara* spread" is as follows: in the absence of taking up the *prastara*, there would be a repeated picking up from its place and putting it back down; to prevent that, the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) which were laid around for the *ātithyā* offering should be left exactly as they are, and not everything should be brought back again and again. Thus, nothing further is to be employed. This is the sense of the sūtra.

Since the spreading of the *barhis* grass and the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) for the *ātithyā* offering are established by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) as being the same as those for the *upasad* offerings and the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, the composition of the heavy sūtra beginning with "the *barhis* of the *ātithyā*" and ending with "the *śayāḥ* and *paridhayaḥ*" would be redundant if it merely served to establish that the *barhis* is spread and the *paridhis* are laid. Therefore, it must be admitted that this sūtra conveys two distinct meanings.

And Āpastamba has stated two views regarding the meaning: "The *prastara* [grass-bundle], the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), and the *barhis* [sacrificial grass] that have been spread for the *ātithyā*, the *upasad*, and the *agnīṣomīya*—these same [items] constitute the enclosing sticks; this is one view. The portion ending with "those same *prastara* and enclosing sticks" was explained by the commentators with the intention that there is a repetition of the ritual action. However, the portion beginning with "that which has been spread" (*tatstīrṇam*) and so forth was intended to show the absence of repetition. The word *paricitāḥ* means "encircled" (*parihitāḥ*); this is a Vedic usage.

The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) used for the *upasad* rites is provided with a spread layer (*stīrṇaprastara*), and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are laid down. However, regarding Agni and Soma, because of the difference in location, a repetition of the rite is prescribed by the Sūtra. The sequence of performance should be understood as intended according to the "spread-layer" view, similar to the procedure for the *gṛhamedhīya* offering. Since the purpose would have been accomplished merely by stating that "the sacrificial grass which was used for the *ātithyā* is [used] for the *upasad*s and the *agnīṣomīya*," the repeated use of the word "that" (*tat*) also indicates a specific meaning.

The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice is indeed the same as that used for the *ātithyā* offering; its spreading is to be performed only in that specific location which serves the purpose of the altar (*vedi*), not across the entire great altar (*mahāvedi*). Therefore, only within the space between the *uttaravedi* and the *havidhāna*—as far as the grass is spread for the sake of the animal during the *ātithyā* day—is there the performance of duties pertaining to the altar. It is with this very intention that the author of the Sūtras will state: "To the west of the *uttaravedi*, he spreads the sacrificial grass with the mantra."

By this [statement], the exclusion of the entire area of the great altar (*mahāvedi*)—which constitutes the western portion of the *uttaravedi*—is effected. The mention of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice is for the purpose of excluding the *savanīya* and other sacrifices. Consequently, it should be understood that the rites pertaining to the altar (*vedi*) in the *savanīya* and subsequent sacrifices are to be performed on the *mahāvedi* itself. This is clearly stated in another Sūtra: "In the *agnīṣomīya*, the intermediate space between the *uttaravedi* and the *havirdhāna* sheds is the non-circumambulatory altar (*asaṃcara vedis*); there [take place] the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), the spreading of the grass (*bahiḥstaraṇa*), and so forth."

The word "agnīṣomīya" is in the locative case. By the term "asaṃcara," both the northern part [of the sacrificial ground] and the door are indicated. Here, "saṃcara" refers to ordinary (worldly) movement; thus, "asaṃcara" means a place where no such movement occurs. This is a qualification of the specific intermediate region between the *uttaravedi* and the *havirdhāna*. The mention of "upasad" implies that the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) accompanied by the *prastara* bundle is spread only during the *upasad* rites, and not even at the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice.

Therefore, since it is established by the qualification "on the sacrificial grass" (barhis) that the placing of the prastara must occur immediately after the spreading of the barhis for Agni and Soma, the placing of the prastara does not take place there, but rather in its own proper place. Such ancient cities that have come together and approached one another become dilapidated; likewise, those rivals who have approached and joined with their own [kin] become scattered for the sake of the sacrificer—such is the *Upasat* sacrifice. We shall explain its *tantra*, that is, the collection of its ritual procedures. Since it is a *khaṇḍatantra* (a partial or fragmentary ritual manual), the meaning is that we shall speak after having condensed the *tantra* intended as a duty from various scriptural sources (*śruti*).

Regarding those Asuras, there were three cities; in this regard, a well-known narrative concerning the *upasad* rites is established. The connection between these cities is well known in the Skanda Purāṇa, the Padma Purāṇa, and other Purāṇas.
In that [city], clarified butter (*ājya*) was the sacrificial oblation (*havis*).

Since the fact that the clarified butter (*ājya*) serves as the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is already established by its application (*viniyoga*) later on, this statement is for the purpose of making it known that this sacrifice is indeed *apūrva* (unprecedented). By this, it is established that here too, only as much as is explicitly stated should be performed. If it is objected: "In that case, since we shall explain everything that is done there, why was a statement not made here [at the outset] just as it was in the case of the *Prāyaṇīyā*?"—the answer is: no.

Since novelty (*apūrvatva*) is also necessary here with respect to the *hautra* ritual procedure (*tantra*), the statement "whatever is performed there, that we shall explain"—which serves to exclude the novelty regarding the *hautra* procedure—is undesirable in the present context; therefore, its non-mention is itself highly logical. Consequently, even the archetypal (*prākṛta*) *hautra* procedure beginning with "devāyo" is excluded. Thus says Āśvalāyana: "Now, at the *upasad*, there are the mutterings (*japa*) pertaining to the ancestors."

Jaimini also states in the sixth (seventh) section of the tenth chapter that this sacrifice possesses the quality of being *apūrva* (unprecedented). He does so through four sūtras: "In the *upasads*, the ritual action should be only as much as is stated; or rather, there is a prohibition of the remainder because of its subordinate status by means of the *nauveṇa* [formula]; or rather, there is no prohibition because of the re-introduction after having been prohibited; or rather, it is not a sacrifice (*anijyā*) because the principal deity does not desire the remainder."

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: regarding the Upasads, it is stated, "They have no Prayājas, they have no Anuyājas. Because of the prohibition of the Prayājas and [Anuyājas], it would follow that everything else mentioned [in the ritual context] should be performed; this is the meaning of the first Sūtra. As for the meaning of the second Sūtra: "He pours the Āghāra-libation with the *sruva* ladle for the sake of the discernment of the sacrifice"—thus the *sruva*-ladle is enjoined. From the word *sruva*, the suffix *ac* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). Thus, the meaning becomes "possessing the *sruva*" (*sauvavat*).

The term *strīvaditi* (as in the case of a woman) is, by virtue of its fitness, a qualifier of the sentence through the relation of being the object to be expressed (*pratipādyatā*). Thus, the meaning becomes: "by means of the sentence that prescribes the *yūpa-āghāra* [the sprinkling on the sacrificial post], namely, 'He performs the *āghāra* with the *suvega* ladle for the sake of the sacrifice's discernment. By the word *śeṣa* (remainder), an action other than an unprohibited action and an action other than one not specifically enjoined is denoted.

Since it possesses the quality of being devoid of qualities (*aguṇavat*), and since its own substratum possesses the quality of being the manifestation (*prajñapti*) of the existence of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), this sentence—which establishes the substratum of the *su*-suffix—effects the negation of the remaining rites. One might suspect that the mention of the substratum is for the purpose of reviving (*pratiprasava*) what was previously prohibited by the rule "not another oblation before [this]," and thus argue that there is no negation of the remainder; however, this is not so, because the third sūtra serves to revive what was prohibited.

In this context, there are three principal oblations—the Āgneyī, the Saumī, and the Vaiṣṇavī—and the *aupasadā* oblations beginning with "yā te agne" are also prescribed. However, since the *āghāra* (libations) and others are not mentioned, there arises a doubt as to their absence. To address this, a prohibition would otherwise follow; therefore, this statement is made as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*). Thus, the phrase "he pours the *āghāra*" is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all the archetypal (*prākṛta*) elements.

The meaning of the fourth sūtra is as follows: Regarding the "remainder" (*śeṣa*)—that is, the collection of oblations other than those offered to the primary deities—it is neither a *homa* nor a *yāga*. This is because there is a prohibition against offering any other oblation for the sake of bestowing the fruit upon the three primary deities; thus, the other oblations are not desired by the primary deities and are therefore not conducive to the granting of the fruit. When what is prohibited is performed, the intended fruit of the rite does not arise at all, as the primary deities do not possess the capacity to grant the desired fruit in that context. The deities are Agni, Soma, and Viṣṇu.

Since their status as deities is already established by the observation of injunctions later on, this statement is intended to ensure that all three deities are understood as primary. By this, the suspicion that Agni and Soma might merely be deities of the *ājyabhāga* offerings is dispelled. The entire consecration formula is simply "Thou art curd" (*dadhir asi*).
The ritual procedure for the *upāṃśuyāja* has been explained.

*Kalpa* means "manner" or "type. Due to similarity, it is a modification (*vikāra*). Since the status of being a modification of the *upāṃśuyāja* is established by the two sūtras—"In case of conflict, the commonality of the oblation prevails"—and since [the loudness] is intended merely to inform others, the loudness of the *āśrāvaṇa*, *pratyāśrāvaṇa*, *saṃpraiṣa*, *vaṣaṭkāra*, and *praṇava* would otherwise apply; however, because the text "We shall proceed with the *upasad*s in a low voice" prescribes low-voiced performance for the entire *upasad*, that loudness is set aside and low-voicedness is obtained. Thus, one proceeds with the *upāṃśuyāja* which has clarified butter as its oblation in a low voice.

Regarding that [Upāṃśuyāja], the *āśrāvaṇa* and *pratyāśrāvaṇa* are in a loud voice (*uccais*), while the *yājyā*, the *puronuvākyā*, the *sarpaḥ*, and the *vaṣaṭkāra* are in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), as is the designation of the deity. This statement is intended to set aside even that [general rule] regarding the Upāṃśuyāja. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and the *vaṣaṭkāra*," the *āgūḥ* and the *praṇava* are included. Thus Āśvalāyana says: "The *āgūḥ*, the *praṇava*, and the *vaṣaṭkāra* are in a loud voice everywhere. Furthermore, he states another distinction regarding loudness: "The tones of the *tantra* [portions] of the Upāṃśu [offering] are high-pitched (*uccāni*), while those of the *tantra* portions of the Upāṃśu [offerings] themselves are soft (*mandrāṇi*)."

Because the *upasads* have the *upāṃśu* (whispered) mode as their standard procedure (*tantra*), these [mantras] possess loudness (*uccaiḥ*) characterized by a low-pitched tone (*mandrasvara*). Nor should it be argued that the scriptural injunction, "We perform the *upasads* in a whispered manner" (*upāṃśūpasadā carāmaḥ*), refers only to the principal acts (*pradhāna*). For if that were so, since [the loudness] would already be established as a modification (*vikāra*) of the *upāṃśuyāja*, the scripture would become purposeless. Thus, once it is established that the rule pertains to both the principal acts and their subsidiaries, it must be understood that this Sūtra is required precisely to set aside the whispered nature established by other scriptural texts concerning the *āśrāvaṇa* and related rites.

The *praṇava* belongs to the *puronuvākyā*. However, in the case of the *sāmidhenī* verses and similar contexts, the communication to another is achieved by means of the name itself, just like the *āśrāvaṇa* and *pratyāśrāvaṇa* of the *mārutī* offering within the *Rājasūya*. And that name [is conveyed] precisely by the snapping of the middle finger and the thumb of the hand. Alternatively, in this context regarding the *preṣa*, one must accept that there is no *upāṃśutva* (whispering) because the purpose is to communicate to another. But in the case of the *āśrāvaṇa* and *pratyāśrāvaṇa* of the *mārutī* offering, although the purpose is to communicate to another due to the specific scriptural injunction (*vacana*), there is indeed *upāṃśutva*.

But the instruction for making others understand is indeed through speech alone; for in the context of the *sāmidhenī* verses, the scripture states, "We shall proceed with the *upasads* in a low voice," thereby declaring that even the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) are to be performed in a low voice. Furthermore, from the Āśvalāyana Sūtra—"The ancestral offerings (*pitryopāsana*) are with their own ritual procedure"—it follows that they must indeed be in a low voice. Even here, the snapping of the middle finger is for the purpose of fully cognizing the *praṇava*. As for the position regarding the non-low tone mentioned by Āśvalāyana, it does not apply here because it contradicts the Śruti. [End of Chapter] Accompanied by the *Jyotsnā* commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa: Having added fuel to the fires, he binds together the sacrificial faggot (*idhma*) consisting of sixteen pieces of wood.

The purpose of the statement regarding the addition of fuel to the fires (agnyanvādhāna) should be understood as being like that of the Prāyaṇīyā offering. The binding (sannahana) is indicative of the sweeping (saṃmaraṇa). This...

And according to the view that "the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) which were laid around during the *ātithyā* sacrifice consist of sixteen pieces of wood, they remain exactly the same during the *upasads*," the phrase "having added fuel to the fires" (*agnīnanvādhāya*) is intended to ensure there is no interruption in the bringing of the fuel-bundle (*idhma*). Therefore, the cutting of *darbha* grass for the purpose of strewing and so forth occurs immediately after the bringing of the fuel-bundle, and not at this point. However, it is not for the purpose of indicating that the *paurṇamāsī* (Full Moon) ritual procedure (*tantra*) applies here; for that [application] is established by the very mark (*liṅga*) of the presence of the *upāṃśuyāja*, as stated in the Sūtra: "The modification [of the model] is understood through a mark due to similarity."

The mantra for the gathering of the fuel (idhma-saṃbharaṇa) is modified as follows: "When you, having assumed the form of a tortoise, entered the trees, then I gather you together in sixteen ways, well-gathered. I follow one kindling-stick (samidh) for the sake of the life of the sacrifice; I gather the fire-stirring stick (upaveṣa), well-gathered. Or, with the intention of referring to the *upaveṣa*, it may simply be "I follow [it] in its movement" (*anusaṃcarāmi*). However, regarding the view that they are not yet encircled (*aparihitatva*), it has already been stated previously that the gathering of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) is separate from the fuel and is without a mantra.
Since they have already been gathered, there is no gathering performed with a mantra.

Having prepared the Veda, strewn around the fires, washed his hands, and spread out the *ulaparājī* grass, he arranges the vessels for the clarified butter according to their purpose: the wooden sword (*sphya*), the small ladle (*sruva*), the large offering spoons (*sruk*), the pot for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), and whatever else is required.

The purpose of the restatement ending in the *ktvā* suffix in the phrase "having made this *veda*" (*vedaṃ kṛtvā*) should be understood as being similar to that of the *prāyaṇīya* [offering]. The making of the *upaveṣa* [wooden chip] does not take place even at the time of the employment of the vessels, because it serves no purpose there. The section beginning with "having strewn the fires" (*agnīn maristīrya*) and ending with "having strewn the *ulaparājī* grass-bundle" (*ulaparājīm astīrya*) has already been explained. "According to the purpose" (*yathārtham*) means according to the requirement; that is, without exceeding the purpose or requirement. "Vessels for the clarified butter" (*ājyapātrāṇi*) refers to those vessels intended for the clarified butter. The mention of "clarified butter" (*ājya*) is for the sake of specifying those vessels already mentioned that are intended for the clarified butter.

This is intended to indicate a specific sequence: first the performance of that which has been mentioned, followed immediately by the performance of the other vessels not so mentioned. The inclusion of the term "according to purpose" (*yathārtha*) regarding the *ājyapātra* (ghee-vessels) is for the sake of including the use of the *niṣecanapātra*, even though it was not explicitly mentioned. The mention of the *sphya* (wooden sword) and so forth is to prevent the *agnihotrahavaṇī* from being included in the group with the *kapāla* (potsherds) and *śūrpa* (winnowing basket)—which would otherwise follow from their exclusion [from the ghee-vessels]—and to ensure that the *sphya* and others are used immediately after the use of the *ājyapātras*, since they are not themselves *ājyapātras*.

[Objection: "In that case, for the sake of brevity, one should simply say: 'the wooden sword (sphya), the butter-vessels (ājyapātra), and whatever else is required. Thus, the separate mention of each item would be redundant; since everything is related to the butter, they will all be included among the 'butter-vessels' (ājyapātra). Furthermore, there would be no need to include the pouring-vessel (niṣecanapātra) for the purpose of its specific use. [Reply: True. However, by virtue of their commonality as butter-vessels, they constitute a collective group consisting of the butter-vessels.

Because [if they were grouped otherwise], there would be the occurrence of dual compounds (dvaṃdva) such as "the one vessel and the wooden sword" (mekam pātram sphyaś ca); therefore, they are mentioned separately. However, for the three vessels included under the expression "with which purpose," there is a dual compound: "the Agnihotra-ladle and the Darbha grass. This is because in another Sūtra, the use of Darbha grass is prescribed for the sake of forming a dual compound. There is also a dual compound: "the Veda and the Veda-cutter" (vedam vedānam). Alternatively, there is the formation of dual compounds as follows: "the Veda together with the Agnihotra-ladle" and "the Darbha grass together with the Veda-cutter."

Alternatively, the *vedāgra* and the *vedānta* constitute a single substance, because the latter is produced from the former. Therefore, it should be understood that *agnihotrahavaṇī* and *vedāgra-vedānta* form a single *dvandva* compound. Together with the pouring vessel (*niṣecanapātra*), the *darbha* grass alone serves as the object of the *dvandva*. If it is asked: "In that case, let it be simply 'the wooden sword (*sphya*), the *sruva*-ladle, and the butter-vessels (*ājyapātra*)'; for what purpose is the mention of the *sruc* and other implements?"—this is true; however, they are mentioned here in order to state that the *sruc* ladles, being a collection, constitute a single vessel.

In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the seventh book]—the *juhū*, *upabhṛt*, *dhruvā*, and *ājyasthālī* form pairs (*dvandva*) in this very manner. The mention of the *ājyasthālī* is for the purpose of excluding the *niṣecanapātra* (the pouring-vessel), because that vessel is used first; it might otherwise be used along with the *stugbhiḥ* (the stirring-sticks), so its use is prevented. The remaining *niṣecanapātra* is indeed for its own specific use as required. The phrase "that which serves a purpose" (*yena cārthaḥ*) is intended to include the use of vessels other than the *ājyapātra*.

The singular number in the word *yena* refers to the collection of vessels; by this, the acquisition of three vessels is established. If it referred to a single vessel, only one vessel would be employed, and there would be no employment of the other two, even though they have a purpose.

[The ritual procedure is: having made the *pavitra*-strainers, he issues the direction, "O Sacrificer, restrain your speech"; while restraining his speech, he touches the vessels; once they have been sprinkled, he releases his speech.

Having performed the *pavitra* rite, one issues the command, "The sacrificer shall restrain his speech. Because of this statement, even though it serves an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose, the *praṇītā* waters are not [required here]. Since Kātyāyana has already mentioned them in that context, this effort is intended for their exclusion. Regarding the rule, "One releases the speech with the *haviṣkṛt* [call]," because there is no specific time [for it], and since the vessels have been sprinkled and the ritual acts must be performed while restraining speech—even among those archetypal acts included by the *codaka*—[these acts] do not occur in the interval; thus it is said, "when they have been sprinkled" (*prositeṣu*). "Restraining speech" (*vāgyataḥ*) means one who has restrained his speech by means of speech; [this refers to] the hand.

The contact with the palm is *samarśa*. By the phrase "in the case of those things over which sprinkling has been performed" (*prokṣiteṣu*), the following items are included: "Thou art for Dakṣa, thou art of the forest"; "The Rakṣas is burnt away"; "May the god Savitṛ impel you"; "O flawless ones..."; "O divine waters, cleanse yourselves for the sake of the gods. There is no address to the Brahman priest with the words "O Brahman, I shall sprinkle," because the sprinkling of the sacrificial vessel is not mentioned in the *Brahmatvasūtra* regarding the sprinkling of the oblation and the fuel and grass.

Because there is no procreation [of offspring], even the formal invitation (*āmantraṇa*) should not be performed, as it conforms to that [absence]. Alternatively, the sprinkling of the vessels (*pātraprokṣaṇa*) is included by means of the word "and" (*ca*). In this view, even here the invitation "O Brahman, I shall sprinkle" (*brahman prokṣiṣyāmi*) takes place. Here, prior to the sprinkling, the sacrificer equips the sacrifice with the sacrificial implements.

Having taken up the wooden sword (*sphya*), he removes the *stambayajus* from above the hair of the strewn altar (*vedi*). Having performed the final tracing of the boundary (*parigrāha*), he proceeds with the formal direction (*saṃpraiṣa*).

The *stambayajus* (the sacrificial cutting of grass) is performed with the mantra alone, because its purpose is for that specific rite. The touching of the altar (*vedy-abhimarśana*) and the sweeping of the altar (*vedi-sammārjana*) are not performed, because the altar is already covered by the *veda* grass-bundle. The "hairs" are the *darbha* grasses spread out; having placed *darbha* over them, one removes the *stambayajus* as in the archetype (*prakṛti*). In this case, the formula "May the sky rain for you" does not apply, because the altar is covered by the *veda* and remains uninjured. The call (*preṣa*), "O men, [prepare] this," is also omitted, because there is no further preparation of the altar. The digging up and scratching are not performed, because they are impossible.

The phrase "having taken up the northern enclosure" (*uttaraṃ parigrāhaṃ parigṛhya*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to exclude both the sweeping (*samārjana*) and the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) with the mantra "thou art a support" (*dhā asi*), but it does not intend to exclude the first enclosure (*pūrva-parigrāha*). This is because the word "only" (*eva*) indicates that it serves merely to exclude the subsequent [elements] situated in the middle. (*It excludes the consecration alone.*)

Since the purposefulness of the restatement is established by its very nature as a reiteration, it is improper to assume that it serves to exclude two forms of the "taking up" (parigraha), namely the prior and the subsequent. The meaning of the injunction "He proceeds with the call 'Prokṣaṇīs, bring them! is that he issues this very call immediately after the taking up of the subsequent parigraha.
[The portion within the brackets is not present in manuscript *ka*. Chapter 4, with the commentary Jyotsnā by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa:
He issues the call for whatever else there is besides the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and the binding of the wife.

The meaning is that he issues the *saṃpraiṣa* (direction) for whatever ritual action other than the spreading of the *barhis* grass and the binding of the wife’s girdle. For example: "Set down the *prokṣaṇī* waters; place this [ladle] near; cleanse the *dhruvā* and the *juhū*; bring the clarified butter. In the case where [the *barhis*] has not been spread, the touching of the altar (*vedi*) and the sweeping of the altar certainly take place, because the altar remains uncovered. There is no removal of the *stambayajus* from the hair [of the altar], because the altar is both covered and strewn with grass. "May it rain upon you" (*varṣatu te dyauḥ*) certainly occurs, because the altar is covered and strewn.

The injunction "imāṃ narā" (O men, this [altar]) indeed occurs even when the construction of the altar (*vedi*) has already taken place, because the act of preparing the altar exists. Likewise, the formula "dhā asi" (Thou art the supporter) occurs during the digging and scratching of the ground because it is applicable there. The invitation "purā krūrasya" (Before the cruel [act]) is indeed set aside by the force of the scriptural statement. Even in the alternative where [the altar] is already strewn, the injunction remains exactly the same. Nor should it be argued: "Since the placing of the grass outside is required, how can such an injunction be applicable here?"

Since the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is for the purpose of preparing (*upapādana*), and since even the absence of the *bahiṣprokṣaṇa* itself establishes its non-existence, it is possible to employ the *preṣa* exactly as it is recited. Thus, the [grass] should be spread after taking it from the place where it was set outside, without having been prepared at all.

Nor should it be argued that even sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) exists in the case where [the grass] is already spread, since the placing (upasādana) is for the sake of that; and likewise, since the previously mentioned directive (praiṣa) would be useless here, let there be a directive containing the word "barhis" alone—such as "Place the sprinkling water (prokṣaṇī), place the barhis, cleanse the sacrificial ladles, and bring the clarified butter"—in the case where it is already spread. This must not be said.

Since it is improper to sprinkle again a vessel that has already been sprinkled during the *ātithyā* rite, the vessels are retained for as long as one lives; thus, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of those vessels would have to be repeated with every ritual performance (*pratitantra*). However, because it has already been stated—by prescribing the repetition of the refinement of the vessels themselves—that such refinement ceases elsewhere, and because it is established by the principle of Jaimini in the first section of the twelfth chapter that when a sacrifice is taught as a completed act, its performance is not repeated in each ritual cycle since it has already been performed, [the refinement does not recur].

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: regarding the injunctions for the origin (*utpatti*) of the sacrifices—the *Ātithya*, the *Upasads*, and the *Agniṣomīya*—such as "the *barhis* [grass] is outside the *ātithyā*," the question arises whether the acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) performed upon that *barhis* should be repeated with each ritual procedure (*tantra*) due to the difference in performance. In the reading *niṣṭhitakarma*, the meaning of the preceding Sūtra is that the act concerning the *barhis* is determined to be common (*sādhāraṇya*) to all.

The meaning of the subsequent sūtra, however, is as follows: because the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth, have already been performed, they are not to be performed again. For that reason, there is "instruction regarding that" (*tadupadeśa*); *tadupadeśa* means instruction concerning that. By the word *tat*, the commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is understood. Since there is instruction regarding that commonality with the sacrificial grass, the purificatory rites connected to it are also to be performed only once in common; they are not to be performed separately for each individual ritual action (*prati-prayoga*).

Since the door is common [to both rites], the performance of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other acts at the very time of the *ātithyā* is mandatory; however, this is not an indispensable requirement for the *upasads* and so forth, because they have not yet been reached at that time. For this very reason, because the *ātithyā* comes first, it is the primary cause (*nimitta*), while the other two are understood to be incidental (*prasaṅgin*). Once the exclusion of the external sprinkling is established, the fetching of the grass (*upastaraṇa*) for that purpose is also excluded; thus, there is all the more possibility for the utility of the injunction as it was originally recited.

If it is argued that since the binding of the wife (*patnīsanahana*) is impossible here, its absence is already established and thus the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is redundant—this is true; however, there is no redundancy because it serves to indicate that the binding of the wife does indeed take place here in certain cases.
Having performed whatever [rites] precede the taking of the clarified butter (*ājyagrahaṇa*), he takes [the butter] from the *dhruvā* vessel itself.

Prior to the taking of the clarified butter (*ājya*), excluding the striking outside, the girding of the wife, and the *vyāghāraṇa* sprinkling, whatever ritual action begins from the placing of the *prokṣaṇī* waters—ending with the phrase "having supported it with the Veda upon the *dhruvā* ladle which is established on the ground"—that having been performed, he takes the *ājya* in the *dhruvā* itself. By the use of the word "itself" (*eva*), the taking of *ājya* in the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles is excluded. By this, the cessation of the ritual actions beginning with the movement of the *sruva* spoon up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings is stated.

And likewise Āpastamba says: "One should not offer another oblation before [the first]; one should perform the *āghāra* libation alone. The formula beginning with "O Agni, Lord of the House, come near" is recited on both occasions. Having consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* waters and addressed the *brahmā*, he sprinkles the fuel and the altar, pours out the remainder of the *prokṣaṇī* water, and having cast back the two strainers (*pavitra*) into the fire and consecrated the fire, he places the first *āghāra*-fuel stick and sets down the *dhruvā* ladle and the *sruva* spoon, modifying the mantra "This has sat down" accordingly.
