He consecrates the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the mantra: "Thou art Viṣṇu; thou art the abode of Viṣṇu; thou art that of Prajāpati."

The sequential enumeration is for the purpose of excluding what has already been mentioned. However, the removal of the *ājyasthālī* (the vessel for clarified butter) certainly takes place, because the *vedī* requires it to be empty for the purpose of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and because otherwise drops of sprinkling would fall into the clarified butter. By the act of addressing (*āmantraṇa*), the formal permission (*prasava*) is also implied; otherwise, the very act of addressing would be rendered meaningless. In the phrase "the fuel (*idhma*) and the altar (*vedī*)," the word "and" (*ca*) serves to indicate mutual conjunction.

Because [the altar] is covered by the *vedi*, one might suspect the omission of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*); therefore, the statement "of the *vedi*" is made to prevent that. Nor should it be said that this matter applies only to the case where [the *vedi*] is not strewn; for since the rule for sprinkling is observed even for the *vedi* that has been strewn at the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, it is proper to assume the same here as well, and thus a restriction [of the rule] would be inappropriate. By the sequence [of actions] expressed in "having poured out the remainder of the sprinkling water and having cast back the two strainers," the offering of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is set aside.

Even under the view that [the altar] has already been strewn, this very point holds true. By the rule "having cast the *pavitra* [strainers] and consecrated the fire," the offering of the *prastara* to the *brahmán* and the formal establishment (*kalpana*) of the *āhavanīya* fire are excluded by this sequence. The purpose of establishing the *āhavanīya* is accomplished simply by the placing of the fuel-sticks (*idhmādhāna*), because the oblation here is so small. However, if the *āhavanīya* must strictly maintain its essential form, then it must certainly be performed after the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājyābhimantraṇa*), as it is necessary. But if it is impossible to remain until that point, then it should be performed right here.

Alternatively, the cessation [of the ritual] occurs simply through the concomitance of the *ulmuka* (fire-brand) and the *udūhana* (shoveling) for the sake of the *anuyāja* offerings. Even in the case where the altar is not strewn (*anāstīrṇa*), the procedure beginning with "the knot in front within the altar" (*antarvedi purogranthi*) and ending with the sprinkling of the knot (*pratyukṣaṇa*) does not take place. Although the knot is new, there is no sprinkling because the tying of the knot was performed without a mantra. The mantra is used only at that binding which serves to carry the cut *barhis* grass to the sacrificial ground (*vihāra-deśa*). The same applies to the carrying as well.

Since that is not the case in the present context, there is no mantra for the binding and the carrying. Accordingly, Jaimini states in the first pāda of the twelfth adhyāya: "If it be argued that [the mantra applies] to the binding and the carrying as before, we say no, because they serve a different purpose. This pair of sūtras will be explained on the occasion of commenting upon the sūtra: "Having added fuel to the fires, he binds the under-laying of the *ātithyā* altar."

In the case where [the altar] is not strewn with grass (*astīrṇatva*), the laying down of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) and the enclosing of the *paridhis* (enclosing sticks)—as prescribed in the injunctions beginning with "having taken up the *tṛṇaidimantīya*," etc.—is excluded by the purpose [of the ritual]. Furthermore, even in the case where it is strewn, there is no sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) because it has already been sprinkled. It has already been stated previously that the tying of the central knot (*purogranthi*), etc., is also not performed.

Having silently loosened [the cord] outside, having taken up the sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara) together with the enclosing sticks (paridhi), having silently inserted the two strainers (pavitra) into the grass-bundle, and having silently handed it over to the Brahman priest, having placed a blade of grass between [himself and the altar], and having stretched the cord diagonally, he silently spreads the sacrificial grass for the New and Full Moon sacrifices in the prescribed order. There is also the preparation of the Āhavanīya fire. Because there is no offering of the Anuyāja oblations, there is no burning away of the fire-brand (ulmuka).

Having taken up the *prastara* (grass-bundle), he lays the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) around [the fire], and so forth, up to the placing of the fuel-stick for the eastern libation (*pūrvāghāra-samid*). However, the placing of the fuel-stick for the northern libation (*uttarāghāra-samid*) does not occur in either case. Because the enclosing sticks have already been laid down, there is no touching of this [fire]; for, according to the Śruti—"Indeed, the rising sun, by its rays, drives away the evil spirits from the east"—the fire possesses the nature of an enclosing stick (*paridhi*) due to the similarity in its function of destroying obstacles. Thus, it is like the enclosing sticks laid down for the guest-offering (*ātithyā*), which are utilized elsewhere.

The consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) performed during the *ātithyā* [offering] will also be for the sake of utility here; thus, the statement regarding the consecration is intended to dispel the doubt that there might be a cessation of the consecration at this point. The use of the gerund (*lyap*) in "having consecrated" (*abhimanvya*) is for the purpose of indicating the absence of any temporal interval. Having performed the other consecration with "Sūryas tvā," one places the first *āghāra*-fuel-stick with "Vītihotraṃ tvā" immediately without any lapse of time.

In the absence of the injunction for placing the *ādhāra-samidh* (the fuel-stick for the supporting libation), there would only be the placement of the *dhruvā* and *sruva* ladles after the consecration of the fires; furthermore, the application of the *ādhāra-samidh* itself would occur only at the time of the primary fire-installation (*ādhāna*). To prevent this, it is stated: "having placed the first *ādhāra-samidh*. By the rule, "having placed the first *ādhāra-samidh*, he places the *dhruvā* and *sruva*," the placement of the two *vidhṛti* blades within the altar (*antarvedi*) as prescribed by Āpastamba is set aside according to this sequence. That the two *vidhṛtis* remain in their original state is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this.

When [the grass] has not been spread outside, then the two *vidhṛtī* are also to be placed silently, and likewise the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) remain unenclosed. But when it has been spread, then the two *vidhṛtī* must certainly be in that same state, and the enclosing sticks must certainly be enclosed; this is how it should be understood. Furthermore, when taking up the enclosing sticks again and again for repeated use, the re-enclosing of the enclosing sticks is performed with the mantra alone.

Regarding the word *pūrvām* (the first) in the phrase *pūrvāmādhārasamidhamādhāya* ("having placed the first fuel-stick for the Āghāra-libation"), it functions as an adjective qualifying the fuel-stick (*samidh*), meaning "the first," i.e., situated in the eastern direction. By this, it is indicated that the placement of the *sruva*-ladle for the Āghāra-libation is necessarily fixed toward the east. Furthermore, this is understood from the force of the term *ādhārasamidh*. For the meaning of the compound *ādhārasamidh* is "the fuel-stick that serves as the limit for the completion of the Āghāra-libation."

By qualifying it as "prior" (*pūrva*), its location in the eastern direction is obtained; consequently, the priority of the ritual action for which the fuel-stick (*samit*) is intended is also established. However, the meaning of *pūrvām* is not "the first," because since that [priority] is already obtained through the very connection with the *sruva*-ladle as the support, prescribing "firstness" would result in redundancy. For this very reason, it was not stated as "*pūrvādhārasamidham ādhāya*" (having placed the prior support-fuel). The exclusion of the "subsequent support-fuel" (*uttarādhārasamit*), however, follows simply from the absence of any mental operation [to include it].

The mention of the *ādhāra* (supporting ladle) is for the purpose of placing it upright; the mention of the *samidh* (fuel-stick) is for the purpose of excluding its similarity to the fifteen fuel-sticks used for kindling. Consequently, it does not measure two spans (*dvipāda*). He places the *dhruvā* and the *sruva* [ladles] with their respective mantras. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), he also places the *ājyasthālī* (clarified butter pot). The meaning is that he employs the mantra containing the plural form of the word *etāḥ* ("these have sat down") because of the plural ending, and he employs the mantra containing the singular form of the word *eṣā* ("this has sat down") because of the singular ending.

Regarding the phrase "tā viṣṇo," here too the singular form "tāṃ viṣṇo" must be employed. Since these ladles (srucaḥ) which have sat in the world of the well-done—[the formula] "tā viṣṇo pāhi" being shown as a single modification in one instance by virtue of having a single referent—it follows that the same method applies elsewhere. The meaning is that he consecrates the clarified butter (ājya) with the formula "viṣṇave tvā," which is characterized by the singular form "viṣṇave" in place of "viṣṇave stha," specifically [with the words] "vaiṣṇavaṃ dhāma prājāpatyam."

Accepting that the plural number has the sense of "repetition" (*punaḥ*), the demonstration of *ūha* (modification) in both cases is intended to preclude the application of the mantra as qualified by the use of the plural ending. However, the formula beginning with "the butter-pot together with the *sruva*-ladle" (*sasruvām ājyasthālīm*) remains unchanged. For this very reason, the suffix *-lyap* is not employed in Satyāṣāḍha’s *Śrautasūtra*. Here, the sacrificer touches the butter placed nearby with these [mantras]: "This sacrifice," "O Agni, may my splendor... (*mama agne varcaḥ...*), and "May the earth be the Hotṛ" (*pṛthivī hotā*).
Having set down the Veda, he gives the direction for the *sāmidhenī* verses; then, having divided the entire fuel-wood into nine parts, he places it on the fire.

Having placed the *veda* grass-bundle, he issues the call for the *sāmidhenī* verses; this restatement of the sequence is intended to preclude the spreading of grass around the edge of the altar (*vedyanta*). As for the preparation of the *hotṛ*'s seat, it should be prepared by the *hotṛ* himself for his own sake. Alternatively, following the natural sense of the restatement, it need not be prepared at all; rather, it should be prepared by the *adhvaryu* himself precisely at the time of the *hotṛ*'s sitting down. The syntactical connection is: "Having placed the *veda*, having divided the sacrificial grass into nine parts, he issues the call for the *sāmidhenī* verses."

In that context as well, the phrase "for the sake of the *sāmidhenī* verses" (*sāmidhenībhyaḥ*) is construed with both [parts of the sentence]: "Let us worship for the sake of the *sāmidhenīs*" and "having divided [the fuel] for the sake of the *sāmidhenīs*, he issues the call for the *sāmidhenīs*. In both instances, the dative case in *sāmidhenībhyaḥ* expresses purpose (*tādarthya*). Consequently, the meaning becomes: "Having divided [the fuel] for the purpose of the *sāmidhenīs*, he issues the call for the purpose of the *sāmidhenīs*"; the word "the Hotṛ" (*hotāram*) is to be supplied as the object. The division prior to the call for the *sāmidhenīs* serves an invisible spiritual purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Regarding the *sāmidhenīs*...

The instruction for the purpose is: "Recite the invitatory verses for the fire being kindled. By the phrase "having divided this ninefold," it is understood that there are exactly nine *sāmidhenī* verses here; these will be shown further on. In the expression "having divided [the fuel] from the *sāmidhenīs*," because of the word "divided" (*pratīti*), the division is equal. In that context, equality of division consists precisely in each consisting of a single piece of wood, as no other [division] is possible. And thus, during the nine *praṇavas* of the *sāmidhenīs*, he throws in nine pieces of wood.

The remaining six pieces of wood are thrown in for the purpose of fuel alone by means of the addition of the ninth piece of wood; they are not thrown in as being connected with the *sāmidhenī* verses. The intended meaning there is that two pieces of wood are thrown in solely with the intention of being fuel (*indhana*), and not with the intention of being connected with the *sāmidhenī* verses. This meaning is obtained from the further employment of the word *idhma* (fuel); otherwise, its use would be redundant.

By this [rule], two pieces of wood (*kāṣṭha*) are to be thrown into each of the first six *praṇavas*, and three are thrown together into the *paridhānīyā*; or else, one is thrown into the third, sixth, and ninth *praṇavas*, while two are thrown into each of the other six—thus the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) of certain [teachers] is rejected. The sacrificer’s duties (*yājamāna*) are according to the archetype (*prakṛti*). There is no mention of "O gods" or "O ancestors. Regarding this, Āpastamba states a specific rule for the *hautra*: "There are three or nine verses to be recited in succession (*parāc*)."

The first three verses are the original (prākṛtī) ones, or those prescribed by Āśvalāyana. They are recited *parācī*, that is, without repetition, as in the original ritual. It should be understood that if the *hautra* belongs to the Yajurveda, the procedure prescribed by Āpastamba or Āśvalāyana should be adopted.

When the deities have been invoked, having offered the *upavāja* to Agni and poured the *sruvāghāra* libation, he gives the command: "O Āgnīdh, cleanse the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the fire three times each. Once they have been cleansed, he chooses the *pravara* (the ancestral invocation) as in the Mahāpitṛyajña, saying, "O Hotṛ, sit down. Then he takes eight portions from the *dhruvā* ladle into the *juhū* and four into the *upabhṛt*.

When the deities of the Hotṛ-offerings have been invoked, having fanned the Āhavanīya fire with the Veda-grass-bundle three times, this fanning is for an invisible (transcendental) purpose; for it is observed that in the Avabhṛtha rite there is fanning with water once the deities have been invoked. Having taken clarified butter from the Dhruvā vessel with the Sruva-spoon and supported it with the Veda-grass-bundle, he pours the Srauva Āghāra-libation eastward with the formula, "To Prajāpati Manu, svāhā. Having poured the Srauva Āghāra-libation, he gives the call for the cleansing (saṃmārga).

Regarding the statement, "When [the fire] has been cleansed (*saṃmṛṣṭe*), one should choose the most excellent [offering]," although the injunction (*praipa*) for that purpose is already established by the mere fact of the cleansing, the recitation of the injunction is intended to ensure that the injunction does not take the form, "O Agnīdh, cleanse the fire three times" (*agnim agnītriḥ saṃmṛḍḍhi*), since the subsequent use of the singular "cleansed" (*saṃmṛṣṭe*) indicates that the cleansing pertains to the fire alone. One might object: "But in that case, the singular number in 'cleansed' (*saṃmṛṣṭe*) would be contradicted. This is not so.

There is no contradiction because [the singular number] is intended to indicate an alternative view—that the wiping applies to that fire alone and not to the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*). The assumption that the singular number refers to the genus (*jāti*) is itself rejected on the grounds that it would render the recitation of the injunction (*praiṣa*) purposeless. Thus, two positions are established: that the recitation of the injunction is intended to indicate that the wiping applies to the enclosing-sticks as well, and that the singular form "is wiped" (*saṃmṛṣṭaḥ*) is intended to indicate that the wiping applies to the fire alone and not to the enclosing-sticks.

In the view that there is no wiping (*saṃmārga*) of the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), the injunction from the Śruti—"O Agnīdh, wipe the fire three times"—and the sequential prescription of "having offered the *āghāra* with the *sruva*, offer three oblations directed forward," would result in the exclusion of both the wiping and the choosing of the priests (*pravaraṇa*). To prevent this, both are prescribed. The *sruva-āghāra* ends with the replenishing of the *dhruvā*. He chooses the priests as in the Mahāpitṛyajña; this is one Sūtra. As in the Mahāpitṛyajña, [the formula] is "Sit down, O Hotṛ."

The meaning is that just as by the words "the best of speakers" (*vānpravara*) the selection of the *āghāra-hotṛ* is terminated, so too is it done here. The repetition of the phrase "having said, 'Sit down, O Hotṛ! is for the purpose of ensuring there is no interval of time between this and the statement "he takes eight [spoonfuls] from the *dhruvā* into the *juhū*. After the word "from the *dhruvā*," the word "ghee" (*ājyam*) is to be supplied. He takes eight [spoonfuls] of the ghee connected with the *dhruvā* into the *juhū*, and four times into the *upabhṛt*.

The filling of the ladles occurs only during the *jū* (juice-offering) libations, not during the libations from the *upabhṛt*. One should not leave any residue in the *dhruvā*. However, for one who performs the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvattin*), he takes up the two ladles ten times and five times respectively, according to the sequence.
He sets them down, and the Hotṛ causes them to be taken up.

If the *yājuṣa* form of the *hautra* exists, it should be performed according to the *yājuṣa* method alone. The word division is *ādāpayati*. This is a causative (*ṇijanta*) form. The word *adhvaryum* is to be supplied as the object. From the *pravara* formula, "Sit down, O Hotṛ," it is understood that the Hotṛ remains standing up until this point; for him who is standing there, the act of sitting down occurs. The word *nucau* connects with both [the preceding and following] by way of the "lamp at the threshold" (*dehalī-dīpa*) maxim. Here, the placing of the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles is done silently (*tūṣṇīm*), because after the placing of the *dhruvā*, it is not appropriate to place those two with mantras.
When it is said, "O Adhvaryu, pour the ghee-filled ladle into my mouth," he takes up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, steps across once, and performs the sacrifice to the three deities.

The word "south" (*dakṣiṇā*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Āpastamba has likewise recited this. Because of the use of the present tense in the word *ucyamānaḥ* ("being spoken"), the taking up of the two ladles occurs at the very same time as the utterance of this sentence. Although the taking up of the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* is already established by the general rule in the statement "the Hotṛ causes [the Adhvaryu] to take the two ladles," the specific mention here—while the words "O Adhvaryu, bring the two ladles full of ghee" (*ghṛtavatī madhvaryo srucāv āsyasva*) are being spoken—is intended to prevent the application of Āpastamba’s rule, which states that the taking up occurs when the word *ghṛtavatī* alone is uttered.

By this, the opinion of Āśvalāyana and others—that the *jhukādāpana* (the formal request for permission) is solely for the purpose of departing—is also refuted. The word "once" (*sakṛt*) is stated to prevent the performance from being repeated for each individual sacrifice. The meaning is clear. Here, the sacrificer should recite the *pañcahotṛ* formula.
He issues the call for the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*) for the first offering from the north, and for the other two from the south.

The single crossing-over is prescribed for the purpose of the three sacrifices; in that context, since it would follow that even the *puronuvākyā* associated with the first sacrifice must be performed only after the crossing-over, this statement—"He issues the command for the *puronuvākyā* of the first [sacrifice] from the north"—is intended for that purpose. Furthermore, because of the statement "having crossed once" and because the rule for returning (*pratyākramaṇa*) is prescribed after all the sacrifices, it is for the sake of all the sacrifices.

Since it is impossible for one who has passed beyond the middle [of the altar] to return to it, this statement—established by implication for the sake of the two subsequent sacrifices—is intended for all sacrifices: even though returning to the middle after having passed beyond is impossible, one should come from the north along the front of the Āhavanīya fire for the purpose of the *puronuvākyā* and the *saṃpraiṣa*; having given the *saṃpraiṣa*, one should go south along the front of the Āhavanīya for the *āśrāvaṇa* and so forth; and for the purpose of the *puronuvākyā* and the *saṃpraiṣa*, one should again come from the north along the front of the Āhavanīya.

Even for one who has arrived, there is no such thing as "returning" (*pratyākramaṇa*). This is because the conventional usage of "returning" applies only when one comes back by the very same path by which one went. Furthermore, since the verbal root *kram* (to step) signifies the act of stepping with the feet, its capacity refers specifically to the movement of the feet; thus, it transcends the altar (*vedi*). Regarding the movement toward the Āhavanīya fire from the north, he says: this is not of the nature of a foot-step characterized by the transgression of the space immediately preceding the Āhavanīya, but rather it is simply pure movement.

Therefore, since there is no contradiction in proceeding from either side, there would be no fixed rule as to whether one should go to the north or to the south; in order to preclude this, it is specified that "to the south" applies to the other two [verses]. "To the north" means to the north of the altar (*vedi*), or alternatively, to the north of the deity of the first sacrificial act. It is called a *puronuvākyā* because the Hotṛ priest recites it before the invocation of the deity, according to the Vedic text: "One indeed invokes with the *puronuvākyā*. Alternatively, it is a *puronuvākyā* because it announces the sacrifice to the deity beforehand, according to the Vedic text: "He indeed invokes him with the *puronuvākyā*."

The meaning is that he recites the *puronuvākyā* of the first [verse], that is, the introductory verse of the first; or alternatively, after "the *puronuvākyā* of the first," the word "hotṛ" (the priest) is to be supplied; or else, the accusative case here should be understood in the sense of the dative. He sacrifices to Agni with one half of the clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle, and to Soma with the other half. This is clear.
Having brought what was in the *upabhṛt* into the *juhū*, one should sacrifice with that to Viṣṇu.

The statement "having brought it into the *juhū*" is for the purpose of bringing everything; it means that not even a single drop should be left behind. The phrase "with that" (tena) means "with what has been brought into the *juhū*. The inclusion of the word "with that" is intended to prevent the doubt that the sacrifice to Viṣṇu might be performed with only half [of the butter]—due to the recurrence from the previous sūtra of the term "with half" (*ardhena*)—and instead ensures that the sacrifice to Viṣṇu is performed with the entirety of what was brought from the *upabhṛt* into the *juhū*. Because this is a modification of the *upāṃśuyāja*, the formula "Thou art the piercer" (*dabdhir asi*) serves as the consecratory recitation (*anumantraṇa*) for all [the offerings].

These three sacrifices are performed facing inward (pratyaktas), according to the Śruti: "Three oblations are indeed directed outward. Regarding the performance of these oblations, there is a difference of opinion: Baudhāyana’s Sūtra states, "The offering of the oblations [is as follows]," while the Dvaidhasūtra records that Śālīki says, "One should conclude the oblations facing westward. Furthermore, this is clearly stated in the Kalpasūtra: "In the eastern half, in the middle, and in the rear. "Concluding" (saṃsthāpana) means bringing to completion. This is established by both the Śruti and the Dvaidhasūtra concerning the oblation. [End of] Chapter 4, with the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

By the word "sound" (śabda), the action consisting of the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* is to be understood. Even though the office of the *hotṛ* priest is present here, the reading of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses follows that of the Āśvalāyana school alone.
Having stepped back, he offers the *upasad* oblation with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), reciting: "O Agni, that body of yours which is devoid of desire... etc.

Regarding the statement "the Upasad [offerings]," it is explained that one offers with clarified butter from the *ājyasthālī* (butter-pot). In the verse beginning "O Agni, that body of yours which is the *ayāśayā*," there are two mantras—namely, those consisting of the *ayāśayā* and *harāśayā* forms—which, together with the *tanū* (body) word indicated by the *anuṣaṅga* (supplying of omitted words), form a set of three mantras when combined. Thus, the meaning is that one performs each individual Upasad offering with each of these mantras as indicated by their respective opening phrases (*pratīka*). The mention of "each" (*anu*) is for the purpose of indicating the repetition of the offerings. The mantra concludes with "thou hast struck away, svāhā."

In this context, the word *svāhā* is indeed recited. To demonstrate the application of the *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation), Jaimini also stated in the first pāda of the second adhyāya that "the *anuṣaṅga* is the completion of the sentence, because it functions equally with all [the principal elements]," by means of this sūtra. The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: that which effects the completion or conclusion of a sentence is the *anuṣaṅga*. This is because it functions equally (*tulyayogitva*) with all the principal elements (*śeṣin*), due to the sameness of the cause for its connection. Since it is connected to the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), the clarified butter (*ājya*) belongs specifically to the sacrifice.

The author of the *Bhāṣya*, however, says "the clarified butter is unprecedented" (*apūrva*). In this regard, the root [of his argument] must be considered. It has already been stated that the acts of disposal (*pratipattikarma*) may be performed or not; all other ritual procedure (*tantra*) is indeed set aside because it is not sequentially prescribed (*ananukramaṇāt*), and because of the restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyāna*) in the *Brāhmaṇa* passage beginning with "only three *sāmidhenī* verses are to be recited," and so forth. For this very reason, even the expiations (*prāyaścitta*) occasioned by the omission of subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) that might have fallen in between are also set aside.

And so Baudhāyana says: "At the end of the ritual, they should proceed with the *upasads* as if in haste; they should not pay heed to what has been left undone. By this it is shown that the procedure here is indeed rapid, and not moderate. However, the expiation related to the principal rite (*pradhāna*) certainly takes place. The oblation connected to that, however, is performed with the clarified butter from the *ājyasthālī* (butter-pot) alone. They wash their hands with the *madantī* waters; the *brahmā* priest unties the King [Soma], they cause him to swell, and they conceal him as previously described—with the right hands turned upward in the forenoon, and with the left hands turned upward in the afternoon.

Although it could have been stated more concisely as "the washing of the hands, the *viṣṭepana*, the *āpyāyana*, and the *nihavana* are as before," the separate prescription of the washing of the hands and the *viṣṭepana* is for the purpose of making known that the washing of the hands subsequent to the *tānūnaptra* rite is delayed and that its performance by the *brahman* priest is not mandatory.

Alternatively, the re-statement "they wash their hands with *madantī* waters" is for the purpose of indicating that the *madantī* waters here are distinct; it is not the same as those used during the *ātithyā* ceremony. As for the application of the statement "the *brahmán* causes the King to descend," it is exactly as explained immediately above. *Madantī* means heated water. The mention here is for the purpose of indicating the proper occasion for the duties of the *brahmán*. Just as the phrase "as before" is used for the sake of reciting the respective mantras.

With those whose right hands are turned upward, [he touches] their left hands; with those whose left hands are turned upward, [he touches] their right hands. "The waters gladden the Agnīdh" (*agnīnmadantyāpā3*), etc., applies here as well. Thus Āpastamba says: "The formula beginning with 'The waters gladden the Agnīdh' (*agnīnmadantyāpā3*) is performed because of its connection to the *anuvacana*. He issues the command: "O Agnīdh, announce the wives of the gods; O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā!"

This is clear. Regarding the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, in the seventh book: after the call (*praisha*) "O Āgnīdh, recite for the wives of the gods," the explanation of the wives of the gods (*devapatnī-vyākhyāna*) must be performed. To address the inquiry as to how this is done, he says:
"Vāc is the wife of Vāyu"—having sat down behind the Gārhapatya fire, the Āgnīdhra recites the names of the wives of the gods, or [the formula] "The cow of Indra."

To the west of the Gārhapatya fire, sitting down very close to the Gārhapatya, he recites the mantras that designate the wives of the gods (*devapatnī*). These are contained in the section beginning with "The army of Indra" (*senendrasya*). "Recitation" (*vyākhyāna*) means reading word by word (*vākyaśaḥ*). The ellipsis to be supplied is simply that one should say [the mantra] immediately after the words "dhenā vā" (or "dhenā"). Thus, the meaning becomes that it should be recited continuously (*saṃtataṃ*). For if the term "recites" (*vyācaṣṭe*) were to carry over [from a previous rule], there would arise a contradiction between two positions regarding its being intended for continuous recitation.

Now, one must accept that the expression "atha vyācaṣṭe" (then he explains) refers specifically to continuous recitation through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because figurative indication is simpler than the necessity of supplying missing words (*adhyāhāra*). Where there is the statement "he explains," there is indeed recitation word by sentence (*vākyaśaḥ*). And where the author of the Sūtras has performed a continuous recitation of a mantra that was [originally] recited word by sentence, there it is simply continuity.

However, as for the lack of restriction (*aniyama*) elsewhere, according to the method stated in the introductory section (*upoddhāta*), this statement—established here through the same principle of optionality (*vikalpa*)—indicates that where all the mantras contained in a section (*anuvāka*) are employed in a single context, there is no restriction; but in cases such as the employment of mantras from the *pavamāna-anuvāka* and others, the recitation of the *vāsaḥśas* [formula] itself is fixed.

The lowing voice (*dhenā*) belongs to Indra; the path (*pathyā*) to Bṛhaspati; speech (*vāk*) to Pūṣan; consecration (*udīkṣā*) to Soma; the earth (*pṛthivī*) to Agni; the *gāyatrī* to the Vasus; the *triṣṭubh* to the Rudras; the *jagatī* to the Ādityas; the *anuṣṭubh* to Viṣṇu; the *virāj* to Varuṇa; the *paṅkti* to the Sacrifice; *anumati* to Prajāpati; faith (*śraddhā*) to Mitra; procreation (*pramūti*) to Savitṛ; the ray (*marīci*) to Sūrya; Rohiṇī to the Moon; Arundhatī to the Ṛṣis; lightning (*vidyut*) to Parjanya; the four quarters and the four intermediate directions; day and night.
Agriculture, rain, prosperity, honor, water, herbs, and the sun—these are the wives of the gods; such is the reading in continuous sequence. He states the duty of the Subrahmaṇya:
the Subrahmaṇya priest invokes the Subrahmaṇyā.

The *subrahmaṇya* is the reciter of the *sāman* that rests upon the *subrahmaṇyā-om* formula; he invokes the *subrahmaṇyā*. The meaning is that he approaches Indra by means of the *sāman* resting upon the *subrahmaṇyā-khyā* formula. In other words, he addresses Indra with the word *subrahmaṇyā* and so forth for the purpose of the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing). Alternatively, the meaning is that he should chant the *sāman* resting upon the *subrahmaṇyā-khyā* formula for the sake of summoning Indra. Thus, "subrahmaṇyā" is the name of the *sāman* produced from this *subrahmaṇyā-om* formula.

The feminine gender designation, however, is due to its being a qualification of the specific speech-form known as the *subrahmaṇyā*; for there is a scriptural text stating, "Speech indeed is the *subrahmaṇyā*. Āpastamba states regarding the location for the invocation of the *subrahmaṇyā*: "He invokes the *subrahmaṇyā* on the *utkara* heap; the sacrificer follows it with the same mantra as before. Lāṭyāyana and Drāhyāyaṇa state: "Standing in front of the southern door of the eastern door. That ritual procedure is to be understood from its own respective sūtra. These [rites] are performed following the *upasad* days.
"Following each Upasad, following each Upasad"—the meaning is that these rites are to be performed after every Upasad.
Thus, for three nights, he proceeds with the Pravargya and Upasad rites in the evening and in the morning.

Thus far, the general procedure for the *upasad* has been described. Now, the number of *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, as well as the number of days, is stated: the combination of three nights is called *trirātra*. According to the rule *ahaḥ-sarvaikadeśa-saṃkhyāta-puṇyācca rātreḥ*, the suffix *ac* is applied to the word *rātri* when it follows a numeral, due to the recurrence of the word "numeral" (*saṃkhyā*) from the preceding rule *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ*. By the rule *dvigurekavacanam*, it takes the singular form.

In a *dvigu* compound denoting a collective (*samāhāra*), neuter gender applies according to the rule "that [compound] is neuter. A *dvigu* is a compound preceded by a numeral, based on the sūtra "a *dvigu* is a compound preceded by a numeral. Here, the word *rātri* (night) refers to a day (*divasa*), due to its co-occurrence with the words *sāyam* (evening) and *prātaḥ* (morning). Now, one might object: "In that case, it should simply be said 'tryahaṃ' for the sake of brevity; since the goal can be achieved by a direct path, a circuitous one is improper. Thus, for what purpose is the expression 'trirātram' used? This is true.

It was stated in that manner to indicate the absence of fault even when the ritual action is performed at night after the *upasad* has been initiated, because there is no futility due to its necessity. However, the fault regarding the *vaṣaṭ*-call during the day is established by the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra*. As for the fact that the *pravargya* may be performed at night even though it has not yet been formally commenced, this point will be established by the very *jñāpaka* (indicative mark) that is to be mentioned in the *Pravargya-sūtra*. This procedure that has been described pertains to the morning time, as it is the one that is immediately present.

That same [procedure] applies to the other performances as well. In that context, because the word "evening" (sāyam) immediately brings to mind the performance associated with the previously mentioned morning time, it is mentioned first. [The sequence is: on the first day, evening; on the second day, morning and evening; and on the third day, morning and evening. In this manner, the *pravargya* and the *upasads* constitute the *pravargyopasada*; the meaning is that he proceeds with these two. The singular number is used with reference to the *adhvaryu*, who is the primary agent. [He performs them] in the forenoon with the two forenoon rites, and in the afternoon with the two afternoon rites.

The phrase "he proceeds with the *pravargya* and the *upasads*" is understood as a continuation [of the previous rule]. "Well-forgone-morning" (*supūrvāhna*) means a very good morning; "well-later-day" (*svaparāh*) means a very good afternoon. By the word "well-forgone" (*supūrva*), the time consisting of the first half of the forenoon is taken; by the word "well-later" (*svapara*), the time consisting of the second half of the afternoon is taken. Even there, the two *ghaṭikās* following [the division] and the two *ghaṭikās* before sunset are to be abandoned. Here, the division is either twofold or threefold. Those occurring in the forenoon are "forenoon-related" (*paurvāhnikyau*); those occurring in the afternoon are "afternoon-related" (*āparāhnikyau*). He states the rule for the performance of the *upasat* oblations:
With the mantra, "O Agni, that body of yours which is fond of offerings," one offers the *sruva*-ladle-oblations at evening and morning on the first day.

The analysis of the compound *sāyamprātaḥ* is simply "evening and morning. According to the *vārttika* stating "there is no fixed rule regarding *dharma* and so forth," this form is correct; *dharmādi* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. When two words denoting both times are used together, the word *sāyam* (evening) is generally placed first. In that regard, in the *agnihotra* oblation and similar rites, it remains exactly as it is; there, the commencement is seen to begin specifically with the evening.

Regarding the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, Āśvalāyana states that one should offer the prepared *haviṣya* food both in the evening and in the morning; yet, even though "evening and morning" is mentioned, it is observed that the commencement begins with the morning in accordance with other authorities. This is also the case here [in the present context]. (Note: Variant reading *vakreṇa*).

86.7.658. Since the ritual begins precisely at dawn, it must be stated that one performs the *pravargya* rite in the evening in accordance with that [dawn] commencement. Although this could have been expressed directly, the general indication serves to make known the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): "The specific meaning is understood through the explanation; for there is no lack of definition due to doubt. Therefore, because the explanation regarding the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) takes the form of its commencement in the evening, the specific understanding arises that the evening is indeed the point of commencement.

In the Vaiśvadeva offering, the sequence is indicated by the mantras "To those who wander by day" for the daytime and "To those who wander by night" for the nighttime; furthermore, because of the sequential appearance of the words "day and night" in the two subsequent [mantras]—"Desiring the oblation by day and night"—it is understood that the commencement must specifically begin with the morning. In the Agnihotra, because of the sequential appearance of the mantras "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā" and "Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā," it is understood that the commencement must specifically begin with the evening.

In the present context, although the sequence is observed in both ways, there is the sequence of the mantras as follows: "Agni is light, svāhā; Sūrya is light, svāhā," and so forth; and the sequence for the specific application of the mantras is as follows: "With 'svāhā to you for the rays of Sūrya,' he places [the offering] in the morning; with 'svāhā to you for the stars,' [he places it] in the evening"; and the sequence for the injunction regarding time is as follows: "With the two [offerings] belonging to the forenoon in the forenoon, and with the two belonging to the afternoon in the afternoon."

In this context, the purpose of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is that, by way of explaining the superiority of the signs supporting the commencement in the morning over the signs supporting the commencement in the evening, one understands the specific distinction that the commencement belongs to the morning alone. Therefore, in the present case, although "evening and morning" (*sāyaṃprātaḥ*) is read in accordance with the majority of manuscripts, the sequence "morning and evening" (*prātaḥsāyam*) is established. This is for the purpose of demonstrating the elided connection (*anuṣaṅga*) of the word *tanūḥ*.

Since the rule was not established by the preceding sūtra which prescribes the *upasad* oblations, this sūtra is for that purpose. That [oblation] whose offering (*pradāna*) is made with the *sruva* ladle is called *sruvapradānā*; this word is in the feminine gender, accusative case, singular number. This is a technical name (*saṃjñā*) for the *upasad* oblation; it is a term based on both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). While one might simply say "she offers" (*juhoti*), the specific expression "*sruvapradānām*" is used because there is a particular distinction in this case.

This [act] consists of the imitation of the action of discharging an arrow. Accordingly, another Sūtra states: "With the mantra, 'O Agni, that seat of thine which is in the air' (yā te agne'yāśayā), he offers this oblation with the *sruva* ladle, as if discharging an arrow. The meaning is that on the first day, during the performance of the first *upasat*, one offers the oblations with the *sruva* using the mantra "yā te agne'yāśayā" for both the morning and evening rites.
On the second day, one uses the mantra "yā te agne rajāśayā."

The phrase "he offers with the offering-spoon" (*sruvapradānāṃ juhoti*) continues [from the previous rule]. On the second day, the second *upasad* day, he offers with the offering-spoon during both the morning and evening performances of the second *upasad*, using the mantra: "O Agni, that body of yours which dwells in the dust" (*yā te agne rajāśayā tanūḥ*). Since the connection (*anuṣaṅga*) of the word "that" (*sā*) was demonstrated in the preceding mantra, its application here is also implicitly shown by the sense of the context. On the third day, [he offers] with the mantra: "O Agni, that body of yours which dwells in the heat" (*yā te agne harāśayā*).

Here too, the [rules] beginning with "non-eternal" (anīti) apply. On the third day—that is, on the day of the third *upasad*—one offers the *nūvan* oblations at both the morning and evening performances of the third *upasad* with the mantra: "O Agni, that which is thy heat-dwelling... (*yā te agne harāśayā*). The ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) in this mantra is indeed recited in the Śruti.
Although [the word] "yadi" (if) seems disconnected, [it is explained as follows]:
"If they should fight in front, one should offer [the oblation] after placing iron in the first [ladle]."

If the forts of the enemies of a Kṣatriya who is performing a sacrifice should fight against him along with his own [forces], or if the enemies should desire [to seize] the forts, then, having placed iron—made of black metal—into the clarified butter for the first *upasad* oblation and having cast it in, he should offer the oblation with the mantra: "O Agni, that body of yours which is the iron-natured (*ayāśayā*). Silver-gold (*rajata-hiraṇya*) is [placed] in the middle one; in each of the middle ones, having placed silver-gold into the clarified butter for the middle *upasad* oblation, [he should offer with the mantra]: "That body of yours..."

One should offer an oblation with the mantra: "O Agni, the body that dwells in the dust. The mention of *hiraṇya* (gold) is intended to demonstrate that the designation *hiraṇyapada* (the gold-footed) applies to silver as well; for there are also indicative marks such as, "All gold was silver; it became gold of inferior color," where the word *durvarṇa* (inferior color) denotes silver. Since the word *hiraṇya* can denote both gold and silver, there might arise the doubt as to which kind of *hiraṇya* is to be taken here; the mention of silver is used to remove that doubt. [In the case] of the *uttamā* (highest/last) [offering], [one uses] *harita* (green/gold).

In the *uttamā* [offering], having placed green [gold] into the clarified butter used for the *upasad* oblation with the mantra, "O Agni, that body of yours which dwells in gold (*harāśayā*)," one should offer the oblation. The word "green" (*harita*) refers specifically to gold, as indicated by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "All gold is green," and also by the indicative mark, "From them, he milked Soma into a green vessel.
According to some teachers, this rule applies if they should fight in battle;
that is to say, if the enemies of a Kṣatriya sacrificer should fight in battle—that is, should engage in combat—then this is the procedure, according to the opinion of certain teachers.
The ritual procedure not connected with a sacrifice is [called] *kalpa*. 13.

The meaning is this: if no other means exists, then there is a connection with the sacrifice; however, if another means does exist, there is no connection with the sacrifice at all. This meaning is obtained through the force of the prefix *sam*. Having performed the two midday *Pravargya* and *Upasad* rites belonging to the forenoon, one proceeds eastward from the front of the *Prāgvaṃśa* hall, takes three steps toward the east, and drives in a peg; that [peg] is in the western half of the *Vedi*.

By the suffix *lyap* in the word *pracarya*, it is indicated that [the subsequent action] must occur immediately after the construction of the altar (*vedi*) and the sacrificial shed (*vimāna*). Consequently, the bestowing of the vow (*vratapradāna*) and the covering with *udumbara* branches (*parivāsayati*) follow immediately after that.

From the point where the southern cord originating from the eastern edge of the *prāgvaṃśa* (front hall) intersects with the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord, one drives a peg three *prakramas* away along the direction of the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord; that peg should be placed at the intersection of the southern cord originating from the western edge and the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord on the western half of that peg—this becomes the middle [peg]. The construction of the altar (*vedi*) takes place right here, because it has already been observed in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) prior to the measurement of the altar.
[One measures: "I measure thee, the milk-rich cow of the gods, the good milker, the unswerving; may Indra drink the Soma."
This word is redundant.

Having stepped thirty-six steps eastward with the formula, "May there be security for us," he drives in a wooden pin (śaṅku) in the eastern half. This is from the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, in the seventh book.

The word "to see" (vedeḥ) is understood from the previous context. Starting from the first mark dug at the edge of the altar, one measures thirty-six steps eastward along the line of the altar; having measured these, one drives a peg into the point where the north-south line and the east-west line intersect in the eastern half of the altar. That becomes the central point of the eastern half of the altar. The mantra is recited only once.

Having stepped fifteen steps south and fifteen steps north from the western peg, one drives in two pegs; these are the two hips. Having stepped twelve steps south and twelve steps north from the eastern peg, one drives in two pegs; these are the two shoulders.

The word "prakramān" (steps) is carried over from the preceding sūtra before the word "prakramya" (having stepped). Since measurement is already established by the Śulba-sūtra itself, the statement here is for the purpose of ensuring the application of the mantra even in measurements involving the hips and other parts. If this sūtra were intended merely as an injunction for independent measurement, it would result in an inconsistency, because measurement would be impossible without the method prescribed in the Śulba-sūtra.

Therefore, regarding the instruction "fifteen to the south," one first takes one step with the mantra and then takes the others silently, for the sake of obtaining the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by the mantra. The same applies to "fifteen to the north," and also to "twelve to the south and twelve to the north. In this way, including both hips and both shoulders on the spine (*pṛṣṭhyā*), the repetition of the mantra five times is established. [The word] *paścārdhya* means that which exists in the rear half; therefore [it is so called].

The term *pūrvādhyardha* means "that which exists in the eastern half"; the suffix *-ya-* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *diś* (Pāṇini 4.3.54). The reading *paścārdhāt pūrvārdhāt* is indeed a corruption. This is known from the *Śulbasūtra*: "In the case of the Soma-altar (*saumikī vedi*), it is understood that there are three hundred *pada*s or *prakrama*s as the transverse side at the back, thirty-six as the longitudinal side, and twenty-four as the transverse side at the front. From this sūtra, it is understood that even in the measurement of the altar, *pada*s are interchangeable with *prakrama*s.

Regarding this, the manifold nature of the *pada* (step) is stated in the *Śulbasūtra*: "In the case of the *pada*, the *yuga*, the *aratni*, the *viyati*, and the *śamyā*, there is freedom of choice among these measures for the purpose of measurement, because the meaning of the word is subject to doubt (*viśayitvāt*). "Because it is subject to doubt" means because it is of many kinds. Baudhāyana says that a *pada* is ten *aṅgulas*; he also says that a small *pada* is ten *aṅgulas*. Kātyāyana says that a *pada* is twelve *aṅgulas*. These three types of *padas* are optional alternatives to the common worldly *pada*.

These same [measures] doubled or tripled are the *prakramas*; by this very measure of the *prakrama*, the measurement is made for the *soma* sacrifice involving the piling of the sevenfold fire-altar (*agniciti*). However, measurement by *padas* does not occur here, because the area required for the fire-altar (*agni-kṣetra*) would be impossible [to fit]. Thus, the increase of twenty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in the sevenfold fire-altar has been explained. Regarding the piling of the fire-altar, however, some maintain that there is an optional choice (*vikalpa*) among all the measures of *pada* and *prakrama* according to one's preference.

Others, however, maintain the following rule for measurement in the piling of the fire-altar (*agni-citi*): by means of twenty-finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) or a step (*prakrama*). In the case of a single-fold fire-altar, [the measurement] is by twenty-finger-breadths; in those of two-fold up to five-fold, it is by twenty-four finger-breadths; in those of six-fold up to twelve-fold, it is by thirty finger-breadths; or by a worldly double-step (*dvipada*); and in those of thirteen-fold and so on, it is by thirty-six finger-breadths, and so forth—in all these cases, the fires [are measured] by forty-five finger-breadths.

In that case, they arise according to the *prakrama* (step), and there an increase in the Veda (altar) should be made in accordance with the fire-altar, since this has been demonstrated in the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*). For example, in the fifty-fold fire-altar, a staff of fifty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) serves as the substitute for the *prakrama*; in the one-hundred-and-one-fold altar, it is eighty finger-breadths, and so forth. Having measured that [the Veda] by the method of Śulba, one fixes pegs here and there for the purpose of encircling it with a cord.
Having prepared the altar with a measurement made diagonally, he stretches a cord around it clockwise.

"Diagonally" means by means of a diagonal cord; "measurement" refers to that which is to be accomplished by one cord or multiple cords according to the method stated in the *Śulba-sūtra*. Having prepared the altar with that measurement, he—meaning he encircles—the sacrificial ground (*vedi-kṣetra*) by means of a cord (*spandyā*), winding it all around clockwise once pegs have been driven into the four corners. "Diagonally" (*akṣṇayā*) is an indeclinable.

In this context as well, the term does not signify "clockwise" (prādakṣiṇya), since that is already established by the technical rule (paribhāṣā) itself; rather, it signifies "conformity" (anukūlya). The proof for this meaning has already been demonstrated. Thus, it is established that one stretches [the cord] firmly in such a way as to be conducive to making the edge of the altar known.
One stretches along the *pṛṣṭhyā* line.

Although the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord was already laid down previously for the purpose of establishing the altar (*vedi*), its continued utility is nevertheless indicated here. Even if that altar is destroyed after the measurement (*vimāna*) is completed, the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord must be laid down once again; its purpose is stated as: "having spread the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) continuously along the *pṛṣṭhyā*. The word *pṛṣṭha* denotes the middle. A rope situated in the middle is a *pṛṣṭhyā* rope; the suffix *ya* is applied according to the rule beginning with *dig-ādi*.

By the statement "one should measure by diagonal measurement," the method of laying out [the altar] is indicated. The procedure for this is set forth in the *Śulbasūtra*: "The diagonal cord (*akṣṇayā rajju*) consists of three and four units; with these multiplied three times, the two shoulders (*aṃsau*) are formed, and with them multiplied four times, the two hips (*śroṇī*) are formed. Regarding this: when the transverse cords (*tiryag-mānī*) consist of three and four units, the shoulders are formed by those three, four, and five-unit cords when they are multiplied three times—that is, when they are laid upon one another. The hips are formed by those same cords multiplied four times.

Just as the *trikā* cord is repeated three times, the *dvādaśikā* four times, the *ṣoḍaśikā* three times, and the *pañcikā* three times, making a *viṃśikā*; by these three cords—repeated three times, namely the *dvādaśikā*, the *ṣoḛśikā*, and the *viṃśikā*—the two shoulders (*aṃsau*) are to be measured. By these same four cords—repeated four times, namely the *pañcadaśikā*, the *viṃśikā*, and the *pañcaviṃśikā*—the two hips (*śroṇī*) are to be measured. Thus is the layout performed with these six cords.

Another method is stated in that very same place: "The diagonal cord (*akṣṇayā rajju*) consists of a twelve-unit and a five-unit [cord] and a thirteen-unit [cord]; with those doubled, the two shoulders (*aṃsau*) are formed; with those [same cords], the two hips (*śroṇī*) are formed. Yet another method is also stated in that very same place: "The diagonal cord consists of a fifteen-unit and an eight-unit [cord] and a seventeen-unit [cord]; with those, the two hips are formed; the diagonal cord consists of a twelve-unit and a thirty-five-unit [cord] and a thirty-seven-unit [cord]; with those, the two shoulders are formed."

Another alternative method is also stated in that same *Viṃśikā*, in the eighteenth section on the summary: "Having fixed the two ends at the two ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, having extended [the cord] southward by fifteen [units], one drives in a *śaṅku* (peg). Likewise from the north; those two are the two hips (*śroṇī*). With the cord reversed, having extended it by fifteen [units], one drives in a twelve-unit *śaṅku* from the north; those two are the two shoulders (*aṃsau*). This is the measurement described using a single cord."

This is the method for laying out the altar (viharaṇa). This is an elaboration of the measurement described as "as long as the length" (yāvadāyāma). Furthermore, in that same [text] it says: "There are this many altars for the layout of the altar-sites"; the meaning is that there are this many [altars] without any reduction (cheda). Moreover, in that same [text] it says: "The great altar (mahāvedi) consists of one thousand minus twenty-eight paces (pada)"; the mention of *pada* here is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the *prakrama* (step).

The method for counting is also stated in that very same place: "Starting from the southern half, one should mark twelve [units] on the southern cord; having shifted the cut, one should lay down [the bricks] on the other side. That [shape] is a long square; one should observe it thus arranged. Starting from the southern half, one should mark the cord at twelve [units] to the south of the westernmost spine.

One should place the long triangle, measuring thirty-six [units] by twenty-seven, inverted on its northern side at the southern corner. It becomes a long rectangle with thirty-six units as its east-west dimension and twenty-seven units as its north-south dimension; one should count it as such. When those two, twenty-seven and thirty-six, are combined, they become nine hundred and seventy-two. Now, for the easy understanding of the ritualists, these verses (kārikās) are composed: "The altar is measured either by three kinds of *pada*s or by *prakrama*s."

First, on the fire-line (vahni), there is one and a half [units]; on the moon (niśākara), one and a half [units] of the fire-line; on the half-moon (sārdhacandra), one and a half [units] of the half-moon; on the fire (anala), half [a unit]; on the crescent (candraka), half [a unit]; on the black path (kṛṣṇavartman), half [a unit]; likewise, on the half [unit], one and a half crescents; on the one and a half Vedas (vede), likewise half [a unit]; on the moon (candra), half [a unit]; and on the one and a half carriers (vāhika), half [a unit]. Thus, including the lower part, there are twenty-one pegs (śaṅku) along the back line. These should have sharp points and be fine, firm, and straight.

The side-measure (pārśvamānī) is declared by Padiśami; the cross-measure (tiryamānī) is proclaimed as sixteen [units] and twenty [units] by Akṣiṇa. First, at the fifth [mark], the southern hip-line is established; likewise, the northern hip-line is proclaimed from Budha. Then, having fixed the cord for the side-measure from the east to the west at the eye-mark, the wise man should perform the ritual layout (viharaṇa) for the two Mahāvedi altars. At the end, in the fourteenth [mark], is the southern [corner] of the Mahāvedi.

Thus it is declared for twelve [parts], and the same is recorded for the northern [side]. Now, having shifted the two cords, the subsequent distribution by rope is as follows: in the second and seventh [spaces] from the south, the southern hip of the *sadas* is considered to be; in the tenth and eighth [spaces], the northern hip of that [same structure] is proclaimed. In the third and tenth [spaces] on the right, the *audumbarī* pillar is at the lower station; in the fourth and twelfth [spaces] on the right, the fire-hearth (*dhiṣṇya*) of the *praśāstṛ* is said to be. To the north of that, the southern [hearth] is proclaimed for the sake of the *hotṛ*'s fire-hearth.

To the north [of the Hotṛ’s hearth], there should be a half-hearth joined to it; likewise, another half-hearth to its north. To the north of that are the hearths for the Śaṃsin, Pautrī, and others, numbering as many as the Vedas. All these hearths are one span (prādeśa) in measure, with an interval of one span between them. The measurement of the Acchāvāka’s hearth should be slightly more than that. And in the fifth and sixth [spaces] to the south is the southern shoulder of the Sadas. [Chapter 683, Section 4, Paṭala: With the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.]

The eighth [mark] is said to be on the tenth [line], and the shoulder of the *sadas* is on the eleventh. On the sixth and fifteenth [lines] is the hip of the *havirdhāna*, and the southern [hip] is on the fifth. (14) In the same way, the northern hip of the *havirdhāna* is proclaimed; the *mānīya* [mark] is on the eighth and sixteenth [lines] on the south. (15) Likewise, the wise one has declared the *āgnīdhra* hearth on the northern [side]. Now, the method of laying out both is demonstrated. (16) [It is done] with the side-measuring cord between the great altar (*mahāvedi*) and the end-cord of the southern [section].

At the intersection to the north, the middle point is recorded at twelve finger-breadths; there, one should fix a peg for the Mārjālīya hearth at the junction of the northern edge of the Mahāvedi and the line called pārśvamānī. At the intersection to the south, the middle point is recorded at twelve finger-breadths; there, one should fix a peg for the Āgnīdhra hearth at the ninth and seventeenth steps, and with a half-step to the south.

The center of the *uparava* situated in the direction of Prabhañjana is proclaimed [to be] two *prādeśas* from that middle of the *uparava*. The center of the *uparava* situated in the direction of Rakṣodhipati is proclaimed [to be] two *prādeśas* from that middle of the *uparava*. The center of the *uparava* situated in the direction of Aparājita is proclaimed [to be] at the tenth and eighteenth steps, and one and a half [steps] to the south. The center of the *uparava* situated in the direction of Vītihotra is proclaimed [to be] two *prādeśas* from that middle of the *uparava*.

These [measures] are declared to be one span (prādeśa) long with an interval of one span; at the twelfth and the twentieth [finger-breadths], the southern shoulder is five [units]. Then, the northern shoulder of the altar (dhāna) is likewise proclaimed to be the same. Now, having fixed the cord as the lateral measurement from east to west at the axle-end (akṣiṇaka), the wise ones should perform the subsequent ritual layout (viharaṇa). At the twelfth and the twentieth [finger-breadths], the southern shoulder of the small altar (laghuvedi) is declared to be five [units]; the northern one is likewise remembered to be so.

In the sixth and the fifteenth [steps], the southern *laghuvedi* (small altar) is established; likewise, in the five [steps] following, the northern *laghuvedi* should be so. This measurement may also be performed using a cord laid in reverse. Now, the alternative method for the two corners (*aṇīyas-pura*) is demonstrated here: the southern shoulder (*dakṣiṇa-aṃsa*) is established at the four [steps], and the northern one is likewise declared to be so. According to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, the southern hip (*dakṣiṇā śroṇi*) is thus, and the northern one is considered to be exactly the same.

Some have declared that the *yuga* (the distance between the two poles) is ten *padās* in length. In this view, which applies to the three Vedas and the *Aśvalāyana* school, the southern hip (*śroṇi*) is thus; likewise, the northern one should be so, and it is described in this very manner. Alternatively, it may be a *yuga* in length on all sides, but it must not be smaller than that. At the location of the eastern end-mark (*aṃśa*), the pit for the sacrificial post (*yūpāvaṭa*) is prescribed. Now, the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) for the *Āgnīdhra* hearth is shown: from the western corner-stake (*śaṅku*) of the altar (*vedi*), one measures toward the north by the distance of the sun (twelve *padās*).

The mark of the *mahāvaya* and the mark of the northern shoulder—between these two marks is a cord, and there is also a mark in the middle. (34) There is also a mark in the middle of the cord at the northern edge of the great altar (*mahāvedi*). Between these two [marks] as well, there should be a cord; then, to the west, having established a gnomon (*śaṅku*), (35) the mark made at the sun [position] and a cord of that same measure should be laid out to the north; there, a clear mark is to be made. (36)

From the northern shoulder of the great altar (mahāvedi), the thread should be extended; likewise, from these two [shoulders], the thread should go to the end of the altar. Having made a mark in the middle at a distance of two and a half padas to the front, and having struck [lines] like a square, a mark should be made behind as well. Having constructed a pavilion there, one should enclose it with mats. One should make a door on the south, sixteen finger-breadths wide; alternatively, its width may be one aratni, or there may be no door at all.

However, there is no enclosure at all on the right side. This method has been demonstrated for the case where the pavilion is straight. Now, the method for the case where the pavilion is curved is as follows: Having made a mark in the middle of the cord at the northern edge of the great altar (mahāvedi), one should proceed according to that cord two and a half paces to the east and likewise to the west; thereafter, it should be like the abode of Śaṃsu. The curvature should be exactly as that of the great altar.

The curvature of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) is also [an option]; thus two alternatives are recorded. When the supreme bliss (paramāna) is the altar (vedī), then the sacrificial hall (sadas) and other structures should be constructed according to the measure of a *pada*, as declared by the wise. If the *prakrama* consists of two *padas* totaling ten *aṅgulas*, then the sacrificial hall and other structures must be made according to the measure of a *pada*. If the *prakrama* consists of either twelve or fifteen *aṅgulas*, [the same applies]. [Chapter 410] Accompanied by the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

The height of the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* should indeed be one *aratni*; likewise, when measuring according to the dimensions of the body, the doors should also be measured accordingly. They should be exactly one *bharana* in measure; thus has this measurement been declared. These verses have been set forth for the easy understanding of those engaged in sacrificial rites. 4–48.

He performs that [rite] in the same manner as in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa), except for what pertains to the bending [of the grass-bundle]. Having performed the pressing, he prepares the altar (vedi) according to the measurement of the bending, following the procedure of the New and Full Moon sacrifices. By the statement "as in the darśapūrṇamāsa," it is understood that the ritual prior to the digging up [of the earth] is indeed the archetypal (prakṛta) one; the specific instruction (praiṣa) mentioned in the *Acchidra-prapāṭhaka* does not apply here. Just as in the New Moon sacrifice, the second space is to the east of the altar, and it is stated that one throws the *stambayajus* from the north. By this very [rule], the location for taking the *stambayajus* is also explained: from the eastern half of the middle third of the altar.

Regarding this, Baudhāyana says: "One draws out the *stambayajuḥ* from the *uparavas*. Here, the word *kāla* signifies location; Kātyāyana states explicitly: "One draws out the *stambayajuḥ* from the location of the *uparavas*. One performs the actions beginning with "This for him," etc., up to the digging, excluding the *saṃnamana* (concluding formula), using the wooden sword (*sphya*), the *vighana*, the rib-bone (*parśu*), and the axe (*paraśu*).

The connection is made by modifying the words to "they perform the *pedi*. Āpastamba, however, has stated this quite clearly: "Because this rite is specific (*vaiśeṣika*), the specific expiation (*śreṣa*) mentioned in the *Ācchidrika* section of the *Prapāṭhaka* applies here alone. It is as follows: 'O men, come and prepare this altar, which possesses wealth, possesses the Rudras, and possesses the Ādityas—the famous earth of heaven—by means of which this sacrificer shall not suffer harm, at the impulse of the god Savitṛ.'"

Regarding this mantra, the addition of *yad viśvadevyāvatīm* and so forth, which was mentioned by Baudhāyana, should not be incorporated, as that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Rather, only that addition which is connected to a required subsidiary act (*aṅgakarma*) should be incorporated. This principle is to be observed everywhere. By the rule *yathārūpam itaraḥ*, the author of the Sūtra has stated the application (*viniyoga*), yet because it was not explicitly stated, it is optional (*kṛtākṛtaḥ*). The status of being a *preṣa* (directive) follows from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the word *kṛṇuta*. In this context, the *parikarmins* (attendants) are the ones to whom the directive is addressed.

Therefore, they alone are the performers. Just as in the injunction "make the *prakṛtis*" the plural number indicates that the attendants (*parikarmika*) are the performers, so too here this command refers to the purpose of making the *vidhana*, striking the clods of earth, and so forth. Here, the *sphya* is merely a common (worldly) tool because it is to be discarded. The *vidhana* is a mallet; alternatively, it is the rib-bone of an ox. The *paraśu* is an axe. *Sphayana* is the spreading out of the clay; with the *vidhana* one strikes the clods of earth and such; with the *pardi* one cuts grass; and with the *paraśu* one cuts the roots.

At the conclusion of the three rites beginning with the *vidhana* [rite], the word "animal" (*paśu*) refers to a female, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra: "The intellect has gone forth; she goes to the sacrificial grass. He places the *smaya* and other implements exactly as they were previously known, because they will be used later. The *sphyā* is a wooden sword; however, for those items not intended for offering, it is made of *dhāraṇa* wood according to the forthcoming paribhāṣā-sūtra, or in its absence, from a tree suitable for sacrifice. The *vidhana* is likewise. In the absence of that, a branch of the *āyapsī* tree is to be taken, as it is suitable due to its resemblance to that shape.

Now, the *parvan* (joint) is severely censured. Since Yājñavalkya has severely condemned the practice of *asvarya* (lack of self-restraint), stating that one should not even perform a duty if it is hated by the world (*asvaryaṃ lokavidviṣṭaṃ dharmam apy ācaret na*), and since Satyāṣāḍha, in his *Śrautasūtra*, states that this [practice] should not be performed, the learned take only an iron animal in its place. Even when the *parvan* is made of iron, the use of the word "animal" (*paśu*) in the mantra is not contradictory; for it is well known in the world that "an axe is made of iron" (*paraśur āyasamayaḥ*).

"The four-tufted young woman, well-formed, with ghee as her face, stands in the midst of the world; upon her two birds are seated—of these two, the gods have assigned their respective portions. This is the consecration to be performed by the Adhvaryu priest. Thus says Āpastamba regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

Having performed everything except the bending [of the grass] prior to the northern boundary-line (parigrāha), he consecrates [the earth] with the mantra: "The young woman with four locks, well-formed, with ghee as her face, in the midst of the world; upon her sit two birds of beautiful wings; of those two, the gods have established their domain. The connection is made by modifying the verb to "he makes the altar" (*vediṃ karoti*). According to the *Āpastamba-sūtra*, because the word *vedi* is used in the context of the preceding [text], only the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) is to be understood, and not the great altar (*mahāvedi*).

Otherwise, there would be an inconsistency regarding the shared agency (*samānakartṛkatva*) understood from the suffix *-lyap* in the expression "he makes the altar after having consecrated it" (*vediṃ kṛtvābhimantrya*). Nor can it be argued that the connection with the preceding sūtra—"they make the altar with the *sphya* [sacrificial wooden sword], the *vidhana*, and the axe"—is such that the word "altar" (*vedi*) refers only to the *mahāvedi* (the great altar), because this would entail that the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) has a performer other than the *adhvaryu*, in order to maintain the requirement of shared agency. And this is not an acceptable conclusion (*neṣṭāpatti*).

Since the interpretation of [the action] as having a primary agent is logically consistent, it is inappropriate to postulate a figurative or external agent; for this very reason, the subsequent sūtra—"He causes [the altar] to be covered with Udumbara branches or Plakṣa branches"—is correctly understood as an injunction pertaining to the Uttaravedi. Let this discussion of the Āpastamba-sūtra stand. The sūtra "With the Sphya and the wooden sword" is indeed merely a supplement to the construction of the original (prakṛta) altar.

By such injunctions as "he cuts that which the wooden sword (*sphya*) surpasses," "having scraped off the uppermost layer with the *sphya*, he throws it onto the rubbish heap (*utkara*)," and so forth, the status of the *sphya* as the instrument (*karaṇa*) is established. However, since it is unsuitable here due to the great size of the altar (*vedi*), other implements such as the *vidhanas* are also enjoined as means for accomplishing their respective tasks. The mention of the *sphya* is for the purpose of including the ordinary (worldly) *sphya*. When the altar is constructed by an assistant (*parikarmika*), this *sphya* belongs specifically to the *iṣṭi* rites, not to the archetypal (*prākṛta*) ritual.

The word *ca* (and) serves to include the performance of the ordinary (*prākṛta*) altar-construction. Therefore, having performed the ordinary rites up to the digging, he performs this specific (*vaiśeṣika*) rite. Nor should it be argued that the particle *ca* has the sense of including what was not previously mentioned; for in the subsequent mantra for worship, "The wooden sword is well-being" (*sphyaḥ svastiḥ*), only four [objects] are prescribed for worship, and thus nothing beyond those four is possible. Having performed that which precedes the northern boundary-line (*parigrāha*), he constructs the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) measuring ten paces, according to the ritual procedure for the northern altar.

The phrase "yat" (that which) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to prescribe the time for preparing the *uttaravedi* as obtained through the injunction of transfer (*codaka*). From "He digs with [the mantra] 'At the impulse of God Savitṛ'"—referring to the *śakulā*, the *vyaṅgulā*, the *caturaṅgulā*, the *sītāmātrī*, and so on—up to "he causes that [dirt] to go to the *utkara*," it is like the *darśapūrṇamāsa*. The optional rule, "one who desires cattle [should have] a *purīṣa* brought from elsewhere," belongs to the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself, according to the statement of the learned: "Optional rites find their place in the archetype."

Having performed whatever ritual action precedes the measurement of the *uttaravedi*, he constructs the *uttaravedi* according to the method and procedure described in the *Paśusūtra*. In this regard, the specific distinction here is that it measures ten *pada*s.

The method for this ritual placement is stated in the *Śulbasūtra*: "It is known from the *Some* [sacrifice] that it becomes ten paces wide; that is described as being by means of a single cord, or by a fifteen-part [cord]. Having extended it by half, one should mark the two hips (the western corners). While measuring it with a yoke, or having measured it with steps, one should delimit it with a *śamyā*. The word "tataḥ" is the suffix *tasi* used in the sense of the genitive case; it means "of that," namely, of the *uttaravedi*. It is ten paces on all sides in terms of its area.

The *yuga* (yoke) is also ten *padās* in length; its measurement is four *aratnis*. It is like a bamboo pole. Some say it is an independent measurement; in their view, the *yuga* consists of eighty-six *aṅgulas*, based on the *Śulbasūtra* statement: "They call eighty-six [aṅgulas] a *yuga*. Here, the mention of the *yajamāna* (sacrificer) is for the purpose of excluding the *adhvaryu* (officiant).

Having measured the extent with a *śamyā*, leaving space for the *vedīpāvaṭa* (the pit for the sacrificial post) in the eastern half of the Veda, he measures out the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) with the *śamyā*. Having placed the *śamyā* to the east, pointing toward the north, [he recites] "May it be the acquisition of wealth for me," and so forth. Regarding the construction of the northern altar, he states another alternative:
"Some say it should be narrower in the east."

"Shorter, shorter. According to the *Śulbasūtra*: "In a square [altar], one should reduce the side-measures at the front by virtue of the force of the scriptural statement (*śruti*). Reduction means decrease. By implication, it is established that one should increase the two rear side-measures by the same measure as the reduction made in the front.

Just as the measurement of the hip (*śroṇi*) of the great altar (*mahāvedi*) consists of thirty *pada*s or thirty *prakrama*s, its fifth part consists of six *pada*s or six *prakrama*s; its depression (*hāma*) is to the east. To the west, it is thirty *pada*s or thirty *prakrama*s according to that same principle. By this, in the case where one leaves eight *pada*s in front and twelve *pada*s behind, it occurs as follows.

To the north of the northern shoulder (*aṃsa*) of the altar, at a distance of one *prakrama*, there is the pit (*cātvāla*); to the west, there are twelve mounds (*utkara*), or they may be of unlimited size.

"Cātvāla" is a future designation based on the purpose of the ritual preparation. To the north—meaning to the north of the Uttaravedi—one should measure one *prakrama* (if the school follows the measurement by *prakrama*) or one *pada* (if the school follows the measurement by *pada*), and having measured that, one should determine the southern shoulder (*dakṣiṇāṃsa*) or the middle of the southern line of the Cātvāla. In accordance with that, one should delineate the Cātvāla to the north, measuring one *śamyā*, as a square. "The Cātvāla measures one *śamyā*"—so says Baudhāyana.

By the word *śamyā*, only the measurement consisting of thirty-six *ala*s is intended, and not the shape of a *śamyā* as well. This is because that shape, lacking straightness, is unsuitable for drawing lines; furthermore, since it is included within that [measurement] by the injunction "he makes the *uttaravedi* by means of the *kalpa*," and because it serves as the means for that [measurement]. Although the [location of the] *cātvāla* is already established by the rule "the *cātvāla* is at a distance of one *prakrama* to the north of the northern edge of the *vedi*," just like the actions of tracing lines and so forth, its mention here again is for the purpose of measuring with the *śamyā*.

Regarding the phrase "the northern [altar] equal to the *vedi*," this refers only to the *mahāvedi*, not to the *uttaravedi*. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the *cātvāla* pit being situated within the middle of the *mahāvedi*. If it is argued that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of indicating the location of the *utkara* heap, we say no; for that purpose is already established by the rule alone—"the *utkara* is twelve [steps] from the *cātvāla*"—and thus a restatement would be redundant.
