One should therefore measure twelve steps either from the western edge or from the center of the *cātvāla*, and there one should establish either the edge or the center of the *utkara*.

The *utkara* consists of two paces; this is because another sūtra states, "the *utkara* is two paces. The word "exists" (*vidyate*) means "is present. By the phrase "or even unlimited," it is made known that one may also take an indefinite measurement exceeding [the standard]. The meaning of the word "unlimited" (*aparimita*) was stated by Kātyāyana: "unlimited is that which exceeds the measurement. "Exceeding" (*bhūyaḥ*) means "more. In the case of measuring by paces, having measured twelve paces starting from the middle of the *asvāla*, the *utkara* should be prepared right there in the middle.

Furthermore, in the case of measuring by *pada*s, twelve *pada*s do not fit from the western edge of the *āvāla* (water-pit), because it would be impossible to locate the *āgnīdhīya* shed. In the case of measuring by *pada*s, the *āgnīdhīya* shed is also measured by the *pada* unit alone. All the characteristics of the altar (*vedi*) are to be performed on the *utkara* (heap of earth) for the purpose of placing the sacrificial implements; and these are to be performed according to the method of *kāṇḍānusamaya* (performing all actions for one item before proceeding to the next).

Furthermore, when another substance is connected with that purpose, there is an "entry of the ritual properties" (*dharmāveśa*); according to the Sūtra, this means the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the ritual properties in the case of the *utkara*. When another substance—in the form of the *utkara*—is connected with that purpose, namely the act of placing (*āsādana*) which is connected to the altar (*vedi*), and is not [otherwise] connected by the scriptural statement (*vacana*), there is an entry of the ritual properties; the meaning is that there is an entry, that is, an acquisition, of the properties pertaining to the locus of placing. And in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, there is a scripturally enjoined placing of the whey (*vājina*) upon the *utkara*.

Since the *āmikṣā* dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *āmikṣā* dedicated to the Viśvedevas, the requirement to place the *vājina* on the rubbish heap (*utkara*) applies here as well. The author of the Sūtra has included the placing of the *vājina* on the rubbish heap as an example in this very Sūtra: "He places the *vājina* on the rubbish heap; they tie the animal to a enclosing-stick (*paridhi*). The example, "they tie the animal to a *paridhi*," is utilized in the Soma-related Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
Between those two [the *vājina* and the *paridhi*] is the path for moving about on the altar (*vedi*).

*Antareṇa* is an indeclinable. Regarding *tau*, the accusative case is used because of the rule *antarāntareṇayukte*. The meaning is that between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, there is a path (*saṃcara*) connected to the altar for the purpose of entering and exiting. On this point, Āpastamba says: "The Adhvaryu, the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Agnīdhra, and the Dṛśīkas should pass between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*; or [between] the *āgnīdhra* and the *cātvāla*. Some say that during the *prasuta* [offering], the Dṛśīkas should pass on all sides."

Here, the mention of the *adhvaryu* is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *hotṛ*s and others by way of the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so"): if this rule applies even to those who merely look on, what need is there to mention those who actually recite? Those who look on are the observers. Regarding the statement, "Those who are outsiders are the observers," two types of outsiders are seen from the *Avivākya* [section]: the external and the internal. Among these, those observers who are internal should always move about with him and perform their exiting and entering.

Alternatively, the meaning is that on the day of the Soma pressing, once the Soma has been pressed, the *dṛśīkavaḥ* may move about as they please. Some maintain that because of the expression "on all sides," there is no fault even in passing between [the *āgnīdhra* and the *catvāla*].
According to some, [the path] is from east of the *āgnīdhra* to west of the *catvāla*;
by this, movement even to the west of the *utkara* is permitted.
He causes it to be covered with *udumbara* branches.

By "branches" (*śākhābhiḥ*) is meant those branches that are sprouts of the *udumbara* tree; the plural number indicates three or more. Āpastamba has prescribed covering with either *udumbara* branches or *plakṣa* branches, stating, "He causes it to be covered with *udumbara* branches or *plakṣa* branches. This statement is intended to exclude both that option and the alternative prescribed in another *sūtra*, which is covering with *darbha* grass. This concludes the procedure for the middle *upasad* day.

It is for this very reason that in the sūtra—"Having performed the *pravargya* and the two middle *upasad*s, having stepped three steps eastward from the *prāgvaṃśa*, he drives in a peg; that [peg] is in the western half of the altar"—the phrase "by the two middle ones" (*madhyamābhyām*) is stated. Otherwise, the construction of the altar would occur on the first *upasad* day. This is because the word "on the following day" (*śvobhūta*) connects specifically with the passage "He causes it to be covered with *udumbara* branches," which occurs precisely on the middle *upasad* day.

[The fifth chapter: Together with the *Jyotsnā* commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. Only the statement "he causes [the altar] to be covered" would suffice; however, the rule "having performed the two final morning *pravargya* rites" follows from the force of the injunctions pertaining to the subsequent and final [rites]. To exclude all of this, the text specifies "with the two middle ones. Thus, the phrase "on the following day" (*śvobhūte*) is indeed to be construed with what follows. If it is objected that the mention of "on the following day" is redundant since it is already established by the phrase "with the two final ones," we say no.

The injunction "he causes [the fire] to be covered with *udumbara* branches" is meaningful only for the purpose of indicating that this too occurs on the very day of the middle *upalādana*; otherwise, its performance might occasionally occur even on the following day.

Nor should it be argued that, even when the altar (*vedi*) is being constructed during the middle day of the *upasada* rites, one should adopt the syntactical connection as "on the next day he causes [the altar] to be covered with *udumbara* branches," and thus perform only this much on the following day—namely, causing it to be covered with *udumbara* branches—while the subsequent morning rites (*uttama-paurvāhnikī*) and so forth are to be performed on the day after that. For such an assumption of a division within the middle day would be entirely improper, as it contradicts the entirety of the sūtras.

Nor should it be argued that in the expression *śvobhūte*, because it marks the end of a section (*khaṇḍa*), its connection must be with what precedes; for this rule lacks necessity due to exceptions such as *yathārthaṃ havirdhānayoḥ prāgvaṃśasya* and *sadohavirdhānayoḥ*. Furthermore, the designation of a "section" (*khaṇḍa*) is based solely on the will of the venerable Teacher (*Bhagavadācārya*), as there is no fixed measure for a "breath" (*ucchvāsa*).

*Channām* means she causes [the sacrificial shed] to be covered; she passes the night without activity, or rather, she guards it. The word *parikarmibhiḥ* (by the attendants) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. By the phrase "she guards the covered [shed]," the protection of the sacrificial branches (*śākhā*) is also understood; for without the protection of the branches, the protection of the [shed] in its specific form would not occur. This meaning is obtained through association with the word *śvobhūta* (on the following day). Immediately after this follow the *pravar-gya* and *upasada* rites of the afternoon.

Thus, because it is established that one performs the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites three times, both in the evening and in the morning, they are not mentioned here [separately]. Āpastamba has stated this clearly: "In the interval between the middle *pravargya* and *upasad*, they prepare the altar (*vedi*). On the following day (śvobhūte), having performed the two final *paurvāhṇika* (forenoon) *pravargya* and *upasad* rites and having given the half-vow (*ardhavratam*), he then immediately performs the two *āparāhṇika* (afternoon) *pravargya* and *upasad* rites.

"On the next day" (*śvobhūte*) means on the day following the middle *upasad* day, that is, on the day designated as "tomorrow. If it were stated merely that "having performed the *pravargya* and the two morning *upasad*s on the next day," then—given that the twelve *upasad*s for the *ahīna* sacrifices are established by the scriptural injunction, "The *upasad*s of the *sāha* [one-day sacrifice] are three; those of the *ahīna* are twelve"]—the middle *upasad* day would [be affected].

Since the ritual acts beginning with the measurement of the altar and ending with its covering are applicable on any one of the first three days of the four-day period, the rule "having performed the Pravarṇya and Upasad rites in the afternoon" would apply even on the days following the covering of the altar; the expression "with the last two" is stated in order to preclude that.

And thus, even though the altar (vedi) is constructed during the four days of the middle *upasad*, it is established by the rule—"having performed the *pravargya* and *upasad* at that very time on the final day of the twelve *upasad*s"—that this occurs only then, and not on the days following the day of the altar's construction. The restatement beginning with "with the two last" (*uttamābhyām*) is for the purpose of prescribing the performance of the *avakāśa-upasad* immediately upon the offering of the *ardhavata*.

It should be understood that the statement "on the next day" (*śvobhūte*) is intended to demonstrate that the ritual, beginning from the final *pravargya* and *upasad* performed in the morning and afternoon in the *havirdhāna* shed and ending with the sacrificer guarding the King Soma, is to be accomplished in a single day. Otherwise, because of the connection indicated by the gerund (*lyap*) in the phrase "having performed the *pravargya* and *upasad*" (*pravaryopasadyamānam*), there would be no fixed rule as to whether the remainder of the ritual up to the driving away of the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*) is to be completed on the day of the final *upasad* or on the following day. This is according to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha.

Therefore, the expression "on the next day" (*śvobhūta*) is indeed necessary. And half of that [period] is the *avatta* (portion taken out). Regarding the phrase "one teat on the subsequent two days," in the *Yājamāna-sūtra*, the word "half" refers to half of what is prescribed for the one-teat rite on the final *upasad* day. The meaning is: "Having lifted the *pravargya* vessel, he proceeds to the *upasad* if it is the former. That is to say, if the *pravargya* is the former—that is, the first—relative to the *upasad*, then the *upasad* is to be performed after the lifting of the *pravargya*.

Having bestowed the half-vow, having carried forward the fire according to the procedure for the fire, having placed a tuft of wool in the fire-place and established the fire, he drives away the calves for the evening milking intended for the curdled milk (āmikṣā) for Mitra and Varuṇa.

The remaining portion is *ardhavatam*. The word division is *āmer iti*. If the word division were *agneḥ iti*, it would mean "by the manner of fire" (*agnerāvṛtā*), which would be incoherent; for no such manner of fire is required here. If it is asked, "Even with the word division *āger iti*, how is the meaning coherent?", it is replied: *āgeḥ* means "of this [fire]"; that is, of that fire (*tasyāgneḥ*), meaning of the carrying forth (*praṇayana*) connected with fire.

Thus, by the method of supplying the elided *am*, the meaning becomes "having led the fire" (*agniṃ praṇīya*). And that [meaning] is both consistent with the performance of the rite and non-contradictory. Nor is there a contradiction with the gender indicated by the suffix of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*); for, since the assumption of the word-division as *agneḥ* (genitive) is stronger due to its consistency with the performance and its non-contradictory nature, while the status of being a secondary derivative ending in a single syllable and the masculine gender are weaker, the assumption of the form *āgneya* is appropriate, and thus there is no contradiction.

The word *āvṛt* denotes a manner or procedure. "Having brought forward the fire according to the *āvṛt* of Agni"—that is, by means of the procedure for bringing forward the fire beginning with the leading forth (*praṇayana*) and kindling (*upasthāna*), and ending with the placing of the enclosures made of *pautudrava* wood, or ending with the incense of *guggulu* and *sugandhitejana*—the meaning is: having performed the ritual procedure for bringing forward the fire which has Agni as its object. Although the sense of "having brought forward the fire according to the *āvṛt* of Agni" would have been understood from that alone, the explicit mention of "Agni" here is for the purpose of indicating that the commands (*praiṣa*) and so forth occur only when the fire is entirely blazing.

The statement, "having placed a tuft of wool (*ūrṇāstukā*) on the fire-altar (*agnyāyatana*)," is intended to exclude *guggulu* and *sugandhitejana*. For whiteness and the state of being produced from the interior of the horn of a ram (*petva*) certainly apply [to these two substances as well]. Alternatively, since the *Paśu-sūtra* states, "he pours them out all at once on the northern shoulder," it follows that the pouring out of the *guggulu*, *sugandhitejana*, and the tufts of wool would occur simultaneously; therefore, this instruction is for the purpose of pouring out the tuft of wool separately on the fire-altar. In this case, the mantra must be repeated.

The preceding and following restatements are intended precisely for this purpose. If only one of them were restated, the sequence of the ritual performance would remain doubtful. A *petva* is a castrated ram; the tuft of wool (*ūrṇāstukā*) found between its two horns is seen in the *paśusūtra*, and it should be understood in the same way here. Alternatively, the prescription is given specifically to demonstrate the distinction that while there is the placing of the tuft of wool itself, there is the scattering (*nivapana*) of the other two. Even in this view, because of the difference in the actions, the repetition of the rite is established.

Of such a ram (*vṛṣṇi*), which has never at any time had its wool clipped, the wool-fiber (*ūrṇāstukā*) located in the space between the two horns is to be taken. [This concludes] Chapter 1. The act of sowing (*nivapana*) is like seeds being sown in a field; such is the ritual action. "Depositing" (*nidhāna*), however, simply means placing. Although the term *āyatana* (site) is used, there is no restrictive rule that the deposit must be in the northern navel (*uttaranābhi*); rather, it is intended to convey the meaning that the site may be anywhere at all. The "fire-place" (*agnipada*) refers to that portion of the site where the fire is established, and not any other part. That [place] consists of both the area shaped like the northern navel and the central region other than that.

For in other treatises (*śāstra*), it is stated that the central region itself is the location for the fire during the *gā* rite. The installation of the fire begins with "Thou art the nest of Agni" (*agneḥ kulāyam asi*) and continues up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). These [mantras] are indeed the ancillaries (*aṅga*) of the installation itself. There is no contradiction in regarding something as non-intervening even when it is separated by that which does not intervene; as Āpastamba says: "He brings forward the fire as in the *paśubandha*. When the *Yājuṣa* *hautra* is present, all the *hautra* here is specifically *Yājuṣa*.

That which has Mitra and Varuṇa as its deities is *maitrāvaruṇī*; for that [curd-mixture], *āmikṣāyai*, this fourth case ending is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthya*). In the expression *sāyadohāya* as well, the fourth case is used in the sense of purpose. The meaning of the sentence is: "that which is the evening milking intended for the sake of the *āmikṣā*. He drives away the calves, separating them from their mothers, silently. Since the preparation of the branch is accomplished by means of the removal of the calves, the fetching of the branch must be performed first. The term *kṣetrāvaruṇyāḥ* is an adjective qualifying the *āmikṣā*, intended to prescribe the deity.

In the mantras for fetching the branches, there is modification (*ūha*) according to the specific purpose. Having poured curds into hot milk and boiled it, that solid substance which results is *āmikṣā*. For the Śruti states: "This *āmikṣā* is indeed the form of the egg. That which has become liquid is the *vājina*; for the Śruti states: "The *vājina* is indeed semen.
[One gives] the calf to Indra for the *dadhigharma* (curd-milk offering).

*Indrāya indrārthaṃ dadhidharmaḥ*: "For Indra, for the sake of Indra, the *dadhidharma*"; it is to be prepared with curds (*dannā*). Regarding *dadhidharma*, [the term] is either *dadhnaḥ dharmaḥ* ("the nature of curds") or *dadhnaḥ dharmaḥ* ("the nature of curds"). Alternatively, by the word *dharma*, an action characterized by protection is expressed. Or, it is that in which the nature (*dharma*) of curds consists of flowing (*kṣaraṇa*). It is a word established through both etymological derivation and conventional usage (*yogarūḍha*). And this qualification is intended to resolve the expectation—arising because it is impossible to determine the deity from the mantra to be used as the means for the *dadhidharma* oblation, which will be mentioned later, namely, "Him whom they call Indra, him whom they call Varuṇa"—as to which deity should be accepted.

The *dharma* (the milk) is for the sake of the *dharma* (the ritual); she whose [udder] is pained is called *dharmaduh*. The meaning is that one drives away her calf. This too is done silently. However, the fetching of the branch is indeed accompanied by a mantra, because the substance of the *dadhi-dharma* offering is to be given with the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to indicate an unexpressed collection, showing that for the sake of the *dadhi-graha*, the *sāya-doha* (evening milking), and so forth, the driving away of the respective calves from their respective cows must be performed.

For this purpose, the taking of the *śālā* (the vessel) is done silently, because there is no ownership of what is offered with the *vaṣaṭ* call. Even though the *śṛtātaṅkya* (the boiled milk) is indeed offered with the *vaṣaṭ* call, nevertheless, its purpose is merely for mixing and not for the sacrifice itself; therefore, there is no fault.
According to some, all [the offerings] belong to Indra.

Due to the proximity of the *āmikṣā* dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa, the word "all" (*sarva*) refers to the *savanīya* sacrificial offerings consisting of parched grains (*dhānā*) and so forth. Having set aside the deity Mitra and Varuṇa who belong to the *savanīya āmikṣā*, Indra takes the place of that deity by virtue of the context; thus, here itself, the *āmikṣā* is included among the materials to be offered together with the *dhānā*s and other *savanīya* offerings. As for the deities: for Indra accompanied by the Haris, one offers the *dhānā*s; for Indra accompanied by Pūṣan, the groats (*karambha*); for Sarasvatī Bhāratī, the *parivāpa* grains; and for Indra... [the *āmikṣā*].

Setting aside those offerings which are to be prescribed by the sūtra "the cake on eight potsherds" (*puroḍāśamaṣṭākapālam*), Indra’s status as the deity is optionally enjoined in their place: Indra takes the place of Mitrāvaruṇa for the *āmikṣā*; Indra, devoid of the quality of "possessing bay horses" (*harivat*), [takes the place] of the parched grains (*dhānā*); Indra, devoid of the quality of "possessing a roar" (*ghoṣavat*), [takes the place] of the groats (*karambha*); and Indra takes the place of Sarasvatī and Bhāratī for the fried grains (*parivāpa*) and parched rice-flakes (*lājā*).

Indra alone is the recipient of the *puroḍāśa*. As for the phrase "the calf for Indra, for the *dadhigharma*, [and] for the *dharmaduho*," the connection with Indra is obtained simply through the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "for Indra" from the preceding *sūtra*. If one asks, "What is the purpose of the word 'Aindra'?"—it is true that it serves this purpose: if the *sūtra* were composed without the word "Aindra" as "all [offerings] belong to him," there would be no fixed requirement for the word "Indra" to recur, and consequently, everything would be seized by doubt and fall into incoherence.

It should not be argued that this sūtra ought to have been placed before "the calf for the one who milks the *dharmadughā* for Indra and for the *dadhidharma*," so that the word "Indra" would possess its proper significance. For if it were placed earlier, then even in the case of "the calf for the one who milks the *dharmadughā* for Indra and for the *dadhidharma*," the phrase "he drives away [the calf]" would necessarily have to be included there as well, resulting in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). He performs the subsequent tracing around [the altar] while it possesses fire.

The locative case in *agnivatī* is used in the sense of the accusative. *Anivata* is an adjective qualifying the subsequent measurement (*parimā*). By the statement, "They led them eastward with Agni, southward with the Vasus, westward with the Rudras, and northward with the Ādityas," it is shown that the eastern boundary was already established prior to the measuring out of the altar-site (*vedi*) by means of Agni.
One does not step upon the site after it has been measured out but before it has been sprinkled, until the spreading of the grass.

Having been enclosed by the subsequent enclosure and sprinkled, he does not step upon or stand upon the altar until the spreading [of the grass]. The expression "enclosed" is stated to demonstrate that there is no prohibition against stepping upon it prior to the subsequent enclosure. From the expression "until the spreading," it follows that the prohibition against stepping upon the sprinkled altar begins from the point where one touches it with the wooden sword facing westward and continues until the end of the spreading.

By this, it is established that one sprinkles the ground, sweeps the altar, sprinkles for the purpose of strewing, and then strews. Regarding the phrase "until the strewing" (*ā āstaraṇāt*), the prefix *ā* denotes inclusive limit (*abhivyāpti*). Consequently, the prohibition against stepping upon un-sprinkled materials lasts until the completion of the entire strewing. This is merely a restatement of a scriptural injunction from another recension (*śākhāntarīyā śrutiḥ*).

The wood intended for the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the Great Altar (*māhāvedi*) have been prepared; one sprinkles the wood, the altar, and the grass three times each with water silently (*tūṣṇīkābhiḥ*).

Those things for which the *sutyā* (the Soma-pressing) is the purpose or objective are called *sutyārthāni*. Regarding the phrase "prepared for the Mahāvedi," the term *māhāvedikaṃ* means that sufficient sacrificial grass (*barhis*) has been prepared for the covering of the Mahāvedi. In the expression "wooden materials for the *sutyā*," the word *upaklṛpta* (prepared) is to be construed by changing its grammatical number to the plural, as in "they have been prepared. The word "by the attendants" (*parikarmibhiḥ*) is to be supplied as the agent. *Sutyā* is so called because the Soma is pressed (*sūyate*) or crushed (*kaṇḍyate*) therein; alternatively, it is the ritual action in which the Soma is pressed or crushed.
