Thus, by the term *sutyā*, there is the inclusion of all ritual acts connected with the day known as the *sutyā*. Consequently, even for those rites arising after the *avabhṛtha*—such as the *udayanīyā-iḍā* and others—the same sacrificial wood (*kāṣṭha*) is to be used. Because of the qualification "for the sake of the *sutyā*," the preparation of the wood is solely for the purpose of the *sutyā*; it is precisely these [woods] that are sprinkled (*prokṣaṇa*) in this manner. Due to the external qualification "belonging to the great altar" (*māhāvedika*), the connection of the *sutyā*-purpose does not apply there, because of contradiction. By this, it is understood:

The firewood intended for the *gnīṣomīya* sacrifice consists of entirely separate pieces; for these, there is no sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) in this manner [as previously described]. Rather, because the *Dharmasūtra* prohibits the placing of un-sprinkled fuel on the fire—stating, "one should not place un-sprinkled fuel on the fire"—the sprinkling is merely a common worldly act performed with pure water, done silently (*tūṣṇīm*). In both cases, the word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the previously unstated connection to that specific day and the taking up of the vessel.

Even though this is a new injunction (*apūrva*), the mention of the ritual items (*padārtha*) is intended to show that the sequence is indeed the same as the original model (*prakṛta*). The repetition "three times each" (*tristriḥ*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the number three applies to each individual item. The phrase "with those [waters] over which nothing has been recited" (*tūṣṇīkābhiḥ*) is for the purpose of obtaining the consecration of the *prokṣaṇī* waters as prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. Since the taking up of water is already established by its very nature as the means for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), the explicit statement "of water" (*adbhiḥ*) is for the purpose of making known that the consecration mentioned in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* is optional (*pākṣika*).

Thus, two alternatives are established: sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) either with water consecrated according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, or with ordinary (laukika) water. If it were stated simply as "silently" (tūṣṇīkābhiḥ), one might occasionally suspect that the meaning intended was that the sprinkling is optional—meaning it could be done silently, or otherwise with something else such as a liquid substance. To prevent this, the word "or" (vā), which would have served to clarify the meaning, has been omitted; instead, the term "with water" (adbhiḥ) is employed to establish the option through an implied indication.

For it should be understood that there is an option here due to mutual contradiction. From the use of the past participle "upaklṛptam" (prepared), it is understood that the preparation must be performed by the attendants (*parikarmibhiḥ*) even before the commencement of the performance associated with the day of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice. Because of the prohibition against stepping upon the altar (*vedi*) without having sprinkled it, one should sprinkle the area near the southern hip (*dakṣiṇaśroṇi*) of the great altar (*mahāvedi*), and standing upon that very spot, [one should perform the rite] there with the mantra.

Having spread the *barhis* grass on the outer area and having sprinkled the front part, one should take one's stand upon that spot; having performed the spreading of the *barhis* on that spot with the mantra, it should be understood that this sequence is to be carried out until the end. By this, the direction of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) here also becomes toward the west (*pratyag-apavarga*). In the rule, "He silently sprinkles the firewood, the altar, and the *barhis*," the two words "true" (*satya*) and "pertaining to the great altar" (*māhāvedika*) from the preceding sūtra are carried over. He silently spreads the *barhis* on the altar in the same manner as in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

The statement "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*) is for the purpose that the application of the mantra *devabarhirūrṇamradasam*—which would otherwise occur by virtue of the rule "as in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices"—should not take place. By the rule "as in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," such ritual details as covering with grass, spreading from west to east, covering the roots with the tips, and spreading without overlapping are obtained. Furthermore, Baudhāyana has prescribed a five-aṅgula width for the spreading of the *stotra* and for the *sadas* and *havirdhāna*; since this is not contradictory and serves a visible purpose, it must certainly be accepted.
"Those who kindle Agni and spread the sacrificial grass in succession—those for whom Indra is a youthful friend"—some recite this as the *staraṇī* verses. 15.

Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the seventh praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. Regarding the term *staraṇī* (the spreading verse): it is derived from the root *stṝ* with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), according to the rule *yuvoranākau*. Because it has the marker *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. The indication of the feminine gender in the word *staraṇī* is because this mantra is singular; the meaning is that this *ṛc* serves the purpose of spreading.

Thus ends the fourth chapter of the seventh book in the *Jyotsnā* commentary, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—the son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was himself the son of Okopāha Śrīmad Amiṣṭoma-yājin, Sāhasrāgni-yukta Vājapeya-yājin, Sarvatomukha-yājin, and Dviṣāhasrāgni-yukta Pauṇḍarīka-yājin—which serves to alleviate the distress of learned men caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the ocean of the *Sūtras* of the venerable Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
7.5 Now begins the fifth chapter of the seventh book.

When the two carts with circular wheels, which have been prepared and previously employed, have had their old knots untied and washed, they make them new. Having made them provided with covers and fitted for yoking, and having stationed them in front of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, he offers an oblation on the northern altar with the verse, "They yoke the mind."

Regarding the term *upaklṛpti* (preparation): because it is a designation of an accomplished fact (*bhūtanirdeśa*), the preparations must be made prior to the commencement of the performance of the rites connected with the day of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice. Due to the dual number, there are two carts (*anasī*). Those two carts, which have wheels shaped like circles and which were previously employed for other tasks, are referred to as "those previously used. Having untied the old, ancient, and previously fashioned thongs (*pradhī*) of those two carts, and having washed them—having washed them at the *havirdhāna* sheds—they tie new, fresh knots. The word "the ritual assistants" (*pārekarmiṇaḥ*) is to be supplied as the subject.

*Charitavatī*, *kaṭavatī*, *yugyakṛte*. *Yugyakṛte* means "for the yoke" (*yugya*) and "made for it" (*kṛta*), hence *yugyakṛte*. This is an adjective qualifying the cart (*śakaṭa*). Regarding the word *yugya*: by the word *ca* (and) in the sūtra *yugāhe khalayavamāṣatilavṛṣabrahmaṇaśca*, which serves to include words not explicitly mentioned therein, the word *yuga* is included; from this word *yuga*, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "suitable for that" (*tadarha*) to form *yugya*. *Kṛte* means "made," i.e., rendered capable of performing its function through the application of new axles and other parts.

Having placed such a cart in front, near the eastern hall (*prāgvaṃśa*)—specifically in the eastern shed (*prāgavaṃśa*) itself—he stations the southern [cart] to the south and the northern [cart] to the north, so that they stand without being separated. Then he offers an oblation on the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) with the verse beginning, "They yoke the mind" (*yuñjate manaḥ*). The mantra ends with "pariṣyati. Because this is enjoined as an *āhuti* (an offering), the exclamation *svāhā* is used. By the mere fact that the carts have been prepared, the two wheels are understood to be parts of the cart.

Furthermore, since [the circularity] is already established in the case of the *maṇḍalacakra*, this statement does not merely enjoin that the two wheels (*cakra*) must have the form of a circle; rather, its purpose is to demonstrate a specific meaning: that the wheels should be circular in form just as the solar disc (*ravimaṇḍala*) is without gaps. By this, there is an exclusion of wheels that possess a hollow interior characterized by the term "gap" (i.e., wheels with a central hole). By the phrase "previously employed," it is indicated that only those wheels made for ancient purposes, such as travel or household tasks, are to be accepted.

If [the new ones] are unavailable, one should take only the new ones. Regarding the specific rule when they have been used previously, he says: "Having untied their old knots... By saying "having washed them, they make them new," the term "newness" (navatva), common to both old and new, indicates fitness for the task at hand. The use of the word "having made" (kṛtvā) is for the purpose of indicating that the Adhvaryu is the agent; for this very reason, the requirement of a single agent for the *ktvā* suffix is also justified. Furthermore, there is the establishment [of the knots] without interruption.

[Chapter 550] Accompanied by the *Jyotsnā* commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. The *Stamghana* states: "Along the front of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, on both sides, they pass between the *pṛṣṭhyā* cords. Kātyāyana says: "He places [the two carts] in the *havirdhāna* shed; he supports the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord on both sides at a distance of one *dharanī*; having washed them, they face eastward, enclosing the hall on both sides, with the southern one being larger. In the *Mānava Sūtra*, there is another specific rule: "He places the wheels outside the altar and supports them within the altar.
The mention of the *auttaravedika* (northern altar) is for the purpose of excluding the *śālāmukhīya* fire mentioned by Baudhāyana and Kātyāyana.

With a portion of the third part of the dust from the footprint—[the formula being] *devaśrutau*—she, the wife, with her right hand turned upward, thrice anoints from front to back the southern shaft of the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart; she does the same for the northern one.

The *havirdhāna* is that in which the oblation called *soma* is placed (*dhīyate*) or established; it is designated as "southern" because it is connected to the southern direction. This is the meaning of the term *cidvitam*.

Having removed the wheel from such a *havirdhāna* cart, he anoints the southern axle-pin with his right hand, palm upwards, three times, starting from the lower part and moving toward the upper part, while sitting close by facing away [from the pin]. After the anointing, he joins that [wheel] to it. Having done exactly the same for the northern *havirdhāna*, he joins its wheel. Because the substances are distinct, there is a repetition of the mantra. The mantra ends with the word "vaśī."

The mention of the "wife" (patnī) is for the purpose of excluding the Adhvaryu. The mention of "south" (dakṣiṇa) is for the purpose of marking at the time of preparation itself—indicating "this is the southern one" and "this is the northern one"—and to indicate a specific placement such that one is to the south of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and one is to the north, rather than being placed only to the south or only to the north of the *pṛṣṭhyā*.

If it were stated that "the one placed on the south is the southern [pole] and the one placed on the north is the northern," then since this would already be established by the fact of the arrangement being oriented toward the north (udaksaṃsthatva), the employment of the words "southern" and "northern" would result in redundancy. The mention of the *havirbhān* (the axle-end) is intended to demonstrate its purpose for the cart. The term "southern" (*dakṣiṇām*) is an adjective qualifying the axle-end (*akṣadhur*), in order to exclude the northern axle-end.

In the case of *pākpūrabdhūḥpayām anaḥ*, the suffix *bh* (forming *-bha*) does not apply as a compound-ending because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the word *anas*. This is because this [word] is connected with *akṣa*. *Akṣa* refers to the horizontal wooden shaft situated between the two wheels; that part where the wheel is fixed is called *akṣa*. The term "with the right hand" (*dakṣiṇena*) is a qualification of the hand, intended to exclude the left. Alternatively, "with the right hand" serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that one anoints it with the right hand and not with the left either. [This would follow] if "with the right hand" were not stated.

The mention of "right" (dakṣiṇa) is intended to prevent the possibility that even a woman might perform the anointing. The inclusion of the term "upturned" (uttāna) is for the purpose of excluding the downward-turned position. Since the hand alone is well-known as the instrument for anointing and is the most appropriate [tool], the word "hand," which serves as the substantive, is not explicitly stated. Baudhāyana specifies a particular distinction regarding the hand, stating it should be "turned forward" (prāc). According to the rule "where there is a single substance," the mantra is recited only once. Regarding the sequence for returning to the *havirdhāna* shed, Baudhāyana has prescribed: "While following [the sacrificer], the wife follows behind, taking a third part of the footprint."
According to some, she anoints all [the axles].

However, "all" refers only to the axles and not to the wives, because the word "all" does not necessarily imply plurality, and because it would contradict the rule that "actions for the sake of others should be performed by one person. Therefore, she anoints only the principal [axle]. For this anointing is a refinement of the axle, and its primacy is established by the scriptural injunction: "The eldest [wife] alone [anoints] with the eldest [axle], and not the others. This is from the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha.

Furthermore, according to the scriptures, the work for the sake of others must be performed by the eldest wife alone and not by another; therefore, when she is absent, it should be understood that whichever [wife] is the eldest among those present is the one intended. Here, "eldest" refers to seniority established by marriage, not by age. The source for this should be sought elsewhere. The meaning is that he anoints all the yoke-pins together with the mantra. By this, it is established that in the previous ritual option (*pūrvakalpa*), the anointing of the two rear yoke-pins is done silently (*tūṣṇīm*). Moreover, because it serves a visible purpose, this is necessary. According to some, it should be done with clarified butter (*ājya*).

The word *ca* (and) serves to indicate a conjunction of actions. The meaning is that one should bring another portion of clarified butter (*ājya*) onto that spot and perform the anointing of the pole (*dhūr-añjana*) with that mixture. Alternatively, the conjunction means that after first performing the anointing with the [first] portion alone, one then anoints it again with the clarified butter alone. In this latter case, there is a repetition of the mantra. According to the view of some, the conjunction is mandatory; such is the intended meaning of the Sūtra. By this, it is established that according to the view of others, it is conditional (*naimittika*).

If the footprint is dry, one must certainly apply collyrium by mixing it with clarified butter (*ājya*). In the event of the footprint being lost, one must take soil from a pure place, mix it with clarified butter, and certainly apply collyrium. Alternatively, having mixed other soil with ordinary clarified butter and applied collyrium with that, one must also certainly perform the application of collyrium with another [substance] that has been consecrated. At this point, the wife, her task having been completed, returns to her own place.

And it has been stated by Baudhāyana: "They lead the wife. The plural number is for the purpose of including any one of the attendants (*parikarmin*), the *unnetṛ*, or others. He issues the command: "Recite for the two *havirdhāna* carts as they are being moved forward," or "Recite for them as they are being moved forward"; the word "the Hotṛ" is to be supplied [to the verb]. Regarding this very point, the invocation is stated by Baudhāyana: "The two go toward the Hotṛ. The plural number is for the purpose of including any one of the Brahman, the sacrificer, or the *adhvaryu*. In this matter, the specific *hautra* (duties of the Hotṛ) is indeed that of Āśvalāyana.

When the first [verse] has been recited three times, they move the two carts forward while lifting them up with the mantra, "Go forward. Since the Hotṛ priest has already stood by, it is the first verse that is recited three times. Āpastamba has stated this quite clearly: "When the first [verse] has been recited three times. With the mantra, "Go forward," they lead the two carts forward, holding the two poles of the draft-animals with their right hands. The prefix *pra-* indicates that the carts should be led in such a way that there is no jarring impact against the wheels or other parts of the cart during the movement.

Those expressed by the plural number refer only to the constituent parts (*avayava*) and not to the attendants (*parikarmiṇaḥ*), because they constitute the ritual action (*karma*) like a mantra. In the term *samudgṛhṇantaḥ*, the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) indicates that the act of lifting up (*samudgrahaṇa*) occurs simultaneously with the setting in motion of the breath (*prāṇa*). Therefore, for as long as the breath is set in motion, for that long the lifting up continues. In the word *samudgṛhṇantaḥ*, the prefix *sam-* has the sense of grasping firmly (*dārḍhyena*), while the prefix *ud-* has the sense of grasping upwards (*ūrdhvagrahaṇa*). The mantra ends with *jīhvaratam*. If the axle should creak, he consecrates it with the mantra: *suvāg deva duryān āvada*.

If the axle makes a loud noise due to friction with the wheel, then he consecrates it with the mantra "suvāg" (O fair-tongued one). The word "axle-noise" (*akṣaśabdam*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence], because it is seen in the Agnicayana section that one consecrates the axle-noise with the mantra "akrandad agniḥ" (Agni cried out). And this [consecration] is for the purpose of driving away the Rakṣases, according to the Śruti: "In that he utters [the sound] here, he recites 'akrandat' for the sake of striking down the Rakṣases.
Because of the singular number [in the mantra], the Adhvaryu alone is the performer here, and not the Pratiprasthātṛ either.

Where he steps onto the altar, having placed gold at the edge of the altar on the northern track of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, he offers an oblation with the verse, "This [step] Viṣṇu... (RV 1.22.17).

Baudhāyana says that one should dig up [the ground] with the wooden sword (*sphya*), sprinkle it, place gold upon it, strew [sacrificial grass] all around, and then offer the oblation. At whatever place the two minds (*manasī*) step onto the altar—that is, having stepped onto the altar and proceeded there—at that very spot, on the northern track of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, meaning on the path of the northern wheel at the edge of the altar, [one offers]. The mantra ends with the word "pāsuraḥ. In the word "tad" [in the mantra], the locative case ending is elided according to the rule *supāṃ suluk...* (Pāṇini 7.1.39).

Because of the dual number in the word *avakrāmataḥ*, the stepping down (*avakramaṇa*) of the two [officiants] occurs simultaneously. Here, the mention of "right" (*dakṣiṇa*) and the mention of "left" (*uttara*) in the subsequent sūtra are for the sake of establishing the sequence: the oblation based on the northern track of the southern *havirdhāna* cart must first be performed by the Adhvaryu, and the oblation based on the southern track of the northern *havirdhāna* cart must be performed by the Pratiprasthātṛ immediately thereafter. Otherwise, there would be no fixed order here.

The word "end" (*anta*) is intended to include the area adjacent to the edge of the altar (*vedi*). Since the *pratiprasthātṛ* is mentioned later on, the *adhvaryu*—who is established as the agent by the general rule (*paribhāṣā*) "the *adhvaryu* [acts] according to the Yajurveda"—is the performer in the preceding case.
The *pratiprasthātṛ*, however, performs the subsequent part beginning with "irāvatī dhenumatī."

The term *pratiprasthātṛ* is etymologically significant (*anvartha*). He is called the *pratiprasthātṛ* because he stands (*tiṣṭhati*) for the sake of sacrifice following (*anu*) the *adhvaryu*. Alternatively, the prefix *prati-* conveys similarity; thus, he is the *pratiprasthātṛ* because he stands for the sake of sacrifice like the *adhvaryu*. The reading "of the subsequent" (*uttarasya*) alone is appropriate, as it is dependent [on a preceding rule]. The reading "in the subsequent" (*uttarasyām*), however, is indeed incorrect; for since the subsequent [action] is already obtained through the extension (*atideśa*) implied by the word "thus" (*evam*), the inclusion of that specific mention would result in redundancy. The mention of the *pratiprasthātṛ* is intended to exclude the *adhvaryu*.

The mantra ends with the word *mayūkhaiḥ*. In both cases, the ritual procedure (*dharma*) for the *darvihoma* applies. There is no fault in passing between the two fires. The return is made by that same path. Because it is enjoined by the root *hu* (to sacrifice), the utterance *svāhā* is used.
The Adhvaryu performs the rites of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, and the Pratiprasthātṛ performs those of the northern one.

This *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) is intended to indicate that where the dual number is heard and there is no division of the mantra, there is indeed conjunction (*sāhitya*). In cases other than this, however, the exclusion of conjunction occurs precisely because of its absence. An example of such a case is the "driving in of the wooden stake" (*methīnihanana*). This is mentioned separately from the others due to the difference in its specific property (*dharma*).

Since the specific object to be qualified—the *havirdhāna* cart—is already obtained from the context itself, the repeated mention of "the *havirdhāna*" is intended to indicate that [the following actions] apply specifically to the southern *havirdhāna*: one places the *droṇakalaśa* with its fringe and filter behind the axle; the *āhavanīya* fire in the northern interior; the *pūtabhṛt* vessel on its very front beam; and the three *ekadhanā* jars behind the axle. Because these vessels are connected to their respective *havirdhāna* carts, this general rule (*paribhāṣā*) would otherwise apply here as well; however, let it not so apply, but rather—

The application of this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) should occur only in the context of rites that effect the consecration of the *havirdhāna* shed; however, since the employment of the vessels (*pātraprayoga*) does not constitute a rite for the consecration of the *havirdhāna*, this technical rule does not apply here. This is the purpose [of the statement]. (11. Ja. Sa. A. 'paṇācakrama iti). [End of] the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [Book] 7.698.

"Drive away the fear of the enemy; turn back the wheels; go to the house of Soma, to the assembly of Indra"—with these words, at the rear third of the altar, the Hotṛ mentally drives away the fear of the enemy with his foot, as does either the Adhvaryu, the Sacrificer, or the Brahman.

The Adhvaryu, the Sacrificer, or the Brahman [is the one who] faces the danger. When the Hotṛ’s duty has been performed according to the Yajurvedic procedure during the *ṛtu* and *śastra* recitations, the Hotṛ, having gone behind the Veda—that is, the Mahāveda—at a point where a third part is removed (meaning either the rear third or the front third), utters a mantra mentally and drives away the danger pertaining to the people (*janya*) with his foot, by means of a gesture of repelling or by scattering dust; this is the meaning.

In this case, the removal [of the danger] is accomplished by the recitation of the mantra alone, specifically by the mantra beginning with "ācchidrikena" and ending with "gacchatam. This is an optional alternative (vikalpa). Furthermore, that fear pertains only to the ritual action (*karman*) and not to the *hotṛ*, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), or the *brahman*. This option is obtained from the natural sense of the context. Here, although the specific limb of the foot is not specified, there is no fixed rule because of the absence of the word "right" (*dakṣiṇa*). Regarding the meaning of the word *hotṛ*: the very act of invoking [the deities] by saying "Bring such-and-such! Bring such-and-such! constitutes the *hotṛ*-ship of the *hotṛ*.

The etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) as "one who offers" (*juhoti iti hotā*) is not employed in various contexts because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaktatvāt*). Regarding that, he states the optional officiants (*kartṛ*) with the words beginning "the *adhvaryu*," and so forth. The etymology of the word *adhvaryu* was stated on the occasion of explaining the sūtra: "The *adhvaryu* should select the Soma. The etymology of the word *yajamāna*, however, will be stated in the *Agniṣṭoma-yājamāna-sūtra*. The etymology of the word *brahman* was stated on the occasion of explaining the sūtra: "They wash their hands with the *madantī* waters; the *brahman* causes the King [Soma] to tremble."
To the west of the Uttaravedi, having stepped back three steps toward the west, they both place their chariot-navels on either side of the Pṛṣṭhyā line, saying, "May you two rest here."

The *uttarā* (northern) altar is the *uttaravedi*. "Northern-ness" (*uttaratva*) signifies excellence (*utkṛṣṭatva*). This excellence arises from its being the locus for numerous ritual procedures (*tantra*), such as those pertaining to the *iṣṭi*, the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*), and the Soma sacrifice, due to its possession of superior qualities (*guṇādhikya*). This is seen from the fact that in the mantra "I am the northern, the most excellent" (*uttarāham uttaraḥ*), which occurs within a hymn intended to overcome rival wives, the word *uttara* carries the sense of excellence. The term is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍha*). "Facing west" means having a western orientation (*pratyaksaṃsthān*). The mention of "three" is for the purpose of excluding four or more.

The word *prati* is used to indicate that the steps (*prakrama*) are to be taken in succession. The prefix *vi-* implies an increase in measurement beyond the measure established by whichever foot or step was previously used, according to the requirements of the desired result. Here, the "western part" refers to the area to the south and north of the post situated at the western edge of the *uttaravedi*. The accusative case in *pṛṣṭhyām* is justified by the rule: "The accusative is used in connection with *amitaḥ*, *paritaḥ*, *samayā*, *nikaṣā*, *hā*, and *prati*."

Just as the two *havirdhāna* carts stand at three *prakrama*s behind the *uttaravedi*, which increase in size toward the north, so too they place the two carts on both sides of the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord; the northern wheel-nave of the southern cart and the southern wheel-nave of the northern cart are positioned on either side of the *pṛṣṭhyā*.

The nave is that middle plank upon which the navel is made; this is known from the indicative mark (liṅga) in the phrase "in the middle of the nave. They place [the two wheels] upon the wheel-supporting planks situated on those two planks. By being situated as the support for the wheels, they are not situated on the ground; this is the meaning. This is done for the sake of the two remaining wheels of the two Havirdhāna carts, in accordance with this very requirement.

By the rule *ugavādibhyo yat*, the suffix *yat* is applied; then, by the rule *nābhi nabhaṃ ca*, the word *nābhi* undergoes the substitution of *nabha*. The vowel *ā* of *nābha* is shortened. "Of the earth" (*pṛthivyāḥ*) is the end of the mantra. He states that there is no fixed rule regarding the measurement of the intermediate space: "According to the purpose, [they leave] the interval between the two *havirdhāna* sheds" (16). They create an interval. "According to the purpose" (*yathārtham*) means according to the requirement; "according to the purpose" (*yathārtham*) means not exceeding the purpose. This is a compound in the sense of "not overstepping the meaning" (*padārthānativṛtti*). The meaning is that an interval greater than the requirement should not be made between the two.
With the mantra "Thou art Vaiṣṇava; may Viṣṇu support thee," they prop it up.
The remainder [of the sense] is that they prop it up with two supporting wooden beams (*upastambhana-kāṣṭha*).
These two are elevated at the front.
The support should be made in such a way that the two poles of the cart are elevated at the front; this is the meaning.

With the verse containing the word "blessing," *divo vā viṣṇav uta vā pṛthivyāḥ*, the Udgātṛ strikes the southern joint of the southern *havirdhāna* cart behind [the axle]. With the verse *viṣṇornukam*, the Pratiprasthātṛ strikes the northern joint of the northern cart behind [the axle].

The meaning is: "with such a *ṛc* characterized by words expressing a prayer for blessings (*āśīḥ*)," that is, one containing words whose purpose is to pray for a blessing. [The relevant verse is: "Fill both hands with many desirable things; bestow them from the right and from the left"—these are the words expressing a prayer for a blessing. The mention of "words expressing a blessing" is for the sake of ensuring knowledge [of the text]. In the absence of such knowledge, the expiation for a breach of the *yajus* formula is that an oblation should be offered on the southern *hotṛ*-fire with the mantra "Bhuvaḥ svāhā. The specific mention of "the southern *havirdhāna*" is for the purpose of following the Brāhmaṇa text.

The mention of "of the northern" (*uttarasya*) is indeed necessary to prevent the recurrence of the phrase "of the southern *havirdhāna*" from what follows. In the expression "the southern *karṇātarda*," the word "southern" is for the purpose of excluding the northern *karṇātarda*. By the term *karṇātarda*, the wedge used for joining the two poles (*iṣā*) is denoted. In the form *karṇātaīm*, the accusative case is used according to the rule *enapā dvitīyā*. A *methī* is a firm pillar intended for binding.

In the phrase "uttaraṃ karṇātardam," the inclusion of the word *uttaram* (the upper) is for the purpose of excluding the right [ear]. The phrase "merthī nihanti" is supplied as an ellipsis. The first mantra ends with "savyāt" (from the left), and the second ends with "ghorugāya. By the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the words "viṣṇoryāṇi pravocam," the designation *āśīrpadam* applies to "viṣṇornukam" as well.

Alternatively, the designation *āśīrpad* is heard and applicable specifically to this [verse] beginning with "divo vā viṣṇu"; accordingly, in the Sūtra as well, this designation applies only to "divo vā," and not to the subsequent one. In this view, the term's status as a *yogarūḍha* (a word formed by both etymological derivation and conventional usage) should be understood.

With the words "viṣṇordhruvamasi," they two fasten these two there. There, they lead these two carts through the ear-holes of those two posts. The prefix *ni-* expresses the sense of "fastening. Binding (*bandhana*) means encircling with a rope.
With the formula "Thou art the fixed point of Viṣṇu," the two of them make two knots; these two knots become well-known.

They make the knots on the two ropes that have been wrapped around. These two knots are well-known and firm, because the knotting of the Sadas and Havirdhāna sheds—which were previously made—is intended by the author of the Sūtras to be undone later with the mantra "of the garment" (vastrasya); thus, they remain "well-known" until that point. Having pulled the pins (śamyās) upwards, they wrap them around from above so that it is well-fastened.

Having pulled them upward and fixed the lower rings, they should wrap them with a rope from above so that they do not fall; the meaning is that they should wrap them firmly. Āpastamba states the scriptural authority for their being upright: "It is known from scripture that the divine oxen carry [the burden] while facing upward.
They fix the boundary pillars.

Those who deserve the extremity are the "paryantya" (border-dwellers). The suffix *yat* is applied here because they belong to the class beginning with *daṇḍa*, and not because they exist at the extremity (*paryante bhavāḥ*), for there is no such location there. Alternatively, "existence" (*bhavana*) should be understood here as the nature of being; and that existence should be known as prospective (*bhāvinī*). They dig two-pronged pillars—that is, stakes.

Regarding the injunction, "One desiring heaven should perform the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite with the *sādyaḥkratu*; they proceed with the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* [sāmans]; the *havirdhāna* and *āgnīdhra* sheds are made of *aśvattha* wood; and they are provided with wheels according to the rule," because of this restriction to the *aśvattha* tree, the trees for the pillars here are unrestricted and should be understood as any sacrificially suitable (*yajñiya*) trees. Here too, the phrase "as in the case of creation" (*yathā sṛṣṭavat*) follows. Just as there is a path of movement in front of the *khara*, so that the path of movement (*saṃcara*) is in front of the *khara*, the connection is with the preceding word "he measures" (*minuta*).
Having driven two posts in front of the *havirdhāna* [shed], and having placed a bamboo beam (*vaṃśa*) upon them with its top pointing north, he lays down the bamboo beams facing east.

By the phrase "having driven two posts in front of the *havirdhāna*," it is understood that these two posts are to be situated near the front of the *havirdhāna* shed, positioned such that they are at the edge of the *havirdhāna* pavilion. Furthermore, these two posts are located in the middle of the pavilion and serve as the primary supports for the structure.

Having placed a bamboo pillar (*vaṃśa*) with its top-end [pointing] upwards—meaning one whose upper end is like a *mudga* bean—upon those two pillars, he places transverse beams (*vaṃśa*) with their tips pointing eastward all around so as to cover [the space].

He places the middle roof-cover (*chadis*) upon it with the formula, "Thou art the back of Viṣṇu. The others [roof-covers] are placed silently on top of the remaining [beams], because they are remnants. Regarding this, Āpastamba says: "The other two roof-covers are placed silently on top."
With the formula, "Thou art the forehead of Viṣṇu," he encloses the *rarāṭī* in front.
That is to say, at the front—the region where the door is to be made—he encloses it; the meaning is that he covers it from above. He describes its nature:
a reed (*tejanī*) for the *rarāṭī*, made of *eṣī* grass, straight and slender in the middle, he fastens it to the bamboo beam.

The *tejanī* is a stick. As it is stated in the Baudhāyana [Śrautasūtra]: "Of the *tejanī*, at both ends... and "The fourth joint is the *śalya*, the leaves are the *temana*"; and "Soma is the *śalya*, Viṣṇu is the *temana*. In the Brāhmaṇa and Sūtra manuscripts, the reading *aṇukāṇḍa* is found as a short form. Also in the [Baudhāyana] Śrautasūtra: "The *śalya* is the hair of the face, Viṣṇu is the *temana*. [End of] Paṭala 150, together with the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 701. In the [Baudhāyana] Śrautasūtra also: "The *śalya* is the hair of the face, Viṣṇu is the *temana*."

And this [rarāṭī] is made of *iṣīkā* grass; it is in the form of a stalk produced from the *iṣīkā* plant. It is directed eastward (*prācī*), meaning extended toward the east. It has slender joints (*aṇūkāṇḍā*), meaning its nodes are not thick. It is long and unbroken. It is stretched out and expanded in the middle. In some manuscripts, the reading is exactly the same. Having made a hole in the middle, it is strung on a cord. Such a *tejanī*-shaped *rarāṭī* he ties to the upper ends of the two eastern doorposts which stand in the place of the gateway.
He fixes the two ends of the *rarāṭī* with the formula: "You are the two nostrils of Viṣṇu."

He fastens the *rarāṭī* rope to the beam situated at the eastern edge, which is fixed upon the two pillars at the northern end; the prefix *vi-* here signifies "binding. Having bent it downward, he ties it. They then lay down mats and splinters in the intervals between the roof-coverings (*chadiṣ*).

They spread mats, grass coverings, and bamboo-sticks; having repeatedly spread them, they settle them within the intervals between the skins—meaning they fix them by aiming at each respective intermediate space, placing them one below the other. The word "and" (ca) is for the purpose of including the gathering of grass. Here, because the plural number is heard, the attendants (*parikarmiṇaḥ*) are the agents. *Tejanī* means staffs.
As before, having tied the mats together with certain staffs, they place them there in the openings; this is the meaning. They call these the "interior-locaters" (*antarvartāḥ*).

Those which are bound and joined with these splinters (*tejanī*) are called *antarvat*. The meaning is that they are designated by the word *antarvat* in the Brāhmaṇa with the phrase, "he makes them *antarvat* by means of exclusion.
"O lover of songs, [surround] thee with songs"—with this [verse], the two [priests] enclose [the cart-shed] on all sides;

the word "sacrificial oblation-holder" (*havirdhāna*) is to be supplied. Because of the dual number, [the agents are] the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ. "On all sides" (*amitaḥ*) means toward their respective portions; they enclose, that is, they cover [it]. The mantra ends with the word *juṣṭaye*.

They make two doors, one in front and one behind. The word "ca" (and) follows immediately after the word "dvāre" (doors). Thus, the meaning becomes: "they make two doors, one in front and one behind. The word "ca" also serves to include the making of large windows (*gavākṣa*). They make two doors, one in front and one behind—that is, the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ make the one situated in the eastern direction as the front door and the one situated in the western direction as the rear door. Regarding this, he states a specific detail:
the Adhvaryu sews up the southern door-opening, and the Pratiprasthātṛ [sews up] the northern one.

This sūtra has been composed so that the previous technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) may apply here as well to the term *havirdhāna*. By the rule *madyāditvāḍḍhak*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied to the word *dvāra*; thus, by this direction, the meaning becomes "by means of that door. Here, "existence" (*bhavana*) does not mean production (*utpatti*), because that is impossible; rather, it refers to existence (*sattā*). And that [existence] is to be understood here as future (*bhāvinī*). Furthermore, this is a qualifier for the two door-posts (*dvārasthūṇā*). The Adhvaryu ties around the southern door-post, and the Pratiprasthātṛ ties around the northern door-post.

Regarding the sewing with the formula *viṣṇoḥ syūrasīti*, Baudhāyana explains the sewing as follows: "Then, having taken hold of a handful of Kuśa grass at the southern door-post, he sews it through with a needle. With the formula *viṣṇoḥ syūrasīti*, the Adhvaryu sews the southern door-post, and the Pratiprasthātṛ sews the northern one. Although this is established by that much alone, the two actions—*sīvyati* (he sews) and *sīvyataḥ* (they two sew)—are mentioned for the purpose of indicating the two alternative options.

Since the preceding sūtra prescribes sewing around [the bundle] in sequence, while the subsequent sūtra prescribes sewing it together, there is a contradiction which results in an option (*vikalpa*). However, the mantra applies to both cases according to the "lamp-in-the-hall" analogy (*dehalī-dīpanyāya*). The meaning is that, having passed a cord through the holes of the *darbha* grass, one sews the *kuśa* blades together so as not to let them slip out.
With the mantra "Thou art the firmness of Viṣṇu," the two of them make knots; these two [knots] become well-known.

The meaning is clear. Regarding the injunction that "the Adhvaryu should untie the first knot he ties," the Brāhmaṇa states that if he does not untie it, he will die from urinary retention (*ameha*); thus, the tying of the knot is well known because the scripture mentions the fault in its failure to untie. The Sūtrakāra has indeed prescribed the untying at the end of the previously tied knots of the *sadas*, the *havirdhāna*, and so forth. *Amehena* means by the obstruction of urine.

Therefore, wherever the first knots are located, all of them should be identified and subsequently loosened; this is the intended meaning. By the phrase "surpassing the wisdom of Viṣṇu," this mantra is made optional. Alternatively, the application previously stated remains the very same as this application:
"Thou art Vaiṣṇava, for Viṣṇu thee"—with these words, they touch the *saṃmita* (measured).
The word "measured" (*saṃmita*) implies the measured *havirdhāna* (sacrificial shed); this is the sense.

"Viṣṇu is praised for that heroic deed, like a terrifying wild beast roaming on the mountains; in whose three wide strides all the worlds abide"—with these words, he steps forward from the measured *havirdhāna* shed.

From the *saṃmita* and the *vimita*. From the *havirdhāna*—that is, from the *havirdhāna* shed where the oblation called Soma is placed or established—they go out toward the east. The words "the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ" are to be supplied as the subject, because it is they alone who are present in this context. The reading is clearly *prāk* (eastward). If the reading were *prāc*, it would function as an adjective qualifying the agents; in that case, there would be the grammatical error of requiring a dual ending, as in *prāñcau*. The rest is clear. Having gone out, they mutter [the mantra]. The muttering should be performed by them whether they are seated or standing.
Having stepped forward three steps toward the east, he should mutter [the formula]; so say some.
Thus ends the fifth paṭala in the seventh praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

Even in the case of the *prakrama* (stride) being measured, the term *prakrama* is derived from the etymology "that which is stepped upon" (*prakramyate*), and thus it refers here specifically to the foot-step. This is because of the wording of the mantra: "In whose three strides on the thighs... and because it is known from the rule of Māradaivāja that "he strides three times," and also because of the singular number. Regarding the construction of the *havirdhāna* (sacrificial cart-shed), Āpastamba states the specific detail: "The *havirdhāna* is higher in front and lower at the back."

Some maintain that because the *uparava* ritual is imminent, even though there is no purpose for the Adhvaryu’s exit [from the *āgnīdhra*], he should perform the *uparava* ritual at this very time for the sake of an invisible merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), and having done so, re-enter and then perform the *uparava* ritual. Others, however, say that for the sake of a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), the Adhvaryu exits at the time of measuring out the *āgnīdhra* shed; the other [the Pratiprasthātṛ] exits right here. They further state that the sūtra will prescribe an exit for the sacrificer as well, and his exit should likewise be like that of the Adhvaryu. In reality, however, [the exit occurs] right here at the *āgnīdhra*.

It is more logical that the departure of both occurs together at the very time of the *vimāna* rite; however, regarding the fact that the sacrificer’s departure occurs only after the sowing of the *viṣṇiyas*, the supporting evidence will be stated in the *Yājamānasūtra*.

Thus ends the fifth chapter of the *Jyotsnā* commentary, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—the son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was himself the son of Okopāha Śrīmad Amibhiṣṭoma-yājin Sahasrāgni-yukta Vājapeya-yājin Sarvalomukha-yājin Dviṣāhasrāgni-yukta Pauṇḍarīka-yājin—written to pacify the lamentations of learned men seeking to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the ocean of the sūtras of the venerable Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin. Chapter Five. 5.
7.6 Now, the sixth chapter of the seventh book:

In front of the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, there are four *uparava* pits in the intermediate directions; they are a span wide at the opening, separated by a span, a cubit deep, hollowed out below, and separated above.

The inclusion of the word *dakṣiṇa* (southern) is for the purpose of excluding the northern [side]. If only "of the southern" (*dakṣiṇasya*) were stated, it might refer to the wheel as well, since that too could potentially be the substantive (*viśeṣya*). Furthermore, because the genitive case can sometimes signify proximity (*sāmīpya*), the meaning could also be "in front of that part of the axle which is attached to and situated near the southern side"; this should not be the case. Rather, so that it may be understood as being "in the middle," the term *havirdhāna* (the oblation-holder) is included. "In front of the axle" (*puro'kṣa*) means "ahead of the axle" (*purastād akṣasya*).

By interpreting the genitive case as having the sense of proximity (*sāmīpya*), [the location] is precisely near the axle. And thus, it results that they are below the southern *havirdhāna* cart. Āpastamba states this very point clearly: "Below the southern *havirdhāna*, in front of the axle, he makes four *uparavas* in separate locations, with a span (*prādeśa*) for their mouths and a span for the intervals between them. There are four *uparavas*; this is the general proposition. They are those in which there is a sound (*ravaḥ*) or noise above, near (*upa*) the tips.

In the intermediate directions—namely, the corners of Agni (southeast), Īśāna (northeast), Nairṛta (southwest), and Vāyu (northwest)—there are those whose openings (*mukha*) measure a *prādeśa* (span); these are called *prādeśamukha*. Those whose intervals (*antarāla*) between the directions measure a *prādeśa* are called *prādeśāntarāla*; the meaning is that even the measurement of the interval is a *prādeśa*. Those whose dimension is the length of an arm (*bāhu*) are called *bāhumātra*. They are *saṃtṛṇṇa*, meaning they are properly joined together below; they are *vidhṛta*, meaning they are all kept separate above. [This concludes] the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Sāyaṇa Mādhava, [Book] Seven, [Chapter] One.

The taking up of the spade (*abhri*) and the tracing around (*parilekhana*) have been explained in the context of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). The meaning is that just as the taking up of the spade with the mantra "Of the god... and the tracing around with the mantra "Traced around... were explained and stated in the ritual pertaining to the sacrificial post, so too should they be performed here. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the fact—unmentioned here—that the digging of the pit (*avaṭa*) is to be performed by another agent. He states the sequence for the tracing around: having traced around the southern [corner] of the two eastern [lines], he traces around the northern [corner] of the two western [lines]; then the southern [corner] of the two western [lines] and the northern [corner] of the two eastern [lines].

Of the two front [holes], the southern one is situated in the south-east (āgneyī); of the two rear ones, the northern one is situated in the north-west (vāyavī). Of the two rear ones, the southern one is situated in the south (naiṛtī); of the two front ones, the northern one is situated in the north-east (aiśānī). By this, the sequence mentioned in another sūtra—"the others in a clockwise direction, ending in the north"—is set aside.
In this manner, their ritual actions are performed in successive order.

Thus, the sequence described for the drawing out [of the lines] applies to those other [depressions]; these are their ritual actions. Since it was previously stated independently that they are "a cubit deep," the digging to a depth of one cubit is performed silently immediately after the drawing out. Furthermore, it was already indicated earlier that this is to be performed by another agent. The state of being perforated and the state of being separated must be accomplished immediately following the digging to a depth of one cubit.

Āpastamba has clearly stated this meaning: "They are perforated at the bottom and unbroken at the top; one should cause them to be dug silently to the depth of an arm. The syntactical connection is: having caused them to be dug silently to the depth of an arm, they become perforated at the bottom. However, Baudhāyana has described the digging to the depth of an arm and so forth as being performed by the Unnetṛ, preceded by a formal command (*praiṣa*) for the purpose of digging to that depth. It has been stated that their rites are performed in this successive order; he now states those rites: "I dig out the Rakṣas-slayers, the spell-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu," with these words he digs them out.

He digs the *uparavas* slightly more than a cubit (*bāhumātra*) deep. During the digging, there is the ritual touching of water (*udakasparśa*), which is prescribed by the Smṛti. He digs them with the formula: "I dig out the Rakṣas-slaying, strength-winning, Viṣṇu-related [holes]. The loosening of the dug-up earth is called *nivedana*. Regarding this, some authorities desire the touching of water.
With the formula, "Thou art great," he strikes the wooden mallet (*abhri*).

Once the earth has been loosened, he strikes it and then presses down (*upagṛhati*). This much alone is the mantra; however, "bṛhannasi" is not the full mantra, but rather a citation of the opening words of the mantra "bṛhannasi bṛhantam indrāya vācaṃ vada," because that full mantra would contradict the grammatical gender (the word *abhri* being feminine).
With the formula, "Thou art Virāj," he lowers his arm, or both arms;

for the mantra ends with the words, "driving away the rival. This is known from the indication of the subsequent sūtra which states, "he lowers the arm with each successive mantra. "He lowers" means that, being bent down, he brings his arm or both arms near to the excavated clay.
With the formula, "Here I dig out that hidden charm (valaga)," he throws up the loose earth.

He throws the dust into another vessel; this is the rule for the Pratiprasthātṛ. According to the view that "the lowering is by the arm," the throwing of the dust is done with one hand alone; according to the view that "the lowering is by the arms," it is done with both hands. The mantra ends with "nicaravāna.
He pushes [the stone] down into the pit of the uparava with the formula, "Idam enam adharam karomi" (I make him lower).
"In the vicinity of the *uparava* cavities, on all sides, he 'presses down' (*avabādhate*), which means that having bent down, he strikes with his hand. The mantra ends with the words *bharātīyati*.
He carries it away [with the words] 'The *valaga* has been cast out,' carrying it from the secret place in a vessel."
With the formula, "The malevolent one is pressed down," he pours [the earth] into that place where he intends to prepare the *khara*.
A *khara* is a square mound for the purpose of placing the Soma vessels; its dimensions are established by practical necessity, and it is four-cornered. "Pouring" (*nivapana*) means casting down.
With the formula, "By the Gāyatrī metre, the *valaga* is pressed down," he presses down with a hoe into the cavity of the *uparava*.
The meaning is that he grasps it firmly from below, i.e., he presses it down.
The same applies to the others;

"in the *uparavas*" is the ellipsis. Thus, the procedure beginning with digging and ending with the firm grasping applies to the other *uparavas* as well. Regarding this, he states the specific distinction:
With each successive mantra he lowers the arm, and with each successive meter he restrains it.

The mantra "thou art a sovereign" (*samrāḍ asi*) is superior to the preceding one; with it he lowers the arm for the second time. The mantra "thou art self-ruling" (*svarāḍ asi*) is superior to "thou art a sovereign"; with it he lowers the arm for the third time. The mantra "thou art all-ruling" (*viśvārāḍ asi*) is superior to "thou art self-ruling"; with it he lowers the arm for the fourth time. This is an illustration of the position that [he lowers] both arms. [The mantra] "brother... [is used].

The ends of the three mantras—*vyāghra*, *abhimātihā*, and *viśvāsāṃ nāṣṭrāṇāṃ hantā*—should be understood in their respective order. Regarding the statement that "one seizes [the victim] with each successive metre," since only the *gāyatrī* metre is recited in one's own Vedic branch (*śākhā*), there arises the question of which subsequent metres are to be taken. In response to this expectation, he says:
the metres recited are the *gāyatra*, the *traiṣṭubha*, the *jāgata*, and the *ānuṣṭubha*.

The word "they say" (*mavantīti*) is the ellipsis. They are recited in another *śākhā*; in another *śākhā*, four [metres] are recited, not only the *gāyatra* metre alone as it is recited in one's own *śākhā*. Here, the mention of the *gāyatra* is with reference to other *śākhās*. Alternatively, this is also to indicate that there is the following position: that by the *gāyatra* alone all [the others] are included. Thus says Āpastamba: "Or the first in all [cases]. The first is the *gāyatra* metre.

The sacrificer touches the southern one of the two front holes with the formula, "Thou art the sovereign ruler" (*virāj asi*); the Adhvaryu touches the northern one of the two rear holes with the formula, "Thou art the universal ruler" (*samrāj asi*).

This touching is for the purpose of distinguishing them from one another. Of the two front ones, the southern is the *uparava* situated in the region of Agni; he touches it. Of the two rear ones, the northern is the *uparava* situated in the region of Vāyu; the Adhvaryu—[the word] "touches" (*avamṛśati*) being understood from the subsequent context—[touches] it. As before, there are two formulas at the end of these two.

"Touch these for long life and for splendor! You are the treasure-store of the gods; drive away hatred! May you ward off whatever hatred we have committed. This which has been deposited here belongs to the gods; shine forth, illuminating the four quarters, making our other rivals low!"—thus he touches it from below.

"Feeling [them] correctly from below, one another" (*adhastātsamyakparasparam mṛśataḥ*). The reading "feeling these life-forces" (*saṃmṛśatīmānāyuṣaḥ*) is indeed a corruption. In such a reading, there would be a discrepancy between the two actions caused by the prefixes: in one case it is *avamṛśati* (he touches down), while in the other it is *saṃmṛśati* (he touches together). Therefore, the reading "touching these life-forces" (*saṃmṛśa imānāyuṣaḥ*) alone is appropriate. Āpastamba has also stated the reading in that very way. The word *samṛśa* is merely a portion of the mantra; for the accusative form *imān* cannot have its expectancy satisfied without a corresponding verbal action.

Where there is a designation [of the fruit] as being "together" (*saha*), even there, because the dual number is inappropriate, the fruit belongs only to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). As for the letter *p* [in the word *patnī*], it is for the sake of the ritual action; however, since the fruit is meaningful with respect to their master, it belongs only to the officiating priests—this is what was stated regarding the fruit, and this [particle] serves to draw that [point] forward.

[The ritual procedure is: "With the words *svarāḍ asi*, the sacrificer touches the southern [post] of the two rear ones; with the words *viśvārāḍ asi*, the Adhvaryu touches the northern [post] of the two front ones."

The western *uparava* is situated in the south; the eastern *uparava* is situated in the north-east. The rest is to be explained as before. The end of these two mantras is as before. "They touch [the *uparavas*] as previously" means that by the phrase "as previously," the mantra "Touch these, O Āyus" and the lower region are obtained. "He touches as previously" is simply a corrupt reading.

"What is here? asks the sacrificer. "Blessing," replies the Adhvaryu. "May that be mine," says the sacrificer. In the phrase "What is here?", the Adhvaryu is to be addressed; in the phrase "May that be mine," the sacrificer is to be addressed. Here too, the question and the reply are made with the hands placed below. "O you who are slayers of Rakṣas, slayers of secret spells, I sprinkle you, belonging to Viṣṇu. With these words, he sprinkles the Uparava holes three times with water containing barley grains.

"With barley-mixed water" (*yavamadbhir yavamiśrābhiḥ*). Since there is no obstacle to accepting any of the three possible analyses—*yavaḥ yayau āsu*, *yavaḥ āsu*, or *yavāḥ āsu santi*—the mixture may be with one barley grain, two barley grains, three, four, or even more. There is no restriction regarding the number of barley grains. Because of the mention of "with water," the previously mentioned refinement (of heating) does not apply here. The reading *tribhiḥ* is also seen in some manuscripts; this very reading is the correct one.

Because simultaneous sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of all [the uparavas] is impossible by rule; because the sequence is established here as well by the statement, "Thus their rites are performed in successive order"; and because in another Sūtra, Kapa alone is explicitly mentioned. Furthermore, the mantra for the uparavas should be treated as a *tantra* (common to all) because of the plural number in common usage, for Jaimini has stated this point in two Sūtras: "It is not [a *tantra*] because of its connection [to individual acts]," and "Since there is no perception of distinction among non-connected acts, there is a single recitation because of the unity of time."

The mantra for the *uparava* holes would be governed by the rule of the plural number; for just as in common usage the plural may be employed even when referring to a single thing, so it is here as well—this is the meaning of the preceding sūtra. Because the mantra is "conjoined" (*saṃnipātī*), that is to say, because its nature is to be conjoined with the beginning of the ritual action, and because the nature of the mantra and the beginning of the action is to be conjoined—as long as there is a mantra of instrumentality (*karaṇamantra*)—there is a rule that the action must begin at the end of the mantra. Thus, the commencement of the digging is conjoined with the end of the mantra; therefore, that mantra alone serves that purpose and not others.

The plural number of the word *suparvāṇām* (of the well-jointed) is sufficient to serve its purpose. The instrumental case ending of the mantra becomes a plural expression because it repeatedly grasps such specific distinctions. Therefore, it should be understood that only the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the mere grammatical relation (*kāraka*) are intended, while the plural number is employed for the sake of repetition (*pūjārtha*) even when referring to a single object. Nor should it be argued that, on this basis, the plural number in the word *pāśān* (the nooses) would also be unintended.

Since the intention to express plurality is in no way possible here, there is no occurrence of the anomaly found in the *Pāśādhikaraṇa* due to the disparity with the illustrative example. Those rituals where there is no coincidence (*saṃnipāta*) between the end of the mantra and the beginning of the action are "non-coincident rituals" (*asaṃpātikarmāṇi*). In these, the distinction is that the end of one coincides with the beginning of the other; this distinction does not exist in the case of a non-performative mantra (*akaraṇamantra*). Therefore, because the specific distinction is not grasped and because both share the same time, the non-performative mantra is uttered only once.

Therefore, the meaning of the subsequent sūtra is that there is no repetition [of the mantra], but rather a return [to it]. This is found in the fourth quarter (pāda) of the eleventh chapter. Regarding the reading "three times, three times" (tris-tris) in the sūtra, it means once with the mantra and twice silently for each uparava. The plural number used for the mantra should be understood as being for the sake of honor, like the plural number used for the fires (agni). Even when the reading is simply "three times," the mantra is used only once because it is sufficient; however, if it were insufficient, there would be a repetition of the mantra in accordance with the completion of the action.
He pours down water containing barley-grains [with the formula]: "I pour down the Rakṣas-slayers, the Vālaga-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu."

He pours water mixed with barley into the *uparava* holes. In all cases, there is a repetition of the mantra. He throws a grain of barley [into each hole] with the mantra, "Thou art barley" (*yavo'si*). Since the mantra "Thou art barley" is heard in the singular, the phrase "he throws a grain of barley" (*yavaṃ prāsyati*) also uses the singular. This singular number is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*); therefore, many barley grains themselves are to be thrown. And so says Baudhāyana: "Then he causes barley grains to fall into these [holes] with the mantra: 'Thou art barley; drive away our hatred, drive away our enemies'. "Throwing" (*prāsana*) means casting in. Here... [text fragment]. 708. [End of section] 1. sa. ga. śeṣana. || 708 ||

The word *pra* (forth) indicates casting away, as if striking; this is indicated by the indicative marks (*liṅga*) in the mantras "Drive away from us hatred" (*yavayāsmad dveṣaḥ*) and "Drive away the enemies" (*yavayārātīḥ*). The mantra ends with "the enemies" (*arātīḥ*).
With the words "I spread out the Rakṣas-slayers, the charm-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu," he spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) facing eastward.

In this context, it should be understood that the word *barhis* denotes a species of grass and not a consecrated object (*saṃskāra*). Consequently, acts such as cutting and so forth are not *barhis*-dharmas (ritual properties of the sacrificial grass). Thus, Jaimini states in the first chapter, fourth quarter: "In the case of *barhis* and clarified butter (*ājya*), because the words are used even when there is no consecration, they are not [restricted] by that term."

The meaning of the term *mūtra* (the word "barhis") is as follows: Since the word is applied even in the technical ritual usage (*yājñika-prayoga*) based on the mere genus (*jāti*) when there is no specific refinement (*saṃskāra*), and because it conforms to the sense of the sentence "he cuts that which is *barhis*" in the passage "he goes beyond," and since otherwise one would fall into the error of an excessively strained interpretation, the word is not based on refinement (*saṃskāra-nimittaka*). [The text says: "With *prācīna* grass—that is, with grass whose tips point eastward—he strews the lower regions; he makes them covered. [And:
"Saying 'I offer oblations to the slayers of demons, the slayers of spells, belonging to Viṣṇu,' he offers oblations with the *sruva* ladle while placing gold in between."

Having placed gold beneath [the offering] in each of the upper sacrificial pits (uparava) in sequence, and having likewise placed it in the middle, he makes an oblation with the *sruva* spoon, making the gold the target of his offering. Because the act is enjoined as an *oblation* (*juhoti*), the utterance of *svāhā* is required; this follows the ritual procedure of a *darvihoma*. [The offering is made] between the two fires. There is no fault in walking [between them]; one returns by that same path. The mention of the *sruva* is for the purpose of excluding the *juhū* ladle.

With the formula, "I sprinkle you, the two slayers of Rakṣases, the destroyers of spells, belonging to Viṣṇu," he sprinkles the two pressing-boards made of Udumbara, Kārṣmarya, or Palāśa wood; they are planed, joined at the front with their edges flush, and at the back either joined or not joined, being perforated at the back by two, three, or four finger-breadths.

Since the word *phalaka* is neuter in gender, the reading should be *vaiṣṇave* (neuter dual); however, the feminine form found in the subsequent mantras must be justified as being archaic (*chāndasa*). Some read: *rakṣohaṇau valagahanau prokṣāmi vaiṣṇavī*. Those two upon which Soma is pressed—that is, squeezed—are the *adhiṣavaṇe*; and those two boards are the *adhiṣavaṇe-phalake*.

He sprinkles those two wind-boards simultaneously with water consecrated by this mantra, because of the dual number [in the mantra] and because it is possible [to do so]. He states their nature with the words beginning "audumbare" (made of *udumbara* wood). "Audumbare" means made from a modification of the *udumbara* tree; the suffix *aṇ* is used here in the sense of a modification according to the rule for the *bilva* group. "Kāmayamaye" means made from a modification of the *kārmarya* tree (the *śrīparṇī*). The suffix *mayaṭ* is applied invariably here according to the rule "nityaṃ vṛddha-śarādibhyaḥ," because it belongs to the *śara* group. "Pālāśe" means a modification of the *palāśa* tree.

The suffix *ap* is optional here by the rule *palāśādibhyo vā*. They are like two door-panels (*kapāṭa*) joined on all sides. "Pradhimukhe" means those two whose faces are the *pradhī*, which are the planks of the wheel shaped like a bow. "Saṃhite" means joined together or closely attached; such are they at the front. "Samāpikarte": the word *api* here indicates a certain distinction regarding the cutting, and that [distinction] consists in smoothness (*ślakṣṇya*). Those two whose cutting is characterized by smoothness are "samāpikarte."

In such a case, it occurs afterwards; or rather, it has the sense of being "proper. By this, it is established that a proper cutting must be performed, and that indeed consists in the state of being smooth (*ślaiṇya*). By this, it is covered at the back, facing the *pradhi*. At the middle of the western edge of the two *kalaka*s, there is an interval of one of the measures, such as three fingers or more. In the expression "by three fingers," the word "by measure" is to be supplied.

The same applies here for [an increase] of two finger-breadths or four finger-breadths. And this [increase] may be either horizontal or transverse. Thus the meaning is as follows: on the southern plank, the carpenter should have a cut made at the western and northern edges—measuring one, one and a half, or two finger-breadths in size—for the purpose of joining them into a uniform square. On the northern plank, however, it should be done in the same manner at the western and southern edges.

In the case of the *tiryag* (horizontal) measurement, it becomes a long quadrangle (*dīrghacaturaśra*). By this, its connection with the subsequent [measurement] is excluded. Regarding the completion [of the altar], whether it is not joined by two, three, or four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) at the back—since it could have been stated simply as "at the back"—the separate formulation of the sūtra should be understood as being for the purpose of making known that the lack of connection (*asaṃhitatva*) is not an absolute rule (*anityatā*).

*Saṃtardana* is the act of joining together; it refers to the two [wooden] parts that have been cut so as to be equalized, and for the sake of a firm union, one should plane the areas to be joined thin and then join the one over the other—this is *saṃtardana*. Having made corresponding holes in the upper edge of the southern plank and the southern edge of the northern plank, one should insert a wooden pin (*kolaka*) into the hole at the upper edge of the southern plank, and those two pins...

Some say that the phrase "in those characterized by that" means one should insert [the wedge] into the hole located at the southern edge of the two pressing-slates (*adhiṣavaṇaphalaka*); thus, they hold that [the practice applies] only when the slates are joined. Others say that in the case of an unjoined [pair], meaning one devoid of joining, there is an option based on personal choice; for while the Vedic text states, "In a long *soma* sacrifice, they are joined for stability," and the *Ahīnasūtra* states, "The two pressing-slates are joined in an *ahīna* sacrifice," the rule of joining is mandatory in an *ahīna*, whereas here [in a *sattra*], they maintain the option is optional.

In fact, there is indeed an established option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*) regarding the *saṃtardana* (joining together) in the *prakṛti* (archetype): it is not performed in the *dīrghasoma* sacrifice denoted by that term, but it is performed in the *ahīna* sacrifice. Although length exists even in the *prakṛti* relative to [the *agniṣṭoma*], nevertheless, because the length pertaining to the *soma* depends on other *soma* sacrifices, the *saṃtardana* is displaced to the *vikṛti* (modification). Thus, in the third chapter, third pāda, Āpastamba states: "The *saṃtardana* should exist in the *prakṛti*, like the purchase (*krayaṇa*), because there is no loss [of its purpose]."

Just as in the case of the purchase [of Soma], because there is no loss of purpose due to the non-omission of the act, the piercing [of the sacrificial post] should take place in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Just as among the various items for purchase—such as cloth, gold, and so forth—even though the purchase is accomplished by one alone, the others, being offered according to the scriptural injunction, contribute even more to the completion of the act; thus, just as there is no loss of purpose regarding the cloth and other items, so too, because the archetype is not deficient in its assistance, the piercing is not omitted.

Although pressing is possible on both types of stones, since the capacity for cooking exists, when the *saṃtāna* (the continuous striking) is resorted to, ease in the act of pressing is obtained rather than a loss of purpose; thus, because its purpose is not lost, the *saṃtāna* should exist in the archetype (*prakṛti*). In this manner, the sūtra of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been explained by the Teacher.

The Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), however, has explained this by taking the example of the "purchase" (*krayaṇa*), reasoning that because the purpose is not interrupted in the continuous series, it should apply to the archetype (*prakṛti*); since both the piercing (*satardana*) and the non-piercing are possible as alternatives—just like the purchase—it is logical for the piercing to be included even when the non-piercing occurs. Thus, having established the alternative based on the analogy of the purchase, he concludes that there is no distinction, and therefore there is an upward extension (*utkarṣa*) to the *saṃsthās* and the *dvirātra* and other sacrifices; this is the final position (*siddhānta*). On this point, the Sūtra states: "Or rather, there is an upward extension because of the mention of a specific distinction."

The meaning [of the previous argument] is that because the specific characteristic of having long hair exists only in the *saṃsthās* (the completed forms of the sacrifice), the shaving should take place only there and not in the *prakṛti* (the archetype), as that characteristic is absent in the archetype. [The author] refutes the position stated in the Sūtra—"or [it is] on account of the agent"—which suggests that by taking the length [of the hair] as residing in the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), it is reintroduced into the *prakṛti* itself; for that specific characteristic of length is caused by the agent, since the agent is the sacrificer, and thus the characteristic of length is caused by him, being dependent upon the sacrificer. [The author refutes this] by stating "on account of the ritual" (*ṛtutaḥ*).

Or rather, because an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would otherwise be untenable, according to the Sūtra "it would be so because of the unaccountability of the explanatory passage," the meaning is that since the explanatory passage is untenable, the distinction is caused by the *ṛtu* (seasonal sacrifice) itself, and not caused by the name. Thus ends the seventh section of the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha. Baudhāyana also says: "Now, these two boards for him are to be joined together in a long *Soma* sacrifice; they are unjoined in a one-day (*ekāha*) sacrifice; he places them joined together."

With the formula, "I place you two, the slayers of Rakṣases, the destroyers of secret spells, belonging to Viṣṇu," he covers the *uparavas* with the two *adhiṣavaṇa* planks—two with the southern one and two with the northern one.

He covers them simultaneously with both hands using the two *adhiṣavaṇa* planks; that is, he conceals them. Regarding this, there is a specific detail: he covers two *uparavas* with the southern *adhiṣavaṇa* plank and two *uparavas* with the northern *adhiṣavaṇa* plank—meaning two with the southern and two with the northern. By this, it is understood that the measurement and the purpose of the two [planks] are equal.

By this, the possibility that—due to the acquisition of wood—one might cover all three with a single plank and cover only one with another is precluded. The mantra is recited only once, because it is impossible for there to be two dual-numbered formulas. The statement, "He covers the *uparavas* with those two," by means of the reference through the pronoun *tābhyām* ("with those two"), establishes the identity of those two; furthermore, the subsequent mention of the "two pressing-planks" (*adhiṣavaṇaphalake*) is intended to indicate the optional nature of the requirement for their specific characteristics, such as being made of *udumbara* wood, which were mentioned immediately prior.

By the statement, "two on the south, two on the north," it is understood that the covering is to be performed in an upward orientation (udaksaṃstha), and not in a forward orientation (prāksaṃstha). If it were stated simply as "one [on one side], two [on the other], one [on the other], two [on the other]," then the forward orientation might also occur as an alternative; it is for this very purpose that the rule is stated in this manner.

With one [piece] he covers the southern [side], and with one the northern; since the state of being oriented toward the north is already established by this much alone, this statement is for the purpose of identifying "this is the southern plank" and "this is the northern," and to indicate that a mark must be made beforehand. The words ending in the third case, *dakṣiṇena* and *uttareṇa*, signify the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Regarding the statement by Baudhāyana that "one should encircle these with stakes," he has prescribed the stabilization with six stakes for the purpose of preventing movement; since this serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), it must indeed be performed. The method for the placement of the stakes has also been stated by him: "two in front, two behind, and two on both sides to prevent movement. This means: two stakes in front of the two [posts], two behind the two, one to the south of the southern [post], and one to the north of the northern [post].
"O you two who slay the Rakṣases, who destroy the secret spells, belonging to Viṣṇu, I pile you around," with these words he piles it around with the loose earth from the upper mound.

The phrase "on the two pressing-boards" (*adhiṣavaṇaphalake*) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the object]. "Auparava" means belonging to the *uparavas*; with that *auparava* earth—that is, with clay—one "fills," meaning one surrounds or encloses it on all sides. In the case where the boards are perforated (*saṃtṛṇṇa*), there is only a single act of filling. In the case where they are not perforated (*asaṃtṛṇṇa*), it is indeed distinct [for each board]. Although, according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā-sūtra*) stating that "when there is a plurality of substances, the mantra is repeated," the repetition of the mantra would thus be required in this case, nevertheless, because the mantra possesses a dual number indicator (*dvivacana-liṅgatvāt*), it occurs only once.
"O you two who slay the Rakṣases, who destroy the Valagas, belonging to Viṣṇu, I strew [you]," with these words he strews around [the fire] with Darbha grass.

The phrase "adhiṣavaṇaphalake" (the two pressing-boards) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Since the use of *darbha* grass in the context of strewing (*paristaraṇa*) is so well known that it is established by the very sense of the matter, the explicit mention of *darbha* is for the purpose of including a specific type of grass that is devoid of flowers, and for the purpose of including the qualification of having uncut tips. The meaning is that one covers all around the area with *darbha* grass; or alternatively, the meaning is that one encircles [it] on all sides. Here too, the distinction between being perforated (*saṃtṛṇṇa*) and not being perforated (*asaṃtṛṇṇa*) should be observed as previously explained.
The circumambulation is established by the general rule.
[Kha. 1] "The two pressing-boards (adhiṣavaṇaphalake) are slayers of Rakṣasas, slayers of Valagas, belonging to Viṣṇu"—with these words he consecrates them.
The remainder of the phrase refers to the two pressing-boards. The meaning is clear.
"Having struck down the Rakṣas, having struck down Bala, I sprinkle [it] as belonging to Viṣṇu"—with these words he sprinkles the hide for pressing (*adhiṣavaṇacarma*).

That is the hide upon which Soma is pressed (*sūyate*) or extracted (*kaṇḍyate*). Because the word "with" (*abhi*) is absent, this is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the waters intended for sprinkling. He describes the nature of the hide:
it is the red hide of a bull, with the hair on the upper side, shaped like a vessel for pouring, so that it is suitable for the pressing.

*Lohita* means red. *Ānaḍuham* refers to that which belongs to or is a product of the ox (*anaḍuh*). That upon which the hair is located [is "upariṣṭāl-loma"]. That by which the Soma juice is poured out—that is, brought outside—is the *āsecanam* (pouring-vessel); that which possesses this is *āsecanavat*. By the term *āsecanavat*, its bowl-like shape is understood. By the phrase "for the purpose of pressing" (*abhiṣavāya*), the dimension established by the context is indicated. *Upāptam* means sufficient. In the reading *upāttam*, the meaning is "utilized.
In both cases, the word *yathā* has the sense of "as much as" (*yāvat*); these are all qualifiers of the hide (*carman*).
"Having slain the Rakṣases, having slain the Valagas, I spread what belongs to Viṣṇu"—with these words he spreads [the skin] over the two pressing-boards;

the word "skin" (*carman*) is understood [from the context].
