Regarding the specific characteristics of the skin, Āpastamba states: "The pressing-skin is made from that [animal skin] on which the Soma has been measured; it is rough, trimmed all around, provided with four flaps, and capable of receiving liquid poured upon it. The meaning of this is: the pressing-skin should be made from a portion of that skin on which the Soma was measured; and it is to be rough, not soft. It is "trimmed all around" (*parikṛta*), meaning cut evenly on all sides; it has "four flaps" (*catuṣpuṭa*), those flaps in which the strainers (*grāvan*) are placed.
By this it is understood that four compartments (puṭas) are to be made in the four cardinal directions or the intermediate directions.
Upon that [altar], he places four pressing-stones (grāvan), with their upper surfaces level and arranged so as not to strike one another; the fifth is placed in the middle, being the broadest.

Upon that skin which has been spread out: although the word *prāva* refers exclusively to a stone, nevertheless, because its specific form will be described later, the term *prāva* here should be understood as referring to the well-known stone characterized by a particular shape used as an instrument for grinding. He states its number: "four. Regarding the word *saṃ* in the expression *saṃsādayati*, it indicates the sense that they should be placed down in such a way that, like those placed on a high shelf (*ūrdhvamānava*), they do not fall.

Regarding this, he states the distinction: "upward-facing ridges, types of threshing-sledges. The word *sānu* signifies the summit or peak. Those whose ridges (*sānu*) consist of minute portions of form are "upward-facing ridged" (*ūrdhva-sānu*); that is to say, those [stones] which possess such ridges. The broad surface is the "mouth," and that itself is the instrument for threshing. "Types of threshing-sledges" (*āhanana-prakāra*) refers to those things upon which there are methods (*prakāra*) by means of which (*ānanāya*) one threshes (*āhanyate*).

The meaning is that for the purpose of striking and threshing, a specific object in the form of a stone must be conceived as the name "upara. The *upara* is a stone serving as the substratum for the threshing. In the middle of the hide, one places the *upara*, which is the thickest part. Because the word "in the middle" is used independently, its placement is separate [from the hide].

Because it is impossible to place [the ladle] together with the four [other vessels] due to the great size of the *uparasthālī*, it is commenced separately. According to the rule *atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau*, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added to the word *pṛthu* in the sense of "exceedingly"; by the rule *ra ṛto halāderlaghoḥ*, the *ṛ* is replaced by *r* when *iṣṭha* follows; and by the rule *ṭeḥ*, the final *u* is elided when *iṣṭha* follows, whereby the form *prathiṣṭham* is produced.

The statement "the fifth" is intended to demonstrate that even a stone characterized by its specific shape, which serves as the base for the threshing, possesses the quality of being a *grāvan* (pressing-stone). The purpose is that the expiation prescribed by the rule, "If the pressing-stone should break," applies even when it is the upper stone that breaks.
[One should recite] "Thou art great" for each one.

By the phrase "one by one" (*ekaikaśas*), the meaning understood is as follows: having first silently placed the four pressing-stones (*grāvan*) and then the upper stone (*upara*) in the middle, he subsequently places each pressing-stone in the directions starting from the east in order, and the upper stone in the middle, with the mantra. Otherwise, because the singular number is heard in the mantra—"I gather thee, well-gathered"—the word "one by one" (*ekaikam*) would be redundant, as it would apply individually to each handful (*muṣṭi*), just as in the case of the handfuls themselves.

Thus it is understood that the result of placing [the vessels] simultaneously is a distinct unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and the result of placing them one by one is a different unseen merit. In this regard, since it is impossible to perform the simultaneous placement in the directions starting with the east, the rule for placing them on the upper hide prescribes their placement at the southern and northern ends, as well as the western and eastern ends of the hide.

In that regard, the simultaneous placing [of the stones] is such that with the right hand one stone is placed on one edge of one of the two [skins], and with the left hand one stone is placed on one edge of the other; thus they are placed simultaneously. The placing of each individual stone also occurs only upon the skin, because it will be prescribed later that "having turned the pressing-stones (grāvan) face-to-face upon the upper [skin]" (*upara*), the upper skin serves as the substratum.
Having turned the pressing-stones face-to-face upon the upper skin, he sprinkles them with the formula: "I sprinkle you, the Rakṣas-slayers, the Valaga-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu."

The mouth by which the *soma* is rubbed should have a thick region and be made of solid stone; it should measure one and a half *prādeśas* in length. It should be circular, fine at one end and thick at the other. The circumference of the mouth is said to be six finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*), while the thickness is its width. The *aga* is the fine region; this indeed is the characteristic of the *grāvan*. Thus say the learned authorities.

Āpastamba also states regarding the measurement of one span (*prādeśamātratva*) and the object denoted by the term "mouth" (*mukha*): "Upon that [altar], they place four pressing-stones (*grāvan*), each a span in size, with their upper surfaces level and their faces turned outward," and he adds, "the mouths are the larger parts. "Larger" (*sthavīyasi*) means more substantial or broader. Lāṭyāyana and Drāhyāyaṇa state: "Having made those [stones] with their larger parts on the inside, these are the mouths. In the passage, "He sprinkles [them] after having placed the stones facing each other upon the *upara*," the word *upara* is used in the locative case (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*).

By this, the facing upwards mentioned by Āpastamba is excluded. Since there is no definition provided for "upara," its length and width are determined by the requirements of the purpose; its shape may be either square or circular. "Saṃmukhān" means facing [the sacrificer]; because of the use of the plural number, they are sprinkled simultaneously. Regarding the sprinkling here, since there is no mention of the word "adbhiḥ" (with water), the consecration of the water intended for sprinkling indeed takes place.

In front of the support of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, he fastens a bundle of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the purpose of the *stotra* chants. Thus says Baudhāyana: "Then, in front of the support of the southern *havirdhāna*, he fastens a handful of sacrificial grass for the sake of the *stotras*.
In front of the support, he constructs a square mound (*khara*) from the earth of the *uparava* pits, as large as he deems sufficient for the vessels.

Thus ends the sixth chapter in the seventh book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. This is the [earth] for the *uparavas*; it is the earth (*purīṣa*) from that *uparava*. This is for the purpose of distinguishing it from the fourfold earth. In the phrase "of the earth of the *uparava*," the genitive case denotes a part-whole relationship (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). The meaning is: "by means of a portion of the earth of the *uparava*. Alternatively, the genitive may have the sense of the instrumental. In the first view, a portion of the earth of the *uparava* must necessarily be set aside for the purpose of smearing the *khara* (mound). In the second view, the entire earth of the *uparava* is used solely for the construction of the *khara*.

Regarding the purpose of the plastering: the plastering is done with ordinary earth. On that part of the wood with which the cart was supported, he constructs right there nearby a square, four-cornered platform known as the *khara*. The *khara* is square because its front and rear parts are conventionally designated as the "shoulders" (*aṃsa*) and "hips" (*śroṇi*). He states its dimensions with the words beginning "as large as... and so forth.

The meaning is that, having determined that all the Soma-vessels—the *camasa* cups related to the Soma and those for the *pariplu* [ladle]—are to be placed upon a *khara* (mound) of this specific dimension, one constructs the mound accordingly. By this, the absence of a fixed rule regarding the measurement is indicated. Since no instruction is given concerning its height, there is no fixed rule for that. Furthermore, the *khara* must be made with *purīṣa* (clay/earth) unmixed with anything else, so that the clay may adhere to the bases of the vessels.

This mixing with water is established by implication (*arthāpatti*). A space must be left behind the *havirdhāna* shed for the sake of movement (*saṃcara*), according to the Sūtra stating, "so that there is a path of movement in front of the *khara*," and from the Brahman’s Sūtra, "having gone around in front of the *khara*, he sits down to the south. Āpastamba states this clearly in this very context: "He leaves a path of movement in the front."

Regarding the phrase "in front of the support" (*agreṇopastambhanam*), the reference is to the southern [post] because it is the one present at hand and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in the sūtra concerning the status of the Brahman priest. Āpastamba states clearly: "In front of this very *havirdhāna* cart, he makes a square mound (*khara*) with stones from the *uparava* pits, as much as he considers sufficient for the Soma vessels."

Thus ends the sixth chapter of the seventh book in the *Jyotsnā* commentary, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—the son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was the grandson of Okopāha Śrīmad Amibhiṣṭoma-yājin, Sāhasrāgni-yukta Vājapeya-yājin, Sarvatobhadra-yājin, and Dviṣāhasrāgni-yukta Pauṇḍarīka-yājin—on the *Śrīmad Bhagavat Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra*. This commentary, known as *Jyotsnā*, serves to alleviate the distress of learned men caused by their inability to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within that ocean of sūtras. ||6||
714. *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[Seventh Praśna, Seventh Paṭala]:

Now, in the seventh Praśna, the seventh Paṭala. To the north, one erects the Āgnīdhrīya shed; half of it is within the altar and half is outside the altar. They construct a measured hall with its ridge-pole facing east (*prācīnavaṃśa*), with the approach from the south.

In the word *uttarataḥ*, the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the locative case; thus, it means "in the northern region. From the word *ānīva*, the suffix *cha* is applied in the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*) according to the rule *vṛddhāccha*; this results in the substitution of *iy* for the vowel. Having driven a peg into the middle of the eastward line situated at the northern edge of the great altar (*mahāvedi*), one performs the layout of the square according to the method stated by Śulba-sūtra, using the measurement of the full extent. In that regard, the specific detail is: "half [of the area] inside the altar, half outside."

Half [of the *magnīdhra* shed] is within the altar (*antarvedi*), meaning it is in the middle of the altar; half is outside the altar—this alone is the injunction. The phrase "half within the altar" is for the purpose of restating what is heard in another recension (*śruti*). Such a scriptural statement (*śruti*) is to be inferred from another branch (*śākhāntara*). Just as in one's own branch, regarding the performance of the *havir-nirvāpa*, the rule "the fourth [portion] is silent" is the injunction and "with the three *yajus*" is the restatement, so it should be understood here. Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*).

Since the altar (*vedi*) serves all purposes, it follows that the entire pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is included within the altar; however, because the requirement of the injunction is specifically for the portion outside, the rule "half outside the altar" is understood as the actual injunction. Consequently, by implication, the rule "half inside the altar" is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Furthermore, the length and width of this [altar] are characterized by the strength of its dimensions. Baudhāyana, however, [states]: "Now, the northern part of the great altar..."

From the corner of the *daṇḍa* (the measuring cord) at the altar, they step eighteen steps toward the west; there they measure out the *Āgnīdhra* shed so that its middle would be exactly halfway across. Then, having leveled it, they enclose it, making its door on the south side. He states a specific measurement: "Bringing it along the side of the *Āgnīdhra* shed, [it should be] one *aratni* behind. "He erects the *Āgrīya* post to the north" is the general proposition.

The mention of the word *vimita* (enclosed shed) is for the purpose of indicating that this [shed] should be constructed immediately after the measuring out of the Great Altar (*mahāvedi*). Because of the statement, "He measures out the Āgnīdhra fire-shed to the north," the measurement must be performed right here. Alternatively, the mention of *vimita* is intended to indicate another possibility—that the measurement should be performed immediately following the measuring out of the Great Altar without any interval—or to exclude the simultaneity of the measurement with the enclosure. They measure it out; they enclose it.

In both of the first two positions, the enclosure (*pariśrayaṇa*) is right here. To the south means in the southern region; it is called a "path" (*upacāra*) because it is the path by which the ritual action consisting of exiting and entering is performed. Regarding the door and its measurement, Bādhūla says: "He erects the Āgnīdhra shed to the north. Half of the altar is inside and half is outside. They construct a measured hall (*vimita*) with its long side facing east, measuring one *aratni* or sixteen *aṅgulas*. They make the door to the south."

In another Sūtra, it is stated that the enclosure (*pariśrayaṇa*) should be made excluding only the southern direction. Consequently, two alternatives are established: either a door must be made for the sake of the path, or the enclosure itself should not be made toward the southern direction. In the word *upacāram*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied by the rule *akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām*. Because the suffix is *nit*, there is *vṛddhi* of the first vowel of the root. Thus, *dakṣiṇataupacāram* is a compound word, just as in the expression *uttarataupacāro 'gniḥ*.

Regarding the term *uttarataupacāra*, it should be understood that it is a compound word (*samastapada*) because of the *avagraha* (word-break) as *uttarataḥ-upacāraḥ*. Āpastamba also mentions [the shed] as having four pillars. Since there is a rule regarding the use of *aśvattha* wood for the six-day sacrifice of the Sādhyas, there is no restriction on the tree here. Like the *āgnīdhīya* shed, the *mānālīya* shed is also described by Baudhāyana; the specific distinction here is its being *uttarataupacāra* (approached from the north), and by this the *mānālīya* is explained, as it says, "they make its door facing north."

From the front edge to the rear limit of the altar, at a distance of three steps or an indefinite distance, he measures out the *sadas* with its beams oriented toward the north; it should be situated further to the south, as far as one considers sufficient for the sacrificial fires (*dhiṣṇiya*), the officiating priests, and the attendants.

Immediately after the word "sadaḥ," the phrase "he measures" (*minoti*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Starting from the middle peg (*śaṅku*) of the western edge of the *vedi*, one should lay down three pegs toward the east, arranged in an eastern direction, and there place a peg. That [last] peg marks the western limit of the *sadas*; starting from that point, one should construct the *sadas* with its beams running northward (*udīcīnavaṃśam*). By the term "with its beams running northward," the elongation of the *sadas* from south to north is indicated. It is called *sadas* because the officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*) sit (*sīdanti*) therein for the purpose of consuming the Soma; thus, it is a word whose meaning is established both etymologically and by conventional usage (*yogarūḍha*).

"To the south" means in the southern part; "more westerly" (*pratikṛṣṭatara*) means exceedingly westerly. According to the rule *dvivacanavibhajyopapade tarabīyasunau*, the suffix *-tara* is used here in the sense of excellence (*atiśaya*). "Westerliness" (*pratikarṣa*) refers to distance. In this context, "excellence" consists of one *pada* in the case where the measurement is by *padas*, and it consists of one *prakrama* in the case where the measurement is by *prakramas*. In the case where the measurement is by *prakramas* consisting of twenty-four *aṅgulas* and so forth, it should be made equal to one *aratni* in accordance with the custom of Sāṃkāśya.

Āpastamba states the reason for the contraction [of the southern part]: "At a step to the south of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, he erects the Audumbarī post in the middle of the *sadas*; he should contract the southern part of the *sadas* so that there is no obstruction to the *saṃkāśana*. This means: he erects the Audumbarī post in the middle of the *sadas* both in length and in width; he erects the Audumbarī post at a step to the south of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line in such a way that the southern portion is expanded so as to remain in the middle of the *sadas*.

If one asks, "Why is this so? [it is] so that there may be no contradiction with the visibility (*sāṃkāśya*) of the *śālāmukhīya* and other fires. For otherwise, it would be obscured by the *audumbarī* post. The term *avirodham* is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) according to the rule for the absence of meaning [i.e., *avyayaṃ vibhakti-samīpa...*]. By the rule beginning with *yāvad-ṛ-vibhyaḥ*, the fact that the measurement is established by its own sense is demonstrated. The measurement of the *sadas* is exactly eighteen *parārdhas*.

There is no fixed rule [regarding the size], but it should be understood that—due to the requirement of accommodating the placement of the *viṣṇya* and other elements—it may be either less or more than eighteen *padās*. This is to be seen as an option between the two measurements stated in the *Śulbasūtra*: "The *sadas* is nine *aratnis* across and twenty-seven *aratnis* extending northward," and "According to some, it is eighteen [across]. Āpastamba, however, states: "It is nine *aratnis* in width and twenty-seven *aratnis* in length, or it may be of unlimited size."

The term *aparimita* (unmeasured) denotes a measurement greater than that which has been stated. By the phrase "as far as the two *ṛtvij*s [can reach]," even a measurement less than eighteen *aratnis* is obtained. The measurement—whether in units of *pada* or *prakrama*—should be calculated in such a way that the entire *sadas* is situated within the middle of the altar (*vedi*). Since the *Śulbasūtra* prescribes a north-south length by stating "twenty-seven [units] extended toward the north," the word *tiryak* (transverse) here must be understood as referring specifically to the east-west direction. That [measurement] becomes nine *aratnis* in dimension.

Even in the case of the "unlimited" (aparimita) side, it becomes nine *aratnis* wide; with a measurement of either twenty or twenty-four *prakramas*, it is eighteen *aratnis* to the north and twenty-seven *aratnis* to the south. The location, however, has been stated in the *Prayoga-sūtra*. The method for its construction is stated in the *Śulba-sūtra*: "That which was described as having one cord and fifteen [units]—one should draw the corners by subtracting nine and using four and a half [units]. Here, the *pṛṣṭhyā* line runs northward. This concludes the *Śrauta-sūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [seventh book].
To the south of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, at the middle of the *sadas*, is the pit for the *audumbarī* post.

Here, the *pṛṣṭhyā* line is to be taken as facing east, because of its association with the term "south. Having measured one *prakrama*—or, according to the view that measures by steps, one step—straight from the southern region of the *pṛṣṭhyā* and immediately adjacent to it, the pit for the *audumbarī* post is located; the meaning is that it lies in the middle of the *sadas* both in length and in width. This is because of the statement "in the middle of the *sadas*," and [the measurement] must conform to that.

The Bhārgava [priest] should not measure the stride (*prakrama*) or the step (*pada*) on the back part or the southern region; by this, Sāṃkāśya is protected. The *audumrī* is made from the wood of the *udumbara* tree; its *avaṭa* is a pit.
The taking up of the wooden sword (*abhri*) and the tracing around have been explained in the section on the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

The meaning is that just as the taking up of the wooden sword (*abhri*) with the formula "For thee, O god... and the tracing around the pit (*avaṭa*) with the formula "It has been traced around" were explained and stated in the context of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the rites pertaining to it, so too should they be performed here. One digs the pit right here; for since the taking up [of the *abhri*] and the tracing around are intended to establish the boundaries of the pit, and since that [tracing] is for the purpose of digging the pit, the act of digging the pit is effectively accomplished right here, as it has already been indicated, and as Bharadvāja has explicitly stated: "Having dug, he sprinkles."

The word *ca* (and) here serves to include the unspoken directive (*praiṣa*) concerning digging. That directive is simply: "O Āgnīdh, dig the pit for the Udumbara post. Because there is no mention of the "upper part" (*upara*), the portion of the directive beginning with "measured by the upper part" (*upara-saṃmitam*) is omitted. Consequently, it is established that the digging of the pit is to be performed by the Āgnīdhra. However, Baudhāyana has stated that the digging of the pit for the Udumbara post is to be performed by the Udgātṛ, preceded by a directive. Furthermore, he has specified this particular detail: "the removal of the loose earth (*purīṣa*) is to take place first. The pit is to be dug according to the extent of the [post's] base.

With the words "For the day," he sprinkles [the grass] from the far side toward the near side. Starting from the region of the tip on the far side, he sprinkles it toward the root on the near side; this is for the purpose of placing that [grass] whose pit is at the front. This [grass] must be placed with its tips facing east. For if it were placed with its tips facing north over the pit, the sprinkling would result in ending toward the south; since ending toward the south is highly contrary to the requirement of ending toward the west in rites for the gods, this is clear. Āpastamba has stated this explicitly: "Having placed it in front of the pit, facing east."

For this very reason, the view that the tip should face westward or southward is refuted. He also says, "one should wash it silently. Here, the sequence is "the top," "the middle," and "the root"; thus, the meaning of the statement "he sprinkles from the further side toward the near side" is that he sprinkles in that specific order. The inclusion of the phrase "to the sky" (*dive svāhā*) is for the purpose of showing the sequence of the mantras; it does not mean that this mantra alone is the instrument of the sprinkling, nor does it indicate that the other two [mantras] are optional alternatives.

By means of that mantra—“For heaven thee, for the intermediate space thee, for the earth thee”—and with a single effort, the meaning “he sprinkles it from the further side towards himself” is established. Baudhāyana states this very point: “He sprinkles it from the further side towards himself with [the formula] ‘For heaven thee, for the intermediate space thee, for the earth thee. Since the *audumbarī* pillar was introduced previously, it is referred to by the pronoun *tām* (it).

Alternatively, the meaning is that one sprinkles the three parts of the udumbara post with three mantras: "To the sky, thee! for the top; "To the intermediate space, thee! for the middle; and "To the earth, thee! for the root. This has been stated quite clearly in this very way by Bharadvāja and others. The statement "downwards from above" is intended to set aside another sequence observed in the case of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). According to Baudhāyana, there is an addition: that the sprinkling occurs with the three mantras prior to the actual pouring of water.
A certain specific detail has been stated: "This post made of Udumbara wood, having been washed and brought forward, rests before the pit (avaṭa). It is brought forward by way of the *tīrtha*.
The pouring down of water, the scattering of barley, and the spreading with sacrificial grass (*barhis*) have been explained in the section on the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

The pouring out of water with the mantra "The world is emptiness," the scattering of barley with "Thou art barley, keep [the demons] away," and the spreading of the sacrificial grass (barhis) with "The seat of the Pitṛs"—all this is to be performed here in the same manner as was explained and stated regarding the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) in the ritual acts pertaining to the *yūpa*. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the mixing with barley, which was not explicitly mentioned in the context of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). And it has been stated by Bharadvāja: "He sprinkles the Udumbara post with sprinkling waters mixed with barley. Thus, there is indeed a mixing with barley.

"Rise up, O Lord of the Forest, in harmony with the divine *barhis*!"—with these words, he raises [the sacrificial post] together with the *udgātṛ* priest, using either "Support the sky! or [the former]. That which has its "ear" (*karṇa*) facing east at the time of raising is called "eastward-eared" (*prācīnakarṇī*). A "karṇa" is a small branch; he raises it so that its root is situated toward the eastern part. This is an option based on specific circumstances (*vyavasthitavikalpa*): in one performance one mantra is used, and in others another. Even in that case, in the first performance the first mantra is used, and in the others the latter.

It is precisely to make this known that the mantra belonging to another recension (śākhā) is cited first, followed by the one found in one's own recension which is read in this very context. By this, it is established that even the mantra belonging to one's own recension is connected to the ritual action. Where only the mantra from another recension is cited and not even that of one's own recension, there an implied option (vikalpa) exists.

The mantra for propping up is *varuṇastvottamnātu* from another recension (*śākhā*), while *varuṇasya skambhanam asi* belongs to one's own recension. According to the two sūtras—"the mantras for the purpose of the sacrificial ritual [are taken] from other [recensions]" and "according to their form"—the mantra *varuṇasya skambhanam asi* belonging to one's own recension would be obtained. However, since it is impossible to employ both in a single performance, they result in an option (*vikalpa*). This option is optional (*āpika*).

In this case, regarding the first application, there is no restrictive rule (niyama) that "this very mantra must be used here" or "this very one in others"; rather, the application (viniyoga) is optional (aicchika). It is precisely to demonstrate such a distinction that the text does not mention the application of mantras from one's own Śākhā in the case of the *upastambhana* (supporting) and other rites, whereas it does mention them in the case of the *audumbarī-ucchrayaṇa* (raising of the Audumbara post). Such is the difference between an implied option (*ārthika-vikalpa*) and a scripturally stated option (*vācanika-vikalpa*). Nor should one fear a contradiction with the Sūtra which establishes the restrictive rule for accepting the adopted position—namely, *prakramāt tu niyamyate* ("But [the mantra] is restricted by the commencement")—because that Sūtra pertains exclusively to the context of the *vaimṛdha* sacrifice.

Furthermore, the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* states: "The form, the time, the non-extinguishing [of the fire], the deity, and likewise the cooking—these very options that were established at the beginning shall indeed always remain. This shows that the rule regarding the adoption of a specific option applies only to these five items and does not extend to other optional matters. Nor should it be argued that the mention of these five is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all other optional elements; for there is no evidence to support such an illustrative intent.

Even though the remaining mantra lacks the status of being a cause that produces a result (*phalopadhāyakakāraṇatā*), its causality should be understood as existing by its very nature (*svarūpasat*), like a staff standing in a forest. If it is impossible for him to perform the swelling himself, he causes it to swell. This meaning is obtained through the intended sense of the causal suffix (*ṇic*). "The Udgātṛ is one who sings the *udgītha* portion; together with him, they cause the *audumbara* posts to stand up"—this is the meaning. The second mantra ends with the word *dṛśha*. (Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, Seventh Praśna).

With the mantra, "May Dyutāna Māruta set thee up," he places [the post] into the pit; or rather, he has the pit dug by his attendants at this point. The mantra ends with the word *dharmaṇi*. "Placing into the pit" means fixing it there. Here too, the phrase "together with the Udātṛ priest who holds the cord with its end pointing eastward" is understood to apply. Āpastamba states clearly: "With the mantra, 'May Dyutāna Māruta set thee up,' he fixes it together with the Udātṛ priest holding the cord with its end pointing eastward. The procedures for smearing around (*paryūhaṇa*), protecting (*parirakṣaṇa*), and sprinkling around (*pariṣecana*) have been explained in the section on the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

The threefold ritual consisting of the sprinkling with loose earth while reciting *brahmavani tvā*, the encircling with the Maitrāvaruṇa’s staff while reciting *brahma dṛha*, and the circumambulation from left to right with water while reciting *unnambhaya*—this triad has been explained and described in the context of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and its related rites; the meaning is that it should be performed here in the same manner.
Having placed gold in its ear or at the forked branch (*viśākha*), he makes an oblation with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) while reciting: *ghṛtena dyāvāpṛthivī āpṛṇethāṃ svāhā*.

*Karṇa* means the base of a small branch. *Viśākha* is a specific qualification of a particular part of the *audumbarī* post; it refers to that part from which branches have departed (*vigatā śākhā yasmāt*). Such is the nature of this component. The meaning is that one places gold there and offers an oblation. Alternatively, it means "in that part from which a distinguished branch [has emerged]. According to this interpretation, the placing of gold occurs on that specific component where a large branch is located. The inclusion of the word *nu* is for the purpose of excluding the *juhū* ladle.

The word *abhi* (towards) is used here either to indicate that the oblation must be performed directly over the *audumbarī* post, aiming specifically at the gold placed thereon, or to signify facing toward the *audumbarī*. Since the utterance of *svāhā* is already established by the injunction to "offer" (*juhoti*), the explicit mention of *svāhā* is intended to clarify a specific point: that while the *svāhā* is to be made only when the clarified butter (*ājya*) has reached the root [of the post], the *avasāvana* (pouring out) must be performed even earlier, at the very moment the mantra begins. Thus says Kātyāyana:

"—*svāhākāra* when [the oblation] has reached the ground. This means that once [the clarified butter] has reached the ground, the *svāhākāra* (the utterance of *svāhā*) must be performed. Because the mantra is short while the ritual action is long, and because at the time of beginning the mantra the act of pouring down (*avastrāvaṇa*) cannot yet have commenced, the action does not take place here at the end of the mantra. By this, the acceptance of the rule stated by Āpastamba—"In the case of an *āghāra* (pouring) and a continuous stream (*dhārā*), there is a connection with the beginning"—is made known.
By this, the following point is also established: here, the recitation of the mantra is to be done in a slow (*vilambita*) manner.

He causes [the ghee] to flow down as far as the root. [The prefix] *ā* here signifies pervasion (*abhivyāpti*). The meaning is: having pervaded the base of the Audumbarī pillar. Thus, starting from the top and reaching down to the base, he causes it to flow along the Audumbarī; for when the clarified butter has flowed down as far as the base, it necessarily reaches the ground, because those two are connected. And so, the meaning is that the *svāhā*-utterance is made precisely there where the butter, having reached the base, has reached the ground.
The tallest pillars are measured to be exactly the height of the sacrificer, so that they stand well.

The meaning is that the Udumbara post is as high as the sacrificer, measured by the sacrificer, reaching as far as the height of his shoulders. Some say it is "measured by the sacrificer" including the portion buried in the ground, because it is seen [so] in the case of the sacrificial stake (yūpa). Others say it is "measured by the sacrificer" starting from the part buried [in the ground]. There is no evidence for such a restriction.

It is logical that the Audumbarī pillar should be exactly the height of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) together with the portion to be buried. By the term "as tall as the sacrificer" (*yajamānamātrī*), the vertical measurement of the Audumbarī is indicated; its thickness, however, is established solely according to the requirements of the ritual materials (*dāya*). This has been stated quite explicitly by Bharadvāja: "The Audumbarī pillar, when erected, is as tall as the sacrificer among pillars."

From the example, "The other [acts] should be performed by one [person], just as one sows with a single potsherd, and the *audumbarī* [pillar] becomes equal to the sacrificer," the height of the *audumbarī* is to be understood. This example pertains to the context of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*). In that case, when several sacrificers are present, the *audumbarī* becomes equal to one sacrificer—whichever he may be—either the one designated as the *gṛhapati* (householder) or the primary sacrificer.

The *audumbarī* post is measured according to the sacrificer; "measured by that" means having that same dimension. They are called *varṣiṣṭhāḥ* because they are "most grown" (*atiśayena vṛddhāḥ*). Regarding the suffixes *-tama* and *-iṣṭha* used in the sense of excellence (*atiśāyane*), when the suffix *-iṣṭha* is applied to the word *vṛddha*, the word *vṛddha* undergoes the substitution of *varṣa* according to the rule "priyasthirāsphirobahulaguruvṛddha... (Pāṇini 6.4.157). The word *vṛddha* is a synonym for "ancient" (*purātana*), and it indicates "firmness" (*dāḍhya*). Thus, the meaning is that they are exceedingly firm.

The *sthūṇās* are pillars with two branches. Since specific measurements for those on the periphery are prescribed later on, and because of their similarity to the *audumbarī* post, it follows from the statement "measured to the height of the sacrificer" that the middle pillars are primarily intended here. Because of the dual verb "they measure," the pillars situated in their respective sections must be measured together by both [the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ]: the three pillars on the southern side by the Adhvaryu, and the three on the northern side by the Pratiprasthātṛ.

Because multiplicity follows from each individual [post] and because that [multiplicity] culminates in three, there are three times three. When there is a greater purpose, there may be more as well; the meaning is that the pillar should be made so that the seat becomes very firm and very solid.
He fixes the final one, reaching up to the navel, near the Udumbara post.

The term *paryantya* means "those existing at the limit" (*paryante prānte bhavāḥ*). The suffix *-ya* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *diś* (Pāṇini 4.3.54). Here, "existence" (*bhavana*) does not mean "origination," as that is impossible; rather, it refers to "being" (*sattā*), and that which is yet to be (*bhāvinī*) is what is intended to be grasped. Alternatively, the term *paryantya* may be derived from the sense of "possessing a limit" (*paryantam ahanti*). According to the rule *khalayavabhāṣatilavṛṣabrahmaṇaśca* (Pāṇini 5.1.7), the suffix *-ya* is also applied after the word *paryanta*, by virtue of the particle *ca* ("and") which serves to include items not explicitly mentioned in the list.

The meaning is that they are "measured by the navel," which signifies having a measurement starting from the feet up to the limit of the navel. There is no fixed rule that when a single measurement is established, the suffixes *mātra* and *daghna* must be used according to the distinction between horizontal and vertical orientation. The phrase "he fixes all the pillars facing the Audumbarī pillar" means he fixes them so as to be directed toward the Audumbarī; that is to say, they are bent toward the Audumbarī. In this context, being bent is itself what constitutes being "facing," as there is no other possible mode. [He] fixes them... so it says.
Because of the mention of the *kavaca* (armor), all the enclosing stones (*paryantya*) must be measured by the Adhvaryu alone; the word "well" (*suṣṭu*) from the preceding formula also applies here.
One should measure the Sadas shed low for one who desires rain, and high for one who does not desire rain; some authorities record the opposite.

This measurement is not eternally fixed; therefore, one should construct the *sadas* slightly higher for a sacrificer desiring rain, and slightly lower for a sacrificer desiring drought. The desire for rain arises when there is no rain, while the desire for drought arises when there is excessive rain. Furthermore, this should be understood as applicable when the *Soma*-preceded fire-installation (*somapūrvādhāna*) is performed during the rainy season, in accordance with the scriptural injunction: "Whenever the sacrifice approaches him, then he should install [the fires]; that indeed becomes his foundation. (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.1.2).

*Nīcaiḥ* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) meaning "low" or "in a low tone. *Uccaiḥ* is an indeclinable meaning "high" or "in a high tone. When heard in the sense of "in the Ṛgveda," the sacrificer desires it; likewise, this applies to the permanent constituent parts of the sacrifice, according to the sūtra: "But those which the word 'kāmayati' (he desires) causes to be heard. Here, the root *kam*.

Upon hearing the *dhātu* [the section of the Veda], a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) must be made here by the sacrificer: "Desiring rain, I shall perform [the rite] with the Sadas at a low level," or "Desiring drought, I shall perform it with the Sadas at a high level. The word *kāmayati* is derived from the verbal root *kam*. The suffix *śtip* is applied according to the rule (or *vārttika*) "The indication of a verbal root is by means of *śtip*. Some authorities transmit the matter in reverse; the meaning of the word "reverse" is that the result which belongs to the former [rite] belongs to the latter, and the result which belongs to the latter belongs to the former.
It should be understood that this refers to the low and high levels of the Sadas, as well as the low and high levels of the Audumbara pillars.
Nine roof-coverings have been prepared.
This preparation occurs even before the commencement of the performance connected with this day. The meaning is clear.
Having laid down the northward-pointing beams, he lays down the eastward-pointing beams.

The plural in *vaṃśān* (bamboo poles), *veṇūn* (reeds), and *vaṃśān* is not intended to be significant; therefore, the placement may be of a single bamboo pole or reed, or of two bamboos or two reeds. *Udīcaḥ* means with their tips pointing north (*udagagrān*), and *prācaḥ* means with their tips pointing east (*prāgagrān*). *Ādhānam* means placing or fixing them. With the formula *aindram asi*, he places three middle roof-coverings (*chadīṃṣi*) facing northward. There is a repetition of the mantra because of the singular number [in the original instruction]. With the formula *aindram asi*, he places each of the middle roof-coverings facing northward. This much alone is the mantra. Bhāradvāja says: "With the formula *aindram asi*, he places each of the middle roof-coverings upon [the others]."
With the formula, "Thou art the seat of Indra," he lays down three southern [roof-tiles], and with "For the shelter of all people," three northern ones.
By this it is stated that the *sadas* consists of nine roof-tiles. In both cases, there is a repetition of the mantra because of the singular number.
He arranges the southern and northern ones facing toward the *audumbarī* post.

The meaning is that he makes the southern roof-coverings those with their tips pointing north, and the northern ones those with their tips pointing south, so that they all lie above [the central post]. The purpose of this is that they face toward the Audumbarī post. The prefix *sam-* signifies firm joining.
The optional roof-coverings for one desiring splendor, as explained in the Brāhmaṇa—"one should erect nine coverings for one desiring splendor"—are also subject to his own choice.

The Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "One desiring splendor (*tejas*) should measure nine [roofs]" and so forth explains the optional rites (*kāmyāni*) mentioned for specific desires. Among those desires, such as splendor and the like, one should adopt the side (*pakṣa*) associated with whichever desire one has. In the term *yāthākāmī*, the suffix *ṇini* denotes habituality. Since the verbal root *kam* (to desire) is heard here as well, the sacrificer must form a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), according to his inclination, in this manner: "Desiring such-and-such, I shall construct the *sadas* hall with such-and-such a number of roofs."

The position of nine coverings is also permanent. Because of the force of the permanent injunction—"one should measure nine for the Agniṣṭoma"—and because of what Bharadvāja has stated, "nine coverings," in the case of the alternative of six coverings, there should be three each in the middle, the south, and the north, according to the principle that "it should be equal, as nothing specific has been heard. [End of] Seventh Paṭala, with the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 721.

In the case of those who give eleven roof-coverings, there are five in the middle because the middle region is primary, and three each on the other two sides. In the case of those who give fifteen roof-coverings, there are five each everywhere, according to the principle that "it should be equal in all respects when there is no specific scriptural instruction. In the case of those who give seventeen roof-coverings, there are seven in the middle because the middle region is primary, and five each on the other two sides.

Regarding the case of a hall (*sadas*) with twenty-one roofs, there should be seven in each instance, as it would be equal since nothing specific is heard [in the scripture]. Even so, due to the inequality of the ritual acts, they would be unequal; for in the purchase (*parikraya*), the designations and injunctions heard do not apply to the act of purchase itself, because of the observation of a distinction and because of the principle of "thus [is] prosperity" (*abhyudaya*). This principle was demonstrated by Jaimini in the third section (*pāda*) of the tenth chapter.

The meaning of the first sūtra is as follows: since there is no specific scriptural statement to the contrary, the distribution [of the sacrificial fee] should be equal. The word "api vā" (or rather) excludes this equality; the distribution is not equal, but rather, due to the inequality of the work—where for one person the work involves great effort and for another it involves little effort—the distribution is according to the effort, because of this inequality of work. This is the meaning of the second sūtra. In the case of hiring, they would be unequal; that is to say, they would not be equal, nor would there be an equal distribution.

In response to the inquiry as to in what domain there is inequality among these [rules], he says: "in the case of purchase" (*parikraye*). This means "in the domain of purchase. By this, it is demonstrated that in domains other than purchase, where no specific rule is heard, there is indeed equality. He states the reason for the inequality: "on account of designation and injunction" (*samākhyāvidhibhyām*).

In the sentence, "On the twelfth day, having initiated the Gṛhapati, the Adhvaryu initiates the Brahman," and so forth, it is stated: "He initiates the half-sharers (ardhinaḥ), he initiates the third-sharers (tṛtīyinaḥ), he initiates the quarter-sharers (pādinaḥ). Here, because we observe the usage of the term *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* and others for those designated as "third-sharers" (*tṛtīya-samākhyayā*), the term *āgnīdhra* and others for those designated as "quarter-sharers" (*pādi-samākhyayā*), and the term *potr* and others for those designated as "half-sharers" (*adhi-samākhyayā*), and because such usage is impossible without a connection to the [respective] shares, that which is given to the primary priests such as the Brahman constitutes their "half."

The rule is established that a third portion is to be given to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin and others, a fourth portion to the Āgnīdhra and others, and [the remainder] to the Potṛ and others. A prescription inferred from titles such as "half-sharer" (*ardhin*) and so forth is called a "prescription based on title" (*samākhyā-vidhi*). In the Vedic text (*śruti*) that establishes this, the disparity [in shares] is justified by the context of hiring (*parikraya*), but it is not justified in the case of rituals other than hiring. This disparity arises from a specific [textual] distinction, as seen in the *Abhyudayeṣṭi* (the sacrifice for prosperity) with the scriptural passage: "Those who may be the middle ones, those one should give to Agni Dātṛ," and so forth.

This is because it demonstrates a specific instance that serves as a point of comparison. In this regard, for those seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtu*) where there is no fixed rule regarding the number of roof-coverings (*chadis*), if one accepts the principle that optional (*kāmya*) elements are to be inserted into the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself according to the requirements of each particular form, then among those nine roof-coverings, neither the other alternative options nor the optional state of having nine coverings would apply.

They place mats and splinters between the coverings; these they call the *antarvartas*. With the verse, "O lover of songs, may the songs encompass thee," the two attendants cover [the altar] on both sides and make the eastern and western doors. The Adhvaryu sews up the southern door-panel, and the Pratiprasthātṛ the northern one, with the formula, "Thou art Indra’s seam. They make knots with the formula, "Thou art Indra’s firm [knot]," and these two remain well-known.

With the formula "Thou art the firm one of Indra," they touch the firm part of Indra; this is an alternative to the previously mentioned [formula]. The rest of the description of the dimensions of the *dhavirdhāna* (grain-holding shed) and the *vimāna* (measuring) is to be explained [elsewhere]. [Variant readings: 1. kha. ga. read *pavābhyudayaṣṭau*; 722 refers to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha.
They both touch the measured (*saṃmita*) [shed] with the formula "Thou art for Indra, for Indra thee. The measured (*saṃmita*) is that which has been constructed (*vimita*), namely the *sadas*.

[This applies] to the *prāgvaṃśa* (fore-hall), the *sadas*, and the *havirdhāna* [sheds]. "Sāṃkāśinam" means common. It is derived from the root *saṃ-kāś* with the suffix *lyuṭ* because it belongs to the *nandī*-class; the substitution of *an* for the *yu* and *vu* vowels is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule *yuvoranākau*. If the reading is "sāṃkāśanam," it should be justified by adding the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), so that *saṃkāśanam* becomes *sāṃkāśanam*. However, the reading distinguished by the long vowel *ī*—namely, "sāṃkāśinam"—is indeed an archaic (*ārṣa*) one. *Sāṃkāśanam* means "manifestation," "being seen from all sides"; this [manifestation] is common to these [structures].

The meaning is that just as one standing in a single place can see everything, so too should their doors be made with straightforwardness (*ājavena*). The mention of the *prāgvaṃśa* (fore-hall) without a compound is based on the fact that it is not fixed—due to the absence of a door at the front of the *prāgvaṃśa* caused by the requirement of a single door in any of the directions (south, west, or north) depending on the specific desire—and because it is characterized by both permanence and impermanence.

"Before the *soma* sacrifice has been concluded, the Adhvaryu, having entered the *havirdhāna* (soma-shed) by the eastern door, should not exit by the western door; if he should exit, he should mutter: 'This Viṣṇu strode across.'"

The meaning is that while the ritual procedure (*tantra*) connected with the Soma sacrifice remains unestablished—that is, while it is incomplete—the completion of the Soma-related *tantra* occurs only at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). Although there is no direct connection with the Soma at the *avabhṛtha*, there is nevertheless a connection by way of the vessels smeared with the dregs (*uñjīṣa*) of the Soma; therefore, the prohibition indeed persists until the *avabhṛtha*.

Bādhūla states this very point: "The Adhvaryu, having entered the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door, should not exit by the western door; if he should exit, he should mutter 'idaṃ viṣṇuḥ'. The word division is *ā-avabhṛthāt*. Its meaning is "until the *avabhṛtha* [concluding bath]. This is an illustration of the prohibition stated by Āpastamba: that one should not enter by the western door and exit by the eastern door.

And thus, the rule results that one must exit by the very same door through which one entered. If this [rule] were not based on the word [of the scripture], then the mention of the *adhvaryu* would be for the purpose of excluding the other priests (*ṛtvij*). Therefore, this prohibition applies only to the *adhvaryu*. Nor should it be argued that since the *pratiprasthātṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, and *unnetṛ* are also *adhvaryus*, this prohibition extends to them as well; for that would result in a contradiction with the singular number [used in the term *adhvaryu*].

If the inclusion of the Pratiprasthātṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Netṛ were intended, then one would have stated it here just as one did in the passage "the Adhvaryus chant 'udgītha'" (*tām adhvaryava udgṛṇanti*). Since it was not stated thus, the prohibition applies only to the Adhvaryu. By this, the assumption that the singular number is used with reference to the class (jāti) is refuted. This should also be understood in the case of the subsequent sūtra. Having entered by the rear door of the *sadas*, he should not exit by the front; if he should exit, he should mutter the formula while rising: "Ojasā saha uttiṣṭhan."

The phrase "while the Soma has not yet been settled" (asaṃsthite some) continues [from the previous rule]. This is an elliptical reference to what Āpastamba stated: that one should not enter the *sadas* by the eastern door and exit by the western door. This prohibition also extends up until the *avabhṛtha* (concluding purificatory bath). Thus says Bādhūla: "Until the *avabhṛtha*, the Adhvaryu, having entered the *sadas* by the western door, should not exit by the eastern door; if he should exit, while rising, he should mutter the mantra, 'With vigor... In the expression "until the *avabhṛtha*" (*āvabhṛthāt*), there is also a word-division (*padaccheda*).

In this case as well, the rule is established that one must exit by the very same door through which one entered. Regarding this, Āpastamba states [in the seventh paṭala]: "The exit is by the same way. This results in a restrictive rule. Because of the word *yadi* ("if"), even this recitation (*japa*) is contingent upon a specific occasion (*naimittika*). Immediately after the measuring out of the Sadas, and before the Soma sacrifice has been concluded, the Adhvaryu should not step across the Sadas toward the west. And thus says the Śruti: "The Adhvaryu should not cross toward the west of the Sadas while the Soma sacrifice is not yet concluded."

In this context as well, only the *somasaṃsthā* rites up to the *avabhṛtha* bath are to be understood. [The rule states: "The Adhvaryu should not pass behind the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths toward the Hotṛ. Thus, even in the *sadas*, he should not go by passing over the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths. However, according to the alternative view that "he may go toward the Hotṛ," there is no fault even if he passes over the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths. Regarding this, the Śruti also says: "The *dhiṣṇiya* hearths are indeed the vital breaths; if the Adhvaryu were to pass behind the *dhiṣṇiyas*..."

"If he were to glide past [the Hotṛ] while facing him, he would draw away the vital breaths and would be liable to die; for this [Hotṛ] is indeed the navel of the sacrifice. The Hotṛ is the out-breath (prāṇa) and the Adhvaryu is the in-breath (apāna). If the Adhvaryu were to glide past the Hotṛ while facing him, he would place the out-breath into the in-breath, and he himself would be liable to die. In this matter, one must accept the position already adopted to the very end. Otherwise, by adopting only one side [of the argument], one would arrive at a state where there is no fault at all. In the rites connected with the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths, it is forbidden to go beyond the *dhiṣṇiyas*.

Since proceeding beyond the *hotṛ* priest is forbidden during other rites, this is a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*). Regarding this, some teachers recite the following concerning the *uparava* rite: "That which was previously stated regarding the *uparava* rite should not be performed there, but rather it should be performed at this time"—this is the meaning of what some teachers say.
Having brought earth from the *cātvāla*, he scatters it upon the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths, making them either square or circular.

Having dug again below the *cātvāla* for the sake of the soil (*purīṣa*), he brings that soil from there—either by carrying it or by having it brought—and scatters it, meaning he constructs the *dhiṣṇiya* altars. The accusative case in "fourth" (*caturthe*) may be used in the sense of the dative; thus, the meaning becomes that he scatters it at those respective places for the purpose of the *dhiṣṇiyas*. Alternatively, the accusative may be used in the sense of the locative; thus, the meaning becomes that he scatters it upon the locations of the *dhiṣṇiyas*. "Scattering" (*nivapana*) means the depositing of soil in those respective places. [He scatters] from the *cātvāla* onto the *dhiṣṇiyas*.

Regarding the statement in the Śruti, "That which he scatters," this refers specifically to the *nivapana* (pouring down). This is because of the explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) that "other sacrificial implements (*vigṇiya*) are poured down. Then Baudhāyana says: "He asks for the wooden sword (*sphya*), a water-vessel, earth from the *cātvāla*, and sand; having taken these, [he says] 'bring them,' digs with the wooden sword, sprinkles water, and pours down the earth from the *cātvāla* and the sand; then he makes it non-porous (*ānāśin*) by means of the sand. Here, "non-porous" (*ānāśin*) means "shining" (*prakāśavat*).

And those hearths (dhiṣṇiyas) are either square or circular. Thus it is understood from the Śulbasūtra regarding the hearths: "They are the size of a piśīla; they are square, according to some, and circular, according to others."

If it is assumed that the measurement of the *piśīla* mentioned in the *Śulbasūtra* applies to the *viṣṇiya* hearths of the Soma sacrifice—on the grounds that it was anticipated by the maxim of the "lion's glance"—then, in accordance with the requirement of spatial accommodation (*samāveśa*), the *viṣṇiya* hearths should be constructed according to the measure of any one of the five types of *piśīla*. In this view, there is no space of one *prādeśa* between them, because such a space is impossible. And this refers to the case of measuring by *pada*. In reality, however, this *piśīla* measurement applies only to the *viṣṇiya* hearths of the fire-altar (*āgnika*), not to those of the Soma sacrifice.

Regarding the mention of both "square" (*caturaśra*) and "round" (*parimaṇḍala*), since these two terms are employed here for the purpose of precluding the fixed measurement of *piśīla* used in Soma rituals, they serve a meaningful function. In this view, the measurement is extremely small—namely one *prādeśa* (span)—and that too is applicable here; furthermore, a measurement of one *prādeśa* is observed in other scriptural texts.

Even the state of having an interval of one span (*prādeśa*) is seen in another sūtra within this very context. This refers to the position where the foot-measure is fifteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). In the positions where the foot-measure is either ten or twelve finger-breadths, the interval may be even less, depending on the requirements for the arrangement. In the position where it is merely a *piśīla*, the determination of the interval should be understood as being according to the requirements for the arrangement.

Regarding that, they say the *piśīla* is fivefold: the first is the space between the two arms; the second is a clenched fist; the third is the span of the two hands joined at the tips of the fingers; the fourth is thirty-two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*); and the fifth is thirty-six finger-breadths. Some say the sixth is a cubit (*piṃśat*). In the case of it being circular, its measure is determined by the area. The same applies to the measure of a span (*prādeśa*). According to the view that one should not go beyond the *hotṛ*, when pouring [the grain], one faces west or north. According to the view that one should not go beyond the *dhuriṇī* [posts], one faces north only.
With the words "Thou art all-pervading," he [places] the Āgnīdhrīya fire in the Āgnīdhra shed so that there is a passage to the north of it within the sacrificial altar.

The *āgnīdhrīya* hearth is located at the *āgnīdhra*. That [space] and its building together constitute the *āgnīdhāgāra* (the Āgnīdhra shed). Alternatively, it is the *āgnīdhra’s* shed, hence *āgnīdhāgāra*. In that [shed], the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth is to be constructed. And that [hearth] is to be made such that, when one passes by the middle of the altar toward the northern side, there remains a space for passage sufficient so that the foot does not touch the ground on the path leading to the site; this is the meaning. [Thus ends the section on] the *āgnīdhra*.

By the word *śaraṇe ramam*, the suffix *raṇ* is applied to express "in the house" (*gṛhe*) due to the sense of "delighting" (*ramam*), and from that [word] the suffix *cha* is added according to the rule *buddhāc chaḥ*. The substitution of *iy* occurs for the final vowel of that [suffix]. The word *agāra* signifies a house. The mantra ends with *pravāṇaḥ*.

[The phrase] *antar-sadasam itarān* refers to the others, namely the *viṣṇiya* priests such as Maitrāvaruṇa and the rest. The term *antar-sadasam* means "within the *sadas*" (*sadaso madhye*). This is an *avyayībhāva* compound. The suffix *ṭac* is added at the end of the compound because it belongs to the *śarad*-class.
With the formula "Thou art fire," [he measures] one pace on the *pṛṣṭhyā* line behind the opening of the *sadas*. This is the *hotrīya* [dhiṣṇiya].

The meaning is that this *hotrīya* hearth (*dhiṣṇiya*) is located behind the opening of the *sadas*, at a distance of one pace from the western side of the eastern opening. "Hotrīya" is the name of a specific *dhiṣṇiya*. According to the rule prescribing the technical designation "vṛddha" for "the place of names" (*nāmadheya*), or according to the statement that "the name itself may be designated as vṛddha," the word *hotrīya*—being the name of a specific *dhiṣṇiya*—is subject to the designation "vṛddha. Consequently, by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ*, the suffix *cha* is applied, and its *ik* portion is replaced by *īya*.

By the statement, "proximity consisting of movement itself" is intended; by the phrase "within the assembly hall," the other opening is excluded. Here, the word *bila* (opening) denotes a door, because no other opening is possible due to the proximity of the assembly hall. The mantra ends with "havyavāhanaḥ.
With the words "śvātro 'si," [he places] the *hotrīya* fire to the south of the *maitrāvaruṇa*.

In the view where the measure begins with a step of fifteen *aṅgulas*, since there is the possibility of an interval of one *prādeśa*, the interval between the twelve-*aṅgula* step and the *prādeśa* would be equal; thus, the interval would be measured at exactly that much. And so, by the use of the suffix *-ena* in "to the south" (*dakṣiṇena*), even here, only that much proximity is intended to be expressed. In the view where the measure of the step is either ten or twelve *aṅgulas*, since an interval of one *prādeśa* is impossible, the interval is as much as is required for the purpose.

In the view that the *ghṛṇiyas* consist merely of the *piśīla*, the interval is indeed no less than a *prādeśa*. The same should be understood regarding the *viṣṇiya* fire-places as well. The two divine *praśāstṛs* are Mitra and Varuṇa. Because this [human] *praśāstṛ* is equal to Mitra and Varuṇa by virtue of being a human *praśāstṛ*, or because he performs their ritual duties, or because he recites the *ājyā-praiṣas* belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa, he possesses the status of a Maitrāvaruṇa. The status of *praśāstṛ* belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa; [thus it is said]: "Mitra and Varuṇa are the two *praśāstṛs*. *Praśāstṛ*...

This is recorded in the *pravaraṇa* formula: "The *praśāstṛ* belongs to Maitrāvaruṇa alone. This is another name for him, because he issues the *praiṣa* (direction) for the *prasthitayājyā*. Its meaning is: he who instructs (*śāsti*) all the *praiṣas* with excellence (*pra*). It ends with the word "pracetāḥ.
To the north of the *hotrīya* [fire], they go eastward, while the others go northward.

In this case as well, the determination of the intervening space should be understood as before. The proximity of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s hearth (dhiṣṇya) to the Hotṛ’s hearth is intended to be exactly as much as that intervening space exists. This same principle is to be applied to each subsequent pair. Nor should it be argued that, on the strength of the suffix *-pratyaya* [in the compound], one might assume all the hearths are actually joined to the Hotṛ’s hearth, just as in the injunction: "One makes the altar of the measure of a *vanamātrī* behind the Āhavanīya fire."

Since it is impossible for all [the priests] to be simultaneously in contact with the *hotṛ*-seat, such a conceptualization is far-fetched; furthermore, it contradicts the statement "extended as far as Umā. Nor does this contradict the suffix *-pratyaya*, because what is intended here is proximity only to the extent of the interval between the *hotṛ*-seat and the other seats, which is the only way the situation allows.

Nor should it be argued that the *hotṛ*-hearth should simply be contiguous with the *maitrāvaruṇa* and *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* hearths because such contiguity is possible, and that the same should apply to the others as well to establish their mutual homogeneity; for if there were no intervening space, it would result in the impossibility of passing to the north of the Vasu-hearths. Nor should it be argued that the intervening space should merely consist of a few finger-breadths (*aṅgula*); for a space of such limited measurement is unfit for the act of walking. And thus, by whatever intervening space...

It is established that the space between [the hearths] must be made such that there is no striking with the foot at the time of going to the site; for, in the case where the measure of the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths begins at fifteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) per step, the intervals would be less than one span (*prādeśa*). Otherwise, sitting down would be impossible due to the rule of non-support. Nor can this undesirable consequence be accepted.

This is because, in view of the conflict with the rule of sitting for the sake of the primary and subsidiary acts—which involves maintaining the ritual marks (*aṅka*)—it is more appropriate that there be a conflict regarding the mere proximity to the sacrificial hearths (*dhiṣṇya*), characterized by the nine-year-old [calf] and so forth. Alternatively, in the passage "to the south of the *hotrīya* [hearth], to the north of the *hotrīya*," the accusative case has the sense of the genitive. The two words "dakṣiṇena" and "uttareṇa" are indeclinables (*avyaya*) that resemble case-endings, meaning "to the south" and "to the north. Thus, when proximity is not required, the establishment of the intermediate space (*antarāla*) in the middle is achieved.

In the case where the measurement of the footprint (*pada*) is either ten or twelve *aṅgulas*, the reduction of the *dhāraṇa* (the distance between the footprints) must be accepted provisionally for the present, in accordance with the reduced measurement of the footprint necessitated by the lack of available space. If the learned (*śiṣṭas*) perform it in this way now, then—depending on the specific time of sitting at the *śālāmukhīya* fire—the *sarvaprāyaścitta* (all-expiation) oblation is to be offered, or not, as follows: if there is an interval of time between each sitting, it is to be offered separately; if there is an interval other than that [between sittings], it is to be offered once; and on the day of the *sautya* sacrifice, it is to be offered, or not. They should stand facing north.

The statement "Let them chant the *udgītha*" is intended to indicate the following sequence: to the north of the *hotṛ*’s hearth (*dhiṣṇya*) is the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*’s hearth with an interval; to the north of that is the *potṛ*’s hearth with an interval; to the north of that is the *neṣṭṛ*’s hearth with an interval; and to the north of that is the *acchāvāka*’s hearth with an interval. This is the meaning.

By this, the claim that the eastward extension belongs directly to the *hotṛ*-hearth alone, while the surrounding nature is for the sake of proximity to all [hearths], is refuted. He states those denoted by other terms:
"Thou art *tutha*" for the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*; "Thou art *uśij*" for the *potṛ*; "Thou art *andhāri*" for the *neṣṭṛ*; "Thou art *avasyu*" for the *acchāvāka*—[these are] more distant.

Regarding the term *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*, there is an addition [to the rule] for the ablative case (*pañcamyāḥ*), resulting in the absence of elision (*aluk*). The *śastras* prescribed in the *Brāhmaṇas* are metaphorically called *brāhmaṇas*; one who recites (*śaṃsati*) those is a *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*, a specific type of officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). The ablative case is used in the sense of the accusative precisely because of this addition. Furthermore, the word *brahman* refers to the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī* in a specific context, as seen in the injunction for the *prasthitayājyā* at the *brahmayajña*. One who protects (*pāti*) the sacrificer through his prayers is a *potṛ*, another specific type of officiating priest.

And there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this point in the *Potṛ-prasthitayājyā*: "O Maruts, of great splendor, he in whose dwelling you drink from heaven—he is the most well-guarded person. [The term] *neṣṭṛ* is correct by virtue of the *Uṇādi-sūtra*: "The words *naptṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, *bhrātṛ*, *jāmātṛ*, *pitṛ*, and *hita* are [formed] as irregular derivations (*nipātana*). Regarding the specific application of the rule for the suffix *-na* (in *patnī*), [the term] *neṣṭṛ* means "one who leads the wife" (*patnīm nayati*). This [term] also is correct by virtue of the aforementioned *Uṇādi-sūtra*.

By the word *accha*, the hymn beginning with *accha vo agnim avase* is indicated. He speaks toward that [hymn] most excellently (*ātyantam samīcīnam vakti*), thus he is the *acchāvāka*, a specific officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). His *dhiṣṇiya* (altar-hearth) is "more proximate" (*pratikṛṣṭataram*) or "superior" (*adhikataram*) than the other *dhiṣṇiyas*; this is the meaning. Since no measure for that superiority is prescribed there, something slightly more should be done for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Because a visible purpose is impossible here, it serves an unseen purpose. However, according to Vāsiṣṭha and Vādhūla, the measure of superiority is—

However, they state a specific rule: "The *dhiṣṇiya* of the Acchāvāka should be four finger-breadths larger than all the other *dhiṣṇiyas*. The concluding formulas are, in order: "O Viśvavedas, the sage, the destroyer of the enemy, may he be honored"; and for the Mārjālīya: "Thou art the purifier. This [Mārjālīya] is outside the *sadas*, in the southern half of the altar, level with the Āgnīdhrīya, so that there is a passage to the south within the altar.

*Mārjālīya* refers to that place where the vessels are cleansed (*mṛjyante*) and purified (*śuddhāni kriyante*). The suffix *ālīyac* is applied to the root *mṛṣ* (meaning "to cleanse") by the *uṇādi* sūtra *mṛjerālīyac*. The compound *bahiḥsadasam* is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*), meaning "outside of the assembly hall" (*sadasaḥ bahiḥ*). The suffix *ṭac* is added at the end of the compound because it belongs to the *śaradādi* group. The mention of *bahiḥsadasam* ("outside the assembly hall") is intended to prevent the *mārjālīya* from being included within the *sadas* itself, as this would follow from the recurrence of the word *itarān* ("others") in the previous rule. Thus, it is specified as being outside the *sadas*.

The statement "in the southern half of the *vedi*" is intended to exclude [the altar] from the northern half of the *vedi*, even though it is situated outside the *sadas*. The phrase "level with the *āgnīdhrīya*" is for the purpose of excluding the extreme proximity (*pratikṛṣṭataratā*) mentioned in the preceding sūtra. If it is asked: "In that case, for the sake of brevity and because of its primary status, one should have specified 'level with the *hotṛ-dhiṣṇiya*' here to exclude that same extreme proximity; why then is the non-primary and cumbersome *āgnīdhrīya* mentioned? The answer is: no, because of the *āgnīdhrīya*... [text fragment ends].

The purpose of taking up that [measurement] is for the sake of achieving equality by means of the northern cord (udaksūtra) for both the *dhīyamānī* and the *mānī*; since that is not possible at the *hotṛ-dhiṣṇya*, the meaning resulting is this: having laid down the northern cord from the middle of the western edge of the *mahāvedi*—starting from the *āgnīdhra* shed—to the middle of the eastern edge of the southern edge of the *mahāvedi*, the *mānī* shed should be constructed there. This is the conclusion of the equal measurement. [End of] Paṭala 727/710, with the commentary Jyotsnā by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

In the expression *bhīyeṇa*, the instrumental case is used according to the rule *tulyārthairatulopamābhyāṃ tṛtīyā'nyatarasyām*. This should be understood as being like the previous [sūtra]: "The movement takes place to the south within the altar" (*dakṣiṇenāntarvedi saṃcaro bhavati*), just as it is stated in the subsequent sūtra: "The movement takes place to the north within the altar" (*yathottareṇāntarvedi saṃcaro bhavati*). Baudhāyana has stated that the Āgnīdhra shed is five *aratnis* in size; the Mārgalīya shed is also described as being the same, and it should be constructed if possible.

The measure of one *aratni* is possible only in the case of the *prakrama* [step] starting from twenty-four *aṅgulas*, and not otherwise. It should be understood that in the case of the *prakrama* ending at twelve *aṅgulas*, it is simply the measure of a *pada*.
The *raudra-anīka* formula is appended everywhere.

The meaning is that he joins—the *yonayati*, which means "he applies"—the portion of the mantra containing the word *raudra* (fierce), which possesses the word *raudra* and contains the word *anīka* (face/front), to all mantras, including those at the end and those in the middle. That portion is: "O Agni, protect me with your fierce face; hide me; do not harm me. The explicit meaning is that he joins this portion to the ends of each respective mantra. In the term *raudramanīkam*, the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for the *arśa-ādigaṇa* to express the sense of the possessive suffix *matup*.

By this, the exclusion of the two terms *kevala-raudra* and *anīka*, which are otherwise redundant, is established. If the term *kevala-raudra* were used [alone], then by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating that "one should know the end of the preceding [section] by the beginning of the succeeding one," it would be understood that [the section] ends at each respective measure (*mātrā*), and consequently, any mantra containing the word *raudra* might follow immediately thereafter. However, the mantra containing the word *raudra* in one's own Vedic branch (*śākhā*) consists of a single section (*anuvāka*) beginning with "brahmaṇā tvā śapāmi."

If only the word *anīka* were used, there might be an application (*anupaṅga*) of the phrase "with whatever army" (*yasya kasyacid anīkavatā sainānīkena*) to any mantra containing that word; and this must not happen. Rather, it is intended that the application be only of the mantra qualified by both words: "O Agni, protect me with a fierce army, nourish me, do not harm me"—this very mantra being present in this context.

Because the final mantra ends with "bahirasi buniya," the rule for *anuṣaṅga* (the carrying over of a word) is intended to prevent the assumption that the [word] must be supplied only there, since it is recited at the end. This applies to all mantras except the final one; however, in the case of the final one, it is already explicitly recited. Here, because the word *raudra* is a specific qualifier of the *anīka* (army/division), and not because of the [general] word *raudra*, the phrase "with the *raudra-anīka*" is to be supplied everywhere by this straightforward method alone.

In order to establish that the subsequent application (*anuṣaṅga*) here is qualified by the phrase "the fierce army" (*raudram anīkam*), which occurs in the context of the accomplishment of the sacrifice, the statement "the fierce army" is made; for it is necessary to know that this *anuṣaṅga* is so qualified. In the absence of such knowledge, one must offer an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) consisting of a goat (*yama*) and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) into the southern fire.
Regarding this, some authorities prescribe the spreading of the altar (*vedistaraṇa*).

The meaning is that some teachers say: "That which was previously mentioned as the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) should not be performed there, but rather it should be performed at this time. Nor should it be argued that because of the scriptural injunction, "He spreads the northern grass over the [other] grass" (*uttaraṃ barhiṣa uttarabarhiḥ stṛṇāti*), the spreading performed previously is obligatory while the second spreading here is optional—out of fear of rendering the scripture meaningless. For since this scriptural passage can be rendered meaningful by referring to the spreading of the *barhis* for the sake of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, it is improper to assume a second, unprecedented (*apūrva*) act of spreading. Regarding this specific spreading, he states the distinction:
He does not strew grass upon the high altar (uttaravedi), the sacrificial mound (khara), the sounding-holes (uparava), or the hearths (dhiṣṇiya). || 21 ||

Thus ends the seventh paṭala in the seventh praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. In the phrase *uttaravedim iva*, the word *iva* (like) must be supplied as having a sense of comparison. The meaning is that just as one does not strew [grass] upon the *uttaravedi* in the preceding case, so too here, in this strewing, one does not strew upon the *khara*, the *uparavas*, or the *viṣṇiya* hearths. Otherwise, it would follow that the *uttaravedi* is to be strewn during the strewing mentioned previously; and this is not an acceptable conclusion.

Because that [altar] is not seen anywhere as being spread out as a delightful place for the *uttaravedi*, and because it is impossible due to the presence of the fire (*agni*) there; thus ends the work composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita—who was a performer of the *Agniṣṭoma* sacrifice, a performer of the *Vājapeya* sacrifice accompanied by a thousand fires, a performer of the *Sarvatomukha* sacrifice, and a performer of the *Pauṇḍarīka* sacrifice accompanied by two thousand fires—within the *Śrīmad-Bhagavat-Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.

In the commentary named *Jyotsnā*, which pacifies the distress of learned men caused by the failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the ocean [of the scriptures], this is the seventh section of the seventh chapter. 7.
7.8 Now begins the eighth chapter of the seventh book.
He commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya*).

"Agni and Soma" are *agnīṣomau*. That which has Agni and Soma as its deity is *agnīṣomīya*. He commences—that is, he begins—the ritual procedure for that animal, the entire collection of rites beginning with the kindling of the fires (*anvādhāna*). The causative suffix (*ṇic*) here is used in its own sense (i.e., reflexively).
The ritual procedure for that [animal sacrifice] is explained by the *Nirūḍhapaśubandha*.

The meaning is as follows: the animal is bound in a rite where it is "bound" (*nirūḍha*) by its own [specific] nature; that rite is called the *Paśubandha*, and by means of that rite, the ritual procedure—the method—of the *Agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice is explained, that is, stated.

In that regard, this is the ritual procedure for all animals: the animal offering is a modification of the morning milk-offering due to the similarity of time; likewise, the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) belongs to Agni and Indra-Agni, and this remains unchanged in their modifications.
