In the case of the *agnīṣomīya* animal and its modifications, the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is made of *aśvavāla* grass, the crosswise-stick (*tiraścī*) is made of sugarcane, and there are additional enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *kārya* wood beyond those of *pūtudāru*. [The calls are: "Prompt for the omentum and fat of such-and-such"; "Prompt for the cake of such-and-such"; "Prompt for the oblation of such-and-such"; and he gives the general call for the deity of the animal sacrifice, [specifically] for the one dedicated to Indra.

Regarding the Sārasvata sacrifice and its modifications, the rule for the performance (*pracaraṇakalpa*) is that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśapaurṇamāsika*). This is stated in the sūtra which makes known the relationship between the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*) of animal sacrifices. By the passage beginning with "of the Āgneya and Aindrāgna," etc., the status of the five animals as archetypes is demonstrated. The Āgneya and Aindrāgna are the Savanīya animals in the Agniṣṭoma and Ukthya terminuses; their ritual procedure is unmodified—neither deficient nor redundant—and is exactly as described for the Nirūḍha sacrifice. That which is said for those two applies likewise to the animal sacrifices that are their modifications.

The animal sacrifice for Agni and Soma (agnīṣomīya) is to be observed on the fast-day; its modifications on the fast-days include the *nirūḍha* [animal sacrifice], the *adhika* [additional] rites, the *cavāla*, and so forth. That which was performed previously at the *ātithyā* [guest-offering] and outside the *ātithyā* belongs to the *upasads*; thus, by the rule "that belongs to the *agnīṣomīya*," it is stated that these are indeed for the sake of the *agnīṣomīya*. Therefore, in its modifications as well, it is exactly the same. In the *nirūḍha*, the *savanīya*, and their modifications, regarding the carrying forward of the fire (*praṇayana*), the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are made of *pūtudru* wood, not of *kārmarya* wood.

Since those [details] are obtained for them through the Agniṣomīya sacrifice itself by means of the forest [text], it has been stated that the specific details established by other recensions do not exist in the Nirūḍha. [End of] Chapter 8. This very point—that they likewise do not exist in the Savanīya offerings due to other scriptural authorities—has been stated by the phrase "this is unmodified."

By the rule, "The ritual procedure for the performance [of the sacrifice] belonging to the New and Full Moon [offerings] applies to those [sacrifices] dedicated to Indra, to Sarasvatī, and to their modifications," the application of the Maitrāvaruṇa priest is excluded from the cake-offerings and oblation-offerings of the *upāṃśu* sacrifice. Among these, the *agnīṣomīya* and other sacrifices are, in part, modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *nirūḍha*; furthermore, while these are the archetypes (*prakṛti*) for the *ādhvaryava* ritual, the *nirūḍha* is the modification.

With reference to the *nirūḍhapaśu* (the independent animal sacrifice), since its *hautra* (functions of the Hotṛ priest) and other duties are prescribed in its own branch (*svaśākhā*) with the words "they immolate it," it serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*) for all those animals—whether occasional (*naimittika*), optional (*kāmya*), independent (*svatantra*), or obligatory (*nitya*)—to which these [rites] are extended. Likewise, having obtained the specific *ādhvaryava* (functions of the Adhvaryu priest), such as the measurement of the altar (*vedimāna*) and so forth, from direct instruction (*aupadeśika*), they are extended to others; and having obtained the *ādhvaryava* rites of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice through extension (*atideśa*), it also becomes the archetype for its modifications (*vikṛti*).

By the statement "This is the ritual procedure for all animals," it is demonstrated that this very injunction is common to all animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*); it is not by this that an extended application (*atideśa*) is being made. Rather, the injunction for the *savanīya* [animals] belonging to Agni-Soma is mixed with those of the Soma sacrifice; therefore, having been extracted from that, it is explained as applying specifically to the *nirūḍha* [animal sacrifice], which is obtained through extended application. That [procedure] is common to all. The one pertaining to the *agnīṣomīya* and others is based on direct instruction (*aupadeśika*), while for the others it is based on extended application (*ātideśika*).

Those specific mantras belonging to other recensions (śākhāntarīya), such as "I dedicate this which is pleasing to Indra and Agni" (*indrāgnibhyāṃ tvā juṣṭam upākaromi*), which are heard in the *Nisala* [text], are to be extended (*ūhya*) by rule of transfer (*atideśa*) to the animal sacrifices dedicated to Sūrya and Prajāpati, beginning with the *Āgneyī-aiṣomīya*. Herein is the established rule (*vyavasthā*): among the animals included within the ritual framework (*tantra*), the *Āgneyī-aiṣomīya* and others alone serve as the archetypes (*prakṛti*) due to their similarity.

In that regard, among those performed at the *aupavasathya* stage, the *āgneya* and others are the models for those performed at the *sutyā* stage. Even though the *āgneya* and *aindrāgna* are equal [in status], the determination is made on the strength of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) ritual procedure. For those whose animal-cakes are modifications of the *āgneya* cake, the *āgneya* *savanīya* is the archetype (*prakṛti*). However, for those whose animal-cakes belong to dual deities or multiple deities—and thus, by virtue of having names consisting of two or more syllables, are modifications of the *aindrāgna* cake—the *aindrāgna* itself is the archetype.

Those [offerings] to multiple deities whose names consist of four syllables—such as the *puroḍāśa* for Agni-Soma—which have the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) as their archetype, are also modifications (*vikāra*) of the *savanīya* cake for Agni alone. Having directly adopted the extension (*atideśa*) of the properties of the eight-potsherd cake for Agni to the eleven-potsherd cakes for Agni-Soma on the basis of similarity, one must here effect the fulfillment of the modification based on the similarity indicated by the *Sūtra*. This is to be understood as an instance of a fixed modification (*vyavasthitavikāra*).

Regarding the animal sacrifices dedicated to Indra, those *paśupuroḍāśas* (animal-cake offerings) follow the procedure of the *aindrāgna-puroḍāśa*; thus, the *savanīya* [cake] has the *aindrāgna* as its archetype (*prakṛti*). According to the rule, "Except for the deities of the archetype, as in the case of the *saumya-caru* and the *aindra-puroḍāśa*," although the two cakes dedicated to Soma and Indra are expressed by a singular number, they do not possess the status of being modifications (*vikāra*) of the *āgneya*. Furthermore, according to the rule, "Neither the other [the *saumya*] nor the *aindrāgna* [is a modification] of the *agnīṣomīya*," the *aindra* and *saumya* [cakes] are established as distinct.

Although, because it falls within the category distinct from the modifications (*vikāra*) of the Āgneya sacrifice, there might be an option (*icchā*) for it to be a modification of both due to the presence of the word *vā* (or), and one might accept that the word *vā* has the sense of a restricted alternative (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*)—such that the Aindra [offering] is exclusively a modification of the Aindrāgna and the Soma is exclusively a modification of the Agnīṣomīya—nevertheless, the Saumya and other offerings of the *sautya* day are indeed modifications of the Āgneya, due to the similarity of their ritual characteristics (*kapāla-dharma*). "The deities belonging to the archetype" (*prakṛti-devatāḥ*) refers to those deities residing in the archetype; [the compound means] "from those deities belonging to the archetype."

For the state of being the deities of the archetype belongs to the triad of Agni, Indra, and Soma. In this regard, the distinction is that Agni’s status as a deity exists both independently and as a co-occurring deity, whereas for Indra and Soma, it exists only through their association with Agni. Elsewhere, apart from these archetypal deities—as in the case of "the *saumya* [oblation] and the *aindra* cake"—the word *iti* is intended to include Indra as a deity characterized by the quality of being free from enemies (*vaimṛdha*). For this very reason, [it is said] "the archetypal deity..."

The plural number in the word *tāmyaḥ* is thus consistent. Now, one might object: "Since Indra—even when qualified by the specific attribute named Vaimṛdha—is non-different from Indra, he would be grasped by the word 'Indra' alone; consequently, since plurality is impossible in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there would be the fault of inconsistency. This is not so. Just as in the case of Indra and Mahendra, there is indeed a distinction here as well, and thus plurality is possible; therefore, there is no inconsistency.

The portion pertaining to the deities of the archetype (prakṛti) belonging to both Indra and Soma is precisely what is understood by the phrase "to the deities of the archetype" (*prakṛtidevatābhyaḥ*). Although the Āgneya [oblation] also possesses a connection to the deities of the archetype, it is nevertheless not included in that phrase "to the deities of the archetype."

Just as in the case of the statement "the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) belongs to both Soma and Indra," since both are mentioned, it has been established that the properties of the Agni-related [sacrifice] do not apply to the animal sacrifice dedicated to Soma. Because of this generality, compared to that, Indra—as a constituent part—is specific; thus, by virtue of being stronger and by virtue of having a name consisting of two syllables, the animals dedicated to Soma and Indra in the Aśvamedha possess the properties of the Indra-Agni [sacrifice], whereas those animals dedicated to Indra that are prescribed in other ritual contexts [possess their own specific properties].

The modifications of the animal sacrifice for Indra (*aindra-paśu*) belonging to the *savanīya* [offering] in the *ṣoḍaśin* ritual formation are those which have Sarasvatī as their deity; these are modifications of the Agni-related animal sacrifice (*āgneya-paśu*). Some maintain that the status of being a modification of Sarasvatī arises from the similarity of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). However, other deities of Sarasvatī, as well as those with female deities, are modifications of the female sheep (*meṣī*) dedicated to Sarasvatī belonging to the *savanīya* in the *atirātra* formation—excluding the *anūbandhyā* sacrifices dedicated to Mitra-Varuṇa, Sūrya, and others.

And because it will be stated in the subsequent sūtra located in the section on the *anubandhyā* (the animal to be bound after the Soma sacrifice) that "it also exists," this indicates that there is no similarity (*sājātya*) here; however, elsewhere it certainly does exist—such is the established rule (*vyavasthā*). Therefore, the five animals beginning with the *āgneya* and *aupavasathya*, as well as the *paśu* for the *savanīya*, are established as the archetypes (*prakṛtis*) for those included within the Soma ritual framework. But for those excluded from the Soma ritual, the *nirūḍha-aindrāgna* is the archetype. Thus, all five animals possess directly perceived characteristics (*pratyakṣadharma*), and according to the *hautra* (the office of the Hotṛ priest), they are the modifications (*vikṛtis*) of the *nirūḍha*.

The *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ priest), which is obtained through both the general rules of the *ādhvaryava* and the specific rules of the *hautra*, is established—despite being applicable to all—as restricted solely to the sphere of the offerings of the omentum (*vapā*), the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and the animal (*paśu*) dedicated to Indra and Sarasvatī, by way of precluding the activity of the Maitrāvaruṇa priest according to other scriptural injunctions. As for the animals performed during the *aupavasathya* day and those performed on the day of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*), the view that they serve as archetypes (*prakṛti*) "as the case may be" should be understood as intending an optional alternative (*aicchika-vikalpa*). Let this incidental discussion suffice.

The *Iṣṭi* is stated to be the archetype (*prakṛti*); the rule for it has been explained by means of the *Nirūḍhapaśubandha*. It should be understood that this Sūtra was composed by the venerable Teacher with the intention that, according to the *Hautra*, the *Nirūḍha* alone serves as the archetype for all animal sacrifices (*paśu*).
The *Ṣaḍḍhotṛ* and the *Paśviṣṭi* do not exist as constituent parts (*aṅga*) [of the archetype].

Regarding those subsidiary animal sacrifices (*aṅga-paśu*) that follow the internal procedure (*antastantra*), as well as the principal sacrifices (*aṅgin*) from the *agnīṣomīya* up to the *anubandhya*, which share the same place, time, and fires—in these cases, the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula is not employed, because its purpose is to mark the commencement [of a rite]. Since the commencement of those [subsidiaries] is accomplished by the very commencement of the principal sacrifice, so too the animal-offering (*paśviṣṭi*) does not take place, because the commencement of the deities' forms is already accomplished by the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering.

As for those [sacrifices] which belong to external systems (*bāhyatantra*), as well as those occurring at different places and times—such as the *vāyavyapaśu*, the *pañcapaśu*, the *sautrāmaṇīpaśu*, and so forth—even though they may somehow possess the status of auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* and the *paściṣṭi* certainly do not exist in them. If it is argued: "One need only say that 'the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* and the *paściṣṭi* are not found,' because their non-existence follows from the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself; therefore, the word 'non-existent' (*abhūta*) should not even be employed," this is true. However, [it is used] for the following reason: [The full argument continues: ...because the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* and the *paściṣṭi* are not mentioned in the context of the *vāyavyapaśu* and the others, whereas they are mentioned in the context of the *savanīya-paśu*. Therefore, the word "non-existent" (*abhūta*) is employed to indicate that these two rites are absent from the former contexts. Furthermore, the mention of the word "non-existent" serves to exclude the possibility that the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* and the *paściṣṭi* might be considered auxiliary parts of the *vāyavyapaśu* and other such sacrifices through the principle of "transference" (*codaka*). Thus, the word "non-existent" is indeed necessary.

In order to demonstrate that the phrase "being a constituent part" (*aṅgabhūta*) has the sense of a reason (*hetu*), [the author] states: "Because of the necessity of the material cause (*upādāna*) among them. Since the animal is a constituent part, this prohibition regarding the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* and the animal-sacrifice (*paśviṣṭi*) applies; however, this prohibition is not prompted solely by the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice. By this, the absence of the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* and the animal-sacrifice is established even for animals such as the *savanīya*. Furthermore, the use of the singular number becomes justified.
The singular number is used with reference to the class [of vessels]. Thus Āpastamba says: "The Ṣaḍḍhotṛ and the Paściṣṭi do not exist among the subsidiary [rites].
Having added fuel to the fires, he binds the enclosing sticks of the Ātithyeṣṭi to the fuel-bundle.

The statement regarding the *agnyanvādhāna* (the adding of fuel to the fires) is for the purpose of refuting the prohibition of the *agnyanvādhāna* mentioned in other sūtras. The verbal suffix in the expression "one should add fuel to the fires" (*agnīnanvādadhīta*) initiates the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya-paśu*). Since Baudhāyana states that one should bring a branch after having performed the *ātithyā* and *upasada* rites, and since this is a modification of the *sānnāyya* [offering], it is said that the bringing of the branch should not take place; this is the purpose [of our statement].

The meaning is this: for a liquid substance is to be purified by means of a branch, whereas a solid substance does not cease to be a substance that shares the same ritual function simply because the specific action [of purification] is absent. Furthermore, since it has been stated that only the *barhis* used for the guest-offering (*ātithyā*) serves the purpose of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, the fetching of that [specific] *barhis* is precluded. However, the *barhis* intended for the *utkara* must indeed be fetched on that very day. As for the *prastara*, one fetches it alone; the "only" (*eva*) in the upcoming sūtra excludes only the *barhis* intended for the altar (*vedi*).

In this context, the fires to be added (*anvādheya*) are the *auttaravedika*, the *śālāmukhīya*, and the *dakṣiṇāgni*; the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires are also to be added. There is no addition of the *prājahita* fire, but rather only that of the *śālāmukhīya*. According to the *Paśusūtra*, which states that "this [fire] from which [the fire] is carried forth is the *āhavanīya*, and that [from which it was taken] is the *gārhapatya*," the *gārhapatya* status is attributed specifically to the *āhavanīya* in the archetype (*prakṛti*), thereby indicating the cessation of the former *gārhapatya*.

In this context, by the word "therein" (atra), it means that [the Gārhapatya fire] belongs to that very rite, and not to the Agnihotra oblation which falls within it. The word "therein" (atra) should also be applied to the forthcoming sūtra: "They conclude the duties of the Śālāmukhīya for the Gārhapatya rites; in that [fire], the Gārhapatya rites are performed. Otherwise, [the rule would apply] to the Agnihotra prescribed for the Kuṇḍapāyināmayana sacrifice, where it is enjoined: "He performs the Agnihotra for a month."

Even in the case of the *darvihoma*, since it is obtained through a succession of *codaka* (transferred injunctions) in the form: "from the Jyotiṣṭoma [comes] the Dvādaśāha; from the Dvādaśāha [comes] the Gavāmayana; from the Gavāmayana [comes] the Kuṇḍapāyinām ayana," the cooking (*śrapaṇa*) should take place at the Śālāmukhīya fire itself. Although in this particular *darvihoma* there is no direct application of the Śālāmukhīya fire either by its own rule or by a primary *codaka*, nevertheless, because the Śālāmukhīya is obtained through the *codaka* in the Kuṇḍapāyinām ayana, it must be understood that its application exists even for the cooking of the sacrificial oblation (*haviḥ*) belonging to the *darvihoma*, which is a secondary wave (*taraṅga*) of that same injunction.

Therefore, the phrase "herein" (*atrety evam*) must necessarily be stated. Thus, by the word "herein," it refers to the act [of cooking] as "Agnihotra," just like the cooking of the *bhurija* and *gārhapatya* fires obtained through the transfer of names within the *Kuṇḍapāyināmayana* sacrifice. And so, in the first section (*pāda*) of the twelfth chapter, he states this very point with the following sūtra: "And the cooking of the Agnihotra should not take place on the *Śālāmukhīya* fire, because the *Prājahita* fire is already present."

The sense is that it is logical for the *śālāmukhīya*—which serves another purpose—to be set aside by the *prājahita*, which possesses a specific name (*nāman*). As for the meaning of the sūtra, it is indeed clear. Although the precedence of the named [fire] is established by the very principle of the seventh book (*sāptamika-nyāya*), this sūtra should nevertheless be understood as intended to refute the objection of "incidental application" (*prasaṅga*).

The general rule—that "that from which the fire is carried forth is the Āhavanīya, and that [from which it is] brought forth is the Gārhapatya"—is set aside by the specific rule stating, "they assign the Śālāmukhīya for the duties of the Gārhapatya; in that [fire], the Gārhapatya duties are performed. Thus, it must be stated that the laying of the fires (ādhāna) here pertains specifically to the Śālāmukhīya, the Āhavanīya, and the Dakṣiṇāgni.

Because the word "here" (*atra*) in the Sūtra—"This is the Āhavanīya; that from which it is carried forward is the Gārhapatya"—is applied specifically to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka-karman*), this rule does not apply to the Soma sacrifice (*saumika-karman*). Therefore, since it is necessary to formulate this Sūtra for the purpose of extending its application there as well, and because there is no common subject matter (between the two contexts), the relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhaka-bhāva*) is simply impossible.

"This is the Āhavanīya here; that from which it is carried forward is the Gārhapatya"—this is the scope of that sūtra. "They conclude the animal sacrifice (pāśuka-karma) with the Śālāmukhīya fire; in that [fire], the Gārhapatya rites are performed"—this is the scope of that sūtra, namely the Soma sacrifice (saumika-karma). Thus, due to the difference in their respective scopes, there is no relationship of sublation (bādhya-bādhaka-bhāva) between them here.

Alternatively, for the purpose of demonstrating that the subject matter of the *Paśu-sūtra* (the section on animal sacrifices) is concerned with the underlying cause (*hetu*), there is the sūtra: "They assign the *Śālāmukhīya* fire to the duties of the *Gārhapatya*; in it, the duties of the *Gārhapatya* are performed. Since the scriptural texts (*śruti*) assign and employ the *Śālāmukhīya* for the sake of the *Gārhapatya* duties within the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka-karman*), therefore, because those duties are accomplished by means of the fire, the duties of the *Gārhapatya* pertaining to the Soma sacrifice (*saumika*) are also performed in that very same [fire].

Because of the mention of "fuel" (*idhma*) as an established fact, it is understood that the fetching of fuel must be performed here. However, the binding of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the *Atithyā* offering should be performed after the fetching of the fuel, rather than at the place prescribed by the archetype, because that would subvert the [new] rule. Alternatively, the binding of the sacrificial grass may take place at the very time of taking up [the materials]. Or else, the word "also" (*api*) should be supplied after the word "enclosing-sticks" (*paridhīn*); by this, the binding of the sacrificial grass is also established at its original (archetypal) place.

And Āpastamba says: "He silently binds the sacrificial post for the guest-offering (atithyā), and those same [materials] serve as the enclosing sticks (paridhi) and the fuel (idhma) for the animal sacrifice. Here too, the phrase "he binds silently" is understood to carry over. In the first pāda of the twelfth adhyāya, Naimini also states this through the two sūtras: "If it is argued that the binding and the carrying are likewise [for the animal sacrifice], no, because they serve another purpose," and "In the binding and the carrying, there is a combination of these two. Binding and carrying constitute the compound *saṃnahanaharaṇam*; in that binding and carrying...

The word "thus" (*tathā*) refers back to the repetition of the mantra mentioned in the preceding sūtra, based on the principle that "the mantra is repeated because of the difference in location. By the word "no" (*na*), this repetition is negated. The primary purpose of bringing [the fire] to the sacrificial site (*vihāra-deśa*) is the binding and taking up; by the word "other" (*anya*), any purpose other than those is expressed. That [purpose] consists in reaching the altar (*vedi*); such is the meaning. If it were also for the purpose of reaching the altar, then in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the mantra would have been employed even when [the fire] was being led toward the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires.

Likewise, even when the tying of the knot for the deities (*devāgranthi*) is applicable during the girding (*saṃnahan*), if it is performed again silently, one should not ask what the deciding factor (*vinigamaka*) is regarding the rule "not [after] reaching the place of recreation" (*na ca vihāradeśaprāpaṇātavaitayoḥ*). For the deciding factor is simply the priority of occurrence (*prathamopasthiti*), as this is more parsimonious (*lāghava*).

Thus, this is the distilled meaning of Jaimini’s sūtra: although the repetition of the mantra is generally required according to the principle stated in the sūtra, "The mantra is repeated because of the difference in location," such repetition is precluded here. For the binding and carrying of the sacrificial grass (barhis) are intended for the purpose of bringing the cut grass to the sacrificial ground; since those two acts—binding and carrying—are performed in the archetype (prakṛti), the mantras associated with them are not repeated in the present case.

For this very reason, even the *saṃbharaṇa-mantra* does not apply to the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*). After the gathering of the wood for the *sāmidhenī* verses, there is a separate gathering performed silently. Therefore, in the *saṃbharaṇa-mantra*, the phrase "three enclosing-sticks" (*trīn paridhīn*) is omitted; likewise, the modification "twentyfold" (*viṃśatidhā*) and the name "the circulating ones" (*saṃcarāḥ*) are also dropped. Alternatively, with the intention of referring to the *upaveṣa* and the *dhr̥ṣṭi*, one may simply say "the circulating ones" (*saṃcarān*). Regarding the term "he brings near" (*upaniyati*), because of the prefix *upa*, the joining of the enclosing-sticks occurs specifically above the fuel-sticks (*idhma-samidh*).
In this case, they silently bring a branch of the *lakṣa* tree. However, some bring it silently according to the rule for the outer ritual (*bahir-dharma*).
Having strewn around the fires, washed his hands, and spread out a layer of *ulapa* grass, he arranges the vessels used for animal sacrifice as required.

In this context, those fires which have been directly added (anvāhita) are these very ones: namely, the Uttaravedi fire, the Śālāmukhīya fire, and the Pradakṣiṇa fire. According to the view of Sāyaṇa and others, these two [the Śālāmukhīya and Pradakṣiṇa] are also included. Since there is no formal adding of fuel (anvādhāna) for the Āhavanīya fire, there is no strewing of grass (paristaraṇa). The section beginning with "having strewn around the fires" (agnīn paristīrya) and ending with "having strewn" has already been explained. [This concludes the section from the *Jyotsnā* commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.]

In this context, it is understood from the very absence of an injunction for making a *veda* that the *veda* which was made for the purpose of preparing the great altar (*mahāvedī*) remains in use until the final purificatory bath (*āvabhṛtha*). However, since the preparation of a *veda* is specifically enjoined at the *avabhṛtha*, there is a separate *veda* for that occasion. The phrase "according to the purpose" (*yathārtham*) means according to the requirement. This statement is intended to declare that, although the vessels for the medicinal herbs (*auṣadha-pātra*) would otherwise apply by extension (*atideśa*), they have no further use here.

The statement "pāśukāni" (belonging to the animal sacrifice) is for the purpose of including the use of items related to the animal sacrifice, such as the knife (*svadhiti*), the oblation of fat (*vasāhoma*), the *havirnīya* vessel, the splinter from the sacrificial post (*yūpaśakala*), the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), and the gold splinter (*suvarṇaśakala*). If it is objected that the word "pāśukāni" need not be stated because that is already established by the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself, we say no. This is because its purpose is to exclude the use of the *pracaraṇī* spoon as prescribed by Āpastamba. Nor should it be argued that since the rule for its use is prescribed specifically for the *mṛtyā* sacrifice, its exclusion here is already implied by the context, and thus the statement "pāśukāni" would be redundant. [This is not so, as the explicit mention serves to prevent any ambiguity regarding the scope of the ritual application.]

Since the *sutyā* sacrifice occurs first, according to the rule for its performance, the *prakaraṇī* spoon would, by the principle stated by Āpastamba, employ its own seventh [finger-breadth] measure; thus, the present text finds its purpose as a means to preclude that application of the *dhruvā* spoon. Furthermore, it is shown by the phrase "belonging to the animal sacrifice" (*pāśukāni*) that the accomplishment of the *somaprāśitra* is not [included here].

And likewise, in the first section of the twelfth chapter, Jaimini states: "In the case of vessels, there would be *prasaṅga* (incidental application), because they serve the purpose of the *homa*; or rather, it is proper that there be no *prasaṅga* because they are not specifically enjoined; for there is a contact with the scriptural word. Just as in the preceding section, where the *mahāvedi* serves as a substitute for the archetypal (*prakṛta*) altar, so too in the case of vessels—even those such as the *juhū*—there would be *prasaṅga*, because they also serve the purpose of the *homa*.

The meaning is that the oblations (*homāḥ*)—namely, the rites such as the *homa* performed with the *juhū* ladle and other implements belonging to the *iṣṭi* sacrifice—are accomplished by those very implements belonging to the *soma* sacrifice; this is the sense of the preceding sūtra. As for the meaning of the subsequent sūtra: the term *nyāyya* (proper) refers to the *juhū* and other implements which do not deviate from the purpose (*kārya*) consisting of the *homa* and so forth. The suffix *-ya* is applied according to the rule *dharmapathyarthanyāyādanapete* (Pāṇini 4.4.92). The word *vā* serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The meaning is that the *juhū* and other implements alone are the performers of the *homa* of substances other than *soma*, and there is no accomplishment through incidental application (*prasaṅga*) by means of the *camasa* cups. Why?

Because they are not employed [independently]. The vessels are employed [for the sake of the sacrifice], yet they are employed for their own sake. When a subsidiary (aṅga) is employed, there is no further employment of the archetypal (prākṛta) element as a substitute for that debt. Since the archetypal constituent (padārtha) possesses its status as a constituent by that very form, when there is an employment of a subsidiary characterized by that [form], it is proper that even upon the loss of a quality (guṇahāni), the [archetype] should be obtained. And indeed, in the case of "he places the oblations on the altar" (vedyām havīṃṣy āsādayati), it is precisely by way of being an altar (veditva)—that is, by way of being a subsidiary characterized as an altar—that the archetypal altar is indicated.

In that case, when there is an application [of the vessels], it is logical that even if a quality is lost, there would be the consequence [of using the vessel] for its attainment. Here, however, there is no application of the *juhū* and other vessels as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) by virtue of their being common vessels for the *camasa* cups, such that there would be a lack of application; rather, they function as subsidiaries by virtue of being *juhū*s and so forth, according to the injunction "one offers with the *juhū*. Consequently, since the subsidiary in the form of the *juhū* itself is not applied [by the *camasa* rule], there is an application of the original vessel for the sake of performing the subsequent rites with the *juhū* and other vessels that are to be performed again.

And thus, this is the distilled meaning: by the word "nyāya" (reasoning/logic), the subject matter at hand—the ritual acts such as the *homa*—is denoted. Those things, such as the *juhū* ladles and so forth, which do not deviate from those [acts]—that is, which are not separated from them in the absence of a subverting scriptural injunction—are employed specifically in those very *soma* and *iṣṭi* rituals. However, it is not through a common property, such as the mere state of being a vessel, that the *juhū* and other implements are employed; rather, how is it that their application is established by the *grahas*, *camasas*, and so forth?

However, the *juhū* and other vessels are employed by virtue of their specific qualities, such as being a *juhū*, and not by virtue of the general quality of being a "vessel" (*pātra*). Therefore, there is no establishment of *prasaṅga* (incidental application). This is the meaning of the second sūtra. As for the meaning of the third sūtra: the statement "the vessels [beginning] with the *juhv*" is intended to include all vessels commonly referred to as *pātras*, including the *sphya* and others; otherwise, it would serve to exclude the *pracaraṇī*. Thus, the meaning of the third sūtra has been set forth.

53–734. *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—Seventh Praśna: The necessity of the mention of "belonging to the animal sacrifice" (*pāśuka*). Since the *svadhiti* (cleaver) and other implements are unique to the animal sacrifice, there might be a doubt that only those [implements] are to be employed; to preclude that, the word "vessels" (*pātrāṇi*) is used.

Having performed that which precedes the taking of the clarified butter (*ājya*), and having brought [the fire] back, he takes the clarified butter for the animal sacrifice over the *Gārhapatya* fire.

Having taken four portions each in the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, he pours a third part of the clarified butter into the curd, and so forth—this refers to the manner in which the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) is performed. The word "gārhapatye" (in the Gārhapatya fire) is a locative ending, which connects with the verb "pratihṛtya" (having brought back). "Pratiharaṇa" means bringing back toward oneself. The term "gārhapatye" functions as a locative of proximity; the meaning is that having brought [the ladles] back toward the vicinity of the Gārhapatya fire, he takes the sacrificial portions for the animal (*pāśukāny ājyāni*) right there. In the form "pratihṛtya," a causative sense (*ṇic*) is to be understood as being inherent.

Otherwise, since the carrying [of the fire] westward would already be established by the rule "one takes the *pāśuka* *āghāra* oblations in the *gārhapatya*," the statement "having turned back" (*pratihṛtya*) would result in being redundant. The *prokṣaṇī* water-vessel is placed at the western third of that portion of the ground which is strewn with sacrificial grass (*barhis*) extending as far as the *ātitheyī* vessel. Here, the *pracaraṇī* ladle is not used at the time of the formal arrangement of the vessels, because its use is prescribed only for the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing).

At the time of taking the clarified butter (*ājya*) from the *pracaraṇī* ladle, one does not take [any portion] first, because that too is prescribed only for the *sutyā* day; nor at the end, because that is prescribed specifically at the time of the *vaitaraṇa* oblation.
Thus, with the words "So, do thou praise," the *brahmán* places the King [Soma] upon his lap.

When the Adhvaryu has performed the ritual action ending with "He pours water [into the *ājya-sthālī*]," the term *upastha* refers to a specific type of seat consisting of a particular arrangement of the feet. The meaning is that he places—or establishes—the King Soma upon that. Although this would have been established by the Brahman’s own sūtra, the repetition here is for the purpose of knowing the sequence of the performance: that the taking up of the pressing stones and other implements occurs immediately after the King Soma is placed in the lap, and not prior to it.

In this context, the mention of the mantra is intended to exclude the alternative of silence (*tūṣṇītvam*) which would otherwise apply under the view that no mantra is recited. Alternatively, there may be a word-division (*padaccheda*) here as *atra* [meaning "in this"]. The meaning is: anyone other than the *brahman* priest—whether he be one standing among the group of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) or another person—places the King [Soma] upon his lap. And this role of the *brahman* is optional according to the rule to be stated later in the *Brahmatvasūtra*: "He places the King upon the lap of the *brahman*, or anyone other than the *brahman* who is an officiating priest."
Even in this explanation, the recitation of mantras is required for the sake of the officiating priests (ṛtvij) other than the Brahman priest; otherwise, the state of silence would persist.

[The text continues: "They take up the pressing-stones, the Vāyavya cups, the Droṇakalaśa vessel, the goblets, the sacrificial grass for the guest-offering (ātithyā), the fuel-wood, the clarified butter, and they lead forward the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma."

Immediately after the word "ādadata" (they take up), the word "parikarmiṇaḥ" (the attendants) is to be understood as the ellipsis. The plural number here is used with reference to the collective group of agents. It is accepted that the leading [of the animals] by means of a rope, after having bound those beginning with the horse and ending with the ram, is also included. If it is argued that the injunction for taking them up is therefore redundant, [we reply: no, because that [leading] is already accomplished solely through the breaking [of the ropes]. If it is further argued that since the injunction for taking them up is established by the very sense of the matter, the explicit statement is useless, [we reply: true.

Because it is placed on the lap of the king immediately after he has performed the Brahma-rite, the purpose is to make known that the taking [of the Soma] must occur right then and not previously, even though one might have lain down; thus there is no redundancy. The *grāvāṇaḥ* (pressing-stones) are well-known. The *vāyavyāni* are upward-pointing vessels. A jar shaped like a wooden trough (*droṇa*) is a *droṇakalaśa*. [End of] Chapter: With the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

And the staff is four finger-breadths long, either circular or square, its dimensions not fixed, serving as a substitute for the purpose [of the fire-pan]. Therefore, the author of the Sūtra has stated that the *doṇa* altar may also have either a square or a circular shape. Regarding these [staffs], since there is a statement to be made later—"those whose wood is not specified are of *vikaṅkata* wood"—they are made of *vikaṅkata*. In its absence, they are made from any sacrificial tree other than the elephant-tree (*vāraṇa*).

However, by the rule *ahomārthāni tu vāraṇasya*, since it is stated that vessels not intended for *homa* are made from the *vāraṇa* tree, and because the *droṇakalaśa* is indeed intended for *homa*, the prohibition of the *vāraṇa* tree applies to it by implication. Yet, the *kalaśa* is not made of clay (*mārtika*), for there is a scriptural prohibition: "One should not offer an oblation in what is made of clay" (*mṛnmayam āhutim ānaśe*). In the case of *dharma*, however, the use of clay for the vessel used in *homa* is expressly enjoined. As for the *camasas*, their characteristics will be described later.

The *pāva* and other implements previously employed have been sprinkled with water. The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the guest-offering (*ātithyā*) is tied up and prepared silently, together with the *prastara* bundle. The fuel (*idhma*) is also tied up, including the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) used for the guest-offering. The clarified butter (*ājya*) has been poured into the ladles and placed in the vessel; likewise, the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) is in its respective vessels. The animal (*paśu*) dedicated to Agni and Soma—the one by which the King [Soma] was welcomed as a guest through the ear-grasping ceremony performed by the sacrificer—is prepared. The particle "ca" (and) serves to include items not explicitly mentioned.

Then the *parikarmiṇaḥ* (attendants) take up the *khuvāsa*, the *spālī*, the *bhṛt*, the *ādhavanīya*, the *pariplava*, the *ekadhana* jars, the *pajhe-janī* jar, the *vasatīvarī* jar, the *daśāpavitra*, the *udacana*, and so forth. If there is a *prāyaścitta-paśu* (expiatory animal sacrifice), those two [jars] are also taken. Regarding the statement "they lead them along" (*anunayanti*), only the previously mentioned items such as the boat (*nau*) and so on are connected here. The meaning is that the *parikarmiṇaḥ* lead—that is, cause to reach—the fire, Soma, the *pātra*, and the rear portion. Even though the *idhma* (sacrificial fuel) was already moistened by the *ātithyā-mahiṣī* (hospitality cow), because of the specific mention of "leading along" (*anunayana*) here, it is again taken up as before.

They bring the wife and set the carts in motion; the connection [of the sentence] is "they bring the wife. This very *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) is "they bring the wife" (*patnīm ānayanti*). For this reason, the insertion of another word between a prefix and a verb, as prescribed by the rule *vyavahitāśca*, is not contradicted. The plural number is intended to include those who are to be circumambulated, and these consist of three or more. Furthermore, this bringing [of the wife] is from the *patnīśālā* to the *śālāmukhīya*. The bringing by many people serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). The connection is "they set them in motion after having brought her" (*ānīyānupravartayanti*).

"Setting in motion" (*pravartana*) means leading forward. This *śruti* (scriptural injunction) is also being restated here. The lack of contradiction despite the intervention of other words is to be understood here as well, just as before. Here, "carts" (*anas*) are mentioned; by the plural number, [the carts] beginning with the *pratyagni* are included. Because of the word "after" (*anu*), it is the setting in motion of the carts. These are placed near the *śālāmukhīya* fire or toward the northern side, according to their use. When the carts have been fully prepared, the attendants shall carry the sacrificial offerings and other materials.

And that [process] extends from the north of the great altar (mahāvedi) as far as the eastern limit of the assembly hall (prācīmaṇṭapa). Because of the plural number, many priests perform the circumambulation. By this, it is indicated that there is no yoking of oxen for the purpose of leading [the cart]. They set the carts in motion together with the materials required for the rites to be described hereafter, based on the indicative mark (liṅga): "Whatever belongs to him, he goes to the heavenly world (suvarga loka) along with that."

They cause the sacrificial implements to follow after her; according to the *Naudhāyasūtra*, "by whatever sacrificial implement she possesses, with that they settle down behind the fire. By "sacrificial implement" (*śastra*) is meant a sacrificial utensil, that is to say, a vessel for the sacrifice. Āpastamba states that following with the implements applies to the *yāyāvara* (the wandering ascetic). Therefore, it is understood that according to this view, for the *śālīna* (the settled householder), there is only the fire produced by friction (*nirmanthya*). Satyāṣāḍha, in his *Śrautasūtra*, describes the manner of leading out the wife: "The Brahman’s wife shall go forth," thus the Neṣṭṛ leads the wife out.

The Neṣṭṛ priest, together with the attendants, leads the wife forward from her place toward the Śālāmukhīya fire for the Vaisarjana oblations, using the mantra: "May the Brahmanaspati go forth. The meaning of the word *utthāpya* (having raised) is derived from the prefix *ud*. By the rule that "particles have multiple meanings," it is understood that if she is standing, she should be made to sit down and then raised before being led forward; she is not to be led while remaining in that [standing] state. Alternatively, the prefix *ud* may signify "slowly.
The mantra concludes with the words, "Sit down according to your color.
Then, as she is being led forward, she mutters the formula: "And I am a willing follower."
The *neṣṭṛ* brings [the wife] while being attended by the assistants; this is a qualification of the wife. "Viśā iha" is the end of the mantra.
Having sat down to the west of the *śālāmukhīya* fire with the words "suprajasas tvā vayam," he mutters the mantras belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

Sitting down very close to the rear part of the Śālāmukhīya fire, he mutters those mantras pertaining to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśapaurṇamāsika*), beginning with "O householder" (*gṛhapate*). The word "wife" (*patnī*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. The suffix *ṭhan* is applied by the rule "madhyātmādeṣṭhaṃ bhaviṣyati," and there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) for both parts of the compound according to the rule for the *anuśatikādi* group. By the word "not reciting" (*na japati*), the acts of worship (*upasthāna*) and so forth are excluded, and in their place, this muttering (*japa*) is prescribed by this rule. However, for the two mantras "O you of good offspring" (*suprajāstva*) and "May my sons... (*mama putrāḥ*), there is only the natural muttering (*japa*) itself.
They assign the Śālāmukhīya fire to the duties of the Gārhapatya; in it, the Gārhapatya rites are performed.

The "face of the hall" (*śālāmukha*) is the eastern part of the hall (*prāgvaṃśa*). That which is situated there is the "hall-faced" (*śālāmukhīya*), namely the householder, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). The fire associated with him is the *gārhapatya*. Its association with the householder is due to its being produced by him. To avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), [the suffix] *-īya* must also be accepted for other cases. Since the Vedic scriptures (*śruti*) derive their injunctions from the duties of the *gārhapatya*—that is, the *gārhapatya*-rites—for the sake of those *gārhapatya*-rites, they depend upon them.

The meaning is that all those vital points (*marman*) which belong to the *gārhapatya* fire are performed upon that *śālāmukhīya* fire. Since the hall (*śālā*) in the form of the *prāgvaṃśa* has already been established, the term *śālāmukhīya* applies specifically to the original *āhavanīya* fire located at its entrance. Because the entire hall has not yet been completed, the fire situated on the *uttaravedi*—even though it is located at the entrance of that [hall]—does not possess the status of *śālāmukhīya*. If the fire on the *uttaravedi* were to have the status of *śālāmukhīya*, it would contradict the statement that "they proceed toward the east."

Therefore, the original *āhavanīya* fire itself possesses the status of the *śālāmukhīya*. For this very reason, during the carrying forth (*praṇayana*) of the sacrificial vessels (*havirdhāna*), the fire that serves as the locus for the oblation with the mantra "I yoke the mind" is designated by the term *auttaravedika* (the northern altar fire) alone, and not by the term *śālāmukhīya*. Alternatively, the meaning is this: the performers settle upon—that is, they establish—the *śālāmukhīya*, which is the original *āhavanīya* known by that name, as the functional equivalent of the *gārhapatya*; the word "performers" is to be supplied to complete the sense.

In this context, there are two types of restrictive rules (*niyama*): first, that they carry forward only the *Śālāmukhīya* fire for the *Gārhapatya* rites, while the ancient *Gārhapatya* fire is not carried forward; second, by the subsequent rule, the *Āhavanīya* rites are performed with the [newly established] fire, and even though it serves as the *Āhavanīya*, they carry forward the *Śālāmukhīya* only for the *Gārhapatya* rites and not for the *Āhavanīya* rites as well. Here, the *Gārhapatya* rites intended are those pertaining to the Soma sacrifice (*saumika*), and not those pertaining to animal sacrifices (*pāśuka*).

Among those [fires], however, it is established by this very sūtra that "this is the Āhavanīya here; that from which it is carried forward is the Gārhapatya. If one asks: "Is this not already established even by the sūtra 'this is the Āhavanīya here; that from which it is carried forward is the Gārhapatya'? For what purpose, then, is this statement?"—it is true. By the word "here" (*atra*) in the phrase "this is the Āhavanīya here," [the fire] in the *pāśubandha* sacrifice is indicated.

Since this [fire] is already established for *kakarma*s (the rites of the *soma* sacrifice), it is not established for anything other than that; therefore, it is necessary to compose this sūtra in order to establish its application even there. When two kinds of *gārhapatya* fires are present after the *abhipraṇayana* (carrying forward) in the *saumika* rites, and a doubt arises as to which *gārhapatya* rite should be performed, it is restricted that only the *śālāmukhīya* fire is connected with the *gārhapatya* rites.

The Soma-related rituals belonging to the Gārhapatya fire commence precisely with the carrying forward of Agni and Soma; therefore, this technical definition (paribhāṣā) is established here. [Objection: If that is so, then the word "Gārhapatya" itself should be used in each respective instance, as the application of the Śālāmukhīya fire will follow from the definition alone. [Response: The mention of the "Prāsaṃśa" in the Audayanīyā rite is intended solely to exclude the status of being the Gārhapatya from the Śālāmukhīya and the status of being the Āhavanīya from the Uttaravedika fire.

If it is asked: "Since the prevention of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding objects that ought to be enjoined in this manner is thus established, for what purpose is the term *śālāmukhīya* employed here and there?"—the answer is no. For although all subsequent rites (*uttara-karman*) are without distinction characterized as belonging to the Soma sacrifice (*saumika*), the inclusion of the term *śālāmukhīya* in various places serves a specific purpose; namely, the necessity of it to indicate that the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) pertains specifically to those particular rites. Thus, its employment is meaningful.

For, according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "they resort to the *śālāmukhīya* fire for the duties of the *gārhapatya*," and that "the duties of the *gārhapatya* are performed in it," only those rites connected with a sacrifice are understood here. Therefore, since the placing of vessels and other acts prompted by the *savanīya-puroḍāśa* are indeed connected to the *savanīya-puroḍāśa* sacrifice, the *śālāmukhīya* fire is obtained [for them] as a matter of course; thus, there is no requirement for anyone to fetch it. For this very reason, the twenty-one-fold [fire] is taken at the *udayanīyā* sacrifice.

In the case of acts such as the *vaitaraṇa-homa* and others, which are distinct from speech and unconnected with the sacrifice, if it were merely stated that "one offers in the *gārhapatya* fire," then—since the *gārhapatya* is heard directly in the revealed scripture (*śruti*) in each respective instance—the term would refer only to the original *gārhapatya*. To prevent this, the mention of the *śālāmukhīya* is necessary. Where there is no direct hearing of the word *śālāmukhīya*, as in the case of the employment of vessels and the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) used for the *savanīya* sacrifice, the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) finds its application.

The mention of the *śālāmukhīya* fire in rites other than the sacrifice—such as the *vaisarjana* and others—which are not connected to the sacrifice, is intended to exclude [the use of] the *gārhapatya* fire in the rule "the wife [stands] before the *varaśe* from the *gārhapatya*," by specifying that only the *gārhapatya* already established there is meant. If it is argued that this is already established by the statement, "this is the *āhavanīya* here, from which it is carried forward; that is the *gārhapatya*," we say no.

Because the word *ati* used in that context in this sūtra demonstrates that it refers exclusively to the *pāṃśuka* (dusty) [fire], and since the *savanīya-puroḍāśa* sacrifice lacks the quality of being *pāṃśuka*, the *parimāṣā* rule—"In the absence of the *pāramāṣā* [fire], they resort to the *śālāmukhīya* as the *gārhapatya*; in that [fire], the *gārhapatya* rites are performed"—is necessarily required to establish it. It should not be argued that this same *parimāṣā* rule also suffices for the *vaisarjana-homa* and other such rites.

If that were the case, it would follow that the mention of the *śālāmukhīya* fire in various contexts would be without any basis. Nor should it be argued that there should likewise be no mention of any specific fire in the *vaisarjana-homa* and other such rites; for by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating "oblations are offered in the Āhavanīya," the Āhavanīya fire would necessarily be obtained there as well.

Based on the Sūtra stating, "They follow the Śālāmukhīya for the Gārhapatya rites; in it the Gārhapatya duties are performed," one might conclude that the commencement of the Gārhapatya functions in the Śālāmukhīya begins only with the carrying forward of the Soma (*somapraṇayana*), and not with the placing of the fires (*anvādhāna*). However, if such an interpretation were accepted, there would be no *anvādhāna* at all for the Śālāmukhīya as the Gārhapatya, because its status as the Gārhapatya would simply not exist [prior to that point].

If this were accepted as the desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), it would follow that there is no *anvādhāna* (the ritual piling of fuel) for the *śālāmukhīya* fire, which is not utilized in the primary rite (*prakṛtakarman*). If one were to accept this here as well, then since the *āgnīdhrīya* fire—which originates from the *śālāmukhīya*—is also being utilized, it would follow that it too has not been formally established (*ananyāhitatā*), resulting in a great logical inconsistency. Therefore, it is well-established that this [text] must indeed have the purpose of providing a reason (*hetuparatvam*).

Even though the *āhavanīya* fire is present in the portion of the *āgnīdhrīya*, we must proceed exactly as Āpastamba did regarding the possibility of anger (*kopopapatti*) there, because at that very moment the invisible merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is transferred from the *gārhapatya*.

By this [explanation], those such as Dhūrtasvāmin, Māṇḍāraka, and Rudradatta—who, being ignorant of the intention of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Bharadvāja-sūtra*, describe a meaning contrary to the *Āpastamba-sūtra*—are refuted. For the *Āpastamba-sūtra* states in the section on the carrying forward of the fire related to the Soma sacrifice: "This is the *āhavanīya* of the Soma from which it is carried forward; that is the *gārhapatya*. However, according to the opinion of Satyāṣāḍha and Bharadvāja, it should be understood that the rites of the *gārhapatya* take place only after the carrying forward of the fire to the *āgnīdhra*.
He issues the command: "Summon those who have taken the fast-food (*sam-pivratān*)."

The attendants (*parikarmiṇaḥ*) or the reciters (*ṛtvijaḥ*) are the ones to be sent here. Furthermore, the word *api* (also/even) signifies those kinsmen with whom the vow (*vrata*)—performed together with the sapinda relatives—is appropriate, namely, eating from a single cooking-pot (*ekapāka*). Alternatively, the word *api* has the sense of equality; thus, it refers to those whose vow consists of the same act of eating from a single cooking-pot. The meaning of the command is "unite yourselves for the duration. Because it serves the purpose of moving toward another state, it is *udātta*. The prefix (*upasarga*) is construed with the verb.

According to the rule *vyavahitāśca*, the intervention of another word between a prefix (*upasarga*) and a verb is not contradictory. Since this injunction belongs to another recension (*śākhā*), it certainly possesses the character of a Vedic mantra (*chandaḥ*).
They summon the dependents (*amātya*) of the sacrificer.

The meaning is that they accompany and assist the *yajamāna*’s *amātyas* and *jñātis*. The phrase "attendants (*parikarmiṇaḥ*) or *ṛtvijas*" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. The plural number is used to include any one of the various types of attendants. In the word *sahayante*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied according to the rule *ni-sam-upa-vi-bhyaḥ haḥ*. In the reading *amātyāḥ*, the nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative. The word *amātya* refers to those who share the same cooking place, the same lineage, and the same clan (*gotra*). The *yajamāna* takes hold of the *adhvaryu*; the wife takes hold of the *yajamāna*; and the *yajamāna*’s *amātyas* take hold of the wife.

The sacrificer takes hold of the *adhvaryu*, and the wife takes hold of him. Although the reference to the sacrificer is already established by the word "him" (*tam*), the explicit mention of "the sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is made again to dispel the doubt that—since the pronoun "him" is a general term (*sarvanāman*) referring to whatever is present in the mind, and since he [the sacrificer] was the first to appear—the wife might take hold of him [the *adhvaryu*] even though he is not currently in close proximity. This is done to ensure that she takes hold of the sacrificer himself.

In the passage, "The sacrificer, the wife, and the sacrificer's attendants," since the reference to the wife is already established by the word *tām* (her), the explicit mention of the word *patnī* (wife) again is for the purpose of including all wives in the case where there are multiple wives.

Otherwise, by taking the word "that" (*tat*) as referring to the primary [act], and based on the scriptural injunctions "the others are not without the eldest" and "the ritual must be performed with the eldest alone and not with another," the eldest alone would be the one to perform the *anvārambha* (touching/assistance) due to her primacy; let this not happen, but rather, all [wives] should participate here—this is for that purpose. [End of Maṇḍala 2, Paṭala 1] [This is] accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha. 739. It should be understood thus.

All wives, both those of the same caste (*savarṇā*) and those of a different caste (*asavarṇā*), touch the one who is being measured out. All the female relatives (*jñāpapatnī*) touch him. Because of the mention of "wives" (*patnī*), in the case of one who has married after the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), since his wife lacks connection with that *ādhāna*, she is not included by virtue of being a "wife"—for according to Pāṇini’s rule, "the state of being a wife (*patnītva*) is occasioned by connection with a sacrifice, and the husband's [status] is through connection with the sacrifice"—but rather she is included solely by virtue of being a female relative (*jñāpatnī*).

In the phrase "the attendants (*amātyāḥ*) of the one being led away (*yanamānasya*)," the inclusion of the term *yanamānasya* is for the purpose of excluding the *adhvaryu*. "Attendants" refers to brothers, sons, and so forth; specifically, the wives of brothers, sons, and others, as well as unmarried daughters. Married women are not included because their lineage has shifted to another family (*gotrāntara*). This is based on the rule: "The attendants touch only the wife, not one another. Thus, [the attendants] are the attendants of the one being led away who is accompanied by his wife.

Having covered them with an unwashed cloth, having taken four portions of clarified butter in the *pracaraṇī* ladle, having tied a piece of gold to the fringe of that cloth intended for covering, having placed it in the clarified butter, and having fastened the end of the cloth to the handle of the *sruk* ladle, he offers the two *vaisarjana* oblations on the *śālāmukhīya* fire. He offers the first oblation with the verse, "O Soma, you [protect us] from those who harm our bodies," and the second with, "May the swift one, enjoying the clarified butter, partake of it; Svāhā!"

"Those" refers to the ministers, the sacrificer, and so forth; by the use of the word "those," it is understood that the Adhvaryu should not conceal himself. Having covered [the head] with a cloth characterized by such qualities as being slightly worn, new, and white—meaning having thoroughly covered it with a cloth sufficient for the purpose of veiling—the head is covered first, for when the heads are covered, the ministers are considered covered, since the head is the most important among all the limbs.

The meaning is that one should cover [the ladle] in such a way that its handles are not visible; this is the excellence [of the procedure]. A *pracaraṇī* is so called because by means of it an unprecedented (*apūrva*) oblation is performed. Having taken four spoonfuls of clarified butter with the *sruva* for that *pracaraṇī*, one should place gold upon the fringe (*daśāñcala*) of the cloth used for covering it. Then, having tied the end of the cloth to the handle of the *pracaraṇī*—that is, to the *sruva*-handle—and holding it firmly so that it does not move, [one proceeds].

The intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*) is released at the *śālāmukhīya* fire by means of two offerings known as the *vaisarjana* (releasing) oblations; he offers them. Therein, the first *vaisarjana* oblation is with the mantra "O Soma, having made [thee] sweet... (*svara soma tanūkṛtya*). The second is with "May Apnu enjoy it" (*juṣāṇo apnur*). Having performed the placement of the vessels for the purpose of the offering, the preparation of the strainer (*pavitra*), the consecration of the *prokṣaṇī* waters, the taking up of the *sruva* and *sruca* ladles, and the other purificatory rites such as the wiping of the ladles, the [oblations] must be performed. The mention of "for the sake of covering" is intended to exclude any other garment.

The statement "in the fringe" (*daśāyām*) is for the purpose of excluding the edge that is devoid of a fringe. Because of the use of the locative case in "in the fringe," the binding is performed with either a thread or a blade of *darbha* grass during the fringe, but not by the fringe itself. Furthermore, this gold [ring] is either in the shape of a bracelet or has a hole; it is as follows: just as when one says generally, "Bring a jar," only a suitable jar is brought, so it is here. In the case of the option with a hole, having threaded a string through it, it should be bound to the fringe with that string.

By the singular number in "ten," the binding is to be done upon a single heifer (*baśā*). Alternatively, the singular number is used with reference to the genus; by this, binding upon all ten heifers is established when possible. The mention of the *Śālāmukhīya* fire is for the purpose of excluding the *Uttaravedi*, which—by the general rule that "offerings are made in the Āhavanīya with the *juhū* ladle"—would otherwise take the place of the Āhavanīya. Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra: [In the seventh book] he performs the remainder of the clarified butter (*ājya*).

The first oblation is with clarified butter (ājya) measured by two drops; the second oblation, however, is with clarified butter measured by only a single drop. "He makes the remainder of the clarified butter [measured] by a *nuvada* [of the ladle]" means that he sets it aside. The first mantra ends with "varūthāya svāhā," while the second is recited in its entirety. Because of the act of setting aside the remainder of the clarified butter, it is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, "May the Lord of the clarified butter enjoy it, svāhā!"—that the second oblation consists of a single drop of clarified butter.

The recitation of the entire mantra is solely for the purpose of clearly demonstrating the characteristic mark (*liṅga*). Baudhāyana has stated this matter quite explicitly: "Then, with the *sruva* ladle, he causes [the butter] to flow into the *āhuti*. Since two *āhutis* are prescribed by the Sūtra—namely, "having taken four portions in the *pracaraṇī* ladle, she offers the *vaitarjanī*"—there is no acceptance of this [procedure] mentioned by Baudhāyana.

He causes the fires to be carried forth from the *śālāmukhīya* fire-altar; he prepares the sand for the supporting-wood (*upayamanī*) and lifts up the fuel-stick (*idhma*). He takes hold of the supporting-wood while it is being held [in place]. Having given the command, "Recite for Agni and Soma as they are being carried forth," or rather, "Recite for them as they are being carried forth."

The fire that is being led forward is ignited in the *śālāmukhīya* [hearth]. The term "in the *śālāmukhīya*" is stated in order to set aside the removal [of the fire] that would otherwise be required for the sake of the primary *gārhapatya* fire. Sand—that is, gravel—is used as the supporting fuel (*upayamani*). He holds those blazing fires with those supporting fuels in such a way that they are supported by a vessel so as to be capable of being held; the particle "eva" (only) has the sense of restriction. By this, the meaning is that he prepares sand alone as the supporting fuel.

Nor is it improper to abandon the well-established sense of the particle *ca* as "conjunction" (*samuccaya*) and accept its function as "exclusion" (*avadhāraṇa*), such that one might say: "And thus, other [substances] are indeed different from sand. For it is more appropriate here to take it as having the sense of exclusion, because of Baudhāyana’s statement, "He scatters the *upayamani* [sand]," which implies that only sand is suitable for scattering, and because of Āpastamba’s statement, "Having made the *upayamani* with sand," which indicates that sand alone is used for the scattering.

Even those sacrificial fuels (*idhma*) which are set ablaze are called "fuel" only when they have attained the state of a composite whole; it has been shown that this term is not based on a specific ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*). One lifts the fuel, having gathered it together, and holds it aloft. One brings near the sand held in a shallow dish over the ignited fire. One brings it near—that is, one holds it close—for the purpose of covering the fuel, so that the fire being lifted does not scatter, nor fall down from below.

The meaning is that the fuel (idhma), being held by the supporting ladles (upayamanī) when they have approached, is positioned above. The rest is clear. Here, although both the Hautra and Yājuṣa-hotra manuals exist, only the Āśvalāyana manual is to be followed.
When [the verse] has been recited three times, they proceed eastward with Agni first or with Soma first, according to the mantra "This Agni of ours... (ayaṃ no agniḥ).

Because it has already been established, it is not recited three times, just like the first [verse]. Regarding this, Āpastamba stated: "In the case of the verse being recited three times... Those for whom Agni is the first city (pūḥ) are "Agni-first. In this view, after Agni comes Soma, and after that, the Adhvaryu, Brahman, and Yajamāna are included by virtue of the specific statement. Those for whom Soma is the first and foremost are "Soma-first."

In this view, behind the *soma* is the *agni*, and behind that is the place where the *adhvaryu* and others proceed. They go facing east (*prāñcaḥ*), with their faces turned toward the east, reciting the mantra "This is our *agni*. This mantra belongs to three [of the officiants]. Some say it also belongs to the wife. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says in the *Kauntha*: "They should proceed while remaining completely covered up to the *āhavanīya* fire. The word division is *ā-āhavanīyāt*. The meaning is "up to the *āhavanīya* fire. Baudhāyana also states: "They follow the impulse of the *hotṛ*."

In another treatise (*śāstrāntara*), because of the injunction that "the garment (*vāsaḥ*) [used] for the Vaiśarjana oblation belongs to the group of Adhvaryus," the Adhvaryu must take possession of that garment; since it is impossible for one to take what has not been given by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the act of giving is established by implication. However, the Mīmāṃsakas argue that this scriptural statement is not authoritative because it is rooted in greed; thus, they claim there is no taking of the garment by the Adhvaryu, and consequently, no giving either. This principle was stated in the third section (*pāda*) of the first chapter (*adhyāya*) by the sūtra: *abhininayanaṃ tu darśanāt* (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.25).

Regarding the conflict between these two types of scripture, the view of the Bhāṣyakāra (Śabara) is that the phrase "in the absence [of conflict], there would be inference" is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to the preceding sūtra itself; thus, according to the Vārtikakāra, there is indeed a distinction, and this difference should be understood. When there is a conflict with Śruti, only that scriptural statement which is independent of other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) is authoritative, and not a Smṛti statement, because only when such a conflict exists does Smṛti serve as an indicator (*anumāpaka*) of Śruti. Thus, the meaning of this sūtra—"in conflict it would be independent; in its absence, there is inference"—is as follows.

"Because of the observation of a cause" (*hetudarśanāt*) means because of observing a cause in the form of agitation. This refers to the meaning of the sūtra "because of the observation of a cause," which brings together the causes mentioned in the preceding sūtra. "In order to win over" (*vājasātāv*) is the end of the mantra.
They conciliate according to the purpose.

The attendants (*parikarmīṇaḥ*) lead the sacrificial implements (*prāvādīni*) according to their purpose, without wavering from the correct order; that is to say, they lead the *prāvādīni* first. Since these are to be placed at the beginning of the *māvādīni*, they lead the *prāvādīni* forward. After that, the *ātithyā-vedī*. For that [altar], the task of its initial strewing has presented itself. After that, they lead the fuel-sticks (*idhma*). For that [fuel], the task of placing it upon the fire has presented itself immediately thereafter. After that, the clarified butter oblations (*ājyāni*).

Immediately after those very [acts], because the oblation-form body (homarūpakāya) presents itself, and because it is employed immediately after the *māva* and so forth, there is the leading away (*nayana*) of these [priests]. The statement "they lead them away from the *avana*" is thus expressed; due to the plural number, it refers to the assistants (*parikarmin*).
The ministers follow along.

The meaning is that they follow after these other objects. Since following along (anvārambha) was prescribed previously and it was prescribed later that "the attendants return by the same way they came," the fact that the attendants follow the teacher is already established; therefore, this statement serves as a restrictive rule (parisaṃkhyā) regarding the commencement of the mantra after the oblation, indicating that there is merely a following along and not even the act of holding on (anvārambha). Because it is intended to convey a favorable disposition, the instruction is simply, "Follow along.
They lead the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma.

"The ministers follow" (anugacchantyamātyāḥ)—this subsequent statement indicates that the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma is led along with the ministers; because of the word "animal" (*paśu*) in the expression "they lead along," and because of the plural number, the attendants (*parikarmiṇaḥ*) are meant. For this very reason, the superior strength of the animal is understood.
Having established this fire on the Āgnīdhrīya altar, he offers an oblation in the Āgnīdhra shed with the verse containing the word "lead" (*naya*), namely: "O Agni, lead... (*agne naya*).

The meaning is that one should place this fire, which has been brought forward (*praṇīta*), facing the *viṣṇya* hearths; the prefix *prati-* is used to indicate placement facing oneself in the middle [of the hearths]. In this case, there is no facing northward, as one must face eastward; for there is a prohibition stating, "He does not turn away from the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*)."

Having smeared the fire-altar with cow-dung, having scraped it up with the wooden sword (*sphya*), and having sprinkled water upon it, this fire is to be established; for there is a rule stating that "this is universal," meaning that wherever the fire is to be established on an altar, there the smearing with cow-dung, scraping, and sprinkling must be performed. Having recited "O Agni, lead us... (*agne naya*), [the offering is made] because of the presence of the word "lead" (*naya*); indeed, there is also a Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating, "One offers in the *āgnīdhra* with the verse containing 'lead' (*nayavatī*)."

And this qualification is for the sake of identifying the specific knowledge; in the absence of such knowledge, the expiation for a breach of the *yajus* formula must be performed in the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*). The purpose of mentioning the *ṛc* is to be understood as previously stated in the case of the rule "he measures with a verse in the *aticchandas* meter. Although the identity of that [fire] is established by the mere statement "he offers into it," the explicit mention of "the Āgnīdhra" is intended to show that the fire established upon the *dhiṣṇiya* altar of the Āgnīdhra is designated as the *Āgnīdhra*.

The purpose of the designation [of these offerings as *vaisarjana*] is to ensure the recognition of this specific fire in passages such as, "He offers in the *āgnīdhra*, which is the body of the sacrifice. The word *vidha* marks the end of the mantra. Because they are enjoined by the root *hu* (to offer), the utterance *svāhā* is required. Although the two offerings are yet to be described, they are indeed designated as *vaisarjana*. According to the Śruti: "These *vaisarjana* offerings are offered for the sake of the heavenly world. He offers two in the *gārhapatya* fire; the sacrificer has two feet, [it is] for stability. He offers one in the intermediate space; he thus ascends the atmosphere. He offers one in the *āhavanīya*; he thereby causes him to go to the heavenly world. He performs the remaining rites with the clarified butter.

Two [ladles] indeed remain; of these two, one is measured by the *sruva* [ladle]. The meaning is that he offers an oblation with the words "O Agni, lead... and leaves behind a quantity of clarified butter (*ājya*) measured by the *sruva*. They set down the pressing stones (*grāvan*), the Vāyavya cups, the *droṇakalaśa*, and the *camasa* cups. The word "in the Āgnīdhra fire-hall" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the *somasthālī*, the *pūtabhṛt*, the *ādhavanīya*, the *pariplu*, the *ekadhana* jars, the *pannejana* jar, the *vasatīvarī* jars, the *daśāpavitra*, and the *udacana*. As for the *sruva*, its use is concluded by its being carried away along with the *sruc* ladles.

They carry the others across; here, "across" (*ati*) means "beyond. Thus, even before the *āgnīdhra* hearth, they carry the other items—the *ātithya* grass-bundle, the fuel-wood, the clarified butter, the *sruva*-ladle, and the animal—as far as the *uttaravedi*. In the case of the expiatory animal sacrifice, those two are also carried first. Or rather, the word "across" (*ati*) has the sense of "in front of. In this case, for the other items, the carrying is done directly from the cart. Alternatively, there is a reading "they carry the others along with" (*anuharanti*), which implies that for the others as well, the leading forward (*anunayana*) is indeed performed. Having gone around the north of the *āgnīdhra* hearth, he offers on the *auttaravedika* mound with the mantra: "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely."

The mention of *viṣṇiya* is for the purpose of excluding the *maṇḍapa*. Since it is possible that the term "having gone around" (*parītya*) might imply going to the *āgnīdhra* fire—understanding the meaning as "having circumambulated the *āgnīdhra*, having gone to the south, he offers"—the mention of *viṣṇiya* is made to prevent that. [This is] because it serves to specify the location. Going toward the *auttaravedika* fire is implied, since the oblation cannot take place without it. [Maṇḍana Paṭu: This is accompanied by the commentary named *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Mahāmahopādhyāya. Page 743. Line 2: Variant *kha* and *va* read "grahaṇa". [End of Maṇḍana Paṭu. Because it is restrictive in nature. The movement toward the *auttaravedika* is implicit, as the oblation is impossible without it.

In this case, the *sajyā* [cord] is not used later because there is no further application; Āpastamba has stated quite clearly: "With the mantra 'O Viṣṇu, stride out widely,' he offers the entire remainder of the clarified butter. The word *tira* marks the end of the mantra. Because it is enjoined by the verb *juhoti*, the utterance *svāhā* is required.
The attendants return by the same way they came.

"Yathetam" means "not deviating from that [path]. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound. The meaning is that they should return by the same path by which their departure was previously made; they should not go back by a different route. However, those who take the *ājya* and *barhis* materials remain near the northern direction until those respective items have been used up. The leader of the animal for Agni-Soma also remains stationed there from the time of the *upākaraṇa* rite. If the animals for Indra-Agni and Viṣṇu are present, the leaders of those two also remain stationed there from the time of their respective *upākaraṇa* rites. Having set down the *sura*, *sitā*, and other items, all of them may then depart.
With the verse, "Soma goes forth, the knower of the way," the Brahman priest causes the King [Soma] to enter the *havirdhāna* shed by means of the western door.

The word "saumya" (belonging to Soma) is to be explained as before. "Prapādayati" means he causes him to enter. The statement here is for the purpose of establishing the sequence of the performance: that the entry of the Adhvaryu into the *havirdhāna*, which is about to be described, occurs at the very moment the King is being led in, and not prior to it.

In the *Bālasvasūtra*, it is stated: "Having taken the King [Soma] from the Adhvaryu with the Saumya verse, 'somo jigāti gātuvid,' he enters the *havirdhāna* by the western door; having offered the King and performed the sacrifice, he returns, crosses over the northern altar from the west, and sits down to the south"—thus, the handing over of the King to the Adhvaryu is prescribed as being performed by the Brahman priest himself. By this [present rule], however, the status of the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛtva*) is prescribed.

And likewise, having himself recited the mantra, Brahmā should cause the King’s entry into the Havirdhāna shed by any attendant through the eastern door, and cause the offering of the King [Soma] to be made to the Āśvinas. Thus, due to the contradiction between these two [options], there is an option (vikalpa). Here, because of the mention of the mantra alongside the non-mention of the mantra, silence (tūṣṇīkatva) might also occur in one alternative; therefore, this is stated in order to preclude that.
