Or, "abro" may be taken as a word-break (padaccheda) here as well; the meaning, however, is clear.

Even in this interpretation, the statement regarding the leaf requires the understanding of [the action] being distinct from the *brahman*. Here is the summarized meaning: according to the first explanation, when the offering is made by the *adhvaryu* priest, the phrase "of one who has attained prosperity through the former [means]" does not apply; rather, it applies only when the offering is made by the *brahman* priest.

However, according to the second explanation, it is precisely when the agency of a priest other than the *brahman* is accepted that the phrase "of one who has attained prosperity through the former" becomes applicable, and not when the agency belongs to the *brahman*.
[The phrase is: "of one who has attained prosperity through the former."

The term "by way of the door" (*dvāreṇa*) carries forward the subject specified in the preceding sūtra. "One whose prosperity has departed" (*gataśrī*) refers to one who has lost his fortune. For such a sacrificer, according to the stated rule, the King [Soma] is to be brought in by the eastern *havirdhāna* shed. According to the established principle of the scriptures that "roots meaning 'to go' mean 'to reach'," it should be understood that a verbal root signifying motion here signifies reaching. The word *gataśrī* refers to those three types of persons mentioned in the Śruti: "There are indeed three who have attained prosperity: the learned Brāhmaṇa, the Vaiśya, and the Kṣatriya."

[The following] should be recited: "O bright one, student of the three Vedas! O Ahibuniya, protect my mantra, which the seers who know the three Vedas know—the Ṛks, the Sāmans, and the Yajus; for that is the immortal glory of the virtuous. This refers to one qualified as a *prāmaṇī*. An anointed Kṣatriya is a *rājanya*. These three enter through the eastern door. The word "āsam" marks the end of the mantra.

Following the formula, "I go along the wide mid-region," the Adhvaryu enters by the eastern door and spreads a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and its hair upward in the interior of the southern Havirdhāna cart, saying, "Thou art the seat of the Ādityas."

Here too, the term "by way of" (*dvāreṇa*) has its substantive (*viśeṣya*) understood by ellipsis. The reading *anvihī* (come along) found in one's own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā*) might otherwise apply; to prevent that, the reading *anvemī* (I am following) is used. The statement "by the eastern [door]" (*pūrveṇa*) is for the sake of restriction: whether the sacrificer is one whose prosperity has departed or one whose prosperity has not departed, he enters the sacrifice by the eastern door alone, and not according to the previous arrangement. The mention of the *adhvaryu* is for the purpose of excluding the *brahman*. The mention of the "southern" [door] is for the purpose of excluding the "northern. The rest is to be performed as in the purchase of the Soma.
He places [the vessel] upon it with the mantra: "The king Aditi has sat down in his own seat.
This also should be explained as before.

Having consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* waters, having addressed the *brahman*, having sprinkled the fuel and the altar, having poured out the remainder of the *prokṣaṇī* water, and having thrown back the two strainers (*pavitra*), he spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) behind the *uttaravedi* with the mantra, just as in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

The sequential enumeration is for the purpose of excluding what has already been mentioned. Having consecrated the water with the mantra "O Waters, you are divine," and having addressed [the Brahman priest] with the words "O Brahman, I shall sprinkle," the invitation (*āmantraṇa*) also implies permission (*prasava*), because otherwise the act of addressing would be rendered meaningless. The mention of the *vedi* (altar) is intended to prevent the omission of the *iṣṭika-prasava* (the sacrificial invocation), as it would otherwise be obscured by the word "Veda. Here, the *vedi* is intended to be of such a dimension where the spreading of the grass outside [the altar] is to be performed; it does not refer to the entire great altar (*mahāvedi*).

[The word] *dirīvaḥ* [is used] because they have been sprinkled (*prokṣita*). Since sprinkling has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), once the invisible merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by the sprinkling has been realized, there is no further need for sprinkling; thus, just as there is no need for the purpose of sprinkling, it would be impossible to do so again because spreading [the grass] has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭakārya*). Once the spreading is accomplished, one might suspect that because there is no longer any sprinkling, the spreading should be performed without reciting the mantra. To ward off that doubt, [the author says] "by means of the mantra" (*mantreṇa*).

Furthermore, regarding the absence of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) at the originative injunction (*utpatty-upadeśa*) of the sacrifice, Mīmāṃsaka Jaimini himself stated in the first section (*pāda*) of the twelfth chapter that "it should be performed for each [instance] because of the difference in the application of the established ritual" (*niṣṭhita-karma-prayoga-bhedāt pratitatra kriyeta*). This sūtra was explained by Śabara in his commentary on the sūtra: "The *barhis* [grass] belongs to the *Atithyā*, that to the *Upasads*, and that to the *Agnīṣomīya*. In this explanation, it is stated that the taking up of the mantra occurs only when there is a specific requirement for the sprinkling of the *barhis*.

Therefore, it is understood that this reading, which includes the word *bahiṣpad* [in the compound], is merely a modern interpolation. Even though there is a difference in location (*deśapṛthaktva*), the mantra is repeated. [End of Section]. This is accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. By the sūtra beginning with "iti" in the first quarter of the twelfth chapter, even Jaimini has stated that the spreading (*staraṇa*) is to be performed with a mantra; the meaning of the sūtra is indeed quite clear.

Because of the commonality of the *bahiḥ* grass, this [objection] arises as a consequence; it is stated [in response] that by the phrase "due to the separation of place" (*deśapṛthaktvāt*), it is understood that this spreading is not for the sake of the external object (*bahir-artha*), but rather that one spreads the altar (*vedi*) with the *bahiḥ* grass. This is because of the accusative case-ending and because it serves a purpose; thus, it is for the sake of consecrating the location of the altar. Furthermore, "here" (*iha*) refers to the two locations near the eastern hall (*prāgvaṃśa*) and the northern side; therefore, the spreading is for that purpose, and the mantra, being a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that act, is also repeated.

In the absence of repetition, the placing of the *āgneya* and *saumya* sacrificial oblations (*havis*) on the altar would be defective due to the deficiency of the altar itself. Or, even if the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is for the sake of the exterior, such that the oblations are placed directly upon the spread grass, nevertheless, because of the repetition of that [spreading], there must be a repetition of the mantras that are its subsidiaries; otherwise, the oblations would be placed on grass that has been spread without mantras. Consequently, [the mantra] "He ties the front knot" (*antah puro granthim*) and so forth ceases after the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).

When the sacrificer has silently grasped the *prastara* (grass-bundle), he applies the two strainers (*pavitra*) with the formula, "I place the out-breath and in-breath [in you]. By the gerundive suffix *-lyap* in the word "having applied" (*apisūjya*), the handing over of the *prastara* to the Brahman priest and the preparation of the *āhavanīya* fire-altar are indicated. Consequently, it is established that one should spread the *barhis* (sacrificial grass) only after having held the *prastara*. Because it is separated by the greatness of the *stotra*, there is no dependence on the parts taken up [within the *stotra*]. However, the spreading of the *śulba* (cord) certainly takes place.

Because that [space] is not an obstruction due to being outside the *barhis* (sacrificial grass), the statement "to the west of the *uttaravedi*" is intended to show that this *barhis* is to be spread in the area immediately adjacent to the *uttaravedi*, and not in both directions from the edge of the *uttaravedi* as is the case with the *barhis* used for the Soma sacrifice. By the suffix *-ena*, the entire western portion situated outside the *uttaravedi*, starting from the *havirdhāna* shed, is excluded.

Thus, the meaning established is that one spreads [the grass] outside, starting from the region near the Uttaravedi up to the Havirdhāna shed. Now, one might object: "Should there not be the application of the injunction for spreading [grass] as in the Soma sacrifice, as well as the attainment of the mantra *itvāsyā ādhāya*? Let this not happen; rather, let there be only the original (prakṛta) mantra. If this is argued, we say no.

Since this *barhis* (sacrificial grass) is used exclusively for the sake of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), it is impossible for the ritual properties of the spreading (*staraṇa*) belonging to the Soma sacrifice to apply to it; therefore, there is no purpose served by their exclusion. And thus it has been stated that this is the purpose: by the rule "of the Darśapūrṇamāsa," the ritual properties such as the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* are extended [to the animal sacrifice]. If it is asked, "But will not the mantra also be obtained by this very rule? What is the point of the word 'mantra'?"—this is true;
however, because we observe a deviation in the case of the Soma-sacrifice spreading, there would be no way to ensure its application without the explicit statement "by the mantra."
When the clarified butter (ājya) has been set down, one proceeds with the "measuring out of the sacrificial post" (yūpa-sammāna).

By this, it is indicated that the sequence beginning with the *anuyāja* offerings and ending with the *udvāsana* is implied. After the strewing of the altar (vedi), there is the strewing of the *plakṣa* branch upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Thus it is stated in the *Kātyāyana-Śrautasūtra*: "He strews the *plakṣa* branch upon the sacrificial grass. The "measuring out of the sacrificial post" refers to the ritual action of fixing the post in its base (the *agniṣṭhā*) by means of fire; all actions characterized by that are termed "measuring out of the sacrificial post. One proceeds with that—that is, one performs it—starting from the taking up of the wooden sword (*sphya*) with the mantra "Of the god... (*devasya tvā*) and ending with the grasping of the cord (*raśanā*).
He dedicates the animal to Agni and Soma. Its form has been explained;

that which has its [ritual] procedure explained is "of explained form. The meaning is that, while touching the animal with the large outer branches of the sacrificial grass, he makes a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) directed toward the deities Agni and Soma. By the phrase "its form has been explained," it is made known that the very same animal which was cooked for the King’s hospitality (ātithyā) is the one to be dedicated, and not that a different animal is to be brought for the purpose of dedication.

1.746. Regarding the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha: If it is argued that, such being the case, one should simply say "that has been explained" and thus the mention of its "form" (*rūpa*) is useless—no; for among all the characteristics mentioned, such as "red," "black-and-white," and "red-and-white," these colors must necessarily be understood for their significance. The purpose is that when an animal endowed with all the prescribed characteristics is obtained, the requirement is not fulfilled merely by its being red and so forth.

In some cases, for the sake of fulfilling the purpose, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must indeed be performed even in the common language (*prākṛta*). However, it should be understood that if, by virtue of obtaining such an animal, one takes hold of one specifically characterized by its being made of iron (*lohavat*) and so forth, there is no expiation. Regarding the characteristics of the goat (*chāga*), [it is stated] in the *Kātyāyana-pariśiṣṭa*: "Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the auspicious characteristics of goats, and likewise the inauspicious ones; I shall declare them hereafter. [A goat may be] of one color, of two colors, or likewise of many colors."

The goat that is reddish-brown (rohita) is indeed the sixth; it shall uplift one's lineage. That goat which has a white face, a black neck, and a white belly is the most excellent form among animals; one desiring cattle should sacrifice it. A goat resembling the color of madder, whose two horns are four finger-breadths long, is named Pālaka; such a goat protects great wealth. A deformed, dwarf, or impotent goat—these three types of animals accomplish the great sacrifice, and one obtains a great fruit.

In the sacrifice, that goat whose mark is on the right side is indeed named Sārthaka; he bestows the fruits of all desires. That goat whose white mark is on the right side is known as Vinaya, the subduer of enemies. A white-and-black goat is for the *pratiṣṭhā* rite, and a black goat with white [marks] is established for the *pratiṣṭhā*; these two goats are established by the sacrificer for the sake of stability. [The goat] that is lame, bent, having six curls, possessing curly hair, and pot-bellied [is also specified].

A goat that is entirely hairless in color is a "Nimba," which accomplishes all goals; likewise is one with ears like iron, O Puṣpaka, if these two features are present. Furthermore, one with ears shaped like a plowshare, or ears like ginger, or one whose seven hooves are flat on the sole, or one with ears like a *śuṇṭhā* plant—such a goat brings the destruction of daughters, the loss of sons, and even death. If three of its legs are of one color and the fourth is otherwise, that goat is named "Musalī"; it destroys the family from below.

Kālāla has black sides and stands upon white feet. The goat named Vaiśravaṇa attends upon Nabhāga; he was born old, with waning vigor and diminished strength. Having performed the *pravara* selection according to tradition, he chooses the Soma-offering priests (*saumika-ṛtvij*) with the *āśrāvaṇa*, *ṛtu-praiṣa*, and other formulas.

"Having performed the *pravara*," "having performed the ordinary *pravara*. The phrase "having performed the *pravara*" is a restatement (anuvāda) intended to indicate the previously mentioned rule. By means of that, the ritual procedure beginning with "having offered the introductory oblation (*upākṛtya*), he offers five [oblations]" becomes established. This restatement is also for the purpose of prescribing a specific rule in the form of an expansion of the Soma sacrifice. The meaning of "having performed the *pravara*" is: having performed the divine and human selection (*varaṇa*). The term "repeatedly calling for the *āśrāvaṇa*" (*āśrāvyāśrāvya*) refers to the act of calling for the *āśrāvaṇa*. This *ṇamul* suffix is used here in the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇye*).

Therefore, "prativaraṇa" (the counter-selection) refers to the *āśrāvaṇa* (the call for assent). "Āmīkṣṇya" means repetition. Because it is connected with the *āśrāvaṇa*, the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* (the response) is also considered a *prativaraṇa*. Baudhāyana has clearly stated both the *āśrāvaṇa* and the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* individually: "He selects the Hotṛ in the well-known manner."

[The Adhvaryu] causes [the Maitrāvaruṇa] to announce: "Oṃ, cause to hear! Let there be hearing! O Mitra and Varuṇa, the two Praśāstṛs, from the office of the Praśāstṛ—such-and-such is the human [name]," thus he utters the name of the Maitrāvaruṇa. Then he causes [the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin] to announce: "Oṃ, cause to hear! Let there be hearing! Oṃ śrauṣaṭ! Indra is the Brahmā, from the office of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin—such-and-such is the human [name]," thus he utters the name of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; by means of this sūtra beginning with these words and ending with "they may be either associated or unassociated in the ritual framework."

The *ṛtupraiṣas* are the calls (*praiṣas*) containing the word *ṛtu*, intended for the drawing of the *ṛtugraha* cups; they are to be recited by the Maitrāvaruṇa priest. "Beginning with those" means beginning with the *ṛtupraiṣas* and so forth—that is, having the *ṛtupraiṣas* as their opening formulas. "Belonging to Soma" (*saumika*) means these belong to Soma; the meaning is that he chooses these officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) connected with the Soma sacrifice, namely the *ṛtuyājins* (those who perform the *ṛtu* offerings), such as the Hotṛ and others, who will be mentioned hereafter. Here, the word *ṛtu* refers to the *ṛtugraha* cups. They are called *ṛtvij* because they sacrifice (*yajanti*) those [cups]. The meaning is that the officiating priests intended here are specifically those who perform the *ṛtugraha* offerings.

Since their status as belonging to the Soma sacrifice is established by context and the sense of the matter, this statement serves to establish the identity of one person with multiple roles: "He who is the Hotṛ is the Adhvaryu, he is the Potṛ; he who is the Udgātṛ is the Neṣṭṛ, he is the Acchāvāka; he who is the Maitrāvaruṇa is the Brahman, he is the Pratihartṛ; he who is the Prastotṛ is the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, he is the Prāvastut; he who is the Pratiprasthātṛ is the Agnīdh, he is the Unnetṛ; the Gṛhapati is the Gṛhapati, and the Subrahmaṇya is the Subrahmaṇya. This is according to the sūtra situated within the section on the Kuṇḍapāyināmayana sacrifice, which establishes the multiplicity of functions for a single individual.

To ward off the objection that—even though there are multiple sacrifices—only a single selection (*varaṇa*) is sufficient because the agent is one and the same, [the text specifies] "pertaining to the Soma rites" (*saumikān*). This is intended to indicate that, despite the identity of the individual agent, the selection is made for each individual *yajyā* (offering verse) by taking up the agency in relation to the Soma; thus, this selection belongs specifically to the Soma rites and not to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*). By this, it is also understood that even independent animal sacrifices are modifications (*vikāra*) of the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice]. [This is] because they are modifications of the Agniṣomīya.

Since only the Hotṛ, Agnīdh, Adhvaryu, Pratiprasthātṛ, Maitrāvaruṇa, and Neṣṭṛ are possible for the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka-karman*)—namely, the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma—their selection (*varaṇa*) would necessarily follow; therefore, the qualification "pertaining to the Soma sacrifice" (*saumika*) is meaningful only as a means to exclude them, and not otherwise. As for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Acchāvāka, they are simply impossible in the animal sacrifice; thus, there is no possibility of their selection at all.

And thus, it is established that even the extension (*atideśa*) of the *āgnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice] applies optionally to independent optional sacrifices (*kāmya*) whose deities have four-syllable names, as well as to similar *savanīya* offerings and the *anubandhyā* cow. Regarding the general proposition, "One should choose the Soma-offering priests with the *āśrāvaṇa*, the *ṛtu-praiṣa*, and so forth," when the expectation arises as to how this is done, [Satyāṣāḍha] states in his Śrautasūtra:
"With the formula 'Indra from the office of the Hotṛ, together with Heaven and Earth,' [he chooses] the Hotṛ."

The phrase "indraṃ hotrāt sardiva ā pṛthivyāḥ" means that he chooses this very Hotṛ priest for the Soma sacrifice; it refers to the beginning of the seasonal invocation (*ṛtu-praiṣa*). The reading with the instrumental ending, "indra hotrātmasajadina ā pṛthivyā," is indeed a corrupt reading. This is because the genitive construction is appropriate here—just as "divaḥ" is a genitive compound, so too "pṛthivyāḥ" must logically be a genitive—and because in the *ṛtu-praiṣa*, the genitive is heard in the passage: "indra hotrātmasajūr diva ā pṛthivyā ṛtena somaṃ pibatu hotaryaja."

Otherwise, there would be the consequence of contradiction with other reciters (*bhaṣāri*). Nor should it be argued: "In this *Indra-ho* formula, since there is no reading of the nasalized (*anunāsika*) vowel, how can that which possesses the nasal (*sānunāsika*) have the status of being a *ṣādi*? For the nasalized quality is generally a characteristic of the *Yajus* (sacrificial formulas), and it is precisely the *ṣādi* characterized by the *Yajus*-dharma that is to be accepted here. Indeed, there is no rule that even when following the *ṛtupraiṣa* (invocations to the priests) which lack the nasal, the *ṣādi* must likewise be devoid of it; for the dharma of the *Veda* (the *Yajurveda*) takes precedence.

For nasalization (*sānunāsikatva*) and non-nasalization (*niranunāsikatva*), being distinct properties, do not establish the absence of the *ṛtu* status or the subsequent state [of the *hotṛ*]. This is because, in the *mṛgāreṣṭi*, there would result the simultaneous application of both [nasal and non-nasal] to the deities such as Agni and Ahomuk. Thus, since the absence of *ṛtu* status exists in both cases, it is established that one must indeed perform the *praśya* (the act of looking/invoking). "Having cast away the grass with the wooden sword (*sphya*), he chooses the subsequent [priests]. The meaning is: having chosen the *hotṛ* by means of the *ṛtu-praiṣa* and so forth, and having cast away upon the altar itself the grass held together with the *sphya* while standing on the altar, he—having become one who is without the *sphya* joined with the *saṃnaina*—must necessarily choose the subsequent [priests] as they are about to be mentioned.
From the Āgnīdhra fire he [obtains] Agni; from the Āgnīdhra office, the Āgnīdhra priest—this is well known.
From the office of the two Adhvaryus, the two Aśvins [obtain] themselves as the Adhvaryus and the Pratiprasthātṛ.

Because the *adhvaryu* acts as the one who chooses himself, there is the reference "himself" (*ātmānam*). Here, the word "and" (*ca*) serves to indicate mutual conjunction, since no other [option] is possible.

[He chooses] Mitrāvaruṇa as the *praśāstṛ* from the *praśāstṛ*-office; Indra as the *brahmán* from the *brāhmaṇá*-office, i.e., the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*; the Maruts as the *potṛ* from the *potṛ*-office; and the *gnās* (goddesses) as the *neṣṭṛ* from the *neṣṭṛ*-office. This is clear.

"Agni is the leader of the divine clans; this sacrificer, pressing the soma, is [the leader] of human beings. For these two, the household-fire has shone forth as their inseparable bond. Go ye both! Let not Vāyu seize your offerings. May you two, blending yet not blending, unite with your bodies"—with these words [he addresses] the sacrificer.

This procedure applies to the Prāṇa [offering], and it is indeed unprecedented. Although the Soma-related [procedures] have been stated without distinction, only those intended for the purpose of the seasonal sacrifices (cāturmāsya) are to be adopted. This is because the selection (varaṇa) is made only of eight [priests] and because of its connection with that [specific context]. Thus, this selection is for the purpose of the seasonal sacrifices; therefore, there is an exclusion of this selection in the animal sacrifice (pāśuka).

Regarding this, some say that the word *sunvat* applies only to the selection (*varaṇa*) at the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*), whereas on the day of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, there is simply an elision of the word *sunvat*. Their reasoning is based on the indication of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) in the form *sunvan*, which denotes a present meaning. Others, however, maintain that after the carrying forward of the fires and Soma (*agnīṣomapraṇayana*), the word *sunvat* comes into use; and since the present tense can be applied to what is proximate to the present according to the rule "the present may be used for what is near," they hold that by taking up this sense of the present, there is no elision. This is precisely the intended meaning of the author of the Sūtra.

The meaning is that each person who has been chosen (*pravṛta*) offers two oblations immediately after his own selection, using these two mantras: "May I be beloved of speech" (*juṣṭo vācaḥ bhūyāsam*) and "With the Ṛg-verse, may I be beloved of the hymn" (*ṛcā stomaṃ juṣṭo bhūyāsam*). According to the general rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "where one enjoins a rite by means of a group of mantras, one should not offer for each individual mantra," there are two oblations. Since the first [mantra] already contains the *svāhā* exclamation, the offering is made with that very *svāhā*; no other *svāhā* should be employed at the end of the second mantra.

Thus, the offering concludes with the utterance of *svāhā*. In the second [offering], there is indeed the utterance of *svāhā* at the end. Since the *svāhā*-utterance does not occur at the beginning, these oblations are performed according to the rule for offerings accompanied by *davihī*. Although the general rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "oblations are offered into the Āhavanīya fire with the *juhū* ladle" would apply to this offering, because the *juhū* is already occupied and because this offering belongs to the Soma ritual, the offering is made with the *pracaraṇī* ladle, as it is connected to the Soma. The offering related to the animal sacrifice is made with the *vasāhomahavaṇī* (the vessel for the fat-oblation).

By the repetition "pravṛtaḥ pravṛtaḥ" (at each selection), these two oblations are to be offered by all those belonging to the four *yānas* immediately after their respective selections (*pravara*). Even the *hotṛ* and others must offer them according to the ritual rules of the *Yajurveda*. Because these two oblations are caused by the act of selection (*pravaraṇa*), Āśvalāyana has given them the technical name "selection-oblations" (*pravṛtāhuti*) in the rule: "He offers the selection-oblations, [saying] 'O you who make the *ṣaṣaṭ* call. The author of the *Sūtra* also indicates this naming by the rule: "At each selection, he offers. Having offered, the *adhvaryu* chooses the subsequent [priests].

Immediately after having performed the *adhvaryu*-duties, he chooses the subsequent [priests]. The intention is that he should not wait for the *pravṛtāhuti* offerings of the *pratiprasthātṛ*. He chooses the subsequent ones, beginning with the *maitrāvaruṇa*. Some authorities prescribe the *pravara* formulas at the *savanīya* sacrifice.

The meaning is that some teachers state that although the performance of the *pravara* (invocation of ancestors) is prescribed for the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, it should not be performed there, but rather only at the *savanīya* animal sacrifice. There is no *pravara* for the *acchāvāka* because there is no scriptural injunction [to that effect]. Therefore, the two *pravṛtāhuti* offerings are also not made for him. Regarding the *pravṛtāhuti* offerings, Āśvalāyana states: "The others, excluding the *acchāvāka*, are the *vaṣaṭ*-makers. Since the *acchāvāka* is himself a *vaṣaṭ*-maker, he would otherwise be subject to the rule for the *pravṛtāhuti* oblation; thus, the exclusion "the others, excluding the *acchāvāka*" is made.

The author of the Sūtra will indeed state that the Adhvaryu, the Pratiprasthātṛ, and the sacrificer (yajamāna) are also directly the *vaṣaṭ*-utterers (*vaṣaṭkartṛ*) in one view, by means of the sūtra: "Or he himself, having sat down, performs the sacrifice. The *pravaras* are those who invite (*pravriyante*) the performers of the seasonal offerings (*ṛtuyājins*) for the purpose of the seasonal offerings; even though the seasonal offerings take place at the *sutyā*, the selection (*varaṇa*) occurs at the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice because of a specific scriptural injunction.

Āpastamba states the specific rule for the selection (*pravaraṇa*) of the *hotṛ* and others: "In all cases, the utterance of the name is in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), while the words 'this one is human' (*mānuṣaḥ*) are spoken aloud (*uccaiḥ*). The meaning of Āpastamba’s Sūtra is that in all selections, having first uttered the person's name in the nominative case in a low voice, he says aloud, "This one is human. In the selection of the *adhvaryu*, the formula is: "I and so-and-so Śarman are the two humans."

Some, however, claim that one should mention even one's own name—as the Adhvaryu priest does—saying, "The two humans, so-and-so Śarman and so-and-so Śarman"; but this is trivial. For the Smṛti prohibits the mention of one's own name: "One who desires his own welfare should not utter his own name, the name of his teacher, the name of one who is extremely wretched, nor the names of his eldest child or wife. Furthermore, it is improper to mention a name without an explicit statement to that effect. For this very reason, the author of the Sūtra used the indirect reference "one's own self" (ātmānam). Therefore, the reference should be made using the word "I" (aham) alone.

In the selection of the sacrificer (*yajamānapravaraṇa*), because the designation is accomplished by these very words, "this [is] the pressing sacrificer," there is no mention of the sacrificer's personal name. When the omentum (*vapā*) has been offered, he issues the command: "O Subrahmaṇya, summon the Subrahmaṇyā! The Subrahmaṇyā becomes that which pertains to father and son (*pitāputrīyā*).

"When the omentum of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma has been offered" means when the omentum of the *paśu* for Agni-Soma has been offered. The singular number is not intended to be restrictive; therefore, even when there are animals for Indra-Agni and the Aśvins, the *subrahmaṇyā* invocation occurs immediately after the omenta of those two as well, and not after the offering of the omentum of the Agni-Soma animal alone. Following that, the omentum-offering (*vapā-yāga*) for the animals of Indra-Agni and the Aśvins takes place. "When it has been offered into the fire" means when it has been cast into the fire with the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance.

By the phrase "when the omentum has been offered," the ritual action beginning with "taking up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles" is indicated, which occurs when it is said, "O Adhvaryu, place the butter-smeared ladle."

Although it might be argued that since the giving of the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa is prescribed specifically for the *nirūḍhapaśu* sacrifice immediately after the *pravaraṇā*, that same rule should apply here as well, nevertheless—based on the statement "he gives the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa once the Soma has been purchased"—the Soma must already have been purchased before the gift is made. Since the sacrificer has already given it [to the priest] at that point, it is impossible to give it again. Therefore, there is no act of giving here; rather, after the purchase of the Soma, the staff is to be accepted from the sacrificer by the Maitrāvaruṇa using the mantra: "May I become one whose hooves are unshod, not shod."

Since the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) is a constituent part of both the preceding and the subsequent rites, both of them are included. Thus Āpastamba says: "When the omentum has been offered, having performed the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*). Because it occurs in the middle [of the sequence], the subsequent offering of the omentum should also be understood as being included in this sūtra. However, there is no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśukī*), because of the prohibition: "In all Soma-related sacrifices, iṣṭis, and animal sacrifices, one does not give the *anvāhārya*."

Since it has already been explained that the mention of the *anvāhārya* rice serves as an indicator for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), and since the intention there was also explained that the purchase [of the officiants] is accomplished by the fee of the principal rite alone; furthermore, because of the natural sense of the *Yajamāna-sūtra* of the animal sacrifice—which states, "When the omentum (*vapā*) has been offered, he gives a boon, or he should lead three cows as the fee"—the giving of the fee certainly takes place.

If it is asked how this is so, it is explained as follows: According to the sūtra, "When the omentum has been offered, he gives a boon," the giving of the boon occurs prior to the sprinkling (mārjana), and the sprinkling follows thereafter; this should be understood to apply here exactly as it was established for the animal sacrifice (paśu). In the phrase "three [cows]," the cows are the subject, and because there are two verbal actions, the giving of the boon is distinct. The giving of the boon prescribed by the rule "he gives a boon" belongs to the *sarvatis* alone. Likewise, the gift of three cows also belongs to them alone.

In the phrase "or three," the word *vara* (boon) is carried over from the preceding portion "he gives a boon. Its meaning is that he should give either a boon or three cows. [Note: The variants *kha* and *ga* read *riprahasī*; *sa* and *ga* read *na ti*. This is the end of the section (*a0paṭalaḥ*). The rules for the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) pertaining to the *iṣṭi* do not apply to the giving of the boon; rather, the gift is made simply by saying, "I give you a boon. The rules for the giving of sacrificial fees pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*) apply here, because the word *dakṣiṇā* occurs later in that context.

If the single purpose of this sūtra were that "if one gives a boon, one should lead away three sacrificial gifts," then it would have stated simply: "when the omentum has been offered, one should give a boon or lead away three sacrificial gifts. But it has not been stated in that way. Therefore, it must be said that "he gives a boon" is distinct from "or three [gifts]. And thus, the first giving of the boon does not constitute the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā) pertaining to the animal sacrifice; consequently, there is no prohibition against it.

It should be understood that the injunction regarding the granting of a boon (*varadāna*) in the *Paścaikādaśinī-sūtra* is consistent only with this method and not otherwise. Alternatively, the word *vā* here has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Regarding the animals used in the Soma sacrifice, there is a specific scriptural statement: "They carry the fire forward; they lead the wife away; they move the sacrificial utensils after them. Now, this *dhiṣṇiya* hearth of his is left behind; it broods, and being liable to become Rudra, it is capable of destroying the offspring and cattle of the sacrificer."

When they lead the consecrated animal northward, then one should take the fire for cooking the animal from that [Ahavaniya fire]; by doing so, he makes it a sharer. The Ahavaniya is indeed the sacrificer; when they take the fire for cooking the animal from the Ahavaniya, they are pulling away from the sacrificer. Therefore, that [fire] itself should remain, or one should produce a secondary fire (anvāhāryapacana) for the sake of the sacrificer’s own integrity. The purpose of taking the fire for cooking the animal from the Prājahita fire is the accomplishment of its status as a sharer; this cannot be achieved without establishing its non-sharer status [in the other case].

Therefore, in order to demonstrate this, there is a scriptural passage beginning with "the fire facing east" and ending with "having calmed it. The meaning of this scripture is as follows: first, the fire situated in the *gārhapatya* located in the western direction is led for the first time to the *sālāmukhīya*, which was formerly the *āhavanīya*; immediately thereafter, it is led from that place as well toward the east. This is what is expressed by the phrase, "they carry the fire facing east."

They also lead the wife, who is situated in the *patnīśālā* located in the western direction, toward the *śālāmukhīya* fire, which is the former *āhavanīya*. The carts situated near the western *gārhapatya* are also moved forward in succession by a span (*prādeśa*). As soon as all this is accomplished, the specific location (*viṣṇiya*) of that former *gārhapatya* is vacated and becomes empty.

And that fire, moreover, thinks in its mind, "I shall bring about the ruin of the sacrificer. While so thinking, that Rudra becomes cruel and becomes capable of pacifying—that is, destroying—the offspring and cattle of the sacrificer. By means of the scriptural passage beginning with "when the animal has been gratified" and ending with "for the sake of attaining his own nature," the justification for [the animal's] participation in the rite is established.

When, at that time, they lead the animal—which has been gratified and satisfied by the *prayāja* offering-verses known as the *āprīs*—toward the north, facing northward, then at that moment one should carry fire from the *gārhapatya* hearth situated toward the west to the place where the animal is to be cooked. By that very act of carrying, one makes this [fire] possessed of a share in the flames of the western *gārhapatya*. From that, it should be understood, there is no destruction of offspring.

One might ask: "Why not simply carry the fire for cooking the sacrificial animal (paśuśrapaṇa) from the Āhavanīya itself? Anticipating this objection, the scripture shows the fault in that practice through the passage beginning with, "The sacrificer is indeed the Āhavanīya. If one were to drag the fire away from the Āhavanīya, this would constitute a dragging away (*vikarṣa*) of the sacrificer himself; for the Āhavanīya, being the primary fire, is of the very nature of the sacrificer. Therefore, either that same [Gārhapatya] fire, or the *prājahita* fire, should be used for the purpose of cooking; or else, having produced some fire by churning or by common means, one should perform the cooking with that.

This being the case, the sacrificer becomes free from distress and established in his complete essential nature. Therefore, in the statement "he should take away his animal-cooking fire," the word "his" (tasya) refers to that very same person who was referred to by the preceding word "he" (saḥ). This is also to be understood by reflecting upon the scriptural injunctions such as "they carry forward the eastern fire. Thus ends the section composed by Satyāṣāḍha in the Śrautasūtra, [Book 7].

And likewise Baudhāyana says: "He should indeed be [the fire]"; thus they prescribe the ancient Gārhapatya. This rule applies to the Savanīya animal sacrifice as well, because it is equally a subsidiary part of the ritual, being similar to the Dīkṣā-animal sacrifice. In the Nirūḍhapaśu sacrifice, however, because of the specific mention of the word *svāhā*, the offering must be brought from the Āhavanīya fire alone.

Regarding this, Vādhūla says: "The procedure from the pouring of the oblation up to the *āprī*-verses is the same; it is stated that 'they lead the consecrated animal northward. Once the *pāyasya* has been offered, having performed the ritual purification (*mārjana*), he issues the command: 'O Subrahmaṇya, call the Subrahmaṇyā litany for the Father-and-Son [sacrifice]'. It is also stated in the Āpastamba-Prāyaścitta-sūtra: "'When they lead the consecrated animal northward'—thus it is said. The meaning is that the passage beginning with "As for the animal" and ending with "those who would tear the animal apart," which is taught in the Brāhmaṇa, is to be followed in this sūtra.

The circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*), however, is performed with the fire-brand (*ulmuka*) from the northern altar alone. Herein is the specific detail: after the circumambulation, the Āgnīdhra enters the *prāgvaṃśa* shed by the eastern door along the edge of the northern altar; taking fire from the old Gārhapatya, he carries it out through the eastern door, leads it north of the Āgnīdhra hearth to the vicinity of the animal, and places it before the animal. When the animal has gone toward the place of immolation (*śāmitradeśa*), he deposits it to the north of the animal there.

Having brought a portion [of the fire] toward the Āhavanīya along with the omentum (*vapā*), one should cast it back into the old Gārhapatya by that same path. Some, however, proceed along the southern edge of the altar, enter the shed through the southern door, take the fire from the old Gārhapatya, turn to the right, exit through the southern door, lead it south of the Mārjālīya fire between the Brahman and the sacrificer, pass between the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the Āhavanīya, carry it near the animal, and then carry it in front of the animal.

When the animal has gone toward the region of the *sāmitra*, they place [the portions] there to the north of the animal. Having brought back a portion together with the omentum (*vapā*) toward the fire, they say that one should throw it into the old *gārhapatya* by that very same path. That is incorrect, because it contradicts the rule of circumambulation (*prādakṣiṇya*) and because it contradicts the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) that "the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) is approached from the north."

Having released the animal from the side of the churning [fire], prior to the verse "paśum" (the animal), he silently churns near the *āhavanīya* fire; having kindled it and placed it in some vessel, he strikes it in front of the animal and sets it down to the north of the animal in the *śāmitra* location. Having brought a portion of that along with the omentum (*vapā*) in front, he should discard it in a pure place outside the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*). For this churning, two ordinary pieces of wood from the forest are used.

In the term *pitāputrīyā*, the word *pitṛ* includes mothers as well through the grammatical device of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member of a class), such that "fathers and mothers" are understood. Furthermore, within that, both the group of paternal ancestors and the group of maternal ancestors are to be understood by the words *pitṛ* and *mātṛ* respectively. By the word *putra*, daughters are also included through *ekaśeṣa*, where "sons and daughters" are understood as simply "sons. This [term] is also an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for grandsons and great-grandsons. That [lineage] in which fathers and sons are celebrated is...

The meaning is that the *subrahmaṇyā* formula becomes like that of a father and son. "Loosen [the girdle], O sacrificer; loosen the fist," thus they address him by name, saying: "May the *subrahmaṇya* invoke the *subrahmaṇyā* for you together with your fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, sons, and grandsons. All of this has been clearly stated by Baudhāyana in the form of a formal injunction (*praiṣa*). "Loosen" means make it slack.

For the full understanding of the Subrahmaṇya, after the *praiṣa* (directive), one must simply say, "The Pitāputrīyā [Subrahmaṇyā]. However, according to Āpastamba and Bādhūla, the directive itself is: "O Subrahmaṇya, call the Pitāputrīyā Subrahmaṇyā. It is recited in that manner. The procedure for calling the Pitāputrīyā Subrahmaṇyā is to be seen in the sūtras of Lāṭyāyana and Drāhyāyaṇa. The purpose of mentioning the name is to be seen in the Nidāna-sūtra.

In the *Nidānasūtra* it is also stated that one should not utter the names of women, such as one's mother and others. According to this view, in the compound *pitāputrīyā* ("mother and daughter"), there is no application of the *ekaśeṣa* rule [to form a dual). One should not utter the names of those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*) or unchaste women (*pravaṇitā*). [End of Maṇḍala 1] Accompanied by the commentary *Bhaktajyotsnā* by Gopīnātha.
In the afternoon, he takes up the *vasatīvarī* waters from flowing streams.

The third part of the day when it has been divided into three, or the fourth part when divided into five, is here called "afternoon" (aparāhṇa); in that time, one takes the *vasatīvarī* waters—waters known by the name *vasatīvarī*. Regarding this, he states a specific qualification: "of flowing [waters] (*vahantīnām*). By this, stagnant waters and the like are excluded. There is also a prohibition in the Śruti: "One should not take from stagnant waters. However, if flowing waters are not available in any way, even stagnant waters may be taken.

Because Baudhāyana demonstrates a specific rule—that one does not take [water] from stagnant sources by standing against the current—it is permitted to take even from stagnant sources when flowing water is unavailable. The purpose of these [waters] is to serve as an additive for the Soma. And the author of the Sūtra will state: "having added the *vasatīvarī* waters. In the phrase "having added the *vasatīvarī* waters," the qualification "*vasatīvarī*" is used for the sake of identifying these specific waters.

Regarding the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of *vasatīvarī* in the Śruti: "The gods, indeed, divided the sacrifice among themselves at the Āgnīdhra shed. What remained over, they said, 'Let this dwell (*vasatu*) with us now. That is the reason for the name *vasatīvarī*.

Once upon a time, the gods, staying in the Āgnīdhra shed, divided the sacrificial implements—the vessels and other articles used in the sacrifice—saying, "This is mine. Then, regarding what remained after everyone had taken their respective portions, they said to one another: "Let this remnant remain common to us all for now; we shall make our division in the morning."

Because it was said by the gods, "Dwell here" (*vasasva*), therefore, through that connection, the name *vasatīvarī* was established; thus, the waters containing those [qualities] are called *vasatīvaryah*. From the sacrifice, whatever watery substance remained after being distributed, that very substance was requested by the gods, saying, "This watery substance is for our sake"—the word *nu* being used for emphasis, meaning "exclusively for our sake. Because they were requested [with the thought], "May it dwell right here near the *Śālāmukhīya* fire immediately after the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) to Agni and Soma," the waters possess the quality of being *vasatīvarī*. He takes such waters.

Such is the meaning. In the phrase *vahantīnām*, the genitive case functions as an ablative (*pañcamyarthe*) or as a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). Regarding this, Āpastamba states a specific rule: "When [the Vasatīvarī water] has been called for, he takes it from the flowing waters that have struck against a mountain, using a jar. Both *girimitāḥ* and *vahantīnām* are qualifying attributes. The meaning is: he takes [the water] from those rivers which, having burst through a mountain, flow forth. He should not pass over the nearest flowing waters.

One should not cross over, nor step beyond, the nearest flowing waters. This means that one should abandon even the nearest flowing waters if they are devoid of qualities, and should not accept waters that are distant, even if they are distinguished by their qualities. Those dwelling on the shore of the ocean should not drink the ocean's waters because of their saltiness. There is also a prohibition in the Śruti: "Therefore, they do not drink from the ocean; for they regard it as [the source of] procreation. [This applies also to] the shadow of a whirlwind.

In this context, "shadow" (*chāyā*) is that which is not produced by human effort; it is created by clouds. "Heat" (*ātapa*) means warmth. The meaning is that one takes [the water] at the junction of the cloud-shadow and the heat. The Śruti also says: "One takes it at the junction of the shadow and the heat. In the word *chāyāyaiḥ*, the dative case is used in the sense of the genitive. In the word *ātapatani* (or *ātapat*), the form ending in *ni* (or *ta*) is a term denoting heat; *ātapat* is the singular genitive of that word.
Since the junction depends upon the objects of both terms, even in the absence of the word *ca* ("and"), the conjunction is established by implication.
Having created the shadow of a riverbank, a tree, or of oneself.

In the absence of the shadow of a cloud, one should take it at the junction of the shadow and the sunlight of any sacrificial object—such as the bank of a river, grass, a shrub, or a tree—or, in the absence of any other means, by casting the shadow of one's own body under a forest canopy or some such thing. The meaning is that one takes it at the junction of such a shadow and the sunlight. This is because the phrase "at the junction of the sunlight and the shadow" from the Sūtra continues to apply here. The portion "at the junction of the sunlight... is understood to carry over.

Āpastamba has also stated all of this: "If one does not find the shadow of a cloud, [one should perform it] in the shadow of oneself, a tree, or a riverbank. He describes the method of drawing [the water]:
"Standing against the current, he fills the jar or the pot with the words, 'O waters, you are full of oblation.'"

*Apām pratīpam*. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound. Due to its status as an *avyayībhāva*, it is neuter. The meaning is "facing the water. Here, "facing the water" means facing the current. The word *pratīpam* is to be construed with *tiṣṭhan* (standing) itself. The fact that the jar (*kumbha*) or the pitcher (*kumbhī*) faces the water is understood from the prefix *abhi* alone. The sense is that the jar or the pitcher, standing facing the water, fills [itself] by being held facing the water.

In the word *pratīpam*, the vowel *ā* of the word *āpaḥ*—which has received the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) by the rule *chadir-upasargebhyaḥ apa īt*—is replaced by the long vowel *ī*. According to the Baudhāyana Sūtra, there is a jar (*kumbhaḥ*) without breasts and a jar (*kumbhī*) with breasts; in that case, the jar has either two or four breasts. That the jar or the pot (*kumbhī*) possesses firmness is established by its very suitability for the purpose. Baudhāyana states this quite clearly: "Now, he asks for that jar which is solid" (*vīḍita*). Regarding the meaning of the word *vīḍita*, it is stated in the Karmānta section: "By this, it is simply said to be 'firm' (*dṛḍha*)."
If the sun should set while the *vasatīvarī* waters have not yet been drawn, one should take water from the jars belonging to a Brāhmaṇa who performs many sacrifices (*bahuyājī*).

By the word "if" (*yadi*), it is indicated that this is an occasional (*naimittika*) rite. If, while the *vasatīvarīs* remain undrawn, the sun sets—that is, goes down—then one should take those waters which are in the jars (*kumbhya*) belonging to a Brāhmaṇa who performs many sacrifices; "belonging to the jars" (*kumbhyāḥ*) means those waters existing within the jars. Here, "existence" (*bhavana*) refers to presence. By the term "performer of many sacrifices," the Soma-sacrificer is meant, for he is the one who has already drawn the *vasatīvarīs*, as is indicated by the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) [of the text].

From the Āpastamba Sūtra, "It is known that one who performs the Soma sacrifice becomes a *bahuyājī* (one who sacrifices much)," and from the Bhāradvāja Sūtra, "The Brāhmaṇa who is a *bahuyājī* refers to a performer of the Soma sacrifice," it follows that [the term] does not mean one who performs many sacrifices [for others], because that is prohibited. In the phrase "from the house" (*gṛhāt*), the ablative case has the sense of the locative. By the word "house" (*gṛhe*), such an interpretation as "having brought [the water] from there, going near the flowing rivers, and drawing [it] there" is excluded. In the expression "of the *kumbhyās*" (*kumbhyānām*), the genitive case is used for the ablative.
If they should not find that fire, they should take gold and go to where there is water; holding the light above and placing the gold in between, he takes it when the bride-price has been given.

Regarding that person who performs many sacrifices: by the word "yadi" (if), it is shown that the rule beginning with "having taken fire and gold" and ending with "he takes [the water] when it is placed in his hand" is conditional. "Na vindeyuḥ" means they would not find or obtain [it]. Just as at the time of taking the Vasatīvarī waters, if the sun sets while the fire is being kindled, then the taking of the waters in the jars must be performed specifically at the house of one who performs many sacrifices; this is according to [the section on] the Bahuyājin (Ma. Paṭalaḥ) accompanied by the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

The exclusion of flowing waters has been made; even in this alternative view—that "if one should not find that [flowing water]"—the general indication "wherever there may be water" was made precisely to suggest this. Alternatively, it is to suggest that one should go and take the water wherever water is present, whether flowing or non-flowing, and that one need not travel a great distance for the sake of flowing water alone.

At the time of taking up the *basatīvarī* waters, when the sun has set, one should abandon the flowing waters (*vahantī*) and take them from a well located within the precincts of many vehicles; by the force of this rule for taking them, it is understood that even though the purpose is not directly perceived, they must be taken while remaining close at hand because of the possibility of danger at night. By this, it is also understood that one who has gone halfway on the road for the purpose of taking the flowing waters should remain there.

Due to some obstacle, a delay occurred such that he was unable to perform the ritual before sunset; in that case, having quickly returned to the village and stayed there for the time required to complete the *agnihotra* sacrifice along with its ancillaries, he should take the fire and gold and proceed toward a place where water is available—whether flowing or stagnant—and having made the offering of the fire and gold at that spot, he should turn back and depart from there.

If, however, he should go away while actually taking hold of the fire and the gold, then he must turn back from that very place and proceed toward the spot where water is found. It is with this intention that the author of the Sūtra employs the prefix *parā* in the word *pareyāt*, as it signifies "turning back. Regarding the phrase *taj jyotir upariṣṭād dhārayan*: the word *tat* means *sat* (being); by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the locative case-ending.

By the mention of the word "light" (*jyotis*), he indicates a certain specific detail here: that the light should be made such that it can be seen clearly and without obstruction. Thus, this is understood: having kindled a torch in the ordinary fire brought there, one should perform the grasping of the *vatsa* while staying in its light. "Holding it above" means holding it above the water-pot (*kumbha*) or the small jar (*kumyī*).

The meaning is: "in such a way that it is favorable for the drawing of the *vasatīvarī* waters. Āpastamba states: "One should draw [the water] while holding a firebrand above. By the use of the present participle (*dhārayan*), simultaneity with the main action is indicated; from the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) alone, the identity of the agent is understood. "Having placed gold" means having interposed or deposited it in the *kumbha* or the *kumbhī*. Or rather, "having deposited gold"—this is precisely what Āpastamba says.

In the Śruti as well, an option is stated: "One should take [the cup] either with light (jyotis) or having placed gold (hiraṇya) [within]; thus one takes it together with the bright (saśukra). Here, *śukra* means brilliance (*tejas*). However, according to the Sūtrakāra’s view, there is indeed a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of both light and gold; the intention is that the word *vā* signifies conjunction. In this regard, the Śruti from another recensional branch (*śākhāntara*) should be cited. When the *vara* has been given—that is, when the *vara* has been bestowed upon himself by the sacrificer—the Adhvaryu goes forth; such is the meaning. This concludes the occasional (*naimittika*) rite. With the formula, "I set thee down in the seat of Agni Apannagṛha," he sets it down to the west of the Śālāmukhīya fire.

The meaning is clear. The mantra ends with the word *dhatte*. This concludes the procedure for taking the *vasatīvarī* waters. Regarding that, since the second part of the day is divided into three parts, if there is ample time remaining after the offering of the omentum (*vapā*), then there are two methods. In that regard, one method is as follows: having commenced the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the animal cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) after the omentum offering, when the third part of the day arrives, one should stop from the point where the previous action ended, take the *vasatīvarī* waters, and then resume the ritual from the point where it was left off. This is the first method.

Another [teacher] maintains that after the offering of the omentum (*vapā*), one should pause for the purpose of awaiting the third watch; when that has arrived, having first taken the *vasatīvarī* waters, one begins the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the animal cake-offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*). However, if the third watch has already passed due to delay during the very offering of the omentum, then after the offering of the omentum, one should first take the *vasatīvarī* waters and then [proceed with] the ritual procedure for the animal cake-offering.

756. The commencement of the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha should be undertaken as follows. Āpastamba has clearly stated that the commencement of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) occurs only after the drawing of the *vasatīvarī* waters. This should be understood to apply even in the case of the fivefold division. The pouring out (*nirvāpa*) of the oblation intended for the animal-cake offering and other rites must take place within the original shed (*śālā*) itself; it is not to be performed there incidentally once the two carts known as the *havirdhāna* have been set in motion.

Regarding the statement, "He pours out [the grain] to the west of the *gārhapatya* fire," this is because the original location—namely, the two *havirdhāna* carts—is not established here. Furthermore, the injunction "He pours out from upon the cart" remains valid even when another cart is brought in. Nor should it be argued that, since the two *havirdhāna* carts (which are accompanied by mantras) are stationed on the great altar (*mahāvedi*), they must be led to the wife's hall (*patnīśālā*). This is because, in the absence of any obstacle to bringing in another cart, the ritual can be accomplished by that very means; thus, it should be understood that leading the carts already stationed on the great altar is improper.

And likewise, Jaimini states in the first pāda of the twelfth adhyāya through three sūtras: "The two [cart-poles] should serve for the purpose of pouring the oblation because they have already been employed; or rather, there is no accomplishment [of the purpose] because the location is different. There would be a contingency of deficiency due to the deficiency of the primary [act], and because of the observation of carts. Thus he says.

Those two carts upon which the oblation (*havis*)—consisting of *soma* juice—is placed or established are the *havirdhāna*s; they alone should accomplish and fulfill the task consisting of the pouring out (*nirvapaṇa*) for the sake of that pouring out, because they have already been employed for the purpose of the *soma* ritual, and there is no reason to abandon what has already been employed.

Nor should it be argued that because the act of pouring out (*nirvapaṇa*) is performed "upon the cart" (*adhi*), as stated in the scripture, the cart is the material cause (*upādāna*); whereas in the case of pouring out from the two *havirdhāna* carts, since they are not the material cause, the act of pouring out would result in being defective (*viguṇa*). This is because even the two *havirdhāna* carts possess the nature of a cart (*anatva*), and thus, by virtue of having the form of a cart, they serve as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*). Furthermore, since the pouring out is accomplished by means of the two *havirdhāna* carts—which themselves have the nature of a cart—there is no absence of the cart being the material cause, and consequently, there is no occurrence of defectiveness.

The sense is that since it is improper to perform a subsidiary act (*aṅga*) again for the sake of its specific quality when it has already been applied, there is no fault here—just as there is a reduction in measurement in the case of the *vedi*—in the loss of the characteristic of being "to the side of the Gārhapatya fire. This is the meaning of the first Sūtra. Because of the difference in location—that is, because of the difference in place—the performance of the act of pouring out (*nirvapaṇa*) is accomplished.

For in the Havirdhāna shed, the location for the offering (nirvāpa) is obtained by its original form (*prakṛti*); however, because it is impossible for the offering and the Havirdhāna shed to occupy the same space behind the Gārhapatya fire, the original function of the offering is not rendered ineffective by the two Havirdhāna carts. Furthermore, the injunction "he offers from the cart" (*anasaḥ*) is fulfilled even when the cart is brought into proximity. Nor should it be argued that the two Havirdhāna carts, which are stationed on the Mahāvedi with the *mantras*, should instead be led to the Patnīśālā.

Since there is no obstacle to taking up [the mantra] from within the recitation itself, the matter is resolved by that alone; therefore, it is improper to establish the *yoninaya* (the placement of the womb) as in the case of the *manava*. If one were to accept this [latter view], then the turning forward of the *havirdhāna* cart performed previously with the mantra "O Soma, come forward to the sacrifice" (*prācī prehi adhvaram*) and the subsequent placing of it performed here with the mantra "Rejoice here" (*ramethām*) would both become purposeless. Furthermore, if one were to perform the turning and placing again, such repetition would be unscriptural, and thus the *soma*, which is the primary element, would in every respect be rendered defective.

From that deficiency, there would follow the contingency of non-deficiency; for nowhere is non-deficiency ever seen to result from a deficiency in the primary element. Therefore, the leading forward (*nayana*) is not at all logical. In the phrase "the contingency of deficiency" (*vaiguṇyaprasaṅga*), the word *prasaṅga* denotes an undesirable consequence (*āpatti*).
When [the sun] has set, one proceeds with the animal ritual (*paśutantra*) beginning with the *saṃvāda* [formula].

The meaning is: "when the sun has gone to its setting, i.e., when it is no longer visible. By this, the time prior to that is excluded. [The ritual] does not take place at all starting from the conversation prior to sunset, but only after it. Therefore, after the Paśupuroḍāśa sacrifice, one must simply cease for the remainder of the day. Even if [the time] has lapsed due to a delay in the Paśupuroḍāśa sacrifice after sunset, there is no fault; thus it is established. [End of] Paṭala 750, with the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

The dialogue beginning with "O Śamitr, the oblations are cooked" is the point from which the animal ritual (*paśutantra*)—the entire collection of rites related to the animal sacrifice—is commenced; that is to say, starting from this dialogue, the animal ritual begins. Having taken five portions into the *juhū* ladle and having taken the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) and the *upabhṛt* ladle, [he proceeds]; this is connected specifically to the dialogue, because its connection to that is indicated in the *Paśusūtra* and because the taking of those items is for use later on.
He carries the collected portions (*samavatta*) either to the south or to the north of the *havirdhāna* cart.

Of that animal victim, the collection of portions for the *paśu-īḍā* is designated by the term *samavatta*. And it should be understood from the usage of the Sūtra-author that this *samavatta* is placed in the *paśu-īḍā* vessel.
The sacrificer does not consume the portions; some, however, record that he does consume them.

"They are eaten" (*bhakṣyante*) refers to the "eatings" (*bhakṣāḥ*). By the word *makṣa*, the portions such as the *iḍā* and the heart that have been cut off are denoted; "of the eatings" (*bhakṣāṇām*) is the ellipsis. The sense is that there is a scriptural statement for both cases: "therefore it should not be eaten" and "therefore it should be eaten. Thus, the eating of the *iḍā* and so forth is established by extension (*prasaṅga*) from the Soma sacrifice, because we see the observation, "Having eaten the *ājya-iḍā*, they cease," and because of the sūtra, "Some recite [the rule] regarding eating. Consequently, the eating of the *iḍā* must indeed be performed by the Adhvaryu and others.

Jaimini also says the very same thing in the first section (pāda) of the twelfth chapter: "If it be argued that the eating of the remnants is likewise [for the purpose of disposal], we say no, because it serves another purpose. The eating of the remnants is for the purpose of the ritual disposal (*pratipatti*) of the remains, not for the purpose of satiation (*ānati*). Therefore, their requirement is not satisfied by the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of the primary sacrifice alone; this is what is established by the sūtra: "If it be argued that the eating of the remnants is likewise... [The ritual concludes] with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings; the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice is completed.

That which has its conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings is called *patnīsaṃyājānta*. Although the completion of the ritual action (*karmasaṃsthā*) is already established by the statement "it ends with the *patnīsaṃyājas*," the repeated mention of "it concludes" (*saṃtiṣṭhate*) is for the purpose of indicating that the rite should be brought to a close even by means of the concluding acts (*pratipattikarma*). Therefore, the concluding acts are indeed to be performed with their respective mantras; however, the final disposal of the Veda (*vedapratipatti*) does not take place here.

Since it has been stated that the holding [of the Soma] lasts until the completion of the *sutyā*, and since the Agniṣomīya [animal sacrifice] is already obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself, this repetition is intended to demonstrate that the disposal rites (*pratipattikarma*) are mandatory specifically for the Agniṣomīya, but not for those on the days of the *sutyā* connected with the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), such as at the end of the *patnīsaṃyāja*. When the Yajurvedic *hautra* (officiant's duties) is present, the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākyā*) for the omentum (*vapā*) are: "O Agniṣoma, whoever today... and "O Agniṣoma, whoever shall worship you with the oblation..."

"O Agni and Soma, he who offers the oblation... and "O Agni and Soma, you perceive that power of yours... are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* for the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*). "O Agni and Soma, this [oblation] is well-prepared... and "O Agni and Soma, enjoy the presented oblation... are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* for the limbs (*aṅga*). For the Aindrāgna animal sacrifice, however, "The pure, newly-born hymn today... and "He slays Vṛtra and wins booty... are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* for the omentum (*vapā*). "Both of you, O Indra and Agni, for the sake of the people... is for the animal-cake. Āvṛ...

"O singer, like a prayer," etc., are for the limbs. Now, for the animal sacrifice to the Aśvins—the invitatory and offering verses for the omentum are: "The chariot has come hither; it has spread across the two worlds and over the five regions. For the cake-offering to the animal, the verses are: "With your own horses and glory, you have encompassed splendor," and "He who is your charioteer, O lords of the chariot, [who rescued] Bhujyu when he was cast down. For the limbs, the verses are: "Whose chariot-horses... and "The charioteer [rescued] Bhujyu. The entire *paśuhautra* (the priest's duties regarding the animal) follows the *pājaṣa* model. If there are two animals, the modification (*ūha*) is made with dual endings; if there are three animals, with plural endings. (Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Book 7, Chapter 5, Section 8).
One carries away the *vasatīvarī* waters during the night, from all sides but not from the front.

That time in which living beings go to rest is denoted by the word "night" (*niśā*). Some maintain that the first half of the night is to be understood by the term "night. Others say it is only the second watch (*yāma*). Still others say it includes the third watch as well. According to the first view, the carrying away of the *vasatīvarīs* occurs even in the first watch; according to the second and third views, however, it does not occur in the first watch—this is the distinction. The night connected with the day of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice is to be understood here, because of its proximity.

Furthermore, by the use of the qualification "of this" (*etasyāḥ*)—as in Āśvalāyana’s statement, "Now, for this night, [there is] the *vināsa*-offering"—the unity of the night, which serves as the substratum for both the *pāśuka-tantra* beginning with the *saṃvāda* and the portion of the *saumya-tantra* beginning with the *bodhana*, is demonstrated. He carries [the fire] around the altar on all sides (*pari*). Regarding the present context, he states the intended meaning of the word "carrying around" (*pariharaṇa*): "not in front, but on all sides. Or rather, the scriptural injunction itself, "he carries it around on all sides," is being cited here.

By the word "on all sides" (*sarvataḥ*), although the act of warding off [the *rakṣases*] would also apply to the eastern part, the intention is as follows: just as the sun accomplishes the function of the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*)—which consists in the destruction of the *rakṣases*—in the eastern quarter, so too here, by the scriptural statement, "He moves them around on all sides for the destruction of the *rakṣases*," it is understood that the sun will indeed accomplish the function of the *vasatīvarī* waters' movement—which consists in the destruction of the *rakṣases*—in the eastern quarter. Now, [one might object]: "But the sun is indeed... [and so forth].

If it is argued that this [statement]—"it wards off the demons from the front"—is inconsistent because the removal of the *vasatīvarī* waters is performed at night (when the sun has set), and thus it is impossible for the sun to ward off demons since its rising cannot occur, we say no. This is because the term "rising" (*udyan*) is accepted as meaning "about to rise" (*udyantsyann*); for instance, in the injunction, "One should offer an eight-potherd cake to Agni Rakṣohan."

The phrase "the *rakṣas* might seize [them]" refers to the necessity of performing the laying of the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) at night during the *iṣṭi* dedicated to Agni Anīkavant. According to the view of some, namely the statement "they proceed with rays," this applies to the laying of the enclosing-sticks which—by implication—falls at night in connection with the *iṣṭi* for Agni Anīkavant. Since, according to that procedure, it is possible here as well to effect the destruction of the *rakṣas*, there is no lack of relevance. This is a general proposition.

Alternatively, the phrase "not from the front" (*na purastāt*) is to be construed only with the subsequent part. Thus, the injunction is simply this much: "He steps out from all sides, but not from the front. Its purpose is that he steps out from "all sides," meaning from all the extremities of the directions, but not from the area in front, because there is no carrying around (*pariharaṇa*) there. By implication, this statement refers to those who are uninitiated (*adīkṣita*). The syntactical connection is: "Having said, 'Step out,' he carries around the *vasatīvarī* waters.
Having said, "Step out," the sacrificer and his wife remain within the altar (*antarvedi*).

In the word *patnī* (wife), the singular number is not intended to be significant because it resides in the subject (*uddeśya*). Therefore, when there are multiple wives, all of them should remain within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*). In the case of the *sattra* sacrifices, since even the *asvin* priests are initiated (*dīkṣita*), they too must remain within the altar. Because the Adhvaryu is the one who performs the carrying around of the *vasatīvarī* waters, he does not remain within the altar. The particle *ca* serves to indicate mutual conjunction. He does not carry [the water] past one who is uninitiated.

This prohibition is the reason for not allowing those who are uninitiated (adīkṣitāḥ) to go outside; its meaning is that one must not allow an uninitiated person to pass by. [Maṇḍala 6, Paṭala] Together with the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa: He describes the manner of carrying around: "Having taken the pitcher and placed it on his left shoulder, having passed behind the Āhavanīya fire, having carried it out through the southern door, and having carried it along the southern edge of the altar, he places it on the northern corner of the southern high-altar (uttaravedi) with the formula, 'O ye waters, belonging to the portion of Indra and Agni.'"

In the phrase "having taken the *kumbha*," the word "from another" (*anyasmāt*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. By this, it is established that the offering of the *kumbha* must be performed by someone other than the *adhvaryu*. Otherwise, since the act of taking would already be established by implication through the words "having placed upon the *samya*," the explicit statement would be redundant. The mention of the *kumbha* is an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *kumbhī*. The term "left" (*savya*) is used without further qualification in order to ensure its internal proximity to the *atyāśitavarī* waters. The mention of the "shoulder" (*aṃsa*) is intended to exclude the side (*pārśva*).

The term *atirātra* has the sense of "concealment" (*antardhāna*); that is, the *ādheya* (the fire to be established) should be established after having concealed something. Alternatively, *prājahita* means that which was previously the *gārhapatya* fire, and which was set aside (*nahita*) or abandoned during the principal rites such as the carrying forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*); this is its meaning. In this view, the word is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍha*). The long vowel is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) usage. Regarding the word "having gone" (*gatvā*), because of the statement "having passed over" (*atikramya*), one must go beyond the rear part of the *gārhapatya* fire. "By the southern door" means by way of the southern entrance.

The prefix *upa* indicates a specific sense of bowing down. "Carrying out" (*nirharaṇa*) means leading out through the door. Having carried the *vasatīvarī* waters around while aiming toward the edge or extremity of the southern great altar (*mahāvedi*), he pours them out on the southern shoulder of the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) with the mantra: "O Indrāgnī, you who possess your own portions."

Taking the pitcher and placing it on his right shoulder, he returns by the same way he came, carries it out through the northeast door, and having carried it around along the northern edge of the altar, he sets it down on the northern hip of the northern altar with the formula: "You are the portions of Mitra and Varuṇa."

Regarding the phrase "on the right shoulder" (*dakṣiṇe 'ṃse*), the mention of "right" is for the purpose of establishing the intermediate position of the *vasatīvarī* waters. The mention of "shoulder" (*aṃsa*) is for the purpose of excluding the side (*pārśva*). This [carrying] is prescribed only for this specific case when entering by the north-eastern door according to one's desire, and not otherwise. In its absence, the carrying out is by the north-eastern or the northern door.

Having taken the jar and placed it on the left shoulder, having caused [the water] to enter by way of the *tīrtha*, he deposits it in the *āgnīdhra* fire-hall with the formula: "You are the portions of the Viśve Devas."

The word *tīrtha* refers to the space between the *vedi* and the *utkara*, as well as the space between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, according to another sūtra which states: "Between the *vedi* and the *utkara*, or between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, [it is] the *tīrtha*. Regarding the ritual action at the *cātvāla*, the former is the *tīrtha* and the latter is the *cātvāla*. The *āgnīdhra* is near the *āgnīdhra-dhiṣṇya*. *Jāgṛti* refers to the end of the mantra.

Having taken the water-pot and placed it on the left side, [the rule] "having entered by the *tīrtha*"—by this much alone, since the entry by the *tīrtha* for one who has not yet grasped it is already established, the specific mention of the word "taking" (*ādāya*) indicates that even in other cases, entry by the *tīrtha* applies even to that which has not been grasped by the hand. By this, the entry by the *tīrtha* for animals such as cattle becomes established. Furthermore, from this statement here, it follows that when one is unable to carry oneself due to some object, entry by the *tīrtha* is not restricted.

If it is argued that since the status of being "internal" (*antaraṅga*) is already established by the general rule (*paribhāṣā*)—"the limbs of the sacrifice are internal, while the performers are external"—the repeated mention of "left and right" (*savyadakṣiṇa*) in various places for the sake of establishing internality is redundant, this is true; however, it is intended to indicate that the sacrificial limb (*yajñāṅga*) taken up by the performer is internal here alone, and not elsewhere. If this were stated only here, there would be the risk of a lack of restriction in other instances distinct from this one; therefore, the expression "left and right" is used in those respective places.

They dwell here; they dwell only here and not elsewhere. In the word *vasanti*, the suffix *ṇic* is applied to the root *vas* (to dwell) with the sense of "causing to dwell. Thus, it becomes *vāsayanti* (they cause to dwell). The term *adhvaryu* is a singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*), because the plural number is used for honorific purposes. Alternatively, there is a remainder [in the compound] meaning "the Vasatīvarī waters are to be caused to dwell by the four Adhvaryus. This is based on the Śruti: "He causes them to dwell near; this indeed is the unconquerable part of the sacrifice; whatever is the unconquerable part of the sacrifice, that very thing he causes these [waters] to dwell near. These are the Vasatīvarī waters.

He issues the command: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā! and [the Subrahmaṇya responds]: "The Subrahmaṇyā is like a daughter to her father. This [response] is to be recited for each animal sacrifice.
