He issues the command: "Let them milk the cow that provides the *vratadhuk* (fast-milk) for the sacrificer’s *āśira* (curd-mixture); let them milk the one that provides the *patnī-vrata* (wife’s fast-milk) for the *dadhi-graha* (curd-offering); let them milk the one that provides the *gharma-dhuk* (hot-milk cow) for the *dadhi-gharma* (curd-heat offering); let them prepare the warm milk for the Maitrāvaruṇa without heating it further; and let them prepare the curd for the Āditya-graha by heating it thoroughly."

The cow that yields the *vratadoha* (fasting-milk) for the sacrificer, she he should milk for the *āśira*—that is, for the sake of the *āśira* (the mixture); the *āśira* is the curdled milk (*mathita-dadhi*). The cow that yields the *vratadoha* for the wife, he should milk her for the *dadhi-graha*—that is, for the purpose of the *dadhi-graha*; the cup to be drawn with curds is the *dadhi-graha*. By this, it is understood by implication that the sacrificial offering consists of curds. The cow that yields the *dharmaduh*—that is, the cow that yields the substance related to the *dharma* (the Pravargya rite)—he should milk her for the *dadhi-dharma*.

The object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by means of curd is a specific ritual act (*karman*) designated as "Dharma"; thus, the meaning is "for the sake of that [act]. Here too, according to the method just mentioned, the substance itself is understood to be curd. [The phrase] "of this [milk], which is heated and not yet coagulated (*anātañjyam*)," refers to the fact that there is no coagulation (*ātaścana*) for it while it remains in that state; such milk [is intended] for Maitrāvaruṇa—that is, for the sake of the Maitrāvaruṇa priest. It is drawn forward from "make" (*kuruta*), or alternatively, it is drawn back from "let him make" (*kurutāt*).

That which is boiled (*śṛta*) is indeed *ātañcyam* (curdled with whey); however, when it depends upon the coldness of the base (*budhna*), it is not called *śṛtātañcyam*. Such curd is to be prepared for the Āditya-graha—that is, for the purpose of the Āditya-graha. The word "kuruta" is the first person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*). In the case of the curd for the Badhiga-graha and the curd for the Dhruva-vessel, there is no requirement for the form of *śṛtātañcyam*.

When the performance of either the *ājyagraha* or the *somagraha* is intended to be carried out according to its specific procedure, then the milking for the *dadhigraha* is omitted; because of the absence of the *dadhigraha*, the milking is not performed. In the case of the *avārya*, the milking for the *dadhidharma* is omitted; because of the absence of the *dadhidharma*, the milking is not performed. For the sake of the *maitrāvaruṇapayas*, the milk of any cow whatsoever may be used; for the sake of the *śṛtātaṅka*, the milk of any cow whatsoever may be used.

In the view that the agent of the milking for the three purposes beginning with the *āśira* is the same as the agent of the milking of the Maitrāvaruṇa’s milk—namely, the phrase "he milks the heated *manāṭakya* milk for the Maitrāvaruṇa"—the agent here is likewise indefinite, just like the agent of the milking for the three purposes beginning with the *āśira*. However, in the view that the word "milks" (*duhat*) from the subsequent passage is to be construed here, the agent is specifically the Pratiprasthātṛ, because of the singular number. [End of] the first section, together with the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha.

The Pratiprasthātṛ alone is the performer of the milking for the sake of the Āditya-graha, as well as the milker for the sake of the *dadhi* (curds) required for the *adhyardha-doha*, just as before. The performance of the five milkings takes place right here, in accordance with the ritual injunctions (*praiṣa*). The milking for the sake of the *savanīyāmikṣā* (the curdled milk for the Soma-pressing) occurs at this very time, because the production of the *sānnāyya* (the oblation of milk and curds) requires two days. The Pratiprasthātṛ alone is the performer of the milking for the *savanīyāmikṣā*, because since the morning milking has him as its performer, it is logical that this [milking] related to it should likewise have him as its performer.

The preparation of the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) stands in the place of the *anubandhyā* cow; otherwise, it would be impossible [to perform the rite]. In this case, it is performed with ordinary milk, because in the Kali age, the immolation of a cow is prohibited. In that context, there are five milkings performed silently (*tūṣṇīm*). For the sake of the *saknīyāmikṣā*, there is one milking accompanied by mantras. For the five milkings, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) beginning with the fetching of the branch is indeed without mantras. Because of the statement, "It should be heated but not placed on the fire," only heating is to be done. Having added [the curdling agent] to the milk for the purpose of coagulation (*ātañcana*), the transgression occurs.

If this were accepted as the desired conclusion, however, the injunction "he mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk" would fail to establish boiling (śrapaṇa) where milk is the instrument. Thus, since the exclusion of curdling agents follows from the very purpose [of the mixture], the statement "it is not to be curdled" indicates the application of the ritual properties of milking, such as the fetching of the branch and so forth. And that [milking] is performed silently, because the milk lacks the inherent nature of being an offering-substance (*pradāna*). For this very reason, the ritual properties pertaining to the purchase do not apply.

And likewise, in the fourth pāda of the ninth adhyāya, Jaimini states this same point through such sūtras as: "But because the cooking [of the vessels] is not [otherwise] established, there would be an injunction for the purpose of offering; or rather, it is a subordinate element (guṇa) because it serves the purpose of cooking. Regarding the statement, "He mixes the vessel for Mitra-Varuṇa with milk," since mixing milk with Soma serves a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārtha) by way of preparing the offering, whereas if it were for the sake of purifying the Soma itself, it would result in an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that the milk is an ingredient to be offered. However, since there is no fault in postulating an invisible purpose on the strength of the accusative case-ending (dvitīyā-śruti), the milk is not to be offered.

"Tvam" [is used] for the purpose of offering the milk and other substances for cooking. For the sake of the *savanīya* curd (*āmikṣā*), the ritual procedure (*tantra*) beginning with the fetching of the branch (*śākhā-haraṇa*) is indeed accompanied by mantras. Alternatively, at the outset, the fetching of the branch is performed for all [substances] in sequence, distinguished by whether it is with or without mantras. In that same sequence, the making of the *upaveṣa* [wooden chip] is likewise performed; likewise, the discarding of the three-fold grass-strainer (*trivṛt-pavitra*) is likewise performed; and likewise, the milkings are performed in sequence. "May we milk a hundred autumns from Mitra and Varuṇa."

"O Mitra and Varuṇa, may these cows delight you here; speak for us to Mitra and Varuṇa. May the oblation yield much Indra-power for Mitra and Varuṇa; [may it be] the offering for the gods, O Mitra and Varuṇa. With Soma I stretch you out; [I offer] curds for Mitra and Varuṇa. This is the modification for the *savanīyāmikṣā* (curdled milk for the pressing). At the very time of bringing the *śākhā* (branch) and the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick), the various tasks must be performed for the sake of full understanding. Alternatively, the milking for the *savanīyāmikṣā* takes place first; thereafter follow the five milkings without mantras.

In accordance with this very principle, there is the fetching of branches, the making of the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick), and so forth. When all the milkings have been performed, the calves are driven away in the morning for the sake of equal curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*).
The *āgnīdhra* priests remain adorned.

By this, residence in the *sadas* is excluded. Āpastamba has stated the prohibition regarding the call for milking (*dohārthapraiṣa*) with the words, "One should not fast in the *sadas*. Regarding the term "unadorned" (*akṛta*), the ornamentation refers only to human [ornaments] and not to divine ones. These have been described by Vaikhānasa: "Endowed with golden ornaments, with bright garments and ointments, and graced with fragrant flowers—this is called divine ornamentation. That same [ornamentation], when devoid of flowers but including collyrium, is remembered as human."
"This is declared to be the ancestral ornament, devoid of ointment. [Thus ends the eighth chapter of the seventh book of the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha.
In the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, they cause the wife to wake.

"O Vinasta, you must perform the vigil for this night. Having thus enjoined his wife to the vigil, they should both sleep. However, sleeping is not something that must necessarily be done. Nor should it be argued that sleeping is mandatory because of the injunction to wake [the sacrificer], since otherwise the injunction would be rendered purposeless; for the injunction to wake only becomes effective when sleep is actually present, and thus there is no lack of purpose for the injunction. In the phrase "they keep watch," the instigators are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). In the *havirdhāna* shed, the sacrificer protects the King (Soma); he protects him. 25.
Thus ends the eighth paṭala in the seventh praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

The mention of the *havirdhāna* (soma-cart) serves to distinguish the protection of the King Soma even when he is elsewhere; the meaning is that just as servants guard a king, so the sacrificer, together with his attendants (*parikarmins*), protects King Soma with one-pointed attention from the *dasyus* and the dogs. The explicit mention of the "sacrificer" is for the purpose of excluding the *adhvaryu*.

The reason for composing this as a separate *sūtra*—when it could have been made more concisely within the *Yājamāna-sūtra* itself by simply stating, "While awake, he protects the King [Soma] in the *havirdhāna* during the night"—is to convey the following meaning: in cases such as the nights of the second day of the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice or the *ahīna* sacrifices, when one is not awake, protection must be performed by another; whereas when one is awake, one may protect the King oneself or have him protected by another. Thus, when one is not awake, he must certainly have it done by another. It is for the purpose of making this point known that this was written separately.

The repetition is for the purpose of indicating the conclusion of the question. Thus ends the eighth chapter of the seventh book in the commentary named *Jyotsnā*, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—the son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was the grandson of Okopāha Śrīmad Agniṣṭomayājī, Sāhasrāgni-yukta Vājapeyayājī, Sarvatomukhayājī, and Dviṣāhasrāgni-yukta Pauṇḍarīkayājī—which serves to alleviate the distress of learned men caused by the difficulty of discerning the hidden jewels of meaning within the ocean of the *Śrīmad Bhagavat Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra*.
This seventh question is complete. 8.1 Now begins the eighth question; therein is the first chapter:
they wake up at the dead of night.
Reciting each preceding verse followed by each succeeding one, and then with the first [verse] alone,
some offer oblations against the failure of the sacrifice (*yajñārti*).
He then commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *savanīya* animal sacrifice.
The ritual procedure for this is explained by that of the Nirūḍhapaśubandha sacrifice.

No sacrificial grass (barhis) is used; he brings only the prastara-bunch according to the ritual rule for sacrificial grass. At the time of arranging the vessels, he first places the *pracaraṇī* ladle.
At the time of taking the clarified butter, having taken four portions with the *pracaraṇī* ladle, he takes [the butter] for the subsequent offerings.

Having consecrated the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*), having addressed the *brahmán*, and having sprinkled the fuel, the altar, and the *prastara* grass-bundle, he pours out the remainder of the sprinkling waters, inserts the two strainers (*pavitra*) back [into the vessel], and having set down the *prastara*, he sets down the offering-ladles (*sruk*).
He touches the *āgnīdhra* hearth with the formula: "May this Agni of ours create wide space."
With the verse "Viṣṇu strode through this," [he offers] in the Havirdhāna shed;
with "O Agni, you purify the life-spans," [he offers] the ladles;
with "May there be an addition," [he offers] the Vāyavya vessels.
Rising with vigor, he goes together to the assembly hall.
He arranges the vessels on the *khara* mound.

He assigns them according to their form with these formulas: "Agni is the deity, Gāyatrī the metre," and so forth; the remaining vessels are assigned with the formula, "Who yokes you? May he yoke you."
On the right shoulder [of the altar], he places the cups for the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma [libations]: the southern one for the Upāṃśu and the northern one for the Antaryāma;
or alternatively, the eastern one for the Upāṃśu and the western one for the Antaryāma.
Between these two, he places the Upāṃśusavana pressing-stone with the formula, "For the diffused breath (vyāna) thee," having joined it together with the Upāṃśu cup.
The cups for the two deities are turned inward: the cup for Indra and Vāyu has a garland around it; that for Mitra and Varuṇa has two corners; and that for the Aśvins has four corners.
Behind these are the two cups for the Śukra and Manthin offerings: the southern one, made of Bilva wood, is for the Śukra; the northern one, made of Vikaṅkata wood, is for the Manthin.

Behind those are the two Ṛtu-cups made of Aśvattha wood, with bases like a horse's hoof and openings on both sides: the southern one belongs to the Adhvaryu, and the northern one to the Pratiprasthātṛ.
On the southern hip [of the altar] he places the vessel for the Āgrayaṇa;
on the northern hip, the vessel for the Ukthya and the Ukthya cup, which has a horse-hoof-shaped bottom.
Between these two, he places three Atigrāhya cups facing northward.
In front of the support of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, he places the *āditya* vessel and the *āditya* cup, both with bottoms shaped like a horse's hoof.
In front of the support of the northern *havirdhāna* cart, on ground that has not been leveled, he places the *dhruva* vessel.
On the northern shoulder [of the altar], he places the four-cornered *dadhi* cup made of *udumbara* wood.
In the middle, he places the floating vessel;
and according to the available space, eleven cups made of Nyagrodha or Rauhītaka wood.
The *tsaru* or *atsaruka* [trees]:
*rohī*, *rohitaka*, *plīhaśatru*, *dāḍimapuṣpaka*,
*gāyatrī*, *bālatanaya*, *khadira*, and *dantadhāvana*.
The *rohī* and the *rauhitaka* tree are masculine terms for the *caitya* and the *vaṭa* tree respectively.
The *camasa* cup without lines is prescribed for the *hotṛ*, that which is wiped clean for the *brahman*,
that which is wiped downward for the *udgātṛ*, and that which is wiped at the side for the *svāmin*.
"The wise should fashion the cup for the Prastotṛ with a single line;
they should have the wooden scraper made for the Neṣṭṛ, and the Āgnīdhra’s should possess a handle;
one should make the footprint of the Ayājya as the mark for the Acchāvāka. Thus it is said.
The Vāyavya ladles are a span in length, with raised backs and curved in the middle;
the *pariplava* ladle is shaped like the handle of a common spoon.
Of these, those whose wood has not been specifically prescribed are made of *vikaṅkata*; however, those not intended for use in the fire-oblation (*ahomārtha*) are made of *vāraṇa*.

With the formula, "I yoke the earth for thee together with light," he yokes the *droṇakalaśa* equipped with its fringe-filter behind the axle of the southern *havirdhāna*. With the formula, "I yoke Vāyu for thee together with the intermediate space," he places the *ādhavanīya* in the interior of the northern [cart].
With the formula, "I yoke speech for thee together with the sun," he places the *pūtabhṛt* on the front pole of that very same [cart].
He touches the spoons with the formula: "The three Ekadhanā jars are behind the axle; I yoke the three separate ladles for thee, O Sūrya.
At this point, some authorities prescribe the employment of the pressing-skin and the pressing-stones.

Having turned the stones so that they face each other upon the lower stone, he addresses them with the formula: "Dwellings of the waters, embryos of the cosmic order, guardians of the world, falcons, guests of the mountains, peaks, protectors like those sent forth—by your voice call Indra; by your roar drive away disease; you are yoked, carry [the sacrifice] to the heavenly world, bring the sacrificer forward."
He offers in the Āgnīdhra fire with the formula, "Protect me from the seat-mantra.
With the two verses, "For the heart thee! For the mind thee!", he causes the King [Soma] to descend onto the pressing-stones between those [fires].
According to some, one who desires heaven should offer the Pañcahotṛ oblation in the Āgnīdhra fire.
Before speech is uttered, he begins the Prātaranuvāka for one who has gone abroad, [thinking] "for the sake of his enemy. Having issued the summons, he gives the direction:

"O Brahman, recite for the gods who come in the morning; O Subrahmaṇya, restrain your speech; O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; O Pratiprasthātṛ, pour out the grains for the Savanīya offerings. Thus he issues the commands.
The Pratiprasthātṛ undertakes the rites for the Savanīya offerings, beginning with the setting out of the vessels; he arranges the vessels for the vegetable oblations according to their purpose:
two potsherds for roasting, eight for the *puroḍāśa*, and a vessel for the *āmikṣā*.

At the time of the pouring out, he pours out the parched grains (*dhānā*) for Indra Harivat, the groats (*karambha*) for Indra Pūṣaṇvat, the fried grains (*parīvāpa*) and parched grains (*lājā*) for Sarasvatī Bhāratī, and the *puroḍāśa* on eight potsherds for Indra.
Having sprinkled the rice grains with the *vibhāga* mantra, he divides them; he threshes half of them and sets aside half for the sake of the parched grains (*lāja*).
With the first *kapāla* mantra, he places two potsherds for the roasted grains and two for the parched grains.
Having placed eight potsherds for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), he prepares the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) for Mitra and Varuṇa according to the ritual procedure for *āmikṣā*.
He roasts the grains and parched grains with the mantra used for placing the pot on the fire.
They remain there without being scorched.

Having performed everything prior to the decoration, he divides the grains with the division-mantra; having made half of the flour into groats according to the procedure for flour, he mixes them together with the mixing-mantra, and that becomes the *karambha*.

When the verse "In those unadorned [women], Dawn has appeared; the sacrificial animal has been brought forward; Agni has been established according to the season" is being recited, he offers a fourfold-drawn portion of ghee with the verse "May Agni hear my call along with the fuel.
Having taken another fourfold-drawn portion...

Holding a handful of *darbha* grass, he issues the command: "O *Hotṛ*, go for water! O *Camasādhvaryu* of the Maitrāvaruṇa, come hither! O *Ekadhanins*, come hither! O *Neṣṭṛ*, lead the wife forward! O *Unnetṛ*, wait at the *cātvāla* with the *Hotṛ*'s cup and the *vasatīvarī* waters!
The *Maitrāvaruṇa-camasādhvaryu* takes his cup and comes hither;
the *Ekadhanins* come hither, taking three or more uneven numbers of *ekadhana* jars.
Saying, "Come, come," the *neṣṭṛ* leads the wife forward.
At the place where he can hear the Hotṛ reciting the *prātaranuvāka*, the Adhvaryu should take the water;
if they are at a distance, he should draw it up and take it at the place where he hears the Hotṛ.
Having thrown a blade of grass into the waters with the mantra, "O divine waters," he offers an oblation of four ladlings,
or he performs the remainder [of the rite].
Or, if there is already a blade of grass present, he offers the oblation upon that very blade.
With the mantra, "Thou art a furrow," he causes the oblation to overflow with *darbha* grass.
With the mantra, "For the imperishability of the ocean, I draw you up," he draws up the [milk] not smeared with ghee using the cup of the Maitrāvaruṇa;
he does the same for the *ekadhana* waters with this very same mantra.
With the formula, "To the Vasus, to the Rudras, to the Ādityas," the wife takes up the *pannejani* waters.
Those who bring the vessels bring them forward;
with that same mantra, the Neṣṭṛ leads the wife away.

Having entered the *sadas* by the eastern door, having gone around the front of the *praśāstrīya* hearth, he places the *pannejanī* waters for the wives behind the *naiṣṭra* hearth with the formula: "To the Vasus, to the Rudras, to the Ādityas.
Or [he says]: "O Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, these are your *pannejanī* waters; protect them!
The others go to the *cātvāla*.

"May Varuṇa unite you; may Indra unite you; may Dhātṛ unite you; may Bṛhaspati unite you; may Tvaṣṭṛ and Viṣṇu, bestowing [blessings] with progeny, grant wealth to the sacrificer. May the yokes be made fit for the yoke-poles according to their respective positions. Having thus touched the *hotṛ*’s cup and the *maitrāvaruṇa*’s cup above the *cātvāla* pit, he pours the *vasatīvarī* waters into them.
Having poured some of the *vasatīvarī* waters into the *hotṛ*’s cup, he pours it into the *maitrāvaruṇa*’s cup; from the *maitrāvaruṇa*’s cup, he pours it back into the *hotṛ*’s cup.
He anoints both the Hotṛ’s cup and the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup with the *pracaraṇī* ladle, modifying the beginning of the mantra to "May he anoint you" (*saṃ vo 'naktu varuṇa*).
They approach the vicinity of the Hotṛ.
The Hotṛ asks the Adhvaryu three times: "O Adhvaryu, have you drunk? (*adhvaryo 'vepā3*).

He responds three times, "I have offered the oblation. If there is a remnant, he performs the *kratukaraṇa* (concluding oblation) with the *pracaraṇī* ladle, reciting the verse, "O Agni, that mortal whom you protect... If no remnant exists, he takes another fourfold portion and offers it all.
He places the *pracaraṇī* ladle on the front beam of the southern *havirdhāna* cart.
For one whom he should desire, "May he be impotent," he places it below that [beam]. He causes the waters to enter the *havirdhāna* by the eastern door.

Among those [waters], he places the *hotṛ*’s cup in front of the axle on the northern track of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, touching it [to the others]. He places the other [cups] in the northern *havirdhāna* according to available space.

While [the waters] are being poured into the *hotṛ*’s cup, he causes the sacrificer to recite: "You are the *nigrābhya*s; you are heard by the gods; you are bright, bearers of brightness; you are pure, bearers of purity; satisfy my life! These become the *nigrābhya*s. || 4 ||
Thus ends the first paṭala in the eighth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the second paṭala in the eighth praśna:
He proceeds with the Dadhigraha offering.

"Thou art taken with a support; for Prajāpati, thee, the luminous, I take thee, the luminous," with these words he takes the *dadhi-graha* (curd-offering) in the *dadhi-graha* vessel. "O Indra, [ward off] the mind of the hater," with these words he carries it forward. "For out-breathing thee, for in-breathing thee," with these words he offers it. One should take the *ājya-graha* (ghee-offering) for one desiring splendor; one should take the *soma-graha* (soma-offering) for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
The ritual procedure for these two is explained by that of the *dadhi-graha*.
"One should take the *dadhigraha* for one who desires cattle"—thus [it is prescribed] both as a permanent rite and as an optional one.
When about to take the *somagraha*, he draws out as much of the King [Soma] as he deems sufficient for a single draught;
he ties it up with a cord and sets the other [portion] aside.

Having poured that [mixture] into the *upara* stone and mixed it with the *vasatīvarī* waters, he consecrates it with the mantra: "We have increased you... Then, with the *grāvan* stone as required, he presses [the Soma] while reciting: "The gods, seeking favor, made three kindling-sticks for the immortal one from the moving youth; of these, they assigned one to the mortal as enjoyment, while two went toward the hidden world.
He consecrates or catches the first shoot of the juice being pressed with the mantra: "May it leap unto me."
With the mantra, "The drop has fallen," he consecrates the droplets.
This is the ritual procedure for all pressings;
this same pressing-mantra applies to this very one as well.
Having grasped it with his hand containing gold, standing facing the east, he offers it in the eastern part of the southern half, or in the eastern part of the northern half.
Wherever this is done, there all Soma offerings are performed;
having offered them, he either makes an offering of the remainder.

Having entered the *sadas* by the eastern door, sitting in front of the *hotṛ* facing west, he looks at [the soma] with the formula, "Thee, the one who watches over men," and consumes it with the formula, "The delightful overcomer.
When bringing the portion himself, he begins with the consumption formula starting from the act of looking.

When it is brought by another, he awaits it with "Come, O portion! Having received it with "May I grasp thee with the arms of the Aśvins," and having looked at it with "Thee, the one who watches over men," and having recited "The delightful overcomer," he continues with "Of the Vasu-group, O Soma-deity."

At the morning pressing, they consume all the Soma with the formula, "Of that drunk by Narāśaṃsa"; at the midday pressing, they consume all the Soma with the formula, "Of the Soma belonging to the Rudra-group," and the Nārāśaṃsa cups with the formula, "Of that drunk by Narāśaṃsa"; and at the third pressing, they consume all the Soma with the formula, "Of the Soma belonging to the Āditya-group," and the Nārāśaṃsa cups with the formula, "Of that drunk by Narāśaṃsa.
Whatever [formula] precedes the "Vasu-group" formula, he attaches it everywhere.
Some authorities transmit the [formula] as universally applicable: "May Vāgdevī drink of the Soma.
Having consumed the Soma, they touch themselves with the mantra: "Impel my limbs, O Lord of Tawny Steeds!
"The small, stainless lotus-city situated within the highest heaven; within that, too, is a small sky free from sorrow—that which is inside it should be meditated upon."
Having washed the vessel at the Mārjālīya mound, he places it in its proper station.
This is the procedure for all Soma vessels;
however, in the case of the Grahas, there is the requirement of including gold.
The consumption [of the soma] occurs through both the oblation and the pressing, not by either rite alone.
The vessels for the *dadhighraha*, the *aṃśu*, and the *adābhya* are common;
one proceeds with the *aṃśu*.

He takes as much of the King (Soma) as he deems sufficient for a single drawing; he sets aside the remainder to be used later. Having placed that [portion] upon the lower stone and moistened it with the *vasatīvarī* waters, he draws [the Soma] while breathing out and then breathing in, chanting the *Vāmadevya* in his mind, or with the verse of the *Vāmadevya*: "With what [splendor] has the Wondrous One come to us? If he is unable to draw it without pausing, he places a hundred-measure (*śatamāna*) piece of gold upon it and draws it while giving a choice gift.
Having touched it with a hundred-measure weight of gold, he covers it with gold. He carries it away with the mantra, "May Indra and Agni bestow splendor upon me.
He offers the oblation without pausing, reciting, "When they have indeed run after this."
The Pratiprasthātṛ sprinkles the Adhvaryu with water.
He proceeds with the *adābhya* cup.

Having plucked three stalks from the King [Soma] that are tied together—without letting them touch one another—with the formulas beginning "May the Vasus pull you forth," he pours them into another vessel, either from curds or from the *nigrābhya* waters, saying, "O bright one, I shake your bright [essence] into the *māndā* waters. Into that [vessel], he causes these stalks to overflow three times clockwise.
The remaining options are four, five, or seven times.

He takes [the draught] with these verses: "I take thy bright [essence] with the bright; Agni at the morning pressing; the All-gods at this third pressing of the seers"—at the end of all [these verses], the *upayāma* formula is employed.
With the verse, "Into him the fierce ones have drawn [the Soma]," he carries it away.
He consecrates [the bull] with the mantra, "The lofty form of the bull shines forth, great.
He offers the oblation with the mantra, "Soma is the leader of Soma," and sets aside the recognized stalks.
Thus ends the second paṭala in the eighth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the third paṭala in the eighth praśna.
Having taken up the *upāṃśusavana* pressing-stone with the mantra "devasya tvā," he restrains his speech until the drawing of the Āgrayaṇa cup.
He consecrates [the stone] with the mantra, "Thou art the pressing-stone.

Having placed it upon the *adhiṣavaṇa* (pressing-skin) with its surface facing upward, he measures out the King [Soma] with these mantras, beginning with "For Indra, thee, the slayer of Vṛtra," just as at the purchase [of Soma], except for the act of gathering together.

Having poured out the King [Soma] into one part of the *adhiṣavaṇa*, he takes up as much as he deems sufficient for a single cup; he sets the remainder aside. Having placed that [portion] upon the lower millstone (*upara*) and having moistened it with the *vasatīvarī* waters, he pours in the *nigrābhya* waters with the mantra, "Ye are refreshing, conquerors of Vṛtra."
He consecrates [the Soma] with the mantra, "O Soma, that light of yours which is in heaven.
Some authorities prescribe this consecration as occurring earlier.

Having grasped six stalks of the King (Soma) that have been touched [by the pressing stones] and placed them aside without letting them touch one another, and having taken the other stalks, he holds the pressing stone above them and, while not holding the stalks below, causes the three verses of the *dhotṛ*’s cup to flow around it three times from left to right—eastward, westward, northward, and southward; this constitutes the *nigrābha*.

Having placed them down and moistened them with the *vasatīvarī* waters, he lifts up the pressing-stone with the words, "Do not fear, do not tremble," and addresses the two pressing-boards with the verse, "O Dhiṣaṇās, being firm.

Then, with the formula, "Sinless we, sent by Indra, [approach thee]; may Vāyu be thy portion; may Mitra be thy portion; may Varuṇa be thy portion; Soma the King is unslain," he strikes [the stone] upon that spot where he sees a root, a blade of grass, or a piece of wood, provided the ground is level.
According to some teachers, he presses after having placed a blade of grass in between.
Having performed the first pressing eight times, he approaches the *nigrābha* water as before.
Having covered the *upāṃśu* vessel with two of the soma stalks already taken up, the Pratiprasthātṛ holds it from the north.
With the words, "Flow pure for Vācaspati, O vigorous one," the Adhvaryu pours soma into it with his joined palms.
In this manner, the second and third pressings are performed.
Alternatively, he presses the second time eleven times and the third time twelve times.

Having set aside the previous stalks, he covers the vessel with two other stalks for the second pressing and pours water over it; with two others for the third pressing, he pours Soma into the vessel at the second pressing with the verse, "The god of the gods," and at the third pressing with the verse, "Make our nourishments honey-sweet."
He does not set it down.
He rises with the words, "Thou art made ready for thy own self.
He proceeds with the words, "The wide atmosphere."
Having passed beyond the Hotṛ to the north. || 7 ||
With the words, "May Manas offer thee," he stands over the northern junction of the enclosing sticks.

Having brought [the ladle] along the northern junction of the enclosing sticks, he offers a straight, long, and continuous oblation toward the south-east with the formula, "Svāhā! May the well-born one offer thee to Sūrya."
With the formula, "For the gods, for the rays of light, thee," he wipes the internal smear on the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*).
If he should desire, "May Parjanya be rainy," it is explained in the Brāhmaṇa.
He pours the residue into the Āgrayaṇa vessel.
"This is your womb; for breath, you!"—with these words he sets down the vessel.

Into it he places a stalk of *aṃśu* grass, and it remains there until the third pressing. However, for one performing a malevolent rite (*abhicāra*), having drawn the cup, he should set it down with the formula, "I set you down in the breath of so-and-so. Having taken it up with a verse addressed to Savitṛ, and having consecrated it with the mantra, "Kill so-and-so; then I shall offer you," he offers it with the verse: "In the exhilaration of the intoxicating, joy-inspiring [Soma], may so-and-so become false."
He should not sit without breathing until the Hotṛ has called;
if he is far away, he should remain standing until darkness falls.
He pronounces the name of one whom he hates.

"Devāṃśo yasmai tveḍe"—that is the truth; it is not subject to fluctuation. With the formula "phaṭ," he offers that ray of his which has struck him by way of a fracture, whether it clung to his chest, his garment, or his arm.
They sit down around for the great pressing: the Adhvaryu in the east, the Pratiprasthātṛ in the south, the Neṣṭṛ in the west, and the Unnetṛ in the north.

He takes from the King (Soma) as much as he considers sufficient for the morning pressing; he sets the remainder aside. Having placed that [portion] upon the lower stone, he pours the *uśīka* water over it with the formula, "O divine Soma, you who are invincible... He adds one by one at each pressing those shoots which are *ādābhya*, with the formula, "O Soma, that invincible name of yours, the watchful one... And he adds two by two of the *upāṃśusavana* stones.

Having placed them upon the lower stone and poured the *vasatīvarī* waters over them, he presses with the pressing-stones using his right hands as required, and they proceed to the *nigrābha* ceremony as before.
In this manner, the second and third pressings are performed.
They pour the king [Soma], pressed three times, into the Ādhavanīya vessel.
In this manner, the second and third rounds (paryāya) are performed.

Having prepared the King [Soma] well-pressed during the final pressing and having squeezed it through the strainer, he places the pressing-stones facing each other on the uppermost stone and removes the *ṛjīṣa* from them;
he thus makes the stones have the *ṛjīṣa* as their mouth.
The Udgātṛs place the *droṇakalaśa* vessel upon the stones, facing the east.
They draw him down below the senses. || 8 ||

"Your purifier is spread out, O Brahmaṇaspati; as the lord, you encompass all living beings on every side. One whose body has not been heated by austerity does not enjoy that, being raw; only those who have been cooked and carry it attain it. With this [verse], the Udgātṛ priests, having spread it out, hold the purifier with its fringes pointing northward. The Adhvaryu consecrates it with this very same [verse]. The sacrificer makes his navel [mark] upon it.
And with the Hotṛ’s cup, he causes a continuous stream to flow into it.
The Unnetṛ pours from the Ādhavanīya vessel into the Hotṛ’s cup using a ladle.
He draws the cups while the stream is still flowing.
"Thou art taken with a support; restrain within," [with these words] he takes the Antaryāma cup.
Its ritual procedure is explained by that of the Upāṃśu cup.

Having passed to the south of the Hotṛ, [saying] "May speech favor thee," he stands at the southern junction of the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*). Having moved along the southern junction of the enclosing-sticks, [saying] "Svāhā! To thee, O well-born one, for Sūrya," he offers [the oblation] straight forward, upward, straight, long, and continuous.

He does not wipe the smear on the enclosing-stick (paridhi), nor does he pour the residue from the Āgrayaṇa vessel. He sets down the vessel with the formula, "This is thy womb; for out-breathing thee! He does not place a stalk of grass into it.
Between them, with the formula "For the diffused breath (vyāna) thee," he places the Upāṃśusavana pressing-stone, touching it [with the stone], together with the Upāṃśu vessel.

For one whom he desires, "May he be liable to die," he should place the two [stones] without touching each other; for one whom he desires, "May he attain a full lifespan," he should place the two touching each other.
He offers both after sunrise, without hurrying.
Hastening, one should offer the Upāṃśu cup before sunrise and the Antaryāma cup after sunrise;
according to some, both should be offered before sunrise.
Thus ends the third paṭala in the eighth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the fourth paṭala in the eighth praśna:
One should draw the cups beginning with the Aindravāyava when the Rathantara-sāman is used.
In a rite with the *bṛhat* as the *sāman*, one should draw the cups beginning with the *śukra*. In a rite with both *sāmans*, one may act according to preference.
Or, if the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* is connected to the modified (*vaikārika*) form, one should draw the cups beginning with the *aindravāyava*.
"Let one who has the eldest as his kinsman draw [the cups] beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu," so it is said in the obligatory rite;

"one who is afflicted by disease should draw [the cups] beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu"—these optional extractions have been explained in the Brāhmaṇa, and regarding them, one may act according to one's desire.
They are drawn before the Aindravāyava cup and, once set down, are deposited.
He draws the Aindravāyava;
having recited "O Vāyu, come forth," he holds up the vessel with "Thou art taken with a support; for Vāyu, thee! and into that he pours [the juice].
Having recited "Indravāyū," he moves the cup away; then, having recited again, "Thou art taken with a support; for Indra and Vāyu, thee! he takes it up once more.
With that part of the strainer which has not been used, he wipes it around, and sets it down in its place with, "This is thy womb; for the two who are in harmony, thee!
Those cups taken with a support are drawn with a Yajus formula at the front, and those taken with a support are drawn with a Ṛc verse at the back.
The cleansing of all the *grahas* and their placement according to their source [is as follows]:

with the verse, "This for you, O Mitra and Varuṇa," he places the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa; with the verse, "May we, having won through wealth, rejoice in you both, O gods, with the oblation, as cows do with pasture," and with the verse, "O Mitra and Varuṇa, bestow upon us that cow every day, one that does not kick," he mixes it with warm milk and places it down.
With the verse, "This is the longing one," he mixes the *śukra* cup with gold.
With the verse, "As of old," he mixes the *manthin* cup;

for at those invocations where one offers with power, you two, like swift horses, win the prize through your skill. He who is of great valor, with his arrows, has mixed this [libation] toward the goal, as it were, while grasping it in his hand. Thus, avoiding the defilement of himself and the other cups, he mixes the *manthin* with parched grain flour.
With the formula, "The gods who are eleven in heaven," he takes the *āgrayaṇa* from the vessel; or else, with the formula, "Thou art the *āgrayaṇa*," he takes it first with the *upayāma* formula.
He draws [the Soma] with two streams.

Having poured a portion of the Soma that is in the Āgrayaṇa vessel into another vessel, he makes the second stream. For one performing sorcery, he should use as the *puroruc* [introductory verse]: "Saramā found the breach of the mountain; she made a great, ancient path for us to travel together. She led the way for those who move on good feet among the flowing waters; knowing [her way], she went first toward the roar."
"Thirty-three" is for one who has rivals.

Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa cup, he utters "him" three times—softly at first, then loudly, and then very loudly—and says "Soma purifies itself" three times—softly at first, then loudly, and then very loudly. 10.

"He purifies himself for this *brahman*, he purifies himself for this *kṣatra*, he purifies himself for this sacrificer who presses the Soma; he purifies himself for food and vigor, he purifies himself for the waters, the plants, and the trees; he purifies himself for heaven and earth, he purifies himself for well-being, he purifies himself for spiritual luster, he purifies himself for the sacrificer, he purifies himself for my preeminence. Having thus consecrated the Soma, he releases his speech and draws the *atigrāhya* cups:
the one for Agni with "O Agni, you purify our lives," the one for Indra with "Rising up with vigor," and the one for Sūrya with "The traverser, visible to all."

"His vigor blazed forth when Indra rolled out both worlds like a hide. "His banners, his rays, have become visible among the people, shining like fires. With these two [verses], having settled the *dhruva* vessel, he causes the King [Soma] to flow through [the filter] as much as he considers sufficient for the morning pressing. The stream ceases; having pressed [the residue], he sets down the filter.
Having poured into the Ādhavanīya vessel the contents of the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup and a portion of the Ekadhana waters, he pours a portion through the filter into the Pūtabhṛt vessel.
From this point forward, only that which has been poured through the filter is placed into the Pūtabhṛt. He then draws the Pavamāna cups.
With the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; for Prajāpati thee," he should touch the Droṇakalaśa; with "For Indra thee," the Ādhavanīya; and with "For the Viśve Devas thee," the Pūtabhṛt.
As they go out, they maintain contact with one another.
The Prastotṛ takes hold of the Adhvaryu; the Pratihartṛ, the Pratihartṛ; the Udgātṛ, the Udgātṛ; the Brahman, the Brahman; and the sacrificer, the sacrificer—so say some authorities.

Where an action is prescribed as an auxiliary to the agent but no specific direction is given, it should be understood that the right hand is to be used, for it is the hand that brings actions to completion.

Having crept out, [he offers] with the verses: "Thy drop which falls," "Three drops of thine which fall," and "Thy stalk, that which is within and that which is beyond the sky; may this god Bṛhaspati pour that together as wealth. Having offered the Vaipruṣa oblations and the Saptahotṛ formula, they move northward, bowing low, for the *barhiṣpavamāna* laud. "The Gāyatra path, the Vasus as the deity; by the path of the wolf, the one who does not stray, may I safely reach the Vasus. "May Speech, going in front, go at the head, going straight"—with these words, the Adhvaryu first creeps forward, slightly shaking a handful of sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
Having sat down to the south of the *cātvāla* pit and looking at the *cātvāla* from within the altar, they chant the *vahiṣpavamāna* laud.

While handing a handful of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) to the *prastotr*, he introduces the chant with the formula: "Vāyu is indeed the maker," and [the *adhvaryu* continues]: "Speech has been released; Indra’s power has been released; turn back, O priests! Approach, O sacrificer!
This same procedure is followed for all the *pavamāna* lauds.
"Turn hither!"—with these words [the priests address] the other hymns from the *barhis*.
While the *bahispavamāna* is being chanted, the Brāhmaṇas approach it together; they repel what is hateful. || 12 ||
Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the eighth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

Now begins the fifth paṭala in the eighth praśna: "O Āgnīdhra, distribute the fires; strew the sacrificial grass; prepare the *puroḍāśa* cakes; O Pratiprasthātṛ, come with the animal victim!"—thus he gives the command as he rises while the *stotra* is being chanted.
Having entered the *havirdhāna* shed, he worships the cups with the verse, "O Viṣṇu, you are our nearest," and touches the vessels.
The *āgnīdhra* priest, having brought embers from the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth, distributes them over the *dhiṣṇiya* altars according to where they were originally placed, using those same formulas.

The *adhvaryu*, having taken the King Soma into the fourfold cup and the fivefold-drawn clarified butter, sits facing west in front [of the shed] and sprinkles the *dhiṣṇiya* altars with the butter according to where they were originally placed, using those same formulas.
He offers the Soma to the Āhavanīya, the Āgnīdhrīya, the Hotrīya, and the Mārjālīya fires, and the other fires with clarified butter.
He utters the *vaṣaṭ* call while passing over [the fires].
The consumption of the Soma has been explained.
Having continuously strewn the sacrificial grass (barhis) along the spine [of the altar], the Āgnīdhra prepares the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa).
He proceeds with the animal victim.
The Adhvaryu draws the cup for the Aśvins with the verse, "O ye two, that whip of yours which is honey-sweet..."
Having spread a base of ghee from the *droṇakalaśa* with the *pariplava* ladle and having drawn [the juice] from the *pūtabhṛt*, he pours an oblation over it from the *droṇakalaśa*.
This is the ritual procedure for all the *grahas*.
Having set that down and having encircled the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with a triple-twisted cord, he dedicates the animal victim for Agni belonging to the *savanīya* offering.
There is no fixed rule regarding its form.
When the omentum has been offered, they proceed to the procession; having approached by way of the openings for the cups, they move forward together.
"Two oceans" refers to the *droṇakalaśa* and the *ādhavanīya*.
With "The two firm ones," he addresses the *pūtabhṛt* vessel; with "Encompassing Agni," he addresses the entire *soma*.

With "For my out-breathing (prāṇa)! he [offers] the Upāṃśu vessel; with "For my in-breathing (apāna)! the Antaryāma; with "For my diffused breathing (vyāna)! the Upāṃśusavana stone; with "For my speech (vāc)! the Aindravāyava cup; with "For my will and insight (dakṣakratu)! the Maitrāvaruṇa cup; with "For my two eyes (cakṣus)! the Śukra and Manthin cups; with "For my hearing (śrotra)! the Āśvina cup; with "For my self (ātman)! the Āgrayaṇa; with "For my limbs (aṅga)! the Ukthya; with "For my life-span (āyus)! the Dhruva; with "For my vigor (vīrya)! the Atigrāhya cups; and with "For my luster (tejas)!", "for my strength (ojas)!", and "for my splendor (varcas)!"—with these, according to their respective forms, he joins everywhere the formula: "O giver of splendor, purify yourself for splendor. || 13 ||

With the formula, "Thou art the belly of Viṣṇu," [he touches] the *droṇakalaśa*; with "Thou art the belly of Indra," the *ādhavanīya*; and with "Thou art the belly of the All-gods (*viśve devāḥ*)," the *pūtabhṛt*. In every case, he appends the verse, "O giver of splendor, purify yourself for my splendor. With the formula, "Who art thou? What is thy name? he looks at the entire King Soma without distinction.
One who desires prosperity, one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), one who is ill, one desiring food, or one practicing sorcery should look [at it].
With the formula, "The wooden sword (*sphyah*) is well-being," he deposits the implements used for making the altar on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) according to their respective forms.
"O you worthy of sacrifice, performers of sacrifice, stay!"—with these words [he addresses] all [the priests].
"May Heaven and Earth be near me"—[this refers to] Heaven and Earth.
"Near the place of praise"—[this refers to] where they chant the *bahiṣpavamāna* hymn.

He approaches the *droṇakalaśa* with "Upakalaśa"; the Soma with "Upasoma"; Agni with "Upāgni"; the gods with "Upadevāḥ"; the sacrifice with "Upayajña"; and the *hotṛ*s with "Upahave hotrā upahvayantām.

He appends [the formula] everywhere according to its form: "hvayatām," "hvayetām," and "hvayantām. He stands near the *āhavanīya* fire with the words: "Homage to Agni, the slayer of Makha; may the glory of Makha not depart from me."

"Obeisance to Rudra, the slayer of Makha; having paid obeisance, protect me"—with these words [he addresses] the Āgnīdhra fire. "Obeisance to Indra, the slayer of Makha; do not destroy my sensory power and my vigor"—with these words [he addresses] the Hotrīya fire. "Obeisance to Yama, the slayer of Makha; having paid obeisance, protect me"—with these words [he addresses] the Mārjālīya fire.
"Be firm, O you two loose ones"—this refers to the two pressing-boards.
According to some, he looks at heaven and earth with the formula "Heaven and Earth! He joins the word "protect" (pātu) everywhere:

"May the god Sūrya protect me from celestial distress," [with which] he addresses Sūrya; "Vāyu from the intermediate space," [with which] Vāyu; "Agni from the earth," [with which] Agni; "Yama from the fathers," [with which] Yama; "Sarasvatī from men," [with which] Sarasvatī. He appends "protect" (pātu) in each case.

With "Homage to the two goddesses at the doors," he pays homage to the two door-posts; with "Homage to the assembly," the assembly; with "Homage to the lord of the assembly," the lord of the assembly; with "Homage to the eyes of the friends who go before," the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); with "Homage to heaven," heaven; and with "Homage to earth," the earth.

With "O serpent of the son-in-law's house," he throws away a blade of grass or a clod of earth from where he is about to sit, touches water, and sits down with the formula, "May I go along the downward and upward paths. Having moved forward to the assembly hall (*sadas*), he should gaze toward the southern half [of the altar] with the words, "Come, O fathers."
Here he instructs the animal victim.
While being cooked, it remains lying around all the pressings, or it is cooked at the third pressing.
8.6 Now begins the sixth chapter of the eighth book.
Having placed the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) and having taken portions from them equally, he proceeds with the offering.

Having spread a layer [of ghee] in the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, having taken the portions, and having poured ghee over them, he issues the two calls: "Recite the invitatory verse for the cakes for Indra at the morning pressing," and "Prompt the Hotṛ to recite the offering verse for the cakes set forth for Indra at the morning pressing."
Having poured the contents of the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*, he issues the calls: "Recite for Agni" and "Prompt for Agni" at the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
The *prāśitra* and the *iḍā* are prepared; having taken the *prāśitra*, he does not take the *iḍā*.
For the offerings to the dual deities, for the two *marutvatīya* cups, for the *āditya* cup, for the *sāvitra* cup, and for the *hāriyojana* cup, there are both invitatory and offering verses.
In the other Soma offerings where there are *yājyās*,
both the *āśruta* and *pratyāśruta* calls, as well as the *yājyā-saṃpraisha*, have been explained.
In those [offerings] that possess *puronuvākyās*, the *puronuvākyā-saṃpraisha* is likewise explained.
Having taken up either a *graha* or a *camasa*, he causes the announcement (*āśrāvayati*) to be made as in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
Standing in the *āgnīdhra* shed facing south and holding the wooden sword (*sphya*), the *āgnīdhra* priest responds with the counter-announcement (*pratyāśrāvayati*). This has already been explained.
However, the *saṃpraiṣas* (directions) and the *yājyās* (offering verses) consist of the *ekadhanas*.

There, having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* and after the response has been given, the Adhvaryu issues the direction to the Maitrāvaruṇa, saying, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for such-and-such"; he then urges the Hotṛ.
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers the oblation; when the second *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, having offered, he brings forward the portion for consumption.
This is the ritual procedure for all Soma offerings.

In the cups for the dual deities during the seasonal offerings, as well as in the Āditya cup and the Sāvitra cup, there is no *anuvaṣaṭkāra*. Regarding the Śukra and Manthin cups and the Pātnīvata cup, it is optional.
They proceed with the dual-deity offerings.

The Pratiprasthātṛ takes a portion of the Aindravāyava cup as a secondary draught (*pratinirgrāhya*) using the Āditya vessel, saying: "Thou art taken with a support; for Vāyu, for Indra and Vāyu, thee!"
And he takes a second [cup] from the *droṇakalaśa* with the formulas: "Thou art taken with a support; thou art the seat of the dice."
The Adhvaryu takes the cup for Indra and Vāyu from the *droṇakalaśa*, and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the King Soma as the *pratiprasthāya* portion by means of the *pariplu* ladle.
Having gone out, he pours the *āghāra* libation with the *pariplu* ladle while reciting, "May this sacrifice be a peaceful one, O Gods," so that it becomes offered like the *upāṃśu* cup.
He issues the summons: "Recite for Vāyu and Indra-Vāyu! Prompt for Vāyu and Indra-Vāyu! Thus he gives the command.
They offer at the *vaṣaṭ*-call; they offer again at the second *vaṣaṭ*-call.

The Pratiprasthātṛ pours the residue from the Adhvaryu’s cup into his own; the Adhvaryu pours a portion of that into the Pratiprasthātṛ’s cup. With the words "For the gods, thee," the Pratiprasthātṛ pours the residue from the Āditya-vessel into the Āditya-sthālī. || 15 ||
With "O Viṣṇu, wide-strider," he covers [the vessel].
With "In me is wealth, in front is wealth," the Adhvaryu hands the portion to the Hotṛ.
With that same formula, the Hotṛ receives it.
In this manner, they proceed with the two subsequent [mantras] according to the respective deities.
For the two subsequent [mantras], he does not draw from the *droṇakalaśa* vessel, nor is there an *āghāra* libation for the two subsequent ones.
With each subsequent mantra, he draws once and both offer once.

With each subsequent [pouring], the Pratiprasthātṛ pours the residue into the Aditya vessel; with that very [residue] he covers [the vessel] at every instance. With each subsequent [pouring], the Adhvaryu hands the portion for consumption to the Hotṛ; with this same [formula] the Hotṛ receives it:

"I have performed [the rite] for the sons of Diti, for Aditi, who provide wide shelter, who are great and possess protective armor—those whose abodes are established according to their stations, and whom all beings worship with various [offerings]"—or he covers [the vessel] at every instance with this [formula].
If he should desire, "May evil befall him," then having drawn first with the Pratiprasthātṛ, he should offer while standing first; having offered first, he should set it down.
If he should desire, "May I be of equal strength with my rival," they should draw simultaneously, offer simultaneously, and set them down simultaneously.
According to some, one should draw [the Soma] at the time of the *dhārāgraha* (the first stream). At this point, he removes the vessels.

If he should desire, "May I remove from the village him who is in the village, and place in the village him who is outside the village," then the Adhvaryu should remove the vessel with the formula: "This one, the son of such-a-one and grandson of such-a-one, I remove from such-a people. The Pratiprasthātṛ should set down the vessel with the formula: "This one, the son of such-a-one and grandson of such-a-one, I set down in such-a people. This is the ritual procedure connected with the sacrifice.
Having poured the *ādhavanīya* vessel into the *pūtabhṛt*, and having wiped the jar with the fringes (*daśā*), he turns it face down.

The Hotṛ, Brahman, Udgātṛ, Sacrificer, and Sadasya are the "central performers" (*madhyataḥ kāriṇaḥ*). The Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, Acchāvāka, and Āgnīdhra are the "Hotṛ-assistants" (*hotrakāḥ*).
Both [the sacrificer and the priests] are cup-holders; for all of them, there is a separate cup-attendant (camasādhvaryu) for each person.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the eighth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.

Now begins the seventh chapter in the eighth book. He issues the command: "Recite for those being drawn out; draw out the cups following that of the Hotṛ; make them bright on both sides; O Adhvaryu of the Acchāvāka’s cup, do not you draw [your cup]; O Pratiprasthātṛ, prepare the wood-shavings, both sprinkled and unsprinkled; O Unnetṛ, cause the Soma to flow forth. Thus he gives the direction.
He draws ten goblets, headed by the *hotṛ*’s goblet, but not those of the *acchāvāka*.
The *unnetṛ* uses the *pariplava* ladle: having made an under-layer of butter from the *droṇakalaśa*, having drawn [the soma] from the *pūtabhṛt*, he pours [butter] over it from the *droṇakalaśa*.
This is the procedure for all the goblets.
While that hymn is being chanted as they have set forth, when it has been concluded, the two of them take up the two cups with the *sāvitra* formula:
the Adhvaryu takes the *śukra* cup and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the *manthin* cup;
the Camasādhvaryus take up their respective goblets.

With the two sprinkled chips, they cover [the cups] for the Śukra and Manthin [deities], saying: "Śaṇḍa and Marka are driven away along with him whom we hate. With the two unsprinkled chips, they scatter dust beneath [the cups] and take hold of them with those very chips.

The Adhvaryu carries the Śukra cup, saying: "Thou art praised, O nourisher of people; may the gods who drink the Śukra lead thee forth. The Pratiprasthātṛ carries the Manthin cup, saying: "Thou art praised, O nourisher of people; may the gods who drink the Manthin lead thee forth.
Some authorities prescribe that they both carry them together; they proceed, saying: "The wide atmosphere!"

"Join the life-span; quicken that for me! Join the out-breath; quicken that for me! Join the in-breath; quicken that for me! Join the diffused breath; quicken that for me! Join the eye; quicken that for me! Join the ear; quicken that for me! Join the mind; quicken that for me! Join the speech; quicken that for me!"—with these words, they join their forearms or the vessels at the front of the *havirdhāna* sheds. With the formula "Thou art unassailable," they step upon the high altar (*uttaravedi*) with both thumbs.
Moving around it in opposite directions, they circumambulate it.

"O bright one, of bright luster, go around, procreating offspring rich in heroes"—with these words the Adhvaryu carries [the cup] by the south. "O churning one, of churning luster, go around, procreating offspring rich in progeny"—with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ carries [the cup] by the north.
"May you two quicken; enjoy the honeyed [draught] on a good path"—with these words the sacrificer consecrates them while standing in front of the Āhavanīya fire.
They stand facing west, on both sides of the sacrificial post, to the east [of it].
Then the cup-attendants (camasādhvaryus) move toward the east.

The Adhvaryu joins [the cups] with the formula, "The bright one, with bright luster, has come together from heaven and earth," and the Pratiprasthātṛ joins them with, "The stirred one, with stirred luster, has come together from heaven and earth"; they join either their forearms or the vessels together. || 17 ||

You two are life; bestow life upon me, bestow life upon the sacrifice, bestow life upon the lord of the sacrifice. You two are breath; bestow breath upon me, bestow breath upon the sacrifice, bestow breath upon the lord of the sacrifice. You two are sight; bestow sight upon me, bestow sight upon the sacrifice, bestow sight upon the lord of the sacrifice. You two are hearing; bestow hearing upon me, bestow hearing upon the sacrifice, bestow hearing upon the lord of the sacrifice. O you two gods, Śukra and Manthin, bring them into order.

"O divine subjects, arrange yourselves; bestow upon us human food and vigor, breath in the cattle, and offspring both in me and in the sacrificer"—with these words they both consecrate [the two chips].

They both place the two sprinkled chips [on the fire]: the Adhvaryu says, "Thou art the support of the Śukra; this is thy fuel, O Śukra; by it mayest thou be kindled," and the Pratiprasthātṛ says, "Thou art the support of the Manthin; this is thy fuel, O Manthin; by it mayest thou be kindled."

"Rebuffed is Śaṇḍa, rebuffed is Marka; both Śaṇḍa and Marka are driven away along with him whom we hate"—with these words, having touched water, they throw out the two unsprinkled [portions] outside the altar.

"Prompt the Hotṛ for the Soma-pressings of the morning, which are bright, stirred by churning, and dripping with sweetness; for Indra, the Somas have been set forth! Having thus issued the command—"O Camasādhvaryus of the central officiants, offer the cups at the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*; O Camasādhvaryus of the Hotrakas, having offered each once, replenish them from the *śukra* vessel and return"—they all offer simultaneously at the *vaṣaṭ*.

"He is the first Saṃkṛti Viśvakarman; he is the first Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni; he is the first Bṛhaspati, the wise one—to that Indra I offer the pressed [juice], svāhā!"—thus says the Adhvaryu. "To that Mitra I offer the pressed [juice], svāhā!"—thus says the Pratiprasthātṛ. Some prescribe both [libations] as having the *vaṣaṭ* call repeated (*sānuvaṣaṭkāra*); some [prescribe them] as not having the *vaṣaṭ* call repeated (*ananuvaṣaṭkāra*); others [prescribe] only one of the two as having the *vaṣaṭ* call repeated.

Having drawn out a coal from the Āhavanīya fire outside the enclosing sticks toward the north-east, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers this residue of the *manthin* cup as a complete oblation into it with the formula, "This is thy portion, O Rudra.
At the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call, the Camasādhvaryus of the central officiants offer their portions.
He issues the command: "Let the Hotṛ’s cup go forward; let the Brahman’s, the Udgātṛ’s, the Sacrificer’s, and the Sadasya’s go forward!"
They set down the sacrificial portions.
He sets down the *śukra* cup like that of the *sūda*.
Having each offered once, the *camasādhvaryus* of the *hotrakas* return after pouring [the remnants] over the *śukra* cup.
With these [soma portions], the Adhvaryu proceeds.

Having taken the cup of the Maitrāvaruṇa, he issues the command, "O Praśāstṛ, recite the offering-verse! Having offered it at the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ*, he hands it over to the Camasādhvaryu and carries it to the Sadas for consumption.
He proceeds in the same manner with the subsequent [cups]. || 18 ||
"O Brahman, sacrifice!"—thus [he addresses] the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; "O Potar, sacrifice!"—thus the Potar; "O Neṣṭar, sacrifice!"—thus the Neṣṭar; "O Āgnīdhra, sacrifice!"—thus the Āgnīdhra.
Having taken his cup, he goes to the Sadas and announces to the Hotṛ: "The Āgnīdhra has sacrificed. The Hotṛ replies: "He has performed a blessing; he will cause us to drink Soma."
The Adhvaryu’s portion for consumption arises from the oblation and the pressing; that of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterers from the *vaṣaṭ* call; and that of the *camasins* from their designation.
The *vaṣaṭ*-utterer consumes first, then the Adhvaryu, and finally the *camasin*.

In the case of an interruption between two oblations, an interruption between two consumptions, or an interruption between two *vaṣaṭ* calls, there is consumption of the remainder and the taking up [of the vessel]. This also applies when two [portions] not taken separately come together.
The consumption of Soma is indeed prescribed for the Vaiśya and the Rājanya.

If a non-Brāhmaṇa should desire to drink Soma, he should fetch *udumbara* shoots, crush them, mix them with curds, and strain them. Then, when he draws out the other cups, he draws this cup of the sacrificer from that same [supply]. When he offers the other cups, he takes a portion of this [cup] with a young blade of Darbha grass, removes a coal from the Āhavanīya fire within the enclosing sticks, and offers it with the formula, "I am thou. When he consumes the other cups, the sacrificer consumes this cup. They consume the cups belonging to the dual deities.
The Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Pratiprasthātṛ—
thus in this sequence—
they desire the invitation (upahava) from one another.
"Upahvayasva" (invite) is the invitation;
"Upahūtaḥ" (invited) is the response. Whenever they might consume [the food] at the same time, they should seek an invitation from one another.

He consumes the Aindravāyava cup twice, and each of the other two cups once. He places the Aindravāyava cup upon the vital breaths at the front; he places the Maitrāvaruṇa cup upon the eyes at the front; and he places the Āśvina cup upon the ears by moving it all around. Having consumed all of them, they do not release their hold until the pouring down [of the remnants].

Having poured all the remnants into the Hotṛ’s cup, he places a piece of the sacrificial cake in the vessel for Indra and Vāyu, the curd-mixture in the vessel for Mitra and Varuṇa, and the parched grains in the vessel for the Aśvins. He sets these down on the northern track of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, where they remain until the third pressing.
Having performed the cutting-off, he places the *iḍā* portion before the Hotṛ.
As it is being invoked, the cup-bearers (*camasādhvaryus*) lift up their respective cups.
He holds the *hotṛ*’s cup so that it touches [the others].
They consume the portion when it has been invited, as they do in the archetype.
He places a fragment of the *iḍā* for the *acchāvāka*, after the [portion] has been consumed and he has performed the purification.
He proceeds with the Vājina offering as in the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. || 19 ||
He commences the rites for the *savanīya* offerings beginning with the *mārjana* (sprinkling), as in the case of the *paśupuroḍāśa* at the *nirūḍhapaśubandha*.
The cup-bearers consume [the soma] according to their respective cups; the formula for their consumption has been explained.
The Hotṛ, being first among all, consumes once from each [cup], and twice from his own cup again.

The Adhvaryu consumes twice from those [cups] that have been brought forward and have already been consumed; the Hotrakas consume once each at the end. Without having consumed all of them, they cause them to swell with the mantra, "Swell up! Let [the essence] come together unto thee! Thus they become the Nārāśaṃsa cups.

He places them behind the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, extending toward the north. He places the two cups of the *neṣṭṛ* and the *āgnīdhra* between [the two carts]. The *acchāvāka* sits down in front of his own *dhiṣṇya* hearth, outside the *sadas*.
For him, [the *hotṛ*] takes a fragment of the sacrificial cake and says: "O *acchāvāka*, speak what is to be spoken by you.
When it is said by the *acchāvāka*, "Call the Brahmins hither for us, O Brahmins," he issues the command: "This *acchāvāka* desires an invitation; O *hotṛ*, invite him."
When he recognizes that the Hotṛ has called upon him, at that moment he takes the cup of the Acchāvāka and issues the command: "Recite for the one being filled!

When that [verse] has been concluded, he issues the command: "Acchāvāka, recite the offering prayer! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers; at the subsequent *vaṣaṭ* (anuvaṣaṭ), having offered, he brings the portion for consumption.
He does not consume it together with that [cup].
He does not desire an invitation to this [cup].
If he were to desire an invitation to this, he should simply say, "Consume it.
Having consumed it and performed the swelling rite, he places the two cups between those of the Neṣṭṛ and the Āgnīdhra.
This very [cup] is henceforth the place for the Acchāvāka’s goblet. ||20||
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the eighth book of the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra*.
Now begins the eighth chapter in the eighth book.

They proceed with the *ṛtugraha* cups—either twelve, thirteen, or fourteen. If there are twelve, they offer all the oblations separately; if there are thirteen, two of them together; if there are fourteen, the first two together and the last two together.
The cups are drawn while still in the vessel.
The remnant of each preceding one is poured over each succeeding one.

"Thou art taken with a support; for Madhu thee!"—with these words the Adhvaryu draws the first cup with his own vessel; "Thou art taken with a support; for Mādhava thee!"—with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ draws the subsequent one with his own vessel.
They take hold of the interlocking [vessels]:
the Adhvaryu first and the Pratiprasthātṛ second.
The Adhvaryu uses each preceding mantra, while the Pratiprasthātṛ uses each succeeding one.
The Adhvaryu moves along the south and the Pratiprasthātṛ along the north;
they should not pass one another.
He encircles the Adhvaryu with the cup as he enters and with the vessel as he goes out.

The Adhvaryu gives the command with the word "Ṛtu" three times; the Pratiprasthātṛ responds three times. Having turned the mouths of the two vessels upside down, the Adhvaryu gives the command with the words "With the Ṛtus" twice; the Pratiprasthātṛ responds twice. Again, having turned the mouths upside down, the Adhvaryu gives the command with the word "Ṛtu" once; the Pratiprasthātṛ responds once.
When it is said, "O two Adhvaryus, sacrifice," the Hotṛ issues the command, "Sacrifice!
or he sacrifices himself after sitting down.
The Pratiprasthātṛ pours the residue from the Adhvaryu’s cup into his own; the Adhvaryu pours a portion of that into the Pratiprasthātṛ’s cup.
They consume [the soma] by means of the Pratiprasthāna formula:
the Hotṛ twice, and each of the others once.
At the *vaṣaṭ*-call of whichever [deity], they offer; that very [portion] each of them consumes.
Having washed the vessel at the Mārjālīya fire, he places it in its proper station. || 21 ||

With the verse, "O Indra and Agni, come to the pressed [juice]," he draws the draught for Indra and Agni from the *kalaśa* vessel using his own cup, which has not yet been consumed, accompanied by a *śastra*.
Having set it down and sat down facing east in front of the *hotṛ*, he introduces the *śastra* with the formula, "The *iḍā* is the invoker of the gods.
At the moment when the *hotṛ* calls out to him, he responds at that time with "Śoṃsāmo daiva," or "Śoṃsāmo daivodhāmo daiva."
Rising and turning to the right, he first receives the response (*pratigara*), facing [the reciter] at first and thereafter standing upright or slightly stooping.
This applies at all pauses and at every *praṇava*.
He does not omit [the response] after a half-verse.
The *nābhi* does not respond;
he utters both [responses] during the *vyāhāva*: "śoṃsāmo daiva" and "othāmo daiva. Wherever the *hotṛ* should pause, he should announce: "othāmo daiva."
This is the ritual procedure for all the vessels (*śastra*).

Having swallowed the *śastra*, he takes up the cup; the *camasādhvaryus* [take up] their cups. He issues the command: "O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice the Soma! They shake the *nārāśaṃsa* cups following the *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* calls.
The consumption of the cups and the *nārāśaṃsas* has been explained.
And [the same applies] to the swelling and the placing of the Nārāśaṃsa cups. || 22 ||
With the verse, "O you who protect men, supporters of the people," he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup from the *kalaśa* vessel using the *śukra* cup, accompanied by its *stotra* and *śastra*.
Having set it down, he introduces the *stotra*; that has been explained.
When the *stotra* is concluded, he introduces the *śastra*; that has been explained.

Having thrown away the *śastra*, he takes up the *graha* and the *camasa*s. He issues the call: "O Adhvaryus, for the reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice the Soma! The procedure for the shaking of the vessels has been explained; the consumption of the *graha*s and *nārāśaṃsa*s involves consuming the entire contents.
There is no replenishing or setting down [of the vessels]. They proceed with three *ukthya-vigraha* offerings.
"Thou art taken with a support; for Mitra and Varuṇa, thee!"—with these words, he draws the third portion for Mitra and Varuṇa from the Ukthya-vessel using the Ukthya-cup.
"This is thy womb; for Mitra and Varuṇa, thee!"—with these words, he deposits it in its place.
"Thou art a renewed oblation," he says, touching the vessel again.
He draws eleven cups, with the cup of Maitrāvaruṇa as the principal one.
He draws the cup for the Acchāvāka before the cup for the Āgnīdhra; the *stotra* and *śastra* take place.
Having responded to the *śastra*, he takes up the *graha* cup and issues the command to the *camasādhvaryus*: "O reciter of the *uktha*, offer the Soma! || 23 ||

Having offered [the portion] with the formula, "I fill thee, who art dear to the gods, for the gods, for the prosperity of the sacrifice, as one who is beloved," he pours the residue of the draught into the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup. Having touched it outside the Sadas, if the Adhvaryu should desire, "May I endow myself with the glory of the sacrifice," there are various ways of pouring it out explained in the Brāhmaṇa; regarding these, he may act according to his wish.

The Maitrāvaruṇa drinks first from all [the cups], drinking once each time; he drinks twice from his own cup, and the Adhvaryu drinks once from that which has been drunk by him twice; the Maitrāvaruṇa drinks the third time.
Thereafter, the Pratiprasthātṛ proceeds with the two subsequent Ukthya-vigrahas, accompanied by Stotra and Śastra, according to this same ritual procedure.
At the second [libation], he performs the drawing and setting down with the formula, "For Indra thee! He touches the vessel again with the formula, "Thou art the oblation again.

While pouring out the cups, beginning with that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, he leaves over the King Soma for one cup-group. He pours the residue from the draught-cup into the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin's cup; the Pratiprasthātṛ does not consume it.
At the third [libation], he performs the drawing and setting down with the formula, "For Indra and Agni thee!"

He does not touch the vessel. Having drawn the cups beginning with that of the Acchāvāka, he draws the entire King Soma, giving the command: "Do not leave any remainder; having wiped the two jars with the fringes of the cloth, turn them upside down."
He draws the cups beginning with that of the Acchāvāka; he draws the entire King Soma, not leaving any remainder.
Having wiped the two jars with ten stalks, he turns them face down.
He pours the residue from the draught-cup into the Acchāvāka’s cup; the Pratiprasthātṛ does not consume it.

When the ritual has concluded with the words, "May Agni protect us at the morning pressing," he offers the oblation; he then issues the command, "O Praśāstṛ, give the impulse! and the Praśāstṛ says, "Crawl forward!"
The morning pressing concludes; the morning pressing concludes. || 24 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the eighth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra. This eighth book is complete. [Chapter 10] Accompanied by the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 763
Now begins the eighth question;
therein is the first chapter:
they awaken at the dead of night.

"rātremahānbhāgo mahārātraṃ; tasmin mahārātre rātryā yo mahān bhāgas tasmin"—this is the meaning. This is a compound according to the rule for *mayūravyaṃsaka* and similar formations. The suffix of the compound (*samāsānta*) and the elision of the first member (*pūrvapadalopa*) occur because it belongs to that class. In such an interpretation, if the two Soma-pressings were to be performed together, the phrase "he should commence the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) for the great night" found in the Śruti—where the discrepancy in grammatical case (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) caused by the difference in gender between the words *rātri* and *mahat* serves as the supporting evidence.

The analysis of the compound as "mahatī cāsau rātriḥ" (this is a great night) is simply not possible here. If "greatness" were a qualifier of the night, then that greatness would reside in the night; however, such greatness caused by duration is entirely impossible in the spring, because the nights become progressively shorter. Greatness among the nights occurs only during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*). If that were the case, the awakening ceremony would have to take place only when the nights are actually long; and since the awakening is for the purpose of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*), it would consequently have to be performed at that very time.

Or rather, the performance [of the ritual] should take place only during the spring night, because that [night] alone is significant. Since that would contradict what is under discussion here, such an analysis of the compound is not appropriate in this context. By this, one should see that the baseless fabrication—which claims that just as the dative *rātriyai* in the immediately cited scripture functions in the sense of a genitive, so too the locative case-ending in the word *mahatī* must signify a genitive, and that even the masculine gender should be altered accordingly to conform to this—is refuted.

In this context, by the word "great" (*mahat*), the third part of the night is intended. If one asks what the restrictive rule (*niyāmaka*) is for such a definition of "greatness," it is the very sūtra that will be stated later: *svaramāṇas tv anudita upāṃśu udite 'ntayāmam ubhayānudita ity ekeṣām* ("But [the mantra] is recited loudly when [the sun] has not yet risen; it is whispered when [the sun] has risen; according to some, until the end of the watch, it is both [whispered and loud] when [the sun] has not yet risen"). By this alone we understand that the ritual action—whether ending with the *upāṃśu* or ending with both—must be understood as occurring during the "not-yet-risen" period, in accordance with that duration of time.

By this, it is also understood that [the time] must be understood as consisting of the first portion of the third division of the night. Now, one might ask: "For what purpose is this sūtra, since its meaning is established by implication alone? No; for even though the officiating priests (ṛtvij) are swift performers of their duties, they might otherwise understand [the time] to be at some other point—not before or after this specific moment. Therefore, this sūtra is intended to establish a restrictive rule (niyama).

[Objection: "Even so, O Great King, it is established by the mere fact that 'the ritual acts commence'; there is no need for the statement regarding awakening. [Reply: No, because its purpose is to indicate a specific relationship. Only where there is the instruction regarding awakening is there the commencement of the *prātaranuvāka* before the utterance of speech, and not elsewhere.
