Therefore, it is established that on the twelfth day—specifically the first *sutyā* day known as the *Prāyaṇīyātirātra*—the commencement of the *Prātaranuvāka* for the second *sutyā* day must be performed even when the sun has already risen, because there is no requirement for the ritual of waking (*bodhana*).

By this, it is demonstrated that the view held by some—that on the basis of another scriptural authority stating "wherever the Hotṛ recites the Āśvina[-śastra], there the Maitrāvaruṇa should recite the Prātaranuvāka," the Pratiprasthātṛ alone must perform the rites of the second Soma-day until the Adhvaryu is released from his previous duties, and once the Adhvaryu is released, he himself begins from that point—is not acceptable to us.
In such a manner they commence the ritual acts, so that the Prātaranuvāka occurs before speech has been uttered.

Just as the *prātaranuvāka* (morning recitation) begins prior to the speaking—that is, before the utterance—of humans or birds, so too, in accordance with that, the ritual acts such as the *yajñatanū-homa* (oblation for the body of the sacrifice) and others commence; this is the meaning of "they begin. Furthermore, the commencement of the rite must be performed by those who have already purified themselves; otherwise, there would be no entitlement (*anadhikāra*) to perform the ritual. Some maintain that only those who have bathed should perform the rite.

Others maintain that they are indeed considered *ācānta* (one who has sipped water) once they have washed their hands and feet. Furthermore, it should not be argued that because the *Kalpasūtras* state that after the conclusion of the ritual, having washed their hands and feet, they proceed to the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) by way of the space between the *āśvāla* and *āloka*, and that they approach the sacrificer under the *ānībhra* tree merely by washing their hands and feet, there is no requirement for bathing to gain eligibility for the rite, and that daily bathing occurs only at its prescribed time. This is because [the texts] speak of eligibility for the ritual through the mere washing of hands and feet.

By the statement of Yājñavalkya, "One should not practice that which is contrary to oneself and hated by the world," even the position stated in the Sūtra is set aside. Thus, in the Smṛti, "Having bathed, one should perform the rites," it is declared that only one who has bathed has the qualification (*adhikāra*) to perform the rites; therefore, following the general rule (*sāmānyaśāstra*), it is proper that the rite should be performed according to the specific Sūtra alone. However, it should be understood that this bathing is without mantras (*amantraka*). As for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsti*), however, it must be performed at its own proper time in the middle period.
"Prajāpati, blind with his mind, sought [the sacrifice]"—with these thirty-three mantras known as *yajñatanū* (limbs of the sacrifice), he offers oblations in the Āgnīdhra fire.

Having prepared the clarified butter (*ājya*) according to the Smārta rite, the offering is performed according to the rules of the *davihoma*. The meaning is that he offers thirty-three oblations to be accomplished by those thirty-three mantras beginning with "Prajāpati, with his mind. Among them, the first has four feet; the thirteenth and the thirtieth have three feet; the others have two feet. According to the lexicon, "twenty and so forth" take the singular number. He states a specific detail here:
"Having recited each preceding [verse], one offers with each succeeding one, beginning with the first:

'Prajāpati, blind with the mind, went toward the Soma'—this is the first sacrificial body (yajñatanū). 'Dhātṛ, at the consecration'—this is the subsequent sacrificial body. In this regard, the meaning is that having recited and joined the first sacrificial body, 'Prajāpati, blind with the mind, went toward the Soma,' one offers it with the subsequent sacrificial body, 'Dhātṛ, at the consecration. In the same way, having joined the second sacrificial body, 'Dhātṛ, at the consecration,' one [offers] with the third sacrificial body, 'Savitṛ, at the maintenance.'"

Having joined the third sacrificial body with "Savitṛ [is joined] with the *bhṛti*," and the fourth with "Pūṣan [is joined] with the *somakrayaṇī*," and so on, up to the thirty-third sacrificial body. It is precisely for this purpose that there is repetition (*vāpsā*) in both cases. This joining is indeed in the form of a *saṃhitā*. He states the means for achieving the number thirty-three in the oblations: "With one, indeed, as the first. The particle *nu* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). Thus, the thirty-third oblation is offered with only the very first verse.

The statement "with one" (*ekayā*) would mean that, having recited the final sacrificial body (*yajñatanū*), one offers with the first sacrificial body; for, in relation to the final one, the first is "subsequent" due to its immediate succession, while the final one is "prior" due to its preceding it—this being in accordance with the sūtra rule: "having recited each preceding [verse], [one offers] with each subsequent [verse]. Alternatively, according to the principle that "the final [syllable] is elided and there is expansion," it might mean "with the final sacrificial body characterized by the recitation"; to prevent this from being the case, the word *eka* is used in the sense of "exclusive" (*kevala*).

The mention of "with the first" is for the purpose of precluding the application of the final [verse] alone by that same logic. Because it is enjoined by the word *juhoti* (he offers), the utterance *svāhā* is used. Where it says "with a group of mantras," according to the Pāraskara-Māṣya, it is done with each individual mantra. According to some, one offers in relation to a sacrificial mishap (*yajñārti*). [End of the first section of the Paṭala] Together with the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. Page 765. (Note: The bracketed text *rayai| [1pra0paṭalaḥ]* and the reference to the commentator appear as marginal or structural notes in the source.)

"From the *yajñāti* of the sacrifice"—that is, from the *yajñāti*. *Yajñāti* means excessive destruction (*ativināśa*), that is to say, *ava*. By this, according to the opinion of certain teachers, even the occasional (*naimittika*) nature of this oblation is established. Regarding the term *yajñāti*, it bears the designation of a *karmapravacanīya*. Consequently, it is established that the meaning is "an oblation performed for every *yajñāti*. Now, one might object: "Is not this oblation caused solely by the *yajñāti* consisting in the absence of waking during the third part of the night associated with the *rātrisattra*?"

When the oblation (*homa*) occasioned by this [specific] transgression is due to take place, because the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is more powerful as it serves the purpose of rejoining [the sacrifice], one should first perform the expiation and subsequently perform the obligatory rite. Thus, in the Soma ritual system (*somatantra*) itself, whenever there is an unspecified lapse (*yāvineṣa*), this expiation is to be offered; however, it is not to be performed in the Pāśuka or Āgniṣṭomika systems.

In the subsequent sūtra, by the mere statement "he initiates the procedure (*tantra*) for the *savanīya* animal," the knowledge that this is the *pāśuka-tantra* (the ritual procedure pertaining to the animal sacrifice) is already established; nevertheless, the inclusion of the word "animal" (*paśu*) serves to indicate that the offering of the "limbs of the sacrifice" (*yajñatanū-homa*) is indeed connected to the *soma-tantra*, and that in the absence of a specific injunction, this very offering is the one to be performed. Furthermore, due to its superior capacity for removing defects, even the *sarvaprāyaścitta* (universal expiation) must be offered. From the expression "one who has committed a single [fault]" (*ekapātin*), it is understood that the nature of being an expiation is only optional (*pākṣika*).
He initiates the procedure for the *savanīya* animal.

The animal sacrifice belonging to each pressing-day (*savanīya-paśu*) occurs on every day of the *sautya* [pressing] period; he begins—that is, commences—the entire sequence of ritual acts for that animal sacrifice. Its procedure (*kalpa*) has been explained by [the rules for] the *nirūḍha-paśubandha* (the independent animal sacrifice).

Regarding that *savanīya* [animal sacrifice]: other matters have already been explained in the context of the *āgnīṣomīya*. The *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* offering and the *paśviṣṭi* do not exist here, because the animal sacrifice is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the ritual. Since the ritual actions up to the leading forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) have already been performed, they are omitted. Furthermore, there is an absence of the *anvādhāna* (kindling of the fires) due to the prohibition: "In the *savanīya* animal sacrifice, the *anvādhāna* does not take place. By the rule stating "starting from the *prāyaṇīyā*," there is an absence of the entering of the forest (*vanopāyana*) and so forth.
No sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is used; he brings only the *prastara* (grass-bundle) according to the ritual procedure for the *barhis*.

The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the animal sacrifice is brought from elsewhere; however, the sacrificial grass for the rubbish-heap (*utkara-barhis*) certainly exists. Now, one might object: "By the very word 'only' (*eva*) in the rule 'he brings only the *prastara* according to the ritual procedure of the *barhis*,' the exclusion of other *barhis* is already established. Why, then, is there this further prohibition stating that 'no [other] *barhis* exists'? If this is asked, the answer is no. If it were merely stated, "He brings the *prastara* according to the ritual procedure of the *barhis*," the exclusion of other *barhis* would not necessarily follow. Rather, such a statement would only effect an exclusion regarding the specific ritual procedure applied to the *barhis* during its bringing. It would not preclude the existence of other *barhis* altogether. Therefore, the explicit prohibition is necessary to ensure that no other *barhis* is used at all.

And thus, since there would otherwise be a silent bringing [of everything], it is necessary to have a prohibition in order to exclude that. If it were merely stated, "It does not exist outside," then the exclusion of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) from being outside would also follow; therefore, the statement "He brings the *prastara*" is for the purpose of excluding that. The word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "he brings only the *prastara*" connects with the word "brings" (*āharati*). Thus, the meaning becomes: he brings it by means of the ritual procedure for the *barhis* (sacrificial grass) alone, and not even the binding-cord.

In this very manner, the particle *eva* becomes meaningful; by it, that which was established as a binding (*saṃnahanam*) through Āpastamba’s sūtra—"He binds these [grass-blades] outside, or he does not bind the *prastara* outside"—and which was indicated by the commentators as a supplementary rule, is excluded. The preparation of the cord (*śulvakaraṇam*) is solely for the purpose of the *utkara* (the rubbish heap) and not for the sake of the *prastara*. For the purpose of the *utkara*, one performs everything from the preparation of the cord up to the end with the words "may it not stand upon thee."

"I am gathering well-prepared materials; I gather them well-prepared. (Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Book 8, Chapter 7, Section 66). This [formula] does not exist for the *śulba* because of its very non-existence. "Around the womb" (*abhito yoni*)—this also does not exist for the same reason just mentioned. In the case of the external gathering of the *utkara*, it is precisely this [formula]: "Āpas tvām" and "Indrasya svā"; having placed these two at the beginning of the *prastara*, he performs them for the *utkara* and the *barhis*. From "Bṛhaspater mūrdhā harāmi" up to the end of the placement, both are performed together.

In the mantra "urvantarikṣaṃ prehī" (go through the wide atmosphere), there is no modification (*ūha*). This is because the action of going is connected only to the self (*ātman*), and thus a connection with anything external is impossible. The intended connection with the self is as follows: "O Self, having gone toward the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the purpose of cutting it—as if through the wide atmosphere—return from there and go forth (*prehi*), that is, proceed specifically toward the place of sacrifice. Now, one might ask: "Why not let the connection here be with the sacrificial grass itself? What is the obstacle? To this it must be said: [The obstacle is that] the action of going cannot logically belong to the grass. Since the grass is stationary, it is impossible for it to perform the act of moving; therefore, the action of going must necessarily be attributed to the agent who is capable of such movement. Consequently, the mantra is addressed to the self. Furthermore, since the self is the primary factor in the ritual procedure, it is logical that the mantra should relate to it. Thus, there is no need for modification. Therefore, the mantra remains as it is.

In the preceding case, there is indeed such a modification because of deviation [from the archetype], because the mantra is seen to be an instrument for the act of placing, and because the agent of the act of placing is singular. In the phrase "He sat upon the seat of Aditi" (*ādityāḥ sada āsīdat*), the dual ending occurs as "you two sat" (*āsīdatam*) precisely because it expresses two external objects. Likewise, in the two phrases "attaining the world of the gods" (*devaṃgama*) and "I place you on the back of Aditi" (*ādityāstvā pṛṣṭhe sādayāmi*), the form "you two are world-attainers" (*devaṃgame sthaḥ*) and "I place you two on the back of Aditi" (*ādityā vāṃ pṛṣṭhe sādayāmi*) are the respective modifications.

He brings the handful called *paribhojanīya* (for personal consumption) along with the handful of *mūlparājya* (root-clarified butter), silently and in the natural manner. In the view that this is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, everything mentioned in the *Paśusūtra*—such as the horse-hair (*āśvavāla*) *prastara*, the *aikṣavī* crosswise-stick, and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made of *kāmayamaya* wood—is indeed present, replacing those made of *pūtudāru*. However, there is no *barhis* (sacrificial grass) at all; for there is no obstacle to the application of the prohibition "there is no *barhis*" here as well.
At the time of arranging the vessels, he employs the *pracaraṇī* ladle first.

By the phrase "at the time of arranging the vessels" (*pātrasaṃsādanakāle*), the spreading of grass (*paristaraṇa*), the washing of the hands (*pāṇiprakṣālana*), the spreading of *ulapa* grass, and the duties of the Brahman and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) along with their respective assistants are indicated. Alternatively, "at the time of arranging the vessels" means "the place for arranging the vessels. Thus, the meaning becomes that the use of the *pracaraṇī* ladle occurs at the place where the vessels are arranged. Furthermore, the use of the word "time" (*kāla*) to denote "place" (*deśa*) is observed in the Baudhāyana Sūtra, in such passages as "that is the time (place) of the *uparava* holes."

And that [place] for the *pracaraṇī* ladle is precisely the northern border-line of the *śālāmukhīya* fire-altar, because it belongs to the Soma sacrifice. Now, one might object: "Is not the place for arranging the vessels used in the *vaiṣṭika* and *pāśuka* sacrifices the very same as that for the *saumikī pracaraṇī*? And if so, how can there be a difference in location? This is true; however, they assign the *śālāmukhīya* to the duties of the *gārhapatya*, because of the scriptural statement: "In that [fire], the duties of the *gārhapatya* are performed. Therefore, the [place] for the *pracaraṇī* of the Soma sacrifice...

Because the *śālāmukhīya* fire is a vessel related to the *karṣman*, the *pracaraṇī* ladle is employed independently immediately to its north; it is not used in the place obtained by the sequence [of the *pāśuka* vessels] according to the rule of pairing (*dvaṃdvatva*), because a difference in location would otherwise result. As for the *veda*, that which is prepared for the sake of the *mahāvedī* itself is spread with *darbha* grass to the north of the *śālāmukhīya*, and upon it one arranges the *pāśuka* vessels as required. Therein, one arranges the *pracaraṇī* as an additional item.

And that [grass] becomes the first among the *juhū* and other ladles. According to the principle that "interpolated elements (*āgantūnām*) are placed at the end," it follows immediately after the connection with the original *snūkā* (the grass-bundle), and there is no absence of the use of the sacrificial vessels (*satapātra*). [In the case of] the *prastara-sambharaṇa* (the gathering of the grass-bundle), because of the absence of the performance of the *uttaranidhana* and so forth, there is no laying down [of the bundle]. However, in the case of gathering the grass outside the *utkara* (the rubbish heap), this very [bundle] is lost because of its disappearance due to the absence of the *prastara*. [Notes: 1. *kha*, *ga*: It is heated. 2. *kha*, *ga*: Because of the absence of the laying down characterized by the *uttaranidhana* and so forth during the gathering of the *prastara*. 3. *kha*, *ga*: But in the gathering of the grass outside the *utkara*, this very [bundle] is lost because of its disappearance due to the absence of the *prastara*. 4. *ā*: [End of section]. 5. *kha*, *ga*: [End of section].

Some perform the *pretamiyatra* (the rite for the deceased) at this point; that is not correct. [The word] "first" (*prathamām*) is used to prevent the application of that [rite] to this [offering]. By using the word "first" (*prathamām*) instead of "firstly" (*prathamam*), the intention is to convey that primacy belongs only to the *sruva*-ladles, and not primacy over all the vessels.

The use of the term *sugraha* (well-grasped) is for the purpose of indicating that this [ladle] is indeed the *vasāhomahavanī* (the vessel for the fat-oblation), and not merely something that performs the function of a *juhū*. Consequently, when the *juhū* is occupied with the Soma sacrifices, it becomes the *pracaraṇī* (the working ladle) during the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), just like the *vasāhomahavanī*. Thus says Bharadvāja: "In the Soma sacrifice, [the work is done] with the *pracaraṇī*. This means that while the *juhū* is occupied, this [ladle] takes over the duties of the oblation. For this very reason, it is made of *pālāśa* wood. If one asks what the result of these two [specifications] is, it is to establish the specific distinction among vessels that perform the functions of the *juhū*.

In the absence of cooking, there is the requirement for the vessels to be made of *vaikaṅkata* wood and for the vessels in the form of the *juhū* ladle to be made of *pālāśa* wood. It should be understood that if even those vessels performing the function of the *juhū* were to possess the form of the *juhū*, then the general rule (*paribhāṣā*) enjoining *vaikaṅkata* wood would be rendered purposeless due to having no scope of application. Since there is no taking up of the *juhū* in the *pracaraṇī* ladle used for the *vaisarjana-homa*, it does not consist of *pālāśa* wood; rather, it consists of *vaikaṅkata* wood as established by the general rule. One does not employ the sacrificial post-staff (*daṇḍa-yūpa*), because it has already been employed elsewhere. Nor does one employ a chip of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-śakala*), because there is no purpose for it.
At the time of taking the clarified butter, having taken four portions with the *pracaraṇī* ladle, he takes [the butter] for the subsequent verses.

By the phrase "at the time of taking the clarified butter (*ājyagrahaṇakāla*)," the animal ritual (*pāśuka karma*) beginning with the preparation of the strainers (*pavitrakaraṇa*) and ending with the purification of the clarified butter (*ājyotpavana*) is indicated. There is no selection of the *brahmán* priest (*brahmavaraṇa*). At the same time as [the offering], one silently cleanses the *pracaraṇī* ladle first, just like the *juhū*, and then wipes the *juhu* and other spoons. Although the *pracaraṇī* serves the function of a *juhū*, its cleansing is performed silently because it is not connected with the *vaṣaṭ*-call, just like the *vasāhomahavanī*. However, for the *upabhṛt* and the *dhruvā*, the cleansing is accompanied by mantras, because there are separate mantras for them.

Regarding the *prayoga* (the ritual procedure), because of its primacy in the taking of the clarified butter (*ājya*), by the logic of "inclusion within" (*pratyāhāra-nyāya*), primacy applies even to the *samārga* (cleansing) which falls in the middle of that sequence. The fourfold portion taken with the *pracaraṇī* ladle is for the sake of the *apūrva-homa* (the primary oblation); therefore, it is taken silently into the fire. As for the subsequent portions, one takes them in the *juhū* and other ladles for the animal sacrifice; this is the meaning. Because the *pracaraṇī* is first, the *juhū* and others are considered "subsequent" (*uttara*) in relation to it. The taking of the clarified butter for the *sphyā* occurs only on the path (*varman*), as there is no specific statement to the contrary. Or else, it may be taken in the *āgnīdhra* fire.

According to the *Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra*, some teachers hold that one takes the clarified butter (*ājya*) for the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice in the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, for the *savanīya* sacrifice at the *āgnīdhra* shed, and for the *anūbandhyā* sacrifice on the *uttaravedi*. Alternatively, it may be near the *uttaravedi*. Another view, expressed by the same author as an option, states: "Some say one takes the clarified butter for the *savanīya* and the *anūbandhyā* behind the *uttaravedi*. This statement regarding the time of taking the butter is intended precisely to indicate the existence of these alternative options; in this particular case, the word "time" (*kāla*) should be understood as referring to location.

Having consecrated the sprinkling waters (prokṣaṇī), having addressed the Brahman priest, and having sprinkled the fuel (idhma), the altar (vedi), and the grass-bundle (prastara), he pours out the remainder of the sprinkling waters, inserts the two strainers (pavitra) back [into the vessel], places the grass-bundle down, and then sets down the offering-spoons (sruk).

The enumeration has been stated for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*). By means of the address (*āmantraṇa*), the impulse (*prasava*) is also implied; otherwise, the address itself would result in being meaningless. This is understood from the statement: "Having sprinkled the fuel (*idhma*), the altar (*vedi*), and the grass-bundle (*prastara*), he pours out the remainder of the sprinkling water. By this, the sequence beginning with "the knot in front" and ending with the "sprinkling" (*pratyukṣaṇa*) is set aside. *Śāṅkhāyana Śrautasūtra*, composed by Śāṅkhāyana, [Eighth Praśna]. (Note: The numbering and bracketed text appear to be part of the source formatting.)

Having poured out the remainder of the *prokṣaṇī* water and wiped the two *pavitra* blades, one proceeds in this sequence; thus, by the formula "Thou art the tuft of Viṣṇu," the taking up of the *prastara* is postponed. However, the untying of the knot certainly takes place, because without it, the wiping of the *pavitra* blades would be impossible. For this very reason, being subordinate to that [untying], it does not constitute an interruption.

Having inserted the two strainers (*pavitre*) and having placed the *prastara* [on the altar]—in this sequence, the handing over of the *prastara* to the Brahman, the separation by means of grass-blades, the spreading of the cord (*śulba*), the drawing out of the fire-brand for the *anūyāja* offerings, the preparation of the *āhavanīya* fire, the placing of the two kindling-sticks for the *āghāra* libations, and the setting down of the two separating-reeds (*vidhṛtī*) are omitted. Because the area is already separated by the strewn sacrificial grass (*barhis*), there is no need for separation by grass-blades; likewise, there is no spreading of the cord either.

Since its absence is established simply by the fact that it does not pertain to the outer spreading (*bahirāstaraṇa*), which is a constituent part of that [act], the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the cord (*śulba*) consists merely in its being laid down together with the grass-bundle (*prastara*). Furthermore, the exclusion of the two acts—digging up for the sake of the *anuyāja* offerings and the mental construction of the *āhavanīya* fire—is due to their very nature; however, the exclusion occurs at this specific time. Therefore, these two must indeed be performed after the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājyābhimantraṇa*). If they were performed here [earlier], the sequence would be subverted. Nor should it be argued that there should simply be an omission (*lopa*) of these two.

Since proceeding without the *ālambha* (touching) is in every respect improper for him, even the placing of the *ādhāra* and *samidh* must occur only after the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the clarified butter (*ājya*). Because there is no offering (*pradāna*) of the *prastara* (grass-bundle), there is likewise no taking it back (*pratyādāna*). Alternatively, the two firebrands (*ulmuka*) intended for the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice and the subsequent offerings (*anuyāja*) should be placed together as a single unit; the subsequent offerings for the *savanīya* animal sacrifice should then be performed with those two. Furthermore, the preparation of the *āyatanīya* (the altar-ground) is also omitted precisely because it is concomitant with that [preparation of the firebrands].

Thus, when the two fire-sticks intended for the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice have already been prepared, they are to be placed in that very manner. In this ritual procedure (*kalpa*), there is a modification (*ūha*) as follows: "From that fuel-wood (*idhma*), I gather you well-prepared in eighteen parts; I follow one fire-stick (*samidh*) as the life of the sacrifice; I gather the fire-stirrer (*dhṛṣṭi*) well-prepared. However, the placing of the two *vidhuti* sticks remains exactly as it is.

Since the procedure is already established by the fact that one proceeds with the placement of the *prastara* and so forth after inserting the *pavitra*, the composition of the heavy sūtra—"having placed the *prastara*, he places the ladles (*sruc*)"—is intended to make it known that the placement of all the ladles here occurs specifically upon the *prastara*. Thus, it follows by implication that the "placing" (*āsādana*) consists essentially in the act of spreading (*āstaraṇa*). The statement "he places the ladles" is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Therefore, the acts of sprinkling [the grass], discarding the *sthālīpāk* vessel, the *pṛṣadājya* vessel, the invitation to the *sruva*-ladle, and the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājyābhimarśana*) take place exactly as before. In the view that this is a modification of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, everything including the *barhis* grass is performed exactly according to the archetype (*prakṛti*). In this alternative, the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the two separating blades (*vidhṛti*) are also present.
He touches the *āgnīdhra* altar with the mantra: "May this Agni of ours create wide space."

When the sacrificer has performed the touching of the clarified butter (*ājyābhimarśa*) with the *pañcahotṛ* formula beginning with "This is the sacrifice," he touches the *maṇḍapa* brought by the *āgnīdhra*. The word *maṇḍapa* refers to a shelter for people; as the lexicon states: "*Maṇḍapa* (not feminine) is a shelter for people. In this context, its nature as a shelter for people exists only in a space connected to a covering placed above a bamboo beam which is itself set upon four pillars—not merely in the covering alone, nor in the ground alone.

In cases such as "having sat down at the Āgnīdhra," "having sat down at the Havirdhāna," or "having sat down in the Sadas," the power (denotative capacity) resides specifically in the qualified [entity] alone. For it is established by the maxim that "a substance which has a past or future utility is fit for consecration" (*bhūtabhāvyupayogaṃ hi dravyaṃ saṃskārārham*); thus, although the consecration (*abhimarśana*) is equally applicable to both the ground and the cloth-covering because their utility—past or future—is identical, nevertheless, the touching belongs to the ground alone. This is because, since it is impossible to touch both simultaneously, there is a sublation (*bādha*) regarding the qualifying factor [the cloth].

By the maxim of "not grasping that which has not been qualified," the conclusion rests upon the qualified object alone. Even though sitting down is possible on a mere covering, it is nevertheless not included by the word "maṇḍapa" because such a person is unfit for the ritual act.

Although, in the cases of "having entered the Āgnīdhra," "having entered the Havirdhāna," and "having entered the Sadas," the act of entering also applies to the open space (*avakāśa*), nevertheless, because it is impossible to sit down in an open space, it is not denoted by the word *maṇḍapa*. Nor should it be argued that even that [sitting] is possible through the power of yoga-meditation; for even if that were so, since such a thing is not useful for the ritual action, it cannot be included in the present context. By touching one part, the entire *maṇḍapa* becomes touched.
The simultaneous recitation of the *abhimarśana* (touching) and the mantra occurs in all cases. The mantra ends with *vānasātā*.
Regarding the phrase *idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame*, [it is used] at the *havirdhāna* (sacrificial cart shed).

The word *abhimṛśati* (he touches) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Because the substances are distinct, there is a repetition of the mantra. The mantra ends with *pāramuraḥ*. In the reading where it says *havirdhānam*, since the shed (*maṇḍapa*) is a single unit, the mantra is recited only once.

With the verse *agna āyūṃṣi pavase*, [he touches] the *sruva*-ladles. Regarding the *sapti* (the horse-like ladle), among those [ladles] for which a single touch with one effort is possible, the mantra is recited once; otherwise, there is a repetition of the mantra. Because the substance [of the *sruca*] is a single unit, the mantra is recited once, or the touching may be done sequentially. There is also a touching of the *pracaraṇī* ladle, because it contains the clarified butter (*ājya*) that has been taken up. There is no touching of the *vasāhomahavanī* (the vessel for the fat-oblation), because it does not contain the clarified butter that has been taken up. The mantra ends with the word *ducchunām*. For the *vāyavya* cups, there is the insertion of the word *bhūyaḥ*.

Among all the *vāyavya* vessels, the mantra is recited only once for as many *vāyavya* vessels as can be touched simultaneously with a single effort; otherwise, there is a repetition of the mantra. Regarding the term *vāyavyāni*, because the substance is one, either the mantra is recited once or the touching is done sequentially. The *vāyavya* vessels are the upward-facing cups (*ūrdhvapātra*). Because of the specific mention of *vāyavyāni*, he does not touch the *camasa* cups, due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) from the separate statement: "whether it be a *vāyavya* vessel or a *camasa*. However, he does indeed touch the cooking pots (*sthālī*).
There are four *sthālī* vessels, according to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) "those which hold the Soma-draughts. "The first drink" (*pūrvapeya*) marks the end of the mantra.
"Rising with vigor" (*uttiṣṭhann ojasā saha*) refers to the *sadas*.

Here too, as before, the word *sadas* refers only to the ground. In the reading "the oblation-holder" (*havirdhānam*), the word *havirdhāna* also refers only to the ground. "The pressed juice" (*sutam*) marks the end of the mantra.

He places the vessels on the mound that has been prepared previously. "The vessels" refers to those about to be mentioned. According to another Sūtra, they are to be washed; however, because of the specific wording and the absence of a general rule, they are not to be turned with their openings downward. This is a general declaration.
With the formulas, "Agni is the deity, Gāyatrī is the metre," one assigns them according to their respective forms; the remaining ones are assigned with the formula, "Who yokes you? May he yoke you."

"In accordance with their form and their characteristic mark. This means that for the Upāṃśu, Antaryāma, Aindravāyava, Maitrāvaruṇa, Āśvina, Śukra, Manthin, Āgrayaṇa, Ukthya, and Dhruva cups, these ten mantras are to be employed in sequence according to their respective characteristics. All these mantras are complete. As for the remaining vessels, such as the *ṛtupātra* and others, the mantra "kastvā" (Who you? is used for them. In that regard, he states the sequence for the employment of all the vessels:

On the right shoulder are the cups for the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma [libations]: the southern one belongs to the Upāṃśu and the northern one to the Antaryāma. "Upāṃśu and Antaryāma" refers to those two known by the names Upāṃśu and Antaryāma. By stating "the southern for the Upāṃśu and the northern for the Antaryāma," the specific mention of "southern" and "northern" is made first for the purpose of marking them; this excludes the possibility of their being placed in the opposite positions. Alternatively, the former belongs to the Upāṃśu and the latter to the Antaryāma.

The first [stone] is placed toward the eastern direction; the other toward the western direction. By this, they come to stand facing each other. "Agni is the deity, Gāyatrī the metre" and "Soma is the deity, Triṣṭubh the metre"—these are the two mantras in sequence.
Between them, with the formula "For the through-breath (vyāna) thee," he joins the Upāṃśusavana pressing-stone, which has been rubbed together, with the Upāṃśu cup.

Regarding the word *te* (them), [the accusative case is used] by the rule *dvitīyā 'ntarāntareṇayukte*. "Them" means between the two vessels, namely the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma vessels; that is, in the middle of those two vessels. The *upāṃśusavana* stone is that by which the Soma for the Upāṃśu libation is pressed—that is, extracted—by rubbing; he sets down that pressing-stone so that it touches the Upāṃśu vessel with the mantra, "For the Vyāna, thee! Because the name *upāṃśusavana* is given as a distinct, etymological designation, this stone is indeed different [from the others].

Therefore, in the passage "having turned the other pressing-stones toward one another, he sprinkles," this sprinkling does not apply here. Because it is the *upāṃśusavana* stone, there is contact with the *upāṃśu* vessel alone, and not contact with the *antaryāma* vessel. Even though the two vessels are situated facing each other, the *upāṃśusavana* stone is indeed on the northern side. Thus says Āpastamba: "With the mantra 'Thou art great,' [he places] the *upāṃśusavana* stone between those two stones, facing southward, in contact with the two vessels."

By the rule "touched with the *upāṃśu* cup," since contact is prescribed with only a single vessel, the contact between two vessels mentioned by Āpastamba is thereby precluded. The determination of the orientation of the cups, however, should be understood as being exactly as before.
The cups for the dual-deities (*dvidevatya*) face westward: the cup for Indra and Vāyu has a garland around it, that for Mitra and Varuṇa has two corners, and that for the Aśvins has four corners.

The meaning is as follows: they are placed facing west. When the two vessels are arranged toward the north, the *upāṃśusavana* stone is placed behind them; when the vessels are arranged toward the east, the *antaryāma* vessel is placed behind them. When the vessels are arranged toward the north, one begins from the north of the *antaryāma* vessel; when the vessels are arranged toward the east, one begins from the north of the *upāṃśusavana* stone. Thus, one sets out the vessels for the dual-deity offerings (*dvidevatya*) facing west.

The word "other" (apara) has not been employed here—just as in the case of the usage of the vessel to be mentioned later—in order to demonstrate that there is no fixed rule regarding the position; and this employment of the word "other" is indeed appropriate. [End of] the first section of the chapter. [This is] accompanied by the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. Page 771. The employment of the word "other" is indeed appropriate.

Otherwise, it should be understood that if the two vessels were positioned side-by-side (*pratyaksa*), the performance of the *dvidevatya* vessel at the rear part connected to the *upāṃśu* and *antaryāma* vessels would be impossible due to the intervening space occupied by the *antaryāma* vessel; thus, everything [the ritual procedure] would be subverted. "Surrounded by a *srak*" means that which has a *srak* all around. By the word *srak*, the *rāsnā* (girdle or rim) is meant. The meaning is that there is a *rāsnā* all around the lower region below the opening of the upper vessel. Regarding *ājagāvat*: the term *ājaga* (or *ājagā*) is a technical convention used by the ritualists (*yājñika*) for the *anāgas-stana* (the breast-like part of the ladle).

Two [strands] are applied to the *ājagava* [bow]; likewise, here too, there are two [strands] for the heat (*tāpa*), so it is said. And those two are to be made from the lower part of the *pātravila*. There is a lengthening by the rule "of *mati*, *vacas*, *anajira*, etc. That which has two handles (*sakthi*) at its corners is *dvi-sakthi*. The vessel (*pātra*) for the *aindravāyava* cup—that is, the *aindravāyava* libation—becomes *paritr̥ṅ*. The vessel for the *maitrāvaruṇa* cup—that is, the *maitrāvaruṇa* libation—becomes *ājagāvat*.

The meaning is that the vessel for the Āśvina cup belonging to the Aśvins has two corners (*dvisrakti*). The reading *dviḥsrati* with the visarga is indeed a corruption. The mantras for the three [cups] follow in order: Indra is the deity and Jagatī the metre; Bṛhaspati is the deity and Anuṣṭubh the metre; the Aśvins are the deities and Paṅkti the metre. Regarding the other two vessels for the Śukra and Manthin cups: the southern one is made of Bilva wood for the Śukra, and the northern one is made of Vikaṅkata wood for the Manthin.

The meaning is that after the drinking of the Āśvina cup, he employs the vessels for the Śukra and Manthin cups in another location. According to the maxim that "an injunction or a prohibition applies to what immediately precedes," the "other location" must be understood as the place immediately following that of the Āśvina. By the statement beginning with "the southern one made of Bilva wood," the established order of precedence is set aside. Although it would have been sufficient to say "the southern and the northern," the specific phrasing "the southern and the northern" is intended to serve as a marker for the preceding sequence.

The *baiśva* [cup] is made of *bilva* wood; the *vaikaṅkata* [cup] is made of *vikaṅkata* wood. Āpastamba says "in a stream" (*pravāha-gat*), which means "equal. Now, one might object: since the *manthin* vessel being made of *vikaṅkata* wood would be established by the general rule (*paribhāṣā*) alone, the explicit mention of *vikaṅkata* here is redundant. If it is argued that the mention of *vikaṅkata* is necessary to prevent the recurrence of *bilva*—given that only "the southern [cup] is *vailva* for the *śukra*, the northern for the *manthin*" were stated—then [the answer is as follows]: in the other case...

In the rule "The cup for the *śukra* is on the right, that for the *manthin* on the left; [the cup] for the *vaiśvadeva* is first," the word "first" (*ādya*) must indeed be included in the sūtra in order to exclude the possibility of using a *bilva* wood vessel. Furthermore, by including the term "of *vikaṅkata* wood" (*vaikaṅkata*), the brevity resulting from the reduction of two syllables is achieved. If it is asked: "Why was the phrase 'the *bilva* is first' omitted, and why was the inclusion of the word 'of *vikaṅkata*' adopted?"—the answer is as follows.

Regarding the composition of such a rule by the Teacher, the inclusion of the phrase "those which are of unassigned wood, namely of *vikaṅkata*" is for the purpose of making known the non-constant nature of the *vikaṅkata* wood in vessels other than the *manthi*, as established by the *paribhāṣā*. This was stated by Āpastamba: "Of those [vessels], those whose wood is not specified should be made of *vikaṅkata*, or whatever tree is fit for sacrifice and bears fruit. The two mantras follow in sequence: "Sūrya is the deity, *bṛhatī* is the metre," and "Candramas is the deity, *satobṛhatī* is the metre."

Others [place] two seasonal cups made of *aśvattha* wood, with bases shaped like horse's hooves and openings on both sides; the southern one belongs to the *adhvaryu*, and the northern one to the *pratiprasthātṛ*.

The other two, belonging to the *manthin* cup, are made of *aśvattha* wood—meaning they are fashioned from the *aśvattha* tree—with bases like the hoofs of a horse at their roots; or rather, "those whose bases are like the hoofs of a horse. Their mouth is a channel for pouring. The *vilāhi* is that by which the Soma, having been mostly offered in the oblation, is poured out for consumption; it is positioned straight between these two cups. This is the meaning.

From this very statement, it is understood that even the other vessels have their openings facing the same direction. By the rule, "The southern one belongs to the Adhvaryu, the northern to the Pratiprasthātṛ," the irregular placement is excluded. The purpose of composing the long sūtra is as before. Here too, Āpastamba says, "facing east. The mantra *kaḥ svit* is used here. Because the substances are distinct, the mantra is repeated.

The Āgrayaṇa-sthālī is placed on the southern hip of the mound (*khara*). The Āgrayaṇa-sthālī is on the southern hip of the mound; its deity is the Viśvedevas and its metre is the Uṣṇih. [The vessels] made of clay are to be employed.
On the northern [side], he places the Ukthya-vessel and the Ukthya-cup, the bottom of which is shaped like a horse's hoof.

On the northern hip of the mound, he places the Ukthya-vessel; Indra is its deity and the Kakubh is its metre—thus it is employed. In this very manner, he then places the Ukthya-cup to the north. Between those two, facing northward, are the three Atigrahya cups.

Those two [pātras] are connected with the *sthālī* and the *āprīyaṇa-ukthya*. It should not be argued that there is a reference by means of that word (*tacchabda*) based on the commonality of being vessels, such that it refers specifically to the *ukthya-sthālī* and the *ukthya-pātra*, and consequently, the *atigrāhya* vessels are to be employed only between those two; for a reference to two vessels of the same class is more appropriate than a reference to two vessels of different classes, since a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) refers to what is present in the mind. Furthermore, the commonality of being *sthālīs* does not exist between the *ukthya-pātra* and the other vessel.

Because they differ in form and function from the *sthālī*, it is established that the cups for drawing the *atigrāhya* offerings must be used between two *sthālīs*, and not between the *ukthya-sthālī* and the *ukthya-pātra*. Āpastamba states clearly: "The three *udacatimāhya* cups are placed between two *sthālīs*. The term *udaśvī* is used to exclude the state of being arranged in a forward direction (*prāksaṃsthatā*).

Since the number three will be established later through its very application (*viniyoga*), the explicit mention here of "three" is intended to indicate that these vessels are used in conjunction with one another in close contact; or alternatively, it is to indicate that when these *atigrāhya* cups are indeed used, their placement must be oriented toward the north (*udaksaṃstha*). Consequently, this indicates that in the *Vājapeya*, where there are seventeen *atigrāhya* cups, there is no rule requiring them to be placed facing north. For these vessels associated with the *atigrāhya*s, since they serve as the instruments for the ritual action (*karmakaraṇa*) by their very nature, a reversal of order is impossible, and thus the purpose of [the specific order] is not particularly significant. The performance is carried out with the repetition of the mantra beginning with *karatva*.
In front of the support of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, one places the *āditya*-vessel and the *āditya*-cup, the bottom of which is shaped like a horse's hoof.

By the phrase "in front of the support," it is understood that the *atigrāhya* cups are to be used behind the *khara* (the mound) in accordance with the support; for the Śruti states, "The other *grahas* are set down upon the *upayama*. From this, it is also known that a single *khara* must be made so as to be joined with the support. The *āditya* vessel is placed to the north of the *āditya* cup. The mantra beginning with "karatva" is to be repeated because of the distinctness of the substances.
In front of the northern *havirdhāna* cart, on ground that is not strewn (*anupopte*), one places the *dhruva* vessel.

By the phrase "in front of the support" (*agreṇopastambhanam*), it is indicated that the *dhruva* vessel should be used as being directly attached to the support. The mantra is: "The earth is the deity; Virāj is the covering. That place which is in the form of a mound (*khara*) made with the soil from the *auparava* holes is called "strewn" (*upopta*); different from that is "not strewn" (*anupopta*). [End of page 473, line 150] [This text is] accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

In this context, the mention of "not being sprinkled" (anupopta) is for the purpose of indicating that the *khara* itself—which, according to the scriptural statement "others are sprinkled after [the *khara*] has been sprinkled"—is the object of the sprinkling; it serves to demonstrate that the use of all vessels other than the *dhruvā* occurs on that very same *khara*.
On the northern shoulder [of the altar], there is a four-cornered *audumbara* vessel for the *dadhi-graha*.

The term *audumbara* is used to exclude wood from the *vikaṅkata* tree. The word *catuḥsrakti* (four-cornered) is stated to exclude circularity; however, a mouth (*mukha*) is indeed present there as well. *Kastveti* is the mantra. In specific sacrifices such as the *ṣoḍaśin*, one employs the vessels associated with them, such as the *ṣoḍaśin* cup and others, at the point where the *bāhyaka* cups are used. According to the principle that "interpolated elements are placed at the end," their use occurs after the *āgrayaṇa* vessel with the mantra *kastveti*. Their use is on a single *khara* (mound), because of the scriptural injunction: "The other *graha*s are on the strewn [mound]."

The *anupopta* (unstrewn) ground is for this very *dhruva-sthālī* (the *dhruvā* vessel), because by the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vacana*), the strewn (*upopta*) ground is established by the very nature of the ritual procedure for all other vessels mentioned or unmentioned. The meaning of the word *upopta*, however, has already been stated previously.
[One places it] in the middle, floating.

"In the middle" means in the center of the *khara* (the sacrificial mound). "Pariplā" means it moves or floats like a boat in the midst of the Soma juice; thus, it is "pariplā," meaning it is like a boat in the midst of the Soma juice. The word *plava* denotes a boat and is exclusively masculine. Its status as a vessel-name ending in a long vowel is established by the statement of the author of the *Sūtras*. That the masculine word *pra* refers to a boat is supported by the Śruti: "When he places that which is the *saṃyānī* on the fire-altar, he places this very boat for the fires."

By the word *pariplu*, the throwing of a boat-like vessel into the middle of the Soma juice for the purpose of crossing appears to be intended. That [act] must be performed as part of the grasping of the *paṣamāna* cup. And it has been stated by Baudhāyana: "Having thrown the *pariṣṭhu* vessel, he consecrates his hands with a mantra. The word *pariṣṭhu* is a synonym for *pariplu*. The meaning is that he employs the vessel in the form of a *pariplu* in the middle of the *khara* (Soma-stand) while reciting a mantra; or rather, he prepares it for the purpose of the *āghāra*-type oblation.
According to the available space, there are eleven cups made of Nyagrodha or Rauhītaka wood; they may have handles or be handleless.

The term "eleven" (*ekādaśa*) should be understood as restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇa*), for the purpose of excluding a higher number. By this, it is established that the *camasa* used for the purpose of holding the *dhruvā* vessel is not to be employed. Otherwise, the number would simply be twelve. The mention of "eleven" applies to the case where there is a *sadasya*. In the absence of a *sadasya*, there are only ten. By the phrase "as space permits," the lack of restriction regarding their positions is indicated. *Nepodha* is a synonym for *rohītaka*, which is a banyan tree with small leaves. As it is said by Amara:
"The *rohī* is the *rohitaka*, the enemy of the spleen (*plīhaśatru*), and the one with pomegranate-like flowers (*dāḍimapuṣpaka*)."
The son of Gāyatrī and Bala, Khadira, is the tooth-cleansing wood.

By this, the denotation of the instrumental case has been stated; nevertheless, since the *karañja* tree is not suitable for use here because it is a tree unfit for sacrifice, one must accept the fact that the word *vaṭa* denotes a tree in general—as stated in the *Viśvakośa*: "The words *rohī*, *rauhitaka*, *caitya*, and *vaṭa* refer to trees, and are masculine"—as this alone is useful in the present context. Nor can it be argued that, since the words *naiyagrodha* and *rauhītaka* denote the same object by virtue of signifying the category delimited by "tree-ness," the option (*vikalpa*) indicated by the word "or" (*vā*) is untenable. This objection is to be refuted as follows: [the author of the *Śrautasūtra*] Satyāṣāḍha has composed... [the rest of the sentence is omitted].

Since another Sūtra states "naiyagrodha" and "audumbara," and by accepting the very meaning of the restrictive particle *eva* as an exclusion of the term *audumbara*, there is no possibility for an alternative option (*vikalpa*) to arise, and thus no inconsistency exists. The mention of *naiyagrodha* is not for the purpose of excluding the *karaja* tree, nor is the mention of *rohītaka* for the purpose of excluding the *naiyagrodha* alone; rather, it is established that only the banyan tree known as *rohītaka* is to be taken.

In the absence of these, any sacrificial tree (*yajñiya-vṛkṣa*) other than the well-known *vaṭa* and *udumbara* is permitted; in the absence of even that, it is established that anything else may be used. [The cups] may have handles (*sadaṇḍa*), or be without them. In the word *assahakān*, the suffix *kap* is used in its own sense (to form a noun). They are called *camasas* because the Soma juice is drunk (*camyate*) or consumed (*adyate*) by the *hotṛ* and others therein. Regarding their shape, some authors of the *Sūtras* maintain that they are square and their dimensions are established by practical necessity. Baudhāyana and others, however, state that they are one span (*prādeśa*) long and have openings four finger-breadths wide.

In that regard, for the *asarumā* (the post without a socket), the characteristics, designations, and ritual functions of the types of men (*puruṣajātāni*) are to be applied. However, for the *sarumā* (the post with a socket), the specific characteristics of the types of men are to be applied to the staffs (*daṇḍeṣu*). The source for this is the *Mānava-sūtra*, which states: "At the support-point of the southern [post], at the end of the *camasa*-shaped part, there are various types of *sarumā* posts made of *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, or *rohītaka* wood. Furthermore, regarding the southern *havirdhāna* cart, the lower part of the seat is called the *avālamba*; there, ten *camasa* vessels made of *nyagrodha* wood [are placed].

The meaning is that he employs those [sacrificial vessels] which have handles (sarumataḥ), i.e., those whose handles possess the characteristics described for various types of cups (camasa), arranged according to their respective shapes. Thus, the Kaṭha-sūtra states: "Ten cups with handles (savṛntān), including the *prāṅga* cup, downwards. This means that the handle is rooted in the base (*vṛtamūla*).

The characteristics of the *camasa* cups are described in the *Mānava-sūtra* and the *Kaṭha-sūtra*: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the characteristics of the *camasa* cups. In substance, they are vessels of specific dimensions: the *camasa*s have stalks (*daṇḍa*) four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in girth, four finger-breadths in height, six *aṇu*s in width, and one span (*prādeśa*) in length. On their stalks there are marks: the *camasa* of the Hotṛ has no line; that of the Brahman is known as 'wiped upwards'; that of the Udgātṛ is 'wiped downwards'; and that of the Sacrificer (*khāmin*) is 'wiped at the side'."

"A single line should be made for the *stotṛ* and the *maitrāvaruṇa*; two lines are prescribed for the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, and three lines are said for the *potr*. One should cause a notch (*abhri*) to be made for the *neṣṭṛ* and the *āgnīdhra*, provided with a peg (*mayūkhavān*). Then one should make the mark of the *acchāvāka* as the footprint of a goat. Thus [it is said]. "Without a line" means that the *hotṛ*'s staff is devoid of lines. "Polished and smoothed" means that the upper part of the staff is further thinned out; this is for the *brahman*. Thus is the meaning.

Now, the lower part of the handle (*daṇḍa*) which has been polished, planed, and made thinner is the cup (*camasa*) of the *udgātṛ*. On the sides—that is, on the sides of the handle—which have been polished, planed, and made thinner, is the cup of the master, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). That which has a single horizontal line upon its handle is the cup of the *prastotṛ*. That which has three horizontal lines upon its handle is the cup of the *potr*. The cup of the *neṣṭṛ* has a wooden scraper (*kāṣṭhakuddāla*) on its handle.

The meaning is that one should have the ladle (laka) made in that shape; for according to the lexicon, *adhi* means a wooden shovel (*kāṣṭhakuhāla*). The meaning is that a crest (*mayūkha*) should be made by the wise on the handle of the *āgnīdhra-camas* and the *praśāstṛ-camas*. The meaning is that the *dvirekha* (two-lined) belongs to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin—that is, one upon whose handle there are two horizontal lines.

One should make the staff of the *khaga* sharp; this is the meaning. Regarding the staff of the *acchāvāka*, one should make it like the footprint of a goat; thus it has been explained in that commentary (*bhāṣya*). Alternatively, the author of that commentary has also stated that, beginning from the cup of the *hotṛ* and ending with the cup of the *acchāvāka*, one should increase the lines on the staffs by one for each, until there are ten lines. Contemporary experts have stated as follows: "The staff of the *brahman* should be square, while that of the *hotṛ* should be circular."

"The sacrificial ladle of the sacrificer should be square; that of the Udgātṛ, circular; that of the Praśāstṛ, planed smooth; that of the Brahman-praśastṛ, unplaned; that of the Potṛ, forked at the tip; that of the Neṣṭṛ, turned to the right; that of the Acchāvāka, provided with a handle; and that of the Āgnīdhra, pronged. That of the Sadasya is turned to the left—such are the characteristics of the *camasa* (ladles). Thus [it is said]. "Squareness" and so forth are the attributes of the handles of the *camasas* of the Brahman and the others, respectively. "Square" means four-cornered; "circular" means round.

*Pṛthvanaḥ*: that which has a broad (*pṛthu*) and thick (*sthūla*) tip. *Tryanistrikoṇaḥ*: triangular. *Avataṣṭaḥ*: sharpened at the bottom. *Uttuṣṭaḥ*: sharpened at the top. *Viśākhī*: having two branches at its tip. *Dakṣiṇāvṛtaḥ*: sharpened on the right side. *Sānā*: possessing a line at its tip. *Mayūkhaḥ*: a sharp point; the suffix *ka* is added to the word *mayūkha* in the sense of identity. *Savyāvṛtaḥ*: sharpened on the left side (the northern side). The source for this should be sought. *Vāyavyāni*: those belonging to Vāyu, which are a span (*prādeśa*) in length, with a flat top and curved in the middle.

By this, the essential form of the vessel known as the *vāyavya* is presented. "Measuring a span" (*prādeśamātrāṇi*) means having the dimension of a span. Here, having divided the specific region of the tortoise (*kācha*) measuring a span into three parts, the first part is designated by the word "upper" (*ūrdhva*). By the word "middle," the middle part is indicated; the remaining lower part follows by implication. Since a span consists of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), its division into three parts results in each part being four finger-breadths in length.

In that regard, the uppermost portion, taken up by the word *urva*, is the *sānu*; by the word *sānu*, the shoulder (*aṃsa*) is expressed. In the middle portion is the *sanamana* (the bending). By implication, in the third, lowermost portion is the shape of a *budhna* (base). In this way, the form of a mortar (*okhalī*) is demonstrated. As for the thickness of the vessel, it is according to its length. These characteristics belong to the *vāyavya* vessels—those known as *vāyavya*—by which the Soma juice is drawn for the sake of Vāyu.

In the *Mānavasūtra*: "The [vessels] for Vāyu are one span (*prādeśa*) in measure, with their middles joined, and dug out by a third part. That which has a measure of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) is "one span in measure" (*prādeśamātra*); they are circular and one span high. Those whose middle is constricted and joined [to the base] are "with their middles joined" (*saṃlagnamadhyāni*). "Dug out by a third part" means excavated by a third portion, having square holes; thus it was explained by the commentator. In the *Kaṭhasūtra* as well: "The [vessels] for Vāyu are one cubit (*hasta*) in measure or one span in measure, with a third part excavated."

Regarding the *sthālīs* (pots), although they are designated individually as "the *sthālī*," this definition does not apply even to their being *vāyavya* (dedicated to Vāyu). This is because, according to the scriptural indication (*śrutiliṅga*) stating, "There are four *sthālīs*, namely the *somagrahaṇī*s (Soma-receiving pots)," the *vāyavya* nature pertains specifically to these. Furthermore, due to the qualification "four-cornered" (*catuḥsrakti*) applied to the *dadhighraha* vessel, the other *vāyavya* vessels have a circular shape. Just as the handle of a ladle (*sruc*) is straight, so too is the *pariplava* (the revolving spoon).

"Without a staff" means devoid of a staff. The meaning is that their form is as it is when they are completely stripped of anything that would constitute a staff. Among those [trees], whichever have unspecified wood are of *vikaṅkata* for purposes other than the *homa*, but those of *vāraṇa* are for the *homa*.

Among those vessels, those whose wood has not been specified—*anādiṣṭa* means "not specified"; *anādiṣṭa-vṛkṣāṇi* refers to those [vessels] whose wood is not specified; "vessels" is the word to be supplied as the subject. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "The vessels whose wood is not specified belong to the *vikṛta* (modified sacrifice). Because of the statement later on that they are "for the purpose of *homa*," it is understood that the vessels for *homa* whose wood is not specified belong to the *vikṛta*. The word *tu* ("but") is used for the sake of distinction. Some say that in the vernacular language, *vikṛta* is known as *mutayī*.

Others say it is *heṅkala*. Or, as in "the elephant is the warder-off of the wind. In that context, among those [implements] such as the *upāṃśu* and others which are not specified as being made of a particular wood for the purpose of offering (*ahomārtha*), there is the property of being made of *vaikaṅkata* wood. Those [implements] not specified as being of a particular wood for the purpose of offering are: the cup (*camasa*) connected with the *tānūnaptra* rite, the wooden sword (*sphya*) which serves as a means for constructing the altar in connection with the *soma* performed by the assistant priests (*parikarmin*), and the *vidhṛti*; these three alone are [made of *vaikaṅkata*] in the archetype (*prakṛti*). If it is argued that this [cup] also has the purpose of offering because of the optative suffix in the word "juhomī" (I offer), then in that case, it is indeed made of *vaikaṅkata* wood.

In this view, the plurality [of cups] becomes meaningful because it pertains to the vessels connected with the *tantra* of the Soma that has undergone modification (*vikṛti*). Even though the cup (*camasa*) connected with the *tānūnaptra* rite is made from the *vāraṇa* tree, the vessels connected with the *tantra* of the modified Soma are indeed made from the *vāraṇa* tree; these will become manifest in their respective places. Because the sentences are numerous and primary, this is established as a general rule (*paribhāṣā*), and not at the specific occasion of the cup connected with the *tānūnaptra*.

Nor should it be argued that since the application of the *pātra* [vessels] related to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* occurs at the time of the *prayoga*, the *paribhāṣā* "there is one [application] everywhere" (*tatraikaṃ sarvatra*) should be stated after that; for even if the matter were settled in this way, the effort of formulating the *paribhāṣā* again would be useless. This is because the formulation of the *paribhāṣā* in both places serves a purpose: it functions as a restrictive rule (*parisaṃkhyā*) intended to exclude the *tantras* of the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*) and other such rites from the *iṣṭika* and *saumika* *tantras*. Therefore...

This rule does not apply to the *samavattadhānya* (mixed grain) placed in the *māī* vessels, nor to the *vāyavya* vessels used for taking the *surā* liquor related to the *gharaka-sautrāmaṇī*, nor to the *vāyavya* vessels used for taking the milk-related offerings in the *kaukilī-sautrāmaṇī*. Thus, it is established that this restriction—that [the *vāraṇa* wood] is only for the purpose of *homā* (oblations), while [the *pālāśa* wood] is only for the purpose of *mahā-homā*—does not hold true.

Regarding the pronoun *teṣām* (of them), one must accept that it refers to all vessels by taking it as referring to those present in the mind; it should not be taken as referring only to the *vāyavya*, *avamasa*, and *pariplava* vessels by taking it as referring to what is immediately proximate. For, since it is impossible for any of these [proximate vessels] to have the purpose of non-homa (*ahoma*), the [interpretation] would result in incoherence. Those whose purpose or motive is *homa* are "homārtha"; those which are not homārtha are "ahomārtha. Here, *homa* is understood in its general sense, common to both the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*adhāna*) acts.

And thus, the *droṇakalaśa* must indeed be made of *vikaṅkata* wood; likewise, the *camasa* used for the sprinkling (*vyāghāraṇa*) must also be made of *vikaṅkata*. However, although the *droṇakalaśa* serves the purpose of an oblation (*homa*), there is no restrictive rule that it must be made of *vikaṅkata*. This is because the instruction regarding the [use of] trees occurs after the general rules on trees have been established. Therefore, it may be made from any sacrificial tree whatsoever.

Regarding this, Āpastamba says, concerning the *droṇakalaśa*: "There is no restriction as to the tree for it, provided it is made from a *vāyavya* [tree]. However, there is this much distinction: while the *droṇakalaśa* is made from a *bailva* (wood-apple) tree, in the case of the *vāyavyas*, one may take any sacrificial wood (*yajñiya-vṛkṣa*) if a *vaikaṅkata* is unavailable. It should be understood that this restriction does not apply to the *droṇakalaśa*; by this, it is demonstrated that the *droṇakalaśa* is not necessarily earthen (*mārktika*).
With the formula, "I yoke the earth for thee with light," he places the *droṇakalaśa*, together with its fringe-strainer (*daśāpavitra*), behind the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart.

The *droṇakalaśa* is so called because it is filled with grain measured by a *droṇa*, according to the measurement established by common usage; it is cooked [or prepared] to such a capacity. A *droṇakalaśa* is that in which the *kalās*—the portions or particles (*kaṇāḥ*)—of the *droṇa*, that is, of the grain measured by a *droṇa*, reside or are contained. Thus Yāska says: "The *kalaśa* is so called because the *kalās*, the portions, reside in it. It is not, however, characterized by a neck shaped like a conch (*kambu-grīvā*) and so forth, because of the traditional practice of the ritualists (*yājñika*). This is because it will be stated later: "He takes the *droṇakalaśa* from the *pariplu* [ladle]."

The meaning of *parivāśam* is indeed "to float around" or "to cross over on all sides. This is because there is no possibility of entry into a *droṇakalaśa* that possesses a neck like a *kambu* (conch-shell) or similar features; therefore, the practice of the ritual experts (*yājñika*) is that the *droṇakalaśa* is either square or circular. By the very mention of "successive" (*uttarottara*), the doubt regarding the lack of restriction—namely, whether in the previous case it refers to the southern one or in the previous case it refers to the southern or the northern—is excluded.

"Behind the axle" (*paścād-akṣa*) means behind the axle. Having placed two *daśāpavitra* strainers—referred to by the two previously mentioned [terms]—into the middle of the *droṇakalaśa*, one employs them together with it; this is the meaning. Because of the mention of "lying face down" (*nyakta*), the employment is specifically of that which is turned face up (*uttāna*). The same applies to the *ādhavanīya* and the many vessels (*aneka-dhana*). Of the northern [vessel]...

By the very *paribhāṣā* (technical rule), "by [the word] *dinā* [is indicated] the end of the preceding [mantra] in the performance," it is made known that the complete recitation of the mantra ending with the word *mantrānta* is intended so that the *paribhāṣā*—"one should effect the ritual act with the end of the mantra"—may take effect. By this, it is established that the application occurs at the very moment of uttering the verbal action-word *yunajmi*. This should be understood to apply likewise to the other three mantras as well.
With the mantra, "I yoke Vāyu together with the intermediate region for you," one places the Ādhavanīya jar in the northern *nīḍa*.

The inclusion of the word *uttara* (upper) is for the purpose of excluding the *rakṣin* (protector). The *ādhavanīya* is that vessel into which the Soma—having been shaken, squeezed, and filtered—is poured; its correctness is established by its belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. With the formula, "I yoke the speech together with the sun," one places the *pūtabhṛt* on its forepole.

That statement is not intended in a literal sense. Otherwise, since the subsequent *havirdhāna* shed would already be obtained by mere continuity, the reference to it would result in being purposeless. Regarding the phrase "the *pavamāna* great jars," since the *mādhavanīya* and *samr̥t* will also be described later as being of the nature of jars (*kalaśa*), these two are indeed jars. Therefore, they possess the quality of being made of clay and the shape of a jar. This is clear from the *Kaṭha-sūtra*: "The *ādhavanīya* and *samr̥t* are two jars without lids."

There is some difference between a *kumbhī* and a *kalaśa* based on their shape: a *sthālī* has a wide base, a narrow mouth, and a short form; whereas a *kalaśa* should be understood as having a narrow base, a wide mouth, and a long form. The meaning is that one places the purified [liquid] in such a place which is "pradhura"—that is, where it is firmly established so that when the vessel is placed there, it does not fall. The suffix *a* is applied at the end of the compound according to the rule *bhakṣapūrabdhṛthāmānakṣe*.

This [meaning] is obtained by splitting the word as *anakṣa*. 778—In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: [The word *adhas* signifies a location adjacent to and connected with the *nīḍa* (the bottom of the vessel). The extracted meaning is: "One places the *pūtabhṛt* vessel in a specific location that is extensive and horizontal, situated near the *nīḍa*. By means of the particle *eva*, [it is excluded from] the mere northern *havirdhāna* which is not connected to the *nīḍa*.

This serves to exclude a location that possesses horizontal beams as well as the *cubuka* (front part) of the *havirdhāna* shed mentioned in another Sūtra. By this it is understood that where the particle *eva* is not heard, even what is stated in another Sūtra may be combined [with the present rule]; but where it is heard, that alone is restricted, even if the other possibility exists. The term *pūtabhṛt* is an etymological designation (*anvarthā saṃjñā*). It is called *pūtabhṛt* because it "bears" (*bibharti*) only the purified (*pūta*), that is, the strained (*gālita*), Soma.

The master will say: "He lowers one part of the *pūtabhṛt* into the *ādhavanīya*; thereafter, the *pavitra* is lowered into the *pūtabhṛt*. Both the *ādhavanīya* and the *pūtabhṛt* are made of clay, as stated in the *Baudhāyana*: "The *ādhavanīya* and the *pūtabhṛt* are like a cooking pot (*sthālī*). From the word *sthālī*, their being made of clay is understood.
Behind the axle, he touches the three *ekadhana* vessels with the formula: "I yoke the three; the three [vessels] of the sun, apart," and he touches the ladles (*srucaḥ*).

The phrase "of the northern *havirdhāna*" continues to apply [here] because of its association with the axle-base (*akṣapada*). "Behind the axle" (*paścādakṣam*) is an *avyayībhāva* compound. The mention of "three" is for the purpose of restriction, so that the use of the *ekadhanā* vessels occurs only behind the axle for three [of them]. By this, it is established that the other *ekadhanā* vessels may be used as appropriate. One should not, however, be deluded into thinking that there are only three *ekadhanā* vessels, for it is said: "Having taken the *ekadhanā* pots, which have at least three, they run forward."

This is because it would result in a contradiction with the *Varuṇapramāṇasūtra*. There is no contradiction with the indicative mark (*liṅga*). For when three *ekadhana* vessels are to be used after the axle, the contradiction regarding the indicative mark is avoided by the repetition of the mantra in this manner: "In which [vessel] among these should the mantra be applied? Thus, the meaning is that for the purpose of seeking Soma, there are waters called *ekadhana*, and their jars are made of clay. The word *ekadhanān* refers to the jars containing those waters; the reading is indeed without the visarga.

In the *Sūtra* stating "he touches the *sruk* ladles," because there is no instruction for a mantra and because the touching is seen to be a secondary act (*pradharmābhimarśa*), the touching of the *sruk* ladles is performed with the formula "I yoke you for the sake of long life. The reading "he touches the *udīcīna* [ladles], as before" is indeed consistent with the *Sūtra*. Alternatively, the mantra "I yoke you, O drops, for the sake of the sun" (*yunajmi tilo vicaḥ sūryasya te*) is for the purpose of touching the ladles; for Baudhāyana has prescribed this mantra for the touching of the ladles that have been arranged.

Therefore, it must be understood that the three [ladles] to be used subsequently are intended as a single unit. It should not be argued that because the *abhimarśana* (touching) consecration is also necessary for the *ājyapā* (butter-drinking) ladles, there would be a conflict with the gender [of the singular] when combined with them; for since the *upabhṛt* and the *dhruvā* are intended as one through their commonality of being "supporters" (*upabhṛt*), the number three is established, and thus there is no conflict with the gender.

There is no touching [of the *pracaraṇī*] because it lacks connection with the sacrifice. Since the quality of "leaking" (*sravatva*) exists in this [ladle] as well, there is an insistence that it too must be touched; however, by virtue of its similarity to the *upabhṛt* and *juhū*, and with the intention of expressing their unity, the triad [of ladles to be touched] is indeed established. As for the *vasāhomahavanī*, there is no touching because it is empty. Some say that the touching of the *srucaḥ* (ladles) is performed silently (*tūṣṇīm*).
Regarding this, some authorities prescribe the purpose [of touching] as being for the sake of the *adhiṣavaṇa* skin and the pressing-stones (*grāvan*).

Regarding the pressing-boards, the subsequent rubbing, the sprinkling of the pressing-stones, the spreading [of the skin], the placing of the strainers, the making of the upper stone face-to-face with them, and their sprinkling—what has been prescribed there [in the previous section] should not be performed then; rather, some teachers (ācāryas) prescribe that it should be performed at this time. "Some" means they say so. This concludes the fifteenth section (paṭala). [This is] accompanied by the commentary named Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa. 771.

The purpose of the *adhiṣavaṇa* skin is precisely its being spread out as a covering; since sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is for that purpose, it too is included [in the compound]. As for the vessels (*grāvāṇaḥ*), their purpose is indeed the placing down (*āpsādana*); since even the sprinkling characterized by being directed toward them is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of them, and because it is connected to them, they too are included here. However, "purpose" (*prayojana*) is not a separate category of meaning (*padārthāntara*). Otherwise, since it has not been mentioned elsewhere, the demonstration here of the specific time as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) would be untenable.

Therefore, it should be understood that only the spreading [of the grass] and the placing [of the vessels] are to be grasped by the word "purpose. And this has been stated by Āpastamba: "I sprinkle the pressing-stones, which are slayers of demons and destroyers of spells, belonging to Viṣṇu."

Having sprinkled the hide with the formula, "O you Valaga-removers, I sprinkle you, belonging to Viṣṇu," and having spread the pressing-boards with their hair-side up using the formula, "O you Valaga-removers, slayers of Rakṣases, I spread you, belonging to Viṣṇu," they place upon it four stones—one span high and shaped like a hammer—along with a fifth stone in the middle which is the broadest, with the formula, "O you Valaga-removers, slayers of Rakṣases, I set you down, belonging to Viṣṇu. By this [procedure], the doubt regarding the application of the *karasvati* mantra as the instrument is removed.
[This objection] is refuted. Here, the word *iti* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). It is a conjunction with the employment of the Vāyavya vessel and so forth.

[The Adhvaryu] addresses the lower stones, turning them face-to-face, with the mantra: "The abodes of the waters, the embryos of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*), the guardians of the world, falcons, guests of the mountains, like protectors sent forth—O Vāc, with your sound, call Indra; drive away disease! You are yoked; carry [him]; bear the sacrificer to the heavenly world! Thus he consecrates them.

Since the act of facing [the deity] serves respectively as the purpose for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and consecration (*abhimantraṇa*), and according to the principle that "accessories (*guṇa*) repeat with each primary (*pradhāna*)," the second act of facing also indeed takes place, because it is not interrupted by the sprinkling in the middle.
He offers an oblation in the *āgnīdhra* fire with the mantra: "Protect me from the seat-mantra."

The taking [of the *ājya*] from the *āgnīdhra* vessel is for the purpose of precluding the *āhavanīya*. Since the *juhū* and the *pracaraṇī* are occupied, this oblation is performed with the *sruva* ladle using the *ājya* from the *ājyasthālī*; some say it is from the *apūrva-ājya*, but the source for this must be examined. Nor should it be said that the oblation should be made with a portion of the *ājya* in the *pracaraṇī* by means of that very ladle; for since the pouring out of this *ājya* will be prescribed later, its use for the oblation here is impossible. "Abhiśastyai" is the end of the mantra. With the two [mantras], "For the heart thee! For the mind thee!", he brings down the King [Soma] onto the pressing stones between them.

With the two mantras, "I have brought thee for the mind; O King Soma, come, descend," he leads [the Soma] between the two poles, through the middle of the two poles, and when they are facing each other, he brings it down and places it upon the pressing-stones. Because it is characterized by the *anuṣṭubh* meter, the first mantra ends with *yaccha*; consequently, the second mantra begins with "O King Soma, come."

Āpastamba states clearly: "Here, between the two poles (īṣe), he brings down the King (Soma) with these two [formulas]: 'For the heart thee, for the mind thee, O King Soma! Baudhāyana also says: "Between the two poles of the southern Havirdhāna cart, he brings down the King with these two [formulas]: 'For the heart thee, for the mind thee, O King Soma! Come, descend! [Note: The text contains various manuscript variants indicated by the letters kha, ga, and ka. This concludes the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [the eighth book].

"One desiring heaven should offer the Pañcahotṛ [formula] in the Āgnīdhra fire," so say some. One should offer that material called the Pañcahotṛ with the formula "O Agnihotra," according to the ritual procedure of an *āvi-homa*, as before; this offering is indeed performed by means of a reed (*veṇu*). Because it serves the purpose of an offering, the Pañcahotṛ includes the *graha* (libation). The mention of the Āgnīdhra is for the purpose of excluding the Āhavanīya. "One should offer" is one complete sūtra; "one desiring heaven" is another. By this, both its obligatory nature and its optional nature are established.

Āpastamba clearly states the meaning: "They prescribe the Pañcahotṛ [offering] at the Āgnīdhra fire for one desiring heaven, as if it were obligatory.
