On this occasion, regarding the matter of the oblations, Āpastamba states a specific technical rule (paribhāṣā): "One offers the middle Soma-oblations, the subsequent oblations, and the cake-oblations; one does not offer from this side the Soma-oblations."

Those which are the principal oblations of the Soma, the clarified butter, the animal victim, and the sacrificial cakes—these he offers in the middle of the *ḍoḥ* (the central part of the fire). Those that are the subsidiary portions of the clarified butter, such as the *ājyabhāga* and the *sviṣṭakṛt* offerings, he performs according to the original model (*prakṛti*). As for the Soma oblations, he offers them on both sides; wherever in whichever direction a specific oblation is prescribed, he offers it there on the periphery of the fire—this is the meaning of the phrase "not in the middle.
Before the utterance of speech, he commences the *prātaranuvāka* (morning litany).

Formerly, the speech of humans or birds was uttered; [therefore] one begins the *prātaranuvāka* before the birds have begun to call. Thus Āpastamba says: "One begins the *prātaranuvāka* before the speech of men or before the birds have called. Āśvalāyana has stated that the calling of the birds alone is the occasion for the commencement of the *prātaranuvāka*: "At the time of the dawning of that night, from the first sound of the birds, the *prātaranuvāka* is commenced. [The word] *pravaditoḥ* [is used] by Mādhava.

The suffix *tosun* is applied according to Pāṇini’s sūtra *kṣaṇestheṇ*. "Prātar-anjayate" means the *prātar-anuvāka*; its *upākaraṇa* (commencement) is the initiation of the Hotṛ for that purpose. From the word *upākaraṇa*, a similarity to the *śastra* appears to be indicated. Thus, the *pratigara* (response) is established here. The manner of the *pratigara* is clearly stated by Āpastamba: "With the words 'I respond to your recitation with my mind,' he addresses the Adhvaryu."

Having said this, the meaning is that the *adhvaryu* responds to the *pratigara*. If it is asked, "How can this be so, given the absence of a *stotra*? it is replied: the singing of the *viśvarūpa* chants by the *chandoga*s constitutes the *stotra*, and the *vasatīvarī* waters constitute the *graha*; through that alone, the complete fulfillment of all requirements is achieved.

Baudhāyana also states in the *Karmānta*: "What indeed is the division of the *vāsatīvara* [water] into *stotra* (laud) and *śastra* (recitation)? Its *stotra* division occurs in the *viśvarūpā* verses, and its *śastra* division occurs in the *prātaranuvāka* (morning litany). Now, one might object: "But surely the *viśvarūpā* verses do not exist elsewhere than in the *jyotiṣṭoma*. Since Lāṭyāyana and Drāhyāyaṇa have stated that the *viśvarūpā* chants occur only in the context of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the absence of the *stotra* would entail the absence of the *prātaranuvāka*. This is not so.

Because it is conceived in this very way—that what is performed in the archetypal sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, which are mentioned extensively in the *Chāndogya*, also assists in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*); and there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because there is an absence of over-extension since such [archetypal] mention does not exist elsewhere.

From the mantra for the *viśvarūpā* chant—"The hundredfold speech, the thousandfold song; the *gāyatrī*, the *triṣṭubh*, the *jagatī*; all forms are gathered together; the gods have fashioned the ether"—it is understood that even in its modified form (*vikṛti*), that *viśvarūpā* chant provides assistance within the four archetypal sacrifices (*prakṛti-kratavaḥ*) consisting of the *agniṣṭoma*, *ukthya*, *ṣoḍaśin*, and *atirātra*, which are themselves the archetypes (*prakṛti*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*. In the case of this doubt, the meaning is stated for that purpose: the word *śata* signifies the infinite. This is because of the Nirukta [statement]: "The hundred (*śata*) is the infinite. That which has a hundred words—that is, words whose meanings are infinite—is a *śatapadī*; such speech I join (*yuñje*), that is, I employ, for the sake of liberation. The word *sahasra* also signifies the infinite.

The essential meaning is this: since there is a path in the form of a "thousandfold course" (*sahasravartanī*) from which infinite modifications (*vikṛti*) proceed, I sing within those very Agniṣṭoma and other rites that serve as the archetypes (*prakṛti*). By that [archetypal singing] alone, the assistance is accomplished even in the modifications; such is the intended sense. The term *sahasravartanī* occurs when the locative case-ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk...* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). In these [archetypes], there are the Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī meters—this is an illustration including other meters as well.

By this, other *chandas* (metres) are also included here. The meaning of the mantra is: "All forms whatsoever, which consist of transformations, have been gathered together; in these, the gods, Indra and the others, made for themselves *okas*, that is, dwellings, for the purpose of receiving their respective portions. Alternatively, the word *apākaraṇa* has the sense of "commencement" alone. Regarding the *pratigaraṇa* (response), it is based on a scriptural injunction (*vācanika*). Kātyāyana states that the Adhvaryu should remain awake during the *prātaranuvāka* (morning recitation), though he also mentions the option of sleeping. This [sleeping] should be understood as applicable when staying awake is impossible, such as when one's enemy is away on a journey.

The genitive case is used for the object of hatred (*dveṣya*), namely the enemy, in the sense of the locative (*saptamī*). And that [genitive] has the sense of a cause (*nimitta*); that is to say, when the one who is hated exists, it is caused by him, meaning it is caused by his destruction. The meaning is that he begins the *prātaranuvāka* (morning litany) when the night has "passed away" (*proṣitāyām*)—that is, when it has been spent or completed. In the Dhātusūtra, in the rule *upa puṣa pluṅ dāha*, the word *dāha* (burning) indicates destruction. By this, the sense "when it has perished" or "when it has come to an end" is obtained.

"O Brahman, recite for the gods who come at dawn; restrain your speech; O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; O Pratiprasthātṛ, pour out the grains for the Savanīya offerings," thus he issues the command.

The *prātaryāvāṇaḥ* are specific classes of deities, having the forms of Agni, Uṣas, and the Aśvins; the meaning is that one should recite the *prātaranuvāka* for the purpose of their arrival. Here, the *hotṛ* is the one to be urged (*preṣya*). Baudhāyana has made this direction for the urging (*preṣya*) quite explicit: "O *hotṛ*, recite the *anuvāka* for the gods who come at dawn. Regarding the *savanīya*s: those which exist at the *savana* (pressing) on the day of the Soma sacrifice are the *savanīya*s; these are the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*s). The authority for using the term "cake" (*puroḍāśa*) here even for parched grains (*dhānā*) and other such items is the *savanīya-puroḍāśa*.

This will be explained in the section on the sacrifice (*yāga*). Just as the attendants perform the ritual according to the sequence of the recitation, there is no rule regarding the "father-and-son" (*pitāputrīya*) nature of this *subrahmaṇyā* invocation, because of the absence of a statement to that effect. The *pratiprasthātṛ* priest undertakes the rites for the *savanīya* offerings, beginning with the setting out of the vessels; he employs the vessels for the vegetable offerings (*oṣadhi*) according to their respective purposes.

Since [the procedure] is already established by the term *apeṣaṇa* (grinding), the mention of the *pratiprasthātṛ* is for the purpose of excluding the *adhvaryu*. Otherwise, it would follow that the mere act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) is performed by the *pratiprasthātṛ*, while everything up to the production of the other implements would be performed by the *adhvaryu* during the *savanīya* sacrifice. Therefore, the mention of the *pratiprasthātṛ* is indeed necessary to exclude the *adhvaryu*.

The statement "of the *savanīya*s" (782) in the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). It establishes that the duties connected with the *savanīya* offerings are to be performed by the Pratiprasthātṛ alone, and not those pertaining to the Soma sacrifice (*saumika*). Thus, it is established that in rites such as the *śṛṇotomi*, the performer is exclusively an Adhvaryu priest. Alternatively, the statement "of the *savanīya*s" indicates that the Pratiprasthātṛ is restricted to the *savanīya* offerings alone; while he is fixed for these, he is not so restricted for other true [offerings], such as the *saumya* and others which are excluded.

By this, it is established that the Pratiprasthātṛ, like the Adhvaryu, is also the performer of the offerings of cooked rice (caru) for Soma and others in the alternative case. The fact that the offering of the Soma-caru has the Pratiprasthātṛ as its performer is clearly stated by Baudhāyana himself: "O Pratiprasthātṛ, offer the cake on one potsherd (ekakapāla) to Varuṇa; prepare the portion for the Soma-offering. In this context, the mention of the Pratiprasthātṛ is for the purpose of restriction. Therefore, [the Madhyandina school...]

It is established that in the case of the morning and third pressings (*savana*), there is also the possibility of another person performing the rites. And according to the *Baudhāyana-sūtra*, it is the *Āgnīdhra* who performs them because of the statement "having been seen. Due to the injunction beginning with "the placing of the vessels" (*pātrasādana-prabhṛtīni*), there is the cessation of the washing of the hands and the strewing of the *ulaparājī* grass. Alternatively, there is the cessation of the strewing of the *ulaparājī* alone, because that [act] has already been performed.

Regarding the washing of the hands, he says, "May I be able for the work for the gods," because a consecration (*saṃskāra*) residing in the person by way of capacity is necessarily required; thus, it must certainly be performed. Accordingly, Āpastamba states: "He undertakes the rites beginning with the washing of the hands for the *savanīya* offerings. "Undertakes" means "begins. The phrase "according to the purpose" (*yathārtham*) means according to the requirement. Since the mention of "plants" (*oṣadhi*) is intended to exclude those belonging to animal sacrifices (*pāśuka*), by this [mention] the sacrificial oblations (*havir*) of the *iṣṭi* are indicated.

Therefore, there is the employment even of those items not connected with the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture). The meaning is that one should employ those things which, though not employed for the sake of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), are nonetheless purposeful. And these are: the winnowing basket (*sūrpa*), the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), the wedge (*śamyā*), the mortar (*ulūkhala*), the pestle (*musala*), the lower grinding stone (*dṛṣad*), the upper grinding stone (*upala*), the *vājinapātra* (vessel for the whey), the two *kuṭaru* vessels, the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), the *prāśitra-haraṇa* (vessel for the priest's portion), the *praṇītā-praṇayana* (vessel for carrying forward the consecrated water), the original *iḍā-pātra*, the *dadhi-pātra* (curd vessel), the *āmikṣā-uddharaṇa-pātra* (vessel for drawing out the curd-mixture), the *vājinoddharaṇa-pātra* (vessel for drawing out the whey), and the vessel for the parched grains (*dhānā*).

The vessels for the *karu*, the vessel for the *artha-pātra*, the vessel for filling the *artha-pātra*, the *aiṣa-gamadantī* vessel, the vessel for dividing [the cake] into four parts, the vessel for the flour-smeared fragments (*piṣṭalepa*), and the vessel for the husks (*phalīkaraṇa*)—these are the ones. The *āgnihotraṇī*, *sruva*, *juhū*, *upabhṛt*, *ājyasthālī*, and *upaveṣa* belong specifically to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*). Since it is observed that there is an injunction for the re-use of the *veda* even after it has been employed at the animal sacrifice, it is not used again here; for the injunction regarding its re-use pertains specifically to the *paśupuroḍāśa*, and thus its application occurs only there. Therefore, there is no employment of the *veda* in this case.

Having prepared the *pavitra* strainers, he issues the command, "Restrain your speech," for the *Paśusūtra* states, "Restraining his speech, he cleanses the vessels. Since there is an absence of the *praṇītā* waters in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), and since there would otherwise be no incidental benefit here, the bringing forward of the *praṇītā* waters indeed takes place.

One commences the rites for the *savanīya* offerings beginning with the measuring (*mānana*), because these are extended to them by the subsequent rule regarding the *nirūḍhapaśubandha* sacrifice; since the measuring, the flour-smeared oblation (*piṣṭalepa-homa*), the fruit-oblation (*phalīkaraṇa-homa*), and the release of the potsherds (*kapāla-vimocana*) are established for these as well, it is necessary that there be a distinct set of *praṇītā* waters for the sake of the *savanīya* offerings. Nor should it be argued that this [rule] pertains to a different subject matter, for there is no evidence to justify such a restriction.

Alternatively, if no other [liquids] were available, one might purify whatever [liquids] exist with the *yajus* formula and mix [the flour] with them; thus, the statement "he mixes" is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) for an emergency situation, according to the Sūtra, which implies that there is indeed an absence of *praṇītā* water. If it is asked what the scope of this rule is, it is said: by means of the prohibition of *praṇītā* and because the suffix *-ktvā* indicates immediate sequence, the scope of this rule consists of those rites that, while lacking *praṇītā*, incidentally require *praṇītā*—such as the *savanīya* offerings, the *devikā* offerings, and the *devasū* oblations within the animal sacrifices of the Soma ritual.

By the word *āpat* (emergency), this [rule] applies to a situation of distress, not everywhere as being equal in status to the *praṇītā* water. If it is argued that by this very sūtra, since the prohibition would be established even in cases such as the *avabhṛtha* and the *vaiśvānarīya*, the statement "he pours it together with the *yanus* and *ṛtubhiḥ*" found here and there would be redundant—this is true; however, because it is an *apūrva* (novel) injunction, that statement is necessary to prevent its application in those respective places where it might otherwise occur. [End of] Chapter 1, Section 150, accompanied by the *Jyotsnā* commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

783. This is because [the mixing] is established by the very fact that the *puroḍāśa* would otherwise be impossible without it. Nor should it be argued that the defect remains as it was; for since the statement is justified as being intended to enjoin the purification (*utpavana*) by means of the *yajus*, there is no persistence of that defect. Furthermore, in the case of the *paśupuroḍāśa* connected with the *nirūḍhapaśu* sacrifice, the mention of the *praṇītā* water is intended to exclude the mixing with waters purified by the *yajus*. As for the *upaveṣa*, although it serves the purpose of the animal sacrifice, its removal (*udāsana*) occurs only at the conclusion of the animal ritual procedure (*paśutantra*).

If it is argued that, in this way, since there would be no act of pouring out the refined [grain] and no act of discarding the *upaveṣa* stick, the plural number in the phrase "he performs the rites" (*karmāṇi pratipadyate*) would be untenable, we say no. This is because the plural number is justified by taking into account two distinct rites consisting of the two offerings of the flour-smear (*piṣṭalepa*) and the husks (*phalīkaraṇa*). Thus, the kneading of the dough is established as being done optionally with those very [husks] produced by the *yajus*-formula. And so says Bharadvāja: "He bakes the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) with those [husks] produced by the *yajus*-formula."

And Baudhāyana, standing by the animal cake (paśupuroḍāśa), says: "He mixes the flour with the remainder of the sprinkling water (prokṣaṇī) as much as is required for the Savanīya offerings. Since the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick) is mandatory for the purpose of removing the embers to the *śāmitra* fire during the animal sacrifice, the task is accomplished by that very *upaveṣa*. Having divided the tips of the *vedāgra* into four parts, he employs one portion in the vessels used for the animal sacrifice; with that same portion, he wipes the ladles (*srucaḥ*) and discards it. The other portion is to be employed here.

By that same [ladle], the horse’s vessel (*vājinapātra*) and the *prāśitra* portion are likewise treated. He discards that very [ladle]. From what remains, two portions are to be used respectively for the cleaning of the *prāśitra* at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) and the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*); he discards those two in their respective places.

Regarding the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) and the kindling-wood (*samidh*), although they have been employed in the animal-sacrifice vessels, they are to be divided and used in the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), or in the *piṣṭalepa* and *phalīkaraṇa* oblations included within the *savanīya-puroḍāśa*. He specifies the particular vessels:
two potsherds for roasting, eight for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and a pot (*sthālī*) for the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*).

Those two *kapālas* (potsherds) which have the purpose (*artha*) or objective (*prayojana*) of parching grain (*dhāna*) and frying grains (*lāja*) respectively are *bṛhatī* (large). Their largeness is due to their suitability for the task. The word *kapāla* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as a part of a jar (*sarāva*). Therefore, those who employ a *sarāva* as a *kapāla* are to be disregarded. Since the number two is already established by the dual ending in the phrase "two *kapālas* for the purpose of [the sacrifice]," the inclusion of the term "two" (*dvi*) indicates that both belong to the same class (*sajātīyatva*). By this, it is established that they must be of equal size (*tulyaparimāṇatva*).

One who desires *āmikṣā* [says] "the pot," meaning that the object qualified by its specific form is what is denoted by the word "pot" (*sthālī*), and it is precisely that which is intended here, and not a jar (*kumbhī*), a bowl (*śarāva*), or the like; this is for the purpose of conveying such a meaning.

At the time of the offering, one offers parched grains (*dhānā*) to Indra accompanied by the Haris, a gruel (*karambha*) to Indra accompanied by Pūṣan, parched barley-flour (*parivāpa*) and fried grain (*lāja*) to Sarasvatī Bharatī, and a cake on eight potsherds (*puroḍāśa-aṣṭākapāla*) to Indra.

The phrase "at the time of the offering" (nirvapaṇakāle) is to be explained as being part of the *ātithyā* [rite]. By the passage beginning with "he offers parched grains (*dhānā*) for Indra, the possessor of bay horses (*harivat*)" and ending with "on eight potsherds" (*aṣṭākapālam*), the expectation regarding which deity corresponds to which substance is removed. Now, one might object: should it not simply be stated "for Indra, a sacrificial cake" (*indrāya puroḍāśam*)? As for the quality of being "on eight potsherds," that is already established by the rule "the cakes are intended for the fire" (*aṣtau puroḍāśārthāni*). [Response: No. [Note: The text fragment provided ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument regarding the specific details of the ritual offerings.]

[The opponent objects: "It is already established; thus, the statement 'eight-potherd' (*aṣṭākapālam*) is redundant. [The author replies: No, because it serves to inform [the practitioner] that in the alternative view where the cake is not dedicated to all the gods (*sarvendra*), the *puroḍāśa* dedicated to Indra (*aindra*) is indeed eight-potherd and does not become eleven-potherd. Its application, however, follows from the well-known rule that an *aindra-puroḍāśa* is everywhere eleven-potherd. The terms such as *dhānā* (fried grains) and so forth function by taking on their future designations.

When various grains and various seeds are brought together, there is, according to the measurement [of the ritual], one mortar, pestle, winnowing basket, and black antelope skin. There is no distinction between each seed regarding these four items—the mortar and so forth—and the two, the grinding stone and the muller, which are included by the word "and" (ca). The pouring out (*nirvāpa*) and the taking out (*udvāpa*) are performed according to the specific location. However, for the purpose of separating and winnowing, by virtue of their functional capacity, they are carried out with a separate vessel for each individual seed.

The six *adhivāpas* (pourings) should be understood as occurring in succession; the pouring into the black vessel (*kṛṣṇāninna*) and the simultaneous pouring (*saṃvāpa*) occur according to different locations, and so forth. The Brahman and the Sacrificer remain exactly as they were. The application of the mantra regarding the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) is as follows: "For skill (*dakṣa*), thou art of the wood" (*vānaspatya*), and so on. Having placed two vessels to the west of the *Śālāmukhīya* fire, one draws the sacrificial grass (*saṃya*) from the south, and so forth. All the mantras pertaining to the cart (*śakaṭa*) are to be repeated. This applies only in the case of using separate carts, and not otherwise.

In the case where the cart is divided [into two parts], the vessel is likewise divided; in the case where the cart is not divided, the vessel is also not divided. In this latter case, there is no repetition. On a single undivided vessel, the barley is placed to the south and the rice to the north. It is the same even in the case of the spilling [of the grain]. There is a repetition of the mantra "urjaṃ dhat-sva," because it is impossible to perform the touching simultaneously according to the *paribhāṣā* sūtra: "Mantras that are capable [of being performed together] are performed together; those that are incapable are performed separately. The mantra "payo mayi dhehi" is recited only once.

He recites "bhapahatara rakṣa" only once. Having explained the *daśahotṛ* formula and placed the two strainers (*pavitra*) upon the awn-end of the grain, he forms a handful with the words "yacchantām" and silently pours water into the offering-spoon (*sruk*). He pours out the barley with the formula: "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I pour thee out, agreeable to Indra accompanied by the Haris. He pours out the barley again with the formula: "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I pour thee out, agreeable to Indra accompanied by Pūṣan."

With the formula, "May they yield; for you, O god... for Sarasvatī, for Mārutī, [I offer]," he pours out the *vrīhi* rice in the northern part of the winnowing basket. With the formula, "May they yield; for you, O god... for Indra, [I offer] what is pleasing," he pours out the *brīhi* rice. According to some teachers, all [the grains] belong to Indra; thus, in the case of the alternative mentioned in the preceding sūtra where everything belongs to Indra, one uses "for Indra" (*indrāya*) everywhere.
Once the grains have been sprinkled, he divides the *vrīhi* rice with the division-mantra, threshes half of it, and sets aside half for the purpose of parched grain (*lāja*).

The formula *idaṃ devānām* is repeated; because it is impossible [to utter it] simultaneously with the *sparśa* [touching], it is repeated. The formula *idamu naḥ saha sphātyai yata* is also repeated for the very same reason of impossibility. The rites beginning with *idamahaṃ* and ending with the *skannānumantraṇa* are each performed only once. The formula *urv antarikṣamanvihi* is also performed only once. Regarding this, some perform an *ūha* (modification), but that should be seen as refuted by the refutation of *ūha* in the case of the *savanīya-paśu* sacrifice in the mantra *urv antarikṣa prehi*.

With the mantra "O Ādityas, I place you in the lap," he places [the vessels] simultaneously with the [already] prepared mantra. [He says: "O Indra, accompanied by the bay horses (harivant), protect the oblation; O Indra, accompanied by the spotted horses (pṛṣanvant), protect the oblation; O Sarasvatī, O Bhāratī, protect the oblation; O Indra, protect the oblation. Thus, according to the respective deity, he circumambulates... [ga], and he gives away the wooden sword (sphya). [End of Section 1, Chapter 785] [This concludes] the section titled Jyotsnāvyākhyā composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa.

In the case of the *sarvendratva* (all-pertaining to Indra) view, [the formula is] simply: "O Indra, protect the oblations. Regarding the [animal] with the *śūka* [tail-hair], and so forth: at the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), [the formula is] "With the god's [power], I sprinkle you, acceptable to Sarasvatī, to Mārutī, to Indra, to the tawny one, to Indra accompanied by Pūṣan, to Indra. In the case of the *sandritva* (all-pertaining to the joint) view, [the formula is]: "With the god's [power], I sprinkle you, acceptable to you, to Indra. Having thus sprinkled the sacrificial food (*havis*) while the vessels have been sprinkled, the distribution mantra is: "May you two separate according to your respective portions."

Having divided the rice grains with this mantra—"This for Sarasvatī and Bhāratī, and this for Indra"—he threshes each respective portion for the two deities in due order, after the pounding of the barley, for the sake of the second *puroḍāśa* cake. He sets aside half of the non-shattered rice grains, keeping them well-protected. The ritual procedure (*tantra*) extends from the taking of the black antelope skin up to the placing upon the mortar. The taking of the pestle is performed as part of that same procedure.

According to the Sūtra—"He calls for the *haviṣkṛt* at the first seed-grain, or he releases his speech at the last"—the call for the *haviṣkṛt* occurs at the very first seed-grain, and one releases his speech when the command for the threefold husking (*triṣphalīkaraṇa*) is given at the final seed-grain. Since the calling of the *haviṣkṛt* is already accomplished by the taking up of the first seed-grain, there is no further need for a repeated call due to a lack of purpose. If the release of speech occurs precisely at the command for the threefold husking of the first seed-grain, then the threshing of the others may be performed without restriction.

The intention of the Sūtra is that [the action] would otherwise be non-scriptural (avaidha). Furthermore, threshing is for the purpose of producing the state of rice-grains (taṇḍulībhāva); since the removal of the husks (phalīkaraṇa) results in that very state of being rice-grains, these [actions] are connected and terminate with a single result. Therefore, in this case, the "non-simultaneous performance" (kāṇḍānuprasamaya) is to be understood. The disposal of the husks (tuṣa-nivapana), however, is performed by a single common ritual procedure (tantra). Thus says Bharadvāja: "At the end of all [the grains], he disposes of the husks. By this same [principle], the pouring out of the wash-water (prakṣālana-ninayana) is also explained.

The analysis is as follows: the injunction "one should husk them three times" applies to each individual grain; the reason for this has already been shown previously. Having washed [the grains] and combined them, one pours out [the water] together. Having performed the washing and pouring out for the barley, the procedure for the rice follows. The statement regarding the *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) is intended to prevent a division prior to the *adhi-vapana* (pouring out), which would otherwise be observed for the purpose of dividing the *caru* and *puroḍāśa*; however, a division prior to the threshing is indeed appropriate.

Regarding the production of parched grains (*lāja*) from rice that still possesses its husks, there might be a doubt that the mantra [prescribed] for the division [of the grain] prior to its scattering (*avivapana*) would not apply here; to dispel that doubt, it says "with the formula for division" (*vibhāgapatreṇa*). He threshes the rice intended for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). He sets aside and preserves half of what remains for the purpose of the parched grains. From the mention of "rice" (*vrīhi*) and the mention of "half," it is understood that the roasted grains (*dhānā*) and the flour-mash (*karambha*) are made of barley (*yava*). This is because the word *dhānā* is well-known in common usage for roasted barley grains.

The fact that the *puroḍāśa* consists of barley—which was optionally obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction)—is here set aside. As for the nature of the *karambha*, the author of the Sūtra himself will explain it. The word *parivāpa* is indeed a synonym for *lāja* (fried grain). Having performed the rites beginning with the taking of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) and ending with "they scatter [the grains]," he sets down the flour-residue (*piṣṭalepa*) in its designated place. With the first mantra for the potsherds (*kapāla*), he places the potsherds for the *dhānās* and the *lājās*.

Since there are many *kapālas* (potsherds), multiple [rites] would result through the application of optionality (*vikalpa*). In that case, the placing (*upadhāna*) is performed by the first [mantra] alone. These two *kapālas* are to be placed first, according to the properties of the first *kapāla*; once their purpose has been accomplished, the others cease to apply. If it is asked: "Is it not the case that the application of the first mantra for the placing of the first *kapāla* is established simply because it is proximate (*upasthitatvāt*)? For what purpose, then, is the mention of 'first' (*prathama*)?"—this is true.

Regarding the statement, "having placed the pot with the first *kapāla* mantra," since there is no general rule (*paribhāṣā*) governing the placement of the pot or the placement of the *kapālas*, the specific mention of "with the first *kapāla* mantra" is for the purpose of making it known that the placement of the first *kapāla* must occur wherever that mantra is prescribed, and not elsewhere; because of that inclusion, [it applies] to the animal-cake offerings (*paśupuroḍāśa*) in the Aśvamedha sacrifice.

He offers the Mṛgāra sacrifice consisting of ten oblations, beginning with "To Agni, the deliverer from distress, a cake on eight potsherds," following the sequence of the first [offering] of the *pracetasaḥ*. [Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, 8th Praśna, 786]The Mṛgāra sacrifice consisting of ten oblations, beginning with "To Agni, the deliverer from distress, a cake on eight potsherds," he offers, following the sequence of the first [offering] of the *pracetasaḥ*.

The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the animal-cake offerings (*paśupuroḍāśa*) and the *mṛgāreṣṭi* are "taptāḥ. Since it is prescribed that the *sviṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* portions are common to both, and because no specific ritual procedure (*tantra*) is stated for the *mṛgāreṣṭi*, the placement of the single potsherd (*ekakapāla*) is accomplished by using whichever one of the two potsherd-mantras is available—namely, the first mantra used for placing the potsherds for the parched grains (*dhānā*), as there is an absence of a specific injunction [for this case]. Thus, the practical application is established.

The mention of "taking the potsherd" (*kapālagrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of making it known that the recollection of the mantra for placing the potsherds (*kapālopadhāna-mantra*) is necessary here prior to the actual placing of the potsherds. Having performed the rites beginning with "madantīradhiśritya" (having heated the boiling water) and ending with "dhṛṣṭirasi" (you are the bold one), up to "ekasthāpya" (having placed them together), he proceeds. Here, only a charcoal capable of performing the function [of heating] is used. Having kindled it with fuel, he makes it possess a flame suitable for the splitting of the grains (*dhānā*) upon the potsherd; thus, with the first potsherd... *dhruvam* (firmly).

Having placed [the first] potsherd with the mantra, thinking "it is burnt," he turns back the embers over it; then, having again turned back the embers and so forth, and having placed a potsherd for the sake of parching like the potsherds for the *dhānās*, thinking "it is burnt," he turns back the embers over it; then, having again turned back the embers and so forth—just as in the case of placing the potsherds for the *āgneya-puroḍāśa*—he places eight potsherds for the *aindra-puroḍāśa* and proceeds to push the embers [over them] in sequence.

Some say that what is produced from the pan used for roasting grain (*kenidbharjana-kapāla*) does not become burnt; this is incorrect, because the visible purpose consisting of heating must necessarily be required. Some also say that the placing of embers (*aṅgārādhyūhana*) with the formula "of the Bhṛgus" applies only to those pans intended for the *puroḍāśa* cake; this too should be understood as refuted by the present [text]. For the two pans intended for parched grains (*dhānā*) and roasted grains (*lājā*), there is a modification (*ūha*) of the formula to "heat yourself. Although non-intervention is indicated by the suffix *-tyap*, nevertheless, since the placing of embers is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the laying down of the pan, the non-intervention is not sublated by the rule that "there is no intervention by that which is a subordinate part."

Alternatively, the beating [of the grain] occurs after the preparation of the *āmikṣā*; the bringing of the potsherds (*kapāla*) for the purpose of placing them there—according to the rule "one should place the potsherds for the sake of *dhānās* and *lājās*"—is intended to dispel the doubt that the status of being a potsherd (*kapālatva*) exists only up to the point of the beating (as implied by the earlier statement "two potsherds for the sake of beating"), and not thereafter; thus, the acquisition of the potsherds is established only up to the point of the beating.
Having placed eight potsherds for the *puroḍāśa*, one prepares the *maitrāvaruṇī āmikṣā* according to the procedure for the *āmikṣā*.

The meaning is that one prepares the *āmikṣā* dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa (*maitrāvaruṇī*) according to the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for the *āmikṣā* dedicated to the Viśvedevas. In the expression "one prepares the *āmikṣā*," the mention of *āmikṣā* is intended to demonstrate that the term *payasyā*—found in the Vedic text "Mitra and Varuṇa [are worshipped] with *payasyā*" and in the forthcoming sūtra "the *payasyā* belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa"—refers to the *āmikṣā* itself, and not to some other distinct substance called *payasyā*.

In this very context, the preparation of the *āmikṣā* occurs first, and not the placing of the *puroḍāśa* on the fire; for the placing of the *dhānās* and *lājās* is prescribed prior to their roasting. Otherwise, the statement of the reverse order would be inconsistent. Therefore, it is established that the preparation of the *āmikṣā* takes place immediately after the morning milking (*prātardoha*), and the pouring together (*saṃvapana*) and other rites follow thereafter.

In this regard, the sequence of the ritual application is as follows: having caused the milk to be milked before dawn according to the injunction beginning with "nirūdham" and ending with "saṃpṛcyadhvam," he places barley and rice grains into another vessel while reciting the mantra, purifies them with the *hovovāra* strainer saying "utpunāmi," and likewise places parched rice (*lāja*) and wild rice (*vīhi*) into [the same] vessel, purifies them, and then, while reciting the mantra, places the ground flour into it and purifies it. Then [he proceeds] with "samāpa" and so forth.

Having performed the rites for the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) up to the stage of forming the lump, and having removed the embers from the two potsherds intended for the fried grains (dhānās) and the parched grains (lājās) respectively, he removes the embers by means of the potsherds themselves. [End of Paṭala 787, Section 150] He roasts the fried grains and the parched grains with the mantra used for placing the oblation on the fire.

The mantra for placing [the vessel] on the fire is "Thou art the Law (dharma), the life of all" (*dharmo 'si viśvāyuḥ*). With that mantra, he carries the parched grains (*dhānāḥ*) and the fried grains (*lājān*). This sūtra is intended to ensure that this mantra applies specifically to the carrying (*bharjana*), rather than to the placement of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) upon the potsherds—just as it would otherwise apply to the throwing of barley-grains or rice into the two potsherds—and that its application occurs only during the act of carrying. Therefore, the mantra is to be repeated for as long as the carrying continues.

Regarding the mother’s food, one should say: "An agreeable procedure must be commenced. Thus it is established that modification (*ūha*) must be performed because the mantra "Thou art dharma" (*dharmo'si*), which contains a singular number, is unsuitable for the present context. In that regard, for the barley-grains, [the formula is] "Ye are dharma, possessing all life" (*dharmāḥ stha viśvāyuṣaḥ*); likewise for the parched grains (*lājāḥ*) and the rice-grains (*vrīhayaḥ*, it is) "Ye are dharma, possessing all life. Or rather, it remains as in the archetype: "Thou art dharma, possessing all life," because they are enjoined collectively as a single unit in the case of the *parivāpa*.

In this view—that by the word *dharma* (the sacrificial substance) the oblation itself is praised, and not the rice grains which constitute its parts—it should be understood that there is no modification (*ūha*) even in the case of roasted grains (*dhānā*). For roasted grains and boiled grains, there is neither the first smearing nor the subsequent inference [of the offering], because such actions are impossible for them. The circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*), however, applies to all of them, because it is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) and because it is possible for them. But for the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*), it does not apply, because it possesses unique ritual properties (*apūrvadharma*). As for the flaming [of the oblation], it applies only to the cake (*puroḍāśa*), and not to others, because it is impossible for them. The formula "O Agni, you... certainly applies.

Because heating all around is necessary as it is conducive to cooking; the reading *saṃ brahmaṇā* does not exist because it is impossible [in this context]. However, *avidahantaḥ śrapayata* certainly exists, since that meaning was disregarded in the archetype (*prakṛti*). The reading *ya* (or *pa*) is simply a corruption, or else it should be understood as having a causative suffix (*ṇijanta*). The word *lāja* ends in the plural and is masculine according to the rule on gender instruction (*liṅgānuśāsana-sūtra*) stating "wives, fried grain, and parched rice" are plural.
They lie around without being scorched.

The prefix *upa-* here signifies "excessively. Until the removal [of the embers], they should remain lying down, situated upon their respective potsherds (*kapāla*). Because of the statement "without being over-burnt," they should be baked in such a manner that excessive burning does not occur. Since a slight amount of burning is unavoidable, it is not to be avoided. However, in the case of the Mahāpitṛyajña, because of the Vedic injunction that "the grains (*dhānā*) are of many forms," even some excessive burning is not a fault.

Otherwise, its manifold nature would be untenable; for the pouring of water toward the Gārhapatya fire must take place only from behind it, since the Mahāvedi has already been strewn, and because Baudhāyana states: "One should pour [the water] behind the Gārhapatya and toward the Āgnīdhra.

Having performed that which precedes the decoration, one divides the grains with the division-mantra, prepares half of the flour into groats according to the procedure for flour, and mixes them together with the mixing-mantra; that becomes the *karambha*.

Having wiped the *vājinapātra* (the vessel for the whey) and the *prāśitraharaṇa* (the vessel for the portion to be consumed) with the prepared *vedāgra* grass-blades, and having discarded them, he removes the parched grains (*dhānā*) and other items from the fire. Because there is no placing [of the grains] upon the fried grains (*lāja*), there is likewise no removal of the husks (*aśārā*). If the modification (*ūha*) of the mantra for placing [the offering] on the fire has been performed, then there is also a modification of the mantras beginning with the invitation (*animantraṇa*). The formula "This [is for] the army" (*idam ahaṃ senāyāḥ*) applies only to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). [Note: The variants *kha* and *ga* indicate that the *paiṣa* (directive) exists; *kha*, *ga*, and *va* indicate the meaning of the directive.]

With the modified formula, "O Sūryajyotis, measure out for great power," or as in the archetype, he consecrates the *dhānās* (parched grains). Likewise, with the modified formula, or as in the archetype, he consecrates the *lājās* (fried grains). Having consecrated the *puroḍāśa* (cake) exactly as in the archetype, he spreads a layer [of ghee] in the vessel intended for the *dhānās* with the modified formula, "May it be pleasant for you," or as in the archetype; likewise, having spread a layer in the vessel intended for the *lājās*, he [spreads it] in the vessel for the *pāyasam* (milk-rice) with the formula, "May it be pleasant for thee."

Having strewn [the grains], he silently spreads an underlayer [of ghee] upon the two vessels for drawing out the *āmikṣā* and the *vājina*. There is no pouring of ghee over the parched grains (*dhānās*) here. He pours ghee over the fried grains (*lājās*) with the formula: "May Agni, whose source is ghee, swell! Be well-mixed, be well-blended; you who are fair-formed, finders of wealth, the splendor of cattle—I pour ghee over you, acceptable to Sarasvatī and Pārvatī. Or [he may do so] silently. In the case of the view that [the sacrifice] belongs entirely to Indra, the pouring of ghee is done silently.

Having silently sprinkled the *puroḍāśa* with clarified butter, he sprinkles the *āmikṣā* with the formula "He who is your self... and then sprinkles the *vājina*. With the verse, "The guardians of the world have been moistened; the mothers of prayers emerge cooked," he removes the grains from the potsherd. In this case, there is either the elision of the word *prapasnupada*, or, in the alternative view, the modification (*ūha*) to *prathasnavaḥ*; or again, there may be no modification at all. With the formula, "Sit upon this, be established in the immortal, the essences of barley, being well-disposed," he places them in his own vessel which has been spread with a base of butter.

Or there may be no modification; or the setting down [of the grains] is done silently. Regarding the mantra for the removal of the parched grains (*lāja*), "O scatterers," if one follows the path of modification, the distinction lies in the mantra for the removal of the vessel. He places them in his own vessel upon that which has been spread out, with the words: "May they sit therein, may they be established in the immortal, the essences of rice, being well-disposed. Or there may be no modification. He removes the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) as in the archetype. Then, having removed the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) with the word "Dṛśhā," he likewise removes the vessel.

Then, having performed the application of collyrium (*añjana*), the counting (*saṃkhyāna*), and the removal (*udvāsana*) of the two *kapālas* in sequence with the formula "Irā bhūtiḥ," he performs these same acts for the *kapālas* of the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*). Having performed those items which precede the decoration (*bhalaṃkaraṇa*), he divides the roasted grains (*dhānāḥ*) into two equal portions according to the prescribed path, saying, "Go apart! and designates the deities: "This for Indra accompanied by Hari; this for Indra accompanied by Pūṣan. According to the view that all [the offerings] belong to Indra, he simply says "for Indra" in both cases.

The statement "with the distribution mantra" is intended to exclude silence. Just as all the grains (*dhānāḥ*) are to be sprinkled with clarified butter (*ājya*), so too is there an aspersion here over the grains, because they are a modification of the *tūṣṇīm-mantra*. Thereafter, he prepares the groats (*karambha*) from half [of the flour]. Alternatively, the aspersion of the grains occurs either immediately after the production of the groats, or the groats are prepared immediately following that. The procedure for the flour—the manner of its preparation—is according to the ritual rule for flour (*piṣṭānām āvṛt*). Black... [text ends]

In that manner, he performs the half-establishment (*ardhādhāna*) consisting of the *nināda* (loud sound) and so forth, as well as the parched grain (*saktu*). In the second alternative, the black sacrificial post (*kṛṣṇājinam*), the *śamyā*, and the grinding stones (*dṛṣad-upalā*) would remain in their respective positions. The flour of barley is called *saktu*; the word *saktu* is always used in the plural, just like the word *piṣṭa* (flour). With the mixing-mantra, "I mix you for the sake of procreation," he mixes [the flour] with clarified butter (*ājya*) by means of this mantra, blending it in such a way that it becomes saturated with butter.

The meaning is that when the kneading (*saṃyavana*) takes place, that object becomes designated as the *karman* (the ritual action). The explicit statement "with the mantra for kneading" is intended to dispel the doubt that—since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the bringing of the dough-balls (*piṇḍa*) serves a visible purpose, whereas here that purpose is absent—the mantra should be omitted. However, some hold that the phrase "with the mantra for kneading" is merely an illustration; by it, the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) of the clarified butter (*ājya*) from the beginning should also be performed.

The modification [of the mantra] is: "O clarified butter, be united with clarified butter; O Agni, with the essence of the herbs; flow together with the world that possesses vigor, being full of sweetness, with that which is sweet. Then, from that very [vessel], the heated clarified butter is poured out onto the hide and the skin. Having brought it with the mantra, "Thou art born all around," he pours it over with "Be thou mixed with the clarified butter," and stirs it together with "May he generate thee. This is trivial, because there is no evidence for its being intended as a mere secondary indication (upalakṣaṇa).

This *ājya* is indeed that which was [prepared] for the *auṣṭika* [offering]. Some say it is the *ājya* of the *apūrva* [offering]; others say it is that which has been heated by the *yajus* formula. Āpastamba clearly states that the pouring over [of the *ājya*] occurs after the division: "At the time of removal, having removed the parched grains (*dhānā*), and having divided them with the mantra of division, he mixes half of them with *ājya*; the other half he makes into flour-cakes according to the procedure for ground meal. Here, the mixing (*saṃyavana*) is indeed nothing but the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*), yet a slight distinction should be observed due to the connection with a different term; it consists in the form of a pervasive smoothness.

Āpastamba also states: "They call a mixture of *mantha* 'karambha'. Since this is the case, the designation *parivāpa* for parched grains (*lāja*) is established by implication alone; thus, there is no need for an explicit definition. Āpastamba, however, states explicitly: "*lājānaḥ parivāpaḥ*. By means of this etymological name—whereby they are called *parivāpa* because their scattering (*vāpa*) occurs all around (*paritaḥ*) like that of barley (*naptamaya*)—the term denotes parched grains. From these parched grains...

Only the fingernails are suitable for removing the husks [of the parched grains], not the mortar; otherwise, the parched grains would be broken into pieces. Since such a fact is established through common worldly experience, it is not explicitly stated [in the rule]. This has been clearly stated by Āpastamba: "He removes the husks from the parched grains with his fingernails; he performs the functions of the mortar and the pestle with his nails. "Removal" (saṃharaṇa) means extraction (apoddharaṇa). For the purpose of separating the husks in order to perform the *savanīya* ritual, he performs the functions of the mortar and the pestle with his nails.

When the time for their inspection and sprinkling has arrived, then, having performed everything from the sounding of the black antelope horn up to the sprinkling of the *upara* stones, he places the pressing-stones (*adhiṣavaṇāni*) upon them with the formula, "Ye are the stones; may Aditi acknowledge you for men. Having placed them, he mutters over them as in the archetype: "Ye are the stones; ye are for men; may these well-prepared [stones] prepare this oblation for the gods. Then [he recites]: "May I strike down the demon, the drinker of the sky."

Having removed the husks and having carried them away to a heap, he should pour out the *varṣavṛddha* grains, recite the formula "O *varṣavṛddhas*, stay! and then mutter the mantras for sifting and winnowing. He consecrates the husks with the mantra, "The enemies have been blown away. Thus says Bharadvāja: "In that regard, the mantra for pouring in, the mantra for threshing, the mantra for pouring out, and the mantra for winnowing are performed; the properties of the mortar and pestle should be applied to the hands."

Then, with his hand, he pours in the husks because the potsherds have been prepared. Some, however, claim that the word *lāja* (fried grain) applies even to those with husks, and therefore there is no removal of the husks; but this is not correct. For rice with husks lacks the fitness for sacrifice, it contradicts common worldly usage, and Āpastamba and Bharadvāja have explicitly stated the removal of the husks. In the *aupāsana* domestic fire offering, the fact that rice grains serve as the means of sacrifice by their very nature is based on scriptural injunction (*vacana*).

When the verse "In those not adorned, the dawn has appeared; the sacrificial animal is ready; the fire has been established according to the season" is being recited, he offers a fourfold-drawn portion of ghee while reciting the verse, "May Agni hear my call with the fuel."

"Unadorned" (*analaṃkṛtāḥ*) means "not adorned"; this is an adjective qualifying the *puroḍāśa* cakes. Thus, the meaning is: "let them sit upon the unadorned *puroḍāśas*. In the phrase "unadorned," the word *pratiprasthātṛ* (the assistant priest) is to be supplied as the subject. Here, by the term "adornment" (*alaṃkaraṇa*), pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*) is intended through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and not the anointing (*abhyañjana*) or smearing (*upāñjana*) performed with the mantra "May the gods purify you" (*devas tvā pavitreṇa*).

Otherwise, since the absence of that [ornament] would already be established here by the ornament itself which is to be prescribed later on, the statement "not having been adorned" (*analaṃkṛta*) would be redundant. And thus it is established that the phrase "the fire is indeed a quality" (*guṇo hyagniḥ*) serves as a restriction regarding the person.

*Adupā* and *ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.129). Regarding the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: although the injunction is already established by the mere phrase "while [the verse] is being recited" (*iti śasyamānāyām*), the inclusion of the long introductory term (*dīrghapratīka*) indicates that this offering pertains only to the first half of the verse being recited, and not to the second half as well. The explicit statement "in this [verse]" (*etasyām*) is intended to inform us that even when the verse is recited three times, this offering is to be made only during the first repetition, and not during the second or third repetitions.

The meaning is as follows: since this word [etad] is a pronoun (sarvanāman), it refers to the primary subject; and because the first pouring (āvṛtti) is the one first presented and is self-evident, and because the oblation consisting of four portions (caturgṛhīta-homa) is the primary element by virtue of being the renunciation of the substance, it is logical that the connection with the primary act—the oblation—belongs to the first pouring, which is the primary instance. The specific expression "this [is] the four-fold taken" (etaccaturgṛhītam) is intended to indicate that the five-fold taken (pañcagṛhīta) is also applicable in some cases. "Havaṃ me" is the end of the mantra. Because it is enjoined by the root *hu* (to sacrifice), the utterance *svāhā* is required.

Furthermore, having taken four portions, while holding a handful of *darbha* grass, he issues the command: "O Hotṛ, come forward! O Camasādhvaryu of Maitrāvaruṇa, come forward! O Ekadhanins, come forward! O Neṣṭṛ, lead the wife forward! O Unnetṛ, wait at the *cātvāla* with the Hotṛ’s cup and the *vasatīvarī* waters! Thus he gives the direction.

The subsequent statement is for the purpose of connecting with what precedes it; thus, it is established that the praise expressed in the first half of the verse—namely, "it was not an ornament"—is indeed expected here as well. However, there is no expectation here for the word *etasyām* (in this [verse]), because two things are impossible in the first half, and because the act of "taking" (*grahaṇa*) is secondary in relation to the "offering" (*homa*). The mention of "four times taken" (*caturgṛhīta*) is for the purpose of excluding the "five times taken" (*pañcagṛhīta*) which might otherwise apply by default. The mention of a "handful" (*muṣṭi*) implies the binding of the *darbha* grass. The root *iṣ* denotes motion.

"O Hotṛ, go forth toward the waters with your mind; go toward the waters"—this is the meaning of *apa iṇya*. Alternatively, O Hotṛ, addressing the waters that are to be brought forward, recite the verse beginning with "pra devatrā," etc.; or rather, the meaning is "pray for the waters as your desired object," for in the world, a desired action is properly performed when directed toward water. Regarding "of the Maitrāvaruṇa," it means pertaining to the Maitrāvaruṇa priest. "Camasādhvaryo" is an address to the Camasādhvaryu, who is the Adhvaryu responsible for the offering from the cups (*camasa*).

"O Camasādhvaryu of Maitrāvaruṇa, come with your own cup! Likewise, O Ekanins—those who possess waters in single-vessel measures—come running together with the Ekadhana vessels; that is to say, come along with the Sastha-sthālī. O Neṣṭṛ, bring up the wife holding the Pannnejani water-vessel."

Āpastamba makes this great point clear: "With the words 'Come forward,' the Neṣṭṛ leads the wife forward; or with the words 'Come forward,' she, holding the *pānnanī* vessel, comes forward. The Unnetṛ pours the Soma juice into the cups from the water. O Unnetṛ, together with the *camasa* and the *vasatīvarī* waters, go toward the *cātvāla*; the meaning is that you should sit down right near the *cātvāla*, facing the *cātvāla*.
The Camasādhvaryu of the Maitrāvaruṇa takes up his cup and hastens [toward it].

The phrase *apa iṣya hotar* ("O Hotṛ, impel [the gods] away") is not explicitly stated because its purpose—the request for the Hotṛ—is already evident and does not require further elaboration. However, this sūtra is intended to demonstrate a specific point of meaning: since it has not been mentioned that the Maitrāvaruṇa should run forward together with the *camasa*-adhvaryu, he might otherwise run forward alone; rather, it is to ensure that his running forward occurs only together with the *camasa*. Thus, the sūtra serves to clarify this particular detail.

The Maitrāvaruṇa-camasādhvaryu [takes] the cup of the Maitrāvaruṇa; the Maitrāvaruṇa-camasādhvaryu [takes] the cup of the Maitrāvaruṇa. Having taken that very one, the Maitrāvaruṇa [proceeds]. [Chapter 15, Section 711–150: Paṭala] accompanied by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa’s Jyotsnā commentary:
Taking up three or more odd-numbered vessels for the ekadhana waters, they run forward.

*Tisro'varāḥ* means those which have three or fewer (i.e., less than three) parts; *tāsyavarādhīḥ*. The word *ardha* signifies a part. These [pots] are uneven (*ayugma*). Regarding the phrase *ekadhanāsthālīḥ*, it is a single compound word. The attendants take up the pots containing the waters known as *ekadhana* and pour them out one by one. The plural number is used because many persons perform the action. Each attendant must not carry two pots with his own two hands; rather, each individual attendant carries only one pot.

Since it has been stated that fetching water with the left hand is always prohibited by tradition (*smṛti*), a distinction between persons is necessary for that purpose. By the word "odd" (*ayujaḥ*), an even number is excluded. Regarding the rule for the limit of the odd numbers, Āpastamba has stated: "Behind this very *havirdhāna* cart, one should place three, five, seven, nine, or eleven *ekadhanas*. Baudhāyana also has specified a particular instruction: "The *ekadhanas* are odd in number, with one as the minimum and eleven as the maximum."
The arrangement of the three *pramṛtis* of uneven number is determined by their position: five in the *ukthya*, seven in the *ṣoḍaśin*, nine in the *atirātra*, and eleven in the *aptoryāma*.
With the words "Go forth! Come out!", the *neṣṭṛ* leads the wife away.

Since it is already established by the word *śreṣeṇa* that the agent is the leader (*netṛ*), the mention of the *neṣṭṛ* is intended to demonstrate that "leading" (*nayana*) itself is the meaning of the word *neṣṭṛ*. The *neṣṭṛ* causes her to rise and leads her [to the altar]. From the word *ut*, he causes her to rise and leads her. The meaning is that even though she was previously seated for some reason, he causes her to rise with the mantra and leads her. Āpastamba states: "Holding her who stands at the place of the *pannejani* (foot-washing water)."

As for the claim made by some—that because of the statement regarding the remaining space for movement, "since everywhere one proceeds by going around the Āgnīdhra fire to the north, there is thus a passage to the north within the sacrificial enclosure"—this is trivial. For it would result in the absurdity of prescribing a movement to that specific location during the Vaisarjana-homa and other rites. Therefore, it should be understood that [the rule] applies only where it is specifically prescribed, and not elsewhere. By this, the statement of the ancients—that the wife is led back by way of the Vaisarjana path—is refuted.

In the case of many *palyas*, all of them are poured out in succession with the mantra ending in "mā mā hiṃsīḥ" (do not harm me). Since the purpose of the action of the *unnetṛ* is clearly understood from the *praisha* (direction), there is no need for a separate formula. Regarding this, Āpastamba states a specific rule: "They go along the *tīrtha* while reciting the mantra. This means that everyone proceeds through the space between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*.
The Adhvaryu should take the water at the spot where he can hear the Hotṛ reciting the *prātaranuvāka*.

The meaning is that in whichever place he stands for the purpose of drawing water, if he hears the *prātaranuvāka* being recited by the Hotṛ in the morning, then and there in that very place the Adhvaryu should draw the water. According to Āpastamba, this refers to flowing water (*vahantīnām*). The specific mention of the "Adhvaryu" is to exclude the Neṣṭṛ. Regarding the fault incurred if one does not hear the *prātaranuvāka* at the time of drawing the water, the same author says: "If he does not hear it, he becomes deaf; his speech is indeed cut off."
"His speech is indeed cut off; he becomes mute"—so says the Ṛṣi. Now, if one asks what should be done if there is no water within that distance, the author states the remedy for that contingency:
"If it should be far away, he should draw it up from afar and take it where he can hear the Hotṛ."

If the *prātaranuvāka* recitation cannot be heard by one standing at a certain distance, then water should be carried from a place where it exists to a location within that same distance such that the *prātaranuvāka* can be heard while standing there; having brought another supply of water and placed it there, one should perform the ritual. Thus, the hearing of the recitation itself is essential.

In the *Maitrāyaṇīya Brāhmaṇa*, it is stated: "Wherever one might overhear [the recitation], one would become deaf"; the sense is that this is for the purpose of removing that defect. This is a general proposition. To address the inquiry as to how this is so, he says:
"Having thrown a blade of grass into the water, he offers the fourfold-drawn oblation with the mantra 'O divine waters... (devīr āpaḥ).

Regarding the water that is to be taken up, the mention of "grass" (*tṛṇa*) is for the purpose of restriction; having thrown it—that is, having cast it—[into the water]. Because of the singular number, there is only one blade of grass; the singular number is used with reference to the genus (*jāti*). The word *etad* (this) should be understood as having its locative case-ending elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk...* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). Thus, the meaning becomes "in this [grass]. And so, it is established that one offers the oblation precisely while aiming at the grass.

"Having taken another fourfold portion"—since the previously taken portion was indeed fourfold, the mention of "taken" (*gṛhīta*) is for the purpose of indicating that it is obtained by implication; furthermore, in the *Rājapūya* sacrifice, one takes the water-drawings with the *Vaiśvadeva* verses consecrated by sprinkling: "O divine waters, you are the protectors of the people, the bestowers of sovereignty; grant us sovereignty, svāhā! Having offered the *Sārasvata* water with this, he takes [the other portions] with the same formula: "From here, O God... This is even though it is prescribed by the rule "on the others, 'to the god,'" for the purpose of obtaining the fourfold portion at the *Āhoma*.
The end of the mantra is "you are the portion, svāhā. Or he performs the remainder.

The meaning is that one offers all that has been taken up or makes a remnant; having offered a fourth part, one leaves behind three parts. This is because [the offering] must be performed while the substance remains in its original form for the sake of being suitable for taking up. Even when there is an offering of the whole, it must indeed be left over for the purpose of anointing. This is because the upcoming sūtra, "He offers all that," by using the word "all," indicates that no part of the original substance itself is to be omitted.

Regarding the requirement that the substance for anointing must be sufficient for the entire act, it has been stated by the ancient commentators in the sūtra "He three times anoints the *dhruvā* with the *juhū*" that this applies everywhere. Therefore, since the purpose exists here, one must certainly set aside a quantity sufficient for the anointing.
Alternatively, if there happens to be grass already present before [the offering], he offers into that very grass;

the meaning is that if grass is naturally available prior to the throwing away of the grass (*tṛṇaprāsana*), then having used that to steady the ladle, he offers into it, and the throwing away of the grass need not be performed specifically for the sake of the oblation.
With the mantra "Thou art a furrow" (*kārṣir asi*), he causes the oblation to overflow with *darbha* grass.

Because of the word "with *darbhas*" (*damaiḥ*), there is a loosening of the handful. He causes the clarified butter related to the oblation to overflow; that is, he pushes it away or removes it from the place of taking, meaning he moves it to a distance. "Mṛdham" is the end of the mantra.

With the mantra "For the imperishability of the ocean, I draw you up" (*samudrasya vo 'kṣityā unnaye*), he draws up [the butter] from those [vessels] not smeared with ghee using the cup of Maitrāvaruṇa.

The pouring out of the oblation (āhuti) does not serve an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), but rather has a visible purpose consisting in its being conducive to the taking up of the unsmudged portions (avṛtalipta). To demonstrate this, [the text says] "of the unsmudged portions. Therefore, it is established that if the taking up of the unsmudged portions were impossible by means of the pouring out of the oblation, then the pouring out of the oblation must be performed again with a mantra. [This concludes] the first section (paṭala) from the work accompanied by the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. Page 793.

"He draws with the cup of Maitrāvaruṇa" means he takes it out. For this very reason, the genitive case is employed in the sense of a part-whole relationship (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). By this, it is established that as much water as can be drawn by the cup of Maitrāvaruṇa should be taken. Nor should it be argued that all the ghee-dripping waters are to be drawn into another vessel using the cup of Maitrāvaruṇa, and that the genitive here should instead be understood as an accusative; for there is already the employment of the *ekadhana* waters and the *apanejanī* (ablution) waters.

Because it is utterly contradictory to assume that the genitive case has the sense of the accusative when the grasping of all [the vessels] is impossible, and because such an assumption would be irrelevant to the context; this much alone is the mantra.
By this very mantra, [the procedure applies] to the *ekadhana* waters.

The word "he takes" (*gṛhṇāti*) is the remainder [of the sentence]. By the phrase "standing in the ocean" (*samudrastha*), the meaning is that he takes [the Soma] into the *ekadhana* vessels—that is, the jars intended for the *ekadhanas*. Because of the use of the locative case, it is understood that the taking is performed with another vessel. The particle *eva* (only/just) is for the purpose of excluding the mantras mentioned by Āpastamba, such as "I take the essence of the swift-moving Soma," as well as the mantra mentioned by Baudhāyana, "I take you, who are pleasing to Indra," and other mantras mentioned in other *sūtras*.

By this, it is shown that the procedure stated by him is indeed acceptable to us as well. Consequently, the taking [of the water] with the cooking-pots (*sthālī*) is established as an alternative option.
"To the Vasus, to the Rudras, to the Ādityas," [with these words] the wife takes the *pannejanī* waters.

The mention of the *patnī* (wife) is for the purpose of distinguishing her from the *adhvaryu*. Those by whom the feet are led forth—that is, washed—are called *pādenanyasta*; the meaning is that he takes [the liquid] from the vessel of the *paścanī* with the mantra, "To the Vasus. And this act of the *pādenana* is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the wife; therefore, the taking from each respective vessel must be performed by all the wives as well. Āpastamba says, "They stand facing [the sacrificer]. The end of the mantra is simply, "I take [this] for the sacrifice, which is the *pādenana*. Bhāradvāja and Bhāradvāja likewise recited it in that very way. Those who bring the vessels, they bring them in.

Whichever person brings whichever vessel, he alone brings that very vessel, neither in reverse order nor anyone else at all. The bringing of the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup is established by implication as being performed by him, because of his status as the *camasādhvaryu* for that specific cup. Regarding the rule "those who bring the vessels bring them [to the Hotṛ]," this restriction applies specifically to the vessels; thus, just as in the case of the fetching of the *vasatīvarī* waters for the Hotṛ's cup, there is a restriction that the bringing must be performed by the *unnetṛ*.
By this, it is established that the bringing of the *vasatīvarī* waters is performed by the *parikarmika*, and the bringing of the *hotṛ-camasa* is performed by the *camasādhvaryu* of that [cup];
with that same mantra, the *neṣṭṛ* leads the wife forward.

By the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "by that very [path]," the alternative reading mentioned by Āpastamba—"come hither" (*ehi*)—is excluded. Alternatively, by the word "that" (*tena*), the path is referred to; thus, the meaning becomes "by that very path by which she was brought. By this, it is demonstrated that the return is strictly dependent upon the path of arrival and is not a matter of personal choice. Regarding the mantra, only that mantra which was observed at the time of arrival is to be employed here.

The statement "by means of the mantra" is for the purpose of excluding the state of being *tam* (the Adhvaryu). Just as there is no formal command (*praiṣa*) regarding the bringing back of the water intended for the *pannejanī* libations, there is likewise an absence of a command regarding the returning; thus, since the *neṣṭṛ* would not otherwise be reached [for this duty], the rule that "the Adhvaryu performs with the Yajurveda" might apply by way of the general principle (*paribhāṣā*). To prevent that from occurring, and so that the duty may belong to the *neṣṭṛ* alone, this is stated.

Having entered the *sadas* by the eastern door, having gone around the front of the *praśāstrīya* hearth, and [having gone] behind the *naiṣṭrīya* hearth, he places down the *pannejanī* waters for the wives with the words, "To the Vasus, to the Rudras, to the Ādityas."

The phrase "the path itself is always without limit" and "by that very path" implies that the path extending as far as the *prāgvaṃśa* (eastern hall) is also obtained; this is what is excluded by the present [text]. By the suffix *-ena* in *agreṇa* ("in front of") and the suffix *-ena* in *apareṇa* ("behind"), the proximity of those two words to the objects of both actions is made known. Now, one might ask: "In this case, regarding the location of the *praśāstṛ*, there is a qualifier ending in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), whereas regarding the location of the *neṣṭṛ*, there is no qualification by connection with the *neṣṭṛ*; thus, what is the significance of these two?"

It is said: In the case of the *praśāstṛ* and the *dhiṣṇya*, the requirement is fulfilled by its mere existence (*sattā*), and not even by its physical presence; however, in the case of the *neṣṭṛ* and the *dhiṣṇya*, even its presence is not required. To demonstrate that such a disparity exists, a derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is employed in one instance, while in the other, the term is used as a relative (*saṃbandhin*). The words *dhiṣṇiya* and *dhiṣṇya* are synonyms. Therefore, it should be understood that no consideration regarding the brevity or prolixity of the terms—such as between the words *ghaṭa* and *kalaśa*—is relevant here.

The grammatical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) also states that one should not pay heed to a discussion regarding the relative weight (*guru-lāghava*) of synonymous terms. [For example,] in the case of "to the Vasus, to the Rudras, to the Ādityas," because the word "I take" (*gṛhṇāmi*) serves as the indicator for the act of taking, and the phrase ending with "I take" (*gṛhṇāmi*) serves as the indicator for the act of placing, it might follow that the act of placing (*sādana*) consists only of the words "for the sacrifice, I place the *pannejani* waters. Let this not be so; rather, let the entire sequence beginning with "to the Vasus, to the Rudras, to the Ādityas" and so forth serve as the indicator for both the taking and the placing.

The purpose here is that there may be the application of a single mantra through modification (*ūha*) as "I take you" (*gṛhṇāmi*) for the act of taking, and through modification as "I set you down" (*sādayāmi*) for the act of setting down. Accordingly, the recitation of the two mantras is as follows: the recitation of the mantra for taking is: "From the Vasus, from the Rudras, from the Ādityas, from the Viśve Devas—I take you, the foot-washing waters; for the sacrifice I take you, the foot-washing waters."

"I set down for you the foot-washing waters for the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and the Viśve Devas; I set down for the sacrifice for you the foot-washing waters"—this is the recitation at this point. When the wife comes and enters the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, the Neṣṭṛ sits down right there in the *sadas*.
Or [he says]: "O Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, these are your foot-washing waters; protect them. This is clear.
The others go to the *cātvāla* pit. || 3 ||

The wife, the Neṣṭṛ, the Netṛ, the Hotṛ, the Camasādhvaryus, those who bring back the Vasatīvarī waters (excluding the one who performs the *parikrama*), the Adhvaryu, the Brahman, the sacrificer, the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Camasādhvaryu, and the Ekadhanins [participate].

"May Varuṇa unite you; may Indra unite you; may Dhātṛ unite you; may Bṛhaspati unite you; may Tvaṣṭṛ and Viṣṇu, bestowing with progeny, grant wealth to the sacrificer. According to their respective positions, they are joined by their positions. [End of] Paṭala 170, from the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

With the mantra ending in "kalpantām," having touched together the *hotṛcamasa* and the *maitrāvaruṇacamasa* above the *cātvāla*, he pours out the waters known as the *vasatīvarī*. The meaning is that by means of those two cups—the *hotṛcamasa* and the *maitrāvaruṇacamasa*—he pours them into each other; the word "vi" (apart) indicates a mutual pouring. The prefix "sam-pari" is used here to denote simultaneity, as in the expression "he sleeps with his mouth open."

Therefore, it is established that contact (*saṃsparśa*) exists for as long as there is mutual bringing together. This meaning is clear from another Sūtra: "The Adhvaryu pours the *vasatīvarī* waters while the *tṛca* cup and the Maitrāvaruṇa cup are in contact upon the *cātvāla* mound. The term "in contact" (*saṃspṛṣṭayoḥ*) is a locative absolute; by this, simultaneity is indicated. Due to the use of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the act of contacting has a different agent. The presence of a different agent is indeed appropriate to avoid the impossibility [of self-contact].

It is understood that a touch must be performed such that the northern part of the Hotṛ’s cup, held in the right hand with its handle pointing eastward, and the southern part of the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup, held in the left hand with its handle pointing eastward, become joined together. This is a general proposition. To address the inquiry as to how this is done, he states the specific detail:
having poured some of the Vasatīvarī waters into the Hotṛ’s cup, he pours them into the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup; and from the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup, he pours them into the Hotṛ’s cup.

The term "of the *vasatīvarī*s" is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). Having poured a portion of the *vasatīvarī*s sufficient for the *hotṛ*-cup into the *hotṛ*-cup—that is, having mixed it—[the Adhvaryu] pours from that *maitrāvaruṇa*-cup [into the *hotṛ*-cup]. He pours half from that *maitrāvaruṇa*-cup into the *hotṛ*-cup. This act of pouring is the ritual procedure of "pouring out" (*vyānayana*). Because of the hearing of the ablative case ending (*pañcamī*), the pouring out is not performed with another vessel, but rather the pouring out is done from those two [cups] themselves. "May he join them together"—this is the mantra for the pouring out from the *kāṭa* [vessel]. [This applies to] the *hotṛ*-cup and the *maitrāvaruṇa*...

There is a mantra for pouring from the *maitrāvaruṇa* cup into the *ruṇacamasa* and for pouring from the *maitrāvaruṇa* cup into the *hotṛcamasa*. There is no mantra for the pouring out (*niṣecana*), because that does not have the nature of a drawing-out (*vyānayana*). For this very reason, a different verbal root is employed. By the prefix *ni-*, the filling is indicated; by the word *strāvaṇa*, it indicates a small amount being drawn out repeatedly for the purpose of preventing spilling. Here [ends section] 55.

Pāraskara states a specific rule: "Having recognized that they are moving along together, one pours from the Maitrāvaruṇa cup into the Hotṛ cup, or conversely, from the Hotṛ cup into the Maitrāvaruṇa cup.
One anoints both the Hotṛ cup and the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with the *pracaraṇī* spoon, modifying the beginning of the mantra to "May he anoint you all" (*saṃ vo 'naktu*).

In place of the mantra *saṃ vo dadhātu*, he employs the mantra beginning with *saṃ vo 'naktu*. The intended meaning is that he uses the word *anaktu* in place of the word *dadhātu*. By the words *hotṛcamasa* and *maitrāvaruṇacamasa*, the waters contained therein are indicated, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra *saṃ vo 'naktu*. Thus, it is the anointing of the waters alone, not [the vessels]. [End of] Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, [Eighth Book, Section on] the Two Vessels.

Because the substances are distinct, there is a repetition of the mantra. That [ladle] from which the *tuṣṇīkagraha* (silent drawing) was first taken is the one used here for the performance; it is not any other. By this, it is established that the ladle intended for the *vaitarjana-homa* is not used here. Regarding the reading "mantrādīn" with a plural ending, it is indeed a corrupt reading.
They approach the presence of the Hotṛ.

*Antika* means "near. The statement regarding approaching the vicinity is for the purpose of [reaching] the elevated area and so forth; however, this approach to the vicinity is established for the Adhvaryu by the rule of questioning. Here, there is a specific sequence in the *Mānava Śrautasūtra*: "They bring up the *havirdhāna* shed; in front [of it], the vessels belonging to the Maitrāvaruṇa, the vessels belonging to the Hotṛ, the *vasatīvarī* waters, and the *savanīya* jars in successive order. Then the Hotṛ asks the Adhvaryu three times: "O Adhvaryu, have you obtained water? The meaning of the question is: "O Adhvaryu, have you obtained water? The protracted vowel (*pluti*) is used in the question.

He replies three times, "utemanannamuru te. The phrase ending with "utemanannamuru" is the citation of the opening words (*pratīka*). The response-verse itself ends precisely at "utemanannamu. The phrase "utemāḥ paśya" is its explanation. For this very reason, the traditional explanatory statement, "vāvaitavāha," is consistent. This is clearly stated in the *Bāṣkala-śākhā* as well: "Just as the Adhvaryu replies 'utemanannamu,' so indeed does he say 'utemāḥ paśya'."

Thus, in accordance with the two scriptural passages, [the author] explains that "see" (*paśya*) means "see the highest food" (*uttamam annam*); this is intended to refute the view that the two sentences ending with those words constitute a single sentence. Regarding the two occurrences of the word *yatra*, the second sentence is an explanation of the first sentence, but it does not have the purpose of explaining the phrase "burning of the wind" (*vāta-dāha*).
