Because there is no pair of *iti* particles in the present context, there is only one sentence for the sake of providing a reply. As for the meaning of "burning of the wind," however, it will be explained later.

The subsequent sentence is indeed an explanatory gloss upon the first sentence. Therefore, the intention is that one does not employ only the phrase "he obtained food" (*uta annam avārīt*), but rather recites this entire sentence. The word *vāva* is used for emphasis. It is not merely that he obtained it; moreover, he fully attained those [cows]. Even when something is at a distance, its existence alone constitutes "obtaining," yet "full attainment" (*upa-sam-prāpti*) exceeds that mere existence.

"O Hotṛ, do not place your trust merely in my word; rather, look at these [fires] standing before you. This is the meaning of what the Adhvaryu must say: "Look at these great ones," or "Look at these. Regarding the sequence, the questions and answers are paired: there is one answer for each individual question, and not three answers following a set of three questions.
If a remnant remains, he offers the *kratu-karaṇa* oblation with the *pracaraṇī* ladle, using the verse beginning, "O Agni, the mortal whom you [protect] in battles... (RV 10.104.11).

The mention of the *pracaraṇī* spoon is for the purpose of a general rule (*paribhāṣā*): in all rites other than the *vaisarjana-homa*, this very *pracaraṇī* is to be used; however, in the *dākṣiṇa-homa*, it is the *vaisarjana-homīya* [spoon]. Furthermore, since there is an extended application (*atideśa*) regarding the *dākṣiṇa-homa* stating "just as in the *vaisarjana*," by that very rule, the *vaisarjana-homīya pracaraṇī* would be obtained [for the *dākṣiṇa-homa* as well]. The *ṛtukaraṇa* is so called because by means of it the ritual cycle (*ṛtu*) is performed. This technical designation (*samākhyā*) is for the sake of conventional usage, as seen in such expressions as "fifteen-fold *sadas*" or "having offered the *ṛtukaraṇa*."

Regarding the statement "or he performs the remainder," another alternative was mentioned previously; in that case, if a remainder is possible, then he offers all that is left. The mantra ends with "śaśvatīriṣaḥ. Because it is enjoined by the root *hu* (to sacrifice), the utterance *svāhā* is required. [Chapter 150] With the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa: 797. If no remainder exists, he states the procedure: having taken another fourfold portion, he offers all of that.

If the clarified butter (*ājya*) is non-existent—either because it was not used as the remnant of the *ājya* or because the remnant that was prepared has been lost—then one should take another four-spoonful (*caturgṛhīta*) of clarified butter and offer all of that butter. The mention of "four-spoonful" is for the purpose of indicating that even when only a portion of it is employed, one must still take exactly four spoonfuls, and not a quantity determined by what remains after previous employment.

Since the performance of the *sarvahoma* (offering of all) is already established by the absence of any intention to offer more and the absence of any further application (*viniyoga*), this statement is for the purpose of making known a specific meaning: that the offering of everything must be made in such a way that not even a single drop remains. The inclusion of the word "that" (*tat*) is for the purpose of indicating that whatever else has been taken up must be offered here without any residue. By this, it is established that there is no restriction regarding other [substances].
He places the *pracaraṇī* ladle on the front of the southern *havirdhāna* cart.

The mention of the *havirdhāna* (the cart for holding the oblation) is intended to indicate that the two *daśāpavitra* strainers connected with the Soma, as well as the *camasa* cups and other implements, should be set down here in this very place, just like the *pracaraṇī* ladle.
Regarding the rule "for whom one should desire, 'May he be impotent,' [one should place it] below him":

if a sacrificer (*yajamāna*) who is performing the sacrifice desires that a certain enemy should become impotent—that is, a eunuch or neuter—he should place the *pracaraṇī* below the southern *havirdhāna*. Alternatively, the meaning is that he should place it below that lower part.

He causes the waters to enter the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door. The causative suffix (*ṇic*) in "he causes to enter" indicates that this action is performed by an attendant; thus, it is established that all [the priests] enter together.
Among those [waters], he places the *hotṛ*-cup, touching it [to the others], in front of the axle on the northern track of the southern *havirdhāna* cart.

When those *vasatīvarī* waters have been brought forth, this [water] is placed nearby just as the oblation called *soma* is contained within the *havirdhāna* cart; indeed, it is itself an oblation, and through its mixing with *soma*, it possesses a connection to the primary oblation known as *soma*. As for the result: in the event of the destruction of the *hotṛ*’s cup (*hotṛcamasa*), one should take the *vasatīvarī* waters to the *āgnīdhra* pit and, having poured some of the *vasatīvarī* waters into the *hotṛ*’s cup with the mantra "May he unite you" (*saṃ vo dadhātu*), one should then pour a small amount into the *maitrāvaruṇa*’s cup.

The origin [of the rule] is as follows: "Having anointed the cup of the Maitrāvaruṇa and the Hotṛ with the *pracaraṇī* spoon, he places it in front of the axle. The mention of the specific injunction (*vidhi*) is intended to indicate this particular meaning: that for those cups belonging to the Maitrāvaruṇa, there is no anointing because it has already occurred. "In the northern track" means near the northern track; the phrase "in front of the axle" (*purokṣam*) is used to exclude the area behind the axle, even though the space near the northern track extends that far.

The phrase "on the northern path" (*uttarasyāṃ vartanyām*) is used to indicate the region situated in front of the axle, devoid of the northern track. The waters contained in the *hotṛcamasa* (the Hotṛ’s cup) are those within the cup itself; their contact is through the medium of the cup, not direct contact, because such would be impossible and because it would result in spilling. "Touched" (*āspṛṣṭam*) means either completely touched or slightly touched. This is more than merely touching the *havirdhāna* shed. [Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram—8th Praśna]
The others [the *ekadhanā* vessels] are placed according to available space in the northern *havirdhāna* cart;

that is, all those other than those contained in the *hotṛ*-cup are placed near the northern *havirdhāna* according to available space. The *ekadhanā* vessels are placed behind the axle, while the *vasatīvarī* waters are placed in front of the axle. Thus says Āpastamba: "The *vasatīvarī*s are below the northern *havirdhāna*, in front of the axle; the *ekadhanā*s are behind the axle. In this regard, the specific detail from Āpastamba is that three *ekadhanā* jars are placed behind the axle, while the others are placed according to available space.

"You are the *nigrābhyā* waters, heard by the gods; you are bright, bearers of the bright; you are purified, bearers of the purified; satisfy my life!"—with these words he makes the sacrificer recite over the *hotṛ*'s cup; they thus become the *nigrābhyā* waters. || 4 ||

Thus ends the first paṭala in the eighth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. "Right there," meaning in the vicinity of the *hotṛcamasa*, indicates observation by proximity. Accordingly, Maudgalya says: "He causes the sacrificer to recite while he is looking at them. The mention of the "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is for the purpose of excluding the wife. He states another particular detail as well: "Having grasped that *nigrābhyā* water so that it almost spills over [his] chest, he causes the sacrificer to recite. The grasping [of the water] may or may not have been performed, depending on which [water] serves as the cause in the *hotṛcamasa*.

The recitation has been performed; the meaning is that those waters become "nigrāmyāḥ" (subdued), that is, they are brought under control. The purpose of this designation is seen in such passages as "śvātrāḥ stha vṛtraturaḥ," where one sprinkles [the Soma] with the *nigrāmyā* waters, and so forth; it serves to identify these specific waters. The terms "śukrāḥ śukrabhṛtaḥ" and "pūtāḥ pūtabhṛtaḥ" are optional alternatives to those found in other recensional branches (*śākhāntara*), being replaced by the corresponding terms found in one's own branch.

Thus ends the first paṭala of the eighth praśna in the Jyotsnā commentary, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—the son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was himself the son of Śrīmad Agniṣṭomayājin Sāhasrāgniyukta Vājapeyayājin Sarvatomukhayājin Viṣāhasrāgniyukta Pauṇḍarīkayājin—on the *Śrīmad-Bhagavat-Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*. This work is intended to alleviate the distress of learned men caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within that ocean of a sūtra. ||1||
8.2 Now begins the second chapter of the eighth book. He proceeds with the *dadhighraha* (curd-offering).

It is called a *graha* because it is "taken" (*gṛhyate*). That ritual action in which there is a *graha* consisting of curd is the one named *dadhighraha*; he "proceeds" (*pracarati*) by means of that, meaning he performs it. Here, by the word *pracāra*, only the sense of performance is intended, not the sacrifice itself, because it lacks the status of being mediated by the *vaṣaṭ*-call. By the word *graha*, the substance is meant here; this is a general declaration. 1.
"Thou art taken with a support;

for Prajāpati, the luminous, I take thee, the luminous," with these words he takes the Dadhi-graha (curd-libation) in the Dadhi-graha vessel. "O Indra, [ward off] the mind of those who hate us," with this he carries it forward. "For out-breathing thee, for in-breathing thee," with these words he offers it.

That which was performed on the previous day is here [referred to as] "curd" (*dadhi*). In the expression "he takes the curd-cup" (*dadhighraṃ gṛhṇāti*), the word *dadhighra* refers to the substance (the curd), just as in the expression "he brings the Agnihotra. Since the act would be accomplished by the mere statement "he takes the curd," the inclusion of the word "takes" (*graha*) is for the purpose of including the wiping with the *śākhāpavitra*. He carries it toward the Āhavanīya fire for the sake of the oblation. The endings of the three mantras—"To heaven thee! To the atmosphere thee! To the earth thee!"—are respectively: "I bind thee" (*taṃ naddhi*) and "I offer" (*juhomīti*).

Because it is stated that "he offers," the word *svāhā* occurs at the end of the final mantra intended for the oblation. Sitting behind the Āhavanīya fire, the offering is made with any corner of the cup used for drawing the soma. Since this is a unique rite (*apūrva*), the rules of the *darvihoma* do not apply. From this point until the Āgrayaṇa draught, one should draw the cups in a low tone (*upāṃśu-svara*); from the Āgrayaṇa onwards, in a loud tone (*upabdimat-svara*). Thus says the Śruti: "Those cups which he draws prior to the Āgrayaṇa, those he should draw in a low tone; those which are subsequent, those he should draw in a loud tone."

According to the two rules stated in the *Prātiśākhya*—"The *upāṃśu* [whispered] recitation is without sound (*aśabda*) and without mental application (*amanaḥprayoga*)," and "The *saśabda* [audible] recitation is accompanied by resonance (*upabdimat*)"—one should proceed according to those two accents as appropriate. The accent for the *Āgrayaṇa* [cup] is indeed the same. This *Dadhigraha* is not occasional (*naimittika*). Nor should it be argued that its occasional nature follows from its being prescribed in the event of a displacement of deities; for, in the absence of the word "if" (*yadi*), no such occasion (*nimitta*) is perceived. Thus, it is obligatory (*nitya*).

And likewise, Jaimini [states] in the fourth chapter, fourth quarter: "The *dadhi-graha* (curd-offering) is occasional (*naimittika*) because of its connection with a scriptural injunction; it is also constant (*nitya*) because of the word 'eldest' (*jyeṣṭha*), and because of its universal form (*sārvarūpya*). Or rather, it must be constant, for those two [statements] are explanatory praises (*arthavāda*) since they have no connection with the ritual act and because there is no interruption. The meaning of the first sūtra is: the *dadhi-graha* is occasional precisely because of its connection with a scriptural injunction regarding the occasion of an interruption (*antarāya*). In the phrase "because of the word 'eldest'," the word "word" (*śabda*) refers to praise.

"Because [the cup] has the word 'eldest' (*jyeṣṭha*) as its praise; or rather, because it possesses the word 'eldest,' meaning it is characterized by that term; or else, the word 'eldest' denotes primacy because it is grasped first. Thus, the meaning of the second sūtra is that there is both occasional (*naimittika*) and permanent (*nitya*) status. And because of its universal form—since Prajāpati is all the deities—it has permanence even due to its identity with all deities; this is the meaning of the third sūtra. [The texts state: 'One should take the *ājya* cup for one desiring splendor; one should take the *soma* cup for one desiring Vedic luster.'"
The word "kāmyau" (desirable) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
For those two—the *ājya* and *soma* cups—the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is explained by that of the *dadhi-graha*.

Regarding those two, the *ājya* and *soma* cups: the ritual method (*prakāra*) of the *dadhi-graha* applies here; namely, the rule that "the *dadhi-graha* vessel is made of Udumbara wood and has four corners" is applicable. Furthermore, the meaning is that for these two, the formula beginning with "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, the luminous, for Prajāpati the luminous," and ending with "For out-breath thee, for in-breath thee," and concluding with "He offers [it]," is likewise applicable.

"One should take the *dadhi-graha* for one desiring cattle"—this applies to both the obligatory (*nitya*) and the optional (*kāmya*) rites. By the sentence "one should take the *dadhi-graha*," there is an obligatory injunction; and by the subsequent sentence "one should take the *dadhi-graha* for one desiring cattle," there is an optional injunction through the hearing of the result. Thus, the meaning is that in both cases it is the *dadhi-graha* alone, and not the other two. Now, what is the case here? In the expression "in the obligatory" (*nitye*), the reference is primarily to the state (*bhāva-pradhāna*). After the word "obligatory," the particle "also" (*api*) is to be supplied.

And thus the meaning is as follows: although the *dadhi-graha* (curd-cup) is obligatory, it nevertheless proceeds even when its desirability is established by the scriptural mention of a result, such as "one desiring cattle should take the *dadhi-graha*. Therefore, while the *dadhi-graha* possesses both forms [obligatory and optional], it is established that the *ājya-graha* and *soma-graha* are exclusively optional; the letter *pa* [in the original text] should be regarded as a corruption (*apabhraṣṭa*).

Because the *ājyagraha* and *somagraha* are optional (*kāmya*), their placement is only in the archetype (*prakṛti*) and not in the ectype (*vikṛti*). Likewise, the optional *dadhighraha* is placed only in the archetype when performed for the sake of obtaining a husband. However, it should be understood that the obligatory (*nitya*) *dadhighraha* is placed in both [the archetype and the ectype]. Regarding the *ājyagraha*, it is either a previously unestablished (*apūrva*) offering or one belonging to the sacrifice of the cake-offering (*aiṣṭika*). In the view that it is *apūrva*, the drawing is done with the vessel itself; in the view that it belongs to the cake-offering, the drawing is done with the *sruva*-ladle as far as the *dadhighraha*.

The touching of water occurs after the vessels have been set down and before the taking of the clarified butter (ājya) to fill the cup. In this regard, because the verbal root *kam* (to desire) is heard in the texts, when there is a desire, the sacrificer must make a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) according to his wish, such as: "Desiring prosperity, I shall take the Āgrayaṇa cup"; "Desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), I shall take the Soma cup"; or "Desiring cattle, I shall take the Dadhi cup. This is because of the rule: "The sacrificer desires that which is heard [prescribed] for the entire sacrifice; likewise in the case of the obligatory sacrifices, he desires those things which the scripture causes him to hear through the use of the verb *kāmayati*."
When about to take the Soma, one takes up as much of the King (Soma) as one deems sufficient for a single drawing (*graha*).

Because of the prefix *apa-*, the taking is to be performed from the King who has become a mass and serves as the source (*apādāna*), but it is not the taking of the entire King. Alternatively, the prefix *apa-* expresses the manner of the taking; that is, the Soma is to be taken in such a way that it is held by a ladle (*hadas*) or a handful (*muṣṭi*). In this regard, the measure of the King to be taken is stated by the phrase: "as much as one deems sufficient for a single drawing."

Since the matter could have been stated with brevity simply as "he took the king who was standing there with a focused mind" (*ekagrahāyātaṃ rājānam apādatta*), the composition of a heavy sūtra is intended to convey a specific rule: namely, that if sufficiency (*paryāpti*) is not established by the ablative (*apāta*), then another [case] may also be sufficient; however, it is not the case that sufficiency is restricted solely to the ablative. Thus, it is for the purpose of making this known. "He is seized" (*gṛhyate*)—oh, what flavor!

The term *ekaśamā* means "only" (*kevala*). It is determined that by this much Soma—just what has been obtained for the sake of the *graha*—the juice is secured; that is, the meaning is that one should take up exactly that amount of Soma, whether or not the vessel becomes completely full.

Since it is established by implication that the Soma obtained for the purpose of a single cup (*ekagraha*) is the source (*apādāna*), the statement "he considers [it] as obtained for a single cup" is intended to show that the rule to be stated later—"one desiring rain should draw all the cups full"—is an optional (*kāmya*) prescription regarding the fullness of the cups; it does not apply here, but rather, in the absence of such a desire, just as there is no drawing from above for the stream-cups (*dhārāgraha*), so it is here as well.
He places the other [cup] back down.

The meaning is that he places back in its own place what remains after having taken up the other [portion] for the sake of holding it single-handedly (*ekagraha*). Because of the statement "he takes it back" (*pratyupanahati*), the placing down occurs only after untying the binding. Having held the Soma in his hand, while still sitting, he performs the re-binding and places it down. If, while sitting, he is unable to do so in this manner, then he hands it to another, performs the re-binding, and places it down.
Having placed it upon the lower stone (*upara*), having sprinkled it with the *vasatīvarī* waters, and having consecrated it with the mantra "You have grown strong for us... (*avīvṛdhaṃ vaḥ...*)—

Having placed that which was taken from the bottom, the one above it, and the broadest one in the middle—the fifth—having thus deposited them as characterized by the marks, he dwells there. Having approached and mixed them with the *ṛc* verses, the meaning is that he consecrates the mixture with the mantra, "O Soma, for the pressing. This concludes the section [of the chapter]. [End of] the eighth section, accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa.

"The gods, the seekers, have prepared three kindling-sticks for the mighty, immortal one as he moves around. Of these, they assigned one as enjoyment to the mortal; two have gone to the world of the hidden. Thus [it is said]. With the pressing-stone (*grāvan*), he presses according to the purpose—that is to say, from among the four [stones] taken up excluding the *upāṃśusavana*, with whichever one is appropriate, according to his inclination, until as much juice as is required is produced; the meaning is that he makes it loose by pounding, in accordance with the extraction of the juice, during the pressing.
With the mantra "May he leap unto me," he addresses or recovers that first drop which spills when the Soma is being pressed; this applies to what has spilled.

Because of the mention of the "first" [drop], this expiation is not required for the spilling of the second or subsequent drops; in those cases, one should simply recover the spilled drop silently. The end of the mantra is "from the joint. With the mantra "The drop has spilled," he consecrates the scattered droplets.

"Vibhūṣo nindavaḥ" and "saptahotrāḥ" mark the end of the mantras. This consecration (*anumantraṇa*) is for one who is a *vimat* (a learned Brahmin), not for one who is not a *sat* (a virtuous person). This is the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for all pressings (*abhiṣava*). The meaning is that this rule—beginning with the bringing near (*upamantraṇa*) and ending with the consecration (*anumantraṇa*)—applies to all pressings associated with the cups beginning with the *aṃśu*, as well as to the great pressing (*mahābhiṣava*).

This is the mantra for the pressing (*abhiṣava*) in this very [case]. Since the rule "this is the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for all pressings" applies, this mantra would also apply to the mantra "three times for the *yaha*"; however, its exclusion is made for pressings related to cups (*graha*) such as the *dhruva*, and for the great pressing (*mahābhiṣava*). The meaning is that this pressing-mantra "three times for the *yaha*" applies only to this specific pressing and not to other pressings. He states a general rule (*paribhāṣā*):
Having taken hold of it with his hand containing gold, while standing facing the east, he offers it in the eastern part of the southern half, or in the eastern part of the northern half.

Having taken the Soma that has been pressed equally, having taken it in a vessel—with the hand together with gold; this has been explained in the section on the purchase of Soma. Since the requirement "having taken it with the hand together with gold" is already obtained through its recurrence in the subsequent sūtra, the explicit mention of "with gold" (*sahiraṇyena*) here is for the purpose of providing a basis for the gold. Consequently, "with gold" functions as a qualification of the cup itself. By virtue of its association with gold, the act of resting upon gold (*hiraṇya-śrayaṇa*) is what is actually enjoined. In the expression *sahiraṇyena*, the instrumental case denotes the sense of accompaniment.

The meaning is that he stands together with that cup (graha) along with the gold. The southern half is in the south-eastern direction; the northern half is in the north-eastern direction. Wherever it is thus, there all Soma-offerings are performed.

In those Soma-offerings where this procedure—beginning with "standing facing east," and so forth—is prescribed, there the oblations of the entire Soma from each respective vessel are all the Soma-oblations; the offering of the whole Soma must be performed, and no remnant is to be set aside. Because of the statement "where it is thus, there [it is so]," this rule for the offering of the entire Soma applies only to such a procedure; elsewhere, it is according to the specific injunction.

The meaning is that in whichever place—whether in the eastern part of the southern half or in the eastern part of the northern half—the *homa* is performed, all the *soma*-oblations must be offered in that very same place. Following the words "all *soma*-oblations," the verb "he offers" (*juhoti*) from the preceding sūtra is to be supplied. Nor should it be argued that this [verb] should instead connect with the word "having offered" (*hutvā*) from the subsequent [sūtra], because that would result in the word "having offered" being left without a proper syntactical connection.

Nor should it be argued that even if there is a connection with the subsequent sūtra for the sake of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), that same defect remains; for since this can be justified as a restatement (*anuvādaka*) of a specific injunction, the defect does not persist. The purpose of the restatement, however, is to show that in the case of the *homa* (offering) itself, the act of making a remnant (*śeṣakaraṇa*) is secondary (*gauṇa*), because its purpose is for consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*). Thus, the making of a remnant refers to a small amount of Soma, while the *homa* is of the greater portion. Having offered, he makes a remnant—this is clear.

Having entered the *sadas* by the eastern door and sat down facing west in front of the *hotṛ*, he looks [at the Soma] with the mantra, "Thee, O watcher of men... (*nṛcakṣasaṃ tvā*), and consumes it with the mantra, "The delightful overcomer... (*mandrābhibhūtiḥ*).

According to the general rule (*paribhāṣā*)—"When not specifically stated, the Adhvaryu is the performer"—the Adhvaryu alone is the agent. His entry into the *sadas* is for the purpose of consumption, based on the scriptural statement, "They consume in the *sadas*. Because of the injunction "in front of the *hotṛ*," the *hotṛ* must remain seated behind his own altar (*dhiṣṇya*) until the completion of the Soma consumption.

Alternatively, regarding the passage "having entered the *sadas* by the eastern door, [he goes] past the *hotṛ*," one must accept the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) as follows: "having entered the *sadas* by the eastern door, [he goes] past the *hotṛ*," in order to avoid contradiction with the *Hautra-śāstra*. Thus, the meaning becomes: "having gone to the *sadas* past the *hotṛ*, he enters the *sadas* by the eastern door. In this way, since there is no possibility of connecting the phrase "past the *hotṛ*" with the word "seated" (*āsīna*), there is no contradiction with the *Hotṛ-śāstra*.

Nor should the redundancy of the word *purastāt* (in front) be suspected; for since *purastāt* here refers to the eastern part of the *sadas*, there is no such redundancy. This very word *purastāt* indicates that one should not go behind either the *sadas* or the *hotṛ*-altar (*hotṛdhiṣṇiya*). By implication, the *hotṛdhiṣṇiya* alone serves as the limit in all instances of consumption (*bhakṣa*), and not each respective altar (*dhiṣṇiya*), because it would result in a contradiction with the rule "they consume [the soma] at the *āgnīdhra* in the *sadas*," which would otherwise be impossible.

The point is that, because the Hotṛ is the primary priest and is the first to be present, it is logical that his position alone should serve as the limit. Now, one might object: "Is not the statement 'in front of the Hotṛ' redundant? Its purpose would be to exclude entry through the western door for one who has already entered by the eastern door of the *havirdhāna*. If this is argued, we reply: no, because that [exclusion] is already established by the prohibition, "When the Soma sacrifice is not yet concluded, the Adhvaryu, having entered the *havirdhāna* by the eastern door, must not exit by the western door. [This is said] regarding the Hotṛ... [End of fragment].

"Sa. and so forth. [This section belongs to] the sixth chapter (paṭala) of the second book (dvitīya-kāṇḍa), accompanied by the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa. Because it is necessary for the purpose of approaching in close proximity, [the mantra] ending with "prathamaḥ rūpeṣu" is the first; that ending with "āyuṣe varṣase" is the second. Here, there is merely a demonstration of the mantra to be recited later; therefore, this mantra "vamumadgaṇasya" applies here as well.

"One should partake [of the Soma] by means of the *bhakṣa-mantra* beginning with the inspection (*avekṣaṇa*)," so says the upcoming injunction. Furthermore, the contradiction with the word "all" (*sarva*) in the statement, "At the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), they partake of all the Somas with the formula, 'Of thee, O Soma, belonging to the Vasu-group and having Soma as thy deity,'" is also resolved in this manner. Otherwise, just as in the case where the contradiction with the rule "he should rise after touching the Audumbarī post" is resolved by restricting the meaning of the word "all" in the rule "the entire [post] is to be wrapped," such a restriction would result here as well. Now he states the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*): "One who partakes [of the Soma] himself, having performed the inspection and so forth, proceeds by means of the *bhakṣa-mantra*."

Whoever, having himself brought [the portion] from wherever it may be, begins with the inspection—referring to the rite prescribed as "having inspected"—that person proceeds with such a mantra characterized by the indicative mark of consumption (bhakṣa-liṅga), namely "mandrābhibhūtiḥ"; the meaning is that he consumes it.

From such sūtras as "Taking up, he proceeds," which establish that the acts of taking up and consuming have a single agent, and because of the specific injunction later on that [the portion] is brought by another, the act of taking up oneself is already established here; nevertheless, the explicit mention of "himself" (svayam) is for the purpose of conveying this meaning: whoever is the consumer, he himself, while taking up his own portion, proceeds with the consumption-mantra beginning with the inspection (*avekṣaṇa*).

By this, it is established that for the Pratiprasthātṛ and others as well, this same rule applies when they take their respective portions. Alternatively, "taking himself" (*svayamāharan*) is a qualification of the *makṣa* (the portion). In the phrase "taking himself," the suffix *vit* is applied according to the rule *vijupe chandasī*; then, by the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*, the suffix *vin* is added to the root *hṛ*. And by the rule *kartari kṛt*, this suffix denotes the agent. Thus, the meaning is: "that in which there is one who takes himself" (*svayamāharaḥ*), i.e., the agent of the act of taking himself.

They themselves bring the food and partake of it with the *bhakṣa-mantra* beginning with "avekṣaṇa" (inspection) and ending with "bhakṣa" (consumption). The letter *na* is archaic (*chāndasa*). Alternatively, according to the rule "of verbal roots, nominal stems, genders, persons, tenses, consonants, vowels, and agents," it should be understood that the *śatṛ* suffix is used archaically in the sense of the absolutive (*ktvā*) to denote a prior time. By this, the simultaneity of the bringing and the eating is precluded.

In the case of consuming [the Soma] by one's own agency, the procedure beginning with the inspection (*avekṣaṇa*) and so forth is accomplished solely through the mantra; likewise, in the case of consumption by another agency, the procedure beginning with the waiting (*pratīkṣaṇa*) and so forth is of that same nature. Since the two acts of "having entered the sacrificial hall" (*sadaḥ praviśya*) and "seated facing west in front" (*purastāt pratyaṅ āsīnaḥ*) are not accomplished by means of a mantra, they are common to both cases. As for the phrase "in front of the Hotṛ" (*agreṇa hotāram*), since it is possible only in this very instance of consumption, it applies here alone and not to other consumptions. In the expression *bhakṣam aṇan*, the inclusion of the word *bhakṣa* (consumption) serves to delimit the portion ending with *bhakṣayāmi*.

This is stated in order to demonstrate the *yoga* (connection). The expression "beginning with the *avekṣaṇa*" (looking) is intended to exclude the *manana* (mental recitation) mentioned by Bhāradvāja—namely, that even in the absence of *pratīkṣaṇa* (waiting for permission) and *pratigrahaṇa* (acceptance), one should simply recite these mantras while intending, "May I eat [this] wherever I may eat"—thereby setting aside that specific mental recitation. In this context, the *upahāna* (invocation/permission) certainly takes place; for there is a prohibition in the Śruti and in the Āpastamba-sūtra stating, "Soma must not be drunk by one who has not been invited (*anupahūta*). Furthermore, that *upahāna* belongs specifically to the Adhvaryu, because he is the primary agent due to his role as the performer of both the oblation (*homa*) and the pressing (*abhiṣava*).

The *pratiprasthātṛ* and the *adhvaryu* are the two beings to be invited (*upahāna*), and this mutual invitation is the rule for this portion. Because of the reason already stated, the invitation of the *pratiprasthātṛ* by the *adhvaryu* would otherwise follow; to preclude that, the Sūtra says: "Wherever they may eat at the same time, they should desire the invitation from one another. From the analysis of the compound (*yogavibhāga*) with the suffix *mat*, it should be understood as a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix, as in the word *padmanābha*.
