He awaits [the offering] being brought by another with the words, "Eat! Having received it with "May I be united with you through the arms of the Aśvins," and having looked at it with "Thee, the one who beholds men," he recites "The delightful, the overpowering... and concludes with "Of the Vasu-group, Soma is the deity. At the morning pressing, they consume all the Soma portions; the Nārāśaṃsa cups are consumed with the formula, "Of that drunk by Narāśaṃsa..."

The term *āhiyamāṇam* does not indicate that the act of waiting is simultaneous with the bringing [of the fire]. Here, by the word *prati*, "facing toward" is meant; thus the meaning is that he looks toward that end. This is indicated by the sign (*liṅga*) of the word *ehi* ("come"). Because of the singular number in *pratīkṣate*, the one who performs the waiting for his own axle is the Adhvaryu alone, and not the Brahman and others who perform the waiting for their respective axles. Alternatively, the reading *pratīkṣante* (with the plural ending) is indeed more appropriate.

The reading in the singular number is indeed improper because it contradicts the plural number used later on. Nor can it be argued that why should the order not be reversed; for since the injunction regarding eating is required by all [the priests], such a reversal is impossible to maintain. Furthermore, because the act of offering depends upon the bringing [of the portion] by another agent, it is impossible for it to be directly expressed, and thus there is an absence of the *śyan* suffix. Alternatively, the singular number itself may be considered acceptable; one should accept whichever of these two views is appropriate here.

The meaning of the phrase *ananataḥ sannautitvā* is "having sat down without bending. The term *anudravarṇa* has already been explained previously. *Sarvatomāḥ* refers to all those *soma* offerings; they are the ones being consumed, as indicated by the plural number, namely the Adhvaryu, Pratiprasthātṛ, Brahman, and Neṣṭṛ. The Sadasya is also included here. This same mantra is used by the Hotṛ and others for the consumption of the *camasa*. This is because it will be stated later that "the mantra for their consumption has been explained."

The specific distinction to be stated hereafter is that, following the taking of the mantra, there is no further rite until the end of the *anudravaṇa*. In this context, the inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of dispelling the occasional doubt that this rule applies only where many performers consume many portions of *soma* connected to a single ritual action at one time. The first mantra ends with *ḍhayo'si*; the second is of the same length; the third ends with *khyeṣam*; and the fourth ends with *varcasaḥ*.

The fifth recitation is for the Narāśaṃsa group: "O divine Soma, knower of the mind, belonging to the morning pressing, having the Gāyatrī metre, sung by Indra, full of sweetness; being invited, I, who am invited, partake. And for the Narāśaṃsa consumption mantra: "Of that which was drunk by Narāśaṃsa, O divine Soma, knower of the mind, belonging to the morning pressing, having the Gāyatrī metre, drunk by the Fathers, full of sweetness; being invited, I, who am invited, partake. This is the recitation of the Narāśaṃsa consumption mantra.

Regarding the consumption of the *makṣa* (honey-mixture), there is this distinction between bringing it oneself and having it brought by another: when bringing it oneself, the recitation of the consumption mantra is performed without the *anudrava* (the call for haste); when having it brought by another, the recitation is performed with the *anudrava*.

In the third chapter, second section, Jaimini also states that the designation "bhāsa" for the *anuvāka* beginning with "mahī" must be established through the presentation of both direct and indirect commonality. He does so via two sūtras: "The *anuvāka* has the purpose of recitation (*bhakṣa*) by virtue of both indicative mark (*liṅga*) and designation (*samākhyā*); there is a displacement [of the mantra] from its place due to its form and the instruction, because the purpose is enjoined. The indicative mark is the word "bhakṣa" (recitation), and the designation is the ancient name "Bhakṣānuvāka."

The first meaning of the Sūtra is that there might be a desire for consumption even of this entire Anuvāka of Bhalehu. Regarding that Anuvāka, *liṅga* is the unique indicative mark found within the mantra that makes known the specific action; *upadeśa* is the statement that enjoins that mantra. Even in the absence of *liṅga*, the application is determined by these two [through the process of exclusion]. [End of] the second section of the eighth chapter, accompanied by the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

The meaning of the second sūtra is that *viniyoga* (application) occurs because [the mantra], despite not explicitly stating the action such as the grasping of the substance (*artha*), is enjoined and therefore must be performed. Thus, the application of the mantras beginning with "mahī" and ending with "hinva me" is solely for the purpose of summoning [the deity] and looking upon [the offering], whereas the application of the mantra "mandrābhibhūtiḥ" alone is for the act of consumption (*bhakṣa*). Some maintain that this mantra "mandrābhibhūtiḥ" extends only as far as the word "tṛpyatu" (may [the deity] be satisfied). That is not correct.

Because of the mention of a subordinate quality (*guṇābhidhāna*), there would be only one mantra beginning with "mandra" and so forth, due to the connection between those two; this is because it would contradict the rule of Jaimini found in the second quarter of the third chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]. Since satisfaction is mentioned as a subordinate quality of the consumption (*bhakṣa*) by the word "be satisfied," there would be only one mantra beginning with "mandra. The meaning is: "because of the connection"—that is, the existence of the "connection" (i.e., the relation) between those two, namely satisfaction and consumption, which is of the nature of a cause-and-effect relationship.

Furthermore, satisfaction (*tṛpti*) possesses the status of an effect, while the act of consuming (*bhakṣa*) possesses the status of a cause, because it brings about satisfaction. Since satisfaction is not an object to be performed, the application (*viniyoga*) of the mantra lies solely in the illumination of the consumption characterized by satisfaction.

At the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), they consume all the Soma with the formula, "Of the troop belonging to Rudra, O Soma-deity," and the Nārāśaṃsa cups with, "Drunk by Narāśaṃsa. At the third pressing (*tṛtīya-savana*), they consume all the Soma with the formula, "Of the troop belonging to Āditya, O Soma-deity," and the Nārāśaṃsa cups with, "Drunk by Narāśaṃsa."

"O divine Soma, knower of the mind, of the midday pressing, belonging to Rudra-vadanasya, having the *triṣṭubh* meter, drunk by Indra, full of sweetness, being invited—I, being invited, partake. This is the recitation of the mantra for consuming all the *soma* at the midday pressing. "O divine Soma, knower of the mind, of the midday pressing, having the *triṣṭubh* meter, drunk by Narāśaṃsa, drunk by the ancestors (*pitṛ*), full of sweetness, being offered—I, being invited, partake. This is the recitation of the mantra for consuming the *nārāśaṃsa* cups.

"O divine Soma, belonging to the Āditya-group, knower of the thought, of the third libation, having the Jagatī metre, drunk by Indra, full of sweetness, being invited—I, being invited, partake. This is the recitation of the mantra for consuming all the Soma at the third libation. "O divine Soma, drunk by Narāśaṃsa, knower of the thought, of the third libation, having the Jagatī metre, drunk by the ancestors, full of sweetness, being invited—I, being invited, partake. This is the recitation of the mantra for consuming the Nārāśaṃsa cups.
The purpose of including the word "all" (*sarva*) should be understood as previously explained. In this very manner, Baudhāyana and Bhāradvāja recite the mantras;
that which precedes the *vasumadgaṇa* formula is appended everywhere.

The meaning is that the mantra beginning with *yo mandrābhibhūtiḥ* and ending with *āyuṣe varcase*, which precedes the mantra *vasumadgaṇasya*, is to be applied everywhere—just as in the case of the *rudravat* and *ādityavat* groups—to all three *narāśaṃsa* mantras, even for one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*). It does not mean, however, that this mantra is merely a supplement to the *vasumadgaṇasya* mantra alone. In the word *yad*, the suffix *soluk* is applied by the rule *supāṃ suluk...*; the same applies to *tad*.

Alternatively, this is the meaning: the phrase "bhalehi" (drive forth) following "vasumadgaṇa" (the group of Vasus) does not merely apply to that specific rite; rather, its application extends even beyond the groups of Paśus, Rudras, Ādityas, and Maruts. The singular number is used for metrical reasons (*chāndasa*). Or else, the meaning is that starting from "bhohi," the rite involving the "vasumadgaṇa" and so forth occurs everywhere—that is, in the context of all three *savanas*—and not only in the morning *savana*. In this context, the prefix *anu* has the sense of "also."

In the sense of "possessing wealth" (*dhanadhāmatī*), it should be understood by the wise that grammarians have accepted the polysemy of verbal roots even in the case of the root *bhū*; by that same principle, it must necessarily be accepted here as well without any logical flaw. Furthermore, [the mantra] is recited exactly as "of that which was drunk by Indra" (*anindreṣv indrapītasya*) because this very passage establishes that the consumption is performed only for that which has not been modified (*anūhita*). Nor is there an absence of being drunk by Indra in the Soma offerings not dedicated to Indra.

It should not be said that this is contradictory; for by resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that sacrifice (*savana*) in which Soma was drunk by Indra"—and by accepting it as a qualification of the *savana*, there is no contradiction. Thus, in the second quarter of the third chapter, Jaimini states: "But [the name] applies to all, according to Aitaśāyana, because of the purifying power of the portion (*bhakti*); for there is eligibility for the *savana*."

"Ekamantrya" means having a single mantra for all the portions (*bhakṣas*). Those [portions] which have this quality are "ekamantra"; their state is "aikamantrya. Even though there are multiple deities, the portions themselves possess "aikamantrya," which is simply the state of having a single mantra for a single deity. This is because all the mantras consist of drinking preceded by the act of devotion (*bhakti*), and that drinking of the Soma is performed by Indra alone. For, since the qualification for the *savana* (pressing) pertains to the three pressings, the text reads "drunk by Indra" (*indrasya pītasya*) with reference to all three; therefore, because they are to be drunk preceded by devotion, there is indeed "aikamantrya."

The meaning of the sūtra is that for all [mantras], the opinion of the sage Aitiśāyana applies. The mention of Aitiśāyana in the sūtra is for the sake of honor. By this, Jaimini’s view—that based on the specific indication of gender in the sūtra *liṅgaviśeṣanirdeśāt* (JS 3.2.31), non-Aindra cups have no mantra when the ritual procedure is common—along with the occasional mantra-less consumption, as well as his "replacement" (*ūha*) theory in the sūtra *punarabhyunnīteṣu sarveṣām upalakṣaṇaṃ dviśeṣatvāt* (JS 3.5.24), is refuted.

By the removal of the *ūha*, however, in the case of the *pātnīvata* offering, it is as before; one should, however, indicate Tvaṣṭṛ because of his drinking, and the "thirty" because they are for another's sake, and the *vaṣaṭkāra* because of the agent, as in the previous case. But the prohibition of the meters is set aside because they apply to all [verses]. As for the six sūtras in the second quarter of the fourth chapter beginning with "In the case of the *aindrāgna*, however, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) would prevail," their objects are already refuted by the very sense [of the argument]. Therefore, it is established that one consumes even those not dedicated to Indra with the formula, "Of what has been drunk by Indra."

"Of the man, of the Hotṛ, of the hope"—or alternatively, "those for whom the hope was made by the man," thus they are *narāśaṃsāḥ*; these are the deities. Soma drunk by these deities is "drunk by Narāśaṃsa."

In this context, "Indra-Agni" and "the Viśvedevas" are the deities of the *nārāśaṃsa* cups associated with the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*); "Indra accompanied by the Maruts" and "Mahendra" are the deities of the *nārāśaṃsa* cups associated with the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdinasavana*); and "the Viśvedevas" are the deities of the *nārāśaṃsa* cups associated with the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*). These are the deities designated as *nārāśaṃsa*. Soma, when drunk by these [deities], becomes precisely "drunk by the *narāśaṃsa*" (*narāśaṃsapīta*). It is only through such a procedure that the mantra for consumption (*bhakṣamantra*)—"the deity of the Soma drunk by the *narāśaṃsa*"—is logically established, and not otherwise.

Since the sacrifice is accomplished even by [the Soma] being shaken, it also becomes "drunk by them" (pitṛpīta). Regarding the term *pitṛpītasya*, the etymology is simply "that which has been drunk by the ancestors" (*pitṛbhiḥ pītaḥ pitṛpītaḥ tasya*); it does not have an etymology like the word *indrāpati* (husband of Indra), such as "that in which Soma has been drunk by the ancestors. This is because both the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* and the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, having read the text as *teṣu pitṛbhirbhakṣitasya* ("of that which has been consumed by those ancestors"), establish its status as having the characteristic mark of the ancestors (*pitṛliṅga*).

They are mentioned in the *Bāḍhaca* (Ṛgveda) scripture as follows: "The *Umā*s are indeed the Pitṛs at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*); the *Ūrjā*s at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina*); the *Kāvyā*s at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*). Thus he makes the Pitṛs themselves partakers of the pressings. The meaning of "making them partakers of the pressings" (*savanabhājaḥ*) is that he makes them sharers of the Soma in each pressing. They are also mentioned in the *Chandoga* (Sāmaveda) scripture in the passage beginning, "There are indeed three kinds of Pitṛs: the *Avamā*s, the *Aurvā*s, and the *Kāvyā*s," and so forth. According to the *Bāḍhaca* method, the Pitṛs are the *Umā*s and *Ūrjā*s in the first two pressings; according to the *Chandoga* method, they are the *Avamā*s and *Aurvā*s.

Here there is an alternative view. Even according to the third *savana*, the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are indeed the deities of the *kāvyas*. Therefore, this is what is meant: "The ancestors are the deities of the *nārāśaṃsas*. Regarding the number of *nārāśaṃsas*, it is stated that the morning *savana* has two *nārāśaṃsas* and the midday *savana* has two *nārāśaṃsas*; however, the statement "the [third] *savana* has one *nārāśaṃsa*" is not found in Jaimini’s Sūtra. It appears that this has fallen into the text by error. 807

"The third pressing has one *nārāśaṃsa* cup. Āpastamba also says: "In the first two pressings there are two *nārāśaṃsa* cups; in the third pressing there is one *nārāśaṃsa* cup. Lāṭyāyana and Drāhyāyaṇa also state this with a specific qualification: "The *nārāśaṃsa* cups are the second ones in the [first] two pressings, and the third one in the third pressing. This means that in the first two pressings, the second and third *nārāśaṃsa* cups are present, while in the third pressing, only the second one is present.

The Teacher, however, will explain each specific application in its proper place: at the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana), there are two Nārāśaṃsa vessels; at the midday pressing (mādhyandina-savana), there are three Nārāśaṃsa vessels; and at the third pressing (tṛtīya-savana), there is one Nārāśaṃsa vessel. Having sipped [the water] from these vessels, they should not rinse their mouths with the Soma itself, because it is not considered "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa). As Āśvalāyana has stated regarding the absence of rinsing: "They quote the tradition that 'they do not become impure by means of Soma. Furthermore, the sipping is performed from the vessel while it is still touching the mouth.

Having accepted that it is the leavings of that [person], for those who have eaten it, there is no immersion; rather, because purity is declared through washing, as in the statement: "Immersion is for those who have eaten [the leavings], but for others, purification is by washing. Also in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra], with reference to the vessels of ascetics (*yati*), it is said: "The purification of these is prescribed by water, like that of the *camasa* cups. Likewise, regarding the *camasa* of the *udgātṛ* and the *sadasya*, some—namely Tulādhāryāyana and Brāhmaṇa—have stated: "If they should become disgusted, they should have separate *camasa*s. Similarly, Kātyāyana says: "One should consume the Soma with the *hotṛ*-cup."

Therefore, there is no fault even in the state of being "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa). However, another opinion holds that several of these [scriptural] indications cannot logically apply to the state of being leftover from a vessel. Why? First, the mention of washing—such as the injunction "having washed away other smears," etc.—is consistent even with the purpose of removing external smears. Furthermore, the analogy of the *camasa* cup is appropriate for that purpose, given the context of the alms-bowl (*bhikṣāpātra*). Even the mention of "disgustingness" is consistent because it refers to the similarity of substances and their pleasant taste.

For indeed, there is a sense of revulsion toward the water remaining in the teacher’s water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) after it has been drunk, as indicated by the phrase "from the *camasa* [of the teacher]. Furthermore, this is not established by that very word *kamaṇḍalu*, since consumption is possible even when the pot has not been touched. Likewise, Baudhāyana has made known the very nature of the water-pot as being like a *camasa*: "Just as the *camasa* is considered pure due to its connection with Soma, so too the water-pot is pure due to its connection with the heat of the waters. Therefore, purification, therefore drinking, and therefore sipping (*ācamana*) are prescribed. Thus it is said.

Therefore, it is proper to sip [the water] using a vessel, either by taking it from another vessel as one does with a ladle, or by using a vessel whose rim has not been touched by the mouth. In this way, both requirements are fulfilled: the *hantakāra* (the ritual offering) is drunk, and the vessel remains non-defiled (*anucchiṣṭa*). However, although this is not the preferred view, if one drinks after having taken it through negligence, there is a slight loss; yet there is no failure regarding the primary rite, because no specific expiation (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed for that particular act is present here. The conclusion is simply that the general expiation applies. This may be so.

The primacy belongs to one side alone. If it is asked why, it is said: from the sentence "one should consume the *camasa*," contact with the mouth is obtained. Regarding the word *camasam*, there is a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for what is contained within it, but not for what has been extracted from it; for even in the case of figurative indication, it is improper to abandon a proximate meaning to adopt a remote one. As the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda has stated: "Even in figurative indication, proximity and remoteness certainly exist."

Furthermore, the meaning is obtained even from the nominal stem *camasa* alone. This is because the word *camasa* is etymologically explained in the *Bahvṛcabrāhmaṇa* and other texts within the rule "atyavi-cami-tami-nami-rabhi-labhi-nabhi-tapi-pati-pani-pani-mahibhyaḥ asac," as in: "Soma is drunk (*camyate*) and consumed (*bhakṣyate*) in this [vessel], therefore it is called a *camasa*. This has also been stated by the authors of the *Dhātuvṛtti*. [Note: Variants include *yajati* for *camati* and *pinasa* for *camasa* in some manuscripts.]

This is because Satyāṣāḍha, in his *Śrautasūtra*, has stated exactly this; and because the Mīmāṃsakas, while explaining the consumption (*bhakṣa*) by means of the designation (*samākhyā*) in the passage, "In the cups (*camasa*), due to the connection with the designation, since that is the cause," have also stated exactly this; and because Rudradatta has likewise said, "Its status as the *Brahmacamasa* is precisely this: that the Soma is consumed in it by the Brahman"; and because it is stated in the same way in the work of Rāmasvāmin.

Moreover, the *sūtra* stating that "there is washing in the *mārjālīya* [shed] of those things that have been eaten" is also an authority here, because the suffix *-ka* is prescribed in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) by the rule *kto'dhikaraṇe ca dhrauvyagatipratyavasānārthebhyaḥ*. Furthermore, the mention of "of the remnants" (*ucchiṣṭānām*) in the *Bhāradvāja-sūtra*—which states that "there is washing in the *mārjālīya* of the remnants of those things that have been eaten"—is also an authority here. Moreover, the expression of disgust found in the *Drahyāyaṇa* and *Lāṭyāyana-pūtra*, namely, "if they should feel disgust, there should be separate cups," is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*) here.

If it were taken as "having been lifted," then in the context of the *vībhatsā* (disgust), it would result in the loss of its foundational basis (*nirmūlatva*). Furthermore, the passage from the Vedic commentary (*vedabhāṣya*) on the rule "it is a *daśapeya*"—namely, "in this [rite], Soma is to be drunk by ten [priests] from a single vessel"—is also supportive here. The same applies to the mantras beginning with "the residue in the two cups" (*ucchiṣṭaṃ camvoḥ*), as seen in Uvaṭa’s commentary (*ūr-bhāṣya*). Moreover, this is also clear in the *Kalpataru* commentary on the *Uttaramīmāṃsā* sūtra: "If it is argued that it is impure, no, because of the word [of the scripture]. This is the general direction.
Some authorities record the mantra "May the goddess of speech drink of the Soma" (*vāgdevī somasya pibatu*) as being universal (*sārvatrika*).

The term "universal" (sārvatrika) refers to that which exists in place of the mantra for consuming all [offerings] everywhere. The teachers transmit such a mantra as this; the explicit meaning is that in place of all [deities] beginning with Vasumat and Ṛṇañcaya, there is the mantra: "May the Goddess of Speech drink of the Soma."

They argue that since all [mantras] beginning with "makṣahī" share the commonality of being "consumable" (bhakṣa) by virtue of their designation as such, one thing of the same class necessarily excludes another of the same class; thus, they claim there is an exclusion of all [mantras] beginning with "bhakṣehī. This is not correct, because it is impossible for those mantras to exclude one another due to their distinct purposes.
Having consumed the Soma, they touch themselves with the mantra: "hinva me gātrā harivaḥ... [and so forth].

The statement "having consumed the Soma" (*somaṃ bhakṣayitvā*) in this mantra is intended to demonstrate that the self-touching (*pratyabhimarśana*) occurs both when consuming what has been brought by others (*anyāhṛta-bhakṣaṇa*)—due to the indicative mark of digestion in the mantra "may my speech not go beyond the navel"—and also during the consumption with the *vāgdevī* mantra. Otherwise, since the principle of the application of all consumption mantras applies only to the case of consuming with the long mantra, this self-touching would occur only there; thus it should be understood.
By the word "self" (*ātman*), the heart is meant.

Within the heart, there is a small, stainless lotus-city situated in the midst of the body, as firm as a stone; within that too is a small space, free from sorrow—it is that which is within it which should be meditated upon.

Thus, although the Supreme Self (paramātman) is all-pervasive according to the Upaniṣad, the heart alone is described as its locus for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*). Alternatively, the navel may be intended here due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra; however, since direct measurement of the Self is impossible, the word "touching" (*prati*) prescribes the touching of the skin covering the lotus of the heart as a means for the contemplation of the Self. Regarding the phrase "having crossed over" (*atigā*), it is the end of the mantra. Having washed the vessel at the *mārjālīya* shed, he places it in its proper station (*āyatana*).

The word *mānalīya* has already been explained. *Pātram* refers to the vessel for the insects (*makṣapātra*). However, the washing (*prakṣālana*) is done with the hand alone. This is because of the prohibition by Āpastamba in the section on the Agnihotra: "The gods do not eat that which has been washed with meat. [End of] the first Paṭala. [This is] accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. The prefix *pra-* indicates a thorough washing; in the word *prakṣālya*, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is included within the root itself.

By this, it is established that the washing is to be performed by the *parikarmika* (assistant). However, Baudhāyana has stated that the washing of the two *ṛtu* cups and the *śukra* cup is to be performed by the *pratiprasthātṛ*; this [rule] should be accepted as an alternative (*vā*) for these. The placing [of the cups] in their respective seats (*āyatana*) is to be performed by the *adhvaryu* alone, according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā-sūtra*) stating, "The *adhvaryu* [acts] with the *yajus*. "In their own seats" means in their respective places. This is the procedure for all *soma* vessels.

"Having washed the vessel for the *māna* libation, he places it in the sanctuary"—this is the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for all *soma* offerings. The word "it occurs" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Since the preceding section began with the *avarīṣ* libations, one might think that this procedure applies only to those *soma* offerings not connected to the [preceding] context; therefore, the inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is intended so that this procedure may apply to all *soma* offerings belonging to every *ṛtvij* who partakes in the drinking of *soma*. The compound *sarvasomānām* is analyzed as follows: *sarveṣām* (of all) + *somāḥ* (the *soma* offerings) = *sarvasomāḥ* (all *soma* offerings); [then] *teṣām* (of those) + *sarvasomānām* (of all *soma* offerings).

The plural number in the word *somānām* is due to the distinction [of the cups] because they are taken with reference to those respective [deities]. Although the point is established by the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) alone, the formulation of the sūtra in its more elaborate form is for the purpose of excluding the cup for *surā*. Consequently, in the case of the *surā* cup, there is neither the washing of the vessel nor the placing [of it] in its proper place.

Alternatively, the meaning of the statement "this is the ritual procedure for all Soma-libations" is as follows: having entered the *sadas* by the eastern door, the Hotṛ sits facing east; looking at the *nṛcakṣas* [cup] with the words "svā," he recites "mandrābhibhūtiḥ" and so forth. This ritual procedure, beginning thus and ending with the settling in the seat (*āyatana-sādana*), applies to all Soma-libations. Since this procedure is established as being connected to the participants who consume the Soma, it follows by implication that it is also performed by those same participants.
However, in the case of the *grahas*, there is the requirement of including gold.

In this context, however, the word *tu* (but/only) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). The word "there is" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Thus, the sentence becomes: "The state of being accompanied by gold (*sahiraṇyatā*) exists only in the case of the cups (*graha*). The meaning is that the state of being accompanied by gold, which was previously mentioned in a general manner, occurs only in the case of the *grahas*—namely, the *somagrahas*, the *somameha*, the *aśvadābhyas*, and so forth—and not elsewhere, such as in the case of the *camasas*.

By the phrase "with gold" (*sahiraṇyena*) in this sūtra, which prescribes standing facing the east, it is established that the mere act of placing gold in the *camasa* cups does not occur; however, other requirements such as "standing facing the east" and so forth certainly do apply to the *camasa* cups. From the preceding sūtra, the term "of all Soma [vessels]" (*sarvasomānām*) must be carried over. Consequently, there is no requirement for gold in the *surā* cups.
Furthermore, the consumption (*bhakṣa*) results from both the oblation (*homa*) and the pressing (*abhiṣava*), and not from either action alone.

The phrase "of all [the cups]" (*sarvasāmānām*) continues to apply here. The particle *ca* (and) has the sense of *tu* (but). The syntactical connection is: "But the consumption [is determined] by the *homa* and the *abhiṣava*. The word "it is considered" (*mata*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Thus, the commonality regarding the *camasa* cups is established. "Homa" and "abhiṣava" form the compound *homābhiṣavau*; [the consumption is determined] by those two, *homa* and *abhiṣava*. This is intended to refute the notion that each is an independent cause, rather than [determining it] by either one of the two acts alone. These...

The meaning is that the consumption [of the soma] by the Adhvaryu, Pratiprasthātṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Unnetṛ is understood to occur only through both the offering (*homa*) and the pressing (*abhiṣava*) combined, and not through either one alone; for the Vedic text—"Having pressed [the soma], having offered it in the Āhavanīya fire, and having gone back westward, they consume it in the *sadas*"—states that the act of consumption has the same agent for both [actions]. Therefore, [this applies] to the cups belonging to the morning and midday pressings.

In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: [Regarding the eighth book—] in the case of the *savanamukhīya* cups, the *yojodgātṛ* cup, the *yajamāna* cup, and the cups involving over-pouring (*atimāha*), although there is pressing (*abhiṣava*), there is no consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*) because there is no offering (*homa*). Likewise, for the Pratiprasthātṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Unnetṛ, there is no consumption in these cases because there is no offering. However, in the *bhadāmya*, *mahābhadāmya*, and so forth, although there is an offering, there is no consumption because there is no pressing. Similarly, regarding the cups (*camasa*), it should be understood accordingly that there is no consumption for those who do not draw the cups (*acamasa-van*), and so on.

However, in the case of the *savanamukhīya* cup associated with the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), since there is indeed an offering (*homa*) as well, the consumption (*bhakṣa*) certainly takes place.
The vessels for the *dadhighraha*, the *aṃśu*, and the *adābhya* are common;
the word "common" (*samāna*) means "equal," not "one and the same," and therefore there are indeed three vessels. This point is indicated by the Sūtra—

Thus, there is a brief explanation of the three vessels. And Āpastamba has stated the distinctness of the *aṃśu* and *ādābhya* vessels from the *dadhigraha*: "On the northern shoulder [of the sacrificial post] is the *dadhigraha* vessel made of *udumbara* wood with four handles; the *aṃśu* and *ādābhya* vessels are indeed like the *avaśrū*. In that regard, according to the view of Āpastamba, there is a difference in the ritual application: there is one vessel for the *dadhigraha* and one for the *aṃśu* and *ādābhya*, making two vessels in total.

According to the opinion of the Teacher (Ācārya), there is a distinction in the ritual procedure (*prayoga-bheda*) such that there is one vessel for the *dadhi-graha*, one for the *āśvin*, and one for the *āgrayaṇa*, thus making three vessels in total. According to the school of Āpastamba, however, based on the sūtra stating, "One should take the *soma-graha*; this itself shall be the [sole] vessel," there is only one vessel even in the case of the *soma-graha*. But according to the Teacher's view, it should be understood that even here there are indeed three vessels; thus, there is a mention of "three. Their "sameness" (*tulyatva*) consists in their being of the same kind (*sajātīyatva*), and that sameness of kind is due to both being made of *udumbara* wood and having four corners.

One joins the cup for Aṃśu in close proximity to the cup for the Dadhigraha. One [cup] belongs to the Āditya [graha]. These two are to be employed facing west and facing east, respectively, to the north and in front of the Dadhigraha cup. The mention of the "Dadhigraha" is an elliptical designation for the Soma and Ājya grahas. In the case of the Ājya grahas, the disposal of that cup consists of throwing it into the fire; this occurs immediately after the offering. However, in the case of the Soma grahas, the disposal of one of them consists of discarding it once it has been smeared.

And he will state at the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) that "whatever is smeared with Soma [is to be discarded]. Since the vessel for the *dadhi-graha* is not smeared with Soma, according to the method taught by Baudhāyana and Āpastamba, it is simply to be cast away.
He proceeds with the *aṃśu* cup.

"He proceeds with the *aṃśu* [cup] by means of the rite to be accomplished by the *aṃśu*"; that is to say, he performs those rites which are to be accomplished by the *aṃśu*. This is a general proposition (*pratijñā*). This proposition is intended to exclude the status of being a subsidiary to the *pālikas* mentioned in other Sūtras. Furthermore, this taking of the *aṃśu* cup is not a subsidiary to the *savana* (pressing), but rather a subsidiary to the *Soma* sacrifice itself. Therefore, there is no repetition at each pressing. And the Teacher will demonstrate this by the expression "the midday pressing beginning with the pressing" (*abhiṣavādi-mādhyandina-savanam*), using the term "beginning with the pressing" (*abhiṣavādi-padena*). Jaimini also states: "The *aupānuvākya* [rite] regarding the cups and bricks is a subsidiary to the pressings and the piling (*citis*) because it is not connected to a specific context (*anārabhya-vāda*). The *aupānuvākya* is a statement established outside of any specific ritual context.

He takes up as much of the *rājā* (king) as he considers sufficient for a single draught; he sets aside the remainder. Having placed that [portion] upon the lower millstone (*upara*) and having moistened it with the *vasatīvarī* waters, he draws [the soma], breathing out and then breathing in his vital breaths, while mentally chanting the *Vāmadevya* hymn.
He takes up the *rājā*; having placed it upon the lower millstone and moistened it with the *vasatīvarī* waters—this is the statement: "We have increased you... etc.

1kha, ga, [Sad-bhāṣāṅka]: Chapter Two, together with the commentary Jyotsnā by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. [The phrase "as much as he considers sufficient for one draught"] is for the purpose of excluding the act of measuring (*mantraṇa*). It must certainly be stated that "he places it down for each person who has been led forward. Otherwise, there would be an exclusion even of taking a quantity sufficient for a single vessel (*graha*). Consequently, the optional full-draught (*pūrṇagraha*) might also occasionally occur; to prevent this, this [phrase] must certainly be stated.

The statement "he places it down immediately" must also certainly be stated because it falls within the middle [of the sequence]; otherwise, there would be the cessation of this as well. The repetition of the section beginning with "he takes up the King [Soma]" and ending with "he pours in the Vasatīvarī waters" is indeed purposeful. In the passage, "Having inhaled and exhaled the breaths once-poured [Soma], while mentally singing the Vāmadevya hymn, he draws [it]," the phrase "once-poured" is syntactically connected only with "he draws."

When the *nimitta* (the causal factor) exists, one performs the subsequent pouring with the two verses beginning with "ā mā skāndrapsa" and "śvityañca. The word "sakṛdabhiṣutasya" is in the accusative case, though it appears in the genitive in the Brāhmaṇa text. If the genitive were accepted here, then—since no other meaning is possible except for the sense of a part (*avayava*) in this context—the term would have to refer to a portion of the Soma already pressed; however, since there is no use for such a portion, it would result in its mere disposal, which would be contradictory. Therefore, the genitive is used only in the sense of the accusative.

"Of one who has been impaled," so says Āpastamba. Having once—meaning a single time—expelled the breaths forward until they have gone outside, and having drawn back the breaths, he should [sing] the Vāmadevya Sāman, seen by Vāmadeva, with the verse "kayā naḥ"; because of the mention of "mentally," the operation of the lips, palate, and other organs is restricted.

Although the *sāman* is sung upon a triplet (*tṛca*), nevertheless, because it will be stated in the subsequent sūtra that only one verse which serves as the source (*yoni*) of that *sāman* is to be taken as its representative, it is understood that this *sāman* consists of a single verse (*ekarcam*). Although "without pausing" (*anavānatā*) is not explicitly mentioned here, it is understood that the taking up of the *aṃśu* cup is indeed "without pausing," because it is heard in the context of the *aṃśu* ritual that "he takes it without pausing," and because it is virtually stated in the subsequent passage: "if he were unable to take it without pausing. "Without pausing" means without breathing in between.

Although it is said that "the Udgātṛ [sings] by means of the Sāmaveda," and thus the singing of the Sāman belongs to the Udgātṛ, nevertheless, because the drawing of the cup (*grahagrahaṇa*) is performed by the Adhvaryu, the present participle *gāyan* (in the phrase *gāyann aśvināv adhvaryur upayamyopāṃśupātreṇa*) indicates that the Adhvaryu is the one singing. This is because the simultaneity of the singing and the drawing of the cup is heard in the text, and because the common agency (*samānakartṛkatva*) is heard in the phrase *vasatīvarībhir upasṛjya*. Nor should it be argued that, since the drawing of the cup is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the portion-drawing (*aṃśagraha*), everything up to the words *vasatīvarībhir upasṛjya* must belong to the Udgātṛ alone—just as in the case of the taking up of the King Soma (*rājopādāna*). This is not so.

Where there is a connection with the *māna* (measuring), that action is performed by the *udgātṛ*; this rule is shown to have an exception (*vyabhicāra*) in the sentence "The *adhvaryu* measures out the *nava* [graha]," which prescribes a praise (*stuti*) performed with the *parimāṇā-sāman*. Furthermore, from the scriptural text—"If the *adhvaryu*, while taking the *āśu* [cup], should fail, he should lead [the sacrifice] for both the *adhvaryu* and the *yan-māna*; if he should succeed, it would succeed for both; he takes it without pausing; that indeed is the *aspardhi* [non-contentious]"—it is clearly understood that the *adhvaryu* is the performer of the taking of the *āśu* cup.

Because, by virtue of the mere connection with the *sāman*, it would be utterly unnecessary to assume that the act of drawing the *aṃśu* cup—which is prescribed for all [priests]—has as its performer the *udgātṛ*, who is neither mentioned nor established [in this context];
or rather, [the cup is drawn] with the verse of the *Vāmadevya*: "With what [splendor] has the Wondrous One come to us? (*kayā naś citra ābhuvat*).

The connection is with the verse of the Vāmadevya [Sāman]: "kayā naś citra ābhuvat. Since it is established that the *ṛc* produced from the Vāmadevya is to be taken because it serves as the source for the other Vāmadevya [chant], the specific citation of the *pratīka*—"kayā naś citra ābhuvat"—is intended to ensure that there be no arbitrary selection of any one of the three verses belonging to the Vāmadevya Sāman (whether it be its source-verse or the other two), but rather that this very verse alone be taken.

This is for the purpose that it may be so. Here, because the suffix *śānac* in the word *gāyamānaḥ* (singing) denotes the present tense, the simultaneous utterance of the formula *upayāmagṛhīto 'si* with a low (*upāṃśu*) tone—whether mentally or otherwise—is precluded by its very impossibility.
If one is unable to draw [the cup] without pausing, one draws it after placing a hundred-māna piece of gold upon it and giving a choice gift (*vara*), while reciting: *ā naḥ prāṇa etu parāvataḥ*.

By the phrase "this very [act]," it is shown that everything up to the covering with the *vyāna* is contingent (*naimittika*). By the phrase "one would not be able to take [the breath] without pausing," the occasion (*nimitta*) is indicated; "would not be able" means one would lack the capacity. "A hundred measures" (*śatamāna*) refers to that which consists of a hundred measures. Regarding the nature of the measure, a Smṛti states: "The measure is said to be two *guñjās*, or even a single *guñjā. The application of these two is determined by one's capacity or incapacity.

By the etymological derivation *mīyate 'neneti mānam* ("that by which something is measured is a measure"), the word *māna* refers even to a vessel such as a *sapivaṭavī*. This position [of using a vessel] is for one who is extremely poor. Such gold (*hiraṇya*) or fine gold (*suvarṇa*) is placed upon it; "placing" (*vyavana*) means holding it in the intermediate state between the exhalation and inhalation of the breath. After the placing, when the boon is granted, the remainder is simply "the placing" (*yanamā*), because only that [gold] has the qualification for being given. And this has been stated in the Sūtra.

It has been stated in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa-yājamāna-sūtra*: "The preparation of materials, the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and the recitations (*japa*) belong to the sacrificer. Āśvalāyana also says: "He gives; [this refers to] the sacrificer. Kātyāyana also says: "In the acts of giving, recitation, the commencement, the observance of vows, and the measurement [of the altar], one should cause the sacrificer to rejoice. In the third chapter, eighth section, Jaimini also states: "The hiring of services belongs to the owner (the sacrificer), because it serves the purpose of the ritual action; for others, it may be so by virtue of a specific scriptural injunction. This is established by these two [sūtras].

The meaning of the first sūtra is as follows: "The hiring [of priests] consists of the giving of fees and so forth to the officiating priests; this belongs to the patron who is performing the sacrifice, because that sacrifice—along with its auxiliary parts—is for his sake, since it is for the sake of the patron. For if the hiring did not belong to the patron, it would be impossible for the auxiliaries to be performed by him. Regarding the others: "But for the officiating priests, it should be so because of a scriptural statement; however, in the case of those other than the patron, the giving [of fees] occurs by virtue of a scriptural statement."

The meaning of the second sūtra is as follows: examples such as "the ox is to be given by the *hotṛ*" should be understood; the core point is that, according to the scriptural statement, one's own property must be caused to be given by the *hotṛ*. Regarding the nature of the *vara* (bride-price), Āpastamba states: "Cows are the *vara*, another is the *ativara*; a milch-cow is the *vara*, another is the *ativara*; goats are the *vara*, another is the *ativara*. This is applied in the context of the lineage of the three *varas*. In another sūtra it is said: "A cow is the *vara* for a Brāhmaṇa, a village for a Kṣatriya, and a horse for a Vaiśya."

There is also another alternative mentioned by Smṛti: "One should know a four-year-old, healthy cow to be the *vara*; others have declared that which is the best among sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) to be the *vara*. The meaning is this: among those things such as gold and so forth that are given as *dakṣiṇās*, that object which is the most excellent (*variṣṭha*)—being of the highest value—is what other teachers have called by the word *vara*. Paiṅgya says: "A *suvarṇa* weighing even a single *guñjā* is the *vara*."

The determination of these options is based on one's capacity or incapacity; the word "grasps" (gṛhṇāti) is to be understood as "grasps with the rays" (aṃśubhiḥ), because that alone has been introduced [in the context]. When the blowing over [of the vessel] with gold has been performed, at the time of grasping the cup, the defect caused by holding one's breath—which consists in the shortening of life—is destroyed; this is the meaning.

And so says the Śruti: "He draws [the cup] without drawing breath; this is his support. He covers it with gold. Gold is indeed immortality, and breath is life; by means of life, he thus covers immortality. It is a *śatamāna* [weight]; man has a hundred years of life and a hundred powers; verily, he becomes established in life and power.
Having touched it with a *śatamāna* weight of gold, he covers it with gold.

Having touched that *tamaṃsu* gold, which is accompanied by a *śatamāna*—that is, another piece of gold of such a measure—and having thoroughly brought it into contact with the gold, he covers it with gold. Here, because of the inclusion of the word "together" (*saha*), it is understood that another piece of gold must be taken for the purpose of being in conjunction with the *śatamāna* gold; and that [other gold] here is specifically of silver, not of gold. In the *Baudhāyanīya*, the connection with silver is clearly seen in this context.

In the phrase "with a *śatamāna*," the word *hiraṇya* (gold) also connects as its qualifier. Furthermore, this *śatamāna* of gold is indeed distinct from the previous *śatamāna*, because the word *śatamāna* is mentioned again. Otherwise, it would have been referred to by the pronoun *tena* (by that) together with the word *hiraṇyena* (with gold). Nor should it be argued that the mention of the word *śatamāna* is for the sake of securing the status of being a *śatamāna* in the case of silver; for since the word *śatamāna* cannot syntactically connect with silver, such a status cannot be secured.

The connection of the word *śatamāna* with silver occurs only through a compound of this specific form—namely, [the genitive tatpuruṣa] "silver possessing a śatamāna"—and not otherwise. Indeed, such a compound does not exist in the present case. Nor should it be argued that, due to a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanā*), the opposite might hold—that is, that among the acts of sprinkling, touching, and covering, the form "silver" is secondary while "gold" is primary in the sense of being a collective whole; for gold, consisting of *suvarṇa*, is indeed primary, and it alone is employed for the primary ritual function.

However, since silver and gold function as subordinate elements (*gauga*), their association constitutes a subordinate effect (*rūpagauṇakārya*); thus, because such a method of determining the distinction (*vinigamaka*) is obtained, it is impossible to argue the opposite. Nor should it be asked: "What is the proof for the nature of gold in silver?"

"Silver became gold; that [silver] became the gold of Urvaṇa; that became gold of excellent color (suvarṇa). Because of such scriptural passages as "all gold is silver," and because of the Sūtra stating "silver is gold in the middle [layer]," it is understood from the use of the causative form *saparśayet* that the touching with gold must be caused by another [priest], and not that the Adhvaryu himself should perform the touching. Alternatively, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) may be used in its own sense (*svārthe*). In this latter case, the Adhvaryu [is the agent].

Because of the word *sam* (together), the contact [of the hands] must be made by covering all parts. The repetition of the word *hiraṇya* (gold) is for the purpose of excluding silver. From the statement "he covers," its circular shape is understood. Following the *aṃśu* oblation, that [gold] must indeed be employed in the house, as there is no mention of giving it away. The mantra is used during the blowing over. The end of the mantra is *prāṇāya tvā*.
He carries it with the mantra: *indrāgnī me varcaḥ kṛṇutām*. From this point onward, the rule is obligatory. He carries it toward the *āhavanīya* fire. The end of the mantra is *aśvinā*.
When [the mantra] "dadhanvevā yadīmanu" occurs, he offers the oblation without pausing (*anavānam*).

"Without pausing" is an elliptical expression for the absence of both inhalation (*prāṇa*) and exhalation (*apāna*). Prajāpati is the deity here. Āpastamba has stated this clearly: "With the verse 'dadhanvevā yadīmanu,' which is addressed to Prajāpati and is *anirukta* (unspecified), he offers while breathing out and breathing in through the *vyāna*. "Unspecified" (*anirukta*) means devoid of a specific gender marker. This meaning is also seen in the Śruti, in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice at the *kṛtva-aṅga* rite: "He takes [the vessel] with the *anirukta* verse addressed to Prajāpati."

The *abhivyānana* (sniffing) belongs only to the followers of Āpastamba and not to us, because the author of the Sūtra mentions it specifically in connection with the drawing [of the cup]. In the event of an inability to offer the oblation, the previously mentioned expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for *abhivyānana* itself applies. Thus says Āpastamba: "If he is unable to draw or to offer, when the boon has been granted, he should draw and offer. Regarding this, the commentators have stated that there is indeed a combination (*samuccaya*) of the previously mentioned acts, such as *abhivyānana* and so forth. The mantra ends with "as if a wheel has fallen. The Pratiprasthātṛ sprinkles the Adhvaryu with water.

The mention of "with water" (*adbhiḥ*) is for the purpose of precluding other consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*). The mention of the *adhvaryu* is for the purpose of excluding the sacrificer, the *brahman*, and the wife. Sprinkling toward oneself is "sprinkling back" (*pratyukṣaṇa*). This is indeed obligatory (*nitya*), because there is no word indicating that it is contingent (*naimittika*). In the case where the remnant is used, the consumption (*bhakṣa*) is as before. He proceeds with the *adābhya* cup.

"He performs the rite known as the *adābhya*," meaning he carries out the ritual procedure designated as the *adābhya*. Regarding its etymology, it is stated in the Śruti: "Because the gods overcame the Asuras with the *adābhya*, therefore the *adābhya* is called *adābhya*. This is a general proposition. This proposition serves to exclude the alternative views mentioned in other Sūtras. Now, he states the specific injunction:

With the formulas beginning "May the Vasus draw thee forth," he draws out three stalks from the King [Soma] that has been tied up, ensuring they do not touch one another; having poured them into another vessel—either into curds or into the *nigrābhya* waters—with the formula "O bright one, I shake thy bright [essence] into the *māndā* [waters]," he causes these stalks to float around it three times clockwise with those same formulas.

The expression "with these" (*etaiḥ*) is for the purpose of excluding the singular number [of *aṃśu*]. Regarding the phrase "O divine Soma, you are the desirous one," although the number three is already established by the forthcoming sūtra stating that "one should press each of those *aṃśu*s belonging to the *adābhyas* at every pressing," the explicit mention of "three" is intended to preclude the possibility of other numbers. This is because, since it is possible to understand the meaning as "pressing each *aṃśu* separately at each pressing through the repetition of the respective formulas," a number such as four might otherwise be assumed; therefore, this is said to exclude that. "Three" (*trīn*): those which possess three [parts] are "triads" (*triyas*); [the word refers to] those three.

By the word *tri*, three mountains are intended here. Regarding the rule *iṭa kiṭa kaṭī gatau* (DhP 1.985–987), one adopts the position that there is a *praśleṣa* (splitting) of the vowel *ī* [from the root *kaṭī*]. Based on that, the suffix *vip* is applied to such a root because it belongs to the *saṃpadādi* group. In the form *tri*, due to the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), there is the fault of *savarṇa-dīrgha* resulting from the combination of the vowels *i* and *ī* within the root. However, the augment *tug*—as prescribed by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti tug* (Pāṇini 6.1.71)—does not occur because the short vowel *i* is absent. Thus, *trīś ca trīś ca trīś ca* becomes *trīn*.

Regarding this, Baudhāyana says: "Having made [spaces] between the fingers. Kātyāyana says: "Two by two, between the fingers. Kaṭha says: "He attaches them to the left hand, two by two, not touching each other. "Upehi" is the end of the mantra. *Pravṛhaṇa* means drawing away.

If it is argued that this statement is redundant—since the taking up of the cups (graha) will be prescribed later on, and because if the pouring of either curd or whey were done into the Ādāmya vessel, it would be impossible to take the cup later; therefore, by the very nature of the situation, the taking must occur in another vessel—then that is true. However, there is no redundancy because the purpose is to indicate the lack of restriction: that the taking may occur in *any* other vessel whatsoever, rather than being restricted to a specific form such as a Vāyavya or a Camasa.

In general, because of the word "vessel" (*pātra*), there is no fixed rule regarding its shape. This curd here is worldly (secular), and it is prepared for this very purpose. The *nigrābhyā* waters, which were in the *hotṛcamasa* and have been gazed upon by the sacrificer, are poured out—that is, made to flow—into that vessel. In the case of the pouring of the *nigrābhyā* waters, one should understand that there is a change in gender in the word "in them" (*tāsu*). The mention of "by these" (*etair*) is intended to preclude the idea that the sprinkling might be done with only a single mantra, since the remaining eleven [mantras] would then be optional alternatives (*vikalpa*).

From this very statement, it is established—also in accordance with the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "rites [are performed] with single mantras" (*ekamantrāṇi karmāṇi*)—that each individual action is to be performed with each individual mantra. These [actions] are to be performed starting from the front. Since the counter-clockwise direction (*prādakṣiṇya*) is already established by the technical rule itself, the explicit mention of "clockwise" (*pradakṣiṇa*) is for the sake of indicating favorability; the meaning is that one should pour [the liquid] around so that it becomes fluid and favorable to the *dadhi* oblation. The prefix *anu-* is intended to convey the sense that the pouring around is performed specifically with reference to such favorability.
"Parishanah" means for the sake of being all-encompassing. By that, the circumambulation established by "paribhāṣā" becomes established.
"Four times, five times, or seven times"—the remaining [terms] have the sense of alternatives (*vikalpa*).

If the state of liquefaction is not achieved by immersing [the object] three times, these rites are performed four times, four times, five times, five times, seven times, and seven times. The suffixes *kṛtvas* and *vār* denote repetition. In the case of "three times" (*tris*), there are three actions with three mantras; in the case of "four times" (*catur*), there are four actions with four mantras; and the same applies to the cases of "five times" (*pañcakṛtvas*) and "seven times" (*saptakṛtvas*).

In the alternative views beginning with "three times," the remaining mantras are nine, eight, seven, and five respectively. Those which remain serve as optional alternatives (*vikalpa*) according to their respective positions among these four views. The statement that "the remaining ones are for the purpose of option" is intended to preclude the application of all mantras in all views, which might otherwise be inferred from the rule: "Let them pull [the horse] forward with each mantra, beginning with 'O plants,' and ending with 'with the Gāyatrī metre.'"

"Indeed, this is a secret name of the waters, namely *ādhāva*. When he says, 'O bright one, I pour the bright [Soma] into your *māndā* waters,' he wins rain from heaven by means of the secret name of the waters. Thus, in the Śruti, the word *ādhāva* is stated to be a name of the waters. Because the mantras bear the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the *ādhāva*, Baudhāyana has also given the name *ādhāva* to the mantras themselves, as seen in the Sūtra: "He pours [the Soma] with twelve *ādhāvas*."

Āpastamba has also given the name *ādhavana* to the *aṃśu* shoots: "Having placed the well-known *ādhavana* shoots in a vessel made of *uśīka* wood, he pours each one into the great pressings at each pressing with the respective formulas: 'O divine Soma, with the Gāyatrī metre... He states the formula for the drawing here: "I take thy bright [portion] with the bright; Agni at the morning pressing, Viśve Devas... [End of section 2, variant readings ka, ga, niṣicya]. This is from the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, eighth book.
He draws [the cup] with these verses beginning, "The gods [draw] this third pressing for the seers. In all [these verses], there is finally the *upayāma* formula.

By these mantras ending with "Thou art taken with a support" (*upayāmagṛhīto 'si*), he draws [the juice] in very small quantities; this is the meaning. Since the verse beginning with "O bright one, thee... (*śukra te*) also has the form of a *triṣṭubh* meter, the *upayāma* formula is indeed at its end. By the word "of all," the inclusion of the verse beginning with "I take thee, the bright one, with the bright [Soma], in the form of a cow, with the rays of the sun" is necessarily accepted, because drawing [the cup] is impossible without that verse.

In this regard, regarding the doubt as to how there can be a calculation of feet (*pāda*) since the *kaca* [verse] is not bound by feet, or what kind of meter (*chandas*) would exist if such were the case—it is said: "I take your bright with the bright" (*śukraṃ te śukreṇa gṛhṇāmi*) is one foot; "with the form of the sun through its rays" (*rūpeṇa sūryasya raśmibhiḥ*) is another. Therein, the first foot consists of eleven syllables, formed by the two vowels *i* and *ā* having attained unity through the *yaṇ*-substitution. The second foot consists of ten syllables, based on the conception of the doubling of syllables in the letter *ri* within the word *sūrya* (as *riya*).

Thus, the definition of the *triṣṭubh* is established by the *Piṅgala-sūtra*, "The *triṣṭubh*s are [of eleven syllables]," and by the scriptural statement, "The *triṣṭubh* has three [feet] of eleven syllables. Due to the deficiency of one syllable, it becomes a *nirṛṣṭubh*, according to the *Piṅgala-sūtra*: "By a deficiency or excess of one [syllable], they become *nirṛt* and *ij* [respectively]."

*Riya* consists of two syllables through the contemplation of duality; *ghṛṇi* consists of two syllables; *sūrya* consists of three; and *āditya* consists of three. This is the eight-syllabled foot of the Sāvitra mantra, consecrated with glory—so says the Śruti. Furthermore, there is authority for this in the Piṅgala Sūtra, which states that a foot [of a Vedic meter] is "complete" when it has [the required number of] syllables. This is well known in the case of the Gāyatrī, where the syllable *ṇya* becomes two through the contemplation of duality as *ṇiya*. This is also clear from the Nyāsa and other such texts.

And thus, because it is embraced by the characteristics of the nivṛti-gāyatrī meter, it is established that this mantra also possesses the nature of an *ṛc*. The ends of the mantras are: "With the rays, together with the bees, may we abide in good thought; may the third ones lead us" (*raśmibhiḥ saha makṣāḥ sthāma sumatau syāma tṛtīyo nayantu*);
and "Into him the fierce ones have driven" (*āsminn ugrā acucyavuḥ*).
He carries [the vessel] toward the Āhavanīya fire; the end of the mantra is "unfailing" (*asaścat*).
He recites the mantra, "The bull’s lofty form shines forth, great...
This is clear.
He offers the oblation with the mantra, "Soma is the precursor of Soma," and sets aside the well-known stalks.

Thus ends the second paṭala in the eighth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. In that same sequence in which [the shoots] grew, he places them, well-known by that very order, for the purpose of pressing, having pounded them. "To Soma, svāhā"—this concludes the mantra. Here, the oblation is indeed to be performed without remainder, because, in the absence of pressing, the disposal (pratipatti) consisting of consumption is impossible.

Āpastamba states the remaining details regarding the Aṃśu and Adābhya cups: "The Adābhya cup is to be drawn by one who has enemies; the Aṃśu cup is for those desiring prosperity. These two are not to be drawn in every sacrifice, but [only] in the Vājapeya, the Rājasūya, a Sattra, a Sāhasra, or a Sarvavedasa sacrifice. One should draw them for him who is very dear and well-prosperous. Since they are optional (kāmya), their application is only in the archetype (prakṛti). [End of] the third Paṭala of the Vājapeya and so forth, together with the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha.

These two should be taken only at the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), not at all the original and modified sacrifices (*prakṛti-vikṛti*). However, if the sacrificer should be one who is well-pleased with this Adhvaryu and well-tested, and possesses auspicious qualities, then for him these two may be taken at will even at all the original and modified sacrifices.

Thus ends the second chapter of the eighth book in the *Jyotsnā* commentary on the *Śrīmad-Bhagavat-Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—the son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was himself the son of Śrīmad-Amiṣṭoma-yājin, Sāhasrāgni-yukta-Vājapeya-yājin, Sarvatomukha-yājin, Dviṣāhasra-Aptoryāma-yukta-Pauṇḍarīka-yājin—written to alleviate the distress of learned men caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within that ocean of a manual. 2.2.

8.3 Now begins the third chapter of the eighth book. Having taken up the *upāṃśusavana* pressing-stone with the formula "devasya tvā," he restrains his speech until the drawing of the *āgrayaṇa* cup. The specific mention of the word "grāvāṇam" (the pressing-stone) is intended to show that even though it is distinct from the four stones placed upon the *droṇakalaśa*, its shape here is exactly like theirs; furthermore, it indicates that the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for breaking this stone is also the same as for those others. The use of the gerund "ādāya" (having taken) implies simultaneity, as in the expression "he sleeps with his mouth open. This meaning has been stated quite explicitly by Āpastamba: "Taking it up, he restrains his speech."

Therefore, it is appropriate to describe this as having the same meaning as the *Āpastamba Sūtra*, and not to describe it as being in disagreement with it. Here, by the injunction for restraining speech (*vāgyamana*), it is understood that elsewhere there is no fault in uttering articulated speech (*vyākṛtavāc*) as much as is required during the interval; however, here, even such utterance constitutes a fault—this distinction is discerned. This explanation should be applied everywhere. One restrains—that is, controls—one's speech from the time of taking [the vessel] until the drawing of the *Āgrayaṇa* cup. The word division is "ā āgrayaṇāt. The mantra ends with the word "ādadaḥ" (taking).

He consecrates [the pressing stone] with the mantra, "Thou art the pressing stone," ending with the words, "thou art possessed of rain. Having placed it upon the *adhiṣavaṇa* [pressing-skin] with its upper surface facing upwards, he measures out the King [Soma] with these mantras, beginning with "For Indra, thee, the slayer of Vṛtra," just as at the purchase [of Soma], except for the act of piling up [the stones].

That is the *upāṃśusavana* stone. On the skin used for pressing (*adhiṣavaṇa*), by the mention of "pressing-vessel" (*adhiṣavaṇa-grahaṇa*), the *upara* stone mentioned in another Sūtra is excluded. Having placed it with its ridge facing upward and having fixed it, he measures out the King [Soma] with the five formulas beginning with "For Indra, thee, the slayer of Vṛtra. The purpose of employing this specific term is as before. The statement "with the mantras" is for the purpose of indicating that there is also an alternative view according to which every single measurement is performed with all the mantras.

In the Śruti, the fact that the word "yajus" appears five times in the singular number is the authority for this view. The word "abhi" is used in the sense of measuring over the *upāṃśu* vessel at its end, just as in the case of the purchase (*kraya*). Thus, according to the rule from Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra: "He measures five times with the *yajus*, and five times silently. Because of the extension (*atideśa*) from the purchase rite, he measures five times with the *yajus*, and the measurement occurs by virtue of the injunction: "five times silently."

In the absence of an extended application (*atideśa*), one would have to measure five times—once with each of the five mantras—and then measure another five times in the same manner using those very same mantras; thus, there would be ten measurements. To prevent this from occurring, the statement "just as in the purchase" (*yathā kraya*) is made.

The statement "other than the gathering together" (*anyad-upasamūhanāt*) means that those [stalks] which remained after the purchase and were set aside separately might otherwise be taken again here by that same rule; this is not to be so. Rather, it is for the purpose that there be no remainder when the stalks are measured within the ten measures themselves. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: having combined the measured and the remaining *rājāna* [soma], one measures it such that five bundles are tied with a mantra and five bundles are tied without a mantra—thus, "other than the gathering together."

By way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), [the rule] applies to all [fingers] except the thumb; with the hand containing gold, one supports the back of the entire [hand] with whichever finger is extended—the fifth not being used by that same [finger] which was used for the first, but rather by that very same [finger] for the tenth. All this is extended [by analogy]. The spreading of the cloth does not occur later, because it is set aside by the specific injunction: "Having placed it upon the *adhiṣavaṇa* boards."

Having poured out the King (Soma) from one part of the pressing-vessel, he takes as much as he considers sufficient for a single cup; he places the remainder back into the vessel and sets it aside. Having placed that [portion] upon the lower stone and moistened it with the *vasatīvarī* waters, he pours in the *nigrābhya* waters with the formula: "Ye are refreshing, subduers of Vṛtra."

Having poured out the King [Soma] from one empty portion of the pressing-skin—that is, having moved him away from the measured area—he takes [the Soma] from there. The explanation for the section beginning with "as much as for a single draught" and ending with "having mixed it with the *vasatīvarī* waters" is as before. The *nigrābhya* waters have been explained previously; he mixes [the Soma] with them. "May Soma drink" is the end of the mantra. The addition of a portion of the *nigrābhya* waters continues until the great pressing (*mahābhiṣava*). The conclusion occurs at the final pressing.

Āpastamba has stated quite clearly: "One should not touch [the *hotṛcamasa*] with only a part of the nose. Having set aside a portion of the *nigrābhyā* waters in the *hotṛcamasa* for the purpose of the *nigrābha*, one pours the remaining *nigrābhyā* waters into another vessel and then causes them to flow around the *hotṛcamasa* three times clockwise. Whenever there is an addition of *nigrābhyā* waters, at that time a corresponding amount of *nigrābhyā* waters from the other vessel is brought into the *hotṛcamasa*.

For all those [soma portions] situated in the *hotṛcamasa*, the repeated taking up of the *nigrābhyā* waters at the time of the *niyābha* would be inconsistent; for when the *nigrābhyā* waters have been exhausted, they are replenished by the *vasatīvarī* waters, since the latter are their source (*tadyoni*). In this case, no mantra is used at all, because since the action consisting of the pouring out (*vyānayana*) does not exist, it is impossible for [the mantra] to have that as its purpose.
He consecrates [the soma] with the mantra: "O Soma, that light of yours which is in heaven...
The end of the mantra is: "...I have spoken to the giver."

Some authorities prescribe the consecration (abhimantraṇa) first; its priority is in relation to the act of bringing near (upasarpaṇa). Its immediate sequence follows the act of bringing near. Some authorities prescribe it in the reverse order; even though [the desired result] is accomplished by that much alone, nevertheless, one might suspect here merely a reversal of the mantras. To prevent that, and so that there may also be a reversal of the actions themselves, such a sūtra is necessary. (ŚB 3.1.2.19–310). [This is] accompanied by the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

Having taken six shoots from the king [Soma] that have been touched by the hand, having set them aside without touching them, and taking the others, while holding the pressing-stone above and not below the shoots, he causes them to flow around the Hotṛ’s cup three times clockwise, saying "eastward, westward, northward, southward"; this constitutes the *nigrābha*.

There is no contact for one who has been approached by the domestic [cups]; this is the well-known procedure for all six, following the increased sequence. Regarding the others—those distinct from the [preceding] ones, such as the plural forms and so forth—the word "above" (upariṣṭāt) implies "of the Hotṛ’s cup. The *grāvan* is the *upāṃśusavana* stone. Holding the *grāvan* below, and holding the stalks (*aṃśu*) other than those previously taken—which are distinct from the six and are attached to the *upāṃśusavana* stone—below, he causes them to flow around three times clockwise with the mantra beginning "eastward, westward" (*prāgapāg*).

The phrase "he causes [them] to flow around clockwise" (*pradakṣiṇamanu pariplāvayati*) has already been explained. Here, the clockwise direction indicated by the word *pradakṣiṇa* should be understood as follows: just as by rubbing those stalks against those *nigrābhyā* waters, a connection with their juice (*rasa*) is produced, so it is here.

[Objection: Is it not the case that because the *aṃśu* stalks alone are present nearby, the connection must be "above those very [stalks]," and thus the meaning becomes "holding the pressing-stone above the *aṃśu* stalks already taken"? And in this way, the supplement to the *hotṛcamasa*, which was not mentioned previously, would indeed be incoherent. [Response: No, for if that were so, the phrase "below" (*adhastāt*) in the word *anitya* would result in being redundant. That juice which is produced by stirring the *niyābhyā* stalks is designated as *nigrābha*. The mantra ends with "O Mother, come down! (*amba niṣvara*).

Having placed them [the soma-stones] upon the lower [pressing-board] and having moistened them with the *vasatīvarī* waters, he lifts up a pressing-stone (*grāvan*) while reciting, "Do not fear, do not tremble," and he consecrates the two pressing-boards (*adhiṣavaṇaphalaka*) with the mantra, "O Dhiṣaṇās, you who are firm. [The stones] are accompanied by the liquid known as *nigrābha*. The mantra "Do not fear, do not tremble" is of this extent alone; the mantra ending in "do not harm me" belongs to the "O Dhiṣaṇās" formula. After the moistening with the *vasatīvarī* waters, having lifted the pressing-stone with "Do not fear," he consecrates the two pressing-boards with "O Dhiṣaṇās. Because of the dual number in the grammatical mark and because of their physical possibility, the mantra is used only once.

"O sinless one, we have been sent by Indra; let Vāyu be yours, let Mitra be yours, let Varuṇa be yours; Soma the King has slain [the enemy]. At that place where he sees a root, a blade of grass, or a piece of wood, he strikes [the post] there on level ground.

In whichever place he perceives any one of the king’s roots or something suitable, he strikes first in that very spot. Because of the word "equal" (*sama*), he strikes after making [the enemy's position] equal; that is to say, he strikes in such a place where the majority of the king's constituent parts (*aṃśu*) are joined with his own root. "Wood" (*kāṣṭha*) means a small piece of wood. "Clod of earth" (*loṣṭa*) is a corrupt reading, because it is improper for a clod of earth to have contact with a king, and it must therefore be rejected.

Or if there were previously grass, wood, or a root at that spot, [he should place it] there, according to the agreement with the Āpastamba Sūtra; and because of the agreement with the Mānava Sūtra: "If he does not find a root, he should place grass or wood in between. If he does not find—that is, does not obtain or does not know—the root, meaning the root-part of the *soma*, [he should use] a clod of earth (*loṣṭa*). (Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, composed by Satyāṣāḍha).

[8. The Eighth Light—The Non-perception of the Root of the Present Soma is Based on Ignorance, and Thus Knowledge Exists Here in the Element of Attainment. Likewise, the failure to find the root of the present *soma* is indeed due to ignorance; thus, knowledge exists here in the element of attainment (*labhadhātu*). Accordingly, one does not find the root, yet one perceives it and strikes first at that location. And so says the *Mānava-sūtra*: "One presses at the root. The meaning of this is that the first blow for the purpose of pressing is directed at the root-portion of the *soma*, and not at the tip.

If he does not see the root of the *soma*, then if he sees grass, he presses it there. In the absence of grass, he sees a piece of wood; and in the absence of both grass and wood, he presses while interposing either grass or a piece of wood—this is the meaning. In that pressing, the earth should be continuous so that one would not perceive [the gap]—this is the meaning. Therefore, the meaning of the *Mānava-sūtra* is that one should press that *soma* after interposing grass, such as *darbha*, or a piece of wood.
According to some, "he presses after interposing grass."

The meaning is that, according to the opinion of some teachers (*ācārya*), one should press [the Soma] only after placing a blade of grass in between, even when there is an absence of any one of the [stems] beginning with the root, or during the second and subsequent strokes. Because of the mention of "some" (*ekeṣām*), the placement of a blade of grass is not mandatory in the event of the absence of any one of the [stems] beginning with the root, nor during the second and subsequent strokes. The term "blade of grass" (*tṛṇam*) is illustrative and includes a piece of wood as well.
Having pressed eight times in front, he approaches the *nigrābha* [vessel] as before.

"Aṣṭaukṛtvaḥ" means eight times. In the expression "aṣṭaukṛtvaḥ," the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is applied according to the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ kriyābhyāvṛttigaṇane kṛtvasuc* to denote the counting of repetitions of an action. The absence of the case-ending (*vibhaktyaluk*) is Vedic. The mention of "first" (*agre*) is with reference to the alternatives that will be stated for the second and third rounds. When the occasion arises, [the Adhvaryu] approaches the *nimābha* [spot] as before, having performed the two [mantras]: "O drop, do not spill" (*ā mā skanda drapsa*) and "Do not spill" (*mā skanda*). Having covered the *upāṃśu* vessel with two of the stalks already taken, the Pratiprasthātṛ holds it from the north.

In the midst of the six *aśū* (spikes) that have been taken up previously, arranged in their known order and placed without touching one another—of which two are at the beginning and two are at the end—the Pratiprasthātṛ, sitting to the north of the cup, takes hold of it with his right hand from the south; that is to say, he supports that cup.
With the mantra, "O Vājin, flow pure for Vācaspati," the Adhvaryu pours Soma into it with his joined palms (*añjali*).

When that Upāṃśu cup, with its two portions concealed within it, has been held by the Pratiprasthātṛ, the mention of "with joined palms" (*añjalinā*) is intended to exclude pouring with only one hand. The explicit mention of the *adhvaryu* is for the purpose of excluding the Pratiprasthātṛ. It should not be argued that the *adhvaryu*’s role as the performer of the pouring is already established simply because the acts of covering, lifting, and pouring cannot be performed by a single person; therefore, what is the purpose of mentioning the *adhvaryu*?

The mention of the *adhvaryu* is necessary to prevent the application of the rule "he marries" (*upayacchati*)—which, through the assumption of a verbal root suffix (*vitaṇi*), implies that the three actions have a single agent—to these [other rites]. Here, the *āghāra* libation does not take place because there is no scriptural injunction for it. Furthermore, the *pavitra* filter is not used for the cups ending with the *antaryāma*; the proof for this will be stated later in the section [Paṭala 28, Kāṇḍa 21] according to the commentary named *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha. [Note: 1. ka. ga. yo'trājñā; 28 21 paṭaka; gopīnāthamahakṛtajyotrāṇyākhyāsamatam]

He himself will state [later] that it should be placed in this very spot. Regarding this, Āpastamba says in the sixth book: "We purify the filter; there is no placing [of the vessel]. "Gamyas tiptaḥ" is the end of the mantra. Thus is prescribed the second and third pressing.

Thus, having measured [the soma], by means of the procedure beginning with the *upasarjana* and ending with the *nigrābhopāyana*. The rest is clear in meaning. He now states a specific optional alternative:
Or alternatively, he presses the second time eleven times and the third time twelve times.

According to the Brāhmaṇa, it is stated that there should be eight pressings at each pressing; this [following] option is also provided for that. Having set aside the previous stalks, he covers the vessel with two others and pours [the juice] during the second pressing; with two others, he does so during the third pressing.
