At the second pressing, he pours the Soma with the mantra, "The god of the gods... (devo devānām); at the third pressing, with "Make our refreshments honey-sweet" (madhumatīr na iṣaḥ kṛdhi).
By this [sūtra], the fixed distinction between the second and third pressings (*abhiṣava*) is stated. The meaning of the sūtra is indeed clear:

"He does not set it down. Regarding the vessel already taken—the measurement of all the vessels and their setting down according to their respective origins—once the drawing of the *aindravāyava* cup has been mentioned, the fact that the previous cups are not to be set down is understood precisely from the formulation of this general rule (*paribhāṣā*). Thus, the prohibition "he does not set it down" is for the purpose of removing any suspicion that, despite being unestablished, it might be established as a property of the cup (*grahadharma*). Because the prohibition is enjoined by a specific injunction, even the wiping (*parimārjana*) does not take place.

Nor should it be questioned why, in the case of the Soma-draughts, there is no prohibition of the placing (*āsādana*) of the *aśvadābhyas* as well, just as there is a prohibition of placing for these [other] draughts. This is because, since these draughts are taught independently (*anāramyādhīta*), there is no possibility of their being obtained through the *apūrva* (the transcendental result). Furthermore, this is intended to indicate that in the case of the *dhārāgrahas* other than the *aśva-upāṃśu*, even silent placing (*tūṣṇī sādana*) may occur. Because it is enjoined in conjunction with that [placing], the wiping (*parimārjana*) is also included. The same should be understood regarding the *antaryāma-graha*.
He rises with the formula, "Thou art made thy own" (*svāṃkṛto'si*). This is clear.
He proceeds with the words, "The wide atmosphere. The mantra ends with "follow after" (*anvihi*). Here, it does not end with "come hither" (*āvihī*) as in the cooked [offering].
Having passed to the north of the Hotṛ, he stands by the northern junction of the enclosing sticks with the words, "May Manu [protect] thee from the Tvaṣṭṛ."

"Having gone," "having abandoned," and "having passed beyond"—these words mean that the Pratiprasthātṛ, having moved only a short distance beyond the northern region of the Hotṛ, proceeds to the next area. Having taken up the Mahāvīra vessel with the formula, "Thou art made acceptable (svāṃkṛta)," he steps forward. He goes, but not by placing his feet in the northern region of the Hotṛ at the time of going; this is for the purpose of indicating the absence of such a specific restriction regarding the placement of the feet.

Having led [the ladle] along the northern joint of the enclosing-sticks, he offers [the oblation] straight, long, and continuous, directed toward the south-east, with the formula: "Svāhā! To thee, O auspicious one, to Sūrya!"

Since the purpose is already accomplished by the phrase "he follows that very junction," the further statement "the junction of the northern enclosing-stick" (*uttara-paridhi-saṃdhi*) indicates that the placing down (*anvavasthāna*) and the drawing out (*nirharaṇa*) occur simultaneously. "Having drawn it out" means having brought it into the sacrificial pit (*sāṃnāhya*). "Towards the south-east" means as far as the direction of Agni (the southeast). By implication, this means making a continuous stream starting from the direction of Vāyu (the northwest). The word "straight" (*ṛju*) is for the purpose of excluding any curvature.

The length [of the offering] extends from the western direction at the edge of the fire to the western direction at the very edge of the fire, reaching as far as the *āpothī* line. The shortness [of the offering] occurs during the *homa* when it is from the western direction at the center of the fire to the western direction at the very center of the fire. The mention of "length" is for the purpose of excluding this [short form]. The mention of "continuous" (*saṃtata*) is for the purpose of precluding an interruption in the middle. Regarding the exclamation "svāhā": although the *svāhākāra* occurs at the beginning of the mantra such as "to Sūrya," it certainly occurs at the end as well.

And it is not the case that the *svāhākāra* (the utterance "svāhā") is recited only before [the mantra]; for there is the recitation of *svāhā* after [the mantra] as well. It is not that Sūrya alone possesses the quality of having the *svāhākāra* before it and the quality of having the *svāhākāra* after it; therefore, one must explain how there can be a *svāhākāra* at the end here, given the intervention by multiple words. Where there is no intervention between the word denoting the deity and the word *svāhā*, it is precisely in such cases that this *purastātsvāhā* (having *svāhā* before) mentioned in the Śruti applies.

The status of being the *svāhākāra* will be established by way of a specific restriction for what follows, and not for everything. It is understood that where there is a connection between multiple words, the preceding *svāhākāra* does not have the sense of "offering" (*pradāna*). Otherwise, there would result the undesirable consequence of the final *svāhākāra* alone [having that sense] in the case of "svāhā'dhim ādhītāya svāhā. Nor should it be suspected that each of these three mantras—beginning with "svāhā'dhim ādhītāya svāhā"—is intended to refer to two separate mantras.

"One offers twenty-one Vaiśvadeva oblations"—this statement would contradict the number twenty-one if there were more than three mantras. Therefore, there are indeed only three mantras. This very fact serves as the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that the first *svāhākāra* must be understood as occurring immediately before the word for the deity, and not separated from it by the beginning of a mantra. Thus it is said: "viśa."

In the sūtra located in the section on the *vasā-homa* (fat-oblation), the phrase "in all cases" (*sarvatra*)—found in the passage beginning "To the eastern directions," "to the southern directions," "to the western directions," "to the northern directions," "to the intermediate directions," and "to the upward directions"—is intended to ensure that the word *svāhā* is applied at the end of the mantra "ghṛtaṃ ghṛtapāvānaḥ," which otherwise contains the *svāhā* call only in its middle. Furthermore, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this is found in the statement: "At the middle *svāhā* call, he should throw [the remains] outside."

With the formula, "For the gods, for the rays of light, thee," he wipes the internal smear on the middle enclosing-stick. This is clear. If he should desire, "May Parjanya be rainy," it is explained in the Brāhmaṇa.

If he should desire, "May Parjanya be a showerer," he should wipe [the vessel] with the palm facing downwards; thus he brings down rain. If he should desire, "May he be a non-showerer," he should wipe it with the palm facing upwards; thus he holds back the rain. This is explained in the Brāhmaṇa. The meaning is that, depending on the difference in desire, the palm of the hand may be either downward-facing or upward-facing during the wiping. This [act] is also obligatory. Whatever remains adhering to the vessel, he pours that residue into the Āgrayaṇa-sthālī.

The pouring of the entire residue from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel is performed by means of the genitive case, which denotes a part of the whole. This has been stated quite explicitly by Āpastamba: "One should pour the entire residue of the *āgrayaṇa* [into the *droṇakalaśa*].

He sets down the vessel with the formula, "This is thy womb; for breath thee. Because the entire residue has been poured out, he sets down the empty vessel; that is to say, in its very place. This has been stated quite explicitly by Āpastamba: "With the formula, 'This is thy womb; for breath thee,' he sets down the empty vessel in its place. Having placed a piece of *aṃśu* in it, one should mix it at the third pressing and press it."
He places the *aṃśu* stalk upon that [fire] and it remains there until the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*).

This *aṃśu* is indeed for the sake of the third pressing; therefore, only as much of it as is sufficient for the third pressing should be taken. And thus, this *aṃśu* consists of four joints (*parvan*). Elsewhere, the *aṃśus* are generally three-jointed or two-jointed; for it is established by the hearing of another scripture (*śāstra*) that "three-jointed or two-jointed *aṃśus* are to be taken. If this one is destroyed, another must be taken.

In the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), after the drawing of the Āditya cup, if there is no portion of this *aṃśu* [Soma], then, due to the absence of other Soma, one should have some nearby Soma brought by any person, whether a *prothaka* (one who carries forth) or a seller of Soma; having given something to him, it should be pressed. In the absence of that, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) consisting of the pressing of *phālguna* plants and so forth becomes established.

But for one performing malevolent magic (*abhicara*), having taken up the vessel, he should set it down with the words, "I set thee down in the breath of so-and-so. Having taken it up with a verse addressed to Savitṛ, and having consecrated it with the mantra, "Kill so-and-so; then I shall offer thee," he offers it with the words, "In the exhilaration of the intoxicating, joyous [Soma], let so-and-so be rendered false! The term *abhicarati* means "one who performs malevolent magic"; the meaning is "of the sacrificer who performs malevolent magic directed toward an enemy. The word "but" (*tu*) is used to indicate that the ritual action beginning from this point and ending with "he offers it on his chest or arm" is an occasional rite (*naimittika*).

Having drawn the *upāṃśu* cup according to the procedure beginning with "Of the god thee" (*devasya tvā*) and "The *upāṃśu* [cup], the mind, the presser," and ending with "Make our food full of honey" (*madhumatīrna iṣaḥ kṛdhi*), one should place it in its very receptacle while reciting "I place thee in the breath of so-and-so," substituting for "so-and-so" the name of the enemy in the genitive case ending in *-śarman*. Even though the placing [of the cup] is otherwise prohibited, its placement is prescribed for the purpose of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). The meaning of the mantra is: "I place thee in the breath of so-and-so. That [cup] thus placed is the *upāṃśu* [cup].

With the mantra "O Svā, you have arrived with the groats," he should take [the vessel] up to the end of the formula "I take it from Sāvitra's breast," and perform the rites ending with the standing up and the settling down. In the phrase "amuṃ na hi," the word *amuṃ* (that one) should be replaced by the name of the person one hates, ending in the suffix *-śarman* and in the accusative case; for example, "Amukaśarmaṇaṃ na hi" (I bind Amukaśarman). The word *atha* in the mantra indicates immediate sequence.
[End of section]. Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Book Eight. [Note: The text fragment ends here.]

One should not entertain the thought, "I shall not offer this immediately after having performed the *dhyāna*," nor should one recite the mantra for the offering of water. In the mantra *praharṣiṇo*, in place of the word *asau*, one should insert the name of the victim ending in *śarman* in the nominative case; for example: *praharṣiṇo madirasya made mṛṣā amukaśarmā astu svāhā*. In place of *svāhā tvā sumanasaḥ*, there is this mantra for the oblation intended for malevolent magic (*abhicāra*).

After the oblation, having performed the rites beginning with the smearing and wiping up and ending with the pouring of the remnants, he should place the vessel with the mantra: "This is thy womb; for breath thee! Having uttered the mantra, "I place thee in the breath of such-and-such," and having set down that vessel, he should cover it with a blade of *aṃśu* grass. Regarding this, a specific rule is stated by Āpastamba: "Then he should offer [the libation] while stepping forward, saying: 'In the intoxication of the exhilarating drink of the great seer, let such-and-such be false! Having offered it, he should set it down, saying: 'I place thee in the breath of such-and-such. He should remain seated until the end of the rite without breathing."

The meaning is that from the time of sitting down until the completion of the oblation (*homa*), one should remain seated without breathing or letting the breath go outside. The suffix *tosun* is applied according to the rule *māvalakṣaṇe stṛvad-car-iha-tumi-jani-bhyas tosun*. Furthermore, this requirement of remaining seated until the end of the oblation applies specifically to a person who is nearby and hostile; for a different rule will be stated regarding one who is at a distance.
If he should be far away, he should remain standing until sunset.

"Until he is exhausted. The phrase "not breathing" (*aprāṇan*) continues [from the previous rule]. For one whose enemy is far away, [the recitation] lasts until the end of the oblation (*homaparyanta*); it is not merely "not breathing," but even longer than that. Its limit, however, is exhaustion; even while standing at the very place of the oblation, he recites the name of the enemy. In this rite of sorcery (*abhicārika*), the meaning is that he recites the enemy's name using the sixth, second, and first case endings respectively in place of the words *amuṣya*, *amum*, and *asau*.

"O Deva, O Aṃśu! For whomsoever I praise you—that be true and unfailing. By this stratagem (bhaṅgyena), may that [enemy] be struck down. Phaṭ! That ray of yours which is clung to his chest, garment, or arm—him I offer as an oblation. The meaning of the mantra is: "O Deva, O Aṃśu! For whomsoever I praise you—that be true and unfailing; may it be unswerving and unobstructed. By this stratagem (māyena)—meaning a deed beneficial for the destruction (māyana) of the enemy—may so-and-so (Amukaśarmā) be struck down by this rite about to be described. Phaṭ! The syllable *phaṭ* here takes the place of the *svāhā* exclamation.

The meaning is that he should offer (*jahoti*) with the mantra ending in *pari*—namely, "that stalk of his which was struck down during the stage of pressing while the presser was pressing, or which clung to his chest, his garment, or his arm"—provided that it has been offered, poured, and the vessel set aside. If it has not clung [to him], then this offering does not take place; this is the established sense. He places that stalk into it; it remains there until the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*). Thus ends the specific ritual procedure employed for the purpose of exorcism (*abhicāra*). This very [rite] is intended here.

— [Tṛpaṭa] accompanied by the commentary of Gopīnātha Makṛtājyokhā. 25. The composition of this sūtra—"he first mentions the name of the one he hates in order to make known the *śuhoma*"—is intended to indicate this. This concludes the occasional (*naimittika*) rite. Now the primary (*prakṛta*) procedure is stated:
they sit down around for the great pressing (*mahābhiṣava*); the Adhvaryu in the east, the Pratiprasthātṛ in the south, the Neṣṭṛ in the west, and the Unnetṛ in the north.

The greatness of the pressing (*abhiṣava*) is due to its being performed for the sake of the *savana* (pressing) and because it is performed by both the *sadasya* and the *adhvaryu*. The dative case [in *mahābhiṣavārtham*] denotes purpose; thus the meaning is "for the sake of the great pressing. The term *pari* means "facing each other," and not "all around," as that is already established by what will be stated later, beginning with "to the east of that" (*tasya purastāt*). The phrase "to the east" (*purastāt*) and so forth is intended to exclude the intermediate directions.

When it is sufficient for the purpose that "all the Adhvaryus sit down around [the Soma] for the great pressing in order according to the directions," the composition of this elaborate sūtra is for the sake of establishing the sequence of their sitting: first the Adhvaryu sits in the east, then the Pratiprasthātṛ to the south, then the Neṣṭṛ to the west, and then the Unnetṛ to the north. These locations—east and so forth—are to be understood in relation to the King (Soma), in order to facilitate the pressing.

He takes from the King [Soma] as much as he considers sufficient for the morning pressing; he sets the remainder aside in a vessel. Having placed that [quantity] upon the lower millstone, he pours it out with the formula, "O divine Soma, you who are invincible. Of those portions which are invincible (*ādābhya*), he adds one at each pressing, reciting: "O Soma, that invincible name of yours which is watchful," and likewise two at a time from the Upāṃśu-pressings.

The passage ending with *samupare nyupya* has already been explained. Previously it was stated, "having brought one large [vessel] for the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*)," and that stood as the rule for the sacrificial session (*sattra*). Here, however, there is a specific distinction: the statement "as much as he thinks sufficient for the morning pressing" is intended either to remove the suspicion that this is merely a formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) rather than an actual pressing (*abhiṣava*), or simply to specify the quantity required for the morning pressing. As for the word *ādāmyāḥ*, the division is *ā-dāmyāḥ*. The absence of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) or the long vowel resulting from the *pūrvasavarṇa* rule is for the sake of the meaning.

Among those portions which belong to me as non-connected [to others], he places each single portion, one by one, at each pressing (*anusavana*) according to the sequence of extraction; for the sake of the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavanam*), he causes it to touch that King [Soma]. This placing (*apisarjanam*) is not a mixing (*melanam*) with the King, but rather merely a touching. Otherwise, the subsequent statement regarding "placing upon the lower stone" (*upare nivānam*) would become inconsistent. There are three mantras ending with *apehi*.

Among these, some say that with the first mantra he pours the first *aṃśu* at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), with the second the second at the second [pressing], and with the third the third at the third [pressing]. That is not correct; for from the statement "with these [mantras]... of the King [Soma]"—just as in the case of the *upāṃśu* [cup]—it is understood that the Sūtrakāra intended them to be used in the same order as the mantras themselves. If the Sūtrakāra had intended a plurality of distinct mantras, then [the word] "thus" (*evam*) would have occurred just as before.

By means of the *uśik* [verse], O divine Soma, with the *gāyatrī* metre, enter the beloved abode of Agni; as one who possesses power, O divine Soma, with the *triṣṭubh* metre, enter the beloved abode of Indra; as our friend, O divine Soma, with the *jagatī* metre, enter the beloved abode of all the gods. Thus, it is stated that there is only one [verse] for each of these three purifications (*anupavana*). Regarding the portion called *ādābhya*, this too is indeed part of the *abhiṣavaṇa* (pressing).

O friend! 26. This is understood from the very context of Satyāṣāḍha’s composition of the *Śrautasūtra*. From the root *pū* (to purify), with the suffix *lyuṭ* (ana) in the sense of instrument or locus, we derive *pavana*. Then, with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of action (*bhāva*), we have *pāvana*. That which is purified at the time of drawing is a *pavana*; those which are *pavana*s are *pāvana*s. "The *upāṃśupāvanas*" means the purifiers of the cup known as the *upāṃśu*. Thus is the meaning.

Among them, two by two are joined together even without [the recitation of] mantras, because there is no instruction for mantras [in this case]. Here too, for the reason already stated, "joining" (apisaṃhana) means merely touching. Or, in the phrase "two by two," the word "and" (ca) connects [to the previous rule]. And between those two, the mutual joining occurs with the mantra: *uśig asi...* for the two Āgrayaṇa cups; and with the mantra: *yat te soma adābhyam nāma...* for the Upāṃśusavana stone and the Āditya cup. There is a repetition of the mantra for each respective cup.

Having placed them in the lower [mortar], having moistened them with the *vasatīvarī* waters, and having pressed them as required with the pressing-stones using the right hands, they proceed to the *nigrābha* rite as before.

Having taken those shoots used for the *upāṃśusavana* stone and having piled them up on the upper [stone], he pours them near the king [Soma] placed above; then, having moistened [the Soma] with the *paśvatīvarī* waters, [he presses]. Regarding the mention of "with the right hands" (*dakṣiṇaiḥ pāṇibhiḥ*), the inclusion of the word "right" is intended to exclude the alternative found in another *sūtra*, namely, "they press with both hands. If it is objected: "This [procedure] should be stated only for the pressing for the sake of the *soma-graha*s, because by the rule 'this is the ritual procedure for all pressings,' it would already apply here as well," [we reply:]...

It is said: it should be understood that the sūtra "with right hands" (dakṣiṇaiḥ pāṇibhiḥ) was composed here specifically to preclude the restriction of using only the right hand in places other than the Great Pressing (mahābhiṣava). Therefore, even if the right hand lacks the capacity [to press continuously], one must press with the right hand alone, pausing again and again. Elsewhere, the pressing of Soma for the *graha* vessels, the *śulba*, and the *upāṃśusavana* may be performed with the left hand as well.

This also is established: in the case of a *mahābhiṣava*, if the southern [fire] is entirely incapable, it does not occur here either; however, for the purpose of expiation due to the transgression of the rule, a sacrifice of thirty-three *yajñatanū* oblations must be performed. Furthermore, regarding the *sarvaprāyaścitta*, there is no expiatory oblation in *abhiṣavas* other than the *mahābhiṣava*, because there is an absence of such rules in those cases.

In the passage, "The great pressing-festivity (mahābhiṣava) is thus the rule for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)," the plural number found in the mantra, "naro yatte duduhuḥ dakṣiṇena," [is significant]. The word *naraḥ* is the nominative plural of the noun *nṛ*. The mention of the hand (*pāṇi*) is for the purpose of demonstrating that it must be accompanied by gold. Accordingly, Āpastamba states: "He sprinkles, takes, and offers with a golden-handed [person]"; this is an absolute injunction (*atyantapradeśa*). *Pradeśa* means a prescription; an absolute prescription is an *atyantapradeśa*.

The meaning is that the rule is universal, stating that "the one with golden hands (Hiraṇyapāṇi) performs the Soma-pressing and so forth. As long as [the procedure continues], all [participants] press the Soma and undergo the *nigrābha* rite by means of the four [verses] other than the *upāṃśu-savana* verse, according to the purpose and according to the requirement. Because of the plural number, it refers to all. By the phrase "as before," the rule beginning with the taking of the *aṃśu* stalk and ending with "that becomes the *nigrābha*" is obtained. The pulling out [of the stalk] (*prabṛhaṇa*) does not apply to the *paṅka* [verse], because that is intended solely for the *upāṃśu* [cup].
Some maintain that these two verses, "O drop, do not fall upon me" (*ā mā skāndrapsaśca*), belong to the Adhvaryu alone.

In this manner, the second and third pressings are performed. Thus, the meaning is that the second and third pressings are performed with the fat (vasā), the subordinate offerings (upasarjana), and the *nigrābha* water. When the occasion arises, [the formula] is: "O drop from the sky... [04:: : 25 1 2 :: 3]. They pour the King Soma, which has been pressed three times, into the *ādhavanīya* vessel. [This concludes the section] regarding the incapacity of the southern [vessel], together with the commentary (*jyotsnā*) composed by Gopīnātha Maṣṭaka. Page 827. Three times-pressed King Soma is poured into the *ādhavanīya*.

"Squeezing and pouring" means [the act of] sprinkling. Regarding this, a specific rule has been stated by Āpastamba: "The Adhvaryu pours the mixed [Soma] into the *udañcana*; the Unnetṛ, having lifted it between the two poles (*iṣe*), pours it from the north into the *ādhavanīya* vessel; this indeed is the place of Soma. The meaning of this is as follows: Having thus poured the mixed [Soma] into the *udañcana*, he takes it up. The Unnetṛ, having lifted that which has been taken up along the path between the two poles, goes to the north of the *ādhavanīya* and pours it into that vessel.

"The path of the *paśutīvarī* waters—which serve as subordinate elements—and of the pressed *soma* is indeed this [same one]. This too must certainly be accepted because it is not contradictory. In that context, the mere pouring together (*saṃsiñcana*) is performed by the *adhvaryu*. Because it would contradict the *sūtra*, the pouring into the *ādhavanīya* vessel is not exclusively the duty of the *adhvaryu* alone—as it might be for the followers of Āpastamba—but rather it is the duty of all the *adhvaryus*, since the plural form "they pour together" (*saṃsiñcanti*) is used. For this very reason, the view that it is the duty of the *netṛ* (the leader) alone is also refuted.
Thus are the second and third turns (*paryāya*) prescribed.

The second and third rounds are performed according to the procedure ending with the pouring together (*saṃsiñcana*). Thus, there is a reversal, and it becomes a "great pressing" (*mahābhiṣava*). Āpastamba also clearly states this point: "In the reversal"—having well-prepared the King Soma for the final pressing, having squeezed it through each strainer (*pavitra*), and having turned the pressing-stones (*grāvan*) face-to-face on the upper stone, he removes the dregs (*ṛjīṣa*) from them.

The *ṛjīṣa* is produced from the *supa* (the dregs) and is collected entirely. Having made the King [Soma] the *madhavanīya* vessel, he purifies it with the *daśāpavitra* strainer. In the *madhavanīya* itself, having placed the *prapīḍana* (pressing-stones) upon the *upara* stones and having turned them toward each other as before, he removes the *ṛjīṣa* from those vessels; "removes" here means that he distributes it. At the final pressing, when the *nigrābha* formula is recited, the *nigrābhyāḥ* waters contained in the *hotṛcamasa* cups are completed together with the stalks (*raśanā*).
He makes the mouths of the *ṛjīṣas*.

Āpastamba states that those whose mouths are divided by the *ajīpa* are called "those with wide-mouthed plows" (*ṛṇīṣamukha*); such ones he makes [the subjects], meaning he provides them with fodder. *Vāsaḥ* means a garment. The Udgātṛ priests place the *droṇakalaśa* facing eastward upon the pressing-stones (*grāvan*).

"Prāñcam" (eastward) is an adjective qualifying the *droṇakalaśa*, intended to exclude the alternative option of "udañcam" (northward) mentioned in the *Chandoga* [sūtra]. The term "udgātāraḥ" refers specifically to the Udgātṛ, Prastotṛ, and Pratihartṛ, and not the Subrahmaṇya as well; for in the *Chandoga-sūtra*, by virtue of the plural number, only those three are understood. When the cups (*pātras*) have been turned toward one another, they place the *droṇakalaśa* facing eastward upon them, establishing it above according to the procedure stated in their own sūtra beginning with "ṛtapātram" and so forth. They then draw it downward below the axle. || 8 ||

"Below the axle" (*akṣasyādhaḥ*) means [the part] below the axle; this is a compound with the elision of the middle member (*avyayībhāva*). They pull [the cart] by way of the lower part of the axle to support or establish it. The word "Udgātṛs" (the chanters) is understood from the preceding [text].

"Your filter is spread out, O Brahmaṇaspati; as the Lord, you go around all living beings on every side. He whose body has not been heated [by austerity], being raw and impure, does not reach that [filter]."—[Thus ends the portion] composed by Śāṣṭhāvin in the *Śrautasūtra* [(Mañcanapraśna)].
"The cooked ones indeed enjoy it; those carrying it have attained it"—saying this, the Udgātṛ priests, having spread out the filter with its fringes facing north, hold it over that [vessel].

In that jar, having spread out—that is, having extended—the *pavitra* filter with its fringes pointing northward, they hold the corners so that the liquids may be drawn; this is the meaning. This is the demonstration of the rule for the *udgātṛ*; since there are alternative readings due to the existence of various branches of the *Sāmaveda*, and because the *ṛc* is employed in certain cases, this very reading is intended even when the fringes of the *pavitra* point eastward. It is for the purpose of ensuring that the *pavitra* has its fringes pointing northward that this single verse is intended.
With this very [verse], the *adhvaryu* consecrates [the vessel].

The meaning is simply "by this very [means]," namely by that which has been spread out and held by the milk-mixers (*payogātṛ*). This indicates that the *pavitra* used here belongs specifically to the *Sāma-veda* branch and not to that contained in the *Āraṇyaka*. Furthermore, the performance of the *śānti* rite as prescribed in the *Pravayasūtra*—namely, "thus in the rites"—does not apply here. The word "being spread out" (*vitatyamānam*) is to be supplied as the object, as indicated by the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the term *pavitra*. The sacrificer makes his navel its size.

Regarding that fringe-filter (*daśāpavitra*): at the time of spreading it out, one makes its "navel" (*nābhi*). This is stated to be performed by the Adhvaryu priest; for this very reason it is so specified, lest it fall into meaninglessness. Thus, the option is established that either the Adhvaryu or the Pratiprasthātṛ makes the navel. Alternatively, the suffix *ṇic* should be understood [implying causation]. In this way, the instigation by the Adhvaryu is established as being performed by the Pratiprasthātṛ. The word *nābhi* has already been explained. And with the *hotṛ*-cup, he causes a continuous stream to flow into this [filter].

The word "ca" (and) follows immediately after "lāvayati" (he causes to flow). Thus, the meaning becomes: "He gives the sacrificer a name; he himself causes the stream to flow. Because the word "ca" is placed in the middle [of the two actions], it is inferred that this very *śruti* (Vedic text) is being restated. Alternatively, the letter "pa" has the sense of conjunction (*ādhāraṇa*). In this view as well, the word "yajamāna" (sacrificer) continues to apply. The meaning of the *sūtra* is clear.
From the *ādhavanīya* vessel, the *unnnetṛ* pours [the soma] into the *hotṛcamasa* using a ladle (*udacana*).

The mention of the *udgātṛ* is for the purpose of excluding [the *udgātṛ*] from the preparatory duties (*parikarma*), but not for the purpose of excluding the *adhvaryu*, because the exclusion of the latter is impossible since he is inherently engaged in other tasks. An *udañcana* is simply a cup (*camasa*) used for drawing the Soma; thus it is said, "the *udvadhana* cup. Regarding this, Āpastamba states a specific rule: "A continuous stream should be poured out, for it is known that his desires become fulfilled; however, one should break the stream for him whom [the sacrificer] hates.
This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the result, meaning that the desires of this sacrificer shall be accomplished.

He draws the cups from a flowing stream; "from a flowing one" is the appropriate reading. What is the meaning of "prāpat"? [It refers to] the direction of the flow. The phrase "sravatyā dhārāyāḥ" (from a flowing stream) uses the ablative case in the sense of the source. The meaning is: he draws the cups while they are being poured out from a flowing stream. Since the cups beginning with the Aindravāyava are qualified by the attribute of being "fine" (aṇvī) streams, in the Antaryāma cup, the stream must indeed be large.

In the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, however, it should be understood that the Antaryāma cup does not possess the status of being a *dhārāgraha* (a draught from a continuous stream). These rules extend up to this point regarding the *dhārāgrahas*.
[The formulas are: "Thou art taken with a support; hold within" for the Antaryāma; "rejoice" marks the end. The word "he takes" (*gṛhṇāti*) is carried over from the preceding sūtra.
The ritual procedure for this [cup] has been explained by the rule for the *upāṃśu* cup.
The conclusion of this sūtra consists merely in the rising and the moving forward. However, there is a specific distinction here regarding the mantra for the rising:

"Thou art well-disposed; make our nourishments honey-sweet; [grant] all powers, both celestial and terrestrial. Otherwise, if one were to take only as much as is seen in the *upāṃśu* rule—namely, "Thou art well-disposed"—then the phrase "make our nourishments honey-sweet" would be rendered purposeless, despite its being recited in the context. By the statement "the ritual procedure is explained by that of the *upāṃśu*," the rule beginning with "having passed beyond the Hotṛ to the north" and so forth is obtained; he states the following specific modification to supplement that.

Having passed the Hotṛ to the south with the words, "May speech choose thee," he stands by the southern junction of the enclosing-sticks; having brought [the ladle] along the southern junction of the enclosing-sticks, he offers [the oblation] straight, long, and continuous, directed eastward and upward, with the formula: "Svāhā! To thee, O well-born one, to Sūrya!"

The mantra "vāktvā'ṣṭu" (may speech protect you) is an alternative to "manastvā'ṣṭu" (may mind protect you), which belongs to one's own Vedic branch (*sva-śākhā*). Now, the portion "manastvā'ṣṭu" is indeed a remainder (*śeṣa*) of the *potṛ* priest's formula. Furthermore, the phrase "svāhā vā subhavaḥ sūryāya" indicates a difference in the final part of the mantra from the preceding one. Thus, it is established that the mantra "devebhyastvā marīcipebhyaḥ" is a remainder of the *homa* mantra itself, as no other application (*viniyoga*) for it is possible.

From the east, the front, and the northeast, up to the limit [of the altar]. By the statement, "The ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is explained by the *upāṃśu* [muttering]," this is already established. Regarding the rule "he should not offer [the oblation] long and continuous," it is for the purpose of excluding the optional (kāmya) practices mentioned in other Sūtras, such as: "If he should desire, 'May [the sacrificer] be short-lived,' he should offer the first half; if he should hate someone, he should offer that person's portion with a broken [interruption].

He does not wipe the smear on the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*), nor does he pour the residue (*saṃpāta*) from the Āgrayaṇa vessel [into the Gārhapatya], provided that the entire [offering] is sacrificed. In the case where the sacrifice is performed with a remainder, the disposal (*pratipatti*) consisting of pouring out the residue indeed takes place at the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsya*).
"This is your womb; for out-breathing, you!"—with these words he sets down the cup.
The Antaryāma cup is set within the cups; the setting is in its proper place.
He does not insert a stalk of grass.

[This is] the eighth [chapter]. 1. [The text reads] *sthānāga* in manuscript *ka*; 2. *tyānaṃ mannaḥ* in manuscript *kha*. [End of section]. According to the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [in the eighth book]:

Between those two, with the formula "For the through-breath (*vyāna*) thee," he places the Upāṃśusavana pressing-stone, touching it with the Upāṃśu vessel. These two are the vessels for the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma [libations].

If he should desire of someone, "May he be short-lived," he should set down the two cups for him without touching each other. If he should desire of someone, "May he live his full span of life," he should set them down for him so that they touch each other.

Regarding whichever sacrificer he should desire, "May he be short-lived and not reach old age," the Adhvaryu should set down the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups for that sacrificer at the *kata* (the wooden frame) without touching each other and without touching the *pāṃśusavana* stone. Regarding whichever sacrificer he should desire, "May he live a full and complete span of life," the Adhvaryu should set them down for that sacrificer at the *kata* so that they touch each other.

In this regard, according to the maxim that "censure does not function to censure, but rather to praise," the purpose of the censure of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is solely to extol the final position (*uttarapakṣa*). Since the Adhvaryu priest has been obtained through a purchase, how could he desire anything detrimental to the sacrificer? Therefore, because the two are not connected by virtue of the excellence of the placement (*sādana*) as expressed in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), there is no single purpose; thus, the latter optional ritual procedure is also obligatory (*nitya*).

This position is distinguished from the obligatory [rite] by the mere contact with the *upāṃśu* vessel alone. Although the verbal root √kam (to desire) is heard here, it does not constitute a *saṃkalpa* (formal resolve), because the desire does not reside in the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). If the desire were directed toward someone whom the sacrificer hates—according to the rule "the sacrificer should desire whomsoever he hates"—then, since the desire would not belong to the sacrificer himself, there would indeed be a *saṃkalpa* prompted by that desire.
Both [offerings] are offered at sunrise, without hastening.

The meaning is this: even when the *prātaranuvāka* has concluded, if there is no knowledge of the accents regarding the performance of the ritual, such an Adhvaryu, not hurrying, offers the *upāṃśu* and *antaryāma* cups after sunrise;
however, if he is hurrying, he offers the *upāṃśu* before sunrise and the *antaryāma* after sunrise.

The word *tu* (but) has the sense of distinguishing from what precedes it. Even though there is haste, one takes the Antaryāma cup only when [the sun] has risen; for although both cups are taken at sunrise, by virtue of its capacity to bring about the completion of the pressing (*savana*) at its own time, one should take the Upāṃśu cup only before sunrise. Thus, there is a twofold restriction here. It should be understood that taking both [cups] at sunrise is meaningful only in this manner, and not otherwise. According to some, both are to be taken before sunrise. (Sūtra 9)

Thus ends the third paṭala in the eighth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. In this [section], the drawing of the cups for Indra-Vāyu and the others is prescribed at sunrise; however, in accordance with how much light has appeared, the drawing of the Antaryāma cup may take place even before sunrise. It is said: "When even a mere line of the sun is visible through its rays, one should know that it is risen; there, one should perform the oblation. Thus, the time for sunrise prescribed here for the Agnihotra is the same. The meaning is clear.

Thus ends the third chapter of the eighth book in the *Jyotsnā* commentary—composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was himself the son of the illustrious Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin, a performer of the *Agniṣṭoma*, the *Sāhasra-Agni*, the *Vājapeya*, the *Sarvatomukha*, and the *Pauṇḍarīka* sacrifices—written to alleviate the distress of learned men caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the ancient Vedic tradition.
8.4 Now, the fourth chapter in the eighth book:
One should draw the cups beginning with that for Indra and Vāyu when the *rathantara* is the *sāman*.

The *rathaṃtara* is the *sāman* [chanted] upon which that Soma resides; thus he is "one whose *sāman* is the *rathaṃtara*. That draught for which Indra and Vāyu are the deities is the *aindravāyava*. Those among the draughts whose first extraction is this one are the *aindravāyavāgrayaṇa*; the meaning is that one should offer such draughts. It is the opinion of some Āryas that in the first performance, the *rathaṃtara-sāman* must be used. Accordingly, Āpastamba says: "Some say that one should not bring forward the *bṛhat-sāman* without having first performed the *rathaṃtara-sāman*. Because of the expression "some say," it is stated that this is not an absolute rule. When the *bṛhat-sāman* is used, the *śukra-agra* [draughts] are offered.

The meaning is that one should draw the *śukra* cups—those whose [deities] are the *śukra* graha and others such as the *śukrāyās*—at the *bṛhatsāmnī* soma sacrifice. In this version, having first drawn the *śukra* itself after the *antaryāma*, having mixed it with gold, having placed it in the hand of another, having drawn the *aindravāyava*, having wiped it and set it down in its place, having drawn the *śukra*, having wiped it and set it down in its place, having drawn the *maitrāvaruṇa* and mixed it with boiled, cooled milk, and having set it down, [one proceeds] from the drawing of the *manthin* cup onwards in the same manner.

The sequence of application is as follows: Nor can it be said that here there is an injunction for a modification (*vikāra*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*. This is because the qualification "having the *rathantara* as its *sāman*" is impossible for the *jyotiṣṭoma*, since other *sāmans* exist therein and thus [the term] lacks the capacity to differentiate it; furthermore, it is impossible for [the injunction] to apply to the entirety of the *jyotiṣṭoma*. Therefore, due to the equality [of the two cases], it cannot be stated that the injunction for the *aindravāyava* cup is based on the *rathantara-sāman* of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, nor can it be stated that the injunction for the *śukra* cup is based on the *bṛhat-sāman*.

If the *Soma* sacrifice were characterized by the *Rathantara-sāman*, one should draw the *Āindravāyava* cups; if it were characterized by the *Bṛhat-sāman*, the *Śukra* cups. Since the two words "if" (*yadi*) appear here, and because this scriptural statement is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it follows that the word "Soma" is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* itself. However, its status as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*)—by way of excluding other applications and thereby excluding the mutually contradictory *Rathantara* and *Bṛhat* *sāmans*—is to be understood as logically consistent.

And likewise, in the third pāda of the second adhyāya, Jaimini states in two sūtras: "But a subordinate element (guṇa), because it is connected with a sequence, prompts a different action, since its connection is not a part of the whole; however, for the sake of the purpose [of the injunction], the oneness of one [action] is stated, because it is a sentence concerning a subordinate element."

The meaning of the second sūtra is as follows: although there is a distinction in the indicative marks (*liṅga*)—such as the *ṛksama*, the *bṛhatsāman*, and the *ubhayasāman*—within the single Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, this is composed by means of various recensions (*pāṭha*). Because of this difference in the nature of the indicative marks, for the purpose of establishing the application of the ritual procedure (*apratāprayojana*), it is stated that there is indeed oneness (*ekatva*), namely, the state of being directed toward a single sacrifice (*ekakratuparatva*). Since these examples are "quality-sentences" (*guṇavākya*), the qualities such as the *aindravāyava* and *āgrayaṇa* are intended for that [single sacrifice]; therefore, the sentences concerning them are quality-sentences. For this reason, there is indeed oneness directed toward a single sacrifice; this is the meaning of the second sūtra.

[First: But the meaning of the sūtra is that the Rathantara-sāman and so forth are attributes of the sacrifice because of their connection with it. A previous connection with the Jyotiṣṭoma would indicate that this is merely a modification of the same ritual action. Why? Because the connection—namely, the connection with the Rathantara-sāman—is understood as being established by a restatement of something already existing; since such a connection is impossible within the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, it must belong to a different action.

In the case of the *ubhayasāman* (the sacrifice having both Sāmans), there is freedom of choice (*yāthākāmī*). That sacrifice in which both Sāmans—the Rathantara and the Bṛhat—are present is called an *ubhayasāman*; in that case, there is freedom of choice, meaning one may proceed according to one's desire, whether by having the Aindravāyava cup first or the Śukra cup first. Since this [option] is impossible in the archetype (*prakṛti*), its application is restricted to sacrifices such as the *Sarvapṛṣṭha* and the *Āptoryāma*.
One should take the Aindravāyava first when there is a connection with the *pṛṣṭha* chants in a modified (*vaikṛtika*) sacrifice.

When there is a connection with the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra]—that is, in conjunction with the *pṛṣṭha*—in whichever name it occurs, such as in the tenth section within the seventeenth chapter [of the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*]: "A Vaiśya desiring prosperity should sacrifice with the *agniṣṭoma*, having the *kava* and *bṛhat* as the *sāman*s," or likewise: "In the *rājana-sāmans*, one should take the cups beginning with the *aindravāyava* for the *mahāvrata*";
the meaning is that "one whose elder relatives are living should take those beginning with the *aindravāyava*" applies both to the obligatory (*nitya*) and the optional (*kāmya*) rites.

The phrase "the elder brother" is followed by the ellipsis "is surpassed by the younger. This [sequence] is "leftward" (vāmā) because, having introduced the statement, "When the Aindravāyava cups are drawn, they indeed reach the end of the sacrifice," and then concluding with the mention of the Aindravāyava-first sequence in the words, "Therefore the Aindravāyava cups are drawn," and because of the placement of the Aindravāyava cup at the beginning, it is established that the Aindravāyava is indeed the first. Furthermore, since in another recensional text (*śākhā*) a fruit is heard for the obligatory rule—namely, "He obtains an elder brother"—it follows that even in the optional injunction, the Aindravāyava is indeed the first. This is the meaning.

The term *jyeṣṭhabandhu* means "one whose paternal uncle is senior. On this point there is a scriptural authority (*śruti*): "The younger does not overstep the elder. This [rite] is optional, because it begins with "One who desires... and concludes with "...the younger does not overstep the elder. Here, the desire is precisely for the avoidance of the transgression committed by the younger.

These optional extractions (*grahaṇa*) have been explained in the Brāhmaṇa as "One suffering from illness should extract [the cups] beginning with the Aindravāyava"; regarding these, one may act according to one's own desire.

The sick person is one who suffers from disease. Regarding the sequence of the *dhārāgraha* (the stream-cup) offerings, it is not the case that the *aindravāyava* cup comes first; rather, the *aindravāyava* cup remains in its own original position. Nor should it be argued that there is no basis for the rule "one desiring that the vital breaths should proceed in their proper order" being established as the subsequent injunction for the *kāmyāgratā* (optional precedence), because the connection with the fruit belongs specifically to those *dhārāgraha* cups themselves as qualified by the particular precedence (*agratā*).

Regarding this, Jaimini states in the fifth pāda of the tenth adhyāya: "But in the case of a connection with a desire, there should be a displacement from the beginning because of the scriptural statement. However, when the *śukrāmanthinau* cups are present, they remain in their own place, because the fruit is assigned only to the state of not having obtained the *śukra* and *manthin*. Therefore, that [displacement] is displaced from the very beginning. And regarding this, in the fifth pāda of the tenth adhyāya, the rule is: "And in the case of subsequent [elements], the word 'not' (na) should be as before, starting from that point. [This concludes the section] composed by Gopīnātha, accompanied by the commentary named Jyotsnā.

Since the *aindravāyava* and other cups (*graha*) are the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), it is not the case that the priority of the *śukra* cup (*śukrāgratā*) is enjoined as a result [of the sacrifice]; rather, there is no displacement [of the sequence] from the very beginning. Thus, Jaimini states in the fifth section of the tenth chapter: "Because the place for the *aindravāyava* cup has already been established at the front. Due to the plural number in the word *gṛhṇīran*, the priority of the *maitrāvaruṇa* cup pertains to the sacrificial session (*sattra*). This is the reasoning regarding the *āśvina* cup.

The extraction of the Maitrāvaruṇa cup and the subsequent cups from a portion of the *āgrayaṇa* vessel is prescribed by the text itself according to the following procedure: having first poured [the soma] into the *āgrayaṇa*, having performed the pouring into the *droṇakalaśa*, having taken a portion of that same [soma] through the *pavitrapūtabhṛt* (the filter and the *pūtabhṛt* vessel), having spread an underlayer [of ghee] from the *droṇakalaśa*, and having drawn [the soma] into the *pūtabhṛt*, one pours [ghee] over it from the *droṇakalaśa*. Thus, the extraction prior to the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant is expressly stated. Then, after the oblation of the *antaryāma* cup, the Maitrāvaruṇa cup and the subsequent cups are likewise [extracted].

Having performed the rites beginning with the pouring of a portion of the *dhanas* into the *ādhavanīya* and *āvanīya* vessels, up until the drawing of the *āśvina* cup, and having performed the rites beginning with the drawing of the *aindravāyava* cup up until the drawing of the *dhruva* cup, one should stop the stream, press [the vessel], and set down that filter. The procedure for the presentation of the *savanīya* animal victim and so forth is the same as before. The method for the drawing of the *śukra* cup has already been explained.

In the case of the *āgrayaṇa* [cup], having taken the *manthin* cups and having taken the *aindravāyava* cup, immediately after its placement, one places the *manthin*; then, following the placement of the *kṣetrāvaruṇa*, *śukra*, and *āgrayaṇa*, there is the taking and placing of the *āgrayaṇa* and so forth. Regarding the *āgrayaṇa* and the *ukthya-anatana*, first these two are taken, not the *aindravāyava* and the others. Since these options concern desired objects, they are optional (*kāmya*). He describes the nature of the *maitrāvaruṇa*, *āśvina*, *śukra*, *manthin*, *āgrayaṇa*, *ukthya*, and *anatana*: they are drawn before the *aindravāyava* and, once placed, are set down.

The *saṃsādana* (placing) of the Aindravāyava cup occurs once it has been drawn; Naimini also holds this because there is no distinction [regarding the time of placing]. The drawing is not the commencement of the offering (*pradāna*), as it is like the cutting of portions (*avadāna*); rather, that [offering] is performed after all the cups have been drawn. Therefore, there is no anticipation of the offering. Thus says Mīni: "And the offering is like the placing. He describes the procedure under discussion: "He draws the Aindravāyava.
This general statement is intended to dispel the suspicion that it refers only to optional (*kāmya*) rites.
Having recited "O Vāyu, come hither" (ā vāyo bhūṣa), he holds the vessel under [the stream]. With the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; for Vāyu thee," he draws [the Soma] into it.

"Holding under" (upayamana) means restraining or supporting near the stream. The meaning is that he draws into that vessel, which is held beneath the stream, Soma measuring half of the vessel minus a fourth part.
Having held the vessel under with "Indra and Vāyu," he again holds it under; with the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; for Indra and Vāyu thee," he draws [the Soma] into it once more.

Having moved it away from the stream—that is, having set it aside—one takes the upper half. The statement "taking it up again" is for the purpose of precluding the division of the vessel. Since this is already established by the phrase "taking it up again," the specific mention of "in that [vessel] again" is intended to exclude the vessels dedicated to Indra and Vāyu.

In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [the purpose of the phrase] "he takes it again" (*tasmin punargṛhṇāti*)—which would have been established by that alone—is to prevent the recurrence of the same state as previously described: namely, that at the time of the *punarabhiṣavaṇa* (re-pouring), there is merely a re-pouring into the *vāyavya* vessel, whereas the *aindravāyava* drawing is made from a broken vessel. By stating "he takes it again" (*punarevopayacchati*), it is indicated that even for a vessel that has been set aside (*dhārāto dīkṛta*), the drawing must be performed precisely at the time of the drawing itself, and not merely below the stream (*dhārāyā avastāt*).

It should be held in the middle near the stream at the very time of reciting the mantra, so that it may remain thus; for this purpose, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage concerning the drawing of the portion for Vāyu: "O Indra, having bent her down in the middle, he divided her; therefore this speech is called 'divided' (vyākṛtā). Therefore, this [portion] is drawn for Indra in the middle. Two [cups] are drawn for Vāyu, for he chose two boons. Having wiped it around with the unwoven filter, he deposits it in its place with the formula: "This is thy womb; to you two who are well-disposed, svāhā! (eṣa te yoniḥ sajoṣābhyāṃ tvā).

By the term "not covered," the exclusion of that which is held over the *droṇakalaśa* is effected. By the use of the word "by that" (*tena*), the wiping mentioned by Āpastamba and stated in the *Mānava-sūtra* is restricted to the *daśāpavitra* alone. "In its own place" (*āyatane*) means in its proper location. Regarding the cups (*graha*), however, according to the previously stated technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), there is a mixing with gold in all cups. Whether this [mixing] has been performed or not will be explained later. He states the technical rule:
"Those cups taken with the *upayāma* formula are taken with a *yajus* [formula]; those taken with the *upayāma* formula above [the vessel] are taken with a *ṛc* [verse]."

Because the general rule (*paribhāṣā*) is formulated after the drawing of the *aindravāyava* cup, it does not apply specifically to the *aindravāyava*. Thus, even though the *upayāma* formula "indravāyubhyām tvā" occurs later in the text, the meaning of the word "anu" here is simply "having recited [the formula]," and not for the purpose of connecting it with the *upayāma* itself. Otherwise, since the drawing of the cup would already be possible at the time of the mental connection with the *upayāma*, the action prescribed in the middle—namely, the act of taking up the vessel (*pātropayamana*)—would result in being purposeless.

Regarding the phrase *anuṣṭhāya*, if it is not accepted as meaning "having recited," then since there would be no possibility of a difference in time when the vessel is brought forward at the same time as the recitation, it would lack purpose. The suffix *-tyap* signifies simultaneity alone, and not immediate succession; otherwise, a logical inconsistency (*toṣa*) would arise. The term *purastādupayāmāḥ* refers to those cups for which the formula "Thou art taken with a base" (*upayāmagṛhīto 'si*) is recited first, prior to the verses (*ṛc*), in the case of those cups. In other words, it means those cups for which the formula is recited before the verses.

Those cups which are of such a kind are "taken with the Yajus"; the meaning is that their taking is performed by means of the Yajus formula. Those cups for which the *upayāma* (the supporting ladle) is mentioned subsequently are "those whose *upayāma* follows later"; this refers to those cups for which one should recite the mantra "You are taken with a support" (*upayāmagṛhīto 'si*) immediately after the mantra [of the cup's specific rite]. Those cups which are of such a kind are "taken with the Ṛc"; the meaning is that their taking is performed by means of the Ṛc verse.

The *upayāma* formulas are recited before the *yajus*; they are taken at the end of the *yajus*. This is because [the Soma] is not lost (*riṣṭāt*) in this way, whereas it would be lost through the *upayāma* alone. By this, the meaning of "never neglecting" (*kadācana prayucchan*), "the cooked milk and curd," "the sacrifice of the gods approaches," and so forth, as well as the fact that "Soma takes all"—namely, the taking of the Āditya cup and the *adābhya* cup—is established through the recitation of the *upayāma* formula. Thus, the *upayāma* is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of both types of cups. This is proven.

In the sixteenth question, in the sixteenth section, regarding the verse "viṣuvanyudgaṃ jātavedasam," he takes the seventh draught from their midst for Manu. [End of Chapter 40] — accompanied by the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha.

Regarding the verses "vācaspataye viśvakarmaṇa ūtaye" for the Vaiśvakarmaṇa cup in the Viśvajit sacrifice, and "mahīm su mātaram" for the Āditya cup on the following day—as prescribed by this sūtra—when the first Viṣuvat day occurs, the Saura cup is drawn with the verse beginning "atiprā viśvāni" and the Vaiśvakarmaṇa cup with the verse beginning "atiprā. On the subsequent Viṣuvat day, when the Āditya cup is drawn, one should pour it out using the upayāma formula because of the mention of the "upayāma" vessel. The term "upayāma" refers to the earth in the form of a vessel, as indicated by the portion of the verse: "upayāmagṛhīto'si. By means of the "upayāma" portion, the earth is described as the vessel.

And thus says the Śruti: "He says, 'Thou art taken with a support' (upayāma); this [earth] is the support; therefore, people do not lead this [earth] away from its support. The meaning of the mantra is: "O Soma, thou art taken by means of the support, that is, by the earth itself. There is also the wiping of all the cups and their placement according to their source (yoni).

Since the plural number in the word *grahāṇām* (of the cups) already establishes this, the inclusion of the term *sarva* (all) is for the purpose of a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). By means of that, it follows that wiping (*parimārjana*) is established even for cups such as the *ukthya* and others, which are distinct from the *dhārā-graha*. Because of the formulation of this technical rule, there is no wiping in the case of the preceding cups. As for the injunction "one wipes the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), it does not mean that the wiping applies to only one specific cup due to the singular number; rather, because the cup in general is the object of reference, the wiping applies to all cups.

If, however, singularity were also enjoined, there would result a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) because two things—the cup (*graha*) and the number—would have to be enjoined simultaneously. Alternatively, if it were intended to exclude [other cups], that too would entail a syntactical split. Therefore, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of singularity. And thus Jaimini states in the first section of the third chapter: "The mention of singularity is connected to the cup, because of its connection with the Vedic text. Furthermore, the inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the underlying logic (*nyāya*). As for the meaning of the Sūtra: since the text says "he cleanses the cup," the cleansing applies to only one cup because of the connection with the singular number; it does not apply to all cups, because in the Vedic text, the connection is specifically with the singular number.

The measuring (*parimāṇana*) is not obstructed by that [rule], because it was already stated in the preceding section. The mention of the *graha* (cup) is for the purpose of excluding the *camasa* (scoops). There is no non-intentionality regarding the form of the singular number; rather, there is indeed an intentionality regarding its form. Since an injunction is impossible without a subject (*uddeśya*), there is no reason for the non-intentionality of its essential nature. Thus, there is no cleansing (*samārjana*) in the case of the *camasas*.

And likewise, in the first section (pāda) of the third chapter, Jaimini states in two sūtras: "Or, because of the purificatory rite (saṃskāra), there would be no restriction among the subordinate elements (guṇa); or rather, there would be a restriction of the purpose, because it is connected with the Vedic text, since that [text] is the authority for the word. The meaning of the first alternative is as follows: on account of the purificatory rite—namely, the act of cleansing (saṃmārga)—there would be no restriction regarding the subordinate qualities such as being a *graha* (cup) or being a *camasa* (bowl); thus, in this case, there would be no restriction based on the specific nature of being a *graha* or a *camasa*. Consequently, the cleansing would apply to the *camasas* as well. This is the sense of the first position.

In the subsequent sūtra, the word *khalu* serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Here, the restriction of the meaning is as follows: the non-dual [reality] delimited by the two properties of the cup (*graha*) and the bowl (*camasa*)—which consists of both the cup and the bowl—is connected to the Vedic text (*śruti*) through the term "cup" (*graha*), such that the connection with the text is "one wipes the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*), and not "one wipes the bowl" (*camasaṃ sammārṣṭi*). Therefore, because of the connection with the text regarding the cup, and because that connection with the text regarding the cup is based on verbal authority (*śabdapramāṇa*)—that is, it is accessible solely through the Word (*śabda*)—this is the meaning of the second sūtra.

By the word *yoni*, the cause (*kāraṇa*) and the locus (*āyatana*) are intended. "Yoni and yoni" becomes "yonī" (in the dual); "not transgressing the *yoni*" means "according to the *yoni*. Thus, the meaning is: according to the causal mantra and according to the locus. It is well known that the word *yoni* denotes "cause"; however, its denotation of "locus" is seen in the Vedic scripture: *yoniṣ ṭa indra niṣade akāri* ("O Indra, a seat has been prepared for you to sit upon"), which means "I have made a place for your entering."

At the time of drawing [the cups], Baudhāyana has stated that the primary [action] takes place first in the water at the bottom; this too should be performed everywhere whenever there is a possibility of a visible purpose. Because this rule is established here, there is no wiping (*parimārjana*) for the cups ending with the Antaryāma. The word "ca" (and) serves to include the non-recitation of the *ṛc* and the *upayāma*. [End of] the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Eighth Book. [Section 1]

With the verse, "O Mitra and Varuṇa, this [is for you]," he prepares the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa. Having mixed it with warm milk that has been boiled, he deposits it with the verse: "May we, having won through wealth, rejoice in you both, O gods, as cows do in pasture and fodder; O Mitra and Varuṇa, bestow upon us every day that cow who does not kick away. Thus he deposits it.

"Thus, O Indra, he who offers the vessel"—this [verse] is recited as a refrain for all the *graha* offerings. Regarding "the *maitrāvaruṇa*," the word "having taken" (*gṛhītvā*) is to be supplied immediately after. In the passages beginning with "This indeed is Mitra and Varuṇa," the mantras are understood to be those connected to the respective *graha* vessels according to their specific designations. "That *maitrāvaruṇa* [cup]" means: having mixed it with warm milk—that is, with the milk previously prepared by milking—[one should mix it]. "Warm" (*śṛta*) means boiled; "warm" (*śīta*) means cooled. [The meaning is: having mixed it with that milk.

If it were stated merely as "śūna" (hot), there would be the fault of overcooking; for that reason, it says "śītena" (with cold). If it were stated merely as "śītena," there would be no heating; for that reason, it says "uṣṇena" (with hot). The word "śata" refers to cooking, based on the Pāṇinian rule: "paraḥ śata-pāka" (cooking more than a hundred times). Just as with the deities, according to their respective mantras—there is a mantra for taking [the vessel] at each respective drawing, a mantra for seating [the deity] characterized by the mark of that respective deity at each respective seating—and thus there is a rule for the application of all the drawings.

The mantras for the Maitrāvaruṇa draught are as follows: "This [is] for Mitra and Varuṇa," "O Mitra and Varuṇa," "Thou art taken with a support," and "For Mitra and Varuṇa. "This is thy womb; O ancient one, come hither"—these are the mantras for the Maitrāvaruṇa draught. "This is thy womb; O Nābhya, come hither"—this is the mantra for the depositing. With the verse "This is the longing one," he mixes the *śukra* draught with gold. The word "the *śukra*" implies that it has been "taken" immediately thereafter. Because it is stated here, "he mixes with gold," whereas previously it was not mentioned, the mixing with gold is understood to be optional. "Thou art taken with a support; for Śaṇḍa," and "This is thy womb; protect the truth"—these are the two mantras for the taking and the depositing.
The remainder [of the mantra] is: "Take that Manthin cup with the words 'as of old'.

"In which invocations, offering like a mind, you two, speeding along, win over the enemies by your power"—[this refers to the verse]. "He who, possessing great manly strength, has mixed his aim with the arrows while grasping them in his arms"—with these words, he mixes the Manthin with groats, not defiling himself nor the other cups.

"You are taken with a support; for Marka you [are taken]; this is your womb; protect the breath"—thus are the formulas for the drawing [of the cups]. The groats (*saktu*) are parched grains. It is established there by the very text. Likewise, it is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the phrase "he entered. Here, since the groats are prescribed to be offered in the *Śrotriya* fire, they must be produced outside the sacrificial enclosure (*vihāra*). Baudhāyana has stated that the offering of the groats is indeed from the common (*laukika*) fire, and that on the preceding day itself. For that purpose, he has stated the injunction: "Prepare both the butter and the groats."

"Do not scatter yourself; do not scatter the other vessels while causing them to be scattered"—this is the meaning. [The phrase] "do not scatter yourself" [is explained as follows]: From the statement "and the other vessels," it is understood that in a windy place, the scattering of the flour-meal (saktu) would generally occur, and that would be detrimental due to the mutual mixing of the Soma with the other sacrificial offerings (havir).
