Therefore, after touching other oblations (*havīṃṣi*), the king [Soma] must be touched only by those who have washed their hands. After touching the king, [one may touch] the other oblations... and according to the *Vādhūla* and other sūtras: "One should not consume the other oblations with Soma without having touched water. In the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*: "Having touched the clarified butter (*ājya*), one should touch water; likewise when touching the curd and the Soma. And in the *Chandoga-sūtra*: "One should not touch the clarified butter without having touched water; likewise, one should touch the clarified butter [after touching] the king [Soma] everywhere."

Āśvalāyana also, in various places, has prescribed the *udakaparṇī* (water-sprinkler) before the contact with the King [Soma] occurs, stating "one who has already touched water. For these many [verses], the *upāṃśu* (whispered) tone is used; for the *sthālī* and *āgrayaṇa* [vessels], one uses either "ye devā divyekādaśa stha" or "āgrayaṇo 'si" with a *purastādupayāma* formula.

The mention of the *sthālī* (pot) is for the purpose of excluding [the use of] the *āgrayaṇa-sthālī*, because the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—which states that "the Viśve Devas [delight in] the great"—indicates that [the pot] should not be used at the time of the *āgrayaṇa*. He draws [the Soma] with the *sthālī*; he offers it with the *vāyavya* cup. Therefore, they milk the animals with one vessel and receive them with another; thus the sacrificer attains distinction. This is both for the sake of what is enjoined by the Śruti and for the sake of performing the great imitation (*mahānukaraṇa*) by means of the *sthālī*.

"O gods, you who are eleven in heaven, you who are eleven upon the earth, you who dwell in the waters, eleven by your greatness—O gods, enjoy this sacrificial food! You are taken with a support (*upayāma*). This is the mantra for the first wing. "You are taken with a support; you are the Āgrayaṇa, the self-supporting. Quicken the sacrifice, quicken the lord of the sacrifice; protect the pressings! May Viṣṇu protect you; protect the people, protect the sensory power (*indriya*). This is the mantra for the second wing.

By this, the suspicion that the formula *āgrayaṇo 'si* is a supplement belonging specifically to the *upayāma* performed above is dispelled. The connection is rather with the *purastādupayāma* formula, as in *āgrayaṇo 'si*. Because of the qualification "with the *purastādupayāma*," it is indicated that the preceding mantra possesses the character of an *upariṣṭādupayāma*. Āpastamba states this clearly: "With the mantra *ye devā divi...* [one offers] either with the *upariṣṭādupayāma* or with the *purastādupayāma* formula."

Since it is already established by the statement "those with the *upayāma* before [the formula] are taken with the *yajuḥ*, and those with the *upayāma* after" that this applies here, the explicit mention of "with the *upayāma* before" is intended to show that because a single *upayāma* occurs in the middle and thus connects to both, both mantras are likewise accompanied by the *upayāma*. Consequently, there is no case where one [mantra] is accompanied by the *upayāma* while another is devoid of it; rather, for whichever is devoid of the *upayāma*, its taking would occur precisely by means of the *upayāma*, and not at the end of either the *bhakṣa-mantra* or the *yajuḥ*.

In order to exclude that [interpretation], it follows that in both cases the conclusion of the mantra (*mantrānta*) is to be understood as occurring at the end of each respective [portion]; thus it is established that the conclusion of the mantra does not occur here through a single *upayāma*.
He draws [the soma] with two streams;
this general proposition is intended to signify the conjunction of the two streams.
Having poured a portion of the Soma that is in the Āgrayaṇa vessel into another vessel, he makes the second stream.

In the manuscript of the Sūtra, the reading is *niṣicya*. (838) According to the *Bhīma-sūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the section on the eightfold measurement]—it is understood from this that the cavity of the *upāṃśu-pātra* is wide and deeper. It is also known that the oblation (*homa*) is half [of the vessel], and the pouring down (*avanayana*) is half of that. This constitutes one-fourth of a part. The meaning is that, having poured it into whichever other vessel is available, one performs the second stream (*dhārā*) with that.

Saramā found the breach in the mountain; she, the ancient one, established a great path for those who walk together. The swift-footed one led the way among the flowing waters, the first to know the sound, stepping toward the ford. One performing a rite should employ this *puroruc* (introductory verse). That which is stated before the mantra used for the purpose [of the rite] is called its *purog* (predecessor). Where, upon the occasion of an oblation, a specific verse is taken up, there it is designated by the term *puroruc*. This is seen in the following: *vidadyatī saramā rugṇamadrermahi pāthaḥ pūrvyaṃ sadhriyakkaḥ | agraṃ nayatsupadyakṣarāṇāmacchā ravaṃ prathamā jānatī gāt ||* (One should recite: "Saramā found the breach in the mountain; she, the ancient one, established a great path for those who walk together. The swift-footed one led the way among the flowing waters, the first to know the sound, stepping toward the ford. [The commentary continues: It is said that what precedes the mantra for practical application is termed *purog*. Where a specific verse is selected as the basis for the act of pouring the oblation (*abhidhāra*), it is introduced by the technical name *puroruc*. This is observed in the following: ... [text fragment] ... seen.

Regarding the *ukthya* cups being drawn first for one who is practicing sorcery against another: "One should draw the *ukthya* cups for one who is being practiced against; for all his vital breaths and senses are indeed in the *ukthya* vessels. Thus, he overpowers him with his entire power. He should use the *puroruc* verse: "Sarasvatī has led me forward to gain. For Sarasvatī is speech; thus, he overpowers him with speech. He says, "May we not go to desolate fields. By this, he does not go to the desolate fields of death.

"One who practices sorcery" (*abhicaran*) refers to one who performs sorcery directed toward an enemy. For such a sacrificer, one should employ these *puroruc* verses. This is because they are composed with the word "ruj" (to break). Here, since there is no mention of the *upayāma* formula in the revealed text (*śruti*), it should be understood that the taking [of the cup] occurs by means of the *upayāma* itself. The phrase "thirty and three" is for one who has rivals (*bhrātṛvyavat*).

The *bhrātṛvya* (rival) possesses the vessel; the previous ritual procedure (*kalpa*) serves only to cause him harm. This [present procedure], however, is for the purpose of counteracting the harm done by him—this is the distinction. Here, the word "āgrayaṇa" occurring after "atītya" is a supplement (*śeṣa*) specifically to the *upayāma* formula. This is because, as before, there is no word indicating an option (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, in this mantra "āgrayaṇo 'si," since there is no word indicating the counteraction of harm caused by the rival (*bhrātṛvya*), its application is impossible. The mantra for the placing (*sādana*) is exactly as before.

Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa cup, he utters "him" three times—first softly, then loudly, and then very loudly—and says "Soma purifies itself" three times—first softly, then loudly, and then very loudly. 10.

The statement "having taken the Āgrayaṇa" is intended to exclude the suspicion that the following mantra is for the occasional (naimittika) taking of the Āgrayaṇa alone. By this, it is established that the mantra applies to the regular (nitya) taking of the Āgrayaṇa as well. Since the *hiṃ* sound has various forms such as *hai*, *hā*, and *am*, the reading *him* is for the purpose of encompassing all these desired forms. Furthermore, because the word *uccaiḥ* ("loudly") is heard here, the word *śanaiḥ* ("softly") refers to the pitch of the voice (*svara*).

"Softly," "loudly," and "clearly"—these are said to be the low (*mandra*), middle (*madhyama*), and high (*tāra*) pitches. By the words "softly," "loudly," and "clearly," the three pitches for the three *hikāra*s are already established; however, the inclusion of the word "first" (*prathamam*) and the two words "immediately after" (*anantaram eva*) indicate that one should first perform [the *hikāra*] three times softly, immediately followed by [three times] loudly, and immediately followed by [three times] clearly, rather than following a sequence such as once softly, then loudly, and then clearly. By this, it is also established that there is no repetition (*nirāvṛtti*) for each individual pitch.

The *suṣaḥ* [is used] with *sūruḥ*, *apekṣapā*, and *suplutā*; in the case of *somaḥ parataḥ*, it should be understood in exactly the same way. [End of section 10, Paṭala: Together with the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Mahāmahopādhyāya.

"He flows for this priesthood; he flows for this nobility; he flows for this sacrificer who presses [the Soma]; he flows for food and vigor; he flows for the waters and the plants; he flows for the trees; he flows for heaven and earth; he flows for well-being; he flows for spiritual luster; he flows for the sacrificer; he flows for my preeminence"—having thus consecrated the Soma, he releases his speech.

The Soma has been drawn. He releases his speech immediately after the consecration mantra (*abhimantraṇa*). Then follows the placement: "This is thy womb; for all-pervading Viśve Devas thee. By the phrase "he releases his speech," it is taught that one should maintain the mental realization, "My speech is released," but it does not mean that actual speaking must be performed at this point in the middle of the ritual.

Regarding the etymological explanation of *bhāgyana*: Speech departed from the gods; not remaining with them, she went away. When Speech had departed, the gods silently took up the *mahān* [libation]. She thought, "They are excluding me. She returned to the *āgrayaṇa*; that is why the *āgrayaṇa* is so called. He draws the *atigrāhya* cups.

The meaning is that one takes [the draughts] from the house known as Asigrāma. This is a general proposition (*pratijñā*). Furthermore, this proposition is intended to exclude the partiality mentioned in other Sūtras. It is not the case that there is a specific statement—such as "one should take [them] at the Ukthya" or "they are to be taken at the Viśvajit Sarvapṛṣṭha"—wherein the extension (*atideśa*) would apply only to that particular instance and not to other modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*). Otherwise, if the extension were made only for both cases in the statement "one should take [them] at the Ukthya" and "they are to be taken at the Viśvajit Sarvapṛṣṭha," then [the specific rule] would be rendered useless.

It must be stated that the sentence "they are to be drawn at the *agniṣṭoma*" indeed requires [the rule] for the sake of restriction (*niyatattva*). Since a uniform injunction (*samānavidhāna*) is necessary for the engagement of those desiring specific qualities (*guṇakāma*), the repetition [of the injunction] constitutes a uniform injunction; therefore, there is no cessation of extension (*atideśa*) elsewhere. As Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 10.1.5 states: "In the case of the *saṃsthā* [terminuses], because they are taught as modifications (*vikṛti*), there should be exclusion. [The cups are]: the *āgneya* with the verse "O Agni, you purify our lives" (*agna āyūṃṣi pavase*); the *aindra* with "Arising with vigor" (*uttiṣṭhann ojasā saha*); and the *saurya* with "The swift one, visible to all" (*taraṇir viśvadarśataḥ*).

"Thou art taken with a support; for Agni, the radiant, thee!"—"This is thy womb; for Agni, the radiant, thee!"—thus for the taking and placing of the Āgneya cup. "Thou art taken with a support; for Indra, the radiant, thee!"—"This is thy womb; for Indra, the radiant, thee!"—thus for the Aindra cup. "Thou art taken with a support; for Sūrya, the radiant, thee!"—"This is thy womb; for Sūrya, the radiant, thee!"—thus for the Saurya cup. The taking [of the cups] occurs at the end of the Ṛc verses.
"His vital energy blazed forth when he rolled out both worlds like a hide, Indra. "His banners, his rays, have become visible among the people, shining like fires," with these two [verses].

1. Regarding the sentence: 42. In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Āpastamba—[(Ma0Pra): If the sacrificer should desire, "May the Adhvaryu always uproot this person, the son of such-and-such, from the lineage of such-and-such, out of such-and-such a clan," he should uproot the *dhruva* [ladle] from that place with the mantra: "I uproot this person, the son of such-and-such, from the lineage of such-and-such. Then, with the mantra: "I settle this person, the son of such-and-such, in the lineage of such-and-such," he should settle that *dhruva* back in its very same place.]

Whoever [performs this rite] against an enemy—having uprooted me and cast me down, or having driven me away from the village to the place of the enemy—does so by this method. "Utkhedana" means pulling up or lifting upwards. For the purpose of causing distress (*utravedana*), in the mantra, the word "amuṃ" (that one) is replaced by the name of the enemy. "Āmuṣyāyaṇa" is his name derived from his *gotra*. As previously stated, "āmuṣyāyaṇa" is indeed expressed by means of the father's name. In the phrase "the son of such-and-such" (*amuṣya putraḥ*), the mention of "amuṣya" refers to the name of that father.

In the phrase "amuṣyā viśaḥ," the word *amuṣya* refers to the name of the village (*grāmanāman*), and the word *viś* denotes the people (*mānavācin*). The reading found in the Sūtra—"idamahamamuṣyāmuṣyāyaṇamamuṣyāḥ putramamuṣyā viśa urikhadāmi"—appears to be a corrupt reading. Why? It is said: one should observe that the genitive form *amuṣya*, which expresses a part of a compound name, does not include the father’s name; therefore, the mention of the mother’s name alone, without the father’s name, is seen to be inconsistent.

In this regard, the reading up to the word *viś* should follow the recension of Āpastamba as follows: "This one, [named] so-and-so, the descendant of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, from such-and-such a clan (*viś*). Accordingly, the mantra becomes: "This Viṣṇugupta, the descendant of Vena, the son of Citra, from the clan of Kāśi—I uproot him. However, the reading of Āpastamba is "I uproot" (*udūhāmi*). Since there is no contradiction here, the reading "I uproot" (*udūhāmi*) need not be adopted.

Alternatively, in this mantra, "I place this one of such-and-such [name]," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) should be understood as having the sense of the accusative (*dvitīyārthe*). Furthermore, the reading "I place this one, the descendant of such-and-such, the son of such-and-such, in such-and-such a clan" is likewise a corrupt reading, for the same reasons stated previously. Even here, the reading follows the version of Āpastamba, since the entire mantra remains undivided. And thus the mantra becomes as follows: da.

"The army of Śūrasena, protected by Mahāmitra; I set down the son of so-and-so in such-and-such a clan. By the word "this" (*idam*), the vessel is indicated. The mantras become complete as follows: "May they [the gods] settle this vessel—belonging to so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, in such-and-such a clan—for me to place upon the earth. But for the subsequent mantra, it is: "In order to set down the son of so-and-so, belonging to so-and-so, in such-and-such a clan, I set down this vessel. Here too, the genitive and accusative cases are to be understood [as appropriate].

The word *punaḥ* (again) is intended to indicate that this placing (*āsādana*) occurs at the very same place as the first placing; it does not suggest the prior existence of a permanent placing, for that is already established by the force of the injunction regarding the cutting (*utpavana*). The result is revealed by the passage beginning with "that which is the village," etc. Regarding this, a specific rule is stated by Āpastamba: "If one should act thus, he would disturb the primary life-force; therefore, with that mantra, he should pass [the grass] over and over. By this, he means: "with the mantra 'this I [place],' [he should do so]. The meaning is that he should cause the grass to descend from above, starting from the bottom of the vessel on the ground, until it reaches the surface.
Having settled the *dhruva* vessel, he pours out for the King [Soma] as much as he considers sufficient for the morning pressing.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the statement "having caused [the sacrificer] to sit down" is redundant? If you argue that its purpose is to terminate the entitlement to perform occasional rites (*naimittika-karma*), then we must necessarily state that the very purpose of demonstrating such a meaning—namely, that once the desire for the fruit has been fulfilled, the occasional rite ends with that point—is already established by that [statement] itself; thus, [your objection] is true. [Response: This is so because, in the *Mādhyandina* recension, [this is established] in the eleventh section (*paṭala*). [Commentary by Gopīnātha, titled Jyotsnā: Accompanied by the commentary of Gopīnātha. Note: The text provided contains a fragment of a discussion regarding ritual procedure (*kalpa*) concerning the termination of occasional rites after the fulfillment of a specific desire, citing the *Mādhyandina* tradition. The bracketed portions indicate the structure of the argumentative dialogue and the identification of the commentator. The phrase "nyāpattau mādhyaṃdine" likely refers to a specific rule or principle (*nyāya*) applicable in the Mādhyandina school. The mention of "gopīnāthamākṛtajyotsnāvyākhyāsametam" identifies the specific commentary being referenced. The "11.paṭaka" indicates the eleventh chapter or section. The use of IAST diacritics (e.g., *naimittika*, *karma*, *siddhi*) follows the instructions. The translation aims for fluidity while preserving the technical terminology of the ritual science (*śrauta-sūtra*).

If [the Soma] spills while being carried, one should perform the expiation beginning with, "O Sky, you are the giver of life; grant me firm life," and so forth. Having set it down with the *sādana* mantra, one then proceeds to filter the King [Soma] excessively (*atipāvayati*). This is likewise at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*). One filters the King excessively; the remainder of the sentence is "in the *droṇakalaśa*. This is because that [vessel] alone is present and because there is no other purpose. This statement refers to the lack of temporal interval [between the spilling and the expiation]. In the term *atipāvayati*, the prefix *ati-* signifies excessiveness. As much as was [filtered] at the morning pressing...

It is considered "not obtained" (*nāyāpta*) due to this association. From the word *pāvayati* ("he purifies"), by means of the *aśāpavitra* (the filter), the purpose of the pouring is the purification of the stream itself; it is not the pouring down of Mitra from the stream. For this very reason, he will state further on: "The stream ceases; he has cast out the water from the filter. Regarding the specific measure for pouring more soma into the *droṇakalaśa*, Kātyāyana has stated: "Having made the *droṇakalaśa* half-full..."

But Baudhāyana has stated that one should place the *droṇakalaśa* on top [of the *pūtabhṛt*]. One takes up [the water] in the same manner as far as the *pāvan* [verse]; this should be understood as taught in the *Bahvṛcasūtra*, which considers it to be performed with a single effort. When the stream ceases, having pressed [the filter], he sets down the *pavitra*.

By the phrase "he restrains [the flow] and holds it," its continuity until the end is indicated. By this, it is established that the holding of the stream must be performed even at times other than the actual drawing [of the Soma]. Regarding the statement "having squeezed the *pavitra*—that is, the *daśāpavitra*—right into the *droṇakalaśa* itself, and having placed the *pavitra* in the southern *havirdhāna* cart," the indicative authority (*jñāpaka*) for this has already been stated.
And having poured a portion of the *ekadhana* waters from the cup belonging to the Maitrāvaruṇa into the *ādhavanīya* jar, he pours a portion through the *pavitra* into the *pūtabhṛt* jar.

In the phrase "the portions belonging to the Maitrāvaruṇa cup" (*maitrāvaruṇa-camasīyāḥ*), the word *ca* (and) is for the purpose of pouring out together both the portions belonging to the Maitrāvaruṇa cup and a single portion of the *ekadhana* waters. Thus, there is a pouring out of all those portions belonging to the Maitrāvaruṇa cup; the pouring out of a single portion of the *ekadhana* waters is as described above. Accordingly, Āpastamba states: "The *ekadhana* waters are poured out according to their purpose, and all the portions belonging to the Maitrāvaruṇa cup are poured out into the *bhakṣaṇīya* vessel."

The meaning is that he pours out as much [of the Soma] as he considers sufficient for the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) to increase its flavor. He pours it into the *pūtabhṛt* vessel—meaning he causes a portion of the *ādhavanīya* to flow into it—in such a way that the filter (*pavitra*) remains hidden or internal to the action; that is, having bent down, he causes it to reach there for the sake of the *pavamāna* cups. A single portion is sufficient for the drawing of the *āśvina* cup.

For the purpose of raising and pouring out the groups of *camasa* vessels, such as those belonging to the Śukra and Manthin cups, the Sūtrakāra prescribes the pouring out (*avanayana*) prior to the lifting of the *camasa* groups; he says, "having wiped the *kalaśa* with ten [fingers], he pours it down. Because the drawing of the Āśvina cup serves a very minor purpose, the pouring out is likewise minimal. Since the pouring from the Ādhavanīya vessel is to be prescribed immediately before the lifting of the *camasa*s, it is understood that this pouring serves solely the purpose of drawing the Āśvina cup.
Thereafter, one pours into the Pūtabhṛt vessel only across the filter (*tiraḥpavitra*).

Having wiped the *ādhavanīya* and *pūtabhṛt* vessels with the fringes [of the filter] and having poured [the soma] into the jar, he pours [it] down here. Now, if this is so, then even in that case [of the *āghāra*], one should simply say "across the filter" (*tiraḥpavitram*). Since the meaning is already established by that, for what purpose is a heavy sūtra composed for its own sake?

If it is argued that [the ritual procedure] for the Mādhyandina-savana and the Tṛtīya-savana is explained by the Prātaḥsavana—[that is,] since the Mādhyandina-savana is established by the very extension (*atideśa*) from the Prātaḥsavana as stated in Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra (Book 8), and since the [procedure] for the Tṛtīya-savana is explained by the Mādhyandina-savana, [one might conclude] that there is no need for a separate extension from the Mādhyandina-savana; we say no, because the extension from the Mādhyandina-savana is not established in the same way as the extension from the Prātaḥsavana.

This is because the pouring from the *pūtabhṛt* [vessel] into another vessel across the *pavitra* [filter] is meaningful, as it serves to indicate that the state of being purified (*pavitratā*) is not required [for the Soma already in the *pūtabhṛt*]. If it is argued that, in that case, the designation "purified" (*pūtabhṛt*) for the *pūtabhṛt* would be untenable, we reply: we do not say that unpurified Soma is poured [into the *pūtabhṛt*], which would make this designation untenable; rather, a portion of the Soma from the *āghāra* vessel is poured into another vessel across the *pavitra*.

"Let him pour out that purified Soma with that same vessel while the strainer is still not removed; thus we say he pours it out as if for the *pūtabhṛt* [purified-holder] vessel. In this way, the Sūtra becomes purposeful, and the designation *pūtabhṛt* is also not untenable; thus all is well.
He draws the *pavamāna* cups.

The cups of the *pavamāna* are the *pavamānagrahas*. These will be described in the subsequent sūtra; the meaning is that one takes them. Furthermore, this technical designation is for the sake of clear understanding in such passages as, "Having worshipped the *pavamāna* cups, the *kalaśas*, the *śukra* and *manthin*, the *āgrayaṇa*, and the *ukthya* with the *grahāvakāśa* formulas. The compound is precisely of the form: "the cups of the *pavamāna*," namely *pavamānagrahāḥ*.

Having drawn the *pavamāna* cups, the fault in performing the *upākaraṇa* (preliminary rite) for the *pavamāna* is demonstrated in the Brāhmaṇa: "The *pavamāna* cups are drawn; now, if one were to perform the *upākaraṇa* for the *pavamāna* without having drawn those [cups]—namely, the *droṇakalaśa*, the *ādhavanīya*, and the *pūtabhṛt*—he would cut off the *pavamāna*. As it is being cut off, the breath (*prāṇa*) of the Adhvaryu would follow and be cut off. [The Adhvaryu] should touch the *droṇakalaśa* with the formula: "Thou art taken with a base; for Prajāpati, thee! the *ādhavanīya* with: "For Indra, thee! and the *pūtabhṛt* with: "For the All-gods, thee!"

The phrase "held with a support" (*upayāmagṛhīto 'si*) also follows for the two subsequent [verses]. Thus Āpastamba clearly states: "All [the cups] have supports at the beginning. The meaning is that the term "support" (*upayāma*) is to be supplied for the two subsequent verses just as it was for the first. By means of these mantras, the mere touching (*abhimarśana*) constitutes the "taking" (*grahaṇa*) here; for this very reason, there is no "placing" (*sādana*) either. When touching is performed with these [mantras], the two previously mentioned defects do not occur, and furthermore, the attainment of the animal's vital breath (*prāṇa*) is secured.

And so says the Brāhmaṇa: "With 'Thou art taken with a support; for Prajāpati, svāhā! he should touch the Droṇakalaśa; with 'For Indra, thee! the Ādhavanīya; with 'For the Viśve Devas, thee! the Pūtabhṛt. Thus he extends the Pavamāna [libation], attains a full lifespan, does not die before his time, becomes possessed of cattle, and obtains offspring. Some say that there is no wiping (of the vessels) because they are drawn from a continuous stream (*adhārāgraha*). That is not correct, because it would contradict the inclusion of the word "all" in the rule: "There is wiping of all the cups" (*sarvagrahāṇām parimārjanam*). As they go out, they hold onto one another. (11)

In this context, the prefix *niḥ* has the sense of "outward" with respect to an external object; thus, the meaning becomes "moving outwards," that is, from the *havirdhāna* (the oblation-holder). The suffix *-śatṛ* in the word *niḥsarpantaḥ* ("moving out") indicates that the act of taking hold (*samanvārambha*) occurs at the time when they are in the process of moving out. This taking hold is performed sequentially and not all at once, because it is impossible to do so simultaneously. Furthermore, the term "moving out" (*niḥsarpantaḥ*) is a qualification of the *prastotṛ* and the other priests, but it does not apply to the *adhvaryu*, since there is no one else for him to take hold of.

The prefix *sam-* implies inclusion; as in the case of "one who has been seized" (*samanvārabdha*), it means that among those who have been seized, there should be no interruption. This is from the *Paṭala* [of the ritual manual], accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

For it is heard in the scriptures regarding the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) that: "If the Udgātṛ should lose his connection while they are proceeding together, the sacrificer would be deprived of the sacrifice; that sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*) is to be concluded without a sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇa*), and another [rite] is to be undertaken. Whatever he intended to give in the previous [rite], he should give that here. The priests (*ṛtvij*) should perform the sacrifice for him. Since no specific expiation is mentioned for the loss of connection by the Brahman or the sacrificer, there is only the general expiation consisting of the *anudravaṇa* and the *yajñatanū-homa*.
Thus, even in these two cases, there must be a proper holding of the connection.

The Prastotṛ takes hold of the Adhvaryu; the Pratihartṛ, the Prastotṛ; the Udgātṛ, the Pratihartṛ; the Brahmā, the Udgātṛ; and the sacrificer, the Brahmā—according to some, the sacrificer [takes hold of] the Brahmā.

In the preceding sūtra, it was stated generally that "they take hold [of one another]"; this present sūtra is intended to address the inquiry as to who exactly takes hold. Now, an objection may be raised: since it is established by the very use of the pronoun *tat* (him) that the Prastotṛ takes hold of the Adhvaryu, the Pratihartṛ of him, the Udgātṛ of him, the Brahman of him, and the sacrificer of him—according to some authorities even the Brahman of the sacrificer—a further specification is redundant. This is not redundant.

If it is argued that, since the word *tat* (that) is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) and thus primarily refers to what is proximate, it might—by taking its primary sense as referring to what is mentioned immediately—refer to the Adhvaryu alone, and therefore a further specification is necessary to exclude that possibility, [the answer is] no; for this can be accomplished by a concise sūtra such as: "The Adhvaryu, Prastotṛ, Pratihartṛ, Udgātṛ, Brahman, and Yajamāna touch him."

If it is argued that once the reference to the *adhvaryu* is established, the repetition of the instruction is unnecessary, and thus its redundancy remains as before—this is true. Nevertheless, if that were the case, the *anvārambha* (the act of touching) would occur even at a single time; since the repetition is required to prevent this, it is not redundant. Thus, it is well-established that the repetition of the instruction is indeed necessary to exclude the reference to the *adhvaryu*.

The sequence stated by the *Chandogas* is as follows: "The *Prastotṛ* should join the *Adhvaryu* as he goes out; the *Udgātṛ* [should join] that *Udgātṛ*; the *Pratihartṛ* [should join] that [Udgātṛ]; the *Brahman* [should join] that [Pratihartṛ]; and the sacrificer [should join] that *Brahman*. According to the statement of *Āśvalāyana*, "the *Maitrāvaruṇa* and the *Brahman* are always [to follow] behind the *Chandogas*," the *Praśāstṛ* is also excluded. Furthermore, the statement "he takes hold again" (*punaranvārabhate*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Alternatively, this statement is intended to indicate that it is an independent injunction (*svatantra-vidhi*), namely: "those going out together should take hold of one another."

To satisfy the expectation of "whom do they follow? the remainder [of the sentence] is "those connected with the *pavamāna*. Thus, the sequence stated by the *Chandogas* is obtained, and the *Praśāstṛ* is also included in the *sarpaṇa* (creeping). And he comes after the *Chandogas*, according to the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra*: "The *Maitrāvaruṇa* and the *Brahman* always follow behind the *Chandogas*. However, the sequence mentioned in the subsequent *sūtra* is intended as an independent alternative view.

For this very reason, the different expression "merely takes hold" (*kevalam anvārabhate*) has been employed. Even in this alternative (*kalpa*), there is indeed firmness in the taking hold (*anvārambha*), because an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed for its failure. In both alternatives, the taking hold is performed with the right hand alone; for the taking hold is primary due to being the first to present itself, and it is logical that the primary [hand] should have a connection with the primary [right] hand. That taking hold in which there is firmness is of two kinds: qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) or simple (*kevala*).

If the commencement of the *anvārambha* (touching) intended is indeed performed with the right hand, then it is a qualified *anvārambha*. If this *anvārambha* is accepted, the oblation for the purpose of moving forward (*sarpaṇa*) is performed with the left hand alone. However, if the mere *anvārambha* is accepted, then because the *anvārambha* for the first movement is present at the outset and is thus primary, it is performed with the primary right hand.

Having merely touched [the sacrificer] with the hand at the time of the oblation, while the right hand maintains its contact, one should firmly touch him again with the left hand; then, releasing the contact made by the right hand, one performs the *homa* for the purpose of moving forward (*sarpaṇa*) using only the right hand. When the contact is maintained by the left hand, one should again firmly touch him with the right hand, release the contact of the left hand, and recite "The path of the Gāyatrī," and so forth. This first alternative is thus easily understood.

In both cases, one must act with great care so that no deficiency occurs. In this regard, the right hand holds primacy, according to the statement of Āśvalāyana: "When a single limb is mentioned, one should understand the right [limb] in the absence of a specific instruction.
Where an action is prescribed for the performer but the [specific] limb is not stated, the right hand should be understood there as the one that brings the rites to completion.

And so it is stated in the *Chāndogya-pariśiṣṭa*: "When it is said, 'The sacrificer [is] the Brahman,' or 'the opposite,' there would be a reversal for everyone; lest that happen, for this reason the statement 'some say the sacrificer is the Brahman' is made.

Having stepped out and offered the drops with the verses, "Thy drop which falls," "Thy drop which falls," "Thy stalk, and that which is beyond, and that which is in heaven, before"—"may this god Bṛhaspati pour that together as wealth"—and having offered the Vaipruṣa oblations and the Saptahotṛ formula, they proceed toward the north, bowing low, for the *Bahiṣpavamāna* chant.

The expression "having crept out" (*niḥsṛpya*) is for the purpose of indicating the absence of any temporal interval. By this, the *homa* prescribed in their own *sūtra* must be performed by the *udgātṛ*s first, and not in the middle. It is also for the sake of establishing a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). Therefore, those who are the agents of the creeping out (*niḥsarpaṇa*) are the same as the agents of the *vaiṣasaptahotṛ-homa*, and they are also the agents of the *tarpaṇa* for the sake of the *bahiṣpavamāna*. The word "three" (*tisraḥ*) is for the purpose of grasping the mantras; the feminine gender is specified to indicate the number. There are three mantras ending with the word *juhomi*.

The fourth [section] is from the Sūtra. Immediately after "vaipuṣān," the word "homān" (oblations) is to be supplied as the remainder. These four oblations named *vaiḍghaṣā* are for the purpose of making good (*devatrākaraṇa*) the spilled *vaipuṣa* [portions]. Because it serves the purpose of an oblation here, the *saptahotṛ* formula is included along with its *graha*. Since there is no statement saying "having recited mentally," the *savana-svara* (the accent of the pressing) alone is used here. However, Āpastamba has read "having recited mentally" even in this instance. In the word *saptahotāram*, the letter *gha* should be regarded as a corruption.

Because of the grammatical connection in the phrase "having offered, they glide forward" (*hutvā sarpanti*), the *homa* (oblation) must be performed by all [the priests] alike. By this, one should understand that the alternative view stated by Kātyāyana—that the *vainuṣān-homas* are performed by the Adhvaryu—is refuted. In the case where the Maitrāvaruṇa also glides forward, his procedure is likewise the same. When the sacrificer belongs to the Sāma-veda branch, the *homa* must be performed by the Udgātṛs and the Brahman according to the method prescribed in their own *sūtras*, and not even according to the method prescribed in the *sūtra* of the Adhvaryu.

When the sacrificer belongs to the *Kṣākhin* branch, the oblation (*homa*) must be performed by the Brahman and the Udgātṛs according to the procedure prescribed in their own *Sūtra*. Even in the case of the *Maitrāvaruṇa-tarpaṇa* (the feeding of the Maitrāvaruṇa), it should be done by him in that same manner and not even according to the procedure prescribed in the *Adhvaryu-sūtra*. When a sacrificer belonging to either the Sāmavedic or the Ṛgvedic branch performs the rite according to the *Satyāṣāḍha-sūtra*, the two oblations must be performed by the Udgātṛ, the Brahman, the sacrificer, and the Maitrāvaruṇa. However, by the Adhvaryu, [it is performed] in all cases... [text fragment].

It should be understood that this is according to the procedure stated in the *Adhvaryu-sūtra*. "Facing north" (*udañcaḥ*) means facing the north. By the word "gliding" (*pralāya*), the gliding movement without recitation is indicated. The phrase "for the sake of the *bahiṣpavamāna*" is for the purpose of showing the objective; by this, it is understood that the holding-on (*anvārambha*) continues until the sitting down for the sake of the *bahiṣpavamāna* stotra.

The *bahippavamāna* is so called because it is chanted outside (*bahiḥ*) while the *pavamāna* [laud] is being praised; or alternatively, it is called *bahippavamāna* because it purifies even those who have gone to an external state (*bahir-bahir-bhāva*). Regarding the specific manner of their crawling, Āpastamba says: "They crawl with their heads bent down, as if gliding, as if creeping; they move like hunters pursuing a deer, for the sacrifice is indeed like a deer. Thus, they proceed as if moving stealthily, as if going by way of concealment.

Likewise, they were as if hissing with their tongues protruding, and with heads bowed down, they were like hunters desiring to see a deer. Here, the hunters are the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are the object of comparison (*upameya*). Similarly, the deer is the standard of comparison and the sacrifice (*yajña*) is the object of comparison. The Brāhmaṇa scripture records the sacrificial nature of the sacrifice: "The sacrifice fled from the gods, having assumed the form of a black [antelope]. A black antelope is a deer.

"The Gāyatra is the path; the Vasus are the deity. By way of the wolf, the one that does not stray from the path, may I safely reach the Vasus. Let Speech go first, going straight. Saying this, the Adhvaryu creeps forward first, slightly shaking a handful of sacrificial grass (barhis).

The status of the two mantras as the instrument (*karaṇatva*) is based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*). In the phrase *pūrvaḥ pūrvasmin*, the word *pūrvaḥ* [is formed] by the substitution of *mu* for the locative case ending according to the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*. The term "place" (*pradeśa*) should be understood here as the substantive (*viśeṣya*) by virtue of its suitability. From the mention of "grasping with the fist," the binding of the reins is understood. The expression "as it were" (*īṣadiva*) means "slightly similar. By this, the intermediate state during the shaking is indicated. Through the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) in the word *vidhunvan*, the simultaneity of the shaking and the gliding is expressed. The mind also [proceeds] along the very same path.

In this context, the mention of the *adhvaryu* is for the purpose of clarifying the following explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "The *adhvaryu* is the first to be yoked; therefore they say the *stoma* must be yoked by him. 'Let the straight-moving [horse] go in front, bestowing glory upon me from the gods, and entering into my vital breaths and those of the cattle and myself, the sacrificer,' he says; thus he yokes speech at the mouth of the sacrifice. Indeed, a structural flaw (*vāstu*) is created in the sacrifice when they proceed to the *bahispavamāna* chant without having drawn the cups."

By the word "previously" (*pūrva*), in accordance with the requirement for uninterrupted contact during the following-up (*anvārambha*), he goes three or four steps forward to the east, at the very beginning. This moving forward (*sarpaṇa*) belongs to the Adhvaryu alone because of the singular number [in the mantra]; the mantra also belongs to him alone because it is connected to the act of moving forward. Then all of them go toward the north. The end of the mantra is "and the sacrificer. Having sat down to the south of the *cātvāla* pit and looking at the *cātvāla* from within the altar, they chant the *bahis-pavamāna* hymn. Having sat down to the south of the *cātvāla* and looking at the *cātvāla* from within the altar, they chant the *bahis-pavamāna* hymn.

And thus the meaning is as follows: having first sat down in accordance with the proximity of the *cātvāla*, afterwards all [the priests] should be there; this is the sense. If the three steps consisting of the *prakrama* were to the north of the site of the *uttaravedi*, then this [interpretation] should be seen as purposeful. Nor should it be asked why the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is not made in this way: "Having sat down to the south of the *cātvāla*, looking toward the *cātvāla*, they chant the *bahiṣpavamāna*. This is because of the suffix *-tva* in the subsequent sentence.

This is because it would result in a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*). To explain: the act of seating pertains to all [the chanters], whereas the praise pertains only to the *udgātṛ*. Thus, since not all those seated are performers of the praise, there would be a lack of connection. Nor should it be argued that the act of seating pertains only to the *udgātṛ*; for that would entail the impossibility of the others being seated. Therefore, the aforementioned method alone is correct.

By the use of the present participle *avekṣamāṇāḥ* ("looking at"), the simultaneity of the looking at the *cātvāla* pit and the chanting of the *bahiṣpavamāna* is established. By this, the Chāndoga recension’s reading "looking at the junction of heaven and earth" (*dyāvāpṛthivyoḥ saṃdhim īkṣamāṇāḥ*) is excluded. After the word *stuvate* ("they chant"), the word *udgātāraḥ* ("the Udgātṛ priests") is to be supplied as the subject. There is no following along (*anvārambha*) after the sitting down; in a *sattra* sacrifice, because all are sacrificers (*yajamāna*), there is no dispersal (*avisarpaṇa*) of the Hotṛ and other officiants.

In this matter, the position that "the *brahmán* is the sacrificer" (*yajamānaṃ brahmā*) alone must be adopted, in order to maintain consistency with the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra*, which states: "The *maitrāvaruṇa* and the *brahmán* always recite the *anuvākyās*; between these two, the others undergo initiation. It should not be argued that the *hotṛ*'s *sarpaṇa* (creeping) does not take place because of the *Dvādaśāha-sūtra* rule stating, "All [officiants] should perform the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) provided they do not conflict with their priestly duties (*ārtvijya*)," for there is a contradiction between that [creeping] and the priestly duty consisting of the *hotṛ*'s sitting within the *havirdhāna* shed.

If, however, the Hotṛ himself should be the sacrificer, [the rule] "he should go up to the seat" applies; for there is a Brāhmaṇa text stating this, according to Āpastamba. Because of that specific injunction, the general rule is set aside. Regarding the statement "the officiating function (ārtvijya) is stronger when there is a conflict," one should look to the general Sūtra of the Āpastambīya twelve-day sacrifice which provides that specific rule. In other cases, the inclusion occurs precisely between the Chandoga and the Brāhmaṇa.

According to the Āśvalāyana-sūtra—"After the Chandogas, the Maitrāvaruṇa and the Brahman are constant; between those two, the other initiated priests [are seated]"—the order among the others follows their primary and secondary status. Even there, although the Maitrāvaruṇa is secondary in relation to the Hotṛ, his position immediately after the Chandogas belongs to him alone, as per the Āśvalāyana-sūtra: "After the Chandogas, the Maitrāvaruṇa and the Brahman are constant; between those two, the other initiated priests [are seated]."

The others follow after the Maitrāvaruṇa. Their sequence is as follows: the Hotṛ [addresses] the Maitrāvaruṇa; the Pratiprasthātṛ [addresses] the Hotṛ; the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin [addresses] the Pratiprasthātṛ; the Acchāvāka [addresses] the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; the Neṣṭṛ [addresses] the Acchāvāka; the Āgnīdhra [addresses] the Neṣṭṛ; the Grāvastut [addresses] the Āgnīdhra; the Unnetṛ [addresses] the Grāvastut; the Potṛ [addresses] the Unnetṛ; the Subrahmaṇya [addresses] the Potṛ; and the Gṛhapati [addresses] the Subrahmaṇya—the Gṛhapati being the sacrificer (yajamāna). Thus he addresses the Gṛhapati, the sacrificer.

The householder sacrificer [offers] to Mitra and Varuṇa; the householder sacrificer [is] the Hotṛ. It should be understood that the Sadasya is not included here, as he has been specifically enumerated elsewhere in the Sūtra for the Sattra.

Saying, "Vāyu is indeed the doer," while handing a handful of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) to the Prastotṛ, he introduces the Stotra with the formula: "Speech has been released, speech has been released; Indra’s power has been released. Return, O priests! Approach, O Sacrificer!"

He gives the fist held in his hand to the *prastotṛ*. While giving it, he begins the *stotra*. By the use of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) in the word "giving" (*prayacchan*), the simultaneity of the handing over of the fist and the commencement of the *stotra* is established. "He begins" (*upākaroti*) means he initiates it. Vāyu asks: "Is the mantra for handing over the fist outside [the cart]? Indeed, the commencement of the *stotra* occurs at the very same time as the handing over of the fist outside; or rather, since Vāyu is the agent, the mantra belongs specifically to the commencement of the *stotra*.

The offering of the outer handful is indeed silent. At the very moment of that offering, the commencement of the Stotra is with the words "vāyavyai te. "Asaj saṃbhāti" is the second mantra for the commencement itself. Thus it is established that the commencement is performed by means of these two mantras. This mantra "upāgarta dhvam" is also for the purpose of commencement and is added to all Pavamāna chants. [End of] Paṭala 410, accompanied by the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa.

Immediately after "upāvartadhvam," the word *iti* is to be supplied. Immediately after "abhisarpa yajamāna iti," the phrase *saṃpreṣyatīti* is to be supplied. This *praiṣa* (directive) ending with "upāvartadhvam" belongs to the *udgātṛ*s for the purpose of commencing the *stotra*. "Abhisarpa yajamāna" is the directive addressed to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). "Upāvartadhvam" means "turn toward [us]," that is, turn near to us and face us in order to praise.

The meaning is that, being seated nearby (*upa-samīpe*), you should "take hold of" (*anvārabhadhvam*) the *mahīpavamāna* chant; or rather, O sacrificers, come forward toward the Udgātṛs for the purpose of chanting the *praṇava*. By this it is known that even after the release from the "taking-hold" (*anvārambhavisarga*), wherever a further "taking-hold" occurs, the sacrificer should remain seated right there until the final command (*praiṣa*).
This applies to all *pavamāna* chants in this manner.

The meaning is: "in the manner beginning with 'O Pavamānas, carry [the sacrifice] thus' and ending with 'approach, O sacrificer. By this it is known that in the other *stotras*, the *upagāna* (choral response) must be performed by the sacrificer while seated in his own place.
With the words "turn hither," the other *stotras* are addressed by means of the two *barhis* blades.

The term *upādhyam* indicates the end [of the formula]. By this, everything beginning with "vāyur hi kartā" (for Vāyu is the agent) occurs. Through this, the exclusion of the portion beginning with *amita panamāna* is established. Alternatively, the dedication (*upākaraṇa*) consists merely of the words *upāvartadhvam*. In this view, there is a suspension of the portion ending with *vāyur hi kartā*, and also the suspension of the part ending with *asapatna indrasaho 'si*. However, the suspension of the phrase *abhisarpa yajamāna* remains here as well. The word *bahiḥ* is for the purpose of preventing the grasping of a handful [of grass] from outside.

The remaining *bhājyā* verses, the *pṛṣṭha* chants, and the stotras beginning with the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* and the *ṣoḍaśin*, he introduces; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. During the *bahiṣpavamāna* chanting performed by the *udgātṛ*s, the *upagātṛ*s must perform the *upagāna* (accompaniment). Thus says the Śruti: "Neither the Adhvaryu nor the Brahman should perform the *upagāna*; if the Adhvaryu were to perform the *upagāna*, he would hand over his speech to the Udgātṛ, and his speech would become liable to fail. Since there is a prohibition of *upagāna* for these two, it follows that the *upagāna* exists and is performed solely by the chanters (*ṛtvij*s).

Āpastamba clearly states the number of those who join in the singing (*upagātṛ*): "While [the Sāman] is being chanted, the sacrificer joins in the singing; there are four or more singers, but not the Adhvaryu. This means that while the *bahiṣpavamāna* is being chanted, the sacrificer first joins in the singing, and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) also join in, provided they are four or more in number. Since the priests would otherwise have the status of singers without distinction from the Adhvaryu, leading to the possibility of the Adhvaryu also performing the singing, the rule "not [the Adhvaryu]" serves as a prohibition. [This concludes the section on] the manner of joining in the singing.

Bharadvāja said: "Five, including the sacrificer, sing along; the priests sing 'Ho! and the sacrificer sings 'Om'. In the seventh section of the third chapter, Jaimini also states: "And the singers [are those other than the Adhvaryu], because of the observation of indicative marks. The meaning of the sūtra is that the prohibition—"the Adhvaryu should not sing along"—would be untenable if there were no prior application [of the practice]; therefore, it indicates that those other than the Adhvaryu are the ones who sing along. The word "and" (ca) serves to draw in the sense of the statement, "others do not shine."

Some Chāndogas state the opposite: "The sacrificer says 'Om,' and the priests [respond]" (iti yajamāna omityṛtvija iti). According to another Sūtra, which prohibits those other than the Adhvaryu group from singing along (*upagāyeyuḥ*), the *upagātṛ*s (accompanying singers) are those distinct from the Adhvaryu group. However, in the Uttara-mīmāṃsā, in the section on the "Inclusion of Qualities" (*guṇopasaṃhāra-pāda*), the statement that "the priests sing along" (*ṛtvija upagāyanti*) has been cited as an example.

Regarding the manner of accompanying, the Chāndoga-sūtra states: "The accompanying singers, at least four in number—some being more, even up to six—should sing along with the syllable 'Hāṃ' in a low tone, standing behind the Udgātṛ at a distance of less than half [the space]."

In the phrase "those who approach according to the purpose of the *bhadram*," the word "upagās" (those who sing along) is required. [From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Eighth Book: "They begin together with the continuous recitation. The meaning of this is as follows: behind the *udgātṛ*s, that is, in the western part near the *udgātṛ*s, those whose lowest portion consists of three are called "three-lowest-portioned" (*tryavarārdhāḥ*). "Upagās" means those who sing along (*upagātāraḥ*). One teacher maintains that the "upagās" consist of those who have four as their lowest portion. By the term "six-higher-portioned" (*ṣaṭparārdhāḥ*), the limit for the number of participants is indicated.

If they [the singers] are half of my [number], or a quarter, or six parārdhas—that is the meaning—then by means of this syllable (akṣara) which is about to be mentioned, they should chant along with it. He states that syllable as "ho. They should chant with the syllable "ho" in a low tone (*mandrasvara*), continuously and without interruption. They should begin at the *nidhanas* (concluding phrases) which are to be uttered together; there is also a pause (*ārama*) within the *nidhanas*. The extracted meaning is: they should chant while filling the intervals between the *prastāva* and other divisions with this syllable.

The *upagāna* (accompaniment) of the sacrificer is likewise exactly the same. There is no *upagāna* prior to the *nidhana*, because there is no interruption [of the chant]. This applies to all *stotras*.
While the *bahiṣpavamāna* is being chanted, the Brāhmaṇas approach it from all sides; they drive away the one whom they hate. || 12 ||
Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the eighth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

While the *bahiṣpavamāna* is being chanted, the Brāhmaṇas, having assembled together, approach facing [the singers]; that is to say, they sit down near the *gātṛ*s (singers). This approaching (*sarpaṇa*) is for the sake of purification. And so says the Śruti: "Therefore, one who knows this should approach the *bahiṣpavamāna*; the *bahiṣpavamāna* is indeed a purifier; he thus beholds his own self. By the use of the present participle (*stūyamānam*), contemporaneity is indicated. Thus, [they sit] near the singers at the same time as the chanting.

It follows that "sitting down" (upaveśana) is established. And that [sitting] occurs either at the very beginning or immediately after the first section (prastāva), because it is what presents itself [first]. However, even if sitting down in close proximity does not occur until that point, the hearing [of the mantra] takes place only at such a distance that hearing would occur for those who are seated; it does not take place at such a distance that hearing would not occur for those who are seated.

Otherwise, it should be understood that the fruit—consisting of the removal of all external impurity as taught by the Veda and produced by hearing [this mantra]—would not come to pass. Some authorities have stated that if the chanters (udgātṛs) perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) with water drawn from a well for the sake of destroying all sins, it is equal to the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. He says "the hateful one" to show that it serves not only the purpose of destroying sin, but also has the result of overcoming those who are hostile.

"Parisādhante" means he becomes hateful; "paribādhanam" refers to his harassment and oppression. Thus ends the eighth [chapter] in the commentary named *Jyotsnā*, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—the son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was the author of the *Śrīmad-Bhagavat-Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra-vṛtti*—which, like the moonlight, assuages the distress of learned men caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the ocean [of the Sūtras].

While rising after the chanting has been performed,

"Make the offering!"—this is the *praisha* (direction) addressed to the *Āgnīdhra*. "O Pratiprasthātṛ, come with the animal; come, O Bhāgachit!"—in the expression "come with the animal," the *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form) applies according to Pāṇini 6.1.94 (*omāṅośca*). By the word "stuta" (praised), the time for the *praisha* is indicated. With the words "having risen" (*utthāya*), the simultaneity of the rising and the *praisha* is shown, but not a relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgin*) between the rising and the mantra. Therefore, it is understood that the performance of the ritual act does not coincide with the end of the mantra.

Likewise, Jaimini also states in the third chapter, second quarter, by the ninth sūtra, "so also in the releasing of speech" (*tathā tyāna-visarjane*). The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: in the injunctions "rising, arrange the fires" and "utter the word 'do' [O priests]," the connection in both cases is solely for the purpose of time, and not for the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅga*) or a benediction (*āśīḥ*). The word "likewise" (*tathā*) indicates that the same applies to the invocation (*āhvāna*); it serves to carry forward the sense of the previous section—that the connection is for the purpose of time.
Having entered the *havirdhāna* shed, he worships the cups with the mantra "O Viṣṇu, you are our nearest" and touches the vessels.

Since no specific distinction is made as to whether it is "from the east" or "from the west," entry is by either door. Exit is by the very same door through which one entered. Entry here may also be through a window, as there is extreme proximity to the door; this is because the word "door" was not explicitly used. Regarding the cups (*graha*)—the Soma juices drawn for Indra-Vāyu and others—the cups of the *pavamāna* [laud] are also included here. As for the claim that "the vessels are those which hold the Soma, and only those that are not empty [are meant]," that is incorrect.

This is because it contradicts the remainder of the sentence: "that which dries up while he is lying down. The word *ca* (and) serves to draw in the mantra. From the word *saṃ*, there is contact with the palm of the hand; the mantras apply to the cavities of the vessels by way of their function. "*Akṣitam*" is the end of the mantra.

This is the fruit: they go away from the Brahmin with [verses] directed away; they praise with [verses] directed away; then he returns and stands near the Vaiṣṇavyā [verse]. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; thus he draws the sacrifice toward himself. "Thou art our nearest one, O mighty one, grant us the highest [blessing]; thy streams, dripping with honey, milk out the imperishable," he says. "Whatever of this [Soma] that lies down has dried up, that very part of it he causes to swell by means of this [verse]. Soma that has remained in the vessel for a long time is called "lying down" (*śayāna*).
Having brought embers from the Āgnīdhrīya fire, the Āgnīdhra priest distributes them over the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths according to the same formulas as when they were originally scattered.

The coals, free from smoke, consisting of portions of the fire-wood, and sufficient for the purpose of distributing [the fires] to all the hearths (*dhiṣṇiya*), are taken up in the heating-vessel (*tāpātra*). Having taken them up, he pours them out upon the hearths with those very same mantras used for the pouring out of the hearths. The phrase "as poured" (*yathānyuptam*) means "exactly as poured," that is, not exceeding what was poured; it is used to indicate that just as it was in the case of the pouring out (*nivapana*), so it is also in the case of the distribution (*viharaṇa*). Here, the expression "as poured" is required.

1ka, ga. *śrāntaka*; 2 ka, ga, pa. *paṃkṛtvā*. 1. [This is] the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the eighth section]: By this, the necessity of moving [the fires] to each respective hearth (*dhiṣṇya*) is established. By this, the optionality [of the movement] is excluded. He moves the *dhiṣṇya* fires; that is, he establishes them in their respective places. One does not move [the fire] to the Āhavanīya, because of the occurrence of the fault of contact with the fire.

The Āgnīdhra should silently take embers from the Āgnīdhra hearth and, having placed one portion with the mantra "Thou art pervasive" (vibhūr asi), place it on the Hotṛ’s hearth with the mantra "Thou art the bearer" (vahas i). To avoid the fault of interruption, he should carry them together along the north of the Āgnīdhra hearth, passing between the sacrificial posts while carrying the portions, and having gone to the front of the post, [he should place them] to the south.

Having approached the Mānīḍīya hearth from this side, he should deposit [the grains] near the Praśāstṛ’s hearth with the mantra "Thou art auspicious" (*śvātro 'si*). Having returned by the same way he came, he should deposit them at each of the hearths beginning with that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin and ending with that of the Acchāvāka, using their respective mantras. Having gone back to the Mānīḍīya hearth as before, he should deposit all [the grains] upon the Mānīḍīya with the mantra "Thou art pure" (*śundhyur asi*). There is an option between facing westward or facing northward, just as in the case of the pouring out (*nivapana*). The kindling of all the fires of the hearths is for the purpose of the sprinkling (*vyāghāraṇa*).

Because it is stated that they "hold" [the grains] during the third *savana*—as indicated by the term *dhāraṇa* (holding)—it is understood that there is no fault even if the grains are lost after being held during the other two *savanas*. By the phrase "just as they were sown," it is also understood that the spreading [of the fire-altar] occurs only upon the dust-hearths (*pāṃsudhiṣṇiya*), and not upon those designated for other purposes, such as the *vahippavamāna-stotra* and so forth. Thus says Āpastamba: "He scatters [the grains] upon the dust-hearths; thereby they become 'sown according to their order' (*yathānyupta*)."

The statement "with those very same mantras" is for the purpose of excluding silence (*tūṣṇīkatva*). The mention of the *Āgnīdhra* is for the purpose of excluding the *Adhvaryu*. In this case, the application of the mantras—similar to that at the *raudrānīka*—is optional (*kṛtākṛta*), because there is no specific scriptural injunction to the contrary.

Having taken the King Soma into the fourfold cup (*catuścamasa*) and the fivefold-oblation (*pañcagṛhīta*) of clarified butter, the Adhvaryu, sitting facing west in front [of the hearths], sprinkles the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths with those same mantras, according to how they were previously assigned.

The mention of the *adhvaryu* is for the purpose of excluding others. "Four by four" means that eleven cups are to be filled in the *camasa*. It is called a *camasa* because it is the means of drinking. In the phrase "and the five-fold taken ghee," the word "and" (*ca*) signifies simultaneity; thus, it is established that the fetching of both must be performed by the *adhvaryu* alone. Following the word "ghee" (*ājya*), the term "taken" (*gṛhīta*) is understood. The taking of the King [Soma] into the *camasa* is done with the *pariplava* ladle.

The taking of the clarified butter (*ājya*) is performed with the *pracaraṇī* ladle—the one with which the *kratukaraṇa* oblation was offered—not with the one intended for the southern oblations. Regarding this, the very indicator has already been stated in the sūtra: "He first employs the *pracaraṇī* and the *kūrca*. Sitting down—that is, seated—in front of the *dhiṣṇya* hearths, facing westward, he establishes the *viṣṇiya* fires in that same sequence as the shaving of the hair. Here, because of the mention of "sitting," it is understood that in another alternative, he may also be standing during the ritual arrangement (*viharaṇa*).

The statement "behind" (*parastāt*) is intended to exclude sitting on the right side of the *dhiṣṇya* altar facing east. The statement "facing west" (*pratyak*) is intended to exclude the lack of a fixed rule regarding facing west during the ritual distribution (*viharaṇa*); by this, facing north also occurs as an alternative during the distribution. The statement "with those very same mantras" is for the purpose of excluding the silent (*tūṣṇīka*) option mentioned by Āpastamba. Here too, the addition of the mantras used for the *raudrānīka* [rite] is optional, as there is no specific injunction; however, in the final mantra, [the word] "Bhava" [is used].

Because it is recited thus in the Śruti. Here, the restriction (*niyama*) is twofold: "by those [verses] alone" and "by those mantras alone. In the first restriction, the result is the exclusion of other optional mantras mentioned by Baudhāyana, such as *pravāhaṇāya svāhā* and so forth; this is the meaning of the word "only" (*eva*). In the second [restriction], the result is the exclusion of silence (*tūṣṇīkatva*) as prescribed by Āpastamba. Since it is enjoined by the term "supporting" (*vyādhāraṇa*), it does not possess the characteristics of a *parihoma*. [End of] Chapter 150, accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Mahāmahopādhyāya.

In this case, the *rājā* (king Soma) is to be taken from either the *droṇakalaśa*, the *ādhavanīya*, or the *pūtabhṛt* vessel, because there is no specific rule [to the contrary]. If the taking of the *rājā* from the *droṇakalaśa* alone had been intended, then Āpastamba would have stated "the *rājā* from the *droṇakalaśa* with a ladle," just as he stated elsewhere regarding the taking of Soma from the *droṇakalaśa* for the purpose of the *āghāra* libation—namely, "O Gods, may this sacrifice (*adhvara*) be [successful]! Since he did not say that here, there is no fixed rule.
However, Āpastamba states that in this instance, the Soma is to be taken specifically from the *droṇakalaśa* for the purpose of the sprinkling (*vyāghāraṇa*).

One pours the *soma* upon the Āhavanīya, the Āgnīdhrīya, the Hotrīya, and the Mārjālīya fires; the others with clarified butter (*ājya*). This distinction regarding the *soma* applies to those [fires] for which it is intended, but it is not a restriction on the order of the pouring itself. For the sequence of the ritual action is already established by the rule: "He pours over the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths. Therefore, following the order of the scattering, one pours over the Āhavanīya, Āgnīdhrīya, and Hotrīya first, and subsequently from the Praśāstrīya up to the Mānolīya. The Uttaravedi is the location of the Āhavanīya; because it was scattered first, the pouring over the Āhavanīya takes place first. With clarified butter means with the butter contained in the *pracaraṇī* ladle.

"By means of the *pravaraṇa* [invitation], he passes over the others—the *praśāstṛ*-related and those belonging to the *acchāvāka*, namely the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths; this is the meaning. He utters the *vaṣaṭ* while passing over that *dhiṣṇiya*. Having passed over the *māna-līya dhiṣṇiya*, he approaches it slightly and then utters the *vaṣaṭ*. Some authorities transmit the *vaṣaṭ* as *vaṣaṭ*, some as *vauṣaṭ*, some as *vāpaṭ*, and some as *vāṭ*; the meaning is that among these four types of *vaṣaṭ*-utterances which will be described in the section on the *Yājuṣa-hotra*, he utters the *vaṣaṭ* with one or another of them. Alternatively, the meaning is that he utters the *vaṣaṭ* while passing over that *dhiṣṇiya*."
The consumption of the Soma has been explained.

Having entered the *sadas* by the eastern door and sat down facing east in front of the Hotṛ, he looks at [the Soma] with the mantra "O thou who art watched by men" (*nṛcakṣas*) and consumes it with "The mild one, the overcomer" (*mandrābhibhūḥ*), meaning that which was spoken by Indra. Here too, the act of smelling (or tasting) certainly takes place even in the absence of a co-consumer, because of the prohibition: "Soma must not be drunk by one who has not been invited. With "Do not harm me" (*hinna me*), he touches himself; having washed the vessel at the *mārjālīya*, he places it back in its proper place.

Since that [act] is enjoined by the word "employment" (*vyāpāraṇa*), it lacks the nature of a *homa* (oblation); therefore, this Sūtra is intended to prevent the application of the rule for eating (*bhakṣa*) which is occasioned by a *homa*.
Having strewn the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) continuously along the spine of the altar, the Āgnīdhra prepares the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*).

The word *āgnīdhra* connects with both [the preceding and following terms] according to the principle of the central gem (*madhyamaṇinyāya*). Alternatively, one might argue that it belongs to the latter, because the connection occurs first there. To refute the doubt that—since in the archetype (prakṛti) the spreading of the grass and the decoration of the sacrificial cake are performed by the Āgnīdhra priest, and this is observed here as well—the injunction here should follow suit and thus the command (*preṣa*) would serve its own purpose—it is stated that the mention of "continuous" (*saṃtata*) is for the purpose of precluding any interruption.

"Anupṛṣṭhya" means along the *pṛṣṭhya* [chant] itself. In this view, because there is an intervention by the *vaṣaṭ*-call in the midst of the many oblations, each individual oblation is indeed the cause [of the subsequent action]. Therefore, it should be understood from the Sūtra: "For every [oblation], there is a taking up and a consuming. Consequently, the rules "silently to the south" and "silently to the north" are set aside.

The mention of "outside" (*bahiḥ*) is for the purpose of excluding the spreading of dry *darbha* grass. With the mantra "Of the sacrifice you are the continuity...," one begins from the *gārhapatya* fire and proceeds as far as the site of the *āhavanīya*. Thus Āpastamba says: "With the mantra 'Of the sacrifice you are the continuity; for the continuity of the sacrifice I spread you; for the continuity of the sacrifice,' one spreads the *barhis* grass continuously along the back from the *gārhapatya* up to the *āhavanīya*. Here, even though parched grains (*dhānā*) and other items are present, the term *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake) applies [to the whole] because of the plural number.

Some desire the washing of the hands with the mantra "yāmiṣe" prior to the spreading of the outer covering. For the decoration of the roasted grains (*dhānā*), there is a modification of the mantra: "May the divine Savitṛ anoint you with honey. For the others, it is as in the archetype (*prakṛti*). The pouring of the *āmikṣā* is the decoration. Having performed the decoration, the Āgnīdhra ceases his activity.

Regarding this, Baudhāyana states the specific detail: "Then this Āgnīdhra, having sat down to the north of the Gārhapatya fire, spreads [the sacrificial grass] fivefold in the vessel; he places the *puroḍāśa* cake in the middle, having spread [grass] beneath it and poured [clarified butter] over it; to the east [he places] the *ānās*, to the south the *karambha*, to the west the *parivāpa*, and to the north the *āmikṣā*.
He goes with the animal sacrifice; the remainder is that he comes together with the *savanīya* animal. [He acts] precisely according to the direction.

The Adhvaryu draws the Aśvin cup with the mantra: "O your whip, which is honey-sweet... The formula for the drawing is: "Thou art taken with a support; for the two Aśvins, svāhā! This explicit mention is intended to show that, like the cups for Indra-Vāyu and others, this too is a *dhārā-graha* (a stream-drawing), and thus its greatness (*mahattva*) is indeed established. Consequently, the wiping (*saṃmārjana*) prescribed by the rule "he wipes the cup" is also accomplished here. The specific mention of the Adhvaryu is for the purpose of excluding the Pratiprasthātṛ. He describes the method of drawing:
having spread a base [of ghee] from the *droṇakalaśa* with the *pariplava* ladle, having drawn [the soma] from the *pūtabhṛt*, he pours [ghee] over it from the *droṇakalaśa*.

The term *pariplavayā* (with the ladle that moves back and forth) carries over to the subsequent passage as well. Consequently, both the drawing out (*unnayana*) and the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*) are performed with the *pariplu* ladle. The mention of *pariplavayā* is for the purpose of excluding the *uccha* vessel. The mention of the *droṇakalaśa* is for the purpose of excluding the *ādhavanīya*. Following the words "from the *droṇakalaśa*," the phrase "having taken the Soma" is to be supplied. The prefix *ud-* signifies abundance.

Although the order of the manual recitation (*mantrapāṭhakrama*) places the Āśvina cup as third, nevertheless, because the Vedic sequence (*śrautakrama*)—which states, "When the *ṛk-pavamāna* has been chanted, the Āśvina is drawn"—is stronger than the order of the manual recitation, the Adhvaryu priest draws the cups at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*). Furthermore, based on the Śruti text, "When the tenth [cup] is drawn, that which is the Āśvina, he offers it as the third," the drawing of the Āśvina cup occurs here. Jaimini also [states]: "The displacement of order is due to purpose and verbal expression, because of the specific nature of the Śruti and because of the predominance of the purpose."

Furthermore, among the cups that have been set down, the tenth cup is the Āśvina cup and the third place is for the oblation; thus, when it is said, "When the Āśvina is taken as the tenth, one offers it as the third," the meaning of the words "tenth" and "third" found in the Śruti must be understood. From the pouring out (*upastaraṇa*) and the sprinkling (*abhicāraṇa*), this is known: the primary drawing (*unnayana*) is up to the brim; for those desiring rain or suffering from illness, it is up to the point of filling. The pouring out and the sprinkling are done with a very small amount. And so on.
Ga. ja. ma. says: "na. davana" | 855 55. This section [paṭalaḥ], together with the commentary named Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha, extends this procedure elsewhere as well:
"This ritual rule applies to all the cups (grahas)."

The meaning is: [the procedure applies] to the Ṛtumukha cups, the Āpanna cup, the *apunargraha*, the *somātireka* cup, the *ṣoḍaśin*, the *prājāpatya*, and so forth. The meaning is that this aforementioned ritual method (*kalpa*) or mode of performance is applicable. Since the term "of the cups" (*grahāṇām*) is in the plural, all cups would already be included; however, the explicit mention of "all" (*sarva*) is intended to exclude the *āśvina* cup from this rule, as it is to be taken by the *adhvaryu* alone, whereas the present rule establishes a convention regarding all cups except for those specifically designated for the *adhvaryu*. Having set that [cup] down and having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-twisted rope (*trivṛt*), he dedicates the animal victim for Agni belonging to the *savanīya* sacrifice.

Since the act of settling [the cups] is already established by the general rule "according to their origin" (*yathāyonisādana*), the specific statement "having settled them in their respective places" (*tatra sādayitvā*) is intended to ensure that there is no interval of time between the settling and the subsequent wrapping (*parivyayana*). "This is your womb; for the two Mādhvīs" is the mantra for the settling. The mantra "I unyoke these two at dawn" (*prātaryujo vimuñceyam*) is an alternative to "O Kaśā, of you two... (*yā vāṃ kaśā*). With the mantra "I unyoke the two yoked at dawn," the grasping [of the cups] occurs; "This is your womb; for the Aśvins, you" is the corresponding mantra for the settling.

"Having loosened the previous cord with a triple-stranded cord according to the procedure prescribed for the *nirūḍhapaśubandha*—beginning with the taking of the cord of the god [Savitṛ] and so forth—one encircles the sacrificial post at the level of the navel; this means that one dedicates the animal to be sacrificed at the Soma-pressing (*savanīya-paśu*). Nor should it be argued that this cord does not belong to the animal because it would result in an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) if it were merely an accessory (*aṅga*) of the post; for even if it is an accessory of the post, a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭa*) consisting of binding is possible. Furthermore, since the second case-ending (*dvitīyā-vibhakti*) is heard, it is logical that the encircling of the post with the cord has the post itself as its purpose."

And likewise, Jaimini states in the fourth chapter, fourth pāda: "The girdle should be made of a single cord, not of three, because there is no injunction [to that effect]. Some take up a single previous cord and wrap it around [the sacrificial post]; that is not correct, because the statement regarding its repetition would otherwise be purposeless. Furthermore, it is clearly stated by both Kātyāyana and Baudhāyana: "Having taken up the previous one... Even though it is used for the Savanīya sacrifice, it is not repeated, because it is a consecration (saṃskāra) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). As for the *svaru* chip, however, it is taken up with the mantra only once at the beginning.

Because of the statement "the *svaru* for each sacrificial post" (*pratiyūpaṃ svaravaḥ*), the *svaru* is common to all posts; this is clear from the explicit scriptural injunction in the Agniṣṭoma itself. From the formula beginning with "Of the god... (*devasya tvā*) up to the end of the house-naming, there is either the wiping (*unmārjana*) or the looking forward (*apraprekṣaṇa*). The animal intended here is the goat (*aja*), because no other species is mentioned and because of another scriptural passage stating, "They begin the Agniṣṭoma with the *āmeya* animal.

There is no restriction regarding its form. Regarding that Savanīya animal, there is no restriction of form—meaning there is no restriction such as being red (*lohita*) and so forth; it does not exist here. This too is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that the Agniṣomīya is the archetype (*prakṛti*).
When the omentum has been offered, they proceed to move forward, having worshipped with the *grahāvakāśa* formulas, and then enter the procession.

The *uttaraparivapya* oblation and the measuring at the *cātvāla* pit indeed take place. This is because the offering of the omentum (*vapāhoma*) occurs after those two. It also applies to the *vara* (boons), since the granting of boons is explicitly prescribed in the *Paśvekādaśinī-sūtra*. "The complete offering" (*sarvahuta*) is an addition. [This concludes] the end of the mantra. 16. There is no omission here, as there is no statement to that effect. As they are about to enter the *sadas*, their movement toward their own seats for the purpose of sitting down is established.

They are about to perform that [rite]. They provide space (*avakāśayante*) by illuminating the meaning; thus, the *mantras* are called *avakāśas*. The *grahāvakāśas* are those *mantras* which provide space—that is, illumination—for the *grahas*, or in which there is the space/illumination of the *grahas*. Starting from "Two oceans... up to "the wooden sword (*sphyas*) is the sacrificial grass (*sastris*)," these *mantras* are designated as *grahāvakāśas*. Having worshipped the *pūtabhṛt* and other jars, they "approach" (*saṃprasanti*), meaning they enter the *sadas* together. This is a general declaration.

Because of the statement "they will press [the Soma]," when the Ukthya vessel is taken on account of the excellence of the Soma, there is an absence of *pratarpaṇa* (refreshment), and consequently the cessation of the *grahāvakāśa* and the *upasthāna* (worship). Due to the plural number, the *adhvaryu*, *pratiprasthātṛ*, and *yajamāna* perform the *upasthāna* and *tarpaṇa* according to the procedure of the *adhvaryu*. For the *unnetṛ*, the *upasthāna* and *sarpaṇa* are performed according to the procedure of the *adhvaryu*. The *upaveśana* (sitting down) also belongs to the *sadasya*; for the *sadasya* as well, it is exactly the same.
