By the phrase "those who are about to move forward" (*prasṛpsyantaḥ*), this worshipful salutation (*upasthāna*) is intended for all those who perform the act of moving forward (*prasarpaṇa*), whether they are endowed with both the duties of the *Neṣṭṛ* and the *Āgnīdhra*, or by means of the *Adhvaryu's* function alone. Consequently, because the *Brahman* is also a performer of the movement, he too performs the salutation; as for the duties of the *Hotṛ* and others, or the *Udgātṛ* and others, these should be understood according to their respective branches (*śākhā*) as appropriate.

The two oceans refer to the *Droṇakalaśa* and the *Ādhavanīya* jars; the meaning is that one worships both simultaneously with the mantra recited once. Regarding the phrase "they pass over the other by means of a bridge": *neṣṭrāgnīdhayor ubhayānvitayoḥ hariṇā ādhvaryaveṇa vā | prasṛpsyanta ity anena ye ye prasarpaṇakarās teṣām idam upasthānam, tena brahmaṇo 'pi prasarpaṇakartṛtvād upasthānam, hotrādīnām udgātrādīnāṃ ca karma śākhānusāreṇeti yathāyathaṃ draṣṭavyam | dvau samudrāv iti droṇakalaśādhavanīyau | sakṛd uktena mantreṇa dvau yugapad upatiṣṭhanta ity arthaḥ | setunā atiyanty anyam iti |*
The phrase "the two firm ones" (*dve dradhasī*) refers to the *pūtabhṛt* vessel; the words "O noble lady" (*nāryā*) mark the end of the mantra;
and the words "encompassing Agni" (*paribhūr agnim*) refer to the entire *soma*.

The word "they attend upon" (*upatiṣṭhante*) is the remainder [of the sentence]. The end of the mantra is *tasya ta idaṃ unmūnaḥ*. That which is both "all" (*sarva*) and "Soma" (*soma*) is "all-Soma" (*sarvasoma*). Here, the word "all" denotes all types [of Soma], as in the expression "he eats all kinds of food. Because the substance is a single unit, one recites the mantra once for the attendance upon the entire Soma. The inclusion of the word "all" is for the purpose of attending upon the Soma located in the *graha*, the *droṇakalaśa*, the *ādhavanīya*, and the *pūtabhṛt* vessels.

With "For my out-breath (prāṇa)! he [offers] the Upāṃśu cup; with "For my in-breath (apāna)! the Antaryāma; with "For my diffused breath (vyāna)! the Upāṃśusavana stone; with "For my speech (vāc)! the Aindravāyava cup; with "For my will and insight (dakṣakratu)! the Maitrāvaruṇa cup; with "For my two eyes (cakṣus)! the Śukra and Manthin cups; with "For my hearing (śrotra)! the Āśvina cup; with "For my self (ātman)! the Āgrayaṇa cup; with "For my limbs (aṅga)! the Ukthya cup; with "For my life-span (āyus)! the Dhruva cup; with "For my vigor (vīrya)! the Atigrāhya cups; and with "For my brilliance (tejas)!", "for my strength (ojas)!", and "for my luster (varcas)!"—he joins these respectively according to their form. Everywhere he appends the formula: "O giver of luster, flow for luster. || 13 ||

The remainder [of the sentence] is simply that they "stand near" immediately after the *samit*. In the word *antaryāma*, there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the vessel, because [the soma] has already been offered. Alternatively, the absence of initial *vṛddhi* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). By that, the form *antaryāmam* is established. [Paṭala 857, 550]. This is accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa. The word "vessel" (*pātram*) is to be supplied by virtue of suitability. Also in the case of *cakṣā me*, it is exactly as in *varcedā varcase pavasva*.

Regarding the rule in the Sūtra, "With the formula *varṣodā varcase pavasva*, one joins [the mantra] everywhere," the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) indicates that even here the singular reading alone is to be applied. However, due to the distinctness of the substances (*dravyapṛthaktvāt*), there is a repetition of the mantra. In this ritual procedure (*kalpa*), the dual form *cakṣuyāmi* should be understood as being mutually correlative. This interpretation is established by the natural force (*svarasa*) of the Sūtra; it sets aside the dual-form reading mentioned in the Śruti, namely *vakadau varcase pavethām*.

In this ritual procedure (*kalpa*), because there is a dual gender [in the term *atigrāhya*], the mantra is used only once. For the *atigrāhya* cups, however, the mantras are repeated: "For my strength, O drop, flow for splendor; for my luster, O drop, flow for splendor; for my vigor, O drop, flow for splendor; for my splendor, O drop, flow for splendor. These three mantras for the three *atigrāhya* cups are respectively correlated with the phrase "for my strength," and thus stand as alternatives to that single formula. The use of the plural pronoun "by these" (*etaiḥ*) is intended to exclude the possibility of treating them as a single unified mantra.

Since the sequence is established by the very nature of the context, the expression "in the order they appear" (*yathārūpam*) is intended to demonstrate that in the case of the Vājapeya sacrifice, among the *aindrātigrāhya* cups, there is a repetition of only the second mantra and not of the final one. The meaning is that the portion "varṣodā varcase pavasva," which follows the word *mā*—which is a substitute for the word *asmad*—is to be supplied (*anuṣakta*) everywhere, that is, in all the mantras.

With the formula, "Thou art the belly of Viṣṇu," [he addresses] the *droṇakalaśa*; with "Thou art the belly of Indra," the *ādhavanīya*; and with "Thou art the belly of the All-gods (*viśve devāḥ*)," the *pūtabhṛt*. To every [formula], he appends the phrase, "O giver of splendor, purify yourself for my splendor. This is well known. With "Who art thou? What is thy name? [he addresses] the entire King Soma without distinction.

"They attend upon [him]"—this much [is said]. "This [cup] of yours, O [Indra], is wiped clean"—this is the end of the mantra. The purpose of including the term "all" (*sarva*) is as explained previously. The meaning is that the mantra is "without distinction" (*aviśeṣa*), because there is no specific feature in the act of attending (*upasthāna*) characterized by repetition—which would otherwise arise from differences in ritual properties such as being dedicated to Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyava*), or from differences in properties such as being a cup (*graha*) or residing in a pitcher (*kalaśastha*).

Thus it is established: "The attendance upon all the kings occurs by means of the mantra recited only once; there is no separate attendance by taking up each individual king. By this, it is understood that in the previous case of attending all the kings, there is a repetition [of the ritual].
One who desires prosperity, one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), one who is ill, one who desires food, or one who is practicing sorcery (*abhicaran*) should gaze [at the assembly].

"One desiring to prosper should gaze; one desiring Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*) should gaze; one who is ill should gaze; one practicing exorcism (*abhicaran*) should gaze"—these are the ritual rules (*kalpa*) found in one's own recension (*svaśākhā*). "One desiring food (*annādya*) should gaze" is a rule from another recension (*śākhāntarīya*). Since this is shown here as an optional rite for a specific desire (*kāmyakalpa*), the preceding act of standing nearby (*upasthāna*) does not possess the quality of being optional.

In place of the word "this" (*idam*), one should insert the mention of the respective object of desire: "O Unmindful One, [take] his form; O Unmindful One, [take] his Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*); O Unmindful One, [take] his life-span (*āyus*); O Unmindful One, [take] his food (*annādya*); O Unmindful One, [take] the vital breaths of that person [amuṣya]. Baudhāyana also has clearly demonstrated these modifications of the mantras associated with the desire for prosperity and so forth, even in the absence of a desire for food. In the absence of a specific desire, the mantra is modified according to one's own [intent]. Here, the desire... [is fulfilled].

In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, when the crop has ripened, the act of looking (*avekṣaṇa*) must also be performed; however, in the absence of a specific desire, there is only the act of standing near (*upasthāna*) and not the looking—this is the distinction. This meaning is understood from the use of a different word and from the singular number. This looking belongs to the sacrificer alone, as it is stated generally.

Since it is established in all schools of thought that the fruit of the action accrues solely to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and because of the Sūtra which states, "The sacrificer desires those things which the [text] causes to be heard," [the fruit belongs to him]. If it were to accrue to the *maitrāvaruṇa* priest as well, then [the Sūtra] would have said, "he should say 'let them look'. By this, the view that the result pertains to the *adhvaryu* is also refuted. Here, the reading is intended merely to illustrate the syllables. Having performed the mixing with the desire for existence as the objective, the looking must be performed by the sacrificer.

The sacrificer desires those [objects] which he desires; this is known from the Sūtra: "He causes them to be heard. The mantras ending with this are designated as *grahāvakāśa*. Regarding the mantras that follow this, he states their application (*viniyoga*) as follows:
"The wooden sword (*sphya*) is the blessing (*svasti*)," etc.; thus, the implements for preparing the altar are deposited upon the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) according to their respective forms.

The meaning is that those implements for which the word *vedi* (altar) and so forth have been used—those *vevikaraṇas* (implements characterized by the word *vedi*)—are properly deposited (*saṃnyastāni*), and they remain present according to their respective forms and genders. By the formula "The *sphya* is the blessing," one deposits the *sphya*; by "The *vidhana* is the blessing," the *vidhana*; by "The animal is the altar (*vedi*)," the animal; and by "The axe is the blessing," the axe. This is the meaning of the term "according to form" (*yathārūpam*). The prefix *sam-* signifies that the depositing is done separately.

The word *yastāni* (having laid down) serves to exclude [the implements] from being placed in a storehouse (*nidhāna*). The prefix *ni-* has the sense of non-contact (*asaṃsarga*). The laying down of the wooden sword (*sphya*) and other implements on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) is to be performed by an attendant (*parikarmika*), as indicated by the natural force of the term *saṃnyastāni*. Otherwise, he would have said *saṃnyasya* (having laid down).

From this point onward, there is the proceeding and sitting down; because there is no such proceeding for the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*) and the third pressing (*tṛtīya-savana*), the construction of the altar, the standing near [the Sadas], and so forth—up to the looking at the southern part of the Sadas—do not take place, since the purpose is accomplished by the proceeding for the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) alone; this is the sense. However, the standing near the *prahāvakāśa* occurs in the two subsequent pressings because of a specific scriptural injunction and because it is a consecratory act (*saṃskāra*) for the cups (*graha*).
"O you who are worthy of sacrifice, makers of sacrifice, stay!"—this applies to all [pressings].

"They stand near" (*upatiṣṭhante*)—this much [is the rule]. "You must go" (*iyadhvam*) is the end [of the section]. The distinction between these two is that the former was a standing near (*upasthāna*) in the form of individual parts (*vyaṣṭi*), while this is in the form of the whole (*samaṣṭi*). All four [implements], beginning with the wooden sword (*sphya*), are included.
"May Heaven and Earth stand near me" (*upa mā dyāvāpṛthivī*) refers to Heaven and Earth.
The phrase "they stand near" (*upatiṣṭhante*) is to be supplied everywhere. The meaning is that they stand near while intending Heaven and Earth.
"And they worship" (*upāstāca*) refers to where they chant the *bahiṣpavamāna* hymn.

The phrase "where they chant the *bahiṣpavamāna*" is intended to demonstrate the meaning of the word *āstāva*. The ellipsis is "they worship that. [They worship] the *droṇakalaśa* with "near the jar" (*upakalaśa*), Soma with "near Soma" (*upasoma*), Agni with "near Agni" (*upāgni*), the gods with "near the gods" (*upadevā*), the sacrifice with "near the sacrifice" (*upayajña*), and the *hotṛ*-priests with "may the subordinate *hotṛ*s call upon us for invocation" (*upahave hvayantām*).

"They attend," so it is said. Soma has indeed been pressed, because that is the subject under discussion. And it resides in the eleven cups and three jars; it remains on the northern altar (uttaravedi) itself, because it is the primary element as the locus for the Sautya sacrifice. "Become gods. [550] [This is] from the work of Gopīnātha Maṭṭa, titled Jyotsnā-vyākhyā. There are thirty-three: namely, the eleven fore-offerings (prayāja), the eleven after-offerings (anuyāja), the eleven offerings to the Upayājas, and Prajāpati as the Vaṣaṭ-call.

In this context, even though they are inherently great, the deities are intended [to be addressed]; by the word *yajña* (sacrifice), the sacrificial implements such as the oblation (*havis*) and clarified butter (*ājya*) are meant; and by *hotrakāḥ*, the Maitrāvaruṇa and other officiating priests. Because of the proximity of the *droṇakalaśa* (the wooden trough), these are all indeed invocations (*upasthāna*) of those very things employed in the ritual. To prevent the omission of the word *mā* (not), the reading "there, there" (*tatra tatra*) is included. Even though it is mentally present for the one who is qualified (*adhikṛta*), the desire for completion is satisfied by that alone, as if saying "the gods are near the sacrifice."

Nor is there any acceptance of an intervention by the noble *samādhi*, because the meaning is that it serves as a non-distinctive indicator for the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself, which remains unaltered even when intervened upon. By this, the view of some who attach the word *mā* (prohibitive particle) to both the beginning and the end simply because it is heard there is refuted.
One attaches [the verb] according to its form—such as *hvayantu*, *hvayetām*, or *hvayantu*—in every instance.

The sense is that one should not entertain the doubt that "because of the dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) of the word *hvayate* even though it is proximate, there might be an inappropriate connection in some places, and therefore the ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) will be established"; for by virtue of semantic competency (*sāmarthya*), one must accept only a transformed connection (*vipariṇatānvaya*). And this transformed connection is stated by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): "The modification of case endings occurs due to the purpose of the sentence" (*śānirarthādvibhaktivipariṇāmaḥ*). The meaning is that in all cases—that is, in all mantras—the verb is supplied (*anuṣajati*), i.e., becomes connected, in accordance with the form [of the deity], such as the singularity inherent in the deity.

Regarding the mantras for the *bhāstotra*, the *kalaśa*, the *sāman*, and the *agni-yajña*, they are recited as "haryatām" because they are expressed in the singular. For the *dyāvāpṛthivī* [heaven and earth], it is "yajatām" because they are not expressed in the plural. For the *devān* [the gods], it is "yantām" because they are expressed in the plural. Although it would have been possible to read "haryetām," "igatām," or "yantām" according to the sequence of the deities to be worshipped (*upastheya*), nevertheless, such a reading is stated because there is no contradiction in following the sequence of the verbal forms (*vacana*) themselves. Furthermore, in the final mantra, because of the addition of the word "upahava," the root *i* (from which *iyate* is derived) is recited again in accordance with that.
"Oblation to Agni, the slayer of Makha! May the glory of Makha not depart from me," [with these words] he stands worshipping the Āhavanīya fire.

In the phrase "one should stand near" (*upatiṣṭheta*), the meaning is not merely standing nearby for the sake of imitating a Brahmin; rather, because the mantra contains the word *namaḥ*, its meaning is salutation (*namaskāra*). Thus, since the word *namaḥ* occurs at the very beginning of the mantra, the performance of the gesture of bowing (*natimudrā*) begins from that point and continues until the conclusion of the mantra. Furthermore, the entire recitation of this and the subsequent mantras to be mentioned is intended to prevent the physical act of salutation from being performed by oneself at the end of the mantra.

By this [verse], having thus paid homage to them, the meaning of the Śruti—that he is the breath of his own self—is established. The fourth mantra, however, is that very one from the Sūtra. From the statement "he worships again," it is understood for the purpose of indicating that the worship of all [deities] beginning with the *sphyu* and ending with the *hotṛ* is a single ritual act. By this, it is established that the worship must be performed while standing at the eastern door of the *havirdhāna* shed itself, and not by going near each individual [deity].
[The mantra is: "Homage to Rudra, the slayer of Makha; having paid homage, protect me"—[this is directed toward] the *āgnīdhra*.

Because of the proximity of that which is to be honored, there is the touching of water. The word "he stands near" (*upatiṣṭhate*) is the understood remainder. The explanation here should be seen as being the same as before. [The Brahman priest] also recites the *vedha* formula. From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: "To Indra, the slayer of Makha; do not destroy my sensory power and my vigor"—this is for the *hotrīya* fire.

In this context, the word *hotrīya* refers specifically to the fire (*agni*) by means of a secondary indicative mark (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its location, because of the proximity of the *āgnīdhra*. Since one must attend to the location itself, it is more appropriate to attend to the fire situated there. Thus, it is established that the *hotrīya* fire is to be maintained until this point. The same should be understood for the *mānīya* fire as well, or rather, these two [fires] refer to the *dhiṣṇya* fires, since attendance to them is also observed. In this alternative view, there is no maintenance [of the fire].
Regarding the *mārjālīya*: "Homage to Yama, the slayer of Makha; having paid homage, protect me"—this has been explained.
"Ye two are firm, ye two are loose"—this refers to the two pressing-boards.
"He worships them," so it is said. "May no harm reach us"—this is the end of the mantra.
According to some, he gazes at heaven and earth.

This is clear. [The formula] "May the god Sūrya protect me from celestial distress" refers to Sūrya; "Vāyu from the intermediate space" refers to Vāyu; "Agni from the earth" refers to Agni; "Yama from the ancestors" refers to Yama; and "Sarasvatī from humans" refers to Sarasvatī. The word "protect" (pātu) is appended everywhere, as in "may he protect" (pātu).

Immediately after "Sarasvatīm," the word "upatiṣṭhate" (he worships) is to be supplied. This applies everywhere, meaning in all the mantras beginning with "vāyurantarikṣāt" and so forth. The use of the term "ghoṣā" is for the purpose of excluding the necessity of supplying words by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). The mention of *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation) is intended to prevent the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "ahasaḥ. In the mantra "yamaḥ pitṛbhyaḥ," there is no touching of water, because the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are not the primary object of the action. For this very reason, the sacred thread is also not worn over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*). The verb "pātu" is supplemented; that is to say, it is understood as being supplied from the preceding context.

With "Obeisance to the two divine door-panels," he pays homage to the two doors; with "Obeisance to the assembly hall," the assembly hall; with "Obeisance to the lord of the assembly hall," the lord of the assembly hall; with "Obeisance to the eye of the friends who go before," the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); with "Obeisance to heaven," heaven; and with "Obeisance to earth," the earth.

The two door-posts of the *sadas* are the two pillars of the door; the end of the mantra is "Mā mā saṃtāptam" (May you not burn me). By the word *sadasaspati*, the Brahman priest is meant. Thus Āpastamba has clearly stated: "With 'Obeisance to the Lord of the Assembly' [one addresses] the Brahman. The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are fifteen, excluding himself; they are sixteen when the *sadasya* (the sixteenth priest) is included.

With the words "O son of a remarried woman," he throws away a blade of grass or a clod of earth from where he is about to sit, touches water, and sits down with the mantra: "May I go along the downward and upward paths."

In whichever spot he intends to sit—that is, where he will perform his sitting—he should cast away from that place whatever grass or clod of earth (loṣṭa) there may be, saying: "O son of a remarried woman (daidhiṣavya), depart! According to the general rule, this is done toward the north. Āśvalāyana says it is done with the little fingers. He then sits down there, reciting: "From the low ground and from the high ground, I have gone forth."

Regarding this, the rule for the positions of the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ is shown in another Sūtra: "The Adhvaryu sits on the right side of the sacrificial grass-bundle, and the Pratiprasthātṛ on the left. Their sitting is indeed within the *sadas*. The Unnetṛ sits to the north of the Pratiprasthātṛ.

According to the view that the sitting down occurs specifically at the *unnata-havirdhāna*, the procedure for the *unnetṛ* is as follows: having performed everything up to the worship (*upasthāna*) of the *hotraka* priests, one throws away a blade of grass or a clod of earth with the formula, "O Ahi Vaidhiṣavya," at the place where one is about to sit down; then, having touched water, one recites "unnivataḥ" while looking upwards—this much constitutes the rule for the *unnetṛ*. The intermediate rites beginning with the worship of the *āhavanīya* fire and ending with the worship of the Earth do not apply to him, because these [rites] are only possible at the time of entering the *sadas*.

The author of the Sūtra will demonstrate the place for the *namāna* in the *Yājamānasūtra*. He will demonstrate the place for the *brahman* in the *Brahmasūtra*. The place for the *sadasya* is stated in another Sūtra: "To the south of the *audumbarī* pillar is the *sadasya*. Baudhāyana also says: "To the south, facing north, the *brahman* and the *sadasya* sit down. From the previous Sūtra, the word *audumbarīm* carries over here, as in: "The *udgātṛ*s sit around the *audumbarī* itself.
The word *pākataraḥ* is the end of the preceding [Sūtra]; *adhāraḥ* is the end of the following [Sūtra].

Having crept forward to the sacrificial hall (*sadas*), he should look toward the southern half [of the altar], saying, "O Fathers, come hither. Here, the sequence is reversed from the usual order—first the action is shown, followed by the mantra—in accordance with the *Brāhmaṇa*. The looking (*parekṣaṇa*) continues until the completion of the entire mantra; it is not a simultaneous conjunction with the end of the mantra, nor is it for the sake of mere illustration. Having crept forward to the hall and completed the act of creeping forward ending with sitting in the hall, he looks while standing right there, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*) or having it worn normally (*upavītin*), with palms joined (*baddhāñjali*); this is the meaning of the prefix *parā-* [in *parekṣeta*].

The joining of the palms (*añjali*) is for the purpose of honoring the ancestors. Thus says the *Brāhmaṇa*: "Having thus paid homage to them, one should enter the sacrificial assembly (*sadas*) for the sake of one's own security. The mantra ends with the words "may you be abundant" (*bhūyās ta*). According to the view that the sacred thread is worn over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), one should touch water while wearing it as a sacrificial cord (*yajñopavītin*). Regarding the plural form "they enter" (*saṃprasarpanti*): when about to enter, one should worship [the deities] at the openings of the vessels; this plural usage applies here. However, in the subsequent instances—where it says "he worships," "he gazes," or "he sits down where he is to sit"—the singular form is used.

By these two [statements], two positions are indicated: from the plural number, that the status of being the performer of the *upasthāna* belongs to them (*ṛtvij*); and from the singular number, that the status of being the performer of the *upasthāna* belongs to the *adhvaryu* alone. In this case, regarding the fruit, since it pertains to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), it is logical that it belongs to him alone, because it serves the purpose of the performance and is thus connected to the one who is engaged in it. And so, in the third chapter, eighth section, Jaimini states: "But the fruit is for their sake; it should belong to the master [of the sacrifice] because it is for his benefit."

The fruit—namely, the result consisting of freedom from distress and so forth—is for the sake of the ritual action (*karmārtha*), serving as a means for the performance of the rite. With respect to the master (*svāmin*) who is the recipient of the fruit, it possesses purposefulness (*arthavattva*) in the form of not obstructing his own ritual duties, and it serves a purpose (*prayojanatva*) in the form of being conducive to his own desired ends. Thus, for those officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), this fruit comes about precisely through their state of being *avigāmin* (non-deviant). And so, in accordance with the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), it is logical that they are indeed *avigāmin*. [End of section].

The word "but" (*tu*) in the sūtra is intended to indicate the distinction from the previous section, where it was established as a settled conclusion that the fruit—such as *varcas* (splendor) and so forth—is connected to the agent because it is mentioned in connection with the instruments, as in the case of the instrumental mantras beginning with "O Agni, [grant] splendor to me. The phrase "because the fruit is mentioned in connection with the instruments" refers to that prior discussion.

In the view that the Adhvaryu should perform the worship of the Āhavanīya and other fires, the inspection of the Yāvā and Pṛṣi vessels, the discarding of the Jhoṣṭa, the touching of water, the sipping of water (ācamana), and the looking at the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) while standing behind [the altar] should be done alone; however, the rest should be done together—this is either for the sake of illustration. [From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Eighth Book:
Here he dissects the animal victim.

It should be understood that the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is included [in the root *śam*]. By this, the sense becomes "he causes the slaughterer to cut up the animal" (*śamitāraṃ paśuṃ viśāsayati*). By this, it is also established that the command (*praiṣa*), "O slaughterer, cut up the animal" (*śamitaḥ paśuṃ viśādhi*), must likewise be uttered by the Adhvaryu priest at this very point. Consequently, the time for cutting up the animal as stated in the *Paśusūtra*—namely, "having released his speech with the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he cuts up the animal"—is set aside. Here, he cuts up the animal at this specific time, and not at the time following the release of speech triggered by the command, "O preparer of the oblation, come for the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*)."
While being cooked, it remains lying over all the pressings, or it is cooked at the third pressing.

The term *śrapyamāṇaḥ* (being cooked) is an adjective qualifying the sacrificial animal (*paśu*). By the phrase "it lies around all the pressings" (*sarvāṇi savanāni pariśete*), it is understood that it remains lying down while being cooked—until the time of the final offering—so that it becomes well-cooked, neither undercooked nor overdone. Regarding the reading *pariśerataḥ*, the plural number should be understood as Vedic (*chāndasa*), because it would otherwise contradict the singular form *śrapyamāṇaḥ*.

Even in this view—that [the animal] is cooked at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*)—the dismemberment (*viśasana*) takes place right here, and only the cooking is to be commenced at the time of the commencement of the third pressing. Thus ends the *Śrīmad-Bhagavat-Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was the grandson of the venerable Okopāha, a performer of the *Agniṣṭoma*, a performer of the *Sādyaskra*, a performer of the *Vājapeya*, a performer of the *Sarvatomukha*, a performer of the *Aptoryāma*, and a performer of the *Pauṇḍarīka*.

Thus ends the fifth chapter of the eighth [section] in the commentary named *Jyotsnā*, which pacifies the distress of learned persons caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the ocean [of the *Tantrāloka*]. 5.

8.6 Now begins the sixth chapter of the eighth book. Having placed the *puroḍāśa* cakes down and having taken portions from them, the Adhvaryu proceeds with the offering together with the Pratiprasthātṛ. After the Pratiprasthātṛ has placed the struck *puroḍāśa* cakes, the Adhvaryu takes portions from those *puroḍāśas* along with them and proceeds. In the word *jātāya*, it should be understood that the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is elided; thus it is established that the striking must be caused to be performed by the Pratiprasthātṛ. Accordingly, Āpastamba states: "At this point, the Pratiprasthātṛ places the *savanīya* offerings. The rule concerns only the portion regarding the simultaneous taking of portions (*sahāvadāna*); the term "proceeds" (*pracarati*), however, is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).

Although the *pracaraṇa* (the act of proceeding) is to be accomplished by multiple agents, the *samavadāna* (the taking of portions) is performed by the Adhvaryu alone. Consequently, since it is impossible for the *pracaraṇa* and the *samavadāna* to share a common locus of multiple agents (*aneka-kartṛ-sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the sentence would otherwise be untenable; it is precisely to avoid this inconsistency that the singular number is used. As for the reason why the Pratiprasthātṛ brings [the portions], it is simply due to the prohibition: "While the Soma sacrifice has not yet concluded, the Adhvaryu must not pass behind the *sadas*. [The portions] rest with the Āgnīdhra.

He places [the vessels] down. And thus says Baudhāyana: "Then, having taken hold of these [vessels], having brought them in through the eastern door, having gone around the north of the *sadas*, and having carried them around the north of the *āgnīdhra* and the *viṣṇya* hearths, he places them within the altar."

Now, this [offering] is to be announced by the Āgnīdhra. Since the agency of the Āgnīdhra is understood in this sūtra through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) from the preceding sūtra which sets forth the removal [of the oblations], beginning with "having sat down near the Gārhapatya fire, he should spread fivefold [the butter] in the *pāyī*," it should be seen that the Āgnīdhra is the performer here. The placing of all [the offerings] is done silently. He places the *āmikṣā* and the *vājina* silently in the middle of the *vedirāsa* on the southern corner of the *vedi*. Then he places the *vājina* silently on the *utkara*.
By the statement "having taken portions together, he proceeds," the individual sacrifice is excluded. He states the manner of that:

Having strewn the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles with clarified butter, having taken the portions, and having sprinkled them with clarified butter, he issues the direction: "Recite the invitatory verses for the morning pressings for Indra; announce the offerings of the morning pressings for Indra as they are presented. He thus issues the summons.

Since the acts of spreading the base (upastaraṇa) and pouring over (abhighāraṇa) are already established by the rule "having taken a portion from the *juhū*, he takes a portion for the *upabhṛt*," the author of the Sūtra formulated the rule as "having spread [the base] in the *juhū* and *upabhṛt*, having taken the portions, he pours over them" in order to exclude (*parisaṃkhyātum*) the re-pouring (*pratyabhighāraṇa*) and the equalizing of the *prastara* and the *barhis*. Where there is an interruption of time caused by the main sacrifice between the taking of the portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt*—which is for the sake of the principal offering—and the [subsequent] act, only in that case is there a re-pouring for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice.

On the basis of the force of the *jñāpaka* (indicative mark) stating that "where it is not so, there is no re-sprinkling," it is established [as follows]: when it is stated, "having spread [ghee] in the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt*, having taken the portions, and having sprinkled [them with ghee]," the spreading, taking of portions, and sprinkling might be performed in the *juhū* first and then in the *upabhṛt*, which would constitute *kāṇḍānusamaya* (performance by groups). To prevent this and ensure instead that *padārthānusamaya* (performance of individual items) occurs—namely, that the spreading, taking of portions, and sprinkling are performed together for both the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt* simultaneously—the two, *juhū* and *upabhṛt*, are mentioned in a compound.

And thus: having spread the *upastaraṇa* (under-layering) in the *juhū*, immediately after the *upabhṛt*, having again spread the *upastaraṇa* in the *juhū*, one should—just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*)—take portions from the *dhānās*, *karambha*, *parivāpa*, *puroḍāśa*, and *āmikṣā* in sequence: twice for those who offer four portions (*caturavattin*), or three times for those who offer five portions (*pañcāvattin*). Immediately thereafter, taking portions from the *upabhṛt* and the other [vessels], one should take once each for those who offer four portions, or twice each for those who offer five portions, for the *sviṣṭakṛt*. Having likewise taken [the portions] from what was in the *juhū* once...

The performance is established as follows: "He sprinkles twice that which is contained in the *dupabhṛt* [ladle]. It should be understood that by the use of the suffix *-lyap* (in the word *abhighārya*), only this single option—"he gives the call" (*saṃpreṣyati*)—is intended here, and not the two other options of "about to cut off" (*avadāsyat*) or "while cutting off" (*avadyan*). Then, having given the *puronuvākyā* call for the morning pressing (*prātaḥsāvasya*), having stepped across, and having called for the announcement (*āśrāvya*), when the response has been given, he gives the *yājyā* call for the morning pressing. The sacrifice is performed according to the archetype (*prakṛti*).

In the case of the *avadāna* (cutting) and the *pratyabhighāraṇa* (re-anointing), there is a modification (*ūha*) according to the specific purpose, as in the case of roasted grains (*dhānā*). Even in a sacrifice dedicated to Indra as the deity, one takes into account the distinction between deities at the time of pouring out the oblation (*nirvāpa*); thus, the blessings contained in the consecratory formulas (*anumantraṇa-mantra*) are appropriately combined for the sacrifices involving those respective substances. Accordingly, regarding the *sadana* (seating) offerings, Bharadvāja states: "The ritual procedure (*tantra*) consists of the grasping of the deities; the blessings should be combined, especially when there is a mixture of various substances. The particle *ca* has the sense of "also" (*api*), and it signifies the possibility of such a ritual act.

Immediately after the word "saṃsṛṣṭa" (mixed), the word "yāga" (sacrifice) is to be supplied as the remainder. The reason "because of the diversity of substances" (*nānādravyatvāt*) refers to the combination of blessings (*āśīḥ-samuccaya*). The meaning is: "because of the diversity of substances," that is, because of the diversity of the deities and the substances. The word "nirvāpa" (offering of the oblation) is to be supplied as the remainder. This [reasoning] is for the sake of establishing the combination of blessings for the two principal sacrifices in the Varuṇapraghāsa and other rites. But here, it is caused by both. In that case, the recitation of the consecration formula (*anumantraṇa*) is established as follows: "By the sacrifice to the gods, may I become possessed of power and an eater of food; may I be possessed of power and an eater of food."

In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [in the eighth praśna]: "May I attain the power of Indra, the eater of food, the possessor of power"—thus for one who sacrifices to Indra. "The victory..."—thus for one who sacrifices to Mahendra. "May I attain victory and greatness"—thus [he says]. However, according to the view that all [offerings] belong to Indra alone, for one who sacrifices to Indra, the formula "the possessor of power" (*indriyāvī*) occurs five times; for one who sacrifices to Mahendra, however, in place of the fifth occurrence of "the possessor of power," he says "victory" (*jemānam*).
According to the view that they are combined, having uttered "the possessor of power" once, he says "victory."

Having poured the contents of the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū*, he issues the two calls for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering: "Recite for Agni" (*agnaye 'nubrūhi*) and "Prompt for Agni" (*agnaye preṣya*). The recitation of these calls is intended to demonstrate the absence of the word *sviṣṭakṛt* from them; it serves to negate the possibility that this sacrifice might also be considered primary because of the absence of a call containing the term *sviṣṭakṛt*. Consequently, there is a single pouring of the oblation and a double sprinkling of clarified butter, and the subsequent consecration formula is as follows: "May I, through this sacrifice to the gods, become long-lived and attain stability through the sacrifice. This [formula] is thus associated with the *sviṣṭakṛt*.

There is no returning [of the ladle] because there is no further purpose; "aupabhṛta" means that which exists in the *upabhṛt* (the supporting ladle). Here, "existence" (*bhavanam*) means being present or existing. "Having turned over the *mudgā*" means having poured out the contents. The word "having turned over" (*paryasya*) signifies immediate sequence; therefore, it should be understood that the command (*preṣa*) follows immediately after the turning over, and not simultaneously with it as Āpastamba has stated. Regarding the words "bū" and "pre," there is prolation (*plāvana*), according to Pāṇini’s sūtra:
"In the case of *hi*, *preṣya*, *abhi*, *upa*, *deśa*, *ava*, and *ha*, the initial vowel [is prolated]. This should be understood everywhere in this manner.
The *prāśitra* and the *iḍā* are both performed; having taken the *prāśitra*, he cuts off the *iḍā*. [Objection:

Should it not have been stated here simply that "the *prāśitra* is performed," since the act of cutting will be established by the rule to be stated later, namely, "having cut [the portion], he places the *iḍā* for the Hotṛ"? If this were so, and these two tasks were accomplished by that alone, for what purpose is the injunction for cutting the *iḍā* and its prohibition made? [Response: True; it is for the purpose of excluding [any other] portions belonging to the sacrificer (*yajamāna-bhāga*). Because of that [injunction], [other portions are excluded].

It should not be argued that the prohibition is already established by the sūtra itself—"He does not cut off the sacrificer's portion"—and thus the fault remains as it was; for in the *kṛtsna-tantra* (the complete ritual procedure), the cessation [of the rule] is understood through the statement "he does not cut off the sacrificer's portion," because the *savanīya-puroḍāśa* sacrifice—which occurs in the midst of the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka-tantra*)—is brought forward there, and since it belongs to the complete procedure (*kṛtsnatva*), the prohibition "he does not cut off the sacrificer's portion" does not apply here either, resulting in the attainment of the cutting off of the sacrificer's portion.

Because that [portion] is necessary for the purpose of completing the distribution (*parisaṃrūpaṇa*), there is no state of deficiency in it. In the view that "the oblation belongs to Vaiśvānara," the giving of the *prāśitra* from the *āgneya* cake occurs only after the removal (*virujya*) of the *parivāpa*, while for the others it occurs without removal. In the view of some that "he causes the *prāśitra* to be taken from the *āgneya*," the *prāśitra* is taken only from the *parivāpa* and not from the others.

Having caused the protector of the clarified butter and other oblations to shake [them], and having washed his hands which were smeared with clarified butter, he proceeds to the *saumika* ritual; this applies everywhere.

In the offerings to two deities—the two Marutvatīya cups, the Āditya cup, the Sāvitra cup, and the Hāriyojana cup—there are both the invitatory verse (anuvākyā) and the offering verse (yājyā). The word "and" (ca) is used in each case to indicate that for every sacrifice there is a pair of verses; this is intended to ensure that those familiar with the presence of invitatory and offering verses do not lose track of their number. [End of Section 150, Paṭala] According to Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa’s Jyotsnā commentary: In the other Soma offerings, there are only offering verses (yājyās).
The meaning is clear.
Regarding both types [of offerings], the *āśruta* (the call for assent), the *pratyāśruta* (the response), and the *yājyā-saṃpraisha* (the command for the offering verse) have been explained.

This applies to both those [offerings] joined with a *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā*, as well as those that are alone. The *āśruta* is the call for assent (*āśrāvaṇa*), the *pratyāśruta* is the response (*pratyāśrāvaṇa*), and the *yājyā-saṃpraisha* is the command for the offering verse; the meaning is that this entire collection consisting of the *āśruta*, *pratyāśruta*, and *yājyā-saṃpraisha* has been explained and stated according to the general rules (*paribhāṣā*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
In the case of those [offerings] accompanied by *puronuvākyā* verses, the *puronuvākyā-saṃpraisha* is prescribed;

the phrase "it has been explained" is understood to carry over. Its meaning is as stated in the sūtra located within the section on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*): "Recite for such-and-such deity according to the respective deity.
Having taken up either a cup (*graha*) or a goblet (*camasa*), he causes the announcement (*āśrāvayati*) to be made, just as in the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

If one were to call for the *āśrāvaṇa* (the formal announcement) without holding onto either the *pad* (the footstep-mark) or the *camasa* (the cup), he would fall away from his own self; therefore, one should call for the *āśrāvaṇa* while holding onto it, so that he does not depart from his own self—this is the meaning of the word "holding onto" (*anvārambha*) in the Śruti. The sense is that it is indeed taking hold (*ādāna*), and not merely touching (*anvārambhamātra*). By the phrase "as in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," there is a comprehensive inclusion of the three types of *āśrāvaṇa* belonging to the ritual procedure: *āśrāvaya*, *astu śrauṣaṭ*, and *yaja*. Otherwise, [in this context] Prajāpati contended with the gods and Asuras, and subsequently the sacrifice was created; in this section, the *soma-pra...* [is discussed].

Since it has been stated that the *āśrāvaṇa* (the call "Oṃ śrāvaya") consists precisely of the form "Oṃ śrāvaya" which binds the instruments, its application alone would follow; therefore, the statement of extension (*atideśa*) is necessary to prevent that [undesired result]. Herein lies the distinction in the Brāhmaṇa: "He who knows the firm foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the Adhvaryu stands firm indeed. From whatever place he might think, 'I shall offer without stepping forward,' standing there he should say [the call]; this, indeed, is the Adhvaryu’s [foundation]."

Firm establishment belongs to him who knows thus; he indeed becomes firmly established. If one were to offer while stepping forward, there would be a loss of firm establishment; therefore, the offering should be made by one standing in the same place, for the sake of firm establishment. As for the Adhvaryu, if he converses with anyone else, he becomes as it were empty; his own Vāyavya cup becomes empty, and his own Camasa becomes empty. If he were to cause the *āśrāvaṇa* call to be made without grasping either the Vāyavya cup or the Camasa, it would become empty; therefore, having grasped it, he causes the *āśrāvaṇa* to be made, so that it does not become empty.
Standing in the Āgnīdhra shed facing south and holding the wooden sword (sphyá), the Āgnīdhra calls for the response; that has been explained.

Since the procedure for the *āśrāvaṇa* (calling for the response) and *pratyāśrāvaṇa* (response) in the *āmikṣā* house would have been established by the rule "as in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices" alone, the repetition of this cumbersome statement regarding the *āśrāvaṇa*, *pratyāśrāvaṇa*, and so forth serves to indicate that if these are performed otherwise than prescribed, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is specifically connected to the *soma* ritual system, and not the general expiation of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*. Furthermore, the prescription of all these details—such as facing south, standing, and holding the wooden sword (*sphya*)—is for the purpose of establishing them as a new, independent injunction (*apūrva*).

By that, the blowing and binding [of the bellows] are suspended. The mention of the *āgnīdhra* is for the purpose of obtaining both types of expiation. And the mention of the *adhvaryu* is for the sake of the subsequent [rite], and that is by way of modification. Regarding the *satyāṣāḍha-viracita-śrautasūtra* (in the eighth section):
"The *ekadhanas*, however, are the *yājyās* for the *saṃpraiṣas*."

"Ekadhana" refers to those for whom there is a single *pradhāna* (primary element) as their wealth—that is, their defining characteristic (*svarūpa-bhedaka*). Here, the word "wealth" (*dhana*) is understood to refer to the essential nature [of the objects], in accordance with the meaning of the Sūtra. Alternatively, the meaning is: "those in whom the essential nature, which serves as the differentiator, is deposited (*dhīyate*) or resides. Its grammatical correctness is established by its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group. Thus, because they are differentiated here by the difference in their essential natures, they are indeed both distinct and non-distinct, and not of a single uniform form. "Parimeyyajjā" means belonging to those who are subject to measurement (*parimāṇa*).

This means the *praiṣas* (directions) related to the sacrifice. In the word *yajyā*, the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule for the class beginning with *diś*. *Yājyās* are simply *yajyās*; here, there is no further suffix added to the base meaning. The syntactic connection is that the *praiṣas* for the *yājyās* are the *ekadhanās*.

In that context, the Adhvaryu, having called for the announcement (*āśrāvya*) and once the response has been given (*pratyāśrāvite*), issues a direction to the Maitrāvaruṇa, saying "Direct [the Hotṛ] for such-and-such," and he [the Maitrāvaruṇa] then urges the Hotṛ.

The mention of the *pūrvapradhvaryu* (the first *adhvaryu*) is for the purpose of including the *pratiprasthātṛ*. This sūtra pertains to the *yājyā* (offering verses) and the *praśas* (incitements). In the phrase "amuṣmai," the word denoting the deity in the dative case is to be uttered. The statement "amuṣmai preṣya" is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the entire incitement (*praśa*), including the call for the *āśrāvaṇa* (the announcement), such as: "O [priest], for the morning pressing, for the one possessing the *śukra* cup, the *manthin* cup, and the honey-drinker. The meaning is that the *Maitrāvaruṇa* impels the *Hotṛ* to utter the *yājyā* by means of this incitement.

This elaboration [of the ritual] is intended to demonstrate that for Soma, there is no direct dependence on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa). With this very intention, in this same section, after the creation of Prajāpati, the gods, and the asuras, the sacrifice was created; therein, the elaboration of the *āśrāvaṇa* and other rites is repeated:
"When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers; having offered when the secondary *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he carries away the portion for consumption.
This is clear.

This is the ritual procedure for all *soma* offerings. The meaning is: this applies to all those *soma* offerings beginning with the one for Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyava*). "When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers; when the secondary *vaṣaṭ* (*anuvaṣaṭ*) is uttered, having offered, he takes [the remnant] for consumption"—this being the rule for all *soma* offerings, since by this rule the secondary *vaṣaṭ* would apply everywhere, someone states an exception: "In the case of the double-deity cups (*dvidevatya*), the seasonal cups (*ṛtugraha*), the Āditya cup, and the Sāvitra cup, there is no secondary *vaṣaṭ*. For the Śukra and Manthin cups, as well as the Pātnīvata cup, it is optional (it may or may not be performed)."

The rule regarding the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* applies exclusively to the *śukra* and *manthin* cups; its performance or non-performance is subject to this specific condition. However, for the sake of the *madhyataḥkārin* cups, that [offering] is indeed obligatory by implication. For what purpose is this stated in the *sūtra*? It is for general knowledge. The recitation of this *sūtra* is mandatory at the time of the ritual action. If this is not performed, there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for a breach of the *yajus*. The fruit here, however, is purely transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*) in the *dakṣiṇāgni*. This technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) is established here because it relates to the subsequent pouring [of the oblation] accomplished by the *vaṣaṭkāra*. They proceed with the offerings to the dual deities (*dvidevatya*).

This introductory sūtra is intended to focus attention on the fact that the incidental matter is now concluded and the ritual acts to be performed hereafter are being stated. The purpose of this technical designation is evident in such passages as "they consume the double-deity cups" and "in the seasonal cups, in the Āditya cup, and in the Sāvitra cup, there is no *anuvaṣaṭkāra*. The meaning is clear. [End of Paṭala 150]. With the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa: To address the inquiry "How [is this done]?", he says:

"Thou art taken with a support; for Vāyu, for Indra and Vāyu, thee!"—with these words, the Pratiprasthātṛ takes a portion of the Aindravāyava cup as a *pratigrāhya* (counter-pouring) using the Āditya vessel.

The instrumental case in "ādityapātreṇa" is used in the sense of the locative (*saptamy-arthe*), because it is impossible for the Āditya vessel to be the instrument for taking a portion of the Soma already contained in the Aindravāyava vessel. The meaning is that he takes [this] by drawing it out as a counterpart to the previous [portion], hence it is called *pratini-grāhya*; "he takes that" is the sense. Even if the reading is *pratinihyam*, the meaning remains the same.
And he takes a second [draught] from the *droṇakalaśa* with the formulas: "Thou art taken with a support; thou art the seat of the dice."

The meaning is that with the mantra, "Thou art taken with a support; thou art the seat of the dice," he takes [the soma] by repeatedly seizing the second *pratinigrāhya* from that very *droṇakalaśa*. Or, the particle *vā* is used in the sense of *naḥ* (us). Here, the meaning of the word *pratinigrāhya* should be understood as "that which is seized again and again" (*pratirūpatayā nitarāṃ gṛhyate*). In all instances, the word *pratinigrāhya* should be understood as ending in the suffix *ṇamul*; thereby, repetition in the act of taking is established according to the circumstances. The taking is performed with the fingers (*pariplavayā*). The end of the mantra is: "I take thee with the two eyes."
The Adhvaryu takes the cup for Indra and Vāyu from the Droṇakalaśa, and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the King Soma as the counter-pressing portion by means of the dipping-spoon.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "from the *droṇakalaśa* [he takes] with the *pariplavā* [ladle], and the King [Soma] as well. The particle *ca* (and) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). From the very statement regarding the taking of the *pratinigrāhya* cup immediately after the *mahottara*, it is understood that a portion of the *aindravāyava* cup is drawn while it remains in its own place. In the phrase "and from the *droṇakalaśa* [he takes] the King [Soma] with the *pariplavā*," the word "takes" (*ādatta*) is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). In the phrase "the *pratinigrāhya* for the Pratiprasthātṛ," there too the word "takes" carries over. By the force of the statement regarding the taking, it is also understood that the placing down (*āsādana*) is likewise enjoined.

And that [offering] is indeed [performed] without a mantra, because there is no mantra. There is also a wiping with the *daśāpavitra* (the fringe of the woolen filter), according to the sūtra: "The wiping of all the cups.
Having gone out, he makes the *āghāra* offering with the *pariplava* ladle, saying, "May this sacrifice be a harmless one, O gods," so that it becomes offered in a whisper (*upāṃśu*).

Regarding the phrase "having gone out," the word "from the *havirdhāna* [shed]" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The mention of "having gone out" is for the purpose of establishing the basis (*ādhāra*) through the specific act of going out. Regarding the phrase "he pours the *āghāra* with the *pariplu* [ladle]," the word "the Adhvaryu" is indeed to be supplied as the ellipsis; for since the King [Soma] intended for the *āghāra* has already been taken by the Adhvaryu himself, the Adhvaryu's role follows by implication. By this, the possibility of the Pratiprasthātṛ performing it—on account of his proximity—is precluded.

The statement, "He pours the libation with the *pariplavā* [ladle]," is intended to prevent the following misconception: that the taking up of the King [Soma] in the *pariplavā* is for the purpose of the *vyāghāraṇa*, and that the pouring of the libation (*āghāraṇa*) is performed with that same cup. To avoid this, it means: "In whatever manner the *upāṃśu-upāṃśu* cup is offered, in that same manner he pours the libation. That manner begins with "he follows along the northern enclosing-stick" and ends with "he offers continuously.
The mantra "Hail to thee, O well-born Sūrya! is set aside by the specific mantra, "The sacrifice is indeed the Adhvara."
The reading should be understood as *pratinimādhyam*. 1. Not so; it is *niṣkṛtya*. 1. According to R., Ja., Sa., Na., and Tu., it is *nirṇāyam*. 868. From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha:
"Recite for Vāyu and for Indra-Vāyu; command for Vāyu and for Indra-Vāyu"—thus he issues the formal command (*saṃpreṣyati*).

The call for the *puronuvākyā* (invitatory verse) is indeed from the north of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line; and that belongs to the Adhvaryu alone, because of the singular number [in the formula]. Standing facing east with the gold [plate], he offers in the eastern part of the southern half, or in the eastern part of the northern half—by this general rule, both the facing-eastward and the standing are established for both [priests]. By this, it is established that the offering must be performed by the two [priests] standing facing east, to the south of the *pṛṣṭhyā* and behind the fire.
The Pratiprasthātṛ stands to the north of the Adhvaryu, who is to the south of the *pṛṣṭhyā*.
They offer when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, and they offer again when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered again.
This is the eighth [section]. The Pratiprasthātṛ pours the residue (*saṃpāta*) from the Adhvaryu’s cup into his own; the Adhvaryu pours a portion of that [residue] into the Pratiprasthātṛ’s cup.

Because of the statement "he pours the residue," it should be understood that the Pratiprasthātṛ must pour only a small amount. Because of the statement "he pours a portion," it should be understood that the Adhvaryu must pour a larger amount. The pouring of the residue by the Pratiprasthātṛ into his own cup is in accordance with the requirement for the consumption of the Soma; the pouring of a larger amount by the Adhvaryu is in accordance with the essential nature of the act of consumption itself. Thus it should be seen.
With the words, "For the gods thee," the Pratiprasthātṛ pours the residue into the Āditya vessel. || 15 ||

In this context, if the word *saṃpāta* were intended to refer merely to the residual portion of the substance itself, it would result in the inconsistency of applying the term *saṃpāta* to the vessel of the Pratiprasthātṛ, since a large quantity remains there. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: having caused [the substances] to flow together (*saṃpātya*), the pouring down (*avanayana*) must be performed. The fruit here is indeed transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*).
He covers [the vessel] with the formula, "To Viṣṇu, the wide-strider."

From the preceding sūtra, the word *pratiprasthātṛ* (the assistant priest) and the word *ādityasthālī* (the vessel for the Āditya cups) are carried over by modification from their respective positions. Because they are present [in the context], the injunction is made specifically with the Āditya cup. All of this has been clearly stated by Āpastamba: "O Viṣṇu, O Urukrama, this is your Soma; protect it"—with these words, the Pratiprasthātṛ covers the Āditya-sthālī with the Āditya cup. As for the mantra, it is employed by Āpastamba at the final covering, whereas for us, it is not so.
The only distinction for us, however, is that [the mantra] is prescribed by the Sūtrakāra for the closing of the lid (*sapidhāna*). "Mā 'vaḷyad" is the end of the mantra.
"Mayi vasuḥ puro vasuḥ"—with these words, the Adhvaryu hands the portion to the Hotṛ for consumption.

The notion that what remains in the cup of the *graha* is to be consumed arises from its having reached that state. The mention of the *adhvaryu* is for the purpose of excluding the *pratiprasthātṛ*. "Protect my speech"—this is the end of the mantra. Regarding this, Āpastamba states a specific rule: "Having taken the *praharaṇa*, having quickly passed by the *hotṛ*, [the *adhvaryu* says] 'Māthi vasuḥ, puro vasuḥ' and asks the *hotṛ* about the *graha*. The *hotṛ* accepts it with those very words. And this should be understood as belonging to the *yājuṣa-hautra* (the ritual procedure of the *hotṛ* according to the Yajurveda). [Gopīnātha Maṭṭa’s Jyotsnā Commentary, Volume 6, Section 869]

In this manner, they proceed with the two subsequent [verses] according to the respective deities. Regarding the phrase "with the two subsequent," the word "with the two cups" (*grahābhyām*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. The two subsequent [cups] are those for Kṣetrapati and Varuṇa, and that for the Aśvins. The expression "according to the deity" is stated in order to prevent the application of the *praisha* formulas—such as "Recite for Mitra and Varuṇa" and "Prompt for Mitra and Varuṇa"—which might otherwise be obtained by extension (*atideśa*).
One does not take [the draughts] from the *droṇakalaśa* for the two subsequent [deities], nor is there an *āghāra* libation for the two subsequent ones.

By the phrase "not [with] the two following *doṇakalaśas*," the taking of the *pratinigrāhya* cups is excluded. The meaning is that for the other two [cups], there is no [recitation of] "O gods, may this sacrifice be prosperous.
With each subsequent mantra, he takes [the cup] once and both offer [it] once.

Regarding the single taking, the successive mantras are: "Thou art taken with a support; thou art the heated one" (*upayāmagṛhīto 'sy ūṣat-tad asi*) and "Thou art taken with a support; thou art the famous one" (*upayāmagṛhīto 'si śrutasad asi*). The statement "both offer once" is intended to preclude the performance of the *vaṣaṭ*-offering which might otherwise be obtained by the rule "thus with the two following [mantras]."

With each subsequent [pouring], the Pratiprasthātṛ pours the residue into the Aditya vessel; with that very [residue] he covers it at every instance. At the pouring of the residues, the mantras become increasingly higher: "For the Viśvedevas thee! For all the gods thee! He covers it with this very [formula]: "To Viṣṇu, to Varuṇa. According to Āpastamba, this mantra is for the final covering; the word "eva" (only) is for the sake of excluding repetition. The meaning is that it applies in both cases everywhere. With each subsequent [offering], the Adhvaryu hands the portion to the Hotṛ; with this very [formula] the Hotṛ receives it.

In the offering of the *makṣas*, the subsequent mantra is: "May the Vasu who bestows wealth find his place within me; may the Vasu who gathers [all things] find his place within me. Or, he covers everything with the mantra: "I have performed [this rite] for the sons of Diti, the sons of Aditi, who possess wide protection, great shelter, and vast defense—those whose abodes are established according to their stations, and whom all beings worship with various [offerings] in every world.
This is clear. He now states the optional ritual procedure (*kalpa*).

If he should desire, "May evil befall him," then having first taken [the cup] with the Pratiprasthātṛ's vessel, he should offer while standing in front; having offered first, he should set it down. Because of the word "if" (*yadi*), this desire pertains to one who is departing on a journey. If the sacrificer, while departing, should desire, "May evil thoroughly befall this hateful Devadatta," then—at the time of setting down the vessels—he employs those three Vāyavya cups from the Pratiprasthātṛ's vessel (*pratiprasthāna*) upon the mound (*khara*). At the time of drawing the cups for the dual deities, each preceding one belongs to the Adhvaryu.

Having seized [the offering] with the mantra used for seizing one who is to be restrained, he should offer it while standing. Then, after the oblation, having poured out the remnants (*sampāta*), he should set it down as prescribed. Since the vessel is held by oneself during the performance, and because it is impossible to perform the subsequent rites while holding it, it is handed over to another's hand until the completion of the oblation. Although the status of "standing" is already established by the very nature of the rite accomplished by the *vaṣaṭ*-call, the explicit statement "standing" is for the sake of what follows.

Therefore, it is established that one should perform the placing (*āsādana*) while standing as well. The meaning is that one should offer the oblation (*juhuyāt*) and sacrifice (*yajet*). Although it would have been simpler to state, "Having taken the eastern [cup], having offered the eastern [oblation], he should place it," the separate statement, "Standing at the east, he should offer," indicates the existence of the pouring of the remnants (*saṃpātāvanayana*) and the covering (*apidhāna*). If it were stated simply, "Having offered at the east, he should place it," the *ktvā* suffix would convey the absence of intervention (*avyavahitatva*), thereby excluding those two [actions]; therefore, the separate statement is made.

It is understood that, beginning with the placing [of the Soma] immediately after the *homottara* (the subsequent oblation), one takes it up again, starting from the pouring of the remnants (*saṃpātāvanayana*). Here, "placing" (*āsādana*) refers merely to depositing it on the northern cart (*uttaradhi*), and not to depositing it in its own specific place (*svāyatana*), because that would be impossible without entering the *havirdhāna* shed. Furthermore, it is inappropriate for this procedure to be carried out without the formal entry into the *havirdhāna*. From the statement "in each case, the former [first]," it is understood that this rule applies to the Adhvaryu as well immediately thereafter.
If he should desire, "May I be of equal strength with my rival," they should draw [the cups] simultaneously, offer them simultaneously, and set them down simultaneously.
"With his rival"—that is, with one who is hateful; "of equal strength" means of equal power. "Simultaneously" means together.
According to some, one draws [the cup] at the time of the *dhārā-graha*.

Because it falls under the category of a *saṃdeśa* (an incidental instruction), this is an alternative view regarding the optional injunction itself. The meaning is that, according to the opinion of some teachers, at the time of drawing the *dhārā* (the stream-offering), the Pratiprasthātṛ draws the *pratinigrāhya* cups from those two-deity vessels either before or immediately after the time of drawing them by means of the stream.
In this case, he sets aside the vessels.

Here, the meaning is "in this optional injunction" (kāmye vidhau), or alternatively, "at this time. In the first interpretation, there is an exclusion of the obligatory rule (*nityavidhi*); in the second interpretation, there is an exclusion of the time of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath). "The vessels" refers to those for the *pratinigrāhya* offerings. "He discards" (*utsādayati*) means he destroys (*vināśayati*). The word "discarding" (*utsādana*) is seen in the sense of destruction in the passage: "In former times, the Kṣatriya power was discarded by Rāma of the unextinguished fire (*anagnyena*)."

From the very injunction "he removes the vessels," it is understood that in the preceding case there were separate vessels for the sake of the *pratinigrāhya* cups; from the statement "he removes them," it is understood that this procedure applies only to the optional (*kāmya*) rite.

If he should desire, "May he who is in the village be driven out from the village, and may he who is outside the village be established in the village," then the Adhvaryu should set down the vessel with the formula, "Here I drive out so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, from such-and-such a clan"; the Pratiprasthātṛ should set down the Pratiprasthāna vessel with the formula, "Here I establish so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, in such-and-such a clan. This is the ritual procedure connected with the sacrifice.

The mention of the *adhvaryu* is for the purpose of excluding the *pratiprasthātṛ*. The vessel of the *pratiprasthātṛ* is the *pratiprasthāna*. The manner of reciting the mantras here is also to be understood as being the same as previously described. The sūtra “the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is not connected with the sacrifice” has been explained. Having poured the *ādhavanīya* into the *pūtabhṛt*, and having wiped the jar with the fringes (*daśā*), he turns it face down. [Note: The numbers 1., 21., and 150 refer to variant readings or citations from manuscripts (ja, sa, a, da, na, pa, ma) by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa in his commentary Jyotsnā.]

The *kalaśa* is that which is called the *ādhavanīya*. Having wiped it with the fringes (*daśā*) of the filter, and having sprinkled it, one turns it upside down; the meaning is that one makes it face downwards. Since the mention of the *ādhavanīya* is already established by the reference "having wiped it with the fringes," the explicit statement of "*kalaśa*" is for the purpose that both of these [the *ādhavanīya* and the *pūtabhṛt*] may be understood by the plural form of the word "*kalaśa*" used in the phrase "the *pavamāna*-cups and the *kalaśas*."

The Hotṛ, the Brahman, the Udgātṛ, the Yajamāna, and the Sadasya are the central performers; the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the Potṛ, the Neṣṭṛ, the Acchāvāka, and the Āgnīdhra are the assistant priests (hotrakas).

"Those who act in the middle" (*madhyataḥkāriṇaḥ*) means those whose nature it is to perform their duties in the midst—that is, between—the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), beginning with the *adhipra*, during their coming and going. It is a worldly axiom that those who are principal are placed in the middle, while those who are subordinate are placed at the sides. Alternatively, the designation "those who act in the middle" is intended for the sake of clear identification in the context of the *maitrāvaruṇa* and others performing the *hotraka* duties, as in the passage: "The *camasādhvaryus* [should] offer the cups at the *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* calls."
In passages such as "O cup-officiants of the Hotrakas, having offered once each," the term *hotrakāḥ* is used for the sake of conventional usage.
All of them are cup-holders (*camasinaḥ*), and for every one of them there is a cup-officiant (*camasādhvaryu*). || 16 ||

Thus ends the sixth chapter in the eighth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. The meaning is that the *hotraka* priests are those who perform the duties in the middle during the *upayāja* offerings. For all the *camasins*, "per person" (*pratipuruṣam*) means for each individual; the meaning is that there are eleven *camasādhvaryus*, one for each cup-bearer. In the absence of a *sadasya* priest, there are exactly ten *camasādhvaryus*, because of the absence of the [eleventh] cup itself.

Since the offering of two *camasa* cups can be accomplished with two hands, and since this task can likewise be accomplished by five *camasādhvaryu*s—or even six when the *sadasya* is included—the statement "there is a *camasādhvaryu* for each person" is intended to preclude the number five. Furthermore, there is a scriptural passage from another recension (*śākhā*) stating: "Let him not offer; let one [person] alone [offer] two *camasa* cups with two hands."

The author of the *Nimitta* [the Bhaṭṭa school] also stated this same point through two sūtras: "But in the case of origination, because of the scriptural mention of plurality" (*utpattau tu bahutvaśruteḥ*) and "Because of the observation of indicative marks regarding the number ten" (*daśatvaliṅgadarśanāt*). The meaning of these will be explained later. Thus [ends the work] of Gopīnātha, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita—who was himself the son of Śrīmad Agniṣṭomayājin, Sāhasrāgniyukta-vājapeyayājin, Sarvatomukhayājin, and Viṣāhasrāgniyukta-pauṇḍarīkayājin, known as Okopāha.

In the commentary named *Jyotsnā*, composed by Dīkṣita, which serves to alleviate the distress of learned men caused by their failure to obtain the hidden jewels of meaning within the ocean of the *Śrīmad-Bhagavat-Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*, the sixth *paṭala* of the eighth *praśna* is concluded. Now begins the seventh *paṭala* of the eighth *praśna* in the *Śrauta-Sūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha.

He issues the command: "Recite for those being drawn out! Draw out the cup of the Hotṛ! Make them bright on both sides! O Acchāvāka’s cup-bearer, do not draw out [your cup]! O Pratiprasthātṛ, prepare the splinters, both sprinkled and unsprinkled! O Unnetṛ, make the Soma increase! Thus he gives the direction.

This directive, "anu hī," is addressed specifically to the Praśāstṛ, in accordance with the *Hautra* scripture. In the phrase "unnīyamānebhyo 'nuvīhi," the word "unnīyamānebhyaḥ" (to those being lifted) is a qualifier of the cups (*camasa*s). The dative case is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*). Because of the qualifier "unnīyamānebhyaḥ," this directive is occasioned by the act of lifting. The meaning is: "Recite the *unnīyamāna-sūkta* for the purpose of the lifting of Soma."

"O *hotṛ-camasa* [cup-bearers], fill yourselves up!"—this means: O *camasādhvaryus* of the *brahmā* and others who have become assistants to the *unnetṛ*, you must fill your respective cups after the *unnetṛ* has drawn [the soma] for the *hotṛ-camas*. The sequence is as follows: the *brahmā*, the *udgātṛ*, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the *sadasya*, the *maitrāvaruṇa*, the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*, the *potṛ*, the *neṣṭṛ*, and the *āgnīdhra*. Regarding the drawing [of the soma], he states a specific rule: "Make them bright on both sides."

"Those in which there is *śukra* (the bright Soma) at both ends—beginning and end—are called *ubhayataḥśukrāḥ*. Perform [the rites] with such [stones]. *Śukra* refers to the Soma residing in the *droṇakalaśa*. O *adhvaryu*, you have drawn that cup belonging to the *acchāvāka* from the *acchāvāka*’s position. *Mā niṣedhaḥ* means "do not restrain. That is to say, do not stop the drawing of the *acchāvāka*’s cup. Arrange near [the altar] these *prokṣitāprokṣitāḥ*—that is, sacrificial wood-shavings (*yajñiyavṛkṣaśakalān*) that have been both sprinkled and unsprinkled, and which are capable of serving as covers and supports."
The meaning of the command is: "O Unnetṛ, draw up the Soma, making it sufficient for the morning pressing and mixed with the *ekadhanā* waters.
He draws ten cups, headed by the *hotṛ*'s cup, excluding the *acchāvāka*'s cup.

"Those for whom the *hotṛ*-cup is the principal are the *hotṛcamasamukhyās*; [the text refers to] them. By this, the meaning of the word *anu* (after/along) in the phrase "you should pour out after the *hotṛ*-cup" (*hotṛcamasamanūnayadhvam*) is demonstrated. The sense is that, having first poured out the *hotṛ*-cup, one subsequently pours out the other ten cups everywhere. The number "ten" is used in the case where there is a *sadasya* (presiding priest). Here, since the number ten serves as a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*), when the question arises as to which cup's pouring out is to be excluded, [the answer is given]: "except for the *acchāvāka*-cup."

"He leads up the other cups except for the *acchāvāka* cup" means that he does not lead up the *acchāvāka* cup at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*). By this, the meaning of the formula "O *camasādhvaryu* of the *acchāvāka*, do not pour out your own [cup]" is demonstrated.

The *unnētṛ* takes [the draught] from the *droṇakalaśa* with the dipping-spoon (*pariplava*), pours it out into the *pūtabhṛt*, draws it up, and then pours [clarified butter] over it from the *droṇakalaśa*.

By this, the meaning of the mantra "O you two with white shoots on both sides, grow" is shown. Although it would have been sufficient to say "the spreading of the base, the bringing forward, and the sprinkling," as in the case of the taking up of the Āśvina cup, the full statement is made again for the purpose of indicating that here the *kāṇḍānusamaya* (sequential performance by sections) is strictly required. The mention of the *pariplava* (revolving ladle) is for the purpose of excluding the *udacana* (the vessel used for pouring out). Furthermore, the mention of the *droṇakalaśa* (wooden trough) here is not redundant.

This is meaningful because it serves to indicate that even after the pouring from the *ādhavanīya* vessel has occurred simultaneously with the declaration of the *uttāna* [formula], and following the spreading of the base (*upastaraṇa*) and the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) for all the *camasa*s, there remains a time for the pouring into the *pūtabhṛt*. If it is objected: "But surely, there is a mutual contradiction between the view that the action is performed by the *camasādhvaryu*s—indicated by the plural number in the injunction 'Pour after the *hotṛ*'s cup' (*hotuścamasamanūnayadhvam*)—and the view that it is performed by the *unnetṛ* alone," we reply: True. However, the use of the plural number is justified by taking the *camasādhvaryu*s as assistants.

Immediately after the drawing of the cups (*camasonnayana*), the Pratiprasthātṛ prepares the wood chips for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), both those that have been sprinkled and those that have not. The sprinkling is performed with the hand alone, because of the injunction regarding the preparation of the *pavitra* strainers. And that [sprinkling] is done with the palm turned upwards; for there is a traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating: "The sprinkling must be performed with the hand turned upwards. This is the procedure for all the cups;
the meaning is that this very same procedure for drawing applies to all the cups.
While that hymn is being chanted as they set forth, once it has been concluded, they take up the two cups with the Sāvitra formula.

The term *prasthāna* refers to the placing [of the fire] upon the *uttaravedi*. And it has been stated by Baudhāyana: "Having gathered [the fires], he places them upon the *uttaravedi*. Regarding the phrase "when the *sūkta* is being carried forth" (*prasthite... sūkte*), the ellipsis to be supplied is "once it has been completed. Now, the locative case used for the second case is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*). Thus, the meaning becomes this: when the *soma* juices have been set forth (*prasthiteṣu someṣu*), he completes the *sūkta* that is being carried forth. The word "completes" (*samāpayati*) is to be supplied for the sake of establishing the syntactical connection.

Beginning from the *unnayana* (filling) up until the *sādana* (placing), the *praśāstṛ* should recite the hymn (*sūkta*) in such a way that its completion occurs. The statement "in which [cup] it is girt" (*yasmin parihitaḥ*) is for the purpose of indicating that the placing of the two cups (*grahau*) occurs only after the girding, and not simultaneously with the girding. By the word "in that" (*tasmin*), the hymn being brought forward is referred to. The mantra beginning with "Sāvitra, of the god... and ending with "...from the taking" (*ādānakaraṇavādāt*) is used. "The two great, bright, and intoxicating ones" (*mahau śukrāmandhinau*).
"Ādadāte" (they both take) is the dual number; "the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ" is the ellipsis. To the inquiry "How? he says:
"The Śukra [cup] the Adhvaryu, the Manthin [cup] the Pratiprasthātṛ.
This is clear.
The *camasādhvaryu* priests take up the cups;
that is to say, the *camasādhvaryus* bring forward the cups that have been placed upon the *uttaravedi*.

They cover the *śukra* and *manthin* vessels with two sprinkled wood-shavings, saying: "Driven away are Śaṇḍa and Marka along with him whom we hate. With two unsprinkled shavings, they sweep away the dust from beneath [the vessels] and likewise support them with those two.

These two wood-shavings (*śakala*) are sprinkled; likewise, there are exactly two that are unsprinkled. Otherwise, there would be six—either sprinkled or unsprinkled. No, it is not so; they are well-stated. In this entire compound word, although the possibility of plurality exists, the duality of the two types of wood-shavings is fixed. This statement, "by means of the two sprinkled ones," serves both to demonstrate such a meaning and to show the application (*viniyoga*) of the wood-shavings that are about to be used. [This is from] the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [the eighth book]. In this complete term, even if the possibility of plurality were present, the duality of the two kinds of wood-shavings is certain; and in order to indicate this meaning and to demonstrate the application of the wood-shavings that are to be employed, the expression "by means of the two sprinkled ones" is used.

The mention of the two *śakala* wood chips is for the purpose of removing doubt. The two planets [the cups] are the *śukra* and the *amanthin*.
