By the word "he covers" (*apidhatte*), the preparation of the two *śakalas*, which are suitable for covering, is indicated. The purpose of the statement "with the two un-sprinkled ones" (*aprokṣitābhyām*) is to be understood in the same way as the statement regarding the sprinkled ones. The mantra "The two *śaṇḍa* and *marka* are driven away, along with him whom we hate" belongs to the *pratiprasthātṛ* as well. With the two un-sprinkled *śakalas*, they both shake off—that is, remove—the dust located in the lower part of the vessel.

The word "adhvaryū" [is used], with "the Pratiprasthātṛ and [the Adhvaryu]" being the understood sense throughout all these duals here. With those two very [vessels] that have been sprinkled, they take hold; they perform the *upayamana* (supporting) of the *śukra* and *manthin* vessels. The particle *ca* is for the purpose of including the mantra. Alternatively, this [means]: "With those two [vessels] below, which have been sprinkled, they take hold"; the particle *ca* is for the purpose of including the hands. And there exists in the Śruti text, "Having grasped them, they go out facing eastward," the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the verbal root *grah*.

And thus, having grasped [the vessels] from above and below with the right hand, the meaning is established that they go out facing east, with their faces turned toward the east. In this mantra, the person to be hated is indicated only in a general form and not by name, because the word "adāś" (giver) is absent. "Apanuttau" means repelled or driven back. "Stuto 'si janadhā devāstvā śukrapāḥ praṇayantu" (You are praised, O sustainer of people; may the gods who drink the *śukra* lead you forth)—with these words, the *adhvaryu* takes the *śukra*. "Stuto 'si janadhā devāstvā manthipāḥ praṇayantu" (You are praised, O sustainer of people; may the gods who drink the *manthin* lead you forth)—with these words, the *pratiprasthātṛ* takes the *manthin*.
The taking away of the foremost portion of each of these two offerings will be performed right there, as it is the principal act. The separate mention of the mantras is due to their distinction.
Some authorities prescribe the recitation of those two mantras as they go: "Wide is the mid-region."

Some reciters of the Vedic branches (śākhins) transmit the two mantras, "stuto'si" and "janadhā," as the acts of taking up [the cups] (*ādāna*). The meaning is that they declare this. In this view, the *sāvitra* mantra is excluded. In this alternative, the mantra for the bringing [of the cups] is "urvantarikṣam. "macchataḥ" means they go together with the *śukra* and *manthin* cups. Because it is well-known, the end of the mantra is "avihi. Āpastamba also states clearly: "They move forward [with the words] 'urvantarikṣamanvihi'."

"Join the life-force; quicken it for me! Join the out-breath; quicken it for me! Join the in-breath; quicken it for me! Join the diffused breath; quicken it for me! Join the eye; quicken it for me! Join the ear; quicken it for me! Join the mind; quicken it for me! Join the speech; quicken it for me!"—with these words, they join their forearms or their vessels at the front of the two *havirdhāna* sheds.

"In front of the *havirdhānas*" means in the vicinity of the two *havirdhānas*, that is, at their fore-parts. Since the word *havirdhāna* is in the dual number, it refers specifically to the two carts and not to the shed (*maṇḍapa*). Standing near the fore-part of the southern *havirdhāna* the *adhvaryu* and near the fore-part of the northern *havirdhāna* the *pratiprasthātṛ* join together—meaning they yoke or connect—the two *aratnis* or the two vessels. *Aratni* here refers to the hands; the vessels refer to those of the *śukra* and *manthin* cups.

This [rite] is an alternative to what was stated by the Brāhmaṇa: "The Brahman-saṃghāta. [Sūtra 19.7]: With the formula, "Thou art unassailable," they step upon the Uttaravedi with both thumbs. Here, the "thumbs" refer specifically to those of the feet, because of their association with the act of stepping. The mantra remains exactly as it is. The middle voice (ātmanepada) is used despite the change in subject. By the very sense of the action, the movement toward the Uttaravedi is established.

Moving around while "viparihantau" [the two of them] means moving about while pressing or scratching—that is, while scratching with their thumbs—the *uttaravedi* altar on all sides. "Viparihantau" is an archaic (ārṣa) term. Specifically, they move around the *uttaravedi*, scratching it with their thumbs. Such are the two Umās who move around the *uttaravedi*. The specific quality here consists in continuity. Moving around (*viparikramaṇa*) refers to descending from the vicinity of the *uttaravedi*.

"Generating offspring rich in heroes, go around with the bright [cup], O you of bright luster!"—with these words, the Adhvaryu carries it by the south. "Generating offspring rich in progeny, go around with the stirred [cup], O you of stirred luster!"—with these words, the Pratiprasthātṛ carries it by the north.
The terms "by the south" and "by the north" here imply "around the Uttaravedi," as this is understood from the preceding sūtra.
"May you two quicken; partake of the honeyed [mixture] on a good path"—with these words, the sacrificer consecrates [the cups] in front of the Āhavanīya fire.

The word "great" (*mahā*) alone is the remainder [of the compound], due to the context and because it is in the dual number. Here, the prescription regarding the vehicles and drinks is for the purpose of indicating the occasion. The phrase "the Āhavanīya fire by means of the vehicle" refers specifically to the act of driving; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the fire] being placed in front of the footprints.
On both sides of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), two [men] stand facing westward from the east.

In the phrase "in front" (*purastāt*), because the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is proximate, it is that very post which is connected [to the verb] through a modification of the grammatical form. There is no connection with the *āhavanīya* fire, for otherwise the word "in front" would remain redundant. "Facing west" (*pratyak*) means they stand facing the west; "they remain bent over" (*avanatau*) means they remain standing slightly stooped.
"Behind, facing east" refers to the *camasādhvaryu* priests.

Regarding the word "behind" (*paścāt*), the phrase "of the Uttaravedi" is to be supplied as the remainder. By implication, they face east (*prāñcaḥ*); that is, they are facing eastward. Although for some there might occasionally be a facing north (*udag-mukhatā*) based on the sūtra "or [they may be] facing north," the word "eastward" is used to preclude that. The verb "they stand" (*avatiṣṭhante*) is to be supplied as the remainder. According to the established rule (*parimāṣā*), their standing is such that they are not arranged along the water-side. The Adhvaryu joins his two forearms or two vessels with the mantra: "United from heaven and earth, the bright one, with bright luster. The Pratiprasthātṛ joins his two forearms or two vessels with the mantra: "United from heaven and earth, the stirred one, with stirred luster. || 17 ||

The two mantras spoken by the Brahman priest, ending with "saṃjajñānau diva ā pṛthivyā," are to be recited as alternatives for these two. The meaning is clear. I 1 kha, 't' etā| 4 Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha: [Eighth Book]...

You are life; bestow life upon me, bestow life upon the sacrifice, bestow life upon the lord of the sacrifice. You are breath; bestow breath upon me, bestow breath upon the sacrifice, bestow breath upon the lord of the sacrifice. You are sight; bestow sight upon me, bestow sight upon the sacrifice, bestow sight upon the lord of the sacrifice. You are hearing; bestow hearing upon me, bestow hearing upon the sacrifice, bestow hearing upon the lord of the sacrifice. O you two gods, Śukra and Manthin, bring about harmony.
"O divine clans, prepare yourselves! Bestow food and vigor upon us; bestow vital breaths upon the cattle, and progeny upon me and the sacrificer"—with these words they both consecrate [the cups].

This consecration belongs only to the two cups, Śukra and Manthin, not to the two wooden sticks (araṇis). Therefore, even when the two sticks are joined together, the consecration applies only to the two cups.

They place two sprinkled wood-shavings (śakala) [into the fires]: the Adhvaryu with the formula, "Thou art the support of the Śukra; O Śukra, this is thy fuel-stick; by it mayest thou be kindled," and the Pratiprasthātṛ with the formula, "Thou art the support of the Manthin; O Manthin, this is thy fuel-stick; by it mayest thou be kindled."

Because there is an absence of an injunction for an oblation (*juhoti-codanā*), there is here neither the utterance of *svāhā* nor the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*). In the mantra, the word *samit* signifies merely fuel-wood, as in the mantra "O Agni, you are kindled by the fuel-stick" (*samidhā samidhyase*), which contains the word *samit*. Thus, there is neither an offering nor an omission of the mantra. Regarding the placing of the wood-shavings (*śakala-abhyādhāna*), one may optionally use the two mantras prescribed in the Brāhmaṇa: "Thou art the fuel of Śukra" (*śukrasya samid asi*) and "Thou art the fuel of Manthin" (*manthinaḥ samid asi*). Having thrown away the two un-sprinkled [shavings] outside the altar with the mantra, "Śaṇḍa is cast out, Marka is cast out; Śaṇḍa and Marka are driven away along with him whom we hate," and having touched water, [the ritual continues].

*Śaṇḍa* is cast out; *Maka* is cast out; *Śaṇḍa* and *Maka*, together with *Amuṣmin*, are cast out—this is an option according to what is stated in the Brāhmaṇa. In this context of the Brāhmaṇa, in place of the word *amuṣmin*, the name of the enemy is to be uttered in the instrumental case (*-ā*). In the Veda, [the text says] "the two Mahāvedis"; outside, in the northern direction, the two splinters (*śakalau*) are thrown away. After the words "having touched water," the word "they stand" (*tiṣṭhataḥ*) is to be supplied. By the phrase "then, having touched water," a different, previously unstated act of touching is enjoined.

The act of touching water (upasparśana) is already established by the Smṛti rule: "One should touch water during the acts of cutting, splitting, discarding, and self-reflection. However, what is prescribed here is that specific instance caused by discarding. Therefore, while one [act] is established by Smṛti as a constituent part of the ritual, the other is not. Thus, the impossibility of a common agent (samānakartṛkatva) is also resolved. Having touched water... [kha. sāniyā | 2 kha, yayā | ga. tvayā | 877. sapaṭalaḥ] [This concludes] the section with the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

"Every morning, for the Prātaḥsavana, for Indra, announce the Soma juices that have been set forth—the bright, the stirred, the honey-dropping! O Camasādhvaryus of the central performers, offer the oblations at the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *vaṣaṭ* calls! O Camasādhvaryus of the Hotrakas, having offered once each, replenish from the *śukra* vessel and then withdraw!"—thus he issues the command.

This touching of water occurs after the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* (the response "Astu śrauṣaṭ"). The *bhaiṣa* (command) must be uttered in the singular number; for according to the *paribhāṣā-sūtra*: "The Adhvaryu, having caused the *āśrāvaṇa*, when the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* has been made, issues the command to the Maitrāvaruṇa, saying 'Prompt for so-and-so' (*amuṣmai preṣya*)."

Taking either a *graha* or a *camasa*, he causes the announcement (*āśrāvayati*). This is explained by the sūtra stating that it is "as in the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices," where the *Āgnīdhra*, standing in the *Āgnīdhra* shed facing south and holding the wooden sword (*sphya*), responds with the counter-announcement (*pratyāśrāvayati*); thus, the procedures for the announcement and counter-announcement apply everywhere. "O *Praśāstṛ*: at dawn, indeed at dawn—of the morning libation (*prātaḥsāva*) belonging to the morning, those [cups] which have the *Śukra-graha* and the *Manthin-graha*, and whose contents flow as honey, are called *madhuścutaḥ* (honey-dropping)."

The meaning is that he should direct the *hotṛ* priest to employ, by means of the *yājyā*, the Soma juices—which have become thus (i.e., purified), are for Indra, and have been drawn from the *havirdhāna* shed at the place of drawing up—once they have reached the *uttaravedi*. And thus, when the cups (*camasa*) have been brought to the *uttaravedi*, it is established that the *maitrāvaruṇa* should issue the direction (*praiṣa*). According to the *sūtra*, "He directs the *maitrāvaruṇa* with 'Direct [the *hotṛ*] toward so-and-so'," the direction is indeed addressed to the *maitrāvaruṇa*; subsequently, the *maitrāvaruṇa* impels the *hotṛ* to recite the *yājyā*.

"He impels the Hotṛ," according to the Sūtra; "impelling" (codana) means instigation. This should be understood generally throughout. Those who perform in the middle are the Hotṛ, Brahman, Udgātṛ, Yajamāna, and Sadasya; their Camasādhvaryus [are mentioned]. Then there are those designated by the term *hotraka*, beginning with the Maitrāvaruṇa and ending with the Āgnīdhra, for whom there is an offering at both the *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* calls. Their Camasādhvaryus, having offered at the first *vaṣaṭ* call alone, [take] from that small portion of the bright Soma located in the Droṇakalaśa vessel and pour it into the cups of the *hotraka*s.
"O you [cup-bearers], having been led up by the chief [Adhvaryu], come down—that is, approach—into my presence. This is the meaning of the *saṃpraiṣa* (direction).

When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, they all offer simultaneously. "All"—meaning the Adhvaryu, the Pratiprasthātṛ, the cup-bearers of the Madhyataḥkārin, the cup-bearers of the Hotrakas, and the Adhvaryus—all together, at the very moment the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered by the Hotṛ, offer the oblation; such is the meaning.

"He is the first fashioner, the creator of all; he is the first Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni; he is the first Bṛhaspati, the wise one. To that Indra I offer the pressed [soma]—svāhā! Thus says the Adhvaryu. "To that Mitra I offer the pressed [soma]—svāhā! Thus says the Pratiprasthātṛ.

The reading *mitrāya* belongs to another recension (*śākhāntara*). Or rather, [the deity] is Pārakṣudra for both [recensions]. Although a connection with Mitra is understood in the Manthin oblation, nevertheless, because the remainder of the sentence—*tau devā apanadyātmana indrāyājuhavur iti* (those two gods, having set him aside, offered [the Soma] to Indra themselves)—indicates that the *yājyā* verse has Indra as its characteristic mark (*liṅga*), and because the call (*praiṣa*)—*indrāya somān prasthitān preṣya* (Prompt the offering of the Soma set forth for Indra)—makes it clear that the deity is Indra, [the deity of the Manthin cup is Indra]. Thus ends [the section]. Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, 11.3.8–11.3.878.

[In the eighth question: The moon alone is the deity; "Mitra" is merely a qualification of Indra, because he is a friend (*mitra*) by virtue of being the sovereign of the gods. Thus, in this case, Indra himself, as qualified by that attribute, is the deity. Therefore, the relinquishment (*tyāga*) here is made with reference to the deity mentioned in the mantra, namely: "To Mitra, to Indra, this [be offered]."

Even though the qualified [deity] is the deity, according to the view that the qualified is not distinct from the pure [deity], there is no contradiction with the fact that the essential nature of Indra as the deity remains intact; thus, there is no conflict with the supplementary passage, "Those gods did not exclude Indra from themselves," nor with the *praisha* (direction) for the *yājyā* characterized by the mark of Indra: "Direct [the Hotṛ] to offer the Soma set forth for Indra. Furthermore, even though the *śukra* and *manthin* cups have their own *yājyās*, their offerings are accompanied by mantras because of a specific scriptural injunction. Accordingly, Āpastamba states: "The offering of the *śukra* and *manthin* is performed after reciting the respective *pratinigada*."

The meaning is that even for those who have the *śukra* and *āmādhi* as their *yājyās*, there is an offering accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ* call. The recitation of the word "svāhā" is intended to dispel the doubt that they might not perform the *svāhā* call on the grounds that the *vaṣaṭ* call already exists. The mantra is recited in such a way that the *vaṣaṭ* call and the *svāhā* call occur simultaneously.

Some authorities prescribe both [the *yājyā* and the *anuvākyā*] as being accompanied by the *anuvaṣaṭ* call; some prescribe them as being without the *anuvaṣaṭ* call; and others prescribe one of the two as being accompanied by the *anuvaṣaṭ* call.

"Having offered at the *vaṣaṭ*-call, offer again at the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*-call"—by this very statement, since both [libations] are established as having the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*-call (*sānuvaṣaṭkāra*), the repetition "some teachers recite them as having the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*-call" is for the purpose of demonstrating that this specific position is the one favored by Bāla Ācārya. Some teachers hold that they are without the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*-call (*ananuvaṣaṭkāra*), meaning both libations are devoid of the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*-call. Other teachers hold that only one of the two cups—the *śukra* or the *manthin*—is accompanied by the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*-call.
In this way, three positions are established.

Having drawn out a coal from the Āhavanīya fire outside the enclosing sticks toward the north-east, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers this residue of the Manthin cup as a complete oblation upon it, saying: "This, O Rudra, is thy portion."

"In the north-eastern direction" means in the *īśānī* (northeast) quarter; the sense is that it belongs to Rudra, because Rudra is the presiding deity of the northeast. The production of the embers takes place on the altar itself, within the enclosure (*paridhi*). This is clear from another sūtra: "Having drawn out embers from the *āhavanīya* fire inside the enclosure, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the residue of the oblation entirely into them with the mantra, 'O Rudra, this is your portion'. In the expression "from the *āhavanīya*," the ablative case denotes the source. The embers serve for the support of the oblation.

It should be understood that when it is stated in general terms, "Bring a jar," a jar that is indeed without cracks is brought; so it should be seen here as well. Having extinguished [the fire] and having removed [it] from the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*): since the *āhavanīya* fire is established by its association with the enclosing-sticks and its connection to the oblation, the explicit mention of the *āhavanīya* is for the purpose of indicating a specific meaning—that the charcoal to be taken must be one situated in close proximity to the spot where the offering of the *manthin* was performed. Upon that extinguished charcoal:

The expression "in that" (*tasmin*) is for the purpose of indicating its capacity to sustain the oblation; or alternatively, it is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that the pouring out of the embers is for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), by establishing that the offering must indeed be made in the *āhavanīya* fire. The expression "this" (*etam*) is for the purpose of making known that the entire remnant is intended; thus, it is established that the offering is not to be made from a single portion of what remains. The mention of "melted butter" (*mandha*) is for the purpose of excluding the *śukra*.

If it is asked: "Since the pouring out [of the remnant] is already established by the very statement 'he sets down the Śukra vessel,' what is the purpose of mentioning the *manthin* [vessel] here, given that this would exclude the *saṃsrāva-homa* (offering of the remnant)? The answer is: Because it is possible for the *manthin* to be an alternative option (*pakṣāntara*), one might suspect that a complete offering (*sarvahoma*) of its contents could also occur here. To prevent that, the mention of the *manthin* is necessary. The term *saṃsrāvya* is derived from the root *sru* with the suffix *ṇamul*, meaning "having poured out [the remnant] repeatedly. *Prati*... [text fragment].

The mention of the *prasthātṛ* is for the purpose of excluding the *adhvaryu*. The expression "entirely offered" (*sarvahuta*) is intended to show that the offering must be performed in such a way that not even a single drop remains. It is an adverbial modifier meaning "in such a manner that all the soma becomes offered in that action. Because it is enjoined by the root *hu* (to sacrifice), the utterance *svāhā* is required. Since the soma possesses a unique transcendental power (*apūrva*), the ritual rules of the *darvihoma* do not apply. This is a concluding rite (*pratipatti-karma*). Because the deity of the oblation is Rudra, there is the touching of water (*udakasparśa*).

The fact that [the vessel] has Rudra as its deity is known from the wording of the mantra, "O Rudra, do not seize this [victim]," and from the Brāhmaṇa passage stating, "In that case, Rudra does not regard the victim as his own. Regarding this, Āpastamba states a specific rule: "It is known that this is an 'ārtapātra' (a vessel causing distress), namely the *āmanthipātra*; one should take it away from whichever officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) one might hate. The sense is that because this vessel causes distress, one should not bring it into the presence of those who have performed the *tanūnaptra* rite, but should set it down right there in its own place.

In the Brāhmaṇa as well: "They say, 'O expounder of Brahman, why does he not consume the vessel of the Mandhī? [The answer is: 'Because it is a vessel of distress (ārtipātra). For if he were to consume it, the Adhvaryu would become distressed; therefore, he does not consume it.
At the second *vaṣaṭ*-call, the Camasādhvaryus of the central officiants offer their libations. This is clear.

"Let the cup of the Hotṛ go forward; let the cup of the Brahman go forward; let the cup of the Udgātṛ go forward; let the cup of the Sacrificer go forward; let the cup of the Sadasya go forward," he issues the command.

*Pretu* means "go forth with excellence. The excellence in going consists precisely in the immediate sequence following each respective *homā*. Although the *prastotṛ* and *pratihartr̥* are connected to the *udgātṛ*'s cup (*udgātṛcamasa*) according to the view of Jaimini, and even though they are connected to the *subrahmaṇya*, the singular number is used because the *udgātṛ* alone is primary. In the alternative view where the *sadasya* is included, the phrase is *prasadasyasya*. In expressions such as *prabrahmaṇaḥ*, the word *etu* (let him go) is to be construed after the prefix *pra-*; in *brahmaṇaḥ* and so on, the word *camasa* is to be construed immediately after.

And thus this meaning is established: "Let the cup of the Brahman go forward; let the cup of the Prastotṛ go forward; let the cup of the Yajamāna go forward; let the cup of the Sadasya go forward. However, the reading of the *praiṣa* (direction) remains exactly as it was recited. He explains the purpose of the *praiṣa*: "They carry the portions (*bhakṣas*) to the *sadas*.
The word *sadaḥ* is in the accusative dual. The meaning is that the *camasādhvaryus* carry those Soma-portions—the cups belonging to the Hotṛ and others ending with the Sadasya—toward the *sadas*.
He places the *śukra* cup with the word *sūda*.

The word *sūda* signifies "remainder"; thus, he places the cup for the *śukra* draught [with that word]. The remainder [of the action] is indeed that they should not move away, because the *śukra* cup belongs to the *adhvaryu*. It is in its very place. And so says Āpastamba: "Having placed the *śukra* cup in its place with the word *sūda*..."
The *camasādhvaryus* of the *hotṛkā*s, having offered once each and having poured a portion of the *śukra* into [their respective cups], withdraw.

Regarding the *hotṛkā*s beginning with the Maitrāvaruṇa: the *camasādhvaryus*, having offered their own individual cups once each, pour a small amount of the *śukra*—the Soma located in the *droṇakalaśa*—into their own respective cups from that vessel, and thus approach the presence of the Adhvaryu.
By means of those [cups], the Adhvaryu proceeds with the ritual.

Furthermore, it has been reconsidered: whatever duty is related to me (the Adhvaryu) is obtained for them by the designation *camasādhvaryu* (cup-priest); the mention of "Adhvaryu" is for the purpose of excluding that [designation]. Since the word "Adhvaryu" applies to them only figuratively (*gauṇa*), the sense is that their agency occurs only when the primary [application] is impossible. This point was also stated by Jaimini in the sūtra: *camasāṃścamasādhvaryavaḥ samākhyānāt* ("The cup-priests [perform] the cups because of the designation").

Having taken up the cup of Maitrāvaruṇa, he gives the command, "O Praśāstṛ, recite the offering prayer! Having offered it at the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *anu-vaṣaṭ* calls, he hands it over to the Camasādhvaryu and brings the portion for consumption to the Sadas.

In this case, there is the *āśrāvaṇa* (call for the response) after having taken hold of the cup (*camasa*). The specific distinction here is that once the response (*pratyāśrāvaṇa*) has been given, he takes it and issues the *praiṣa* (direction). Since the status of the Adhvaryu as the agent in this action is established by the very injunction "he hands it over to the Camasādhvaryu," the mention of the "Adhvaryu" in the preceding [text] might lead one to suspect the following meaning: that after the Maitrāvaruṇa-Camasādhvaryu has performed the offering, he hands it over to some other Camasādhvaryu whatsoever. To preclude this, [the text specifies the Adhvaryu]. In this manner, he proceeds with the subsequent [cups]. 18.

By the word "thus" (evam), it is extended by analogy that, having touched each respective cup, after the *āśrāvaṇa* has been responded to (*pratyāśrāvite*), one takes up each [cup], issues the *preṣa*, and at the *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* calls, offers it to the respective *camasādhvaryu* and brings it back to him always. Regarding this, he states the specific rule for the *preṣas*:
"O Brahman, sacrifice! for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; "O Potar, sacrifice! for the Potar; "O Neṣṭar, sacrifice! for the Neṣṭar; and "O Āgnīdh, sacrifice! for the Āgnīdh.

The *praiṣas* (directions) such as "O Maitrāvaruṇa, sacrifice," "O Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, sacrifice," and "O Āgnīdhra, sacrifice" have also been fully explained; they are now excluded [from this context]. The inclusion of the two [directions] "O Potṛ, sacrifice" and "O Neṣṭṛ, sacrifice" is because they follow in the established sequence. The meaning is clear. The word "he directs" (*saṃpreṣyati*) is the remainder [to be supplied] everywhere.
Having taken his cup, he goes to the *sadas* and announces to the Hotṛ: "The Āgnīdhra has sacrificed."

Regarding that Āgnīdhra cup: the statement "taking that cup" (tasya camasam ādāya) is for the purpose of [the Adhvaryu] carrying it himself. "He" refers to the Adhvaryu; the word "his" (tasya) serves to refer back to the Adhvaryu who holds the cup in his hand. By this, it is established that the placing of the Āgnīdhra cup occurs only after the question and answer have been completed, and not prior to them. This is intended to remove the doubt as to whether the Hotṛ’s cup might be excluded. The use of the genitive case indicates dependence upon the [preceding] action.

Being thus questioned by the Hotṛ, he replies, "He has indeed sacrificed" (ayāḍ), meaning "he has sacrificed" (ayākṣīt) in answer to the question; this is the established sense. The meaning of the sentence is: "The Āgnīdhra has sacrificed" (ayāḍ agnīd āgnīdhre). The Hotṛ replies, "He has performed a good deed, he will cause us to drink Soma. This refers to the subsequent duties of the Anuṣahotṛ. In connection with the consumption of the Soma (bhakṣa), he first states the relevant technical rule (paribhāṣā). [End of Section 7, Paṭala 1, from the Jyotsnā commentary by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.]

The *adhvaryu*’s portion for consumption arises from both the oblation (*homa*) and the pressing (*abhiṣava*), as well as from the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call by those who utter it, and from the designation (*samākhyāna*) of the cup-bearers (*camasin*).

By this, the causes for the various portions are stated. From the combination of both the oblation and the pressing, there is the consumption for the *adhvaryu*. The mention of the *adhvaryu* is for the sake of illustration; therefore, the consumption by the *pratiprasthātṛ* and others also occurs only through the combined performance of both the oblation and the pressing.

Now, one might object: since it is already established that the consumption [of the Soma] occurs through both the *homa* (offering) and the *abhiṣava* (pressing), and not by either action alone, the statement here is redundant; for its purpose would merely be to indicate that the cause is the combination of both *homa* and *abhiṣava*, lest there arise the doubt that it might not apply. To prevent such a doubt, this statement is necessary. Thus, those who possess cups (*camasa*) are called *camasins*. By virtue of this designation, there are the *hotṛ-camasa*, the *brahman-camasa*, the *udgātṛ-camasa*, the *yajamāna-camasa*, the *sadasya-camasa*, the *praśāstṛ-camasa*, and the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsi-camasa*.

The *potṛ-camasa*, the *neṣṭṛ-camasa*, the *acchāvāka-camasa*, and the *āgnīdhra-camasa*—this designation of "cup" (*camasa*) is based on the same principle as the word *kapiñjala* (partridge), namely that the consumption [of Soma] is occasioned by it. This very thing constitutes its status as the *brahmā-camasa*: that the Soma is consumed (*camyate*) in it for the sake of the *brahman*, because no other relationship has been set aside. As it is stated in another *sūtra*: "And what would that 'cup-ness' (*camasitā*) be, if there were no other relationship?"

In the phrase "and from the *vaṣaṭ* call of those who utter the *vaṣaṭ*," the word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include the *anuvaṣaṭ* call; therefore, the *anuvaṣaṭ* call is also an independent cause for consumption. Āśvalāyana states that the *anuvaṣaṭ* call is also a separate cause for consumption: "There is consumption at every *vaṣaṭ* call, but the subsequent [consumption] is silent.

He describes the specific order of consumption for the *adhvaryu* and *pratiprasthātṛ* (who perform the *vaṣaṭ*-occasioned consumption due to the acts of offering and pressing), for the *vaṣaṭ*-utterers (who perform consumption occasioned by the *vaṣaṭ* call), for those whose consumption is occasioned by their office titles (*samākhyā*), and for the *camasins* (those who consume from the cups).
The one who utters the *vaṣaṭ* first consumes [the offering], and after him, the *adhvaryu*—the latter being the one who holds the cup (*camasī*).

The one who pronounces the *vaṣaṭ* is the first; he consumes first. After that—that is, immediately following the consumption performed by him—the *adhvaryu* [consumes]; the mention of the object (*arthagrahaṇa*) is an indication for the acts of offering (*homa*) and pressing (*abhiṣava*). "Latter" (*jaghanya*) means being at the end (*jaghane bhavaḥ*); the meaning is that in the act of consuming, the holder of the cup (*camasī*) is the latter. Where many [persons] are assembled for the purpose of consuming in a single vessel due to the convergence of causes such as the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ*, among them, the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ* is the first and consumes first, not the *adhvaryu* and the others.

Because of the Vedic revelation, "The first portion belongs to the one who utters *vaṣaṭ*," and because of the further revelation, "Therefore, the one who utters *vaṣaṭ* is the first to consume all the sacrificial portions," as well as from the indicative mark (liṅga), "May they eat the oblation first," the priority belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer alone, even by virtue of the sequence of causal factors (*nimitta*), since the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance precedes the *homa* (offering). Nor should it be suspected that the Adhvaryu priest has priority because the pressing of the Soma (*abhiṣava*) occurs before the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance; for that [pressing] alone is not the determining factor.

But at the very end, the consumption [of the Soma] based on the designation (*samākhyā*) is [excluded], because that designation is weaker than other alternatives since it must be inferred. In the alternative view where [the Hotṛ] himself sits down and sacrifices—namely for the Hotṛ, Praśāstṛ, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, Acchāvāka, Āgnīdhra, and [the Pratiprasthātṛ]—there is a consumption occasioned by the *vaṣaṭ* call for the Hotṛ and the Pratiprasthātṛ. For the Sacrificer, there is consumption only when occasioned by the *vaṣaṭ* call. In the case of a very large oblation, for the Pratiprasthātṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Unnetṛ, there is consumption only when occasioned by the act of offering and pressing.

4.682. [In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, in the eighth book—] for the Hotṛ, Praśāstṛ, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, Acchāvāka, and Āgnīdhra, [the right to consume the Soma] is based both on their respective titles and on other causes. However, for the Brahman, Udgātṛ, Yajamāna, and Sadasya, it is based solely on their titles, as there is an absence of any other cause. Even in the case of the Hāriyojana cup, where there is no basis in a specific scriptural injunction (*vacana*), all [of these] partake. Therefore, following the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), the sequence is: first the Adhvaryu, then the Camasins.

Although "the one who has drunk" (*pītavān*) could have been used, the term "unfortunate" (*adhanya*) is employed to indicate that the consumption in one's own cup, caused by the title [of office], occurs only at the time following the drinking after the *homa* and *abhiṣava* performed by the Adhvaryu; it does not mean that the consumption by the cup-bearer (*camasin*) in his respective cup occurs immediately after the Adhvaryu has finished drinking from that specific cup.

Furthermore, there is consumption for every remnant and for every taking up [of the cup] when there is an interruption between two *homas* by a *vaṣaṭ*-call, or an interruption of the consumption by a *vaṣaṭ*-call, or an interruption between two *vaṣaṭ*-calls by a *homa*. And there is consumption when there is a conjunction of two [cups] that were not taken up together.

The "interruption by the *vaṣaṭ*-call between two oblations" (*homayoḥ madhye vaṣaṭkāravyavāya*) means the absence of the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ*-call at the same time as the oblation. "Interruption by the consumption" (*bhakṣavyavāya*) means the absence of the recitation of the mantra at the time of consumption. The "interruption by the oblation between two *vaṣaṭ*-calls" (*vaṣaṭkārayoḥ madhye homavyavāya*) means the absence of the oblation at the time of holding the *vaṣaṭ*-call. In both cases, "for every remnant" (*pratiśeṣam*) means for each respective remnant. "For every taking" (*pratigrahaṇam*) means for each respective taking. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction with the term "for every remnant."

In the phrase "of both the *homau* and the *vaṣaṭkārau*," the dual number is used in both instances with the intention of referring to the two offerings (*homau*) dedicated to two deities; therefore, this applies even when there are many [deities]. By the word *homa*, it is precisely the sacrifice (*yāga*) that is meant, because of the proximity of the term *vaṣaṭkāra*. Because of the mention of the word "interruption" (*vyavāya*), the taking of the remainder (*pratiseṣa-pratigrahaṇa*) and the consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*) are occasional (*naimittika*) with respect to the Veda.
And [this applies] when there is a conjunction of two [offerings] that have been separately drawn (*nānā-gṛhītau*).

Here, the letter *dhakāra* also signifies "even" (*api*). The meaning is that even when two oblations—which were not grasped together, but were grasped separately, and are now grasped at one and the same time—are separated by a *vaṣaṭkāra* or a consumption (*makṣa*), or when there is a separation between two *vaṣaṭkāras* or two oblations, this rule applies: namely, the remnant is to be taken up again and consumed. This occurs, for example, in the case of the *marutvatīya* offerings and others where the cups are drawn individually.

It is precisely to demonstrate this that the statement is placed here, setting aside the section on expiations (*prāyaścitta*), as it concerns only those deities associated with proximity and so forth.

Regarding the consumption of Soma by Vaiśyas and Rājanyas, there is the rule that the word *avaśyam* (necessarily) must be placed first in a compound. He states another perspective concerning the Soma-consumption of Rājanyas and Vaiśyas:

If a non-Brāhmaṇa should desire to drink Soma, he should fetch *stibhinī* shoots of the *nyagrodha* tree, grind them, mix them with curds, and strain them. When he draws out the other cups, he then draws out this cup of the sacrificer from that same [supply]. When he offers the other cups, he then takes a portion of this [grain] with a young blade of *darbha* grass, turns out a coal from the Āhavanīya fire within the enclosing sticks, and offers it with the formula, "I am thou. When he consumes the other cups, the sacrificer then consumes this cup.

By the phrase "if he should desire to drink," the primary position is that there is no consumption at all for the Rājanya and the Vaiśya; the desire to drink is merely incidental. This is the method [to be followed] if there is a desire to drink; it follows by implication that it does not apply if there is no desire to drink. Āpastamba states: "If one should officiate for a Rājanya or a Vaiśya, and if he should wish to cause him to vomit the Soma. And this has indeed been indicated by the author of the Sūtra through the use of the word *yajamāna* (sacrificer).

A non-Brāhmaṇa is one other than a Brāhmaṇa—namely, a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya. Although a Śūdra is also a non-Brāhmaṇa, he is excluded precisely because he lacks the qualification for Vedic study and for the performance of those rites prescribed for them. This is because the *Dharmaputra* states that initiation (*upanayana*), the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), and the fruit-yielding rites pertain only to those other than Śūdras; furthermore, the Śūdra is prohibited from sacrifice by the Vedic text: "Therefore, the Śūdra is unqualified for the sacrifice."

Jaimini also stated a prohibition by means of the sūtra: "Because there is no distinction [of caste] among the four varṇas. However, Niṣādas and Ārapakas have the right [to perform sacrifices] because of a specific scriptural injunction. Why would one not follow the scriptural injunction? For there is no overstepping of a scriptural injunction.

The *nyagrodha* is the banyan tree; its *stibhinyas* are the fruits or the sprouts. At the time of purchase, having purchased them according to the rules of purchase; at the time of swelling, having swollen them; at the time of carrying forward, having carried them forward; at the time of bringing down, having brought them down; and after the consecration of the King (Soma), having ground them properly upon another skin with other stones according to the rules of pressing—having mixed them with curds like Soma, and having squeezed the Soma-like liquid mixed with curds through another *daśāpavitra* filter into the vessels intended for that purpose.

At the time of the *unnayana* (filling up), having drawn from the *soma*-juice collected in the *vadhū* vessel into the *camasa* used for measuring, and after all the *camasas* have been offered at the *vaṣaṭ*-call, he takes that *camasa* in his left hand; immediately thereafter, taking a portion of the filled *camasa* with a young blade of *darbha* grass, he sets down a large ladle (*mahāra*) capable of holding the offering to the north of the *āhavanīya* fire within the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), and offers it with the mantra: "I am thou, thou art this; may we both be sweet."

"lokakṛj jātavedāḥ" is the end of the mantra. Since the complete recitation is not available, this oblation must be recited phrase by phrase (*vākyaśas*). Because it is enjoined by the root *hu* (to sacrifice), the word *svāhā* occurs at the end of the mantra. Jātavedas is the deity Agni, as indicated by the indicative mark (*liṅga*). The meaning is that after all the portions to be consumed have been eaten at the time of consumption, the sacrificer eats immediately thereafter. Furthermore, because some of the characteristics of Soma are directly prescribed and because vessels such as the *kalaśa*, *ādhavanīya*, *śukra*, and *apavitra* are mentioned, the characteristics of Soma are obtained here.

Therefore, at the time of purchase, the rules for purchasing apply; there is no *ohana* (the ritual act of pouring water over the Soma), because this [act] serves solely an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose. However, at the time of swelling (*āpyāyana*), the swelling does indeed take place, because this serves a visible (*dṛṣṭa*) purpose. Regarding the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) and the bringing down (*upāvaharaṇa*), these two also certainly occur, since they serve visible purposes in the form of being conducive to the pressing (*abhiṣava*) by means of remaining in close proximity. At the time of the pressing, the ritualists state that the mantras pertaining to the pressing also apply.

The Mīmāṃsakas, however, hold that the purificatory rites such as *abhiṣava* (pressing) apply equally (*samānavidhāna*) even to the occasional *kala-camasa*, because there is no difference in its being a means for the *apūrva* of the Jyotiṣṭoma. To this, [the Siddhāntin] replies: since it is impossible for a permanent purificatory rite to have an occasional *phala-camasa* as its locus, and because the occasional [element] is not present at that time, there is no equal application of the rule. Thus, the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* states: "The occasional [rite] shall not have an equal application because of its inequality. This means that whenever [the occasion arises], [the occasional element is not subject to the same rules].

By this, the meaning is "at which time. The reading "when he draws up the other cups" (*yadā'nyāṃścamasānnunayati*) is indeed straightforward. In the same way, two readings should be understood for the following two cases as well. The word *atha* signifies immediate succession. By this, it is established that the drawing [of the fruit-cup] occurs immediately after the drawing of all the cups, neither in its own place nor prior to them. By the word *etad* (this), the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) is referred to. This reference is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

Therefore, immediately after this, he infers that it is not always the case that the sacrificer partakes [of the remainder]. Thus, from this juice of the fruit (phalarasa). This very purpose applies to the two subsequent uses of the word "atha" (now/then). The word *taruṇa* refers to a blade of grass (*yava*). The rule is that one should throw [the scrapings] with two blades of Darbha grass, because it is well-known in that very way. Because of the singular number, there is only one blade of Darbha. This instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) denotes accompaniment (*sāhitya*).

And thus there is this traditional rule: "One offers with a vessel in the shape of a *dāka* accompanied by young *darbha* grass. Alternatively, the word "young" (*taruṇa*) refers to the *dāka* vessel itself; in that case, the meaning is that the offering is made with *darbha*. In this view, the vessel shaped like a *dāka* is not the instrument for the oblation, but rather the firm *darbha* grass itself. In this view, the offering consists of more than just parched grain. Or else, the word "young" denotes a clump; thus, the meaning becomes that one offers with a clump of *darbha* grass.

Even in this view, there is merely the act of consuming (*trāvaṇa*). Wherever there is a sacrifice upon the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, in that very place this oblation is to be offered. However, in the case of the shaking (*kampana*), this is not an oblation, but rather the shaking itself. The genitive case in the word *etasya* (of this) should be understood as intending the cup together with the remaining *nārāśaṃsa* vessels. Therefore, wherever there is total consumption of the Soma by others, there too there must be total consumption by him [the sacrificer]. In that case, there is a modification (*ūha*) of the mantras containing the characteristic marks of Soma, because even in the archetype (*prakṛti*), such modifications are a constant feature.

There is no modification (*anūha*) for the occasional rites (*naimittika*) in the *Bāhvṛcya*, because of the injunctions regarding the consumption of the Soma and other acts by means of [formulas] such as "when [it is] left over," which bear the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of Soma; and also because the juice of the *vaṭa* tree is praised by the word "Soma" in the passage, "This King Soma is, as it were, hidden, namely the *nyagrodha*.
They consume the cups belonging to two deities (*dvidevatya*).
This [statement] is intended to establish the application within the context of the archetype (*prakṛti*). When there is an expectancy as to who is to be included by this plural number, he says:
The Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Pratiprasthātṛ.
The sense is that the connection of the Pratiprasthātṛ is mediated by the *saṃpāta* (the residue of the oblation). To demonstrate the sequence, he says:
"In this order."

In this very way, wherever there is such a successive order, they are thus "successive" (*anupūrvāḥ*). This same order is universal in the method; it is for that purpose alone, and this is merely a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). The meaning is that this same order applies everywhere in both the invitation (*upahava*) and the consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*);
they desire the invitation from one another.

Since *anyonya* is treated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the usage of the locative case ending in *anyonyasmin* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). The meaning is that they should desire—that is, they should perform—the mutual invitation (*upahava*). The scriptural reason for this should be understood here from the prohibition: "Soma is not to be drunk by one who has not been invited; indeed, by drinking Soma without an invitation, one becomes deficient. Mutual authorization is the *upahava*; without performing it, Soma must not be drunk. By the phrase "by a Soma-drinking without an invitation," the meaning is that one becomes "deficient" (*vyardhuka*), that is, one whose nature is devoid of satisfaction (*vigata-tṛṣṇā-śīla*). He states the form of the mantra for the invitation:

"Upahvayasva" (invite) is the *āmantraṇa* (invocatory formula). The word "of the mother" (*mātraḥ*) is the ellipsis, as indicated by the masculine gender. The meaning is that the mantra by which one is addressed—that is, made present before [the deity] or invited to partake—is called *āmantraṇa*. By implication, this means that the name of the person for whom the *upānman* (invitation) is intended must be mentioned in connection with the ritual action. Otherwise, it would not be known by whom the invitation is being performed through this [formula].

This has been clearly stated by Āpastamba: "He addressed him by means of the ritual name, saying, 'O so-and-so, come hither; O so-and-so, do thou favor us. In that context, the address consists of "O Praśāstṛ, do thou favor us" and "O Brahman, do thou favor us. This is known from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the phrase "O Praśāstṛ, O Brahman, sacrifice! He states the nature of the response mantra: "The response is 'Thou art favored' (*upahūtaḥ*). It is called a "response" (*prativacana*) because one responds with it; as before, the remainder is simply that it is a mantra.
"Wherever they might eat at the same time, they should desire an invitation (*upahava*) from one another.

"The same time" means simultaneous. Thus Āpastamba says: "Those who eat together in the same *prāya*, they should desire an invitation from one another. By the etymology "that which goes with excellence" (*prakṛṣṭa-gati*), the word *prāya* refers to time; this is because of the expression "wherever... at the same time. He considers that in the case of offerings to two deities (*dvidevatya*) and so forth, the occasion for the invitation is indeed distinct, and that consists in the state of using a single vessel. Thus Āpastamba says: "And those who [eat] from a single vessel."

By the word "vessel" (*pātra*), the Soma contained therein is indicated; or it may be analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose [share] is a single vessel. The meaning is "the Soma situated in a single vessel. The consumption of the *atigrāhya* cups serves as an illustration of consumption based on designation (*samākhyā*). Examples of the "single vessel" category should be understood accordingly as the *dvidevatya* offerings and so forth. Here, there is the consumption of the remnant of the *āghāra* libation. Even in the absence of a formal participant in the consumption, an invitation (*upahava*) is required here, because of the prohibition: "Soma must not be drunk by one who has not been invited. And that [inviter], due to proximity, is the Hotṛ priest. He consumes the *aindravāyava* cup twice, and each of the other two cups once.

Āpastamba states that [the Adhvaryu] does not call out "Obeisance" (anutsunantau) for the vessel; likewise, there are two ṣaṭkārās here and the *iḍā*. The other two, the Maitrāvaruṇa and the Āśvina, perform them once each; the sense is that this is because there is only one ṣaṭkāra and one oblation (*homa*).

Regarding this, Āpastamba, having stated "they consume" (*bhakṣayanti*) or "he consumes" (*bhakṣayati*) for those two who consume the *aindravāyava* cup twice, and having said "once each time," he himself provides an explanation of the alternative options: "for those [in the case] where it is 'they consume' (*bhakṣayataḥ*), the meaning is that the Adhvaryu and [the other] have taken it; and for 'he consumes' (*bhakṣayati*), the meaning is that each one [consumes] it. By this, the meaning of the singular number is established: whoever is the consumer here, he alone consumes it.

In the reading "bhakṣayanti" (they eat), however, the Pratiprasthātṛ’s consumption is also included, even though it is not explicitly mentioned, due to the force of this plural number. There is no doubt at all regarding a reading ending in the dual number in our Sūtra. The repetition "sakṛtsavan" (once at each pressing) follows the duality of the cups.

[The procedure is: first, the cup for Indra and Vāyu is held near the breaths; first, the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa is held near the eyes; and the cup for the Aśvins is carried around on all sides and held near the two ears.

The phrase "he eats" (*bhakṣayati*) or "they eat" (*bhakṣayanti*) also carries over here, following the previous recension. In the Brāhmaṇa, with the desire to prescribe a specific rule for the Āśvina cup, the word "in front" (*purastāt*) was restated after the two preceding [cups], namely "the avoidance of all around" (*sarvataḥparihāram*). He performs an imitation of that very [rule] here;
it should be understood that the reading "he has performed" (*kṛtavān*) found in all manuscripts is an error.

1. From that [it follows]. [Variant: *sya tat*. 112.1.886. The author of the Sūtras [states] "the cup for Indra and Vāyu first," and so forth. Because of the plural number in the word "prāṇeṣu" (in the vital breaths), both the nostrils and the mouth are included. It is well known that when both nostrils are blocked, the clear utterance of speech does not occur at all. Therefore, because these two also possess the capacity for the utterance of speech, they too are included.

Nor should it be argued that, because of the Vedic text "He does not speak before him," the word *prāṇa* refers only to the mouth, and that the plural number is justified by the inclusion of the nostrils as well. For such an assumption is improper unless there is no other way to explain the passage; it is a resort of those who have no other recourse. Due to the mention of the suffix *ṇamul*, each individual [organ] is to be understood. This is stated by Āśvalāyana: "After the invitation (*upahava*), [he smells], saying 'O Adhvaryu, may you partake,' and having smelled with the two nostrils."
"Having avoided it from all sides, he avoids it head-on. This [word] also ends in the suffix *ṇamul*. Therefore, here too, the act of avoidance occurs twice.
"Having consumed all," [this continues] until the non-dropping [of the cup], with the words "not dropping" [implying] the limit.

Immediately after "all," the remainder is "at their respective times. In the phrase "until the non-dropping," the former limit is the consumption by all. Thus Āpastamba says: "When they have not yet dropped [the cup], they consume the Aindravāyava; they consume it once each, or they consume it together."

Having poured all the remnants into the Hotṛ’s cup, he places a fragment of the sacrificial cake into the vessel for Indra and Vāyu, the curdled milk into that for Mitra and Varuṇa, and the parched grains into that for the Aśvins; these he sets down on the northern track of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, where they remain until the third pressing.

The placement [of the vessels] is for the sake of attention. Regarding the *payasyā* (curdled milk) and *āmikṣā* (coagulated milk), the phrase "he places [it] in the vessel of the Maitrāvaruṇa" follows from the previous context. "Vartanī" refers to the path of the cart wheels; here, the term "path" (*prāya*) signifies the act of placing, because it conforms to the placement along the wheel-path. The prefix "ā" [in *ā-tṛtīyāvanāt*] indicates inclusion up to the third pouring. Here, during the third pouring, while the verse beginning with "kayā naścitra ā bhuvat" is being recited, [the thought arises]: "May we be united at dawn."

The *prasthātṛ* priest, having separated the vessels for the dual-deity offerings (*dvidevatya*), having carried them away to a distance, and having washed them at the *mānala* fire-altar, shall place them in their respective places through the eastern door. Herein lies the third stage of the ritual action involving the washing and setting down of the vessels. The plural number in the phrase "they lie around" (*pariśerate*) is used because there are three vessels containing the sacrificial oblations (*havirviśiṣṭapātra*). Since the text explicitly mentions the washing and the placing of the vessels while they still contain the *havis*, those very vessels, being thus not empty, should remain set down lying around.
This is for the continuity of the sacrifice (*yajñasya saṃtatyai*); so says the *Brāhmaṇa*.
Having performed the cutting-off (*niravadāya*), he places the *iḍā* portion before the *hotṛ*.
*Grahaṇam* means taking up; it signifies that one places [the vessel] down or offers it.
The *camasādhvaryus* lift up their respective cups while the *iḍā* is being invoked.

"While the *iḍā* is being invoked" means they lift up—that is, they restrain—the cups in the vicinity of the *iḍā*, each *camasādhvaryu* restraining his own cup. As before, [this refers to] the eighth section of the sixth chapter, accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha.

He holds the *hotṛ*’s cup so as not to touch it; the *camasādhvaryu* of that [cup] holds it so as not to touch it, nor even to come near it. In the previous case, there was merely holding the cup first, but no touching; however, in the case of the *hotṛ*’s cup, there is touching—this is the distinction.
They consume the portion when it has been invited, just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
By the mention of the original subject, the act of eating is suspended, even though a relationship exists between the Pratiprasthātṛ and the Maitrāvaruṇa.
He places a portion of the *iḍā* for the Acchāvāka after they have eaten and performed the ritual purification (*mārjana*).

The expression "when [the *iḍā*] has been consumed" (*prāśitāyām*) is intended to establish the sequence, indicating that the placing of the *iḍā*-portion for the *acchāvāka* must be performed prior to the consumption. In the preceding section, there was no understanding of sequence; rather, this [statement] serves as a general injunction. Furthermore, since the rule that "the wives, with the sacrificer as the fifth, eat the *bhakṣya*" is already established, this statement here serves to show that the *mārjana* (cleansing) occurs only after the consumption of the *iḍā*, and not in the middle, even if another [act] were to apply.

By this it is understood that there is also the eating of another [remnant] in the middle. And that is of the remnant of the sacrificial oblation (*havirucchiṣṭa*). This has been stated by Āśvalāyana: "They eat that remnant of the oblation. However, that [eating] belongs only to the four original [officiants], not to others. But for those who follow the *Saṃhitā* of Āśvalāyana, it certainly does occur, in accordance with his sūtra:
"He proceeds with the whey (*vājina*) as in the Vaiśvadeva [parvan]. (19)

Because the *bhakṣaṇa* (eating) is the primary factor, the singular number is used; however, there is no exclusion of the relationship with others. This is just as in the case of the *vaiśvadeva*, due to the rule of extension (*atideśa*). The word "they move" (*caranti*) refers only to the *vṛṣan* (bull). In this context, there is no displacement (*utkarṣa*). Thus says Āpastamba: "For among these, the subsidiary remainder (*prasaṅga-śeṣa*) does not extend. Regarding these sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśas*), the subsidiary elements that depend on the occasion (*prasaṅga-upajīvya*), such as the *paśu-yūpa* (animal-sacrifice post) and so forth, even when being displaced, do not displace the specific *vājina-caryā* (ritual procedure for the whey) belonging to these.

Why? Because there is no connection between the *pāśuka* [animal sacrifice] rites such as the *anyādhāna* and the specific duties of the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*), such as the *vājinacaryā* and so forth; and since there is no such connection, it is impossible for them to be established through the sequence [of the ritual]. As stated by Jaimini: "Because of the lack of connection with the incidental [elements]. The meaning is that because of the lack of connection, the *vājinacaryā* and other such acts do not apply. One undertakes the rites beginning with the cleansing (*mārjana*) of the *savanīya* offerings, just as in the case of the animal-cake offering in the *nirūḍhapaśubandha*.

The rites involving the flour-smeared remnants (*piṣṭalepa*), the husks (*phalīkaraṇa*), and the *amṛtī* [offering] of the *savanīya* cakes are undertaken; this much alone being sufficient to establish that the rites beginning with the measuring (*māna*) are undertaken, the repetition of the term "undertakes" is for the purpose of indicating that there is also an occasion for the cleansing (*mārjana*) even after the distribution of the whey (*vājina*).
The cup-bearers (*camasin*) consume [the soma] according to their respective cups; the mantra for their consumption has already been explained.

"Without passing over the *camasa*," [refers to] each respective *camasa*. Regarding those *camasins*, the procedure has been explained by the sūtra beginning with "The *makṣa*" (drinking) and ending with "Some recite this as a universal rule. The application has been explained. In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, although one should simply say "*makṣa*," the inclusion of the term "mantra" is for the purpose that whichever of the two optional mantras is chosen by the *adhvaryu*, that same one must also be chosen by the *hotṛ*.

Among all those who consume [the Soma], the Hotṛ priest first consumes it once from each of the cups, and twice from his own cup. The word "again" (punaḥ) is used for emphasis, meaning that he consumes it twice specifically from his own cup. The intention is that since the *anuvapaṭkāra* (the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call) serves as a consecration for the Soma contained within the cups, it is appropriate that the consumption occasioned by that *anuvapaṭkāra* should proceed precisely with the consumption from the cups belonging to one's own presence.

Since there is no partaker [of the Soma] in the *hautṛ-camasa* during the morning and midday pressings, the consumption based on the ritual designation (*samākhyā*) is accomplished by way of a common application (*tantra*).
Regarding the cups that have been refilled and twice consumed, the Adhvaryu consumes them once each.

The meaning here is that for the juices remaining in the cups which have already been consumed twice by the Praśāstṛ and others—once on account of the *vaṣaṭ*-call and once on account of the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ*-call—the Adhvaryu performs a single consumption for each cup, occasioned by both the *yūpa-abhiṣava* (the pressing over the sacrificial post) and the [original] *vaṣaṭ*-call.

The third [consumption] belongs to the *hotraka*s at the end. Regarding the consumption by the *adhvaryu* from the *homābhiṣava* vessel and the consumption by the *camasin*s due to the designation (*samākhyāna*) of the *vaṣaṭ* utterer: "The *vaṣaṭ* utterer consumes first, then the *adhvaryu*, then the other *camasin*s"—by this, the consumption based on designation is established for the *hotraka*s who perform the central rites. As for the mention of "the third [consumption] belongs to the *hotraka*s," if they have already consumed in the middle, then the designated consumption is distinct; otherwise, there is a single performance (*tantra*) of both the consumption occasioned by the *vaṣaṭ* and the consumption based on designation.

This is for the purpose of making known that [the procedure] pertains to the *prakaraṇa* (context). Here, the portion for the *hotraka*s is distinct; because there is a separate individual consumer (*pratibhakṣitr*), these [consumptions] do not form a single ritual complex (*tantra*). However, for the *hotṛ*, the consumption based on designation (*samākhyā*) is separate, due to the absence of a separate consumer. But in the first two pressings (*savana*), because there is no separate consumer, the consumption based on designation occurs by that very [means]. Wherever there is an absence of a separate consumer, there it occurs only by means of the [designation], namely at the end.
Having consumed all [the portions], they cause them to swell with the mantra, "Swell up! May [the essence] come together to thee!"; thus they become the *nārāśaṃsa*s.

The word "evil" (*pāpa*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. "By means of desire" (*lobhena*) refers to the swelling or nourishing with the *vasatīvarī* waters; this is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the text, "he causes to swell. Others say it is performed with a mantra. Likewise, Āśvalāyana says, "they should touch [the cups] with the mantra. Kātyāyana, however, says: "With the two verses, 'Swell up' (*āpyāyasva*) and 'May it come to you' (*sametu te*), they touch the cups that have been drunk, or they pour Soma into them. Baudhāyana, however, regarding the *vasatīvarī* waters, says: "One should cause [the cups] to swell with those brought [waters], and with those one should press [the Soma]. These [cups] become the *nārāśamsa* offerings.

The meaning is that the cups (camasas), having been thus replenished, receive the designation "Nārāśaṃsa" because they have Narāśaṃsa as their deity. He places them behind the axle of the southern Havirdhāna cart, extending towards the north; he places the two cups of the Neṣṭṛ and the Āgnīdhra between [the other cups].

Those *nārāśaṃsa* cups. The rest is clear. He places them between the cups of the *neṣṭṛ* and the *āgnīdhra*. Here, the word "between" (*antarā*) refers by implication to that which is characterized by an interval. And this qualification pertains to the cups of the *neṣṭṛ* and the *āgnīdhra*. The accusative case is used because of the rule "with *antarā* and *antareṇa*, the second case is employed.

The *acchāvāka* sits down in front of his own hearth (*dhiṣṇiya*), outside the *sadas*. By the phrase "in front of his own hearth, outside the *sadas*," it is understood here that the instruction extends only as far as the area outside the *sadas*.

To him he gives a fragment of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), saying: "O Acchāvāka, speak what is to be spoken by you. The reading is indeed *ādadāt* (he was giving); *ādadhat* is a scribal error, meaning "while giving. [The sense is: "O Acchāvāka, speak that which is fit to be spoken by you.
When the Acchāvāka says, "O Brahmins, invite these Brahmins," [the Adhvaryu] issues the command: "This Acchāvāka desires an invitation; O Hotṛ, invite him."
He gives the direction to the Hotṛ upon hearing the word "Oṣe. Here, by the word "direction" (praiṣa), the announcement (āvedana) is meant.
At the moment he recognizes that the Hotṛ is being invited, he takes up the cup of the Acchāvāka and issues the direction: "Recite for the one being drawn out! (unnīyamānāyānubrūhi).

At the time when the Acchāvāka, being invited by the Hotṛ with the mantra "O Hotṛ, invite us; the cows have been invited," does not eat, at that time the Adhvaryu, having taken the Acchāvāka’s cup, issues the call to the Acchāvāka, saying, "Recite for the one being filled. Here, the one who performs the filling is indeed the Adhvaryu of his own cup, not the Unnetṛ.

Āpastamba has stated by way of an injunction: "O Camasādhvaryu of the Acchāvāka, when [the Soma] is being drawn out, draw it out; make it bright on both sides. By this, the Unnetṛ does not have the mantra for the act of drawing out. Having spread a base with water from the Droṇakalaśa using the *pariplava* ladle, he draws [the Soma] from the Droṇakalaśa and pours it over [it]; according to the Sūtra—"This is the ritual procedure for all the cups"—this rule applies to this cup as well.

When that *unnīyamāna-sūkta* has been concluded, he issues the command, "O Acchāvāka, recite the *yajyā*. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the oblation; at the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ* utterance, having offered, he carries away the portion for consumption. This occurs when the *sūkta* being recited by the Acchāvāka has been concluded. The procedures regarding the *āśrāvaṇa*, *pratyāśrāvaṇa*, and so forth, follow the *Parimāṣāsūtra* of the Soma sacrifice. The rest is clear. He does not consume it together with him. [From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Eighth Book, Section 1] (Note: The text contains references to manuscript variants such as *ja. sa. ma. da. 'dayā* and page/section numbers like *890*, which have been omitted from the translation as per instructions.)
Even though the conditions for it exist, there is a cessation of the *bhakṣa* (consumption) for the two officiants (*adhvaryū*) because of a specific statement.
"He does not desire an invitation (*upahava*) in this [case]";
in this instance, the *acchāvāka* does not desire an invitation from the *adhvaryu*.
If one should desire an invitation (*upahava*) toward him, he should simply say, "Eat!
If the *acchāvāka* should desire an invitation toward the *adhvaryu*, then [the latter] should say, "O Adhvaryu, eat!"—this is the invitation for drinking.
Having eaten and caused [the cup] to swell, he places the two cups of the *neṣṭṛ* and the *āgnīdhra* between them.

Because of the prohibition against the *upahava* (invitation), in the absence of an *upahava*, there arises the possibility that the *makṣa* (the portion) itself might not be consumed due to the prohibition: "Soma is not to be drunk [without an invitation]. To prevent this contingency, this statement regarding the consumption and swelling (*āpyāyana*) is made as a qualification for that purpose. Having been swollen by the *māśin* (the Maitrāvaruṇa), the *acchāvāka* places it in his own cup; and the *neṣṭṛ* places his cup between those two cups, which are at the end of the group. The sense is that its place is precisely that which is established by the sequence of the ritual. This very spot is, from now on, the place of the *acchāvāka*’s cup. 20.

Thus ends the seventh chapter in the eighth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. From this point onward, up until the third *savana*, the procedure is exactly the same as that [previously described]. The rest is clear. This *acchāvāka* must be performed by one who is specifically a *baḍhaca* (one belonging to the Ṛgveda). Accordingly, it is stated in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa: "Whosoever among the Brāhmaṇas is a *baḍhaca* and is powerful, he should perform the duties of the *acchāvāka*. [This concludes] the work of Gopīnātha, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was a performer of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice a thousand times, a performer of the Atirātra sacrifice a thousand times, a performer of the Vājapeya sacrifice a thousand times, a performer of the Sarvatomukha sacrifice a thousand times, and a performer of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice a thousand times, and who belonged to the lineage of Okopāi.

Thus ends the seventh paṭala of the eighth praśna in the *Jyotsnā* commentary composed by Dīkṣita, which allays the distress of learned men caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the *Śrīmad-Bhagavat-Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
8.8 Now begins the eighth chapter of the eighth book.

They proceed with the seasonal cups (*ṛtugraha*), using twelve, thirteen, or fourteen [verses]. At twelve [verses], they offer all the oblations separately; at thirteen, two of them together; at fourteen, the first two together and the last two together.

They consume [the portions]. One, Ga... "The infinite... [Maṇḍala-paṭala]. Together with the phrase "in the thirteen others," the word *saha* (together) is connected. When there is a *pariplava* (spoon), the drawing [of the cup] is performed by the Adhvaryu; when there is an *udañcana* (ladle), it is performed by the Pratiprasthātṛ, provided that the Adhvaryu is the receiver. This is because of the absence of a second *pariplava*. Otherwise, it is the reverse. The rest is clear.

In this regard, the application of the three groups [of months] is as follows: In the first group, the Adhvaryu says, "Madhu," and the Pratiprasthātṛ says, "Mādhava"; the Adhvaryu says, "Śukra," and the Pratiprasthātṛ says, "Śuci"; the Adhvaryu says, "Nabhas," and the Pratiprasthātṛ says, "Nabhasya. With these six, he gives the *praisha* (direction), which involves the reversal of the vessels' positions. Then the Adhvaryu says, "Iṣa," and the Pratiprasthātṛ says, "Ūrja"; the Adhvaryu says, "Saha," and the Pratiprasthātṛ says, "Sahasya."

Regarding these four, he issues the command (*preṣya*) with the word "auṣaḥ," which serves as the reversal of the vessel's opening. Then the Adhvaryu says "tapo" and the Pratiprasthātṛ says "tapasya. The command (*praiṣa*) is issued by means of these two mantras. Immediately following this, there is no mention of a simultaneous drawing (*sahagrahaṇa*) or a simultaneous offering (*sahahoma*) anywhere.

Let the Adhvaryu be the eater together with the Hotṛ; the Pratiprasthātṛ alone [is the eater] with the Potṛ; the Adhvaryu with the Neṣṭṛ; the Pratiprasthātṛ with the Āgnīdhra; the Adhvaryu with the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; and the Pratiprasthātṛ with the Praśāstṛ. Following this, there is the overturning of the cups.

The *hotṛ* together with the *adhvaryu*, the *pratiprasthātṛ* together with the *neṣṭṛ*, and the *avayā* together with the *acchāvāka*; the *adhvaryu* together with the *potṛ* [are seated] separately from the *pratiprasthātṛ*. Then, the *pratiprasthātṛ* is likewise separate from the *hotṛ* at the *havirdhāna*. In this very case, he either sacrifices himself after sitting down, or if he accepts this alternative, then at the final *yājyā* there is no offering for the *hotṛ*. Consequently, the *bhakṣa* (consuming) is not joined, and the formula "O Agnīdh, summon [the gods] to sacrifice" (*āgnīd ity etad yaja*) is omitted.

The Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ, facing eastward between the two Havirdhāna carts, hold the Viśvagraha cups in their hands according to the procedure prescribed by Āśvalāyana. After the Adhvaryu has recited the *yājyā* and stood up, the Pratiprasthātṛ should remain seated right there. Having gone to the Uttaravedi for the sake of offering the portion-cups (*avayavagraha*), and having offered them with the *vaṣaṭ* call, he should sit down in the *sadas*. The Pratiprasthātṛ should likewise sit down in the *sadas*.

In this context, there is mutual consumption (bhakṣa) on account of the *vaṣaṭ* call, characterized by the conduct of the *avayuj-pratiprasthātṛ*, through mutual invitation. However, the consumption occasioned by the dual cause consisting of both the oblation (*homa*) and the pressing (*abhiṣava*) belongs only to the *adhvaryu* and not to the *pratiprasthātṛ*. In that case, the consumption first belongs to the *adhvaryu* alone, because he alone possesses the status of the primary performer (*kartṛ*). As for the consumption occasioned by the dual cause of both the oblation and the pressing, it belongs to the *sadasya* alone.

According to the scriptural injunction, "Having pressed [the Soma] with the eleven [verses] over the hide in the Havirdhāna, having offered it in the Āhavanīya fire, and having gone back toward the west, they consume it in the Sadas," and according to the alternative view that "having sat down for self-drinking, one should restrain oneself," the procedure for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is as follows: there is an omission of the *hotṛ*’s recitation. The sacrificer, facing eastward and seated in his own seat, should recite the *yājyā*. At the end of the *vaṣaṭ*-call, in the Havirdhāna itself, he should [approach] the Pratiprasthātṛ alone.

One should perform the consumption [of the remnant] accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ* call. Then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having invited the sacrificer for the purpose of both the oblation and the sprinkling, consumes [the remnant] in the *sadas*. Or, according to the alternative that "he himself, having sat down, performs the sacrifice," this supersedes the role of the Hotṛ. Now, as for the second alternative: if there is a simultaneous oblation of the last two [cups], its procedure is as follows: beginning with *madhuśca* and ending with *sahasya ca*, it is to be performed as before.

Then, having called out "tapaśca" and having offered the oblation at the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, the Adhvaryu returns to the *havirdhāna* shed and stands there. When the Hotṛ has sat down, the Pratiprasthātṛ calls out, "O Adhvaryu, *tapaśca*. —Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Book Eight, Part One. 892. — [End of Section] — [Section on the Aṣṭama-praśna] — [End of
