Having taken [the cup] together with these two mantras, "Thou art taken with a support; thou art Samarya for the sake of Bṛhaspati," the Pratiprasthātṛ, because he was the first to proceed, offers it together with the Adhvaryu at the simultaneous utterance of *vaṣaṭ* and pours down the remnants. Now follows the consumption (*bhakṣa*): therein, the sequence of consumption ending with that of the Acchāvāka is as before. However, in the first consumption, it belongs only to the two who offered the oblation, not to the Pratiprasthātṛ.

In the second consumption, there is the consumption by the Hotṛ and the Pratiprasthātṛ. Or, according to the alternative that "he himself, having sat down, performs the sacrifice," in this case, at the eleventh consumption, the consumption belongs only to the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ as before, and not to the Hotṛ when the *yājyā* is performed by him personally. However, in the case of a *yājyā* related to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the consumption is for the Pratiprasthātṛ and the Adhvaryu together with the sacrificer. Since the Pratiprasthātṛ acted first, his consumption comes first, followed by that of the Adhvaryu.

If, however, the view is that there is a simultaneous offering (*sahahoma*) for the first two [cups], then both the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ, having taken them together with the mantras "madhuśca" and "adhivaśva," and having offered them simultaneously when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, perform the pouring of the remnants (*saṃpātāvanayana*). The call "with the season" (*ṛtunā preṣya*) is given by the Adhvaryu; the call "śukraśca" is for the Adhvaryu, the call "with the season" is the command; the call "śuciśca" is for the Pratiprasthātṛ, the call "with the season" is the command; the call "namaśca" is for the Adhvaryu, the call "with the season" is the command.

"Namasyaśca"—thus the Pratiprasthātṛ [responds]; "Ṛtubhiḥ preṣya"—this is the call (praiṣa). "Iṣaśca"—the Adhvaryu [responds]; "Ṛtubhiḥ preṣya"—this is the call. Then follows the overturning of the cups. "Urjaśca"—the Pratiprasthātṛ [responds]; "Ṛtubhiḥ preṣya"—this is the call. "Sahaśca"—the Adhvaryu [responds]; "Ṛtubhiḥ preṣya"—this is the call. "Sahasyaśca"—the Pratiprasthātṛ [responds]; "Anubhiḥ preṣya"—this is the call. "Tapaśca"—the Adhvaryu [responds]; "Anubhiḥ preṣya"—this is the call. "Auṣaḥ."

Then follows the inversion of the vessels and mouths. The Pratiprasthātṛ [performs] the *tapas* offering; with the call "Prompted by the season," the Adhvaryu offers separately, not together. There is no pouring down of the residue (*saṃpāta*) here, because there is no joint offering. With the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; thou art for Soma; for Bṛhaspati thee," the Adhvaryu takes [the cup] separately and offers it separately. Here too, there is no pouring down of the residue, because there is no joint offering. As for the consumption: the first consumption is together with the Hotṛ; the [subsequent] consumption belongs to the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ.

In that regard, because it proceeds from the mouth [of the Adhvaryu], first the Adhvaryu [acts] with the Neṣṭṛ; afterwards, the Pratiprasthātṛ. Then the Adhvaryu with the Potṛ; the Pratiprasthātṛ with the Neṣṭṛ; the Adhvaryu with the Āgnīdhra. The Pratiprasthātṛ with the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; the Adhvaryu with the Praśāstṛ; the Pratiprasthātṛ with the Hotṛ. Then there is the reversal of the cups. Then the Adhvaryu with the Potṛ; the Pratiprasthātṛ with the Neṣṭṛ; [the Adhvaryu] with the Acchāvāka.

The Adhvaryu: then, together with the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu consumes [the portion] separately. Likewise, the Pratiprasthātṛ also consumes [his portion] separately together with the Hotṛ. In this case, the specific distinction is that for both consumers, there is an invocation of the deity. As for the *yājyās*: the *yājyās* for the first and second offerings, which are performed without mantras, belong to the Hotṛ; for the third, to the Potṛ; for the fourth, to the Neṣṭṛ; for the fifth, to the Āgnīdhra; for the sixth, to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; and for the seventh, to the Praśāstṛ.

In the eighth [turn], [the offering] belongs to the Hotṛ; in the ninth, to the Potṛ; in the tenth, to the Neṣṭṛ; in the eleventh, to the Acchāvāka; in the twelfth, the first *yājyā* belongs to the Hotṛ; in the thirteenth, the second *yājyā* belongs to the Hotṛ. According to the view that "he himself, having sat down, performs the sacrifice," the agency of the final *yajamāna*-priest is set aside. There is also a setting aside of the *bhakṣa* (consumption). As for the performance following this alternative, it has already been stated immediately above. In the fourteenth alternative, [the distribution] is arranged as follows:

The teacher [has described] the first *graha* of the thirteen *graha*-offerings on the fortnight, which is like the *hotṛ-homa* fortnight. Here, the distinction is that the *hotṛ* offering is on the thirteenth day and the *yājyā* on the fourteenth. Now, regarding the consumption (*bhakṣa*): there, at the first consumption, the *hotṛ*, the *adhvaryu*, and the *pratiprasthātṛ* consume [the soma] after inviting one another in accordance with the sequence of the occasion. At the second consumption, the *adhvaryu* [consumes] together with the *potr*. [This concludes] the eighth hundred and fiftieth section, accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa.

At the third portion, the Pratiprasthātṛ partakes together with the Neṣṭṛ; at the fourth, the Adhvaryu together with the Āgnīdhra; at the fifth, the Pratiprasthātṛ together with the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; at the sixth, the Adhvaryu together with the Praśāstṛ; at the seventh, the Pratiprasthātṛ together with the Hotṛ; at the eighth, the Adhvaryu together with the Potṛ; at the ninth, the Pratiprasthātṛ together with the Neṣṭṛ; at the tenth, the Adhvaryu together with the Acchāvāka; and at the eleventh, the Adhvaryu together with the Hotṛ. Having caused the Hotṛ to invoke the *upahava* (invitation), he consumes [the portion] separately.

In the final *bhakṣa* (consumption) of the two [sections] consisting of twelve and thirteen [verses], the *adhvaryu* and the *pratiprasthātṛ*, together with the *hotṛ*, consume [the portions] after having invited one another in sequence. Here, the *praiṣa* (direction) is as in the case of both [the *adhvaryu* and the *pratiprasthātṛ*]. The pouring down of the *saṃpāta* (residue) also occurs in both cases. Regarding the deficiency of mantras in the fourteen-fold version, it should be resolved by the principle that "the loss of the end is an increase. By this same principle, there is a repetition of the final mantra.

For the sake of ensuring commonality among these three positions, the Sūtra states: "At the *vaṣaṭ*-call of whichever [deity], offer the oblation; consume it for that very one. This formulation expresses commonality; therefore, there is no contradiction even if the mutual consumption of portions is reversed. Now, the offerings: "To Indra, Madhu; to Mādhava..."—this is the offering for the first two. "To the Maruts, Śukra—this"; "To Tvaṣṭṛ, Śuci—this."

The renunciations (*tyāga*) are made in this order: "To Agni, the object of homage, this [offering]!"; "To Indra, the object of homage, this [offering]!"; "To Mitra and Varuṇa, the objects of nourishment, this [offering]!"; "To the gods who bestow wealth, the *ūna* ones, this [offering]!"; "To the god who bestows wealth, the *sahama* one, this [offering]!"; "To the god who bestows wealth, the *sahasya* one, this [offering]!"; "To the god who bestows wealth, the *tapas* one, this [offering]!"; "To the god who bestows wealth, the *tapasya* one, this [offering]!"; "To Agni Gṛhapati, the *sas* one, and to Aśhaspati, this [offering]!
They are offered while not yet placed [on the altar]; the meaning is that they are offered while still un-deposited. The term "seasonal cups" (*ṛtugraha*) is to be understood as the subject.
Each subsequent [draught] is taken up facing toward each preceding remnant.

By this very fact it is known that they are offered with their remnants. "Facing" (abhi) means having turned toward; that is the meaning. With the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; for Madhu thee," the Adhvaryu takes the first [draught] with his own cup; with the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; for Mādhava thee," the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the subsequent one with his own cup.

This is clear. They take hold of each other’s positions; they interlace, they should interlace, [they form] an interlacing (*vyatiṣaṅga*). The absence of the *vṛddhi* strengthening in the word *ṇamul*-affixed [form] is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). When the Adhvaryu has gone for the sake of the oblation, the Pratiprasthātṛ takes his place at the door; likewise, when the Pratiprasthātṛ has gone, the Adhvaryu takes his place. This is the meaning of the term *vyatiṣaṅga*. Āpastamba also states this clearly: "They have passed by way of the door. That is, having passed by way of the door, they go past each other and meet one another. The meaning is that elsewhere they proceed individually.
In this regard, the author of the Sūtra will also demonstrate the reason. [The text] states:
"The Adhvaryu is in the east, the Pratiprasthātṛ is in the west.
The Adhvaryu proceeds with each preceding mantra, and the Pratiprasthātṛ with each succeeding one. This is clear. The Adhvaryu moves along the south, and the Pratiprasthātṛ along the north.

The movement of both [the soul and the breath] occurs through the region connected to the *āhavanīya* fire, because the suffix *-tra* (indicating "in both places") is heard in both instances. The reason for this is stated in the Śruti: "It is well known that one enters by the southern path, and it is well known that the other stands firm by the northern path.
Otherwise, they would not be mutually consistent, as each would be restricted to its own specific location. This serves as the causal basis for the sūtra, like a door to a house.

He encloses the Adhvaryu as he enters with the *graha* (cup) and as he goes out with the vessel (*pātra*). By means of this *graha*, he encloses him from below so that he does not go astray; such is the meaning of "enclosing" (*parigraha*). When he goes out, he encloses him with the vessel alone. Here too, the meaning of the word "enclosing" is simply "to hold. Alternatively, he acts in such a way that [the vessel] remains to the north of the *aśvayuj* cup. Or rather, the meaning of the word "enclosing" applies in both cases. Even though there is a remnant (*śeṣa*) present here, nevertheless, because that [remnant] is absent in the offering of the *pradēśa*, the term "vessel" (*pātra*) is used. As for the remnant, however, it is... [text fragment].

The Adhvaryu issues the call with the *ṛtu* formulas three times, and the Pratiprasthātṛ likewise three times. In the fourteen-fold division of the *ṛtupraharaṇas*, this is the rule. Having turned the mouths of the two vessels over, the Adhvaryu issues the call with the *ṛtu* formulas twice, and the Pratiprasthātṛ likewise twice.

This is clear. Of these two vessels, the *mukhaśrūta* becomes the *upāṃśupātra*. In that regard, the meaning is that with whichever *mukha* the first oblation was offered, with that same *mukha* the subsequent oblation is offered. Then, having reversed the *mukha*, the Adhvaryu says "Prompt [the Hotṛ] by season" once, and the Pratiprasthātṛ says so once.
This is clear.
When it is said, "O two Adhvaryus, sacrifice," he issues the command, "O Hotṛ, sacrifice this.

Because of the singular form in "he issues the command" (*saṃpreṣyati*) and because of the general rule (*paribhāṣā-sūtra*) regarding the subsequent [action], this belongs to the Adhvaryu alone and not to the Pratiprasthātṛ.
Or, having sat down himself, he sacrifices.

When it is said, "O Adhvaryus, sacrifice," the Hotṛ issues the command, "O Hotṛ, sacrifice this. This is because, in the case of the singular reading, a contradiction with the *śreṣa* (the ritual sequence) would arise. In this view, the phrase "O Hotṛ, sacrifice this" is omitted. The Adhvaryu and Pratiprasthātṛ [place] the oblations between the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and the southern *avaṇu*; the *patnaḥ* [are placed] to the north of the *pṛṣṭhyā*. ... [End of citation]. [This is from] the Ānandāśrama Saṃskṛta Granthāvalī, Volume 53.

9.1 Now begins the ninth book; therein, the first chapter.
The midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina-savana), beginning with the pressing of the Soma, is performed.
Its ritual procedure is explained by that of the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana).
However, the cups for the dual deities, the seasonal cups (ṛtu-graha), the cup for Indra and Agni, the cup for the Viśvedevas, and the offerings with the *darvi*-ladle do not exist here.
Having poured out the *vasatīvarī* waters, he prepares the *nigrābhya* waters.
They press the entire King Soma.
He gives the turban for the Soma-presser (*grāvastut*) to the one who recites the *soma-uṣṇīṣa*.
Saying "Come hither, come hither," they press [the Soma] while propitiating it.
During the middle pressing of the final round, they press it saying "Bṛhat, Bṛhat.
During the final pressing, when the King [Soma] has been well-prepared, they press it.

"The gods, the pressing-stones, and the Soma-drop have spoken of Indra; they have caused Indra to move from the furthest distance, from this vast intermediate space, from his dwelling place. They have pressed out the vital breath for him; they have pressed out spiritual luster for me. In battle they have slain the Rakṣasas; the oppressors of sacred knowledge have been struck down. With these words, the Pratiprasthātṛ gives thanks to the pressing-stones. At this point, some authorities prescribe the offering of the *savanīya* oblations. At the time of the *dhārā-graha*, having first drawn the *śukra* and *manthin* cups, he draws the *āgrayaṇa* from three streams. Ādhrigu... [text ends]
He should take the third stream after having drawn the Ukthya cup.

They draw the two Marutvatīya cups with the two Ṛtu vessels; the Adhvaryu draws the first with his own vessel, using the mantra "The bull accompanied by the Maruts, the increasing one," and the Pratiprasthātṛ draws the latter with his own vessel, using the mantra "O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, the bull, for the delight.
Having drawn [the Soma], he pours out as much of the King (Soma) as he considers sufficient for the midday pressing.
He stops the stream, squeezes [the Soma], and places the *pavitra* [filter].
The pouring of the *ekadhanā* waters into the *ādhavanīya* jar has already been explained.

Having worshipped the *pavamāna* cups, the jars, the *śukra* and *manthin* vessels, the *āgrayaṇa*, and the *ukthya* with the "cup-observances" (*grahāvakāśa*), they proceed to exit while maintaining physical contact with one another.
Having offered the Vaipruṣa oblations and the Saptahotṛ formula, they proceed to the Mādhyandina Pavamāna; its ritual procedure has been explained by [the rules for] the Bahiṣpavamāna.

The path is in the *triṣṭubh* meter; the Rudras are the deity. He modifies the mantra: "By the unobstructed path, by the wolf-path, may we safely reach the Rudras. Having gone north of the *havirdhāna* shed and having passed around the north of the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth—or by the south or between [the *mārjālīya* and the *āgnīdhrīya*]—the Adhvaryu, the sacrificer, and the Brahman enter the *sadas* through the eastern door and stand in front of the *praśāstrīya* hearth. Having passed around it, the Udgātṛ priests chant the *mādhyandina-pavamāna* stotra.

Whatever else there is besides the leading forward of the animal, he issues the command: "O Pratiprasthātṛ, proceed with the curd-vessel ritual (dadhidharma)"; thus he concludes the command. When the hearths (dhiṣṇiyas) have been spread out and assigned, and when the sacrificial grass (barhis) has been strewn.
Having offered the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa), the Pratiprasthātṛ pours out the oblations for the Savanīya offerings.
Here, the sacrificial cake is on eleven potsherds;
there is no curd-mixture (āmikṣā).
When the vessels have been adorned, the Pratiprasthātṛ proceeds with the Dadhigharma.

With the verse, "As great as are heaven and earth," he takes curds into an Udumbara ladle in the Āgnīdhra shed, saying: "May speech and mind mix you; may out-breath and in-breath mix you; may sight and hearing mix you; may skill and strength mix you; may vigor and force mix you; may life and old age mix you; may the self and the body mix you. You are cooked; you are made cooked; for the cooked one, for the cooked ones, you! Having placed it over the fire in the Āgnīdhra shed, he heats it.
"O Hotṛ, speak what is to be spoken by you," he thus commands.
When it is said, "If it is cooked, offer; if it is not cooked, let it cook," he replies, "The oblation is cooked.

Having taken that [ladle] and gone to the Āhavanīya fire, and having called for the announcement (*āśrāvya*), once the response has been given, he issues the command: "Recite the offering prayer (*yaj*) for the Dadhigharma."

"He whom they call Indra, whom they call Varuṇa, whom they call Mitra, whom they call Truth; he who is the god among gods, born of ascetic fervor—to him, to you, [I offer] svāhā! With these words, he offers at the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
Having offered at the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*-call, he takes away the portion for consumption. Those who are present at the *pravargya* ceremony consume it.
The mantra for consuming [the sacrificial portion] in the forest belongs to him. ||2||
Thus ends the first chapter in the ninth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
9.2 Now begins the second chapter in the ninth book.
Having set out the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) and having taken portions from them together, he proceeds with the offering, giving the call: "For the midday pressing."
Having performed the offering with the *paśupuroḍāśa* cake and having taken portions from it, he proceeds with the *savanīya* oblations.
The *sviṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* portions for both the *paśupuroḍāśa* and the *savanīya* oblations are common.
Having poured the contents of the *ādhavanīya* vessel into the *pūtabhṛt*, and having wiped the jar with the fringes of the filter, he turns it face down.

He issues the command: "Recite for those being drawn; draw the cup of the Hotṛ; make them bright on both sides; O Adhvaryu of the Acchāvāka’s cup, you also draw; O Pratiprasthātṛ, prepare the splinters, both sprinkled and unsprinkled; O Unnetṛ, make the Soma increase."

He draws eleven goblets, headed by the Hotṛ’s goblet; he draws the Acchāvāka’s goblet from the front of the Āgnīdhra’s goblet. "Prompt the [Hotṛ] for the Soma juices set forth for Indra—the exclusive portion of the midday pressing, accompanied by the Śukra and Manthin vessels, dripping with sweetness—[saying] 'Preṣya' (Command!). In the middle [of the sequence].

"O *camasādhvaryu*s of the [main] sacrificers, offer the cups at the *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* calls! O *camasādhvaryu*s of the *hotraka*s, having offered each once, replenish them with the *śukra* juice and then return!"—thus he gives the command. When that which was prior to the further replenishing has been performed, the *hotraka*s, having moved forward with the formulas for advancing (*prasarpaṇa-mantra*s), sacrifice from the cups that have been further replenished. After the Hotṛ has announced, "The Āgnīdhra has sacrificed," and having made the portions available, he places the *iḍā* for the *hotraka*s; the *camasādhvaryu*s lift up their cups as the *iḍā* is being invoked.
He does not set aside a fragment of the *iḍā* for the Acchāvāka.

When the *nārāśaṃsa* cups have been consumed and the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) have been placed to the south of the altar, he offers the *dākṣiṇā* oblations just as the *vaisarjana* oblations were offered.

Having tied a piece of gold to the fringe of the cloth used for covering, and having placed it in clarified butter while leading the end of the cloth up the handle of the offering-ladle, he makes an offering in the *śālāmukhīya* fire with the two verses, "Upwards that" and "The bright," and sets aside the remainder of the clarified butter.
As the fees are being led away, he first steps forward and offers in the *āgnīdhra* fire with the verse containing the word "lead": "O Agni, lead us."
He performs the remaining rites with clarified butter.
Having offered the gold with the mantra, "Go to heaven, fly to the light," he takes it up.
He offers the second oblation with the mantra, "In the forests he has spread out the atmosphere," provided that a draft-animal, a chariot, or a garment is being given away.
"O Prajāpati, these [gifts] are not yours"—with this verse he offers the third oblation if a horse, a man, or an elephant is given as a sacrificial fee.
When the fees have been led away, [the priests] say to the patron of the sacrifice: "The seers have charged you with sin. (3)
With five [verses], he offers the Vaiśvakarman oblations in the Āgnīdhrīya fire.
Having taken the two Marutvatīya portions as they were drawn, he issues the direction: "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra with the Maruts; give the command for Indra with the Maruts!
Having offered them, the two of them move away from the fire.
They consume [the portions] according to the seasons, by means of the Pratiprasthātṛ.
The Hotṛ consumes twice, while the other two consume once each.
Having washed the vessel at the Mārjālīya fire, he places it near the Hotṛ.

"You have been born fierce for victorious power, delightful, most mighty, with abundant pride; even the Maruts strengthened Indra here when his mother bore him as the most excellent hero. With the [verse] "O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, drink here," he takes the third *marutvatīya* cup from the *kalaśa* vessel using one of his own cups that has not yet been consumed, while reciting the *śastra*.
Beginning with the *ṛtupātra*, he responds.
Having responded to the *śastra* with "The hymn is uttered," he mutters this at every [recitation] during the midday pressing.

Having thrown away the blade of grass, he takes up the draught-cup; the *camasādhvaryu*s [take up] the cups. He issues the command: "O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice the Soma! The shaking after [the offering], the consumption of the draught-cups and the *nārāśaṃsa* cups, and their swelling and setting down have been explained.
With either of the two *śukra*-cups, he draws the *māhendra* cup from the pitcher, accompanied by the chant and the recitation.
Having set it down, he introduces the *stotra*; that has been explained. When the *stotra* is concluded, he introduces the *śastra*; that has been explained.
Having thrown back the *śastra*, the *camasādhvaryus* take up the cups;
the other *adhvaryus* take up the *atigrāhya* cups—the *pratiprasthātṛ* takes the one for Agni, the *neṣṭṛ* the one for Indra, and the *unnetṛ* the one for Sūrya.

"O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice the Soma!"—thus he gives the command. He offers the *atigrāhya* cups according to their respective forms with the formulas beginning, "O Agni, full of splendor, [may I be] full of splendor."
With the formulas, "May wisdom be in me, may progeny be in me," they consume the *atigrāhya* cups according to their respective forms.
There is neither the replenishing nor the setting down of all the cups. They proceed with three *ukthya-vigraha* offerings as previously described.
In all cases, the drawing and placing of the cup are performed with the formula, "For Indra thee.

When the rite is concluded, he offers the oblation with the verse, "The All-gods, the Maruts, and Indra—may they protect us. He issues the command, "O Praśāstṛ, impel [the sacrificer]," and says, "Crawl forth!"
The Mādhyandina pressing concludes with the Praśāstṛ. ||4||
Thus ends the second paṭala in the ninth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the third paṭala in the ninth praśna:
The third pressing (savana) is performed beginning with the Āditya cup.
The ritual procedure for him is explained by that of the midday pressing.
Having closed the doors of the *havirdhāna* shed, [the offering is made] when many [enemies] are within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*),
or when his rival is there.
The sacrificer and his wife remain within the altar; then he draws the Āditya cup.
If one whose rival is sacrificing with Soma should draw the Āditya cup, he should stand outside the altar for as long as that cup is being drawn.
He draws a portion of the Soma which is in the Āditya vessel using the Āditya cup with the verse, "Never art thou barren."
"May you never fail us"—with this [mantra], he takes the curd from which the fever has been removed.
"The sacrifice of the gods comes toward us"—with this, he draws all the Soma that is in the Āditya vessel.
"O Vivasvat Āditya"—with this, he mixes the Āditya [Soma] with the Upāṃśusavana stone.
With the formula, "I mix you with that divine rain," he should mix [the soma] with milk or curds from above for one who desires rain; this is directed toward the Āditya cup.
According to some, however, one does not take curds from the middle.
Into that [cup], he places the *upāṃśusavana* pressing-stone.
Having raised it, he approaches with discernment:
if, when it has been run forth, a small amount quickly spills over, Parjanya will be rainy; if [it spills] after a long time, he will not rain. It does not fail.
With the words, "From the ocean to the atmosphere," he causes [the water] to flow out with *darbha* blades;
with the words, "I am above, I am below," he covers it with *darbha* blades or with his hand.

"May the god Sūrya protect me from the gods," with these words he rises; "The sage extends the path of the sacrifice," with these words he carries [the offering]; "To the Ādityas, the beloved, whose abodes are dear, whose vows are dear, the great ones, the lords of the waters, the overseers of the wide mid-air—recite the invitatory verse! To the Ādityas, the beloved, whose abodes are dear, whose vows are dear, the great ones, the lords of the waters, the overseers of the wide mid-air—give the command! Thus he gives the direction and issues the formal call. || 5 ||

Reciting, "O Agni, those which are all your fuel-sticks," he throws *darbha* grass into the Āhavanīya fire and offers the oblation while looking away. For one who desires rain, he should offer with the verse, "Make the earth swell.
Having offered, he must not look back.
He does not utter the *anuvaṣaṭ* call, nor does he consume [the soma]; he sets down the vessel like that of the *sūda*.
Having poured [water] from the *vasatīvarī* waters, he prepares the *nigrābhya* waters.
He should mix the stalk that was in the *upāṃśu* cup into the *ṛjīṣa*; they silently press the *adābhya* stalk and the *ṛjīṣa* over the two *upāṃśusavana* stones.
He does not give the turban to the Grāvastut;
the Pratiprasthātṛ does not approve of the pressing-stones.
Here, some prescribe the offering of the Savanīya oblations.
At the time of drawing the *dhārāgraha* cups, he draws the *āgrayaṇa* from four streams; he makes the fourth stream from the *āditya* vessel.
Having drawn that, he causes the King (Soma) to flow through it as much as he considers sufficient for the third pressing. He stops when the stream ceases, squeezes the filter, and sets it down.

When that [rite] which precedes the *pavamāna* cups has been performed, the sacrificer and his wife, having churned the *āśira* (milk) in the *āgnīdhra* shed and entered the *havirdhāna* shed by the western door, pour the *āśira* into the *pūtabhṛt* vessel through the filter with the four verses beginning, "O gods, look upon us for beauty. Having worshipped the *pavamāna* cups, the jars, and the *āgrayaṇa* cup with the *grahāvakāśa* formulas, they proceed to exit while maintaining physical contact with one another.
Having offered the Vaipruṣa oblations and the Saptahotṛ formula, they proceed to the Ārbhava Pavamāna; its ritual procedure is explained by that of the midday pressing.
The path belongs to the Jagatī; the Ādityas are the deity. He modifies the mantra as: "By means of a wolf-like, non-narrow path, may I reach the Ādityas in safety.

Whatever [ritual action] follows the distribution of the hearths (*dhiṣṇiya*), he issues that command: "O Pratiprasthātṛ, perform the *saṃvāda* (dialogue) regarding the animal sacrifice," thus modifying the conclusion of the call.
When the hearths have not been shifted and have not been leveled, and the sacrificial grass has been strewn, the Pratiprasthātṛ pours out the grains for the Savanīya offerings;
the sacrificial cake here consists of twelve potsherds,
and no animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) is found.
In all cases, some prescribe the *savanīya* cakes as being on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*), some on eleven potsherds, and some on twelve potsherds.

Once the [cakes] have been adorned, the Pratiprasthātṛ proceeds with the ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice (*paśutantra*) beginning from the dialogue. He carries the collected portions (*samavatta*) either to the south or to the north of the *havirdhāna* cart.

The sacrificer does not consume the portions; some authorities prescribe the consumption. Having set down the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and having taken portions from them, he proceeds with the offering. He issues the call: "For the third pressing! Having poured the *ādhavanīya* vessel into the *pūtabhṛt*, and having wiped the jar with the fringes of the filter, he turns it upside down. He issues the call: "Recite for the cups being filled! Fill the cups following the cup of the Hotṛ... make them strong and mixed with milk-curd (*āśīr*). O Adhvaryu of the Acchāvāka’s cup, fill yours as well. O Unnetṛ, cause the Soma to flow forth! Thus he issues the command.

He pours out eleven cups, with the *hotṛ*’s cup as the foremost. At the time of the ritual performance, he proceeds with those [cups] already set forth. He issues the command: "Prompt the offering of the Soma juices set forth for Indra—[Somas] of the third pressing, rich in nourishment, all-pervading, powerful, full of vigor, accompanied by Savitṛ, Bṛhaspati, and the Viśvedevas, strong and accompanied by the *āśis* (blessing). Then he gives the instruction: "O *camasādhvaryus* of the *madhyataḥkārin* priests, offer the oblations at the *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* calls; O *camasādhvaryus* of the *hotrakas*, having offered each once, fill [the cups] again from the strong [Soma] accompanied by the *āśis*, and then return."

"To the falcon, the flyer, svāhā! (7). With these [formulas], he offers the cups that have been refilled. He makes the secondary *vaṣaṭ* calls with the formula, "Obeisance to him who has spontaneously approved.
He consecrates the offerings with the formula, "May the officiating priests be satiated with the honeyed ghee.
The cup-bearers consume [the soma] from their respective cups; the mantra for their consumption has already been explained.

When the *nārāśaṃsa* cups have been placed down, they each take their own cup and set aside three pieces of sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) to the south. Having done that, and having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), and having recited the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula, they mutter the mantras of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, beginning with the offering of the portions and ending with the pouring back of the remnants.

When that has been performed, he draws the *sāvitra* cup from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel using one of these vessels, namely the *antaryāma* cup, with the verse: "O Savitṛ, today [grant] what is desirable... etc.
Having stepped out, he does not set [the cup] down; he issues the summons: "Recite for the god Savitṛ! Prompt for the god Savitṛ!
Having offered the oblation, he does not utter the *anuvaṣaṭ* call nor does he consume [the remnant]; he sets down the vessel as if with clarified butter (sūdavat), with this very formula:
"Thou art taken with a support; thou art a good refuge, a firm foundation."
With an unblessed vessel, he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup from the pitcher along with the Śastra.

While the verse "ekayā ca daśabhiśca svabhūte" is being recited, the Pratiprasthātṛ unyokes the two morning-yoked [steeds] with the formula "vimucyethām. Having released the vessels for the dual deities (dvidevatya), carried them out through the western door, washed them at the Mārjālīya mound, and brought them back in through the eastern door, he places them in their respective positions.
While the verse "pra dyāvā yajñaiḥ pṛthivī ṛtāvṛdhā" is being recited, he responds with the *anyataratomoda* chant: "modā moda iva athāmoda."
Some transmit the procedure in reverse order:
having responded to the *śastra* with "The hymn is for Indra in speech," he mutters [the formula] at every instance during the third pressing.
Having responded to the *śastra*, he takes up the cup; the *camasādhvaryu*s take up the *camasa*s.
He proceeds with that [cup] just as at the morning pressing with the Vaiśvadeva [offering]. ||8||
Thus ends the third paṭala in the ninth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
9.4 Now begins the fourth paṭala in the ninth praśna:
One commences the rites beginning with the setting out of the vessels for the Saumya offering.
He offers a *caru* oblation for Soma.
Having set it down and having taken a portion of clarified butter, he issues the command: "Sacrifice the ghee! and, upon the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.

Standing right here, he first cuts a portion of the *saumya* with his hand, and the second with the *mekṣaṇa* spoon. Having stepped across toward the north, caused the announcement to be made, and received the response, he issues the direction: "Recite the offering prayer for the *saumya*. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, standing facing south, he makes the offering in the eastern part of the southern half. He recites the offering prayer for the clarified butter as before.
Some authorities prescribe that the offering be performed on either side.
Having filled it with clarified butter, they carry it to the Udgātṛs.
Then, saying "It is here, it is here," they look down upon it;
for in it they behold their own self.
One who does not see himself should look [at the reflection] after having made a breach in the wall with the words, "May I be without life-breath; may my mind that has gone away [return].
One who is ill or one who desires food should eat [the reflection]. Or, by whomsoever, though capable of eating food, food is not eaten—that person should eat it.
The Āgnīdhra distributes the blazing fires onto the hearths using wooden sticks.
Having taken up the clarified butter held in nine ladlings, the Adhvaryu sprinkles it over the blazing fires.
He prepares the remainder of the clarified butter, and they maintain the fires upon the hearths.
"Thou art taken with a support; of thee, the son of Bṛhaspati... With these words, he draws the Pātnīvata cup from the Āgrayaṇa vessel using the Upāṃśu vessel.
Having mixed it with the clarified butter remaining from the sprinkling over the Dhiṣṇiya hearths, he does not set it down.
Having gone out, he issues the command: "O Agnīdh, recite the offering prayer for the Pātnīvata."
He offers at the *vaṣaṭ*-call with the formula, "O Agni, accompanied by the wives!
The *anuvaṣaṭ*-call may be performed or not;
according to some, he performs the *anuvaṣaṭ*-call in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).

"O Agnīdh, sit in the lap of the Neṣṭṛ! O Neṣṭṛ, lead up the wife! O Udgātṛ, cause the wife to look at [the Soma]! O Unnetṛ, fill the cups headed by the Hotṛ’s cup! Make room for the Dhruva vessel in the Hotṛ’s cup! Fill the entire King Soma; do not leave any remainder! Having wiped the two jars with the fringes of the cloth, turn them upside down!"—thus he issues the command.

The Āgnīdhra, having stepped out between the Neṣṭṛ and the Dhiṣṇiya fire-altar, consumes [the portion]; or, sitting on the lap of the Neṣṭṛ, he consumes it—but he should not sit on the lap; if he were to sit on the lap, he would become impotent.
He pours out the cups, with the Hotṛ’s cup as the foremost. There are the Stotra and the Śastra.

Having kindled the *ghiṣṇiya* fires, he begins the *agniṣṭoma* chant. Without untying their waist-knots (*nīvī*), making their navels visible as it were, and with their ears covered, all those who are members of the *sadas* remain so from the *sadas*.
According to some, the officiating priests and the sacrificer [are present].
With the verse, "Of thee, the all-encompassing, the all-possessing, the powerful," he causes the wife to be looked at by the Udgātṛ.
Having made the wife's right thigh bare and having exposed the groin, she says, "The gods, the sacrifice... [and so on].
With the words, "Svāhākṛtāḥ samudreṣṭhāḥ," the wife, standing inside the thighs, causes the *pannejani* waters to flow out through the thigh toward the north.
The counting and the incitement are performed for the third *stotrīyā* verse.

While the verse beginning with "svāduṣkila ayam madhumāṃ uta ayam" is being recited, he responds with joy on both sides, saying "madāmoda iva modāmoda iva. From the *āhāva* onwards, the response is established up to the *vyāhāva*.
When it has become dark, the Pratiprasthātṛ consecrates the *dhruva* cup, saying, "mā asi bhūte mā dhāḥ."
"I enclose you with heaven and earth," he says as he encloses it. "May all the gods, belonging to all men, move you forth," he says as he moves the *dhruva* from its place.
"In heaven strengthen the gods; in the intermediate space, the birds," he says as he carries it away.

With the formula, "We lead Soma down with the firm *dhruva* oblation," he pours the *dhruva* into the *hotṛ*'s cup while the *paridhānīyā* verse is being recited, once it has been recited, or at the beginning of the *śastra*. [He does so] either in the middle part or at the end.
Having responded to the *śastra*, the Adhvaryu takes up the *hotṛ*'s cup, and the *camasādhvaryus* take up their cups. He issues the call: "O reciter of the *uktha*, offer the *soma*s!
The consumption of the cups has been explained.
The two [fires] do not serve as the place for replenishment or for the establishment of the fires.
From the command, "O Āgnīdh, bring the embers for the after-offerings," one commences the ritual pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka-karman*).
If there is an *anūbandhyā* cow, one does not offer the *svaru* at the end of the *anūyāja* offerings, nor do they proceed with the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*).
When the enclosing-sticks have been cast into the fire, having offered the residue, they proceed with the Hāriyojana cup.
With the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; thou art the bay steed, the yoker of bays," the Unnetṛ draws the entire Āgrayaṇa juice as the Hāriyojana from the Droṇakalaśa.
Having roasted it with many grains of parched barley, he does not set it down.

Having placed it upon his head and gone out, he issues the two calls: "Recite for Indra, the possessor of bay horses; give the command for Indra, the possessor of bay horses! Or [he says]: "Recite for the Soma-grains; give the command for the Soma-grains that have been set forth!
Having stepped forward and said, "You are the two bays, the grains for the two bays," he utters the *vaṣaṭ* at the moment of the call.
He offers at the *anuvaṣaṭ* call; having offered, he brings the portion for consumption.

All of them, having divided it equally and having sought permission from the *unnetṛ*, consume the roasted grains (*dhānā*) with the formula, "O divine Soma, [thee] whose sacrifice is well-performed," making a *ci-ci-ṣā* sound.
They do so by biting them, without breaking them, making hollows in the grains, and thus clearing away the husks.
"May you be filled; may I be filled," saying this, they spit upon the grains on the high altar and scatter them, or [they say], "For wealth, for prosperity.
In the Āgnīdhra shed, they consume drops of curd while reciting, "I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan."

Having poured out the *camasa* cups one by one until only a single portion of Soma remains, having spread out the green *dūrvā* grass, and having intensified the flavor by producing its juice, they smell the juice of the Soma washed in water with the mantra, "O Soma, whose deity is the Waters," and then they pour it into the *cātvāla* pit.
With the *minda* oblation, "Whatever flaw has occurred in my self," they worship the Āhavanīya fire.

"You are the expiation for sin committed against the gods; you are the expiation for sin committed against men; you are the expiation for sin committed against the ancestors; you are the expiation for sin committed by oneself; you are the expiation for sin committed by another; you are the expiation for every sin—of whatever sin I have been conscious and whatever sin I have been unconscious of, you are the expiation for that sin.

With each of these formulas, they place wood-shavings into the Āhavanīya fire. "Both are young seers, the lords of the law through truth. "O Lord of the Law through Truth, we release our bonds of friendship. With this, they dissolve their bonds of friendship.
When the Veda has been stroked, they perform the *saṃyāja* offerings for the wives.

When the Veda has been spread, the Adhvaryu, having taken nine portions of clarified butter, stands upright within the altar and, with the *juhū* ladle, offers nine *samiṣṭayajus* oblations into the Āhavanīya fire while reciting the formula beginning with "dhātā rātiḥ."

If he should desire, "May he be short-lived," then, while standing obliquely or bent over, he offers silently with the *sruva* ladle at the conclusion [of the rite] with the verse, "This is the third pressing of the seers.
He issues the command, "O *praśāstṛ*, give the impulse! and says, "Crawl forth!"
The third pressing concludes with the Praśāstṛ. || 12 ||
Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the ninth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the fifth paṭala in the ninth praśna: He commences the ritual procedure for the avabhṛtha bath.
In this regard, we shall explain whatever is performed:

having added fuel to the fires, having prepared the Veda-grass mat, having strewn around the fires, having washed his hands, and having spread out a layer of *ulapa* grass, he arranges the vessels according to their purpose; however, he does not carry forward the *praṇītā* waters.
At the time of the offering, he offers a cake on one potsherd to Varuṇa.
He mixes it with water purified by a sacrificial formula.
Once it has been covered, having poured out the scrapings from the water-vessel, he proceeds with the formal summons.

Whatever else there is besides the fuel and the sacrificial grass and the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings, for that he gives the *saṃpraisha* command. Having performed what precedes the taking of the clarified butter and having returned,
he takes the portions of clarified butter at the Gārhapatya fire.

Having taken all [the portions] four times, or twice in the *upabhṛt* ladle, and having adorned the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), he places it on the northern shoulder [of the altar] for the final bath (*avabhṛtha*). He sets aside the sacrificial cake, the clarified butters, the *audumbarī* post, the two pressing-boards, the dust from the *khara* mound, the dregs (*ṛjīṣa*), and whatever else is smeared with Soma—except for the four Soma-vessels: the *āgrayaṇa* vessel, the *ukthya* vessel, the *āditya* vessel, and the *dhruva* vessel. He offers the oblation in whichever fire he has cooked [the cake], reciting: "O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation..."
When the *avabhṛtha* has been performed, he gives the direction: "O *prastotṛ*, sing the *sāman*s! Together with the wife, they all chant the *nidhana* of the *sāman* three times.
Having gone to the *cātvāla* pit, they say, "For King Varuṇa has made wide space," or they say this while departing from the *cātvāla*.
They exit toward the north between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara* heap.
It is prescribed that they proceed toward all directions for the *avabhṛtha* bath.
According to some, however, one should not move toward the north.
In the middle of the country they perform the second *nidhana* of the *sāman*; at the edge of the water, the third.
Upon seeing the water, they mutter: "A hundred physicians are yours, O King, a thousand.
They step upon the edge of the water with the words: "The noose of Varuṇa has been stepped over."
Standing after having immersed themselves in the water, they proceed with the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath).
When the deities have been carried away, he pours water [into the ladle], offers the *sruva*-oblation, and issues the command to the *āgnīdh*: "Wipe the water three times!
Once it has been wiped, he throws a blade of grass into the water.
With the words, "The face of Agni has entered the waters," he pours the butter from the *sruc* ladle.
He chooses the *pravara* (invocation of ancestors) in the same manner as during the *upasads*. The *pravara* consists of only the word "tiṣṭha" (stand).
He performs the *prayāja* offerings excluding the one for the *barhis* grass.
He does not pour the butter from the upabhṛt ladle into the juhū. The two ājyabhāga offerings contain the word "ap".
Having performed the ritual with those two, he sacrifices to Varuṇa from the puroḍāśa cake.
Having taken the entire sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) as an oblation, he sacrifices to Agni and Varuṇa as the *Sviṣṭakṛt* deities.

He issues the command: "O Āgnīdhra, sprinkle the water once. He performs two after-offerings (*anūyāja*) without the *barhis* grass. He issues the call for the first after-offering: "Sacrifice to the two gods; sacrifice! and for the latter: "Sacrifice!"
This much is performed:

"O King Soma, those dear limbs and well-hewn joints of yours which they have severed with the pressing-stone—unite them with clarified butter and cause them to grow; being free from sin, may we utterly destroy our evil. "O divine Soma, that which the men, moving their arms, have caused the pressing-stone to cast down upon you, and that which they have milked from you with the right hand—that may swell for you, that may heal for you. That skin of yours which they have pierced, and that womb, and when you are displaced from your station, you yourself yearn [for it]."

"O Soma, let that be protected by you; may it be our bond in the highest heaven. Having met with the milk, he has cast off his body; its color becomes one thing after another. In that [Soma], we are invited; we are yours. Grant us a share in the assembly, O you of all forms. With these four verses, he offers the *ṛjīṣa* over an Udumbara branch. He does so with five, seven, nine, eleven, or thirteen [verses].
Having filled the ladle with the *ṛjīṣa*, he dips it into the water while reciting: "In the ocean is your heart."
With the mantra, "O Soma, whose deity is the waters, for that which has been washed in the waters," he smells or touches whichever drop of the [soma] drops rises up.
With the mantra, "O Avabhṛtha, thou art Nicaṅkuṇa," they drive away the Avabhṛtha bath.
With the mantra, "O divine waters," they stand in worship.
They purify themselves with the mantra "sumitrā naḥ. || 14 ||

"O Unnetṛ, bring forth! Bring forth! These most honey-sweet songs rise up; these hymns of praise go forth, ever-conquering, winning wealth, with unfailing aid, like chariots seeking booty. Like the Kaṇvas, like the Bhr̥gus, like the suns, they have attained everything that was to be attained"—with these words he gives the command to the Unnetṛ.

"Rise up, bestowing offspring and luster; you have been sent forth for wealth and for sacrifice. Embrace the Gāyatrī metre; thus may we be fragrant in our homes. With this, the Unnetṛ causes the vessels to be filled, with the Hotṛ at the head and the sacrificer at the head.
"Varuṇa’s noose is cast off," with these words he tosses [the grass] toward the edge of the water; "Varuṇa’s noose is thrown back," with these words, having tossed it toward the edge of the water,
they hold fuel-sticks of Udumbara wood.
Reciting "We have drunk Soma;
we have become immortal," they return without looking back, preceded by the Unnetṛ.
They perform the ritual purification (mārjana) outside the cow-pen.
With the words, "Fuel art thou; may we prosper," they place fuel-sticks on the Āhavanīya fire. With the words, "I have followed the waters," they pay reverence [to the fires].
In the same way, the wife, having placed a fuel-stick on the Gārhapatya fire, pays reverence. || 15 ||

9.6 Now begins the sixth chapter of the ninth book. One commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *udayanīyā* offering in the *prāgvaṃśa* hall. Its ritual rules (*kalpa*) have been explained by analogy with the *prāyaṇīyā* offering.
He binds on the anūyāja fuel-stick.
In the same pot in which he cooks the prāyaṇīya offering, and with the residue remaining therein, he cooks [the anūyāja] using that same stirring-spoon.
He girds the wife.
He does not take clarified butter into the *juhū* ladle if there are no *prayāja* offerings;
the *prayājas* may be either performed or not performed.
He sacrifices to the deity with clarified butter, reciting the *pathyā svasti* hymn as the supreme blessing.
He does not set aside the cooking-pot, the scrapings, or the stirring-spoon.
He does not leave a remnant for the *dhruvā* ladle.
The entire [rite] is established.
He commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *anubandhyā* cow.
Its ritual method (*kalpa*) is explained by that of the *nirūḍhapaśubandha*.
He dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa;
or three: one of two colors to Mitra and Varuṇa, one of many colors to the Viśvedevas, and one with a white back to Bṛhaspati.
He proceeds with the offering to the Viśvedevas in a low voice from the center; both the *āśrāvaṇa* and the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* are also in a low voice, while for the other two [offerings] they are loud.
Having offered the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) for the Anubandhyā cow, he subsequently offers the divine oblations (daivikāni havīṃṣi),
offering a cake on twelve potsherds to Dhātṛ, exactly as prescribed in the tradition.
These sacrificial porridges (carus) are cooked in milk within the Soma-vessels.
The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the *iḍā* portion for the animal-cake of the *anūbandhyā* cow and for the *devikā* oblations are common.
He recites the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*) addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa,
and the formal call (*saṃpraiṣa*) also takes place.
At the end of the after-offerings (anūyāja), he offers the *svaru* splinter; he proceeds with the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*) as previously described.

Some authorities prescribe the curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa (*maitrāvaruṇīmāmikṣā*) in place of the *anūbandhyā* animal sacrifice, beginning with the offering of the oblation. It concludes with the *iḍā* portion.
Having untied the first knots of the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds, he moves the *havirdhāna* carts northward outside the altar.
With the verse, "That which is lent and not returned," he causes the *āhavanīya* fire to fast upon the altar;
with the *gārhapatya* fire, the wife [fasts] in the *prāgvaṃśa* hall.
With the three verses beginning, "This common dwelling-place, I give it back to you," he consecrates the rising smoke.

If he thinks that he has acted as if mixed up while wandering about, he should offer groats with his joined palms into the forest fire, saying: "O all-devouring, all-consuming one, I sacrifice unto thee!
He then deposits the fires onto separate kindling woods: the *prājahita*, the *gārhapatya*, the *dakṣiṇāgni*, and for one who has attained prosperity, the third, the *śālāmukhīya*.

Having moved away either toward the east or the north and having prepared the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), he performs the *udavasānīyā* offering, consisting of a cake on eight potsherds or five potsherds for Agni.
Everything for him is performed in a low voice up until the final after-offering (*anūyāja*).
Some authorities prescribe the *pūrṇāhuti* (full-oblation) in place of the *udavasānīyā* (concluding offering), with the mantra: "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely.

When that [offering] is completed, whether at night or after some time during the night, at that very moment he should offer the evening *agnihotra*; the morning oblation is offered at its proper time.
The Agniṣṭoma is concluded. || 17 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the ninth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the seventh chapter in the ninth book:
The Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśin, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma are modifications of the Agniṣṭoma by means of additional qualities.
One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Ukthya.
Its ritual procedure is explained by that of the Agniṣṭoma.
The Sadas has fifteen roofs.
Having performed the *kratu-karaṇa* oblation with this very mantra, he wipes the internal smear on the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*).
At the Ukthya sacrifice, he immolates the second *savanīya* animal dedicated to Indra and Agni.

At the third pressing, at the time of drawing the *dhārāgraha* cups, having drawn the *āgrayaṇa*, he draws the *ukthya*. While pouring out the *agniṣṭoma* cups, he leaves over the King Soma for three sets of cup-bearers. "Pour out the entire King Soma; do not leave any over"—this [instruction] is omitted. Having wiped the two jars with the fringes of the cloth, he turns them face down; this [action] is also omitted.

Regarding these *agniṣṭoma* cups, whichever is the final group of *saṃsthāna* cups, while lifting that, he issues this command. Having proceeded with the *agniṣṭoma* cups, they proceed with the three *ukthya-vigraha* [cups] as before. By the phrase "as before," the entire procedure pertaining to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) is obtained.
He modifies the first drawing and placing of the cup with the formula, "For Indra and Varuṇa thee," and [the second with] "For Indra and Bṛhaspati..."
With the formula "For the two Ṛbhus, thee," he offers the second; with "For Indra and Viṣṇu, thee," the third.
One who desires vigor [should offer] with the Ṣoḍaśin cup.
Its ritual procedure is explained by that of the Ukthya.

He purchases Soma from her who has a small body, is short (meaning *śuṇṭhā*), and whose ears hang down over her eyes (*adhīlodhakarṇā*). Although the [purchase] for the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice is already established by the general context, the explicit mention of "from her" (*tasyāḥ*) indicates that such a purchase of Soma occurs only in the optional (*kāmya*) case, not in the obligatory (*nitya*) case. From this very indicative mark, its obligatory nature is also understood. *Śuṇṭhā* means having a small body, i.e., short. *Adhīlodhakarṇā* means one whose ears hang down (*lambamāna*) over (*adhi*) the eyes; or alternatively, one whose other color (*varṇāntara*) is upon the ear.
While drawing out the cups for the *agniṣṭoma*, he leaves the King Soma in excess over the three groups of cups.
"Draw up all [the Soma] for the King; do not leave any remainder. Having wiped the two jars with the ten [fingers], he sets them down; thus it is omitted.
While drawing up whichever group of *saṃsthāna-camasa*s is last, he issues this command regarding the *agniṣṭoma-camasa*s.
Having proceeded with the *agniṣṭoma-camasa*s, they proceed with the three *ukthya-vigraha*s as previously described.
With "For Indra and Varuṇa, thee," he performs the first drawing and placing; with "For Indra and Bṛhaspati, thee," the second; and with "For Indra and Viṣṇu, thee," the third.
One who desires vigor should [draw] the Ṣoḍaśin cup.
The ritual procedure for that [sacrifice] has been explained by means of the Ukthya.
He purchases Soma with a piece of ginger from which the *lodhra* has been removed.

Having moved away either to the east or to the north and having prepared the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), he offers the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice: a cake on eight potsherds or on five potsherds for Agni.
For this sacrifice, everything is performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) up until the final after-offering (*anūyāja*).
Some authorities prescribe the *pūrṇāhuti* (full-oblation) with the formula "Stride out widely, O Viṣṇu" as the substitute for the *udavasānīyā* (concluding oblation).

When that [concluding rite] is completed—whether at night or after a certain portion of the night has passed—one should then offer the evening *agnihotra*; the morning *homa* should take place at its proper time.
Thus the *agniṣṭoma* is concluded. || 17 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the ninth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Now begins the seventh chapter in the ninth book:
The Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśin, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma are modifications of the Agniṣṭoma by means of added qualities.
The *sadas* has seventeen roofs.
At the time of arranging the vessels, he places the four-cornered *ṣoḍaśin* cup made of *khadira* wood on the northern shoulder [of the *sadas*].
Having offered the *ṛtukaraṇa* oblation, he touches either the *droṇakalaśa* or the forehead-band (*rarāṭī*) with this very same mantra.
At the *ṣoḍaśin* [sacrifice], he immolates as the third *savanīya* victim a bull for Indra.
He draws the *ṣoḍaśin* cup with one of these [verses]: "Mount [the chariot], O slayer of Vṛtra!
Prior to the last *ukthya* round, in the first two pressings, he draws it from the *droṇakalaśa*.
At the third pressing, after all the Ukthya rounds have been performed, [the ritual proceeds] from the Āgrayaṇa vessel.

"Since there is no other born who has entered all the worlds—Prajāpati, in harmony with his progeny, he attends the three lights; he is the Ṣoḍaśin. He is the Brahman who is seasonal, renowned by the name Indra among the host. For your great assembly, I shall proclaim your two bay steeds. I win for you, the seasonal one, the desirable exhilaration of the conqueror—Indra by name, who like ghee beautifully pours forth [his power] with his bay steeds.
Renowned is the host; may the songs enter you, whose form is golden. With these verses, at every drawing of the cup, he consecrates the Ṣoḍaśin.
While drawing up the cups, beginning with the cup of the Acchāvāka, he pours out the *rājā* (Soma) for one group of cups. Having performed the ritual with them, he proceeds with the *ṣoḍaśin*.
When the sun has reached the midpoint, he introduces the *ṣoḍaśin* chant with gold and two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
He holds a white horse in front, or one that is reddish-brown or black. They chant while handing over gold. The *śastra* recitation contains the word "bay" (*hari*).
After the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses, he responds with the formula in alternation: "Thus we shall rejoice as if in joy; let us rejoice as if in great joy.
In the case of *anuṣṭubh* verses, the response is established as usual.
Having responded to the recitation (*śastra*), he takes up the cup, and the *camasādhvaryus* take up their goblets.
"O reciter of the uktha, sacrifice the soma-libations," he thus issues the command. || 1 ||
"O Indra, lord of lords, you are the lord of the gods; make me, long-lived and radiant, a lord among men"—with these words he offers the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.

"Indra the sovereign and Varuṇa the king—those two first made this your portion; I consume it as their subsequent portion; may Speech, being pleased, be satisfied with the Soma"—with these words he consumes the draught from the cup.
"With the group [of verses] beginning with 'ādityavat' for the cups;
'anustup-chandasaḥ'—thus he modifies the *bhakṣa*-mantra.
One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) [should perform it] by means of the Atirātra sacrifice."
The ritual procedure for that [Soma sacrifice] has been explained by means of the *ṣoḍaśin*.
The *sadas* has twenty-one roofs.

He does not offer the *kratukaraṇa* oblation, nor does he touch the *droṇakalaśa* or the forehead-band (*rarāṭī*). Reciting only this sacrificial formula (*yajus*), he enters the two *havirdhāna* sheds; such is the extent of the *kratukaraṇa*.
At the Atirātra sacrifice, he offers a ewe dedicated to Sarasvatī as the fourth Savanīya victim; according to some, it is a ram.
While drawing the goblets for the Ṣoḍaśin cup, he leaves over the Soma-king for thirteen groups of goblets.
Having proceeded with those, he proceeds with the nocturnal rounds.
"Thou art taken with a support; for Indra thee, for the overcoming of the nights!"—with these words, he draws each principal cup.

There are the *stotra* and the *śastra*. He draws the first cups, headed by the *hotṛ*'s cup; the second, headed by the *maitrāvaruṇa*'s cup; the third, headed by the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*'s cup; and the fourth, headed by the *acchāvāka*'s cup.
That was the first watch of the night.

In this same manner, the second and third watches of the night were performed. Having performed those rites, he proceeds with the rituals beginning from the setting out of the vessels for the Āśvina cup; he offers the two-potherd cake for the Aśvins.
Having approached him, he draws the *saṃdhicamasas*, of which the *hotṛcamasa* is the chief. There are the *stotra* and the *śastra*. 20.
The *saṃdhi-stotra* is the *rāthantara* consisting of three verses;
the *āśvina-śastra* follows.
Once the sun has risen, the Adhvaryu, having recited the *paridhānīyā* verse for the *āśvina*, takes up the *hotṛ-camasa* cup, and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes up the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
The *camasādhvaryu*s take up the cups.
He issues the direction: "Recite for the Aśvins the *tiroahniya* Soma-draughts; give the call for the *tiroahniya* Soma-draughts set forth for the Aśvins."
The Pratiprasthātṛ offers the cake together with the Soma cups as a complete oblation.
He modifies the *bhakṣa*-mantra by adding "of the Paṅkti metre.
One who desires cattle should perform the Aptoryāma sacrifice.
The ritual procedure for this [sacrifice] has been explained by that of the Atirātra.
While drawing the *saṃdhi* cups, he distributes the King [Soma] over four sets of cup-rows.
There are four sets of cup-rows provided with *stotra*s and *śastra*s, beginning with the Hotṛ’s and the Maitrāvaruṇa’s...

The procedure for the performance with the *saṃdhicamasas* of Varuṇa, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and the Acchāvāka has been explained. He modifies the *bhakṣa*-mantra [by adding] "atichandāś chandasaḥ" (of the Atichandas metre).

"O Āgnīdh, bring the embers for the supplementary offerings"—starting from this point, the rites pertaining to the animal sacrifice are performed identically in all forms of the sacrifice up until the morning Agnihotra.
Thus ends the seventh paṭala in the ninth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the eighth paṭala in the ninth praśna:
The sacrificial animals for the seasonal sacrifices (kratupaśu) and those belonging to the group of eleven (aikādaśina) are subject to option.
In their combination, the constituent parts of the ritual procedure manifest; they do not manifest [independently], but recur with each refinement according to the purpose.
There is modification (ūha) according to the specific requirement.
Having offered the oblation for the sacrificial post (yūpāhuti), one begins with the eleven [posts], starting with that nearest the fire (agniṣṭha).
He cuts the sacrificial posts, the *anūpaśaya*, and the *pātnīvata*. This is optional with respect to a single post.
Having measured a cord eleven times the length of a chariot axle, he measures out the altar with a twenty-fourth part of that cord; it serves as a substitute for the *prakrama* step.

Having encircled the sacrificial post standing nearest the fire (*agniṣṭha*) with two cords, he encircles the eleven sets of cords at the *agniṣṭha* post and leaves them there. On the following day, having drawn the cup for the Aśvins (*āśvina*), he erects the sacrificial posts.
Some authorities prescribe the measurement [of the posts] on the previous day.
The taking up of the spade (*abhri*) is performed once as a common procedure (*tantra*), but the tracing around [the ground] is repeated.

Having traced around the southern [post] starting from the one standing near the fire (agniṣṭha), he traces around the northern one; thus, alternating, he traces them so that they end toward the north.
The intervals between the sacrificial posts (yūpa) are the measure of a chariot-axle, or he measures them equal to the altar (vedi).
He follows each [post] with one of the same kind; he causes the entire [set] to be prepared one by one, beginning from the ointment, and performs the second meal.
There is a *svaru* for each sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
One who desires the world of the ancestors should fix it so that it is level with the top [of the post].
One who desires the world of men should have it measured at the middle by a girdle;
one who desires sensory power should have it measured by the *caṣāla*;
one who desires a firm foundation should have all [the parts] equal.
Those three middle [posts], he should interlink for one desiring cattle; verily, by offspring he interlinks him with cattle.

For whomsoever he should desire, "May he be liable to die," for him he should set up the *gartamit* [post] with its northern half the tallest, and the others shorter. For one desiring heaven, he should set up the southern half the tallest, and the others shorter and shorter. For one practicing sorcery, the *ārāgra* [post] should be the tallest among them, and the others shorter and shorter.
For one who desires rain, he should have the post standing nearest the fire the shortest,
and the others progressively longer;
for one who has rivals, he should arrange them crosswise, alternating between short and long.

If he should desire, "May the common people (viś) be more powerful than the nobility (kṣatra)," he should erect those [posts] to the south of the *agniṣṭha* post, making them successively taller and taller.

If he should desire, "May the nobility be more powerful than the common people," he should erect those [posts] to the north of the *agniṣṭha* post, making them successively taller and taller. || 22 ||

The upper parts [of the stakes] should be equal in length; the middle sections, the girdles, and the caṣālas should be equal in width. Having encircled the upaśaya-stake with two girdles, one should place it at the front of the southernmost sacrificial post (yūpa).

If he should practice sorcery, he should place the upaśaya-stick pointing eastward with the formula: "I place this so-and-so, the son of such-and-such, under Indra’s thunderbolt. At the time for the animal sacrifice, he dedicates to Agni a black-headed animal at the *agniṣṭha* post; to Sarasvatī, a ewe to the north; and to Soma, a brown one to the south. In this alternating manner, he dedicates the animals of the southern row: to Pūṣan, a dark-grey one; to Bṛhaspati, a white-backed one; to Viśve Devas, a speckled one; to Indra, a ruddy one; to the Maruts, a brindled one; to Indra-Agni, a composite-colored one; to Dhūr, a dark-red one; to Savitṛ, a white one; and finally, to Varuṇa, a long-haired ram.

If he should desire, "May he who has been excluded regain his position, and may he who is excluded be reinstated," he should sacrifice a victim to Varuṇa in the place of the one for Indra, and a victim to Indra in the place of the one for Varuṇa; thus, he who was excluded regains his position, and he who was excluded is reinstated.
If he should desire, "May the subjects become bewildered," he should intermingle the animals; thus, he indeed bewilders the subjects.
If he were to sacrifice a victim to Varuṇa on the west side, Varuṇa would seize the subjects; therefore, he sacrifices facing north on the south side, away from the west.

He points out a wild animal or a mouse while lying down, saying, "This animal is for you. If he hates someone, he should point that person out; if he does not hate anyone, he should say, "The mouse is your animal.

For all [the animals], there are separate sacrificial grasses (*barhis*), omentum-spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*), cooking-pots (*kumbhī*), heart-spikes (*hṛdayaśūla*), and *plakṣa* branches. The carrying forward of the fire (*agniharaṇa*) is common (*tantra*). The final fore-offering (*prayāja*) is the *adhrigu*; likewise, the first secondary offering (*parivapya*) is at the end. There is the oblation for the slaughtered animal (*saṃjñaptahoma*), the casting away of the ropes (*raśanānām udasana*), the second secondary offering (*parivapya*), the throwing into the fire of the omentum-spits (*vapāśrapaṇīnām anupraharaṇa*), the supplementary oblation (*abhihoma*), the purification (*mārjana*), and the granting of a boon (*varadāna*). || 23 ||
For each [animal], the *manotā* verse is recited, or [the offering is made];
the three portions (*tryaṅga*) and the collected scrapings (*samavatta*) belong to all [the animals]. For each [animal], he offers the *vasāhoma* at the half-verse (*ardharca*).
He performs the *upayaj* offerings with the entrails of all [the animals]. And they perform the *saṃyājana* of the wives with the tails.

When the omentum of the *anūbandhya* cow has been offered, having measured out a sacrificial post for the *pātnīvata* offering in front of the *śālāmukhīya* fire—its height reaching below the navel, with its top-ring (*caṣāla*) and two ropes—he dedicates to Tvaṣṭṛ a bull that is hairy, tawny, and multicolored.
Having released the animal after the fire has been carried around it (paryagnikaraṇa), one should complete the remainder of the rite with clarified butter (ājya).

If there is a Kāpeya set of eleven animals, there are two for Indra on both sides of the one for Agni: [one] for Sarasvatī, [one] for Soma, and [one] for Pūṣan to the north; and [ones] for Bṛhaspati, Viśve Devas, Maruts, Savitṛ, and Varuṇa to the south.
The followers of Kapi know this [set]; one should sacrifice it at the end of an Atirātra.

In the Ahīna sacrifices, because of the connection with the indicative mark, she (the cow) becomes other than those belonging to the Sattra. One should understand the cattle suitable for the cows by means of the names of cattle: "bull," "stallion," "barren cow," "cow that miscarries," "milch cow," "calf," and "ox."
[The offerings] are more independent.
In the case of animals dedicated to a single deity, provided they are not interspersed with animals dedicated to other deities, the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) is common; it is indeed common. 24.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the ninth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
This ninth book is complete,
together with the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha.
Now begins the ninth question;
therein is the first section:
the midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina-savana), beginning with the pressing of the Soma, is performed.

The *abhiṣava* (pressing) is the great pressing (*mahābhiṣava*). That [rite] beginning with the pressing—meaning that the midday extraction (*mādhyandina-savana*) is extended, commenced, and performed—is explained by its ritual procedure (*kalpa*) according to the morning extraction (*prātaḥsavana*).
The meaning is that the ritual procedure for this midday extraction has been explained and stated in the manner of the morning extraction.

The cups for the dual deities, the seasonal cups, the Aindrāgna cup, the Vaiśvadeva cup, and the *darvihomas* are not found [in this context]. Since these would otherwise be obtained from the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), they are prohibited by this [text]. The *darvihomas*, beginning with the *dadhi-graha* and ending with the *antaryāma*, are also not found.
Having poured [water] from the *vasatīvarī* waters, he prepares the *nigrābhya* waters.

Having poured [the water] from the *vasatīvarī* vessels into the *hotṛcamasa*, and having taken water from the *vasatīvarī* vessels with the *hotṛcamasa* along with sand, he makes them *nigrābhya* by means of the formula "You are *nigrābhya*s.
They press the entire King [Soma].
The meaning is that there is no pressing of Soma in the third pressing, because of the scriptural statement: "In the third pressing they press the *ṛjīṣa*."

He gives the Soma-turban to the Grāvastut priest; "having loosened the King [Soma]" is the understood remainder. That is to say: "Having loosened the King [Soma], he gives the Soma-turban to the Grāvastut. Āpastamba recited it in exactly this way: "The King [Soma] being bound, [the Adhvaryu] silently causes him to descend from the binding-strap; having loosened him, having wiped that skin, and having placed the entire King [Soma] upon the lower stone, he gives the garment used for the striking of Soma to the Grāvastut. And this is not a gift, but rather something to be taken back from him again, as its place of storage is well known.

"By the words 'the sacrificer puts on the garment that removes the Soma,' a disposal (*pratipatti*) is indicated; for the placement of the garment used for wrapping the Soma is well known. Also, by the words 'the wife wraps the Soma,' a disposal is indicated. Regarding this, Āpastamba says: 'Without being prompted, the Grāvastut priest recites the *grāvastotrīyā* verses. The word 'Grāvastut' is the remainder [of the sentence]. The meaning is that there is no formal call (*praiṣa*) for the pressing of the Soma when the Grāvastut has already performed his duty. The ritual procedure is explained by the rule regarding the morning pressing;
thus, the pressing stones (*grāvan*) placed beneath the skin are treated in the same way. He states the specific detail regarding that:"
They press [the Soma] while propitiating with the words "hither, hither" (*ihā-iha*).
This means they speak loudly, "hither, hither. Because of the prefix *sam*, there is a repeated utterance of this word as many times as the pressing lasts, and not merely reciting it twice.
The reading in the manuscripts of Ja and Ma is *ubhayatīti*. 904
In the middle pressing of the final round, they press with the mantra, "Bṛhad-bṛhat.

The repetition of the word "they press" (*abhiṣuṇvanti*) here indicates that this is specifically the mantra for the pressing itself, and not merely the act of preparation. Consequently, it is established that the ritual action occurs at the end of the mantra; whereas in the previous case, the pressing was simultaneous with the recitation of the mantra—this is the distinction.
Regarding the phrase "when the excellent pressing has been well-prepared for the King":

the meaning is that when the excellent pressing is complete—meaning when all the Soma juice has been extracted—and the King [Soma] has been well-prepared. The mention of "in the excellent pressing" (*uttame 'bhiṣave*) is intended to exclude the possibility that the "well-preparation" might apply to every individual pressing; otherwise, it would have to be performed at each one. Furthermore, the mention of "when the King has been well-prepared" (*susaṃbhṛte rājani*) is intended to exclude the possibility that the preparation might occur before the pressing is finished and immediately after the pressing has begun.

"The gods, the pressing-stones, and Indu have spoken of Indra; they have caused Indra to move from the furthest distance, from this vast intermediate space, from the firmament. They have pressed out for me the essence of life, they have pressed out spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) for me. They have slain the demons in battle; the oppressors of sacred knowledge have been struck down. Thus the Pratiprasthātṛ gives thanks to the pressing-stones.

The *anumodana* is a fondling in the form of play, consisting of recitation accompanied by sport; and that is performed separately for each of the four [cups]. The mantra is recited only once, because of the use of the plural number. Then, having turned toward the *upara* [cup], he performs the rites beginning with "having made [the breath] face-to-face" and ending with the *māvasvadhyūhana*. Regarding this, some authorities prescribe the offering (*nirvapaṇa*) of the *savanīya* [cakes] at this very time. Because of the explicit statement "at this time," it is understood that this is not the time prescribed for what follows, nor is it the time for what precedes; therefore, it is considered that the preceding time is also valid. And this has been stated by Baudhāyana: "One should offer all the *savanīya* cakes at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) itself."

From that point, the ritual pertaining to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is concluded. Regarding the two subsequent pressings (*savana*), one should proceed with the potsherds by means of the non-sowing and the piling-up (*adhyūhana*) alone, for the procedure is established from that point onward. Thus, indeed, when the *savanīya* offerings of the midday pressing are being set out, one should say, "At the hymn (*stotra*) of the minor *vaiśvadeva*"; and at the third pressing, regarding the *savanīya* offerings, one should simply say, "At the hymn of the *māhendra*. At each pressing, one proceeds by means of the piling-up within the shed.

The meaning is that the placing [of the oblation] upon the potsherds occurs at the very same time as the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) for the two subsequent *savanīya* offerings. "At the *stotra* of the minor *vaiśvadeva*" means at the first *stotra* of the *ājya* [offering]. Regarding the doubt as to where the *savanīya* offerings connected with the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) are located, the phrase "at the *māhendra-stotra*" means that its time is the *māhendra-stotra*. By this much, the existence [of the offerings] during the three periods of time is established.

At the time of drawing the streams, having first drawn the Śukra and Manthin cups, he draws the Āgrayaṇa from three streams; he forms the third stream from the Ādhavanīya vessel after having drawn the Ukthya cup.

Immediately after having taken the Jyotiṣmat cup, he brings the Pratiprasthātṛ close at hand for the purpose of drawing the Marutvatīya cup; this is the remainder [of the sentence], intended to indicate that the agents are the same as understood from the context. The third stream is made from the Ādhavanīya vessel by means of pouring out. And here, the sequence of "prior" and "subsequent" is with respect to the order of the mantras. By the words "having first taken the Śukra and Manthin cups," it is indicated that the time for this very [action] is now.

By the extended application (atideśa) stating, "His ritual procedure is explained by that of the morning pressing," this rule would also apply to the midday pressing—namely, that one should draw the cups beginning with the Indravāyava at the Rathantara-sāman and those beginning with the Śukra at the Bṛhat-sāman—in order to avoid such a contingency. The mention of "each day" (amaham) is for the purpose of showing that this applies to every occasion. One should draw the two Marutvatīya cups using the two Ṛtu-vessels; the Adhvaryu draws the first with his own vessel, reciting, "The bull, increasing, accompanied by the Maruts," and the Pratiprasthātṛ draws the second with his own vessel, reciting, "O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, the bull, for our delight."

In this context, the sequence of "prior" and "subsequent" is with respect to the order of the mantras. The cup dedicated to the deity Marutvat is called *marutvatīya*; this is an epithet of Indra. The suffix *-cha* is applied according to Pāṇini’s sūtra: *dyāvāpṛthivī-śunāsīra-marutvad-agnīṣoma-vāstoṣpati-gṛhamedhāc cha ca*.
Having drawn [the Soma], he pours out as much of the King [Soma] as he considers sufficient for the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*).

The [procedure] has been explained in relation to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*). Here too, the phrase "having taken" (*gṛhītvā*) is a reiterative reference that connects with what follows. The ellipsis "the Adhvaryu" is supplied after "having taken," in order to establish that the Adhvaryu is the agent of both the taking and the pouring out.
The stream ceases; having pressed [the filter], he sets down the *pavitra*.
