This also has been explained in relation to the morning pressing.

The pouring of the *ekadhanas* into the *ādhavanīya* has been explained. The use of the term "of the *ekadhanas*" here is intended to indicate the absence of the *varuṇapraghāsa-camasas*. This has been explained by the sūtra: "Having poured a portion of the *ekadhanas* into the *ādhavanīya*, he pours a portion across the filter into the *pūtabhṛt*. The meaning is that this has already been stated. Having worshipped the *pavamāna-grahas*, the jars, the *śukra* and *manthin* cups, the *āgrayaṇa*, and the *ukthya* with the *grahāvakāśa* formulas, they proceed forth while maintaining physical contact with one another.

In this context, by the suffix *tyap*, there is the status of "approaching" (*upasthānatā*) due to the act of emerging (*niḥsarpaṇa*), but not due to the act of advancing (*prasarpaṇa*). Therefore, here the approaching belongs only to the Adhvaryu, the Brahman, and the Āgnīdhra, but not to the Pratiprasthātṛ, because for the latter there is no emerging. Regarding the approach to the Pavamāna cups, the approach to the water-jars (*kalaśa*), and the mere approach to the Śukra, Manthin, and other vessels, neither the sequence of ritual actions (*padārtha-krama*) nor even the order of the items themselves is intended to be significant here; rather, it is only the sequence of the mantras that prevails in this case.

Having performed the worship of the first *pavamāna* cup, and having performed the worship of the *śukra*, *manthin*, and other cups, he performs the worship of the jars (*kalaśas*). With the verse "Two oceans," he worships the *droṇakalaśa* and the *ādhavanīya*, which are the two *pavamāna* cups. With "Two supports," he worships the *pūtabhṛt*, which is the *pavamāna* cup for the great sacrifice. With "With the two eyes," he worships the two cups, the *śukra* and the *manthin*. With "For my self," he worships the *āgrayaṇa* cup. With "For my limbs," he worships the *ukthya* cup.

The worship of the jars (*kalaśa*) is performed with these mantras in sequence: "The belly of Viṣṇu," "The belly of Indra," and "The belly of the All-gods. There is also the set of six beginning with "Come near to the jar" (*upa kalaśo yata*). This is because it is included by the word "and" (*ca*), which serves to collect what has not been explicitly mentioned. By this very [word "and"], the worship for the Marutvatīya offering, namely "Paribhūr agni" and "Who art thou? What is thy name? (*ko 'si ko nāma*), is also included.

There is no ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) for the Āhavanīya fire, the *dhruva* ladle, the *atigrāhya* cups, and so forth, because they have already been attended to during the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*).

Having offered the *vaipruṣa* oblations and the *saptahotṛ* formula, they proceed to the midday *pavamāna* chant; the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for this is explained by that of the *bahiṣpavamāna*. || 1 ||

The *vainuṣas* and the *saptahotṛ* have been explained in the context of the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*). For the sake of the midday *pavamāna*, they proceed to the *mādhyandina-pavamāna*; they enter the *sadas*. Regarding that midday *pavamāna*, he states a specific mantra here:

"The path is *triṣṭubh*, the Rudras are the deity; by way of the wolf, by the path that does not lead astray, may we safely reach the Rudras"—with this, he adapts the mantra. This is the sixth [section].

Having gone to the north of the *havirdhāna* shed and having passed to the north of the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth, or alternatively to the south of the *mārjālīya* hearth; then, having passed between the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna*, one goes to the south of the *mānīkīya* hearth—this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "or between," the words "between the *havirdhāna* and the *mārjālīya*" are to be supplied by implication due to the force of the context. Here, the two "or" (*vā*) particles are intended to indicate that both options are primary alternatives.

Having entered the *sadas* by the eastern door, the Adhvaryu, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and the Brahman stand [there]; having gone around the front of the *praśāstrīya* hearth, the Udgātṛs chant the Mādhyandina Pavamāna.

Having entered the *sadas* by the eastern door, the *adhvaryu*, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and the *brahmā* stand [there] after having circumambulated the *praśāstrīya* hearth (*dhiṣṇiya*) from the front; such is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). Here, "standing" means sitting down. Alternatively, the phrase "having circumambulated the *praśāstrīya* hearth from the front" connects with the subsequent sūtra. In this alternative view, more is stated in another sūtra, namely, "to the south of the *audumbara* post"; since there is no contradiction, that too should be performed.

Regarding that which is other than the bringing of the animal: he issues the command, "O Pratiprasthātṛ, proceed with the curd-rite (dadhidharma)"; he concludes the command at this point. [The opponent asks: "Is it not the case that the command 'O Pratiprasthātṛ, come with the animal' constitutes the bringing of the animal, and therefore he should issue the command for what is other than that? [The author replies: It is not merely that much of a command; rather, he concludes the command at the words "O Pratiprasthātṛ, proceed with the curd-rite," meaning that he brings it to a close there. Because of the statement "he shall issue the command" (*saṃpreṣyati*), and because of the *paribhāṣā* sūtra stating "the Adhvaryu [acts] by means of the Yajurveda," and because no specific exception is mentioned, the Adhvaryu is the one who utters the command.

When the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths have been distributed and assigned with the mantras beginning with "vibhūrasi," and when the Adhvaryu has performed the distribution as before with the Soma taken in four ladlings and the clarified butter taken in five ladlings, and while the remnants remain in the *mārjālīya*— here, having previously entered the *havirdhāna* shed before the distribution, the worship of the cups (*graha-upasthāna*) is performed with this very mantra, "viṣṇo tvam naḥ," and the wiping of the vessels (*pātra-saṃmarśa*) is likewise performed.
[This occurs] when the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) has been strewn.
The meaning is that the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) has been spread by the Āgnīdhra.
Having offered the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), the Pratiprasthātṛ pours out the *savanīya* offerings.

In the previous case, according to the alternative of pouring out the *savanīya* offerings, the Āgnīdhra also performs the decoration of the cakes here. In the previous case, according to the alternative of pouring out the *savanīya* offerings, only the offering of the animal-cake took place here.
In this case, there is a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) on eleven potsherds.

However, because the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) is a modification of the offering to Agni (*āgneya*), it possesses only the eight potsherds as obtained from its archetype. Here, at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina savana*), there is no curdled milk (*āmikṣā*).

The ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for that [offering] is explained by the rule regarding the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*); thus, by this [rule], the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) would also be obtained, and the prohibition is intended to prevent that. The meaning is clear. Once [the Soma vessels] have been adorned, the Pratiprasthātṛ performs the *dadhigharma* rite. Here, the adornment of the *savanīya* [cakes] is performed at the time of the pressing. The singular verb "he performs" (*carati*) refers to the Pratiprasthātṛ alone, because he is the primary agent; the reading with the plural ending is merely a scribal error.
With the verse beginning "As great as are heaven and earth," he takes curd into an Audumbara ladle within the Āgnīdhra shed.

The mention of the "shed" (agāra) is for the purpose of excluding the taking of the Dadhigharma [offering] by one who is seated near the Viṣṇiya mounds or even outside the pavilion. The mention of the "ladle" (sruk), however, is for the purpose that the cleansing (saṃmārjana) should be performed silently, just as with the Juhū ladle.

"May speech and mind season you; may out-breath and in-breath season you; may sight and hearing season you; may skill and strength season you; may vigor and power season you; may life-span and old age season you; may self and body season you. You are cooked; you have been made cooked; for the cooked one, for the cooked ones, you! Having placed [the oblation] on the Āgnīdhrīya fire, there is no spreading of the base [of ghee] nor pouring over it, because it has not been so prescribed. He issues the command: "O Hotṛ, speak what is to be spoken by you."
Sixth. When it is said, "If it is cooked, offer it; if it is not cooked, let it simmer," he replies, "The oblation is cooked.
In the phrase "when it is being said," the word "he" (*saḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder. This is from the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha. [9th Praśna]

Having taken that [ladle] and gone to the Āhavanīya fire, after the call for attention (*āśrāvaṇa*) has been made and the response (*pratyāśrāvaṇa*) received, he issues the direction: "Sacrifice the Dadhigharma. The statement "having gone to the Āhavanīya" indicates that the call for attention must occur immediately after the departure, and no interval of time should be allowed between them; it is precisely for this purpose that the mention of the *āśrāvaṇa* and *pratyāśrāvaṇa* is made. He issues the direction: "Sacrifice the Dadhigharma. The word "Pratiprasthātṛ" is to be supplied as the subject, because of the context.

"He whom they call Indra, whom they call Varuṇa, whom they call Mitra, whom they call Truth; he who is the most divine among the gods, born of ascetic heat—to him [I offer] you, to them [I offer] you, Svāhā! With these words, he offers at the *vaṣaṭ* call.
This is the sixth [offering].
Having offered at the subsequent *vaṣaṭ* call, he carries away the portion for consumption.

The word "towards the Hotṛ" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. The meaning is that those who are engaged in the Pravargya rite—the Ṛṣikas—consume that Dadhidharma. This is a restrictive rule (niyama) for those who consume it; it is not an extension of the ritual properties (dharmātideśa) of the [ordinary] consumption, because there is no statement such as "as in the Pravargya. Nor are these the properties of the Dharmasacrifice, because the Dadhidharma is prescribed as a primary action (karma). Therefore, there is no request for permission (upahavayācana).
In the forest, this is his mantra for the consumption [of the sacrificial food] which is to be recited.

Thus ends the first chapter in the ninth book of the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra*. Regarding that *dadhidharma* (curd-rite), the *bhakṣamantra* (consumption mantra) is the section consisting of the *anuvākas* recited in the *Āraṇyaka*, the forest-text; this is what is meant by "it is stated. Which one? It is the *anuvāka* beginning with "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ mayi. He will state in the *Pavitra-sūtra*: "They consume the *dadhidharma* with the *anuvāka* 'bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ'. In this consumption mantra, there are the preceding and following *śāntis* (propitiatory verses).

And likewise, the *Pravāhaṇa* [Brāhmaṇa] states: "Having touched the *madantī* waters and having performed the propitiation (*śānti*) with the first *anuvāka*, one should study; and having studied, one should perform the rites with the last [anuvāka]. Because of this extension (*atideśa*) by the word "thus" (*evam*), there is also the touching of the *madantī* waters here. This mantra is modified by the mantra mentioned in the Brāhmaṇa, beginning with "In me is that great power (*indriya*)" and ending with "May speech, having rejoiced, satisfy itself on Soma. In this alternative, there is no propitiation (*śānti*).

Regarding this, Āpastamba specifies a particular rule: "Having recited 'mitro janān yātayati' and 'pratimitraḥ', they touch the region of the navel while consuming [the curds]. Since there is no contradiction and because the author of the Sūtra also intends the application of the mantra, this too must be accepted. In a sacrifice where the *pravargya* rite is not performed, there is no *dadhidharma* (curd-rite). It has been stated: [Ga, i, ca, ja, jha, ma, da read *pravarya*; ṅa, ra, vi, paṭalaḥ; accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* by Gopīnātha].

By nature, Āśvalāyana maintains that one should look at the *pravaradeva*s during the *dadhidharma* rite; however, Āpastamba has stated an alternative (*vikalpa*) by means of the sūtra: "Having described the *dadhidharma*, [he says] 'there is another [view]: it should not be performed in the *apravargya* sacrifice. The meaning of this is that the *dadhidharma* should not take place in the *apravargya* ritual.

Thus ends the first chapter of the ninth book in the *Jyotsnā* commentary, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—the son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was a performer of the Aṣṭāha, Śrīmad-Agniṣṭoma, Yājisāhasra, Aptoryāma, Tājapeya, Sarvatomukha, Dvisāhasra-Aptoryāma, and Pauṇḍarīka sacrifices—on the *Śrīmad-Bhagavat-Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*, which pacifies the distress of learned men caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within that ocean of a manual. ||1||
9.2 Now begins the second chapter in the ninth book.
Having placed the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) and having taken portions from them together, he proceeds with the offering, giving the call: "For the midday pressing! (mādhyandinasya savanasya).

Having placed the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) offered by the Pratiprasthātṛ, and having taken portions from those cakes together, he proceeds with the offering. The nature of the taking of the portions has already been explained in the context of the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana). The singular number in the word "pracarati" (he proceeds) is intended to indicate that the Adhvaryu is the principal officiant. In place of the words "prātaḥ prātaḥsāvasya," one should substitute "mādhyaṃdinasya savanasya. Thus, he issues the command using the modified directive formula (praiṣa-mantra). This command is directed toward the Praśāstṛ.
Having performed the offering with the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) and having taken the portions together, he proceeds with the Savanīya offerings.

Because of the statement regarding the performance [of the rite] with the *paśupuroḍāśa*, the *paśupuroḍāśa* is indeed obligatory. By this, the non-obligatory status mentioned by Āpastamba is set aside. There is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for its obligatoriness: "They proceed with the omentum at the morning pressing, with the *puroḍāśa* at the midday pressing, and with the animal cake at the third pressing. This very conclusion applies even to the Bahvṛcas. Regarding the *paśupuroḍāśa* and the *savanīya* offerings, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* are common. The meaning of the morning pressing has already been explained.

Having poured the *ādhavanīya* [vessel] into the *pūtabhṛt*, and having wiped the jar with the fringes [of the filter], he turns it face down. This too has already been explained in that very place. He issues the command: "Recite for those being filled! Fill the cups following the *hotṛ*'s cup! Make them bright on both sides! O *acchāvāka*-cup attendant, you also fill yours! O *pratiprasthātṛ*, prepare the wood-shavings, both sprinkled and unsprinkled! O *unnetṛ*, increase the Soma! Thus he preps the ritual.

Because there is a specific distinction among the three [sets of cups], the entire recitation of the *praisha* is performed for the sake of its full comprehension. In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [it is stated]: "He draws eleven cups, with the *hotṛ*-cup as the first; he draws the *acchāvāka*-cup from before the *āgnīdhra*-cup. This much is the distinction here; everything else is the same. The word "eleven" refers to the intention regarding the *sadasya*.

"Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the Soma-pressings set forth for Indra—the portion belonging exclusively to the midday pressing, accompanied by the *śukra* cup, the *manthin* cup, and dripping with honey. O *camasādhvaryus* of the performers, sacrifice at the central [call], both at the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*. O *camasādhvaryus* of the *hotrakas*, having sacrificed once each, replenish from the *śukra* cup and return," thus he gives the command. When that which was prior to the further replenishments has been performed, the *hotrakas* have moved forward with the formulas for advancing; they then sacrifice the Soma that has been further replenished.

The word *punaḥ* (again) is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). Prior even to these [subsequent] *unnetas*, when that ritual action has been performed, the mantras beginning with "Homage to Agni, the sacrificer" (*namo 'gnaye makhanne*) are the *prasarpaṇa-mantras*; having approached the *sadas* while reciting these, the approach to the *sadas* concludes with the crossing to the southern half. Here too, the word *punaḥ* serves solely to emphasize; that which was prior to the subsequent *unnetas*.

The meaning of the phrase *tasmin kṛte* is this: when that [preṣaṇa] has been performed—that is, when it has been uttered prior to the *abhyunnīta* cups—at this juncture occurs the *prasarpaṇa* (approaching) of the *hotṛ*-priests. It is for this very purpose that the entire [section] is recited. Even though they have already sat down according to the procedure prescribed in the Āśvalāyana-sūtra, this re-approaching (*punaḥ-prasarpaṇa*) concerning the Yājuṣa *hautra* is based on a direct scriptural injunction (*vācanika*).

Having announced "The Agnīdh has sacrificed," and having made the portioning-off, he places the *iḍā* for the Hotṛ. While the *iḍā* is being invoked, the cup-bearers (*camasādhvaryu*) lift up their cups.
Because of the mention of "announcing" in the phrase "having announced to the Hotṛ," the portioning-off occurs at the very moment of uttering "samadramakaḥ," and not immediately thereafter.
He does not set aside a fragment of the *iḍā* for the Acchāvāka.

This restatement is intended solely for the purpose of prescribing such a specific rule; the meaning, however, is clear. By the statement "The ritual procedure is explained by [the rules of] the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*)," the placement of the *iḍā*-portion was obtained, and that is now precluded by this [rule]. "They consume according to their cups" (*yathācamasam*); for them, the consumption mantra has been explained. "According to the cup" (*yathācamasam*) means not exceeding the respective cup. This has already been explained during the morning pressing.

When the Nārāśaṃsa cups have been consumed and the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) have been placed to the south of the altar, he performs the Dākṣiṇa offerings just as the Vaiṣarjana offerings were performed.

The word "to the south" (dakṣiṇena) indicates that the sacrificial gifts are situated in a place adjacent to the altar. "Vedi" refers to the Mahāvedi. The Dākṣiṇa rites are those actions consisting of oblations employed for the sake of the sacrificial gifts. By the phrase "just as the Vaiṣarjana offerings," the touching of the attendants (amātyānvārambha) is extended by analogy. [End of Second Paṭala] With the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

Having tied gold to the fringe of the cloth used for covering, having placed it in clarified butter, and having drawn the end of the cloth up along the handle of the offering-ladle (*sruc*), he offers two oblations in the *Śālāmukhīya* fire with the two verses, "Upwards that" (*ud u tyam*) and "The bright" (*citram*), and prepares the remainder of the clarified butter.
This has already been explained.
While the fires are being led forth, the Adhvaryu first takes his place and offers an oblation in the *Āgnīdhra* fire with the verse containing the word "lead," "O Agni, lead us" (*agne naya*).

While the [sacrificial] fires were being led by the attendants toward the Āgnīdhra pavilion, the first [priest], having arrived and gone ahead, said, "Lead [it] brokenly," because it is composed of the word *naya* (lead). Just as in the case of the *vaisarjana* [offerings], where by the mere mention of "the [fires] for the dismissal," the acts of tying gold to the fringe of the covering cloth and leading the end of the cloth along the axle are established even without the explicit statement, "having led the end of the cloth... regarding these constituent elements (*padārtha*).

Furthermore, the repetition here of the ritual items is for the purpose of specifying that they belong only to the two preceding oblations, and not to the *nayavatī* [verse] nor to the *vaisarjana* oblation. Consequently, the *vaisarjana* oblation occurs even with the *nayavatī* verse. For this very reason, Āpastamba stated that the holding of hands (*anvārambha*) is optional, saying: "Or, while they hold hands together, he offers in the *āgnīdhra* fire with the verse beginning 'O Agni, lead...
He then performs the remaining rites with clarified butter.
Clearly:
"Go to heaven, fly to the sky!"—having offered the gold, he takes it up.
The grammatical connection is: "Having offered, he takes up the gold. The meaning is that he takes up the gold from the place where it was poured.
"Across the forests he has stretched the intermediate space"—this is the second [offering], if a wagon, a chariot, or an upper garment is given.
If a wagon or a cart is given by the sacrificer, or if a chariot or an upper garment—a skin-cloth—is given, then this is the second oblation.
"O Prajāpati, these beings of yours..."—this is the third [offering], if a horse, a man, or an elephant is given.

If a horse, a man, a slave, or an elephant is given by the sacrificer, then this is the third oblation: "When the sacrificial fees have been led away, the seers say that the lord of the sacrifice has been struck by sin. With five [verses], he offers the Vaiśvakarman oblations on the Āgnīdhrīya fire.

When the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) have been led away by this or that person, while those fees are being carried off, the seers say of the lord of the sacrifice (*yajñapati*), "He has been struck by sin. Thus, on the fifth day, he offers the Vaiśvakarman oblations during the *anvāhārya* ritual. On the fifth offering, there is the character of being dedicated to Viśvakarman according to the principle of the *sāṣṭi* [or *sāṣṭika*] rule. Regarding "the lord of the sacrifice," "the terrible seers," "the non-other Soma-drinkers," "those who consume," and "homage to the ancestors"—thus Bharadvāja clearly states at the end.

These rites consisting of oblations are *vaiśvakarmaṇa*, belonging to Viśvakarman; these are the *vaiśvakarmaṇa* rites. He offers them on the *āgnīdhīya* fire. The mention of the *āgnīdhīya* is for the purpose of excluding the *āhavanīya*. Here, the pause (end of a section) is set aside according to the recensional text (*pāṭha*). Pauses are determined in accordance with how far the word *viśvakarman* extends in the passage, because this has been clearly stated by Bharadvāja.
[Note: This refers to Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Ninth Book.]

"Having taken up the two Marutvatīya cups according to how they were drawn, [the Adhvaryu] issues the directions: 'Recite the invitatory verse for Indra accompanied by the Maruts; give the command for Indra accompanied by the Maruts!

'According to how they were drawn' means that the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ take up the two Marutvatīya cups without transgressing the order. According to the technical rule (paribhāṣā-sūtra) stating 'The Adhvaryu acts with the Yajurveda,' it is the Adhvaryu alone [who gives the directions].
Having offered them, the two of them pour out the remnants."

Having offered the *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* calls, they both pour out [the remnants]. The Pratiprasthātṛ pours the residue into the Adhvaryu’s cup; the Adhvaryu pours a portion of that into the Pratiprasthātṛ’s cup—the meaning is that they both perform the pouring of the residues. In the term *vyavanayete*, the prefix *vi-* is intended to indicate the distinction between this pouring of residues and that performed during the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*).

And that distinction between the two is one of uniformity, not a distinction consisting in the Adhvaryu bringing both [portions] together while the Pratiprasthātṛ brings only a single portion from one side; such is the nature of the difference here. The meaning is that just as in the case of the Ṛtugraha cups they consume with the Pratiprasthātṛ's participation, and just as in the case of the Ṛtugrahas there is consumption first from the Pratiprasthātṛ’s cup, so it is here as well.

The *hotṛ* drinks twice, while the other two drink once each. The *hotṛ*’s drinking twice is caused by the *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* calls; the drinking of the other two, the *adhvaryu* and the *pratiprasthātṛ*, occurs once each, being caused by the oblation and the pressing. Since the *adhvaryu* acted first, his drinking comes first, followed by that of the *pratiprasthātṛ*. Having washed the vessel at the *mārjālīya* fire-altar, he places it near the *hotṛ*.

"In his presence, near him, you were born fierce for victorious power, delightful, most mighty, with abundant pride; even the Maruts strengthened Indra here, when the Mother bore the Hero as the most excellent. With the [verse], "O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, drink here," he draws the third *marutvatīya* cup from the *kalaśa* vessel using one of his own cups that has not been consumed, while reciting the *śastra*.

Since the alternative (*vikalpa*) is already established by the word "or" (*vā*), the mention of "either one" (*anyatara*) is for the sake of restriction: in the modified rites (*vikṛti*), the mantra is "janithāḥ," whereas in the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*), it is "indra marutvaḥ. The phrase "with one's own undiminished vessel" has its purpose demonstrated in the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*). Two *marutvatīya* cups have been drawn; this is the third *marutvatīya* cup, intended to ensure the necessary knowledge that "this cup is accompanied by a recitation" (*śastravat*) at the time of its drawing. In the absence of this knowledge, the expiation for a breach of the *yajus* formula is performed in the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*). Beginning with the *ṛtupātra*, he responds with the *pratigara*.

"Having taken hold" means having grasped. Here, the meaning of the word *ālambha* (taking hold) is simply grasping with the hand; for it is impossible for the Adhvaryu, while standing, to perform the primary meaning of the word *ālambha* at every response (*pratigara*). The meaning is: having taken the *ṛtupātra* vessel in his right hand, he responds to the *śastra*. "The *uktha* has been spoken"—having responded to the *śastra*, he mutters this everywhere at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*).
This is clear.

Having thrown back the *śastra*, he takes up the *graha*; the *camasādhvaryus* [take up] the *camasa*s. He issues the command: "O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice the Soma! The shaking [of the vessels] after [the offering], the consumption of the *graha*s and the *nārāśaṃsa*s, and the swelling and setting down of the *nārāśaṃsa*s have been explained.

Since one could have achieved brevity by stating in the sūtra simply, "like that of the Aindrāgna [cup], including the *śastra* and the *nārāśaṃsa*s," the fact that the sūtra is composed in this more elaborate manner implies that the recitation of this sūtra is mandatory immediately after the *śastra* response. If this were not done, the expiation for a breach of the *yajus* formula would be performed in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with the mantra, "Bhuvaḥ svāhā"; this result is indeed invisible (*adṛṣṭa*), as a visible result is impossible here.
With either of the two mantras, "Great is Indra who [rules] by might" or "Great is Indra, like a hero," he draws the Māhendra cup from the *kalaśa* vessel, accompanied by the *stotra* and *śastra*.

Since the alternative (*vikalpa*) is already established by the word "or" (*vā*) itself, the inclusion of the term "either one" (*anyatara*) is for the purpose of specifying the particular arrangement (*viniveśa*). In the *rathantara* [sāman], the cup is taken with the first [verse], and in the *bṛhat*, with the second. This was stated by Baudhāyana: "In the *bṛhat-pṛṣṭha* [rite], [the verse] 'mahān indro nṛvad' [is used]. However, in the case of the *ubhayasāman* [rites], it is like the sequence of the cups (*grahāgra*). There is no restriction regarding the meters such as *vairāja* and others. In the alternative arrangement, the phrase "dvibarhāḥ" is also a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the *bṛhat*. By this, the claim made by some that there is an equal option (*tulyavikalpa*) is refuted.

Regarding the statement, "Some prescribe the offering of the *savanīya* oblations here at the third pressing," the inclusion of the word "here" (*atra*) in the sūtra to be cited later indicates that the time for the offering of the *savanīya* oblations occurs even after the drawing of the *māhendra* cup. Therefore, in this view, the offering of the *savanīya* oblations takes place at this point. Baudhāyana also has stated the offering of the third-pressing *savanīya* oblations at this stage, and that has already been demonstrated previously.

Bhāradvāja and others say: "In this case, one should perform the pressing for the third pressing (*tārtīyasavanika*); one should offer the *savanīya* cakes and the *saumya* [caru]; one should pour the *āśir* milk for Agni. This is one view; another is that there is only a single third pressing. Regarding the phrase "possessing the *stotra* and *śastra*," its purpose has been shown in the context of the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*).

Having set it down, he introduces the *stotra*; that has been explained. When the *stotra* is concluded, he introduces the *śastra*; that has been explained. This has been explained in the context of the morning pressing.

Having responded to the *śastra*, the *camasādhvaryus* take up the cups and the *graha*. Although it would have been more concise to state, "At the recitation of the *vaiśvadeva*, [there are] the *śastra-graha* and the *nārāśamsa*," the purpose of composing the aphorism (*sūtra*) in its elaborate form is to ensure that the reading of the *sūtra* is mandatory. The *sūtra* has already been explained. The phrase "having responded to the *śastra*" also has a demonstrated purpose.
The other *adhvaryus* take the *atigrāhya* cups: the *pratiprasthātṛ* takes the one for Agni, the *neṣṭṛ* the one for Indra, and the *unnetṛ* the one for Sūrya.

By the term *adhvaryu*, the Pratiprasthātṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Unnetṛ are meant, according to the sūtra: "The Adhvaryu, the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Neṣṭṛ, and the Unnetṛ—these are the Adhvaryus. The occasion for the taking of these cups has been shown by Āpastamba: "The *atigrāhya* cups are taken after the Māhendra cup. This means that the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the *atigrāhya* cup dedicated to Agni, the Neṣṭṛ takes the one dedicated to Indra, and the Unnetṛ takes the one dedicated to Sūrya. (Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, Book 9).

"O reciter of hymns, sacrifice the Soma!"—with these words he issues the command; then he offers the *atigrāhya* cups according to their respective forms with the formulas beginning, "O Agni, full of splendor, [make me] full of splendor."

The mantra "O Agni, you who possess splendor" (*agne tejasvin*) is for the Pratiprasthātṛ at the offering of the *atigrāhya* cup dedicated to Agni; the mantra "O Indu, you who possess splendor" (*indau māsvin*) is for the Neṣṭṛ at the offering of the *atigrāhya* cup dedicated to Indra; and the mantra "O Sūrya, you who possess radiance" (*sūrya bhrājasvin*) is for the Unnetṛ at the offering of the *atigrāhya* cup dedicated to Sūrya—this is the meaning of the term *yathārūpa*. The occasion for these offerings has been clearly stated by Āpastamba: "When the [cup] for Mahendra has been offered, they go [to the next stage] according to the rule of the subsequent offerings. However, there is no *vaṣaṭ*-call for this. Why? Because in the Āpastamba-sūtra...

They say "jhūyanta" because of the act of killing. Because of the singular number in "ukthaśā yaja somasya" and because of the difference in deities, there is then an *anuvaṣaṭkāra* for the Māhendra cup. With the formulas "Mayi medhām," "Mayi prajām," and so forth, they consume the *atigrāhya* cups according to their respective forms.

"May Agni bestow wisdom upon me, offspring upon me, and splendor upon me"—with these words, the Pratiprasthātṛ consumes the portion belonging to Agni. "May Indra bestow wisdom upon me, offspring upon me, and sensory power (*indriya*) upon me"—with these words, the Neṣṭṛ consumes the portion belonging to Indra. "May Sūrya bestow wisdom upon me, offspring upon me, and radiance (*bhāsa*) upon me"—with these words, the Unnetṛ consumes the portion belonging to Sūrya; such is the meaning of the words according to their respective forms. "Speech, which is the subduer of the dull," is the common designation for both.
Since the Adhvaryu is the performer of the consumption occasioned by the pressing, the invitation (*upahvāna*) must be performed by all three.
The two vessels for the *āpyāyana* (swelling) do not become "all-consuming" (*sarvabhakṣa*). This is clear. They proceed with three *ukthya-vigrahas* as before.

As stated by the word "purastāt" (before), the following are obtained: the drawing of the third portion from the *ukthya* vessel into the *ukthya* cup; its placement in the *āyatana*; the touching back of the vessel; the sequential drawing of the Soma into the three cups, beginning with the respective *śastra*-reciter's cup and ending with the eleven *camasa*s; the filling of the *āgnīdhra-camasa* and the *acchāvāka-camasa* first; the commencement of the *stotra* and *śastra*; and the rites beginning with the response to the *śastra* and ending with the consumption (*makṣa*). Regarding this, he states the specific rule:
at every instance, the drawing and the placing are modified [respectively] with the formula "For Indra, thee! (*indrāya tvā*).

Having set aside the deities Mitrāvaruṇa and Indra-Agni, the deity Indra alone is prescribed. A mantra containing the word "Indra" applies in all three cases. In that regard, the mantra for the drawing [of the cup] is: *upayāmagṛhīto 'si* ("Thou art taken with a support"). The mantra for the setting down is: *eṣa te yonir indrāya tvā* ("This is thy womb; for Indra thee"). That by which something is drawn is called the "drawing" (*grahaṇa*); that by which something is set down is called the "setting down" (*sādana*). These two are specific to the mantra. When the sacrifice is completed, he offers with the mantra: *viśve devā maruta indro asmān*.
The morning pressing has been explained. [In the text] "g, ca, 'rī" they perform [the rites]. [Adhyāya 1, Paṭala 915. Together with the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa:
Having issued the command, "O Praśāstṛ, impel! he says, "Crawl forth! O Praśāstṛ; thus the midday pressing is concluded. ||4||

Thus ends the second chapter in the ninth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. Completed. Thus ends the second chapter of the ninth book in the commentary named Jyotsnā, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—the son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was the grandson of Śrīmad Agniṣṭomayājin, Sāhasrāgniyukta, Vājapeyayājin, Sarvatomukhayājin, and Viśāhasrāgniyukta Pauṇḍarīkayājin—written to alleviate the distress of learned men caused by the failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the ocean of the venerable Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. || 2 ||
9.3 Now begins the third chapter of the ninth inquiry.
The third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) is performed beginning with the Āditya cup.

This statement is made even though it is already established by the initial injunction for the Āditya cup; its purpose is to indicate that if one, through confusion, performs the rite starting from "having poured from the *vasatīvarī* waters" while forgetting the Āditya cup, then after completing the procedure pertaining to the Āditya cup up to "he sets down the vessel like a cook," one must perform again the rite starting from "having poured from the *vasatīvarī* waters," even though it has already been done. It is not sufficient merely to perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed for such a transposition.
The ritual procedure for him is explained by that of the midday pressing;
this is clear.
Having closed the doors of the *havirdhāna* shed, when many [priests] are inside the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*).

"Having covered" means having closed. When many people are seated inside the altar (*antarvedi*), then the closing of the doors is performed and not otherwise. By the word "many," those who are ignorant of the ritual and numerous in number are included here by the plural. Thus Āpastamba says: "Having closed both doors of the *havirdhāna* [shed] when there are many people on the altar.
Or, "when his rival":
when the sacrificer’s rival or enemy is seated inside the altar, then too the doors are to be closed.
The sacrificer and his wife sit within the altar; then he draws the Āditya cup.

Although the sacrificer’s presence within the altar is already established, this specific statement is for the purpose of prescribing that they both sit in the middle portion of the altar, which consists of the *havirdhāna* shed. Because there is no compound, their joint action (*sāhitya*) is not intended. The word "atha" (then) signifies the sequence following the sitting by both agents within the altar. If one whose rival is performing a Soma sacrifice should perform one himself, he should stand outside the altar for as long as the other draws the Āditya cup. *Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra*, Ninth Book.

When an adversary (*bhrātṛvya*) has entered within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*) among many people, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) should likewise remain outside for as long as that soma-pressing for the adversary’s sacrifice continues; this is the meaning. Āpastamba states this matter clearly: "But at the sacrifice of an adversary, while the Āditya cup is being drawn, one should stand outside. The meaning of Āpastamba’s sūtra is that when one has gone to the sacrifice of an adversary, one should stand right there outside the altar at the time of the drawing of the Āditya cup.
With the mantra "kadācana starīrasi," he draws a portion of that soma which is in the Āditya vessel using the Āditya cup.

Here, the soma residing in the Āditya vessel consists of the remnants from the libations for the dual deities (*dvidevatya-graha*). With the mantra "kadācana prayucchasī," [he takes] the curd from the heated milk-vessel (*śṛtātaṅkyam dadhi*).
He pours out that curd which was previously prepared for the purpose of the Āditya-graha, [reciting] "The sacrifice of the gods approaches. He takes all the Soma that is in the Āditya vessel;

he takes all the Soma remaining from the libations to the dual deities (*dvidevatya*). [He does so] with the formula, "With a support from above, I take thee. According to the general rule (*paribhāṣā*), the phrase "thou art taken with a support" (*upayāmagṛhīto 'si*) appears at the end of these mantras.

With the formula, "O Vivasvat, O Āditya," he mixes the Soma with the *upāṃśusavana* stone for the sake of the Āditya cup; that is, he stirs—meaning he causes to mingle—the Soma taken in that vessel and the curds. With the formula, "I mix thee with that which is divine rain," he should mix the Āditya cup with milk or curds from above for one who desires rain.

After the final lunar eclipse mentioned above, the sacrificer who desires rain should form the following resolution: "I shall perform the mixing (*śrayaṇa*) with milk or curd after the final lunar eclipse. This is based on the *Darśapūrṇamāsa-yājñika-sūtra*, which states: "He mixes [the soma] with what he desires" and "he causes it to boil. Regarding the rule "he does not take curd from the middle," according to the view of certain teachers, there is an omission of the taking of curd for the boiled milk (*śṛtātaṅkyadadhigrahaṇa*), as indicated by the passage "never failing" (*kadācana prayucchatīti*).
Upon that [stone], he places the *upāṃśusavana* pressing-stone.

When the *āditya* cup has been drawn, he places that stone called the *upāṃśusavana* on top of it. Regarding this, the northerners do not recite the *pāvana* verses; that is indeed consistent with reason.
Having lifted it up, he attains higher knowledge.

Having taken that Upāṃśusavana stone from that Āditya cup, one should discern the future rain from it. Regarding this, he says: "If, when it has been struck, a drop falls quickly, Parjanya will be rainy; if [it falls] after a long time, he will not be rainy. [End of] the Sixth Paṭala, accompanied by the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa.

If a small drop of the surging, overflowing *soma* juice should quickly fall or descend, then the rain-cloud (*parjanya*) will be one that rains; if [the drop falls] after a long delay, it will be one that never rains—this is the meaning of the word "knowledge" (*vijñāna*). The grammatical construction is: "if it should descend after a long time.
It does not perish.

The remainder is simply "I am. Regarding the wiping and the settling according to their source, which is obtained through the general rule (*paribhāṣā*), the settling is prohibited by this [text]. However, the wiping certainly takes place, as there is no statement prohibiting it. As for the pressing-stone (*grāvan*), one settles it indeed because of the requirements of the ritual, and because of Baudhāyana’s statement: "He throws the *upāṃśusavana* stone onto the pressing-stones. With the words "From the ocean, from the atmosphere," he causes [the sun] to move with *darbha* grass;
that is, he causes the sun to move or churns it with *paribhojanīya* *darbha* grass.
Saying, "I am above, I am below," he covers it with darbha grass or with his hand.
Furthermore, by the act of taking up the *darbha* grass again, other *darbha* blades are meant, and not those previously taken up. With his right hand, he covers—that is, he shields—the sun's orb.
He rises with the mantra: "May the god Sūrya protect me from the gods.
This is clear.
"The poet extends the path of the sacrifice"—thus he brings [the offering].
"He leads it toward the one who speaks the higher word"—this is the meaning.

"To the Adityas, the beloved, whose abodes are beloved, whose vows are beloved, the great ones, the lords of Sarasvat, the overseers of the wide mid-air—recite the invitatory verse! To the Adityas, the beloved, whose abodes are beloved, whose vows are beloved, the great ones, the lords of Sarasvat, the overseers of the wide mid-air—give the command! Thus he gives the *saṃpraiṣa* (the formal direction). || 5 ||
This is the eighth [section]. With the mantra, "O Agni, those which are all thy fuel-sticks," he throws *darbha* grass into the Āhavanīya fire and offers the oblation while looking elsewhere.

This mantra connects only with the primary act of offering (*homakriyā*), and not with the throwing of the *darbha* grass. As for what some say—that the throwing of the *darbha* grass is done with the mantra while the offering is silent—that is trivial; because it contradicts the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the phrase "of the clarified butter as the oblation" (*āhuti ghṛtasya*), and because it is more logical that the mantra connects with the primary act of offering itself. (Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, Ninth Book, Section 118).

One who desires rain should offer oblations with the mantra, "Unfold the earth" (*unnambhaya pṛthivīm*). This serves as a substitute for the mantra "All those of yours" (*yāste viśvā*). Because it occupies that place, the primary act of offering is its function; thus, even in the absence of an explicit indicative mark (*liṅga*), its application is established by the rule of substitution. Here, the sacrificer desiring rain must form a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Desiring rain, I shall offer the Āditya-graha oblation with this mantra, 'Unfold the earth. Having offered, he should not look back.
One should not look at the offering even until it has been placed down, much less at the time of the oblation itself.

He does not perform the *anuvaṣaṭ* call, nor does he consume [the remnant]; he places the vessel like a *sūda*. "Remnant" (*sūda*) means what remains. The prohibition "he does not perform the *anuvaṣaṭ* call" is for the purpose of focused attention (*avadhāna*). The consumption [of the remnant] would otherwise be established by virtue of the occasion of the oblation and the pressing; the statement "he does not consume" is intended to preclude that. Even in the absence of consumption, there might be no setting aside of the remnant; therefore, the phrase "like a *sūda*" is used. Since the setting aside of the remnant is already established by its subsequent application, this specific statement is for the sake of ensuring focused attention.
Having drawn [water] from the *vasatīvarī* waters, he prepares the *nigrābhya* waters;
that is to say, by this procedure, he places the *nigrābhya* waters in the *hotṛ*'s cup after having drawn them from the *vasatīvarī* waters.
He should mix the stalk (*aṃśu*) which is in the *upāṃśu* vessel into the *ṛjīṣa*; they silently press the *ābhyā* stalk and the *ṛjīṣa* into the *upāṃśusavana* stones.

Even when these ritual objects have been placed [on the pressing stones], they press silently together with them, saying "iha-iha" (here-here); this also occurs here. This is because of the sūtra stating, "Its ritual procedure is explained by that of the Mādhyandina pressing. Nor should one suspect a contradiction with the statement "they press silently," for the utterance "iha-iha" does not function as an instrument of the pressing. However, "bṛhat-bṛhat" is not used, because that functions as an instrument of the pressing and is thus set aside by the injunction "silently.
He does not give the turban to the Grāvastut priest.
This is a prohibition of what is obtained through extension from the midday pressing (*mādhyandinasavana*):
"The Pratiprasthātṛ does not approve of the pressing-stones.
This too is a prohibition of what is obtained through extension from the midday pressing.
Regarding this, some authorities prescribe the offering of the *savanīya* oblations at this very time;
that is to say, neither at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*) after the drawing of the *māhendra* cup, nor at the later time subsequently prescribed.
At the time of the continuous stream-offering (*dhārā-grahaṇa*), one draws the *āgrayaṇa* from four streams, making the fourth stream from the *āditya* vessel.

The three streams have been described in the Mādhyandina Śastra; the specific distinction here is that there is a fourth stream from the Āditya vessel, as in the case of the Soma-presser. [From] the Āditya vessel [means] with the Soma contained in the Āditya vessel. Having taken that, he causes the King (Soma) to flow through until he considers it sufficient for the third pressing; he stops the stream, squeezes out the filter, and sets it down. This Sūtra is for the purpose of recording the recitation as part of the ritual procedure. In the absence of this recitation, the expiation for a breach of the Yajus formula is performed on the southern fire.

When that [rite] which precedes the Pavamāna cups has been performed, the sacrificer and his wife, having churned the *āśira* (milk-mixture) in the Āgnīdhra shed, enter the Havirdhāna shed by the western door and pour the *āśira* into the *pūtabhṛt* jar through the filter with the four verses beginning, "O Gods, provide us with beauty."

Having poured from the *pavamāna* [vessel] into the *āghavanīya* either the entire mass or a portion of it prior to the *nābhi*, and having purified it with the *pavitra* filter, he pours it out; when that ritual act has been performed, [he does so] in the *āgnīdhra* shed, in the *āgnīdhra* pavilion. Regarding the presence of multiple wives (*patnībahutve*), only the principal wife performs the churning and the pouring into the *pūtabhṛt* vessel, not all of them. Because of the statement "with four [verses]," the pouring out occurs at the end of all the mantras. This sets aside the general rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "ritual acts consist of single mantras. [The phrase] "having entered the *havirdhāna*" refers to this...

The verb "stands" (*tiṣṭhati*) is to be supplied [after *anantaram*]. Therefore, in this case, who is the wife? In the subsequent passage, both are the agents. Thus, the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) would otherwise be untenable; this contradiction between the preceding and following sections is resolved by this supply of the verb. As for the mention of the *āśira* (curd-mixture) in the subsequent passage, the remainder of the sense is "having divided that. In this way, the mention of the *āśira* in the subsequent section for the purpose of division becomes purposeful. By the word *pavitra*, the *daśāpavitra* (the fringed filter) is meant.
Having worshipped the *pavamāna* cups, the jars, and the *āgrayaṇa* vessel with the *grahāvakāśa* formulas, they proceed to move out while maintaining contact with one another.
This is to be explained as being like the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*).
Having offered the *vaipruṣa* oblations and the *saptahotṛ* formula, they move toward the *ārbhava-pavamāna*; its ritual procedure is explained by that of the midday pressing. || 6 ||

Because of its connection with the deities of the third *savana*, it possesses the quality of being "manifest" (*ābhava*); thus, the term "third-*savana* [laud]" (*tātīyasavanika*) is applied to the *pavamāna* as well, since the third *savana* is "manifest" by means of that [quality]. By the extension (*atideśa*) from the midday *pavamāna*, it is obtained that one should go around to the north of the *āgnīdhra* and *viṣṇiya* hearths, or to the south of the *mārjālīya*, or between them.
The path belongs to the *Jagatī* meter and the Ādityas are the deity; one modifies the mantra, "By a path not obstructed by a wolf, may I safely reach the Ādityas," to fit the context.
This modification is called *ūha*.

Whatever [is required] other than the spreading of the *dhishṇiya* hearths, he issues that command: "O Pratiprasthātṛ, perform the dialogue regarding the animal sacrifice. He concludes the command with this much: "Spread this sacrificial grass; prepare the cakes for the offering; O Pratiprasthātṛ, perform the dialogue regarding the animal sacrifice. This much is established here by the Sūtra. If the words "O Pratiprasthātṛ, perform the dialogue regarding the animal sacrifice" were not uttered, [the sequence of the] *viṣṇiya*...

In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the ninth book]—once it is established that the meaning is "he gives the command for everything other than the spreading [of the fires]," this specific statement is intended to exclude the possibility that the Pratiprasthātṛ might perform the *dadhidharma* rite due to the extension (*atideśa*) from the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdinasavana*).

When the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths have not been spread apart and have not been addressed with mantras, and when the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) has been strewn, the Pratiprasthātṛ pours out the *savanīya* offerings.
When the *āmīṣa* grass has been strewn, the Pratiprasthātṛ pours out the *savanīya* offerings. This too is one time for the pouring out of the *savanīya* offerings.
In this case, there is a cake (puroḍāśa) on twelve potsherds.

Since the ritual procedure for the third pressing is explained by the extension of the rules from the midday pressing—as indicated by the statement "the ritual procedure here is explained by the midday pressing"—the injunction for the curd-mixture (āmikṣā) does not apply; thus, the prohibition of the āmikṣā is also established here.
Furthermore, the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) is not present.
Because the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) is also obtained through the extension (*atideśa*) from the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdinasavana*), a prohibition is made [of its performance].

Regarding this, some authorities prescribe the cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) for all the pressings, some on eleven potsherds, and some on twelve potsherds. Here, the middle position is that found in one's own recension (*svaśākhā*): "One should offer cakes on eleven potsherds at the morning pressing, cakes on eleven potsherds at the midday pressing, and cakes on eleven potsherds at the third pressing, for the sake of the regularity (*salomatva*) of the sacrifice. The other two positions belong to other recensions.
When the animals have been adorned, the Pratiprasthātṛ proceeds with the animal ritual (paśutantra) beginning from the *saṃvāda* (the dialogue).

Although the offering (*nirvāpa*) took place previously, the adornment occurs here specifically because it follows the sequence of the *praisha* (directions). Having taken five portions of clarified butter into the *juhū* ladle, he proceeds with that animal ritual—which begins with "O Adhvaryu, bring the *pṛṣadājya*... and ends with "he places the heart in its known location"—meaning he consecrates them. The performance beginning with the placing of the *pañcahotṛ* vessel and so forth belongs to the Adhvaryu by virtue of his authority.
He carries the collected portions (*samavatta*) either to the south or to the north of the *havirdhāna* cart.

He carries around the *samavatta* (the collected portions) of that animal victim, having brought it from the *jhuṅga* (the place of the *jūhu*) and the *iḍā*, either to the south of the *havirdhāna* shed or to the north. They carry it around on all sides.
The sacrificer does not consume the portions; however, some authorities prescribe the consumption.

By the use of the plural "portions" (*bhakṣān*), there is a prohibition against the consumption of the *iḍā*, the remnants of the oblation, and the portions belonging to the sacrificer. On the alternative view that there is consumption, there is indeed consumption of all of these.

Having placed the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) down and having taken portions from them together, he proceeds with the offering while giving the call: "For the third pressing. Having had the cakes brought by the Pratiprasthātṛ and having placed those cakes down, he proceeds by taking portions together from those cakes. [Chapter 3, Section 10] Together with the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

Having poured the *ādhavanīya* [vessel] into the *pūtabhṛt*, and having wiped the jar with the fringes (*daśā*), he turns it face down. He issues the direction: "Recite for those being drawn up; draw up following the cup of the Hotṛ... make them strong and mixed with milk (*āśīrvat*); O *acamasa*-adhvaryu of the Acchāvāka, pour your portion; O Unnetṛ, manifest the Soma. This entire passage is recited because there is a specific purpose within the instruction. By the word *tīvra*, Somas that are exceedingly pungent and sour are meant. By the word *āśīrvat*, those mixed with milk (*āśir*) are meant. He draws up eleven cups, with the cup of the Hotṛ as the foremost.
[The section on] the *gata* [is concluded].
"He proceeds with those very [chamasa cups] that have already set out at the time of the *pracaraṇa*" means:

he proceeds with such *camasa*s as have already set out at the time of the *pracaraṇa*, having reached the point of departure toward the *uttaravedi*; the meaning is that he proceeds with these existing cups, and not with others previously [used].

"Prompt the offering of the Somas set forth for Indra—belonging to the third pressing, abounding in wealth, abounding in power, abounding in strength, possessed of vigor, accompanied by Savitṛ, Bṛhaspati, and the Viśve Devas, and strong with the *āśis* (invocation)—O Camasādhvaryus of the middle-performers, sacrifice at the *vaṣaṭ* and *anu-vaṣaṭ* calls! O Camasādhvaryus of the Hotrakas, having sacrificed once each, fill up from the strong, *āśis*-endowed [Soma] and return!"—thus he issues the command.

Because there is a specific distinction within the *preṣa*, the entire recitation belongs to the *preṣya*. Here, regarding the cups of the *hotraka*s, the *camasādhvaryu*s offer them only once each; they face southward and not eastward. Other oblations are offered facing east, because of the statement concerning the connection between the *śukra* and *manthin* cups: "The *śukra* and *manthin* [cups] are offered facing west. When the *unnīyamāna-sūkta* has been concluded and the other cups have been taken up by the *camasādhvaryu*s, the *adhvaryu* takes up his own cup; this is because there is no mention of the two *graha*s [in this context].
"To the hawk that flies, svāhā!"—with these [formulas] he offers the portions that have been drawn again, [reciting] "Obeisance to him who has spontaneously approved," at each subsequent vaṣaṭ-call.

Regarding the phrase "by these, moreover" (*etaiḥ punar*), the word "moreover" (*punaḥ*) has the sense of "also" (*api*); this should be construed immediately after the word "abhyunnīta" (re-offered). Thus, the meaning becomes: "He offers with these mantras those [portions] that have been re-offered. By including this purpose, the *hotṛ-camasa* (the cup of the Hotṛ priest) is also included. Therefore, the first mantra is: *śyenāya patvane svāhā* (Hail to the flying eagle!). With this, the offering from the *hotṛ-camasa* is performed. The other six mantras are to be understood as belonging respectively to the cups of the Praśāstṛ and the other priests.

This meaning is obtained from the symmetry (*sāmya*). When there is an inquiry as to how that symmetry is established, [the answer is] seven mantras and seven performers. Thus, the seven mantras become connected with the seven *camasa* cups. In the application (*viniyoga*) of the collection of mantras, the application was not made by saying "with six"; nor was it stated that the remainder is for the purpose of an option (*vikalpa*). And so, the Teacher, by not abandoning his own style in this way, [composed the rule] exactly thus: "by these six" (variant readings: *mūtri*, *ga*, *gha*, *saiḥ*, *ṣaḍbhire*; 2. *ga*, *ya*).

In the *Māna-sūtra* (Sū. 522), it is indicated that seven mantras are connected with seven [objects]; this very meaning is implied. And so says Jaimini: "It should be equal, because nothing has been heard [to the contrary]" (*samaṃ syādaśrutatvāt*). The meaning is that, since no specific distinction is heard, there is indeed equality. Āśvalāyana also stated this paribhāṣā: "When there are many [objects], the assignment of many [mantras] follows the principle of immediate succession."

Pāṇini also, for the sake of utility within his own grammar, formulated a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule), namely: "The designation of equals follows their respective order" (*yathāsaṃkhyamanudeśaḥ samānām*). And thus, this very interpretation here is correct, and no other. [He performs] the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*-offerings with the formula: "Homage to you who have been spontaneously praised. This refers to the oblations employed during the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*-calls. He consecrates the offered oblations with the mantra:

"May the officiating priests be satisfied with the honey and the clarified butter. The meaning is that he recites the mantra while aiming at each of the oblations individually after they have been offered.
The cup-bearers consume [the soma] according to their respective cups; for them, the consumption mantra has been explained.

This explanation pertains to the midday pressing. In this pressing, in the Hotṛ’s cup, the consumption based on the designation (*samākhyā*)—which consists of the essence of the stalk used for the Adhvaryu’s drawing and pressing—is distinct and does not achieve its result through a single ritual application (*tantra*). By the words "Having drawn the strong, the swelling [soma], turn back," it is understood that the drawing from the *punarbhṛt* vessel itself should be performed only once.
When the Nārāśaṃsa goblets have been placed down, they each take their own cup and set aside three pieces of sacrificial cake from the south.

In this way, the word *anu* (after/along) must be supplied immediately after "their own cup" (*svaṃ camasaṃ*). Alternatively, the sūtra may be corrupt; for in that case, the accusative case is indeed appropriate. Āpastamba has read it exactly thus: *svaṃ svaṃ camasamanu nyanta iti*. The repetition (*vīpsā*) in the phrase *śrī strīn* is intended to indicate that the agency extends over all the cups. They place—the term "placing" being performed silently—the fragments connected with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) from the remnants of the oblation (*haviḥśeṣa*) to the south of each respective cup, using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the path of the ancestors). They deposit them there in silence.

Since the recitation (*japa*) of mantras beginning with those for giving is what is being prescribed here, one should remain wearing the sacrificial thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*). This is because the rule for wearing it over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) is prescribed later on. Otherwise, the prescription for worship would have been made after first prescribing the *prācīnāvīta* position; however, it was not done in that way. Therefore, during the worship of the fragment of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa-śakala*), one must indeed wear the sacrificial thread over the left shoulder.

The construction might sometimes be understood as "having made the *prācīnāvīta* [arrangement], they perform the worship (*upāsante*)," and thus there might arise the doubt that the *prācīnāvīta* arrangement should also apply to the act of worship itself. To dispel this doubt, the phrase "having performed that" (*tatkṛtya*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the worship. Having performed that worship—wherein "that" (*tat*) means "those" (*tāni*), referring to those acts of worship; the plural ending is due to the rule *mu-pām mu-luk*; the plural number is intended to indicate the plurality of agents—having done that, having assumed the *prācīnāvīta* arrangement and explained the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula, they mutter the mantras of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, beginning with the offerings and ending with the propitiation.

Those who perform the ritual worship with a fragment of the *puroḍāśa* cake, having placed their sacred threads over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), having explained the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula with "Sūrya te cakṣuḥ," and having recited it word by word ending with "na vāgvo veti"—for this very expiation it is heard in the scripture (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.7.2.1). Also, because of its application in the Sūtra, and because it is not for the purpose of an oblation, there is no drawing of the cup (*agraha*) here.
