The explanation of the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula is performed right beside the *camasa*. "O Grandfather, [Name], and those who follow you—this is for you. O Great-grandfather, [Name], and those who follow you—this is for you. O Great-great-grandfather, [Name], and those who follow you—this is for you. O divine waters! Here, O Fathers, according to [the ritual]... *svāhā*, [to the steam]... "The Fathers have rejoiced. O Grandfather, [Name], wash yourself. O Great-grandfather, [Name], wash yourself. O Great-great-grandfather, [Name], wash yourself. O Grandfather, [Name], look upon this.

O Adhyakṣa, Grandfather [Name] Śarman! O Adhyakṣa, Great-grandfather [Name] Śarman! These [are for you], O Pitṛs... Homage to you, O Pitṛs, for the essence; O Pitṛs, homage to you... Homage to you, O Pitṛs, for the vital strength; O Pitṛs, homage to you... Homage to you, O Pitṛs, for the life-force; O Pitṛs, homage to you... Homage to you, O Pitṛs, for the *svadhā* offering; O Pitṛs, homage to you... Homage to you, O Pitṛs, for the wrath; O Pitṛs, homage to you... Homage to you, O Pitṛs, for the non-terrible.

"Full of vigor," "Arise, O Fathers," "Go forth, O Fathers," "May they go, O Fathers," "The mind has returned," "May he come back to us," "O Fathers, [give] us again," "They have eaten, O Prajāpati"—these are the mantras for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, beginning from the giving of the gift and ending with the *patyāyana* (re-entry). These are indeed to be known; the ritual action (*karman*) itself is not [explicitly stated here]. Regarding the giving of the garment and the pouring out of the water-vessel, there is only one mantra. It is established that for the sacrificer, this refers to his own ancestors. For the other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), however, it refers only to their own respective ancestors.

According to Āśvalāyana, one should worship [the ancestors] of one's own paternal line, because that is what he stated. However, in the opinion of Kātyāyana, the mention of "the sacrificer’s fathers" (*yajamāna-pitṛ*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all [ancestors]. Thus says his sūtra: "Or [one worships] the sacrificer’s fathers, because there is no modification in that regard. The meaning of Kātyāyana’s sūtra is as follows: since the sacrificer is the seeker of the fruit, he alone has the entitlement (*adhikāra*) in rites intended to yield results; the word "or" (*vā*) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that one should perform the rite for the sake of one's own paternal ancestors.

In this alternative, the application of the mantras is as follows: "To the father of the sacrificer, [Name] Śarman; to the grandfather of the sacrificer, [Name] Śarman; to the great-grandfather of the sacrificer, [Name] Śarman; to the paternal grandmother of the sacrificer, [Name] Śarmā; to the paternal great-grandmother of the sacrificer, [Name] Śarmā; to the paternal great-great-grandmother of the sacrificer, [Name] Śarmā. Thus is the employment of the mantras.

Even in the absence of the specific word *asau* (so-and-so), because the word *ataḥ* exists within the mantras of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, a designation by name takes its place here as well. This is due to the scriptural injunction: "They mutter the mantras of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. In this regard, even if the sacrificer or all those performing the rites such as the offering of the cake-shards (*śakala*) and the worship (*upāsana*) have their fathers living, the ritual of offering the cake-shards and so forth must still be performed specifically with reference to the grandfather, the great-grandfather, and the great-great-grandfather.

"Upon [the father's] old age, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), when he has renounced the world (saṃnyasta), or when he has fallen [from his caste], the son himself should give [the offerings] to those very same persons to whom the father would have given. From this statement, and from the Maitrāyaṇīya-Pariśiṣṭa statement: "At a wedding, upon the birth of a son, at a Śrāddha for the ancestors (pivya), at a Soma sacrifice, at a sacred ford, and when a Brāhmaṇa arrives—these six occasions [for śrāddha] occur while the father is still living. By the phrase "at a Soma sacrifice," what is meant is a rite dedicated to the ancestors that occurs within the context of a Soma sacrifice; that is the meaning.

In this same way, those whose father is still living must also perform this rite for their own father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, or for the sacrificer's father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. If, by chance, the fragments of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) are lost, then there is an omission; in that case, the entire expiation (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed for the omission of the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) must be offered into the fire.

But when the father and paternal grandmother are alive, then it should be performed with reference to the great-grandfather, the great-great-grandfather, and the great-great-great-grandfather. If all three are alive, then there is an omission [of the rite]; in this case, there is no performance of the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*), because there is no transgression.
When that has been done, he draws the Sāvitra cup from the Āgrayaṇa vessel using one of these cups belonging to the Antaryāma, reciting either "vāmam adya savitar" or another [of these verses].

The meaning is: when the collection [of mantras] beginning with the *śakala-upāsana* and ending with the *ajapā* has been performed as a whole (*kaṇi*). By the phrase "when that has been performed," it is indicated that this is not a ritual act (*adhyayana-karma*), because it is not something to be tasted (*acamasitvāt*); this is the intended sense. This serves as an illustration for all those who do not taste the cup (*acamasinaḥ*). From the statement "by one of these," it is understood from the Śruti that three mantras are recited here, and that the drawing of the cup (*grahaṇa*) must be performed by whichever one [mantra] among them.
One should pour out the *sāvitra* cup—that is, the cup dedicated to the deity Savitṛ—from the *āgrayaṇa*.

He does not set it down after having gone out; rather, he issues the summons: "Recite for the god Savitṛ! Prompt the offering for the god Savitṛ! From the statement that he goes out at this point, it is understood that in other cases where there is no specific instruction, the prompts (preṣas) occur even while standing in the *havirdhāna* shed. Here, the rule is that [the action] occurs only after going out. The same applies elsewhere as well. The rest is clear.
Having offered the oblation, he does not utter the *anuvaṣaṭ* call, nor does he consume [the portion]; he sets down the vessel like the *sūda*.

In the case of the two *devagṛha* cups, and for the *āditya* and *sāvitra* draughts, the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* does not occur; this prohibition is established by the sūtra itself, yet it is stated here so that its application may be understood immediately. Since the consumption of the *akṣa* (residue) is normally obtained as a consequence of the *homa* and the *abhiṣava*, this is a prohibition [of that]. The statement "he sets down the *sūdakapātra*" is for the purpose of excluding all other *homas*. With the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; thou art good refuge, thou art well-established," he draws the *vaiśvadeva* cup from the *kalaśa* along with the *śastra*, using that very same cup which has not been consumed.

Since the prohibition "one does not consume" (*na bhakṣayati*) already establishes this, the inclusion of the word "not having consumed" (*abhakṣitena*) here is for the purpose of making it necessary to know that at the time of taking the *graha*, this *sāvitra* cup has not been consumed, and therefore the *vaiśvadeva* cup is taken in that very same [unconsumed] state. In the absence of this, the expiation for a breach of the *yajus* formula, namely *bhuvaḥ svāhā*, must be offered into the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*). The purpose of the term "accompanied by a *śastra*" (*śastravantam*) has already been demonstrated regarding the *aindrāgna* cup in the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*).

While the verse "With one and with ten, you are self-existent" is being recited, the Pratiprasthātṛ unyokes the two yoke-horses of the morning; he then unhooks the vessels for the dual-deity offerings, carries them out through the rear door, washes them at the Mārjālīya mound, brings them back in through the front door, and places them in their respective stations.

While this ṛc is being recited, [the Adhvaryu] should release the two yokes with the mantra, "May I be released from the bond of the morning. Having released the vessels for the two deities from the northern side, and having approached the western door of the *havirdhāna* shed, he should wash the vessels. [Then], having entered by the eastern door of the *havirdhāna*, he places them each in their respective position. The mention of the *Pratiprasthātṛ* is for the purpose of excluding the *Adhvaryu*.

With the *upātanya* [chant], he carries away the *dhṛpā* together with the *puṅkha*. And it is clearly stated in another *sūtra*: "Having held the vessels of the two deities near his mouth, he carries them away. Regarding the prefix *ni*, the meaning is understood from the force of the prefix as being for the purpose of carrying away (*nirharaṇa*).

When the verse beginning with "O Heaven and Earth, you who increase the cosmic order through sacrifices" (*pra dyāvā yajñaiḥ pṛthivī ṛtāvṛdhā*) is being recited, he responds with the *anyataratomoda* chant: "Modā moda ivothāmoda" (Rejoice, rejoice, indeed, O rejoicing one).

In this connection, regarding the *prastāva* and *udgītha*, there is a joy (*moha*) at the beginning; the *praṇava* (the syllable *Om*) is the joy that arises. There is joy on one side or the other. Where there is excessive joy in one [part], that sound is called "joy from the other side" (*anyataratomoda*). Some authorities record the opposite order: first the *prastāva*, then the *medha*, these two being the *praṇava* and the *mohānoda*. This very *pratigara* occurs immediately after the *apādāna*; its purpose is for the sake of the *ṛc* (verse). The seventh case ending is used in the sense of the fifth. Beyond those, however, the *pratigara* remains exactly as before. This is the specific distinction regarding the domain of the *anuvacana* and *hotṛ* duties.
Having responded to the *śastra* with "The hymn has been spoken for Indra," he mutters [the formula] at every third pressing;
this applies to all three *ukthya* pressings.
Having responded to the *śastra*, he takes up the cup, while the *camasādhvaryu*s take up the goblets.

Regarding the statement "vaiśvadevam mahānārāśamsam" (the Vaiśvadeva [cup] and the great Nārāśamsa), the recitation of the *śastra* at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) follows the injunction of the *Gopatha-brāhmaṇa*. That very *śastra*, beginning with the *abhihiṅkāra* and so forth, which is prescribed in the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra*, is what occurs here; this is for the purpose of making known that it is not applied by way of the *prakṛti* (archetype). The necessity of the reading of this sūtra—namely, "he takes the cup and the *camasa*s, excluding the *camasādhvaryu*s"—is found to have no other purpose than this. For instance, the taking of the cup and the *camasa*s is already established by the very statement that will be mentioned immediately after "the Vaiśvadeva at the morning pressing" (*prātaḥsavane vaiśvadevam*).
He proceeds with that in the same manner as at the morning pressing with the Vaiśvadeva offering.

Thus ends the third paṭala in the ninth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. By this Vaiśvadeva-maha, the meaning is that one proceeds with this Vaiśvadeva-maha just as one proceeds with the drawing of the Vaiśvadeva cups at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*). Since the two *preṣa* (directions) here are also identical, a complete extended application (*atideśa*) has been made. And this is not for the sake of the *nārāśaṃsa* cups; rather, it is for the purpose of extending the rule and its properties according to the Śrauta-sūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha. By this, it is established that all the cups (*camasa*) are to be consumed entirely (*sarvabhakṣa*), because of the statement: "The third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) is accompanied by the *nārāśaṃsa* cups."

Thus ends the third chapter of the ninth book in the *Jyotsnā* commentary, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—the son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was a performer of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice involving two thousand [animals], a performer of the Sarvatomukha sacrifice involving one thousand [animals], a performer of the Vājapeya sacrifice involving one thousand [animals], and a performer of the Aṣṭāpāha Śrīmad-Amiṣṭa sacrifice—for the purpose of quelling the distress of learned people caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the ocean of the venerable Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtras.
9.4 Now begins the fourth chapter of the ninth book.
One commences the ritual acts of the Saumya sacrifice, beginning with the setting out of the vessels.

By the phrase "the preparation of the vessels and the cleansing," the rites beginning with the *anvādhāna* (placing of the firewood) up to the taking of the seat for the *brahmán* priest are not excluded. Regarding this, according to the *sūtra* "he [the Adhvaryu] goes to his place" (*padanāvayuḥ*), the Adhvaryu performs the action; however, according to the *sūtra* of the teacher Kātyāyana, "because of the connection with the drawing of the *karṣu*," there is also the option of the Pratiprasthātṛ performing it. In this regard, the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) is shown in the *sūtra*: "The Pratiprasthātṛ undertakes the rites for the *savanīya* offerings, beginning with the preparation of the vessels."

Since no specific details regarding the vessels used for urine have been taught, and because there is no strict adherence to a particular style, two alternatives are presented: either with mantras or silently (*saumyam*). Thus, there is a twofold division: Baudhāyana holds that it should be accompanied by mantras, saying "it belongs to Pūṣan," whereas Śālīki holds that it should be silent. It has been stated that one proceeds with the rites beginning from the placing of the vessels (*pātrāsādana*); those vessels are as follows.

He places the *carusthālī* (pot for the cooked rice), the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), and the *ulūkhala* (mortar) and *musala* (pestle); the *pātrī* (small vessel) for the purpose of scattering and pouring; and also the vessel for carrying the *praṇītā* water. He brings forward the *praṇītā* waters in the form of a stream, as prescribed by the injunction "he pours forth the *praṇītā*s," because there is no prohibition against the singular number and because there is no specific rule regarding the joining [of the waters] with the *juru-pūnāmiḥ*. The vessel for the *madantī* (hot water) is also brought because it is conducive to the cooking. There is an absence of the *kuṭa*, *dṛṣad*, and *upalā* (upper and lower grinding stones), due to the absence of any requirement for them.

Furthermore, according to the statement of Bharadvāja: "Just as a bundle [of grass] is placed upon a substance, so too is there the pouring out from the *caru*, the *samāhanana* (threshing), and the *māṣya*. In the view that the *śamyā* (wooden pin) is used for the *samāhanana*, even that [the *sphya*] is absent. There is the cessation of the *sphya*, the *agnihotrahavaṇī*, the *piṣṭapeṣaṇārtha-mekṣaṇa*, the *veda*, the *pātraharaṇa*, the *iḍāpātra*, the *anvāhāryasthālī*, the *yoktra*, the *catuṣkaraṇapātra*, the *upaveṣa*, and so forth. This is established by the very fact that the *āmādana* (offering) for the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*) has already been obtained; for this very reason, it was not stated [separately] as being for that purpose.

Having performed the purification, he should perform the bringing forward of the *praṇītā* waters with the mantra if he follows the view that includes mantras; if he follows the view that excludes mantras, he should do so without the mantra.
He offers the *saumya* sacrificial porridge (*caru*).

The offering (nirvāpa) is indeed accompanied by mantras; likewise, even in the case of the silent (tūṣṇīṃ) method, the procedure from the taking up of the Agnihotra-ladle (agnihotrahavaṇī) until the entrustment (paridāna) remains the same. The deity is connected [to the act] merely by the pouring out (vipi), as in the case of the Maṣṭi. In the case of the method with mantras, the ritual action ends with the triple-shelling (triphalīkaraṇa). [End of section] Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa’s Jyotsnā commentary. In the case of both the mantra-accompanied and mantra-less methods, it is performed without the *mavara* [formula]. From the taking up of the *dhṛṣṭi* onwards, in the mantra-accompanied method it is with mantras, and in the mantra-less method it is without mantras.

O Mother, on both sides of the altar, regarding the two strainers (*pavitre*), it is indeed silent (*tūṣṇīm*) because of the contradiction with the *chandas* [metres]. For the *prastara* is the sacrificer, and the two strainers are the out-breath and in-breath (*prāṇāpānau*); thus, [the text] says, "I place the out-breath and in-breath in the sacrificer. This is established as the rule. In the case of the view that includes the mantra, the pouring of the clarified butter (*abhighāraṇa*)—beginning with "The sun is light" (*sūryo jyotiḥ*) and so forth—is likewise silent, because even the waters are modifications of Agni and Soma.
Having placed that [offering]...

Having placed [the offering] down; having placed it down, the statement regarding the placement at the beginning of the sacrifice is established for the purpose of enjoining the *ājyabhāga* offerings subsequent to the placing of the *sāmidhenī* verses. "After placing [it], one performs the ghee-sacrifice as a single portion.
Having taken a portion of the ghee, he issues the command, "Sacrifice with the ghee," and having offered it when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.

The meaning is "of the clarified butter" (*ājyasya*). Alternatively, it is a partitive genitive; the meaning is "a portion of the clarified butter sufficient for the sacrifice. Having taken that [portion]—either fourfold according to the rule for the *caturavatta* or fivefold according to the rule for the animal sacrifice—and having stepped across to the south, called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, and received the response (*pratyāśrāvita*), he offers with the *vaṣaṭ* call while saying, "Of the clarified butter, svāhā. Because its substance is clarified butter, it is to be recited in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). Āpastamba also clearly states its low-voiced nature: "With clarified butter, one performs the *saumya* offering in a low voice on both sides."

"Or one recites the other [formula] in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). Since the quality of being *upāṃśu* is already established by the very nature of the *upāṃśu* [rite], the repetition is for the purpose of ensuring that *all* [parts] are *upāṃśu*; this has been explained in the *Savyākhyātaniryākhyāna*. By this, the rule regarding the *savana-stotra* is set aside. Because it is for the purpose of making [the deity] known to another, one recites "aloud" (*uccaiḥ*) during the *āśrāvaṇa* and *pratyāśravaṇa*, according to the sūtra: "Except for the *pravara*, the *saṃvāda*, the *āśravaṇa*, and the *saṃpreṣa*. By this method, the word *dhṛtasya* (of the clarified butter) is indeed *upāṃśu*. However, the determination of the deity is to be known from the *yājyā* verse.

In that regard, those other [verses] not mentioned by Āśvalāyana—namely, "O Soma, entering together with the fathers" (*soma pitṛbhiḥ saṃviśāna*) as the *yājyā* for the offering to Soma—and the two *ghṛta-yājyās*: "The one who has performed his task, seated upon the back, has entered into the darkness; may his bay horses, glowing in heat, carry him to his station" (*kṛtākṛtno pṛṣṭho abhivartaḥ śritaḥ tamasya dhāma tapasyā harito vahantu*); and "They have offered the clarified butter to the gods of gods" (*ghṛtaṃ nirṇijānaḥ devadevān*); and [the verse] beginning "O Viṣṇu, stride forth" (*uru viṣṇo vikramasva*) for the sake of our protection. They proceed with these in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).

Even though the ritual action is performed, it does not extend beyond the lord of the sacrifice; otherwise, one would fall into error. Thus, "O Viṣṇu, your great abode is dear"—this is the *dhṛtāhuti* (offering of clarified butter) with its *yājyā* verse, belonging to the *ghṛtayāga* (butter-offering). It has been stated that "O Viṣṇu, stride forth" is the *yājyā* for the subsequent *ghṛtayāga* dedicated to the deity Viṣṇu. In either case, the deities are those associated with the *āviṣṇu* [formula].

Standing right here, he first cuts a portion of the *saumya* [oblation] with his hand, and the second portion with the *mekṣaṇa* spoon. Having stepped across toward the north, caused the announcement to be made, and received the response, he issues the direction: "Recite the offering-verse for the *saumya*. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, standing facing south, he makes the offering in the eastern part of the southern half of the fire.

Because the author of the Sūtra prescribes the *prācīnāvīta* mode of wearing the sacred thread for the *saumya* offering, there is an option (*vikalpa*) based on the rule that "in other cases there is no fixed rule. Āpastamba (Śrautasūtra 1.12.8) states: "He performs the *saumya* offering with the *prācīnāvīta*; he says 'with the *prācīnāvīta*' and 'with the left hand'. Since the rule "with a stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) for the *caru*s" would imply that even the subsequent portioning should be done with the spoon, the hand is prescribed there to set aside the spoon for the first portioning.

The statement "the response is with the *mekṣaṇa*" is for the purpose of removing the doubt regarding the lack of a fixed rule. The mention of "standing facing the north" is for the purpose of indicating that the sacrifice is performed while standing in the northern direction. The mention of "having been addressed (*āśrāvaṇa*) and having responded (*pratyāśrāvaṇa*)" is for the purpose of making known that among the three ways of addressing, the first way is the one employed here; the mention of the response is because it is connected to the act of addressing.

The phrase "as if with the *vaṣaṭ* call" refers to the view that giving at an improper time is like the *vaṣaṭ* offering; it is for the purpose of refuting that position. [The rule] "standing in the north" means that even in a sacrifice, one should perform the rite standing facing the east, according to the sūtra "facing the east. By implication, the *āgnīdhra* priest faces north. Since it would naturally follow that he stands facing the fire, the explicit statement "standing" indicates that he should face the fire even when the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) sacrifice is being performed.
The statement "one offers in the southern region" is for the purpose of specifying the location already established by the archetype (prakṛti), namely that one offers upon the Āhavanīya fire;
it is as before: "Sacrifice with ghee. The remainder is "the ghee-sacrifice" (ghṛtayāga).
Some authorities prescribe that the offering should be made from either side;

the meaning is that it may be done with the face toward the mirror or otherwise. For the *saumya* (soma-related) portion, there is no *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and so forth. This is because, according to the rule of Āpastamba—"Having stepped back after the shaving has been performed, having poured clarified butter over the *caru* and saying 'I offer this to you'"—the stepping back and the pouring of clarified butter over the *caru* exclude the *sviṣṭakṛt* and subsequent offerings.
Having filled it with clarified butter, they carry it to the Udgātṛ priests.

That [cup] is for Soma. By means of the renunciation of the *āhavanīya* fire, because of the statement "to the Udgātṛs," that Soma-cup is indeed brought forth; they carry it away and present it. The plural number is used for the purpose of including any one of the groups of officiating priests (*adhvaryu-gaṇa*) who are to perform the task.
Having been set down, they look at it, saying, "It is here."

The word "udgātāraḥ" (the Udgātṛs) is the remainder [of the sentence], because they alone are nearby and because their name is mentioned multiple times. This is made clear by the statement: "The Udgātṛs look at it when it has been placed on the seat. However, some ritualists (kalpāntarakārāḥ) maintain that this looking belongs to the Adhvaryu because it is prescribed in his section; to refute that, the mention of the "Udgātṛs" is included. As for the Śruti text, "They look at the purifier, which is indeed Soma," the sense is that this too pertains to the Udgātṛs, for it is said: "In that [Soma], they behold themselves."

"O Udgātṛs!"—thus [he says]. This is for the purpose of mixing [the waters] while moving toward the east in two [successive] movements. "Pariśrāvayan" means having bent down. Regarding the end of the Sūtra: "He who does not see his own reflection would be likely to die. Having performed the *abhidardī* rite, he should look [into the water] with the mantra: "My mind which has gone away... [End of] Paṭala 1, Chapter 1. Together with the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa.
Baudhāyana: "He who does not see his own self would be likely to die; having performed the *abhidardī*, he should look [into the water] with the mantra: 'My mind which has gone away...'"

While looking at that [mirror], he should look at himself without blinking, reciting the mantra: "May no others perceive my form; may I perceive the forms of others. May I not see death; may death not see me. Having made this avoidance of death, may my mind which has gone away return to me; may what was lost to me return. As it is stated by Baudhāyana: "He looks at himself, having become motionless. He says: "I have given, I have given, I have given, I have given. This is what was stated by Baudhāyana.

Having made it fragrant with cardamom, one should smell it while reciting the verse: "O Gāneshati, having become dark, come hither. When this is done, the clarified butter (*ājya*) becomes more abundant, for its increase is indeed visible. Regarding the boiled offerings (*śṛta*), the purpose of looking at them has been stated: "He whose mind has wandered away should look [at them], [reciting]: 'That mind of mine which has gone afar, that which has gone to the distant regions—may King Soma restore that within us.'"

The mind does not appear as if it has departed; even Āpastamba says that he whose mind has departed would see [it], for the mind does not become something that has gone away. Furthermore, anyone else who is absent-minded appears as if empty, according to the venerable Vyāsa. One who is ill or one who desires food should eat [of this].

"O, alas! I have fallen into disease. For one who desires food, O gentle one, he should eat the *saumya-caru*. With the formula "I am performing this act for the hearing of the *kamidhātu*," he should make the resolve: "I shall consume the *saumya-caru*. Or, for one who is emaciated by fear, cold, wind, or hunger, and who desires food, or one who is capable of eating food but does not eat it—he should eat [the *caru*] after making that resolve.

If any man who is capable of eating food and traveling by boat does not eat food due to some obstacle, he is likely to die because of that very act; this is the remainder [of the sense]. This is an occasional (naimittika) rite. The reading without *visarga* is an error. With sticks (*śalākā*), the Āgnīdhra priest distributes the blazing fires among the various hearths (*dhiṣṇiya*). "With the sticks of the sacrificial grass and the fuel, together with the *āprī*-verses, having taken up the sticks, he distributes them. Distribution (*viharaṇa*) means placing them in their respective positions within the hearths.
Having taken the *ājya* (clarified butter) drawn nine times, the Adhvaryu sprinkles it over the blazing fires.

This sprinkling applies even to those fires that have not yet been established, such as the Āhavanīya and the Hotrīya; it is not performed with Soma. For this reason, it is specified as "drawn nine times. The statement "again, they settle" is intended to ensure that the fires are blazing at the time of the sprinkling. Due to the absence of Soma, there is no consumption (*bhakṣa*). In the manuscript copies of the Sūtras, there is a lacuna. [From the *Baudhāyanaśrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Ninth Book, First Section: He performs the remaining rites with the *ājya*; they maintain the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths.
[He takes] the *viṣṇiya* cups. With the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; of thee, pressed by Bṛhaspati... he draws the *pātnīvata* cup from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel using the *upāṃśu* cup.
The end of the mantra is: "I take thee, belonging to the *patnīvat*s."

Having mixed that [oblation] with clarified butter by pouring it over the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths, he does not set it down. It is "mixed with the *pātnīvata*" (*pātnīkta*); that which has the wives as its portion is the *pātnīvata*, and thus it is the *pātnīkta*. Here, the specific qualification is that Agni is the *patnīvān* (the one accompanied by the wives). The *yājyā* verse is from the *Liṅgānuśāsana*: "With these, O Agni... The mention of "clarified butter" (*ājya*) is intended to show that when he mixes the *pātnīvata* with clarified butter, he takes it in a vessel made of *karkandhu* wood; it is clarified butter that has been heated, not thickened clarified butter. Having gone out, he issues the command: "O Āgnīdh, recite the offering prayer for the *pātnīvata*."
The departure for this [offering] has already been indicated.
He offers when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered with the words, "O Agni, accompanied by the wives!
The end of the mantra is, "O Soma, drink the sixth portion along with them."
The *anuvaṣaṭkāra* is both performed and not performed;

the *karisaka* is both performed and not performed. Since the author of the Sūtra has prescribed that the word *patnīvata* is to be uttered in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), it is indeed [performed] inaudibly.
According to some, one performs the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* in a low voice.

Even though the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* is performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), the portion from "O Agni, drink the Soma" (*agne vīhi*) until the end is indeed in a low voice, but "vauṣaṭ" is uttered aloud. He issues the command: "O Agnīdh, sit in the lap of the Neṣṭṛ; O Neṣṭṛ, lead up the wife; have the wife gaze at the Udgātṛ; O Unnetṛ, fill the cups headed by the Hotṛ’s cup; provide space for the *dhruvā* in the Hotṛ’s cup; pour out the entire King (Soma); do not leave any remainder; wipe the two jars with the fringes [of the cloth] and set them face down. Thus he gives the direction. 9.

"Sit upon the lap; sit there for the purpose of consuming the Soma. [The Neṣṭṛ] should lead the wife near the Udgātṛ for the sake of counting. "In response to the *hiṅkāra* made by the Udgātṛ, cause the wife to count"—that is to say, at the time of the utterance of the *hiṅkāra*, he should cause her to look on.

Lāṭyāyana and Drāhmāyaṇa have stated exactly the same: "At the *hiṃkāra* of the *yajñāyajñīya*, the Udgātṛ should look at the wife; at the *nidhana*, he should sprinkle water on the wife's right thigh; when the third *stotrīyā* verse has been introduced (*prastuta*), he should pour out all that water. Regarding the doubt as to when the Udgātṛ should look at the wife if the *yajñāyajñīya-sāman* does not exist in another *ṛc*—and thus there is no *hiṃkāra*—he says: "But in the absence of the *hiṃkāra*, the Udgātṛ should look at the wife at the time of the *pratihāra*."

The meaning is: "Make room for the pouring of the *unneta*’s cup and the *hotṛ*’s cup into the *camasa*s, and for the pouring of the *dhruva* [cup] into the *hotṛ*’s cup. This is the remaining instruction (*praisha*) following the *nyāhāva*. Regarding the statement "the *āgnīdhra* sits in the lap of the *neṣṭṛ*," he explains its meaning: "The *āgnīdhra*, having stepped out between the *neṣṭṛ* and the *dhiṣṇiya* altar, partakes [of the soma]; or, sitting in the lap of the *neṣṭṛ*, he should not sit in the lap. If he were to sit in the lap, he would become a eunuch (*klība*). Gopīnātha Mahāmahopādhyāya’s *Jyotsnā* Commentary. Chapter 5, Section 10. Text with Commentary. End of Section. End of Chapter.
