Having stepped out, entered, and sat down, he eats while sitting on the lap (*upastha*) [of the Neṣṭṛ] or sitting near it. He eats while sitting on the Neṣṭṛ’s lap. Now, it was previously stated that he sits on the Neṣṭṛ’s lap, but now it is said that he does not sit on the lap; how is this stated in contradiction to what preceded? True, both [positions] are difficult to reconcile. Therefore, due to this contradiction, an option (*vikalpa*) has been made by the author of the Sūtra. In the phrase "he sits on the Neṣṭṛ’s lap" (*neṣṭurupastha āsīdet*), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used in the sense of the seventh case (*saptamī*).

And this has been demonstrated by the author of the Sūtra himself. The locative ending in *upasthe* indicates location; proximity is expressed by the phrase *antarā neṣṭāraṃ viṣṇiyaṃ cāgnīdhro vyavasūpya*. Regarding the statement *agnīdheṣṭur upastham āsīdet*, some hold that when one is not actually sitting on the lap (*upastha*), the portion *upastham āsīdet* is elided. Others maintain that since the word retains its sense of proximity, the locative case remains valid even then, and thus there is no elision. The term *klībaḥ* means neuter. He draws the cups, of which the Hotṛ’s cup is the chief. This is the sixth [section].
The Stotra and Śastra are performed. This is clear. Having kindled the fires of the Dhiṣṇiya hearths, he introduces the Agniṣṭoma Stotra.

The mention of the *agniṣṭoma* cup is intended to indicate that this is the principal chant (*stotra*) employed in the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice. Without untying their waist-knots (*nīvī*), they remain with their navels visible; all of them keep their ears covered. They do not loosen their waist-knots. Making their navels as if barely visible, they stand with their ears covered and their mouths closed. The inclusion of the word "all" is for the purpose of ensuring that even those who have entered the ritual space but are not otherwise connected to the specific action must also have their heads covered. He states this very point:

Those who are members of the assembly (*sadas*), belonging to the *sadas*, namely those who sit in the assembly (*sabhāsada*), they too appear with their ears covered. "Belonging to it" (*sa-sambandhitva*) means simply being one who has entered the *sadas*. The meaning of the genitive case is "relationship.
According to some, this includes both the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the patron (*yajamāna*).

All the *avina* birds are also covered with ear-flaps (*karṇaprāvṛta*), but this does not apply exclusively to those connected with the *stotra*; for this reason, the term "all" (*sarva*) must be understood as carrying over here as well. Since there is no fixed rule regarding the *yajamāna*’s connection with the *stotra*, there is an option (*vikalpa*). By the phrase "of some" (*ekeṣām*), the option for the *yajamāna* is indicated. It was already stated previously in the first section that the mention of "of some" is for the purpose of indicating a secondary alternative (*mala-karaṇārtha*). [End of] Satyāṣāḍha’s *Śrautasūtra*, [Book] 1, Chapter 112. (End of volume)
With the words, "O you who possess all, belonging to all, possessing manly vigor," he causes the wife to be looked at by the Udgātṛ.
At this point, the Neṣṭṛ is the one who performs the directions.
Having bared her right thigh and exposed the groin, the wife [recites], "I sacrifice to the gods."

The right thigh is not to be offered to the Kṛtyā; many [offerings] are made for the sake of union with the one who has gone to the highest place. Hence the plural number. Regarding the locus, it is the instrument. Here, in the Ātmanepada, the means for the manifestation of this [state] is stated: "When the husband is away, the manifestation of the wife occurs through the non-appearance [of the husband]; thus it is known. Just as there may be a desire for her, so when she is dressed accordingly, she becomes one whose face is unclouded (*ahātamukhī*), one whose face is unfaded (*amlānamukhī*); the meaning is that her husband’s wives become [manifest]. Thus it is.
With the formula, "Svāhā-consecrated, dwelling in the ocean," the wife, standing inside the thighs, causes the *pannejani* waters to flow out through the thigh toward the north.

*Usīcī*, *udākhe*, *ūrugā*, *daligenā*, and *dāmane*; the *pananīya* [verse] causes the transition to the next interval. Here, the proponents of the position state that there is only one [verse]. Or rather, he proceeds with his hand alone, but does not sing from another interval; this is the meaning. The counting and the introductory proceeding (*upapravartana*) are performed for the third *stotrīyā* verse.

The third *stotrīyā* verse belongs exclusively to the first turn (*paryāya*). Regarding the expression "at the end" (*agre*) in the phrase "at the last *stotrīyā*," it should be understood from the *Chandoga-sūtra* that the third *stotrīyā* is indeed connected to the first turn. Here, the prefix *ā-* denotes inclusion (*abhividhi*); the meaning is "up to the third turn. The substance is milk. This [rite] is repeated as a consecration of the wife (*patnī-saṃskāra*) and as a disposal (*pratipatti*). When the offering of the *raśanā* (rope) has occurred for one wife, there is an omission of the taking up of the *manī* and of the rites connected therewith.

Regarding the *āgnimāruta* [śastra], Āpastamba states a specific rule: "One should respond (*pratigṛṇāti*) to the *āgnimāruta* with the word *amba* at the beginning. *Amba* means quickly. In the *Āśvalāyana* [Śrautasūtra] as well, it says: "The *āgnimāruta* begins with *su*. *Su* means extremely quickly. Another specific rule is stated here by Āpastamba: "Recognizing the verse *āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*, one responds while pouring water. This means that during the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, one responds while pouring down water.
The *Āśvalāyana* [Śrautasūtra] says: "While touching the water and having his head uncovered, he responds while holding on [to the Adhvaryu]."

While this verse, "Sweet indeed is this, and honeyed is this," is being recited, he responds with joy on both sides, saying, "As if from intoxication, joy! As if from joy, intoxication! This established response continues from the *āhāva* up until the *vyāhāva*.

In the phrase "etasyāṃ śasyamānāyām," the locative case functions as an ablative. Therefore, beginning from this verse while it is being recited (*śasyamānā*), the *pratigara* (response) occurs. Starting from this *ṛc*, the *pratigara* consists of the "joy on both sides" (*ubhayatomoda*). Even in the *upayama* form of the *pratigara*—as in "madāmoda iva ra yodāmoda"—the *pratigara* possesses the quality of joy on both sides because of the word "moda. This *ubhayatomoda* *pratigara* extends from the beginning up to the *āhāva* (call), specifically until the middle *āhāva* belonging to the *svāduṣkilīya* verses.

The *svāduṣkiliya* chant proceeds; the *vyāhāva* is said to be the call. Immediately after the *vyāhāva*, there is the continuation of the word "of the preceding" (*pūrvatanasya*). After the word "upwards" (*ūrdhvam*), the particle "and" (*ca*) is to be supplied. Thus, even above the *āhāva*, the *pratigara* (response) consists of "ubhayatomoda" alone. The *pratigara* is established from the *vyāhāva*. The meaning is that starting from the *vyāhāva*, the *pratigara* becomes established—that is, it is well-known. [450th Paṭala] Accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha.
"You are the existent; place me in the existent," with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ consecrates the *dhruva* cup.

The mention of the Pratiprasthātṛ is for the purpose of distinguishing him from the Neṣṭṛ and Unnetṛ, since there is no difference between these two in their status as Adhvaryus. As for the distinction of the Adhvaryu himself, it will follow simply from his being otherwise occupied. The mantra ends with "may I become great. He encloses [the cup] with the formula, "I enclose you for Heaven and Earth."

He grasps the *dhruva* with his joined palms (*añjali*). This is because it is seen [in other texts] that "having grasped it with his joined palms, he remains," and because Āpastamba has explicitly stated, "he grasps it with his joined palms.
With the mantra, "May the All-gods, the Vaiśvānaras, move you forth," he moves the *dhruva* from its place.
"Moves" means he causes it to shift from its own position. The prefix *pra-* signifies moving quickly. The mantra ends with the word "move them forth" (*pracyāvayantu*).

"Strengthen the gods in heaven, the birds in the intermediate space"—with these words he carries [the Soma]. This means he carries it toward the *hotṛ*’s cup. "The earthly ones... is the end of the mantra.

With the words, "We lead Soma down with the firm oblation for the sake of the firm one," he pours the *dhruva* [Soma] into the *hotṛ*’s cup while the *paridhānīyā* verse is being recited, once the recitation has begun, or at the beginning of the *śastra*. [He does so] in the middle of the [cup], or finally.

Regarding the phrase "while it is being recited," this refers to [the recitation] from beginning to end. By the phrase "when it has been recited once," the middle round (paryāya) is indicated. Thus, five positions are established: at the beginning of the recitation, in the middle of the recitation, or at the end of the recitation. Having responded to the recitation (*pratigīrya*), the Adhvaryu takes up the Hotṛ’s cup, and the Camasādhvaryus take up their cups. He issues the command: "O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice the Soma-juices! The purpose of responding to the recitation has already been shown; the remaining portion of the Sūtra also has its purpose demonstrated.
The consumption of the cups has been explained;
that is to say, it has been explained by the sūtra beginning with "The cup-bearers consume according to their respective cups" and ending with "the third [group] are the Hotrakas."
The two [fires] do not serve as the means for swelling [the grains] because they are not used for the *ārāśaṃsa* offerings; this is the intended meaning.
From the point when the *agnīd* says, "Bring the embers for the *upayaja* offerings," one commences the ritual procedure pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka-karma*).

This is clear. 1 Ga. i. ca. ja. ma. da. read *nāccyāva*. 118. 934. At the end of the *anūyāja* offerings, he offers the *svaru* splinter; they do not proceed with the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*) if there is an *anūbandhyā* cow.
This is an indicative mark for the *vāhana-bandhya* (the animal to be bound for transport).

When the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) have been thrown into the fire, having offered the residue (*saṃsrāva*), they proceed with the *hāriyojana* cup. The mention of "having offered the residue" is for the purpose of making it known that the residue-oblation (*saṃsrāvahoma*) is a subordinate part of the throwing of the enclosing sticks. This is a restatement because [the cup] follows immediately after the Soma. Indra is yoked by this [cup] for the sake of returning to his own place; thus, it is the *hāriyojana*. The *hāriyojana* is the cup belonging to Indra. The meaning is that one draws that cup at the end of the residue-offering, once the rite consisting of the throwing of the enclosing sticks has been performed.
"Thou art taken with a support; thou art the bay one, the yoker of bays"—with these words, the Unnetṛ draws the entire *āgrayaṇa* [portion] as the *hāriyojana* from the *droṇakalaśa*.

Here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative. Because the *sthālī* (vessel) containing the *soma* for the *āgrayaṇa* is a small vessel, whereas the *droṇakalaśa* is a large vessel, it is impossible to draw [the former] from the latter. Thus, he draws the entire *āgrayaṇa*—all the *soma* contained in the *āgrayaṇa-sthālī*—into the *droṇakalaśa* as the *hāriyojana*.
Having mixed it with many parched grains (*dhānā*), he does not set it down.

In this context, "dhānās" (parched grains) refers specifically to worldly [grains]. Yava-grains are called *dhānās*. Baudhāyana also stated in his injunction: "Prepare the single *dhānā* for the Hāriyojana cup. Having placed [the cup] upon the head and having gone out, he issues the formal command (*saṃpraśya*): "Recite the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for Indra accompanied by the Haris; give the impulse (*preṣya*) for Indra accompanied by the Haris," or alternatively, "Recite the invitatory verse for the *dhānās* and Soma; give the impulse for the *dhānās* and Soma that have been set forth. Regarding the word *śīrṣan*: it means "on the head" (*śīrṣi*). The locative case ending is elided according to the rule *vibhāṣā śiśyoḥ*. Thus, *śīrṣannadhi* means "upon the head" (*śīrṣṇa upari*). By the expression "having gone out" (*upaniṣkramya*), it is indicated that this formal command is issued only after one has stepped outside the *havirdhāna* shed.

"Ye are the tawny ones; the grains for the two tawny ones"—having stepped forward with this, he offers at the *vaṣaṭ*-call and at the subsequent *anu-vaṣaṭ*-call. Having offered, he carries away the portion for consumption. "Having stepped forward" (*vikramya*) means performing various strides, moving the feet repeatedly forward and backward. The reason for this is stated in the Śruti: "For by stepping forward, Indra slew Vṛtra; [it is done] for prosperity. This stepping forward is performed silently after the *vaṣaṭ*-call. The offering is made with a mantra: "To Indra, svāhā! because of the indicative mark of the word *svāhā*. He carries away the portion; he carries the portion toward the *sadas* hall.

Having divided that [Soma] equally among all, they seek the invitation from the Unnetṛ and, with the formula "O divine Soma, those who have sacrificed the Yajus," they eat the parched grains (dhānās) while making the sound *ci-ciṣā*.

Here, the acquisition of the portion for eating is based on the explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*), and thus applies even to those other than the Hotṛ and the Unnetṛ, despite the absence of a specific occasion. For the Hotṛ, the right to eat is occasioned by the *vaṣaṭ*-call; for the Unnetṛ, the eating is occasioned by the pressing (*abhiṣava*); for the others, it is based on the explicit statement. Then the Hotṛ, the Unnetṛ, and the others proceed with the Hāriyojana cup. [End of Chapter 3] — With the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa. Page 935.

The meaning is that all of these [priests], having placed the parched grains (dhānā) together with the Soma that has gone to the *hāriyojana* vessel into another vessel, have made them equal in measure. The prefix *prati-* signifies "facing toward. With the words "O Unnetṛ, invite! they all invite the Unnetṛ; then, with the mantra "O divine Soma, [this is] for you," having made the sound *ci-ci-ṣā*—the meaning being "having made it"—[that is,] *ci-ci-ṣati* is an imitation of the sound, having made such a sound, they cause the essence to flow into the heart from the parched grains; they swallow only the essence.
Without biting or breaking [the grains], making depressions in the parched grains, they consume [them] without leaving any residue.

Having bitten the parched grains (*dhānā*) without crushing them—that is, without causing them to break—they make the grains flat with their teeth, creating depressions only at the thick parts of the grains; that is to say, they make the thick parts depressed. Having extracted [the juice] from them, they drink it; this is the meaning of "extracting and drinking.
Having spat the parched grains onto the high altar (*uttaravedi*) while saying, "O you who are to be filled, fill me," or [alternatively], "For wealth, for prosperity," they scatter them.

The meaning is that they sow [the seeds] after having spat and made a *thūtkṛta* sound near the *uttaravedi*, having extracted the essence from the drinks. By the word "āpūryāḥ," this is optionally replaced by "ramyai svā. Regarding this, Āpastamba has stated: "Then they sip water (*ācamana*)," because they have become impure (*ucchiṣṭa*) due to the consumption of the *bhānas*. They consume drops of curd in the *āgnīdhra* shed with the mantra: *dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam*. By the word *ipsa*, the thickened upper layer of the curd is denoted.

Having poured out the *camasa* vessels one by one, leaving only the single *ekadhana* vessel remaining; having spread out the green *dūrvā* grass, intensified it, and produced its juice; and having smelled the juice of the Soma washed in water with the mantra "Thou art for the deity Soma," they carry it to the *cātvāla*.

Having placed the remaining portions of the *ekavanas* in order into the *sañciti* cups, having pressed and crushed the *hariṇī*, *hastinī*, and *dūrvā* grasses therein, and having made them into a paste, they produce the essence (*rasa*) by extracting it from the *dūrisanā*. Having produced that essence, the cup-holders (*camasins*) pour it into the water with the mantra "of the washed one" (*dhautasya*), causing it to flow down with force; then they pour it out according to their respective cups with the formula "having poured it out according to the cup. This ritual action belongs to the cup-holders and not to others.
It is considered that [the Soma] belongs to the Adhvaryu and the others. Āpastamba has stated that the place for consumption is either behind the *cātvāla* pit or in the *āstāva*.
With the mantra, "Whatever injury has occurred to my self," they worship the Āhavanīya fire with the *mindā* verse. || 11 ||

[The rule applies] to both those who blow [the breath] and those who do not blow. Here, there is only one *mindā* (defect), because of the singular number. [Variants noted: *saṃdaraśyā* (ka.ga.ba.ja.ba.ka.); *niriva* (ka.ja.sa.ma.da.); *gīrvāḥ* (ga.pa.ja.sa.ma.da.); *māyatī* (pa.ja.sa.ma.); *veneti* (ga.pa.). 936. The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[Ninth Book].

"You are the expiation for sin committed against the gods; you are the expiation for sin committed against men; you are the expiation for sin committed against the ancestors; you are the expiation for sin committed by oneself; you are the expiation for sin committed by another; you are the expiation for every sin; you are the expiation for that sin which I have committed knowingly and that which I have committed unknowingly. With each of these formulas, they place wood-shavings (*śakala*) upon the *āhavanīya* fire. The explicit statement "with each formula" is intended to prevent the following misconception: because of the particle *iti*, one might think there is only a single mantra and that the placing of the shavings occurs only at its conclusion. This is not to be so.

"Both young poets, the bestowers of truth, lords of the law; O lord of the law of truth, let us release our friendships. With these words they release their friendships. Here, the release of truth is the release from malice. Beyond that, there is either no malice or malice; however, there is no injunction that one must necessarily practice malice. When the Veda has been touched, they perform the *saṃyāja* offerings for the wives.

When the Veda has been touched by the sacrificer, they perform the *saṃyājya* offerings for the wives. After the oblations of the remnants (*saṃsrāva-homa*) upon the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), there is the consumption of the remains of the sacrificial food (*haviḥ-śeṣa-prāśana*), and then the *patnīsaṃyājās* performed after the touching of the Veda; this much is the sequence here, which is the specific distinction from the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Having taken nine portions of clarified butter (*ājya*) while the Veda is spread out, the Adhvaryu, standing upright within the altar (*antarvedi*), offers the nine *samiṣṭayajus* oblations into the Āhavanīya fire with the *juhū* ladle, reciting "dhātā rātiḥ... and so forth.

By the statement "on the strewn altar" (*stīrṇe vede*), the specific distinction here from the archetype (*prakṛti*) is that the time for spreading the altar-grass (*vedastaraṇa*) is at this point—prior to the *samiṣṭayajus* offering and after all the expiatory oblations (*sarvaprāyaścitta-homa*). The mention of the *adhvaryu* is for the purpose of restriction: only the *adhvaryu* offers, and not the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) by means of taking hold from behind (*anvārambha*). This statement is intended to exclude the sacrificer, as there is a rule in another *sūtra* regarding the sacrificer's taking hold from behind at this point. The mention of "within the altar" (*antarvedi*) is for the purpose of excluding the ritual characteristics of a *davihoma*.

Although the upward [offering] is already established by the archetype (*prakṛti*), this statement is for the purpose of making it known that in other offerings consisting of *āhuti*s, this [upward direction] also optionally applies. The mention of *juhū* is for the purpose of excluding the *dhruvā* vessel which is obtained from the archetype. Although there is no immediate practical purpose here in mentioning the *āhavanīya* fire, nevertheless, it must be assumed that its purpose is purely transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*), serving as a reminder at the time of performance that "this offering of all nine *samiṣṭayajus* oblations is to be made in the *āhavanīya*."

In the absence of this recollection, the expiation for the breaking of the *yajus* formula is the offering of "Bhuvaḥ Svāhā" into the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire. He offers nine *samiṣṭayajus* oblations; the meaning is that he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* with nine verses (*ṛc*). Regarding this, there is also the scriptural statement: "He offers six *ṛc*s and three *yajus*s. Among these, the first six are *ṛc*s and the remaining three are *yajus*s. The Śruti also says: "He offers six *āmmyāṇi* and three *yajus*s. [The term] *āmmyāṇi* refers to the *ṛc*s; the reading *āmmyāṇi* is a Vedic (Chāndasa) form used in place of the expected *ṛgmmyāṇi*.

In these *ṛc*s, the *svāhākāra* (the utterance "svāhā") is established by general rule; however, in the *yajus* formulas, the *svāhākāra* is explicitly recited. [Chapter 450] This is accompanied by the *Jyotsnā* commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. The bringing of the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) occurs at the *ajyoktra* (the binding with clarified butter); likewise for the *somasya phalīkaraṇahoma* (the offering of rice-huskings) and the *sārasvata homa* (the offering to Sarasvatī), etc. As stated by Bharadvāja: "It is the same up to the *samiṣṭayajus*.
If one should desire of someone, "May he be liable to die," then for that person, while standing obliquely or bent over, one should silently offer [the oblation] with the *sruva* ladle.

Regarding the *samiṣṭayajus*: if a sacrificer should desire that his enemy be "pramāyukaḥ"—meaning prone to sudden death—then for such a sacrificer desiring this, the performance [of the rite] is as follows: with the *sruva* ladle held crookedly—that is, with its handle bent—he stands. Thus, both the crookedness and the standing are prescribed in relation to the object of the desire. By the word "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*), it is prescribed that the mental aspect applies to the mantras, thereby setting aside the requirement of whispering (*upāṃśutā*). By the phrase "or having offered" (*praho vā*), the alternative of having already offered is prescribed.

By the word *nihma*, the curvature of the sides is indicated; by the word *prala*, the curvature of the back—these two are the defects. The rest is clear. Here, there is no throwing away (*anupraharaṇa*) of the *bahiṣ* grass, because a specific rule will be prescribed later for burning the altar (*vedi*) with the words "he burns the altar. This follows the principle of the *hṛdayaśūla* rite. There is the release of the sacrifice (*yajñavimoka*) by the Adhvaryu. Regarding the phrase "the pot which... some desire this to be the release of the *saumya-sthālī*; that is not so, because it had already been released previously.
Furthermore, one should not postpone what is incidental (*prāsaṅgika*), according to the maxim: "because of the lack of connection [to the main purpose]."
When [the ritual] has concluded with the words, "This is the third pressing of the sages," he offers the oblation.

Because of the expression "when it has concluded" (*saṃsthita*), the remainder of the ritual action following the *samiṣṭayajus* must indeed be completed. From the bringing forward of the *anubandhyā* cow until the removal of the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*), and ending with the worship of the sacrificial post (*yūpopasthāna*), the procedure is the same, including the gratification of the Brahmins. Thereafter, the expiations for Soma (*somaprāyaścittāni*) occasioned by the spilling of Soma, as well as other expiations prescribed in other scriptures according to the specific cause, are to be performed here before the *savanīya* animal sacrifice. The explanation, however, is exactly the same here as it was for the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*).
"O Praśāstṛ, give the impulse!"—thus he issues the command; "Crawl forth," says the Praśāstṛ; thus the third pressing is concluded.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the ninth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

This too has been explained as occurring at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) alone. Thus [ends] the commentary composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita—who was a performer of the Agniṣṭoma, the Sāhasra, the Bājapeya accompanied by the thousand-fold fire-offering, the Sarvatomukha, and the Pauṇḍarīka accompanied by the two-thousand-fold fire-offering—on the venerable Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

In the commentary named *Jyotsnā*, which pacifies the distress of learned men caused by the failure to obtain the jewels of hidden meanings contained within the ocean of the *Vājasaneyi-saṃhitā*, this is the fourth chapter of the ninth book. Now begins the fifth chapter of the ninth book of the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha.
He initiates the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).

Now, although the point was already established by the mere statement, "We shall explain whatever is performed there at the *avabhṛtha*," the composition of this heavy sūtra—namely, "He initiates the *satra* with the *avabhṛtha*"—is intended to indicate that the application of the rule "we shall explain whatever is performed there" pertains specifically to the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the Adhvaryu, and not to the ritual procedure of the Hotṛ. Therefore, in the case of the mantra "O Waters, [you are] greatness," it occurs; however, the mantra "Bhūḥ, I enter [the waters]" and so forth does not occur, because of the absence of the *vedi* (altar).
As for what is performed there, we shall explain that.
The procedure for the *gṛhamedhīyā* and the *prāyaṇīyā* has already been explained.
Having added fuel to the fires, prepared the *veda*, strewn around the fires, washed his hands, and spread out a layer of *ulapa* grass, he arranges the vessels according to their purpose.

Regarding the absence of the statement concerning the wood-piling (*vanavata*) at the *agnyanvādhāna*, its application would follow from the sūtra: "We shall explain whatever is performed therein. For the sake of establishing that [application], the explanation has already been provided in the context of the *prāyaṇīyā* sacrifice. As for the modification according to time: if it is the *paurṇamāsī* ritual framework, one uses "jyotiruttamaṃ yajñāya" and "imāmūrje praviṣṭāḥ"; if it is the *āmāvāsyā* ritual framework, one uses "jyotiruttamam adya yajñāya... and "imāmūrjaṃ yathātithi."

In both cases, the specific detail that "the oblation is adorned" is exactly the same. There is no taking up of the vow (*vrata*), because the vow previously undertaken has not yet been released; this is to avoid its loss. There is also no bringing of the *nemi* and the *barhis*.

Having taken the sacrificial grass (barhis) in silence, heated it over the fire, cut the *paribhojanīya* grass, and taken it up; having taken the *vedāgra* blades from the *paribhojana* grass and fashioned a *veda* with them, he strews around [the fire] with the mantra: "For both of you, for the sake of the ritual. Having sprinkled his hands and strewn the *ulaparājī* grass with the mantra, "Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice," he arranges the washed vessels upon the *darbha* grass according to their respective places and purposes, placing them near the fire. Some say [the vessel] is the *ulaparāji*.

The purpose of the weaving has already been shown in the context of the *prāyaṇīyā* sacrifice. Here, due to the suffix *ktvā*, the employment of the vessels occurs immediately after the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Because the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) is the final remainder of the entire rite, there is no preparation of the seats for the Brahman and the sacrificer; this is because their seats are already established by those prepared for the sake of the *sutyā*. Furthermore, there is only one potsherd (*kapāla*) for the *sapatha* offering, owing to its great significance.

The Agnihotrin [prepares] these many vessels: a black antelope skin, a wooden pin (śamyā), a mortar, a pestle, a lower grinding stone, an upper grinding stone, a large ladle (sruva), an offering-ladle (juhū), a supporting-ladle (upabhṛt), a stirring-ladle (dhruvā), a vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī), a winnowing basket (kuṭara), a vessel, a stirring-stick (mekṣaṇa), the sacrificial grass-bundle (veda), a vessel for hot water (madantīpātra), a fire-brick (upaveṣa), a pouring-vessel (niṣecanapātra), the tips of the sacrificial grass (vedāgra), a pair of garments, and a branch of the Udumbara tree. There is no formal selection of a Brahman priest; the purpose is accomplished by the very selection of the principal officiant. The sacrificer’s wife takes her seat. Then follows the preparation of the purifier (pavitra) for the Brahman with the mantra beginning "O Lord of Speech" (vācaspati).
He does not carry forward the Praṇītā waters.

"O Brahman, shall I carry forward the waters?"—"No," he replies; for there is no carrying forward of the *praṇītā* waters, as their carrying forward has been prohibited. "He should restrain his speech"—this much alone is the injunction here. [End of Paṭala 150] With the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa: At the time of the offering, he offers a cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) to Varuṇa.

"May they lie down for skill, or for service. "Burnt away [is the evil]... [With these words,] he does not let go of the one who is about to release [the animal]. By the phrase "at the time of the Nirvapaṇa," the existence of the verses beginning with "may they lie down" is indicated. He offers the one-potsherd cake dedicated to Varuṇa with the formula, "I offer what is pleasing to Varuṇa. O Varuṇa, the oblation is savory. "I sprinkle what is pleasing to Varuṇa."

The sprinkling of the vessels with the formula *śundhadhvam*, the taking up of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), and so forth—the ritual procedure ending with the *bheṣa* (the scattering of grains)—is obtained as the archetypal *tantra* even in the absence of an explicit statement, because otherwise the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) itself could not be accomplished. The placing [of the vessel] on the fire is performed with the *madanti* verse. The placing of the potsherds for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is done with the very first mantra: "Be heated by the *bhṛgus* and the *aṅgirases*; be heated by their austerity. The scattering of embers, the heating of the vessels, and so forth, up to the sifting of the flour, are performed.
He mixes [the flour] with the water purified by the *yajus* formulas.

Having taken pure [water] into any vessel whatsoever, one should pour it out with the *gāyatrī* mantra—"Devo vaḥ savitā" recited foot by foot—once with the mantra and twice silently; having thus drawn [the water] from them with the *sruva* ladle, one pours the flour [into it] with the words "samāpaḥ" (meaning "unite with the waters"), and so forth, beginning with "adbhyaḥ pariprajātāḥ stha. There is no division nor specific designation, because the purpose is already served. The purpose of the rule for pouring out the *yajus* has already been demonstrated in the context of the preparation of the *savanīya* offerings; therefore, it should be understood from there.
Having poured out the water for sprinkling (*āpyalepa*), he proceeds with the formal command (*saṃpraieṣa*).

By the word "having covered" (*abhivāsita*), the covering of the ashes with the Veda in its proper form is called "covering" (*abhivāsana*). By this [instruction], the cessation of the command "cook without burning" (*avidahantaḥ apayata*) is effected. Even without a formal command, the cooking characterized by non-burning must be performed here. The mention of "pouring out the water for sprinkling" is for the purpose of removing the doubt that the spreading [of grass] on the Great Altar (*mahāvedi*) might have ceased; it is for the sake of preventing that cessation. Having silently taken up the *syama* [ladle], he proceeds with the formal command. After the pouring out of the water for sprinkling, there is only the formal command, not the [spreading of grass].
The suffix *-tya* is used for the purpose of illustration, as in the expression "the altar is made of *stamba* grass.
He issues the command regarding whatever else there is besides the fuel (*idhma*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.

Where there is the carrying away of the *stambayajus*, it is only there that the taking up of the wooden sword (*sphya*) accompanied by its mantra occurs, and not elsewhere, because [the mantra] is an ancillary part of that [act]. In this regard, the injunction from this Sūtra is as follows: "Place the *prokṣaṇī* waters; cleanse the *sruva* ladle and the *sruk* spoons; bring the other [utensils] here. Although the placing of the *prokṣaṇī* waters has no visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) here, nevertheless, the placing must certainly be performed for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), because it is distinct from the fuel (*idhma*), the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and the girding of the wife (*patnīsanahana*).

Then, having placed the *pavitra* strainers inside the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle, he performs the rites beginning with "He purifies the mind" (*apa mano yati*) and ending with "He touches this" (*ayaṃ parimṛśati*), followed by the formulas beginning with "You are sharpened" (*niśitāḥ stha*) and ending with "The craft of heaven" (*divaḥ śilpam*). Taking the darbha blades for wiping and the udumbara branch, he heats them silently (*tūṣṇīm*), wipes the *juhū* and other ladles silently, heats them again silently, rinses them, and places them near the ladles. He throws the wiping blades into the fire silently. This is understood from the forthcoming sūtra. There is no wiping of the *prāśitra* portion, because that [portion] does not exist at all.
Having performed that which was to be done prior to the taking of the clarified butter (*ājya*) and having brought it back, he takes the *ājya* at the Gārhapatya fire.

Having performed the ritual actions up to "May Pūṣan open your opening" (*pūṣā te bilaṃ viṣyatv*), and so forth, before the taking of the *ājya*, he brings the *ājya* back near the Gārhapatya. "Bringing back" (*pratiharaṇa*) means carrying it back after turning around. He takes the *ājya* to the north of the Gārhapatya.
All [portions] are taken four times; or twice in the *upabhṛt* ladle.

Furthermore, regarding the *upabhṛt* [ladle], it should indeed be stated as "twice taken" (*dvigṛhītam*) for the sake of brevity; such a statement is intended to exclude the "five-fold taking" (*pañcagṛhītam*) which might otherwise apply optionally by virtue of the archetypal model (*prakṛti*), as in the case of the *juhū* and other ladles. In the *upabhṛt*, one takes four portions with the formulas beginning "For the Brahman... (*brahmaṇas tvā*). It is understood that the subsequent prohibition—"one does not pour together from the *upabhṛt*" (*nopabhṛtaḥ samānayate*)—is solely for the purpose of the [subsequent] pouring together, and not for the purpose of the *svāhā*-utterance.

Therefore, because there is no connection with the *aupabhṛta* clarified butter (*ājya*) for the *prayāja*s, the first fourfold-drawn portion intended for the *prayāja*s is omitted. In the view that "there are two [drawings] in the *aupabhṛt*," the drawing is performed twice using the two formulas, "For Viśve Devās" and "For good heroic power. As in the archetype (*prakṛti*), this applies when there is an increase. Having removed the *ājyasthālī* along with the *sruva* and the *veda*, its removal elsewhere is established by the requirements of the purpose.

"Self-power (svadhā) to the ancestors, ūm. This [formula] is used because the disposal of the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*) that have been set down is mandatory. The throwing away of the two strainers (*pavitra*), however, is done silently on the altar itself, since there is no *prastara* [bunch of grass]. The mantra is used only for the throwing away of the *prastara*. For there is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating: "The *prastara* is indeed the sacrificer; the two strainers are the out-breath and in-breath; thus he bestows out-breath and in-breath upon the sacrificer himself.
Having adorned the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), he places it on the northern shoulder [of the altar] for the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).

By the statement "having adorned the sacrificial cake" (*alaṃkṛtya puroḍāśam*), this injunction beginning with "this for the army" (*idaṃ hāsenāyā*) is obtained. In this case, there is no filling of the cavity (*āmipūraṇa*), because the entire [cake] is not to be offered as the principal oblation, and because of the mention of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. On the northern shoulder of the *uttaravedi*, one collects the materials to be cast into the *avabhṛtha* bath; that is, he brings them together in one place. He says exactly this:

The sacrificial cake, the clarified butters, the Udumbara post, the two pressing-boards, the dust from the mound, the dregs, and whatever else has been smeared with Soma—except for the four Soma-vessels, namely the Āgrayaṇa vessel, the Ukthya vessel, the Āditya vessel, and the Dhruva vessel.

By the phrase "whatever is smeared with Soma," the skin used for pressing and other such items are included. There is no measuring of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) upon this [Soma-vessel], because it is an original (apūrva) act. Since the number four is already established by the mere mention of "from the four Soma-vessels," its explicit mention here serves to indicate that, in the case of the offering of the Devikā-havīs, the four vessels must be moved away from that place and set aside elsewhere in a known manner; furthermore, among those, first the Āgrayaṇa vessel should be placed, then the Ukthya vessel, and so on.
The *ādityasthālī* is placed first, then the *dhruvasthālī*; they are to be set down in this very sequence, for the purpose of establishing such an order.
He offers with the mantra, "O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation," into whichever fire he has cooked [the offering].

In this rite, the second oblation is offered with the mantra: *atrāvabhṛtha nica kuṇa*. The third oblation is offered with: *namo rudrāya vāstoṣpataye*. And it has been stated by Āpastamba: "With the mantra *āyurdā agne haviṣo juṣāṇaḥ*, one should offer at the Avabhṛtha (concluding bath), and also with *atrāvabhṛtha nica kuṇa*. [And] *namo rudrāya vāstoṣpataye*. [At the place] of arrival and of departure; in the garden and in the retreat; in the turning point and in the forest. [End of] Chapter 150. Accompanied by the commentary of Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

"Whoever protects it, let him strike it down"—this [is the mantra]. Regarding this, because the *sūtrakāra* has assigned the mantra for the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) elsewhere, there is no application of it to the oblation (*āhuti*). As for the mantra "namo rudrāya," since it has not been specifically assigned elsewhere, its application here follows from the general rule of paribhāṣā; or rather, its application is to the silent recitation (*japa*), and that occurs after the oblation. For the scriptural indicative mark (*śrutiliṅga*)—"in that fire he offers"—which serves as the basis [for the application], is found in the passage: "He who departs from this world is cut off from immortality."
If the cooking is performed on the *gārhapatya* fire, then this oblation belongs to the *gārhapatya*; if the cooking is performed on the *āhavanīya* fire, then it belongs to the *āhavanīya*.

When the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) has been performed, [the vessel] is placed upon a seat made of *udumbara* wood; it is called "on the seat" (*āsanya*) because it is situated upon the seat, as if on a throne.

"O Prastotṛ, sing the Sāmans," he thus commands. Together with the wife, they all three times reach the *nidhana* (concluding syllable) of the Sāman. The *nidhana* is a distinct division (*bhakti*) of the Sāman. The word "three times" (*tris*) is construed with the verb "they reach" (*upayanti*); thus, the phrase becomes "they reach [it] three times. The meaning of "they reach it three times" is that they conclude it three times. In the command (*preṣa*), the plural form "Sāmans" (*sāmāni*) refers to the singing of the Sāmans to be performed at each of the three locations; therefore, the command itself is established as being uttered only once.

"Indeed, King Varuṇa has made wide space," they say. Regarding this, the meaning of the first position is that they say it after having gone to the *cātvāla* pit, or that they say it while departing from the *cātvāla*, or that they say it after having gone near the *cātvāla* and standing in its vicinity. The meaning of the second position is that they say it while departing—that is, while going out—from the seat [of the *cātvāla*].
They exit toward the north between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*.
In both cases, they exit between the *catvāla* pit and the *āhavanīya* fire, facing northward.
It is traditionally taught that the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) may proceed in any direction.

In this matter, whichever direction they head toward becomes the east (*prācī*); the respective locations for the various rites must be determined in accordance with that. The same mantra applies to all. That it also applies to the wife is obtained by the continued application of the preceding sūtra, "together with the wife" (*saha patnyā*).

"One should not travel by the northern [road]," so say some; that is, by the road going toward the north. This is a qualification of the path. The meaning is that, according to the opinion of certain teachers, one should not travel by the northern road.
In the Middle Country, they employ the second *nidhana* of the *sāman*, and at the edge of the water, the third.

The meaning is clear. Having seen water, they mutter: "A hundred are your physicians, O King, a thousand... For all [the officiants], there is the muttering because of the plural number; in the case of the reading with the singular number, it belongs to the Adhvaryu alone; in the case of the reading with the plural number, it belongs to the wife as well. 1. Not in Nivī. 2. Ga. Va. *prasya vi*. 3. Ga. Ca. *dutiri*. 7 1 942 Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra—[9th Praśna].
"Varuṇa’s noose has been stepped over," [with these words] they step upon the edge of the water.
Having gone to the edge of the water, everyone stands facing the water. Plunging into the water and remaining there, they perform the *avabhṛtha* rite.

"Stepping into the waters, stir the waters. By means of this [formula], while standing, the sacrificer and his wife perform their stepping forward and stepping back at the beginning of the *āghāra* offerings and other rites. To the south are the Brahman, the sacrificer, and the wife; to the north is the *Āgnīdhra*; behind is the Hotṛ. In the middle, one should place the sacrificial oblations, held by someone in another vessel, upon a high seat, a platform, or a stool. All stir the waters. Even before being addressed, the Hotṛ, having silently sipped water outside, remains seated.

Thinking, "The gods [know] that greatness," he sips water, puts on the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavīta*), and sips water again. He stands upon the edge of the water, thinking, "The noose of Varuṇa is loosened. Then, having stirred the water, he stands and does not move toward the place of immolation (*avabhṛtha*).
When the deities have been invoked, he sprinkles water, pours the *sruva*-libation, and issues the command to the *agnīdh*: "O Agnīdh, cleanse the water three times!"

When the deities have been invoked (*oḍhāsu* = *āvāhitāsu devatāsu satīṣu*), this [is the procedure] for the *yājuṣa-hautra*. According to the sūtra, "When the deities have been invoked," the *hotṛ* must perform the invocation of the deities: "O Agni, come! O Soma, come! O Varuṇa, come! O gods who drink the clarified butter, come! O Agni and Varuṇa, the two *sviṣṭakṛt*s, come! According to the sūtra, "When the deities have been invoked," one should perform only the simple invocation of as many deities as there are; the recitation of the remainder of the *nigada* is not required. He sprinkles water upon the *vedī* with the *upavāja*.

This fanning is for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Having covered the *nau-āghāra* [channel], he causes the *dhruvā* ladle to swell. This swelling of the *dhruvā* is because of the force of the prohibition: "The *dhruvā* being emptied... The Adhvaryu gives the command: "O Āgnīdhra, sprinkle the water three times. Then, having been thus commanded, the Āgnīdhra sprinkles the water standing in the *prauga* shed three times with the modified mantra. That modification is as follows: "O Water, winner of the prize (*vājajit*), you shall flow toward me; winning the prize, may you cause me to win the prize; O winner of the prize, make me a winner of the prize for the sake of obtaining food.
After the water has been sprinkled, he throws a blade of grass into it.

By the word "cleansed" (*saṃmṛṣṭa*), the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*) is indicated. Because the term "cleansed" is used as a past participle, it signifies that after the cleansing, the wiping is performed in water. The meaning is that [the vessel] has been cleansed by the *āgnīdhra* priest with the prescribed and appropriate [means]. Since there is an absence of fire-cleansing implements here, one takes the darbha grass intended for the surrounding-sweeping (*pariṣecana*) along with the *sphyam* (wooden sword) and performs the same action with them as was done with the *sphyam*.

Regarding this, Bharadvāja has stated: "When an action is enjoined, one should produce the substance [required], as in the case of the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, where there is the sweeping of the fires. The term *gṛhamedhīya* is an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *avabhṛtha*, the *upasad*s, and other rites that lack the sweeping of the fires. Once the ritual procedure has been performed by the *āgnīdhra*, he throws a blade of grass into the waters while aiming toward the location of the *āhavanīya* fire. All oblations are to be offered upon this grass.

"He offers the *barhis* upon the foundation of the oblations for their stability; thus he offers upon that which possesses Agni," so says the Śruti. In the mantra "Thou art the world, O wide-spreading, [name] of the sacrificers, obeisance!"—where there was the word "Agni," the word "water" (*udaka*) is substituted. This is because the word "Agni" here refers to the Āhavanīya fire, and since the Āhavanīya is absent here, water occupies its place. Furthermore, because the word "sacrificer" (*yaṣṭṛ*) is an adjective qualifying that [fire], and since the word "water" is neuter, the adjective "sacrificer" must be modified in accordance with it.

[Chapter 943, Section 550] Together with the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. The word [saprathas] should also be used in the neuter gender. However, in the case of the mantra "saprathā namo devebhyaḥ," the modification (*ūha*) is "sapratho namo. The word "saprakāḥ" ends in a long vowel (is *sānta*). When it functions as a qualifier for water, it takes the neuter gender as "saṃpratha. [The formulas] "svadhā pitṛbhyaḥ," "mudde hyagnistvā," "upabhṛdehi devastvā," "suyame me," and "agnāviṣṇū" are not present [in this context].

Due to the absence of the altar (*vedī*), there is an absence of the stepping upon it, the attack prompted by that, and the mantra associated with it. [The mantra] "Thou art the station of Viṣṇu" does not exist, because of the absence of the crossing-over. There is an absence of the standing still and the mantra associated with it. [The injunction] "the right foot within the altar," and so forth, is omitted due to the absence of the altar.
He pours the clarified butter into the ladle with the mantra: "The face of Agni has entered the waters."

The *sruc* is that which is accomplished by the *sruc*. Here, there is no modification (*ūha*) of the word "Agni," because it reveals the deity to whom the oblation is being offered. Having offered, he says, "He breathes after. He lifts up the *sruva* with the words, "O Great Light! There is no returning [to the altar] because of the absence of the formula "Protect me from harm. The renunciation (*tyāga*) is: "This for Agni. There is a modification: "Speech is yours, belonging to Agni. [He offers] with "Well-anointed... O Leader of wealth, to the one rich in heroes, Svāhā! Through sacrifice... Having set down the two *srucs*, [he concludes].

Having gathered the grass blades at the place where the faggot-bundle (idhma) was tied and having taken them onto the *sphya*, [the Adhvaryu says]: "Who will announce this for the Adhvaryu? Who will announce this for the Agnidh? [The Brahman replies: "O Brahman, I shall cause the announcement for the *pravara*. [The Adhvaryu says: "O Vācaspati... o3m... mānā3... ā 3 śrā3... astu... O Hotṛ, stand! This is the sequence of the performance.
As in the *upasads*, so does he choose the *pravara*. "Stand"—this much constitutes the *pravara*.

Regarding the phrase "sauda hotar" [in the context of] the *upasad* rites, because that [formula] is sublated here, the specific modification is "tiṣṭha. There is an elision of the section beginning with "agnirdevo hotā" and ending with "mānuṣaḥ. Nor should it be argued that if the *pravara* (the invocation of ancestral priests) is elided, the standing and other acts intended for the *pravara* would also be elided; for by the rule stating that the *pravara* consists merely of the word "tiṣṭha," the existence of such a *pravara* is indicated, and thereby its constituent parts—the standing and so forth—are also indicated.

Beginning with the words "The gods, the ancestors," and extending up to "Make me known among the gods for long life and splendor"—this portion of the mantra belongs to whichever ṛṣi I am related to; because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that "I do not exclude him from whom I am [descended]," one understands that this refers to one connected to a *pravara* distinguished by the proclamation of such a ṛṣi. In the present case, however, since there is an absence of such a *pravara*, the omission of this portion of the mantra is indeed appropriate.

By the mere word "tiṣṭha" (stand), the status of being a *pravara* (ancestor) for the purpose of ritual practice is established by the author of the Sūtra; and once the status of being a *pravara* is established, its capacity to produce the fruit [of the rite] is also established. Thus, whatever portion of the mantra intended for requesting the fruit related to the *pravara* is not contradicted here, that much must indeed be performed, including the words: "O Napāt, announce me among the gods for long life and prosperity. [The Hotṛ continues: "May Agni, the invoker, know the deity; may he who is rich in ghee sacrifice. He sacrifices the *prayāja* offerings excluding the *barhis*."

When it is said, "O Adhvaryu, O Adhvaryu, place the ladle [with] so much [ghee]," he takes the *jāghani* (tail-portion) and performs the *prayāja* offerings excluding the *barhis*. Because they are subordinate to the *prayājas*, there is no taking of the *anuyāja* portions. [The mantra is: "May Pṛthivī be the Hotṛ... etc. Those *prayājas* from which the *barhis* has departed are the *apabarhiṣaḥ* *prayājas*. The meaning is that there are four *prayājas* without the *barhis*. He does not pour [the ghee] together from the *upabhṛt* [ladle].

One does not pour from the *upabhṛt* during the *prayājas*, because its purpose is for the *barhis* (the sacrificial grass), and that [purpose] is absent in the archetype (*prakṛti*). From this very fact it is known that the pouring [of ghee] is solely for the sake of the *barhis*, and not even for the sake of the *svāhākāra*. Therefore, it is understood that in the archetype, the clarified butter (*ājya*) must be left as a remnant. Here, one sprinkles the *dhruvā*, the *vāruṇa* cake, and the *upabhṛt* with the remnant of the *prayāja*s;
this is obtained because the disposal of the remnant is mandatory.
The two *ājyabhāga* offerings are accompanied by the *apsu-mant* verses.

The two [deities] who release [the waters] are those denoted by the word *apsu*; they are addressed in the verses, "O Agni, thou art the seat among the waters" and "Soma has spoken to me in the waters.
Having performed the ritual for these two, he sacrifices to Varuṇa from the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

The statement "one should proceed with those two" is intended to mean that the performance must be carried out using only those [formulas] containing the word *ap* (water), and not with the optional *puronuvākyā* verse related to the second *ājyabhāga*—namely, "O Soma, you are the bull, the strengthener"—which is recited in the context of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices; or else, it is for the purpose of avoiding the performance of occasional (*naimittika*) expiations (*prāyaścitta*) in the interim. If one asks, "Where then should it be performed? the implication is that it should be performed at the end of the *anūyāja* offerings. Regarding the *agnihotra*, the sacrificer performs the *puroḍāśa* sacrifice to Varuṇa.

In this case, there is no offering of the entire portion, because it will be prescribed for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering alone. Having spread the *upastaraṇa* (under-layer) of clarified butter, having replenished the *dhruvā* vessel, and having touched [the oblation] with the mantra "Mā bheḥ" (Do not fear), he takes two portions; he does not replenish the *dhruvā* for the sake of the subsequent pouring. Having sprinkled [the oblation] twice with the mantra "Yad akṛtāni" (Whatever was done imperfectly), he offers the invitation to Varuṇa. After the call for the *āśrāvaṇa* and the response, the performance of the Varuṇa sacrifice proceeds: the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) and the offering verse (*yājyā*) are "imaṃ me varuṇa śrudhi" and "tattvā yāmi brahmaṇā," respectively. [The formula is: "To Varuṇa, this [offering]. [The concluding formula is: "By the sacrifice to the god Varuṇa, may I become an eater of food."

Having taken the entire *puroḍāśa* as an oblation, he sacrifices it to Agni and Varuṇa as the *Sviṣṭakṛt*. The performance of this is as follows: having spread a base of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle, he does not replenish the *dhruvā* vessel. Having taken the entire *puroḍāśa*, he pours clarified butter over it twice; in both instances, he does not replenish the *dhruvā*. The completion of the *prauga* section occurs with these two pourings of butter. [The Adhvaryu says: "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni and Varuṇa as the *Sviṣṭakṛt*. After the *āśrāvaṇa* and the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* have been made, [the Adhvaryu says: "Sacrifice to Agni and Varuṇa as the *Sviṣṭakṛt*. The performance of the *Sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice consists in making the offering while aiming at the north-eastern part of the altar.

"O Agni Varuṇa, release us from our bonds; svāhā! We worship Agni and Varuṇa, the two Sviṣṭakṛts. May Agni have sacrificed to the dear abodes of Agni; may he have sacrificed to the dear abodes of Soma; may he have sacrificed to the dear abodes of Varuṇa; may he have sacrificed to the dear abodes of the gods who drink the clarified butter. May he sacrifice to the dear abodes of Agni and Varuṇa, the two Sviṣṭakṛts. May he sacrifice to the great oblation. O Agni, be our nearest protector; svāhā!"—this is the specific modification for the Hotṛ.

"I have sacrificed to Agni and Varuṇa with the Sviṣṭakṛt offering. "By the sacrifice to the gods, Agni and Varuṇa, who are the Sviṣṭakṛts, may I, long-lived, attain firm standing through this sacrifice. "May Agni and Varuṇa protect me from ill-sacrificed offerings; may Savitṛ protect me from those who speak evil; may he who is near and far drive away my enemies; by that, may I be victorious. Having observed the place where the Vaiśvānara oblation was offered, he pours out the washing water. He issues the command: "O Āgnīdhra, sprinkle the water once."

In this case as well, the sweeping (*saṃmārjana*) is not established even in the absence of the expression "swept" (*saṃmṛṣṭa*). [The sweeping is performed] with those very *paribhojanīya* blades by those [same persons]. Having taken water from the water-vessel, he sprinkles it over the blades with the formula: "May they conquer the enemies, may they conquer the adversaries, may they conquer the challengers, may they conquer the attackers, for the sake of victory, for the sake of food-eating, for the sake of food-enjoyment. He silently throws the sweeping-blades into the water. Here there is no [recitation of] "He who is the lord of beings," because of the contradiction with the formula "That which has been offered, Svāhā! Nor is there [the recitation regarding] the altar and the fire, because of the contradiction.
He performs two after-offerings (*anuyāja*) without the *barhis* grass. He issues the call for the first after-offering as "Sacrifice to the two gods!

Sacrifice! and for the latter as "Sacrifice! The Udgātṛ priest holds the *mahāhavis* oblation. Having brought the clarified butter intended for the after-offerings, he consumes it with that [butter] while excluding the *barhis*. He performs the after-offerings excluding the *barhis*, which has been removed. He issues the call for the first, initial after-offering as "Sacrifice to the two goddesses! and for the latter after-offering as "Sacrifice! Because the first after-offering involves two sacrifices (*dviryaji*), there are two sacrificial calls (*yajyā*). Because the latter involves a single sacrifice (*ekayaji*), there is only one sacrificial call.
"Let there be no tasteless [offering] for this sacrifice at the morning recitation (prātaranuvāka) and the day [rite]; let there be no *nārāśaṃsa* cups at the *iḍā*-offering.
This much is performed;
nothing further is to be done for the sake of the *kautsa* rite.

O King Soma, those dear limbs of yours which they have severed with the pressing-stone, and your joints which have been hewn, heal them with clarified butter and cause them to grow; being thus made whole, may we utterly destroy our sin. O God Soma, that part of you which the men, moving their arms, have caused the stone to strike down, and that which they have milked with the right hand—let that swell for you and let that be restored for you. As for the skin they pierced and the womb, and when you were displaced from your station, you yourself felt it within.

"O Soma, may that [essence] be protected by you for us; may it be our bond in the highest heaven. Having entered the body with the milk, one color after another arises within it. In that [body], we are invited and belong to you; grant us a share in the assembly, O you of all forms. With these four verses, he offers the *nīṣa* (the dregs) over a branch of the *udumbara* tree, using five, seven, nine, eleven, or thirteen [verses].

He offers oblations with the *svāhā* utterance at the end of each respective verse as prompted by the injunction. Immediately after the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) of the ladles with the verses, he should not offer with a vessel that has not been cleansed; rather, he should offer with the Udumbara branch—whose cleansing is obtained from another [textual] source—and with ordinary curd. He offers over the *ṛṇīṣa* (the wooden ring) with five, seven, nine, eleven, or thirteen [verses], the separate mention of these numbers being for the purpose of excluding an equal number. Some say it is with clarified butter (*ājya*), because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) "he pours out the essence of the clarified butter."

That is incorrect, because it would result in a contradiction with the direct statement of the text (*dṛtivacana*), and because the word *ājya* (clarified butter) can apply to the *dadhi* (curds), just as the word *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) does. Having filled the ladle with the residue of the Soma (*ṛjīṣa*), he dips it into the water with the mantra: "In the ocean is thy heart. (Satyāṣāḍha Śrautasūtra 9.4.6).

Regarding the term *anīṣasya*, it refers to a part [of the vessel]. By means of that single part, the ladle (*sruk*) is filled. It is the *pracaraṇī* ladle, because it alone is connected with the Soma; or else, it may be another ordinary (*laukika*) one. In the case of adopting an ordinary ladle, this one is also employed during the use of the *avabhṛtha* vessels. The sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and the wiping (*saṃmārjana*) are performed silently, just as with the *juhū* ladle. One causes the ladle, which has been filled by a portion of the *anīṣa*, to descend into the waters—that is, one immerses it in the water.
Of that which has been washed in the water, whatever drops rise up addressed to the deity Soma, he consumes them with his nose or touches them.

"Po bhindūnām uccarati": [the drop] rises, moves upward from the sun due to the wind. "Bhindūnām": among the drops; because of its greatness, that drop which leaps up—that drop one consumes with intense concentration (*avadhāna*), or touches. Since that drop cannot remain once it has reached the vital breath (*prāṇa*), its touching is [described as such]. "Avabhṛthanicaṅkuṇa": they cast the *avabhṛtha* (the final purificatory bath) together.

Because of the plural number, the Adhvaryu, Pratiprasthātṛ, Netṛ, and the Sacrificer (*yajamāna*) cast it together; they throw the collection of substances used for the *avabhṛtha* into the water. This is the meaning.
They stand near [the water] with the verse, "O divine waters" (*devīrāpaḥ*).
Because of the plural number, all those who recite the Yajurveda do so.
They purify themselves with the verse, "May we be well-friends" (*sumitrā naḥ*). || 14 ||

As before, all [the verses] belong to the Yajurveda. He issues the command to the Unnetṛ: "O Unnetṛ, carry us across to the further shore; these most honey-sweet songs rise up; the hymns of praise go forth like chariots seeking booty, winning wealth, providing inexhaustible aid, and striving for victory—just as the Kaṇvas, the Bhr̥gus, and the Sūryas have attained everything that is most desired.

The word *vakṣīya* ("carry us") is a qualification of the Unnetṛ. [The phrase] "carry us across" means "lead us upward, across the waters, toward the further shore. The words beginning with *madhumattamāḥ* ("most honey-sweet") are qualifications of those being carried across, intended to express their greatness.

"Rising up, bestowing progeny and splendor, they have sent you forth for wealth and sacrifices. Embrace the Gāyatrī metre; thus may we be fragrant in our homes. With this, the Unnetṛ causes the Hotṛ, the sacrificer, and others to ascend first.
All of them, including the sacrificer's wife, do so. The mantra is recited only once, because of the indicative mark of the plural "rising up" (*udeta*).
With the words, "The noose of Varuṇa is cast off," he wades back to the edge of the water.

He stirs the water standing at the boundary of the mantra-limit. Having cast [the grass] toward the edge of the water with the formula, "The noose of Varuṇa is cast away," [he concludes]. The meaning is that one should cast water standing at the final boundary-line (*antima-sīmā*) with the forepart of the foot. Maudgalyāyana states this very point: "Having turned back, he casts [the water] toward the edge of the water with the forepart of the foot" (*prapadena*). Regarding the gerund *pratyasya*, the sense is "without looking back," as in the phrase "they return without looking back. Because of the plural number, it indicates that all participants perform the casting; likewise, in the phrase "they return without looking back," it applies to all. They hold *audumbara* fuel-sticks (*samidh*).

All the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and his wife hold a single *udumbara* fuel-stick (*samidh*). The plural number in the word "fuel-sticks" (*samidhaḥ*) is intended to refer to the multiple participants.
Reciting the verse "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal," they chant the *mahīyā*.

The name of this verse, "apāma soma," is *mahīyā*. The purpose of this designation has been explained; it is used here in the phrase "the lifting is the *mahīyā*" so that this specific verse may be understood. Because of the plural number, the recitation is performed by all.
Placing the Unnetṛ at their head, they go forward without looking back.

Having placed him at the head and having prepared the seats for all, they go toward the place of the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) without looking back; that is to say, they return toward the sacrificial ground (vihāra).
They perform the ritual purification (mārjana) in the cow-pen beyond.

The *goṣṭhī* is the dwelling place of the cows; in the region situated beyond that, in front of it, all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and his wife pay their respects. Regarding this, Bharadvāja states that they recite the mantra "sumitrā na āpa oṣadhayaḥ santu. They place fuel-sticks (*samidh*) upon the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra "edho 'sy edhiṣīmahi. Then, having taken them from the Uttaravedi, each places his own Audumbara fuel-stick upon the fire, first the sacrificer, and then all the officiating priests, using that same mantra on the Uttaravedi fire itself.
They stand worshipping with the verse, "I have followed after the waters.
They worship according to the sequence of placing the fuel-sticks.
In this same manner, the wife, having placed [fuel] on the Gārhapatya fire, stands worshipping. || 15 ||

Immediately after that, at the end of all the recitations, there is the kindling of the fires (*ādhāna*) and the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) performed by the wife. The word "thus" (*evam*) is for the purpose of indicating that these two acts—kindling and attendance—must be performed by her in the same manner as they were performed by the husband. The mention of the *gārhapatya* fire is intended to set aside the rule that would otherwise apply based on the location of the *uttaravedi*. In that context, the mantra "O Agni, come with milk; unite me with luster" undergoes modification (*ūha*).

Thus ends the fifth chapter of the ninth book in the *Jyotsnā* commentary, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—the son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was a performer of the *Agniṣṭoma*, *Vājapeya*, *Sarvatomukha*, and *Pauṇḍarīka* sacrifices, and who was endowed with the title "Śrīpada"—written to alleviate the distress of learned men caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the ocean of the *Hiraṇyakeśi-Śrautasūtra* of the venerable Satyāṣāḍha.
[End of the Ninth Book] [Note: The fragment "ga. ca. hīyāmitya" and "satyāpāṭhaviracitaṃ śrautasūtra-" appear to be scribal or editorial marks indicating the end of the section.]
9.6 Now begins the sixth chapter of the ninth book. One commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *udayanīyā* offering within the *prāgvaṃśa* hall.

The rule applies to that portion which is merely the *prāgvaṃśa*. Therein, one infers the commencement of the rite. This is the rule regarding the *praśana* (eating/consumption). "This is the *āhavanīya* fire from which [the fire] is carried forth; that is the *gārhapatya*"—by these two sūtras, it is established that the *śālāmukhīya* fire serves the functions of the *gārhapatya*, and thus the *gārhapatya* rites are performed there. Consequently, the displacement of those two—the *āhavanīya* and the *gārhapatya*—which would otherwise have been located on the *uttaravedi* and in the *śālāmukhīya* respectively, is effected by this [rule].

By this, it is established that one does not deviate from the very ordinary (prākṛta) [rites]. In that regard, the statement "he commences the sequence" (*tantraṃ prakramayati*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*); even in this *iṣṭi*, there is no novelty (*apūrvatā*) concerning the office of the *hotṛ*, but rather it concerns only the constituent parts. This is precisely what the expression "he commences the sequence" signifies.
The ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for that [Udayanīyā] has been explained by means of the Prāyaṇīyā;
the ritual procedure—that is, the method beginning with the *anvādhāna* and so forth—of that Udayanīyā has been explained and stated by way of the Prāyaṇīyā.
He binds the *anūyāja* fuel-stick.
Herein lies the distinction from the *prāyaṇīyā* [offering]; the meaning is clear.
In whichever pot he cooks the *prāyaṇīyā*, in that same pot—without emptying it—he cooks [the offering] with that same stirring-spoon.

The meaning of the phrase "when there is no *niṣkāsa*" is as follows: *niṣkāsa* refers to the remnants of the oblation (*haviḥ*). Therefore, there is no contradiction with the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
He girds the wife;
the sense is that the *yoktra* (girdle) has already been discarded.
If the *prayāja* offerings are not to be performed, one does not take clarified butter into the *juhu* ladle;
this is clear.
The *prayāja*s may be either performed or omitted.

Although this sacrifice is complete, the statement "if there are no *prayāja*s" is made to indicate that the performance of the *prayāja*s is indeed optional; for even though optionality might otherwise be understood from the mere fact of their being performed or not, the explicit statement "the *prayāja*s are performed or not performed" is used for that purpose. Regarding the sequence of deities in that sacrifice, he states the distinction:
one sacrifices to the deity Pathyā Svasti last with clarified butter (*ājya*).

The distinction here is that the sequence of deities is Agni, Soma, Savitṛ, Pathyā Svasti, and Aditi; however, the sequence of locations follows the respective order of those deities. Thus Āpastamba says: "In those very places, for those who chant the Āgnimāruta [laud], the first goes to Pathyā Svasti and the last to [Agni]. This is for the sake of clarity. [End of] the section on the deity. [This concludes] the chapter composed by Gopīnātha Mahāmahopādhyāya, accompanied by his commentary Jyotsnā. 951. First, he proceeds to Pathyā Svasti, and the last to [Agni].

The meaning of the Āpastamba Sūtra is that one should worship in that very place whichever deity was previously invoked. Furthermore, another specific detail is stated in the Āpastamba Sūtra: "Those which were the *yājyās* of the *prāyaṇīya* [offering]," as it has been said. The reversal of the *puronuvākyās* and *yājyās*, as declared in the Brāhmaṇa, is also to be observed; this is the meaning of the Āpastamba Sūtra.
One does not set down the cooking pot (*sthālī*), the scrapings (*niṣkāsa*), or the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*). The intention is that there is no further purpose for them at this stage.
One does not leave a remainder of the *dhruvā* vessel,
because there is no further purpose for it;
it is completed in its entirety.
This statement is intended to exclude the *śayama* [the animal to be immolated].
One commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *anubandhyā* [the animal to be bound after the sacrifice].

Here, the expression "one commences the procedure" is stated for the purpose of indicating that the commencement of the procedure must take place immediately after the *udayanīyā* [concluding offering], without any intervening interval until its completion.

The ritual procedure for that [animal sacrifice] is explained by [the rules of] the *nirūḍhapaśubandha*. The ritual procedure—the specific method—for that *anūbandhyā* cow is explained as being like the *nirūḍhapaśubandha*, the *aindrāgna*, the *saurya*, or the *prājāpatya*. It is called *anūbandhyā* because she is bound (*badhyate*) after the sacrifice (*yajñam anu*), that is, at the conclusion of the sacrifice; the vowel is lengthened. According to the rule "the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* and the animal-offering (*paśviṣṭi*) are not considered parts [of this]," the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* and the animal-offering do not take place.
He dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa.

*Vaśā* means a barren cow; that is a cow (*gauḥ*). Accordingly, Āpastamba has stated two *praiṣas* (directions) involving a cow: "Recite for the omentum and fat of a barren cow for Mitra and Varuṇa," and "Direct [the Hotṛ] for the omentum and fat of a barren cow for Mitra and Varuṇa. The word *vaśā* may also be used in place of *gauḥ*. By the use of the word *paśu*, it is understood here that the feminine gender is intended by the word *go*.

Regarding the *preṣa* (direction) for the portions of the oblation (*havir-avadāna*), Āpastamba states: "In this manner, at the portions of the oblation, he modifies the end [of the formula] to 'of the oblation' (*haviṣaḥ*). This means that in place of the word *meṣa* ("ram") in the formula for the omentum (*vapā*), the word *haviṣaḥ* ("oblation") is substituted. Among the five types of sacrificial animals (*pañcapaśu*), because it possesses two syllables and a specific number of phonemes, the *āgnīṣomīya* animal is indeed the archetype (*prakṛti*) for this. Therefore, in its modifications (*vikāra*), such as the *āśvavāla* grass-bundle (*prastara*) and the two *vidhṛtī* made of *aiṣīka* grass, and the *adhi* made of *kāma* wood, and the two *pautudārava* [wooden sticks].

"Prompt for the omentum and fat of such-and-such; prompt for the cake of such-and-such; prompt for the oblation of such-and-such"—these are the rules prescribed in this sūtra that apply here. Here, because the animal is female, the modification (*ūha*) "of such-and-such" (*amuṣyāḥ*) takes the place of "of such-and-such" (*amuṣya*); this is the distinction. According to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [the animals are]:
three of two colors for Mitra-Varuṇa, one of many colors for the Viśvedevas, and one with a white back for Bṛhaspati.

The animal dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa (maitrāvaruṇī) has two forms and two colors. The one dedicated to the Viśvedevas (vaiśvadevī) has many forms and many colors. The one dedicated to Bṛhaspati (bārhaspatyā) has a white back (śitipṛṣṭhā)—that is, a white back—and there are thus three such animals. Although the animal with a white back may also have two forms, its possession of the color white on the back is fixed; therefore, the distinction lies in its having two forms. The word "iti" (thus) serves to indicate that regarding the *anubandhyā* animal for Bṛhaspati, there is also another alternative. By this, the red-colored (*rohitavarṇa*) animal mentioned by Āpastamba as "the red one for Bṛhaspati" is also established as an option.
He performs the Vaiśvadevī offering in a whisper from the center; both the *āśrāvaṇa* and *pratyāśrāvaṇa* are also in a whisper, while the other two are performed loudly.

If [the recitation] is in the middle, then only the *vaiśvadevī* portion is in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), and not the beginning or the end. By this, it is understood that there is also a mode of sacrifice where [the entire portion] is at the beginning and the end. According to the rule "except for the *pravara*, the *saṃvāda*, and the *āśrāvaṇa* and *saṃpraiṣa*," the loudness (*uccais*) of the *āśrāvaṇa* which was established by that [rule] is set aside by this [present rule]. The mention of *āśrāvaṇa* in this sūtra is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*. The word "also" (*api*) is for the purpose of indicating that the *saṃpraiṣas* are also in a low voice.

However, this [procedure]—consisting of methods such as snapping the fingers with the hand—is postulated because of the force of the injunctions laid down by the author of the Sūtras and because there is no other way to communicate to others; that is, [it applies] in contrast to the other two offerings, those dedicated to Mitrā-Varuṇa and Bṛhaspati. This statement is intended to exclude the doubt that [the procedure] might be optional.

Regarding the fact that the *anubandhyā* (the final animal sacrifice) belongs to one's own side, and that there is such a specific modification and such an inclusion, Āpastamba says: "They do not perform these [sacrifices] everywhere—[only] at the Vājapeya, the Sādyaskra, the Sattra, the Paśubandha, or when all one's property is given away (*sarvavedasa*). Furthermore, another distinction regarding this position is stated in that very same place: "He who desires, 'May my sacrifice be full of sap,' he should sacrifice these three *anubandhyā*s. By this desire, however, the performance is prescribed everywhere; "full of sap" means vigorous.

In this rite, the carrying forward of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is performed according to the ritual procedure for the *barhis* (sacrificial grass). There is an absence of the use of the wooden sword (*sphya*), the cord (*raśanā*), and the spit (*śūla*). The taking up of the animal fat (*pāśuka-ājya*) occurs only in the northern direction, because there is no pressing (*mardana*) of the soma. In all mantras containing masculine nouns, there is a modification (*ūha*) to the feminine gender: "Recite for Mitra and Varuṇa the omentum (*vapā*) of the cow (*goḥ*)," and "Command [the Hotṛ] regarding the fat (*medas*) of the cow for Mitra and Varuṇa"—this is the modification. "Recite for Mitra and Varuṇa the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) of the cow."

"Prompt the [hotṛ] for the cake of the cow for Mitra and Varuṇa. "Recite the invitatory verse for the oblation of the cow for Mitra and Varuṇa. "Prompt the [hotṛ] for the oblation of the cow for Mitra and Varuṇa"—these are the *praiṣas* (directions). In all these directions, the word *paśoḥ* ("of the animal") may be used immediately after the word *goḥ* ("of the cow"). Having offered the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) of the *anūbandhyā* cow, he subsequently offers the *daivika* oblations.
These belong to the *devikās*; the meaning is that they are related to the deities of the *devikās*.
"He offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Dhātṛ," as it is traditionally handed down in the scripture.

He offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Dhātṛ; a pap (caru) to Anumati, a pap to Rākā, a pap to Sinīvālī, and a pap to Kuhū—these are the five. Āpastamba clearly recited "five" twice. He says: "He offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Dhātṛ, a pap to Anumati, a pap to Rākā, a pap to Sinīvālī, and a pap to Kuhū"; this is how it is handed down in the tradition. These pap-offerings are cooked in milk in the Soma-vessels.

In the *pātra* vessel is a cake on twelve potsherds.
