In the *āmrapaṇa-sthālī* is a *caru* for Anumati; in the *ukthya-sthālī* is a *caru* for Rākā; in the *āditya-sthālī* is a *caru* for Sinīvālī; and in the *vasatīvarī-sthālī* is a *caru* for Kuhū—this is the meaning. For the animal-cake of the *anūbandhyā* cow and for the *devikā* oblations, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* portions are common;
this is well known.
He recites the *puronuvākyā* addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa;

this is clear. The specific statement that he "recites the *puronuvākyā* addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa" is for the purpose of making it known that, whereas in the archetype (*prakṛti*) there is one [verse], here there is a triad, and this applies specifically to the modification (*vikṛti*) just shown.
Furthermore, there is also a formal call (*saṃpraiṣa*).

This sūtra is intended to indicate that [the animal sacrifice] is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice specifically, and not a modification of the *sarasvatī* sacrifice by taking the commonality of "femininity" (*strītva*). Just as with the Soma sacrifice, in the Aśvamedha there are fifteen white barren cows (*vaśā*) as the *anūbandhyā* animals; since the rules for the *anūbandhyās* are extended (*atideśa*) to them as well, the *saṃpraiṣa* (direction) occurs there too because of this extension. Thus it is in all those *anūbandhyā* sacrifices.
At the end of the *anūyāja* offerings, one offers the *svaru* and proceeds with the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*) as previously described.
This is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the throwing away of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
Some prescribe the curdled milk (āmikṣā) for Mitra and Varuṇa in place of the Anūbandhyā cow, beginning with the offering of the oblation and ending with the Iḍā. It concludes there.

By the word *sthāna* (place/position), it is indicated that the function of the *anūbandhyā* cow is performed by means of the *āmikṣā*, even though this *āmikṣā*-rite is [ordinarily] minor. Furthermore, because the slaughter of cows is prohibited in the Kali age—according to the verse: "In the Kali age, one should avoid these five: the Agnihotra, the slaughter of a cow, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), the Śrāddha for those who have died abroad, and procreating a son through the husband’s brother"—the sacrifice must indeed be with *āmikṣā*. Due to the inherent force of the term *sthāna*, this [āmikṣā] does not serve as a mere substitute (*pratinidhi*) for the cow.

The meaning is that [the sacrifice] begins with the *havirātipra* and concludes with the *iḍā*. That which has its conclusion (*saṃsthā*) at the *iḍā* is called *iḍāntā*. Since the term *iḍāntā* alone would already establish that the sacrifice is concluded (*saṃsthita*), the further use of the word *saṃsthita* is for the purpose of indicating that the conclusion is necessary even by means of a ritual of disposal (*pratipattikarma*). Consequently, it is established that the *aninaya* sacrifice must be performed, as it consists of the disposal of the substance already produced. And thus Maradvāja says: "When the substance is produced, there is no failure of the rite."

Āśvalāyana also states: "From the *ājyabhāga* offerings up to the *vājin* offering. By this, it is indicated that as many rites as are necessary for the production of the sacrificial substance (*havis*) must be performed, and no other ritual framework (*tantra*) such as the *anvādhāna* is required. Here, the *āmikṣā* is made with ordinary curd, because there is no mention of the evening milking (*sāyaṃdoha*). The *khaṇḍeṣṭi* is designated as *āmikṣā*. Following that is the sacrifice with the *devikā-havis* offerings.

By means of the entire sequence of ritual acts beginning with the *anyānvādhāna* and ending with the *brāhmaṇatarpaṇa*, there is no single *tantra* for both [the *devikāhavīs* and the *sākamedha*], because their essential natures (*svarūpa*) are contradictory. Āpastamba, however, desires the performance of these [offerings] as a subsequent rite (*anuniṣṭhā*), stating: "After that, he offers the *devikāhavīs*. Baudhāyana states an exception here: "The *devikās* are performed with clarified butter (*ājya*)," according to the tradition of Āñjīgavi. Bharadvāja says another thing: "When one is about to prepare the *āmikṣā*, [one performs] the *devikās* with clarified butter. In the case of the *ājya* option, the sacrifice is performed according to the procedure (*dharma*) of the *aindrāgna* and *āśvina* offerings.

The *sviṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* portions are common to the offering for the extinguishing [of the fire] as well; thus Āpastamba, referring to the *āmikṣā* sacrifice, states: "But the *sviṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* are common. This too should be accepted when one is unable [to perform the full rite], because the word "only" (*eva*) is not heard [in the rule].
Having untied the knots first tied to the *sadas* and *havirdhāna* sheds, he should carry the *havirdhāna* carts northward outside the altar.

Having led the Āhavanīya fire from the southern of the two *havirdhāna* sheds to the outside of the *sadas* and *havirdhāna*—that is, from those *sadas* and *havirdhāna* structures—he releases the knots first tied to the *sadas*, the *havirdhāna*, and the two *havirdhānas*, so that they may not become entangled. By this it is known that the first knots are to be recognized [as such].

If one should untie the first knot, he would not pass urine; through retention [of urine], his life-span would perish. Therefore, because the defect is heard in the Śruti, "He who [unties] the knot of Savitṛ," the untying of the knot is necessary. "Amehena" means by the obstruction of urine. Having drawn it out toward the north—that is, having led it out without causing any obstacle—one burns it upon the altar from the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra, "Whatever debt remains unpaid."

Regarding the statement "he burns the altar" (*vedim upoṣati*), since it is impossible for the altar itself to undergo destruction of its essential form (*svarūpa-nāśa*) when the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) has been spread upon it, the term refers by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to the fire situated thereon. By this, the burning of the sacrificial grass spread on the altar is established, and not of the altar itself. This is because the Brāhmaṇa text—"When he spreads [the grass], and if he were to depart without having burned it"—prescribes the burning specifically of the spread sacrificial grass.
[The wife] [remains] in the *prāgvaṃśa* hall from the *gārhapatya* fire.

From this very Sūtra it is understood that the throwing away of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) at the *udayanīyā* sacrifice does not take place until after the *samiṣṭayajus* oblation. The wife must perform the fasting (*upoṣaṇa*) of the *udayanīyā* sacrificial grass that has not yet been thrown away. The verbal root *upa-vas* (from which *upoṣaṇa* is derived) signifies "burning. The prefix *upa-* indicates proximity or staying near.
With the three verses beginning "I give thee around this common dwelling-place" (*etaṃ sadhastha pari te dadāmi*), he consecrates the rising smoke.
The meaning is that he consecrates the smoke arising from the burning of the sacrificial grass as it rises upward.

With the mantra, "O all-devouring, all-consuming one, I offer thee," he should sacrifice parched barley flour (*saktu*) with his joined palms into a forest fire, if he thinks he has acted as if mixed [with good and evil]. The word *sakta* is conventionally used for parched barley flour; it is always plural in form because it refers to a multitude. Here, [the commentary] says: the parched flour is made from those very same barley grains, because they are intended to be employed in the sacrifice. If he thinks that he has performed the sacrifice as if mixing the right and the wrong, then he should sacrifice ordinary parched barley flour into the forest fire—that is, into a fire set by a hunter.

The Śruti also says: "If one should offer [the oblation] in a forest fire as if it were mixed with the sacrificial call (*codanā*), this very forest fire is indeed Vaiśvānara; he himself makes it palatable. Regarding this, a specific rule has been stated by Āpastamba: "It is said that there are two kinds of *vidhānī*. The meaning of this Āpastamba-sūtra is as follows: for one who desires to know his own good and evil fortune within a year, this rite—which is not connected to a formal sacrifice and follows the sequence of ritual portions—is shown to be applicable to a Brāhmaṇa. The word "Brāhmaṇa" is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence.

And that Brāhmaṇa says: "On the Ekāṣṭakā of the middle of the ten-day period, having baked a cake of four śarāvas, one should approach a thicket with it in the morning; if it burns, there will be great merit; if it does not burn, there will be sin. By means of this very knowledge, the seers of old used to enter upon the long sacrificial session (dīrghasattra). Regarding that, he himself will explain the Ekāṣṭakā in the Gṛhya-sūtra: "We shall explain the Aṣṭakā: the eighth day of the dark fortnight following the full moon of Māgha is what they call the Ekāṣṭakā."

We shall now explain that which is called the *Aṣṭakā*, the permanent collection of ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*). It generally occurs under the asterism Maghā; thus, it is the full moon day of the month of Māgha, meaning the full moon of the month of Māgha. The teachers call the eighth day of the dark fortnight immediately following that [full moon] the *Ekāṣṭakā*. The word *eka* signifies "principal"; thus, it is the principal *Aṣṭakā*. Just as in the term *kapuruṣa*, the "best man" is expressed.

If it is asked, "In relation to what is this preeminence [of the eighth day]? it is said: in relation to all those four eighth days that occur during the four dark fortnights of the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons. For what purpose is this statement? It is for the sake of prescribing the ritual on the day preceding and the day following that [eighth day]. If this were the case, one should simply have said, "on the seventh day, by means of the Anarādhās. If so, then the word *aṣṭakā*—due to its connection with time—is used here to refer to the ritual; and this is for the purpose of making known that this very [eighth day] is the primary element among the *aṣṭakā*s and so forth.

What is the purpose of making this known? [It is] so that, through the common designation (*samākhyā*) and the desire for the *Aṣṭakā* sacrifice, the ritual action may proceed; furthermore, [it serves] to establish its primacy and its fixed nature. [Otherwise, one might think] "the *Dolī* [offering] is on the *Ekāṣṭakā*" or "the purchase [of Soma] is accomplished on the *Ekāṣṭakā*. It is for the sake of ensuring the correct understanding of this [act] that this specific qualification is provided for this very *Ekāṣṭakā*: "on the *Amāvāsyā* (New Moon). For she (the *Amāvāsyā*) indeed ordains and initiates the days of the year.

According to the Śruti, "Those who are about to undergo initiation for the sake of the year-long sacrifice (saṃvatsara) should be initiated on the Ekāṣṭakā day. On that day, having prepared a cake mixed with four handfuls of barley flour and cooked it until it is thoroughly soaked in its own juices, one should set it alight in the forest. If that cake burns brightly, one should know that there will be the greatest merit and auspiciousness; in the opposite case, there will be peace. Thus, in ancient times, the Ṛṣis, having performed this test, would initiate others only when [the omen] was favorable for long-term sessions.

One consigns the fires into separate fire-drills: the *prājihita*, the *gārhapatya*, the *dakṣiṇāgni*, and the *śālāmukhīya*; for one who has attained prosperity (*gataśrī*), there is a third. By the phrase "for one who has attained prosperity, a third," it is understood that this refers specifically to the *āhavanīya* when it is not yet established. By the term "consigns" (*samāropayate*), the consigning into oneself (*ātmasamāropa*) is also intended here, because—as in the statement of Māpastamba—there is no subsequent mention of "taking out the embers" (*nirmadhya*). And do not think otherwise... [End of Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Ninth Book].

Having moved to the east or north and prepared the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), he performs the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice, offering either an *āgneya* cake on eight potsherds or on five potsherds. The meaning is that he performs this *udavasānīyā*, which is the sacrifice of departure (*udavasānā-iṣṭi*). This sacrifice consists of the rites beginning with the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) and ending with the satiating of the Brahmins. The option of eight potsherds belongs to another recension (*śākhā*), while the option of five potsherds belongs to one's own recension. Regarding this, he states a specific rule:
"Everything for it is performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) until the final after-offering (*anūyāja*)."

Regarding that cake on eight potsherds or five potsherds: by the word "all" (*sarvam*), the low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutā*) is prescribed for the entirety of the principal rite together with its accessories, including the *āśrāvaṇa*, *pratyāśrāvaṇa*, *vaṣaṭkāra*, and so forth. The communication to others is by means of a designation (*saṃjñayā*). [The prefix] *ā* [is used] in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*). Therefore, the meaning of the phrase "until the final *anūyāja*" is as follows: from the final *anūyāja* onwards, the accent remains the original (*prākṛta*) one; this is the sense.

Regarding this, Āpastamba mentions a specific distinction: "If it is a cake on five potsherds, the two *saṃyājyā* verses are [those of] Gāyatrī; if it is a cake on eight potsherds, they are [those of] Paṅkti. He has also stated a specific rule for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*): "The fee is an ox, or half an ox, or gold. Āśvalāyana also states the rules for the re-establishment of the fires (*paunarādheyika*): "The rite of re-establishment is an unmodified form. Some authorities prescribe the *pūrṇāhuti* with the mantra "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely" in place of the *udavasānīyā* offering.
Āpastamba says: "Having filled the ladle (*sruva*) with twelve portions of clarified butter, standing between [the fires]..."
As long as it remains during the night, or for however much of the night, at that very time one should offer the evening Agnihotra; the morning oblation is likewise offered at its proper time.

The *iṣṭi* is the *udavasānīyā*. "As long as that night" means for the duration of the night. In this context, the night is of two kinds: long and short. On either of these two nights, one concludes with whatever portion of the night remains. By the word "kiyat" (how much), the lack of a fixed time limit is indicated. "Kiyadrātra" refers to that period of time during which [the sacrifice] remains unfinished. When it is completed, one should then offer the evening *agnihotra*, even though its proper time has passed, because the secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) has not been exceeded. One offers the morning [oblation] at the very same time when the next day arrives.

But at this time, what is the occasion (*prasaṅga*)? There is indeed an occasion. For there is a scriptural injunction (*śruti*) stating that "at the end of the *udavasānīyā* [offering], there is the evening and morning oblation," and because of the opinion of the author of the Sūtras. As Baudhāyana says: "He offers the evening and morning *agnihotra* at every [sacrifice]. The intention of the Sūtra-author, however, is as follows: the scriptural injunction regarding the evening oblation is for the purpose of permitting a secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) for the regular evening oblation when its primary time has passed. The scriptural injunction regarding the morning oblation is likewise a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the morning oblation that occurs by way of incidental connection (*prasaṅgāt*).

Therefore, it is not an injunction for a previously unknown *agnihotra*. For this very reason it has been stated: "At the time [of the morning], the *prātar-homa*. However, some say that these two *agnihotras* conclude with the *soma* sacrifice, because of the subsequent statement: "The *agniṣṭoma* concludes with the *soma*. Likewise, regarding the *udavasānīya*, Kātyāyana says: "At the end of that [sacrifice] is the evening oblation; [the morning oblation] is either permanent or concluded with the *soma* sacrifice, due to proximity and lack of contradiction, according to the Śruti text concerning the morning oblation."

In their view, even if the Agnihotra has not yet commenced, the *daśahotṛ* and other rites must be performed according to the rules of the *daśahotṛ* etc., as long as life lasts; this is because [the time for them] has arrived. Jaimini also stated in the seventh section (pāda) of the sixth chapter: "Because the time for initiation (*dīkṣā*) has been prescribed, when it is exceeded, there is a postponement of the obligatory rites because their time has arrived; or rather, there is an advancement [of the rites], because the reason [for the postponement]—namely, being initiated—is no different [from the reason for their performance]."

The meaning of the first sūtra is as follows: because the time for initiation (*dīkṣā*) remains due to divine providence, and because [the sacrifice] is not yet completed, there is no postponement even when fixed rites are omitted, since their proper time has arrived. The word "or" (*vā*) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The meaning of the second sūtra is: because one is initiated and because the initiation has not been relinquished, there must indeed be a postponement; for the reason is no different from the previous case. In that situation, there is no compensatory oblation (*pratihoma*), just as in the previous cases, and this is also because of the predominance of the time factor.

In this regard, the meaning of the first sūtra is as follows: just as when the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice is postponed due to a divine cause (*daiva*), there is no compensatory offering (*pratihoma*) for the preceding oblations prior to the *avabhṛtha* sacrifice, so too there is no compensatory offering for the subsequent oblations when the *udavasānīyā* is postponed due to a divine cause. This is because time is the primary factor. The meaning of the second sūtra is that since time is the primary factor, one should perform the evening *agnihotra* at whatever point the [sacrifice] is completed—whether it be at night or after some portion of the night; thus, even for this reason, no compensatory offering is prescribed.

Furthermore, Jaimini states: "The prohibition [applies] after the *bhavabhṛtha* and before the *iṣṭi*. This means that there is a prohibition of the *iṣṭi*, which serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*) for the concluding rites. Elsewhere, he says: "If there are *pratihomas*, then the *sāyamagnihotra* and subsequent offerings should be performed; however, the *prātar* [offering] is [performed] on the sixteenth day. Thus, due to a delay caused by either divine or human circumstances, when the *udavasānīyā* is postponed to the following day, the statement regarding the latter applies: the *sāyam* homa must be performed, not the *pūrva* (morning) one.

Because one has no authority to perform the *agnihotra* after the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice [of the *punarādheya*], this meaning is obtained from these two sūtras of Mīmāṃsā. There is also a scriptural statement (*śruti*): "Having performed this [sacrifice] for the sake of the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*), one should offer the *agnihotra*. However, the *sarvaprāyaścitta* (universal expiation) must indeed be offered because of the postponement of the *udavasānīyā*. But in that case, due to the influence of the ritual (*kratu*), there is no expiation, as in the case of the *atirātra*. Regarding this, Bhāradvāja says: "If the *agnihotra* offerings have been omitted at the time of rising, should one offer them again or not?"
The Agniṣṭoma is concluded. || 17 ||

Thus ends the sixth chapter in the ninth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra. The statement, "The Agniṣṭoma is completed," is intended to declare that the two Agnihotra offerings are subsidiary parts of the Soma sacrifice. The meaning is clear. Thus concludes the commentary composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita—who was himself the son of the venerable Āmiṣṭomayājī, Sāhasrāpri, Yuktapājapeyayājī, Sarvatomukhayājī, Dvisāhasrāmiyuktapauṇḍarīkapājī Śrīmad Bhagavat Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin—on the Śrīmad-Bhagavat-Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.

Thus ends the sixth chapter of the commentary named *Jyotsnā*, which pacifies the distress of learned men caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the ocean of the Veda, concerning the ninth book of the *Mānava Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha.
Now begins the seventh chapter of the ninth book.
The *Ukthya*, the *Ṣoḍaśin*, the *Atirātra*, and the *Aptoryāma* are modifications (*guṇavikāra*) of the *Agniṣṭoma*.

Thus, first of all, the Agniṣṭoma—defined by the author of the Sūtras as that which is delimited by the pervading property of being a Jyotiṣṭoma, and which is further delimited by the sub-class property of being an Agniṣṭoma inherent within the Jyotiṣṭoma—is explained as having the Agniṣṭoma *saṃsthā* (concluding form) as its fundamental archetype (*prakṛti*) for the group consisting of the Ahīna and other sacrifices, as indicated by the Sūtrakāra’s use of the term "Agniṣṭoma" in such passages as "one desiring all objects [should perform] the Agniṣṭoma. Now, the other *saṃsthās* are explained.

In this regard, first, what is the arrangement of its constituent parts? One view is that there are three; another view is that there are four. Regarding the state of being three: "If it is an *agniṣṭoma*, he offers the *tāpalikā* oblations; if it is an *ukthya*, he wipes the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*); if it is an *atirātra*, he enters while reciting the *yajus*. Also: "If the *soma* sacrifice beyond [the *agniṣṭoma*] should be an *ukthya*, one should perform the *ukthya*; if it should be an *ukthya*, one should perform the *atirātra*. And: "As much as one attains through the *agniṣṭoma*, so much does one attain; as much as one attains through the *ukthya*..."

It should be understood that "he attains it" means he attains it as long as he does not attain it at the *atirātra*, and so forth. Now, regarding the fourfold [sacrifice], it is said: "Neither the *agniṣṭoma*, nor the *ukthya*, nor the *ṣoḍaśī*, nor the *atirātra* [is attained]. Yet, "they first undertake the *agniṣṭoma*, then the *ukthya*, then the *ṣoḍaśī*, then the *atirātra*. It should be observed that "he did not attain them by the *agniṣṭoma*, he did not attain them by the *ukthya*, he did not attain them by the *ṣoḍaśī*, and he did not attain them by the *atirātra*," and so on. In this regard, some ritualists (*kalpakāra*) have adopted the three-day period (*tritvakāla*).

Regarding this, it has been stated by Lāṭyāyana, Drāhmāyaṇa, and others that the sacrificial terminuses (*saṃsthā*) of the independent Jyotiṣṭoma are the Agniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Atirātra, and so forth; however, other teachers, such as Āśvalāyana and others, have enumerated these four terminuses within the section on the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Thus, while various opinions were floating about, the Teacher demonstrates the fundamental form (*prakṛti-saṃsthā*) according to his own view by means of this sūtra: "The Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśin, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma are modifications (*guṇavikāra*) of the Agniṣṭoma. Āpastamba also holds this same view. In this regard, the intention of the author of the sūtras is as follows: the Agniṣṭoma alone is the original archetype (*maulika-prakṛti*) of all Soma sacrifices. As he will state in the first section of the *Saptadaśasavana*: "The Agniṣṭoma is the archetype of all rituals (*sarvakratu*)."

However, other forms such as the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña* and others are merely modifications of the qualities (*guṇavikāra*) of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices themselves; they are not entirely different rites (*karmāntara*), just as *tri-kaṭuka* and similar substances are not distinct from their base ingredients. For example, the *Agniṣṭoma* is the archetype (*prakṛti*) for the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other *Iṣṭomas*; the *Ukthya* is the archetype for the *Gavām-ayana* and other *Ukthyas*; the *Ṣoḍaśin* is the archetype for the *Vājapeya* and other *Ṣoḍaśins*; and the *Atirātra* is the archetype for the *Viśvajit* and other *Atirātras*.

Regarding the *Aptoryāma*: in the twelfth section of the seventeenth book [it is stated], "One desiring cattle should perform the *Aptoryāma*, because from whomsoever cattle might fall away, for that reason there are eleven animals. Its nature as a *Sava* sacrifice will be explained in the thirteenth section of the thirteenth book within the *Sava* section by this very sūtra: "The *Aptoryāma* has been explained. Thus, its nature as a *Sava* also belongs to this [sacrifice]; here there is merely an extension of the name. And so, those [rites] which have all the *Pṛṣṭhas*...

The *stomas* of the *viśvajit* are indeed [characteristic] of a specific modified (*vaikṛta*) *atirātra* sacrifice named *asoryāman*, belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*). Therefore, those who maintain that there is no *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice by the name *aplāyaryāma* mentioned in the section on the *sava* (as found in Gopīnātha Maṭṭa’s *Jyotsnā* commentary) are refuted. For even this [sacrifice], due to the mention of the *jyotiṣṭoma* as its final form (*saṃsthā*) here and because it falls within the scope of the archetype, certainly possesses the status of being an archetype itself.

Bharadvāja also, having introduced the Jyotiṣṭoma here and stated, "These five are the archetypal forms (prakṛtisaṃsthā): the Agniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśin, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma," concludes at the end by saying, "The Jyotiṣṭoma is completed after covering the tail of the sacrifice. Therefore, there indeed exists the Jyotiṣṭoma in its archetypal form as the Aptoryāma.

Now, one might object: "The teachers Gautama and others teach seven forms (*saṃsthā*) of the Soma sacrifice—namely, Agniṣṭoma, Atyagniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśī, Vājapeya, Atirātra, and Aptoryāma—as the seven forms of the Soma sacrifice. Among these, the latter six are merely modifications (*guṇavikāra*) of the first, the Agniṣṭoma. For what reason, then, are the Atyagniṣṭoma and the Vājapeya not included [in this list]? If this is asked, the answer is no; for the intention here is to enumerate only those forms of the Jyotiṣṭoma that constitute its archetypal (*prakṛti*) structure.

But this does not apply to the mere *saumika* sacrifice or to the mere modification of the quality of the *agniṣṭoma*. In that regard, first of all, the *atyagniṣṭoma* is not the archetype (*prakṛti*) of any sacrifice; nor is the *vājapeya* an archetype, because the *jyotiṣṭoma* is the archetype of the *vājapeya* due to the latter’s possession of the seventeen-fold chant (*saptadaśatva*). Therefore, it is indeed correct that these two are not mentioned [as archetypes]. Thus, it is established that the five-branched *agniṣṭoma*, which is the *jyotiṣṭoma*, is the archetype of all *sāman*-based sacrifices.

Likewise, it should be understood that the Agniṣṭoma is the archetype (*prakṛti*) of all sacrifices; this is the intended meaning. Nor should it be argued that because we shall explain the fire-altar (*agni*) as being for the sake of subsequent sacrifices—since the mantra "sa uttarakratvarya" prescribes its application to subsequent rites—the construction of the *uttaravedi* altar would be established even in the Agniṣṭoma. This is not so, because Āpastamba’s Paribhāṣā-sūtra explicitly states: "In the Agniṣṭoma there is the *uttaravedi*; in subsequent sacrifices, the fire-altar. Furthermore, since the Ukthya and other sacrifices are modifications (*vikāra*) of the Agniṣṭoma, the prohibition of the fire-altar construction applies to the Ukthya and others as well.

Because these [sacrifices] do not have the *agniṣṭoma* as their archetype (*prakṛti*) and because they are subsequent sacrifices (*uttarakratu*), they possess a form modified by specific qualities (*guṇavikṛta*). Nor should it be argued that the *Āpastamba-sūtra* statement, "The *uttaravedi* is not in the *agniṣṭoma*," intends the five *śākhā*-archetypes, while its mention of "in the subsequent sacrifices" intends their modifications (*vikāra*). For otherwise, the exclusion of the *ṣoḍaśin* vessel in the rule "except in the *sādyaskas*, the *vājapeya*, and the *ṣoḍaśin*" would be untenable. Furthermore, one should not argue that the *ṣoḍaśin* should be construed as a qualifier of the *vājapeya* in the phrase "from the *vājapeya* which is a modification of the *ṣoḍaśin*."

It should be qualified by the absence of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because of the statement of the learned: "A qualification is meaningful when there is both possibility and deviation. For there is no *vājapeya* sacrifice that is not a modification of the *ṣoḍaśin*, such that the qualification would be meaningful by way of excluding it. Does this mean, then, that the *uttaravedi* is obtained only in the *ukthya* and other sacrifices? Not so; it is obtained in all modifications (*vikṛti*) by way of option (*vikalpa*).

In the eleventh section of the seventeenth chapter, a restrictive rule is observed: "One who desires honor (apaciti) should perform both Sāmans with the two 'honoring' [verses], using the two wing[-verses] for one who is building the fire-altar (agnicit). Furthermore, Baudhāyana states: "Or rather, one should bring the sacrificial days even for those who do not build the fire-altar. Therefore, it is established that the construction of the fire-altar (agnicityā) indeed occurs optionally even in the Ukthya and other rites. That sacrifice which has its conclusion (saṃsthā) together with the Ukthya rounds (paryāya) is called the *Ukthya*. That which has its conclusion by means of the *Ṣoḍaśin* chant and recitation is called the *Ṣoḍaśin*.

That sacrifice which remains after the night has passed is the *Atirātra*. It has been stated that the *Āptoryāma* status of the *Āptoryāma* [sacrifice] arises from its completion; thus, the etymology of *Āptoryāma* is explained. Alternatively, according to the view of Baudhāyana, because "one causes the Soma to overflow from the Āgrayaṇa vessel," it is called *Āptoryāma* because the overflowing (*āpta*) of the [excess] Soma occurs within this [sacrifice].

This is stated by Baudhāyana: "The gods, while going toward the *aptoryāman*, said, 'This one has been overfilled; what shall we do with it? That is why the *aptoryāman* is called *aptoryāman*. For it, they prepared these *stotras*. The distinction between the regular rites (*nitya-karma*) and the terminuses (*saṃsthā*), as well as the meaning of the word *saṃsthā*, should be seen in my *Saṃskāramālā* and in the introductory section (*upoddhāta-prakaraṇa*) of my work *Itopayogin*.
One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *ukthya*.

Those desires are dependent upon qualities; therefore, they exist only when qualities are present, not when qualities are absent. Gautama, however, [mentions] the following: conception, the rite for a male child, the parting of the hair, birth rites, naming, the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, and initiation—these four [Vedic stages].

The seven forms of domestic sacrifice (*pākayajña-saṃsthā*) are: the *prāyaṇīya*, the union with one’s wife for the sake of bathing, the five great sacrifices (*pañca-mahāyajña*), the *aṣṭakā* rites, the *pārvaṇa* rite, the *śrāddha*, and the [offerings on the full moons of] Śrāvaṇī, Āgrahāyaṇī, Caitrī, and Āśvayujī. The seven forms of oblation sacrifice (*haviryajña-saṃsthā*) are: the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*), the new and full moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the *āgrayaṇeṣṭi*, the *nirūḍhapaśubandha*, and the *sautrāmaṇī*. The seven forms of Soma sacrifice (*somayajña-saṃsthā*) are: the *agniṣṭoma*, the *atyagniṣṭoma*, the *ukthya*, the *ṣoḍaśī*, the *vājapeya*, the *atirātra*, and the *aptoryāma*.

Thus, these forty sacraments (saṃskāras) and eight personal qualities (ātmaguṇas)—compassion toward all beings, tranquility, freedom from envy, purity, lack of fatigue, auspiciousness, lack of miserliness, and absence of anger—are prescribed. Since the scripture declares the fruit [of these] as "he who possesses these forty sacraments and eight personal qualities attains union with Brahman," they are optional (kāmya). Furthermore, since the scripture declares the fault [of their omission] as "he who does not perform those sacraments becomes more sinful," their obligatory nature (nityatva) is also stated. Therefore, these possess both the quality of being optional and the quality of being obligatory. His ritual procedure is explained by that of the Agniṣṭoma.
Regarding that Ukthya sacrifice, he states a specific rule:
"The Sadas has fifteen roofs.
This is a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi).

Having performed the *ṛtukaraṇa* oblation with this very mantra, he wipes away the internal smear on the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) with the mantra: "O Agni, [protect] me in battles... Having offered that oblation known as the *ṛtukaraṇa*, which is to be accomplished by the mantra "O Agni, [protect] me in battles...", he performs it with this very mantra: "O Agni, [protect] me... At the Ukthya sacrifice, he immolates the second *savanīya* animal dedicated to Indra and Agni.

The combination [of the Ukthya] with the Savanīya animal is understood from the second statement. However, the mention of the Ukthya again within the section on the *ukṣan* (bull) is for the purpose of indicating that there is also the alternative view of non-combination (*asamabhyuccaya*). For this very reason, Āpastamba stated: "Some recite it as being like a combination. This is the position of another school (*śālāntarīya*). In our own branch (*sva-śākhā*), however, in the context of the Vājapeya, each ritual conclusion (*saṃsthā*) is shown by means of a single animal. At the third pressing, at the time of the *dhārā-graha*, having drawn the Āgrayaṇa cup, one draws the Ukthya.

Sixth [section]. Seventh Paṭala. Accompanied by the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa. 959. Regarding this, he states a specific rule: "While drawing out the Agniṣṭoma cups, he leaves over the King (Soma) for three sets of cup-groups.
At the time of drawing out the Agniṣṭoma cups, he leaves over—that is, makes surplus—the King (Soma) for the sake of three sets of cup-groups, meaning for the purpose of the three groups of cups.

"Draw up all for the King; do not leave anything deficient. Having wiped the two jars with the ten [fingers], he turns them upside down—thus it is omitted. The word *ca* here has the sense of "and. Now, he formulates a technical rule (paribhāṣā) relevant to this:
regarding the summons (*saṃpraiṣa*) for the Agniṣṭoma cups, whichever is the final group of cups for the concluding rites (*saṃsthāna*), while drawing those up, he issues this summons.

"Having wiped the ten jars with the formula *etatsarvaṃ rājñām unnaya mā'tirīriṣaḥ*, he should set them down face-down. This means that the portion consisting of the call (*praiṣa*) should be uttered there while pouring out each group of *camasa*s (cups) as they are completed—that is, as each group of *camasa*s reaches its conclusion. The repetition "each and every one" (*yo yaḥ*) is used to indicate that this applies to the groups of *camasa*s at the conclusion of all sacrifices. Having performed the ritual with the *agniṣṭoma* cups, they proceed with the three *ukthya* offerings just as before.
By the phrase "as before," the entire ritual procedure pertaining to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) is obtained. Regarding this, he states the specific detail:
with the formula "To Indra and Varuṇa, thee," he modifies the first drawing and placing; with "To Indra and Bṛhaspati, thee," the second; and with "To Indra and Viṣṇu, thee," the third.
This is clear.
One who desires vigor should perform the Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice. "Vigor" means strength.
Its ritual procedure has been explained by that of the Ukthya.

Regarding that *ṣoḍaśin* [sacrifice]: he purchases Soma for it with a female rhinoceros (*śuṇṭhī*) whose ears hang down over her eyes. Since the *ṣoḍaśin* is already established by the general context (*adhikāra*), the explicit mention of "for it" (*tasya*) indicates that such a purchase of Soma applies only to the optional (*kāmya*) view, not to the obligatory (*nitya*) view. From this very indicative mark, its obligatory nature is also understood. "Female rhinoceros" (*śuṇṭhī*) means one of small body, that is, small in stature. "Whose ears hang down over her eyes" (*adhīloṣakarṇā*) means one whose ears hang down (*adhi-upari lambamāna-karṇā*) over the eyes; or alternatively, one whose ears have a different color (*varṇāntara*) above the ear. 1. *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, 4.5.8.10–12. (Note: The commentary reflects the style of Śabara Svāmin or a similar Mīmāṃsā commentator.)
The *sadas* has seventeen roofs.
This is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*).

At the time of arranging the vessels (*pātrasaṃsādana*), one places the four-cornered *ṣoḍaśin* cup made of *khadira* wood on the northern shoulder [of the altar]. According to the principle that "the placement of adventitious items occurs at the end, after the regular arrangement," one places it at the end, in the available space, with the mantra "kastve" (who art thou?). Among those [vessels], whatever materials have not been specified for the modification (*vikṛti*) are not for the purpose of offering (*ahomārtha*). However, by the rule "those of the *vāraṇa* tree are for the purpose of offering," since the *vaikaṅkata* wood would otherwise be obtained, the term "*khadira*" is used to preclude that. The shape of a mortar (*ulūkhala*) is obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*), but that is set aside by the phrase "four-cornered."
Having performed the *ṛtukaraṇa* oblation with this very mantra, he touches either the *droṇakalaśa* or the forehead-band (*rarāṭī*).
This is clear.
At the *ṣoḍaśin* [sacrifice], he immolates the third *savanīya* victim for Indra Vṛṣṇi.

The Vṛṣṇipā [says]: The purpose of taking the Ṣoḍaśin cup is like the purpose of taking the Tanūnapāt cup. One takes the Ṣoḍaśin with one of these [mantras], beginning with "Mount [the chariot], O slayer of Vṛtra.
That is, with any one of these six mantras.
Before the final Ukthya round, in the first two pressings, he draws from the Droṇakalaśa; after having proceeded with all the Ukthya rounds, in the third pressing, he draws from the Āgrayaṇa vessel.

In the two preceding pressings: at the morning pressing and at the midday pressing. The rest is clear. "Than whom none other has been born superior, who has entered into all beings—Prajāpati, in harmony with his progeny, he, the sixteenfold one, attends upon the three lights. He is the Brahman who is timely; known by the name Indra in the assembly, I shall proclaim your two bay steeds at the great sacrifice. I win for you, the eager one, the desirable exhilaration that is timely—he who, like Indra, pours forth the beautiful ghee with his bay steeds."
With the verse, "The troop has been heard; may they enter thee, O thou of golden form, with songs," he consecrates the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at every drawing.
By the phrase "at every drawing," it is meant that there is a consecration for each individual drawing.
While pouring out the cups, of which the cup of the *acchāvāka* is the chief, he pours out the King [Soma] in excess for one group of cups.

The narrative has already been explained. 10.6.70 [Paṭala]: Having performed the rites with those [vessels], he proceeds with the Ṣoḍaśin cup. This is accompanied by the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha. 961.

The singular number in the statement, "He proceeds with the cups having the *acchāvāka*’s cup as their chief," is intended to refer to the *adhvaryu* as the primary agent. The reading in the plural, however, is straightforward. If it is objected: "But then, the grammatical identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) indicated by the suffix *-lyap* in the phrase 'having proceeded with those [cups], he proceeds with the *ṣoḍaśin* cup' would be untenable; for the proceeding with the cups headed by the *acchāvāka*’s cup is performed by the *pratiprasthātṛ*, whereas the proceeding with the *ṣoḍaśin* is performed by the *adhvaryu*. This is true.

Immediately after the phrase "having performed [the rite] with them," the word "standing" (*sthita*) must be supplied in reference to the *pratiprasthātṛ* priest in order to maintain grammatical consistency regarding a common agent. Otherwise, the shared agency would be untenable. According to the view of Baudhāyana, however, in the position that one draws [the cups] at each pressing (*savana*), there are three [cups] for the purpose of drawing at each respective pressing during the first [pressing], while the latter three are optional alternatives to those very same ones. When the sun has half-set, he introduces the *ṣoḍaśin* chant with gold and two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
The meaning is that when the sun, having entered its conjunction (*samaya*), is setting, there is the commencement of the hymn of praise (*stotropa-karaṇa*).
He holds a white horse in front, or one that is reddish-brown, or black.

The word "purastāt" (in front) denotes the proximate region. The word "udgātṛbhyaḥ" (to the Udgātṛs) is the ellipsis [of the recipient]. "Aruṇa" means red in color; "piśaṅga" means the color of yellow pigment (gorocana). The meaning is that it possesses both of these colors. The rule regarding the location for tethering the horse is stated by Lāṭyāyana and Drāhyāyaṇa: "Dhānañjayya says a black horse should stand at the eastern door of the Sadas facing west; Śāṇḍilya says [it should be] at the western [door] facing east."

In every case, when there is an absence of the prescribed horse, the remedy for that has been stated by those two [authorities] as "in its absence, any [animal whatsoever]. This means that in the absence of the specified horse, any [animal] may be used; there is no restriction regarding the species in this instance. However, if there is an absolute absence of the horse itself, then the substitute has been stated by those same two authorities as "either a cow or a bull in the absence of a horse. Here, "cow" refers specifically to a bull because of its similarity to the female gender [of the original term]. Gold is praised as being traditional.

Having received the gold given by the *adhvaryu*, and having passed it from one to another at the time of singing their respective portions, they praise [the deity]; the word "the *udgātṛ*s" is to be supplied by implication. It is also stated by Lāṭyāyana and Drāhyāyaṇa: "Whosoever recites a part of the *sāman* should hold the gold; when they reach the *nidhana*, either the *udgātṛ* alone or all of them should touch it.
The *śastra* contains the word "hari"; the word "becomes" is to be supplied. The meaning is that the *śastra* consists of a collection of words containing the term "hari."
After the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses, he responds with the formula: "Othā moda iva mada-madāmoda ivomatheti," alternating [the response] for each verse.

Those verses in which the singing has been performed by the *udgātṛ*s are called *stotriyas*; the verses following them are called *anurūpas*. Immediately after both these types of verses, he responds with: "Othā moda iva mada-madāmoda ivomatheti. (Note: The variants *yantyaru* (Ja, Sa, Na) and *dāyya* (Ka, Ga, Ca, Dha) are noted in the manuscript readings.)

In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, beginning with the verse "ā svā vahantu harayaḥ" and proceeding through the sequence of final *praṇavas*, there is an alternating pattern: at the conclusion [of each verse], one says "othāmoda iva madaḥ," followed by a *praṇava*; then "modāmoda iyomathā. This sequence continues through the *anuṣṭubh* verses. This established method for the *anuṣṭubh* verses is understood from the Sūtra as the rule for the *pratigara*. Thus, the *pratigara* is established for the *anuṣṭubh* verses.

The *praprava* is a *triṣṭubh*, and beginning with "iṣam" (the *anuṣṭubh*), the well-known response (*pratigara*) is "dhāmoda iva"; the meaning is that the response is "śyāmora. The singular form "response" (*pratigara*) is used with reference to the class [of responses].
Having responded to the *śastra*, he takes up the cup; the *camasādhvaryus* [take up] the goblets. He issues the command: "O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice the Soma! || 19 ||

The statement regarding the weapon (*śastra*) has its purpose already demonstrated; or rather, here too, it serves the purpose of ensuring there is no interruption. Furthermore, the recitation of the *sūtra* here is not something previously seen.

[The priest] offers the *ṣoḍaśin* cup with the mantra: "O Indra, Lord of lords, you are the lord of the gods; make me, the long-lived and radiant one, the lord among men. He offers it at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* with this mantra; the offering at the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ* call is performed silently.

"Indra the sovereign and Varuṇa the king—those two first partook of this portion for you; following their example, I partake. May Speech, being pleased, be satisfied with the Soma. With these words, he partakes of the cup—the cup of the *ṣoḍaśin*. The genitive case in "of the cup" (*grahasya*) is used in the sense of the accusative. The meaning is that he partakes of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, which was previously consumed on account of the *ṣaṭkāra* formula uttered by the Hotṛ, and on account of the pressing and offering. [He partakes] of the cups [along] with the group beginning with Ādityavat.

Regarding the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, [the rule] "Indra and the Sovereign" (*indraśca samrāṭ*) always sets aside the regular consumption. However, the sacrificer and others consume the *camasas* with the very same formulas used for the regular [consumption], beginning with "The earth... (*mahī*). He modifies the consumption formula by saying "of the *anuṣṭubh* metre" (*anuṣṭup chandasaḥ*).

The meaning is that he substitutes the word "of the *anuṣṭubh* metre" in place of "of the *jagatī* metre. For example, it becomes: "O Soma-deity, of the troop accompanied by Āditya, of the third pressing, of the *anuṣṭubh* metre, drunk by Indra"—thus the measure is established.
One who desires spiritual luster should perform the Atirātra sacrifice;
this is clear.
Its ritual procedure is explained by that of the Ṣoḍaśin.
Regarding that Atirātra sacrifice: [This is] the seventh section, accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa.
The *sadas* has twenty-one roofs;
this is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

He does not perform the *kratu-karaṇa* oblation, nor does he touch the *droṇakalaśa* or the *rarāṭī*. Reciting only this sacrificial formula (*yajus*), he enters the two *havirdhāna* sheds. The meaning is that the *kratu-karaṇa* consists of just this much; that is, it consists merely of reciting the formula while entering the *havirdhāna* sheds. The point is that here neither the oblation nor the touching constitutes the prescribed ritual act. Just as there was a combination [of acts] in what was previously stated, here a negation of such a combination is effected by this [text]. At the *atirātra*, he immolates the ewe for Sarasvatī as the fourth *savanīya* victim; according to some, it is a ram.

The ritual procedure (*pracaraṇakalpa*) here belongs to Sarasvatī; according to the Sūtra, "In the [sacrifice] for Indra and in that for Sarasvatī, the ritual procedure is that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices. This means that all *yajus*-precepts apply to the principal offerings, while there is an absence of activity by the Maitrāvaruṇa priest.
While drawing the cups of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, he leaves over the King Soma for thirteen groups of cups.

While drawing the cups for the *ṣoḍaśin*, one combines the three rounds [of the ritual] to form twelve groups of cups; the group related to the *āśvina* is the thirteenth group of cups. Thus, there are thirteen groups of cups, and for their sake, one sets aside the King [Soma], making it an excess (*atirikta*). Regarding the phrase "while drawing the cups for the *ṣoḍaśin*," since this is a restatement as if it were obligatory (*nityavat*) in the preceding sūtra, it shows that the *ṣoḍaśin* is obligatory. If it is asked: "But previously it was stated as being optional (*kāmya*); how can both of these be consistent?"

There is nothing here that is difficult to reconcile, because even that which is obligatory—like the *dadhi-graha* (curd-offering)—is not incompatible with being optional (*kāmya*). However, some scholars have established the optionality of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup in this context due to perceived contradictions and the observation of other scriptural injunctions.
Having performed [the rites] with those, he proceeds with the rounds of the night (*rātri-paryāya*).

If it is objected that the grammatical coreferentiality (*samānakartṛkatva*) in the phrase "having performed [the rite] with those" is untenable—since the performance of the *ṣoḍaśin* offering has the Adhvaryu alone as its agent, whereas the subsequent rounds (*paryāya*) have both priests as their agents—the answer is true. However, since one's own Sūtra states that even for all the rounds the agency belongs exclusively to the Adhvaryu, there is no lack of coreferentiality. Indeed, a lack of coreferentiality would only arise if both priests were the agents;
but because the Sūtra does not prescribe the Pratiprasthātṛ for the latter two rounds, such a lack of coreferentiality does not exist here.
"Thou art taken with a support; for Indra thee, for the passing of the night," [with these words] he draws each principal cup.
The repetition (vīpsā) is for the sake of all the sets of cups. "Having drawn," is the ellipsis, as it follows from the context.
The *stotra* and *śastra* chants take place.
[This is] the sixth [chapter]. And: "Not this contradiction... 1.964. Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra—[Ninth Praśna]:

He draws out the first [vessels], having the Hotṛ’s cup as their chief; the second, having the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup as their chief; the third, having the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s cup as their chief; and the fourth, having the Acchāvāka’s cup as their chief. "The first" means the first group. In the same way, [he draws] the second, third, and fourth groups.
That is the first *rātriparyāya*, a session connected with the night. By the word *paryāya*, the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns are meant.
In this manner, the second and third *rātriparyāyas* are prescribed.
This is the sixth [section].
Having performed those [rites], he proceeds with the rites beginning from the setting out of the vessels for the Āśvina [offering] and offers the two-potsherd cake for the Aśvins.

Here too, because of the impossibility of [the action] having a single agent otherwise, and due to the absence of an explicit statement regarding the Pratiprasthātṛ, the setting out of the Āśvina vessel and so forth belongs to the Adhvaryu alone. The vessels consist of the pair of potsherds, the winnowing basket, the black antelope skin, the mortar and pestle, the lower and upper grinding stones, the bowl, and the stirring-spoon. The formation of pairs is as follows: for the sake of pairing, a blade of grass is placed together with the two potsherds, and the winnowing basket and the black antelope skin form a pair.

The mortar and pestle form a pair; the grinding stone and millstone form a pair; and with the *kuṭaru* (winnowing basket), there is a grass-blade for the sake of forming a pair. The pot-ladle (*mekṣaṇa*) and the vessel form a pair; and with the vessel for the *madantī* water, there is a grass-blade for the sake of forming a pair. Because of the presence of the clarified butter (*ājya*) intended for the Soma, that very butter-pot exists, and that indeed is the clarified butter. Since the purpose consisting of the mixing of the dough exists, the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* waters must certainly be performed.

The vessels for the *prāśitra*, the *iḍā*, the vessel for the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*), the vessel for the flour-smear (*piṣṭalepa*), and the vessel for the husks (*phalīkaraṇa*) do not exist here, because they are incomplete and there is no purpose for them. The pouring out (*nirvāpa*) is accompanied by mantras; at the time of pouring, [one says]: "I pour out what is pleasing to the Aśvins. [One says]: "O Aśvins, protect the offering; I sprinkle you who are pleasing to the Aśvins. The sprinkling of the vessels and so forth follows the *yavāgrayaṇa*. If this is performed after that, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) consists of barley alone.

Because there is no such statement here as "he offers the *bohimya* sacrificial cake," [the procedure is as follows]: at the end of the three-fold husking, having placed the boiling water (*madantī*) on the fire, he sets down two potsherds with the two *āghāra* formulas, up until the pouring out of the water. Having set it down—that *āśvina* sacrificial cake—having placed it on the altar according to the rule for setting down, with the words "O dear seat, sit down, O guest, with a dear name" (using its dear name), because its name consists of two syllables, it is a modification of the *aindrāgna* cake; for this very reason, the pouring of clarified butter over it is done silently.
He draws the *saṃdhicamasas* (junction-cups), of which the *hotṛcamasa* is the first.

They are called *saṃdhicamasas* because they are produced at the junction of day and night; he draws them because they have been drawn [previously], as is evident from their very nature. There are the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns. 20.
The sixth [chapter]. [Ga. and Ca. read *viyudvāsya*]. [This is the Saṃ-paṭala], together with the *Jyotsnā* commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.
The *sandhi-stotra* (junction-stotra) is the *trivṛt-rāthantaram*.

By the word *trivṛt*, the number nine is expressed. In the term *rāthantaram*, the suffix *a* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). The meaning is that the *rathantara* [sāman] should be sung by the Udgātṛ priests nine times.
The *āśvina* recitation (*śastra*).

That whose deity is the Aśvins is called *āśvina*. The meaning is that the Hotṛ recites the *śastra* dedicated to the Aśvin deities. Regarding this, Āpastamba, Āśvalāyana, and others state: "It consists of more than a thousand [verses].
Once the sun has risen and the Hotṛ has concluded the *āśvina* recitation, the Adhvaryu takes up the Hotṛ’s cup (*hotṛcamasa*), and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes up the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

"When the sun has risen, one undertakes the rites dedicated to Sūrya," so says Āśvalāyana. Having donned the garment dedicated to the Aśvins, after the conclusion of the recitation of the *āśvina* śastra, the Adhvaryu takes up the Hotṛ's cup, and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes up the *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to the Aśvins; and here the particle *ca* is used in the sense of "and."

Furthermore, since the Pratiprasthātṛ would otherwise be obtained later through the general injunction for the Pratiprasthātṛ, this specific statement is made to indicate that in each of the three sequences (pakṣa), there is also the agency of the Pratiprasthātṛ in the rites preceding the pouring out, preparation, and placing of the *āśvina* cups—rites which are connected to all three sequences and specifically to the final two groups [of verses] at the commencement of the *stotra* and *śastra*. By this, non-contradiction with the sūtras of Āpastamba, Baudhāyana, and Bharadvāja is established.

In the phrase *paridhāya*, the suffix *ṇic* (causative) must be intended in order to establish a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). Since the Pratiprasthātṛ is prescribed at this very point, it is understood that prior to this, there was no activity on the part of the Pratiprasthātṛ. Consequently, two alternatives are established here:
the Camasādhvaryus take up the cups;

and the respective Camasādhvaryus take up the cups other than the Hotṛ’s cup, because the Adhvaryu is already occupied with the Hotṛ’s cup. His [the Adhvaryu’s] duty regarding the cup ends there. This is understood.
"Recite for the Aśvins the *tiroahniya* Soma-libations; give the command for the *tiroahniya* Soma-libations that have been set forth!"—thus he issues the direction.
They are called *tiroahniya* because they are performed on the day following [the previous one] by means of a hidden connection (*saṃdhi*). And this is an adjective qualifying the Soma.
Together with the Somas, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) as a complete oblation.

The *sarvahuta* is performed in its entirety. Having taken the *juhv* and *upabhṛt* ladles and having returned [to the altar], all [the subsequent rites] proceed as prescribed. The rules regarding not turning back (*aparyāvartana*) and so forth do not apply here, because there is no single-pot offering (*ekakapāla*). Since it is expressly stated in the text, the entire portion is to be offered.
He modifies the *bhakṣa* mantra by saying "of the *paṅkti* meter."

The meaning is that in the mantra, "ādityavadgaṇasya somadevate matividastṛtīyasya savanasya patricchandasa indrapītasya," a modification (*ūha*) of the *saṃnāma* (the collective name) must be performed. [Note: 1ca. reads *tā veti*; 2ca. reads *ṇā gṛhītatvā*]. According to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, one who desires cattle should perform the *aptoryāma* sacrifice;
"cattle" refers to cows, horses, and so forth.
The ritual procedure for that [Aptoryāma] has been explained by means of the Atirātra;
the method and form of that Aptoryāma have been explained and stated.
While drawing the Saṃdhi-cups, he pours out the King [Soma] in excess over four sets of cups.
The *gatāpa* [is performed];
there are four groups of cups (*camasagaṇa*) accompanied by *stotra* and *śastra*, belonging respectively to the Hotṛ, the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and the Acchāvāka.

The statement, "He leaves over the King [Soma] for four groups of cups," establishes the fourfold nature of the groups by that much alone; the mention of "the groups of cups belonging to the Hotṛ, the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and the Acchāvāka" is for the purpose of ensuring the recollection that at the time of the surplus of the King [Soma], there are four groups of cups accompanied by *stotra* and *śastra*—one group for the Hotṛ, a second for the Maitrāvaruṇa, a third for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and a fourth for the Acchāvāka.
This is because there is no other purpose [for this specific enumeration].

The procedure for their performance with the *saṃdhi-camasa*s has been explained. This is the sixth [section]. Here, Āpastamba states a specific rule: "One draws from the Āgneya [cup] the first [series], from the Aindra the second, from the Vaiśvadeva the third, and from the Vaiṣṇava the fourth. These are the qualifiers of the groups of *camasa*s. The sense is that Agni and the others—mentioned in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "they do not reach [the end] because of the *stoma*"—are indeed the deities of each respective group of *camasa*s. Another specific rule is also stated by him: "The procedure for their performance is like that of the *saṃdhi-camasa*s; this is one view."

Alternatively, just like the *saṃdhicamasa*, the *āśvina* cups alone constitute the *stotra* and *śastra* for all [the rounds]. The meaning is that because the subsequent groups are modifications (*vikāra*) of the *saṃdhicamasa*, they follow its pattern. This has been stated by Baudhāyana: "Now they say that all the *stotra* and *śastra* should indeed be *āśvina*; that which exceeds the latter part of the night is the *āśvina*. There is one [verse] consisting of three, fifteen, seventeen, and twenty-one [verses]; their deities are Agni, Indra, the Viśvedevas, and Viṣṇu."

Maradānaśva says: "In that context, four *stotra*s and *śastra*s dedicated to the Aśvins, along with their respective *yājyā*s, are prescribed. Āśvalāyana has also stated that the *śastra*-sūktas for the Aśvins include their *yājyā*s; however, the *stotriya*s and *anurūpa*s are made to be addressed to Agni and others, so that both [the texts of Śāṅkhāyana and Āśvalāyana] may be honored. In this regard, the ritual procedure for the *saṃdhicamasas* is as follows: the two calls (*saṃpraiṣau*) are 'Recite the invitatory verse for the Soma-draughts of the Aśvins' and 'Direct the Hotṛ to recite the offering verse for the Soma-draughts of the Aśvins. It should not be understood as 'for the hidden [Soma-draughts],' because these Soma-draughts are for the sake of the concealment of the *saṃdhi*."
He modifies the *bhakṣa-mantra* (the mantra for consuming) by substituting "Aticchandas" for "Chandas":

"O Soma-deity, belonging to the troop of Adityas, with Aticchandas as the metre, drunk by Indra, of the third pressing, [partake]..."—this is the meaning of the modification (*ūha*) to be made in the mantra. [End of Paṭala 80] Together with the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa:

From the words "O Āgnīdhra, bring the embers for the supplementary offerings (*upayāja*)" onwards, all the rites pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka-karmāṇi*) are performed identically in all sacrificial terminuses (*saṃsthā*), up until the morning *agnihotra*. 21.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the ninth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

The meaning is that the rites connected with the animal sacrifice—beginning with "He should fetch various plants" and ending with the morning Agnihotra—are performed identically in all sacrificial sessions (saṃsthās). This indicates that even the morning Agnihotra is a subordinate part (aṅga) of this [animal sacrifice].

Thus ends the seventh chapter of the ninth book in the commentary named *Jyotsnā*, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—the son of Gaṇeśa Dīk� performer of a thousand Agniṣṭomas, a performer of Vājapeyas, a performer of Sarvatomukhas, and a performer of Pauṇḍarīkas—who was commissioned [by his father]; and which, by extracting the hidden jewels of meaning from the ocean of the venerable Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra, serves to dispel the distress of learned men caused by the darkness [of the original text].
9.8 Now begins the eighth chapter of the ninth book. The animal sacrifices of the *kratuyāgas* and the *ekādaśina* groups are subject to option (*vikalpa*).

Thus, the *Jyotiṣṭoma*s—consisting of the *agniṣṭoma* and other terminuses (*saṃsthā*s)—which serve as the archetype (*prakṛti*) for all *soma* sacrifices, have been explained. Now, the *ekādaśina* groups, which serve as the archetype for all classes of animal sacrifices, are being explained. Because there are eleven animals in each group, they are called *ekādaśina*; those occurring therein are the *ekādaśina* sacrifices.

Which, then, are these? They are those mentioned in the Anuvāka: "The one for Agni is black-necked; the ewe for Sarasvatī; the ram for Soma; the dark one for Pūṣan; the white-backed one for Bṛhaspati; the speckled one for Viśvedevas; the ruddy one for Indra; the spotted one for the Maruts; the one with a white spot on its forehead for Indra-Agni; the one with a white mark on its forehead for Savitṛ; and the castrated goat for Varuṇa. As for the animal sacrifices belonging to the *kratuyajñas*, they have already been described previously in connection with their respective ritual forms (*saṃsthās*). Both of these [types of animals] are taught separately in the various recensions (*śākhās*) within the *prakṛti* (archetypal sacrifice) itself, because they serve the same purpose and function as subsidiaries.

In their combination, the constituent parts of the tantra become manifest; they cease to be manifest as individual items, yet they recur with each ritual preparation for the sake of the perceptible purpose.

When there is a combination of these eleven [animals] in a simultaneous performance (*sahaprayoga*), those auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) which are not directly perceived (*adṛṣṭa*) and which are capable of benefiting all [the animals] by being performed once become *tantra*; they are performed only once, such as the *prayāja* offerings and others which provide remote assistance (*ārādupakāraka*). However, those that are perceptible (*pratyakṣārtha*), meaning those whose purpose or utility is directly observed, and which effect a visible benefit, are repeated (*āvartante*), because a *tantra* arrangement is impossible for them.

For example, having performed the *upākaraṇa* for all [animals], one dedicates (*niyunakti*) them all, and thereafter sprinkles (*prokṣati*) them all; thus, since the sprinkling can have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), its performance as a single ritual act (*tantra*) is established. Furthermore, it is logically settled that whatever is the order of the animals, that very same order applies to the *upākaraṇa*, the dedication, and so forth. This has been clearly stated by Āpastamba: "The consecrations are according to the injunction" (*yathācodita-saṃskārāḥ*).
There is modification (*ūha*) according to the specific object.

Since it is a general rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "in a modification (*vikṛti*), there is modification of the text according to the actual requirement," one might fear that this would preclude modification in the archetype (*prakṛti*); therefore, the repetition of the term "modification" is used. Consequently, [the formulas] such as "Come with the cattle," "Converse with the cattle," and "May the cattle not abandon me" are indeed modified.
Having offered the *yūpāhuti* (sacrifice to the sacrificial post), he cuts eleven sacrificial posts, beginning with the central one (*agniṣṭha*), as well as the *upaśaya* and the *pātnīvata*.

Because of the explicit mention of the *yūpāhuti`, it is offered even for the initiated sacrificer (*dīkṣita*), despite the prohibition regarding the *yūpāhuti`. And that offering is performed only once, because it is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakārin*), thus applying to the *upaśaya* post as well.
There is an option regarding the single sacrificial post (*ekayūpa*).

This single post is optionally substituted for the group of eleven posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*) by virtue of its commonality with both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). Regarding the domain of the consecrations of the post, Bhāradvāja states: "For all [posts], there is the bringing of the chips (*śakala*), the cutting (*avaścana*), and the oblation (*homa*). It has been stated that one cuts the *upaśaya* (the leaning post) and the *pātnīvata* (the post for the wives of the gods). In that context, the rites for the purpose of cutting—such as "he takes the remainder of the clarified butter (*ājyaśeṣa*) and the *sruva*-ladle," and so forth, including those ending with the cutting, such as "he recites 'atyanyān agām' (*I have surpassed others')"—are to be repeated for each individual post.

According to the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*), "they appear" means they become manifest, and "they disappear" means they return to their original state through re-construction; thus, the measuring and the carving apply to each individual piece. The removal of the first chip applies to all [pieces], because it is for the purpose of the pit (*avaṭa*); since there is no pit for the *upaśaya* (the spare piece), its offering is performed in place of that [chip] everywhere. This is clearly stated by Āpastamba: "The offering of the chips includes the removal and the cutting."

Since the purpose of the *śakala* (wood chip) is for the subsequent consecration (*saṃskāra*), there is no *śakala* for the *upaśaya* (the spare post), because the *upaśaya* is not placed in the pit. Thus, it is established by implication that the entire [post] is to be planed and nothing is to be left over for the sake of the *upaśaya*; this was not explicitly stated by the author of the Sūtra. Āpastamba has stated this clearly: "He planes the entire *upaśaya*. As for the meaning of the word *upaśaya*: it lies (*śete*) near (*upa*) its respective sacrificial post; it is not placed in the pit. One cuts the *pātnīvata* post in exactly the same manner.

It indeed has another [measurement]. Because it will be stated later that "below the navel," one cuts a piece of that size reaching down to the navel. And because it will be stated later that "without a *caṣāla*," it is devoid of a *caṣāla*.
Having measured a rope that is ten *ratha-akṣas* long and eleven spans wide, one measures out the altar with a twenty-fourth part of that rope; it serves as the place for the *prakrama* steps.

At the time of measuring the altar (vedi), one takes a cord of one hundred and four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and multiplies it ten times; then, one adds an eleventh cord to it. That length of cord over which the eleven base-ends (upamūla) will be situated is the eleventh cord. These [measures] are optional. [End of Section] Accompanied by the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

The *daśarathākṣa* (the axle of ten chariots) consists of eleven *uparamitā*s; the twenty-fourth part of that is composed of forty-nine *alā*s minus five *tilas*. With a staff of that measure, one should construct the altar (*vedi*)—this is the meaning. This cord, measured by twenty-four parts, serves as the equivalent of a *prakrama* (step). The meaning here is that this very cord constitutes the *prakrama*, and not the "two-footed" or "one-footed" *prakrama* mentioned in the *Śulbasūtra*.
Having girt the central post (*agniṣṭha*) with two ropes, he girds the eleven-fold set of ropes (*ekādaśinīraśanā*) upon the central post and leaves them there.

Having measured the post that stands near the fire (the *agniṣṭha*), he binds it all around simultaneously with two cords. In this case, there is a dual modification (*dvivacana-vikāra*) regarding the taking up of the cords. The formula "thou art the encircler" (*parivārasī*) is not recited, because it refers specifically to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Then, having bound and wrapped the remaining ten cords—namely, one cord for the animal sacrifice (*ekapaśinī*), the cord related to the eleven [cords] (*ekādaśinī*), and the cords for the eleven [animals] (*ekādaśinīraśanā*)—around the *agniṣṭha* post, he causes them to be blown upon.

The remaining eleven ropes remain wrapped on that very day until such time as their application occurs, specifically at the post standing nearest the fire (agniṣṭha). On the following day, having drawn the Āśvina cup, he erects the sacrificial posts.
This is understood.
Some authorities prescribe the preparation on the preceding day.

This means that some teachers say one should have [the sacrificial post] set up together with the *agniṣṭha* [post] on the previous day. In this view, one does not wrap the cord around the *agniṣṭha* post; rather, the posts remain already encircled. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction regarding the non-abandonment of the posts, since the measurement for the wrapping—which begins from the bottom—is not yet completed.
The taking up of the spade is common to both days, but the act of tracing around [the ground] is repeated.

This statement is intended to demonstrate the very principle already stated—that those things which do not manifest [in their proper order] are repeated. The rule for tracing [the lines] is repeated. This statement is intended to demonstrate the principle that those things which do manifest as perceptible objects are not repeated. Regarding the specific sequence in the tracing, he says: "Having traced the southern one starting from the *agniṣṭhā* (corner post), he traces the northern one; thus, by alternating, he completes them ending toward the north."

This specific order of sequence is intended to set aside the rule of "ending toward the north" (*udagapavarga*) which would otherwise apply by the general technical definition (*paribhāṣā*). [The procedure is as follows: Having marked out the southern sacrificial post-hole (*yūpāvaṭa*), he marks out the northern sacrificial post-hole. Then, from the southern post-hole, he marks out the one to its south; then, from the northern post-hole, he marks out the one to its north; then again to the south of that, and then again to the north of that.

In this manner, he marks out as many sacrificial post-holes as there may be—up to ten—with five to the south and five to the north. The mention of "ending toward the north" (*udagapavarga*) means that having performed the work for the southern [hole], he performs it for the northern one so that they conclude toward the north; the sense is that he does not conclude toward the south merely because that was the starting point. The intervals between the sacrificial posts are equal to the axle of a chariot. *Śatapatha Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha (Ninth Book).

The axle is one hundred and four *aṅgulas* long; according to the *Śulbasūtra*, "the transverse axle is four hundred [aṅgulas]. Four hundred means four more than one hundred, that is, four hundred. Thus, the axle becomes one hundred and four *aṅgulas* in length.
Or, he measures it as equal to the altar (*vedi*).

"The altar is as large as [the space] twenty-four [steps] across from east to west. This means that on an altar established according to the standard dimensions, one traces eleven sacrificial post-holes (*yūpāvaṭa*). However, one does not [trace them] with a cord of ten *ratha-akṣa* [units]; rather, having taken a cord of eleven *upara* [units], one measures out the altar by a twenty-fourth part of that [cord]. The divisions [of the altar] take the place of the *prakrama* [step]. Such is the description of the measurement of the altar; on it, the injunction is that one traces eleven sacrificial post-holes. One performs each [action] in sequence with its corresponding class [of objects]; one completes each [item] entirely, beginning from the anointing up to the removal of the double-strand rope (*dviraśana*).

An action prescribed by a single injunction is of one kind; that is, a single instance of an action is of the same class as another instance being performed because they share the same purpose and connection, and not because it is that very same individual instance. For it is not possible for what was performed in a previous instance to be accomplished later [if it were the same]. Therefore, since there is a difference between individual instances (*vyakti*), the genus (*jāti*) must necessarily be denoted. Its manifestation, however, consists merely in its being prescribed by that particular injunction.

Among the ritual objects (*padārtha*) that are to be prepared, one proceeds by following each individual object in sequence with a single action of the same class (*sajātīya*), and immediately thereafter, likewise, with an action of a different class (*vijātīya*). To "proceed" (*sameti*) means to perform (*sananāti*). This specific order is designated as the "sequential arrangement of ritual objects" (*padārthānusamaya*). In this regard, the action of measurement (*parilekhana*) is performed for each individual object in the very same order as the digging of the pit (*avaṭakhanana*), the washing of the sacrificial post (*yūpaprakṣālana*), and the sprinkling (*mokṣaṇa*), and so forth.

Then, for each [deity] individually, he performs the rites beginning with the pouring out of the remainder of the sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇī*) and ending with the *śakalābhihoma*. This is because, since they serve the purpose of consecrating the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), they constitute a single ritual act. He performs the entire collection of rites, from the *ājyāvekṣaṇa* (gazing at the clarified butter) up to the *pariṇayana* (carrying around), according to the method of *kāṇḍānusamaya* (grouping by sections). With the intention that there is no contradiction regarding the intermediate release (*utsarga*) and based on the explicit statement of the sacrificer, he describes this *kāṇḍānusamaya* by means of the sūtra beginning with "the whole for each" and ending with "he concludes."

He describes the procedure up to the point where it says, "From the beginning of the anointing and the beginning of the yoke-halter, he winds two halters each around [the post]," ending with the rule for the *sthaviman* (the uppermost part). "Apavarga" means completion; the meaning is that it leads to its conclusion. And the Mīmāṃsakas say: "But because of the scriptural statement, the actions beginning with the anointing (*añjana*) continue until the winding of the halter (*parivyayaṇa*). In that case, since there is no burying of the *upaśaya* (the auxiliary post), the purificatory rites for the pit (*avaṭa-saṃskāra*) are omitted. However, all the rites for the *pātnīvata* post will take place later on. There is one *svaru* (wooden chip) for each sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is the motivator for the *svaru* (wooden chip), but not for the anointing of the animal; therefore, they do not exist for each individual animal—this is the sense. Regarding the sons of heaven, the taking up of the *svarus* that have been placed near is done by way of a common procedure (*tantra*); they measure them out according to the rule: "They are of equal size. However, the grasping of the intermediate space is done with a span (*aratni*), and there is no separation of the posts because of the *upaśaya* (the spare post). [From the commentary of Gopīnātha, titled Jyotsnā: One should fix the post level with the top for one who desires the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*).

That in which the girdles (*raśanā*) alone are equal and the upper parts [of the sacrificial posts] are equal is called "equal with the upper part" (*sopara-samita*); this means for one desiring the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*). That which is measured by the girdle and measured equally in the middle is for one desiring the world of men (*manuṣyaloka*). That in which the girdles alone are equal and the middle sections of the sacrificial posts are also equal—this is called "equal with the middle" (*madhya-samita*), and it is said that one who desires the world of men should choose this. In this world of men, the maternal uncle and others are considered equal. Thus, one who desires the world of men is so designated.
One that is equal to the *caṣāla* for one who desires sensory power.

That among which the *caṣāla*s are equal is for one who desires sensory power; "sensory power" (*indriya*) refers to the sharpness of the senses, and one who desires that is called "one who desires sensory power.
One that is equal in all respects is for one who desires a firm foundation.

The phrase "minuyāt" (one should measure) is to be supplied everywhere as a remainder. Regarding the expression "uparāṇām" (of the upper ones), it is to be understood that [the measurement] applies to the upper parts of the waters. From this [context], the intermediate measurement and the measurement by the *raśanā* (girdle) follow; that is, the horizontal measurement of the intermediate parts and of the *raśanās* is also derived from this. As for the measurement by the *caṣāla* (cupola), that refers to the equality of the width of the *caṣāla*.
