To this effect, the authoritative *sūtra* will be stated later, beginning with "uparāṇi āyāmataḥ" (the upper parts by length) and ending with "prathinnāścaṣālāni" (and the *caṣālas* by breadth).

Those three middle [posts] he should interlace for one desiring cattle; thus he interlaces him with offspring and cattle. He should make those three middle posts equal for one desiring cattle; he should interlace the others around the middle ones. Those others which are separated by one [post] from the middle ones do not become equal, but rather they remain unequal. By this interlacing, he makes the sacrificer specially interlaced, exceeded, and prosperous with offspring and cattle—this is the meaning.
On both sides, starting from the center, they are separated by one [post] each; they are not equal, but rather alternate—this is what Āpastamba says.
For one whom he desires, "May he be liable to die," he should set up his posts as if in a pit: the northernmost one should be the tallest, and the others shorter.
This refers to the post of that sacrificer whom he desires to be "pramāyuka"—that is, one prone to sudden death.

One should measure the extent of the eleven sacrificial posts (*ekādaśinī*) by means of a pit (*garta*). He describes the nature of the pit-measurement with the words: "The northernmost is the tallest, and then the others are shorter. This is a technical term. That which exists in the northern half is "northernmost" (*uttarārdhya*); that which is "tallest" (*varṣiṣṭha*) is the largest. The word "atha" indicates sequence: after the northernmost has been made the tallest, the others are to be made progressively shorter.
One should set up the southernmost as the tallest for one who desires heaven, and then the others as shorter and shorter.

In this context, "tallest" (*varṣiṣṭha*) refers to height. Because of the hearing of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) in the expression "shorter and shorter" (*hasīyaso hasīyasaḥ*), it is made known that for the others there is a progressive shortening by some degree; whereas since there is no such repetition heard in the preceding case, there is no progressive shortening, but rather an equal shortness. For one practicing sorcery against an enemy, among those [stakes], the one at the Agni-sthāna is the tallest, and the others are successively shorter and shorter.

The nature of the *ārāma* (altar-stones) is stated by this sūtra: "Among them, the one in the center is the largest (*varṣiṣṭha*), and the others are progressively smaller (*hasīyasaḥ*). Here too, the term *varṣiṣṭha* refers to size. Because of the repetition [of the comparative suffix] as before, the others are each slightly smaller than the preceding one. Āpastamba clearly states the nature of the *ārāmas*: "The middle one is elevated, while the two ends are gradually lower."

The one at the place of the fire (agniṣṭha) is high; from that point on, they gradually become lower in sequence toward the ends on the south and the north. This is the meaning of the term *ārāgrā*: it is so called because its middle part is like the end (*āgra*) of a spoke (*āra*). By the word *āra*, height is expressed. For one who desires rain, [the altar] should be even-flowing; among those [altars], the one at the place of the fire should be the shortest, and the others should be progressively longer and longer.

Among those sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), the one at the end (*aniṣṭha*) is the shortest; the others are longer than it, each subsequent one being longer than the preceding. By means of this repetition (*vīpsā*), "longer and longer," it is indicated that each post other than the final one is successively longer. The word *atha* (then) signifies sequence: after the final post has been made shorter, the others are made longer in successive order. "Properly causing to flow down" (*samyag-avasrāvaṇam*) refers to [rain] from a high place, from the sky, flowing down as if into a depression on the earth—that is, upon which the rain flows down evenly. Rain is the act of raining (*varṣaṇam*).
One who has rivals should interlace the short and the long in reverse order.

"Interlacing the short and the long" means that they should be joined with each one separated by an interval; this is the meaning. Āpastamba states this matter clearly: "For one who has rivals, [the stakes] are interlaced on both sides starting from the *agniṣṭha* stake, with each one separated by an interval; thereby they become equal, while the others are unequal—this is the interlacing.
If he should desire, "May the peasantry be more powerful than the nobility," he should erect those to the south of the *agniṣṭha* stake as progressively taller and taller.

If the sacrificer should desire, "May the Vaiśya class be more powerful than the Kṣatra class," then the Adhvaryu should erect those sacrificial posts which are to the south of the *agniṣṭha* post, making them progressively taller and taller in successive order. If he should desire, "May the Kṣatra be more powerful than the Viś," then he should erect those which are to the north of the *agniṣṭha* post, making them progressively taller and taller. || 22 ||

If the sacrificer should desire that the *kṣatra*—the power of the Kṣatriya caste—be more powerful and stronger than the Vaiśya caste, then he should erect those posts which are to the north of the *aniṣṭhā* (the last post) in a progressively increasing order, making each subsequent one taller than the preceding; this is the meaning. Among the remaining [posts], there is a decrease in height. [End of Paṭala 80] This is accompanied by the commentary named Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa. The upper parts should be equal in length, the middle parts and the girdles (*raśanā*) should be equal in width, and the *caṣāla* ornaments should be equal in breadth.

The upper parts are equal in length; the middle sections and the girdles are equal in their horizontal dimensions; and the *caṣāla* rings are equal in breadth and thickness. This sūtra applies to these [measures]: "One should measure [the post] level with the top," "level with the girdle," "level with the middle," and "level with the *caṣāla*. Having encircled the *upaśaya* (the spare post) with two girdles, one should place it in front of the southernmost sacrificial post.

One should place the *upashaya* (the lying-post) in front of the southern sacrificial post (*dakṣiṇāya-yūpa*), which is situated in the southern half and turned toward the south. Or, according to Āpastamba, one may place it to the south [of the post].

If one intends to practice sorcery (*abhicara*), one should place the *upashaya* facing eastward with the formula: "Here I lay down so-and-so, the son of such-and-such, with the thunderbolt of Indra."

In this *abhicāra* rite, the placement [of the fire] is indeed directed toward the east; however, it is not by way of a permanent rule (*nityatā*), because the author of the Sūtra has prescribed its eastern orientation only for this specific context. Therefore, the eastern orientation mentioned in the *Āpastamba-sūtra* does not apply as a permanent rule for the placement [of the fire]. In the expression "this one" (*amum*), there is the inclusion of the conventional name ending in the singular accusative case. And that [name] refers to the *śarman* of a Brāhmaṇa, according to the *Vasiṣṭha-sūtra*: "That by which one is addressed. By the term "āyuṣyāyaṇam," there is the indication of the name employed for the body.

As in the *Vāsiṣṭha* [sūtra]: "By which one it is distinguished" (*vyavayita*)—thus, according to the *Vāsiṣ�ṭha-sūtra*, the application of the conventional name [is restricted] to this very context and not to other names.

At the time for the animals, he dedicates to Agni a black-headed animal at the *agniṣṭha* post; to Sarasvatī, a ewe to the north; to Soma, a brown one to the south. In this manner, by way of transposition, [he dedicates] those on the southern side: to Pūṣan, a dark-grey animal with a white back; to Bṛhaspati, a variegated one; to the Viśvedevas, a reddish-brown one; to Indra, a ruddy one; to the Maruts, a speckled one; to Indra-Agni, a composite one; to Dhūr, a pale-red one; to Savitṛ, a white one; and lastly, to Varuṇa, a ram.

One whose head is black is *asitaśīrṣa*. By the word *ava* (or *āva*), the face is also indicated. *Meṣī* is well-known [as a female sheep]. *Babhru* is tawny. *Nābha* is entirely black. *Śinipṛṣṭha* means having a dog-like back. *Śilpa* is salt-colored. *Aruṇa* is reddish. *Kalmāṣa* is a color other than black, marked with black spots. *Saṃhita* is a color mixed with other colors. *Adhorāma* is one whose belly region is black. *Petva* is a ram from which the male organ has been removed.

At the southernmost post, near the Agni post, he dedicates the animal for Agni, which has a black head; at the northern post, a ewe for Sarasvatī; at the southern post, a brown one for Soma; at the post to its north, a dark-grey one for Pūṣan; and at the southern post, a white-backed one for Bṛhaspati.

120.974. According to the *Satyāṣāḍha-vicitra-praśna-sūtra*, [the procedure for the ninth chapter]: To the northern sacrificial post, one dedicates a Vaiśvadeva animal of variegated color; to the southern post, an Aindra animal of ruddy color; to the northern post, a Māruta animal with black knees; to the southern post, an Aindrāgna animal that is well-knit; to the northern post, a Sāvitra animal of a tawny hue; and to the southern post, a Pārṣṇa animal that is castrated. Having thus alternated them in this manner, he dedicates these animals, ending with those on the southern side.

Having thus offered each subsequent animal, while performing the dedication of each southern one, he also dedicates the other animals beginning with those for Pūṣan. In that regard, since the completion [of the rite] is established through the sequence of transposition, the repetition [of the rule regarding] ending toward the south is for the purpose of ensuring such completion even in cases where there is a set of eleven animals at a single sacrificial post (*ekayūpa*). There is no restriction regarding the orientation toward the east or other directions at the time of dedicating these animals.

Since its status as the last is established by implication alone, the explicit mention of "last" is for the purpose of ensuring that even when there is an exchange of positions—as prescribed by the rule, "If one desires, 'May he who has attained [prosperity] be ousted, and may he who is ousted attain it,' let him sacrifice a Vāruṇa animal in the place of the Aindra, and an Aindra in the place of the Vāruṇa"—it is the Vāruṇa alone that remains the last. Thus, he who had attained prosperity is ousted, and he who was ousted attains it.

If the patron (yajamāna) should desire that he who is known as his enemy—having been excluded and having obtained a kingdom—be excluded and fall from his sovereignty; and that he who has been excluded by him be understood [as the one] to obtain sovereignty, then in such a rite performed by that patron, the Adhvaryu should sacrifice a Varuṇa animal in the place or station of Indra, and sacrifice an Indra animal in the place of the Varuṇa animal. This is the result for him who is known [as the enemy].

He who is excluded is excluded; he who is excluded understands [this]. This has already been explained by the statement regarding desire: "If he should desire, 'May the subjects become confused,' he should intermingle the animals"; thus, he indeed causes the subjects to become confused.

"If the sacrificer should desire, 'May the subjects be bewildered; may the subjects fall into confusion,' then he should perform the animals with each one separated by an interval. This is called the *vyatipaṅga* (interchange). For example: having brought forward the victim for Agni at the *agniṣṭha* post, he brings forward the victim for Soma at the northern post; then the ewe for Sarasvatī at the southern post, the victim for Bṛhaspati at the northern post, the victim for Pūṣan at the southern post, the victim for Indra at the northern post, the victim for Viśve Devās at the southern post, the victim for Indra-Agni at the northern post, the victim for the Maruts at the southern post, and the victim for Varuṇa at the northern post, and finally the victim for Savitṛ at the southern post."

This is the interlocking (*vyatiṣaṅga*) of the animals. In this ritual form, there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the rule "the spotted ram for Varuṇa is the last"; or rather, here there is merely an interlocking of positions. Regarding the view that the animals themselves should be dedicated (*upākaraṇīya*) in their proper sequence, there is a sublation of the rule "ending toward the south. He states the result of this with the words, "He thus deludes the progeny. For if one, when struck down, were to sacrifice a [ram] for Varuṇa among the waters, Varuṇa would seize his progeny; he sacrifices facing north from the south, so that he is not struck down.

If he desires wealth, the word *apām* (of waters) is in the genitive case used in the sense of the accusative. "In front" (*samukham*) means near, specifically near his own house. Thus, [from Paṭala 810], according to the commentary by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa: if a sacrificer should desire that those who have gone in various directions might come back to him, he should sacrifice a victim to Varuṇa facing eastward; for at that time Varuṇa would seize his offspring. Because of the scriptural mention of the fault, "Varuṇa would seize his offspring," he should instead dedicate it facing westward.
To this extent, this fault does not apply to one who has offered [the animal]. He sacrifices from the south toward the north;

or rather, he points out another wild animal, such as a mouse, as a substitute, saying, "This is your animal. He should point out whichever animal he hates; if he does not hate anyone, he should say, "A mouse is your animal."

One should point out a wild animal, such as a gavaya or a mouse, as being "the animal," by means of the cognition of its being an animal, saying: "This animal of yours has been laid low; this is your animal. Alternatively, one may point out whoever one hates as being the animal, saying: "So-and-so is your animal. If one does not hate anyone, and there is no one to be hated, then one should say: "The mouse is your animal."

But for one who hates even though he is constantly being hated, there is no hatred [in return]; for him, the designation is simply "beast" (*paśu*), and it is not optionally considered as any one of the *gavaya* or other such animals. When there is merely hatred and he himself is not being hated, then the former rule alone applies. When he is being hated and he is also hating, then the rule is optional. Even when that [hatred] exists, if he is not being hated, then the same rule applies. For all [animals], there are sacrificial grasses (*barhis*), omentum-spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*), pots (*kumbhī*), heart-spits (*hṛdayaśūla*), and *plakṣa* branches.

The plural number in *bahir* and other terms is used with reference to the collection of animals; the meaning is that the *barhis* and so forth are provided for each individual animal according to the rule. The carrying forward of the fire (*agniharaṇa*) is common (*tantra*); likewise, the *adhigu* formula, the first *prayāja*, the final *parivapya*, the *saṃjñaptahoma*, the discarding of the ropes (*raśanā*), the second *parivapya*, the throwing into the fire of the omentum-spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*), the *abhihoma*, the *mārjana*, and the granting of the boon (*varadāna*). || 23 ||

These days belong to all the animals by way of a single performance (*tantra*). According to the principle that "the subsidiary (*guṇa*) is repeated for each primary (*pradhāna*)," [the ritual] recurs when there is a difference in substance (*dravyabheda*), as in the case of taking the clarified butter (*ājyagrahaṇa*), cutting the grass (*lavana*), and spreading the strew (*staraṇa*). This is because the taking of the clarified butter and so forth apply here as well due to the difference in substance among the various animals. Since it would follow that acts such as the bringing forward (*abhiharaṇa*) would have to be repeated for each animal, their performance is prescribed collectively in these [days].

In this regard, the sequence of ritual actions is as follows: having bathed all the animals, he takes two *vīpī* (grass-bands) while repeating the mantra "For you, O seeker (*iṣe tvā*)," and [takes] a branch of *kṣa* wood with "You are the upper garment (*upavīra asi*). He dedicates the black-headed animal to Agni with "I dedicate you, who are dear to Agni," and leads it near the *āgnīdhra* fire. He places the two prepared *bahiṣpavamāna* grass-bands down. Then, with "For you, O seeker (*punariṣe tvā*)," and so forth, and "I dedicate you, who are dear to Sarasvatī," and so forth, he dedicates the ewe to the northern post of the *amiṣṭha* [animal].

Having placed two well-known outer grass-bunches [on the altar], he dedicates the animal for Soma at the southern sacrificial post with the formula beginning "For food, thee! and ending "I dedicate [thee] to Soma, svāhā. Having placed two well-known outer grass-bunches, he dedicates the animal for Indra-Agni at the northern post with the formula beginning "For food, thee! and so on; the verse "The waters have come...
and "May it not be hated by those who hate us" is required here.

With the formula, "I dedicate thee, acceptable to Pūṣan," he dedicates a dark-colored animal for Pūṣan at the northern post of the central (agniṣṭha) stake; having set aside two recognized blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he repeats the formula beginning with "For food, thee" and, with "I dedicate thee, acceptable to Bṛhaspati," he dedicates a white-backed animal for Bṛhaspati at the southern post of the central stake.

Having placed the two recognized outer skins aside, he again [recites] "For food, thee," and so forth, and at the northern post of the one standing nearest the fire, he dedicates the Vaiśvadeva animal with the formula: "I dedicate thee, acceptable to the Viśve Devas. Having placed the two recognized outer skins aside, he again [recites] "For food, thee," and so forth, and at the southern corner of the one standing nearest the fire, he dedicates the Aindra animal with the formula: "I dedicate thee, acceptable to Indra," and so forth. Having placed the two recognized outer skins aside, he again [recites] "For food, thee," and so forth, [dedicating] to the Maruts... acceptable to thee.

Saying "I dedicate," he dedicates the spotted animal for the Maruts to the north of the post standing nearest the fire (*agniṣṭha*). Having placed two known blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) down, and saying again "For food, svāhā," and so forth, "I dedicate you, acceptable to Indra and Agni," he dedicates the combined animal for Indra and Agni to the south of the *agniṣṭha* post. Having placed two known blades of sacrificial grass down, and saying again "For food, nay," and so forth, "I dedicate you, acceptable to Savitṛ," and so on, he dedicates the downward-facing animal for Savitṛ to the north of the *agniṣṭha* post.

Having placed [the animal] on the *bahiṣī* mat while it is being recognized, he again performs the ritual act of dedication (*upākaraṇa*) for the one standing near the fire (*agniṣṭha*), beginning with "For food, thee! and ending with "I dedicate you, acceptable to Varuṇa," specifically the ram belonging to Varuṇa (*petva vāruṇa*) to the south. Then, once the animals have been dedicated, having made the designation of wild animals or the designation of the person who is to be hated as the sacrificial victim at the *upaśa* post, and having performed the dedication, he offers five oblations. According to the rule stating that "the procedures (*tantra*) and the mantras apply to this offering," the offering is performed by way of a single common procedure (*tantreṇa*).

In that context, because there is a plurality of animals, the modification (*ūha*) of the words denoting the animals into the plural form occurs everywhere: *suvarga yāta*, *pratitiṣṭhata*, *niṣkrītā ime*, *yan su*, *vadhyamānān*, *upākṛtāñchaśamānānyad*, and *apiyannu pāthaḥ*. Some authorities maintain that this modification applies even to the word "living" (*jīva*). Then follows the churning; it is performed as a common ritual procedure (*tantra*) for all, according to the Sūtra stating "the procedures are shared when possible," since the fact that [the churning] serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) is established through direct perception.

The sequence beginning with the taking up of the rope with the *sāvitra* formula and ending with the tethering (*niyojana*) is performed for each animal individually. This is because of the sūtra stating, "Those acts whose purpose is directly perceptible are repeated for each individual object. However, according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "those acts joined together form a single unit," and the sūtra stating that one completes the entire set for each [animal], there is a *kāṇḍānumeya* (section-by-section) performance. The tethering of the animal to the south of the sacrificial post follows the previously mentioned order. One performs the rites beginning with the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and ending with the upward sprinkling (*upokṣaṇa*) beneath the post for each animal in succession.

Because they all share the common purpose (*prayojana*) of making [the animal] pure (*medhya*), they possess the quality of being conjoined (*saṃyuktatva*). Due to this conjunction, the status of "object" (*karmatva*) belongs specifically to the ritual items (*padārtha*) beginning with the sprinkling from below and ending with the *upokṣaṇa*. This is established by the sūtras: "One should complete each one in its entirety" (*kṛtsnamekaikamapavarjayati*) and "But those that are conjoined have a single completion" (*saṃyuktāni tv ekāpavargāṇi*). Regarding the mantra for the omentum (*vapā*), there is a modification (*ūha*): "May he enjoy this" (*svadatainām*). Having poured the clarified butter from the ladle (*sruc*) and having stepped back, one performs the rites for all [the animals] in sequence, starting with "This is your breath" (*se te prāṇa*) and ending with "The lord of the sacrifice has attained his blessing" (*saṃ yajñapatirāśiṣā*). This is because the ritual item consisting of the act of generating [the fire] (*ajanarūpapadārtha*) is singular.

Therefore, the ten *prayāja* offerings—beginning with the *dhruvā*, the *samit*, and the *añjana*—constitute a single performance (*tantra*). This is because of the sūtra stating, "The subsidiaries (*aṅgāni*) are capable of being performed as a *tantra*. Nor should it be argued that these do not form a *tantra* because the final *prayāja* is specifically prescribed as a *tantra*; for since the final *prayāja* serves to consecrate the substance already prepared in the form of the *vapā* (omentum) and is thus proximate to the main act, it would directly benefit the sacrifice, and there might arise a doubt that it must be repeated every year. To prevent this, the statement [of the sūtra] is necessary.

However, because the other *prayājas* lack direct auxiliary status—due to their being *saṃskārakas* (purificatory acts) of substances in the form of omentum (*vapā*) and due to the absence of immediate proximity—their repetition is not established; therefore, the Teacher did not compose a sūtra for their arrangement. Immediately after the ten *prayāja* offerings, one first anoints the *svaru* with the *juhū* and then the *svadhiti*, and then performs for the *āgneya* animal sacrifice the rites beginning with the anointing of the head and ending with the anointing of the tail. The *svadhiti* is indeed only one.

Furthermore, its repeated application of collyrium is because it was previously employed for the first animal when the clarified butter had not been prepared. In this manner, having performed the respective procedures such as the anointing of the head and so forth for all the animals, he performs for each one individually in sequence, beginning with the anointing of the head and ending with the anointing of the buttocks.

At the conclusion of handing over the knife to the *śamitṛ*, he hands the *svaru* to the *śamitṛ* for insertion into its respective place in due order; he inserts the *svaru* into its proper position, because the manual for animal sacrifice (*paśusūtra*) prescribes the insertion of the *svaru* immediately after handing over the knife to the *śamitṛ*. Until the completion of the insertion, the *svarus*, being clearly identified in their sequence, should remain placed right there.

The carrying of fire around [the sacrificial objects] (*paryagnikaraṇa*) is performed once for all (*tantra*), as it is possible to do so according to the rule that "that which is capable of being common is performed as a *tantra*. The injunction (*praiṣa*) is modified as follows: "Recite for those for whom the fire is being carried around" (*paryagnimpaḥ kriyamāṇebhyo 'nubrūhi*). As for the claim made by some that the fire being carried around is not denoted by the word "fire" (*agni*) and thus the modification is invalid—that is incorrect; for in such expressions as "he performs the *paryagni*" or "having performed the *paryagni*," the neuter gender would otherwise be untenable.

[Objection: But even for you, in the case of the *paryagni* rite being performed on the animal, there would be an inconsistency regarding the masculine gender in the scriptural injunction, "he offers [the oblation] when the *paryagni* is being performed," because it should then read, "when the *paryagni* is being performed on [it]. [Response: This fault does not exist. In that context, since the animal is the substantive (*viśeṣya*), there is no contradiction with the masculine gender. Therefore, the modification (*ūha*) is indeed appropriate: "The *paryagni* rite is performed with the fuel-stick taken up once for this such-and-such animal. In that regard, the *paryagni* rite is repeated for each animal, according to the sūtra: "The separation of the two [fires] is repeated."

In that context, regarding the *apāvya* oblation for animals distinguished by the numbers one, six, and eleven during the first *paryagnikaraṇa*: the first *apāvya* oblation is performed at the first [turn], the second *apāvya* oblation at the sixth, and the third *apāvya* oblation at the eleventh. This is because of the use of the present participle in the phrase "while the *paryagni* is being performed. Therein, for the animals that have been dedicated (*upākṛta*) and are being pacified (*śamāna*), the modification (*ūha*) is as before: "May they go to the path of the gods while still alive."

Having released the animals one by one and having consecrated them, the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* (response) is given, followed by the *upapreṣa*: "O Hotṛ, announce the oblations to the gods. This call is made only once. According to the Sūtra, "The ritual procedure (*tantra*) is performed for all," the touching of the animals outside [the altar] with the mantra, "O wealthy ones, enter the beloved abode of the Lord of the Sacrifice," is done for each animal individually because it is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the animal. As for the view held by some that the touching should be performed only for the primary animal, that is incorrect.

Furthermore, because it contradicts the sūtra stating "the ritual procedure (tantra) is not extended," and because the commencement [of the rite] by means of the *āśrāpaṇī* and *plakṣa* branches for each individual animal is established by the very nature of the purpose; for the commencement of one animal with the *āśrāpaṇī* and *plakṣa* branches intended for another animal cannot serve the purpose of the consecration (*saṃskāra*). By this, the view that the simultaneous commencement (*samit*) is possible through a single ritual procedure (*tantra*) for as many animals as possible is also refuted. This is because the invitation of the sacrificers (*yanamānānimantraṇa*) is extended through a single ritual procedure, according to the sūtra: "The ritual procedure is not extended."

In this context, the distinction in the mantra is that "the sacrificer [performs] the sacrifice with various breaths through the animals. Regarding the carrying of the fire, it is a *tantra* (common/shared) action because of the sūtra stating "the carrying of the fire is for Agni. Furthermore, since this fire has the purpose of cooking and thus serves a perceptible end, it is not separate; therefore, according to the sūtra "it is repeated," although one might expect it to be performed for each individual animal (*pratipaśu*), the statement "the carrying of the fire is a *tantra*" establishes its commonality.

The point is that when the single fire is carried forward, because the visible purpose—namely, the act of cooking—is more powerful, the invisible fruit consisting of the destruction of obstructive spirits (*rakṣas*) is also accomplished. There is no restrictive rule (*niyama*) that one must follow [the fire] for as long as it is being carried to the *śāmitra* location, because there is no such statement.

Regarding the leading forth of the animals, Baudhāyana states the favor [of the ritual procedure]: "Just as [the Adhvaryu] holds onto the *pāśrapaṇī* (slaughter-stick) belonging to the Āgneya animal, the other assistants lead the others separately toward the north, one after another, without letting them touch each other. The holding onto [the stick] occurs individually for each; it is not performed by the *śamitṛ* (the slaughterer) or by the assistants collectively. The *adhrigu* formula is recited as a single unit (*tantra*). Although this rule would have been established by the principle that "when the substances are separate, the action is repeated," this statement is made nonetheless.

In this regard, the ritual procedure following the *Yājuṣa-hautra* is as follows: "O divine immolators (*śamitāraḥ*), [drive] the victims toward the lords of the sacrifice (*medhapatibhyaḥ*) and the sacrifices (*medhebhyaḥ*). Let the mother [Earth] receive them with favor. Drive them northward. Let the Earth receive their bodies whole. O 978. 7 | . 0 [This is from] the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the ninth book]: Let their skins be stripped so that they are not torn, nor even the sinews, nor the flesh; let the butcher move the knife between the ribs."

"Make their chests like hawks, their shoulders like *praśas* [sacrificial knives], their flanks like *chalāda* [a kind of animal], and their haunches like those of the *kaśyapa*. Let their thighs be flawless, their knees like those of the *kava*, and their ankles like those of the *nekaparṇa*. Let there be sixty ribs for them; let each limb be measured accordingly. Their smallest parts are not to be omitted; let these animals be offered with the *upaśaya*. 'The navel is the measure, the fat is the oblation'—these are the portions not to be carried forward," so says Āśvalāyana, as well as "before the *purastāt*" and "one [portion] also."

He himself, as the primary officiant, leads the animals to the slaughterer; for the Vājasaneyi-śruti states that he leads them to the slaughterer by leading each one in turn, seizing it by the neck. To the north of the *pātvāla* (the pit) is the place of the slaughterer (*śāmitra-deśa*). Having placed the *golmuka* (the firebrand) there, he places the various limbs of the animal—whether in a forward direction (*prāksaṃstha*) or a transverse direction (*udaṅsaṃstha*)—after they have been prepared. The instructions for the slaughter (*saṃjñapana-praiṣa*) apply collectively, according to the rule that "the common elements (*tantra*) are shared. [The formula is: "O you who are not deceiving, make them ready; let them be slaughtered; let them lie down; let them be quiet!"

There is no modification (*anūha*) of the word *śakya* because it qualifies the action. According to the Sūtra, "The *tantra* [mantras] are used for those who are not dependent on the sacrificer," they are recited as follows: "O you who know the self, having known the self, go to the heavenly world; O you who know the worlds, having known the worlds, go to the world; O you who know the way, having known the way, go to the path; O you who know the refuge, having known the refuge, go to the protection. Neither shall you be hidden, nor shall you be harmed. May the evil-doers fall there into your portion."

The invitation to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings for the wives is as before. The inspection of the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) is performed once for all (*tantra*), because there is only one portion of speckled butter, whereas this [other offering] is a consecration of the speckled butter itself. The invitation for the occasional performance (*naimittika-karaṇa*) is also performed once for all, according to the sūtra: "They extend the *tantra* to those who are capable. The modification (*ūha*) is: "He who hates us—do not delight in him; O sinless ones..."

The qualification "prior" (pūrva) is used because the final fore-offering (*uttama-prayāja*) occurs before the prior *parivapya* oblation; thus, there is a mention of the final fore-offering first, followed by a mention of the prior *parivapya* oblation immediately thereafter.

This group of four, which follows in sequence, is prescribed out of order immediately after the *saṃjñapta-homa* and before the *raśanodāsana*, the *uttama-prayāja*, and the *pūrvapariṣyahoma*, in accordance with the sequence of the ritual actions. This is for the purpose of demonstrating that the first item must be performed in proximity [to its related elements]: namely, that the *agniharaṇa*, the *adhigupraiṣa*, and the *uttama-prayāja* are to be taken together, as is the *pūrvapariṣya*. Thus, they occur by being taken up together, beginning with the *agniharaṇa*, the *adhigupraiṣa*, and the *uttama-prayāja*.

Alternatively, the construction is as follows: since the word *tathā* is seen later on, it is established that the word *yathā* in the preceding passage must be supplied as having the sense of an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). And that [supply] applies only to the first two items, not even to the *tattama-prayāja*. This is because the priority of the *prayāja* over the primary sacrifice is well-known according to all schools of thought.

The word *agrimatayā* (by way of being foremost) connects with both [sides] according to the maxim of the lamp at the entrance (*dehalīdīpanyāya*). The meaning is: "Just as that is the best among these two items, so too is the first *parivapya* oblation. Alternatively, this word is supplied (*adhyāhāra*) only for the proximate item: "Just as that is the best *prayāja*, so too is the first *parivapya* oblation. At the end, the two actions are presented in reverse order to demonstrate that they must be performed: the *saṃjñapta-homa* and the action of depositing the cords upon the *cātvāla* pit after their removal.

In these two cases, there is the grasping of the *karma* (the ritual action). According to the principle that "the repetition of subordinate elements occurs for each primary act (*pradhāna*)—such as the pouring out of the omentum (*vapā*), its offering, the throwing into the fire (*anupraharaṇa*), the *srāva* libation, and the *mārjana* and granting of the boon (*varadāna*)"—and according to the *Pariśiṣṭa-sūtra* stating that "it repeats when there is a plurality of substances," this *sūtra* is introduced when [the action] is reached at the end of each respective *haviryajña*. "O you two, make us free from fear... "...the faults. [Notes: 1. *ga*: *paṇatvā*; 2. *ka*: *vitiṣa*; 3. *ka*, *ga*: *caṃya*; 4. [blank].

[With the words: "O Spiṭa, [be gracious]; O Gopīnātha, [be gracious]; O Madva, [be gracious]; O Jyotis, [be gracious]. Having offered these two expiations (*prāyaścitta*) according to other Sūtras, they should be understood here as being illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*). "O Saprajñādhyakṛt, be gracious"—this expiation is for the occasion of unintentional ignorance (*akāma-saṃjñāna*).

Death resulting from the consciousness of being unwilling [to die] is self-evident. Having fled, [the sacrificer] says, "Be gracious. There is a repetition of the mantra for raising up one who has sat down. In the *saṃjñaptahoma* mantra, there is a modification (*ūha*) regarding the two animals: "Whatever lowing the two animals have made, or whatever they have bent with their feet... [The sacrificer says: "O preparers (*śamitāraḥ*), approach! Release the animals from the nooses. 'I make the enemy subject; upon him whom we hate, I fasten the nooses.'"

Having passed that cord through each respective single-pronged pin, their placement in the *cātvāla* pit is performed by a common procedure (*tantra*). From the sūtra, "They serve a common purpose for the immolation," the bringing of the full vessels and the subsequent rites up to the cleansing are performed by a common procedure. From the sūtra, "The rites that serve a common purpose are repeated for each animal," the act of swelling [the vessels] with the formula, "May speech swell," is repeated for each animal. From the sūtra, "The rites that do not serve a common purpose are repeated for each individual," the pouring out of the remnants is performed by a common procedure. From the sūtra, "They serve a common purpose for the immolation," the rites beginning with the placing of grass between [the animal and the ground] and ending with the cutting of the omentum are repeated for each individual animal.

"O herb, protect her"—this is the modification for the ewe. The cutting out of the omentum is dedicated to the deities. I cut out [the omentum] acceptable to Agni; thee, acceptable to Sarasvatī; thee, acceptable to Soma; thee, acceptable to Pūṣan; thee, acceptable to Bṛhaspati; thee, acceptable to the Viśve Devas; thee, acceptable to Indra; thee, acceptable to the Maruts; thee, acceptable to Indra and Agni; thee, acceptable to Savitṛ; thee, acceptable to Varuṇa.

Or rather, for all [the fires], [the term] "uncut" applies. Having made all the non-living parts into hands and having smeared all the solid parts with blood, and having set them down in their known places, he discards them simultaneously at the end. Regarding that, there is a *tantra* (common procedure) for the urine, as it is said, "The funeral pyres (*amaśānī*) are capable of being performed there. For the cooking of the non-living parts, there is heating separately by division. The carrying of the firebrand (*ulmuka*) is a *tantra* just as before, because of the statement, "The carrying of the firebrand is a *tantra*."

In the view that there is a division [of the fires], having brought about the unification of all the fires, the bringing of that firebrand (*ulmuka*) is performed by means of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*), for the reason shown immediately below. Regarding the mantra "The wide atmosphere, O Agnihotra," some say [it applies here], but that is refuted in the case of the bringing of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the *savanīya* offering. The re-grasping [of the fires] is as before; the taking back [of the fires] is by means of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*) alone, according to the sūtra: "The *tantra* is divided because of the fear of injury. The casting away of the firebrand (*ulmuka*) is also by means of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*) alone, for the reason shown immediately below.

The seizing of the omenta and the first offering of them: the Pratiprasthātṛ cooks them together. Then, the placing of each respective omentum is beneath the *agra* (fore-offering). The *abhihoma* (libation over) is performed with the *staraṇa* (spreading). This is because it is enumerated among the rites to be accomplished for this [sacrifice]. In the *prāduṣkaraṇas*, the *stokasaṃpraisha* (direction regarding the drops) is common (*tantra*). The placing of the cooked meat is also common. [The formula is: "O you who are the selves among the animals, having indeed become consecrated by Soma, go to the gods; being well-bound, [go] for the sake of the sacrificer, do not harm me. Or rather, there is no modification (*anūha*).

The setting aside (*udvāsanam*) is also performed by means of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). He places each [omentum] upon a branch of the *plakṣa* tree on the southern shoulder of the altar (*vedibhāga*), with the formula "Be firm" (*dṛhata gā*). The placement and the mantra differ according to the different branches. The procedure for the insertion of the omentum-spits (*vapāśrapaṇī-pravṛṇam*) recurs; for the Sūtra states, "If they do not suffice, they are repeated. The portion belonging to the sacrificer (*yājamānam*) is as follows: "May these [spits] be fit for the senses... may we obtain the gods through these... may the cooked [omenta] also be roasted. "This [Agni] is the Hotṛ..."—this is the touching of the omentum-covering (*vapāvarmātyabhimarśaḥ*).

Having performed the rites from the *bhūgādāna* up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings according to the archetype (*prakṛti*), he sprinkles [the clarified butter] twice over [the oblation] in due order with the remainder of the *prayāja*. At the time of the performance, having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, and when the response has been given, he offers the fat of the omentum of the goat to Agni with the formula: "To the gods, svāhā! To the first-drinkers! In this very place, there is the first *parivapya-homa*.

Likewise, according to the sūtra *tathā pūrvaḥ parivapya*, [the call is] "Prompt for the fat of the ewe for Sarasvatī. In the view that the five animal sacrifices (*pañcapaśu*) are the archetype (*prakṛti*), the procedure for the performance (*pracaraṇakalpa*) in the sacrifice to Indra, the sacrifice to Sarasvatī, and their modifications follows the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśaparṇamāsika*); thus, all [the calls] are exactly as previously stated. There is no activity of the Maitrāvaruṇa priest regarding the principal oblations (*pradhānahavis*). In the view that they are modifications of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, it is like the archetype. In this view, [the calls are] as follows: ...

From the sūtra beginning with "The *pomiya* [is used] for its modifications; the *prastara* is of *ācivāla* grass, the two *vidhṛtis* are of sugarcane," and ending with "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for such-and-such a portion of such-and-such an oblation," these characteristics of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice are obtained for all animals in the *palala* [offering]. [With the formula: "By the sacrifice to the goddess Sarasvatī, may I nourish speech and food. [For Soma: "To Chāga..."

Through the sacrifice to the god Soma, may I become powerful. To Pūṣan, [I offer] the portion... Through the sacrifice to the god Pūṣan, may I become prosperous and possessed of cattle. To Bṛhaspati, [I offer] the portion... Through the sacrifice to the god Bṛhaspati, may I become powerful. To the All-gods, [I offer] the portion... Through the sacrifice to the All-gods, may I be endowed with vital breaths. To Indra, [I offer] the portion... Here, in the New and Full Moon sacrifices, there is an option for the ritual procedure; in the other case, that of the offering to Agni-Soma: through the sacrifice to the god Indra, may I become powerful.

*Maruñcaśchā*—for the Maruts, I offer the goat (*chāga*). *Indriyānī bhū*—for Indra and Agni, I offer the goat. *Mendrigāvī*—for Savitṛ, [recited] in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). [Then] aloud: *Chāga*—in all cases, [the word] "Savitṛ" is recited in a low voice, according to the *Cāturmāsya-sūtra*. Regarding other words denoting deities as well, Āśvalāyana has stated that they are to be recited in a low voice: "The words *ādadhat*, *saṃjuṣat*, *karat*, *agrama*, and *ud* belong to the deities."

This procedure will become clear in the ritual application (*prayoga*) of Maitrāvaruṇa. [The formulas are: "May I be endowed with the power of the god Savitṛ... and "Of the ram...". Here follows the *uttaraparivapya-homa* (the offering of the subsequent scrapings): "May I be endowed with the power of the god Varuṇa... The throwing of the omentum (*vapā*) and the fat (*vasā*) is performed with the *tastra*. The *jaha* (the formula for the drops) is: "O drops, go to the Maruts. There is also the pouring of the remnants (*saṃsrāvaṇa*). The sprinkling (*mārjana*) takes place at the *cāvāla* pit according to the *tantra* rule. For it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *tantra* applies to those that are capable of being shared."

Then follows the performance of the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) offerings. There is the pouring out (nirvāpa) of the cakes for the deities beginning with Agni and ending with Vāstoṣpati. All these animal-cakes consist of rice and are prepared on either eleven or twelve potsherds (kapāla). Their placing upon the potsherds is according to the specific rules of their respective modifications. Among them, the cake for Agni is performed according to the archetype (prakṛti). Since the cakes for Sarasvatī, Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, Mitra, and Varuṇa are also modifications of the cake for Agni, their placing upon the potsherds is performed according to the rules of the eight-potsherd cake of Agni.

The [procedures] for the *saumya* and *vaiśvadeva* offerings are like those for the *agnīṣomīya*. Those for the *aindra*, *māruta*, and *indrāgna* offerings are like those for the *āgneya*. [The Adhvaryu says: "O slaughterer, supervise the entrails; do not let them fall into the fire; bring the kidneys, the peritoneum, and the fats together. Then, for the purpose of cooking the animal, the placing of the firewood on the hearth (*tantra-dhṛyādāna*) is performed in sequence, followed by the placing of the pots (*kumbha-adhiśrayaṇa*), the adding of fuel (*parīndhana*), and the pouring of the contents (*āvapana*), all in sequence. Next, the consecratory formulas (*anumantraṇa*) for the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) sacrifices are recited in sequence: "Eater of food" (1); "May I nourish speech with the eating of food" (2).

"Vṛtrahā (the slayer of Vṛtra) is possessed of prosperity, possessed of cattle, and an eater of food; may I attain union with the vital breaths. Indriyāvin (possessed of sensory power), eater of food; Indriyāvin, eater of food; Indriyāvin, eater of food; eater of food, eater of food. These are the consecratory formulas (anumantraṇas) in sequence. "O animal, converse!"—this is the call used for the conversation. Having taken one five-fold portioned ladle (pañcagṛhīta) in the Juhū, and having taken the Pṛṣadājya (spotted butter) and the cooked oblation (śṛtahavīḥ)... [End of Adhyāya Paṭala]. Accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

There is no modification (*anūha*) [in the formula]. Since Āśvalāyana stated that there is no modification regarding the word "oblation" (*havis*) in the passage, "The navel is the measure; the fat is the oblation," and because of the statement in the *Āpastamba-sūtra* located in the section on the *Anūbandhyā* sacrifice—"He modifies [the formula] up to the end of the word 'oblation' (*haviṣaḥ*)"—[it follows that the modification applies only to that specific term].

Having extracted the first heart from its own *hṛdaya-śūla* and placed it in the first *kumbhī*, he sprinkles it with *pṛṣadājya* while reciting "saṃ te manasā manaḥ. Having sprinkled the animal (*paśu*) with this, he follows the rising steam with the formula "svāhoṣmaṇo'vyathiṣyāḥ. He then sprinkles the animal that has entered the *kumbhī* with the formula "yasta ātmā. Then, having returned, he again takes five portions of *pṛṣadājya* as before and proceeds toward the fire silently; there is no recitation of the *saṃvāda*.

Some, however, say that others bring forward the fivefold-grasped clarified butter and the speckled butter. As before, for the heart, there is the extraction from the heart-spit and so forth, ending with the pouring over [the offering] with the formula "He who is the self. In this manner, having lifted up each pot for the third and subsequent animals, he places each one in its respective branch of the *plakṣa* tree in sequence by means of the *pañcahotṛ* formula. In the mantra "Make firm the cows, make firm," there is no modification (*ūha*), but rather repetition alone, according to the Sūtra: "They do not divide; they repeat."

In the mantra "He who is the self," there is a modification (*ūha*). These immortal senses are three; with these, the animals offered themselves to Indra. By them, the gods [were satisfied]; may they be established in me as cooked offerings. This sacrifice is the protector and the Hotṛ. Regarding these two, when they both occur here, there is either a common procedure (*tantra*), non-separation (*avibhava*), or repetition (*āvṛtti*).
For each of them, the *manotā* verse is repeated.

For each individual animal victim, one repeats the procedure beginning with "He spreads [the butter] under [the ladles]" for the *juhū*, the *upabhṛt*, the *vasāhomahavanī*, and the *samavattadhānī*, up until the end of the sacrifice; this is because of the sūtra rule: "If one is unable [to complete all at once], one repeats. Since the rule "or the *manotā*" would otherwise necessitate the mandatory repetition of the *manotā* hymn as well, he states an option regarding that *manotā* hymn.

Alternatively, the connection with the Sūtra is as follows: the Sūtra is composed for the purpose of providing an option regarding the *manotā* mantra, stating that "at the time of the cutting (*avadāna*) of each respective animal, the *manotā* is repeated. The requirements for the *muhūpamṛta*, the *sāhomahavanī*, the *samavatta-dhānī*, the *upastaraṇa*, and so forth, are established by their own inherent purpose. As for the *manotā*, its repetition at the time of the cutting is established by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the text: "of the oblation being cut. Consequently, because it is separated from the time of the actual sacrifice (*ijyā*), there is a repetition for each animal; thus, the recurrence is established by the very nature of the matter.

And it has been stated clearly by Āpastamba in the Paribhāṣā-sūtra: "The repetition of the *manotā* [verse] occurs when there is a difference in time. Here, the sense is that repetition takes place due to the difference in the present time. However, the alternative of non-repetition has also been mentioned by Āpastamba with the words "or rather, not so. Thus, since both positions are desired by the author of the Sūtra, he has formulated the rule accordingly. If it is asked how simultaneity is maintained in that [repetitive] position, the answer is: it is true.

The *manotā* mantra belongs to the Agni-related [sacrifice]; however, at the time of the cutting of the portions (*avadāna*) from other animals, it is not capable of effecting the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the deity of another oblation. It is only at the very same time as the cutting of the portions from the Agni-related animal that it is capable of effecting the consecration of the deity of the Agni-related oblation, because there is a single deity. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, for all [the animals], the three parts (*tryaṅga*) and the collected portion (*samavatta*) are [to be offered].

This Sūtra is intended to convey that the cutting of the limbs for the sake of the *viṣṭakṛt* offering occurs only after the principal portions have been offered, and not during the sacrifice itself. There is the placing of gold dust in the *upabhṛt* ladle and the final sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*). However, for the portion intended for the deities, it occurs immediately after each respective part. Regarding the term *samavatta*, the cutting of the *iḍā* also takes place at that very time; the final sprinkling, however, occurs at the end. For each individual part, one proceeds in sequence until the end of the *jyā*. At the half-verse of each respective [verse], he offers the *vasāhoma* (fat-oblation). [From] the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [the ninth book].

One should place the remaining portion in another vessel for the sake of the *dig-homa* (oblation to the quarters); for it has been demonstrated by the author of the Sūtras themselves in the very Sūtra stating that "because the *dig-yāga* serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), the ritual procedures (*tantra*) do not vary. Āpastamba has stated this clearly: "Having poured out the remainder, one performs the sacrifice toward the quarters. Having combined the deposited remnants into one, the *dig-homa* is performed as a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). The pouring out of the remainder is solely for the sake of establishing the unity of the *dig-homa* procedure; otherwise, it would result in its being rendered useless.

By the statement, "The portions of all [the limbs] and the *samavatta*," it is already implied by the sense that the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice occurs at the end of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*). Since the sacrifice to Vanaspati is a modification of the *sviṣṭakṛt*, it is also almost evident by implication that its sacrifice likewise takes place in the vicinity of the *sviṣṭakṛt*. Āpastamba has stated this explicitly: "At the final animal sacrifice, [he offers] to Vanaspati and the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
He performs the *upayaja* offerings with the entrails of all [the animals].

The intention is that the statement "of all" (*sarveṣām*) is for the purpose of establishing [the rule], in order to dispel the doubt that the *upayāja* might be performed with the omentum of the first animal alone—since it is the first to be present because the others have not yet been offered—and thus [the rule] would apply only to that one. For each individual offering, there is indeed independence [of the mantra]. In all the mantras, the modification (*ūha*) is: "Go to the ocean, svāhā! In the *svaru*-offering, the modification is: "O you who are born from the wood... In the case of the *anūbandhyā* cow, there is no *svaru*-offering to Agni.
And they perform the *saṃyājana* of the wives with the tails (*jāghanī*).
The intention is that this is for the purpose of disposal (*pratipatti*).

When the omentum of the Anūbandhyā cow has been offered, one should measure out the sacrificial post for the Pātnīvata animal in front of the Śālāmukhīya fire—measuring it below the navel, without a top-ring, and with two ropes—and having consecrated it, one dedicates to Tvaṣṭṛ a bull that is hornless, hairy, tawny, and multicolored. Having released it after the fire has been carried around it, one should complete the remainder of the rite with clarified butter.

When the omentum of the animal to be immolated has been offered and the principal sacrifice of the *āmikṣā* has been performed, the ritual for this animal begins. That which has Tvaṣṭṛ as its deity is called *tvāṣṭṛ*. By the statement, "He cuts the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) for the Pātnīvata," it is shown that the deity here is qualified by the attribute "having wives" (*patnīvat*). That which has the deity Patnīvant is the *pātnīvata*.

To demonstrate that even when applied as a qualifier, this designation (*saṃjñā*) functions with respect to this very sacrificial post (*yūpa*), both types of this designation are employed in the revealed scripture (*śruti*): "The sacrifice becomes desirable through the omentum (*vapā*), undesirable through the *vaśā*; then he proceeds with the *pālīvata*. He proceeds at a proper ford; thus this [animal] of his becomes for the gods the one belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ. And: "He releases the *pātnīvata* which has been set aside," and so forth. By the phrase "in front of the *śālāmukhīya*," it is indicated that its performance (*pracāra*) takes place precisely at the *śālāmukhīya*. This is clearly stated.

"It is known that they proceed with the *māpastamna* and the *śālāmukhīya* fires. Thus it is stated that, as in the case of the *codayanīya*, the entire ritual procedure (*tantra*) takes place in the eastern sacrificial enclosure (*prāgvaṃśika-vihāra*). Here, because the fire has been carried forth (*vihṛta*), the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) and other such items are omitted as their purpose is already served. However, the altar (*vedi*) is prepared according to the *dāśika* (sacrificial) rite. Furthermore, those original (*prākṛta*) consecrations intended for the *anūbandhyā* sacrifice are also performed, such as the spreading of grass around the *prājahita* fire, the pouring of clarified butter, the spreading of the *uparājya*, and so forth. As for the measurement of the *naivāra* [grain], it is as much as...

[Ma-paṭalaḥ] Together with the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa. "He measures it out" means he measures it to a limited extent. Since the status of being a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) entails the requirement of a top-ring (*caṣāla*), the explicit statement "without a top-ring" (*acaṣālam*) is made. Because this animal sacrifice is a subordinate part of the *ekādaśinī* (the set of eleven animals), two ropes would not otherwise be required for its sacrificial post; this statement is intended to ensure that two ropes are provided. Having measured it according to the rule beginning with "Having measured it... whatever craft the carpenter has employed," and having thus established it, [he proceeds to] the cutting of the post.

Immediately after the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), one offers to Tvaṣṭṛ—the deity belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ—at that very post. Since the phrase "having approached the post" (*yūpam abhyaitya*) mentioned in the *Patnīsaṃyāja* section demonstrates that even the qualification "belonging to the wives" (*patnīvat*) is connected to the animal, it is established that Tvaṣṭṛ qualified by the "wife-possessing" attribute is the deity here. In all cases, the modification (*ūha*) is as follows: "I dedicate you, who are dear to Tvaṣṭṛ, who possesses wives. By the word "with testicles" (*sāṇḍam*), the possession of both testicles is indicated.

By the word "lomaśam" (hairy), the meaning is that [the animal] possesses abundant hair; by "piṅgalam" (tawny), it means having many forms; by "bahurūpam" (multiform), it means possessing a tawny color due to an abundance of tawny parts; and by "saddha(ntaṃba)durūpam" (of various forms), it means having variegated colors. Having brought forward that animal thus offered, one should conclude—that is, complete—the remainder of the ritual procedure using clarified butter as a substitute, with the formula: "O Tvaṣṭṛ, husband of Patnī, I loosen this for you. This is based on a direct scriptural injunction (vācanika). And thus it is.

The *kumbhāśalā* and other such items, as well as the *saṃjñapta-homa* and other rites, are dispensed with because their purpose has been fulfilled. There is an omission of the *adhigava*. Regarding the method for completing the rite with the remainder of the clarified butter (*ājya*), Āpastamba has clearly stated: "One should cut portions from the clarified butter of the *dhruvā* vessel as many times as there are portions to be cut from the animal. Whatever portion of the animal there may be—such as the omentum (*vapā*), the heart, and so forth—one should cut from the *dhruvā* clarified butter in place of each of those. For those who follow the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvattin*), three portions are taken each time. However, the pieces of gold (*hiraṇyaśakala*) are indeed common to all cases without distinction.

Elsewhere, Āpastamba states a distinction: "The clarified butter (ājya) possesses the characteristics of the animal sacrifice. In that case, the clarified butter takes on the ritual properties of the animal sacrifice. He will state this very point in the *Paribhāṣā*: "It should have those properties. Therefore, for the clarified butter occupying the place of the omentum (*vapā*), the *preṣa* is: "O Patnīvata, [offer] the fat of the goat's omentum to the Lord of Sacrifice (*Sviṣṭakṛt*). The same should be understood for the *paśupuroḍāśa* and the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) as well. Likewise, the *homam* is simply: "O Knower of Beings (*Atavedas*), go to the gods with the omentum."

In this manner, the *prayāja*s, *anuyāja*s, *samiṣṭayajus*, and so forth, belong exclusively to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*) and are not those of the archetype (*prākṛta*). Regarding this, another alternative has also been stated by Āpastamba: "Or rather, one should conclude the rite once the *paryagnikaraṇa* (the circumambulation with fire) has been performed. That is to say, having completed up to the *paryagnikaraṇa*, one should abandon the remainder of the animal ritual procedure; one should not, however, complete the remainder with clarified butter (*ājya*). One should complete the remainder of the *paśupuroḍāśa* and the *anūbandhyā*. Thus, when the entire procedure is concluded at the end of the *paryagnikaraṇa*, or when the independent rite is finished, one should complete the remainder of the *anūbandhyā*.

If the *kāpeyī* eleven-animal sacrifice (*ekādaśinī*) is to be performed, there are two animals dedicated to Indra on both sides of the one dedicated to Agni; [then] those for Sarasvatī, Soma, Pūṣan, and Bṛhaspati [are on the north], while those for Viśve Devās, the Maruts, Savitṛ, and Varuṇa are on the south.

The *ekādaśinī* as prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā*) has already been explained. Now, the specific details mentioned in another branch regarding this *kāpeyī* eleven-animal sacrifice are shown: the *kapayas* are a group of seers (*ṛṣis*); the sacrifice seen by them is the *kāpeyī*. If that is intended to be performed, then, having formally dedicated (*upākṛtya*) the animal for Agni at the central sacrificial post (*agniṣṭha*), the two animals for Indra are to be dedicated at the southern and northern posts.

Then, on the northern sacrificial posts, one should dedicate the animals for Sarasvatī, Soma, Pūṣan, Bṛhaspati, and Kṛpākṛt; and on the southern posts, those for Viśve Devās, the Maruts, Savitṛ, and Varuṇa. The alternating arrangement and the orientation toward the south are as before. There is no offering to Indra-Agni. The Kāpeyas know this [set]; one should sacrifice it at the end of the Atirātra.

Immediately after the word *mālamata*, the particle *iti* should be supplied. Regarding this very *ekādaśinī*, those who are residents of the Kapi region (*kāponām antavāsinaḥ*) or students of the *Kāpeya* recension (*kāpeṭyādhyāyinaḥ*) know thus: "One should sacrifice that [set] at the end of an *atirātra*. Now, what is this rite called the "end of an *atirātra*" (*atirātracarama*), in which this [set] is to be sacrificed? He clarifies it: "It occurs in the *ahīna* sacrifices, because of the connection with the indicative mark (*liṅga*)."

That *kāpeyī* sacrifice is to be attached only to the *ahīna* sacrifices, because of the reason of its connection with the term "mark" (*liṅga*). Here, the status of being the cause for the word "sound" (*śabda*) is not applicable, since the finality of the *ahīna* is clearly demonstrated by the word "last" (*carama*). Therefore, the author of the Sūtras has set aside the word "sound" and employed the word "mark. The intention of the Teacher is that the term "mark" applies where the finality results from the sense (the result).

That by which the intended object, whose final nature is to be known, is indicated (liṅgyate) is a "mark" (liṅga). This means that wherein the meaning is not perceptible but is [known] through the word; the sense is: wherein there exists its conjunction, that is, its connection. Since the final *atirātra* is the mark, there exists a connection with it; for this word "final *atirātra*" is applied to those very [sacrifices] because they are the ultimate *atirātras*.

As he will state in the seventeenth *praśna*, in the thirteenth *khaṇḍa*: "The *ahīnas* begin with the *dvirātra* and end with the *ekādaśarātra*, having the *atirātra* at the end. Now, one might object: in the *sattras* as well, it is not distinct that they have the *atirātra* as their final element, because they have *atirātras* at both ends. As he will state in the first *khaṇḍa* of the eighteenth *praśna*: "The *sattras* have *atirātras* at both ends. Therefore, that [rule] ought to apply to them as well. To this, he says: "In the case of the *sattra*, it is otherwise."

That which is fit for *satras* is "sattrīyā"; the other, distinct from the *kāpeyī*, is only for *satras* as prescribed in its own branch, and not the *kāpeyī* in *satras*—this is the meaning. The intended sense is that for those [schools] for whom only the fact of being the final day of the *atirātra* is the distinguishing factor—and not even the fact of being the first day of the *atirātra*—for them alone is the *ekādaśinī* joined with the *kāpeyī* excluded. Now, in the eighteenth section of the sixteenth book, titled "The Preparation of the Animal Victims" (*paśuklṛpti*), there is a single [verse] situated within the context of the *gavāmayana*.

Having introduced the *daśīrṇī* [sacrifice] which has commenced, he will state regarding those [animals]: "Among them, there are the *gavyā* animals; an extra animal for Viṣṇu, a dwarf bull for Indra at the twenty-one-fold [stoma], a cow for the Viśvedevas at the twenty-seven-fold, a milch-cow for Heaven and Earth at the thirty-three-fold, its calf for Vāyu at the first *chandoma*, a ewe for Aditi at the middle, a ewe for Mitra-Varuṇa at the last, a hornless bull for Prajāpati at the *avivākya*, and a bull for Agni at the *mahāvrata* as the concluding sacrifice. These are the *liṅgāyanika* animals mentioned in the Sūtra as the *gavyā* animals; among these, which are they?

When there is an expectation as to what constitutes "belonging to cattle" (*gavya*), he specifies here the animals belonging to the *ekādaśinī* (the group of eleven) beginning with the *prasannā*: "one should understand the animals belonging to cattle by their names: the bull, the steer, the cow, the heifer, the milch-cow, the calf, and the ox."

Since these other animals also have names belonging to the bovine species (*go-jātīya*), these animals are indeed bovine (*gavya*). Regarding the phrase "wherever...": where there is the scriptural statement, "bovine animals are sacrificed," and where there is the rule stating, "animals other than the bovine," one should understand—that is, recognize—those [as the ones intended]. The others [are to be understood] by their own [names].

One should recognize other animals—those distinct from the goat and the cow—by their own respective names alone, and not by many names; for this purpose, this sūtra is established so that it may be understood that several individuals of the same class are included, rather than [individuals] of different classes. In the case of those animals dedicated to a single deity and distinguished from those dedicated to other deities, there is a common animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa). || 24 ||

Thus ends the eighth paṭala in the ninth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. Regarding the Vājapeya sacrifice, in the eighteenth section of the seventeenth praśna, oxen are prescribed as the sacrificial animals (*paśavaḥ*). Concerning these, the same sūtra—beginning with "for all of them, per animal, there are many *bahiṣpavamāna* [verses], the omentum-cooking spits," and ending with "the granting of the boon"—has been repeated. The purpose of this is to indicate that the *paribhāṣā* (general rule) stating "in the case of animals dedicated to a single deity, when they are dedicated to a single deity and not to other deities" is not universally obligatory.

This indicates that even in the case of animals dedicated to a single deity, there is a *puroḍāśa* for each individual animal. "Those for which no other deity intervenes"—that is, those separated by another deity—are "ananyadevatāḥ. The meaning is that for such animals dedicated to a single deity, there is only one *puroḍāśa*. The repetition [of the word] is intended to signal the conclusion of the inquiry.

Thus ends the eighth chapter of the ninth book in the commentary named *Jyotsnā*, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—the son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was himself the son of Śrīmad Ananta Dīkṣita, a performer of the Aṣṭāpadasacrifice, the Sāhasrāgni, the Vājapeya, the Sarvatomukha, and the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifices, and a builder of the thousand-fire altar (*sāhasrāgnicit*)—which serves to alleviate the distress of learned men caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the ocean of the *Śrīmad-Bhagavat-Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*. This concludes the ninth book.
[The *Satyāṣāḍha-Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha. 986. [End of volume/section].
10.1 Now begins the tenth question. Therein is the first chapter.
Therein is the first chapter.

The sacrificial terminuses beginning with the Agniṣṭoma have been declared, as well as the set of eleven sacrificial animals and the set of eleven sacrificial posts. Now, in order to draw the attention of the student, [the author] introduces the duties of the sacrificer required for the Agniṣṭoma and other rites, which are yet to be explained.
We shall explain the *yājamāna* (the duties of the sacrificer) pertaining to the *agniṣṭoma*.

The mention of "of the *agniṣṭoma*" is intended to indicate that "Agniṣṭoma" is the primary name of the rite; thus, its connection is direct with this very action (*kriyā*), namely the *pakṣya* [sacrifice], and not with the terms *jyotiṣṭoma* or *soma*. However, the purpose of mentioning those two terms prior to the word *agniṣṭoma* is to convey such a meaning.

Although by the rule *yaj-deva-pūjā-saṃgati-karaṇa-dāneṣu* (Pāṇini 1.3.56), which prescribes the meaning of the root *yaj*, and by the rule *saṭ-śānac-au* (Pāṇini 3.2.124), which prescribes the substitution of *śānac* for the present participle suffix *laṭ*, the word *yajamāna*—thus derived—is understood to denote the agent of actions such as the worship of deities and the enjoyer of the fruit through the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), nevertheless, due to the inseparability of etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), it is understood specifically as one who enjoys the fruit of the sacrifice itself.

Because the term *yajamāna* is observed to be applied even to those who are merely participants (*aṅga*) in the rite, and because it is not seen to apply to one who merely performs the worship of the gods; therefore, in a ritual performed by officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), he alone who is the enjoyer of the fruit is denoted by the word *yajamāna*. Nor is [the term] seen to apply to one who enjoys the fruit of mere action, for there is an absence of usage in cases such as initiation (*upanayana*) and other duties of customary conduct (*sāmayācārika*), even though there is an enjoyer of the fruit therein. That which is the action of the sacrificer is what constitutes being a sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

Even the wife (*panyā*) is included here because she possesses the status of a sacrificer (*yajamāna*), as indicated by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra; therefore, her ritual action (*karman*) is also to be understood here. Thus, the analytical statement (*vigrahavākya*) is as follows: "That which is the ritual action of both the [male] sacrificer and the wife is what is meant by 'sacrificial' (*yājamāna*)."

Although it has been established that the rites prescribed in the various Vedas have specific performers—such as the *hotṛ* and others—designated by names like "Hotṛ-Veda" and so forth, nevertheless, when those [restrictions] are set aside by specific authorities (*viśeṣa-pramāṇa*), the status of the husband and wife as performers in certain cases arises; this is what is now being determined. Here, first of all, even prior to the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), the preparation of the materials and the appointment of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) must be performed, for without them, the rite is not accomplished. Thus, the preparation of the substances is described.

The giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) by the patron, celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and the recitation of prayers (*japa*) are included. This has been clearly stated here by Baudhāyana in his Kalpasūtra: "One who is about to sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma procures a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) and a black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*)," and so forth. Kauntha also says: "He procures beforehand a spread of grass, a *vaśa*-branch, animal fat, a vessel for clarified butter, a bowl, a jar, a *kurīra* [head-net], and so forth."

Even in the case of a conflict [of views], [the text says]: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the Agniṣṭoma. Regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say: "One should not initiate the King (Soma) and the sacrificer unless they have been purified. After procuring all the necessary materials, one should purify oneself along with one's wife through the performance of Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, the recitation of the Gāyatrī, oblations of sesame seeds, breath-control (prāṇāyāma), the Kushmāṇḍa oblations, the Gaṇahoma, pilgrimages to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā), visiting the Setu, and so forth; then, permitted by the Brāhmaṇas and having pacified all enmities, one should make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa).

Because of the Vedic injunction, "An action must be performed by one who is pure," and because of the Vedic injunction, "One becomes purified and fit for ritual action," one must perform the prescribed expiations—whether combined or not combined—as appropriate to the offense, for the sake of eligibility. Furthermore, according to the Smṛti, "One who is free from enmity toward all beings shall become eligible for sacrifices. Now begins the tenth book; therein, the first chapter:
We shall explain the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) in the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Having caused the King (Soma) to be brought forward before the consecrations, he distributes it;
that [distribution] is concluded at the consecrations.
He chooses sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who are Brāhmaṇas and not descended from *ṛṣis*, one by one.

The Hotṛ, Maitrāvaruṇa, Acchāvāka, and Grāvastut are the Hotṛs; the Adhvaryu, Pratiprasthātṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Unnetṛ are the Adhvaryus; the Brahman, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Āgnīdhra, and Potṛ are the Brahmans; and the Udgātṛ, Prastotṛ, Pratihartṛ, and Subrahmaṇya are the Udgātṛs.
The Sadasya is the seventeenth. Then he chooses the officiating priests (ṛtvij).

"Agni is the divine, the divine Hotṛ; may he be my Hotṛ"—with these words, he chooses the divine Hotṛ in a low voice. "So-and-so is the human one; I choose him as the Hotṛ"—with these words, he chooses the human Hotṛ aloud. In the same way for the others, he chooses the divine one in a low voice and the human one aloud.

"Āditya is the divine Adhvaryu; may he be my divine Adhvaryu, and this one here is the human [Adhvaryu]; I choose him as the Adhvaryu. "Candramas is the divine Brahman; may he be my divine Brahman, and this one here is the human [Brahman]; I choose him as the Brahman. "Parjanya is the divine Udgātṛ; may he be my divine Udgātṛ, and this one here is the human [Udgātṛ]; I choose him as the Udgātṛ. "Ākāśa is the divine Sadasya; may he be my divine Sadasya, and this one here is the human [Sadasya]; I choose him as the Sadasya."

"The divine waters are the Sadasyas; may they be my Sadasyas. These are the human ones; I choose them as the Sadasyas. Thus he chooses the Sadasyas. "The rays are the divine Hotrāśaṃsins; may they be my Hotrāśaṃsins. These are the human ones; I choose them as the Hotrāśaṃsins. Thus he chooses the Hotrakas. "The gods are the divine Camasādhvaryus; may they be my Camasādhvaryus. These are the human ones; I choose them as the Camasādhvaryus. Thus he chooses the Camasādhvaryus. || 1 ||
If he should cause [the sacrifice] to be performed without having honored them, he becomes joined with sin.
Or rather, he chooses these very ones: the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Brahman, and the Udgātṛ.
Then he requests the Kṣatriya for the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*).
If he gives [the land], he says to him, "May you become possessed of a place for sacrifice. If he does not give, he says, "On whatever place for sacrifice I know, on that I cut you down.
Then they cause him to utter these words.

"You have struck down speech; speech will abandon you," says the Hotṛ. "You have struck down breath; breath will abandon you," says the Adhvaryu. "You have struck down mind; mind will abandon you," says the Brahman. "You have struck down sight; sight will abandon you," says the Udgātṛ. "You have struck down hearing; hearing will abandon you," say the Hotrakas. "You have struck down the self; the self will abandon you," says the Sadasya. "You have struck down the limbs; the limbs will abandon you," say the Camasādhvaryus.
"You have struck down Prajāpati; Prajāpati will abandon you," [says one] to the sacrificer. "You have struck down the beings; the beings will abandon you," [they say] to all.
Then the officiating priests (ṛtvij) request the sacrificial ground (devayajana).
"Agni is my Hotṛ; may he grant me the sacrificial ground," he says in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). "O Hotṛ, give me the sacrificial ground," he says aloud (*uccaiḥ*), which pertains to humans.
In this way, regarding the others, he pronounces the name of the deity in a low voice, but that of the human in a loud voice.

"May Āditya be my Adhvaryu; may he grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods. O Adhvaryu, grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods!"—thus [he addresses] the Adhvaryu. "May Candramas be my Brahman; may he grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods. O Brahman, grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods!"—thus [he addresses] the Brahman. "May Parjanya be my Udgātṛ; may he grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods. O Udgātṛ, grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods!"—thus [he addresses] the Udgātṛ. "May Ākāśa be my Sadasya; may he grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods. O Sadasya, grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods!"—thus [he addresses] the Sadasya. "May the Waters be my Hotrāśaṃsinīs; may they..."

"May the Hotrāśaṃsinīs grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods; may the Hotrāśaṃsinīs grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods," [he says] to the Hotrakas. "May the rays, O Camasādhvaryus, grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods; may the Camasādhvaryus grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods," [he says] to the Camasādhvaryus.
Having requested, "We have come to this place of sacrifice on the earth," he settles upon the sacrificial ground (devayajana).
It should be level, well-established, covered with plants, not saline, not fragile, not occupied by others, not barren, and not prone to crumbling;
it should slope toward the east, or toward the north, or toward the northeast.
Because it extends all around to another spot; he does not leave over a space in front merely the size of the sacrificial ground,
but rather as far as the range of a throw of the *śamyā*.
One who has attained prosperity should sacrifice on ground that is level; this applies to both obligatory and optional rites.
One performing malevolent magic should sacrifice on ground that is very elevated; one being falsely accused should sacrifice on ground that is hidden.
"He should cause him to sacrifice on a *purohavis* sacrificial site"—thus are the optional sacrificial sites explained in the Brāhmaṇa; regarding these, he may act according to his desire.
One undergoes initiation in the afternoon.
He who desires, "May I be an ascetic," undergoes it in the forenoon.
