Having assigned what belongs to him for the sake of the sacrifice, they eat from the remainder; or, if it has not been assigned, they do not eat of it until the Agniṣomīya offering.
He mutters "May you attain the auspicious higher worlds" at every stage while the hair is being shaved.

He recites "Golden-colored, pure, purifying... (RV 9.1.67): "The golden-colored, pure, purifying waters have moved forward after piercing Vṛtra, leaving behind all impurity. A hundred filters are indeed spread out for them; by means of these, may the god Savitṛ purify us. And with "May the mothers, the waters, cleanse us," he bathes in a lake containing conch shells after having placed gold [in the water], or he bathes in standing waters. Some say he bathes in a pool that has hair and is open, or he bathes in a reservoir.
"From the waters, pure and purified, I come," he says as he steps out after bathing;
having touched water and sipped it, he performs the ritual rinsing.

"Thou art initiation; thou art the body; may I clothe thee, who art auspicious and pleasant"—with these words he puts on a large, unwashed garment of linen. And [he says], "Thou art the body of Soma; protect my body.
And [he says], "Thou art the garment of the Sun; thou art the girdle; bestow vigor upon us"—with this he arranges its girdle around himself.

With the words, "For strength, thee," he eats, [thinking] "Place strength in us"; this refers to whatever is dear to his mind, such as clarified butter mixed with curds or honey, used as a sprinkling. Having eaten his fill, he thereafter observes the vow with less and less food.

With the formula, "Thou art the milk of the earth," he clarifies the fresh butter from a cow using two bunches of *darbha* grass. With the formula, "Thou art the bestower of luster; bestow luster upon me," he anoints himself with it, first the face, then the other limbs in the direction of the hair; thus he becomes well-anointed.
With the formula, "Thou art the eye of Vṛtra," he applies collyrium made from Mount Trikakud.

In its absence, he should smear each [eye] three times, beginning with the right one first, using any available means— such as an arrow-shaft with its tuft, a blade of *darbha* grass, or a bunch of *darbha* grass— without rubbing inwardly;
or he may smear the left eye twice.
According to some, he sprinkles it twice on the right side and once on the left;
he does not sprinkle it again.

While being purified, he mutters: "Of thee, O Lord of the Purifier, with the purifier," and the section beginning with "May the Lord of Thought purify me, may the Lord of Speech purify me, may the divine Savitṛ purify me," and also the hymn "The purifying one, whose path is light."
Thus ends the first chapter in the tenth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the second chapter in the tenth book:
"O gods, we invoke you," with these words he recites while entering the *prāgvaṃśa* hall by the eastern door.
Having touched water with the formula, "Thou art lightning," he steps across to the south behind the Āhavanīya fire and sits down to the south.
This is his path of movement until the Soma-pressing.
He consecrates the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "Indra and Agni, Heaven and Earth."
Within the altar, he touches the white and black streaks on the spread black antelope skin with the formula, "You two are the artistic forms of the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda.

He ascends the mound to the south with the formulas, "Thou art a good refuge," and "O God, this prayer of one who strives for skill," as well as "The good protector, the earth, the faultless heaven," or "I have ascended this good ship."

"I have ascended the consecration, the consort of immortality; by means of the Gāyatrī metre and the sacred word (*brahman*), I have established the cosmic order (*ṛta*) in truth. "It has been established in immortality; both the cosmic order and truth have become mine; I have become light; I have gone to the sun; I have gone to the heavenly world, to the back of the firmament, to the summit of the radiant sky. Having thus ascended, he murmurs this. With the black antelope skin, he covers his right shoulder, saying, "Thou art the protection of Viṣṇu. With a cloth, he wraps his head, saying, "Protect me from the gaze of the stars."
With the formula, "For the plowing, for good crops, thee," he digs up a clod of earth from the altar with the presented black antelope horn.
With the formula, "For the plants with good fruit, thee," he scratches his head.
With the formula, "O horn, for the sake of scratching—that knot of his which itches in the heart, that itch of his which is in the mind," he [scratches] the remaining limbs.
"May the divine tree be well-established; standing upright, protect me until the end"—with these words, he takes up the staff. ||5||

Agni is consecrated; the earth is the consecration. By that consecration with which Agni was consecrated—by which consecration Agni was consecrated—may that consecration consecrate me. By that consecration I am consecrated. Vāyu is consecrated; the intermediate space is the consecration. By that consecration with which Vāyu was consecrated—by which consecration Vāyu was consecrated—may that consecration consecrate me. By that consecration I am consecrated. Āditya is consecrated; the sky is the consecration. By that consecration with which Āditya was consecrated—by which consecration Āditya was consecrated—may that consecration consecrate me. By that consecration I am consecrated.

By that consecration I am consecrated; the moon is consecrated, the stars are the consecration—by that consecration with which the moon is consecrated, may that consecration consecrate me. By that consecration I am consecrated; King Varuṇa is consecrated, the waters are the consecration—by that consecration with which King Varuṇa is consecrated, may that consecration consecrate me. By that consecration I am consecrated; King Soma is consecrated, the plants are the consecration—by that consecration with which King Soma is consecrated...

By that consecration (*dīkṣā*) by which King Soma was consecrated, may that consecration consecrate me; by that consecration I am consecrated. Breath is consecrated, speech is the consecration; by that consecration of breath, [breath] is consecrated. By that consecration by which breath was consecrated, may that consecration consecrate me; by that consecration I am consecrated. Prajāpati is consecrated, mind is the consecration; by that consecration of Prajāpati, [Prajāpati] is consecrated. By that consecration by which Prajāpati was consecrated, may that consecration consecrate me; by that consecration I am consecrated. [May it be so] through my speech.

May my speech be consecrated for Agni; may my breath be consecrated for Vāyu; may my eye be consecrated for Sūrya; may my mind be consecrated for Prajāpati. May Heaven and Earth, Day and Night, Agriculture and Rain, Splendor and Reverence, Waters and Herbs, Light and Truth—may these all consecrate me as I am being consecrated. Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ! Truth is my self; faith is mine.

Having recited the *Keśinī-dīkṣā* formula: "The earth is my foundation, austerity my support, faith and truth my householder," he says *svāhā*, and wipes two fingers with the formula, "Svāhā! [I take hold of] the sacrifice with the mind. With "Svāhā! To heaven and earth," he wipes two; with "Svāhā! From the wide atmosphere," two; and with "Svāhā! I take hold of the sacrifice from the wind," he clenches his fists. Then, with "Thou art the mistress of the sacrifice," he releases four fingers, and with them he acts as he pleases while restraining his speech.
If he should speak while distracted, having recited the verses addressed to Viṣṇu, Agni and Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, and Bṛhaspati, as well as the *vyāhṛtis*, he restrains his speech again;
he speaks no falsehood and eats no meat.
He does not approach a woman; he does not sit on high;
he does not spit.
He does not rinse his teeth; he does not display his teeth; he does not smile with his face bent down, but rather smiling while covering his mouth.
Seeing something impure, he mutters: "The mind is unbound.
When being rained upon, he mutters: "O waters, bestowing strength, grant us vigor.
He dwells in the consecrated hut to the south of the sacrificial ground.
He sits or lies down on nothing other than a black antelope skin.
Neither should the sun set nor rise while he is elsewhere than in the consecrated shed.
He should void urine and excrement only at night, or during the day in the shade.

Desiring to urinate, [he recites] "This is thy sacrificial body," and having struck a clod of earth or something else with the horn and taken it, he voids his urine [with the mantra]: "I release the waters, not my offspring; O releasers from distress, being consecrated by Svāhā, enter the earth. Having touched water and sipped [water], he replaces it [with the formula] "Be born upon the earth" or "Be born from the earth.
A Śūdra does not sit down behind him.
He may converse with a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya;
he does not rise for anyone,
nor does he offer salutations.
Everyone should indeed salute him, and he should salute everyone.

If conversation with a Śūdra should occur for him, he should say to one of these [preceding] castes, "Address this man thus. If conversation—that is, dialogue—with a Śūdra should occur or happen for this initiated person (*dīkṣita*), he should say to one of these—namely, the Brāhmaṇa, Rājanya, and Vaiśya mentioned immediately above, excluding the Śūdra—even though the word *varṇa* (caste) applies to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras alike.
Speaking worldly speech, he places at the end of the names [of the deities] the words *vicakṣaṇam* and *canasitam*.
He does not cook, he does not give, and he does not offer any oblation whatsoever, except for those connected with the sacrifice.
On that day, having been consecrated (*dīkṣita*), he remains awake through the night.
The vow does not take effect [immediately].
Having seen the constellation, he releases his speech silently. He restrains his speech at the moment when the one who bestows the vow gives him the command.

"Those words which are in the bull of cattle, those which are in the Sun, those which are in the Bright One—at their head, send them forth; according to your respective portions, may those auspicious words return to us here.
With these words, he worships the rising Sun.
Once the Sun has risen, he issues the command: "Perform the vow!"
In this manner, he observes the vow at sunset, at midday, and at midnight. Those who have not been initiated do not see him while he is observing the vow.
Milk is for a Brāhmaṇa, barley-gruel for a Rājanya, and curdled milk (āmikṣā) for a Vaiśya.
One should offer either milk or barley-gruel;
if one desires curd, they should prepare this curd for him.
If he should eat [the sacrificial food], they should mix parched grains for him, or they should mix barley meal for him, or they should mix clarified butter for him.
Or alternatively, he may consume one of the oblations of the Agnihotra.
These rules for the fast-food (vrata) apply to all social classes.
For all the *upasad* rites, there are the rules regarding the cups (*stanakalpāḥ*).

He consecrates the bronze vessel used for the offering of the fast-food (*vratapradāna*) with the mantra: "Thou art wide-extending, the supporter of people; as one who has his own portion, protect me.
He washes his hands with the mantra: "We direct our divine thought."

He observes the vow with the mantra: "O gods born of mind, joined by mind... He drinks water with the mantra: "Become auspicious when drunk, O you who are worthy of sacrifice; O waters, be very gracious in our womb and belly; full of nourishment, multiform, and sinless, be auspicious for our drinking. He drinks whenever he has not yet drunk or whenever he feels thirsty. He lies down to the south of the Āhavanīya fire, facing the east.
He should lie on his right side;
he should not lie on his back,
nor should he turn his back toward the fire.
"O Agni, watch well," he says as he approaches the Āhavanīya fire when about to sleep.
"May all the gods turn toward me," he says as he turns back, should he turn back.

"May mind come back to me; may life come back to me; may sight come back to me; may hearing come back to me; may breath come back to me; may intention come back to me; may thought come back to me; may reflection come back to me. May Vaiśvānara, the undeceivable guardian of my body, remain within me, warding off all misfortunes. May Vaiśvānara, the sustainer of all, the source of welfare for all, drive away all misfortunes. May he protect us from harm by day and by night. Having awakened, one mutters: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows.
If one should utter a word unfit for a consecrated person (*adīkṣita-vāda*), one should recite: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows."
Having released his fists and speech, this mode of conduct begins from the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [initiation] sacrifice.

He does not break his staff, nor does he walk about after having unfastened the black antelope skin; he scratches himself with the black antelope horn and smiles while covering his mouth—these observances (*vrata*) begin from that point of application. 8.
Thus ends the second paṭala in the tenth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the third paṭala in the tenth praśna:
"Pūṣan is with the gain," [with these words] he instructs those who bring the gains.

For twelve days he practices begging for alms; when the period of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is unlimited, he may accept as much as he desires, but when it is limited, [he accepts] gold, a garment, a cow, a horse, a goat, and a ram—up to as many cows as are permitted, and one each of the other species. He accepts these with the formulas beginning "Thou art the moon," according to their respective forms.
One appends "The god Savitṛ... everywhere.
With "For Vāyu thee," one should designate whichever among them might be lost.
With "For Varuṇa thee," one designates that which has sunk into the water.
With "For Nirṛti, thee," [he addresses] one that has collapsed;

with "For Rudra, thee," one bitten by a serpent; with "For the Maruts, thee," one struck by a thunderbolt or lightning; with "For Indra, thee," one killed by a ram; with "For Yama, thee," one killed by Mahādeva; and with "For Death, thee," one killed by an unknown cause of death.
Having encountered such a cow that has been designated [for sacrifice], the sacrificer must not let it roam among the cattle.
If he should set out, having consigned the fires into the two separate kindling woods (*araṇī*), he proceeds by chariot;
if a chariot is not available, [he proceeds] with a part of a chariot.
If he crosses waters that are navigable by boat, he crosses having placed both the kindling woods and the chariot together [in the boat].
If he crosses or carries away the waters by means of a cart that cannot float, or if he should plunge into them, he should plunge with the formula, "O divine waters!
While treading upon a clod of earth, he crosses over from this shore to the further shore with the formulas: "May I follow the unbroken thread of the earth; you are the bridge of the waters."
"Be born from the earth. (9) He places either sand or clods of earth in the middle and on both banks, or he does so with the formula, "Be born from the earth.
Some authorities prescribe the formal selection of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) at this point.
Having touched the central pillar of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, he mutters this mantra.
Having been initiated for one night, he purchases the King [Soma] on the second day, the third day, the fourth day, or for an indefinite period.
He hands over the purchased portion to the wife with the words, "Thine be the portion," or "Thine be the wealth.
He sits to the south of the King as he is being purchased.
When the Soma has been purchased, he hands over the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa priest—
either on that day or when the pressing for the following day is being performed.
With the verse "The birds, the fair-winged," he uncovers [the head of the sacrificer], first the head and then the other limbs in successive order.
"Come to us as a friend, bestowing good friendship"—with these words, he embraces the King who has been placed upon his lap; thus he truly takes hold of him.
"Up with life!"—with this he rises. "The wide mid-air"—with this he proceeds.
Having reached the cart, he hands over the King (Soma) to the Adhvaryu.
He gazes at the King as it is being carried toward the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, saying: "Homage to the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa!
He touches the *tānūnaptra* vessel, saying: "May the Lord of Consecration approve my consecration."
Having entered upon those three vows, he eats that which the Adhvaryu does not smell.
With the formula, "O Agni, lord of vows," he enters the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*).

He draws his girdle tighter and makes his fists tighter; he becomes one whose vow is heated. He performs the rites requiring water with the *madantī* (boiling) waters. 10. The washing of the hands, the swelling [of the cups], and the concealment have been explained.
He observes the vow with the formula, "O Agni, that body of yours which belongs to Rudra.
On this day, the extent of the vow is that of the consecration (*dīkṣā*);
from this point onward, the ritual procedure for the vow is that of the *aupasadā*.
On this night he observes the vow with four breasts; on the middle day, with three breasts; on the night [of the middle day], with two breasts; and on the last day, with one breast.

"One should undertake the intermediate consecration (avāntaradīkṣā) that is sharp as a needle"—thus are explained the optional measures of the vows according to the Brāhmaṇa; regarding these, one may act according to one's desire. Having stepped out before the Havirdhāna shed from the measured space with the words, "Viṣṇu is praised for his heroic deeds," he worships the Dhiṣṇiya hearths with those same mantras, in the order they were originally assigned.

"You are the sovereign, O Kr̥śānu," [he says] regarding the Āhavanīya fire; "You are the one seated in the assembly, O Pavamāna," [he says] where they chant the Bahiṣpavamāna; "You are the swift-moving, O Nabhasvant," [he says] regarding the Cātvāla pit; "You are unswept, O preparer of oblations," [he says] regarding the animal-cooking fire (Paśuśrapaṇa); "You are the abode of Truth, O Suvar-jyotis," [he says] regarding the Audumbarī post; "You are the light of Brahman, O Suvar-dhāman," [he says] regarding the seat of the Brahman priest; "You are the goat, the one-footed," [he says] regarding the Prājihita Gārhapatya fire; "You are the serpent, O Budhniya," [he says] regarding the Śālāmukhīya fire; "You are the Kavya, O carrier of the Kavyas," [he says] regarding the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.

With the formula, "Thou art the heap, all-encompassing," he addresses the rubbish-heap (utkara); with "Thou art the ocean, the bearer of all," the Sadas; with "Thou art the Sadasya, the robber," the place of the Sadasya; and the phrase "the fierce face" he attaches everywhere. || 11 ||
Thus ends the third paṭala in the tenth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the fourth paṭala in the tenth praśna.

At the time when the Brahman priest causes the King (Soma) to enter the Havirdhāna shed, he enters the Havirdhāna by the eastern door and addresses the King who has been placed upon the cart with the mantra: "O divine Savitṛ, this is your Soma... and so forth.
Saying "I am this man among men," he turns to the right;
saying "Homage to the gods," he makes a reverential salutation with joined palms toward the east; saying "Svadhā to the ancestors," he makes it toward the south;
saying "Here I depart from the noose of Varuṇa," he steps out.
With the words, "May I be renowned as one of good fortune," he looks over the entire sacrifice; with the words, "The light of Vaiśvānara," he gazes at the Āhavanīya fire.
With the formula, "O Agni, Lord of Vows," he releases the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*).
He loosens his girdle more widely and makes his fists more loosely.

"May the sacrifice be *svāhā*! Release it into speech and into the wind! Having thus released his fists and his speech, he thereafter moves with his hands as he pleases. The other duties of the consecrated (*dīkṣita*) continue;
he remains awake during this night.
From this point onward, the ritual procedure for the vow does not apply to one who has undergone the consecration (*daikṣa*).

With the *saptahotṛ* formula, he touches the King Soma placed upon the pressing stones. He follows after those waters wherever they lead him into the *havirdhāna* shed; whatever glory there is becomes inclined toward him.
He gives twelve heifers that have calved for the first time, pregnant, along with a garment made of animal hide, to the *adhvaryu* at the *aṃśu* cup; likewise at the *adābhya* cup.
Once the *dhruva* vessel has been drawn, he does not urinate until the pouring down [of the soma].
Before the *bahispavamāna*, he mutters the *vyāhṛtis*—"Do the *hiṃ*-call for Vasvī; chant the *prastāva* for her; may she be secured for me"—and the *daśahotṛ* formula.

"You are a falcon, having the Gāyatrī as your metre; I take hold of you; may you, possessing well-being, carry me across," [with these words] he takes hold of [the sacrificer] while the [Sāman] is being chanted, or during the middle *stotrīyā* verse. With the formula, "Of the praised, you are the praised," he consecrates all the *stotras* as they are being praised, saying for each, "The praised, the praised."
With the formula "Thou art the weapon of weapons," he [addresses] all the weapons.
With the verse "We choose those possessed of power," he appends [the formula] everywhere.
While the offering for Indra and Vāyu is being made, with the formula "Thou art the earth, the best of rays," he worships the sun.

When the offering for Indra and Vāyu has been made with the verse "O Indra and Vāyu," he should press his thumb [into the cup] if he desires to rival one who is superior; if he desires to rival one who is inferior, he should press a finger against the thumb.
With the verse "O Mitra and Varuṇa, who... he [presses the thumb] when the offering for Mitra and Varuṇa is made; with "O Aśvins, who... when the offering for the Aśvins is made.
With the verse "Of thee, O Lord of Wealth, whose heroism is unbroken, we, joined with Indra," he takes hold of the *śukra* cup as it is being offered.
When they bring him a cup, he consumes it just like the other cups.
When the command "O Gṛhapati, sacrifice" is uttered, he issues the direction "O Hotṛ, sacrifice this," or he sacrifices himself after sitting down.

Thinking, "May it be secured for me," he mutters the *vyāhṛtis*, the *Caturhotṛ* formula, and the *Pañcahotṛ* formula before each of the *ājya* stotras, saying: "Make the *hiṃ* for Jyotis; chant the *prastāva* for it.

Thinking, "May it be secured for me," he mutters the *vyāhṛtis*, the *Caturhotṛ* formula, and the *Pañcahotṛ* formula before the midday *pavamāna* stotra, saying: "Make the *hiṃ* for Iḍā; chant the *prastāva* for it.
He touches the one being praised, saying: "You are the Suparṇa, having the *triṣṭubh* metre; I take hold of you; lead me safely across. || 13 ||
The touching of Śukra has been explained.
When the Nārāśaṃsa cups have been set down, she stands to the south of the altar and gives the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās).
These consist of twenty-seven cows, twenty-four, sixty, a hundred, a thousand, twelve hundred, or all one's possessions, or an unlimited number.
Barley-meal, rice, sesame, and beans; gold, a garment, and a goat without dust—these are the prescribed items.
A wagon, a chariot, a cloak, a horse, a man, or an elephant are the non-prescribed items.
Taking gold and clarified butter, he approaches them with the words: "By means of your form, I approach your form."
"May Tvaṣṭṛ, the all-knowing, distribute among you," saying this, he steps into the middle and distributes [the portions]:
twelve each for those who perform the central work, six each for the Ṛṣis, four each for the third-tier workers, three each for the footmen;
in this manner the remainder is distributed.
The Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Brahman, and Udgātṛ are the central performers (*madhyataḥkāriṇaḥ*).

The Maitrāvaruṇa, Pratiprasthātṛ, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and Prastotṛ are the "half-sharers" (*ardhinaḥ*). The Acchāvāka, Neṣṭṛ, Āgnīdhra, and Pratihartṛ are the "third-sharers" (*tṛtīyinaḥ*). The remaining ones are the "quarter-sharers" (*pādinaḥ*).
With the verse, "This gift of thine, O Agni, comes, distilling Soma," he brings them after they have been distributed.

From the front of the *prāgvamśa* hall, behind the *sadas*, to the south of the *āgnīdhrīya* fire, and between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), he releases them toward the north. He consecrates those going along with the formula: "Go by the path of Truth, O you who have the moon as your sacrificial fee."
Thinking, "May I today win over a Brāhmaṇa, a seer and the descendant of seers," he takes gold and a portion of the sacrificial fee and approaches the Āgnīdhra fire.
With this same mantra, he gives the gold and the portion of the sacrificial fee to the Āgnīdhra.
He gazes at the Sadas hall, saying, "Behold the light; behold the mid-air."

"Go among the gods, given by us"—with these words, the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇās*) enter the *sadas* through the eastern door. He gives the most excellent gold to a descendant of Atri with the same mantra used at the *āgnīdhra*.
If such a person is not available, he should give that fee to one who is of noble lineage (*ārṣeya*), learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*), and whose father is also learned in the Vedas.

Then he assigns the portions of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*): "O Brahman, I give you the mind; I redeem it with this," he says to the Brahman seated on the Brahman’s seat. Whatever he intends to give, he assigns that to the Brahman, saying, "I give this. In the same way to the others: "O Hotṛ, I give you speech; I redeem it with this," he says to the Hotṛ seated on the Hotṛ’s seat.
"O Adhvaryu, I give you the breath; I redeem it with this," [he says] to the Adhvaryu seated in the Havirdhāna shed.
"To the Udgātṛ, seated upon the Udumbara post: 'I give you the eye; with this I redeem it.
To the Hotrakas, seated within the Sadas according to their respective Dhiṣṇiya hearths: 'I give you the ear; with this I redeem it. And to the Pratiprasthātṛ, seated in the Havirdhāna shed.
He gives according to his faith to the Sadasya, to the Camasādhvaryus, and to the Prasarpakas."
"I give myself to the Sadasya; I redeem him with this," [he says] to the Sadasya seated within the *sadas* while the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇās*) are being presented.

"I give my limbs to you, O Camasādhvaryus; I redeem them with this," [he says] to the Camasādhvaryus seated in the *havirdhāna*. "I give my hair to you, O Prasarpakas; I redeem it with this," [he says] to the Prasarpakas seated in the southern half within the *sadas*.
The thought "I am giving this" follows him everywhere.
He does not give out of fear,
nor to one who merely asks.
Not to the Kaṇvas or Kāśyapas;
not to lute-players and singers; nor to one who is not an officiating priest.
Not to a kinsman; not to one who has not approached [for instruction];
not to one who is not a Śrotriya.
Not to one who is not a Brahmin;
he should give it to one who knows the Vedas.
To whomsoever else might reject it when being given, or to one whom [the giver] hates, to him he should give that sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
He should accept it with another [verse].
At the very least, he gives it to the *pratihartṛ* or to one who is an Ātreya.
He should not give it when the two *marutvatīya* [stotras] have been recited.
If he should give [the gift], he should do so when the omentum of the Anūbandhyā cow has been offered, or at the Udavasānīyā sacrifice in the Iṣṭi.
Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the tenth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the fifth paṭala in the tenth praśna.

When the sacrificial fees have been led away, he unfastens the black antelope horn and throws it into the *caṭvāla* pit with the mantra: "The healing medicine of the swift-moving deer, which overcomes hereditary disease, has driven it away in all directions with its horn. He also throws it with the mantra: "The tawny deer has stepped over you with his four feet; may there be no serpent, no viper. At the *Rathantara* [Sāman], he gives a choice gift;
at the *Vāmadevya*, he gives a choice gift.
He gives a choice gift at the Niṣkevalya.

He takes hold of the Āditya cup as it is being offered, saying: "Utter the *hiṃ* for long life; chant the *prastāva* for that; may it be secured for me. Prior to the Ārbhava Pavamāna, he mutters the five Vyahṛtis and the Pañcahotṛ formula.

"You are the earth, having the *jagatī* as its meter; I take hold of you; lead me safely across. With these words, he takes hold of [the sacrificer] while the latter is being praised. When they have set down his own cup, he places three fragments of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) to the south.

Having done that, and having arranged the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), and having recited the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula, he mutters the mantras of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, beginning with the offering and ending with the departure.
At the Yajñāyajñiya [stotra], he gives a choice gift.
Prior to the Agniṣṭoma-stotra, he mutters the vyāhṛtis and the Saptahotṛ formula.

"You are Subhū, the best of rays, beloved of the gods, to be fully accomplished. May the gods enter into you, O Subhū! You are *iṣas*, you are *tveṣas*, you are *nṛmṇas*, you are *yahvas*, you are *vrata*, you are *svas*, you are *cāraṇas*, you are *śūdra*, you are *ārya*. Of that *iṣas* of yours, of *tveṣas*, of *nṛmṇas*, of *yahvas*, of *vrata*, of *svas*, of *cāraṇas*, of *śūdra*, and of *ārya*, may I enjoy [the fruit]. Just as you, O Sūrya, are all-visible (*viśvadarśata*), so may I become all-visible. Thus [he concludes] the Agniṣṭoma.
Having completed [the rite], he worships the sun; if it should have set, he worships the Āhavanīya fire itself with the formula used for worshipping the sun.
A drop of curd;
Soma in the waters;
the propitiation of Mindāyū.
The placing of the wood-shavings and the dismissal of the companions.
When the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations have been offered, he strides the Viṣṇu-steps with the verse in the Jagatī meter: "With Agni as my god, may I conquer the armies."

"Bestowing support upon the mother, the supporter suckling the mother—may he bestow upon us abundance of wealth, food, and vigor," [saying this] as he steps out, he pulls up the Audumbara post. "Away with thy wrath, O Varuṇa," [saying this], having unfastened the black antelope skin, he throws it into the *catvāla* pit.
With the two verses, "Upwards that one" and "The bright one," he worships the sun; if the sun has already set, he worships the Āhavanīya fire itself with the worship of the sun.
The ritual for the final bath (*nidhanopāyana*) has been explained,
as well as the sprinkling (*mārjana*) with the *sumitriyā* formula.

Having removed the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) with the words, "May I not be deprived of power, pre-eminence, and excellence," he sprinkles it and sets it aside, provided it was not already laid down previously.

With the verse, "May Sumitrā lead us," the two of them, having entered [the water] together without sinking and remaining with their heads above the surface, bathe and wash each other's backs while swimming against one another.
With the verse, "I loosen thy bonds," the sacrificer unfastens his girdle;
with the verse, "This I untie," the wife unties the noose of her waist-band.
Having washed the girdle, the sacrificial cord, the net, and the two garments of the consecrated, the sacrificer puts on the Soma-enclosing cloth, and the wife puts on the Soma-covering cloth;
they both wear these new garments once the sun has risen.
These are given to the Adhvaryu at the concluding oblation. || 17 ||
The lifting up has been explained, as well as the placing of the fuel-sticks and the standing in attendance.

Having sat down at the entrance of the hall by the western side, and having taken five portions of clarified butter into the *juhū* ladle, he places a black antelope skin on his lap and offers the oblation with the formula: "May Indra bestow upon me power, seniority, and preeminence.
He either spreads out the black antelope skin or makes it serve as a support for the *sruk* ladle.
Or else, the grinding of the oblation:
he thereby establishes it once again in the consecration itself.
He should give it either to his son or to a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*).
If [the vow] has not been formally released previously, he enters upon the vow at the *udayanīyā* offering.

When the omentum of the *anūbandhyā* cow has been offered, the sacrificer has his hair and beard shaved on the southern shoulder of the altar within an enclosure; here he gives away whatever he intends to give.
The *svaru* and the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*), as well as the worship of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-upasthāna*), have been explained.
He gives a pair of cattle in the *āmikṣā* offering dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.
While the *saktu* oblation is being offered, he worships Agni with the verse, "May this [Agni] come before us through the sky."
He gives a draft-ox, or oxen, or gold at the *udavasānīyā* offering, reciting "O Lord of the Clouds, you who are such as you are" for Vāyu, and "O God, the Increaser" for Āditya.
At the *pūrṇāhuti*, he gives according to his ability.
When the *ṣoḍaśin* stotra has concluded, he gives that very horse or a mule as the sacrificial fee.
Thus ends the fifth paṭala in the tenth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
10.6 Now begins the sixth paṭala in the tenth praśna:
One who is about to accept a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), or having already accepted it, breathes out seventeen times.
One should recognize a cow by its sacrificial grass (barhis), or a horse by [its fodder];
a man by his food;
and a bed by its fragrance and pleasant conversation.

He rises toward the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). The sacrificial grass is indeed the dear abode of the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*); he becomes dear to the sacrificial gift, and the sacrificial gift comes to him. The gods once caused Varuṇa to perform a sacrifice. For whichever deity they brought the sacrificial gift, that deity was distressed by it. They said, "Let us receive [the gift] while turning away; thus the sacrificial gift will not distress us. They received it while turning away, and from then on the sacrificial gift did not distress them. He who, knowing this, receives the sacrificial gift while turning away, the sacrificial gift does not distress him. This is the receiving [of the gift] while turning away.
He shows them to the southern women who play stringed instruments. || 19 ||

At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I receive you. May King Varuṇa lead you, O divine Dakṣiṇā. For Agni, gold; through it may I attain immortality. May there be strength for the giver, and may there be bliss for me, the receiver. Who has given this to whom? Desire has given it to desire. Desire is the giver; desire is the recipient.

O recipient! Enter the ocean at will; I accept you with desire. O Desire, this is for you! O Desire, may the son of Aṅgiras, Utāna, accept you. For Soma, a garment: The Gnas cut it out; the Apas stretched it; the Varutris wove it; the Adhiyas dyed it. For Rudra, a cow; for Varuna, a horse; for Prajapati, a human; for Manu, a bed; for Tvashtar, a she-goat; for Pushan, a sheep; for Nirriti, a mule and a donkey; from the Himalayas, an elephant; for the Gandharvas and Apsarases...

[He offers] a garland as an ornament to the Viśvedevas; grain to Vāc; food to Brahmán; boiled rice to the Ocean; water to Uttāna Āṅgiras; and a chariot to Vaiśvānara. With the verse addressed to Vaiśvānara: "Vaiśvānara has mounted the firmament, the back of heaven, as of old, being praised by those of good thoughts. Like the ancients, he generates wealth for the living; the watchful one goes around the common path," he accepts the chariot with this verse to Vaiśvānara.
He places the Sāvitra formula at the beginning of each [gift], and at the end he adds the supplementary formula: "By this may I attain immortality. (20)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the tenth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
10.7: "For one year, one of the four shall not eat"—this is the observance for the employment of the Caturhotṛ formulas.
He who desires, "May I become much, may I procreate," should go to the forest and offer the Daśahotṛ formula with either a deficient or a full ladle upon a clump of Darbha grass.

He who is not successful in obtaining offspring or cattle should put on a garment of bark, drink [only] hot water for twelve nights, and sleep on the ground. On the morning of the twelfth day, having gone out toward the east, he should breathe out and breathe in; then, having explained the *Daśahotṛ* formula, he should breathe out with the words, "Go to Indra, svāhā!

One desiring a son should sacrifice to the wives of the gods for a year. Between the wives of the gods and Tvaṣṭṛ, one desiring a son should offer oblations with four *Yajus* formulas. If a son is not born after a year, one should disregard that and have him perform the sacrifice with the *Caturhotṛ* formula.

If a king has been deposed when a battle is joined on barren soil where no roofs are visible, he offers the first oblation with four-drawn ghee using the *Caturhotṛ* formula, and the second oblation with the *Graha* formula; or alternatively, having mentally recited the *Caturhotṛ*, he offers half with the former *Graha* and half with the latter. Whatever they may find there shall be the sacrificial fee; some prescribe a hundred.
One desiring offspring should have him sacrifice with the *Caturhotṛ*;
its ritual procedure for the oblation is the same as that.
The sacrificial fee is a choice gift.
One desiring cattle should cause him to sacrifice with the Pañcahotṛ formula.

With clarified butter taken four times, he offers the first oblation with the Pañcahotṛ formula; the second with a vessel (graha). Or alternatively, having recited the Pañcahotṛ formula, he offers half with the first vessel and half with the second.
For this [sacrifice], these are the four sacrificial fees: a horse, gold, a garment, and a cow.
One who has rivals should have him perform the sacrifice with the *saptahotṛ* formula using the oblation and the cup without a fee.

If one should become worse off after the completion of the sacrifice, he should offer the first oblation with the *saptahotṛ* formula using clarified butter taken in four ladlings, and the second with the cup.

Those [formulas] connected with the sacrifices have been explained. One performing sorcery should offer the *daśahotṛ* formula in a self-made salt-flat or a fissure, pronouncing "phaṭ" as the *vaṣaṭ*-call. If a learned Brāhmaṇa who possesses knowledge should fail to attain fame, he should go to the forest, tie up a bunch of *darbha* grass, seat a Brāhmaṇa to his right, and loudly recite the *caturhotṛ* formulas together with the *graha*s, the *svāhā*-utterances, the *saṃbhārayajus* formulas, the wives, and the response-mantras. Or else, he may recite only the *caturhotṛ* formulas; to that Brāhmaṇa who sits to his right, he should give a boon.
It is known from the sacred tradition: "Whatever one gives to him there, whatever fame he attains, that Varuṇa seizes."

If they should expel him while he has been chosen for the office of the *ṛtvij*, he should offer the *daśahotṛ* formula with clarified butter taken four times, or—according to some—with nine ladlings, standing in front and facing west, reciting it backwards and with distinct pauses; thus he causes his vital breaths to perish. If they should restore him, he should offer the *daśahotṛ* formula with clarified butter taken four times, or—according to some—with nine ladlings, sitting behind and facing east, reciting it in the natural order and without pauses; thus he restores his vital breaths for him. At the beginning of each season, one should perform an expiation: "Speech is the *hotṛ*," and at the beginning of each season, one should offer the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula.
He who desires, "May I become more abundant," should employ the Daśahotṛ. He who desires, "May a hero be born to me," should employ the Caturhotṛ.
He who desires, "May I possess cattle," should employ the Pañcahotṛ.
He who desires, "May the seasons be favorable to me," should [employ] the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ.
He who desires, "May I be a drinker of Soma, a sacrificer with Soma; may one who drinks Soma and sacrifices with Soma be born to me," should [employ] the Saptahotṛ.

He who desires, "May I be beloved," or for whom he desires, "May he be beloved," should fashion for him this *sthāgara* ornament, and having adorned his face with the Daśahotṛ on the south, the Pañcahotṛ behind, the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ on the north, and the Saptahotṛ above, as well as with the *saṃbhāras* and the wives, he should go half-way toward her; thus he indeed becomes beloved.

Among those [mantras], those which are heard for the purpose of an oblation (homa) should be employed together with the planetary deities (sagraha) and the exclamation "svāhā" (sasvāhākāra); however, those which are not for the purpose of an oblation are without the planetary deities and without the "svāhā" exclamation. Those which are recitations (japa) and those belonging to the sacrificer (yājamāna), when connected with a sacrifice (kratusaṃyukta), belong to one who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni) in both cases; those not connected with a sacrifice belong to both. || 22 ||
Thus ends the seventh paṭala in the tenth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the eighth paṭala in the tenth praśna:
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the Brahman priest belongs to the Vasiṣṭha lineage.
Or whoever should study the *stomabhāga* verses;
or when the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) perform the transmission of the sacrifice to one another—
so long as the priestly office (*ārtyijya*) is carried out by means of the *ṛc*, so long does the sacrifice reside in the *hotṛ*s alone.

As long as there is activity among the Adhvaryus by means of the Yajus, so long does it remain there; as long as there is activity among the Udgātṛs by means of the Sāman, so long does it remain there;
wherever the sacrifice comes to rest, it rests within the Brahman alone. Thus the sacrifice becomes established.
Therefore, during this disappearance, the Brahman priest should remain restrained in speech.
If he should speak out of negligence, he should mutter a verse addressed to Viṣṇu and the *vyāhṛtis*, and then restrain his speech once more.

[This applies] while the King (Soma) is being measured, while the fire is being prepared, while the Great Altar (*mahāvedi*) and the Northern Altar (*uttaravedi*) are being constructed, while the King is being carried forth, while the Soma is being pressed, and while the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant is being performed.
When the fire-pan is being prepared, when the rites pertaining to the pan are being performed, when it is being placed upon the fire,
and while the fire is being measured out.
While being ploughed; while being sown;
while the altar is being constructed.
And during the accumulated rites (*saṃcita-karman*):
while these rites are being performed at their proper time, he sits to the south—
while the fire is being carried forth, while the fire is being led forward, and while the two *havirdhāna* carts are being moved.
When the fire-pan (ukhā) is being prepared for assembly, when it is being carried,
and when the Nairṛta bricks are about to be laid down.
When the city fires are being carried forth;
when the Vasatīvarī waters and the Savanīya offerings are being brought forward; and when they are being drawn back.
And they should descend for the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
And when these rituals are being performed at the appropriate times, he goes to the south.

While the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds are being constructed, he goes between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), passes to the rear of the *uttaravedi*, and sits down to the south. He remains seated until the time of the *vaisarjana* offerings.

When the *vaisarjana* oblations are about to be offered, he returns by the same way he came, goes around the north of the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth, enters the *prāgvaṃśa* hall through the eastern door, passes to the rear of the *śālāmukhīya* fire, and sits down to the south.
With the words, "Thus do thou praise," he places the King (Soma) upon his lap.
He remains seated until the *vaiśarjana* oblation is offered. Once the *vaiśarjana* has been offered, he follows after the fire,
or he goes before it.

Having reached the Āgnīdhrīya shed, he sits down to the south and remains seated until the Vaisarjana oblations are offered. When the Vaisarjana oblation has been offered, having handed over the King Soma to another, he goes around the north of the Āgnīdhrīya hearth, takes back the King Soma, and enters the Havirdhāna shed by the western door with the verse addressed to Soma, "Soma goes forth, the knower of the way. Having handed the King Soma to the Adhvaryu, he returns by the same way he came, passes to the west of the Uttaravedi, and sits down to the south.
He remains seated until the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma.
Once the omentum has been offered, he performs the ritual purification (*mārjana*).
While the *vasatīvarī* waters are being taken up, he restrains his speech until the *subrahmaṇyā* formula.
When they awaken at the dead of night, he awakens.
Once the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) has been commenced, he restrains his speech until the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*).

When the *savanīya* offerings are being introduced, he enters the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door, goes around the front of the *khara* mound, and sits down to the south. He remains seated until the time of the *āgrayaṇa*.
While the cups (*graha*) are being drawn, he restrains his speech until the drawing of the *āgrayaṇa* cup.
When they proceed to the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant, he follows along, maintaining contact with them as they move.

When it is said, "I shall satisfy the Brahman," [the Adhvaryu] says: "O God Savitṛ, you have declared this; impel it and perform the sacrifice! Bṛhaspati is the Brahman. Do not depart from the long-lived Ṛc nor from the body-protecting Sāman. May your blessings be true, may your intentions be true. Speak Ṛta and Satya! Praise in the impulse of the god Savitṛ—Om, praise! With these words he gives the impulse (*prasauti*). This is the ritual procedure for all the Stotras.
[He recites: "Thou art a ray; for dwelling, thee, quicken the dwelling! Thus he places the thirty-one *stomabhāga* verses, each subsequent one following the previous, in each Stotra.

There are twelve [stotras] in the Agniṣṭoma, thirteen in the Atyaṣṭoma, fifteen in the Ukthya, sixteen in the Ṣoḍaśin, seventeen in the Vājapeya, twenty-nine in the Atirātra, and thirty-three in the Aptoryāma.

When the Bahiṣpavamāna has been chanted, he returns by the same way he came, passes beyond the northern altar from the west, and sits down to the south; he remains seated until the offering of the omentum (vapā) of the Savanīya animal sacrifice.

When the omentum has been offered and he has performed the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), he enters the *sadas* by the eastern door, goes around the front of the *praśāstrīya* hearth, and sits down to the south; he remains seated until the conclusion of the rite. When they bring him his goblet, he consumes it just as he does with the other goblets.
He restrains his speech during the *stotra* and the *śastra*.
When the pressing session has concluded, he departs by the way he came.
Thus is the procedure for the movement between sessions and the office of the Brahman priest prescribed for the two subsequent pressings.
All other ritual acts beyond this are prescribed for the Brahman priest in the *Ādhvaryava* [section] of the Brāhmaṇa.
Thus has the office of the Brahman priest for the sacrificial sessions been prescribed; this is the office of the Brahman. 25.
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the tenth book in the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
The tenth book is completed.
[986] The Śrauta Sūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha.
10.1 Now begins the tenth question. Therein is the first chapter.
Therein is the first chapter.

The sacrificial terminuses beginning with the Agniṣṭoma have been declared, as well as the eleven animals and the eleven sacrificial posts. Now, in order to draw the attention of the student, [the author] introduces the duties of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) required in the Agniṣṭoma and other rites, which are about to be explained:
We shall explain the *yajamāna* (duties of the sacrificer) for the *agniṣṭoma*.

The mention of "of the *agniṣṭoma*" is intended to indicate that "Agniṣṭoma" is the primary name of the rite; thus, its connection is directly with this very action (*kriyā*), namely the *pakṣya* [the sacrifice], and not with the words *jyotiṣṭoma* or *soma*. The purpose of this is to make known that these two terms [precede] the word *agniṣṭoma*.

Although, by the rule *yaj-deva-pūjā-saṃgati-karaṇa-dāneṣu* (Pāṇini 1.3.66) and the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacau* (Pāṇini 3.2.124), which prescribes the substitution of *śānac* for the present suffix *laṭ* after the root *yaj*, the word *yajamāna* is formed to denote the agent of actions such as the worship of deities—and since it is an ātmanepada verb, it would imply one who enjoys the fruit—nevertheless, due to its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) established through etymological connection (*yoga*), it is understood specifically as one who enjoys the fruit in a sacrifice other than his own.

Because the term *yajamāna* is observed to be applied even to those who are merely participants (*aṅga*) in the rite, and because it is not seen to apply to one who merely performs the worship of a deity, therefore, in a ritual performed by officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), he alone who is the enjoyer of the fruit is denoted by the word *yajamāna*. Furthermore, one does not see the term used for anyone who merely enjoys the fruit of the action; for there is an absence of usage for the term in cases such as the initiation (*upanayana*) and other rites governed by conventional conduct (*sāmayācārika*), even though there is an enjoyer of the fruit therein. That which is the ritual act of the *yajamāna* is what constitutes being a *yajamāna*.

Even the wife (*panyā*) is included here; because she possesses the status of a sacrificer (*yajamāna*) based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, her ritual action (*karman*) must also be understood as being comprised within this context. Thus, the analytical statement (*vigrahavākya*) is as follows: "That which is the ritual action of both the [male] sacrificer and the [female] sacrificer is what is meant by 'sacrificial' (*yājñika*)."

Although it has been established that the rites prescribed in the various Vedas have specific performers—such as the *hotṛ* and others—as determined by the designations of the *Hotṛ-veda* and so forth, nevertheless, when those rules are set aside by specific authorities (*viśeṣa-pramāṇaiḥ*), the status of the husband and wife as performers in certain instances arises; this is what is now being determined. Here, first of all, even prior to the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), the preparation of the ritual materials and the appointment of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) must be performed, for without these, the rite is not accomplished. Thus, the preparation of the substances is described.

The giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) by the sacrificer, celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and the recitation of prayers (*japa*) are included. This has been clearly stated here by Baudhāyana in his *Kalpasūtra*: "One who is about to sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma procures a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) and a black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*)," and so forth. Kauntha also says: "He procures beforehand a spread of grass, a *vaśa* plant, an animal, clarified butter, a vessel, a bowl, a jar, a *kurīra* head-net," and so forth.

Regarding this point of divergence, [the author] says: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the Agniṣṭoma. Baudhāyana used to say: "One should not initiate the King (Soma) and the sacrificer without having first seen [an auspicious omen]. After ensuring the completeness of the ritual materials, one should purify oneself along with one's wife through the performance of *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, the recitation of the *gāyatrī*, sesame oblations (*tila-homa*), breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), the *kūśmāṇḍa* oblations, the *gaṇa-homa*, pilgrimages, visiting sacred fords (*setu-darśana*), and so forth; then, permitted by the Brahmins and having pacified all enmities, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).

Based on the Vedic texts stating, "Action must be performed by one who is pure," and "One becomes purified and fit for action," it follows that for the sake of eligibility, a sequence of expiations—either combined or uncombined according to the nature of the offense—must be performed. Furthermore, based on the Smṛti stating, "Being free from enmity toward all beings, one becomes eligible for sacrifices," there is no eligibility for one who harbors such enmity. [Chapter 1, Section 150] Accompanied by the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

If it is objected: "Since the applications for one who would practice malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) are taught in such passages as 'if he should practice malevolent magic,' how can there be no qualification for an enemy?"—it is replied: Even for one who practices malevolent magic, if he is an enemy of all people, there is indeed no qualification, because he stands outside the scope of the scriptures. All of this purification must be performed for the sake of establishing qualification; furthermore, rites such as the pacification of planets (*grahaśānti*) and the pacification of water (*udakaśānti*) must be performed so that the rite one intends to undertake may reach completion without obstacles.

Since sins obstruct auspicious deeds—even those performed with devotion—and since even contrary acts bring about ruin through both visible and invisible means, therefore, for the removal of all those ancient and unknown sins which cause one's downfall and cannot be remedied by mere ritual acts, an expiation must certainly be performed; at the very least, even one who is incapable must certainly perform the *kuśmāṇḍa* oblation alone.

"One should offer the *māṇḍa* [oblation]; thereby one attains the worlds of the gods"—thus it is stated in the Śruti that it is extremely purifying. And this purification has been described by Baudhāyana in the *Karmānta*: "One who is about to perform the *agniṣṭoma* should make himself 'straight' (*prajya*), by whatever means his welfare may be secured, he should secure his welfare. "Straight" (*prajya*) means a bow from which the string has been removed; the meaning is that one makes oneself fit for one's own task through the accomplishment of purity, just as a bow is made fit for its purpose when the string is removed.

The meaning is that one should perform virtuous action by means of that which is comprised of the methods for pacification, tranquility, and so forth, such that the action becomes free from obstacles. Having first honored and satisfied all the cultured persons (*śiṣṭas*) residing in one's vicinity with due respect, the rite should be performed with their permission. Regarding this, there is a Vedic scripture: "Therefore, if one who is unlearned, lacking faith, and devoid of self-restraint performs a sacrifice, it goes only to Śaṃyu Ārhaspatya, not to the prosperity of the sacrifice."

In the *Baudhāyana-paribhāṣā* it is also stated: "Having obtained the permission of those Brāhmaṇas who are present there, they perform [the rites]; whatever he performs becomes successful for him. All of this applies to the *somapūrvādhāna* (the establishment of the sacred fires preceded by the Soma sacrifice) prior to the actual installation. As for one who has previously established the fires (*āhitāgni*), having performed the *haviryajñas*, if he has not performed the *pākayajñas*, he should perform them as well before performing the *agniṣṭoma*.

But when that sacrifice has been performed once, then even if it is impossible to perform it [again], one should perform the Agniṣṭoma after merely performing the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). And thus says the *Karmāntasūtra*: "Those obligatory rites (*nitya-karmāṇi*) which have passed their appointed time (*utthita-kālāni*), one should either perform them or seek permission for them. "Obligatory rites" refers to those rites that must be performed; "which have passed their appointed time" means those whose time has elapsed, i.e., those not yet performed. "One should perform them" means one should carry them out.

"Anujñāpayeta" means that if one is unable to perform all [the rites] together, one may proceed even without that [full performance] by means of permission; by this it is indicated that the sequence is not intended here. And it has been stated by Āśvalāyana: "Having performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, then the Iṣṭis, the Animal sacrifice, and the Cāturmāsyas, then the Soma sacrifice; or else, having performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one may perform them according to what is possible, or even before the Soma sacrifice, one by one. "Yathopapatti" means according to what is possible; the sense is that the sequence is not intended here.

The *iṣṭi* sacrifice is performed at dawn (*āyaṇa*), and the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) is performed at midday (*nirūḍha*). This is also an indicative reference to the *sautrāmaṇī*. Regarding *haviryajñas*, it should be understood that if the prescribed time exists for the second or subsequent performance, they are to be carried out; if the time does not exist, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed. On the day prior to the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), in the afternoon, the *nāndī-śrāddha* preceded by the worship of the *mātṛkās* should be performed. This is because of the Smṛti rule stated by Bodhāyana: "But the *ānikam* [is] from the afternoon. On that very night—

The water-appeasement (*udakaśānti*) and the binding of the *pratisara* amulet should be performed according to the injunctions of Baudhāyana; these two may be done either separately or within a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). Because it is a subsidiary part of that [rite], the mounting of the fire (*anurāropaṇa*) is also included. It should be understood that while there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*) in the non-performance of the water-appeasement, the binding of the *pratisara*, and the mounting of the fire, there is an abundance of merit (*phalādhikya*) in performing them. On the day of the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), the worship of Gaṇapati and the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) must be performed prior to the actual resolve.

The bathing, purifying, sipping of water (ācamana), bowing, and sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) should also be performed together, according to what is stated in the *Baudhāyana-dharmasūtra* within the *Satyāṣāḍha-śrautasūtra*. Then, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) either in the morning or at midday; for the Sūtra states: "In a complete sacrifice, the sacrificer desires that which is heard, and he causes whatever he desires to be proclaimed."

In the *Triminarmā*, the teacher [Śabara] employs the terms *jyotiṣṭoma*, *soma*, and *agniṣṭoma* in the sentence of formal resolve (*saṃkalpavākya*). While one ought simply to say "the *agniṣṭoma*," the author of the Sūtras—by using two names in the statement, "One desiring heaven, intending to sacrifice with *soma*, shall sacrifice with the *jyotiṣṭoma*"—cannot be presumed to have a purpose for uttering these multiple names other than an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). And that [unseen merit] is possible only through the utterance of the triad in the sentence of formal resolve, and not otherwise.

In this context, by the word *agniṣṭoma*, there is a specification of the sacrificial form (*saṃsthā*); by the word *jyotiṣṭoma*, there is a specification of the fourfold *stoma*; and by the word *soma*, there is a specification of the substance. The inclusion of the phrase "with the *pravargya*" in the first performance is for the purpose of determining the adoption of one or another of the optional ritual elements. Because of the primacy of the *sāman*, there is also a specification of "with such-and-such a *sāman*. Regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), since many types of offerings, numbers, and substances have been prescribed, the specification of the number and the substance to be given serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*).
Having brought the King Soma forward before the initiations (*dīkṣās*), he serves it.

By using the plural form *dīkṣābhyaḥ* instead of the singular *dīkṣāyāḥ*, it is made known that this procedure is primarily intended for the view of multiple days of initiation due to the great abundance of hardship; we shall clarify all of this in the subsequent sūtra. According to the view that the purchase (*krayaṇa*) takes place on a mountain, there is no bringing forward; however, since the serving occurs by going there itself, it is stated [in the text] specifically regarding the purchase of Soma.

Regarding the term *āhārya*, because of the use of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), it means that which is to be brought by attendants and the like; it does not mean that he should not bring it himself, nor that it should not be brought by Śūdras. Nor should it be argued that it must be brought by Kṣatriyas alone and not by Brāhmaṇas, on the grounds that since touching is strictly prohibited for them in the Smṛtis, bringing [the items] is all the more forbidden. This is because that prohibition refers specifically to touching without a valid reason, and thus does not intend to prohibit this particular act. As it is said: "A Brāhmaṇa should himself fetch the sacrificial fuel, flowers, Kuśa grass, and so forth."

"One who brings [Soma] from a Śūdra, or one who has purchased it, falls low while performing the ritual. Since this statement by Śātātapa, which prohibits bringing [Soma] from a Śūdra, includes Soma and other substances under the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the prohibition against bringing Soma for the purpose of sacrifice is also established. The word "king" (*rāja*) is used to indicate the royal honors (*rājopacāra*) accompanying the bringing of the king; these include the sounds of chariots, umbrellas, fans, conchs, musical instruments, and so forth. He "surrounds" (*pariveveṣṭi*) means he causes [the Soma] to be honored; since the purification (*pāvana*) was performed by the deity whose essence is Soma, the *pāvana* must be performed.

Āpastamba states, "with *pāyasa-odana*. This means with rice-milk (*odana*) sprinkled with milk (*payas*). Thus, the two combined constitute a single substance; a distinction between separate substances is not intended. Otherwise, the word "and" (*ca*) would have been mentioned. In the reading *pāyasaudanena*, rice cooked in milk (*payasi śṛta odanaḥ*) is to be understood. Regarding this, there is a specific detail in another Sūtra: "Having brought the King [Soma] daily in the morning and evening, and having worshipped King Soma with the formula 'Obeisance to King Soma,' one should serve him with *pāyasa-odana*."

In this context, the worship consists precisely of the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*) and ending with dismissal (*visarga*). This is because worship is impossible without invocation, and the act of purchase and so forth is impossible without dismissal. Indeed, as long as the presence of the deity (*devatāsattva*) persists, acts such as purchasing, threshing, and the like cannot take place. As for the application of the term "king" (*rāja*) seen here and there, that should be understood as referring merely to the mental conception (*bhāvanā*). However, in this case, because the status of being a deity arises specifically through the performance of the ritual of worship, dismissal is indispensable.

[Chapter 188] Accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. What is it? Otherwise, there would be no way to manage the rites such as the *kāya*. Since worship is untenable without invocation (*āvāhana*), invocation is also indispensable. For this very reason, dismissal (*visarjana*) is likewise required. Although dismissal, being included among the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), serves to complete the worship, [the rule] "having worshipped, he serves food" implies that dismissal is included within the ritual services of worship.

Although it follows that the food should be served after the dismissal [of the deities], since the presence of the deities no longer exists after the dismissal, it would be impossible to serve them; therefore, the serving must be performed prior to the dismissal. In this view, the substance for the *naivedya* offering is indeed distinct. The serving, however, takes the place of the "great offering" (*mahopahāra*). Alternatively, by the word "having worshipped" (*saṃpūjya*), worship ending with the lamps is intended. The phrase "he serves with milk-rice" is for the purpose of the *naivedya* itself. In this case, there is no separate "great offering," though the remaining ritual services (*upacāras*) certainly follow thereafter.
It is excluded from those initiations (*dīkṣā*).

That serving [of food] is excluded during the initiations—that is, on the days connected with the initiations; the plural number is used with the intention of referring to multiple initiations, such as two or more. Therefore, even in the case of a single initiation, there is indeed an exclusion of the serving. "Is excluded" means it becomes ceased. By this plural number, it is also understood that the position of multiple initiations alone is primary, because of the great amount of hardship involved.

For indeed, without austerity involving an abundance of affliction (*kleśa*), sin—which brings about suffering—is not destroyed; just as in the world, there is no healing of poisonous wounds without incision, so it is here. Nor should it be argued that the austerity prescribed for the *adhvaryu* priest in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice—such as "he does not eat for three days, he does not eat for three days"—is inappropriate, because, being of the nature of suffering, it is fit to be performed by hired laborers (*parikrīta-puruṣa*). Furthermore, it should not be said that such austerity is improper for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) because, due to its very nature as suffering, it lacks the character of being a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the enjoyer of the fruit.

Since austerity (*tapas*), although consisting of suffering, can serve as a purificatory rite for the master (*svāmi-saṃskāra*) by virtue of its power to destroy that sin which produces suffering and acts as an obstacle to the attainment of the fruit that is of the nature of future happiness; regarding this point, the authors of the *Kalpasūtras* have cited an indicative mark found in the supplementary portion of the scripture (*vākyaśeṣa*): "When the initiated one becomes emaciated..."

Then he becomes fit for sacrifice (*medhya*): when there is nothing remaining within him, then he becomes fit for sacrifice; when the blackness of his eyes disappears, then he becomes fit for sacrifice; when his skin and bone are joined together, then he becomes fit for sacrifice. He is seen as fat, yet he sacrifices emaciated; that which wanes of his limbs, it is known, he offers as an oblation (*juhoti*). "Wanes" (*mīyate*) means "decreases. Jaimini also [states]: "And austerity [is a means], because the fruit is accomplished thereby, as in the world."

This is stated by the two sūtras beginning with *vākyaśeṣaśca* and *tadvat*. The word "and" (*ca*) connects the term *yājamāna* from the sūtra *yājamānāstu tatpradhānatvātkarmavat* [JS 3.8.1], which is applied here by changing the number and gender accordingly. Thus, the sentence becomes: "And austerity (*tapas*) belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). This is because, since the result is yet to be accomplished, austerity serves as a means to achieve that result by removing the evil (*durita*) that obstructs the production of the result. This is established in the world: he who is the enjoyer of the fruit is the very same one who performs the austerity.

The meaning of the phrase "and the supplementary statement is likewise" (*vākyaśeṣaśca tadvat*) is that the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) is also equal to worldly means of knowledge (*laukikapramāṇa*), and not merely a worldly means of knowledge alone. By this, the following doubt is removed: since austerity (*tapas*) consists of suffering, it is appropriate for it to be performed only by persons who have been purchased [for the rite] because of its painful nature; consequently, due to its very quality of being pain, it lacks the inherent capacity to be a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the enjoyer of the fruit. Therefore, it is not proper for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) [to perform it]. These two sūtras are located in the eighth quarter (*pāda*) of the third chapter (*adhyāya*).

The supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa) begins with: "When the initiated one indeed becomes emaciated, then he becomes fit for sacrifice," and so forth. If it is argued that the prohibition is redundant because the phrase "prior to the initiations" alone is sufficient to ensure its non-performance on the days of initiation, we reply: True; however, there is no redundancy because that statement serves to indicate that the [prohibited] acts must be performed even on days such as the *prāyaṇīyā*, which are distinct from the days of initiation.

And likewise Āpastamba states: "Having brought the King (Soma) here, they serve him with milk-rice until the purchase. The meaning of "here" (*atretyasya*) is "immediately after the twelve *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas. By the phrase "until the purchase" (*ākrayāt*), the serving of food on the days of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is also implied; it is only that much which is prohibited by this [text]. Since the word "serves" (*parivaveṣṭoti*) is in the singular in the Sūtra, only the sacrificer (*yajan*) is meant, not the wife nor the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). On the first day of initiation as well, the bringing of the food and the serving do indeed take place.

By the statement "one does not look back," only the evening worship and the serving of food associated with the days of initiation (*dīkṣā*) obtained from other sūtras are prohibited. By this, the objection that the prohibition would otherwise have no scope in the case of a single initiation (*ekadīkṣā*) is resolved. Even on the day of departure (*prāyaṇāśā*), worship and the serving of food take place only in the morning, not in the evening.

By the word "prior" (*ākkrāya*) in the phrase "prior to the purchase" (*ākrāya*), since the necessity of performing that [act] before the purchase is established, its cessation after the purchase is established by implication alone. Here, the attendance upon the king is to be performed by means of the mantra "Behold this, O King" (*sakṣedaṃ paśya*). This is because the author of the Sūtra has demonstrated the principle that for mantras not otherwise assigned, their application should be made according to their indicative power (*liṅga*), as stated in the manner of Āpastamba. Thus is the application in that Sūtra.

It is not [performed] because it is already accomplished by the act of making known and will be refuted later; or rather, the *upasthāna* (reverential standing) occurs after the determination (*adhyavasāna*) of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*). Viyāraṇya holds that the words beginning with *sakṣa* are designations for Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya, and that the *upasthāna* belongs to those very deities.
He chooses sixteen Brahmin priests who are not descended from seers (*anārṣeya*), one by one.

Since the entitlement of Brāhmaṇas alone is already established by Smṛti, the explicit mention of "Brāhmaṇas" again is for the sake of emphasis. Alternatively, since there is a Vedic text stating, "Therefore, the officiating priests (ṛtvij) of the Vājapeya sacrifice [should be Brāhmaṇas]," it might be suspected that a Kṣatriya who has performed the Vājapeya sacrifice could also be eligible here; this statement is intended to exclude that possibility. Or else, since there are seventeen other Camasādhvaryus besides the Ṛtviks, this is for the purpose of enjoining the selection of Brāhmaṇas alone as those Camasādhvaryus, even though they are not among the [principal] Ṛtviks.

The office of officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) belongs to all three castes, since there is no difference in their learnedness. As for the rule that "officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) is for the Brāhmaṇa," this restriction stated in the Smṛti is for the sake of the person's spiritual welfare; therefore, its transgression does not result in a deficiency in the ritual (*ṛtuvaiguṇya*). This being the position, [the author replies]: Having commenced with the words "We shall explain sacrifice," the Sūtra-author’s traditional teaching (Smaraṇa) that "the office of officiating priest belongs to Brāhmaṇas" indicates the restriction as being integral to the sacrifice itself. For this very reason, it is said in the *Rāmāyaṇa*: "He whose officiating priest is a Kṣatriya is, especially so, a Caṇḍāla."

"How can the divine sages (*surarṣi*) be the partakers of his sacrificial oblation (*havis*) in the assembly?"—this means that the *suras* are the deities (*devatā*) and the *ṛṣis* are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Since the deity is not a consumer, the intent is precisely that there is a deficiency in the sacrifice (*ṛtuvaiguṇya*). Likewise, the statement, "The sacrificial oblation of one who employs a king, a brewer, or a sacrificer for a low-caste person perishes," also serves only to indicate a deficiency in the sacrifice. By this, those who have entered the livelihood of Kṣatriyas and others are also refuted.

Regarding the statement "the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) belongs to the Brāhmaṇas," one should also consider the indicative marks (*liṅga*), such as "the sacrificial oblation (*havir*) belongs to the Brāhmaṇas" and so forth. Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the office of the officiating priest belongs to the Brāhmaṇas alone. The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the mention of the Brāhmaṇas is intended to exclude Kṣatriyas and others even in times of distress (*āpad*). The office of the officiating priest belongs to the best of the twice-born (*dvijottama*), but not to the Kṣatriya or the Vaiśya; for the rule that the office of the officiating priest belongs to the Brāhmaṇas is indeed recorded as being for the sake of the sacrifice itself (*kratvartha*).

Thus say the Miśras. In the fourth quarter of the twelfth chapter, Naimini also states in the sūtra: "The office of officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) may belong to all castes because of their capability. Kātyāyana also says: "Brāhmaṇas are the officiating priests, because of the prohibition [of the office] for the other two [castes] and because of the observation [of it] for the other two. The meaning of "because of the prohibition of the *makṣa*" is as follows: "A non-Brāhmaṇa should not drink [the soma], for they heat it over the fire; therefore, a non-Brāhmaṇa should not drink. This is the sense of the prohibition regarding the *makṣa*.

And thus, since the rule for the *homa* (oblation) of the portion belonging to the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas is not [intended as] a consumption, the prohibition of eating is established. "There are two kinds of gods: the gods who are [the deities] themselves, and those Brāhmaṇas who are learned (*śuśruvāṃsaḥ*) and well-versed in the Vedas (*anūcānāḥ*), who are the human gods. For them, the sacrifice is divided into two parts: the oblations belong to the gods, and the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) belong to the human gods, the Brāhmaṇas who are learned and well-versed. Thus, by means of the oblations the gods are satisfied, and by means of the sacrificial fees the human gods, the Brāhmaṇas, are satisfied. It is for the Brāhmaṇas alone...

This is the scriptural evidence regarding this matter: the word *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee) occurs in the sense of purchase (*parikraya*). Therefore, the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) belongs to Brāhmaṇas alone. There is also a Smṛti text: "Of his six duties, three are his means of livelihood: teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts from the pure. In the phrase "of the six duties," the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). "Of him" refers to the Brāhmaṇa, because he alone was introduced in the preceding context.

If one’s livelihood cannot be sustained otherwise, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and accepting gifts may be performed; however, these are not required when one’s livelihood is already secured. The sense is that there is no sin (pratyavāya) incurred by not performing them. "Those who know their own *ṛṣis* are *ārṣeyas*. Thus, the *Vādhūla-Vaikhānasa* [Sūtra] states: "He chooses those who are *ārṣeyas*, namely those who know their own *ṛṣis*. By this, those whose lineage (*bāndhava*) is unknown are excluded. Furthermore, those who have heard [the Veda] are *ārṣeyas*. For the Śruti says: "This Brāhmaṇa is an *ṛṣi* and an *ārṣeya* who has heard [the Veda]. The *ṛṣis* are the seers of the mantras.

And so the etymologists [say]: "A seer (*ṛṣi*) is so called because he saw the hymns," says Aupamanyava; "Since the Brahman descended of its own accord upon them while they were performing austerity, they became seers; that is the seer-hood of the seers. Some teachers also state the definition: "Those whose lineage of seers is unbroken up to the tenth generation are 'of seer-descent' (*ārṣeya*). An "learned man" (*śuśruvān*) is one who has studied the three Vedas along with their meaning, or one who has studied at least his own Vedic branch. According to others, [the term refers to] Brāhmaṇas of seer-descent, as per another scriptural tradition.

This is an illustration of various characteristics [of those who should not be chosen]. They are demonstrated here as follows. In that regard, the *Dharma-sūtra* states: "One does not choose a priest (*ṛtvij*) who is not learned (*ananūcāna*), nor one who is bargaining. One who has studied and can expound the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) is called *anūcāna*. "Not" (*na*) + *anūcāna* = *ananūcāna*. One does not choose a priest who is *ananūcāna*. The meaning is: nor one who is haggling over how much should be given. The two negative particles (*na*) indicate the absolute necessity of choosing a learned priest.

The statement in the *Dharmasūtra* is for the purpose of making it known that even in the *aupāsana*, *homa*, *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka*, *vaiśvadeva*, and other such rites, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are of this same nature. It is understood from this that in these [rites], there is indeed the status of being an *ṛtvij*.
