Śāṅkhāyana also says: "One who is about to sacrifice with *soma* chooses four priests who are *ārṣeya*, *anūcāna*, and *ṛtvij*."

Bharadvāja also states: "In the spring, one who is about to perform the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice chooses as ṛtvij priests Brāhmaṇas of noble lineage (ārṣeya), who are either young or old, learned in the Vedas (anūcāna), free from physical defects, and possessing unimpaired speech. Āpastamba likewise says: "One should choose as ṛtvij priests Brāhmaṇas of noble lineage, who are either young or old, learned in the Vedas, possessing unimpaired speech, and free from physical defects. "Young" means youthful; they alone are suitable for the rite at hand.

For this very reason, they are neither too old nor children. Being between thirty and sixty years of age constitutes "old age" (*sthaviratva*). By these two [terms], the capacity for performing ritual acts is indicated. Since children and the elderly would lack proficiency in ritual action, the mention of both "the young" and "the old" is made.

This statement is made again, even though it was already established by the rule "one should not appoint a priest who has not studied [the Veda]," because there are two kinds of *anūcāna*: one who has studied the Vedas (*vedānūcāna*) and one who is proficient in ritual action (*karmānūcāna*). Among these, a person who has merely studied the Vedas is not prohibited if he lacks the capacity [to perform the rites]; however, since a person proficient only in ritual action might be eligible due to his capacity, this rule is intended to ensure that there is a prohibition even for one who lacks both types of proficiency. According to Bharadvāja, an *anūcāna* is one who has not deviated from the path.

By this, the inclusion of both types of *anūcāna* (those who have studied the Veda) has been demonstrated. Those whose speech is directed upwards—meaning those capable of producing sound through the three locations of the chest, throat, and head—are called *ūrdhvavācaḥ*. "Those not lacking limbs" means those with unimpaired limbs. Āśvalāyana says: "He chooses officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who are neither deficient nor redundant in their limbs, [both] on the mother's side and the father's side," as was stated previously; "one should choose young priests," so it is said in one place, as was stated previously.

By this [passage], the Sūtra has been demonstrated: "Those who, on both sides—maternally and paternally—through ten generations, have maintained learning and austerity and through meritorious deeds, would lead neither side to non-Brahminhood; [this applies] to the paternal side alone," so says one [teacher]. Lāṭyāyana and Drāhmāyaṇa also state: "The officiating priest (ṛtvij) and others should be learned in the Vedas (anūcāna), of good conduct, not deficient in limbs, nor having redundant limbs, born of a pure lineage, neither too dark nor too fair. Therefore, they are called *ṛtvij* because they sacrifice (*yajanti*).

And thus it is stated in the *Nirukta*: "The next eight [words] are names of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Why 'ṛtvik'? Because he impels (*īraṇa*) the sacrifice; or, according to Śākapūṇi, because he performs the sacrifice (*yajī*). In the *Chandoga-śruti*, an etymology is also given by another method: "Prajāpati desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate. He beheld the sacrificial office (*ṛtvij*) within himself and created the officiating priests. Because he created them through the sacrificial office, they are called 'ṛtviks'—this is their status as ṛtviks. The word *ṛtvik* is derived from the root *ṛ* (to go) and the suffix *dhṛk*.

The terms *ārṣeya* (descendant of a seer) and *anūcāna* (one who has studied the Vedas) have already been explained. The word *su* is used in the sense of praise. By the word *caraṇa*, action (*karman*) is meant; thus, in the expression *sādhucaraṇaḥ*, the meaning is "one whose actions are praiseworthy. *Vāgmī* means one capable of speaking. The refinement (*saṃskāra*) of speech consists in the knowledge of words, their meanings, and logic. For he who utters refined speech is *vāgmī*; likewise, he who does not speak much meaningless speech is also *vāgmī*. The suffix *-min* is applied according to the rule *vāco minic*.

For one who speaks excessively and meaninglessly is not an eloquent speaker (*vāgmī*); rather, he is called talkative (*vācāla*) or loquacious (*vācāṭa*). This is because of Pāṇini’s rule: "The suffixes *ālaC* and *aṭac* are used for one who speaks much. Furthermore, according to the Vārttika stating "these should be stated [to apply] to that which is contemptible," these two suffixes have the sense of contempt. The established meaning is: one who, when questioned, gives an answer in accordance with logic, thereby cutting through doubt when a conflict of opinions has arisen.

"Deficient" (*ūna*) means lacking; one whose limbs (*aṅga*) are deficient is "deficient-limbed" (*nyūnāṅga*). One who is not deficient-limbed is "not deficient-limbed" (*anyūnāṅga*). "Excessive" (*atirikta*) means having more than the norm; one whose limbs are excessive is "excessive-limbed" (*atiriktāṅga*). One who is not excessive-limbed is "not excessive-limbed" (*anatiriktāṅga*). The deficiency and excess of limbs are established by the characteristics of men as taught in the *Sāmudrika* treatises. One for whom there are two [limbs] equal in each respective measurement is "possessing pairs" (*dvayasas*); the meaning is that they are neither deficient nor excessive even in comparison to that.

Regarding the term *pramāṇa* (measure), according to Pāṇini’s rule *dvigossaṃjñā-mātracaḥ*, the suffix *taddhita* *yat* is applied in the sense of measure; from that, the suffix *tasi* is added. The suffix *tasi* after the simple suffix *yat* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). [The animal should be] not too black, i.e., not excessively black; not too white, i.e., not excessively white. The words *kṛṣṇa* and *śveta* denote both color and age; thus, it means not too young and not too old. [This concludes] the first section (Paṭala) with the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

They also state the definition of the sacrificer (*yājya*): "And the sacrificer is designated by the first three [qualities]. The sacrificer (*yājya*) is the one who performs the sacrifice, that is to say, the patron (*yajamāna*). He too possesses such characteristics as those of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). He is designated by the first three qualities; this is a rule where the case-ending is elided. The mention of "qualities" is for the purpose of indicating that the qualities should be understood according to their respective order for both the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya.

Baudhāyana states that the selection of the officiants is known from the *Brāhmaṇa*: "The priests shall be Brāhmaṇas endowed with noble birth, lineage, learning, and conduct; they must be free from defects, without moles, not having crossed a moat, not being *antaga* (those who have reached the end), not being *atyanta* (excessive), not being unlearned, and not being the sons of a plowman (*hāleya*), a donkey-driver (*vāleya*), a daughter's son, a son of another's field, a son born of a pregnant bride (*sahoḍha*), a son of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*), or a son of a remarried woman (*anunāvara*), nor those with two ancestral lineages (*dvipravara*). The *adhvaryu* shall be of the Aśiras family, the *brahmā* of the Śiṣṭha, the *hotṛ* of the Viśvāmitra, the *udgātṛ* of the Ayāsya, and the *sadasya* of the Kauṣītaka; they shall be Vasiṣṭhas, Bhṛgus, or Āṅgirases, possessing noble birth, conduct, and learning."

Some say that these are the criteria for selection: one should choose those whose limbs are unimpaired; one should not choose an *adhvaryu* who has deformed nails, nor a *brahmā* who suffers from white leprosy (*kilāsa*), nor a *hotṛ* who is impotent, nor an *udgātṛ* who has crooked teeth, nor a *sadasya* who is afflicted by *śipiviṣṭa*. "Yoni" refers to a pure origin; "gotra" refers to a noble lineage; "śruta" refers to Vedic study; and "vṛtta" refers to conduct. Those who are endowed with these qualities are "qualified. "Those with unimpaired limbs" means those whose limbs are not deficient. "Not having three scars" (*atrikiṇinaḥ*): those who possess three scars are "trikiṇins," and they are excluded [by the term *atrikiṇinaḥ*].

*Kiṇas* are marks appearing on the body produced by wounds, blows, and the like. Here, by the word *tri-kiṇa*, what is intended are the calluses (*kiṇas*) produced by wrestling, donning armor, snapping bowstrings, or carrying heavy loads. The meaning is that they should not possess even a single such callus among these. This is an illustration; it should be understood that they should also not possess marks produced by the repeated practice of activities not prescribed [by the scriptures].

They shall not cross the moat; that is, they shall not be sea-farers who have crossed the ocean’s boundary—the moat being the limit, namely the tide-line of the sea. This is the meaning. They shall not be "goers to the end" (*antaga*); "end" (*anta*) refers to a border region or a land of barbarians (*mleccha*). Those who go there are "goers to the end," and it is meant that they shall not be such. Furthermore, they shall not be "goers to the end" in the sense of approaching the lowest caste (*anta-varṇa*), that is, approaching a Śūdra woman; they shall not be such either.

The term "end" (*anta*) is used figuratively; it means that those who approach women who should not be approached (*agamyā*) would also not be [eligible]. Those who do not have an end (*anantāḥ*)—meaning those who do not belong to the aforementioned lineages (*deśanātāḥ*)—would not be [eligible]. Those born of a Śūdra woman would also not be [eligible]. Those who have not studied the Vedas (*ananūcānāḥ*)—that is, those who are not *otriyas*—are not to be chosen. Those who live by performing agriculture with a plow are *hāleyās*. Those who live by selling wool, fine hair, and so forth, are *vāleyās*.

At the time of giving away a daughter in marriage, [the thought] "the son who is born of her shall be my son"—with this intention, a daughter is given; the sons born of such a daughter are called *putrikāputras*. Those born in another's field by a paramour are called *parakṣetras*. One who is given while still in the womb along with his mother at the very time of the wedding is called *sahoḍha*. One born of a maiden who has not yet been married is called *kānīna*. The eldest brother who is subordinate to his younger brother is called *ānunāvara*.

The meaning is that one who is born in one *gotra* but has been given away into another *gotra*—one who thus possesses two lineages (*dvipravara*)—should not be chosen as a priest, just like a plowman (*hāleya*) and others. The alternative view, namely that they may belong to the *Vasiṣṭha*, *Mudgala*, or *Aṅgiras* [lineages], is to be understood as applying when there is the presence of specific marks (*liṅga*) characteristic of those respective *gotras*. Whatever is the *gotra* of the principal [ancestors] is the same for each triad of men belonging to those respective groups. And this refers to the position that restricts the *gotra* to the principal [ancestors]. "Pure origin" (*yoni*) means a pure birth; "conduct" (*vṛtta*) means proper behavior.

The meaning is that some teachers state that *vidyā* (knowledge) and Vedic learning are the authoritative means for determining eligibility (*varya-tā-prayojaka*). The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include proficiency in ritual action (*karma-kauśalya*). The sense is that if one should choose those who are endowed with such knowledge, ritual action, and proficiency, then one chooses only those whose limbs are not impaired. The mention of "womb" (*yoni*) and so forth is for the purpose of making known that there is no restriction regarding lineage (*gotra*).

*Kunakhī* refers to one who has deformed nails; *akunakhī* is one different from that. *Kilāsa* is a specific type of leprosy (skin disease); *akilāsī* is one different from that. *Ṣaṇḍa* means a eunuch; [the term here refers to] one different from that. *Karāla* refers to one with a hoarse voice and a distorted face; *akarāla* is one different from that. *Śipiviṣṭa* is a specific kind of disease.

The demonstration that the *adhvaryu* and other priests must not have deformed nails (*akunakhitva*) and so forth—even in the event of an extreme transgression—is for the purpose of making known the gravity of this defect: namely, that those characterized by such faults must be abandoned altogether in the performance of their respective duties. The mention of "deformed nails" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for having hands marked by scars or wounds. As stated in another *Smṛti*: "The husband should always avoid officiating as a priest (*ārtvijya*), eating at a *śrāddha*, undertaking a journey, or bathing in the ocean while his wife is in her menses."

Garga also says: "One should avoid shaving, officiating at sacrifices (*ārtvijya*), travel, anointing the body, worshipping deities in another's house, and bathing in the ocean, if one's wife is menstruating. Śāṭyāyani states: "The husband of a menstruating woman should avoid travel, officiating at sacrifices, eating at a *śrāddha*, bathing in the Indus (*sindhu*), as well as anointing the body and shaving. In another Smṛti it is also said: "When a woman in his household is either menstruating or pregnant..."

"The sage Gālava declared that one is not fit for a sacrifice or for being chosen [as a priest]": here, the mention of "sacrifice" (*yajña*) is an elliptical reference (*upalakṣaṇa*) to Śrauta rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and to Smārta rites. Devala states: "Upon the death of a great preceptor (*mahāguru*), however, one should not perform any optional (*kāmya*) rite, nor officiate as a priest (*ārtvijya*), nor practice celibacy (*brahmacarya*), nor perform a *śrāddha*, nor likewise any ritual for the gods. Some maintain that this refers to the period prior to the *sapiṇḍana* ceremony; others hold that it applies even after that.

In the *Saṃgraha*: "Brahmins associated with Telāṅga, Karṇāṭaka, Kaliṅga, and Vaṅga, as well as those from Mathurā—even if they are devotees of Śambhu—should certainly not be honored at a *śrāddha*, a wedding, or a sacrificial cooking. The source for this should be investigated. As for the statement in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "One should not offer the oblation (*havis*) to one of the same lineage, nor should a maiden [be given], nor likewise the oblation," the commentators on the *Smṛti* maintain that since it is read within the section on *śrāddha*, it refers exclusively to that subject.

Baudhāyana says: "Every officiating priest (ṛtvij), having put on a new garment, being pure, cleansed, fit for sacrifice, free from sin, observing celibacy, and relying on his assistants, should look [at the fire] until the fourth [day]. In the Saṃgraha: "Those who are disciplined, devoted to good conduct, masters of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, free from pride, envy, and the like, and devoid of hypocrisy and partiality. [This concludes] the tenth section of the Pākayajña chapter, together with the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

"Those who are tranquil, self-controlled, learned in the Vedas (anūcāna), belonging to a lineage of seers (ārṣeya), possessed of eloquence and mental composure, free from defects, most righteous, virtuous, speakers of truth, endowed with celibacy (brahmacarya), bathed graduates (snātaka), skilled in all ritual acts, looking [at the rites] up to the fourth generation, wearing unwashed garments, pure, and purified Brāhmaṇas—these are traditionally declared to be the officiating priests (ṛtvij) for the rituals. Thus, the meaning of the word *ṛtvij* is: those who, at the prescribed time, perform sacrifices—that is, they engage in activities conducive to the sacrifice.

It should be understood that this is because a sacrifice, which consists of the relinquishment of material substances, has the sacrificer as its agent. Furthermore, in the application of the term *adhvaryu* therein, mere selection (*varaṇa*) is not the cause, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of the *camasādhvaryus*.

Nor is there any contradiction here with the number seventeen in the statement, "There are seventeen *ṛtvij*s for the gentle *saumya* sacrifice," a sacrificial rite (*yajña-kratu*). Nor is the statement "there are seventeen *ṛtvij*s" a partial restatement (*avayuti-anuvāda*) intended to praise the fact that the number of priests in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* is four, in the *cāturmāsya* five, in the *paśubandha* six, and in the *saumya adhvara* seventeen—thus making seventeen the total sum of the parts. Consequently, it must be said that the status of being a *camasādhvaryu* arises by taking the act of appointment (*varaṇa*) as the cause.

The rule that "wherever a large number is mentioned, it is a partial restatement (*avayutyānuvāda*)" applies only to cases such as "he chooses one," "he chooses two," or "he chooses three," and so on, because in all those instances a large number is actually mentioned. However, in the present case, since no large number is mentioned, the quality of being a specific portion of a number is not even perceived; therefore, it is impossible to claim that this is a partial restatement. Thus, it is established that the mere act of choosing (*varaṇa*) is not the cause [for the application of the ritual].

If it is asked what [the reason] is for that, it is said: because that very thing does not exist, even that cannot be stated. Nor should it be argued that, since the *camasādhvaryus* are to be chosen from among those who perform the intermediate functions (*madhyataḥkārin*) based on the designation (*samākhyā*), and because there is an absence of choosing by the *yajanamāna* (sacrificer) regarding them, let the quality of "being chosen by the *yajanamāna*" simply persist in the general sense and cease to apply specifically to the *camasādhvaryus*.

Since the designation (*samākhyā*) is established merely by the performance of the ritual acts connected to the seven priests (*saptahotṛ*), those [Camasādhvaryus] also possess the act of choosing (*varaṇa*) as their duty because the sacrificer performs the choosing; furthermore, since the choosing is never seen to have the priests (*ṛtvij*) as its agents, there is no exclusion of the Camasādhvaryus [from that category]. Why do you thus frighten me with the technical language of the established system (*prasiddhabhāṣā*) regarding the limbs? I am not afraid, for I obtain a specific distinction of choosing pertaining to the Brahman and other priests. And that [distinction] is to be inferred from the force of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in the mantra used for the choosing of the Camasādhvaryus.

And that indicative mark (*liṅga*) is the ray (*raśmi*); that this alone is the "word" (*pada*) will be explained later. That this very thing constitutes the non-primary status of being a priest (*ṛtviktva*) will also be explained later. The intermediate generality of "being chosen" (*varaṇa*), which persists among the *brahmā* and others but is excluded from the *camasādhvaryu*s, is the cause for the word *ṛtvij*. Sacrificing at the ritual (*ṛtuyajana*) residing in the *brahmā* and others is likewise the cause for the word *ṛtvij*, just as the state of being the *itihartṛ* residing in the animal is the cause for the word *itihartṛ*. And thus, because its constituent parts are well-known and because of the scriptural mention of a number, the word *ṛtvij* is caused solely by the specific act of sacrificing at the ritual.

And thus, there is no abandonment of the well-known etymological power of the word's components, nor the undesirable consequence of postulating an unseen secondary power (*adṛṣṭa-śakti*); nor does there arise a contradiction with the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) that ordains the formation of the noun *ṛtvij* from the root *yaj* with the suffix *kvip* (as in *ṛtvig dadhṛg...*); nor is there a contradiction with the traditional legal text (*smṛti*) stating, "An *ṛtvij* is called one who performs the sacrifice. Furthermore, the scriptural statement regarding the number seventeen (*saptadaśatva-śruti*) becomes logically established, and the injunction for the formal selection (*varaṇa-vidhi*) comes to have its meaning well-known: just as much as is expressed by "he selects the sacrificers" (*yājakān vṛṇīte*), so much is expressed by "he selects the *ṛtviks*" (*ṛtvijo vṛṇīte*).

Therefore, there is no lack of well-known meaning for the words. However, if they were based on the act of choosing (*varaṇa*), there would be a lack of well-known meaning for words such as *yūpa* (sacrificial post) and others, as well as a reversal of the syntactical construction; and this is not logical. Since words such as *adhvaryu* lack a conventional meaning, those very persons who are designated by the master of the sacrifice through their roles as *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, and so forth—based solely on determination—are what are meant by the terms *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, and the rest. [This concludes] the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [in the tenth praśna]. The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the tenth praśna]—there is a lack of well-known meaning for the words, and furthermore, there would be a reversal of the syntactical expression. And this is not proper. But because words such as *adhvaryu* lack conventional usage, those very individuals who are determined by the master of the sacrifice through their functions as *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, and so on, are indeed the ones referred to as *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, and the rest.

Therefore, because its constituent parts are well-known and because of the scriptural mention of a specific number, the word *ṛtvij* is caused solely by the particularity of officiating at a sacrifice. In this way, the over-extension [of the term] to the *camasādhvaryus* is avoided. The detailed exposition should be consulted in the original source (*ākara*). Jaimini states all of this in the seventh section (*pāda*) of the third chapter: "The status of being an *ṛtvij* belongs to all [participants] because there is no distinction in their ritual function," and "it is not so, because of the restrictive enumeration."

Even though the meaning of the *Adhvaryu-sūtra* is "because there is no distinction" (*aviśeṣāt*)—that is, because where there is no distinction, it is "without distinction"—and this [term] is a qualification of the phrase "from the performance of the ritual action" (*karmakāryāt*), meaning "from the state of being a performer of the ritual action" (*karmakārya*) due to the status of being a ritual agent (*karmakartṛtva*); the meaning of the preceding sūtra is that because there is no distinction—that is, because the performance of the ritual action is equal for all including the *camasādhvaryus*—there is the status of being a priest (*ṛtviktva*) for all of them. It is not [the case that] the *camasādhvaryus* [are excluded].

The meaning of the subsequent sūtra is that the state of being a *brahmā* and so forth does not exist [in the case of the *udgātṛ*] as it does for those who have attained the status of *brahmā* and others, because of the restrictive enumeration of the number seventeen. Terms such as "the *udgātṛ* is one who sings the *udgītha*" are designations based on ritual action (*karmanimitta*). However, in the case of the *brahmā* and others, [the titles arise] from "expanding" (*vṛhaṇāt*) through ritual action—that is, by means of overseeing (*avekṣaṇa*), binding, and regulating. Furthermore, the *brahmā* and others are also [designated] as "hotṛ" through etymological derivations such as "he is the Brahman."

The Adhvaryu priest joins the sacrifice; Agni brings the gods, as in the formulas "O Agni, bring the gods" and "O Agni, bring Soma," he thus causes the gods to be brought by means of Agni. Regarding the statement "he joins the sacrifice," since there exists another agent, the number of agents would be determined by the task—namely, however many are required to accomplish the ritual action at that point—rather than being restricted to this specific number, because no such distinction is perceived. This is the meaning of the sūtra.

At the time of the choosing (*varaṇa*), since it is impossible for [the act] to have the ritual action (*karman*) as its motive, it must be stated that the choosing itself is the motive. For multiple choosings do not coexist in a single person, because they serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). Indeed, the choosing of one who has already been chosen does not serve a visible purpose. Therefore, because the choosings and the names which are their motives have non-overlapping domains, the distinction among performers—both as many as there are choosings and as many as there are names—is an auxiliary element of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*).

Jaimini stated all of this in the third chapter, seventh section: "In that case, there should be no restriction on the number of performers, because there is no specific distinction. Therefore, the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is accomplished by that many performers. By this, the view that the term [refers to] a single person performing the action like a cook or a butcher is refuted, because these designations are not heard at the time of undertaking the action nor at any time subsequent to it. For the formal selection (*varaṇa*) is a request made prior to the commencement of the action, and in the *satra* sacrifice, that selection ceases due to the disappearance of its purpose.

Even in the absence of formal appointment (*varaṇa*), the conventional usage—such as "having initiated the Adhvaryu and the Gṛhapati"—is observed. And that [usage] would be inexplicable without accepting that the cause [of the designation] is intention (*saṃkalpa*); therefore, one must necessarily accept that intention is the cause. For even in the archetype (*prakṛti*), intention alone is the cause; for he who, though present, does not desire [the office], does not become a Hotṛ, an Adhvaryu, or the like. Therefore, since the appointment is enjoined in the archetype, it is the intention itself, conjoined with that [appointment], which is the cause.

In the case of *satras*, however, it is merely figurative (*bhākta*), because we observe the use of terms such as "adhvaryu" and so forth therein. Nor should it be thought that this is unseemly due to such inconsistency; for by the force of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*), precisely such usage is indeed seemly. Indeed, there is no evidence whatsoever for the terms "hotṛ," "adhvaryu," and so on, to be used in a figurative sense in the *satras*.

Furthermore, if there is an insistence that it must exist with absolute uniformity of form, then the cause is indeed the mental resolve (saṃkalpa). At the commencement of the sacrifice, whoever resolves for himself the state of being the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, and so forth, he is designated by such terms as "Hotṛ" and "Adhvaryu. [End of] Chapter 130, with the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

And so the author of the *Pārtika* will state in the section concerning how all [the priests] attain the status of *ṛtvij* through their performance of ritual acts: "In the *satras*, because the requirements of being chosen (*varaṇa*) and being supported (*bharaṇa*) are not needed, there is no deficiency even without those two, since they are not required. In that case, the status of *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, and so forth is established by mere eligibility alone.

Among the *sūtras* of Jaimini, after the initial *sūtra*—"The number [of officiants] should be indefinite, because there is no specific distinction"—and having inserted several other *sūtras* in between, the subsequent *sūtra* was composed: "All [are entitled to the office of] an *ṛtvij* because of their lack of distinction from those performing the ritual action. Here, the word *ṛtvij* refers primarily (*mukhya*) only to the sixteen [officiants], since they alone are enumerated in that preceding *sūtra*. However, since the seventeenth, the *sadasya*, is also enumerated in certain views, he too is included as a primary *ṛtvij*.

Nor should it be argued that since the *camasādhvaryus* (cup-bearers) also perform the selection accompanied by mantras, they too must possess the status of primary priests (*ṛtvij*). For, since the *camasādhvaryus* are constantly engaged in their duties, if one were to include them along with the others when determining the number, the mention of the number sixteen would result in a contradiction. The same applies to the occasional mention of the number seventeen.

For this very reason, the Mīmāṃsakas have established the conclusion that the word *eka* (one) is used as a cause for a specific sacrifice to the Master (*bhartṛ-yajana*), because the number [of cups] is not heard in the scriptural injunction regarding the well-known parts [of the ritual]. However, the selection (*varaṇa*) accompanied by mantras, even in the absence of the previous selection, serves a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) based on the context (*pāñcikam*). Since an independent selection is prescribed, it is also understood from this that the *camasādhvaryus* are distinct from the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Thus, Jaimini states in the seventh section of the third chapter: "And the *camasādhvaryus* are separate, because of their designation."

The meaning of the Sūtra is that the *camasādhvaryus* are distinct because they are designated as separate from the three [classes of priests]: "the *camasādhvaryus* of the *madhyataḥkārins*," "the *camasādhvaryus* of the *hotrakas*," and so forth. Furthermore, their status as auxiliary members (*aṅga*) is established by the indicative power of the mantra (*mantraliṅga*); just as the sun is the principal entity and its rays are its constituent parts, so too the *camasādhvaryus* are the constituent parts of the *adhvaryu*. Since it is impossible for the *adhvaryu* alone to perform the libations from all the *camasa* cups at once, these [priests] are appointed as his subordinates (*taccheṣatvena*).

For this very reason, they have the designation "camasādhvaryu" (cup-attendants). For this same reason, it is established that whatever specific distinction exists among the *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, and others does not exist among them. For this reason as well, their status as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is secondary. As for their number, the author of the Sūtras himself will state: "For all [of them], there is a cup-attendant for each person. Jaimini also states in the third chapter, seventh section: "But at the origin, because of the plurality of the word."

Regarding the rule "one should choose the *camasādhvaryu*s," since plurality is heard in the originative injunction (*utpatti*), the meaning is that there are indeed many *camasādhvaryu*s. Furthermore, the fact that there are ten is established through the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*). Once plurality is established, as to how many there are among the many—there being no fixed rule and three being the default minimum—it must be ten because of the ten cups (*camasa*s). Since there is no evidence for a higher number, there are exactly ten.

Nor should it be argued that since a single person can offer from two cups simultaneously using both hands, how is it that there must be ten *camasādhvaryu* priests even when there are only ten cups? The point is that one should not offer from two cups with both hands at once; for this is prohibited in other recensions (*śākhāntara*), and because of the rule that an action must be performed with the right hand, offering with both hands is improper.

In the *Daśapeya*, which is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, there is a statement in the remainder of the injunction: "Ten by ten they follow each cup," followed by the phrase "There are ten *camasādhvaryu* priests. From the observation of this indicative mark (*liṅga*), which takes the form of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the number ten, the meaning is that the number ten applies to the officiants in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Nor should it be argued that the status of being a *camasādhvaryu* priest is merely figurative (*gauṇa*) and therefore not established.

In the absence of universal ownership (*sarvasviktva*), the selection (*varaṇa*) accompanied by mantras would be untenable, and furthermore, the performance of the cup-offering (*camasayāga*) would be impossible; moreover, for the sake of obtaining the status of a *pratiprasthātṛ*, that [universal ownership] must necessarily be admitted. It is precisely to indicate this that the author of the Sūtra used the term "all" (*sarva*). Due to the absence of primary ownership, the *japa*, the *abhimantraṇa*, the *janana*, and the *tānūnaptra* and so forth do not apply to them at all.

This is not a restrictive rule that only those who are chosen with a mantra are the primary officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). For if it were, it would result in the absence of such priests in rites like the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). If one were to accept that consequence, it would be impossible for them to act as the primary performers of the sacrifice. Therefore, this is established: among the *camasādhvaryus*, there is no primary status of being an officiating priest at all.

The mention of "sixteen" is for the purpose of excluding the *sadasya*, or else to demonstrate that even in the case of choosing four priests, their status as non-*ṛtvij*s is equal to that of those chosen without a mantra. By this, it is established that the observance of vows (*vrata-caryā*) indeed occurs in all cases, even for those chosen without a mantra. The expression "one by one" is intended to exclude a collective choice. This choice is purely worldly and distinct [from the ritual], because of the inclusion of the scriptural statement: "O Agni, choose him again."

For this very reason, even the statement "one by one" (ekaikaśaḥ) becomes appropriate. Otherwise, since the purpose [of the selection] would already be accomplished through the distinctness of the mantras in the case of the selection accompanied by mantras, the statement "one by one" would be redundant. This applies to the selection of the *hotraka* priests and the selection of the *pratiprasthātṛ* and others.

Furthermore, because the specific ṛc, yajuḥ, tiṅ, and noun designations for each respective person are not indicated within the mantras, and because it would be impossible to carry out the procedure through the "selection without mantras" (*amantraka-varaṇa*) alone—since titles such as "Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin" cannot be known from the mantras themselves—the "selection without mantras" is indeed necessary. By this, it is also understood that the *somapravāka* should bring all the other priests to the house of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and perform the invitation there.

And this first selection (*varaṇa*) is common to all. However, the second selection accompanied by a mantra applies only to the four [officiants] in the case of the fourfold selection; for those other than the *mahartvij*, their requirement is fulfilled by the first selection alone. It should be understood that for the *hotṛ* and others, the second, worldly selection is indeed required for the purpose of the mantra-consecration (*mantra-saṃskāra*).

The Hotṛ, Maitrāvaruṇa, Acchāvāka, and Grāvastut are the Hotṛs; the Adhvaryu, Pratiprasthātṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Unnetṛ are the Adhvaryus; the Brahman, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Āgnīdhra, and Potṛ are the Brahmans; and the Udgātṛ, Prastotṛ, Pratihartṛ, and Subrahmaṇya are the Udgātṛs.

The term "hotṛ" is used [in the plural] in order to establish the designation "hotṛ" for the Maitrāvaruṇa, Acchāvāka, and Grāvastut as well; the purpose of this is that, in the passage "the second is the hotṛ," the Maitrāvaruṇa is included by the mention of the word "hotṛ. Furthermore, under the view that the selection (*varaṇa*) of all [these priests] is accompanied by mantras, the mantra for the selection of the hotṛ is also applied during the selection of the Grāvastut. Similarly, the term "adhvaryu" [is used in the plural] to include the Pratiprasthātṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Unnetṛ as well.

For the sake of establishing the designation "Udgātṛ," the Adhvaryus take up that [cup] in such injunctions as "the Adhvaryus should drink four [cups]," whereby the Pratiprasthātṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Unnetṛ are included; furthermore, when there is the selection of the Pratiprasthātṛ and Unnetṛ, the mantra for the selection of the Adhvaryu is applied. Similarly, in the term "Udgātṛs," the inclusion of the Prastotṛ, Pratihartṛ, and Subrahmaṇya is for the sake of establishing the designation "Udgātṛ" for them as well.

In such cases as "The Udgātṛs move the Droṇakalaśa forward" and "They lift it up and pull it down below the axle," there is the inclusion of both the Prastotṛ and the Pratihartṛ. Furthermore, in the selection (*varaṇa*) of the Prastotṛ, Pratihartṛ, and Subrahmaṇya, the mantra of the Udgātṛ is employed. Regarding the performance of all duties, the sequence of officiants (*gaṇakrama*) is as follows: first the four principal priests (*mukhya*), then the four *adhina*s, then the four *tṛtīyina*s, and then the four *pādina*s; such is the order.

The common purpose for establishing the fourfold designation—namely *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, *brahmā*, and *udgātṛ*—should be understood as follows: by this enumeration, the total number [of officiating priests] is also determined. Furthermore, by this, the status of the *camasādhvaryus* as *ṛtviks* is also excluded. The inquiry as to who constitutes the "sixteen possessors" (*ṣoḍaśinaḥ*) is also fulfilled by this. In the third chapter, seventh section, Jaimini also states: "But there is a restriction [regarding the sacrificial fee] because of its connection with the scriptural injunction; he gives the fee to the *ṛtviks* and to the *agnīdh*."

[Section 1, Chapter 1] Accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. If it is recited together with the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) in such a manner as "he gives to the Brahman, he gives," then because the final resolution is "he gives to the Agnidh priest, to the Brahman priest," etc., there arises a connection based on grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) through the scriptural mention (*śruti*) of the word "priest" (*ṛtvij*). From that, the meaning of the Sūtra is that there would be a restrictive rule (*niyama*) that the status of being a priest belongs only to those starting from the Agnidh.
The Sadasya is the seventeenth.

The statement regarding the "seventeen" is intended to demonstrate that for this person as well, the status of being a *ṛtvij* (priest) is primary—just as it is for the *hotṛ* and others—and not a lack of primary *ṛtvij*-status like that of the *camasādhvaryu*s. This is because, in the *sūtra* prescribing the ritual selection (*varaṇa*) accompanied by mantras, the selection of the *sadasya* is ordained after the selection of the *udgātṛ*; therefore, the selection follows that sequence and does not occur after the selection of the sixteen *ṛtvij*s. Bharadvāja states: "The Kauṣītakins record the *sadasya* as the fifth great priest (*mahartvij*)."

One should choose seventeen Brahmins who are of noble lineage (*ārṣeya*) and learned (*ṛṣi*); since the inclusion of the *sadasya* (the presiding priest) is already accomplished by this much alone, the separate mention [of him] is intended to indicate his non-obligatory status. This has been stated by both Āpastamba and Āśvalāyana: "The followers of Kauṣītaki record the *sadasya* as the seventeenth. Those same two authorities have stated the purpose of the *sadasya*: "He becomes a supervisor (*upadraṣṭṛ*) of the rituals. Supervision (*upadraṣṭṛtva*) consists in the capacity to reflect upon what is well-done and what is ill-done.

Āśvalāyana states that the Kauṣītakins prescribe the *sadasya* as the seventeenth [member], and having said this, he cited the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) which serves as authority for this point: "He whom the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) fashion in many ways," as stated in two *ṛg*-verses. Regarding the existence of the *sadasya*, there is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in our own branch of the Veda: "The seasons became the *sadasyas*. Here, the plural number is used in accordance with the plurality of the seasons. However, the fourfold number of *sadasyas* mentioned by Baudhāyana is not accepted by the Teacher (Āśvalāyana).

Because it is shown that the *sadasya* is the seventeenth, as in the expression "the seventeenth [member] of the assembly," and because there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the independent injunction for the prince's appointment for the purpose of constant supervision;
then he chooses the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

The word "with mantras" (*mantraiḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. The word "atha" (then) signifies immediate succession after all worldly selection (*laukika-varaṇa*). Therefore, having performed the worldly selection of the *hotṛ*, his very same selection with mantras must be performed immediately thereafter. In this way, for the *adhvaryu* and others as well, it is established that there is no "sequential performance by parts" (*padārthānusamaya*) here, but rather only "sequential performance by sections" (*kāṇḍānusamaya*). Furthermore, it serves to indicate the primacy [of the mantra-based selection].

By this, it is also established that even among those who have become one's father or among humans, there must indeed be a formal selection accompanied by mantras in order to obtain the consecration of the mantra.

The *Śāṭyāyanins* have stated that there is a threefold classification of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) based on their status as human-beings, ancestors, or gods: "Those who are chosen for each specific ritual by [the patron] himself are 'human-beings'; those who are chosen by the ancestors and so forth, yet accepted by [the patron] himself, are 'ancestors'; and those who are chosen by [the patron] himself for the sake of lifelong rituals are 'gods'. He has also described their nature in this same way. In this context, one must necessarily accept that the word *ṛtvij* applies to both the secondary and primary types alike.

Otherwise, there would be an absence of their performance of vows (*vrata-caryā*) and the impossibility of the formal selection accompanied by mantras (*samantraka-varaṇa*). Furthermore, it has already been stated previously that primary priestly status (*mukhya-ṛtviktva*) cannot be accepted, as it would result in the contradiction of having to adopt either sixteen or seventeen priests. The former selection is worldly (*laukika*); this [present one] is with mantras, for the sake of accomplishing a transcendental purification (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*) through the mantra. The sequence of the worldly and the mantra-accompanied selections is indeed distinct and different.

"Divine" means pertaining to the gods; "human" means pertaining to humans. In place of the word "this one" (*asau*), he utters the name that has been given by the father or others for the sake of worldly transaction with the Hotṛ priest. And that name should end in *śarman*, because of Baudhāyana’s statement, "The name of a Brāhmaṇa ends in *śarman*," and because of the Vāsiṣṭha Sūtra, "By which [name] one is transacted with. The phrase "by which one is transacted with" is intended to exclude names derived from lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and so forth from having the suffix *śarman*.

*Varaṇa* (the choosing) means the performance of an inclination conducive to carrying out one’s own duty as an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), preceded by honoring and worshiping; therein, the presence of the *sambhakṣaka* (the partaker of the soma-residue) is for the sake of a specific refinement (*saṃskāra*). The mantra for choosing the divine Hotṛ is: "Agni is the divine Hotṛ; may he be my Hotṛ. The mantra for choosing the human Hotṛ is: "I choose so-and-so as the human Hotṛ. From the indicative mark (*liṅga*) itself, [it follows that] this is the choosing of the divine Hotṛ.

Since the purpose of the preceding mantra will already be accomplished [by the general rule], its repetition is for the sake of demonstrating the reason: "because he is the divine *hotṛ*, therefore one should choose him in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). The same applies to the rule "the human [should be chosen] loudly" (*uccaiḥ*). Although the word *upāṃśu* appears to be syntactically connected with the choosing of the divine *hotṛ*, nevertheless, because the word *upāṃśu* refers to a pitch (accent), and since that pitch is a property of the mantra, it cannot be connected directly with the act of choosing itself; rather, its connection must be understood as being with the mantra which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the act of choosing.
And thus there is this statement: "Having recited the mantra 'abhir deva' in a low voice (upāṃśu), one should choose the divine Hotṛ. The same applies in subsequent cases as well.
Thus, in the other instances, one chooses the divine [Hotṛ] in a low voice and the human [Hotṛ] loudly.

Since the choice of both divine and human [priests] would be established by the mere statement "so for the others," the repetition—"he chooses the divine, he chooses the human"—is intended to make known that in the silent (amantraka) choosing during the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites, this very mental visualization (*abhidhyāna*) is mandatory, namely: "This is the divine Agni, the Hotṛ; this is the human [Agni]. If only "so for the others, he chooses the divine and the human" were stated, there might be the exclusion of the low-voiced (*upāṃśu*) and loud (*svaiṣṭhya*) [recitations]; to prevent that, those two [terms] are mentioned.
"In the others" refers to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), such as the Adhvaryu and so forth.

"The Sun is the divine Adhvaryu; may he be my divine Adhvaryu, and this one here is the human [Adhvaryu]; I choose that Adhvaryu. "The Moon is the divine Brahman; may he be my divine Brahman, and this one here is the human [Brahman]; I choose that Brahman. "Parjanya is the divine Udgātṛ; may he be my divine Udgātṛ, and this one here is the human [Udgātṛ]; I choose that Udgātṛ. "Space is the divine Sadasya; may he be my divine Sadasya, and this one here is the human [Sadasya]; I choose that Sadasya."

"The divine waters are the members of the assembly; may they be my *hotrāśaṃsins*. These are the human ones; I choose them as the *hotrāśaṃsins*," [he says] regarding the *hotrakas*. "The rays are the gods; they are the divine *camasādhvaryus*; may they be my *camasādhvaryus*. These are the human ones; I choose them as the *camasādhvaryus*," [he says] regarding the *camasādhvaryus*. || 1 ||

From the indirect indication in the mantras, "choose him," it is understood that the selection is made through some intermediary and not directly. Because he is the one present at hand, the author of the Bhāṣya, with the intention that it refers specifically to the Soma-pravāka (the Soma-invoker), has stated in his commentary—along with his followers, the authors of the Prayogas—that the selection is made through the Soma-pravāka. This is because, in the cases of the giving, the recitation, the touching, the choosing of the bridegroom, and the authority of the vow, the sacrificer is the one perceived. [1st Paṭala, Jyotsnā Commentary by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa] 1001. Selection through the Soma-pravāka is declared; [this applies to] the giving, the recitation, the touching, the choosing of the bridegroom, and the authority of the vow, wherein the sacrificer is the one perceived.

This must be disregarded because it contradicts the *Ditikaatyayana-sutra*. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the indirect reference by means of the word "that" (*tat*) occurring in the mantra would be inconsistent; for, by referring with the word "that" to the divine Hotṛ priest Agni and mentally connecting it with the meaning of the word "you" (*yuṣmad*), one can avoid the charge of inconsistency through the identification of the referents of the words "that" and "you," resulting in the sense: "I choose that very same divine Hotṛ priest, you, as my own. Thus, the possibility of resolving the inconsistency exists.

In this way, the contradiction with the *Kātyāyana-sūtra* is fully resolved. The word *bhadaḥ*, however, is employed for the purpose of mentioning their respective names. Furthermore, the mention of the name in place of the word *bhadaḥ* is established by the sūtra located in the section on the announcement (*āvedana*), which states: "And when [the officiant] has arrived, he mentions the name. The meanings of the terms *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, *brahmán*, and *udgātṛ* have already been shown previously. A *sadasya* is one who exists in the assembly (*sadas*). Here, "existence" (*bhavana*) means being present (*sattā*, *vidyamānatva*). This is a term that is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*).

The suffix *ya* is applied according to the rule beginning with *digādi*. By this word *sadasya*, it is understood that the sitting (*upaveśana*) of one who belongs to the assembly (*sadasya*) is intended. Alternatively, *sadasya* means "one who is good (*sādhu*) in the assembly" or "beneficial (*hita*) to it. Here, by the word *sada*, the entire ritual action performed within the sacrificial hall (*sada-maṇḍapa*) is indicated; because of its connection to that [hall], its quality of being "good" or "beneficial" should be understood. *Hotra* refers to the means of offering, namely the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance; those who recite or speak that loudly are called *hotrāśāsinaḥ*.

Furthermore, in the view that the Hotṛ priest himself sits down and performs the sacrifice (*yajate*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the term [to the sacrificer or the Adhvaryu]; for since it has already been stated that the choosing of the Hotrakas constitutes the choosing of the Hotrāśaṃsin priests, and since it is shown by the passage "The Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, Acchāvāka, and Āgnīdhra are the Hotrakas" that the application of the word *hotraka* is restricted to these six—namely, the Maitrāvaruṇa and the others—there is no over-extension of the term to the Hotṛ, the sacrificer, or the Adhvaryu.

And thus, the Hotṛ, Yajamāna, and Adhvaryu are not included by the term *hotrāśaṃsin*. By this, even the suspicion that—despite the Hotṛ, Yajamāna, and others having been chosen with their respective mantras—a further choice is required for the sake of the mantra-consecration characterized by the mark of *hotrāśaṃsin*—is also refuted. The word *amī* is the nominative plural of the pronoun *adas*.

In place of the word *amī* (these), having taken the names of the six *hotṛ* priests ending in *śarman* in their respective order using the first case plural form in compound, he should choose them with the formula: "I choose these human ones as the reciters of the *hotṛ* formulas" (*mānuṣāstān hotrāśasino vṛṇe*). For example: "I choose Keśavaśarman, Nārāyaṇaśarman, Mādhavaśarman, Govindaśarman, Viṣṇuśarman, and Kṛṣṇaśarman as the human reciters of the *hotṛ* formulas. Alternatively, the word *śarman* may be used only once at the end of all [the names].

The sequence here should be understood as follows: Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, Acchāvāka, and Āgnīdhra. And thus, the plural form "itibahuvacanānta" refers to the meaning of the word *yuṣmad* (you). This same principle is to be observed in the mantra for the selection of the Camasādhvaryus as well. Here too, in the selection of the Camasādhvaryus, the sequence should be taken as: Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Brahman, Udgātṛ, Prastotṛ, Mānasadasya, Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, Acchāvāka, and Āgnīdhra.

The *camasādhvaryus* are those who are connected to the *namasa* (the *namasa*-cup). Here, the relationship is one of the nature of the supported and the supporter (*dhārya-dhāraka-bhāva*). And that supporting is for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*) and so forth. However, for the *pratiprasthātṛ* and others, it is by way of their respective primary officiating roles (*mukhya-adhvaryu*).

In that regard, the selection of the Pratiprasthātṛ and the others is performed by using the very terms "Adhvaryu" and so forth—specifically, the Pratiprasthātṛ with the mantra of the Adhvaryu, the Prastotṛ with the mantra of the Udgātṛ, the Pratihartṛ with the mantra of the Udgātṛ, the Grāvastut with the mantra of the Udgātṛ, the Unnetṛ with the mantra of the Adhvaryu, and the Subrahmaṇya with the mantra of the Udgātṛ. Nor should it be argued that, for the sake of identifying the Pratiprasthātṛ and the others, one should also employ the terms "Pratiprasthātṛ" and so on following the terms "Adhvaryu" and so on.

Since the knowledge of the Pratiprasthātṛ and others is obtained through the very act of their selection (*varaṇa*), there is no reason to employ additional words that would disrupt the essential nature of the mantra by being redundant. Following the selection of the *hotraka* priests, the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha (10.2) prescribes the selection of the Pratiprasthātṛ and others. This is because, compared to the secondary cup-bearers (*gauṇacamasādhvaryu*), the Pratiprasthātṛ and others are primary officiants (*mukhyartvik*); therefore, it is logical that they should be selected first.

Immediately after the worship of the King [Soma], the *somapravāka* must necessarily be chosen by the officiant (*ṛtvij*) for the purpose of issuing the invitation. He is called the *somapravāka* because he speaks (*vakti*) to the officiants in order to determine their engagement in the sacrificial duties (*ārtvijya*) favorable to the Soma sacrifice. From this very name, the purpose of the *somapravāka* is understood. Furthermore, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the existence of the *somapravāka* in the statement: "In the *sādyaska* sacrifices, horse-chariots with well-groomed horses and seven *somapravākas* run."

The Lāṭyāyana, Drāhyāyaṇa, Mānava, and Āśvalāyana [Śrautasūtras] prescribe this as a constant rule. Therefore, one must certainly choose a person named Somapravāka for the purpose of addressing him. And he [is chosen] silently, because no specific mantras are taught for it. His worship with perfumes and other offerings, as well as the giving of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to him according to one's ability, should take place; or alternatively, the giving of the dakṣiṇā may occur at the time of the actual distribution of fees.

The procedure for the selection of the *somapravāka* and so forth is as follows: After the worship of the King (Soma), the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) chooses him, saying, "In this sacrifice, be you the *somapravāka*. When he has replied, "So be it," the sacrificer honors him with perfumes, garments, and other offerings, and says to him, "Procure Soma from the other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*s). Sent by the sacrificer, the *somapravāka* approaches each priest who possesses the aforementioned qualities, brings them all to the sacrificer’s house, and there performs the formal invitation.

In that regard, the formal request (*āmantraṇa*) for the *praṇava* is as follows: "The Soma sacrifice of [Name] Śarman will take place; therein, you must perform the duties of the Hotṛ, the duties of the Adhvaryu, the duties of the Brahman, the duties of the Udgātṛ, the duties of the Praśāstṛ, the duties of the Pratiprasthātṛ, the duties of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the duties of the Prastotṛ, the duties of the Acchāvāka, the duties of the Neṣṭṛ, the duties of the Āgnīdhra, the duties of the Pratihartṛ, the duties of the Grāvastut, the duties of the Unnetṛ, the duties of the Potṛ, and the duties of the Subrahmaṇya. If the Sadasya is included, "the duties of the Sadasya" should be added.

In this sūtra, *hotrābhyaścha*, the word *hotrā* refers specifically to the *hotrakas*. Accordingly, the suffix *cha* is applied only to the *praśāstṛ*, *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, *potṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, and *acchāvāka*, and not to the *pratiprasthātṛ*, *prastotṛ*, *pratihartr̥*, *unnetṛ*, or *subrahmaṇya*. From the word *grāvastut*, however, the suffix *cha* is applied by the rule *vṛddhāccha*. From the word *brahman*, the suffix *tva* is applied by the sūtra *brahmaṇastva*.

However, it should be understood that the suffix *aṇ* is applied in a general sense after the words *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, and *gātṛ*. Regarding this, one mode of questioning—concerning "What is the sacrifice? Who are the officiating priests? What is the sacrificial fee?"—is set forth by Āpastamba, Āśvalāyana, and others. In the response sentences, a specific rule is stated by Āśvalāyana: "The association [of the names] with auspicious [terms]. Thus: "Such-and-such is an auspicious sacrifice; such-and-such Śarmans and others are auspicious officiating priests; the cows are auspicious sacrificial fees."

Another method of questioning has been stated by Āpastamba: "He asks him: 'Who are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); who are they that sacrifice for [others]? Is it not an *ahīna* [sacrifice]? Has the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) not been abandoned? Are the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) auspicious? The mention of the *Chandoga-brāhmaṇa* here is intended to indicate an option. The examination of the priests is for the purpose of removing doubts regarding defects in the sacrificer, such as having sacrificed for outcasts (*patita-yājita*). The examination of the current [priests] is also for the purpose of removing doubts regarding their incapacity due to having consumed [forbidden substances]."

[Chapter 150, with the commentary Jyotsnā by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa: "One who intends to perform [the sacrifice] should cause [the animals] to be led forward one by one. According to the opinion of Bhāradvāja, the recitation (japa) is obligatory even for one who is not himself performing the sacrifice. The cattle-herder, the attendants, the Dhātṛ, the Śamitṛ, the Dhruvagopa, the Dohya, the Soma-vendor, a woman for the purpose of seeking sacrificial materials (haviṣyeṣaṇa), two women for the purpose of driving the cows for the Agniṣomīya animal, and the Prasarpakas and Upagātṛs—these should be prepared right here.

The *paśupāla* is the guardian of animals to be sacrificed, of living beings such as cows and other livestock intended for sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), of milch-cows, and of oxen used for carrying the king’s vehicles; this person is a Vaiśya, because his livelihood consists of that work. The *preṣyās* are those who carry out the tasks assigned to them, such as the *sanīhāras* and others, as well as the attendants (*parikarmins*) who bestow the vows. The term *sanīhāra* refers to those who bring back (*haranti*) the wealth obtained through begging (*sani*). By this it is understood that the materials required for the sacrifice have already been requested beforehand.

These [officiants] are Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas. Regarding the *sanīhāra* (the procurement of materials), a distinction is stated by Baudhāyana in the *Dvaidha-sūtra*: "Then he sends out the *sanīhāras*; except for the *ugra* and the *śūdra*, so says Baudhāyana; except for the *ugra*, so says Śālīki; all [castes] may do so for the success of the sacrifice, so says Aupamanyava. The *dhātṛ* is a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra who protects the sacrificial materials. The *śamitṛ* is the one who performs the immolation of the animal; he may be either a Brāhmaṇa or a Śūdra.

"He gives that arm to the Brāhmaṇa, if he is not a Brāhmaṇa"—this is from the Sūtra. "The Śamitṛ, exerting himself, gives the arm; that arm the Śamitṛ gives to a Brāhmaṇa if he himself is not a Brāhmaṇa"—this is the meaning of the Sūtra. From this very indicative mark, it follows that this person is indeed distinct from the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

Based on the scriptural statement, "The Adhvaryu turns his back as the animal is being slaughtered," it follows that among the Adhvaryu and his assistants, one, two, or all of them may perform the act of slaughtering the animal according to the requirements of the ritual. In this regard, the view of Jaimini is that if there is one person, it is the Pratiprasthātṛ; if two, they are the Pratiprasthātṛ and the Neṣṭṛ; and if three, they are the Unnetṛ as well—this is to be understood. Thus, it is stated in the seventh section (pāda) of the third chapter, in the relevant sūtra: "And the Śamitṛ [is distinct], because of the difference in designation."

The meaning of the word *śamitṛ* (the immolator) is "one who pacifies" or "one who slaughters. Although, in this context, the role of *śamitṛ* would logically belong to the Adhvaryu himself because the duties of the *śāmitra* are designated as part of the Adhvaryu’s office (*ādhvaryava*), nevertheless, since it is stated that the Adhvaryu must turn his back upon the animal being slaughtered, his status as *śamitṛ* is untenable; therefore, someone closely associated with him, such as the Pratiprasthātṛ or another, becomes the *śamitṛ*.

Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the scriptural injunction: "One should give the *kloman* and the *vaikartana* to the *śamitr*; if he is not a Brāhmaṇa, one should give them to a Brāhmaṇa. For there is no contradiction if the meaning is taken as: "If the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) should be a non-Brāhmaṇa, such as a Kṣatriya or others. Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the two statements—the prohibitive one stating "the *śāmitra* [duty] belongs only to Brāhmaṇas," and the prescriptive one stating "the *śamitr* may be a member of the three [upper] castes" or "the potter may be the *śamitr*."

Since it is possible to resolve the contradiction by allowing these Smṛtis to apply only where the Adhvaryu’s assistants are unavailable, the requirement for them is established. Among them, the Sūtrakāra himself has pointed out the Śamitṛ, the Dhruvagopa, the milkman, and the Soma-seller; thus, their appointment is already settled. Furthermore, since Āpastamba, Bharadvāja, and others have mentioned the Upagātṛs (chorus-singers), their appointment is likewise established.

However, regarding the procurement (*upakalpana*) of the others, it should be understood that there is no fixed rule even according to the view of the ritualists (*yājñika*). As for the *dhruvagopa*, even according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, he is indeed a different person based on the statement, "the prince guards [the cows]"; thus, his procurement is mandatory. Regarding the *śamitṛ* (the immolator), procurement is required according to the ritualists' view, but not according to the Mīmāṃsaka view. Furthermore, because he is distinct from the milker (*dogdhṛ*), the milker's procurement is also [required]. Since the Soma-seller (*somavikrayin*) is included within the category of officiants (*karmāntaḥpātī*), his procurement is [required] according to all views.

In the case of the appointment of the *paśupāla* (cattle-tender) and others, because there is no origination [of the act] as in the case of the *śamitṛ* (slaughterer) regarding the path (*adhvan*) and so forth, there is an absence of a connection with the name at the time of origination. For a mere name is not a differentiator; rather, it must be heard at the time of origination. This name is not heard at the time of origination in the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Book Ten, Chapter One. Since there is no origination of the *śamitṛ* due to the absence of a formal selection (*varaṇa*), just as in the case of the path, the point is that a name alone does not effect a distinction.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: the *śamitṛ* (the slaughterer) is distinct [from the other priests] because of the difference in the word "śamitṛ," or because of the specific function. The word "or" (*vā*) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). As for the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is found in the section on the duties of the Adhvaryu priest, where it is stated: "The *śamitṛ* holds [the animal] by the neck. Furthermore, there is no connection with its origin in the absence of a Brāhmaṇa [text]. However, in the Kali age, since there is a prohibition against the performance of the *śāmitra* rite for Brāhmaṇas—according to the rule "and the *śāmitra* belongs only to the Brāhmaṇas"—it must be a Śūdra alone. The *dhruvagopa* is the one who protects the *dhruva* vessel.

That he is a *rājaputra* (king’s son) has already been stated by the author of the Sūtra. Therefore, the milker is a Kṣatriya, acting as the one who performs the milking for the purpose of understanding the vow (*vrata*). And he may be either a Brāhmaṇa or a Śūdra. Since there is a prohibition against a Śūdra performing the milking specifically related to the Agnihotra—namely, "A Śūdra should not milk the Agnihotra"—there is no restriction regarding other types of milking. Furthermore, this Śūdra is specifically a cowherd (*gopa*), because the Smṛti states that "the good Śūdras are the cowherds and basket-makers," thus describing him as generally suitable [for such tasks] and because his livelihood is derived from that occupation.

If the *brāhmaṇa* is the one who performs the milking, it is indeed proper. As for the seller of *soma*, the Sūtrakāra has already stated previously that he may be either Kautsa or a Śūdra. Since the sale of *soma* is likewise prohibited in the Kali age, such a person nowadays must be a Śūdra. Furthermore, it has already been stated that this person is distinct from the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). For the purpose of grinding the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), the woman may be either a Brāhmaṇī or a female slave (*dāsī*). However, for the purpose of carrying the fire and the *agnīṣomīya* animal, as well as for carrying the *agnīṣomīya* materials, she must be a Brāhmaṇī woman.

They are called *prasarpakas* because they move forward (*prasarpati*) to resolve doubts regarding the purpose of the sacrifice. These are indeed Brāhmaṇas, as they are the recipients of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). As for their place of seating: as long as the ritual action takes place within the *prāgvaṃśa* (the eastern hall), they remain in that very *prāgvaṃśa*; from the time of the fire-piling (*agnipraṇayana*) onwards, they sit in the vicinity of each respective rite. That assembly where learned and disciplined men sit during a sacrifice is termed a *yajñasamsthā*.

This has been stated in the *Rājadharmas*: "Three assemblies are to be known: one for *dharma* and one for *karman*; likewise, Rāma, these have been proclaimed by the wise. By the word *dharma*, both judicial procedure (*vyavahāra*) and expiation (*prāyaścitta*) are meant. The hall constructed for that purpose is the assembly for *dharma*. This is the first assembly. Furthermore, the hall for the sake of ritual action, such as sacrifices and the like, is called the assembly for *karman*. This is the second.

The hall where the king sits together with Brahmins, attendants, soldiers, and others is called the *rājasabhā* (royal assembly). This is the third court. These three assemblies have been proclaimed—that is, described—by learned Brahmins. The number of members of the assembly has been stated by Bṛhaspati: "That assembly in which there sit seven, five, or even three Brahmins who know the worlds, the Vedas, and the Dharma, is equal to a sacrificial session (*yajñasad*). Thus it is said.

In another Smṛti it is also stated: "If learned men, such as the four [classes of experts] and others, are seated there from which the Dharma has emerged, then that should be known as a *samiti*. Here, the term *prasarpaka* refers to learned and disciplined Brāhmaṇas who are seated in the sacrificial hall (*yajña-śālā*) for the purpose of the sacrifice; they should be understood as being of the highest rank among the twice-born (*vipra-bhūtayaḥ*). From the commencement of the sacrifice until its conclusion, their mandatory seating in the hall serves as the witness (*sākṣya*) for the ritual act.
[Chapter 150] Accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. It has already been stated previously that among the *ṛtvij*s, any who are singers (*upagātṛ*) are six in number.

Day and night were the two attendants of the animal sacrifice; the *muhūrtas* became the messengers; Death was the slaughterer (*śamitṛ*); the Lord of the People (*viśāpati*) was the preparer (*śamitṛ*); the Guardian of the Pole Star (*dhruvagopa*) was *Saha*; and *Ākṛti* was the sacrificial cake (*havir*). Indeed, both Hunger and Thirst brought the fuel (*idhma*) for them. This sequence is found in the *Viśvasanāmayana* [section], and the assignment of these [functions] occurs right here. Nor should it be argued that because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating "the seasons are the singers" (*ṛtavā upagātāraḥ*), there must also be a separate assignment of distinct roles for these [seasons].

In all their views, because the non-difference of the sacrificer is established, there is no basis for [assuming] a distinction. According to the Mīmāṃsaka view, since the statement "the singers of the Ṛgveda are the inviters" is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it lacks authority regarding its own literal meaning—just like [the statement] "Indra is the slayer of Vṛtra, the breaker of cities"—and thus cannot lead one to postulate a difference among the singers. Even though there is authority regarding the literal meaning in the view of the Pāṭhika school, it should be understood that there is non-difference due to the scriptural injunction. And the vow of the sacrificer and the priests lasts as long as the ritual action.

This has been stated in the *Baudhāyana-prāyaścitta-sūtra*: "In all cases, they prescribe the vow for one who is sacrificing, [including] the non-eating of meat and [abstaining from] women. This was also stated by Āśvalāyana: "They should not eat meat nor approach women until the end of the *kāṭhaka* section. The plural number is used with reference to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). There is also another specific prohibition in the *Baudhāyana-prāyaścitta*.

In the *Śāṅkhāyana Śrautasūtra* it is stated: "The office of the *ṛtvij* (priest) does not exist elsewhere [than in specific rites]; there is no combination [of priests] other than for the *mahāvrata*; and there is no officiating on behalf of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) except in the case of a *sattra* sacrifice. This combination—where the one who is the *hotṛ* is also the *adhvaryu*—is prescribed specifically for the *Kuṇḍapāyināmayana* sacrifice. Because that [sacrifice] is a *sattra*, this applies only there and not elsewhere, such as in *ahīna* sacrifices or *ekāha* sacrifices. Likewise, the officiating on behalf of the sacrificer is also restricted in this way. The honor of the *ṛtvij*s must be performed with the *madhuparka*.

Regarding this, Viśvāmitra states: "One should cause the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) to perform their duties after honoring them with *madhuparka*; if one causes them to perform them without honoring them, he is afflicted by some poison. In the *Dharmasūtra*, [the term] *gomadhuparkārhī* refers to one who is worthy of the cow and the *madhuparka*: "A Vedic scholar (*vedādhyāyin*), a teacher (*ācārya*), a *snātaka*, a king, or one endowed with righteousness (*dharmayukta*) is worthy of the cow and the *madhuparka*. The meaning is that he is worthy of those two—the cow and the *madhuparka*. In such a compound (*dvandva*), there is a greater cow than the cow included within the *madhuparka* itself.

"Vedādhyāyī" (one who studies the Veda) is an epithet for the Ācārya and others. This implies that if the Ācāryas and others have studied the entire Veda, then a cow superior to the madhuparka should be given, and nothing else. By this it is understood that even those such as Ācāryas who have studied only a portion of the Veda are indeed to be honored with the simple madhuparka alone. Alternatively, the compound may be analyzed as "gomadhuparka," meaning a madhuparka accompanied by a cow; however, the absence of the gift of an additional cow is even more certain.

Furthermore, there is a specific rule in the *Dharmasūtra*: "To the teacher (*ācārya*), the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the graduate (*snātaka*), the father-in-law (*śvaśura*), and the king. This means that for these individuals—the teacher and others—distinguished by the aforementioned qualifications, who have arrived after the lapse of one year, worship with the *madhuparka* accompanied by a cow must be performed. By this *sūtra*, the time limit is established: the cow is to be given only to the *vidyā-snātaka* and the *vidyāvratasnātaka*, and not to the *vratasnātaka* alone.

From this sūtra it is understood that the *madhuparka* is occasioned by the attainment of specific qualities, such as being a teacher of the Dharma in each preceding case. In this regard, the *madhuparka* for a teacher of the Dharma should be seen as occurring after the initiation (*upanayana*), for a chosen priest (*ṛtvij*) after his selection, for a *snātaka* at the conclusion of the return home (*samāvartana*), for a father-in-law at the conclusion of the raising of the deity-image (*devakotthāpana*), and for a king at the conclusion of his consecration (*abhiṣeka*). According to the principle that "the occasional rite follows each respective occasion," having chosen a priest, he speaks of the *madhuparka*:

From the Āśvalāyana-sūtra: "He should go to meet [the guest]"; from the Chāndoga-sūtra: "The sacrifice [is performed] again and again"; and from the Baudhāyana-sūtra: "Now these are the persons—maternal uncle, father-in-law, paternal uncle, maternal uncle, teacher, king, one who has completed his Vedic studies (snātaka), and a dear guest—who, having arrived within the year, one should honor with the same rites used for a bridegroom at every ritual act;
if one causes [the guest] to perform [the rite] without honoring him, he becomes joined with sin."

Thus, from Viśvāmitra’s statement regarding the hearing of the fault incurred by failing to perform the *madhuparka* offering at every sacrifice, it follows that the presence of those who have become gods (*devabhūta*) and those who have become ancestors (*pitṛbhūta*) is possible outside of ritual time after a year has passed; however, this is not the case for those who have become human (*manuṣyabhūta*), because their status as officiants (*ṛtvik*) cannot possibly persist beyond the performance of the ritual. According to the opinion of Vaijavāpa, since the four offices of the *hotṛ* and other priests are combined in a single person, when a period of impurity (*āśauca*) falls upon the sons and others belonging to that person while they are engaged in those offices, other [substitutes] for them must be brought in.

This should be understood as referring to the case of those who have become gods (*devabhūta*) or ancestors (*pitṛbhūta*). The impurity (*āśauca*) prescribed for a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*) upon the death of his patron (*yājya*), which has been recorded in the Smṛtis, applies specifically to those who have become gods or ancestors. Likewise, the impurity resulting from the death of the patron should be understood to apply only to priests who have become gods or ancestors. For learned men (*suvidvāṃsaḥ*), there is an absence of impurity only after the *madhuparka* offering has been received. It is certain that once a priest has accepted the *madhuparka* from the patron, he does not incur impurity even if it should subsequently descend upon him.

Thus, according to the *Brāhma* [Smṛti]. From the implication of the text itself, it follows that where there is no *madhuparka*, impurity (*āśauca*) certainly exists. Regarding this, some hold the view that the *madhuparka* does not occur at all in the *Ādhāna*, *Iṣṭi*, or *Paśubandha* sacrifices, but only in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other such rites. The intention of this opinion is that since the formal selection (*varaṇa*) accompanied by mantras occurs only in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and so forth, the *madhuparka* is present there; whereas in the *Ādhāna*, *Iṣṭi*, and *Paśubandha*, because the mantra-accompanied selection is absent, the *madhuparka* is not performed. However, the opinion of others is that the *madhuparka* is required in all cases.

The intention of this view is that there is no evidence for the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) being intended solely for the selection accompanied by mantras. This view is trivial, because the statement "having chosen the *ṛtvij*s" is made as a restatement (*anuvāda*) precisely to demonstrate that the honey-mixture is indeed connected with the selection accompanied by mantras, and because no other purpose is possible. Furthermore, the honey-mixture at great gifts (*mahādāna*) and the like is based on explicit scriptural injunction (*vācanika*). The Vaikhānasa-sūtra also mentions the honey-mixture even in the context of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*); that too is purely based on scriptural injunction.

"What speech indeed would one not carry out? There is no burden too heavy for a word. Although in the statement—"The commencement [of a rite] is the *varaṇa* (formal invitation) in a sacrifice; the *saṃkalpa* (resolve) in a vow or a sacrificial session (*sattra*); the *nāndīśrāddha* at the beginning of a marriage and so forth; and the preparation of the cooked food in a funeral feast (*śrāddha*)"—the *varaṇa* alone appears to be the cause for the absence of ritual impurity (*āśauca*), nevertheless, because the *varaṇa* and the *madhuparka* (honey-mixture offering) are interconnected, the term *varaṇa* includes the *madhuparka* as well. Therefore, there is no contradiction with Bāṇa’s statement, "of him who has accepted the *madhuparka*."

This absence of impurity for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) lasts only as long as the ritual action continues. For those initiated by a priest and those performing sacrificial rites, as well as for those observing the *sattra* vows, celibates (*brahmacārin*), donors, and knowers of Brahman—likewise, in cases of giving, marriage, sacrifice, battle, or the destruction of a country, and even in times of dire distress, immediate purification is ordained; so says the traditional text. [Chapter 150] — Along with the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

In the statement, "The sacrifice begins with the taking [of the bride]," it should be understood that the taking [of the bride] is indeed accompanied by mantras, so as to maintain syntactic consistency with the statement regarding the reception of the *madhuparka*. By this, the impurity (*sūtaka*) caused by the non-commencement of a rite—as taught in the Viṣṇu-smṛti passage: "In sacrifices, marriages, *śrāddhas*, burnt offerings (*homa*), worship, and recitation (*japa*), there shall be no impurity once they have begun; but where they have not begun, there is impurity"—applies even to those who have accepted a formal proposal (*varaṇa*) according to worldly custom. The mention of *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) here is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for death-impurity (*mṛtaka*) as well.

Regarding the phrase "the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) from the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) who has received the *madhuparka*," the term *ṛtvij* must be understood as being applied specifically on account of a particular sacrificial function.
