Consequently, the *madhuparka* is not offered to the *gharmādhvaryu* priests; rather, they receive merely an honorific offering (*pūjā*) consisting of perfumes and other items. Furthermore, for the sacrificer as well, there is no suspension of ritual purity (*āśauca*) only for as long as the ritual action lasts. This is because of the immediately preceding scriptural statement: "For the initiated priest (*dīkṣita*) and [the sacrificer], there is no impurity. And also because of the rule: "After the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering] in the sacrifice, one does not perform penances such as the *kṛcchra* while engaged in the rite. Here, *dīkṣiṇyāḥ* refers to the *dīkṣaṇīyā*.

The plural number in the phrase "of those initiated" (*dīkṣitānām*) refers to the *satra* sacrifices. This [impurity] also occurs only after the commencement [of the sacrifice], according to the statement: "There is no birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) when the sacrifice has commenced; however, there is birth-impurity when it has not commenced. Here too, the meaning of the word "commencement" is restricted to the formal selection (*varaṇa*), as established by the rule: "The commencement is the selection in a sacrifice. If [the impurity occurs] before the selection following the initial resolve (*saṃkalpa*), then there is indeed a cessation [of the ritual]. As for the *nāndī-śrāddha*, it is performed beforehand and serves for use up until the twenty-first day.

According to the scriptural statement: "In a sacrifice lasting twenty-one days, ten days [are required]; in marriage, six; and in the *caula* and *upanayana*, three days—the *nāndī-śrāddha* is prescribed. Furthermore, for one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*), there is an absence of impurity (*āśauca*) even during non-ritual times prior to the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath). This is because of the statement: "Likewise, for a learned man who has received initiation in a great sacrifice, there is no birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) for him until the *avabhṛtha* bath. The meaning of the word "likewise" (*tadvat*) is that he is like a member of a sacrificial session (*satrin*), a student (*brahmacārin*), and others who possess immediate purity (*sadyaḥ-śauca*).

One by whom initiation (*dīkṣā*) has been received is "initiated" (*dīkṣita*); that the state of being initiated occurs after the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice has been performed was already stated previously. "Trividyā" refers to knowledge consisting of three parts; one who studies or knows that is a "Vidya," meaning one who has studied the three Vedas or possesses knowledge of the three types of rituals expounded therein. For such a sacrificer—until the *Avabhṛtha* bath in the great sacrifice, such as the *Agniṣṭoma* and others, has been completed—the performer of the sacrifice remains in a state of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*). This is the meaning.

By the phrase "in that same manner," immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*) is extended [to this case]. By this, the absence of impurity (*āśauca*) is established even during times when no ritual act is being performed. To prevent over-extension (*ativyāpti*)—since the status of having taken initiation (*dīkṣitatva*) and the status of being a performer of the *amṛtasnāna* exist even during the Cāturmāsya, Sautrāmaṇī, and other such rites—the term "great sacrifice" (*mahāmakha*) is used. By the phrase "of one who has taken initiation," the prior limit is indicated. Consequently, it follows that the absence of impurity occurs only during this interval, even at times when no ritual act is being performed, and not before these two limits.

If it is argued that the phrase "of one who has taken up the swing" (*gṛhītadolasya*) alone would suffice—since in the *Cāturmāsya*, *Sautrāmaṇī*, and other rites, the contingency [of the ritual application] is already avoided by the absence of initiation (*dīkṣā*) itself, and thus the qualification "Great Sacrifice" (*mahāmakha*) is redundant—this is not so. Because the verbal root *dīkṣ* has multiple meanings, the sense of "sacrifice" (*ijyā*) is also present there; therefore, the qualification "Great Sacrifice" is necessary to exclude that case.

By this qualification, "of one who possesses knowledge," it is established that for one who merely has faith—even if initiated (*dīkṣita*) during a great sacrifice (*mahāmakha*)—there is indeed impurity (*āśauca*) prior to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). Accordingly, having performed the bath required by the cause of impurity before the commencement of the ritual, and having dried the collection of ghee and garments, one should don ashes and begin the rite. After the completion of the rite, one becomes subject to impurity once again. Thus, there is a bath at the beginning of each performance of the rite.

If one is unable to maintain the vow, then after bathing, having washed the garment, the girdle, the black antelope skin, and so forth, and having put on another garment while the one intended for initiation is still wet, one should wear that dry garment with the mantras: "Thou art the body of Agni; thou art the body of Soma. Then, having fastened the girdle with the mantra: "The bond of the Sun is our protection," and having applied fresh butter to the eyes and rubbed them, once the girding has been performed with that same washed girdle, [the next stage] is reached.

He performs the ritual action; likewise the merchant, and so on until the cessation of impurity. This is postulated because it cannot be explained otherwise. In such a postulation, the very mention of the injunction (*vidhi*) is the indicator, for otherwise this [text] would result in being meaningless.
Or rather, he chooses these very persons: the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Brahman, and the Udgātṛ.

Alternatively, one may choose only the four principal priests; this much alone serves to establish the inclusion of the four—namely the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Udgātṛ, and Brahman—as mentioned by Āśvalāyana. Furthermore, this is intended to exclude the view that the Brahman should come first as stated by Āśvalāyana, as well as the view that the Adhvaryu should come first as stated by Bhāradvāja in the passage: "Choosing four, or all of them, he chooses the great officiating priests: the Adhvaryu, the Hotṛ, and the Udgātṛ. Therefore, everything stated therein regarding the manner of choosing and so forth is indeed to be combined [into a single comprehensive rule].

The word *etac* (this) includes the *sadasya* as well because of his primary status; the particle *ca* is used to exclude him from that [specific] exclusion. The particle *eva* (only) is for the purpose of excluding the equal invitation (*samaprakavaraṇa*) of others. For these [others], the invitation is indeed without mantras. It should be understood that in the case of the view of equal invitation for all four, the *madhuparka* worship is performed for those four alone, while for the others there is merely worship with garments, ornaments, perfumes, and so forth.
Then he asks the Kṣatriya for the place of sacrifice (*devayajana*).

We shall explain the duties of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*); because of this heading, the sacrificer alone is the agent in every instance. The word *apa-* has its primary meaning as "always" (*nitya*). By this, it is established that even when a site for the sacrifice (*devayajanadeśa*) is already available, the act of requesting it is obligatory. This is because Āpastamba mentions the request even for a king who possesses such a site. Likewise, for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who does not receive gifts (*pratigraha*), the request is also obligatory. Regarding the mantra for the request for the sacrificial site, Āpastamba says: "Reciting the mantra, 'O God Varuṇa, grant me a sacrificial site,' one should request a king."

"If he gives [the land], say to him: 'May you become possessed of a sacrificial ground (devayajana)'; if he does not give, say to him: 'If I know a sacrificial ground, upon that I cut you down'—this is the meaning of 'yadi' (if). 'Enam' refers to the giver. After 'na cet' (if not), the word 'dadāti' (he gives) is to be supplied. If he does not give—thus indeed Āpastamba has stated. Even though the text ends with 'ced dadāti' (if he gives), the word 'tam' (him) is supplied; for this [text] is found as 'adātāram' (one who does not give), and that [reading] is merely a scribal error."

13.3... *Rama*. "Veda, give this to him. 5. *Ja*, *Sa*, *Ma*: *Śyenā* | [Folio 150] Together with the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa: 1009. The purpose is that if one gives with faith only when asked, then at that very moment there is the blessing, "May he become a possessor of a sacrificial ground (*devayajanavat*). If, however, it is due to persistence or fear of public censure, then there is no such blessing. "Whatever sacrificial ground I shall designate"—this is the counter-statement for one who is about to speak thus. Then they cause him to speak aloud.

The word *apaśabda* has the sense of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*). By this it is meant: "In that which I know as the *devayajana*, I cut you off"—this invocation by the *hotṛ* must be performed immediately after [the cutting], and not simultaneously with it or prior to it. [The phrase] "him, the non-giver" refers to the curse (*abhiśāpa*) here; for this is indicated by the characteristic marks (*liṅga*) of the mantras to be recited later, such as "having seized the speech, he shall abandon it. The meaning is: by means of the speech and other faculties set forth in the mantras for the invocation to be recited later.

The plural number is used with reference to the *hotrā*s (priestly offices) that are about to be described; this is a general proposition. Alternatively, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in "abhivyāhārayanti" is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). The *hotrā*s to be described are the objects of the action. It should not be argued that the *ṇic* suffix cannot be assumed to have its own sense (*svārtha*) because there is no other way out (*nāgatikāgati*), since the sacrificer is the instigator (*prayojaka*) of the assistant priests (*napānavijaḥ*). This is because, just as the agency of uttering the words resides in the *hotṛ* and others, the sacrificer’s agency in that same act will be explained later, and thus it is impossible for him to be the object of his own instigation. Therefore, the *ṇic* is indeed used in its own sense. He states the manner in which this occurs:

"You have struck down speech; speech will abandon you," said the Hotṛ. "You have struck down breath; breath will abandon you," said the Adhvaryu. "You have struck down mind; mind will abandon you," said the Brahman. "You have struck down sight; sight will abandon you," said the Udgātṛ. "You have struck down hearing; hearing will abandon you," said the Hotrakas. "You have struck down the self; the self will abandon you," said the Sadasya. "You have struck down the limbs; the limbs will abandon you," said the Camasādhvaryus.

"You have struck down Prajāpati; Prajāpati will abandon you," [he says] regarding the sacrificer. "You have struck down all beings; all beings will abandon you," [he says] regarding everyone. The mention of the Hotṛ and the others is for the purpose of ascertaining their connection with their respective mantras; otherwise, there would be no thorough knowledge of which mantra belongs to whom, such as "the first belongs to whom? or "the second belongs to whom? All those mentioned, beginning with the Hotṛs, and those not mentioned, such as the sacrificer's attendants and so forth, are included. The invocation is performed in this very order. Having thus addressed them, he then requests another:
"Now he requests the officiating priests (ṛtvij) for the sacrificial ground (devayajana)."

Although the *devayajana* (sacrificial ground) belongs to [the king] himself, nevertheless, there can be no request directed toward the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) without the permission of Rāma. The word "ṛtvijaḥ" is in the accusative plural. Here, the meaning of the word "request" (*yācana*) consists precisely in the act of obtaining permission from the Hotṛ and the other priests. Āpastamba, however, states that the request directed toward the priests is to be performed by the king, using such formulas as: "O King, as far as the sacrificial ground extends, he shall be my Hotṛ; he is my Hotṛ; O Hotṛ, give me the sacrificial ground," and so forth.

At that juncture, he goes to the place of sacrifice (*devayajana*) for the purpose of requesting it. If it cannot be obtained even there, one should perform the *Traidhātavīyā* sacrifice, which is prescribed by the rule: "He who, having said 'I shall sacrifice,' does not sacrifice, should sacrifice with the *Traidhātavīyā*. According to the view that the selection of the priests (*ṛtvij-sampādana*) occurs at the very time of the formal invitation (*varaṇa*), some hold that this applies even when a priest is unavailable.

In reality, the preparation of the sacrificial ground (*sāmanya-upakalpana*) is just like the conceptualization of the sacrificial site for the gods (*tatvika-devayajana-kalpana*) prior to the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). Thus, there is neither the *dhātavīya* sacrifice nor the lapse consisting of the failure to remember the commencement of the ritual (*kratvanārambha-rūpa-vibhreṣaḥ*). Baudhāyana has stated this clearly in the Vaidhasūtra: "One should not undergo initiation (*dīkṣeta*) without having seen the sun and the moon. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include the collection of materials such as the sacrificial site and the vessels.

[The mantras are recited as follows: "May Agni, my Hotṛ, grant me the sacrificial site for the gods"—this is whispered (*upāṃśu*); "O Hotṛ, give me the sacrificial site for men"—this is spoken aloud (*uccaiḥ*).

Immediately after the word *upāṃśu* (in a whisper), the phrase "he asks for the sacrificial ground" (*devayajanaṃ yācate*) is understood by virtue of its presence in the general introductory sūtra. It is directed toward each [person] individually because of the specific indicative marks (*liṅga*) for each. The term *mānuṣam* (human) is an adjective qualifying the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*). It cannot be an adjective qualifying the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), because in the mantras there is no mention of the names of individual humans, which would render that interpretation untenable. Consequently, it follows by implication that prior to this, there was an asking for the divine sacrificial ground (*daivya-devayajana*). This [request for the human ground] serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

Since the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is a property of sound, its application pertains only to the mantras used for requesting the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), and not to the act of requesting itself. Therefore, the sentence becomes: "Having uttered the mantra in a whisper, he requests the divine sacrificial ground. The same applies to the phrase "the human" (*mānuṣa*). This should be understood everywhere in this manner.
Thus, in the other cases as well, he pronounces the name of the deity in a whisper, but loudly for the human [sacrificer].

The statement "so it is with the others" is made because the matter is already established by that much; the specific injunction "he pronounces the name of the deity in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), [but] loudly for a human being" is intended to demonstrate that this is an alternative method alongside the previous one. What is the former, and what is the latter?

If this is asked, it is replied as follows: In the two preceding mantras, there is the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) and loud (*uccaistva*); however, here, the whispered and loud qualities apply specifically to the names. Thus, it should be understood that in the preceding mantras, the names of the deities are whispered while the remaining portions of the mantras are necessarily loud; whereas in the subsequent mantras, the human names are loud while the remaining portions of the mantras are necessarily whispered.

Although it would have been sufficient to say simply "human" (*mānuṣam*) for the sake of brevity, the use here of the more cumbersome genitive form (*mānuṣasya*) indicates that the name of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) should also be included. For example: "O *Amukaśarman*, human [priest], give me this sacrificial ground for the gods," and so forth. "Name" (*nāmadheya*) means "name" (*nāma*); the suffix *-dheya* is added in the sense of the word itself according to the rule *bhāgarūpanāmabhyo dheyaḥ*. "Addressing" (*abhivyāharaṇa*) means specifically the recitation [of the name], because of its association with the word "deity" (*devatā*).

Names such as "hotṛ" and so forth are not names of humans, but rather are employed in the context of officiating at sacrifices (*ātvijya*). Following the word "mānuṣasya," the term "nāmadheya" from the compound *devatānāmadheyam* (meaning "the name of a deity") is understood to carry over. In the phrase "he utters the name of the deity" (*devatānāmadheyam abhivyāharati*), it is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound—namely, "the name of the deity" (*devatāyā nāmadheyam*)—which is adopted for the sake of brevity; it is not a non-co-referential *bahuvrīhi* meaning "that in which there is the name of the deity."

However, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, if the word denoting the deity were intended to mean "mind" (*manas*), it would result in the same state of tautology as before, since it would function as a single unit with the preceding term; therefore, a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound alone is appropriate. Thus, the rule "He pronounces the name of the deity in a low voice, [saying] 'Of the divine and of the human'" must necessarily be accepted in this way, even while acknowledging that it intends an alternative view; enough has been said on this point. [From the tenth Paṭala, accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 1011

"Āditya is my Adhvaryu; may he grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods. "O Adhvaryu, grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods"—thus [he addresses] the Adhvaryu. "Candramas is my Brahman; may he grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods. "O Brahman, grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods"—thus [he addresses] the Brahman. "Parjanya is my Udgātṛ; may he grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods. "O Udgātṛ, grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods"—thus [he addresses] the Udgātṛ. "Ākāśa is my Sadasya; may he grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods. "O Sadasya, grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods"—thus [he addresses] the Sadasya. "The Waters are my Hotrāśaṃsinīs; they..."

"May the Hotrāśaṃsinīs grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods; may the Hotrāśaṃsinīs grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods," [he says] to the Hotrakas. "May the rays, O Camasādhvaryus, grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods; O Camasādhvaryus, grant me a place for sacrifice to the gods," [he says] to the Camasādhvaryus.
This is clear.
Having requested [the site] with the words, "Having asked for this, we have come to the place of sacrifice on the earth," he settles upon the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*).

A *devayajana* is that place where the gods are worshipped, or alternatively, it is a *devayajana* because it is the sacrificial ground (*yajana*) of the gods. He settles there together with the fires and the prepared materials for the Soma sacrifice, meaning he goes there for the purpose of dwelling, preceded by water-pots. This is because in the injunction "having followed after, he should settle," the act of settling is seen to have that specific meaning; and also because of the mantra, "We have come to the god-frequented place. The end of the mantra is "may we rejoice. The plural number in "we have come" (*aganma*) refers to the wife and the attendants.

Therefore, the ministers also should be present; this inclusion of the ministers is intended to indicate their presence. However, it is not so with the wife, because without her, the sacrifice itself would not exist. Her journey toward the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), however, is already established by virtue of the fact that the wife is enjoined to hold onto the kindling woods (*araṇyanvārambha*). Precisely because the sacrificer is the principal agent, the singular number is heard in this *Brāhmaṇa* passage: "He who sacrifices comes to the sacrificial ground of the earth."

The phrase "having requested" (*yācitvā*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to refute the position stated by Āpastamba—that one should not request a sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), but rather simply stand near the deities saying, "May he see this. Because of the suffix *-kvā*, [the act of requesting] is an ancillary part of the determination of the sacrificial ground (*devayajanādhyavasāna*). Therefore, when the determination of the sacrificial ground is postponed, this [requesting] is also postponed; thus, the acts such as the formal depositing of the fires (*samāropaṇa*) occur even before the request for the sacrificial ground. In this context, the determination of the sacrificial ground applies to the view that "one undergoes initiation (*dīkṣate*) in the forest and sacrifices in the forest."

It should be understood that this refers to the view that "one undergoes initiation (*dīkṣate*) in the forest for whatever one intends to perform hereafter. Previously it was stated that "one settles upon the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*). In response to the inquiry as to what the characteristics of such a sacrificial ground are, he says:
"That which is level, well-established, possessed of herbs, not saline, not fragile, not infested [by pests], not barren, and not crumbling away."

The connection with the preceding [text] is as follows: "That which is the site for the creation [of the sacrificial ground], that which is the path of the gods (*devayānana*), and that which becomes the place of sacrifice (*devayajana*), one settles upon. It is well-established and beautifully adorned; it is a place where, by means of qualities such as being soft and level, the mind of one staying there finds delight. And thus says Baudhāyana: "A hall is caused to be built on a *devayajana* that is pleasing (*juṣṭa*). The meaning of "pleasing" (*juṣṭa*) is "agreeable" (*abhirucita*). Furthermore, it should be understood that the phrase "not obstructing the movement of all" is also to be supplied according to the requirements of the context.

In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, the qualifications of the sacrificial site (*devayajana*) are to be construed with what precedes. "Like plants" (*oṣadhivat*): that place where plants end with the ripening of their fruit; the vowel *va* is used here according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). "Not saline" (*anūṣaram*): that place where saline soil (*ūṣa*) or alkaline earth (*smṛtsā*) is not found. This is because of the prohibition: "One should not settle on a naturally formed saline wasteland (*iriṇa*). Since the word *iriṇa* refers specifically to such a saline spot, there is also a reading in some places as *anūkharām*.

The meaning of the word *anūkharā* is "that which is devoid of *ūkhara*"; *ūkhara* refers to land devoid of the production of grain. *Abhaṅgura* means that where breakage by river currents and the like is not possible; this is a characterization of being without holes (*asuṣira*). *Amucira* means without cracks. *Anupahata* means that which is not damaged by fire, the presence of outcastes, and so forth. *Aniriṇa* means that where grass and such do not grow is *iriṇa*; other than that is *aniriṇa*.

*Avisaradāre*: where the splitting (*dāraṇa*) of trees by the falling of [large] branches (*visṛndāra*) is not possible—that is *avisaradāra*. Since the prohibition of such splitting is already established by the very phrase "one's own arm" (*svamaṅguri*), there is no need for a separate prohibition here. Even if the reading were *avisṛndārī*, the meaning would remain the same. It should be [a place] sloping toward the east, sloping toward the north, or sloping toward the northeast.

Regarding what was previously stated as "level" (*sama*), three alternatives are now considered here: where the ground slopes toward the east (*prācīna-pravaṇa*) and is depressed toward the north (*kramanimna*); where it slopes toward the north (*udīcīna-pravaṇa*) and is depressed toward the east; and where it slopes toward the northeast (*prāgudak-pravaṇa*)—that is, toward the intermediate direction between east and north—and is depressed toward the northwest (*kramanimna*). The quality of being well-established (*pratiṣṭhita*) and so forth, however, is common to all four alternatives, since there is no other ground surrounding it.

The meaning is that one should accept such a *devayajana* (sacrificial ground) from which there is another site (*sthalāntara*) on all sides, extending infinitely; it does not mean that one leaves over more than just the *devayajana* itself. Regarding the phrase "in front of the *devayajana*" (*purastāt devayajanasya*), the word "merely" (*mātra*) indicates that there is no fault in leaving over an area slightly less or greater than the measurement of the *devayajana*. The prohibition against leaving over more than the measure of the *devayajana* is for a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), as a visible result is impossible [otherwise]. He states an alternative view:

"Or as far as the throw of the *śamyā*": the meaning is that he does not leave [the ground] beyond the distance at which the *śamyā*—when thrown—comes to rest. This is an alternative to the rule, "He does not leave [the ground] beyond the extent of the sacrificial site (*devayajana*) in front. Regarding the rule, "One who has attained prosperity should sacrifice on level ground," this applies both to the obligatory (*nitya*) and the optional (*kāmya*) rites.

In the phrase "as far as level" (*yāvatsamam*), the word "on all sides" (*sarvataḥ*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis; for the Śruti states, "that which stands equally on all sides. The meaning is that a sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) is designated as such only to the extent that it is level and firmly established. Whether in the case of a mandatory injunction (*nityavidhi*) or a contingent injunction (*kāmyavidhi*), the sense is that for one who has attained prosperity (*gataśriyaḥ*), that very sacrificial ground which is firmly established is the one to be used.

The essential meaning is as follows: that which is established by its own nature, characterized by the marks beginning with "T" [Paṭala 15] and ending with "gopīnāthabhakṛtajyotsnāvyākhyāsametam" (accompanied by the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha), and extending up to "śamyāprāsa," is common to both those who have attained prosperity (*gataśrī*) and those who have not; this is the definition of the *devayajana* (the sacrificial ground). Furthermore, "one who has heard much" (*śuśruvān*) refers to one who has studied the three Vedas, while "one who has attained prosperity" (*gataśrī*) refers to one who possesses wealth.

In the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa*, it is clearly stated that those who study the three Vedas are designated by the term "Śrī. By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word *grāmaṇī* as "one who leads" (*nayatīti*), the village headman is referred to; whereas one who is consecrated as a Kṣatriya is called a *rājanya*. One who has attained (*gatā*) prosperity (*śrīḥ*) is "Gatīḥ," according to the scriptural principle that "those [roots] which signify 'going' also signify 'attaining'."

Āpastamba states a specific rule regarding the *devayajana* (the sacrificial ground): "Or, where many Brāhmaṇas may perform [the rites] together—that indeed is a *devayajana*. It is known from tradition: 'Where one, having established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), performs a sacrifice, he sacrifices on a *devayajana*. Or again, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is indeed the *devayajana*; for if one gives excellent sacrificial fees, he sacrifices on a *devayajana*—so say some. In this context, regarding the *devayajana*, when many Brāhmaṇas are present as members of the assembly (*sadasya*) or witnesses, they [recognize] that "this is a proper place for your ritual activity."

Even in the absence of the characteristics described therein, it may serve as a *devayajana* (sacrificial ground). The sense is that this quality is more important [than the specific features]. Thus, regarding the section on the *devayajana*, the Brāhmaṇa states: "For all these gods indeed take pleasure in those who are Brāhmaṇas. Wherever one performs the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) after bringing the fires from elsewhere and performs the sacrifice (*yajati*), that very place is a *devayajana*, even if it lacks the aforementioned characteristics. This ritual procedure applies to the *ādhāna* preceded by the Soma sacrifice.

Alternatively, wherever one establishes and places the fires and performs the sacrifice, that very place is a *devayajana* (sacrificial ground), even in the absence of the characteristics previously mentioned. According to this view, the procedure is as follows: having established the fires in a location not incompatible with the *prāgvaṃśa* hall—specifically a portion of the *devayajana* itself—and having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) right there, one should perform the rites beginning with the honoring of the King and ending with the *madhuparka*, and then proceed toward the hall. The underlying sense is: what need is there for any further consideration of the qualities of a site already presided over by the fires?

If someone were to know cows possessing the required characteristics, then, even when there is a large assembly and an abundance of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the absence of a *devayajana* (a site for sacrifice) would render the ritual ineffective; this is the intended meaning. These alternative positions should be understood as applying only when a *devayajana* endowed with the aforementioned characteristics and graces is unavailable. However, if both [the site and the fees] are present, it becomes conducive to superior merit—this follows by implication. One should perform the *abhicāra* (malevolent) sacrifice when there is great infamy; one who is being falsely accused should perform it in secret.

Having repeatedly cut down—that is, having repeatedly felled—the trees, they should prepare the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*); this is what is meant by "excessively. Āpastamba has used the term *nirvakhya* as a synonym for the phrase "one performing sorcery (*abhicaran*) should sacrifice. He describes its nature as follows: "In that place where they would carry away trees and anthills, or even dig them up"—the essential meaning is that they should prepare the sacrificial ground by cutting down the trees and digging up the anthills, so that it is not new.

"In a secret place, in a secret forest, in a place abounding in secrecy"—that is to say, in a forest. They designate the performer of the *Yama* sacrifice as one who commits sin; when he is being thus accused, his "secret forest" becomes a sacrificial ground for the gods—this is the meaning. Regarding this, Āpastamba states a specific rule: "One should cause the person being accused to sacrifice in a secret forest; they should perform the *Pṛṣṭha* chants out of sight; everything should be performed in a whisper; one should sacrifice on dry land. That which is done so that people do not see it is "out of sight"; one should cause the accused person to sacrifice in such a manner.

Even his back would become invisible; they should not chant their own *ṛc* verses [aloud]; the entire principal rite, along with its auxiliary parts, should be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*); the meaning is that one should sacrifice on a raised ground. Āpastamba states another distinction: "Where a path lies between the water and the place of divine worship, one should perform the sacrifice there if he desires, 'May the sacrifice be more accessible. Even for one traveling by boat... the ritual—

120. Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra—[End of the Fifth Praśna]: Now, therefore, follows the ritual for the sacrificial ground (devayajanakalpa). He seeks out such a sacrificial ground: one that is sloping toward the east or the north, not saline, not previously used for sacrifice, free from pits, and abounding in herbs where various kinds of herbs grow close together; it should be inclined toward the northeast so that water flows away, yet not too steeply so that one cannot find another sacrificial ground nearby to its east.

Kātyāyana states: "They desire a place for the sacrifice to the gods that is highest, level, and imperishable; from this [place], they prepare a sacrificial ground that is slightly sloping toward the east, free of anthills, where those learned in the Vedas have removed the roots of plants, and having cleared it, they construct the sacrificial shed."

Lāṭyāyana and Drāhmāyaṇa state: "The sacrificial ground for the gods (*devayajana*) should slope toward the northeast, be covered with grass, and be treeless; it should be level in the east and have water nearby. There should be a large tree or a great road rising up at its edge, and there should be no higher ground within a short distance. For rites involving malevolent magic (*abhicaraṇīya*), the sacrificial ground should be the opposite of this, and the path for the gods should be from high ground down to the water. "Covered with grass" means abounding in grass and herbs. "Treeless" means that in which there are no trees. "Level" means where the ground is not uneven.

To the east of this sacrificial ground (devayajana), there should be water; in the absence of that, in the absence of water, there should be a well (udapāna). A great path (mahāpatha) is a road leading to another region. That which has an elevated spot (sthalatara) nearby on all sides and no depression (ara) is a sacrificial ground. The word "ca" is used in the sense of "but"; however, there should not be even a mere sacrificial ground in front of—that is, in the eastern part of—the sacrificial ground. The characteristics previously mentioned, when reversed, are the defects (kṣaya) in places intended for the performance of hostile rites (āmica-raṇīya).
And there should not be another high place too close to it; the meaning is that the ground in front [of the altar] must not be inverted.

Regarding the statement, "One should cause him to sacrifice on a level sacrificial ground (devayajana) with offerings in front," these optional sacrificial grounds have been explained in the Brāhmaṇa; one may choose among them according to one's desire.

Beginning with "One should lead [the fire] to a place for sacrifice where oblations are offered first" (*purohaviṣi devayajane*) and ending with "it indeed comes to pass" (*bhavaty eva*), that Brāhmaṇa passage has been explained. Those optional rites (*kāmyāni*) which fulfill desires have been stated; among them, the term *yāthākāmī* means that one may adopt whichever alternative is desired according to one's wish. Āpastamba also says, "The optional places for sacrifice are those where oblations are offered first. Baudhāyana also says, "A hall is constructed on a favored place for sacrifice; one should lead [the fire] to a place for sacrifice where oblations are offered first"—of these, the latter is preferable.

If one should desire, "May the subsequent sacrifice incline toward him; may he thus conquer the heavenly world," one should cause him to go to a place for the divine sacrifice where oblations are first offered. "One should cause him to go to a place for the divine sacrifice where oblations are first offered" is the injunction (*vidhi*). One who possesses the desire, "May the subsequent sacrifice incline toward him; may he lead him to the heavenly world," is the qualified performer (*adhikārī*). The definition of a place for the divine sacrifice where oblations are first offered is given by the section beginning with "For whom the Hotṛ [recites] the morning litany" and ending with "he beholds."

The fruit [of this] begins with "upainamuttara" and ends with "muvargaṃ lokaṃ jayati. A sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) where one reciting the *prātaranuvāka* simultaneously beholds Agni situated in front—the fire on the northern altar (*auttaravedika*), which is further east than that—as well as the impurity of rivers, ponds, and so forth to the east of that, and the risen sun in the eastern direction facing him, is called a *purohavir*.

The subsequent sacrifice, beginning with the Ukthya-offering, shall lead the sacrificer toward himself and cause him to attain the radiant world of heaven; this is the meaning of the Adhvaryu’s desire that he should perform the sacrifice at such a "devayajana" (sacrificial ground). By the term *prātaranuvāka* (morning recitation), the *ājyānuśastra* (the Ājya-recitation) is intended, and not the actual *prātaranuvāka*, because the latter must be completed before sunrise. Otherwise, it would contradict the statement: "He gazes upon the sun. [End of Patala 150] [This concludes] the commentary composed by Gopinatha.

Alternatively, by the word "Āditya," its associated light is primarily intended. The injunction is: "One who has rivals should go to a reached *devayajana* (sacrificial ground). By the phrase "one who has rivals," the qualified performer (*adhikārī*) is indicated. From "Or he should touch it upon the path" up to "this indeed is a reached *devayajana*," the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is provided. From "He indeed obtains" up to "he obtains," the result (*phala*) is stated.

On the path to the *prauda* (the elevated ground), having observed that it has indeed become *prauda*, one should construct the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) in such a way that there is contact with it by means of the *ādhi*. Between the sacrificial ground and the pit (*garta*), one should leave just enough space for a cart or a chariot to pass; this is what is meant by "contact with the *ādhi*" (*adhisparśa*). This very thing is called the "attained" (*āpta*) sacrificial ground; the meaning is that one attains or conquers [prosperity] thereby. One should cause him who desires cattle to sacrifice on a sacrificial ground that is raised in one place.

"One should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice on a sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) that is elevated in one place" is the injunction (*vidhi*). "One who possesses cattle" is the qualified person (*adhikārī*). "Indeed, from a sacrificial ground elevated in one place, Ahirbudhnya releases cattle for him" is the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). "It should be elevated between the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* [sheds]; this indeed is the sacrificial ground elevated in one place" is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). "He becomes possessed of cattle" is the result (*phala*).

The *havirdhāna* shed is situated closer to the east from the *prācīnavaṃśa* hall than the *uttaravedi* altar is to the west. That place which is higher than both of these is called "elevated on one side" (*ekonnata*). One desiring heaven should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice on an elevated sacrificial ground (*devayajana*). "One should cause him to sacrifice on an elevated sacrificial ground" is the injunction (*vidhi*). "One desiring heaven" is the qualification (*adhikāra*). "From an elevated sacrificial ground, indeed, they went to the heavenly world" is the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

The definition [of the site] begins with "between the Āhavanīya fire and... and extends up to "...this is indeed the elevated place for the sacrifice. The result is that "one goes to the heavenly world itself. The meaning of "elevated" (*unnata*) is that place where there is an elevation among the three intermediate spaces between the four [structures]: the *uttaravedi*, the *havirdhāna*, the *sadas*, and the *āgnīdhra*. "One who desires stability should have the sacrifice performed on a stable sacrificial ground"—this is the injunction (*vidhi*). "One who desires stability" is the qualified person (*adhikārī*).

The definition [of the sacrificial ground] begins with "This is firmly established" (*etad vai pratiṣṭhitam*) and ends with "level" (*samam*). The result is that one stands firm upon it. That this very [ground] possesses permanence was stated previously by the author of the Sūtras. It was also stated previously that even for one whose prosperity has departed, this alone is the *devayajana* (sacrificial ground). The meaning is that it is level on all sides—that is, in every location—being neither elevated anywhere nor depressed anywhere. The injunction is: "One should dig where various plants are intertwined."

By this very [passage], the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is also stated. The qualified person (*adhikārī*) is one who desires cattle. The fruit (*phala*) begins with "this [is] for cattle" and ends with "he indeed becomes possessed of cattle. The meaning is that one should cause a person desiring cattle to sacrifice in a place where seeds of barley, wheat, millet, rice, and so forth—which are mutually distinct—are grown together. Although the name of this sacrificial ground for the gods (*devayajana*) is not explicitly mentioned, its name must nevertheless be inferred from its characteristics as "the sacrificial ground for the gods consisting of various intermingled plants."

It is well known that worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is not possible without a name. Regarding the injunction: "If one should desire, 'May I cause his sacrifice to be firmly established,' he should officiate for him at a sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) that is firmly established; he should officiate for him at a sacrificial ground that is firmly established," the person possessing such a desire is the qualified performer (*adhikārī*). The definition of a firmly established sacrificial ground is given by the passage: "This indeed is the firmly established sacrificial ground which is level and true."

The fruit [of this] is that one obtains a sacrifice where one may dwell permanently. A *nityavāsya* is a specific type of *rākṣasa* who obstructs sacrifices. Regarding the phrase "in a place devoid of unevenness": it refers to a site connected to the earth that is level, free from grass and the like, which has been accepted as such. "One desiring distinction (*vyāvṛtkāma*) should cause him to sacrifice at a place of distinction" means: "one desiring distinction should cause him to sacrifice at a place of distinction. This is the injunction. One desiring distinction is the qualified person (*adhikārī*). *Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram*, Tenth Book, Chapter Ten, Section Six. 1016. This is the injunction. One desiring distinction is the qualified person.

The definition [of the ritual] begins with "in a vessel or in a tree" and ends with "this indeed is the distinguished state of the host of gods. The result begins with "free from evil and the rival" and ends with "they deliberate. Regarding the meal with kinsmen indicated by the vessel and the marriage indicated by the ascetic practice (*tapas*): that person whom his relatives, friends, and others deliberate upon—that is, doubt about—is one who desires the removal of the evil, such as censure, which is the cause of that doubt; he is "one desiring distinction" (*vyāvṛtkāma*).

The meaning is that one should lead him to that sacrificial ground known as *vyāvṛtta*. The meaning of "sacrificial ground known as *vyāvṛtta*" is a place where the ground slopes downward (*pravaṇa*) and descends toward the east from the *auttaravedika* *āhavanīya* fire, and where the ground slopes downward and descends toward the west from the *gārhapatya* and *āgnīdhra* fires. There, one is separated—that is, freed—from evil and from enemies.

Regarding this sacrificer, his relatives, friends, and others deliberate and doubt both at the communal meal characterized by the *pātra* vessels and at the marriage characterized by that same term. "One desiring prosperity (*bhūtikāma*) should cause him to sacrifice on a prepared (*kārya*) sacrificial ground (*devayajana*); one should cause him to sacrifice on a prepared sacrificial ground"—this is the injunction. One desiring prosperity is the qualified performer (*adhikārī*). By the word "prepared" (*kārya*), its definition is also stated. "A man indeed becomes prepared"—this is the result. "Prepared" (*kārya*) means it should be made elevated by means of clay, stone, and so forth.

By the phrase "he indeed becomes," [the author] shows that a person who has undergone the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) such as the initiation (upanayana) and so forth must be elevated; therefore, this is the appropriate fruit for him. "He indeed becomes" means that he certainly attains sovereignty (aiśvarya). In that regard, among sacrificial grounds (devayajana) that are naturally high, low, or neither, the states of being high and low should be understood as non-artificial (akṛtrima); however, in the absence of such [natural sites], they may also be artificial (kṛtrima).

When the *devayajana* (the sacrificial ground) is being accepted as deficient by one unit, the measurement from the *prāgvaṃśa* (fore-hall) up to the pit for the sacrificial post (*yūpāvaṭa*) must be performed silently using the standard measure, in order to achieve the required height between the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna*. This same procedure applies to those [deficiencies] that are to be avoided according to the characteristics. However, in the case of what is to be done, the entire area should be raised with earth, gravel, and so forth, until it is made sufficiently high. [This concerns] the censure of one who has accepted a deficient sacrificial ground.

The excellence of others [is established] by way of the principle that "disparagement does not function to disparage, but rather to praise that which is to be praised. How could an *avayuj* priest, being hired by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), desire anything undesirable for the sacrificer? In the phrase "or he might perform the sacrifice for him" (*apa vā yājayet*), the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used in its own primary sense (*svārthe*).

Regarding the injunctions: "If one should desire, 'May he be victorious,'" "one who has rivals and desires cattle," "one who desires heaven," "one who desires stability," or "one who desires cattle"; and regarding the injunction: "If one should desire, 'I would cause his sacrifice to be seized by death,'" "one who desires distinction," or "one who desires prosperity"—in these cases, a transposition of case endings and verbal suffixes is to be understood. In this view, the desire becomes an attribute of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and the grammatical discrepancy (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is thereby avoided. [The term] *nirgati* [refers to the end of the section].

Furthermore, the application of one who has already accepted a *devayajana* (sacrificial ground) in rites of sorcery (*abhicārika*) becomes established. Moreover, the objection—namely, how the desire of the officiating priest (*adhvaryu*) could serve as the motive for employing a desirable *devayajana* when the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) has no such desire—is also refuted. In this context, the "womb of the holy ford" (*tīrthagarbha*) and so forth are mentioned for the purpose of prohibiting the acceptance [of gifts] at such places. Regarding this, the *Amarapurāṇa* states: "Taking the flowing current as the limit, for a distance of four cubits [on either side], Nārāyaṇa is the master; never is there any other master."

"In that regard, one should not accept [water] even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat. Here, "the flow" (*pravāha*) is an elliptical expression for the limit of the water. Therefore, in all cases at sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*) such as Puṣkara, lakes, ponds, and the like, the prohibition applies within a distance of four cubits measured from the edge of the mud. [Chapter 7, Verse 1] (Paṭala 150) — accompanied by the *Jyotsnā* commentary composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa. 1017. Regarding the rule for drinking: "On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, as far as the water extends..."

"One should recognize the *garbha* (the central area) as extending that far; beyond that is called the *tīra* (the bank). In this context, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, even if there is no rain and consequently no increase in water, the region should be understood to extend up to that limit. This is just as, in the injunction "one performs the *upāṃśuyāja* between the two *puroḍāśas*," the location is indicated even in the absence of the two *puroḍāśas*. Furthermore, the extent of the *tīra* is stated in the *Brahma-purāṇa*: "The area extending one hundred and fifty cubits from the water is called the *tīra*."

In the *Skanda Purāṇa* it is said: "The sacred field (*kṣetra*) is declared to extend for a distance of one *gavyūti* all around the bank. Here, charity, recitation, and fire-offerings [yield fruit] as they do in the Gaṅgā; of this there is no doubt. Thus, on each of the two banks, the sacred field measures two *krośas*, which is the extent of a *gavyūti*. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "All sins without exception do not cross the boundary of the Gaṅgā; they flee in the ten directions like deer upon seeing a lion. The boundary of the sacred field extends for one *yojana* across both banks."

The prohibition against accepting gifts applies to well-known rivers. Regarding highly renowned rivers such as the Gaṇḍakī and others, the learned (śiṣṭas) maintain that there is a prohibition even on the banks for a distance of one hundred and fifty cubits on both sides. However, the prohibition regarding a "sacred field" (kṣetra) pertains specifically to the Gaṅgā, because it is only in reference to her that the term "field" is mentioned [in the relevant texts]. As for the statement in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "Where Mahādeva and Svayaṃbhū are present, and where there is a penance grove—that should be known as a 'Field of Siddhi' (Siddhikṣetra), extending for three yojanas in every direction."

"On each side it is one and a half *yojanas*, meaning three *yojanas* all around. This is for the sake of emphasizing the excellence of the place at the time of death, not for the purpose of prohibiting the acceptance of gifts. However, when the reading is "one and a half *yojanas* on all sides," then it is equal to what is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*. While performing sacrifices in the fields of sacred sites (*tīrthas*) yields great fruit, there is indeed a fault for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). "One should not accept gifts at a sacred site even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat; even a creature overcome by lust protects its mother alone."

"Accepting a gift at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) is indeed the selling of the sacred ford. When the Gaṅgā is sold, Janārdana is sold; when Janārdana is sold, the three worlds are sold. For that evil-minded person who, though born of a low caste, takes pleasure in accepting gifts at a sacred site, there is neither the next world nor this world. Thus says the *Pādma Purāṇa*: 'Taking the flowing current as the boundary for four cubits, Nārāyaṇa is the master there; no one else is ever the master.'"

In that case, one should not accept [the gift], even if one’s life-breaths are at the throat. This is because the Baudhāyana Śrautasūtra states that there is a fault in an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) accepting a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Greed (*laulya*) means covetousness. However, in this instance, accepting [the gift] is not a fault. Thus says the Vāmana Purāṇa: "An excellent twice-born man who accepts elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, a bed for the deceased, seats, and so forth, as well as a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), commits no sin when he has fallen into times of distress."

"He who accepts a cow consisting of penance, along with land and mountains, from a fallen Pāṇḍāla in Kurukṣetra, or at a monthly *navaśrāddha*, shall attain the state of a ghost. Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, in the *Pāga*: "A Brāhmaṇa should always accept gifts from a virtuous person; however, he should avoid a horse, a gem, a mother-of-pearl shell, sesame, and iron. This concludes the section on livelihood (*vṛtti*). Now, this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is stated in full.

Regarding this, the Lord of Yogins (Yogīśvara) states: "Dwelling in a cow-pen for one month as a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), subsisting on milk alone and constantly engaged in the recitation of the *Gāyatrī*, one is purified from the acceptance of improper gifts (*asatpratigraha*). Manu states: "Having drunk only milk in a cow-pen for one month and being composed in mind, one who has accepted [improper gifts] is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts (*asatpratigraha*) by reciting the *Sāvitrī* three thousand times. In both of these statements, the word division is *asatpratigrahāt*.

By the use of the accusative case in the word *māsam* (for a month), which denotes continuous duration (*atyantasaṃyoga*), it is understood that the thousand-fold repetition extends over every single day. As for the recitation (*japa*) and the milk-vow (*payovrata*), they should be performed either individually or combined, according to the gravity or lightness of the offense. Regarding this, the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* states: "All terrible offenses arising from accepting gifts are purified by the *Pavitreṣṭi* sacrifice; sometimes by the *Aindravaiṣṇava*, the *Mṛgāreṣṭi*, or the *Mitravindā*. By means of the *Devī-lakṣahoma*, one is purified even from the acceptance of forbidden gifts."

Thus, it should be understood that [this applies] when any one of the place, time, substance, or agent is defective. Following this same method, an increase in the severity of the penance (*prāyaścitta*) should be calculated for the occurrence of three or four such defects together. Some maintain that it is equivalent to the previously mentioned recitation of the *Gāyatrī* one hundred thousand times. Since accepting gifts at a sacred site (*tīrtha*) is prohibited even though the gift exists, it is indeed considered the acceptance of an improper gift (*asat-pratigraha*). Consequently, the penance remains exactly as stated above.

In that regard, although the acceptance of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) as part of the ritual is prohibited at the *tīrtha*, it should be understood that a mitigation of the penance (*prāyaścitta*) is to be assumed because of its being prescribed by rule (*vaidha*). Furthermore, since the mandatory enkindling of the two kindling woods (*araṇī-samāropa*) is specifically ordained for the performance of the departure on the day of the *Prāyaṇīya* sacrifice, it is indicated that there is no fixed rule regarding other times.

Regarding this, Baudhāyana prescribes the consignment [of the fires] into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*): "Having performed either the New Moon sacrifice or a sacrifice under a [specific] lunar mansion, one consigns the fires into the two *araṇīs*. Then, having approached the sacrificial hall (*śālā*), having gone around the north side of the hall, having entered the hall by the eastern door, and having established the Gārhapatya fire in its place, one spreads the fires and enters the Vaiśvadeva chamber through the middle door. Kātyāyana says: "Having consigned [the fires], having taken hold of the front part of the sacrificial hall pillar, and holding the two *araṇīs* in his hands, he should say: 'We have come here.'"

Regarding the two alternatives: as for the carrying of the fires, Baudhāyana says that one should carry them by means of the *anvāhāryapacana* fire; Śālīki says that one should consign them into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*). Vādhūla also says that one should consign the fires either into the two kindling woods or into one's own self, and then carry them by cart or lead them visibly toward the hall. When carrying them by cart, there is no requirement for the ritual breathing-in (*anucchvāsa*) and so forth.

If there is storage (*saṃnidhi*), even without a cart (*śakaṭa*), there is the carrying away of the perceptible items; if the departure occurs within three breaths (*ucchvāsa*), that indeed constitutes the carrying away of the perceptible items even without a cart. However, if the departure extends beyond the fourth breath, there must be a re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*). When the materials for the ritual are being carried away, there is no instruction regarding the breaths; nor is there the offering to Vāstoṣpati (*vāstoṣpatīya*) or the *avasita-homa* at the conclusion, because this journey is considered a mere fragmentary act (*karthita*). Regarding this [journey], some maintain that these two [offerings] do take place.

Regarding the specific procedure for returning to the sacrificial hall (*śālā*), there is a difference of opinion in the *Dvaidha* [text]. Baudhāyana used to say that one should settle in the hall at midday; the waters should go first, followed by the sacrificer, the *rājñī* (queen), and the two kindling woods (*araṇī*). On this point, Śālīki used to say: "One may settle in the hall either in the forenoon or in the afternoon, provided that one intends to complete the *ākvaḥ* and the *iṣṭi* offerings.
Immediately after settling in the place of sacrifice (*devayajana*), he performs the ritual fire-distribution (*agniviharaṇa*) in the consecrated altars smeared with cow dung.
He undergoes the initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the afternoon.

The *saṃbhārayajus* and so forth take place in the afternoon, because they constitute the initiation (*dīkṣā*) alone. That the statement "one who is about to be initiated" refers to the practitioner (*sādhaka*) has already been shown previously. However, the *kuśmāṇḍahoma* takes place in the forenoon, because it is an ancillary part of that [initiation] alone. According to the Sūtra—"In his own skill, from 'I am the Truth' until the end, there is the muttering of the *pratyagāśis* before the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, because it effects the act of kindling"—Āpastamba [prescribes it] before the *dīkṣaṇīyā*.

Regarding the statement, "One should worship the Āhavanīya fire with the *kṣaṇīyā* [verse]," there is no contradiction even in its application to the act of worship (*upasthāna*), because that worship has already been shown in the introduction (*upoddhāta*) to possess the nature of a *mātra* (mantra). The meaning of the Sūtra is clear:
he who desires, "May I be an ascetic," should perform this in the forenoon.

This is an optional alternative (*kāmyapakṣa*). Alternatively, this desire is not independent; rather, because there is an excess of time regarding the observances of one initiated on that day, it is merely a praise of initiation in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇadīkṣā*). This is known from the observation of another scripture stating: "He, being restrained in speech and performing austerity, remains [seated]. From the two rules for initiation in the forenoon and the afternoon, it is understood that the division of time referred to by the terms "forenoon" and "afternoon" here is the same division as that [prescribed elsewhere]. And that division is either a twofold division or indeed a single division.

Regarding the division into two parts, as expressed by the words "the forenoon belongs to the gods and the afternoon to the ancestors," there is an inclusion of two portions through the terms *pūrvāhṇa* and *aparāhṇa*; therefore, the division into two parts is accepted. Likewise, even in the division into three parts—as in "the forenoon belongs to the gods, midday to humans, and the afternoon to the ancestors"—there is an inclusion of two portions through the terms *pūrvāhṇa* and *aparāhṇa*; therefore, the division into three parts is also accepted. [This applies to the day] consisting of the morning (*prātaḥ*), the time when cows are gathered (*saṅgava*), the midday (*madhyāhna*), the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), and the evening (*sāyāhna*).

Having assigned—that is, having pointed out—the sacrificial materials (*havya*) of this initiated person, such as the clarified butter (*ājya*), the animal victim (*paśu*), the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and so forth, for the sake of the sacrifice; that is, having indicated: "This sacrificial material, consisting of clarified butter, animals, sacrificial cakes, and so on, is for the purpose of the sacrifice; from among these, this much shall be used here in the sacrifice, and this much for the purpose of the sacrifice, the Brāhmaṇas shall eat from the remainder"—having thus assigned it. Here, the causative sense (*ṇic*) is intended within the term *nirādiśya*; thus, "having caused the assignment" (*nirādeśya*) means "having caused the pointing out" (*nirādeśana*) to be performed. In this context, the sacrificer is the one to be prompted (*prayojya*), and the officiating priests are the prompters (*prayojaka*).

By this, the meaning that "one's own purpose must be accomplished without assigning [the task to others]" becomes established. Otherwise, there would be an impossibility of common agency (*samānakartṛkatva*) between the two [verbs] *nirādiśya* (having assigned) and *bhuktvā* (having eaten). In the expression *anirādiśya*, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is also included internally; thus, *anirādeśya* means "without having caused [others] to assign. If there is a desire on the part of all—the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the rest—that "everyone here should eat," then one should cause the assignment to be made and then eat.

If there is no desire [to eat], then one should neither cause the *nirādeśana* (the formal assignment) to be performed nor should one release [the remainder]. By stating "having assigned [it], from the remainder one eats," this much alone is intended; it is not that one does not eat without having assigned it. This inclusion is for the purpose of establishing the meaning of the Vedic distinction (*ārṣika-vyatireka*), in order to make known that while these two positions are independent, the acceptance [of the remainder] is dependent on desire. Otherwise, the redundancy would be difficult to avoid. The portion remaining from the substance determined as being for the sake of the sacrifice is denoted by the word *śeṣa* (remainder).

He states the limit for the prohibition of eating: "prior to the Agniṣomīya. This means prior to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice. And that [sacrifice] ends either with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings or with the offering of the omentum (vapā). Accordingly, the Dharmasūtra states: "At the conclusion of the Agniṣomīya alone, the initiated one may eat; or when the omentum has been offered, or when the King [Soma] has been purchased, they may eat from the remainder of what was designated for the sacrifice—so says the Brāhmaṇa. The phrase "or when the King has been purchased" refers to this alternative case in the event of the eater's incapacity.

The *saṃsthā*—the completion—of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice: only when that has occurred may the initiated one eat food related to the initiation (*dīkṣita*), even in the absence of a specific instruction; however, it is not [permitted] before that, except where there is a specific instruction. Alternatively, it may be when the omentum (*vapā*) of the *agnīṣomīya* animal has been offered, or when the King Soma has been purchased. These options are to be determined according to whether there is an emergency or no emergency. If it is designated for the sake of the sacrifice, it may be eaten even before these occasions.

In this context, the statement regarding the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is as follows: when there is an instruction concerning the purpose of the sacrifice, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is the one who employs [the materials]. However, when there is an instruction concerning other purposes, the state of being employed belongs to the clarified butter (*ājya*), the animals, the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), and so forth. [The thought is: "This [substance] is for the sake of the sacrifice; among these, this much will be used in the sacrifice, and only this much is for the sake of the sacrifice; the remainder is for the *havirdhāna* shed. In such an instruction, the state of being employed does not belong to the clarified butter, the animals, or the sacrificial cakes.

"This substance is for the sake of sacrifice; among this, so much shall be used in the sacrifice and only so much is for the purpose of the sacrifice; from the remainder, all [the participants] should eat"—these two sentences constitute the *nirādeśana* (assignment). The *nirādeśana* for the sake of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), being dependent on the context where the priests are the agents, is non-permanent (*anitya*). The second, however, because it has the Brahmins as its own agents and because it is necessary for them, is indeed permanent (*nitya*). It should be understood that only in this manner does the injunction in both cases become purposeful, and not otherwise.

"He undergoes initiation in the afternoon"—from this [statement], because of the subsequent injunction, it is understood that the disposal (*nirādeśana*) of the materials used for the rites beginning with initiation is mandatory. Since even the *samrāḍdhu* and other items serve the purpose of initiation, the same applies to them as well. Thus, there is no fault in consuming the clarified butter remaining from the *Kūśmāṇḍa* oblations after it has been set aside, even in the absence of its disposal following the initiation.

Regarding eating food that has not been designated for one's own specific kin: the expiation for eating food that has not been designated or inspected is stated in the *Āpastamba Smṛti*: "A twice-born man who eats sacrificial food (*yajñiya-anna*), food from a *navashrāddha*, food at a communal gathering (*saṃgraha*), or food during the first pregnancy of a woman, shall perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. "Sacrificial food" (*yajñiya-anna*) refers to food related to a sacrifice. For consistency with the *Sūtras*, the inedibility of such sacrificial food should be understood as lasting until the completion of the sacrifice, or specifically until the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma (*āgneya-aupomīya*). "Gathering" (*saṃgraha*) refers to marriage.
He mutters "May there be well-being; may [the days] following be better" at every instance while the hair is being shaved.

The inclusion of the word "everywhere" (sarvatra) is for the purpose of ensuring that this recitation applies even to the shavings of hair connected with the *samāvartana*, the *caula*, and the *godāna* ceremonies; and also to the shaving performed without a mantra when the *anubandhyā* victim's omentum has been offered and the sacrificer’s hair and beard are shaved on the southern shoulder of the altar; and also to the shaving in the *Aśvamedha* sacrifice described as: "He shaves his hair and beard, pares his nails, cleanses his teeth, bathes, and puts on a new garment," which is likewise without a mantra.

Or rather, it is for the purpose of bringing about the recitation of the mantra "svastyuttarāṇyaśīya. Because of the use of the present participle "upyamāna" (being sown), the recitation occurs while the shaving is actually being performed—neither before nor immediately after. Even if there is impurity, the recitation of the mantra takes place because of this specific injunction. This much alone constitutes the mantra.
Once the barber's work is finished, he cleanses his teeth with a stick made of *udumbara* wood, taking care not to produce blood.

"There is no barber’s work; [it is performed] in that barber’s work. By the expression "in the barber’s work" (*nāpitakṛtye*), it is understood that this act of shaving has the Adhvaryu as its agent. If the barber were the agent, the usage "when the barber’s work is completed" (*nāpitakṛtye kṛte*) would be inconsistent. Furthermore, if the barber’s agency had been intended, the author would necessarily have said, "when the barber’s work has occurred" (*jāte nāpitakṛtye*). The author of the Sūtra did not state it in that way. Therefore, this shaving is indeed performed by the Adhvaryu.

The mention of *audumbara* (fig wood) is for the purpose of excluding other trees and copper. Since no distinction is specified, either wood or a leaf may be taken. *Danta* means the teeth; *dhāvate* means he cleanses them. Furthermore, this cleansing of the teeth is a mandatory ritual act (*karmāṅga*), not merely for the sake of removing bad breath and the like, because that [purpose] is already accomplished by the morning tooth-cleansing, or by twelve mouthfuls of water which serve as a substitute for the tooth-stick when it is prohibited due to forbidden lunar days and so forth.

Because this tooth-cleaning is enjoined by Vedic injunction (*vaidha*), the prohibition found in the *Smṛtis* regarding the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and other such occasions does not apply here. As for the Smṛti statement: "The initiated, the student (*brahmacārī*), the ascetic (*yati*), and the widow should always use a tooth-stick, but on the new moon day they should avoid it"—that refers specifically to initiation into mantras (*mantradīkṣā*). One who has received mantra-initiation should perform the cleaning of teeth, using sticks four finger-breadths long, but he should avoid it on the new moon day.

This is because of the agreement with the statement in the *Tantra*, and not because it refers specifically to the initiation (*dīkṣā*) connected with a sacrifice; for otherwise, there would arise a contradiction with the Vedic injunction, "He brushes his teeth" (*dato dhāvate*). Thus, when the initiation has not yet taken place, the brushing of the teeth certainly occurs. Regarding the specific rule for brushing the teeth, Āpastamba states in the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: "Thereafter, he should brush his teeth with a twig in an upward direction."

The meaning is that one should first clean the upper teeth and afterwards clean the lower teeth. Regarding the dimensions of the tooth-stick (*dantadhāvana-kāṣṭha*), the *Kaurma* states: "The tooth-stick should be as thick as the middle finger, twelve finger-breadths in length, and possessed of its bark; one should brush with its tip. This [measurement] is for one with uneven teeth; for others, however, it should be as thick as the tip of the little finger.
"Fine for one with even teeth, medium for one with even teeth, and coarse for one with uneven teeth—thus is the tooth-stick of three kinds," according to the statement of Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu [also says]: "The wise say that the wood for a Brāhmaṇa should be twelve finger-breadths long."
"For those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, it is nine, six, and four finger-breadths [respectively].
Thus says Garga: "The measurement for women is four finger-breadths; there is no doubt in this matter.
This is used by the wife for cleaning her teeth. Regarding the cleaning of the teeth, Vyāsa says:
"Having thoroughly washed his feet, hands, and face, being well-composed, he should lift his right arm and place it between his knees," so says [the text].
Āśvalāyana states: "He should discard the wooden tooth-stick in the southward direction (rākṣasī), or having wiped it clean, in a pure place."
Having wiped and washed [the tooth-stick], Viṣṇu says: "From the east, there is happiness from the chewing of the tooth-stick, as well as bodily health;
in the south, however, there is hardship, and in the west, defeat."
"In the north, however, there is the loss of cattle, women, and attendants;
but in the north-eastern quarter, one shall obtain all desires. Thus [says the scripture].
Aṅgiras says: "One should chew the tooth-stick after washing it, and one should discard it only after washing it."

"This mantra beginning with 'āyuḥ' is prescribed for the consecration of the branch. And that mantra is found in the Purāṇa: "O Lord of the Forest, grant us long life, strength, fame, splendor, progeny, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence."

The mantra for brushing the teeth, as stated in the Purāṇas, is: "For the destruction of foul odors from the mouth, for the purification of the teeth, and for the clearing of phlegm from the body, I perform the brushing of my teeth.

Alternatively, one may brush the teeth silently. This mantra is used when there is a suspicion of foul odor in the mouth; otherwise, it should be done silently. Śaunaka describes the duties following the brushing of teeth:

"Afterwards, one should perform the cleaning of the teeth with twelve mouthfuls of water. "Red" means blood. "Without entering or exiting"—the word "damya" (the animal to be tamed/initiated) is understood as the subject, because it is that which is present in proximity. If, after the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering has been performed, blood should flow out and come within the range of vision, then, since all the duties of the initiated (*dīkṣita*) have already commenced, the recitation of the mantra "O Rudra, to the waters, svāhā! takes place. [End of Paṭala 27, Section 150, accompanied by the commentary Jyotsnā by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 1023. All the duties of the initiated being in effect, the recitation "O Rudra, to the waters, svāhā" occurs.

If that [tooth-cleaning] has not been performed, there is no recitation (japa) because the duties of one who is consecrated (dīkṣita) have not yet commenced. If what has emerged from the teeth goes back into the stomach, then one must perform an expiation (prāyaścitta) and carry out the subsequent rite; for if that is not done, there is a lack of qualification to perform it. Therefore, tooth-cleaning should be performed in such a way that blood does not come out. And that expiation is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "In the case of intentionally eating hair, nails, or blood, there is a three-night fast; if unintentionally, a single day's fasting."

With the verse, "Golden-hued, pure, purifying," he bathes in a stagnant pool after having placed gold within a lake containing conch shells: "The golden-hued, pure, purifying waters, having pierced Vṛtra and cast off impurity, have flowed forth; for them there are a hundred spread-out filters—by means of these may the god Savitṛ purify us. And with the verse, "May the Waters, our mothers, cleanse us," he bathes.

These are the mantras for bathing. The bath is performed only once at the end of the *manaḥ* [mantra]. This statement is intended to prevent the doubt that, as is well known elsewhere, there might be an inclusion here of the four mantras or the entire section (*anuvāka*) beginning with the word *ripram*. The third [mantra] ends with *ripram*. If one does not bathe in flowing water, but only in stagnant water, then one should bathe after placing gold within that water.

Alternatively, when Hari is present, one bathes having placed gold within those very waters that are "sthāvara" (stationary). They are "sthāvara" in the sense of being non-exhaustible (*aśoṣyāḥ*), because of the proximity of the word *ha*. According to the interpretation where "sthāvara" means "having ceased movement," the bathing may take place even in a pond or a lake. In this view, the previous explanation becomes consistent with the meaning here.

Regarding the bath for the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*), it is stated in the *Smṛti* that it yields great fruit when performed in a natural pond (*devakhāta*), a river, the Gaṅgā, or at a confluence: "Whether in a natural pond, a river, the Gaṅgā, or even at a confluence, a bath performed for the sake of initiation is declared to yield great fruit. The term "rivers" refers to the twelve great rivers, such as the Godāvarī and Bhīmā. Accordingly, the *Brahmapurāṇa*, concerning the great rivers, states: "The Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Veṇikā, Tāpī, and Payoṣṇī are proclaimed to be on the southern side of the Vindhya mountains."

"The Bhāgīrathī, Narmadā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Viśokā, and Vitastā are situated to the north of the Vindhya. Thus [it is said]. The Bhāgīrathī, Godāvarī, and Veṇā—these three have gone [to the ocean]. And likewise the Brahma Purāṇa states: "Three rivers of great merit—the Veṇā, Godā, and Nāhī—having reached the earth from the body of Hari (Viṣṇu), are indeed celebrated as the Gaṅgā. There is an alternative reading: "having reached the earth from the portion belonging to Hari and Īśa (Śiva)."

The meaning is that from the feet of Hari, the Lord, the navel reached the earth. The word *śaṅkha* indicates clear water. From the word *śaṅkha*, the suffix *ini* is applied in the sense of "possessing. Thus, *śaṅkhin* means "that which possesses water as clear as a conch" (*śaṅkha*); this is the meaning. A lake with deep water is called *sahana*. The term *śaṅkhinī* is an adjective qualifying the lake (*hrada*). He states another method: *Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram*—[In the tenth book, he describes an alternative method:]

Regarding the phrase "he bathes in that *tīrtha* which is hairy (*lomaśa*) and open (*avakāśa*)," some say he bathes in that *kuṇḍa*. That water is "hairy" (*lomaśa*) where there are grasses; it is "hairy" because hairs (*loman*) are found therein. The word *loman* here refers to grass, as seen in the passage, "From the hairs, he offers the *adhistambayajus*. The suffix *śa* is used in the sense of possession according to the rule *lomādi-pāmādi*. "Open" (*avakāśa*) means that which has *avakās*, i.e., moss (*śevāla*). Some explain it as *śaro'vakā* (reeds and moss), citing the *liṅga* [of the Veda] such as "the reed and the moss. That which has an expanse (*āśa*)—that is, pervasion (*vyāpti*)—by means of the *avakās* is "open" (*avakāśa*).

Alternatively, it is called *avakāśa* because there is space (*avakāśa*) therein; the suffix *ac* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) because the word begins with *aś*. That is to say, it is a place where one may descend easily. The meaning is that one should bathe in such a true sacred ford (*sattīrtha*) where people bathe; however, there is no rule that one must bathe only in those [tīrthas] of great majesty. Indeed, if they are available, bathing in them is even more meritorious. Or, the meaning is that one should bathe in a *kuṇḍa*, which is a trench (*droṇī*) characterized by those features.

The repetition of the word "snāti" (he bathes) in the middle of this [sūtra] is for the purpose of showing that this is an independent alternative view (*pakṣāntara*). In the phrase "he bathes in a *kuṇḍa*," the expression "having placed gold [in it]" (*hiraṇyam avadhāya*) is understood by means of "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) syntax. Thus says Āpastamba: "Having placed gold in a *kuṇḍa*, he bathes in it; this is the Vājasaneyaka tradition. Therefore, according to the Vājasaneyi-mata, this bathing is to be performed specifically in a well (*kūpa*).

Regarding the specific procedure for going to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), Baudhāyana said: "In the case of going to a *tīrtha*, one should turn to the right and go to the other *tīrtha*; one should turn back with the hands facing away [from the body]. On this point, Śālīki said: "Having turned back with the hands facing away, one should go from here to the *tīrtha*, and then turn to the right from there. "From here" means from the place of shaving; "from there" means from the place of the *tīrtha*.
