If the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) is far away, then the following expedient is prescribed by Baudhāyana: "Now, if the *tīrtha* is distant, they prepare two straw-mat enclosures to the north of the hall; the eastern one for the sacrificer and the western one for his wife. They make the doors of these two facing east. Therein he causes water-jars to be placed. The meaning is that he causes water-jars to be placed within those two straw-mat enclosures by the attendants for the purpose of bathing.

In this ritual, beginning with the words "where the waters are pleasant and easy to plunge into" and ending with the entire section of the *anuvāka* "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ," the complete procedure for bathing (*snānatantra*) takes place. Regarding that bathing denoted by the term "plunging into" (*avagāhya*), which consists of "where the waters are pleasant and easy to plunge into," the three mantras beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ" are prescribed for the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*). The word "having plunged into" (*avagāhya*) here has the meaning "having bathed" (*snātvā*).

Regarding the phrase "having bathed" (*snātvā*) in this *anuvāka*, the meaning of the word *snāna* is taken to be "having honored" (*mānayitvā*). This interpretation of these two words within the sūtra that prescribes bathing is established in the *Saṃskāraratnamālā*; it should be consulted there. When the midday bath and the bath for the purpose of initiation coincide in time, the midday bath is accomplished by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*). Having bathed with the mantra, "Having emerged from the waters, pure and purified, I come," he performs the *udghāha* (submerging).

The repetition of the word "bathe" (*snāsva*) is for the purpose of excluding the *tarpaṇa* (libation) which is an ancillary part of the bath. Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) "emomi," this is the mantra for the immersion (*udgāhana*). Immersion (*udgāhana*) means returning to the bank. Then, with the words "Whatever water has been defiled by me," he pours out water on the bank, dedicating it to Yakṣman. However, in the previous case where the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice is not performed, there is simply an absence of the midday bath. Following that, there is the twice sipping of water according to the Smṛti rules. [End of the first section of the Paṭala] Having touched water and having sipped water. 3. With the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 1025. Having touched water and having sipped water. 3.

In some cases "water" is not mentioned, while in others it is; where it is not mentioned, one should use the water after purifying it, whereas where it is mentioned, one does not [purify it]. This is a universal rule. Since the word "water" is absent in the present context, it is established that one should take water in a vessel, purify it with two strainers (*pavitra*), and then touch it with the hand.

Regarding the term *ācamya*, the word division here is *ā-ācamya*. It is not intended that this refers merely to the sipping of water as established by the authoritative texts of the Smṛtis; rather, the prefix *ā* indicates that something more is involved. Thus, the meaning established is that one takes a handful of water in a vessel and consumes it all at once with the hand alone. By this, one becomes pure within. Accordingly, the Śruti states: "He eats the waters; thus he becomes pure within."

Baudhāyana says that one should cover [the head] with the edge of the garment. If this sipping of water (*ācamana*) is performed while remaining within the water, then the midday ritual (*mādhyāhnika-karma*) is to be performed here; however, if the sipping is performed after coming outside, it should be understood that the midday ritual is to be performed at the conclusion of the arrangement of the *nīvi* as will be described later. As for the *brahmayajña*, it must be performed in the morning itself, prior to the commencement of the sacrifice. He puts on a large, unwashed linen garment with the mantra: "Thou art the consecration (*dīkṣā*), thou art the body; may I clothe thee, who art auspicious and pleasant," and with the mantra: "Thou art the body of Soma; protect my body."

The words *kṣauma* (linen) and *ahata* (unbeaten/new) have already been explained. Here, by the word *mahat* (great), the thickness (*sthaulya*) of the garment is expressed, since its length is established by implication. Thus, the garment here is thick, meaning it is firm; by this, the exclusion of a fine (*sūkṣma*) garment—which would lack firmness—is accomplished. This is a representative citation (*pratīka*) ending with the word *sanvi*, belonging to the section of the Ācchidrika-prapāṭhaka beginning with "Thou art initiation (*dīkṣā*), thou art the womb of austerity. Furthermore, this mantra is prescribed by Āpastamba for the act of putting on the garment.

"Thou art the body; thee, such as thou art"—this is the second [mantra] from the Sūtra. "Thou art the body of Soma; protect my body"—this is the third from the *Saṃhitā*. Thus, there are three mantras for the act of girding. Moving clockwise is established by the general rule (*paribhāṣā*). Baudhāyana has indeed read: "He puts on a new, unwashed garment, moving clockwise. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include this together with the two preceding [mantras]. Alternatively, the word "and" is intended to include the *Ācchidrika* mantra: "Thou art consecration (*dīkṣā*), the womb of austerity (*tapas*)."

In this alternative view, the sequence is as follows: first, there is only this single mantra, "Thou art consecration; thou art the body"; second, the mantra ending with "Thou art consecration of austerity" (*dīkṣāsi tapasaḥ*); and third, the mantra "Thou art the body of Soma; protect my body," followed by the action of putting on a large, unwashed linen garment. Then, with the mantra "Thou art the garment of the Sun; thou art the girdle; bestow vigor upon us," he arranges its girdle around him.

The meaning is: "Thou art like the garment of the Sun. By this, the doubt as to how the garment can belong to the deity Sūrya when it belongs to the deity Soma is dispelled. Of him [the sacrificer] who has put on the garment: the meaning is that one should subsequently arrange the knot of the wrapped cloth for the purpose of concealing the inner part and for the sake of making the edge of the garment visible. The prefix *pari* signifies the sense of distribution (*dāya*). The singular number in the word *nīvim* is used in the sense of a genus (*jāti*). In that regard, among the four folds of the waist-cloth (*kaccha*), two folds are denoted by the term *nīvi*.

In this context, the lower garment (*paścātkaccha*) comes first because it is primary. As stated by Gārgya: "If a man performs any optional rite (*kāmya-karman*) with his lower garment untied (*muktakaccha*), all of that becomes futile due to the exposure of his private parts. This is from the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha.

It should not be said that the *macātra* [the waistband] is the primary element here; for by the reason of its revealing the secret parts, it is understood that the *nīvī* itself is the primary one. It should be observed that because of the mention of "optional" (*kāmya*), this rule applies specifically to optional acts, and not to obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) ones. Due to the singular number, the mantra is recited only once; and that [recitation] is over the first *nīvī*.

One should not spread out the lower garment (*paridhānīyavastra*) to the right for the purpose of wearing it; rather, facing either east or north, one should put it on. All the rules from the *Smṛti* texts—such as "the knot (*nīvī*) should be arranged facing forward or toward the south," and so forth—should be applied here. By the mention of "sipping water" (*ācamya*), it is understood that the wearing of the garment is connected to the consecration (*dīkṣā*) within the waters.

Therefore, on the afternoon of the *daśapeya* sacrifice, he undergoes initiation for the *daśapeya*. In place of the [usual] initiation in water, the sacrificer puts on a golden ornament with six or twelve lotus-petals (*puṇḍarīka*). By this—namely, by the initiation in water which ends with the non-wearing [of clothes] and by the putting on of the lotus-ornament—the cessation of the garment is established, as if by the removal of the garment, there is also the cessation of the "garment-initiation" (*vāsodīkṣā*).

He eats [the food] with the formula, "For strength (*ūrj*) thee," or "Bestow strength upon us," or whatever is dear to his mind, such as curd mixed with clarified butter or honey, used as a condiment.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: whatever is dear to his mind—whether it be *sīmiśra* (sour milk mixed with grain), curd, or honey—that he eats, having approached [it] with the thought "this is light" (*bhāti*). Because of the constant relationship between the pronoun *tat* and the verb *ad*, the word *tat* is understood as referring to the food (*ārṣikaḥ tacchabdānvayaḥ*). The meaning is that he eats whatever food is among the collection of edible things that is dear to his own mind (*manasa ātmanaḥ*), not to the sacrificer (*yajamānasya*), because the demonstrative pronoun *idam* (in the sense of "this") cannot refer to himself, and because the word *manas* would otherwise be redundant.

The fact that *manas* denotes the self (*ātman*) is observed in such passages as "you have found the self by means of the self" (*ātmānam ātmanā veda*). Some maintain that what is dear to the mind is only food fit for sacrifice (*haviṣya*). Others hold that the statement "what is dear to the mind" is intended to ensure the consumption of all sacrificial food whatsoever.

Just as in the case of legumes (*masūra*), stalks (*vṛntāka*), and so forth—which, although not inherently unfit for sacrifice (*ahaviṣya*), are prohibited on specific lunar days (*tithi*)—there is permission to eat them at other times when such eating is prompted by desire (*rāga-prāpta*); likewise, since this meal is prompted by desire and yet also constitutes a constituent part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*), the statement "that which is dear to his mind" must be explained in this very way: that because the prohibition applies to specific lunar days, the permission does not extend to other times, and therefore this statement is intended to ensure its attainment [at those other times].

However, the possibility of eating *all* *haviṣya* food is entirely irrelevant here, as it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to include onions (*palāṇḍu*) and other such items. If one were to accept this [over-extension], then since eating onions and similar things constitutes a cause for re-initiation (*punarupanayana*), there would be a constant transgression in the interim. Nor should it be argued that this statement is intended to enjoin the eating of all *haviṣya* foods other than those [specifically prohibited]; for it is more reasonable to understand it as referring to the eating of only a small amount of *haviṣya* food in comparison to this [prohibition]. Furthermore, it should not be argued that the absence of fault must be inferred here simply because the act is prescribed.

Since there is no explicit statement [to that effect], rather than postulating numerous faults, it should be considered how—given that the word *ātman* refers to the mind (*manas*) in this context regarding those non-eatable items for which no penance is prescribed—the word *manas* can instead denote the *ātman*. This remains to be examined.

Even though the word *hari* denotes a horse in the context of the *dheśamda* (the *dhe-śam-da* formula), the word *aśva* does not denote a horse; for it is logical to establish the absence of defects regarding the ritual items (*padārtha*), whereas there is indeed a prohibition against eating lentils (*masūra*), eggplants (*vṛntāka*), and so forth, based on specific lunar days (*tithi*). By this [text], the time and the specific mantra are prescribed for a meal that is prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*).

The word *sarpiḥ* denotes ordinary clarified butter (*ājya*). For this very reason, the author of the Sūtra provided the qualification "with [butter] for the sake of consecration" (*saṃskārārtha-sarpiṣā*) regarding the pouring over the milk that has been heated (*sāyadoha-abhighāraṇe*) with silent [mantras]. The meaning is: having poured either curd or honey upon it, one eats that which remains mixed with the clarified butter. In the reading "curd and honey" (*dadhi madhu ca*), there is a conjunction of both; because there is no compound, the two are not necessarily simultaneous.

This sūtra demonstrates that among those substances which are exceedingly dear to the mind, the consumption of at least one of them is necessary. The expression "dear to the mind" is stated so that, in the event of not consuming what is dear to the mind, one incurs a scriptural expiation (*śrautaprāyaścitta*); and since no specific [expiation] is mentioned, it is simply the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). Here, the curd may be either from a cow or from a buffalo. Here, the honey must be *saudra* (from bees), and not *mākṣika* (from flies), because the hearing of defects such as being a great sinner (*mahāpātakin*) is recorded regarding the consumption of the latter. One should consume either the curd or the honey.

The rule is "what? (kam). By this, curd and honey alone are for the purpose of sprinkling (abhyupaseka), but not milk; however, that [milk] is for eating independently. Alternatively, the rule is that curd or honey is only for sprinkling. By this, curd and honey are only for sprinkling; it should be understood that milk is for both purposes. In the first alternative, [curd and honey] are for both purposes: as sprinkling and independently as food. But ghee and oil are to be regarded as being only by way of mixing. One becomes satiated.

Because of the use of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the word *āśita*, the instigators (*prayojaka*)—such as ministers and beloved kinsmen—and the one to be instigated (*prayojya*)—the sacrificer—are indicated. Thus, the meaning is: "he eats much until satiety," being impelled by ministers, beloved kinsmen, and so forth. However, the two words *ā* and *aśita* were not separated in that manner by the makers of the *pada-pāṭha*. The meaning "he piles up much until satiety" is obtained from the Śruti text: "As far as his vital breath (*prāṇa*) extends, with that he overcomes the enemy. [Objection: But is this statement redundant?

If it is argued that this is established by the very statement of the *Dharma-sūtra*: "Eight morsels are prescribed for a sage (*muni*), sixteen for a forest-dweller, thirty-two for a householder, and an unlimited number for a student (*brahmacārin*); [and] 'The fire-maintainer (*āhitāgni*), the ox, and the student—these three succeed only when they are infinite; their success does not belong to those who have limited [intake]'", which was made for the purpose of setting aside the rule regarding the number of thirty-two morsels concerning the householder mentioned in the *Dharma-sūtra*, we reply: True.

"The measure of food has been prescribed for as long as one remains comfortable. Eating in deficient measure, however, does not lead to strength, nourishment, or vigor; rather, it becomes the cause of all wind-related diseases (*vātaroga*). Furthermore, eating in excessive measure quickly provokes all the *doṣas*. Thus, having stated the defects of eating too little or too much in the medical treatise of Vāgbhaṭṭa, [it is said]: 'One should fill two of the stomach's quarters with solid food and one with drink; one should leave the fourth quarter empty as a refuge for the wind and other [humors]. "

1028. The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the tenth book]—by this [statement], the measure of food is declared. And thus, since one must eat while leaving one part of the stomach for the sake of digestion and so forth, this [sūtra] is purposeful as a means of making known that the meal here should be greater than the meal established in Āyurveda by a quantity equal to an additional fourth part (the *caturthīśa*) intended for the sake of digestion and so forth. Eating more than this would cause bodily suffering.

Otherwise, it would be contradictory due to the risk of indigestion (*ḍāha*). Therefore, one should release [the food] only after preserving a certain portion for the sake of wind (*pavana*) and other bodily humors. Regarding the phrase "the measure of enjoyment has been specified," there is also a reading: "the measure of the *mātrā* has been specified. Even with this reading, by the term *mātrā*, eating itself is understood.

Once the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering has been performed previously, because the duties of the initiated (*dīkṣita*) have already commenced, the prohibition contained in the sūtra—"He does not offer any oblation other than those connected with the sacrifice"—also applies to the Vaiśvadeva offerings and the breath-offerings (*prāṇāhuti*). If the initiated person is the primary performer of the Vaiśvadeva, the Vaiśvadeva must indeed be performed by others using food cooked for their own sake, provided they have his permission.

After the entry into the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, since the duties of the initiated (*dīkṣita*) have not yet commenced, the prohibition [of the Vaiśvadeva] does not apply; therefore, the Vaiśvadeva must be performed by the sacrificer himself. Likewise, the *prāṇāhuti* offerings also take place. The mantra "ūrje tvā" is intended solely for the purpose of eating, as it applies regardless of whether the prohibition is in force or not; it is not intended for the *prāṇāhuti*. This mantra "ūrje tvā" is combined with the mantra of the first *prāṇāhuti*, because the latter serves a human purpose (*puruṣārtha*).

Some maintain that because of the difference in purpose—since this [mantra] pertains to the ritual (*ṛtu*) while the other pertains to the year (*arṣa*)—the mantra "neither by day nor by night" cannot serve as a substitute for the *prāṇāhuti* mantras. Others, however, say that this very mantra takes the place of the five [offerings], since the prohibition "he offers no offering whatsoever except those connected with the sacrifice" excludes offerings intended for human ends (*puruṣārtha*); therefore, it must be for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*) alone. Of these, the former view is trivial.

Regarding the first [position], because of the combination with the *prāṇāhuti* mantra, since one or the other would be separated, there would be no immediate connection with the action (*kriyā-saṃnipāta*), and thus it could not function as an instrument (*akaraṇatva*). Furthermore, because they constitute the subject matter of distinct scriptures, there is no instruction regarding a single instrument—as in the case of "by two" or "by three. Moreover, if the *prāṇāhutis* were not prohibited for the sake of human goals (*puruṣārtha*), then since the *prāṇāhutis* themselves would be non-existent, the statement that "this very mantra [should be used] in place of all the *prāṇāhutis*" would be utterly inconsistent; therefore, the second position is also trivial.

Therefore, it is concluded that the mantra applies only to the food itself and not to its location as a seat for the *prāṇāhuti* offerings. [The mantras] do not indeed become redundant. Because they take the form of an oblation (*āhuti*) by virtue of being offered with reference to a deity, the prohibition "he does not offer any oblation" (*na kāṃcanāhutiṃ juhoti*) applies here as well, without any contradiction. However, the sprinkling (*pariṣeka*) and the invitation (*animantraṇa*) do indeed occur, because those two are not offered with reference to a deity. From the sūtra "wherein there is one substance," the mantra is recited in its entirety. From this point onward, he consumes smaller and smaller portions as his fast-food (*vrata*).

The word "in the initiations" (*dīkṣāsu*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. "Lesser and lesser" (*kanīyaḥ kanīyaḥ*) means increasingly small; the meaning is that starting from the initiation, one undertakes the vow until the completion of the initiation. This has been clearly stated by Āpastamba: "He should eat in such a way that, thereafter, he may undertake a lesser and lesser vow during the initiations. This is for the sake of accomplishing the necessary functions of the body; for as there is an increase in the bodily functions, so too is there an increase in purity (*medhyatā*).

And likewise Āpastamba says: "When the initiated one becomes emaciated, then he becomes fit for sacrifice; when there is nothing remaining within him, then he becomes fit for sacrifice; when the blackness from his eyes disappears, then he becomes fit for sacrifice; when his skin and bone become joined together, then he becomes fit for sacrifice. One should be fat when being initiated, but emaciated when performing the vow; it is known from scripture that whatever of his limbs wastes away, that indeed he offers as an oblation."

In the third chapter, eighth section (pāda), Jaimini also states: "And austerity [is not required], because the fruit is already established, as in common worldly usage" (Jaiminisūtra 3.4.10). And: "The supplementary statement is likewise. These two sūtras were explained during the commentary on the sūtra: "That [restriction] ceases during the initiations. [This refers to the day of] the *medha*, which is the sacrifice (*yajña*). [This concludes] the tenth paṭala, together with the moonlight-like commentary composed by Gopīnātha. 1029. 3. And the remainder of the sentence is to that effect. These two sūtras have been explained on the occasion of the commentary on the sūtra: "That [restriction] ceases during the initiations. [The term] *medhya* means *medha*, which is the sacrifice; [it refers to] that day.

Even during the state of initiation (*dīkṣā*), when one who is emaciated is among those who have undergone initiation and consume food, [the food] is as if offered into the fire itself. Therefore, one must consume [only] with an emaciated body. By this also it is known that the position favoring an abundance of initiations is extremely praiseworthy. From this it is further understood that the injunction "he becomes emaciated" refers to multiple initiations and not to a single initiation; in the case of the latter, however, one should eat only what is necessary to sustain life in order to produce some degree of austerity.

In this context, the emaciation caused by disease is excluded, as it is the emaciation resulting from the reduction of ritual vows that is intended; for we see the scriptural injunction: "One who is fat should be initiated. This cooking for the purpose of eating must be caused to be performed by another, neither by oneself nor by one's wife. Thus says Baudhāyana: "Then he causes the *pratipānīya* (food for consumption) to be brought to these two; they both eat of it. It is well known that one must eat only after having offered [the food] to the Lord.

And this [food] is to be eaten by the husband and wife alone; no Brāhmaṇa is to be fed here either, because this meal serves the purpose of the consecration (*dīkṣita-saṃskāra*) for them, and thus there is an absence of any other feeding. For this very reason, the prohibition "one should not eat alone" does not apply here. With the mantra "Thou art the milk of the earth," he clarifies the cow’s fresh butter using two bundles of *darbha* grass. With the mantra "Thou art the bestower of splendor; bestow splendor upon me," he anoints himself with it—first the face, then the other limbs in the direction of the hair. Thus he becomes well-anointed.

The mention of "cow" (*gavya*) is for the purpose of excluding [milk] from buffaloes and other such animals. The prefix *sam-* has the sense of "properly" (*samyak*); and that [quality of being proper] connects with the act of churning. In the word *udyotī*, the remainder of the sense is "for the purpose of purification. Baudhāyana states that placing [the milk] in a vessel of ten fingers' width is specifically for the purpose of purification.

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "Then this butter of his, having been stirred, rests upon a vessel of water" (*udaśarāva*): although the root *yudh* has the meaning of "mixing," since that [action] requires two entities as its objects and no other such entity is possible in the present context, the root *yudh* cannot have that meaning here; therefore, it must mean "stirring. It is precisely to demonstrate this specific meaning that the word *ut* is employed. In the case of stirring, clockwise rotation (*pradakṣiṇya*) is established by technical convention (*paribhāṣā*). The mention of the word "together" (*saha*) is for the purpose of restriction.

By this, the meaning established is that one should take up only as much oil as is sufficient for anointing the limbs with that very same [quantity], and nothing else should be taken up. Or, the purpose of the expression "by that" (*tena*) is to indicate that if, by chance, one forgets to stir [the oil] after the anointing has been performed and remembers it immediately thereafter, one should take up more, stir it, and perform the anointing again with that.

It is with the hands alone that he anoints, because of their inherent capacity, and not with two bundles of *darbha* grass, as there is no scriptural authority for that. Regarding this, Bodhāyana has stated quite explicitly: "Having rubbed [the ointment] together with his two hands, he first anoints the face. Here, the locative case in the word *agre* is used in the sense of the ablative; thus, the meaning becomes "he anoints starting from the front of the face. That is to say, starting from the front of the face—that is, from the head—he anoints the face. By this, the forward direction (*parācīnatā*) of the anointing is demonstrated.

And likewise, Āpastamba states: "The face is repeated three times in the forward direction; so too the neck. Because it serves as the support for the face, it is indeed connected to the face. Furthermore, because of the subsequent mention of the "natural order" (*anuloma*), even though the parts from the head down to the neck do not strictly (in the primary sense) fall under the designation "face," they are nevertheless designated by that term in a figurative sense. Otherwise, since there is no hair on the neck, there would be no inclusion of it anywhere at all.

*Anulomam* means that which follows the direction of the hair (*yanmukhāni*). The meaning is that the oil is applied to the other limbs by facing toward them, starting from the 130th to the 1030th [sections] of the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha. Alternatively, by the word "mouth" (*mukha*), only the primary mouth itself is intended. The word "front" (*agra*) signifies sequence. In the phrase "the limbs starting from the head down to the neck, and the other limbs in their natural order" (*anulomam*), there is an inclusion of both. The word *anuloma* means "in successive order."

It is thus established that the anointing (abhyaṅga) should be performed by him starting from the head and proceeding down to the feet. "The others" refers to those other than the face; in the former ritual procedure these are the hands and so forth, while in the latter they are the head and so forth. Because of the separate mention—"the face first in the direction of the hair, and the other limbs"—there is a distinct mantra for the anointing of the face. For the anointing of the other parts, there is a single recitation of the mantra when possible, and a repetition of the mantra when impossible.

"He becomes well-anointed (svabhyaktaḥ)," meaning he is anointed in such a way that he becomes well-anointed. The prefix *su-* indicates that the ghee (*navanīta*) should come into contact with all parts [of the body]. The verbal root *añj* preceded by the prefix *abhi-* expresses the sense of "anointing" (*abhyaṅga*), while the same root preceded by the prefix *ā-* expresses "application" (*añjana*). The meaning of the term *abhyaṅga* is the contact of ghee with every part [of the body]; the meaning of the term *añjana* is the contact of collyrium specifically with the eyes.

To this extent, the force of the prefix (*upa*) is obtained, as in the case of words such as *prahāra* (a blow). Since it is impossible for one to thoroughly perform the anointing of one’s own entire back by oneself, the word *su* (well/thoroughly) also brings about the fact that it is performed by another. Regarding the lack of a fixed rule concerning the agent in that context, Baudhāyana states the restriction: "They anoint each other's backs.
He applies collyrium with a preparation made from the Trikakud mountain, [reciting]: "Thou art the eye of Vṛtra."

"Traikakuda" means that which originates on Mount Trikakuda; [the meaning is] "by such collyrium," implying "one who is afflicted. The word "bhakṣiṇī" (she who consumes) is to be supplied as the subject, due to the proximity of the action of applying collyrium. "Pāhi" (protect) is the end of the mantra. If that [specific collyrium] is unavailable, [it may be done] with whatever [collyrium] is at hand.

Since it would have been simpler to state merely "by that [ointment] made from *traikakuda* or by some other [ointment]" (*tasmin avidyamāne anyena vā*), the inclusion of the words "not being present" (*tasminnavidyamāne*) is for the purpose of preventing the possibility that there might sometimes be an equal option between any other ointment whatsoever and one distinct from that made from *traikakuda*. If it is objected: "In that case, one should simply say 'not being present, by another' (*tasminnavidyamāne anyena*); thus, the rule 'by whatever [other]' (*yenaiva kenacit*) is redundant," the answer is: True.

Since there is no lack of purpose (vaiyarthyābhāva) in this case—because it serves to indicate the understanding that the rule "when there is a substitute, one must first take that which is of the same genus (*sajātīya*), and only thereafter another" does not apply here—it follows that, among the various types of collyrium (*añjana*), only that produced from stone (*śailaja*) should be taken as the substitute at the outset due to its extreme similarity. Furthermore, the absence of the rule "in the absence of even this, one may use lamp-soot (*kajjala*)" is thereby established for this context.
Using a reed-shaft with its tuft, or a blade of *darbha* grass, or a bunch of *darbha* grass, he anoints each [eye] three times from the inside outward, beginning with the right eye first.

"Tūlam agrebhyo mūlebhyaḥ svāhā" (To the tips, to the roots, svāhā); this is because of its association with "roots. Some say it means "flower" (*puṣya*); that is not correct, because in the *Oṣadhi-homa* mantras of the Aśvamedha—"to the herbs svāhā, to the roots svāhā, to the tufts svāhā, to the stalks svāhā, to the shoots svāhā, to the flowers svāhā"—the separate mention of "flower" would otherwise be illogical. Therefore, the meaning is "with the tips," as stated by Jayanta-svāmin. [Chapter 150] — Accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

It occurs [as follows]: *śareṣīkā* is a stalk of the grass called *śara*; by that, or else *darbheṣīkā*, which is a stalk of *darbha* grass; or by a *darbhapuñjīla*, which is a cluster of *darbha* stalks. Since the tip of a *darbha* stalk lacks the capacity for the act of applying collyrium (*añjana*), the application is done with the base [of the stalk] alone. The quality of being "with cotton" (*satūlatva*) applies only to the *śareṣīkā* and the *darbheṣīkā*. It is precisely to indicate this that the word *vā* (or) has been placed in the middle. Alternatively, *tūla* means *kārpāsa* (cotton); the meaning is "by that which is accompanied by it."

The inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*) in the middle [of the compound] indicates that, because the feminine gender (*strīliṅga*) is used in the Śruti as "with a tuft" (*satūlā*), only the *śareṣīkā* (reed-tuft) and the *darbheṣīkā* (Darbha-grass tuft) possess equal status. The *darbhapuñjīla* (bundle of Darbha grass), however, possesses only a secondary (*gauṇa*) status. It should be understood that the result is this: in the absence of a *śareṣīkā*, the *darbheṣīkā* is to be taken precisely as the primary substitute; yet even when a *darbhapuñjīla* is present, it is not to be taken, because it lacks that same status. Internally means so that it does not protrude externally. That is, starting from the anus up to the end.

Without rubbing [the collyrium] and without turning back, he applies it three times to the right eye and three times to the left; this is the meaning. The mantra is recited only once for both eyes. Regarding the sequence there, he states: "The right first. Or, he may apply it twice to the left.

In all these alternatives, the mantra is recited only once for both. The application of the collyrium three times to the left was obtained from the preceding sūtra; in that regard, the optionality of doing it twice is prescribed by this [sūtra].
"Twice on the right, once on the left," according to some;
"both three times on the right and three times on the left, or twice"—this which was previously stated is an independent alternative view expressed here.
He does not, however, pour out [the water] again.

The collyrium should be applied continuously with a single effort; since it is impossible to do so, the phrase "he does not apply [it] again" means he does not place it back into the eyes for the sake of continuity. Alternatively, the word *punaḥ* (again) has the sense of "much. In this case, the meaning of *niṣecayati* is "he causes to go out," and thus the sense becomes "he does not cause much to go out," which implies [only a small amount] from the eyes.

Regarding the specific procedure for the application of collyrium, Baudhāyana says: "Then, having placed that ground ointment upon a stone slab, and sitting facing west while he faces east, he anoints his right eye with his left hand using a reed-shaft together with its tuft. While being purified, he mutters the verse, "O Lord of Purity, with thy purifier... and the Anuvāka beginning with "May the Lord of Thought purify me, may the Lord of Speech purify me, may the divine Savitṛ purify me," and [the verse] "The Purifier, whose path is light. (4)
Thus ends the first chapter in the tenth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

The initial *ca* (and) is intended to indicate that although there is oneness [of the ritual], there is a triad of mantras; this triad is appropriate because a distinction is observed in the Ārṣeya section. Furthermore, Jaimini has also accepted that a scriptural meaning determined in one place applies elsewhere as well, provided there is no sublation.

Just as in the injunction "the *prāyaṇīya* oblation is a *caru* like the sun," where the word *caru*, though denoting a cooking vessel, is determined to mean boiled rice (*odana*) by virtue of the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) "with rice," so too in cases such as "a *sūrya-caru*," even in the absence of a supplementary statement, it has the meaning of boiled rice; so it is here as well.

Regarding the statement in the *Ādhvaryava-sūtra*, "He joins [the formula] 'With the flawless strainer' everywhere," the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the formula beginning with "With the flawless [strainer]" is to be applied to all three [somas]. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and this Anuvāka, 'Pavamāna, the winner of heaven,'" the particle *ca* (and) should be construed after the word *anuvākam*. The use of the pronoun *etat* (this) is intended to demonstrate that this Anuvāka destroys even the secret sins (*rahasya-pātaka*), thereby establishing its well-known nature as the ultimate purifier.

And this matter has been stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "By reciting daily these—the *Pāvamānī* verses, the *Kautsa*, and the *Puruṣasūkta*—one is liberated from all sins. The *Pāvamānī* verses are the Ṛgvedic hymns found in the *Pavamāna-anuvāka*. For the sake of purification, their recitation should be performed every day. Accordingly, the Smṛti states: "He who recites daily the *Rudrādhyāya*, the *Pāvamāna*, and likewise the *Pūrva-nārāyaṇa*, is liberated from sins."

The word "ca" (and) serves to include [these rites] together with the preceding mantras. The *adhvaryu* priest should perform the *pāvamāna* [recitation] with sufficient space so that the reading of all those respective mantras may occur throughout the three *pavana* sections. There is a single recitation of the *pavamāna-anuvāka* sentence by sentence. Thus [ends the work of] Gopīnātha, the son of Gaṇeśadīkṣita, who was a descendant of Okopāha Śrīmad Āśiṣṭoma-yājin Sāhasrāmi-yukta Vājapeya-yājin Sarvatomukha-yājin Dvisāhasrāmi-yukta Pauṇḍarīka-yājin.

Thus ends the first section of the tenth book in the commentary named *Jyotsnā*, composed by Dīkṣita, which alleviates the distress of learned men caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the ocean of the venerable *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha.
10.2 Now begins the second chapter of the tenth book. Reciting, “O gods, we invoke you,” he murmurs while entering the *prāgvaṃśa* hall by the eastern door.

The mention of the “door” is for the purpose of excluding a window. By the use of the present participle (*praviśan*), it is understood that the murmuring occurs simultaneously with the act of entering. The end of the mantra is: “We invoke those worthy of sacrifice.”
Having touched water with the formula "Thou art lightning," he passes behind the Āhavanīya fire to the south and sits down on the southern side.

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites, there is the taking up of a visible representative (pratīka). By this, the end of the mantra becomes "May faith be in me. [End of the sixth section]. This is accompanied by the *Jyotsnā* commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. Seating occurs to the south, facing north, because otherwise it would result in the southern fire being placed behind him. Baudhāyana also clearly states: "He should seat him to the south, facing north. However, if there is only one door, entry is through that same door due to the force of the context. His path of movement remains exactly thus until the *Sutyā*.

The term *saṃcara* means a path. In the phrase "until the pressing" (*ā sutyāyāḥ*), the prefix *ā* denotes inclusion. Since it has been determined that in the case of the rule, "As long as the Soma sacrifice is not concluded, the Adhvaryu, having entered the Havirdhāna shed by the eastern door, must not exit by the western door," the meaning is that the pressing lasts until the *avamṛtha* bath; therefore, the same determination applies here as well. This path is for ritual purposes; however, for ordinary (worldly) movement, the path follows one's convenience, such as passing in front of the Āhavanīya fire or behind the Gārhapatya fire, and so forth.

By the force of the injunction specifying a particular limit in the phrase "until the Soma-pressing" (*ā sutyāyai*), the movement for the sake of ritual acts—such as the *udayanīya* offering and others that follow the completion of the pressing—is by the *āhavanīya* fire to the east; however, it is not by the *āhavanīya* fire to the west as obtained through general extension (*atideśa*). Otherwise, since there would be no distinction between the two movements obtained through specific and extended injunctions, the injunction specifying the particular limit would be rendered meaningless. This is because of the governing heading: "We shall explain the duties of the sacrificer" (*yājamānaṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ*).

O King, the employment of the word *tat* (that) as a reference to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*)—upon obtaining [the status of] a sacrificer—is for the purpose of making known that the sacrificial acts belonging to the period prior to this [point] belong to the wife (*patnī*) as well. In that regard, it has already been stated in the commentary on the *Ādhvaryava-sūtra* that there is no shaving (*vapana*) for the wife. Due to the absence of shaving, the muttering (*japa*) of "May I attain prosperity through the subsequent [acts]" (*svastyuttarāṇyaśīya*) is also not performed. At the immersion (*udgāhana*), there is a modification (*ūha*) of the mantra to "Pūm. Baudhāyana says "Sūṣṇīm. He consecrates the *Āhavanīya* fire with the mantra: "Indra-Agni, Heaven-Earth... (*indrāgnī dyāvāpṛthivī*).

The mantra ends with *santaṃ pāhi*. After entering the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, if the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice is to be performed, one performs it there; immediately thereafter follows the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the Āhavanīya fire. The reasoning supporting this is demonstrated in the sūtra: "Some authorities prescribe that after entering that *prāgvaṃśa*, one should perform the *dīkṣaṇīyā* here. Following this, the *dīkṣā* oblations are offered. After the offering of the *dīkṣā* oblations, the sacrificer must mutter the mantra: *pātaṃ prāṇaṃ manasā 'nvāramāmahe*.

This is because of the sūtra stating, "The mantras whose blessings are directed inward [are used] when there is no action or instrument. Since Āpastamba has assigned the sixth *dīkṣā-huti*, known as the *pūrṇāhuti*, for the purpose of consecration (*anumantraṇa*), one should perform this consecration with this mantra while the sixth *dīkṣā-huti* is being offered. Furthermore, it was already demonstrated in the introduction that consecration (*anumantraṇa*) also possesses the character of an action.

Within the altar (*antarvedi*), upon the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) that has been spread out, he touches the white and black stripes [of the skin], saying, "You two are the forms (*śilpe*) of the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda."

The mention of "within the altar" (*antarvedi*) is for the purpose that the touching of the *rājī* (the line) should not occur in all cases, such as when spreading the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) for the sake of the corpse; this is so it shall not happen there. The mention of "black" (*kṛṣṇa*) is for the purpose of excluding the touching of the *rājī* on a tiger skin. The *rājī* is a line. The touching of both the white and black lines occurs simultaneously, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra: "You two are artistic forms" (*śilpe sthaḥ*). "Touching" (*ālambhana*) means contact. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says: "On the white [line] the thumb is placed, and on the black [line] a finger."

In the case of a division, there is another distinction: "the contact between the white and the black. Baudhāyana says that one should touch the white with the thumb and the black with a finger, thus touching both the white and the black; Śālīki says that one should touch the junction with the thumb alone; and Upamanyava says that one should touch these two with a single finger. "Pṛtha" means thirteen fingers. "Of the sacrifice, upward" is the end of the mantra. (Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, 10th Praśna, 1034).

With the words "Thou art well-protecting," he ascends from the south onto the ashes; and with the verses "This prayer of the one seeking instruction, O God," "The good protector, the earth, the blameless heaven," and "I have boarded this good ship."

The mantra is simply "suśarmāsi" (Thou art a good refuge). The preceding *ca* is for the purpose of connecting it with the subsequent mantra; the subsequent *ca* is for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the first mantra. "Imām ahaṃ sunāvam āruham" (I have mounted this good ship) is an alternative (*vikalpyate*) to "sutramāṇam" (the good protector). In the phrase "dakṣiṇatas," *tas* has the sense of the ablative case (*pañcamyartha*), meaning "from the southern region. In "masat," *tas* has the sense of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyārtha*), meaning "with the hip-region or the anus-region. Baudhāyana states: "Having bent the right knee, he recites [the mantra]."

"I have ascended the consecration (*dīkṣā*), the consort of immortality, with the *gāyatrī* metre and with the sacred word (*brahman*). Order has been established in truth. Having said, "It has been established in immortality; order and truth have become mine; I have become light; I have gone to the sun; I have reached the heavenly world, the back of the firmament, the summit of the radiant sky," he recites this while ascending.

The explicit mention of "having ascended" is intended to ensure there is no temporal interval between the act of ascending and the recitation; by this, it is established that the actions beginning with "he places a garland on the head of his wife" occur immediately after the recitation.

With the mantra, "Thou art the protection of Viṣṇu," he covers the right shoulder with a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). The purpose of specifying "black" is as previously stated; the purpose of specifying "right" has already been explained. The prefix *pra-* indicates that the covering of the shoulder must be performed so as to encompass all its parts. The mention of the "black antelope skin" is for the purpose of excluding the garment mentioned by Āpastamba. The end of the mantra is "yaccha. With the mantra, "Protect me from the glare of the stars," he wraps the head with a cloth.

In this context, "cord" (*pāśa*) refers to the form of a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), as its use for wrapping the head is established by common worldly usage. Its clockwise direction (*prādakṣiṇya*) is established by general convention. Baudhāyana and Āpastamba state explicitly: "One wraps the head with a turban clockwise. If a cloth in the form of a turban is unavailable, any other [garment] may be used. For this very reason, Āpastamba’s mention of the *Vājasaneyaka* should be understood as providing an option.

In the case of a conflict, an explicit option (*vikalpa*) has been stated: "Now he wraps his head with a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*) while circumambulating it"—this is the *sūtra* of Baudhāyana; "He should be covered by a garment (*vāsas*) alone," says Śālīki. Since no specific distinction is mentioned, it is understood that both views are acceptable to the Teacher (*ācārya*). The word *uṣṇīṣa* is well known to refer to a long cloth; *veṣṭana* means wrapping.

"One should not uncover [the head] before the purchase of the Soma," because a fault is heard in the scripture regarding the removal of the garment prior to the purchase; and because the garment is praised as being the form of the womb for the consecrated one who is the embryo—stated thus: "The consecrated one is indeed an embryo; when he covers himself with the garment, therefore embryos are born covered"—and because of the indicative mark from the sūtra to be mentioned later, "He uncovers the head first, and the other limbs in due order"; and because the covering of the sacrificer with the garment is stated independently as "Then he covers the sacrificer with the garment."

From the injunction, it is established that first there is the covering of all parts of the body including the head with a cloth (*vāsas*), and immediately thereafter the wrapping of the head with a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*). Regarding the contraction of the portion of the cloth located on the head, Baudhāyana states: "Having drawn back the ends of the garment, he wraps the head with the turban from left to right" (*pradakṣiṇam uṣṇīṣeṇa śiro veṣṭayati*). *Proṛṇavana* means covering or wrapping.

The black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), which has been placed upon the right shoulder, must be removed by covering [the body] with a garment, because otherwise it would be impossible to cover the right shoulder. That the consecrated person (*dīkṣita*) is of the nature of an embryo is explained in detail in the *Bāḍhaca Brāhmaṇa*: "The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) indeed make him an embryo when they consecrate him. The *ulba* is the membrane resembling a cloth that envelops the embryo; the *jarāyu*, however, is the substance that serves as its outer covering. In this context, that [covering] takes the form of the black antelope skin.

Therefore, after the upper garment (*prāvaraṇa*), the body must be covered with a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). And it is stated in another Sūtra: "The head is wrapped with a cloth; having covered the body with a black antelope skin and having drawn [the skin] over the one who is lying down, [the priest] digs up a clod of earth from the altar with a black antelope horn. In this way, the state of being pregnant is established for the initiated one.

Regarding the fault in drawing water before the purchase of Soma, the Śruti states: "If one draws water before the purchase of Soma, the offspring of people would be prone to miscarriage. "Prone to miscarriage" (*parāpātukāḥ*) means having the nature of falling away prematurely. Therefore, its generation after the purchase of Soma, and consequently the uncovering with a cloth, is entirely appropriate. Thus says the Śruti: "When the Soma has been purchased, he uncovers [the water]; then indeed it is born. Uncovering (*aporṇavanam*) means opening or revealing.

Furthermore, just as when people have a desire to see someone of high status, such as a king, those standing nearby remove the curtain of the assembly with their hands and the like, so too does this occur. And thus says the Śruti: "Just as one pushes aside [the curtain] toward a superior, so indeed is that. By this act of covering, it is indicated that at this time there is an emergence from that [state].
With the dedicated black antelope horn, he digs up a clod of earth from the altar, saying: "For cultivation thee, for good harvest!"

The mention of "bestowed" (*pratta*) is for the purpose of excluding [the use of] the black antelope horn. By the mention of "bestowed," it is also understood that the bestowing of the black antelope horn must be performed only after the wrapping of the head with a cloth. Due to the order of the mantra recitation, the sequence beginning with the girding of the waist-belt (*mekhalā-parivyayaṇa*) and ending with the binding of the wife (*patnī-sannahana*) must precede the covering of the right shoulder. Regarding the phrase "from the altar" (*vedeḥ*): one digs up—that is, loosens—any clod of earth (*loṣṭa*), any lump of soil, belonging to the altar. Here, the word "altar" (*vedi*) is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) to refer to the region of the altar.

It has already been demonstrated in the sūtra *loṣṭair-unnanti* that the reading *loṣṭam* is indeed appropriate. Alternatively, the meaning is "they strike as if [striking] a clod of earth," just as a clod of earth is split by a blow; thus, it refers to clay. Since it is well known in the world that the splitting of clay occurs through scattering [it], the present rule prescribes that its splitting occurs by means of a blow.

If it is argued that, for the sake of brevity, one should simply say "they dig up the altar" (*vedim uddhanti*), we reply: True. However, if one says "they dig up the altar" (*vedim uddhanti*), it implies digging up the altar by way of all its constituent parts; whereas if one says "they dig up the sacrificial ground" (*vediṃ uddhanti*), it implies digging up only a certain portion. Since there is thus a difference in the essential nature of the act—here, only a partial excavation being intended—the principle of brevity is not a determining factor in this case. To provide an interpretation based on such a forced construction would result in the undesirable consequence (*lopa*) of omitting the term entirely when the word *loṣṭa* (clod) is absent. And this is not an acceptable conclusion.

Since it is improper to assume an elision when an interpretation that avoids elision is possible in some way or another, so says the *Nidānasūtra*: "Non-elision is more logical than elision. And this should be understood as applying to matters concerning invisible results (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Nor should it be argued that, just as there is an elision of the meaning in the case of the phrase "he scratches his head" (*śirasi kaṇḍūyate*) which is about to be mentioned, the same should apply here; for in that case, the meaning is already established in the statement "when the head exists" (*satyāṃ śirasi*) from the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha.

Because, unlike the explicit statement of the Lopākara-pakāpastambīya school, such an explicit statement is absent in the present case, it is impossible to assume [the practice] in that manner; furthermore, because the natural sense of the Baudhāyana-sūtra indicates that it must be performed even in the absence of itching. [As it says: "With the words 'For the plants with good fruit,' he scratches his head."

In the view that this [act] has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), the meaning is that one performs scratching on the head or on some other part of the body. According to Baudhāyana’s statement, "He scratches the *godāna* (the hair-lock) on the right," although there is no attainment of a visible purpose due to the mention of a restricted location, it is indicated that scratching must indeed be performed. However, in the case where the visible purpose is attained—as in the view of Āpastamba who states "he scratches" (*kaṇḍūyate*)—there is simply an omission of the act. Both views are acceptable to the author of the Sūtra.

Nor should it be argued that, under the view that the mantra serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), its application to other instances of scratching would be impossible due to a lack of a basis for such application; for there exists a specific *paribhāṣā* sūtra as the basis: "Because the purpose is distinct, the mantra for scratching is repeated. Furthermore, the statement ending in the locative case, "on the head" (*śirasi*), supports the meaning that scratching occurs wherever on the head there is an itch, rather than implying that the entire head must be scratched.

In the view that the mantra serves no visible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*), there is an injunction for scratching the head using this specific mantra alone. In the view that it serves a visible purpose (*iṣṭārthatva*), the injunction pertains only to the portion consisting of the mantra; the injunction for scratching, however, is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). When one scratches the head, one scratches with the mantra "supippalābhyas tvā" alone; when one scratches other limbs, one does so with the mantra "viṣāṇe". In both views, scratching begins on the head first, and only thereafter on the other limbs.

When multiple purposes arise at different times, there is a repetition of the mantra. Thus states the Sūtra: "Because the purposes are distinct, the mantra for scratching is repeated. This distinctness of purpose here is caused by the lapse of time. However, in the view of Jaimini, even when there is a lapse of time, there is no repetition. Accordingly, the Sūtra in the fourth quarter of the eleventh chapter states: "In the case of scratching, [there would be] a separate act every day because of the difference [of time]; or rather, there should be unity of the injunction because it is a single performance."

In the act of scratching, because the suffering to be removed by the action of scratching, the mental formation (*saṃskāra*) for the removal of that suffering, and the various ignorances (*ajñāna*) are distinct, there is a repetition for each limb. Here, the word "action" (*karman*) refers both to the technical sense of "that which possesses a result produced by an activity" and to the activity itself as the meaning of the verbal root.

And thus, if one accepts that [the mantra] refers to the primary action (*karma*) characterized by possessing a fruit non-different from the action itself, then the logical connection is that because the actions—which possess fruits produced by the act and consist of the head and other parts—are distinct, there is a repetition of the mantra for each instance of scratching. However, if it refers to the action in the form of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*), then the logical connection is that because of the difference in actions for each part during the scratching, there is a repetition of the mantra. This is the meaning of the previous sūtra.

The meaning of the subsequent sūtra is as follows: "From oneness" (*aikakāt*) means from that state where there is only one single action; for that reason, the injunction (*codanā*)—namely, the injunction "one should scratch"—is indeed a unity and not a plurality. This is the distilled meaning: sufferings are not distinct [in themselves], nor is the removal of suffering intended as an end in itself, nor is it a mere embellishment (*saṃskāra*), by which there might be a distinction between them. Rather, scratching is performed in order to make the self—one whose mind is afflicted by the pain of itching—free from the pain of that itching.

Therefore, since the removal of all suffering is performed here for the sake of that very Self—because there is no other fruit than that—for as much suffering as remains unremoved, so much suffering arises within the Self; and by that [removal], it is further established that the Self alone is of such a nature. *Ka*, *cha*, *mi* | 7 | 1 [2nd Paṭala] | This is accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha. 1037. "Single action" (*aikakarmyam*) means the state of being a single action (*ekakarma*); for that reason. "Single action" is an adjective qualifying scratching. Scratching does not become divided by the difference between one limb and another.

When scratching constitutes a refinement of the body (*aṅga-saṃskāra*), then that [refinement] would be distinct from this [ultimate goal]; therefore, even the refinement of the body does not occur. Rather, a refinement arises in the self (*ātman*) itself through the removal of suffering residing within the self. The cessation of itching in the body is merely a means (*dvāramātra*). Indeed, one is observed to apply effort with the intention of removing all suffering whatsoever by which suffering arises in the self once it has been removed; for when the scratching is finally accomplished, the goal is achieved.

And for this very reason, there is indeed a unity of the cooked rice (*audana*), and no distinction is made by means of the *ātman*. Therefore, because no specific difference is perceived, it does not become that [distinction].
Regarding the two horns, the knot that was in his ankle is [placed] on the two horns; "that which was in his heart, the mind, that which was in his ankle"—these are the remaining limbs.

The meaning is "in the remaining parts. By this, it follows that scratching occurs only on certain parts of the limbs such as the hands, and not on all parts; thus the meaning remains as previously stated. By the word "head" (*śiras*), only the head itself is intended; therefore, regarding the forehead and other parts [of the head], the mantra is simply *viṣāṇe viṣāṇyā*, and not *supippalābhyas*. Since scratching the eyes is already implied by the purpose [of the rite], one does not scratch them with the black antelope horn, because it is unsuitable for that purpose.

One should not scratch with the hand, because of the scriptural warning that those who do so become afflicted with skin diseases (*pāmā*) and other ailments. If one asks, "How then should it be done?"—the answer is that one should tie a bundle of black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*) with a cord and scratch with that; in this way, the scratching is to be performed. The mention of the "limbs" (*aṅga*) is intended to indicate the preeminence of the head, even though it is but one limb.

Consequently, regarding the rubbing (*udvartana*) prescribed by the rule "having rubbed [him] with the bathing-paste," it is established that because of its preeminence, the head is to be rubbed first, and then the other limbs.
"May the divine tree be well-established; standing upright, protect me until the end," with these words he takes up the staff. ||5||

As long as the act of acceptance (*pratigrahaṇa*) has not been performed, the meaning of the term "giving" (*dāna*) is not established; likewise, without giving, the meaning of the term "acceptance" remains unestablished. Thus, the simultaneity of the giving and acceptance of the staff is indeed required by the sense of the matter. Consequently, it follows that the mantra for its performance must be recited beforehand.

Agni is consecrated; the earth is the consecration. By that consecration with which Agni was consecrated—by which consecration Agni was consecrated—may that consecration consecrate me. By that consecration I am consecrated. Vāyu is consecrated; the intermediate region is the consecration. By that consecration with which Vāyu was consecrated—by which consecration Vāyu was consecrated—may that consecration consecrate me. By that consecration I am consecrated. Āditya is consecrated; the sky is the consecration. By that consecration with which Āditya was consecrated—by which consecration Āditya was consecrated—may that consecration consecrate me. By that consecration I am consecrated.
By that consecration (dīkṣā) was the moon consecrated; the stars are the consecration. By that [consecration]—[the text continues]. Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra—[Book Ten].

The moon is consecrated by that consecration by which the moon is consecrated; may that consecration consecrate me; with that consecration I am consecrated. King Varuṇa is consecrated; the waters are the consecration; by that consecration King Varuṇa is consecrated; by that consecration by which King Varuṇa is consecrated, may that consecration consecrate me; with that consecration I am consecrated. King Soma is consecrated; the plants are the consecration; by that consecration King Soma is consecrated; by that consecration by which King Soma is consecrated, may that consecration [consecrate me].

May he initiate me with that initiation; I am initiated. Breath is the initiate; speech is the initiation; by that initiation of breath, may I be initiated. By that initiation of breath by which breath was initiated, may that initiation initiate me; with that initiation, I am initiated. Prajāpati is the initiate; mind is the initiation; by that initiation of Prajāpati, may I be initiated. By that initiation of Prajāpati by which Prajāpati was initiated, may that initiation initiate me; with that initiation, I am initiated. May my speech be initiated by speech for Agni, having been completely consecrated; may my breath be initiated by breath.

To Vāyu, for the sake of unification: may my eye be consecrated by the eye; to Sūrya, for the sake of unification: may my mind be consecrated by the mind. To Prajāpati, for the sake of unification: may Heaven and Earth, Day and Night, Agriculture and Rain, Splendor and Honor, Waters and Herbs, Light and Truth—may these all consecrate me as I am being consecrated. Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ! Truth is my self, faith is my dwelling, austerity is my foundation; faith, truth, and the householder—thus [he addresses] Keśinī.

Having recited the *dīkṣā* formula, "Svāhā! The sacrifice with the mind," he rubs two fingers; with "Svāhā! To Heaven and Earth," two [more]; with "Svāhā! From the wide atmosphere," two [more]; and having formed a fist with "Svāhā! I take hold of the sacrifice from the wind," he releases four fingers with "Thou art the mistress of the sacrifice" (*iṣṭrīḥ stha*), and with them he moves as he pleases while restraining his speech.

Japa consists of the *saṃbhāra*, the *yajus*, the *homa*, and that which follows. The mention of *Keśinī* in relation to that sound is for the purpose of knowledge (*jñāna*). In the absence of such knowledge, the expiation for the violation of the *Yajus* formulas is to offer an oblation into the *Dakṣiṇāgni* fire with the mantra "Bhuvaḥ Svāhā. By the word *dīkṣā*, the mantras containing the term *dīkṣā* are indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). The specific deities such as Agni and others who receive the *dīkṣā* are precisely what is denoted by the word *keśa*. *Keśinī* is thus an epithet qualifying *dīkṣā*.

When the substantive (*viśeṣya*) is denoted by the mantra-word through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is also denoted by that word through secondary signification. [For example], based on the etymology "what is heaven (*svarga*)? Its lords are the hair (*keśāḥ*)," the word *keśa* denotes the gods. Therefore, it is a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*). Since the substantive, the word *dīkṣā*, is feminine, the suffix *ḍīp* is applied to the qualifying word *keśin* in accordance with the gender of the substantive. The fact that the word *ka* denotes heaven is stated in the *Haimakośa*: "1. *sa.*; 2. *ja*, *jha*, *ma*; and *ca*. [Note: The numbers and letters refer to specific citations or definitions within the commentary.]

[Chapter 2, Part 2] Accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 1039. The word *ka* is declared to mean Brahmā, the Self (*ātman*), wind (*anila*), the sun (*arka*), fire (*agni*), Citrā, the enemy (*ari*), the sun (*yama*), and a banner (*ketu*). It is used for Viṣṇu’s vehicle (*vāhana*), the ocean (*abdhi*), white-eared (*sitakarṇa*), Vasu, and shaking (*dhuta*). It is also well-known in the sense of quarrel (*kalaha*), and is considered to mean "who" (*praśna*) as well as "what" (*artha*). Furthermore, it signifies heaven (*svarga*), a wheel (*cakra*), a friend (*mitra*), purity (*śuddhi*), pleasure (*smara*), and time (*kāla*). Among all the gods, the status of being the Lord of Heaven (*svargeśatva*) is established from the term *tridiveśa* (Lord of the Third Heaven) just as much as from the term *keśa* (Lord of the Sky).

The singular number is intended to denote the class (jāti). Since it is impossible for the act of recitation (*japa*) to exist within the initiation (*dīkṣā*), which consists of observances, vows, and so forth, one must accept by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that the term refers to the mantras that serve as the instruments for that initiation. The etymological meaning is as follows: *keśinī* is that [initiation] in which the "hairs" (*keśāḥ*)—that is, the gods such as Agni and others who receive the initiation—are present; in other words, it is that in which these [deities] exist as the subjects to be propounded in the mantras that constitute its means. This is the *keśinī-dīkṣā*.

Beginning with "The grandson of the past is the Adhvaryu; the earth is the consecration (dīkṣā); by that consecration with which Agni was consecrated—by that consecration I consecrate you," and ending with "may they consecrate you as you undergo consecration," the Adhvaryu, looking at the sacrificer, mutters the collection of mantras found in the Ācchidrika section of the Prapāṭhaka. Because of the use of the word *yuṣmat* ("you"), this [sacrificer] is the grandson of the Adhvaryu.

In the phrase "having muttered the *dīkṣā* [formula], Keśinī," the suffix *-lyap* signifies that the agent of the action of forming the fist (*muṣṭikaraṇa*) is the same as the agent of the action of muttering (*japa*). Consequently, since the formation of the fist must be performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) alone, it is established that the muttering must also be performed by him. Thus, the wife's agency is excluded. The basis for the fact that the formation of the fist is indeed the sacrificer’s duty alone will be explained later, based on the particle *ca* in the passage: "he moves about at his pleasure with them and restrains his speech."

Regarding the phrase "two fingers are joined" (*jatī*), although it is stated in general terms, two fingers from each of the two hands are to be understood; the same applies to the subsequent [fingers]. The sequence is as follows: first the two little fingers, then the two ring fingers, then the two middle fingers, and finally the clenching of the fists of both hands.

Nor should it be said that the procedure must be exactly as follows: first two fingers of the right hand—the little finger and the ring finger; then the middle finger and the index finger; then the little finger and the ring finger of the left hand; and finally the closing of the fists of both hands. For such a performance is improper, as it contradicts the maxim *samaṃ syādaśrutatvāt* (the rule should be equal when there is no scriptural statement to the contrary). The term *nirbhujati* means he makes them bent (*saṃbhugna*), that is to say, he brings them together. This state of being bent occurs simultaneously for each pair of fingers.

Simultaneously: the joining of the thumb together with all the fingers bent inward constitutes a fist; "making that" means its accomplishment. By this, the bending of the two index fingers is also shown by implication; otherwise, the rule for forming a fist would be untenable without them. The word *muṣṭī* is in the dual number because the Padakāras have applied the particle *iti*, which indicates the status of a *pragraha* (a specific type of pause). Thus, the formation of fists occurs with both hands. *Eṣṭrīḥ stha* is the Vedic mantra from the Sūtra.

There are two [fists] for each of the two hands; thus there are four, and not just one. Otherwise, the subsequent injunction regarding the release of the two fists—“having released the fists and speech”—would be untenable. Furthermore, Āpastamba clearly states: “two [fists], or on either side. The release (*utsarga*) also occurs simultaneously, because of the plural number in the mantra “of the two goats” (*eṣṭroḥ*). [The phrase] “by those released” (*tābhir utsṛṣṭābhiḥ*) follows from the statement “according to one’s pleasure” (*yathāsukham*), which refers to those by which [the sacrifice] is released.

Those [fingers] by which it is possible to perform the acts of sipping water (ācamana) and so forth with ease should be released. These, however, are the little finger and the ring finger. It is established by experience that if the little finger and the ring finger are not released, their contact with the thumb causes pain. Therefore, only these four—the little finger and the ring finger—are to be released. This is because in the phrase "having released the fingers" (aṅgulīr utsṛjya), the word *catasraḥ* (four) appears in the feminine gender.

Although the inclusion of the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*) would have been established by the rule for "taking the fingers" (*aṅguligrahaṇa*)—since the word *aṅguli* does not inherently denote the feminine gender—the separate mention of "fingers" (*aṅguli*) is intended to demonstrate that the thumb is not included among the fingers in certain cases. This is based on the Vedic text: "Ten [fingers] for killing, ten toes for drinking," where even though the thumb is included as a finger, it is seen to be mentioned separately in the passage: "If he should desire to produce both, he should take hold of the thumb together with the fingers, as if [seizing] the hair. Thus, it shows that the thumb is not to be grasped within the category of the fingers.

By this, the release of the thumb and the little finger mentioned in the Vājasaneyaka should be understood as refuted. The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "he restrains his speech" (*vācaṃ ca yacchati*) indicates that [the restraint] is prescribed as being conjoined with the closing of the fingers. Therefore, the restriction of speech applies only to the one who forms the fist; thus, there is no requirement for the wife to restrain her speech. He states the expiation for the lapse of the restraint of speech:
"If, through negligence, he should utter [speech], having recited the verses addressed to Viṣṇu, Agni-Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, and Bṛhaspati, as well as the *vyāhṛtis*, he restrains his speech again."

By the word "yadi" (if), the character of being contingent upon a specific occasion (*naimittikatva*) is indicated. "Prāmattaḥ" means one who would utter [the syllables] out of negligence; that is, he should pronounce the *vāk* (speech). However, if the utterance occurs due to the influence of negligence of the intellect, then the recitation (*japa*) of those mantras should be performed twice or thrice—this is the literal meaning. But when it is said that the meaning of "prāmattaḥ" is specifically "one who is insane," then there is only a single recitation of these mantras. Regarding the utterance caused by negligence: "If, in some way, there should be a lapse in the restraint of speech during the recitations and so forth..."

"One should utter a Vaiṣṇava mantra or remember the immutable Viṣṇu"—this statement from the Smṛti is to be accepted. Furthermore, this prohibition against vocal utterance refers to matters other than those pertaining to the means of sacrifice (*yajñasādhana*). Thus Āśvalāyana says: "In an emergency (*āpad*), one should mutter 'Āto devā avantu naḥ' or any other Vaiṣṇava [mantra]. He further states: "Other than the means of sacrifice. Here, "in an emergency" means having transgressed the rule; "means of sacrifice" is an adjective qualifying speech.

Speech that is a means for sacrifice (*yajñasādhana*) is that which exists for the purpose of accomplishing the sacrifice and for the avoidance of what remains incomplete; the meaning is that it is the restraint of speech beyond this. *Vaiṣṇavī* refers to the well-known verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ. Alternatively, either of the first two verses of the section beginning with "agnāviṣṇū mahi tadvām" is *āgnāvaiṣṇavī*. Following those, either of the two subsequent verses, "pra ṇo devī" or "ā no divaḥ," is *sārasvatī*.

Then, from among these three verses beginning with *tataḥ parāsām*, *bṛhaspate juṣasva naḥ*, and *evā pitre bṛhaspate*, one or another belongs to Bṛhaspati (*bārhaspatyā*). The word *iti* here has the sense of "in this manner" (*prakāra*). By this, the recitation of the triad of mantras beginning with *anājñāta* is established. The word *anu* here is intended to indicate that these mantras are for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the lapse of silence (*vāgyama*), and must be performed *before* the recitation of the mantras. Nor should it be argued that this connection [to the purpose] may occur at the very time of the mantra recitation itself.

Because it is impossible to contemplate this [the mantra] while the sound is obstructed by the contemplation of the meaning of the mantra; for since contemplation is of the nature of cognition, two cognitions cannot arise at one and the same time. Alternatively, it is to show that these mantras have the form of recitation (*anuvacana*). Therefore, there is only monotony of pitch (*ekaśrutya*). Since there is no mention of the word "having muttered" (*japitvā*), there is no rule regarding the fourfold intonation (*cātuḥsvarya*). It is precisely for the sake of avoiding the rule of fourfold intonation that the word "having muttered" is omitted and the word "reciting" (*anucyet*) is used instead.

The *vyāhṛtis* may be used either collectively or individually, both separately and together. This is because there is no statement here indicating a mandatory combination. Furthermore, since it is stated in the *Brahmatva-sūtra* for the *iṣṭi* and *paśubandha* sacrifices—"If one should speak out of negligence, having muttered a verse addressed to Viṣṇu and the *vyāhṛtis*, he should again restrain his speech"—this refers specifically to the office of the *brahmán*. Likewise, in the *Agniṣṭoma-brahmatva-sūtra*, that which is about to be performed pertains solely to the *brahmán*.

In this context, what is prescribed pertains exclusively to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). As for the *adhvaryu* and other priests, however, there is no restrictive rule that they must remember Viṣṇu solely by means of the *vaiṣṇavyṛc* mantra; rather, it may be done even by uttering His name—this is another such means. It is with this very intention that [the name] is not mentioned in the *Ādhvaryava-sūtra*. And that other means was stated in the *Smṛti*: "If there should be a lapse in the restraint of speech during the *japa*s and so forth, how should one proceed? One should utter a *vaiṣṇava* mantra or remember the imperishable Viṣṇu. This was mentioned incidentally. He does not speak untruth.

Since the prohibition of false speech is already established by the general prohibition [of lying] from the time of the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) until the end of life—specifically by the particular rule "one should not speak untruth"—the repetition of the prohibition is for the purpose of making it an integral part (*aṅga*) of ritual action (*karman*). Consequently, there are three types of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) here: first, an expiation occasioned by the failure to observe the general prohibition which applies to all persons; second, an expiation occasioned by the failure to observe the particular prohibition which applies specifically to those who have undertaken the relevant vows.

This third [act] is for the purpose of not maintaining the prohibitions that constitute parts of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*). For the first [of these], there is a Smārta expiation; for the latter two, there is a Śrauta one, and that is double [the former]. This triad must be performed. Among them, the Smārta expiation is stated by Vṛddha-Parāśara: "Having sneezed, spat, or spoken untruths, O Brahmin; having uttered the word 'patita' (outcaste), one should touch the right ear. Upon seeing the moon or the sun, one should recollect the *Brahmayajñī* [mantra]."

Vṛddhaśātātapa states: "Having sneezed, spat, or put on a garment, a wise man should sip water (ācamana). He should perform ācamana, touch the back of a cow, and look at it; whichever of these is possible first, and in the absence of that, the next. This should be understood to apply when water is unavailable or when one is occupied with other tasks. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "For speaking abusively or untruthfully, there shall be fasting for three nights or one night. Thus, other penances mentioned in the Smṛtis should also be consulted from their respective sources.

In this regard, the classification should be understood according to whether one is capable or incapable, whether there is desire or lack of desire, and whether there is practice or non-practice, as well as the degree of slightness or non-slightness. Vedic expiations (*śrauta-prāyaścitta*) differ based on the distinction between verbal falsehood (*śabdānṛta*) and material falsehood (*arthānṛta*). Among these, regarding verbal falsehood, the *Sārasvateṣṭi* sacrifice was taught by the venerable Patañjali; regarding material falsehood, only the *Vrātyastoma* is prescribed. However, in the case of Smārta [expiations], the same applies to both types of falsehood.

Although the second expiation is accomplished by way of *prasaṅga* (incidental application) through the first expiation alone, nevertheless, because the Śrauta prohibition is stated here again, repetition (*āvṛtti*) itself is established. This is precisely the purpose of this prohibition. [From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, in the section on the *Dana* sacrifice:
"He does not eat meat."

The mention of "meat" (*māṃsa*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for [other forbidden items] such as honey and the like, because Āpastamba includes them among the things prohibited. This is a prohibition of the consumption of meat obtained through worldly attachment (*rāga-prāpta*); it is not a prohibition of its consumption when it is prescribed by Vedic injunction (*vaidha*).
