Just as in the case of the scriptural rule "one should not harm any living beings," where ordinary violence is prohibited but that which pertains to sacrifice is not—because it is enjoined—so it should be understood here as well.

This prohibition against eating meat other than that of a widow applies to other ages (*yuga*); however, in the Kali age, since the eating of meat is prohibited altogether, such [specific] meat is simply not available. Furthermore, because there is an absence of any prohibition against sacrifice in the Kali age, there is likewise no prohibition against eating the meat associated with it. [The following are also permitted: theft, initiation for others, the human sacrifice (*naramedha*), the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), the taking of *surā* liquor in the *sautrāmaṇī* rite, unhusked grain, a cow as a sacrificial animal, meat at a *śrāddha*, and honey.

By means of such specific prohibitions regarding the Kali age, the absence of a prohibition for the *agniṣṭoma* and other sacrifices, as well as for animals other than cows—such as goats—is clearly demonstrated.

[The rule] "he does not approach a woman" applies even during her fertile period (*ṛtu*), because a penance is prescribed for the emission of semen in the passage: "if one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) should spill [his seed]. Thus, approaching the wife by the husband is suspended only for half [the duration]. In that regard, if the emission occurs intentionally, the penance to be mentioned later—"if one who is consecrated should spill"—applies; however, if it is unintentional, [the penance is]: "whatever of my milk here [has been spilled], may that be for the sacrifice."

The expiation prescribed by Āpastamba—"I shall speak that again, as one pours Soma over the Agnihotra"—should be understood as the rite for consecrating the spilled semen. This consecration must be performed after having sipped water (ācamana). Accordingly, another Sūtra states: "Having sipped water, he consecrates the spilled semen. If one who is initiated (*dīkṣita*) should spill it, it refers only to his own wife and not to another woman; in that case, however, the expiation mentioned in the Smṛti—namely, "the student who has violated his vow"—also applies.
There is a prohibition regarding one afflicted by disease. He does not sit upon [a high seat].

He does not sit or lie down on a seat higher than [his teacher’s]. The mention of the seat is for the sake of illustration; indeed, Āśvalāyana says simply, "then he may lie down. He does not spit—that is, he does not discharge saliva from his mouth.

He does not brush his teeth; he cleans his teeth with [twigs]. It should be understood from the Smṛti that when the brushing of teeth is prohibited, twelve mouthfuls of *gaṇḍūṣa* (water-rinses) should be performed in its place, and by that alone the purification of the mouth is achieved.
He does not display [his teeth].
The term "data" (having given) is understood to carry over. "Āviṣkaraṇam" means making manifest or revealing. [Chapter 2, Part 2] Together with the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa:
1043. One should not smile while looking down; one should smile while covering the mouth.

Even when laughter is provoked by some cause for mirth, one should not smile; one should not even manifest a slight smile. The word *smaya* is derived from the verbal root *smi*, meaning "to smile slightly. By the prohibition of a slight smile, the prohibition of loud laughter is established all the more strongly through the logic of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) principle. Furthermore, the prohibition of laughter without cause is already established by the *Dharmaśāstra*.

If even a slight smile cannot be restrained, then one should simply smile while covering the mouth with the hand; this is indicated by the Vedic text: "He scratches himself with a black antelope horn and smiles while covering [his mouth], for the protection of offspring. *Gopīthā* means protection. The word is correctly formed through a specific irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the *Uṇādi-sūtras*. Furthermore, another result is stated in the *Pravaya-brāhmaṇa*: "Therefore, one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) should smile while covering [his mouth], for the maintenance of his splendor (*tejas*)."

These prohibitions apply to the wife as well, because of the indicative mark [in the text] "of her" (*tasyāḥ*). If there is a lapse in the restraint of speech (*vāgyamana*) by the wife, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is simply the recollection of Viṣṇu. This is because of the general statement: "If, in any way, there should be a lapse in the restraint of speech during the *japa* and other rites, one should utter a Vaiṣṇava mantra or remember the imperishable Viṣṇu. Since another means exists, it is improper to assume the recitation of a specific mantra [other than the remembrance of Viṣṇu]. However, the two mantras, "abaddhaṃ manaḥ" and "undatīr balaṃ dhatta," do not apply here.

This is because of the Sūtra statement: "The duties of the wife consist of celibacy and the recitation [of mantras]. Nor should it be argued that, by this logic, there should likewise be an absence of nail-clipping, tooth-cleaning, bathing, wearing clothes, eating, applying collyrium, purifying [the breath], and so forth; for the word *tasyāḥ* (of her) in the phrase "this very same conduct for her until death" was employed precisely for the purpose of including those aforementioned duties. Otherwise, its redundancy would be unavoidable.

Nor should it be argued that some other means must be postulated to avoid this redundancy; for apart from such a postulation, it is impossible to conceive of any interpretation consistent with other sūtras. This applies to the view of silence (*tūṣṇī-pakṣa*). However, in the case of the *ūha*-view, there is the modification (*ūha*) of the bathing mantra to "I am purified" (*pūto 'smi*). In the *ūha*-view, these two recitations (*japa*) indeed take place. In the alternative where there is no recitation (*japa*), it should be understood that the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
Upon seeing something impure, one recites: "The mind is unbound."

Upon seeing impure things such as filth, excrement, or urine, or those who are fallen, outcastes (caṇḍālas), or women in their menses, if there is no lapse of time between sightings, one recites the mantra only once even if one has seen them more than once. However, if there is a lapse of time, the mantra is recited separately for each instance. If all these are seen simultaneously at the same time, one recites it only once.

Regarding the sūtra in the fourth pāda of the eleventh adhyāya which states, "And likewise in the cases of dreaming, crossing a river, being rained upon, and the recitation of mantras over impure things," the distinction to be observed is as follows: in the cases of dreaming, crossing a river, and being rained upon, there is no repetition of the rite even when there is a difference in time. However, in the case of the recitation of mantras over impure things, since it occurs at one and the same time even when several impure objects are seen simultaneously, there is an absence of repetition due to the lack of a difference in time; this specific point should be understood.

In the case of being addressed while impure, since the very sight is the cause, there must be a repetition whenever one sees something impure at different times, even according to the Mīmāṃsaka view. By the word "thus" (evam), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) from the section concerning scratching (*kaṇḍūyana*) is extended by analogy. The meaning of the Sūtra is indeed clear. Some maintain that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and the looking (*avekṣaṇa*), both of which are prescribed by Smṛti. "Mā mā hāsīḥ" is the end of the mantra. 1044. While being rained upon, he mutters: "Undantīr balaṃ dhatta. (The flowing waters bestow strength. Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram—[10th Praśna]—While being rained upon, he mutters: "Undantīr balaṃ dhatta. (The flowing waters bestow strength.)

The recitation (*japa*) is performed while facing the one being sprinkled with the word "abhi" [of the mantra]. By the use of the suffix *śānac* in the term "vṛṣyamāṇa," it is indicated that the recitation occurs simultaneously with the sprinkling. According to the view of the ritualists (*yājñika*), if there is no interruption in time, the recitation is performed only once. However, according to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, it should be understood that even if there is an interruption in time, there is no repetition. "Nirvadhiṣṭa" is the end of the mantra. To the south of the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), he dwells in the hut of the initiated person (*dīkṣita*). || 6 ||

The *vihāra* is that place where the sacred fires are maintained, such as the *prāgvaṃśa* and other structures; having constructed the *dīkṣitāgāra* (the hall for the initiated) not far to the south of it, he performs the *vihāra*. From this very [text] it is understood that the *dīkṣitāgāra* must be made to the south of the *vihāra*. Here, *vihāra* means that which one performs for the purpose of passing the time, consisting of virtuous conversation, discourse, listening to the *Purāṇas*, and deliberation on the meaning of the Vedas. By the phrase "to the south of the *vihāra*," sitting in one's own fixed seat (*svāyatana*) is excluded. By the suffix *-ena*, proximity is indicated, thereby excluding distance.

The mention of the "initiated's house" (*dīkṣitāgāra*) is intended to exclude wandering about in any other hall or place whatsoever. Regarding the duties of the initiated, another Sūtra states: "He should not engage in worldly talk; he should avoid the sentiments of poetry (*kāvyarasa*); he should not sing; he should not weep; he should not be a spectator of dancing. Poetry is the work of a poet (*kavi*), and it is of many kinds—such as drama (*nāṭaka*), epic (*ākhyāyikā*), and farce (*prahasana*)—as shown in the *Agni Purāṇa* and other texts; he should avoid that. He should avoid the ten types of aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others. Elsewhere, he sits or lies down only on a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). This is clear.
The sun should not set upon him, nor should it rise, anywhere other than the *dīkṣitavimita* (the consecrated shed).

The *dīkṣitavimita* is the shed for the sake of the consecrated; that has already been shown to be in the eastern part. Therefore, "elsewhere" means in another place: while he is consecrated, the sun should not set upon him, nor should it rise upon him. The essential meaning is that during the sun's setting or rising, he should not go outside the *dīkṣitavimita*, but should remain right there. Regarding this expiation, Āpastamba says: "When [the sun] has set, he should mutter the verses addressed to Varuṇa (*vāruṇī*); when [the sun] has risen, those addressed to Sūrya (*saurī*)."

And furthermore, at sunset, he recites the verses addressed to Varuṇa: "O gamblers, whatever we have done here... (*yaściddha te yatkidedam kiāvāsa*); and at sunrise, the three verses addressed to Sūrya: "Up from darkness," (*udvayaṃ tamasaḥ*), "That bright one," (*tyaṃ citram*). At sunrise, he also recites the verses addressed to Varuṇa: "Loosen the highest bond, O Varuṇa," (*uduttamaṃ varuṇa*), "For our sake, O gambler, whatever we have done here" (*tannāyāṃ yatkidedam kiāvāsa*); and the verses addressed to Sūrya: "Up that bright one of the gods," (*udu tyaṃ citraṃ devānām*), and "The seven bay mares, the traverser, visible to all" (*sapta svā haritastaraṇiviśvadarśata*). According to the opinion of Bhāradvāja, the phrase "the traverser, visible to all" (*taraṇirviśvadarśata*) is not included.

Āpastamba says: "Honey, meat, women, untruth, sleeping on a high bed, spitting, going out at an improper time, and staying away from the sacrificial hut of one who has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*)—these are the vows. "Improper time" (*vikāla*) refers to the twilight periods and other times unfit for going out. "Staying away" (*pravāsa*) means spending a night elsewhere. The phrase "from the sacrificial hut of the consecrated" connects with both [parts of the compound] according to the *kākākṣinyāya* (the maxim of the crow's eye). The meaning is: one should not go out from the sacrificial hut at an improper time, nor should one stay elsewhere overnight after having gone out from it. In all cases of transgressing these vows, the *Vātapatī* [penance] applies.

The specific penances, however, are as prescribed. Āpastamba has stated the penance for vomiting and so forth: "Whatever undigested food has been cast out by me, or whatever has been improperly remembered; may Agni, Soma, and the Earth restore that again into my self. Having vomited or having sneezed, the food that is eaten at night does not protect one from hunger in the morning. [End of Second Paṭala, Section 2] — together with the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

"1045. Therefore, do not harm me; for that [death] is not seen in heaven," he says when having eaten food in a dream. "To the Rudriyas, to the waters, svāhā!"—having seen blood gushing forth, he says this out of disgust. "The waters, consecrated by svāhā, have entered the earth"—this refers to the *sthūhāna* (the discharge). "The tears, named *kṛpāṇā*, [have entered]"—this refers to the *tapasyā* (the sweat). The remainder of the formula is simply "he mutters"; there is no continuation of the phrase "do not permit [it] to go."

Regarding the phrase "having eaten food in a dream," since a dream-object is impossible during the waking state, it is impossible to recite the consecratory formula (*anumantraṇa*) for it. Because there is an inconsistency in one instance, the word "he mutters" (*japati*) is the only [word] that remains as the remainder for all cases. In the passages beginning with "the *stūhāna*," the word "having seen" (*dṛṣṭvā*) is also to be construed. Both types of tears—those born of sorrow and those born of joy—are included, as there is no distinction made.

Regarding the offering of a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati [with the injunction], "If one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should suffer distress or shed tears," some maintain that because this is not occasional (*anaimittika*), and because an occasional rite is equal to a permanent (*nitya*) one, the prohibition—"he does not offer any oblation other than those connected with the seasonal sacrifices" (*ṛtusaṃyuktābhyaḥ*)—excludes only oblations used for the seasonal sacrifices, and thus there is no prohibition regarding the *Jñātabhṛtī* sacrifice. This is not correct; because this rite is recited in the section on expiations (*prāyaścitta-prakaraṇa*), it is connected to the sacrifice just like the *Apāmārga* sacrifice, as its purpose is the removal of misfortune (*āpanirdhātārthatva*).

For without the removal of defects, the subsequent ritual action cannot take place; therefore, this *iṣṭi* indeed becomes the *pūrṇāhuti*. *Stūhānam* refers to phlegm and other secretions flowing from the nose; *anu* refers to the water flowing from the eyes; and *svedaḥ* is the water produced from the body. Bhāradvāja states: "If one should go out by a door other than [the prescribed one], he should enter by that same door and recite, 'Idam Viṣṇur... (RV 1.22.17).

Āpastamba states: "One should not release speech before the appearance of the stars; if one should release it, having muttered 'O Agni, you are the protector of the vow,' he restrains his speech. The statement "one should not release speech before the appearance of the stars" is a restatement (anuvāda) intended for the prescription of an expiatory rite (prāyaścitta), because it was previously stated that "he remains restrained in speech while performing austerity until the rising of the stars."

In the Śruti, however, after demonstrating the fault—stating that "one should not release speech before the stars; for if one were to release speech before the stars, he would cut off the breath"—and having prescribed the rule to release speech only after the rising of the stars, it further states as an expiation: "If he should release it, he should recite a verse addressed to Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; thus by means of the sacrifice he continues the sacrifice. Thus, only the mere recitation of a Vaiṣṇava Ṛk is prescribed as the expiation.

In the morning, however, if he should utter the speech of one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*), [the rule] "O Agni, you are the protector of vows" should be recited; then, having released his fists and his speech, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) to be mentioned later is to be observed. Āpastamba states: "One should not put on the garment of one who is consecrated, nor should one proclaim his evil. Since this prohibition applies even to those who are not consecrated, no one at all should put on a garment discarded by him for the sake of consecration; the meaning is that one should not proclaim any fault of his, whether it be real or unreal. One should void urine and feces only at night, or during the day in the shade.
One should void urine and feces only at night, not during the day. However, if one is unable to restrain them, one may do so even during the day; but in that case, one must do so in the shade.

In this regard, the *Dharmasūtra* states: "One should void urine and feces far from one’s dwelling, toward the southern direction or the south-western direction; or, if it is near the dwelling, one should avoid doing so after sunset. One should avoid using stones, clods of earth, or living plants and trees for the cleansing of urine and feces. Furthermore, while impure, one should avoid uttering the names of the deities. Parāśara says: "Then, having risen in the morning, one should first attend to the evacuation of feces and urine."

"Beyond the range of an arrow-shot to the southwest, and even further from the ground... (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 132.2.1046). This *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha states: "One should perform the voiding of urine and excrement at a distance from one's dwelling. The term "at a distance" (*dūrāt*) refers to a distance during the day, not during the night, because of the possibility of danger. With this very intention, Devala says: "One should never go far at night for the purpose of voiding feces or urine."

Śaunaka also says: "In the event of danger to life, one may perform the *utsarga* (voiding) even at night, even in the house. Regarding feces and urine, one should not do so during the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*). Thus Devala states: "One should always perform [the voiding of] feces and urine, but one should avoid it during the twilights. In the *Dharmasūtra*: "One should avoid covering the head during the day while performing the act of voiding feces or urine; however, having covered the head, one may void feces or urine."

Furthermore: "One should not perform the acts of urination or defecation on a staircase, on a difficult path, or likewise in water. One should avoid spitting and sexual intercourse while facing fire, the sun, water, a Brāhmaṇa, or deities. One should avoid the acts of urination and defecation while facing these. Furthermore: "One should eat food facing the east; for defecation, one should face the south; one should urinate facing the north; and one should wash one's feet facing the west. Here, "uccāra" refers to the act of defecation.

The rules regarding the voiding of urine and feces are to be known from the *Smṛtis*. In this regard, one should adopt the very position that specifies the southern direction or the south-western direction for those staying in a dwelling. Even when outside the house, one should not do so near the door.

Although there is a general prohibition of all shadows in the rule, "One should avoid the act of voiding urine or excrement in the shadow," nevertheless, because specific Smṛti texts state, "Nor in the shadows of those upon whom one depends," it is only that [specific] shadow which is prohibited, and not the prohibition of shadows from umbrellas and the like. That shadow which is not prohibited is what is intended here; it is precisely in such a shadow that the act of voiding urine and excrement is prescribed, as indicated by the phrase "by day or in the shadow."

The "shadow for subsistence" (*upajīvyacchāyā*) is that in which travelers and others rest. However, in this case, it is precisely the negation of such a shadow; even the non-negation of the shadow of a cloud and so forth is due to its being unavoidable, so let this remain as an irrelevant digression. Desiring to urinate, [the sacrificer] says, "This is thy sacrificial body," and having struck a clod of earth with his horn or something similar, and taking it, he voids urine while reciting: "I release the waters, not offspring; O ye who release from distress, being consecrated by *svāhā*, enter the earth. Having touched water and sipped it, he replaces the clod with the formula, "Be born from the earth," or "Be born of the earth."

"Desiring to urinate" means wishing to perform the act of urination. Since it is established by the very indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra "I release the waters" that this injunction pertains merely to the discharge of urine, the statement "desiring to urinate" is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). It means: one who desires to do *only* urine and not feces; therefore, this injunction does not apply when there is a flow of urine occurring at the time of discharging feces. [The cow] may be given with her horn or even with another [implement]; there is no restriction that she must be given only with her horn.

Because there is no mention of the word "given" (*pratta*) as in the case of "throwing up a clod of earth" (*loṣṭoddhanana*). A "clod" (*loṣṭa*) is a lump of clay. When the word "something" (*kiṃcit*) refers to something other than a clod, such as grass and so forth, then Āpastamba has indeed recited: "Having taken up either grass or a clod. Since taking [the water] is already established by the subsequent act of depositing it, the explicit statement "having taken" (ādāya) indicates that the passing of urine and feces must be performed only after having taken [the water]. Because the previous section began with the phrase "desiring to pass urine" (mūtra-cikīrṣan), and because of its suitability, the "passing" (prasrāvaṇa) refers specifically to the discharge of urine. It is established by the Smṛti that after performing the purification of the organ by discharging [urine], one should perform the washing of hands and feet and the ritual rinsing (ācamana). "Having touched water" (apa upaspṛśya) means having touched water; "having rinsed" (ācamya) means having performed the Vedic (śrauta) ritual rinsing.

Regarding the statement "having touched water, one should sip water" (*apa upaspṛśya ācāmet*), since it is impossible for two distinct acts to occur without a separate mention [of each], the word *upaspṛśa* denotes mere touching; it should not be taken to mean "sipping water," which is the meaning of the word *ācamana* as stated in the lexicon: "sipping water (*upasparśa*) is the act of *ācamana*. In certain instances where the word *ap-* (water) is employed in the sense of water—such as in sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), sipping (*ācamana*), and so forth—it is used; in others, it is not. The reason for this is as follows: where the word is employed, there is an absence of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as *utpavana* (purification by straining); where it is not employed, such purificatory rites are present.

With the mantra "From the earth arise," he places back exactly where that clod of earth or grass and so forth were taken from; or alternatively, with "Arise from the earth. There is a defect in the mantra here caused by the nasalization (*anunāsika*) and the *visarga*. Immediately after taking up the clod, one should wear the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) around the ear and so forth. Wearing it before the taking [of the clod] is not appropriate, as it would contradict the scriptural injunction: "One who performs the ritual action should be wearing the sacred thread. Nor is it the case that the taking [of the clod] is indicated by the suffix *-lyap* in the word "ādāya" (having taken).

For us, there is no occurrence of a contradiction regarding immediate sequence, because "immediacy" (*avyavahitatva*) is not intended here as a strict requirement. Furthermore, the wearing of the *yajñopavīta* on the ear is not an interruption, as it is conducive to the act of voiding urine or feces. As for ritual sipping (*ācamana*), it is somehow prescribed even while maintaining the fist for some reason; however, some hold that there is no fault in releasing the fist for the purpose of sipping, while others maintain that there is. The rule for purification must indeed be performed after releasing the fist. Regarding this, some say that no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is required.

Others maintain that immediately after that, having performed the expiation for releasing the fist, one should again form the fist with the mantra. One should perform urination and defecation only after placing the staff and the black antelope skin [on the ground]. Thus Āpastamba says: "One should not release [the staff] from the hand nor [the skin] from the body; having placed them down, one should perform urination and defecation.
A Śūdra does not sit behind him.

A Śūdra does not enter or approach this consecrated person (dīkṣita). Here, the prefix *anu* has the sense of prohibiting entry preceded by aiming toward [the person]. By this, it is understood that there is no prohibition against accidental entry. He may converse with a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya.

The meaning is that one should speak correctly with these [persons]. By this enumeration, the prohibition against conversing with women and Śūdras is established. Āpastamba states all of this clearly: "One should not converse with a woman or a Śūdra, nor should one follow after him. The meaning of the *Āpastamba Sūtra* is that one should not converse even with a woman who is not a Śūdra; nor, even out of a desire for great assistance, should one follow after this Śūdra; or alternatively, the meaning is that while he is traveling, a Śūdra should not follow after him.

The second meaning of the phrase "one should not approach him" is in accordance with our Sūtra: there is no fault even in conversing properly with venerable persons such as one's mother and others, as this is seen in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts. Because of the prefix *sam-*, only improper conversation is prohibited; by this, it is established that there is no fault in speaking a few words for the sake of a necessary purpose. Furthermore, the singular number and the masculine gender in the word "Śūdra" are not intended to be restrictive (*avivakṣita*), because they reside in the subject of the statement (*uddeśya*).

"Therefore, many Śūdras and even women should not approach [the sacrifice]. Regarding the matter of conversing with a Śūdra, Āpastamba states an exception: "One may converse with a Śūdra at will, provided he is one who is not suspected of having committed a sinful deed; this is the teaching of the Śāṭyāyanaka. The meaning is that one may converse as one pleases with someone who has not been heard of or determined to be a perpetrator of such faults as approaching forbidden women (agamyāgamana) or theft.

The mention of the *śūdra* is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for women as well. As for those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*), because they desire sin by their very birth, conversation with them is forbidden. However, conversation is not prohibited with those who desire only minor sins. If it is asked: "But since conversing with impure persons, even Brāhmaṇas and others, is forbidden by the Smṛtis, what is the distinction in the case of a *śūdra*? It is replied: Conversation with those such as Brāhmaṇas who do not desire sin is prescribed during intervals between ritual acts, such as listening to the *Mahābhārata* and other texts.
"One should spend the remainder of the day in the company of learned and beloved persons"—thus it is said; and likewise, "it is not ordained for a Śūdra, nor even for one who is learned.
He does not rise to greet anyone.

Upon seeing any learned person—whether a father or other elder, an elderly man, or even a wise one—who has arrived, he shall not perform the act of rising to welcome them. This is a prohibition of that which would otherwise be required by the Smṛti.

One should not fail to offer salutation to one’s father and mother, as well as to one’s paternal grandfather and grandmother, the great-grandfather and his wife, and the maternal grandfather and his wife; likewise to one’s paternal uncle, maternal uncle, brother, and father-in-law; and to one’s preceptor (*ācārya*), the one who performs the initiation (*upanetṛ*), and the giver of food; as well as to the teacher (*upādhyāya*), the expounder of the treatises on ethics (*nītiśāstra*), the protector from fear, the trusted friend, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), and the elderly; and one should salute those endowed with learning and modesty, as well as those possessed of wisdom.

The meaning is that one should not greet or pay homage to those such as the *ābhīrāḥ* who are mentioned in such Smṛti texts as being worthy of salutation (*abhivādyāḥ*). Āpastamba states: "According to the Śāṭyāyanaka, one greets [them] but does not perform the formal salutation (*abhivādayate*) toward the teacher (*ācārya*), the father-in-law (*śvaśura*), and the king. When greeted by others, he utters blessings for them but not for himself; even when the teacher and others have arrived, he does not greet them, much less anyone else. Since a greeting from a king to a Brāhmaṇa is impossible, the prohibition regarding the greeting of a king refers here specifically to the act of prostration (*namaskāra*), which is synonymous with the term "greeting" (*abhivādana*) in the context of the words used by Āpastamba for the teacher and so forth.

Everyone indeed should salute him, and he should salute everyone. All those who are initiated (dīkṣita) should be saluted by him; his father and others, as well as others, should salute him. Even though he is not to be saluted, he should nevertheless offer a blessing to all of them. In a formal salutation, a Brahmin should be addressed with the words, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one" (*āyuṣmān bhava saumya*). At the end of his name, the letter *a* should be pronounced with a protracted vowel (*pluta*), following the preceding syllable. One should speak according to this definition. Or, one may perform a bow (*namaskāra*) as is appropriate.

The prohibition "he shall not greet" means that even if he is older, he must not perform the salutation first himself; rather, it should be performed only after they have done so—this is the summarized meaning. The particle *eva* (only) is to be construed immediately after the word *abhiṣadet*. Āpastamba states: "The consecrated one is like fire; therefore, one should not touch him, nor should one utter his name. This is a rule for others [not initiated].

One should not seize this initiated person by the name; rather, one should perform a mere address using honorific terms such as "mo" and so forth. While there is a perceptible fault in physical contact, there is none in the mention of the name. Furthermore, the praise of Agni is not the sole reason for [avoiding] mere contact, but it also applies here: he is to be saluted even by those who are themselves worthy of salutation, and blessings must be bestowed upon them by himself.

For this very reason, the *Śāṅkhāyanaka* states immediately after [the rule]: "One does not greet a teacher, a father-in-law, or a king. This prohibition applies even to officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) regarding contact other than that which is prescribed by rule.
If one should come into conversation with a Śūdra, he should say to one of these castes: "Look at this man in such a manner."

Conversation—that is, dialogue—with this initiated person (dīkṣita) may occur together with a Śūdra. This refers to those mentioned immediately above—the Brāhmaṇa, Rājanya, and Vaiśya—excluding the Śūdra. Although the word *varṇa* applies to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—as in the statement, "The Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra are the castes (*varṇas*), but the first three are twice-born"—[the present rule concerns the former three].

According to this statement by Yājñavalkya, since the Śūdra class falls within the category of prohibition, it is impossible for him to be included by that word; therefore, only Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are meant. If a conversation were absolutely necessary, then one should conduct the conversation by placing any one of these—Brāhmaṇa, Rājanya, or Vaiśya—in front, saying: "Explain this to this Śūdra in this manner," meaning, "Speak to this Śūdra in this way."

Speaking common speech, he places *vicakṣaṇa* and *canasita* at the end of the names. "Speaking common speech" means speaking—that is, intending to speak or being prepared to speak—speech that has the form of worldly entities (*bhāvārūpā*). [The suffix -vat in] *kapilavatī* is used in the sense of proximity to the present tense (*vartamānasāmīpye*). Thus, the meaning is that he places *vicakṣaṇa* and *canasita* at the very end of those names which serve for calling and so forth; he joins them there. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), both are to be combined with each individual name, as in: "O Devadatta, *vicakṣaṇa-canasita*! (or "O *vicakṣaṇa*-Devadatta, O *canasita*-Devadatta!").

Āpastamba states a specific distinction: "For a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, [the mantras] are *canasita* and *vicakṣaṇa*. The meaning is that these two [mantras] apply to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya respectively. For a Brāhmaṇa, however, there is indeed a combination of both. By the phrase "speaking common speech," the secondary nature of speaking the vernacular is indicated; thus, it is established that one should speak in Sanskrit as the primary rule, and only when it is impossible to do so may one use the vernacular.

And so Āpastamba says: "By means of *pariṇaya*, she speaks human speech. *Pariṇaya* is that which is led (*nīyate*) everywhere, in all places, in a uniform manner; it is the correct word (*sādhuśabda*). By means of that, they speak even worldly speech. (Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra 10.5.0). The meaning is that one should speak only with correct words, and not otherwise.

There is also scriptural authority (*śruti*) on this point: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not speak in the speech of a barbarian (*mleccha*); for he who uses an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) is indeed a barbarian. The extracted meaning is that one initiated [for sacrifice] should not speak in a regional dialect consisting of incorrect words. Regarding the use of common worldly speech, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is simply that pertaining to the local community. The terms *vicakṣaṇa* and *canasita* do not apply to the names of deities, but rather to the names of humans.

And so Baudhāyana says: "Declare those names of deities as they have been told; then, declaring those which are not names of deities as they have been told, say at the end, 'Bestow the Vicakṣaṇa. Those which are not names of deities are such as 'man' (mānuṣa) and so forth, but not Kṛṣṇa, Gaṇeśa, Śiva, Māskara, and the like, because these are indeed designations of deities."

Bodhāyana has also stated the usage of *cana* and *sita-vicakṣaṇa* even in ordinary speech: "One should speak words that are *canasita* or *vicakṣaṇavat*. The application of the suffix *-matup* and the others is according to their respective positions: the first [suffix] at the beginning, and the second at the end.

Alternatively, this is the meaning of the Sūtra: when about to utter common human speech (*laukikī mānuṣī vāc*) and names (*nāmadheya*), one places the word *vicakṣaṇa* at the beginning and the word *canasita* at the end, respectively. That is to say, when about to speak common speech, one places the word *vicakṣaṇa* first; and regarding names, one places *canasita* finally, at the very end. Or rather, there is a conjunction of both in each case. In that regard, concerning the domain of speech, there is a conjunction of both at the beginning; concerning the domain of names, there is a conjunction of both at the end.

The expression *vicakṣaṇam canasitam* is a citation of the nominal stems (*prātipadika*); the case endings are not intended. Having first uttered "O wise and pleasant one" (*vicakṣaṇa-canasate*) in order to engage in ordinary conversation, one may then speak as one pleases. The use of the vocative phrase "O wise and pleasant one" (*ḍiṣṭha-vicakṣaṇa-canasate*) is for the purpose of addressing someone. Bhāradvāja says that one should address him as "O pleasant and wise one" (*canasita-vicakṣaṇa*).
He does not cook, he does not give, and he does not offer any oblation (*āhuti*), except for those connected with a sacrifice.

The meaning is that one does not perform cooking not connected with a specific purpose. And that [cooking] is for the sake of guests and so forth. There is no fault in having it cooked by another. By the prohibition, "A Brāhmaṇa shall not dwell in his house hungry," when a Brāhmaṇa arrives seeking lodging and has a desire to eat, food must certainly be given; therefore, cooking is established as necessary for that purpose.

In that regard, having prepared the food himself and given it to a guest for their meal, one attains the status of being the actual performer of the cooking due to the excellence of the fruit resulting from the particular effort involved; this [status] is what is here prohibited. "He does not give" means he does not perform the act of giving that is connected with a sacrifice.
Candrasena sacrificed with sacrifices involving abundant food and abundant sacrificial fees.

Thus, because the gift of food (*annadāna*) is seen in the *Purāṇas*, and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) from this sūtra—"they do not eat without having assigned [the food]"—the gift of food certainly takes place. "He does not offer any oblation whatsoever" means he offers no oblation at all. Of what kind? One that is prescribed other than those connected with a sacrifice (*kratu*). In the expression "connected with a sacrifice," there is a collective compound (*ekaśeṣa*): *kratusaṃyukta* (masculine), *kratusaṃyuktam* (neuter), and *kratusaṃyuktā* (feminine) become *kratusaṃyuktāḥ*. Because there is no distinction in their defining characteristic, there is no [gender-based] remainder here; [the neuter form is used]. Neuter...

And furthermore, there is [the rule]: "With another word, except for those connected with a sacrifice" (Pāṇini 2.4.13). In the case of [the compound] *sakamanapuṃsakena*, the formation as a singular collective (*ekavadbhāva*) is optional; therefore, its absence [as a compound] occurs. By this, cooking (*pāka*) and giving (*dāna*) are also included. This inclusion is necessary; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a prohibition applying even to cooking and giving that are connected with a sacrifice. In the case of cooking, being connected with a sacrifice is indeed the basis for the prohibition; the same applies to giving and offering (*homa*).

By stating "to those connected with the *kratu*" (*kratusaṃyuktābhyaḥ*)—rather than using the expressions "to those prescribed for the seasons" (*ṛtuvihitābhyaḥ*) or "to those [connected] to the seasons" (*ṛtubhyaḥ*)—it is made known that this prohibition does not apply to the cooking, giving, and oblations performed for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), because even these are connected to the *kratu* by way of restoring what has been destroyed.

Furthermore, if it were stated as "those prescribed for a sacrifice" (*kratuvihitānyāḥ*) and "for the sake of a sacrifice" (*kratvābhyaḥ*), then since the prohibition of cooking, giving, and offering (*pākadānahoma*) would apply to everything except a sacrifice, and because such a prohibition is impossible in the case of those very acts [of cooking, etc.], one would necessarily have to admit that the scope is restricted to things other than those; this would result in the fallacy of making the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) redundant. Moreover, since it is impossible for the cooking, giving, and offerings performed for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) to possess the quality of being "for the sake of a sacrifice" (*kratvarthatva*) or "prescribed for a sacrifice" (*kratuvihitatva*), there would be the fallacy of failing to include those acts which are nevertheless indispensable as means for connecting with the sacrifice (*kratusaṃdhāna*).

Therefore, it must necessarily be accepted that such a statement is intended precisely for the purpose of collecting these various expiations (prāyaścitta). Regarding the word "saṃ" (collective), among these prescribed expiations consisting of cooking, giving, and offering, that [expiation] alone occurs which cannot be accomplished without one of these three; however, that which can be accomplished [without them] does not occur at all.

Just as in a case where a penance is prescribed as being of the nature of a cooked offering (*pākātmaka*), a gift (*dānātmaka*), a burnt offering (*homātmaka*), or by another mode such as recitation (*japādi*)—and since the removal of the fault is possible through any of these alternative modes—it follows that [the specific forms] do not necessarily occur. However, if the daily worship of the deity (*prātyahikadevatārcana*) is performed together with a burnt offering (*homa*), then because of the prohibition "he does not offer any oblation whatsoever" (*na kāñcan āhutim juhoti*), it must be performed without a burnt offering, and not together with one.

The mention of "oblation" (*āhuti*) is indicative of any mere casting of a substance intended for a deity; by this, the *tarpaṇa* (water libation) and the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice are also excluded. However, because of the specific mention of "oblation," there is no prohibition of the placing of fuel-sticks (*samidādhāna*), even when performed for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Even according to the view that the sacrifices to the gods, ancestors, and spirits consist only of the formulas "Svāhā to the gods," "Svadhā to the ancestors," and "Namaḥ to the spirits"—and do not include the *vaiśvadeva*—there is still a prohibition of these as well, since they are not connected with a formal sacrificial rite (*akratusaṃyukta*).

The *manuṣyayajña* (offering to humans) does not even occur [in this case] with the thought "I shall kill for the sake of humans," because it lacks the nature of an oblation (*āhuti*) connected to a ritual (*kratu*). However, by his command, it certainly occurs for another. In the *Baudhāyana-prāyaścitta-sūtra*, other prohibitions are also mentioned: "One should not give, one should not offer oblations, one should not cook, one should not recite [mantras]," and so forth; they say that from the very beginning one should divide [the food], and furthermore: "One should not enter [the water], nor should one wear a garment [therein], nor should one let a garment float away."

By the statement "one should not plunge into water," the *vāruṇa* bath is excluded, but the *āgneya* and other baths are not excluded. Furthermore, the *brahmayajña* (study of the Vedas) does not take place; for although it is of the nature of study, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) beginning with "When one studies the Ṛgveda, one satisfies the gods with oblations of milk" establishes that it is of the nature of an oblation, and because of the use of the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*). Nor is there retention-study (*dhāraṇādhyayana*), because in the *Hemādri* and other Smṛtis, non-study is prescribed during a sacrifice, stating: "For the initiated and for Brahmins, [non-study lasts] until the end of the *anūbandhyā*."

There is a suspension of the *aupāsana-homa*, the *sthālīpāka*, the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, the *aṣṭakā*, the *śravaṇākarma*, the *pratyavarohaṇa*, and other such rites—whether they be obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or monthly (*māsika*)—as well as the purificatory ceremonies (*saṃskāras*) such as the tonsure (*caula*) and the initiation (*upanayana*). Furthermore, by the very prohibition that "a pregnant woman shall not undergo consecration" (*na garbhiṇī dīkṣeta*), the suspension of the *puṃsavana*, the *sīmanta*, and the *jāteṣṭi* is already established.

As for that which is stated in Baudhāyana’s *Prāyaścitta-sūtra*: "Now, when ten days have passed for a woman who has given birth (*sūtikā*), having performed purification as prescribed, one should employ the wife in the ritual acts; her son or a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) should perform those acts, while the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) should mutter the mantras"—this should be understood to apply to the state of being a *sūtikā* during a ritual act. It should be known that the possibility of this occurs in a sacrificial session (*satra*) lasting a year. [This is because] by the rule, "He does not offer any oblation other than those connected with the sacrifice," he is without a sacred fire (*anihotrin*).

In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Krion 1052, Chapter Ten: Prohibition of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, their modifications, the Paśubandha, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, the Āgrayaṇa, and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices when they are performed as repeated practices (*abhyāsa*). The same applies to the *Kṣāmavatī* offerings, the *Hiraṇyanābha*, the *Oṣṭhacat* and so forth. Although giving (*dāna*) is prohibited, nevertheless, garments, ornaments, and ointments must indeed be given, as seen in the *Rāmāyaṇa* and other texts. It will be stated later that the giving away of a maiden (*kanyādāna*) also takes place.

This prohibition regarding cooking, giving gifts, and *homa* offerings extends up until the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath); however, the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsti*), the recitation of hymns (*stotra-pāṭha*), and so forth, certainly do take place, because they do not consist of cooking or *homa*. In a sacrificial session (*sattra*) lasting a year, if a woman has given birth, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with *puṃsavana* must be postponed and performed later; *homa* should not be performed among these, because it is more appropriate to omit a single part than to omit everything. The wise should accept whatever is stated here as correct. [The text continues: the prohibition of the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) and so forth for the husband of a pregnant woman...

However, [the husband] must wait for at least six months. Accordingly, Dakṣa, while prescribing the duties of the husband of a pregnant woman, states: "But when six months have passed, one should not perform the tying of the girdle (initiation); one should avoid the establishment of the sacred fires, the *gayāśrāddha*, and shaving. The mention of the "establishment of the sacred fires" (*agnyādhāna*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for obligatory rites such as the Soma sacrifice and others. Likewise, Gālava says: "The husband of a woman whose pregnancy is manifest [should avoid] traveling by sea, carrying a corpse, shaving, and sexual intercourse."

"In the same way, with such effort, one should not perform sacrifices at sacred fords (tīrtha) such as Gayā, nor the ritual of consecrating a dwelling (vāstuvidhi). Thus, it explicitly states the prohibition of sacrifice; here, "sacrifice" refers specifically to the Soma sacrifice and others. Another Smṛti text also clearly states this while describing the duties of the husband of a pregnant woman: "When six months have passed, he should not perform the offering into the fire (agnyādhāna); he should avoid sacrifice, initiation (dīkṣā), pilgrimage to sacred fords, and the Śrāddha at Gayā."

By the statement "one should not [perform it] once six months have passed," it is implied that there is no fault in performing it within the interval of those six months. Regarding this, some say: "The prohibition against re-consecration (*anyādhāna*) and other rites after a month has elapsed is intended to indicate an excessive degree of fault; therefore, even prior to that time, if the opportunity arises, one must certainly observe the prohibition. On that day, the consecrated person keeps watch through the night;
the meaning is that on whichever day he is consecrated, on that very night he remains awake.
It is not a vow; it consists of drinking milk. The rest is clear.
Having seen a star, he releases his speech silently.

The singular form "nakṣatram" (the asterism) is used in the Śruti even though a plural is heard [elsewhere], in order to indicate that if even one [asterism] is seen, the purpose of the Śruti is thereby accomplished. Regarding the phrase "vrataṃ kṛṇuta," although it serves both the purpose of commanding others and the purpose of releasing speech, since the release of speech exists here even if the purpose of commanding others is absent, there arises a doubt that the rule "vrataṃ kṛṇuta" might apply; to prevent this, the word "tṛṣṇām" (thirst) is used.

The meaning is that the conjunction is solely for the purpose of time, and not for the relationship of principal and subordinate (aṅga-aṅgin). And thus says Jaimini: "In those two cases, rising and dismissal. The word "eva" (only/specifically) is for the purpose of excluding the alternative mentioned by Baudhāyana. [End of Second Paṭala, Section 2] *Jyotsnā* Commentary by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. Page 1053.

According to Baudhāyana, when the stars have risen, the sacrificer, having fastened on a black antelope skin and having gone out by the eastern door, stands in front of the hall and releases his speech with the formula, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ, make the vow. The particle *eva* (only) indicates that this specific rule must be adopted here as a restrictive injunction; by the word *vrataṃ kṛṇuta*, there is the exclusion of only that [formula] which was present in the context of the *sūṇī*.

On the first day, there is no vow; he releases his speech either silently or with the *vyāhṛtis*. This cessation of the *pālīkṣya* as taught by Vādhūla and others is indicated by the word "only" (*eva*). Having covered his body with a black antelope skin with the neck pointing upwards, this rule mentioned therein is also to be adopted.
He restrains his speech at the time when the one who bestows the vow gives him the command. || 7 ||

At the very time when [the Adhvaryu] issues the command to the initiated sacrificer, "O initiated one, restrain your speech," at that same time the wife also restrains her speech. Here, the meaning of the word *asmin* (at that) is "immediately following" (*adhyavahita-samīpa-kāla*). Thus, this is intended to indicate that she restrains her speech as soon as she hears the word *patnī* immediately after the command "O initiated one, restrain your speech," and not only after hearing the specific words "O wife, restrain your speech. By this...

It is also understood that the restraint of speech is coextensive with the time of the *praiṣa* (the call) for the *anuyāja*. In the phrase "at that time," the mention of "time" is for the purpose of excluding "place"; by this, the restriction that the restraint of speech must occur only in the same place where the *praiṣa* was given is thereby removed.

If it is argued that this very sūtra is redundant because the time associated with the rising of affection (prema) is already established by the rule, "Having sent forth [the cow], while the sun is still above the trees before its rising, he gives the command for the milking," we reply: True. However, it serves a purpose as a means of indicating that there is also another alternative time. That other time is stated in the Baudhāyana-sūtra: "Then, before the disappearance of the stars, having given the command, he says, 'O you who have restrained your speech, milk the cows.'"

When the firewood for the purpose of kindling is ready, standing to the north of the Āhavanīya fire, he issues the call: "Make the fires radiant! O consecrated one, restrain your speech! O wife, restrain your speech! Having issued this call, they both restrain their speech and cause the cows to be milked, saying, "O, let them yield [milk]. According to another Sūtra, the word "upayusam" is used. He worships the rising sun with the verse: "Those words of animals that are in the bull, those bright ones that are in the sun—send them forth; may they, being auspicious, return to us here according to our respective shares."
The prohibitory injunction "one should not look at the rising sun" is set aside in this case. The mention of the "sun" (āditya) is for the purpose of excluding the rays and the dawn.
He issues the command: "When the sun has risen, perform the vow.
At the conclusion of the command, there is the release of speech.
The same applies when [the sun] has set.
By the word "thus" (evam), the injunction "perform the vow" (vrataṃ kṛṇuta) and the release of speech (vāgvisarga) are extended by analogy.
He consumes the fast-food (vratayati) at midday and at midnight.

Midday (*madhyandina*) is the middle portion of a day divided into three or five parts; midnight (*madhyarātra*) is the middle portion of a night divided into three or five parts. At the time of the sun’s turning, since any kind of eating whatsoever is prohibited by the *Smṛti*, this constitutes the vow for times other than those.

In that regard, according to the system of three parts, the time subsequent to the final two *ghaṭikās* of the first half of the day is the time for the vow (*vratakāla*). According to the system of five parts, the time subsequent to the first two *ghaṭikās* of the first half of the night is the time for the vow. This is the extracted meaning: it is the same for the night as well.

Regarding this, Āpastamba states another alternative: "Or, having passed the human time—namely, the evening milk in the latter part of the night and the morning milk in the afternoon—so says one [teacher]. That is, he consumes the fast-food after that "human time" has elapsed, which is the period generally when humans eat, both by day and by night, beginning from midday. The evening milk is for the night-fast, and the morning milk is for the day-fast. Those who are not initiated do not see him while he is consuming the fast-food.
Baudhāyana says that he consumes the fast-food after enclosing [the area] with a screen.

Milk for a Brāhmaṇa, gruel for a Rājanya, and curdled milk (āmikṣā) for a Vaiśya. "Milk" means cow's milk; "gruel" means thin rice porridge; "āmikṣā" is well known [as curdled milk]. The meaning is that these observances (vrata) are to be followed according to one's respective caste. Nor should it be argued that this observance is solely for the benefit of the person (puruṣārtha), because its purpose is visible (dṛṣṭārthatva). Rather, since no visible result is possible for a restriction that is already established, it is more appropriate that it serves the purpose of the sacrificial transcendental potency (kratvapūrva). And thus Jaimini states in the third pāda of the fourth adhyāya: "But for substances intended for an action, the consecration (saṃskāra) should be a property of the sacrifice."

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: *kriyārtha* means the purpose of action (*kriyāyā arthaḥ*). By the etymology "that which is sought after" (*arthyate*), the word *artha* denotes the fruit (*phala*). Those persons for whom the purpose is solely the fruit of action are "those whose purpose is action" (*kriyārthānām*). Of what kind of things? Of "substantial things" (*dravyāṇām*), that is, of those possessing substance (*dravyavatām*). In the term *dravyāṇām*, the possessive suffix *ac* is added according to the rule for the *ārśa-ādi* group.

Their status as substances is established by scripture (*śruti*), namely: "Milk is the fast-food for the Brāhmaṇa, gruel for the Rājanya, and curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for the Vaiśya. Their consecration (*saṃskāra*) consists of the form of the milk and so forth; thus, it would be a duty of the sacrifice (*ṛtudharma*). The second sūtra, which is supplementary to this, stands as a separate point: "They would remain distinct," meaning that the persons enjoined by the injunctions—"milk for the Brāhmaṇa, gruel for the Rājanya, curdled milk for the Vaiśya"—[would remain distinct].

[The words] would not remain distinct; they would reach a state of fixed determination. In this context, the word *rājanya* refers to all Kṣatriyas, and not merely to an anointed (consecrated) Kṣatriya. This is because it is observed as such in the section concerning the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice (*Aveṣṭyadhikaraṇa*), and because it is recited between the Brāhmaṇas and the Vaiśyas. Regarding this point, Āpadeva also stated in the second chapter, third section (*Adhyāya 2, Pāda 3*), in the sūtra: "In the *Aveṣṭi*, because of its connection with the sacrifice, it is said to have the ritual as its primary element."

In the Rājasūya sacrifice, the following offering is prescribed under the name *Aveṣṭi*: "The king, as the performer, offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, with gold as the sacrificial fee; [he offers] a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra, with a bull as the sacrificial fee; a pap to the Viśvedevas, with a reddish-brown cow that has calved for the first time as the sacrificial fee; a pap to Mitra and Varuṇa, with a barren cow as the sacrificial fee; and a pap to Bṛhaspati, with a white-backed bull as the sacrificial fee. *Piśaṅgī* means reddish-brown in color. *Paṣṭhīhī* is a cow pregnant with her first calf; some say she is four years old. *Vaśā* is a barren cow.

"The white-backed" and "the dark-backed" refer to the ox (*go*). The phrase "he offers" (*nirvapati*) is to be supplied everywhere. Although, based on the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating "there are the Aveṣṭis of the quarters," [one might think] this refers to the sacrifice known as the *Aveṣṭi*, and although the plural number in that explanatory passage intends each individual sacrifice, here there is no contradiction because it refers to the ritual action consisting of the collection of oblations named *Aveṣṭi*. Alternatively, the singular number may intend the genus (*jāti*).

In this *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice, if a Brāhmaṇa should undertake it, he should place the oblation for Bṛhaspati in the middle and, having offered each oblation, pour the clarified butter over it; if a Rājanya, the oblation for Indra; if a Vaiśya, that for the Viśvedevas. Regarding the mention of "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth in those sentences connected to them, it is stated that this refers to a distinct sacrifice (*kratu*) which is the primary act. Why? Because of its connection with the term "sacrifice" (*yajña*). This is the meaning of the Sūtra: "Only for the Kṣatriya."

The detailed explanation should be understood from the original source (*ākara*). These substances, such as milk and the rest, remain eternal even when other substances are present. Thus, Jaimini states in the eighth quarter of the sixth chapter: "Likewise, [the rule applies] to eating, the *praisha* command, clothing, the *saṃjñapta-homa*, and aversion. The example for "eating" is: "Milk is the vow (*vrata*) of the Brāhmaṇa"; this means that even when other substances exist, milk and the like alone are used in the vows. The example for the *praisha* command is: "O Agnīdh, spread the fires," and so forth; this refers to the meaning of the command even when it is understood from another source.

Examples should be observed as follows: the injunction "one puts on unwashed clothing" applies even when another garment is present; the *saṃjñapta-homa* (the oblation at the immolation) with the mantra "that which has made the animal long-lived" is performed even in the absence of the act of making it long-lived; and the mantra "he who hates us and whom we hate" is recited even when there is no actual person to be hated. Because there is no perception of a specific occasion (*nimitta*), and because the accomplishment of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the rule cannot be achieved by any other means, it is considered mandatory (*niyata*).

In the Sūtra, the word *tathā* (so/likewise) serves to carry forward the word *niyataṃ* (necessarily) from the preceding Sūtra, for the sake of its meaningfulness. The rest is clear. The *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) should be made with ordinary curds because of its solid consistency. Since there is praise of the *pākayajña* (cooked sacrifice) regarding the *āmikṣā* used in the context of vows, the ritual rules (*dharmas*) pertaining to the *āmikṣā* do not apply here. He states the substance common to all social classes (*varṇas*):
"One should offer either a single portion of milk or barley-gruel."

One should consume as a fast-food (*vrata*) the milk of a single cow; that is "single-milk" (*ekadugdha*). Alternatively, having cooked groats (*yavāgū*) in the milk of a single cow, one should consume that as the fast-food. This is a rule from another Vedic branch (*śākhāntara*). Āpastamba states this clearly: "One should consume either groats or single-milk as the fast-food"—thus some teach it without reference to specific castes; however, others consume milk itself as the fast-food. But one should not do it that way; rather, having cooked groats in milk, one should consume them as the fast-food.

In this context, because only one milking is mentioned, it follows that even for one who subsists on milk alone (*payovrata*), much milk may be taken; if there are many [cows], then *āśira* (curdled milk) should be prepared from them. Regarding this, Āpastamba states another specific rule: "If the cow providing the vow-milk gives little, one should have another milked; if there is no other, one should mix it with water and cook it. If there should be no milk at all, one should cook barley-gruel (*yavāgū*) in water and consume it as the vow-food; at the very least, one should consume *pippala* fruits, but one must never fail to consume the vow-food, so that the *agnihotra* remains uninterrupted."

"Pippalas" are fruits, or "vohayas. In the absence of all [other options], one should even consume fruits, but one must not omit [the vow], because the vow is praised as being like the *agnihotra*; this is the sense. The word "iti" is for the purpose of indicating the scriptural source (*śruti*). Likewise, Bhāradvāja states that it is understood [from scripture]: "So that the *agnihotra* may not be interrupted. If one should desire curd, they should prepare this curd for him. "Dadhīyāt" means if he should desire curd; having curdled this very [milk], they should prepare this curd for this sacrificer, for the sake of the sacrificer. The plural number is used for the purpose of including any one of those who are capable of performing the task.
If he should desire food, they should pour parched grains (*dhānā*) for him, or they should pour barley-meal (*saktu*) for him, or they should pour clarified butter (*ghṛta*) for him.

If, while possessing sharp strength, he should desire edible food, then at the time of his vow, for the sake of not interrupting his vow, they should pour—that is, they should add—any one of these substances, such as parched grains, into that very vow. The two occurrences of the word *yadi* (if) are for the purpose of showing that these are optional alternatives (*samavikalpa*). This is the offering.

The mention of "anuvitā" (in succession) serves to indicate that the protection of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is maintained only as long as one focuses on the sequence [of the substances], and not beyond that. Although the brevity of the Sūtra would have allowed for the formulation "one should scatter parched grains (*dhānā*), flour (*saktu*), or ghee (*ghṛta*) for him," the separate statement "one should scatter for him" was accepted at the outset to show that whichever substance was initially chosen must be used until the end; in its absence, only its substitute (*pratinidhi*) is to be taken, and not another prescribed substance such as rice or barley.

This is for the purpose of making it known. *Dhānāḥ* are roasted barley grains; *saktavaḥ* are flour made from parched barley. In case of extreme inability [to procure these], even boiled rice (*odana*) may be used. And so says the Brāhmaṇa: "If he should think, 'I shall perish,' he should consume boiled rice, roasted grains, flour, and ghee, so that he does not perish. Or else, he should consume one of the sacrificial oblations (*havir*) of the Agnihotra.

From among the oblations of the *agnihotra*, one should consume a single substance as a fast-food (*vrata*). Even if rice and other such items are exhausted, one should consume that [single substance]. This implies that even rice is included among these. Because of the prohibition, "One does not eat meat," one should exclude meat from these [fast-food substances]. Āpastamba states clearly: "One should consume a single [substance] from the *agnihotra* oblation, excluding meat. The use of the singular number is for the purpose of prohibiting mixing [of substances].
These rules for the fast-food (*vrata*) apply to all castes; the meaning is that these rules for the fast-food are common to all castes.
Regarding all *upasad* rites, there are rules for the arrangement of the "breasts" [of the milk-vessel]:

"milk for a Brāhmaṇa, gruel for a Rājanya, and curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for a Vaiśya," and so forth; such a rule is intended for the *dīkṣā* (initiation). However, in the *upasad* rites themselves, the rule of the milk-fast (*payovrata*) applies without distinction to all social classes (*varṇa*), because the arrangements of four breasts and so on are prescribed therein. These [arrangements] will be demonstrated specifically in the context of the *upasad* rites.

Furthermore, when there is a doubt as to whether one must necessarily observe a vow (vrata) regarding milk and other substances that might not be fit for consumption, or whether one need not, Jaimini states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the eighth section of the sixth chapter: "But that which is purposeless would be non-obligatory" (*anarthakaṃ tvanityaṃ syāt*). For in such a case, due to the occurrence of illness in the sacrificer, a conflict with the ritual (*ṛtu*) could arise; therefore, because it would conflict with the primary rite (*pradhāna*), the vow should not be observed. The meaning of the sūtra is this: that vow which becomes purposeless due to the risk of causing the omission of the primary rite would be non-obligatory (*anitya*).

"Thou art wide-extending, the sustainer of people, the one who provides his own portion; protect me," with these words he consecrates the bronze vessel (*kaṃsa*) which is the offering of the vow (*vratapradāna*).

The mention of the *kaṃsa* is for the purpose of excluding the cup (*camasa*) mentioned in other Sūtras. It is called *pradāna* because it is "given by means of this"; thus, the offering of the vow is the *vratapradāna*.
With the verse, "We direct our divine thought," he washes his hands.
"Sprinkling" means washing. "Asadaśaḥ" marks the end of the mantra. He undertakes the vow with the mantra: "The gods who are born of mind, yoked by mind..."

"Namaste-bhyaḥ svāhā"—this is the end of the mantra. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says: "Having enclosed [the area], he causes her to consume it"; and "Having caused her to consume it once silently, he causes her to consume it again. At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ pours [the remainder] into his wife's vessel and gives it to her for consumption; she consumes it after enclosing [the area]; and having silently rinsed [the vessel], he returns it to her. This is also stated in the *Jyotsnā* commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa on the second section of the second chapter.

In the case of the *odanānuvrata* rite, since the vow (*vrata*) is a sacramental refinement (*saṃskāra*), the sprinkling (*pariṣeka*) and the consecration by recitation (*anumantraṇa*) of the rice (*odana*)—which is the object of that vow—necessarily occur because they too are sacramental refinements. Furthermore, because [the rice] lacks the nature of being cooked, given away, or offered as a sacrifice (*homa*), the *āpośāna* (sipping of water) also necessarily occurs. One drinks water with the mantra: "O waters, you who are worthy of sacrifice, may you be auspicious when drunk; may you be very kind within our womb, our belly. Rich in nourishment, many-formed, and sinless, be auspicious for our drinking. This is done when the water has been drunk, or when one feels thirsty again.

When water has been specifically drunk by someone who, out of devotion, has brought and offered it, thinking "this must not be refused," then even a small amount should indeed be drunk with this mantra. For the *Smṛti* states that milk, water, and betel-leaf are said to be "not to be refused": "A twice-born man who refuses these becomes a sinner. Since the fault of refusal is thus heard in the *Smṛti*, if one insists that the reading must be "yadāpītam" (when it has been drunk), then—

The meaning should be understood as follows: "May you, the waters, having been drunk, come face-to-face, reach [me], and be brought by someone for the purpose of drinking. Since the drinking of water immediately after the drinking of milk is prohibited in the medical scriptures (Vaidyaka-śāstra), it should be understood that even when one is thirsty, water should be drunk only after waiting for some time. This mantra is not intended solely for the drinking of water during a religious vow (*vrata*), but rather for all instances of drinking. "O Waters, may you be auspicious when drunk; may you be very gracious within our womb-like belly."

"O you who possess refreshing water, free from disease, sinless, and auspicious, be for our life! Having thus taken the vow, he touches the region of his navel; and having drunk water, he mutters [the mantra], so says Āpastamba. The wife, however, takes the vow silently. Thus says Āpastamba: "The wife takes the vow silently in her own place. Baudhāyana also states: "Having enclosed that space, she takes the vow silently. The washing of the hands and the drinking of water are also performed silently because of their connection to that [vow].
To the south of the Āhavanīya fire, he lies down facing east; he lies down with his head toward the east.
"He lies on his right side"— this is to be supplied [to the previous statement]. He should not lie on his back.
Sixth: Āpastamba also states that one should not turn down (*nyaṅ*). One should not turn away from the fire;
that is, one should not turn around with one's back toward the fire. Here, the prefix *pari-* signifies proximity.

In this context, it should be understood that the reading is *yadā pītam* according to the first commentary. (Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Book 10, Chapter 5): "O Agni, do thou watch well"—with these words, one who is about to sleep (*svapsyan*) worships the Āhavanīya fire. "About to sleep" means intending to go to sleep. This rule applies where staying awake has not been specifically prescribed. According to the view of the ritualists (*yājñika*), however, there is a repetition of the worship of the Āhavanīya every time one wakes up during sleep. According to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, since the worship is performed by intending to sleep for the entire night, there is no repetition.

If it is argued that, because they have stated that this [act] has for its object the mantras which constitute the means of performance (*karaṇa*), this [rule] refers only to the cessation of the mantras alone and not to their ancillary parts (*aṅga*) as well, then it should be observed that even in their view, there is indeed a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the *upasthāna*.
"The Viśvedevas have turned toward me" (*viśve devā abhi mām āvavṛtran*); thus he turns around, provided he should turn around.

Regarding *apaparyāvartanam* (turning away): turning one's back [is the act]. By the word "yadi" (if), it is understood that the *upaparyāvartanam* (turning toward) must be performed with the mantra; this itself is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). *Upaparyāvartanam* is the act of turning so as to face the fire. The mantra ends with the word "rādhasā."

"May mind come back to me; may life come back to me; may sight come back to me; may hearing come back to me; may breath come back to me; may intention come back to me; may thought come back to me; may reflection come back to me. May Vaiśvānara, the undeceivable protector of my body, remain within me, warding off all misfortunes. May Vaiśvānara, the sustainer of all and the source of all well-being, drive away all misfortunes. May he protect us from harm by day and by night. Having awakened, one mutters: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows."

The phrase *yad* (or *yā*) *apaparyāvarteta* has its syntactical connection either here or with what precedes it. After the word *naktam*, the verb *japati* (he mutters) must be supplied. In this view, the ritual turning around (*upaparyāvartanam*) accompanied by the mantra ending with *viśve devā abhi mām āvavṛtran* is indeed obligatory. Nor should it be argued that the phrase *na ca tvam agne vratapā asi*, which is muttered upon waking, should also have its connection right here; for there is no benefit in combining them [with the preceding]. However, if the connection were with what precedes, there would simply be an omission [of the mantra].

The statement "having awakened, he mutters" indicates that the water is for the purpose of awakening as an ancillary to the act of awakening; by this, it is established that since there is no sleep on the day of waking, this recitation does not take place at night. The prefix *prati* is used to indicate that this recitation occurs only in a state of complete wakefulness. The word *ījyaḥ* marks the end of the mantra.
One should recite "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows," if one should utter a word [contrary to] the vow of consecration (*adīkṣita-vāda*).

The statement "Again, O Agni, you are the guardian of vows" (*punastvam agne vratapā asi*) is for the purpose of enumerating [the recitation of] the verse addressed to Viṣṇu beginning with "O mind, come back again" (*punar manaḥ*). Because of the statement "he should follow," there is an absence of muttering (*japa*). By that, the rule of fourfold intonation (*cātuḥsvara*) is established here. The avoidance of speaking barbarisms (*mleccha*), indistinct speech, laughter, and so forth, constitutes "speaking what is unfit for one who has not been initiated. Having released his fists and his speech, the phrase "you are the guardian of vows, O Agni" connects with what precedes it.
This procedure begins with the *dīkṣaṇīyā* (initiation offering).

The ritual rules beginning from "if he should speak out of negligence" up to "having released his fists and speech" are designated by the term "procedure" (*vṛtti*). This [procedure] ends here. [End of Chapter 1059, Section 1] With the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

He is not cut by a staff, nor does he walk about after having put on a black antelope skin; he scratches himself with a black horn, and he smiles while covering his mouth—these are the vows beginning with the "use" (of the items). || 8 ||

Thus ends the second chapter in the tenth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. By the giving of the staff, the staff [is consecrated]; by the mounting of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), the black antelope skin; by the giving of the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*), the horn; and by the wrapping with the garment, the use of the garment [is established]. These and those following are the observances (*vratas*). "The staff is not to be broken" and "having fastened the black antelope skin, one does not walk about"—these are prohibitions. The latter two are injunctions. These observances last from the commencement of the use of each respective item until its relinquishment.

He is not cut by a staff, nor is he separated from the staff. Having set aside the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), he should not even take a step. He should scratch himself only with the black antelope horn, and never with his nails or other means. The meaning is that, while residing in the sacred place, he should laugh only after covering his mouth.

Thus ends the second chapter of the tenth book in the *Jyotsnā* commentary, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—the son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was himself the son of Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—on the *Śrīmad-Bhagavat-Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*. This work is intended to alleviate the distress of learned people caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the ocean of that Sūtra.

10.3 Now begins the third chapter of the tenth book. With the words "Pūṣan, [bring] the gains" (*pūṣā sani*), he instructs the *sanīhāras*. *Sani* is wealth obtained through begging; those who carry away from here and there whatever substance has been begged for are the *sanīhāras*, and it is them that he instructs—that is, he urges them on—saying, "Go to such-and-such a person and such-and-such a person. By this it is known that the material required for the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) has already been begged for previously. The long vowel is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). A *Dvaidhasūtra* demonstrating specific types of *sāhāra* was already stated at the occasion of preparing the cattle-pen, the ewes, and so forth.

He practices begging for alms for twelve days; when the period of consecration (*dīkṣā*) is unlimited, he may beg as much as he desires. If this is the determination of one who has not yet gathered the necessary materials—that even during the middle of the sacrificial consecration he will certainly obtain materials by begging—then this same procedure applies. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says: "Then he sends forth messengers for the requisites; whomever he thinks will not refuse him, to him he sends first. *Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram*, Tenth Book. (Note: The text provided contains a fragmentary citation from the *Śrautasūtra* regarding the sending of messengers for ritual materials.)

In this regard, there are two modes: in the rite of initiation (*dīkṣākalpa*) lasting twelve days (*dvādaśāha*), there is the practice of wandering for alms (*bhikṣācaryācaraṇa*); in rites of initiation lasting one day or more, it is according to one's desire and in accordance with the time. Even in rites of initiation lasting a single day or similar durations, the practice of wandering for alms must certainly be performed. This practice of wandering for alms is for the sake of providing sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth. Regarding this, Bharadvāja says: "One should beg for twelve days for the sake of sacrificial fees. Even when wealth is present, begging is indeed obligatory.

And likewise, Jaimini states in the eighth quarter of the sixth chapter by means of the two sūtras: "The begging for purchase [is required] when [the substance] is not available, as in common worldly practice," and "Or it is fixed because it serves a purpose. The meaning of this section has already been demonstrated in the context of the purchase of Soma.
