He states the substances to be begged for: gold, clothing, a cow, a horse, a goat, and a sheep; and as many cows as are prescribed, one of each of the other species.

The meaning is that they become as many as are limited by the ultimate extent, sufficient, and complete in number. Regarding "of the others"—namely gold, clothing, horses, goats, and sheep—the term "of the others" is a qualification of the genus, intended to indicate that there are other items as well, and that these also have a corresponding measure. These consist of both those specifically assigned and those not so assigned. Specifically, the items to be mentioned—consisting of gold, clothing, sheep, wool, a chariot, an upper garment, a horse, a man, and an elephant—are included here as the unassigned ones. (Note: *adhīvāsa* refers to an upper garment).

One accepts those [gifts] with the formulas beginning with "candramasi," according to their respective forms. The acceptance of the six gifts, beginning with gold, is performed with these six verses. When any of the six items, beginning with gold, are present, one should accept that specific object at the time of uttering the corresponding part of the mantra containing its specific indicative mark (*liṅga*). Regarding the concern that if any one among these is not present, the mantra should be used silently because it is impossible for it to serve as the means for accepting all the objects, this statement [of the Sūtra] refutes that; therefore, these mantras are indeed distinct.

The acceptance of that specific substance which is present occurs by means of the food alone used for that purpose; there is an omission of the remaining items. Alternatively, the word *air* (or *ebhiḥ*) refers back to the *sanīhāra* (the collected materials), and having taken up the phrase *āhṛtāni* (brought forth), it is connected with that. These refer to gold and the other items. By these mantras, according to their form—that is, according to their indicative marks (*liṅga*). Gold is [offered] with the mantra beginning *candramati*, because in the Vedic lexicon (*Nighaṇṭu*), the word *candra* is listed as a name for gold in the passage: "Gold is bright (*hema*), the moon (*candra*), and the golden disk (*rukmam*)."

Because of the observation that "candra" means gold, the word *candra* here refers to gold. "Vastram asi" [means] a garment. "Ustrā asi" [means] a camel; the word *ustra* denotes a cow. Due to the feminine gender indication, the mantra applies only to a female cow. However, for a male bull, the acceptance is performed silently (*sṛṣṇīm*), because there is no modification (*ūha*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*). According to Ālekhana, because a modification is seen in the archetype—the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*)—in the phrase "adya mūtyām," there may be a modification as "usra asi.
In this way, when a horse, a goat, or a sheep is present, one should know there are two positions: with modification or without modification. The mantras end with the words "mama bhogāya bhava."
The phrase "devaḥ savitā" is appended everywhere;

that is to say, in all the mantras. The word "āyuṣā" constitutes the end of the appendage here. Since no specific mantras are taught for the other substances, their acceptance is performed silently. Now, as for that which is not specifically prescribed by the Brāhmaṇa: "Thou art of Prajāpati; [I accept] mine..."

[The Sixth Paṭala] Together with the commentary named *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa: 1061. "May it be for my enjoyment"—thus he accepts it; so says Baudhāyana. Regarding the mantra beginning with *devaḥ savitā*, there is an option (*vikalpa*) to append either *prājāpatyam asi* or *mama bhogāya bhava*.
With the formula *vāyave tvā*, one should designate whichever of those [cups] might be lost.

Among those cows obtained as a gift, whichever cow should perish, one should dedicate that one [to Vāyu]. "Perishing" (*nāśa*) is of two kinds: that caused by theft or by becoming invisible to the range of sight, and that caused by death, which consists in its being entirely useless to the owner. Both of these are included here. Baudhāyana states clearly: "Having gathered them together, they guard them; whichever among them perishes or dies, one dedicates it with the words, 'To Vāyu, Svāhā!
Dedication (*anudeśana*) is the formal resolution (*saṃkalpa*) for the sake of the deity associated with the mantra. Regarding a cow that has died by drowning in water, he states a specific mantra:

"To Varuṇa thee!"—[this is said] for one submerged in water. "Submerged" means dead; by the act of submerging, death caused by water is indicated. Now, why is the expression "died in water" omitted and the expression "submerged in water" used? It is so that this mantra might apply even to one who has been carried away by water due to some unknown cause, lest this mantra [be restricted only to those actually dead]; rather, let this very mantra, "To Death thee," be applicable. The word "should assign" (*anudiśet*) is the ellipsis. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says: "Whether she is in the water, or in a snare, or [intended] for Varuṇa—to her [he should assign it]."
The term "anudiśati" (he assigns) is to be connected with every [subsequent clause].
Regarding the phrase "nirṛtyai tvā" (for Nirṛti, you):

it refers to one who has collapsed, or one who is so weakened as to be incapable of moving, or one who is emaciated. Baudhāyana says that this applies to her whose joints have become loose such that she is unable even to rise, or who is falling apart, or who falls into a pit; [in such a case], he should assign her with the words "nirṛtyai tvā."

With "To Rudra thee," [he offers] for one bitten by a snake; with "To the Maruts thee," for one struck by a thunderbolt or lightning; with "To Indra thee," for one killed by a ram; with "To Yama thee," for one killed by Mahādeva; and with "To Death thee," for one killed by an unknown death.

[The cow] struck by a wind accompanied by a pleasant sound and dust; "aśani" means lightning. The word "vā" is used in the sense of "api" (also), "api" (even), or to indicate disregard. A "meṣka" is a lowly creature, such as a tiger and the like. "Struck by Mahādeva" means struck by a thunderbolt (ghara). Regarding the phrase "by an unknown death," here it is by indication (lakṣaṇayā) that a certain specific disease which has become the cause of death—an unknown one—is intended. Thus says Āpastamba: "With the mantra 'To Yama thee,' [one offers for a cow] dead from an unknown consumption (yakṣman)."

According to the view of our own teacher (ācārya), the dedication (*anudeśana*) is performed with the formula, "To Yakṣman the Unconscious," or "To Death. According to the view of Āpastamba, however, it is performed with the formula, "To Yama. This is the distinction.
Having found the animal thus dedicated, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) shall not let it roam among the cows.

If the sacrificer should find it again after the dedication has been made, he must still not let it roam among the cows; the meaning is that he should not take for his own use that which was dedicated for the sake of the deity. The mention of the "sacrificer" implies that there is no fault if the animal is taken for personal use by someone other than the sacrificer.
This sūtra does not appear in all manuscripts.

In all manuscripts, there is the word "ṣaḥ. Regarding the verse beginning with "varuṇāya tvevāsu manām," [it is stated]: "yā" (1062). This Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the tenth book]—by this, the giving of it to another is also indicated.

And so Baudhāyana says: "Now, if they should find that [cow] which was lost, how should it be? It should be as if it had already been assigned; this is one view. At the conclusion of the rite, he should obtain a more excellent recipient and give her along with the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās); this is another view. Or, he should sacrifice with her to Vāyu; this is yet another. The meaning is: at the end—that is, upon the completion—of the rite, he should obtain a more excellent, that is, a superior, recipient; to him he should give her, who has not yet been formally assigned, together with the sacrificial fees.

From the use of the plural "with sacrificial fees" (*dakṣiṇābhiḥ*), it is understood that three or more individuals of the twice-born classes are to be given [the fees]. In the Kali age, because of the prohibition of cow-sacrifices, the sacrifice to Vāyu does not take place. The completion of the day occurs at the conclusion of the dismissal of the *sanīhāra* (the cloud of smoke).
If he should set out, having consigned the fires into separate sets of kindling woods (*araṇī*), he proceeds by chariot.

Now, if one should set out from here—that is, should make a journey—one places the fires upon separate kindling woods (*araṇīs*) and proceeds by means of a chariot; that is, one goes. From this injunction regarding the departure, it is understood that there is also an alternative involving consecration at home (*gṛhadīkṣā*). The procedure for the placement of the fires has already been shown previously. [Objection: For the purpose of the chariot-injunction, it should have been stated simply that "one proceeds by means of a chariot"; the phrase "having placed the fires upon separate kindling woods" need not be mentioned, since that is already established by the previously mentioned injunction for the placement of the fires.

If it is argued that the statement "having placed the fires upon separate churning-sticks (*araṇī*)" would thus be redundant, this is true; however, its purpose is not redundancy, as it serves to exclude [the performance of] the *Vāstoṣpati* oblation and other such rites. In the case of maintaining two fires permanently, or four in the case of the *Samyāvasathya* fire, or three or five in the case of maintaining the *Āhavanīya* fire permanently—one should place the fires upon two pairs of separate churning-sticks using the prescribed mantra. If the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) is present, one should also place that fire [upon the sticks] and then depart. The two churning-sticks for the *Gārhapatya* fire are consecrated (*saṃskṛta*), while those for the others are ordinary (*laukika*).

Because of the expression "separately," the re-establishment (*samāropaṇa*) occurs for each fire, using two sets of *araṇi* wood in the order of the original installation (*ādhāna*). The mention of the *araṇi* is for the purpose of excluding the mental re-establishment (*ātmasamāropaṇa*). Re-establishment is the placing of the fire into the *araṇis* by heating them; and that placement is like the grasping of the fire within oneself through mere meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), since the primary [physical] fire is not present. For each fire, there is a repetition of the mantra.

The prefix *sam-* indicates that the placing [of the fire] should be done in such a way that it reaches as far as the parts constituting the locus of the fire within the forest; it is like the heating [of the forest] extending to every part. Precisely because of this injunction for the formal placing (*samāropa*), the act of physically carrying [the fire] is excluded. The mention of a "chariot" (*ratha*) is for the purpose of excluding a cart (*śakaṭa*). The wife should perform the placing while maintaining her hold [on the husband]. Upon crossing a boundary or upon crossing a river, both must maintain their hold. Even at the time of the formal lowering (*avaropa*) [of the fire], the wife maintains her hold.

Beginning with the act of consigning [the fires] and ending with the act of depositing them, this is the primary ritual procedure (*mukhya-kalpa*). "This is your womb" is the mantra for consigning [the fires].
If a chariot is not available, [the consigning is done] together with a part of the chariot.

The word division is *avidyamāna* (not existing). In the absence of a chariot (*ratha*), one takes some part of it and proceeds with that; for the purpose of carrying all the equipment such as vessels and so forth, there are indeed other carts (*śakaṭa*). In that case, although mounting upon the cart itself would logically follow, it is precluded by the purpose [of the journey]. Alternatively, in the expression "he proceeds by means of a chariot" (*rathena prayāti*), the instrumental case in *rathena* is to be understood as being connected with the word *tena* ("with that"), and not as having the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

In this case, the journey together with the *syena* (hawk) occurs only by means of both feet. On the chariot, the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) are placed. [End of the eighth paṭala] Accompanied by the *Jyotsnā* commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa:
If he crosses waters that are navigable by boat, he places the kindling woods and the chariot on board and crosses over together with them.

If he crosses waters that are navigable by boat, he should take the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) and the chariot; having placed them in that very boat in which he himself crosses, he crosses accompanied by them. The reading "ādāya" (having taken) is indeed a corruption. In any case, one must never effect a separation from the chariot or a part of the chariot. Thus says Āpastamba: "With the two kindling woods, or with [many] kindling woods—some say so—one should not be separated from the chariot or a part of the chariot. Here, the word *araṇī* is in the accusative plural. If the waters are non-navigable, he crosses and carries them by means of the chariot.

If there are no boats by which one may cross, then one crosses and carries the fire-sticks (*araṇis*) oneself by means of a chariot alone. Even in this case, there is no breaking apart of the chariot’s parts, such as the wheels.
If he should plunge into the waters, he should do so with the mantra "O divine waters... (*devīr āpaḥ*).

If the waters on the path are such that they must be crossed on foot, then since the risk of being defiled by impurity arises at the moment of entering that water, he should perform the rites beginning with "O divine waters... and "O son of the waters... (*apāṃ napāt*) and then proceed. The mantra concludes with "I shall step forth" (*kramiṣam*).
"May I follow the unbroken thread of the earth; you are the bridge of the waters"—saying this, he crosses over by crushing a clod of earth. "Clod" (*loṣṭa*) means a lump of clay;

"crushing" (*vimṛgan*) means trampling it, that is, pulverizing it for the sake of reaching the further shore. The word *loṣṭam* is used in the singular to denote the class; thus it is implied that if other [clods] are required, others may also be taken. The crushing is for the purpose of throwing [the clod] continuously. The prefix *vi-* is intended to indicate continuous throwing. "Having made a bridge, one should stand"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"Arise from the earth" (pṛthivyāḥ saṃbhava). || 9 || He places sand or clods in the middle and on both banks, or [he places them] with the mantra "Arise from the earth.

Sand (*sikatā*) refers to clay-dust; clods (*loṣṭā*) refer to lumps of clay. He places—that is, he throws—sand or three lumps of clay in the middle part and on both banks; the meaning is that he casts them in these three locations. There is a repetition of the mantra due to the difference in location. Furthermore, when returning to the water, there is a repetition of the rites such as immersion with the mantra "O divine waters" (*devīr āpaḥ*).

And regarding this, Maradvāja states: "In the context of mantras, there is repetition when there is a plurality of substances, a plurality of purposes, or a plurality of locations—as in the cases of scratching, sleeping, crossing a river, being rained upon, and addressing a person in the midst [of a group]. However, in the view of Jaimini, there is no repetition. Accordingly, in the fourth quarter of the eleventh chapter, that sūtra states: "And likewise in the case of scratching, sleeping, crossing a river, being rained upon, and addressing a person in the midst. This sūtra has been explained.

Regarding the occasion for reciting the mantra "The mind is bound to the carriage" upon seeing something impure, there is a distinction between mantras based on whether they include or exclude the *visarga* (the final *s*). Because these rules for departing (*prayāṇadharma*) are mentioned in the section concerning the duties of the initiated (*dīkṣita*), they are not intended to apply to the departure of one who is not initiated. Baudhāyana states: "They release the fast-food (*vrata*) and bind the two calves of the two cows that provide the fast-food; whatever is to be placed [on the fire], he places it. He further says: "And having taken [the implements]... (with the variants *ja*, *ha*, *na*, *da*, *ca*).

1064. From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the tenth praśna]: Now, as he is going along, he reaches the place for the vow (*vratavelā*) after placing the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) to the north and having enclosed [the area] to the south, he undertakes the vow; he silently provides grass and water. According to the *Dvaidhasūtra*: "Now, as he is going along, he reaches the place for the vow..."

"Having churned the fire and spread it out, one should observe the vow," says Baudhāyana; "having placed the two kindling woods (araṇīs) to the north and having enclosed [the area] to the south, one should observe the vow," says Śālīki. That same [teacher] says: "Then, wherever he intends to settle, there he settles. That same [teacher] says: "Then, when he is about to perform a sacrifice, there he settles with the formula, 'We have come to this place of sacrifice on earth,' up to the end of the section."

Regarding this departure, Bharadvāja states another particularity: "He mutters daily, as he sets out, 'He purifies himself for these [waters],' 'He purifies himself towards the waters,' ending with 'He purifies himself towards the quarters.
Some prescribe the settling upon the sacrificial ground at this point."

He who would settle here should set out; he who does not [set out] from the beginning does not proceed. He who, having been initiated elsewhere, should then settle at the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), he indeed should set out. But he who sets out at the very outset, having already settled upon the sacrificial ground and being initiated there, does not set out from that point. The sense is that the purpose of the setting out is for the sake of settling at the sacrificial ground, and since that has already been accomplished.

Baudhāyana, however, permits departure for the purpose of selecting another sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) even during the consecration (*dīkṣā*), provided that security and well-being (*yogakṣema*) cannot be ensured there. Thus runs his sūtra: "Now, therefore, follows the deliberation regarding departure: either the consecrated person encounters insecurity elsewhere, or he is not yet consecrated at the [original] sacrificial ground. The meaning is that some teachers say that the selection of the sacrificial ground mentioned previously should not be performed then, but rather must be done at this time.

Since it is already established by implication that the selection of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) occurs only after the departure, this statement is intended to make known that these ritual duties of departure (*prayāṇadharma*) must be performed specifically at this selection of the sacrificial ground and not previously.
Having touched the central king-post (*sthūṇārāja*) of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, he mutters this mantra.

At this time, during the settling upon the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), this specific detail is stated by him: "the king of the pillars" (*sthūṇārāja*) means the most excellent pillar among the pillars; the word *rāja* expresses excellence. The suffix *ṭac* is applied according to the rule *rājāhaḥ-sakhibhyaṣṭac*. Because there are many pillars serving as the central support (*meḍhī*), the qualification "middlemost" is added.

The term *enam* (this) is a qualifier for the mantra, intended to demonstrate that this ritual rule does not apply to the determination of the sacrificial ground (*devayajanādhyavasāna*) performed according to the *Āgnika* section—where it will be stated that one determines the sacrificial ground with the mantra "Apeta vīta" once the duration of the initiation (*dīkṣāparimāṇa*) has been completed. The inclusion of the word *mantra*, even though the specific form of the mantra is already obtained from the context of the recitation (*japa*), is for the purpose of making known that the practitioner must perform the recitation preceded by the mental realization: "This mantra is for the purpose of determining the sacrificial ground.
One remains initiated for one night and purchases the King [Soma] on the second, third, fourth, or an indefinite number of days.

The meaning is "that which has passed. The same applies to the three-day periods and so forth. Five-day periods and those exceeding four days are to be included under the term "unlimited" (aparimita). However, the three-day, two-day, and four-day periods are the primary ones; the others are secondary. To demonstrate this, the mention by the terms "three-day," "two-day," and "four-day" refers specifically to the options of three-day, two-day, and four-day consecrations (dīkṣā). [Chapter 340] Accompanied by the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 1065. Three-day, two-day, and four-day periods. By the words "three-day," "two-day," and "four-day," the inclusion is of the options for three-day, two-day, and four-day consecrations.

The term "unlimited" (*aparimita*) refers to the other durations, such as five days and so forth. However, the twelve-day initiation (*dvādaśāha-dīkṣā*) option is superior even to the options of one, two, three, or four days of initiation. Furthermore, the unlimited initiation option should be understood as superior even to the twelve-day initiation option because of the greater intensity of austerity (*tapas*). This is the established rule.

If [the rule] were already established by the statement, "There may be one initiation, two, three, four, or an unlimited number," this specific declaration is for the purpose of demonstrating that—from the *prāyaṇīyā* offering up to the pouring of water connected with the *ātithyā*—these rites take place on the very day of the *upasad*s, and not on the day of the initiation (*dīkṣā*). He mutters these two mantras, "I am that" and "Being invoked," prior to the *prāyaṇīyā* offering, according to the sūtra: "The mantras are those containing blessings directed toward oneself. However, Āpastamba has prescribed them as a ritual salutation (*upasthāna*); thus, they may also be employed in that manner.

The mantra *ekaniṣke* is to be recited during the steps taken following the footprint of the cow for the purchase of Soma (*somakrayaṇī*), according to the sūtra *yathārūpam itaraḥ*. Furthermore, the *upahoma* offerings are restricted by their indicative marks (*liṅga*), according to the Bharadvāja-sūtra: *acchidrā upahomāś ca liṅgān niyamyante*.

"May Viṣṇu follow you, O Ekaniṣka; may Viṣṇu follow you from the *hotrās*," [the sacrificer] says while following them as they step out. According to the Āpastamba-sūtra, "at the seventh step he mutters, 'O friends, the sevenfold... may we not be separated,'" the word "pada" (step) in the locative singular case is understood here by changing the grammatical form to refer to the step being taken as they exit. By the rule, "he mutters mantras containing blessings for himself that do not have an action or an instrument," the author of the Sūtra has demonstrated that these are mantras recited by the sacrificer.

The application (*viniyoga*) of the first six [verses] is for recitation (*anuvartana*), based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) "Viṣṇus tvānv-etu. However, because the last one contains a blessing directed toward oneself (*pratyagāśīṣṭva*), according to the view of the author of the Sūtra, it is indeed a *japa* (muttering). Furthermore, since this application is not explicitly stated in the Sūtra, its performance is optional (*kṛtākṛta*).

He gives the gift (*pratta*) to the wife with the words "tava te rāyaḥ" or "tava te rāyaḥ. This Sūtra—"He gives it to the wife; she places it in the house"—has already been explained in the context of the Sūtra itself.
He sits to the south of the King while he is being purchased.

From this statement, it is understood that in other rites there is merely his presence, but no rule regarding sitting specifically to the south. This should be observed everywhere wherever such a statement occurs.
Once the Soma has been purchased, he hands the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa.

In the sūtra, "Having offered [the oblation] with the verse 'The sacrificial posts [are yours], O King, at the Āhavanīya fire,' he cuts the sacrificial post," the determination of the time is already clearly demonstrated. By this giving of the staff, the Adhvaryu's agency—which is obtained through extension (*atideśa*) from the *Nirūḍhapaśu* sacrifice—or the timing of the *Maitrāvaruṇa*'s direction (*praiṣa*), is set aside. The *Maitrāvaruṇa* receives it [the staff] with the formula: "May I, being unscathed, become scathed."

Furthermore, this giving of the staff (*daṇḍa*) does not constitute the actual employment of the staff; rather, it is primarily intended for the Maitrāvaruṇa priest by virtue of being mentioned in the dative case. The accusative case in the word "staff" (*daṇḍam*), however, denotes an object that is not desired by the agent. And since its purpose is merely to serve as a support, the act of giving is for the sake of the staff itself. Thus, Jaimini states in the second pāda of the fourth adhyāya: "The giving of the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa is [merely] incidental, because his purpose has already been fulfilled; or rather, it is a functional act (*arthakarma*) because of its connection with the agent, as in the previous case."

"And because it is seen to be connected with the ritual action (*karma-yukta*), like the throwing away (*prāsana*) of the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*). Because its purpose has been fulfilled—that is, because its function has been accomplished—meaning its utility has arisen. And that purpose is established by the injunction "he initiates him with the staff" (*daṇḍena dīkṣayati*); since that [purpose] has already occurred, the handing over of the staff to the *Maitrāvaruṇa* is merely a disposal (*pratipatti*). This is the meaning of the first sūtra.

The handing over of the staff (*daṇḍapradāna*) to the Maitrāvaruṇa is not a disposal (*pratipatti*); rather, it is a productive act (*arthakarma*), meaning an action whose purpose is visible (*dṛṣṭārtha*). He states the reason for this: "Because of its connection with the agent" (*kartṛsaṃyogāt*). This is because of the connection—that is, the relationship—between the one standing still and the recitation of the *praiṣa* (directions). Since the staff serves as a support for one who stands still while performing the recitation of the *praiṣas*, it is purely for a visible purpose, just like [the staff] previously used for the purpose of mixing (*saṃyavana*).

This giving of the staff for the sake of Maitrāvaruṇa is also the motivator of the staff; this is the meaning of the second sūtra. It is connected with the ritual action because it has the form of an objective support (*ālambana*), and because it is seen [in scripture] as being connected with that action, as in the statement: "The staff follows after the three [formulas]. "Observation" (*darśana*) means that by which something is seen or known; thus, it is observed—that is, known—through the injunctive statement (*vidhivākya*). Therefore, it becomes connected with the ritual action; this is the meaning of the third sūtra. [This occurs] either tomorrow or when the *sutyā* sacrifice is being performed.

This [act] also has the sacrificer as its agent. By the very phrase "one who is not a cutter" (avikṣuraḥ), the acceptance [of the staff] by the Maitrāvaruṇa is indicated. It is ordained by this [text] that the giving of the staff must be performed at some point prior to the time for the duties of the Maitrāvaruṇa, beginning from the commencement of the performance connected with the day of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.
With the verse "The birds, the fair-winged ones" (vayaḥ suparṇāḥ), he uncovers [his head], first the head and then the other limbs in successive order.

*Pratyaporṇate* means he uncovers. *Aya* is for the sake of indicating sequence (*krama*). *Anupūrvam* means in due order. The meaning is that those parts, beginning with the trunk (*skandha*), which were previously covered and bound together, are to be uncovered in their proper sequence. Here, by the word "head" (*śiras*), one should understand the head alone in its primary sense (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*), because it alone is suitable for being covered; it does not include the mouth, eyes, or nose even in a secondary sense (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*), because covering them is impossible and would contradict the ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*).

For it is not possible to recite the mantra or to look while the mouth and both eyes are covered; nor is it possible to cover even the nose alone because it is situated within the two eyes. Furthermore, covering the feet is not possible because it would be incompatible with walking. Thus, by the word "others" (itarāṇi), those parts other than these [mouth, eyes, and nose] are intended. Baudhāyana says: "The sacrificer, having sprinkled himself with water, gives the turban to the Kautsa or to an attendant."

Regarding the giving of the staff, a mantra is stated by Āpastamba: "He hands the consecrated's staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa [with the words], 'I give thee to Mitra and Varuṇa, the directors; may I be unharmed, unseparated, and undivided. The mantra ends with the word "bound" (*baddhān*). [Then,] with the mantra, "O Mitra, come to us, bestowing good friendship," he embraces the King (Soma) who has been placed upon his lap, as if taking hold of him.

The meaning is that the Adhvaryu priest [says], "O King, enter Indra's thigh," and thus the King is seated upon the thigh; "upagṛhīta" (embraced) means as if held against the chest. The verbal root *svaj* signifies embracing, and it is well known in the world that such an embrace occurs at the chest. The word "upasvaja" is a locative form denoting the chest. In the term "upasvana," the prefix *upa* conveys the sense of intensity (*atiśaya*). It is the chest itself that embraces with intensity. The particle *eva* (only/itself) connects immediately after the word "upasvaja."

Here too, the prefix *upa* has the sense of "properly joining. [ŚTṚ0 Paṭalaḥ] Accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 1067. Here, "joining" (*śleṣaṇa*) means grasping. Because the word *eva* is recited between the prefix and the verb, it is understood that this Vedic text itself is authoritative. This much alone is the mantra. "O Adhvaryu, have you performed [the rite]?"—this is the question directed toward the Adhvaryu.

When the Adhvaryu has given the northern [spot] with "āśaka," the question "How did he attain it? is asked again. These two questions are prescribed by the Adhvaryu-sūtra; they apply in the case of the *girī-jayaṇa* rite, and not otherwise.
He rises with "udāyuṣā.
"Amṛtā anu" is the end of the mantra.
He proceeds with the words, "The wide atmosphere. The mantra concludes with "Follow after.
Having reached the cart, he hands over the King [Soma] to the Adhvaryu.

From the statement "having reached the cart" (*śakaṭaṃ prāpya*), it is understood that the King is handed over by the Adhvaryu precisely where he remains after the black antelope skin has been spread, and not after he has come into the Adhvaryu’s own vicinity. Furthermore, having moved a short distance from the place of rising, he proceeds silently even beyond that until he reaches the cart. And the mantra "Thou art Subrahmaṇyā" (*sā'si subrahmaṇye*) is for the invocation of the Subrahmaṇyā.

And likewise Āpastamba states: "In all *subrahmaṇyā* recitations, the sacrificer, having taken hold of the *subrahmaṇyā*, mutters: 'Thou art the *subrahmaṇyā*; the earth is thy foot. Thou art the *subrahmaṇyā*; the intermediate space is thy foot. Thou art the *subrahmaṇyā*; the sky is thy foot. Thou art the *subrahmaṇyā*; the quarters are thy foot. Beyond the dust (the sun) is thy fifth foot. Do thou milk for us food, strength, splendor, sensory power, Vedic luster, and the enjoyment of nourishment.'"

The meaning is that in all instances where [the *subrahmaṇyā*] differs due to differences in time, the officiant says "O Subrahmaṇyā, Om! and the sacrificer mutters, "Thou art the Subrahmaṇyā. By the rule, "The other [the sacrificer] acts according to the form [of the mantra]," the author of the Sūtra has also stated its application (*viniyoga*). Furthermore, its status as a duty of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) is established by the *Darśapūrṇamāsa-yājamāna-sūtra*: "He mutters those mantras which contain blessings directed toward himself and which do not serve as instruments for the ritual act. Its application to the summoning of the *subrahmaṇyā* is established through indicative power (*liṅga*). With the mantra, "Homage to the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa," he gazes at the *prāgvaṃśa* hall while it is being carried forward.

He gazes directly toward the King [Soma] as he is being carried forward and brought into the *prāgvaṃśa* hall; from the word *prati*, direct orientation (*āmimukhya*) is understood. "To Sūrya, recite! is the end of the mantra.
"May the Lord of Consecration favor my consecration"—with these words, he touches the *tānūnaptra* vessel.

The prefix *sam-* signifies together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). The prefix *ava-* indicates the act of bowing down at the moment of touching. "Do not place [me]... is the end of the mantra.
In that regard, having undertaken the three vows, he consumes [the portion] provided that the Adhvaryu does not smell it.

Having undertaken the three Aupasada vows, while performing the ritual procedure, he consumes it after repeatedly dividing and setting it aside, provided there is no desire on the part of the Adhvaryu to smell it. In this alternative, there is a repetition of the mental vow for each individual vow. [In the case of] both, there is a combination. However, if there is a desire to smell it, this consumption does not take place.

Regarding this, Kātyāyana states a specific rule concerning the *tānūnaptra* ceremony: "Having covered [the vessel] with something other than earthenware, he gives it mixed with the *vrata*-milk to the initiated one in the afternoon; if there are many, to the *gṛhapati* (householder). The meaning is that, having prepared it so as to be mixed with the *vrata*-milk, he gives it to the initiated one using a non-earthenware vessel such as one made of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) or another material. Here, by the mention of the "initiated one," the wife is excluded. Since in a *sattra* all participants are initiated, and thus the giving would apply to everyone, he specifies: "if there are many, to the *gṛhapati*. He enters the intermediate initiation (*avāntaradīkṣā*) with the formula: "O Agni, lord of vows..."

"O Lord of Vows, may the vows of us two who observe them be fulfilled"—this is the end of the mantra. The term *dīkṣā* refers to those duties (*dharmāḥ*) prescribed from the time of the consecration (*dīkṣā*) up until the departure on the day of the *Prāyaṇīya* offering; their relinquishment (*visarga*) occurs at the *Avabhṛtha* bath. Within that interval, the additional duties beginning with "the girdle more tightly around me" (*saṃtarāṃ mekhalām*) are designated by the specific term *antaradīkṣā* because they arise in the middle; one "approaches" or takes them upon oneself—this is the general proposition.
He tightens the girdle more closely; he makes his fists tighter; he becomes one whose vow is heated; he performs the rites requiring water with the *madantī* waters. ||10||

The meaning is: "more closely," "more tightly," and "more firmly. This is because of Kātyāyana’s Sūtra: "Having touched the *madantī* waters, make the fist and the girdle (*mekhalā*) more firm. "Properly" means he draws them together and causes them to adhere. In the phrase "make the fists more closely" (*saṃtarā muṣṭī kuruta*), the word *saṃtarā* is used in the dual sense (*saṃtare*). By the rule *supāṃ suluk...* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), the dual case-ending is replaced by the vowel *ā*. If the reading is *saṃtarām*, it should be understood as a singular form used in the Vedic style (*chāndasa*). Alternatively, *saṃtarām* may be regarded as an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

Regarding the statement, "it belongs to one who has heated [the water]," it is understood from this injunction that among the various locations and vows, some specifically cool vow must be adopted. The meaning is that one should perform the worldly duties involving water—such as purification (*śauca*) and sipping water (*ācamana*)—using those very heated waters called *madantī*; likewise, one performs the ritual acts included within the ceremony using heated water on the *gārhapatya* fire. The intention is that the scriptural mention of "conquered by the *madantī* waters" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the injunction regarding the cleansing (*marjana*).

One protects oneself by means of the *dīkṣā*, and one protects oneself even more thoroughly by means of the *avāntaradīkṣā*. He tightens the girdle more closely; for offspring is closer to oneself than the body of one who has undergone the heat [of initiation]. Regarding the statement in the Brāhmaṇa, "He wins with the boiling waters," it should be understood that the fruit of the *avāntaradīkṣā* is the protection of the wife. "He makes his fists tighter"—this is the injunction from another recension (*śākhā*).
The washing of the hands, the swelling [of the Soma], and the concealment have already been explained.

The washing of the hands is explained and prescribed by this sūtra: "They wash their hands with the *madantī* waters. The swelling [of the Soma] is explained by this: "Saying 'aśśura aśśu,' they all cause it to swell with their hands containing gold. The *nihnavana* (concealment) is explained by this: "Having touched water while the [Soma] is being tied back, they perform the *nihnavana* over the *prastara* grass-bundle, placing their left hands downward and their right hands upward, saying 'iṣṭā rāyaḥ'. Since the touching of water is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the *nihnavana*, that [touching] also takes place.

It is appropriate to say, "when there is a desire to smell. [This concludes] the *paṭala* composed by Mopīnātha, together with the *Jyotsnā* commentary. The meaning is that one performs the vow (*vratayati*) with the mantra, "O Agni, that which is your Rudra-body," in place of the mantra, "Those gods who are born of the mind"; thus, "To that of yours, svāhā! is the end of the mantra.
On this day, the measure of the vow is that of the *dīkṣā*.

The meaning is as follows: whatever is the measure of the vow of this day—the vow connected with the day itself—is the same as that which was prescribed for the *dīkṣā* by the rule, "leaving one teat remaining"; this remains so even when it pertains to the days of the *upasad*s, because it occurs at a time prior to the commencement of the *upasad*s.
From this point onward, the ritual procedure for the vow is that of the *upasad*s.

This *upasad* is the *aupāsada*. Therefore, beginning after the evening vow (*vrata*) of this day, there occurs the ritual procedure for the vow (*vratakalpa*), the manner of the vow. From this point forward, starting from the evening vow of this day, one enters into the *aupasadavrata* by means of that very same vow-observance (*vratapati*), together with the previous mantra; such is the meaning. As for the fact that the vow of this current day is performed by means of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of another [day], even though the initiation is to occur at a later time, it becomes measured by the duration of this day; because the state of being a vow is thus declared, it is indeed the initiation itself that is the vow.

But as for the mantra, since this divine [mantra] has no fixed limit, even though one has already recited "O Agni, that which is your Rudra-like body," and "O you who are ashes," this very same mantra is prescribed for the vow.

Baudhāyana has stated quite clearly in the injunctional formula: "Tighten the girdle more closely; make the fists tighter; become firm. Having poured out the *madantī* water and having purified it, he says: "O Agni, that which is your Rudra-form (*rudriyā tanūḥ*), with that protect us; to that of yours, *svāhā*! Following this, regarding the instruction "Observe the vow from here on," he states—anticipating the question of what the mantra for the previous vow is—"That which is your [form], O Agni," and so forth. The meaning is: "The mantra for the previous vow was the *pūrvavrata*; release that. Thus, when there is an expectation as to what the mantra is, he says: "That which is your [form], O Agni," etc.

By this, the meaning is: "Starting from here, take possession of the forest. Because it is recited after the *nihavana*, this view holds that it occurs immediately following the *nihavana*. While fasting, one observes the vow for this night with the four-breasted cow; the wife also observes the vow with the four-breasted cow alone. This meaning is clear from the *Mānava-sūtra*: "On the first day, [the cow] has four teats; on the middle [day], two teats; on the last day, one teat. From the dual form "with the four-breasted," [it follows that] on the first [day]... [aupavasathya].

The meaning is that on the day of the *sadas*, the wife of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) partakes in the fast-food (*vrata*). "Four-breasted" (*catuḥ-stana*) refers to those two [vessels] which have four teats each. Kaiyaṭa states that in the context of compound formation (*vṛtti*), numerals possess a distributive sense, as in the case of *sapta-parṇa* ("seven-leaved"). Thus, the meaning is that the fast-food of the sacrificer is measured by four teats, and that of the wife is exactly this much. This sūtra is employed as an authoritative source regarding this specific matter—that the fast-food of the sacrificer and his wife is limited in this way. He now states the measurements for the fast-food of the sacrificer and his wife during the *aupasadha* days:
On this night he observes the vow with four teats; on the middle day with three teats; at night with two teats; and on the final day with one teat.

On whichever day one takes this first portion with the verse, "O Agni, that Rudrian body of yours," on that night—meaning on that very night—one should perform the *tri-stana* (three-teat) extraction on the middle *aupasadāha* (day of the Upasad rites), the *dvi-stana* (two-teat) on the night, and the *eka-stana* (one-teat) on that night; [and] the *eka-stana* on the last, the final *aupasadāha*. The middle and the last [extraction] should be understood as being prepared at dawn (*uṣas*). [From] the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[10th Praśna].

"One should undergo the intermediate initiation at the edge of the ploughshare"—thus have the optional measures of vows been explained in the Brāhmaṇa; regarding these, one may act according to one's desire.

He who desires, "May I have prosperity in this world," should undergo the *ārāgra* intermediate initiation; this is one optional measure of the vow. He who desires, "May I have prosperity in yonder world," should undergo the *parovarīyasī* intermediate initiation; this is another. First one [day], then two, then three, then four—this indeed is the *ārāgra* intermediate initiation; for him, there is prosperity in this very world. First four, then three, then two, then one—this indeed is the *parovarīyasī* intermediate initiation.

"In this very world, it becomes beneficial for him"—thus, in due order, the nature of these two is demonstrated in the Brāhmaṇa. Therein, the first is the *ārāgrā* intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*), and the second is the *parovarīyasī*. That which has a mouth as small as the tip of an awl (*ārā*)—an iron goad used for driving oxen—is called *ārāgrā*. Regarding the term *parovarīyas*, the word *para* here is intended to signify the beginning because of its excellence; that which is *varīyas* (greater) at the beginning is *parovarīyasī*.

The *ardhaka* is characterized by prosperity; this is the fruit of these two. These two measures of the *aupasada* vow connected with the initiation (*dīkṣā*) are optional (*kāmya*). "For the calf has one teat as its portion; then he undertakes the vow for one teat, then for two, then for three, then for four"—this is one form of the vow.

The name and the fruit of this [vow] are stated in the Brāhmaṇa itself: "This indeed is the vow named Kṣurapavi; by it one drives away the rivals already born and those yet to be born; moreover, by means of the lesser, one attains the greater. First he observes the vow on four teats, then on three, then on two, then on one—this is the "one" (ekam). The name and the fruit of this too are stated in the Brāhmaṇa itself: "This indeed is the vow named Sujayana; it is asceticism leading to heaven; moreover, one is truly procreated with offspring and cattle."

"Bhiriti. These two are also optional (*kāmya*). These four have been explained by the Brāhmaṇa as optional measures of the vow (*vrata*) that accomplish one's desires; they are the specific forms of the vow according to different sequences. The meaning is that one should adopt whichever measure of that vow one desires. Having gone out from the *havirdhāna* shed which has been measured out with the words "pra tad viṣṇuḥ stavate vīryāya," he worships the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths with those same mantras, in the order in which they were scattered.

"From the measured [space] to the two-measured [space]. By this *lyap*-suffix (the gerundive ending), this is made known: he should remain seated right there at the *havirdhāna* shed until this point; the abandonment of the connection with the *audumbarī* post and the *abhihoma* offering must be performed by one seated in that very place. "With the same mantras" means with those very mantras by which the *adhvaryu* performed the pouring out (*nivapana*). "As poured out" (*yathānyuptam*) means not exceeding the manner in which they were poured out; the meaning is that he worships the hearths (*dhiṣṇiyas*) and the altars (*āyatanas*) exactly as they were poured out. By this, the possibility of acting according to one's own preference (*aicchikatva*) is excluded.

Or rather, it is for the purpose of conveying the meaning that one should worship immediately after what has been scattered by the *adhvaryu*. By the mere statement "he worships" (*upatiṣṭhate*), the fact that the worship is accompanied by mantras is established, since worship is impossible without mantras. And those mantras, because they are presented within the context of the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths, are precisely those beginning with "Thou art pervasive" (*vibhūrasi*).

And thus, since the leaves beginning with "vibhūr asi" are obtained from the very meaning of the text, this statement—"some recite these very [formulas] as both upasthānas and vyāghāraṇas"—is intended to exclude the optionality of the *upasthāna* mentioned by Āpastamba. The word "eva" (only/just) is to be construed immediately after "upatiṣṭhate" (he worships). [End of Section 340, Paṭala 1071] [This text is] accompanied by the commentary Jyotsnā composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

"You are the sovereign, Kṛśānu," [with these words] he addresses the Āhavanīya fire; "You are the one who sits in the assembly, the purifying one," when they chant the Bahiṣpavamāna; "You are the swift one, possessed of the clouds," the Cātvāla pit; "You are unpolished, the maker of oblations," the animal-cooking fire (Paśuśrapaṇa); "You are the abode of Truth, the light of heaven," the Audumbarī post; "You are the light of the Brahman, the abode of heaven," the seat of the Brahman priest; "You are the goat, the one-footed," the Prājihita Gārhapatya fire; "You are the serpent, dwelling in the depths," the Śālāmukhīya fire; "You are the one belonging to the ancestors, the carrier of the offerings to the ancestors," the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.

With the formula, "Thou art the heap, all-encompassing," he addresses the rubbish-heap (utkara); with "Thou art the ocean, the bearer of all," the Sadas; with "Thou art the Sadasya, the robber," the place of the Sadasya; and the phrase "the fierce face" he attaches everywhere. || 11 ||

Thus ends the third chapter in the tenth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. [The term] *āhavanīya* refers to that situated on the northern altar (*auttaravedika*), because it is mentioned separately from the *śālāmukhīya*. Following the statement "where they chant the *bahiṣpavamāna*," the word *tam* (accusative singular, masculine) must be supplied; this is due to the constant syntactic connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tat*, and because the verb *upatiṣṭhate* (he stands near/worships) is transitive and requires an object. Since it qualifies a specific location, the word is in the accusative case and masculine gender. Now, if it is asked: why not simply say "the *āstāva*" as in "O Pavamāna, you are the one to be surrounded" (*pariṣadyo 'si pavamāna*) for the sake of brevity? It is replied that the meaning of the term *āstāva* is not established by such a usage alone.

If it is argued that this [sūtra] is redundant because the matter is already established by the Adhvaryava-sūtra stating, "where they praise with the *bahispavamāna*," that is true; however, its inclusion is purposeful for the sake of making known that there is a certain further distinction in the meaning of the word *āstāva* here compared to the meaning of the word *āstāva* as previously mentioned. For instance, in the previous case, the single object denoted by the word *āstāva* is common to all sacrifices.

In the one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*) such as the *agniṣṭoma*, [the place for the *upasthāna*] consists of the area near the *cātvāla*; in the multi-day sacrifices (*ahīna*) such as the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), it consists of the area near the *cātvāla* on the first *sautya* day, and from the second *sautya* day onwards, it consists of the *sadas*. Thus, in each case, there is only one location. However, by this word *āstāva*, which refers to the subject of the *upasthāna*, both locations—the *cātvāla* and the *sadas*—must be understood in the context of the *ahīna* rituals such as the twelve-day sacrifice, and not the *cātvāla* alone.

Otherwise, the impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the *upasthāna* rite would exist only in the vicinity of the *cātvāla* pit and not in the *sadas*; yet it is desired that the impression exist in both places. Thus, the intended distinction should be understood. Due to the difference in location, there is a repetition of the verse "asi pavamāna" for those seated in the assembly (*pariṣat*). On the first *sautya* day, the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant is performed in the vicinity of the *cātvāla* pit, whereas on the other days, it is performed in the *sadas* itself.

This matter has been demonstrated by Lāṭyāyana and Drāhyāyaṇa: "They should chant the Bahiṣpavamāna in the Sadas, except on the first day of the Ahīna sacrifice. The *cātvāla* is well-known. The place where the animal victim is cooked is the *paśuśrapaṇa*. The meaning of the word *prājihita* has been shown in the sūtra concerning the carrying around of the *vasatīvarī* waters. The mention of the *gārhapatya* fire is intended to demonstrate that the word *prājihita* refers specifically to the old *gārhapatya*.

Otherwise, there would be no resolution to the doubt as to whose this designation (*saṃjñā*) is. Thus, it is established that wherever the term *prājahita* occurs, it must be understood as referring specifically to the *purāṇagārhapatya*. The hall (*śālā*) is called the *prāgvaṃśa*; that which is situated at its mouth, i.e., its front part, is the *śālāmukhīya*. The rest is clear. The phrase "one joins the *raudramanīka* everywhere" is to be explained as before.

Thus ends the third paṭala of the tenth praśna in the *Jyotsnā* commentary, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—the son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita, who was himself the son of the illustrious Agniṣṭoma-sacrificer, performer of the thousand-fire Vājapeya, and sacrificer of the Sarvatomukha and the two-thousand-fire Pauṇḍarīka—written to alleviate the distress of learned men caused by their failure to obtain the jewels of the hidden meanings contained within the ocean of the *Śrīmad-Bhagavat-Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
10.4 Now begins the fourth chapter in the tenth book.

At the time when the Brahman priest causes the King [Soma] to enter the Havirdhāna shed, he enters the Havirdhāna by the eastern door and consecrates the King Soma, who has been placed upon the cart, with the formula: "O divine Savitṛ, this is your Soma."

"At whatever time"—that is, at that very time—the bringing [of the King Soma] occurs. "Having taken up the King, Soma goes forth, knowing the way"—with this verse addressed to Soma, having entered the *havirdhāna* shed by the western door, one should hand over the King to the *adhvaryu*. This is an illustration of what is stated in the *Brahmasūtra*. The word "nearby" (*āsannam*) is used to exclude the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the King who is not nearby. The mention of the "cart" (*śakaṭa*) is for the purpose of excluding the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).

Sitting to the north of the cart while facing east, he should perform the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*). In this case, there is no requirement to face north; for the accomplishment of the ritual act consisting of the consecration while seated to the side—provided it is done facing east in accordance with the scriptures—is established, whereas facing north would contradict the scriptures and lack justification. Here, performing the action to the left of the king constitutes a contradiction of the scriptures. "Upagā" marks the end of the mantra. He then turns clockwise, reciting: "I, a human being, [protect] human beings."

And this [offering] is not a fault, because it is impossible to avoid placing it behind the king, even to the north of the cart. "With increase of wealth" (*saha rāyaspoṣeṇa*) is the end of the mantra.
He makes a salutation with joined palms facing eastward, saying "Homage to the gods" (*namo devebhyaḥ*); facing southward, he says "Svadhā to the ancestors" (*svadhā pitṛbhyaḥ*).

[He makes] the *añjali* facing east, with its fingers pointing eastward. Because in the archetype (the *prakṛti*) it is seen that "he makes the *añjali* facing east for the gods with the front of the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles," here too the phrase "with the front for the gods" is to be supplied. By implication, this means "with the front for Soma"; and by the mantra "Svadhā to the Pitṛs," [he makes it] facing south, meaning to the right. 3 1 ka. This is the fault. [Chapter 40] Accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa.

1073. Regarding the rule *dakṣiṇād āc*, there is an infinite application. "Dakṣiṇam" means "toward the south. The phrase "he makes the *añjali*" is understood from the context. Baudhāyana says "downward" (*nyac*), which means "toward the cart" (*śakaṭānyañc*).
He steps out with the formula, "Here I [release myself] from the noose of Varuṇa";
the word "from the *havirdhāna* cart" is supplied by implication.
With the words, "May I be renowned as one of good color," he looks upon the entire sacrifice; with the words, "The light of Vaiśvānara," he gazes at the Āhavanīya fire.

Since this requirement is already established by the rule "as in the Darśapūrṇamāsa" regarding the looking at all the sacrificial fires (*sarvayajñānuvīkṣaṇa*) and the looking at the Āhavanīya fire (*āhavanīyaparekṣaṇa*), this more elaborate statement is intended to make it known that even though there is no Brāhmaṇa text for these two acts in one's own Śākhā, such a Brāhmaṇa exists clearly in another Śākhā. The purpose is the necessity of knowledge. By the word *yajña*, the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) is to be understood here; thus Āpastamba says: "He looks at the entire sacrificial ground. In that context, the meaning of *pareti* (looking beyond) is "standing right there"; thus the meaning becomes: the looking which must be performed while standing is *parekṣaṇa*.
With the mantra, "O Agni, Lord of Vows," he releases the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*).

He loosens his girdle more widely and opens his fists more widely; this means that he should abandon those intermediate duties previously undertaken in the manner about to be described. This very process is called the release of the intermediate consecration. The conclusion of the mantra is: "O Lord of Vows, according to our respective vows, [fulfill] the vows of us two who observe them. He states the procedure for that: "He loosens his girdle more widely and opens his fists more widely."

He draws the girdle together so that it becomes very loose; the meaning is that he pulls the girdle [tight] so that it becomes very loose. He makes his fists very loose. The word *vitarām* is to be explained like *saṃtarām*.
Having released his fists and his speech with the words, "Svāhā! Release the sacrifice into speech and into the wind," he thereafter moves about at ease with both hands as he pleases.

The division [of the mantra] occurs by supplying the word *iti* immediately after *svāhā yajñam*. The mantra *vāci vāte visṛja* is indeed distinct. Thus, with the first [mantra], there is the release of the fist; with the second, the release of speech. The particle *ca* serves to conjoin [the second] with the release of the fist. The mantra *svāhā yajñam* begins with *svāhā yajñaṃ manase* and ends with *vātād ārabhe*.

Āpastamba has stated such a matter as follows: "He loosens the girdle more widely; he opens his fists more widely. Regarding this, some authorities prescribe the handing over of the staff. [The student recites: "Svāhā! I take hold of the sacrifice with the mind; Svāhā! from heaven and earth; Svāhā! from the wide atmosphere; Svāhā! I take hold of the sacrifice from the wind"—with these words he loosens his fists. Or, "Svāhā! I release my speech into speech and the wind"—with this, he releases his speech. Alternatively, because of the single introductory formula, there is only one mantra: "Svāhā! I release my speech into speech and the wind."

In this view, the mantra must be repeated during the release of the two fists and the release of speech, because the substances are distinct. One releases that speech which is normally restrained during the *saṃdhyā* rites; "as one pleases" means according to one's own will. "From here onwards" means starting from this point, namely the release of the intermediate initiation (*avāntaradīkṣā*). The rest is clear. This sūtra concerns the release of the intermediate initiation. 2074.

This release of the fist is merely for the sake of meaning; immediately thereafter, another fist must be formed silently for the purpose of sustaining the sacrifice. This is stated to prevent the possibility that the other duties of the consecrated (*dīkṣita*) might be performed together with that [release].
The other duties of the consecrated continue.

In the Sūtra stating, "This conduct begins from the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [initiatory offering]," the duties beginning with "if he should speak out of negligence" and ending with "if he should speak what is unbecoming of one initiated, having released his hands and speech" are designated by the term "conduct" (*vṛtti*). That same conduct is what is referred to here by the word "other. This other conduct of the initiated continues; it is not the case that there is a release of even that conduct which began at the start of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice at the time of the intermediate release of the initiation.
He remains awake during this night.

Because this word (*etad*) is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), it refers by means of the pronoun to that night which is connected with the *anūyāja* offerings of the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya-paśu*). Therefore, the keeping of the vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) occurs on this very night, and not on the second and subsequent nights of the twelve-day sacrificial session (*dvādaśāha*) or other *ahīna* sacrifices. Otherwise, if the vigil were performed every day during the performance starting from the second *sutyā* day, there would be extreme physical exhaustion. Nor is the protection of the King impossible; for that can be accomplished through others as well.
Regarding this matter, the explanation for the sacrificer protecting the King [Soma] in the Havirdhāna shed has already been demonstrated in that very sūtra:
"From this point onward, there is no observance; rather, it is the ritual procedure for the *daikṣa* [initiation]."

The phrase "this night" follows by adapting the wording [from the previous rule]. Thus, the meaning is that on this night there is no vow (*vrata*). Beyond this point, if it has not yet occurred, then this is the place for initiation; the meaning is that this is the place related to initiation, the ritual procedure for the vow, and the manner of the vow connected to initiation. And this should be understood as applying when the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) has not taken place due to an obstacle. This applies likewise in the *ahīna* sacrifices and during the second and subsequent nights of the Soma pressing (*sutyā*). With the *saptahotr* formula, he touches the King [Soma] placed upon the pressing stones.

In the phrase "near the pressing-stones," the word "by the Adhvaryu" is to be supplied as the ellipsis, because the act of placing [the vessels] is prescribed for the Adhvaryu alone. Here, the *saptahotṛ* formula is used for the sake of the cups (*graha*), and that is the *mahāhavis*. "Ayāsya is the Udgātṛ"—this concludes the Hotṛ-mantra.
Wherever one causes the waters to enter the *havirdhāna* shed, he follows after them; whatever glory becomes inclined toward him, he attains it.

"At which [time]" (*yatra*) means at that time when he follows after those waters—that is, he enters the two *havirdhāna* sheds; this is because of the statement "he follows them" (*tā anu*), which implies entry through the eastern door. Since "where" (*yatra*) was stated previously, the word "then" (*tadā*) is to be supplied by implication. Thus, the meaning becomes: at the very time he causes the waters to enter the *havirdhāna*, at that same time he enters after them. For him, the sacrificer, glory (*yaśas*) becomes inclined toward him (*upanāmukam*).

The prefix *upa* signifies proximity; by means of that, it indicates contiguity (*nairantarya*). In the word *nāmukam*, the suffix *ukañ* is applied to the root *ṇamu* (as shown in the Dhātupāṭha sūtra "ṇamu prahṛtve śabde ca"), which here conveys the sense of being bent or directed. Due to the *nit* designation, there is vṛddhi of the first vowel. By the inclusion of the letter *ca*, the sense of being well-known (*khyāti*) is also combined. It must always be piled in such a way as not to be bent away; this is an epithet of fame (*yaśasaḥ*). [End of the fourth paṭala] Accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 1075. It must be piled so as not to be bent away, which is a qualification of fame.

The meaning is that fame becomes known continuously toward this sacrificer; that is, he attains it. The indication of the meaning as "existence" (*sattā*) is merely illustrative, because in cases such as "heaven arises from sacrifice," meanings such as "is produced" (*utpadyate*) are observed. In the present context, however, since it is joined with an accusative case-ending, it must be understood specifically in the sense of "causing to reach" (*prāpaṇa*). Although the suffix *ukañ* is not explicitly mentioned in the *Uṇādi* sūtras, nevertheless, in technical names, the verbal roots themselves and the suffixes following them [are used].

"One should infer a suffix from the grammatical operation; this is the rule regarding *uṇādi* suffixes. By the force of this rule, even though the suffix *ukañ* is not explicitly prescribed here, it can be inferred. This is indeed a scriptural text (*śruti*) belonging to another recension (*śākhā*) that is being cited here. This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) praising the act of following along (*anuprapadana*). The presentation of this explanatory passage is intended to demonstrate the necessity of knowing such explanatory passages. In the event of ignorance of them, an expiation for a corruption of the *yajus* formula must be offered into the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire with the word "Bhuvaḥ.

Furthermore, one gives twelve cows, or six-year-old heifers, or pregnant ones, as well as a garment worn at the waist (*kṛttyadhīvāsa*), to the *adhvaryu* priest; the same applies to the *evamādabhya* vessel.

The cows are those that have recently calved; the *paṣṭhauhīs* are five-year-old cows. The term "pregnant" (*garbhiṇī*) is an epithet for the *paṣṭhauhīs*. According to Āpastamba, one gives a *paṣṭhauhī* that has conceived for the first time. A leather garment (*carma-paṭa*) is intended for use as a bed or seat, obtained through a ritual act; some maintain that this must specifically be made of elephant hide. The term *aṃśu* refers to the *aṃśu-graha* vessel. Since the giving of even a Brahmin is observed in another Sūtra, the word *adhvaryu* is included here to exclude the Brahmin.

Since it is already established by the mere statement "he gives [the two] shares at the *ādāmya*," the explicit mention of the extension (*atideśa*) rule "in this manner" is for the purpose of making known that what was given as the two shares between the gift of twelve cows and the gift of a six-year-old cow should be given in the same way at the *ādāmya* as well; there is no difference in form between these two. The word "and" (*ca*) serves either to indicate mutual conjunction or to include the gold mentioned in another *sūtra*.
Once the *dhruvā* vessel has been taken up, he does not void urine until the pouring down (*āvanayana*).

Since the Smṛti prohibits the suppression of the urge to urinate with the injunction, "One should not suppress the urge to urinate," and since such suppression is unavoidable, one might argue that observing this prohibition is impossible to achieve over an extremely long period of time; and if so, for what purpose is there a prohibition of the impossible? This is true, however, because it is intended to ensure that if one urinates in the interim, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed at the conclusion of the sacrifice. That expiation consists of the *Vrātapatīṣṭi* sacrifice. By this, understand that there is no expiation for urinating during other ritual acts.
"Perform the *hiṃ* for Vasvī; chant the *prastāva* for her; may she be secured for me"—with these words, before the *bahiṣpavamāna*, he mutters the *vyāhṛtis* and the *daśahotṛ*.

These *vyāhṛtis* may be recited either individually or all together. The *daśahotṛ* begins with "Consciousness is the ladle" (*cittiḥ sruc*). It is not included [in the previous rule] because it does not serve the purpose of an oblation. The word "and" (*ca*) here serves to indicate their mutual conjunction, as no other possibility exists. He then takes hold of the chant being performed, saying:
"You are a hawk, having the *gāyatrī* metre; I take hold of you; may you bring me safely across. (12) He takes hold of the chant while it is being sung.

Aiming at the *bahiṣpavamāna* while it is being praised, he begins—that is, he touches—the *udgātṛ*s; this is indeed the touching of the *udgātṛ*s. In other words, keeping in mind that its nature consists in the touching of the *bahiṣpavamāna*, he performs the touching of the food. From the present-tense indication "while it is being praised" (*stūyamānam*), it is understood that he begins with the *udgātṛ*, the *prastotṛ*, and the *pratihartr*, who are the agents of the praise.

At the time of the recitation of each respective *bhakti*, one maintains contact with that specific *bhakti* until its conclusion. However, in the case of the *bhakti* consisting of the *nidhana*, one must necessarily maintain contact with all of them simultaneously by some means or other. For the sake of accomplishing the sacrificer’s single simultaneous contact, the hands should be joined together in one place. Since the option "or in the middle" (*uttaratra madhyamāyāṃ vā*) is mentioned later, it is understood from the inclusion of the middle *stotrīyā* as an alternative that, in the present instance, the first [verse] itself is to be taken.

"Being praised" (*stūyamānam*) is an adjective qualifying the *bahiṣpavamāna*. This mantra is named "the ascent" (*anvāroha*). Thus, the Śruti says: "He who [knows] the ascents of the *pavamānas*," and so forth. Or, it may refer to the middle *stotrīyā* verse; in that case, the word "being praised" is supplied by changing its gender, as is the word "he takes hold" (*anvārabhate*). Consequently, the syntactical connection is as follows: "At the middle *stotrīyā*, taking the *bahiṣpavamāna* as his mark, he takes hold of the breaths. Āpastamba, however, simply states: "He mutters the *anvāroha*."

With the formula, "Of that which has been praised, you are the praise," he consecrates every *stotra* as it is being praised. The connection is that he consecrates all the *stotras*, each one as it is praised. The repetition of the word "praised" (*stutaṃ stutam*) is for the purpose of terminating the scope of the term "being praised" (*stūyamāna*). If it were merely stated, "He consecrates all the *stotras* that have been praised," there might be a doubt that the consecration occurs only once after the completion of all the *stotras*; it is said thus in order to prevent that. [End of section on] *stuta*.

It will suffice merely to say that "having been praised, he consecrates the praise" (*stutaḥ stotram anumantrayate*); however, this interpretation of the statement—just like the previous interpretation of the preceding sūtra—is not for the purpose of obtaining the qualification of touching (*anvārambha*) those who are being praised. By that [interpretation], it is established here as well that "having praised, he touches all those being praised by means of the formula *stutam asi*," which was previously stated regarding the *udgātṛ*s. Furthermore, that touching is not possible in either the first or the middle [verse], because it has already been occupied by the preceding [formula].

In that context, the *anvārambha* (taking hold) is performed with the verse, "Thou art the impeller (*ina*), connected to the *pavamāna*, having the *gāyatrī* metre. Regarding the rule "in the first [verse]," this *anvārambha* is not possible in the first verse; nor is it possible in the middle verse according to the alternative view; nor is it in the other verses—meaning it is not in just any verse whatsoever. The term "being praised" refers to the *stotra* (laudatory hymn), indicated by the present participle suffix *śānac*.

In the passage "He consecrates each praise with 'Thou art praise,'" the recurrence of the phrase "of the praised, thou art praise" is established by implication alone; for since the primary purpose of the consecration (anumantraṇa) is the utterance of the mantra, no other mantra is taught here. Alternatively, it may be intended to dispel the doubt that the *pavamāna* chants might be included among the *stotras*. Regarding the formula "Thou art a recitation (*śastra*"), it applies to all recitations. The remainder of the sentence—"he consecrates each recitation"—is to be understood through contextual fitness (*yogyatā*).

Since this is not found in the manuscript of this Sūtra, it must be investigated whether this Sūtra exists or not. [Chapter 450] • Together with the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa: 1077.
One appends "indriyāvanto vanāmahe" everywhere.

The meaning is: "and in all the *śastra* recitations. Now, one might object: since there is only a single mantra for the recitation accompanying the *stotra*, it should have been stated as "in the preceding" (*pūrva*) for the sake of its application [to subsequent ones], rather than as "in all" (*sarva*), because there is no multiplicity of mantras. [We reply: Just as there is an application to the second and subsequent *stotras* following the recitation accompanying the first *stotra*, so too shall there be an application to the second and subsequent *śastra* recitations.

If it is asked, "And why is there such a statement as 'in all cases'?"—the answer is: True; because there is no pointlessness in such a statement, as it serves to indicate that the *anuṣaṅga* (supplying of a word from a previous context) applies even to the first, second, and subsequent [sections], thereby preventing the restriction [of its application] to only those [specific instances]. If it is asked, "What is the fruit of this indication?"—[the answer is: even though the *anuṣaṅga* is accepted for the *dhiṣṇya-viharaṇa* (spreading of the altars) and the *vyāghāraṇa* (sprinkling) connected with the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*), [it would not apply] to those connected with the midday libation (*mādhyaṃdinasavana*) and the third libation (*tṛtīyasavana*).

The necessity of accepting the *anuṣaṅga* (the syntactic connection of a word from a preceding sentence) arises in the cases of the *viharaṇa* (spreading out) and *vyādhāraṇa* (supporting) of the *bandhu-dhiṣṇya*. This should be understood in other instances as well. By this very principle, it is also known that where there is no explicit statement of *anuṣaṅga*, the *anuṣaṅga* may or may not be applied.
When the offering for Indra-Vāyu is being made with the mantra "Thou art the earth, the best of rays," one worships the Sun.

The term "being offered" (*hūyamāna*) refers to the present tense suffix *śānac*; thus, the worship of the Sun (*ādityopasthāna*) occurs while the oblation is being performed. The mantra "thou art a supporter" (*dharasi*) is also to be employed specifically for the cup dedicated to Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyava*), because the teacher [Baudhāyana], as well as Āpastamba and Baudhāyana, have not prescribed its application to the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa (*maitrāvaruṇagraha*). The mantra concludes with "protect my out-breath" (*apānaṃ me pāhi*). When the cup for Indra and Vāyu has been offered, one should press down the thumb: if one is competing with someone superior, one should press the finger with the thumb; if with someone inferior, [one should press the thumb with the finger].

In the passage beginning with "yo na indravāyū," since it is impossible for the *śastra* (recitation) of the Sāvitra cup to be complete without expectation [of a supplement], the subsequent portion beginning with "abhi dāsati" is supplied by implication (*ārthika*). For this very reason, it is not explicitly recited. The same applies to the passage beginning with "yo no mitrāvaruṇau. In the case of "yo no 'śvinā," however, it is indeed recited as it stands. The repetition of the mention of the Aindravāyava cup is intended to cover the section starting from "yo na indravāyū" up to "yadi pāpīyase."

This is not merely occasional (*naimittika*), for the Sūtra must be understood as ending with "yo na indravāyū" (he who [is] for Indra and Vāyu) after the offering has been made to Indra and Vāyu; then, by carrying forward from the previous Sūtra the phrase "upatiṣṭhate ādityam" (he worships the Sun), the action must be rendered complete. Thus, the worship of the Sun following the oblation, performed with the mantra "yo na indravāyū," is indeed obligatory (*nitya*); the occasional nature is merely a restriction (*avabādhanamātram*). Furthermore, this is done silently (*tūṣṇīm*) because no mantra is prescribed. This is stated in order to dispel the doubt that it might be merely occasional. "Avabādhanam" means pressing down or suppression.

The word *ava* has the sense of "bending down. By the word *yadi*, the conditional nature (*naimittikatva*) is indicated. *Śreyasā* means by something superior, such as wealth and so forth; *spardhā* means rivalry or conflict, which is to say, hatred. *Pāpīyasā* means by something inferior, such as poverty and so forth. The phrases *yo no mitrāvaruṇau* [are used] in the offering to Mitra and Varuṇa, and *yo no'śvinau* in the offering to the Aśvins. After the oblation has been offered, one should press the thumb with the finger if one is competing with someone superior, and the finger with the thumb if competing with someone inferior; this is understood to apply to both cases from the preceding sūtra.
In the manuscript of the Sūtra designated as *ḍha*, this *anuṣṭubh* verse does not exist. (Variant:
*ka* and *cha* read "everywhere" [*sarvatra*]). M 1078. From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, in the tenth book, sixth chapter:
"With the words, 'O Lord of Wealth, may we, joined with Indra, partake of your unbroken and heroic power,' he touches the *śukra* cup while it is being offered."
[He consumes] the *śukra*, the *śukra* cup.

"At which [time] he brings him the cup, at that [time] he consumes it. From the word *yatra* ("where/at which"), the word *tadā* ("then/at that") is to be supplied by implication. Thus: "At which time he brings him the cup, at that time he consumes it. *Yatra* means "at which time. *Asmai*—the dative case used in the sense of the ablative—means "from this," i.e., from the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ* call (*vaṣaṭkartṛ*). When the *camasādhvaryu* brings the cup, his own cup (*svacamasa*), into his presence for the purpose of consumption, then he consumes that cup according to the procedure beginning with the verse *mahī* and ending with *hinva me*.

"O divine Soma, belonging to the Vasu-group, knower of the mind, of the morning pressing, having the *gāyatrī* metre, drunk by Indra, full of sweetness, being invited—I, invited, partake," is the mantra for the consumption at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*). "Drunk by Narāśaṃsa, O divine Soma, knower of the mind, of the morning pressing, having the *gāyatrī* metre, drunk by the ancestors, full of sweetness, being invited—I, invited, partake," is the mantra for the consumption of the *nārāśaṃsa* cups at the morning pressing.

The ritual act of swelling (*āpyāyana*) is performed excluding the *manārāśaṃsa* cups; the consumption (*bhakṣa*) is based solely on the name [of the cup] and not otherwise. Where there is an absence of one who consumes, there the Adhvaryu performs the invitation (*upāhvāna*). The mantra for consumption at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*) is: "O Soma-deity, belonging to the troop of Rudra, knower of the mind, of the midday pressing, having the *triṣṭubh* meter, drunk by Indra, full of sweetness, being invited, I, being invited, consume thee."

"O divine Soma, of thee who art drunk by Narāśaṃsa, who knowest the mind, belonging to the midday pressing, having the Triṣṭubh metre, drunk by the Pitṛs, full of sweetness, and invited—I, being invited, partake. This is the mantra for the consumption of the Nārāśaṃsa cups at the midday pressing.
