"O divine Soma, of thee who belongest to the troop accompanied by the Ādityas, who knowest the mind, belonging to the third pressing, having the Jagatī metre, drunk by Indra, full of sweetness, and invited—I, being invited, partake. This is the mantra for the consumption [of the cups] at the third pressing.

"O divine Soma, I, being invited, partake of that which has been drunk by Narāśaṃsa, which is known by the wise, which belongs to the third libation, which has the *jagatī* meter, which has been drunk by the ancestors, which is honey-sweet, and which has been invited"—this is the mantra for consuming the *nārāśaṃsa* cup at the third libation (*tṛtīyasavana*). The meaning is that he consumes his respective own cup (*svacamasa*) in this manner. The word "cup" (*camasa*) means the Soma present within the cup; the pronoun "that" (*tat*) refers back to that very [Soma], because it is mentioned in conjunction with the act of consumption.
It is just like the other cups.
The other cups have been consumed by the Brahman and the others; the connection with the preceding [text] is that he consumes that cup in such a manner (yathā) and by that method (yena prakāreṇa).

When it is said, "O Gṛhapati, sacrifice," he issues the command, "O Hotṛ, sacrifice this," or he sacrifices himself after sitting down. By the use of the present participle in the word "ucyamāne" (being spoken), this command (*praiṣa*) occurs at the very time of that speech; or else, having sat down himself—that is, having sat down in his own place and being seated facing east—he sacrifices. "Sitting down" (*niṣadana*) means taking a seat; [this refers to] the sacrificer being seated.
In the manuscripts Ṅa, Ja, Sa, and Sa, the reading is *anvārabheta*. [Chapter 450] Together with the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa. 1079.

The explicit mention of "he should sit down" (*niṣīdet*)—despite the fact that sitting down is already established by the term "his own place" (*svāde*)—is for the purpose of conveying this specific meaning: that having performed the ritual removal (*nirasana*) with the mantra, he sits down with the mantra as well. Furthermore, those two [mantras] to be employed must be precisely those connected with the *Yājuṣa-hautra* of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), because they are related specifically to those two. For this very reason, there is the use of the *parasmaipada* ending in the word "he sacrifices" (*yajati*). Here, facing the east is established for the sake of being oriented toward the sacrifice. And the *yājyā* here consists specifically of the *ṛtu-praiṣa*.

Saying, "For the sake of light, perform [the rite]; for that, chant the Prastāva; for that, may it be secured for me," he mutters the Vyāhṛtis and the Caturhotṛ and Pañcahotṛ formulas before each of the Ājya-stotras.

The *ājya* chants are the *āvr̥t* stotras connected with the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*), by means of which the gods went toward the battle (*āji*) against the Asuras. Thus says the Chāndogya Śruti: "Because they went toward the battle (*āji*), that is the reason for the *ājya*-nature of the *ājyas*. Here, *āni* means "to the battle"; "of those *ājyas*" means among those *ājyas*, "one by one" (*ekaikam*)—that is, of each one of them. In this context, the word *ājya* is shown to refer to the stotra; thus, the construction is: "before each one of the four *ājya* stotras. These [syllables] are either the individual *vyāhṛtis* or all of them together.

Because they serve the purpose of the *ahoma* (non-offering), the *cātuḥsvarya* (fourfold intonation) is not fixed for the *agraha* and *asvāhākāra*, nor for the *cātuḥhotṛ* and *pañcahotṛ*. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include them with what precedes. Because they are recited as *japa*, the fourfold intonation is indeed obligatory.

One recites the *vyāhṛtis*, the *cātuḥhotṛ*, and the *pañcahotṛ* before the *mādhyaṃdina-pavamāna* chant, [saying]: "Perform the *hiṃ* for the *iḍā*; sing the *prastāva* for it; may it be secured for me.

If only the phrase "before the *mādhyaṃdina-pavamāna*" were stated, there would be the exclusion of the *vyāhṛtis* and the others; to prevent that, the words "the *vyāhṛtis*" and so forth are included.
"You are a Suparṇa, having the Triṣṭubh as your metre; I take hold of you; carry me safely across," with these words he takes hold of [the horse] while it is being praised. || 13 ||
Immediately after the word "being praised" (*stūyamānam*), the term "purifying" (*pavamānam*) is to be supplied by changing the grammatical case. The rest is to be understood as before.
The touching (*anvārambhaṇa*) of the *śukra* cup has been explained.

By this sūtra—"With the words 'O Lord of Wealth, of good heroism, we, united with Indra, [touch] thee who art unbroken,' he touches the *śukra* while it is being offered"—the aforementioned touching has been explained; such is the meaning.
When the *nārāśaṃsa* cups have been consumed, she stands to the south of the altar and gives the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

"Altar" here refers to the *mahāvedi*. Standing near it to the south—using the suffix *-ena* to indicate proximity—she gives the cows as the sacrificial fees. She specifies those fees as follows: twenty-seven, twenty-four, sixty, a hundred, a thousand, twelve hundred, all one's possessions, or an unlimited number.

"Twelve hundred" means one hundred plus twelve. "Veda" is a word for wealth ending in a vowel; it signifies "all one's possessions," meaning everything one owns. Regarding this, the experts in logic (Nyāyavidaḥ) maintain that [the term] consists of land, persons, and cattle. In this regard, there are two sūtras by Jaimini in the sixth chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]. [Variant readings: ṅa. ja. a. a. read "śataṃ dvādaśaśata sahasraṃ sarva-"].

In the seventh section of the tenth book of the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, it is stated: "In the gift of all one's property (*sarvasvadāna*), everything [is included] because there is no distinction; or rather, that over which one has mastery, because [giving] anything else is impossible," and also, "Land should not be given, because it is common to all. Even in the *Agniṣṭoma*, the gift of all one's property is prescribed as an optional alternative; therein, everything including father, son, and so forth, must be given because there is no distinction, and since the father is one's own, he is denoted by the word *sva* (one's own).

However, ownership exists in the same manner toward sons and others; since ownership also exists in wealth, that too must be given. Thus, because there is no distinction among these [categories], "everything is to be given"—this is the meaning of the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra. That object whose nature is ownership, which is the referent of the genitive case, and which possesses the capacity for relinquishment characterized by mastery—that object is here denoted by the word *sva* (one's own).

The meaning of the Siddhānta-sūtra is this: "And that [gift] is indeed wealth," because only wealth is fit for giving, whereas other objects are impossible to give as they cannot be transferred. Since the word "one's own" (sva) implies that even land is fit for giving, the following objection arises regarding the possibility of giving land: "Land is not to be given," because it is distinct from all other things belonging to oneself. It is not merely one's own property; for a sovereign ruler, there is no ownership of the great earth in the absolute sense, but rather a relationship with it by way of sovereignty, consisting of protecting the country, collecting taxes, and exercising governance.

Therefore, the meaning of the subsequent sūtra is that even a sovereign ruler of the great earth (*mahāpṛthivīmāṇḍalika*) would not withhold his domain. And he will state later: "that which is other than land and persons. Regarding this, Āpastamba states a specific rule: "Or, having excluded the eldest son, he gives away all his property (*sarvavedasa*). The meaning of this is: while giving away all his property, he gives a share to the eldest son and then gives the remainder. Another specific rule stated by him is: "He gives a thousand [cows] with a horse as the foremost in the case of *sarvavedasa*."

A mule born from a she-ass and a donkey is to be given in all cases; however, it is mandatory when the sacrificial fee consists of a thousand or one's entire property (*sarvavedasa*). Thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "Therefore, one who is fit for the sacrifice is fit for either the *sarvavedasa* or for a thousand. In this context, the options of a hundred, a thousand, and so forth as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) are primary, while the lower numbers such as seven and so on are secondary and intended for those who are not wealthy. For one who is capable, there is a fault in resorting to the secondary options.

And so says Bādhūla: "One who possesses ten cows sacrifices with Soma; one who possesses seven cows becomes worse off after sacrificing with Soma. According to another *sūtra*, "A constant rule in the archetype is that the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of one hundred and twelve [cows]. Also, in the *Ātharvaṇa-vaitāna-sūtra*: "One who has little property should sacrifice with one cow. "One who has little property" means one who has little wealth. Some say that having given seven cows, one should pay the price to complete the number of either one hundred, one thousand, or one hundred and twelve.

In reality, however, all seven [cows] should be given to all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) solely for the purpose of enjoyment established by an agreement regarding time. They, in turn, should avoid violence and divide them among themselves for mere enjoyment based on mutual agreements regarding time, just like the acceptance of cows connected with a sacrifice (*iṣṭi*). The same should be understood in the cases of twenty-one, twenty-four, and sixty [cows], as well as in the cases of one hundred, a thousand sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), all one's property (*sarvavedasa*), or an unlimited amount.

The justification for the division among the priests is established by its very nature. Regarding the meaning of the word *aparimita* (unlimited), one should conceive of it only to the extent that equality is achieved. From the mantra for acceptance, "May it be for my enjoyment in the moon," it follows that even the solicitation of wealth must be performed for the purpose of giving to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). A specific rule regarding this has been stated by Āpastamba: "When the *nārāśaṃsa* cups have been set down, he gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), much and unlimited.
"Much" means abundant; and "unlimited" refers to wealth whose measure is not fixed—this is the remainder of the sense.
Mash, rice, sesame, and beans, as well as gold, clothing, and a goat—these are prescribed as the offerings.

These [items] are prescribed as they can be obtained. By forming a compound in the phrase *manthaudanatilamāṣāḥ*, it is indicated that when these are given, the gift consists of all four together, not just one of them. This gift of *mantha*, rice, sesame, and beans is to be divided into a hundred parts according to its essential nature and then distributed. If possible, an equal number of gifts of gold, clothing, and other items should also be given in accordance with that division.

If that much cannot be obtained, then only what has been acquired should be given. Some say that for the sake of completing the remaining number, it should be divided by means of its value; however, it is more appropriate [to give] merely as used previously. A chariot, a garment, a horse, a man, or an elephant are "unassigned" (aniyuktāni).

The word division is *aniyuktāni*. *Anaḥ* means a cart; *rathaḥ* is well known [as a chariot]. *Adhīvāsaḥ* is a costly leather garment used for bedding and seating. *Puruṣaḥ* means a slave; this is also indicative of a female slave (*dāsī*). Here, by the hearing of the particle *vā* ("or"), the absence of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) among these items is indicated. In this context, the gift of a maiden is also prescribed for any officiating priest (*ṛtvij*); the rule in the Sūtra states: "One should bestow [the maiden] upon the priest at the sacrifice."

Eight forms of marriage are mentioned in the *Dharmasūtra*; among them, this third type of marriage is described. In a "divine" (*daiva*) marriage, when the sacrificial ritual has been spread out and the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is performing his duties, one should give the daughter to him—provided that he is not a *sapiṇḍa* relative and does not share the same *pravara* lineage. This is the meaning of the "divine" marriage.

Since the matter would be established by the mere statement that "one should bestow [the fee] upon the deity, the sacrifice, and the officiating priest," the inclusion of the word *tatra* (therein) indicates that only the great *saumika* rite is intended here, and not the minor *naiṣṭika* and *pāśuka* rites. This is because of the expression "one should bestow" (*pratipādayet*), and because of the singular form "to the priest" (*ṛtvije*), which implies bestowal upon only one person; thus, this is not the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) associated with those [minor rites]. Furthermore, this bestowal occurs after the giving of the principal sacrificial fee.

And likewise Baudhāyana says: "When the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are being led forth, one should give [the bride] at the very end. "One should give" means "one should bestow. Regarding the acceptance [of the bride], a specific mantra has been stated by that same author in the Gṛhyasūtra: "Now, if she has been given along with the sacrificial fees, one should accept her with these six verses in their respective meters, beginning with *Prajāpatiḥ striyām yaśaḥ*. The mention of her being "given along with the sacrificial fees" is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that the bestowing of the girl does not constitute a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the sacrifice.

And this mantra for receiving a gift (*pratigraha-mantra*) is not contradictory even for us. It should not be argued that there is a contradiction with the sūtra stating, "He shows [the gift] of those ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*) which are accompanied by mantras (*sāmnī*)," because this specific mantra for receiving a gift—which was not recited by the author of the sūtras within the section on the reception of ritual fees—cannot possibly be the subject of the sūtra "He shows [the gift] of those ritual fees which are accompanied by mantras," and thus there is no contradiction.

The prohibition that "one who is initiated (dīkṣita) does not give" does not apply to the giving away of a maiden included within the sacrificial context, due to the force of the scriptural injunction. However, the giving must be performed according to the prescribed rule for the complete bestowal of a maiden. As for the gift of gold and other items which constitute an ancillary part of the maiden’s bestowal, since this is enjoined by the verb "to give" (dadāti), the prohibition certainly applies to it. Furthermore, the recitation of the auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana), the formal choosing of the bridegroom (kanyāvaraṇa), the verbal betrothal (vāgdāna), and the offering of the honey-mixture (madhuparka) are all dispensed with.

The specific fruit of this particular form of marriage has also been stated by Āśvalāyana: "To the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) when the ritual is performed, one should give after having adorned [the bride]; that god purifies ten ancestors and ten descendants on both sides. This which has come down from the *Prasanna* [tradition] has been stated; let us now return to the subject at hand. Regarding the specific items [to be given], a distinction has been stated by Āpastamba: "A ram, a goat, a cow, a horse, a human, an elephant, clothing, a cart, a chariot, boiled rice, a stirred drink (*mantha*), beans, sesame seeds, rice, barley, and a donkey—these are the additional items, which are not fixed."

Regarding the *nīti*: the term "additional" (*adhika*) is stated in order to dispel any doubt that there might be an option (*vikalpa*) between these and the previously mentioned southern sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). The term "indefinite" (*aniyata*) is stated in order to dispel any doubt that there might be a mandatory combination (*samuccaya*) as if they were obligatory. These materials, as described, are given in addition to the aforementioned sacrificial gifts when one has the capacity; the sense is that by giving this many, the sacrifice becomes more meritorious. Taking gold and clarified butter while reciting, "By means of your form, I approach your form," he approaches. *Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra*, Book 10, Chapter 8.2.1082.
"He approaches those sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) facing them"; the meaning is that he goes toward those sacrificial gifts.
"May Tutha, the all-knowing, distribute you"—having stepped into the middle, he distributes them.

Having stepped into the middle, that is, having entered into their midst, he distributes them. "He should spread them out with a black antelope skin," says Āpastamba. "With the tail," says Baudhāyana. The meaning is that he spreads them out with the tail of the black antelope skin so that they may be divided into four parts.

Twelve shares each for those who perform the central rites (*madhyataḥkārī*), six each for the *ṛṣis*, four each for the third-tier priests (*tṛtīyin*), and three each for the fourth-tier priests (*pādin*). Those to whom a share belongs from the central rites are called *adhinah*. The same should be understood for the terms *dvitīyin* and *pādin*. Regarding this, Āpastamba states: "Whatever he gives to the *adhvaryu*, half of that goes to the *pratiprasthātṛ*, a third to the *neṣṭṛ*, and a fourth to the *unnetṛ*; by this very rule, the distribution to the others is declared. Thus it is for the remainder as well.

By the word "remainder" (śeṣa), the neck-tendons (*manyā*) and so forth, as well as the anus and so forth, are denoted. This [distribution] is to be understood as occurring when these [parts] exist. When a division of the anus and so forth is possible, the division is like that of a cow; when it is not possible, some say it is by way of the price (*mūlya*). Others say it is by way of the mere enjoyment (*upabhoga*). It is more reasonable [to say]: "The Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Brahman, and Udgātṛ are the central performers (*madhyataḥkārin*)."

The enumeration of these [officiants] is for the purpose of excluding the *sadasya*. If it is argued that this is already established by the forthcoming separate injunction, "to the *sadasya* according to faith" (*yathāśraddham sadasyāya*), and therefore the composition of this sūtra for the sake of excluding him is redundant—this is true; however, the sūtra "to the *sadasya* according to faith" serves a purpose by way of precluding the suspicion that there might be an excess of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

The Maitrāvaruṇa, Pratiprasthātṛ, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and Prastotṛ are the "half-sharers" (*ardhinaḥ*); the Acchāvāka, Neṣṭṛ, Āgnīdhra, and Pratihartṛ are the "third-sharers" (*tṛtīyinaḥ*); and the remaining ones are the "quarter-sharers" (*pādinaḥ*).

In response to the inquiry, "Who are those who receive the *adhibhāga*, the *tṛtīyinaḥ*, and the *pādinaḥ*?", this sūtra is provided. By the word *śeṣa* (remainder), the *grāvastut*, *unnetṛ*, *potr*, and *subrahmaṇya* are denoted. By the word *pāda*, a fourth part is denoted. He brings [the portions] as they have been divided, with the mantra: "O Agni, this is your gift, flowing with Soma. The sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are thus divided. The rest is clear. He states the purpose of bringing [them]:

He releases them toward the north, between the front of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall and the rear of the *sadas*, to the south of the *āgnīdhrīya* fire, and between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).
The purpose here is the release. "Toward the north" means facing north.
He consecrates them as they go with the formula: "Go by the path of Truth, O you whose sacrificial fee is silver."

They are going. The rest is clear. [Chapter 10] Accompanied by the *Jyotsnā* commentary composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa, [page 1083]: "May I today attain a Brāhmaṇa who is a seer (*ṛṣi*) and a descendant of seers (*ārṣeya*)," saying this, he takes the gold and the share of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā-bhāga*) and approaches the Āgnīdhra fire-shed. This mantra is for the purpose of approaching the Āgnīdhra. A seer (*ṛṣi*) is the Veda; its student is an *ārṣeya*, one who knows its meaning. According to the scriptural statement: "This Brāhmaṇa of mine is a seer and a descendant of seers, who has heard [the Vedas]."
With this very mantra, he gives gold and the portion for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the *Āgnīdhra*.

"With this very mantra" means with the mantra intended for the purpose of going toward the *Āgnīdhra*. The rest is clear. For each entry, there is a repetition of the mantra by the *Āgnīdhra*. He gazes at the *Sadas* hall with [the mantra]: "Behold the heaven; behold the intermediate space."
"By the members"—this marks the end of the mantra.
"Go among the gods, O sacrificial gift, given by us"—this is for the dakṣiṇās. "Behold"—this is carried over from the preceding sūtra. "Prepared"—this marks the end of the mantra.
Having entered the *sadas* by the eastern door, he gives the most excellent gold to the descendant of Atri (*ātreyāya*) with that same mantra which was used for the *āgnīdhra*.

An *ātreyāya* is one born of the Atri lineage. In the absence of a pure *ātreyāya*, [it may be given to] one born of the four groups belonging to him, namely Gaviṣṭhira, Vādbhūta, Kama, and Mudgala. To him he gives "most excellent gold"—that is, superior gold in comparison to other gold previously given; it is not merely superior in weight or measure. "With that same mantra" means with the very same mantra with which it was given at the *āgnīdhra*.

If that person is not available, one should give that sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to someone who is an *ārṣeya* (descendant of sages), learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*), and the son of one learned in the Vedas.

If such a person born of the Atri lineage, or one born of his four specific groups, is not available—that is, if they cannot be found—then anyone at all who is an *ārṣeya*, learned in the Vedas, and the son of one learned in the Vedas, is eligible. One who knows both the *ṛṣi* (the sage) and the meaning [of the Veda] is an *ārṣeya*. For the Śruti declares: "This Brāhmaṇa is indeed an *ṛṣi* and an *ārṣeya* who has heard [the sacred texts]. Regarding the term *anūcāna*, Bhāradvāja states: "One who does not deviate from the path is *anūcāna*."

The meaning is that one who is himself a learned Vedic scholar (*anūcāna*) and whose son is also a learned Vedic scholar, and for whom the characteristic mark exists here—namely, that he is "possessed of a father" (*pitṛmantaḥ*) and "descended from a father" (*paitṛmatyaḥ*)—to him one should give that sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) intended for the sake of Atri. Regarding this, Āpastamba states a specific rule: "In his absence, one should give it to one who is of a noble lineage (*ārṣeya*) and well-connected (*saṃhita*). The term *saṃhitaḥ* means one whose lineage is continuous through his father and so forth.

Then he assigns the portions of the sacrificial fees to the officiating priests: "O Brahman, I give this to you; with this I redeem myself," saying "I give this" to the Brahman seated on the Brahman's seat; whatever he intends to give, that he assigns to the Brahman.

"O Brahman, I give this mind to you; I redeem it with this,"—with this mantra, having given the mind itself to the Brahman seated on the Brahman’s seat, he intends (saṃkalpayati) that which he is about to give—a cow or another object—as a ransom for the mind given to the Brahman, saying "I give this" for the sake of its release from the Brahman. This is the gift to the Brahman.
In the same way, [the gift] is made to the others.
The meaning is that this is the instruction for the subsequent assignment (*anudeśa*) of the ransom.
[One says: "O Hotṛ, I give you speech; I ransom it with this," [addressing] the Hotṛ as he sits upon the Hotṛ’s seat.
"I give this to you"—in this very manner the assignment is made everywhere. And the author will state: "I give this" is to be understood everywhere.
"O Adhvaryu, I give you the breath; I redeem it with this," [he says] to the Adhvaryu seated in the Havirdhāna shed.
The same as before.
"I give you the eye, O Udgātṛ; I redeem it with this," [he says] to the Udgātṛ seated upon the Udumbara post. The same as before.
"O Hotṛ-priests, I give you hearing; I redeem that with this," [he says] to the Hotṛ-priests as they are seated according to their respective hearths within the Sadas.

By the rule "to those seated according to their *viṣṇiya* [seats]," the act of sitting within the *sadas* is already established; however, the explicit mention of "within the *sadas*" (*antaḥsadasam*) is for the purpose of indicating two alternatives: either sitting near the *viṣṇiya* seats or merely sitting within the *sadas*. This does not apply to the *āgnīdhra*, because for him there is no sitting in the *sadas* at all. The *hotrakas* are the Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, Acchāvāka, and Āgnīdhra, as indicated by the sūtra: "to those seated according to their *viṣṇiya*."

However, for the Pratiprasthātṛ and others, because they share the same designation as the primary officiant (the Adhvaryu), the mantra belonging to him is indeed theirs; yet their order should be understood from the sequence of the "half-and-a-third" quarters and the sequence of the Hotṛ-group. For example: "O Adhvaryu, I give you breath; I redeem it with this"—this is for the Pratiprasthātṛ.

"To the Udgātṛ: 'I give you your eye; I redeem it with this. To the Prastotṛ: 'I give you your speech; I redeem it with this. To the Prāvastut: 'I give you your breath; I redeem it with this. To the Unnetṛ: 'I give you your eye, O Udgātṛ; I redeem it with this. To the Subrahmaṇya: 'I give you your eye, O Udgātṛ; I redeem it with this. Finally, to the Pratihartr: 'I give you your eye, O Udgātṛ; I redeem it with this. And [he gives] to the Pratiprasthātṛ as he sits in the Havirdhāna."

By the use of the word "ca" (and), it is also for the Unnetṛ; for the Subrahmaṇya, who is seated near the Hotṛ or within the Sadas; also for the Grāvastut, who is seated near the Hotṛ or within the Sadas; and for the Prastotṛ and others, while they are seated in their respective places. Āpastamba clearly states regarding one who is unable [to go]: "He should give to the Ṛtviks seated within the Sadas, and to the Adhvaryu at the Havirdhāna shed.
Although the Neṣṭṛ is an Adhvaryu, nevertheless, because he is a Hotraka, the gift is given to him while he is seated near the Viṣṇuyaśas.

He gives according to his faith to the *sadasya*, the *camasādhvaryus*, and the *prasarpakas*. By the phrase "according to his faith," it is understood that he should give what is outside the regular sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Āpastamba makes this meaning clear: "Except for the sacrificial fees, [he gives] to the *camasādhvaryus*, the *prasarpakas*, and others. By the word "as much as" (*yāvān*), the lack of restriction regarding the quantity is also indicated. He says to the *sadasya*: "I give myself to you; I redeem myself with this," and thus presents the sacrificial fees to the *sadasya* while he is seated within the *sadas*.
"Flour! O Camasādhvaryus, I give you my limbs; I redeem them with this," [he says] to the Camasādhvaryus seated in the Havirdhāna shed.
This is clear.
"I give you the hairs of the *prasarpakas*; I redeem them with this [gift]," he says to the *prasarpakas* seated in the southern half of the *sadas* inside the *sadas*.

This is clear. Although the *sadasya* is also the seventeenth among these, nevertheless, by virtue of a specific injunction, he receives a share in the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) associated with the ritual procedure.
The phrase "I give this" is to be appended everywhere.

This statement is an instruction; likewise, it is intended to ensure that the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is accomplished through the recitation of the mantra itself, so that the resolve may indeed take effect.
One does not give out of fear;
nor does one give to an unworthy recipient even out of apprehension of danger.
He does not give to one who asks;
he does not give to one who asks and approaches him, nor to one who does not approach him; nor does he give to those belonging to the Kaṇva and Kāśyapa lineages.

Giving is prohibited for those who belong to two *gotras* and whose *pravara* is Kaṇva-Kāśyapa; giving to such a person is forbidden. The reason is stated in the *Nigama*: "One should know Kaṇva to be deaf, and one should know Kāśyapa to be one-eyed. However, in reality, this reason is questionable. Even if they possess physical deficiencies, because their power is inconceivable, the scriptural injunction itself is the sole refuge in this matter. [Gifts] are not to be given to lute-players (*vīṇā-gāthin*). They are not to be given to those who live by means of the nose or the mouth (*ghoṇā-māthā*). *Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram*, 10th Praśna, 11.137.1086.
Not to one who is not a priest (*ṛtvij*).

If someone has entered the sacrificial assembly but is not a priest, one should not give [the sacrificial fee] to him, provided he is not learned in the recitation of his own Vedic branch (*śākhā*). Āpastamba states this meaning clearly: "One should not give to a non-Brahmin, nor to a Brahmin who is unlearned; however, one may give even to a non-Brahmin who possesses knowledge. Whatever knowledge he knows, by that [gift] he acquires it. Among the members of the three higher castes, one should give to whoever possesses meaningful knowledge and not to anyone else, provided he knows the Vedic branch; by means of that sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he attains it. Therefore, the essential point is that knowledge alone is the basis for the eligibility to receive a gift.

Not to a kinsman; "kinsmen" (*jñātayaḥ*) refers to those of the same lineage (*sajātīya*) as well as relatives (*saṃbandhin*). Regarding this, Āpastamba has stated that the cause [of success] is the knowledge of the meaning along with the text—*yo ha vidyā veda tayā'varundhe*—and not merely the knowledge of the form alone; this is the distinction. Not to one who has not approached [the teacher].

One should not give [the sacrificial fee] to one who has not entered the assembly (*sadas*). The intended meaning is that one should not give it to one who, due to a lack of utility in ritual action and knowledge, is unfit to enter the *sadas*. The reason for this—that "whatever knowledge he knows, by that he attains"—has been stated by Āpastamba in every instance. "Not to one who is not a *śrotriya*. A *śrotriya* is one who has studied the Veda. This means one should not give it to one who possesses only the knowledge of music (*gāndharva*) and so forth; that is, one should not give it to one who possesses only the knowledge of music and the like, nor to one who has not studied the Veda.
Not to a non-Brahmin; the general rule is that it should be given only to a Brahmin and not to anyone else. One should give it to one who knows the Veda.

If one should give it to another caste, the meaning is that it must be to one who has studied the Veda along with its meaning. Āpastamba has stated this matter clearly: "It should not be given to a non-Brahmin, nor even to a Brahmin who is ignorant; however, one may give it to a non-Brahmin who possesses knowledge, for by means of that [gift] he acquires whatever knowledge he possesses. Regarding the specific fruit of giving to a learned descendant of ṛṣis (ārṣeya), Āpastamba says: "Whatever [gift] is given to a learned person, by that one attains the heavenly world.
If someone else should reject a gift being offered, one should give that sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to someone whom one hates.
If anyone should reject a sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) being offered—that is, if one does not desire it—one should give that rejected gift to one whom he hates; this is the meaning.
He (the recipient) would then accept it with another [attitude].

He is the recipient; the word *ha* is used in the sense of certainty. He should receive it together with another sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*). In the expression *pratigṛhṇīyāt*, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is inherent; therefore, the meaning becomes "he should cause him to accept it. This meaning is in accordance with the *Stambasūtra*. [From the Fourth Paṭala, accompanied by the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa, page 1087.]

And that Sūtra says as follows: "If another person should not desire the cow being given away, one should give it to him whom [the sacrificer] hates, along with other wealth. If [the cow] is rejected by everyone, he should either graze her together with his own cows or take her for himself, thinking, "I shall graze her separately"; having thus become inauspicious, she would surely bite [him]. Therefore, one should give her to someone whom [the sacrificer] hates. Āpastamba states this same point: "If he should cause the unexpended sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be grazed among the cows, or if he should take it back, it would drive him away like a female jackal.
Finally, he gives it to the Pratihartṛ priest or to a descendant of Atri.

One should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Pratihartṛ at the end; or to an Ātreya at the end. In the case of giving to an Ātreya at the end, the gift to the Pratihartṛ occurs in the third [round], in the fourth position.
One should not give after the recitation of the two Marutvatīya [śastras].

If the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*) for the two cups dedicated to Marutvat has been recited, then from that point on, nothing should be given; the meaning is that it must not be given by the sacrificer to anyone who arrives, even to one who is qualified [to receive it]. Nor should it be accepted by recipients. Here, "giving" is used as an elliptical expression for both giving and receiving. Āpastamba states this matter clearly: "When the verse for Marutvat has been recited, then it is neither to be given nor to be received. If one should give it, one may do so after the omentum of the *anūbandhyā* cow has been offered, or at the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice.

Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the tenth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. When the omentum (vapā) of the Anūbandhya cow has been offered, one should give [the gifts] and they should accept them. Here too, "giving" is indicative of both giving and accepting. Āpastamba states this meaning clearly: "When the omentum of the Anūbandhya has been offered, one should give and they should accept. If the option of *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) is chosen, it is after that sacrifice. Alternatively, the meaning is that one should give when the Udavasānīyā iṣṭi is completed. This refers to the option of the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation).

After the giving of all the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the *somapravāka*, an external fee should be given according to one's faith, following the giving of the fees to the *prasarpaka*s; this is because it is seen in the *Upasti-brāhmaṇa* of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*. To the *sadasya*, if there is the capacity, an external object equal to half or a fourth part of the total sacrificial fee should be given according to one's faith. Nārada says: "Even in times of misfortune, the son of the Sun (the priest) should likewise cause another to complete the rite."

"He shall take from that [gift] what has been assigned as his fee. Thus it is said. "Another" means one distinct from the other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Manu says: "If an officiating priest chosen for a sacrifice should abandon his own duty, a share corresponding to his work must indeed be given to him by the performers. (1) [Variant readings: *anū* in ka, ca, cha; *anyāyāṃ va* in ka, ca, cha, da. When the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) have been distributed, if he should abandon his own duty... [End of fragment]. *Note: This is a translation of the Sanskrit fragments provided, specifically focusing on the rules regarding the distribution of sacrificial fees and the duties of officiating priests.*

"One should receive one's share only for what has been performed and have it carried out by another. Furthermore, Manu says: "If a priest abandons a sacrificer, or if a sacrificer abandons a priest who is capable and not dissatisfied with the work, the punishment for both of them shall be one hundred [paṇas]."

Thus ends the fourth chapter of the tenth book in the *Jyotsnā* commentary, composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita—son of Tanūnaga Dīkṣita and disciple of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita—who is himself a performer of the *Agniṣṭoma*, the *Sāhasra-Agni*, the *Cājapeya*, and the *Sarvatomukha* sacrifices, as well as the *Dvi-sāhasra-Agni* and the *Pauṇḍarīka* sacrifices; a work intended to alleviate the distress of learned men caused by their failure to obtain the hidden jewels of meaning within the ocean of the *Śrīmad-Bhagavat-Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtras*.
10.5 Now begins the fifth chapter in the tenth book.

When the sacrificial fees have been led away, he releases the black antelope horn and throws it into the *caṭvāla* pit with the mantra: "The healing medicine of the fleet-footed deer, which [removes] the hereditary disease from the heads, has driven it away in all directions with its horn. He throws it with the formula: "After you the deer, the antelope, has stepped out with his four feet; may there be no snake, nor a *pṛdāku*!"

The mantra "of the deer, the swift one" (*hariṇasya raghuṣyataḥ*) is for the unfastening of the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*). Regarding the rule "when the [sacrificial] furrows have been led south, he throws the black antelope horn into the *cātvāla* pit," the recollection of this Brāhmaṇa passage is necessary to indicate that it must be performed at the time of the ritual application. In the phrase "he throws it into the *cātvāla*," the word "the black antelope horn" (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇām*) from the preceding sūtra is understood by ellipsis.
He gives a boon in the *Rathantara* [Sāman].

This is for the purpose of showing that this [gift] is performed only when the *pṛṣṭha* chant is the *syaṃtara*, and not in the case of the *bṛhat* and other chants. If Āpastamba has stated a specific rule here—"He pays homage to the ṛtvij priests"—the meaning is that he pays homage to those who have received and led away the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). It should be stated in general that he gives the choice gift (*vara*) at the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ.

If the granting of the boon had been intended generally for all the *pṛṣṭha* chants of the Hotṛ, then it would have been stated simply as "he grants a boon upon the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ. But that was not done; therefore, this is indeed for the sake of this specific purpose:

"He grants a boon during the Vāmadevya. The purpose of mentioning the Vāmadevya is similar to that of mentioning the Rathantara. "To the Udgātṛs" means to the Udgātṛ and the Prastotṛ; this is the granting of the boon. [End of Paṭala 150] accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Maṭṭa. 1089.
He gives a boon at the *niṣkevalya*;

that is, at the liturgical recitation (*śastra*) called the *niṣkevalya*. The word "at the *hotr*" is used by implication. The statement "he gives a boon again and again" is intended to make it known that even in the absence of the *rathantara-pṛṣṭha* [stotra], the giving of the boon for these two [recitations] still occurs; thus, one should not entertain the doubt that they are taught as being invariably conjoined (*saṃniyoga-śiṣṭa*).
He touches the *āditya-graha* cup while it is being offered.
This is clear.

He mutters the five vyāhṛtis and the Pañcahotṛ formula before the Ārbhava-pavamāna, saying: "For long life, perform the *hiṃ* for it; praise it; may it be secured for me. The meaning has already been explained.
"You are the earth, having the *jagatī* metre; I take hold of you; lead me safely across"—with these words, he takes hold of [the sacrificer] as he is being praised.
This too has been explained.
Where they set down their own goblet, he offers three pieces of sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) to the south.

In this context, the reading "svara-svam" and "trīn-trīn" with the repetition (*vīpsā*) in both instances is indeed merely an error; it should be understood that otherwise the formulation of that particular sūtra would be rendered purposeless. Therefore, this sūtra is properly established as referring exclusively to the actions performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

Having done that, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), and having explained the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula, he mutters the mantras of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña beginning from the giving [of the oblation] up to the end of the invocation.

The reading with the plural ending in both instances—*upāsyanti* (they worship) and *japanti* (they mutter)—is indeed merely an error, for the reason stated immediately above. Now, one might object: "Since the matter is already established by the reading containing the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) within the *Ādhvaryava-sūtra* and by the plural reading itself, the statement here is intended to indicate association with the *ṛṣis*. Therefore, this [rite] occurs separately, immediately after the offering of the *ṛtvij*-pindas;
he gives the gift (*vara*) at the *yajñāyajñiya* [stotra], or to the *udgātṛ*s during the *udgāna*."

Before the Agniṣṭoma stotra, he mutters the Vyāhṛtis and the Saptahotṛ formula. It is said "before the Agniṣṭoma stotra" because the Yajñāyajñiya is the concluding stotra of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. "Thou art Subhū, the best of rays, dear to the gods, to be accomplished; may the gods, being well-disposed, enter into thee. Thou art the brilliant one; thou art the radiant one."
In the manuscripts *ja* and *jha*, the reading is *upāntīti*.

1. In *ca*, *ja*, *sa*, and *pa*, it is *svara svaṃ*. 2. In *ca*, *ja*, *sa*, and *na*, it is *nte cīnīnpu*. 37. In *ca*, *ja*, *a*, and *pa*, it is *upāsyanti*. — *i*, *ja*, *jha*, *a*, and *sa*: *sadha*. 5. *cha*: *suno*; *ca*: *subhavo*; *ja*, *a*: *suto*; *sa*: *suvo*. 3. The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the tenth book (*daśamapraśne*)].

"You are manliness; you are the mighty one; you are the vow; you are the light; you are the wanderer; you are the Śūdra; you are the Ārya. Of that manliness of yours, of that impetuous one, of that mighty one, of that vow, of that light, of that wanderer, of that Śūdra, and of that Ārya—may I enjoy [the fruit thereof]. "Just as you, O Sūrya, are visible to all, so may I become visible to all. Having completed the Agniṣṭoma, he worships the Āditya; if [Sūrya] has already set, he worships the Āhavanīya fire with the same prayer used for the worship of Āditya. || 16 ||

By the statement "having completed the Agniṣṭoma," it is understood that whichever *ṛtusamsthā* (concluding form of the sacrifice) is performed, having completed and finished each one with the specific *sāman* prescribed for that particular *samsthā*, the worship (*upasthāna*) of the Sun must be performed immediately thereafter. If the Sun has set, one worships one's own Āhavanīya fire while maintaining the mental conception (*bhāvanā*) of it as the Sun. It should be known that this applies only where this specific injunction exists; otherwise, there is simply an omission of the Sun-worship.
The *Hāriyojana* [cup] has been explained by the Sūtra beginning with "then all [the priests] divide it equally" and ending with "for wealth, for prosperity. This has been explained and stated.
The *dadhigraha* (curd-draught).
It has been explained and stated by this sūtra: "In the Āgnīdhra shed, they consume the *dadhigrahas* with [the mantra] 'I have performed the service for Dadhikrā.
The *apsuṣoma*.

The cup named *apsuṣoma* is so called because its ritual action is performed in water. This technical term has been explained by Lāṭyāyana and Drāhyāyaṇa with the passage beginning, "The cups named *apsuṣoma* are full of water at the site of the *cātvāla*; green grass is strewn upon them," and so forth. The ritual action starting from "the remnants of the *ekadhana*" up to "they pour [the water] into the *cātvāla*" is designated by the word *apsuṣoma*.
The worship with the *minda* verse is explained and stated by the sūtra ending with, "They worship the Āhavanīya fire with the *minda* verse, 'Whatever injury has occurred to my self... etc.

The placing of wood-shavings (*śakalābhyādhāna*) has been explained and stated by the Sūtra beginning with "He places wood-shavings on the Āhavanīya fire with each mantra starting from 'For the expiation of the sin committed against the gods'" and ending with "he places the wood-shavings.
And likewise, the dismissal of the friendship (*sakhyavisarjana*).

The meaning is that this has been explained by the sūtra beginning with *ubhā kavī* and ending with *sakhyaṃ visṛjante*. The word *ca* (and) serves to include this together with the previous rites. 1. *vāraṇo'si* (in Da.); 2. *vāraṇasya* (in Ja, Ḍha); Ja, Sa, Pa read *yadāsta*; 4. *suhomaḥ* (in Ṅa, Ja, Śa, Ḍha). [150 Section] Together with the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa:
When the *samiṣṭayajus* offerings have been sacrificed, he strides the Viṣṇu-steps with the verse addressed to Jagatī: "With Agni as the god, may I conquer the armies."

By the formula "huteṣu samiṣṭayajurṣu," this indicates that all preceding ritual actions—both those pertaining to the cake-offering (*pauroḍāśika*) and those pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*)—are archetypal (*prākṛta*). These *saumika* Viṣṇu-strides, known as the *Jāgata*, are those which are stepped with the Viṣṇu-striding mantras. While stepping out, he digs up the Audumbara post with the mantra: "Bestowing support upon the mother, the supporter suckling the mother; may he bestow upon us increase of wealth, food, and vigor."

The meaning is that, for the sake of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), he causes the *audumbarī* pillar to be raised from its place while departing, as indicated by the present participle in "niṣkrāman" (*departing*), which implies that the uprooting of the *audumbarī* occurs at the very same moment as his departure.
Having untied the black antelope skin with the mantra "O Varuṇa, let go of thy wrath," he throws it into the *cātvāla* pit;
the meaning is that immediately after the uprooting of the *audumbarī*, he releases it from his own body in silence and casts it into the *cātvāla* with the mantra.

With the two verses, "Upwards that one" (*udu tyam*) and "The bright face of the gods" (*citraṃ devānām*), he worships the Āditya, provided that [the sun] has already set; otherwise, he worships the Āhavanīya fire itself with the worship of the Āditya.

This rule applies only where this specific statement occurs; it has already been stated previously that elsewhere there is simply an omission of the worship of the Āditya. The worship of the Āditya is performed with the two verses, "Upwards that Jātavedas" (*udu tyam jātavedasam*) and "The bright face of the gods has risen" (*citraṃ devānām udagāt anīkam*). The rest is clear. The procedure for entering the *nidhana* has been explained.

Together with their wives, they all perform the *nidhana* (concluding chant) of the *sāman* three times: the second *nidhana* at the middle of the site, and the third at the edge of the water; this is what is stated by these [rules] as being explained in the *Sūtra*. Regarding the *sumitriyā* purification: because of the feminine gender indication in "sumitriyā," it is understood that this mantra is to be known as a part [of the ritual]. The mantra "sumitrā na āpa oṣadhayaḥ sanvat" is the "sumitriyā. The construction is "sumitriyā mā avanantu" (may those who are well-disposed protect me). This is explained by the statement "mārjayante" (they purify themselves) with the words "sumitrā na āpaḥ"; this is what is meant by "stated."

Thinking, "Lest I be deprived of my preeminence and excellence among the senses," he unties the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), sprinkles it with water, and sets it down, provided it was not already laid down previously. By the statement, "If it was not laid down previously," the optional nature of the laying down of the black antelope skin at the *cāvāla* pit is indicated. Thus, it is understood that this setting down occurs only if it was not already laid down before. Having stepped forward together while reciting "sumitrā naḥ," they bathe without submerging themselves, with their heads together, and wash each other's backs, plunging against one another in opposite directions.

Bathing is of two kinds: that consisting of immersion and that consisting of splashing. Among these, bathing consisting of immersion is merely the washing of the body; whereas that consisting of splashing results from submerging oneself within the water. Regarding that, there is no prohibition here for bathing consisting of immersion.

By that, bathing is accomplished merely by sprinkling water on the body. Even regarding householders, he will say: "One should perform immersion in the waters including the head. Chāgaleyana and Drāhyāyaṇa have stated in this very context: "Having touched water, they should sprinkle themselves [with it]. Furthermore, according to the natural sense of the Sūtra, after prohibiting bathing in the form of immersion, it says: "The two of them dive, plunging [into the water]. As for what some say—that "without immersing themselves, they bathe while drying their clothes"—that is worthless.

This is because it contradicts the subsequent sūtra which states, "they wash each other's backs. Washing means cleansing; since it is difficult for one to do that on one's own back, this [sūtra] is intended to prescribe another as the agent, and not for the purpose of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā).

Because they have not yet been attained [by initiation], because they are already established by Smṛti texts such as "even one who does not wish to do so should wash his feet three times and himself three times," and because Bharadvāja has explicitly stated in the Sūtra, "they cause all the marks of the initiated to fall away," that even the stainless [impurity] born from the initiation into butter (navanītadīkṣā) and the like is to be purified; and also because of the indicative mark of the mantra, "the austerity [is] the releaser for the initiation into semen (śukra)," it is therefore logical that all the limbs (aṅgas) are indeed to be purified.

Regarding this, Āpastamba has stated the application of the mantra *yad id dīkṣe* as follows: "With the thought 'Whatever the seers consecrated with their mind, by which the vital breaths, the other worlds, splendor, and the senses were established—those waters which are the releasers of the bright consecration and of austerity, may they release the sense-power within me,' he should sprinkle [the water] with his ring finger on the head. The word "on the head" (*śirasi*) is understood as the ellipsis. Since it has been stated by the rule *yathārūpam itaraḥ* that even for mantras not explicitly assigned, an application must be made according to their indicative marks (*liṅga*), this application is accepted by us as well.

The meaning of this *sūtra* is that by the mere act of splashing water, one is considered bathed including the head; thus, having plunged in and immersed oneself, one is bathed together with the head. "Moving against the current" means agitating the water while moving toward the flow of the water. The rest is clear. With the mantra, "I loosen your girdle," the sacrificer unfastens his *mekhalā*.
"Bhavamṛdhe viṣepyate" means he becomes free from distress (*vinasyati*). "Devatāsu" marks the end of the mantra.
"I shall loosen this"—thus [speaking], the wife [loosens] the noose of the girdle (*yoktrapāśa*).

Although one should simply say "the wife [loosens] the girdle" (*yoktraṃ patnī*), by using the word "noose" (*pāśa*), it is established that the wife loosens the girdle which has become a loose noose.
Having washed the girdle, the girdle-string, the net, and the two garments of the consecrated, the sacrificer puts on the Soma-wrapping cloth, and the wife puts on the Soma-enclosing cloth.

Having immersed [the garment] for the purpose of cleansing, the sacrificer alone [performs this], because of his entitlement. That by which the measured Soma is bound is the *sopānahana* (Soma-binding cloth); that by which it is finally wrapped around is the *somapariśrayaṇa* (Soma-covering cloth). Because of the entitlement and because of the subsequent mention of the word "wife" (*patnī*), since the sacrificer’s participation in the former case is already established, this is intended to make known the following meaning: at the very time when the wife puts on the garment for the Soma-covering, at that same time the sacrificer also puts on the garment for the Soma-binding.
Thus, they both arise wearing their respective garments.

To the sacrificer and his wife (or wives): the meaning is that these two, wearing unwashed garments, return toward the region near the water's edge. And they are given to the Adhvaryu at the Udayanīyā offering. [Chapter 550, with the Jyotsnā commentary by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa, page 2093] 17.
Those two garments [are mentioned]; the rest is clear.
The *unnayana* (the drawing up of the Soma) has been explained.

It was explained and stated by the sūtra beginning with "O Unnetṛ, draw up more Soma" (*unnetar vasīyo na unnaya*) and ending with "he draws up [the cups] starting with those of the Hotṛ, or starting with those of the Anvāhāryapacana fire."

*Mahīyā* means *mahīpājapa* (the recitation of the *mahīpā* verses). The nominative reading alone is appropriate. It has been explained—that is, stated—in the Sūtra beginning with "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal" (*apāma somam amṛtā abhūma*) and ending with "they recite the *mahīyā*" (*mahīyāṃ japanti*). Here, by the force of the context, the application of these two verses—beginning with "We are debtless in this world" (*anṛṇā asmin*) and "We are debtless in the other" (*anṛṇāḥ parasmin*)—after the recitation of the *mahīyā*, has also been stated; that too is acceptable to us. [Then follows] the placing of the fuel-sticks (*samid-abhyādhāna*).

The meaning is that this has already been explained by the sūtra "They hold the *audumbarī* posts with the *nidhana*s" (*audumbarīḥ sanidho dhārayante*) and by the sūtra "With the mantra 'May we prosper below him,' they stand near the Āhavanīya fire kindling it" (*adho'syedhiṣīmahītyāhavanīyamabhyādadhānāstiṣṭhanti*). Furthermore, the ritual action beginning with "The noose for Varuṇa is released" (*pratiyuto varuṇāya pāśaḥ*) and ending with "Having gone to the water's edge" (*udakāntaṃ prasya yāya*) is also indicated as being connected [to the preceding] by the gerund suffix (*lyap*).

The taking up of the Unnetṛ priest as the leader, the returning without looking back, and the ritual of purification (*mārjana*) performed at the boundary stone (*parīmāṣṭhe*) are also included here because they fall within the interval.
And there is also the act of standing in attendance (*upasthāna*).
The meaning is that this has been explained and stated by the sūtra: "They worship with [the verse] 'I have followed fear...

Sitting to the west of the Śālāmukhīya fire and having taken five portions of clarified butter into the *juhū* ladle, he places a black antelope skin on his lap and offers the oblation with the mantra: "May Indra bestow upon me power, preeminence, and excellence.

The meaning is that he offers it into the Śālāmukhīya fire together with the portion taken up. Since the act is enjoined as an *āhuti* (offering), the word *svāhā* is used here. Indra is the deity, as indicated by the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra.

He causes the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) to be brought forward, or he causes it to be brought forward; in this instance, the word division is *āpayate* (causes to reach). The particle *vā* is inserted in the middle according to Pāṇini’s sūtra *vyavahitāśca*. The construction is *prāpayate vā* (or he causes it to reach). The meaning is that he causes it to be brought for the purpose of lying down, sitting, and so forth—that is, he should employ it for the sake of lying down, sitting, and the like.
Or, he performs the placing of the offering-ladle (*sruc*).

The meaning is that one should perform the fixing of the attention upon that black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). [Variants: *mahīyām*; *davātī*]. From the preceding sūtra, the word "perform" (*kuruta*) is understood to carry over: "Or, the grinding of the oblation (*havis*) [is performed] upon it. That is, one performs the grinding of the oblation upon that black antelope skin, having set aside the original black antelope skin.
By means of this very initiation, he establishes him once again;
because of the word "again," it is an initiation for one's own sake. The rest is clear.
Or rather, he should give this to his son or to a religious student (*brahmacārin*).

For the sake of initiation and so forth for a son; for the sake of providing a bed and water for a student. If it has not been cast forward previously—if it has not been cast forward previously—then at that very time these concluding rites, beginning with the oblation, are performed.
At the concluding oblation (udayanīyā), he undertakes the vow.
This is clear.

When the omentum of the Anūbandhya victim has been offered, the sacrificer has his hair and beard shaved on the southern hip of the altar within an enclosure; here he gives whatever he intends to give.

Shaving the feet at night is because of the *śrauta* [tradition]. Here, by the phrase "he gives," the gift of a cow is intended specifically as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) related to the animal sacrifice, and not as a mere gift (*vara*). By the phrase "whatever he intends to give," the lack of restriction regarding the type of substance is indicated; it may be gold or a cow. The *svaru*, the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*), and the worship of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) have already been explained.

By the word *svaru*, the action connected with the *svaru* is indicated through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). This has been explained by the *Pāśubandha-kathānamāna-sūtra*, beginning with "Like the horns of horned animals" and ending with "he worships the *svaru*. By the word *hṛdayaśūla* as well, the action connected with it is expressed. This has been explained by the *Pāśubandha-avayava-sūtra*, beginning with "they proceed with the heart-spit" and "having struck [it] without touching," and ending with "they worship with 'I have followed what was to be followed'. [The *yūpa*...]
"Desiring the post, [he offers] with the verse 'goodly strength'"; this has been explained and stated in the *Pāśubandhikayanamānasūtra*:
"He gives a pair of bulls in the *āmikṣā* offering to Mitra and Varuṇa.

Since a pair of bulls is mentioned here as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it follows from the statement "in the case of the primary *anūbandhyā* sacrifice, a pair of bulls is given," that an additional substance must be offered; thus, it is established both by the *Āpika* (the supplementary section) and by common worldly practice. The meaning of the *sūtra* is clear.
While the offering of parched flour (saktu) is being made, he worships Agni with the mantra: "This one for us through the sky...

Because of the use of the present participle "being offered" (hūyamāne), this worship takes place at that very moment while the Adhvaryu is performing the offering of parched flour. "Asat" is the end of the mantra. He worships Vāyu with "Thou, O Lord of the Sky... and Āditya with "O Increaser of the Gods... and so forth.
In the *saktuhoma*, the phrase "while being offered" (*hūyamāne*) is understood from the context. The mantra ends with "do thou" (*kṛdhi*). The final mantra ends with "well-being" (*svasti*).

At the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice, one gives either a bull (*anaḍvāham*) or a pair of oxen (*anaḍuho*), along with gold. By the expression "either a bull or a pair of oxen," there is an option regarding the number; however, the gold is to be added to both cases. The term *udavasānīyā* refers to the sacrifice performed for the purpose of departing; the meaning is "in that [sacrifice]."
Regarding the *pūrṇāhuti*, [the offering] is according to one's capacity;
by this, the lack of restriction on the material is stated.
When the *ṣoḍaśin* stotra has concluded, he gives that very horse or a mule as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). ||18||
Thus ends the fifth paṭala in the tenth praśna of the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

By the rule "that very horse," the giving of that horse for which the holding [of the reins] by the udgātṛs in front [of the sacrifice] at the time of the stotra was prescribed is made known. Or one may give as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) a mule born from a female donkey and a male horse.
10.6 Now begins the sixth chapter of the tenth book.

Regarding the rule: "Intending to accept a sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*), or having accepted it, one breathes out seventeen times"—because of the future tense in the word "intending to accept" (*pratigrahīṣyan*), the breathing out seventeen times occurs at the very beginning. By the word "having accepted" (*pratigṛhya*), it is indicated that it occurs immediately thereafter. This is the position of another Vedic school (*śākhā*). "Breathing out" (*apānanam*) means the downward movement of the breath through the lower opening.
One should go toward a cow or a horse with sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

"Sacrificial grass" means a handful of grass. The meaning is that one should approach the cow being given or the horse being given by going toward it with a handful of grass held in the mouth. The two disjunctive particles (*vā*) in the phrase "one should go toward a cow or a horse with sacrificial grass" are for the purpose of recalling the Brāhmaṇa text.
[One should go toward] a man with food.

A "person" (*puruṣa*) is one of human birth, whether a male slave or a female slave. Regarding this, Āpastamba has stated that even in the case of an elephant, the act of returning [the gift] is performed by this same [formula]; that too is acceptable to us, because the mention of "person" (*puruṣa*) is intended to include the elephant as well. [This is from] the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Saṃtyāpāḍha—[in the tenth praśna]:
"And with perfume and with a pleasant word, [he approaches] the bed."

"Perfume" (*gandha*) refers to fragrant substances such as sandalwood, garlands, and the like. "Pleasant speech" (*priyodya*) means speaking kindly. The two occurrences of the word *ca* (and) are intended to indicate that the offering of perfume and pleasant speech occur simultaneously, rather than merely being presented in succession. The word *tat* (that) is used in the treatises (*śāstra*) to refer to a woman by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The gift of a woman is [permitted] only in the Vājapeya sacrifice.

In that context, since female slaves are prescribed as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), this does not apply to a girl being given according to the *deva*-wedding rite, because she is not being given as a sacrificial fee. The evidence that the girl is not being given as a sacrificial fee is the word "present" (*pratipādayet*) found in the *Dharma-sūtra*, which states: "One should present [the fee] to the officiating priest. Now, if she were given along with the other sacrificial fees, one would accept her.

The injunction regarding the acceptance [of the gift]—namely, that "this [gift] should be given together with the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*s) according to the meters, using these six verses beginning with *yā prajāpatiḥ striyām yaśaḥ*"—as found in the Baudhāyana-sūtra, as well as the prescription of a different mantra for the acceptance, serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*). By this, it should be understood that this rule pertains specifically to the acceptance of female slaves connected to the Vājapeya sacrifice, and not to the acceptance of a bride as treated in the section on the divine marriage (*daiva-vivāha*) within the general ritual framework of the sacrifice.
Consequently, the claim made by some that this rule applies solely to the acceptance of a bride in general should be regarded as refuted.

He rises toward the sacrificial grass (barhis); for the sacrificial grass is the dear abode of the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā), and thus he becomes dear to the sacrificial gift, and the sacrificial gift comes to him.

"Carry [the offering] toward the sacrificial grass (barhis); the horse or the ox stands facing it. Regarding this, he states an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) as the underlying reason, beginning with "The sacrificial grass is the dear abode of the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*)" and ending with "therefore the sacrificial gift comes to him. The word *vai* has the sense of expressing a reason. For (*hi*), because the sacrificial grass is the dear abode—the dear place—of the sacrificial gift consisting of a cow or a horse, therefore, when that [grass] is offered, he becomes dear to the sacrificial gift consisting of a cow or a horse.

When one has attained self-restraint (*niyama*), the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) comes to this recipient; that is, the sacrificial fee—whether in the form of a cow or the form of a horse—becomes favorable. It does not mean that the cow-form of the sacrificial fee proceeds to strike him, nor that the horse proceeds to kick, strike, or bite him; such is the meaning of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). The inclusion of this explanatory passage here is for the purpose of demonstrating the necessity of knowledge (*jñāna*). Furthermore, this applies specifically to the case of the sacrificial fees consisting of cows or horses, and not otherwise.

The gods indeed caused Varuṇa to sacrifice for them. For whichever deity he brought a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), that deity was pierced by it. They said, "Let us receive [the fees] with a turning away; thus the sacrificial fee will not pierce us. They received them with a turning away, and from then on the sacrificial fee did not pierce them. He who, knowing this, receives the sacrificial fee with a turning away—the sacrificial fee does not pierce him.

For this purpose, the gods, having become the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), certainly caused Varuṇa to sacrifice—that is, they performed the sacrifice for him. That Varuṇa bestowed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) upon whichever deity, synonymous here with "divine being" (*devatā*), had become an officiating priest; he then struck that deity away from the sacrificial fee. Thereupon, the gods held a mutual deliberation;
since the word *lattā* does not exist in the Sanskrit language, it is appropriate to say "striking with the foot" (*pādaprahāra*).

[The tenth Paṭala] accompanied by the Jyotsnā commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 1097. "Having turned away, one should accept," meaning that the acceptance is performed by designating another person as the recipient; this is the "turned-away acceptance. The intended meaning is this: for whatever deity each sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā-dravya) belongs to, the acceptance of it must be performed by designating that deity through the mantras to be mentioned hereafter. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "To Agni..."

"He says, 'Gold! For gold belongs to Agni; thus he accepts it with its own deity. The meaning of the remainder is easy to understand. The recitation of this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) here serves the purpose of making knowledge necessary. He prescribes the acceptance [of the gift] after having turned away, as taught by the explanatory passage:
"Acceptance after turning away.
The method of accepting after turning away has already been explained previously.
He shows them to the southern women who play stringed instruments. || 19 ||

The meaning is that the cited Śruti passage, beginning with "The gods indeed caused Varuṇa to sacrifice with sacrificial fees consisting of the ritual procedures of the Tantras," sets aside the ordinary manner of accepting gifts and demonstrates a specific mode of acceptance. The phrase "having set aside" (vyāvṛtya) refers to the acceptance of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) which was occasioned by the opening statement "they caused [him] to sacrifice. And the intention is that the mantras are intended for that very purpose; thus he says, "of those belonging to the Tantras. He states the mantras for the acceptance:

At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I receive you. May King Varuṇa lead you, O divine Dakṣiṇā. For Agni, gold; through this may I attain immortality. May there be strength for the giver, and may there be bliss for me, the receiver. Who has given this to whom? Desire has given it to desire; desire is the giver, desire is the recipient.

O Recipient! Enter the ocean at will; with desire I accept you. O Desire, this is yours. O Desire, may Utāna Āṅgirasa accept you. For Soma, a garment: the Gnas cut it out, the Apsarases wove it, the Varutris spun it, and the Adhiyas dyed it. For Rudra, a cow; for Varuṇa, a horse; for Prajāpati, a human being; for Manu, a bed; for Tvaṣṭṛ, a goat; for Pūṣan, a sheep; for Nirṛti, a mule and a donkey; from the Himavat, an elephant; for the Gandharvas and Apsarases.

With a garland as an ornament for the Viśvedevas, grain for Vāc, food for Brahmán, rice-porridge for Aṅgiras, water for Samudra, and a chariot for Uttāna Āṅgirasa; with the verse addressed to Vaiśvānara: "Vaiśvānara has ascended the firmament as of old, to the back of heaven, being praised by those of good thoughts. Like one of old, he has generated wealth for living beings; ever-watchful, he goes around the common path," he accepts the chariot with this verse dedicated to Vaiśvānara.

Immediately after the words *vayo dātre*, the word *bhūyāt* is an additional Sūtra-text; the reading devoid of it is an alternative. The mantra for the gold ends with *gṛhṇātu*. At the end of the Sūtra-mantra, *nāstvā'kṛntannapaso'tanvata varūtraṃ vayannavadhiyaḥ... na kṣiṇāṃ dā...* (as in the text of Satyāṣāḍha), the phrase *tenāmṛtatvamaśyām* is appended. *Note: The text provided contains some scribal errors and fragments from the commentary of Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra. The translation reflects the intent of the ritual procedure.*

The application (*viniyoga*) of these mantras in the act of acceptance (*pratigraha*) is according to their indicative mark (*liṅga*). Among these as well, there is *anuṣaṅga* (supplying an ellipsis) because of similarity. In that regard, an adaptation (*ūha*) must be made according to the actual object—such as "by that," "for that," or "thus"—if a cart is given in a particular rite, then the adaptation "to Tvaṣṭṛ" or "not by name" (*anāmnā*) must be performed. However, in the case of the donkey and the mule, when they are given, the mantras are fixed; the mantra is always "the mule [is] not [by name], the donkey [is] not [by name]."

However, since ornaments are unsuitable for a wretched Gandharva, the ornamentation belongs to the Apsarases. "Grain" refers to rice, barley, and so forth. "Food" refers to that which is edible, such as honey, clarified butter, and the like, because "newly cooked rice" (*navodana*) is mentioned separately. In the case of a chariot, there is a combination with the verse dedicated to Vaiśvānara. For an inanimate object, the mantra is simply: "May Utāna Āṅgīrasa accept you."

And so says the Śruti: beginning with "Of that [gift] of the son of Aṅgiras, Uttaṇa, who accepted it while not possessing life-breath," and concluding with "If one who knows thus accepts a gift while not possessing life-breath, then the eighth sense departs from him who accepts it without knowledge," and continuing with the passage starting "Whatever here... and ending "...he accepts it by means of this very [mantra]; it does not harm him," the mantra for accepting non-living substances is prescribed: "May Uttaṇa, the son of Aṅgiras, accept you."

Regarding this, Āpastamba also says: "Having cooked [the food], he should receive all that which is not a living being while lying on his back, O son of Aṅgiras; or whatever may be without a prescribed mantra. The meaning of this is: one should receive whatever other substance there may be that is not a living being while lying on one's back; or it may be that which has no prescribed mantra; whereas for gold and the like, which do have prescribed mantras, they are to be received with those respective mantras themselves.
For all [gifts], he places the Sāvitra mantra at the beginning of each, and at the end, he appends the formula: "By this may I attain immortality. (20)

Thus ends the sixth chapter in the tenth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra. In all cases, the *sāvitra* [formula] comes first. The *sāvitra* mantra begins with "Of the god Savitṛ... and ends with "...the right hand. He bestows it; he yokes it. Following this, the mantra beginning with "By that may I attain immortality... and ending with "...may he accept" is recited at the end. [The materials are: gold for Agni, a garment for Soma, [wool] which they cut out for Nāsatyas and wove for Varuṇa.

The nine intellects asked: "To Rudra, a cow; to Varuṇa, a horse; to Prajāpati, a human; to Manu, a deer; to Tvaṣṭṛ, a goat; to Pūṣan, a sheep; and from Himavat, a mule and a donkey—these are the perpetual [sacrificial animals]."

"To the elephant [be given]; to the Gandharvas and Apsarases, garlands and ornaments; to all the gods, grain; to Speech, food; to Brahman, boiled rice; to the Ocean, water; to Uttāna Āṅgirasa, a vehicle; to Vaiśvānara, a chariot. "Vaiśvānara has ascended the firmament as of old, to the back of heaven, being praised with hymns by those of good thoughts. He, the watchful one, goes around the common path, bringing wealth to the sacrificer who offers first. These are the primary portions of mantras for receiving gifts (*pratigraha*).

Before all of these [mantras], the Sāvitra [mantra] is used. "By that may I attain immortality"—this is the subsequent addition (*anuṣaṅga*). Āpastamba has designated the portion to be added at the end as *anvādhi*, stating: "In every case, the Sāvitra is at the beginning, and the *anvādhi* is at the end. Just as in the first mantra, in the second and subsequent mantras as well, the Sāvitra mantra—beginning with *devasya tvā* and ending with *dakṣiṇaḥ*—is added at the beginning.

The meaning of "at the end, above" is that there is an *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation) of the mantra "tenāmṛtatvamaśyām" at the very top. Regarding the term *anvādhi*: it is so called because the primary portion of the *pratigraha-mantra* (the formula for receiving) is subsequently (*anu*) placed (*ādhīyate*) or applied (*yojyate*). [This concludes the section from the *Saṃhitā-paṭala* accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 1099. *Anu* means after; *mukhyaḥ pratigrahamantrāṃśaḥ* means the principal part of the receiving mantra; *ādhīyate* means is placed; *yojyate* means is joined; thus it is called *anvādhi*.

Āpastamba states the specific [mantras] for the garment: "The *apasaḥ* cut you; the *tanvaḥ* stretched you; we [wove] you as a protector"—he joins this to the end of the *vāsaḥ* [mantra], before the word *vāsaḥ*. This means that he joins this [mantra] after the *sāvitra* [mantra] and before the word *soma*. Consequently, the *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation) of "with that he touched" (*tenāpṛścat*) occurs even in our own *sūtra*. This is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); by it, the phrase "with that [he attained] immortality" (*tenāmṛtatvam*) is supplemented after the word "vigilant" (*jāgṛviḥ*).
10.7 Now begins the seventh chapter of the tenth book.

Now, in the immediately following chapter, the author will describe the optional and occasional applications of the *caturhotṛ* formulas; furthermore, regarding their study, there is a vow of observance for the *caturhotṛ* formulas which states: "One should not eat with any of the four for a full year."

Regarding the rule that "one of the four [students] eating together shall not eat for a year," this refers to the application of and study of the *Caturhotṛ* formulas; indeed, "application" (*upayoga*) is synonymous with study. Thus Āpastamba states: "One of the four shall not eat for a year; this is known as his vow (*vrata*), for one who is reciting the *Caturhotṛ* formulas. This vow is understood to apply to one who is reciting—that is, studying—the *Caturhotṛ* formulas. Regarding a specific detail here, Āpastamba says: "The form... (rūpa-pā...).

"The sacrifice for one who has not maintained the sacred fires is the *daśahotṛ*. The meaning of this is: "sacrifice" (*iṣṭi*) refers to a ritual (*yajña*). What is being stated here is that these applications of the *caturhotṛ* formulas belong to the Śrauta rites, yet they also apply to one who has not maintained the sacred fires. In that regard, for one who has maintained the fires, the offering is made in the *āhavanīya* fire; for one who has not maintained them, it is in the *aupāsana* fire. He who desires, "May I become many, may I procreate," should go to the forest and offer the *daśahotṛ* formula with either an empty or a full ladle upon a clump of *darbha* grass.

One who desires two things—thinking, "May I be pre-eminent among many in terms of wealth or knowledge," and "May many offspring be born to me and they may procreate"—should go to the forest and, having gone there, offer oblations with these two full ladles (*pūrṇapātrābhyām*): into the *āhavanīya* fire for one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), and into the *aupāsana* fire for one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). [He states another desire: *Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram*, Daśama-praśna, Chapter 10.1.100. [The text continues with the ritual details.]

He who would not succeed through offspring or cattle should put on a garment of bark, drink [only] hot water for twelve nights, and sleep on the ground. On the morning of the twelfth day, having gone out toward the east, he should breathe out and then breathe in; having explained the *Daśahotṛ* formula, he should breathe out with the words, "Go to Indra, svāhā! and then breathe in.

He who would not prevail with his cattle through affection would certainly not be a hero; here there is a conjunction of the desires for progeny and cattle. This is its preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*): a choice sword and a thick cloth. Regarding the word "heated" (*tapta*), the remainder of the sense is simply "water. Āpastamba recited this quite clearly: [the water] is indeed below the ground, not above.

Before the vow is completed, on the morning of the twelfth day, one who maintains the sacred fires should rise facing the east, go to the place of sacrifice, and perform *prāṇa* and *apāna*. *Prāṇa* is the upward movement of the breath; *apāna* is the downward movement of the breath. Then, without breathing in and abandoning speech, having explained the *Daśahotṛ* formula and recited it word by word, he should exhale while reciting the mantra "To Indra, Svāhā!"—the meaning being that he should release his breath.
One desiring a son should sacrifice to the wives of the gods for a year.
