The phrase *senendrasya* belongs to the section concerning the wives of the gods (*devānām paśnyaḥ*). One desiring a son should perform this for a year; the meaning is that one should offer oblations every day for a year with these mantras.

Between the four *yajus* formulas and the wives of the gods, one desiring a son should sacrifice for a year. If a son is not born after a year, one should disregard that and have him consecrated by means of the *caturhotṛ* formulas.

The connection of the *saṃvara-saraśan* occurs in both cases, because the desire for a son (*putrakāma*) is mentioned in both. Therefore, the four [verses] beginning with "by four" (*caturbhiḥ*) constitute distinct rites within the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*. One should offer oblations with the four [verses] beginning with "of Indra" (*senendrasya*), etc., inserting Tvaṣṭṛ between them; and at each joint (*parvan*) of the sacrifice, one should offer four [oblations] while counting the four *yajus* verses. Upon the completion of the sentences, the performance begins again from the beginning.

One who desires a son should offer oblations in this manner. The use of the word *yajati* (he sacrifices) instead of the word *juhoti* (he offers) in the formula of intention (*saṃkalpa-vākya*) is for the purpose of employing the root *yaj*. Therefore, in the formula of intention, one should employ the phrase exactly as "I shall sacrifice" (*yajeyam*), rather than "I shall offer" (*hoṣyāmi*). If, after a year, the desire for a son is not fulfilled by birth, then beyond that point, disregarding this specific rule, one should cause him to be sacrificed with the *Caturhotṛ* formulas. The performance of the sacrifice with the *Caturhotṛ* formulas is for the purpose of completing the ritual procedure.

When a king has been deposed and a battle is joined on barren ground that is open and without a roof-covering, he offers the first oblation with ghee taken in four ladlings and the *Caturhotṛ* formula, and the second oblation with the *Graha* formula; or else, having mentally recited the *Caturhotṛ*, he offers half with the first *Graha* and half with the second. Whatever they may find there shall be the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); some authorities prescribe a hundred [cows].

When a battle has commenced and is raging, like an enemy captured and surrounded, in a place where the sky is obscured by dust and even the roofs of houses are not visible—in such a location, one offers the first oblation with the *Caturhotṛ* formula and the subsequent one with the *Graha* formula. Even in the scope of this specific injunction, the word "or" (*vā*) prescribes an alternative method. In this regard, there is this much distinction: the first part of the *graha* consists of the words "O Vācaspati, with the fourth [portion] of mind, following the previous [portion], with the greatest accumulation of the voice of speech, you shall bestow what is desirable upon the sacrificer"—this is the first part of the *graha*. The subsequent part of the *graha* is that which is recited later: "Vācaspati makes the Soma flow for him; Indra drinks the Soma for the sake of power, Svāhā! Since it is enjoined that one should offer at the end of the first part, the utterance of *svāhā* must be employed there; however, it has already been recited in the latter part.

The word "half" (*ardham*) applies to both cases, with the word "of clarified butter" (*ājyasya*) understood as the remainder. Whatever wealth one may obtain there in battle, a portion of that should be taken away and given as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Some teachers say that exactly one hundred [coins] should be given; this is the meaning.
One desiring offspring should cause [the sacrifice] to be performed by means of the *Caturhotṛ* formula.

The suffix *ṇic* is used in the sense of "should cause to perform" (*yājayet*). Therefore, the meaning becomes: "one desiring offspring should sacrifice. The purpose for employing the causative suffix (*ṇi*) is as explained previously.

The ritual procedure for that [offering] is the same as that for the *khila* sacrifice, beginning with "where no roof-covering is seen" and ending with "towards the north. Regarding this, he states a specific detail:
the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a choice gift (*vara*).
The rule that "whatever [gift] they may know there, from that the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given," as some authorities recite, is set aside by this [injunction].
One desiring cattle should cause the sacrifice to be performed with the Pañcahotṛ formula; the procedure for the offering is as previously described.

With ghee taken four times, he offers the first oblation with the *pañcahotṛ* formula, and the second with the *graha* formula; or alternatively, having recited the *pañcahotṛ*, he offers half with the former *graha* and half with the latter.
The explanation is the same as before. Regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) here, he states the specific detail: for this [offering], these are the four fees—a horse, gold, a garment, and a cow.
Regarding that *pañcahotṛ* oblation, he states another method:
"One should cause a person who has rivals to sacrifice with the *saptahotṛ* [formula] by means of the *graha* and the oblation without a sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇena*).

The oblation is the *saptahotṛ* oblation. The two rules—"he offers half with the former *graha* and half with the latter"—are stated here under the names *graha* and *homa*. The term "without a sacrificial fee" is a qualification of the *saptahotṛ*. He states another method: "The high-pitched [sound] mentally... [Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, 10th Praśna, 139.1102].

If anyone should become worse off after the completion of a sacrifice, he should offer the first oblation with four ladlings of clarified butter using the *saptahotṛ* formula, and the second oblation with a *graha*.

If a sacrificer should desire that, upon the completion—meaning the conclusion—of the sacrifice, he himself should become more wretched and hateful, then [the rite] beginning with "with ghee taken four times" should be performed.
Those [rites] connected with the sacrificial ritual have been explained.

One establishing the sacred fires should place the lower fire-drill with the *daśahotr* formula. Having risen [from that], he should offer the *agnihotra* with that very same formula. When about to pour out the oblation-material, he should recite the *daśahotr*. When about to recite the *sāmidhenī* verses, he should recite the *daśahotr*. He should recite the *daśahotr* before the *sāmidhenīs*. He should recite the *daśahotr* during the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant, and the *caturhotṛ* during the midday *pavamāna* chant.

The meaning is that those [formulas] which are stated in their respective contexts by injunctions such as "the Pañcahotṛ at the Ārbhava-pavamāna," "the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ at the Pitṛyajña," and "the Saptahotṛ at the Yajñāyajñiya-stotra" have been explained within those respective contexts.

One who performs sorcery should offer the ten *caturhotṛ* formulas in a self-made salt-flat or a cleft in the ground, uttering "phaṭ" instead of "vaṣaṭ. If a learned Brāhmaṇa whose knowledge and fame are not flourishing should desire [success], he should go to the forest, tie up a bunch of *darbha* grass, seat a Brāhmaṇa to his right, and loudly recite the *caturhotṛ* formulas together with the *graha* cups, the *svāhā* calls, the *saṃbhārayajus*, the wives, and the response mantras. Or else, he may simply recite the *caturhotṛ* formulas; to that Brāhmaṇa who sits to his right, he should give a boon.
It is known from the sacred tradition: "Whatever one gives to him there, whatever fame he attains, that Varuṇa seizes."

*Amicāra* is said to be a rite intended for the slaying of an enemy. *Iriṇamukhara* is a region that is naturally so, not produced by human effort; *pradara* is a fissure in the earth. One performs the *vaṣaṭ* with "phaṭ. The reading is indeed "phaṭ" and not "vaṭ," because of the Vedic revelation (Śruti) stating, "One performs the *vaṣaṭ* with whatever is harsh in speech. The harsh utterances of speech are demonstrated in the Āraṇyaka Śruti as: "khaṭ-phaṭ, kill, cut, pierce, strike, kaṭ"—these are the harsh utterances of speech.

The word *phaṭ* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all harsh sounds of speech. The meaning is that one performs the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance with any one of these, and offers the oblation (*juhoti*) in place of the *svāhā*-utterance with any sound such as *khaḍ*. Āpastamba states this meaning clearly: "With whatever is harsh in speech, he utters *vaṣaṭ*; by means of the very harshness of speech, he cuts him down; it is known that he meets with immediate destruction. Because of the mention of the *brāhmaṇa*, this rule does not apply to the *kṣatriya* and *vaiśya*. *Vidyā* means the Veda. *Yaśas* means the renown of being a learned scholar (*śrotriya*).

The meaning is that these two do not reach or attain the one who knows. That knower, having risen and tied a darbha-bundle to his right side, having seated any brahmin there, recites loudly; by this, the requirement of whispering (*upāṃśu*) obtained from the *yajurveda* is set aside. Here, because of the injunction "loudly" (*uccaiḥ*), this does not apply elsewhere. He should explain—the *caturhotṛ*, *daśahotṛ*, *saptahotṛ*, *ṣaḍḍhotṛ*, *pañcahotṛ*, and *caturhotṛ* formulas—reciting them word by word.

"Preceders of Soma," "O Lord of Speech, by the power of speech," "O Lord of Speech, with unbroken speech," "O Lord of Speech, whose name is heart-knower"—these and similar [formulas] are accompanied by those cups (*graha*). In the commentary, because the utterance of *svāhā* was not obtained [in the original], it says "together with *svāhā*" (*sasvāhākārān*). By the phrase "with the *agniyajus* formulas," the mantras contained in that section of the *Anuvāka* are intended; [the offering] is accompanied by those. By the section of the *Anuvāka* beginning "The army of Indra," the wives are intended; [the offering] is accompanied by those. By the section of the *Anuvāka* beginning "Of the god," the mantras known as "receptions" (*pratigrahaṇa*) are intended; [the offering] is accompanied by those.

The mantras for receiving the gifts (*pratigrahaṇa-mantra*) should be understood as including their continuations (*sānuṣaṅga*). Alternatively, the meaning is that these are not the *grahastotra*, *āhāva*, *saṃbhārayajus*, *patnī-pratigrahaṇa*, or mantras [of the Caturhotṛ formulas]. To the Brāhmaṇa who sits on the south side, one should give the *vara* (the choice); a four-year-old cow is the *vara*. Whatever glory (*yaśas*) reaches him there—whatever desired glory he seeks—that glory Varuṇa gives; such is the meaning. "It is known from Śruti" is the remainder of the sentence.

If they should expel him while he has been chosen for the office of the *ṛtvij*, he should offer the *daśahotṛ* formula in the *āgnīdhra* fire with clarified butter taken four times; according to some, with butter taken nine times. Standing in front, facing west, and reciting it backwards, word by word, he causes his very vital breaths (*prāṇa*) to perish. If they should restore him, he should offer the *daśahotṛ* formula in the *āgnīdhra* fire with clarified butter taken four times; according to some, with butter taken nine times. Sitting behind, facing east, and reciting it forwards, without breaking the flow, he restores his vital breaths to him.

If those acting on behalf of the sacrificer should dismiss this man from his office as *āvijya* while he is still free from fault, then he, desiring to strike back at them, should offer the *daśahotṛ* formula into the *āgnīdhra* fire. He should begin from the end and recite the *yajus* formulas in reverse order (*pratiloma*), pronouncing the syllables without elision (*anudravaṇa*). He should pause at each *yajus* and pronounce the syllables with distinct separation (*vigrāha*). "Cutting off" (*upadāsa*) means expulsion; "instruction" (*upaśikṣaṇa*) means reinstating him in the office of *āvijya*. In this way, the *daśahotṛ* becomes recited in the natural order (*anuloma*) and without separation. Alternatively, for the sake of expiation, one should offer the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula at the beginning of each season, saying, "Speech is the *hotṛ*."

By the word *prāyaścitta*, purification (*śuddhi*) is indicated here. A person desiring purification should recite the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula at the beginning of each season; by virtue of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), this applies for as long as a year. He who desires, "May I become more abundant than many," should employ the *daśahotṛ* formula. Being more abundant than many—meaning more abundant than many [beings] such as progeny and cattle—he should employ it, that is, he should offer it. Here, "employment" refers specifically to the oblation (*homa*) with clarified butter (*ājya*) using the *caturhotṛ* formula.
He who should desire, "May a hero be born to me," he [should employ] the Caturhotṛ;
a hero is a virtuous son.
He who should desire, "May I be possessed of cattle," he [should employ] the Pañcahotṛ.
"Domestic animals" refers to cows, horses, and so forth. (Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, 10th Praśna, 1104):
"He who should desire, 'May the seasons be favorable to me,' he [should employ] the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula.
The meaning is: 'May the seasons come to me as auspicious, each nourishing its own respective quality.'"
He who desires, "May I be a drinker of Soma and a performer of the Soma sacrifice; may one who drinks Soma and performs the Soma sacrifice be born to me," [should employ] the *saptahotṛ* formula.

Regarding the phrase "may he be born as a performer of the Soma sacrifice," the suffix is used in the sense of the future (*bhaviṣyad-artha*) while retaining the form of the past tense (*bhūtavat-pratyaya*), according to the rule that "suffixes [can denote] a connection with the root [in various tenses]. The separate mention of "drinker of Soma" (*somapa*) is because drinking Soma is for the benefit of the person (*puruṣārtha*), even though it occurs within the context of the Soma sacrifice itself. For this very reason, it is stated in the scriptures: "Those two indeed grant him the drinking of Soma (*somapītha*)," and "he is worthy to drink the Soma," and so forth.

He who should desire, "May I be beloved," or for whomsoever he should desire, "May he be beloved," for him he should fashion this Sthāgara ornament; having adorned its mouth with the Daśahotṛ on the south, the Pañcahotṛ behind, the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ on the north, and the Saptahotṛ above, and with the *saṃbhāras* and the wives, he should go half-way with it, and he indeed becomes beloved.

If one should think, "May I be dear to another," or if one should desire of another person, "May he be dear to me," for him [the officiant], having placed this ornament made with the substance called *sthāgara*—intended for anointing and so forth—in front of him, and standing facing him in the eastern and other directions, having recited the *Daśahotṛ* and other formulas word by word, and having performed the consecration according to such a procedure, [he should perform it] with those materials (*saṃbhāra*) consisting of the consecrated fires.

Having performed the rites with the mantras designated as *saṃbhāra* and having adorned his face with the forms of *puṇḍraka* and other ornaments using the mantras designated as *patnī*, he should go to the place of the woman he desires to subjugate. Whether it be himself or another who is desired by another, once he has gone to that place, he becomes beloved. The word *uha* is used in the sense of certainty (*niścaya*).

Among those [mantras], those heard for the purpose of *homa* should be employed together with the *graha* vessels and the *svāhā*-utterance; however, those intended for non-*homa* purposes are without *graha* vessels and without the *svāhā*-utterance.

Now, the author of the Sūtra himself provides a general explanation of the Caturhotṛ formulas concerning both the subject matter at hand and that which is not. Among those Caturhotṛs, those four which are heard in the context of the *caturhotṛ* offerings—being prescribed for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*) along with the exclamation *svāhā*—should be employed there. Those which are heard for the purpose of the *graha* (libation cups) should be used without the *svāhā* call; that is, they are devoid of the *graha* and lack the *svāhā* call. They should be employed in that context.

Although it is established that [the formulas] lack the *svāhākāra* because they are intended for the *ahoma* (non-oblation), this statement is made so that one might not suspect that—even though the *svāhākāra* is recited at the end of the mantras during their application in the *cāturhotrīya-upadhāna* and also during the *cāturhotra-cayana*—the *svāhākāra* is nonetheless primarily intended for the four *hotṛ*s.
Furthermore, those [formulas] which are *japa*s and those which are *yājamāna* [rites] are also connected with the sacrifice (*kratu*).

Regarding the *japas*: those *japas* belonging to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) are to be employed by the sacrificer; thus, there is a distinction between *japas* that are to be employed by the Adhvaryu and others, and those to be employed by the sacrificer. However, for those *japas* belonging to the sacrificer, there is only the property of being employed by the sacrificer. To demonstrate this difference in ritual characteristics (*dharma*), two instances of the word "which" (*yat*) are used. [Note: Variants exist in the reading and manuscripts.

Those [rites] of one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) belong to both [the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer], provided they are not connected with a specific sacrifice (*akratu-saṃyukta*). 22.
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the tenth book in the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra*.

Among those four [sets of formulas], those connected with sacrificial rites (*vihāra*) belong to one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), as in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices where one undertakes them, such as the *caturhotṛ* formulas and others. However, those not connected with sacrificial rites—such as the *daśahotṛ* and others, found in passages like "He who desires, 'May I procreate'" and "The learned Brāhmaṇa whom one knows as glory"—belong to both the one who has established the fires and the one who has not. For one who has established the fires, the oblation is performed either in the *āhavanīya* fire or in the *aupāsana* fire, according to the specific rule of the ritual.

For one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), all [rites] are performed in the *aupāsana* fire alone. Āpastamba has stated another specific rule: "One should also officiate for one who has failed in a sacrifice (*yajñavibhraṣṭa*) by means of the *saptahotṛ* formula, using either four portions of clarified butter or the first cup, with half [the portion] in the latter [cup]. In that regard, he will explain the "one who has failed in a sacrifice" in the *Vidhyaparādhaprashna*: "One who, having commenced [a rite], is unable [to complete it] is one who has failed in a sacrifice. Among these, for one who has failed in an *iṣṭi* or animal sacrifice, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is indeed another *iṣṭi*, according to the rule: "He who should be one who has failed in a sacrifice..."

But for one who has failed in the *soma* sacrifice, it is indeed the *soma* [rite]. And [the author] will state in the seventeenth book (*Saptadaśapraśna*) that "one who has failed in the sacrifice [should sacrifice] with the seventeen-fold [stoma] to Agni. This [present rite], however, occurs for one who has failed in the *agnihotra* because of the commonality of being a burnt-oblation (*havis-homa*). Because the sacrificer has failed regarding the oblation. Beyond that, however, the *Tantumatī* [offering] is prescribed. This same rule is to be understood for failure in the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* and for failure in the *pārvaṇa-pākayajña*.

Thus ends the seventh paṭala of the tenth maṇḍala in the *Jyotsnā* commentary—composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita (who was the author of the *Śrīmadbhagavat-satyāṣāḍha-hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra-bhāṣya*, the ocean in which the jewels of deeply hidden meanings were submerged, and who brought relief to the distress of learned men seeking those gems)—on the seventh [chapter] of the tenth book.
10.8 Now begins the eighth chapter in the tenth book:
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the Brahman priest belongs to the Vasiṣṭha lineage.

One born of the Vasiṣṭha lineage (*gotra*) becomes the Brahman priest in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. By this, there is no restriction regarding the Vasiṣṭha lineage in the rites of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*), the *iṣṭis*, and the animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*). Even if one belonging to the lineages of the gods, the spirits, or the ancestors has been accepted [as officiant], if a non-Vasiṣṭha is accepted as the Brahman priest for the fire-installation and so forth, then another person of the Vasiṣṭha lineage must be accepted for the sake of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites. There is no rule stating that the very same person who was accepted for the fire-installation and so forth must also serve in the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites. Furthermore, the Śruti in the context of the Soma sacrifice states: "Therefore, a Brahman of the Vasiṣṭha lineage should be appointed."

In this context, the Vāsiṣṭhas are those who have a single ṛṣi; according to the *Pravara-sūtra*, "other than Upamanyu, Parāśara, and Kuṇḍina," the primary Vasiṣṭha and his descendants—namely Upamanyu, Parāśara, and Kuṇḍina—are included here. Because they are his descendants, they are designated by that same name (*tatsaṃjñayā*), and because of their existence as such (*tatsattayā*), they are indeed Vāsiṣṭhas even through their *pravara*. *Note: The text contains two parenthetical markers (1 ka cha and 1106) which appear to be manuscript or editorial notes and have been omitted from the translation.*

The rule "the Vasiṣṭha [should recite] the *brahma* [portion]" is prescribed for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; it applies in the same way to their archetypal forms, namely the *iṣṭi*s and the *paśubandha*s. Some maintain that the term "Vāsiṣṭha" refers specifically to one who is a descendant of Vasiṣṭha. However, in reality, because of the statement "it is the Jyotiṣṭoma," the restriction of being a Vāsiṣṭha applies only to the Jyotiṣṭoma; elsewhere there is no such restriction. Thus, what was stated—that anyone at all may recite the *stomabhāga*s—is indeed correct. Whoever should study the *stomabhāga*s [may do so].

The meaning is that whoever else, moreover, knows the *stoma* chants, the *āgāna* melodies, and the sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) such as "For the dwelling place thee! Invigorate the dwelling place!", along with their purpose and application—that person shall be the *brahman*. For this very reason, it is stated by Āpastamba:
"They perform the tradition of the sacrifice for one another. Or rather, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) carry out the sacrificial tradition for each other.

Respecting one another and being mutually devoted, each following whichever scripture belongs to them—whether it be the *Śāstra* that establishes the *Hautra* for the *Hotṛs*, the *Āśvalāyana Śāstra* which applies to unstated cases, the *Śāstra* that establishes the *Ādhvaryava* for the *Adhvaryus*, or the *Śāstra* that establishes the *Audgātra* for the *Udgātṛs*—they resolve mutual contradictions through reasoning and practice the traditional system of sacrifice (*yajña-saṃpradāya*), that is, the established limits of performance pertaining to the sacrifice, exactly as they should.

The meaning is that the *ṛtvij* (priest) or the *pravartaka* (initiator) may be the *brahmā*, or one who has mastered all the *sūtras* may be the *brahmā*. To the extent that the office of the *ṛtvij* is performed by means of the *ṛc* verses, to that extent the sacrifice resides in the *hotṛ*s alone.

By the word "as far as" (*yāvat*), the duty pertaining to the *hotṛ* priest is expressed. Through the *ṛc*, through the *Anūkta* (the supplementary portion of the *Ṛgveda*), and through the entire ritual activity pertaining to the *hotṛ*—to whatever extent that ritual extends—the sacrifice pertaining to the *hotṛ* becomes fully accomplished. Alternatively, the meaning is that for as long as the priestly function (*ārtvijya*) is being performed by means of the *Ṛgveda*, for that long the sacrifice remains established among the *hotṛ*s themselves.

The sense is this: if there is a deficiency in his ritual action, the stability of the sacrifice does not exist therein; the sacrifice becomes deficient, and its fault falls upon the Brahman priest because of his superior strength and because of the absence of the aforementioned qualities.
This applies as long as [the rite] pertains to the Adhvaryus through the Yajus formulas;
this is clear.
To the extent that there is chanting among the Udgātṛs, to that extent [the sacrifice is complete].

This too is clear. And thus, the meaning is that the sacrifice becomes perfected by means of the threefold knowledge (*trayi vidyā*). It is also stated in the Paribhāṣā: "It is performed with the three Vedas. Wherever the sacrifice has reached its conclusion, the sacrifice remains established in the Brahman alone.

By the phrase "wherein those," the threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*) is understood. For one who performs a sacrifice prescribed by the threefold knowledge, the silence (*mauna*) practiced during that sacrifice is such that through this very silence, the sacrifice becomes complete unto Brahman. The meaning is that this silence itself is the primary action of Brahman. Furthermore, this is for the sake of one-pointedness of mind regarding actions directed toward perceptible ends. Therefore, Āśvalāyana says, "not speaking much, with the mind fixed on the sacrifice," thus stating the state of having the mind fixed on the sacrifice. [End of Section] Accompanied by the *Jyotsnā* commentary composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 1107

Therefore, during this *antardhi* (the interval of cessation), the *brahmán* priest should maintain silence (*vācaṃyama*). After the word *antaḥ*, the particle *ca* is to be supplied. For that reason, [this applies] to the sacrifice consisting of those various rites accomplished by the three Vedas. By the term *antardhi*, the time of the cessation of the ritual is expressed; the meaning is that even there, the restraint of speech (*vāgyamana*) occurs. And thus says the *Chāndogya*: "The sacrifice indeed rests in the *brahmán*; at that *anta* (end/cessation), the *brahmán* should remain silent. If he should speak out of negligence, having muttered a verse addressed to Viṣṇu and the *vyāhṛtis*, he restrains his speech once again.

If one should utter speech out of negligence while distracted, he should recite the *vaiṣṇavī* verse, namely "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" (This [is] Viṣṇu). Having muttered this ṛc, or having muttered all the *nyāhṛtis* together, he should again restrain his speech; such is the meaning. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the *vaiṣṇavī* verse. [The occasions for this are: when the King [Soma] is being measured; when the fire is being prepared on the Great Altar (*mahāvedi*) and the Northern Altar (*uttaravedi*); when the King is being carried forth; when he is being pressed; when the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant is being chanted;
when the fire-altar site is being prepared according to the *śulba* rules; the rest is clear.
While the fire-pan (ukhā) is being prepared, and while the rites pertaining to the fire-pan are being performed—

namely, the "bringing together of the fire-pan" (ukhābharaṇa), which is the gathering of the clay for the fire-pan, and the "making of the fire-pan" (ukhākaraṇa), which refers to the rituals beginning with the mixing [of the clay]—
and while it is being set forth.
When the *ukhā* is being prepared; the word "and" (*ca*) serves to connect this with what precedes.
When the fire is being measured;
that is, when it is being measured with a staff upon ground where the fire has not yet been established.
While being ploughed;
while the fire-altar site is being ploughed with a wooden ploughshare; while being sown.
When the sowing of seeds is being performed in the fire-altar site;
when the altar-pile is being constructed;
when all the layers are being laid down.
And regarding the accumulated rites (*saṃcitakarman*):
as many accumulated rites as there are, such as the *saṃcita-māmimṛśati* and so forth—
in these rites, while they are being performed at the proper time, he sits to the south.

He specifies those very acts as they are performed at their respective times: the meaning is that he sits to the south while they are being performed at their own proper times. When the fire is being carried forth, when the two *havirdhāna* carts are being moved, and when the king is being carried on the cart and the fire on the northern altar (*auttaravedika*) is being brought forward—the rest is clear.
"When the fire-pan (ukhā) is about to be prepared.

By the use of the future suffix in "when the fire-pan is about to be prepared," going toward the clay for the sake of the fire-pan is understood. This has been clearly stated by Āpastamba: "Go toward the fire-pan. The meaning of "toward" (accha) is "go facing toward the place where the clay is dug.
And also, "while it is being carried."

While she is being carried toward that fire-pan (mukhā) by the sacrificer, who has fastened her around his neck with the Viṣṇukrama formulas, [the text says] "let them place the Nairṛti bricks," meaning "let them place the Nairṛti iṣṭakas. The plural number is intended to include the Adhvaryu, Pratiprasthātṛ, Brahman, and Sacrificer; for although there is no direct connection with the Pratiprasthātṛ, Brahman, and Sacrificer in the act of placing [the bricks], nevertheless, the plural is used here by relying merely on their general connection with the piling of the fire-altar (agnicayana).
Regarding the *cityagni*s being carried forth:

the bricks intended for the altar are the *cityagni*s. In the phrase "of the *cityagni*s," the word *agni* refers to the means of constructing the altar. Regarding the carrying forth of the *cityagni*s which is prescribed by such injunctions as "recite for the *cityagni*s being carried forth," he likewise sits to the south.
[He also sits to the south] when the *vasatīvarī* waters and the *savanīya* offerings are being taken away.

By the term *savanīya*, the *ekadhana* waters are understood, because they serve that purpose at each pressing (*savana*). [The phrase] "as they go, as they go back," and "while being brought"—that is, while the *vasatīvarī* waters and the *savanīya* offerings are being brought at their respective times. Among these, the time for bringing the *vasatīvarī* waters is after the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) of the animal sacrifice to Agni-Soma; the time for bringing the *savanīya* offerings is after the *prātaranuvāka*.
And let them both descend for the *avabhṛtha* bath.
Facing the place of the *avabhṛtha*, they should descend—that is, proceed—toward that location while the action of going is about to be performed, with the verse "For wide [is the space], O King.
And while the suns are rising.

While these rites are being performed at the appropriate time as they commence and proceed, he moves to the south. He goes to the south of those, such as the Adhvaryu, who are moving. Āśvalāyana states that he is always to the south of all rites, whether they are fixed or moving. It should be considered why the rites related to the fire are recited without interruption, or why they are recited according to the sequence of the ritual; the reason for this inverted order of recitation is to be reflected upon. [Chapter 80] Accompanied by the commentary *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa. 1109.

While the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds are being prepared, he goes between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara* heap, passes behind the *uttaravedi*, and sits down to the south. He remains seated until the time of the *vaisarjana* offerings.
He remains seated until the *akṣapittāhāna* formula is recited.

When the *vaisarjana* oblations are about to be offered, he returns by the same way he came, goes around the north of the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth, enters the *prāgvaṃśa* hall through the eastern door, passes behind the *śālāmukhīya* fire, and sits down to the south.
This is clear.
With the words "Thus do thou worship," he places the King (Soma) upon the lap;
"lap" here means the lap [or the interior].
He sits by [the fire] until the *vaiśarjana* oblation.
This is clear.
Once the *vaiśarjana* oblation has been offered, he follows after the fire as it departs.

"Having first gone out," says Āpastamba. After the *gārhapatya* oblation has been offered, having first gone out from all [the fires], he goes toward the fire along the path beyond the *prāgvaṃśa* hall in the ritual procedure where Soma is the first. Or he may go first;

for when Agni is the first, he goes out after the clarified butter (*ājya*) and proceeds toward the fire. Otherwise, it would contradict the rule: "Whether with Agni as the first or with Soma as the first, they proceed eastward."

Having reached the Āgnīdhrīya shed, he sits down to the south and remains seated until the Vaisarjana oblations are offered. Once the Vaisarjana has been offered, having handed over the King Soma to another, and having gone around the north of the Āgnīdhrīya hearth, he takes back the King Soma with the verse "Soma goes forth, knowing the way," and enters the Havirdhāna shed by the western door. Having handed the King Soma to the Adhvaryu, he returns by the same way he came, crosses to the west of the Uttaravedi, and sits down to the south.
Regarding the handing over to another: Āpastamba has clearly stated—“Having reached the Āgnīdhra fire-shed, he hands over the King (Soma) to the Pratiprasthātṛ. The rest is clear.
He sits by [the sacrificer] until the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) of the Agniṣomīya animal;
here, because it is an inclusive limit (*abhividhi*), the meaning is "up to and including the offering of the omentum."
When the omentum has been offered, he performs the ritual purification (*mārjana*).

He purifies himself together with everyone at the *cātvāla* pit; "the priests, including the Brahman, purify themselves at the *cātvāla*," so says Āśvalāyana. Regarding the *vasatīvarī* waters being drawn, he restrains his speech until the *subrahmaṇyā* call.

The meaning is "up to the Subrahmaṇyā invocation. Here too, there is an inclusive limit (āṅ). He awakens while they are awakening during the late night; the word "first" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Since the act of awakening is established by implication alone, its purposefulness is achieved solely through the prescription of its priority. Without supplying the word "first," the sūtra would indeed be redundant.

When the *prātaranuvāka* has been introduced, he restrains his speech until the *paridhānīyā* verse. Here too, because it is an inclusive limit (*abhividhi*), it includes everything up to and including the *paridhānīyā*. When the *savanīya* offerings are being brought forward, he enters the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door, goes around the front of the *khara* mound, and sits down to the south. He remains seated there until the time for the *āgraha* cups.
The time for the *graha* offerings begins from the point where it is said, "He proceeds with the *dadhi-graha*.
While the *grahas* are being drawn, he restrains his speech until the drawing of the *āgrayaṇa*.
The word division is "until (*ā*) the drawing of the *āgrayaṇa*. This means up to the point of the *āgrayaṇa* drawing; *ā* is used here in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*).
While the others are proceeding with the *bahis-pavamāna*, he proceeds while maintaining physical contact with them.

Regarding the *vaimuṣa-homa* and the *saptahotṛ-homa*, there is an option—namely, that "the sacrificer [maintains contact] with the Brahman priest" according to some authorities—which should be understood here as well, as it was stated in the *āvayava-sūtra*. Following such a procedure, the Brahman priest also proceeds while maintaining contact.

When it is said, "I shall satisfy the Brahman," [the Adhvaryu] gives the impulse: "O God Savitṛ, he has declared this to you; impel it and sacrifice it! Bṛhaspati is the Brahman. Do not depart from the long-lived Ṛc, nor from the body-protecting Sāman. May your blessings be true, may your intentions be true. Speak Ṛta and Satya! Praise in the impulse of the god Savitṛ: *Om, praise!*" Thus he impels. The complete recitation of the *saṃhitā* mantra is for the purpose of joining it with the *stomabhāga* mantra. With that, the joining occurs by means of the sentence of authorization: "*...oṃ, praise!"* Impulsion (*prasava*) is the sentence of authorization.
This is the ritual procedure for all the *stotras*.
It is clear.
With the formulas, "Thou art a ray; for habitation thee; quicken the habitation," he places one after another of the thirty-one *stomabhāgas* in each *stotra*.

There are exactly thirty-one *stomabhāga* verses. Therefore, in the *aptoryāma*, there is a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of another [verse]. And thus is the rule regarding the number. And this being so, even when there is an excess of hymns (*stotra*) caused by an overflow of Soma, one should proceed with those respective hymns in that very manner; [the *stomabhāgas* are not added]. Here, the repetition occurs at the end of the pressing (*savana*), not in the two preceding pressings. In the third pressing, they are inserted as additional [verses].

Having entered the northern part of the *toreva* [enclosure], when the *Udgātṛ*s or the *Prastotṛ* say for the sake of the *Bahiṣpavamāna*, "O Brahman, we shall chant the *stotra*," he recites the mantra, "O God Savitṛ, this is yours. Because of the use of the present participle "being spoken" (*ucyamāne*), this mantra is recited at the very same time as that address, or even before the address; and at that moment, he gives the impulse with the words, "O Sāman, chant! (*o stṛta*).

The meaning of the word *ādadhati* (they place) is that they join the mantra for the *stoma* immediately after "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ" and before "Oṃ, let him be praised. The repetition (*vīpsā*) is for the purpose that each individual mantra should be applied in sequence to each respective *stotra*. He states the number:

twelve in the *agniṣṭoma*, thirteen in the *atyagniṣṭoma*, fifteen in the *ukthya*, sixteen in the *ṣoḍaśin*, seventeen in the *vājapeya*, twenty-nine in the *atirātra*, and thirty-three in the *aptoryāma*.

The teacher has stated that one should take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup even at the *agniṣṭoma*; this very [sacrifice] was mentioned by Āśvalāyana as the *atyagniṣṭoma-stoma*. Thus, this sacrifice named *atyagniṣṭoma* is inferred. By the statement "he should take it for a *rājanya*," a sacrifice performed by a king is indicated. Since Gautama includes it among the forty *saṃskāras* as something obligatory, it should be understood as mandatory for a *brāhmaṇa* as well. The meaning is clear.

While the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant is being performed, he returns by the way he came, passes to the west of the *uttaravedi*, and sits down to the south. He remains seated until the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice. "By the way he came" means according to the path taken; here, the prefix *ā-* signifies inclusion, meaning that he remains until the point of the omentum-offering. Once the omentum has been offered, having performed the ritual purification (*mārjana*), he enters the *sadas* by the eastern door, circumambulates the *praśāstrīya* hearth to its front, and sits down to the south. He remains seated until the conclusion of the rite.
By the word *saṃsthāna*, the completion of the *savana* is expressed.
Where they bring him a cup (*camasa*), he consumes it just like the other cups. This has already been explained in the *Yājamāna-sūtra*, which has the same meaning.
He restrains his speech during the *stotra* and the *śastra*, until their completion; [he does so] until the completion of the *śastra* at the end of the sacrifice.
When the *savana* has concluded, he goes out again by the same way he came.
The meaning is that he exits by the very same way through which he entered the assembly hall (*sadas*).
Thus prescribed are the *saṃcara* (the path) and the office of the *brahman* for the two subsequent pressings (*savana*).

*Saṃcara* means the path; "and the other [is] the office of the *brahman*"—both are included according to the principle of the *mobaḍīvaī* [maxim]. This is the cause [for the rule]. [End of] the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha. 1112.
From this point on, the other rites are prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa as belonging to the Adhvaryu alone.

Therefore, the meaning is that the rites other than those already mentioned—such as the choosing (*varaṇa*), the *japa*, the *tānūnaptra*, and the *upasthāna*—are prescribed as belonging to the Adhvaryu; he should perform them like the Adhvaryu. Thus is the office of the Brahman priest (*brahmatva*) for the various sacrificial terminuses (*saṃsthās*) ordained. || 25 ||

Thus ends the eighth chapter of the tenth book in the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. In this manner, the office of the Brahman priest is prescribed for all the sacrificial forms (saṃsthās). The repetition [of the concluding phrase] is intended to indicate the completion of the book. Thus [ends the work] composed by Gopīnātha Dīkṣita, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita—who was himself the son of Śrī Padagnistoma-yājin, Sāhasrāgni-yukta-vājapeya-yājin, Sarvatomukha-yājin, and Sāhasrāgni-yukta-pauṇḍarīka-yājin Okopāḍa—and who, through his commentary, has dispelled the distress of learned men caused by their failure to obtain the hidden jewels of meaning within the ocean of the venerable Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
The eighth chapter of the tenth question in the commentary known as the *Jyotsnā* on the *Śāmikā*. || 8 ||
The tenth question is completed. We shall now explain the fire-altar (Agni). 1.

That [piling] is for the sake of subsequent sacrifices, except for the Sādyaskra, the Vājapeya, the Ṣoḍaśin, and the Sārasvata Sattra; or it may be according to what has been taught for the Agnicit-stoma. In the Rātri-sattras that include the Mahāvrata, the repeated piling (punar-citi) is for the purpose of what is not otherwise heard [in the texts]. || 2 ||

Alternatively, while the fire is being maintained, he should touch the altar within the *vedi* with the formula: "May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit firm. Or, having laid down three *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks, the rule for their laying is as follows: the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, the *sāman*, the *purīṣa*, and the *viśvajyotis*. In this manner, the second is prescribed with *purīṣa*, and the third likewise.

Or alternatively, there are three *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks and all the *viśvajyotis* bricks; the rule for their laying out is as follows: first the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, then the *sāman*, then the *purīṣa*, then the *viśvajyotis*. Thus is the second layer prescribed. But in the third layer, the *viśvajyotis* is first; then the *purīṣa*; then the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; then the *sāman*. 4.
Desiring that [sacrifice], having chosen the officiating priests on the new moon day, the full moon day, during the waxing fortnight, or under an auspicious lunar mansion, he should proceed.

"O gods whose priest is Bṛhaspati, O first-born gods of the gods, exert your power among the gods! As the first among the second, as the second among the third—thrice eleven, thirty-three—may I take hold of you; may I be able to accomplish this which I am doing. Svāhā! With these words, he offers the oblation. || 6 ||

Having cleansed the *juhū* and the *sruva* ladles and having taken either four or eight portions of clarified butter, he, standing upright within the altar, offers one oblation with the Sāvitra verses beginning with the Yajus verse "yuñjānaḥ prathamaṃ manaḥ" as the eighth.

If one should desire of someone, "May he become worse off," he should offer each oblation for that person individually. If one should desire of someone, "May he become more prosperous," he should offer all the oblations for that person while reciting them in their entirety.

If he should desire, "May I endow the meters with the glory of the sacrifice," he should make the final [verse] one containing a *ṛc*. If he should desire, "May I endow the sacrificer with the glory of the sacrifice," he should make the final [verse] one containing a *yajus*.
With the verse, "Fulfill the hymn with the Ṛc," he offers the northern oblation with butter taken four times.

With the four formulas beginning with "devasya tvā," he takes up the spade (*abhri*). It may be made of *khadira* wood, or of bamboo, or of spotted wood; it may be hollow or solid, sharpened at both ends or sharpened at one end only; or it may be made of *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *arka*, or *śamī* wood. Or it may be made from any tree that bears fruit, being a mere fist-sized, or a span (*prādeśa*) long, or an elbow-length (*aratni*), or an arm’s length (*bāhu*), or a fathom (*vyāma*) long, or of unmeasured size. (Section 1, Sutra 11)
Having taken the horse's halter with the mantra, "They have grasped this rein of the Eternal Law," he fastens it to the horse with the mantra, "O courser, run forward swiftly!"
Silently, having taken hold of the donkey, [he says] to the two of them: "Yoke the donkey, you two! Thus [he addresses] the donkey. || 13 ||
With the three verses beginning "yoge yoge tavastaram," they proceed eastward, preceded by the horse, to where they intend to dig for the clay.
With the words, "Come hither for Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras," he should address that person with whom he has come into contact; looking away, he points him out. 15.
Or [he may say]: "We approach Agni Purīṣya in the manner of Aṅgiras.
Facing the rising sun, he stands near an anthill, saying: "We shall carry Agni Purīṣya in the manner of Aṅgiras."
In this regard, some recite: "We bear Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras. || 18 ||
"Agni has looked upon the forefront of the dawns," with these words he steps forward from the mound of the ant-hill. || 19 ||

Having arrived, he makes the horse step upon the clay-digging pit with two verses beginning, "O steed, having come from the path of the prize," and "O steed, having stepped upon the earth. || 11.1.20 ||
With the words, "The sky is your back," he cleanses the back of the horse. || 21 ||

"Trample those who attack; let the enemies be beneath [your feet]. Stand like Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, conquering the waters and the lands. With these words, he meditates in his mind upon him whom he hates, [placing him] beneath the horse's feet. || 22 ||
With the two verses beginning "He has stepped forth" (RV 10.189.2) and "He has stepped out" (RV 10.189.3), they cause the horse to step out from the place where the earth was dug.
With the words, "O divine waters, flow forth," he pours water into the footprint of the horse.
Having placed gold in it, he offers a single oblation with two verses containing the word "mind" (manasvatī), namely: "I sprinkle Agni," and "I sprinkle thee. || 25 ||
With the three verses beginning "Take away the water, take away the gold, O lord of the sacrifice," he traces around the clay pit with the wooden shovel, making it wider on the outside. || 26 ||
He digs with two [mantras], beginning with "devasya tvā. || 27 ||

With the formula, "Thou art the back of the waters," he brings a lotus leaf; with this same formula, he wraps it around. Above that, to the north of the clay-digging tool, he spreads a black antelope skin with the formula, "Ye two are a shelter, ye two are a protection. (Section 2) With two verses, he spreads it with the neck toward the east and the hair upward; the lotus leaf is on top, and the handle is underneath, turned face-upward. || 28 ||
Having touched the clay with the mantra, "Thou art the one worthy of being carried; thou art the sustainer of all. (29)

He collects the black antelope skin and the lotus leaf with three Gāyatrī verses beginning, "Thee first from the lotus," for a Brāhmaṇa; with the following Triṣṭubh verses for a Rājanya; and with Jagatī verses for a Vaiśya. 11.1.30.
If he should desire, "May he become more prosperous," for him he should collect [the earth] with both types of verses: with *gāyatrī*s and with *triṣṭubh*s.
"Be born, O noble one!"—with these words he consecrates the prepared [mixture]. 32.
With the words, "May Vāyu Mātariśvan place [the breath] within you," he pours water into the pit for the clay.

Having enticed the digger of the clay and having lifted it up, he, being well-born, fastens the ends of the black antelope skin with the mantra "With light, O well-born one," using a triple-stranded cord made of muñja grass or arka fibers.
He rises with two verses beginning, "O Moon, arise at this well-performed sacrifice. (35)
"Thou art born as the embryo of the two worlds," with these words he carries [the fire]. || 36 ||
With the words, "Be firm, O thou of strong limbs," he places [the mortar] upon the back of the donkey. || 37 ||
With the three verses beginning "Let the steed go forth, neighing," they return without haste, preceded by the horse. || 39 ||
With the words, "We bring Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras," he should address that person with whom he has come into contact; if he does not see him, he points him out. 11.1.40.
To the north of the monastery, having enclosed a space, he brings down [the fire] among flowering and fruiting plants with two verses: "O plants, receive this fire; let it come. || 41 ||
With the verse "vi pājasā," he loosens [the cord]. || 42 ||

With the two verses, "Mitra, having united the earth... and so forth, he unites [the altar] with the materials for union: with potsherds from a ruined site, charcoal from bamboo, husks of rice, the decoction of *palāśa* leaves, and ground pebbles; with the hair of a black antelope skin, both with and without hair, and whatever else he considers suitable for strengthening half [of the altar]. (Section 3) 44.
With the words, "Thou art the head of Makha," he forms a lump [of clay]. || 45 ||
With the words, "You two are at the feet of the sacrifice," he consecrates both the black antelope skin and the lotus leaf.
With the four verses beginning with "The Rudras, having gathered the earth," he offers the funeral cakes. || 47 ||
For one who has many wives, the chief queen makes the fire-pan with four verses beginning with "May the Vasus fashion you. (48)
The Adhvaryu [performs] for one who has a single wife. || 49 ||
With these very *yajus* formulas, the sacrificer consecrates the [oblation] as it is being prepared. || 11.1.50 ||
He performs either a threefold elevation or a fivefold elevation. || 51 ||
Making it one span (prādeśa) in height, one cubit (aratni) in width, and one fathom (vyāyāma) in circumference, or making it of unlimited size, he raises four corners toward the four directions.
Or he makes it circular. || 53 ||
One who practices malevolent magic should fashion [the sacrificial post] with nine edges.
With the formula, "Thou art the girdle of Aditi," he makes a girdle at the middle part or at the opening. 55.
At the junction of the *aśrī* and the *rāsnā*, he forms two, four, six, or eight breasts. || 56 ||
"May Aditi grasp your opening," with these words he makes the opening. || 57 ||
Having fashioned it with the verse "kṛtvāya sā mahīmukhām," he establishes it upon the sand in the north. || 58 ||
From that very same clay, he silently fashions the Aṣāḍhā brick, marked with three lines and square in shape. || 59 ||
Having placed horse-dung on the *gārhapatya* fire, he fumigates the *ukhā* with horse-dung while reciting the seven meters, beginning with: "May the Vasus fumigate thee. (Khaṇḍa 4) 11.1.60.

Having dug a pit in front of the Gārhapatya fire with the mantra "Aditi the goddess [has prepared] thee," and having spread it with red cooking materials, he places the *ukhā* (pot) upon it with the mantra "The wives of the gods [have placed] thee. || 61 ||

Having silently placed the Aṣāḍhā brick upon it and covered it with the red cooking materials, he cooks [the rice] from the Gārhapatya fire with the six verses beginning, "The goddesses Dhiṣaṇās thee. || 62 ||
With the verse, "Of Mitra, the supporter of the people," he attends to the rice being cooked with a rite dedicated to Mitra.
"May Savitṛ, the god, lift you up," with these words he lifts up the cooked [grain].
Saying, "Filling the earth, the quarters, and the intermediate directions," he establishes it upon the sand from the north. || 65 ||

"I entrust this fire-pan to Mitra so that it may not break; may she not be shattered," thus having entrusted it to Mitra, he anoints the pan with goat's milk while reciting four Vedic meters, beginning with "May the Vasus fashion you. || 66 ||

Taking seven, twenty-one, or twenty-four beans, he goes toward the head of a man—either that of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who has been killed by an arrow or struck by lightning—and having placed the beans upon it.

Having cut off the head of the man with the words, "This is he who you are; this is your head," he replaces it in the place of the head with a termite-mound split into seven parts, saying, "By this, may you be possessed of a head here. || 68 ||

With three verses concerning Yama, he sings around [the horse]: "He who alone is the ruler of this earthly realm that is within the belly; the king whose fame for victory is unassailable; by whom the waters, the rivers, and the deserts were made firm, as was heaven and earth—Yama the king stands over the gift of horses that have golden girths, well-yoked, golden-horsed, iron-shod, and inexhaustible. (69)
Some say that one should recite [the mantra] while taking [the food]. 11.1.70.
Thinking, "May this serve as enjoyment for our arm," he takes up the human head. || 71 ||
"O Agni, rise up from the mother, the earth," he says as he brings [the fire]. || 72 ||

"Agni goes around the threefold sacrifice like a charioteer, he who bestows [gifts] upon the gods"—this is the verse beginning with "the sage, lord of booty. With the three verses beginning with "The god Agni has gone around, the slayer of demons, the driver away of disease; driving off all enemies, burning the *rakṣas* at all times," he performs the *paryagni* (carrying fire around). Having smeared it with clay, he sets it down. (Section 5) 73.
Thus ends the first paṭala in the eleventh praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter in the eleventh book.
One sacrifices animals to the Fires and to Kāma: a horse, a bull, a ram, and a hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati; these are castrated. || 1 ||

He recites twenty-one or twenty-four *sāmidhenī* verses continuously. Having recited the eleven original ones, he recites the ten verses addressed to Agni beginning with, "May the years, O Agni, and the seasons increase thee. He recites [the following]: "I have sent forth my speech, seeking strength; may the one who eats today accept my songs. Will Apāṃnapāt, the swift impeller, make them well-adorned? For he shall take pleasure in them. For Apāṃnapāt has stood upon the lap of the prostrate ones, upright in his own glory within their lap."
"Both most beloved dwellings, he moves toward and away from them, knowing [them]"—thus there are three verses containing the word *apsu*; if they become twenty-four, [that is the rule]. || 2 ||
"May it be more abundant there, and hereafter in the realm of Yama"—this one should recite for a person suffering from illness. || 3 ||
"Bṛhaspate savitar bodhaya enam" (O Bṛhaspati and Savitṛ, awaken him) is for one who is not afflicted by disease.

"O Agni, for great wealth and for the sake of giving, we kindle thee. Praise the two great ones, Heaven and Earth, who are worthy of being praised, for the office of the Hotṛ-priest. With the verse beginning "Upward from out of darkness," he concludes with the one containing light. || 5 ||
He pours the butter-oblation with the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning."
"His fuel-sticks rise upward"—thus the Āprī verses become the Prayāja offerings. || 7 ||
The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the oblations dedicated to Agni are *triṣṭubh* verses addressed to Agni. || 8 ||
The verse beginning with "yaḥ prāṇata" belongs to Prajāpati.
The animal cake (paśupuroḍāśa) belongs either to Vaiśvānara or to Prajāpati and consists of twelve potsherds. || 11.2.10 ||
The established [rite] is concluded. ||11||
Alternatively, having released the animals dedicated to Agni after they have been carried around the fire, he cuts off their heads, smears them with clay, and sets them aside.
He throws the headless trunks into the water. || 13 ||
He concludes with the Prājāpatya [offering].
Or rather, in place of all these, he should immolate a white, hornless goat for Vāyu Niyutvat.
The ritual procedure for that has been explained by means of the Prājāpatya rite. || 16 ||
The *vāyumatī* and *śvetavatī* verses are the invitatory and offering formulas (*yājyānuvākye*) for the omentum (*vapā*). || 17 ||
The sacrificial cake on twelve potsherds belongs to Vāyu accompanied by the Niyuts, or to Paśu as a deity, or to Vaiśvānara, or to Prajāpati. || 18 ||
The rite is accomplished; it is concluded. || 19 ||
Having smeared it with clay, he places the head of the Vāyavya [vessel] upon it. (Section 6) 11.2.20.
Thus ends the second chapter in the eleventh book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the third chapter in the eleventh book.

Having performed that which was prescribed prior to the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, he offers the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice consisting of either two or three oblations: a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu, or a *caru* of ghee for Agni and Viṣṇu; a *caru* of ghee for Aditi; and a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara as the third [oblation], if the year-long maintenance has not yet been completed.
At the time of the initiation oblations, having offered five oblations pertaining to the *adhvara* sacrifice with the formulas beginning "To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, svāhā!",
he offers six oblations pertaining to the fire (*agni*) with the formulas beginning "Ākūtim agnim," and the seventh with "Viśve devasya netuḥ."

Having performed that which precedes the making of the fist, he spreads a layer of *śaṇa* grass or *muñja* grass inside the *ukhā* and then places the *ukhā* upon the embers of the Āhavanīya fire with two verses: "Do not break, do not be harmed. || 3 ||
"O Maitrāyaṇī, heat this fire-mouth with embers! Thus he heats it around. || 4 ||
Saying "dravanna," he places a betel nut, having scraped it and anointed it with ghee, into that [ladle]. || 5 ||
And muñja grasses. || 6 ||
Whoever should desire prosperity, whoever would prepare the fire-pan (ukhā), for him that very [fire] should be used; however, one who has lost his fortune should establish the fire by churning.
If he should desire, "May I produce a rival for him," he should bring [the material] from elsewhere and place it [on the fire].
[The story] of Ambarīṣa, who desired food. || 9 ||
One should have a forest fire carry away [the earth] from where he desires: "May a hero be born to me in my kingdom. ||11.3.10||
[One should offer oblations] from the tip of a tree for one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). || 11 ||
[The offering] for one desiring food is by means of roasting. || 12 ||
One who is performing the optional fire-ritual (kāmya-agni) should not add fuel to the Āhavanīya fire.
Once it has been produced in the ukhya fire, he causes it to follow after the āhavanīya fire.

With the words, "From the highest gathering," he places a fuel-stick of *udumbara* wood; with the words, "From the furthest distance," a stick of *vaikaṅkata* wood; and with the words, "That wonderful [work] of Savitṛ, the most excellent," a stick made of *śamī* wood. || 15 ||
Some prescribe a sacrificial ladle made of *śamī* wood for the first [offering] and one made of *vaikaṅkata* wood for the latter.
With the three verses beginning, "Sit down in the lap of this mother," he worships the chief of the newborn. || 17 ||
With the five verses beginning "O Agni, whatever [thou hast]... (RV 3.22.1–5), he places upon the fire a faggot of Udumbara wood that has been cut with a back-cutter.
One should perform the *tailvaka* [rite] against one who practices malevolent magic; by means of that, they become his seizers. || 19 ||

With the verse, "By means of your two tusks, [O Agni], [seize] the thieves," he places a fuel-stick of *Ficus religiosa* (Aśvattha) on the fire; with the verse, "Those who among men are thieves... he places one of *Flacourtia ramontchi* (Vikaṅkata); and with the verse, "He who acts as an enemy toward us... he places one made of *Prosopis cineraria* (Śamī). As he places them, he meditates in his mind upon the destruction of him whom he hates. (11.3.20–21)
"O Brahman, I have condensed [the ritual] for them, or perhaps I have gone too far," he says, and with these words he places two fuel-sticks of Udumbara wood upon the topmost [fire].
Then he makes the sacrificer recite: (Section 7) || 23 ||

"Brahman and Kṣatra are our companions; the Brahman indeed quickens the Kṣatra, and the Brahman quickens the Kṣatra of the Kṣatriya. When they perform heroic deeds together, [the Brahman] quickens the Brahman of the Brāhmaṇa. Thus he mutters. || 24 ||

"As the mother bears her son, so shall the earth bear Agni Purīṣya; the fire-pan (ukhā) shall bear him in its own womb. With these words, Prajāpati Viśvakarman, in harmony with all the gods and the seasons, shall yoke it—thus he places the ukhā upon a sling made of muñja grass, having six or twelve suspension-strands. 25.

With the two verses, "O Agni, yoke those [steeds] of yours... and "The one with twenty-one ribs, the gold-encrusted, woven with threads," the sacrificer, sitting within the altar (antarvedi), having turned it over so that the gold plate (rukma) is visible, fastens the one with twenty-one ribs on the outside; he places the one with the rib-protectors (nirbādha) underneath.
With the verse "naktoṣāsā," he fastens on the black antelope skin.
With the mantra "viśvā rūpāṇi," [he unties] the loops of the sling. || 28 ||
Or alternatively, having fastened the carrying-sling, he fastens the black antelope skin.
"Thou art Suparṇa, Garuḍa," with these words he gazes at the fire in the ukhya vessel.
"You are Suparṇa, the Garuḍa; go to heaven," with these words he lifts it up. || 31 ||
Holding [the vessel] above the navel, he strides four Viṣṇu-strides toward the east, saying, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu. || 32 ||
He consecrates the fire-pan with the mantra, "Akrandad Agni. || 33 ||
With the four verses beginning "O Agni, you who turn toward us," he turns clockwise.

Having brought [the fire] with the verse, "I have brought thee," he worships it; if he should desire of someone, "May he possess a kingdom," he should meditate upon him mentally, saying, "May all the subjects desire thee. || 35 ||
With the verse "uduttamam," he unties the loop of the sling. || 36 ||
"Great and upright, he has stood at the head of the dawns"—with these words, having released [the horse], he worships it. || 37 ||

The Audumbarī stool is one cubit high, with a head-piece (anūcya) one span long and feet one span long; it is woven with Muñja grass or covered with wooden planks and smeared with clay. [The sacrificer] sits upon it with the formula, "Sit thou in the lap of this mother. Upon that [stool], he deposits the Ukhyā fire with four verses.
Or on sugar. || 39 ||
"Some recite that one should worship with the *haṃsavatī* [verses].
Thus ends the third chapter in the eleventh book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
Now begins the fourth chapter in the eleventh book.
One undertakes the ritual acts beginning with the forming of the fist. ||1||
With the verse, "By which the gods went upward to the light," he kindles the fire in the *ukhya* pan with pieces of wood a span long.
It is always ablaze. || 3 ||
Saying, "O Lord of Food, give us food," he who is about to undertake the vow places a fuel-stick of Udumbara wood upon the Satra-jyokhya fire while performing the vow.

"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the Gāyatrī metre, I place thee, the night-brick; by that deity, mayest thou sit firm like Aṅgiras"—with these words he worships the fire at the head of the altar in the evening. || 5 ||

"At the impulse of God Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the Gāyatrī metre, I place thee, the day-brick; by that deity, mayest thou sit firm like Aṅgiras"—thus in the morning.
On the following day, he worships with the Vātsapra hymn consisting of eleven verses beginning, "Agni was first born from out of heaven. 7.
Thus, [the rule applies] always from the time of purchase. || 8 ||
On the previous day he strides the Viṣṇu-strides; on the following day he worships with the Vātsapra hymn. Thus [it is said]. 9.
On the day when he is about to establish the sacred fires, on that very day he should combine both [the rites]; he should either proceed with them together or perform the worship separately.

If, while the fire is being carried forward, this god should think ill of the subjects, one should offer three fuel-sticks with these three verses: "O Agni, bring us physicians! You are the black-pathed one; you are our worshipful Hotṛ. O Agni, be our physician among the gods, O bearer of oblations! You are the bearer of oblations to the gods; we invoke you as physicians, we kindle you as physicians; be a physician for us among the gods. || 11 ||

If, while the *ukhya* fire is dying down, he should desire, "May it rain," he should offer three fuel-sticks with these three verses: "Sūrya plunges into the waters with his rays, winning the prize, the darkness; be aware, O singer, you who increase our life-force! He who has measured out the ends of heaven and earth with his ray, he has filled both worlds with his greatness. "You come weaving the thread with your most excellent steeds; you spread it out, O God, as you bestow wealth. The rays of Sūrya, shaking [the darkness], have driven away the gloom like a skin. With these three verses, he should place three fuel-sticks upon the fire.

If, while the fire is being carried forward, he should desire, "May it not rain," he should offer three fuel-sticks with these verses: "His banners have appeared; his rays extend over the people, shining like fires" (RV 7.3.1); "Swift, visible to all" (RV 7.62.1); and "The golden ornament of heaven, far-seeing, rises up, reaching its goal, swift and radiant. Now indeed, impelled by Sūrya, men go forth to their tasks, performing their works" (RV 7.60.1–4). With these [verses], he should place the three fuel-sticks upon the fire. || 13 ||

If anything should be lost while the *ukhya* fire is being carried, he worships it with the three verses beginning "O Agni, who comest hither... It is known from tradition: "He surely recovers that [which was lost]. (Kaṇḍikā 9) 14.
Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the eleventh praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the fifth chapter in the eleventh book:
"Oṃ, may all the gods lift thee up"—with these words, he lifts up the fire-pan (ukhya).
With the four verses beginning "Sit down in the lap of this mother," he places the cart on the island.
Having silently seated the other two fires, he proceeds with the verse: "O Agni, go forth, full of light... (RV 10.87.2). || 3 ||
He consecrates the axle with the mantra, "Akrandad Agni."

Having resolved upon it, he places a fuel-stick of Udumbara wood, anointed with clarified butter, into the Ukhyā fire with the verse addressed to the guest, "Serve Agni with this fuel" (*samidhāgnim duvasyata*), using a *gāyatrī* for a Brāhmaṇa; a *triṣṭubh*, "Forward, forward goes this Agni" (*pra prāyam agniḥ*), for a Rājanya; and a *jagatī* for a Vaiśya. || 5 ||
In the kindling, the vow, and the resolve, as well as in all those [rites] where [the fires] are brought together, he first places a log anointed with ghee.

If the fire-pan (*ukhā*) should sink into the ashes, he takes the pan, goes to the edge of water, and with these two verses—“O Great One, descend into this well-made, well-fashioned, golden vessel with a thousand spikes; enjoy the honeyed spring, the wide expanse; enter your oceanic seat! and “Suck this honeyed breast of the waters, which is swollen in the midst of the lake; enjoy the honeyed spring, the wide expanse; enter your oceanic seat!”—he brings the pan down.
With the three verses beginning, "O divine waters, receive this ash," he causes the ash to enter the water.
Having taken up some of the ashes and having propitiated with the two verses beginning with "By means of the ashes [I have propitiated] the womb," he places it back into the fire-pan (ukhā).
He returns with two verses: "Again, vigor! Together with wealth! (RV 10.191.3) and [the following]. || 11.5.10 ||
"May the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus kindle you again," with these words he adds fuel.
"By awakening, that is awakening. (Khaṇḍa 10) He worships with two verses containing the word "awakening. 12.

For one who has been initiated, the constant immersion in water after entering the ashes serves the purpose of purifying those for whom the *iṣṭakā* offerings have been performed from those for whom they have not been performed. || 13 ||
One who desires cattle should perform [the rite] in the dung.
One who is a traveler may scatter [the hair] in water. || 15 ||

"He should be consecrated for three nights; he should be consecrated for six nights"—these optional rules for consecration have been explained in the Brāhmaṇa; regarding them, one may act according to his desire.

He prepares the bricks for one who has been initiated during the ritual procedures of initiation lasting for months and so forth; for others, he does so before the initiation in the former case, and after the animal sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati in the latter case.
The bricks are made of clay, level, and square. Of these, three are Maṇḍaleṣṭakās; they have straight lines, turned to the right, and turned to the left, and are marked with three lines. ||18||
They cook the *lauhini* cakes with fire produced by friction. || 19 ||
He does not place a black one, nor a spotted one, nor a mottled one. || 11.5.20 ||

A lotus leaf, a golden plate, a golden man, two offering-spoons, seven naturally perforated pebbles, golden bricks, five ghee-bricks, a clump of *dūrvā* grass, a tortoise, a mortar, a pestle, a winnowing basket, stones, the heads of sacrificial animals, and the head of a serpent—these are the bricks not made of clay. || 21 ||

The mantras for the fire-altar extend as far as its measurement; the *lokapṛṇā* bricks are according to the purpose. One building the altar for the first time should pile it knee-high with a thousand bricks; for the second time, navel-high with two thousand; for the third time, mouth-high with three thousand. Each subsequent one is larger than the preceding.
One who desires heaven should pile the great, vast, and immeasurable [fire-altar]; this is the Vājasaneyaka. 23.
When the duration of the initiation has expired, he settles upon the sacrificial ground with the words, "Go forth, depart! (apeta vīta). || 24 ||

Having removed the site of the funeral pyre with mere effort, [he prepares] a square or circular space. With the verse "Go away, depart," he stirs it with a yellowish branch of the *palāśa* tree, sprinkles it with water, and scatters sand with the formula, "Thou art the ash of Agni. (Khaṇḍa 11) 25.
"Thou art consciousness, the upholder of desire," [with these words] he [offers] the saline earth.
He pours them out while meditating in his mind: "That which he gave away, that blackness in the moon—may it be here. ||27||
Having mixed together the saline earth and the sand with the verse, "Those dear bodies of yours," he spreads them out along the lines. ||28||
"You are piled; you are piled around"—with these words, he encloses the site of the Gārhapatya altar with twenty-one pebbles. || 29 ||
He forms three triplets of Saṃhitās.
With the four verses beginning "This is that Agni," he places four bricks facing eastward upon the Gārhapatya altar during its piling.

With the two verses, "O Agni, the *iḍā*" and "This is your seasonal womb," he places two bricks joined upwards in the east; with the two verses, "Thou art the layer" and "Thou art the surrounding one," he places two [bricks] joined upwards in the west. With the thirteen *lokampṛṇā* bricks beginning with "Fill the space, fill the gap," he covers what remains.
With two mantras at a time, he lays down each individual *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick.
Having placed it on the front [altar] with the *sūdadohas* formula, he touches it.
In all the iṣṭakās, he places the tayādevata formula at the end. || 35 ||
A black horse, or else a dark-grey one, stands to the north. || 36 ||
Having taken earth from the *cātvāla* pit with that [ladle], he spreads it over [the altar] while reciting the verse, "Upon the back of heaven" (*pṛṣṭo divi*). || 37 ||
That is the layering. || 38 ||
One who is building for the first time should build with five layers; one building for a second time, with three layers; and one for a third time, with a single layer. || 39 ||
The ritual procedure for one who maintains a single funeral mound is permanent. (Section 12) 11.5.40.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the eleventh book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
Now, the sixth chapter in the eleventh book:
With the four verses beginning with "samitam," he pours the fire-pan (ukhya) onto the Gārhapatya altar-site.
As a mother [lifts] her son, he takes down the fire-pan from the sling. || 2 ||
In this very context, some authorities prescribe the filling [of the vessel]; one should not look at it when it is empty.
With the verse "That which is on the other side of this dust," he takes up the sling for Vaiśvānara.

Taking three black *nairṛti* bricks baked with husks, a sling, a gold thread, and a stool, and having carried them to the south-western intermediate direction, he lays them down facing away from him, not touching one another, on a self-made salt-flat or in a crevice, with the mantra: "Obeisance to thee, O Nirṛti... (TS 4.2.5.1).
(He lays down the noose upon it with bricks.)
With these three verses beginning with "yasyās te asyāḥ krūra āsan juhomi," he offers [the oblations] moving away from himself, without touching [the previous ones], ending toward the south.
(7) He does not perform the *tad-devatya* offering. (8)
With the words, "O Goddess Nirṛti, that which you have bound," he suspends the sling.
Here he places the stool and the gold-threaded cord.
With the verse addressed to Vaiśvānara, "That which is beyond this region," he sprinkles water around [the fire].
"Salutation to Bhūti," with these words he circumambulates [the fire] from left to right. "May the goddesses be auspicious for our aid," with these words they purify themselves.

"Carrying strength, with a wealthy mind and good intellect, I go to my home, rejoicing in my heart, full of luster. With an eye that is not terrible, but auspicious, may I look upon my kin as I rise up from the houses"—thus they go forward without looking back. 14.
With the words, "The dwelling-place, the gatherer of riches," they worship either the Āhavanīya fire or the Gārhapatya fire. 15.

When the *prāyaṇīya* offering has been performed, having set down the King (Soma) and prepared the altar, he digs a pit in the middle of the fire containing a green clump of darbha grass with its roots; then, taking five portions of clarified butter with the *juhū* ladle, he offers five oblations upon the darbha clump while lifting it up with the verse, "May the year be in harmony with the days. || 16 ||
He measures the fire-altar with a bamboo staff as long as a man with his arms raised. || 17 ||
There are three persons facing east, four facing north, and the wings and tail are each one person's length across. || 18 ||
The self consists of four persons; with the cubit-measure, he extends the right wing from the south. || 19 ||
The tail at the back is one span or one cubit; the northern wing on the left side is one aratni.

"O Earth, be pleasant, thornless, and a place of rest; grant us wide-spreading shelter. With these two verses, beginning with "baḍ itthā parvatānām," they step upon the prepared fire-altar. (Section 13) || 21 ||
"Bind the thongs together," he commands.
He digs a pit with a smooth interior and a wide mouth.
"Pour the inexhaustible water upon the well," [with these words] he pours water from the pit into the trenches. (24) In them, they cause the oxen to drink. (25)

With the formula, "The goad for their impelling, the hoof of the bird, the driver's whip, the palm-leaf fan, the leather thong, both frogs as the two yoke-horses"—thus he extends the pair consisting of the yoke and the plough.

With the two verses beginning "They yoke the ploughs," he yokes the plough—either with six oxen, twelve oxen, or twenty-four oxen. With the two verses, "They yoke the ploughs" and "May Pūṣan yoke, may Savitṛ yoke, may Bṛhaspati yoke you with the brilliance of Agni and the luster of Sūrya," he yokes [the plough]; according to some, this applies to a team of six or twelve oxen. 27.

With the mantra, "We know the names of you all—the two camels, the two bilva-wood [yokes], and the two fastenings; O yoke-straps, you who are skilled in the mixture of the sweet drink"—he consecrates the harnessed animals.

"brahmajajñānam" (Rigveda 2.3.10) is this [verse]. "The first [soma-pressing] of yours which has not been reached, in which they perform the rites—do not deceive our heroes therein; I place that before you. "Flow forth for the winning of booty, overcoming the obstacles; to cross over the enemies, you go like a debt-collector. "In the thousand-streamed [soma], those honey-tongued and unceasing ones have sounded together from the vault of heaven.
His watchful, restless spies do not close their eyes; at every step there are bridgers with nooses. Thus he offers the protective brahman-formulas. (29)

"He has arisen, winner of cattle, winner of wealth, winner of horses, winner of gold, encompassed by pleasant speech; with his one-wheeled chariot, may Savitṛ go around the earth, filling it with a portion of vigor"—with these words he raises the plough. || 11.6.30 ||

Thou art named the thief, the thirteenth month; thou art Indra’s armor, thou art Indra’s protection, thou art Indra’s shield. Into thee I enter. Be thou my refuge and my armor. I enter the Gāyatrī with my hair; I enter the Triṣṭubh with my skin; I enter the Jagatī with my flesh; I enter the Anuṣṭubh with my bones; I enter the Paṅkti with my marrow. This is the thick, formidable armor of Indra and Agni, which even the all-gods, the heroes, cannot pierce.
"May that protect us, may that protect us from all sides; O long-lived ones, O gods, may we reach old age"—with these words they step upon the fire-altar which has been constructed. || 31 ||
He plows with two [verses], beginning with "The plough, sharp-pointed... (RV X.101.3–4).
The plowmen drive the oxen.
He ploughs over the head of the tail.
Turning to the right, he plows three furrows each time, reciting: "O you who are like a cow that milks all desires, milk [the field] for me! || 35 ||
