He gazes toward Sītā. || 36 ||
With the formula, "Ghṛtena sītā," he touches the spaces between the furrows.
He draws the northern wing from the southern wing. || 38 ||
From the southern hip to the northern shoulder, and from the northern hip to the southern shoulder; or otherwise, he completes twelve [sections]. || 39 ||
In the middle, it becomes divided. || 11.6.40 ||

"Be released, O inviolable ones, paths of the gods! We have crossed to the further shore of this darkness; we have attained the light, we have gone to the sun. Having said this, he unyokes the oxen on the right shoulder, or on the left, and releases them toward the east or the north. || 41 ||
He gives them to the Adhvaryu priest. || 42 ||
He pours out fifteen water-cups. || 43 ||
Twelve [fingers] for the secondary furrows, and three for the primary furrows. || 44 ||
With the fourteen verses beginning "The plants that have been born," he sows the herbs: seven are cultivated plants and seven are wild plants.
Domestic animals sow along the furrows in ploughed land; wild animals do so in unploughed ground. || 46 ||
If one cannot obtain any of the medicinal herbs, one should sow barley mixed with honey in their place. || 47 ||
Or he should meditate mentally [on it], saying: "Thou art sown by me. || 48 ||
When it has been obtained, he ties it to the first piece of firewood that comes along. || 49 ||
(One should bind together those branches of trees that bear fruit and sprinkle them with water as fuel. 11.6.50.
Having performed that which precedes the guest-offering (*ātithya*), he piles up clods of earth from the four directions with the four verses beginning, "May the progenitor not harm us. (51)
Those who have passed from internal variety into external variety. || 52 ||
"May I take from here food and strength"—with these words, he should fetch a clod of earth from that direction in which his enemy may reside.

He should proceed in such a way that there may be final liberation in that direction; he scatters the northern altar after having performed as much as is required for the fire up to the pouring of the sprinkling water. 54.
With the six verses beginning "In front of you, fame and vigor," he scatters sand.
With the formulas, "You are piled; you are piled around," he encloses the site of the Āhavanīya altar with an unlimited number of pebbles, just as he did for the Gārhapatya altar.
With twenty-one [verses], for one desiring cattle. || 57 ||
For one who has rivals, [the chant] is with the Triṇava [stomas]. || 58 ||
One should measure with immeasurable [units]. || 59 ||
With the two verses addressed to Soma, "Swell up" (ā pyāyasva) and "Be united" (saṃ te), he spreads out the sand.

Alternatively, one should perform the *vyūha* (interchange) for a Brāhmaṇa with a *gāyatrī*, for a Rājanya with a *triṣṭubh*: "The Soma has been pressed, the ruddy bull, the tawny one; like a king, the wondrous one has bellowed toward the cows. Purifying himself, he goes around the woolly filter; like a falcon, he sits upon his ghee-filled womb"—this [verse] is in the *jagatī* meter for a Vaiśya. || 61 ||

If he should desire of someone, "May he be without cattle," he should scatter pebbles and sand for him without measuring them out. If he should desire of someone, "May he be rich in cattle," he should scatter pebbles and sand for him after measuring them out.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the eleventh book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
Now begins the seventh chapter in the eleventh book:
One undertakes the ritual acts beginning with the Ātithyā.

Having performed the first two morning *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, he arranges the bricks of the first layer on a red bull's hide, which has its neck toward the east and its hair facing upward, in front of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall.
Or alternatively, there may be three *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks, and all [the others] are *viśvajyotis*. || 3 ||

Having sprinkled them with clarified butter using a handful of the tips of *darbha* grass and having lifted them up, he issues the command: "Recite for the fire-places being carried forth," or "Recite for those being carried forth."
When [the verse] has been recited three times, they go eastward with the horse at their head.

Having reached the *uttaravedi*, he touches it with the formula: "May Prajāpati seat thee; by that divinity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit thou firm. Then, having taken the fire into himself with the two verses, "I take into myself that Agni who is ours" and [the second verse], he touches the *svayaṃciti* (self-piled altar) with the verse: "O Agni, those logs of thine, those abodes of thine... (6).
The Adhvaryu piles the fire-altar with bricks; or the sacrificer, or the Brahman himself, when piling the fire-altar, takes the fire into his own self and does not touch it once it has been piled. 7.

Turning to the right, he places them on the south; turning to the left, he places them on the north. Straight lines run from west to east. He places three parallel lines running eastward in the middle.

"He places them facing westward"—this is a statement regarding the rows (*gaṇa*). "He places one facing eastward, he places one facing westward"—this is a statement regarding the orientation of the agent. He places some bricks facing westward in the front; others facing eastward in the rear, according to the rule of completion (*apavarga*). By virtue of the scriptural injunction, he places them on the wings, the tail, the two hips, and the two shoulders. (11.7.10)
A white horse stands to the south. || 11 ||
Having touched that, he lays down the bricks. || 12 ||
With the verse addressed to Indra, "Indraṃ viśvā avīvṛdhan," he should place a brick upon the stepping-stone.
Or the fire may be placed to the north or behind [the sacrificer]. || 13 ||
"Speech has entered my mouth, breath into my nostrils"—reciting this, he steps upon the fire at all instances of stepping upon it. || 14 ||
With the verse addressed to Varuṇa, "I approach the principles, adoring with the sacred word," he makes an offering in the Śālāmukhīya fire.
With the words, "He has overcome all hostile armies," he makes the horse, facing eastward, step upon a bunch of darbha grass with its right forefoot. || 16 ||
With the verse, "When you were first born, crying out," he leads the horse around clockwise. || 17 ||
While it is being held on the right side, he places a lotus leaf with its stalk downward and face upward upon a clump of darbha grass with the formula, "Thou art the back of the waters. || 18 ||

"You are the source of austerity; with all prayers I place you, the flawless one, for the winning of kinsmen. You are the source of immortality, the source of sacred knowledge (brahman), the source of sovereignty (kṣatra), the source of the earth, the source of the intermediate space, the source of heaven, the source of the quarters"—thus [he says]. || 19 ||
With the verse "Brahma jajñānam," he places a gold plate with its lower side facing downward upon a lotus leaf.

With the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning," he touches the golden man who is facing eastward and lying on his back to the south of the gold plate with the words, "The drop has fallen," and then he sings over him with the Puruṣasāman. || 21 ||
He worships with the three names of serpents beginning with "Homage be to the serpents. || 22 ||
With the five verses beginning "kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ," he sprinkles the man diagonally, just as [he sprinkles] the high altar (uttaravedi).
On both sides of the person, he places two ladles filled with ghee and curds, [saying]: "I settle thee with the brilliance of Agni. || 24 ||

Having placed a southern brick made of *kārṣmarya* wood, filled with ghee, with the formula, "I settle thee, belonging to Indra, by his vigor," and a northern one made of *udumbara* wood, filled with curds, he worships them with the two verses beginning with the word *mūrdhan*.

Alternatively, having laid them down silently, he worships with the two verses containing the word *mūrdhan*; according to some, having laid them down with the two verses containing *mūrdhan*, he worships with the two *yajus* formulas.
He pours gold over [the altar] according to the dimensions of each person.

(Section 17) || 27 || Having touched the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone with the formula, "Thou art firm, O Varuṇa," and having caused a horse to smell it, he places it in the middle of the fire-altar together with an unlearned Brāhmaṇa, using the formula, "May Prajāpati seat thee upon the back of the earth, thee that art wide-extending," and with the *vyāhṛti*, "Bhūḥ. || 28 ||
Having offered the oblation with the words, "I offer into consciousness," he breathes over the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.
An ignorant Brāhmaṇa gives a boon—one, two, or three [times]. 11.7.30.

"Thou art brilliance; grant me brilliance; grant me the earth; protect me from the earth," [with these words] he lays down a gold brick (*hiraṇyeṣṭakā*). "The earth, whose fortress is the waters, is pervaded by food; men are its guardians," [with these words] he lays down a circle-brick (*maṇḍaleṣṭakā*). "Thou art the *bhūḥ*, the seed of the world; thou art the bricks, the heavenly world; with my mind I ascend after thee. "Thou art the *suvar*, the seed of the world; thou art the bricks, the heavenly world; with my mind I ascend after thee. With these two [formulas], he lays down two bricks for the ascent (*anvāroha*).

With the two verses beginning "Growing forth from joint to joint," he places a clump of *dūrvā* grass together with its clod of earth, with its tips uncut, so that its tip reaches the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone.

Having placed two pieces of gold on both sides of the Vāmabhṛt brick with the formula "O Agni, those splendors of thine which are in the sun," he lays down the Vāmabhṛt brick with the two [verses] beginning with "O Agni, those splendors of thine which are in the sun. (33)
"Virāḍ jyotir adhārayat"—these three [verses] are for the pourers of seed. || 34 ||
Two [teachers] prescribe one [rite]. || 35 ||
One should place those [bricks] in the first layer for a youth; in the middle [layer] for one of middle age; and in both the first and the last [layers] for an elderly man.

"May Bṛhaspati settle you on the back of the earth, the luminous one"—with these words [he places] the Viśvajyotis. "Thou art the path of Agni," and "Thou art the path of the gods"—these two are the Saṃyānī bricks. "Madhu and Mādhava"—these two are the Ṛtavyā bricks. They have the same deity. || 37 ||
He places the *avakā* plant upon all the seasonal layers.
He lays down the *gharma*-brick; the mantra for it is recited in the *pravargya* ritual. (39)

"The Aṣāḍhā [brick] with its mark above; the Aṣāḍhā of the one he hates with its mark below. With the verses: "O Agni, those moist wombs of thine which are nest-like; those drops of thine, O Agni, and those navels; those bodies of thine, O Agni, named 'Strength'—with all these, being in harmony, mayest thou sit down here with thy body among offspring," and with the verse "The winds blow honey for the one who follows the Law," he anoints the tortoise with curds mixed with honey. (Section 18) 41.

Go to the depths of the waters; let not the sun scorch you, nor Atri Vaiśvānara. Looking upon the creatures with no ill intent, may the divine rain attend you. Glide along the three oceans, the self-watering ones; O Bull among bricks, lord of the waters, go through the worlds.

Having consecrated it with the mantra, "Go there where the ancestors have gone, clothing yourself in soil, to your own womb as is fitting," he places it facing eastward while alive, facing westward, with the two verses, "The great heaven and earth for us" and "The four quarters. He surrounds it with *avakā* plants, covers it with a net, and drives stakes around it. 42.

"O mortar, whatever you are joined with in every house, here speak most brilliantly, like the drum of the victorious! With these words, he places the mortar and pestle on the southern buttock of the altar.
The mortar is made of Udumbara wood, one span in length, four-cornered; the pestle is of unlimited size. || 44 ||
"And indeed, O Lord of the Forest, let the wind blow upon your tip. Then, saying, "O mortar, press out the Soma for Indra to drink," they fill [the mortar] with all kinds of herbs and pound them. 45.
In the middle of the fire-altar, he places a mortar and a pestle with the verse, "That supreme abode of Viṣṇu"; or he places the pestle with the verse, "Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu."
"O Viṣṇu, from heaven!"—with these words [he takes] the winnowing basket. || 47 ||
He fills the fire-pan with sand. || 48 ||
With curd, honey, or clarified butter. || 49 ||

If one should desire of someone, "May he be hungry," one should place for him a deficient [brick]. If one should desire of someone, "May he eat food that does not fail him," one should place for him a full [brick]. || 11.7.50 ||

Sewn by the gods with immortality, the sister has come; he has placed the fire-pan upon the altar. May Agni, who was longed for by the ancient seers and is full of wisdom, perform that here—thus, taking up the pan, [he says] "Thou art firm, thou art the earth," and "O Earth, sit upon the earth; Mother, sit upon the Mother; pleasant one, sit upon the pleasant one. We pray for the great majesty of the gods’ creative power, for Agni, the wise one, in his dwelling places and seats."

Vaiśvānara, the all-pervading through sacred prayer, the foundation of the hymn, established in the soil; you are kindled with fuel as the well-kindled Agni, the immovable one in his dwelling-place and seats. Vaiśvānara, the all-pervading through sacred prayer, I establish as the foundation of the hymn in the soil. The sages, bestowers of vital strength, have approached him with the proper measure—Agni, invoked in his dwelling-place and seats.

"Vaiśvānara, who is all-pervading through the sacred word, the foundation of the hymn, the purifying one, the honored one. "Thou art the firm earth; by that deity, like Aṅgiras, be thou firm"—with these words, he places the fire-pan (ukhā) in the middle of the fire-altar. ||51||
According to some, [he should place it] above the mortar.
With the two verses beginning "O Agni, yoke those which are yours" (RV 6.16.43–44), he offers one oblation into the fire-pan (ukhā). (Sūtra 53)

He throws pieces of gold into the vital breaths of the human head: with "For the Ṛc, thee! on the right eye-socket; with "For the Lustre, thee! on the left; with "For the Shine, thee! on the right nostril; with "For the Light, thee! on the left; with "This has become the vigor of the entire world" on the mouth; with "Agni, by his light, is full of light" on the right ear; and with "The golden disk, by its splendor, is full of splendor" on the left.

"Like rivers, the streams flow together"—having thus filled the human head with curds mixed with honey that have been boiled with *ātaṅkya*, and having taken it up with the formula, "Thou art a thousandfold, for a thousand thee," he places it face upwards in the fire-pan (*ukhā*) with its chin pointing eastward, while anointing it with milk with the verse, "Anointing the solar embryo with milk. (55)
With the two verses beginning "That bright one" (*udu tyaṃ citram*), he makes offerings upon the two axles.
He lays down the heads of animals. || 57 ||

If he should desire of someone, "May he be without cattle," he should lay down [the animal heads] facing in all directions for him. If he should desire of someone, "May he be rich in cattle," he should lay them down facing together for him. If he should desire of someone, "May his food be less," he should lay down the animal heads closer together for him. If he should desire of someone, "May his food be equal," he should lay them down on both sides of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick for him. If he should desire of someone, "May his food be more," he should lay them down at the ends, having spread them out for him. 58.

With the verse, "The course of the wind," he places [the brick] facing westward in front of the horse; with "The eternal drop," facing eastward behind the bull; with "The protector of Tvaṣṭṛ," facing northward to the south of the ram; or to the north of the ram, facing southward; with "The fire which is of fire," facing southward to the north; and with "Of the dwelling," facing northward to the south. Without interrupting these by other rites, moving clockwise around them, he pays homage to each direction.

"Do not harm this two-footed one," for a human; "Do not harm this single-hoofed one," for a horse; "This ocean," for a bull; "This woolly one," for a ram; "For the goat belongs to Agni," for a he-goat. || 59 ||
Now, if the head belongs to Vāyu. || 11.7.60 ||
Having placed [the fire] in the primary place by all [means], he worships it with all the utsargas. || 61 ||
Or rather, having placed each [implement] in its respective place, he worships it with the formula for its relinquishment.
With the formula "Homage be to all," he places one of these [bricks] on the northern shoulder; he places the serpent's head facing away from the animal heads.
Or rather, he should merely recite the sacrificial formula (yajus) and not actually place [the brick].

Mā is the metre; its deity is Agni and the Earth; with that Ṛṣi, with that Brahman, with that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! Pramā is the metre; its deity is Vāta and the Intermediate Space. Pratimā is the metre; its deity is Sūrya and Heaven. Asrīviś is the metre; its deity is Soma and the Quarters. Virāj is the metre; its deity is Pūṣan and the Eye. Gāyatrī is the metre; its deity is Bṛhaspati and the Goat. Triṣṭubh is the metre; its deity is Indra and Gold.

The Jagatī is the metre; its deity is Prajāpati, the Bull. The Anuṣṭubh is the metre; its deity is Varuṇa, the Bull. The Uṣṇih is the metre; its deity is Mitra, Āyu. The Paṅkti is the metre; its deity is Parjanya, Agriculture. The Bṛhatī is the metre; its deity is Parameṣṭhin, the Horse. With these verses—twelve in number, repeating them three times, thus making thirty-six—with that Ṛṣi, with that Brahman, with that Deity, saying, "Sit firm like Aṅgiras," he piles the layer in the form of a man facing westward in front.
A human head becomes its head. || 66 ||
Having placed that [brick] down, he worships with the Puruṣa hymn: "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet"—thus with Nārāyaṇa as the Puruṣa. (Section 21) 67.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the eleventh book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.

Now begins the eighth chapter of the eleventh book. He lays down the *apasyā* bricks. With the formula, "In the wave of the waters I settle thee," he places five in the east facing west. With the formula, "Sit in the ocean, the seat," he places five in the south facing north. With the formula, "In the seat of the waters I settle thee," he places five in the west facing east. With the formula, "The *gāyatrī* metre," he places five in the north facing south. (1)

The gods who took hold of the sacrifice from among the gods—may Gāyatrī, knowing the way, lead them to the heavenly world, milking out immortality. Those who establish the lights, ascending to the world of immortality—may they go, knowing the way and understanding the sacrifice, to the world of the well-done. Those sacrificial animals that have come together toward the womb of the sacrifice—the sages, the wise ones, understanding the sacrifice, place them in the world of the well-done.

The path that is extended as the way of the gods, which is held apart by the Vedic meters—by that he has ascended to heaven and the intermediate space, taking hold of the sacrifice and the world of the well-done. That sacrifice which is fashioned over heaven and earth with a thousand streams—by means of it, may the sacrificer go safely to the back of heaven; thus [he says] regarding Aditi. (There are) five gold bricks: four in each direction and one in the middle. 2.

"Adoration to Āyu, svāhā! Adoration to Yoṣkṛta, svāhā! Adoration to Yoṣyatvan, svāhā! Adoration to Viṣṇu, svāhā! Adoration to Bṛhaspati, svāhā!"—with these [formulas], five gold bricks are placed: four in each direction and one in the middle.

"O Agni, the Trivṛt is your head; that, O Agni, is my head. The Pañcadaśa are your two arms; those, O Agni, are my two arms. The Saptadaśa is your body; that, O Agni, is my body. The Ekaviṃśa are your two thighs; those, O Agni, are my two thighs. The Triṇava are your two knees; those, O Agni, are my two knees. The Trayastriṃśa is your foundation; that, O Agni, is my foundation. With these [formulas], he places [the bricks] on the head, the wings, the tail, the hips, and the shoulders.

"O Agni, the Trivṛt is your head; with it, protect me. O Agni, the Pañcadaśa are your two arms; with them, protect me. O Agni, the Saptadaśa is your body; with it, protect me. O Agni, the Ekaviṃśa are your two thighs; with them, protect me. O Agni, the Triṇava are your two knees; with them, protect me. O Agni, the Trayastriṃśa is your foundation; with it, protect me. With these words, the sacrificer consecrates the bricks as they are being laid down. (Khaṇḍa 22) 3.

Born from the waters and from the essence of the earth, he came into being from Viśvakarman. Tvaṣṭṛ, fashioning his form, enters him; that is the entire birthplace of the Puruṣa in the beginning. Having placed this [brick] here with the words, "Thou art the seat of the Ṛtás, the seat of Truth, the seat of brilliance, the seat of luster, the seat of glory; thou art praised," [he continues]: "Thou art a foundation; for the sake of the foundation thee! For the sake of the foundations thee! Sit upon the foundations! Thou art gain; for the sake of gain thee; may I gain!"

You are wealth; for the sake of wealth, may I find you. You are power; for the sake of power, may I be able. You are prosperity; for the sake of prosperity, may I flourish. You are action; for the sake of action, may I perform it. You are a joy; for the sake of joy, for the joys, sit as a joy. Protect the sovereignty; swell the sovereignty; quicken the sovereignty; restrain the sovereignty; make firm the sovereignty. You are sovereignty; for the sake of sovereignty, for the sovereigns, sit as sovereignty. I settle you among all earthly beings.

I settle you in all the intermediate spaces; I settle you in all the celestial realms; I settle you among all the gods; I settle you in all the waters; I settle you in all the plants; I settle you among all the trees; I settle you in all the directions. Sit in heaven!

You are the winner of heaven; you are the winner of armies; you are the winner of much; you are the conqueror; you are the winner of all; you are the winner of everything; you are the ever-conquering; you are the winner of wealth; you are the radiant one; you are the widely radiant one; you are the preeminent radiant one. I set you down as the thunderbolt that slays rivals. I set you down as the thunderbolt that slays those who seek to harm. I set you down as the thunderbolt that slays enemies. I set you down as the thunderbolt that slays sorcerers. I set you down as the thunderbolt that slays Piśācas. I set you down as the thunderbolt that slays Rākṣasas.

I set down for you, O Indra, this thunderbolt that slays enemies, slays foes, slays rivals, and slays Asuras. You are the rising; you are the one who has risen; you are the one about to rise; you are the stepping forward; you are the one stepping forward; you are the step already taken. You are the crossing over; you are the one crossing over; you are the crossing already accomplished. You belong to heaven; you are heaven. Sit upon the impulse; sit upon vigor; sit upon fortune; sit upon wealth; sit upon prosperity. Sit upon the earth worthy of sacrifice; sit upon the back of Viṣṇu; sit upon the station of Iḍā; sit upon the one rich in ghee; sit upon the swelling one.

Sit in the *saṃvatsara*; sit in the *parivatsara*; sit in the *idāvatsara*; sit in the *udvatsara*; sit in the *vatsara*. Sit in one; sit in ten; sit in a hundred; sit in a thousand; sit in ten thousand; sit in a hundred thousand; sit in a million; sit in ten million; sit in a hundred million; sit in a billion; sit in ten billion; sit in a hundred billion; sit in the middle; sit in a trillion; sit at the end; sit in the supreme number (*parārdha*). You are swelling; for the swelling one, for the swelling ones, for the swelling, sit!

"Thou art *ṛta*; for *ṛta* thee, for the *ṛtas* thee, sit in the *ṛta*. Thou art truth; for truth thee, for the truths thee, sit in the truth. Thou art the junction; for the junction thee, for the junctions thee, sit in the junctions. Thou art the union; for the union thee, for the unions thee, sit in the unions. Thou art the attainment; for the attainment thee, for the attainments thee, sit in the attainments"—with these two sections he lays down the *ṛṣi*-bricks.

"This one was in front"—with these words, he lays down fifty *prāṇabhṛt* bricks: ten in each direction, ten transversely, and ten in the middle. Having laid down the outermost [brick] on the outside, he lays down the innermost [brick] on the inside.
"East is of the quarters; spring is of the seasons"—with these words, he places fifty apānabhṛt bricks, placing each outer one after having placed each inner one, just as he did with the prāṇabhṛts.
He lays down the *viṣūcī* brick, which sustains the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the in-breath (*apāna*).

You are the Earth by birth, a cow; you have conceived Agni as your embryo—unite with me! You are the Sky by birth, a cow; you have conceived Āditya as your embryo—unite with me! You are the Stars by birth, a cow; you have conceived the Moon as your embryo—unite with me! You are the Waters by birth, a cow; you have conceived Varuṇa as your embryo—unite with me!

"You are Auṣadhī by birth, a cow; she bore King Soma as her embryo—be united with me! You are Vayovir by birth, a cow; she bore [Agni] Jarāṃdhanas as her embryo—be united with me! You are Virāj by birth, a cow; she bore the King [Soma] as her embryo—be united with me! With this Anuvāka, he lays down the Vaśa bricks. 9.

"O divine brick, you who are life-giving and restful; may you always settle upon me as a wife settles upon her husband. "O divine brick, you who are the giver of out-breath, the giver of in-breath, the giver of diffused breath, the giver of sight, the giver of hearing, the giver of the earth, the giver of the intermediate space, the giver of heaven, the giver of the celestial realm (*svarga*), the giver of maidens, the giver of young women, the giver of matrons, and you who are restful; may you always settle upon me as a wife settles upon her husband. With this section of the text, he lays down the *upaśīvarī* bricks. (11.8.10)

"Ye are purposeful; ye have attained the station of Agni; with the most brilliant splendor, I take you by means of the deities. Ye are bright, full of vigor; belonging to Indra the powerful, I take you by means of the deities. Ye are sovereign mistresses, full of brilliance; belonging to the Ādityas, the gods, I take you by means of the deities. Ye are delightful, victorious; belonging to the Viśvedevas, the gods, I take you by means of the deities. Ye are sustainers of the kṣatra, full of vital force; belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa through the sacred word (Brahman), I take you by means of the deities."

"Ye are established in the cow-pen, resting on high; with the sacred word (brahman) of Bṛhaspati and with the deities, I take you. Having filled twelve jar-bricks (*kumbheṣṭakā*) with water, he places one jar and one pot for each mantra, following the furrows in every direction, using this *anuvāka* beginning with "The golden-colored, pure, purifying ones... There are four in the middle.

"Rest in the sky; exert yourself in the intermediate space"—with these words, he places in the center of the bricks a pap of wild rice (*naivāra*) cooked in milk, dedicated to Bṛhaspati, within a water-jar.
"For your splendor, for your luster, for your sight, for your light, for your seed, for your offspring"—with these words, he throws two gold chips each into the two [fires].

"O Agni, you, the bull, the one who is observant..."—having thrown a bull-shaped piece of gold onto the layer, he touches it with the *klṛpti* formula, thinking, "He shall pile up the layer and the non-layer. (Section 24) || 14 ||

Whatever has been piled by you, O Agni, whatever has been piled by you, whatever was deficient here, or whatever was in excess—may all the gods and the Aṅgirases pile it; may the Ādityas fill your layer. Those logs of yours, O Agni... [the layer] and the non-layer... May we, O Agni, be possessed of wealth, sufficient for the sacrifice and for the sacrificial fee. May the pressing-stone speak over the stalk of Soma; may we serve Indra with the pressed drop. Bestow upon us, O Jātavedas, increase of wealth and strength.

May we set down the sacrifice, rich in honey and full of kind words; let us press the Soma and serve you with the sacrifice, O Śakra. We have heard that you are the lord of riches; O Agni, Lord of Wealth, come among me with food consisting of cattle, horses, abundant nourishment, and gold. May Heaven and Earth milk for you their milk; may the serpent glide along with water. With Prajāpati I satisfy myself; my soul was empty—[fill it] with Rudra.

With the seven verses beginning, "To him who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants—Rudra who has entered all beings—to that Rudra, O gods, let there be homage," he touches the *svayamcit* (self-piled) altar and covers it with the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks. || 15 ||
With two mantras each, he lays down one *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick each. || 16 ||
Having placed it with the former formula, he touches it with the *sūdadohas* verse. || 17 ||
In all the bricks, he places the *tayādevata* formula at the end. || 18 ||

A black horse, or one that is dark-brown, stands to the north; having touched it and having brought earth from the *cātvāla* pit, he spreads it out with the verse, "Thou art asked about heaven" (*pṛṣṭo divi*). || 19 ||
That becomes the layer. || 11.8.20 ||

The fire that is within the waters, that which is in Vṛtra, that which is in man, and that which is in stone; that which has entered into all beings—to those fires let this be offered. The fire whom they call the eater of oblations, whom they call desire, whom they call the giver and the receiver; he who is the most divine among the gods, born of austerity—to those fires let this be offered. "He who is asked in heaven"—this is the verse. Soma who is within, who is within the cows, who has entered into birds and who is in wild beasts.

"May this oblation be for those fires which entered into bipeds and quadrupeds; for those by whom the chariots of Indra were fashioned, who is Vaiśvānara and who belongs to the Viśvedevas; for that wise and powerful one who prevails over many attackers—may this oblation be for those fires. Having laid down each layer of the altar with the six verses beginning "For him whose food is the bull, whose food is the cow," he makes the offerings. (21)
In this manner, from this point upward, all [bricks] beginning with the Ṛṣabha are piled and performed identically. || 22 ||

With a *gāyatrī* verse addressed to Agni, he should touch the first layer; with a *triṣṭubh*, the second; with a *jagatī*, the third; with an *anuṣṭubh*, the fourth; and with a *paṅkti*, the fifth. For all of them, the second [verse] is the *dhāmacchat*. "O Agni Jātavedas, many are your abodes"—this is the *dhāmacchat* [verse]. "O Agni, being born, bring the gods here for him who has spread the sacrificial grass; you are our Hotṛ, worthy of praise. "We have approached with a great mind the youngest one who has shone forth, well-kindled in his own dwelling."

Between the two wide worlds, Citrabhānu (the one of wondrous light), well-invoked on all sides, faces every direction. He is the maker of wisdom, the ordainer, the perfecter of the sacrifice—Agni, the Hotṛ, the most pervasive thought. Men choose you alone for the small oblation and likewise for the great; no other than you do they choose. Like Manu, we establish you; like Manu, we kindle you. O Agni, O Aṅgiras, like Manu, worship the gods for the one who seeks the gods. For Agni, the lord of all people, bestows the prize-winning steed upon the one who desires it.
"Agni for wealth, self-sustaining; he, being pleased, goes to the noble; bring nourishment to the singers"—these are the verses that are recited. || 23 ||
There are six *upasad* days. || 24 ||
He piles the fire-altar with the *anupasada* rites; one layer (*citi*) is piled each day, and the final layer takes two days. || 25 ||
There are three sets of four-breasted vows; likewise, there are those with three breasts, two breasts, and one breast. || 26 ||

Having performed the afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites, and having led the white horse clockwise around [the altar] while reciting, "When you first cried out at birth," they dwell, they dwell. (Section 25) 27.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the eleventh book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Thus ends the eleventh book in the Satyāṣāḍha-sūtra. 11.

The Manuscript Catalogue for the Edition. Now, out of gratitude, the names and designations of those who have kindly provided manuscripts of this *Hiraṇyakeśi Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, along with its commentary *Prayogacandrikā*, for the purpose of this edition are being made public: The manuscript designated as (Ka. contains the commentary alone, belonging to Bhaṭṭa Raghunātha Dīkṣita, surnamed Daṇḍavatī.

The Telugu-script manuscripts: (kha.)—marked as such, belonging to Daṇḍavata Upādhyāya Śivadīkṣita; complete. (ga.)—marked as such, belonging to Ve. Śā. Saṃ. Śaṃkaradīkṣita Tāpasakara; complete. (gha.)—marked as such, belonging to Ve. Śā. Saṃ. Gurunāthadīkṣita Mulagundakara; containing questions 11–14, 327 folios. (ṅa.)—marked as such; containing only the root text (mūlamātra); questions 11–12, 117 folios.

This is the complete [text] of Ve. Śā. Saṃ. Dhundhirāja Dīkṣita Somayājī Bāpaṭ, residents of the village of Pācavaḍa (Sātārā), who are adorned with the title *Śrotriya-Cūḍāmaṇi* and are performers of Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*). (Ca.)—marked as such—contains the root text (*mūlamātra*) only; it is complete. This is the root text only of Ve. Śā. Saṃ. ‘Aṇṇabhaṭṭa Abhyaṅkara’, residents of Puṇyapattana. (Cha.)—marked as such.

Questions: (11, 12, 15, 24, 25). A portion is missing in the manuscript (Gauri Maṇḍal, Mysore Oriental Library), which is written in Nāgarī script from Devanāgarī and is designated as "Ja. It contains only the root text (*mūlamātra*). Questions (21, 22) belong to Ke. Brahmaśrī Kāśīnātha Śāstrī Somayājī Vāī, who is adorned with the title *Dharmamātaṇḍa* and the surname *Lele*. This is the list of reference manuscripts.

6. Now, out of gratitude, the names and designations of those individuals who, with hearts solely inclined toward the welfare of others, have provided manuscripts of the *Hiraṇyakeśi Śrauta Sūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha for the purpose of this edition, are presented as follows: The manuscript designated as (Ka. contains the text from the eleventh praśna up to the end, belonging to Vaidika Rājaratna Vāmana Raghunātha Bhaṭṭa Ḍoṅgare of Puṇyapattana.

The date of its transcription is Śaka year 1709. The manuscript designated (kha. consists of 220 folios and is incomplete; it belongs to Rā. Rā. Kuśābhāū Abhyaṅkara Vakil. The manuscript designated (ga. consists of 163 folios and is incomplete; it belongs to Ve. Rā. Vināyakaśāstrī Vāīkara. The manuscript designated (gha. consists of 247 folios and is incomplete; it belongs to Ve. Rā. Bālaśāstrī Abhyaṅkara, whose residence is Vāī. (ṅa.)...

Thus, twenty manuscript copies—including the one titled *iti saṃjñitam* (numbered 301), which consists of 301 folios and is fragmentary—of the practical manuals (*prayoga*) for the Hiraṇyakeśī school’s fire-altar construction (*cayana*), horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), royal consecration (*rājasūya*), the *Kāṭhaka*, optional animal sacrifices (*kāmyapaśu*), expiations (*prāyaścitta*), and so forth, were provided by Ve. Mū. Rā. Bhāskara Kṛṣṇabhaṭṭa Limaye Dīkṣita for the purpose of consultation; their residence is in Pune.

They have rendered great assistance in the work of editing the *Prayogacandrikā*. 6–7. An alphabetical list of the works and authors cited in Mahādeva Śāstrī’s commentary on the *Prayogacandrikā*: *Aṣṭādhyāyī*—composed by the sage Pāṇini. *Agnipurāṇa*—composed by the great seer Vedavyāsa.

The Atharvaveda; the Atri-smṛti; the Āṅgirasa-smṛti; the Amarakoṣa; the Śrauta-paddhati composed by Anantadeva; the Dīpikā (the Āpastamba-Śrauta-prayoga) composed by Aṇḍilācārya; the Āpastamba-smṛti; the Āpastamba-sūtra; the Āśvalāyana-smṛti; the Āśvalāyana-sūtra; the Udgātṛ-paddhati composed by Rāmakṛṣṇa Tripāṭhī; the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā with the commentary of Sāyaṇa; the Ekāgni-kāṇḍa with the commentary composed by Haradatta; and the Aitareya-brāhmaṇa with the commentary of Sāyaṇa.

The Aitareya Āraṇyaka with the commentary of Sāyaṇa; the Auśanasasmṛti; the Kapardikārikā; the commentary on the (Āpastamba) Śrautasūtra composed by Kapardisvāmin; the Karmāntasūtra; the Karmapradīpa composed by Kātyāyana; the Kaśyapa Saṃhitā; the Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra with the commentary of Karka; and the Kṛṣṇayajurveda Saṃhitā with the commentary of Bhaṭṭabhāskara.

The Brāhmaṇa of the Kṛṣṇayajurveda—1; the Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇayajurveda; the Mantra-Brāhmaṇa of the Kṛṣṇayajurveda; the Kāśīkhaṇḍa (from the Skanda Purāṇa) together with the commentary by Rāmeśvara Yogin; the Kaṇva Saṃhitā with the commentary of Sāyaṇa; the Sūtra of Kātyāyana; the Smṛti of Kātyāyana; the Kauṣītaki Sūtra; the Khādira Gṛhyasūtra with the commentary of Rudraskanda; and the Gṛhyasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha with the commentary of Mātṛdatta.

The Gṛhyasūtra (of Āśvalāyana), accompanied by the commentary composed by Gopīnātha; the *Candrikā* ritual manual compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī; the Gṛhyasūtra composed by Āpastamba, together with the commentary (*bhāṣya*) of Kapardisvāmin; the Gṛhyasūtra accompanied by the commentary (*vṛtti*) composed by Haradatta; the [Gṛhyasūtra] together with the practical manual (*prayogavṛtti*) of Aṇḍilācārya; [the Gṛhyasūtra] accompanied by the commentary (*bhāṣya*) of Sudarśanācārya; and [the Gṛhyasūtra] together with the commentary composed by Mahādeva Yajvan.

*Gṛhyasaṃgraha* (Chandoga); *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* (Āśvalāyana); *Gṛhyaratnakaṇṭhabhūṣaṇa* by Vaidikasārvabhauma; *Gobhilagṛhyasūtra* accompanied by the commentary (*bhāṣya*) of Candrakānta Bhaṭṭācārya; *Gotamasūtra* accompanied by the commentary (*bhāṣya*) of Maskarī; *Gotamasūtra* (Kriyākāṇḍa); *Gotrapravaranibandhasaṃgraha* composed by Candracūḍī Bhaṭṭa; *Saṃskāranirṇaya* (Āpastamba Gṛhya); and *Candrikā*, a manual on Śrauta rites.

*Chandogapariśiṣṭa*—with the commentary by Nārāyaṇa and the *Candrakānta-vṛtti*. *Naimini Gṛhyasūtra*—accompanied by the commentary of Bhaṭṭa Kumārila. *Jaimini Śrautasūtra* (Pūrvamīmāṃsā)—with the *Śābarabhāṣya*. *Jaimini Nyāyamālā*—composed by Mādhavācārya. *Jaimini Sūtravṛtti* (Jyotiṣa). *Tattvamuktāvalī*—composed by Nanda Paṇḍita. *Tantrarahasya*—composed by Rāmānujācārya.

The Taittirīya Saṃhitā with the commentary of Mādhava; the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa with the commentary of Mādhava; the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka together with the Tribhāṣyaratna on the Taittirīya Prātiśākhya; the Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana composed by Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara; the Dattakamīmāṃsā composed by Nanda Paṇḍita; the Dattakacandrikā composed by Kubera; and the Dattakaustubha composed by Anantadeva.

*Dattakasāra* by Dattaka; *Daśanirṇaya* composed by Vaidikasārvabhauma; *Dakṣasmṛti*; the *Dānakhaṇḍa* (of Hemādri); the *Baudhāyana-gṛhyasūtra* accompanied by the commentary of Rudraskanda; *Dharmapradīpa*; *Dharmapravṛtti*; the *Dharmasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha with the *Vaijayantī* commentary by Mahādeva; the [Āpastamba-dharmasūtra] together with the *Ujjvalā* composed by Haradatta; and the [Bodhāyana-dharmasūtra] with the commentary of Govindācārya.

Thus [ends] the Vaikhānasa [text]. —Today indeed, [I offer salutations] to Him whose lotus feet are worshipped by hosts of gods beginning with Indra, the lord of the circle of infinite millions of universes adorned with the multitude of the auspicious and infinite virtues of the True One; to Him whose divine incarnations, resplendent with rows of pure titles sung by the forest-dwelling sages and ascetics whose minds act as bees at the nectar-flood of intense bliss trickling from those feet; and who has fulfilled the desires of all His devotees...

Having girded his loins with the fulfillment [of his purpose], he possesses the majesty of knowledge blossomed through the excellence of a pure intellect obtained by the grace and favor of the venerable Supreme Lord; he has rendered fruitful the entire circle of the earth; and he has whitened the circumference of the quarters with stainless fame sung by the Sarasvatī of learned men, which attained its expansion through the multitude of virtues—wisdom, benevolence, integrity, and prosperity—that were honored in assemblies esteemed by various distinguished scholars shining over the whole surface of the earth.

Today, before all the venerable scholars residing throughout the entire circle of the earth—those who are worthy recipients of supreme honor, whose feet are worshipped by the lotus-like heads of all the virtuous, who have reached the further shore of the vast ocean of all the Vedas and Shastras, and whose intentions are freed from the shackles of false learning by the skillful mastery of the entire collection of arts—I shall now offer this new introduction.

Our mind yearns to announce this auspicious and novel tidings with a few introductory words, which have blossomed through the sweet and playful splendor of the Goddess of Speech—the deity of divine eloquence—who is intensely eager due to the fresh and surging excellence of our devotion, and who is the very abode of the favor of Sarasvatī.
Therefore, let the minds of all learned people, refined by the play of discernment, turn toward this present subject from among the multitude of various matters currently under consideration.

Having respectfully requested with joined palms that you would deign to lend your attention to the portion of my address concerning the report of this new event, we now begin to introduce our own subject matter by way of a preamble: "O all you virtuous ones! It is indeed well known to your honors—who follow the path of all Vedic dharma and are endowed with noble conduct."

Since the Veda, which is the primordial seed of all speech, is the very form of the Lord, this very point is here briefly analyzed: "That lotus of the world was entered by that very Viṣṇu, who illuminates all qualities; within it, he himself became the Creator consisting of the Veda, whom they call the Self-born (Svayambhū). Thus it was stated by Maitreya.

The Self-Existent One (Svayambhū), who is Viṣṇu himself in manifest form, shines eternally together with the manifestations of the knowledge produced from Himself—namely, the Vedas, Upavedas, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, Upapurāṇas, Vārttā, Daṇḍanīti, Ānvīkṣikī, and so forth. From that very Lord, whose nature is knowledge and who serves as the material cause, the manifestation of the Vedic sciences occurred. He created from His mouth the Vedas known as Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan; and He established in due order the sacrificial weapons, the ritual worship, the hymns of praise, and the rites of atonement.

"From his eastern face, he brought forth Āyurveda; from his southern face, Dhanurveda; from his western face, Gāndharvaveda; and from his northern face, Sthāpatyaveda. The Lord, the all-seeing, created Itihāsa and Purāṇa as the fifth Veda from all his faces" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa, Third Skandha). By such passages, it is shown that the Blessed One taught those Vedas—which are eternally established and identical to His own nature—to Brahmā through His inconceivable power and formal initiation (*vaidha-dīkṣā*).

This very point is stated in the Śruti: "He who in the beginning created Brahmā and who indeed imparted the Vedas to him. By this scripture, it is said that he manifested the eternally established Vedas—which reside within himself in an extremely subtle form as the *praṇava* and the *mātṛkā*—through the mouths of Brahmā in their gross forms as the *Ṛg* and other Vedas. For this very reason, it is said: "The divine speech, consisting of the Vedas, which is without beginning or end and eternal, was emitted by the Self-born in the beginning; from it all activities proceed."

This is because of the Smṛti, and because of the Śruti: "By speech, which is multiform and eternal" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.11). Thus, the eternity of the Vedas is established. As for what was said—"The Ṛg-verses and Sāman-chants were born" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.11)—there too, it should be understood that there is merely a manifestation (*āvirbhāva*), since the root *jan* signifies becoming manifest (*prādurbhāva*). If it is asked, "What then is the status of the Vyāsa-sūtra, 'Because [Brahman] is the source of the scriptures' (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.3)?"—in that context, the word *yoni* should be understood as meaning "means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, that sūtra—"I ask you about that person known from the Upaniṣads" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26)—teaches that Brahman is to be known through the Upaniṣads. Furthermore, scriptural passages such as, "In this very way, O Maitreyī, the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, etc., are the breath of this great Being" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.10), also refute the notion of the Vedas having a temporal origin. For the intent of the Śruti is precisely this: that the Lord, like exhalation and inhalation, has effortlessly manifested the Vedas which were already present within him.

But surely, even if Brahman is the agent of manifestation through its own play (*līlā*), it does not thereby follow that the Vedas have Brahman as their material cause (*upādāna*). And if that were the case, how could they not be of human origin (*pauruṣeya*)?

Furthermore, even though those Vedas are the work of Brahman, they do not possess what is called "human authorship" (*pauruṣeyatva*). For if human authorship were defined merely by being produced by a person, then even for one who considers himself a Mīmāṃsaka, the Vedas would face the consequence of losing their authority; this is because, although the individual phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal, the specific sequence (*ānupūrvī-viśeṣa*) is produced by a person. Moreover, if the status of being non-human (*apauruṣeya*) were established solely on the basis of the eternity of the phonemes, then even worldly sentences such as "tat tvam asi" (That thou art) would consequently have to be considered non-human.

Therefore, being composed after perceiving an object through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—that is, being of human origin—is not the cause of the defect characterized by dependence. And this [human authorship] does not apply to the Vedas, because the meaning of the Vedas is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition. Indeed, this very point has been demonstrated by the Śruti through the analogy of breathing. For instance, although breathing arises from a person, it is not produced by the person's intention to act, since it is observed even during deep sleep.

Thus, although the entire Veda arises from Brahman—which is of the nature of knowledge and serves as its material cause—it is not produced by a desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) on the part of Brahman; for the meaning of the Veda is not an object of any means of valid cognition other than the Veda itself. By this method, according to the principle that "the qualities of the cause indeed initiate the qualities of the effect," the eternity of the Vedas manifested from Brahman is established, just as the eternity of Brahman—their cause—is established.

1. [3] At the very beginning, these Vedas existed in a subtle state in the form of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om). From that *praṇava*, the manifestation of the *mātṛkā*s occurred; those very *mātṛkā*s are what are called the "enumeration of syllables" (*akṣara-samāmnāya*). From that very enumeration of syllables, all eighteen branches of knowledge, beginning with *Ānvīkṣikī*, were likewise produced through the door of Brahman.

This very point was stated by Maitreya to Vidura in the third book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, beginning with: "He created from his mouth the Vedas known as Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan," and continuing through: "Logic (Ānvīkṣikī), the Triple Veda (Trayī), commerce (Vārtā), and likewise the science of government (Daṇḍanīti)," up until the end: "O dear one, [these proceed] from the Self that is the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman). Among those eighteen branches of knowledge, each has spread out infinitely due to its countless sub-branches.

Now, those eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) are briefly presented here according to the sequence of enumeration and so forth: therein, the Vedas are fourfold, distinguished as Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharvan. The six auxiliary sciences of the Veda (*vedāṅga*) are phonetics (*śikṣā*), ritual manuals (*kalpa*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), etymology (*nirukta*), astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*), and metrics (*chandaḥviciti*). The four secondary auxiliaries (*upāṅga*) are the Purāṇas, the expansion of logic (*nyāyavistara*), hermeneutics (*mīmāṃsā*), and the treatises on law (*dharmaśāstra*).

Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, and Arthaśāstra—these four constitute the Upavedas; thus, when combined, there are eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyās*). Among these, the Upapurāṇas are included within the Mahāpurāṇas. Within the Nyāya system, the Vaiśeṣika system is included. Within Mīmāṃsā, Vedānta is included. And within Dharmaśāstra, the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa, as well as Sāṃkhya, Pātañjala, Pāśupata, Vaiṣṇava, and other systems, are included.

Thus, there are these eighteen forms of knowledge (*vidyā*), which constitute the systems of Dharma for those who hold to the existence of the sacred truths (*āstika*). All other systems of Dharma belonging to non-Vedic (*adeśin*) schools are included within these very ones. In this manner, the distinction between the various systems that serve the ultimate goal—either directly or indirectly—by means of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedopākaraṇa*), has been shown merely by way of direction. Now, the cause for the distinction in the essential nature of these systems [will be explained].

First, the distinction of purpose is stated briefly: therein, the Veda is a non-human (apauruṣeya) statement that establishes Dharma. It consists of Mantras and Brāhmaṇas. As it is said [in Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra, Paribhāṣā]: "The name 'Veda' applies to both Mantra and Brāhmaṇa. The nature of these two has been explained elsewhere. Among them, the Mantras are those which illuminate the substances and deities that serve as the instruments of ritual performance. They are of three kinds, distinguished as Ṛc, Yajus, and Sāman. The Atharvaveda is included within these three...

Because they are included within [the aforementioned categories], they are not mentioned separately. Thus, the *mantras* have been defined. The *Brāhmaṇa*, which consists of the exposition of the *mantras*, is also threefold: that which takes the form of an injunction (*vidhi*), that which takes the form of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and that which is distinct from both. Regarding these, the detailed distinctions between the definitions of injunctions and so forth should be understood from other sources. Furthermore, this *Brāhmaṇa* is of eight kinds. As it is stated in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*: "Itihāsa, Purāṇa, Vidyā, Upaniṣads, Ślokas..."

"The Sūtras, Vyākhyānas, and Anuvyākhyānas are indeed His very breaths. Among these, *itihāsa* is that which sets forth narratives. *Purāṇa* is that which describes the prior states of the universe. *Vidyā* refers to those teachings that set forth the knowledge of the self for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*). That which sets forth the secrets of the deities to be meditated upon is the *Upaniṣad*. Those mantras that are recited in verse-form are *ślokas*. A *sūtra* is that which sets forth a condensed meaning. A *vyākhyāna* is that which sets forth an expanded meaning.

The *Anuvyākhyāna* is that which brings about the clarity of the *Vyākhyāna*. These are the *Brāhmaṇas*. Furthermore, the *Śikṣā*, *Kalpa*, *Rahasya*, and so forth, serve precisely to establish the status of being auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) of the Veda; for there exists a relationship between the *Mantra* and the *Brāhmaṇa* as the explained (*vyākhyeya*) and the explanation (*vyākhyāna*). And this has been established by the authors of the *Vṛtti* in their commentary on the Sūtra: "That which is based on the wording of the Mantras" (*māntravarṇikam*). Thus, the Veda—consisting of the *Karmakāṇḍa*, *Guṇakāṇḍa*, and *Brahmakāṇḍa*—is the cause of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.

And that [Veda] is divided into three forms—the duties of the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Udgātṛ—for the purpose of defining the distribution of royal rituals. The Atharvaveda, however, as the fourth Veda, although it establishes the duties of the Brahman priest remaining from the triad of Vedas, is indeed useful for all purposes by teaching rites such as those for pacification (*śāntika*), nourishment (* pauṣṭika*), and malevolent magic (*abhicārika*). Due to differences in the teachings of various teachers, there exist numerous distinct branches (*śākhā*) for each Veda.

That knowledge is to be understood from the Vedic treatise known as the *Caraṇavyūha*. Now, the purpose of the six Vedāṅgas, beginning with Śikṣā, is stated. Among them, Śikṣā and Vyākaraṇa are employed for the sake of correctly understanding the pronunciation of phonemes and the grammatical correctness of words, respectively. Nirukta is employed for the sake of knowing the meaning of the mantra-texts.

In that regard, the *Nirukta* indeed demonstrates the meaning of Vedic words by defining the fourfold categories of speech—nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), particles (*nipāta*), and prefixes (*upasarga*)—through etymological analysis. Likewise, since the *Ṛgveda* mantras are characterized by meters such as the *anuṣṭubh* bound in quarters, and because scriptural condemnation is heard for those who do not know them, the *Chandoviciti* (metrics) composed by Piṅgala is useful for the knowledge of meter. Similarly, the *Jyotiṣa* (astronomy/astrology) composed by Āditya and others is useful for knowing the proper times for Vedic rites such as the *darśa* sacrifice.

Thus, for the sake of understanding the specific sequence of Vedic performances through the integration of qualities from other recensions (*śākhā*), there is the utility of the *Kalpasūtras* composed by Āśvalāyana, Sāṃkhyāyana, Satyāṣāḍha, Āpastamba, Baudhāyana, Vādhūla, Bharadvāja, Vaikhānasa, Agniveśya, Jaimini, Mānava, Varāha, Maitrāyaṇīya, Kātyāyana, Pāraskara, Lāṭyāyana, Bāhyāraṇa, Gobhila, Khādira, Kauśika, and others. In this manner, the six [aids] have been defined.

The specific purposes of the Vedāṅgas. Now, the specific purposes of the four Upāṅgas are stated briefly. Among them, the Purāṇas—expounding upon the primary creation, secondary creation, the Manvantaras, the genealogies, and the histories of the dynastic lineages—were composed by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa. These number fifty-four, categorized as Mahāpurāṇas, Upapurāṇas, and Upopapurāṇas.

The sole proper purpose of those Purāṇas is the demonstration of knowledge regarding primary creation, secondary dissolution, and so forth, as well as the engagement in the practice of the True Dharma (saddharma). Nyāya is the science of logic (ānvīkṣikī) composed by Gautama; its purpose is the attainment of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) through the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) derived from the enumeration, definition, and examination of the sixteen categories (padārtha), beginning with the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and the objects of cognition (prameya). The Vaiśeṣika treatise composed by Kaṇāda and others likewise has as its objective the exposition of the seven categories.

And it has been stated previously that this [Nyāya] is included within Nyāya itself. Mīmāṃsā is of two kinds: Dharmamīmāṃsā and Śārīrakamīmāṃsā. Among these, Dharmamīmāṃsā consists of twelve chapters (*dvādaśādhyāyī*) and sixteen chapters (*ṣoḍaśādhyāyī*). Dharmamīmāṃsā begins with "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*) and ends with "Just as the *yājyā*-prompting, just as the *yājyā*-prompting" (*yathā yājyasaṃpreṣo yathā yājyasaṃpreṣaḥ*), composed by the venerable Jaimini. Its utility lies in the thorough understanding of the arrangement of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), preceded by the knowledge of the means of valid cognition for Dharma (*dharmapramāṇa*) and so forth. And Śārīrakamīmāṃsā—
Regarding that subject, specific points to be stated separately here we shall explain further below.

[5] Starting from "Then, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*) and ending with "Non-return, on account of the scriptural word; non-return, on account of the scriptural word" (*anāvṛttiḥ śabdādanāvṛttiḥ śabdāt*), the venerable Bādarāyaṇa has composed [this work], which presents the logical principles (*nyāya*) expounding the investigation known as *śravaṇa*, which is the cause for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the identity of the individual soul and Brahman. And the purpose (*prayojana*) of that [work] is the direct realization of the unity of the individual soul and Brahman.

Thus, the Dharmaśāstras composed by Manu, Yājñavalkya, Viṣṇu, Yama, Āṅgiras, Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, Śātātapa, Parāśara, Gotama, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Hārīta, Āpastamba, Uśanas, Nārada, Vyāsa, Kātyāyana, Bṛhaspati, Devala, Nārada, Paithīnasi, and others, establish the specific duties of the castes and stages of life through their systematic classification. The very purpose of these works is the precise knowledge of the specific duties pertaining to the castes and stages of life.

Thus, the *Mahābhārata* composed by Vyāsa and the *Rāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki are renowned as historical narratives (*itihāsa*). As was stated previously, these two are included within the category of *Dharmaśāstra*. Similarly, the science of mantras common to all deities, as formulated by Śrī Mahādeva, Brahmā, Gautama, and others, is also included within the *Dharmaśāstra*. Its purpose is the attainment of one's desired fruits from one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Thus has been described the distinction in the purposes of the four auxiliary sciences (*upāṅga*).

Now, the specific purposes of the four Upavedas are briefly stated. Corresponding to the four Vedas, there are four Upavedas in their respective order. Among them, Āyurveda—the Upaveda of the Ṛgveda—was composed by Brahmā, Prajāpati, Aśvin, and others, and it consists of eight sections (*sthānas*): Sūtra, Śārīra, Indriya, Cikitsā, Nidāna, Vimāna, Kalpa, and Siddhi. Furthermore, the science of erotics (*kāmaśāstra*) is also included within Āyurveda itself, since Suśruta mentions the science of erotics under the name *vājīkaraṇa*.

Thus, the purpose of the entire Ayurveda is the knowledge of disease, its causes, the cessation of disease, and the means for that cessation. And this [purpose] is indeed conducive to liberation (*mokṣa*), by way of producing bodily health which serves as a means to liberation. In the same way, the Dhanurveda is an Upaveda of the Yajurveda; it consists of four quarters and was composed by Viśvāmitra. The purpose of the Dhanurveda is the performance of one's own duty (*svadharma*) by Kṣatriyas, warfare, and the protection of subjects from wicked bandits, thieves, and the like.

Thus, the Gāndharva Śāstra, which is an Upaveda of the Sāmaveda, was composed by the teacher Bharata. In it, manifold subjects are expounded through the distinctions of dance, song, and instrumental music. The deity of that Gāndharvaveda is the attainment of perfection in propitiating the gods, non-conceptual meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi), and so forth. Furthermore, the various treatises on aesthetics (rasa-śāstra) were likewise composed by Bharata himself and are included within the Gāndharvaveda; these consist of descriptions of aesthetic flavor (rasa), literary style (rīti), verbal and semantic ornaments (śabdālaṃkāra and arthālaṃkāra), as well as the hero, the heroine, and other dramatic elements.

Now, the Arthaśāstra is the Upaveda of the Atharvaveda; its purpose is the attainment of all worldly happiness. Furthermore, in accordance with that very [Arthaśāstra], the Nītiśāstra was also aphorized by Manu and others, and composed by Kāmandaki and others. It is manifold through its divisions such as peace and war (*saṃdhivigraha*). Its purpose is precisely proficiency in all worldly transactions.

In this manner, various treatises—namely the treatise on horses (*aśvaśāstra*), the treatise on elephants (*gajaśāstra*), the treatise on arts and crafts (*śilpaśāstra*), the treatise on cookery (*sūpaśāstra*), and the treatise on the sixty-four arts (*catuḥṣaṣṭikalāśāstra*)—have been composed by various sages such as Śālihotra and others. The specific worldly purpose of each of these should be observed. Thus, the eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), along with their purposes, have been briefly stated by way of naming them.

In this very way, the various divisions of the systems (*prasthāna-bheda*) that are concordant with the Vedas have been demonstrated: namely, the Sāṃkhya scripture composed by the sage Kapila, the Yoga scripture composed by the sage Patañjali, the Pāśupata scripture fashioned by the Lord Paśupati, and the Vaiṣṇava scriptures such as the Pāñcarātra composed by Nārada and others. Indeed, in this manner, the body of the Blessed One, who consists of the mass of the Vedas, is described as being composed of knowledge (*jñānamaya*).

Thus, because the entire order of creation, origin, and so forth, proceeded from this very Brahman who consists of the Veda, everything is faultless. Now, let us return to the subject at hand. Regarding what was previously stated—that the Lord consisting of the Veda is enumerated among the *aṅgas* (limbs) and *upāṅgas* (subsidiary limbs)—a certain clarification concerning that matter is now presented. Starting with the words, "Whatever Ṛg-verses they studied" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 2.9), and continuing with "the Purāṇas and the Kalpas" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 2.9), the term *kalpas* refers to these [Kalpa texts].

"Mādhava states that the *Kalpasūtras* are those which set forth the practical applications (*prayoga*). Likewise, it is said in the *Gopatha Brāhmaṇa* of the Atharvaveda: 'In this manner, all these Vedas were created together with their *Kalpas*' (GoPūPra 2.5). Similarly, in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*: 'To him he said: "Two kinds of knowledge are to be known," so indeed say those who know Brahman—the higher (*parā*) and the lower (*aparā*). "

"In that regard, the lower [knowledge] consists of the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvaveda, Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, Chandas, and Jyotiṣa. Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable is attained" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.5). Here, *kalpa* means a *sūtra*, a treatise; the meaning is that *kalpa* refers to the sequence of things to be performed. This is discussed in the section on the inherent authority of the *Kalpasūtras* (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.7).

Regarding the dispute as to whether the *Kalpasūtras* are authoritative as independent works or as dependent ones, and upon considering whether they are of human origin (*pauruṣeya*) or not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), we maintain that the *Kalpasūtras* and similar texts possess authority as independent works precisely because their authority would otherwise be untenable. This is because postulating a separate source for them would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and because of the traditional Smṛti statement: "The Veda has six limbs."

This is the presentation of the position [of the opponent]: since the Kalpasūtras are observed [to exist], it is difficult to establish the meaningfulness of these authoritative Vedic statements if they were of human origin; for designations such as "Satyāṣāḍhīya" and so on can be explained in the same way as "Śākala" and other such names; and because there is seen to be an injunction for the study of the Kalpas themselves in the passage, "The Purāṇas and the Kalpas" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.9.10).

The refutation of that [position] is as follows: since the names such as *Satyāṣāḍhī* and others involve a firm recollection of an author, it is impossible for them to be based solely on oral transmission; thus, their human origin remains unimpaired. Furthermore, because it is necessary to compose even those works directly based on perception—such as the *Kalpas*—using easily understood words for the sake of summarizing what is difficult to comprehend, and because their status as objects of the injunction for the eternal *Brahmayajña* is also justified by the eternity of the tradition, the entire collection of *Kalpasūtras* is not an independent authority.

The absence of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is also a single indicative mark for the non-Vedic nature of the *Kalpa* [texts]. Furthermore, the purpose [of this argument] is to establish the lack of authority of the *Kalpasūtras* regarding those matters taught by direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣaśruti*), such as "on the new moon day" (*amāvāsyāyām*, Śrautasūtra 1.3.19), which are present in portions of the text such as "the entire dark fortnight" (*sarvo'parapakṣaḥ*, Khādiragṛhyasūtra 7.1). In this regard, the example cited by the author of the Bhāṣya, namely "the entire dark fortnight," should be considered.

Furthermore, since it is established by direct perception that both the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) constitute the time for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), there is no [separate] *pathikṛt* offering for the transgression of the time of the New and Full Moon sacrifices. This is because the *pathikṛt* offering is prescribed as a quality (*guṇa*) for the very *āyayāga* belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices, following a censure of the common performance (*tantra*) of the two. This is understood from the scriptural text of another recension cited by the Sūtrakāra and others, beginning with "Now, for some, what is the separation of this? (*atha keṣāṃ vivā etasya*, ŚB 15.3.2), which conveys the censure [of the separate performance]. Indeed, [it is not so].

By the logic of censure (*nindānyāya*), there is praise for the quality of being the performer of the path (*pathikṛt*). Furthermore, since the state of having a common ritual procedure (*samānatantratā*) is inferred as being accepted in other recensional branches (*śākhāntara*) through an alternative option, and because this is supported by statements such as "vā" (in *Saṃhitā Śrautasūtra* 15.14.3) which are consistent with Satyāṣāḍha’s text, and because otherwise it would be untenable, the performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices is possible even at another time.

Furthermore, one should observe that the claim made in the *Vārtikas* and other works—that sūtras such as "Or both, because there is no distinction" (*Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra* 3.8.4)—are invalid because they contradict the Śruti and are rooted in fallacious reasoning, is itself untenable. Moreover, we shall relate some account of the life of this author of the Sūtras named Satyāṣāḍha: on which riverbank and in which field did he reside?

It is understood from the *Skandopapurāṇa* that the great sage Satyāṣāḍha, born in the lineage of the great ṛṣi Vaiśampāyana, lived on the eastern side of the Sahya mountain, in the field of Paraśurāma, or on the banks of the Haraṇakāśī river. Once, the sage Satyāṣāḍha beheld the most venerable Vedavyāsa approaching his hermitage. Having offered him hospitality according to tradition and once he was comfortably seated, he asked: "Among the gods, who is the most excellent?"

Then, having understood from his own mouth that Śiva alone is supreme, he went to Kāśī to perform penance. Thereupon, Śaṅkara, being well-pleased by his austerity, appeared before him and bestowed upon him his desired boons. Thus, having obtained divine vision through the grace of Śiva, the sage Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin became honored everywhere; this is indeed well known to those who are conversant with the Vedas.

And many followers of that [school] reside in the region of Paraśurāma (in various places). In that Sūtra, the subject matters are summarized as follows: "Having received the branch from the sage who was the propagator of the Veda known as the Yajus and who had acquired its meaning from his teacher Vyāsa, the eminent sage [Tittiri], possessing a body in the form of a partridge bird, divided his own branch and taught it to the lords of sages. The venerable Hiraṇyakeśin is the one named Satyāṣāḍha."

The *Kalpasūtra* known as the *Saptaviṃśati-praśna* (Twenty-seven Questions) is now presented. In the first two questions, the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are described in great detail. In the third, the establishment of the sacred fires (*Ādhāna*) along with its ancillaries and the *Agnihotra* are treated. In the fourth, the animal sacrifice (*Paśubandha*), and in the fifth, the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices. In the sixth, the measurement of the sacrificial vessels for oblations (*Haviryajña*) and the rules for one who is away from home (*Pravāsa-vidhi*) are given. With three subsequent questions, he set forth the duties of the *Adhvaryu* priest for the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. In the tenth question, he taught the duties of the sacrificer (*Yājamāna*), the office of the *Brahman* priest, and the rules regarding sacrificial fees (*Dakṣiṇā*).

In the second book (praśna), the construction of the fire-altar (agnicayana) and the collection of materials for the hearth (mukhā-sambharaṇa) and so forth are treated; in the thirteenth, the Vājapeya sacrifice; and in the fourteenth, the Aśvamedha. Then, in the fifteenth book, expiation (prāyaścitta) is explained in detail, as well as the Agnihotra, the sacrifices pertaining to the iṣṭis, those pertaining to the animal sacrifice (pāśuka), and likewise those pertaining to the Soma sacrifice. In the sixteenth, however, the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha), the Mahāvrata ritual, and the Gavamayana are discussed. Then, in the seventeenth book, the performance of the one-day (ekāha) and multi-day (ahīna) sacrifices is set forth. Subsequently, in the eighteenth book, various forms of sacrificial sessions (satra) are described.

In the nineteenth and twentieth [sections], there is the determination of the domestic rites (*gṛhyakarman*). Then, in the twenty-first book (*praśna*), there are the determinations regarding the *hautra* and the *pravara*. In the twenty-second book, the optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) and the optional animal sacrifices (*kāmyapaśu*) are taught. In the twenty-third, the *kaukilī*, the *sautrāmaṇī*, and the *kāṭhaka* [rites] are treated. In the twenty-fourth, the *pravargya* rite along with its expiations (*prāyaścitta*) is likewise presented. In the twenty-fifth, there is specifically the determination of the application of the sacrificial enclosures (*vihārayoga*). In the twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh, however, all duties (*dharma*) are explained without exception.

Thus is the summary of the meaning of all questions in general. Furthermore, sacrifice is threefold: *havir-yajña*, *soma-yajña*, and *pākayajña*. The performance of *havir-yajña* consists of the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the Āgrayaṇa, the Animal Sacrifice (*paśu*), the Cāturmāsya, the Piṇḍayajña, and the Sautrāmaṇī. The waves of the *soma-yajña* are the Agniṣṭoma, Atyagniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśin, Vājapeya, Atirātra, and Aptoryāma. The *pākayajña* includes the Homa, the Pākayajñas, the Avamāśrāddha, the Mādhyāvarṣa, and the Aṣṭakās.

"The Śravaṇākarma and the Agrahāyaṇī are recorded by the wise as *pākayajñas*. Thus has the venerable Satyāṣāḍha explained the *śrauta*, *gṛhya*, and *sāmāyācārika* dharmas in his Sūtra consisting of twenty-seven chapters (*praśnas*). Now, [one might ask]: "Dharma is a purposeful matter characterized by an injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*, Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.2).

2) Since the inclusion of both types of injunction—those that are indirect (*parokṣa*) and those that are direct (*aparokṣa*)—is found here, it is logical that the investigation into the authority of the indirect Vedic sentences follows immediately after the investigation into the authority of the direct Veda, which consists of injunctions (*vidhi*), mantras, and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, this "indirectness" is not from the perspective of Manu and others, but rather from our own perspective; for them, even those [mantras and so forth] are indeed direct (*pratyakṣa*).

However, there is no fault in this, because those specific passages—which serve as the source for the Smṛtis of Manu and others—were contained in dispersed Vedic branches (*viprakīrṇa-śākhā*). Consequently, Manu and the others did not commit them to writing in their own Smṛtis, as they did with their own [Smṛti] compositions, out of fear that the tradition might be interrupted. This is the underlying idea: in the injunctive statement "One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied" (*Tai. Āraṇyaka* 2.15), because the study is qualified by the term "one's own," it refers to the study of a branch obtained through one's own lineage within a single Veda. As it is said: "Having mastered one Veda, two Vedas, or even three Vedas, in due order... [and so forth].

From this statement, the study of all branches (*śākhā*) belonging to other Vedas is also enjoined. Consequently, it is understood that for those studying the *Kṛṣṇayajus* branch, the study of the *Śuklayajus* branches contained within the Yajurveda is prohibited; likewise, for those studying the single branch transmitted through their own lineage within the Ṛgveda, the study of other branches contained within that same Veda is prohibited. Furthermore, in the section concerning the "Combination of Qualities" (*guṇopasaṃhārādhikaraṇa*) [2.4],...

2) Regarding the dharma common to all Vedic branches (*sarvaśākhīya*), its performance must be carried out by everyone provided there is no contradiction; however, when a contradiction exists, a regulated option (*vyavasthitavikalpa*) and so forth have been determined. Thus, although the dharmas belonging to other branches are not directly perceived because it is impossible to study the texts of those other branches, their performance is nevertheless necessary based on the conviction that, upon examining the *smṛtis* of Manu and others alone, there must exist some such scriptural statement regarding them within another branch.

In this regard, if Manu and others were to study even those sentences belonging to other recensions (*śākhā*) that they had personally realized, then the injunction "One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) should be studied" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.15) would be violated. For according to the view of the authors of the Kalpa-sūtras such as Śālīki and Sāṣāḍha, it is the unseen potency (*apūrva*) that bestows the fruit [of ritual action]. Superficially, there is no acceptance of a Lord (*īśvara*). The deity consists of mantra and does not possess a physical body. There is an absence of supersensuous pleasure. The entire Veda is devoted solely to ritual action (*kriyā*).

Saṃsāra is beginningless, like the seed of a banyan tree. Liberation through ritual action (*karma*) is simply the attainment of heavenly bliss. The potency of a word resides in that which is connected to an action. This is the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyātivāda*). All cognition is indeed valid knowledge (*pramā*). The Self (*ātman*), distinct from the gross body, is ultimately eternal. By performing duty (*dharma*, i.e., *karma*) with the understanding that it is for the Supreme Lord and without desire for reward, one attains purity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); through this, by means of the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self, one attains the liberation of absolute isolation (*kaivalya*). This is the view of Vyāsa, the teacher Satyāṣāḍha, and the established doctrine of the Brahma-kāṇḍa.

In other scriptures, there exist as many books that are exceedingly profound and difficult to penetrate; since those [qualities] are not inferior even in this Kalpasūtra, we, being of little knowledge, are unable to fully determine its profundity and such characteristics.

Regarding this *Satyāṣāḍha-sūtra*, there exists a detailed commentary titled *Vaijayantī* composed by Bhaṭṭa Mahādeva, born of the ancient Kauśika lineage, which extends up to the end of the first six books (*ṣaṭka*). From the seventh book onwards, up to the end of the tenth, a commentary named *Jyotsnā* composed by Gopīnātha Bhaṭṭa is available and has been published.

From the eleventh question onwards, there follows another new commentary entitled *Prayogacandrikā*, compiled independently by Mahādeva Dīkṣita Somayājī. Having informed the honorable Vināyaka Gaṇeśa Āpaṭe, B.A., and the honorable Dattātreya Viṣṇu Āpaṭe, B.A., that this work has now begun to be printed and will soon be published in parts:

For the sake of the longevity, health, and prosperity of the administrators of the Ānandāśrama, he respectfully prays to the Lord Umāramaṇa and Ramāramaṇa. On the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, on a Monday, in the Śaka year 1849, the year Prabhava, at Puṇyapattana, Daṇḍavat Upādhyāya Kaṇḍamaṇḍanācārya Mahādeva Dīkṣita, a performer of Soma sacrifices and resident of Dhāravāḍa village, [composed] this introduction to the Satyāṣāḍha Cayana Sūtra.

Having paid homage to Satyāṣāḍha, Mahādeva, for the delight of the virtuous, extends by his grace this auspicious manual on the making of bricks (*iṣṭakākaraṇī*). Now, the methods for making the bricks of the second type of *śyena* altar, which consists of a single form (*ekavidha*), will be described. Regarding that, first is the measurement of the man’s size (*puruṣapramāṇa*): "Having made the seventh part of the threefold measure the standard for the man, one should proceed [with the layout]," so says the *Śulbasūtra* (25.9).

Whichever is the seventh among all the types of fire-altars (vidhas) that exist, that is the "seventh-maker" (saptamakaraṇī). Having placed that in the position of a man (puruṣa), one should construct the wings and tail from one's own side using it. This is the meaning: if the fire-altar is of one type (ekavidha), one should divide it into fifteen parts, combine two portions, and having made them into a square, place its measurement in the position of a man; using this, one should construct the wings and tail. One should proceed in exactly the same way for those of two types and so forth.

The seven operations consist of four thousand and eighty. The square of that [number] is one crore, six million, six hundred thousand, four hundred and sixty-four. Having calculated the eightfold square of the number of persons by multiplying it by eight, adding half of the previous heap, dividing that by fifteen, doubling the result, and taking its square root, one obtains the number of persons.
