In the case of decrease (*apacaya*), because there is an absence of *aratni* and *prādeśa* measures, there is no conjunction with a half-unit; the other [measure] is like that of increase. Now, the method for bringing forth the *puruṣa*: the finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) of the seventh part of the threefold measure (*vidhā*) are 120. These, multiplied by thirty-four (*34*), become sesame seeds (*tila*), which are 4,080. These sesame seeds, multiplied again by those same units, become squares (*varga*), designated as 16,640,640. When these squares are divided by 150, the resulting figures are 1,109 and 760.

When the obtained figures are doubled, the principal figures are 2, 2, 1, 9, 5, 2, 0. By following the method for calculating the square root—namely, "having discarded the square root from the last odd place among these figures, one should set down twice that [root] in the even places; having subtracted the square of the quotient from the next odd place, and so on"—the resulting root figures are 1, 4, 8, 9. These are the *tilas*.

When these thirty-four *bhaktas* have been subtracted, forty-three *aṅgulas* and twenty-seven *tilas* remain. According to the rule that "the remainder at the base is increased by one," when the single unit of the remaining *tila* is added, there are forty-three *aṅgulas* and two *tilas*. This constitutes the measure of one type of *agni-puruṣa*. By this very measurement, according to the method taught in the *Śulba-sūtra*, the dimensions of the fire-altar, the preparation of bricks, and so forth, are to be performed. In this regard, the procedure is as follows: the *puruṣa* measures thirty-three *aṅgulas* and twenty-eight *tilas* (43 aṅgulas, 28 tilas).

Twenty-one fingers and twenty-one *tilas* (21 + 31) constitute one *puruṣa*. Ten fingers and thirty-two *tilas* (10 + 32) constitute one-quarter of a *puruṣa*. Six fingers and nine *tilas* (6 + 9), increased by eight *tilas*, constitute one-eighth of a *puruṣa*. Five fingers and sixteen and a quarter *tilas* (5 + 16¼) constitute one-seventh of a *puruṣa*.

Five *tilas* (5); one-sixteenth of a *puruṣa*, which is two *aṅgulas* plus twenty-five *tilas* (2; 25); one-eighth of a *puruṣa*, which is fifteen *aṅgulas* plus eighteen *tilas* (15; 18); one-fourth of a *puruṣa* with a slight excess, which is seven *aṅgulas* plus twenty-six *tilas* (7; 26); half of that one-fourth with a slight excess, which is sixteen *aṅgulas* plus fourteen *tilas* (16; 14); three times one-eighth, which is four *aṅgulas* plus twenty-five *tilas* (4; 25).

[2] Ten *aṅgulas* and fourteen *tilas* (14; 14) is the long side of the brick for the wings (*pakṣeṣṭakā*). Ten *aṅgulas* and one *tila* more than ten *tilas* (10; 11) is the short side of the brick for the wings (*pakṣeṣṭakāhrasvakaraṇī*), namely two *aṅgulas* and twenty-two *tilas* (2; 22). The seventh and eighth parts of the wing-side measure five *aṅgulas* and twenty-three *tilas* (5; 23). The length of the wing is ninety *aṅgulas* and thirteen *tilas* (90; 13), with fourteen *tilas* added...

The length of the wing excluding the tip is thirty-nine fingers and twenty-four *tilas* (39 24/79). The diagonal of the wing (*pakṣakaraṇī*) is eighteen fingers and eighteen *tilas* (18 18/79). The diagonal for bending the wing (*pakṣanamanī*) is forty-six fingers and eighteen *tilas* (46 18/79). The diagonal of the whole (*aṣṭādaśakaraṇī*) is eighteen fingers and eighteen *tilas* (18 18/79). In this procedure, some of the measurements cited are used for the bricks (*iṣṭakā*), while others are for the measurement of the fire-altar (*agni*).

Now, regarding the making of the bricks: therein, first, the bricks of the second Śyena altar are of six types—the *ṣoḍaśī*, the half-bricks (*ardha*), the quarter-bricks (*pāda*), the wing-bricks (*pakṣa*), the middle-wing bricks (*pakṣamadhyīyā*), and the end-wing bricks (*pakṣānīyā*). Among these, first is the *ṣoḍaśī*. The rule states: "One should construct the *ṣoḍaśī* with four [panels]: three eighth-parts and one fourth-part with a specific addition. The meaning of this is: one should produce the brick named *ṣoḍaśī* by means of four wooden boards.

By the eighth [unit], there is one plank measuring five finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) plus sixteen *tilas* and a quarter; by three eighths—that is, by a unit tripled by the eighth—there is one measuring sixteen finger-breadths plus fifteen *tilas* less a quarter; these two are the side planks (*pārśvaphalaka*). By the fourth [unit] measuring eleven finger-breadths minus half a *tila*, there is one crosswise; by the fourth with its specific addition measuring fifteen finger-breadths plus eighteen *tilas*, there is one diagonal crosswise; these two are the cross planks (*tiryakphalaka*). Thus, there are four.

With these slabs, the *ṣoḍaśī* should be made; the same should be understood for what follows. Now, the *aṣṭakās*: "The half-brick (*ardheṣṭakā*) consists of three, two, four, and a fourth with a remainder. The meaning of this is as before. Four *caturtha*s (fourths) are 10 *aṅgulas* and 32 *tilas*. Thus, two [such] fourths with a remainder amount to 15 *aṅgulas* and 18 *tilas*; this constitutes one [half-brick]. In this way, there are three slabs. With these, the *ardheṣṭakā* should be made. This is triangular. Now, the *pādeṣṭakās*.

"By three [parts], one with a quarter, and two with a quarter plus a fraction," so it is said. The meaning is as before. One part consists of four *aṅgulas* and thirty-two *tilas*. Two parts consist of seven *aṅgulas* and twenty-six *tilas*. In this way, the *pādeṣṭakā* (quarter-brick) is to be made from three slabs; this too is triangular. Now, the *pakṣeṣṭakās* (wing-bricks): "The *pakṣeṣṭakā* is by four [parts], two quarters, and two sevenths. The meaning is as before.

The fourth [side] consists of ten *aṅgulas* and thirty-two *tilas*; these two are the side-panels (*pārśva-phalaka*). The seventh consists of six *aṅgulas* and nine *tilas*; these two are the cross-panels (*tiryak-phalaka*). With these four panels, the wing-brick (*pakṣeṣṭakā*) is to be made. Having first made it a long rectangle, one should subsequently bend it.

The author of the Sūtra describes the method of bending: "The seventh [measurement] from the side-line is the transverse measure, and the fourth man’s-length is the cross-measure; one should extend the construction by means of that diagonal cord. [1] The seventh is the measurement for bending. [2] And so on. [3] The meaning of this is as follows: having constructed a long square with four planks according to the previously mentioned method, one should fasten a cord at the eastern end and another cord at the northwestern (Vāyavya) corner, and then pull it with force by means of the cord.

Just as when the drawing is performed, the *pakṣakaraṇī* between the two side-measures (*pārśvamānī*) becomes equal [to the diagonal] by means of straightness—measuring five fingers plus twenty-three *tilas* less some fraction—one should draw it accordingly. However, the interval between the two transverse-measures (*tiryaṅmānī*) remains exactly one-fourth of a *puruṣa*; there is no reduction in that, but rather only in the interval between the two side-measures. And thus, starting from the northwest corner and extending to the southeast corner, there are fourteen fingers plus twenty-five *tilas*, i.e., 14 25/64 fingers.

There are twenty-five [units]. From the southwest corner up to the northeast corner, there are ten fingers and ten sesame seeds (10 aṅgulas + 10 tilas). Now, regarding those in the middle of the wings: "those in the middle of the wings" refers to four [units], two, and two sevens; the meaning is as before. In the fourth [row], there are ten fingers and thirty-two sesame seeds (10 aṅgulas + 32 tilas); these two are the side planks (*pārśva-phalaka*). In the two sevens, there are twelve fingers and seventeen sesame seeds (12 aṅgulas + 17 tilas); these two are the transverse planks (*tiryak-phalaka*).

In this manner, the middle of the wing should be made with four planks. Having thus formed a long rectangle, one should subsequently bend it. Regarding the method of bending, the author of the Sūtra states: "One should bend the planks by means of the seventh [measurement] for the wing-bending. The meaning of this is: one should bend the middle portion of the two planks consisting of thirty-two units of the previously mentioned square. Now, when the bending has been performed in the middle, the two parts of the wing-measure of the wing-line—

It becomes equal by means of the seventh [measurement], which consists of five fingers plus twenty-three *tilas* less some small amount; one should bend it accordingly. The distance between the two transverse lines (*tiryaṅmānyoḥ*) is indeed exactly one-fourth of a *puruṣa*. One should effect both the elevation and the depression in the middle portion of one of the transverse planks by means of the seventh [measurement], which consists of two fingers plus twenty-two *tilas*, for the wing-measuring lines (*pakṣanamanyāḥ*) which consist of eighteen fingers plus eighteen *tilas*. Such is the summary of this.

Having placed one *pakṣeṣṭakā* with its southeast corner raised, one should join another to its south with its northeast corner raised. One should remove those two from the central plank where they meet. When this is done, there arise six-cornered [bricks] beginning with the *pakṣeṣṭakās*, which are unlimited in number. Now, regarding the *pakṣāgrīyās*: one [is made] with three [parts], one with a fourth, one with a fourth and a seventh, and one with a fourth and a slightly larger seventh; the meaning is as before. The fourth [part] consists of ten *aṅgulas* and thirty-two *tilas*.

This is the side-board (*pārśva-phalaka*): seventeen and seven-sevenths finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and seven sesame-seeds (*tila*). These two transverse boards (*tiryak-phalaka*) are twenty-one and twenty-seven-sevenths finger-breadths and twenty-seven sesame-seeds respectively. Thus, the wing-structure (*pakṣānīyā*) should be constructed with these three boards. Having thus established one wing at the northeast-elevated corner, one should join it to the front board located in the eastern part, which measures twenty-one and seven-sevenths finger-breadths. One should then remove the two middle boards that have been joined together.

When this is done, there arise five-cornered bricks measuring both one wing-brick (*pakṣeṣṭakā*) and half of eight bricks (*aṣṭaka*). Thus, there are six types [of bricks]. In the case of the thousand-fold altar (*sahasraciti*), the respective numbers for each of the six types of bricks are as follows: sixteen *ṣoḍaśī* bricks (192), half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*) (104), quarter-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*) (168), wing-bricks (*pakṣeṣṭakā*) (464), middle-wing bricks (*pakṣamadhyīyā*) (24), and end-wing bricks (*pakṣāgrīyā*) (48). These are the total counts (1000). The shapes of these bricks are demonstrated as follows: first, those of the *ṣoḍaśī*, the half-brick, and the quarter-brick...
Of the half-bricks—of the side-bricks. [4] This illustration pertains to the shapes, dimensions, and quantities of the bricks used in a specific sacrifice.

Now, regarding the Gārhapatya hearth-mounds, one view is that they should be square, while another is that they should be circular. Among these, the instruments, shapes, and measurements for the square version will be stated: 22 fingers, 13 fingers, and 24 finger-breadths; the Gārhapatya bricks are 105 in number. The Gārhapatya bricks are 105 in number.
Aṃ. 13, Ti. 24: The form of the *dhishṇiya* hearths shall be thirty-two finger-breadths; [the seat] of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin is eight finger-breadths. Aṃ. 8.
The Āgnīdhrīya hearth is constructed by combining [the measures] from 8 aṅgulas (ŚB 8.8), 12 aṅgulas (ŚB 12),
and 8 aṅgulas (Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin 1.8). It is constructed by combining 8 aṅgulas (ŚB 8), 8 aṅgulas (ŚB 8), and 8 aṅgulas (ŚB 8).

Now, the constructions of the *praśāstṛ*, *potr̥*, *neṣṭr̥*, *acchāvāka*, *śamitr̥*, *cātvāla*, and *avabhṛtha* hearths are presented, along with their shapes and dimensions. Regarding the shape of the eight hearths beginning with that of the *praśāstṛ*: [the measurement is] 12 *aṅgulas* in total; 56 for the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*;
2 for the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*.

Aṃ. 12: The shape of the *mājalīya* sacrificial hearth bricks. [Fig. 6: Combined. Aṃ. 12, Saṃbhūca. Aṃ. 8, Aṃ. A. 12, Poona Līl, work 6895. [6] All the bricks, beginning with those for the *ṣoḍaśin*, should be made with a height of six *aṅgulas* plus three and a half sesame seeds (*tilas*). Due to shrinkage during baking, there will be a reduction in their dimensions; at the time of laying them down, one should fill that [reduction] with *purīṣa* (clay).

There are eleven *brāhmaṇācchaṃsi-dhiṣṇiya* bricks; among them, nine are *hotṛ-dhiṣṇiya* bricks and two are *hautraka-dhiṣṇiya* bricks—thus making eleven. Alternatively, there may be no construction of the *praśāstṛ*-dhiṣṇiya and the others at all, since their purpose is fulfilled by the *hotṛ* and *mārjālīya* dhiṣṇiyas alone. We have presented this here according to traditional practice. Thus, there are five constructions of the dhiṣṇiyas in the fire-altar of a single type (*ekavidha*).

The hearths (*adhiṣṇiya*) other than the *gārhapatya* are each twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) square. There is a mutual space of eighteen finger-breadths between them; in the *sadas*, there is a space of twelve finger-breadths to the south and north of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line. To the south of the *hotṛ*'s hearth is that of the *praśāstṛ*; to the north are those of the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, *potṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, and *acchāvāka*. The *āgnīdhrīya* and the others are situated in their respective places. Now follows the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*).

In that regard, for a sacrificial ground (*sāgnikī*) provided with fires, the measurement is according to the two-foot step (*dvipadakra*) of the Veda. In the case of a single-altar site (*ekavidha*), however, the foot-measure is twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). The temple layout (*vimāna*) is according to the twenty-four finger-breadth step (*caturviṃśaty-aṅgulātmaka-prakrama*). First, having prepared a plot of land suitable for the divine sacrifice (*devayajana*), measuring fifteen *ratni* in length and thirty *ratni* in width, one should drive stakes (*śaṅku*) into the middle of the eastern and western boundaries and stretch a cord between those two stakes. This cord is designated as the *pṛṣṭhyā*.

From the western peg, a peg is fixed sixteen *prakramas* to the east along the spine-line. From the first peg, a peg is fixed six *prakramas* to the south; likewise to the north. From the second peg, a peg is fixed six *prakramas* to the south; likewise to the north. Thus, the *prāgvaṃśa* hall is sixteen *aratnis* in length and twelve *aratnis* in width. From the front of the *prāgvaṃśa*, a peg is fixed three *prakramas* along the spine-line. This peg marks the western boundary of the great altar (*mahāvedi*).

Now, regarding the *mahāvedi*: starting from the peg (*śaṅku*) at the eastern limit of the previously mentioned altar, there are twenty pegs extending along the spine-line (*pṛṣṭhyā*). Including the two boundary pegs—the one at the end of the spine-line and the one marking the eastern limit—there are twenty-two. To illustrate: the first is the boundary peg; then follow [the intervals] in the sequence: three, six, one, one, earth (one), moon (one), two eyes (two), moon (one), pair (two), and fire (three).

"In one [unit] (1), two (2), one (1), two (2), likewise in one (1), likewise in two (2), one (1), one (1)—in these stages; together with the first, there shall be twenty *śaṅkus* here. (Thus,) one should drive in *śaṅkus* at intervals of these numbers of *prakramas*. Then, having made a single rope thirty-six *prakramas* long with loops at both ends, one should make a mark on it at the sixteenth *prakrama* for the purpose of drawing [the line].

In this [measurement], the sixteen-unit cord is the transverse measure, and the twenty-unit cord is the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayā rajju*). One should make another cord twelve *prakrama*s in length with loops at both ends; this is designated as the "twelve-unit" (*dvādaśikā*) cord. At the time of constructing the temple (*vimāna*), having stretched the twelve-unit cord across the desired pegs, one should stretch the thirty-six-unit cord between those same two pegs, fasten the loops, and determine the locations to be described hereafter.

Having extended a sixteen-finger cord from the first peg, having fastened two thirty-six-finger cords at that very spot, and having placed a sixteen-finger cord to the west, one should pull it toward the mark; thus, the fifteenth peg is to the south of the first peg. Likewise to the north. This is the western boundary of the Great Altar (*mahāvedi*). The same sequence should be understood for the front of the pavilion (*vimāna*) as well. To the south of the second peg, at ten steps, there is a peg; to the north, at eight steps, there is a peg. This is the western boundary of the assembly hall (*sadas*).

To the south of the third and fourth hearths (*dhiṣṇiya*), at a distance of twelve *aṅgulas*, is the conch (*śaṅkha*). Likewise to the north. This hearth of the Hotṛ is one *aratni* in extent and is perfectly square. An interspace of eighteen *aṅgulas* remains between them. To the south of the Hotṛ’s hearth is that of the Praśāstṛ; to the south of that is the seat of the Brahman (*brahmasadana*). To the north of the Hotṛ’s hearth, the hearths of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Acchāvāka are to be constructed in the same manner as the Hotṛ’s hearth.

From the sixth peg, as before, one should measure out the *sadas* hall. From this very peg, at eleven *prakramas* and seventeen *prakramas* to the north, there are two pegs; this marks the western boundary of the *āgnīdhra* shed. To the south of the eighth peg, at twelve *prakramas*, there is a peg; this is the central peg of the *mārjālīya* shed. Likewise to the north; this is the central peg of the *āśīdhīya* shed. To the south of the ninth peg, at four and a half *prakramas*, there is a peg; likewise to the north.

This is the western boundary of the Havirdhāna shed. To the north of the tenth peg, the Āgnīdhra shed is constructed as before. To the north of the thirteenth peg, at a distance of fourteen prakramas, there is a peg; this is the utkara (mound of excavated earth). Then, one should exchange the two loops of the thirty-six-fold cord. To the south and north of the fourteenth peg, the Havirdhāna shed is constructed as before. To the north of the twentieth peg, at a distance of fifteen and a half prakramas, there is a peg.

This is the *śāmitra* post at the eastern edge; twelve *prakramas* to the south of it is another post, and likewise to the north. These two are the corners of the great altar (*mahāvedi*). This is the eastern boundary of the great altar. From this very post, thirteen *prakramas* to the north is another post; this marks the southern limit of the *cātvāla*. To the west of the *havirdhāna* shed, having left one and a half *prakramas* [behind] and having left two *prakramas* minus a quarter on both sides, one should construct a square measuring one *aratni* on each side.

This is the location for the *uparava* holes. Having thus measured out the great altar (*mahāvedī*), the *sadas*, the *havirdhāna*, the *āgnīdhra* shed, the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths, and the *cātvāla* pit, one should encircle them with a cord. When they have been encircled, their combined measurement is as follows: the great altar is thirty-six steps in length from west to east, thirty steps wide at the rear, and twenty-four steps wide at the front; it is thus an irregular quadrangle in shape.

The Havirdhāna shed is eighteen steps long from north to south and nine steps in width; however, the Havirdhāna is nine aratnis wide and nine [aratnis] in length. The Āgnīdhra shed is six steps in length and six steps in width. The antaḥpātya markers are twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) square. The Cātvāla pit is the measure of a śamyā. The place for the Audumbarī post is one step to the south of the spine-line in the middle of the Sadas.

The post-hole (yūpasthāna), however, is to the east of the great altar (mahāvedī), outside the altar (bahirvedi), at the eastern edge, half inside the altar and half outside the altar. To the west of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall is the wife’s chamber (*patnīśālā*), with its width and length as large as possible. Now, for the measurement of the fire-altar (*agnivimāna*): having made a step (*prakrama*) consisting of one-fourth of a man plus eleven finger-breadths minus one and a half sesame seeds, as previously described, one should measure the fire-altar by that unit. For example: in front of the sixteen stakes among the twenty-two stakes previously fixed, one should drive down eleven stakes.

The sequence there is as follows: [In the measures of] sixteen, two, one, earth (1), moon (1), moon (1), moon (1), one, earth (1), moon (1), one, moon (1), and moons (1), one should strike the Śaṅkaras and Śaṅkhakas. Having thus struck them, one should make a single rope consisting of twenty-five steps with loops at both ends; on that rope, which measures twelve steps, one should make a mark for the purpose of pulling. On this [rope], the twelve-step [measure] is the transverse rope (*tiryagrajjū*), and the thirteen-step [measure] is the diagonal rope (*akṣṇayārajju*).

This [line] is designated as the "twenty-five-fold" (*pañcaviṃśatikā*). At the time of measuring out the palace, one should measure it in such a way that this line falls exactly between the two loops of the twenty-five-fold cord at the desired pegs. The convention of "first" and so forth begins with the sixteenth peg. Now, the measurement of the palace.

One who suspects [the measurement to be] sixteen [units] should fix one noose from the *pañcikā* and another where it becomes equal; having fixed [the second], one should fix a twenty-five-unit noose upon those very two pegs, lay down a twelve-unit [noose] transversely, pull it toward the mark from the side, and fix a peg at four *prakramas*. Likewise on the north side. This is the tip of the tail. In this same manner, the procedure for the front part of the temple (*vimāna*) is to be understood. To the south of the second peg, a peg is fixed at one *prakrama*, and likewise on the north.

This is the first point where the tail tapers off (*pucchāpyaya*), at three *prakramas* to the south of the fourth peg (*śaṅku*)—that is, at the third peg. The same applies to the north; this is the other point where the tail tapers off. In this way, the tail becomes eight *prakramas* wide at the tip, two *prakramas* wide in the middle, six *prakramas* wide at the base, and five *prakramas* in length. From this very peg, at seven *prakramas* plus two *mūlas* and twenty-five *tilas* to the south, there is a peg. This marks the extent of the wing (*pakṣa*).

To the south of this gnomon, at a distance of one *prakrama*, there is a gnomon; this is the tip of the wing (*pakṣāgra*). Likewise, there are three gnorons to the north. Thus, from the third gnomons starting from the fifth, there are three gnorons each to the south and to the north. When this has been done, the body (*ātman*) is one and a half *puruṣas* in length and one *puruṣa* in width; the two wings are one *puruṣa* in width and seventy-nine *aṅgulas* plus fourteen *tilas* in length. Furthermore, the tips of the wings have a length of one *puruṣa* and a width of one *prakrama*.

Then, at a distance of one *prakrama* to the south of the tenth peg, there is a peg; likewise to the north. Similarly, at a distance of one *prakrama* to the south and north of the eleventh peg, there is a peg. This is the location of the head (*śiras*). When this has been done, there are four squares, each measuring one *prakrama*, at the head. Therein, in the first two squares, one should draw a line in the right-hand square starting from the northeast corner (*īśānakoṇa*) up to the northwest corner (*nirgatikoṇa*), thereby dividing it into two parts diagonally; then, one should discard the southeast part.

Having drawn a line from the southeast corner (āgneyakoṇa) to the northwest corner (vāyavyakoṇa) of the northern square, one should abandon the northeast portion (īśānabhāga). Having likewise made four squares of four *prakrama*s each for both wings, in the squares of the southern wing, one abandons the northeast portion by proceeding as in the case of the head-square of the southern [main] square. In the squares of the northern wing, one abandons the northeast portion by proceeding as in the case of the northern square situated at the tip of the head. Now follows the folding of the wings (*pakṣasaṃnamana*).

Here, having made a single cord eight *prakramas* in length with loops at both ends, and having made a mark in its middle for the purpose of pulling it, one should fasten the two loops to the pegs at the southern wing’s end and the western extremity, and pull [the cord] toward the east by means of the mark. Wherever the mark falls, there one should drive a peg. Likewise, having fastened the two loops to the pegs at the southern wing’s end and the eastern extremity, and having pulled [the cord] as before, wherever the mark falls, there one should drive a peg.

When this is done, the eastern side becomes elevated and the western side depressed. The same applies to the vimāna of the northern side as well. Then, one should cause it to vibrate on all sides and encircle it. This determination of the meaning and logic of the Sūtras for the Kalpasūtra has been composed here by the sage Satyāṣāḍha according to the *Prayogacandrikā-vṛtti*. May this work, offered by me for the pleasure of the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva), be like a crest-jewel; for He indeed accepts whatever is offered by His devotees.

Thus ends the introduction to the *Satyāṣāḍha-cayanaprayoga*. Immediately thereafter, having reversed the two loops of the eighth cord, [one fixes] three pegs to the south and to the north. The back... *The Satyāṣāḍha Śrautasūtra* (Questions 11–14). *Oṃ tat sad brahmaṇe namaḥ*.
The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, together with the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.
Now begins the eleventh book;
therein is the first chapter:

I bow to Viṣṇu, the Lord, who is existence, consciousness, and bliss, infinite and the destroyer of the elephant of sin—the one to whom offered action leads to its fruit, and to whom offered [action] leads even to liberation from bondage. O Soul of the three Vedas, Soul of the three fires, Soul of the three Lords, Soul of the qualities of Nature, You who are the reflection corresponding to the three states of the individual soul and the Soul of the threefold images—protect me from misfortune! [I bow to] the Lord of Sages, whose bliss is the true, conscious, and blissful joy of all the preeminent Siddhas joined with those to be disciplined...

With joy, I bow to my preceptor named Hiraṇyakeśin, who knows the meaning of the Sūtras and is an ocean of compassion. I praise my preceptor Gaṇapati, as well as Maheśāna together with Gaurī, who bestow both birth and knowledge; and I praise Viṣṇu along with Padmā. The Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and its officiating priests have been described in the tenth Praśna; the Cayana ritual will be explained in the eleventh and twelfth [Praśnas].

But surely the Vaikhānasa teachers teach seven forms of the Soma sacrifice: "The Agniṣṭoma, Atyagniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśī, Vājapeya, Atirātra, and Aptoryāma—these are the seven forms of the Soma sacrifice" (Vai. Śrī. 1.1).

Among those, even the latter six are modifications of the qualities of the first, the Agniṣṭoma; therefore, by what distinction are the Atyaṣṭoma and Vājapeya not included? If this is asked, the answer is no, because it is intended here that only the forms (*saṃsthā*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma which constitute the archetype (*prakṛti*) are enumerated, and not merely any Soma-form or merely any modification of the qualities of the Agniṣṭoma. In that regard, the Atyaṣṭoma is not the archetype of any rite, and the Vājapeya is not an archetype.

Nor is it the Jyotiṣṭoma, because the Vājapeya consists entirely of seventeen [stomas]. Therefore, it is indeed correct that these two are not included. Thus, it is established that the five-branched Agniṣṭoma is the archetype (prakṛti) of all Soma sacrifices. Likewise, one should understand the intention to be that the Agniṣṭoma is the archetype of all rituals (kratūnām). And [it is said]: "We shall explain the fire-altar; it serves the purpose of the subsequent rituals."

Since the subsequent sacrificial purpose regarding the fire is prescribed by the sūtra to be stated hereafter, the *uttaravedi* is established by implication for the *agniṣṭoma*; thus, the venerable Āpastamba states in his *Paribhāṣā-sūtra*: "The *uttaravedi* is used in the *agniṣṭoma*; in the subsequent sacrifices, the *mahāvedi*. (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra, Praśna 11, Paṭala 6; Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, Pāraskara 4.7).

8) Thus, because of this explicit statement, one might argue that since the Ukthya and other sacrifices are modifications (*vikāra*) of the Agniṣṭoma, the prohibition of the piling of the fire-altar (*agni-citi*) should apply to the Ukthya and others as well. However, this cannot be said, because those sacrifices, by virtue of their modified forms characterized by specific attributes (*guṇa-vikṛta*), are not *anagniṣṭoma* (non-Agniṣṭoma), and because they belong to the category of subsequent sacrifices (*uttara-kratu*). Nor can it be argued that the Āpastamba-sūtra—“The Uttaravedi [is used] in the Agniṣṭoma”—refers to the Pañcaśākha as the archetype (*prakṛti*), whereas the phrase “in the subsequent sacrifices” refers to its modifications (*vikāra*).

Otherwise, there would be the inconsistency of excluding the *ṣoḍaśin* [cup] from the *vājapeya* sacrifice, as stated in Āpastamba Paribhāṣā-sūtra 4.8: "Except for the *sadyaskr* and the *vājapeya* with the *ṣoḍaśin*. Nor should it be argued that the term *ṣoḍaśin* should be applied as a qualifier of the *vājapeya*, such that the meaning is "from the *vājapeya* which is a modification of the *ṣoḍaśin*"; for since there is no deviation [of the *vājapeya* from being a modification of the *ṣoḍaśin*], the qualifier would be redundant. As it has been said by Abhiyukta: "A qualifier may be meaningful when both possibility and deviation exist."

For there is no Vājapeya sacrifice that does not possess the sixteen-fold chant (*ṣoḍaśin*), such that the qualification would be meaningful by way of excluding it. [Objection: Is the *uttaravedi* then obtained in the Ukthya and other sacrifices? [Reply: Not so. It is obtained in all modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) optionally. This is because a restrictive rule is observed in the passage: "One desiring honor should perform the two Apaciti sacrifices with both *sāmans*, using the two *pakṣinyaḥ* bricks accompanied by the piling of the fire-altar" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 17.11).

And because of Baudhāyana’s statement: "Or one may perform the sacrificial rites without fire. Therefore, it is established that even in the Ukthya and other sacrifices, the piling of the fire-altar (agnicityā) indeed occurs optionally. Now, in order to announce the ritual procedure for the piling of the fire-altar—which is desired in the subsequent seasonal sacrifices—he makes a formal declaration to focus the attention of his pupils:
"We shall explain the fire-altar (agni). || 1 ||

The word *agni* would be understood as the name of a sacrifice because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) in the form of references associated with the *stotra* and *śastra*, such as "the *agni-stotra*" and "the *agni-śastra*. Since the *stotra* and *śastra* have a single connection with the ritual (*kratu*), the word *agni* in the sentence concerning the *stotra* and *śastra*—by virtue of the force of what would otherwise be untenable—indicates through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) merely that which is connected to those two, namely the sacrifice. Thus, the word *agni* has the status of a name for a sacrifice in the "Injunction of the Knower" (*vidvadvākya*). We shall explain this; the meaning is that we shall state it clearly.

Now, it is heard in scripture: "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire"; likewise, there are these other statements: "Then, therefore, they sacrifice after the fire with the Agniṣṭoma," and "him [they sacrifice] with the Ukthya," and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt: is this "he piles the fire" an injunction for a sacrifice, or is it an independent injunction for a mere refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the fire, or is a subordinate element (*guṇa*) being enjoined in relation to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices? For that purpose, one must determine whether the word *agni* is the name of a sacrifice or a term denoting a substance.

In this case, unlike the *añcandābhyas*, because there is no further mention in the context (*prakaraṇa*), there is no connection with a ritual (*kratu*). In the absence of such a connection, the mere act of consecration (*saṃskāra*) would be purposeless as an independent rite. Therefore, the injunction "one should make the fire" (*agniṃ kuryāt*) is an injunction for a sacrifice (*yāga*). Furthermore, the term "he piles" (*cinoti*) is a restatement of what is already established by the sentence "he piles the fire with bricks" (*iṣṭakābhir agniṃ cinute*), just like the verb "he offers" (*nirvapati*). But how can there be an injunction for a sacrifice when there is no hearing of the *yat* suffix (the optative marker)?

It is said: when the action has already been determined by another injunction as "one should establish the fire" (*agniṃ kuryāt*), then in the sentence "Now, therefore, they sacrifice after the fire with the Agniṣṭoma" (*athāto 'gnim agniṣṭomenānuyajanti*), which is intent on prescribing the *saṃsthā* (concluding rite), the word *agni* is understood to denote the sacrifice in its origin, because it is restated (*anuvāda*) by the verb *yajati*. Even if this is not a prescription for the *saṃsthā* itself, but rather [means] "they sacrifice after the fire with a sacrifice that has the Agniṣṭoma as its *saṃsthā*," nevertheless, the fire is the object of the sacrifice (*yājyatva*).

It is not possible for one thing to be perceived as another; just as when one says "Yajñadatta follows Devadatta," it is understood that Devadatta also goes, because otherwise following would be impossible—so too, the status of the fire as a sacrifice is established precisely through the act of following (anuyajana).

To the objection that, therefore, it must be an injunction of a sacrifice (*yāga*), the following is stated: In this context, only the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of piling (*cayana*) is enjoined for the fire (*agni*). Its connection with a ritual (*kratu*) would be established by such sentences as "Now, therefore, the fire" (*athāto 'gniḥ*). This word *agni* is conventionally fixed (*rūḍha*) upon the flame; it is certainly not a designator of a sacrifice. For the word *agni*, due to its extreme conventional fixity, and because it lacks the characteristics of being a name of a sacrifice—namely, the criteria of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), being mentioned alongside the act (*tat-prakhyatā*), and being designated as such (*tad-vyapadeśa*)—does not attain the status of a sacrifice-name. Therefore, this consecration of piling is enjoined for the flame itself.

And regarding that *saṃskāra* (consecration), there are passages devoted to its connection with the seasonal rites (*ṛtu*), such as "Therefore, they subsequently sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma. Here, the word *agni* refers to the fire consecrated by the piling (*cayana*) due to the context. The prefix *anu* denotes the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices that occur subsequent to the piling. Thus, the meaning is: "One should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma and others in the fire consecrated by the piling. However, even here the word *agni* is not in grammatical apposition with the root *yaj*, which would [otherwise] make it a name (*nāmadheya*).

Furthermore, sequence does not necessarily belong only to those things that are of identical form, since it is observed even between heterogeneous elements in cases such as "he enjoys the cooked food" (*pākam anubhuṅkte*). Therefore, in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, this is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*).

That [fire-altar] is for the sake of subsequent sacrifices, except for the Sādyaskra, the Vājapeya, the Ṣoḍaśin, and the Sārasvata Sattra; or it may be according to the instruction regarding the Agniṣṭoma-stoma. In the Rātri-sattras that include the Mahāvrata, the re-piling (punar-citi) is for the purpose of what was not previously heard.

And that fire does not occur in the *paridṛśin* sacrifice nor in the *vājapeya*, which is a modification (*vikāra*) of it, because it is not mentioned there. In the *sādyaska* sacrifices, there is an absence of piling (*cayana*) because completion on the same day is impossible. In the *sārasvata sattra*, no fire is piled because of the lack of stability. Therefore, other than these, the fire is present in the subsequent seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtu*). Since the fire is prescribed in the subsequent seasonal sacrifices, the *uttaravedi* (northern altar) mentioned in the context (*prakaraṇa*) is used there; from that, [the fire] is carried forth from the *āhavanīya*.

In the subsequent sacrifices (*uttareṣu kratuṣu*)—those to be performed after the *agniṣṭoma*, excluding the *sādyaskra* and others—in the modifications (*vikṛti*) such as the *agniṣṭut* and *jyotiṣṭut* where the fire-altar is not prescribed by a general rule (*anārabhyādhīta*), the fire is piled up. Upon that altar, the *āhavanīya* fire is brought forth. Regarding these, some say that since the *uttaravedi* (high altar) is obtained in certain cases through specific injunctions, such as "It is with the piling of the fire-altar; it is with two wings having the piling of the fire-altar," there is no fixed rule for other instances.

Regarding the statement, "For Agni is piled upon the *uttaravedi*," this *agni*, taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*), enters the archetype (*prakṛti*) by way of the *uttaravedi*, just as the *khadira* wood [enters] by way of the *sruva* ladle. Since the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) is already established in the archetype, the *praṇeya* fire is to be established on the northern navel (*uttaranābhi*) based on the Ṛgvedic text: "Agni is indeed the Hotṛ of the gods; his own world is that which is the northern navel."

Thus, the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), which concludes with the *uttaravedi*, will serve the purpose of the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), just like the rule of seventeen-foldness (*sāptadaśya*). Regarding this, Āpastamba says: "The *uttaravedi* is [used] in the Agniṣṭoma; in the subsequent sacrifices, the fire-altar [is used]" (ĀpŚS Paribhāṣā 4.8). In that very context, the piling of the fire-altar will take place in the Jyotiṣṭoma when it is performed in the form of the Agniṣṭoma. As it is said: "Now, therefore, they sacrifice to that Fire by means of the Agniṣṭoma, to him by means of the Ukthya, to him by means of the Atirātra, to him..."

"By means of a two-night [sacrifice], by means of that three-night [sacrifice]," and so forth. Therefore, since the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) and the subsequent altar-ground (*vedi*) are optional even in the archetype (*prakṛti*), they remain optional in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) as well, just as in the archetype. For this very reason, when the contingency of optionality arises in all modified sacrifices, the restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*)—"He is one who possesses the piling of the fire-altar; [he performs] with two altars accompanied by the piling of the fire-altar"—is justified, just like the case of the animal-cake made of rice (*vrīhimaya-paśupuroḍāśa*).

In the case of the *dvigava* and other such sacrifices, the injunction for the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) is non-instructional (*anādeśika*), being intended for the accomplishment of subsidiary desires (*guṇakāma*) and the like. Now, an objection: the fire-altar is enjoined by a detached statement (*anārabhyavāda*); it is applied to both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and certain ectype (*vikṛti*) sacrifices by means of a specific sentence, as in: "Now, therefore, they sacrifice after the fire with the Agniṣṭoma; him with the Ukthya; him with the Atirātra; him with the Trirātra," and so on, up to the Dvādaśarātra. This same fire-altar is not taught by such a sentence in those ectypes where it is absent, such as the Ṣoḍaśin and the Vājapeya. In that case, what [is the rule]?

There is a doubt as to whether [the *atigrāhya* cups] should be performed by virtue of the extended injunction (*codaka*) or not. Similarly, there are great cups called *atigrāhya* heard of in the archetypal rites (*prakṛti*), which are also prescribed in certain ectype rites (*vikṛti*) with the instruction: "One should take them at the *ukthya*, one should take them at the *ṣoḍaśin*, one should take them at the *viśvajit*. There is a doubt as to whether these too are to be taken in other ectypes or not. On this point: "By the extended injunction, the *atigrāhya* is not prescribed for the ectype; for if it were so, its mention in certain [specific ectypes] would be purposeless."

Therefore, for the sake of its meaningfulness, it is postulated that there is a specific location (pradeśa) for it; by this, wherever its instruction occurs, action takes place only there and not elsewhere. It is said in reply: The application of this [mantra] is certain through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), just like other auxiliary elements (*aṅga*). Since the purpose of the *codaka* is complete, the fact that it is heard in certain instances is merely for the sake of establishing the general injunction (*sāmānyavidhi*); it would not prevent its extension (*atideśa*) otherwise. If there were a general injunction, what would be the purpose of the initiation of those seeking specific qualities (*guṇakāma*)?

In those modifications (*vikṛti*) for which [the rite] is prescribed, there is an identical injunction (*samānavidhāna*) as in the archetype (*prakṛti*). However, in other modifications, the application occurs through the rule of transfer (*codaka*), and thus the injunction is not identical to that of the archetype. Furthermore, the purpose of this identical injunction is that qualities intended for the fires (*agnyāśritaguṇakāma*), such as "One desiring heaven should pile the *śyenacit*," are operative even in those modifications.

For those desiring specific qualities (guṇakāma) resort to the archetypal fire (prakṛtāgni), and since the archetypal fire is common to both the archetype and its modifications (vikṛti), the application of those desiring qualities occurs even in the modifications because it serves as their substratum. However, in those modifications where there is no explicit injunction, those desiring qualities do not apply—or rather, they cease—according to the principle that "there is a cessation [of the archetype] due to the difference in the ritual acts" (karmabheda). Thus, while there is indeed a scriptural mention in certain modifications for the purpose of applying those desiring qualities, one cannot on that basis postulate the absence of extended application (atideśa).

Therefore, there is an extension (*atideśa*). On this point, some say: "The *agni* mentioned outside of any specific context (*anāramyādhīta*) cannot find a place in the archetype (*prakṛti*) because it would conflict with the *uttaravedi* prescribed within that context. And since what is not part of the archetype is not extended to the modified rites (*vikṛti*), its application to the modifications occurs only through direct instruction (*upadeśa*); thus, by virtue of the lack of such instruction, the *agni* is not to be piled in the *ṣoḍaśin* and *vājapeya* sacrifices. This is incorrect, because the *agni* is prescribed in the archetype as well by the sentence concerning the *agniṣṭoma*.

However, that [reference] will not be intended for the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice as a modified form (*vikṛti*), because it contradicts the context (*prakaraṇa*) within the sixth chapter concerning the archetype (*prakṛti*). Indeed, it is not proper to restrict a sentence by means of a context. Furthermore, since the status of being an *agniṣṭoma* belongs to the archetype alone—whereas for the modified forms it depends on their own extended application (*atideśa*)—it is the archetype itself that is denoted by this term.

And here the principle of the *sāptadaśya* (seventeen-foldness) does not apply; for while the connection of the *sāptadaśya* with the *sāmidhenī* verses is understood through direct syntactical statement (*vākya*), its connection with the sacrifice (*kratu*) would have to be inferred. However, the connection of the *pāñcadaśya* (fifteen-foldness) with the context (*prakaraṇa*) is already established, and thus its relative strength [of authority] is appropriate. Furthermore, the word "Agniṣṭoma" denotes the sacrifice itself, so its connection [with the *vāravantīya*] is effected by syntactical statement and cannot be set aside by the context. Therefore, since the fire-altar exists in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) as well.
In that regard, since it is impossible in the *sadyaskra* sacrifices and in the *Sārasvata* *sattra*s, let Agni not be piled at will; however, in the *ṣoḍaśin* and the *vājapeya*, he must be piled.

Alternatively, while the fire is being maintained, he should touch the altar within the *vedi* with the formula: "May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm. Or, having laid down three *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks, the rule for their laying is as follows: the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, the *sāman*, the *purīṣa*, and the *viśvajyotis*. Thus prescribed are the second and the third layers, including the *purīṣa*.

Or alternatively, there are three *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks and all the *viśvajyotis* bricks; the rule for their laying out is as follows: first the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, then the *sāman*, then the *purīṣa*, then the *viśvajyotis*. Thus is the second [layer] prescribed. But in the third [layer], the *viśvajyotis* is first, then the *purīṣa*, then the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, and then the *sāman*. 4.

Among the small pebbles known as *śarkarā*, that which possesses a hole naturally, without human effort, is the *svayamātṛṇṇā* (self-perforated stone); one should place that here. The *viśvajyotis* (all-light) bricks are to be placed with mantras containing the word *viśva* (TS 4.4.6). One should place those three in the first, middle, and highest layers respectively. The rest is clear. 3 || 4 ||
Desiring that [sacrifice], having chosen his officiating priests on the new moon day, the full moon day, during the waxing fortnight, or under an auspicious lunar mansion, he should proceed.

Because it serves as the substratum for the fire (*agni*), the brick altar (*iṣṭakā-sthaṇḍila*) is called *ṛtu*; through association with that, the season (*ṛtu*) is also called *āśir*. This is according to the statement of Āpastamba: "One who is about to establish the fire" (*āpa0 śrau0* 16.3.1). One who is about to establish that fire becomes one who intends to sacrifice with a *ṛtu* characterized by the form of the altar (*sthaṇḍila*). Since that fire is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the Soma sacrifice, there is here an interconnection (*nyatiṣaṅga*) with the auxiliaries of the Soma. Furthermore, because that fire is taught independently (*anāramyādhīta*), it possesses a separate result from the auxiliary of the Soma.

Regarding the purpose of the *uttaravedi* (high altar), it is heard in the *prakṛti* (archetypal rite) during the *praṇayana* (carrying forward of the fire): "The *nābhi* (navel) of that [altar] is this very *uttaravedi*. However, in the *agni-citya* (fire-altar piling) ritual, there is the placing [of the fire] upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* (self-perforated brick). Therefore, because it is not for the sake of a specific desire (*akāmyatvāt*), it serves the purpose of the *vikṛti* (modified rite). If it were for a desire (*kāmya*), like the *godohana* vessel and others, it would find its place in the *prakṛti*. Thus, one who is about to sacrifice with that ritual characterized by the fire-altar [performs it].

Āpastamba states: "One performs the collection of the *ukhā* on the new moon day, the full moon day, or the *ekāṣṭakā*. The *ekāṣṭakā* has been explained by the author of the Sūtra as being the eighth day after the full moon of the month of Māgha. Regarding that *aṣāḍhā* brick—which is drawn out and placed in the center—some followers of other recensions (*śākhās*) recite specific ritual rules (*dharmas*). In that case, the *ukhā* is performed silently; those mantras containing the characteristic marks of the *ukhā*, such as "O you two *ukhās*" (*dhatūkhe*), and so forth, are excluded, just as a mantra containing the characteristic mark of rice (*vrīhi*) is excluded when barley (*yava*) is used.

Regarding this, Baudhāyana states the materials: "One who is about to collect the fire-pans (ukhās) prepares a horse and a donkey, their two reins made of muñja grass or of kuśa grass, fire accompanied by a Brāhmaṇa, clay that has been prepared and is fit for use, a mound from an anthill, a black antelope skin, two lotus leaves, a yoke-halter, a water-jar, gold, potsherds from an old jar, gravel, unground ointment, wool from a black sheep, wool from a Vaiśya’s black antelope skin, and a seventeen-year-old [bull]."

"The auspicious rite is performed with the slaughterhouse as its primary locus. Having sacrificed with the *āmāvāsya* oblation, or under an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), one should dig a pit in front of the hall at the place where the *śamyā* markers are set. One smears that [pit] with earth prepared for the purpose. One levels it with the surface of the ground. Therein he places a black antelope skin, two lotus leaves, a yoke-halter, a water-pot, and gold. (Baudhāyana Śrautasūtra 10.1).

Having said, "In this matter, I shall sacrifice with the Karma-Jyotiṣṭoma, the Vikadruka, the Agniṣṭoma accompanied by the piling of the fire-altar (*agniciti*), with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), so that I may attain the heavenly world," he performs the selection of the *Soma-pravāka* and other rites beginning with the [selection of] the *Vidyut*. Then, at the conclusion of the request for the sacrificial ground (*devayajana-yācñā*) or at the conclusion of the worship of the deities (*devatopasthāna*), those who are the performers of the principal rite (*pradhāna*) are the same as the performers of the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*), according to the principle that "the place for the subsidiaries is the same as that for the principal. Furthermore, the selection of the *Ṛtvij*s and so forth is performed prior to the request for the sacrificial ground, because of the statement in another *sūtra*: "The principal rite is together with its subsidiaries" (*Āpastamba-pariśiṣṭa* 2.39). || 5 ||

"O gods whose priest is Bṛhaspati, you gods who were born first among the gods, exert your power among the gods! You who are first among the second, second among the third—thrice eleven, thirty-three!—I take hold of you; may I be able to accomplish this which I am doing. Svāhā! With these words, he offers an oblation. || 6 ||

Having spread out the fires for the purpose of collecting the fire-pans (*ukhā*), Baudhāyana also says here: "They strew [the grass] around; the Brahman and the sacrificer sit down to the south" (*BaudhŚS* 10.1). In the injunctions regarding oblations, the offering is made with the utterance of *svāhā*. Regarding the rule of the instruments as well, it should be understood from the technical definitions: "The oblations are offered into the Āhavanīya fire with the *juhū* ladle. The deities are the gods. 6.

Having cleansed the *juhū* and the *sruva* ladles, and having taken either four or eight portions of clarified butter, he offers one oblation with the Sāvitra formulas while standing upright within the altar (*antarvedi*), reciting the verses beginning with "yuñjānaḥ prathamaṃ manaḥ" (YV 33.8–15), with the Yajus formula as the eighth. [End of Paṭala 7] The cleansing of the *juhū* and *sruva* is performed silently; however, according to the Commentator (Bhāṣyakṛt), it is accompanied by mantras as in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

The oblation with eight portions taken up (*aṣṭagṛhīta*) is prescribed in another Vedic branch (*śākhā*). However, the oblation with four portions taken up (*caturgṛhīta*) is stated in our own branch, as seen in the injunction: "He offers with what has been taken up four times" (*Caturgṛhītena juhoti*, Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.1). Starting from "Yoking the mind first" (*Yuñjānaḥ prathamam manaḥ*) and ending with "O God Savitṛ, this sacrifice of ours" (*Imam naḥ deva savitar yajñam*), he—standing between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires—offers a single oblation with those verses of which the *yajus* is the eighth, i.e., those for which the *yajus* is the eighth.

Savitṛ is the deity. || 7 || Here, this must be considered: should one offer the oblation after reciting each individual mantra, or rather, after reciting all the sentences (mantras)? In this regard, he shows both the rejected and the accepted positions in succession: "If one should desire that someone be worse off, one should offer for him [the oblation] one by one. If one should desire that someone be better off, one should offer for him after reciting them all in succession. || 8 ||

"Pāpīyān" means one who is exceedingly wicked, that is, a pauper; "vasīyān" means one who possesses more wealth. || 8 || Here, this further point must be considered: should one recite the *yūpa-āṣaṇ* formulas and, having made the *yajus* verse "imaṃ no deva savitaḥ" the seventh, subsequently make the *ṛc* verse "deva savitaḥ" the final one? Or, having made this *ṛc* the seventh, should one make that *yajus* the final one? In this regard, he shows the two positions—the one to be rejected and the one to be accepted—in sequence:

If he should desire, "May I endow the meters with the glory of the sacrifice," he should make the *ṛc* the final element. If he should desire, "May I endow the sacrificer with the glory of the sacrifice," he should make the *yajus* the final element. (9)

"I shall offer" means "I shall unite" the fruit of the sacrifice with the glory of the sacrifice. Since a *ṛc* verse is bound by meters (*chandas*), if it were placed at the end, the fruit of the sacrifice would go to the meters. However, because a *yajus* formula is devoid of meters, the fruit of the sacrifice does not go to the meters; rather, it goes only to the sacrificer. Therefore, the meaning is that one should place the *yajus* last. "This is the desire of the Adhvaryu," says the Commentator. This is the principle: a praise for the injunction that the *yajus* is the eighth [element]. || 9 ||
With the verse, "Fulfill the hymn with the Ṛc," he offers the northern oblation with butter taken four times.
The phrase "he offers an oblation" (āhutiṃ juhoti) is understood to carry over. Agni is the deity. 10.

With the four formulas beginning with "devasya tvā," he takes up the spade (*abhri*). It may be made of *khadira* wood, or of bamboo, or of spotted wood; it may be hollow or solid, or sharpened at both ends, or sharpened at one end only; or it may be made of *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *arka*, or *śamī* wood. Or it may be made from any tree that bears fruit, being a mere handful in size, or a span (*prādeśa*) long, or a cubit (*aratni*) long, or an arm’s length (*bāhu*) long, or a fathom (*vyāma*) long, or of unlimited size. (Sūtra 11) [From the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha] 91.1–5.

Beginning with the mantra "devasya tvā" and ending with "ānuṣṭubhena tvā chandasādade 'śirasvat," he takes up the fire-drill (the wooden churner), which may be made of *khadira* or *veṇu* wood, using these four mantras. It should be variegated, marked with black spots, either hollow within or solid (not hollow). The word *kṣṇu* is derived from the verbal root *kṣṇu*, meaning "to sharpen," and thus denotes sharpness. Both ends of the drill must be sharpened by a carpenter; such a tool, being sharp on both sides, should be prepared.

Alternatively, *pālāśī* means made of *parṇa* wood; *audumbara* refers to the *jantuphala* tree; *arka* is well-known; and *śamī* is the *ghaṇṭā*. In the absence of these, the meaning is that whatever sacrificial tree (*yajñiya-vṛkṣa*) is "fruit-bearing" (*phalāvah*), its branch should be used. However, the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) explains that it is called "fruit-bearing" (*phalāvah*) because it bears many fruits. Among trees, there is one that is fruit-bearing; and even among those that are not fruit-bearing, the bamboo (*veṇu*) is the most preeminent bearer of fruit.

Because it is endowed with many grains resembling wheat at the completion of the year of the bamboos beginning with Brahmā, this [altar] should be made with speed and vigor. A *vyāma* is equal to four *aratnis*; it should be made of this much extent. It prescribes the state of being "unmeasured" (*aparimita*) as the absence of a fixed measure, stating: "It is unmeasured" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.1). Now, as for those mantras associated with numbers...

In such passages as "He takes up the spade with four [verses]" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.1), there is likewise an option as previously stated; however, due to the force of the number, there is a combination (*samuccaya*). For the number four, being an auxiliary of the ritual action, cannot be fulfilled unless there is a combination. In this regard, it is determined by the power of the statement regarding the number that the mantras employed previously function as causes through the medium of a purificatory act (*saṃskāra*), while the final one functions directly. Therefore, there is a combination. || 11 ||
Having taken the horse's halter with the mantra, "They have grasped this rein of the Eternal Law," he fastens it to the horse with the mantra, "O spirited steed, run forward! || 12 ||
That by which a horse is designated—being bound and held—is this very thing called the "horse-halter" (aśvābhidhānī). 12.
Having silently taken hold of the donkey, he says, "Yoke the donkey, you two," regarding the donkey. || 13 ||

The section ends with the mantra "bharantam asmayum. Without reciting any mantra, one should take the donkey's halter and then address the donkey with the mantra "yuñjāthām" (Yoke ye two). Because it was employed here for a lowly task, even in the world today the donkey is more base than the horse; for only washermen and the like show it respect, whereas kings, ministers, and others do not. || 13 ||
With the three verses beginning "yoge yoge tavastaram," they proceed eastward with the horses leading, to where they intend to dig for the clay.

The section ends with "acchehi. Because of the use of the plural number in the word "gacchanti" (they go), the Adhvaryu, the Brahman, and the Sacrificer are meant. "With the horse first" means that they go to that place where the clay for the bricks is located; the horse goes first, then the donkey, and then the others. In this regard, [the ritual procedure for] the horse and the donkey... [end of fragment]. [Note: The final portion of the provided text appears to be a fragment of a commentary title: *Mahādevaśākhisa-kālatapa-yoga-candrikā-vyākhyā-sametam*.]

Āpastamba clarifies the precedence in going: "If one should desire that there be a reversal of fortune (*pāpavasyasa*), they should go with the donkey first" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 16.1.12). It is well known that the donkey is inferior to the horse; therefore, so that the two do not travel together as equals, they should lead the horse in front. Thus, the Brāhmaṇa states: "They lead the horse first. || 14 ||
With the mantra, "Come hither to Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras," he should address one whom he hates; not looking at him, he points him out. 15.

While going toward the clay pit, if one should encounter anyone who is hateful on the way, then one should recite this mantra. Even if one does not see the hateful person, one should still recite it while mentally designating him. || 15 ||
"Let us go to Agni Purīṣya in the manner of Aṅgiras," or so [it says].
The word "or" (vā) is intended to indicate the opinion of another Vedic school.
At the rising of the sun, he approaches the mound of the anthill with the formula: "We shall carry Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras. || 17 ||

That portion of the anthill which has grown prominent by its elevation is this *vapā*; from among such *vapās*, having slightly lifted the tip of that *vapā* which faces the rising sun, he worships that *vapā* with this mantra. ||17||
In this regard, some recite: "We bring Agni Purīṣya, like Aṅgiras. || 18 ||

Just as it was at the time of departure, so it is also at the time of arrival. In that context, the reading is "we shall carry" (*bhariṣyāmaḥ*); here, however, the distinction is "we carry" (*bharāmaḥ*). Although this is not the proper time for the arrival, nevertheless, because it has arisen in the mind through the context, this mantra is recited; one should transpose it to a later point. Some followers of other Vedic branches recite this injunction. || 18 ||
"Agni has looked upon the summit of the dawns," with these words he steps forward from the mound of the ant-hill. || 19 ||
He goes near an anthill. || 19 ||
Having arrived, he causes the horse to step upon the clay pit with two verses: "O steed, having come from the path of the prize," and "O steed, having stepped upon the earth. || 11.1.20 ||
They cause him to step upon the mouth with his right forefoot. || 20 ||
With the words, "The sky is thy back," he cleanses the back of the horse. || 21 ||

(These words within the *dhanuścīnā* are not recited by some. 1. *ka.* reads *tadā*; 2. *ka.* reads *syodetoḥ tām uddhatyopa*; 3. *kha.* reads *ma iti*. 1. The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: He touches [it] on all sides. || 21 ||

"Trample those who attack; let the enemies be beneath you! Stand like Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, conquering the waters and the lands"—with these words, he meditates in his mind upon him whom he hates, [placing him] beneath the feet of the horse. 22.
Whomever he hates as "Devadatta," him he meditates upon with his mind as being beneath the hoof of a horse.
With the two verses beginning "He has stepped forth" (utkrāma) and "He has stepped out" (udakramīt), they cause the horse to step out from the place where the earth was dug.
The place where earth is dug is called a *mṛtkhana*; from that [place], one should cause the horse to emerge facing north. || 23 ||
Saying, "Release the divine waters," he pours water into the footprint of the horse.

He pours water onto the right hind hoof of the horse; "supippalā" is the end of the mantra. (24) Having placed gold upon it, he offers a single oblation with two verses containing the word "manas," namely: "I sprinkle Agni" and "I sprinkle thee. (25)

The recitation of *svāhā* follows from the injunction for the *juhoti* oblation. Agni is the deity. Having placed gold upon the ground, one should offer the oblation upon it. Vaikhānasa says it should be with clarified butter taken up once; others say it should be with that which has been taken up [once]. (21) Having set aside the gold, he traces around the excavation for the clay with the water-pot using the three verses beginning with "parivāja patiḥ," making the outer line larger. (26)

"Śuciḥ" is the end of the mantra. Having taken up—that is, accepted—the gold, there is a circum-inscription with each mantra, according to the statement: "He circum-inscribes with the Gāyatrī; he circum-inscribes with the Triṣṭubh; he circum-inscribes with the Anuṣṭubh" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.3). Each successive outer line is larger; that is, the circum-inscription with the Gāyatrī is innermost, while those with the Anuṣṭubh and Triṣṭubh are progressively further out. || 26 ||
He digs with two [mantras] beginning with "devasya tvā. || 27 ||
"purīṣyam aṅgirasvat khanāmi" is the end [of the first mantra]. Then the act of digging consists of two parts, with one action accompanied by two mantras. || 27 ||

With the formula, "Thou art the back of the waters," he brings a lotus leaf. With this same [formula], he encircles it. Above that, to the north of the clay-digging tool, he spreads a black antelope skin with the hair upwards, saying, "Ye two are a shelter; ye two are a protection. With two verses beginning with "mekā," he spreads the second lotus leaf with its neck pointing eastward and its hair facing upward, beneath which the handle [of the digging tool] lies face-upward. (Section 2, Paṭala 1) — [This is from] the *Payogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.

Since this [lotus leaf] expresses an existing object that is already present upon the waters, he brings this lotus leaf with a corresponding mantra. He wraps it again with this same [mantra] used for the wrapping. With the two mantras beginning "You are a shelter" (*śarma ca stha*), he spreads the black antelope skin and the lotus leaf to the north of the place where the clay is dug; the meaning is that the lotus leaf is placed face upwards so as to be above the black antelope skin. || 28 ||
Having touched the clay with the mantra, "Thou art the one worthy of being carried; thou art the sustainer of all. (29)
The consecration of the earth-digger. || 29 ||

He collects [the materials] on a black antelope skin and a lotus leaf with three Gāyatrī verses beginning, "I collect thee first from the lotus," for a Brāhmaṇa; with the following Triṣṭubh verses for a Rājanya; and with Jagatī verses for a Vaiśya. (11.1.30)

Although only these three *gāyatrī* verses beginning with "tvāmugra" are recited here, they are nevertheless stated as an option in the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) of Āpastamba and others, such that "one may [use] four. In the case of the four-verse version, the count should be completed together with the previously mentioned mantra, "purīṣyo 'si viśvabharāḥ. Some, however, throw [the earth] onto the black antelope skin and the lotus leaf with the verse "tvāmagne puṣkarād adhi. For a Brāhmaṇa, he gathers [the materials] with either four or three *gāyatrī* verses.

When [the rite] is performed with three verses, then one begins with "O Agni, from the lotus... and uses three verses. When [it is performed] with four verses, then one begins with "Thou art he who... and uses four verses. Alternatively, they say: "The first one churned thee out, O Agni. By means of that very person who perceived him, he thus collects him; this is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the word "him" (*yam*). In the same manner he consecrates [the fire], and in the same manner he collects it. The instruction is to use four verses.

He repeats the third verse, "O Pāthya, thee," twice; likewise the seventh. With the *triṣṭubh* verses beginning with "Sit down, O Hotṛ," he performs the fourth [rite]. By means of these four [verses], starting with "Be born, O noble one," he causes the gods and men who have gathered there to be procreated—so says the indicative mark (*liṅga*). The fourth [verse] is a *triṣṭubh*, and the touching of the clay is performed in the same manner. With the three verses beginning with "The protector of this people that does not perish," and the fourth being "Soma has been pressed. (30) Now he prescribes the optional combination:
If one should desire, "May he become more prosperous," for him one should collect [the materials] with both types of verses—both Gāyatrīs and Triṣṭubhs. || 31 ||

"May he become more powerful and wealthy"—thus is his gathering performed with both *gāyatrī* and *triṣṭubh* verses. Among these, through the *gāyatrīs* there is the attainment of splendor (*tejas*), and through the *triṣṭubhs* there is the attainment of sensory power (*indriya*). [From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, 11th Praśna:
"For you have been born, O noble one"—with this verse, he consecrates the gathered materials. (32)
The touching of the gathered clay is performed so that the pit in the earth-digging site is filled with other clay such that it is no longer perceived as a hole. || 32 ||
With the words, "May Vāyu Mātariśvan place [the breath] within you," he pours water into the clay pit.
One should pour water into the place where the earth was dug; "for you" marks the end of the mantra. || 13 ||

Having enticed the clay-digger and taken hold of him, he, being well-born, fastens the ends of the black antelope skin with a triple-stranded cord made of muñja or arka grass, with the mantra: "With light, O well-born one. || 34 ||

The enticement is for the purpose of deluding him. Having raised up all the edges of the black antelope skin, [he recites] "O well-born one" (*sujāta*). According to Āpastamba (*Āpastamba Śrautasūtra* 10.16.1–2, 25): "With a cord made of linen, or of *mūñja* grass, or of *arka*. He binds [the horse] with a cord made of linen—that is, a fresh garment—or of *mūñja* grass, or of *arka*, that is, made from the *devarūpikā* plant. 34.
He rises with two verses beginning, "O wood, stand firm at the well-performed sacrifice. (35)

The section ends with "vi hvayāmahe. Having taken up the fire bound by these two Ṛg-verses characterized by Savitṛ, he should rise. Since it is stated in the second mantra, "devo naḥ savitā," these two are Sāvitrī verses; he rises by means of these. Thus Āpastamba says: "He rises by means of two Sāvitrī verses. (35)
"Born art thou, the embryo of the two worlds," with these words he carries [the fire]. || 36 ||
Ending with "kanikradad gāḥ," he carries [the horse] near the donkey. || 36 ||
With the words, "Be firm, O one of sturdy limbs," he places [the fire] upon the back of a donkey. || 37 ||
"Carrying the soil," thus ends [the mantra]. He places the clay upon the back of the donkey. || 37 ||
"Be auspicious to the subjects," with these words he consecrates the one who is near. || 38 ||
The section ending with "vanaspatīn" [is recited]; he consecrates that which has been placed [therein]. || 38 ||
With the three verses beginning "Let the steed go forth neighing," they return without haste, preceded by the horse. || 39 ||
"Truth," thus [ends the section]. They return to the sacrificer's house with the horses leading, proceeding without haste; however, they do not have the donkeys leading. || 39 ||

"Let us bring Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras"—with this mantra he should address the one with whom he has come into contact through an enemy; [the text] explains that he points him out while looking at him. [Commentary: When there is contact between the sacrificer and an enemy, he addresses him with that mantra. If there is no physical contact, then after reciting the mantra, he points him out with the second [part of the formula], saying, "Devadatta. [This concludes] Paṭala 1, accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* composed by Mahādeva Śāli. This has been explained. [End of section 4.]
To the north of the monastery, having enclosed a space, he brings down [the fire] onto flowering and fruit-bearing plants with two verses: "O plants, receive this fire; let it come hither. || 41 ||

The section ends with the words, "He has sat down in common dwelling" (*sadhastham āsadat*). In a place near the northern side of the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), which is enclosed and covered with mats, he brings down—that is, places—the plants, such as rice, barley, and others, both domestic and wild, among which there are flowers and fruits. He brings them down with two verses: "O plants, receive him; do not harm him" (*oṣadhayaḥ pratigṛhṇītākṣitam etam*, Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.6). Thus concludes the sacrificial ground; according to the principle, it becomes secular (*laukika*) thereafter because there is no further purpose for the sacrificial ground. || 41 ||
With the verse "vi pājasā," he loosens [the cord]. || 42 ||
The section ends with the word *praṇītā*. He unties [the animal] which was bound with a rope. || 42 ||
With the three verses beginning "O Waters, you are indeed the source of happiness," he pours water [into the vessel]. 43.
And [the passage] ending with "not" is the Brāhmaṇa on the statement: "He pours out with three [verses]" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.6). ||43||

With the two verses beginning "Mitra, having united with the earth," he unites [the altar] with the materials for unification: with potsherds from a ruined dwelling, charcoal from bamboo, husks of rice, the decoction of *palāśa* leaves, and ground pebbles; with the hair of a black antelope skin that has no hair, and whatever else he considers suitable for strengthening half [of the altar]. (Section 3) 44.

The formula ends with *chandasāṅgirasvat*. He mixes the clay. With two [verses] he mixes it with the *saṃsṛjanyā* substances, which are strengthening materials. *Arma* is a place devoid of villages; therein, those potsherds (*kapāla*) he mixes with purified flour, with charcoal from bamboo reduced to powder, with the husks of rice, with the powder of *palāśa* decoction, with ground gravel, and with the hair of a black antelope skin, both long and short hairs—he thus mixes the clay.

Whatever other clay is obtained, half of it is for the purpose of strengthening that which is already firm; whatever else there is of the sacrificial material, such as powder and so forth, all of this is mixed together to form the "mud. In this context, the mixing with the causes of the vessel, such as potsherds and the rest, is explained in the Brāhmaṇa: "He mixes it with potsherds, he mixes it with gravel, he mixes it with hairless [substances], he mixes it with the hair of the black antelope skin" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.6). || 44 ||
With the words, "Thou art the head of Makha," he forms a ball of clay. || 45 ||
O _______________ 14. The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha [Book 11]: the meaning has already been explained. 4.
With the words, "You two are the feet of the sacrifice," he consecrates both the black antelope skin and the lotus leaf. 46.
"He strikes [the earth] and grasps [the clod] with his soft thumb," says Āpastamba.
(56) He offers the rice-balls with the four verses beginning, "The Rudras, having gathered the earth... (57)
"Until the end of the verse beginning with *garbhe ā*," [says] Āpastamba: "He hands over the hand" (*ĀpaŚrSū* 16.24). ||47||
For one who has many wives, the mahiṣī prepares the ukhā with four verses beginning with "May the Vasus fashion you. (48)
The section ends with "to her who is moving. If the sacrificer has many wives, he gives [the garment] to the principal queen (mahiṣī). || 48 ||
The Adhvaryu [performs the rite] for one who has but a single wife. || 49 ||

The Adhvaryu priest, having a single wife, hands [the materials] over to the sacrificer. With these very same Yajus formulas, the sacrificer consecrates [the sacrifice] as it is being performed. 11.1.50.
The sacrificer gives his consent with the sacrificial formulas (yajus) beginning with "Vasavas tvā. || 60 ||
He performs either a threefold elevation or a fivefold elevation. || 51 ||

The *uddhi* is a specific upward projection. Just as one vessel is placed upon another, and upon that yet another vessel—thus forming three tiers (*kakṣyā*)—so too this single pan (*ukhā*) should be made with three tiers. This is the meaning of "he makes it five-tiered.

... Measuring one span (*prādeśa*) in height, one cubit (*aratni*) in width, and one fathom (*vyāyāma*) in circumference, or even of unlimited size, he raises four corners toward the cardinal directions.

It is one *prādeśa* in height; one *aratni* in width; and one *vyāyāma* in circumference. A *vyāyāma* is four *aratnis*. It may be unlimited beyond the *vyāyāma*, or five *prādeśas* on the inside, or the measure of an arrow (*iṣumātrī*). As Āpastamba has said: "It is five *prādeśas* or the measure of an arrow, if there are five animals," according to the Vājasaneyins (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 16.2.8). Regarding the sacrifice with five animals, the rules of the Vājasaneyins and others are also applicable.
Even when performing the rite for five victims, he makes the *ukhā* according to another recension; he makes its four corners with clay, not triangular. Or he makes it circular.

It is circular; when it is circular, it has the dimensions of the *gārhapatya* fire-altar. The sacrificer is grasped by means of his two arms. Regarding the specific qualifications [of the sacrificer], he prescribes a specific number of corners: "One who practices sorcery (*abhicaran*) should make it nine-cornered. (54)
And so says the Brāhmaṇa: "One who practices malevolent magic should make [the fire-altar] nine-edged" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 6.2.6). || 14 ||
With the formula, "Thou art the girdle of Aditi," he makes a girdle either around the middle or at the opening [of the vessel]. 55.
At the junction of the aśrī and the rāsnā, he forms two, four, six, or eight breasts. || 56 ||

When there are two [lines] at the junction and meeting point of the *aśrī* and the *rāsnā*, then they are in the east alone. When there are four, then one in each direction. When there are six, then two in each of two directions. When there are eight, then two in each of all four directions. He makes it either square (*caturasrā*) or circular (*parimaṇḍalā*), having six nipples (*ṣaṣṭanā*). All this has been set forth by the Brāhmaṇa: "He makes it with two nipples; he makes it with four nipples; he makes it with eight nipples" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.6). Thus ends [section] 16.
"May Aditi grasp your opening," with these words he makes the opening. || 57 ||
"Vilamantaścidam || 1.7 ||" Having performed this, he places it upon the sand in the north with the verse, "Having made the earth its mouth. || 58 ||
He places it; he establishes it in the sand to the north of that place where it was prepared. || 68 ||
From that very same clay, he silently fashions the Aṣāḍhā brick, marked with three lines and square in shape. || 59 ||

He who makes the *ukhā* (fire-pan) makes that very same [pan] as the *aṣāḍhā*. From the clay of the *ukhā*, he makes it four-cornered for the four-cornered fire-altar, but not for the *śyena* and other altars; in those cases, he makes the characteristic mark in the middle of the bricks just as [prescribed], whereas the *vyālikhitā* (the cross-lined brick) is obligatory. || 19 ||
Having added horse-dung to the *gārhapatya* fire, he fumigates the *ukhā* with horse-dung while reciting the seven meters, beginning with: "May the Vasus fumigate thee. (Khaṇḍa 4) 11.1.60.
Ka. Here also; 2 Ga. equal to a Brāhmaṇa; 3 Kha. square; 4 , 32 Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra—[11th Praśna]

The dung of a horse is *aśvaśakṛt*. With seven mantras, beginning with "O Vasus, you [protect] this," he fumigates the *ukhā* pot with horse-dung; thus, a single act of fumigation is performed with many mantras. Similarly, other acts that are spoken of with many sentences (many mantras) are treated in the same way. In this case, the horse-dung from the mounting-place (*āroha*) is removed from the *gārhapatya* fire for the fumigation of the fire-altar.
