This is the rule: the fumigation and the cooking take place from the *gārhapatya*; and there is a relinquishing of it (the original dung), even though there is no specific injunction for such relinquishment. 6.

Having dug a pit in front of the Gārhapatya fire with the mantra "Aditi, the goddess," and having spread it with red-heated materials, he places the fire-pan (ukhā) upon it with the mantra "The wives of the gods. || 61 ||

To the east of the Gārhapatya fire, he prepares a pit that is red in its constituent parts; having spread over the ground with those materials for baking the pot—such as cow-dung, sugarcane leaves, and so forth, which have been baked until they are red—he places the pot into that pit with the formula, "For the sake of the gods. (11)

Having silently placed the *aṣāḍhā* brick upon it and covered it with the red cooking materials, he cooks [the oblation] from the *gārhapatya* fire while reciting the six verses beginning with "The goddesses Dhiṣaṇās thee. (62)

Because of the statement "the *tṛṣṇā* [fire]," having placed the *aṣāḍhā* brick while restraining speech, when the *aṣāḍhā* is [handled] with mantras, then the *ukhā* [pot] is done silently (*tūṣṇīm*). And the commentator states that all preparatory rites, such as fumigation and so forth, are performed silently. Because of the statement "silently" regarding the placing [of the fire], the principle is that no unordained rite is performed. The placing of the *aṣāḍhā* is indeed silent because the *ukhā* is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the mantras; therefore, the covering, the mention of "red cooking-pot," and the mantra are omitted.
In this context, based on the observation of the text "He cooks with six" (*TaiSaṃ* 5.1.7), he smears [the vessel] from the *gārhapatya* fire into the mouth of the fire. || 6 ||
With the verse, "Of Mitra, the supporter of the people," he attends to the rice being cooked with a rite dedicated to Mitra.
The meaning is that, O Mairya, one attends to the cooking vessel while it is being heated by means of blazing fire and so forth. || 63 ||
"May Savitṛ, the god, lift you up," with these words he lifts up the cooked [offering].
"Facing the cooked [food]," ending with "according to one's ability. || 64 ||
Saying, "Filling the earth, the quarters, and the intermediate directions," he establishes it on the sand from the north. || 65 ||
Ending with the words "Thou art firm," he establishes it upon the sand from a place to the north of the ashes. || 15 ||

"O Mitra, I entrust this fire-pan to you; may it not be shattered"—having thus entrusted it to Mitra, he besmears the pan with goat's milk while reciting the four Vedic meters, beginning with "May the Vasus fashion you. || 66 ||

— 1. The lifting up [of the *ukhā*] by means of seeing, etc. 3. Variant: *ajakṣī* (goat’s milk). 0 — 1. Paṭala: Accompanied by the commentary *Yogacandrikā* composed by Mahādeva Śāli. Again, the handing over (*paridāna*) is for the sake of protection. Regarding the *ukhā* of Mitra: here, while remaining silent, the *aṣāḍhā* brick is lifted out. This is based on the Āpastamba Sūtra: "Having silently lifted out the *aṣāḍhā*" (ĀpaŚrSū 16.2.23). And with the mantra "The Vasus [are yours]," the sprinkling with goat's milk is performed to remove the heat.

By this, the fire-pan (*ukhā*) becomes firm when sprinkled with milk. Because in the world [the use of] non-milk is the cause for warding off all diseases, it is also stated in the Veda: "This earth is indeed related to Agni; that which is non-milk... Thus, its supreme nature is declared. He prescribes the means of sprinkling: "He sprinkles with non-milk; for it is the supreme... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.7). || 16 ||

Taking seven, twenty-one, or twenty-four beans, he seeks out the head of a man—either a Rājanya or a Vaiśya—who has been killed by an arrow or struck by lightning; having placed the beans upon the head of that male.

Having taken seven or twenty-one *māṣa* beans, he goes toward a human head—either that of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya—who has died either pierced by an arrow or struck by lightning. Alternatively, having taken twenty-one *māṣa* seeds and carrying them with him, he should go to obtain a human head. Thus it has been stated by a Brāhmaṇa: "With twenty-one *māṣas*, he approaches the human head" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.1.8).
This is because of the indicative mark [in the scripture]: "Having scattered beans upon it and having made its head pure, he carries it away" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.8). ||67||

Having cut off the head of the human [effigy] with the words, "This is he who you are; this is your head," he replaces it in the place of the head with a sevenfold-cleft anthill mound, saying, "By this, may you be possessed of a head here. || 68 ||

With the words, "This one who is you," he cuts off the head of the man. With the words, "By this, may you be provided with a head here," he places a seven-holed date-palm heart in the position of the head. ||18||

With the three verses of Yama’s song—beginning with "He who alone is the ruler of this earthly world," "The king whose fame is renowned as a breaker of obstacles," and "By whom the waters, the rivers, the deserts, by whom the sky and the earth were made firm; he, King Yama, presides over the gift of horses that have golden girths, well-yoked, golden-hoofed, and iron-shod"—he sings around [the horse].

Those verses in which Yama is sung are the *yamagāthās*. They are those recited by Kauṣṭhya and others in the *pitṛmedha* section of the *Āraṇyakakāṇḍa*. Regarding the number of these required *yamagāthās*, the text prescribes: "He sings around with three" (*tai0 saṃ0* 5.3.8). This means that while turning his head to the right, he sings around—that is, recites—the *yamagāthās*. According to some, he recites while bringing [the materials] together. (Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin, 11.1.70)

Regarding the *yamagāthā*: it refers to one who has set out for birth [as a professional singer]. That Brāhmaṇa who, having abandoned sacrificing for others (*yājana*), teaching (*adhyāpana*), and receiving gifts (*pratigraha*), maintains his livelihood solely through singing—for such a Brāhmaṇa, one should not give anything that is prescribed by the scriptures. For, because he consumes that wealth after making it impure through the mere art of singing, and excludes it from rites for the gods and ancestors (*devapitṛkārya*), therefore, nothing should be given to him.

In this context, as an incidental point, he shows a certain prohibition regarding human purpose: "Therefore, [wealth] should not be given to a singer, for the song consumes it" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.8). || 70 ||
Thinking, "May this serve as an object of enjoyment for our arms," he takes up the human head. || 71 ||
The seizing of a human head. || 71 ||
"O Agni, rise up from the mother, the earth," with these words he brings [the fire]. || 72 ||
The term "human head" (puruṣaśiras) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. || 72 ||

"Agni goes around the threefold sacrifice like a charioteer, he who bestows [gifts] upon the gods"—this is the verse beginning with "The sage, lord of strength. With the three verses beginning, "Agni, the god, has gone around, the slayer of demons, the driver away of disease; driving off all enemies, burning the Rākṣasas at all times," he performs the *paryagni* rite. Having smeared it with clay, he sets it down. (Section 5) 73.
Thus ends the first paṭala in the eleventh praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. || 1 ||

The head, having been brought [to the cremation ground], is encircled with fire once by means of ordinary (laukika) fire while reciting the three verses beginning with *pari triviṣṭayadhvaram*. According to the Commentator (Bhāṣyakṛt), it should be done thrice. Or, it may be done with the Gārhapatya fire. By means of ordinary methods, such that worms do not arise, one should smear the head with black earth and set it aside. There is no fault of touching a corpse, because of the direct injunction. However, some perform a bath along with their clothes. || 73 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the eleventh book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.
11.2 Now begins the second chapter of the eleventh book.
One sacrifices animals to the fires and to Kāma: a horse, a bull, a ram, and a goat with testicles; they are hornless goats dedicated to Prajāpati. They possess testicles. || 1 ||

"Desires" (*kāmāḥ*) are those things desired, such as sons, cattle, and so forth; "sacrifices" (*āgrayaḥ*) are the means for attaining them. Sacrifices or desires are one... [the rest of the sentence].

3. Paṭalaḥ] Accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* composed by Mahādeva Śāstrī. By the statement [“...kāmaḥ”], desire (*kāma*) is the subordinate factor (*guṇa*). One should sacrifice [the animal] on the new moon day, the full moon day, in proximity to a festival (*parvan*), or under an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). It is prescribed in the Brāhmaṇa: “He places the five heads of animals, such as the blind one, etc. (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.9). In that regard, even in the section concerning the fire-altar (*agni-prakaraṇa*), it is stated: “Prajāpati created Agni” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.5.1).

10) Thus, the placement of the five animal heads is to be understood. The *muskaras* are animals together with their testicles. First, he dedicates to Prajāpati a hornless (*tūpara*) animal that is devoid of horns. After them, he dedicates to the fires for the sake of desire (*kāma*) a bull (*ṛṣabha*), a ram (*vṛṣṇi*), and a goat (*bastā*). According to the Vājasaneyins, however, when there is an option regarding the human [victim] among the animals, then at that time the head of a man is to be severed.

In this context, regarding the construction of the altar for the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), there is a cord four *akṣas* long and five *uparas* long; the measurement of the altar is known by means of one-third of that cord. This is because it is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *ekādaśinī*. However, some perform only the *saumika* [altar]. Since it is not employed in the immediate context of the *ekādaśinī*, and because it shares common features with the independent (*nirūḍha*) Soma sacrifice, it is also a modification of the *nirūḍha*. Furthermore, the specific ritual details (*vaiśeṣika-dharma*) of the *ekādaśinī* are applicable here, as the animal sacrifice for Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya-paśu*) is the fundamental archetype (*mūla-prakṛti*) for the ten [animal sacrifices].

In this context, regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśukarma*), one says, "I shall sacrifice with an animal," and then performs the *ṣaḍhotṛ* offering. However, some do not perform the *ṣaḍhotṛ*, on the grounds that it is merely a subsidiary (*aṅga*) element. According to them, the *ṣaḍhotṛ* is not to be performed when one intends to sacrifice with an animal. Furthermore, even the *vidyut* offering—which is prescribed for those intending to sacrifice with Soma—is not to be performed by them. Although they do not intend to sacrifice [with the animal], the *ṣaḍhotṛ* and the *vidyut* are nevertheless performed because the animal sacrifice has the *Nirūḍhapaśubandha* as its archetype (*prakṛti*). However, these are not performed here in the *udavasānīyā* and subsequent rites.

The touching of water for Soma and Aryaman has already been performed; it is not done again here for Soma. That very point is established by way of incidental discussion: having set aside the fire and brought forth another, one performs the subsequent rites—such as the bringing of the branch, the offering for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and so on—in the manner of the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice. There is the cutting of five sacrificial posts. Having prepared the *veda*, one prepares the altar (*vedi*) and the *uttaravedi*; the carrying forward of the fire and other rites are like those of the animal sacrifice. The dedication (*upākaraṇa*) of the animal dedicated to Prajāpati is performed with the formula: "I dedicate you, who are dear to Prajāpati."

"For the fires, for desire, I dedicate you who are pleasing"—thus [the formula] is for the others: the horse, the bull, the ram, and the ewe. Likewise, the binding [is performed with]: "For Prajāpati, I bind you who are pleasing; for the fires, for desire, I bind you who are pleasing. Likewise [are performed] the sprinkling and other rites. In this context, having accepted the combination of these *sāmidhenī* verses with the archetypal (*prakṛta*) *sāmidhenīs*, he prescribes the *sāmidhenīs* characterized by a specific number.

He recites twenty-one or twenty-four *sāmidhenī* verses continuously; having recited the eleven original ones, he recites the ten verses addressed to Agni beginning with "May the years, O Agni, and the seasons increase thee. He recites [the verse]: "I have sent forth my prayer, seeking strength; may the eater of food accept my songs. Will Apāṃnapāt, the swift impeller, make them well-formed? For he shall take pleasure in them. For Apāṃnapāt has stood upon the lap of the prostrate ones, upright in his own glory within their lap."

"Both most beloved dwellings, he moves toward and away from them, knowing [the way]," thus there are three verses addressed to the waters; if they become twenty-four, [then... 2. May it be so in that world—thus ends the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [Book] 11, [Section] 1.

If [the patient] is ill, he should perform [the ritual] with the verse beginning "O Yama" (RV 10.14.1). For one who is not ill, he uses the verse beginning "O Bṛhaspati, O Savitṛ, awaken him" (RV 10.36.14). With the verse "O Agni, for great wealth, for the sake of giving, we kindle thee" (RV 10.128.1), and with "Praise the two great ones, Heaven and Earth, the bulls, for the office of the Hotṛ" (RV 10.110.9), and with the verse "We have risen up above the darkness" (RV 1.50.10)—which is full of light—he performs the concluding rite (paridhāna).

"May we kindle [thee] for the sake of giving. For the *hotṛ*-function, he establishes the great earth as the seat of power (*indriyā*). With the verse "Upwards from the darkness... (*ud vayaṃ tamasaḥ pari*), he concludes with the verse containing the word "light" (*jyotiṣmatī*). Because of the statement that there are "twenty-one or twenty-four *sāmidhenī* verses recited in a continuous sequence," one should first recite eleven verses beginning with "Obeisance to the winds" (*pra vo vājāḥ*) for the first and last [verses]. Then, for other lineages (*gotra*), there is the set of eleven verses beginning with "He offers" (*ājuhotā*). For the Vasiṣṭhas and the Kṣatriyas, however, there is the set of eleven verses beginning with "Thou, O Varuṇa" (*tvaṃ varuṇa*).

Having recited the eight verses beginning with *samāstvāgne* (TS 4.1.7), the ninth verse for one who is not ill is *bṛhaspate savitar bodhayainam*; for one who is ill, the ninth is *amutra bhūyāt*. The twentieth is *rāye agne*, and the twenty-first, *ud vayaṃ tamasas pari*, is the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*).

When there are twenty-four verses, one should recite eleven *prākṛta* verses and nine *āgnikī* verses as before; then, having recited the three *apsumatī* verses beginning with "upemasṛkṣi," the *jyotiṣmatī* verse "udvayaṃ tamasaspari" serves as the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*). As for what was stated by the Commentator—that in the case of the twenty-four-verse version, one should omit the three *dhāyyā* verses mentioned in another recension, such as "upemaṃ vājayuḥ," and thus complete the count of twenty-four by using ten *prākṛta* verses and ten *āgnikī* verses beginning with "samāstvā agne"—that is incorrect. [The verses should be recited] forward, not repeated. (Sūtras 2, 3, 4, 5)
He pours the libation from the ladle with the verse: "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning."
The substitution for the support is "Hiraṇyagarbha. || 6 ||
"His kindling-sticks are turned upwards"—thus the Āprī verses become the Prayāja offerings. || 7 ||

Although there are indeed only eleven *prayāja* offerings, nevertheless, because the second and third mantras are fixed according to the distinction of persons, the number twelve of the mantras is not contradicted. And that restriction has been shown by the author of the Sūtra: "The second *prayāja* is for Narāśaṃsa for the Vasiṣṭhas and Śunakas; for other lineages (*gotra*s), it is for Tanūnapāt. (7)
The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the oblations dedicated to Agni are *triṣṭubh* verses addressed to Agni. || 8 ||

The three *triṣṭubh* verses addressed to Agni for the gathering [of the fire], "Sit down, O Hotṛ," and the three verses of Yājñasena beginning with "Thou art the source of the sacrifice"—these are the layers of the altar. || 8 ||
The verse beginning with "yaḥ prāṇata" belongs to Prajāpati.

The meaning is that these two are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the animal dedicated to Prajāpati. In that context, there are six verses as *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*: two verses for the omentum (*vapā*), two verses for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and two verses for the oblation (*havis*), beginning with "To Prajāpati, of the goat's omentum. The formal call (*praiṣa*) is: "For the Agnis, for Kāma, of the horse, the bull, and the ram—of their omenta and fat. [End of] Paṭala 1, accompanied by the commentary *Yogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.

The oblation is performed with the mantra: "O Agni, O Indra, go to the gods with the omenta. Although these *ṛc* verses have been stated in the singular number, they accomplish the purpose for many fires, because of the statement: "They are *triṣṭubh* verses addressed to Agni. (9)
The animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) for Vaiśvānara, belonging to Prajāpati, consists of twelve potsherds. It concludes once it has been prepared.

That which belongs to Prajāpati is severed from Vāyu; yet, because the animal victim belongs to Vāyu, one does not fall away from Vāyu. Because there is a cake (puroḍāśa) for Prajāpati, one does not fall away from Prajāpati. As for the cake that is prepared on twelve potsherds, by that [cake] one does not fall away from Vaiśvānara, the deity prescribed in another recension; for Vaiśvānara is indicated as an alternative option. 10–11.
Alternatively, having released the animals dedicated to Agni after they have been encircled by fire, he cuts off their heads, smears them with clay, and sets them aside.

The phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) is intended to indicate the position of another Vedic school (*śākhāntara*). Here, this must be considered: are the *āgneya* animals not to be sacrificed at all; or, having consecrated those animals, should one release them after the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite; or, should one carry out the rites until their completion? Not the first, because it would result in the total non-acquisition of the sacrificial animals. Not the second, because by abandoning them midway, it would result in the sacrifice being incomplete.

Not the third [alternative], because here, due to the fact that the horse, the bull, and the ram have already lost their essence (*sāra*), it would follow that they could not be placed upon the future *cit* (altar-pile). To avoid these three defects, it should be done as follows: by means of the touching (*ālambha*) and the releasing (*utsarga*), the first and third defects will not occur; and by completing the rite with a hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati (*prājāpatya tūpara*), the middle defect—consisting of the failure of the sacrifice—will also not occur. Alternatively, after death, having offered the *saṃjñapta-homa* for those that have been immolated, one cuts off their heads, smears them with clay, and sets them aside. || 12 ||
He throws the headless trunks into the water. || 13 ||
He throws headless trunks into the waters. || 13 ||
He concludes with the Prājāpatya offering.
Having concluded with the Prājāpatya, the ritual recitations (nigamas) belong to that [offering] alone, not to the fires.
Alternatively, in place of all these [offerings], one should sacrifice a white, hornless goat to Vāyu Niyutvat.

He who possesses horses of the specific kind known as *niyuts* is called *niyutvān*. To him one should sacrifice a white goat that is hornless (*tūpara*). Alternatively, Vāyu Niyyutvān may take the place of the five sacrificial animals.
The ritual procedure for that is explained by the rule pertaining to the Prājāpatya sacrifice. ||16||

Its ritual procedure is like that of the established animal sacrifice (*nirūḍhapaśubandha*), because its injunctions are similar to those of the lightning-sacrifice (*vidyudṛṣṭi*); it is performed with five animals. The *āprī* verses and the *ādhāra* oblation are likewise like those of the five-animal sacrifice. The invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) and the offering verse (*yājyā*) for the omentum (*vapā*) are those containing the word "Vāyu" and the word "Śveta," respectively.

This is the Yājuṣa Hautra (the portion for the Hotṛ priest). The verses beginning with "pīvo'nnā rayivṛdhaḥ" are addressed to Vāyu and consist of two *śvetavatī* verses; this is because of the presence of the word "vāyu" in the mantra "te vāyave samanasaḥ," and the presence of the word "śveta" in "śvetaḥ siṣakti. The meaning is that these two, addressed to Vāyu and containing the word "niyutvat," serve as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* for the deity of the offering. ... [The cake] addressed to Vāyu and containing the word "niyutvat" belongs to the deity of the animal sacrifice; or there is a twelve-potherd *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to Vaiśvānara or Prajāpati. It concludes with the established ritual.

The meaning is clear. Regarding this, it has been discussed in the Brāhmaṇa: "Three [offerings] for Vāyu, three for Prajāpati" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.5.1). Vaikhānasa maintains that an animal sacrifice for Vāyu should be performed and a cake (*puroḍāśa*) for Prajāpati. However, as for the twelve-potherd cake made for Prajāpati, by means of it, the deity prescribed in another recensional branch is intended; whereas Vaiśvānara is designated by means of the attribute of Agni.

"For him, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds as a *paśupuroḍāśa* to Agni Vaiśvānara" (*Āpastamba Śrautasūtra* 16.2.12). Thus, even deities other than the deity of the animal sacrifice increase the deity of the animal sacrifice. Therefore, there is an exclusion of the [formula] "they have grown strong by means of the *puroḍāśa*. However, our reading is: "Oṃ, they have grown strong by means of the cups" (*grahaiḥ*). By this it is known that the cups themselves are the deities; therefore, the deities of the cups cause the deities of the animal sacrifice to grow strong.

For this very reason, the Śruti has been recited: "Otherwise, however, they would have said, 'They prospered with the *puroḍāśas* for the cups (*graha*s)'. And whichever animal is sacrificed in a sacrifice that lacks the [Agni-Viṣṇu] qualification—whether it be the *agnīṣomīya*, the *savanīya*, or the *anūbandhyā*—for that [animal], a *puroḍāśa* on twelve potsherds dedicated to Vaiśvānara alone is prepared. Agni is the deity qualified by [the word] *vaiśvānara*; here too, [he is] Vaiśvānara. But the Commentator explains that by virtue of the specific scriptural statement, Agni is Vaiśvānara [only] in other cases, whereas here he is simply Vaiśvānara.
Thus, the entire [rite] is established; it is completed. (18, 19)
Having smeared it with clay, he places the head of the Vāyavya [pot] upon it. (Section 6) 11.2.20.
Thus ends the second chapter in the eleventh book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

Having cut off its head, after touching it and smearing it with clay, the head of the Vāyu-deity is established. Having sacrificed with that Vāyu-animal, or with five animals, because the ritual procedure (*vidhāna*) is the same. For one year, there is the avoidance of meat-eating, the avoidance of sexual intercourse with women, and the avoidance of sleeping on elevated beds. Even when the sacrifice is performed before a full year has passed, the commentator (*bhāṣyakṛt*) states that the Vāyu-vows are still suspended for one year. And there is a combination of all these with the duties pertaining to the fire-possessor (*sāgnika*). (Note: *ga. mucchya* appears to be a scribal error for *samuccaya*.)

3rd Paṭala: [This work is] accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 26. This is the rule (*nyāya*). Alternatively, one may consume meat and sleep on a raised bed; however, one must not approach a woman. "In this manner for a year," so says the Vājasaneyaka. Thus ends the animal sacrifice dedicated to Vāyu. Thus concludes the second Paṭala in the eleventh Praśna of the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra-vyākhyā*, compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin, titled *Prayogacandrikā*. 11.3 Now begins the third Paṭala in the eleventh Praśna.

Having performed that which was to be done prior to the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*, he offers the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice consisting of two oblations or three oblations: a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu, or a pap in ghee for Agni and Viṣṇu; a pap in ghee for Aditi; and a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara as the third [oblation], provided he has not maintained the fires for a full year. (1) At the time of the *Dīkṣā* offerings, having offered the five *Ādhvarika* oblations with the formulas beginning "To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, svāhā," he offers the six *Āgnika* oblations with the formulas beginning "Ākūtim agnim. He offers the seventh with the verse "Viśve devasya netuḥ... (2).

Having first performed the ritual acts pertaining to the recipient of the gift (*dakṣiṇīya*), there follows the assignment of materials, the *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas, the dismissal of the fire, and the crushing of the *soma*. Having set aside the *saptahotṛ* formula, one should establish the fire for the sake of the sacrifice; then follow the *āgnāvaiṣṇava*, the *āditya*, and thirdly the *vaiśvānara* offerings. For a sacrificer who has not maintained the sacred fires for a full year, the *vaiśvānara* offering takes place even before the *āgnāvaiṣṇava*; according to the commentator, it occurs before the *āditya* because of its immediate sequence.

Agni, however, possesses the quality of Vaiśvānara, according to the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) and the indicative mark of the mantra (*mantraliṅga*). From the wording of such mantras as "The *caru* for Agni-Viṣṇu [is] in ghee" and "Ghee is his womb; he rests in ghee," ghee belongs to Agni. Rice grains (*taṇḍula*), on the other hand, are dear to Viṣṇu, according to the scriptural statement: "Those which are the smallest, those [he offers] to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. Therefore, because it is dear to both, the *caru* should be prepared with ghee. That *caru* of which Aditi is the deity is called *āditya*.

Having first prepared the oblation for Agni and Viṣṇu, this *caru* for Āditya is to be made as the second oblation. The Brāhmaṇa prescribes the maintenance of the fire in the pan (*ukhya*) for a year: "He who piles the fire-altar without having maintained the fire in the pan for a year... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.5.1). Without that maintenance, the piling of the altar is equivalent to the miscarriage of a fully developed fetus; consequently, the sacrificer would die.

Therefore, a man who is unable to maintain [the fire] for a full year, and who desires to perform the *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial gifts) after three, six, or ten nights even before the completion of the year, should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara; for that Agni Vaiśvānara is of the nature of the year. Just as in the world a fetus fully developed over the course of a year is born easily at the proper time, so too, by means of this sacrifice, having reached the year, he becomes one who has piled the fire-altar when the time arrives; consequently, he does not die.

He praises the threefold nature of the oblations prescribed for the *hāva*: "These oblations become threefold" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.5.3). Here, since there is the presence of the *yājuṣa-hautra*, [the number] is seventeen according to the method stated in the *Yājuṣa*.

The *Sāmidhenī* verses are as follows: "Agni is the first among the deities" (*agniragne prathamo devatānām*) and "O Agni and Viṣṇu, you two are the highest and greatest" (*agniśca viṣṇo tam uttamaṃ mahaḥ*); these are the *Yājyā* and *Anuvākyā* for Agni and Viṣṇu. "May Aditi protect us" (*aditirna uruṣyatu*) and "The great Mother" (*mahīmu ṣu mātaram*); these are for Aditi. "Vaiśvānara with his aid, he who is touched in heaven" (*vaiśvānaro na ūtyā pṛṣṭo divi*); this is for Vaiśvānara. The *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice concludes with the *Ājyeḍā*. The rule is that the division into three parts applies to the offerings for Āditya and Vaiśvānara.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, explains that at the end of the *iḍā* offering for the clarified butter (*ājya*), the Brahman priest eats his portion, performs the ritual worship (*upasthāna*), and then departs. The construction of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, the shaving of the hair, and so forth—extending up to "outside [the hall] to the north"—take place prior to the *dīkṣā-hutis*. Having performed everything up to the point of "he sits down near the Āhavanīya fire," the *dīkṣā-hutis* are offered. All optional injunctions are also available here. The *adhvara* is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

In the *adhvara* sacrifice, there are those [oblations] pertaining to the *adhvara*: "To Prayer, to Impulsion, to Agni, Svāhā!"—thus with the *veṇu* [reed]; four [oblations] with the *sruk* ladle, and the fifth with the *sruva*. Having offered six oblations pertaining to Agni beginning with "The Form, Agni," and having likewise offered them together with the *pūrṇāhuti*, there is the pouring over [of ghee]. According to the *bhāṣya*, however, there is a replenishing [of the ladle] with the mantra. The seventh is the *pūrṇāhuti* with "Of Viśve Devāḥ, the Leader... Because of the mention of "the seventh," the sacrificer follows it with the mantra "Vātam prāṇam... (Wind is the breath).

Now, an objection: by virtue of the archetype (*prakṛti*), six initiation-oblations (*dīkṣā-āhuti*) are obtained for the fire-sacrifice, and their six mantras are likewise obtained from the archetype itself, such as "To Ākṛti, to Prayuja, to Agni, Svāhā" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 1.2.2), and so forth. For the fire-sacrifice, there are other six mantras, such as "Ākṛtim agnim prayujam svāhā," and so forth; and these are enjoined for the purpose of initiation, according to the rule: "He initiates with six [oblations]" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.3.1). Furthermore, a repetition of the initiation-oblations is heard in the scripture: "He offers twelve [oblations]."

In this regard, there is a doubt: are the archetypal (*prākṛta*) mantras set aside by the modified (*vaikṛta*) mantras, or are they combined with them? In that case, because of direct recitation and direct scriptural statement, the modified mantras should set aside the archetypal mantras, since they serve the same purpose.

Although there is repetition of the oblations because of the statement, "He offers twelve," nevertheless, since only the modified (vaikṛta) oblations—those specifically enjoined by direct scriptural statement—are intended as oblations (by virtue of subverting the archetypal mantras obtained through the rule of extension), it follows that the twelve oblations are to be performed with those [modified ones] alone when repeated; to this we reply: the modified [mantras] are not heard in the direct statement for the purpose of the oblation itself. Rather, their status as auxiliary elements of the oblation is established by force of their being for the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*).

And because it is performed only once, its purposefulness is established; therefore, the archetypal [acts] are to be combined with the modified ones, not sublated. In the injunction "He causes [the sacrificer] to be initiated six times," the purpose of initiation is heard; and since that [purpose] is achieved through the oblations by means of the signs of the *svāhākāra*, it is inferred that [the archetypal acts] pertain to the oblation in order to establish their status as being for the sake of initiation.

Since the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is accomplished by the six oblations (*homa*) performed only once, there is no authority for their repetition (*abhyāsa*) or for the annulment of the original (*prākṛta*) rule; therefore, by virtue of the repetition, because there are twelve oblations, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of both the original and the modified mantras. [End of] Paṭala 1, 2, 3, accompanied by the commentary *Payogacandrikā* composed by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 25.

Having performed that which precedes the making of the fist, he spreads a layer of *śaṇa* grass or *muñja* grass inside the *ukhā* and then places the *ukhā* upon the embers of the Āhavanīya fire with the two verses: "Do not break, do not be harmed. || 3 ||

The action of the fist is the making of a fist; and previously [it was said], "having made two fists" (*saṃ. sū. 1.2.6*). Having performed that making of the fist, where one offers the *avakā* grasses and so forth, these are the *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas, ending with: "He does not weary this Adhvaryu" (*saṃ. śrī. 7.1.3*). A *śaṇa* is a particular kind of bird; its *kulāya* means its nest. *Muñja* refers to pieces of reed; having covered the interior of the fire-pan (*ukhā*) with them, he places the outer pan upon the Āhavanīya fire with the two verses beginning, "Do not break, do not be harmed. The mantra ends with the word "in this" (*asmin*). || 3 ||
"O Maitreya, heat this fire-mouthed [vessel] by surrounding it with embers. || 4 ||
One should place fuel on all sides, circumambulating it with embers.
Saying "dravanna," he places a betel nut, having scraped it and anointed it with ghee, into that [ladle]. || 5 ||

In the *Sasyāmukhā* [fire], one throws a small piece of wood from the *kramuka* tree; having scraped the *kramuka* wood and sprinkled it with ghee, one casts it [into the fire]. It is stated by Vaikhānasa that one should cast the *kramuka* in the form of powder into the *mukhā*. || 5 ||
And muñja grasses. || 6 ||

The meaning is that he places [the fire] together with the mouths [of the hearth]. (6) However, for one who has lost his prosperity (*gataśrī*) and desires to regain it, the text prescribes the re-establishment (*pravṛjana*) after removing the churned fire (*mathitāgni*), as before:

"He who desires prosperity, or he who would prepare the *ukhā* [fire-pan], for him that very [fire] should be used; having churned [a new fire], one should place it for one who has lost his prosperity. (7)

"The fire that arises in the *ukhā* when it has been heated on the *āhavanīya*—that alone is to be used for one desiring prosperity (*bhūti*), and not the fire produced by friction. 'This one arises; this indeed becomes self-existent (*svayaṃbhū*),' [Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.9]. Therefore, since this fire arises in the *ukhā* and is produced spontaneously without depending on friction, it is called 'self-existent. This being so, the sacrificer certainly attains prosperity. || 7 ||

He prescribes another method for the *adhvaryu* who hates the sacrificer: "If he should desire, 'May I produce an enemy for him,' he should bring fire from elsewhere and place it [in the pan]. (8) Regarding this, the *Satyāṣāḍha Śrautasūtra*, Book 11, states: If the *adhvaryu* should desire with respect to someone, "May I produce an enemy for him," he should bring fire from another location, such as another house, and cast it into the pan (*ukhā*). When that is done, he produces an enemy without delay. Next, he prescribes another fire for a specific desire. (8)
[The story] of Ambarīṣa, who desired food. || 9 ||

The worldly vessel made of iron or other materials used for frying vegetables and the like with clarified butter and so forth is called *ambarīṣa*. When that [vessel] is heated, a powerful flame arises within the pan of clarified butter. Then, having taken the fire from there, it is placed into the *ukhā* (cooking pot). For in the world, food such as vegetables and the like is held in that *ambarīṣa*; therefore, because this fire shares the same origin (*samānayonitva*) as the desired food, the sacrificer indeed obtains food. || 9 ||
One who desires, "May a hero be born to me in my kingdom," should take [the fire] from a forest conflagration. || 11.3.10 ||

*Pradāvya* is a forest fire. Therefore, it is said that [the fire] from an *udukhya* [vessel] is for one who desires, "May a hero like Dhanañjaya be born in my kingdom. Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "The taking [of fire] from a *pradāvya* is for the chief [officiant]. [Fire] from the tip of a burning tree is for one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). 11. 15... [End of section].

The phrase "having brought from it" continues [to apply]. For a sacrificer desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he should bring burning coals from a tree and place them upon the *ukhā* pot. || 11 ||
[The offering] for one desiring food is by means of roasting. || 12 ||

...In this case as well, there is the elliptical extension (*anukarpa*) of the phrase "having brought it back, he should place it. *Bharjana* means a frying pan; the meaning is that having abandoned [the grains] where they were, one should bring them back from that place and place them upon the *dhānās*. || 12 ||
One who is performing the optional fire-sacrifice (kāmya-agni) should not add fuel to the Āhavanīya fire.
Even when performing the optional fire-installation (kāmya-agni), the sacrificer does not perform the heating of the fire in the Āhavanīya. || 13 ||
Once it has been produced, he follows it [to the fire] and leads it toward the Āhavanīya.
Air... for the sake of meditation; on the side of the kindling, that which has arisen in the fire-pan (ukhā) follows the fire in the pan (ukhya) to the Āhavanīya. 14.

With the verse, "From the highest gathering-place," he places a fuel-stick of *udumbara* wood; with the verse, "From the furthest distance," a stick of *vaikaṅkata* wood; and with the verse, "That wonderful [work] of Savitṛ, the most excellent," a stick of *śamī* wood. (15) Some prescribe the *śamī* stick first and the *vaikaṅkata* stick afterwards. (16)
Having kindled it, he throws [the fuel] into [the fire]. 15 || 16 || 4.
[End of] Paṭala 3: Accompanied by the *Payogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.
With the three verses beginning, "Sit thou in the lap of this mother," he worships the Agni who has been born. 17.
"May he not sit upon me," and so forth; here, with three verses, there is the worship of the powerful one who has been born. 17.
With the five verses beginning "O Agni, whatever [thou hast]... he places upon the fire a faggot of Udumbara wood that has been cut with a back-cutter.

The section ends with the words *dadhāmy āsye*. With the mantras beginning with *yad ala*, he should place a fuel-stick (*samidh*) made of wood that has not been cut by an axe (*aparaśu-vṛkṇa*). Alternatively, at the end of the five [mantras], he should offer once a single piece of *udumbara* wood—or something else that has not been cut by an axe—that is broken by hand alone, as the primary fuel-stick (*mukhya idhma*), using tools such as a knife (*vāsī*).
18. For one who practices sorcery (*abhicarataḥ*), he should make [the fuel-stick] from *tailvaka* wood; through this, the seizers (*grāhukas*) become his equals. 19.
A bundle of fuel for the *tilaka* sacrifice consists of *telvaka* wood; some say it consists of much *gālava* wood. 19.

With the verse, "With thy two tusks, O Agni, crush the thieves," he places a fuel-stick of *Ficus religiosa* (aśvattha) on the fire; with the verse, "Those who among men are thieves... he places one of *Flacourtia ramontchi* (vaikaṅkata); and with the verse, "He who acts as an enemy toward us... he places one made of *Prosopis cineraria* (śamī). As he places these, he meditates in his mind upon the destruction of him whom he hates. (11.3.20–21)

The syntactical connection is that he places fuel-sticks (*samidh*) everywhere. The meaning is that at the time of placing those fuel-sticks, the Adhvaryu priest meditates in his mind upon the slaughter of whichever sacrificer he harbors hatred toward.
"At my sacred knowledge (*brahman*) has been sharpened; or rather, it has surpassed theirs"—with these words, he places two final fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood.
The phrase "I am" [is used] at the end. The remainder of the instruction is that he should silently offer two fuel-sticks (*samidh*) made of *udumbara* wood. || 22 ||
Then he makes the sacrificer recite: (Section 7) || 23 ||
At the end of the *rākṣoghna* hymn in the *uttama* [section], he should cause the sacrificer to recite the two final verses beginning with "saśitaṃ me. He then mutters:

"Brahman and Kṣatra, you two are our allies; the Brahman indeed quickens the Kṣatra, and the Kṣatra quickens the Kṣatra of the Kṣatriya and the Brahman of the Brāhmaṇa, as they perform heroic deeds together. (24)
This is clear.

|| 24 || "Like a mother her son, may the earth—the fire-pot—bear Agni Purīṣya in her own womb. Being in harmony with all the gods and the seasons, may Viśvakarman, the Lord of Progeny, yoke that [fire-pot]. With these words, he places the fire-pot in a sling made of Muñja grass, having six or twelve suspension-strands. || 25 ||
There are six feet for the sling made of *muñja* grass; he places the fire-pan upon that which has six or twelve [feet]. He should employ such a means that the sling is not burned. || 25 ||

With the two verses, "O Agni, yoke those [steeds] of yours... and "The one with twenty-one knobs, made of gold, strung on a cord," the sacrificer, sitting within the altar (antarvedi), having turned it over so that it is visible with the words "The golden ornament (rukma) shining forth," fastens the one with twenty-one knobs on the outside; he places the one with the knobs facing downward underneath.

The "Nirbādha" (unobstructed) are specific parts resembling pustules that, by becoming depressed or elevated on a golden plate, cause complete pain to the person who touches them. That gold plate (*rukma*) upon which there are twenty-one such [parts] is called the "twenty-one-fold treasure" (*ekaviṃśatinidhi*); one should fashion such a gold plate. It is "woven with threads" (*sūtrota*), meaning it is marked with lines (*lāṅgita*) upon the thread.
With the mantra beginning "dṛśāno rukmaḥ," the sacrificer, having first marked the internal pustule from above, subsequently forms the external pustules. || 26 ||
With the verse "naktoṣāsā," he fastens on the black antelope skin.
With the verse "naktoṣāsā," he places a black antelope skin over his arms.
"Viśvā rūpāṇi"—with these words, [he unties] the loops of the sling. || 28 ||
The word "he fastens" (pratimuñcate) is understood to carry over from the previous verse. He fastens the loop of the carrying-net around the neck. || 28 ||
Or alternatively, having fastened the carrying-sling, he fastens the black antelope skin.
Or rather, the meaning is that it is recited exactly as it is read in the traditional textual transmission (samāmnāya). || 29 ||
"Thou art Suparṇa, Garuḍa," with these words he gazes at the fire in the ukhya vessel.
[This is] primarily the observation of that which is indeed immovable. || 30 ||
"You are Suparṇa, the Garuḍa; go to heaven," with these words he lifts it up. || 31 ||
The meaning is clear. || 31 ||
Holding [the vessel] above the navel, he strides four Viṣṇu-strides toward the east with the formula, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu. || 32 ||

Holding the *ukhya* fire above the navel, he strides four *viṣṇukrama* steps toward the eastern direction while facing east, with the mantra "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇoḥ kramo’si*) ending each step with the words "him whom we hate. [32] He consecrates the *ukhya* fire with the mantra, "Agni has cried out" (*akrandad agniḥ*). [33]
With this verse beginning "He cried out," he consecrates that fire with a mantra. || 33 ||
With the four verses beginning "O Agni, you who turn towards us," he turns clockwise.

The phrase "viśvataspari" marks the end [of the verse]. He turns clockwise with four [verses], "together with the fire"—this is the remainder [of the instruction]. Regarding the turning, he prescribes clockwise motion: "He turns toward the south" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.2.1). "Toward the south" means by way of clockwise motion; keeping the southern side [of the fire] on one's right, the circumambulation starting from the left side is clockwise motion. Because of the presence of superior capability in the right side of a person, the turning is performed following that very principle. || 34 ||

Having brought [the fire] with the verse, "I have brought thee hither," he worships it; if he should desire of someone, "May he possess a kingdom," he should meditate upon him mentally, saying, "May all the people desire thee. (35)

He shows that in the first quarter of this mantra, the fetching of the fire is understood as being well-known: "He says, 'I have brought you hither,' for he indeed brings him hither" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.2.1). Regarding the second quarter, he states that stability is established through positive and negative concomitance: "He says, 'Stand firm, unshakable,' for the sake of stability" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.2.1).

In the third quarter [of the verse], the prosperity of the subjects (*prajāsamṛddhi*), and in the fourth quarter, the stability of the kingdom (*rājyasthairya*), he shows in sequence: "May all the people desire you"—by saying this, he causes him to prosper through the people; "may the kingdom rest upon this one"—by saying this, he makes the kingdom firm in him. "Through the people" means through the subjects. "Him" refers to the sacrificer. "Upon this" refers to the sacrificer. "He makes" (*akaḥ*) means he performs (*karoti*).

At the time of reciting the fourth foot [of the verse], he prescribes a mental meditation concerning the patron (*yajamāna*) for a specific desire: "Regarding whomsoever he should desire, 'May he possess sovereignty,' he should meditate upon him mentally; he indeed becomes sovereign" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.2.1). If the Adhvaryu should desire that a certain patron attain kingship, he should meditate upon him at the time of pronouncing the fourth foot. Some, however, explain: "Having silently [carried the throne] as far as the vicinity of the throne-seat (*āsandi*), he worships it with the mantra, 'I have brought thee hither' (*ā tvā ahārṣam*)."

And [the mantra] "The great one has arisen at the head of the dawns. But in the Bhāṣya, he explains: "The first [mantra], 'I have brought you,' is for the purpose of bringing [the fire]. The worship of the second fire is performed silently after having brought it; this is because of the composition of the Vaikhānasa Sūtra: "For one whom he should desire, 'May he be the lord of the kingdom,' the meditation for him is: 'O Devadatta, place this kingdom upon [him]. (35)
With the mantra "uduttamam," he unties the loop of the sling. || 36 ||
He lowers the loop of the sling from the neck. || 36 ||
"Great and upright, he has stood at the head of the dawns"—with these words, having released [the horse], he worships it. || 37 ||
The meaning has been explained. || 37 || [From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha:

On an Audumbara throne (āsandi) with a head-piece one cubit (aratni) long, with legs one span (prādeśa) long, bound with Muñja grass, either spread with wooden planks or smeared with clay, he places the Ukhya fire upon it with four verses, [reciting]: "Sit thou in the lap of this mother. || 38 ||

Because the *audumbarī* throne (*āsandi*) has been introduced as the subject at hand, it is that very object which is referred to by the word "in it" (*tasyām*). The passage ends with "bṛhat. One should establish the primary fire upon the *audumbarī* throne with the verses beginning "Sit down, O Mother," and so forth. Alternatively, "audumbarī" means made of *udumbara* wood. "In the throne" (*ādityasyām*) refers to the seat. It is one whose head-piece (*śīrṣaṇya*) and side-boards (*anūcya*) are a span (*prādeśa*) in measure, and whose legs are also a span in measure. Its weaving is done with cords of muñja grass, or it is covered with wooden planks (*phalaka*).

It is not woven with *muñja* grass and is smeared with clay; the meaning is that it is done in such a way that both [the fire and the clay] are not burned. With the four verses beginning "Sit upon the lap of this mother," he places the *ukhya* fire within it. || 38 ||
Or on sugar. || 39 ||
"He settles them with three [verses]" (ĀpŚS 16.4.17), says Āpastamba; or he settles them with the *śakvarī* [verse]. 39.
"Some recite that one should worship with the *Haṃsavatī* [verse]," thus they hand down.
(Section 8) || 11.3.40 || Thus ends the third chapter in the eleventh book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.

The followers of the *Aukīya* branch prescribe the worship with the *Haṃsavatī* verse, "The swan dwelling in purity" (*haṃsaḥ śuciṣat*). || 40 || Thus ends the third chapter in the eleventh book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. *Mana*.
11.4 Now begins the fourth chapter in the eleventh book.
One undertakes the ritual acts beginning with the forming of the fist. ||1||

From the making of the fist (*muṣṭikaraṇa*) onwards, he begins to perform the rites belonging to the Soma sacrifice. This is the sequence of rites for the first day of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Having caused the *saṃbhārayajus* formulas to be recited, he covers the fire-pan (*ukhā*) with a mat of hemp or a mat of *muñja* grass and prepares the fire for the pan (*aukhyam agnim*). (Śrautasūtra 11.3.3).
With the verse, "By which the gods rose upward through the light" (*yena devā jyotiṣordhvā udāyan*), he kindles the fire in the pan with pieces of wood a span (*prādeśa*) long. (2)

With the verse *yena devāḥ*, [he places] fuel-sticks of the size of a span (*prādeśa*) [into the fire], because the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is the subject under discussion; however, the Commentator (*bhāṣyakṛt*) says it is the Adhvaryu. (In another manuscript, there is a variant reading: *adhvaryuṇaiva*. [The fire] burns constantly. [Chapter 4, Section 1: Together with the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 31: It burns always.
"Because of the statement of Āpastamba: 'He always burns eternally' (16.19); and because of the Vaikhānasa [sūtra]: 'He indeed, the glorious one, burns only at the time of the vow' (3). 4.
"O Lord of Food, give us food"—saying this, one who is about to undertake the vow places a fuel-stick of Udumbara wood upon the *satra* fire, which is maintained for the duration of the vow.

When he is about to take up the vow (*vrata*), the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) anoints a fuel-stick (*samidh*) made of *udumbara* wood with a milky substance for the sake of the vow and then inserts it [into the fire]. Because of the use of the locative case in the word "in the vow" (*vrata*), the vow is taken by the sacrificer either at midday or at midnight. This concludes the section on the four-footed [animals]. 4.1.4.1.4.

"By the impulse of God Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the Gāyatrī metre, I place you, the night-brick; by that deity, may you sit firm like Aṅgiras"—with these words he worships the primary fire in the evening. "By the impulse of God Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the Gāyatrī metre, I place you, the day-brick; by that deity, may you sit firm like Aṅgiras"—with these words [he worships] in the morning.
The meaning is that he worships the fire in the *ukhā* pot. || 6 ||6||
On the following day, he worships with the Vātsapra hymn consisting of eleven verses beginning, "Agni was first born from the sky. 7.

"On the second day, he worships with the Vātsapra" (LŚS 5.2.1). The hymn beginning with "divaḥ parīti," which was studied by the great seer named Vatsaprī, is called the Vātsapra; with that, he should worship Agni. || 7 ||
Thus, [the rule applies] always from the time of purchase. || 8 ||
In the manner thus described, up to the point of "purchase" (kraya). || 8 ||
On the previous day he strides the Viṣṇu-steps; on the following day he worships with the Vātsapra hymn. Thus [it is said]. 9.

"On the previous day" means on the first day he performs the Viṣṇu-strides; "on the following day" means he worships with the Vātsapra hymn. While it might be understood that both the Viṣṇu-strides and the Vātsapra occur on the first day, it is stated [in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.2.3]: "On the previous day he strides; on the following day he worships. However, some perform both—the Viṣṇu-strides and the Vātsapra—on the first day.

"On the second and subsequent days, they perform the Viṣṇukrama on the second day and the Vātsapra on the third, always alternating them until the day of the purchase of the Soma. On the day of the Soma-purchase, however, both are performed: first the Viṣṇukrama and afterwards the Vātsapra. (9) [Note: The reading "te'pi" is found in the text. The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha and others—[16] "On the day when one is about to establish the sacred fires, he should combine both [rites]. He should step forward and then stand in worship. (11.4.10)
On whichever day he is about to perform the sacrifice, on that day he should combine the Viṣṇukrama and the Upasthāna of those two.

If, while the fire is being carried forward, this god should think ill of these creatures, [the priest] should offer three fuel-sticks with these three verses: "O Agni, bring us physicians! You are the form of the one whose path is black; you are our invoker, worthy of praise. O Agni, be our physician among the gods as the bearer of oblations; you are the carrier of offerings to the gods. We invoke you, the physician; we kindle you, the physician. Be our physician among the gods. || 11 ||

While the [Agnihotra] is being offered in the Āhavanīya fire situated in the *ukhā* [pot], if this god Agni-Rudra should become angry with the creatures and seek to harm them, one should offer three fuel-sticks (*samidh*) with the verses addressed to Agni containing the word "miṣ" (ĀpŚS 16.1.28), placing each stick with its respective mantra. || 11 ||

If, while the *ukhya* fire is being carried, he should desire, "May it rain," he should offer three fuel-sticks with these three verses: "Sūrya plunges into the waters with his rays, winning the prize; he awakens the singer as the increaser of life. "He who has measured out the ends of heaven and earth with his ray, has filled both worlds with his greatness. "Thou goest weaving the thread with the best bearers; thou art spreading it out, O God, for the sake of wealth. The rays of Sūrya, shaking [the darkness], have driven away the gloom like a skin. With these three verses, he should place three fuel-sticks upon the fire.

If, while the fire is being established or maintained, anything belonging to the sacrificer should be lost, and if he should desire, "May Parjanya rain," he should place three fuel-sticks with each mantra from those dedicated to Sūrya—that is, having Sūrya as their deity—among which the word *raśmi* (ray) occurs; these are the *raśmivatyaḥ*. He should offer them one by one. || 12 ||

If, while the fire is being carried forward, he should desire, "May it not rain," he should offer three fuel-sticks with these verses: "His banners have appeared; his rays extend over the people, shining like fires" (RV 7.3.1); "The swift one, visible to all" (RV 7.62.1); and "The golden ornament of heaven, far-seeing, rises with its goal afar, swift and radiant; now indeed, impelled by Sūrya, men go forth performing their tasks and their duties" (RV 7.63.2–4). || 13 ||

1. I shall explain. 2. Ka: "That is new. [Chapter 6] Accompanied by the commentary *Payogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śākhin. If one should desire, "May Parjanya not rain," [he should offer oblations] with excessive rain [as the result]. Those [oblations] which have Sūrya as their deity are *saurya*. The word *dhānāḥ* (parched grains) exists; they are radiant (*bhrājasvatī*). With those three, he should place three fuel-sticks (*samidh*) on the fire for each mantra. And also [with the mantra]: "His rays have become visible" (*adṛśram asya ketavaḥ*). ||13||

If anything should be lost while the fire is being carried, he worships it with the four verses beginning "O Agni, who returnest" (*agne 'bhyāvartin*). It is known from tradition: "He surely finds that very thing. (Section 9, Sūtra 14)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the eleventh book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.

If anything belonging to the sacrificer should be lost while the *ukhya* fire is being carried or maintained, he should worship the *ukhya* fire with the four verses beginning with "O Agni, returning one" (*agne 'bhyāvartin*). According to the Śruti, "He recovers that which was lost. This same [rite] applies even in the case of the loss of gold, because of the injunction regarding the time for carrying it away. Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the eleventh praśna of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.
11.5 Now, the fifth chapter in the eleventh book.
With the verse, "May all the gods lift thee up," he lifts the *ukhya* fire.

... on whichever day, while the consecrations (*dīkṣā*) are in progress, he should set out toward the vicinity of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*). Regarding this, Āpastamba has stated quite explicitly: "On the day he should set out" (ĀpaŚrSū 16.4.35). In this case, the consecration is obligatory in the house, because of the injunction for setting out in another *sūtra* and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra. He lifts up—that is, he raises—the fire-pan (*ukhya*). || 1 ||
With the four [verses] beginning "Sit down in the lap of this mother," he places the cart on the island.

"Upon the cart he places the *ukhya* fire," says Āpastamba. That cart which has two poles is the *dvīṣa*; on that *dvīṣa* cart [he proceeds]. He does not travel by chariot; the cart is the substitute for the chariot. That in which the *mauga*—the mouth—is placed, or in which the *ukhya* is established with three [fires], is the cart. There is an *upasthāna* (reverential standing) with verses containing the word "horse. Here too, the act of setting out belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).
Having silently placed the other fires, he sets out with the mantra: "O Agni, go forth, full of light... (VS 11.57). 3.

In the archetype (prakṛti) of the Agnihotra and Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is not prescribed that one should deposit the Āhavanīya fire into the mouth of the vessel [for transport], and the Gārhapatya and Dakṣiṇāgni fires behind the *havis*-vessels; nor is it prescribed that one should deposit the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires onto two separate pieces of wood and then proceed by chariot. 3-_________________

The author of the Bhāṣya states that the *sāmnāyya* and *āvāsathya* [fires] belong only to the Full and New Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), and not elsewhere. "The other two are silent" means they belong to only those two fires, because of the rule regarding their formal installation (*samāropaṇa*). For the verse "From the auspicious, may we go to the better," the substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) at the time of kindling is "Come, full of light. ||3||
He consecrates the axle with the mantra, "Agnir akrandat."
If a sound arises for the eye, then there is a consecration; crossing a river is as in the natural state. || 4 ||

Having resolved [upon the ritual], he places a fuel-stick of *udumbara* wood, anointed with clarified butter, into the *ukhya* fire-vessel with the verse containing the word "guest" (*atithivat*), using the *gāyatrī* verse "Worship Agni with fuel" (*samidhāgnim duvasyata*) for a Brāhmaṇa; with the *triṣṭubh* verse "Forward, forward this Agni" (*pra prāyam agniḥ*) for a Rājanya; and with a *jagatī* verse for a Vaiśya. || 5 ||

The mantra for the departure (*prayāṇa*), however, belongs to the sacrificer as well. This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the words "O Agni, go forth, full of light," which the sacrificer speaks with reference to Agni. Likewise, even in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is the indicative mark: "May Bṛhaspati be your leader" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 1.2.4). Having reached this sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), he enters the sacrificial ground together with the fires, saying, "I have attained this."

In this case as well, having placed the Gārhapatya and Dakṣiṇāgnis in their respective places, and having first caused the Ukhyāgni to rest upon the Gārhapatya, he does not wrap himself [with the cord], or rather, [he wraps it] behind. When the journey has concluded—meaning it is finished—with the verse "Worship Agni with fuel" (*samidhāgnim duvasyata*), the sacrificer himself, as one who has undertaken the journey, places that [Ukhyāgni] which has been moistened from the root up to the top; it is not [placed] by another, because the acts of moistening and placing are performed by a single agent.

In this way, for a Kṣatriya, the placing with a Triṣṭubh verse anointed with ghee is: "This Agni is the lord of the people" (*ayaṃ so agnir yo havyavāṭ*). For a Vaiśya, it is with a Jagatī verse: "The guardian of the people" (*janasya gopāḥ*).
At the kindling, the undertaking of the vow, and the settling [of the fire], when all these [verses] are brought together, he places the first one anointed with ghee.

"When the gods rose up from the fuel, from the light"—this refers to the kindling woods being placed upon the *ukhya* fire. Vaikhānasa says that if the sacrificial ground is reached at the time of midday, then the sacrificer, having poured clarified butter over them, first places the eastern [wood], followed by the fuel and the conclusion of the vow. This is because there is no deviation from the prescribed time.

If the fire-pan (*ukhā*) should sink into the ashes, he takes the pan, goes to the edge of water, and with these two verses—"O buffalo, descend into this golden vessel, well-made, of good ritual order, and thousand-spiked; enjoy the honeyed spring, the wide expanse; enter your oceanic dwelling"—and "Suck this honeyed breast of the waters, which is swollen in the midst of the lake; enjoy the honeyed spring, the wide expanse; enter your oceanic dwelling," he brings down the pan from the fire.

Regarding the passage beginning with "He places ashes upon the *ukhā*," this applies to anyone other than the Adhvaryu. "May the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus kindle you again," with these words he adds fuel.
The Adhvaryu, according to Vaikhānasa; "He rekindles the Āhavanīya fire," according to Āpastamba and Baudhāyana. ||11||
"By awakening it is awakening"—thus [he says]. (Khaṇḍa 10) He worships with two verses containing the word "awakening. 12.

He awakens it with the mantra; he indeed awakens this fire with the mantra "sa bodhi. The southern part of the Āhavanīya fire is the place where the sacrificer stands to perform the *upasthāna* (reverential salutation). Therefore, here too, he stands and performs the *upasthāna* while remaining in the southern region. 12.

For one who has been initiated, the constant immersion in water after the *iṣṭakā* offerings have been performed serves the purpose of avoiding contact with those for whom the *iṣṭakā* offerings have not yet been performed. || 13 ||

The meaning is that when the ash has increased, one should perform the immersion of the ash into the water; once the bricks have been prepared, the immersion of the ash becomes a constant requirement. As for those [bricks] not yet prepared, it means they are used together with the clay for the purpose of mixing for the sake of making bricks. ||13||
One desiring cattle should perform [the rite] in excrement. || 14 ||

However, for one desiring cattle, the mixing with ashes should be done in earth containing feces, not in water; on this point, both the author of the Sūtras and the commentators maintain that it must indeed be in feces, but Satyāṣāḍha does not hold this view. Furthermore, the rule regarding "silent" and "made of clay" applies to the two optional rites even for one desiring cattle.

A Yāyāvara should shave [his hair] in the waters. 15.
A *yāyāvara* is one whose nature is to wander. A *yāyāvara* should cast even the ashes of his sacrificial fires into the waters alone when they have become excessive. || 15 ||

"He should remain consecrated for three nights; he should remain consecrated for six nights"—these optional rules for consecration have been explained in the Brāhmaṇa; regarding them, one may act according to his desire.

Initiation (*dīkṣā*) consists of the acceptance of rules such as shaving the head and so forth. Regarding the initiation connected with the fire being piled (*cīyamāna*), thirteen optional forms are modified: three nights, six nights, seven nights, eight nights, nine nights, ten nights, eleven nights, twelve nights, thirteen nights, fourteen nights, fifteen nights, seventeen nights, twenty-four nights, thirty nights, one month, four months, eight months, and twelve months. These optional initiation rituals are stated in the section beginning "O Agni, by means of initiation" (*agne dīkṣayā*, Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 6.6.7), and they may be performed according to one's desire.

In this rite, having performed the rites up to the kindling of the *ukhya* fire with the verse "atra yena devāḥ," he loosens his fingers with the formula "ayāṅgulīr nyañcati svāhā. Having performed the release of speech (*vāgvisarga*) at the rising of the stars with the formulas beginning "yajñe manasaḥ svāhā," they take up two pieces of wood at midnight: the first is an *audumbara* fuel-stick with the formula "te no dehy anaparoḍavaḥ," and the second fuel-stick with the formula "rātrim iṣṭakām. Then follows the washing of the hands up to the touching of the navel. Thereafter, the sending away of the cold (the cessation of the ritual activity) and the keeping of vigil for that night are performed. || 1 ||

Then, at the time of sunrise, there is the release of speech after the vow of silence and so forth, and the worship with the *vātsapra* hymn. At midday, having placed the fuel-sticks with the mantra "O Lord of Food, give us food" (*annapate 'nnasya no dehi*), the second brick is brought forward. Then follows the washing of the hands and so forth, ending with the touching of the region of the navel. Then, under a tree, the placing of the fuel-stick and so forth; the night is the second brick, and the fuel-stick is the third. Then he says: "O Agni, well-portioned householder."

While about to sleep, he performs the *vanīyābhimarśana* (touching the embers): "O Agni, you are the protector of vows for one who is unawakened; may all the gods turn toward me. He mutters, "Punarmana" (*punarmana*). At dawn, there is the restraint of speech (*vāgyamana*), and at sunrise, its release (*visarga*). [He performs] the *rukmaprabhoccama*, the *viṣṇukrama* strides, and the worship with the *haṃsavatī* verses. He performs the kindling of the fire-pan (*ukhya*) by repeatedly inflaming it with pieces of wood the size of a span (*prādeśa*).

While performing the midday vow, on the day when the *iṣṭakā* bricks have been prepared, there is the worship with the *vātsapra* hymn; this is the rule for the nights. On whichever day the purchase of the Soma occurs, on that day [one performs] the *viṣṇukrama* and the *vātsapra*.

One makes the bricks for the consecrated person during the ritual procedures of consecration lasting for months and so forth, prior to the consecration; for others, it is after [the consecration], following the animal sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati.

One prepares the bricks for the consecrated sacrificer during the rules for consecration lasting a month and so forth, specifically in the first fortnight of the months and so on. For one whose consecration lasts a month, he prepares the bricks in the first fortnight; for one [consecrated] for all four months, in the first two months. Likewise in the case of a year-long consecration, it is in the first six months. However, for one whose consecration lasts three days and so forth, he prepares the bricks after the animal sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati or Vāyu.

The bricks for the mandala have straight lines; they are arranged with a clockwise turn and a counter-clockwise turn, and are marked with three lines. Regarding clay bricks, there is no fixed measurement here. Specifically, in the Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra it is stated: "They may be the size of a foot, the size of a cubit, or the size of a thigh-bone" (ĀpaŚrSū 16.4.20). This rule regarding the size of a foot or a cubit does not apply to golden bricks; their dimensions are unrestricted.

Regarding those made of clay, however, the *Mānava-Brāhmaṇa* explains them as being "four-part-aṇūka" (*caturbhāgīyāṇūka*). "A quarter-measure" (*pādamātrāḥ*) means having the measure of a quarter. Or, a quarter is a *pada*; or rather, a *pada* itself is a quarter. Those having the measure of a cubit (*aratni*) are four fingers (*aṅgula*) less than a cubit, or they are the bone of the thigh (*ūrvasthi*). These too are exactly twenty-four fingers, because two *bhūlya*s (finger-breadths) have the same meaning [as one *aṅgula*]. "Aṇūka-measure" (*aṇūkapramāṇāḥ*) means having the measure of an *aṇūka*. An *aṇūka* is a quarter of a man, consisting of eighteen fingers.

The lines of those bricks are to be drawn with a reed; the lines are to be drawn turning from left to right (pradakṣiṇāvṛt), and likewise turning from right to left (apradakṣiṇāvṛt). Furthermore, there are three lines, the ends of which are bent three times. This rule regarding the lines applies specifically to this [set of] bricks:
they cook the red ones with fire produced by friction (nirmanthya). 19.

He does not place a black one, nor a spotted one, nor a mottled one. || 11.5.20 ||

"Khaṇḍā" refers to [the cow] according to Vaikhānasa and Āpastamba. A *khaṇḍā* is one whose single part is even slightly broken. A *kṛṣṇā* is one that is black even in a single spot, or is of another color. A *lohitā* (red) is a *lakṣmaṇā*. These should not be offered, because they are prohibited by the Śruti. Even as substitutes, the *khaṇḍā* and others are not employed, due to the prohibition. The Commentator says: "He uses the *khaṇḍā* only as a substitute; having performed the expiation with 'Bhuvaḥ' in the Dakṣiṇāgni, he should proceed. (20)

A lotus leaf, a gold plate, a golden man, two offering-spoons, seven naturally perforated bricks, gravel, golden bricks, five ghee-bricks, a clump of *dūrvā* grass, a tortoise, a mortar, a pestle, a winnowing basket, stones, the heads of sacrificial animals, and the head of a serpent—these are the bricks not made of clay. || 21 ||

A lotus leaf is a *puṣkaraparṇa*. The "golden" (*rukma*) is that very one which was held by the sacrificer at the time of the *viṣṇukrama* steps. The "golden man" (*hiraṇmaya-puruṣa*) is one fashioned from gold. The two *sruva*-ladles are made of *kāmya* wood and *udumbara* wood respectively. There are seven naturally fissured pebbles. The golden bricks (*hiraṇyeṣṭakā*) are unlimited in number. The five ghee-bricks (*ghṛteṣṭakā*) are lumps of clarified butter. A cluster of *dūrvā* grass and a cluster of *haritaka* grass.

The mantras [for the bricks] extend as far as the fire-altar; the Lokampṛṇā bricks are according to the purpose. One building it for the first time should pile one of a thousand [bricks] reaching to the knees; for the second time, one of two thousand reaching to the navel; for the third time, one of three thousand reaching to the mouth. Each subsequent one is larger than the preceding.

*Kjānu* means knee-height. *Sāhasra* means that which has a measure of one thousand. One who is building for the first time should pile the fire-altar knee-high, consisting of one thousand bricks. One piling it for a second time should pile it navel-high, consisting of two thousand bricks. One piling it for a third time should pile it mouth-high, consisting of three thousand bricks. Alternatively, *sāhasra* is a collection of bricks numbering one thousand; or, the fire-altar produced by one thousand bricks is *sāhasra*. He who piles the fire-altar for the first time should make it *sāhasra*.

Piling it a second time, one makes it double; piling it a third time, one makes it triple. Likewise, there is an increasing height for each successive layer—the first, second, and third—so that each subsequent one is larger. By this rule of repetition, the number for the fourth and subsequent layers is explained as being more than three thousand; in that case, the sense is that "one should not pile it larger [than that]. || 22 ||
One who desires heaven should pile up the great, vast, and immeasurable [altar]; this is the Vājasaneyaka. 23.

The "large" [altar] is constructed according to the rules with more than three thousand bricks; it is immeasurable and innumerable. For one desiring heaven, there are three thousand. This is the Vājasaneyaka, which is the scripture of the Vājasaneyins. This rule is not obligatory because it is optional (kāmya). However, a smaller [altar] than that is not obtained later; for the Brāhmaṇa states: "Having piled the larger, one should not pile the smaller. || 23 ||

When the duration of the initiation has elapsed, he settles upon the sacrificial ground with the formula, "Go away, depart! (apeta vīta). Having dug up the site for the altar to the extent of a vyāyāma (the distance of a man's arms extended), whether it be square or circular, he stirs it with a yellowish branch of the *palāśa* tree while reciting, "Go away, depart!"; then, having sprinkled it with water, he scatters sand over it with the formula, "Thou art the ash of Agni" (agner bhasmāsi).

When the period of initiation (*dīkṣā*) has concluded—that is, when its duration is completed—and after waking up, the recitation (*japa*), and the release of speech (*vāgvisarga*) have been performed, as well as the *viṣṇukrama*, *vātsapra*, and *somānaddāna* rites; the Commentator, however, explains that [the Adhvaryu] also gives the vow (*vrata*). With the formula, "Go away, depart," he measures out a square or circular space four *aratnis* on each side for the site of the Gārhapatya hearth using a bamboo rod; with the formula, "Go away, depart," he performs its excavation. The term "he sows" (*nivapati*) is understood to carry over. The word ends with "may it be" (*bhūyāt*). The fact that plants are the cause of nourishment and the cause of the birth of offspring is to be understood by way of sacrifice (*yajña*), as seen in *Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.9.3. || 26 ||

A mixture of saline earth and sand is prepared; with twenty-one pebbles, the encircling of the Gārhapatya altar is performed while reciting, "Ye are piled, ye are piled around. (29)
He forms three triplets.

The three *tisṛs* become one; according to the principle that there is a repetition of the mantra for each of those [pebbles], and because they are designated by the word "sit" (*sīdanti*), the author of the Bhāṣya says, "it is a *san*-mantra. In this context, because the Gārhapatya altar is the subject under discussion, he places four Prāṅganā bricks in the middle of the fire-altar.

With the two verses, "O Agni, the *iḍā*" and "This is your seasonal womb," he places two bricks upright in the front; with the two verses, "Thou art consciousness" and "Thou art encompassing," he places two bricks upright and joined at the back; and with the remaining thirteen *lokapṛṇā* bricks, beginning with "Fill the space, fill the gap," he covers the rest. || 32 ||

With the mantra, "O *iḍā*, this is your womb," he places [the first brick] in front of the fire-altar. He places two bricks facing each other (*samīcī*) and two facing away (*pratyandrī*). On the second layer (*prastāra*), he places two bricks lying crosswise (*tiraścī*), one pointing north and the other south. In this same manner, he places them behind. This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the text: "He makes the quarters firm with those two facing each other on the first layer and those two lying crosswise on the second layer. The commentator states that on the first layer there are two in the eastern southern corner, and two in the northern and southern [corners]; on the second layer, there are two in the eastern northern corner and two in the western [corner]. He covers the remaining space with thirteen bricks.
With two mantras each, he lays down one *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick.

Or he performs it facing north, placing each *lokapṛṇā* brick with two verses. Having placed it with the former [formula], he touches it with the *sūdadohas* verse.

Taking three black *nairṛti* bricks baked with husks, as well as a sling, a gold plate with a thread, and a stool, he carries them to the south-western intermediate direction; then, on a self-made salt-flat or in a crevice, he lays them down facing away from him, not touching one another, with the mantra: "Homage to thee, O Nirṛti. (5)

Those bricks whose deity is Nirṛti are called *nairṛtyaḥ*. Since husks (*tuṣāḥ*) belong to Nirṛti, whose presiding deity is the Rākṣasas, they constitute her portion. For this very reason, when preparing the bricks, the mantra for scattering the husks is recited as: "Thou art the portion of the Rākṣasas. Furthermore, the color of the deity Nirṛti is black; therefore, for the sake of conformity with her, one should prepare the bricks baked with husks and of a black color.

Alternatively—Nirṛti is the deity; those [stones] which belong to her are Nairṛtyas. Having taken three black stones together with husks, he takes up the carrying-sling (*śikya*). The Adhvaryu, the Brahman, and the Sacrificer go toward the south-western intermediate direction. "Homage to Nirṛti, the well-born"—this refers to a self-made spot, meaning a place of saline soil (*kṣāramṛttikā*); or in a cleft, that is, a place that has split open by itself. The rest is clear. || 5 ||

He places the bricks above the sling-noose with the three verses beginning "Into that which was thy," facing away without turning back, not touching one another, ending toward the south. Alternatively, "he beholds" (*vicaṣṭe*) is the end of the mantra. He places them either in a natural hollow or in a cleft, according to the Brāhmaṇa: "In a self-made pit or in a cleft" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.2.4).)

"Self-made" means produced by oneself alone, and not brought from another place and piled like bricks at a construction site; on such a saline wasteland (*iriṇa*), a barren soil (*ūpara*), or a fissure (*pradara*)—that is, a hole in the earth—one should lay down three black bricks. Regarding the location for laying the bricks: it is that spot situated where, having set aside the upper part of the net (*jāla*) upon the sling (*śikya*), one observes the lower part in the form of a loop (*pāśa*). He prescribes the number of bricks: "He lays down three" (TS 5.2.4).

"Facing away, not touching one another, ending toward the south"—from this observation [it follows that] a person facing south should, having laid down one brick, then lay down a second to the south of it, and then a third to the south of that.
He does not perform the *tayādevatam* rite. || 8 ||
