Regarding the rule *nitimava yanate* (Pāṇini 6.2.1), because the mantra contains a characteristic mark of a deity (*devaliṅgaka*), it is [treated as] addressed to that deity.
He places the sling over [the victim], reciting: "O Goddess Nirṛti, what you have bound... (RV 7.59.12). || 9 ||
This Sūtra and its commentary exist in manuscript *ga*.
[End of] Chapter 188y-6. Accompanied by the commentary *Mayūkhacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 43.
He covers these bricks with a network of bamboo mats (*śikya*). 9.

At this time, he places the stool (āsandī) and the cord for the gold plate (rukma-sūtra). At this time, he places the stool and the cord of the twenty-one-fold gold plate; and he consecrates the bricks that have been laid down with the verses beginning, "May she not go beyond the limit," or over the pebbles. 10.6.10.
With the verse, "That which is on the other side of this dust," he sprinkles around [the fire] with a verse addressed to Vaiśvānara.
Ending with "svāhā," he sprinkles around those very same [fires]. || 11 ||
With the words "Homage to Bhūti," he turns clockwise;
[this] clockwise circumambulation is for those very [deities]. 12. 12.
They perform the ritual sprinkling with the verse: "May the goddesses be auspicious for our protection. || 13 ||
"With water" is the ellipsis. || 13 ||

"Carrying strength, wealthy-minded and wise, I go to my home rejoicing in my mind, full of luster. With an eye that is not terrible, but auspicious, may I look upon my kin as I emerge from the houses. Thus they return without looking back. 14.
Without looking back, they turn back from those bricks; so do the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer. || 14 ||
With the words, "The dwelling-place, the gatherer of riches," they pay homage to the Āhavanīya fire, or to the Gārhapatya. 15.

Regarding the worship with a mantra, it should be understood that either the worshipper or the object of worship is intended; for it is seen in the Brāhmaṇa: "They worship the Gārhapatya fire" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.2.4). || 15 ||

When the *prāyaṇīya* offering has been performed, having placed the King (Soma) [on the altar] and having prepared the altar, he digs a pit in the middle of the fire containing a green clump of darbha grass with its roots; then, taking five portions of clarified butter with the *juhū* ladle, he offers five oblations upon the darbha clump while lifting it up with the mantra: "In harmony with the years, with the months... etc. (VS 8.24). || 16 ||

Beginning with the words, "He initiates the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *prāyaṇīyā* [offering]" (ŚrīSū 7.2.5), and concluding with the words, "It is either ending with the *svāhā*-utterance or complete," he undertakes the Soma-related rites beginning with the pouring out of the King [Soma]. He proceeds to perform the actions such as [the preparation of] the red bull's hide at the site of the *uttaravedi* or the *uparava* holes (ŚrīSū 7.1.4).

Then, having prepared the altar, he places a bundle of Kuśa grass—along with its roots, as it were—of such color, in the center of the fire; having established it there, he subsequently offers oblations of clarified butter into it, performing the renunciation (tyāga) according to the specific characteristics of each mantra. ||16||
15. Or rather, "not looking behind" means not turning his gaze back.
Now he prescribes the measurement of the ground for the burial (asicyana):
"He measures the fire-altar with a bamboo staff as long as a man with upraised arms. (17)

Even a man standing above an object with his arm outstretched is unable to ask about it. One should measure the bamboo pole. Or else, one measures the shed for the purpose of piercing it according to the measurement of the sacrificer’s outstretched arm. || 17 ||
There are three persons facing east, four facing north, and the wings and tail are of the measure of a person in width. || 18 ||

Starting from the tail, one leaves a span toward the east and draws four lines toward the north; starting from the southern wing, one leaves a cubit and completes [the lines] on the northern wing. The wings and the tail are each the measure of a man.
The self is four men; with a cubit, he extends the right wing from the south. || 19 ||
The four men are the self (ātman). With an *aratni*, he extends the right wing by twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) on the right side.
With a span (*prādeśa*) or a cubit (*vitasti*), [he extends] the tail behind; with an *aratni*, the left wing on the left side. 11.6.20.

In this way, O Uttara, he increases the upper wing. The increase at the tail-end is by twelve *aṅgulas*, or the tip [of the tail] is by a *vitasti* (span). A *vitasti* consists of a middle finger and a thumb when extended; even then, there is no other reason [for deviation]. The filling out is done with soil alone. In another Sūtra, only modifications such as the "single-fold" (*ekavidha*) and others are heard: "One should indeed pile it as sevenfold; for the natural fire-altar is sevenfold; from that upwards, they are increased by one each—so says the Vājasaneyaka."

(Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 16.5.31). "The natural fire is indeed sevenfold," it is said; [the phrase] "vaṣaṭ astu tubhyam" refers to those [fires]. That which has a single measure is "one-fold" (*ekavidha*). "Fold" (*vidha*) is a term for a person (*puruṣa*). In the first layer, the fire is one person's height, measuring five *aratnis*. The second is two persons; in this very manner, increasing by one person each time, it continues up to the one-hundred-and-one-fold. Starting from "sevenfold" and ending with "wings and tail."

The *araṇi* and the *prādeśa* are according to the number stated in the scripture, as is the vertical measurement of the bricks. Having deprecated the one-fold and other types of fires, another scriptural passage enjoins that "the seven-fold fire alone is to be piled first. The term "seven-fold" (*saptavidha*) means "original" (*prākṛta*), that is, "natural" (*prakṛti*), because it is recited with reference to that [first fire]. Starting from the seven-fold, up to one hundred and one, there is the "one-hundred-and-one-fold" (*ekaśatavidha*). Some, however, explain it as: "that which exists in the original is 'original' (*prākṛta*)."

This scriptural statement of the Vājasaneyins is due to the non-permanent nature of the additional injunction; for repetition in an injunction is non-permanent. "This is the opinion of the Vājasaneyins," so says the author of the Bhāṣya.

(20) [Paṭala 6] With the two verses, "O Earth, be pleasant, thornless, and a place of rest; grant us wide protection" and "Thus indeed [is the dwelling] of the mountains," they step upon the measured fire-altar. (Khaṇḍa 13) (21)

The Adhvaryu, the Brahman, and the sacrificer step forward with two Ṛg-verses. According to the author of the Bhāṣya, because of the mention of the *vimita* (the sacrificial shed), they step forward the entire distance as far as the *vimita* extends.
"Bind the thongs together," he commands.
The Adhvaryu issues the command; "Akṣitam" (the end) is the conclusion. Regarding the farmers, the author of the Bhāṣya says it is "saṃveṣa" (the gathering). 22.
He digs a pit with a smooth interior and a wide opening, saying, "A pit with a smooth interior. || 23 ||
A farmer digs a pit—a hollow space situated within troughs made of wood or stone; he digs that very pit, which is called an *āhāva*, or rather, he digs the troughs themselves. || 23 ||
"Pour out the undecaying water from the well," with these words he pours water into the pits and the furrows. (24) In them they give drink to the oxen. (25)

The repetition of the mantra occurs at each response (*pratyāhāva*), because the substances are distinct. At those responses, the Adhvaryu causes the oxen to drink, as in the case of [the *valīvarda*]. However, the Commentator supplies the word "plowmen" (*kīnāśāḥ*), meaning that the oxen are the plowmen (or farmers). 24, 25.

He extends the pair of plow-shares with the formula: "The impulse and the restraint, their bird-like hoof, the goad, the palm-leaf, the thong, and both the frogs—yoke them as a pair. Thus he spreads out the double-plow.

The joining together of those very thongs (*varatrā*) is their fastening and their yoking. The *antaryāma* is the intermediate cross-piece (*antarākhaṇḍakūṭa*), the pole (*īṣā*), and the shaft of the plow (*lāṅgaladaṇḍa*). The *khagalya* is the chin-piece (*cubuka*), the *śarpha* is the ring (*valaya*), and the *aṣṭrā* is the *tāla* or the snout-piece (*tuṇḍaka*). The *pratīnāha* is the *pratisīra*, which is the collection of ropes and the two thongs; these are the two "frogs" (*maṇḍūkyau*) belonging to the netter (*vāgurika*). He extends the two pairs of oxen for the purpose of plowing. The *yuga* is the yoke and the *lāṅgala* is the plow; thus, he extends the pair-yoke-and-plow (*yugalāgala*) for the purpose of yoking—this is the meaning. || 26 ||

With the two verses beginning "They yoke the ploughs," he yokes the plough—either with six oxen, twelve oxen, or twenty-four oxen. With the three verses, "May Pūṣan yoke them, may Savitṛ yoke them, may Bṛhaspati yoke you with the brilliance of Agni and the luster of Sūrya," he yokes it; according to some, this is for a team of six or twelve oxen. 27.

With two or three verses beginning with "sīrā yuñjanti," he yokes the plough; the mantra is recited once, because its purpose is the yoking of the sun (the plough). When it is drawn by six oxen, there are three yokes. The same applies in subsequent cases. However, in a single yoke, there is no mention of the poles (*dhanu*) in the text found in manuscript *ga*.
[Variant: *vā sarim*].

46. "They spread out many [oxen]," so it is said. However, some say that because of the mention of "the two yokes" (*yugau*), two [oxen] are obtained for the purpose of plowing. He prescribes the number of oxen: "He plows with six oxen" (5.2.5). A *ṣaḍgava* is a plow to which six oxen are harnessed, bound to three yokes arranged in the form of three girths (*kakṣyā*).

They establish another alternative: "Or else, with a twelve-yoked [plow]" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.2.5), and so forth. A plow to which twelve oxen are yoked—those being mentioned in the six sections—is a *dvādaśagava*; the meaning is that one plows with such a plow. In this manner, the alternative up to twenty-four [oxen] is to be understood. || 27 ||

With the verse, "Of the two camels, of the two bilva-wood [yokes], and of the two binding-thongs—for all of you we know the name: 'O straps, you who are skilled in carrying sweet drink,'" he consecrates the harnessed animals.
The consecration of the yoked [oxen] begins with "uṣṭārayoḥ" and ends with "kīlālapeśasaḥ. || 28 ||

"Brahmajajñānam" is this [verse]. "The first [soma] which you have not obtained, in which they perform their rites—do not deceive our heroes here; I place that very thing before you. "Flow forth for the winning of booty, overcoming the obstacles, so that you may cross over our enemies; you go like one seeking to recover a debt. "In the thousand-streamed [soma], those whose tongues are honey, unceasing, have resounded from the vault of heaven.
His watchful ones do not close their eyes; they are restless, and at every step there are bridgers with nooses"—thus he offers the protective armor of the *brahman*. 29.

"Brahma jajñānam" is the first [verse]. "Puro dadhe," ending thus, is the second. "Ṛṇayā na īyase," ending thus, is the third. "Setavaḥ," ending thus, is the fourth. "Brahmavāṇī" is the name of the oblation. Because protection is performed by these mantras just as armor protects, they are called "brahmavarmāṇi" (the Brahma-armors). || 29 ||

"Rising up, winner of cattle, winner of wealth, winner of horses, winner of gold, surrounded by pleasant speech—may Savitṛ with his one-wheeled chariot go over the earth, filling it with strength and a share of vigor," with these words he raises the plough. || 11.6.30 ||
He raises the plough for the purpose of yoking it. || 30 ||

Thou art named Malimluca, the thirteenth month; thou art Indra’s armor, thou art Indra’s protection, thou art Indra’s shelter. Into thee I enter. Be thou my protection and my armor. I enter the Gāyatrī with my hair; I enter the Triṣṭubh with my skin; I enter the Jagatī with my flesh; I enter the Anuṣṭubh with my bones. [End of Paṭala 6] [Included here as part of the source text: Accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 47.

"I enter the row with my marrow. May the thick, formidable armor belonging to Indra and Agni, which even the heroic Viśvedevas cannot pierce, protect us; may it protect us from all sides. O gods, may we, being long-lived, reach old age. With these words, they step upon the measured fire-altar.

"Thou art named Malimluca"—this is the stepping over of the fire by the Adhvaryu, the bull, and the Kīnāśa, ending with the words, "May we, O gods, reach old age. However, the Commentator says that the Brahman and the Sacrificer step over [the fire]. Some, however, say that the first oblations are the *brahmāṇi* (Brahman-protective formulas), while those beginning with "Thou art named Malimluca" are the *varmāṇi* (armor-protective formulas). The seven oblation-mantras ending with "May we, O gods, reach old age" constitute the *varmāṇi*. They silently step over the measured fire.
He ploughs with two [verses], beginning with "The plough, sharp-pointed... (RV 4.57.1–2).
[The mantra] ends with "dhattam. With two [mantras], the Adhvaryu plows. || 32 ||
The plowmen drive the oxen.
"Farmers and Vaiśyas indeed strike," says Vaikhānasa. (33)
He ploughs over the head and the tail.
Starting from the question, he draws [the fire] upward above the head; by saying "the head," he metaphorically refers to the eastern fire.
Turning to the right, he plows three furrows each time, reciting: "O you who are like a cow of plenty, grant our desires! (RV 10.169.1).

In front of the two wings, reciting "kāmaṃ kāmadughe," he mutters while turning clockwise. There are three furrows each, which are the tracks of the plough; these he ploughs so that they do not intersect. [The mantra] ends with "prajābhyaḥ. || 35 ||
He gazes at Sītā. With the formula "Sītā by ghee," he touches the spaces between the furrows.
He touches it. (36) (37). He states a specific method for drawing [the cord]:

he draws the northern wing from the southern wing. (38). From the southern hip to the northern shoulder, and from the northern hip to the southern shoulder; or otherwise, he completes twelve [units]. (39).

Starting from the right wing and extending as far as the northernmost point, there is one furrow (*sītā*). Again, starting from the left wing, the second furrow is to the east of that [first]. Again, starting from the right and extending as far as the north; to the east of that [second], starting from the southern hip (*śroṇi*) and extending as far as the northern shoulder (*aṃsa*)—these three furrows belong to the northern side. Likewise, from the northern hip to the southern shoulder, or conversely; to the east of the northern hip.

He pulls the northern shoulder from behind the southern [shoulder]. There is a repetition of the mantra "Kāmam," because the substances are distinct. He turns around so that it results in a complete turning toward the *vihāra*, [saying]: "O wish-fulfilling cow, [grant] my desire."

48. Or alternatively—starting from the tail up to the head, he should plow three furrows; likewise, starting from the right wing up to the left wing, he should plow three furrows; likewise, starting from the southern hip up to the northern shoulder, he should plow three furrows; and likewise, starting from the northern hip up to the southern shoulder, he should plow three furrows. In this manner, twelve furrows are completed.
In the middle, it becomes divided. 40.
At the time of plowing, a line should be drawn across the middle of the space between [the furrows].

Having released the oxen with the mantra, "Be released, O inviolable ones; you are the paths of the gods. We have crossed to the further shore of this darkness; we have reached the light; may we go to the sun," he releases them on the southern shoulder of the altar, or on the northern, facing either east or north.
"Be released," [is the formula] for the unyoking of the oxen on the right shoulder; or "on the left shoulder," if it is the reverse. || 41 ||
He gives them to the Adhvaryu priest. || 42 ||
Having led those cows that have been released either northward or eastward, the sacrificer then gives them to the Adhvaryu. He accepts them with the unmodified formula: "A cow for Rudra."
He pours out fifteen water-cups. || 43 ||
"Apastamba says that one pours out fifteen water-vessels."
Twelve [fingers] for the furrows, three for the ploughed ground. || 44 ||

"The Adhvaryu pours water-vessels onto the ploughed furrows," so says Vaikhānasa. "Water-vessels" means vessels containing water; there are twelve of them on the ploughed ground—one for each furrow—and one on the unploughed area. 44.
With the fourteen verses beginning "The plants that have been born," he sows the herbs: seven are cultivated and seven are wild.

The mantra ends with "for well-being" (*ariṣṭatātaye*). There are seven cultivated plants: sesame, beans, rice, barley, millet (*priyaṅgu*), panic seed (*aṇu*), and wheat. There are seven wild plants: bamboo, *śyāmāka* millet, *nīvāra* millet, castor seed (*tila*), *gavīdhuka*, *markaṭaka*, and *gārmuta*. For each plant, whether cultivated or wild, there is one mantra for the purpose of sowing, according to the injunction seen in the text: "He sows the plants" (*oṣadhīr vapati*; Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.2.5). || 45 ||
Domestic animals sow along the furrows in ploughed land; wild animals do so in unploughed ground. || 46 ||

As stated by Āpastamba: "Seven [grains] are for the village on ploughed ground; seven [grains] are for the forest on unploughed ground" (ĀpŚS 16.6.15). Regarding that, he prescribes a specific location for the village grains: "He sows on ploughed ground" (TS 1.1.5). He sows the village grains on ploughed ground; likewise, the seven forest grains are on unploughed ground. The remaining mantras are optional alternatives. [End of Chapter 16] If one cannot obtain those [specific] herbs, one should sow barley mixed with honey in their place. (47)
Whatever herb is not found among those of the village or the forest, let barley mixed with honey take its place; may it depart [from me]. 17.
Or he should meditate mentally [on it], saying: "Thou art sown by me. || 48 ||
Regarding the phrase "uptā me 'si" (you are sown by me), one should mentally contemplate the name of that grain, such as rice or sesame, which is not currently available. || 48 ||
When [the fire] has been obtained, he ties it to the first piece of fuel that comes along. || 49 ||

When the act of sowing has been accomplished and completed, whatever first fuel-stick (idhma) arrives during that Upasada, he ties this [formula] to that fuel-stick and casts it along with the fuel. || 49 ||
(Those among the trees that bear fruit—one should bind them to the fuel-wood and sprinkle them.

Those among the trees (*vanaspati*) that bear fruit—meaning those trees which have fruits as their sole [product], such as the *vaṭa* (banyan) and the *udumbara*—of these also, those which are desired to be well-fruited, he binds to the fuel-wood (*idhma*). The statement "he should sprinkle them when the first [oblation] has been offered" is for the purpose of indicating the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*). And the throwing [into the fire] is with this [verse]. || 10 || || 11.6.50 ||

Having performed that which precedes the guest-offering (*ātithya*), he piles up clods of earth from the four directions with the formula, "May the progenitor not harm us," for those [clods] which have fallen outside the enclosure from within the enclosure.

Those clods which have fallen outside the fire-altar site during the plowing—meaning, those that fell outside the boundary of the measured field—should be brought back inside. Or rather, at the time of plowing, those clods which have fallen in various directions outside the fire-site from the bamboo-framed enclosure (vimita), one should bring those clods from those directions and join them to the field. According to the Bhāṣya: "With these [mantras], there is the bringing of clods in each direction, one by one. || 11 ||
52. ... Regarding the fourth [offering], he prescribes a certain specific detail:
"I take from here food and vigor"—with these words, he should bring a clod of earth from that direction in which his enemy may reside. 53.

If this person should hate one who has performed the fire-sacrifice (agnicayana), he should take a clod of earth from whatever direction that person resides, using the mantra: "Iṣam ūrjam" (Food and strength). || 53 ||
The *Dhanuścin* is a text contained within [the *Śulba-sūtra*], found in manuscript *Gha*. ... [The commentators] explain: "The *Śrauta-sūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—... [In the eleventh *praśna*:

One should proceed in such a way that the completion (*apavarga*) occurs in that direction; one pours out the *uttaravedi* altar. Having performed as much as is required for the fire up to the sprinkling (*vyāghāraṇa*), [one completes it]. || 54 ||
One should construct the *uttaravedi* in the ordinary manner. Behind that *uttaravedi*, the fire-altar (*agni*) is piled.
Clearly, with the six verses beginning "O Agni, your fame... (*agne tava śravo vaya*), he scatters sand.

"O Agni, thy fame and vigor..."—with these words he scatters the sand, pouring it down with six mantras; he applies these mantras as follows: "O Agni, thy fame and vigor... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.2.6), and so forth. || 55 ||
With the formulas, "You are piled; you are piled around," he encloses the site of the Āhavanīya altar with an unlimited number of pebbles, just as he did for the Gārhapatya altar.

"Ye are piled, piled on the further side," with these words, using an unlimited—that is, an uncountable—number [of bricks], the enclosing of the Āhavanīya altar is performed; just as for the Gārhapatya, there are three layers each joined together. However, there is no recitation of the mantra "vanamasi. Alternatively, by the etymological derivation that they are made or produced from within the *śara* grass, the name *śarkarā* (pebbles) has come into being. Regarding the pebbles (*śarkarā*), he states the optional number for one desiring cattle:
"With twenty-one [pebbles] for one desiring cattle. (57)

The word "should measure" (*parimimuyāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. "Trisapta" refers to those pebbles (*śarkarā*) of which there are three sevens; that is to say, by those numbering twenty-one. One should measure them—that is, having measured them, one should set them down. (17) Now he states another optional number for one who has rivals: "With twenty-seven [pebbles] for one who has rivals. (58)

The phrase "he should measure" (pāriminuyāt) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Those which have three groups of nine are called *triṇava*; the meaning is that they number twenty-seven. (18) He states another alternative: "He should measure with an unlimited [number of bricks]. (59)

Some say that "one who desires immeasurable wealth" (*aparimita*) is one whose desire is immeasurable; or alternatively, one who wishes to obtain all desires is one whose desire is immeasurable. [Chapter 11, Section 6, Sūtra 60: With the two verses addressed to Soma, beginning with "Swell up, unite [with us]" (*āpyāyasva saṃ ta*), he spreads out the sand.

The phrase "viśve" marks the end [of the first verse]. That *ṛc* in which Soma is perceived as the deity is a *saumī* (verse dedicated to Soma). This [Soma] is perceived in the verse beginning with "viśvataḥ soma"; and "amṛtāyaḥ soma" is perceived in the following verse. With that *saumī* verse, one should spread out in various ways the previously poured sand.

Alternatively, one should arrange the *vyūha* for a Brāhmaṇa with a *gāyatrī*, for a Rājanya with a *triṣṭubh*: "The Soma has been pressed, the ruddy bull, the tawny one; like a king, the wondrous one has bellowed toward the cows. Purifying himself, he goes around the woolly filter to sit upon his ghee-filled womb like a hawk. For a Vaiśya, it is with a *jagatī*: [61]

The word *api vā* indicates an alternative to the previously mentioned position. One should spread the sand with the verse *ā pyāyasva sametu te*. The subsequent Triṣṭubh verse, *saṃ te payāṃsi*, is for the purpose of spreading [the sand] for a Kṣatriya. For a Vaiśya, the spreading is done with the Jagatī verse, *asāvi somaḥ*. Now, he confirms the pouring around (*pāraśrayaṇa*) by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): "If one should desire of someone, 'May he be without cattle,' one should spread the pebbles and sand for him without measuring them out. If one should desire of someone, 'May he be possessed of cattle,' one should spread the pebbles and sand for him after measuring them out. (Section 15, 62)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the eleventh book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

He will prescribe the covering over of the sand already poured down. Desiring that the sacrificer be without cattle, the Adhvaryu should spread out the sand without having placed pebbles around it. When that is done, because of the absence of a surrounding boundary (*pāraśrayaṇa*), he destroys the seed of the sacrificer in such a way that it goes astray in an unenclosed place; consequently, he becomes one who possesses no cattle—this is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). The positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is the opposite of this.

Therefore, for the sake of obtaining cattle, the spreading of sand must be performed preceded by the encircling with pebbles; this is the essential meaning. Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Eleventh Book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśisūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.
11.7 Now begins the seventh chapter of the eleventh book.

One undertakes the rites beginning with the *ātithyā* (guest-offering). [Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.7.3.17]—starting from this point until "he completes the remainder of the *dhruvā* [ladle]" and "the *ātithyā* ends with the *iḍā*" (ŚB 1.7.3.11)—these are the sacrificial rites pertaining to the ground (*maumika*). 1.

Having performed the first two morning *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, he arranges the bricks of the first layer on a red bull's hide, which has its neck pointing eastward and its hair facing upward, in front of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall.

Having performed the Upasad rite ending with the Subrahmaṇyā formula on both sides of the Pravargya-apasads—if the Upasad occurs later—then, not far from the front of the Prāgvaṃśa hall, upon the hide of a red bull that draws a cart, which has its neck facing east (*prācīnagrīva*) and its hair facing north (*uttaraloman*), he places the first set of bricks that were previously prepared; having gathered them together, he deposits them.
Or alternatively, there may be three naturally perforated bricks (svayamātṛṇṇā) and all the Viśvajyotis bricks. || 3 ||
Alternatively, the meaning is that he settles three *svayamātṛṣṇā* bricks and three *viśvajyotis* bricks. || 3 ||

Having sprinkled them with clarified butter using a handful of the tips of *darbha* grass and having lifted them up, he issues the command: "Recite for the fire-piles being carried forth," or [alternatively], "Recite for those being carried forth."

"Bṛhaspati shall settle you upon the back of the earth"—with these mantras, those [bricks] which are laid down are referred to. By a "handful of darbha-tips" (*darbhāgramuṣṭi*) means by a large handful of darbha tips. Having sprinkled [them] variously with clarified butter (*ājya*), one raises them up in all places; this is the optional view of some teachers. There are three *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks and three *viśvajyotis* bricks; for it is impossible to lay down the remaining *iṣṭakās* (bricks) without first laying these down.

Regarding the fires of the city intended for the piling of bricks, the Śruti text is heard as an option: "Recite the invitatory verse (*anuvaha*) for those being brought from the *stamba*," or "Recite the invitatory verse for those being led forward (*praṇīyamānebhyaḥ*). || 4 ||
When [the verse] has been recited three times, they proceed eastward with the horse at their head. || 5 ||
When the first [verse] has been recited three times, the Adhvaryu, the Brahman, and the Sacrificer proceed, placing the horse in front.

Having reached the Uttaravedi, he touches the Uttaravedi while reciting: "May Prajāpati settle thee; by that divinity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit thou firm. Then, having taken the fire into himself with the two verses, "I take into myself that Agni who is ours... and "O Agni, those logs of thine, those abodes of thine...", he touches the Svayamciti (the self-heaped altar).
He touches the *uttaravedi* altar. [End of] Chapter 7. [From the *Yogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī:

The Adhvaryu piles the fire-altar (*agni*) with bricks; or the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), or the Brahman himself, when piling the fire-altar, takes the fire within himself and does not touch it once it has been piled. 7.

"Either the Adhvaryu or the sacrificer piles the fire with bricks," says Āpastamba. Those ritual acts which are auxiliary to the piling (*citya*), such as the preparation of the fire-pan (*ukhā*) and the *vāyavya* offerings, are performed by the Adhvaryu alone; therefore, it is said "with bricks. If one asks how the rites such as the bringing forward of the bricks (*iṣṭakā-praṇayana*) are to be performed: when the sacrificer piles the fire himself, he does not take hold of the fire, nor does he touch the fire-pile that he himself has built; furthermore, the Adhvaryu does not pass between his own body and the fire.

The Adhvaryu priest, having taken Agni into himself, should pile the fire-altar; for such is the statement of the Adhvaryu. Now, one might object: regarding the bricks (*iṣṭakābhiḥ*) which serve as the means for the piling of the fire-altar, must they necessarily consist of clay or brick? This is because the word *iṣṭakā* is seen to be used in both senses: it denotes a genus, like the word *ghaṭa* (pot), or it denotes a specific shape, like the word *vedi* (altar).

Since the basis for the application [of the term "brick"] is not distinct even in those things made of clay, this being the prima facie view, it is established that [the term refers to] only those produced by churning, because of the supplementary statement: "Since earth and water are the primordial material of fire, why then is the fire built with earth and water? (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.6.4), and because the cooking prescribed in the injunction "they bake the bricks with fire produced by churning" would otherwise result in having an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). As for the fact that in the root text the status of the word *iṣṭakā* as denoting a genus was rejected in favor of its denoting a configuration (*ākṛti*), and that this was proven after presenting another doubt regarding its meaning—that has been disregarded as being neither very useful nor appropriate. || 7 ||

Turning to the right, he places them on the south; turning to the left, he places them on the north. Straight lines run from west to east. He places those with three furrows in the middle, facing east. "He places them facing west"—this refers to the rows within the groups. "He places one facing east, he places one facing west"—this refers to the orientation of the performer's face. He places others facing west in the front, and others facing east in the rear; these are statements regarding the completion of the work. According to the scriptural injunctions, he places them on the wings, the tail, the two hips, and the two shoulders. (Śulba Sūtra 11.7.10)

Where it is heard in the ritual manuals (*gaṇa*) that "one lays down [bricks] facing east" and "one lays down [bricks] facing west," and where it is further stated that "others [are laid down] facing west in front," there the discussion concerns the *rīti* (the flow or arrangement). Where it is heard that "one lays down [bricks] facing east" and "one lays down [bricks] facing west," there, due to the absence of a literal face, the discussion concerns the "face" of the person laying down the bricks. In the case of the *paścāccauḍā*, it is said: "One lays down the last [brick] facing west at the back."

Regarding the Jaimini Sūtra (14.1.19), "nanu gaṇeṣu," which states, "He lays down [bricks] facing east, he lays down [bricks] facing west," and so forth—where, by referring to a group (*gaṇa*) of bricks, qualities such as facing east are enjoined—it is argued that since square bricks lack a "front" (*mukha*), the designation "facing east" and so on is applied to the bricks only insofar as they are to be laid down by an agent facing east. To this, the reply is: although a single brick cannot possess a front and so forth, when many bricks are being laid down, there arises the possibility of their arrangement lacking a specific order; therefore, rules such as "they must indeed end toward the east" are prescribed. Thus, even though the individual bricks lack a literal front, the term is used figuratively based on the orientation of the entire group.

*Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—... [11. Rules for Restriction (*niyamārthā vidhayaḥ*): For this very reason, regarding the statement "he offers the other *anuyāja*s facing west," in its supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) it says, "he concludes with the last one facing east; by means of the last one he joins them together from here. Since facing west would otherwise be obtained here, the fact that the final one faces east is justified precisely by the joining of the others to it at the end. ...

Now, an objection is raised: "In the passage, 'He places the last brick facing eastward from behind; therefore, the wife sits facing eastward from behind' (14.1.2), since the previously stated principle applies, the theory of the bricks being like a row (*rīti*) would follow. To this we reply: In the case of groups (*gaṇa*), such a [row-like] arrangement is possible; however, here it is impossible because there is only one [brick]. Furthermore, because the supplementary portion of the Vedic text (*vākyaśeṣa*) explains this by way of the agent's own state—stating "facing forward from the front" (*purastāt pratyakṣam*)—this is a metaphorical description (*mukhavāda*) of the agent himself. Thus, "facing forward from the front" is a metaphorical description of the agent, whereas "facing westward from the front" is a metaphorical description of the ritual action (*karman*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that even in the passage, "In front he lays down others facing west; behind he lays down others facing east," this too is a figurative statement regarding the agent's face? For the meaning of the phrase "behind... facing east" has already been determined in the preceding section, and because of proximity [to that context]. [Reply: This being the prima facie view, we respond: These two rules indeed prescribe the specific manner of completion for many bricks. Therefore, because we observe a praise of the arrangement of the *nakṣatra* bricks in the passage, "Therefore, one should cover the *nakṣatra*s which are both facing east and facing west," [the directions refer to the bricks themselves]. 8 || 9 || 10 ||
A white horse stands to the south. || 11 ||
To the south of the fire. || 11 ||
Having touched that, he lays down the bricks. || 12 ||

Having touched that place where a white horse stands, he lays down a brick. To the north, however, having caused a furrow to tremble, he lays down loose soil; such is the Vedic text cited by the author of the Sūtras. It is also obtained [as an alternative] that two horses should stand on both sides—one black to the north and one white to the south—and having touched them, he should lay down the bricks. || 12 ||

One should place the brick for the stepping-stone with the verse addressed to Indra, "All have magnified Indra," while proceeding from the north or from behind; for the fire is approached from the north or from behind.

With the mantra, "O Indra, all have magnified thee," he places a brick there, thinking, "I shall ascend by way of the northern side of the junction of the tail. This refers to the space within the *vidhā* bricks; that is to say, inside the *puruṣa* bricks of the fire-altar. He places the brick at the point where one steps upon it during the ascent. Or rather, he should place the brick corresponding to the step on the northern wing. If the ritual procedure is from the north, or if the stepping occurs from behind, he places the brick at the tail.

"He steps upon it while piling up the subsequent layer," according to the scriptural statement; thus, it occurs only at the first layer (*cit*). Some, however, maintain that "the father piles up a brick for the purpose of stepping upon the layer. That is not so, for such a method of piling is not found even in the Sūtra. || 13 ||
"May speech be in my mouth, breath in my nostrils"—reciting this, he steps upon the fire at all instances of stepping upon it. || 14 ||

The section ends with *hiṃsāri*. The ascent (*ārohaṇa*) occurs with the mantra *vāṅma āsan* in all five layers (*citi*). Regarding the descent (*pratyavarohaṇa*), it is understood from another Śruti text that this procedure follows after the scattering of earth (*purīṣa*) has been performed. For us, however, [the ascent] occurs only once, because of the statement: "Having piled [the altar], he ascends seven times. Having offered the oblation with *saṃsthā yāmi*, he mutters *vāṅma āsan* while ascending.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, [interprets] "he mutters the Pratyavarohaṇa" as referring to the sequence taught in another Vedic branch within this same ritual order; thus, having recited the *pratyavarohaṇa* on the fifth layer after having laid down the *purīṣa*, this too is based on another scriptural authority. 14.
With the verse addressed to Varuṇa, "tattvā yāmi brahmaṇā vandamānaḥ," he makes an offering in the Śālāmukhīya fire.

"Pramoṣīḥ svāhā. Varuṇa is the deity. This is an oblation in the Śālāmukhīya fire. The taking of the Śālāmukhīya fire as a subsidiary part of the piling (cayana) is intended so that the oblation does not take place in the Cit fire-altar. || 15 ||
With the words, "He has overcome all hostile armies," he makes the horse, facing eastward, step upon a bunch of *darbha* grass with its right forefoot.

Now, thinking "the speech has indeed been attained," he causes [the horse] to mount together with the horse, facing eastward—that is, with its face turned toward the east—with the verse "abhyasthād viśvāḥ. He makes it step upon the bunch of darbha grass with its right foot. || 16 ||
With the verse, "When you first cried out at birth," he leads the horse around clockwise. || 17 ||
Having led the horse around clockwise, he makes it step upon the bunch of darbha grass once again with the verse, "When you neighed. || 17 ||

While it is being held on the south side, he places a lotus leaf with its stalk pointing downwards and its face upwards upon a clump of darbha grass, with the formula: "Thou art the back of the waters. || 18 ||
With the formula, "Thou art the back of the waters," he places a lotus leaf with its stalk downward upon a bunch of darbha grass in the horse's footprint, with its face turned upward. 18.

"Thou art the source of austerity; with all holy thoughts I place thee, the flawless one, for the winning of kinsmen—thou art the immortal womb, the womb of the Brahman, the womb of the Kṣatra, the womb of the earth, the womb of the intermediate space, the womb of the sky, and the womb of the quarters. Or [so it is said]. 19.
Or, by means of this mantra, one should perform the anointing with the addition of the leaf. || 19 ||
With the verse "Brahma jajñānam," he places a gold disk with its lower surface unobstructed upon a lotus leaf.

The section ends with *vi vaḥ*. With the verse *brahma jajñānam*, he places a gold disk (*rukmam*)—which has a perforation at its bottom—upon a lotus leaf. That which was present at the time of the Viṣṇu-strides, that is this. He places the gold disk so that its opening is toward the north; the gold disk is the very form of the Sun. This mantra is enjoined for this purpose in the Brāhmaṇa: "With the verse *brahma jajñānam*, he places the gold disk" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.3.7), and so forth. [From] the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin, the eleventh Praśna.

With the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning," he touches the golden man, who is facing eastward and lying supine to the south of the gold plate, with the words, "A drop has fallen"; then he sings over him with the Puruṣasāman.

With the verse "Hiraṇyagarbha," he places upon that golden plate a golden, gold-made man, facing east with his head to the east and lying supine, to the south of the opening. While being released from that [bond], he, facing east, places him as the door; he places that golden man, who is within the sun, as the form of the Puruṣa. He sings the *puruṣasāman*; if the Udgātṛ does not wish to perform that singing of the *puruṣasāman*, [he may omit it].

The Adhvaryu alone sings the *sāman* chant "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ," as does the sacrificer. When about to perform the piling of the altar, he performs the touching of the man with the formula, "The drop has fallen. || 21 ||
He worships with the three names of serpents beginning with "Homage be to the serpents. || 22 ||
Ending with "Homage to the serpents," he performs the ritual service for the person against darkness. || 22 ||
With the five verses beginning "kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ," he sprinkles the person diagonally, just as [he sprinkles] the high altar (uttaravedi).
5. [The altar] ending with the *śamyā* is for the support of the person, like the *uttaravedi*. 4–23.

He places two ladles filled with ghee and curds on either side of the man [the image], with the formula: "I settle thee with the splendor of Agni. He places the southern one, made of *kārṣmarya* wood and filled with ghee, with the formula: "I settle thee with the vigor of Indra," and the northern one, made of *udumbara* wood and filled with curds. Having placed them, he worships them with the two verses beginning with the word *mūrdhan*.

Regarding this, it says: "He places [the two ladles] upon the two pits" (*Leṅga Saṃhitā* 1.2.7). Because of this observation of the injunction, he shows the specific characteristics of those two ladles: "The southern one is made of *kārmarya* wood and filled with clarified butter; the northern one is made of *audumbara* wood and filled with curds. *Kārmarya* is a particular tree named *śrīparṇa*; a certain ladle made from it is made of *nūka* wood and is filled with ghee. A certain [ladle] is made from *udumbara* wood, and that is filled with curds.

Since the laying down of the two bricks (*khuc*) characterized by these specific qualities is prescribed as a single act, one should not suspect a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). To ward off the suspicion that these might be like the laying down of other bricks—which would require the use of mantras—or that they might be ordinary worldly speech, the *Brāhmaṇa* states: "He lays them down silently" (*tūṣṇīmupaddhāti*, Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.2.7). Because no mantra is traditionally handed down for this purpose, these two are not fit to be laid down with a *yajus* mantra.

It prescribes a specific direction for these two: "The southern one is made of *kārmarya* wood, the northern one of *udumbara* wood; therefore, that [heavenly world] is higher than this [earth]" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.2.7). Since the *udumbara* post, which represents the heavenly world, is placed in the northern direction, therefore in the world as well, that [heavenly world] exists as the upper portion, higher than this earth. And that specific direction—

Āpastamba has stated this clearly: "To the south of the person, [he places] a ladle made of Kārmarya wood filled with clarified butter; to the north of the person, [he places] one made of Udumbara wood filled with curd" (ĀpŚS 16.7.5). With the verse *agnirmūrdhā*, there is the worship of the ladle made of Kārmarya wood; with the verse *bhuvo yajñasya*, that of the one made of Udumbara wood. || 24 || 25 ||

Alternatively, having laid them down silently, he worships with the two verses containing the word "head" (*mūrdhanvatī*); according to some, having laid them down with the two verses containing the word "head," he worships with the two *yajus* formulas.

Alternatively, there is silence for the laying down of those two; "with the two verses beginning with *mūrdhanvatī*, one performs the worship"—this is one view. "Having laid down the one made of *kārmarya* wood and the one made of *udumbara* wood with the two verses *agnir dhā* and *bhuvo yajñasya*, one worships with the *yajus*-verse *agneḥ tvā*, *indrasya tvā*"—this is another view. Or else, some reciters of the Vedic branches state that there is either the silent laying down or the laying down with *ṛc*-verses, while the worship is performed with a *yajus*-verse. || 26 ||

Regarding the placing of the gold plate (*rukma*) upon the upper part [of the altar], as in the case of the *uttaravedi* for the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*), it says: "He sprinkles the gold plate; according to the person. (Section 17) || 27 ||
One should pour the clarified butter over the gold in the manner of a man. || 27 ||

Having touched the naturally perforated stone (*svayamātṛṇṇā*) with the mantra, "Firm art thou, O Varuṇa," and having caused a horse to smell it, he places it in the middle of the fire together with an unlearned Brāhmaṇa, using the mantra, "May Prajāpati seat thee on the back of the earth, the wide-extending one," and with this *vyāhṛti*, "Bhūḥ. (28)

With the mantra "Thou art firm," he touches the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone; having caused the horse to drink water and mounted it, even one who does not know the mantras, having been taught them, performs the placing together with it, beginning with "May Prajāpati seat thee on the back of the earth," and having said "sat," it is placed with "bhūḥ."

Alternatively, although the *svayamātṛṣṇā* (the naturally perforated brick) was not constructed by men, its status as a brick is primary; with this in mind, its priority among the principal bricks is stated in the Brāhmaṇa: "The first brick being laid... (5.2.8), and so forth. Here, one should place the *svayamātṛṣṇā*, consecrated by mantras, into the hand of an ignorant Brāhmaṇa. Then, that Brāhmaṇa and the Adhvaryu priest together should lay it down—this is the meaning. || 28 ||
Having offered the oblation with the words, "I offer into consciousness," he breathes over the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.

"Oblation, Svāhā! Viśvakarman is the deity. Having offered thus with the thought, "I offer into the layer," he performs the act of breathing upon it by blowing air from his nostrils over the clarified butter. 29.
An ignorant Brāhmaṇa gives a boon—one, two, or three. 11.7.30.

He who, being himself ignorant, lays down the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick—he is capable of meeting with misfortune. Therefore, to avoid this, one should offer a boon (*vara*) to the Adhvaryu priest. By the word "boon" (*vara*), a cow is meant because of its excellence. There are three options prescribed: three, two, or one. 30. — *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [11th Praśna]—

"Thou art brilliance; grant me brilliance; grant me the earth; protect me from the earth," [with these words] he places the gold brick. "The earth has a wide enclosure, it is filled with food; men are its guardians," [with these words] he places the mandala brick. "Thou art the earth, the seed of the world; thou art the bricks, the heavenly world; with my mind I ascend thee. "Thou art the sky, the seed of the world; thou art the bricks, the heavenly world; with my mind I ascend thee. With these two formulas for ascending, he places two bricks.

With the mantra, "Thou art brilliance; grant me brilliance," he lays down a golden brick (*hiraṇyeṣṭakā*). Earthen bricks are laid even above the vyoṣṭakās at an indefinite location, and material bricks (*dravyeṣṭakā*) are placed in the pit. According to Āpastamba, the numbering should be completed by the earthen bricks alone, as indicated by the statement, "Thus this layer consists of two hundred [bricks]. This is also supported by the indicative mark (linga) in the text: "Whatever sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is performed prior to the iṣṭakā-bricks. With the mantra, "The earth is the city, with food," he lays down the maṇḍaleṣṭakā; its status as a maṇḍaleṣṭakā is established by the mantra itself.

According to Baudhāyana, however, the *maṇḍala* is drawn upon the *maṇḍaleṣṭakā*, and the *ṛṣabha* is drawn upon the *ṛṣabheṣṭakā*. According to Āpastamba, however, there is the view that the names of the bricks are not based on specific characteristics (*animittāni*), as in the case of the "self-brick" (*ātmeṣṭakā*). Regarding the two [bricks] with the formula "Thou art the earth" (*bhūr asi*) used for the ascending steps (*anvāroha*), they are placed near the brick of the stepping (*ākramaṇa*). || 11 ||

With the two verses beginning "Growing forth from joint to joint," he places a clump of *dūrvā* grass together with its clod of earth, with its tips uncut, so that its tip reaches the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone.

With the two verses beginning with "From joint to joint" (*durvāstambamūlam*... *saha loṣṭena*), he places the root of a green clump of *durvā* grass together with a clod of earth upon the brick so placed, in such a way that it reaches as far as the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick itself. || 32 ||
Having placed two pieces of gold on the two ends of a brick, he lays down the Vāmabhṛt brick with the two verses beginning, "O Agni, those splendors of thine which are in the sun... (VS 15.2–3).

"Prabāhuk" means level. Having placed two pieces of gold on the brick at the same spot, he establishes the Vāmabhṛt brick with the two verses, "O Agni, those [flames] of yours which are in the sun... (VS 15.47–48). || 33 ||
"Virāḍ jyotir adhārayat"—these three [verses] are for the pourers of seed. || 34 ||
"One should place three [bricks] for the shedders of semen"—this is the remainder [of the rule]. According to Vaikhānasa, this is done with three mantras. || 3 ||
Two [schools] recite them as one. || 35 ||
Certain [Vedic] schools transmit [the text]: "Two [bricks] from Aditi. [End of] Chapter 7.
[This is] accompanied by the *Payogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.
One should place those [bricks] in the first layer for a youth; in the middle layer for one of middle age; and in both the first and the last layers for an old man.

The rule for these is as follows: for a young man, there are two *citi*s (layers) of the first [altar], and he has no third; for one of middle age, all three are in the middle *citi*; and for an old man, there is one in the first *citi* and one in the fifth, called the *svarāṭ*. "His seed, once emitted, he grasps from both sides by means of these two," so it is said because of the praise of Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*). However, Āpastamba has stated that one may place only one of them: "With the *yajus*-formula, he places both this [earth] and that [heaven]."

"With the mind, the middle one" (Āpa. Śr. Sū. 16.7.20). This is for the purpose of prohibiting [the use of a mantra] when laying down a brick belonging to an enemy. One lays down both the earth and the sky with a *yajus* formula. The rule for the first and third [bricks] is that they are to be laid down in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), because those two are praised as the earth and the heavenly world. The middle one is the second; that one he lays down with the mind—[specifically] with the *yajus* formula itself: "The ancient light... (36).

"Bṛhaspati may settle you on the back of the earth, the luminous one"—with these words [he places] the Viśvajyotis brick. "Thou art the path of Agni, thou art the path of the gods"—with these words [he places] the two Saṃyānī bricks. "Madhu and Mādhava"—with these words [he places] the two Ṛtavyā bricks. They have the same deity. || 37 ||

"May Bṛhaspati seat thee, O Viśvajyotis"—this refers to the *praṇītā* water. "Thou art the wife of Agni"—this refers to the *saṃyānyā* offering. "Madhu and Mādhava"—these two are the seasonal offerings (*ṛtanyā*), having the same deity. 37.
He places the Avakā plant upon all the seasonal layers.

Having placed [the bricks] on all the seasonal layers (*ṛtavyā*), he places two *avakā* plants behind; upon those two, he places [the brick]. "He should look at the *avakās*," say some—thus says Āpastamba (ĀpŚS 16.7.22). || 38 ||
He lays down the *gharma*-brick; the mantra for it is recited in the *pravargya* ritual. || 39 ||
The mantra recited in the Pravargya ritual is: "The sun [arose] from the vigor of this [Agni], who is to be placed as the Gharmestiṣṭakā. (39)

"The Aṣāḍhā [brick] with its mark above; the Aṣāḍhā of the one whom he hates with its mark below. "O Agni, those moist wombs of yours, those which are nest-like; those drops of yours, O Agni, and those navels; those bodies of yours, O Agni, named 'Strength'—with all these, being in harmony, may you sit down here upon the bodies of living beings," [he says regarding] the Kulāyinī. 40.

He places the Aṣāḍhā brick, prepared together with the fire-pan, using two formulas: "Thou art the invincible (aṣāḍhā)" in the middle, and "the unscratched" in the middle. He places it so that it lies above the scratched brick. And thus it is said in the Brāhmaṇa: "Whom..."

60. Regarding the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: [In the case of one] who desires, "May I become more prosperous," he places the *sthā* bricks so that they are marked above (*upariṣṭāc-cyālikhitā*). For one who desires, "May he become worse off," they are to be placed below (*adhastāt*) those [bricks]; this is for the purpose of prohibition regarding the *cyālikhitā* bricks. Furthermore, the two mantras recited in the *Pravargya* ritual, "O Agni, those which are *kulāyinī*s" and "The moist wombs," are also [to be used here]. 40.
With the three verses beginning "The winds carry honey for the one who follows the cosmic order" (*madhu vātā ṛtāyate*), he anoints the tortoise with curds mixed with honey. (Section 18) || 41 ||
"May they be ours"—ending thus; with three [verses], he offers [oblations] from the tortoise with curd mixed with honey. || 41 ||

Go to the depths of the waters; let not the sun scorch you, nor Atri Vaiśvānara. Without malevolence, look upon the creatures; may the celestial rain attend you. Glide along the three oceans, the self-watery, the worthy ones—the worlds—O Bull, Lord of the Waters, Master of the bricks.

Having consecrated it with the mantra, "Go there where those of old have passed away, wearing the soil, each to his own womb according to his nature," he places it facing eastward while alive and facing westward, using the two verses, "The great heaven and earth for us" and "The four quarters. He surrounds it with *avakā* plants, covers it with a net, and fixes it in place with stakes. || 42 ||

Having prescribed the consecration of the deposited [brick] with the mantra, "Go to the depth of the waters," he deposits it with the two verses beginning, "The four quarters of the earth. He places a living tortoise facing west in front of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, while the performer faces east. According to the *Āpastamba Sūtra*, one may optionally deposit it with the verse, "The four quarters... It is wrapped in *avakā* plants, covered with a net stretched over it, and pinned down with stakes so that once deposited, it does not move.

The Brāhmaṇa prescribes the quality of being endowed with life for the tortoise to be placed [as a foundation]: "Verily, this is made into a cemetery" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.2.8), and so forth. It will be stated later that the heads of the deceased animals—the horse, the bull, the ram, and the he-goat—are to be placed upon it; thus, this site becomes a cemetery indeed. By placing a living tortoise, the sacrificer does not become one who builds a cemetery. Furthermore, the tortoise that is there is "vāstavya," meaning fit for habitation, because the earth rests upon the back of the tortoise; therefore, the meaning is that the placement of the tortoise is for that very reason. || 42 ||

"O mortar, whatever you are joined with in every house, here speak most brilliantly, like the drum of the victors"—with these words, he places the mortar and pestle on the southern buttock of the altar.
He places the mortar and pestle on the southern hip [of the altar] with the mantra; because they are made of wood, there is a repetition [of the action]. [Section 7, Paṭala:
The mortar is made of Udumbara wood, a span (prādeśa) in length, and four-cornered; the pestle is of unlimited size.

That which is a part of the *udumbara* tree is *audumbara*. A mortar (*ulūkhala*) measuring a span (*prādeśa*) in length and unmeasured in thickness—that is *audumbara*. He prescribes the primary material for the mortar in the passage beginning with: "It is made of *udumbara*" (*Tai. Saṃ. 5.2.8*). || 14 ||
"O Lord of the Forest, may the wind blow upon the tip of you; and now, O mortar, press out the Soma for Indra to drink!"—having thus filled [the mortar] with all kinds of herbs, they pound them. 45.

Having filled [the mortar] with the seven village and seven forest herbs, he performs the placing [of the mortar] silently with the mantra "uta sma ta... (RV 10.89.1), because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra "press the Soma, O mortar" (*sunu soma ulūkhala*). He specifies the particular location:

in the middle of the fire, he places the mortar and pestle with the mantra "that is Viṣṇu’s highest step" (*tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam*); or alternatively, he places the pestle with the mantra "behold the deeds of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇoḥ karmāṇi paśyata*).

"He places them in the middle" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.2.8); such is the Brāhmaṇa passage. He places the mortar and pestle in the middle of the fire-altar; because the materials are distinct, the action is repeated according to the principle that even in the case of a single mantra, [the act is performed for each object]. However, in the case of two mantras, he should place the mortar with the mantra "That of Viṣṇu... and the pestle with the mantra "The deeds of Viṣṇu...". || 16 ||
"O Viṣṇu, from heaven!"—with these words [he addresses] the winnowing basket. || 47 ||

With the verse "O Viṣṇu, from heaven... ending with "...the abode of blessings," he pours [the grain] into the winnowing basket; with the verse ending "...from truth, O Āditya," [he pours it] into the fire-pan. (17) Regarding the filling of sand for the fire-pan that is to be placed [on the hearth], he says:
"He fills the fire-pan with sand. (48)
The meaning is clear. || 18 ||
With curd, honey, or ghee. || 49 ||

The word "fills" (*pūrayati*) is understood [from the previous rule]. Having sewn the two edges together, one fills the *ukhā* with clarified butter, honey, sand, or all of these. One fills it after mixing it with clarified butter; for there is no prohibition against looking into an empty vessel, since Āpastamba has stated that even when it is empty, there is no impurity (*śuc*) or lack of purity. After the filling, one pours milk into it; however, some authorities prescribe the filling only after the *saṃnivāpa* (the pouring in of the mixture) has been performed. This, therefore, is the sequence. || 49 ||
He praises the filling by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*):

"If he should desire of someone, 'May he be hungry,' he should place for him one that is deficient. If he should desire of someone, 'May he eat food that does not fail,' he should place for him one that is full. (11.7.50) ...In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: When a fire-pan (*ukhā*) that is filled with sand but slightly deficient is placed, the sacrificer becomes hungry, lacking food, and prone to hunger; this is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). However, when it is placed with the sand fully filling it, he eats food that does not fail—that is, food that never diminishes.
This is the positive concomitance (anvaya). || 50 ||

"Stitched together by the gods with immortality, the sister has come; he has placed the fire-pan upon the altar. May Agni, who was longed for by the ancient seers and is full of wisdom, perform that here according to the truth. Having taken up the pan, [he says] "Thou art firm, thou art the earth," and "O Earth, sit upon the earth; a mother upon a mother; gracious upon the gracious. We pray for the great majesty of the gods’ creative power—the wise Agni in his assembly-place, in his dwellings."

Vaiśvānara, the all-pervading one, through sacred prayer—him who is established as the foundation of the *stoma* and the source of the soil; you are kindled with fuel, O Agni, the immovable one in his station within the sacrificial seats. Vaiśvānara, the all-pervading one, through sacred prayer—I have established him as the foundation of the *stoma* and the source of the soil. The sages, bestowers of vitality, have measured him out with their measure and placed Agni, the invoked one, in his station within the sacrificial seats.

"Vaiśvānara, who is all-pervading through the sacred word, the foundation of the hymn, the purifying one who is honored. "Thou art firm, O Earth; by that deity, like Aṅgiras, be thou firm"—with these words, he places the fire-pan (ukhā) in the middle of the fire-altar. ||51||
He places; he establishes. || 11 ||
According to some, [it should be placed] above the mortar.
"May the earth settle upon the earth"—with these words he places the *ukhā* pot upon the mortar; thus says the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa. 52.
With the two verses beginning "O Agni, yoke those that are yours" (*agne yukṣvā hi ye tava*), he offers one oblation into the fire-pan (*ukhā*). (Sūtra 53)
When the fire-pan has been placed upon the hearth, the oblation is offered; Agni is the deity. 53.

He throws pieces of gold into the vital breaths of the human head: with "For the Ṛc, thee! on the right corner of the eye; with "For the Lustre, thee! on the left; with "For the Light, thee! on the right nostril; with "For the Radiance, thee! on the left; with "This has become the vigor of the whole world" on the mouth; with "Agni, by his light, is full of light" on the right ear; and with "The golden disk, by its splendor, is full of splendor" on the left.

Chapter 7: Accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. Regarding that human head, the Śruti prescribes the casting of gold chips (*hiraṇyaśalka*) into its apertures, such as the mouth, stating: "He casts gold chips into the vital breaths" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.2.9), and so forth. One should cast the gold chips into the apertures, such as the mouth, which are the locations where the vital breaths circulate. This is to be understood likewise in the texts of Āpastamba and others. 54.

With the verse, "The streams flow together like milch-cows," he fills the human head with curds mixed with honey that have been boiled with *ātaṅkya* [a specific medicinal plant]; then, having taken it up with the formula, "Thou art thousandfold, for a thousand thee," and anointing the solar embryo with milk, he places it face upwards in the fire-pan (*ukhā*) with its chin pointing eastward. ||55||

The section ends with *āsām*. With the intention expressed in the mantra, "May I be worthy of the honey" (*ahaṃ madhavyo'sāni*, ŚB 5.2.9)—meaning, "May I become fit for partaking in the sweet essence"—one should fill this human head with curds mixed with honey. In this context, there are two kinds of curds: one that thickens by itself through the addition of silver or other substances, and another produced by churning boiled milk. Of these, that which is produced by churning milk is fit for sacrifice; therefore, one should fill it with precisely such [curds].

The Vājasaneyins record that for all the animal heads, such as those of the horse and others, there is the casting of gold fragments and their filling [with earth], exactly as with the human head. Having taken the human head with the formula "A thousandfold," he places it in the fire-pan (*ukhā*) with the formula "O Aditya, the womb, the milk. It is explained that it is placed facing east, like a bow, with the chin directed forward; this means it is placed face upwards. The meaning is that the performer places it while facing the east. || 55 ||
With the two verses beginning "That bright one" (*udu tyaṃ citram*), he makes an oblation upon the two axles.

The oblation is performed with the two verses concerning Sūrya; Sūrya is the deity. Alternatively, he offers [the oblation] on the right shoulder-blade with the verse beginning "citram," and on the left with the verse beginning "ā prā dyāvāpṛthivī. || 16 ||
He lays down the heads of animals. ||57||
He places the heads of animals as supporting blocks. || 17 ||

If he should desire of someone, "May he be without cattle," he should lay down [the bricks] facing away from one another for him. If he should desire of someone, "May he be rich in cattle," he should lay them down facing toward one another for him. If he should desire of someone, "May his food be less," he should place the heads of the animals closer together for him. If he should desire of someone, "May his food be equal," he should place them on both sides of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* for him. If he should desire of someone, "May his food be more," he should scatter them at the ends for him.

If one should desire, "May he become devoid of cattle," [the heads] should face away (*parāṅmukha*) and be turned sideways (*viṣacīna*). This is a prohibition regarding the human head, not an injunction. His cattle turn sideways; all [animals], such as horses and others, flee. [The heads] should be facing together (*samīcīna*) and not turned away. The injunction regarding the human head is thus praised. When they face together, the animals—horses and others—come toward the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) in his vicinity. Consequently, he becomes possessed of cattle.

He places them thus in the very vicinity of the sacrificer. Similarly, regarding what follows: "If one should desire that there be little food for him, the animal heads should be placed closer together, with a narrower interval between them"—this is stated for the purpose of prohibition. One should place [the bricks] in the middle of that fire-altar, starting from the year, such that they are equal and not deficient; [that is,] in all four directions.

If one should desire, "May there be food," then having dug out the earth from the four directions at the ends [of the altar], the placement [of the bricks] should be made; that is, at the very ends of the directions. Therefore, there shall be food; from that, food is obtained, and there will be abundant food. ||18||

With the verse, "The course of the wind," he places [the brick] facing west in front of the horse; with the verse, "The eternal drop," facing east behind the bull; with the verse, "The protector of Tvaṣṭṛ," facing north to the south of the ram; or alternatively, to the north of the ram; with the verse, "The fire which is of fire," facing south to the north; and with the verse, "Of Vasta," facing north to the south. Without interrupting these with the *utsarga* formulas, while moving clockwise around [the altar], he pays homage to each direction. With the verse, "Do not harm this two-footed one," he pays homage to the man.

"Do not harm this one-hoofed [creature]"—this for the horse; "this ocean"—this for the bull; "this woolly [creature]"—this for the ram; "for the goat is indeed the birthplace of Agni"—this for the he-goat. || 59 ||

With the verse, "May he not abandon us," he places the horse's head facing westward, with his own face turned toward it, in front of the fire, facing the head of the man. With the verse, "The unceasing drop," he places the bull's head facing eastward, with his own face turned toward it, behind the fire, facing the head of the man. With the verse, "The protector of Tvaṣṭṛ," he places the ram's head facing northward, with his own face turned toward it, to the south, facing the head of the man.

With the verse, "The fire which is in the sun," he places the head of a goat facing southward and toward the fire from the north; these heads stand there, reaching one another without any gap between them. Regarding the domestic animals, as for the wild ones—such as the *mayu* and others that correspond to their forms—he will speak of them in the context of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). For the worship of the human head, [he uses] the verse, "Do not harm this two-footed one";
for the horse, "Do not harm this one-hoofed one"; for the bull, "This ocean..."; for the ram, "This ewe..."; and for the goat, "For the goat is... (VS 25.1–6). || 19 ||
Now, if it is the head of the Vāyavya [offering], [then... || 11.7.60 ||
Having placed [the fire] in its primary place by all [means], he worships it with all the utsarga offerings. || 61 ||

The meaning is as follows: if the head of another [deity] were to be placed in the position of all [the deities], then, having placed the human head in the position of the principal [deity] using the *upadhāna* mantras for all [the others], one should place it in the fire-pan (*ukhā*) with all these [mantras]: "ādityaṃ garbhaṃ," "vātasya dhājim," "ajasramindram," "varūtriṃ svaṣṭaḥ," and "yo agniragneḥ. Then, having performed the eye-opening rite on the two temples with "citraṃ devānām," there occurs the ritual worship (*upasthāna*) by means of the *utsarga* formulas for all [the deities]. || 60 || 11 ||
Alternatively—[the text reads] "Ṛcam eva" [verse alone], [as found in] the *Yogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Devaśākhin:
"Or rather, having placed each [brick] in its respective position, he worships it with the renunciation (utsarga) of that very [brick]. (62)

Alternatively, having offered oblations with two half-verses at the place where the human head was deposited, there is an adoration by means of its [the head's] ritual dismissal (*utsarga*). The meaning is that, in this manner—excluding the fire-offerings for the horse and so forth—the adoration is performed by means of the ritual dismissal after the depositing has been completed. || 62 ||
With the formula "Homage be to all," he places one of these [bricks] on the northern shoulder, with the head of a serpent; [he places it] crosswise with the heads of animals.

Or, according to the principle that "rites performed with a single mantra [constitute a single act]," the placing of the heads of the serpents is done with the single verse, "Homage be to the serpents. Here, one should not face the heads of the animals directly. 63.
Or rather, he should merely recite the *yajus* formula and not actually place the brick.

One might say: "Since it is stated that one does not mutter [the mantra] with the fourfold tone (*cātuḥsvarya*), one should not place the *sarpaśiras* brick. However, it must indeed be placed, because of the repeated statement: "In that he places it... (*Leṅga Saṃhitā* 5.2.9). In the original ritual (*prakṛti*), this is obligatory. In the modified rituals (*vikṛti*) such as those of a single type (*ekavidha*), and in cases where there is a modification of qualities, it is said: "If he recites a Yajus formula, by that it is pacified" (5.2.9). For the author of the Sūtra, however, in such instances, when a fruit is indicated in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), there is an injunction for one who desires that fruit. "Radiance" (*sadīpti*) is the fruit of "pacification" (*śānti*).

Mā is the metre; its deity is Agni and the Earth. By that seer, by that Brahman, by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! Pramā is the metre; its deity is Vāta and the Intermediate Space. Pratimā is the metre; its deity is Sūrya and Heaven. Asrīviṣ is the metre; its deity is Soma and the Quarters. Virāj is the metre; its deity is Pūṣan and the Eye. Gāyatrī is the metre; its deity is Bṛhaspati and the Goat. Triṣṭubh is the metre; its deity is Indra and Gold.

The Jagatī is the metre; its deity is Prajāpati, the Bull. The Anuṣṭubh is the metre; its deity is Varuṇa, the Bull. The Uṣṇih is the metre; its deity is Mitra, Āyu. The Paṅkti is the metre; its deity is Parjanya, Agriculture. The Bṛhatī is the metre; its deity is Parameṣṭhin, the Horse. With these verses—twelve in number, recited three times, making thirty-six—with that Ṛṣi, with that Brahman, with that Deity, saying, "Sit firm like Aṅgiras," he piles the layer in the shape of a man facing westward in front.

With the formulas beginning with *mā chandaḥ*, he piles up twelve remaining bricks, repeating them three times, ending toward the west (*pratyag-apavargam*), because of the statement in the Vaikhānasa text: "The bricks are facing westward. Regarding this [altar], the head of the Puruṣa becomes its head. (Śatapatha Śrauta Sūtra, composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Book 11, Chapter 66).

The author of the Commentary states that she fashions it so that the entire form of a human being is produced, and the human head is placed in its proper position, with the feet forward, the face upward, and the hands upon the thighs. 66.
Having placed that [brick] down, he worships with the Puruṣa hymn, beginning with "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet," [identifying him] as Nārāyaṇa. (Section 21) 67.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the eleventh book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.

The sacrificer worships that [altar] with the verse, "Thousand-headed is the Puruṣa," facing westward. Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Eleventh Book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.

11.8 Now, the eighth chapter in the eleventh book. He lays down the *apasyā* bricks. With the formula, "I settle thee in the movement of the waters," he places five in the east, facing west. With the formula, "May he sit in the ocean, the seat," he places five in the south, facing north. With the formula, "I settle thee in the seat of the waters," he places five in the west, facing east. With the formula, "The *gāyatrī* metre," he places five in the north, facing south. (1)

The *apasyā* bricks are those whose form consists of mantras containing the word "water" (*ap*). One should lay them down as follows: twenty *apasyā* bricks with the mantra, "In the waters, thee; in the wave, I settle thee. Five are placed to the east of the fire-altar, ending toward the west. Five are placed to the south of the fire-altar, ending toward the north, with the mantra, "Sit in the ocean, in the seat. Five are placed to the west of the fire-altar, ending toward the east, with the mantra, "In the seat of the waters, I settle thee. To the north of the fire-altar, ending toward the south, [five are placed] with the mantra, "Gāyatrī is the metre.
On the two wings and the tail, [the bricks are laid] beginning with the mantra, "In the ocean, in the seat," and so forth.

The gods who grasped the sacrifice from among the gods—may Gāyatrī lead them on, she who knows the way, milking out immortality in the heavenly world. Those who establish the lights, ascending to the world of immortality—may they go forth, knowing the way and understanding the sacrifice, in the world of the well-done. Those sacrificial animals which have come together toward the womb of the sacrifice—the sages, the wise ones, knowing the sacrifice, place them in the world of the well-done. That path which is stretched out... (ka).
[This is] the eighth chapter [of the Suvarga]. Accompanied by the *Mahādevaśāstrisaṃphalisaṃprayogacandrikā* commentary:

"The path of the gods (*devayāna*) proceeds, separated by the meters (*chandas*). By it he has ascended to heaven and the intermediate space, having grasped the sacrifice and the world of the well-performed deed. That sacrifice, with a thousand streams, which was fashioned over heaven and earth—by that may the sacrificer go safely to the back of heaven; may Aditi [protect him]. With these [mantras], five gold-bricks (*hiraṇyeṣṭakā*) are placed: four in each direction and one in the middle.
With each mantra beginning with "ye yajñam," he places a gold brick in each direction; one in the middle.

"Oblation to Āyu! Oblation to Yoṣkṛta! Oblation to Yoṣyatvan! Oblation to Viṣṇu! Oblation to Bṛhaspati!"—with these [formulas], five golden bricks are placed: four in each direction and one in the center.

"O Agni, the Trivṛt is your head; that, O Agni, is my head. The Pañcadaśa are your two arms; those, O Agni, are my two arms. The Saptadaśa is your self (ātman); that, O Agni, is my self. The Ekaviṃśa are your two thighs; those, O Agni, are my two thighs. The Triṇava are your two knee-bones; those, O Agni, are my two knee-bones. The Trayastriṃśa is your foundation; that, O Agni, is my foundation. With these [formulas], he places [the bricks] upon the head, the wings, the tail, the two hips, and the two shoulders.

"O Agni, the Trivṛt is your head; with it, protect me. O Agni, the Pañcadaśa are your two arms; with them, protect me. O Agni, the Saptadaśa is your trunk; with it, protect me. O Agni, the Ekaviṃśa are your two thighs; with them, protect me. O Agni, the Triṇava are your two knees; with them, protect me. O Agni, the Trayastriṃśa is your foundation; with it, protect me. With these words, the sacrificer consecrates the bricks as they are being laid down. (Khaṇḍa 22) 3.

With the formula, "To Āyu, svāhā! there is the laying down of five gold bricks in their respective places. With the formulas beginning, "Threefold art thou, O Agni," there is the laying down of these five clay bricks either on the head or, according to the opinion of some, in whatever place is available. For the sacrificer, there is the consecration of the bricks once they have been laid down with the formula, "Threefold art thou. || 3 ||

"Born from the waters and from the essence of the earth, he arose from Viśvakarman. Tvaṣṭṛ, fashioning his form, entered him; that was the first birth of the Puruṣa, the entire universe. Having placed this brick, [he recites]: "Thou art the seat of the Ṛtus; thou art the seat of Truth; thou art the seat of splendor; thou art the seat of luster; thou art the seat of glory; thou art the one being praised. Thou art a foundation; for the sake of the foundation, thee! For the sake of the foundations, thee! Sit in the foundations! Thou art a gain; for the sake of gain, thee! For the sake of gain, thee! [Satyāṣāḍha-viracitam Śrautasūtram—11th Praśna]

May I win. You are acquisition; for the sake of acquisition, may I find you. You are power; for the sake of power, may I be able. You are prosperity; for the sake of prosperity, may I flourish. You are action; for the sake of action, may I perform it. You are a joy; for the sake of joy, for the joys, sit as a joy. Protect the ruling power (*kṣattra*); swell the ruling power; quicken the ruling power; restrain the ruling power; fortify the ruling power. You are the ruling power; for the sake of the ruling power, for the sake of the rulers, sit in the ruling power.
