I settle you in all earthly realms; I settle you in all intermediate spaces; I settle you in all celestial realms; I settle you among all the gods; I settle you in all the waters; I settle you in all the plants; I settle you among all the trees; I settle you in all the directions. Sit in heaven!

You are the winner of heaven; you are the winner of armies; you are the winner of much; you are the victorious one; you are the winner of all; you are the winner of everything; you are the ever-victorious; you are the winner of wealth; you are the radiant one; you are the widely radiant one; you are the preeminent radiant one. I set you down as the thunderbolt that slays rivals. I set you down as the thunderbolt that slays those who seek to harm us. I set you down as the thunderbolt that slays enemies. I set you down as the thunderbolt that slays sorcerers. I set you down as the thunderbolt that slays Piśācas. I set you down as the thunderbolt that slays Rākṣasas.

I set down this Vajra of Indra, which slays enemies, slays foes, slays rivals, and slays Asuras. Thou art the rising; thou art the one who has risen; thou art the one about to rise; thou art the one treading upon; thou art the one treading; thou art the treading; thou art the one stepping together; thou art the one stepping together; thou art the stepping together; thou art leading to heaven; thou art heaven. Sit upon the impulse; sit upon strength; sit upon fortune; sit upon wealth; sit upon prosperity; sit upon the earth worthy of sacrifice; sit upon the back of Viṣṇu; sit upon the station of Iḍā; sit upon the one rich in ghee; sit upon the swelling one.

Sit in the *saṃvatsara*; sit in the *parivatsara*; sit in the *idāvatsara*; sit in the *udvatsara*; sit in the *vatsara*. Sit in one; sit in ten; sit in a hundred; sit in a thousand; sit in ten thousand; sit in a hundred thousand; sit in a million; sit in ten million; sit in a hundred million; sit in a billion; sit in ten billion; sit in a hundred billion; sit in the middle; sit in a trillion; sit at the end; sit in the supreme limit (*parārdha*). You are swelling; for the swelling one, for the swelling ones, for the swelling, sit!

Regarding the clay bricks according to their respective places: "another has come into being" (is one). There are seven [bricks] with the formula "in the seat of Truth" (*ṛtasadasī*); five with "you are a resting place" (*sanirasi*); the sixth is "the joyous one" (*gūrda*). There are six with "protect the ruling power" (*kṣatraṃ pāhi*). There are ten beginning with "I settle you among all earthly beings" (*viśveṣu tvā pārthiveṣu sādayāmi*) and ending with "sit in heaven" (*divi sīda*). There are eleven beginning with "you are the light-finder" (*svarṣiḥ asi*) and ending with "you are the radiant one" (*prabhāḍasi*). There are seven "Vajras" beginning with "slayer of rivals" (*sapatnahanam*). There are eleven beginning with "upward" (*udasi*). There are ten beginning with "sit upon the earth" (*ipisīda*). There are six "Years" (*saṃvatsarāḥ*) beginning with "sit in the year" (*saṃvatsare sīda*).

There are ten verses beginning with *ekasyāṃ sīda*. There are six verses beginning with *pinvamānā*, ending with the *saṃpat* formula. Those who do not prescribe the act of settling (*sādana*) have these as separate sections (*anuvāka*) in another recension (*śākhā*). For those, however, who do prescribe the settling, the number of sections is not stated. All of these are called "seer-bricks" (*ṛṣīṣṭakā*). Some, however, say that the sections themselves are the seer-bricks, because they are recited in the midst of the mantras of the first [section] beginning with *citraṃ tvā*. After having laid the seer-bricks of the first [section] beginning with *agne*, one lays the space-filling bricks (*lokaṃpṛṇā*).

"Those very same *prāṇabhṛt* bricks, beginning with the *gaṇas*, etc. Furthermore, a division of the *gaṇas* is not logical, because of the opinion of Baudhāyana and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra: "If one should lay them down as a single unit. However, some perform the laying down of the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks and so forth even on the first layer (*prastāra*) of the fire-altar, and they also perform the laying down of the *purīṣa* (filling soil) for the *ṛṣabha* brick, based on the statement: "The layer ends with the *purīṣa*. And afterwards, they perform the second layer; they should make it end with the *purīṣa* on that very same layer.

Such, however, is the intention of the author of the Sūtra: that there are two layers (citayaḥ) consisting of two sets of stars (dvipastārāḥ), not in the *sāhasra* [fire-altar]. Some, however, maintain that by omitting the *ṛṣīṣṭakā*s, the additional rule is non-obligatory; thus they perform [the rite] with "This is the earth" (*ayaṃ puro bhuvaḥ*) even in the first fire-altar. Nevertheless, a difference in the number of groups (*gaṇabheda*) certainly arises; therefore, the application of the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks occurs in the second or third fire-altar, because the author of the Sūtra has prescribed them specifically for the first layer (*cityā*). || 4 ||

"This one was in front, O Earth"—with these words, he lays down fifty *prāṇabhṛt* bricks: ten in each direction, ten transversely, and ten in the middle. Having laid down the outermost brick on the outside, he lays down the next innermost brick on the inside.

He lays down fifty bricks called *prāṇabhṛt* with the formula, "This one in front is the earth. He lays them down ten by ten in each direction, but crosswise and obliquely. Ten are in the middle; having laid those crosswise within the fire-altar, he subsequently lays down the outer ones behind.

Alternatively, he states that the placing [of the bricks] is to be accomplished with these mantras: "He places the *prāṇabhṛt* [bricks]" (*Leṅga Saṃhitā* 5.2.10), etc. Having been enjoined generally, he now enjoins them specifically: "With 'This one here before' (*ayaṃ puro bhuvaḥ*), he places [a brick] in the east; by means of these [mantras], he supports the vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself. With 'To the south, Viśvakarman' (*ayaṃ dakṣiṇā viśvakarmā*), he places [a brick] in the south; by means of these, he supports the mind (*manas*) itself. With 'To the west, Viśvavyacās' (*ayaṃ paścād viśvavyacāḥ*), he places [a brick] in the west; by means of these, he supports the eye (*cakṣus*) itself. With 'This one above, light' (*idam uttarāt suvaḥ*), he places [a brick] in the north."

"By these two he supports the ear itself; 'the mind above'—by these two he supports speech from above" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.9.10). —In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: ... [In the eleventh section, he prescribes the number of bricks to be placed in each direction: "He places ten at a time" (5.2.10). One should place ten bricks for each mantra, repeating it ten times.

Regarding the curvature in this placement, the text prescribes: "He places them crosswise" (5.2.10), and so forth. When one begins in the southwest and concludes in the northeast, there is straightness; when one begins in the southwest and concludes in the northwest, there is curvature. It is the same here as well. This is what is expressed by the term "crosswise" (*akṣṇayā*). Furthermore, regarding the passage "He places the breath-supporting bricks" (1.4.18), one must discern whether, as before, it serves as a reference to the mantra, or for the purpose of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), or for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*).

However, another aphorism is stated for the purpose of explaining other grounds [for secondary usage]. For in that case, there is the actual application of the word "destruction" (*bhū-nāśa*). Here, however, because those possessing the characteristic (*liṅgin*) are formless, the word functions solely through its inherence (*samavāya*) in them. Indeed, in a group consisting of living beings (*prāṇabhṛt*), there is inherence of living beings; and even in a group consisting of both living and non-living beings, there is inherence of living beings—thus, by virtue of this similarity, the word "moon" (*śaśabhṛt*) is applied. Thus it is said: "By means of accomplishment, genus, similarity, praise, characteristic, and abundance—these six grounds, the figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) of words is established everywhere. (Verse 5)

"The eastern direction of the directions, the spring of the seasons"—with these [formulas], he places fifty apānabhṛt bricks, placing each subsequent one further outward after having placed each preceding one further inward, just as he did with the prāṇabhṛts. || 6 ||

He lays down the *apānabhṛt* bricks with the formula, "The eastern direction is supported by the out-breath," just as he did the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks. They are laid down across the quarters and diagonally on the outside. Having first laid down the previously mentioned *prāṇabhṛt* bricks in the inner space, he should now lay down these *apānabhṛt* bricks, known as the *saṃyats*, in the outer space. He prescribes the *prāṇabhṛt* and *apānabhṛt* bricks in a reversed manner:
"He lays down the *prāṇabhṛt* and the *apānabhṛt* bricks in opposite directions."

Since there is a reciprocal reversal of the sequence between the outgoing breath (prāṇa) and the incoming breath (apāna) among living beings, therefore, even in the world, prāṇa and apāna are of mutually opposite natures: outward movement is prāṇa, and inward movement is apāna.
With this Anuvāka beginning with "āyuṣaḥ prāṇaṃ saṃtanvi," he, being self-restrained, lays down [the bricks]. (Section 23) 8.
"From life to breath," says Āpastamba; these are twelve continuous [recitations], occurring at no fixed place.

You are the Earth by birth, a cow; you have conceived Agni as your embryo—unite with me! You are the Sky by birth, a cow; you have conceived Āditya as your embryo—unite with me! You are the Stars by birth, a cow; you have conceived the Moon as your embryo—unite with me! You are the Waters by birth, a cow; you have conceived Varuṇa as your embryo—unite with me!

"You are Auṣadhī by birth, a cow; she bore King Soma as her embryo—do you unite with me. "You are Vayovir by birth, a cow; she bore [Agni] Jarābodhin as her embryo—do you unite with me. "You are Virāj by birth, a cow; she bore the King [Soma] as her embryo—do you unite with me. With these verses from this Anuvāka, he lays down the Vaśā bricks. (Paṭala 71, Section 8–9) This work is accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.

Beginning with "Thou art the earth," there are seven *vaśā* bricks; Āpastamba says there are five *vaśā*s. "O divine brick, thou who art the giver of life, the one who lies close by—may she, like a wife to her husband, always lie close to me in my dwellings. "O divine brick, thou who art the giver of out-breath, the giver of in-breath, the giver of diffused breath, the giver of sight, the giver of hearing, the giver of the earth, the giver of the intermediate space, the giver of heaven, the giver of the sun, the giver of maidens, the giver of young women, the giver of virgins, the one who lies close by—may she, like a wife to her husband, always lie close to me in my dwellings. With this *anuvāka*, he lays down the *upaśīvarī* bricks. (Śulba Sūtra 11.8.10)
The meaning is clear. || 10 ||

"Ye are purposeful; ye have stood firm, gone on the path of Agni. With the most brilliant splendor, I take you with the deities. Ye are bright, full of vigor; I take you, belonging to Indra the powerful, with the deities. Ye are sovereign mistresses, full of splendor; I take you, belonging to the Ādityas the gods, with the deities. Ye are delightful, victorious; I take you, belonging to the Viśvedevas, with the deities. Ye are sustainers of the kṣatra, full of might; I take you, belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa through the sacred word (brahman), with the deities."

"Ye are dwelling in the cow-pen, ye are standing on high; with the sacred word (brahman) of Bṛhaspati and with the deities, I take [you]. Having filled twelve jar-bricks (*kumbheṣṭakā*) with water, he places one jar and one pan (*kumbhī*) for each mantra, following the furrows in every direction, using this Anuvāka beginning with "Golden-hued, pure, purifying..."—six jars and six pans in each direction. Four are placed in the middle.

According to the author of the Bhāṣya, the mention of "one who has set out on a journey" (*sthādhvagata*) is for the sake of the water, and the filling of the *kumbha* and *kunbhī* vessels occurs simultaneously. This is because the mantras are expressive of the waters, and because of the principle that when one is unable [to perform all at once], the filling is done one by one. Furthermore, two bricks of the *kumbha* have the same deity.

From the recension of the Vājasaneyins: "You are a shelter and you are a protection; by the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I set you down, full of sweetness. By that deity, O Aṅgirases, sit ye down. Thus he places them in front of the fire according to the order in which they were laid out. To the west is the *kumbha* (pot) and to the east is the *kumbhī* (cauldron). "For light, you two"—with these words, he throws a piece of gold into each of them, according to Āpastamba and Vaikhānasa.

And because the mantra has a dual ending for both the *kumbha* and the *kumbhī* simultaneously; thus, by this reason, the filling, the placing (*upadhāna*), and the throwing of gold chips are performed with the subsequent mantras, each in its respective direction. Two are placed to the south, likewise two to the west, and two to the north—the *kumbha* to the south and the *kumbhī* to the north, following the furrow (*anusītam*). In all cases, the *kumbha*-bricks remain situated upon stones underneath—since he places them beneath the fire when he says, "He places water beneath the fire" (TS 5...).

6-2) Thus, from the other side as well, it is exactly the same: a *kumbha* to the west and a *kumbhī* to the east; a *kumbha* to the north and a *kumbhī* to the south. In the middle, however, there are four; they are paired two by two according to their respective deities. In the three furrows (*sītā*) situated in the eastern direction, there is a pair consisting of a *kumbha* and a *kumbhī*. The same applies to the other directions. This is stated: "He places the others in pairs, four in the middle for stability" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.6.3).
Of the twelve, eight have been placed in the four directions; now one should place the remaining four in the center. And that serves for support and for firmness. || 11 ||
"Rest in heaven; exert yourself in the intermediate space"—with these words, he places in the middle of the bricks a *naivāra* (millet) pap cooked in milk for Bṛhaspati in a water-jar.

The word "he places" (*upadadhāti*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. With the formula "May he rest in heaven" (*divi śrayatu*), the placing of the *naivāra* [grain] occurs; by means of the dedication to Bṛhaspati, the cooking of the *naivāra* oblation takes place in the common (*laukika*) fire. According to the Commentator (*bhāṣyakṛt*), the cooking is performed in the *gārhapatya* fire. Some, however, explain that the twelve verses beginning with "Golden-colored ones" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*) and ending with "the mothers" (*mātaraḥ*) are employed for the placing of the two pots (*kumbha-kumbhī*), while the remainder [of the text] constitutes the consecration of the *naivāra* grain; thus, one should perform the standing near (*upasthāna*) of the *naivāra* with the formulas "For him, enough! (*tasmā aram*) and "Rest in heaven, in the intermediate space" (*divi śrayasvāntarikṣe*), which is the placing of the *naivāra-caru* oblation. || 12 ||
"For your heat, for your luster, for your sight, for your light, for your seed, for your offspring"—with these words, he throws two gold chips each into the two [fires].

With the mantra "For splendor, you two," he anoints the two pieces of gold, because the mantra is in the dual number and applies simultaneously to both the water-pot (kumbha) and the cooking-pot (kumbhī).

"O Agni, you, the bull, the observer..."—having thrown a bull-shaped piece of gold onto the layer, he touches it with the *klṛpti* formula, [thinking] "he shall pile the layer as a layer. (Section 24) || 14 ||

The *ṛṣabha* brick is placed first, even out of sequence, for the sake of stability; for it is said: "In each layer (*cityā*), one places the *ṛṣabha*. And the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks are for the purpose of filling, according to the indicative mark: "Fill the world, fill the gap. With the formula, "O *lokaṃpṛṇā*, thou art the *sūdadohas* of this [Agni]," he covers the entire Agni with the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks. The Śruti states: "One should make all the colors of the bricks. He does not, however, apply colors such as white or yellow.

The lines are called *varṇas*. [End of] Chapter 8. This is accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. Because it is enjoined thus in another Śruti: having placed gold upon the altar (*citi*), he touches it with the mantra "Cittiśca cittiśca. "Citiklapti" is the name of this [mantra]. || 14 ||

Whatever has been piled by you, O Agni, whatever has been piled by you, whatever was deficient here, or whatever was excessive—may all the gods and the Aṅgirases pile it; may the Ādityas fill your layer. Those logs of yours, O Agni, [are] the piling and the non-piling. O Agni, may we be possessed of wealth, sufficient for the sacrifice and for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). May the pressing-stone speak over the stalk of Soma; may we serve Indra with the pressed drop. Bestow upon us increase of wealth, O Jātavedas; grant us a portion of strength, full of sweetness and truth.

We establish the sacrifice; let us press the Soma. O Śakra, may we serve you through this sacrifice. We have heard that you are the lord of riches, O Agni, Lord of Wealth; come among me for food that is rich in cattle, rich in horses, abundant in nourishment, and rich in gold. May Heaven and Earth milk for you their milk; let the serpent glide along with the water. Through Prajāpati I satisfy myself; my self was empty.

Having touched the *svayamcit* (self-piled) altar with the seven verses beginning, "The Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants—the Rudra who has entered all beings—to that Rudra, O gods, let there be homage," he covers it with the *lokapṛṇā* bricks. || 15 ||
Beginning with "yatte'citam," he touches [the altar] with these eight verses and covers the entire fire-altar with the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks.
With two mantras at a time, he lays down each individual *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick. || 16 ||
Having placed it with the former [formula], he touches it with the *sūdadohas* verse. || 17 ||
Having touched it with the [verse] "cittimacittiṃ," he then touches it while reciting these eight verses beginning with "acitam. || 16 || 17 ||
In all the iṣṭakās, he places the tayādevata formula at the end. || 18 ||
In the case of the laying of bricks, at the end of the mantra, the formula ends with: "By that deity, sit thou firm in thy own place. || 18 ||

A black horse or a dark-grey one stands to the north. Having touched it and having brought earth from the *cātvāla* pit, he spreads it out with the verse, "Thou art asked about heaven" (*pṛṣṭo divi*). That constitutes the layer (*cit*).

He stands to the north of the fire, beginning from the black [bricks] for the filling-in (upadhāna), or the white one. Having touched him and having brought earth from the *cātvāla* pit, he spreads the earth over it with a verse addressed to Vaiśvānara; he does not lay them down in this manner. "With a verse addressed to Vaiśvānara he lays down the *prabheda*," so says the Śruti. The piling (*cit*) ends with the earth-filling. Having uttered the *pratyavarohaṇa* formula, "Speech is in my mouth," [the rite is concluded]. || 19 || 20 ||

The fire that is within the waters, that which is in Vṛtra, that which is in man, and that which is in stone; that which has entered into all beings—to those fires let this be offered. The fire whom they call the eater of oblations, whom they call desire, whom they call the giver and the receiver; he who is the most divine among the gods, born of austerity—to those fires let this be offered. [The verse] "He who is questioned in heaven" follows. That Soma which is within, which is within the cows, which has entered into birds and which is in wild beasts.

"May this oblation be for those fires which entered into bipeds and quadrupeds; for that fire by which the chariots of Indra were brought together, which is Vaiśvānara and which belongs to the Viśvedevas; for that wise and powerful one who overcomes many attackers—may this oblation be for those fires. Having laid down each layer (*citi*) with the six verses beginning "For him whose food is the bull, whose food is the cow," he makes the offerings. (21)

Having laid down each layer (*citi*) with the six verses beginning "He who has entered within the waters" (*yo apsvantarnirita*), he offers an oblation upon the topmost layer, ending with the *purīṣa* (filling soil). The deity for all [these offerings] is Agni. Some say that one should place gold upon the layer itself and offer [the oblation] over it.
In this manner, from this point upward, all [bricks] beginning with the Ṛṣabha are piled up; they are performed identically. || 22 ||
In all the funeral rites about to be described, the rituals beginning with the *ṛṣabha* [offering] are indeed common to all.

With a *gāyatrī* verse addressed to Agni, he should touch the first layer; with a *triṣṭubh*, the second; with a *jagatī*, the third; with an *anuṣṭubh*, the fourth; and with a *paṅkti*, the fifth. For all [verses], the second [part] is the *dhāmacchad*. "O Agni Jātavedas, many are your abodes"—this is the *dhāmacchad*. "O Agni, being born, bring the gods here for him who has spread the sacrificial grass; you are our invoker, worthy of praise. "We have approached with a great mind the youngest [Agni], who has shone forth, well-kindled in his own dwelling."

The one of variegated luster between the two wide worlds, well-invoked from all sides, facing every direction—Agni, the creator of wisdom, the ordainer, the fulfiller, the Hotṛ, the most pervasive thought; thee alone, the common [priest] of the small oblation, do men choose for the great [sacrifice], none other than thee. Like Manu, they establish thee as the treasure-store. [End of Paṭala 8] [From the *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī, Chapter 75]

"O Agni, like Manu, let us kindle thee; O Aṅgiras, like Manu, sacrifice to the gods for the one who seeks the gods. For Agni, the lord of all people, bestows a prize-winning steed; Agni [bestows] wealth that is self-sustaining. Being pleased, he goes toward the noble; bring nourishment to the singers"—these are the verses as they are recited. 23.

"Agni, one offers many oblations with the seventh [verse]," says Āpastamba. "He performs the laying down of the bricks for the altar," says Vaikhānasa. "One should touch the first layer with a Gāyatrī verse addressed to Agni," so says the Brāhmaṇa. When the offering has been made, he touches the first layer with that [verse] which has Agni as its deity and is in the Gāyatrī meter. He touches the second with a Triṣṭubh; the third with a Jagatī; he touches the fourth with an Anuṣṭubh; he touches the fifth with a Paṅkti.

With the Gāyatrī verse addressed to Agni beginning with "O Agni, thou who possessest many abodes" (agne bhūrīṇi) and "O Agni, bring the gods hither" (agne devān iha āvaha), he should touch the first layer; in that recensional tradition, these verses ending with [the word] "pavate" are prescribed in another Śākhā. || 23 ||
There are six *upasads*. || 24 ||
The Upasad days become six through their connection with the fire-altars; likewise, the Soma days become six through their connection with the piling of the altar. || 24 ||
He piles the fire-altar with the *anupasada* rites; one layer (*citi*) is piled each day, and the final layer takes two days. || 25 ||

For two days he performs the oblation with each of the two worship-mantras. He piles the fire-altar for two days without the *upasad* rites; the last layer (*citi*) is performed thus, according to Āpastamba. "Without the *upasad*" means following the *upasad*. The commentator states: "When the *upasad* is completed, he piles the fire-altar, and the *pravargya* follows after. The author of the Sūtra intends that one piles the fire-altar after having performed the *upasad* in this manner. The last layer is concluded by two [days].
There are three vows with four breasts; likewise, there are those with three breasts, two breasts, and one breast. || 26 ||

There are three vows with four teats; the vows of the night of the day of purchase (krayadivasa) consist of these. Thus, there are three vows with three teats, three vows with two teats, and one vow with one teat on the day of the Agniṣoma sacrifice.

Having performed the afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites, and having led the white horse clockwise around [the altar] while reciting, "When you first cried out at birth," they dwell [there], they dwell. (Section 25) 27.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the eleventh book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
Thus ends the eleventh book in the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha. 11.
Now begins the first chapter of the twelfth book.

Regarding all the layers (*citi*), the morning and afternoon *pravargya* and *upasad* rites are explained; the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites at the beginning, the afternoon ones at the end, the layer-offering (*citihoma*), and the leading around of the horse have been described. On the following day, he piles the second layer.
With the verses beginning "dhruvakṣitiḥ" and "dhruvayoniḥ," he places five Āśvinī bricks: four in each of the cardinal directions and one in the center.
With the verse "In harmony with the seasons," he lays down five seasonal bricks pertaining to the Aśvins.

He places [the bricks] around in succession, saying: "Protect my out-breath; protect my in-breath. He lays down five *ṛtavyā* bricks dedicated to Vāyu with the formulas, "Thou art the path of Vāyu," and "Thou art the path of the gods, O Vāyu. Two *saṃyānya* bricks follow. Two *ṛtavyā* bricks follow with the formulas, "Śukra and Śuci. These two have the same deity. 4.

He lays down five *apasyā* bricks belonging to Vāyu; he places them along the circuit. He lays down four bricks with the formula "The support, strength..."; he places the one containing the word *mūrdhan* (the head) to the east of the last [brick]. || 5 ||

"Tryavir vayaḥ"—these five [bricks] he lays down on the south as *vayasvinī* bricks; "paṣṭhavāḍ vayaḥ"—these five on the west; "vasto vayaḥ"—these five on the north as *siṃhavatī* bricks. Alternatively, he places the brick with "vasto vayaḥ" on the southern shoulder and the one with "vṛṣṇir vayaḥ" on the northern shoulder. He places the brick with "vyāghro vayaḥ" on the right wing and the one with "siṃho vayaḥ" on the left wing. The brick with "puruṣo vayaḥ" he places in the middle. 6.
The section beginning with Ṛṣabha and ending with Citya has been explained. || 7 ||
On the following day, he piles the third layer. (Section 1) 8.

Having touched the *svayamātṛṇṇā* with the mantra, "O Indra and Agni, you who are unshakable," and having caused a horse to smell it, he places it in the middle of the fire-altar together with an ignorant Brāhmaṇa, using the mantra, "May Viśvakarman seat thee on the back of the atmosphere, thee who art expansive," and with this sacred utterance (*vyāhṛti*), "Bhuvaḥ."
Having offered with the words, "I offer consciousness," into the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone, he then recites; the learned Brāhmaṇa gives a boon. || 12.1.10 ||

"Thou art light; give me light. Thou art the intermediate space; protect me from the intermediate space"—with these words he lays down the gold brick (*hiraṇyeṣṭakā*). "The sky has entered the intermediate space with sacred power (*brahman*); the Maruts are thy guardians"—with these words he lays down the circle brick (*maṇḍaleṣṭakā*). He places the two *anuretas* bricks and the two *sica* bricks. "May Viśvakarman settle thee, the luminous one, on the back of the intermediate space"—with this he lays down the *viśvajyotis* brick. "Thou art the paths of the intermediate space; thou art the intermediate space of the gods"—with these words he lays down the two *saṃyānī* bricks. (1.1)
Nabhas and Nabhasya, Iṣa and Ūrja—these four seasonal deities (ṛtavyā) consist of two pairs, each pair being a single deity. || 12 ||
"You are the queen of the eastern quarter"—thus [he addresses] five [bricks] pertaining to the quarters: four in each direction and one in the middle.
Having first laid down ten Vairāja bricks with the formula, "Protect my life. (14)
He lays down thirty-six *bṛhatī* bricks: twelve to the south with the formula "The *mā* metre," twelve to the west with "The *pṛthivī* metre," and twelve to the north with "Agni as the deity. (15)

With the formula, "Thou art the head, the sovereign," he places seven Vālakhilya bricks in front, facing westward; with the formula, "The restrainer, the sovereign," he places seven behind, facing eastward.
With the formula "Svāhā to the Earth," he lays twelve elemental bricks (bhūteṣṭakā). || 17 ||
"From the eastern quarter I set thee down"—with these words he places five self-bricks: four in the cardinal directions and one in the middle. (Khaṇḍa 2) || 18 ||
With this Anuvāka beginning with "Indro dadhīco asthabhiḥ," he lays down ten bricks that are recited over the Atharvaśiras. || 19 ||
The section beginning with Ṛṣabha and ending with Citya has been explained. 12.1.20.
On the following day, he piles the fourth layer.
He lays down the bricks with these two sections beginning with "The swift one, the threefold, is the portion of Agni," according to the Brāhmaṇa.
"Antarikṣa! For the intermediate space, thee!"—with these two [verses], there are two *saṃyājyā* offerings.
*Sahaś* and *sahasya* are the two seasonal months; they share the same deity. || 24 ||
With the verse "ekayā'stuvata," seventeen creations [are described]. || 25 ||
"This is indeed she who first shone forth"—thus [he recites] fifteen dawns. || 26 ||

"O Agni, drive away our born enemies"—with these words he places [the brick] in the east; "those born by force"—in the west; "the forty-fourfold hymn-form"—in the south; "the sixteenfold hymn-form"—in the north. || 27 ||
Having spread loose earth over the brick with the formula, "The loose earth of the earth, whose name is apsa," he places the *purīṣavatī* brick in the middle of the fire-altar. || 28 ||
The [funeral mounds] ending with the *citya* have been explained starting from the *ṛṣabha*. || 29 ||
On the following day, having performed the morning rites, he piles the fifth layer.
With the formulas "The *chandas* is eva, the *chandas* is varivas," he lays forty *virāj* bricks, ten in each direction, diagonally.
"Thou art a ray; for habitation thee, quicken the habitation"—with these [formulas] there are thirty-one *stomabhāga* bricks, seven in each direction and three in the middle. || 32 ||

"O King, the eastern direction is yours"—with these words, he places five *nākasad* bricks, four in each of the cardinal directions and one in the center. Having subsequently placed the last one facing eastward, he places five *coḍā* bricks among the *nākasads* with the mantra "This one in front, the golden-haired one. Having placed those, he builds the circular layer (*vṛttā citiḥ*).
Tapaśca and Tapasya are the two seasonal deities who share the same ritual status. (Section 3) || 34 ||
"Thou art the one belonging to the gods; thou art the goddess-devotee of the gods"—with these words, two *saṃyānī* (steeds) [are addressed]. 35.
"May Prajāpati settle you on the back of heaven, the luminous one," [with these words] he places the Viśvajyotis brick. Here he lays down the Retahsic bricks of the elder. 36.

"May the unconquered heaven, pervaded by immortality, be your protectors—O Ādityas"—with these words [he places] the Maṇḍaleṣṭakā. "Thou art light; grant me light; grant me heaven; protect me from heaven"—with these words [he places] the Hiraṇyeṣṭakā. || 37 ||
Having performed the afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites, they dwell [there] after having led a white horse around clockwise while reciting, "When you first cried out at birth... (RV 10.72.6).
He lets three Audumbara fuel-sticks, each a span long, soak in clarified butter. || 39 ||
On the following day, having performed the morning Pravargya and Upasad rites with the two final [formulas], he piles the Yājñasenī layer as the remainder of the fifth layer.

He places three Gāyatrī verses containing the word "mūrdhan" (head), beginning with *agnirmūrdhā*, in the east. To the north, he places three Triṣṭubhs; to the south, three Jagatīs; to the west, three Anuṣṭubhs; and to the north, three Bṛhatīs, Uṣṇihs, Paṅktis, Akṣarapaṅktis, and other such diverse metres (*viṣurūpāṇi chandāṃsi*), placing them according to available space. Right here he places the Aticchandas verse, having placed the Dvipadā as the last one.

Having touched the *svayamātṛṇṇā* with the formula, "I settle thee in the seat of Āyu," and having caused a horse to smell it, he places it in the middle of the fire-altar together with an unlearned Brāhmaṇa, using the formula, "May Parameṣṭhin settle thee on the back of heaven, thee that art expansive. He does so with this *vyāhṛti*, "Suvaḥ. Having offered an oblation upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* with the formula, "I offer the layer," he breathes out. On the northern shoulder, he places the *vikarṇī* brick with the verse, "Snorting like a horse eager for fodder.
He places neither the *svayamātṛṇṇā* nor the *vikarṇī* over other bricks. || 43 || 44 ||
With this Anuvāka beginning with "O Agni, come to us with cattle," he lays down the Gociti layer; there are a thousand bricks measuring one foot (pāda).
One who desires cattle places them on each of the middle layers. (Section 4) 46.
Thus ends the first chapter in the twelfth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter of the twelfth book.
"O Indra and Agni, I yoke you with a yoke-mate, with a yoke-mate"—with these [verses] he yokes eight yoke-mates. || 1 ||
"You are named Ambā"—thus [she spoke] to the seven Kṛttikās. ||2||
With the five verses beginning "Thou art the wind from the front, the winner of rain," he places [the vessels] down while moving around them in succession. ||3||
"Salilāya tvā," "Sarṇīkāya tvā"—these are the eight Āditya bricks. || 4 ||
With the formula, "For the Ṛc thee! For the Ruc thee! he places five ghee-bricks, moving around them in successive order.
"Yaśodāṃ tvā yaśasi sādayāmi"—with these words, he places five Yaśodās.
"Bhūyaskṛd asi, varivaskṛd asi"—these are the five Bhūyaskṛt [bricks]. ||7||
"Thou art seated in the waters, thou art seated in the falcon"—these are the five forms of Agni. || 8 ||
"Upon the wealth of the earth I set thee"—with these [verses] there are five Draviṇodās.
"Protect my out-breath; protect my in-breath"—these are the six formulas for long life. 12.2.10.
"O Agni, that which is your supreme heart-name"—this is the Heart-mantra of Agni. || 11 ||
"Whether it be a year or not a year"—these are the seven seasonal verses. 12.
With this Anuvāka beginning with "agninā viśvāṣāṭ," he lays down the bodies of Indra. || 13 ||
With this Anuvāka—"Abhīṣāt, Abhiṣavī, Abhivayas, Ūrdhvavayas, Bṛhadvayas, Savayas, Sahvān, Sahamāna, Sahasvān, and Sahīyān"—he lays down the names of Indra.
With "Prajāpati beheld the horse with his mind," he [lays down] thirty-three bodies of the sacrifice.
"Jyotiṣmatīm tvā sādayāmi"—with these words, he places twelve Jyotiṣmatī bricks.

"I settle you among the red clouds; I settle you among the ruddy clouds; I settle you among the white clouds; I settle you among the blue clouds; I settle you among the black clouds"—thus are the five clouds. 17.
With this Anuvāka beginning with "The Kṛttikās are the lunar mansion," he places eight asterism-bricks on his shoulders. ||18||
He appends "O Agni, with splendor" to all [the verses]. || 19 ||

"Full [is] afterwards"—having first laid down the full-moon brick, he lays down each subsequent earlier one after each subsequent later one, up to the Viśākhās. "What the gods placed in thee"—having first laid down the new-moon brick behind, he lays down each subsequent later one after each subsequent earlier one, ending with the Apabharaṇīs.
"Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre"—these eight [verses] are the *sarits*. || 21 ||
"Viśvakarman is the lord of the quarters"—with these [formulas], one places five golden bricks: four in each direction and one in the middle.
With the formulas, "For breath thee! For sight thee! he places four naturally perforated pebbles in each direction; [the one-year-old bull is prescribed as the image of the year]. || 23 ||

"O Agni, come for the feast! We choose Agni as our messenger. By means of Agni, Agni is kindled. May Agni strike down the Vṛtras. O Agni, we meditate upon the effective hymn that touches the heavens today. Of the divine wealth..."—these are the forms of the five days. [Then he lays down the Vrata brick.]

With the formula "To him of a hundred weapons," he places five *ājyānī* bricks; with "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra," he places four *vajriṇī* bricks in each direction. Some recite five [bricks] together, and he modifies the mantra with the words "He who is above us. || 25 ||

"O Agni, bestow glory upon the glorious one"—with these four *rāṣṭrabhṛt* verses he lays down the bricks. He places a *gāyatrī* verse in the east, a *triṣṭubh* in the south, a *jagatī* in the west, an *anuṣṭubh* in the north, and a *paṅkti* in the middle. He places a *gāyatrī* in the south; in this manner all are laid down in successive order. Everywhere the formulas begin with "Agni is the head," "Of the world," "The guardian of the people," "Thee, O most renowned," and "O Agni, that horse today. These are the verses as they are recited. (Section 6) 26.
Thus ends the second chapter in the twelfth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Now begins the third chapter of the twelfth book.

With the mantra, "Thou art the measure of a thousand," he sprinkles the fire while moving clockwise around it with a thousand gold chips, two hundred at a time for each direction; in the center, he sprinkles facing east with the final two hundred.
"O Agni, may these bricks of mine be milch-cows"—with this [formula], he makes the bricks into milch-cows. || 2 ||
He touches [the altar] with the Aiḍikī brick; the verses for the forest-dweller (Āraṇyaka) become the invitatory formulas (Anuvākyās).

He offers the Śatarudrīya oblation with either a gruel of wild sesame (jartila) or a gruel of gavīdhuka seeds, or with flour of gavīdhuka seeds mixed with wild sesame and clarified butter, or with deer’s milk, or with goat’s milk. Standing upright on the northernmost brick, using an Arka leaf, he divides these Anuvākas into three parts and offers them: with the first Anuvāka and eighty oblations at knee-height; with another eighty at navel-height; and with the remaining eighty and as many more as there are prior to the *avatāna* verses, at mouth-height—making a thousand oblations in total.

He offers thousands—that is, innumerable—descents of the ten guardians (daśāvata). [He offers] with "Homage to the Rudras who are in heaven" at the height of the mouth; with "Homage to the Rudras who are in the intermediate space" at the height of the navel; and with "Homage to the Rudras who are on earth" at the height of the knees.
In a place free from traffic, he discards the *arka* leaf. ||6||
One should place [the sacrificial portions] at the entrance of one whom he hates; whichever animal stands first shall meet with misfortune. (Section 7)
The Brāhmaṇa of the Śatarudrīya. ||7||

With the verse, "Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants," he offers a *gāvīdhuka* pap cooked in milk as an oblation to Rudra; he places it upon that brick upon which he performs the *śatarudrīya* offering. || 8 ||
One should give three bows obtained without asking to a Brāhmaṇa.

With the formula, "May the Vasus protect you with the Rudras from the east," he sprinkles the fire with clarified butter while moving clockwise around it, addressing each direction; in the center he uses the final formula, facing eastward. With the formula, "O Rudra, that bow which is yours in front," he worships [the fire] by moving clockwise around it, addressing each direction with salutations; in the center he uses the final formula, facing eastward. (12.3.10)
Taking a water-pot and placing a stone [within it], he goes around the fire three times from left to right, sprinkling water while reciting, "In the stone, strength. || 11 ||

Having set down the water-pot, he goes around three times sprinkling water behind him. If he should practice sorcery, he pours out the pot at the southern buttock, saying, "I destroy the breath of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so," and he pronounces the name of the one he hates.

He worships with the back-ribs: with the *gāyatra* [sāman] from the front; with the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* [sāmans] the two wings; with the *yajñāyajñīya* as the *ṛtusthā* [sāman], the tail; he sings the *vāravantīya* on the southern hip and the *vāmadevya* on the northern; furthermore, he sings the *prajāpateḥ sāman* upon the verse for each wing. || 13 ||

"The sacrifice has been offered by the Bhṛgus; may it be accompanied by blessings from the Vasus. Of that which has been offered and enjoyed, may I partake in the wealth. With these words, he causes the sacrificer to recite during the milking of the Stotra and Śastra.
The Hotṛ recites the *saṃcita-ukthya* with the verse, "Father Mātariśvan.
If the Hotṛ does not desire it, the Adhvaryu [recites it]. || 15 ||
In this regard, some authorities prescribe cows as the instrument [of the sacrifice]. (Section 8) 16.
Thus ends the third paṭala in the twelfth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now, the fourth chapter in the twelfth book:

Having tied together an *avakā* plant, a frog, and a branch of reed-grass to a long bamboo pole, he drags the fire [with it] seven or eight times with the formula: "With the *avakā* plant of the ocean, O Agni, we encircle thee. || 1 ||
Having followed [the frog] and lured away its life-breaths, he places all [the parts] together in a heap of dust. || 2 ||
One should touch that person whom one hates. || 3 ||

Creating for himself an easy path for his departure, the sharp-horned bull, blazing brightly, looking back toward his ancient dwelling place, Agni has stretched out the celestial thread. You, O Agni, are our thread and our bridge; you are the path that leads to the gods. By you, O Agni, may we ascend to the heights, and then may we rejoice in the communal feast with the gods. Giving their leave to the descendant of Manu, they looked upon the straight path.

The Maruts have delighted in this sacrifice—the rain of the gods, the nectar, the finder of heaven. Turning back into the midst of the world, transforming the various forms of progeny, may Saṃvatsara, the Supreme Lord who maintains his vows, protect our sacrifice from beyond the realm of space. May Parivatsara grant us progeny; may Dhātṛ, being well-disposed, grant it. "May many [progenies], together, manifold, of all forms, yet bound by a single vow, enter into me"—with these words he offers the five *anvāroha* oblations. (Section 9) ||4||
"I have stepped upon the earth; may my vital breath not forsake me"—with these words, he puts on the two sandals made of black antelope skin, or at least one of them.
With the two verses, "This is the gathering-place of the waters" and "Homage to your heat and your flame," he steps over the fire.

Having taken five portions of clarified butter into the *juhu* ladle, he sprinkles it crosswise over the fire with the five formulas beginning with "To the seat of man, vaṭ! just as over the *uttaravedi*. 7.
With the two verses beginning "ye devā devānām," he sprinkles water mixed with curds and honey around the fire using a handful of darbha grass.
Having made the tortoise-spotted [mark], he descends with the words, "Givers of out-breath, givers of in-breath. || 9 ||
Having taken five portions into the *juhu* ladle, he offers one oblation to Agni Anīkavat with the two *saṃhitā* verses beginning, "Agni with his sharp flame" and "He with his host. (12.4.10)

Having filled the *sruk* ladle with sixteen portions, he offers the various *vaiśvakarmanī* oblations with the two hymns beginning "ya imā viśvā bhuvanāni juhvat," or else with all [the verses] together.

If he should desire of someone, "May he be released from evil for a long time," he should offer each oblation separately for him. If he should desire of someone, "May he be released from evil quickly," he should offer all of them for him after reciting them in succession. || 12 ||

"Salutation to the ocean, the wise one, the lord of rivers!"—if he should find him in water, he should take water in his cupped hands and offer it into the waters. This is the ritual procedure when not connected with a formal sacrifice. (Section 10) 13.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the twelfth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Now begins the fifth chapter of the twelfth book.

Having performed the final afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites, he places three pieces of wood that have been soaked in ghee into the Āhavanīya fire with the three verses beginning, "Lead him toward the north."
With the verse, "May all the gods lift you up," he raises the fire. ||2||
With the six [verses] beginning with "May the goddesses of the five directions protect the sacrifice," he carries [the fire]. || 3 ||
With the hymn of ten verses beginning with "The swift one, sharpening [his weapons]," the Brahman—or the Maitrāvaruṇa or the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin—follows from the south with the Apratiratha hymn. ||4||
With the two verses beginning, "This celestial chariot stands in the midst of heaven," he places a stone upon the Āgnīdhra altar.
With the four verses beginning "All have magnified Indra," he goes as far as the tail.
With the five verses beginning "Along the eastern direction," they step toward the fire.

Having filled a ladle made of Udumbara wood with milk or curds from a black cow that has a white calf, he offers one oblation upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone while reciting the two *saṃhitā* verses: "Night and Dawn... and "O Agni, thousand-eyed...".

(8) While the verse "Sit down first upon the womb rich in wool" is being recited, he establishes the fire upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone with three verses beginning with "Thou art the fair-winged Garuḍa," or with two. (9)

"O Agni, shine forth, kindled before us"—with these words he places a fuel-stick of *Audumbara* wood; "we would worship thee in thy highest birth, O Agni"—with this verse he places a stick of *Vikaṅkata* wood; "the wonderful [splendor] of Savitṛ, the most excellent"—with this verse he places a stick of *Śamī* wood. Some prescribe the *Śamī* stick first and the *Vikaṅkata* stick afterwards. (Section 11) 12.5.10.
With the verse "O Agni, bring that today," he offers oblations using the *akṣarapaṅkti* meter.

Having cleansed the *juhū* and the *sruva* ladles, and having filled the *sruk* with either four, eight, or twelve portions of clarified butter, he offers the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verse, "Seven are thy... (RV 10.53.6).
While offering that [oblation] here with the thought, "May he be [present]," one meditates mentally upon Agni from the various directions. || 13 ||
He commences the ritual procedure for the Vaiśvānara [offering]. We shall explain therein everything that is performed. 14.
Having prepared the Veda, strewn around the fires, washed his hands, and spread out a layer of *ulapa* grass, he arranges the vessels according to their purpose.
He does not lead those who are already led. || 16 ||
At the time of the offering, having offered a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara, he offers seven cakes on seven potsherds each to the Maruts. || 17 ||
When treated with silence, the Maruts become submissive. || 18 ||
He mixes [the grains] with those purified by the Yajus formulas. Having poured out the water for sprinkling after it has been scented, he proceeds with the formal summons. || 19 ||
He gives the command regarding whatever else there is besides the sacrificial fuel and the sacrificial grass, and the binding of the wife.
Having performed that which was previously done before the taking of the clarified butter, he takes it in the *dhruvā* ladle itself.

Having consecrated the sprinkling waters (prokṣaṇī), having addressed the Brahman priest, having sprinkled the altar, and having poured out the remainder of the sprinkling waters, he places the two strainers back [into the vessel] and sets down the Dhruvā ladle and the Sruva spoon. || 22 ||
He concludes the mantra with "eṣā'sadaditi. || 23 ||
He consecrates the clarified butter with the mantra: "Thou art Viṣṇu's; thou art the abode of Viṣṇu; thou art Prajāpati's.
(Section 12) Having placed the Vaiśvānara oblation, he places the Māruta oblations.
He causes the announcement for Vaiśvānara to be made loudly. || 26 ||
He offers the entire oblation without turning away. || 27 ||
Sitting down, he offers the Māruta oblations with his hand, whispering "such-like" and "other-like," as a group, while making them all-encompassing offerings.
Having recited each preceding group, he offers with each succeeding one.
Having recited the final group of names—*svatavān*, *praghāsī*, *sāṃtapana*, *gṛhamedhī*, *krīḍī*, *sākī*, and *ūrjiṣī*—he offers with the first [verse]. || 12.5.30 ||
Having offered the oblation with the verse, "The divine hosts, the Maruts, follow Indra," he worships [the fire]. || 31 ||

If he desires, "May I destroy the ruling power with the common people," he recites three or four words of the verse to be recited in the village (*grāmya-anuvākya*), and offers the oblation with the remainder of the verse to be recited in the forest (*āraṇya-anuvākya*).
Thus, with three [verses] from the beginning as recited in sequence for the *anuvākyā* in the village [ritual], so too with the three subsequent groups, just as before. ||33||

If he should desire, "May I destroy the common people with the power of the ruling class," he should place six groups [of syllables] within the six word-intervals of the *anuvākya* verse recited in the forest; then, having muttered the *vākya* among the villages, he offers the remainder of the *vākya* with the forest-verse.

Thus, with the first three [verses] as they were recited at the beginning in the village [ritual], by means of the invitatory verse (anuvākyā), and just as with the preceding ones, so it is with the three subsequent groups.
He does not give the command; he does not wipe [the spoon]; he does not offer the after-offerings (anūyāja). || 36 ||

If one should desire, "May this Kṣatriya fall from his own station," he should cause a part of the chariot-stand or the chariot itself belonging to that group of *anuvākyās* recited in the forest to be broken; this is a ritual procedure not connected with a sacrifice. (Section 13) ||37||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the twelfth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Now begins the sixth chapter in the twelfth book.

He offers the Vasordhārā oblation with clarified butter using a ladle made of Udumbara wood, reciting "O Agni and Viṣṇu, being in harmony... and following it with "Vāja and my impulse and my... continuously until the completion of the mantra. ||1||

If one should desire, "May I cut off his vital breaths and his food," he should offer for him with interruptions. If one should desire, "May I continue his vital breaths and his food," he should offer for him continuously. ||2||
Whatever clarified butter may remain, having cooked the Brahma-rice in it, he should feed four Adhvaryus and give them four milch-cows as sacrificial fees.
Having cooked four śarāvas of rice, he feeds him that with its condiments. || 4 ||

He offers the Vājaprasavīya oblations. There are seven cultivated plants and seven wild plants. Having liquefied the various foods separately, he offers each kind of food with one verse at a time using a ladle made of Udumbara wood, reciting fourteen Ṛg-verses beginning with "This impulsion of strength (vāja) flows well. || 5 ||

Now I shall praise the drinker, the one of great ordinances, the mighty power, by whose force Trita shattered Vṛtra limb from limb. O sweet Soma, O honeyed Soma, we have chosen thee; be our protector. Come to us, O Soma, as a gracious friend with thy gracious aids—bringing delight, not to be hated, a most kind friend, free from duplicity. These juices of thine, O Soma, are spread throughout the realms, resting in heaven like the winds.

These [gifts] of yours, O *pitu* (Soma), you bestow; these most delicious things of yours, O *pitu*, flow forth. The swift ones, like horses with powerful necks, hasten toward the chariots. In you, O *pitu*, the mind of the great gods is fixed. By your beautiful banner, he struck the serpent with his power. When you have gone there, O *pitu*, into the expanse of the mountains, even then, O sweet *pitu*, come sufficiently for our enjoyment. Whatever essence of the waters and plants we may consume, O *vātāpi*, become fatness for us.

"O Soma, that portion of yours which consists of milk, of curd, and of barley—O Vātāpi, become fat! O porridge, O herb, become fat; O kidney, O healer, become fat! O Vātāpi, become fat indeed! We have prepared you, O Pita, with our words, as cows prepare their offerings. For the gods you are a feast-companion; for us you are a feast-companion. Having thus offered it repeatedly, he should pour the remnants into the vessel. (Section 14) 6.
Or alternatively, he should make a fuel-stick from that very food at the beginning of which he offers the oblation.
While the sacrificer is seated on the Audumbarī post at his station, he sprinkles him, who is touching the fire, with the remnants of the oblations while he is upon the black antelope skin.
On the right wing of this black antelope skin, he should seat a Brāhmaṇa; on a tiger skin, a Rājanya; and on a goat skin, a Vaiśya who desires cattle. || 9 ||
Some recite [the text] as if it were eternal. 12.6.10.
"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I consecrate you with the sovereignty of Bṛhaspati"—thus for a Brāhmaṇa. || 11 ||
"I consecrate Indra with sovereign power," [he says] for a Kṣatriya; "I consecrate Agni with sovereign power," for a Vaiśya. ||12||
Standing in front facing west, he pours water over the head of the one seated behind him facing east, letting it flow down as far as the mouth.
Having filled a ladle made of Udumbara wood with milk or curds from a black cow that has a white calf, he offers an oblation with the verse, "Night and Dawn. ||14||
With the six sections beginning with "ṛtāṣāḍ ṛtadhāmā," he offers twelve *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations using clarified butter taken ten times.
Having recited the formula in its proper sequence, he offers the first oblation with the words, "Svāhā to him! (paryāyamanudrutya tasmai svāheti). ||16||

"To them, Svāhā!"—with this he offers the northern oblation. "O Lord of the World," with this he offers five oblations at the front of the chariot. Or, in ten rounds, he offers into the Āhavanīya fire over the head of the chariot while it is being held there. According to some, he offers using the head of the chariot itself. (Section 15, Sūtra 17)
They carry the collected chariot to the Adhvaryu’s dwelling; they lead after it three horses, or four, according to some authorities.
He gives them, together with their chariots, to the Adhvaryu. || 19 ||
"Thou art the ocean, thou art possessed of wind"—with these words, he offers three oblations of the names of the winds with his joined palms.
Or with a pouch made of a black antelope skin. || 21 ||

With the five sections beginning with *agna udadhe yāta iṣuryuvā nāma*, he offers five oblations of clarified butter, moving clockwise around the fire while facing each of the directions; with the final section, he faces the east in the center. With the six sections beginning with *samīcī nāmāsi prācī dik*, he offers six great oblations of curds mixed with honey. He offers the "serpent-oblations" as prescribed, and he offers the three "luster-oblations" (*ruca*) with the verses beginning *yāste agne sūrye rucaḥ*. || 22 ||
Having offered five oblations of ghee with the mantra "suvarṇaṃ gharmo 'svāhā," he should offer the Arka oblations. || 23 ||
He undertakes the ritual acts beginning with the spreading of the sacrificial altar. || 24 ||

With this Anuvāka beginning with "mamāgne," he piles the Dhiṣṇiya hearths with bricks, one by one according to each mantra. He completes each Dhiṣṇiya with a single mantra. He lays down eight bricks on the Āgnīdhrīya hearth; according to some, there is a stone as the ninth.

Twelve or twenty-four [verses] in the Hotṛ’s seat; eleven or twenty-one in the Praśāstṛ’s seat; six in the Mārjālīya; eight in the others. (Section 16) “For thy glory the mountain opened apart; thou didst release the herd of cows, O Aṅgiras. With Indra as thy ally, O Bṛhaspati, thou didst unbind the ocean that was encompassed by darkness. O Bṛhaspati, whatever the enemy deserves to surpass—[with these words] he releases the victim. With these three verses addressed to Brahman, he recites in the Brahman’s seat. “Yama has supported the earth; Yama has supported this entire world.”

Whatever is in the presence of Yama, whatever breath is preserved by Vāyu—just as there are five, six, or fifteen seers (ṛṣis)—he who knows Yama should speak thus, as does the one seer who truly understands: "By the three *trikadruka* libations he falls; the six wide ones, this one great [hymn], the *gāyatrī*, the *triṣṭubh*, and all the meters—all these are placed in Yama. With these three verses addressed to Yama at the *mārjālīya* altar, [one recites]: "We, performing the sacrifice, invoke for protection the fierce Rudra, the fulfiller of the rite, the wise one."

Far from us be his divine wrath; we choose instead his benevolence. May we attain your favor through sacrifice to the gods, O bounteous Rudra, lord of heroes who rule over men. Being gracious, come toward our people; let our heroes be unharmed. We offer this oblation to you.

With the three verses addressed to Rudra, "Be gracious to us, O Rudra, and grant us happiness," he gratifies the *havya* at the *cātvāla*. With the eight [verses], "Gratify the *havya*, mix the *havya*, cook the *havya*, boil the *havya*; you are the *havya*; for the *havya* you, for the *havyas* you, sit in the *havya*," [he offers] at the *śāmitra*. With the three verses addressed to Varuṇa, "May your wrath depart from us, [O Varuṇa], let the highest [bond] go away; I implore you with prayer, adoring you," he performs the *avabhṛtha* (final purificatory bath). They proceed with these [verses]. He throws the *khaṇḍā*, the black [spots], and the *lakṣmaṇā* marks onto the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), as well as the remaining [parts].
Having performed that which precedes the erecting of the sacrificial post, he erects either a single post or eleven posts.
On the previous day, he erects among them the one standing nearest the fire.

Or at this very point; or on the following day. Having offered the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, he subsequently offers the oblations of the Devasū, beginning with "To Agni Gṛhapati," according to the traditional recitation. For the animal-cake and the oblations of the Devasū, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* portions are common. (Section 17) || 29 || 12.6.30 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the twelfth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Now begins the seventh chapter of the twelfth book.
At the time for the animal sacrifice, he dedicates eleven animals to a single sacrificial post, or to eleven posts.
At the morning pressing, he touches the fire with three verses beginning, "I yoke Agni with power and ghee."

At the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), having looked at a golden vessel filled with honey weighing a hundred mānas, which has been prepared, with the verse "The bright [face] of the gods," and having caused the horse to smell it at midday, he gives it to the Brahman priest.
One should give auspicious sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Adhvaryu priest.
If he were to pile other [bricks] for him, he would not satisfy [the sacrificer] with sacrificial gifts; he would deprive him of his fire. || 5 ||

When the animal dedicated to Agni has been brought forward for sacrifice, while the *stotra* is being performed—either when the *prastāva* has been chanted or when one verse has been sung—he touches the fire with two verses beginning, "In the ocean is your heart."
He offers a single oblation for the release of the fire with the verse, "This breast, full of vigor, which has been drawn by the Hāriyojana, do thou suck," or with the verse, "I unloose thee. (7)
He offers eleven *samiṣṭayajus* oblations. ||8||

Having offered the nine oblations pertaining to the sacrifice, he offers the tenth and eleventh with the mantra: "May Agni, who has been worshipped, into whom offerings have been poured, and for whom the *svāhā* has been uttered, carry us across; may this oblation be well-offered, *svāhā*, this is homage. (9)
When the omentum of the Anūbandhyā cow has been offered, he offers the Ākūtis with the formulas of this Anuvāka, verse by verse, starting from "Whatever intention [I have] has flowed forth. (12.7.10)
"O Agni, I have obtained you with my mind"—with these words, as he is about to depart, he worships Agni with the Āpti formulas.
With the mantra "The fires that belong to the soil," he worships whichever of his own fires he beholds. || 12 ||
Having seen the fires of others, [he performs the rite] with the three verses beginning "upa tvā'gne dive dive" for those others. ||13||
Having piled the fire-altar, he should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī and with the curdled milk (āmikṣā) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.
Having piled the fire-altar, for one year he should not descend toward anyone, nor should he eat birds. || 15 ||
It rains for as long as he lives. He must not run; he must not approach a woman; and having piled a second fire-altar, he must not approach the wife of another. || 16 ||
Having piled the third [fire-altar], he should not approach any woman, nor should he approach his wife.
If, after piling the fire-altar, one does not shine within that year, he, when undertaking a sacrificial session (*kratu*), should pile the fire-altar consisting of a single layer (*ekacitīka*).
"Salilāya tvā," "Sarṇīkāya tvā"—these are eight distinct mantras. || 19 ||
The *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks are laid according to their actual form; then the loose soil (*purīṣa*). 12.7.20.

If one who has piled the fire-altar does not find a firm foundation within this year, he should, when commencing a sacrificial session (*kratu*), pile the fire-altar in a single layer (*ekacitīka*) with the five separate mantras beginning with "Saṃyac ca pracetāś ca. The *lokapṛṇā* bricks are placed according to their respective positions. Then follows the loose soil (*purīṣa*).

Furthermore, we shall explain *citi*. It is heard in three senses: either in the sense of hearing (*śravaṇa*), or in the sense of prosperity (*samṛddhi*), or in the sense of continuity (*saṃtāna*). ||22||
We shall explain for the purpose of the outflow [of the sacrificial water]: "If one should sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, or with an animal sacrifice, or with Soma. (23)
Having moved to another spot immediately adjacent to where his previous fire-altar was piled, he should sacrifice.
Alternatively, there are eight separate mantras beginning with "yenarṣayaḥ" and eight *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; then the loose soil (*purīṣa*).

On the following day, there are eight bricks with various mantras and eleven *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; then the loose soil (*purīṣa*). On the following day, these [same] bricks with various mantras and twelve *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; then the loose soil. Now we shall explain those for the sake of prosperity: he who, having piled the fire-altar, does not prosper within that year, should, when undertaking a sacrificial session (*kratu*), pile a fire-altar consisting of three layers. With the verses "For the flood (*salila*) thee, for the surging (*sarṇīka*) thee," there are eight bricks with various mantras and eleven *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; then the loose soil.

On the following day, these various mantras and twelve *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; then the *purīṣa* (filling soil). On the following day, these various mantras and thirteen *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; then the *purīṣa*. But for one piling the third fire-altar for the sake of continuity, on the third layer there are eight various mantras beginning with "yenarṣayaḥ" and an unlimited number of *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; then the *purīṣa*. (Section 19) 26.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the twelfth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Now begins the eighth chapter in the twelfth book.
We shall explain the optional fires; their modifications of form have been explained in the Brāhmaṇa.

There is a connection with the purpose and there is no fixed rule regarding its application; "one desiring cattle should pile the fire-altar with *chandāṃsi*. One should pile the fire-altar with those *chandāṃsi* which are [prescribed] in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Eight *gāyatrī* verses containing the word "head" (*mūrdhanvatī*) he places in the east. || 2 ||
"One desiring heaven should pile the Śyenacit. It takes the form of a hawk with curved wings and a spread-out tail. ||3||
One who desires, "May I be possessed of a head in yonder world," should pile the Kaṅkacit. Having the form of a heron with an outstretched neck, he becomes possessed of a head.
"One desiring stability should pile the altar in the shape of a tortoise with four furrows," so he plows four furrows joined together in each direction.
"One who has rivals should pile the *prauga-cit*," it is said; it takes the form of a cart.
One who desires, "May I drive away my born enemies and those yet to be born," should pile the *ubhayataḥprauga* altar; it has the shape of a cart on both sides, like a cart with its face turned away.
"One who has rivals should pile it in the form of a chariot wheel"; thus it is circular. || 8 ||
"One desiring food should pile the Drona-cit. Now, there are indeed two kinds of Dronas: square and circular; in this matter, one may act according to one's preference.
Afterwards, it becomes a *svaru* because of its conformity [to the sacrificial post]. || 12.8.10 ||

"One desiring cattle should pile the *samūhya*"; thus he lays down the bricks while piling them together. (11) According to some, having dug in the four directions from the *catvāla*, he throws the earth from those places onto [the altar]. (12)
"One desiring a village should pile the Paricāyya altar"; thus he encircles the central naturally perforated brick (svayamātṛṇṇā) clockwise with clusters of bricks.
"One desiring a village should pile the *paricāyya* and the *upacāyya*"; thus it is stated by means of the *paricāyya*.

One who desires, "May I prosper in the world of the ancestors," should pile the funeral mound in the shape of a cemetery. It may be square or circular; according to some, it should be like the great altar for the ancestors (mahāpaitṛkī vedi); according to others, it should be triangular. (Section 20) 15.
We shall now explain the Tāpascita [Agnicayana]. || 16 ||
He remains consecrated for one year. || 17 ||
When the year has returned, he purchases the King. || 18 ||

Before the Upasads, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, one on eleven potsherds to Indra, one on twelve potsherds to the Viśvedevas, a pap to Bṛhaspati, and a cake on three potsherds to Viṣṇu; having performed the Upasads continuously for a year, he piles the fire-altar.
Two months for each funeral pile, with four at the last; there are vows lasting three months, consisting of four teats, and likewise those of three teats, two teats, and one teat. 12.8.20.

One should pile the fire-altar for a year using that *sūkta* of the Ṛṣis which is dedicated to Agni. With each individual *sūkta* among those dedicated to Agni that appear in the *Daśatayīs*, one places a single brick.
The various mantras are measured by the *sūktas*; the *lokaṃpṛṇās* are according to their purpose. ||23||

When the Upasads have been performed, in the third year he should sacrifice with either the Abhijit or the Viśvajit. We shall explain the [sacrifices] characterized by a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*sahasradakṣiṇā*) and the giving away of all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*). [This applies] for each successive period of fasting (*parivāsa*). (Section 21) 24.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the twelfth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Thus ends the twelfth book in the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.

76: *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—In the afternoon, when there is danger, the two [rites] belonging to the afternoon are performed. Having performed the supplementary rite (*pravopasaṅkhyā*) with those two, and having circumambulated a white horse from left to right, one begins [the work] starting either to the east or to the north of the altar (*citi*), proceeding clockwise; they dwell there and cease from their ritual duties. However, the Commentator explains that once the offering of the vow (*vratapradāna*) has been made at midnight, they dwell there after completing everything up to the leading around of the horse (*aśvapariṇayana*). Some, however, say that the leading around of the horse is an integral part of the "dwelling" (*vasati*). Therefore, there is no leading around of the horse on the fifth layer (*citau*).

But that marriage ceremony is a constituent part of the Truth (Satya); because it belongs to that context, it is therefore performed on the fifth [lunar day]. The repetition is for the purpose of concluding the inquiry. || 27 || Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Eleventh Book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. Thus ends the Eleventh Book in the commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*. || 11 ||
12.1 Now begins the first section of the twelfth book.

Regarding all the layers (*citi*), the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites are explained as follows: the two morning rites are performed at the beginning, and the two afternoon rites, along with the *pravargya*, *upasad*, layer-offering (*citihoma*), and the leading around of the horse (*aśvapariṇayana*), are performed at the end. On the following day, he piles the second layer.

On the following day, at dawn, having performed the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites of the forenoon (*paurvāhnikībhyām pravargyopasadbhyām pracarya*), and having performed those two—the *pravargya* and the *upasad*—at the conclusion of the *subrahmaṇyā*, he piles the second layer (*dvitīyāṃ citiṃ cinoti*). If he collects the bricks of the first layer, then that is done; thus, there is a carrying forward of the fire (*praṇayana*) for each layer. However, the touching of the *uttaravedi* altar is performed only once.

Because it is an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the *citi*, the taking of the fire (*agnigrahaṇa*), the self-piling (*svayaṃcityā*), the touching (*abhimarśana*), and the offering at the *Śālāmukhīya* fire are performed only once, as they are for the sake of the *araṇi*. Regarding the rule, "When about to pile the bricks, one should touch a white horse; when about to pile the loose earth (*purīṣa*), a black one"—since the touching of the horse is an auxiliary to the *citi*, and because of the statement, "He recites [the formula] while ascending her at every *citi*," this [touching] also occurs at each individual *citi*.

[In the alternative case: When, however, the position is taken that there are three *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks and three *viśvajyotis* bricks, then there is no further leading forward (*praṇayana*). Two horses are stationed on either side: a black one to the north and a white one to the south; then, having sacrificed the white one— || 1 ||
With the verses "dhruvakṣitir dhruvayoniḥ," he lays down five Aśvinī bricks: four in each direction and one in the middle.

The bricks to be laid down with mantras associated with the Aśvins are the *āśvinī* bricks. According to the injunction, "He lays down the *āśvinī* bricks" (*TaiSaṃ* 5.3.1), one should lay down the *āśvinī* bricks. He prescribes their number: "He lays down five," and so forth (*TaiSaṃ* 5.3.1). Five are placed in the eastern half of the fire-altar.

With the formula *sajūrṛtubhiḥ*, he lays down five seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*) belonging to the Aśvins. [This concludes] Paṭala 1 of the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. Behind the Aśvinī bricks, he lays down the five seasonal bricks with the formula *sa-ṛtubhiḥ*. Among these seasonal bricks, there is no omission (*apakāma*). He lays them down in pairs; four are placed in the middle for the sake of stability (*dhṛti*), according to the governing rule: "He places the Avakā plants upon them."

Alternatively, he prescribes the laying down (*upadhāna*) to be accomplished with these mantras: "He lays down the seasonal bricks" (*ṛtavyā upadadhāti*, Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.3.1), and so forth. This laying down is for the sake of providing the seasonal periods, beginning with spring, with the capacity for their respective functions. He prescribes the number of bricks: "He lays down five" (*pañcopadadhāti*, Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.3.1), and so forth; this is because the winter and the cool season are combined, resulting in five seasons. ||3||

He places [the bricks] around without leaving a gap, saying, "Protect my out-breath; protect my in-breath. He lays down five *ṛtavyā* bricks dedicated to Vāyu with the formulas, "Thou art the path of Vāyu," and "Thou art the path of the gods, O Vāyu. Two *saṃyānya* bricks are laid down with the formulas, "Śukra and Śuci," and two *ṛtavyā* bricks. These have the same deities. 4.

"Protect my breath," [he says]; behind [the first set], there are five breath-supporters (*prāṇabhṛt*). "Spread out the waters," [he says] for the water-bricks (*apasyā*); thus says Āpastamba. Having circumambulated the fire, he places them one by one in each direction, according to the Śruti. However, as for the statement of Bharadvāja, "If he should place them all in one place," the meaning of that Śruti is an alternative (*vikalpa*) provided by him. And there are two *saṃyānī* bricks with the formula, "Thou art the path of Vāyu. And there are two seasonal (*ṛtavyā*) bricks, namely "Śukra" and "Śuci"; their placement on the ground is as before. || 4 ||

He places five *apasyā* bricks, dedicated to Vāyu, along the [eastern] edge; he sets them down while moving around [the altar]. He places four bricks with the formula "Support, vigor," and one with the word "head" at the front.

The five *apas* bricks are laid down with the formulas beginning "Apasinvā" (*apasinvā*); this is the laying of the eastern quarter. There are four *vayas* bricks with the formulas beginning "Viṣṭambho vayaḥ" (*viṣṭambho vayaḥ*); according to the Commentator (*bhāṣyakṛt*), these are placed starting from the east and ending toward the west. The bricks to be laid with mantras containing the word "mūrdhan" (head) are called *mūrdhanvatī*. Because those to be laid in the eastern direction are accomplished by mantras containing the word "mūrdhan," it follows that for the fire being built in the shape of a bird, its head also comes to be in the eastern direction; such is the detailed explanation in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*). || 5 ||

"Tryavi vayaḥ"—five [bricks] with these verses, containing the word *vayas*, he places on the south; "paṣṭhavād vayaḥ"—five on the west; "vasto vayaḥ"—five containing the word *vayas*, he places on the north, [these being] the *siṃhavatī* bricks. Or rather, he places [the brick] on the southern shoulder with "vasto vayaḥ," and on the northern with "vṛṣṇir vayaḥ. He places [the brick] on the southern wing with "vyāghro vayaḥ," and on the northern with "siṃho vayaḥ. [The brick] with "puruṣo vayaḥ" he places in the middle. 6.

"O you who possess the vigor of a ram," [he places] on the southern hip of the five-layered fire-altar; "of a bull"—these are the five [on the northern hip]. "Of a goat"—one on the southern shoulder; "of a ram"—on the northern shoulder. "Of a ewe"—one on the southern wing; "of a he-goat"—on the northern [wing]; "of a man"—in the middle. 6... 78. The section beginning with the bull and ending with the layering has been explained. 7. *Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa* (or *Śrautasūtra*) composed by Satyāṣāḍha. 12.
The section beginning with the bull and ending with the layering has been explained. 7.

In the Vāmana [rite], the procedure beginning with the bull and ending with the *nitya* sacrifice is the same; however, the specific difference is that the second [offering] is performed with a *triṣṭubh* verse. Having performed the afternoon *pravargya* and *upasads*, the leading forth of the horse (*aśvapariṇayana*) is carried out, ending thus with the conclusion of the *citya*.
On the following day, he piles the third layer. (Section 1) 8.

On the following morning, having performed the forenoon rites up to the Subrahmaṇyā formula and having touched the white horse for the third layer while reciting "May speech be in my mouth," [he proceeds]. || 8 ||

Having touched the *svayamātṛṇṇā* with the mantra, "O Indra and Agni, you who are unshakable," and having caused a horse to sniff it, he places it in the middle of the fire-altar together with an ignorant Brāhmaṇa, using the mantra, "May Viśvakarman seat thee, the expansive one, upon the back of the intermediate space," and with this *vyāhṛti*, "Bhuvaḥ."

Having touched the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick that has been brought forward with the mantra, "O Indra and Agni, [lead] those who are wavering," he proceeds otherwise with the bringing forward of the bricks starting from the third layer. Having caused the horse to step upon those *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks while standing on the altar-site itself, he places them down with the mantra beginning, "May Viśvakarman settle thee," and ending, "By thy own deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm; become. || 9 ||
Having offered into the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone with the words, "I offer consciousness," the learned Brāhmaṇa, while reciting the subsequent verses, bestows a boon.

Having offered with the ladle, saying "I offer with consciousness," both into the naturally perforated stone and elsewhere, he remains there without breathing out while another recites the *anuvyākhyāna*. The instruction is: "Sing the Sāman; grant a boon. And with his knee raised, he lays down [the bricks]. 10.

With the formula, "Thou art light; give me light; thou art the intermediate space; protect me from the intermediate space," he places the gold brick (*hiraṇyeṣṭakā*). With the formula, "The sky has entered the intermediate space through the holy power (*brahman*); the Maruts are thy guardians," he places the circle brick (*maṇḍaleṣṭakā*). He places the two *anuretas-sic* bricks with the formula, "Thou art the two wide-extending ones. With the formula, "May Viśvakarman settle thee, the luminous one, on the back of the intermediate space," he places the *viśvajyotis* brick.
