With the formulas, "Thou art the path of the intermediate space" and "Thou art the path of the gods in the intermediate space," he places the two *saṃyāni* bricks. (1.1)

With the formula "Light art thou," he lays down a golden brick; with "Upon the sky," the circle-bricks; all of these are "seed-shedders" in the middle layer. With "May Viśvakarman settle thee," one of the *praṇītā* bricks is the "all-light" (*viśvajyotis*). With "Thou art the support of the atmosphere," two *saṃyānī* bricks [are laid]. 11.

*Nabhaḥ* and *Nabhasya*, *Iṣaḥ* and *Urjaḥ*—these four seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*) consist of two pairs of identical deities. [End of] Paṭala 1. This is accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śākhin. Regarding the four seasonal bricks, *nabhaḥ* and *nabhasya*, etc., there are two pairs with identical deities. There is also the laying down in a hollow; he lays them down two by two. However, some perform the laying down of the four [bricks] together. || 12 ||
"You are the queen of the eastern quarter"—thus [he addresses] five [bricks] pertaining to the quarters: four in each direction and one in the middle.

The bricks to be laid with mantras containing directional words are the *diśyā* bricks. One is placed in each direction, starting from the east in the middle; for the Śruti states: "Thou art the heap, the eastern direction," and so on, as he lays down five *diśyā* bricks (ŚB 5.3.2). || 13 ||
Having first laid down ten Vairāja bricks with the formula, "Protect my life," [he proceeds].

To the east of the fire. These [bricks] are to be understood from the Brāhmaṇa and other Sūtras, beginning with: "He places ten *prāṇabhṛt* bricks in front. They are called *prāṇabhṛt* because one recites mantras containing the word *prāṇa* at the time of their placement. In this very context, he praises the word *jyotis* in the final mantra: "He places the last one as possessing light" (*TaiSaṃ* 5.3.2). A brick to be placed with a mantra joined by the word *jyotis* is *jyotiṣmatī*. According to the statement of the Commentator, that which is final is indeed the "last" (*uttama*). || 14 ||
He lays down thirty-six *bṛhatī* bricks: twelve to the south with the formula "The *mā* metre," twelve to the west with "The earth metre," and twelve to the north with "Agni the deity. (15)

Just as the *bṛhatī* is praised among the meters, so too are the bricks called *bṛhatī* praised; thus says the author of the Bhāṣya. One lays down three hundred and sixty *bṛhatī* bricks, beginning from the south of the fire, then from the west, and then from the north.

He prescribes these very bricks for specific directions: "With 'The Mā [meter],' he places one on the south; therefore we move toward the right. With 'The Earth [is] the meter,' he places one on the west, for the sake of stability. With 'Agni is the deity,' he places one on the north; the *ajira* is indeed vigor (*ojas*), so he bestows vigor on the north. Therefore, one who attacks from the north conquers" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.2). He prescribes the number of bricks obtained through the recitation of the mantras: "They amount to thirty-six," and so forth (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.3.2). || 15 ||

With the formula, "Thou art the head, the sovereign," he places seven Vālakhilya bricks in front, facing westward; with the formula, "The controller, the sovereign," he places seven behind, facing eastward.

Seven *vālakhilya* bricks are placed starting from the east and ending toward the west; seven are placed starting from the west and ending toward the east. Alternatively, because they were first perceived by the sages named *vālakhilyas*, the bricks themselves are called *vālakhilyas*. Through the number seven inherent in these bricks, there is a correspondence with the seven apertures of the head; furthermore, by having one set of seven in the east and another set of seven in the west, there is a correspondence with the two apertures situated below due to the similarity of the two groups of seven.

He prescribes the division of the mantras for the two sets of seven: "Thou art the head, the sovereign" he places in the east; "The controller, the sovereign" in the west (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.3.2). || 16 ||
With the formula "Svāhā to the Earth," he lays twelve elemental bricks (bhūteṣṭakā).
There are twelve *bhūteṣṭakā* bricks, as recited in another *śākhā*. (17) In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [Chapter 12]:

"With the formula, 'I settle thee with the eastern quarter,' he places five *ātmeṣṭakā* bricks: four in the cardinal directions and one in the middle. (18) This has already been explained. With this *anuvāka*, "Indra [armed] with the bones of Dadhyañc," he lays down the ten *atharvaśiras* bricks. (19)
He places ten bricks, each exceeding [the others] by one, upon the head. || 19 ||
The lineage beginning with Ṛṣabha, ending with Citya, has been explained. 12.1.20.

From the *ṛṣabha* chant up to the marriage of the horse, and ending with the *citya* altar, it is as before; however, the specific difference is the touching of the third layer (*adhiti*) with the *jagatī* metre.
On the following day, he piles the fourth layer.

On the following day, having performed the morning Pravargya and Upasad rites ending with the Subrahmaṇyā invocation, he piles the fourth layer. Having performed the Aśvālambha rite, he mutters the formula: "May speech be in my mouth. Otherwise, however, there is for that layer the bringing forward of the bricks and so forth.
He lays them down according to the Brāhmaṇa with these two sections beginning with "The swift one, the threefold, is the portion of Agni. (22)

As stated for the Brāhmaṇa, so too for the *upadhāna* (the laying down of bricks) in the east, south, west, and north. In the first section (*anuvāka*), there are four cycles (*paryāya*); in the second section, there are three. [The formulas are: "The swift one, the supporter, the shining, the rushing, the overcoming, the splendor, the heat, the womb, my vigor, the gatherer, the foundation of the season-killer, the vault; of Agni, of those who look upon men, of Mitra, of Indra, of the Vasus, of the Ādityas, of Aditi, of the god Dhātar, of the Yavas, of the Ṛbhus—the turning."

Regarding this, the author of the Viniyogasaṃgraha states as follows: "One should place eighteen [bricks] diagonally, joined with the *stoma*s; one should place the remaining ten bricks of Agni diagonally, designated by the *stoma*s. (22)
"Antarikṣa! For Antarikṣa, thee!"—with these two [verses], there are two *saṃyājyā* offerings.
"That they lay down the *saṃyānī* bricks, the *saṃyanīs*—so says the Brāhmaṇa. || 23 ||
Saha and Sahasya are the two seasonal [deities]; they share the same deity with her. || 24 ||
The meaning is clear. || 24 ||
With the verse "ekayā'stuvata," seventeen creations [are described]. || 25 ||

The bricks to be laid down are those associated with mantras containing the verbal root *sṛj* (to create); the meaning is that one lays down the "creations" (*sṛṣṭi*). Now, regarding the doubt as to whether the word *sṛṣṭi* in the rule "He lays down the creations" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.17) is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) or an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), [the answer follows]. [End of] Chapter 6. [This work is] accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 41.

In this case, because of the connection with a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the absence of being part of a single syntactical unit with another injunction (*vidhyantaraikavākyatvābhāva*), and its own meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), it is an injunction (*vidhi*). The mantras containing the indicative mark *sṛṣṭi* are enjoined for the purpose of placing the bricks (*upadhāna*). Not so. Since they are already established by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*) alone, an injunction of these mantras is not possible. If that were the case, it would result in a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*). In that situation, since many mantras are already applicable through the context, by enjoining the *sṛṣṭi*-mantras, the others would be excluded.

Furthermore, that [view] would entail three defects, and there would be the consequence of the other enumerated mantras becoming purposeless. Therefore, it is the act of placing (*upadhāna*) itself that is to be enjoined here. The phrase "the creations" (*sṛṣṭīḥ*), however, is merely a restatement of the mantras obtained through their indicative power (*liṅga*), for the sake of making the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—"one wins exactly what has been created" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.3.4)—coherent; such is the intention of the Bhāṣya. Some, however, support the injunction of the mantras themselves.

For there is no exclusive indicative mark (*liṅga*) in such passages as "They praised with one [verse]" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 4.3.10) that would establish their application to the piling up (*upadhāna*). Because the indicative marks are common [to other contexts], the bricks would also apply to the seizing (*grahaṇa*), placing (*āsādana*), and so forth; therefore, there is scope for an injunction [specifically regarding the piling]. Even if the piling were already established by implication, the direct injunction will be purposeful in order to connect them specifically with the middle layer (*madhyamaciti*). For the author will state later: "But in the middle [layer], because of the scriptural statement, they possess the *Brāhmaṇa*."

Furthermore, the injunction regarding the *sṛṣṭi* [hymns] in this Sūtra need not necessarily be accepted as mandatory, because the purpose is merely to state the grounds for applying the term figuratively (*guṇavṛtti*). What, then, is the quality (*guṇa*) here? It is abundance (*bhūmā*). For abundance exists in the collection of *sṛṣṭi* hymns, and it also exists in the collection of both *sṛṣṭi* and *asṛṣṭi* hymns. Since there is an abundance of *sṛṣṭi* hymns in the section beginning with "They praised with one" (*ekayā'stuvata*, Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.3.10), the word *sṛṣṭi* is applied by virtue of that similarity. || 21 ||
"This is indeed she who first shone forth"—thus [ends] the fifteen *vyuṣṭi* verses. || 26 ||

The word *vyuṣṭi* means that which especially shines forth and destroys darkness; it refers to the time of dawn (*uṣaḥkāla*). The bricks to be placed with mantras containing words expressive of that [time] are the *vyuṣṭi*-bricks. The meaning is that one should place those [bricks]. || 26 ||

"O Agni, drive away our born enemies"—with these words he places [the brick] in the east; "those born by force"—in the west; "the forty-fourfold hymn-form"—in the south; "the sixteenfold hymn-form"—in the north. || 27 ||

The phrase "he places afterwards" (paścādupadadhāti) carries over [from the previous rule]. He prescribes this placement to be accomplished with these mantras: "O Agni, destroy our born enemies" (agne jātān praṇudā naḥ sapatnān)—with this he places one in the east; "those born with force" (sahasā jātān)—with this he places one in the west; "the forty-fourfold hymn-form" (catuścatvāriṃśaḥ stomaḥ)—with this he places one in the south; "the sixteenfold hymn-form" (ṣoḍaśaḥ stomaḥ)—with this he places one in the north. (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.3.5), and so forth. || 27 ||
Having spread loose soil over the brick, he places the Purīṣavatī brick in the middle of the fire-altar with the formula: "Thou art the loose soil of the earth; thy name is Ap. || 28 ||

The text prescribes this placement as something to be accomplished with a mantra: "He places the *purīṣavatī* bricks in the middle; the middle indeed belongs to the self (*ātman*); thus he piles the fire-altar together with its self" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.3.5). Having spread the *purīṣa* (filling soil), these are placed upon it; therefore they are called *purīṣavatī*. Or rather, they are so called because the *purīṣa* exists in the middle of the self—that is, within the belly of the body consisting of cows and other such forms. Thus, by virtue of being *purīṣavatī*, he piles the fire-altar as one that is "with-self," meaning accompanied by a body. || 28 ||
The [funeral rites] ending with the piling of the altar (cityanta) have been explained starting from the case of Ṛṣabha. || 29 ||

The rites beginning with the *ṛṣabha* and ending with the *citi* are performed; those ending with the leading around of the horse are as before. Having touched the fourth layer with an *anuṣṭubh* verse, on the following day, after performing the morning rites, he piles the fifth layer. 12.1.30.

On the following day, at dawn, having performed the rites of the forenoon and [reached] the end of the *subrahmaṇyā* litany, there is the fifth layer (*citi*). Having touched a white horse and muttered the formula, "Speech is in my mouth," [the procedure] otherwise for the fifth layer, beginning with the bringing forward of the bricks, is the same. With the formulas, "The *chandas* is light, the *chandas* is space," he lays forty *virāj* bricks, ten in each direction, diagonally.

The remainder [of the sentence] is that one should place the bricks called *virāj* on the fifth and highest layer (*city*). This is to be seen in the Brāhmaṇa: "He places the *virāj*s on the highest layer; indeed, he makes the *virāj* the highest" (TS 5.3.5). He prescribes the number of bricks for each direction: "He places ten in each [direction]" (TS 5.3.5). To prevent them from forming a straight row, he prescribes their curvature: "He places them crosswise" (TS 5.3.5). || 31 ||
"Thou art a ray; for dwelling thee, quicken the dwelling"—thus [he lays down] thirty-one Stomabhāga bricks, seven in each direction and three in the middle. || 32 ||

The *raśmi* and others are the *stomabhāga* bricks; the bricks to be placed with these mantras are also called *stomabhāgas*. Having prescribed this generally by saying "he places them," he now praises it in a specific form: "He places seven in each [direction] for the sake of possessing strength (*savīryatva*); three in the middle for the sake of stability (*pratiṣṭhiti*)" (TS 5.3.5). By placing seven in each of the individual directions, there is strength and firmness;
by placing three in the middle, there is stability and steadfastness—this is the meaning. || 32 ||

[He places the bricks with the formulas: "The eastern direction belongs to the kings," [and so on]. There are five *nākasad* bricks; four are placed in each of the four directions and one in the middle. Having subsequently placed the last one facing east, he places five *coḍā* bricks among the *nākasads* with the formula, "This one in front, the golden-haired one. Having placed those, he builds the circular layer (*vṛttā citiḥ*). [End of] Chapter 1. [This work is] accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. Page 83.

*Nāka* means heaven (*svarga*). Those by whom it is attained or reached are called *nākasat*. Thus, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in a mantra: "May they establish the sacrificer upon the back of the *nāka*, in the heavenly world" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 4.4.2). The bricks to be laid with these mantras are also called *nākasat*. Regarding the meditating upon the enemy with half [of the mantra], Āpastamba has formulated the rule: "Meditating upon the enemy in his mind, [he lays] the last one facing eastward from the west" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 17.1.4.5).

Having made them with the fifth [verse] and having thrown excrement upon them while remaining silent, he says, "This one in front is Hārakeśa," and places five *coḍā* bricks on top of them; that which faces west is placed at the back. He places [the next set] with the words, "This one behind is Viśvavyacāḥ. He meditates in his mind upon someone he hates as he places the five *coḍā*s, saying, "I place Devadatta in the jaws. The word *coḍā* is derived from the verbal root *cūḍ*, meaning "to cover."

Because they serve the purpose of covering the openings above the celestial dwellers (*nākasad*), these bricks are called *cauḍās*. The meaning is that one lays down five *cauḍās*, as there are five in number. Regarding the specific meditation to be performed at the time of laying them down, the text prescribes: "Whomever he may hate, while laying [the brick], let him meditate upon him; verily, from these very deities he cuts him off, and he quickly goes to ruin" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.3.7). Whatever person the sacrificer hates, that enemy the Adhvaryu priest should meditate upon while performing the laying down.

By that [act] during the meditation, he cuts off this one whom he hates from those very deities, such as Agni Senānī and others; he severs him completely. "He meets with immediate affliction; he attains death at that very moment. He prescribes the placement of the five *coḍas* upon the *nākasads*: "He places the *nākasads* on the north; just as one brings a wife and seats her in the house, so it is in that case" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.3.7). The *nākasads* represent the household, and the five *coḍas* represent the wife.

Regarding this, the text prescribes the finality of that brick which is to be placed with the third mantra, "tatrāyaṃ paśyāt": "He places the last one behind, facing east; therefore, the wife sits behind, facing east" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.3.7). The meaning is: because he places the brick to be laid down facing east in the western direction as the very last one, therefore the wife, standing in the western direction, sits facing east toward the Gārhapatya fire. || 33 ||
Tapaḥ and Tapasya are the two seasonal deities who share a common ritual status. (Section 3) 34.

The Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), however, explains it thus: "With the spring alone he piled its eastern wing"—thus, in the first [season], the eastern wing of the fire-altar is piled; in the second, on the southern wing, with the words "with the summer [he piled] the southern wing"; on the tail, in the third, with the words "with the rainy season [he piled] the tail"—thus there are two near the tail; and with the words "with the autumn [he piled] the northern wing," [he piles] near the northern wing; and with the words "with the winter [he piled] the middle," he explains that the two bricks named Hemanta and Śiśira are placed in the middle.

In this regard, both the placing [of the image] and the favoring [of the devotee] have been described (and their sequence has also been stated); however, according to the Vaikhānasa tradition, it is done according to the available opportunity. || 34 ||
"Thou art the [path] of the gods; thou art Devayānī of the gods"—with these words, two *saṃyānī* (conveying) vessels are used.

The meaning has been explained. || 35 || From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: [In the twelfth book: "May Prajāpati settle thee on the back of heaven, the luminous one"—with these words, he lays down the *viśvajyotis* (all-light) brick. Here he places the *retahsic* (seed-shedding) bricks of the elder. || 36 || "Thou art the unconquered heaven, pervaded by immortality; the Ādityas are thy guardians"—with these words, he lays down the *maṇḍaleṣṭakā* (circle-brick). "Thou art light (*suvar*), grant me light, uphold the heaven, protect me from the heaven"—with these words, he lays down the *hiraṇyeṣṭakā* (gold-brick). || 37 ||

... Or rather, there is another sequence for the laying down [of the bricks]: having laid down the five *coḍā* bricks ending with [the verse], the two *saṃyānyau* [bricks] with the formula "Thou art the path of the gods"; the two *utavye* [bricks] with "Tapaśca tapasyaśca"; the *viśvajyotis* [brick] with "May Prajāpati settle thee on the back of heaven"; the *retaḥsic* [brick] with "Svarāḥ jyotiḥ"; the gold brick (*hiraṇyeṣṭakā*) with "Thou art the light of heaven"; the *maṇḍala* [brick] with "Thou art the unconquered by the gods"; the *vikarṇī* [brick] with "Thou art the step of the gods"; and the *svayamātṛṇṇā* [brick] with "May Parameṣṭhin settle thee on heaven"—thus it is stated in the Āpastamba Sūtra; this indeed is the sequence for the laying down. || 31 || 37 ||

Having performed the afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites, they dwell [there] after having led a white horse clockwise around [the altar] with the verse, "When you first cried out at birth... (RV 10.97.1).
The [third] section is concluded. || 38 ||
He soaks three fuel-sticks of Udumbara wood, each a span in length, in clarified butter. || 39 ||
He throws fuel-sticks of Udumbara wood into the clarified butter. || 39 ||
On the following day, having performed the two final morning Pravargya and Upasad rites, he piles the Yājñasenī layer as the remainder of the fifth layer.

On the following day, at dawn, having performed the morning rites, it is stated that there remain two layers of the fifth *citi*, and the last *citi* is [the seventh]. The meaning is that he piles the *Yājñasenī*—so called because it originated in the lineage of a certain man named Citra and was seen by one named Yajñasena. || 40 ||

He places three Gāyatrī verses containing the word "mūrdhan" (head), beginning with *agnirmūrdhā*, in the east. To the north, he places three Triṣṭubhs; to the south, three Jagatīs; to the west, three Anuṣṭubhs; and to the north, three Bṛhatīs, Uṣṇihs, Paṅktis, and Akṣarapaṅktis—these being the various forms of meters (*viṣurūpāṇi chandāṃsi*)—placing them according to the available space. Right here he places the Aticchandas verse, having placed the Dvipadā as the last one.

Agnibhūti: One places three *gāyatrī* verses in front; likewise, one should place the subsequent meters, three by three. [End of] Paṭala. [This is] accompanied by the commentary titled *Prayogacandrikā*, compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 45.

"Dadhāti" [is the rule] according to Āpastamba and Vaikhānasa. Triṣṭubhs are on the south; Jagatīs on the west; Anuṣṭubhs on the north; Bṛhatīs, Uṣṇihs, Paṅktis, and Akṣarapaṅktis—these, beginning with the Bṛhatīs, should each consist of exactly three verses, as space permits. Any additional Akṣarapaṅkti is for the purpose of providing an option. However, the Aticchandas verse, "Agnirhotāram," is in the middle. As for the Dvipadās, they are at the very end, in the tail; for it is stated in the *Chandovicitibhāṣya*: "At the time of the ritual, one does not intend [to use] the Dvipadās. || 11 || 42 ||

Having touched the *svayamātṛṇṇā* with the formula, "I seat thee in the seat of Āyu," and having caused a horse to smell it, he places it in the middle of the fire-altar together with an unlearned Brāhmaṇa, using the formula, "May Parameṣṭhin seat thee on the back of heaven, thee, the wide-extending. He does so with this *vyāhṛti*, "Suvaḥ. Having offered an oblation upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* with the formula, "I offer the layer," he breathes out. On the northern shoulder, he places the *vikarṇī* with the verse, "Snorting like a horse eager for fodder.
Neither the *svayamātṛṇṇā* nor the *vikarṇī* should be covered over by any other bricks. || 43 || 44 ||

Having touched the *praṇītā* waters with the formula, "I settle thee in the seat of Āyu," and having caused the naturally perforated stone (*svayamātṛṇṇā*) to be reached by a white horse, some say that while still mounted he performs the act of smelling [the stone]. Having led the horse near it, he should place it down together with an unlearned Brāhmaṇa using the mantra, "May Parameṣṭhin settle thee on the back of heaven," ending with, "By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit in the light. Having offered an oblation upon it with the formula, "I offer consciousness," he causes the breath of exhalation to be led away by the wind of his own breath.

The *varadāna* (granting of boons), the *sāman*, and the *praiṣa* (direction) are performed; there is no *upadhāna* (placing) with those two. With the verse "prothad aśva" (the neighing horse), he places the *vikarṇī* brick upon the northern shoulder. These two—the *svayamātṛṇṇā* and the *vikarṇī*—are the *viṣṭambhe*; one does not place any other brick upon them. 43–44.

With the section beginning "O Agni, come to us with cattle," he lays down the *go-citi* (the layer of cattle). There are a thousand bricks measuring one foot (*pāda*) each. One who desires cattle lays them down in every middle layer (*citi*). (Section 4) 46.
Thus ends the first chapter in the twelfth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra. || 1 ||

He lays down the bricks with the Anuvāka beginning with *agne gobhir na ā gahi*, reciting one mantra for each brick. This Anuvāka is repeated again and again until a thousand [bricks] have been laid down. When the thousand is complete, the remaining verses (*ṛc*) should be omitted. This rule is so that the number does not exceed a thousand fires. In other cases, beyond a thousand, he recites the first verse twice for a sacrificer desiring cattle; this is the name of the "Gociti" (the layer of cows). This pertains to the fire that is being piled. [End of] Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Book 12.

The meaning is that one should not place the *purīṣa* (filling earth) on those [bricks] which measure a *yāda*, whether they are in the first, the middle, or the fifth layer. Thus ends the first chapter in the twelfth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.
12.2 Now begins the second chapter of the twelfth book.
"O Indra and Agni, I yoke you with the yoke-fellow," [with these words] he yokes eight yoke-fellows. || 1 ||

The *sayuj* mantras are those by which one joins Agni with the deities. The bricks to be laid down with those mantras are also called *sayuj*, as seen in such passages as, "When he lays down the *sayuj* [bricks]" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.3.9). || 1 ||
"You are named Ambā"—thus [she spoke] to the seven Kṛttikās. ||2||
Seven Kṛttikās with an unequal [number]. || 2 ||
With the five verses beginning "Purovātasaniḥ asi," he places [the cups] around [the fire] while seeking rain. ||3||

The bricks to be laid with mantras associated with the "rain-giver" (*vṛṣṭisani*) are the *vṛṣṭisani* bricks. Holding one brick in his hand, he should circumambulate the site of the piling (*cayana*) clockwise and then place it. In this manner, following the sequence of circumambulation, he places one in each direction and one in the center. The Venerable Śruti ordains that the placing [of the bricks] be done by moving around [the site] in order, lest—if he were to place them all at once—a single season should rain. Thus, she prescribes that placement after having moved around [the site] step by step. 3.
"Salilāya tvā," "Sarṇīkāya tvā"—these are the eight Āditya bricks. || 4 ||
The bricks to be laid with mantras containing the word "āditya" are the Āditya-bricks.
With the formula, "For the Ṛc thee! For the Ruc thee! he places five ghee-bricks, moving around them in successive order.

The "butter-bricks" (*ghṛteṣṭakā*) are likewise lumps of clarified butter. Since the Sūtrakāra has enumerated them among those not made of clay, they are not earthen. Regarding these as well, he prescribes—as before—that each individual brick must be placed while proceeding in a clockwise direction: "He places them by going around; thus he bestows splendor upon it without omission" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.3.10). || 5 ||
"Yaśodāṃ tvā yaśasi sādayāmi"—with these [formulas], he places five Yaśodās.
One should place them individually. The Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "Yaśodā upadadhāti" (He places the Yaśodās) [is the authority].
"Bhūyaskṛd asi, varivaskṛd asi"—these are the five Bhūyaskṛt bricks. ||7||

Even words that do not denote form are said to be "formless" [in this context]. As it is said: "Thou art seated in the waters, seated in the hawk; with this [formula], O Agni, one wins the desired form by means of form" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.3.10). The meaning is that by the recitation of words denoting other forms, one attains Agni himself who is endowed with the appropriate form. || 8 ||
"Upon the wealth of the earth I settle thee"—with these words [he offers] five [oblations] for Draviṇodas. || 9 ||
There are five *draviṇodās*. Because they are to be placed with mantras containing the word *draviṇodas*, their name is *draviṇodās*. 9.
"Protect my out-breath; protect my in-breath"—these are the six life-prolonging formulas. 12.2.10.
There are six *āyuṣyā* bricks. These bricks are called *āyuṣyā* because they are to be laid down with mantras containing the word "life" (*āyus*). || 10 ||
"O Agni, that which is your supreme heart-name"—this is the Heart-mantra of Agni. || 11 ||
"O Agni, that which is thy highest name"—this is one [verse]. The intention is that it should be placed in the middle because of the similarity of the heart.
(11) "Those which are the non-goers"—these are the seven seasonal verses. (12)
Since words such as *etadyāvat* and others are connected with the seasons (*ṛtu*), the bricks to be placed by means of them are also called *ṛtavyā*. || 12 ||
With this Anuvāka beginning with "agninā viśvāṣāṭ," he lays down the bodies of Indra.

The *indratanu*s (the bodies of Indra) are twenty-two. Words such as "Viśvāṣāṭ" and others denote specific bodies of Indra; the bricks to be placed with mantras containing those [words] are the *indratanu*s. || 13 ||
With this Anuvāka—"Abhīṣāc, Abhiṣavī, Abhivayās, Ūrdhvavayas, Bṛhadvayas, Savayas, Sahvān, Sahamānas, Sahasvān, and Sahīyas"—he lays down the names of Indra.
There are ten names of Indra beginning with "Abhīṣāc."
"Prajāpati sought the horse with his mind"—thus [he recites] the thirty-three sacrificial bodies. 15.
The bricks to be laid down, which consist of mantras containing words that designate the body of the sacrifice, are the "bodies of the sacrifice" (yajñatanu). || 15 ||
"Jyotiṣmatīṃ tvā sādayāmi"—with these words, he places twelve Jyotiṣmatī bricks.
The bricks to be laid with mantras containing the word "jyotismatī" are the jyotiṣmatīs; and those mantras are recited in the Āraṇyakāṇḍa. || 16 ||
"I settle you in the red clouds; I settle you in the ruddy clouds; I settle you in the white clouds; I settle you in the blue clouds; I settle you in the black clouds"—thus are the five clouds. 17.
In brief, there are five kinds of living beings. || 17 ||
With this Anuvāka beginning with "The Kṛttikās are the lunar mansion," he lays down eight Nakṣatreṣṭakās on the shoulders [of the altar]. (18) 18. According to the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha:
Nakṣatreṣṭakās are those bricks which are to be laid down with mantras containing the word "nakṣatra" (lunar mansion). (18)
He appends "O Agni, [thou art] the lights" to all [the verses]. || 19 ||

"O Agni, you are the splendors of Prajāpati, Dhātṛ, and Soma"—this [formula] is used only at the first [layer]. According to the explicit statement "the connection with all [names] is by ellipsis," this applies either in our own Sūtra or in another Sūtra. (19)

"Full [moon] afterwards"—having first laid down the full-moon brick in the east, he lays down each subsequent one further to the west, up to the Viśākhā constellation. "That which the gods bestowed upon thee"—having first laid down the new-moon brick in the west, he lays down each subsequent one further to the east, ending with the Apabharaṇī constellation.

He places the *pūrṇā* brick behind [the central brick]—that is, the *paurṇamāsī*; he places it in front of the fire-altar. He places the *nakṣatra*-bricks starting from the east, ending toward the west, and they are not touching one another. Having placed the first one with the formula, "The *kṛttikā*s are the lunar mansion; for the sake of the *jyotis* (light)," ending with "for thee," he places each subsequent one up to the two *viśākhā*s. To the south of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, he arranges them so that there is a continuous row (*rīti*).

Having placed the brick with the verse "yat te devā adadhuḥ" behind the *uraḥ* (chest) on the new moon day, he places the subsequent *nakṣatreṣṭakā*s (stellar bricks), beginning from the first among them prior to the *apabharaṇīs*, with the constellation Anurādhā and the deity Mitra. This is done without combining them with the *apabharaṇīs*, as previously described. Alternatively, regarding the specific distinction in this placement: if he were to place them touching one another, it would lead to rain; he should meditate upon the world [of rain], for Parjanya might become non-rainy. Therefore, they should be placed without touching.

"He places [the bricks]; he thus creates a world for rain; Parjanya becomes a showerer" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.3.1). When there is mutual contact between the bricks, the place of rain is covered, and therefore Parjanya becomes devoid of rain. But when there is no contact, that gap becomes the locus of rain, and thus Parjanya becomes "magha," one who is habitually raining.

It prescribes another specific detail regarding the placement: "He places some bricks facing west in the east, and others facing east in the west; therefore the constellations revolve both eastward and westward" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.1). One should place the bricks representing Kṛttikā through Viśākhā on the southern side of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, beginning from the eastern direction and ending toward the west.

One should place the bricks beginning with Anurādhā and ending with Apamṛtyu on the northern side of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, starting from the western direction and ending toward the east. Between the two rows situated to the south and north of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, one should place the brick called Amāvāsyā in the western direction in a uniform manner. Between the two rows situated to the south and north of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, one should place the brick called Paurṇamāsī in the eastern direction in a uniform manner.

Since this is so, therefore even in the world the constellations revolve such that on the southern side of the celestial sphere they face westward, while on the northern side they face eastward. || 20 ||
15. "It applies to all [verses]. [From] *Paṭala* 2: *Mahādevaśāstrī-saṃkalita-prayogacandrikā-nyākhyā*. 89.
"The eight verses beginning with *hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre*" are the *sarits* (streams). 21.
The meaning is that one places eight bricks with the verse beginning "hiraṇyagarbha" as the rivers. || 21 ||
"Viśvakarman is the lord of the quarters"—with these [formulas], one places five gold bricks: four in each direction and one in the middle.
One should place the gold bricks in each direction collectively.

With the formulas "For breath thee! For sight thee! he places four naturally perforated pebbles (*svayamātṛṇṇā*) in each direction; [the image of the year is prescribed here as a three-year-old bull]. || 23 ||

"For breath thee, for sight thee—with that deity; for the diffused breath thee, for sight thee—with that; for the downward breath thee, for sight thee—with that; for speech thee, for sight thee—with that"—with these [formulas] he lays down four *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks. ||23||

"O Agni, come for the feast! We choose Agni as our messenger. By Agni is Agni kindled. May Agni strike down the Vṛtras. O Agni, we meditate upon the hymn that is effective today, reaching unto heaven—of the divine wealth. These are the forms of the five days. [Then he lays down the Vrata brick. 24.

The five forms recited in other *śākhās* are stated here: "In this [context], he places the vow (*vrata*)," as mentioned in another *śākhā*. The same applies in the case of Āpastamba as well. || 24 ||

With the formula "To him of a hundred weapons," he places five *ājyānī* bricks; with the formula "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra," he places four *vajriṇī* bricks in each direction. Some recite five [bricks] together, and he modifies the mantra with the words "He who from above. || 25 ||

The bricks to be laid down with mantras containing the word *ajyāni* are the *ajyānayas*; one should lay these down. The injunction is seen in the Brāhmaṇa: "He lays down the *vajriṇīs*" (TS 5.7.3). Those *vajriṇī* stones are laid down in each direction. [The mantra] "Who [would harm] us from above" is used without compounding. According to another recension, the fifth is [laid down] by one holding an arrow: "From above, the malevolent one would seek to harm us. || 25 ||

"O Agni, bestow glory upon the glorious one"—with these four *rāṣṭrabhṛt* verses he lays down [the bricks]: a *gāyatrī* in the east, a *triṣṭubh* in the south, a *jagatī* in the west, an *anuṣṭubh* in the north, and a *paṅkti* in the middle. The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[12th Praśna] (Note: The text enclosed in brackets in the original source is not present in the Sūtra reading.)

He places the *gāyatrī* [verse] on the south; in this same sequence all [the verses] are placed. In every case, these are the verses as they are traditionally recited: "Agni is the head," "Of the world," "The guardian of the people," "Thee, O most glorious one," and "O Agni, that horse today. (Section 6) || 26 ||
Thus ends the second chapter in the twelfth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.

"O Agni, glorious one..."—thus [he recites] the four *rāṣṭrabhṛt* verses before the fire; he piles them up on all sides with gold bricks, so says Āpastamba. Regarding the piling: "Whoever piles the fire that faces in all directions... as stated in the Brāhmaṇa (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.7.4). He piles a *gāyatrī* verse toward the east: "O Agni... a *triṣṭubh* toward the south: "O Agnis, of your sacrifice... a *jagatī* toward the west: "The guardian of the people... and an *anuṣṭubh* toward the north: "Thee, most rich in glorious fame..."

"In the middle of the row, 'O Agni, that horse today... This Agni, facing all directions, is built with golden bricks. Thus ends the second chapter in the twelfth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.
Now begins the third chapter in the twelfth book.

With the formula, "Thou art the measure of a thousand," he sprinkles the fire toward each of the directions while moving clockwise around it with a thousand pieces of gold, using two hundred at a time; in the middle, he uses the last two [hundred] while facing eastward.

The measure for the thousand is "thousandfold" (*sahasrasya pramā*). With other mantras, such as *hiraṇyaśnaih*, he stands up; with two hundred, he sprinkles the crane (*vaka*) in each single direction, like the sprinkling of clarified butter (*ājyaprokṣaṇa*). The mention of "thousand" implies that there is no modification (*anūha*) even for two thousand and so forth, because words such as "thousand" denote an unlimited number. || 1 ||
"O Agni, may these bricks of mine be milch-cows"—with this [formula], he makes the bricks into milch-cows. || 2 ||
Standing at the end of the hip [of the altar] with this mantra, he prepares the bricks for the *dhenu* (cow) on the northern side; "the sacrificer makes the cow," so say Vaikhānasa and Bharadvāja.
He touches [the altar] with the Aiḍikī brick; there are the Āraṇyaka invitatory verses (anuvākyās).

The *aiḍikī citiḥ* (the brick-layering pertaining to the *iḍā*) consists of the section beginning with "Thou art Agni, thou art Vaiśvānara. With this, the Adhvaryu touches the fire. Thus says Āpastamba: "Having touched the fire with the *aiḍikī citiḥ*, the Adhvaryu [performs the rite]. By that [text], the making of the cow (*dhenukaraṇa*) belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). The repeated mention of the Adhvaryu is for the purpose of touching. 3. Paṭala. [This concludes] the commentary known as the *Payogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 91. 3. Thus ends the third section.

He offers the Śatarudrīya oblation with a gruel of wild sesame (jartila) or a gruel of gavīdhuka seeds, or with the flour of gavīdhuka seeds mixed with wild sesame and clarified butter, or with deer’s milk or goat’s milk, using an Arka leaf while standing upright upon the northernmost brick. Having divided these Anuvākas into three parts, he recites them: with the first Anuvāka and eighty [oblations] at knee-height; with another eighty at navel-height; and with the remaining eighty and as many more as there are prior to the *avatāna* formulas, at mouth-height—[making] thousands.

He offers thousands—that is, innumerable—descents of the ten directions. (4) With the formula, "Obeisance to the Rudras who are in heaven," he offers at the height of the mouth; with "Obeisance to the Rudras who are in the intermediate space," at the height of the navel; and with "Obeisance to the Rudras who are on earth," at the height of the knees. (5) He throws away an Arka leaf in a place free from traffic. (6)

*Śatarudrīya* is the name of the ritual act. "Many Rudras are employed" means this. *Jatilāḥ* are wild sesame seeds. With their gruel (*yavāgū*)—or with *kasaka* (wild grass), barley, *gavīdhuka* seeds, or indeed with wild sesame seeds themselves, or with the flour of *gavīdhuka* seeds, or with *kuśa* grass, barley, and ghee—the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*) performs it. And some say that this [gruel] should be old ghee.

Facing north, he performs the oblation of wild animals with goat’s milk in the northern part of the fire-chamber, in the northwestern corner of the northern wing, or in the *vikā* (the space between the two wings). Or, on the northern shoulder of the fire-altar, or in the third *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone, it is secured in such a way that the fire is not stepped upon; there is no formal procession (*pracāra*). According to Vaikhānasa, one offers with a continuous stream of ghee while moving around the altar counter-clockwise (*apradakṣiṇam*). This is based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating, "He thus pacifies it completely."

Even for the Vājasaneyins, because of the explicit statement, "Thus [the offering] is to be made continuously," the oblation is not performed with the end of the mantra. For those whose Anuvākas are divided into three parts as "namaste rudra manyave" and so forth, there are three oblations ending with "sahasrayojane. With the subsequent [mantras], "jānudanena," "nābhidaghnenā," and "āsyadaghnenā," there are three [more] with "namo rudrebhyo ye pṛthivyām" and so on.

"Having offered oblations at the mouth-deep, the navel-deep, and the knee-deep [depths], he causes the sacrificer to recite those [verses] which are the last in the collection. Thus the sacrificer is made to recite these very [verses]. This is the procedure for the Taittirīyas. Alternatively, beginning with "Homage to the first-born," he offers oblations at the knee-deep [depth] with the formula "Homage to the carpenters, svāhā! In all cases, the Rudras are the deities. Beginning with "And homage to you, the cartwrights," he offers oblations at the navel-deep [depth] with the formula "Homage to the well-armed one, svāhā!"

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, states that after offering with "Obeisance to Svāyudha, svāhā," one begins the subsequent section with "To Sudhanvan. Starting from "And to Sudhanvan" and continuing up to "mouth-deep," one offers with the remaining group of mantras; then, prior to the descents (*avatāna*) mentioned before, having offered with "Of them, Īśāna... mouth-deep, the ten descents are offered with the uncompound form "Thousands, by the thousands. Some, however, say there are eleven descents. —Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [Chapter 12]—

Some recite, "Let us go to other forests. The *anvāroha* formulas are for the purpose of providing an option. With the formula, "Homage to the Rudras who are on earth," he [places the fire] knee-deep; with "Homage to the Rudras who are in the intermediate space," navel-deep; and with "Homage to the Rudras who are in heaven," mouth-deep. He causes the sacrificer to recite these very *anvāroha* formulas.

One should offer these [oblations] with their mantras reversed: "Obeisance to the Rudras who are in heaven," while eating from the mouth; "Obeisance to the Rudras who are in the intermediate space," while eating from the navel; "Obeisance to the Rudras who are on earth," while eating from the knee—ending thus with "I place you in my jaw. Or alternatively, as it is said: "He offers the Śatarudrīya" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.3). The word "hundred" (*śata*) indicates an unlimited number. That chapter in which an unlimited number of Rudras are expounded is the Śatarudrīya.

*Jartila* refers to wild sesame seeds; *gīdhuka* refers to wild wheat. Alternatively, one may offer oblations with goat’s milk. Because this plant grows from a mass of goat’s hair (*ajārōma*) that is worthy of worship (*arcanīya*) and adoration (*pūjya*), this stationary being acquired the name *arka*. One should offer oblations with that *arka* leaf. In this regard, the division into three parts should be performed as follows: the first part begins with "Obeisance to you, O Rudra" and ends with "and obeisance to you, the lords of the assembly."

The second part begins with *namo aśvebhyaḥ* and ends with *āvāryāya ca*. The third part begins with *namaḥ prataraṇāya ca* and is accompanied by the verse *ya etāvantaḥ*. For all three oblations, the holding of the fuel-stick (*samidh*) at heights such as the knee and so forth, in sequence, is explained by means of hand gestures. The Adhvaryu priest should cause either the sacrificer or himself to recite the mantras beginning with *namo rudrebhyaḥ*. The discarding of the Arka leaf occurs in a place where animals do not roam. (4) (5) (6). He states the place for the discarding of the Arka leaf:

One should cast [the offering] upon the path of one whom he hates; whichever animal stands first [to pass over it], that one meets with misfortune. (Section 7) This is the Brāhmaṇa of the Śatarudrīya. 7.

One should discard a *tarkaparṇa* leaf in the path where the sacrificial animals pass by that man whom the sacrificer hates. Whichever animal, having been discarded, stands first—preceding the other animals—and steps forward, that one shall perish. This is the meaning of the *brāhmaṇa* of the *Śatarudrīya*. || 7 ||

With the verse, "Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants," he places a *gāvīdhuka* pap cooked in milk—dedicated to Rudra—upon that brick over which he has offered the *Śatarudrīya*. (8) He should give a bow with three arrows to a Brāhmaṇa, having asked for it from no one. (9) While walking around the fire clockwise, he sprinkles it with clarified butter in each direction, saying: "May the Vasus protect you from the east along with the Rudras. (10)

In the middle [of the rite], facing east with the final verse, he worships each direction with salutations while circumambulating to the right, reciting "O Rudra, that bow which you hold in front," and so forth; in the middle, facing east with the final verse. [End of] Paṭala 3. This is from the *Mahādevaśāstra*, accompanied by the commentary *Yogacandrikā*. 5.

The formula beginning with *yo rudro agnau* is dedicated to Rudra, having Rudra as its deity. With this *yajus*, one places a single brick on the northern-western corner; this same brick is placed at the end of the entire layering. One should deposit it on that final brick. Upon it, a sacrificial porridge (*caru*) of *gavidhuka* grass is established. Or, on another brick, upon which one offers the *Śatarudrīya*. Stones are buried for those who follow the *Āsaniya* [tradition].

Having placed [the fire-pan] knee-deep, the Taittirīyas also perform the piling of the altar and other rites once the touching of water has been completed. The sacrificer gives the bow with three arrows to the Adhvaryu; it is not something requested, nor is it something performed as a ritual act. "That which, O Rudra, is thy bow in front"—this is the prayer for the sacrificer alone. 8, 9, 10.
Taking a water-pot and placing a stone [upon it], he goes around the fire three times from left to right, sprinkling water while reciting, "Strength upon the stone. || 11 ||
The Adhvaryu, having taken a water-pot, goes around three times clockwise while reciting, "Strength in the stone... (RV 10.175.1).

Having set down the water-pot, he goes around three times sprinkling [water] behind him. If he should practice sorcery, he pours out the pot on the southern buttock of the altar, saying, "I destroy the breath of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so," and he pronounces the name of the one he hates.

"Having set down the pitcher," that is, having placed the jar; "O stone, let hunger come upon you"—this is the uttering of the name of the enemy. "Let the pain given by you go to him whom we hate"—thus he turns back again three times, because of the scriptural statement: "Three times he moves around from left to right" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.4.4). However, some take up the pitcher again if the sacrificer performs the rite with malevolent intent (*abhicāra*) after returning.

The meaning is that with this mantra, "O Adhvaryu, here I cut short the life of Devadatta, the descendant of Bhṛgu," one should fix the pitcher either in the southern enclosure, in the southeast corner, or in the north. || 12 ||

He worships with the back parts: with the Gāyatra [Sāman] the front; with the Bṛhat and Rathantara the two wings; with the Yajñāyajñīya, established in the seasons, the tail. On the southern hip he sings the Vāravantīya; on the northern, the Vāmadevya. Furthermore, for each wing, he sings the Sāman of Prajāpati over the Ṛc. || 13 ||

The Adhvaryu priest worships that [chariot] from behind with the Sāmans beginning with the *Sāma*. According to the Vājasaneyaka Śruti, "The Adhvaryu should sing those [Sāmans]," or because they are prescribed for the Chandogas. He worships the front part with the *Gāyatra* Sāman, the right wing with the *Rathantara*, and the left wing with the *Bṛhat*; the word *Bṛhat* is placed first according to Pāṇini 2.2.34 (*alpāntaram*). With the *Yajñāyajñīya* Sāman, which stands for the seasons, he worships the tail; and with the *Vāravantīya*, he worships the southern hip.
Some describe it thus: "One worships that fire which is in the north. In place of the Vāmadevya [sāman], one should recite the verse from the Taittirīya [Āraṇyaka].
[End of] Śatapatha-Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Book 12, Section 1 (Ka, Kha).
The highest power of Prajāpati that is beyond the south and beyond himself—that is his resting place there.

"The sacrifice was offered by the Bhṛgus; may it be a bestower of blessings through the Vasus. Of that which has been offered and enjoyed, may I partake in the wealth"—with these words, he causes the sacrificer to recite the formula for the milking of the Stotra and Śastra. || 14 ||
The meaning is clear. || 14 ||
The Hotṛ recites the *saṃcita-ukthya* with "Father Mātariśvan"; when the Hotṛ does not desire it, the Adhvaryu [recites it]. 15.

In the milking of the *stotra* and *śastra*, there is an elliptical extension (*anukarṣa*) of the rule "he causes the sacrificer to recite. When that *stotra* has been chanted, the Adhvaryu causes the sacrificer to recite over it: "Thou art the praise of the praised" (*stutasya stutamasi*). Regarding the *śastra* of the piled fire-altar (*saṃcita agni*), the Hotṛ, standing behind the fire, recites it. If the Hotṛ is unwilling—that is, does not desire—to perform the recitation, the Adhvaryu himself recites it.

Beginning with "The father [is] Mātariśvan," he recites the verses up to "they have fashioned the feet," then pausing, he recites three times this very verse: "Bṛhaspati has proclaimed the exhilarating hymns. This is because of the statement, "He recites [the Śastra] in a continuous flow. Alternatively, the author of the Bhāṣya maintains that since the single verse of the Ṛgvedins, "Agni by his birth [is] a ray of light," is recited [afterward], there is only a single performance. Now, he causes the sacrificer to recite, "Thou art the Śastra. || 15 ||
In this regard, some authorities prescribe cows as the instrument [of the sacrifice]. (Section 8) 16.
Thus ends the third paṭala in the twelfth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
The meaning is clear. || 16 || Thus ends the third paṭala in the twelfth praśna of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.

**Twelfth Praśna, Fourth Paṭala** Then, having tied an *avakā* plant, a frog, and a branch of *vetasa* to a long bamboo pole, he draws the fire across [the altar] with seven or eight [verses], beginning with: "O Agni, we encircle you with the *avakā* of the ocean. || 1 ||

Having tied *avakā* grass, *śaivāla* moss, a branch of *vetasa* or *vajula*, and a frog to a long, immeasurable bamboo pole, he drags it along with a man and a frog; "having tied it to a long bamboo pole" is the rule according to Vaikhānasa. With the seven or eight verses beginning with "Of the ocean," he drags the fire, that is, he scrapes it. Alternatively: this *vetasa* is like the flower of the waters, [situated] in the waters... [End of section 4]. [Section 4] Paṭala: Accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 15.

Because it is being born. And the *avakā* plants, known as *śaivāla*, are the essence of the waters, like the cream on top of curd. Therefore, one should draw out the fire with these two. He prescribes that even the frog is a means for dragging [the fire], together with the two previously mentioned substances: "Whosoever, as the first, approaches the piled fire, his head indeed burns away."

"He drags [the fire] with a frog; indeed, this [fire] is not fit for domestic animals to subsist upon, nor is it beneficial for domestic animals or wild animals; he strikes that very [animal] with grief" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.4). Among cows, buffaloes, and other such animals, whichever animal first steps upon this altar-fire built with bricks and treads upon it with its foot—that animal this fire becomes capable of burning with intense heat. Therefore, one should not perform the dragging with another animal, but rather with a frog.

Furthermore, because the frog (*maṇḍaka*) is not included among either domestic or wild animals suitable for sacrifice, and because its utility is not observed in the world as it is with cattle, buffaloes, and the like, it is not a source of livelihood for anyone. Therefore, when one drags it along, one subjects that very frog to suffering. || 1 ||

Having followed [the frog] until its life has departed, and having enticed it with alluring things, he places it in a heap of refuse. (2) He should touch with water [an object] toward whom he bears enmity. (3)

Dragging it along, he causes it to follow until the life-breaths of the frog have departed; having drawn out all the seats of the vital breaths, such as the nostrils and so forth, he pulls it in such a way that its limbs are no longer recognized, [thinking] "this is the nose," or "these are the eyes. He throws the remainder onto the rubbish-heap (utkara). With these plants, such as the *avakā* and others, the sacrificer should touch whoever he hates. || 2 || 3 ||

Creating for himself an easy path for his departure, the sharp-horned bull, blazing brightly, beholding the ancient dwelling place, Agni has stretched out the celestial thread. You are our thread and our bridge, O Agni; you are the path that leads to the gods. By you, O Agni, may we ascend to the heights, and then may we rejoice in the communal banquet with the gods. Granting their release to the descendant of Manu, they behold the straight path.

"The Maruts have delighted in this sacrifice—the rain of the gods, the immortal, the finder of heaven (*svaḥ*). Turning back into the midst of the world, transforming the various forms of progeny, may Saṃvatsara, the Parameṣṭhin who maintains his vows, protect our sacrifice from beyond the realm of space. May Parivatsara grant us progeny; may Dhātṛ, being well-disposed, grant it. May many [beings], together, manifold, of all forms, yet united under one vow, enter into me. With these words, he offers the five *anvāroha* oblations. (Section 9) ||4||

Having taken five portions with the *juhu* ladle, he should perform the oblation called *anvārohaṇa* on the altar with the verse beginning "svayaṃ kṛṇvānaḥ" (VS 11.70). In all cases, Agni is the deity. 4. With the formula, "I have stepped upon the earth; may my breath not forsake me," he puts on the two sandals made of black antelope skin, or at least one of them. 5. Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra—[12th Praśna] I have stepped upon the earth; may my breath not forsake me—with these words, he puts on the two sandals made of black antelope skin, or at least one of them. 5.
He steps over sandals made from the skin of a black antelope, or he steps over one of them. 5.
With the two verses, "This is the gathering-place of the waters" and "Homage to your heat, to your flame," he steps over the fire.
With two verses addressed to Agni, the Adhvaryu ascends the fire-altar.

Having taken five portions of clarified butter into the *juhu* ladle, he sprinkles it crosswise over the fire with the five formulas beginning with "To Nṛṣad, vaṭ! just as he did over the *uttaravedi*. 7.

The pouring of clarified butter (*vyāghāraṇa*) over the fire—either upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone or elsewhere—is performed with five mantras, according to Āpastamba and Baudhāyana. This is like the procedure for the *uttaravedi*. Regarding the diagonal arrangement, the Brāhmaṇa states: beginning with "To the seat of the Rishis, vaṭ! he pours the butter; he pours it diagonally. Therefore, animals strike their limbs diagonally for the sake of stability. (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.5). || 7 ||
With the two verses beginning "ye devā devānām," he sprinkles water mixed with curd and honey around the fire using a handful of darbha grass.

They conclude with the word *snuvi*. Having gone to the place where the deer was killed, he performs the sprinkling (*avokṣaṇa*) by means of two [verses], taking curds mixed with honey and a large handful of *darbha* grass, and sprinkles the fire in various ways. The Commentator states that a "handful" (*muci*) of *darbha* grass refers to a large handful (*sthūla*). || 8 ||
Having made the tortoise-mark, he descends with the words, "Givers of out-breath, givers of in-breath."

Just as the back of a tortoise is variegated with various spots, so having placed [the fire] in the middle of the back; [reciting] the mantra of one [verse], "The givers of breath, the givers of exhalation," the sacrificer descends silently. 9.

Having taken five portions of clarified butter into the *juhu* ladle, he offers one oblation to Agni Anīkavat with the two *saṃhitā* verses beginning, "Agni with his sharp flame" and "He [the sun] with his face. || 12.4.10 ||
With the two verses beginning "Agniṣṭiṣmeṇa," there is one oblation; Agni Anīkavant is the deity, and knowledge is the *kaṅki*. || 10 ||

Having filled the *sruk* ladle with sixteen portions, he offers the various *vaiśvakarmanī* oblations with the two hymns beginning "He who, offering all these worlds... (*ya imā viśvā bhuvanāni juhvat*), or with all [the verses] together.

Having filled the *juhū* ladle with clarified butter taken sixteen times, he offers the oblations dedicated to Viśvakarman (*vaiśvakarmaṇāni*)—those for which Viśvakarman, the performer of all deeds, is the deity. Beginning with the verse "He who [created] all these worlds," ending with "He placed [him] in the womb of the waters, O Puruṣa, Svāhā!"—this constitutes one [offering]. [End of] Paṭala 5, accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 97.

The oblation (*huti*): beginning with "The father of the eye" and ending with "This one, indeed, is the knower as he truly is," by means of these two hymns—meaning two oblations for each individual hymn. In this regard, the following is considered: Should this Vaiśvakarmaṇa oblation be performed separately for every Manvantara? Or should the two hymns be recited together and the rite performed once? Or should it be performed by reciting each hymn individually?
Among these, he accepts the first two positions as belonging to other Vedic branches (*śākhā*).

If he should desire of someone, "May he be released from evil for a long time," he should offer each [oblation] one by one for him. If he should desire of someone, "May he be released from evil quickly," he should offer all [the oblations] for him after reciting them in succession. || 12 ||

By the gradual performance of oblations with each individual mantra, there occurs a gradual release from sin; however, by the performance of oblations with all the hymns (*sūkta*) together, there is release from sin at that very moment. Furthermore, even when the two hymns are performed separately, their respective efficacy is individually accomplished. Moreover, the duality of the hymns results in stability for the sacrificer. Therefore, the meaning is that this [latter] position alone is superior. || 12 ||

"Salutation to the ocean, the wise one, the lord of rivers"—if he should find him in water, let him take water with his joined palms and offer it into the waters. This is the ritual procedure when not connected with a formal sacrifice. (Section 10) 13.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the twelfth book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.

If one should find this man while he is in the water, it means that a sense of measurement (or a realization) arises. Having taken up a handful of pure water, he should offer it into those very waters in which the fear arose, with the mantra "To the ocean, for wisdom" (*samudrāya vayunāya*), according to the indicative mark of the formula. Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the twelfth praśna of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.
12.5 Now begins the fifth chapter of the twelfth book.

Having performed the final afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites, he says, "Lead him to the north," and places three fuel-sticks that have been soaked in ghee into the Āhavanīya fire with the three [verses] beginning with "ud enam uttarām naya. ||1||
He places; he throws in. The rest is clear. || 1 ||
With the verse, "May all the gods lift thee up," he raises the fire. ||2||

Having cast this *praṇītā* water-vessel and having filled it with sand, he makes the formal declaration: "For Agni being led forward. Having performed the lifting of the fire with the verse, "May all the gods lift thee up," he performs the *uyata-homa* (the offering while moving). 2.

With the six verses beginning, "May the five divine directions protect the sacrifice, may the goddesses protect the sacrifice," he carries [the fire] forth. 3. (Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra—[Book 12, Chapter 5])

The mantra ends with *juṣantām*. When the first [verse] has been recited three times, he carries [the fire] from the Āgnīdhra shed with the words *paśva diśo devīḥ*; this is the remainder [of the ritual procedure]. Even when it is performed with six [verses], there is still a repetition of the fifth. For the Brāhmaṇa states: "He carries it with six; for there are six seasons; verily by means of the seasons he carries it for him" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.6). || 3 ||
With the hymn of ten verses beginning with "The swift one, sharpening," the Brahman—or the Maitrāvaruṇa or the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin—follows from the south with the Apratiratha hymn. ||4||

Standing to the south of the fire, the Brahman—or the Maitrāvaruṇa—follows with the ten-verse hymn beginning "āśuḥ śiśānaḥ. According to the Brāhmaṇa passage, "When the second Hotṛ recites the Apratiratha [hymn]" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.6), the second Hotṛ of the Brahman-group is the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; or, according to Āpastamba, it is the Pratiprasthātṛ. || 4 ||
With two verses beginning "This celestial chariot stands in the midst of heaven," he places a stone upon the Āgnīdhra hearth.

In whatever place the Āgnīdhra fire-pit will be, that place is called the Āgnīdhra; in that place, he places a stone with two verses, "This [stone] from heaven... and "The bright prastara-bunch for the purpose of placing," because of the indicative mark (liṅga) in the verse, "The speckled stone is placed in the middle of heaven. It is placed at the time of placement in the center. 5.
With the four verses beginning "All have magnified Indra," he goes as far as the tail.
The Agnīdhra, having gone out, should touch as far as the tail with these mantras; the second [mantra], however, is without a pause (anavasānā).
With the five verses beginning "prācīm anu pradiśam," they step toward the fire.
Ending with "Svasti," the Adhvaryu ascends the fire-altar with five [verses]. || 7 ||

Having filled a ladle made of Udumbara wood with milk or curds from a black cow that has a white calf, he offers one oblation upon the naturally perforated stone (svayamātṛṇṇā) with the two combined verses: "Night and Dawn" and "O Agni, thousand-eyed. ||8||

Having ascended [the post] at night, with the two *ṛc*s joined together—"O thousand-eyed one" (*sahasrākṣa*) and "The gods have established Agni" (*devā agniṃ dhārayan*)—and with these two joined verses, [he offers]. Others, however, say: "A pause is made; there is no breath-holding (*ucchvāsa*) between the two verses. With these two verses, a ladle full of curd made of *udumbara* wood is offered upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone. Agni is the deity. Having established this, the *brāhmaṇa* regarding the oblation states: "He offers a ladle full of curd made of *udumbara* wood upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā*."
Thus [the scripture] enjoins: "A certain udumbara branch, similar to the *juhū* ladle. (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.7). 8.

When it is said, "Sit first upon the womb, O thou with the tuft of hair," [the priest] places a white-colored stone upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick. Being a *suparṇa* (eagle), Garuḍa sits upon the earth. He establishes the fire upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* with three verses, or with two.

Having heard the call of the Hotṛ, "Sit first upon the woolly womb," [the Adhvaryu] places the animal-related materials (pāśukāḥ sambhārāḥ) while not yet having descended [into the pit], with the formula, "Thou art the life of all" (*viśvāyu-rasi*). For it is stated in the Śruti: "In that he collects these materials. They are placed below the fire, after the fire has been handed over to another [priest]. Because the fire is a modification of the *uttaravedi*, [he places them] with the formula, "Thou art the ash of Agni" (*agner bhasmāsi*), using the materials—guggulu resin, fragrant wood, wool, and tufts—while reciting the three verses beginning with, "Thou art the fair-winged Garuḍa" (*suparṇo 'si garutmān*), upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.

The establishment of the fire is performed with the two verses beginning "ravatyā" and "suparṇo 'si garutmān bhāsāntarikṣam āpṛṇa," or alternatively with the verse beginning "ājuhvāna. If there is no pause [in the recitation], then after the fire has been established in the previous manner, one pours the *upayamanī* sands to the north with the formula "agner asi purīṣam. || 9 ||

"O Agni, shine forth, kindled before us"—with these words he places a fuel-stick of *udumbara* wood; "we would worship thee in thy highest birth, O Agni"—with these words a stick of *vaikaṅkata* wood; "the wonderful [splendor] of Savitṛ, the most excellent"—with these words a stick of *śamī* wood. Some prescribe the *śamī* stick first and the *vaikaṅkata* stick afterwards. (Section 11) 12.5.10.

With the mantra *manuṣvat tvā* (VS 3.27), he performs the act of kindling (*upasamindhana*), because the kindling under discussion is for the purpose of kindling; with the modified mantra *pra iddho agne* (VS 3.28), the *audumbarī* wood is placed [on the fire]. With the modified mantra *vidhema te* (VS 3.29), [he places] the one made of *śamī* wood. The *śamī* wood is placed first, and the modified one is placed afterwards, situated within the *śara* grass. However, some read the text as "in every case, he places a fuel-stick (*samidh*)," [implying that the rule continues to apply]. 10.
With the verse "O Agni, bring that [sacrifice] today with horses," he offers the oblation using the Akṣarapaṅkti metre.
"Having offered two oblations with the verses, 'I offer consciousness, O Agni' and 'That horse today,' [he should proceed]," so says Āpastamba. || 11 ||

Having cleansed the *juhū* and the *sruva* ladles, and having filled the *sruk* with clarified butter taken four times, eight times, or twelve times, he offers the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verse, "Seven are... (RV 10.53.6).

Having filled the *cuca* ladle with clarified butter taken four times, eight times, or twelve times, one performs the ordinary *pūrṇāhuti*. Agni Saptavān is the deity. The meaning is that one should offer with that *juhū* ladle which is full of clarified butter taken twelve times.
While offering it, he meditates mentally on Agni from the quarters, thinking: "May he be here. || 13 ||

The meditation is: "May that Agni who is in the oblations be here by day. Then the Atimuktī verses: "May Agni lead the sacrifice... [1] He places a fuel-stick of Udumbara wood on the fire. [100] The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[12th Praśna].

Regarding the passages beginning with "not knowing," because of the instruction on the carrying forward of the fire (*praṇayana*) as in the *Paśubandha* sacrifice, according to that view, one should prepare the *uttaravedi* up to the sprinkling (*vyāghāraṇa*), deposit the materials belonging to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka-sambhāra*), and then those materials are piled up; thereafter, the *paridhis* are omitted. On this point also, Āpastamba says: "Having performed [the rites] up to the sprinkling of the altar" (*ĀpaŚS* 15.6.1). The phrase "together with the sprinkling of the altar" indicates an inclusive limit (*abhividhi*). Therefore, he states later that the Soma-related ritual acts, such as the spreading of the altar (*vedyāstaraṇa*), follow.

"He proceeds," it is said. He performs the subsequent tracing of the altar (*parigraha*) as in the case of the fire-altar (*agniciti*). Having performed everything up to the inspection (*anuvīkṣaṇa*), he brings a branch and drives away the calves for the *maitrāvaruṇī* curd-mixture (*payasyā*). Within the altar (*antarvedi*), he performs the actions up to the trimming of the leaves of the branch and the preparation of the *upaveṣa*. Having performed everything up to the smearing with cow-dung, he sprinkles the cauldron (*kumbhī*) and sprinkles outside the three-fold altar (*trivedi*) with ordinary water silently.
13. He commences the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the Vaiśvānara offering. Therein, we shall explain whatever is performed. 14.

He commences—that is, begins to perform—the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of Vaiśvānara Agni, which is the collection of its constituent parts: the gathering of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and the *prastara* bundle; when the *dhruvā* ladle is placed upon the *prastara*; the strewn grass, the fuel-sticks for the *āghāra* libation, the first *prayāja* and *anūyāja* fuel-sticks, the three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), and one fuel-stick [for the *sviṣṭakṛt*]; with the mantra "O Agni, bestowing life, do not walk among men," he places the implements used for cutting the fuel-sticks (*idhma-pravṛścana*). 14.
Having prepared the Veda, strewn around the fires, washed his hands, and spread out a layer of *ulapa* grass, he arranges the vessels according to their purpose.

Having prepared the altar, they sweep it; then the work of plastering the shed and the sanctuary is performed, as these were not previously done. Having strewn grass around the fires, he proceeds to perform the rites beginning with the washing of the hands. The meaning is that he employs the vessels according to their purpose, and does not set them out all together as is done in the New and Full Moon sacrifices. || 15 ||
He does not lead those who are already led. || 16 ||
Because of the absence of the liberations and so forth. || 16 ||
At the time of the offering, having prepared a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara, he prepares seven cakes on seven potsherds each for the Maruts.

There are twelve potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara and a seven-potsherd offering for the Maruts. However, some maintain that all the subsequent vessels—excluding the *prāśitra-haraṇa*, the *iḍā* vessel, and the *anvāhāryasthālī*—are the preceding ones. When the time for the pouring of the oblations arrives, having performed the pouring for Vaiśvānara, one should separately pour the seven portions for the Maruts into that same winnowing basket (*śūrpa*).
When treated with silence, the Maruts become submissive. || 18 ||

Because these are performed silently, they are called *vihoma*s (minor oblations). Therefore, the acts such as placing [the grains] near the fire (*upasādana*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and so forth; as well as threshing (*avahanan*), winnowing (*phalīkaraṇa*), washing (*prakṣālana*), looking at [the grains] (*avekṣaṇa*), purifying (*utpavana*), placing the potsherds (*kapālopadhāna*), putting [the vessel] on the fire (*adhiśvayaṇa*), and so on, are each performed separately and silently because they are performed silently.

He mixes [the flour with water] using waters purified by a *yajus* formula. Having poured away the residue of the rinsing-water after it has been covered, he proceeds with the formal summons (*saṃpreṣa*). Whatever else there is other than the kindling of the fires and the binding of the wife’s girdle, he issues the summons for that. [End of Section 12.5.20] *This concludes the fifth chapter of the Mahādevaśāstrī-compiled Prayogacandrikā commentary.*

When the flour has been ground, he mixes it with water purified by the *yajus*-formula. At the time of the formal summons (*saṃpraisha*), he will summon the wife; however, the summons is obligatory, yet the wife remains seated. 19–20.
Having performed that which was previously done prior to the taking of the clarified butter, he takes it from the *dhruvā* vessel itself.
At the time of taking the clarified butter, he takes it from the *dhruvā* vessel alone, because there are no principal offerings (*yājā*) or after-offerings (*anūyāja*).

Having consecrated the *prokṣaṇī* waters, having addressed the *brahman*, having sprinkled the altar, having poured out the remainder of the *prokṣaṇī* water, and having inserted the two strainers back [into the vessel], he sets down the *dhruvā* ladle and the *sruva* spoon. || 22 ||

According to the statement of Āpastamba, "One proceeds with the ritual acts beginning with the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the *prokṣaṇī* waters," it is to be done as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), because of the repeated injunction. Otherwise, the sprinkling of the altar (*vediprokṣaṇa*) would not be performed, as it is stated [elsewhere] that "the sprinkling is done silently" (*tuṣṇīkaṃ prokṣita*). Therefore, it is omitted. This is clearly seen in all cases of the *upasads*. At the time of spreading the grass, one spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) to the west of the fires. There is one kindling-stick for the *āghāra* libation. With the formula "Vītihotra," everything else is according to the archetype. He places the *dhruvā* ladle and the *sruva* spoon either on the *prastara* or on the *barhis*. || 22 ||
He concludes with the mantra "eṣā'sadaditi. || 23 ||
"May these two not be separated"—with this mantra, one consecrates the *dhruvā* ladle and the *sruva* spoon. || 23 ||
"Thou art Viṣṇu; the abode of Viṣṇu; [thou art] that which belongs to Prajāpati"—with these words he consecrates the clarified butter. (Section 12) 24.
"Thou art Viṣṇu"—this is the consecration of the clarified butter belonging to Dhruva. 24.
Having reached the Vaiśvānara [offering], he reaches the Māruta [offerings]. || 25 ||

The rites from the touching of the *kapāla* up to the touching of the *puroḍāśa* are performed as in the archetype (*prakṛti*); however, for the *māruta* offerings, they are performed silently (*tūṣṇīka*), like the modification of the *āgneya* offering.
He causes the announcement for Vaiśvānara to be made loudly. || 26 ||

Now follows the depositing of the *veda*, the strewing around the edge of the altar, and the preparation of the seat for the *hotṛ*. Then follow the *sāmidhenī* verses. The fanning with the *veda* and the pouring of the *dhruvā* libation take place. He does not give the command, "O *agnīdh*, [bring] the enclosing sticks. Even now, he does not rub the enclosing sticks nor the fire. Then follows the proclamation of the divine and human lineages (*pravara*). Nor are the *prayāja* offerings performed, nor is there clarified butter for them. Then the prohibition of the invocation (*āvāhana*) is made. Having performed the ritual, [he proceeds] with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings.

Having spread the base with clarified butter (upastīrya) and having taken portions of the entire Vaiśvānara cake, one silently takes the other sacrificial portions (avadānāni). From that point, the term "portions" (avadānāni) refers to the specific state [of the offering]. One performs the double sprinkling of clarified butter and offers the four-fold portion (caturavatta). Even from a medium pitch of voice, the announcement for the Vaiśvānara offering is heard loudly. || 26 ||
He offers the entire oblation without turning away. || 27 ||
The meaning is clear. || 27 ||

Sitting with his hand [held out], he offers the Māruta oblations, which are of such-and-such and other kinds, in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) by means of a group of many verses. (28) Having recited each preceding group, he offers with each subsequent one. (29) Having recited the last group—"Svatavān, Praghāsī, Sāṃtapana, Gṛhamedhī, Krīḍī, Sākī, and Urjiṣī"—he offers with the first [verse]. (30) *Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra*, Book 12, Chapter 5.30.

Having turned back the *māruta* offerings in a whisper and having offered to Vaiśvānara, the *darvihoma* oblations are performed. Having recited "īdṛṅ cānyādṛṅ ca," the offering is made with "śukrajyotiś ca. In all cases, the Maruts are the deity. Having recited "śukrajyotiś ca," the offering is made with "ṛjic ca. Having recited "ṛtanic ca," the offering is made with "dhuniś ca" according to the *Āraṇyaka*. Having recited "dhuniś ca," the offering is made with "ṛtadhā satyamdhā. Having recited "ṛtaś ca satyaś ca," the offering is made with "svatavāś ca."

Having recited "And the self-strong one," the oblation is made with "Such as these. Having recited "Such as these," the oblation is made with "Such and otherwise. Or, the oblation is performed by groups. Nevertheless, the fourth section belongs to the Āṇhya, and the sixth is the self-strong one. Or rather, he encircles [the fire] on all sides with the Māruta and Vaiśvānara verses. In the Āpastamba tradition, however, the sixth is "The self-strong one," and the oblation is made with "Measured together"; this is the connection (*anuṣaṅga*). There is no further recitation; the connection ends with "May the human [verses] follow, svāhā! at the conclusion of the connection.

Alternatively, there are five groups (*gaṇa*) recited in the *apratya* mantras; another group, "the Shaker" (*dhuni*) and "the Dark One" (*dhvānta*), is recited in the *Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa*; and one group beginning with "Self-strong" (*svatavān*) is mentioned in other Sūtras. Therefore, in the Brāhmaṇa, there are seven [groups], as seen in the number of sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*): "The Maruts are indeed seven groups; thus he wins the people group by group" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.7).

Regarding the recitation of mantras at the time of the *homa*, he prescribes a specific rule: "He offers oblation by repeating each group [of mantras] after the preceding group" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.4.7). When, having offered with the first group, he offers with the second group, he then recites the first group and subsequently offers with the second group.
