Likewise, having recited the second group, he should offer with the third group. (28, 29, 30)
Having offered the oblation with the words, "The divine hosts, the Maruts, follow Indra," he worships [him]. || 31 ||
The word "the sacrificer" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. ||31||

If he should desire, "May I destroy the ruling power (kṣatra) with the common people (viś)," he recites three or four words of the group of verses to be recited in the village (*grāmya-anuvākyā*), and offers the oblation with the remainder of the verses to be recited in the forest (*āraṇya-anuvākyā*). (32) Thus, for the first three [groups], it is as prescribed; for the village-recitation verses, as was done previously, so it is with the three subsequent groups. (33)

If he should desire, "May I destroy the common people (viś) by means of the ruling power (kṣatra)," then having placed six groups of syllables within the six intervals between the words of the *anuvākya* verse pertaining to the forest (*āraṇya*), and having muttered the *vākya* in the villages, he offers the remainder of the *vākya* with the forest-verse. [End of] Chapter 6. Thus, with the first three [verses], it is as recited; with the village-*anuvākya*, it is as before; likewise with the next three groups.

If the sacrificer should desire, "May the Kṣatriyas be more powerful than the Vaiśyas," then from the *prāma* section of the *anuvāka*, he should take three or four words—or even fewer—and the word *īc*. Even such [words] are subsequently mentioned in the *araṇye’nuvākyā*; beginning with the fifth sentence, or the fourth, the oblation (*homa*) is performed according to the *nāma-anuvākyā* (or *kośeṣeṇa*). Having thus performed the oblation with these three, the subsequent oblation in the *araṇye’nuvākyā* is performed with [those words] alone.

Just as previously [it was said], "having recited three or four words for each of the three groups," and so forth; in the same way, one should offer the subsequent [verses] with three [groups]. If one should desire, "May the Vaiśyas be more powerful than the Kṣatriyas," then, having offered according to the recited text starting from the beginning with each group of three, six groups are inserted into the six intervals between the words of the *Āraṇyaka* section. The group beginning with *dhuniśca* and *īdṛṅca* is thus called a group.

Having recited "dhvāntaś ca," one says "śukrajyotiś ca" and "dhvanaś ca ṛtajic ca. Having recited "dhvanayaś ca ṛtaś ca," one says "vilimpaca. Having recited "vilimpaca," one says "īdṛkṣāsaḥ. Having recited "vikṣipa," there is again an oblation with the *Āraṇyaka* alone. Just as with the preceding [verses], the oblation is performed with the subsequent groups as well. The author of the Bhāṣya states that the Vaiśvānara [oblation] concludes with the Māruta oblations. "Ugraś ca dhuniś ca" is an optional [variant]. || 32 || 33 ||
He does not give the summons; he does not wipe [the ladle]; he does not offer the after-offerings. || 36 ||

He does not issue the *saṃpraisha* command, "O Brahman, let us proceed," and so forth. He does not wipe the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) nor the fire. He does not go toward the after-offerings (*anūyāja*). At this time, having taken the clarified butter for the sake of the after-offerings, the rule is that everything must be performed except for what has been prohibited. Because the Vaiśvānara sacrifice is a modification (*vikāra*) of the Āgneya sacrifice, the Sūtra-author has stated accordingly: "He does not issue the *saṃpraisha* and he does not wipe. And [he recites]: "Having offered to the Maruts, [he offers] the *nāriṣṭha* oblations; this is the oblation for Vaiśvānara."

Due to the loss of purpose (*arthalopa*), there is the omission of the rites beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and ending with the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*). The spreading (*vyūhana*) is performed with the two *vājavatī* verses. If the *prastara* has been used for the sake of the *dhruvā*, then [the procedure continues] as in the archetype up to the end of the pouring together (*saṃsrāva*). But if it has not been so used, then [it continues] until the throwing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi-praharaṇa*), because of the statement that the *sūktavāka* is the offering prayer (*yājyā*). From there, it proceeds as in the archetype up to the end of the pouring together. Then, from the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings onwards until the feeding of the Brahmins, it is as in the archetype. || 36 ||

If one should desire of a Kṣatriya, "May he fall from his own abode," then for him, one should dismember the chariot-stand or the fire-altar belonging to that group of verses recited in the forest; this is a ritual procedure not connected with a sacrifice. (Section 13) ||37||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the twelfth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.

If one should desire that a king or the royal kinsmen be slain by their own kṣatra-power, or that other kṣatriyas be slain by their own [power], or that he [the king] should fall away from his [position] and be led by enemies to another country—then, in the forest, he should recite [the mantra] for three nights or for a day and night. [Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram—12th Praśna]

"Go to hell!"—with these words he causes the fire to be carried [on the cart]. If this cart used for carrying the chariot is indeed that very cart, then he makes it defective by means of the *anuvākyā* in the forest. Or rather, "some other part of it. This rule, not connected with the sacrifice, is for all purposes. Thus ends the fifth chapter in the twelfth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*, compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. *** **Note:** The phrase *tadaraṇye'nuvākye(ke)na vyaṅgaṃ karoti* appears to contain a textual corruption or archaic usage. A more standard interpretation might be *tad araṇye'nūcyena vyaṅgaṃ karoti* ("he makes it defective by means of what is recited in the forest"), though the precise ritual application remains subject to specific Vedic exegetical tradition. The concluding sentence clarifies that this is a general injunction (*vidhi*) applicable beyond the immediate sacrificial context. The final title identifies the work as the *Prayogacandrikā*, a practical manual for ritual performance.
12.6 Now begins the sixth chapter in the twelfth book.

He offers the Vasordhārā oblation with clarified butter using a ladle made of Udumbara wood, reciting "O Agni and Viṣṇu, being in harmony" and following it with "May strength be mine, may impulse be mine," continuing the stream of offerings without interruption until the conclusion of the mantra.

When the Vaiśvānara [offering] is completed, he offers a fourfold-drawn portion [of ghee] with the verse, "O Agni and Viṣṇu, being of one accord... (RV 7.99.7). He takes a ladle made of Udumbara wood, as long as the span of his arms, smeared with clay, provided with a pouring-spout at the back, and fills it with clarified butter; thus says Āpastamba. (ĀpŚS 17.6–17)

The Audumbarī ladle is made of Udumbara wood, measuring one *vyāyāma* (the distance between the tips of the outstretched arms) or four *aratnis* in length. It is smeared with clay so that it does not burn; subsequently, its pouring-hole (*āsecanam*) is on the western side of the handle. Having filled the mouth of the ladle—which is held horizontally—with clarified butter, a single *pūrṇāhuti* (full oblation) is offered, beginning with the mantra "vājaśca me. The stream [of ghee] must be continuous and uninterrupted throughout the entire recitation of the mantras until their conclusion.

"Bhuvanaḥ svāhā" and "Adhipatiḥ svāhā"—thus there is the utterance of *svāhā* in each mantra. He offers the *ardhendrāṇi* oblations ending with "Vānaśca me svāhā" and "Prasavaśca me svāhā," for the Śruti states: "He offers twelve sets of twelve" (*Leṅga Saṃhitā* 5.4.8). However, the Commentator [Śabara] maintains that the *svāhā* occurs only at the end. This follows the opinion of the author of the Sūtras. The Mīmāṃsakas, however, hold that from the word "Marutvān" onwards, there is a continuous stream [of offerings].

For instance, in the injunction "he offers a continuous stream of *vasordhārā*," because of the word "continuous" (*saṃtata*), and because that term denotes simultaneity (*sāhitya*), and because simultaneity requires more than one [element], while the ritual action (*karman*) is singular, this simultaneity is expressed as a conjunction of actions. Therefore, in this case, there is a simultaneous occurrence (*saṃnipāta*) of the mantra and so forth with the action and so forth. This would indeed be so if it were a single action; however, here there are twelve distinct sets of twelve offerings, as indicated by the number [in the text "he offers twelve times twelve"]. It is the non-interruption (*aviccheda*) of these [actions] that is denoted by the word "continuous."

Because [the act of] offering (*juhoti*) is already included among those [actions], there is no requirement for the simultaneity (*sāhitya*) of the mantra and the ritual action, as the mantra is not explicitly enjoined [as a simultaneous factor]. Furthermore, the term *saṃtatam* (continuous) applies even when there is no interruption, and not only in the sense of simultaneity. Therefore, in this case as well, the previous [interpretation] alone should hold. With the desire to explain the sequence, he prescribes:

"If one should desire, 'May I cut off his life-breaths and his food,' he should offer the oblations for him with intervals (*vigrāham*). If one should desire, 'May I cut off his life-breaths... [End of section 1.05, from the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary by Mahādeva Śāstrī].
Thinking, "May I not break the continuity," one should offer oblations for him in a continuous stream. ||2||

Thinking, "May I sever the vital breaths and the food of this sacrificer," the Adhvaryu priest, while hating him, should offer this oblation by separating the mantra in the middle. However, he who desires the continuity of the vital breaths and of food should offer the oblation continuously. This is the logical principle for the purpose of prohibition; [the term] *avayukāmaḥ* refers to one who desires disjunction, according to the author of the Bhāṣya. || 2 ||

Whatever clarified butter (ājya) may remain, having cooked Brahma-rice (brahmaudana) in it, he should feed four Adhvaryu priests and give them four cows as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). Having cooked rice sufficient for four śarāvas, he feeds him that as a side-dish (vyañjana).

Whatever clarified butter (*ājya*) remains in that *sruva* spoon, in that very butter a four-*śarāva* measure of boiled rice (*odana*) is cooked. According to the common worldly principle, four Brāhmaṇas should consume it; this is established by the specific instruction regarding "four Brāhmaṇas. However, the author of the *Bhāṣya* maintains that the cooking takes place on the *gārhapatya* fire. A "four-*śarāva*" is a four-*mallaka* measure. Having cooked the rice, the clarified butter remaining from what was left over after the oblations—which was not struck [by the ladle] as a continuous stream—serves as a condiment for that rice.

Although the mention of "Brāhmaṇas" is without distinction, nevertheless, only those who are ordinary [priests], such as the Adhvaryu and others, are intended. The sacrificer should give four cows to those who have eaten the *prāśitra* (the portion of food) and those who have finished their meal. Even if a side-dish (*vyañjana*) is eaten with clarified butter that has already been drawn out, it is nonetheless cooked in clarified butter. 3–4.

He offers the *vājaprasavīya* oblations. There are seven cultivated plants and seven wild plants. Having liquefied the various foods separately, he offers each kind of food with one verse at a time using a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, reciting fourteen verses beginning with "This impulse of strength (*vāja*) flows well. (5)

The collection of oblations in which the word *vājaprasava* occurs is the *vājaprasavīya*; he offers that. Therein are seven sacrificial portions (*māṣyāḥ*) of herbs and the seven previously mentioned *āravāḥ*. The author of the Bhāṣya states that one should prepare separate food-offerings for the substances of both domestic and wild animals by means of clarified butter (*ājya*). The rule is that they should be prepared in such a way that they become liquid. Some perform the offering after making the uncooked items liquid with clarified butter.

Others, however, maintain that the word *anna* is also found in the sense of "sowing," as they say, "he sows food upon food. That is not correct; it will be explained later. The word *anna* applies to that [which is produced] as "that food. Having offered the domestic [grains] with each verse using a ladle made of *udumbara* wood—beginning with "The impulse of strength (*vāja*) has impelled this"—he then offers the wild [grains] with the verse, "Strength (*vāja*) for us, sevenfold. Some hold that the seven domestic [grains] are sesame, beans, rice, barley, millet, lentils, and wheat.

Veṇu, śyāmāka, and so forth are the wild grains cited as examples. There are fourteen oblations for the sake of the abundance of both types of grain. He prescribes the offering of each one with a single mantra: "He offers of every kind of food" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.9). This oblation is performed in this manner for the purpose of obtaining those respective foods. To set aside the *juhū* ladle which is obtained by general rule (*codaka*), he prescribes another means: "He offers with a *sruva* spoon made of *udumbara* wood" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.9). || 5 ||

I shall now praise Food, the one of great laws and mighty power, by whose force Trita shattered Vṛtra limb from limb. O sweet Food, O honeyed Food, we have chosen you; be our protector. Come to us, O Food, as a gracious one with your gracious aids—bringing delight, free from malice, a kind friend, most auspicious and without guile. These juices of yours, O Food, are spread throughout the realms, resting like the winds in heaven.

These [gifts] of yours, O *pitu* (food), you bestow; these most sweet things of yours, O *pitu*, flow forth like chariots with well-fed horses and strong necks. In you, O *pitu*, the mind of the great gods is set. By your beautiful banner, he struck the dragon with his power. When you, O *pitu*, have gone there, clothe yourself among the mountains. Right here, O honeyed *pitu*, come to us for our enjoyment. Whatever portion of the waters and the plants we consume, O *vātāpi*, become fatness for us.

"O Soma, that portion of yours which consists of milk, of curd, and of barley—O Vātāpi, become fat! O herb, become gruel; be fat, O kidney-like [portion], O healer! O Vātāpi, become fat! Having offered with the words, "Thee, the feast-companion for the gods; thee, the feast-companion for us," he should pour the remnants from each offering into the vessel. (Section 14) 6.
Having offered [the oblations] with the *hunvā* formula, he pours down the remainder of the *saṃpāta* from the southern ladle for all the foods.
Or alternatively, he should make the fuel-stick from that food of which he first offers an oblation.
This is a restatement of what is taught in another recensional branch (śākhā).

He sprinkles with the remnants [of the oblations] the sacrificer, who is seated upon the Audumbarī post at the sacrificer’s station, while he maintains contact with the fire on the black antelope skin. Or, on the right wing of that same black antelope skin, he sprinkles a Brāhmaṇa; on a tiger skin, a Rājanya; and on a goat skin, a Vaiśya who desires cattle. Some authorities prescribe this as a regular (obligatory) rite.

"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I consecrate you with the sovereignty of Bṛhaspati"—thus for a Brāhmaṇa. "I consecrate Indra with sovereignty"—thus for a Rājanya. "I consecrate Agni with sovereignty"—thus for a Vaiśya. Standing to the east, facing west, he sprinkles him who is seated to the west, facing east, from the head down to the mouth, allowing the water to flow down along the face.

On the southern side as well, having established an *audumbara* throne at the place where the worship was performed with the *prajāpater hṛdaya* mantra, he spreads upon that throne a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) with its neck toward the east and the hair facing upward. Having seated the Brāhmaṇa upon that black antelope skin so that he is sitting facing the east, and having stood while holding onto him, he sprinkles him with the remaining residues of the oblations. For a Kṣatriya, he does so upon a tiger skin.

With a goat-skin, one consecrates a Vaiśya; with a black antelope skin, a Kṣatriya who desires spiritual luster—and likewise a Vaiśya; and with a ram’s skin, even a Brāhmaṇa who desires prosperity. Having recited the mantra beginning with "Of the god," he sprinkles a Brāhmaṇa with the words: "With both hands, I sprinkle you with the sovereignty of Agni. Having recited as before, he sprinkles a Kṣatriya with the words: "I sprinkle you with the sovereignty of Indra. Having recited as before, he sprinkles a Vaiśya with the words: "I sprinkle you with the sovereignty of Bṛhaspati."

"‘Some recite the reversal of the mantras’ (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 17.4), so says Āpastamba. The author of the Bhāṣya, however, states: ‘He consecrates him with the formula: “By the impulse of the divine Savitṛ, by Sarasvatī the controller of speech, with the controller’s control, may I consecrate you with sovereign power. He is consecrated at the Māhendra hymn. Just as in the Agnicayana, this very Vājapeya reading is shown; but here, there is a direct textual recitation.’”

"I consecrate you with the sovereignty of Agni," he says; "this indeed is the equal [consecration] of Agni" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 5.6.3)—thus it is read explicitly in the Brāhmaṇa. Standing facing west while the sacrificer sits facing east, the Adhvaryu, having smeared [the vessel], causes the remnant of the oblation to flow down as far as the mouth. Regarding this, Āpastamba shows the greatness of the one thus consecrated: "They say that he must indeed not be addressed; for one who has performed the Soma sacrifice does not descend to anyone" (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 17.7.6).

Regarding this, other exponents of the Veda belonging to different recensions say: "Only this much remains to be performed for the consecrated one. Once consecrated, the sacrificer does not descend before any elder, even one he has seen; throughout his life, he should not rise [in salutation]. This is the rule for the consecration. 10, 11, 12, 13.
Having filled a ladle made of Udumbara wood with milk or curds from a black cow that has a white calf, he offers an oblation with the verse, "Night and Dawn... (RV 1.72.1). ||14||
Agni is the deity; the oblation of curd is found in another Vedic branch. 14.

With the six sections beginning with "ṛtāṣāḍ ṛtadhāmā," he offers twelve *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations using a ladle filled by drawing [the ghee] ten times. Having recited each section, he offers the first oblation with the formula "svāhā to him" (*tasmai svāhā*). He offers the subsequent oblation with the formula "svāhā to them" (*tābhyaḥ svāhā*). With the verse "O Lord of the World" (*bhuvanasya pate*), [he offers] at the front of the chariot. [Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram—Book 12, Question 604...]

He offers five oblations. (Khaṇḍa 15) Or he offers ten times in successive turns upon the Āhavanīya fire over the chariot-head which is being held there. According to some, he offers using the chariot-head itself. 17. They carry the chariot, with its contents collected together, to the Adhvaryu’s dwelling. They lead after it three horses, or four according to some. 18. He gives those [horses] along with the chariot to the Adhvaryu. 19.

He offers eleven oblations of desire (*kāma*) in six turns with the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* mantras, ending each turn with the words "atāṣāṛtadhāmā, ūoṃ nāma. Having uttered [the mantra] once, he says "to him, svāhā!"—this is the first oblation. With "to those two, svāhā! comes the subsequent oblation. The division is the same for the following turns as well: "Vastāṣāṛtadhāmā Agni is the Gandharva; may he protect this spiritual power (*brahman*) and political power (*kṣatra*); to him, svāhā!"

"May the herbs, the Apsarases named Ūrj, protect this Brahman and Kṣatra; to them, Svāhā!"—let there not be such a connection of meaning in this division. Because of the force of the traditional recitation (*paripāṭha*), it is not proper to perform the mantra otherwise than as it is recited, unless there is a specific reason. One does not infer [a change] because it expresses meanings, as in the case of the *kṛti* suffix; therefore, a modification (*ūha*) is made in the *vikṛti* (modified sacrifice) because of the presence of the *chandas* (metre) as in the *prakṛti* (archetype). "O Lord of the World"—this is the locative case among the synonyms.

"‘Bhuvanasya pataḥ’—with this [verse] he offers the seventh oblation," so says Āpastamba. This scriptural injunction prescribes the ritual sequences (*paryāyas*). Another scriptural injunction, "He offers the thirteenth oblation," prescribes the individual offerings (*āhutis*). Thus, because the two scriptural statements have the same purpose, this explains that following each sequence, the first offering is made with "Svāhā to him" (*tasmai svāhā*), and the subsequent ones with "Svāhā to them" (*tābhyaḥ svāhā*). In this way, there are five offerings at the front of the chariot.

Some say: "One should offer oblations while the chariot-seat (*sthaviśira*) is being carried. When five oblations have been offered with the *daśāmiva* formulas, they lead [the chariot] to the Adhvaryu’s dwelling while it is being carried above the Āhavanīya fire at the front of the chariot. Carrying it while holding it up, they do not pull it; they lead three horses behind the chariot. If it is a six-horse chariot, there are three yokes. Or four, if it is a four-horse chariot. He gives the three horses and the chariot to the Adhvaryu.

The acceptance of horses is separate, as is that of the chariot; nor is there modification (*ūha*) [of the mantra], because mantras serve both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*). For the sacrificer, when the occasion arises, [offers] either three mares or two mares. 15 || 16 || 17 || 18 || 19 ||
"Thou art the ocean, thou art possessed of wind"—with these three names of the wind, he offers oblations with joined palms, or with a fold of black antelope skin.

"Thou art the ocean, possessed of breath"—with this [formula], the wind itself is offered three times with joined palms (*añjali*). For it is not possible to take a portion (*avadāna*) of this wind. However, the Commentator [Śabara] says: "Three offerings of clarified butter (*ājya*) with joined palms. Or rather, the offering to the wind is made using the fold of a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), and not with joined palms. The instruction also states that the wind itself is offered here. [End of Section 20–21, Chapter 1, together with the *Payogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 109

With the five sections beginning, "O Agni, come from the ocean," he offers five oblations of clarified butter, moving clockwise and proceeding toward each direction; with the final section, he faces the east and offers the oblation in the center. With the six sections beginning, "Thou art the converging one, the eastern quarter," he offers six great oblations of curds mixed with honey. He offers the three *ruca* oblations as prescribed for the *sarpa* offerings, with the verses beginning, "Those splendors of thine, O Agni, which are in the sun. || 22 ||

With the verse *agna udadhe*, he offers five oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) without joining the formulas. It is said that "Vāyu is the source" refers to the oblations of clarified butter. With the formula *samīcī nāmāsi prācī dik*, he offers six oblations of serpents (*sarpāhuti*) using curd mixed with honey. Having circumambulated without joining the formulas, he makes offerings toward each direction facing the fire. He offers the fifth and sixth oblations while facing eastward, subsequently from behind and above; this means he performs them while moving around [the fire]. With the formula *hetayo nāma stha*, he offers the six great oblations (*mahāhuti*), just as the oblations of serpents were offered with curd mixed with honey. [He offers] the three *ruca* verses beginning with *yāste agne*. 22.
Having offered five *arkāhuti* oblations with the mantra "suvarṇagharma svāhā," || 23 ||
Afterwards, he offers oblations of *arka* with clarified butter alone.
He then proceeds with the ritual acts beginning with the strewing of the altar.

Then, having strewn it thickly with sacrificial grass (bārhas) facing eastward—according to the statement of Vaikhānasa—and having performed the Saumika rites beginning with the spreading [of the altar] up to the pouring out [of the earth] for the hearths (dhiṣṇiya), one should carry out the piling of the fire-altar (cayana) after having prescribed the rules ending with the passage: "Those who are visible from all sides may pass through. This concludes the section on the piling [of the altar] along with the sowing and the atonement. 24.

With this Anuvāka beginning with "mamāgne," he piles the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths with bricks, using one mantra for each brick. He completes each *dhiṣṇiya* with a single mantra. He lays down eight bricks at the Āgnīdhrīya hearth; according to some, there is a ninth, a stone. At the Hotrīya hearth, there are twelve or twenty-four; at the Praśāstrīya, eleven or twenty-one; six at the Mārjālīya; and eight in the others. "For thy glory the mountain opened wide; O Aṅgiras, thou didst release the stall of the cows."

"O Bṛhaspati, with Indra as our ally, we have pushed back the ocean enveloped in darkness. "O Bṛhaspati, that which the enemy deserves to surpass... "Thus, O Father..."—with these three verses addressed to Brahman, he performs the rite in the seat of Brahman. "Yama has supported the earth; Yama has supported this entire world. To Yama belongs all this..."—thus ends the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, in the twelfth book.

That which stood firm, protected by the breath of life—just as there are five, six, or fifteen seers—he who knows Yama should speak; for as the single seer understands it: "With the *trikadrukas* he falls; the six wide ones, this one great [space]; the *gāyatrī*, the *triṣṭubh*, and all the meters—all these are placed in Yama. With these three verses addressed to Yama, [one should worship] at the *mārjālīya* fire: "We, seeking success through sacrifice, invoke for our protection the fierce Rudra, the fulfiller of the rite, the wise one."

Far from us be his divine wrath; we choose instead his gracious favor. May we obtain your favor through sacrifice to the gods, O bounteous Rudra, ruler of heroes! Being well-disposed toward us, grant prosperity to our people; let our heroes remain unharmed. We offer this oblation to you.

With the three verses addressed to Rudra beginning, "Be gracious to us, O Rudra, and grant us joy," he gratifies the oblation at the *cātvāla* pit, saying: "Make the oblation ready, prepare the oblation, cook the oblation, boil the oblation; you are the oblation; for the sake of the oblation, for the sake of the oblations, sit in the oblation. With the eight [verses] at the *śāmitra* fire, he says: "O preparer of the oblation... and with the three verses addressed to Varuṇa beginning, "May your wrath depart from us," "Up from the highest," and "That I implore of you, praising you with prayer," they proceed with the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath). He throws the broken pieces, the black ones, and the *lakṣmaṇā* plants onto the rubbish heap (*utkara*), as well as the remaining [portions].

"O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations"—with this *anuvāka*, according to some, one brick is laid down for each *ṛc*, with a mantra for each. However, according to another scriptural tradition (*śrutyantaram*), "those with golden hair set aside each hearth (*dhiṣṇiya*) with a single *ṛc*. But for the Taittirīyas, after stating, "As for the fact that he lays down the *vihavyā*s," it says, "he lays them down on the *hotṛ*'s hearth" (*TaiSaṃ* 5.4.11). The use of the plural "the *vihavyā*s" indicates that at each [hearth] he builds using many bricks, equal in number to the measure of the hearth.

Regarding the stone in the Āgnīdhrīya fire-altar, there is no fixed rule that the eight bricks must be square or long; rather, the laying down is performed with nine verses beginning with "māgnaye" (RV 10.188.1–9). However, the stone is placed in the middle, and one verse is omitted. After the bricks have been laid, the piling proceeds in order: the Hotrīya, Prāśāstrīya, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsīya, Pautrīya, Neṣṭrīya, and Acchāvākīya hearths; thereafter follow the Brahmasadana and Mārjālīya hearths.

When there are twelve *hotrīyas*, then the fifth and the tenth [verses] are repeated twice. When there are sixteen, then the fifth is repeated four times and the tenth as well. When there are twenty-one, then each [verse] is repeated twice, but the last one three times. When there are twenty-four—[this sūtra is found in both the Vyāsa and Pustaka manuscripts]—then [the procedure is as follows]. [Note: In manuscript *ga*, it says "The teachers, however" (*ācāryāstu*). [End of] Chapter [Number], together with the commentary *Śyogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 111.

The fifth [verse] and the tenth are repeated eight times; in this way one should complete the count. There are eleven bricks for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s hearth, six for the Mārjālīya, and eight each for the other Dhiṣṇiya hearths. Regarding the laying down [of these], even though they are not specifically prescribed, the Dhiṣṇiyas may be either square or circular. Some, however, say that in cases of modifications of qualities, they are circular.

For each of those hearths (*dhiṣṇiya*), as many pebbles (*śarkarā*) as there are bricks to be laid down—including those for the *pāraśrita*—are likewise used for the purpose of surrounding them. Having performed the laying of the *acchāvāka*’s hearth and having laid five bricks in the seat of the Brahman, he lays the sixth with the verse beginning "vihavyās tava śriye" (VS 15.28). He lays the seventh with "bṛhaspate ati yad aryo arhāt" (VS 15.30), and the eighth with "bṛhaspateḥ sam ajayat" (VS 15.31). Having laid the *vihavyā* verses on the *mārjālīya* hearth, he lays three more with the verse "yamo dādhāra" (VS 15.62) repeated thrice.

Having placed five *vihavyā* bricks in the *cātvāla*, the sixth is with the verse "tveṣam" (VS 17.89). The seventh is with "asyāśyāmate" (VS 17.90). The eighth in the *cātvāla* is with "mṛḍā no rudra" (VS 16.2). In the place of the *śamitṛ*, eight are placed with the *yajus* formulas beginning "havyaṃ prīṇīhi" (VS 17.91–98). Then, having gone to the place of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), one places five *vihavyā* bricks; then one lays down three with "ava te heḍa" (VS 13.24), "uduttamaṃ" (VS 13.25), and "tattvā yāmi" (VS 13.26). Having first performed the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*), the laying down of the bricks follows here at the *avabhṛtha*; the performance of the *avabhṛtha* together with its subsidiaries takes place at that time.

The Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), however, [states]: "One offers oblations upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the stability of the offerings. Since the bricks are a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) for the sacrificial grass, they are employed at that very time; they are not placed at this time. "At this time" refers to the logical rule (*nyāya*). Even though they have been placed at this time, as substitutes for the grass, the grass is discarded by this very [act]. Those bricks which are broken, black, or have some mark but are not red everywhere—these he throws into the rubbish-heap (*utkara*). He also throws into the rubbish-heap those remaining bricks that possess [defective] qualities. || 25 || 26 ||

Having performed that which precedes the erecting of the sacrificial post, he either erects a single post or eleven posts. Of these, he raises the one standing nearest the fire (the *agniṣṭha*) on the previous day.

That which occurs prior to the erection of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is the preliminary rite (*pūrva-karma*). [The formula] "O Lord of the Paths, homage be to you; do not harm me"—with these words he approaches it, and so forth, as previously described, having consecrated the clarified butter (*ājya*) according to the unmodified procedure of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. Although there are eleven posts, the measurement is nevertheless by means of the altar (*vedi*) alone, and not by the axle of a chariot. Or he makes a single post. At the time of the *Agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, there are eleven [posts], measured by the altar according to the ritual rules for the *Ekādaśina* set.

In the case of one who has piled the fire-altar (*agniciti*), the measurement of the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) is restricted to that which is commensurate with the altar (*vedi*); thus, the measurement by the axle of a chariot (*rathākṣavimāna*) is not obtained for those posts. That post which stands nearest the fire (*agniṣṭha*) he erects on the previous day at the time of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice. How is the rule of being commensurate with the altar obtained? It is stated again: "But those [posts] which, starting from the *agniṣṭha*, are raised after the *āśvina* cup has been drawn. This is because the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) share the same time as the principal (*pradhāna*). Or rather, it is at the very time of the *agnīṣomīya*. Even those who divide the altar into eleven parts starting from the *agniṣṭha*—this is the rule for the one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*). 27–28.

Either at this very point, or on the following day, having offered the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, he subsequently offers the oblations of the Devasū sacrifice, beginning with "To Agni Gṛhapati," according to the traditional recitation. (Khaṇḍa 17) The *Sviṣṭakṛt* and *Iḍā* portions for both the animal-cake and the oblations of the Devasū are common. 12.6.30.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the twelfth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.

The meaning of *ahīna* is "on the morrow" (*śvas*). Or rather, the raising of as many sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) as there are animals to be immolated on the morrow. For example, in the *dvirātra* (two-night rite), five [animals] are immolated on the first day and six on the following. In the *trirātra* (three-night rite), however, there are three animals on the first day, but the raising of only two posts occurs; the animal for Agni (*āgneya*) is immolated at the *agniṣṭha* post itself. On the second day, there are four posts and four animals, and likewise on the third. In this manner, the division is applied elsewhere among the *ahīna* rites as well. That, moreover, is the direct division.

If there were to be a set of eleven sacrificial posts (yūpaikādaśinī), the raising [of the posts] would occur on subsequent days and not on the first day, because the post standing near the fire (agnīṣṭha) already exists. On the days starting from the second, one post is raised each day. In long-duration sacrifices (dīrghasatra), only the animal is repeated and not the raising of the posts, because they have already been raised. Furthermore, due to the injunction of an option stating "or on the morrow," the raising is permitted even in rituals such as the Virātra at the time of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.

Since the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma serves the purpose of all the Soma sacrifices, either all the animals of the *ekādaśinī* group are tied to a single sacrificial post (*yūpa*), or that post belongs to them alone as the final one. At the very time of the offering to Agni and Soma, it is encircled with two ropes. There is a sacrificial chip (*svaru*) for each animal, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating, "He pierces the animals with the sacrificial chips."

Having offered the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma, he offers eight oblations to the divine powers (*devasū*): "He offers a cake on eight potsherds of black rice to Agni Gṛhapati; a *caru* of millet (*śyāmāka*) to Soma Vanaspati; a cake on twelve potsherds of quick-growing rice to Savitṛ Satyaprasava; a *caru* of *gavidhuka* seeds to Rudra Paśupati; a *caru* of wild rice (*nīvāra*) to Bṛhaspati Vācaspati; [and a cake] to Indra Jyeṣṭha."

"One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds of *mahāvrīhi* rice to Mitra the True, a pap of *āmba* grains to Varuṇa the Lord of Dharma, and a pap of barley to Aryaman" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.8.10). Those that ripen in exactly sixty days are the *āśutrīhyaḥ*. The *mahāvrīhi* has large grains. The *āmbas* are a specific kind of grain; some say they are lotus seeds. In this context, if a Yajurvedic Hotṛ is present, [the mantra is] "O Agni, you are the great... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā).

• 3–4 11) The *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses mentioned in this *anuvāka* are to be taken [for the animal sacrifice]. However, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* portions are the same; because the *paśupuroḍāśa* is the primary offering, the *sviṣṭakṛt* has Agni as its deity, and thus it applies to the *devasū* offerings as well. Furthermore, the consumption of the *iḍā* is performed with Maitrāvaruṇa as the sixth [participant]. || 29 || 30 || Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*, compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.
12.7 Now begins the seventh chapter of the twelfth book.
At the time for the animal sacrifice, he dedicates eleven animals to a single sacrificial post, or to eleven posts.

"When the time for the animal sacrifice has arrived, [the priest] says, 'Bring the animal. He dedicates the Savanīya animal to Agni. Thus says Āpastamba (ĀpaŚrSū 15.2). Having encircled the sacrificial post with the cord in the prescribed manner, the seasonal animals (*ṛtupaśu*) are also obtained; their demonstration is in the seventh chapter."—This is accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.

Regarding the mention of the *āgneya* [animal]: the author of the Bhāṣya, however, maintains that the *āgneya* alone is obtained in the *ukthya* and other sacrifices across all ritual forms (*saṃsthā*) because of its re-enactment; yet this does not harmonize with other recensional branches (*śākhā*). It harmonizes only as being intended to demonstrate the seasonal animal-sacrifices (*ṛtupaśu*). As for the phrase "or in the eleven," it is because of the re-enactment stating, "one erects [the post] measured by the altar. Furthermore, after censuring the separation of the sacrificial posts in the case of the eleven by saying, "If one were to erect the eleven separately," the unity of the post for the eleven is then enjoined.

Regarding the term *ekādaśinī*, they apply it specifically to that [sacrifice] in which there is a distinction of sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), as in the Śruti: "This *ekādaśinī* is indeed a gathering of forests; it is capable. For the Śruti says: "He sets up the *pātnīvata* post facing westward, to support the sacrifice and for its stability. It is not the case that the *pātnīvata* belongs to a group of eleven animals (*paśvekādaśinī*); rather, it belongs to a set of eleven posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*) alone, since all other posts have animals tied to them. Having thus stated the plurality of the posts, the *upaśaya* (the lying-down post) is also established as a post by the injunction regarding the animal for the *upaśaya*.

It is dependent upon the distinction [of the sacrificial posts]. Therefore, it does not occur in the case of the *ekādaśina* animals tied to a single post, nor in the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice. This has also been stated by Kātyāyana: "The *upaśaya* and the *pātnīvata* [post] exist only in the *yūpaikādaśinī*, not in the *pañcaikādaśinī*. Consequently, in a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*) outside the *soma* sacrifice, because there is no [single] post consolidated there, there is no *pātnīvata*; however, the *upaśaya* is performed because it is contingent upon the distinction of the posts. It is said that the single post is obtained only in the *agnicityā* (the piling of the fire-altar), and it is prescribed therein.

In other groups, however, which exist outside the Tantra, there is indeed a distinction of sacrificial posts (yūpa), because of the indicative mark [in the scripture]: "If one should sacrifice at three sacrificial posts. || 1 ||
At the morning pressing, he touches the fire with the three verses beginning, "I yoke Agni with power and ghee."

Before the Prātaranuvāka, having brought down the Soma onto the pressing-stones, he touches [the stones] with the three verses beginning with "I yoke Agni" (*agniṃ yunajmi*). He thus yokes the fire for the purpose of carrying the sacrifice; however, he does not touch [it] at the end of the mantra. Having stated the fault [that would arise] if one were to recite all five [verses], the author of the Sūtra himself will later state that the touching during the Yajñāyajñīya stotra is indeed a "yoking," using the two verses beginning with "Homage be [to you], do not harm me" (*namo astu mā mā hiṃsīḥ*). This touching is precisely what constitutes the yoking.

At the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), having looked at a golden vessel filled with honey weighing a hundred mānas, which has been prepared, with the verse "The bright [face] of the gods," and having caused it to be smelled by a horse at midday, he gives it to the Brahman priest.

When the time for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has arrived, having performed the ritual act with the formula "tataḥ" (thence), the sacrificer looks at a golden vessel filled with honey made from a *śatamāna* weight of gold, while reciting the verse "citraṃ devānām. Having caused it to be touched by a horse (or having caused the transaction to be made), he gives that golden vessel to the Brahman priest. Its acceptance is governed by the formula "āye hiraṇyam" (Gold has come), because it is made of gold. He gives the golden vessel full of honey; thus, the acceptance is of the vessel, not of the honey. || 3 ||
One should give auspicious sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Adhvaryu priest.

If he piles [the fire-altar], he gives to the *adhvaryu* a beautiful, well-formed, and highly valuable [cow], provided that he piles it. Thus it is said in the *Brāhmaṇa*: "Indeed, the sacrificer himself should pile this [altar]. If someone other than he were to pile it, he would not satisfy him with sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). He who piles his fire should satisfy him with sacrificial gifts; thus he gratifies Agni. (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa) The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[12th Praśna]: [The sacrificer] gives to the *adhvaryu* a beautiful, well-formed, and highly valuable [cow] if he piles [the altar]. And so it is stated in the *Brāhmaṇa*: "Verily, the sacrificer alone should pile this [altar]. If another were to pile it for him, he would not satisfy him with sacrificial gifts. He who piles his fire should satisfy him with sacrificial gifts; thereby he gratifies Agni. (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa)

(Saṃhitā 5.6.9) Thus, the sacrificer alone should perform the act of piling the fire-altar (*cayana*), because the *adhvaryu*’s mantras are connected [to this act]. When the sacrificer piles it, he does not give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). When the *adhvaryu* piles it, then the sacrificer himself should give many high-priced cows to the *adhvaryu*; this is the meaning. The author of the Bhāṣya states that it is not the case that the sacrificer gives only a specific portion of the fee to the *adhvaryu* and not to the *brahmā*. The principle is: "The *adhvaryu* who piles more [than the others] [receives more]."

For one should not substitute the principal sacrificial fee (*pradhānadakṣiṇā*) with subsidiary signs. And the opinion of Baudhāyana is: "At this point, he gives to the Adhvaryu the fee consisting of the *Āraṇyaka-anuvāka*, or a hundred, or a thousand, or for each brick. This means a hundred or a thousand silver coins.
If he were to have others pile [the fire-altar] for him, and he were not to satisfy them with fees, they would take away his fire. 5.
One should satisfy him with sacrificial fees; by that, one satisfies Agni himself.

When the animal dedicated to Agni has been brought forward for the sacrifice, while the *stotra* is being chanted—either when the *prastāva* has been intoned or when one verse has been sung—he touches the fire with two verses beginning, "In the ocean is your heart."

While engaged in the *yajñāyajñīya* chant, once the *prastāva* has been performed with a single verse, he performs the touching [of the fire] with these two mantras: "Homage be to thee; do not harm me" and "O path of homage. || 6 ||
He offers one oblation for the release of the fire with the verse, "This breast, full of vigor, which has been traversed by the Hāriyojana, do thou suck," or with the verse, "I release thee. (7)

Now, regarding the fire, it is heard in scripture: "With 'O Agni, yoke yourself with power and ghee,' he offers; thereby he yokes the fire itself; he yokes it with five [verses]; for the sacrifice has five parts"—this is the yoking of the fire. Likewise: "'Suck this breast, full of vigor, of the waters,' with these words he offers a ladle full of clarified butter; this indeed is the unyoking of the fire. Should this unyoking of the fire take place upon the completion of the primary rites alone, or upon the completion of the primary rites along with their subsidiaries?

If yoga were intended solely for the sake of the primary rite (*pradhāna*), then its release would occur upon the completion of that rite; however, if yoga is intended for the sake of both the auxiliary and the primary rites (*sāṅgapradhāna*), then its release occurs at the very end of everything. In that case, since the fire (*agni*) serves all purposes, the yoga—which is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of that fire—would also serve all purposes. Therefore, having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "its release occurs upon the completion of everything," the author of the *Bhāṣya* established the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that "because of the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), 'the sacrifice is sixfold,' yoga is for the sake of the sacrifice; therefore, its release occurs upon the completion of the primary rite."

And thus, even the selection (*varaṇa*) pertaining to the Soma sacrifice—based on the statement, "If they were to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call without having been selected, the blessing of the sacrifice would go to the enemy"—is, by virtue of its connection with the sacrifice, subject to the same principle as the connection with the flesh-offering (*āmisaṃyoga*); it serves the purpose of the primary sacrifice alone. In that case, at the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), the selection of the Hotṛ, which has been substituted by the Soma-related selection, becomes applicable.

[In this regard, the reading "na 15, dvābhyām abhimarśanaṃ kāla eva stīrṇe vede" is an addition. [End of] Paṭala 7; together with the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. Page 115.

The injunction "one should choose the Hotṛ" becomes logically consistent as a prohibition [only under this view]. Otherwise, since the choosing at the Soma sacrifice serves the purpose of both the primary rite and its subsidiaries, there would be no occasion for a separate choosing at the Avabhṛtha; thus, the prohibition would be meaningless. This is stated as an indicative mark (*liṅga*). Likewise, in the case of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), there is the observation of yoking and unyoking every day: "Day by day he yokes; day by day he unyokes. If the yoking served the purpose of both the primary rite and its subsidiaries, the observation of yoking and unyoking would occur only at the beginning and the end.

Now, even if the *varaṇa* (selection) has the *pradhāna* (principal rite) as its purpose, because the *avabhṛtha* is an *apūrva* (novelty), there arises the question of whether the *vaiṣṭika-varaṇa* (the selection prescribed for the Viṣṭi rites) applies here. Regarding this, someone says: "This is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the novelty itself, suggesting that there would be simplicity (*lāghava*) in the absence of the selection of a *hotṛ*. And that [simplicity] is postulated only when the selection is applicable under the theory of novelty, and not otherwise. We, however, say: even if the *avabhṛtha* is a novelty, nevertheless, the *ājyabhāga*...

Because the *hotṛ* priest exists there and because the selection (*varaṇa*) of the *hotṛ* pertains to both the subsidiaries and the principal rite, that selection serves the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the principal. Indeed, the selection pertaining to the New Moon sacrifice (*dārśika varaṇa*) does not serve the purpose of the principal alone, as it lacks a connection with the [specific] sacrifice [in question]. Therefore, even in the absence of an extended application (*atideśa*), since the selection of the *hotṛ* has the *ājyabhāga* offerings as its purpose, it certainly applies to the *avabhṛtha* bath; thus, the prohibition is appropriate.

Considering this explanation of the section by the author of the *Bhāṣya* to be untenable, the author of the *Vārttika* has described the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in reverse order. The prima facie view is that, based on the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the word "separate" (*vibhṛtha*), the application (*yoga*) is intended solely for the sake of the principal rite. The established conclusion, however, is that since the fire (*agni*) serves all purposes, its application (*yoga*) also serves all purposes; nor can a specific restriction be established on the strength of the remainder of the sentence.

Regarding the injunction for the origin of the *yoga*, since no supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) is present there, its applicability to all [the sacrifices] is understood. However, in the case of the injunction regarding the quality of the number five, a supplementary statement is indeed heard. Yet, that supplementary statement is not sufficient to set aside the applicability to all [sacrifices] as already understood from the origin-injunction (*utpattivākya*). Furthermore, the word "yajña" denotes sacrifice in general, not only the primary sacrifice; therefore, on account of that word, it cannot be restricted to the primary sacrifice alone.

Furthermore, the prohibition of the selection of the *hotṛ* at the *avabhṛtha* ceremony is indeed consistent even if the Soma-related selection (*varaṇa*) pertains to both the subsidiaries and the principal rite. For the Soma-related selection is for the purpose of securing the priest's services (*ānatyartha*), whereas the original selection of the *hotṛ* performed while the officiant is already engaged serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Therefore, it will be stated in the twelfth book that this [Soma-related] selection must be performed in all Soma sacrifices; thus, the prohibition is logical. Moreover, the observation of the "joining and releasing" (*yogavimoka*) performed every day in the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is consistent only with this view.

This statement is for the purpose of injunction (*vidhi*), not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), because otherwise it would be purposeless. Therefore, since the application (*yoga*) and release (*vimoka*) would otherwise be required only once—at the very beginning and at the very end—this statement enjoins the daily application and release. Consequently, the application lasts for the entire year, and the release occurs upon the completion of the whole.

He offers eleven *samiṣṭayajus* oblations. Having offered nine pertaining to the *adhvara*, he offers the tenth and eleventh with the formulas: "May Agni, sacrificed, invoked, and consecrated by *svāhā*, fulfill us; may this oblation, sacrificed, be *svāhā*; homage! (10–11).

According to the injunction, "He offers eleven *samiṣṭayajus* oblations," having offered the nine oblations pertaining to the *adhvara*, he offers [the tenth and eleventh] with the verses beginning "dhātā rātiḥ" and "iṣṭo yajñaḥ. "Iṣṭo yajño bhṛgubhir āśīrdā vasubhiḥ svāhā. Tasya te iṣṭasya vītasya draviṇe ha bhakṣīya svāhā. Some perform this as a single mantra, repeating that very same one twice, because of the statement of Vaikhānasa: "The tenth and eleventh *samiṣṭayajus* are [identical]. [This concludes] the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[Chapter 12].
When the omentum of the Anūbandhyā cow has been offered, he offers the Ākūtis with this Anuvāka, "Whatever flowed forth from intention," reciting one mantra after another.

When the omentum of the Anubandhyā cow has been offered, the hair-shaving performed, and the bath taken, the Pātnīvata offering follows. Upon its completion, there is the release from the Ṛṣabha. (Having filled a ladle made of Udumbara wood with clarified butter, the "non-release" offering is made with the mantra: *imaṃ stanamūrjasvantaṃ dhayāpām*. Thereafter follows the remainder of the animal sacrifice, beginning with the Paśupuroḍāśa. If, however, it is the Āmikṣā, then having offered that, and having performed the hair-shaving, the bath, and the Pātnīvata offering, one proceeds with the Devikā oblations (beginning with the pouring out) and the Saktu-homa.
And when the consecration with smoke has been performed, the Adhvaryu offers ten oblations with the verse beginning "yadākūtāt."
"O Agni, I have obtained you with my mind"—with these words, when about to depart, he worships Agni with the Āpti formulas.

"Baudhāyana says: 'The sacrificer. One should recite that mantra which has been read in the aforementioned manner at the time of departure. Thus he says: 'This indeed is the attainment of Agni; by that very means one attains him. (5-5-7). This very performance of the recitation of the mantra is what causes the attainment of Agni; therefore, the meaning is that by that alone one attains Agni. || 11 ||
With the mantra, "The fires that belong to the soil," he worships whichever of his own fires he beholds. || 12 ||

Some, however, having descended, worship the *citī* with the mantra "O you who are within the *citī*" (*cityāntarman*). The worship begins with "This one before us through the sky" (*ayaṃ no nabhasā puraḥ*) and ends with "You are rain" (*vṛṣṭirasi*), which pertains to the sacrificer. Then follows the worship with the *āptī* mantras: "Those who are pervasive... (*yeśayaḥ purīpyāḥ*). Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the phrase "He makes you subject to me" (*āpaṃ tvāmme vaśayati*), the rule is that "in the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*), the barren cow (*vaśā*) is constant. However, the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*) maintains that there is indeed an option regarding the worship with the *āptī* mantras. The Vaikhānasas and others hold that after consigning the *prājahita* fire, such rites as these are performed. || 12 ||
Having seen the fires of others, [he approaches] with the three verses beginning "upa tvā'gne dive dive" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.4.46). ||13||

Having seen the altar-pile (*citi*) of other sacrificers, he performs the ritual worship (*upasthāna*). Even while about to depart, as long as the sacrificer has not yet determined the location for the *udavasānīyā* offering, [he continues]. However, some say that one should perform the worship of the fires of others for as long as one lives;
having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the *sautrāmaṇī*, and also with the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. ||14||

When the *udavasānīyā* offering has been performed and the fire-altar (*agni*) piled, having completed the seasonal sacrifice (*ṛtu-iṣṭi*) characterized by the qualities of the fire, one should immediately thereafter perform the *sautrāmaṇī*, the *maitrāvaruṇī*, and the *āmikṣā*. Regarding this, the Commentator (*bhāṣyakṛt*) states that it may be done "without [waiting for] a festival day" (*parvan*). However, the logical rule (*nyāya*) is that it should be performed at the time of the upcoming festival day, as this allows the proper timing to be fulfilled. || 14 ||

Having piled the fire-altar, for one year he must not descend toward anyone, nor should he eat birds. [He must observe this] throughout his life while it rains. He must not run, nor approach a woman; having piled a second altar, he must not approach the wife of another. Having piled a third altar, he must not approach any woman at all, or he may approach his own wife.

For one year, he should not descend [from his seat] even for a moment, nor should he rise to greet even his teachers. However, once the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) has been performed, this applies for the rest of his life, even during years when no consecration takes place, because of the emission of semen. For it is said: "These two do not descend toward anyone; let them both ascend. A sacrificer whose Śūdra wife was obtained by purchase likewise does not approach her for one year. There is also a year-long prohibition against eating the flesh of birds.

The brain is the flesh of the head; one who has piled the fire-altar (agnicit) should not run while it is raining during a divine rite for as long as he lives. If, however, he should run out of some forgetfulness, he must return to that very place from which he ran. Having piled a second fire-altar, he should not approach the wife of another caste who has been brought [as a bride] by force, neither for a year nor for as long as he lives, because she is equal to a *rāma* (a woman of low status).

Having established the third fire through the piling ritual (*cityā*), he did not go away from her for even a single year, even though she was of a different caste. A wife of the same caste must necessarily be maintained by all castes, because the entitlement to both [the domestic and sacrificial fires] applies to them. However, for those who have married out of desire, a wife of a different caste is not necessarily to be maintained. (15, 16, 17)
If, after piling the fire-altar, one should not shine during that year, he, when commencing a sacrificial rite, should pile the fire-altar consisting of a single layer.

Having piled the fire and having performed the sacrifice with the *ṛtu*-offerings characterized by the qualities of Agni, if within this year—in which year the fire was piled—there occurs a lack of growth or a decrease in wealth and grain for that person, some say that even those who possess prosperity may perform this rite. In this year, while bringing about the seasons in which the fire was piled, he should pile the fire consisting of a single layer (*ekacitīka*) and a single spreading (*ekaprastāra*), as it is heard in the scripture: "The sixth layer is common to the previously piled fire through its bricks. (18)
"Salilāya tvā," "Sarṇīkāya tvā"—these are eight distinct mantras. The *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks are placed according to their respective positions. Then follows the loose soil (*purīṣa*). || 12.7.20 ||

Having laid down eight bricks on the *uttaravedi* with the various mantras beginning with "salilāya tvā," [one proceeds] on the eastern *tripramāṇā* altar, which is either prepared as before or equal to the previous fire-altar. In the middle interval between the *pravargya* and the *upasad*s, the *citi* (layering) takes place; having performed the rite up to the *vyādhāraṇa* (supporting) as prescribed for each, one concludes according to the archetype (*prakṛti*). On the day of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, after performing the morning rites, the piling (*cayana*) occurs, because of the scriptural statement that this is the "sixth layer. Since it is a constituent part, the specific duties of the fire-altar (*agni-dharma*) are not required.

The properties of the *Agnicayana* cannot be applied to a single part [of the altar]. Because of the masculine designation in the phrase "one should pile a single-layered (*ekacitīka*) or three-layered (*triciti*) [altar]," the *prastāra* (the first layer) is one that is equivalent to that. However, when the cause is the lack of stability—expressed as "having piled the fire-altar, he does not find a firm footing; there are five previous layers, then he piles the sixth layer"—since this is equivalent [to the case of the whole], the properties of the *citi* (layer) are performed for this [sixth layer] as well, but not the properties of the *agni* (fire-altar) such as plowing and so forth. Having performed the *pravargya* and the two morning *upasads*.

Having performed the rites beginning with "He places eight various *lokampṛṇā* bricks for one layer" in the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, and ending with "They lead a white horse in front," there is the touching (*ālambha*) of the white horse. Then follows the mounting of the altar with the mantra "Speech has entered my mouth. Then he lays down eight various bricks with the mantra "For the sake of the water, hail! and so forth. Then he covers them with *lokampṛṇā* bricks. This constitutes the first modification according to the tradition of Bharadvāja.

The touching of the *uttaravedi*, the taking of the fire into oneself (*ātmany-agnigrahaṇa*), the touching of the *svayaṃcit* altar, and the circumambulation with the verse "tattvā yāmi" cease because they have gone elsewhere; everything up to the touching of the *gāyatrī* is as in the first layer (*prathamaciti*). Having performed the afternoon rites, the leading around of the horse (*aśvapariṇayana*) takes place. Then follows the rite of the removal of the fires (*pravodvāsana*) and so forth, as in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. Some, however, maintain that after laying down the *āśvināmantra* bricks, the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks are laid down; then the *purīṣa* (filling soil) is applied; thus they perform everything as prescribed at that very time.

If one who has piled the fire-altar does not find firm support within this year, he should, when commencing a sacrificial session (*kratu*), pile the fire-altar in a single layer (*ekacitīka*) with the five separate mantras beginning, "Saṃyac ca pracetāś ca. The *lokapṛṇā* bricks are placed according to their respective positions. Then follows the loose soil (*purīṣa*).

Within this very year, he either falls from his position or there is no increase for him; thus, while performing the desired seasonal sacrifice (*ṛtu-yajña-kratu*), it would be performed by that [sacrifice]. Therefore, one should pile only a single layer (*ekacitīka*), equal to the extent of the previous fire-altar (*pūrvāgni-pratāra*). This is because of the contradiction in the Śruti: "There are five previous layers, and then one piles the sixth layer. Since the sixth layer is not piled after the fire-altar has been completed, and because it would result in having the same number as the previous layers, the entire procedure of piling (*cayana-vidhi*) applies.

Regarding these two, some [teachers] recite the desires as being reversed: "for a firm foundation" and "for water," instead of "for desire" and "for perversion"; and as for the second, they read "he who does not go" as "the controller and the wise one"—thus some followers of other branches transmit the desires in this inverted order. || 21 ||

We shall explain the *citi* (piling) again. It is heard [in the scriptures] in three senses: either in the sense of non-hearing (*asravaṇa*), or in the sense of prosperity (*samṛddhi*), or in the sense of continuity (*saṃtāna*). We shall explain [it] in the sense of non-hearing: "Whether one should sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, or with an animal sacrifice, or with Soma. Wherever his previous fire-altar has been piled, having settled there again, he should sacrifice. Or else, [he may pile] with the eight verses beginning with "By whom the seers... which are distinct mantras, and eight *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; then the loose soil (*purīṣa*).

Furthermore, it is heard in the scripture that [the *punaściti*] is for the purpose of preventing leakage: "Whatever oblation one offers without bricks, that indeed leaks away; when the *punaściti* is being piled, the oblations become full of vigor in this [fire-altar]. Thus, it is for the purpose of preventing leakage. The *punaścitis* are also for the purpose of prosperity: "One should pile the *punaściti* for prosperity," thus for one desiring prosperity. [End of] Paṭala 7, accompanied by the commentary *Yogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 119.

Regarding the purpose of continuity: "He carries the food up to the third generation," and thus the lineage remains unbroken, and the food persists up to the third generation for one who piles the fire-altar again for the sake of continuity. In that context, the piling is said to be for the purpose of non-flowing: whether he sacrifices with an *iṣṭi* or with *soma*, having moved down to that former fire-altar of his which was already piled, the *āhavanīya* fire is established upon that previously piled fire.

The *iṣṭis* such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and others: at their *anvādhāna*, one goes near the previously piled fire (*pūrvacita*). Having brought it to the previously piled fire, he establishes it there. Having established it in the location of the *vedi*, [he proceeds with] the *gārhapatya* and *dakṣiṇāgni*. When the *iṣṭi* is completed, he enters [the sacrificial ground]. Such is the rule for the obligatory (*nitya*), optional (*kāmya*), and occasional (*naimittika*) rites. As for the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), however, the third part of the fire belongs to the other; the layer (*citi*) situated in its place serves as the site of the *uttaravedi*.

At the time of the *praṇayana* (the leading forth of the fire), the ritual is performed beginning from the *vyāghāraṇa* (sprinkling) up to the end of the depositing of the *saṃbhāras*. Just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), another sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is placed to the north of the [first] post; the rest is the same. In the *Soma* sacrifice as well, just as the eastern altar (*vedi*) belonging to Agni was situated there, so too is the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) located in its proper place; everything else, including the preparation of the posts, is to be understood as in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. This is the rule for the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) *Soma* sacrifices. This is the meaning of the section.

Alternatively, there is no sacrifice after having settled the previously piled fire-altar; one performs the *agnihotra* and the *iṣṭi* only in the house. When the *uttaravedi* has been prepared for the animal sacrifice and the Soma sacrifice—for the animal sacrifice on a *śamyā*-measure [altar], and for the Soma sacrifice on a ten-pada [altar]—once the *uttaravedi* has been completed up to the sprinkling (*vyāghāraṇa*), one brings bricks of the same size as the *uttaravedi*. Having performed the rites from the carrying forward of the fires (*praṇayana*) up to the ascending, and having laid down the eight bricks with the verse "yenarṣayaḥ" as before, and having performed the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks and the rest up to the leading around of the horse (*aśvapariṇayana*), [the first layer is completed].

Having performed the *citi* (the piling of the altar), the bringing forward [of the fires], and so forth, while the materials (*saṃbhāra*) are being held over the fire, one recognizes [the horse] by the verse "ūrṇāvantam" and thereafter proceeds entirely as in the *paśubandha*.

In the *soma* sacrifice, however, having performed up to the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) during the middle *upasad*, one stops at the *uttaravedi* as in the archetype; then, on the following day, having performed the morning rites and the ritual engagement (*vyāpāraṇa*), and having performed from the bringing forward of the bricks (*iṣṭakā-praṇayana*) as before up to the mounting, the piling (*cayana*) is performed with bricks of the same size as those of the *uttaravedi*, and as before, two horses should stand on either side of it.

Having recited the eight various mantras beginning with *yenarṣayaḥ*, and then the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks with the formula *lokaṃ pṛṇa*, one performs the rites from the arrangement of the layers (*citiklapti*) up to the touching with the *gāyatrī* verse, as in the first layer. Then follow the two afternoon rites; the leading around of the horse, the removal of the vessel of hot ashes (*pravarṇodvāsana*), and so forth, are like those in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. During the leading forward of the fire, when the fire is being held over the upper fire, having recognized [the signal] with the verse *avantam*, the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*) are prepared; everything is like the Jyotiṣṭoma. This second procedure is for the purpose of preventing the spilling of the oblation.

Alternatively, while the fire is being maintained upon the *uttaravedi* during the animal sacrifice and the *soma* sacrifice, [the priest] touches the *uttaravedi* with the formula, "Prajāpati has led you. Then, having performed everything from the maintaining of the fires up to the scattering of the *saṃbhāra* materials, he inserts the subsequent rites; this is the third procedure.

Alternatively, there may be four [Svayamātṛṇṇā bricks], or three; regarding their placement: once the Uttaravedi has been prepared, and the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) and other rites have been performed as previously described for the Soma sacrifice or the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), one should place the Svayamātṛṇṇā up to its edge as in the archetype, with the mantra "pṛṣṭo divi. Then follows the throwing of the loose earth (*purīṣa*). When the first Svayamātṛṇṇā has been laid down in this manner, the second is placed in the same way up to its edge. Then, by the rule for the *puru* (or *purīṣa*) layer, the third is placed.

The fifth procedure consists of the filling of earth (purīṣa) up to the end of the horse’s leading around, excluding the layering of bricks. Alternatively, there are three *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks and three *viśvajyotis* bricks; the rule for their placement is as follows: having performed everything as before, when the *svayamātṛṇṇā* has been placed with its edge facing east, one adds the earth-filling (*purīṣa*). Then, the first *viśvajyotis* is placed with the first mantra. Then the second *svayamātṛṇṇā* is also placed; having placed the *svayamātṛṇṇā* with its edge facing east, one adds the earth-filling.

While the second *viśvajyotis* brick is being laid upon the third *svayamātṛṇṇā* with the second mantra, the first *viśvajyotis* is [laid] with the third mantra. Then follows the third *svayamātṛṇṇā*, which concludes the Sāman. Then comes the *purīṣa* (filling soil). Thereafter, having performed the rites beginning with the *catiklapti* and so forth—excluding the *purīṣa*—up to the leading around of the horse (*aśvapariṇayana*), as in the first layer (*prathamaciti*). It is the same regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśu*). However, for the *soma* sacrifice, the procedure is as previously stated. In the *cayana* (piling of the altar), the *khaṣṭī* bricks, which are the *lokaṃpraṇās* and equal in measure to the *uttaravedi*, are laid down.

One should perform the leading forward (*praṇayana*) and so forth as previously described. Then the *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick with the formula "Thou art asked for heaven" (*pṛṣṭo divi*), then eleven *lokaṃpṛṇā*s of the size of the *uttaravedi* and the loose earth (*purīṣa*). Then twelve *lokaṃpṛṇā*s of the size of the *uttaravedi* and the loose earth. Then, from the preparation of the altar (*citiklapti*) up to the end of the piling (*cityanta*), excluding the loose earth and ending with the leading forward of the horse, it is to be done like the first layer (*prathamacityavat*). Others maintain that when the *soma* sacrifice is being performed for the purpose of the *anavaṇa*, one should follow only the procedure for the *lokaṃpṛṇā*s and no other; the other procedure applies only to the animal sacrifice (*paśu*).

Because it is not characterized by the nature of fire-altars (*anagnicitya*), because it lacks the commonality of being a repeated piling (*punar-citi*), and because it is not a first modification (*prathamāvikāra*). As for the rule stated by the Commentator—that "in every case, it is not a first modification"—this refers to the sixth rule regarding the piling for the sake of eating meat. In the case of the piling for the sake of prosperity (*samṛddhi*), one who piles the second fire-altar has sixteen bricks remaining in the second layer. Of these, eight are for the verses beginning with *yenarṣayaḥ* (each with a different mantra), and eight are *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks. Then follows the layer of loose soil (*purīṣa*). Thereafter, from the section on the determination of the layers (*citiklṛpti*) up to the end of the piling, the section on the loose soil is performed as in the second layer. 25.

On the following day, there are eight *nānāmantra* bricks and eleven *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; then the *purīṣa*. On the following day, these *nānāmantra* bricks [number] twelve and eleven *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; then the *purīṣa*. Now we shall explain the rite for the sake of prosperity: he who, having piled the fire-altar, does not prosper within this year, should, when beginning a sacrificial session (*kratu*), pile a fire-altar consisting of three layers (*triciti*). With the formulas "For the flood (*salila*) thee, for the wave (*sarṇīka*) thee," there are eight *nānāmantra* bricks and eleven *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; then the *purīṣa*.

On the following day, these various formulas and twelve *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; then a layer of loose soil (*purīṣa*). On the following day, these various formulas and thirteen *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; then a layer of loose soil. But for one piling the third fire-altar for the sake of continuity, on the third layer there are eight various formulas beginning with "By which the seers... and an unlimited number of *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; then a layer of loose soil. (Section 19) 26.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the twelfth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*, together with the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. [Chapter 7] 121.

Then, when the next day has dawned, nineteen bricks remain: eight with the *yenarṣayaḥ* formulas, eleven *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks with their respective mantras, ending with the *purīṣa*. Then, from the *citiklapti* up to the end of the piling (*cityanta*), the *purīṣa*-spreading is performed as in the third layer. Then, on the following day, twenty bricks remain: eight with the *yenarṣayaḥ* formulas and twelve *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks; having laid down the *purīṣa*, from the *citiklapti* up to the end of the piling, excluding the *purīṣa*, this is equal to the fourth layer for the sake of prosperity.

But the *citi* is said to be for the purpose of continuity (*saṃtāna*). When piling the third *agni*, having placed various mantras upon the third *citi*, he piles eight bricks with the verse "yenarṣayaḥ" (TS 4.3.6.1). The mention of the *uttaravedi* is repeated again and again, [indicating] that it is indeed on the fire-altar itself and not elsewhere. Then, as required, there are the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks and the *purīṣa*; and the *purīṣa* at the end of the piling is like that of the third *citi*. This is for the purpose of continuity.

Now, moreover, they say that for one who maintains the doctrine of *brahman*, the subsequent piling (*punar-citi*) need not be performed. Furthermore, in another Sūtra, it should be understood that because the piling intended for prosperity and the piling intended for continuity are optional, they are non-obligatory. However, the piling for the sake of the sacrificial fire-shed (*anagāra*) is established as obligatory. For all offerings are desired as being accompanied by potency; thus, the prohibition of [the other types] is for the purpose of providing an option. One may pile even that [fire-altar] optionally. This [is the rule] regarding Rudra and all forms of piling the fire-altar.

Just as a sleeping tiger is awakened, so too is this [sacrifice] awakened when it is being performed for the purpose of causing [the deity] to flow forth; therefore, it is not something to be made conscious (*cetanya*). Others, however, say it is "to be made conscious" (*cetavya*); just as a Brahmin, though asleep, is awakened by one offering wealth who says, "A Brahmin is superior," so too here the sacrifice is performed for the sake of awakening the one already conscious.

[Objection]: Regarding such passages as "When it rains while wearing the fire-brands, one should not run" (*Jaiminīya-sūtra* 5.3.10), there arises a doubt as to whether these [observances] take place immediately after the *cayana* (piling of the altar) or at the conclusion of the sacrifice (*kratu*). [The opponent argues: Since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), namely the *cayana*, is an accomplished fact (*bhūta*) that serves as the occasion (*nimitta*), the observances (*vrata*) should commence immediately thereafter, just like the observances for one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). [Reply]: It is not so. The occasion is the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), and the verbal root is subordinate to it. And the cessation of that [efficient force] is indicated by the accomplishment of the result. ...

For here, the cause for the accomplishment of the nature of the piling (*cayana*) is not that; rather, the causal efficient force (*bhāvanā*)—which has that [piling] as its instrument and is devoid of an object—is the cause. And the thing to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) by that [force] is the assistance to the sacrifice. Furthermore, since that [assistance] consists in the maintenance of the ritual until its completion, it remains extended until the end of the sacrifice. Without the cessation of that [maintenance], there is no cessation of the efficient force, because efficient forces culminate in their fruit. However, in the case of the installation of the fires (*ādhāna*), the thing to be accomplished is an unmanifested transcendental result (*apūrva*); and since that is accomplished immediately thereafter, this is the distinction.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the twelfth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin, compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.

The text enclosed within the arch-marked brackets (16--) is to be applied at the conclusion of the commentary on the sūtra. [In the twelfth book, the Śrautasūtra composed by Sāṃtyāṣāḍha, Book 12, Chapter 8. Now begins the eighth chapter in the twelfth book.
Now he shows some optional piling rites:
"We shall explain the optional fires; their modifications of form are explained in the Brāhmaṇa. (1)
The meaning is that we shall clearly explain them. || 1 ||

There is a connection with the purpose and there is no fixed rule regarding its application; "one who desires cattle should pile the fire-altar with *chandas* verses. One should pile the fire-altar with those *chandas* which are used in the archetype (prakṛti). There are eight *gāyatrī* verses. One places [bricks] preceded by those containing the word *mūrdhan*. || 2 ||
