The *Chandaściti* is that fire-altar which is piled with mantras of various meters as recited in the *Anuvāka* beginning with "Agni is the head of heaven, the summit," and not with *Yajus* formulas; one desiring cattle should pile such a fire-altar. Alternatively, the term "Chandaścita" refers to optional modifications of qualities (*guṇavikāra*), for the authors of the Sūtras teach that these are indeed enumerated in the *Śulba*.

Indeed, it is with *chandases* (metres) that all *chandases* are built; for in the place of the *yajuṣmatīs*, the *gāyatrī* and other original metres are employed, and the *yajuṣmatīs* themselves are not performed. Thus, in the place of the *yajuṣmatīs*, there are other metres. || 2 ||
"One desiring heaven should pile the Śyenacit. It takes the form of a hawk with curved wings and a spread-out tail. ||3||

"The sacrificer desiring heaven builds it in the shape of a hawk: 'The hawk, indeed, is the swiftest of birds; having become a hawk, he flies to the heavenly world' (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.11). Among birds, the hawk is capable of flying with extreme speed. "Becoming a hawk" means becoming as swift as a hawk. || 3 ||
One who desires, "May I be possessed of a head in yonder world," should pile the Kaṅkacita altar. Having the form of a heron with an extended neck, he becomes possessed of a head.

"It is built like a *kaṅka* bird," thus it is indeed the *śyena* (hawk) itself. This bird has broader wings than its tail; its body is long, and its head is rounded. "Possessing a head" means having a commendable head. Its head is praised because it is prominent due to its fullness. || 4 ||

"One desiring stability should pile the *alaja*-piled [altar], having four furrows (*sītā*). This means he plows four furrows joined together in each of the four directions. [End of] Paṭala 8. The *alaja* is a specific bird known as the *bhāsa*, similar in shape to a heron (*kaṅka*). It is so called because it is piled like that [bird]. "Having four furrows" refers to a set of four, by way of substituting for the number twelve; thus, there is one [furrow] in place of each of the three [usual ones]. 5. [This concludes] the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 123.
"One who has rivals should pile the *prauga-cit*," it is said; it takes the shape of a wagon.

The *prauga* has the shape of a chariot-front. Having made a square plot of ground twice as large as the extent of the fire-altar from the *sāraṇi* line, one should draw a line from the middle of the eastern side-line toward the west. Between the two lines, the shape of a *prauga* (chariot-front) is seen; it is built in that very form. Thus [it is said]. 6.

One who desires, "May I drive away my born enemies and those yet to be born," should pile the fire-altar with two front-pieces (*ubhayataḥprauga*); it has the shape of a cart on both sides, like a cart facing in two directions.

And that which is extended forward and shaped like the front of a cart, with a *prauga* (chariot-front) on both sides—by means of it, one destroys the brothers already born and obstructs the birth of those yet to be born. || 7 ||
"One who has rivals should pile a fire-altar in the shape of a chariot wheel"; thus it is circular.

It is called the "chariot-wheel-strewn" (rathacakracit) because it is built in the circular shape of a chariot wheel. Āpastamba and Baudhāyana state that one should make the ground circular with a circumference equal to the extent of the *sāraṇi* and the *prādeśa*.
"One desiring food should pile the Drona-cit. Now, there are indeed two kinds of Dronas: square and circular; in this matter, one may act according to one's preference.
For they bring grain into the granary; therefore, one obtains food together with a place for storing grain. ||9||
"Subsequently, the *svaru* comes into being because of its conformity. || 12.8.10 ||
The word "is understood" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 10 ||

"One desiring cattle should pile the *samūhya*"; thus, he piles the bricks while gathering them together. (11) According to some, having dug in the various directions from the *cātvāla*, he throws the earth from those places onto [the altar]. (12)
It is called *samūhya* because it is a great collection (*samūha*). || 11 || 12 ||
"One desiring a village should pile the Paricāyya altar"; thus he surrounds the central naturally perforated brick (svayamātṛṇṇā) clockwise with groups of bricks.
15. In the square [altar]: "One desiring a village should pile the *paricāyya* and the *upacāyya*"; thus it is stated regarding the *paricāyya*. (Śāṅkhāyana Śrautasūtra 12.14)

"One circumambulates the *svayamātṛṇṇā* [brick] in the middle layer with groups of bricks; that is the *paricāyya*," so said Āpastamba. "One desiring a village should pile the *paricāyya*; he indeed becomes possessed of a village," according to the Śruti. For one desiring a village, the *upacāyya* is performed: in the middle layer, one circumambulates the *svayamātṛṇṇā* in the middle with groups of bricks. No *diśyā* [bricks] are placed here. (13.14)

One who desires, "May I prosper in the world of the fathers," should pile a funeral mound shaped like a cemetery; it may be square or circular, according to some, just as the great altar for the ancestors (mahāpaitṛkī vedī) is; according to others, it is triangular. (Section 20) 15.

It is called *śmaśānacit* because it is built like a cemetery (*śmaśāna*); a cemetery is a place for burning the dead. For one who desires, "May there be prosperity in the world of the ancestors," prosperity comes to him in the abode of the ancestors, such as the *barhiṣad*s and others. It may be either circular or square. The great ancestral altar (*mahāpaitṛkī vedi*) has been explained in the context of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices. The rest is clear. Thus, the optional piling rites (*kāmyacayana*) are concluded. 15.
We shall now explain the chapter on Tāpacita. || 16 ||
The meaning is that we shall explain this clearly. || 16 ||
He remains consecrated for one year. || 17 ||

Regarding the statement "there is the piling of the Drona": because they perform austerity upon every portion of this earth, they are called *tapaścitaḥ* (those piled by austerity), such as Kakṣīvanta and others; that fire which has been sacrificed to by them is the *tāpaścita*. In that fire, the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for a year occurs according to the rule. || 17 ||
When the year has returned, he purchases the King [Soma]. || 18 ||
The meaning is that one commences the ritual procedure beginning with the *prāyaṇīya* offering. || 18 ||

Before the Upasads, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, one on eleven potsherds to Indra, one on twelve potsherds to the Viśvedevas, a pap to Bṛhaspati, and a cake on three potsherds to Viṣṇu; having performed the Upasads continuously for a year, he piles the fire-altar.

The *upasad* days are also not [preceded by] the *pravargya*. This is because of the scriptural statement regarding the number twenty-four—"he performs the *pravargya* twenty-four times"—and because of the opinion of Bharadvāja. However, the Commentator [Śabara] states: "The *pravargya* also lasts for exactly one year. Prior to the *upasad*s, when the *madantī* water has been poured out, there is an offering of five oblations: one for Agni, one for Indra, one for the Viśvedevas, one for Bṛhaspati, and a cake on eight potsherds for Śarava-Viṣṇu. In that case, the same procedure applies as when the *prastara* and *paridhi* sticks have already been spread, according to the rule: "those which have been performed... etc.

In the case of the *astīrṇa* (spread) [pakṣa], another procedure is followed: for four months, one oblation is offered with each individual *upasad* mantra. Having performed each *upasad*, the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) and the bricks are carried out as far as possible. [End of Paṭala 8] The rule is stated thus: "Having performed the *pravargya*, they proceed with the *upasad*. Two months are spent on each layer (*citi*); there are four layers in the last month. There are vows (*vrata*) consisting of four milkings, likewise three milkings, two milkings, and one milking. [12.8.20] This concludes the section accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 125. 12.8.20.

Every two months, one layer (citi) is piled, using as many bricks (iṣṭakā) as possible; however, for four months, the highest layer is used. For five months, it is done with four breasts (catustana), and likewise for three months with three breasts (tristana), and so on. ||20||

One should pile the fire-altar for a year using that *sūkta* of the Ṛṣis which is addressed to Agni (the Āgneya-sūkta). (21) Of those *sūktas* addressed to Agni which appear in the *Daśatayīs*, he places one brick with each individual *sūkta*. (22) The bricks have various mantras according to the number of verses in the *sūktas*. The *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks are placed according to the requirements of the situation. (23)

The *Ṛṣis* remain performing the placement for a year by means of the *Āgneya* [bricks]. The *Śruti* itself provides this determination regarding those *Ṛṣis* who are associated with the *Āgneyas*: "The *Āgneya* has Agni as its deity; the altar (*citi*) belonging to Yājñasenī is likewise. Because of the commonality of being an altar (*cititva*), the mantras for each individual altar (*citeḥ citeḥ*) take the place of the previously mentioned rule, and the *Lokampṛṇās* are also included. In the place of the *Lokampṛṇās*, it is "according to the purpose" (*yathārtham*). Now, as for the *purīṣa* (filling soil), it follows the original sequence across all five layers (*citayas*). 21, 22, 23.

When the Upasads have been completed, in the third year he should sacrifice with either the Abhijit or the Viśvajit. We shall explain [the sacrifices] where the sacrificial fee consists of a thousand or all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*). [This applies] for each successive period of fasting. (Section 21) 24.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the twelfth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Thus ends the twelfth book in the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.

But when the third year has arrived, [one should perform] either the Abhijit or the Viśvajit. According to another Śruti, one should sacrifice with "all one's possessions" (*sarvavedasa*) because of its connection with the Viśvajit; this is the established principle (*nyāya*). In that case, the "all-possessions" gift follows after [the Abhijit], whereas the duties of the Viśvajit begin from the *saṃchadi* onwards. The *Chandoga Brāhmaṇa* states: "His sacrificial fee consists of all his possessions. The author of the Bhāṣya holds that the duties regarding "all possessions" apply to both the Abhijit and the Viśvajit. The repetition is for the purpose of concluding the inquiry. || 24 ||

Having condensed [the teachings] into various kinds of efficient *sūtras* that convey much meaning in few words and which capture the intended purpose, he—who expands the faces of logic—has made even a dullard like myself an interpreter of the meaning of his own *sūtras*. Homage be to that Hiraṇyakeśin, who has seen the further shore of the ocean of the Veda so difficult to grasp! May he, the ocean of compassion, who impels away my dullness, constantly grant me an understanding of the course of the meaning of his own *sūtras*. The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[13th Praśna]

The Kaustubha jewel, a definitive exposition of the *Nyāyasūtra*—which stands as the thread for this garland of diverse ritual applications (*prayoga*)—has been composed here by me. May it, situated in the center, please the Lord whose body is the sacrifice (*yajña-vapuṣ*). For He indeed accepts whatever little has been performed with devotion. Thus ends the eighth chapter in the twelfth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. Thus the commentary on the twelfth book is completed. 13.1 Now begins the thirteenth book.
Therein begins the first chapter.

With joy, I bow to the Lord of Sages, the ocean of compassion, the preceptor known as Hiraṇyakeśin, who knows the meaning of the Sūtras, and who is the bliss of true consciousness and eternal bliss, serving all the excellent Siddhas who are intent upon those to be disciplined. I salute my Guru Gaṇapati, the bestower of birth and knowledge; likewise, I bow to Maheśāna with Gaurī, and to Viṣṇu with Padmā. The Cayanakratu has been explained in the eleventh and twelfth chapters; the Vājapeya and Rājasūya will be described in the thirteenth.

Thus, first of all, the *sarvajyotiṣṭoma* has been demonstrated in the *Sūtra* on the principles of the ritual manuals (*satrakṛtyāyasūtra*) as "the *jyotiṣṭoma* [is] for all [desires]" (*saṃ0 śrī0 1-1*). By means of the words "the *agniṣṭoma* [is] for one desiring all [objects]" (*sa0 au0 7-1*), and so forth, the author of the *Sūtra*, having explained the *agniṣṭoma* *saṃsthā*—which serves as the fundamental archetype (*mūlaprakṛti*) for all the subsequent one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*), multi-day sacrifices (*ahīna*), and sacrificial sessions (*satra*) that are about to be described—further explained that the *ukthya*, *ṣoḍaśin*, *atirātra*, and *aptoryāma* are modifications (*guṇavikāra*) of the *agniṣṭoma*, and thus these five *saṃsthās* have been explained (*sa0 au0 7-18*).
Now, in order to explain the remaining single form of the Vājapeya sacrifice—which consists of sixteen modifications—the author makes a formal promise to focus the student's attention:
"In autumn, one should sacrifice with the Vājapeya. (1)

One etymological explanation is that *vājapeya* is so called because Soma, which is of the nature of *vāja*, is the drink (*peya*) in that sacrifice. Another etymological explanation is that since the gods desired to obtain *vāja*—that is, food in the form of a fruit—by means of this sacrifice, it is called *vājapeya* because *vāja* (food) is the object to be obtained (*peya*) by it. Thus, *vājapeya* is the name of the ritual; for its application is not established in reference to a substance or a quality. And it takes place in autumn, as stated in another *sūtra*: "One should sacrifice with the *vājapeya* in autumn. Now begins the thirteenth inquiry.
Therein is the first chapter:
In autumn, one should sacrifice with the Vājapeya.
A Brāhmaṇa or a Rājanya. ||2||
The ritual procedure for that [offering] has been explained by [the rules for] the Ṣoḍaśin. || 3 ||
The seventeenth [stoma] is the whole. || 4 ||
He attains Prajāpati. || 5 ||
There are seventeen initiation days, three *upasads*, and twenty-one [days] for the pressed soma. ||6||

The sacrificial post (yūpa) is seventeen aratnis in height; it is made of bilva wood, or of khadira or palāśa wood, and its ring (caṣāla) may also be made of wheat flour; furthermore, it should be hornless.
When that which precedes the Upasad rites has been performed, the Pratiprasthātṛ prepares the *parisrut* liquor according to the ritual procedure for *surā*.
At the time of girding, he encircles the sacrificial post with seventeen garments.

Having offered the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) for the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, he subsequently offers the oblations of the Devasū rites—namely, "To Agni Gṛhapati," and so forth, according to the traditional recitation. For both the animal-cake and the oblations of the Devasū rites, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the *iḍā* portion are the same. 13.1.10.
"O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice; impel the lord of the sacrifice for the sake of fortune"—with these words, he offers oblations at the beginning of each pressing.
On the day of the Soma-pressing, the priests, wearing golden garlands, perform the ritual proceedings.

At the time of arranging the vessels, he sets out the vessels according to their respective purposes; in place of the single *atigrāhya* vessel for Indra, he sets out five *atigrāhya* vessels for Indra.
(Regarding those [cups] with the former one: Their ritual procedure is explained by that of the *aindra* *atigrāhya* cup. || 14 ||
Having employed the ṣoḍaśin vessel, he employs seventeen Soma-cup vessels belonging to Prajāpati. || 15 ||

The ritual procedure for them has been explained by means of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup. Thereafter, the Pratiprasthātṛ [prepares] seventeen cups for the *surā* libations along with their bases (*upayāma*). At the time of the Soma-cups in the *Atirātra*, at the moment for the *kratukaraṇa* offering, he should take five *atigrāhya* cups for Indra in place of the single *atigrāhya* for Indra, using the five formulas beginning with "Thou art taken with a base; thou art seated among men" (*upayāmagṛhīto 'si nṛṣadam tvā*). || 16 ||
Their ritual procedure is explained by that of the *atigrāhya* cup dedicated to Indra. Having drawn the *ṣoḍaśin*, he draws seventeen Soma cups for Prajāpati.

The ritual procedure for them has been explained by that of the Ṣoḍaśin cup. "kuvidaṅga" is the single *puroruc* for all; [the second is] "ayā viṣṭhā janayan karvarāṇi. (Section 1) The Pratiprasthātṛ takes seventeen cups of *surā* with the *upayāma* formulas. Some authorities prescribe two reversed cups for the taking. 18.

Taking hold of them in an interlocking manner, the Adhvaryu takes the first and the Pratiprasthātṛ the latter. He places the Soma cups to the east of the axle and the Surā cups to the west of the axle. || 19 ||

At the time for the animal sacrifices, he dedicates three seasonal victims. He dedicates a spotted cow to the Maruts; and a ewe to Sarasvatī, one that has no missing teeth. According to some, [the victim to Sarasvatī] is a ram; according to others, it is a ewe and a ram. 13.1.20.
He dedicates seventeen animals sacred to Prajāpati.
The dark-colored ones, however, being hornless, appear as if they were of a single form. || 22 ||
They immolate first those animals that have been carried around the fire, ending with the one dedicated to Sarasvatī; they hold back those beginning with the one dedicated to Sarasvatī for later.

For all [the animals], there is a single set of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), omentum-spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*), cooking-pots (*kumbhī*), heart-spikes (*hṛdayaśūla*), and *plakṣa* branches; likewise, the carrying forward of the fire (*agniharaṇa*), the *adhigu* formula, the final fore-offering (*uttama-prayāja*), the first secondary portioning (*parivapya*), the *saṃjñapta-homa*, the discarding of the ropes (*raśanā-udasana*), the second secondary portioning (*uttara-parivapya*), the throwing into the fire of the omentum-spits (*anupraharaṇa*), the supplementary oblation (*abhihoma*), the sprinkling (*mārjana*), and the granting of the boon (*varadāna*) are performed as a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). || 24 ||
Having offered the two southern oblations, he brings down the chariot with the formula: "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra. || 25 ||
"In the waters is the essence, in the waters is the remedy"—with these words, they bathe the horses in the water. || 26 ||
"Either Vāyu shall yoke thee, or Manu shall yoke thee"—with these words, he yokes the chariot drawn by mares. || 27 ||
He wipes the forehead-strap of the horses, saying, "O Apāṃnapāt, swift-coursing! || 28 ||
He yokes the other sixteen chariots silently. (Section 29)
At the time of the sacrificial fee, he gives seventeen chariots.

He gives seventeen niṣkas, seventeen horses, seventeen elephants, seventeen hundred cows, seventeen yoke-teams of cattle, seventeen vehicles, seventeen beds, seventeen kitchens, seventeen garments, seventeen male slaves, seventeen female slaves, seventeen goats, seventeen ewes, and for each age-group [of animals], seventeen of each; thus he gives seventeen of each. 31.
According to some, one should prepare seventeen sets of seventeen [vessels].
When the sacrificial fees have been assigned, he gives to the Adhvaryu a chariot yoked with a sacrificial formula (yajuryukta). 33.
The remainder is common to both. || 34 ||
In front of the Āhavanīya fire, they station the chariots facing eastward.

The prince, having stationed himself in front of the Āgnīdhra shed on the southern side of the chariot yoked with the Yajus-formula, shoots seventeen arrows in a continuous flight, either eastward or northward.
Wherever the lowest [element] falls, it produces its own characteristic mark. || 37 ||

When that which precedes the offering to Mahendra has been performed, the Pratiprasthātṛ divides the seventeen-platter offering of wild rice into four parts and pours it out for Bṛhaspati; he cooks it in milk. 38.
He places [the vessel] containing clarified butter into the *catvāla* pit. || 39 ||
The prince protects it. || 13.1.40 ||
He buries a piece of wood shaped like a chariot axle in the cātvāla pit. || 41 ||
Upon it he fastens a chariot wheel made of udumbara wood with seventeen spokes. || 42 ||
With the mantra "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," the sacrificer approaches the chariot yoked with the Yajus.
He touches the two wheels of the chariot, saying, "The hooks, the hooks," or he touches the two side-pieces.
"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, through Bṛhaspati, the winner of the prize, may I win the prize"—with these words, he ascends the chariot wheel made of Udumbara wood. 45.
"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may I ascend the highest vault through Bṛhaspati, the winner of the prize"—with these words, the sacrificer mounts the chariot consecrated by the Yajus formula.
"Speak words for Indra!"—thus they cause the drums to resound.
Those who have won the prize mount the other chariots. ||48||
With the words, "O strong ones, winners of the prize, you who will run for the prize," they cause the two draft horses to smell the *naivāra* grain, or all [the animals].

When the drops have been wiped away, he wipes off the smears with the formula, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu. Having mounted the chariot joined by the Yajus, the Adhvaryu takes the horse-whip and, saying, "Thou art a steed, thou art a racer," he strokes the horses from left to right.
Thereafter, the other chariots follow, not closing the distance between them. || 51 ||
With the three verses beginning "O swift steeds, run for the prize," he consecrates those who are running; according to some, with four verses.
He sings the Vājina-sāman on a cart-wheel made of Udumbara wood while it is being turned three times each way. || 53 ||
With the verses beginning, "Agni won speech by means of the single syllable," he causes the sacrificer to recite while the [sacrificial fires] are being run toward.
Having reached the characteristic mark, they circumambulate it to the right. || 55 ||
With the four verses beginning with "May those coursers, hearing our call, come to our invocation," he consecrates the two who are running forward.
According to some, [the rite is performed] with three [verses]. 57.
"May the impulse of strength come to me," he says, and offers the oblation when they have returned.
"This was that true covenant of yours," saying this, he offers a single oblation for the release of the drum.
He touches all of them. || 13.1.60 ||

With the words, "O vigorous ones, winners of the prize, having run for the prize," he causes the two horses yoked to the cart to smell the *naivāra* grains; as before, he wipes away the remnants from their nostrils.
He gives a *kṛṣṇala* each to the *vājasṛt*s. || 62 ||
Having taken them back, he gives them to the Brahman priest. || 63 ||
And the honey-spoon was made from a śatamāna of gold. (Section 4) || 64 ||
Thus ends the first paṭala in the thirteenth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the second paṭala in the thirteenth praśna.
With the words, "Thou art the caul of the Kṣatra," the sacrificer puts on a garment of linen (tārpya). With the words, "Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra," the wife puts on one made of darbha grass. 1.
"Come, wife, let us ascend to heaven," thus the sacrificer addresses his wife; "Let us ascend," the wife replies.
"I shall cause both of us to ascend to heaven," says the sacrificer; "I shall cause both of us to ascend to heaven," says the wife.
With the ten formulas beginning with "May life be perfected through sacrifice," he ascends the sacrificial post by means of a ladder with rungs, or both [the sacrificer and the Adhvaryu] do so.
Having mounted [the chariot], he mutters: "We have gone to the gods, O Heaven. || 5 ||
He offers twelve oblations with the formulas beginning, "Vāja and Prasava."
According to some, there are thirteen. || 7 ||
Some recite [the following verses] before the climbing of the sacrificial post.

"Equal am I with you in life, equal is life with me; equal am I with you in splendor, equal is splendor with me; equal am I with you in offspring, equal is offspring with me; equal am I with you in the increase of wealth, equal is the increase of wealth with me"—having thus ascended the sacrificial post, he gazes at the cups (*grahas*).

The great officiating priests (*mahartvij*) present that [bundle] from their mouths toward each of the directions using long bamboo poles bound together with sheaths of *aśvattha* leaves. According to some, they do so from the head. The Adhvaryu priest places it in the east with the formula, "For the sake of all-feeding food" (*vaiśvamanāya tvā*). The Brahman priest places it in the south with, "For the sake of eating food" (*annādyāya tvā*). The Hotṛ priest places it in the west with, "For the sake of strength" (*vājāya tvā*). The Udgātṛ priest places it in the north with, "For the sake of winning strength" (*vājajityāyai tvā*). (Section 5) 13.2.10.
Having extended his arms toward the slayer, he turns around. || 11 ||
"Thou art this, O King, for a friend; thou art a restrainer, a supporter, a sustainer—for agriculture, for security, for wealth, and for prosperity," with these words he descends. || 12 ||
In front of the sacrificial post, he spreads out the skin of a he-goat with its neck toward the east and the hair on the upper side.
With the words "Thou art splendor," he places a silver disk upon it.
With the words, "Thou art immortality," he places his foot upon the gold plate.
"Thou art nourishment, thou art procreation," [he says] over the goat-skin.
Therefore, he ascends the stool. || 17 ||
"Mounting to heaven, the Proṣṭhatī, having mounted, she gazes upon the heights according to the will of men"—with these words he addresses him as he mounts. || 18 ||
He undertakes the rites beginning with those dedicated to Mahendra. || 19 ||
Having introduced the hymn of praise for him, he sprinkles [him] as in the case of the piling of the fire-altar (agnicityā).
While the dust is being praised with the seven verses beginning with "anna," he offers the food-oblation, having taken portions from both domestic and wild plants.
During the midday pressing, in the middle *ukthya* round when the *brahmasāman* has been introduced, they immolate here the subsequent animals beginning with that dedicated to Sarasvatī.
He proceeds with their omenta without having first basted them. || 23 ||
Having performed the offering with the omentum of the Sarasvata animal and having taken portions from all of them, he proceeds with the offerings of the omenta of the Prajapatya animals.
He proceeds with the Naivāra offering; it concludes with the Iḍā, beginning from the oblation of the sacrificial material. || 25 ||
The great officiating priests (mahartvijas) are entitled to eat the remnants of the sacrificial oblation. || 26 ||
At the time of the animal sacrifice, he proceeds with all [the offerings] ending with that of Sarasvatī according to their respective deities.

While drawing the cups for the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, he pours out the King [Soma] in excess for one group of cup-bearers. Having performed the ritual with them, he draws the cups, headed by the *hotṛ*-cup, for the additional *stotra*. The *stotra* and *śastra* take place. Having responded to the *śastra*, the Adhvaryu takes the principal cup for the *prājāpatyas*; the other priests take the remaining ones. 28.
The Pratiprasthātṛ, being a Vājasṛt, takes the principal cups of Soma; the Camasādhvaryus take the other goblets. (Section 6, Sūtra 29)

"Ye are mingled; mingle me with prosperity," saying this, the Adhvaryu runs forward with the Soma-cups toward the east; or [he says], "Ye are mingled; mingle me with prosperity. "Ye are separated; separate me from evil," saying this, the Pratiprasthātṛ runs backward with the Surā-cups; or [he says], "Ye are separated; separate me from evil. || 13.2.30 ||

They stand by the Āhavanīya fire with the Soma-cups. He proceeds with the Surā-cups at the Mārjālīya fire. For the Soma-cups, there are the *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* calls. They cause the Surā-cups to vibrate after them. The consumption of the Soma has been explained. || 31 ||
He modifies the consumption mantra by saying, "of the Virāj metre. || 32 ||
On the southern corner of the altar, having divided the Vājasṛts, they consume the Sura-cups. || 33 ||
He proceeds with the after-offerings (anuyājas) when the offering-spoons have been arranged; he proceeds with the deities of those [deities] beginning with Sarasvatī that follow [the preceding ones].
Or rather, one should proceed with the omenta of the other animals at whichever [time] they are performed. || 35 ||
Wherever there are oblations, there he presents the portions for the Māruti offering to the officiating priests from those very oblations. ||36||
Having cut up those portions of the *vājasṛt* priests, which are not to be set aside, they consume them on the southern corner of the altar.
The prince Kakuda eats either Dhruvagopa or Naivāragopa, or both, or the entire Kakuda. 38.
The Vājapeya sacrifice is concluded. || 39 ||
Having performed the Vājapeya sacrifice, one should perform the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
He does not rise up to greet anyone at all. ||41||
It is known that he becomes one who possesses a white parasol. (Khaṇḍa 7) || 42 ||
Thus ends the second paṭala in the thirteenth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the third paṭala in the thirteenth praśna:
A king desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Rājasūya. || 1 ||
One should undergo initiation five nights before the full moon of the month of Taiṣya.
Just as in this [year], in the coming year, on the full moon day of Taiṣya, the initiation for the Abhiṣecanīya Ukthya sacrifice will commence. ||3||
One should perform the Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma sacrifice for the first time.
There is liberation from the five. || 5 ||

Having consecrated the Soma with the mantra, "By thy ray, [I take] thy ray," he silently measures the fruits; then, having measured the Soma with the mantra, "Toward that god... and the fruits silently, he mutters, "For the sake of progeny, etc., I buy thy Soma. Because of the statement, "Thy self is for the cow; by two [cows] for the Rājasūya," the purchase is made with two hundred. There is a sevenfold division of the two hundred among the seven Somas. Twenty-eight [cows] are for each; thus, one hundred thousand [cows] are distributed equally among all the Somas belonging to the Rājasūya, and he gives them day after day. 6.
In the same way, one should lead the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 7 ||
He should arrange it so that its days fall on their proper times; he should assign the remainder [of the rites] accordingly.
Because the Rājasūya sacrifice, the iṣṭis, and the animal sacrifices are enjoined to take place day by day. ||9||
One should understand that there is a distinctness of sacrifices due to the distinctness of their sacrificial fees. || 13.3.10 ||
The separate sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) for the other directions, apart from the encircling of the quarters, constitute a single ritual procedure. || 11 ||
When the next day has dawned, he should sacrifice every day with the Anumata and the subsequent offerings.

"He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Anumati," as it is prescribed in the traditional text. While grinding [the grain], he causes the portion for Anumati to be set aside toward the west and the north. 13.

Those [clay fragments] which fall to the west of the *śamyā* peg, from those he should fashion that cake on one potsherd for Nirṛti (14). Having laid down the potsherds for Ānumata, he lays down the potsherd for Nirṛti (15). Having placed the offering for Ānumata, he proceeds with the rite for Nirṛti (16).
He offers into the Gārhapatya fire with the wooden spoon, saying: "O Vīhi, svāhā! May you accept the oblation" (17).
He fumigates a single firebrand from the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. || 18 ||

Having carried [the material] toward the south-western intermediate direction, having kindled a fire on a self-made salt-flat or in a cleft, he offers it with the formula: "May Nirṛti, being pleased, partake; Svāhā! (Section 8). He offers the oblation to Nirṛti, entirely consumed by fire, with two stalks from a plant that is falling apart. 19.
Or [he may offer it] with his two thumbs, saying: "O Nirṛti, this is your portion. (13.3.20)
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consists of a garment with its ends uncut; it is a black garment with a black fringe.
Having sprinkled water around, they return without looking back. || 22 ||
"svāhā! Homage to him who did this! Having returned, he offers [the oblation] in the gārhapatya fire. ||23||

He proceeds with the permission [of the gods]. Those [grains] that fall toward the north, having gone toward the water, he should dig up an ant-hill with a shell, saying, "I hereby expiate the *kṣetriya* disease of N.N., the son of N.N. With the shell, he offers it into the ant-hill, saying, "I hereby seal off the *kṣetriya* disease of N.N., the son of N.N. He covers it over with the shell or with the ant-hill itself. 24.
"He offers a caru-oblation to Āditya"—this is the last among these [verses]. 25.
Having performed the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, on the following day he offers a caru-oblation to Sarasvatī and a caru-oblation to Sarasvant; a pair of cattle is the sacrificial fee. ||26||
On the following day, he performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; by means of them, he sacrifices for a year.
One does not perform the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice as a substitute. 28.
When the next day has dawned, he performs the sacrifice daily with the offerings beginning with the *indraturīya*.
"He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni," as it is handed down in the tradition. The four oblations are one-fourth of Indra's portion; he should offer them in battle. (13.3.30)
On the night of this very same day, one should perform the sacrifice with five kinds of fuel.
At night, they perform the rite with an oblation of apāmārga plants.
When the evening Agnihotra has been offered, having fetched Apāmārga plants from a pool of water and having ground them into flour, he fumigates a single firebrand from the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with it.

Having carried [the fire] toward the north-western intermediate direction and having established it on a self-made mound or in a cleft, he offers groats of *apāmārga* with a dipping-spoon (*sruva*) made of *parṇa* wood or *arka* wood, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I offer the slayer of the Rakṣas; Svāhā! Or he may say: "I offer for the vigor of Indra; Svāhā! Having cast the dipping-spoon after [the offering] with the words, "The Rakṣas is slain," and having offered with the words, "We have struck down the Rakṣas," he stands worshipping [the fire]. 34.
The bridegroom is the sacrificial fee; whatever you possess, that is the sacrificial fee. || 35 ||

He who fears evil should sacrifice with this very [rite], the Pañcedhmīya. He divides the Āhavanīya fire into four parts toward the cardinal directions; the fifth remains in the middle. Having separately placed fuel on each part, he offers four oblations toward the cardinal directions while walking around them clockwise, reciting "The gods who dwell in the front," etc.; the fifth oblation is offered in the middle.

Having gathered the fuel together in the middle with the verse "The Rakṣas is gathered up," he offers five subsequent oblations with clarified butter taken in five ladlings, beginning with "To Agni, the slayer of Rakṣas, svāhā! A chariot drawn by five oxen is the sacrificial fee, or one drawn by four.
One who fears Rākṣasas or Piśācas should sacrifice with that very [offering]. And whatever he desires, that he should give. || 37 ||
On the following day, one should sacrifice with the oblations of the Devikās.
"He offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Dhātṛ," as it is recited in the tradition; the sacrificial fee consists of a pair of cattle, or a heifer. 39.
According to some, [the forms] *pravītā* and *pravīyamāṇā* [are used]. 13.3.40.
With these [offerings], one who desires offspring or one who desires cattle should sacrifice. || 41 ||

One who desires offspring should have a sacrifice performed for Dhātṛ, placing him in the middle; one who is ill should perform a sacrifice with an animal, placing Dhātṛ at the end, with the sons [acting as priests].
On the following day, he sacrifices daily with the Triṣaṃyukta [offerings].

"One offers an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu"—this is the first *triṣaṃyukta* as it is recited in the tradition; with this, one desiring a sacrifice should sacrifice. "One offers an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma"—this is the middle *triṣaṃyukta* as it is recited in the tradition; they prescribe it for the production of heroes. "One offers a pap to Soma and Pūṣan"—this is the last *triṣaṃyukta* as it is recited in the tradition; with this, one desiring cattle should sacrifice.

"One offers an oblation to Vaiśvānara on twelve potsherds; with that, one who desires a village should sacrifice. [One offers] a pap of barley to Varuṇa"; this pap for Varuṇa is to be exactly one span in every dimension. A trained horse, or one that has been broken in to draw a load, is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Some authorities prescribe that the rites for Vaiśvānara and Varuṇa share the same ritual framework (*tantra*). (Section 10) || 44 ||
Thus ends the third paṭala in the thirteenth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the fourth chapter in the thirteenth book:
On the following day, there are thirteen oblations for the Ratnins.
He offers [the oblation] daily in the houses of the sacrificer's kinsmen.
In whosever house he performs the offering, for that person alone there shall be the distribution of food at the sacrifice and the sacrificial fee. || 3 ||

He offers a *caru* oblation to Bṛhaspati in the house of the Brahman priest; "a white-backed animal is the sacrificial fee," as it is handed down in the tradition. According to some teachers, this takes place in the house of the domestic priest (*purohita*).
An oblation of cooked rice for Bhaga, or for Vāta; a four-year-old female cow with a variegated womb is the sacrificial fee. ||5||
"A pap for Nirṛti"—thus, a pap for Nirṛti, measuring a thumb's breadth on all sides, is prepared. ||6||
Or, [a cake] the size of a thumb-joint, he offers as a sacrifice to Nirṛti with all the oblations.

Having gathered together in one house a carpenter and a chariot-maker, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni; the sacrificial fee consists of all-iron objects. Having gathered together in one house a cow-slayer and a weaver, he offers a cake on three potsherds to Viṣṇu; the sacrificial fee is a white-spotted calf. There is a third offering, a cake on three potsherds to Viṣṇu, at the house of the carpenter and the chariot-maker; the sacrificial fee consists of all-iron objects. According to some, it belongs either to the carpenter or to the chariot-maker.
Having brought together [the materials] in the house of the commander, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni; gold is the sacrificial fee.

In the house of Akṣāvāpa, there is a Raudra oblation of Gāvīdhuka grain; a brindled bull with a white tail-tip is the sacrificial fee, as is either a horse with a white blaze on its forehead, or a rope adorned with tassels for driving away cattle.
With the formula "Svāhā to the path," he offers an oblation in the house of the Pālākala. || 11 ||
They call him the messenger of falsehood; his sacrificial fee is a bow encased in cane. 12.
Three leather bags containing arrows are the sacrificial gifts.

He offers the final oblation for Indra in the house of the sacrificer. Some say it is offered on each successive day. He offers a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra the Good Protector (*sutrāman*), and for Indra the Deliverer from Distress (*aṃhomuc*). In the benedictions of the *sūktavāka*, the Hotṛ recites: "May the King, the slayer of Vṛtra, having become king, slay Vṛtra. || 14 ||
From a branch of the *aśvattha* tree that has fallen of its own accord, he fashions a Mitra-vessel with four corners. || 15 ||
They milk a white cow with a white calf into the skin-bag of a mango tree; that [milk], having solidified by itself, flows forth through the union [of the elements]. || 16 ||
They hang that which has been churned by themselves in the sun. || 17 ||
That ghee becomes melted by itself. || 18 ||

When the rite for Indra is completed, he fashions from a single thickest branch of the *aśvattha* tree that has fallen of its own accord—a branch broken by itself—the vessel for the *caru* offering to Mitra; it is four-cornered and shaped like a *camasa* cup. They milk the cow into a skin-bag (*dṛti*) that has not been used before, or into a new one. The cow is white and joined with a white calf. That [milk] flows through and reaches [the vessel] by means of its own natural death [of the calf]. They place that [curds], churned by itself, in the heat of the sun.

"In this case, the clarified butter becomes self-congealed. This has been made explicit by Āpastamba: "They milk a white cow with a white calf into a leather bag made from the hide of a black antelope; that [butter] congeals by itself through contact with the mixture. That [butter], having been churned by itself, they suspend in the sun. On the full moon day of the month of Taiṣya, they commence the initiations for the Ukthya sacrifice of the Abhiṣecanīya rite. (19)
The initiation offering belongs to Maitrābārhaspatya. || 13.4.20 ||
At the time of arranging the vessels, he arranges them according to their purpose; he places the cooking pot in the place of the potsherds. (kha.11) || 21 ||

At the time of offering, having offered a *caru* for Bṛhaspati, he offers one for Mitra. Or, as when the grains have been husked three times, they separate the rice-grains with the formula for division—those that are without kernels and those that have kernels; according to some, they separate the smallest and the largest grains.

Those which have ears belong to Bṛhaspati in the milk; those which are earless belong to Mitra in the clarified butter. When that [mixture] has been cooked, he then places the vessel for Mitra on top of it.
Having placed it upon that very purifier, he pours [the liquid] which has melted by itself. || 24 ||
Into that clarified butter containing the strainers, he pours the largest grains of rice. || 25 ||
He makes those two, the upper and the lower, resonant together. || 26 ||

The cooking of the oblation is done by half; the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is self-cut; the fuel (*idhma*) is self-made. He settles in a low-lying place; that becomes the self-made altar (*vedi*). He prepares the altar; one half of it is self-made. He cuts one half of the sacrificial grass; he binds one half of it with its own ends. He prepares one half of the fuel. || 27 ||
Alternatively, the altar may be prepared by oneself; the sacrificial grass is to be gathered, and the fuel is to be carried forward. || 28 ||
At the time of the performance, having performed with the offering to Bṛhaspati, he performs with the offering to Mitra.

Or otherwise: a white-backed animal is the sacrificial fee for the offering to Bṛhaspati; a horse for the offering to Mitra, or one that has been harnessed; and that same white cow with a white calf is the sacrificial fee. (Section 12) 13.4.30.
Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the thirteenth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Now begins the fifth paṭala in the thirteenth praśna:
In the same manner, they prolong the initiations (dīkṣās) for the Abhiṣecanīya sacrifice.
Just as when ten nights remain of the year, the Daśapeya sacrifice will take place. ||1||

He purchases the Soma for both the Abhiṣecanīya and the Daśapeya. He sets aside half of the King Soma for the Abhiṣecanīya, and [the other half] he deposits for the purpose of the Daśapeya with either the domestic priest (purohita) or the Brahman priest.

Having offered the animal-cake (puroḍāśa) for Agni and Soma, he subsequently offers the oblations of the Devasū sacrifice, beginning with "To Agni Gṛhapati," as they are recited in the traditional texts. For both the animal-cake and the oblations of the Devasū, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the *iḍā* portion are common.

Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, [the Adhvaryu] makes known the hand of the sacrificer with the formula: "May Savitṛ impel you for all impulses. He says, "This one, O Kurus, is your king," if he is a Kauravya; "This one, O Pañcālas, is your king," if he is a Pāñcāla; "This one, O Bharatas, is your king," if he belongs to both the Kurus and Pañcālas; "This one is your king, O people," to other kings; and "Soma is the king of us Brāhmaṇas," when it has been so stated. || 4 ||
With two verses addressed to Varuṇa, beginning with "This sovereignty has been established for you," the sacrificer wipes his face. || 5 ||
With the formula, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," he strides three steps toward the east as the Viṣṇu-strides.
When that which precedes the offering to Mahendra has been performed, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers a cake on twenty-one potsherds to the Maruts.
He places the skull-bowls with the *gaṇa* formulas. || 8 ||
Having placed [the bricks] in the middle with the *āraṇyaka* formula and the *anuvākya*, he prepares the *āmikṣā* for Mitra and Varuṇa according to the procedure for *āmikṣā*. || 9 ||
With the Vāyavya cups that have been consecrated, he takes the draughts of water.

"O divine waters, you are the offspring of the waters, the givers of sovereignty; grant us sovereignty, svāhā! Having offered this oblation in the Sarasvatī waters, he takes [the water] with this same formula.
Or [he may take it] with the formula "Arthetaḥ stha. In the same way for the others; with whichever [ladle] he offers, with that very one he takes [the portion]. || 12 ||

"You are givers of sovereignty; grant sovereignty, svāhā!"—with these words he appends [the formula] for the purpose of the oblation. "You are givers of sovereignty; grant sovereignty to so-and-so"—with these words he takes [the portion]. 13.

Having entered [the water] either in a man or a beast, [he recites]: "Thou art the lord of waters" (Khaṇḍa 13). Of the oceanic or riverine [waters], one wave falls against the current and another follows the current; he takes that which falls against the current with the words, "Thou art the male wave," and that which follows the current with the words, "Thou art the male army. He takes the stagnant waters with the words, "Ye are the flowing ones."

"Ye who do not flow from a fixed place, but flow around"—with these words [he addresses] the rivers. "Ye waters that overflow, proclaiming your transformation"—with these words [he addresses] the waters that rise up. "Ye who dwell in the cow-pen"—with these words [he addresses] the waters of wells. "Ye who possess the vigor of the Maruts"—with these words [he addresses] the hail-stones. "Ye who possess the brilliance of the sun"—with these words [he addresses] the waters of the heat and rain. "Ye who possess the skin of the sun"—with these words [he addresses] those in which forms are clearly seen. "Ye gentle ones"—with these words [he addresses] the stagnant waters, or those that flow slowly. "Ye powerful ones"—with these words [he addresses] the waters on the back [of the earth].

"You are the Śakvarīs"—this refers to the milk from the udders of the cows. "You are the sustainers of the universe"—this refers to the milk. "You are the sustainers of the people"—this refers to the curd. "You are the fiery splendors of Agni"—this refers to the clarified butter (*ghṛta*), or alternatively, "you are the most excellent, the invincible. "You are the essence of the waters and the plants"—this refers to the honey. He draws sixteen or seventeen portions. || 14 ||
Having taken [the water] with the mantra, "The divine waters, full of sweetness, have been taken," he consecrates it. || 15 ||
"O divine waters, being full of sweetness, mingle with those that are full of sweetness," with these words he pours [the water] together into a trough made of cane.
Regarding this, some authorities prescribe the recitation of the consecratory formula (*abhimantraṇa*).

"Sit down, you who are unassailable"—with these words, he places them between the *dhiṣṇiya* hearth of the Hotṛ and that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin. According to some teachers, he places them behind the *hotrīya* hearth.

Having taken a golden disk (rukmam) with a hundred holes, over which he says, "Thou art uncrushed," he purifies [the milk] three times with it, saying, "I purify your bright [milk] with the bright. || 13.5.20 ||

With the verse, "These [waters] are for our exhilaration, full of splendor, and providing strength," he distributes [the water] into four vessels. (Section 14) [The vessels are] made of Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Nyagrodha wood; he places the remainder in a wooden trough (droṇa). 21.
He feeds the sacrificer with gold, udumbara wood, and curds. ||22||

He anoints [the axle] with one hundred and one bunches of *darbha* grass; according to some, with one hundred. Having anointed the right eye with fifty and the left with fifty-one, the sacrificer puts on a garment made from the bark of *tripana* trees, saying, "Thou art the caul of the Kṣatra. He puts on a white turban, saying, "Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra"; they call this third [garment] "white-pale" (*śvetapāṇḍura*). Having caused him to touch water, he leads the sacrificer out to the outside of the *sadas* while making him recite the *āvida* verses, beginning with "May Agni find us. || 23 ||
"This one [the deceased] announces to you, O Kurus: 'He is your king. With his mind he follows after him; with his mind he rises up after him. || 24 ||
Regarding this, some prescribe a cake on twenty-one potsherds for the Maruts.
"You are the splendor of Soma; may my splendor be like yours," with these words he wraps himself in a tiger skin. || 26 ||

At the front of the Sadas, on the southern door-post, the sacrificer ascends with the formula, "May the biting serpents be driven away. He hands over water for the shaving of his hair. According to some, he hands over a piece of iron. 27.
"The head of Namuci has been cast down"—with these words he pierces lead for the eunuch; and according to some, he pierces him with lead while he himself is a eunuch. || 28 ||
Or, having touched water while reciting, "The head of Namuci has been cast down. || 29 ||

With the words, "Thou art immortality," he places a silver disk upon a tiger skin. With the words, "Lightning, protect me from below," he places a gold disk perforated with a hundred holes upon the head of the sacrificer. || 13.5.30 ||

Having announced [the offering] to these deities, beginning with "Soma the King" and "Varuṇa," and having offered the six previous oblations for the Earth with the formula "To Agni, svāhā!", he performs the six previous *aveṣṭi* offerings for the elements with the formula "To the Earth, svāhā! || 31 ||
"By the splendor of Soma, I consecrate you"—with these words, the Adhvaryu sprinkles [the sacrificer] while the oblation is being offered into the Juhū ladle. || 32 ||

With a ladle made of *parṇa* wood, the Adhvaryu [pours] from the east; likewise the others. With one made of *udumbara* wood from the south, the Brahman or a Kṣatriya; with one made of *aśvattha* wood from the west, a Vaiśya; with one made of *nyagrodha* wood from the north, a friend of the people. He pours [the water] over the gambling-ground from above.
He addresses the one being consecrated with the mantra: "Among the Kṣattras, you are the lord of the Kṣattras. || 34 ||

With the formula, "Protect us exceedingly from heaven," they uncover the garments used in the Rājasūya with the black antelope horn; [the waters] flow out downward and upward. He wipes away those residues of the consecrated king which flow down with vessels.
Having offered the six subsequent Pārtha oblations with "To Indra, svāhā!", he offers the six subsequent Aveṣṭi oblations to the beings with "To the waters, svāhā!".
With the verse, "O Rudra, that supreme name of yours which is secret," he goes northward to where the remnant in the *droṇa* vessel is and offers it in the *āgnīdhra* fire. (Section 16) || 37 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the thirteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Now begins the sixth chapter of the thirteenth book.
"Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra," with these words he brings down the chariot.
With the formula, "By the command of Mitra and Varuṇa, the directors, I yoke you," he yokes the chariot drawn by side-by-side horses.
With the words "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," he mounts the chariot. || 3 ||
"May I conquer in the impulse of the Maruts," he says as he is about to set out. || 4 ||
"Thou hast prevailed," [with these words] the Brahman priest follows from the south with a Triṣṭubh verse. || 5 ||
According to some, the Pratiprasthātṛ takes hold [of the Adhvaryu] from behind.
The archer, a member of the royal class (rājanya), stands positioned to the east or to the north.
He conquers that mind when it has attained [its object] by means of the sense-faculty together with the self. ||8||
Therefore, he shoots these arrows [with the formulas]: "I have won you back," "The mind has reached you," and "Together with my sensory power. Then he turns clockwise. || 9 ||

"This thunderbolt is the best winner of booty; with it may those two sons go to the winning of booty"—with these words, he hands the bow to the wife. According to some, he hands her the end of the bowstring. According to some, the wife pushes away the ends of the bowstring. According to some, she touches the horses. (13.6.10)

"Such is his life; grant me that life," with these words the sacrificer fastens on a jewel of silver. "Thou art vigor," [with this] one of udumbara wood; "thou art a yoke," [with this] one of gold. 11.
Some authorities prescribe that it be made of gold in the middle. || 12 ||
With the words, "Thou art Mitra," he brings down his right arm; with the words, "Thou art Varuṇa," his left. Or rather, it may be the reverse.

With the verse "Together with all the gods," he lowers his hands over the *āmikṣā* dedicated to the Viśvedevas; here he gives these two pieces of gold, one of gold and one of silver, as well as a gem.

"Obeisance to the Mother Earth," saying this, he looks down at the earth while descending. "Thou art the wrath of cattle; may this wrath of mine increase," saying this, he descends wearing sandals made of boar-skin. (Khaṇḍa 17) || 15 ||
With two verses addressed to Varuṇa, beginning with "prati tyannāma rājyam adhāyi," he wipes his face. || 16 ||

In front of the Āgnīdhra shed, they construct a measured mound (khara) four spans deep. To the south, as a preliminary act, he establishes a stool made of Khadira wood upon it with the formula, "Thou art the navel of the Kṣatra. With the formula, "Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra," he spreads a garment woven from hair over it. || 17 ||
He girds [the horse] with the formula "O Viś, do thou strengthen me"; he girds it. || 18 ||
He sits down with the words, "Thou art pleasant. || 19 ||
He addresses him as he sits down: "Sit on what is pleasant; sit on what is easy to sit upon. (13.6.20)
He mounts [the chariot] with the words, "May it not harm you. || 21 ||
He addresses the one who is mounting [the chariot]: "May he not harm you; may you not harm him. || 22 ||
"He sat down, firm in his vows"—with these words, he mutters [the mantra] while seated. || 23 ||

Having offered the oblations for unyoking the chariot into the Gārhapatya fire with the *sruva* ladon, using the formula "To Agni Gṛhapati, svāhā!", he places the chariot upon the chariot-stand together with the charioteer, reciting the verse, "The swan dwelling in purity... (RV 4.40.5).

When the fire has been established, the *saṃgrahītṛ* descends; the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the king, who is not possessed of horses or jewels, sit around him. When they have all sat down, the *brahmán* addresses the *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*): "O King, you are the *brahmán*, you are Savitṛ of true impulsion. He replies: "So be it. In this same manner, he addresses the *hotṛ*, the *brahmán*, or the *udgātṛ*. Each replies with the respective subsequent mantra. || 25 ||
With the formula, "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra," the Brahman then hands over the wooden sword (sphya) to the King; according to some, the Adhvaryu hands it over.

"Thou art this thunderbolt, the best winner of booty. (Khaṇḍa 18) "May I prosper through it," says the king to the domestic priest; the domestic priest to his deputy; the deputy to the jewel-bearers; they hand it down from one to another until finally he gives it to the keeper of the dice. || 27 ||
Having raised up the gaming-ground with that wooden sword, he pours down either one hundred and fifty or five times fifty dice.
Then, saying "The King has won," they cast out four dice, stake four hundred [cows], and play with a six-year-old cow. || 29 ||

Having conquered the regions and attained sovereignty over the cooked rice, saying, "I have become a king," he gives five dice to the sacrificer—[representing] the Brāhmaṇa, the Rājanya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra, and the fifth being the dice itself. || 13.6.30 ||

Having dismissed them as well, he calls those whose names are auspicious: "O you of good fame! for the charioteer; "O you of good fortune! for the distributor of portions; and "O you whose reign is truth! for the attendant. Having called them, he gives the field to the Brahman.
Whatever Brahmā desires, they are the witnesses thereof.

Whichever wife he may desire, thinking, "May her offspring possess the kingdom," for her, having caused her to take hold of the fire-wood placed near the domestic fire (aupāsana), he performs two oblations with the remnants from the vessels—intermingling their names—with the verse, "O Prajāpati, these [beings] are not yours... (Prajāpate na tvadetāni). ||33||
He interchanges their names, saying, "This one is the son of such-and-such a person; that one is the son of such-and-such a woman. || 34 ||
He causes the Śaunaḥśepa narrative to be recited; it consists of verses interspersed with Gāthās, numbering more than a hundred or even more than a thousand. (Section 19) 35.
Seated upon Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Hotṛ priest recites the invitatory verses. || 36 ||
Standing between the two golden bunches of grass, the Adhvaryu responds: "Om" is the response for a Ṛg-verse, and likewise "Tathā" for a Gāthā.
When the Śaunaḥśepa [recitation] has concluded, he gives gold to the Hotṛ; two tufts of kusha grass made of gold to the Adhvaryu.

In this rite, one should proceed with an offering of curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) dedicated to the Viśvedevas, accompanied by a cake on twenty-one potsherds for Vāyu. "Embracing the tiger, they urge on the lion for great good fortune; like the well-offered ocean, they groom the leopard standing in the waters"—reciting this, while performing a malevolent rite, one should split the sacrificial cake in two with the wooden sword (*sphya*). If the wooden sword should stick to it, or if one should wipe it off, from that portion one should cut an oblation for Viṣṇu Urukrama.
In this case, he gives these two pieces of gold: one of gold and one of silver, together with a gem, provided that they were given previously. 13.6.40.
One undertakes the ritual acts beginning with those dedicated to Mahendra. || 41 ||
Having emerged from the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), he offers an oblation into the water with the formula: "To the Son of the Waters, svāhā! (Apām naptre svāhā). || 42 ||
"Omnisvāhā to the Son of Strength!"—thus [he offers] upon a dry tree stump or a clump of darbha grass. || 43 ||
Having returned, he offers [the oblation] in the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "To Agni Gṛhapati, svāhā! (44).
He immolates a barren cow dedicated to Indra as the *anūbandhyā* animal sacrifice.
For that [offering], he prepares a sacrificial cake of wild rice (naivāra) from the four-footed slaughter-ground. || 46 ||
The cart serves as the substitute offering. ||47||
The Abhiṣecanīya sacrifice is concluded. (Section 20) || 48 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the thirteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Now begins the seventh chapter of the thirteenth book.

On the following day, he performs the sacrifice daily with the seven *saṃsṛp* oblations, offering a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, as prescribed in the traditional text. He settles at each sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) one after another. Where the *āhavanīya* fire was previously located, there the *gārhapatya* fire is placed for the subsequent [ground]; however, for the seventh sacrifice, the *āhavanīya* is in the *prāgvaṃśa* hall and the *gārhapatya* is outside.
Then he performs that sacrifice; when it has been completed, in the afternoon he undergoes initiation for the Daśapeya.
In the waters, at the place of the consecration (dīkṣā), the sacrificer puts on a golden garland consisting of six or twelve lotuses.
On that day, having been initiated, he purchases the King (Soma) with ten castrated young bulls.
He does not trade, nor does he carry goods for sale. || 5 ||
He performs yet another purchase. || 6 ||
Before the Upasads, he offers a pap of cooked rice to Soma; between them, one to Tvaṣṭṛ; and after them, one to Viṣṇu.
For these [fires], the Upasad rites and the enclosing sticks (paridhis) accomplish their purpose externally.
The Daśapeya Agniṣṭoma sacrifice consists of seventeen [stomas]; the Vasatīvarī waters are dedicated to Sarasvatī. 9.
The Bhārgava becomes the Hotṛ priest; the Śrāyantīya is the Brahman’s chant (brahmasāman); the Vāravantīya is the Agniṣṭoma chant (agniṣṭomasāman). || 13.7.10 ||
At the time of arranging the vessels, he sets out ten additional *camasa* cups. || 11 ||
At the time of the drawing [of Soma], he draws ten additional cups. 12.

He whose Soma-drinking has been uninterrupted for ten generations is the performer of the consumption; having announced him back from the tenth generation, one hundred Brāhmaṇas who have drunk Soma approach. || 13 ||
Ten persons each consume from one cup.

At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives two golden mirrors to the *adhvaryu*, as prescribed in the traditional text; a bull to the *grāvastut*; a ewe to the *hotṛ*; and a goat to the *subrahmaṇya*. (Section 21) 15.
The Daśapeya sacrifice is concluded. || 16 ||
When that has been completed, he performs the Diśām Aveṣṭi sacrifice.
"One offers an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni"—having sacrificed each oblation according to the traditional recitation, one should pour clarified butter over the offering to Bṛhaspati.
With that [offering], one who desires food or one who desires heaven should sacrifice. || 19 ||

If a Brāhmaṇa is the sacrificer, having placed [the vessel] in the middle and offered oblation after oblation, he should sprinkle it with clarified butter. If a Rājanya, [he should offer] to Indra; if a Vaiśya, [he should offer] to the Viśvedevas. || 13.7.20 ||
On the following day, he should perform the animal sacrifice with two animals.

He sacrifices a large, pregnant ewe to the Ādityas, and a spotted heifer of one year old to the Maruts. He proceeds with the offering for the Maruts in a low voice; both the *āśruta* and the *pratyāśruta* formulas are also in a low voice, while those for the ewe dedicated to the Ādityas are pronounced aloud.
Then, when the next day has dawned, he sacrifices with the six oblations of the Prayuj offerings.
"One offers an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni," as it is recited in the text.
"A chariot-drawing horse from the right side is the sacrificial fee. (24)
On the following day, he offers a sacrificial pap (caru) to Sarasvatī with the six subsequent [verses], as prescribed in the traditional recension.

A bow with three arrows, a dried skin-bag, a staff, and a pair of sandals—this is the sacrificial fee; or alternatively, a horse. According to some, it should be a horse with reddish ears. He sends this to rival kings. || 25 ||
"Having been consecrated, we have become kings," he declares. || 26 ||
He performs the Agnihotra sacrifice for one year. || 27 ||
For the sake of continuity, he should perform there those sacrifices which are not prohibited by the Agnihotra.
At the end of the year, he should sacrifice with the Keśavapanīya Atirātra.

In that rite, there are mantras concerning the shaving; one should have the hair shaved at the beginning with those whose first words [mention it], and at the end with those whose final words [mention it]. Thus concludes the Keśavapanīya.
When that has concluded, he should sacrifice with the Vyuṣṭi-dvirātra.
For him, the Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma constitutes the first day.

The *sarvastoma-atirātra* sacrifice has the *gāyatra* as the *sāman* on the first day and the *traiṣṭubha* on the second. The *rathaṃtara* is the *sāman* on the first day and the *bṛhat* on the second; the *vaikhānasa* is the *sāman* on the first day. The *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice has the *haviṣmat-nidhana* on the first day and the *haviṣkṛt-nidhana* on the second. The first day is for sacrifice on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), and the second is for sacrifice on the following day, or during the waxing fortnight (*āpūryamāṇapakṣa*), whichever two days may be auspicious. 33.
The Agniṣṭoma is the steadfastness of Kṣatriyas; therefore, one should perform it at the end. || 34 ||
There is liberation from the five [elements]. || 35 ||
The Rājasūya sacrifice is concluded. || 36 ||
Having sacrificed with the Rājasūya, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī. (Khanda 23, Sutra 37)
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the thirteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
Now begins the eighth chapter in the thirteenth book.
On the first day of the three-night rite (*trirātra*), having purchased young grass-blades from a eunuch for the price of lead, he ties them in a linen cloth and sets them aside.
He commences the ritual procedure of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.

In this regard, we shall explain what is performed: having added fuel to the fires, having prepared the Veda-grass bundle, having strewn grass around the fires, having washed his hands, and having spread out a layer of *ulapa* grass, he arranges the vessels according to their purpose; he places a cooking pot (*sthālī*) in the place of the potsherds (*kapāla*). ||3||
At the time of the offering, he pours out an abundant quantity of rice for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman.
Having cooked it according to the ritual for *caru*, and having dug a pit in front of the *gārhapatya* fire, he prepares the *parisrut* liquor according to the ritual for *surā*.
With the mantra, "Thee, sweet, with the sweet," he mixes the *surā* with young grass shoots.
He consecrates the mixed [mixture] with the formula: "O Soma, be cooked for the Aśvins; be cooked for Sarasvatī; be cooked for Indra Sutraman. || 7 ||
The stay is for three nights in succession. ||8||
He cuts a single sacrificial post. || 9 ||
It does not create this Veda; once it has been created, it does not produce its meanings. || 13.8.10 ||
He prepares the altar of the Soma sacrifice, measuring one-third [of the size of the previous one]. || 11 ||

At the same time that the Adhvaryu prepares the high altar (uttaravedi), the Pratiprasthātṛ, having brought earth from the pit (cātvāla), prepares a square mound (khara) to the south of the high altar.

At the same time that the Adhvaryu leads forward the Āhavanīya fire, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having taken embers from the Dakṣiṇāgni and having piled them upon the mound (khara), adds fuel to them. ||13||
He does not wash his hands. ||14||
He sets out three cups made of *vaikaṅkata* wood with upward-facing bowls for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman. || 15 ||
A hundred perforated vessels, a cooking pot, a golden ornament, and a hair-strainer. ||16||

Having first performed the rites up to the immolation of the animal, and having extracted the *surā* and poured it into the vessel, he purifies the *parisrut* with a strainer made of hair, saying: "May it purify thy *parisrut*. (17)

"Vāyuḥ pūtaḥ pavitreṇa" is [the mantra] for one who has vomited Soma or for one who has been excessively purified by Soma. "Prāṅ somaḥ" is [the mantra] for one who has been excessively purified by Soma; having placed it upon the head of a pure Brāhmaṇa. (Section 24) 18.

He undertakes the ritual acts beginning with the dedication of the sacrificial animals (*paśūpākaraṇa*). He dedicates a smoke-colored goat to the Aśvins; a ram to Sarasvatī; and a bull, a he-goat, or a wether to Indra. For one who has vomited Soma or for one who has over-poured Soma, a fourth animal is dedicated to Bṛhaspati. || 19 ||
When the omenta have been offered, he gives as the sacrificial fee a golden plate, a bull, and a swift mare. || 13.8.20 ||

Having performed that, he draws the cups of Surā with the Vāyu formulas. The Adhvaryu draws the Āśvina cup with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, faultless, with the faultless, acceptable to the Aśvins. The Pratiprasthātṛ draws the Sārasvata cup with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, faultless, with the faultless, acceptable to Sarasvatī. The Yajamāna draws the Aindra cup with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, faultless, with the faultless, acceptable to Indra Sutraman. || 21 ||
"Kuvid aṅga" is the single introductory verse (puroruc) for all [the offerings].

He mixes the offering for the Aśvins with *kvala*-grain flour; according to some, with jujube (*badara*) flour. He mixes the offering for Sarasvatī with *karkandhu*-flour and lion’s hair; and the offering for Indra with jujube flour and tiger’s hair; according to some, with *kvakala*-flour and wolf’s hair. Or alternatively, the Adhvaryu should mentally meditate on lions, the Pratiprasthātṛ on tigers, and the sacrificer on wolves. 23.

"This is your womb; for the Aśvins you! This is your womb; for Sarasvatī you! This is your womb; for Indra Sutrāman you!"—having thus deposited [the cups] upon the head of a Brāhmaṇa according to their respective forms, he proceeds with the rites beginning with the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*). Having offered the animal-cake for Bṛhaspati, he offers the cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, the cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, and the cake on ten potsherds for Varuṇa.

Having approached them, they take up the cups as they were originally drawn, [saying]: "Recite the invitatory verse for the Soma and the Surā for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman! Having offered the Soma and the Surā set forth for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman, give the command! Thus he issues the formal direction. 26.
He offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered. || 27 ||

Having offered at the *anuvaṣaṭ* call and having proceeded with the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for Bṛhaspati, he purchases a Brāhmaṇa who shall drink the remnants of the cup. He consumes [the remnant] with the formula: "Whatever remains here of the pressed juice, which Indra drank by his powers—that Soma, the King, I consume here with a gracious mind. (28)

"For various indeed are your two seats established by the gods; do not mingle in the highest heaven! You are the powerful Surā, and this is Soma; do not harm me as you enter your own womb"—with these words he addresses him while he is consuming [the draught]. || 29 ||

"I have heard of two paths of the fathers—those of the gods and those of mortals. By these two, this entire world comes together between the former and the latter signs. With these words, he should pour [the mixture] into the mound of an anthill. 13.8.30.
Or he may drink it himself; or he may offer it as a complete oblation (sarvahuti). || 31 ||
Having tied a hundred-holed vessel to the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire and spread it out, they hold it steady; it is covered with a golden plate perforated by a hundred holes.

"May the Fathers rejoice; may we attain the lifespan ordained by the gods, which has Soma as its beginning. May we attain the lifespan ordained by the gods, which is drunk by Indra and is far-seeing. "Whatever of my mind has gone to Yama, or whatever of mine has not returned—by means of King Soma, we establish that within ourselves; may we attain the lifespan ordained by the gods. With these words, he should pour the remainder of the *surā* into that very [vessel]. || 33 ||
He worships the flowing waters with the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses addressed to the Pitṛs. || 34 ||

"O Soma, you are wise with wisdom," [he says]. (Section 26) With three verses, the Adhvaryu [covers] from the east; with the next three, the Brahman from the south; with the next three, the Hotṛ from the west; with the next three, the Āgnīdhra from the north; and with the three verses addressed to Kavyavāhanī [he covers] from above. At this point, he places the perforated pot (*śatātṛṇṇā sthālī*). A Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya should not pay heed [to it]. To lead the southern fire forward, he himself should remain consuming this remnant of *surā* as his sacrificial food (*vrata*). 35.
Having performed the ritual with the animal victims, he proceeds with the sacrificial cakes.
Having completed the *sviṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* offerings for both the animal victims and the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) in a common manner, [he should proceed]. ||37||
They perform the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with spears, māṣa-beans, and vessels. ||38||
The ritual procedure for this is explained by [the rules for] the Soma-consecration bath (avabhṛtha). || 39 ||
The Sāman is not sung. 13.8.40.
Having gone over silently, he offers it with something resembling *māsara* and *ṛjīṣa*. ||41||

"O divine Varuṇa, that bond of yours which has the *gāyatrī* metre and is established in the *brahman*, I release it for you with this; *svāhā*!"—with these words he pierces the cup of the Aśvins. "O divine Varuṇa, that bond of yours which has the *triṣṭubh* metre and is established in the *kṣatra*, I release it for you with this; *svāhā*!"—this is for the cup of Sarasvatī. "O divine Varuṇa, that bond of yours which has the *jagatī* metre and is established in the *viś*, I release it for you with this; *svāhā*!"—this is for the cup of Indra.

"O God Varuṇa, that noose of yours which has the *anuṣṭubh* as its meter and is established in the quarters—him I appease with this; to him, svāhā!"—with these words he offers the perforated pot (*śatātṛṇṇā sthālī*). "O God Varuṇa, that noose of yours which has the *paṅkti* as its meter and is established in speech—him I appease with this; to him, svāhā!"—with these words he offers the spikes (*śūla*). 42.
The response is made by remaining silent. || 43 ||

One should cause him who has vomited Soma to sacrifice. One should cause him who has passed over the Soma to sacrifice. One who desires a kingdom, one who is deprived of his kingdom, one who desires a village, one who desires offspring, one who desires cattle, one who has been overtaken by misfortune, or one practicing malevolent magic against another, should sacrifice with this [rite]. It is prescribed for all consecrations. With this, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya desiring prosperity should sacrifice; desiring prosperity, he should sacrifice. (Section 27) 44.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the thirteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Thus ends the thirteenth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra. ||13||

The Kaustubha jewel—a definitive exposition of the *Nyāyasūtra*—has been fashioned here for this garland of ritual practice (*prayoga*), which is established as a string of aphorisms by Satyāṣāḍha. May it, situated in the center of the body of the sacrifice, bring me satisfaction when offered by me; for He indeed accepts whatever is performed with devotion by His followers. Thus ends the eighth chapter in the twelfth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha, compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. The commentary on the twelfth book is hereby completed.
13.1 Now begins the thirteenth book;
therein is the first chapter.

With joy, I bow to the Lord of Sages, the ocean of compassion, known as the Guru Hiraṇyakeśin, who knows the meaning of the Sūtras and who possesses the bliss of true consciousness and bliss that shines through all the excellent Siddhas joined with those to be disciplined. I salute my Guru Gaṇapati, the bestower of birth and knowledge, and likewise I bow to Maheśāna together with Gaurī, and to Viṣṇu with Padmā. The Cayanakratu sacrifice was explained in the eleventh and twelfth [books]; however, the Vājapeya and Rājasūya will be described in the thirteenth.

Thus, first of all, the *sarvajyotiṣṭoma* has been demonstrated in the *Sūtra-kṛt-naya-sūtra* (Saṃ. Śrī. 1-1). By means of the words "The *agniṣṭoma* is for one who desires all [objects]" (*sarvakāmo 'gniṣṭomaḥ*) and so forth (Sū. Au. 7-1), the author of the Sūtras explained the *agniṣṭoma* *saṃsthā*, which serves as the fundamental archetype (*mūla-prakṛti*) for all subsequent one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*), multi-day sacrifices (*ahīna*), and sacrificial sessions (*satra*). Then, he stated that the *ukthya*, *ṣoḍaśin*, *atirātra*, and *aptoryāma* are modifications (*guṇavikāra*) of the *agniṣṭoma* (Sū. Au. 7-18), and thus explained these five *saṃsthās*.
Now, in order to explain the remaining single form of the Vājapeya sacrifice, which consists of sixteen modifications, he makes a formal promise to secure the attention of the students:
"In autumn, one should sacrifice with the Vājapeya. (1)

One etymological explanation is that *vājapeya* is so called because it is a sacrifice (*yāna*) in which Soma—the food (*vāja*) of the gods—is to be drunk (*peya*). Another etymological explanation is that since the gods desired to obtain *vāja*—that is, food in the form of a fruit—by means of this sacrifice, it is called *vājapeya*, meaning that by which the food (*vāja*) in the form of drink (*peya*) is to be attained. Thus, *vājapeya* is the name of the ritual; for its application is not established in reference to a substance or a quality. And it takes place in the autumn.

"One should sacrifice with the Vājapeya in autumn," because this is stated even in another Sūtra. [Chapter 1] Together with the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī, 128. Regarding this, Baudhāyana states the preparatory materials: "One is about to perform the Vājapeya sacrifice."
