He prepares a black antelope skin, two gold plates with golden borders, a goat-skin, a piece of gold weighing a hundred mānas, seventeen gold *kṛṣṇala* seeds, a golden vessel filled with honey, a chariot wheel of Udumbara wood with seventeen spokes, a wooden frame consisting of seventeen planks for the sacrificial altar, a hornless post four *aratnis* high, a post seventeen *aratnis* high, a bundle of wheat, a turban, wild rice, seventeen *śarāva* measures, seventeen bags of herbs, seventeen *vāyavya* cups, and seventeen [other vessels].

There were seventeen large-bottomed vessels with handles, a hundred and seventeen locks of hair, seventeen gold neck-ornaments (*niṣkas*), seventeen garments, seventeen loads of clothing, seventeen chariots, seventeen drums, seventeen elephants, seventeen female slaves, seventeen swords equipped [with sheaths], and seventeen hundred head of cattle, or perhaps seventeen thousand of each kind of bird; for in that [sacrifice], all kinds of birds were present.

"Twenty-four animals and fifty-one horses—let the Ravādirī be pierced through with weapons; the materials for the Agniṣṭoma are known. "In the latter days of summer, prior to the full moon of Āṣāḍha, he should sacrifice" (BaudhŚS 11.1). The Vājapeya is of two kinds: the Āptavājapeya and the Kuruvājapeya. In this sacrifice, there is no piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*). "One should pile the fire-altar in the Vājapeya," says Baudhāyana; "one should not pile it," says Śālīki (BaudhDhSū).

22-12) Because of the prohibitive statement [in the text], some maintain that even here [the *iṣṭi*] is desired; thus, according to the view of the Chāndogas, the *ācayaṇa* should be performed. For it is stated by Vaikhānasa that the Vājapeya is also a constituent part (*saṃsthā*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma. However, Āpastamba has described the Vājapeya as a separate ritual (*karmāntara*). The status of the Vājapeya as a separate ritual, as well as its twofold nature, [is established]. Among these, the first is called the *āpta-vājapeya*. In that regard, he deduces the rule concerning eligibility for the Vājapeya: "A Brāhmaṇa or a Rājanya. (2)

Because it was performed by Bṛhaspati; for among the gods, Bṛhaspati is the one who identifies with the Brāhmaṇa caste. There is a similarity between the Brāhmaṇa and Bṛhaspati due to their connection with Brahman, based on the etymological derivation: "one who knows Brahman" or "one who speaks Brahman" is a Brāhmaṇa. It was also performed by Indra; for among the gods, Indra is the one who identifies with the Kṣatriya caste. There is a similarity between Indra and the Rājanya (Kṣatriya) due to their connection with *kṣatra*, since both possess the state of *kṣatra*—that is, strength (*bala*).

Therefore, even among humans, the entitlement belongs only to the Brāhmaṇa and the Rājanya, and not to the Vaiśya. For this very reason, Āpastamba says: "In the autumn, one should sacrifice with the Vājapeya; a Brāhmaṇa or a Rājanya who desires prosperity" (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 18.1). || 2 ||
The ritual procedure for that [rite] has been explained by means of the ṣoḍaśin [sacrifice]. || 3 ||

The procedure for that Vājapeya sacrifice follows the ritual pattern of the Ṣoḍaśin, because the Ṣoḍaśin exists [as its model]. Its purpose is stated at the time of the sale of the Soma: "He buys the Soma with a piece of ginger having an *elodhaka* leaf. Alternatively, in the case of seventeen initiation days (*dīkṣā*), the commencement is on the tenth day of autumn; in the case of thirteen initiation days, the commencement is on the fourteenth day. [This is] from both [types of] full-moon festivals. (Note: The reading is *śrutim iti*. This is from the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, in the thirteenth book.

It becomes easy to perform. Then, having offered the morning *agnihotra* and having declared, "I shall sacrifice with the *vājapeya* as an *āpta* [attained] rite," and having declared, "I shall obtain Prajāpati," this is the indication of the fruit; or rather, it is for the sake of prosperity (*ṛddhi*). Or, because of the statement, "Some recite it as a permanent (*nitya*) rite, as if it were permanent," and because in a permanent rite there is no indication of a fruit as if it were permanent, it is for the sake of food (*anna*). The selection of the *somapravāka* and so forth is like that of the *ṣoḍaśin*. At the time of the purchase of the Soma, the purchase is made with ginger (*śuṇṭhī*).

"This is the indication; its essence is even more than this," so said the Soma-seller. "I shall buy it from you for ninety-nine [coins]"—this is the specific detail. "Light for us," and so forth. || 3 ||
The entire [sāman] consists of seventeen [verses]. || 4 ||
All the *stomas* consist of seventeenfold chants (*saptadaśastoma*). ... Alternatively, because of the scriptural mention of a connection with a fruit, he states that a fruit must be postulated:
"He attains Prajāpati. (5)
"He attains Prajāpati" means he attains the station of Prajāpati; indeed, he becomes Prajāpati himself. || 5 ||
There are seventeen initiations, three *upasads*, and twenty-one *prasutas*. 6.

The commencement begins with the statement, "He becomes Soma. Because of the injunction of the three Upasads in the passage, "For twenty-one nights he becomes the pressed Soma," there is no piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*). According to the view of the Chandogas, in that alternative, the mention of the "twenty-first" [night] is a restatement based on the wording of the Brāhmaṇa: "Of that [sacrifice], there are thirteen initiations (*dīkṣā*), the Upasads are passed over, and the pressing (*prasuta*) takes place on the seventeenth day. Alternatively, "There are seventeen initiations, three Upasads, and the pressing takes place on the twenty-first day."

"Alternatively, there are three *dīkṣā*s, three *upasad*s, and the *prasuta* on the seventh day" (*Baudhāyana Śrautasūtra* 11.1). Or rather, "the twenty-first [day]" is another option. Likewise, there are fourteen *dīkṣā*s, six *upasad*s, and the *prasuta* on the twenty-first; this excludes the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) altogether. || 6 ||

The sacrificial post (yūpa) is seventeen aratnis in height; it is made of bilva wood and is four-cornered, or else of khadira or palāśa wood; its upper ring (caṣāla) may also be made of wheat flour; furthermore, it should be hornless (tūpara).

Nor is it eight-cornered; rather, there are four corners facing each direction. Regarding the statement that "the *caṣāla* is made of wheat," since both [options] are supported by scriptural authority (*śruti*), there is an option (*vikalpa*). However, a *caṣāla* made from wheat flour would result in many archetypal features (*prākṛta*) being obtained, such as the corners (*aśri*) and so forth. Alternatively, after performing the *pravargya* rite, they proceed with the *upasad* rites, and so on; at the time of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), one makes the post of *khadira* wood or of *bilva* wood, which has seventeen rings and is four-cornered, while the *caṣāla* is made from wheat flour.

"There is no extra *svaru*," according to the Śruti. There are twenty-three *svarus* for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). There is only one post. Some make a single *svaru* for all the seasonal animals (*ṛtupaśu*); in that case, there are exactly twenty-one. Or, if [a *svaru*] is made for each animal, then there are twenty-three. || 7 ||
When that which precedes the Upasad rites has been performed, the Pratiprasthātṛ prepares the fermented liquor (parisrut) according to the ritual procedure for *surā*.

1.kha. At the time of the purchase of Soma. [Chapter 1] *Mahādevaśākha-saṃkalita-yogacandrikā-vyākhyā-sametam* (Accompanied by the Commentary Yogacandrikā compiled by Mahādeva Śākha). 129. When the purification (*mārjana*) is completed with the mantra, "O Agni, that body of yours which is Rudra-like," the Pratiprasthātṛ prepares the *surā* (fermented liquor), meaning he prepares the *surā* for the sake of the sacrifice. It may be either common worldly liquor or the *payograhā* (milk-offerings) as in the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice. This is because the drinking of intoxicants is prohibited in the Kali age. As in the *Sautrāmaṇī*, it may be either of the nature of an *iṣṭi* (sacrificial offering) or of the nature of a *saumika* (Soma-related rite). The *aiṣṭikī* (offering-type) has been explained in detail in the *Sautrāmaṇī*; similarly here, the *saumikī* (Soma-type) is characterized by the ritual rules (*dharmas*) such as the *kāya* and others.

Regarding the *aiṣṭikī* [offering], one performs the rites beginning with the *klība* [cup] up to the conclusion of the preparation for the *sureṣṭi* and so forth at that very time. Here, the procedure for the *sāman* and other elements is like that of the *Sautrāmaṇī*, using the formula: "I offer you, acceptable to Prajāpati. Or it may be a worldly (*laukikī*) rite. In the case of the *saumikī* [offering], the ritual requirements such as the purchase (*kraya*) and others are not omitted. Since the *surā* is of the nature of *soma*, and because of its syntactic connection with the *somagraha* cups—as per the Vedic revelation stating, "The *surā* cups are indeed *soma* cups"—the measurement of the altar is performed by means of two-footed strides (*dvipadaprakrama*) at the time of measuring the altar.

The mantras for the five roof-coverings of the *sadas* are: "Thou art the seat of Indra," and five times, "For the shelter of Viśvānara"; seven times, "Thou art the seat of Indra"; and for the *uparavas*, the mantra "I dig thee, belonging to Viṣṇu" is used once. During the digging, with the dust from that [pit], the *pratiprasthātṛ* prepares a second square *khara* below and behind the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart for the sake of the *surā* cups. He pours the earth from the *cātvāla* and other pits onto the *iṣṭikās*, and so forth. 8.
At the time of girding, he encircles the sacrificial post with seventeen garments.

When the time for the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma has arrived, having determined [the wood] to be small and large, he encircles the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with seventeen cloths; that is to say, he spreads them around it. According to some, the encircling of the post standing near the fire (*agniṣṭha*) is performed with two cords.

Having offered the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) for the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, he subsequently offers the oblations of the Devasū—beginning with "To Agni Gṛhapati," as they are recited in the traditional texts. For both the animal-cake and the oblations of the Devasū, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the *iḍā* portion are common. 13.1.10.
This indeed is the food. || 10 || Now, regarding the beginning of the ritual acts, he states the Sāvitra oblation:
"O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice; impel the lord of the sacrifice for our fortune"—with this [verse], he offers at the beginning of each pressing. || 11 ||

By means of repetition (*vīpsā*), it is stated that this must be performed at the beginning of all ritual acts (*karman*). At the commencement of all rites, the *sāvitra-homa* is to be performed; these rites have been summarized by the Brāhmaṇa: "At each pressing (*savana*), he offers [the oblation]" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.3.5). Baudhāyana has also cited this for the beginning of various specific rites: "When about to offer the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, he offers the *sāvitra*. When about to offer the *dīkṣā* oblations, he offers the *sāvitra*. When about to offer the *prāyaṇīyā*, he offers the *sāvitra*" (Baudhāyana Śrautasūtra 11.2). It ends with "svadāti naḥ svāhā. Savitṛ is the deity. (11)
On the day of the Sutyā, the officiating priests, wearing golden garlands, perform the ritual proceedings.

Having understood this, O Great King, the officiating priests (ṛtvij), with the exception of the Sadasya, wear golden garlands. Some say that the sacrificer (yajamāna) also wears a golden garland; others do not desire this for the Sadasya. The Sadasya is a permanent member, for it is stated in the Chandoma section: "The Sadasya is the seventeenth; one should elect him separately. (12)

At the time of arranging the vessels, he sets out the vessels according to their respective purposes. In place of the *atigrāhya* vessel for Indra, he sets out five *atigrāhya* vessels for Indra. (The ritual procedure for these is explained by that of the former. The ritual procedure for them is explained by that of the *atigrāhya* vessel for Indra. Having set out the *ṣoḍaśin* vessel, he sets out seventeen *soma* cups for Prajāpati. The ritual procedure for these is explained by that of the *ṣoḍaśin* vessel.

To the west, the Pratiprasthātṛ [places] seventeen cups for drawing the *surā* libations, along with the ritual implements (*kratukaraṇa*). Just as at the time of drawing the Soma cups in the *Atirātra*, he should draw five *atigrāhya* cups for Indra in place of the single *atigrāhya* cup for Indra, using the five formulas beginning with "Thou art taken with a support; thee, the sitter among men" (*upayāmagṛhīto 'si nṛṣadam tvā*). The ritual procedure for these is explained by that of the *atigrāhya* cup for Indra. Having drawn the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, he draws seventeen Soma cups for Prajāpati. The ritual procedure for these is explained by that of the *ṣoḍaśin*.

"kuvidaṅga..."—this is the single *puroruc* for all [the cups], ending with "ayā viṣṭhā janayankarvarāṇi. (Section 1) With the *upayāma* formulas, the Pratiprasthātṛ takes seventeen *surā* cups. Some authorities prescribe two reversed cups. They take them in an interlocking manner: first the Adhvaryu, then the Pratiprasthātṛ. He places the Soma cups in front of the axle; he places the *surā* cups behind the axle.

When the time for setting out the vessels has arrived, after having set out the vessel for the *aindrātigrāhya* from among the vessels in use, he sets out five vessels to its north. The ritual procedure for these—beginning with the type of wood and location—is explained [in the section] on the setting out of the vessel for the *sauryātigrāhya*. Having set out the *ṣoḍaśin* vessel and resolved that they are dedicated to Prajāpati, he sets out those intended for the *soma*-libations. Regarding their ritual procedure, there is a restriction on the type of wood and their square shape.

On another mound, he employs seventeen *upayāma* vessels for the purpose of drawing the *surā* libations; these he employs as being shaped like upright bowls, or shaped like leather pouches (*śulvakośa*), or shaped like *teja* vessels. He draws the libations beginning with the *pariplava* vessel, having performed the drawing of the *aindrāpta-grāhya* and *atigraha* cups, and then the *upayāma* vessels and so forth. He draws the three intermediate ones for the purpose of the cup-drawings, [reciting]: "The cups which have lifted the essence from the further shore"—these two are with the *upayāma* formula at the end. Upa...
1ka. According to their view; kha. Regarding them here. [Chapter 1] Together with the commentary *Yogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 131.

With the five mantras ending with "Thou art seized by Yama," he takes the five Āgrayaṇa cups. Having taken them with the mantra "This is thy womb; for Iḷā thee," he sets them down. Their ritual procedure regarding the space for the cups and so forth is like that of the Aindra cup. He takes the Ṣoḍaśin cup with the verse beginning "By this station" and ending with "I take. Likewise, he takes the seventeen-fold cup. He sets it down with "This is thy womb; for Prajāpati thee. "Somanahā" is their name; their ritual procedure, including the subsequent consecration and so forth, is like that of the Ṣoḍaśin. *Kuvit*... [text fragment].

With *daṅga*, he takes [the vessels]. For the purpose of taking the *surā* cups, he takes the *surā* cups on another donkey using the same *upayāma* formulas and the same vessels as before. With *kuvidaṅga*, however, it is without *upayāma*. This is because it belongs to the section on plants (*oṣadhivikāra*) and is not a primary rite (*apūrva*). Since it is a modification of the *soma* ritual, they prescribe it with *upayāma* in the reverse order, starting from the taking of the *soma* cups with *kuvidaṅga*. With *ayā viṣṭhā*, the *upayāma* formulas are used for the placing of the *surā* cups, but only in the case of the *soma* cups.

Even though the cups for *surā* are neither modifications of the sacrificial materials (*naupadhivikāra*) nor something entirely new (*apūrva*), they do indeed constitute a modification of the *soma*, and thus the *upayāma* (the supporting ladle) and the *āsādana* (the placing) are performed with the same mantras as those used for the *soma*. There is an interlocking sequence (*vyatiṣaṅga*): the Adhvaryu takes the *soma* cups and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the *surā* cups; of these seventeen, the Adhvaryu acts first and the Pratiprasthātṛ afterwards. Such is the rule. The mention of the *soma* cups is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) intended to keep them out of sight, because they are prescribed by the Brāhmaṇa text according to their respective places. 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19.

At the time for the animal sacrifices, he dedicates three seasonal victims. He dedicates a spotted cow barren of calves to the Maruts, and a ewe to Sarasvatī—one that has not yet cut its teeth; according to some, a ram instead of the ewe to Sarasvatī. ||13.1.20||

When the time for the animal sacrifices has arrived, having dedicated three sacrificial animals—the *āgneya*, the *aindrāgna*, and the *aindra* (a bull)—it is stated in another Sūtra that because of the observation of their combination, it is not merely the *āgneya* animal. The *mārutī vaśā* is a barren cow; and the animal for Sarasvatī is a ewe, as indicated by the supplementary statement: "Sarasvatī is indeed speech" (*vāg vai sarasvatī*, Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.3.4). [The ewe] should be one whose teeth have not yet fallen out. Or, prior to the offering to the Maruts, there is the ewe for Sarasvatī, according to the rule: "With the ewe for Sarasvatī, [one performs] the Atirātra" (*sārasvatyā'tirātram*, Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.3.4).

The Sārasvata [sacrifice] has a single form, and Sarasvant is its deity according to the supplementary statement in another recension (śākhā). Baudhāyana cites these injunctions for the animal sacrifices as follows: "Having taken the cup for the Aśvins and having taken the six-fold cord, he approaches the sacrificial post; having set up the post provided with a wooden head-piece (svaru), he then dedicates these animals: one for Agni, one for Indra-Agni, one for Indra, and one for the Maruts."

Āpastamba, however, regarding the offerings to Agni and the others as already established by the general rule (*codaka*), considers them to be mere restatements (*anuvāda*) and cites the injunction for the ewe for Marut and the ram for Sarasvatī: "At the time of the animal sacrifice, having performed the ritual lustration (*upākaraṇa*) three times with *ṛtuparṇa* verses, he performs the lustration of the barren cow for Marut and the ram for Sarasvatī" (ĀpŚS 18.2.12). || 20 ||
He dedicates seventeen animals sacred to Prajāpati.

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the animals dedicated to Prajāpati are performed together. Among these, the subsidiary acts such as the dedication (*upākaraṇa*) and the tethering (*niyojana*) must be repeated for each individual animal. Regarding their repetition, it is not the case that one performs them in their entirety for one animal and then does exactly the same for the next; rather, we shall explain that one begins with any one animal and completes the tethering and so forth from there. In that context, the dedication (*upākaraṇa*) may be begun with any animal and completed anywhere. As for the tethering and the subsequent rites... [Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, 13.2].

Now, there is a doubt: is there likewise no fixed rule in that case, or does the very same sequence in which the performance began apply to what follows? Since there is no restrictive factor, there would be no fixed rule for the second and subsequent items, just as there was none for the first. Alternatively, the sequence may be determined by the order of commencement (*pravṛtti*), because this favors the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Otherwise, there would be an intervention even by those [items] permitted to be added. For the constituent parts (*padārtha*) of each individual animal must be performed in mutual proximity.

Based on the force of the statement, "Having performed the Vaiśvadevī [offering], they proceed with the Prājāpatyas," which implies the accompaniment of other sacrificial elements, one understands that the interval is limited by sixteen items belonging to another [rite] and not by more. Furthermore, since the order is fixed by the sequence of performance (*pravṛtti*), the separation occurs by exactly that many [items]; otherwise, there would be separation even by more. Therefore, the restriction is established by the sequence of performance.

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the animals dedicated to Prajāpati—enjoined at one time by the rule, "Having performed the rite for Vāyu, they proceed with the animals for Prajāpati"—are to be employed together. Since these are remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*), their preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the dedication (*upākaraṇa*) and the tethering (*niyojana*) must be performed separately for each animal. Regarding this, is it that one should complete all the rites for a single animal before proceeding to the next, or should one perform the dedication for all the animals first and then the tethering?

For each individual animal, its own parts are to be taken up without separation; likewise, the *codaka* (the rule of extension) operates here. Therefore, there should be a "section-by-section" (*kāṇḍānumeya*) performance. By the force of the unity understood through the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance), the ritual details (*dharmas*) for each individual animal must be performed in a connected manner. In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the immediate succession (*ānantarya*) of acts such as the *upākaraṇa* was established; here too, that same sequence is obtained for each animal by the *codaka*, which extends it to every individual. Consequently, having completed the entire set of subsidiary sections (*guṇakāṇḍa*)—beginning with the *upākaraṇa*—for one animal, those for the next must then be performed. This is based on the explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*).

But their simultaneity (*sāhitya*) is also justified on the grounds that they are *tantras* (common subsidiaries) providing remote assistance. It is said: "In this case, the simultaneous performance of the animals is enjoined by a direct scriptural statement (*vacana*). That [simultaneity] is not set aside either by the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance) or by the *codaka* (the extended application). Simultaneity based on the *prayogavacana* is merely conceptual, and the *codaka* is an inference. However, by a direct scriptural statement—namely, "Having performed the *vaiśvadevī*, they proceed with the *prājāpatya* [animals]"—the simultaneous performance of the animals is understood. At that very [time]...

When it becomes necessary to perform the introductory rite (*upākaraṇa*) for one animal at a particular moment, the introductory rite for another must be performed at that very same moment; however, because this is impossible, it is simply not done. But in the second moment, there is no reason why another animal should not be introduced. Therefore, having performed the first ritual act (*padārtha*) for all [the animals], the second and subsequent acts should then be performed. Thus, in rites such as the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* where multiple principal offerings (*pradhāna*) occur simultaneously, it is established that the principle is "concomitance of acts" (*padārthānusamaya*), and not "concomitance of groups" (*kāṇḍānusamaya*).

However, where there would be a conflict with the primary act (*pradhāna*) in the case of performing the ritual acts in their individual sequence (*padārthānusamaya*), there the sequence by sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) must indeed be followed. For example, in the *Aśvapratigraheṣṭi* sacrifice, when a hundred or a thousand sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are being cooked, if one were to place them all on the fire and then remove the first one from the oven, it would burn. Therefore, in that case, because it would conflict with the primary act, the sequence of individual acts is not permitted. (5.2.21) ||21||
Regarding those animals, [the text] prescribes two qualities, accepting a split of the sentence:
"They are black, hornless, and uniform in color. (22)

The "uniformity of animals" (*ekarūpatva*) refers to their being endowed with various kinds of horns, tails, and so forth; for it is stated in the *Śeṣa* [of the *Laghu-Prāyaścitta*]: "For thus indeed was Prajāpati at the time of prosperity" (*prajāpatiḥ samṛddhau*). Here, by the word *Prajāpati*, the pre-manifestation state of the Lord (*Īśvara*)—prior to the manifestation of the body of Hiraṇyagarbha—is intended. And that state is indeed darkness alone, according to the Vedic scripture: "Darkness existed, hidden by darkness. Since the manifoldness of the form of the world had not yet arisen, there is uniformity.
According to the Vedic scripture, "One only, without a second," when there is equality between living beings and the Lord of the Universe, prosperity arises. || 22 ||

They immolate the animals previously designated, ending with those for Sarasvatī, after they have been encircled by fire; they hold back those beginning with the animals for Sarasvatī until later. For all of them, there is a common procedure (*tantra*) regarding the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the omentum-spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*), the cooking-pots (*kumbhī*), the heart-spits (*hṛdayaśūla*), and the branches of the *plakṣa* tree. The carrying forward of the fire, the *adhigu* formula, the first fore-offering (*prayāja*), the first *parivapya* offering, and the *saṃjñaptahoma* (the oblation at the immolation) are likewise common.

The removal of the ropes, the second *parivapya* offering, the throwing of the omentum-spits into the fire, the subsequent oblation (*abhihoma*), the purification (*mārjana*), and the granting of the boon are also common.

They immolate the animals beginning with the one for Agni, followed by those for Indra-Agni, Indra, the Maruts, and Sarasvatī, while they are being carried around with fire (paryagnikṛta). When the oblations recited in the text beginning with "having encircled the sacrificial post with the cord three times" have been performed, and the Āgnīdhra has returned, they maintain the eighteen animals beginning with that for Sarasvatī—those for whom the formula "him who is being bound... and so forth applies—right at the place where the sacrificial posts stand. This is because of the indicative mark (liṅga) in the word "for each animal" (*pratipaśoḥ*), and because of the rule in another Sūtra stating "for each animal" (*pratipaśu*).

The undertaking is for the purpose of the seasonal animal sacrifices (*ṛtupaśu*), because the *ekādaśina* (set of eleven) is not the archetype (*prakṛti*) here. The procedure according to Ātreya is as follows: [The Adhvaryu says] "O Agnīdh, spread the fires; O Pratiprasthātṛ, come with the animals. Having taken the cup for the Aśvins (*āśvinagraha*), having encircled the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with a triple-twisted cord (*trivṛt*), and having taken up the wooden pins (*svaru*) together with the formula "Sons of Heaven," he takes all the wooden pins simultaneously. He fixes them down with the formula "I fix you on the ridge of the atmosphere. Then follows the bathing of the animals. Having brought forward the animal for Agni (*āgneya*), he places it upon the prepared sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

That same branch of the *plakṣa* tree is used everywhere; others [use] two outer [leaves]. Having brought forward the victim for Indra-Agni, and having brought forward the ram for Indra, [he says]: "I bring you forth, acceptable to the Maruts"—here, a barren goat (*chāgavandhyā*) serves as a substitute for the cow (*go*). In its absence, a pregnant (*prasūtā*) goat, a ewe (*utrā*), or a she-goat (*chāgā*) serve as mutual substitutes, according to Baudhāyana. (Regarding the substitute for the cow: a barren goat). The ritual formulas (*nigamas*) employ either the word "cow" (*go*) or the word "ewe" (*utrā*).

And from the Āśvalāyana Sūtra: "A ewe without teeth, 'I dedicate you, acceptable to Sarasvatī' (or 'a ram, I dedicate you, acceptable to Sarasvatī'); those for Prajāpati are hornless and dark-colored; 'I dedicate you, acceptable to Prajāpati'—thus, one should first dedicate the seventeen [animals] in this sequence. This is from the Śrauta Sūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [13th Praśna].

Having made marks on the ears of the animals—such as "belonging to Agni" and "belonging to Indra-Agni" for the first, second, and third of the *prājāpatya* group, respectively—and having bound them to the foot-posts, the ritual dedication (*upākaraṇa*) takes place. The same marking is done for the cooking pots, the spit, and the omentum-forks. Having performed the dedication, he offers five oblations.

Knowing [the way], go by auspicious paths; take your stand among the plants with your bodies. Of those over whom [Death] rules—let these reach their sacrificial portion: those who are bound along with the one being bound, those who are wild, those being released, those brought forward, and those striving; whatever has remained alive, let it go to the path of the gods. "Thou art the fire-drill of Agni"—[this concludes] up to the end of the oblation.

Having taken the rope with the *sāvitra* formula, etc., one performs the tethering of the three [animals] to the north with the formulas: "I tether thee, acceptable to Agni," "To Indra and Agni thee," and "I tether thee, acceptable to Indra. To the south, the tethering of the others is performed in sequence for the seventeen [animals] with the formulas: "I tether thee, acceptable to Maruts," "To Sarasvatī thee" (or "To Sarasvant thee"), and "I tether thee, acceptable to Prajāpati. In all cases, the human [agent] follows the ritual rule (*dharma*).

"From the waters, from the plants, I sprinkle you; for Agni, I sprinkle you, acceptable [to him]," and so forth. "For Indra and Agni, for Indra, for the Maruts, for Sarasvatī (or Sarasvant), for Prajāpati, I sprinkle you, acceptable [to them]"—thus for those with marks. Likewise in sequence: "You are the protector, well-prepared. In this same sequence, for the barren cow (*vaśā*) and the pregnant cow (*eṣī*): "Well-prepared indeed, worthy of sacrifice, may he enjoy this."

Having recited "This is the Veda," etc., and having stepped back, he performs four ritual acts in sequence for each animal: "May your breath unite," "O sacrificers, unite," and "May the lord of the sacrifice [unite] with his blessings. Having performed all these, including the smearing of the *dhruvā* ladle and so forth, and having offered the ten *prayāja* oblations, he anoints the *svaru* with the remnant of the *prayāja* using the *svadhiti* knife. The smearing is performed for all the animals in order. He anoints the animal dedicated to Agni with the *svaru* of the one dedicated to Agni-Soma. Having set aside the *svaru*, he again anoints the *svadhiti*.

Then, taking some [ointment] again from his own form, he anoints the second [limb]. Having grasped it again, he does not apply the ointment with *svadhi*. Taking another portion, he anoints the third limb, ending with the act of grasping. In this manner, he anoints all [the limbs]. Having performed the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire) by way of a common ritual procedure (*tantra*) and having released them, there is a modification (*ūha*) as before: "The animals of Paśupati—those whom the gods have chosen, may Svarāj permit them."

There is release according to the *tantra* (the standard ritual procedure). While being released, those who were bound are modified by means of *ūha* (adaptation), beginning with "The Revatī verses [protect] the lord of the sacrifice" and ending with "him [he leads] to the south, westward. Having performed this for each one individually, he proceeds in order for the others. With his two hands, he takes hold of the two *vapāśrapaṇī* (omentum-roasting spits). After the call for the *āśrāvaṇa* has been made and the response (*pratyāśrāvaṇa*) received, having issued the direction to the Hotṛ—"O Hotṛ, Agni has won; Adhrigu has won"—there is the bringing of the firebrands (*ulmuka*) for the purpose of the *śāmitra* (the place where the animal is slaughtered).

In the case of animals to be immolated (*ovadhyagoha*), the [formula] "I dig for a place of concealment" (*khananānām*) is repeated only for the two front feet as they are released according to the various distinctions of the eyes, by means of modification (*ūha*). Some hold that there is a repetition for all the animals; the spreading of the *darbha* grass is done in sequence, and [the formula] "of the earth, well-swept" (*pṛthivyāḥ saṃpūca*) is repeated. Having said, "Make them lifeless, cause them to be quieted," the Adhvaryu turns his back. [He says: "You are finders of heaven; through finding heaven, you are finders of heaven. You are finders of the world; through finding the world, you are finders of the world. You are finders of the path; through finding the path, you are finders of the path. You are finders of refuge; through finding refuge, you are finders of refuge."

"Or indeed, you are not bound; you do not come to harm. You go to the gods with the sacrificial animals. In this [formula], the god Savitṛ shall establish you. Or [the formula] "to the guardians of the quarters" is used for the quarters (*āśā*). There is no modification (*ūha*) for "all the quarters are ours. The Adhvaryu [recites]: "May the breaths of the sacrificer be manifold through the sacrificial animals. "May they go to the path. There is no modification for the verse beginning with "whose head... "The portion of Indra. "He whom we hate—go after him! "Make a sound! [This is said] for one [animal]; "make a sound! for two.

Whatever you have dwelt upon its further shore—whether sitting down, trembling, fleeing, or gathering together—urinate, void excrement, grant us fearlessness, and be gracious toward us from all [directions]. Homage to Rudra! [End of] Paṭala. [This is] accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 135.

The formula *mīḍhuṣe* is used when there are many [animals]. For two [animals], the formulas are: *vāsiṣāyāṃ nyaṣādāthām*, *vepiṣāyāṃ palāyiṣāyāṃ samajñāsāthām*, *nimehathāṃ śakṛtkurutam abhayaṃ kurutaṃ sarvābhyo mṛḍatām*. For one [animal], it is according to the original form. When there are many groups [of animals], they are raised up in sequence according to their kind: *uccha etiṣṭhā*, *unme pratiṣṭhā*, *udvaśāttiṣṭhā*, *yat paśavo māyum akṛta rosi vā padbhir ānate*. In the case of the *agni-māda* verses, there is no modification (*noha*).

"Niṣṭaptaḥ" (Heated): this is the heating of all the omentum-roasting spits together with a branch of the *plakṣa* tree. "O preparers of the sacrifice (*śamitāraḥ*), approach; release the animals from the bonds. The release is performed in sequence with the mantra, "Aditi [releases] the bond. When the bonds have been placed upon the necks, having removed them by means of the primary spit according to the ritual procedure (*tantra*), the Pratiprasthātṛ then leads the wife forward with the repetition of the mantra: "Homage to you, O spreader; go unassailed."

When there are many wives, having recited "O divine waters, you are pure-flowing," and having recited "May speech swell," one performs the rites for the first wife up to the end of "Pure are our paths," and then proceeds with the others in succession. At the end of "Peace to the plants," the pouring out [of the water] is done once for all (*tantra*) regarding the animal sacrifice. Having performed the rite for the first wife starting from "O herb, protect him" up to "I cut [the hair]," one proceeds with the others in succession. For a female animal (*strīpaśu*), the rite extends up to "O herb, protect her; O axe, do not harm her."

Having performed the rite for each animal up to the point where it is "smeared on both sides with blood," once the animal has been immolated, there is no simultaneous disposal of the blood with the formula, "You are the portion of the Rakṣases. Then, following the sequence, the slaughterer performs the extraction of the omentum (*vapā*) everywhere with the formulas, "For *iṣ* thee," and so forth, up to "I cut out what is pleasing to Agni; for Indra and Agni thee; for Indra thee; for the Maruts thee; for Sarasvatī thee [for Sarasvant thee]; for Prajāpati thee—what is pleasing, I cut out. He then covers [the wound] with his fist.

With the formula "Pratyuṣṭam," [he performs] the simultaneous grasping of the sacrificer in sequence; with the formula "Nirdagdham," the handing over to the Pratiprasthātṛ is done simultaneously. With the repetition of the formula "Vāyo vīhi stokānām," there is the placing and stepping over that tip of the *darbha* grass used for the omentum (*vapā*). He throws it down with the verse: "She who has entered into the bodies of living beings as the gods, she who has spread out as the sages."

"O Soma, having become possessed of self and possessed of clarity, go to the gods; do not abandon me, O wise one"—with this [formula], the sprinkling is performed by way of a common application (*tantra*). "Strengthen the cows, strengthen the lord of the cows; let not the patron of the sacrifice suffer harm from you"—some recite this without modification as "he who is your self. Having removed [the vessel] by way of a common application, he places it on the branch of the *plakṣa* tree with the formula "Make the plants bear good fruit," also by way of a common application. The touching of the placed [vessels] is performed alternately, as in the archetype, with the formula "May hostilities be driven away."

"These senses are immortal; by means of their vigor, the animals have fashioned sense-power. Through them, O gods, protect us; let these cooked [portions] rest within me. Some say there is no modification [of the mantra] as "this sense-power. Having offered with the words "O bearer of firmness" (*dhṛtavatī*) and so forth, ending with "Svāhā to the gods," one should perform for all the animals, in sequence, the rites beginning with spreading the base-butter in the *juhū* ladle and ending with the actual offering. Having thus sent forth the command: "Recite the invitatory verse for the omentum and fat of the goat for Agni," [he says] "O Jātavedas... For the second [animal], [the command is] "For Indra..."

For the second [offering], for the goat, of the omentum and the fat—thus give the command, O Jātavedas! For the third, for Indra, of the bull’s omentum and the fat—thus give the command, O Jātavedas! For the fourth, for the Maruts, of the barren cow’s omentum and the fat—thus give the command, O Jātavedas! For Sarasvatī, of the ewe’s omentum and the fat—thus give the command, O Jātavedas! For Sarasvatī, of the ram’s omentum and the fat—thus give the command, O Jātavedas! This is the fifth.

Then, having placed pieces of gold for the sixth [animal], one should recite "To Prajāpati" in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) everywhere, and then loudly say, "Recite the *anuvākyā* for the omenta of the goats with the *Bhedasāman*. Having thus given the command, the modification (*ūha*) is: "O Jātavedas, go to the gods with the omenta. Some, however, say there is no modification. [End of] the explanatory citations from the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [13th Praśna].

The *homa* is performed by way of a common ritual procedure (*tantra*). For all [the portions], there is a consecration formula (*anumantraṇa*) similar to that for the *sāṃnāyya*: "May I nourish speech and food through Sarasvatī. The *parivapya-homa* is performed with the formula "Svāhā to the gods! by way of a common ritual procedure. There is the lifting of the omentum (*vapā*), its removal, and the sprinkling of clarified butter. The casting away of the omentum-spits is performed by way of a common ritual procedure with the formula: "Svāhā to the Maruts, who are in the upward atmosphere. The *saṃsrāva-homa* is performed by way of a common ritual procedure with "(Svāhā) to Prajāpati. And the performance of the offering to Prajāpati is done with low-voiced (*upāṃśu*) formulas, as it has been handed down.

In this regard, because of the Sūtrakāra’s statement, "there is no *ūha* here," [the procedure is as follows]: having stepped out and performed the cleansing of the omentum (*vapāmārjana*), they proceed toward the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) until the end of that section, and so forth. Then, having waited for those two during the drinking of the *ṛtupāna*, at the time of the drawing of the cups, there is the drawing and the worship (*upasthāna*) with the formula, "For my splendor, O cups, draw yourselves; for my vigor, O drops, flow for glory"—this being done in common (*tantra*). From "O abode of Viṣṇu, you delight" (*viṣṇormaha ramasī*) until the end of the departure (*niḥsarpaṇa*), the ritual belongs to Soma. This is the work of the midday pressing: "O God Savitṛ... may he make it palatable for us, *svāhā*."

Savitṛ is the deity. [The ritual procedure] beginning with the wiping of the water-jar (*kalaśodvartana*) with the *hotṛcamasa* from the *vasatīvarī* waters and ending with the authorization of the pressing-stones (*grāvṇām anumodanānta*), the Pratiprasthātṛ shall pour out the *savanīya* offerings. It has been stated that the Pratiprasthātṛ pours out the *savanīya* offerings together with the animal-cake offerings (*paśupuroḍāśa*). The cake-offerings are obligatory; furthermore, his duty follows the sequence of the subsequent rites. He employs seventy-seven potsherds, two potsherds for roasting, a cooking-pot, three winnowing-baskets (*śūrpa*), and (also) two pairs of shallow bowls (*dvandvaśarāva*).

The sounding of the *kṛṣṇājina* and all other [procedures] are as before. (Regarding the pair of large ladles, etc. Alternatively, having touched the three vessels (*pātra*), he takes up simultaneously the *prastha*, the earth, the *audumbara* vessel, the *dakṣāyava*, the *agnihotraṇī*, and the *śarāva*. With the formula "for the sake of the winnowing," he takes up the three winnowing baskets (*śūrpa*), and having placed the two strainers (*pavitra*) upon the winnowing basket, he says: "I pour out what is pleasing to Agni. "To Indra and Agni, what is pleasing... [he pours].

"Acceptable to Indra, acceptable to the Maruts, acceptable to Sarasvatī"—thus for Brāhma [or for Sarasvant]. Having placed the strainers (*pavitra*) upon a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) in which barley has been poured—[the formula is]: "Acceptable to Indra, the possessor of bays (*harivat*), acceptable to Indra, the possessor of speckled mares (*pṛṣanvat*). Alternatively, having placed the strainers upon the previously poured-out grains, [he says]: "Acceptable to Sarasvatī, the daughter of Bharata. Again, having placed the strainers upon the winnowing basket over the poured-out barley, [he says]: "Acceptable to Indra"; again, having placed them upon the grains, [he says]: "Acceptable to Sarasvant," in another winnowing basket.

Having placed the *pavitra* strainers, he pours out the *nīvāra* grains with a shallow bowl, saying "To Bṛhaspati, the acceptable [portion]," twelve times with the mantra and five times silently; then there are eighteen for the subsequent pouring.

"This for the gods," and so forth, like various seeds: "O Agni, protect the oblation; O Indra and Agni, protect the oblation; O Indra, protect the oblation; O Maruts, protect the oblations; O Sarasvatī, protect the oblation; O Indra, Lord of Bay Horses, protect the oblation; O Indra, Lord of the Spotted Cows, protect the oblation; O Sarasvatī, Bhāratī, protect the oblation; O Indra, protect the oblation; O Sarasvant, protect the oblation; O Bṛhaspati, protect the oblation"—thus is the placing [of the offerings].

The sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is performed as follows: "I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni; I sprinkle you, acceptable to Indra and Agni; [I sprinkle] you, acceptable to Indra; [I sprinkle] you, acceptable to the Maruts; [I sprinkle] you, acceptable to Sarasvatī; [I sprinkle] you, acceptable to Indra, the possessor of bay horses (*harivat*); [I sprinkle] you, acceptable to Indra, the possessor of Pūṣan’s horses (*pūṣaśvat*); [I sprinkle] you, acceptable to Sarasvatī, the daughter of Bharata (*bhāratī*); [I sprinkle] you, acceptable to Indra; [I sprinkle] you, acceptable to Sarasvant; [I sprinkle] you, acceptable to Bṛhaspati. Thus is the sprinkling. Following the formula beginning with "Be purified" (*śundhadhvam*), once the mortars have been established, the division is made with the words: "O grains of rice, separate yourselves according to your respective portions."

The longest [piece] is one part; six [pieces] are of equal length; the seventh is the shortest part. Having divided them thus, this is the longest part for Agni, Indra-Agni, Indra, the Maruts, and Sarasvatī (Sarasvant); the shortest part is for Sarasvatī and Bhāratī. [End of] Paṭala 1, accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 137.

Having omitted those [grains], the majority [of the ritual] is performed. Having completed the rites from the pouring of the oblation-material up to the scattering of the rice-grains for the *yavas*, and having likewise completed the rites from the pouring of the oblation up to the scattering of the rice-grains for the *nīvāras*, one sows the *nīvāras* and releases speech with the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*). The dismemberment of all the animals is performed with the formulas: "Do not let the rectum stick," and "Do not let the entrails stick."

Having divided the fire into twenty-three parts along with the sacrificial spikes (*śūla*) and other implements, one should perform the heating (*niṣṭapana*) of all the pots in sequence; having performed the rites from the taking up of the *upaveṣa* until the end of the verse "of the Bhr̥gus" for one pot, one should do the same for the others in order. Having performed the rites from the placing of the two strainers (*pavitra*) upon the grains (*dhānā*) until the touching of the heart for one pot, one should do the same for the others in sequence.

Having performed the rites beginning with threshing for the *nīvāra* grains up to the point of pouring them out, and having husked the rice, barley, and *nīvāra* grains in sequence, one washes all of them separately. Then follows the simultaneous pouring out (*ninayana*). The pouring of the rice-grains (*adhivāpa*) is as follows: "I pour thee out, acceptable to Agni; I pour thee out, acceptable to Indra and Agni; I pour thee out, acceptable to Indra; [acceptable to the Maruts]; I pour thee out, acceptable to Sarasvatī; thou art grain."

Then, having divided the barley-grains according to the original procedure, and having performed the rites from "I pour out what is pleasing to Indra" (*indrāya juṣṭam ādhivapāmi*) up to "make it ready" (*kurutāt*), one proceeds with the taking of the fire-stirring stick (*dhṛṣṭi*) and the subsequent rituals.

Having placed the *kapālas* in sequence—having placed the one for Agni, having placed the one for Indra-Agni, having placed the one for Indra, having placed the ones for the Maruts, having placed the one for Sarasvatī, and [having placed] the one for Sarasvant—and having placed two *kapālas* for the purpose of roasting, and having placed the one for Indra, he places the vessel for the *caru* offering to Bṛhaspati. For all of them, there are eleven *kapālas*. In the placing of the modifications of the Agni-offering, there is a double repetition of the fourth and a triple repetition of the eighth.

"Pouring the boiling waters," and so forth: "I pour together what is pleasing to Agni; I pour together what is pleasing to Indra and Agni; [I pour together] what is pleasing to Indra; [I pour together] what is pleasing to the Maruts; [I pour together] what is pleasing to Sarasvatī; [I pour together] what is pleasing to Sarasvant. Having placed the two strainers in another vessel, he pours in the barley flour with the formula, "I pour together what is pleasing to Indra. Having purified the flours, he purifies the rice grains and the *nīvāra* grains. Having formed a lump, he divides it four times according to the respective portions with the formula, "Separate yourselves according to your shares."

"May I turn away"—these are the two *uttama* verses; they are the specific designation for those two. "This for Sarasvatī" [and "This for Sarasvant"]. Having placed the oblations from the *Āgneya* up to the *Sārasvata* on the fire, he pours in the parched grains (*dhānā*) for roasting with the formula: "You are the supports of all life. Then he pours in the wild rice (*nīvāra*) for boiling onto another pan. Then, having placed the offering for Indra on the fire and having placed the offering for Sarasvatī on the fire, while the milk for Bṛhaspati is heating, he pours in the wild rice grains with the formula: "You are the support."

The [procedures] beginning with the spreading [of the base] apply to all the *puroḍāśas* [of the animal sacrifice]. Having poured out the remnants of the ghee (*māyalepa*), as in the case of the animal *puroḍāśa*, [one says]: "O Giver of Ghee! At the time of taking down [the offering], [one says]: "I pour [ghee] over that which is acceptable to Agni."

Then, silently, [he offers] to Sarasvatī what is acceptable; silently, for the sake of the parched grains (dhānā), to Sarasvatī Bhāratī, what is acceptable; then silently, to Indra, what is acceptable, and to Bṛhaspati, what is acceptable. Having removed the offerings ending with those dedicated to Sarasvatī, and having removed the Savanīya offerings as in the archetype, the removal of the offerings to Sarasvant and Anupāra follows in sequence. At the proper time, the decoration, the taking up [of the vessels], and so forth are performed.

Having performed the *dadhi-dharmabhakṣaṇa* (the consumption of curd as a religious duty), he places the *sāmnāyya* offerings and the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) offerings. There is no placing of the two *sārasvata-naivāra* offerings; having prescribed them as known [from elsewhere], he offers the *āgneya-sārasvatī-lājī* offerings with the formula, "This is the sacrifice," and the *ayaṃ yajña* offering. In sequence: "May Indra and Agni drive away from the worlds him who is weaker than us"; [he offers] the two animal-cakes. "May Indra drive away from the worlds him who is weaker than us"; "May the Maruts drive away from the worlds him who is weaker than us."

May Indra drive away from us those who are weaker; may Indra, accompanied by Pūṣan, drive away from us those who are weaker; may Indra drive away from us those who are weaker. (Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin, 13.13)

"May they drive away [the enemies]! O Agni, my five hotṛs... The Adhvaryu proceeds with the ritual action. The formal call (*saṃpraiṣa*) is: "Recite the invitatory verse for the cake (*puroḍāśa*) for Agni. In the same way, the formal call is: "Recite the invitatory verse for the cake for Indra and Agni," and likewise, the formal call is: "Recite the invitatory verse for the cake for Indra. For the animal-cakes (*paśupuroḍāśa*) of Sarasvatī and Nairṛta, the call is: "Recite the invitatory verse for the cake for the Maruts. For the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), the call is: "Recite the invitatory verse for the cakes for Indra," and so forth.

For the offerings to Agni, Indra-Agni, and Indra, the addressing is as in the archetype: "May I be an eater of food through Indra; may I be an eater of food possessing power through the Maruts; may I be an eater of speech through Sarasvatī. For the *savanīya* offerings, it is as in the archetype. However, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* portions are the same [as in the archetype]. [The procedure begins with] "As they are being lifted up," and so forth. 3–4.
Having performed the two southern oblations, he brings down the chariot with the formula: "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra. || 25 ||

"Go to heaven, fly to the light!"—with these words, ending with "the gold-winged one," [he addresses the chariot]. With the formula, "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra," he brings down the chariot from the *rathavāhana* (the wooden stand). He prescribes the descent of the chariot from that wooden stand—which has been placed there to prepare it for its journey—with the text: "With 'Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra,' he brings down the chariot for the sake of victory; [the enemies] are slain" (BaudhŚS 1.3.5). || 25 ||
"In the waters is immortality, in the waters is healing"—with these words, they bathe the horses in the water. || 26 ||

They do not cause the horses to enter the water while it remains undisturbed. For the bathing at the landing-place (*upaplavana*), there is a repetition of the mantra for each horse. "O ye swift ones" (*vājinaḥ*) is the end of the mantra. Now, regarding the phrase "then he causes the horses to splash about" (*athāśvān palpūlayati*), Baudhāyana and Vaikhānasa both report this. *Palpūlayati* means he causes them to float in the water; that is to say, he washes their bodies. Within the waters exists an essence that wards off untimely death and wards off disease. 26.
"Either Vāyu shall yoke thee, or Manu shall yoke thee"—with these words he yokes the chariot drawn by side-horses. || 27 ||

The section ends with "they place. He yokes a chariot drawn by side-horses (*praṣṭivāhin*). There is a repetition of the mantra for each horse. A chariot drawn by side-horses is yoked with three horses; this is known from the indicative mark (liṅga) that "there are three horses. || 27 ||
He wipes the foreheads of the horses with the formula, "Apāṃnapāt, the swift-racer. || 28 ||

[The word] "but" marks the end [of the previous section]. Now, Baudhāyana also says that its back is wiped; it is wiped. He wipes it again and again. Because it has been purified by the wiping of the back, it possesses fitness for sacrifice. The rest is understood. (24) He yokes the other sixteen chariots silently. (Section 29)
The others, the sixteen *sthān* and *vājasṛt* priests, each yoke their own [chariot] silently; so say some *adhvaryu*s.
At the time of the sacrificial fee, he gives seventeen chariots.

When the time for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has arrived, having approached with the words "May your form [be] my form," and so forth, he divides the chariots and other items into four parts and gives them away with the mantra "Tutho vaḥ. At this time of the sacrificial fee, he gives these very same items joined together; such is the division of the sacrificial fee. He gives either hundreds of cows up to a hundred drums. || 30 ||
Seventeen niṣkas, seventeen horses, and seventeen elephants—[End of] Chapter 13, Section 1: Together with the commentary titled *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. Page 139.

He gives seventeen hundred cows, seventeen ox-carts, seventeen vehicles, seventeen beds, seventeen kitchens, seventeen garments, seventeen male slaves, seventeen female slaves, seventeen goats, seventeen ewes, and for each age-group, seventeen [animals] of that age; he gives seventeen sets of seventeen. According to some, he prepares seventeen groups of seventeen. When the sacrificial fees have been assigned, he gives to the Adhvaryu the chariot yoked by means of a *yajus* formula.
The remainder is common. || 34 ||

A *niṣka* consists of four *suvarṇas*. The *dundubhis* are drums. For the purpose of purchasing the unassigned animals, he gives the sacrificial chariot to the *adhvaryu*; that is to say, one drawn by a side-horse (*praṣṭivāhin*). The portion belonging to the *adhvaryu* is thus restricted; there is no additional share. "More than his share," says the Commentator (*bhāṣyakṛt*). The remainder is common; the remaining sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are obtained by all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

Regarding the portion given to the Adhvaryu—whether it is more or less than the standard—the division is made according to the model (prakṛti), up to the extent of the Adhvaryu's share; that is, the division is equal. The meaning is that the division is indeed equal. Because of the statement of the Chandogas, "One should divide those [fees] equally among the priests," the division is not according to the model. Alternatively, in the case of an equal division, a seventeenth part is obtained as the appropriate share for each. Therefore, the Saptadaśa (the seventeenth, i.e., the Sadasya) is permanent; he too is a great priest (mahartvig).

"One should choose five great officiating priests (*mahartvij*)," so said the venerable Bharadvāja. The formula for the acceptance of gifts is stated in the *Ādhāna* [section]: for the chariot, "Of the god... and for Varuṇa, "The horse..."; for the cart, "Of the god... O Goddess, to the right, the son of Aṅgiras is seated..."; for the elephant, "Of the god... O Goddess, to the right, from the Himavat the elephant... by that [attain] immortality. Having given food, there is the acceptance. For the gold coin (*niṣka*), "For Agni, the gold"; for the female slave, "For Manu, the bed."

The acceptance [of gifts] is performed by uttering words of welcome (*priyavacana*). For a goat, [the formula is] "To Tvaṣṭṛ, thee" (*tvaṣṭre tvā*); for a she-goat, "To Ajā, thee" (*ajāyai tvā*); for a ram, "To Pūṣan, thee" (*pūṣṇe tvā*); for a ewe, "To Avī, thee" (*avyai tvā*). For a garment, [the formula is] "To Nāstya, thee, made by austerity; with thy own body, O thou of beautiful form, they have clothed thee" (*nāstyā kṛtas tapasas svā tanvā rūpayā tvā veṣayan*); for a garment, "To Soma, thee" (*somāya tvā*). For a hundred cows, the acceptance is "To Rudra, a cow" (*rudrāya gām*). For a horse-yoked chariot, it is according to its species. For seventeen drums, the acceptance is "Thee, O supine one" (*uttānas tvā*). Regarding the Vājapeya sacrifice, after prescribing the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as "seventeen chariots, seventeen slave-girls," it is heard [in the scripture]: [the formulas follow].

"He gives the chariot yoked with a *yajus* to the *adhvaryu*. Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the chariot yoked with a *yajus* exclude the share of the *adhvaryu*? In that regard: "Like the two *prākāśas*, the chariot yoked with a *yajus* should be the sublater of his share; however, it is not a sublater, for it is a restriction (*niyama*) of what is already established. Indeed, since the two *prākāśas* are enjoined as something unprecedented (*apūrva*) for the purpose of illuminating the path, it is appropriate that they should sublate the original share [of the *hotṛ*]. But this is not the case here.

In this case, however, seventeen chariots and other distinct substances are prescribed as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the Vājapeya. Therefore, although the giving of the chariot yoked with a *yajus* is already established, it must be given either to the Adhvaryu or to someone else; such is the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha. [13th Paṭala]

The *dhurya* (the pair of draft animals) is restricted [in this context]. Therefore, the meaning is not that "whatever one gives to the *adhvaryu*, that must be yoked by the *yajus*"; rather, it is that whatever one gives which is yoked by the *yajus*, that belongs to the *adhvaryu*. And since the giving of that [animal] is established as occurring only when accompanied by other materials, the restriction applies only to such a case; thus, there is no exclusion of other things to be given. However, regarding the share of the *adhvaryu*, the animal yoked by the *yajus* is restricted according to what has been established. || 31 || 32 || 13 || 34 ||
In front of the Āhavanīya fire, they station the chariots facing eastward.
In front of the Āhavanīya fire, they should station chariots in that place, facing eastward with their fronts turned toward the east.

The prince, having stationed himself in front of the Āgnīdhra shed to the south of the chariot yoked with the Yajus-formulas, shoots seventeen arrows in a continuous volley, either eastward or northward. Where the last one falls, he makes a mark there.

He yokes the chariot. The prince stands at the front of the Āgnīdhra shed. Having fixed an arrow to his bow, he shoots it; he makes it fall down. Where that arrow falls, having gone there, he shoots again. In this manner he should practice seventeen times. Where the last one falls, there he fixes a mark made of Udumbara wood. ||36|| 37||

When that [offering] prior to the one for Mahendra has been performed, the Pratiprasthātṛ divides the seventeen-platter offering of wild rice into four parts and pours it out for Bṛhaspati; he cooks it in milk and places it, mixed with clarified butter, in the Cātvāla pit.

[The ritual proceeds] prior to the *praṇītā*-water being set down, up until the placement of the various *nānā-rāśas*. In this regard, there is a specific detail: having offered with "O Agni, lead us," one offers with "In the riches, across the mid-air; O Prajāpati, not thee... [and] "In the woods, across the mid-air; Varuṇa is the deity. For the remaining two [verses], it is as stated. When the various *nānā-rāśas* have been thus placed, one brings ordinary clarified butter (*laukika-sarpis*) for the *naivāra* [grain-offering] and places it in the *cāvāla* pit. Regarding the *Vājapeya*, it is heard in the scripture: "There is a *naivāra* oblation for Bṛhaspati, seventeen *śarāva* measures, a *caru* cooked in milk."

In the archetype, it is stated, "He pours out four handfuls"; thus, both the number four and the substance of the handful are established. Both of these are extended here by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer). However, it is not possible to produce a *caru* (oblation) measuring seventeen *śarāva*s with only four handfuls. Therefore, since something must necessarily be set aside (*bādhitavya*), is it that both must be set aside—the substance of the handful by the substance of the *śarāva*, and the number four by the number seventeen—or is it only one of them? And even in that case, is there no fixed rule?

Alternatively, there is the conflict between the handful (*muṣṭi*) and the favor (*anugraha*), the number (*saṃkhyā*) and the measure (*parimāṇa*), or the reverse. In that case, since there is no distinction, both are sublated. Even so, because they serve the same purpose, one view is that the substance is connected with the number, and the measure with the number. The number seventeen and the measure of the *śarāva* are for the sake of the sacrificial material (*yāgadravya*), whereas the number four and the handful are auxiliary to the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*). Therefore, they do not directly share a single objective such that both would be sublated by the other.

The meaning is that it is impossible to prepare seventeen *śarāva* measures of cooked rice (*caru*) with only four handfuls; thus, by implication, there is a contradiction. In that case, since the contradiction can be resolved by the sublation of one factor alone, it is not proper to sublate both. Therefore, there must be a sublation of one or the other. Regarding this, the second position is that since there is no specific distinction, there is no fixed rule as to which is sublated. The third position is that because the number is subordinate to the substance, the primary element—the handfuls—should be favored, and thus the number should be sublated. [End of] Paṭala 1, from the *Mahādevaśāstrisaṃkalita-paryogacandrikā-vyākhyā*. 141.

Alternatively, because the status of the handful (*muṣṭi*) as a subordinate element is understood through the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) of the accusative case—which sets aside the connection with the substance that shares the same locus as the definition of the sentence—there is an understanding that both [the handful and the number] are subordinate elements of the action; thus, they are equal. In that regard, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the number is upheld because it is primary, while the handful is omitted because it is secondary. || 38 || 39 ||
The prince protects it. || 13.1.40 ||
A prince guards it, or a brahmin. 40.
He buries a piece of wood shaped like a chariot axle in the *cātvāla*.
"Let it be driven in with a peg made of udumbara wood," said Dehānasa. || 11 ||
Upon it he fastens a chariot wheel made of udumbara wood with seventeen spokes. || 42 ||

Upon that wooden pole shaped like a chariot axle, he fastens a chariot wheel made of udumbara wood with seventeen spokes; for the Vaikhānasa scripture states: "He ties seventeen drums to the northern corner of the altar. (42)
With the mantra "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," the sacrificer approaches the chariot yoked with the Yajus.
One should approach the chariot that is yoked with the Yajus formulas; this is the ritual of honoring the vehicle. 43.
He touches the two wheels of the chariot, saying, "The two hooks, the two hooks," or he touches the two side-pieces.
Some say that the Adhvaryu touches [the ladles] on both sides; others say it is the sacrificer. The mantra ends with "pārayantu. || 14 ||
"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, through Bṛhaspati, the winner of the prize, may I win the prize"—with these words, he mounts the wooden-fig chariot wheel. 45.
"He mounts the chariot," says Baudhāyana; "mounts" means he should ascend. || 45 ||
"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may I, through Bṛhaspati the winner of prizes, ascend the highest firmament"—with these words, the sacrificer mounts the chariot joined with the Yajus formula.
The term "ascends" is carried over [from the preceding rule]. || 46 ||
"Speak words for Indra! they say, as they cause the drums to resound. || 47 ||
They beat the drum at the conclusion of the sacrifice, not the Adhvaryu priest; likewise also in the Āpastamba [Śrautasūtra]. || 47 ||
Those who run for the prize mount other chariots. ||48||
The others mount their chariots silently, without making a sound.
With the words, "May the prize-winners, winners of the prize, run toward the prize," they cause two draft horses to smell the *naivāra* rice; or all [the horses].

"Smell [it]," is the end of the mantra. They cause the two draft-oxen to smell the wild rice (*naivāra*). The mantra is recited only once for the two oxen yoked to the chariot by means of a *yajus* formula. || 49 ||

And from the remnants on the corners of the mouth, he wipes off the smearings with the formula, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu. Having mounted the chariot joined by the Yajus, the Adhvaryu drives the horses with the horse-whip, saying, "Thou art the giver of wealth; thou art the subduer. Thus he strokes the horses from left to right. (Śrautasūtra 13.1.50)

They touch the remnants that remain after the ointments have been applied to the faces and the parts of the harnesses. The Adhvaryu mounts [the chariot] with the *yajus* formula, "O Viṣṇu, thou art homage" (*viṣṇo namo 'si*). According to some, he mounts it silently once it has been yoked. Taking the whip for the horse, the Adhvaryu says, "Thou art a steed, thou art a racer, thou art a prize-winner," and strikes those horses with the whip. || 50 ||
Thereafter, the other chariots follow, not keeping pace with one another. || 51 ||

The others—the king, the Vaiśya, and the chariot-maker—each strike their own [drum] silently. They follow behind the one yoked with the Yajus-mantra, as do the other chariots. However, some maintain that in the absence of Kṣatriyas and others, Brāhmaṇas alone are understood [to perform this]. || 51 ||
With the three verses beginning "O swift ones, run for the prize," he consecrates those who are running; according to some teachers, with four verses.
The sacrificer consecrates the running horses with three or four verses; some say the Adhvaryu does so.
He sings the Vājina-sāman on a cart-wheel made of udumbara wood, revolving three times each way. || 53 ||

When the Brahman has mounted [the chariot], the Adhvaryu sings the *vājina-sāman* and gives the command. For the purpose of its singing, he causes [the chariot] to turn; while the wheel is turning, the singing of the *sāman* is optional. He either sings the *sāman* beginning with "devasyāham... or recites the Yajus formula ending with "...may I go. For one capable of singing the *sāman*, the mantra for the singing is "āvirmā..."; this is known from the Brāhmaṇa: "The *vājina-sāman* is sung" (*te0 prā0* 1.3.6). That *sāman* which belongs to those seeking food (*vājinaḥ*)—the Brahman should sing that.

The specific *sāman* for the giver of food (*annaprada*) is to be found in another recension (*śākhāntara*). Āpastamba clarifies that this singing belongs to the *brahman*: "The *brahman* mounts a chariot wheel made of *audumbara* wood; he says to him, 'Sing the *vājina-sāman*'; he turns the wheel three times clockwise; while it is being turned, the *brahman* sings. (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 18.1.4–11). || 53 ||
With the formula, "Agni won speech by means of the single syllable," he causes the sacrificer to recite the *ujjiti* verses while they are running.

While the horses are galloping, the Adhvaryu makes the sacrificer recite "Agni with one syllable," and having meditated on the *ujjitī*s, he makes him recite up to the end: "He won the stoma. According to Vaikhānasa, [he recites] "The seventeenfold. || 14 ||
Having reached the characteristic mark, they circumambulate it to the right. || 55 ||
"Having reached the Audumbara wood for the race, they turn to the right; those who run toward the axle-pins turn back toward the north," so says the Brāhmaṇa (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.3.6). // 55 //
With the four verses beginning with "May those coursers, hearing our invocation, come to our call," he consecrates the two who are running forward. || 56 ||

The Adhvaryu consecrates the four horses as they gallop back with these [verses]. Thus, following the tradition of the teachers, [ends] the first Paṭala, together with the commentary *Yogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.

The four mantras are divided [into separate units]. However, the teacher Baudhāyana, intending that the portion beginning with *te no arvantaḥ* and ending with *vājino haveṣu* constitutes a single mantra, included the fourth verse beginning with *eṣa sya vājī* within that same group of four. Āpastamba, on the other hand, stated: "With the four verses beginning with *mitadravaḥ*, he follows the horses as they gallop back. || 16 ||
According to some, [the rite is performed] with three [verses]. || 57 ||
The meaning is clear. || 57 ||
"May the impulse of strength come to me," he says, and offers the oblation when they have returned.

He offers with the verse beginning "āmā vānasya" according to the ritual rules of a *darvihoma*. Dyāvāpṛthivī (Heaven and Earth) are the deity. [This is performed] when the horses have returned and have come back. || 58 ||
"This was that true covenant of yours," saying this, he offers a single oblation for the release of the drum.
Having meditated that "this is that truth of yours" is the concluding portion of the *anuvāka* for the releasing of the drum, he offers the oblation; Indra is the deity. 59.
He touches all of them. || 13.1.60 ||
He touches all [the vessels], but there is no oblation.

With the words, "O strong ones, winners of the prize, having run for the prize," he causes the horse-yoked [cart] to smell the *naivāra* [grain]; and as before, he wipes away the smearings from the *praprotha* [nostrils].
He causes the horses and draft animals to drink at the monastery; he wipes the food-leavings from their mouths as was done previously—this is the meaning. || 11 ||
He gives a *kṛṣṇala* each to those who prepare the sacrificial oblation.
According to the statement, "He gives a *kṛṣṇala* at each turn," he gives one *kṛṣṇala* to each of the sixteen; thus, having given to the sixteen... || 62 ||
Having taken those back, he gives them to the Brahman priest. || 63 ||
Having taken that back again, he should give it to a Brahmin. || 63 ||
And a honey-spoon was made from a śatamāna weight of gold. (Section 4) || 64 ||
Thus ends the first paṭala in the thirteenth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

He gives to the Brahman priest a golden vessel filled with honey, measuring one hundred guñjā fruits in weight. Thus ends the first paṭala in the thirteenth praśna of the *Prayoga-candrikā*, a commentary on the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. Now begins the second paṭala in the thirteenth praśna of the Śrauta-sūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha.
With the words, "Thou art the caul of the Kṣatra," the sacrificer puts on a garment of silk; with the words, "Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra," the wife puts on one made of darbha grass.

The *tārpya* is a garment smeared with clarified butter. He prescribes this pair of garments: "He causes the sacrificer to put on the *tārpya*. The *tārpya* is indeed the sacrifice; verily, he endows him with the sacrifice. He causes him to put on one made of *darbha* grass. *Darbha* grass is indeed a means of purification (*pavitra*); verily, he purifies him. He who sacrifices with the *Vājapeya* seeks to win *vāja* (strength/food). *Vāja* is indeed the plants. In that he causes him to put on one made of *darbha*, it is for the attainment of *vāja*. (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa)

(Brāhmaṇa 1.3.7). Because it is a means for the sacrifice (*yajña-sādhana*), it possesses the nature of a sacrifice (*yajñatva*). "This" refers to the body of the wife. For one who has performed the Vājapeya sacrifice and desires to obtain food, food is secured through the form of herbs made of *darbha* grass; such is the meaning. || 1 ||
"Come, wife, let us ascend," thus the sacrificer addresses his wife; "Let us ascend," the wife replies.
With this mantra the sacrificer addresses his wife; "Let us ascend," the wife replies. Thus three times.
"I shall ascend to the heavenly world for both of us," says the sacrificer; "I shall cause both of us to ascend to the heavenly world," says the wife.
The sacrificer speaks at the end; likewise the wife.
With the ten formulas beginning with "May life prosper through sacrifice," he ascends the sacrificial post by means of a ladder with rungs, or both [the sacrificer and the Adhvaryu] do so.

Thinking, "May life be perfected through sacrifice," the sacrificer ascends the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) by means of a ladder provided with seventeen rungs; likewise the wife, and according to some, the *adhvaryu* priest as well. Vaikhānasa says that he ascends that post with ten formulas containing the word "perfection" (*kalpa*), beginning with, "May life be perfected through sacrifice. [That post] is the one referred to by the word *kalpa*. || 4 ||
Having mounted [the chariot], he mutters: "We have gone to the gods, to heaven. || 5 ||

Having reached the sacrificial posts, the sacrificer mutters, "O gods, we have attained heaven (*suvar*)," with the end of the mantra being "we have become [attainers] (*abhūma*). However, in the Bhāṣya it is stated: "He raises his arms, saying 'O gods, we have attained heaven'. This is said by the sacrificer, who intends to indicate the attainment of heaven by means of his raised arms. 5.
He offers twelve oblations with the formulas beginning "Vāja and Prasava. According to some teachers, there are thirteen.

Having meditated upon the rites for the prosperity of cattle (*vājaprasavīya*) with the twelve or thirteen [mantras] beginning with "To Vāja, Svāhā! To Prasava, Svāhā! he offers oblations. The deities are Vāja and others, in those rituals where the words *vāja* and *prasava* are heard as the essence of the mantras; these are the *vājaprasavīya* rites. He prescribes them: "He offers twelve *vājaprasavīya* oblations" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.3.7), and so forth. [End of] Patala 2. This is accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 145.
Some recite [the following] before the climbing of the sacrificial post.
Some reciters of the Vedic branches read that one should offer the *vanaspatyā* oblation prior to the mounting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); this is the meaning. || 8 ||

"Equal am I with you in life, equal is life with me; equal am I with you in splendor, equal is splendor with me; equal am I with you in progeny, equal is progeny with me; equal am I with you in the increase of wealth, equal is the increase of wealth with me"—having thus ascended the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), he gazes at the cups (*grahas*).

"The wife," says the author of the Bhāṣya. [The sacrificer] addresses her as "patnī. The great officiating priests (*mahartvij*) present him from the mouth with horse-tail tufts (*āśvattha*) bound together with bundles of *ūṣa* grass on long bamboo poles; according to some, they present him from the head. With the words, "For the sake of food, for all people (*vaiśva*), for thee," the Adhvaryu presents him from the east with bundles of *āsa* grass. With the words, "For the sake of eating food, for thee," the Brahman presents him from the south. With the words, "For the sake of strength (*vāja*), for thee," the Hotṛ presents him from the west. With the words, "For the sake of winning strength, for thee," the Udgātṛ presents him from the north. (Khaṇḍa 5) 13.2.10.

Having formed a hollow basket-like shape out of *aśvattha* leaves, black earth, and saline soil (*ūṣā*), and having placed it upon the bamboo poles, they strike it while the sacrificer has ascended it, with the mantras beginning "For food, thee! (*annāya tvā*). However, in the *Vaikhānasa-sūtra*, they strike it with leaf-baskets in this manner: "For food, thee!"—the *adhvaryu* from the east; "For the source of food, thee!"—the *brahmā* from the south; "For strength, thee!"—the *hotṛ* from the west; "For the attainment of strength, thee!"—the *udgātṛ* from the north. [This concludes] the digging up of saline soil and its scattering.

Having wrapped [the victim] in leaf-cups made of those [Aśvattha wood], they should strike the patron (yajamāna) as he descends from the raw leaf-cup. For this very reason, Āpastamba says: "They present him to the Piśācas in each direction with cups made of Aśvattha wood—either raw, or filled with ashes, or both; or else, having tied him to long poles by the great priests" (ĀpaŚrSū 18.1.18). According to the Sūtra, they kill him from the front; the meaning is that they strike him facing toward the front. || 10 ||
Having extended his arms toward the slayer, he turns around. || 11 ||
"He turns around toward the slaughterer and the impure one," says Āpastamba; the word "sacrificer" is to be supplied as the subject. || 11 ||

"Thou art this, O King, for a friend; thou art a restrainer, a supporter, a sustainer—for the sake of agriculture, for security, for wealth, and for prosperity," with these words he descends. || 12 ||
When setting out, he descends at the *prapā* (water station); the wife’s ascending and descending are performed silently. ||12||
He spreads a goat-skin over the front of the sacrificial post with its neck pointing eastward and the hairy side upward. (Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Book 13, Section 13).
