Upon that [skin], he places a silver disk with the formula: "Thou art splendor. (Section 14).
Then, having spread out a goat-skin with its neck facing eastward and its hairy side upward in front of the sacrificial post, the Adhvaryu places a hundred-māna weight of gold upon it. 13–14.
With the words, "Thou art immortality," he places his foot upon the gold plate.
Saying, "Thou art immortality," the sacrificer places his right foot upon the gold.
"Thou art nourishment; thou art procreation," [he says] over the goat-skin.
The sacrificer places his left foot upon a goat-skin. || 16 ||
Therefore, he ascends the stool. || 17 ||
Therefore, touching the ground with that skin, he ascends the throne-seat made of Udumbara wood, which is oriented either toward the south or toward the east.
He addresses the one who is mounting with the mantra: "Mounting the heavenly ladder, having mounted it, may you look down upon the sacrificial posts of men. || 18 ||
The Adhvaryu addresses the sacrificer as he ascends with the mantra: "Ascend to the heavenly world, O Proṣṭhinī! || 18 ||
One undertakes the rites beginning with that dedicated to Mahendra. || 19 ||
At this time, he takes up the Māhendra cup. Then follows the commencement of the Stotra: "It has been poured out; it has been poured forth. (19)
Having introduced the hymn of praise for him, he consecrates him, as in the case of the piling of the fire-altar.
Of that sacrificer. || 20 ||

In the *rajas* [layer], while seven verses beginning with "food" (*anna*) are being recited as praise, he performs the food-oblation (*annahoma*), having taken portions from both domestic and wild plants.

Having mixed together wild herbs and seven domestic plants, and having taken portions from them, [he offers] with the seven mantras beginning with "Of the prize-winning... (*vājasyemaṃ*). He performs seven prior food-oblations (*annahoma*). Agni is the deity; the mantras beginning with "Of the prize-winning... have already been mentioned previously. After each oblation, he pours the residue into the cooking vessel; this and other details are to be understood from another Sūtra. However, since the pouring of the remaining residue is not found in our Sūtra, it is understood that such residue-pouring does not occur in this sacrifice, due to the reversal of the sequence. || 21 ||
(At the midday pressing,) during the middle *ukthya* round when the *brahmasāman* has been introduced, here [follow] the subsequent [verses] beginning with those of Sarasvatī.
1. Gold. 2. Chapter. Accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 147.

Venerable sir! 22. He proceeds with their omenta that have not been sprinkled [with ghee]. 23. Having proceeded with the omentum of the Sarasvatī offering, and having taken portions from all together, he proceeds with the omenta of the Prājāpatya offerings. 24. He proceeds with the *naivāra* (millet) offering; it concludes with the *iḍā* portion, beginning from the oblation of the sacrificial food (*havis*). 25. The great officiating priests (*mahartvij*) become partakers of the remnants of the sacrificial food. 26.

"Thou art the praise of the praised," and so forth. At the time of the *atigrāhya* oblation, the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) is performed with the six verses beginning "O Indra, thou who art heated" (*indra unnaya*), either collectively (*tantra*) or individually (*bheda*), adopting the alternative that [the fire] is blazing. When the *brahmasāman* has been introduced during the middle *ukthya* round, O God Savitṛ, this is for thee; there follows the placing of the *sārasvata* and *naivāra* [grains], beginning with "The sacrifice is dear to thee," and so forth, and the performance of those two.

"Having spread [the base] on the *juhū*," and so forth; "Recite the invitatory prayer (*anuvāka*) for the cake (*puroḍāśa*) for Sarasvat," and so forth; "Command [the Hotṛ] for Sarasvat," or "Sacrifice to Sarasvant. "May I be an eater of food through Sarasvat. "Recite the invitatory prayer for Bṛhaspati," or "Command [the Hotṛ] for Bṛhaspati," or "Sacrifice to Bṛhaspati. "May I be an eater of food through Bṛhaspati. Having divided the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering for both, the *prāśitra* and the *iḍā* for both are performed, concluding with the ritual purification (*ārjana*). The great priests shall partake of the remnants of the sacrificial oblation (*havirucchiṣṭa*).

Having adopted the position that [the ritual] should be performed at the proper time (*kāle vai*), the procedure begins with "O God Savitṛ, according to the truth... and so forth, up until the end of the *savana* oblation and the conclusion of the departure (*niḥsarpaṇa*). Thus ends the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*). 22, 23, 24, 21, 26.
At the time of the animal sacrifice, he proceeds with all [the offerings] ending with that of Sarasvatī according to their respective deities.

Now follows the ritual procedure for the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*). "O God Savitṛ, may he make it palatable for us; Svāhā! Savitṛ is the giver. [Then follows] the wiping of the pitcher (*kalaśodvartana*). Thereafter, the taking of the Āditya cup and so forth. Having taken the Āgrayaṇa, the Ukthya cup is taken. Then follows the taking of the Ṣoḍaśin cup.

When these [verses] beginning with *puṣṭyai me* have been recited during the chanting of the Ārbhava Pavamāna, [the Adhvaryu says]: "O Agni, distribute the fires; converse regarding the sacrificial animals. At the conclusion of the worship (*upasthāna*) with the verse beginning *viṣṇo tvaṃ naḥ*, the Pratiprasthātṛ [takes] the hundred oblations (*śata-havis*). [The Adhvaryu says: "O slaughterer, [be] peaceful," and with a wooden sword (*sphyahana*), he sprinkles [the victim] with the formula: "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Agni, with my mind. He brings another speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*). In this same sequence, the sprinkling is performed for all [the victims].

"To Indra and Agni, thee, acceptable; to Indra, thee, acceptable; to the Maruts, thee, acceptable; to Sarasvatī, thee, acceptable; (to Sarasvant, thee, acceptable); to Prajāpati, thee, acceptable"—in this sequence, he sprinkles all seventeen [portions] with clarified butter, saying "I sprinkle. The Adhvaryu [performs the rites] in sequence with the mantra "He who is thy self... With the mantra "Svāhā to the steam," he removes them in sequence with the words "Be firm," together with each respective heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*), and deposits them in sequence with the Pañcahotṛ formula.

The touching of the offered omentum (*vapā*) for all [the deities] occurs in sequence. "He spreads [the grass] under the four," and so forth. Having performed the *āśrāvaya* call with the formula "Indra is the breath of the Agni-related [offering]," the *vasā-homa* (fat-offering) takes place at the half-verse. He brings the remainder elsewhere. Then, upon the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, the oblation is made. Then follows the *manotā* hymn. The procedure for the Indra-Agni offering: the *vasā-homa* at the half-verse; the remainder elsewhere. Again, the *manotā* and so forth. "For Indra, of the bull's oblation. Thus, "Command! The *vasā-homa* at the half-verse; the remainder elsewhere.
Again, the Manotā and so forth; the offering of the bull’s meat for the Maruts; the vital breath belongs to Indra; O God... (Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram—[13th Praśna])

[The Adhvaryu] gives the call for the departure: "For Sarasvatī, of the ewe-offering. Thus he gives the command; at the half-verse, the *vasā-homa* (fat-oblation) is performed. The remainder is otherwise. Again, from the *manotā* onwards: the *vasā-homa* for the fat of the ram-offering for Sarasvatī. Having set aside the remainder elsewhere, [he proceeds] from the *manotā* onwards. For the *prājāpatya* offerings, the *manotā* is performed by a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). Having spread an underlayer of ghee in the *juhū* ladle, having taken all the *prājāpatya* portions together with a piece of gold, and having also taken all the non-limb portions together with the previous limb-portions—

Having taken portions of the *iḍā* from the heaped grain, together with the portions for the *iḍā*-gifts, and having covered the *iḍā*-portion with all the *prājāpatya* fats, one places a piece of gold on top and performs the double sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*). Having poured all the *vasā* (fat) into a single vessel, [the portion] is taken from that. Then follows the *aindra-prāṇa*. Even though all have been offered, one recites for the goat-oblation: "O gods, for protection... [and] "O friends, follow Prajāpati... in a low voice (*upāṃśu*); but "Recite for the oblation of the goats" in a loud voice (*uccais*).

Having thus dispatched [the offerings], there is the *vasā-homa* (oblation of the fat) at the half-verse. Having collected all the remnants (*udreka*) previously set aside, there is the offering to the quarters (*dig-yāga*). At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, the casting [of the oblation] is performed according to the common procedure (*tantra*). And the rule is that one should strike [the fire] with the *juhū* ladle from below. One prepares [the portion] sufficient for the cutting-off (*avadāna*) beforehand. For all [offerings], there is the consecration formula (*anumantraṇa*) as in the case of the omentum (*vapā*). In the common procedures (*tantra*), one covers the fatty parts of the limbs, but not with the fat itself. One should not throw gold therein, nor should one sprinkle clarified butter (*ājya*) over it. [...]

Having offered the fat (*vasā*) at the half-verse, he performs the long and double standing. Without performing the *akṛtya* [rite], he pours the remainder of the fat into another vessel. Having stepped back, there is the sacrifice to the *vanaspati* (the tree) beginning with the *nāriṣṭha* oblation. The procedure for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering begins with "upon the Āhavanīya fire, in the *juhū* ladle," and so forth. [The formula is] "This oblation for Vaiśvānara... followed by the invocation of the *iḍā*, and so on. || 27 ||

While drawing the cups for the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, he pours out the King Soma (the *rājā*) in excess for one group of cups. Having performed the ritual with them, he draws the cups for the supplementary (*atirikta*) stotra, with the *hotṛ*-cup at their head. There are both a *stotra* and a *śastra*. Having responded to the *śastra*, the Adhvaryu takes the principal cup of the *prājāpatya* offerings; the other priests take the remaining ones. 28.

The Soma-related ritual, beginning with the preparation of the *savaniya-puroḍāśa* cake and ending with the washing of the *ṣoḍaśin-camasa*, is completed. Then, he draws the ten cups, of which the *hotṛ-camasa* is the chief; they have been drawn. Thereafter follows the formal command (*saṃpraisha*). According to Āpastamba, one introduces the *bṛhat-stotra* with the formula, "Thou art the Abhijit. This is the *stomabhāga* portion. At the time of the performance, the Adhvaryu takes up the *hotṛ-camasa*, while the Camasādhvaryus and the other officiating priests take up the remaining Soma cups.
The Pratiprasthātṛ, being a Vājasṛt, takes the principal of the Surā-cups; the Camasādhvaryus take the other cups. (Section 6) 29.
The Pratiprasthātṛ takes the chief of the Sura-cups; the Vājasṛt takes the other Sura-cups.

"You are mingled; mingle me with prosperity," saying this, the Adhvaryu moves forward toward the east with the Soma-cups. "You are mingled; mingle me with prosperity... [End of Paṭala]. This is accompanied by the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 149.

"May they be joined," or "You are separated; be joined with evil"—thus the Pratiprasthātṛ [responds] facing westward with the *surā* cups. "You are separated; may you be joined with evil," or "May they be joined. At the edge of the Āhavanīya fire, they stand with the *soma* cups; at the edge of the Mārjālīya fire, he proceeds with the *surā* cups. For the *soma* cups, there are the *vaṣaṭ* and *anuvaṣaṭ* calls. They cause the *surā* cups to tremble after them. The consumption of the *soma* has been explained.

"Ye are for contact," says the Adhvaryu; holding the Soma-cup, he proceeds together [with the others] facing eastward. Having reached the northern altar (uttaravedi) and having stepped across to the south, he stands facing north. The officiating priests (ṛtvij) also stand facing north with their Soma-vessels, as do the cup-bearers (camasādhvaryu). In the event of impossibility, they stand according to available space.

With the formula "O you who are apart," the Pratiprasthātṛ goes westward together with the Sura-cups; having exited by the rear door, entered the Sadas, and exited the Sadas by the rear door, he goes to the Mārjālīya fire. Standing there facing north together with the Vaiśya, at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, the Soma-cups are poured out along with the Camasa-vessels.

"O Prajāpati, you are the overlord of the gods; make me an overlord among men, long-lived and full of splendor—svāhā! With this *ṣoḍaśin* mantra, having offered [the oblation], the Adhvaryu, the Camasādhvaryus, and the other priests perform the offering silently at the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*. And they all cause the vessels of *surā* to shake at both the *vaṣaṭkāra* and the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*. Prajāpati is the deity of the *soma* cups and the *camasa* vessels, and likewise for the vessels of *surā*.
For those belonging to Sūrya and Prajāpati, the mantra is "vibhrāṭ," or alternatively, "mandrā'mibhūtiḥ. (30, 31)
He modifies the *bhakṣa* mantra by adding "of the Virāj metre. || 32 ||
"O you who have the Virāj metre," [he says] regarding the cup. || 32 ||
On the southern corner of the altar, having divided the Vājasṛts, they consume the Sura-cups. || 33 ||

Regarding this, there is a specific rule in the Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra: "They present the portions for the Maruts from the Āhavanīya fire, the Soma-residue, and the cart-wood; and the Vājasādhas present the Surā-cups which are not to be offered as portions. Having cut these out from the corner of the southern altar, they consume them" (ĀpŚS 18.7.8). "Having cut them out from the corner of the southern altar" means having repeatedly sliced them off; this refers to the consumption of the modifications of the Iṣṭi sacrifice, provided that the Surā is consumed after being invoked with an *upahava* (invocation) similar to that used for the *iḍā*. 33.

He proceeds with the *anuyāja* offerings while the *sruks* are spread apart; he proceeds with the deities of the subsequent animals, beginning with Sārasvata. Or rather, he may proceed at the very same point where he proceeds with the omenta of the other animals. At that same place where he proceeds with the oblations, he offers the portions for the *Māruta* offering from the oblations to the officiating priests. Those portions not intended to be cut off, [the *vāja-sṛts*], having been mixed together on the southern corner of the altar, they consume them as the *vāja-sṛts*. —The Śrauta Sūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, 13th Praśna, [Chapter] 34–37.

"Having become Prajāpati and Varuṇa," [with these words] there is the consumption of the Soma cups. If the *surā* is a modification (*vikāra*) of Soma, then, when the Mārjālīya fire has been carried forth, there is the placing of fuel, the strewing of grass, and so forth, as well as the oblation. According to Khānasa, one should consume it on the southern shoulder of the altar (or without dividing it). The consumption of the remainder of the *māruta* [offering] is for all. 34–35.
The prince Kakuda eats either the *dhruvagopa* or the *naivāragopa*, or both, or the entire *kakuda*. 38.

The prince eats the *kakud* (hump), and everyone performs the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). (Although the procedure for those about to sacrifice has already been stated, some explain that there is no fixed order. [The Agnīdh calls out: "O Agnīdh, kindle the fires," and so forth. With all the sections of the rectum (*gudakāṇḍa*), [he offers] with the formula: "Go to the ocean, Svāhā! Go everywhere! At the offering of the *svaru* splinter, [he offers] with the formula: "May your smoke go to heaven, your flame to the intermediate space; fill the earth with ashes, Svāhā!"

From all the tail-ends, four portions are cut off. At the time of taking down the spit, [he says]: "Ye are pure; burn that evil. "May the waters be friendly to us. At the time of attending to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), he takes the cloths from the post and hands them to the *adhvaryu*; for there is a statement of the *Chandogas*: "The cords belong to the *adhvaryu*. Then the *adhvaryu* gives those cloths to the supervisor (*upadraṣṭṛ*); for there is a statement: "Three cloths for the *somapravāka*. Whichever [priest] has gold, he gives to him the corresponding [cloth] used for the garland. || 38 ||
The Vājapeya sacrifice is concluded. || 39 ||

Having performed the rites up to the satiation of the Brahmins, and having concluded with the *udavasānīyā* offering to Agni, the Vājapeya sacrifice is completed. Now follows the ritual procedure for the Kuruvājapeya. Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) at the previously mentioned time, "I shall sacrifice with the Kuruvājapeya," all the aforementioned fruits [of the sacrifice] are attained.

At the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*), having offered the two *dākṣiṇī* oblations into all the *nārāśamsa* cups, and having brought forth the gold while reciting "By your form... and so forth, and having given the full vessel of gold and other gifts, he gives the gift of birds starting with "Of every age... and so forth—seventeen of each kind of bird, a thousand, four hundred and forty-five. Having performed the rites for one [bird] starting from those one year old up to those five years old, ending with the giving of the *camasādhvaryus*, and having given to the *prasarpakas*, [he offers] with the verse, "This is for thee, O Agni... (*etatte agne*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "O Agni, lead us" (*agne naya*) and "Thus from age to age" (*evaṃ vayaso vayasas*), the distribution of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) is equal for all, not only for the *adhvaryu*s. The author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakṛt*) maintains that the *sadasya* is a permanent participant. Furthermore, according to the statement of the *Chandogas*, one who is unable [to give the full amount] gives only seventeen cows; and according to the statement of the *Chandogas*, there are exactly seventeen shares, and he should distribute them equally among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

Having performed the salutation to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and having completed everything prior to the drawing of the *māhendra* cup—including the ritual disposal of the horn (*viṣāṇaprāsana*) with the formula "The lord of the sacrifice," etc.—he brings the *naivāra* (wild rice) mixed with ghee and places it in the *cātvāla* pit. Then, [he draws] the *māhendra* [cup] with the *śukra* vessel. As for the consumption: 1) they should consume it when it has not yet been recited; 2) [the text says] "mālāmatī"; 3) [the text says] "paṭelaḥ. [This concludes] the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin, [chapter] 151.

"Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra," as before. In this case, there is no *ānidhāvana* (the running-in), because it is a refinement of the chariot. Due to the absence of [multiple] chariots and so forth, some desire the *ānidhāvana* with a single chariot in the Kuruvājapeya; however, that is not desired for a Rājanya or a Vaiśya [as they would be the ones driving the chariots of the Vaiśya and the chariot-maker]. All else is as before. Thus concludes the Kuruvājapeya. || 39 ||
Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, he should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī.
Having sacrificed with that, he should perform the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, or the Āmikṣā offering dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.
He does not rise up to greet anyone at all. ||41||
Even when the direct teacher has arrived, one should not descend [from the status of a student] toward anyone else for as long as life lasts; thus says Āpastamba.
It is known that he becomes one who possesses a white umbrella. (Khaṇḍa 7) || 42 ||

Thus ends the second chapter in the thirteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*. Regarding this, Āpastamba has also provided an additional rule: "One should sacrifice either with the Bṛhaspatisava or with the Pratyavarohaṇīya; it is known from tradition that [the sacrificer] becomes one who possesses a white umbrella" (*Āpastamba Śrautasūtra* 18.7.18). If he performs the Pratyavarohaṇa, then he should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava. According to the statement of the Chandogas, the sacrificer remains one who possesses a white umbrella for as long as he lives. 42.
Thus ends the second chapter in the thirteenth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin, compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.
13.3 Now begins the third chapter of the thirteenth book.

The Vājapeya, which consists of a sacrificial session performed by both Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, has been described. Now the Rājasūya, which is a modified form (vikṛti) performed by one class alone, will be prescribed:
"A king desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Rājasūya. (1)

In this regard, the entitlement to the Rājasūya belongs only to a *rājanya* who has not yet performed the *Anīṣomīya* sacrifice (*ānapeya*), and not to one who has already performed it. This is because the fruit of universal sovereignty (*sāmrājya*) is superior even to the fruit of kingship (*rājya*); therefore, it is improper to perform a rite that results in an inferior fruit immediately after a sacrifice that is the means for attaining a superior fruit. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states: "The Rājasūya is for a king, whether he has not performed the *Anīṣomīya* or has performed it" (*Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra* 16.1.12). Furthermore, this word *rājan* is seen in other contexts as being based on the *kṣatriya* caste.

Whatever action is prescribed for him by tradition is called "sovereignty" (*rājya*). Furthermore, it consists of the protection of those respective districts, cities, and so forth. [Objection: Is not the application of the word "king" (*rājan*) based on the connection with sovereignty, as in the case of a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*)? For the word "king" is also applied to a Kṣatriya who possesses that [sovereignty], as in the expression "the people. One who exercises sovereignty is a king. And this being the case, we find the term used in the *Āveṣṭi* sacrifice within the *Rājasūya* itself.

If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, he should place an offering to Bṛhaspati in the middle; having offered each oblation, he should pour clarified butter over it. (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa) 13.152. For a Rājanya, [he should offer] to Indra; for a Vaiśya, to the Viśvedevas. This indicates the eligibility of all three social classes. How is this so? If "rājā" (king) were one who merely performs the function of ruling (*rājya-kartṛ*), then this would be appropriate. To this it is replied: one cannot say that a "rājā" is merely a ruler of a kingdom.

For neither the elision of a suffix nor the restoration of a nominal stem is traditionally taught [in this context]. Rather, the suffix *ṣyañ* is prescribed after the word *rājan* in the sense of an object (*karman*). Therefore, one can say that "the act of a king is sovereignty" (*rājyam*), and thus that "the king is the agent of sovereignty. As for the observation regarding Brāhmaṇas mentioned in connection with the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice, that refers to the *Aveṣṭi* which is prescribed outside of the *Rājasūya* for one who desires food and wealth. As for the claim that the word *rājan* is used for a mere local chieftain (*ekadeśe jāti*) based on etymological derivation (*yoga*), while it applies to a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*) by convention, we reply as follows:

Even in a single instance, usage [of a term] is indeed untenable without the expressive power (*śakti*) of the word. As for universal usage, that occurs through metaphorical function (*upacāra-vṛtti*); one who performs the work of a king is called "king" just like a king. And so it is seen in an identical injunction: "Therefore, one should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha; this Aśvamedha is indeed the sacrifice of a Kṣatriya. Likewise: "Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa sits below the Kṣatriya at the Rājasūya as the sacrificer."

The phrase "by being a *sat* priest" indicates that this applies to a Kṣatriya in the context of the Rājasūya. Within the section on the Rājasūya (*Jaiminīya Sūtra* 4.4.1), all sacrifices—whether *iṣṭi*, animal, or *soma* sacrifices, as well as non-sacrifices such as oblations (*homa*) and gambling (*videvana*)—are heard in the scripture even though they require a fruit. Nevertheless, they are not connected with the fruit of sovereignty (*svārājya*), because according to the principle of the section on the meaning of verbal roots (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*; *Jaiminīya Sūtra* 2.1.2), it is the sacrifice alone that serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the realization of the fruit; thus, it is logical that the non-sacrifices are subordinate (*aṅga*) to it.

Furthermore, because the word *rājasūya* denotes that [entirety] through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), it is the name of that alone. Nor should it be argued that, based on the etymology "that in which the king (*rājā*), i.e., Soma, is pressed (*sūyate*) or extracted (*abhiṣūyate*)," the word *rājasūya* refers only to the Soma sacrifices, and thus the connection with the fruit belongs to those alone; for since the etymology "it is pressed (*sūyate*), i.e., accomplished, by the king (*rājñā*), i.e., the Kṣatriya" is applicable to all [the constituent rites], there is no evidence for restricting the application to the root *yaj*. For this very reason, the king...

The view that the term *rājasūya*—derived from the etymology "wherein a Kṣatriya consecrates himself" (*kṣatriyaḥ sunoti*)—refers exclusively to the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice because of its connection with the consecration at the time of the *Māhendra* stotra, and that therefore only that sacrifice is connected with the fruit, is also refuted. Since the aforementioned etymology allows for the term to apply to all [sacrifices], there is no evidence for restricting the scope of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) [to the *abhiṣecanīya* alone]. Therefore, all sacrifices are indeed prompted by the fruit; thus, the *videvana* and other such acts are extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to the modifications (*vikṛti*) of those sacrifices. || 1 ||
One should undergo initiation five nights before the full moon of the month of Taiṣya.

After the full moon of Pauṣa, when the dark fortnight has passed, on the day of sacrifice—that is, on the first day of Māgha—is the initiation (*dīkṣā*). Thus Kātyāyana says: "The initiation takes place on the day of sacrifice in the [dark] fortnight of Māgha" (Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra 15.1.3). However, according to another Sūtra, at the beginning of spring, on the full moon of Phālguna or on the first day of the lunar month, a Kṣatriya who has been consecrated or has performed his first sacrifice, having offered the New Moon oblation (*āmāvāsya-haviḥ*) together with his wives, performs breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and makes the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).

In this regard, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is as follows: "I shall sacrifice with the Rājasūya, with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of one hundred thousand [cows], so that I may attain the heavenly world"—this is the resolve. (2)
Just as in this [current] year, so in the coming year, on the full moon day of Taiṣya, the initiation for the Abhiṣecanīya Ukthya sacrifice shall commence. ||3||
And that Soma sacrifice [is so called] because of its connection with initiation (dīkṣā).
One should perform the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, specifically the Agniṣṭoma form, for the first time.

Then: "I shall sacrifice with the *pravitra* [strainer]; you are the lightning (*vidyut*). Then follows the selection of the *somapravāka* (the announcer of the Soma) and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*). The *somapravāka* says: "The Rājasūya of Bukavarman is about to take place; therein, the office of the *adhvaryu* must be performed by your honor. When asked, "Is it not an *ahīna* [sacrifice]? the reply is: "The Rājasūya is not an *ahīna*."

Now, it might be argued that since the *rājasūya* shares the common characteristic of being a multi-day session (*ahargaṇa*), it would follow that it is an *ahīna* sacrifice; to this, the following is said. Regarding this, Drāhmāyaṇa has stated: "Except for the three-night [sacrifice] and those beginning with the five-night [session], and other than the *rājasūya* and the *cāturmāsya*s. Therefore, the response is that the *rājasūya* is not an *ahīna*. At the time of the selection of the Hotṛ, the Hotṛ must be a Bhārgava; he chooses him, and not one belonging to the Kaṇva or Kāśyapa gotras. This is because of the scriptural authority of the Brāhmaṇa: "At the Daśapeya, the Hotṛ is a Bhārgava" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.8.20).

Those very same priests are the *pavitra* priests for the entire *rājasūya*. Alternatively, there is a separate selection (*varaṇa*) for each individual ritual action. This is because of Baudhāyana’s statement: "In the *daśapeya*, [the *pavitra* priest] is a descendant of Bhṛgu. Thus it is understood that in the *daśapeya* alone, the *pavitra* priest must be a Bhārgava. Regarding the request for the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), if one follows the alternative view, the king [seeks it] by this very rule: "The sacrificial ground belongs to the king. At the time of the formal depositing (*samāropaṇa*), all the fires beginning with the *gārhapatya* are to be deposited; this includes the depositing of all the fires, as well as the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires. These two are fixed.

According to the scriptural statement, "He is indeed the husband," having offered the *saṃbhāra* oblations, one offers to Soma and performs the serving [of food]. Having fetched *nyagrodha-stibhinīs* (young shoots of the banyan tree), there is the serving of *nyagrodha* fruits. After performing the *saptahotṛ* oblation, one performs the worship with the mantra, "In one's own skill (*dakṣa*). Then follows the *anvādhāna* for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering: "The unextinguished you... and "The food of the dwelling... At the time of bending [the knee], [one recites] "O Vāyu, lord of the earth... At the time of threshing, there is the invocation: "Come, O possessor of the oblation (*haviṣvat*). The selection of priests (*pravara*) is performed according to the lineage of the family priest (*purohita*).

At the time of instruction, because he has previously attained the first and foremost glory; thus, at the conclusion of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, the ritual for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is completed. At the time of the announcement: "This Brāhmaṇa has been initiated—the prince Rājendra, the son of Colavarman. Regarding the vow of barley-gruel (*yavāgūvata*), at the time of the *prāyaṇīya* and *somāyaṇa* rites, he pours out the King Soma upon the right side of the skin. He places *nyagrodha* fruits near it. The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that there is a purpose for the mantras designating Soma by means of the fruit.

According to the principle that "because it is occasional and unequal, there should be no common procedure," there is an exclusion of the mantras for the author of the Sūtra; this is because of the statement, "silently [he performs] the earthen [rite]. Regarding this, there is a specific rule for the purchase of Soma: having consecrated the Soma with the mantra, "By thy spirit (aśu), thy spirit," he measures out the Soma silently; then, having measured the Soma with the mantra, "To that god... (*abhi tyam devam*), he measures out the fruits silently.

With the formula beginning "For the subjects, thee" (*prajābhyaḥ tvā*) and ending with "O Soma, I buy thee" (*soma te krīṇāni*), having purchased [the Soma] with a cow—because of the statement regarding the *Rājasūya*, "The self of that [Soma] is for two"—the purchase is made with two hundred [cows]. There is a sevenfold division of the two hundred cows among the seven Somas. For each [Soma], there are twenty-eight; or, according to another view, twenty-one for each. By the principle of the final increment (*antyavṛddhi-nyāya*), they are placed at the end. [This applies] to the support of the nobles (*kṣatrāṇām dhṛtau*); elsewhere, it is twenty-eight.

He said, "I shall purchase it from you for twenty-one cows. There is the taking of sand for that [purchase], because of the statement, "It is of two forms; for a Rājanya, it is with two forms. Here, [the formula is]: "With twenty-seven cows I purchase it from you," and "Light for us," etc. Having performed the Ātithyā [offering] and having offered the fast-milk (vrata) of barley-gruel, at the time of gathering the materials, he performs the spreading of the sand with the formula: "I release this Bukkavarman, son of so-and-so, into the hands of the Karṇāṭaka Vaiśyas," using the second case ending.

At the time of the installation of the Mahāvīra vessel, [the priest recites]: "O Sword of Dharma, you are the Good Dharma; uphold the powers for me and for others. This is also the nourishment of the fruits. The *upasad* rite is performed in the form of the breasts. The remainder is like that of the Agniṣṭoma. At the great pressing, having employed the *buddha* and *adhvaryu*, he employs the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, as in the *atyagniṣṭoma*. Some do not desire this. In the archetype, the Agniṣṭoma, regarding the *ṣoḍaśin*, there are two *droṇakalaśas*, two *pūtabhṛts*, and two *ādhavanīyas*; some say there is no distinction between the *gāvadharma* and the *manthin*.

Because of the statement of the Bahvṛcas that there is no difference between the hide and the skin; because at the time of carrying forward the *vasatīvarī* waters, one has already gone out by the eastern door due to having attained prosperity (*gataśrī*); at the time of pressing, having performed [the rite] with "For Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra," they descend and prepare only the fruits. Having performed the great pressing and gathered [the materials], having removed the hide and the pressing-stones, having sprinkled the other skin and placed it down, having performed the ritual up to the end of the abode of the waters, or having performed it together at the proper time, having placed the fruits on the other side, [he recites] "eastward, westward," and so forth.

The two verses "nātrāvīvṛdha" and "āmāskān" do not occur here; rather, the two verses "drapsaśca skanda" and "drapsaśca skanda" are used. Some, however, do not accept this. Having thus pressed and squeezed [the juice], he mixes it with ordinary curds and pours it into another *ādhavanīya* vessel. After drawing the *dhruva* cup, the drawing of the *ṣoḍaśin* follows. Then, having set down the *nyagrodha* jar, performed the cleansing, and spread a filter over it, they pour some of the fruit-juice into it. The *ekadhana* waters are used according to the requirements.

Having performed [the rites] for Soma, afterwards, for the fruits, there are two [portions] for the Maitrāvaruṇa cup and so forth, belonging to both [sides]. Then, even for the fruits of the Pavamāna-mahā-etc., having separately performed [the rites] with "You two are the two oceans, you two are the two worlds; [you belong] to Viṣṇu, to Indra, to the All-gods," there is the cessation of "O Soma, you... It becomes "You are the cooked [offerings] for Prajāpati, for Indra, for the All-gods; you are the cooked one. Just as there is a cessation of the rice-mantra upon the employment of barley, so it is here.

At the time of drawing the cups (*camasonayana*), the Unnetṛ draws the sacrificer’s cup (*yajamānacamasa*) with the juice of the fruit. While the cups are being offered from the *droṇakalaśa*—beginning with the spreading of the underlayer (*upastīrya*) and so forth—the *camasādhvaryu* of the three middle-performers (*madhyataḥkārin*) takes a glowing coal from within the altar using a young blade of *darbha* grass while reciting, "I have taken thee from him. With that coal, he offers the cup into the fire. He offers it silently at the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*-call (*anuvaṣaṭkṛte*). At the time of consumption, having looked at it while saying, "Come for consumption," [he recites], "Thee, who art the portion of men... (*nṛcakṣasaṃ tvā*).

"That which remains here, that am I"—thus [the sacrificer] consumes [the remnant]. "May you be auspicious to us," [he says]. "The waters"—thus from the *Bāḍhacavamanā*. In all cases involving the cups of the sacrificer (*yajamānacamas*), the procedure is as follows.
There is liberation from the five. || 5 ||

Apavarga means completion. [End of] Paṭala 1. [This work is] accompanied by the commentary called *Mayūkhacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. Having consecrated the Soma with the mantra "With thy stalk (aṃśu), [I buy] thy stalk," he silently [takes] the fruits. Having measured out the Soma with the mantra "To that god... (abhi tyam devam...), he silently [takes] the fruits. Having muttered the formula beginning with "For the offspring thee" (prajābhyas tvā) up to "I buy thy Soma" (somaṃ te krīṇāni), [he buys it] for a cow; for her is the soul (the price). Because of the statement regarding the Rājasūya, "By two [cows]," the purchase is made for two hundred [cows]. There is a sevenfold division of the two hundred [cows] among the seven Somas.

Twenty-eight [cows] for each [day], or one hundred thousand for each—having divided [the total] equally among all the Soma sacrifices belonging to the Rājasūya, he gives them day by day. (6) In that manner he should lead the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). (7) He should act so that his days have their own proper times. He should assign the remainder. (8)

"At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives five thousand cows as the *pavitra*. [This means] one hundred thousand, or a lakh, in all the *rājasūya*-related *soma* sacrifices, such as the *pavitra* and others, and in the seven *soma* rituals. The rest is clear. At the time of bringing the sacrificial fees, they should be brought in such a way that there is no displacement of the primary elements. This is what is meant: having brought ten or twenty, he gives whatever remains wherever it may be situated.

In the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), having pressed the *ṛjīṣa*, they press the *phala-ṛṣi*. Having divided [the mixture], they pour in the *āśira* (milk), enter by the eastern door, and perform the *āśira*-offering with the *agniṣṭoma* cups. After performing the *ṣoḍaśin* oblation, at the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), the sprinkling of the *phalaka* and the *ṛjīṣa* is done silently; their disposal is performed as a single ritual act (*tantra*). Some say that the touching of the drops of the *phala* is separate and done silently. Following the *anūbandhyā* sacrifice, he offers the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) and also subsequently offers the eight *devasū* oblations. Whether for kings or others, everything else is like the *agniṣṭoma*. 6, 7, 8.
Because the Rājasūya sacrifice, the Iṣṭis, and the animal sacrifices are enjoined to be performed day after day. ||9||

The *iṣṭis* such as the Anumati and others, the *soma* sacrifices such as the Pavitra and others, and the animal sacrifices such as the Mallaka and others—these constitute distinct ritual procedures (*tantra*). Why is this so? Because it is enjoined that they are performed "day by day" (*anvaham*), meaning one by one on each successive day.
From the distinctness of their sacrificial fees, one should understand the distinctness of the sacrifices.

One should understand that there is a plurality of sacrifices (iṣṭi-pṛthaktva) because of the injunction regarding the separate distribution of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā-pṛthaktva) for those [sacrifices] involving the combination of iṣṭis and animal sacrifices (paśu). Others, however, say that in this case there are three *āñścana* cups, three *ābhyas* cups, three *bandhyā* animals, and the *anvāhāryapacana* fire.
The separate sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) other than those for the encircling of the quarters constitute a single ritual procedure (ekatantra). || 11 ||
This is for the purpose of illustration. ||11||
When the next day has dawned, he should sacrifice every day with the Ānumata and the subsequent offerings.

What is the initiation for the Pavitra? There are three Upasad days; on the fifth day is the Soma-pressing; on the following day, beginning with the sixth, he should sacrifice with the eight offerings starting with the Ātumata.

"He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Anumati," as it is handed down in the sacred text. While grinding [the grain], he causes the portion for Anumati to be separated out from behind and from the north. 13.

The *Anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice is not for the purpose of commencing [the main rite], because on the sixth day, after performing the morning *Agnihotra*, one says: "I shall sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*. For this very reason, in cases such as the *Rājasūya*, where the principal rites consisting of *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices are joined with other principal rites, even though [the *Anvārambhaṇīyā*] exists—[Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Book 11].

Regarding their predominance, although there is the possibility of the commencement [of the *ārambhaṇīyā*] even through an activity generated by an intention in the form "May the Rājasūya be mine"—which is an intention characterized by the mode (*prakāra*) of being a Rājasūya, even in the absence of an intention in the form "May such-and-such a sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) be mine"—[the *ārambhaṇīyā*] does not occur prior to that [specific sacrifice], because [the Rājasūya as a whole] lacks the status of being an object of occurrence (*vṛttiviṣayatva*) whose objective reference (*uddeśyatā*) is delimited by the nature of being such-and-such a specific sacrifice (*tattadiṣṭitva*). Nor does it occur prior to the great resolve (*mahāsaṃkalpa*) "I shall sacrifice with the Rājasūya," for that too...

Because there is an absence of being the object of an activity whose objective reference (*uddeśyatā*) is delimited by the nature of those respective *iṣṭi* sacrifices, with respect to being the object of an activity whose objective reference is delimited by the status of being a *rājasūya*. For the nature of being a *rājasūya* is not the delimitor of the "modifiedness" (*vikṛtitā*) as determined by the "archetypality" (*prakṛtitā*) residing in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; for that [nature of being a *rājasūya*] is over-extended (*atiprasakta*), since it exists even in the *soma* sacrifices.

For this very reason, in cases such as the Cāturmāsya or the Āgrayaṇa sacrifices, where the property of being a "Cāturmāsya" and so forth is not over-extended, there is no defect even if one assumes distinct extended applications (atideśa) for each individual sacrifice, provided that [the general property] serves as the delimiting factor of the objective (uddeśyatāvacchedaka). In reality, however, even in the archetype (prakṛti), the status of being a "Darśapūrṇamāsa" is not the delimiting factor of the objective; rather, it is the status of being an Āgneya sacrifice and so forth. Due to the unity of time, however, the performance is carried out by way of a single procedure (tantra). This also applies to the declaration: "I shall sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa."

The meaning is simply: "I shall sacrifice with the Āgneya and the others. Consequently, even in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) such as the Cāturmāsya, that very same nature remains the defining characteristic (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*). Furthermore, because the time is identical, the performance is done by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). As for the expression "with the Cāturmāsya sacrifices," its meaning is likewise "I shall sacrifice with the [four] sacrifices. Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Therefore, in that case, the *anvārambhaṇīyā* indeed takes place at the commencement of that [modified sacrifice].

In the present case, however, although the status of being the sacrifice for that specific [soma-sacrifice] and so forth serves as the delimiting factor (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) for the object of the injunction, the *anvārambhaṇīyā* is not required because the status of being the soma-sacrifice (*saumya*) and so forth also serves as a delimiting factor for the object. For in the archetype (*prakṛti*), by the statement "one who is about to begin the New and Full Moon sacrifices," since the New and Full Moon sacrifices are indicated as qualifiers, at the time of the indication of their status as means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*), there arises a causal capacity (*kāraṇatā*) defined by the effect-ness (*kāryatā*) residing in the apūrva of the archetypal sacrifice.

The qualification of the intended object (*uddeśyatā*) should be understood as being delimited by the delimitor [of the sacrifice] while simultaneously not being delimited by that which is not the delimitor of the aforementioned causal capacity (*kāraṇatā*). Consequently, because such an intended object is absent in the *rājasūya*, the *anvārambhīyā* offering does not apply there. For this very reason, even an intention in the form "May the *agnihotra* and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices be mine" does not constitute an intended object [in the primary sense].

Otherwise, since even the first constituent element (*padārtha*) of the initial performance of the *agnihotra* would be an object of activity characterized by such a [general] objective reference (*uddeśyatā*), the *anvārambhaṇīyā* would consequently have to be performed there as well. Therefore, after that desire [to perform the sacrifice], a desire arises in the form: "May the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices come into being. It should be understood that this very [desire] constitutes the factor of objective reference (*uddeśyatā*). ... Lightning and rain occur at the beginning and end of every ritual action.

The ritual beginning with the *anvādhāna* (placing of the fire-sticks) is for today’s sacrifice: "For this [sacrifice], this nourishment, the sixth... This is the *iṣṭi* offering of the Full Moon (*paurṇamāsa*) ritual. At the time of the preparation of the vessels, there are eight potsherds (*kapāla*); the largest is a single potsherd (*ekakapāla*), and the others are paired, as in the archetype (*prakṛti*). There is also the *anvāhārya* cooking-pot. According to the Śruti: "Anumati is the presiding deity of the Full Moon mixed with the fourteenth day; Sinīvālī is that of the New Moon; and Anumati is that of the Full Moon."

According to the lexicon, "When the moon is deficient in its digits it is Anumati; when full, it is Rākā. Thus, that Anumati is the deity here, and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is the substance; this constitutes one ritual act. It is distinct from the subsequent acts to be described because of the mention of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), as this indicates a modification of the procedure. At the time of the pouring out (*nirvapaṇa*), he pours it out with the formula: "I pour thee out, acceptable to Anumati, with the impulse of the god Savitṛ. [End of] Paṭala. [This is] the *Yogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 5.

Having performed the rites up to the pouring [of the grains] with the formula, "O Anumati, protect the oblations," he recites the mantra over the flour and then pours down—that is, throws—the rice-grains behind the northern of the two water-vessels. || 13 ||
Those [clods of earth] which fall to the west of the sacrificial pin (śamyā), with them he should prepare that single-potsherd offering for Nirṛti.

In this ritual, while the rice grains intended for the *puroḍāśa* cake are being ground, a portion of the flour falls down—that is, drops below—the wooden pin (*śamyā*) placed beneath [the mortar] in order to provide a support in the western direction. That substance consisting of such fragments has *Nirṛti* as its deity; this constitutes another distinct rite, because a separate sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed for it. The grinding is performed with the approval (*anumata*) of the flour. 14.
Having placed [the fire] upon the approved [altar], he lays down the potsherds for the Nairṛta offering. || 15 ||

Having placed [the offering] for Anumati, some say that he places the single-potsherd cake for Nirṛti either silently or with the first mantra; others say he places it with the first mantra. There is a mixing [of grains] for Anumati; this one is not done silently. In another vessel... there is no silent treatment of this one. Having removed both sacrificial cakes, he holds them up. || 15 ||
Having approached, he proceeds with the Anumanam offering toward the south-west.

"By the beloved"—this is the placing of the approved [oblation]; "Thou art the sacrifice; this is the sacrifice; O Agni, for me, with four hotṛs"—this is the touching of that which has been placed. || 15 ||
With the words, "O rice-grain, svāhā! May you enjoy the oblation," he makes an offering in the Gārhapatya fire with the sruva-spoon.
The meaning is that one should offer oblations for the sake of warding off misfortune for the *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer; the deity is Gṛhapati. || 17 ||
He fumigates a single firebrand from the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.

He prescribes the carrying of the brand from the Dakṣiṇāgni fire: "They go with a single brand; for that is the eternal portion. (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.6.1). The word "yuktāḥ" ("joined") is to be supplied [to the verb]. By the word "hi" ("for"), the fact that being joined with a single brand is a reason for its being dear is indicated by another explanatory passage (arthavāda). || 18 ||

Having carried [the material] toward the south-western intermediate direction, having kindled a fire on a self-made salt-flat or in a cleft, he offers it with the formula: "May Nirṛti, being pleased, accept this; Svāhā! (Section 8). He offers the oblation to Nirṛti, entirely consumed by fire, using two stalks from a plant that sheds its parts. 19.

He designates the intermediate region between the south and the west by pointing with his finger: "They lead toward this direction; this is the direction of Nirṛti. In her own direction he causes Nirṛti to be buried" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.6.1). A *iriṇa* is a saline wasteland, and that must be naturally occurring (*svakṛta*), established by itself, not something brought from anywhere and thrown there. A *pradara* is a natural fissure in the earth. Having prepared [the site] there, he offers an oblation to Nirṛti, consuming it entirely. 19.
154. *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—Book 16:
Or [he may offer] with his two thumbs, saying, "This, O Nirṛti, is thy portion. (13.3.20)

The phrase "mumcemamaha" refers to [offering] with the two thumbs, or with the two middle fingers, or with the two index fingers—this is the meaning. Alternatively, he prescribes the offering with the two thumbs in order to set aside the oblation by means of the *juhū* ladle, which would otherwise be obtained through the force of the general rule (*codaka*). || 20 ||
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consists of a garment with its ends unseparated; it is a black garment with a black fringe.

He gives a black garment with a black fringe. He praises the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) prescribed for the principal Brāhmaṇa: "The sacrificial fee is a black garment with a black border. This is indeed the form of Nirṛti. By means of this very form, he expiates Nirṛti" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.1.1). Thus, the black color is the embodiment of the expulsion of Nirṛti, the race of Rākṣasas who are of the nature of evil. ||21||
Having sprinkled water around, they return without looking back. || 22 ||

Having silently performed the sprinkling, they return without looking toward the place of the oblation. He prescribes their return as one in which the back is not shown: "They return without looking back" (*apratīkṣam āyanti*). Having gone out and disappeared—meaning, having become invisible—their return is thus characterized. || 13 ||
"svāhā! Homage to him who has done this!"—having returned, he offers [this] in the *gārhapatya* fire. ||23||

Then, having washed his hands and feet, he returns by the same path by which he came and offers three oblations in the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "Svāhā! Homage! Whatever I have done... There is no utterance of *svāhā* for that [first] oblation, as it belongs to the previous sacrifice. || 23 ||

He proceeds with the permission [of the gods]. Those [seeds] which fall toward the north, having gone toward the water, he should dig up an ant-hill with a shell, saying, "I hereby remove the *kṣetriya* (hereditary disease) of N.N., the son of N.N. With the shell, he offers an oblation upon the ant-hill, saying, "I hereby cover the *kṣetriya* of N.N., the son of N.N. He covers it with either the shell or the ant-hill. 24.

"This is the Veda," and so forth. With the permission [of the Brahman], [the Adhvaryu] says, "O Anumati, sacrifice with Anumati. Through Anumati, may I be an eater of food; the sacrificial fee is a cow. This sacrifice, which brings rain during the Cāturmāsya, is auspicious for me; [the ritual] concludes with the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas.

Having taken those rice grains that have fallen to the north of the *śamyā* and having held them in a shell (*śukti*), he goes to the north, digs out a single horn from the mound of an anthill, touches water, and pronounces the name of the king, including his paternal lineage (*āmuṣyāyaṇa*), as "This [is for] so-and-so, the son of so-and-so," using the patronymic suffix (*āmuṣyāyaṇa*) and the father's name in the genitive case. The practical application here is as follows: "I sacrifice away this weapon of King Indravarman, the son of Indracoḷa; svāhā! With these words, he offers the oblation with the shell.

In the mound of an anthill, having taken the name [of the sacrificer] as before with the mantra using a shell (*śukti*), he places it with that very shell. Some, however, at the time of grinding, take those rice grains that have fallen to the north after being ground; having gone to water and performed the rites beginning with the pouring of water up to the placing of the shells (*śukti-upadhāna*), they then perform the placing of the potsherds (*kapāla-upadhāna*) and so forth. Thus ends section 26. [In the Paṭala: "He offers a pap (*caru*) to Āditya"—this is the last of those [verses] in the subsequent [section]. 25. This concludes the section compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī, accompanied by the *Yogacandrikā* commentary. 159.

On the following day, having performed the *agnihotra*, [he declares]: "I shall sacrifice with the *iṣṭi*," and so forth. This is like the *āditya-cala* of the *Cāturmāsya*. On the following day, beginning with the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), [there is] an offering on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu; a dwarf ox as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The acceptance [of the gift] is: "A cow for Rudra. On the following day, beginning with the resolve, [there is] an offering on eleven potsherds to Agni-Soma, with gold as the sacrificial fee. The acceptance [of the gift] is: "Gold for Agni. On the following day, beginning with the resolve as before, [there is] an offering to Indra.

An eleven-pot-sherd cake; a bull is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). A "bull" is one capable of impregnating, a castrated male. Having completed the *Āgnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice], at that very moment [one performs] the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth. Having performed the *anvādhāna* with two oblations, there is the fetching of the branch. For Indra, the portion for the gods; the procedure of the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā-tantra*); having prepared the *veda*, the making of the altar; the mixing-oblation (*sāṃnāyya-homa*) with barley-gruel (*yavāgū*). At night, the milking: for Indra, the oblation of strength; much milk for Indra and for the gods; curds for Indra; the commencement before sunrise.

At the time of setting out the vessels, there are eight potsherds; all the vessels are those used for the morning milking (*prātardoha*), except for the *anvāhāryasthālī* (the vessel for the Anvāhārya rice), which follows the model of the archetype. [The offering formula is: "I offer this portion to Agni," and so forth; however, there is no morning milking. Everything else is according to the archetype. A bull is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The modification (*ūha*) is as in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice. 25.
Having performed the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, on the following day he offers a caru-oblation to Sarasvatī and a caru-oblation to Sarasvant; a pair of cattle is the sacrificial fee. ||26||

On the following day, at the three-fold [rite], the intention (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth are as before. All the *āgrayaṇa* offerings are made from old rice (*brīhi*) and millet (*śyāmāka*), excluding the two deities Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*). There is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and one for the Viśvedevas; a cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). There is a pap of millet for Soma, and a garment is the sacrificial fee. The offering to Indra-Agni, the one to the Viśvedevas, and the one to Soma—these three together constitute a single sacrifice in the form of the *āgrayaṇa*, joined by three oblations. On the following day, there is a pap for Sarasvatī and a pap for Sarasvant; a pair of cattle is the sacrificial fee. Thus it is said.
There is one sacrifice joined with the oblation for the two deities Sarasvatī and Sarasvat; thus, the Ādityas and the others become six, they become [six]. || 26 ||
On the following day, he performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; with them, he sacrifices for a year. He does not omit the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice.

On the following day, he performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, beginning with the formal resolve: "I shall sacrifice with the Cāturmāsyas. There is neither the Pañcahotṛ nor the Ārambhaṇīyā [introductory] offering. He begins with: "I shall sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva," and so forth. Regarding these Cāturmāsya sacrifices, beginning with the Vaiśvadeva, Āpastamba clarifies that they must occur after the Ānumatī offerings have been performed: "Having sacrificed daily with these [Ānumatīs], he commences the Cāturmāsyas; he should proceed with them for a year."

Regarding these Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the place and time for the first festival, the Vaiśvadeva, have been explained by the author of the Sūtra: "One performs the Vaiśvadeva on ground sloping towards the east," and "One performs the Vaiśvadeva on the full moon day of Phālguna or Caitra. The rest is as before. One does not combine the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice. The options concerning the days and so forth until the end of the month do not apply; the rule applies specifically to every four-month period. [The following is from] the Śrautasūtra composed by Āpastamba, in the sixteenth [chapter], the fifteenth praśna.

On the full moon day of Phālguna, having sacrificed with the Śunāsīrīya [Iṣṭi], and then having sacrificed with the Paurṇamāsa [Iṣṭi] and performed the shaving of the head, he should complete the vows that are auxiliary to the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
On the following day, he sacrifices daily with the Indraturīya and the subsequent offerings.

On that very day or on the following day, there is the possibility [of performing it], according to the opinion of another Sūtra. That ritual in which Indra is indeed the fourth is called *aindraturīyama*. Its status as the fourth is relative to the form of another [deity]; however, in the actual performance, according to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), Varuṇa is the fourth. || 29 ||

Now he prescribes the oblations for the Indra-turīya sacrifice—as it is handed down in the tradition: "He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni. There are four oblations for the Indra-turīya; one should offer them in battle. (13.3.30)

The ritual procedure for the Aindraturīya offering consists of the fetching of the branch, the driving away of the calves, and the formulas as in the archetype; the framework is that of the New Moon sacrifice. At that very time, the evening milking is performed. Having performed the soaking of the rice grains with the formula "O Viṣṇu, this is your deed," there is no further driving away of the calves. In the preparation of the vessels, there are three winnowing baskets (*śūrpa*) and three bowls (*pātrī*); the rest is according to the archetype. Having placed the strainers (*pavitra*) in the winnowing baskets, he pours out the *vrīhi* rice with the formula, "I pour out what is pleasing to Agni," and the *gāvīdhuka* seeds into another basket.

[Offer] to Rudra what is pleasing; again, on another [spike], barley-grains to Varuṇa, what is pleasing. In this very manner, the ritual procedure (iṣṭitantra) continues until the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas. || 30 ||
On the night of this very same night, one should perform the sacrifice with five kinds of fuel.
On the day on which the Indra-turīya rite is performed, having offered the evening Agnihotra that night and having said, "I shall sacrifice with the Pañceṣṭi," [the ritual proceeds].

At night, they perform the rite with an oblation of *apāmārga* plants. (32) When the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, having fetched *apāmārga* plants from a water-reservoir and having ground them into flour, he fumigates a single firebrand from the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire. (33) Having carried it toward the north-western intermediate direction, he kindles it on a self-made salt-flat or in a cleft. (9th Khaṇḍa)

With the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I offer the slayer of the Rakṣas; svāhā! he offers groats of *apāmārga* with a ladle made of *parṇa* wood or *arka* wood. Or [he may say], "I offer for the vigor of Indra; svāhā! Having cast the ladle after [the offering] with the words, "The Rakṣas is slain," and having offered it with the words, "We have struck down the Rakṣas," he stands in worship. (34) A boon is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Whatever one possesses, that is the sacrificial fee. (35)

"Before the Agnihotra has been performed, they proceed with the offering of Apāmārga," so says Āpastamba. "When the twilight has set in, having fetched Apāmārga from near water while the sun is setting, the Adhvaryu alone [performs the rite]. [End of] Paṭala 3, accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 161.

Having prepared the groats, he fumigates them with a single flaming firebrand from the southern fire. Having brought it to the intermediate space between the north and west, in the middle region, he deposits it on a self-made mound or in a cleft. He offers oblations with groats of *apāmārga* using a *sruva* ladle made of *pālāśa* wood, with the mantra "Of the god thee... or "Of Indra thee..."; there is an option regarding the mantra for the oblation. With the words "Slain is the demon," he throws the residue into the fire.

Having performed the ritual worship with the mantra "We have slain the Rakṣas," one should either give away the garment that covered [the fire] at the time of the oblation, or [give it as a gift], because the author of the Sūtra has cited the phrase "the cow is the boon" (*gauḥ varaḥ*), whereby the "boon" is the cow. 32–35.

He who fears evil should sacrifice with this very Pañcedhmīya rite. He divides the Āhavanīya fire into four parts toward the cardinal directions, leaving the fifth in the middle. Having separately piled up the fuel-sticks, he offers four oblations toward each direction while walking around clockwise, reciting "The gods who dwell in the front," and a fifth oblation in the middle. Having gathered the fuel-sticks together in the middle with the verse "The Rakṣas is gathered up," he offers five subsequent oblations with clarified butter taken in five ladlings, saying, "To Agni, the slayer of Rakṣas, svāhā! A chariot drawn by five oxen is the sacrificial fee; or one drawn by four horses. || 36 ||

Having divided the *āhavanīya* fire into four parts, one should draw them out toward each direction; the middle part is the fifth. This [fifth part] belongs specifically to the *dhiṣṇiya* of the *āhavanīya*. Having made the five parts strong with fuel-sticks (*samidh*), and having taken five portions into the *juhū* ladle, one offers according to the respective characteristics in the eastern and other directions with the verse beginning "The gods who sit in the front, led by Agni," using the middle fifth portion. The deities are the gods.

Having gathered all the portions of the Āhavanīya fire together with the formula, "Gather them; protect [them]," and having kindled them with fuel-sticks, he takes another fourfold portion of clarified butter and performs the renunciation (*tyāga*) according to the respective deities: "To Agni, the slayer of Rākṣasas, svāhā! To Yama, the slayer of Rākṣasas, svāhā! To Savitṛ, the slayer of Rākṣasas, svāhā! To Varuṇa, the slayer of Rākṣasas, svāhā! To Bṛhaspati, the worshipful, the slayer of Rākṣasas, svāhā! According to the wording of the mantra: "A chariot drawn by three horses in a line (*praṣṭivāhī*), being carried by three horses as if on a three-legged stand, is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.8.7). || 36 ||
One who fears Rākṣasas or Piśācas should sacrifice with that very [offering]. And whatever he desires, that he should give. || 37 ||
The ritual procedure beginning with "yo rakṣobhyaḥ" is not connected to a formal sacrifice (yajña). The remainder is clear. || 35 ||
On the following day, one should sacrifice with the oblations for Devikā.
Having performed the morning Agnihotra, one should sacrifice with the Deśika-havis offerings.
He offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Dhātṛ, as prescribed in the sacred text. A pair of cattle is the sacrificial fee, or a young heifer. (Śatapatha Śrautasūtra, Book 13, Praśna 162, Section 39).

"Devikāhavirbhir yakṣye," and so forth. [The formula is: "I shall sacrifice with the Devikā oblations; this is the oblation... Some, having said, "I shall sacrifice with the iṣṭi," offer the iṣṭi-oblation: he prepares a cake on twelve potsherds for Dhātṛ, a pap for Anumati, a pap for Rākā, a pap for Sinīvālī, and a pap for Kuhū; a pair of cattle is the sacrificial fee. It concludes with the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas. || 39 ||
According to some, [the forms] *pravītā* and *pravīyamānā* [are used]. 13.3.40.
A cow that has recently calved or one that is pregnant. || 40 ||
With these [offerings], one who desires offspring or one who desires cattle should sacrifice. || 41 ||
By those divine weapons. || 41 ||
One who desires offspring should cause a Dhātṛ sacrifice to be performed, placing the Dhātṛ in the middle; one who is ill should perform a sacrifice with an animal, placing the Dhātṛ at the end.

When [the Soma sacrifice] is completed, there is the animal sacrifice for Dhātṛ; [one declares], "I shall sacrifice with the Paśubandha," and so forth. Some do not accept this. There is the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ offering; having moved away [from the sacrificial ground], there is the Udavasānīyā iṣṭi. The formula for the dedication is simply: "I dedicate thee, acceptable to Dhātṛ. The three subsequent oblations and the one to Agni-Sviṣṭakṛt and Varuṇa are performed on that very same day once the animal sacrifice is concluded. And the author of the Sūtras will explain that procedure later. || 42 ||
On the following day, he sacrifices daily with the Triṣaṃyukta offerings.

In the absence of an animal sacrifice, [the rites] are performed on the Devikā and the following day; or else, according to the opinion of the author of the Sūtra, all five [rites] are performed daily or fortnightly.

"One should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu"—as it is recited in the traditional text, this is the first "threefold-conjoined" rite; with that, one who desires a sacrifice should sacrifice. "One should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma"—as it is recited in the traditional text, they prescribe this as the middle "threefold-conjoined" rite for the production of heroes. "One should offer a pap to Soma and Pūṣan"—as it is recited in the traditional text, this is the last "threefold-conjoined" rite; with that, one who desires cattle should sacrifice.

"One should offer an oblation on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara; one desiring a village should sacrifice with that. 'A pap of barley to Varuṇa'—the pap for Varuṇa is to be exactly one span in every dimension. A draft horse fit for work, or one that has been broken in to pulling, is the sacrificial fee. Some authorities prescribe that the rites for Vaiśvānara and Varuṇa share the same ritual framework. (Section 10) ||44||
Thus ends the third paṭala in the thirteenth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

The ritual procedure for these sacrifices is as follows: "I shall sacrifice with the Iṣṭi," and so forth. The ritual framework (tantra) is that of the Full Moon sacrifice (Paurṇamāsa). [The offerings are: "Acceptable to Agni and Viṣṇu," "acceptable to Indra and Viṣṇu," and "acceptable to Viṣṇu. A dwarf bull is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). As before, the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and other preliminary rites are performed. [End of] Paṭala 1. [This concludes] the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 163.

The oblation: the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the Full Moon sacrifice. [Offerings] to Agni-Soma and Indra-Soma; [an offering] to Soma, acceptable to him (*juṣṭa*). The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a porridge of *śyāmāka* grain, or a tawny cow (*kapilā gauḥ*). At that very time, as before, the mixing and so forth. [Offerings] to Soma-Pūṣan, acceptable to them; to Indra-Pūṣan, acceptable to them; to Pūṣan, acceptable to him. Having poured [the portions] three times onto the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), [he says]: "Separate yourselves according to your respective shares; I pour out what is acceptable to Pūṣan; I mix it. Having placed the two (or three) porridges on the fire, he throws the portion for Pūṣan into the vessel.

A dark-complexioned cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). At that very time, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth: "I shall protect [the sacrifice] with Agni Vaiśvānara; gold pleasing to Agni Vaiśvānara is the sacrificial fee. Having resolved at that same time: "I shall perform the Varuṇa-sacrifice (*varuṇeṣṭi*); a cooking-pot (*sthālī*) measuring one span in height and breadth, pleasing to Varuṇa, is the offering; a horse is the sacrificial fee. Because it is traditionally taught in the mantra for acceptance that "the horse belongs to Varuṇa," the horse has Varuṇa as its deity; [this is done] for the sake of prosperity (*samṛddhi*). (Taittirīya Saṃhitā)

This should be seen in this context (Brāhmaṇa 1.7.2). Now, it has been stated that even when multiple rites that achieve a single result are understood to have their fruits combined, there is a repetition of the auxiliary elements due to a difference in performance caused by differences in place, time, or agent. However, in the present case, no difference of place is mentioned; only a difference in sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) is heard, as for example in the Rājasūya: "He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu; a dwarf is the fee. He offers a pap to Soma-Pūṣan; a dark-colored animal is the fee," and so forth.

In this regard, there arises the inquiry: does a difference in the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) entail a difference in the agent (*kartṛ*), and consequently, due to that difference in the performer, a repetition of the ritual procedure (*prayoga*), or not? Upon reflection, even though there is a difference in the sacrificial fee, there is no evidence for a difference in the agent. For you do not accept a difference in the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) here, since its identity will be established in the subsequent section (*Jaiminisūtra* 11.4.2). Furthermore, a difference in the agent is not pervaded by a difference in the sacrificial fee, as there is a lack of evidence [for such a necessary connection].

Furthermore, in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, even though there is a reversal of the sequence for the *anvāhārya* and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), there is no difference in the agents (performers). By the rule "there are four priests in the Darśapūrṇamāsa," a single, all-encompassing performance by the agents for the six [priests] taken together is enjoined, just as in the case of the Darśa-performance in the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa on level ground. Therefore, although there is a difference in the temporal performance, because the performance by the agents is one, there is the understanding of the unity of the agency.

In reality, however, there is no difference in the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) here either; for, just as in the case of the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice, since they are understood to constitute a single performance (*ekaprayoga*) by virtue of being means to a single result, the fee belongs to the Vāmana and Śyāma sacrifices only when combined. For this very reason, it has been stated that even though the rule "he gives one hundred and twelve [cows] every day" implies a distribution and giving on each successive day, there is nevertheless no difference in the fee therein. Consequently, although the Vāmana and Śyāma sacrifices are established as subsidiaries of their respective primary rites, because they form a single performance when combined, the fee belongs to them only in combination.

This principle is also necessary [in the following case]: when it is argued that the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifices of rice and śyāmāka grain have a common procedure (*samānatantra*) because they are performed by the same Brahmin priest, [we reply that] since the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) serves as a refinement for the agent, it follows the performance in exactly that manner; thus, its power to exclude [the other] is logical. Otherwise, the specific mention of the sacrificial fees fixed for each of those principal rites could not be reconciled in any way. Furthermore, in this case, there is no status of being a collective fee as in the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice, because the word "fee" is heard separately for each, from which their distinctness is understood.

However, in the case of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), because the word *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee) is heard for each [day] individually, their unity is the distinction [from the other cases]. Nor is there a difference in the agent (*kartṛ*) despite the existence of a difference in the sacrificial fees at the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices. [End of section] — Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, 13.164.1.

There is no difference in the agency [of the priests]. Since specific priests are enjoined individually for each sacrifice by their respective designations (samākhyā), such as "the four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in the Darśapūrṇamāsa" and "the seventeen *ṛtvij*s in the Soma sacrifice," the former statement functions merely as an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) in syntactic unity with that other injunction; consequently, it lacks the force of an injunction regarding the performance of the agents. For this very reason, the ritualists perform the formal selection (*varaṇa*) of the priests separately for both the Darśa and the Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

And thus, since a difference in performance is necessary due to the difference in the agency of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), even in the case of the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice included within the *Rājasūya*, when there is a requirement for a sacrificial fee in the performance of the *Aveṣṭi* and other rites performed by Brāhmaṇas and others for the sake of the fruit of food (*annādya*), that very fee—being understood as an auxiliary to those respective primary rites—is presented [to the mind] because it is the most proximate, provided it is possible [for it to apply].

The inclusion [of the fee] is according to the principle of the *Āgneyī* [offering], and not because the *anvāhārya* sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is sublated within the performance of the internal sacrifice; this will be explained later. Or, let it be that [the fee] exists there as well. In any case, it is established that a difference in the sacrificial fees entails a difference in the performance. Thus ends the third chapter in the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*, compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. *** **Note on Diacritics and Terminology:** * *dāgneyīnyāyena*: "by the principle of the Āgneyī [offering]" (referring to the rule where a specific detail from a primary model is extended). * *grahaṇam*: "inclusion" or "adoption. * *antaḥ-kratu-prayoge*: "within the performance of the internal sacrifice" (the main ritual body). * *bādhitāyāḥ*: "sublated" or "set aside. * *anvāhārya-dakṣiṇāyāḥ*: "of the anvāhārya sacrificial fee" (a rice mess given to the priests). * *vakṣyate*: "will be stated/explained" (future passive participle used as a verb). * *astu vā*: "or let it be," "let us grant for the sake of argument. * *tatrāpi sā*: "that [fee] also exists there. * *sarvathā*: "in every way," "in any case. * *dakṣiṇā-bhede*: "in the difference of sacrificial fees. * *prayoga-bhedaḥ*: "difference in the performance/ritual procedure. * *siddham*: "established/proven. * *iti*: "thus" (concluding particle). * *satyāpāṭha-hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra-vyākhyāyām*: "in the commentary on the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra. * *mahādeva-śāstrisaṃkalitāyām*: "compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. * *prayogacandrikāyām*: "in the Prayogacandrikā" (the title of the work). * *trayodaśa-praśne*: "in the thirteenth book/chapter (*praśna*). * *tṛtīyaḥ paṭalaḥ*: "the third section/chapter (*paṭala*). * *|| 3 ||*: "3" (section number).
13.4 Now begins the fourth chapter of the thirteenth book.
Next, the oblations to be performed daily in sequence by the *ratnins* are described. Among these, he prescribes thirteen oblations:
"On the following day, there are thirteen oblations for the *ratnins*. (1)

Those who possess jewels (*ratna*) are called *ratnin*. Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, the Mahiṣī, and others are *ratnin*s. These oblations are dear to the deities presiding over them; therefore, one should go specifically to their houses and offer them. || 1 ||
He offers [the oblation] daily in the houses of the sacrificer's kinsmen.
The meaning is that one should offer [the oblations] separately, day after day, in the houses of the Āghās, beginning with Brahmā. || 2 ||
In whichever house one performs the offering, from that very house the distribution of food and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) are to be taken. || 3 ||
Because the sacrifices are distinct, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is also distinct. || 3 ||

He offers a *caru* oblation to Bṛhaspati in the house of the Brahman priest; "a white-backed [animal] is the sacrificial fee," as it is handed down in the tradition. According to some, it is in the house of the domestic priest (*purohita*).

"ranināṃ havirbhikṣya" and so forth; following the selection (*varaṇa*) for the oblation (*havis*) of the *ranins*, there is the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
