Having separately consigned the fires (*agnisamāropa*), having gone to the house of the Brahman and the great priests (*mahartvij*), having prepared the altar for the New Moon sacrifice (*dārśikī vedī*), and having churned the fire—[this concludes] the fourth section, accompanied by the commentary *Yogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.

Having placed [the offerings] in their respective receptacles and having caused them to descend, one should bring forth for these sacrifices the materials for the pouring out (*nirvāpa*), such as clarified butter, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), and so on, as well as the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and the food for the Brāhmaṇas. [The procedure begins with: "On the full moon day, he offers a pap (*caru*) acceptable to Bṛhaspati," and so forth. A *śitipṛṣṭha* is one with a white back. In this manner, the sacrifice is to be understood everywhere. On the following day, having performed the Agnihotra, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and subsequent rites are to be carried out as before.

Having gone to the house of a Kṣatriya, [he offers] a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra; a bull is the sacrificial fee. On the following day, the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and so forth [are performed]. At the house of the chief queen—the one first married—he offers a cake for Aditi; a man is the sacrificial fee. 4.
An oblation of cooked rice for Bhaga, or for Vāta; in the house, a four-year-old female with a variegated womb is the sacrificial fee. ||5||

On the following day, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is made. A married woman (*ūḍhavā*), a female slave (*dāsī*), or a favorite concubine (*priyatamā vāvātā*) [is the officiant]. An oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) is offered to Bhaga. A cow that has lost her fetus, one whose fetus has been aborted, or a six-month-old calf is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); such is the meaning. || 5 ||
Regarding "the oblation for Nirṛti": the oblation for Nirṛti is on all sides the size of a thumb.

On the following day, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and other rites are performed. A king’s wife who has no son is a *parivṛktī*, one whose purpose is solely for enjoyment; according to some, she is one who has been abandoned by her sons and others. In her house, the oblation for Nirṛti (*nairṛta-havis*) is to be prepared. By prescribing the material as "black" (*kṛṣṇānām*), [the text] prohibits the threshing (*avaghāta*) that would otherwise be obtained through the general injunction. One should offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) made from the rice-grains of black rice (*nīvāra*) that have newly burst forth. And that *nairṛta* pap is to be exactly the size of a thumb on all sides; the meaning is that it must not be larger than that. || 6 ||
Or, [a cake] the size of a thumb-joint, he offers as a sacrifice to Nairṛta, with all [the substances] offered together.

The juncture of the *parvan* [is the time], not the characteristics of the *puroḍāśa*. Because it is enjoined by the root *hu* (to sacrifice) and because the offering is made with the utterance of *svāhā*, this is a *darvihoma*. However, Kātyāyana has stated another alternative in his Sūtra: "He offers with the mantra 'eṣa te nirṛte,' or [he offers] when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered" (Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra 15.3.14–15). A cow with broken horns (*kūṭā*) is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Regarding this, Āpastamba also says: "Some say that the sacrificial cake (*caru*) for Nirṛti is on all sides the size of a thumb-joint" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 18.10.16).

Having brought together a carpenter and a chariot-maker in one house, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni; the sacrificial fee consists of articles made entirely of iron. Having brought together a cow-slayer and a bean-thresher in one house, he offers a cake on three potsherds to Viṣṇu; the sacrificial fee is a white-spotted calf. There is a third offering, a cake on three potsherds to Viṣṇu, at the house of the carpenter and the chariot-maker; the sacrificial fee consists of articles made entirely of iron. According to some, it belongs either to the carpenter or to the chariot-maker.

On the following day, he makes the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth: "I shall sacrifice with the Vaiṣṇaveṣṭi," and so on. A *takṣan*, a *vardhaka*, or a *rathakāra*—the latter being born from a *māhiṣya* father and a *kariṇī* mother—is the one intended. It has been cited that the rite for the *rathakāra* is to be performed in the rainy season. Having gone to the house of either of these two, who share this common status, he offers a cake on three potsherds to Viṣṇu. He gives as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) vessels made entirely of iron—that is, made of all kinds of metal. 8.
Having brought together [the fires] in the house of the commander-in-chief (senānī), he offers an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni; gold is the sacrificial fee.

On the following day, having gone to the house of the Senānī (General), [one offers] a cake on eight potsherds to Indra; gold is the sacrificial fee. On the following day, beginning with the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), [one goes] to the house of the Sūta (Charioteer)—the Sūta being one born from a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother; there, [one offers] a cake on ten potsherds to Varuṇa; a *mahāniraṣṭa* (a castrated bull) is the sacrificial fee. On the following day, at the house of the Grāmaṇī (Village Headman)—so called because he leads the village—[one performs] the resolve and so forth. [One says]: "I shall sacrifice with the Māruta-iṣṭi"; [there is] a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts; a speckled white bull is the sacrificial fee.

Others say [the sacrifice] has few attendants. On the following day, the ritual intention (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth are performed as before. The *kṣattṛ*—literally "one with a staff in hand"—is the superintendent of the inner apartments, the controller of all, also known by the synonym *pratihartṛ*. Or, he may be a minister (*mantrin*). A *kṣattṛ* is one born from a Śūdra father and a Kṣatriya mother; such is his description. In his house, there is an offering to Savitṛ on twelve potsherds. One of mixed caste (*saṃkīrṇavarṇa*), who is degraded (*upadhvasta*), is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). On the following day, the ritual intention and so forth are performed. The *saṃgrahītṛ* is the chariot-yoker.

A *saṃgrahītṛ* is one who collects wealth or the superintendent of the treasury. In his house, [the sacrificer] shall sacrifice with the Āśvina-iṣṭi: a cake on two potsherds for the Aśvins; "two calves born of the same mother" means two young ones from the same womb. On the following day, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth [are performed]. [He thinks: "I shall sacrifice with the Pauṣṇa-iṣṭi. One who receives a sixth part from the subjects as his due from the king is a *bhāgadugha*. In his house, [he offers] a pap (*caru*) for Pūṣan; a dark-colored cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). || 9 ||

In the house of Akṣāvāpa, there is a *raudra* oblation of *gāvīdhuka* grain as a *caru*; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a dappled cow with a white tail-tip, or a mare with a white tail, or a rope from which a horse's mane-hair has been tied. (ŚB 13.4.10)

On the following day, the ritual intention (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth [are performed]. *Akṣāvāpa* is a gambler; in his house there is *gāvīdhuka*, produced from wild wheat (*araṇyagodhūma*). [One offers] a *raudra* oblation of *gāvīdhuka* rice-porridge (*caru*). *Śabala* means variegated in color. *Uddhāra* means having a long tail-hair (*dīrgha-śuṣka*). [The animal] belongs to the *govikarta*. The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a rope made of hair-bundles. It is known that it is a three-year-old calf (*trivatsa*), either miserable (*kṛpaṇa*), covered with hair, or variegated. It is a sword (*asi*) covered with hair, or a *vānī*—a cord woven with hair—used for driving cattle (*govyucchanī*), or a rope for tethering cattle (*dāmatṛṣā*), or a variegated young bull (*vatsatara*).

"A horse with red ears"—thus one [type of gift] is prescribed; these are the specific sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) ordained in the *Āpastamba* tradition. However, some explain it as follows: "Akṣāvāpa" is the name for a thrower of dice or a keeper of dice, that is, a gambler. "Govyucchanī" is a rope used as an aid in hunting. A "go-hiṃsaka" is a hunter. From the houses of both of these, having gathered *gavīdhuka*—wild wheat—from their dwellings, they should place an oblation (*caru*) dedicated to the deity Rudra in the house of the sacrificer. Thus they explain it. 10.
Now, he prescribes the offering of precious articles in the form of an oblation of clarified butter (ājya-homa) to be performed at the house of the messenger:

"To the path, svāhā!"—with this, he offers into the fire at the house of the Pālākalas. They call him the "messenger of falsehood. A bow encased in bamboo is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). [End of] Chapter 4. Three arrows made of leather are the sacrificial fee. [This concludes the section from] the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. Page 167.

The messenger is named *pālāgala*. Likewise, Kātyāyana employed the word "messenger" (*dūta*) in place of *pālāgala*: "May he, enjoying what is seized by the eye, [go] along the path of the clarified butter, as a messenger" (Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra 15.3.13). However, Āpastamba has explained it as referring to a specific sacrificial post (*yūpa*): "He offers in the house of the *pālāgala* with the formula, 'To the path, svāhā! (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 18.10.25), stating that they call the *pālāgala* the "messenger of falsehood."

The meaning is that the teachers say [the messenger] is one who speaks with humility like a *pālāga* tree; or, according to Āpastamba, he is one whose quivers are made of leather, containing arrows, or whose bow is bound with cane. 11, 12, 13.

He offers the final oblation for Indra in the house of the sacrificer. Some say it is offered on each successive day. He offers a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra the Good Protector (*sutrāman*), and [another] for Indra the Deliverer from Distress (*aṃhomuc*). In the benedictions of the *sūktavāka*, the Hotṛ recites: "May the King, the slayer of Vṛtra, having become king, slay Vṛtra. || 14 ||

Having established the fires at home and gone to his own house, he performs the *aindra* rite: having churned the fire and placed it in its hearth, [he thinks] "I shall sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*. It follows the procedure of the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā-tantra*). [He offers oblations] "pleasing to Indra Sutrāman," and "pleasing to Indra Amhomuc. At the *sūktavāka*, the Hotṛ recites the verse, "This king of ours... This constitutes the *hotra* performed according to the Yajurveda. However, according to another *sūtra*, after offering the *nāriṣṭha* oblations, the Adhvaryu recites "This king of ours... A bull is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); some say a gold necklace (*niṣka*) and armor (*kavaca*). 14.

From a branch of the *aśvattha* tree that has fallen of its own accord, he fashions a four-cornered vessel for Mitra. They milk a white cow with a white calf into a leather bag made from the bark of a mango tree; he carries that away himself by means of a yoke. He hangs it out to dry in the sun until it is self-coagulated. That becomes clarified butter which has solidified of its own accord.

When the rite for Indra is completed, he himself prepares from a self-fallen branch of the *aśvattha* tree one very large vessel for the *maitra* oblation; it is four-cornered and shaped like a *camasa*. They milk the cow into a skin-bag (*dṛti*) that has never been used before, or into a new skin-bag. It is a white cow yoked with a white calf. That [milk] flows through by means of its own natural death [of the calf], reaching [the vessel]. That [milk] is churned by itself and placed in the sun's heat.

"Then this clarified butter (ājya) becomes self-congealed. This has been made explicit by Āpastamba: "They milk a white cow with a white calf at the falling of the mango fruit; that [butter] he carries away while it is still in its own form; that, having been churned by itself, they place in the sun's heat. (Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, 13th Praśna).

"In that case, the clarified butter (*ājya*) becomes self-churned" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 18.11.6). When milk is poured into a vessel smeared with the juice of fruit and flowers, it turns into solid curd even without the addition of *ātañcana* (souring agent); and through contact with fruits such as the jujube (*badara*), it overflows and trickles out on all sides like buttermilk. This is what is called "self-churned. There is no cooking here in an earthen vessel; rather, it is cooked in a four-cornered bowl made of *aśvattha* wood, and not in a round one.

And that bowl must not be made from any branch whatsoever; rather, it should be prepared from one that has fallen of its own accord due to the impact of the wind. Having done this, some say [the consecration] is performed with the word "vasat. 15, 16, 17, 18.
On the full moon day of the month of Taiṣya, they commence the initiations for the Ukthya sacrifice of the consecration ceremony.

This has been made explicit by Āpastamba: "On the following day, he commences the initiations for the Abhiṣecanīya Ukthya sacrifice" (ĀpaŚrS 18.11.7). On the following day, having offered the Agnihotra and having declared, "I shall sacrifice with the Abhiṣecanīya," he undergoes the initiation. Some authorities maintain that even those who have already been chosen must be formally chosen again at this point.

In the case of the Tantric school (tantrapakṣa), however, regarding this ritual action (karman), [the procedure] ends with the worship of the deity Varuṇa; there is no formal consigning of the fires (samāropaṇa). Having offered the *saṃbhārayajus* oblations, such as "The clarified butter is the animals," and so forth, there is the serving of Soma and the use of the fruit-cup (*phalacamasaprayoga*) for fruits as well, just like the *pavitra*. He brings what is sufficient for both the *abhiṣecanīya* and the *daśapeya* sacrifices. There is no *saptahotṛ* formula, though some desire it because it serves the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*). The worship is performed with the mantra "In one's own skill" (*sve dakṣe*). || 19 ||
The initiation offering belongs to Mitra and Bṛhaspati. || 13.4.20 ||
The Maitrābārhaspatya sacrifice, which is worthy of the sacrificial fee, is concluded with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings. || 20 ||
At the time of arranging the vessels, he arranges them according to their purpose; he places the cooking pot in the place of the potsherds. (kha.11) || 21 ||

The ritual procedure (*tantra*) beginning with the adding of fuel (*anvādhāna*) for the Full Moon sacrifice is performed outside; it is not cut by the [usual] cutting of the grass. It is self-cut; one does not bring it [in]. The fuel-bundle (*idhma*) is likewise self-made. For these two, the acts of binding and so forth are performed together. The spreading of the cord (*śulba-āstaraṇa*) and so forth for the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is done in the same way for the fuel. At the time of arranging the vessels, there is a vessel for the *bārhaspatya* oblation, a wooden vessel for the *maitra*, and a wooden sword (*sphya*); these are placed in pairs as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), while the other items are arranged accordingly.

At the time of the offering, having offered the oblation for Bṛhaspati, he offers one for Mitra. Just as when the grains have been husked three times, they separate the rice-grains with the *vibhāga* mantra into those that are broken (*karṇa*) and those that are unbroken (*akarṇa*). According to some, they separate them into the smallest and the largest. Those that are broken are for Bṛhaspati in milk; those that are unbroken are for Mitra in clarified butter. [End of] Paṭala 5. [From] the *Mahādevaśāstrisakālataprayogacandrikā* commentary. 169.

When that [mixture] has been cooked, he then places the *maitra* vessel on top of it. Having placed two strainers (*pavitra*) in that [vessel], he pours in what has melted by itself. Into that clarified butter (*ājya*) containing the strainers, he throws the larger rice grains. He cooks those two [portions] together so that they become upper and lower [layers]. The cooking is merely for the sake of ritual form (*dharmamātra*); half [of the mixture] is self-heated, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is self-cut, and the fuel-stick (*idhma*) is self-made; he settles in a hollow place. That becomes the self-made altar (*vedi*).

He prepares the altar; half of it is self-made, and half he cuts from the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Half he binds together from what has been naturally fallen, and half he makes into the fuel-wood (*idhma*). Alternatively, the altar may be entirely self-made; the sacrificial grass is to be gathered, and the fuel-wood is to be collected. At the time of the ritual performance, having performed with the offering to Bṛhaspati, he performs with the offering to Mitra. Or otherwise: a white-backed animal is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the offering to Bṛhaspati; a horse is the fee for the offering to Mitra.
Or one that has calved recently; and that very white cow with a white calf is the sacrificial fee. (Khanda 12) 13.4.30.

Thus ends the fourth chapter in the thirteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*. At the time of the pouring out [of the grain], he says: "To Bṛhaspati, acceptable; to Mitra, acceptable. The division of the husked rice-grains is as follows: "May you two divide them according to their portions. He separates them—those that are cut at the ears and those not cut, those that are most inferior, the smallest, and the largest, the thickest. Having thus distinguished them and placed them separately in different vessels, he proceeds from the taking up of the fire-stirring stick (*dhṛṣṭi*) onwards; having laid down the brick for Bṛhaspati with the formula, "Thou art firm," he lays down the one for Mitra.

He pours milk from a white cow with a white calf; having heated it and purified it, he places the *caru* for Bṛhaspati upon the fire with the mantra "Thou art Dharma," meaning he puts it into a pot within the milk. When it has been slightly boiled, he covers it with a wooden vessel while reciting the mantra.

Having purified the clarified butter that has melted by itself with the *uhya* [ladle], he should pour it into the *maitra* vessel. Having brought water from one side, at that time he pours the other [substances] into it with the formula, "Dharma was. He places those two [vessels] so that one is above and the other below; having placed the *bārhaspatya* below and the *maitra* above, he winds them around with cords, smears them with clay, and thus makes one above and the other below. In this way, they both become cooked together. [With the formulas] "The inner... and "Not burning...", having set down the *bārhaspatya*, he sets down the *maitra*. [He recites: "This sacrifice... and "O Agni, mine... and the *pañcahotṛ* formula.

Thus it proceeds. This is the principal sacrifice (*pradhānayāga*). At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), having placed either a white-backed cow or a horse there, [he recites]: "Thy thousand streams flow forth; with these, [may I cross] the earth, the intermediate space, and the sky; with a white-backed cow, a brown cow, or a white calf, may I overcome death. Some desire the modification (*ūha*) by means of dual speech. — *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Book 13, Question 13.

In this view, "Brahmā" is used in the dual number, while for the others, the plural form is employed: "the white-backed cows, the white cow, and the white calf. For Rudra a cow, for Varuṇa a horse, etc.; and for either one, but not for Bṛhaspati, if there is an omission, a separate sacrifice is performed and again a white milch-cow with a white calf is given. [The ritual proceeds] from "he holds the *dhruva* ladle containing clarified butter" up to the end of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings; and from "to the north of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall" up to the conclusion of the removal of the *sanīhāra*. || 22 || 23 || 24 ||

25 || 26 || 27 || 28 || 29 || 30 || Thus ends the fourth chapter in the thirteenth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. || 4 ||
13.5 Now begins the fifth chapter of the thirteenth book.

Next, the procedure for the second Soma sacrifice, called the Abhiṣecanīya, will be described. Regarding that, he states the initiation (dīkṣā) for the Abhiṣecanīya as obtained by extension from the model sacrifice (codaka): "In the same manner they extend the initiations for the Abhiṣecanīya, so that when ten nights remain of the year, the Daśapeya shall take place. (1)

The time for this is shown in the *Kātyāyana-Śrautasūtra*: "In the fortnight of Phālgunī, on the day of sacrifice (*yajaniya*), he undergoes initiation (*dīkṣate*) for the consecration ceremony (*abhiṣecanīya*)" (KātyŚS 15.3.49). This means that the initiation for the *abhiṣecanīya* takes place on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) following the full moon of Phālguna. From that point onward, the initiation is extended so that the opening ceremony (*prāyaṇīya*) of the *abhiṣecanīya* may occur on the second day after the upcoming full moon of Phālgunī. Thus is the prolongation of the initiation.

He purchases the Soma for both the Abhiṣecanīya and the Daśapeya sacrifices. He sets aside half of the King Soma for the Abhiṣecanīya, and the other half for the Daśapeya, either with the domestic priest (purohita) or with the Brahman priest.

At the stated time, having performed the Prāyaṇīya rite, the purchase of Soma for the Abhiṣecanīya and the Daśapeya takes place together. The treading of the footprint is for both purposes; he places it among the collections, and here [he places] the half-akṣa eye-salve.

Having brought both the Soma and the fruits with ten [cows] for half [the price], the performance is as follows: having purchased the Soma, one also purchases the fruits with that same formula: "I purchase thee, O Soma, with fruits; I purchase thee with a cow. [Reciting] "Her self... or "More than this... and so on, he subsequently purchases it with five hundred cows. [He says: "Light for us! He places two tufts of wool—one for the Abhiṣecanīya and one for the Daśapeya—before the Prāgvaṃśa hall.

Having brought down [the Soma] with the formula, "The subjects are of unbroken lineage," he divides it into two halves—the Soma and the fruits—and having bound them together, he places them in the house of the Purohita for the purpose of the Daśapeya sacrifice. There is no *pravṛñjana* (the heating of the milk), because it is an *ukthya* sacrifice. There are fifteen *chadis* (roof-coverings). Everything from the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) up to the taking of the *vasatīvarī* waters should be performed as previously described. Desiring to prescribe the oblations of the *devasū*, and wishing to state that they occur immediately after the *paśupuroḍāśa* of Agni-Soma, he says: [End of Paṭala 5] [From the *Mayūkhacandrikā* commentary composed by Mahādeva Śāstrin, page 171]

Having offered the animal-cake (puroḍāśa) for Agni and Soma, he subsequently offers the oblations of the Devasū sacrifice, beginning with "To Agni Gṛhapati," as they are recited in the tradition. The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the *iḍā* portion for both the animal-cake and the oblations of the Devasū are the same.

Having offered the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) for Agni-Soma, he subsequently offers the eight oblations of the Devasū; however, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* portion are common [to all]. This is because of the Vājasaneyaka Śruti: "This is the Upavasatha. The Upavasatha is the day preceding the day of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*). Having offered the animal-cake for Agni-Soma, he should then offer the oblations of the Devasū. They are called *sūvaḥ* because they impel (*su*) and authorize; and since they are both gods (*deva*) and *sūvaḥ*, they are the Devasū. Their [offerings] are the Devasū-oblations. *O:* [End of section]

By the rule *supi* (Pāṇini 7.1.82), there is the substitution of *raṇ*. Furthermore, their status as "producers" (*prasavitṛ*) is recorded in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "The consecrations (*sava*) of the gods become heroic for the man. So many indeed are the consecrations of the gods; they themselves bestow those consecrations upon him. They consecrate him" (Lāṭyāyana Śrautasūtra 1.7.4). || 3 ||

Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, [the Adhvaryu] makes known the hand of the sacrificer with the formula, "May Savitṛ impel you for all impulses," saying, "This one, O Kurus, is your king," if he is a Kauravya; "This one, O Pañcālas, is your king," if he is indeed a Pāñcāla; "This one, O Bharatas, is your king," if he belongs to both the Kurus and Pañcālas; "This one, O people, is your king," for other kings; and "Soma is the king of us Brāhmaṇas," is what has been declared. || 4 ||

Before the *paśupuroḍāśa-sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the Brahman priest takes the hand of the sacrificer with the formula: "May Savitṛ impel you for the great sovereignty over the people. He makes it known to the local chieftains (*adhvaranibhyaḥ jānapadebhyaḥ*) with the words ending in: "This one, O Bharatas, is your king," if they are from those localities and he is their king who has performed the *Rājasūya*. [He says: "This one, O Kurus, is your king" if he is a Kauravya and is the king of the Kurus, who are the local chieftains.

"This one is your king, O Pāñcālas," [he says] to the Pāñcāla country-folk; "This one is your king, O Kurus and Pāñcālas," to the Kurus and Pāñcālas. If he is the king of both, [the formula for] the Pāñcālas is "Śabara" with either one of the two [names] added as a group (*varga*). For those other than those mentioned, Āpastamba says: "This one is your king, O Bharatas. The Brahman priest mutters: "Soma is the king of us Brāhmaṇas. || 4 ||
With two verses addressed to Varuṇa, beginning with "This sovereignty has been bestowed upon your name," the sacrificer wipes his face.
The word *ānaṭ* marks the end of the mantra. He wipes his face twice with two [verses] (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 1.7.4).
With the formula, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," he takes three strides toward the east (*viṣṇukramas*).
This has been explained in the context of approaching the chariot during the Vājapeya sacrifice. || 6 ||

When that [offering] prior to the one for Mahendra has been performed, the Pratiprasthātṛ pours out the oblation for the Maruts on twenty-one potsherds. He arranges the potsherds by means of groups (gaṇas). Having placed them in the middle with the group used as the invitatory verse (anuvākyā) for the wild animals, he prepares the curdled milk (āmikṣā) for Mitra and Varuṇa according to the procedure for āmikṣā.

The *puroḍāśa-sviṣṭakṛt* and subsequent rites [are performed]; there is an omission of the *dadhi-dharma* for the sacrificer. Having understood [the time], at the time of setting down the vessels (*pātrāsādana*), the *atigrāhya* cups are not employed. Not in the *ṣoḍaśī* vessel; having performed [the rites] prior to the *māhendra* cup, he offers the cake on twenty-one potsherds (*ekaviṃśati-kapāla*) for the Maruts. And there is the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) for the Viśvedevas. The procedure for that consists of: twenty-one potsherds, the wooden sword (*sphya*), and so forth, in pairs.

In the case where the *savanīya* offerings are to be performed first, there would be no branch (*śākhā*) for those *savanīya* offerings; otherwise, there would be a branch, as well as the fetching of the branch and so forth. At the time of placing the potsherds (*kapāla*) for the Maruts—[with the formula] "To the Maruts, the agreeable"—there are seven potsherds: *īcā*, *nyāṅva*, *etādṛṅ*, *pratiṅ*, *mitāsaḥ*, *samitāsaḥ*, and *samarāḥ*. [Then there are] seven [more]: *dhvaniḥ*, *dhvāntaḥ*, *dhvanayaḥ*, *dhvanayaḥ*, *saḥ*, *nilimpaḥ*, and *vilimpaḥ*; and [the formulas] beginning with "Thou art firm" (*dhruvamasi*), etc., [make up] seven.

Having thus placed twenty-one [bricks], there is the milking for the Vaiśvadeva offering. Having offered the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), there is the bringing of ordinary curds. [The formulas] beginning with "saṃ brahmaṇā" [are recited] as before. 7, 8, 9.

With the *vāyavya* vessels that have been consecrated, he draws the cups of water (*apām grahān*). (10) Having offered an oblation into the waters of the Sarasvatī with the formula, "O divine waters, you are the givers of dominion; grant us dominion, svāhā! he draws [the cup] with this same formula. (11) Or [he may say], "O you who are worthy of sacrifice. In the same manner, with whichever [formula] he offers the oblation, with that very one he draws [the cup]. (12) He appends the words "you are the givers of dominion; grant us dominion, svāhā" for the purpose of the oblation. He draws [the cup] with the formula, "you are the givers of dominion; grant dominion to so-and-so. (13)

Having entered [the water] either at a ford or in a pool, [he recites]: "Thou art the lord of waters" (Khaṇḍa 13). One wave falls against the current, while another follows the current; [he recites]: "Thou art the male wave. He takes that which falls against the current. [This concludes] the section on the *vṛṣasena* [offering], accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 17.

"Ye cool ones," for those that flow along the riverbeds; "ye flowing ones," for those that do not flow from a fixed place; "ye overflowing ones," for those rivers that rise up and are called floods; "ye dwelling in enclosures," for those in wells; "ye of the Maruts' vigor," for hailstones; "ye of solar luster," for those waters that fall as rain during sunshine; "ye of solar skin," for those in which forms are clearly seen; "ye gentle ones," for those standing still or those that flow slowly.

With the formula, "Ye are the Vaśās," he takes [the milk] for the Pṛṣṭhas; with "Ye are the Śakvarīs," for that which is equal to the *gorulbī*; with "Ye are the Viśvabhṛts," for the milk; with "Ye are the Janabhṛts," for the curds; with "Ye are the fiery ones of Agni," or "Ye are the most excellent and unassailable ones," for the clarified butter; and with "Ye are the essence of the waters and the plants," for the honey. He draws sixteen or seventeen [cups]. || 14 ||

Regarding the *vāyavya* vessels: because of the statement, "He takes the great [portion] of water with those *vāyavya* [vessels] produced from trees, scented, and facing upward," one takes sixteen or seventeen *vāyavya* vessels for the sake of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). This should be observed in such passages as *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 1.7.5, where the number sixteen is reached by including a single mantra from another recensional branch (*śākhāntara*). Furthermore, the fact that the sixteen mantras beginning with "ardhet" are both subordinate to the oblation (*homa*) and subordinate to the taking of the vessels (*grahaṇa*) has been established previously.

Because it is stated [in the scripture]: "He stands and offers," and "He draws [the cups] from the flowing waters" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.7.5). In that regard, the text praises the number sixteen, which resides in both [actions], by means of the passage beginning with: "He offers with sixteen [verses]; he draws [the cups] with sixteen" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.7.5), and so forth.

Alternatively, he prepares seventeen vessels made of *vāyavya* wood—or rather, of sacrificial wood as will be described—bringing them from their respective locations and taking them up. He brings water from rivers flowing with the Sarasvatī, water from the ocean, and water from whatever river a man or animal might stand upon; from that spot, he brings the water against the current, drawing it separately from each place. He brings water from wells and should diligently bring water from against the current.

Wherever water has gone, it flows back there and brings it forth. By the mere stirring of great rivers, it brings forth that river which falls into another great river. When it rains while the sun is visible, it brings forth the rainwater. It brings forth water that cannot be dried up. It brings forth any kind of liquid from anywhere: cow’s urine, milk, curd, ghee, and honey.

The taking up of the cups (graha) in sequence near the Āgnīdhra shed is now described: "You are seekers of wealth; O Goddesses, full of sweetness," and so forth, ending with "You are the givers of the kingdom; give us the kingdom, Svāhā!"—this is for the water of Sarasvatī. Since the clarified butter oblation (ājya-homa) consists of pouring over, he offers into that aforementioned water with the Vāyavya [ladle] containing clarified butter. He takes it from that water with the Vāyavya. "You are seekers of wealth... [17...]. This is the Śrauta Sūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [in the 12th Praśna].

"O Goddess, the kingdom has been given; [give] this kingdom to such-and-such"—thus he pronounces the name of the king, having grasped it with the words "given to Rājendravarman," he places it elsewhere. The subsequent [acts] are performed in the same manner. He takes [the portion] with the same [ladle] with which he offers. 10.14.
Having taken [the water] with the words, "The divine waters, full of sweetness, have been taken," he consecrates it with the mantra. || 15 ||

Or again, in a whirlpool, as in the waters of the Śoṇa or other such rivers: "Apāmpati is your lord; O Goddess of Waters, grant [this], svāhā! In water where waves battle against the current: "Vṛṣan is your lord; O Goddess of Waters... In water with waves following the current: "Vṛṣasena is your lord; O Goddess of Waters... In well-water: "Vrajakṣit is your lord; O Goddess of Waters... In water flowing against the current, or in other water: "Marutām-ojaḥ is your lord; O Goddess of Waters... In water that overflows: "Prabhāvatī is your lord; O Goddess of Waters... In a canal...

In the water of rivers, the goddesses are the Hiraṇyās; in the rainwater that falls from the sun, the goddesses are the Sūryavarcasas; in the water of mountain springs, the goddesses are the Sūryatvacas; in stagnant water, the goddesses are the Māndās; in the water of wells, the goddesses are the Vasyās; in the water of ponds, the goddesses are the Vāśās; in the water of cow-pens, the goddesses are the Śakkarīs; in milk, the goddesses are the Viśvabhūtas; in curd, the goddesses are the Janabhūtas.

The meaning is that, having taken [the substances] with the words, "O divine one, you are established in the brilliance of the clarified butter; O divine one, you are established in the essence of the waters and the plants in the honey," he should consecrate them with these mantras. || 15 ||
"O divine waters, being full of sweetness, unite with those that are full of sweetness," [saying this] he pours them together into a wooden trough made of *vetasa* wood.

With the mantra ending in "devīrāpo vananvati" [VS 1.3], he pours the cups together into a trough made of *vetasa* wood. Thus Āpastamba says: "Having poured the cups together into a *vetasa* trough with the words 'devīrāpaḥ'... (ĀpŚS 18.13.21). *Vetasa* is a particular tree born in water; a vessel resembling a *droṇakalaśa* is made from it. The meaning is that one should pour those waters taken in the *vāyavya* cups into that trough. || 16 ||
Regarding this, some authorities prescribe the recitation of consecratory formulas.
The option mentioned in another recensional text [is valid]. || 17 ||

"Sit down, you who are unassailable"—with these words, he places them between the *dhiṣṇiya* hearth of the Hotṛ and that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin. According to some teachers, he places them behind the *hotrīya* hearth.
The passage ends with "dadhatīḥ. He places [the vessels] between the *hotṛ*'s hearth (*dhiṣṇiya*) and that of the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*. 18/19.

Taking up a golden disk perforated with a hundred holes, while reciting "Thou art uncrushed," he purifies [the milk] three times with it, saying, "The bright ones I purify for you with the bright. || 13.5.20 ||

Having placed a *śatamāna* weight of gold in the vessel with the formula ending in "thou art the uncrushed, thou art the giver" (*anibhṛṣṭam asi... dātṛm asi*), [the priest] purifies [the Soma] once with that *śatamāna* using the formula beginning with "The bright ones for you, with the bright one I purify" (*śukrā vaḥ śukreṇotpunāmi*) and ending with "the wise ones" (*citānāḥ*). According to the Commentator (Bhāṣyakṛt), this is done three times; in that case, the formula is: "The bright ones for you, with the bright one I purify, Svāhā! For the Rājasūya, the wise ones; the radiant ones for you... [End of Paṭala 3]. This concludes the *Mahādevaśāstrisaṃkalita-prayogacandrikā-nyākhyā*.

With the three mantras: "I purify you with the essence for the Rājasūya, being gathered; you are immortal, by means of the immortal, svāhā! For the Rājasūya, being gathered," [he purifies them]. || 20 ||

With the verse, "These [waters] are for the sake of exhilaration, for glory, and for strength," he distributes [the water] into four vessels. (Section 14) [The vessels are] made of Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Nyagrodha wood; he places the remainder in a wooden trough (droṇa). 21.

With the mantra ending in "sadhamādo mātṛtamāsvantaḥ," he pours [the mixture] into vessels made of *pālāśa* wood and other materials. Since the mantra is not distinct for each individual vessel, it is repeated for each one. He places the remainder into the *droṇa* vessel. || 21 ||
He feeds the sacrificer with gold, an udumbara vessel, and curds. ||22||
The meaning is clear. || 22 ||

He anoints [the axle] with one hundred and one tufts of *darbha* grass; according to some, with one hundred. Having anointed the right eye with fifty and the left with fifty-one, the sacrificer puts on a garment made from the bark of three types of trees, saying, "Thou art the caul of the Kṣatra. He puts on a white turban, saying, "Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra"; they call this third one "white-pale. Having caused him to touch water, and while making the sacrificer recite the *āvida* verses beginning with "May Agni find us," he leads him out toward the outside of the *sadas*.

Having anointed himself with *darbha* stalks while reciting, "Thou art the caul of the Kṣatriya," he puts on a white garment made of silk (*tārya*) while reciting, "Thou art the womb of the Kṣatriya. A horse has three garments: two for wearing—one white and one of silk—and one as an upper garment. Alternatively, having merely placed a turban on his head, he looks at [the horse] with one hundred and eight (or simply one hundred) *darbha* stalks. He anoints the sacrificer himself with one hundred [stalks].

With fifty [verses] he [anoints] the right eye simultaneously, and with fifty-one the left; such is the alternative order. He should perform these rites in the Āgnīdhra shed. The Adhvaryu touches water, and while making the sacrificer recite the formulas beginning with "Āvidah" and "Saṃjñāna," he leads him out from within by means of the "Avinnaḥ" formula. || 23 ||
"This one, O Kurus, is your king," he announces. He follows after him with his mind; he rises up after him with his mind. || 24 ||

The mention of the king’s name is as follows: "This son of Rājendravarmā, Rājendra-colāyana, [is protected] throughout the entire kingdom," and so forth. Regarding this, there is a specific rule in the *Āpastamba-Śrautasūtra*: "With the mantra 'Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt,' he hands the bow to the sacrificer. With the mantra 'For the slaying of enemies,' he hands over the three arrows. He consecrates the bow being handed over with the mantra "Protect me from behind. While handing it over, the Adhvaryu priest mutters: "Protect me from the front, protect me from behind, protect me from above. [He is also addressed as] Mitra...

The sacrificer raises his right arm with the formula, "Thou art Varuṇa," and his left arm with [the formula], "Thou art Varuṇa" (or alternatively, the reverse). With the verse beginning, "Golden-colored ones," he addresses the two raised arms. He establishes the directions by means of five [formulas] while performing the *arthana* rite. "He places the fuel-stick... (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 14.15.2)—he follows mentally; that is to say, the Adhvaryu follows mentally, not physically. 24.
Regarding this, some prescribe a cake on twenty-one potsherds for the Maruts.

In this context, after the touching of the prepared [grains] for the offerings to the Maruts and the Viśvedevas, one should mentally recite the sequence beginning with "prior to the Mahendra [cup], the cups of water (apām grahān)" and so forth, up to the end of the mental recitation; then, prior to the Mahendra [cup], having covered [the vessels] in this [rite], one should mentally recite the sequence beginning with "the cups of water" and so forth, up to the end of the mental recitation. This continues from the pouring out of the remnants of the Āpya [libations] up to the touching of the prepared [grains]. According to the alternative view that includes the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina*), after the covering together with the *savanīya* [cakes], one should mentally recite the sequence beginning with "the cups of water" and so forth, up to the end of the mental recitation.

Then, having performed the rites pertaining to the Soma sacrifice up to the *upasthāna* (reverential salutation) for Viṣṇu; then [the rites] beginning with the proceeding to the *savana* and ending before the *Māhendra* cup; then, having performed the rites beginning with the installation of the throne (*āsandī*) and ending before the *pāhoma*; and having silently placed the *māruta* cake upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and made it rest there, he pierces the cake with the wooden sword (*sphya*) while reciting the mantra, "Not a tiger... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.2.7). Whatever adheres to the *sphya* and whatever crumbles away, that he offers as an oblation to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa, according to Āpastamba (ĀpaŚrSū 18.15.4).
For one who does not practice sorcery against others, there is no cutting or offering of the oblation. || 21 ||
"You are the splendor of Soma; may my splendor be like yours," with these words he wraps himself in a tiger skin. || 26 ||

"Having placed a throne made of Khadira or Udumbara wood in front of the *praśāstar*’s seat," so says Āpastamba. Having placed the throne, characterized as previously described, in front of the *praśāstar*’s seat, he covers it with a tiger skin, [reciting]: "Thou art the service of Soma... and ending with "...may it be for me. (26)

At the front of the Sadas, on the southern door-post, the sacrificer ascends with the formula, "May the biting serpents be driven away. He hands over water for the shaving of his hair. According to some, he hands over red-hot iron. 27.
Then, having been assisted on the right side by the door-bearer, the sacrificer ascends the throne; the rest is clear. || 27 ||
"The head of Namuci has been cast down"—with these words, he pierces lead for a eunuch; and according to some, he pierces him with that lead as a eunuch. || 28 ||
To a neuter person, one gives a leaden [image]. || 28 ||
Or, having touched water while reciting, "The head of Namuci has fallen," || 29 ||

Āpastamba clearly states regarding the field: "The sacrificer mounts it with his right foot, saying, 'May the biting serpents be crushed. He throws a eunuch's garment toward the west, saying, 'The head of Namuci is cast out,' with his left foot, and they throw a piece of red iron for the removal of hair outside the altar. There is the touching of water for both of them. (29) [End of Paṭala 5] — accompanied by the commentary *Payogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 177.

With the words, "Thou art immortality," he places a silver disk upon a tiger skin. With the words, "Shine forth; protect me," he places a gold disk with a hundred holes upon the head of the sacrificer beneath his feet. || 13.5.30 ||

He pushes [the gold] onto a black antelope skin and wraps it around [the sacrificer's feet]. Then he pushes that [gold] under the two feet. He places upon the head of the sacrificer a golden disk (*rukma*) weighing one hundred *guñjās* and having one hundred holes. Having announced this to the deities with the verses beginning "He has been released" (*asarji saḥ*) and "King Soma, Varuṇa" (*māhendro rājā varuṇaḥ*), and having offered the six preceding oblations to the Earth (*pārthāni*) with the formula "To Agni, svāhā," he offers the six preceding "encircling" (*aveṣṭi*) oblations to the elements with the formula "To the Earth, svāhā. || 31 ||

Having recited [the mantra] and consecrated [the water], he offers six *paryāya* oblations with the formula, "To Soma, svāhā! He offers the *anata* oblations with "To Bṛhaspati, svāhā! and the six *aveṣṭi* oblations for the elements with "To the Earth, svāhā! ending with "To the constellations, svāhā! While standing with his arms raised, [he is sprinkled] upon the seat. This has been stated by Āpastamba: "He consecrates him while he stands with arms raised, in response to the *stotra* of Mahendra" (ĀpaŚrSū 18.15.10).

"By the splendor of Soma, I consecrate you"—with these words, the Adhvaryu sprinkles [the sacrificer] while the oblation is being offered. With a ladle made of *parṇa* wood, the Adhvaryu sprinkles from the east; likewise the others. With one made of *udumbara* wood, the Brahman or a Kṣatriya sprinkles from the south. With one made of *aśvattha* wood, a Vaiśya sprinkles from the west. With one made of *nyagrodha* wood, he sprinkles a friend from the north. He sprinkles from above during the divine consecration.

With the mantra "Somo rājā... marutām anīkaḥ," one standing in front sprinkles [the sacrificer] from the east using a vessel made of *pālāśa* wood. With this same mantra, the *brahmā* priest sprinkles from the south using an *audumbara* vessel; a vaiśya sprinkles from the west using an *āśvattha* vessel; and a *janya* (friend) sprinkles from the north using a *naiyagrodha* vessel. The term *janya* always has the sense of a "friend" (*mitra*), meaning a companion. || 32 || 33 ||
He addresses the one being consecrated with the mantra: "Among the Kṣatriyas, you are the lord of the Kṣatriyas. || 34 ||
The word "adhvaryu" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 34 ||

With that same black antelope horn, the Adhvaryu unties the garments; he discards them on the *utkara* heap with the formula, "Protect [us] beyond heaven. At this time, the procedure must be performed so that the response (*pratigara*) to the recitation (*śastra*) may be reached. The Adhvaryu wipes away with vessels the drops of water that remain on the limbs of the one being consecrated; "whichever person consecrates," says the author of the Bhāṣya. (39)
Having offered the six subsequent offerings pertaining to the earth with "Svāhā to Indra," he offers the six subsequent *aveṣṭi* oblations to the beings with "Svāhā to the Waters. || 36 ||

He offers the *pārtha* oblations and the *aveṣṭi* oblations with the response (*pratigara*). There are six *pārtha* oblations with "To Indra, svāhā! and six *aveṣṭi* oblations for the elements with "To the waters, svāhā! Then follows the response, ending with "The hymn has been spoken. (39)

With the mantra, "O Rudra, that supreme name of yours which is called Krayin," he goes northward to where the remnant in the wooden trough remains and offers it in the Āgnīdhra fire. (Section 16) || 37 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the thirteenth book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.

In this context, the word *svāhā* is supplied [from another passage]. For it is stated in the Śruti: "When he cuts off [the portion] for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, he thereby satisfies him with his own share"; thus, Rudra has the status of a recipient of the remnants (*uccheṣaṇa*). Regarding that very point, [the text] prescribes a specific detail: "He goes out toward the north and offers in the Āgnīdhra fire. This indeed is the direction of Rudra; in his own direction he propitiates Rudra" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.7.8). In this case, one should offer a single oblation.

If one should desire for a brother-in-law (*bhrātṛvya*) that "the kingdom and the subjects shall belong to him," then, having begun the rite with the *pratihita* [fuel-stick] in his *aupāsana* fire, he should offer two *vyatiṣaṅga-homas* from the remnants of the ointments that have been smeared upon the vessels. He offers them with the mantra: "O Prajāpati, let these not be his! He interchanges the names, saying, "This one is the son of so-and-so; this one is the son of so-and-so. According to some, he interchanges the names themselves. This is the specific rule in the *Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* (18.16.19). 37.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the thirteenth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*, compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.
13.6 Now begins the sixth chapter in the thirteenth book.
Now the chariot is addressed with the Vijaya mantra:
"Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra"; with these words, he brings down the chariot. || 1 ||
This has been explained in the section on the Vājapeya sacrifice.
With the formula, "By the command of Mitra and Varuṇa, the directors, I yoke you," he yokes the chariot drawn by side-by-side horses.

In this [work], the *Mayūkhacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin, page 179, ending with the words "by the yoga of the sacrifice": he yokes a chariot provided with three horses, one for each side. He praises such a chariot in another manner: "There are three horses; the chariot is the fourth; there are two charioteers on the left [and right]; thus six are completed" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 1.7.9). The term *savyeṣṭha* should be understood as meaning "standing on the right. Thus, there are two charioteers situated on both sides. 2.
With the words, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," he mounts the chariot. || 3 ||
He goes to the vicinity of the chariot; the sacrificer mounts the chariot, as do the charioteer and the attendants. || 1 ||
"May I be victorious by the impulse of the Maruts," he says as he sets out. || 4 ||
He proceeds. || 4 ||
With the verse beginning "pra sasāhiṣe," the Brahman priest follows from the south with a Triṣṭubh.
To the right, Brahmā goes. ||5||
According to some, the Pratiprasthātṛ should touch [the sacrificer] from behind.
"Anvārambha" means touching. The consecrated prince touches the chariot from behind. || 6 ||
A kṣatriya with his bow stands positioned to the east or to the north; he conquers him [with the mantra]: "I conquer the mind, which has reached its goal, along with the sense-organ. || 8 ||

"O King, you stand before me or to my left at a distance of one arrow-shot. Having conquered him, this [arrow] is released and brought back with the mantra: 'The mind has been fully subdued by the great sense-organ. || 7 || 8 ||
Therefore, he shoots these arrows [with the formulas]: "I shoot against you," "The mind has reached you," and "I have united with the sense-organ"; then he turns clockwise. || 9 ||

He should throw these [arrows] at that nobleman who stands at the distance of an arrow’s length, saying: "The mind has reached [its mark]. There is a repetition of the mantra for each arrow. Saying, "Together indeed with Vāyu," he turns clockwise. || 9 ||

"This thunderbolt is the best winner of booty; with it may those two sons go to the winning of booty"—with these words, he hands the bow to his wife. According to some, he hands her the tip of the bow. According to some, the wife wipes away the tip of the bow. According to some, she touches the horses. (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 13.6.10)
He gives [the portions] to his wife; other alternatives are found in other recensions. || 10 ||

"Such is his life; grant me that life," with these words the sacrificer fastens on a silver amulet. "Thou art vigor," [with these words] an amulet of udumbara wood. "Thou art a yoke," [with these words] a golden amulet. 11.

The mention of the "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is for the purpose of excluding other substitutes. He fastens gems made of silver, copper, and gold. However, according to the author of the *Bhāṣya*, there is a repetition of the mantra in the case of separate [gems]. 11. And [according to] Śāṇḍilyāyana’s *Śrautasūtra*: "Some recite that there is a golden [gem] in the middle. 12.
The meaning is clear. || 12 ||
With the words, "Thou art Mitra," he lowers his right arm; with the words, "Thou art Varuṇa," his left. Or rather, it may be the reverse.
With the words, "Thou art Mitra; thou art Varuṇa," the sacrificer lowers his right and left arms respectively.

With the verse, "Together with all the gods," he lowers his hands over the *āmikṣā* intended for the Viśvedevas; at this point, he gives these two pieces of gold, one of gold and one of silver, as well as a gem.
While mentally measuring the two hands, right and left, over the *āmikṣā* curd for the Viśvedevas, he lowers them. 17.

"Obeisance to the mother Earth," saying this, he looks down at the earth while descending. "Thou art the fury of cattle; may this fury of thine be mine," saying this, he descends upon a boar-skin shoe. (Khaṇḍa 17) || 15 ||
The inspection of the earth is for the sake of the subsequent ritual act. He descends [from the chariot] wearing sandals made of boar-skin and so forth. || 15 ||
With two verses addressed to Varuṇa, beginning with "prati tyannāma rājyam adhāyi," he wipes his face. || 16 ||
For the purpose of purifying the sacrificer. || 16 ||

In front of the Āgnīdhra shed, they construct a measured mound (khara) four cubits wide. To the south, as a preliminary rite, he establishes a stool made of Khadira wood upon it with the formula, "Thou art the navel of the Kṣatra. With the formula, "Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra," he spreads a garment of fine hair over it. || 17 ||

To the east of the Āgnīdhra shed, they construct a four-cornered structure with four openings—some say it has four drains—at another location. They measure out a *khara* (elevated mound) and establish a *harmya* (palatial chamber); this is the meaning. To the south, for the purpose of ritual movement, [they prepare] what is called "the navel of the Kṣatra. Having established upon it a throne (*āsandī*) according to the previously described characteristics, he spreads out—a term meaning he extends—a skin-cloth (*carma-paṭa*) over that throne, which is called "the womb of the Kṣatra," while reciting the *kṛttyadhīvāsa* formula. ||17||
He girds it with the formula, "O earth, do thou strengthen me"; he girds it. || 18 ||
He fastens it; he ties it to the legs of the throne. || 14 ||
With the words, "Thou art pleasant," he sits down. || 19 ||
The sacrificer. || 19 ||
He addresses him as he sits down: "Sit on what is pleasant; sit on what is well-seated. (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 13.6.20)

[The section] on the mounting [of the chariot] with the mantra "May it not harm you" is concluded. [End of Chapter 20]. This is accompanied by the *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. [Chapter] 1.21.
He sits down. || 21 ||
He addresses the one who is mounting [the chariot]: "May it not harm you; may you not harm me. || 22 ||
The [section on] "gone" is concluded. || 22 ||
"He sat down, firm in his vows"—with these words, he mutters [the mantra] while seated. || 23 ||
The Adhvaryu addresses him as he is seated. || 13 ||

Having offered the oblations for unyoking the chariot into the Gārhapatya fire with the *sruva* ladon, using the formula "To Agni Gṛhapati, svāhā!", he places the chariot upon the chariot-stand together with the charioteer, reciting the verse "The swan dwelling in purity... (RV 4.40.5).

With the four [formulas], "To Agni Gṛhapati, svāhā! and ending with "To the strength of the Maruts, svāhā!", he offers the *sthavimīya* oblation. With the mantra "The swan dwelling in the pure place," the charioteer (*saṃgrahītṛ*) properly takes hold of the horse's bridle and stops the chariot drawn by a single side-horse (*praṣṭivāhin*). According to some, up to this point the sacrificer should remain with his arms raised.

When the fire has been established, the *saṃgrahītṛ* descends; the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the king, who is not possessed of horses or jewels, sit around him. When they have all sat down, the *brahmán* addresses the *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*): "O King, you are the *brahmán*, you are Savitṛ of true impulsion. He replies: "So be it. In this same manner, he addresses the *hotṛ*, the *brahmán*, or the *udgātṛ*. Each replies with the respective subsequent mantra. || 25 ||

The previously mentioned officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the chanters (*adhvaryu* and others), and the jewel-bearers (*ratnin*) sit around the king. The *adhvaryu* sits in front; the *brahman* to the south; the *hotṛ* behind; and the *udgātṛ* to the north. There is no fixed rule regarding the other jewel-bearers. When they have all taken their seats, the sacrificer addresses the *adhvaryu* and the *brahman*. The *brahman* replies: "O King, you are the *brahman*; you are Savitṛ of true impulse."

In this manner, he addresses Brahmā, saying, "O Brahmā"; Brahmā replies, "You are the royal Brahmā, you are Indra of true might. Likewise, he addresses the Hotṛ, saying, "You are Mitra"; he addresses the Udgātṛ, saying, "You are Varuṇa. || 25 ||

With the formula, "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra," the Brahman priest hands over the wooden sword (sphya) to the King; according to some, it is the Adhvaryu who hands it over. ||26||
They meditate. Brahmā hands over the wooden sword (sphyam) made of natural wood to the King. || 26 ||

"Thou art this thunderbolt, the best winner of booty. (Khaṇḍa 18) With this [formula], the king says to the domestic priest (*purohita*), the domestic priest to his deputy (*pratihita*), and the deputy to the jewel-bearers (*ratnin*); they hand it down from one to the next in succession until finally they give it to the keeper of the dice (*akṣāvāpa*). [Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram, 33rd Praśna, Section 27]: The king [gives it] to the domestic priest; the domestic priest to his deputy; the deputy to the jewel-bearers—there being no fixed rule regarding the names of the jewel-bearers—and finally he gives it to the keeper of the dice. 27. 145.

With that wooden sword (*sphya*), having dug up the gaming-ground (*adhidevana*), he pours out either three fifties or five fifties of dice. (28) With the words, "The king has won," he then casts four dice; having thus staked four hundred, they play with a four-year-old cow (*ṣaṣṭhauhī*). (29) Having won the rice placed upon the leaf by means of a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, [the priest] gives five dice to the sacrificer with the words, "This king has come to the quarters. (13.6.30)

With that [measure], he should pour out the dice upon the *adhidevana*, the gambling place—that is, within that pavilion. Having leveled it, he should cast the dice. The dice are made of the same material (*sāvarṇa*), of indeterminate size, and exceed one hundred in number. Among them, four are of the measure of a *niṣka*. Those exceeding that [standard] measure are designated as "inferior" (*avara*); they are square, triangular, crescent-shaped, bow-shaped, and circular. Brāhmaṇas and others engaged in the game of dice, having placed the *ṣaṣṭīhī* aside as not being for sale...

"Of my ears, of my horn, of my hoof, of my tail"—having thus resolved in their minds without causing injury, they engage in gambling (*videvana*), meaning they play for stakes. "They speak of boiled rice (*odana*)," as in the case of the *Āgnīdhra* ritual. With that... [resolved] stake, they prepare the sixth oblation of rice; this is the meaning. Such is the manner of gambling: having won the four classes of Brahmins by staking the rice, the King subsequently takes possession of them. The Brahmin takes four squares.

A Kṣatriya [wins] from a triangle; a Vaiśya from a bow-shaped [figure]; a Śūdra from a circular figure. Having thus taken them, he takes several dice of indefinite size and casts them down. He should divide them four by four. Even when they are not yet divided, there are still four [groups]. "The King has come toward the quarters"—this means that he presents the remaining dice to the King. || 28 || 29 || 30 ||

Having dismissed them as well, he calls those with auspicious names: "O you of good fame! for the charioteer; "O you of good fortune! for the distributor of portions; and "O you whose reign is truth! for the attendant. Having called them, he gives the field to the Brahman. Whatever the Brahman desires, they are witnesses to that.

Then the king, whose name is auspicious (*maṅgalyanāman*), calls the men about to be mentioned, beginning with the *suślokas*, and having had the *kṣattṛ* call them, he gives a four-footed field (*catuṣpākṣetra*) to the Brahman. Those named auspiciously (*maṅgalyanāmānaḥ*) act as witnesses (*upadraṣṭāraḥ*) to the field being given; "four-footed" means that which has four feet. Alternatively, he gives the field to the Brahman together with four oxen. 39 || 32 ||

For whichever wife he may desire, "May her offspring possess the kingdom," having caused her to take hold of the fire-wood placed upon the *aupāsana* fire, he performs two *vyatiṣañjanīya* oblations with the remnants clinging to the vessels, using the verse: "O Prajāpati, these [people] are not thine... (RV X.121.10). He interchanges the two names in this manner: "So-and-so, son of So-and-so, grandson of So-and-so. [End of] Paṭala 6. [From the commentary: It is understood that the word *māna*, meaning "measure," is used in common parlance for the *guñjā* seed and similar units. [End of] Paṭala 6. [From the commentary: This is accompanied by the *Paryoga-candrikā* exposition compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 183. He interchanges the two names in this manner: "So-and-so, son of So-and-so, grandson of So-and-so. (Sūtras 33–34)

If one should desire that a son be born to a certain queen, then—whether the domestic fire (*aupāsana*) has been extinguished or kindled—one should have that appointed son take hold of her. Having taken a *lepāñjahvā* ladle placed in a vessel made of *pālāśa* wood or similar material, and having recited the verse, "O Prajāpati, these [worlds] are not yours," he should offer the oblation, saying: "Rājendravarmā, the son of Rājendravarmā, the grandson of Aditidā, the son of Rājendracola (or Rājendracolavarman), *svāhā*. Thus is the second oblation.

Then he interchanges the two names, having uttered the formula ending with "O Prajāpati, may that be ours," [adding] "May we, O Rājendravarman, son of Rājendracolavarman, be lords of riches, Svāhā! This is the first [offering]. Likewise for the second, having uttered the formula ending with "may that be ours," [he says]: "O Aditi, may we, O Rājendravarman, son of Aditi, be lords of riches, Svāhā! Thus [ends sections 33 and 34].
He causes the Śaunaḥśepa narrative to be recited, consisting of Ṛgvedic verses interspersed with Gāthās, numbering more than a hundred or more than a thousand. (Section 19) 35.

"The *śaunaḥśepa* [hymn] is that which was seen by Śunaḥśepa; one should have the Adhvaryu or the Hotṛ recite it. By means of it, he releases him from the noose of Varuṇa" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 1.7.10). This is the Brāhmaṇa. Therein, it prescribes the number of verses: "It consists of more than a hundred" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 1.7.10). "More than a hundred" (*paraḥśatam*) means exceeding a hundred. And the number of verses has been clarified by Āpastamba: "One should cause the story of Śunaḥśepa to be narrated, consisting of more than a hundred verses interspersed with *gāthās*, or even more" (*Āpastamba Śrautasūtra* 18.19.30). || 35 ||
Seated upon Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Hotṛ priest recites the invitatory verses.
The meaning is clear. || 36 ||
Standing between the two golden tufts, the Adhvaryu responds: "Om" is the response for a Ṛc verse, and likewise "Tathā" for a Gāthā.

At the time of the recitation of the Śaunāśepa narrative, the officiant (Yajamāna) should remain silent; he responds "Oṃ" to the Ṛg-verses and "So be it" to the Gāthās. Seated upon a golden cushion, the Hotṛ recites the Śastra; standing upon two golden mats, the Adhvaryu responds. || 37 ||
When the Śaunaḥśepa [recitation] has concluded, he gives a piece of gold to the Hotṛ; two tufts of gold-wool to the Adhvaryu.

When the Śaunaḥśepa [section] has been concluded and the recitation of the *śastra* is finished, the sacrificer gives a golden vessel (*hiraṇyakaśipu*) to the Hotṛ, a golden mat (*hiraṇyakūrca*) to the Adhvaryu, and two garments for the consecration (*abhiṣecanīya*) to the Udgātṛ. || 38 ||

In this rite, one should proceed with a cake on twenty-one potsherds for Vāyu and curdled milk (āmikṣā) for the Viśve Devas. [With the verse: "Embracing the tiger, they send forth the lion for great good fortune; they groom the leopard standing like a well-offered oblation in the waters. While about to cut the sacrificial cake, if one is performing a malevolent rite, one should split it through the middle with the wooden sword (sphya). Whatever part of the cake adheres to the wooden sword or falls away from it, one should offer that to Viṣṇu Urukrama.

Having entered the *havidhāna* shed, there is the performance of the offerings for the Maruts and the Viśvedevas; one should split the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) with the wooden sword (*sphya*), and so forth. ||39||
In this case, he gives these two pieces of gold: one of gold and one of silver, as well as a gem, provided that they were given previously. 13.6.40.

When the *puroḍāśa* has been cut for the *medana*, there is no *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; however, the procedure from the *sviṣṭakṛt* up to the wiping (*mārjana*) is the same. He gives gold—both golden and silver—and a gem to the *brahman*. If he should cut [the portions] beforehand, then [this applies]. || 10 ||
He undertakes the rites beginning with those dedicated to Mahendra. || 41 ||
The ritual procedure beginning with the offering to Mahendra is constant; the offerings of the *atigrāhya* cups are as before. 41.

Having emerged from the *avabhṛtha* bath, he offers an oblation into the water with the formula: "To the grandson of the waters, svāhā! (42). The procedure for the *kalaśa* and *amasa* vessels, as well as the ritual acts associated with secondary results (*guṇaphala*), proceed [as before]. It is the same up to the *avabhṛtha*. Following the *avabhṛtha*, the rite ending with the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) is performed; then, having emerged from the bath, there is the oblation with the formula: "To the grandson of the waters, svāhā! [He also performs] the rite with the *pavitra* [formula]: "That which is thy breath... (42).
"Omnisvāhā to the Son of Strength!"—thus [he offers] upon a dry tree stump or a clump of darbha grass.

The term "juhoti" (he offers) is understood to carry over. [This applies] to an offering made in the interval between the place of the *avabhṛtha* rite and the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), or [an offering] upon a clump of *darbha* grass and so forth. || 4 ||
Having returned, he offers [the oblation] in the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "To Agni Gṛhapati, svāhā! (44).
Having reached the dwelling place, having performed the ritual attendance with the words, "I have followed the waters," he offers oblations into the Gārhapatya fire with the words, "To the fires. 44.

He immolates the barren cow for Indra as the Anūbandhyā victim. For her, he offers a cake on four potsherds made of wild rice (*naivāra*) from the slaughter-ground of the four-footed animal. There is a substitution with a cart. The Abhiṣecanīya sacrifice is concluded. (Section 20)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the thirteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.

The *udavasānīyā* and subsequent rites: one sacrifices an animal dedicated to Indra, a barren cow (*anaḍvāhī*) born from a mare (*sūta-vaśā*). [The offering is made] for Indra with the omentum of the cow, the fat, and so forth. At that [offering], the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) of the sacrificial cake for the animal (*paśupuroḍāśa*) is performed from wild rice (*nīvāra*). (Having thus poured out the sacrificial cake for the animal... [End of section 6]. This concludes the eighteenth [chapter] of the *Payogacandrikā*, a commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.

He offers the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) made of wild rice (nīvāra) from the carcass of a four-footed animal—that is, from the body of a four-footed beast whose meat has been cut for the purpose of sale. From that carcass, he performs the pouring out (nirvāpa) of the animal-cake from the wild rice. Having thus offered the animal-cake, he proceeds with the pouring out and other rites for the eight Devasū oblations of the King [Soma]. The remainder is as before. In this manner, the Abhiṣecanīya sacrifice is completed. 48.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the thirteenth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Sātvāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.
Now begins the seventh chapter in the thirteenth book.
Next, the oblations of the *saṃsṛp* sacrifices, numbering ten, are prescribed:

On the following day, he performs the sacrifices with the seven *saṃsṛp* oblations daily, offering a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, as prescribed in the ritual texts. He settles at each sacrificial ground one after another. Where the *āhavanīya* fire was previously located, there the *gārhapatya* fire of the subsequent sacrifice is established; for the seventh sacrifice, the *āhavanīya* is in the *prāgvaṃśa* hall and the *gārhapatya* is outside.

They are called *saṃsarpas* because they are properly glided toward (*sam-sṛpyante*) or reached by the deities such as Vīryavān and Ambirasa; these are the deities, and their sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) bear that same name. He praises these oblations [as follows]: "The tenfold sensory power and vigor of Varuṇa, the well-shouting one, flew away. That glided along in pursuit (*anusamasarat*). Because it glided along (*sasṛpa*), it is called *sasṛp*. By means of the god Agni, on the first day, he set it in motion again" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.1.1), and so forth.

On the first day, that Varuṇa offered a cake on eight potsherds (aṣṭākapāla) together with Agni, the radiant deity; that is to say, he prepared an oblation for Agni on eight potsherds. On the second day, he offered a pap (caru) together with Vāyu, the impeller. On the third day, he offered [a cake] on twelve potsherds together with Savitṛ, the cause of impulsion. On the fourth day, he offered a pap together with Pūṣan, who is characterized by cattle. On the fifth day, he offered a pap together with Bṛhaspati, who presides over the Brāhmaṇas.

In the sixth [day], he offered a cake on eleven potsherds together with Indra, whose nature is luminosity. In the seventh, he offered a cake on ten potsherds together with Varuṇa, who existed in a past kalpa in the form of his own deity. In the eighth, he offered a mixture together with Soma, the King and sacrificer. In the ninth, he offered a cake on eight potsherds together with Tvaṣṭṛ, who possesses beautiful forms. In the tenth, having offered a cake on three potsherds together with Viṣṇu in the form of the sacrifice, he attained that sensory power (*indriya*).

If the *saṃsṛp* sacrifices were also to belong to the sacrificer, then the meaning of the Brāhmaṇa passage would be that this sacrificer attains sensory power (*indriyasāmarthya*). From this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), one should infer an injunction for the performance of the *saṃsṛps* on separate days for those [sacrifices] already prescribed by originative injunctions (*utpattivihita*). Behind the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) of the upcoming *daśapeya*, following the oblations of the *saṃsṛps*, the location of the *āhavanīya* fire for the final sacrifice is the *daśapeya*. In such a way that it may be at the place of the *gārhapatya* fire in the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, it should be situated behind.
Or seven. [End of] Book 13 of the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha. Section 186. Questions.

The altar should be completely filled. Having performed the *agnihotra* and made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), "I shall sacrifice with the *saṃsṛp* oblations," he offers the *saṃsṛp* oblation for all [the deities]. For all [of these], there is a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) for Agni; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is gold. The location of the *gārhapatya* fire is to the north of the location of the *āhavanīya* fire for the offering to Agni. On the following day, there is a cooked rice offering (*caru*) for Sarasvatī; a heifer (*vatsatarī*) is the sacrificial fee. On the next day, there is a cake on twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*) for Savitṛ; a speckled ox (*upadhvasta*) is the sacrificial fee. The ritual arrangement (*vihāra*) is as before.

On the following day, there is an oblation of cooked rice (caru) for Pūṣan; a dark-colored animal is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). On the following day, there is an oblation of cooked rice for Bṛhaspati; a white-backed animal is the sacrificial fee. On the following day, there is an oblation on eleven potsherds for Indra; a bull is the sacrificial fee. There is an oblation on ten potsherds for Varuṇa; a large castrated bull (mahāniraṣṭa) is the sacrificial fee. For all these offerings, the Āhavanīya fire is used for the first and the Gārhapatya fire for the latter.

The procedure for this has been clarified by Āpastamba: "On the following day, with ten or seven *saṃsṛp* oblations, he proceeds toward the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) of the Soma sacrifice, beginning with the cake on eight potsherds for Agni; thus he settles at each successive sacrificial ground. Where the previous *āhavanīya* fire was, that becomes the subsequent *gārhapatya*. At the last [ground], the *āhavanīya* is to the east of the *yaśas* altar, and the *gārhapatya* is outside" (ĀpaŚrSū 18.10.9). || 1 ||
Now, he states a certain specific time for the eighth, ninth, and tenth oblations on their respective days.

Then he performs that sacrifice. When it has been completed, in the afternoon he undergoes initiation for the Daśapeya. (3) In place of the [usual] initiation water, the sacrificer puts on a golden garland with six or twelve lotuses. (4) On that day, having been initiated, he purchases the King (Soma) for ten castrated young bulls. (5) He does not bargain, nor does he carry [the Soma] around. (6) He performs a second purchase [of Soma]. (7) Prior to the Upasads, he offers a pap of cooked rice to Soma; between them, one to Tvaṣṭṛ; and after them, one to Viṣṇu. (8)

After the *abhiṣecanīya* Soma sacrifice, the *daśapeya* Soma sacrifice is to be performed. On its seventh day, which is connected to the *saṃsṛp* offerings, one *dīkṣā* (initiation) is to be observed. Following that, the three *upasad* days are to be performed. Among these, on the first *upasad* day, prior to the *upasad* sacrifice, one should proceed with the eighth oblation called the *saumya saṃsṛp*. On the middle *upasad* day, between the morning and afternoon *upasad* rites, one should proceed with the ninth oblation dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ.

On the third *upasat* day, having performed the afternoon *upasat*, one should subsequently proceed with the tenth oblation dedicated to Viṣṇu. Within the ritual framework (*tantra*) of the *Daśapeya*, Āpastamba has clarified the performance of the three oblations; beginning with the statement, "In the afternoon, he commences the framework of the *Daśapeya*," it is recited as follows: "There is one initiation (*dīkṣā*). There are three *upasads*. Prior to the *upasads*, he offers the *saumya* portion."

"Between [the Saumya], however, there is an offering to Tvaṣṭṛ on eight potsherds; after it, one to Viṣṇu on three potsherds" (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 18.20.19). Now, in the Rājasūya, ten oblations denoted by the word *saṃsṛp* are prescribed, beginning with the offering to Agni on eight potsherds. Among these, the eighth, ninth, and tenth are those dedicated to Soma, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu. With reference to these, this statement is recited: "Before the Upasads, he proceeds with the Saumya; between them, with the Tvaṣṭra; after them, with the Vaiṣṇava" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.8.1).
