187. This is the *Mayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.

Regarding this Soma-sacrifice within the Rājasūya, the performance of the three [offerings] beginning with the Saumya at the beginning, middle, and end of the Upasads prescribed therein is enjoined by this sentence. When it is argued that, based on this sentence, the Saumya and others are subordinate parts (*aṅga*) of the Upasads, we reply: because the genitive case in the word "of the Upasads" (*upasadām*) is construed with the word "before" (*purastāt*), which denotes time, this sentence is intended to establish a specific temporal relationship for the Saumya and others, and not to establish a relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).

Therefore, one does not perform the *saumya* and other offerings, nor the selection of the principal priests such as the *anumantrayitṛ*. The *Āgneya-paddhati* states: "Having performed the *vāruṇa* sacrifice, on that very day, on the afternoon of the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*), one intends to sacrifice with the *daśapeya*, and so forth. On the first *upasat* day, according to the view that there is a distinction in the selection of priests, one chooses the *bhārgava* as the *hotṛ* on this occasion; neither the *saptahotṛ* nor the serving of Soma is performed.

Having performed the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering and having undergone the shaving of the hair, he performs the bathing and other rites with the mantra "apo asmān" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 1.2.1). At the end of the section beginning with "apo'bhātī" (*ibid.*), instead of that [usual] place, he puts on a garland of twelve lotuses. He fastens a wreath of twelve lotuses upon his body, and not with a mantra, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the text "na maṇiḥ". Then, having divided into three parts the dust collected during the carrying away of the remains (*sanīhāra-prasthāpana*)—starting from the formula "athāsmai saumyamahatam" (*ibid.*)—he deposits it in those [three] houses. The portion starting with "deva sūrya" (*ibid.*) and ending with "prajābhyastvā" (*ibid.*) is omitted.

Having first purchased [the Soma], brought the Soma-fruits from the house of the domestic priest (*purohita*), and performed everything up to the end of the "delaying" (*vilaṃsana*)—beginning with "having grasped them with a linen cloth" (*kṣomeṇa vāsasopasaṃgṛhya*)—he gives them to the Soma-seller. Then, he silently gives the *vatsanarī* [garment]. The formulas beginning with "In us be light" (*asme jyotiḥ*) and "Thou art self-born" (*svajā asi*) are recited; however, the [verses] beginning with "The radiant one" (*svāna bhrājaḥ*) are not. The silent giving of the turban (*uṣṇīṣa*) and the staff (*daṇḍa*) to the Maitrāvaruṇa is performed; the portion beginning with "O Mitra, come hither" (*mitro na ehi*) and ending with "whose path is unbroken" (*acchidrapannaḥ*) is omitted.

In the forests, one should perform the binding of the turban with the mantra "vyantarikṣām. Having placed the Soma-vessel somewhere near the *prāgvaṃśa* hall with his hand, he proceeds with the *ātithya* (guest-offering). Having completed the *ātithya* up to the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), the Pratiprasthātṛ first enters with the mantra "urvantarikṣam" and so forth; having performed the *ātithya*, at the conclusion of the pouring of the *madantī* waters, the ritual action for the Soma begins with the placing [of the vessel] upon the spread-out mat.

For the Upasad rites, there is a *prastara* and sacrificial grass (*barhis*), as well as enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) for Soma; a *caru* of millet (*śyāmāka*) is offered, and a brownish-brown animal is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Having performed the morning *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, he performs the afternoon *pravargya* and *upasad* rites on that very same day and then concludes. On the thirteenth day, having performed the morning rites on the following day, at the conclusion of the *Subrahmaṇyā* litany, he offers a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Tvaṣṭṛ; a white-spotted ox is the sacrificial fee. Then follows the offering to the sacrificial post (*yūpāhuti*) and so forth.

Then, when the fourteenth day has dawned, having performed the morning rites and immediately thereafter having performed the afternoon rites, he offers a cake on three potsherds to Viṣṇu; a dwarf (vāmana) is the sacrificial fee. According to the author of the Bhāṣya, this very sacrifice concludes with the feeding of Brāhmaṇas, while others hold that it ends with the Ājyeḍā offering.
For these [fires], the Upasad rites and the enclosing sticks (paridhis) accomplish the purpose externally.

The *aupasadam* ritual procedure for those sacrifices constitutes their external framework; because it possesses a separate ritual structure (*tantra*) and because there is a scriptural injunction for the sacrifice as a whole, it accomplishes—that is, it encompasses—the requirements such as the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and so forth. || 8 ||
The Agniṣṭoma consists of seventeen [stotras] and is a Daśapeya; the Vasatīvarī waters belong to Sarasvatī. 9.

The pouring out of the *pravarṇa* water and so forth. At the time of taking the *vasatīvarī* waters, when the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) is near the Sarasvatī river, then one takes the *vasatīvarī* waters there. Otherwise, having brought that water, the performer of many sacrifices (*bahuyājī*) places it in a jar (*kumbhī*) and takes it. — *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [13th Praśna], Sūtra 188.

Alternatively—since the term *vasatīvarī* refers to waters flowing in a stream, and because such waters would otherwise be obtained here by extension from the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), the waters specifically belonging to the Sarasvatī are prescribed here. In order to set aside the general characteristics of the *hotṛ* priest and other elements obtained through the rule of extension (*codaka*), he states the specific details:
"The *hotṛ* is a descendant of Bhṛgu; the *brahmasāman* is the Śrāyantīya; the *agniṣṭomasāman* is the Vāravantīya. (13.7.10)

In the phrase "whosoever [is] the Hotṛ," even though that [status] is obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*), he is further specified as being born of the Bhṛgu lineage. Regarding the archetype: since the *Gāyatra* Sāman is prescribed for the *Ājya-stotra* of the *Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, the *Śrāyantīya* Sāman is here enjoined as an exception to that. The *Śrāyantīya* is the Sāman produced upon the verse beginning with "śrāyanta iva sūryam. Furthermore, since the *Yajñāyajñīya* belongs to the *Agniṣṭoma* in the archetype, the *Vāravantīya* Sāman is enjoined as an exception to that.

The Vāravantīya Sāman is produced upon this Ṛc verse: "Come to us, O you who possess the prize" (ave na tvā vāravantam). 10. Now, the manual: from the words "At the great roar" (mahārāje śve) up to the placement of the *pariplava* [ladle], at the time of arranging the vessels, he employs ten additional *camasa* cups. 11.
He employs ten additional cups. || 11 ||
At the time of the drawing [of Soma], he draws ten additional cups. 12.

Likewise, at the time of drawing the cups (*camasonnayanakāla*), because of the statement "ten additional cups," there is an increase in the number of *camasādhvaryu* priests. At the time of consumption, he whose Soma-drinking has been uninterrupted for ten generations is the performer of the consumption; having designated those beyond the tenth generation, one hundred Brāhmaṇas who have drunk Soma proceed forward. (13) Ten [priests] consume each cup individually. (14)

A hundred Brāhmaṇas who have performed the Soma sacrifice and are distinguished by the qualities to be mentioned hereafter enter the *sadas* hall; thus there is an increase in the number of those in the *sadas*. At the time of consumption, they fill the original *camasa*s and, once those have been consumed, the new *camasa*s.

There are a hundred Brāhmaṇas who have performed the Soma sacrifice, ten Soma-sacrificers for each [original cup], who can recount ten generations—down to the tenth person—of unbroken Soma-drinking, saying, "They were such as this. Not merely by such a claim, but because they are learned and exceed the original number, they draw up the largest *camasa*s. (13–14)

At the time of the sacrificial fee, he gives to the Adhvaryu a golden mirror, as prescribed by the traditional text; to the Grāvastut, a bull; to the Unnetṛ, a ram; and to the Subrahmaṇya, a goat. (Section 21) ||15||

Two mirrors made of gold are for the *udgātṛ*. A golden garland is for the *udgātṛ*. A circular golden ornament (*rukma*) is for the *hotṛ*. A horse is for the *prastotṛ* and *pratihartṛ*. Twelve six-year-old heifers are for the *brahman*. A barren cow (*vaśā*) is for the *vaitrāvaruṇa*. A bull is for the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*. Two garments are for the *neṣṭṛ* and *potṛ*. A cart loaded with barley is for the *acchāvāka*. An ox is for the *agnīdh*. According to some, one gives a chariot yoked with a single ox to the *camasādhvaryu*. The rest is clear. 15.

[Chapter] 7. *Mahādevaśāstrī*-compiled *Mayūkhamālikā* with the commentary *Yogacandrikā*. Now, it is heard in the *Rājasūya*: "He gives two *prākāśas* to the *adhvaryu*" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 1.8.18). Some say that *prākāśas* are lamp-posts; others say they are mirrors. Do these two [lamps or mirrors] set aside the entire original sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), or only the portion belonging to the *adhvaryu*? In this regard, because the accusative case in "he gives the two *prākāśas*" (*prākāśau dadāti*) denotes the object of the action, the two *prākāśas* are connected to the act of giving through their status as the recipient (*adhvaryave*). Thus, they set aside only the share of the *adhvaryu*. Why? Because the word *dadāti* ("he gives") is a transitive verb (*sakarmaka*), and it is impossible for the same word to simultaneously denote both the act of giving and its object. Furthermore, since the *prākāśas* are mentioned in the accusative, they are understood to be the objects of the act of giving. Therefore, the *prākāśas* are not the entirety of the sacrificial fee, but rather they replace only that specific portion which belongs to the *adhvaryu*. This is because the *prākāśas* are mentioned in the accusative case, and the *adhvaryu* is mentioned in the dative case. Since the dative indicates the recipient of the gift, the *prākāśas* are understood to be given specifically to the *adhvaryu*. Consequently, they exclude only the *adhvaryu*'s share from the original fee. This is established by the principle that when a specific item is prescribed in connection with a particular priest, it sets aside only that priest's share of the original fee. Thus, the *prākāśas* are the fee for the *adhvaryu* alone. Thus, when the connection with the person (the *puruṣa*) effected by the sentence is set aside, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is a sublation of the entire other object to be given, because the substance to be given is already perceived [as belonging to the priest]. The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that since the connection with the act of giving—established by the hearing of the dative case-ending in "He gives to the Adhvaryu," which denotes the recipient (*saṃpradāna-kāraka*)—cannot be negated, and since there is no contradiction even in the connection with the act of giving as qualified by the recipient, there is a sublation of only the portion belonging to the Adhvaryu. || 15 ||
The Daśapeya sacrifice is concluded. || 16 ||

Having performed the rites with the Agniṣṭoma cups, there is the Ṣoḍaśī offering; [regarding this] the author of the Bhāṣya says it is not a [separate] *homa*. The Daśapeya is a sacrifice consisting of the *agniṣṭoma* *homa*. Having emerged from the *avabhṛtha*, one offers these oblations following the *paśupuroḍāśa* of the *anūbandhyā* animal sacrifice, such as the eight *devasū* offerings, and so forth. Thus the Daśapeya is concluded. || 16 ||
When that has been completed, he performs the Diśām-aveṣṭi sacrifice.

When that [sacrifice] has been completed, having performed the fast for the Daśapeya and having consigned the five fires into the Āhavanīya, he concludes with the Diśām-aveṣṭi; there is no *pūrṇāhuti*. There are no ritual requirements of the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice, such as the cake on five potsherds (*pañcakapāla*) and so forth. Thinking, "This is better than the deficient [sacrifice]," he causes the fires to descend from their hearths and places them back in their respective stations. || 17 ||
"One offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni"—having sacrificed each oblation according to the traditional recitation, one should pour an additional libation over the offering to Bṛhaspati. || 18 ||

"I shall sacrifice with the Diśām-āveṣṭi," and so forth. Today, for the sake of the sacrifice, [the ritual begins with] the Diśām-āveṣṭi oblation, the fetching of the branch, and so on, up to the smearing of the pot (kumbhīlepana). "Pleasant to Agni," "Pleasant to Indra," "Pleasant to the Viśve Devas," and so forth. The morning milking rite follows. The liturgical formulas (nigamas) are addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa. The bringing of ordinary curds is performed with the formula, "Thou art Ghos. After each of the four sacrifices beginning with that to Agni, there is an additional pouring over (abhighāraṇa) at the fifth oblation.
At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), there are gold, a bull, a six-year-old cow, a barren cow, and a white-backed one; this sacrifice concludes with the satiation of the Brahmins. || 18 ||
With that [offering], one who desires food and drink, or one who desires heaven, should sacrifice. || 19 ||
The sacrificer. || 19 ||

If a Brāhmaṇa is the sacrificer, having placed [the vessel] in the middle and offered oblation after oblation, he should pour clarified butter over it; if a Rājanya, [he should offer] to Indra; if a Vaiśya, to the Viśvedevas. 13.7.20.

By means of this very sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), when there is a connection with the desire for [the results of] the *rājasūya*, Brāhmaṇas and others perform it. (20) [From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—Book 13, Question 190...
Now, having prescribed the *āveṣṭi*, he enjoins the ritual of the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) involving two animals:
"On the following day, one should sacrifice with the animal sacrifice consisting of two animals. (21)

On the day that the Daśapeya concludes, on that same day in the afternoon, [the ritual] is performed; according to Baudhāyana and Āpastamba, and by virtue of the Sūtrakāra’s statement, "on the following day," one declares: "I shall sacrifice with the Paśubandha," and so forth. || 21 ||

He immolates a long-eared pregnant ewe for the Ādityas and a spotted heifer of four years for the Maruts. He proceeds with the offering to the Maruts in a low voice; both the *āśruta* and the *pratyāśruta* are also in a low voice, while those for the Āditya are in a loud voice.

The goddess Aditi is her deity; thus she is an Ādityā. "Malhā" means "maṇilā," which signifies being endowed with a dewlap or udder. She is small-bodied (*pṛśni*) or white in color. Since it has been stated more than once that the status of royalty (*rāṣṭratva*) belongs to the Ādityas and the status of the common people (*vaiśyatva*) to the Maruts, the text praises this with the intention of referring to that very point: "He sacrifices an Ādityā cow that is *malhā* and pregnant, and a *pṛśni* heifer belonging to the Maruts. He thereby bestows upon him both the common people and the royalty in harmony" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.8.3).

He praises the order established by the sequence of recitation: "One proceeds with the offering to Āditya first, and with that to the Maruts later" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.8.3). Regarding the act of calling for attention (*āśravaṇa*), having restated the loudness obtained through the *codaka* rule as applying to the sacrifice to Āditya, he enjoins an exception: "One calls for attention loudly for the offering to Āditya; one calls for attention in a low voice for the offering to the Maruts," and so forth. (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.8.3). [...]

Now, the manual (paddhati): There is no *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula, nor the *panviṣṭi* and so forth. The cutting of the three sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) together with the *upaśaya* post occurs at the time of preparing the altar, as in the case of the eleven posts (*ekādaśinī*), beginning with the one standing nearest the fire (*agniṣṭha*). One post is in front of the *āhavanīya* fire; one is at the place where the sacrificial gifts are placed (*dakṣiṇāsasthāna*); and from that, one is at the distance of a chariot-length (*rathālamātra*). The ritual performance takes place at one of these, or at both, depending on whether there is one side or two sides [to the altar]. That is the tenth day. Only one post is in front of the *āhavanīya*.

Therefore, the measurement of the altar (vedi) is determined by seventy-seven fingers and forty-two additional finger-breadths—this being three times the third part of two chariot-axles plus one-third of a fourth finger-breadth. Some say it should be situated at the two shoulders of the sacrificial post (yūpa), being three times the third part of one chariot-axle. Others say the measurement of the altar is seventy-four fingers and two additional finger-breadths, which is three times the third part of half a finger-breadth.

Some say that the *uttaravedi* (high altar) consists of ten parts, because the *ekādaśinī* (set of eleven victims) is its archetype; they desire it to be merely the measure of a *citta* and a *śamyā*. In the arrangement of the vessels: there are six girdles for the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), two ropes for the animals, two pots, two spits, four omentum-roasting spits, and two pairs of *darbha* grass-bundles; the time for the sacrificial posts is like that of the *ekādaśinī*. The raising of the two posts is such that the distance between them is the length of a chariot axle, and the placing of the *upaśaya* (resting-block) is like that of the *ekādaśinī*. Some say that the encircling with the two ropes is performed with the formula, "Come, O two animals."

*Malhā* refers to one whose neck has two fleshy protuberances. One dedicates a *pṛśni*, a *paṣṭhauhī*, and a pregnant cow as the *upavasatha* animals. The term *upaśaya* indicates a mouse. In the *pañcahoma* (fivefold oblation), there is a modification (*ūha*) using the dual number. Once they have been ransomed, [the formula is]: "These two have reached the portion of the sacrifice; go to heaven. At the dedication, while they are being prepared: "The two have drunk. That [formula] for them is in the dual. Of those that have bellowed, may they make *Svarāṭ* and *Amāyu*; cause them to be quieted.
"You two are winners of light; you are winners of light. [End of] Chapter Seven. Together with the commentary *Payogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 191.

"O you two who know the worlds, you have measured out the world; O you two who know the protectors, you have measured out the protector; O you two who know the paths, you have measured out the path. Or rather, you do not dispute this, nor do you suffer harm. O gods, you have indeed reached the various breaths of the quarters. You have drunk from the two animals that are most swift in their desire for food. In trembling, in fleeing, in the act of sitting together, and in urinating, you both void excrement. Fear has been removed from all; be gracious to us. Since you have made the animal long-lived, release the animals from the bonds, O Herb!"

"Protect him from the axe twice; do not [strike] him," and so on. "Those two souls of yours which have entered into the animals, which have taken separate stand—endowed with self, endowed with clarity (ghṛtavat), go; find [him], see [him]; prepare the plants. For the goat's omentum and fat, "To the Ādityas, the omentum and fat... and so on, [this is] loudly (*uccaiḥ*) for Āditya. For the cow's omentum and fat, "To the Maruts, the omentum and fat... and so on, [this is] in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). At the end of the wiping of the omentum, the granting of a boon is prescribed for a pregnant cow and a *ṣaṣṭauhī* (a six-year-old cow).

The performance of the auxiliary rites for the animal-cakes (*paśupuroḍāśa*) and others is like that of the omentum (*vapā*); the remnants are treated like those of the *ekādaśinī*. With the formulas "Go to the ocean, svāhā," etc., the journey [is performed]; with "May the smoke go, svāhā," etc., the rite concludes from the worship of the sacrificial post (*yūpopasthāna*) up to the feeding of the Brahmins. Thus ends the ritual involving two animals. On the next day, the second day, or immediately, one begins with the formula: "I shall sacrifice with the oblations of the Sātyadūtas," and so forth. Regarding the oblation of the Sātyadūtas: "This [offering] of theirs is in me. The procedure follows that of the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyātantra*).

At the time of the offering, [he offers] a cake on twelve potsherds to Pūṣan, beloved by the Aśvins; to Sarasvatī of true speech, a cake on twelve potsherds; and to Savitṛ of true impulsion, a cake on twelve potsherds. "O Aśvins, O Pūṣan, protect the oblation! O Sarasvatī of true speech, protect the oblation! O Savitṛ of true impulsion, protect the oblation!"—and so forth, until the end of the principal sacrifice. [He recites]: "May I become an eater of food through the Aśvins and Pūṣan; may I procreate with offspring and cattle," or for the latter two, "an eater of wealth."

At the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), however, a bow joined with three arrows—the *tisudhanva*—and a dry reed (*śuṣkati*) fashioned for its discharge; both of these are to be given here. This sacrifice concludes with the satiation of the Brahmins. (12) Now, the oblations of the *prayuja* offerings are described:
then, on the following day, he sacrifices with the six oblations of the *prayuja*. (23)
When the oblation for the Sātyadūtas has been completed, they proceed with the thought, "We shall sacrifice with the oblations of the Prayujas," and so forth. This is the oblation of the Prayujas.
As prescribed in the traditional text: "He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni. The sacrificial fee is a chariot-yoke-horse from the right side. || 24 ||

At the time of the offering, [he says] "pleasing to Agni," "pleasing to Soma," "pleasing to Savitṛ," "pleasing to Bṛhaspati," "pleasing to Tvaṣṭṛ," "pleasing to Agni Vaiśvānara," and so forth; at the conclusion of the principal sacrifices, with the exception of the Soma, there is the eating of food.

At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the draught-animal for the chariot—meaning the ox that pulls the chariot or another cart upon which the front of the two chariot-poles is placed—the driver of that chariot-drawing cart, namely the right-hand ox, is to be given away in the first group of six; this is the view of the author of the *Bhāṣya*. This sacrifice concludes with the satiation of the Brahmins. Now, he describes the sacrifice for the second group of six.

On the following day, he offers a *caru* oblation to Sarasvatī with the six subsequent verses, as prescribed in the ritual text. A bow with three arrows, a staff made of dried leather, and two sandals are the sacrificial fees; or alternatively, a horse. According to some, it is a horse with reddish-brown ears. He sends these to rival kings. He makes the announcement: "I have been consecrated; I have become a king."

On the following day, having performed the morning *agnihotra* sacrifice, [the sacrificer] says, "I shall sacrifice with the *prayuj* offerings," and so forth. There are six *caru* oblations: for Sarasvatī, for Pūṣan, for Mitra, for Varuṇa, for Kṣatrapati, and for Aditi—having prepared these as balls (*piṇḍa*), he pours them into the cooking pot with the formula, "Thou art heat (*gharma*)," and so forth. The northern horse that draws the chariot is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Thus says Āpastamba; and in this Brāhmaṇa as well: "He sends forth the messengers; these are the *āvid* verses."

"They make him known" (*āvidam evainam āvedayanti*). Therefore, the injunction must be understood as: "He is not cut off from his messengers" (*ato dūtebhyo na chidyate*, *Lāṭyāyana Śrautasūtra* 1.8.3). He dispatches messengers to rival kings. These messengers are called *āvidaḥ* because they make known (*vedayanti*) and proclaim (*khyāpayanti*) this person's command on all sides (*ā samantāt*). By that very act of dispatching messengers, they cause the sacrificer to attain renown (*āvidam*); for *āvid* means fame (*avikīrti*), derived from the sense that he is made known (*ā samantād vidyate*) and proclaimed—this is what they cause him to reach.

Furthermore, this [sacrificial vessel] is not severed from the leather straps on any side; because spirits (*bhūta*) cannot always be found when one wishes to dispatch messengers, there is no such severance, but rather many messengers are always present nearby. The reason for dispatching these messengers has been clarified by Āpastamba: "Having dipped them [the vessels] into water, he sends them to the rival kings; he announces: 'I have been consecrated as king. (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 18.22.4).

Having descended into the waters containing the *tisṛdhanva* and other sacrificial materials, and having stepped out from there and bathed, he places those items into the hands of a messenger to show them to each of the kings in turn, and dispatches him. That messenger then speaks these words before the kings: "I have been consecrated; I have become the king of you all. || 26 ||

He performs the Agnihotra for a year. (27) This is for the sake of continuity; therein, he should perform those sacrifices which are not prohibited by the Agnihotra. (28) At the end of the year, he should sacrifice with the Keśavapanīya Atirātra. (29) In that rite, there are mantras containing references to shaving; with those mantras containing references to the beginning, he should have [himself] shaved at the beginning, and with those containing references to the end, at the end. The Keśavapanīya is thus concluded. (13.7.30)

The specific ritual duties (*vaiśeṣika-dharma*) of the *Keśavapanīya-atirātra* are now stated. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says: "The *Keśavapanīya-atirātra*, which concludes with the Soma sacrifice, takes place either immediately after the *Abhiṣecanīya* or after one year" (Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra 15.9.26). Thus, the *Keśavapanīya-atirātra* sacrifice is to be performed after two animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*). Having performed the *Abhiṣecanīya* Soma sacrifice, one must observe a vow characterized by not shaving the hair for the duration of one year.

Then, for the purpose of dismissing that [hair], a single Soma sacrifice with a full-moon pressing (paurṇamāsī-sutya) should be performed; that very sacrifice is called the Keśavapana Atirātra. It is called an Atirātra because it proceeds having gone beyond (ati) the night (rātri); it should be performed according to the Atirātra ritual structure. [End of Paṭala] *Mahādevaśāstrī-saṃkalita-prayogacandrikā-vyākhyā-sametam* | 193

Then, for one year, he should offer the Agnihotra and perform the Keśavapanīya sacrifice. For one year, the Agnihotra, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Animal sacrifice, and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices proceed as usual; other obligatory and occasional rites also proceed, but not the optional ones. On the following day, having performed the first shaving, [he declares] "I shall sacrifice with the Keśavapanīya Atirātra," and so forth. It has one initiation like the Pavitra, three Upasad days, and the pressing of Soma on the fifth day.

In that performance, having performed the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, at the time of shaving, one performs the rite with the mantra "O axe, do not harm him" (*svadhite mainam*), and then follows Āpastamba’s procedure beginning with "Those who are long-haired" (*ye keśinaḥ*) and ending with "With which he shaved" (*yenāvapat*). There is an introductory recitation with four verses for the shaving; in place of the verse "The god has moved" (*devaścarati*), there is the cleaning of the teeth and so forth. The *keśavapanīya* sacrifice concludes with an *atirātra* session. The specific detail is that one purchases [the Soma] with twenty-seven cows, saying, "I purchase thee with cows. It includes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup. Some say it is with twenty-eight. Everything else is like the *atirātra*. The procedure for the *phalacamasa* is as before.

When the omentum of the Anubandhya cow has been offered, one performs the removal of the hair with the mantras beginning with "mā te keśān" and ending with "yatsamīnam," and having bathed, this is the ritual procedure; it is entirely like the twelve-day Ahīna sacrifice. 27 || 28 || 29 || 30 ||
When that has concluded, he should sacrifice with the Vyuṣṭi-dvirātra.
When that Keśavapanīya sacrifice has been completed, [he declares], "I shall sacrifice with the Nyūṅkha-dvirātra," and so forth. || 31 ||
For him, the Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma constitutes the first day.

Regarding that *nyuṣṭi-dvirātra* sacrifice: having performed the rites beginning with "He shall establish the Sāvitra fire" up to the preparation of the pebbles (*śarkarā*) and ending with the setting down of the *sanīhāra*, the *samanvārambha-homa* is performed with the mantra "May death depart," and so forth. Some teachers instruct here: "He remains consecrated for twelve days. On the upcoming third day, having performed the *prāyaṇīyā* offering, at the time of purchasing the Soma, [the sacrificer says]: "I shall purchase [Soma] from you with a cow; her soul is more [than enough]. [The seller replies: "I shall sell it to you for ninety-nine cows."

"Some say, 'I shall purchase [the Soma] for fifty-six cows. Then, on the following day, having performed the morning rites, at the end of the *saṃbhārayajus* formulas, he recites, 'The seat of Indra,' and so forth. In this manner, at the conclusion of all the *upasthāna* (reverential salutations), at the time of cutting the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), he measures out thirteen posts, with the one nearest the fire (*agniṣṭha*) as the first, and so on. At the time of preparing the altar, it is like that of the *ekādaśinī*. 'Ten axles of the chariot,' and so forth. On the fifth day, during the *upasat*, having performed the morning rites, the construction of the altar takes place. The consecration is performed with the mantra, 'May he measure.'"

"Catuḥśikhaṇḍā" [is the mantra]. Then, in the center of the site for the *uttaravedi*, [one recites] "kum" and so forth. Having filled the outer lines with curds mixed with honey and with sugar-candy for the purpose of completion, one performs the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites with the two [mantras] belonging to the afternoon. On the following day, having performed [the rites] with the two [mantras] belonging to the forenoon, and having performed the *saṃcita* up to the end of the *ukthya*—beginning with "May Prajāpati seat you"—[one performs] the afternoon [rites]. On the twelfth day, having concluded the *pravargya* and having performed the carrying forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*), the *kāṭhaka* oblations are offered at the end of the *atimukti*.

The twenty-one formulas ending with "asave svāhā" belong to the *chadis-sad* (the roof-covering); they are recited over the two pressing-boards when they are joined together. At the time of the Agniṣoma sacrifice, [the procedure] continues up to the end of the *agredhāna*.

In the Sarvastoma Atirātra, the Gāyatra Sāman is performed on the first day, and the Traiṣṭubha on the second. The Rathantara Sāman is performed on the first day, and the Bṛhat on the second; the Vaikhānasa is the Sāman on the first day. The Ṣoḍaśin is performed on the second day. The first day has the *haviṣmat* as its *nidhana*, and the second day has the *haviṣkṛt* as its *nidhana*. The first day is the day for sacrifice on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), and the second is the following day; or it may be during the waxing fortnight, on whichever two days are auspicious. 33.

When [the Soma] has turned to foam, having employed the *dhruva* vessel, one does not [perform] the *pariṣṭava* and so forth. At the time of the animal vessels, there are fifteen *kumbhīs* tripled [to forty-five], twenty-five doubled [to fifty], five *śūlas*, and five omentum-spits; [there are] pairs of *darbha* blades, beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu. Having taken the cup for the Aśvins with the formula "Come with the animals," he fixes four sacrificial posts (*yūpa*). [The procedure] begins with the anointing and ends with the northern [post], as in the *Aṣṭhādaśī*. Then follows the placing of the *upaśaya* [wood], as in the *Kāpeyyaikādaśinī*.

The animal dedicated to Agni is at the post facing the fire; those for Indra are in the southern and northern [posts]; the animal for Sarasvatī is in the north; the animal for Savitṛ is in the south. Thereafter follows the *upaśaya* (the resting post) with the marking of the rat. At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives ten thousand [cows]. Having performed the rites with the *agniṣṭoma-camasa*s, there is the *ṣoḍaśin* oblation. In the *agniṣṭoma* form, while the *yajñāyajñīya* chant is being sung on the following day, he takes up the *vasatīvarī* waters. When the *sūktavāka* is being recited, the call "Tomorrow is the pressing" (*śvaḥ sutyām*) is given; it concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja*.

The rites beginning with the cutting of the branch dedicated to Mitra-Varuṇa and ending with the smearing of the *kumbhī* are performed during the day. Having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters at night, the milking, the fetching of the animal’s branch, and so forth, up to the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*), take place. At the great night, having awakened [the sacrificer], etc., there are the *atirātra* terminuses together with the *ṣoḍaśin*. In the application of the animal vessels, there are twelve: six *yūpa-raśanās* (rope-bands for the sacrificial posts), six animal ropes, six *kūmyas*, and *śūlas*; the omentum-roasting implements, pairs of *darbha* blades, the *śukra-graha* and so forth, and the formulas beginning with "Come with the animals" (*paśubhiḥ ehi*). Having drawn the cup for the Aśvins, he erects the six sacrificial posts (*yūpas*).

He places them in a continuous line, starting from the south between the *agniṣṭha* and the southern and northern [posts], alternating so that they end toward the north, reaching as far as the two *upaśaya* [yoke-pins]—either by a single performance (*tantra*) or separately. Then follows the cutting of the *upaśaya*. The two girth-ropes (*raśanā*) are wound around [the posts]. On this day, he dedicates the measured [animals] and the *upaśaya*; specifically, on the first day, he dedicates those belonging to the *vaiśvadeva* group.

In the second [round], [the offering is] to Soma in the north; in the third, to Marut in the south and to Pūṣan in the north; again, in the fifth, to Bṛhaspati in the north; then, in the sixth, to Varuṇa in the south. After that follows the indication of the mouse. At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives ten thousand [cows]. The *Kāṭhaka* sacrificial fees are [offered] separately. On the previous day, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) extends up to the *prasarpaṇa*, ending with the *tirohā*.

Having offered the *anūbandhya* victim’s omentum (*vapā*) with the verses beginning "Agnīdīpayaja," one performs the *pātnīvata* ritual, the *paśupuroḍāśa*, and so forth, including these oblations for the deities, up to the *udavasānīyā*. On the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), there is an option regarding the "previous great [rite]" (*pūrvamahāratyādi*). On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), the performance of the "previous great" is prescribed. There is an option regarding the "filling" (*āpūryamāṇa*): on the first [lunar day] it is the former, on the second it is the latter, or on the tenth or eleventh. || 33 ||
The Agniṣṭoma is the steadfastness of Kṣatriyas; therefore, one should perform it at the end. || 34 ||

On the day that the *vyuṣṭi*-dvirātra sacrifice concludes, on that very day the commencement of the *kṣatrāṇāṃ dhṛti* (the firm support of the nobility) takes place; or else, on the second day, the commencement of the aforementioned performance occurs. [The procedure] for the *kṣatrāṇāṃ dhṛti* begins with "I shall sacrifice with the *kṣatrāṇāṃ dhṛti*" and so forth, like the *pavitra* rite. There is one *dīkṣā*, three *upasads*, and the *prasuta* (pressing of Soma) on the fifth day. At the time of the purchase of the Soma, when it is said, "O Gayā, I shall buy thee," [the ritual continues]. [End of Chapter 8, Section of the *Paryoga-candrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 195.

"One purchases [the Soma] with thirty-one mixed [cows]," so it is said; the explanatory passage states, "with twenty-eight cows. At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives five thousand [cows]. Having performed the distribution of the *agniṣṭoma* cups, the *ṣoḍaśin* [cup] follows. Then, beginning with "O Agnīdh, perform the *upayaj* offerings," etc., the *anūbandhyā* cow is prescribed as an alternative in the *rājasūya*. || 34 ||
There is liberation from the five. || 35 ||
The Agniṣṭoma has five concluding rites; it results in the attainment of the fruit, ending with the Udavasānīyā offering. || 35 ||
The Rājasūya sacrifice is concluded. || 36 ||
It stands firm; it is completed. || 36 ||
Having sacrificed with the Rājasūya, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī. (Khaṇḍa 23) 37.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the thirteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.

On the immediately following full-moon day, there is the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice and the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) for Mitra and Varuṇa. Thus ends the seventh chapter in the thirteenth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.
Now begins the eighth chapter in the thirteenth book.

The Rājasūya has been performed by the Teacher; now, as the occasion has arrived, he proceeds to perform the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice—the following is done: on the third night prior [to the main ceremony], having purchased the shoots from a eunuch for the price of lead, he ties them in a linen cloth and sets them aside.

"From the ninth day for three days, [it is] a *trirātra*. Having declared on the ninth day, "I shall sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī," [the ritual proceeds]. With the mantra "Thou art lightning," the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula is performed as in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*). It is established that one purchases the *śaṣpa* (young grass) from a eunuch using lead (*sīsena*). Alternatively, in this *trirātra*, there is first the *sureṣṭi*. Lead is called *loha*. From a eunuch, the *śaṣpa*—meaning hair, young barley, or *tokma* (awned barley)—are purchased; the rice grains (*vrīhayaḥ*) are the size of a *śamyā* (a wooden pin). Both the rice grains and the young barley are called *tokmāni* or *śaṣpāṇi*.
Having tied them in a linen cloth, he places and sets them down; a means is employed so that they do not become dry for three nights. || 1 ||
He commences the ritual procedure of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
He begins the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. Since it is the designation for a collection of constituent parts (*aṅga*), he should undertake its performance. ||2||

In this regard, we shall explain what is performed: having added fuel to the fires, having prepared the Veda-grass bundle, having strewn grass around the fires, having washed his hands, and having spread out a layer of *ulapa* grass, he arranges the vessels according to their purpose. [The procedure] is concluded. 196. In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: 13. He places a cooking pot (*sthālī*) in the place of the potsherds (*kapāla*). 3.

The fire is not abandoned by the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula; in this [fire] the *agnihotra* oblation is performed. Then, on the twelfth day, having offered the morning *agnihotra*, the fire is carried forward (*praṇīyate*) for the sake of the *sureṣṭi*. [The mantra] "thou art lightning" (*vidyud asi*) is not used. Then follows the *anvādhāna*: "I take hold of Agni. The specific difference is: "for four days, follow the life-span of the sacrifice" (*yajñāyuḥ*). "Those who have entered this twelfth day, this sacrificial offering (*havis*) of the Sautrāmaṇī belongs to them within me. Some say, "this desired offering" (*iṣṭaṃ havis*).

When the *anvāhita* recitation has been performed, the bringing [of the fuel] from outside and so forth takes place; however, not the *idhma*. After the decoration of the fire, the strewing (*paristaraṇa*) occurs. Then follows the washing of the hands and so forth. He arranges the vessels according to their purpose, each in its own *sthālī*, and to the west [of them], the *śamyā*, the grinding stones, and the upper and lower millstones. To the further side [he places] the *sruva*-ladle, the *veda*-broom, the *pātrī* vessel, the *ājya-sthālī*, the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* water, the *upaveṣa* for the sake of the *madantī* water, the *vedāgra*, the *mekṣaṇa* stirring-spoon, and the *yoktra* cord. || 5 ||
At the time of the offering, he pours out an abundant quantity of rice for the Aśvins, for Sarasvatī, and for Indra Sutrāman.

When the time for the pouring out [of the grains] arrives, one performs the pouring out and subsequent rites in a common ritual sequence (*tantra*), saying: "I pour out what is pleasing to the Aśvins, to Sarasvatī, and to Indra Sutrāman. [The formula is: "O Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman, protect the oblation! As with the pouring out, so too is the sprinkling; the specific difference is the formula: "I sprinkle. (4)
Having cooked it according to the ritual for *caru*, and having dug a pit in front of the *gārhapatya* fire, he prepares the *parisrut* liquor according to the ritual for *surā*.

Taking the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick), it has the characteristic of being like a potsherd; he places that [pot] over the fire with the mantra "Thou art firm," but not so as to burn it. Having poured out the rice grains, he mixes them with the *praṇītā* waters with the mantra "May the waters unite with the waters. He surrounds them with the boiling water (*madantī*) with the mantra "With water. He places [the vessel] over the fire together with the water with the mantra "Thou art dharma. Without letting [the fire] pass between or burning [the grain], there is no pouring of the water used for smearing, nor is there the preparation of an altar. He should place [the vessel] either on the head of a Brāhmaṇa or on a mound. Having fixed the *sphyā* obliquely and the *sruva* and *srucaḥ* ladles, the wife [should perform] the *sammarjana* (cleansing).

"Sanahyā''jyenodehi," and so forth; [the ritual proceeds] from "āpo bhuvanasya" until the removal of the *caru*. Then, having dug a pit to the east of the *gārhapatya* fire, the vessel (*sthālī*) itself is placed in that pit; the fermentation of the *surā* takes place in that very vessel, and he pours water into it. A large vessel is prepared for the sacrificial offering (*havir*). ||6||
With the mantra, "Sweet thee with the sweet," he mixes the *surā* with young grass shoots.
In this context, rice, barley, and so forth, as well as the sprout and the young grass denoted by the word *śaṣpa*, are indicated. ||6||
He consecrates the mixed [grain] with the formula: "O Soma, be cooked for the Aśvins; be cooked for Sarasvatī; be cooked for Indra Sutraman. || 7 ||
The word "sacrificer" (yajamāna) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 7 ||
The residence is for three nights consecutively. ||8||
1 Bhāgni | 4 Paṭala]. Together with the commentary called *Mayūkhacandrikā*, compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 117.

He likewise ordains the dwelling for three days for [the Soma] mixed with young grass: "It dwells for three nights when mixed; for the purchased Soma dwells for three nights" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.8.5). The three-night dwelling of the purchased Soma is well known elsewhere as well. Thus it is said: "The Gandharva Viśvāvasu stole the Soma while it was being brought in; having stolen it, he dwelt [with it] for three nights. Therefore, the purchased Soma dwells for three nights."

(Tai. Saṃ. 6.1.5). He dwells for three nights in close contact [with the fires]. Then, on the fourteenth day, there is no abandonment of the consecrated fires; the Agnihotra and other rites are performed in those very fires. Then, on the fifteenth day, if the parvan occurs in the forenoon, the Darśa or Pūrṇamāsa sacrifice is performed, and then the Tripaśu (three-animal sacrifice) is commenced. If, however, the parvan occurs later in the day, then having completed [the preliminary rites], the Tripaśu is performed on the fifteenth day, followed by the Darśa or Pūrṇamāsa.

Now follows the performance of the Sauṇāmānī sacrifice based on the *Payovrata*. Having declared, "On the fifteenth day itself, I shall sacrifice with the Sauṇāmānī," one undergoes the *Paṭṭoptā* [observance]; then follows the *Saptahaviḥ-iṣṭi*, the fetching of the branch, and so forth, up to the entry into the sacrificial ground.
He cuts a single sacrificial post. || 9 ||

The rites from the oblation for the sacrificial post (*yūpāhuti*) up to the bathing of the animal are performed according to the archetype (*prakṛti*). However, there is this distinction: at the time of setting out the cups and vessels, the calves are separated [from their mothers] as in the morning milk-offering (*prātardoha*); the animal’s branch is used in place of the *sata* vessel by a woman; the vessels are placed in front of the *kumbhī*; the *kumbhī*, the rope (*abhidhānī*), and the milking vessels are tied together; and at the time of the breaking forth of the *surā*, the rites beginning with "these they perform" and ending with the pouring out of the wash-water are performed as in the morning milk-offering. Furthermore, the *upaveṣa* is made from the animal’s branch, [offering being made] to the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman.

The *nigamas*. Having either placed [the vessel] on the head of the *brāhmaṇa* or on the *khara*, he performs the touching of the seat as in the *darśa* sacrifice, beginning with "Indam indriyam," or having placed it beneath the *khara*, he purifies it with the strainer made of wool through the middle, with the modification "May it purify what has been spilled for you," and then places it in its proper place; the rites from the driving away of the cattle until the end of the cleansing (*mārjana*) are as before.

Alternatively, having taken the portions for the planets ending with Dhruva, and having set aside the Aindra [portion] as before with the verse "kuvidaṅga," and having sprinkled the Prokṣaṇī waters and so forth up to the wiping of the omentum (vapā-mārjana), it is all performed as before. Then, beginning with "he divides the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa)" and so on, everything is as before. However, because of the absence of the Māsarā [offering], that is omitted. Regarding this, there are verses: "Even when there is a milk-offering on the Parvan day, one should drive away the calves from the animal with a branch before the Kumbhī and the Sata have been placed on the mound."

The three strainers, the milking vessels, the donkey, and the head upon the donkey, as well as the wine poured out for the milking rite in the dwelling, the release [of the calf] from the mother—these are likewise [performed]. With a tuft of hair beneath the donkey, there is purification again on the donkey. "For food, thee!"—with this [mantra], the omentum-oblation (*vapā-homa*) and the cleansing (*mārjana*) and so forth are performed as before.

Māsara is a mixture of barley flour with sprouted barley. 198: In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, in the thirteenth book (*praśna*), now follows the ritual for the three animals (*tripaśu*). There is no animal-offering (*paśviṣṭi*) because it has already been encompassed [by the preceding rites]. Regarding the deity of the *surā*, some say it is "Indra Sutrāman" alone; others say it is "Indra" and "another Indra. Therefore, in the *sureṣṭi* following the *paśviṣṭi*, if the *pratipraṇayana* (carrying forward of the fire) has already been performed, one does not perform the *paśviṣṭi* here; rather, the *paśviṣṭi* and the *pratipraṇayana* are performed when the oblations (*havis*) are near.

The bringing of the branches occurs at the *lakṣa-śākhā* (the branch with a hundred thousand knots). From the offering for the sacrificial post (*yūpa-āhuti*) until the taking up of the *capāla*, there are three *svaru* chips; for the scripture states, "I shall not injure the animals with the *svarus*. There is one sacrificial post (*yūpa*). There is neither the *upaśaya* nor the *pātnīvata*.
It does not create this Veda; nor does it produce meanings once [the Veda] has been created beforehand. || 13.8.10 ||
He prepares the altar for the Veda; he does not prepare the Veda itself. Because of the instruction already performed previously, everything is accomplished by that alone. ||10||
He prepares the altar for the Soma sacrifice, measuring one-third [of the size of the previous one]. || 11 ||

One should perform the sacrifice on the third part of the *saumikī* altar. The measurement of the altar is by means of a *prakrama* or by a rod of three *karaṇīs*. With a staff measured at twenty-four *aṅgulas*, [the altar] is ten [parts] to the west and twelve to the east; eight [parts] to the front. Because of the injunction that "the *uttaravedi* is ten paces, or as much as a *śamyā*, as in the *paśubandha*," the eleven [stakes] prescribed directly in this manner proceed accordingly. Therefore, the author of the *bhāṣya* states that the *uttaravedi* is measured by the dimension of a *śamyā*. 11.

At the same time that the Adhvaryu prepares the high altar (uttaravedi), the Pratiprasthātṛ, having brought earth from the pit (cātvāla), prepares a square mound (khara) to the south of the high altar.

At the time when the Adhvaryu prepares the northern altar (*uttaravedi*), the Pratiprasthātṛ takes earth from the pit (*cātvāla*) and makes a mound (*khara*)—a seat of clay—to the north of the southern altar. While the northern altar is being prepared, he silently makes this mound in front of the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, at a distance from the altar. Having taken earth from that same pit, the Adhvaryu makes a second mound for the sake of the *surā* cups on the very altar; the procedure up to the removal of the earth is the same as for the animal sacrifice. || 12 ||

At the same time that the Adhvaryu leads forward the Āhavanīya fire, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having taken embers from the Dakṣiṇāgni and having piled them upon the mound (khara), adds fuel to them. He does not wash his hands.

At the time of the carrying forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*), the Adhvaryu carries the fire for the northern altar (*uttaravedi*). The Pratiprasthātṛ, having taken the fire from the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*) and having deposited it on the mound to the south of the northern altar, silently adds fuel behind it in such a way that no separation occurs [between the fires]. The ritual for the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*), beginning with the bringing of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the northern altar and ending with the strewing around (*paristaraṇa*), as well as the washing of the hands and so forth, continues until the conclusion of the *atimukti* offering.

When the time for placing the vessels has arrived, there is this modification regarding the animal-related items: two ropes for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), three ropes for the animals (*paśu*), three pots (*kumbhī*), three omentum-roasting spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*), and two [skins of] rams and two [skins of] he-goats (*vṛṣṇi*). When there is an Indra-sacrifice, then there is a single pot, spit, and omentum-roasting spit; [the skins of] the ram and the he-goat remain as before. Having thus employed the animal-related items... || 13 || 14 ||
This is the sūtra. [Chapter 8] Together with the *Śyena-candrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin: 199.
He sets out three ladles made of *vikaṅkata* wood, with their bowls facing upwards, for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman. 15.
He places three *ulapa* vessels on the mound (*khara*) for the purpose of taking the *surā* draughts, dedicated to the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutraman. || 15 ||
A hundred-holed vessel made of clay, a golden ornament, and a hair-strainer. ||16||

The distinction is that they prepare a vessel in the shape of a *droṇakalaśa*. It is circular, has a hundred holes, and is made of clay according to the rules for a cooking-pot (*sthālī*). He prepares a *bālavāja*—a filter made of hair, specifically from the pure hair of a cow—for the purpose of washing the *surā* liquor. Some say it is tied to a cloth like a *daśāpavitra* and shaped like the wing or tail of a hawk. He collects the parched grains of *kalavaḍara*, *karkandhu*, and *saktu*; he cleanses the upright vessels as one does the *juhū* and other ladles, and because they are made of *palāśa* wood, they possess the characteristics of a *pātrī*. The clay pot with a hundred holes is the *sthālī*. 16.

Having first performed the acts prior to the immolation of the animal, having pierced the *surā* and poured it into the vessel, he purifies the *parisrut* with a strainer made of hair, saying: "May [Soma] purify your *parisrut*. (17)

Before the removal of the *praśas* (the two wooden pegs), having performed the specific rite therein: the taking up of the two cords with the formula, "I give you two for the God"; the binding [of the horse] with the unmodified formula, "Thou art the encircler"; [and the formulas] "Ye two are the sons of Heaven," and "I take hold of thee, the station of the atmosphere. Having performed thus far, having pierced the ground and placed the *surā* on the head of a Brāhmaṇa or in a pit, he silently [recites] "with what is dear. Some, however, purify the *surā* with a filter made of hair using the formula, "May it purify thy sacrificial trench," beneath the *khara* mound. 17.

With the verse, "The wind is purified by the filter," [he purifies] one who has vomited Soma or one who has been excessively purified by Soma. Having placed the purified [Soma] upon the head of a Brāhmaṇa with the verse, "Forward, O Soma," [he concludes] for the one who has been excessively purified by Soma. (Section 24) 18.

With the verse, "O Soma, turn back," he [addresses] one who has vomited Soma; with "Soma, the wonderful, has turned back," [he addresses] that which has been purified. He places it in its proper place; he places it in the very same spot where it was previously placed. || 18 ||

He commences the ritual acts beginning with the dedication of the sacrificial animals (paśūpākaraṇa). He dedicates a smoke-colored goat to the Aśvins; a ram to Sarasvatī; and a bull, a young male, or a castrated goat to Indra. For one who has vomited Soma or for one whose Soma has flowed over, a fourth animal is dedicated to Bṛhaspati. || 19 ||
He dedicates the animals one by one, as in the case of the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice, and so forth; [with the formulas] "For food, thee! and so forth, and "For the Aśvins, thee!
[and for] the one who has over-poured the Soma, [as prescribed in] the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Chapter 13, Section 1.290.

With the formula "I dedicate the one not enjoyed," he dedicates a smoke-colored ram; with "For food, thee," and so forth; and for Sarasvatī, with "Thee, who art dear to Sarasvatī," he dedicates a ewe—Sarasvatī being the deity, as indicated by the supplementary statement, "Sarasvatī is indeed speech. With "To Indra, thee, who art dear," he dedicates a bull or a ram; others take a peacock and so forth; and with "To Bṛhaspati, thee," the fourth animal is a goat, which is called *somātipavita* because its stomach swelled after it drank Soma that had been over-purified.

[The formula] is *anitya* (non-permanent). Having brought [the animal] near, he offers five oblations: "Go to heaven with the *ūha*; you are established among the plants. "Those for whom [the animal] was purchased, let them go; those who were being slaughtered... But not with the fourth *ūha*: "...releasing those that were brought near, seeking peace. [He recites] from "*agnerjanitram asi*" (Thou art the birthplace of Agni) until the end of the *abhihoma*. Having taken the tethering-rope of the animal with "*devasya tvā*" (Thee, by the impulse of the god...), [he proceeds] from "*paśordakṣiṇe*" (On the right side of the animal) onwards: "*dharṣā mānuṣān*" (Be bold against men...), "*aścimyāṃ tvā juṣṭaṃ niyunajmi*" (I tether thee, acceptable to the horse-goddess); this is the tethering on the right side.

Then, [he says] "For Sarasvatī, thee, acceptable, I bind," [and then] "For Indra, thee, acceptable, I bind. Then he sprinkles [them], beginning with "For the plants, thee" and so forth, and "For the Aśvins, thee, acceptable, I release," and so forth. The three are given water to drink in sequence, beginning with "Thou art the drinker of waters."

Having performed for one animal in sequence the rites beginning with *svāttam*, the placing of the Veda, the pouring of the *sruc* oblation, the *āghāra* libation, and so forth, ending with *sa yajñapatiḥ*; then performing the same for the other two in order; the smearing of the *dhruvā* and all subsequent smearing being done once for all (*tantra*) for all three; having placed the *svadhiti* (cleaver) between [the animals] once; having smeared one [animal] with the *svadhiti*, the smearing of the second animal is performed again with another piece of wood (*śakala*), and the smearing of the third is performed again with another *svaru* together with the *svaru*; and finally, the marking of the *svarus*.

The *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire) for the animals and the *kumbhī* (cauldron) and so forth is performed by way of a common procedure (*tantra*). "O Paśupati, these are your animals; may the gods who follow them grant their approval, O Sovereign Lord. The release is by way of a common procedure. From the point where they are being bound, there is the commencement of the principal omentum-offering and the *vapāśrapaṇī* (omentum-roasting spits). Thus, having performed the sequence beginning with "three times the lord of sacrifice... and ending with "him toward the south" for one animal, some do not repeat it for the other two. For the subsequent animal, they do not repeat the digging of the pit for the sacrificial post, nor the bringing of the firebrand (*ulmuka*).

While [the animals] are being quieted with the formula "O various breaths... and so forth, the pouring out is done by way of a single performance (*tantra*). Then, having touched all [the parts] by way of a single performance, the principal [animal] is grasped from behind by the two *vapāśrapaṇī* [spits]. Following the sequence beginning with the spreading of *darbha* grass and so forth, they quiet [the animals] with the formula: "Making them free from disease, you are finders of heaven" (and so on), up to: "You are finders of the world, you are finders of the path, you are finders of support; indeed, you are not led away. Of the quarters, there are the quarters; of the various breaths... [the formula continues].

The employment of formulas such as "the sacrifice with animals" (*paśubhir yajña*) is not performed collectively for the Goddess’s *śamitṛ*s. The releasing from the nooses is done individually, according to the [text]: "Approach; release the animals from the nooses. Having performed for one [animal] the sequence beginning with "Homage to you, O spreader" (*namas ta ātāna*) and ending with "O divine waters" (*apo devīḥ*), and having performed for one [animal] the sequence beginning with "May your speech swell" (*vāk ta āpyāyatām*) and ending with "Pure are the paths" (*śuddhāś caritrāḥ*), [one performs them] for the other two. Having performed for one [animal] the sequence beginning with "Protect him" (*trāyasvainam*) and ending with "I cut off" (*utkṛntāmi*), [one performs them] for the other two.

Others cast aside [the portion], saying, "This shall be the share of the Rākṣasas, red-edged. [He says: "Uninterrupted is the wealth; I cut thee out, acceptable to the Aśvins. [He says: "To Sarasvatī thee... to Indra thee... With the *tantra* formula, the sacrificer should touch all [the portions] while they are heated. [The procedure] beginning with "a portion of the firebrand" and ending with "without spilling" is performed with the *tantra*. [He says: "O Vāyu, come hither," separately; and also "That which is thy soul," etc. Some [recite] with the *bhī* [variant]: "Those who are thy souls," etc.; [thus] they have entered and taken their stand.

[The verses] beginning with "ātmanvantaḥ" and "supippalāḥ," [are recited]. This is accompanied by the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. [The offerings are made] separately with the formulas "oṣadhīḥ kṛta" and "idam indriyam," starting from the final *prayāja*. Having first performed the *parivapana* and offered the oblations, one proceeds in the sequence beginning with "having spread a base in the *juhū* ladle," etc. The procedure for the omentum (*vapā*) is as follows: "Recite the invitatory prayer for the fat of the omentum of the goat for the Aśvins," and so on; having thus given the direction (*preṣya*), [the offering is made to] Jātavedas. Likewise for the omentum of the ram for Sarasvatī, having thus given the direction; and for the omentum of the bull for Indra, having thus given the direction.

For the offering to Sarasvatī: "By the sacrifice to the goddess Sarasvatī, may I obtain speech and food... For the other two [offerings], it is like the *sānnāyya*. There is the *uttaraparivapya-homa*. The removal of the omentum (*vapā*) and the sprinkling of clarified butter are performed separately, with the formula: "Svāhā! O Nabhas, go to the Maruts. The subsequent oblation (*abhihoma*) is performed as a common ritual procedure (*tantra*). || 19 ||
When the omenta have been offered, he gives as a sacrificial fee a golden plate, a bull, and a swift mare. || 13.8.20 ||

"Once the omenta have been offered, he gives a bull with a gold ornament and a swift mare," says Āpastamba. At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the bull is a draft ox; *sātvarī* means one that moves swiftly; and a mare (*vaḍavā*) is the female of a horse.

And he places it upon the inner altar [with the formula]: "O Brahman, you are the song of the Brahman; for the Brahman have I offered you today; do not harm me, having been offered today; be auspicious to me. With the unmodified [formula], "Swell up, O Aditi," [he says]: "Thousand-streamed, inexhaustible, they have filled the earth, the mid-air, and the sky; they are gold, horses, and mares, most excellent treasures. Death, these Brahmins are your [treasures]; the mares are like swift horses. Some desire the neuter form *napuṃsakena* here.

The word *niṣka* is neuter; such are the various rules of grammatical instruction. The acceptance [of gifts] is as follows: gold for Agni, a cow for Rudra, and a horse for Varuṇa. The purification takes place at the *cātvāla* pit. ||20||

Having performed that, he takes the cups of Surā with the Vāyu formulas. The Adhvaryu takes the Āśvina cup with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, flawless, with the flawless [vessel], agreeable to the Aśvins. The Pratiprasthātṛ takes the Sārasvata cup with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, flawless, with the flawless [vessel], agreeable to Sarasvatī. The Yajamāna takes the Aindra cup with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, flawless, with the flawless [vessel], agreeable to Indra Sutraman. || 21 ||

Because of the statement "having done that," it is according to the archetype (*prakṛti*); thus, the *graha* and *avakāśa* formulas do not occur. The Adhvaryu takes the cup for the Aśvins; the Pratiprasthātṛ or the Āgnīdhra takes the cup for Sarasvatī; the Brahman or the sacrificer takes the cup for Indra. (ĀpŚS 19.2.9)—this is the specific rule in the Āpastamba Sūtra. 21.
"Kuvid aṅga" is the single introductory verse (puroruc) for all [the offerings].
It applies everywhere. (Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—Book 13).

He mixes the cup for the Aśvins with *kvāla* flour; according to some, with jujube (*badara*) flour. He mixes the cup for Sarasvatī with *karkandhu* flour and lion hair; and the cup for Indra with jujube flour and tiger hair; according to some, with *kvāla* flour and wolf hair. Alternatively, the Adhvaryu should mentally meditate on lions, the Pratiprasthātṛ on tigers, and the sacrificer on wolves.

He draws the cup for the Aśvins, mixing it with parched grains of *karañja* and the hair of a lion. He mixes the cup for Sarasvatī with parched jujube fruits and the hair of a tiger (*śārdūla*). He mixes the cup for Indra with parched *karkandhu* fruits and the hair of a wolf (*vṛka*). He mixes these with the powder of their respective fruits. The lion is well known. The tiger is the striped leopard (*dvīpī*). The wolf is well known. In the absence of their hair, one should meditate upon the lion mentally. (23)

"This is your womb; for the Aśvins you! This is your womb; for Sarasvatī you! This is your womb; for Indra Sutrāman you!"—having thus placed [the cups] upon the head of a Brāhmaṇa according to their respective forms. (Section 25) 24.
Having taken up the cups held in the hands and having wiped them all around with the fringe of the antelope skin, he should set them down according to their respective forms. ||24||

He undertakes the rites beginning with the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*). Having offered the *bārhaspatya* animal-cake, he offers the eleven-potherd cake for Indra, the twelve-potherd cake for Savitṛ, and the ten-potherd cake for Varuṇa. || 25 ||

He pours out the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*). Having offered the occasional cake for Bṛhaspati, the pouring out of the others takes place. For that [Bārhaspatya cake], there are eleven or twelve potsherds; for the other cakes, there are three sets of twelve potsherds. The wooden sword (*sphya*) and so forth—all [the implements] are in pairs, just as in the animal-cake sacrifice (*paśupuroḍāśa*). [The formulas for the pouring out are: "I pour out what is pleasing to Indra," "pleasing to Savitṛ," "pleasing to Varuṇa. [The formulas for the protection of the grain are: "O Indra, protect from the Rakṣas; O Savitṛ, protect from the Rakṣas; O Varuṇa, protect from the Rakṣas. The sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is like the pouring out. The oblation...

Having uttered the formula, he gives instructions regarding the animals. Having performed the rites for one animal—beginning with the singeing (*niṣṭapana*) and ending with the cooking of the heart—he then proceeds similarly for the other two. In this regard, there is a specific detail: [he recites] "Do not let the rectum stick," and so forth. Having performed the pouring out (*avahanana*), the placing on the fire (*nirvāpa*), and the spreading of the ashes (*adhi-vapana*), he places eleven portions for Indra. He places twelve for Savitṛ and ten for Varuṇa. He heats the *kamasa* vessels over the boiling water (*madantī*). Having poured away the residue, he says, "O you who are rich in ghee," and so forth. 25.

Having approached them, they take up the draughts as they were previously held: for the Aśvins, for Sarasvatī, and for Indra Sutrāman, [the draughts] of Soma and of Surā. [End of] Chapter 4. [This is] accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. "Recite! he says. Having issued the direction, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the Soma and Surā set forth for the Aśvins, for Sarasvatī, and for Indra Sutrāman," he offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered. ||26-27||

Having silently sprinkled [the vessel] dedicated to Indra, and having adorned it as "pleasing to Savitṛ," he completes the procedure up to the placement [of the vessel] as in the rite for Agni. There is the touching of the vessels dedicated to Savitṛ and Varuṇa with the mantra: "May Indra drive away from us those who have fallen into lesser fortune. Then they proceed with the cups (*graha*). Even those which are modifications of the *juhū*—those cups which they take up—they each take hold of them individually, the Adhvaryu being the one who takes them. The formal call (*saṃpraiṣa*) begins with "To the Aśvins," and so forth. 26–27.

Having offered at the *anuvaṣaṭ* call and having proceeded with the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) dedicated to Bṛhaspati, he purchases a Brāhmaṇa who shall drink the remnants of the cup. He consumes [the remnant] with the formula: "Of this pressed juice that remains here, which Indra drank by his powers—that Soma, the King, I consume here with a gracious mind. (28)

"O Aśvins, [bring] the young Surā"—these are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the offering to all the deities. "O Agni, carry [the oblation] of Soma"—with these words he performs the *anuyāja* (ĀpŚS 19.2.1), says Āpastamba. Having offered at the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*, the procedure continues with the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) dedicated to Bṛhaspati. Then the sacrificer consumes the remnant of the oblation. || 28 ||

"For distinct indeed is the seat ordained for you both by the gods; do not mingle in the highest heaven! You are Surā, the powerful; this is Soma; do not harm me as I enter my own womb"—with these words he addresses the one who is consuming [the Soma]. || 29 ||
The word "yajamāna" (the sacrificer) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 29 ||

"I have heard of two paths of the fathers, and of the gods and mortals; by these two, this entire world meets together between the eastern and the western signs"—with these words, he should pour [the mixture] into an anthill mound, or drink it himself, or offer it as a complete oblation. 13.8.30–31.
Or he should pour the remainder of the vessel into an anthill or into a pit. || 30 || 31 ||

Having tied a hundred-holed vessel to the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire and having spread it out, they hold it; it is covered with a golden disk (*rukma*) that has a hundred holes. (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, Satyāṣāḍha Śrautasūtra, Book 13)

On the southern fire, they hold a hundred-holed pot suspended by cords. Having spread a filter with its fringes pointing northward over its opening, and having placed a piece of gold weighing one hundred mānas within it with the mantra, "That mind of mine which has gone away... (ĀpŚS 19.3.7), so says Āpastamba. On the southern fire or on the mound (khara), some person holds that hundred-holed pot suspended by means of some cord.

Having spread out the filter with its fringes pointing northward over the hole of that [jar], one places a gold piece weighing a hundred mānas into the hole made of wool, [reciting]: "That mind of mine which has gone away... (VS 18.50). || 32 ||

"May the ancestors rejoice; may we attain the life ordained by the gods, which has Soma as its beginning. May we attain the life ordained by the gods, which is drunk by Indra and is far-seeing. That mind of mine which has gone to Yama, or that which has not yet returned—by means of King Soma, we maintain that within ourselves; may we attain the life ordained by the gods. In this [verse], he should pour the remains of the *surā* into that very [vessel]. || 33 ||
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, the Adhvaryu should pour out the remainder of the *surā*.
He worships the flowing waters with the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses addressed to the Pitṛs. || 34 ||
The overflowing vessel stands near with the verses addressed to the cows and those containing the word "pitṛmatī. || 34 ||

"O Soma, you are the wise one," thus [he says]. (Section 26). With three verses, the Adhvaryu [sits] to the east; with the next three, the Brahman to the south; with the next three, the Hotṛ to the west; with the next three, the Āgnīdhra to the north; and with three verses addressed to Kavyavāhinī [he sits] in the middle. Here he places the *śatātṛṇṇā* vessel. A Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya should not take heed [of this]. To lead the southern fire forward, he himself should remain consuming this remnant of *surā* as his sacrificial food (*vrata*). 35.
"O Soma, you are observant; for with you indeed, O Soma, [are we] with the ancestors"—with these words, the Adhvaryu stands facing west in front of the flowing vessel.

To the south, facing north, the *brahmán* [recites]: "I have summoned the fathers who sit on the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣad-pitaraḥ*); the fathers are invited. With these three verses, the *hotṛ* [recites]. To the west, facing east, [the *adhvaryu* recites]: "The fathers who are consumed by fire (*agniṣvātta-pitaraḥ*), those who are consumed by fire and those who are not consumed by fire, enjoying the milk of the cow Abhivānyā. With the three verses beginning with "O Agni, when you carry the maiden" (*yadagne kanyā vahasi*), "O Agni, praised Jātavedas," and "Mātali with the maidens," the *adhvaryu* places the hundred-holed vessel (*śatātṛṇṇā*) upon the southern fire.

For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, the rites beginning with the carrying forward of the fire from the Dakṣiṇāgni and ending with the establishment of the Śatātṛṇṇā vessel do not take place. Having performed the offerings of the animals, he proceeds with the offerings of the sacrificial cakes (puroḍ

Then, once the installation has been performed, having proceeded with the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) dedicated to Bṛhaspati, the Adhvaryu [recites] "O Śamitṛ, the oblation is ready," and so forth, up to "May your mind be united with my mind; I sprinkle you, who are dear to the Aśvins. Having performed this for one [portion], he brings the other *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter) for the two subsequent ones. With the formula "Svāhā to the heat," he performs it in common (*tantra*) for all; then, in sequence, he places them down with the *pañcahotṛ* formula, and in sequence he [offers].

Having touched the *sruva* and having spread [the butter] in the four [ladles], and so forth; in the *upabhṛt*, there is no taking of the portions (*vyāvadāna*), nor is there gold placed on top, nor is there the pouring of fire. Also, when a portion of the *iḍā* has been cut off, having silently poured [butter] over the *yūpa*, he does not sprinkle it with clarified butter.

Having taken up the *āghāra* ladle and touched it so as not to be deficient, he issues the command: "Recite the invitatory verse for the oblation of the goat to the Aśvins. Having thus issued the command and offered the *vasā-homa* at the half-verse, he pours the remainder into another vessel. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, the offering is made; having stepped back, he performs everything as before, including the under-layering (*upastaraṇa*), but without the *viḍāpa*. He issues the command: "Recite the invitatory verse for the oblation of the ram to Sarasvatī. Having thus issued the command, at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, the offering is made; the *vasā-homa* is offered at the half-verse, and he pours the remainder into another vessel.

For the supreme animal, the rites beginning with the spreading of the under-layer (*upastaraṇa*) and ending with "The breath belongs to Indra" are performed according to the archetype (*prakṛti*). [The Adhvaryu] says, "Recite for the oblation of the bull for Indra; thus give the command. At the half-verse, there is the *vasā-homa* (fat-offering). Having collected the remnants, the oblation is made at the *vaṣaṭ*-call, ending with the worship of the quarters (*dig-upasthāna*) beginning with "The quarters, the intermediate directions... There is an after-recitation (*anumantraṇa*) for both [the fore- and after-portions], as in the case of the *sānnāyya*. *Sara...*

Having performed the ritual for the middle [deity] with the formula "By means of Svāti, may I be... and so forth, he proceeds with the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), beginning with spreading the base of clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle. He says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Indra; sacrifice to Indra; may I be possessed of the power of Indra and an eater of food. [For Savitṛ: "Recite the invitatory prayer for Savitṛ; sacrifice to Savitṛ; may I be an eater of pure food through Savitṛ. [For Varuṇa: "Recite the invitatory prayer for Varuṇa; sacrifice to Varuṇa; may I be an eater of food through Varuṇa. Then he should perform the offering to Vanaspati with the *mārjālīya* waters. || 31 ||
Having completed the *sviṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* offerings for both the animal victims and the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) in a common manner, [he should conclude]. ||37||

He cuts portions for the *sviṣṭakṛt* from the *puroḍāśas*, as stated in the injunction: "He cuts portions for the *paśu-sviṣṭakṛt*. Having cut the portion together with the *paśu-sviṣṭakṛt* and sprinkled it [with clarified butter], he performs the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice—previously prepared with a piece of gold—with the formula: "This oblation to Vaiśvānara... Then follows the *prāśitra*; starting from the *bārhaspatya*, the *iḍā* is taken from the *puroḍāśas*. After the *iḍā*, there is the sprinkling [of clarified butter]. For the *puroḍāśas*, everything up to the cleansing (*mārjana*) is performed, excluding the sacrificer's portion.

Then the Āgnīdhra begins the ritual actions concerning the tethering ropes, beginning with "O you who are being led near. There is the offering of the *svaru* wood-chips, beginning with "Go to the ocean, svāhā. They perform the joint sacrifices (*saṃyājana*) for the wives with the *jāpanī* verses. There is no pouring out of the *palpālī* water, nor is there the untying of the yoke-strap here. One should perform the ritual actions up to the end of the "going away" (*upapodvāsānta*). || 37 ||
They perform the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with spears, māṣa-beans, and vessels. ||38||

With "śūlaiḥ" (spits), meaning heart-spits. One prepares the *māsara* according to the procedure for *mṛjīka*. Āpastamba states: "They call the scrapings *māsara*" (ĀpŚS 19.4.8). By the word "and" (*ca*) in "with vessels and [the cup]," the *śatātṛṇṇā* vessel and the cooking pot (*sthālī*) are also included. He offers a cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) to Varuṇa. Regarding the ritual of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath): there is no *paristaraṇī* grass, no *paribhojanī* grass, no *ulaparājī*, and no *veda* mat. Having prepared the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick), the vessels used specifically for the preparation of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) are to be used again.

Having set out the vessels required for the preparation of the *puroḍāśa* cakes, excluding the *agnihotra-havaṇī*, he performs the rites beginning with the preparation of the *pavitra* strainers. Reciting "I pour out what is pleasing to Varuṇa," and so forth, he pours out the remnants of the water used for washing (*āpyalepa*) and sets down the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling waters with the formula, "Be purified by the clarified butter. The clarified butters are taken up; this is the *prāṇa* offering. Having adorned the sacrificial post like that of the *avabhṛtha* bath, he silently places it on the northern shoulder of the altar.
Its ritual procedure is explained by that of the Soma-sacrifice *avabhṛtha*.
