The ritual procedure for the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*) is explained as being the same as that of the Soma sacrifice. Accordingly, he should offer the *avabhṛtha* oblation with the verse, "O giver of life... and "Wide indeed is the King... (RV 1.24.8).
The Sāman is not sung. 13.8.40.
They [the verses] belong to the Sāman-chanting because of the absence of a Prastotṛ.
Having gone over silently, he offers it according to the manner of the *māsara* and the *ṛjīṣa*. ||41||

"O King, you have been born for eternity," [he says]. At the end of the *viṣṭakṛt* or at the end of the *anūyāja* offerings, having performed [the rites], he presents the mother in the form of the *ṛjīṣa*. The sprinkling of the *māsara* is done silently. Having filled the ladle with *māsara*, he submerges it with a mantra; those drops are touched. || 11 ||

"O divine Varuṇa, that noose of yours which has the Gāyatrī as its meter and is established in the Brahmin—by this [offering] I release it from you; to it, Svāhā! With these words, he throws the Aśvin cup. "O divine Varuṇa, that noose of yours which has the Triṣṭubh as its meter and is established in the Kṣatriya—by this [offering] I release it from you; to it, Svāhā! With these words, he throws the Sārasvata cup. "O divine Varuṇa, that noose of yours which has the Jagatī as its meter and is established in the Vaiśya—by this [offering] I release it from you; to it, Svāhā! With these words, he throws the Aindra cup.

"O God Varuṇa, that noose of yours which has the *anuṣṭubh* as its meter and is established in the quarters—this I appease for you with this; to it, svāhā!"—with these words he offers the perforated pot (*śatātṛṇṇā sthālī*). "O God Varuṇa, that noose of yours which has the *paṅkti* as its meter and is established in speech—this I appease for you with this; to it, svāhā!"—with these words he offers the spits (*śūla*). 42.

There is no throwing in of the *acinādi* grasses, the *atrāṇas*, or the cooking pots (*sthālī*) and so forth. Then, with the mantra "I untie this" (*tataṃ imaṃ viṣyāmi*), the wife unties the knot. Having put on other two garments, she throws away the two garments [used for the knot]. With the mantra "O divine waters" (*devīr āpaḥ*), having entered [the water], the wife and the sacrificer, both bathed, run over each other's backs with the mantra "May those waters be friendly to us" (*tanūḥ sumitrā na āpaḥ*). There is no [running] with the *añjalikṛmika* garment, because its purpose is the untying of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). There is no sending of the *unnetaṛ* (water-pourer), because there is no *unnetaṛ*; nor is there the bringing [of water].

The sacrificer puts on two garments, the inner one and the upper one. He worships the sun with the mantra beginning "udyat. [End of Paṭala 8] The bringing back [of the fire] is performed silently. This concludes the section accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 20.1.42–43.

Having reached the edge of the water, they proceed silently with fuel-sticks in their hands. They do not, however, [recite] "He is great. Having gone to the place of the sacrificial enclosure (*vihāradeśa*), all [the priests] perform the rites beginning with "We have placed fuel upon thee" (*edho 'sy edhiṣīmahi*) and ending with "I have followed the waters" (*apo 'nvacāriṣam*). Then the sacrificer performs the rites from the *viṣṇukrama* steps up to the feeding of the Brahmins, as in the *nirūḍhapaśubandha* sacrifice, including the placing of fuel-sticks (*samidādhāna*). Having performed the worship (*upasthāna*) with the verse "Agni has sacrificed" (*āyāḍ agniḥ*), the Brahman priest departs. According to some, the *viṣṇukrama* steps and so forth follow immediately after that. 13.

One should cause him who has vomited Soma to sacrifice. One should cause him who has over-poured Soma to sacrifice. One who desires a kingdom, one who is deprived of his kingdom, one who desires a village, one who desires offspring, one who desires cattle, one who has been superseded by his prosperity, or one practicing sorcery against another—such a person should sacrifice with this [rite]. It is prescribed for all consecrations. With this, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya desiring prosperity should sacrifice; desiring prosperity, he should sacrifice. (Section 27) ||44||
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the thirteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Thus ends the thirteenth book of the Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra. ||13||

The Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice is prescribed for one who has vomited Soma and for one whose Soma has been over-purified (*somātipūta*). Because it is heard in another Vedic branch (*śākhāntara*), the *somātipūta* and the *somavāmī* are indeed Brāhmaṇas; for these two qualifications do not apply to Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas. But surely, according to the Saumaka [text], there is also the injunction regarding the *nyagrodha* tree for those two. Therefore, why should this [Sautrāmaṇī] not take place when there is such over-purification or vomiting of that [tree-juice]? To this it is replied: even if the acquisition of ritual properties (*dharma*) occurs through the assumption of a functional identity (*kāryāpatti*), this is not a property of the Soma sacrifice.

What, then, is the case here? It is the injunction of a different sacrifice for one who has vomited Soma. However, this applies even to members of the three higher castes who have piled the fire-altar (*agnicit*), because of the injunction regarding the connection with the fire. Āpastamba also says: "One should cause the sacrifice to be performed for one who has vomited Soma, one who has passed over the Soma, a king who is being expelled or has been expelled, one who is being consecrated, or one who is being consecrated. One who is being subjected to malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) should perform the sacrifice. So too one who performs malevolent magic, or one desiring leadership, or one desiring offspring, or one desiring cattle. This [sacrifice] is prescribed for all types of consecrations."

"By that [rite], a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or whoever desires splendor (*tejas*) should sacrifice" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 19.4.14). One who desires prosperity (*bhūti*) among the three castes should sacrifice. The repetition [of the concluding statement] is for the purpose of indicating the end of the question. Thus ends the eighth chapter in the thirteenth book of the *Mahādevaśāstrisaṃkalitā* commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*, in the first series. The thirteenth book is complete. 13.13.44.
Now begins the fourteenth question:
"The king shall sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice. ||1||
He who should desire, "May I attain all prosperities," [should perform this].
He settles in a wonderful place of sacrifice for the gods, of auspicious name, where the waters in front of him are pleasant, easy to plunge into, and not turbulent. (3)
On the full moon day of Caitra, one should sacrifice with the Sāṃgrahaṇī iṣṭi; on the subsequent new moon day of that month, one should perform the Saṃjñānī sacrifice.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, he sacrifices a hornless bull of many colors, dedicated to Prajāpati. || 5 ||
On the subsequent new moon night of that period, they bring the great officiating priests from all directions by carriage, not on foot.
Every day they bring the others until the Subrahmaṇyā call. ||7||
He has his hair and beard shaved; he clips his nails; he cleans his teeth; he bathes; he puts on an unwashed garment. ||8||
When the sun is behind the trees, he restrains his speech.
Restraining his speech, he offers the Agnihotra for this night.
The enemies and the givers sit around him; according to some, they are all givers. || 11 ||

"Homage to the Seer, homage to the One who sees nearby, homage to the One who sees from afar; homage to the Proclaimer, homage to the One who proclaims nearby, homage to the One who proclaims from afar; homage to the Hearer, homage to Being, homage to Non-being; homage to what has been born, homage to what is yet to be born; homage to what has come into existence, homage to what is coming into existence; homage to Speech, homage to the Lord of Speech; homage to the Eye, homage to the Ear; homage to Austerity, homage to Brahman"—with these words he worships the rising sun.

When the sun has risen, he worships Agni with the mantra: "Homage to Agni, who dwells on the earth"; Vāyu with: "Homage to Vāyu, who dwells in the intermediate space"; and Sūrya with: "Homage to Sūrya, who dwells in heaven. ||13||
Having placed fuel-sticks of reed (vetasa) upon the fire, he offers eight full oblations with the verse: "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning. || 14 ||
"O gods, exert your prowess among the gods!"—thus [he recites] three verses. || 15 ||
Four kinds of water are collected from the various directions. || 16 ||
In them he cooks the brahmaudana. || 17 ||

Having spread a layer of ghee in a vessel and placed a silver plate upon it, he takes out the *brahmaudana* rice into it, pours abundant clarified butter over it, places a golden plate on top, sprinkles more butter over that, and offers it to four great officiating priests who are descendants of Ṛṣis.
To those who have partaken [of the food], he gives four thousand gold coins (*niṣkas*), four chariots drawn by mules, and these two golden ornaments weighing a hundred *mānas*. (Section 1) 19.
The girdle is made of wood or of muñja grass, and it is twelve or thirteen cubits long; he anoints it with the remnants of the *brahmaudana* rice.
They prescribe the forms of the horse: white, black-spotted, reddish-brown, dappled, or ruddy-brown. || 21 ||
Or he should sacrifice a white animal whose caul is black; it should be a Soma-drinker, the son of two Soma-drinkers.

Those two infants who, when born, were made to drink Soma from the tip of a blade of grass—they become drinkers of Soma. He who is born from those two is the son of the Soma-drinkers. That infant who, when born, is made to drink Soma from the tip of a blade of grass—he becomes a drinker of Soma. || 23 ||
He entrusts the Adhvaryu, who has a mother and a father and is well-trained and bears his burdens upon his back, for the sake of sovereignty. || 24 ||

"O Brahmins and kings, this king is your *adhvaryu*; whatever honor is due to me, bestow that upon him; and whatever medical treatment is yours, let that be his as well. This continues for as long as the king serves as the *adhvaryu* at the sacrifice.

Having taken up the halter with the mantra "Of thee, the god... (devasya tvā), he addresses the horse while it is being led forward with the mantra "They have grasped this halter of the Truth" (imām agṛbhṇan raśanām ṛtasya). || 26 ||
"O Brahman, I shall bind the sacrificial horse for the gods and for Prajāpati; may I prosper through it," with these words he addresses the Brahman priest. || 27 ||
When [the Adhvaryu] has been answered with, "May you prosper through that for the gods and Prajāpati," he addresses the horse with the formula, "Thou art the name-giver. || 28 ||
Regarding this, some authorities prescribe the formal entrustment to the Adhvaryu priest.

They bring a four-eyed dog, bound with a cord of *viṣvaga-vandha* grass. The son of the father’s younger sister leads in front; the son of the mother’s younger sister follows behind, being a *pauṃścaleya* (the son of an unchaste woman), holding a pestle of *saidhraka* wood and having wrapped his knee with a piece of cloth. They plunge into the water—the horse and the dog as well. 14.1.30.

With the words, "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Prajāpati," he sprinkles the horse from the front toward the west. With "To Indra and Agni, thee," [he sprinkles it] from the south toward the north. With "To Vāyu, thee," [he sprinkles it] from the rear toward the east. With "To the Viśve Devas, thee," [he sprinkles it] from the north toward the south. With "To the gods, thee," [he sprinkles it] from below; or with "To all the gods, thee," [he sprinkles it] from above. || 31 ||
Where there is the station of the two dogs, he consecrates that dog, either before the sprinkling or [after it]. (Section 2) 32.
"He who wishes to kill the courser"—with these words, the son of a harlot strikes the dog with a club made of *saidhraka* wood. || 33 ||
Alternatively, on the previous day, one should strike a dog with the verse "paro martaḥ," and having washed the horse's hooves, he washes the right hoof.
With the mantra "I and you, O slayer of Vṛtra," the Brahman priest takes the hand of the sacrificer. || 35 ||
"Exerting thy power, O thou who hast become Indra, come hither," with these words the Adhvaryu makes the sacrificer recite. || 36 ||

They bring the *aiṣīka* grass-bundle. They lift it up from the east toward the west, bound with a triple cord. To it, a fresh branch of cane is fastened. Having spread it out, they hold it supported by two hundred [men] on the south and two hundred on the north.

With this [verse], the great officiating priests sprinkle him from each direction, thinking: "Having sacrificed with this sacrificial horse, may this king slay Vṛtra. With a hundred princes, the Adhvaryu stands to the east, facing westward. [They sprinkle him] thinking: "Having sacrificed with this sacrificial horse, may this king be invincible. With a hundred fierce non-princes, the Brahman stands to the south, facing northward.

"Having sacrificed with this pure horse, may this king become the ruler of this people—possessing many cattle, many horses, many goats and sheep, much rice and barley, much mung beans and sesame, much gold, many elephants, and many male and female slaves; may he be wealthy, prosperous, abundant in the increase of riches, and successful. With these words, the Hotṛ, together with a hundred charioteers and village headmen, stands behind [the horse], facing eastward.

"Having sacrificed with this pure horse, may this king attain a full span of life"—saying this, the Udgātṛ, together with a hundred attendants (kṣattṛ) and collectors (saṃgrahītṛ), causes the horse, which has been sprinkled with water as the sacrificial fee, to step upon the water from the north. Standing, they walk toward the four directions between the place where he stands and the spot where he steps.
With the three verses addressed to Viṣṇu—namely, "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," "pratadviṣṇuḥ," and "divo vā viṣṇave"—he offers three oblations.
With the words, "Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! he consecrates the drops of semen that fall from the horse.
He repeats this section ten times.
According to some, one hundred times; according to others, one thousand times. 42.
According to some, [this occurs] an immeasurable number of times.
He offers the preliminary oblations of the horse with the formulas: "To Agni, svāhā! and "To Indra and Agni! 44.
Having consecrated the horse with the mantra "vibhūrmātra," he releases it with the formula: "Thou art the earth; for the past thee, for the present thee, for the future thee."

He hands it over with the words, "The gods who guard the quarters. For there are a hundred princes worthy of the couch who are the gods guarding the quarters; clad in armor, they protect this [horse]. They follow it, never turning back.

Whichever Brahmin clans they encounter, they should ask them, "How much do you know of the Aśvamedha? Whosoever does not know it, having defeated him, they should cause food and drink to be brought from his family. ||47||
Whatever food is found in the country, that is his food; he dwells in the family of a chariot-maker. (Khaṇḍa 3) || 48 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the fourteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
Now begins the second chapter in the fourteenth book.
Here, with the formula "Dhṛtis, svāhā! he offers four evening *dhṛti* oblations on the four feet of the horse.
To Savitṛ, in the morning, an offering on eight potsherds. || 2 ||

Before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, he offers the horse’s tracks in the Āhavanīya fire with the formulas: "To the sound *īm*, svāhā! To that which has been made with *īm*, svāhā! He offers the forms of the horse with the formulas: "To the dappled one, svāhā! To the black one, svāhā! To the white one, svāhā!"
Some recite [the order] in reverse. || 4 ||
The sacrificial fee is gold weighing one hundred mānas. || 5 ||
While she was thus established, two Brahmins skilled in the lute sang: "You have given," "you have sacrificed," "you have cooked," "you have done that well. ||6||
To Savitṛ Prasavitṛ at midday, there is an offering on eleven potsherds; a silver śatamāna is the sacrificial fee. || 7 ||
To Savitṛ, for the afternoon, there is an offering on twelve potsherds; a gold coin weighing one hundred mānas is the sacrificial fee. ||8||
When that [altar] has been established, he spreads a golden cushion to the south of the altar; upon it the Hotṛ sits down. || 9 ||
To the south are the Brahman and the Udgātṛ priests.
With the front of Hiraṇyakaśipu [he struck] the Hotṛ priest. || 11 ||
The Adhvaryu [places it] upon a golden mat or a wooden board. || 12 ||
To the south, those with lutes and counters are seated nearby. || 13 ||
When they have all sat down, the Hotṛ addresses the Adhvaryu, saying: "Adhvaryo! ||14||
Intending to recite the *pāriplava* and the *bhauvanya*, the Adhvaryu responds with the formula: "Ho! iha hotar! (O Hotṛ, here!). || 15 ||

When the *pāriplava* and the *bhauvanayava* have been completed, he gives the direction: "O lute-players and chanters, sing together with these ancient kings who performed good deeds, [praising] the sacrificer. He shall always give the direction in this manner. (Section 16)

While the evening oblations are being offered, the royal bard, accompanied by the lute, sings: "Thus you donned the skins, thus you fought, thus you slew that enemy in battle, thus you displayed great heroism! 17.

Every evening he offers the *sāyaṃdhṛti* oblations; every morning he sacrifices with the *iṣṭis*. The *pāriplava* and the *bhauvanya* are performed regularly. At the conclusion of the *iṣṭis*, a Brāhmaṇa and a Rājanya play the lute (*vīṇā*) and the drum (*gaṇakī*). When the *iṣṭis* have ceased, he gives them a hundred [cows] and a chariot drawn by mules; according to some, a hundred and a chariot drawn by mules.
This year consists of thirty months. || 19 ||
After eleven months have passed, he binds a horse to an *aśvattha* tree in the cow-pen.
For him, being bound, they bring fodder. || 21 ||
"If one should find the horse afflicted by disease, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni"—thus are the expiations for the horse explained in the Brāhmaṇa. 22.
On the new moon day, he collects the materials for the fire-pan.
The initiation rite consists of the Traidhātavīya offering.
At the time of the initiation oblations, he offers three Vaiśvadeva oblations and four Udgrahaṇa oblations.

"Agni experienced the heat"—these are the *audgrahaṇa* verses. "Svāhā to the intention, to the intended"—these are the *vaiśvadeva* verses. For seven days, he proceeds daily with the *audgrahaṇa* and *vaiśvadeva* offerings. || 26 ||
This very time for the initiation-oblations, having increased, consists of successive Vaiśvadeva offerings. ||27||
All [the oblations] are offered on the final day. || 28 ||
With the mantra "Bhuvo devānāṃ karmaṇā," he consecrates him with the ṛtudīkṣās as he mounts the black antelope skin. || 29 ||
With the mantra, "O Brahman, born as the seed," he worships the principal [fire] that has been produced. || 14.2.30 ||
When the speech has been released, the attendants with lutes and counters [announce]: "The gods have honored this sacrificer," and thus he gives the formal command. 31.
When the *vasatīvarī* waters are being poured out, he gives the final direction to the gods: "At the end of the *sutyā* days, [perform] the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice for Prajāpati. (32)
The altar is twice as large; the fire-altar consists of twenty-one parts. || 33 ||
He proceeds with the Vaiśvānara offering. || 34 ||

He offers a sacrifice consisting of ten oblations, beginning with "To Agni, who is associated with the Gāyatrī, the Trivṛt-stoma, the Rathantara-sāman, and the spring season, [an offering] on eight potsherds. Thus he prepares the Sarvapṛṣṭhyā iṣṭi.
The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are "samiddiśām" and so forth. || 36 ||
"Who yokes you? May he yoke you," with these words he yokes the enclosing-sticks (paridhis).
On the chariot-stand, which serves as the oblation-holder, he erects a sacrificial post made of *rājjudāla* wood, twenty-one cubits in height, so that it stands nearest the fire.
There are two [reeds] made of *pautudrava* wood on both sides. || 39 ||

There are three stakes of *khadira* wood to the south and three to the north; three of *bilva* and *pālāśa* wood to the south and three of *bilva* wood to the north; they prescribe one at the very end, and the *upaśaya* (resting-stake) is of *pālāśa* wood.
He takes the *vasatīvarī* waters, which consist of four portions of water collected from the various quarters. ||41||
On the following day, the Catuṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma sacrifice of the Gotama-Catuṣṭoma type is performed first.
At the time for the animal sacrifices, he dedicates the eleven animals of the Aikādaśina set.

At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he distributes on each successive day, having divided it into three equal parts, that which belongs to the kingdom, whatever else belongs to the Brahmins, and from the wealth consisting of land, the armies, and the men. (43)
The eastern direction to the Adhvaryu, the southern to the Brahman, the western to the Hotṛ, and the northern to the Udgātṛ. || 44 ||
Or rather, [the path] to the east for the Hotṛ, and to the west for the Adhvaryu; the Hotrakas follow this very same [path]. || 45 ||
The day concludes with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings. (Section 6) 46.
Thus ends the second chapter in the fourteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the third chapter of the fourteenth book:
One should construct thirty-six sleeping-places around the Āhavanīya fire.

When the sun has set, having ascended thirty-six steps of the couch, they offer oblations of food throughout the entire night with wooden ladles made of *khadira* wood, using these recitations beginning with "Svāhā to one! || 2 ||
Clarified butter, honey, rice grains, flattened rice, parched grain, groats, fried barley, flour, lentils, and millet grains—with clarified butter and with food. Thus [it is said]. (3)
They offer in alternating fashion: the odd-numbered oblations with clarified butter and the even-numbered ones with food; finally, they offer all with food.
In this regard, some authorities record the application of mantras that have already been employed as well as those yet to be employed. (5)

At dawn they offer with "Svāhā to Uṣas! at the break of day with "Svāhā to the Dawn! when about to rise with "Svāhā to the one about to rise! as he rises with "Svāhā to the rising one! once risen with "Svāhā to the one who has risen! Finally they offer with "Svāhā to heaven! Svāhā to the world! He sets aside the remnants of the food.
The twenty-first [day] is extended as an Ukthya sacrifice; the Mahānāmnī verses are the Sāman.

Between the Āgrayaṇa and the Ukthya, having pressed the worldly Soma, they draw the two Mahiman cups with a golden and a silver vessel. The Adhvaryu draws the first with the golden one, using either the verse "He who breathes" (*yaḥ prāṇata*) or "He who gives life" (*ya ātmadā*). || 8 ||
The Pratiprasthātṛ [offers] the subsequent [oblation] with a silver vessel, with the verse: "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning. ||9||

"The life of the sacrifice flows as dear honey; the father of the gods, their progenitor, the radiant one. He bestows treasure from the secret depths of the two worlds—the most intoxicating, exhilarating, and Indra-like juice. With these words, he fastens a golden ornament upon the necks of the horses. 14.3.10.
"You are a falcon, having the Gāyatrī metre; I take hold of you; carry me safely across," with these words they take hold of the horse's tail.

"May Agni slay the Vṛtras," [saying this] they follow the horse while moving along for the Bahiṣpavamāna chant, or [they do so with the verse] "The steed has stepped forth with his strides; the steed has transcended. Having excluded the Udgātṛ, he chooses the horse for the Udgītha. Mares are kept nearby. When they bray together with these [horses], that is the Udgītha. When they bray back at them, that is the Upagītha. He mutters: "The horse, worthy of sacrifice and fit for the rite, has sung aloud."

With a hundred, or with a hundred-fold, or with a *niṣka*, or with a *śatamāna* [of gold], he addresses the *udgātṛ*: "I shall train the *udgātṛ*; chant after this deity as she chants the *udgītha*. Thus he speaks to the *udgātṛ*. || 12 ||
With the words, "Homage to the King! Homage to Varuṇa! he dedicates the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal at the post standing nearest the fire, using a branch of the cane tree.

The other animals [are tied] with branches of the Plakṣa tree. (Khaṇḍa 17) The black-necked goat for Agni is in front; the ewe for Sarasvatī is on the forehead; the two for Savitṛ are below the forelegs; the two for Sūrya and Yama are on the flanks; the two with hairy thighs for Tvaṣṭṛ are on the hind legs; the two white-backed ones for Bṛhaspati are on the back; the speckled-bellied one for Dhātṛ is on the belly; and the white one for Vāyu is on the tail—these are the animals bound to the horse. 14.
The Rohita, the Dhūmrarohita, and so forth constitute the eighteen [sacrifices]. || 15 ||

Those with black necks are for Agni; the tawny ones are for Soma; the dappled ones are for Savitṛ; the heifers are for Sarasvatī; the dark ones are for Pūṣan; the speckled ones are for the Maruts; the multiformed ones are for the Viśvedevas; and the barren cows are for Heaven and Earth—these are said to be the common animals.

The dappled ones are for Indra and Agni; the black ones are for the Maruts; the hornless ones are for Ka. He sacrifices the first-born to Agni Anīkavant. To the Maruts Sāṃtapanas, he sacrifices the *bāṣka* animals; to the Maruts Gṛhamedhins, the *sāvāta* animals; to the Maruts Krīḍins, the *saṃspṛṣṭa* animals; to the Maruts Svatavantas, the *anusṛṣṭa* animals. These aforementioned are the common sacrificial animals (*saṃcarāḥ*). 17.

The animals for Indra and Agni have prominent horns; those for Indra are multicolored; those for Viśvakarman are brownish-brown, smoke-colored, and shining. For the Soma-drinking Fathers, there are brownish-brown, smoke-colored, and shining ones; for the Fathers seated on the sacrificial grass (Barhiṣad), there are smoke-colored, brownish-brown, and shining ones; for the Fathers consumed by the fire (Agniṣvātta), there are shining, brownish-brown, and smoke-colored ones. Those for Tryambaka are ruddy; some say they are black-spotted.

The white ones are said to be for the Ādityas; these multiform ones are for Indra and Agni; the hornless ones are for the Viśve Devas; those for Śunāsīra are for Śunāsīra; the white ones are for Vāyu (and the white ones are for Sūrya); having thus divided the animals of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices into equal groups, he dedicates them at the other sacrificial posts.
"To Soma, the self-sovereign, two oxen for drawing the cart"—thus he dedicates the animals in pairs, exactly as they are recited in the traditional text, at the very post standing nearest the fire.
When the ritual has been performed with the fire produced by friction, the wives adorn the horse.
Some say it should be surrounded by fire. (Section 8, Sūtra 21)

There are a thousand golden gems, a thousand silver ones, a thousand sea-born or shell-made ones, or a thousand glass ones. Young girls string the glass beads onto the horse's tail-hairs; they fasten the other gems upon its necks. With the word "Bhūḥ," the chief queen fastens the golden ones; with "Bhuvaḥ," the favorite wife the silver ones; with "Suvaḥ," the discarded wife the shell-made ones.

With the formula, "May the Vasus anoint you," the queen anoints the horse with guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter; with "May the Rudras anoint you," the favorite wife with safflower oil (or *kausumbha*); with "May the Ādityas anoint you," the discarded wife with mustard oil; and with "May the Viśve Devas, common to all men, anoint you," the other wives with the original substance. Some authorities prescribe the application of ointment and the fastening of the jewel in reverse order.
With the verse "They harness the ruddy one," he yokes the horse to the chariot. || 24 ||
They harness his two beloved bay horses that cross over the wings; he yokes the two side-horses to the chariot that carries the leader. || 25 ||
"Making a banner for those who have no banner," with these words he raises the flagstaff on the chariot. || 26 ||
With the words "Like a cloud," he puts on the armor. || 27 ||
"With the bow, the cattle"—with these words, he touches the bow.
As if about to speak, she approaches the ear; "It is dear," she says to the bowstring.
They move like the two ends of a bow, as if toward a common woman.
"He is the father of many; many are his sons"—with these words, he fastens the quiver upon his back. || 31 ||
Standing on the chariot, he consecrates the charioteer with the mantra: "He who, standing on the chariot, guides the horses."
"Those with bull-like hooves make a piercing sound," thus [he addressed] the horses. (33)
"O fathers who sit at the sweet draught"—with these words [he addresses] the ancestors. || 34 ||
"He wears the wings of a bird; a deer is its tooth"—with these words he takes up the arrow. || 35 ||
"O straight-flying one, protect us!"—with these words he performs the act of entrustment.

With the words, "They strike the flanks of these," taking up the horse-whip (*aśvājani*), he moves around as if with coils like a serpent; with the words, "He encompasses the arm," he touches [the horse] to the extent of a cubit.
With the five verses beginning "O Lord of the Forest, be firm of limb," [he consecrated] the chariot. || 38 ||
"O you who are not deluded, turn these [carts] back!"—thus they cause the drums to resound. 39.

With the verse, "O Savitṛ, those paths of yours which are ancient," they approach the edge of the water; then, with the verses, "The steed has stepped forth with his strides," and "Do thou thyself, O steed, enjoy the waters," they cause the horse to plunge into the water.

With the verse, "Since the wind has gone to the waters," he turns [the chariot] to the right. At this point, some prescribe the yoking of the draft animals. Wherever it departs from there, it remains standing. 41.
With the verse, "I loosen thy cords," he unlooses the horse. || 42 ||
With the words, "The sky is your back," he cleanses the back of the horse. 43.
"Rathavāhana"—with these words, he places the chariot upon the chariot-stand together with the charioteer.
When it has been placed [on the fire], he descends with the one who collects [the coals]. || 45 ||
They present the horse as it has been brought forward. || 46 ||
"O giver of parched grain! O giver of shade! O giver of glory! May it be mine!"—with these words, the wives take the remnants of the food to the horse.
He who eats what has been sown by his wife obtains offspring and the kingdom. || 48 ||
"The vigorous steed has stepped across with his strides; the vigorous steed has transcended. Heaven is your back, the earth your seat"—with these words, he consecrates the horse. || 49 ||
They employ [the victim] according to how it has been prepared. 14.3.50.
They tie some animals to the horse, others to the sacrificial posts, and they secure the wild animals to the cross-beams.
Having sprinkled the horse, they cause it to drink. || 52 ||
If, while being made to drink, he does not drink, one should cause him to drink [the mixture] with the formula: "The fire was the victim."
"Kindled, he is the maker of ointment for our prayers"—these are the *āprī* verses for the horse. || 54 ||

While the fire is being carried around [the victim], he offers the *apāvya* oblations with the verse: "May the ram protect you with cooked offerings. They immolate the domestic animals that have been encircled by fire and release the wild ones. Of those animals that have been encircled by fire and are paired, they release two at a time:
either a mare and a man, or a mare and a woman.

They immolate the horse upon a golden *hiraṇyakaśipu* and a golden *rukma*, both covered with a garment dyed with turmeric (*tārpya*) and used for ritual purposes. They immolate the other animals on branches of the *plakṣa* tree; they immolate the horse at its root, and the other animals with cords. 56.
While the horse is being slaughtered, he offers oblations with the formulas: "To Prāṇa, svāhā! To Vyāna, svāhā! (57).

Once it has been slaughtered, he offers the Aśvastomīya oblation with the sixteen verses beginning, "When you first neighed at birth," or with thirty-six verses. With the verse, "The steed has stepped out with his strides," the Prastotṛ chants the Yāma Sāman. (Section 10) (58)
Thus ends the third paṭala in the fourteenth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the fourth chapter in the fourteenth book.
With the words, "O Mother, O Ambālī, O Ambikā," the Pratiprasthātṛ leads the wife into the enclosed space.
Having tied up their right tufts of hair, they beat their left thighs, while according to some, they beat their right thighs.
"O you who are the lord of hosts, we invoke you"—saying this, they run around the horse, keeping it to their right.
"May the protectors who stand protect you"—saying this, they mutter it as they walk around, repeatedly going round and round.

Having tied up their left hands, they strike their right thighs with their left hands, or their left thighs with their right hands, according to some teachers. They move three times counter-clockwise and three times clockwise; finally, as before, they complete nine circumambulations. 5.
"O Amba, O Ambāli, O Ambikā!"—with these words, the queen mounts the horse.
Thinking, "Let us both extend our four feet together," they extend their feet. || 7 ||
"May I be you, may you be me; may we both be born of the lineage of Surā; let us lie there interlacing these four limbs"—with these words, she interlaces her feet.
"O fortunate one, dweller of Kāmpīla!"—with these words, the Adhvaryu covers the queen and the horse with a garment made of fine linen.
"Place the bowl between my thighs," he says; thus he joins the organ of generation with the organ of generation. || 14.4.10 ||
"O Amba! O Ambāli! O Ambikā!"—thus he reproaches the queen.
"May he raise her upward"—thus do the wives meditate upon her.
The chief queen censures three times; the wives respond three times with each successive verse of the following [hymn].
They recite all the verses containing the word "surabhi," beginning with "I have performed the praise of Dadhikrāvan. (14)
They purify themselves with the three verses beginning, "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss. ||15||
With two verses beginning "Gāyatrī" and "Triṣṭubh," the chief queen prepares the paths for the sword on the horse using golden needles.

With the next two verses, they fashion the paths for the *vāvātā* cow with silver [spears], and with the following two verses, those for the *parivṛktī* cow with copper or iron [spears]; they fashion the incision-paths for the hornless goat and the *gomṛga* silently.
They smear [the body] with barley flour or wheat flour. || 18 ||
It is understood that this is for the sake of not interrupting the hair. || 19 ||
"Who flays you? Who dissects you?"—with these words he flays the horse's hide. || 14.4.20 ||
There is no omentum of the horse. (Section 11, Sūtra 21)
The fat is called candra; one extracts it. || 22 ||
He rescues the other animals. || 23 ||
When the omenta have been cooked, he places the omenta of the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal upon a mat of Vetasa wood to the north, above the fire.
To the south, on the branches of the Plakṣa tree, [the entrails] of the other animals [are placed]. || 25 ||
In one way, he proceeds with the omenta of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati. || 26 ||

"Recite for the omentum and the fat of the other animals dedicated to Prajāpati, which are marked by the moon. "Give the command for the omentum and the fat of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, which are marked by the moon"—with these words he gives the *saṃpraiṣa* for the omenta of the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal; or he gives the command for the omentum and the fat as they are being presented. || 27 ||

"Recite the invitatory prayer for the omenta and the fat of the *usra*, the goats, and the rams of all the gods. "Prompt the offering of the omenta and the fat of the *usra*, the goats, and the rams of all the gods"—with these words he gives the direction for the other animals; or he says, "Prompt the offering of the omentum and the fat. 28.

Before the offering of the omenta, he first offers the Mahiman cup with the formula, "Svāhā to the gods," or having offered it with the verse, "That greatness of yours which has become manifest among the gods," he performs the remaining rites.

After the offering of the omentum from above, he offers to the gods with "Svāhā! and, having offered either with the verse "That greatness of yours which was manifested upon the earth," he prepares the remnant.
In this very context, the ritual cleansing is prescribed. || 31 ||

Having sat down on both sides of the sacrificial post in front of the Āhavanīya fire, the Hotṛ and the Brahman engage in a theological debate (*brahmodya*); the Brahman sits to the south and the Hotṛ to the north. Now, the questions of the Hotṛ, beginning with "What was the primary consciousness? (*kiṃ svid āsīt pūrvacittiḥ*), are well-known from the Brāhmaṇa. They cause the victim to be slaughtered after the victory of the Brahman.

For Prajāpati, they perform the dismemberment of the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal, using their bones and hair without piercing them crosswise, acting according to the injunction: "Dissect the pig's dissection! || 33 ||
He sets aside the blood of the horse for the sake of the Sviṣṭakṛt offering. || 34 ||
He consecrates him with the hymn of Mahendra, using the throat of a wild ox and the hoof of a horse. || 35 ||
With the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning," he offers six oblations to Prajāpati prior to the consecration.

Six [are recited] above; according to some, the seventh is "He who is Prāṇata. Of the preceding [verses], this becomes the first. Prajāpati moves within the womb; being born, he is manifested in many ways. The wise perceive his source; the ordainers seek the station of the rays of light. He who shines for the gods, who is the domestic priest of the gods, who was born before the gods—to that radiant one of the Brahman, let there be homage. Generating the radiance of the Brahman, the gods [attained] that in the beginning.

He who knows this—of him the gods shall be subject; Modesty and Fortune are his two wives; Day and Night are his two sides; the constellations are his form; the Aśvins are his open mouth. "May I desire what is sacrificed; may I desire that [person]; may I desire everything. He has entered and moves within all beings; he has become the sovereign lord of beings. Within his death he performs the *rājasūya* sacrifice; may that king grant approval for this kingdom. "O Prajāpati"—thus [ends] this [verse].

"These worlds belong to you—the quarters, the intermediate directions, the distant realms, the hollows, and the heights. O Prajāpati, creator of all, you whose wealth is life, accept this oblation of ours, O God!"—this is the last verse of the subsequent [section]. 38.

With the formula, "This one is the eastern quarter," he offers fifty oblations of the Prāṇabhṛt bricks to the east of the consecration; with the formula, "The eastern among the quarters, the spring among the seasons," he offers fifty oblations of the Apānabhṛt bricks to the north.

"The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet"—with these words, he places a golden plate with a hundred perforations upon the head of the sacrificer by means of the Puruṣa, Nārāyaṇa. 14.4.40.

"By the arms of Prajāpati and the earth, by the hands of the intermediate space, I consecrate you as Prajāpati for sovereign rule"—with these words, he consecrates him with the remnants of the *mahiman* cups using vessels made of *parṇa* wood upon a lion skin. || 41 ||
They hold a bull's hide over one who is being consecrated. || 42 ||
With the *āprī* verses addressed to Prajāpati, beginning with "His fuel-sticks rise upward," he takes the hand of the sacrificer.
With the two verses beginning "mṛgo na bhīmaḥ," he wipes his face with the Vaimṛdhī hymns. || 44 ||
With the words, "Through the god Agni may I conquer the hostile armies," he strides the Viṣṇu-strides belonging to the Jagatī meter. || 45 ||

He offers twelve oblations with the formulas, "To Madhu, svāhā! To Mādhava, svāhā! Some say there are thirteen. He offers with the formulas, "To Vasanta, svāhā! To Grīṣma, svāhā! etc. (for the remaining seasons). 46.
He undertakes the ritual acts beginning with the placing of the oblation. || 47 ||
To the north and above the fire, upon a mat of vetasa reeds, they arrange the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal in order, limb by limb, facing eastward. (Section 13) 48.
Or to the south of the western [fire], he should tether the other animals to branches of the Plakṣa tree.
These animals are cooked in various pots; the ritual procedure for proceeding with the omenta has been explained. 14.4.50.
With the verse, "The steed has passed over the strides," he offers the entire oblation of a hornless goat and a forest-deer using a mat of reeds.
With the formula, "To the offered oblation, svāhā! he makes an additional libation over what has been offered. || 52 ||
Those who smell the fragrance of the horse that has been offered as an oblation. || 53 ||
It is known that all of them attain worlds of merit. || 54 ||
Having made the portioning of the clarified butter with the formulas, "With the two tusks of Stegāndu" and "The frogs with their jaws," he offers the oblations after having counted them.
Having offered those pertaining to domestic animals, he offers the *anuvākya* pertaining to the forest; having offered that pertaining to Heaven and Earth, he offers the *aśvastomīya*.

"May we indeed establish these worlds—Indra and all the gods. May Indra, together with the Ādityas, establish for us the sacrifice, our bodies, and our progeny. May Indra, with the Ādityas and the host of Maruts, prepare medicines for us. Having offered the two-footed verses beginning with "O Agni, you are our closest," he offers the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation with cooked horse-flesh and blood. 57.
He offers the first oblation with the neck of a wild ox; the second with a horse's hoof; the third with an iron water-pot or a sacrificial vessel (caru). 58.
The day concludes with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings. (Section 14) || 59 ||
Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the fourteenth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Now begins the fifth paṭala in the fourteenth praśna.
On the following day, the Sarvastoma Atirātra sacrifice, having the Bṛhat-sāman as its final stotra, is commenced.

At the time for the animal sacrifices, he dedicates the animals belonging to the Ekādaśina and those dedicated to Vāyu; having seized as the twelfth an ox, hornless and multicolored, dedicated to Prajāpati, for the sake of all desires.
When the Avabhṛtha has been performed, prior to the Sviṣṭakṛt offering. || 3 ||

Having caused [the sacrificer]—who is a descendant of Atri, bald, moist, pure, with reddish-brown eyes, "clothed in rays" (śipiviṣṭa), and covered with freckles—to descend into the avabhṛtha bath, he offers an oblation upon his head with the formula: "To Jumbuka, svāhā! According to some, [he says] "To Cumbuka, svāhā! He makes a second offering with "To Death, svāhā! and a third with "To the murder of an embryo, svāhā! According to some, [he says] "To the murder of a Brāhmaṇa, svāhā! 4.
To him he gives a hundred yoked with thought. ||5||
According to some, one should yoke a hundred [oxen] to the cart. 6.
Both those who have performed meritorious deeds and those who have committed evil deeds descend together for the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha). 7.
Having emerged from the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), they go to the village holding hands.

There are nine white barren cows for Sūrya as *anūbandhya* (consecrated after the sacrifice), or fifteen. Three are for Tvaṣṭṛ: a kid, a *phalmāṣa*, and a *kikidīvi*—the latter being a *vidīgra*. (Section 15) 9.
The Atirātra sacrifice concludes with the offering for Pātnīvata.

On the following day, he performs the animal sacrifice with three victims on a sacrificial post made of Bilva wood with three branches. He sacrifices to Agni, Indra-Agni, and the Aśvins; he immolates those animals. Alternatively, he may offer the first-born of three-year-old cattle to the Aśvins on the middle branch-post; the middle-born of three-year-old cattle for Ūrj (Nourishment) on the southern branch-post; and the last-born of three-year-old cattle for Pṛthivī (Earth) on the northern branch-post.
Having offered the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa), he performs the Mṛgāreṣṭi consisting of ten oblations, beginning with the cake on eight potsherds for Agni Aṃhomuc.
"Manve agneḥ prathamasya pracetasaḥ"—these are the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyānuvākyā*). || 13 ||
The *sviṣṭakṛt* and *iḍā* offerings for the animal-cake sacrifices (*paśupuroḍāśa*) and the *mṛgāreṣṭi* are common [to both]. || 14 ||
On the following day, he prepares twelve *brahmaudana* offerings day after day; he should sacrifice with twelve *iṣṭis*.
Among them, he gives twelve hundred every day. || 16 ||
With the formula, "Three tawny ones for the spring," he should sacrifice with the seasonal animals according to the season, according to the deity, and as they are recited in the traditional liturgy.
The Aśvamedha sacrifice is concluded. (Section 16) 18.

Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fourteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*. Now begins the sixth chapter in the fourteenth book. The *Puruṣamedha* (Human Sacrifice) lasts for five days. It is performed by a king or a Brāhmaṇa who desires: "May I attain preeminence, excellence, sovereignty, and overlordship over all beings. He should sacrifice with this [rite]. 1. *iti satyāṣāḍhahiraṇyakeśisūtre caturdaśapraśne pañcamaḥ paṭalaḥ | atha caturdaśapraśne ṣaṣṭhaḥ paṭalaḥ | pañcāhaḥ puruṣamedhaḥ | rājā brāhmaṇo vā | yaḥ kāmayeta sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ jaiṣṭhyaṃ śraiṣṭhyaṃ svārājyamādhipatyaṃ gaccheyamiti | sa etena yajeta||1||*
The ritual procedure for that is explained by the rules for the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha). || 2 ||

There are twenty-three initiation days (*dīkṣā*), twelve *upasads*, and five *sutyā* (pressing) days. There are eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) and eleven *agnīṣomīya* animals. The first day is an *agniṣṭoma*, the second an *ukthya*, the third an *atirātra*, the fourth an *ukthya*, and the fifth an *agniṣṭoma*. On the middle day, he dedicates the animals belonging to the *puruṣamedha* (human sacrifice).

Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "It has twelve [days] as its minimum. He undergoes initiation during the winter season. Taking recourse to the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*), when he is about to dedicate the persons [for sacrifice], he offers three oblations to Savitṛ with the verses: "O God Savitṛ," "That of Savitṛ," and "All things, O God Savitṛ. ||4||
Having consecrated the one-year-old heifers, he consecrates the men. || 5 ||
"One consecrates a Brāhmaṇa for Brahmā," as it is handed down in the tradition. Of these, he dedicates forty-eight in the middle.
In the others, eleven each; in the middle one, the remaining eight or ten.

Brahmā praises from the south those excellent men who are not joined with fire, using the Puruṣa-sūkta beginning with "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet," identifying the Puruṣa as Nārāyaṇa.

Having led the men around whom the fire has been carried toward the north and released them, and having offered oblations of clarified butter to those respective deities, they then conclude the sets of eleven victims. ||9||

At the time of the sacrificial fees, he gives in the Puruṣamedha the middle portion of the kingdom, as well as whatever else remains from the wealth of the realm—excluding that belonging to Brāhmaṇas—from the various quarters, from the land, and from the armies. (Khaṇḍa 17) 14.6.10.
Just as in the Aśvamedha sacrifice, a Brāhmaṇa who is the sacrificer should give away his entire property. || 11 ||
There are eleven sacrificial posts and eleven *anūbandhya* animals, dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa, to the Viśvedevas, or to Bṛhaspati.

Having performed the Traidhātavīya and Udavasānīya sacrifices, having consigned the fires into separate kindling woods (araṇis), and having worshipped the sun with the Uttaranārāyaṇa hymn, he may settle in his home and undertake whatever sacrificial rites he may intend to perform. ||13||
The Puruṣamedha sacrifice is concluded. || 14 ||
The Sarvamedha consists of ten nights. He who desires, "May I become all this," should sacrifice with this [Rājasūya]. Its ritual procedure is explained by that of the Puruṣamedha. ||15||
The altar is three times that size, the fire-altar consists of one hundred and one layers, and it is the Agniṣṭut sacrifice.
The Agniṣṭoma is the first day; everything is performed as pertaining to Agni. ||17||
Indra is the one to whom the hymn is addressed; thus, for the second time, everything is performed as dedicated to Indra. ||18||
The third [day] is the Sūryastut Ukthya; everything is performed as pertaining to Surya. ||19||
The Viśvedevas-stotra is the *ukthya*; everything is performed as belonging to the Viśvedevas on the fourth day. || 14.6.20 ||
The fifth [book] is the middle one, the Āśvamedhika; in it, he sacrifices a horse fit for the sacrifice. || 21 ||
The sixth, the middle [book], is that concerning the human sacrifice (puruṣamedha). In it, he immolates pure men as sacrificial victims. || 22 ||
The Aptoryāma is the seventh; in it, he immolates all animals fit for sacrifice.
Having cut off the omentum from those animals possessing one, he offers the omenta after having removed the skin. ||24||
They cut down herbs and trees, both green and dry, and scatter them about. || 25 ||
At the morning pressing, when the Nārāśaṃsa cups have been set down, he offers food after food. 26.

"He offers everything for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything"—thus at the midday pressing; likewise at the third pressing, when the oblations have been offered, the Triṇava is the eighth, the Trayastriṃśa is the ninth, and the Viśvajit Sarvapṛṣṭha Atirātra is the tenth. || 27 ||

At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives the middle portion of the kingdom—whatever wealth other than that belonging to the Brāhmaṇas exists within the [four] quarters—together with land and accompanied by men, just as in the Puruṣamedha, just as in the Puruṣamedha. (Section 18) 28.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the fourteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
Thus ends the fourteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
[2065] In the fourteenth book, the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha.

14.1 Now begins the fourteenth question. With joy, I bow to the Lord of Sages, the ocean of grace, the preceptor known as Hiraṇyakeśin, who knows the meaning of the Sūtras, and who possesses the bliss of true consciousness and eternal bliss, which is the goal for all the foremost Siddhas engaged in disciplining their disciples. I praise my Guru Gaṇapati, as well as Maheśāna together with Gaurī, who bestow both birth and knowledge; and I praise Viṣṇu together with Padmā. Thus, the Vājapeya and Rājasūya sacrifices have been explained in the thirteenth [section]; now, in the fourteenth, he explains the Aśvamedha and Naramedha sacrifices. Now, an objection:

In passages such as "He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.3.12), because the word "king" is absent, it is understood that the three castes alone have the entitlement to perform the Aśvamedha. Thus, for the purpose of destroying sin, one should perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice and its meditative worship.

And thus it is said: "This is indeed the expiation for everything, the remedy for everything; by this the gods crossed over all evil, even the slaying of a Brahmin they crossed over by this. He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice and he who knows it thus crosses over all evil, he crosses over the slaying of a Brahmin" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.3.12).

This performance of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) serves as an expiation for every form of evil, whether it be of the nature of a minor offense (*upapātaka*) or a major offense (*mahāpātaka*). Furthermore, for one afflicted by any disease, the performance of the horse sacrifice is the remedy, by way of destroying the sin that is its cause. For this very reason, the gods of the present age, in their previous human birth, avoided minor offenses such as the killing of a cow and major offenses such as the killing of a Brahmin by means of this horse sacrifice.

Therefore, even now, he who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice crosses over the great sins that lead to rebirth; and also that person who knows this Aśvamedha according to the method prescribed in the scriptures. Knowledge is of two kinds: ascertainment of meaning (*artha-nirṇaya*) and meditative worship (*upāsana*). Among these, the ascertainment of meaning is accomplished through a thorough investigation of words, sentences, and the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The method of worship, however, will be explained in the final section (*anuvāka*) of the seventh book (*kāṇḍa*), beginning with the words: "He who indeed knows the head of the horse... (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 7.9.28). Immediately following the injunction for the *Sautrāmaṇī*, the *Aśvamedha* is prescribed, as its occasion has arrived through the recitation of the scriptural mantras:
"The king should sacrifice with the *Aśvamedha*. (1)

It has been stated in another passage that the word "rāja" (king) applies to a Kṣatriya who has undergone consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Accordingly, [the scripture states]: "The Aśvamedha is indeed a sacrifice for a Kṣatriya; therefore, one who possesses a kingdom should perform the Aśvamedha. Kātyāyana also formulated the rule: "The Aśvamedha is a king’s sacrifice" (*rājayajño’śvamedhaḥ*, Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra 10.20.1). "A king’s sacrifice" means a sacrifice belonging to a king; it does not apply to Brāhmaṇas or Vaiśyas. "Aśvamedha" is the name of a three-night sacrificial ritual (*yajñakratu*).

Āpastamba also states: "A sovereign king (*sārvabhauma*) should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha; even one who is not a sovereign may do so" (ĀpŚS 10.1). "Aśvamedha" is the collective name for all the *iṣṭi*, animal, and *soma* sacrifices. Thus, the Aśvamedha is obligatory for a king. || 1 ||
He who should desire, "May I attain all prosperities," [should perform this]. [End of] Paṭala 1. [This work is] accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 309.

The word "Vājasaneyi-brāhmaṇa" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. That [sacrifice] belongs to one who desires all things (*sarvakāma*). And the attainment of all desires does not occur without the realization of the reality known as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), for desires exist only so long as the body and time persist. Therefore, by the phrase "one who desires all things," it is meant that he is one who seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*). And thus it is said: "He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice indeed attains all desires and enjoys all prosperities."

When all desires [are fulfilled]—conquest for the Brāhmaṇa, prosperity for the King (Kṣatriya), and [prosperity] for the Vaiśya—it follows that the entitlement to the Aśvamedha belongs exclusively to these three social classes. || 2 ||
He settles upon a wondrous place of sacrifice for the gods, of auspicious renown, where the waters in front of it are pleasant, easy to plunge into, and not turbulent.

A holy place (*puṇyasthāna*) is one whose sanctifying name is recognized by its mere mention—such as Puṣkaravana, Gītamavana, Vārāṇasī, Kurukṣetra, and so forth. Therein, the waters are pleasant in front, pleasant to the touch, neither too hot nor too cold in the winter; they are easy to plunge into and have excellent landing-stairs (*sutīrtha*). They are "non-reverberating" (*anapaskarī*): those which, having gone away, do not resound (*apa-ītya na paḥ svaranti*), but flow together, consecrate the earth with their currents, and are free from impurities.

The meaning is that on a ground distinguished by such specific qualities, during the time of the Citrā constellation, he determines the site for the sacrifice to the gods and prepares the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*). On the full moon day of Caitra, having performed the morning *agnihotra* and having declared, "I shall sacrifice with the Aśvamedha; may I attain the heavenly world," he performs the recitation of blessings (*svastivācana*) together with Brāhmaṇas right in his own home. Then, having honored him [the officiating priest] with the selection of the *khoma* garment, the *pravāka*, and the *varaṇa* (invitation), and having worshipped him with the *madhuparka* and other offerings, he should send him forth.

That instructor, having arrived at the palace, said in due order: "O King Indravarman, an Aśvamedha sacrifice shall take place; in that [sacrifice], you shall be the Adhvaryu, and so on, down to the Udgātṛ, for the Nāhīna [rite]. To this, the reply was: "The Aśvamedha is not a Nāhīna. After the recitation of *mahan me vocaḥ*, the royal attendants bring the Adhvaryu, Brahman, and Hotṛ—along with elephants, horses, and other [vehicles]—on foot. Mounted [on their vehicles], they proceed to the royal residence, chanting *devo devam asva...* and so forth. Then, the Madhuparka offering is presented to the Udgātṛs.

Then follows the attendance upon the deity, the *nāndī-śrāddha*, and the bringing [of the guest] on an elephant, horse, or other vehicle. Then he should perform the selection of the *āgnīdhra* priest and the offering of the *madhuparka*. || 3 ||
On the full moon day of Caitra, one should sacrifice with the Sāṃgrahaṇī iṣṭi; on the subsequent new moon day of that same month, one should perform the Saṃjñānī sacrifice.

Thinking, "I shall gather this multitude of people who are required for myself," one performs the sacrifice known as the *Sāṃgrahaṇī*. That sacrifice originates in the text: "One desiring a name [should perform] the *Sāṃgrahaṇī* dedicated to the Viśvedevas. It is called *Sāṃgrahaṇī* because by means of it everything required is gathered (*saṃgṛhyate*). "I shall sacrifice with the *Sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice," and so forth; the oblation for the *Sāṃgrahaṇī* will be explained in the section on optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*). Immediately following that is the New Moon sacrifice (*Amāvāsyā*); on that day, "I shall sacrifice with the *Saṃjñānī*," and so forth.

And that [offering] will be explained in its entirety under the name *Iṣṭi*. These two [rites] are performed for one who is free from desire. [In the] fourteenth [chapter], on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, he sacrifices a hornless bull of many colors, dedicated to Prajāpati.

On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, the Maitrāvaruṇa and the Pratiprasthātṛ cause [the sacrificer] to be brought by means of elephants, horses, and so forth. Then, he should immolate a hornless bull dedicated to Prajāpati, of all colors—that is, one possessed of white, blue, yellow, and other hues—having declared: "I shall perform the animal sacrifice; may I obtain all desires. He should dedicate it with the formula: "I dedicate thee, acceptable to Prajāpati. The remainder is according to the Nirūḍhapaśubandha ritual. 5.
On the subsequent new moon day of that [lunar fortnight], they cause the great officiating priests to arrive from every direction by means other than on foot.

On the new moon day occurring immediately thereafter, the Udgātṛ is brought [to the sacrifice] by means of elephants, horses, and so forth. At that time, while already mounted, he recites "The god shall go to the god," and so on. Upon his arrival, the *madhuparka* (honey-mixture) is offered. Alternatively, having performed the formal selection (*varaṇa*) at this time, the *madhuparka* is offered. On that same day, they bring the great priests (*mahartvij*) without foot-soldiers. The meaning is that the bringing of the great priests occurs on this very day. With the exception of the Udgātṛ, the Āgnīdhra has already been brought prior to the sacrifice; the Maitrāvaruṇa and Pratiprasthātṛ are brought at the animal sacrifice (*paśu*). || 6 ||
Now he states the specific rule regarding the calculation of the days: "Or rather, they bring the other [days] day by day until the Subrahmaṇyā. (7)

Every day they bring the others by means of elephants, horses, and so forth, according to seniority, until the *ā-subrahmaṇyā* [call]. Alternatively, those officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who were chosen in their respective homes—those priests they bring without using foot travel; having prohibited them from walking on foot, the king’s men bring those priests by mounting them upon elephants, horses, and the like. In this regard, the time limit is "until the *ā-subrahmaṇyā*."

On whichever full moon day the Sāṃgrahaṇī sacrifice is performed, starting from that point, when one year has passed, on the new moon day of Vaiśākha in the following year—which is the Traidhātavīya day—one begins with the Dīkṣaṇīyā. Within seven days, once that Dīkṣaṇīyā is completed, the initiation (dīkṣā) is finished over a period of three days starting from the day of its conclusion. Thereupon, on the subsequent Prāyaṇīya day, the Subrahmaṇyā litany proceeds.

The formal invitation (*samāvahana*) of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) must be performed up until the *subrahmaṇyā* litany. This is as follows: on the day of the *sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice, having gone to the respective homes of each priest, they mount the Adhvaryu, Brahman, Hotṛ, and Agnīdhra—who have been selected by the *somapravāka*—upon elephants, horses, and other vehicles, and bring them for the sake of the sacrifice.

On the full moon day of Vaiśākha occurring immediately thereafter, the king’s men bring the hornless bull dedicated to Prajāpati—which has been selected as the sacrificial victim—after having mounted it upon elephants, horses, and other vehicles, while the *somapravāka* has already chosen the *maitrāvaruṇa* and *pratiprasthātṛ*. On the new moon day of Vaiśākha occurring immediately after that, they bring the *udgātṛ* by means of elephants, horses, and so forth; for the sake of the *brahmaudana*, four *mahartvijas* are required, and since the *adhvaryu*, *brahman*, and *hotṛ* have already been brought previously, the remaining *mahartvij* is the *udgātṛ*.

Then it proceeded. On the new moon day of Vaiśākha occurring within the year, they brought the Prastotṛ to the Dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi to chant the Sāman by means of elephants and other conveyances. Thereafter, from the day of the commencement of the consecration (dīkṣā) onwards, on the third and subsequent days, they brought the other eight officiating priests (ṛtvij) every day, mounting them upon elephants, horses, and so forth—namely, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Acchāvāka, Neṣṭṛ, Pratihartṛ, Grāvastut, Potṛ, Unnetṛ, and Subrahmaṇya—and they brought them for the sake of the Soma sacrifice. || 7 ||
[Paṭala 1] Accompanied by the commentary *Yogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 211.

Although this Aśvamedha is, through the medium of being a modification (*vikṛti*) of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), an indirect modification of the Agniṣṭoma, and therefore the shaving of hair and so forth would have been obtained [by extension], nevertheless, it does not occur here in proximity to the initiation (*dīkṣā*). Thus, he prescribes here the shaving and other rites which were not previously obtained and are now new: "He shaves his hair and beard; he clips his nails; he cleanses his teeth; he bathes; he puts on a new (unwashed) garment. (8)

Regarding this, Āpastamba also says: "Having performed the New Moon sacrifice, he proceeds to the sacrificial ground. He has his hair and beard shaved; he trims his nails; he cleanses his teeth; he bathes; he puts on a new garment" (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 20.1–13). "New" (*ahata*) means uncut, i.e., fresh.
When the sun has set behind the trees, he restrains his speech.

"Restraining his speech, he fasts; this is for the protection of the heavenly world" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.8.1). This is the Brāhmaṇa passage. The meaning is that by fasting preceded by the restraint of speech, the heavenly world is protected. || 9 ||
Restraining his speech, he offers the Agnihotra for that night.

They offer the Agnihotra for this night while he remains restrained in speech. Even the morning offering is performed at night; there is no release of speech until before the morning offering. The Agnihotra offering is performed by another officiant. 10.
Both enemies and benefactors sit around him; according to some, they are all benefactors. || 11 ||
"Those who are liberal bestow wakefulness," so says Āpastamba; that is, those liberal ones who cause their friends to be vigilant. || 11 ||

"Homage to the Seer, homage to the Witness, homage to the Observer; homage to the Proclaimer, homage to the Proclaimer-nearby, homage to the Proclaimer-following; homage to the Hearer, homage to Being, homage to Non-being; homage to the Born, homage to the Yet-to-be-born, homage to the Past, homage to the Future; homage to Speech, homage to the Lord of Speech; homage to the Eye, homage to the Ear, homage to Austerity, homage to Brahman"—with these words he worships the rising sun.
With twenty-one prostrations, he worships the rising sun.

When the sun has risen, he worships Agni with the mantra: "Homage to Agni, who dwells on the earth. He worships Vāyu with: "Homage to Vāyu, who dwells in the intermediate space. He worships Sūrya with: "Homage to Sūrya, who dwells in heaven. (Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Chapter 11, Section 13)
The Adhvaryu worships Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya with three verses according to their respective characteristics; some say the sacrificer does so.

Having placed fuel-sticks of reed (vaitasa) on the fire, he offers eight full oblations with the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre" (RV X.121.1), and three oblations with the verse, "Devā deveṣu parākramadhvam" (VS XXII.8).

Now follows the construction of the *prācīnavaṃśa* hall. [The sacrificers recite: "We have come here; these are the paths. Because they have already attained prosperity (*gataśrī*), there is the formal depositing (*samāropaṇa*) of all the fires, beginning with the *gārhapatya*. Having entered the *prācīnavaṃśa* hall for the selection of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana-adhyavasāna*), and having placed a fuel-stick of rattan (*vaitasa*) upon the *āhavanīya* fire, he offers eleven *pūrṇāhuti* oblations: eight with the verse "Hiraṇyagarbha," and [the others with]: "O gods, exert yourselves among the gods, svāhā! O first ones, exert yourselves among the second ones, svāhā! O second ones, exert yourselves among the third ones, svāhā! There are four kinds of water brought together from the various directions. || 16 ||

There are four kinds, consisting of four groups: the rainwater (*vārṣyā*), the well-water (*kūpyā*), the stagnant water (*sthāvarā*), and the flowing water (*vahantī*). These are collected from the four directions, not from a single direction. Alternatively—rainwater, well-water, stagnant water, and flowing water constitute the fourfold classification of waters. This is clearly prescribed in the *Āruṇaketuka* layering of the fire-altar: those waters are to be brought from the four directions, beginning with the east, and not from a single direction. (16)
Regarding the cooking of the rice in the struck waters, it says:
"In them he cooks the *brahmaudana*. (17)
In those waters. || 17 ||

Having spread a base of ghee in a vessel and placed a silver plate upon it, he scoops out the *brahmaudana* rice into it, pours abundant clarified butter over it, places a golden plate on top, sprinkles it with more ghee, and offers it to four *ārṣeya* priests who are masters of the *mahāvrata*.

Having spread [ghee] in the ladle and placed a golden disk (*rukmam*) made of silver or other precious metal on top, he hands it over. The mention of the *ārṣeya* (lineage) is so that, when another person is substituted for the *ārṣeya*, or when the *ārṣeya* is absent or unable to perform the duty, the purpose of the *ārṣeya* may still be fulfilled. [He offers] the *brahmaudana* (the Brahmin’s rice-mess) over the *aupāsana* fire. 18.

To those who have eaten [the sacrificial food], he gives four thousand gold *niṣkas*, four chariots drawn by mules, and these two golden ornaments weighing a hundred *mānas* each. (Section 19) To those four great priests who have eaten [the sacrificial food], he gives four thousand gold *niṣkas*, as well as four chariots drawn by mules and these two golden ornaments. (19)
The girdle is made of wood or of muñja grass, twelve or thirteen cubits long; he anoints it with the remnants of the *brahmaudana* rice.
That which remains as the residue of what has been eaten, staying in the bowl, he anoints his nose with it, because of its firmness (or abundance). || 20 ||

They prescribe the forms of the horse as follows: white, black-spotted, reddish-brown, dappled, or ruddy-brown. Or one may sacrifice a white horse whose womb is black; it should be the son of two "Soma-drinkers" (somapa). Those two who, having been born as infants before they have tasted the tips of grass, are made to drink Soma—they are the "Soma-drinkers. The one who is born from those two is the "son of two Soma-drinkers. That infant who, having been born, is made to drink Soma before he has tasted the tips of grass—he is a "Soma-drinker."

He hands over to the kingdom the Adhvaryu who is well-born on both his mother’s and father’s side, who bears [the burden] on his back, and who is self-controlled. "O Brahmins and kings, this is your Adhvaryu; whatever honor was mine, bestow that upon him; and whatever medical care was mine, let that same medical care be his"—thus he says. The Adhvaryu remains the king for as long as the sacrifice lasts.

The forms of the horse: entirely black, entirely white, and so forth; one that has a mother and a father, one that drinks soma, or the son of two who drink soma—having seized such a horse, after the time for the girding with the rope has passed, the Adhvaryu entrusts it to the King. "O Brāhmaṇas, sit down" is the formula of entrustment. It is a measure of weight (palam). O Kings, this horse is yours; whatever honor is mine, that belongs to you, O Adhvaryus; he performs [this act] for you; let it belong to this part [of the sacrifice].
"As long as this king performs a sacrifice, he is indeed the Adhvaryu for the Udgātṛ; whatever he does, that is done for you. (21) (22) (23) (24) (25)
Having taken the halter with the mantra "devasya tvā," he addresses the horse while it is being led forward with the mantra "imāmagṛbhṇan raśanām ṛtasya."
The girdle is twelve or thirteen aratnis long; [the formula] ends with "I take. Having taken it, one consecrates it with the mantra, "This girdle of immortality I bind," says Āpastamba. (26)

"O Brahman, I shall bind the sacrificial horse for the gods and Prajāpati; may I prosper through it"—with these words he addresses the Brahman priest. (27) 114. According to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin: [In the fourteenth book] the Adhvaryu says—alternatively, having addressed the Brahman with the mantra beginning "O Brahman, the horse..."—(27).
When [the Adhvaryu] has been addressed with, "For the gods, for Prajāpati—thereby prosper!," he addresses the horse with the formula, "Thou art the designator" (abhidhā asi). || 28 ||
With that, he ties it on the mother. || 28 ||
In this regard, some authorities prescribe the formal entrustment to the Adhvaryu priest.
Regarding this, some followers of particular Vedic branches recite the formal entrustment to the Adhvaryu priest.

They bring a four-eyed dog, bound with a *viṣvagbandha* cord. The son of the father’s younger sister leads in front; the son of the mother’s younger sister follows behind, being a *pauṃścaleya*, holding a pestle of *saidhraka* wood and having wrapped his knee with a piece of cloth. They plunge the horse and the dog into the water. 14.1.30.

That dog which has two dot-like marks resembling eyes on the upper part of its own eyes is called "four-eyed" (caturakṣa). In that case, some such dog must be led to the place where the horse is submerged.

Regarding the manner of leading that [horse], Āpastamba says: "They lead forth a four-eyed dog, bound with a *viṣvan* cord. The son of the father’s younger sister leads it in front; the son of the mother’s younger sister follows behind. A *saiyaka* pestle, having wrapped its knee with a piece of cloth (*peśas*), follows behind. They cause the horse and the dog to plunge into the water" (ĀpŚS 20.2.10). The two sons of the sacrificer—the king's—namely the son of his paternal aunt and the son of his maternal aunt, go along. Both go, one in front and one behind, of the dog which is being led while bound on all sides. || 30 ||

With the formula, "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Prajāpati," he sprinkles the horse from the front toward the west. With "To Indra and Agni, thee," [he sprinkles] from the south toward the north. With "To Vāyu, thee," [he sprinkles] from the back toward the east. With "To the Viśve Devas, thee," [he sprinkles] from the north toward the south. With "To the gods, thee," [he sprinkles] from below; or with "To all the gods, thee," [he sprinkles] from above. || 31 ||
With the mantra "To Prajāpati, thee," the Adhvaryu, standing facing west in the eastern direction, should sprinkle [the water]; the same should be understood for the subsequent directions. || 31 ||
Where there is the resting place for the two dogs, he consecrates that as the "dog-place," either before the sprinkling or [after it]. (Section 2) 32.
There is an option [regarding the timing] of whether it is before or after the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa). || 32 ||

"He who wishes to kill the courser"—with these words, the son of a harlot (pauṃścaleya) strikes the dogs with a pestle made of *saidhraka* wood. [End of] Paṭala 1, accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 15.

A tree with a great trunk is one in whose center there exists a core as hard as iron, possessed of colors such as black, reddish-brown, and so forth; its pestle is the means [of accomplishment]. A *puṃścalī* is a wanton woman who behaves with many men but remains fixed upon only one husband; she is a slave-girl (*dāsī*). Her son is a "dog-slayer. The Brāhmaṇa states: "The son of a wanton woman slays" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.8.4). || 33 ||
Or on the previous day, he should cause the dog to bite [the horse] with the verse "paro martaḥ," and having washed the horse's feet, he washes the right foot.

Āpastamba states: "He throws [the horse's hoof-print] beneath the horse with the mantra *paro mataḥ paraḥ śva* while stepping around to the south" (ĀpŚS 20.3.14). However, the author of the Bhāṣya, following another sūtra, has assigned the mantra *yo antam* to the act of killing, and has assigned the mantra *paro martaḥ* to the casting of two dot-like marks resembling eyes upon the lower part of the dog's feet and the upper part of its eyes. || 34 ||
With the words, "I and you, O slayer of Vṛtra," the Brahman priest takes the hand of the sacrificer. || 35 ||
The meaning is that one should take the hand—the right hand—of the king. || 35 ||
"Exerting thy power, O thou who hast become Indra, come hither," with these words the Adhvaryu makes the sacrificer recite. || 36 ||
The meaning is clear. || 36 ||

They bring a bundle of reeds. He spreads it out from the east toward the west, bound with a triple cord. To it, a fresh branch of cane is fastened. They hold it stretched out, two hundred [fathoms] to the south and two to the north.

They bring the *udūha* made of reeds (*eṣīka*). Because of the scriptural statement, "He sweeps this ground from the east toward the west," they sweep it. Bound with a leather thong, a branch of cane (*vetasa*) is fastened to that *udūha*; the meaning is that it is bound by a leather strap. Two hundred men hold up that *udūha* from the south and two hundred from the north; thus, the *udūha* becomes large.

With this [verse], the great officiating priests sprinkle him from each direction, thinking: "Having sacrificed with this sacrificial horse, may this king slay Vṛtra. The Adhvaryu, together with a hundred princes, sprinkles him from the east toward the west. [They do so] thinking: "Having sacrificed with this sacrificial horse, may this king be invincible. The Brahman, together with a hundred fierce non-princes, sprinkles him from the south toward the north.

Having sacrificed with this sacrificial horse, may this king [attain] for these subjects: much cattle, many horses, many goats and sheep, much rice and barley, much mung beans and sesame, much gold, many elephants, and much... (116) — The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Chapter 14, Question 1.

"May he be king for a hundred years," [with these words] the Hotṛ, together with a hundred charioteers and village headmen, sprinkles [the horse] from behind toward the east. "Having sacrificed with this sacrificial horse, may this king attain a full span of life," [with these words] the Udgātṛ, together with a hundred attendants and collectors, sprinkles [the horse] from the north toward the south. He causes the horse, once sprinkled, to step forward toward the water; while standing, they go in the four directions between the place of standing and the place of stepping. (38)

They lead up forty-nine horses facing westward. Standing to the east, facing west, the Adhvaryu sprinkles the horse standing in the water with the mantra, "With this horse... while the other princes stand silently. To the south, the Brahman, together with a hundred unanointed princes, [sprinkles] with the mantra, "With this horse...". To the west, the Hotṛ, facing east, together with the Sūtas and Grāmaṇīs, [sprinkles] with the mantra, "With this horse...".

Together with the *kṣattṛ* and the *saṃgrahītṛ*, the *uddātṛ* [stands] to the north, [saying], "Let us drive the horse by this [path]. He causes it to urinate upon a clump of *ajhaipīka* grass; he causes it to flow [past]. He makes the horse halt in a place devoid of water. The sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is performed only in water, not on dry ground. He makes the horse step onto that spot where it has not previously stood. Between the stopping and the stepping, whatever [spot] was previously flowed past—that is the footprint of the horse as it stands up from the water.

However, some maintain that the four priests—the Adhvaryu, Brahman, Hotṛ, and Udgātṛ—by means of its sprinkling, cause the wind to blow toward the four directions beginning with the east, thereby properly encouraging it from each respective direction.
