The Adhvaryu, accompanied by one hundred princes—sons of Kṣatriyas who have been consecrated and are themselves fit for sovereignty—should stand facing west in the eastern direction and sprinkle him from head to foot.

The mantra beginning with *anena* and ending with *vadhyāt* is for the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). The *ugrās* are the brave warriors. The *sūtās* are charioteers. The *grāmaṇyas* are village leaders or village masters. The *śaṃttāras* are those born from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother. The *saṃgrahītāras* are those who increase the treasury. The rest is clear. ||38||
With the three verses dedicated to Viṣṇu—"idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," "pratadviṣṇuḥ," and "divo vā viṣṇave"—he offers three oblations. || 39 ||
In that foot, there are three Vaiṣṇavī [offerings]. Because they are enjoined by the word "juhoti," the offering is made with the utterance of "svāhā. || 29 ||
He consecrates the horse's droppings as they fall with the formula: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! He repeats this section ten times.

The *stokyās* are those verses recited while consecrating small portions of clarified butter (*avasya stokān*), beginning with: "To Agni, Svāhā! To Soma, Svāhā! (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.1.16); he recites these up to ten. || 10 || 41 || He states the number of the mantras to be recited: "One hundred times," according to some; "one thousand times," according to others. || 42 || [End of] Paṭala 2; accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* by Mahādeva Śāstrī. || 217 ||

Three sections are recited beginning with "To Agni, Svāhā" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.1.15). Among them, eleven mantras are read in the middle section of the Sudhāka. Of these, the last one—"To all, Svāhā"—should be recited at the end because it serves as a conclusion. However, the ten mantras preceding that are to be repeated one hundred times, thereby totaling one thousand. This is the meaning of the phrase "having recited that thousand. Now, he states another alternative regarding the number of mantras: "Some say 'an unlimited number of times. (Sūtra 43)

If one were to recite a limited number by counting it up to a thousand, one would obtain only a limited amount of merit. Therefore, one should recite the Aparimitā without performing any counting at all. || 43 ||
He offers the preliminary oblations of the horse with the formulas: "To Agni, svāhā! To Indra and Agni! (etc.). || 44 ||
Having returned home, he performs the preliminary oblations with the formula "To Agni, svāhā! at each of the Āhavanīya fires.
Having consecrated the horse with the mantra "vibhūrmātrā," he releases it with the formula: "Thou art the earth; for the past thee, for the present thee, for the future thee."

"Vibhūr mātā, prabhūḥ pitā"—having thus caused the sacrificer to recite these names of the horse in its right ear (ĀpŚS 20.5.9), so says Āpastamba. The meaning is that on the second day, after the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), he causes the sacrificer to recite these names of the horse, such as "Vibhūr mātā," etc., in the horse's right ear. With the mantra "Bhūr asi," having again approached the horse, he releases the horse from the two reins; that is to say, he unbinds the binding of the reins. || 45 ||

He entrusts him with the words, "O gods, guardians of the quarters. For there are indeed a hundred princes of royal lineage who are the gods, the guardians of the quarters; clad in armor, they protect him. Following after him, they do not turn back.

"O gods, you who possess hope! With these words, he entrusts [the horse] to the jewel-bearers (*ratnin*). A hundred armored men run after it; they follow the horse without turning back. According to some, there are four hundred. A hundred princes (*rājaputra*), girt with armor and with their charioteers likewise girt, [follow]; a hundred Vaiśyas carrying shields (*viparthin*); and a hundred Śūdras carrying protective coverings (*varūthin*). These become the guardians of the horse. With this mantra, he entrusts the horse to those very princes for the sake of protection.

In this mantra, by the term *āśāpāladeva* (the gods who guard the quarters), one hundred sons of the king consecrated by that title are intended—sons who are *talpyāḥ*, meaning those who sleep on the same couch (*talpa*) as the king. Alternatively, the meaning is: "This [gift] of a hundred belongs to the horse; the *āśāpālāḥ* are the deities mentioned in the mantra who provide protection in the four directions. They are called *devāḥ* because they are characterized by playing (*devana*). This [mention of a hundred] is an elliptical expression for four hundred; it is cited here because of its prominence, as the Brāhmaṇa states: "Four hundred protect" (*catuḥśatā rakṣanti*, Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 3.8.9).

Some give [gifts] to the jewel-bearers; those wearing jewels and armor, equipped and following as attendants, proceed behind the horse. A hundred women of the bedchamber, those who have taken the hand in marriage, princes, sons of princes, Umās, those who live by Umā, mountain-dwellers, those who carry loads, Vaiśyas (merchants), and those who travel on side-paths go along the two sides of the horse, having bypassed the main road.
Those Śūdras who possess protective enclosures and go to the houses to bring fodder for the horse—these are the guardians of the horse. || 4 ||

Whichever groups of Brāhmaṇas they encounter, they should ask them, "How much do you know of the Aśvamedha? Whosoever does not know it, having defeated him, they should cause food and drink to be brought from his family. ||47||

Whichever Brahmin caste they may approach or encounter, they should ask him: "How much do you know of the Aśvamedha—its mantras, its Brāhmaṇa, or its Kalpa? If he knows nothing at all, having defeated him, they shall take from his house the horse's fodder, such as chickpeas and the like, and its drinking water. || 17 ||
Whatever food is found in the country, that is his food; he dwells in the family of a chariot-maker. (Khaṇḍa 3) || 48 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the fourteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.

Regarding this, Āpastamba states: "That which is prepared food for the Brāhmaṇas is their food" (*ĀpaŚrSū* 20.6.17). However, the food of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, as well as that of others, is not to be consumed. At evening time, the horse's stay is in the *sthakāra* house. When the *Subrahmaṇyā* has been summoned and the Lord of Śacī (Indra) has arrived here, it is appropriate that he proceed on foot; therefore, his bringing [to the site] was performed earlier. After the girding and anointing, the Adhvaryu should cause [the horse] to be handed over...

And he shall be king for as long as that sacrifice continues. Then, the men of the sacrificer bring forth a dog, its limbs bound with a fourfold cord, four-eyed and intended [for the ritual]. Those who are discerning describe the dog as "four-eyed" when it is marked by two white spots above the eyes. Then the son of a female slave, holding a pestle made of Sidhraka wood in his hand and with his knees covered in gold, should follow behind the horse.

Then, while causing the horse to enter the waters and releasing the dog into the water where there is no standing place for a dog, the Adhvaryu, being impelled by the call "Slay!", the son of a harlot strikes this dog of his. [This is the section concerning the sacrificial horse of the Aśvamedha, Paṭala 3. Accompanied by the commentary *Yogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 219.

One hundred princes, equipped with armor, shall be his charioteers; one hundred such men, likewise armored and yoked to chariots, shall be his protectors of the cattle. One hundred Vaiśyas shall be the scouts of the road, and one hundred Śūdras shall be the drivers of the wagons. All of them, protecting [the herd] while moving at their own will and never turning back, shall follow as attendants.

When the horse has been tethered, they should ask: "O Brāhmaṇas, how much do you know regarding the subject of the Aśvamedha—namely, the knowledge of the Mantras, the Brāhmaṇas, and the proper timing? Those who know nothing at all should be excluded. Food, drink, and other provisions for the horse should be taken from their [the Brāhmaṇas'] houses; however, prepared food (kṛtānna) here should be accepted from the houses of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. But in the evening, for the horse staying in the house of the chariot-maker (rathakāra), [the following applies]: || 48 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the fourteenth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.
Now begins the second chapter in the fourteenth book.
Here, one offers four evening *dhṛti*-oblations for the horse with the formula: "Dhṛti (Steadfastness), svāhā! at its four feet. (1)

In this context, *dhṛti*—which serves as the tethering post for the horse—is the first among the *dhṛtis* that must be offered into the four feet [of the fire-altar]. Because of the contradiction otherwise, the Adhvaryu priest, having arrived together with the horse, offers the oblation with the clarified butter from the ordinary *ukhā* pot; such is the meaning. ||1||
To Savitṛ, in the morning, an offering on eight potsherds. || 2 ||

The word "he offers" (nirvapati) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. On the following day, the third [lunar day], he should perform the ritual beginning with "to Savitṛ, acceptable" (savitre juṣṭam) and ending with the nāriṣṭha oblations. || 2 ||

Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers the horse’s tracks into the *āhavanīya* fire with the formulas: “To *īṃkāra*, svāhā! To that which has been made with *īṃ*, svāhā! Then he offers the forms of the horse: “To the one with white spots, svāhā! To the black one, svāhā! To the white one, svāhā! 3. Some recite this in reverse order. 4. A gold coin weighing a hundred *mānas* is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

Because of the injunction regarding the time for the secondary oblations (*upahoma*)—namely, "before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering"—Āpastamba says: "He offers with the formula, 'To the coming, svāhā! To the departing, svāhā! and so on. [He offers] with each mantra of the section beginning with "To the letter *ī*, svāhā! [and continuing through]: "To the white one, svāhā! To the black one, svāhā!"—thus forty-eight offerings, plus one additional, ending with "To the All, svāhā! At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), there is a piece of gold weighing a *śatamāna*. 3 | 4 | 5.
While she was thus occupied, two Brāhmaṇas, lute-players, sang: "You have given; you have sacrificed; you have cooked; you have done that well. ||6||

When that morning sacrifice, ending with the satiation of the Brahmins, was completed, a lute-playing bard sang here: "In this manner he constantly gave land and other gifts to the Brahmins; in this manner he sacrificed with the Vājapeya, Rājasūya, and other rites; in this manner he cooked [the meat of] deer and other animals; in this manner he performed what is right—he followed the scriptures and practiced the true path. Thus did the two lute-players sing.
To Savitṛ Prasavitṛ at midday, there is an offering on eleven potsherds; a silver śatamāna is the sacrificial fee. || 7 ||
"I shall sacrifice with the Mādhyandina-istī," and so forth; "to Savitṛ Prasavitṛ, the acceptable [portion]," and so forth, up to the satiation of the Brāhmaṇas. || 7 ||
To Savitṛ Āsavitṛ, in the afternoon, there is an offering on twelve potsherds; a gold coin of a hundred mānas is the sacrificial fee. ||8||
This sacrifice concludes with the satiation of the Brahmins.
When that [seat] has been established, he spreads a golden cushion to the south of the altar; upon it the Hotṛ sits down. || 9 ||

When the first *iṣṭi*, beginning with the *udrāva* and *homa* and ending with the *gāna*, has been completed, [the procedure] for the afternoon *iṣṭi* begins with "to the south of the Āhavanīya," and so forth. || 9 ||
To the south are the Brahman and the Udgātṛ priests.
The ellipsis is "let him sit down upon that. || 10 ||
[He pierced] the Hotṛ priest with the tip [of the weapon] of Hiraṇyakaśipu. || 11 ||
To the south of the Āhavanīya fire, the Hotṛ sits upon a golden cushion; thus says Āpastamba.
The Adhvaryu [places it] on a golden mat or a plank. || 12 ||
"He sits down"—this is the ellipsis. According to Āpastamba, [the sacrificer sits] on a bundle of grass (kūrca) in front of the Adhvaryu in the forest [sacrifice].
To the south, the lute-players and musicians sit down in attendance.
They sit down. || 13 ||
When they have all sat down, the Hotṛ addresses the Adhvaryu, saying: "O Adhvaryu! ||14||
When all have sat down, the Hotṛ addresses the Adhvaryu, saying, "O Adhvaryu! (14).
Intending to recite the *pāriplava* narrative and the *bhauvanya*, the Adhvaryu responds, "Ho! O Hotṛ, here! (15).
"Ho3 Hotar! is the response. || 15 ||

When the *pāriplava* and the *bhauvanayava* have been completed, he gives the direction: "O lute-players and chanters, sing together with these ancient kings who performed good deeds, [praising] the sacrificer! He shall always give this direction in this manner. (Khaṇḍa 4) 16.

When the two [singers] have taken their places and announced themselves, he issues the direction: "O players of the lute and the drum, sing this song as if it were equal to Yudhiṣṭhira and the others. Such is the direction given in the manner described. || 16 ||

While the evening oblations are being offered, a kṣatriya who plays the lute and sings songs says: "Thus you were firm; thus you fought; thus you conquered that battle; oh, what valor he performed! || 17 ||

While the *dhṛtis* were being offered as oblations, the Kṣatriya, accompanied by a lute-player and a singer, [declared]: "He was equal to Māndhātṛ and others; thus he struck down his enemies, he waged war, he engaged in battle," and so forth. || 17 ||

Every evening he offers the *sāyaṃ-dhṛti* oblations; every morning he sacrifices with the *iṣṭis*. The *pāriplava* and the *bhauvanya* are performed regularly. After the completion of the *iṣṭis*, a Brāhmaṇa and a Rājanya play upon lutes (*vīṇā*) and drums (*gaṇaka*). When the *iṣṭis* have ceased, he gives them a hundred [cows] and a chariot-yoked horse; according to some authorities, he gives both a hundred [cows] and a chariot-yoked horse.

Because of the word "constantly" (*nityam*), this refers to the daily evening and morning *homa* offerings and so forth. Thus says Āpastamba: "In this manner, these rites beginning with the *Sāvitra* are performed for a year" (*ĀpaŚrSū* 20.7.2). The accusative case in the word "for a year" (*saṃvatsaram*) denotes continuous duration; therefore, the meaning is "until the end of the year. When the sacrifices have been completed, one should give those two lute-players a chariot yoked with a hundred [cows]. Some reciters of the *Śāntikalpa* read: "A hundred and a chariot yoked with a hundred. || 18 ||
This thirty-first month constitutes this year, according to the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha. 19.

In this manner, the rites beginning with the *sādhiveṣṭi* and ending with the *gāna* are performed daily within the house for one year. Following the *sāvana* [reckoning], the *Sāvitra-iṣṭi* and other rites are performed after the full moon of Vaiśākha that falls in the next year, and even after the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) following that. The meaning is that this year consists of thirty months. || 19 ||
After eleven months have passed, he binds a horse to an *aśvattha* tree in the enclosure.
When the eleventh month is complete, starting from the third day, the attendants of the horse bind the horse to a post made of *aśvattha* wood within a house constructed of the same wood. || 20 ||
They bring fodder for him while he is bound. || 21 ||
The meaning is clear. || 21 ||
"If one should find the horse afflicted by disease, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni"—thus are the expiations for the horse explained in the Brāhmaṇa. 22.

The expiations for a horse that have been explained by the Brāhmaṇas were also formulated as sūtras by Āpastamba: "If one finds that the horse has fallen into a pit, he should offer an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni, a pap to Soma, and an oblation on eight potsherds to Savitṛ. If it is salted, a pap to Pūṣan; and if he considers it to be a great deity, an oblation to Rudra. If it does not return, he should offer an oblation on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara at the lair of wild beasts."

If he should study [the Veda], there shall be a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Amhomuc, milk for Sūrya, and a portion of clarified butter for Vāyu. If he should study [it] with a mare, there shall be a pap for Prajāpati or a cake on twelve potsherds. If it should be lost, a pap for Vāyu. If he should find a victorious army, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra Yātumat. If they should bring [him] by force, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra Prasāhana. If he should become blind, a pap for Sūrya or a cake on one potsherd. If he should fall into a dog’s hole, a pap for Viṣṇu.

"If he should die from an unknown consumption (*yakṣman*), [one should offer] a *caru* oblation for Prajāpati or one on twelve potsherds. If enemies should seize his horse, his sacrifice would be destroyed; therefore, having brought another [horse], they should sprinkle it [with water]. (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 20.8.2). *Uptapasa* is a specific disease that causes intense heat or torment. *Śloṇa* refers to a skin defect. Pūṣan is the healer of that skin defect known as *lauṇya*. Rudra is the great deity, the lord of cattle (*paśūnām adhipatiḥ*). When he takes ill-will toward those cattle, the cattle are afflicted by fever and other ailments.

The meaning is that since the horse has Rudra as its presiding deity by virtue of being an animal, when the *raudra-yāga* (sacrifice to Rudra) is performed, it becomes free from the poison of the disease, just as if treated by its own deity. On the day of the *sutya*, one should perform the *vaiśvānareṣṭi* at the dwelling place of the wild horse (*mṛga-aśva*) known as *stanāman*. One should either think of or mount a mare or a she-ass. Clarified butter (*ājya*) alone is the oblation to be fried. It is like the *upāṃśuyāja* of the *ājyabhāga*. If one mounts a mare...

If he should remember [this], he should offer a *caru* oblation to Prajāpati. If it is not seen anywhere, he should offer a *caru* to Vāyu. If she is *abhītvarī*—meaning she is prone to approaching [him] or she goes to the water—he should sacrifice to Indra. If they should carry her off by force, [he should sacrifice] to Indra Prasaha. [End of] Paṭala 2, accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva. 123.

(kha) If [the horse] is blind, [one should offer] a *caru* oblation to Sūrya. If it should fall into a well, a *caru* to Viṣṇu. If it is afflicted by an unknown disease, a *caru* to Prajāpati. If enemies—that is, foes—should seize this horse, they should bring another of similar appearance, belonging to the same herd, characterized as "having a mother" and so forth, and sprinkle it with water. Having performed the expiation prescribed for lameness and other defects, ending with the formula "To Prajāpati, Svāhā," they should release it and bring another, and so on. 2.2.8.
On the new moon day, he prepares the fire-pan.

"Of this year, after the next [new moon]," says Āpastamba. That new moon which follows the one on which the bringing of the great priests and the Udgātṛ has been performed—from that point until the new moon following the upcoming Vaiśākha full moon, the gathering of the clay for the *ukhā* and other rites take place. This year is calculated by the lunar measure. On that new moon morning, having performed the *pavitreṣṭi* sacrifice with the mantra "bṛhaspatipurohitāḥ," the gathering of the soil for the *ukhā* takes place upon a black antelope skin, and at the proper time, the *hotṛ* sits down with the mantra "sa u lokaḥ."

"By three [verses] for the Rājanya," according to the scriptural statement. Having offered four oblations with the *camasa* [ladle], and having offered the three *vaiśvadeva* oblations with "Svāhā to Ādhi, to Ādhīta, Svāhā," there is a pause. This concludes the *dhrauva* [offering]. Upon completion, there is the gift to the two lute-singers (*vīṇāgāyin*). Thus ends the *Vaikhānasa Sūtra*. The baking of the fire-pan (*ukhā*) and so forth may take place on any day whatsoever. On whichever parvan-day one chooses, one should sacrifice with five animals or with the Vāyavya [offering]. || 23 ||
The initiatory offering (dīkṣaṇīyā) consists of the Traidhātavīya oblation.

The *Dīkṣaṇīyā* [initiation] sacrifice takes place like the fire-sacrifice (*agni*) in the coming spring. On whichever lunar festival (*parvan*) it may be, the preparation of the *Mahāvīra* [vessel] occurs. In the coming spring, the *Prastotṛ* priest is brought [to the site] by means of elephants, horses, and so forth. Having performed the morning *Agnihotra*, he first performs the rites up to the placing of the *Mahiṣī-ukhā* (the buffalo-cow vessel) on the southern side. At midday, beginning with "To Savitṛ, for impulsion" (*savitre prasava*), and so forth, when the *Sāvana* year is completed, there is the *Sāvitra-iṣṭi* and so on.
Having first established the threefold *Ātithyā* sacrifice according to the rule "Clarified butter, animals," and so forth, the rite concludes with the *Patnīsaṃyāja* following the *Dīkṣā*. || 24 ||

At the time of the initiation oblations (dīkṣāhuti), he offers three Vaiśvadeva oblations and four Audgrahaṇa oblations. The Audgrahaṇas are: "By Agni he experienced heat... and so forth. The Vaiśvadevas are: "Svāhā to Ādhi, to the Meditated One, Svāhā! and so forth. For seven days, he proceeds daily with the Audgrahaṇas and the Vaiśvadevas. This period of the initiation oblations is extended; the Vaiśvadevas become increasingly numerous in each subsequent day. On the final day, all [the remaining ones] are offered.

Having performed the rites from "to the north, outside the *prāgvaṃśa* hall," etc., up to "he sits down near the *āhavanīya* fire," he should offer the four *udahaṇa* oblations with the formula, "For intention (*ākūti*), I sacrifice. Then he offers the four [oblations] with "With speech, ma... (the rest being understood). Having offered the three *vaiśvadeva* oblations with "Svāhā to *adhi*, to the one meditated upon (*ādhīta*), svāhā," the author of the Bhāṣya says that one should stop there. On the following day, at the first [pressing], some say that one should offer the four *udahaṇa* oblations or [the four] with "With speech, ma..."; others say that in the subsequent [pressings] one does not offer them with "With speech, ma...". [Then follow] the three *vaiśvadeva* oblations with "To Kāya, svāhā," etc. —The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [Prakaraṇa 14].

On the second day, there are three [offerings] with "Adityā"; on the third, three with "Sarasvatyā"; on the fourth, three with "Kṛṣṇe"; on the fifth, three with "Tvāṣṭre. On the sixth and seventh days, he offers the Audgrahaṇa oblations. The final Pūrṇāhuti is with "Sarvasmai svāhā. He proceeds for six days with the Āgnāvaiṣṇava [offering]. According to the Vājasaneyaka, on the seventh day he performs the Āgneyī offering consisting of three sacrificial portions (*tri-havis*). Thus says Āpastamba. (ĀpŚS 20.8.11)

If there is neglect regarding the commencement of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) on the seventh day, one should offer the *audgrahaṇa* oblations, with the fifth being "By speech, to me. In the case of not practicing [the repetition], having offered "By mind, to me," one performs the six *āgnikī* oblations beginning with "The form, Agni," and the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with "To the Viśvedevas. There are three Vaiśvadeva oblations with "To Viṣṇu, svāhā. The full-oblation is with "To the All, svāhā. In the first three, the *svāhā*-utterance occurs both at the beginning and at the end; for the others, it is only at the end. Some say this applies to every day.

Having offered the four *dṛhaṇa* oblations, there is a meal for the patron (*yajamāna*). This consists of food excluding alkaline substances and salt, because the vow (*vrata*) has been undertaken. Alternatively, it may be performed with the *palaṅga-māṃsa-gāvaiṣṇava* offering. On the seventh day, the *dhātavīyā* rite is performed, followed by the *āgnikī* and the *triviṣkandhā*. 25 || 26 || 27 || 28 ||
With the verse, "For the sake of the gods' work," he addresses with the Ṛtu-dīkṣā formulas the sacrificer as he mounts the black antelope skin. || 29 ||

The formula *bhuvo devānām* is to be joined with the preceding part, *pathyā asi*. [It continues] up to *dakṣiṇāmi*, [then] *vāsi stebhiḥ pathyā asi ādityebhiḥ pathyā asi viśvabhiḥ pathyā asi aśvibhyām*, and so forth. While the sacrificer is mounting the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), he addresses him with the mantra *imām agṛbhṇan raśanām ṛtasya*; it ends with *ahaṃ dīkṣāmanu dīkṣito niśāmya niśāmi*. Having performed the actions from the making of the fist (*muṣṭīkaraṇa*) up to the placing of the fire-pan (*ukhā-pravṛñjana*), because his sacrificial wealth has been exhausted, he worships the fire that has been produced by friction (*nirmanthya*) with the verse *ā brahman brāhmaṇo brahmavarcasī jāyatām*. || 14.2.30 ||
With the two sections beginning with "O Brahman, [give] the seed" (ā brahman jājña bījam), he worships the principal fire that has been produced; there is a cessation of the original [rite]. 30.
When the speech has been released, the attendants with lutes and counters [announce]: "The gods have honored this sacrificer," and thus he gives the command. 31.

When the speech has been released and it is said, "Let the sacrificer perform his vow," the Adhvaryu issues the command: "O lute-players and musicians," and so forth; they sing, "He is equal to Indra. || 31 ||

When the *vasatīvarī* waters are being poured out, he gives the final command to the gods: "At the end of the *sutyā* [Soma-pressing] days, at the *udavasānīyā* [concluding] offering, [this is performed] by Prajāpati. [End of] Paṭala 2, accompanied by the commentary *Yogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. Page 225.

Thus [the ritual proceeds] from the *sadoṣa* dwelling. Āpastamba states: "At the *sutyā*s, at the *avabhṛtha*, at the *udayanīyā*, the *anūbandhya*, and the *udavasānīyā*, the *devara* [is performed] last" (*ĀpaŚrSū* 20.8.17). Thus [it proceeds] from the *aupavasatha*. Regarding the duration of the *dīkṣā*, the performance is based on the three-day (*tryaha*) option as prescribed for the *agni*. Some maintain that the *dīkṣā* and *upasad* periods are like those of the *dvādaśāha*. In that case, the end of the *dīkṣā* occurs in the cool season (*śiśira*); here there are three *dīkṣā*s and six *upasad*s. On the day one sets out, having constructed the *gārhapatya-citi* and performed the *prāyaṇīya* offering, the measurement of the altar (*vedi*) takes place. || 32 ||
The altar is twice as large; the fire-altar consists of twenty-one parts. || 33 ||

"At the time of the altar, the altar is twice [the size]; the fire-altar is three times [the size], or twenty-one-fold"—thus Āpastamba also prescribed in his Sūtra. At the time of the altar, one makes the altar twice the size of the original (prakṛti). The measurement of the altar is by means of the *vikaraṇī*. The diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*) of a square measuring thirty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) is the *prakrama*. The fire-altar is three times [the size] of a man; the *trikaraṇī* is for the man.

The measuring cord for the diagonal of a square measuring one *puruṣa* on each side is three times that length; thus it is the triple-measure (*trikaraṇī*) of the *puruṣa*. A *caturbhāgīyā* brick is made with a fourth part of the body (*ātman*); its quarters are made with a fifth part, and the *pañcamabhāgīyā* bricks with that fifth part, while the *pādeṣṭakā*s are made with half of that. This applies to the *gārhapatya-citi* as well as the *viṣṇiya* hearths, according to the archetype. Having performed the *prāyaṇīyā* sacrifice, having measured the altar and the two fires with a cord, and having measured the altar with the mantra beginning with "the *prāyaṇīyā*, the *dhruva*, the Āditya," and so forth.

At the time of the Soma-purchase, [the sacrificer says]: "I shall purchase from you her soul, or more, up to one less than a thousand. The purchase of the Soma fruits sufficient for three nights is performed. Following the *ātithyā* offering, the measuring of the fire-altar (*agnimāna*) and so forth proceed. With the formulas "Citaḥ stha" and "Saṃ te payāṃsi," the scattering of sand (*sikatānyūhana*) is performed. From the *dhruva* vessel of the *ātithyā* offering onwards, the procedure continues up to the *upavasathya* day, as in the case of the fire-altar. At the evening time, lute-players (*vīṇāgādhinaḥ*) should sing with the verse "Aharahaṃ devaiḥ. At the time of cutting the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), twenty-one posts are prepared.

The Udumbara post is the best; the Laṣmātaka is for that [purpose]. There are three [posts] made of Putudru wood on both sides. There are six made of Bilva, six of Khadira, and six of Palāśa. All are twenty-one cubits long. On the Upavasatha day, the Palāśa posts—the Upaśaya, the Pānīvata, and the Viśāla—are of the standard measurement.
He proceeds with the Vaiśvānara offering. || 34 ||
Agni Vaiśvānara is the calculator of the fires; this sacrifice concludes with the satiation of the Brāhmaṇas. || 34 ||

He offers a sacrifice consisting of ten oblations, beginning with "To Agni, who is associated with the Gāyatrī metre, the Trivṛt stoma, the Rathantara Sāman, and the spring season, [an offering] on eight potsherds. Thus he prepares the Sarvapṛṣṭhyā iṣṭi.

The bringing of branches and so forth, as well as the strewing of grass made of flowers, is like that of the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice; there are fifty-six potsherds and four cooking pots. At the time of the pouring out [of the grain]: "I pour out what is pleasing to Agni, who is associated with the Gāyatrī, the Trivṛt-stoma, the Rathaṃtara-sāman, and the Spring season."

To Indra, associated with the Triṣṭubh meter, the Pañcadaśa-stoma, the Bṛhat-sāman, and the Naiṣka-vala; to the Viśve Devas, associated with the Jagatī meter, the Saptadaśa-stoma, the Vairūpa-sāman, and the rains; [I offer] the *juṣṭam*. To Mitra and Varuṇa, associated with the Anuṣṭubh meter, the Ekaviṃśa-stoma, the Vairāja-sāman, and the autumn; [I offer] the *payasyā*. To Bṛhaspati, associated with the Pakti meter, the Triṇava-stoma, the Śākvara-sāman, and the winter; [I offer] the *juṣṭam*. To Savitṛ... [End of section 14 of the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha].

"To the Āticchandas, to the Trayastriṃśa, to the Raivata, to the Śaiśira, [this is] acceptable; to Aditi, the wife of Viṣṇu, [this is] acceptable; to Agni Vaiśvānara, [this is] acceptable; to Anumati, [this is] acceptable; to Ka, [this is] acceptable," and so forth. Having poured [the remnants] onto the rubbish-heap (utkara), having placed the potsherds according to their respective portions, and having performed the morning milking ritual starting with the heating [of the vessels], [he recites the mantras]: "May you milk the desire-granting [cow]; for Mitra and Varuṇa, for the two Anuṣṭubhs, for the two Ekaviṃśas, for the two Vairājas, for the two Śāradas, the oblation is power. These are the citations (nigamas).

Having formed the *piṇḍa*, he recites "cyāvartadhvam" three times. Alternatively, while chewing [the sacrificial food], he says "vyāvadhvam"; for the *puroḍāśas*, he says "vyāvartadhvam"; for the two *puroḍāśas*, he says "vyāvaṃ. [The rites] from the placing on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) onwards follow. He lays the enclosing sticks (*paridhis*) around with the formula "gandharvo 'si," which is not present here; for this sacrifice, there is no mention of "kastvā" [in place of "kastvā..."]. There is a substitution for those [formulas]. The phrase "asya yajñasya" is to be supplied (*anuṣaṅga*) to all three [mantras]. Here, there is no mention of the name of the deceased, such as "amuṣmai"; rather, one says "kāyānubrūhi" and "kaṃ yaja. The performance proceeds according to the rules of the single-pot-sherd (*ekakapāla*) offering. This sacrifice concludes with the *brāhmaṇatarpaṇa* (satiating the Brahmins) and the *svāhā* offerings beginning with "madhuśca svāhā. || 35 ||
The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are "samiddiśām" and so forth. || 36 ||
This is the Hotṛ-function according to the Yajurveda.
"Who yokes you? Let him yoke you"—with these words he anoints the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*). This has been explained.
In the Havirdhāna shed that serves as the chariot-stand, he erects a sacrificial post made of Rājjudāla wood, measuring twenty-one aratnis, so that it stands nearest the fire. || 38 ||

The Vasordhārā is like the fire. At the time of moving the Havirdhāna, there are two Rathavāhanas for the purpose of the Havirdhāna; they are carts capable of carrying the Rathavāhana. At the time of the preparation of the sacrificial post (yūpa), he erects the one made of Rājjudāla wood, measuring twenty-one cubits, as the central post (agniṣṭha). || 38 ||
The two [reeds] made of *pūtudru* wood are on both sides. || 39 ||
Two [pillars] made of *pautudrava* wood and two made of *devadāru* wood are placed to the south and to the north. || 39 ||

There are three stakes of *khadira* wood to the south and three to the north; three of *bilva* or *pālāśa* wood to the south and three of *bilva* to the north; they prescribe one at the very end, and the *upaśaya* (resting-stake) is of *pālāśa* wood. 14.2.40.
Thus, by means of such transpositions, the measurement [is established]; following that, the placing of the sacrificial grass; then the Agniṣomīya sacrifice. ||10||
He takes the Vasatīvarī waters, which consist of four portions of water collected from the various quarters.

At the end of the *subrahmaṇyā* formula, there are four [offerings], beginning with the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) and the *devasū* oblations; these belong to the deity alone, as stated in the section on the sacrificer’s duties. At the end of the *subrahmaṇyā*, the lute-player sings, saying that he is equal to Prajāpati. 41.

On the following day, the Catuṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is extended; it is the first of the two Catuṣṭomas belonging to Gotama. At the time for the animal sacrifice, he dedicates the animals of the Ekādaśinī set. [End of] Paṭala 3. This is accompanied by the commentary named *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śākhin. 227.

In the Mahārātra, having first performed the *dhruvā* offering for both the *Gotama-catuṣṭoma* and the *Agniṣṭoma*, one uses the *ṣoḍaśi* vessel as in the *Agniṣṭoma*. With the formula "To the heart, svāhā," he pours out the sufficient quantity; then, "I yoke [thee]," and so forth—all is like the *Agniṣṭoma*. At the time of the animal sacrifice, he performs the *savanīya* animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni, or alternatively, the set of eleven animals (*aikādaśina*). || 42 ||

At the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he distributes on each successive day, having divided equally over three days, that which remains from the wealth of the kingdom—excluding the portions for the Brāhmaṇas at the consecrations, the land, the armies, and the men. || 43 ||

When the time for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) arrived, he gave to the Brāhmaṇas, day after day for three days, an equal share of the wealth that had been accumulated from the time the horse was released until it reached the various quarters according to the prescribed rule.
The eastern direction to the Adhvaryu, the southern to the Brahman, the western to the Hotṛ, and the northern to the Udgātṛ. || 44 ||
He gives [the portions] in order to those who proclaim the directions beginning with the east, the worlds, and the paths. || 44 ||
Or rather, [the path] for the Hotṛ is toward the east, and for the Adhvaryu it is toward the west; the Hotrakas follow this very same [path]. || 45 ||

The word *api vā* ("or else") is intended to indicate an alternative option. Furthermore, there is a specific rule in the *Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra*: "He gives the *mahiṣī* to the Brahman; the *vāvātā* to the Hotṛ; the *parivṛktī* to the Udgātṛ; the *pālākilī* to the Adhvaryu"—so it is known (*Āpa. Śr. Sū.* 20.2.10–12). Because of the statement "he gives the *mahiṣī* to the Brahman," the meaning is that he gives their wealth as well. [Regarding the phrase] "the *agnidakṣiṇā* to the Adhvaryu, beautiful women," and so forth. The day concludes with the *Patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. (Section 6) 46.
Thus ends the second paṭala in the fourteenth praśna of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.

At the conclusion of the removal of the horns, while the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* on the *yajñāyajñīya* [verse] is being performed, he pours out the fourfold waters, and so forth; this concludes the *vasatīvarī* [rite]. The day concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, beginning with "With one [verse] the *prastāva* is chanted," and so forth; the meaning is that it is brought to a final close. Thus ends the second chapter in the fourteenth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*, compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. Now begins the third chapter in the fourteenth book. One should construct thirty-six couches around the *āhavanīya* fire.

Having performed the *nasalyavisarga* (the release of the nose-string), they avoid the husks and go toward the water for the purpose of washing the wives' feet. [With] a fuel-stick (*samidh*)... [by means of... 228 ...The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[Book 15, Chapter 6].

He establishes [the fires] with the *hūti* formula. Thus ends the final day. Therein is this distinction: at the *Hāryojana* sacrifice, the call (*preṣa*) is "Tomorrow we shall press the Soma," according to the view of Mahat; according to the view of Āpastamba, it is the *Sūktavāka*. Having heard that, he also issues the call. The chanting is similar to that of the *Prājña-pratinā*. When this has been done, at sunset, he prepares one hundred and eight couches. || 1 ||

When the sun has set, having ascended thirty-six steps of the platform, they offer oblations of food throughout the entire night with wooden ladles made of *khadira* wood, using these sections of the text beginning with "Svāhā to one. (2) [The materials are: clarified butter, honey, rice grains, flattened grains (*pṛthuka*), parched grain (*lāja*), flour mixed with curds (*karambha*), fried grains (*dhānā*), groats (*saktu*), lentils (*masūrī*), and *priyaṅgu* rice grains; these are offered with clarified butter and with food. (3) They offer alternately: on odd-numbered nights with clarified butter, and on even-numbered nights with food; finally, they offer on all nights with both. (4)

Then, having prepared the couches at the southern, eastern, and northern posts, thirty-six Adhvaryu priests, having been formally initiated, offer oblations throughout the entire night with long-handled ladles made of *khadira* wood. [The offerings are: honey; rice grains produced from *vrīhi* rice; flattened grains (*pṛthuka*); parched grains (*lāja*) which are like blooming flowers; parched barley flour mixed with clarified butter (*karambha*); roasted barley grains (*dhānā*); parched rice grains; parched rice flour (*saktu*); and lentils (*masūr*). With these...

In the northern region, there is no such well-known variety of grain by which soup is prepared. However, *priyaṅgu* rice is called *priyaṅga* because its color is like that of gold. Regarding the oblation of ten substances mixed together, it is said: "He offers the ten kinds of food" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 3.8.14). On this point, Āpastamba also states: "They prescribe these four: he offers with clarified butter, he offers with parched grains (*lāja*), he offers with fried grains (*dhānā*), and he offers with flour-meal (*saktu*)."

"‘Ekasmai svāhā’—of these *anuvākas*, the odd-numbered ones are offered with clarified butter (*ājya*), and the even-numbered ones with food (*anna*). With clarified butter at the end" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 20.10.7). Thus, ‘Ekasmai svāhā’: the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth are the odd-numbered ones offered with clarified butter; the second, fourth, sixth, eighth, and tenth are the even-numbered ones offered with food. || 2 || 3 || 4 ||

In this regard, some authorities prescribe the application of mantras that have already been employed as well as those yet to be employed. At dawn, they offer with "Svāhā to Uṣas"; when it has dawned, with "Svāhā to Vyuṣṭi"; when it is about to rise, with "Svāhā to the rising one"; when it is rising, with "Svāhā to the one rising"; and when it has risen, with "Svāhā to the one risen. Finally, they offer with "Svāhā to heaven" and "Svāhā to the world. He sets aside the remnants of the food.

In this manner, having offered oblations for the remainder of the night, one should repeatedly practice these sections (anuvākas). Others say that during the practice or at the conclusion, one should offer with clarified butter (ājya) using each section (anuvāka). "At the end" means at the very end of the entire [section], specifically at the end of those beginning with "To Uṣas, svāhā! and so forth. [End of] Chapter 2: The *Yogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. Page 219.

The ritual procedure (*prayoga*) is as follows: having recited once "to one" (*ekasmai*) and so forth, up to "to the dawn" (*uṣase svāhā*) and so forth, as before, the sequence is reversed. Then, with this [formula], from "vibrant am I" (*vibhūr mātrā*) up to "thirteen others here" (*trayodaśāny iha*), there is the mantra for the release (*utsarga-mantra*): "To Agni, svāhā! and "This is stability, svāhā! and "The mind is the impulse. The mantra for entrustment (*paridāna-mantra*) is "O gods, guardians of the quarters... For the sake of obtaining [the results], there are the thousandfold offerings; the previous oblations are with "To Agni, svāhā!", and after the final oblation with "To the Earth, svāhā!", the initiations (*dīkṣā*) are preceded by "To Agni, svāhā! and so on.

"To the Earth, Svāhā!"—this is the twenty-one-fold initiation (*dīkṣā*). "Of the gods, O Bhūvas!"—these are the fourteen *ut-dīkṣās*. As before, the *vaibura* is joined; "I initiate [you]"—these are the five; "and by the Brahman," "the highest of these"—these two; the *ādiṣṭa* at the end; the *ke nālī*, *patalo*, and *dhṛtayaḥ*; "the sacrifice is turned hitherward," "what has been, what is to be"—these nine; "may the cups come to me"—this is the *sikhā*.

"Unconquered, he overcame the serpents"—thus twenty-four [offerings]. *Svāhā* to Adhidya; to Ajyeta and Kṛṣṇa; to the Oṣadhīs; to the Vanaspatis—[an offering] for the ram; *svāhā* to the Kṛpyās; *svāhā* to the Ambhas; *svāhā* to the Nabhas; *svāhā* to the Mahas. "Homage to the King"—thirteen [offerings]. "Mayo-bhūḥ"—ten [offerings]. *Svāhā* to Prāṇa; *svāhā* to Sitā; *svāhā* to Pṛthivī; *svāhā* to Datvat; "He who gives breath, he who gives the self"—these two are the Mahimā offerings. "Ā Brahma"—the Brāhmaṇa [offering], twelve [in total].

"O Naja, the seed has submitted to the five fires. "May they submit," is the end of the mantra. "To Vāyu it has submitted; to the intermediate space it has submitted. Just as the anus submitted to the intermediate space, so may the Madras submit to me. "To Sūrya, to Candramas, to Varuṇa, to Sāman, to Brahman, to the King, to Sthāna, to Prajāpati it has submitted"—thus it is supplied everywhere. "To the past, svāhā! To the future, svāhā!"—thus are the past and the future.

The verse *yad aṅga prathamaṃ havirmān* is recited with clarified butter and food alternately. With the mantra *ekasmai*, he offers the remainder of the night before the dawn has arisen; with *uṣase*, he does so once when it has dawned; with *vyuṣṭyai*, when it is about to dawn; and with *udite*, when it has risen—he places all the remaining known portions down. While the principal rites are thus proceeding, the Adhvaryu, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters, omits the milkings for the fivefold curd (*pañcadoha*) and other such duties because of the *ukthya* nature of the sacrifice. There is one branch of the *palāśa* tree on the outside, or a branch of the *vetasa*; the rites beginning with the fetching of the branches and ending with the strewing of grass for the *savanīya* offering are performed. [1.5]
The twenty-first [day] is an Ukthya; the Mahānāmnī verses are the Sāman.
Having understood this, O Great King, he extends [the rite]; the Ekaviṃśa Ukthya sacrifice is performed, and he sings the Mahānāmnī Sāman. || 7 ||

Between the Āgrayaṇa and the Ukthya, having pressed the worldly Soma, they draw the two Mahiman cups with a golden and a silver vessel. The Adhvaryu draws the first with the golden one, using either "yaḥ prāṇata" or "ya ātmadā. The Pratiprasthātṛ draws the latter with the silver one, using "hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre."

But having employed the *dhruvā* as the vessel for the *atigrāhya* cups, the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is used on the middle day of the three-night sacrifice; thus, there are two Vāyu-cups made of silver and gold. The *pariplava* ladle and other implements are handled silently. At the time of placing the vessels for the *savanīya* animals, a mat of reeds (*vaitasa*) is used together with the *juhū* ladle. There are forty-two cords for the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), making it a "double-corded" post. For the *upaśaya* post, there are two cords. Thus, according to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, there are forty-four [cords].

There are three hundred and ninety sacrificial animals. There are five hundred and nineteen wooden stakes (*svaru*); one of these has already been employed previously, so it is included in the count. There are five hundred and forty-nine pairs of *darbha* grass blades, and three hundred and ninety jars (*kumbhī*). In the pit, there are, collectively, the heart-spikes (*hṛdaya-śūla*), the omentum-roasting spits (*vapā-śrapaṇī*), and [other implements] for the horse, the hornless goat (*tūpara*), and the gayal (*gomṛga*), similar to the jars; their identifying mark is the word "heart" (*hṛd*), with the modification [*ūha*] being "vetyūha" (*vetyahaḥ*).

Having taken the full measure of the *agniṣṭoma* cup with the formula "I yoke the fire," and having drawn the *śukra* and *āgrayaṇa* cups, he presses the common *soma* silently, mixes it with common water, and draws it with the formula beginning "He who breathes" (*yaḥ prāṇata*) up to the end of the *upayāma*. With the silver cup, using the formula beginning "He who gives life" (*ya ātmadā*) up to the end of the *upayāma*, and with the golden cup, using the formula "The sun is yours" (*sūryaste*), he places the former [cup] down; with the formula "The moon is your greatness" (*candramāste mahimā*), he places the latter down. From the *ukthya* onwards, he proceeds exactly as in the *ukthya* ritual, performing the actions from the anointing of the ladles (*pātra-añjana*) through the wiping (*parimārjana*). He should perform the rites from the *dhārayā* offering up to the *viṣṇu-homa*.

"The life of the sacrifice flows as dear honey; the father of the gods, their progenitor, the radiant one, bestows treasure that is hidden even from the two worlds of self-power. Most intoxicating, exhilarating, the essence of Indra—thus he fastens a golden ornament upon the necks of the horses. (14.3.10)
They fasten a beautiful gold ornament, a specific kind of jewelry, around the neck of the horse. || 10 ||
"You are a falcon, having the Gāyatrī metre; I take hold of you; carry me safely across," with these words they take hold of the horse's tail.

Clinging to the tail of the sacrificial horse, they crawl along; the commencement of the chant is performed with gold. Having gone to the *āstāva* enclosure, the *udgātṛ* priest, having excluded the *hiraṇyakaśipu* (the golden cushion) from the *udgātṛ*, departs; the *udgātṛ* chooses a chariot and a horse.

"May Agni strike down the Vṛtras"—saying this, they proceed to the Bahiṣpavamāna while holding onto the horse, or [they proceed] with the mantra, "The steed has stepped forward with his strides; the steed has transcended. Having excluded the Udgātṛ, he chooses the horse for the Udgītha. Mares are kept nearby. When they make the sound *hiṃ* together with these [sounds], that is the Udgītha. When they make the sound *hiṃ* in response, that is the Upagītha. He mutters: "The horse, worthy of sacrifice and fit for the ritual, has sung forth."

With a hundred, or with a hundred-fold, or with a *niṣka*, or with a *śatamāna* [of gold], he says to the *udgātṛ*: "I shall train myself in this deity; chant after her as she chants the *udgītha*. Thus he addresses the *udgātṛ*. || 12 ||

"Agni is the *dhenu*," says Āpastamba. "Anvārambha" means touching; [the sacrificers] touch the horse. The *prasarpakas* (those who move forward) proceed to the *bahispavamāna* chant. They hold the horse near the mare (*vaḍavā*). The horse utters the sound *hiṃ* toward the mare; that is its *udāna*. ... [The rest is as before. This concludes the first section. [This is from] the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 31.

When the female mules bray in response, that is the *upagāna* (the responsive singing). Having requested a hundred cows and a *niṣka* weighing a hundred *palas*—a *niṣka* being a particular kind of ornament—and having said, "He has sung the *udgītha*," he requests it. Then he gives the command: "This [cow]. With that [cow] weighing a hundred *palas*, he introduces the *bahiṣpavamāna*; this is the substitute for the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). || 12 ||
With the branch of a rattan cane, saying "Homage to the King! Homage to Varuṇa!", he dedicates the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal at the post standing nearest the fire.

The section ends with the words *upākṛtāya*. The girding (*parivyayaṇa*) of the sacrificial posts (*agniṣṭhā*) that lie nearby extends up to the end of those lying near. There are nine sacrificial chips (*svaru*) for each. For the eighteen [posts], there are two hundred and ten [chips]; for the one hundred and twenty-nine [posts] intended for wild animals, he places those chips upon the central post (*agniṣṭha*). Then follows the bathing of the horse and the other animals with the mantra: *iṣe tvā*.

Having taken the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he says, "Upavīri" [referring to] a reed branch (*vetasa-śākhā*). Having said "Upo devān Prajāpatiḥ" at the beginning and "Namo rājñe mayi dhehi" at the end, he says regarding the horse: "I dedicate thee, acceptable to Prajāpati. Having placed it upon the sacrificial grass with the words "Svāhā to the dedicated one," he takes another [branch] with that same mantra and together with the reed branch, [dedicates] the hornless goat (*tūpara*) and the forest-goat (*gomṛga*) with the formula "To Prajāpati thee," and so forth. The horse is well known. The *tūpara* is a hornless goat. The *gomṛga* is the lord of the wild cattle. 13.

The other animals [are bound] with branches of the *plakṣa* tree. (Section 17) A black-necked goat for Agni is at the front; a ewe for Sarasvatī on the forehead; two for Savitṛ below the forelegs; two for Sūrya and Yama on the two sides; two for Tvaṣṭṛ with hairy thighs on the thighs; two for Bṛhaspati, white-backed, on the back; a speckled-belly goat for Dhātṛ on the belly; and a white goat for Vāyu on the tail—these are the animals tied to the horse. 14.

Now, for the sake of the consecratory rites beginning with the *upākaraṇa*, there are many Adhvaryus. Due to the conflict [of duties], each of the three subsequent [priests] acts as an Adhvaryu. He dedicates the domestic and wild animals. While the horse remains motionless, he performs the circumambulations. Once it has been consecrated by the sprinkling and other rites, he dedicates it at the place of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). || 14 ||
The Rohita, the Dhūmrarohita, and so forth—these are the eighteen. || 15 ||

Āpastamba states that some authorities prescribe dividing [the animals] into nine groups of nine each, with Indra and Agni as the tenth (ĀpaŚrS 20.11). Each group consists of one set of eighteen animals. 15.

Those with black necks are for Agni; tawny ones are for Soma; those of a dusty-brown color are for Savitṛ; heifers are for Sarasvatī; dark-colored ones are for Pūṣan; spotted ones are for the Maruts; multiformed ones are for the Viśvedevas; and barren cows are for Heaven and Earth. These are said to be the common (saṃcara) animals. A goat whose neck is black is "black-necked" (*kṛṣṇagrīva*). "Tawny" (*babhru*) means reddish-brown in color. "Dark-colored" (*śyāma*) means of a dark hue. "Spotted" (*pṛśni*) means variegated in color, marked with white spots.

The dappled ones are for Indra and Agni; the black ones are for the Maruts; the hornless ones are for Ka. He sacrifices first-born [calves] to Agni Anīkavant. To the Maruts Sāṃtapanas he sacrifices bāṣkas; to the Maruts Gṛhamedhins, sāvātas; to the Maruts Krīḍins, saṃsṛṣṭas; to the Maruts Svatavantas, anusṛṣṭas. These aforementioned are the common [animals]. 17.

Those with prominent horns are for Indra and Agni; those of many colors are for Indra; those that are brown, smoke-colored, and shining are for the Soma-drinking Pitṛs; those that are smoke-colored, brown, and shining are for the Barhiṣad Pitṛs; those that are shining, brown, and smoke-colored are for the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs; those that are red are for Tryambaka; some say they should be black-spotted.

The white ones are said to be for Āditya; these moving ones are for Indra and Agni; the multiformed ones are for the Viśvedevas; those with prominent horns are for Śunāsīra; the white ones are for Vāyu (and the white ones are for Sūrya); having thus divided the animals of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices into equal groups, he dedicates them at the other sacrificial posts. To Soma the Self-Ruler, two oxen that draw a cart; thus he dedicates the animals in pairs, as they have been enumerated, right at the post standing nearest the fire.

The yoking of their horses [is performed]. Some maintain that the yoking occurs at the post standing nearest the fire (*agniṣṭha*), even for those animals surrounding it; however, the description of the black-spotted animal as belonging to Agni, and so forth, regarding the nostrils (*nāsikāpuṭayoḥ*) and the forehead, is merely based on traditional recollection (*smṛti*). According to the Kṣa branch: having taken for Agni what is pleasing from the northern parts, each its own portion upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), one takes another part: for Pūṣan, the forehead; for Indra, the head-region; for Pūṣan and Indra, the two forelegs; for Agni, the two thighs; for Tvaṣṭṛ, the back—these are the white-backed animals.

"To Bṛhaspati, you two on the sides; to Sūrya, svāhā! To Yama, svāhā below; to Dhātṛ [on the tail] (of the Kāpuṣṭha); to Sūrya, you [on the back]. These are the goats for the Paryaṅgyas. Of the eighteen [animals] in the northern row, having divided them into nine, the remaining ones are for the sacrificial posts [starting] with Rohita on the posts to the north of the Agniṣṭha post—nine in number. On the south of the Agniṣṭha post, the order of dedication (*upākaraṇa*) is likewise in reverse sequence. Regarding "the one for Indra-Agni is the tenth," Āpastamba states that this is an alternative (*vikalpa*), as it is based on the opinions of other Vedic schools.

But for us, there is always one animal in the group: the *rohita* (red), which is red with a tail that is to be offered; the *śivadipti* (brightly shining); the *dhūmrarohita* (smoky-red), which is a faint red; and the *karkandhurohita* (jujube-red), which has the color of the jujube fruit. For these, [the formula is]: "For Prajāpati, thee! [Then there are: the *bakṣuḥ*, which is pale-brown; the *aruṇabhrū*, which is reddish-brown; and the *śukabadhu*, which has a color similar to the *haritaka* (yellow myrobalan). For Ruvā... [End of] Chapter 3. [This work is] accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 233.

Sthā0: *Śyeta* means red-colored. *Śyetākṣa* means having non-red eyes. *Śyetagrīva* is well-known. "For the ancestors, you"—[this refers to] three black barren cows (*vaśā*). "For Varuṇa, you"—three white barren cows. "For Sūrya, you"—those with smoky-colored marks on their foreheads and smoky-colored tails. *Tūpara* means hornless. "For Mitra and Bṛhaspati, you"—*pṛśni* means multi-colored; some say it means white. *Tiraścīnapṛśni* means having a crosswise streak of color; by this, the *ūrdhvapṛśni* (one with an upward streak) is also explained.

To Marut, you who are beloved—[she] with the color of *phalgu* salt, the color of a jujube fruit, or the color of the *pāṭala* flower; [she] with red stripes and red hair; [she] with white spots and red eyes (or white eyes)—for Sarasvatī, you! The spotted one (*pṛṣatī*) is of variegated color; the thick-spotted (*sthūlapṛṣatī*) is not slightly variegated; the well-spotted (*suvrapṛṣatī*) is very slightly variegated—for the Viśvedevas, you! Three dark-brown (*śyāmā*) barren cows (*vaśā*), slightly black—for Pūṣan, you! The ruddy ones (*rohiṇī*) have the color of yellow pigment (*gorocana*)—for Tvaṣṭṛ, you!

[The animals] having ruddy as their mark, marked with the color of twilight. For Indra and Bṛhaspati, you! [The animal] with white forelegs: that which has whiteness in one part of the foreleg, while elsewhere it is otherwise; or that which has whiteness in both parts of the foreleg. For Indra and Vāyu, you! [The animal] with white openings: white in the openings; elsewhere, whiteness in only one opening; or whiteness in all the openings. For Mitra and Varuṇa, you!

Śuddhavāla (pure-tailed), Īpacchulavāla (slightly spotted-tailed), Sarvaśuddhavāla (entirely pure-tailed), Sphaṭikasahaśavāla (crystal-like-tailed); Maṇivāla (jewel-tailed), Śuklāśalavāla (white-spotted-tailed)—these are the three Vaśā (barren cows) of various colors for the Aśvins, svāhā; for Śilpā (the artisans). Viśvabhyaḥ devebhyaḥ tvā (for all the gods, thee). Śyāmīḥ (dark-colored ones), Kumadasanimāḥ (having the appearance of lilies). Parameṣṭhine tvā (for Parameṣṭhin, thee). Śyāmalalāmāḥ (dark with a mark on the forehead), Śyāmapuṇḍrāḥ (dark with a spot). Somāpūṣamyāṃ tvā (for Soma and Pūṣan, thee). Unnata (elevated), Unnatapṛṣṭha (high-backed); Ṛṣabha (bull), Yuvan (young), Vāmana (dwarf), Hasva (short). Indrāvaruṇābhyāṃ tvā (for Indra and Varuṇa, thee). Śitipakṣat (white-winged), Vesarakukṣi (with a speckled belly).

The *śitipad* has been mentioned; *śitimaś* means white-footed. To Indra and Bṛhaspati, [goes] the *śitipad*, the white-lipped, and the white-browed. To Indra and Viṣṇu, [goes] the *sidhma*—one with white spots on the limbs, or one who is white, or one afflicted by the *sidhmala* disease, or a youth; from that, the *uḍupa* falls. Such ones with spotted ears are the *vaśās*. To Viśvakarman, *svāhā*. The *pṛṣodara* and *andhikodara* [go] to Dhātṛ, *svāhā*. The *śvetalalāma*—those with white marks or white forehead-patches—to Indra and Pūṣan, *svāhā*. Those with severed ears, to Yama, [goes] this.

To Soma, svāhā! [The animals] with white limbs, white bodies, or white feet; to Agni Yaviṣṭha, svāhā! [The] *nakula*s, those of the color of a *nakula*; to the Vasus, svāhā! [The] *rohiṇa*s, those of red color; to Aditi, svāhā! [The] *aruṇa*s, those of ruddy color; to the Rudras, svāhā! [The] *dvivarṣa*s (two-year-olds); to Soma and Indra, svāhā! [The] *nabhulalāma*s, those with a mark on the forehead like a *dhela* flower, tawny-colored; to Viṣṇu, svāhā! [The] *śuṇṭha*s, those of small body; to Viṣṇu Urukrama, svāhā! [The] *adhīlaughakarṇa*s, those whose ears have grown over their heads.

To Urukrama, whose strides are wide; Lapsudinah, with hanging dewlaps; to the Ādityas, you—those two-and-a-half-year-old [animals]. To the Aliṣṭhas, you—three-year-old [animals]. Gauralalāmā, marked with white spots on the forehead; gaurapuṇḍrā, marked with white spots on the cheeks; to Indra and Viṣṇu, you. Śitipṛṣṭhā, white-backed; to Indra the King, you. Śitikakuda, white-humped; to Indra the Overlord, you. Śitibhasada, white-rumped; to Indra the King, you. To the Sādhyas, you—four-year-old [animals] that are well-proportioned.

Six-year-old mares for the Viśvedevas; black-spotted ones for Agni and Indra; red-spotted and red-white ones for Aditi; black-spotted and black-white ones for Indrāṇī; ruddy-spotted and ruddy-white ones, the color of twilight, for Kuhū; milch-cows not yet having calved... [from the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, 14th Praśna]

For Rākā, you! The oxen that draw the carts. To Sinīvālī, svāhā! Those with red marks on their foreheads, having red spots, for Agni and Viṣṇu, you! Tawny ones, the color of yellow pigment (gorocana), for Soma, you! Spotted deer, for King Soma, you! Those of the form of *namas*, the color of the sky, for Parjanya, you! Goats with udders on their throats, for Indrāṇī, you! She-goats, for the Ādityas, you! Mālaṅgas, large-bodied, for Heaven and Earth, you! Black ones with marks on their foreheads, for Varuṇa, you!

The red-spotted ones for King Varuṇa; the ruddy-spotted ones for Varuṇa, the destroyer of enemies; the artistic ones for the All-gods; the speckled ones belong to all the deities—those whose [deities] are all the gods, for the All; thus everywhere. Because of the prohibition regarding those with secondary names (*saṃjñopasarjana*), there is no application of the rules for pronouns (*sarvanāma*). For all the deities; the white-spotted ones for Indra and Sūrya.

In this rite, the ritual dedication (*upākaraṇa*) must be performed for each of the three animals beginning with the *rohit* [red deer]. One performs the dedication by dividing eighteen into nine groups of nine; the same applies to the wild animals. They hold these between the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*). Regarding those wild animals that are difficult to capture—such as humans, deer, monkeys, lions, and so forth—one should generally take ten of each, fashion them into various images or representations, and perform the rites from the dedication until the final release (*utsarjana*), according to the *Kaṭha-sūtra*.

The *Mānava Kalpasūtra* states: "One should bind wild animals within the intervals between the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) by means of binding devices. [Specifically: mosquitoes in tubes; snakes in baskets; deer, tigers, and lions in cages; crocodiles, fish, and frogs in jars; birds in nets; elephants in enclosures (*kāra*); and water-animals in boats. The essential meaning is that whatever animals remain in the intervals between the posts, they should be stationed there by whatever specific means is appropriate for them.

... Here, those tracks of wild animals that do not arise [from observation] are to be understood by looking into the *Nigama*, *Nirukta*, *Nighaṇṭu*, and treatises on grammar, etymology, and terminology. Having performed the dedication (*anupākaraṇa*) for the eighteen [domestic animals], he performs the dedication for the wild animals: having said, "I dedicate you, the boar, to Varuṇa, the king; you who are dear to him, with two feathers and a branch of the *plakṣa* tree," [he proceeds]. The black one is the black antelope (*kṛṣṇamṛga*); "I dedicate you to Varuṇa, the king... The *ṛśya* is the horned deer; "I dedicate you to Yama, the king..."

The *gavaya* is a wild ox, hornless and lacking [prominent] horns; for King Ṛṣabha, you! The *gaura* is an exceedingly white deer; for King Śārdūla, you! The *markaṭa* is a monkey; for King Puruṣa, you! The *vartikā* is like a sparrow; the swift *ṭibhi* is for King Śyena, you! The *krimi* (insect) is one that subsists on dung and forms balls of cow-dung; for King Nīlagava, you! The *kuluṅga* is a tusked deer with a harsh cry; for King Soma, you! The *śiśumāra* is a crocodile, a water-dweller; for the Sindhu, you!

The elephant (*hastī*) and the wild elephant (*gaja*)—to Himavat, svāhā! The *mayu*, the *kiṃnara*, or the *kiṃpuruṣa*—to Prajāpati, svāhā! The *ulo*, the frog (*maṇḍaka*), the *so*, and the *halīkṣṇa* (a grass-destroyer; others say a green sparrow)—the *vṛṣadaṃśa* is the cat. These three have the Bhrātṛs as their deities. To each one, "To Dhātr, svāhā!"—thus everywhere. The *śāri* (female parrot) who speaks like a man—to Sarasvatī, svāhā! The white parrot (*śuka*) who speaks like a man—to Sarasvat, svāhā! The forest-dwelling *anaḥ* is the *śarabha*.

The *nakula* is well known. The *śakā* is a fly; [the mantra is] "For Pūṣan, thee... The *krauñca* is a bird with a harsh cry, or the *khañjarīṭa*. [The mantra is] "To Speech, svāhā. The *jhaṣa* is a crocodile with a snout like a horse; [the mantra is] "For the leaf of the Apāna, thee. The *naka* is a long-snouted crocodile; [the mantra is] "For Makara, thee. [End of section 3.1.6] [From] the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. Page 235.

The *stattuṇḍa* is the *graha* (seizer); the *kalīkaya* is the many-footed fish. "For Ākūpāra, you... [the offering]. The *paiṅgarāja* is the *bharadvāja* (crane) with red eyes; "for Yāma, you... [the offering]. The *kutika* is the sea-crow, or the wild cock. "For Bhaga, you... [the offering]. The *ātī* is the female deer (*kuraṅgī*). The *vāhasa* is a creature that carries small shells on its back. The *darvikā* is a water-bird. "For Yāyāta, you... [the offering]. The *cakravāka* (ruddy goose), which roams by day, [is offered] "for the quarters, you... [the offering]. The *ajagara* is the great serpent; "for Bala, for the chariot... [the offering]. The *ākhu* is the mouse.

The *sūkṣayā* is a black buffalo, or a blue fly, or a *jīvañjīvika* (a kind of bird). The *śayaṇḍaka* is a chameleon, or a tree-lizard, or a grasshopper. "For Mitra thee! The *asita* is a black snake; "To Death, svāhā! The *svaja* is raw flesh—specifically that which is born spontaneously in holes and such, or sweat-born, or white, or various kinds of vermin. "To Manyu thee! The *kumbhīnasa* is a sleepy snake. The *puṣkarasāda* is a king of snakes, or a lotus-eater, or a bee.

The *lohitāhi* is a red serpent; [I offer] to Tvaṣṭṛ, svāhā! The *vāhasa* is a small snake; [I offer] to Pratiśrutkā, svāhā! The *puruṣamṛga* is a man-faced deer; [I offer] to Candra, svāhā! The *godhā* is a monitor lizard; the *kālakā* is a chameleon; the *dāvāghāṭa* is a black antelope; [I offer] to the Vanaspatis, svāhā! The *eṇī* is a female deer; [I offer] to Ahaḥ, svāhā! The *kṛṣṇa* is a black deer; [I offer] to Rādhī, svāhā! The *pika* is a cuckoo; the *viṅkā* is a red-mouthed female monkey; the *nīlaśīrṣṇī* is a black-faced female monkey, a *golāṅgūlī*; [I offer] to Aryaman, svāhā!

The *katkaṭa* and the *karkaṭa* [are for] Dhātrī; to you, [I offer] for Sūrya the *balākā*, which is fond of the rainy season. The male deer is the *ṛśya*; the peacock is the *śiravī*; the hawk is the *patrī*. To the Gandharvas, you! The *kapiñjala* bird, which descends from above, [is for] the Vasus; to you! The partridge (*tittiri*), the *tittibha*, and the man-voiced bird (*puruṣavāk*) are for the Rudras; to you! The female red deer (*rohitā*), the *ṛśyastrī*, the *kuṇḍaṇācī*, the house-lizard (*grahagodhikā*), and the wall-fish (*kukhyamatsya*). The *golāttikā* and the *khabarīṭaka* are for the Apsarases; to you! The *samara* and the *śvamara* [are for the same].

The *pṛṣata* is a deer variegated with white spots; [for] the Viśvedevas, you! The *pitva* is a large ant or a tiger; the *nyaṅgu* is a jackal, a deer, or—according to others—a bear; the *kaśa* is a jackal; [for] Anumati, you! The *anyavāpa* is a crow; [for] the half-months, you! The *kaśyapa* is a water-hen (*kvayi*), a *kuṭaru* (a forest lion or a species of owl); [for] the months, you! The *dātyauha* is a crow or a water-hen, according to some; [for] Sinīvālī, you!

The Śitpuṭa bee is for Bṛhaspati; I take you for Bṛhaspati. The Śakā fly is for the Earth; I take you for the Earth. The Pānna is the domestic cricket (*gṛhakalika*). The Kaśa is the female mongoose, the *nakulanāti*, or the very small one. The Mānthīlava is the *samāra* and the water-fowl cock; I take you for the Pitṛs. The Jahakā is the hole-dweller, the *koṣṭā*. Those of the *śalalī* species are for Ṛtavyā; I take you for Ṛtavyā. The Lopā is the cemetery bird; I take you for the Year. The Kapota is the red-footed pigeon. The Owl is the night-hunter (*divābhīta*). The Śaśa is the hare; I take you for Nityā.

The *kṛkavāku* is the domestic cock; "For Savitṛ, thee... The *ruru* is a hornless deer; "For Rudra, thee... The *kṛkalāsa* is the chameleon. The *śakuni* is the crow. The *pippakā* is the *kulāla-śakunika* (the potter-bird); "For Śaranyā, thee... The *hariṇa* is well-known [as the spotted antelope]; "For the Maruts, thee... The *śārga* is the wild sparrow; "For Brahmā, thee... The *tarakṣu* is a specific type of tiger. Some say it is a donkey-like creature with the form of a tiger. It is a specific type of variegated leopard. The *kṛṣṇa* is a dog with four eyes, meaning one that has two spots above each eye.

The *gardabha* (ass) is for Khara; "I dedicate you to the others. The *dhūkṣṇa* (owl) and the white crow are for Agni; "I dedicate you to Agni. The *alaja* (vulture) is for the Atmosphere; "I dedicate you to the Atmosphere. The *udra* (water-fox) and the *mahaḥ* (water-crow) are for Aditi; "I dedicate you to Aditi. The *plava* (diver), the *pariplava* (water-fowl), and the *adya* (heron) are for Aditi; "I dedicate you to Aditi. The *haṃsasāci* (small swan) is for Aditi; "I dedicate you to Aditi. — *Satyāṣāḍhaviracitaṃ Śrautasūtram*, Chapter 14, Section 236.

The *akekīrśā* is a specific kind of cock; [I offer] thee to Indrāṇī, svāhā! The vulture (*gṛdhra*) is well known. The *śitikakṣī* is a vulture with a white breast and belly. The *vārdhāṇasa* is a heron, a water-fowl, or a rhinoceros; [I offer] thee to the Divine Ones, svāhā! The porcupine (*śvāvit*), the hedgehog (*śalalī*), and the weasel (*sūnīroma*); [I offer] thee to Heaven and Earth, svāhā! The *suparṇa* is Garuḍa; [I offer] thee to Parjanya, svāhā! The swan (*haṃsa*) is well known. The wolf (*vṛka*) is the wild dog. The cat (*vṛṣadaṃśa*) has been mentioned; [I offer] thee to the Fire, svāhā! The otter (*udra*) has been mentioned; [I offer] thee to the Iron, svāhā!

The *lopāśa* is a hyena; [the formula] "To Aryaman thee... [is used]. Lions, tigers, and leopards are well-known; [the formula] "To Mahendra svāhā... [is used]. They hold ten buffaloes (*mahiṣa*) at each of the spaces between the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*). Some explain that one should draw ten wild animals—such as the *durga*, the male deer (*puruṣamṛga*), the lion, and the *kiṃpuruṣa*—on a painted cloth and perform the rites from the preliminary dedication (*upākaraṇa*) until the final release (*utsarjana*). This is not correct, because there is no authoritative basis for such a substitution and because it would result in a great loss [of the ritual's integrity].

"The boar for the eastern wing-branch, for Indra the King, thee, the acceptable one... and so forth. These are the wild animals. Among these, there are eighteen animals within the enclosure, depending on the deities of the animals. Three black ones are for the earth; three of reddish-brown color are for the atmosphere, with "svāhā"; three of great breath are for heaven, with "tvā"; three of variegated color and three of speckled color are for lightning, with "tvā"; and three with white spots are for the stars, with "svāhā."

These fifteen goats are for the Agniṣṭha alone. Furthermore, there are the Cāturmāsya animals: three with black necks, three tawny ones, three speckled ones, three heifers, three dark-grey ones, five moving about [the altar], three spotted ones, three black ones, three hornless ones, and three calves born first.

Three with feet, three with calves, three with humps, three born after a long time, mixed, of mixed colors, pregnant, loathsome, followed, unbroken from behind their mothers; or else, those mixed at the end of the rains, and again five beginning with *kṛṣṇāmīvā* and ending with *pauṣṇa*. These: three white ones, three with horns turned forward, three with horns turned back toward the mouth, three multiformed—[I dedicate] you to Viśvakarman.

Smoke-colored in which region? Smoke-colored in which region? Three smoke-colored, three tawny, and the brownish ones—smoke-colored in appearance—in which region? Excessively brownish? Three smoke-colored, three red; "To the deity of the sky, you! The white ones belong to the Ādityas. Again, "the black-necked" and so forth, ending with those belonging to Pūṣan, are five.

These three multiformed ones, three with white limbs, three white ones, and three solar ones—these he places at the Agniṣṭha post itself. Then, as for the two sets of eleven animals belonging to the archetype, beginning with the one for Agni and ending with the one for Varuṇa, he places them at the Agniṣṭha post itself.

In the *Āśvamedhika-parvan*, regarding the *Anīkavat* sacrifice, it is stated: "Red oxen... and so forth. [The animals] are characterized by redness; below the neck, on the lower part of the belly, they are black; they have silver-colored navels, white navels, tawny ones, the color of yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), variegated colors, black goats, and those with one white foot. A ram with testicles like *śāli* rice is also mentioned. ... Now, as for the animals in pairs: the draft animal is the ox (*anaḍvāh*), capable of pulling a cart. The draught-bull is the *balīvarda*.

The two oxen that draw the cart are the bestowers of the eight elements through their lack of restlessness; they are the leaders who pull the yoke with cooperation. The two plow-oxen that draw the plow are like sheep—meaning they are short and small-bodied. This is the pair of riches for the earth. [This concludes the section] from the *Yogacandrikā*, a commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.

Furthermore, for Manu there are two human females (*manuṣī*); for the deity Virāj, two human women who have been remarried (*punarbhū*); for the two draught-oxen that pull the vehicle, two oxen fashioned for the purpose of carrying humans—meaning they were previously yoked to carts for carrying grain and the like, but here they pull a cart for the amusement of princes and others; for Varuṇa, however, there are two barren females of the black antelope species (*kṛṣṇamṛga*); and for the deity Yama, two bulls with upturned horns (*ucchritaśṛṅga*). These two are the "sprinklers" (*ṛṣabha*).

"Parimarau" refers to two animals joined by death; that is, for whichever animal [is sacrificed], if the goat is dead, then that [animal] is also considered dead—thus [it is said] regarding the paired animals in the Āgnicayana. Now, the number of animals is stated: three each for the horse, the hornless goat, and the antelope (*ṛṣya*) make nine *paryaṅgyas*; there are one hundred and eighteen of the eighteen-fold set; fifteen of the fifteen-fold set; one hundred and thirty-five in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; eleven of the eleven-fold set; and furthermore, fourteen for the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), making twenty-two pairs. Thus...

There are one hundred and ninety domestic animals (*grāmya-paśu*). In the *anuvākas* beginning with "The wild ones for King Indra" (*āraṇyā indrāya rājñe*), there are one hundred and eleven; and in "The tawny ones of Kapi" (*yāḥ samtāca kopilānaḥ*), there are eighteen, making one hundred and twenty-nine wild animals (*āraṇya*). Together with the domestic and wild, the number of animals mentioned is one hundred and nineteen. Having performed five oblations, ending with "Agni" (*āgnir iti*), [the ritual concludes]. || 19 ||
When the ritual has been performed with the fire produced by friction, the wives adorn the horse.
The two wives of the Pantaḥ and the Mahiṣī adorn the horse. || 10 ||
Some say that it should be encircled with fire. (Khaṇḍa 8) || 21 ||
The improper time for wearing ornaments has been stated. || 21 ||

There are a thousand golden gems, a thousand silver ones, a thousand ocean-born [gems], a thousand shell-gems, or a thousand glass-gems. Girls weave the glass-gems into the hair-locks; they fasten the other gems upon the necks. The Mahiṣī queen fastens the golden ones with the word "Bhūḥ," the Vāvātā the silver ones with "Bhuvaḥ," and the Parivṛktī the shell-gems with "Suvaḥ."

For each one, there are a hundred maidens as attendants. There are a hundred princesses from the Rāmapurīs, who serve as the place of offspring for the chief queen (*mahiṣī*). There are a hundred daughters of royal slaves (*rājadāsa*) as attendants for the favorite wife (*vāvātā*). There are a hundred daughters of charioteers (*sūta*) and village headmen (*grāmaṇī*) as attendants for the discarded wife (*parivṛktī*). There are fifty [daughters] of charioteers and fifty [daughters] of village headmen serving as slaves.

A thousand each of golden, silver, and ocean-born gems—these gems, consisting respectively of gold, silver, and substances from the sea, such as pearls—are placed upon the hairs (*bāla*). By the word *bāla*, the body hairs (*roma*) are meant. They churn the gems among the hairs with the sound "Bhūḥ"; thus the chief queen (*mahiṣī*) [churns] from the golden [gem] at the mouth up to the region of the neck. Because there is no separation in the repetition of the mantra for the gem. With the sound "Bhuvaḥ," the royal consort (*rājñī*) [churns] from the right side or from the left, until the end of the vessel.

"Suvaḥ! "Parivṛti!"—thus they establish it. 238. The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—... [The remainder of the 14th Praśna]: Then, upon the hair-tufts adorned with gold and other materials, young maidens tie on conch-shell beads. He anoints with clarified butter that portion of the body which has been thus decorated. || 22 ||

With the formula, "May the Vasus anoint you," the queen anoints the horse with guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter; with "May the Rudras anoint you," the favorite wife with safflower oil (or *kausumbha*); with "May the Ādityas anoint you," the discarded wife with mustard oil; and with "May the Viśve Devas, belonging to Vaiśvānara, anoint you," the other [wives] with the original substance. Some authorities prescribe the anointing in reverse order for the fastening of the jewel. 23.

She anoints the buffalo-cow with guggulu and boiled clarified butter, with the mantra, "May the Vasus anoint you. According to Āpastamba, there is an alternative mantra: "With golgulava and surā-liquors. With *kāśāmbava* (safflower-dyed) and boiled *devadāru*, she anoints her with, "May the Rudras anoint you. With *maustakta* (musk-mallow) and boiled [substance], there is a reversal [of the order], with, "May the Ādityas anoint you. The rest is clear. || 23 ||
With the verse "They harness the ruddy one," he yokes the horse to the chariot. || 24 ||
The word "in heaven" marks the end [of the formula]. He yokes the decorated horse to the right side of the chariot. || 24 ||
They harness his two beloved bay horses that fly on opposite sides; he yokes the two side-horses to the chariot that carries the lead horse. || 25 ||
Ending with the words "nṛvāhasa," he yokes the other two horses as companions to that horse. || 25 ||
"Making a banner for those who have no banner," with these words he raises the flag on the chariot. || 26 ||
"Thou wast born with all thy limbs," thus ends [the section]. || 26 ||
With the verse "Like a cloud," he puts on the armor.
They are about to swell. || 27 ||
"With the bow, the cattle"—with these words, he touches the bow.
