With a middle-sized Palāśa leaf, having poured out the insect that has fallen inside the enclosing sticks while reciting the *dyāvāpṛthivī* verse, he should stand over it with the exclamation "bhūḥ."
If one should procure another *sāṃnāyya* offering, or if one should offer the *agnihotra* again after having milked another cow, [he should do so with the verse]:

"Mitra, knowing, ordains the people; Mitra has supported the earth and the sky; Mitra gazes upon the tribes with unblinking eyes. For the sake of truth, let one offer the oblation accompanied by ghee. Having offered the *agnihotra* that was rained upon, he should milk another cow and offer it again.

Having sacrificed to her and bathed after three nights, he should invite her with these words: "I am that [heaven], you are this [earth]; I am the sky, you are the earth; I am the Sāman, you are the Ṛc. Come, let us unite; let us both together deposit the seed for the sake of a male. If, when the first oblation has been offered, the second oblation should spill over, he should offer the first one again with the second, saying: "O Vanaspate, wherever you know the secret names of the gods, there cause the offerings to go. Having added a fuel-stick with this verse addressed to Vanaspati, he should sacrifice again silently. || 46 ||
If the Āhavanīya fire should go out after the first oblation has been offered, he should offer [again] either on a wood splinter or on gold while saying, "Fire in wood, wood in fire. || 47 ||

If, prior to the *prayāja* offerings, a coal should move outside the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) toward the east of the *āhavanīya* fire, it would bring prosperity to both the *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer. If it moves toward the south, it would bring prosperity to both the *brahman* and the sacrificer. If it moves toward the west, it would bring prosperity to both the *hotṛ*, the wife, and the sacrificer. If it moves toward the north, it would bring prosperity to both the *agnīdh* and the sacrificial animals, as well as to the sacrificer.

"O darkness, do not [strike] me; O you who delight in sacrifice, do not [strike] me; O sacrificer, do not [strike] me—let there be homage to you as you advance, homage to you, O Rudra, as you depart, homage where you sit down! Do not harm the *adhvaryu*, do not harm the sacrificer! With these words, he should strike it with the base of the *sruva* ladle. If it should turn back toward the east, [he should say] likewise regarding the other directions: "Do not harm the *brahman*, do not harm the sacrificer!"... do not harm the sacrificer!

With "Sīḥ," he bends the mantra toward the south: "Do not harm the Hotṛ; do not harm the wife; do not harm the sacrificer. Toward the west: "Do not harm the Āgnīdhra; do not harm the cattle of the sacrificer; do not harm the sacrificer. Toward the north: [the same]. (Section 2) 48.

"The thousand-horned bull, Jātavedas, whose back is the Stoma, who is rich in ghee and fair of countenance—may he not abandon us, nor may we abandon him while he is unextinguished; grant us prosperity in cattle and prosperity in heroes. With these words, he casts it into the fire. (49)
Or, having struck [the enemy], he should offer oblations. || 15.1.50 ||

If the fire of one who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni) should not be produced by friction because of the proximity of the [prescribed] time, he should, upon seeing another fire, fetch it, spread it out, offer oblations, and then, without hurrying, churn again.
If he does not find another wife, he should offer oblations into her right ear.
According to some, [the word] "of the unborn" [is used]. 53.
But one should not eat from that [vessel] of an unborn [child]. || 54 ||
One should offer [the oblation] into the right hand of a Brāhmaṇa who has found a goat. || 55 ||
One should not obstruct a Brahmin from staying for the sake of lodging. ||56||
But if he finds a Brāhmaṇa, he should offer [the oblation] into a clump of Darbha grass. || 57 ||
But one should not sit upon Darbha grass.
If one does not find darbha grass, one should offer oblations in water. || 59 ||
But one should not discriminate regarding water, thinking, "This is fit for drinking; this is unfit for drinking. (15.1.60)
One should indeed partake even of that which is unfit for consumption, provided it is water, during this year.
But one should not wash one's feet with water [in that manner]. || 62 ||
These vows are to be observed for one year. || 63 ||
At the end of the year, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati.
If the fire of one who has established the sacred fires should burn his house, [he shall offer] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat.
For one whose fires should become mixed with other fires, or with each other, [he should offer] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vivici.
If the Gārhapatya and Dakṣiṇa fires should become mixed, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vīti.

If both the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires have gone out, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vipṛc; according to some teachers, this applies when both the Gārhapatya and Dakṣiṇāgni fires have gone out.
If he should be consumed by fire, [he should offer] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratabhṛt.
If [the fire] is by means of a corpse-fire, [one should offer] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Śuci; if by means of a birth-fire, [a cake on eight potsherds] to Agni Saṃkusuka. || 15.1.70 ||

The *saṃkusuka*, the *vikusuka*, the *vikira*, and the *viṣkira*—with beans, clarified butter, and *nalada* fuel, we pacify the flesh-eating [fire]. "In this *saṃkusuka* fire we cast away our impurities; we have become pure and worthy of sacrifice; may he prolong our lives"—these are the invitatory and offering verses. (71)
If [the fire is extinguished] by lightning, [one should offer] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Apsumat.

All [the portions] should be offered together to Agni Vivici. Having offered [the portions] to Agni Śuci, he should cause the third [offering], the Vrātabhṛtī, the fourth, the Apsumatī, and finally the Kṣāmavatī, to proceed in order. (Section 3) || 73 ||
Some recite the *vrātabhṛtī* as the second [verse], and the *vrātapatī* as the last. 74.

"Agni, Indra, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Bṛhaspati have made the leaking embryo medicine-free. It has dripped away upon the earth; it does not reach the navel; Nirṛti is driven far away"—with these words, one should consecrate the Agnihotra ladle if it is leaking.

If the moon rises while the sacrificial oblation has already been set out, one should divide the rice grains into three parts: those that are of medium size he should make into a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Dātṛ; those that are the largest he should make into a pap of curdled milk for Indra Pradātṛ; and those that are the smallest he should make into a pap of boiled milk for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. Thus, Agni himself procreates offspring for him. ||76||
If the moon rises while the oblation has not yet been poured out. ||77||
One should offer [the oblation] to those who have suffered failure.
Likewise, when one portion has been set aside and the moon has risen, the remainder is for those who partake in failure.
Having concluded that sacrifice and having driven away the calves, he should sacrifice with the *sāṃnāyya* oblation on the following day.
One who, being a regular performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, should omit either the New Moon day or the Full Moon day, shall offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt.

"The sacrifice of one whose sacrifice is interrupted by the performance of this intermediate offering is indeed severed. One should perform for Agni that same eight-potherd cake for Agni which is offered on the new moon and full moon days, but now for Agni Pathikṛt (the maker of the path). By that very means, he returns again to the path and does not sever the sacrifice; so it is known. (82)

If one who has commenced [the vow] lets the time pass, or if one who has not commenced it [commits an offense], he should offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Agni Vaiśvānara Vratapati. || 83 ||
If one who has established the sacred fires should act as if violating his vows; or if one who has established the sacred fires should go abroad—so say some. (84)

One who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and sheds tears born of distress shall offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Agni Vratabhṛt. Some prescribe the offering to Vratabhṛt for one departing on a journey; others prescribe the offering to Vratapati for the shedding of tears. (85)

"O Agni, you who uphold the vows, being pure, seat the gods here for the sake of carrying the oblation, O Agni! Now, upholding the vows, the protector of vows, undeceivable, ageless, and possessing excellent heroes, sacrifice for us to the gods; bestowing jewels, O Agni, easy to find, protect us that we may live, O Jātavedas!"—these are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. (Section 4) 86.
Thus ends the first chapter in the fifteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Now begins the second chapter of the fifteenth book.
One should consecrate [the bull] with the mantra: "From whatever you fear, from that grant us security; be gracious to all our offspring; homage to Rudra, the bountiful giver. (1)

If the cow of the Agnihotra sacrificer, having been let loose or having been brought near, should sit down, [the priest should recite]: "The goddess Aditi, of all forms, has risen; she has bestowed life upon the lord of the sacrifice, preparing a portion for Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa. Having raised her up and milked her, he should give her to a Brāhmaṇa.

If one should not eat the food of someone, he should beat that person with a stick, crushing it repeatedly, and having raised [the animal], he should make it his own, saying: "May you be blessed with good pasture; may we also be blessed. Eat grass, O inviolable one, at all times; drink pure water as you go. Having torn up a clump of *darbha* grass, he should make [the animal] eat it. || 3 ||

If the cow being milked should bellow or if she should yield blood, one should say, "She has stepped out," and having enclosed a space around the *dakṣiṇāgni*, one should cook it over that fire and offer it in that very same fire. One should give her to a Brāhmaṇa whom one thinks will not return. 4.

"Whatever milk today has clung to the earth, whatever has flowed into the plants, and whatever into the waters—may there be milk in my houses, milk in the cows, and milk in the calves; may I be composed of that milk. Having consecrated it with this mantra, if the milk being milked should spill, one should pour water over it with the verse, "I send you forth to the ocean," and having offered that same [milk] however it may be, and having milked another cow, one should offer again. || 5 ||
Or rather, he may milk that same cow or another; if he should break [the vessel], he should wash another pot and then milk into it, but water must not be poured back into it.

If the milk should spill, or while it is being carried, or while it is being placed on the fire, or once it has been placed on the fire, or while it is being removed from the fire, or once it has been removed, one should milk another cow [into the vessel].

Now, if what has been ladled out should spill—whether once or twice or thrice—one should not heed it, according to some teachers. If, however, what is being ladled out for the fourth time should spill, one should pour the remainder back into the pot, then take four spoonfuls, recite a verse addressed to Varuṇa, and offer the oblation with that verse to Varuṇa. (Section 5) ||8||

If that which has been ladled out should spill, one should ladle it out again and offer it; or else, having recited a verse addressed to Varuṇa over clarified butter, one should make the offering with that Vāruṇī verse. || 9 ||

If what has been hurriedly offered should spill, one should offer again from that same [milk] and then return; [otherwise] one would cut off the sacrifice. Where it spills, having settled that [spilled portion], one should take it up again. Having offered that which is of such a kind and appearance, one should milk another [cow] and offer again. ||15.2.10||

If the eastern [portion] being carried away should spill, one should consecrate it with the mantra, "Thou art offered as the body of Prajāpati for the sustenance of the Viśvedevas," and then, having recited a verse addressed to Varuṇa, one should offer an oblation with that Varuṇa-verse. || 11 ||

If [the oblation] that was carried forward should spill before [the offering], one should lift it up again, pour it out once more, and offer it; or else, having recited a verse addressed to Varuṇa over the clarified butter, one should sacrifice with that verse addressed to Varuṇa. || 12 ||
If, before the oblation has been offered, it should spill, then having offered another oblation of whatever kind and quality it may be, and having milked another cow, one should offer again. || 13 ||

"The sky has leaped; the earth has leaped; the young bull has leaped upon the cows. May all these worlds that have leaped forth cause the sacrifice that has leaped to procreate. From what has leaped forth, the rain-cloud is born; from what has leaped forth, the bull is born. From what has leaped forth, may we procreate"—having thus consecrated the spilled *agnihotra* with this mantra, he should pour water over it. 14.

If it should spill in the evening, one should not eat until the morning offering has been made; if it should spill in the morning, one should not eat until the evening offering has been made. || 15 ||
Divine lightning strikes that person whose *agnihotra* fire makes a crackling sound (*śiriśira*). If he should hate someone, he should say, "May it burn him! (or "May it burn that one!").

If, while the Agnihotra has been placed upon the fire, a dog should run between [the fires], one should take ashes from the Gārhapatya fire and, with the verse addressed to Viṣṇu, "Viṣṇu strode through this," he should sweep away the soot from the Āhavanīya fire; with these very ashes, he fills in the dog's footprint.

If the sun should set upon one whose fire has not been brought forward, or if he should see another fire burning elsewhere, he should bring that fire and enter it; for this is how the fire is established.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for re-establishing the Dakṣiṇāgni that has gone out. ||19||

If the sun should set while the fire of one who has not yet lifted his sacred fires remains unlifted, they should first carry away the *agnihotra* oblation; then they should lift the fire. Alternatively, having tied a piece of gold to a blade of *darbha* grass, someone should go forward first. A *brāhmaṇa* of noble lineage (*ārṣeya*) who knows much should follow behind and lift the fire. Following behind with the *agnihotra* oblation, he should proceed, establish the fire, set down the *agnihotra*, and remain seated without breathing until the end of the day. Having given a gift, offered the oblation, and recited "bhūḥ bhuvaḥ suvaḥ," he should worship [the fire]. He should offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) to Varuṇa. He should sacrifice it with the formula: "O Dispeller of Faults, homage! Svāhā! (15.2.20).
If one should bring [the fire] for the evening Agnihotra at the wrong time, one should offer it in the morning with the formula: "Vastar-namaḥ svāhā. || 21 ||
If, in the morning, one should bring forward the Agnihotra at the wrong time, one should offer oblations with these two mantras to fulfill the proper time and then perform the regular Agnihotra.

Having set down the evening *agnihotra* oblation, he recites "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ" before the offering is made; and having offered it, he sets down the morning *agnihotra* oblation, remains seated without breathing until the fire has gone out, gives a gift, and having offered, he worships with "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ.

He follows the *āhavanīya* fire [to the cemetery], saying, "Agni has looked toward the beginning of the dawns. Having brought forth another fire, he should worship it, saying, "Be secure right here; do not abandon me, nor him, the son of so-and-so. He should offer a *caru* oblation to Mitra.
Some transmit a cake on one potsherd dedicated to Sūrya.
While she remains there, the husband and wife, fasting and restraining their speech, sit for that day kindling the fire.
One should offer the evening Agnihotra with milk; having placed the first [portion] on the fire, one should bring the second.

If the sun should rise while the fire of one who has not yet drawn it out is still unkindled, he should take four portions of clarified butter and go forward first. A Brāhmaṇa of noble lineage who knows much of the sacred tradition should draw out the fire following him. He should follow with the Agnihotra oblation, having established the fire and set down the Agnihotra offering. Sitting in front, facing west, he should offer that which was taken in four portions with the mantra: "May Uṣas with her banner enjoy the sacrifice invited by the gods; [may she accept] the most honey-sweet [oblation] for the gods, Svāhā! Having offered this, he should perform the regular Agnihotra. (Section 7) 27.
For that [transgression], the same ritual procedure for the oblation applies; that is the expiation, which is performed when the morning [libation] has passed.
The difference is only this much: here one does not carry the Āhavanīya fire along. || 29 ||

If the sun should rise upon one whose *agnihotra* has not yet been offered, he should lift the oblation, remain seated without breathing until the sun has set, then offer it and worship with the syllable *bhūḥ*. A choice gift is the sacrificial fee.

If it should happen at the end, he should draw [the fire] out and run toward the east; having placed it down, he should sit until he faints. When he faints, he should then offer an oblation with "bhūḥ svāhā. || 31 ||

If, after he has set out with the thought "I shall offer for this person," the sun should rise while the Agnihotra has already been offered, then according to some, having offered that [second] oblation, he should then demolish [the hearth] and perform the re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya).

If both fires should follow [the sacrificer] when the sun rises or sets, or if they should be lost while mounted on the two kindling woods, there must be a re-establishment of the fires; this is the expiation in that case.
One whose Agnihotra has been interrupted for two or three days should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumat.

"Creating for himself a path easy to traverse and free from retreat, the sharp-horned bull, blazing brightly, looking back upon his ancient dwelling-place, Agni has stretched out the celestial thread. "Thou art our thread and our bridge, O Agni; thou art the path that leads to the gods. By thee, O Agni, may we ascend to the back [of heaven], and then may we rejoice in the communal feast with the gods"—these are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. (35) (Section 8)
Thus ends the second chapter in the fifteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Now begins the third chapter in the fifteenth book.

If the Gārhapatya fire should go out while the Āhavanīya has not gone out, one should extinguish the Āhavanīya, place the embers of the Gārhapatya nearby, and churn the Āhavanīya with the mantra, "From here Agni was first born. Having led it forward, he kindles it with the mantra, "O Agni, sovereign, delight in the chariot, for power, for glory, for vigor, for offspring; you are the sovereign, you are the self-ruler; sit on the good seat; may the two springs of Sarasvatī enkindle you. He should then offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tapasvat, Janadvat, and Pāvakavat.

"Come with your heat among the people, O Agni, as the purifier with your flame; come to this well-recited hymn of mine. "Come to us with your heat among the people, O Agni, as the purifier, shining brightly; bestowing our oblations upon the gods"—these are the invitatory and offering verses (yājyānuvākye). 2.
This very same expiation applies when the Āhavanīya fire has gone out. In this case, one does not follow the Gārhapatya fire; rather, one offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat.
Not for one who practices austerities. || 4 ||

If the eastern fire should go out when the evening *agnihotra* has not yet been offered, some say that one should place the *agnihotra* milk on the fire and ladle it out; others say one should carry it forward with the former fire. Having carried it forward with the former fire, one should follow it with the *agnihotra*. A Brahmin who is highly learned should carry forth the fire. Whatever would be required for a re-establishment (*punarādheya*) of the fires, that he should give as a gift.
If, during the morning Agnihotra, another fire should follow [the first], one should have it followed [to its end], churn out a new fire, take it up, and offer the oblation.
If, however, he should be in haste, he should first settle down by the fire, then draw it out toward the east, and offer the oblation.

But that which is his former fire, he makes it subsequent. Having settled elsewhere, having churned the fire and drawn it out, he should offer the oblation. On the following day, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tapasvat, Janadvat, and Pāvakavat. (Section 9) 8.
According to some, [this applies] when another fire should follow it.

He does not wait for the [proper] time. Then, having churned the fire here and drawn it out, he consecrates it with the verse, "From here Agni was first born," and kindles it with the formula, "O Agni, O Sovereign, delight in wealth; delight in sap, in splendor, in vigor, and in offspring; you are a sovereign, you are a self-ruler; sit on the pleasant seat; may the two springs of Sarasvatī protect you. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat and a porridge of barley to Varuṇa. 15.3.10.

"If one's former fire should go out," so say some; [in this case] one does not observe a specific time. It should be churned from those very same embers. Now, if such embers are not available, one should touch the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) with ashes and then churn; thus he generates him from his own womb. "One whose fire should go out" should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tapasvat, Janadvat, and Pāvakavat, so say some; [in this case] one does not observe a specific time.

One should churn [the fire] from those very embers; or, if there should be only wood-shavings, grass, or ashes, one should touch the two churning-sticks (*araṇī*) with them and churn. Thus he generates him from his own womb. One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tapasvat, Janadvat, and Pāvakavat. || 11 ||

Or, at the place where the desired [deities] follow, he offers these oblations: "To Mitra, svāhā! To Varuṇa, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! To Sūrya, svāhā! To Agni, the ascetic, the one who possesses people, the purifier, svāhā! To Agni, the pure, svāhā! To Agni, the luminous, svāhā! To Agni, the lord of vows, svāhā!"—with the *vyāhṛtis* both separately and combined. 12.
Now, according to some, it is understood that if the Āhavanīya fire should go out before the time for the Agnihotra, one should bring forth another fire.
If at the time of the oblation the *prāṇa* has entered the *udāna*, one should offer it into the *gārhapatya* fire.
If the Gārhapatya fire is the udāna, it has entered the prāṇa in the Āhavanīya fire. || 15 ||
If the Dakṣiṇāgni has gone out, [one should offer] in the Gārhapatya, thinking, "The Vyāna has entered the Udāna. || 16 ||
If all [the fires] should go out, one should churn the fire, carry the Āhavanīya fire toward whichever direction the wind is blowing, and offer an oblation with the formula: "Svāhā to Vāyu! (17).

If they should travel in a windless place, he should churn fire, prepare the sacrificial fires, sit down to the west of the Āhavanīya fire, and himself drink the Agnihotra milk (it is known that this serves as a substitute for the Agnihotra). || 18 ||
If he should offer after sunset, he should offer again once the sun has set. ||19||
If one should offer oblations at the dead of night, one should offer them again at dawn. ||15.3.20||
One whose fire they should carry forth into another fire should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Agnivāt.
He should consecrate them with the mantra: "May you two be of one mind toward us. || 22 ||

One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat. If the fire, having been taken out, should go out before the Agnihotra has been offered, they say that one should take another fire and kindle it without taking out the old one; but that should not be done. Since the portion [of the fire] is taken out in its proper sequence, why should another be taken out? Having brought those very embers back together, one should churn [the fire] with the verse: "From here was Agni first born. (23)
One should offer the oblation with the verse: "Those thirty-three threads which have been stretched out. || 24 ||

If a black bird flies repeatedly over the *agnihotra* while it is being destroyed; or if, when the *agnihotra* has been placed on the fire or the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) has been set out, a man, a dog, a chariot, a cart, or a bull passes between the two fires; or if a cow, a boar, or a ram [passes between them]—in that case, having sprinkled water along [the path], he should lead a cow back along [that same path], [reciting]: "May prosperity increase; may the sacrifice release the lord of the sacrifice from sin through curds and ghee, Svāhā! (25)

Having taken ashes from the *gārhapatya* fire with the verse addressed to Viṣṇu, "Viṣṇu strode through this," he should sweep away [the footprint] from the *āhavanīya* fire and carry it out; with these very ashes, he also fills the footprint and should obliterate both the path and the footprint.

If a cart or a chariot should pass between the two fires, according to some teachers, one does not fix a specific time [for the expiation]. One follows the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "O Agni, that first footprint of yours which was placed down, you have extended its rays along; bring back that wealth-abiding [fire] to us; unite us with your favor, rich in vigor. Having led another fire forward with the mantra: "O Agni, you are far-extending, the beloved, excellent Hotṛ; through you they spread out the sacrifice," he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt (the Maker of the Path).
Furthermore, he should fetch sacrificial grass from nearby, and an ox is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). || 27 ||
One should offer this very [oblation] when the *stotra* is confused; one should offer this very [oblation] when the *śastra* is confused. 28.
Or for one whose fires another's fires might separate, or who himself might separate from his fires. || 29 ||
This [offering] is for one who has died among the people. || 15.3.30 ||

For one who has died abroad, he should offer the Agnihotra with the milk of a cow whose calf has been lost, as long as his physical remains have not yet come into contact with the sacred fires. He spreads out those Darbha grass blades that were pointing northward so that they point southward. Wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītin), he milks the Agnihotra cow and holds a fuel stick beneath [the vessel].
For it is known from scripture: "They hold [the breath] above the gods. || 32 ||
They throw earthen vessels into the water. || 33 ||
They indeed give iron ones. || 34 ||
One should give the sacrificial implements to a Brāhmaṇa. || 35 ||
The stone is indeed the mother of the son. 36.
If one should hear that someone who has not died has died, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Surabhimat.
If the sacrificer should die when the first oblation has been offered, one should pour the second oblation into the southern fire.
Or he should cause him to go to a heap of ashes. (Khaṇḍa 12) || 39 ||
Thus ends the third chapter in the fifteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
Now begins the fourth chapter in the fifteenth book.

If the clarified butter (*ājya*) spills before it has been purified, a piece of gold should be given; according to some, a boon should be given. If it spills while being purified, one should give a living creature. If it spills after it has been purified, a variegated object should be given. (1)
Whatever abundant thing he may have in his house, that he should give.

If [he offers] with "To the Lord of the Earth, svāhā!", he should place that [offering] toward the east at a span's distance; with "To the Lord of the World, svāhā! to the south; with "To the Lord of Beings, svāhā! toward the west; and with "To Being, svāhā! toward the north. With "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he pours it upward, or he consecrates it by reciting, "I pour thee together. || 3 ||
"By the measure, the near-measure, the counter-measure, and the upward-measure of the sacrifice, I encompass thee," with these words he encompasses it. || 4 ||
According to some, he recites "devāñjanamaganyajña" immediately after the *ājya* [verse].

"‘To the Lord of the Earth, Svāhā! To the Lord of the World, Svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, Svāhā!’—with these words one should consecrate what has been spilled; thus it is heard as a rule applying without exception to all sacrificial offerings."

If the potsherd should be lost, he should offer a cake on two potsherds to the Aśvins and a cake on one potsherd to Heaven and Earth. The Hotṛ priest is a Bhārgava; a one-year-old calf is the sacrificial fee. 7.

If it should break before the placing [of the potsherds], he joins it with the formula, "With the Gāyatrī of a hundred syllables, I join thee. Having joined it, he consecrates it with, "The Gharma is unbroken," pours water over it, and then prepares another potsherd. Or, having ground that [shard] and mixed it with other clay to be used for making [the vessel], he unites it with the potsherds while reciting, "May the Gharma go to the gods. This applies if it breaks prior to the placing [of the potsherds]. (8)
Now, if one were to lay down the consecrated bricks with this very mantra: || 9 ||
If, while performing the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, one should cause a potsherd to fall into the fire, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.

One should perform this very offering when a son is born; one should also perform this very offering by one who, being a regular performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, should happen to let the new moon or the full moon day pass by.
One should offer this very same oblation if one should eat of the new grain without having first performed the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice.

He who has established the sacred fires is indeed brought as an offering to the gods; the gods eat his food. If he were to eat of the new grain without having performed the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, he would be eating a portion of the gods that has been set aside for them, and he would meet with calamity.
One whose twin sons or twin cows are born should offer a cake on thirteen potsherds to Māruta. (Section 13) 14.
A man born indeed desires lack of vigor; a cow desires the state of having no calf. || 15 ||
The Gāyatrī is the invitatory verse (puronuvākyā), and the Triṣṭubh is the offering verse (yājyā). || 16 ||
Some prescribe a cake on three potsherds dedicated to Viṣṇu.
One for whom others should perform a sacrifice in their fires, or who himself should sacrifice, should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu.
One should offer a *raudra* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) made from *vāstu* grain at a place where Paśupati might cause harm to cattle.
With this [offering], one should cause the Niṣāda chieftain to sacrifice.

The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consists of either a black antelope skin, a wooden wedge, or a donkey without ears; or a spotted deer, or a deer's hoof-print, or a vessel of śyāmāka grain; or two wooden water-vessels, a winnowing basket, or a bed. For this indeed is his sacrifice.
He who, being a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), should approach a woman, must sacrifice a donkey as an animal offering. || 22 ||
He bakes the animal cake on one potsherd upon the ground. || 23 ||
They should proceed with the portions [of the victim] in the waters. || 24 ||
It belongs to Nairṛta or Prajāpati; according to some, its deity is Rakṣas; according to others, its deity is Yama. || 25 ||
If the oblation of anyone is burnt, Nirṛti seizes that sacrifice; when that oblation has been completed, he should then offer that very same oblation again. || 26 ||

The sacrifice itself is the expiation for the sacrifice; whatever remains as leavings, by that one should bring the rite to completion. He should give that sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to whomsoever he hates; thus he causes that very person to be seized by Nirṛti. || 27 ||
And if he should endure it as described, that itself would be the expiation. || 28 ||
Or if he should not be capable of performing the portions for the sacrificial offerings. || 29 ||
If the oblation intended for a particular deity should be spoiled before it has been offered, one should then bring forth another oblation for that same deity.
In that case, the mantras beginning with the taking up of the *sruva* ladle should be repeated.
(Up until the end, or he might even perish. || 32 ||
But if he should conclude the remainder with clarified butter (ājya) dedicated to the respective deities, [he incurs no fault]. || 33 ||
If all of one’s sacrificial oblations should be lost, or become defiled, or be stolen, one should perform the sacrifice by calculating the deities with clarified butter. 34.
Then he should perform another sacrifice that is not excessive; for a sacrifice is indeed the atonement for a sacrifice. || 35 ||
It is known from tradition that one should consume the spoiled oblation with water. || 36 ||
That which would be unfit as food for the noble ones—one should not sacrifice with that. //37//

Whatever oblation is poorly cooked belongs to Yama as its deity; it goes to Yama alone. Having thus concluded [the rite], one should cook four handfuls of rice on the Anvāhāryapacana fire and feed four Brāhmaṇas.
Among them, one Bhārgava should be the consumer; to them an equal boon should be given. That is the expiation. 39.

If one should sacrifice with a sacrifice that lacks the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), that sacrifice is wasted; a barren cow, not fit for life, should be given as the fee—that is the atonement. 15.4.40.
If they should omit the prescribed sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and give a deficient one, that is the expiation. || 41 ||
If one should invoke a deity that has no assigned portion, one should worship it with clarified butter (ājya) according to how it was invoked, either before or after the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.

If he does not invite his sister, or if he forgets her, he should rise up and invite her mentally, and offer an oblation with the verse: "O gods, whatever we have omitted or overstepped... (RV 10.2.4). ||43||

If the oblation that has been set out should spill, or if the clarified butter that has been taken up should spill, a gift of a bright object should be given; according to some, a boon should be given. 44.
If the portion taken for whichever deity should spill before it has been offered, one should give as a substitute whatever is most abundant in that person's house.
If they should exchange the two oblations, one should offer an oblation with the mantra: "May the mind, as light, enjoy [the offering]. (Section 15) 46.

If for whichever deity there should be an exchange of the portions (avadāna) or the invitatory and offering verses (yājyā-anuvākyā), one should offer a continuous stream of oblations with these two [verses]: "Thou, O Agni, for us" and "So thou, O Agni, for us. This applies in all cases of an omission or an inversion.

If an oblation should spill outside the enclosing-sticks (paridhi), he should say to the Āgnīdhra: "Draw this [spilled butter] together and offer it. He (the Āgnīdhra) should draw it together with his joined palms and offer it, saying: "May the sacrificer not be harmed; may the wife not be harmed; may the sacrifice not be harmed; may the lord of the sacrifice not be harmed—Svāhā! He should give him a full vessel (pūrṇapātra). This is the expiation. 48.

If the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) should fly up or be carried away, one should place it within the altar (*antarvedi*) and address it with this *yajus*: "Why do you fly up? Why have you flown away? Being pacified, come here for the sake of peace. Becoming non-terrible and worthy of sacrifice, sit upon your own seat; do not sit elsewhere, do not harm us! Sent by the gods, be clarified by the brilliance of the clarified butter (*ājya*); do not injure anything of ours! For the sake of the peace of acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*), sit upon this sacred grass (*barhis*). With this *yajus*, he should consecrate it and pour the oblation over it. 49.
Having become so, the sacrificer prospers, for whom they perform this expiation at the sacrifice. (Section 16) || 15.4.50 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the fifteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśī Sūtra.
Now begins the fifth chapter in the fifteenth book.

Men have generated Agni, the praiseworthy one, from the two fire-sticks with their prayers and the movement of their hands—the far-seeing lord of the house, the active one. By means of Agni, Agni is kindled. O Agni, may your mind and light, the thirty-three [deities], enjoy [this offering]. Whatever flaw there is in my mind, whatever in my speech, and whatever in my heart—may this god Bṛhaspati fill that up with wealth. May Viśvakarman, enjoying this oblation, extend this sacrifice together with its continuous threads.

Those dawns that have shone forth and those yet to be sacrificed for, I unite them with the oblation of clarified butter. *Ayāścāgne*, *tvaṃ no agne*, *satvaṃ no agne*. O Gods, may we hear what is auspicious with our ears; O Holy Ones, may we see what is auspicious with our eyes. With firm limbs and bodies, having offered praise, may we attain the lifespan ordained by the gods. May Vṛddhaśravas grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are uninjured, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.

The Maruts, whose horses are spotted, whose mother is Pṛśni, who move in splendor and frequent the assemblies; the Manavas, whose tongue is Agni and whose eyes are the sun—all you gods, come here to us with your protection. A hundred autumns indeed are before us, O gods, in which you have ordained the aging of our bodies; where sons rejoice as fathers, do not harm our life in its midst before we reach our journey’s end. "Enkindled, O Agni..."—with these words, I approach the firmament with my hymns, praising the sage of the hearing ear, the one worthy of sacrifice.

O Agni, grant us that which is fearlessness from what causes fear; O God, ward off the wrath of the gods. Yoke your horses! Make Agni your god with your fires, in harmony with them—the most youthful messenger at the sacrifice. He who is steadfast among mortals, the upholder of *ṛta*, whose head is the heat, whose food is ghee, the purifier, whose face is ghee, whose womb is ghee—Agni, kindled by ghee, for ghee is his food. The rivers, dripping with ghee, carry you; drinking the ghee, worship the gods with a perfect sacrifice.

O Agni, giver of life; these, O Agni; seven are yours, O Agni; may the mind, the light, enjoy [this]; thirty-three; whatever defect there is in my mind; Viśvakarman, I yoke you; I yoke Agni; kindling you... (Section 17) May Agni, being praised, protect us with the gods who are to be praised, those belonging to the earth. May Vāyu, being praised, protect us with the gods who are to be praised, those belonging to the intermediate space. May Sūrya, being praised, protect us with the gods who are to be praised, those belonging to heaven. May Viṣṇu, being praised, protect us with the gods who are to be praised, those belonging to the quarters.

"Agni with the Yajus-formulas, Pūṣan with the Svāhā-call—may they protect this sacrifice; may they protect me; I take hold of you; do you take hold of me, Svāhā!"—with these three Anuvākas, he offers thirty-three oblations in the Soma-sacrifice when no specific expiation is known. || 1 ||
The thirty-three sacrificial bodies [are established] at the Āgnīdhra fire-altar. ||2||

"O Earth, O Bearer of Beings, O Sinīvālī, O Urandhrā; O Ācitti, O Manas, O Bhūvas, O Vivastā"—with these [verses], he offers seven oblations into the Vasatīvarī waters, or when the Savanīya offerings have been poured out.

Having consecrated [the ghee] with the mantra: "Thou art Soma’s ghee, the oblation of oblations, the light of lights; ye are the portion of all the gods," he should pour [the water] together over it or recite the following mantras over it: "May the Maruts pour you together, may Indra, may Bṛhaspati, may this Agni pour you together with life and with strength; may he bestow upon me full vigor. [He should do so] with these seven verses: "The gentle ones, the lowing ones..."; "The waters are auspicious..."; "From that very moment I behold them..."; "O Waters, you are indeed the source of happiness..."; "That most auspicious sap of yours, for that we go gladly unto you. || 4 ||
If at the morning pressing the Soma should be left over before the oblation, they should either pour it back into the cups or offer it as an additional libation.
When [the offering] has been sacrificed, they should cause what remains to be set aside and perform the Stotra and Śastra; that is the expiation.
Having drawn the cups, with the Hotṛ’s cup as the foremost, he introduces the Bṛhat-stotra. || 7 ||
They should chant the hymns containing the word "dhayat" with the verse beginning, "The cow yields milk for the Maruts. (8)
Thinking, "This Soma has been pressed," they should praise with these verses addressed to Indra and Viṣṇu at the Hotṛ's recitation.
The Hotṛ recites the Aindrāvaiṣṇava hymn. || 15.5.10 ||
This very same expiation applies when there is an excess at the midday pressing. 11.

With the verses beginning "Great indeed art thou, O Sūrya," they should chant with the Bṛhat Gaurīvita [Sāman] during the Saura hymns. This very same expiation applies when there is an excess at the third pressing. With the Vaiṣṇava verses containing the word "Śipiviṣṭa," they should chant with the Bṛhat Gaurīvita [Sāman].
If the Soma should be left over at the Agniṣṭoma, one should perform the Ukthya.
If [the sacrifice is] an Ukthya, [he takes] the Ṣoḍaśin; if it is a Ṣoḍaśin, the Atirātra; if it is an Atirātra, [the Dvirātra]; if it is a Dvirātra, [then] only a single stotra. ||14||
In that case, they should chant with the Vaiṣṇava hymns containing the word *śipiviṣṭa*, using either the *Bṛhat* or the *Gaurīvita* melody.

If two Soma sacrifices should be performed simultaneously, having offered the first four *saṃbhārayajus* oblations, one should commence the *prātaranuvāka* at the latter part of the night. When that has been recited and it is said, "Come, O sacrificer," while the sacrificer has taken hold [of the Adhvaryu], he should offer an oblation prior to the morning pressing with the formula: "For lying down, for sitting down, for the overcoming of the Gāyatrī, svāhā! (16)

Having offered the four subsequent *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas, one should offer them before the midday pressing with the formula: "To lying down, to sitting down, to the *triṣṭubh*, for victory—svāhā! Having offered the four subsequent *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas, one should offer them before the third pressing with the formula: "To lying down, to sitting down, to the *jagatī*, for victory—svāhā!"

Having offered the four subsequent *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas, he should offer before the omentum of the *anūbandhyā* cow, saying: "To Saṃveśa, to Upaveśa, to the Anuṣṭubh, to Overpowering—Svāhā! Having offered the four subsequent *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas, he should offer before the *udavasānīyā* oblation, saying: "To Saṃveśa, to Upaveśa, to the Paṅkti, to Overpowering—Svāhā! When the fire is kindled, two oblations are offered with the formula: "O Prāṇa and Apāna, protect me from death; O Prāṇa and Apāna, do not abandon me. || 17 ||
Before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering pertaining to the animal sacrifice, he performs oblations; the introductory verses contain the word "pra," and the Ājya offerings contain the word "pra."
The opening verses (pratipad) consist of those addressed to Marutvat or those addressed to Pūṣan. ||19||

If there should be a *agniṣṭoma* Soma sacrifice further on, he should perform an *ukthya*. If it is an *ukthya*, [he should perform] a *ṣoḍaśin*. If it is a *ṣoḍaśin*, an *atirātra*. If it is an *atirātra*, an *aptoryāma*. If it is an *aptoryāma*, a *dvirātra*. If it is a *dvirātra*, a *trirātra*. If it is a *trirātra*, then only a single *stotra*. 15.5.20.

The Abhijit sacrifice is to be performed for the sake of victory; the Viśvajit sacrifice is to be performed for the conquest of the universe. It consists of all the Stomas and all the Pṛṣṭhas, for the attainment of everything and the securing of everything. The Krośa and Anukrośa hymns are to be performed, as well as both the Bṛhat and Rathantara Sāmans during the invocation of Vasiṣṭha. The Sajanya hymn is to be recited, the Vihavya hymn is to be recited, the Kayāśubhīya hymn of Agastya is to be recited, and the Niṣkevalya hymn of Indra is to be recited—one should chant these. One should make the Abhivarta the Brahman-sāman. "One should perform either the Abhijit or the Viśvajit sacrificial rite," thus he gives the direction.
He should be established as before; or, having pressed [the Soma], they should perform a more extensive sacrificial rite (yajñakratu) with the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās). || 22 ||

The *saṃsava* (simultaneous pressing of Soma) may take place as far as the distance of a chariot's journey, or across a mountain, or across a river; it may be between two people from the same country, or between those from different countries; however, according to some teachers, a *saṃsava* does not exist between two parties who harbor mutual enmity. (Section 19) 23.

If there should be great distress among those initiated, one should kindle a great fire on the Āgnīdhrīya hearth, seat a Brāhmaṇa to the south, place twenty-one barley grains and bunches of *darbha* grass into a full vessel, announce it to the Brāhmaṇa, and address the waters: "You are the Living Ones (*jīvāḥ*); revive this person, so-and-so! You are the Life-Givers (*jīvikāḥ*); revive this person, so-and-so! You are the Fully Reviving Ones (*saṃjīvāḥ*); revive this person, so-and-so! He should respond: "So be it. || 24 ||
With the verse, "Whatever herbs have been born," from this Oṣadhi-hymn, he should sprinkle [the person] with these waters. || 25 ||

He causes them to drink these waters: "May those two, the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma, protect your out-breath and in-breath; may this Upāṃśusavana protect your diffused breath (vyāna); may the Aindravāyava protect my speech; may the Maitrāvaruṇa protect your will and purpose; may the Śukra and Manthin protect your two eyes; may the Āśvina protect your hearing; may the Āgrayaṇa protect your self; may the Ukthya protect my limbs; may the Dhruva protect your life-span; may the Atigrāhyas protect your vigor. Thus he touches [the cups] while saying, "O so-and-so! (26).

He recites in response: "May the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma [cups] protect my out-breath (prāṇa) and in-breath (apāna); may the Upāṃśusavana protect my diffused breath (vyāna); may the Aindravāyava protect my speech; may the Maitrāvaruṇa protect my skill and will (dakṣa-kratu); may the Śukra and Manthin protect my two eyes; may the Āśvina protect my hearing; may the Āgrayaṇa protect my self; may the Ukthya protect my limbs; may the Dhruva protect my vital power (vīrya); may the Atigrāhyas protect [my strength]. When this has been recited in response, [he says]: "O Lord of Prosperity, grant prosperity; [grant] breath through the breaths, and out-breath through the out-breaths."
He offers an oblation with the words: "In the vyāna, place the vyāna; in the udāna, the udāna; in the samāna, the samāna; in speech, place speech back for him. || 27 ||
But he does not provide medicine again. || 28 ||
If he should die before the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), they should perform the fire-avabhṛtha.
Or, having caused him to go to the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) or having brought him back from the avabhṛtha, they should cremate him by collecting his remains with the sacred fires.
This much [is prescribed] for a one-day sacrifice. || 31 ||

In the case of a multi-day sacrificial session (ahargaṇa), however, having said, "Bring wood! Burn it!", they should extinguish a coal from the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni) and burn [the body] with fire produced by friction (nirmanthya). || 32 ||
He places the jar containing the bones on the southern corner of the altar. || 33 ||
The Udgātṛ priests should chant the praise with the three Sārparājñī verses as they are being responded to.

The other officiating priests, led by the Hotṛ, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītinaḥ), should go forward reciting the Yāmya verses, chanting the Sārparājñī verses, tying up the locks of hair on the right side and letting down those on the left, while striking their right thighs, or according to some, their left thighs.
They should walk three times around the Mārjālīya fire, keeping it to their left.
The cups should begin with those for Indra and Vāyu, or else with those for Mitra and Varuṇa; at the end of the Mārjālīya rite, they should pour the portions for consumption together. ||37||
They should take "agna āyūṃṣi pavase" as the opening verse.

Having cremated the bones of one who died without a protector, and having bound them together, those who are his own kin or closest relatives should initiate him in his stead and perform the sacrifice together with him.

In the course of a year, they should perform the sacrifice for the bones. It is an Agniṣṭoma Soma sacrifice; the Rathantara or Gaurivīta Sāman is used, and the Stotra is seventeenfold. As prescribed, when the cup-offering precedes the Stotra, he places the jar containing the bones near it. 15.5.40.
They chant with the Yāma Sāman; the sacrificial fee consists of one hundred and twelve [cows]. (Section 20) ||41||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fifteenth book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
Now begins the sixth chapter of the fifteenth book.

If one should be consecrated for a sacrificial session (*sattra*) and then an illness should arise for him, he should divide the *soma* and perform the *Viśvajit* Atirātra sacrifice, which includes all *stomas*, all *pṛṣṭhas*, and has the entirety of his possessions as the sacrificial fee (*sarvavedasadakṣiṇa*).
From the end-maker (Kṛtānta), one undergoes the fruits of one's actions.
Having scraped [the clay] from the ukhā with those [tools], one should prepare another portion of clay and fashion [it]. || 3 ||
Having drawn [the figures] of the animal heads, he should silently attach them.
When the Āhavanīya fire has been prepared, he silently carries the fire [to it]. || 5 ||
When the fire has been piled up, there is no piling up of the fire at the time of rising from the session. || 6 ||

Having moved the sacrificial ground either to the east or to the north and prepared the ritual space, one should sacrifice with the *Sarvapṛṣṭhī*. One may do so when it is impossible to perform all other sacrifices after having made the formal declaration (*āgūrya*). However, in the case of a *sattra*, one should sacrifice with the *Traidhātavīyā* or the *Viśvajit Atirātra*.

If the Āhavanīya fire should go out while they are pressing the Soma, they should lead it forth from the Āgnīdhra fire; if the Āgnīdhra fire goes out, [they should lead it forth] from the Gārhapatya; if the Gārhapatya goes out, they should churn it out.
One should make the two fire-drills from that wood from which smoke rises.
It becomes a betel nut tree. || 15.6.10 ||
He should give four boons to the Brahman, the Udgātṛ, the Hotṛ, and the Adhvaryu. || 11 ||
If they should steal the un-purchased Soma, another must be purchased. 12.
If [the Soma] has been purchased, one should bring it from whoever is nearest and press it. || 13 ||
One should give something to the Soma-purchaser or to the one who brings the Soma. || 14 ||

If they should not find that [soma], he should press pūtīka plants; if not pūtīkas, then phālguna plants; if not phālgunas, then arjuna plants; if not arjunas, then ādāra plants; if not ādāras, having brought whatever wild herbs are moist, he should press them. (Section 21) 15.

At the morning pressing, there is fresh milk and *pūtīka* plants; at the midday pressing, there is curds and *pūtīka* plants; and at the third pressing, there is boiled milk and *pūtīka* plants. || 16 ||
Alternatively, he mixes all the Soma with curds at the morning pressing; with boiled milk at the midday pressing; and with curds mixed with whey at the third pressing.
The Agniṣṭoma Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara as its Sāman. || 18 ||
One should give a single cow as a sacrificial fee to those very same persons. ||19||

Before the twelfth day, or within a year, he should undergo initiation again for that very same sacrifice. He should give there what he intended to give previously; those same officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should perform the sacrifice for him. 15.6.20.
Now, if the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds should be burnt, the Adhvaryu should preserve the *grahas*, the Udgātṛ the *stotras*, and the Hotṛ the *śastras*. 21.
If the Soma has not been burnt, they should proceed with the ritual according to the established rule.

Āśvalāyana says that they may be performed unenclosed; the meaning is that from the conclusion of the ritual (kṛtānta) onwards, whatever rite has been performed, after that point it follows the general rule (*tantra*). However, when the sacrificial hall (*prāgvaṃśa*) and other pavilions are burnt, one does not go to another place for the *devayajana* (sacrificial ground).
When it is burnt, the expiation for that is the same as that for when it has been stolen.
Thereafter, he gives cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); according to some, five boons.
If the pressing-stone should break, they should chant the *sāman* of the radiant Maruts; according to some, it is the *brahmasāman*.
If the pitcher should break at the morning pressing, they should chant praises on verses addressed to Viṣṇu containing the word *śipiviṣṭa*. || 26 ||
If it should break at the midday pressing, they should perform the Sāman with the *vaṣaṭ* as its finale; if at the third pressing, this very same [Sāman].

If the water-pot should break, some say that one should perform the Brahmasāman with the *vaṣaṭkāra* as its final syllable; however, it is heard in all [the texts] without exception. (Section 22) || 28 ||

Having offered seven oblations with the formulas: "To Asava, svāhā! To Vasu, svāhā! To Vibhu, svāhā! To Vivasvat, svāhā! To Gaṇaśrī, svāhā! To Malimluca, svāhā! To Śūṣa, svāhā!"—and having consecrated [the vessel] with the mantra: "Thou art Indra’s draught; it has been taken, it is to be taken. Thou art the first of the gods. Into thee I enter, together with the draughts, together with the cattle, together with the officiating priests, together with the Soma-vessels, together with the members of the assembly, together with those entitled to the sacrificial gifts, together with the sacrificial fees, together with the sacrifice, and together with the lord of the sacrifice—with whatever is mine. (29)
"Thou for lying down, thou for sitting down"—with these words he offers oblations at each pressing when [the vessel] has been torn.
If it were to cease being praised by all the modes [of chanting], they should chant for the Hotṛ with six verses, and for the others with three each. || 31 ||

If one were to cause the *astuta* (un-praised) [laud] to be completed by means of two turnings, they should chant for the *hotṛ* and the *maitrāvaruṇa* from one [turning], and for the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* and the *acchāvāka* from the other.
If they should chant for the Hotṛ with fifteen [verses] by means of one [stoma], they should chant for the others with three [verses] each.
They should take "agne vivasvad uṣasaḥ" as the opening verse (pratipad) for the offering to the Aśvins.

It is known from the tradition: "If the sun does not rise while the Āśvina Śastra is being recited, one should recite all the hymns of the ten maṇḍalas; one should also set aside a multi-colored animal for Sūrya. This applies when it is known that the sun has not become visible while the Āśvina Śastra is being recited. || 35 ||

If, while they have commenced together and are proceeding, the Udgātṛ should be cut off, the sacrificer would be deprived of the sacrifice; that sacrificial rite is to be concluded without a sacrificial fee, and then another [Udgātṛ] is to be brought in. || 36 ||
In that case, he should give what he would have given previously.

Those very same officiating priests (ṛtvij) should perform the sacrifice for him. Now, if the Prastotṛ should be cut off, the head of the sacrifice would be cut off; [therefore, one should] give a boon to the Brahman priest. || 38 ||
That very same [process] must be performed again. || 39 ||
Now, if the Pratihartṛ should be cut off [from his share], the sacrificer would be deprived of cattle; he should give away all his possessions at a renewed sacrifice. || 15.6.40 ||

If both [the Udgātṛ and Pratihartṛ] are interrupted simultaneously, one should perform the expiation for the Udgātṛ; for the Pratihartṛ, one should offer the universal expiation (sarvaprāyaścitta). || 41 ||
In the case of a severance occurring both before and after [the initiation], he who is the youngest shall perform the universal expiation (sarvaprāyaścitta). || 42 ||
If the Udgātṛ priest should be the last to be cut off, one should give away all one's possessions (sarvavedasa) at a new sacrifice.
If [the Sāman] should be interrupted during the Ārbhava Pavamāna, one should offer the Sarvaprāyaścitta oblation. (Section 24) 44.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the fifteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Now begins the seventh chapter in the fifteenth book.

If the Soma should be exhausted, one should divide the gold into two parts; having placed one half inside the *ṛjīṣa*, one should pour water over it, and having drawn up the other half, one should proceed with the cups.
He should give four boons to the Brahman, the Udgātṛ, the Hotṛ, and the Adhvaryu. || 2 ||

If the Āgrayaṇa vessel should spill or be lost, one should draw [the juice] from the other vessels. If the other vessels should spill or be lost, one should draw [the juice] from the Āgrayaṇa, excluding the Śukra and the Dhruva.
"It is known from scripture that one draws [the draught] from the Droṇakalaśa for all the cups (grahas) that have been spilled or have perished. (4)

If the *dhruva* ladle should spill, he consecrates it with the formulas: "Thou art the giver of life, O *dhruva*; give me life"; "Thou art the giver of splendor, O *dhruva*; give me splendor"; "Thou art the protector of the body, O *dhruva*; protect my body. Having thus consecrated it, he gives a boon. ||5||
If it should break, he divides the gold into three parts; having placed the first part down with the formula, "Svāhā! From heaven, swell!", he causes it to swell.
"Oblation! From the intermediate space, swell!"—this is the second. "Oblation! From the earth, swell!"—this is the third. || 7 ||

O gods, let this sacrifice be a peaceful rite for our plants, for our cattle, and for our wealth; for all that exists, you are the peaceful rite. Swell with abundance, O divine one, like clarified butter! Firm is the sky of the sacrifice, firm is the earth, firm is this entire moving world; firm indeed are these mountains, and firm is this king of the people. Remain right here, do not waver; be immovable like a mountain. Stand firm here like Indra, and maintain the sovereignty here.

"Trample those who attack; let the enemies be beneath you! Stand firm like Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, conquering the waters and the lands. Having consecrated [the pillar] with these four verses—"Indra has made him firm with a firm oblation; for him the gods have spoken in favor, as has this Brahmaṇaspati"—he grants a boon. (Section 25, Verse 8)

If the Nārāśaṃsa cup should spill, the Adhvaryu should draw the subsequent draught. Having offered it at the *vaṣaṭ* and *anu-vaṣaṭ* calls, he causes it to swell with the verse, "Swell up, O most intoxicating one"; by this he causes it to swell, and thereby he makes it partake of the consumption. || 9 ||

At the morning pressing, he should consecrate the spilled Soma with the mantra: "The gods have accepted the sacrifice. At the midday pressing: "The Gandharvas have accepted the sacrifice. At the third pressing: "The ancestors have accepted the sacrifice. At night: "The waters, the plants, and the trees have accepted the sacrifice. With the mantra: "Heaven and earth have accepted the sacrifice," he places the Soma for the day-after-morning pressing after having taken up the Soma. 15.7.10.
If the speckled butter should spill, one should take other speckled butter and offer a single oblation with the two *saṃhitā* verses: "The drop has fallen; may the mind, as light, enjoy it. || 11 ||

If, while performing with the seasonal cups, we two should become bewildered—may the rivers, whose speech is released and which drip with ghee, [protect us]: spring, summer, the honeyed rainy season, autumn, and winter, as well as the two dewy months, may they be sources of bliss for us; may you two dwell together in the two heavens. May Prajāpati produce offspring for us; may Dhātṛ grant us the year. May the Year, turning with the seasons, and may the Lord of Prosperity, bestowing prosperity upon me, grant us abundance.

"O Agni, you are the guardian of the vows of the gods; whatever vows of yours we may violate—Madhu and Mādhava, the two spring seasons—may they protect this sacrifice; may they protect me; following your undertaking, may you undertake mine. Svāhā! With these ten Ṛg-verses and Yajus-formulas, he offers ten oblations. After each oblation, he gives a boon. (Section 26) || 12 ||

If the Soma should spill, one should announce it to the Brahman priest, saying, "O Brahman, the Soma has spilled! Then, having poured water upon the spot where it spilled, he should recite over it: "The divine Savitṛ is to be praised; he is to be invoked by men now at this time of day—he who distributes treasures among mankind. May he grant us here the most excellent wealth. Having thus consecrated it, he should offer an oblation with the verse: "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning... (RV 10.121.1). || 13 ||
If one were to bring forward the cup with a chant before it has been consumed. || 14 ||

"The moon has spoken in favor of the one being urged forward; the Soma juices of both worlds—those celestial and those terrestrial—have flowed together. Having recited this, he partakes of the Soma that has been rained down, saying: "Of thee, who art drunk by Indra, who art rich in sweetness, who art invited—I, being invited, partake. Thus he consumes the Soma that has been sprinkled. || 15 ||

If one should sprinkle [the consecrated] while initiated, [he should recite]: "O Agni, in the waters... and this verse: "O Agni, burn up our enemies within; burn the weapon of the hostile stranger. O Vasu, being observant, burn the ignorant; thy unaging, tireless flames stand forth. O Agni, he who from afar seeks to harm us, or he who, though great as Mitra, plots against us—burn him with thine own unaging, bull-like fires. O most burning one, burn him with thy heat! Let him provide a signal even by night, however far he may dwell."

When the ageless Purifier (Agni) consumes the lords of the forest, no mortal has done harm to your body, O Agni. The monkey devours his own whetted point, like an ox its own skin; when he [the goat] chews up and down through the nights, when he, the unaging one, devours the waters from the lower surface; conquering with his head the songs, with his chest the belly, he devours the stalks with his green mouths—along with these ten Ṛg-verses and Yajus-formulas, he offers ten oblations. For each oblation, he bestows boons. (Section 27)
Having offered ten oblations with the verse, "Whatever offense against the gods," he should sprinkle [the initiate] with the anuvāka beginning, "The blowing one, the world of light. || 17 ||

If the offered and the unoffered Soma should become mixed, one should take out a coal from the Āhavanīya fire within the enclosing sticks and offer the two Somas, both the offered and the unoffered, with the mantra: "For you two, O Indra and Agni, are the seasonal ones of the sacrifice; satisfy yourselves with the conscious [Soma], both the offered and the unoffered! O Indra and Agni, enjoy this Soma, drink it, accept it with pleasure—svāhā! Thus one should offer the two Somas, both the offered and the unoffered. || 18 ||

"O Fathers, let not one who harms our sacrifices, nor a hero, nor one who is our kinsman, nor even one who is a stranger, nor one of evil eye or sinful intent, have power over us. May this oblation reach the gods. With these words, he consumes the two portions of Soma that have been offered. || 19 ||

"May darkness not find the sacrificer, nor the officiating priests, nor these creatures; may it not find him who shall drink this Soma—[this] which has been prepared as both [offerings]. With these words, he addresses the one who is consuming [the Soma]. (15.7.20)

"Seven are the officiating priests, seven the seats; of these, ten fingers, the two Aśvins, and five strengths. May Prāṇa, Vyāna, Apāna, Mind, Intention, Agni, and the Svāhā-offered oblation—the gods eat this! O Prajāpati, none other than you [has created them]. With this mantra, he should pour out the remnants of the portion in the northern half of the eastern half into the Uparava pit. || 21 ||
Or in the eastern part of the southern half. || 22 ||

The sky has flowed; the earth has flowed; this entire world has flowed. All those beings have flowed; may the oblation be born from that which has flowed. May cattle be produced here; may horses be produced here; may men be produced here. May the abundance of wealth, accompanied by a thousand sacrificial fees, settle here. May this sacrifice increase through cattle and horses; may this altar be rich in offspring and heroic sons. May this sacred grass surpass all other grass; may all the gods protect this sacrifice.

Having consecrated the spilled *pṛṣadājya* with these verses beginning "The plants are full of milk" (*payasvatīr oṣadhayaḥ*), having poured water over it, having washed the vessel, and having heated it again, he sets it down. Having placed a hundred-māna piece of gold into it, he takes another portion of *pṛṣadājya* and, while touching it with the verse addressed to Viṣṇu, "May Viṣṇu follow thee for food" (*ekamiṣe viṣṇus tvānv etu*), and then reciting "A drop has fallen" (*drapsaś caskanda*), he causes a horse to smell it and then sets it down.

"Whatever the bird has touched with its beak, O Nirṛti—may Agni, the bearer of oblations and destroyer of ghee, purify all that. This is the expiation for what has been touched by a bird; here the vessel is scraped clean. 24.

"Whatever has been licked by the mouth of a dog, a mouse, or a dog-cooker, O Nirṛti—may the fire, the consumer of oblations, purify all that which is undesirable," with these words he consecrates what has been licked by a beast of prey. This is the expiation for that [case]. (The consumption and so forth are as before. No vessel is used here. (Section 28) || 25 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the fifteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.

One should offer the oblation with the verse, "That which is on the other side of this darkness," if the animal, once dedicated, should tremble, sit down, bellow, stand up, run away, or if it dies while not yet intended for slaughter. With the second verse, "From whatever you have made us tremble with fear, from that grant us security; be gracious to all our offspring; homage to Rudra, the Bountiful One," [one should offer] when it is trembling.
Because of the [scriptural] statement, "Out of fear he sat down," [the mantra] is used when [the deity] has already sat down; this is the second [application].

"O Ustra, stand up! Stand firm! Do not perish! Do not harm this sacrifice or the sacrificer. Place the sacrificer in the world of heaven; be auspicious to us, be auspicious to our bipeds, be auspicious to our quadrupeds"—with these words, he should cause the bull (ustra) to rise. ||3||

"Ucchāga" [is used] for a goat; "unmeṣa" for a ram. "Ūrdhva ū ṣu ṇa ūtaye" is the second [verse]. "Ūrdhvo naḥ pāhy aṃhaso ni ketunā viśvaṃ sam atriṇaṃ daha | kṛdhī na ūrdhvāṃ carathāya jīvase vidā deveṣu no duvaḥ" is the third [verse]. || 4 ||

Because of fear of whom the cows lowed, he performs the second [offering] while they are lowing; because of fear of whom you would have risen up, he performs the second [offering] as he raises it. ||5||

Because of the fear [of whom] you fled—having performed a second animal sacrifice for that which fled and did not return, one of the same form, the same color, the same age, the same lineage, and the same deity—one should complete the rite with that [animal]. || 6 ||
When that specific class is unavailable, goats, sheep, and cows serve as mutual substitutes for one another. || 7 ||
If those [materials] are unavailable, he should conclude the remainder of the rite with clarified butter. ||8||
Because [the cows] stood still out of fear, there is the second [offering] at the immolation when it is not performed intentionally. 9.
"To him who has done this, svāhā!"—with these words he offers the most excellent oblation. || 15.8.10 ||

"Or indeed, you do not die here; [I offer] you to all the quarters, to every quarter. With these four verses, beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss," he should consecrate an animal that has perished, cast it into the water, and then, having brought forward another animal of the same form, color, age, species, and deity, he should complete the sacrifice with it. This applies when an animal of the same species is unavailable. (Section 29) The case of a [sacrificial animal] that has run away has already been explained. 11.

If the cauldron (ukhā) should leak and become useless, one should consecrate the leaking cauldron with the verse: "Agni, the Hotṛ, is the earth, the intermediate space, and the sky; whatever has fallen from there, that reaches Agni alone; it goes away to Nirṛti. Thus he should address the leaking cauldron. 12.
As many times as there are portions of the animal that they do not find, so many times should one take a portion of clarified butter. || 13 ||

If those who have slaughtered an animal should desire that they might meet with misfortune, one should offer an oblation in the Āgnīdhra fire—with the verse beginning "kuvidaṅga" containing the word "namas"—in the case of the Nirūḍhapaśubandha sacrifice, or in the Āhavanīya or Śāmitra fire. 14.
If they should perceive [the fire] as "the eight-stepped one," he offers oblations on the Gārhapatya fire with two verses: "Dhātṛ, Rāti, Sūrya, the god. (15)
Having consecrated [the cow] with the mantra, "O you whose embryo is tawny," he causes the embryo to turn clockwise with the words, "Turn around, turn around."
With the words, "I split thy womb apart," he extracts the fetus from between the hips. || 17 ||

Thinking "let it be outside," he discards the embryo and holds up the vessel for the essence with the verses "The drop that leaps from the thigh," "Viśvarūpa," and "Indu. Having struck down [the spit] into the animal-cooking fire with the *śūla* (spit), he cooks the embryo. ||18||
Having offered the sacrificial cake for Paśupati, he does not [offer] the cake for Heaven and Earth; instead, he offers the embryonic sacrificial cake. || 19 ||

Having cut off the portions of the victim, he should cut one portion from the fetus before the navel and another portion from above; having thus cut them, he places them among the portions for the deities. 15.8.20.
He divides the sacrificial essence (rasa) into three portions: for the deities, for Sviṣṭakṛt, and for the Ādityas.
With the words "one-footed, two-footed," he offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered. || 22 ||
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers the twenty-first [oblation] of the embryo into the south-eastern part with one of the two verses: "O Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa, this name of thine today... || 23 ||
At the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), gold weighing eight prūḍhis is the fee. In the third inner sheath, it is enveloped by a turban; he gives that away. He makes the sheaths loose. ||24||

With one of the two verses, "O Maruts, in whose house [we dwell]... or with the verse beginning] 'By sacrifices, O you who carry the sacrifice,' he offers an oblation of the embryo into the animal-cooking fire. || 25 ||
And he does not utter "svāhā" over the embryo-oblation. || 26 ||
Or else, with the verse, "May the great heaven and earth... he places the embryo upon the cold ashes of the animal-cooking fire.
The embryo as the sacrificial cake. || 28 ||
"I give this youth unto you"—having consecrated [the boy] with these five [verses]. (Section 30) || 29 ||

If the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of one [who has performed the sacrifice] should sprout again, he should offer a ram with testicles, hairy, tawny, and multicolored, as a substitute for the *savanīya* animal; he should then offer an oblation with the verse: "The thirty-three threads which have been stretched out... (RV 10.70.8). || 15.8.30 ||

If a black bird, scattering [the grain], should fly repeatedly over the *havirdhāna* sheds when fear has arisen—if it is possible to sacrifice—then, having taken portions from all the sacrificial offerings and from all the *soma* juices into the *droṇakalaśa*, he offers an oblation with the mantra: "To those gods whose portion this has become, to whom belong the *prayāja*s and the *anuyāja*s; to the gods whose chief is Indra, whose king is Varuṇa, and who have Agni as their hotṛ—*svāhā*! (31)
Furthermore, one should sacrifice in the Abhaya [fire]. || 32 ||

If a failure in the sacrifice occurs on account of the *ṛc*, one should offer an oblation in the *gārhapatya* fire with the word "bhūḥ"; if on account of the *yajus*, with "bhuvaḥ" in the *dakṣiṇāgni*; if on account of the *sāman*, with "suvaḥ" in the *āhavanīya*. If it occurs on all accounts, one should offer a single oblation in the *āhavanīya* using all [three words], or the *brahmán* may offer it.
Or one may meditate with the mind. || 34 ||

"If the Audumbarī pillar should perish or break, one should cut another and raise it with the formula: 'O strength, bestow vigor upon me; stand firm, well-established; supporting the sky and the atmosphere, be steadfast upon the earth—supporter, sustainer, and progenitor. Thus he raises it. || 35 ||
The Adhvaryu, the Sacrificer, or the Brahman priest raises it. || 36 ||
He consecrates it with the eternal *yajuṣ* formula. || 37 ||

If the two *havirdhāna* carts should fall down, the Adhvaryu should lift up the southern one and the Pratiprasthātṛ should support it; the Pratiprasthātṛ should lift up the northern one and the Adhvaryu should support it. 38.
With a verse addressed to Viṣṇu they prop it up; with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu they level it; with a verse addressed to the Aśvins they smooth it down. || 39 ||

With the three *uṣṇih* verses beginning with "O Agni, [grant] booty consisting of cattle," the Adhvaryu offers oblations in the Āgnīdhra fire; the Pratiprasthātṛ offers with the *kakubh* verses. "May Agni, when invoked, be auspicious to us; may his gift be auspicious, O fortunate one, and may the sacrifice be auspicious. May our praises also be auspicious; may our praises indeed be auspicious. Make your mind auspicious for the conquest of Vṛtra, by which you may prevail in battles. By which you may prevail in battles, make our firm bodies manyfold against those who defy us. O Vanaspati, protect us with your aids"—these are the verses as they are recited. (15.8.40)

"Let the head of the sacrifice be restored; let it be made immortal and consisting of the deities; let it be fashioned with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, and let it be restored with one addressed to the Aśvins. Having taken either four or five portions of clarified butter, they both offer the two oblations together.
If the fire-pan belonging to the Āgnīdhra should break while raw, one should scrape it together and make it anew.
If it should break while still uncooked, one should mix another clay with those very potsherds that have been well-ground and fashion [another vessel]. || 43 ||
If the *ukhya* fire should go out, one should lead forward the *āhavanīya* fire; that very same fire is then to be circumambulated again.
A black garment should be given; a black cow, or a black bull, and gold weighing one hundred mānas. || 45 ||
In that he takes the Vasatīvarī waters on the previous day for the Yajñāyajñiya chant of the following day, by that he binds the days together; by that he makes the sacrifice continuous. || 46 ||

In that he recites on the preceding day what is to be chanted on the following day as its corresponding verse (*anurūpa*), by that he joins the day [to the next], and by that he makes the sacrifice continuous. In that he issues the command (*atipraiṣya*), by that he joins the day [to the next], and by that he makes the sacrifice continuous. Thus it is said. 47.

If any one of these is not performed, one should offer this expiation: "Homage to Brahman, homage be to Agni, homage to the Earth, homage to the Plants; homage to Speech, homage to the Lord of Speech, homage to the Great Viṣṇu, I perform [this], Svāhā! One should offer this expiation; one should offer this expiation. (Section 32) 48.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the fifteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Thus ends the fifteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.

Oṃ tat sat. Salutation to Brahman. ... The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.
Now begins the fifteenth book; therein is the first chapter.

I joyfully salute the Lord of Sages, Hiraṇyakeśin, who is endowed with discipline, the foremost among all perfected beings, the bliss of true consciousness and eternal happiness, the knower of the meaning of the Sūtras, and an ocean of compassion. (1) I bow to my Guru, Gaṇapati, the bestower of birth and knowledge; likewise, I bow to Somanātha together with Gaurī, and may Viṣṇu protect me. (2) The Aśvamedha, Brahmamedha, and Sarvamedha were treated in the fourteenth book; now, in the fifteenth book, the expiation for sacrifices (yajñaprāyaścitta) is declared. (3)

The obligatory rites beginning with the Dvādaśāha and ending with the Haviryajña, Somayajña, Rājasūya, and Aśvamedha, which the teachers have explained here, have now been stated. Regarding these, the teaching on expiation (prāyaścitta) is now commenced; an expiation characterized by Vedic revelation is prescribed for the transgression of a rule.

In the Veda (*śruti*), only that which is characterized by the Vedic text itself is taught as expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
