It is heard [in scripture] as "expiation characterized by the Veda" (*śrutilakṣaṇaprāyaścitta*). [The word] *śruti* means "that which is heard. That by which something is characterized or known is its "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*); thus, that whose characteristic is found in the Veda is "Veda-characterized" (*śrutilakṣaṇa*). The locative case in *śrutau* indicates that something is stated in the Veda, but not everything is stated there. Otherwise, it would simply be called "Veda-characterized" (*śrutilakṣaṇa*). What, then, is this expiation? *Prāya* means destruction.

How is *prāya* generally taught? It is taught for the purpose of destroying oneself, as seen in common usage (*loke*). From the verbal root *citī* (meaning "perception"), the word *citta* is derived; because roots have multiple meanings, *citta* is said to mean "rejoining" (*saṃdhāna*). *Prāyaścitta* is the rejoining of a ruined action; thus it is called *prāyaścitta*. The augment *suṭ* is applied to both *citti* and *citta* by rule. Thus ends the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [in the 15th Praśna].

Because the word *vināśa* ends in the vowel *ā*, the form *prāyaścitta* is established through the addition of the augment *suṭ* to both *citti* and *citta*. Furthermore, the augment *suṭ* is justified by the grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) recorded by the author of the commentary on the *Gaṇasūtra*: "The augment *suṭ* is optionally applied to *prāya* before *citti* and *citta*. Thus, the summarized meaning is that the definition of *prāyaścitta* is taught in the revealed scripture (*śruti*). To this, an objection is raised: since all rites are defined either by *śruti* or by *smṛti*, it should not be said that *prāyaścitta* is [defined] by *smṛti*.

To this, the reply is as follows: other ritual acts (*karma*) are characterized by direct scriptural injunction (*śruti-lakṣaṇa*), whereas the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) itself is said to be characterized by scriptural injunction. What, then, is the meaning? Only the characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa-mātra*) of the expiation is taught in the scripture; it is merely a sign (*cihna-mātra*). For example: "The *puroḍāśa* cake is burnt" (*kṣāyati*). "Burnt" (*kṣāya*) means scorched. That is the characteristic mark of the expiation. In the case of the statement "it is burnt," the expiation applies when two or more [cakes] are burnt, not when only a single oblation (*havis*) is burnt.

If one were to understand [the passage] as "if one should perceive eight [or more] calamities," then in the twelfth or sixteenth verse, there would be a conditional rule (*naimittika*) regarding the mere general expiation (*prāyaścitta*). A "rule of action" (*karmavidhi*) is so called because it is enjoined in the event of a transgression of a rule. A "transgression" (*aparādha*) is an act performed otherwise than prescribed; a "transgression of a rule" (*vidhyaparādha*) is a deviation from the injunction. It is in that case of a transgression of a rule—that is, when there is an improper state of affairs—that the expiation is enjoined.

Just as there is an expiation for passing between the two fires without authorization—as in the case [of the rule]: "If one's cart or chariot passes between the two fires"—where there is no such authorization, there is no expiation because it has been prescribed [as permissible]. Furthermore, there is no expiation when traveling for the purpose of a sacrifice. Alternatively, some maintain that this single sūtra means that an expiation characterized by the consumption of food (śana) is prescribed for a transgression of an injunction.

And since there is another specific meaning [to be conveyed], relying on the distinction between the two preceding sūtras, it was stated in the first sūtra that the definition [of the Veda] is merely indicated by the scripture (*śruti*), but not yet its full requirement; whereas by the second sūtra, it was shown that expiation (*prāyaścitta*) occurs when there is a transgression of human action regarding what has been enjoined, but not when there is a change in what has been enjoined by another injunction. Now, it is stated by relying on the unity of the single sūtra.

It is prescribed by the Brāhmaṇa; thus, "prescription" (vidhi) refers to the ritual action. When that [action] is performed otherwise for a purpose other than its intended one, what is prescribed is characterized by direct Vedic revelation (śruti), not characterized by Smṛti, due to the capacity of the injunction. For in a case where both [Vedic and Smṛti authority] apply—such as when the Smṛti-characterized authority exists even in the midst of a rite, because a Smṛti rooted in the Veda is seen regarding the sipping of water (ācamana) as an auxiliary to the rite—it is so [that the Vedic is stronger]. Regarding the fire for the *brahmaudana* rice-porridge, there are three positions: [using] the *aupāsana* fire, or [using] the *nirmanthya* (churned) fire, or all [fires].

Either a portion of the *aupāsana* fire is to be established, or the entire *aupāsana* fire is to be established; or else, in their absence, one may establish the fire produced by friction (*nirmanthya*). Regarding the case of the fire going out (*anugamana*), he states the specific rule: in the case of establishing a portion of the *aupāsana*, if it goes out before the cooking, one should bring back a portion of the *aupāsana* and re-establish it; since no specific expiation has been prescribed, the general expiation applies. If it goes out after the cooking, then having brought back a portion and performed the cooking again, there is neither the granting of a boon nor a formal expiation required.

In all cases where the *aupāsana* fire is used: if it goes out before the cooking is finished, the expiation prescribed by the Smṛtis for the extinction of the *aupāsana* must be performed; having performed the rekindling with the verse "ayāścāgne," and having gathered everything [back], it should be re-established. If it goes out after the cooking is finished, it should be re-established by performing the rekindling procedure as previously described. In the case of the *nirmanthya* (fire produced by friction), if it goes out before the cooking is finished, it should be re-established by producing the fire through friction once again.

If [the fire] has followed [the embers] after cooking, one must again establish the fire by churning and perform the cooking; [then] the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) is required. In the case of the second establishment (*punarādheya*) and so forth, if one follows the view that it is a portion of the *aupāsana* fire, then having brought that portion, all [the rites] beginning with [the recitation of] "taddeśam" should be performed according to the *aupāsana* procedure. In the view of the *tantu* [tradition], having performed the *pathikṛt* oblation, it should be established. In the view of churning (*nirmanthya*), having brought two worldly kindling-sticks (*araṇī*) and churned them, having brought that [fire], it should be established.

However, for one who has already established all [the fires], even that which has been brought from the house of a *śrotriya* must be placed back [in the hearth] during the second establishment (*ādhāna*) and subsequent rites. If he has many wives, he should unite the *aupāsana* fire according to the rules of the *Smṛti*, place a portion of it—or the whole of it—into the [new] hearth, and then perform the *ādhāna*.
[End of] Paṭala 1, accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. Page 263.

In the case of performing all the fire-installations (*sarvādhāna*), there is indeed the omission of the Smārta rites, because their purpose is fulfilled by the Śrauta rites. Some perform the *agnīkaraṇa* and other such rites in the common (worldly) fire, based on the instruction that "the ancestral rite (*paitṛka*) is performed in the Dakṣiṇāgni," and from the statement that "in that very [fire], the *agnīkaraṇa* and so forth constitute a transgression of the rule. However, in the event of a human error, there occurs an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for both Śrauta and Smārta rites. Just as an option (*vikalpa*) is to be observed among sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) and the like which have been set up consecutively and serve a single purpose.

In this case as well, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) between the *khadira*, *palāśa*, and other [woods] when they serve a single purpose; therefore, this is stated: "When a single defect is mentioned, the expiations (*prāyaścitta*) should be combined, because they are connected with distinct purposes. (2)

The expiations that are prescribed for a single fault or a single occasion are to be performed cumulatively. For example: in the case of the *agnihotra* being spilled, there is the recitation of the mantra, "May heaven not spill over the earth"; in the case of an accident (*upasarga*), [there is the recitation], "May the earth rise up in fear"; and regarding fasting, [the rule] "Being invited, one should not eat in the evening"—these constitute a cumulative application. What is the reason? Because of the connection with different purposes. That which is other than a purpose is a "different purpose" (*arthāntara*). The state of being a different purpose is "different-purposedness" (*arthāntaratva*).

Therefore, it is because of internal connection (*āntarayoga*). "Another purpose" (*arthāntara-prayojana*) means that the purpose is distinct from [the previous] purpose. Since the purpose served by the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) is one thing, that served by the approach (*upasarga*) is another, and that served by fasting (*anaśana*) is yet another, there is a combination (*samuccaya*). Even though the purpose of destroying defects (*doṣanirghāta*) is one and the same, nevertheless, because multiple expiations (*prāyaścitta*) are taught for a single occasion, and because an option (*vikalpa*) is improper, the purpose is indeed cumulative.

Because a combination (*samuccaya*) is logically established through their being means (*sādhana*) despite that internal differentiation of types, it is improper to regard them as optional; thus, there is a combination. Just as in the world—wherein one disease in the eyes is cured by collyrium (*añjana*), another is not, and yet another is cured by lying down (*nipātaśayana*)—even though the purpose is the same, namely the removal of disease, there is a combination according to the specific internal differences of the ailments; similarly, even though the purpose is the destruction of defects (*doṣanirghāta*), there is a combination.

An *upadeśa* (injunction) is a statement of fact (*yathārthavāda*); it does not consist of a different meaning, but rather possesses a single purpose (*ekārthatā*). In that case, there is an option (*vikalpa*), not a combination (*samuccaya*). Just as with rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*) and so forth, even in the absence of an explicit scriptural statement regarding a single purpose, since the attainment of the objective is understood from the *arthavāda* itself, an option is appropriate there as well. For example, the *pathikṛt* sacrifice is for the sake of attaining the fruit of heaven, and the *vaiśvānara* sacrifice is likewise. Therefore, because there is an option between these two, a combination is not logical.

Because the instruction for both [the sacrificer and the priest] is free from the fault of being unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), it is performed by both together. It has already been stated previously that these are differences in intermediate effects (*avāntarakāryabheda*). As for the claim that "the injunction located in another recensional branch (*śākhā*) belongs to some [only]," even there, there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*), because the additional injunction is non-obligatory (*anitya*). When the performance belonging to one recensional branch is being taught, one should not say "of some" regarding the inclusion of parts belonging to other recensional branches.

Therefore, where there is an instruction such as "of some" (*ekeṣām*), it is understood that this is an instruction of an additional property (*adhikadharma*) over and above the performance being prescribed; thus, because it is non-permanent (*anityatva*), there is a state of conjunction (*samuccayatva*). When the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are omitted, the *pāthikṛtī* and *vaiśvānarī* [offerings] are prescribed; there is a conjunction of these two. Where there is a relationship of general rule and specific exception (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*), there the general rule is sublated by the specific exception. For example, when the *āhavanīya* fire goes out, the *jyotiṣmatī* sacrifice is prescribed as a general rule.

When the *anvādhāna* has been performed and one follows the *āhavanīya* fire, another oblation is prescribed; there, however, there is a sublation [of the former]. As in the case of the view of some that "the sacrifice went to the gods," even though a combination (*samuccaya*) is possible because the purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), there is only an option (*vikalpa*), since it is presented as an alternative opinion. || 2 ||
169 ... The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—In the fifteenth book (praśna), it states that there are three kinds of expiation (prāyaścitta):
recitation (japa), burnt offering (homa), and sacrifice (ijyā). 3.

The term *ceti* denotes types; it includes other [rites] as well, such as consecration (*anumantraṇa*), attendance (*upasthāna*), adding fuel (*upasamindhana*), and re-establishing the sacred fires (*punarādhāna*), because these too will be described as forms of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). It should be understood that the specific examples given are intended to illustrate their predominance and to indicate their great number. (3) Let these expiations be combined, since they serve different purposes. For what purpose, then, are they performed? To this he says: "They exist for the purpose of destroying faults" (4).

It has been stated that there is a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) in the ritual action. By means of the removal of that [deficiency], they assist the ritual; the meaning is that they render the capacity for the result (*kārya-śakti*) complete. If it is asked, "But how do these [subsidiary acts] have that as their purpose?", the sense is this: when it is said, "This must be performed when such a deficiency occurs," since the remedy for that [deficiency] is required, it is understood that they exist solely for the sake of removing that deficiency. (4) Let it be granted that the removal of defects is their fruit; however, their timing (*kāla*) must also be explained.

Should these rites be performed at the very time of the [main] ritual action, or once the ritual action has concluded, or rather, since sacrifices and the like depend upon specific lunar phases (*parvan*) and so forth, should that particular time be awaited? Regarding this, he says:
"They should be performed immediately after the fault. (5)

The meaning is that, just as in the case of treating a wound and so forth, these [rites] must be performed immediately after the fault; they remove the fault only when done thus, and not otherwise. By this, it is also explained that the performance of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) does not depend on [favorable] lunar mansions, asterisms, and so forth. || 5 ||
But when the fault has been removed, the ritual act is complete in its entirety. || 6 ||

The meaning is that once the fault has been neutralized by such expiation (*prāyaścitta*), the remainder of the ritual action (*karmaśeṣa*) must then be performed. Furthermore, regarding that which was either left undone or improperly performed—whether it be a subsidiary (*aṅga*) or a primary (*pradhāna*) element—it is stated that "it should be done in its entirety" (*kṛtsnam*) so that it may be performed correctly. In this context, a subsidiary element is not performed once the ritual action has already concluded, because it no longer assists the primary act. However, a refinement of the material (*dravyasaṃskāra*) is not performed after the material has already been employed, because its purpose is for that specific utility.

Even the primary [time] (*pradhāna*) when its period has passed is not performed, because that which is performed at the wrong time is as if unperformed. However, it is indeed performed during the secondary time (*gauṇakāla*), since the secondary is to be accepted in the absence of the primary. Therefore, prior to the subsequent *parvan*, there is only the ritual action (*kriyā*) itself in the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). We shall demonstrate this further on. Some, however, explain: "When the defect is removed, the rite becomes whole again; it becomes complete, meaning it becomes capable of yielding its fruit. (6) ...

[Objection: Surely, even if a rite has its defects removed, how can it be fit for its purpose when its capacity has been impaired by the arrival of those defects? For one who is lame because a thorn pierced his foot does not set out upon the path even after the thorn has been extracted. Therefore, since the rite performed [with defects] is useless, there must be a performance of it again.
To this, he says: "There is no repetition of that [rite] because of the non-mention [of such a rule]. (7) [This is] accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 265.

Once that ritual action has been performed, its repetition does not occur except by virtue of a scriptural injunction. Indeed, it does occur by virtue of an injunction, as in: "Having milked one [cow], one should milk another again," or "Then one should perform another sacrifice that is not defective," and so forth. Who, indeed, could know what is to be done or not done regarding a ritual action whose purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), or who could know its capacities or incapacities? Certainly, a blind person does not perceive specific forms.

Therefore, for that [person] whose scripture prescribes repeated application, one may indeed apply it there; however, the capacity for action of the eye will be restored. But where there is no scripture, how could there be repeated application? Yet, in that case, the capacity for action of the very same treated organ—like the eye after the chapter on medical treatment—will be restored. Enough of this digression. (7)
One who has established the sacred fires and is about to depart on a journey should offer oblations with the verse: "To you, O best of Angirases... (RV 10.69.4).

If, due to the disruption of the designation of another consecrated fire (*āhitāgni*) or other such unavoidable causes, one were to depart from home, then one should offer an oblation into the *āhavanīya* fire with the formula "to thee. This is the substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) for the *vāstoṣpatīya* rite. 8.
Having consigned the fires into separate fire-drills, he departs.
The non-obstructive [karmas] are to be superimposed upon the self. || 9 ||
Wherever he may dwell, there he should conclude this sacrifice. || 15.1.10 ||
Wherever he shall dwell, having performed the rites up to the end of the iron oblation (ayasitahoma), he should conclude the sacrifice dedicated to Kṛtānta.

If the Āhavanīya fire of one who has maintained the sacred fires (anvāhitāgni) should go out, he should lead forward another fire with the verse: "Agni has looked upon the forefront of the dawns. Then he offers a spoonful with the formula: "O Purifier, be gracious to him who seeks to win over Agni for the feast of the gods with oblations; Svāhā! (11)

Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* and the *sarvaprāyaścitta*, one should offer an oblation with the verse "idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 9.1.11), says Āpastamba. The mention of the *sruva* ladle is for the purpose of excluding [the *juhū*]. However, if there is another [ladle], one should offer the Vaiṣṇava oblation with the *juhū*. ||11||
Whoever should follow [such a person], this very same penance applies. || 12 ||

Having produced each [fire] from its respective source, the procedure beginning with the *bhūḥ* invocation and so forth is the same. Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya says that both [fires] are established in those very places; however, Devasvāmin maintains that it is only the Āhavanīya [that is established there]. 12.
Having churned [the fire], [he establishes] the Gārhapatya. || 13 ||

Having produced the Gārhapatya fire by friction with the consent [of the authorities], one should perform the expiation exactly as previously stated. Likewise, for the Āhavanīya fire that has attained the status of the Gārhapatya, there is only friction and not the formal leading forth (praṇayana), just as in the case of the animal sacrifice and the Soma sacrifice after the leading forth to the Uttaravedi. || 13 ||
One should repeat [the ritual] excluding the carrying forward of the fire (praṇayana). || 14 ||

Regarding the expiation for the extinction of the *dakṣiṇāgni*, Bharadvāja states in the context of the original rite: "Āśmarathya says one should offer [the oblation] in the *anvāhāryapacana*; Ālekhana says in the *āhavanīya*. However, some maintain that even in the case of the extinction of the *āhavanīya*, when it concerns the *ajastra* fires, one should perform the rite excluding the re-establishment (*praṇayana*), because its entry into the *gārhapatya* implies that the churning alone occurs everywhere. This is incorrect, because there is no distinction made, and because it has been shown that there is no authoritative basis for the *uddhārya* fire also entering the *gārhapatya*.

Or let it be that there is entry into the *tanū* [offering]; even so, the *ajasra* [fires], upon entering, are not struck by the staff because of the specific finality (*antyaviśeṣa*) of the cause for entry, namely their status as *yoni* (sources). Or rather, a distinction must be stated. Therefore, among the rules for leading forward, one leading forward remains for the *ajasra* and the *uddhārya* fires. 14.
That which is the nature of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.

The word "then he should take" (*tata āharet*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. This is for the sake of illustration, because the general introduction states, "whatever breaks the continuity of the recitation," which applies even to the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires; otherwise, that [general rule] would be rendered purposeless. It should be understood that the omission of these two [fires] from the sequence is precisely with this intention. Others hold that it is intended to show their non-permanence. This very expiation for the establishment of the fires (*āhitāgni*) supersedes all other expiations pertaining to the *agnihotra* and so forth within its own domain, because it pertains to a specific case.

However, by the rule "and for whom both [fires] have followed," every other injunction is set aside, because that [latter rule] has a more specific subject matter. For all the rules regarding penance for the following of fires generally apply to cases where one fire has followed—such as when it is not formally established (*avīhita*) or when it is not rekindled (*ananvāhita*)—and they find their scope in cases where only one fire has followed, or in cases where both have followed but are devoid of the *abhinimroka* and *abhyudaya* rites. Therefore, it is logical that this specific rule concerning the following of both fires should set aside those general rules which share the same subject matter. || 15 ||
He should stand worshipping with the word "bhūḥ."
This is clear.
One should mentally mutter the *yajus* mantra associated with the undertaking of the vow. || 17 ||

The word "yajamāna" (the sacrificer) is understood as the subject. This is because of the expression "bopāyanīyam" and because of the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra: "I shall observe the vow" (*vrataṃ cariṣyāmi*, *TaiSaṃ* 1.5.10). Furthermore, because of the praise [of this mantra] in passages such as "This indeed is the continuity of the sacrifice" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 3.7.2), which shows that its purpose is to ensure the uninterrupted continuity of the vow, the meaning is that the sacrificer should mutter that *yajus* verse intended for the commencement of his own vow. || 17 ||

"This is one for you, and another is beyond; enter into union with the third light. Being of beautiful form, become one who enters into union; be dear to the gods in the highest birthplace. With these words, he should collect the fire of one who maintains the *anvāhita* fires as it goes out, from as far as the throw of a yoke-pin (*śamyā*). 18.

The term *āhitāgni* (one who has established the sacred fires) is used to exclude one who has merely undertaken the duty [of maintaining them] (*anyāhitādhikāra*). Regarding the phrase "as far as the throw of the *śamyā*": if, within that distance, any fire should be extinguished or should move away from its place, then one should carry that fire around the *ulmuka* (the fire-brand) and deposit it back into its original place. This has been stated by Āpastamba: "As far as the throw of the *śamyā*, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Sage...
[End of Paṭala]; together with the *Mahādevaśāstrisaṃkalita-prayogacandrikā*. 267.

Having circumambulated three times from left to right with the mantra "nir-iti," he should collect [the embers] with the mantra "idaṃ te. This rule applies even when all the side-fuel-sticks (anvapakṣa) have been used up. As stated by Baudhāyana and Āśvalāyana: "If the Āhavanīya fire should go out, one should extinguish it and throw away the śamyā-stick. However, if a portion of the fire goes out, another rule should be observed, such as: "If a coal should fall outside the enclosing sticks before the Prayāja offerings," and so forth. || 18 ||
One should follow after him as he departs further than the distance of a *śamyā*-throw, and having settled down along the way, one should perform the sacrifice.

The word *paraḥ* (beyond) denotes extreme proximity. One should move away to a point further than the distance of a *śamyā*-throw; having brought the other fires there where that [central] fire is, and having arranged them accordingly, one should dwell there with the sacrificial implements (*vaha-hasta*). || 19 ||
One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt.
The meaning is: where he may dwell; from the vicinity of the path, he should bring [the fuel] from outside. 21. 29.
One should fetch the sacrificial grass (barhis) from those darbha blades that are near the path. || 21 ||
An ox is the sacrificial fee. || 22 ||
But when this desired [topic] falls within the middle of a treatise (tantra), it should be understood as a relevant digression (prasaṅga) concerning that very [subject]. || 22 ||
When the next day has dawned, he should settle down in his home.

Then, on the following day, he should return from whichever place he had previously departed; however, in the case of Soma sacrifices, there is neither departure nor return where there would be an increase in the number of days.
If the calves, having been separated for the sake of a sacrificial oblation, should suckle [the mother cow], one should offer a gruel of barley to Vāyu.

When the calves of all the cows drink up all the milk and leave nothing remaining for the sacrificial oblation, then barley grains should be added; the gruel (*yavāgū*) consisting of soft rice-grains should take the place of the milk. Having been removed from one [of the two] portions, they should suckle [from it].

Although the rice-gruel (*yavāgū*) possesses the properties of the *sānnāyya* because it is dependent upon it, nevertheless, since it has the quality of being a vegetable substance (*oṣadhi*), the ritual acts beginning with the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) and ending with the cooking (*śrapaṇa*) must be performed just as they are for the *caru*. Those acts which serve to produce the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) are performed; however, those prescribed specifically for the *sānnāyya* are omitted due to the loss of their purpose, not because of a scriptural prohibition. Therefore, they are performed here because they are purposeful. Starting from the removal from the fire (*uddhāsana*), whichever of the two *sānnāyyas* occupies the place [of the other], its specific properties apply. Furthermore, there is a separate offering because of the distinctness of the deities.

But when the milk from both milch-cows has been drawn, then there is a simultaneous offering of the two *yavāgū* (gruel) offerings, because they share a single deity. And Bharadvāja says: "In the case of groups of oblations or groups of animals that have the same deity, one proceeds after having divided [the portions] equally. (25)
268. Then, having driven away the calves for the subsequent oblation, he should fast. 269. Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[Book 15, Chapter 2].

The meaning is that, having concluded the *iṣṭi* on that very day and performed the *upavasatha*, one should sacrifice again with the remaining oblation (*pītena haviṣā*). There is no returning to the beginning (*nā'yasyā'vṛttiḥ*), because there is no defect of destruction and so forth; this is also indicated by the scriptural mark (*liṅga*): "Having uncovered the garment for the subsequent oblation" (*uttarasmai haviṣe vasānam apāvṛtya*; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.5.2). In the same way, it should be understood that this applies even to another milking (*doha*) that has not been destroyed. || 26 ||
If the evening milk used as the oblation should suffer damage, one should pour out rice for Indra and fast.

This is because of the removal of the faults [associated with] Ātīnaśin. The mention of Indra is intended to indicate Mahendra as well. Regarding the morning milking, one should proceed by taking portions from this [mixture] without distinction, because of the general statement; otherwise, there would be a contradiction regarding the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for those who sacrifice to Mahendra. Thus, the followers of the Ṛgveda place either the cake for Indra or the cake for Mahendra in its position. Or rather, they are excluded by the mention of the *vāha*.

If the distress occurs at night, then one should use as many vessels as required, set them out, and fast on rice grains. But if it occurs on the following day, then one should set them out immediately and there is no fasting.
Whatever may be available in the morning, one should prepare it as cooked food. || 28 ||

Whatever may be available in the morning that is not spoiled, one should indeed use that which has been heard [in the scripture]; however, since the cake (puroḍāśa) has not been introduced as a substitute for the Sānnāyya, the sense is that even that cake should not be prepared. || 28 ||
Then follows the cake for Indra as the subsequent offering. || 29 ||

The other milk-offering (*doha*) should be a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*); the meaning is that in its place, a sacrificial cake made of husked rice (*nirupta-īḍ*) must be prepared. It should consist of eleven or twelve potsherds (*kapāla*), because it is a modification (*vikāra*) of the offering to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*). Its ritual details (*dharmāḥ*)—both those pertaining to the sacrificial cake and those pertaining to the *sānnāyya* (curdled milk)—are to be understood as previously explained, following the instructions for the consumption (*prāśuśāsana*). || 29 ||
Having taken portions from the Prātardoha here, he proceeds with the ritual. 15.1.30.
Having gathered together and having offered together. || 30 ||
Then, having driven away the calves for the subsequent oblation, he should fast.
This very same [penance] is the expiation for the morning milking when it has met with an accident.
In that case, the fast is not discontinued. || 31 || 32 ||
Having taken portions from the evening milking here, he proceeds with the ritual.

In this *Brāhmaṇa*, as well as in other ritual manuals (*kalpa*), the sacrifice is prescribed for both cases: when there is a deficiency in either one of the two milkings, and when there is a deficiency in both. However, the author of the *Sūtra* will describe that [deficiency] only in the case of both milkings being deficient; therefore, a deficiency in only one is not intended here. But Āśvalāyana provides an exception (anugraha) in this matter, stating: "Just as in the case of a deficiency in either one, they may proceed by pouring out [the milk] or, in its place, using a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Even in the case of a reversal [of the order], there is an exception regarding a deficiency in the evening milking, as follows: having divided the morning-milked milk into two portions, one may curdle one of those portions and perform the sacrifice with it. || 33 ||
Then, having driven away the calves for the subsequent oblation, he should fast.

Then, after the pouring out of the gruel (yavāgū), for the sake of preparing the *sānnāyya*—which is to be performed on the following day for the subsequent oblation—one should again drive away the calves, that is, separate them [from their mothers]. The rest is understood. 34.
If the milk-offering of one who has performed the evening and morning rites should suffer damage, he should cook a five-panful of rice for Indra. || 35 ||

When both [offerings] are reached in succession, one should offer the *puroḍāśa* cakes in order and perform the simultaneous procedure as before. However, when there is a non-sequential arrival of one [offering], or a sequential arrival of the other, or a simultaneous arrival of both, then one should offer a cake on eight potsherds and a *pañcaśarāva* oblation. In this context, the word *pañcaśarāva*—with its nominal suffix elided in the sense of "its measure"—denotes a substance measured by five *śarāvas*.

And he pours that out with a shallow cup (*śarāva*) twelve times—three times with the *triṣṭup* mantra and twice silently. He pours out the twelve-portioned cake; this is established by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that "with twelve mantras [he offers] and the others silently. The mention of Indra here is for the sake of illustration, because of the scriptural statement: "Whether it be for Indra or for Mahendra, it is the same. And the fact that these two oblations are substitutes for the *sānnāyya* is likewise established by the indicative mark: "The plants are indeed milk; milk is milk; verily by milk he secures milk for him" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā).

This is also because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) [in the text] "3-7-1). Therefore, it should be understood that those two also possess the characteristics of the *sānnāyya* (the milk offering), just as before. However, Kātyāyana, having introduced the *pañcaśarāva* (five-platter offering), says: "It is either a substitute (*pratinidhi*) or an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), because of the mention of the deity. If it is for the purpose of expiation, then even after the removal [of the original offering], the characteristics of the *āgneya* and *aindrāgna* offerings apply to the two oblations; this is the distinction. As for gruel (*yavāgū*) and the like, their status as substitutes has already been clearly demonstrated in the Sūtra; thus, the aforementioned rules regarding the *sānnāyya* should be applied accordingly. || 35 ||
One should first worship Agni with a puroḍāśa cake. || 36 ||
Since that [suffix] for the deity is already established by the *taddhita* suffix itself, this restatement is for the sake of the subsequent alternative. || 36 ||
One should worship Indra with the northern [portion] using a five-earthenware vessel. || 37 ||

Having offered only a single five-śarāva oblation to Indra, one should first sacrifice to Agni with that very same offering and then sacrifice to Indra; the meaning is that one should not offer a cake on eight potsherds (aṣṭākapāla) to Tvaṣṭṛ. For in the Brāhmaṇa, the injunction for the sacrifice—"One should offer a five-śarāva of rice to Indra; one should sacrifice to Agni as the first among the deities"—is the rule that establishes the sacrifice for Agni’s eight-potsherd cake; this is the first interpretation. It should be understood that the second interpretation is that the sacrifice to Agni is based directly on the scriptural statement regarding the five-śarāva oblation to Indra.
And in both cases, the offering is intended to be made together at the beginning, provided there is sufficient means.
Then, having driven away the calves for the subsequent oblation, he should fast.
This has been explained. || 38 ||
If on the day of the vow the wife becomes menstruating, he should perform the sacrifice after having excluded her.

The day of the vow (*vrata*) is the day of the vow-food (*vratya*), and that is the day of fasting (*aupavasathya*). Since the instruction for the vow occurs on that very day, if the wife should, by chance, become untouchable (*anālambhukā*) due to her menses, then one should perform the sacrifice omitting her; the meaning is that one should perform the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. Alternatively, the word "vow" (*vrata*) denotes the ritual action, as in the expression "he teaches by means of the vow" (*vrateneti*); thus, the "day of the vow" refers to the specific day fixed for that rite. (From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Book 15, Section 205).

The meaning is that even when his wife is in her courses (*anālambhukā*), he should indeed perform that rite without her. For example: the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices on the festival days (*parvan*), the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), the morning and evening *agnihotra*, and so forth. Because of the expression "on each respective day," whatever is fixed for a specific time is performed therein even when she is in her courses.

This is what is meant: at whatever time, in whatever ritual action there is either a transgression or a penance, and when the primary time has lapsed, that action is performed even for one who is *anālambhukā* (in her courses), but not otherwise. Therefore, optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) and animal and Soma sacrifices are not performed on that parvan day during which she is *anālambhukā*, provided they have not already commenced; however, they are indeed performed on that day once they have been commenced, because of the fixed rule regarding the timing of a rite that has already begun.

By this, the termination at that time of the *apanyādheya* and other rites already commenced is also explained. However, regarding a woman who has begun her menses (*anālambhukā*) while a rite is underway, Kātyāyana states certain specific rules: "The wife, being in her courses, having set aside the forms of initiation (*dīkṣā*), should sit on sand; she should remain standing until the flow ceases, or near the altar at the junction of day and night. At the time of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*), having bathed her with water mixed with cow-urine, he performs the subsequent rites such as the putting on of the garment (*paridhāna*). [This applies to] the procreation."

And for her, bathing and other rites are to be performed after ten nights have passed; however, some say that one should not initiate a pregnant woman, based on the Śruti text: "The fetuses are unfit for sacrifice. [Others argue] that the *anūbandhyā* cow is not excluded because of the context. But regarding a woman who has given birth, even though impurity (*āśauca*) persists, the author of the Dharmaśāstra, Baudhāyana, states that the sacrificer retains the entitlement to perform the *agnihotra* and other rites: "One who is impure should not undertake optional austerity, nor should he sacrifice, nor study the Veda, except for the *agnihotra*, the *darśa*, and the *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices."

Manu has also said: "One should not increase the sacrificial fires nor suspend the rites pertaining to them; and one performing those rites does not become impure, even if he is a kinsman [of the deceased]. Yājñavalkya also says: "The Vaitāna sacrifices and the domestic (Upāsana) rites enjoined by the Śruti must be performed. Likewise, Gautama states: "The obligatory rites are suspended, with the exception of the Vaitāna sacrifices. And Jābāli says: "In the case of birth or death, there is no abandonment of the duties of the Vaitāna sacrifice."...

By this, the Jāteṣṭi (the sacrifice on the birth of a son) is also explained. Regarding that, Bharadvāja says: "How is the Jāteṣṭi performed? 'With the verse *ūrka vā asthāḥ*,' says Āśmarathya; 'One should perform it as soon as the son is born,' says Ālekhana. And Baudhāyana says: "Baudhāyana states that one should offer the oblation when the ten-day period has passed; Śālīki says that one should do so as soon as the birth is known. || 39 ||
One should spread out a water-cord.

Regarding the girdle (*yoktra*), however, Āpastamba says it should be placed at its proper time to the south, with the loop facing east and the cord extending behind the altar, either inside the altar or [outside]; one should place it silently either behind the altar or within the altar. || 40 ||

Having sacrificed to her, when she has bathed after three nights, he should invite her with the words: "I am that [heaven], you are this [earth]; I am the sky, you are the earth; I am the *Sāman*, you are the *Ṛc*. Come, let us two unite; let us both deposit seed for the sake of a male son—to know him, for the increase of wealth, for good progeny, and for great heroism. He invites her at the very moment [of the sacrifice]; that itself is the expiation for that. || 41 ||

If she has passed three nights [without bathing], one should invite her for the purpose of approaching her during her season (*ṛtu*); and that act is solely for the sake of expiation for the ritual, not for the sake of the person. Why? Because, having introduced the subject with the words, "The purpose of this sacrifice is indeed frustrated for him whose wife becomes fit for the slaughter [of the sacrificial animal] on each day" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 3.7.1), it continues: "One should cause her to perform that *iṣṭi*; that itself is the expiation therefrom" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 3.7.1). Thus says the Śruti. (41)

If the *sāṃnāyya* or the *agnihotra* should spill, or if an insect should fall into it, one should go toward the north with a middle or the innermost *palāśa* leaf, pour out the spilling substance into an anthill with a verse addressed to Prajāpati, and worship [the fire] with the syllable "bhūḥ. (42) With that same middle *palāśa* leaf, having poured out the insect that has fallen inside the enclosing sticks with a verse addressed to Heaven and Earth, one should worship [the fire] with the syllable "bhūḥ. (43)

*Viṣyandana* is the downward dripping of [the ghee] that has overflowed due to boiling. The *valmīka-vapra* (ant-hill mound) has already been explained. Having removed it—that is, having made its opening wide—one should pour the *agnihotra* oblation back into its cavity. The word "again" (*punar*) should be understood as referring to the act of pouring back (*avanayana*). One should cause another [substance] to come—that is, produce it—without milking [the cow]. A "worm" (*kīṭa*) is an insect; in the *agnihotra*, the phrase "within the enclosing sticks" (*antaḥ-paridhi*) is an indication of the location. 42, 43.
If he should procure another *sāṃnāyya* offering on another day. || 44 ||
O Bhī, if a worm should fall into the curd or the milk, you would have another brought; the rest is clear.

If one has milked another [cow] and then performs the Agnihotra again, one should offer the Agnihotra with the following mantra: "Mitra, the wise one, ordains the people; Mitra has supported the earth and the sky; Mitra gazes upon the tribes with unblinking eyes; for the sake of Truth, let one offer the oblation accompanied by ghee. Having offered the Agnihotra that was rained upon, and having milked another cow, one should perform the offering again. 45.

Furthermore, because of the specific mention of the *agnihotra*, this rule does not apply to the *sāṃnāyya* offering. Āpastamba states: "If it should rain upon one's *agnihotra*... (*yasyāgnihotram avavarṣet*). "It should rain upon" means that Parjanya rains from above. Having done that—that is, having had it rained upon—one should offer with the *maitrī* [formula]; such is the meaning. This is based on the Śruti: "Mitra [protects] the people" (*mitro janān*, Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.7.2). Thereafter, one should perform the *homa* after milking another cow. However, some desire that one should first perform the *agnihotra* with the mantra "Mitra [protects] the people" (*mitro janān*) for the initial oblation, and then [proceed as usual].

Even then, because of the injunction, "one should again offer the oblation into the other vessel," there is a repetition of both the milking and the offering; however, as for that which occurs before the milking and after the offering—namely, the ritual touching—that remains a single performance (tantra), because it is common to both.

72: ... Śāṅkhāyana-Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[In the 15th Praśna]: If, after the first oblation has been offered, the subsequent oblation should spill over, one should offer the first oblation again with the second, using the verse addressed to the Vanaspati: "O Vanaspati, where you know the secret names of the gods, there cause the offerings to go. Having placed a fuel-stick upon the fire with this verse, one should then offer the oblation again silently. || 46 ||

The *amihoma* is an *uparihoma*. From that very remnant (*śiṣṭa*), the subsequent oblation (*uttarāhuti*) is performed silently in both cases. Then follows the repetition of the *homā* as before. However, when a portion of the subsequent oblation has spilled, that [remaining] oblation is not to be taken up. As he will state: "That which is merely non-oblation is indeed defective," and "In the event of a deficiency in measure, one should complete it with the remainder of that. This same rule applies even when the subsequent oblation falls together with the preceding oblation, because it is effectively spilled and because the principle is the same.
If the Āhavanīya fire should go out after the first oblation has been offered, he should offer [again] either on a wood splinter or on gold while saying, "Fire in wood, wood in fire. || 47 ||

Because the wood from which [the fire] has been churned is the immediate splinter (*śakala*), one should offer into that, or into the gold placed upon it; this means the "subsequent oblation" (*uttarāhuti*). This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra. Thus, Baudhāyana says, "having placed gold on the final splinter. Because of the statement "speaking," the offering occurs in the middle of the mantra, while the *svāhā* exclamation occurs only at the end. From that point, the completion of the remainder follows. In that case, heating and kindling the Āhavanīya fire are dispensed with, as they are impossible.

With the cessation of the heating (*pratitapana*), the very purpose (*uddeśana*) also ceases. However, there is no cessation of the sweeping (*parisamūhana*) and other such acts, because the *śakala* (wood chip) and the gold are prescribed as substitutes for the fire. Even for one whose *āhavanīya* fire is perpetual (*ajastra*), the completion of the *agnihotra* occurs precisely through the substitute, as there is no distinction [in this regard]. Therefore, [one should perform] the churning (*manthana*).

If, before the *prayāja* offerings, a coal should roll out beyond the enclosing stones toward the east of the *āhavanīya*, it would bring prosperity to both the *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer. If it should roll southward, it would bring prosperity to both the *brahman* and the sacrificer. If it should roll westward, it would bring prosperity to both the *hotṛ*, the wife, and the sacrificer. If it should roll northward, it would bring prosperity to both the *agnīdh* and the sacrificial animals, as well as to the sacrificer.

"O darkness, do not [strike] the one intent on sacrifice; do not [strike] the sacrificer. Let there be homage to you as you approach, O Rudra; homage to you as you depart; homage where you sit down. Do not harm the *adhvaryu*; do not harm the sacrificer. With these words, he should strike it with the base of the *sruva* ladle. If it should turn back toward the east, [he should act] thus. [End of Paṭala 1] This is accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śākhin. 274.

In those [other] directions, he modifies the formula to the south: "Do not harm Brahmā; do not harm the sacrificer. To the west: "Do not harm the Hotṛ; do not harm the wife; do not harm the sacrificer. To the north: "Do not harm the Āgnīdhra; do not harm the cattle of the sacrificer; do not harm the sacrificer. (Section 2) 48.

"Bahiṣparidhi" (outside the enclosing sticks) is an indication of the location; this is because of the indicative mark "if [it falls] in front" and because the enclosing sticks are not mentioned in the Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, this rule applies from the time of the *anvādhāna* (the placing of fuel) until the commencement of the *prayāja* offerings. In other cases, however, having silently cast away the embers, one should simply perform the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). "Buddho mūlam": he should crush it, that is, press it down. "Mā tamas" (do not [fall] into darkness)—this is to be combined with all directions. || 18 ||

"The thousand-horned bull, Jātavedas, whose back is the Stoma, who is rich in ghee and fair of countenance—may he not abandon us, may we not abandon him when he is kindled; grant us prosperity in cattle and prosperity in heroes. With these words, he casts it into the fire. (49)
The meaning is clear. || 42 ||
Or, having struck [the enemy], he should offer oblations. || 15.1.50 ||
Having struck [the fire] silently, one should offer oblations with the mantra. || 50 ||

If the fire of one who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni) should not be produced by friction due to the proximity of the time limit, he should, upon seeing another fire, fetch it, spread it out, offer oblations, and then, without hurrying, churn the fire again.

If the fire that has been consigned to the kindling woods (*araṇis*) should not be produced when churned for the purpose of spreading the fires (*viharaṇa*) in proximity to the time of the *agnihotra*—due to being on a journey or other such circumstances—then one should fetch a common (*laukika*) fire, place it in the *gārhapatya* hearth, spread the fires, and offer the oblation. Thus says Baudhāyana: "Now, when the fires have been consigned to the two kindling woods, one should churn [the fire], spread the fires, and offer; or else, having fetched a common fire and spread the fires, one should place the two kindling woods between the fires and offer."

Āśvalāyana also, by stating, "if [the fire] does not arise at the time for the Agnihotra," has made it clear that this injunction refers specifically to the case where the fire has been formally installed (*samārūḍha*). For fire that has merely been carried forth (*anugata*) is not churned for the sake of the Agnihotra; rather, it is the installed fire that is sometimes churned specifically for the Agnihotra during occasions such as a journey abroad (*pravāsa*). Therefore, it is logical that the rule applies to that case. In that situation, when many fires have been installed, whichever specific fire fails to arise when being churned is the one that must be fetched.

This same procedure applies from the time of dwelling [in the sacrificial fires] until the time of the oblation. Regarding the case of following [the fires], whether it be the following of the *gārhapatya* alone or the following of both, whatever rule applies to the non-manifestation of the fire being churned applies to that [specific case].
[Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram—Book 15, Section 274...]

This has been shown precisely in the passage beginning with "both are followed. However, there is another opinion: because the expression "being kindled" (*madhyamānam*) is stated without qualification, this same rule applies even to the case of following [the fire]. Furthermore, in the phrase "proximity of time" (*kāla-saṃnikarṣa*), the proximity to the time of the oblation (*homa*) is understood due to its predominance. Therefore, even in the case of following [the fire], if the time for the oblation is exceeded and the fire being kindled does not arise according to the rule "whose Āhavanīya... and so forth, this very rule certainly applies.

But since there is no attachment to the time of the oblation, the *prāyaṇīya* offerings indeed occur exactly as prescribed. One should churn [the fire] only while awaiting the distant arrival of the future time; otherwise, however, a delay would result. And that is not appropriate within the scope of one's capability—this is the intended meaning. || 51 ||
If he does not find another wife, he should offer oblations into his right ear. || 52 ||

Goats and others are substituted for the fire because of common characteristics such as being primary; as it is stated in the Brāhmaṇa: "The deity Agni was created after him, the Gāyatrī metre, the Rathantara Sāman, the Brāhmaṇa among men, and the goat among animals; therefore these are primary, for they were created from the mouth," and so forth. Consequently, there is no modification of the mantras containing the marks of fire. In that case, however, acts such as digging out, cooking, and heating are excluded due to the absence of another [substitute] entity. Likewise, because of the absence of cooking and taking out, the placing of the Āmāhomas and other offerings in the Gārhapatya fire is also excluded. || 12 ||
According to some, [the word] "of the unborn" [is used]. 53.
But in the case of the *parāgnihoma* ritual, they set it down for the purpose of the oblation. || 53 ||
But one should not eat from that [vessel] of the unborn (aja). || 54 ||

One should not eat any meat, milk, or similar substances that are unrelated to one's own kin. Āśvalāyana states: "If [the animal] was killed for the sake of the ear, there must be an avoidance of meat. (54)
One should offer an oblation into the fire with the verse "ajāma vindan" while holding it in the right hand of a Brāhmaṇa. || 55 ||
The Brāhmaṇa is also explained by means of Ajā. || 55 ||
But one should not obstruct a Brahmin from staying [in one's house]. ||56||
The statement regarding the meaning of "asūrya" is that it refers to what is carried by night.
But if he finds a Brāhmaṇa, he should offer [the oblation] into a clump of Darbha grass. || 57 ||
Regarding this, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "The bunch of Darbha grass is indeed possessed of fire" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 3.7.3). ||17||
But one should not sit upon Darbha grass.
It should be understood that this is not the case elsewhere, because of the scriptural injunction regarding the seat for the purpose of the Brahma-yajña; thus there is no contradiction. || 18 ||
If one does not find darbha grass, one should offer oblations in water. || 59 ||

The sense is that there is no difference between cause and effect. And on this point there is a scriptural passage: "Those who have placed Agni within the womb" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 5.6.1), and so forth. || 59 ||
But one should not discriminate regarding water, saying, "This is fit for drinking; this is unfit for drinking. (15.1.60)
The meaning is that one should not avoid even water that contains living beings. || 6 ||
He says that one should not avoid [the water] even due to a defect in the giver: "One should indeed accept this water for a year, even if it belongs to one from whom food is not to be eaten. (61)
One who is not to be fed is one whose food is unfit to be eaten.
But one should not wash one's feet with water [in that manner]. || 62 ||
The prohibition applies to washing for the sake of pleasure, not even to that for the sake of purification, because only one who is purified has the qualification for ritual action. ||12||
These vows are to be observed for one year. || 63 ||

"Āśmarathya maintains that these vows last for one year; Ālekhana maintains they last as long as one lives," says Bhāradvāja. In his own view, there is no option regarding the one-year duration, because of the indicative mark [in the text]: "Even for one who eats what is unfit to be eaten, this [penance] lasts for a year. There is a scriptural statement: "For one does not exceed the vow for a year. (63) On the completion of the year, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati. (64)
"After a year," says Āpastamba; the conclusion of the vow is by means of the Vrātapatī sacrifice. 14.
An offering on eight potsherds for Agni Kṣāmavat, if the fire of one who has established the sacred fires should burn his house. 65.

Āpastamba says: "If those who precede and follow [the sacrificer] should die in succession, or in the event of a house fire... If both the elders and the young, including the women, should die in continuous succession, then this occasional *iṣṭi* sacrifice is accomplished there, for the house belongs to them; and from the supplementary statement of the text, the desired result is achieved therein: "Thus, none of these dies before his full span of life, nor does a subsequent fire consume his house" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.3). || 65 ||
One for whom the fires are mixed with other fires, or are mixed with each other, [should offer] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vivici.

In the event of contact with others—whether worldly or Vedic—or in the mutual contact of the five fires, this very *iṣṭi* generally takes place; however, in cases of exception (*apavāda*), other rites apply. These [other rites] take place when the fires have been separately established (*vivikteṣu*) through the process of *samāropaṇa* (consignment). Indeed, the mantra for *samāropaṇa* itself will distinguish each respective fire here, just as milk and water are separated. Thus, regarding the procedure for contact, Bodhāyana states: "Having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇiyoḥ*). (66)
If the Gārhapatya and Dakṣiṇa fires should become mixed, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vīti.

Because of the statement "the Gārhapatya and the Dakṣiṇāgni," this iṣṭi does not take place when there is a separate contact with a single portion of those two fires. This same principle is to be observed in the subsequent case as well. || 6 ||
Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra— [Section 16a]:

If the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires [become separated], one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vipṛcu; according to some, this applies when the Gārhapatya and Dakṣiṇāgni fires [are separated]. 68.
"Either the southern [fire] or the Āhavanīya," says Āpastamba; the connection is as before. ||68||
If he should be afflicted by a burning fever, [he shall offer] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratabhṛt.
The logical connection is that "the fires would become intermingled. One who sets fire to [another's] house is a "house-burner" (abhyādāhya). 19.
If [the fire] is by means of a corpse-fire, [he should offer] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Śuci; if by means of a birth-fire, a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Saṃkusuka. || 15.1.70 ||

The syntactical connection "the fires would be mixed" applies everywhere. The *śavāgni* is the fire for the funeral pyre; the *sūtakāgni* is the fire for the purpose of the birth-rite (*jātakarman*). ||7||

The *saṃkusuka*, the *vikusuka*, the *vikira*, and the *viṣkira*—with beans, clarified butter, and *nalada* fuel-wood, we pacify the flesh-eating [spirits]. "In this *saṃkusuka* fire we cast away our impurities; we have become pure and worthy of sacrifice; may he prolong our lives"—these are the invitatory and offering verses. (71)
This is the *yājuṣa* portion of the *hautra*.
If [the house is struck] by lightning, [he shall offer] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Apsumat.
The lightning originates from the thunderbolt. For the other [deities], the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are indeed prescribed in the Vedic recension (*āmnāya*) itself.

All [the oblations] should be offered together; having offered [the first two] to Agni Vivici, he offers [the third] to Agni Śuci. He should cause the third, the *vrātabhṛtī*, to proceed, the fourth, the *apsumatī*, next, and finally the *kṣāmavatī*. (Section 3) 73.

But where all the sacrifices, beginning with the *kṣāmavatī* and ending with the *apsumatī*, would coincide due to the simultaneous occurrence of multiple causes such as a house fire, then even though there is a difference in the sequence of the causes, the sacrifices should be performed according to this very same order. Furthermore, the *vātabhṛtī* sacrifice is added as a third. In that case, having offered the *apsumatī* as the fourth, one should not offer it to the deities beginning with *vipṛgu* and ending with *saṃkusuka*. Then, one should conclude the first sacrifice, the *kṣāmavatī*, at the end. || 73 ||
Some recite the *vrātabhṛtī* as the second [verse], and the *vrātapatī* as the last. 74.

Alternatively, having determined [the appropriate rite] through deliberation, one should offer it to the bearer of the vow (*vratabhṛt*). Then, immediately following that, according to the very sequence just mentioned, [one offers] to those [deities] beginning with *śuci* and ending with *kṣāmavat*. Then, at the conclusion, [one offers] to the *vrātapatī*—this is the meaning. However, when several causal conditions coincide, the sacrifices (*iṣṭis*) take place in their respective order. || 7 ||

"Agni, Indra, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Bṛhaspati have made the leaking embryo medicine. This has dripped away upon the earth; it does not reach the navel, nor does it reach Nirṛti. With these words, one should consecrate the Agnihotra vessel that is leaking. (75)
[Chapter] 1: Together with the commentary *Payogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 277. This is clear. || 79 ||

If the moon rises in the east when the sacrificial oblation has already been set aside, one should divide the rice grains into three parts: those that are of medium size, from them he should make a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Dātṛ; those that are the largest, from them a pap of curdled milk for Indra Pradātṛ; and those that are the smallest, from them a pap of boiled milk for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. Thus, Agni himself procreates offspring for him. ||76||

Having recognized that the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī) is joined with the fifteenth (pañcadaśī)—as when the moon rises on the morning of the full-moon day—and having understood that this is the day for sacrifice, one who has begun the New Moon ritual (darśatantra) should, after the pouring out of the oblation-material (havirnirvāpa), know the true state of affairs. He should divide the grains of the offered oblation into three parts according to their coarseness, medium size, and fineness; he should then prepare a cake on eight potsherds (aṣṭākapāla-puroḍāśa) from the medium-sized grains for Agni Dātṛ. The meaning is that during the acts such as the spreading of the grains (adhivapana) and so forth, one should designate Agni as "Dātṛ" (the Giver).

One should offer the largest [grains] to Indra at the evening milking, and the smallest [grains] to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa at the morning milking. In this regard, the rules for the *caru* (oblation of boiled rice) are explained by those for the *yavāgū* (gruel). Because both the *caru* and the *sāṃnāyya* (curdled milk offering) are cooked and because they occupy the same place, they are modifications of the qualities of those two [offerings]. However, the *puroḍāśa* (cake) is indeed a modification of the *āgneya* (offering to Agni). Regarding the repeated sacrifice (*punarijyā*), there is an option; as it has been said: "One should sacrifice with one [offering], or one should sacrifice with two. This rule does not apply to one who does not perform the *saṃnayana* (the preparation of the *sāṃnāyya*), because of the connection with the *sāṃnāyya*.

And Āśvalāyana says: "In the case of the *sāṃnāyya*, [this applies] when the moon has risen before [the sacrifice]. Bhāradvāja, however, says: "This [procedure] does not exist for one who does not perform the *sāṃnāyya*—this is one view; 'it exists'—this is another. According to the view that it exists, the cooking is performed in water, and the ritual rules are like those for the *dadhi* and the *aindrāgna*. 76.
If the sun rises before the oblation has been poured out. ||77||

The phrase "one should offer to the original deities" is to be supplied [to the preceding rule]. However, when an offering is commenced at a time other than the prescribed time for the *āgneya* sacrifice, a doubt arises: should the offering be made to the original deities (*prākṛtī*) or to the modified deities (*vaikṛtī*)? On this point, Āpastamba maintains that it should be offered to the original deities; in the expression "to the original deities," the number [of deities] is not intended to be restrictive.
One should offer oblations to those who have failed in their prosperity.

"Verily, this [sacrificer] deprives him of progeny and cattle"—by means of this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the cause of the separation is made known; therefore, the oblation offered at sunrise is called *vyūddha* (separated). Those modified deities who partake of that [oblation] are the *vyūddhadevatās*. The meaning is that one should offer [the oblation] to them. || 78 ||
Likewise, when one portion has been set aside and the moon rises, the remainder belongs to those who partake in failure.
"Vinirupta" means half-poured out. In that case, regarding what has been offered, the meaning is that one should pour out the remainder for the very same deity as the original [offering]. ||79||
Having concluded that sacrifice and having driven away the calves, he should sacrifice with the *sāṃnāyya* on the following day.

Now, alternative ritual procedures from other *śākhās* regarding the distinction between what has been set aside (*nirupta*) and what has not been set aside (*anirupta*) are presented for the sake of providing an option: "If the sun should rise upon his oblation that has not yet been taken up, or if he should not expect the performance of the *abhyudita-caryā*, he should divide the rice grains into three parts," and so on, as before.
(Satyāṣāḍha’s *Śrautasūtra*, Book 15, Section 274).

"Then, having driven away the calves for the subsequent oblation, he should fast," so say Bharadvāja and others. "Unuttered" means not yet recited. In the case of what has been unuttered, one should perform the *ādityuditeṣṭi* as before and then perform the sacrifice again. Even in the case of what has been uttered, one should do so only when there is an inability to follow the ritual procedure (*prataścaryā*) about to be described. Or, one should not even intend to undertake the ritual observance (*vratacaryā*). Ritual observance consists in the repeated practice of the fast-day rites (*upavasatha*).

And one should not hope for that [success], meaning one should not desire it by looking at it with the thought, "I shall not be able to perform it. Thus, Kātyāyana states that this applies only when there is an inability to observe the vow (*vrata*). Furthermore, it should be understood that the rule regarding the re-performance of the sacrifice (*punarijyā*) is additional here. Āpastamba says: "Now, if the moon should rise after the oblation has been taken up, that same expiation (*prāyaścitti*) and that same observance of the vow (*vratacaryā*) [apply]."

In the case of what has already been poured out (*nirupta*), the expiation (*prāyaścitti*) is simply the repeated performance of the service (*sevā*) itself; that is, either the performance of the vow (*vratacaryā*) or its repetition on each successive day—this is the meaning. Thus, regarding the matter of what has been poured out, these three alternative ritual procedures (*kalpa*) from other recensions (*śākhāntara*) are stated alongside the procedure mentioned in the immediately following sūtra: namely, one may perform the sacrifice again using the very same original form (*prakṛti*) without modification; or, having performed the *Abhyuditeṣṭi* (the sacrifice for one who has awakened too late), one may sacrifice again according to the original form.

"Or, having extended [the period] by only the fast-day (upavasatha), one should sacrifice with the *pamyā* [cakes]. Regarding this, it is stated in the *Baudhāyanīya*: Baudhāyana used to say, "Having sacrificed with the very established *āmāvāsya* oblations, and having fasted again, on the following day one should sacrifice at the proper time (*kālya*) with those that have not risen [before the moon] and are unimpaired. On this point, Śālīki used to say: "This is the *brāhmaṇaja* sacrifice; having sacrificed with it for the sake of distinction, and having fasted again, on the following day one should sacrifice at the proper time with those that have not risen and are unimpaired"—this too [applies] even when [the extension is] only the fast-day itself.

"...it increased exceedingly. Regarding this practice of observing the vow (*vratacaryā*), Āpastamba states the application as follows: "Having again separated the calves from their mothers after having previously united them, one should set aside on the previous day the milk and curds for the purpose of mixing with the sacrificial offering" (ĀpaŚrSū 9.5.14). All the rites beginning with the placing of fuel on the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) remain exactly as they were performed. However, having reunited the calves with their mothers for the sake of the morning milking, and having again separated them for the sake of the evening milking, one should produce the curds.

Whatever curd-offering (*dadhi-havis*) was produced previously, one should place it in that very vessel and present it. If the morning milk (*prātardoha*) has also been produced, it too should be joined to that same curd as the "after-milking" (*abhidoha*), and not discarded; for that is the correct principle. However, if the *Āgneya* offering, once set aside, is kept and then cooked, it must indeed be discarded, because of the resulting defects such as being unfit for consumption or having become stale. Therefore, one should perform the sacrifice starting from the conclusion of the rites performed on the following day.

But when the moon is perceived after the sacrifice has already been performed, then there is simply a repetition of the sacrifice; for what is performed at an improper time is considered as not performed at all.
One who, being a regular performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, should omit either the New Moon day or the Full Moon day, shall offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt.

This means that one should act accordingly in the Brāhmaṇa and in other ritual manuals (*kalpa*). This is stated there: "One who has commenced the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, having let either of them pass its proper time, should offer an oblation to Pāthikṛt with a bull as the sacrificial fee. Having performed that, the Vaiśvānarī offering must also be performed, because the occasion (*nimitta*) is the same. Furthermore, because of the statement, "Those [rites] prescribed for a single fault," and because both of those are intended for the purpose of remedying the lapse of time, the *Atipannēṣṭi* must also be performed after performing those two. And this has been stated by Baudhāyana.
Having offered this oblation for the evil committed, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara as a counter-sacrifice against the one who has gone astray.
[End of] Paṭala 2, accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 276.

[The author] says: "Diti. He states another alternative view as well. Regarding this, Śālīki said: "Having offered the Pāthikṛta [oblation], one should subsequently offer the Vaiśvānara cake on twelve potsherds with a common ritual procedure (*samānatantra*); one should not perform the *atipannapratiyajña* (the sacrifice for what has been missed). In that case, as long as the time for the subsequent rite has not yet arrived, the *atipannaiṣṭi* (sacrifice for what has been missed) is performed. However, once the time is occupied by the subsequent rite, only the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is performed to restore the eligibility for that [subsequent rite], and it is not the *atipannaiṣṭi*. This is because that which is performed at the wrong time is as good as not performed.

The authors of other ritual manuals (kalpāntarakāra) state that this period is secondary (*gauṇa*) specifically for one who has not performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for having failed [to perform the sacrifice] at the proper time. Bharadvāja says: "One should not let the time for the New Moon (*darśa*) pass until the Full Moon (*paurṇamāsa*), nor the time for the Full Moon until the New Moon. Thus, even when the time has elapsed, one may sacrifice in times of distress (*āpadi*). The author of the Nidāna also says: "In all cases, the waxing fortnight takes the place of the New Moon, and the dark fortnight takes the place of the Full Moon."

Likewise, other scriptural statements such as "one should pass the dark fortnight with the full-moon oblation" and "the bright fortnight with the new-moon oblation" are not recorded here because they belong to different ritual manuals (*kalpa*). It should be understood that this same rule applies even when there is a transgression involving many [offerings]. This *pāthikṛt* cake-offering is performed together with the sacrifice for transgressions; thus the venerable Āpastamba said: "Or, when the rituals are performed in a common sequence (*samānatantre*), the primary one should be performed. (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 9.4.3).

And since that [offering] is desired when [the time] has passed, it is not possible if the time has elapsed entirely; therefore, it is established as being for a figurative (gauṇa) time only. Furthermore, in this alternative, there is no Vaiśvānarī offering, because it belongs to another branch and because the atipanna sacrifice is concluded together with the Pāthikṛta. The same should be understood regarding the two subsequent alternatives. Now, he states the rule from another branch concerning the lapse of one who has already commenced [the rite]:

The sacrifice of one whose sacrifice is interrupted by the performance of this intermediate offering is indeed severed. One should offer that same cake for Agni on eight potsherds which is prescribed for the new moon and full moon sacrifices, but now for Agni Pathikṛt (the Maker of the Path). By means of that very [offering], he returns again to the path and does not sever the sacrifice; so it is known. 82.

If, in the midst of a sacrifice that has already begun, it should be interrupted, and if the *pāthikṛtī* offering were performed in the middle of that sacrifice, then that sacrifice which was previously extended would be severed; nor should it be intended to be completed at the end, because there is no obligation to perform what has already been recognized as defective. Therefore, that very *āgneya* offering which was unswerving (*acyuta*) therein must be performed with the *pāthikṛt* as its quality; by that alone, one regains the path of the interrupted sacrifice, and the sacrifice does not become severed.

And this ritual procedure (kalpa) is to be applied, in the event of a transgression by one who has already commenced [the rite], according to the two previous alternatives, because it belongs to another Vedic branch (śākhā). For one who has not yet commenced, however, only the two former [alternatives] apply, since this [present rule] pertains specifically to the subject of one who has already commenced. || 2 ||
If one who has commenced [the vow] lets the time lapse, or if one who has not commenced it [commits an offense], he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara Vratapati. || 83 ||

The Teacher (Ācārya), however, maintains that even the *pāthikṛtī* [offering] applies when the subject matter has already commenced, as indicated by the statement, "having thus begun this... [which refers to] the removal of time for what has been commenced; whereas the *vaiśvānarī* [offering] applies to what has not yet been commenced. This is not the intention of Āpastamba, because of his general statement and his specific statement [to the contrary]. || 83 ||
28. The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[Fifteenth Praśna]:
"If one who has established the sacred fires should act as if violating his vows; or if one who has established the sacred fires should go on a journey, so say some. (84)

"Failure in the vow" (*vratabhreṣaḥ*) refers to the non-performance of the prescribed conduct. Because of the statement, "On every day or for a month he eats [meat] or approaches a woman" (*Āpastamba Śrautasūtra* 9.1.4), this does not connect with the two preceding [terms]. Therefore, the *vrātapatī* occurs only in the case of failure in the vow and exile that are of indefinite duration. Furthermore, there is another view: the expression from the other *sūtra*, "on the day of the vow" (*vratye'hani*), connects with both [cases], like the eye of a crow.

Baudhāyana says: "If one who has established the sacred fires should act as if he were not so established, this is said to apply from the time of the establishment [of the fires] itself"; Śālīki says: "[It applies] only when the fires have been formally established and the fuel has been added. || 84 ||

One who has established the sacred fires and sheds tears due to distress should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratabhṛt. Some prescribe the offering to Vratapati for one departing on a journey, and the offering to Vratapati for the shedding of tears. (85)

The inclusion of the word *āti* is for the purpose of excluding tears born of joy. Some hold that the letter *d* in *vratabhṛdaḥ* is either Vedic (*chāndasa*) or a scribal error (*prāmādika*). The phrase "on both days" (*pratye'hani*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. Thus say the Bahvṛcas: "Regarding this they say: if one who has established the sacred fires should shed tears on the day of fasting (*upavasatha*). (85)

“O Agni, you who uphold the vows, pure one, seat the gods here for the sake of carrying the oblation, O Agni! Now, upholding the vows, the protector of vows, undeceivable, ageless, and possessing excellent heroes, sacrifice for us to the gods. Bestowing jewels, easy to find, O Agni, protect us that we may live, O Jātavedas!”—these are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. (Section 4) 86.
Thus ends the first chapter in the fifteenth book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.

This is the Hotṛ’s office according to the Yajurveda. Thus ends the first chapter in the fifteenth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*, compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.
15.2 Now begins the second chapter of the fifteenth inquiry.
One should consecrate [the seat] with the mantra: "From whatever you sit in fear, from that make us free from fear; be gracious to all our offspring; obeisance to Rudra, the bountiful. ||1||
The word "that" (tām) is to be supplied as the object. || 1 ||

If the Agnihotra cow, having been let loose for breeding or while being milked, should sit down, [the priest] should make her rise with the mantra: "The divine Aditi, of all forms, has risen; she has bestowed life upon the lord of the sacrifice, preparing a portion for Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa. Having raised her and had her milked, he should give it to a Brāhmaṇa.
