The *āgnihotrī* is the cow that provides the milk for the *agnihotra*. If she, having been let loose or joined [to the calf] for the purpose of milking, should sit down, the Adhvaryu priest makes her stand up. Having milked her, the sacrificer should give her along with the milk to one whose food he does not eat. Regarding this, Āpastamba cites a scriptural passage from another recension: "It is known [from scripture]: 'She casts back upon him his misfortune and his evil' (ĀpŚS 9.2.5)."
And when that has been done, he fastens upon that very [person] the evil characterized by non-turning; "non-turning" means poverty or hunger. ||2||

If one should not eat the food of someone, he should beat that person with a staff until she is bruised or even until she is crushed, then raise her up and make her his own [wife], saying: "May you be blessed with good pasture; may we also be blessed. Eat grass, O inviolable one, at all times; drink pure water as you come. Having torn out a clump of *darbha* grass, he should make her eat it. || 3 ||
The sense is that, having thus caused her—who has been made one's own—to swallow [the offering], one should then milk her for the sake of the oblation (homa). || 3 ||

If the cow being milked should bellow or if she should yield blood, one should say, "She has stepped out," and having enclosed a space around the *dakṣiṇāgni*, having cooked it over that fire, he should offer it in that very fire. He should give her to a Brāhmaṇa whom he thinks will not come back again. 4.

"Go forth, go elsewhere"—this is the *praiṣa* (direction) for the sacrificer and others. One should give [the gift] to someone whom one does not intend to approach—that is, to someone toward whom one will not go for any purpose whatsoever. || 4 ||

"Whatever milk today has clung to the earth, whatever has flowed into the plants, and whatever into the waters—may there be milk in my houses, milk in the cows, and milk in the calves; may I be composed of that milk. Having consecrated it with this mantra, if the milk being milked should spill, one should pour water over it with the verse, "I send you to the ocean," and having offered that same [spilled] milk—however it may be—and having milked another cow, one should offer it again. || 5 ||

Regarding the general spilling of the *agnihotra* oblation, the consecration with the mantra "askāndyauḥ" is prescribed; however, since he will later state that one should effect a union with water using the mantra "unne bhaya," this [present rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that. || 6 ||

1. He who intends to perform that *agnihotra*—according to the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: 1942—or rather, he should milk that same cow or another; if he should break [the vessel], he should wash another pot and then milk into it, but water must not be poured back into it. 6.

If the vessel should break in one part, then, having washed it, one should milk another cow into that same vessel; or one may milk that very same cow, provided she has become full-milked again. But if the vessel is shattered all over, one should bring in a different vessel.

If the milk should spill, or while it is being carried, or while it is being placed on the fire, or once it has been placed on the fire, or while it is being removed from the fire, or once it has been removed—if [the milk] should spill, one should milk another [cow].

The expiation for the spilling of milk while it is being milked has been stated in the preceding sūtra; likewise, [the expiation] for milk and other substances that have already been milked will be explained further on. In this context, the substance for both cases is restricted by this rule. Therefore, there is a specific mention of "while being milked. "What is being carried" means for the purpose of placing it over the Gārhapatya fire. The phrase "of that very kind" and so forth means that whatever remains after the spilling—whether it be a small amount or as much as was left—that must be offered. Now, if what remains is so very little that it is unfit for an offering, then one should have another cow milked over it and offer the mixture with the milk thus poured. || 7 ||

Now, if what has been ladled out should spill—whether once or twice or thrice—some say one should not pay it any heed. If, however, what is being ladled out for the fourth time should spill, one should pour the remainder back into the pot, take four spoonfuls from there, recite a verse addressed to Varuṇa, and offer the oblation with that verse addressed to Varuṇa. (Section 5) ||8||

If [the oblation] spills out gradually or all at once, one should not disregard it; one should offer with only what remains. However, one must certainly perform the expiation for the spilling, because the rule for expiation is prescribed even for the spilling of a mere *āhuti*. If, however, it should spill a fourth time, then one should pour what remains from the *sruva* into the pot and pour it back again into the *sruva*, or else milk it again into the *sruva*. In that context, the mention of "fourth" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) and thus indicates the fifth as well for those who follow the five-fold division (*pañcāvattin*).

By this, it is stated that "the fourth" implies "from the fourth onwards. Likewise, here, because of the statement regarding disregard prior to the fourth, even in the preceding sūtra, the phrase "if the drawn-out [Soma] should spill" is understood to apply only to spilling from the fourth drawing onwards. Since there can be no combination of that [earlier rule] with this one, there is an option (vikalpa). Some, however, establish it as follows: when spilling occurs after the Soma has been drawn once, twice, or thrice, and the Soma drawn from the fourth onwards also spills, then this rule applies; otherwise, it is the former [rule]. || 8 ||

If that which has been ladled out should spill, one should ladle it out again and offer it; or else, having recited over it a verse addressed to Varuṇa, one should offer it with that Varuṇa-verse. If that which has been hurried forward should spill, having offered whatever remains from there, if one were to return, one would break the sacrifice; therefore, having sat down where it spilled, one should take it up again and offer it just as it was, after milking another cow. 15.2.10.

[Paṭala 1] Accompanied by the commentary *Yogacandrikā* composed by Mahādeva Śāli. Regarding the term *udrutasya*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the beginning of an action (*ādikarmaṇi*). It means that having risen up quickly, one has begun to lead [the Soma] forward (*prāṅnetum*). This is because the act of leading forward and so on is taken up later in the text. And it is stated in the Brāhmaṇa: "That which was raised up for Bṛhaspati, set forth for Savitṛ, and being carried away for Heaven and Earth. If that [Soma] which has been raised up should spill, one should sit down there, remain seated, place the vessel (*sthālī*) over the spilled portion, and from that [vessel], once again...

The meaning is that, having taken up what has been spilled, one should offer that very same substance after increasing it; however, one must not produce a separate, different substance from it. That this is the meaning is to be understood from the scriptural text itself, beginning with "whatever of the *udruta* might spill," and so forth. And Baudhāyana explains it thus: "If whatever of the *udruta* should spill, one should sit down and take it up again."

Wherever [the oblation] spills, one should place the vessel right there, pour back the remainder, and having poured it out again, that very same [substance], however it may be, should be offered as a sacrifice. This has already been explained previously. When this has been performed, having recited "Ava te heḍa" and then "Ud uttamam," one should offer an oblation of clarified butter with the verse addressed to Varuṇa. 9 || 10 ||

If the eastern portion being carried should spill, one should consecrate it with the mantra, "Thou art the oblation for Prajāpati’s maintenance," and then, having recited a verse addressed to Varuṇa, one should offer it with clarified butter while reciting that verse to Varuṇa. || 11 ||

But here, because of the qualification "being carried away," as long as one restrains or takes it up, there is a purely original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*). "Prācīnam" means previously commenced; the meaning is: as long as it has been carried away in front. In that case, the mantra for Prajāpati’s recitation is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "akāni. However, the prefix remains exactly as stated.

Therefore, this very substance remaining from the *agnihotra* should be used, and one should not milk another cow and offer again; such is the opinion of Āpastamba. However, according to the final settled view (*siddhānta*), the oblation must be performed again. In that case, if the entire contents have spilled, the vessel must be refilled. If even the vessel is lost, Āśvalāyana prescribes clarified butter (*ājya*) as a substitute, saying: "Thou art the body of Prajāpati, offered upon the All-supporting. Therein, one touches what has spilled and should offer with the remainder. If there is no remainder, one should draw it up again; if there is no clarified butter at all, [one should use a substitute]. Thus ends the section. 11.

If what was brought forward should spill before [the offering], one should lift it up again, pour it out once more, and offer it; or else, having recited a verse addressed to Varuṇa over clarified butter, one should make the offering with that verse addressed to Varuṇa. || 12 ||

"Previously brought forward" means brought forward from the front as a remnant of the placing; the meaning is that it has been led back to its original place. In that case, for what has been placed, because it was previously placed, this same rule applies even when it is being placed. Having not poured it out, one should bring the vessel to the *camas* and, having poured four times, offer it, or otherwise it should be milked over [the vessel], so says Āpastamba. || 12 ||

If, before the offering has been made, what has been poured out should spill, then, having offered again whatever [milk] is of such a kind and of such a quality, and having milked another cow, one should offer once more. || 13 ||

This procedure begins from the placing [of the oblation] upon the *darbha* grass up until the first offering; for it is introduced as "if at the first offering," and because no other limit is mentioned prior to that. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "The [oblation] for Indra and Agni has been placed.
(Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Praśna 15, Section 284).

"Before the first oblation of the fire. This means from the time of the *upasādana* (placing of the ladle) until it has not yet been offered; that is, as long as it remains unoffered. Now, one might ask: since the subsequent limit is already established by the previous statement, why was "before it has been offered" stated here? What is the fault? Previously, because it was understood in some way, the subsequent limit was not explicitly mentioned. Now, however, since it is recited in the *Āpastamba-sūtra*, it is shown exactly as it stands there. Therefore, this is not a point for objection. The procedure for the re-offering and so forth is the same as in the case of a spill (*skandana*). Thus, the production of the substance in the event of a spill of the *Agnihotra* has been explained. Now, he states the expiation (*prāyaścitta*):

"May the sky leap; may the earth leap; may the young bull leap toward the cows. May all these worlds leap; may the leaping sacrifice procreate. From the leaping was born the progenitor; from the leaping is born the bull. From the leaping may we procreate. Having thus consecrated the spilled *agnihotra* offering, he should pour water over it. 14.
He should pour it near and mix it. || 14 ||
If it should spill in the evening, he shall not eat until the morning offering; if it should spill in the morning, he shall not eat until the evening offering. || 15 ||

If the [milk] spills at evening, one should not eat until the morning *āhuti*; likewise until the morning *āhuti* at dawn. This same rule applies to the spilling of all materials for the *agnihotra*. However, when the material is produced [again], the distinction is that instead of the milking with the *abhidohana* formula and so forth, one should bring back another substance of the same kind. || 15 ||
A divine thunderbolt indeed falls upon him whose *agnihotra* makes a crackling sound; he should say, "May it burn that one," naming the person whom he hates.

"Śi-ri-śira" is an imitation of sound. This means that for one whose *agnihotra* sacrifice crackles (*śiriśirāyate*), this falling of the thunderbolt is a bad omen. In that case, the *adhvaryu* priest, having uttered the name of the sacrificer's enemy, should say: "Burn [him], O Devadatta! (*samoṣa devadattam*). The root *oṣ* signifies the act of burning; "samoṣa" is a form derived from that root preceded by the prefix *sam*. || 16 ||

If, while the Agnihotra has been placed on the fire, a dog should run between [the fires], one should take ashes from the Gārhapatya and, with the verse addressed to Viṣṇu, "Viṣṇu strode across this," he should sweep up the soot from the Āhavanīya; with these very ashes, he fills in the dog's footprint.

Scattering ashes here and there while destroying [the fire], and having followed the tracks of the dog, one should fill them with ashes. This expiation applies from the time of placing the vessel on the fire until its removal. Others say it applies until the offering is made; otherwise, the general expiation alone is required. || 17 ||

If the fire of one who has not brought it forth should set as the sun goes down, or if he should see it extinguished while it was burning elsewhere, then, having brought it from there, [the thought] "I shall enter this," is indeed how it is established. || 18 ||

Regarding the statement, "They should bring him [the fire] day after day," which was mentioned in connection with the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern fire): if the sun should set while that fire has not yet been brought, then—without regard for specific origins such as a prosperous household or the like—one should fetch it from wherever it is seen and establish it with the thought, "May I enter this. The word *vā* (or) indicates an alternative. The meaning is that it is prescribed either with the formula "May I enter this" or silently (*tūṣṇīm*). Because of the statement "He should not extinguish it," it should be established silently when the sun rises. || 18 ||
Thus ends the ritual procedure for re-establishing the southern fire that has gone out. ||19||

The meaning is that this very method of *ādhāna* (establishment) applies even to the *dakṣiṇāgni*, although it follows everywhere; this is because of the specific mention of "the *dakṣiṇāgni*. For the *gārhapatya* and *āvasathya* fires, however, the establishment is performed silently (*tūṣṇīm*). As for expiation (*prāyaścitta*), in all cases it is simply the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*), since no specific rule has been stated. || 19 ||

If the sun should set while someone’s fire has not yet been carried forward, they should first take away the *agnihotra* [oblation], and then they should carry forward the fire. Alternatively, having tied a piece of gold to a blade of *darbha* grass, a Brahmin of noble lineage (*ārṣeya*) who knows much of the sacred lore should go out first; following him, he should carry forward the fire. Following him, he should proceed with the *agnihotra*; having established the fire, placed the *agnihotra* oblation, and remained there without breathing until the end of the day, he should give a gift, offer the oblation, and then worship with "Bhūḥ Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ. He should pour out a *caru* offering for Varuṇa and should sacrifice it with the formula: "O Dispeller of Darkness, homage! Svāhā! (15.2.20).

Since it has been stated that the *praṇayana* (leading forward of the fire) must take place before the sun has set behind the trees, this penance (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed for its transgression. Therefore, by the term "taking out" (*uddharaṇa*), the *praṇayana* is indicated, as in passages such as "for whom one should take out fire from the fire," and likewise in Āśvalāyana’s rule: "for whom the *Āhavanīya* fire, not yet led forward, should set. Thus, even when the fire has been taken out but not yet led forward, the penance indeed applies. This has been explained under the *brahmaudana* rite as being for one who knows the meaning of the Veda.

In that very context, one who possesses knowledge (*vedana*) regarding many objects is "one who knows much" (*bahuvid*). Alternatively, the term *bahuvid* is an explanation of the word *brāhmaṇa*, as in the injunction: "A Brāhmaṇa of noble lineage (*ārṣeya*) should perform the extraction [of the Soma]. This is because, in that case, a multiplicity of knowledges is required. It should be understood that for each person, according to the specific source from which their excellence in knowledge arises, there is a superior quality (*guṇātiśaya*) in accepting that particular [knowledge].

In this regard, beginning from the bringing [of the materials] until before the kindling (*uvvaṇa*), once the Adhvaryu has performed the duties of the Āhavanīya fire—excluding those specific rites—a certain attendant of the sacrificer shall carry gold bound with *darbha* grass in front. Following him from behind, the Bahuvid Agni should be lifted up and carried forth according to the prescribed rule. Following that Agni from behind, the Adhvaryu should proceed with the Agnihotra. Then, once the gold has been set down by the attendant, the Bahuvid Agni is established and released. Thereafter, the Adhvaryu places the Agnihotra oblation down. According to another Sūtra, it is said: "It is constant."

This refers to the obligatory *agnihotra* itself, and not to a modified (*vaikṛta*) form that requires a subsequent offering; this is the meaning. Others say that the milk is fixed as the obligatory substance. Then, having performed the placing of fuel on the *āhavanīya* fire and so forth prior to the first oblation, he should remain seated without breathing until he departs from there. Having breathed out and offered the *agnihotra*, and after the touching of water with the formula "Thou art rain" has been completed, he should worship the *āhavanīya* with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" and at that very moment offer the *vāraṇa-cakra*.

"Bharadvāja says: 'Tomorrow it will be better'—one should offer with the formula, *doṣāvastar namas svāhā*. Āśmarathya says that this alone is the obligatory *agnihotra*. Now Ālekhana says: having performed the offering at the proper time with this mantra, one should then perform the obligatory *agnihotra* as before. || 20 ||

If he should carry forward the *agnihotra* for the evening sacrifice when it is past its proper time, he should offer it in the morning with the formula: "Vastar, homage! Svāhā! (21). If he should carry forward the *agnihotra* for the morning sacrifice when it is past its proper time, having offered the two oblations that complete the time with these two mantras, he performs the regular *agnihotra*. (22)

Regarding the Agnihotra, the times for the morning and evening [services], such as the twilights (saṃdhyā), have been prescribed. For the omission of all of these, an expiation (prāyaścitta) is taught. Likewise, Āśvalāyana states that the time for the evening oblation (homa) ends at nightfall (pradoṣa), and that for the morning oblation ends at the time when cows are gathered (saṃgava); he says, "one should not let [the time] pass beyond that. However, the author of the Sūtra has stated alternative times there, beginning with, "when one offers in the middle of the day," and so forth. Similarly, the author of the Upagrantha has also stated: "The entire day is the place for the morning oblation; the entire night is [the place] for the evening oblation."

Bharadvāja also says: "One should perform the evening *homa* before dawn, and the morning *homa* before sunset. By performing it at the proper time and not missing the appointed hour, [the offerings] do not spill over nor are they disturbed; so it is known. Therefore, this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) applies except in cases of distress (*anāpadi*). In times of distress, however, the *homa* itself should be performed until the time for the subsequent [offering] arrives. Once the time for the subsequent one has arrived, the previous one should not be performed, because its proper time has lapsed. As for the expiation in that case, it will be shown further on.

That by which the time is brought about is "to be performed at the [proper] time" (*kālasamāpādanīya*). Having offered that [at the right time], one performs the fetching of the embers and so forth. That very [fire] is intended for some specific purpose in the *agnihotra*; therefore, it is stated that the *agnihotra* is obligatory (*nitya*) in order to exclude that [optional] case. || 21 || 22 ||

Having set down the evening *agnihotra* oblation, he recites "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" before the offering is made; and having offered it, having set down the morning *agnihotra* oblation, he remains seated without breathing until the fire has gone out, then gives a boon, offers the oblation, and worships with "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. He follows the *āhavanīya* fire as it is led away, saying, "Agni has looked upon the forefront of the dawns. Having led forth another fire, he worships it with: "Be secure right here; do not abandon me, nor this man, the son of such-and-such. He should offer a pap (*caru*) to Mitra.

This has been explained by what preceded. "Amum āmuṣyāyaṇam" is the designation of the sacrificer’s name, lineage (*gotra*), and birthplace; for example, "Devadatta, son of Bhṛgu. [End of] Paṭala. Together with the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī:
Some prescribe a cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) dedicated to Sūrya. 27. 24.

The ritual rules for the single-pot-sherd (ekakapāla) offering prescribed for the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice of Sūrya are to be performed; and that [offering] is a modification (vikāra) of the Āgneya sacrifice.
While she remains seated there, the husband and wife, fasting and restraining their speech, sit for that day kindling the fire.

"In the sixth *iṣṭi*, on this day, while kindling the Āhavanīya fire itself, both the sacrificer and his wife remain seated with their speech restrained," so says Āpastamba. The phrase "the Āhavanīya itself" means that they kindle that very same Āhavanīya for the purpose of the evening oblation (*sāyaṃ-homa*). Alternatively, since the kindling of all the fires is prescribed by Āśvalāyana and others, the particle *eva* (itself/only) is used here to exclude that [practice]. || 25 ||
One should offer the evening Agnihotra with milk; having first placed the firewood on the hearth, one should then bring the milk.

The phrase "of two cows" is to be supplied as before; that is to say, according to the method stated in the passage, "One desiring cattle should offer with the milk of two [cows]. In that context, it is understood that the prior act of placing [the vessel] on the fire is for the purpose of providing assistance. || 26 ||

If the sun should rise while the fire of one [who maintains the sacred fires] has not yet been taken out, he should take four portions of clarified butter and go forward first; a Brāhmaṇa of noble lineage who knows much of the sacred tradition should take out the fire following him. He should follow with the Agnihotra oblation, and having established the fire and set down the Agnihotra materials, sitting facing west in front [of the fire], he should offer that four-portioned butter with the mantra: "May Uṣas with her banner enjoy the sacrifice invited by the gods; to the gods, the most honey-sweet, Svāhā! Having offered this, he should perform the regular Agnihotra. (Section 7) 27.

This has been explained by the procedure for the *abhininocana* offering. However, there is this distinction: one should take four portions of clarified butter into the *juhū* ladle in place of gold. Then, once the fire has been established, the *adhvaryu*, having set down the *agnihotra* oblation and sitting to the east of the *āhavanīya* fire facing west, should offer it with the mantra: "O Dawn, with thy banner... (RV 1.92.1). Thus ends [the section]. 27.
For that [omission], the same ritual procedure for the oblation applies; that is the expiation, which is performed when the morning [libation] has passed.

The ritual procedure for the oblation (homakalpa), beginning with "until exhaustion" (*ātamito*) and "not breathing" (*aprāṇan*), and ending with the granting of boons (*varadāna*), is the same as the immediately preceding rule. For both [cases], the expiation consists of the worship of the sun (*ādityopasthāna*) and so forth, up to the oblation of milk (*payasā homa*). "When the morning has passed" (*yat prātar atīte*) means when the morning time has elapsed. || 28 ||
This much is the difference: here one does not carry the Āhavanīya fire along. 29.
The meaning is that in that very fire, there is the Maitra sacrifice along with its oblation. || 29 ||

If the sun should rise while the *agnihotra* has not yet been offered, one should pour out the oblation, sit until the sun has set without breathing, and having offered it, should worship with the syllable *bhūḥ*. A choice gift (*vara*) is the sacrificial fee. 15.2.30.

If one has set out with the intention, "I shall offer when [the sun] has not yet risen," and the Agnihotra remains unoffered while the sun is still not risen, it is just as a woman who has begun to give birth but has not yet delivered might suffer a miscarriage; such is the calamity that occurs. By this, the sacrificer also obstructs himself—the meaning is that he brings suffering upon himself. Consequently, being obstructed for the sake of suffering, he suffers total ruin (*sarvajyāni*) and encounters all kinds of afflictions. Therefore, the sense is that this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be observed. The phrase "until death" (*ātamito'māṇan*) and so forth has already been explained. 30.

If it should happen at the end, he should draw [the fire] out and run toward the east; having placed it down, he should sit until he faints. When he faints, he should then offer an oblation with "bhūḥ svāhā. || 31 ||

"If it should be at the end" means if it should be near the oblation, being caused by that. What is meant? The meaning is: if the rising [of the sun] should occur after the *agnihotra* has been completed, but before the oblation. And so Bharadvāja says: "'If it should be at the end'—this refers to the statement immediately following the *agnihotra*. In that case, having performed everything from the drawing out [of the milk] up to the placing [of the ladle], he should offer the first oblation with the formula: "The exhausted one, *maḥ*, to the breath, *svāhā*. (31)

If, after he has set out with the thought "I shall offer for him," the sun should rise while the Agnihotra has already been offered, then some say that having offered it, one should clear away the ashes and perform the re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya).

When [the thought] "may it be so" has occurred, having offered thus and having formally extinguished that *agnihotra* fire according to the rule, Āśmarathya maintains that the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) must also be performed for him as an expiation; however, this is not the opinion of others—this is the meaning. || 32 ||

If both fires should go out, whether the sun rises or sets [while they are extinguished], or if the fires, having been consigned to the two kindling woods, should be lost, there must be a re-establishment of the fires; that is the expiation in this case. 33.
And because of the statement of Āpastamba: "The sun may set upon this [rite], or it may rise upon it" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 9.2.7). ||33||
One whose Agnihotra has been interrupted for two or three days should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumat.

If four *homa* offerings have been omitted, the *Tantumatī* rite must be performed; or [if] eight [offerings] of the *pāśubandha* have been omitted. If there is an interruption prior to these limits, since no specific expiation (*vaiśeṣika-prāyaścitta*) is prescribed, the general rule applies: the *Saptahotṛ* [rite] is to be performed, according to the text, "One should restore the failed sacrifice by means of the *Saptahotṛ*. Nor should it be doubted that the *Agnihotra* is not a sacrifice, for it would then follow that it cannot suffer from sacrificial failure.

Therefore, because of the praise of this as a sacrifice (*yajña*) in the phrase "of the Agnihotra sacrifice" (*agnihotrasya yajñakratoḥ*), and because Baudhāyana explicitly states that this very [rite] constitutes a sacrificial failure (*yajñavibhreṣa*), it is as stated regarding one who has gone abroad: "Now, if they report to him a sacrificial failure, [he should say], 'You have not offered.
[End of] Patala 3, accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 286.

Thus it is said. Likewise, the author of the *Upagrantha* also stated, introducing his point with "What indeed is this hatred?", saying: "In that Agnihotra sacrifice where the two oblations (*āhuti*) occupy each other's place. Therefore, it is indeed correct that there are seven Hotṛ priests. Furthermore, the determination of the scope regarding the sacrifice for expiation (*yajñavinaṣṭeṣṭi*) has already been shown previously. On this matter, Kātyāyana says: "In the event of an omission of the Agnihotra, one should offer an oblation with the mantra: 'May the mind, as light, enjoy [the offering]' (*mano jyotir juṣatām*)."

Āśvalāyana, referring to the *manasvatī* [verse], states regarding the fourfold-drawn [oblation]: "In the case of the Agnihotra not being offered, one [should perform] a compensatory offering (*pratihoma*). Baudhāyana, however, has prescribed only the compensatory offering in the case where [the fire] has not been properly kindled. As he says: "While the fires are indeed blazing and being maintained, one should count how many Agnihotra offerings have been omitted and offer them in compensation."

The learned scholar should also reflect upon what was stated by Bādarāyaṇa: "Therefore, for one who knows thus, even if they do not offer for one day or two days, it is as if they have offered. In this context, this same rule applies even when there is an interruption of many days beyond four; for no other [rule] is mentioned, and because the additional statement is intended to restrict the suspension of the *iṣṭi* to the period of four days or less.

Regarding this, Bharadvāja states a specific rule for when there has been a long-term interruption of the *homa* and other rites for one who has installed the sacred fire: "When the *homas* are not being offered, how is it that [the ritual] is not lost for those who maintain [the fires] within themselves or in the two kindling woods (*araṇis*)? For two months, if the *Agnihotra* has not been offered and the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices have not been performed, one should perform the *Mahāpathikṛt-iṣṭi* with these offerings: to Agni Pathikṛt, to Agni Vaiśvānara, to Agni Vratapati, and to Agni Ṛtabhṛt. One should sacrifice with the *Pavitreṣṭi*; thus one obtains everything. Thus [he says].

Likewise, having introduced the subject with the words, "if for six months the Agnihotra has not been offered, or if one has not performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," and having stated—as before—the sequence ending with the Pavitreṣṭi, he then declared, "one should perform the Atipavitreṣṭi. Therefore, we consider it an act of extreme rashness when some claim that the sacred fire is destroyed if the offering is interrupted for more than four days. || 34 ||

"Creating for himself an easy path and a place free from retreat, the sharp-horned bull, blazing brightly, looking back upon his ancient dwelling, Agni has stretched out the celestial thread. "Thou art our thread and our bridge, O Agni; thou art the path that leads to the gods. With thee, O Agni, may we ascend to the ridge, and then may we rejoice in the common feast with the gods"—these are the *Yājyā* and *Anuvākyā* verses. (Section 8)
Thus ends the second chapter in the fifteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.

Thus ends the second chapter in the fifteenth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. Now begins the third chapter in the fifteenth book of the *Śrauta-Sūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha. [Book 16, Chapter 15.3] [Note: The numbering provided in the source text appears to contain a typographical inconsistency; the commentary refers to the fifteenth book (*praśna*), while the subsequent section marker indicates the sixteenth book (*praśne*). This translation follows the explicit reference to the "fifteenth book" found in both the sūtra and the commentary title.]

If the Gārhapatya fire should go out while the Āhavanīya has not gone out, one should extinguish the Āhavanīya, collect the embers of the Gārhapatya, and churn the Āhavanīya with the mantra, "From here Agni was first born. Having led it forward, he kindles it with the mantra, "O Agni, sovereign, delight in the chariot, for power, for glory, for vigor, for offspring; you are the sovereign, you are the self-ruler; sit on the pleasant seat; may the two springs of Sarasvatī enkindle you. He should then offer an eight-pot-sherd cake to Agni, the ascetic, the one accompanied by people, and the purifier. ||1||

If, while the fire is being maintained for the sake of a ritual performed with a mechanical device (*yantra*) or in a fire that has been specially prepared, the *gārhapatya* fire goes out, then one should extinguish the *āhavanīya* and *dakṣiṇāgni* fires which have the *gārhapatya* as their source, produce them again according to the prescribed method, and perform either the *tapasvīṣṭi* (the sacrifice for one who has suffered loss) which will be described, or the oblations (*āhutis*). Thereafter, the ritual is completed. Examples include the *darvihomas* such as the *sāvitra*, *sārasvata*, and *caturhotṛ* offerings, as well as the *agnihotra* and the *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices (*paśus*) prior to the *anvādhāna*.

However, subsequent to the *anvādhāna* and at the time of the *homa*, this rule is indeed set aside by those specific expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). It sets aside the rule beginning with "if the Gārhapatya [fire]... because that [other rule] pertains to a specific case. Therefore, even outside of the ritual time, this very same rule applies for one who maintains the perpetual fire (*ajastrāgni*). Alternatively, there is simply an option (*vikalpa*) between those two rules; they do not stand in a relationship of general and specific, because there is no difference in their subject matter (*śamkha*).

The Teacher will state: "According to some, [the rule applies] when one's fire goes out; one need not observe a specific time. It should be churned from those very same embers" (*Śrautasūtra* 15.3). And Bharadvāja says: "Now, according to some: whichever fire should go out, it should be churned from those very same pieces of wood," and so forth.

In this regard, both the *Bahvṛca* and the *Vājasaneyaka*, as well as the *Āśvalāyana*, *Kātyāyana*, and *Baudhāyana*, prescribe that once the *āhavanīya* fire has been maintained, it should be taken up, placed in the *gārhapatya* hearth, and then re-established from there. Concerning the *āhavanīya*, the *Bahvṛca* tradition records the following: "Having collected this entire [fire] together with its ashes and having placed it in the *gārhapatya* hearth, one should then draw forth the *āhavanīya* toward the east. This very same internal reading is also found in the *Vājasaneyaka*.

The same applies in the *Āśvalāyana* and other texts. However, in the *Baudhāyana*, the specific procedure is as follows: having collected everything from the *āhavanīya* fire-vessel, having carried it to the south of the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*), having removed the ashes from both hearths, having smeared them with a lump of cow-dung, having re-established the fires and added fuel, one performs the *praṇayana*. Likewise, regarding the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), a specific rule is stated: one should offer six oblations with the mantras: "Awake, O Agni," "Thou, O Agni, art far-extending," "May the mind, the light, enjoy [the offering]," "Weaving the thread," and "Upwards that bright [sun]. || 1 ||
3rd Paṭala: Accompanied by the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.

"Come with heat among the people, O Agni, as the purifier with your flame; come to this well-recited hymn of mine. "Come to us with heat among the people, O Agni, shining as the purifier; placing our oblations among the gods"—these are the *Yājyā* and *Anuvākyā* verses. (2)
He has gone. This is the office of the Yajurvedic Hotṛ priest. || 2 ||

This very same expiation applies when the Āhavanīya fire has gone out; however, in this case, one does not lead the Gārhapatya fire [to the new site], but offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat.

In each of those cases where the Āhavanīya fire has gone out, one should produce the fire according to the prescribed rule and offer the *jyotiṣmatī* oblation. This applies, for example, in cases such as: "if [the fire goes out] after the evening Agnihotra has been offered," or "if [it goes out] before the time of the *vyoma* [chant]," and so forth. However, where a specific expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is enjoined, that alone is required, as in the case of the *anvāhita* fire and similar instances. Others maintain that by this [rule], the *jyotiṣmatī* is made optional [with the specific expiation].

But surely, by the preceding sūtra, *tapasvatī* is also obtained in each respective case. Therefore, since both are heard in connection with a single fault, is there a conjunction (*samuccaya*)? No, he says: "Not *tapasvatī*. (4)

When one offers the oblation to Jyotiṣmat, then one does not offer to Tapasvat; the sense is that there is indeed an option between these two according to the difference in Vedic recensions (śākhā). Alternatively, this should be construed with the phrase "the sacrifice common to all" as a relationship of general and particular: Tapasvatī is for all fires, while Jyotiṣmatī is for the Āhavanīya fire; thus, the meaning is that there is an annulment (bādha) of Tapasvatī in that specific case.

Regarding the matter of churning, however, according to the rule that "whether it be the Gārhapatya or the Āhavanīya," the *tapasvatī* [verse] alone is used everywhere, not the *jyotiṣmatī*, because of its specific prescription. Otherwise, there would be the consequence of leaving no room for the Āhavanīya. Even in that case, however, there is an option between the two; such is another view. 4.

If the eastern fire should go out when the evening *agnihotra* has not yet been offered, some say that one should place the *agnihotra* milk on the fire and ladle it out; others say one should carry it forward with the original fire. Having carried it forward with the original fire, one should follow it with the *agnihotra*. A Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas should carry forth the fire. Whatever materials were intended for the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*), he should give those away.

Although, because of the statement "even when the Agnihotra has not been offered," this rule should be understood as applying until the morning offering, nevertheless—due to the restriction on the time of removal, namely "having placed the Agnihotra on the fire" or "having drawn it out," and because of the statement that the removal occurs together with the Agnihotra—the limitation of this [rule] to the time prior to that [morning offering] follows by implication. This has been explained by Bhaṭṭa-Uvvaṭa.

The meaning of this is as follows: from the time of the *viharaṇa* (the ritual separation of the fires) until the *adhiśrayaṇa* (placing on the fire) or the *unnayana* (drawing out), once the duties pertaining to the *āhavanīya* have been followed as before—excluding the specific rites of the *āhavanīya* itself—whether the rite ends with the *adhiśrayaṇa* or the *unnayana*, the *bahuvr̥ca-brāhmaṇa* should silently draw out the fire. Then the *adhvaryu*, having performed the rites starting from the conclusion [of the previous] up to the *udvapaṇa* (pouring out), [proceeds].
[Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Praśna 15]

He should not follow the Agnihotra priest who is leading away the *bahuvida* fire. Then, once that [fire] has been established by the *bahuvida*, the sacrificer should give that wealth to him for whom he had set it aside for his own sake, thinking, "I will not give this to anyone else."

By that very wealth which has not been lost, he becomes one who has displaced this Āhavanīya fire from the Gārhapatya. For one who knows much, having given the Agnihotra to another or having deposited it elsewhere, there is either the *anugateṣṭi* sacrifice or the oblations beginning with the *mitrā* offering. Then, having performed the rites of the Āhavanīya that were left undone, the completion of the Agnihotra begins from the point where it was interrupted. This same rule applies even in the case of water, as no specific exception is stated.

Nor should it be argued that, because of the statement "if the Agnihotra has not been offered," the fire in question must pertain only to the fire used for the Agnihotra; for this would be contradicted by the case where it is said, "if another fire should follow after the morning Agnihotra has not been offered," and also by the specific rule elsewhere: "if the fire that has been drawn out should go out before the Agnihotra has been offered. || 5 ||

If, during the morning Agnihotra, another fire should go out, one should follow it [to the place where it has gone], churn out the first fire again, draw out the second fire, and then offer the oblation.

From the time of the morning wandering onwards, until the first offering, the ritual procedure—beginning with the following of the Gārhapatya fire and the drawing out of the Āhavanīya fire, and ending with the *tapasvatī* oblation—is the same as that performed according to the rule "without blowing upon the Āhavanīya," and so forth. Having performed that, one should then offer the Agnihotra; this is the meaning. The repetition [of the procedure] is for the purpose of indicating an alternative limit. || 6 ||
If, however, he should be in haste, he should first settle down by the fire, then lift it up toward the east, and offer the oblation.

If, however, one should hasten due to fear of the lapse of time or other such reasons, then one should designate the Āhavanīya fire itself as the Gārhapatya; having brought the Dakṣiṇāgni and the others to that very spot, one should then draw out the Āhavanīya toward the east and perform the Agnihotra. Thereafter, the production of the Gārhapatya occurs according to the rule beginning with "then [if] the Gārhapatya... (tato yadi gārhapatya...).

But that which is his former fire, he makes it the latter; having settled elsewhere, having churned the fire and taken it up, he should offer the oblation. On the following day, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tapasvat, Janadvat, and Pāvakavat. (Section 9) 8.

The word *jāmi* refers to the previous bliss; it is intended as a praise for the subsequent procedure. *Jāmitva* (redundancy) is a state of lack of excellence caused by repetition. That is indeed *jāmi*, when one performs another fire-altar in exactly the same place where the first was made. Therefore, having gone to another location while the fires are being carried along, and having followed them there, one should churn out another fire according to the rule beginning with "the previous," and having extracted it as before, one should offer the *agnihotra*. Then, on the following day, one should perform the *tapasvatī* oblation. || 8 ||
According to some, [this applies] to one whose other fire should follow after him.
There is an optionality regarding the ritual procedures prescribed in other branches [of the Veda]. ||9||

He does not determine the time. Then, having churned the fire here and drawn it out, he consecrates it with the verse: "From here Agni was first born... [and continues] "O Agni, O Sovereign, delight in wealth; delight in sap, in splendor, and in vigor.

[End of Paṭala 15.3] With the formula, "Thou art the sovereign lord, thou art the self-ruler; sit on the comfortable seat," he kindles it with "May the two Sarasvatīs, the two springs, protect thee. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat and a pap of barley to Varuṇa. 15.3.10.

Alternatively, one need not restrict the time specifically to "morning"; rather, whether in the evening or in the morning, once the Agnihotra has been offered—or even after the fires have gone out and have been followed [back]—the rule beginning with "having first... and so forth shall apply. However, the meaning is that in place of the *tapasvatī* offering, one should offer two *vāruṇa* offerings accompanied by light (*jyotiṣmat*) on a common sacrificial grass mat (*samānabarhis*). Thus, these three alternatives are to be optionally combined with the rule beginning with "for whom the Āhavanīya fire has not been lifted" and so forth, pertaining to the morning time. The last alternative, however, applies even at evening. The rest has been explained. || 10 ||

"Whose fire should go out," so say some; one does not fix a specific time [for this]. It should be churned from those very same embers. Now, if such embers are not available, one should touch the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) with ashes and churn; thus he generates him from his own womb. One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tapasvat, Janadvat, and Pāvakavat—"whose fire should go out," so say some; one does not fix a specific time for this.

He should churn fire from those very same embers; or, if there should be only wood shavings, grass, or dust, he should touch the two kindling sticks (*araṇī*) with that ash and then churn it—thus he generates him from his own womb. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tapasvat, Janadvat, and Pāvakavat. || 11 ||

The pieces of wood remaining after being consumed are called *avakṣāṇas*. If there are such pieces capable of supporting friction, one should take two of them from among those and rub [the fire-drill] upon them. However, if such pieces are not available, then, having avoided contact with the ashes, one should rub [the fire-drill] upon those two *araṇis* (fire-sticks). Having thus prepared the *araṇis*, one generates fire from its own source through friction; for even in the absence of *avakṣāṇas*, the fire resides in the ashes, and it has now been transferred from that location into the two *araṇis*.

And there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the *Tāṇḍya*: "In this very place, indeed, he hid himself. From this very statement, it follows that in the absence of the fire-drills (*araṇi*), even if the fire were churned without the ritual preparation of ashes, it would be as if non-existent because it has not arisen from its own source. Furthermore, the churning of the *Āhavanīya* fire does not take place from the two fire-drills of the *Gārhapatya*, because of the indicative mark: "the fires in the [two] fire-drills of the *Prakṛti*. In all cases, this alone is the origin of the *Gārhapatya*.

And the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) consists of austerity (*tapas*) alone in the case of a false accusation, as in the case of the *anvāhita* fire and others; even where there is no instruction for the bringing forward (*praṇayana*) of the *āhavanīya* fire, the origin [of the fire] is exactly this. As in the *sāvitra* and other ladle-offerings (*darvihoma*), in the *agnihotra*, and likewise at the time of the offering in the animal sacrifices (*paśu*) before the *anvādhāna*, and so forth; and the expiation therein is this very same austerity in the case of a false accusation, such as "if at the time of the offering the *prāṇa* [is obstructed], the *udāna*...
and so on. (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 21... Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, 15th Praśna).

On this point, Stamba says: "If either the Gārhapatya or the Āhavanīya fire should go out, it must be churned from these very embers. Bharadvāja also says: "Whichever of the two fires should go out, it must be churned from those very pieces of wood," and so forth. Likewise, Āpastamba states regarding one who has fuel of dung (*śakaidha*) and fuel of grass (*tṛṇaidha*): "Śakaidha" refers to one whose fuel consists of dried cow-dung (*karīṣa*); similarly, "tṛṇaidha" refers to one whose fuel consists of grass.

Even when the fire has subsided in fuel such as that of the Śaka tree, it should be produced by rubbing the two kindling sticks (araṇī) together with ashes; the sense is that these too possess the capacity for being churned. || 11 ||

Or, at the place where the desired [deities] follow, he offers these oblations: "To Mitra, Svāhā! To Varuṇa, Svāhā! To Soma, Svāhā! To Sūrya, Svāhā! To Agni, the ascetic, the lord of creatures, the purifier, Svāhā! To Agni, the pure, Svāhā! To Agni, the luminous, Svāhā! To Agni, the lord of vows, Svāhā!"—with the *vyāhṛtis* both separately and combined. (Section 10, Sutra 12)

This option applies to every *anugateṣṭi* (expiatory sacrifice for an omission), because of the repeated mention of the term *anugateṣṭi*. Otherwise, he would have simply said, "Or rather, these oblations. Likewise, Āśvalāyana states that there is inclusion for all *prāyaścittaiṣṭis*: "Or rather, it is known that one should offer a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) to each respective deity in place of the *prāyaścittaiṣṭis*. And the Ṛgvedic schools study those very sacrifices as their primary subject matter.
Now, according to some, it is understood that if the Āhavanīya fire should go out before the time for the Agnihotra, one should bring forth another.

Some believe that by the word "ahuta" (unoffered), there is a sublation of the entire [ritual]; that is incorrect, because of the difference in Vedic branches, because the intention refers to a single example, and because a general [sublation] is inappropriate. For if that were intended, he would have used the term "prātar" (morning) alone.

For indeed, when curd is intended to be given to one youth and buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya, there does not occur the statement, "Let curd be given to the Brahmins; let buttermilk be given to Kauṇḍinya"; rather, there occurs the statement, "Let curd be given to Māṭhara; let buttermilk be given to Kauṇḍinya. Thus says the author of the Mahābhāṣya: "A single example does not necessitate a general rule. Therefore, it is logical that [the rule] is for the sake of both times. Now, what is the time for the oblation?

But has it not been stated by the author of the Sūtra that the times for the morning and evening [offerings] begin from the appearance of the stars and so forth? Whichever of those times one offers in, that will be the time, provided it is before the time of the *vyoma* (the sky). What is the meaning? It means "before" the ritual procedure (*tantra*) beginning with the fetching of fuel (*idhma*) is commenced. And thus Kātyāyana, following the time of the oblation, has said: "If the Āhavanīya fire should go out when the vessels have been set down, one should offer in the Gārhapatya [fire], [reciting]: 'The Prāṇa has entered into the Udāna.'"

And what is the time for placing the sacrificial vessels? One should say: at the commencement of the ritual procedure (*tantra*). As Baudhāyana states immediately after the rule for bringing forward the fires: "Then he places those washed Agnihotra vessels to the north of the Gārhapatya fire. However, Vaikhānasa and Bharadvāja state it after the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*): [Agni 3, Paṭala]. [This concludes] the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 275.

"He employs the *hotṛ*-vessels. Therefore, from the time of the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) until the commencement of the ritual procedure, or until the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*pāristaraṇa*), if the Āhavanīya fire goes out, one should carry another fire forward; then either the *anugateṣṭi* sacrifice or the oblations to Mitra and others [are performed]. This rule is the same for the *añjaka* [fire-altar]; because there is no distinction. || 13 ||
If at the time of the oblation the *prāṇa* has entered the *udāna*, one should offer it in the *gārhapatya* fire. || 14 ||

The time for the *homa* has been explained in the preceding sūtra. In that context, if the *āhavanīya* fire should go out, one should offer an oblation of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*) into the *gārhapatya* fire for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), according to the rule beginning with "the breath" (*prāṇa*). Then, having produced the fire according to the procedure beginning with "if the *gārhapatya* or the *āhavanīya*," the *agnihotra* is completed as in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Thus, Kātyāyana states: "Having offered this oblation here, the performance proceeds according to the established sequence. There is no *iṣṭi* (sacrificial offering) for a fire that has gone out here, because of the specific statement regarding the expiation; nor is there an option [between different rites], due to the distinction between Vedic branches (*śākhābhedāt*).

It should be understood that by the rule "for whom the fire has been taken out" (yasyāgnir uddhṛtaḥ), the taking out (uddharaṇa) of this Āhavanīya fire which is to be taken out is also obtained. || 14 ||
If the Gārhapatya fire is the udāna, it has entered the prāṇa; thus [it is placed] in the Āhavanīya. || 15 ||

This has been explained previously. Here, the rule "for whom [the fire] has not gone out in the Āhavanīya" is not intended to apply; for it is prescribed that one should perform the oblation after having made the Āhavanīya alive. However, as for the rule, "Now, according to some, if one's fire should go out, one need not observe the specific time," that indeed applies here as well, because it pertains to all times. || 15 ||
If the Dakṣiṇāgni has gone out, and the Udāna has also gone out, [then one should offer] in the Gārhapatya fire. || 16 ||
Having thus offered the oblation, one should enter; in this manner, having produced [the fire] according to its source, it is to be established. || 16 ||
If all [the fires] should go out, one should churn fire, carry the Āhavanīya fire toward whichever direction the wind is blowing, and offer an oblation with the formula: "Svāhā to Vāyu! || 17 ||

If all the fires are extinguished at the time of the *homakāla*, one should churn the *gārhapatya* fire, place it down, and having drawn out the *āhavanīya* fire toward the wind, one should offer an oblation with the mantra, "Svāhā to Vāyu. Then, having re-established the fires in their respective places, the ritual actions are completed starting from the point where they were interrupted. However, Kātyāyana states that even for the oblation to Vāyu, having drawn it out in its proper place, one should offer it in that very fire; thus, if all are extinguished, one should quickly churn [the fire], draw it out against the wind, offer the oblation to Vāyu, and then perform the sequence of rites as prescribed. (1–7)

If they should travel in a windless place, he should churn fire, prepare the sacrificial fires, sit down to the west of the Āhavanīya, and himself drink the Agnihotra offering; for it is known that "this constitutes a substitute for the Agnihotra. || 18 ||
196. *Śāṅkhāyana Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[19th Praśna]:

If all [fires] should go out while there is no wind, then, having churned the Gārhapatya fire and established the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) in its proper place according to the rule, the sacrificer, having sat down to the west of the Āhavanīya, should himself drink the Agnihotra oblation prepared according to the prescribed rite. Since drinking serves as a substitute for the offering (*pratyāmnāya*), there is no further oblation. Except at the time of the regular offering, in the event of all fires going out, each respective fire is produced again according to the injunctions, and the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is performed accordingly.
But when the sequence is not understood, it should be seen as being according to the order of the fire-installation (ādhāna). || 18 ||
If he should offer the oblation after sunset, he should offer it again once the sun has set. ||19||

If the oblation is offered before sunset, there is a repetition of the entire oblation along with its constituent parts (*aṅga*), because that which is performed at an improper time is as if not performed at all, and because the time for the primary act (*pradhāna*) is also the time for the constituent parts. However, there is no repetition of the *praṇayana* (the leading forward of the fire), because it has already been performed at its proper time. In that case, having performed only as much as "having offered the oblation and touched water," one should worship [the fires] with the mantra, "May you two be of one mind toward us. The remainder of the sentence is "the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires," as is evident from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra.
If one should offer the oblation at the dead of night, one should offer it again at dawn. || 15.3.20 ||

Āpastamba also composed a sūtra stating: "The two [fires] attend [the sacrificer] at dawn; even the oblation before dawn is likewise [performed] for them; having performed the second oblation and the worship, one should worship with this very [verse]" (ĀpŚS 9.3.10). || 20 ||
One whose fire they should carry out from the fire [of another] should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Agnivāt.

If, while the Āhavanīya fire is present, one perceives it to be extinguished and then brings up another fire upon it, one should perform this sacrifice for that person. Now, it is not known whether this expiation (prāyaścitta) is occasioned merely by the act of taking out [the fire], or rather by the act of bringing it forward (abhipraṇayana), since the term "taking out" (uddharaṇa) is seen to apply to both. In that case, if it were occasioned merely by the taking out, then the expiation would apply even to one who, having taken out the fire, realizes its true nature in the middle and fails to install it.

In the case of the opposite, however, it would not apply; therefore, the distinction must be stated. Regarding this, Āpastamba says: "Āśmarathya holds that even if they should somehow lift [the fire] out, there is a penance. Ālekhana holds that if they should tether [the animal] before the fire has been formally deposited, they should follow it [to the burial], and there is no penance" (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 9.3.10). Whether the fire is carried forward or not, if they should somehow lift it out, this very penance applies; such is the opinion of Āśmarathya.

Ālekhana, however, maintains that if [the fire] were not yet established, they would bind it and lead it away; therefore, one should follow this fire once it has been subsequently extracted, for there is no expiation at all. Only a general expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) is prescribed for the extraction of what was not [properly] obtained. Since both these views belong to the teachers, the sense is that one may choose between them as one desires. Furthermore, this rule concerns the extraction of the fires, or rather, the portion specifically indicated by the injunction.

Because of the indicative mark that "one of these two has its portion not specified while the other does," when the fire—whose ritual duties have ceased—is taken out for another purpose and then extinguished, resulting in contact with ordinary (laukika) fire, only the expiation (iṣṭi) occasioned by that contact with ordinary fire must be performed, not the one occasioned by the taking out [of the fire]. || 21 ||
He should consecrate them with the mantra: "May you two be of one mind toward us. || 22 ||
The meaning has been explained. || 22 ||
[Paṭala 3] Accompanied by the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.

One should offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Agni Jyotiṣmat. If the fire, having been drawn out, should go out before the *agnihotra* has been offered, they say that one should light another [fire] and draw it out [again]; however, that should not be done. For what other [portion] should be drawn out when the portion belonging to [Agni] has already been drawn out previously? Having brought together those very same embers, one should churn [the fire] with the mantra: "From here Agni was first born. || 23 ||

In the *Brāhmaṇa*, however, having introduced the passage, "One whose fire, once taken out, should go out before the *agnihotra* has been offered, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.2.4), it prohibits the fetching of the fire (*praṇayana*) and, after censuring it, prescribes churning by means of the verse beginning with "From here, first. In this context, since the censure and prohibition of the fetching of the fire serve the purpose of praising the injunction for churning, the intention of the author of the *Sūtra* is that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between fetching the fire and churning.

And regarding this, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*): "Some indeed should pile that very [fire-altar] on the *uttaravedi* at the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*)"; we shall enumerate those optional alternatives (*vikara*) explained in the Brāhmaṇa. [The text says: "At the animal sacrifice, the Soma sacrifice, the sacrificial session (*sattra*), or when all one's property is given away"—this is the recollection of an option for the very animal sacrifice that was prohibited by the Brāhmaṇa. Likewise, one should observe such things as: "Having taken a portion of the curd, he eats of the boiled milk," or the reverse; and "the wife girds herself while standing," and so forth. And this is the injunction (*vidhi*).

Because of the statement, "When the Agnihotra has not been offered," [the rite] is optionally performed by all the previously mentioned rules pertaining to the time before the first offering. And because of the statement, "He whose fire has been taken out," it does not occur when the fire is unkindled. || 23 ||
One should offer an oblation with the verse: "Those thirty-three threads which have been stretched out. || 24 ||

"Then one should offer an oblation," says Āpastamba; that is, after the *anugateṣṭi*, one offers an oblation either with the verses beginning "mitra... or with the verse "trayastriṃśat tantavaḥ. || 24 ||

If a black bird flies repeatedly over the *agnihotra* while it is being destroyed; or if, when the *agnihotra* has been placed on the fire or the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) has been set out, a man, a dog, a chariot, a cart, or a bull should pass between the two fires; or if a cow, a boar, or a ram [should do so]—in that case, having sprinkled water along [the path], he should drive a cow along it [with the mantra]: "May prosperity increase; may the sacrifice release the lord of the sacrifice from sin through curds and ghee, svāhā! (25)

Some say [the animals are] a black bird, a dove, or a crow. A *dhvaṃsayaṃtra* (a collapsing trap) is that which, while being set, the Agnihotra cow steps over again and again; Āpastamba says this applies when she steps upon the *sānnāyya* (curdled milk offering) while it is being placed on the fire. A "man" (*puruṣa*) is one of the human species. A "cart" (*anaḥ*) is a wagon. A "cow" (*gauḥ*) is one produced in the forest. A "boar" (*varāha*) is well-known; some say it is a village pig. A "ram" (*eḍaka*) is a sheep. A "camel" (*kramelaka*). [Satyāṣāḍhaviracitaṃ Śrautasūtram—15th Praśna]

Thus say others. If any one of these, or all of them together, should go between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires from the time the oblation is produced until its offering, then, having sprinkled water along the path taken by the person and so forth—that is, having sprinkled water following those who have passed through—one should cause a cow to follow and lead her around on all sides; the meaning is that one should make her return by the same way she was led away. According to Āśvalāyana, one should make her pass between [the fires]. 25.

Having taken ashes from the *gārhapatya* fire with the verse dedicated to Viṣṇu, "Viṣṇu strode across this," he should sweep away [the footprint] from the *āhavanīya* fire and carry it out; with these very ashes, he also fills the footprint. He should thus obliterate both the track and the footprint.

One should sweep [the footprint] with a broom; one should make the two footprints of the husband and wife contiguous by means of a nearby space, or one should cause the footprint to disappear. One should destroy the form of the footprint of the man and others. One should cover the footprint with the ashes of the *gārhapatya* fire. Having offered six oblations with the verse "The ointment of the gods" (*devāñjana*), so say Āpastamba and Bharadvāja. (26)

If a cart or a chariot should pass between the two fires, according to some teachers, one does not fix a specific time [for the expiation]. One follows the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "O Agni, that first footprint which was placed for thee, thither thou hast extended thy rays; bring hither that wealth-abiding [fire] and unite us with thy favor accompanied by strength. Having led forward another fire with the verse, "Thou, O Agni, art far-extending, the beloved, desirable Hotṛ; through thee they extend the sacrifice," he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt (the Maker of the Way).
Furthermore, he should fetch sacrificial grass from nearby; an ox is the sacrificial fee. || 27 ||

Because it is expressed as a general rule (*sāmānyavacana*), this injunction is universal; however, it is set aside by the previous injunction regarding its specific subject matter. Likewise, the rule stating that "if a cart or a chariot should pass between the two fires, or between the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna*, one should offer a *pāthikṛtī* oblation as before" is also set aside by the *saumika* (Soma-related) rule, because that latter rule also pertains to a specific domain, occurring after the construction of the *sadas* and *havirdhāna*. Alternatively, there is simply an option (*vikalpa*) between these two, and no relationship of general and particular exists, due to the difference in Vedic recensions (*śākhābheda*).

And likewise, after stating the previous rule, Bharadvāja and Vaikhānasa state an exception: "If a cart or a fire should pass between [the fires], so say some; one does not fix a specific time. This same rule applies to a goat as well, because there is no distinction. Furthermore, it is taught in the Veda: "If a cart, a chariot, or a dog should pass between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires, what is the expiation for that? They say: "One should not take this to heart, for [the fires] are established within his own self. But if he should take it to heart...
Chapter 3: Accompanied by the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.

[Page] 299. One should draw an unbroken stream of water from the Gārhapatya fire, saying: "Stretching the thread, follow the light of the dustless realm" (*tantuṃ tanvan rajaso bhānumanvihi*), up to the Āhavanīya fire. That is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in that case. "As before" means according to the rule: "One should carry it from nearby; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is an ox. Thus is the meaning. || 27 ||
One should offer this very [oblation] when the stotra is confused; one should offer this very [oblation] when the śastra is confused. 28.

Failure to perceive a part of the *stotra* or *śastra*, or perceiving it otherwise, constitutes delusion (*moha*). In that case as well, one should perform this very same *iṣṭi*. However, if they remain unperceived until the conclusion [of the rite], no such *iṣṭi* is required. But if there is a failure to perceive anything at all, then after offering the *sarvaprāyaścitta*, that very same [offering] must be made by those who possess the requisite perception. || 28 ||
Or for one whose fires another should separate from his fires, or who himself should separate from them. || 29 ||

"One should offer this very [oblation]" is the syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*). The plural number in "with the fires" (*agnibhiḥ*) is used either because it denotes a genus or because of their mutual association. This *iṣṭi* belongs to one whose separated fires are interposed by another's fire—whether that other fire has been consigned to the hearth (*samārūḍha*) or not consigned (*asamārūḍha*). Some say it also applies to the person who performs the interposition, even if he is one whose fires have been interposed by a common (*laukika*) fire.
[One should offer] this [oblation] for one who has died among the people. || 15.3.30 ||

When a person has died in another country, one should perform this *iṣṭi* sacrifice in the house immediately after hearing of his death. Regarding this, Bharadvāja states an exception: "Some say that one wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) should offer a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*)" (BhārŚrSū 9.13). || 30 ||

For one who has died while away from home, one should offer his *agnihotra* with the milk of a cow whose calf is to be suckled, until his physical remains have been brought into contact with the sacred fires. He spreads out those *darbha* grasses which were pointing northward so that they point southward. Wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he milks the *agnihotra* cow and holds a fuel-stick beneath [the vessel].

The *abhivānyā* cow has already been explained. One should offer the *agnihotra* with her milk until the cremation of the body. Although that [practice] is prescribed for as long as one lives, nevertheless, by virtue of this specific injunction, it is performed; all other [regular rites], however, cease. Regarding the *bāḍacya* (the fire-pit), after describing the *mṛtāgnihotra* in this very manner, it is said: "Moreover, they say that they should kindle these fires for them without ceasing the offerings until the end of the bodies. In this case, everything should be done silently. Thus say Āpastamba and Bharadvāja.

Regarding the phrase "those which are directed northward" (*ya udañca iti*): this means those *darbha* blades used for the strewing (*paristaraṇa*) in the previous *agnihotra* rite, with their tips pointing north. The mention of "milking" (*doha*) is for the sake of illustration. One should wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) in all cases, because these rites are intended for the ancestors (*pitṛ*). That they are intended for the ancestors is indicated by the scriptural mark (*liṅga*): "He holds [the vessel] over [the fire] for the gods" (*upari devebhyo dhārayati*). || 31 ||
For it is known from scripture: "They hold [the sacrifice] above the gods. || 32 ||
The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [Book 15]:
The meaning is that [the vessel] is held above for the gods, not for the ancestors. || 32 ||
They throw earthen vessels into the water. || 33 ||
"Only the uncooked [food]," says Āpastamba; one should throw all [the remaining items] into the water. || 33 ||
They indeed give iron ones. || 34 ||

The meaning is that he gives or gathers the other sacrificial implements, as expressed in the passage beginning with "He is the giver, he is the gatherer," and so forth. Or, the restriction [in the text] is for the purpose of refuting the opinion of others, as Bharadvāja has said: "Of the son, of the bull, and of the iron [implement]. (34)
One should give the sacrificial implements to a Brāhmaṇa. || 35 ||

At the time of receiving the vessels, the wife or the son should give them to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas. From the very statement regarding the gift, it is understood that they are indeed to be used by the recipient as well. || 35 ||
The stone is indeed the mother of the son. 36.
The meaning is that the stone, the rock, the flint, and so forth, should belong to the son; likewise, Kātyāyana states that they should be "made of stone" (āśmamayāni). || 36 ||
If one should hear that someone who has not died has died, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Surabhimat.
Having heard that Amṛta was dead, and it being determined that he would not die again, they fell before Agni Suramitra. || 37 ||
If the sacrificer should die after the first oblation has been offered, one should pour the second oblation into the southern fire.
The completion of the remainder of the ritual, such as the subsequent oblation and so forth, should be understood according to the principle of the "oblation for the deceased" (mṛtahoma). || 38 ||
Or he should cause him to go to a heap of ashes. (Khaṇḍa 12) || 39 ||
Thus ends the third paṭala in the fifteenth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.

The meaning is that one should pour [the water] there where a heap of ashes from the fires has been deposited. ... Thus ends the third paṭala in the fifteenth praśna of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 15.4 Now begins the fourth paṭala in the fifteenth praśna.

If the clarified butter (*ājya*) that has not been purified spills, one should cut [the vessel] and a boon should be given; so say some. If it spills while being purified, one should cut [the vessel] and give a living creature.

If it spills after it has been purified, a multi-colored object (*citra*) should be given. || 1 || [This concludes] the fifth section, accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. || 381 ||

Regarding the phrase "he should cut [the animal]," the meaning is that one should give grass and such things for the cow, goat, and so forth to chew with its teeth, but not a young [animal]. "Wondrous" means captivating to the heart; "dharma" is the word to be supplied. Likewise, Bharadvāja says, "wondrous wealth. According to some, a "boon" (vara) is to be given; thus says Āpastamba. || 1 ||
Whatever may be abundant in his house, that he should give.
Whatever abundant and easily available items there are in his house, such as barley, wheat, and so forth, he should give those.

If [he offers] with "To the Lord of the Earth, svāhā!", he should place that [offering] toward the east at the span-length [of the ladle]. With "To the Lord of the World, svāhā! toward the south. With "To the Lord of Beings, svāhā! toward the west. With "To Being, svāhā! toward the north. With "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," upward. He either pours it together with the words "I pour you together" or consecrates it with that mantra. || 3 ||

If [the oblation] spills from the *sruc*, one should give a *puṣkala* [of water], pour [it back] with the mantra "saṃ tvā," and then consecrate it; thereafter, [the measurements] are by the span (*prādeśa*). Then, one should pour that which spilled from the *sruc* back into the *sruc* and place it back therein. If it is unfit for pouring back, one should consecrate it [with a mantra]. However, some say: when there is the consecration with "yadā tu devāñ janam agan yajñaḥ," then there are no [measurements by] spans, nor is there the giving of a *puṣkala* and so forth. And this meaning is explained by the explanatory prose (*nigada*) in other ritual manuals (*kalpa*). || 3 ||
"With the measure of the sacrifice—by its forward measure, its backward measure, its corresponding measure, and its upward measure—I encompass thee," with these words he encompasses it.

Then he takes up what has fallen [from the fire-drill]. Having divided it on all sides with a cut-off portion, he measures out spans (prādeśa) upon that spot in every direction. Regarding this, others say "therefore in every direction. A span (prādeśa) is the length between the thumb and the forefinger when they are extended. This is a supplement to the preceding rule, not a supplement to the entire procedure, because the latter is incidental. Therefore, the meaning is: "when the fire has gone to the three [sticks]. || 4 ||
Regarding the verse "devāñjanamaganyajña," according to some, he recites it immediately after the ājya [verse].

According to some, this is a *śākhā* (branch/alternative tradition). The meaning is that immediately after the clarified butter (*ājya*), with reference to the clarified butter, one recites the mantra for consecrating spilled clarified butter: "O gods, the sacrifice has gone to the people" (*devāñjanamaganyajñaḥ*). If it is asked why he recites this consecration, it is because of the statement immediately following that very [passage], and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the words: "having consecrated them as before with these [mantras], 'O gods, the sacrifice has gone to the people,' and so forth. Likewise, Bharadvāja states: "According to some, one should consecrate it with the mantra, 'O gods, the sacrifice has gone to the people' (*devāñjanamaganyajñaḥ*)."

This is what is meant: not only when [the oblation] has gone out, but rather in every case where the clarified butter (ājya) has spilled, consecration with the mantras "The gods have accepted the sacrifice" and so forth is to be performed; these [two] methods are to be treated as optional alternatives. || 5 ||
302. Regarding the sūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha:

"One should consecrate what has been spilled with the formula, 'To the Lord of the Earth, Svāhā! To the Lord of the World, Svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, Svāhā!'—this is heard as applying universally to all sacrificial offerings without exception. [15th Praśna, Section 6]

The meaning is that [the formula] is heard for the sake of all oblations (*havis*) without being extracted as a specific portion for any particular one. However, some say: "Of all oblations" refers to all oblations belonging to the *iṣṭi* sacrifices, because it is heard within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). By the term "without extraction" (*anavayavena*), they intend to express the totality of those very objects. Regarding this, Bharadvāja says: "Some say one should consecrate what has been spilled with 'To Bhūpati, svāhā!'; however, he does not speak with reference to any specific oblation."

And this statement, being general, applies even to those cases where something else has been stated following the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*); there too, it is an option (*vikalpa*) with that [other rule], according to others. Others hold that it is a combination (*samuccaya*), as in the case of "O gods, you have come to the sacrifice" (*devāñjanamaganyajñaḥ*) and so forth. Where it is not specifically stated, it is desired to be obligatory (*nitya*), as in "If one's oblation (*havis*) poured out should spill, or if what was taken for a deity remains unoffered," and so forth. No expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is desired when the oblation spills on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), for it is heard in scripture: "That which spills on the sacrificial grass does not spill."
