Regarding this, Bharadvāja says: "There is no expiation when the *barhis* grass is scattered; so says Āśmarathya. If it should reach the ground, one must indeed perform that expiation; so says Ālekhana. (Bhāradvāja Śrautasūtra 9.13). || 6 ||

If the potsherd should be lost, he should offer two cakes on two potsherds to the Aśvins and one cake on a single potsherd to Heaven and Earth. The Hotṛ priest is a Bhārgava; a one-year-old calf is the sacrificial fee. 7.

Āpastamba says: "Of those engaged [in the sacrifice] prior to the purposeful act. Now, if among those engaged in the ritual, a sacrificial pan (*kapāla*) should be lost or not seen before the purposeful act—namely, before the placing of the *puroḍāśa* cake upon the fire—one should then perform this offering consisting of two oblations (*dvihaviṣkā*). Because of the restriction regarding the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and because of its incidental nature (*prāsaṅgikatvāt*), one should bring as the Hotṛ priest one from the lineage of Bhṛgu who is already part of the main ritual framework (*tantrī*). And since there is no contradiction, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). || 7 ||

If it should break before the placing [of the potsherds], he should join it with the formula, "With the Gāyatrī of a hundred syllables, I join thee. Having joined it, he consecrates it with, "The Gharma is unbroken," pours water over it, then prepares another potsherd—either by grinding that [broken piece] or by making one from other clay to be used for the purpose—and pours it back onto the potsherds with the formula, "May the Gharma go to the gods. This applies if it breaks prior to the placing [of the potsherds]. || 8 ||

If a *kapāla* (potsherd) employed in the ritual should break, it has been stated in the *Āpastamba-śrautasūtra* that one should join it together with substances for joining and offer [an oblation] over it with the verse "The mind is the light" (*mano jyotiḥ*), because that verse contains the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of joining. This same rule applies even when only a single part is broken, as the experts in logic have stated: "Because the purpose is inherent in the whole, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) applies even to a single part. [Then follows the mantra: "Earth has gone to earth...
[This concludes] the fourth section, accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.

Because of the substitution [of the mantra]. However, the Brahman priest merely consecrates it with that [mantra]. Having placed another potsherd upon the *darbha* grass, and having touched it with the singular modification [of the mantra], and having sprinkled it in this manner, one should throw it in the place of the broken [potsherd] with the formula, "May Dharma reach the gods. This applies if the breakage occurs prior to the laying down [of the potsherds]. || 8 ||
Now, if one were to lay down the consecrated [bricks] with this very mantra. || 9 ||

If, however, there is a difference due to the subsequent placement of the bricks, one should place another consecrated brick with this very same mantra; this much is the distinction. Everything else, such as the joining and so forth, is the same. ||9||
If, while performing the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, one should drop an oblation over a potsherd, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.
Its status as a supplementary topic (prāsaṅgikatva) should also be understood from its inclusion within the body of the treatise (tantra). || 10 ||

One should offer this very oblation when a son is born; one should also offer this very oblation if, being a regular performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, one should let either the new moon day or the full moon day pass by.
This procedure has been explained by means of the Pathikṛt procedure. || 11 ||
One should offer this very sacrifice if one should eat of the new grain without having first performed the Āgrayaṇa offering.

It has been stated that one who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni) should not partake of new grain without having performed the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice; even in the case of transgressing this rule, this same expiation applies.

He who has established the sacred fires is indeed brought as an offering to the gods; the gods eat his food. If he should eat of the new grain without having performed the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, he would be eating a portion of the gods that has been set aside for them, and he would meet with ruin.

Now, by this, a censure of the consumption [of food] that serves as the occasion for penance is provided, for the sake of showing reverence toward the penance. For he who establishes the sacred fires (*agnīn ādhatte*) is brought into a connection with the gods; that is to say, he is accepted as their own by the gods who desire their share. Therefore, from this point forward, the gods consume his food. In that regard, if one were to eat fresh food himself without having first offered it to them, one would have eaten the first-cooked portion (*agrapāka*) which was ordained as a share for the gods, and consequently, one would incur sin.

Therefore, one should not let the prohibition against eating pass by. If it is indeed transgressed, one must necessarily offer this [oblation]. Having offered it, one should again perform the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice at its proper time, because this [offering] has eating as its occasion. Furthermore, regarding the transgression of the time, the *Pāthikṛta* and *Vaiśvānara* sacrifices have already been shown previously.
One whose twin sons or twin cattle are born should offer a cake on thirteen potsherds to Māruta. (Section 13, Sūtra 14)
"Two sons born of oneself, two cows, or two men—these should sing," says Āpastamba. (14)
A man born desires lack of virility; a cow desires lack of cattle. (Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram, 16th Praśna, Sūtra 15)

Vīrya is the power of procreation; āśāsana is desire, and by means of that, one performs its function. "Artha" would be indicated [as the meaning]. Thus, the meaning is this: when a man has been born as a *yama* (eunuch), he causes the destruction of virility, and a beast causes the state of being a non-beast. Therefore, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be observed. || 15 ||
The Gāyatrī is the invitatory verse (puronuvākyā), and the Triṣṭubh is the offering verse (yājyā). || 16 ||
"O Maruts, when from heaven... and "That which is your protection"—this is the Hotṛ's office pertaining to the Yajus formulas. || 16 ||
Some prescribe a cake on three potsherds dedicated to Viṣṇu.
He has gone. || 17 ||
One for whom others should perform a sacrifice with fires belonging to another, or who himself should perform a sacrifice, should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu.

If, through negligence, the officiating priests, being extremely inattentive, should perform the sacrifice in another person's fires, then this *iṣṭi* is for both the sacrificer and the one who possesses the sacred fires.
One should offer a *raudra* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) made from the materials of the site (*vāstuma*) where Paśupati might afflict the cattle.
For one whose livestock is killed by fever, there is a sacrificial oblation (caru) for the sake of its pacification; vāstu is a specific type of grain. || 19 ||
With this [offering], one should cause the Niṣāda chieftain to sacrifice.

The one called Niṣāda is born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother; another [view] holds he is born from a Kṣatriya. He is a chief architect (sthapati-mahattara). He is both a Niṣāda and an architect, thus "Niṣāda-architect. Desiring heaven, even he should sacrifice with the Āgneyī offering. ||20||

But surely, since a Śūdra is ineligible for ritual action, how can he have the qualification for ritual, and from where could he possess the sacred fire and the knowledge [of the Veda]? To this, he says:

"A black antelope skin, or a wooden block, or a donkey without ears is the sacrificial fee; or a deer, or a spotted deer, or a vessel of *śyāmāka* grain; or two water-skins, a winnowing basket, or a bed—this indeed is his sacrifice. (21)

A "trap" (*kūṭa*) is a specific means for accomplishing the purpose of one's own work by a *niṣāda*, whose occupation is the killing of wild animals. "Earless" (*akarṇaḥ*) means deficient in ears. A "hare-net" (*hāraṇapotikā*) is a net made of hare-hair, cast by *niṣādas* for the purpose of capturing deer. "Black millet" (*śyāmāka*) refers to black millet that fills a vessel; a "shaphaka" is a deer with hooves as broad as a handful. For she [the deer] was intended for that purpose; therefore, he has authority over her to that extent. And she alone is sufficient for his needs, even if it were to last for a long time.

The meaning is "he shall sprinkle. Some say this refers to the worldly rule; in that regard, one must not forget such [injunctions] as "the *havikṛt* shall run toward the *śūdra*" and so forth. || 21 ||
4th Paṭala: Accompanied by the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 305.
A student (*brahmacārī*) who should approach a woman must sacrifice a donkey as an animal victim.

This rule applies to one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and approaches a woman during the period of his student life (*brahmacarya*), because the section concerns those who have established the fires (*āhitāgni*). Alternatively, it refers to the well-known student (*prasiddhabrahmacārī*) alone, since conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is more powerful [than etymological derivation]. And the *Dharmasūtra* will state: "One who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*) shall sacrifice with a donkey according to the *pākayajña* rite. Nor is this [rule] purposeless, as it serves to provide an option regarding the deity. Furthermore, there is no inconsistency in the statement being made within the context of those who have established the fires; for it is justified as being intended to prescribe a Vedic performance involving a different deity.

Therefore, there is no fault even if [the act] is for the sake of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). This was stated by Bharadvāja: "Regarding the statement, 'If a student (*brahmacārī*) should approach a woman,' whose is this teaching? One view is that it refers to one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*); another view is that it refers to one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). In that regard, for one who has established the sacred fires, the penance prescribed for violating the wife of a teacher (*patny-ādi-prāyaścitta*) should be observed. As stated by the author of the Sūtras: "On the day of the vow (*vratya*), he either eats meat or approaches a woman; if the initiated one (*dīkṣita*) should discharge semen," and so forth. || 22 ||
He bakes the animal-cake on one potsherd upon the ground. || 23 ||

Because of the statement "not on a skull" and because of the absence of the statement "on a skull," one should bake the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) on ground that is devoid of the characteristics of a skull. || 23 ||
They should proceed with the portions [of the victim] in the waters. || 24 ||

They should proceed with the portions (avadāna), such as the omentum (vapā) and others, in the water. The performance of the fore-offerings (prayāja) and other rites should also take place in the water alone, because the subsidiaries (aṅga) must share the same location as the principal rite (pradhāna). They do not go to wherever there is water, as in the case of the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), because there is no scriptural injunction stating "having descended into the waters. Therefore, the waters themselves are to be established in the place of the northern altar (uttaravedi). In that regard, as in the avabhṛtha, the omission of those items whose purpose is lost (arthalupta), such as the [omentum], and the modification (ūha) of the mantras according to the specific requirements, should be understood. || 24 ||
It belongs to Nairṛta or Prajāpati; according to some, its deity is Rakṣas; according to others, its deity is Yama. || 25 ||
The word "donkey" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 25 ||
Nirṛti seizes that sacrifice whose oblation is burnt; when that oblation has been completed, one should then offer that very same oblation again. || 26 ||

"Alakṣmī seizes that sacrifice whose oblation is burnt or scorched; it should not be performed. Therefore, having made clarified butter a substitute for the burnt oblation, one should complete that ritual with the remaining oblations. Having concluded that, one should offer another oblation intended for that same deity—so say Āpastamba and Bharadvāja. Having concluded, one should offer another oblation intended for that same deity within that very sacrificial enclosure (vihāra).

One should sacrifice again with that very same oblation, beginning from the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*), and not with other [oblations] even if they are undamaged; this is the meaning. The intention of the author of the Sūtra is precisely that one should offer that same oblation. However, in the case of the burning of the two milking vessels, because it is a specific (exceptional) case, the expiation for misfortune (*ārtiprāyaścitta*) alone is desired.
306. The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—Fascicle 15:

The sacrifice is the expiation for the sacrifice; whatever may be left over, with that one should complete the rite. To whomsoever one hates, to him one should give that sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); thus one causes that very person to be seized by Nirṛti. 27.

This rule regarding a burnt *puroḍāśa* cake is an alternative to the preceding one. In that case, one should sacrifice with whatever portion remains after the burning. Regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) prescribed for that ritual procedure, Āpastamba and Bharadvāja state that one should give both that fee and the remnant of the oblation to someone disliked. By doing so, the departure of the "sacrifice-seizer" (*yajñagrāhin*) from that [sacrifice] is brought about.
Consequently, the very same sacrifice becomes auspicious and complete; thus, the sense is that a renewed performance of the sacrifice (*punarijyā*) need not be undertaken. ||27||
And if it should be consumed in any manner whatsoever, there must indeed be an expiation. || 28 ||

Āpastamba states: "In all cases of burning. This expiation for a burnt offering (*kṣāma-prāyaścitta*) should apply only when the whole is burnt; it does not apply when only a part is burnt, because that partial burning is unavoidable. As it has been stated by those learned in logic: "But in the case of a burnt offering, [the expiation] would apply when the whole is burnt, because the burning of a single part is unavoidable" (Jaimini Sūtra 6.4.17). || 28 ||
Or if he were not capable of performing the portions for the sacrificial offerings. || 29 ||

Even when not all [of the oblation] has been burnt, if the remaining sacrificial material should be insufficient for the portions to be cut off for the offerings, then it is desired [that more be added]. The meaning is that it should by no means be insufficient for the portions to be cut off. || 29 ||
If the oblation intended for a particular deity should be spoiled before it has been offered, one should then take up another oblation intended for that same deity.

The analysis of the compound is: "that for which there is a portion not yet offered (apratta) to the deity. Bharadvāja maintains that this refers to a "defect" (*vyāpatti*). Furthermore, this term is intended to indicate even unsuitability through destruction and so forth, and it pertains to cases where not all of the oblations (*havir*) are affected. This is because of the statement later on: "If all of one's oblations should be destroyed, burnt, or stolen... Thus, when such a defect occurs, one should offer only that specific oblation which has been spoiled, and not other oblations that were offered together with it and remain unspoiled; this is the meaning.

However, in the case of the destruction of that which has already been offered to the deity—even if the portion for the *Sviṣṭakṛt* has not yet been offered—there is no re-preparation. This is because of the statement "that which has not been offered to the deity" (*aprattadaivata*) and because [the offering] is no longer required. Likewise, Āśvalāyana says, "before the *Sviṣṭakṛt*. Similarly, regarding a defect in the cutting of the portions (*avadāna*), there is the rule: "one should cut again from the original source. In the case of the destruction of the *Sāṃnāyya*, however, only the *Ārti-prāyaścitta* (expiation for misfortune) is desired, because it is a specific rule. As he will say: "The mantras beginning with the taking of the *Juhū* [ladle], etc."

The corruption and destruction of those [substances] have also been explained by that very same [rule]. Regarding this, Bharadvāja says: "The expiations for the *sāṃnāyya* do not apply to the *āmikṣā*. If either one should be spoiled, one should proceed after producing it from whatever source is available. If both should be spoiled, one should proceed with other curd or milk produced with the *yajus* formula. Or, if the *vājina* is spoiled, one should proceed with clarified butter. (30)
In that case, the mantras beginning with the taking up of the *sruva*-ladle should be repeated.

A mantra by which the *sruva* ladle, the *agnihotra-havaṇī* spoon, and so forth are taken up is called a "mantra for taking up" (*khuvādāna*). The statement regarding the recitation of mantras at the commencement of all ritual acts that involve mantras is intended to provide an option for the subsequent rules.
4th Paṭala: Accompanied by the commentary titled *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 307.
(Or until the end, or until it perishes. || 32 ||

Until the end, when the *kaṇi* has been performed, if there is a failure, then only the mantras occurring subsequently should be employed. However, for those occurring previously, the assistance for the ritual is accomplished through a single performance alone; or rather, the very same [mantras] previously employed will be perfected as they recur through their respective functions—this is the sense. (32) But if the deity to whom the offering was given should depart, one should conclude the remainder with clarified butter (*ājya*). (33)

If the portion has already been offered to the deity, then one should complete the remainder, beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, using clarified butter (*ājya*). The meaning is that one should neither procure another oblation nor omit the rite. However, when it is known that even the portion intended for the deity was seen [as a whole] prior to the actual offering, then there must be a fresh production [of the substance], because the act of offering would otherwise be as good as non-existent. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says: "Or rather, there is no fault; for according to the Vedic revelation, 'the gods are not repelled by anything whatsoever. (33)
If all of one's oblations should be lost, or become defiled, or be stolen, one should perform the sacrifice by enumerating the deities with clarified butter (ājya). 34.

However, if in one’s various ritual manuals (*tantra*)—whether involving one, two, or many—the sacrificial oblations (*havis*) for all the deities should, as far as possible, be lost, or become defiled by burning and so forth, or be carried off by hair, insects, and the like, or stolen by robbers; then, having enumerated and counted those deities to whom the oblations were dedicated for the purpose of offering them, one should sacrifice using the *dhruva*-clarified butter as a substitute, exactly according to the original form (*prakṛti*), and not with the characteristics (*dharma*) of the *upāṃśu* [sacrifice], because it is stated that the characteristics of the substitute belong to that [original]. This is also indicated by the scriptural mark (*liṅga*): "The clarified butter becomes the characteristic of the animal sacrifice."

In the event of the destruction of even the clarified butter offerings, one should sacrifice again after taking it up once more from its respective source with the appropriate mantras for each. || 34 ||
Then he should perform another sacrifice that is not excessive; for a sacrifice is indeed the expiation for a sacrifice. || 35 ||

Now, when the sacrifice has been concluded, one should perform that very same sacrifice again, ensuring it is not redundant (*anulbaṇa*) and is unaltered (*avikṛta*). For when a sacrifice is afflicted by misfortune, the re-sacrifice itself is the expiation (*prāyaścitti*). In this regard, concerning the failure of all the oblations (*havir*), this same rule is intended to apply even to the *sāṃnāyya* offerings because they are supplementary to the sacrifice; the expiation for distress (*ārtiprāyaścitta*) is not required. According to the opinion of Āśvalāyana, however, this rule applies only to the invocation (*āvāhana*). Just as when there is a failure of the oblations, having completed the sacrifice with clarified butter (*ājya*) for the deities of the *el̥ā* verses, one performs the sacrifice again.

Likewise, with reference to the repetition of the oblation (*havirāvṛtti*), he says that there is no fault prior to the invocation (*āvāhana*). And likewise [he says], "even for those that have become entirely subordinate" (*atyanta-guṇabhūtānām*). Even for oblations that have become subordinate, if they are completely burnt before or after the invocation, there is a repetition of the oblation; the meaning is that there is a repetition of the sacrifice (*ijyāvṛtti*). || 35 ||
It is known from tradition that one should consume the defiled oblation with water. || 36 ||
But if the sacrificial oblation has become spoiled, one should throw it into the water. || 36 ||
Now, what indeed is this that is called "forbidden speech"? To this he says:
"That which would be unfit to be eaten by the noble ones—one should not sacrifice with that. (37)

308. *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[Fifteenth Praśna]: This is the intended meaning—the occurrence of unfitness for sacrifice. And that is the defect characterized by unfitness for the food of Āryas. One should not sacrifice with that which is corrupted, being a synonym for "defiled. "One should throw it into the waters," he says. Accordingly, Bharadvāja, introducing the topic that the waters consume the defiled oblation (*havis*), states: "How would the oblation be defiled? That which is unfit to be eaten by Āryas—one should not sacrifice to the gods with that. Likewise, Kātyāyana states that what is forbidden to the learned as food is "defiled" (*duṣṭa*).
And Āśvalāyana says: "Sacrificial offerings are defiled by hair, nails, insects, moths, or anything else loathsome. (37)

Thinking that "the oblation which is poorly cooked belongs to Yama as its deity and thus goes to Yama himself," one should stop the sacrifice, cook four *śarāva* measures of rice on the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, and feed four Brahmins. || 38 ||

From the mention of the *havir* (oblation), it is understood that this rule applies to the *caru* and *puroḍāśa* offerings, and not to other modifications [of the sacrifice]. That which is uncooked or improperly cooked is called *duḥśṛta*. Even if that is offered to its intended deity, having become the domain of Yama, it goes to Yama alone. Therefore, the rite commenced with that [offering] should be concluded with that very same oblation; then, having cooked four spoonfuls of rice, one should feed four Brahmins. This is the meaning: this indeed is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for this [fault]. || 38 ||
Among them, one Bhārgava shall be the partaker; to them an equal boon must be given. That is the expiation. 39.
The restriction regarding food based on the rules of Bhārgava applies to all eaters. || 39 ||

If one should sacrifice with a sacrifice that lacks a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), that sacrifice is defiled and does not lead to long life; a barren cow should be given as a gift—that is the expiation. 15.4.40.

When no specific sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed, if one were to perform a sacrifice without giving some rice-gruel or similar offering, that sacrifice becomes as if washed away or burnt; it is fruitless and, as it were, devoid of life. This is because of the Vedic revelation: "The sacrifice is long-lived through sacrificial fees. Alternatively, the meaning is that the sacrifice would become lifeless and detrimental to the longevity of the sacrificer. Thus Vaikhānasa and Bharadvāja state: "The sacrificer would become short-lived. In that case, one should give a field whose value is equal to the intended sacrificial fee. A field rich in all kinds of crops is called *urvarā*. (40)
If they should omit the prescribed sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and give something else instead, that [other gift] shall be the expiation. || 41 ||

Now, if one should perform a sacrifice without giving the prescribed sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), even in that case, the atonement (*prāyaścitta*) is the gift of a similar cow, and nothing else; this is the meaning.

(41) If one should invoke a deity who has no share [in the sacrifice], one should worship that deity with clarified butter (*ājya*) according to how it was invoked, either before or after the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. (42)

If one should invoke a deity not previously enjoined, one should worship that deity in the same order as it was invoked—that is, in the very sequence in which it was invoked—or else after the *nāriṣṭha* oblations have been offered. And because its sacrificial material is clarified butter (*ājya*), it is to be worshipped according to the rules for the *upāṃśu* (whispered) offering. This statement regarding the invocation [is made] in the context of the *nirvāpa*... [end of fragment].
[This concludes] the fourth section, together with the commentary known as the *Payogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 309.

This is also for the purpose of illustrating the taking of the oblation (*haviḥ*) in the form of the *upākaraṇa* (dedication), milking, and so forth, based on the Ṛgvedic scripture which states: "If one should invoke or take [the portion] of a deity who has no share. Therefore, having discarded what has been offered (*nirupta*), dedicated (*upākṛta*), and milked for a deity who has no share, one should proceed in this manner with clarified butter (*ājya*). Kātyāyana, however, says: "Having offered the excess, one may or may not sacrifice it, because it has not been enjoined. In that case, even if there is a mixed offering (*nirvāpa*) of both those with shares and those without shares, the abandonment of the portion belonging to the shareless deity occurs once it has been separated by means of the separation-mantra (*vibhāga-mantra*). || 42 ||
If he does not invoke the sister, or if he forgets her, he should rise up and invoke her mentally, and offer an oblation with the verse: "O gods, whatever we have overstepped. ||43||

If the Bhāginī offering is remembered before the main sacrifice, one should rise at that very moment, invoke [the deities] mentally, and offer an oblation with the mantra "yad vo devāḥ. If it is remembered after the main sacrifice, there is only the oblation; there is no invocation.

If the oblation that has been set out should spill, or if the clarified butter that has been taken should spill, a gift of a variegated object should be given; according to some, a boon should be granted. 44.

From the time of the offering of the oblation until the sifting [of the flour], one should give away living beings. Then follows the "Variegated" (Citra) rite. In both cases, the consecration formula is "bhūpataye. The remainder has been explained. || 44 ||
If the portion taken for whichever deity should spill before it has been offered, one should give as a substitute whatever is most abundant in that person's house.

"Taken for the deity" means that which has been cut off for the purpose of sacrifice; that is, [the portion] set aside. If there is an obstacle regarding another deity, there is either no sacrifice at its own proper time or no offering of the oblation. The passage beginning with "Whatever is in his house," etc., has already been explained. In these circumstances, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) consists solely in giving a *puṣkala* [measure of grain]. When a different deity is sacrificed to from an oblation belonging to another, or when the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses belong to another, one should give a *puṣkala*, then take a fresh portion from what remains and sacrifice again, because the entire oblation is intended for the deity.

Furthermore, according to the statement of Āśvalāyana, "In the case of a defect in the cutting [of the portion], there is a cutting again from the source," this same rule applies when what has been taken for the deity spills; one should consecrate it with "To the Lord of the Earth. However, if the substance taken is different, one should sacrifice after taking that very [other] substance. Likewise, in the event of an interruption regarding another deity, if the rite is remembered while it is still incomplete, the sacrifice or the pouring [of the oblation] must be performed at that very moment. But if the rite is already completed, then starting from the re-establishment of the fires, there is a renewed sacrifice for the sake of the omitted offering. || 45 ||

If one should transpose the two oblations, one should offer an oblation with the mantra: "May the mind, as light, enjoy [the offering]. (Section 15) 46. If one should transpose the deities, the portions cut off (*avadāna*), or the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, one should offer a continuous stream of oblations with these two mantras: "Thou art ours, O Agni" and "So thou art ours, O Agni. This applies in all cases where there is an omission or a transposition. 47.

If the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should transpose the deities—that is, if they should perform them in reverse order, such as first making the offering (*nirvāpa*), the invocation (*āvāhana*), and so forth for Agni-Soma, and then for Agni; or if there is a transposition in the cutting of portions (*avadāna*), such as first cutting from the eastern half and then from the middle—[this constitutes an error]. (From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, 15th Praśna)

Likewise, regarding the oblations such as "He sacrifices to Agni from the Āgnīdhra fire," "He sacrifices to Agni," and "He sacrifices to Agni and Soma," one should employ the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*; or one may employ the *anuvākyā* where the *yājyā* is not prescribed, or the *yājyā* where the *anuvākyā* is not prescribed; or one may employ both when neither is prescribed—this is the rule for the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* in all cases mentioned and elsewhere. However, in the aforementioned specific context, it is treated as an option with the previous rule. In that regard, if there is an interruption in the primary act, having performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), the performance again is shown to be as before.

When even a single constituent part has been omitted, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is considered incomplete; however, that which is capable of providing assistance is still performed. But a refinement of the substance (*dravya-saṃskāra*) is not performed once the substance has already been employed, because its purpose has already been served. Likewise, in a rite accompanied by mantras, once it has concluded, there is only an expiation (*prāyaścitta*); there is no further application of the mantra, nor is there a repetition of the performance from the beginning or until the end, according to the principle stated therein.

And so says Bharadvāja: "In the case of a rite whose purpose has been fulfilled, the application of the mantra is considered as already performed. And Brāhmaṇya has stated: "If there is an interruption in a Yajus formula, Śāṇḍilya maintains that there should be a repetition [of the entire section] in meditative recitation (dhyāna-japya). However, in the case of an interruption in a Homa-mantra, there is a re-offering (punar-homa), except in the case of those offerings where the mantra is recited after the act (pratinigadya-homa). In those cases, however, there is no repetition because the primary focus is on the sacrificial verse (yājyā). || 46 ||

If an oblation should spill outside the enclosing sticks (paridhi), he should say to the Āgnīdhra: "Draw this [spilled butter] together and offer it. He [the Āgnīdhra], having drawn it together with his joined palms, should offer it, saying: "May the sacrificer not come to harm; may the wife not come to harm; may the sacrifice not come to harm; may the lord of the sacrifice not come to harm—svāhā! He should give him a full vessel (pūrṇapātra). This is the expiation. 48.

If the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) should fly up or be scattered, one should place it within the altar (*antarvedi*) and address it with this *yajus*: "Why do you fly up? Why have you flown away? Being pacified, come here for the sake of peace. Becoming non-terrible and worthy of sacrifice, sit upon your own seat; do not sit elsewhere, do not harm us! Sent by the gods, be clarified with ghee and splendor; do not injure anything of ours. For the sake of the peace of our well-being and security, sit upon this sacrificial grass (*barhis*). With this *yajus*, he should consecrate it and pour an oblation over it. 49.

If [the vessel] should fly up from the potsherds or from the cooking pan due to negligence, or if it should break or crack, then one should take it, consecrate it with the two verses beginning "utpatīti," sprinkle it twice with clarified butter, and place it back in its original position. Only the invitation of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and the sprinkling of clarified butter are performed; the removal (*udvāsana*) and other such rites are not.
Having become [thus], the sacrificer prospers, for whom they perform this expiation in the sacrifice. (Section 16) 15.4.50.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the fifteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.

Having become [this], having attained prosperity (*bhūti*), he "prevails" (*prabhavati*), meaning he becomes a lord (*prabhu*) and the master (*īśvara*) of his equals. This demonstration of encouragement is for the sake of showing reverence. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the fifteenth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāpāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.
15.5 Now begins the fifth chapter of the fifteenth book. Now the expiations for the Soma sacrifice are declared:

"Men have generated Agni, the praiseworthy one, from the two fire-sticks by means of their prayers and the movement of their hands—the far-seeing lord of the house, the active one. By means of Agni, Agni is kindled. "O Agni, may your seven [tongues] and your mind, the light, enjoy [the offering]. Whatever breach there is of my mind, or whatever [breach] of my speech, or whatever [breach] of my heart—may this god Bṛhaspati fill that up with wealth. "May Viśvakarman, enjoying this oblation, extend this sacrifice together with its continuous threads."

Those dawns that have shone forth and those yet to come—I unite them with the oblation of ghee. *Ayāścāgne*, *tvaṃ no agne*, *satvaṃ no agne*. O Gods, may we hear what is auspicious with our ears; O Holy Ones, may we see what is auspicious with our eyes. With firm limbs and bodies, having offered praise, may we attain the lifespan ordained by the gods. May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the all-knowing, grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unharmed, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati grant us well-being.

The Maruts, whose steeds are spotted and whose mother is Pṛśni, moving toward splendor, have come to the assemblies. The Manavas, whose tongue is Agni and whose eyes are the sun, may all the gods come here to us with their protection. A hundred autumns, O gods, are indeed near, within which you have ordained the aging of our bodies, wherein sons rejoice as fathers. May we not [be separated from this]—thus says the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [in the 15th Praśna].

"May it not harm the life of the one who goes"—this is the verse beginning with "Preddho agne. With words, I approach the firmament, praising the sage of the hearing ear, the worthy of sacrifice; grant us that from which there is fear so that there may be safety for us; O Agni, ward off the wrath of the gods. Harness [the horses]; make Agni your god, in harmony with the fires, the most youthful messenger at the sacrifice.

He who is steadfast among mortals, faithful to the cosmic order (*ṛta*), whose head is the wind, whose food is clarified butter (*ghṛta*), the purifier, whose face is ghee, whose womb is ghee—Agni, kindled with ghee, for him ghee is the food. The rivers carry you, dripping with ghee; drinking the ghee, sacrifice well to the gods. O Agni, giver of life! O Agni, these [oblations]! O Agni, seven are yours! O Agni, may the mind, the light, enjoy [the offering]. The thirty-three [gods]—whatever flaw there is in my mind, Viśvakarman, I unite you; I unite Agni, enkindling you. (Section 17)

May Agni, being praised, protect us together with the gods of the earth who are worthy of praise; may Vāyu, being praised, protect us together with the gods of the intermediate space who are worthy of praise; may Sūrya, being praised, protect us together with the gods of heaven who are worthy of praise; may Viṣṇu, being praised, protect us together with the gods of the quarters who are worthy of praise.

May Agni protect this sacrifice with the *yajus* formulas, and Pūṣan with the utterance of *svagā*. May they protect this sacrifice, and may they protect me; I take hold of you, and do you take hold of me. With these three sections ending with "Svāhā," one offers thirty-three oblations in the Soma sacrifice when an expiation for an unknown fault is required. || 1 ||

In that context, those specific expiations (*prāyaścitta*) which have not been heard [prescribed] for certain faults constitute the Soma sacrifice known as the *avijñātaprāyaścitta*. This is what is meant: due to human negligence, laziness, and so forth, various other faults generally occur therein; yet they are not all necessarily ones for which specific expiations have been heard [stated], because of their diversity. Therefore, these oblations are offered for the purpose of destroying unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) faults. In this regard, the phrase "ta imaṃ yajñam" and so forth is to be supplied as an *anuṣaṅga* (supplementary addition) to the verses beginning with "agnir na iṃḍitaḥ."

Just as [it is said], "May these protect this sacrifice through the Pārthiva [bricks]," and so forth; likewise, "Agni [protects] this through the Yajus-formulas," and "Pūṣan [protects] this through the Svagākāra [utterances]. || 1 ||
Thirty-three sacrificial bodies [are assigned] to the Āgnīdhra fire.
In this case, there is no requirement to follow each preceding [rule], because it has not been so stated.

"O Earth, O Goddess, O Sinīvālī, O Urandhrā; may thy mind and thy thought be wide-expanded. With these words, he offers seven oblations into the *vasatīvarī* waters, or into the *savanīya* waters when they have been poured out.
(Soma, Paṭala 5, with the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī, Section 3.13).

Having consecrated [the ghee] with the mantra: "Thou art the clarified butter; thou art the oblation of the oblation, the light of lights; ye are the portion of all the gods," he should pour [the water] together while reciting these seven verses: "May the Maruts pour you together, may Indra, may Bṛhaspati; may this Agni pour you together with life and with strength; may he bestow upon me full vitality. And [he should recite]: "The gentle ones, the roaring ones," "The waters are auspicious," "From the beginning I behold," "O Waters, you are indeed the source of happiness," "That most auspicious sap of yours, for that we come unto you. With these seven, he should either pour the water together or consecrate [the ghee] with them. || 4 ||

On each step, there is one oblation. "Bhuvo vivaste" is the seventh [verse]. When the *savanīya* grains have been scattered, or when they have fallen away while being scattered, he should pour them back together and offer them again. But when they are no longer fit to be taken up, then he should consecrate them with a mantra. || 3 || 4 ||
If at the morning pressing some Soma should remain over before the oblation, they should pour it out into the cups or offer it as an additional libation.

If, before the *yoma* at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), they should see [the Soma] remaining in the jars and other vessels, one should pour it into the cups (*camasa*). Or, by means of the *pariplava* ladle and so forth, one should offer it until the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*. However, the secondary offerings (*upahoma*) are performed after that; even if the [main] oblation is not seen, they are offered as long as the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* is reached, because the time for the secondary offerings has not yet passed. And the phrase "before the *yoma*" is understood to refer to the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* offering. || 5 ||
When the oblation has been offered, they should leave the remainder and perform the Stotra and Śastra; that is the expiation. 6.
When the oblation, together with the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*, has been completed, he should then perform the Soma sacrifice accompanied by the *stotra* and *śastra*.
Having drawn the cups, with the Hotṛ’s cup as the principal one, he introduces the Bṛhat-stotra. || 7 ||

The spreading [of the grass] for the cups is from what is left over. Here, because of the statement that "he brings forth the cups," the rule regarding the leftover applies only when there is an excess of Soma sufficient for the entire set of cups; otherwise, it is established that it would merely be the rule for the *aniṃ-nara* and so forth. However, some perform the rule for the leftover even upon the excess of a single oblation, having increased the *ekadhana* waters. || 7 ||
They should chant the praises with the verses containing the word "dhayat," beginning with "gaur dhayati marutām. || 8 ||
The fifth [section], "The Annastobha Portion," has been shown precisely in the injunction regarding the office of the Brahman priest.
Saying, "This Soma has been pressed," they should praise with these verses addressed to Indra and Viṣṇu while the Hotṛ is present.
1. Regarding the reading "paśyet": In these [verses] they should chant the Stotra; not with either of the other two Sāmans. Or else, [they may chant] the Aindraviṣṇavī [verse] at the Agnihotra. 9.
The Hotṛ recites the Aindrāvaiṣṇava hymn. || 15.5.10 ||
He has gone. || 10 ||
This very same expiation applies when there is an excess at the midday pressing. ||11||
If one should see an excess at the midday pressing, this same expiation applies. || 11 ||

With the verse "Great indeed art thou, O Sūrya," they should chant with the Bṛhat Gaurīvita among the Saura hymns. This very same expiation applies when there is an excess at the third pressing. They should chant with the Bṛhat Gaurīvita among the Vaiṣṇava hymns containing the word "Śipiviṣṭa. || 12 ||
Āpastamba says that there is a modification in the *stotra*.
If the Soma should remain over at the Agniṣṭoma, one should perform the Ukthya.

In the third pressing as well, if [the sun] is seen before the *vyoma* [verse], that same procedure for pouring up (*abhyunnayana*) or the subsidiary offering (*upahoma*) is performed. But if it is seen after the oblation has been offered, and if the sacrifice is an *agniṣṭoma*, one should make it an *ukthya*. Therein, having taken the surplus juice to the *āhavanīya* fire and established a stream as in the archetype, he draws the *ukthya* cup from the vessel. Then, the fivefold rite beginning with "of the *ekadhana* waters according to the purpose" is performed. However, the intervals for the cups and the hundred-fold *kāra* are omitted, because of the scriptural statement: "They look at the cups while they are being poured."

Then, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is extended from "He performs the *ukthya* extraction like the morning pressing" up to "O Unnetṛ, [take] the entire *rājāna* [Soma]"; and in the *stotras*, the *stomabhāga* verses are exactly as in the *ukthya*. However, there is no repetition of the twelve-fold hymn-form (*dvādaśa-stoma*), because of the injunction that it is an *ukthya*.
If [the sacrifice] is an Ukthya, [he takes] the Ṣoḍaśin; if it is a Ṣoḍaśin, the Atirātra; if it is an Atirātra, [the Dvirātra]; if it is a Dvirātra, [only] one stotra. ||14||

The phrase "it should be performed" is to be supplied [to the statement] "it remains over at the third pressing. And the entire performance for these [sacrifices], beginning with the drawing of the cups (*graha*), is to be understood as being like that of the *ukthya*. "Only one stotra" means that even at the third pressing, there is only one stotra, just as in the other pressings; it does not mean that there is a subsequent *ṛtu* (seasonal sacrifice). On this point, the author of the Sūtra, following another Vedic branch (*śākhā*), has stated that when an *atirātra* is exceeded, a *dvirātra* (two-night sacrifice) follows, and beyond that, a single-stotra sacrifice. In the *Taittirīyaka*, however, even when an *atirātra* is exceeded, only a single-stotra sacrifice is prescribed.

"That which remains over at the Atirātra is indeed difficult to comprehend," and so forth. This very point has been handed down by the Chāndoga reciters and is approved by the respective authors of the Kalpasūtras. However, the specific textual citations are not written here for fear of prolixity. Therefore, even when there is an excess [of stotras] at the Atirātra, it is appropriate to optionally employ a single stotra. Kātyāyana, having stated that there is a single stotra in that case, says: "Or rather, it is the Aptoryāma. Furthermore, the author of the Upagrantha states that in the Aptoryāma as well, there is indeed only a single stotra.

"Furthermore, in the Atirātra, one should employ only the *gaurikīta* [verses] among those containing the word *śipiviṣṭa*. Now, regarding the *vikṛti* (modified) one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*), the rule for the surplus [stotras] should be understood as being exactly as stated for their respective *prakṛti* (archetype). However, regarding the Vājapeya, the author of the *Upagrantha* has mentioned only a single stotra. Likewise, it is said: "In those [cases], one should perform either the *bṛhannidhana* or the *jumma*. Here, however, Baudhāyana explains the favoring of this entire rule for the surplus of Soma: "Just as for whomsoever there is [surplus] in the morning pressing... [End of fragment].
[This concludes the section from] the *Mayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. Page 315.

Having stated this and other such points according to the Brāhmaṇa, he says: "Thus, when the Chāndogas are desiring [the Soma] during the Bahiṣpavamāna, if they should not desire it, then at the morning pressing, one considers a vessel to be left over for the King (Soma) who has been surpassed. Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa over that [vessel], he holds it underneath; he causes it to flow down over it. As it flows down over it, it becomes entirely Āgrayaṇa. Having uttered the *abhihiṃkāra* over it three times and wiped it around, he sets it down."

Likewise, having stated this very same procedure without modification for the midday pressing as well, [the text] says: "At the third pressing, when there is a surplus, one causes the *hāriyojana* cup alone to overflow here; for no further drawing [of soma] is prescribed. Kātyāyana also says: "Some [hold that] there is a mixing together of what remains from the previous pressing with the subsequent one; desiring that [surplus], it overflows, according to the Śruti. If [the surplus] is from the third pressing, the offering is made after pouring it into the *hāriyojana* cup. As for those [remnants] mixed with the *ṛjīṣa*, their disposal is into the waters."

Now, when according to the opinion of the author of the Sūtra a *dvirātra* sacrifice is performed as an *atirātra*, then the first day should be concluded with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, and the second day should be performed as an *atirātra*. This is because the *ahīna* sacrifices follow the *atirātra* pattern, and because the *dvirātra* sacrifices have the *vyuṣṭi-dvirātra* as their archetype (*prakṛti*). In this same way, other *ahīna* characteristics and *dvirātra* characteristics are to be understood according to their respective archetypes. || 14 ||
In that case, they should chant with the Bṛhat Sāman or the Gaurīvita Sāman over verses addressed to Viṣṇu containing the word *śipiviṣṭa*.
The *tājyasavanika* [chant] is in the *ekastona* [meter]. || 15 ||

If two Soma sacrifices should be performed together, having offered the first four *saṃbhārayajus* formulas, one should commence the *prātaranuvāka* at the great night. When that has been commenced and it is said, "Come, O sacrificer," while the sacrificer has taken hold [of him], one should offer before the morning pressing with the formula: "For lying down, for sitting down, for the overcoming of the Gāyatrī, svāhā! (16)

If there should be a common *sutyā* for two Soma sacrifices, then at the beginning of the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), while the [fire] is being awakened, the Adhvaryu, having recited four *saṃbhārayajus* formulas, performs the commencement of the *prātaranuvāka* at the time of awakening, while the sacrificer maintains contact with him through the sacrificial formulas (*yajurbhiḥ*).

Having offered the four subsequent *saṃbhārayajus* formulas, one should offer them before the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*) with the formula: "To lying down, to sitting down, to the Triṣṭubh, to victory—Svāhā! Having offered the four subsequent *saṃbhārayajus* formulas, one should offer them before the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) with the formula: "To lying down, to sitting down, to the Jagatī, to victory—Svāhā! [The subsequent four *saṃbhārayajus*... Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, Book 16, Chapter on Agni...]

Having offered the *yajus* formulas, he should offer before the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice with the words: "To lying down, to sitting down, to the *paṅkti*, to victory—Svāhā! When the fire is kindled, two oblations are offered with the words: "O out-breath and in-breath, protect me from death; O out-breath and in-breath, do not abandon me. (17)

Thus, at the beginning of each pressing (*savana*), one performs with the four successive *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas; with the next [set], together with the *paṅkti* meter, for the subsequent [pressing]. The sacrifice has five pressings. Āpastamba states: "There are three pressings, the *avabhṛtha*, and the *anūbandhya*" (ĀpŚS 14.7.3). However, there are five [elements] according to the Yajurvedic tradition: the morning pressing beginning with "O Agni, lead us," the midday pressing beginning with the pressing of the Soma, the commencement of the *āditya-graha*, the *avabhṛtha*, and the *anūbandhya*.

The *antya-saṃbhāra-yajus* is employed; each individual *chandas* is [recited]. "The out-breath and in-breath are offered into the two kindling woods"—having performed the recitation (*japa*) of the *vanaspati* formula, [one offers]. || 17 ||
Before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering of the animal sacrifice, he makes oblations; the introductory verses contain the word "pra," and the Ājya-lauds contain the word "pra."

Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering pertaining to the animal sacrifice, the Adhvaryu offers [the oblations]; according to Āpastamba, he mutters [the formulas]. The word "eti" is designated as the word "preti. These are the *ājya* offerings, beginning with that for the Viśvedevas. 18.
The opening verses (*pratipad*) consist of those addressed to Marutvat or Pūṣan. ||19||

The *marutvatī* and *pūṣaṇvatī* verses constitute the commencement of the *ājya* chants; that which is the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s* portion is the *abhivarta*. Both the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans] should be performed. This is the rule for all expiations involving the loss of a *saṃstava*. 19.

If there should be a *agniṣṭoma* Soma sacrifice further on, he should perform an *ukthya*; if an *ukthya*, a *ṣoḍaśin*; if a *ṣoḍaśin*, an *atirātra*; if an *atirātra*, an *aptoryāma*; if an *aptoryāma*, a *dvirātra*; if a *dvirātra*, a *trirātra*; and if a *trirātra*, [he should perform] only a single *stotra*. 15.5.20.

If it is an *agniṣṭoma*, one should perform the *ātma-yajña* (self-sacrifice) together with it, according to the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in the case of a conflict of rituals (*saṃsava*), following the regulations for the conclusion (*saṃsthā*) of that rite. If the conclusion were an *ukthya*, it would be a *para-yajña* (sacrifice for another). If the conclusion were a *ṣoḍaśin*, it would be a sacrifice belonging to one's own branch (*sva-śākhīya-yajña*). In the case of a *saṃsava* between Taittirīyas and those performing an *ukthya*, that excess should be performed as an *atirātra* within the *ukthya*. If the *ṣoḍaśin* were a *para-yajña*, the *atirātra* conclusion should be performed. If it were an *atirātra*, a *trirātra* (three-night rite) should be performed as one's own sacrifice (*sva-yajña*).

Everything is like the Garga-trirātra sacrifice. However, if it were a *parayajña* (a sacrifice for others) lasting three nights, then only one stotra would be increased; or, if there is an excess of one soma-pressing, there would be an increase in the *ukthya* and other rites. ||20||

Chapter 9 — With the commentary *Yogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. The *Abhijit* sacrifice should be performed for the sake of victory; the *Viśvajit* sacrifice should be performed for the sake of conquering the universe. It consists of all *stomas* and all *pṛṣṭhas*, for the attainment of everything and the securing of everything. The *Krośa* and *Anukrośa* hymns should be performed at the invocation of Vasiṣṭha; both the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* chants should be performed. The *Sajanīya* hymn is to be recited, the *Vihavya* hymn is to be recited, the *Kayā śubhīya* hymn of Agastya is to be recited, and the *Niṣkevalya* hymn of Indra is to be recited—one should recite these and perform the *Abhivarta* as the *Brahmasāman*.
"One should perform either the Abhijit or the Viśvajit sacrificial rite," thus he issues the command.

"The Ābhijit or the Viśvajit is [a sacrifice] with all the *pṛṣṭhas*, all the *stomas*, for the attainment of everything, and for the securing of everything," so says the Brāhmaṇa. In the Soma [sacrifice], there are those with both types of meters: the *vairāja*, the *śākara*, and the *raivata*; [the *stomas*] are the seventeenfold, the twenty-onefold, the twenty-sevenfold, and the thirty-threefold. Such is the characteristic of the Atirātra. Regarding the Viśvajit (which has all the *stomas* among the seasons), its recitation [is performed] with the hymn beginning "Mamāgne."

The *kayāśubhīya* hymn, seen by Agastya, should be used for all three libations in the *vaiśvadeva* [śastra]: one should insert it at the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*), after dividing it for the midday libation (*mādhyandinasavana*), and the *agastyasya kayāśubhīya* at the third libation (*tṛtīyasavana*) in the *vaiśvadeva*. According to the method of insertion (*anuproha*), this is their application; Āpastamba has stated that the *tāraśravasa* [chant] should be performed. One should perform the *krośa* and *anukrośa* chants according to the rule. Before the morning libation, he issues the call (*saṃpreṣyati*).

From the morning pressing... the *preṣa* for those reciting the *Chandomas* is "matāditiḥ. This is the *ājyabhāga* in the Viśvajit; that which was stated regarding the *saṃpraiṣa* applies to the *savanīya* offerings and so forth. 2.1.1.
He should be established as before; or, having pressed [the Soma], they should perform a more extensive sacrificial rite with the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās). || 22 ||

Alternatively, it should be established as before; that which was commenced need not be mentioned again regarding the pressing (*abhiṣava*). If there should be a Soma sacrifice of the *agniṣṭoma* type beforehand, then the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) should be brought forward. They should be more abundant than the usual sacrificial fees, or even more numerous than those at the *śakrayajña*. Or, [the fee] is as much as a chariot can travel on its way.

As far as the chariots can travel between mountains or across rivers, so far extends the *saṃsava* (the period of simultaneous Soma-pressing). There may be a *saṃsava* within the same country, or a *saṃsava* in different countries; however, according to some, a *saṃsava* does not exist between two parties who are not at enmity with one another. (Section 19) 23.

Because of the statement, "Indeed, [the sacrifice] goes from one chariot to another," there is no expiation for *saṃsava* (collision) for one who sacrifices over that distance between two chariots. Or, where there may be two mountains, if one goes between them, there is no expiation for *saṃsava*; such a person is called a *girikārī*. Or, if it is a mountain-splitter (*giribhid*), then because he is between those two, there is no fault of *saṃsava* there.

Just as a mountain is surrounded on all sides by great peaks, so too, where there exists a separation between various territories—even within a single kingdom—there is no need for a penance for crossing over. Regarding this, Āpastamba cites another Śākhā: "As far as the boundary extends, whether it be a mountain, a mountain-cleft, or a river...
[Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Book 15].

"If there should be an obstruction by mountains or an interval between two different kingdoms, there is no *saṃsava* [conflict] between those who do not hate one another; for it is stated in the *Kaṅkati-brāhmaṇa*: 'A *saṃsava* does not exist [between such parties]' (ĀpŚS 14.9.4). Furthermore, when one person is in one place and the other in another, there is no fault of *saṃsava* there. The fault of *saṃsava* exists only between those who hate each other. For those who do not hate, there is no expiation for *saṃsava*. This applies even to one who sacrifices within the range of a chariot's path in the world. (23)

If there should be great distress among those who have been initiated, one should kindle a fire on the Āgnīdhrīya hearth, seat a Brāhmaṇa to the south, place twenty-one barley grains and bunches of Darbha grass into a full vessel, announce this to the Brāhmaṇa, and then address the waters: "You are the Living Ones (Jīvās); revive this person N.N.! You are the Life-Givers (Jīvikās); revive this person N.N.! You are the Fully Reviving Ones (Saṃjīvās); revive this person N.N.! To which he should reply. 24.

If a fever should afflict those who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*), that sacrificer (*yajamāna*) must lie down in his own place; he does not perform the duties of the sacrificer. Having taken him up, one should lead him to the *āghī* pavilion. The mantra for leading him around—namely, *pari-pari*—is to be found in the *Āpastamba-śrautasūtra*. We do not possess such a mantra for leading him; rather, it is understood that the leading is to be done silently (*tūṣṇīm*). At the *Āgnīdhrīya* fire-altar itself, he performs the kindling (*upasamādhāna*), the strengthening (*balavatkaraṇa*), and the spreading of the grass-bundle (*pārastaraṇa*); he sits to the south of that bundle of *darbha* grass.

[He says] "śati. Having placed a water-filled vessel facing north upon the *darbha* grass in front of the *āgnīdhrīya* fire-altar, and having thrown twenty-one tufts of *kuśa* grass [there], three mantras beginning with "O you who are named Jīvās" (*jīvā nāma stha tā*) are recited. In the third mantra, one should utter the name of the deceased in the accusative case, saying, "Revive Devadatta" (*devadattaṃ saṃjīvaya*). || 24 ||
With the verse "yā jātā oṣadhayaḥ" from the Oṣadhi-hymn, he should sprinkle [the child] with these waters. || 25 ||
And having sprinkled water from a vessel with the foam of medicinal herbs, [he should perform the rite]. 25.

He causes them to drink these waters: "May those two, the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma [cups], drink your out-breath and in-breath; may the Upāṃśusavana [cup] drink your diffused breath (vyāna); may the Aindravāyava [cup] drink my speech; may the Maitrāvaruṇa [cup] drink your will and purpose (dakṣakratū); may the Śukra and Manthin [cups] drink your two eyes; may the Āśvina [cup] drink your hearing; may the Āgrayaṇa [cup] drink your self; may the Ukthya [cup] drink my limbs; may the Dhruva [cup] drink your life-span; may the Atigrāhyas drink your vigor. Thus he touches [the cups]. || 26 ||
"Moreover, they touch him," says Āpastamba. All touch him. He addresses him by name, saying "So-and-so," while facing him directly.
[End of] Chapter Six, accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. Page 316.

He recites in response: "May the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma [cups] protect my out-breath and in-breath; may the Upāṃśusavana protect my diffused breath; may the Aindravāyava protect my speech; may the Maitrāvaruṇa protect my skill and resolve; may the Śukra and Manthin protect my two eyes; may the Āśvina protect my hearing; may the Āgrayaṇa protect my self; may the Ukthya protect my limbs; may the Dhruva protect my vital strength; may the Atigrāhyas protect my vigor. When this has been recited in response, [he says]: "O Lord of Prosperity, grant prosperity; [grant] breath through the out-breaths, and out-breath through the breaths."
He offers an oblation with the words: "In the vyāna, place the vyāna; in the udāna, the udāna; in the samāna, the samāna; in speech, place speech back for him. || 27 ||

The Adhvaryu responds to the sacrificer; the Vaikhānasa says "the Brahman. Once the response has been made, the mantra for the oblation is "O Lord of Prosperity, [grant] prosperity. Having offered the oblation, one should touch [the cups] as before—so says Āpastamba. However, in the Bhāṣya it is stated that he himself mutters these two [formulas] for the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups. Then the Adhvaryu offers the oblation on the Āgnīdhrīya fire; the touching is performed exactly as done previously, but there is no muttering by himself. This ritual action occurs when [the fire] has arisen on the Āgnīdhrīya, but not previously. || 27 ||
But he does not administer medicine again. || 28 ||
From that, there is cessation. || 28 ||
If he should die before the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), they should perform the fire-avabhṛtha.

If he should die while setting out on the journey, but before the occasional rite (*naimittika*) has been performed, the cremation must take place by one who has not yet piled the fire-altar (*acita*), prior to the *avabhṛtha* bath. Once that occasional rite has been completed, however, [the cremation] is not [performed by one who has not piled the altar], because of the direct injunction. The qualification for the ritual belongs to the sacrificer through his father’s wealth; since he is no longer present, there is no purpose for which that [rite] would be performed. Others, however, say: "It is thrown into the fires," thus [it is] a *bāra*.
Or, having caused [the body] to go to the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) or having brought it back from the avabhṛtha, they should cremate it by collecting [the remains] with the sacred fires.

[One performs the rite] with the *avabhṛtha* mantras, specifically the *avabhṛtha* mantra itself. Alternatively, having led [the sacrificer] to the *avabhṛtha*, at the proper time for the *avabhṛtha* bath, one sprinkles [him] silently, brings him forward, and places the *vara* and the *unnetṛ* in front. Then, the duties of the sacrificer are omitted and cease. Having completed the consecrations and the blessings, such as "He desires long life" (*āyur āśāste*) and so forth, the sacrifice is concluded along with its auxiliary parts by means of his own fires. Those who participate in the *pitṛmedha* rites should cremate [the body] according to the local custom.

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that this same [procedure] applies even upon the departure (that is, death) of the wife, because she too possesses primacy. [Objection: The wife is a subordinate member (*aṅga*); therefore, it does not apply to her. [Response: Thus ends [the discussion on] the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*). 31.
Because this much alone is prescribed for a single-day rite.

But in the case of a multi-day sacrificial session (ahargaṇa), having said, "Bring wood! Burn [the body]!", they should extinguish a coal from the Dakṣiṇāgni fire or burn it with fire produced by friction.

320: ... [From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Book 15] Regarding the *ahargaṇa* (multi-day sacrifice), whether it be a *sattra* (sacrificial session) or an *ahīna* (non-session): having said, "Bring wood; burn him," the Adhvaryu addresses himself as the sacrificer. The meaning of the command is: "Burn that deceased sacrificer according to the rule; burn him and this [body]. Having taken embers from the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern fire) or by means of churning (*nirmanthya*), the cremation of the deceased sacrificer should be performed silently by the relatives (*amātyas*). Once the current day has been completed, others should perform the remaining rites up to the end of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. || 32 ||
He places the jar of bones on the southern corner of the altar. || 33 ||
"And for the sacrificer"—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. || 33 ||
The Udgātṛ priests should chant the praise with the three Sārparājñī verses as they are being responded to.
"The Udgātṛs should praise with the Sārparājñī verses," so he said; [they did so] with three verses. 34.

The other officiating priests, led by the Hotṛ, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītinaḥ), should proceed while reciting the Yāmya verses, chanting the Sārparājñī verses, tying up the locks of hair on the right side and letting down those on the left, while striking the right thighs—according to some authorities, the left thighs.

The officiating priests, led by the *hotṛ*, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītinaḥ*), having twisted and bound the hair on the right side of their heads while leaving that on the left loose, and having pressed down upon their right thighs; according to some, it is the reverse.
They should walk around the Mārjālīya fire three times, keeping it to their left.

They walk three times around the bones counter-clockwise with this mantra, "May [Agni] purify away our sin" (*apa naḥ śośucad agham*). Thereafter, they recite the *Yāmī* verses beginning with "Yama has established... and the *Sārparājñī* verses, because of the indicative mark (liṅga) in the text: "That which was praised, though not properly performed. They chant the *Sārparājñī* verses loudly with uplifted minds. Having bound their left hands and released their right, and having lowered their left knees, they perform that rite for women alone as a substitute with the same mantra, "May [Agni] purify away our sin," and then they proceed facing north.

This person, who places the stone as a boundary (paridhi) to the south of the sacrificers, recites: "This [stone] for the living... by the mountain," etc., having performed the sixteen-fold rites. In families where the lineage is not deficient, they perform the ritual of the day at the very same time as before—having awakened at night after the spreading of the sacred grass (paristaraṇa)—and carry out the ritual procedure (tantra) for that day as it becomes appropriate. || 36 ||
The cups should begin with those for Indra and Vāyu, or else with those for Mitra and Varuṇa; at the end of the Mārjālīya rite, they should pour the portions for consumption together. ||37||

They perform the sweeping together (upasamūhana) for the purpose of the Agniṣṭoma, because of its abundance; therefore, the Stomas are taken from that very [sacrifice]. Likewise, when expiations arise during the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, no other clarified butter (ājya) is set aside. However, some perform the purchase of Soma for this purpose. This Agniṣṭoma is occasional (naimittika); the principle is that others who have died have no entitlement [to it]. At that time, all perform the duties of the sacrificer (yājamāna).

The opinion of the author of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: in the case of the formula "This sacrifice is his," there is an omission of the purificatory rites for the *udgātṛs* and the *prastotṛs*, such as "He desires long life" and so forth. In the *agniṣṭoma* terminuses, in the *soma* sacrifice, the cups (*grahas*) belong to Indra-Vāyu or to Mitra-Varuṇa. In the *yāmya* [stotras], all the *stotras* are performed. While each *stotra* is being chanted, a jar containing bones is placed down. At the *mārjālīya* fire-altar, the portions for the limbs and the principal offerings are brought forward for consumption. || 37 ||
They should take "agna āyūṃṣi pavase" as the opening verse.

The *agna āyāhi* is the commencement of all the *stotras*. Regarding this, Āpastamba states a specific rule: "Their Soma sacrifice should have the *Rathantara* as its *sāman*. They place life-span within themselves; furthermore, it is known that they proceed while casting away evil" (*ĀpaŚrSū* 14.7.22), and so forth. This injunction for the *stotra* pertains specifically to the *Rathantara-pṛṣṭha* [rite]. When this concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja*, their fires are extinguished; having churned [new] fire, they complete the remainder according to the model of the *pitṛmedha* and other such rites, whether it be a *sattra* or an *ahīna*.
Starting from that day which was not observed as a festival, they perform all the rites for the deceased; this is the rule for one who is without a protector during this fortnight of Hari.

If [the sacrificer] is thus without a protector, those who have burnt his bones and bound them together—whichever of his own kinsmen is nearest—should initiate him in his stead and perform the sacrifice together with him.

This much [is done] for one who is without a protector, whereas for one who has a protector, it is because of the statement of the reason: "If he has a protector, having cremated him, saying 'Burn! Burn!', he binds the bones in a black antelope skin with embers from the southern fire, places them [there], and they are not seen even in that [fire]. Some explain that for the son of the deceased or for a uterine brother of the deceased who is consecrated in his stead, there is no shaving during the self-purification (*ātmasaṃskāra*). This is the procedure for him. However, those consecrated ones whose fires have preceded [the death] remain until the completion of the sacrifice.

Those fires for which sacrifices were performed by him remain in his house, and even his obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) are performed there. If he has returned from a journey, he himself performs the service to the ancestors (*pitṛśuśrūṣā*); otherwise, a representative stands in for him along with this [fire], while the other sacrificers remain as such. Those who perform the rites for a deceased sacrificer are considered other sacrificers. (39)

In the course of a year, they should perform the sacrifice for the bones. It is an Agniṣṭoma Soma sacrifice; the Rathantara or Gaurīvita Sāman is used, and the stotra is seventeenfold. As explained [in the ritual manuals], while the stotra is being chanted over the cups, he places a jar containing the bones nearby. 15.5.40.

According to the Śruti, "When a year has been completed, they should perform the sacrifice for the bones," the recitation (*japa*) and the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the patron (*yajamāna*) are omitted, as are the blessings such as "He prays for long life," which are implied by the purpose [of the rite]. However, the *dakṣiṇīyā* [offering] is for the purpose of securing the deities, not for the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*). In the *agniṣṭoma*, the cups begin with those for Indra-Vāyu or Mitra-Varuṇa, and so forth, just as in the previously mentioned bone-sacrifice (*asthiyajña*). But since the *mārjālīya* shed has not yet been constructed, the disposal of the woodworkers' tools takes place on the rubbish heap (*utkara*).

The bone-sacrifice (*asthiyajña*) is performed after twelve months have passed, having completed the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the *udavasānīyā* offering, the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya*, or the *maitrāvaruṇyāmikṣā*. This is the procedure according to the Sūtra-writers. According to the Mīmāṃsakas, however, one performs the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* and the *sautrāmaṇyāmikṣā* separately; just as those initiated for the previous sacrifice perform the *savanīya* together with the *satreṣṭi*, so too does he perform it. He should perform this occasional (*naimittika*) sacrifice when [the patron] has died. Thus ends the fifteenth book of the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha.

Because of the scriptural injunction that [the rites] last for as long as one lives, there is a cessation of the obligatory (nitya) rites. However, the Agnihotra is not performed on the day of death; nor is it performed for four nights, because of the scriptural statement that during those days the fires become "worldly" (laukika). This is also because of the statement of Anupadakāra: "Because they serve to protect the fire. Some, however, maintain that one should continue to maintain the fires. Based on the statement, "In a year, they should perform the sacrifice with the bones," it follows that they will not become worldly. Furthermore, even in the bone-sacrifice (asthiyajña) for a deceased wife, the sacrificer performs the duties of the wife while initiated, but not in the vicinity of the Ishti.
They chant with the Yāma Sāman; the sacrificial fee consists of one hundred and twelve [cows]. (Section 20) ||41||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fifteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra. [Section] 41.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fifteenth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin, compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.
15.6 Now begins the sixth chapter of the fifteenth book.

If, after being initiated for a sacrificial session (*sattra*), one should fall ill, he should divide the *soma* and perform the *Viśvajit* *atirātra* sacrifice, characterized by all the *stomas*, all the *pṛṣṭhas*, and with the gift of all his possessions as the sacrificial fee.

"For the sake of a *sattra*, for the purpose of a *sattra*. Having said, 'I shall sacrifice with a *sattra* devoid of [ordinary] sacrifice,' if he does not perform the sacrifice—based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that 'he who, having said "I shall sacrifice," does not sacrifice'—some authorities prescribe the *dhātavīyā* offering with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), as in the statement, 'Having said here, "I shall join [the sacrifice],"' which is obtained through the injunction (ĀpŚS 14.8.2). Āpastamba says: "That thousand-fold fee should not be given."* *(Note: The text provided contains a contradiction regarding the *sahasradakṣiṇā*; the commentary suggests it should not be performed, while the cited sūtra indicates its prescription. The translation reflects the literal sequence of the provided text.)*

Having been initiated for a sacrificial session (*sattra*), if one should desire to rise up in the midst of it due to a cause such as illness, he should take his own portion of Soma, consign his fires into himself (*samāropa*), and depart. Having gone, he should complete the rite from the very point where it was left off, according to the procedure for a *viśvajit* sacrifice. This is because of the scriptural injunction: "He should sacrifice with an *atirātra*, with all the *stomas*, with all the *sāmans*, and with the gift of all his possessions. Furthermore, for him there is no *agniṣṭut* consisting of seventeen [verses], precisely because of this rule regarding the non-abandonment of the sacrifice.
From the end-maker (Kṛtānta), one undergoes the fruits of one's actions. || 2 ||
*Kṛtānta* refers to Yama. The meaning is that through association with him, one undertakes the duties pertaining to the ancestors (*paitṛmedhika*). || 2 ||
Having scraped [the clay] from the ukhā with those [tools], one should prepare another portion of clay and fashion [it]. || 3 ||

"If he should stop at the consecration (dīkṣā)," says Āpastamba; "he should take the earth from the fire-pan (ukhā), mix it with other clay, fashion another fire-pan silently, and produce fire within it. (3)
Having drawn the heads of the sacrificial animals, he should silently apply them [to the vessels].
Likewise, having taken small portions from the five heads of the sacrificial animals and having attached them to the heads of domestic animals, he anoints them with clay and sets them down. || 4 ||
6th Paṭala: [From] the Mahādevaśāsti, accompanied by the commentary Yogacandrikā. 32.3:
When the Āhavanīya fire has been carried forward, he silently carries the fire [to its place]. 5.

"Once the fire has been carried forward, he should silently carry forward another; according to another view, [he should carry forward] one accompanied by a mantra," says Āpastamba. The phrase "once the fire has been carried forward, [the sacrificer] stands [there]" is to be supplied [to the sūtra]. The rest is clear. || 5 ||
When the fire has been piled up, there is no piling of the fire-altar at the time of rising from that [sacrificial session]. || 6 ||

"For one who stands firm in his duties toward the fire, the piling of the fire-altar (agnicityā) is not required; or he may pile the fire silently; or, according to another view, he may pile it with mantras—so says Bharadvāja. (6)

Having moved the sacrificial ground either to the east or to the north and having prepared the ritual space, one should sacrifice with the *Sarvapṛṣṭhyā*. This is done when it is impossible to sacrifice after having made the *āgūr* for all the *kratavaḥ*; however, in the case of a *sattra*, one should perform the *Traidhātavīyā* followed by the *Viśvajit Atirātra*.
Theft is the mental resolve [to steal], and it is also [the act] by means of speech; this is another [explanation]. The meaning of the Sūtra has been explained previously. || 7 ||

If the Āhavanīya fire should go out while they are pressing the Soma, they should lead it forth from the Āgnīdhra fire; if the Āgnīdhra fire goes out, [they should lead it forth] from the Gārhapatya; if the Gārhapatya goes out, they should churn it out.

The plural number in the phrase "of those who press [the Soma]" (*sunvatām*) is used because it expresses a genus (*jāti*), and not for the purpose of a sacrificial session (*sattra*). For the *āgnīdhriya* fire located on the northern altar (*auttaravedika*), the *śālāmukhīya* fire is the source; however, its kindling is by means of churning (*manthana*). Prior to the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) of the *āgnīdhriya*, the carrying forward of the *auttaravedika* fire takes place from the *śālāmukhīya* according to the rule for the fire that has been carried forward (*anvāhita*). But for that [fire], there is churning according to that same rule. Following the carrying forward of the *auttaravedika* fire, its carrying forward takes place from the *prājahita* fire according to that same rule. The *prājahita*—
