But for the Dakṣiṇa, Sabhya, and Āvasathya fires, the rule regarding the performance of rites according to their original nature applies everywhere.
One should make the two kindling sticks (*araṇī*) from that wood from which smoke rises.

For this very reason, it is said, "one should churn again. In that case, if the fire residing in the wood should go out at the end, one should cut that [wood], prepare two churning-sticks (*araṇī*), and churn. ||9||
It becomes a *kramuka* tree. || 10 ||
The fragments produced from the carving of bows and other objects are *kramuka*; among these, they serve as fuel. || 10 ||
He should give four boons to the Brahman, the Udgātṛ, the Hotṛ, and the Adhvaryu. || 11 ||
The four principal officiating priests are the Mahartvijas. || 11 ||
If they should steal the un-purchased Soma, another must be purchased. 12.
The meaning is that, in the case of theft prior to the purchase, the act of purchase itself must be performed again after the item has been recovered; there is no other penance required. || 12 ||
If it has been purchased, one should fetch it from whoever is nearest and press it. || 13 ||

In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, regarding the theft of the purchased [Soma] in the fifteenth book: "The one who is nearest" (*nediṣṭhī*) means the one closest in space to the Soma; having taken as much as required from him, one should press that very [person's portion]. This is the meaning. || 13 ||
One should give something to the one who brings the Soma or to the seller of the Soma. || 14 ||
To whichever of these two he gives [the gift] according to his faith—either the one who has now stolen the Soma, or the one who was previously the seller of Soma. || 14 ||

If they should not find that [soma], he should press *pūtīka* plants; if not *pūtīkas*, then *phālguna* plants; if not *phālgunas*, then *arjuna* plants; if not *arjunas*, then *ādāra* plants; if not *ādāras*, having brought whatever fresh herbs are available, he should press them. (Section 21) 15.

The *pūtīka* and others are specific types of herbs; the *phālguna* plants are specific types of grasses. In this context, both the *ādāra* and the *phālguna* are combined. Regarding this, there is a specific rule in the *Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra*: "In the absence of *pūtīka*, [one uses] *ādāra* and *phālguna*; and among those, whichever have white wool-like fibers. In their absence, whatever milky herbs there may be, or red *dūrvā* grass, or green *kuśa* grass—this is the *Vājasaneyaka*. At the very end, however, [one may use] rice and barley" (*ĀpaŚrSū* 14.8.13).

In that case, even the *ādāra* and other plants are substitutes for *soma* alone, and not for *pūtīka* and the like, because *soma* is the primary constituent (*aṅga*). Therefore, all those [substitutes] possess its properties and its name. The meaning of "green ones" is that even when nothing at all is available, one should press green stalks of rice or green stalks of barley, but one must not stop before completing the sacrifice. || 15 ||

At the morning pressing, there is fresh milk and *pūtīka* plants; at the midday pressing, there is curd and *pūtīka* plants; and at the third pressing, there is boiled milk and *pūtīka* plants. || 16 ||
The *pratidhuk* and other substances are pressed together with the *pūtīka* plants; the meaning is that the mixing (*śrayaṇa*) is not performed by means of the *pratidhuk* and the rest. ||16||
Alternatively, at the morning pressing he mixes all the Soma with fresh curds; at the midday pressing, with boiled milk; and at the third pressing, with curds mixed with whey.

In all these alternative forms of the substitute, there should be the mixing (*śrayaṇa*) of all the *soma* juices with the *pratidhuk* and other substances. Furthermore, those specific [substitutes] are to be combined with the original mixtures for the *maitrāvaruṇa* and the others. *Pratidhuk* is simply milk that has been milked [the previous day]. Thus says Bharadvāja: "The *pratidhuk* should be merely milk. *Nītam* means butter (*navanīta*). The mixing is performed either with that [butter] mixed with curds, or with curds alone. (17)
The Agniṣṭoma Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara as its Sāman.
Once begun, the season must be completed as an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice with the Rathantara Sāman, even if another final form (saṃsthā) or another Sāman had been previously prescribed. || 18 ||
One should give a single cow as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to those very same [priests]. ||19||

Even though, however, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) will be given to them at the subsequent sacrifice (punarijyā), the meaning is that they shall be given to those very same persons. And thus it is established that at the subsequent sacrifice as well, those very same priests (ṛtvij) are to be employed. || 19 ||

Either before the twelfth day or after a year, he should undergo initiation again for that very same sacrifice. He should give there what he intended to give previously; those same officiating priests (ṛtvij) should perform the sacrifice for him. || 20 ||

This restrictive rule is intended to preclude the appointment of another officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) on the grounds of the misconception that the sacrifice undertaken by means of a substitute is a different ritual altogether. This Brāhmaṇa passage is cited as an example to explain that it prescribes a renewed performance (*punarijyā*); furthermore, a renewed performance is inferred from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in another ritual manual (*kalpa*), which states, "one should purchase the Soma again. There is also a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*): "By means of the sacrifice itself, he desires the sacrifice."

In this regard, let it then be stated: how far does the preceding sacrifice extend, what constitutes the subsequent part, what is its time, and what is its conclusion? Āpastamba has explained all of this: "Having emerged from the *avabhṛtha*, one should undergo initiation for that very same sacrifice before the twelfth [day]. Thus, the preceding sacrifice extends up to the *avabhṛtha*. The subsequent part begins with the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [initiation offering]. As for the time of the initiation, it is from the previous pressing (*sutyā*) until twelve nights have passed. And one should undergo initiation for that very sacrifice whose conclusion is intended.

The meaning is that it was commenced previously. Āśvalāyana, however, has stated that even before [the conclusion], the sacrifice ending with the *udavasānīyā* is completed; as he says: "Having concluded the sacrifice and having departed, one should sacrifice again. Kātyāyana states the alternative: "Either having completed [it], there is a sacrifice again, or [it ends] with the *avabhṛtha*. In that case, one should give that same gift which was intended to be given in the previous sacrifice; one should give that very sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) which was to be given in the prior rite.

By the force of the statement regarding the excellence of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), this injunction applies only to the theft [of materials] after the fees have been distributed. Even in the case of the theft of *rasa* or *paśu* once the fees have been given, the rite is completed by means of a substitute. Likewise, this injunction does not apply everywhere when what was intended is obtained. Thus says Āśvalāyana: "In the event of obtaining Soma, one proceeds according to the original form. And so, for one who has purchased the *pūtīka* plants themselves and then finds those very same ones stolen, this injunction does not apply.

Likewise, this rule applies only when there is a total loss. However, if not all is lost, they should increase what remains by adding another portion and then press it. This entire rule regarding the theft of what has been purchased is intended to show that it also applies to the cases of its destruction or damage, because the principle is the same; for there is also the indicative mark (liṅga): "But when it is burnt, the expiation is that which [is prescribed] for what has been stolen. Likewise, Āśvalāyana says: "When what has been purchased is lost or burnt by the king... (20).
Now, if the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds should be consumed by fire, the Adhvaryu should preserve the *grahas*, the Udgātṛ the *stotras*, and the Hotṛ the *śastras*. 21.

The Adhvaryu priest should keep watch over the planets—those already seized, those not yet seized, those already offered, and those about to be offered; that is to say, he should remain vigilant. || 21 ||
If the Soma has not been burnt, they should proceed with the ritual according to the established rule.

"Having settled upon a sacrificial ground (devayajana) to the side, they may depart from the point where the ritual was completed," so says Āpastamba. At the conclusion of the sacrificial ground, the preparation of the altar and other such acts are performed either silently or with mantras, according to the principle previously stated. Likewise, Āśvalāyana states that these acts may be performed either without a specific ritual procedure (anāvṛt) or with one. The phrase "from the point where the ritual was completed" means that from whatever point in the rite has been finished, the rest follows the general procedure (tantra). However, in the case of burning down the pavilions such as the *prāgvaṃśa*, one does not go to another sacrificial ground. || 22 ||
If it is burnt, the atonement for that is the same as that for what was stolen.
But when the Soma has been burnt, that very same expiation which was prescribed for what has been stolen applies, beginning with the rule "whichever one is nearest" and so forth. ||23||
Afterwards, he gives cows as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); according to some, five boons.

Regarding the statement made there that "one should give a cow as the sacrificial fee," one should give five [cows] in its place. The mention of the bridegroom (*vara*) is for the purpose of obtaining the bullock as well. However, if the required substance is already available, it should be understood that the completion of the rite here also follows the original model. ||24||
If the pressing-stone should break, they should chant the *sāman* of the radiant Maruts; according to some, [they should chant] the *brahmasāman*.

If the *yāva* [wooden beam] should break during the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) before the *ṛc* of the *ṛṣabha-pavamāna*, Āpastamba says that they should chant with the *sāman* of the *dhūtāna-māruta*. Although its status as a *brahmasāman* has not been mentioned by the *Chandogas*, nevertheless, from this very restatement (*anuvāda*), an injunction (*vidhi*) must be inferred. || 25 ||
If the pitcher should break at the morning pressing, they should chant the Stotra over verses addressed to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. || 26 ||

This has been explained in the Brāhmaṇa: "If the *kalaśa* should break at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), they should chant the *stotra* on verses addressed to Viṣṇu containing the word *śipiviṣṭa*; if it should break at the midday pressing (*madhyaṃdina*), they should perform the *Sāman* having the *vaṣaṭkāra* as its finale (*nidhana*); if at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), [they should do] this very same thing. The meaning is that one should follow the Brāhmaṇa exactly as it is. The term "*kalaśa*" here is a reference to a specific part of the *droṇakalaśa* (the wooden trough), just as Satyabhāmā is called Bhāmā, or Bhīmasena is called Bhīma. "*Dīryeta*" means it should break or split. || 26 ||
If it should break at the midday pressing, they should perform the Sāman with the *vaṣaṭ*-call as its finale; if at the third pressing, this very same [Sāman] is to be used.
The final *bhakti* is the *nidhana*; they should sing that *sāman* which has *vaṣaṭ* as its *nidhana*, meaning that for which *vaṣaṭ* is the *nidhana*. ||27||

If the water-jar should break, some say one should perform the *brahmasāman* with the *vaṣaṭkāra* as its finale; however, for all [schools], it is heard in its entirety [without exception]. (Section 22) Having offered seven oblations with the formulas: "To Asu, svāhā! To Vasu, svāhā! To Vibhu, svāhā! To Vivasvat, svāhā! To Gaṇaśrī, svāhā! To Malimluca, svāhā! To Śūṣa, svāhā!", he says: "The draught of Indra has been taken from him; you are the foremost of the gods. I take refuge in you, together with the draughts, together with the cattle, together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), together with the Soma-vessels, together with the members of the assembly (*sadasya*), and together with those entitled to the sacrificial gifts (*dākṣiṇeya*)."

Having consecrated it with the mantra: "May I enter together with the sacrificial fees, together with the sacrifice, together with the lord of the sacrifice—with whatever is mine," [he enters]. 16.29.

One should chant the *sāman* that has the *vaṣaṭkāra* as its finale (*nidhana*) according to the *tāṇḍya* [tradition]. Likewise, when the oblations have been offered with "To *asava*, svāhā!", the sacrificer follows the cracked vessel with a mantra. This rule does not apply to the two subsequent pressings (*savana*s), because in the *Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* (14.8.25) it says, "If the jar cracks during the morning pressing," and because of the statement regarding the subsequent procedure: "at each pressing" (*anusavanam*). || 28 || 29 ||
"For the lying down, for the sitting down," with these words he offers at each pressing when [the vessel] has been split. || 30 ||

Āpastamba states: "With these mantras, at each pressing, one should offer five oblations when [the vessel] has cracked; so say some" (ĀpŚS 14.8.8–5). This ritual procedure pertains to all three pressings; therefore, it is an option in every case. When the expiation has been performed in this manner, one should smear the pitcher with materials fit for rejoining. Thus says Baudhāyana: "If it has become cracked, one should smear it."

If, however, one is unable to hold [the vessel], one should employ another person with a mantra and pour the essence into him. Regarding the procedure when the essence has spilled, Baudhāyana says: "In this case, he causes it to spill from the Āgrayaṇa vessel. But in the case of the *pūtabhṛt* and *ādhavanīya* vessels being cracked, having offered the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*), this same method is to be observed. And so, referring to each of those individually, Baudhāyana says: "If it becomes cracked, it smears it."

Likewise: "From the Āgrayaṇa [vessel] itself, he causes it to flow out here. This same principle applies when the Āgrayaṇa-sthālī is cracked; however, the production of the essence (rasa) occurs from the *kalaśa*. As it has been stated: "When [the Āgrayaṇa] from the *kalaśa*... (10).
If it were to be concluded without being chanted by all the modes, they should chant for the Hotṛ with six verses, and for the others with three each.

"If [the night] has dawned, then by means of the *rātriparyāyas*" (*Āpastamba Śrautasūtra* 14.23.12), says Āpastamba. In the *Atirātra* sacrifice, there are three *rātriparyāyas*, each consisting of four sets of cups (*catuścamasa-gaṇa*). If the night has dawned, then for all three *paryāyas*, they should chant the *stotras* intended for the *hotṛ*'s recitation (*śastra*) with six verses each; the others—the *stotras* intended for the recitations of the Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and Acchāvāka—with three verses each. Thus, a reduction must be made in all twelve *rātri-stotras*.
If one should cause the unstudied [text] to be recited by means of two turns—[reciting] one for the Hotṛ and the Maitrāvaruṇa, and the other for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin and the Acchāvāka.

If [the *stotra*s] are not praised according to both sequences, but are praised according to the first sequence alone, then they would be interrupted; in that case, for the sake of the *maitrāvaruṇa*, they would perform only two *stotra*s, while those for the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* and the *acchāvāka* would be omitted. In the latter sequence, it is the reverse of this. Regarding the middle and the last sequences, their status as "prior" and "subsequent" should be understood in relation to each other. ||32||

—328: ... The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha. In the fifteenth book: If they should chant for the Hotṛ with one [verse] repeated fifteen times, they should chant for the others with three [verses] each. || 33 ||

If, by some turn of events, the *stotra* of the Hotṛ should be interrupted before dawn, they should chant the *stotra* according to the original form (*prakṛti*) with fifteen verses; the others [the other *stotras*] with five. Herein lies this deliberation (*mīmāṃsā*): "Is this injunction [to be followed] only upon the apprehension of the break of dawn, or when the break of dawn has actually occurred? One should say: "Upon the apprehension. Why? Because in the Brāhmaṇas it is recorded as "if there should be a break of dawn" (*abhyudite*). Furthermore, because the mention of the *stoma* (hymn-form) would be untenable if it referred to a state of fixed measure. For the break of dawn is not of a fixed time or measure in all cases.

Therefore, the *stomas* would not be restricted by that [time]. Consequently, when there is dawn (*abhivyuṣṭi*), there is a reduction as a contingent rule (*naimittika*); it is not correct to say it is for the purpose of avoiding non-dawn. This has been stated by the author of the *Upagrantha*: "The *Śāṭyāyani-Brāhmaṇa* says 'at dawn' (*abhivyucchet*) itself; likewise for the Bhāllavins, likewise for the Kālāvins, likewise for the Taittirīyas, and likewise for all, it should be the occurrence of the case-ending [in that very sense]."

Moreover, if it were for the purpose of not shining forth, the *stoma* would have been unlimited; [for] they would have praised in such a way that it might not shine forth—this is what would have happened. For a limitation is not appropriate when the purpose is not to shine forth. By that mention of limitation, however, we know that this ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is indeed connected with the dawning; thus, they should make "O Agni, O radiant Dawn" the introductory verse (*pratipad*) of the *āścina* sacrifice. 34.
They should take "agne vivasvad uṣasaḥ" as the opening verse (pratipad) for the offering to the Aśvins.
It is known from the tradition:
"If the sun does not rise while the Āśvina Śastra is being recited, one should recite all the verses of the ten maṇḍalas; one should offer a multi-colored animal sacrifice to Sūrya. [35]

When the sun does not shine, being obscured by clouds and the like, then, after the *saṃdhi-camasas* have been consumed, a goat of various colors is sacrificed; and therein the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the *savanīya* is applied. The *Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* consists of ten books (*daśataya*), because it has ten divisions (*maṇḍala*). One says "the *ṛc*s of the *Daśatayī*, the *Daśatayīs*" because there is no distinction [between the individual verses and the collection]. He should recite those verses, even if they are difficult, as long as the sun shines. (35)

If the Udgātṛ should be cut off while they have started together and are proceeding, the sacrificer would be deprived of the sacrifice; that sacrificial rite must be concluded without a fee, and then another [Udgātṛ] must be brought in. 36.
That sacrifice is to be concluded with the Udavasānīyā offering. Then, at the immediately following full-moon or new-moon festival, that very same season is to be entered upon again. ||36||
In that case, one should give what one would have given previously.
The meaning has been stated. || 37 ||
[This is the end of] the first chapter, accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* composed by Mahādeva Śāstrin.

Now, let it be granted that these rules apply when there is a severance (apaccheda) of each one individually. But when there is a simultaneous severance of all three, or of two of them, what is the distinction? What is there to be distinguished here, since as many as have been severed, so many expiations (*prāyaścitta*) shall be combined due to the coincidence of the causes (*nimittasannipāta*)? True, they may indeed be combined; however, in every case, the expiation for the *prastotṛ* should be performed without contradiction.

But how can the expiations for the Udgātṛ and the Pratihartṛ be combined when they are contradictory? For it is not possible to combine the offering of no sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇatva*) with the offering of one's entire property (*sarvasvadakṣiṇatva*).

To this he says: "Those very priests shall perform the sacrifice for him. Now, if the Prastotṛ should be cut off [from his part], the head of the sacrifice would be cut off; having given a boon to the Brahman priest... 38.

When there is a simultaneous occurrence of a failure by both the *udgātṛ* and the *pratihartr*, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) applies to the *udgātṛ* alone because of his primacy, and not to the *pratihartr*, due to the contradiction [of their simultaneous fault]. However, when that [expiation] has been performed, there is merely the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). Now, regarding the expiation for the *udgātṛ*s when seven [of them] are excluded from the *pavamāna* [laud]:
"That very [sacrifice] must be performed again. (39)
That very [rite] must again be performed according to the procedure for the selection of priests as previously described. || 39 ||
Now, if the Pratihartṛ should be cut off [from his share], the sacrificer would be deprived of cattle; he should give away all his possessions at a renewed sacrifice.
For the sake of the seasonal sacrificial fee (ṛtudakṣiṇā), one should give away all one's possessions (sarvavedasa).

If both [the Udgātṛ and the Pratihartṛ] are interrupted simultaneously, one should perform the expiation for the Udgātṛ; for the Pratihartṛ, one should offer the universal expiation (sarvaprāyaścitta). || 41 ||

But in the case of simultaneous disconnection, the meaning is that the *udgātṛ* performs the expiation, while the *pratihartṛ* offers the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). Let it be so in the case of simultaneity; however, is this same principle applicable even when the disconnections occur sequentially? No, he says:
"In the case of sequential disconnection, whichever occurs later shall perform the universal expiation. (42)

However, between these two—the earlier and the later—if the later one is set aside, then only the expiation for that later one proceeds; for the other, there is merely the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). This is because the expiation for the later one arises precisely by way of subverting the former. Thus say the Mīmāṃsakas: "In a sequence of earlier and later, the earlier is weaker, as in the case of the archetype" (*Mīmāṃsāsūtra* 6.5.19).

This is what is meant: when the *pratihartṛ* is the one who is last [to fall], then the entire property (*sarvavedasa*) is to be given, but not a further sacrifice (*punarijyā*). However, when the *udgātṛ* is the one who is last, then there is indeed a further sacrifice; it does not mean that only the entire property is to be given in that very same ritual. One should understand that in that case of a further sacrifice, the entire property is to be given. Why is this so? Because in the previous ritual, prior to the disconnection of the *udgātṛ*, the [gift of] the entire property was already established for the *pratihartṛ* upon his disconnection.

In that case, there is also the rule that "one should give as much as was given previously in the [first] sacrifice. And thus say the Mīmāṃsakas: "If the Udgātṛ should be the last [to fall], one should give all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*) in the subsequent sacrifice, just as in the other case" (Satyāṣāḍha Śrautasūtra, Praśna 15, Kāṇḍa 5, Sūtra 20).

However, for those such as the Brahman and others for whom no specific expiation for a disconnection (*apaccheda*) has been stated, the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) alone applies in every instance. 42.
If the Udgātṛ priest should be the last to be cut off, one should give away all one's possessions at a new sacrifice.
This has been explained by the preceding sūtra. || 43 ||
If [the chanting] should be interrupted during the Ārbhava Pavamāna, one should offer the universal expiatory oblation (sarvaprāyaścitta). (Section 24) || 44 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the fifteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.

If [the fault occurs] during the *mādhyandina-pavamāna*, it is exactly this same [procedure]. During the *ārbhava-pavamāna*, one should offer the *sarvaprāyaścitta* (all-expiation) oblation once all [other rites] have been performed. Thus ends the sixth chapter in the fifteenth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.
15.7 Now begins the seventh chapter in the fifteenth book.

If the Soma should run out, one should divide gold into two parts; having placed one half inside the *ṛjīṣa*, one should pour water into it, and having drawn up the other half, one should proceed with the ritual using the cups (*graha*).

Having placed gold into the *droṇakalaśa* and having taken up the *vasatīvarī* waters, one should pour milk into them; that serves as the substitute for Soma. Therefore, for whichever cups (*graha*) or goblets (*camasa*) there is a drawing, after pouring half [of the liquid] into them, the offering is performed as before. ||1||
He should give four boons to the Brahman, the Udgātṛ, the Hotṛ, and the Adhvaryu. || 2 ||
The meaning has been stated. || 2 ||

If the Āgrayaṇa vessel should spill or be damaged, one should draw [the Soma] from the other vessels. If the other vessels should spill or be damaged, one should draw [the Soma] from the Āgrayaṇa, excluding the Śukra and the Dhruva.
[The cup] has gone. It is known that for the planets (grahas) excluding Śukra and Dhruva, as well as for the Kalaśa, the Āgrayaṇa is the source (yoni). Now he states another rule:
"He draws [the juice] from the Droṇakalaśa" is understood to apply to all the grahas that have been spilled or have perished.
[Paṭala 7] With the commentary *Payogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin: 331.

"For all the cups (*graha*), including those for Śukra and Dhruva, when they are spilled or overflowed, the *kalaśa* alone is their source. These four rules are applied as alternatives in various contexts. However, some—interpreting the phrase "for all the cups" as including even the *pavamāna* cups—assert that even for the *pūtabhṛt* and *ādhavanīya*, when they are spilled, their production is from the *kalaśa*.

That is incorrect; for by the separate mention of the *kalaśa* in the passage "whether it be the *rahas* or the *kalaśa*," it is understood that the *pavamāna* cups are not included here under the term "cup" (*graha*). Therefore, like the *kalaśa*, the origin of those two [the *rahas* and *droṇakalaśa*] is from the *āgrayaṇa* itself. As Baudhāyana says with reference to each of them: "He causes it to flow out from the *āgrayaṇa*. However, the origin of the *camasa*s is always from the *pūtabhṛt* alone, because they have that as their source; for all these rules are intended to specify a particular source.

In some cases there is mention of "spilling" (*upadāsa*), and in others mention of "falling and spilling" (*skandana-upadāsa*); this should be understood as being for the purpose of illustrating such types of destruction. Likewise, in all instances where there is a partial spilling of the *soma*, the following injunction must also be applied: "Having taken up the *soma* [again], one should offer it. However, when it spills completely, then one should take it up according to its source with its respective mantra and set it down. || 4 ||

If the *dhruva* ladle should spill, he consecrates it with the formulas, "Thou art the giver of life, O *dhruva*; give me life," "Thou art the giver of splendor, O *dhruva*; give me splendor," and "Thou art the protector of the body, O *dhruva*; protect my body," and then he bestows a boon. ||5||
He has gone. ||5||
If it should break, he divides the gold into three parts; having placed the first part down with the formula, "Svāhā! From heaven, swell up," he causes it to swell.

Having lifted the vessel from the *droṇakalaśa*, he causes it to swell. However, if it should be cracked or incapable of use, then having employed another vessel and poured the remainder of the contents into it, he causes it to swell. But if it has spilled completely, leaving no residue, it must be drawn using the very mantra for drawing.
"Oblation! Be replenished from the intermediate space," thus the second; "Oblation! Be replenished from the earth," thus the third. || 7 ||
The phrase "having held [it], he causes it to swell" is to be supplied by way of ellipsis.

O Gods, let this sacrifice be a holy rite for our plants, for our cattle, and for our wealth; for all that exists, you are the holy rite—swell with abundance like clarified butter, O God! Firm is the sky of the sacrifice, firm is the earth, firm is this entire moving world; firm indeed are these mountains, and firm is this king of the people. Remain right here, do not waver; be immovable like a mountain. Stand firm here like Indra, and uphold the kingdom here.
"Overpower those who attack; let the enemies be beneath you. Stand firm like Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, conquering the waters and the fields.

Having consecrated it with the four verses beginning, "Indra has established this... may he support it firmly with a firm oblation," and "To him the gods have spoken, as has this Brahmaṇaspati," he gives a boon. (Section 25, Sūtra 8)
When the *sanna* has been consecrated by the *adhvaryu*, the sacrificer gives a boon. || 8 ||

If the Nārāśaṃsa cup should spill, the Adhvaryu should draw the subsequent draught. Having offered it at the *vaṣaṭ* and *anu-vaṣaṭ* calls, he causes it to swell with the formula, "Swell up, O most intoxicating one! By this he makes it swell; by this he makes it partake of the consumption. || 9 ||

It has been stated that the *camasa* (cup) is called *nārāśaṃsa* once it has been consumed and replenished. If it should be lost through drying up or other causes, then one should offer the draught—such as the *aindrāgna* and others—which immediately follows the replenishing of the *camasa*, at its proper time, and give it to the *camasādhvaryu*. He, having set aside a portion for consumption, replenishes the cups with that [remaining portion] and shakes them twice; for the purpose of the replenishing is for that end.

At the morning pressing, he should consecrate the spilled Soma with the formula: "The gods have approved this sacrifice. At the midday pressing: "The Gandharvas have approved this sacrifice. At the third pressing: "The ancestors have approved this sacrifice. At night: "The waters, the plants, and the trees have approved this sacrifice. With the formula: "Heaven and earth have approved this sacrifice," he places the Soma that has been drawn on the previous day over the Soma of the current day. (15.7.10)

"Or the oblation may spill," says Āpastamba. "Oblation" refers to the *savanīya* and other such offerings. "At night" means during the night-rounds (*rātriparyāya*). "In the *tiroahni* [rounds]" means in the *saṃdhicamasa* cups. Because of this sequential enumeration, this rule does not apply to the groups of *aptoryāma* cups that follow the *tiroahni* rounds. || 10 ||

If the speckled butter should spill, one should take other speckled butter and offer a single oblation with the two *saṃhitā* verses: "The drop has fallen; may the mind, the light, enjoy it. (TS 3.3.11.4) || 11 ||
"If the speckled butter should spill," says Bharadvāja. (11)

If, while performing with the seasonal cups (*ṛtugraha*), the two [priests] should become confused, [they should recite]: "The rivers, having released their flow, dripping with ghee—spring, summer, the honeyed rainy season, autumn, and winter—may they be auspicious to us. May the two [months of] Nabhas dwell together, overflowing with water. May Prajāpati produce offspring for us; may Dhātṛ grant us the year. May the year, together with the seasons, the protector of the wheel, bestow nourishment upon me, O Lord of Nourishment. "O Agni, you are the guardian of the vows of the gods... [End of Paṭala 7]. [This concludes] the *Mayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. Page 333.

"O you who are [the guardians], if we should violate your vows—Madhu and Mādhava, the two seasons of spring—may they protect this sacrifice; may they protect me; I take hold of you, do you take hold of me, Svāhā! With these ten Ṛg-verses and Yajus-formulas, he offers ten oblations. After each oblation, he gives a boon. (Section 26) || 12 ||

Delusion (*moha*) is the inversion [of perception] regarding the mantra, the face, or the path. In that regard, one offers oblations with the five verses beginning with *visṛṣṭadhenā* and with the thirteen names beginning with *madhu*. || 12 ||

If the Soma should spill, one should announce it to the Brahman priest, saying, "O Brahman, the Soma has spilled! Then, having poured water upon the spot where it spilled, he should recite over it: "The god Savitṛ, who is to be praised, has become manifest; he is now to be invoked by men for this day—he who distributes treasures to human beings. May he grant us here the most excellent wealth. Having thus consecrated it, he should offer an oblation with the verse: "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning... (RV 10.121.1). || 13 ||

The measuring of the *brahman* stone is for the purpose of determining the expiation, like the case of the *skandana* [spilling] and so forth. Regarding this, Āpastamba states: "Having consecrated the *skala* with the verse beginning 'tatrābhūd devaḥ', one should measure the *prādeśas* upon it as before. (13)
If one were to perform the upākaraṇa with a hymn for a cup that has not been consumed. || 14 ||
If one were to introduce the chant for the subsequent group of goblets while this group of goblets has not yet been consumed. || 14 ||

"The moon has spoken in favor of the one being urged forward; the Soma juices of both worlds—those celestial and those terrestrial—have flowed together. "Of that [Soma] drunk by Indra, the honeyed, the invited, I, being invited, partake. With these words, he partakes of the Soma that has been sprinkled over. 15.

Wherever a drop of rain has fallen, that [spot] is sprinkled. However, for this [particular rite], it is understood that the looking is performed silently. "pratyasma pipīṣate" is the mantra for looking; "indurinduḥ" is the mantra for consuming—this should be observed in another Sūtra. But the mantra for consuming is a substitute for the regular mantra. || 15 ||

If he should sprinkle while initiated, [he uses] this [verse]: "O Agni, among the waters... "O Agni, burn up our enemies within; burn the weapon of the hostile stranger. O Vasu, being wise, burn the ignorant; thy unaging, tireless flames stand forth. "May those who are far from us be for us as if near. [End of the section from] the Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha... [15th Praśna]

O Agni, great as Mitra, burn him up with your own ageless, bull-like flames—whoever seeks to harm one who dwells within you. O most burning burner, consume him with your heat! May he provide us a signal even by night, though he dwell far away, when the ageless, purifying one consumes the lords of the forest. For no mortal has done violence to your body, O Agni; the monkey devours his own bristle like an ox its calf-skin. Like a ram, he goes toward and through the nights; he eats the raw flesh of the lower beast in the water.

With these ten Ṛg and Yajus verses—“With his head he conquers the mountains, with his chest the valleys; he shines upon the rays with his tawny horses”—he offers ten oblations. After each oblation, he bestows boons. (Section 27) 16.

The emission of semen into a vagina by one who is in the state of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is "spilling" (*avakiraṇa*). Others say it also refers to intentional emission even outside the vagina. Āpastamba says: "Having offered six full oblations. A *pūrṇāhuti* (full oblation) is an oblation made with a ladle that is completely filled. By the phrase "for each oblation," it is shown that a single horse is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for each individual oblation, not that the fee is to be given after every single oblation has been offered. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the rule "six full oblations," as well as with the observation in such passages as "he gives a sacrificial fee for each brick. 16.

Having offered ten oblations with the verse "Whatever offense against the gods... (or alternatively), he should consecrate [the sacrificer] with this section beginning "The blowing one, [born] of the sun... (RV 9.1.6–7). || 17 ||

He should obtain the consecrations (*abhiṣeka*) by means of the prescribed words. When there is a simultaneous scattering [of grain] with his wife, the oblations (*āhuti*) are performed together, but the consecration for both is separate. However, if there should be an emission of semen in a woman other than his wife or in a non-vaginal opening (*ayoni*), then the rule pertaining to customary conduct (*sāmayācārika*) must also be followed. Having emitted semen in a Śūdra woman or in a non-vaginal opening, he should touch water with verses addressed to the Waters (*ābliṅgābhiḥ*) or with other verses addressed to Varuṇa (*vāruṇībhiḥ*). But if the emission occurs while preceded by purification, the rule already stated applies, beginning with the verse, "That which is mine here from the milk... (*yan me 'tra payasaḥ*). || 15 ||

If the offered and the unoffered Soma should become mixed, one should take out a coal from the Āhavanīya fire within the enclosing sticks and offer the two Somas, both the offered and the unoffered, with the formula: "For you two, O Indra and Agni, are the seasonal ones of the sacrifice; satisfy yourselves with the conscious [Soma], both the offered and the unoffered! O Indra and Agni, enjoy this Soma, drink it, and be pleased—with Svāhā! Thus one should offer the two Somas, both the offered and the unoffered. || 18 ||

When the remnant of a cup (graha) or a ladle (camasa) that has been offered is being brought for consumption, and by some negligence it should fall upon something other than the offering-substance of the cup or the like that was already offered—or if the cup or the like has not been offered at all when there is a remnant of what was offered—then Āpastamba says: "One should give that portion to him as a consumption-offering. Having thus offered that [remnant] after mixing it together, one should give the consumption-offering to him who is generally entitled to consume the remnants of previous offerings. 18.

"O Fathers, let not one who harms our sacrifices, nor one who harms our heroes, nor one who is our kinsman or even a stranger, nor one of evil eye or wicked intent, have power over us. May this sacrifice reach the gods. With these words, he consumes the two portions of Soma that have been offered and those that have not yet been offered. || 19 ||
This is a substitution for the *bhakṣa*-mantra used for the daily [Soma].

"May darkness not find the sacrificer, nor the officiating priests, nor these creatures; may he who shall drink this Soma [be spared]—both [portions] have been mixed and made ready," with these words he consecrates the one who is consuming [the Soma]. 15.7.20.

The word "adhvaryu" is to be supplied as the subject. When the Adhvaryu drinks, then the Pratiprasthātṛ consecrates him with the mantra. Having thus offered the mixed Soma to Indra and Agni, he should again sacrifice to those two deities at their proper time with the portion produced from the *unnīta* (the drawing out), provided that this [portion] was not yet offered when it was taken elsewhere and then transferred. If only a single part of what was offered has fallen into the remnant of the offering and not the whole, then he should sacrifice using only that increased remnant. || 20 ||

"Seven are the officiating priests, seven the seats; ten fingers belong to these [Aśvins], five are the strengths. May the gods eat the oblation offered with 'svāhā': out-breath, diffused breath, in-breath, mind, intention, and Agni. With the mantra, "O Prajāpati, none other than you," he should pour the remnant of the portion upon the *uparava* pit in the eastern half of the northern half. Or, [he may do so] in the eastern half of the southern half.

Damage caused by hair, insects, and the like constitutes a defect (*vyāpatti*). In that case, the vessel should be washed or scraped according to the nature of the defect. Furthermore, another [portion of the] *makha* should not be produced, because it would serve no purpose; rather, it should be disposed of as a residual duty (*pratipatti*) and used for the remaining rites. However, the *nārāśaṃsa* cups must indeed be produced for the purpose of being carried after [the offering]. || 21 || 22 ||

The sky has flowed; the earth has flowed; this entire world has flowed. All those beings have flowed; may the oblation be born from that which has flowed. May cattle be produced here; may horses be produced here; may men be produced here. May the abundance of wealth, accompanied by a thousand sacrificial fees, settle here. May this sacrifice increase through cattle and horses; may this altar be rich in offspring and brave heroes. May this sacred grass surpass other grasses; may all the gods protect this sacrifice. The plants are full of sap... (Satyāṣāḍha-viracitaṃ Śrautasūtram — [15 Praśna])

Having consecrated the spilled *pṛṣadājya* with these verses, having poured water over it, having washed the vessel, and having heated it again, he sets it down. Having placed a gold piece weighing a hundred mānas into it, he takes another portion of *pṛṣadājya* with curds and, touching it while reciting the verse addressed to Viṣṇu, "May Viṣṇu follow thee for the sake of nourishment (*iṣe*)," and then smelling it with a horse, he sets it down. || 23 ||

"Regarding the *sruc* [ladle], Āpastamba says: this rule applies only to that which has entered into contact with the *khuks*. However, for that which is contained in the *sthālī* [pot], the rule is the same as for the clarified butter (*ājya*). In that case, having consecrated what has been spilled with four verses and having thrown the remainder of the spill into water, one should again take five portions from the *sthālī* with the *vaiṣṇavī* formula and set it down with the mantra. (23)

"Whatever [impurity] the bird has wiped away with its beak, O Nirṛti, may Agni, the bearer of oblations and destroyer of ghee, purify all that. This is the expiation for what has been wiped by a bird; in this case, the vessel is scraped clean.

The mantra for the wiping here is "yad apāmṛkṣat," and this is supplemented by the scraping of the vessel; the rest is the same as the other purpose. However, some, based on the wording of the mantra, "with the mouth," having prescribed this rule only for what has been wiped with the mouth of a crow, take [the portion] touched by another limb after discarding it into the water according to the rule for other things, and then take it into the scraped-out *sruva* ladle with its own mantra. ||24||

"Whatever has been licked by a dog, a cat, or a dog-cooker in your mouth, O Nirṛti—may the fire, the consumer of oblations and purifier with clarified butter, cleanse all that which is undesirable. With these words, he consecrates what has been licked by a beast of prey. This is the expiation for that. (The consumption and so forth are as before. No vessel is used here. (Section 28) || 25 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the fifteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.

A "beast of prey" (*śvāpada*) is one whose feet are like those of a dog, such as a dog, a jackal, or a wild cat—a five-toed animal. If [the food] has been touched by such a creature, one should discard it from the middle of the *caṅku* and, having purified another vessel, take [the food] into that. The rest is the same as before. By this very illustration, one should understand the discarding of food touched by outcasts (*patita*), a woman in her courses (*udakyā*), or other impure persons, as well as that which is defiled by the twelve kinds of impurities (*mala*). || 25 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the fifteenth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. [End of Chapter 7].
Now begins the eighth chapter in the fifteenth book.

One should offer [the oblation] with the verse, "That which is on the other side of this dust. If the animal, once brought forward for sacrifice, should tremble, sit down, low, stand up, run away, or if it dies while not yet intended for slaughter, one should offer a second oblation with the verse: "From whatever you have made us tremble with fear, from that grant us security; be gracious to all our offspring; homage to Rudra, the Bountiful. (1)

If the animal should cry out from the time of the *upākaraṇa* until the moment of slaughter, then, having offered with the verse "yadasya... (VS 6.20), one should offer with the verse "yasmād dīṣe... (VS 6.21). Or, according to Āpastamba and Vaikhānasa, one should consecrate the animal with a mantra. It should be understood that at the stage of slaughter, there is a combination of both [the offering] and the inspection with the words "indrasya bhāgaḥ" (VS 6.22). || 1 ||
Because of the statement "from fear whereof he sat down," [the mantra] is applied to the second [offering] when [the deity] has sat down.

The word "he should offer" (juhuyāt) is understood from the preceding context. However, when the animal that has been brought forward sits down, he should offer the second oblation with this modified verse: "From what fear did it sit down? (yatrayā bhīṣā nyaṣadat). The rest is the same as before; this is the meaning. Some, however, because of the rule regarding the *prayāja* offerings that they are performed while the animal stands, desire this injunction to apply only in that case.

"O bull, stand up; stand firm; do not perish; do not harm this sacrifice or the sacrificer. Place the sacrificer in the heavenly world; be a source of well-being for our bipeds and well-being for our quadrupeds"—with these words, he should cause the bull to rise. ||3||

Āpastamba states that once [the student] has sat down, Maitrāvaruṇa should raise him up with a staff. The sense is that this is another specific detail regarding the one who has sat down. Since the word *unaḥ* denotes the bovine species, the mantra remains unaltered as *ganyur ehi*. || 3 ||

"ucchāga" [is used] for a goat; "unmeṣa" for a ram; "ūrdhva ū ṣu ṇa ūtaye" is the second [verse]. "Ūrdhvo naḥ pāhy aṃhaso ni ketunā viśvaṃ sam atriṇaṃ daha | kṛdhī na ūrdhvāṃ carathāya jīvase vidā deveṣu no duvaḥ" is the third. 4.

In the case of goat-skin, however, it is modified to "ucchāga tiṣṭha" and "unmeṣa tiṣṭha. But when there is a change of gender (kśā), disregarding the specific genus, it simply becomes "udvaśa. In that context, because the word "ucchāga" expresses the meaning of the base form (prakṛti), in the modified forms (vikṛti) where there is a plurality of animals or a female animal, the modification (ūha) is made according to the actual facts. However, there is no modification for words such as "nonā," because they are taught specifically for the purpose of the modified forms.
Because of fear of whom the cows lowed, he performs the second [offering] while they are lowing; because of fear of whom you would leap up, he performs the second [offering] as it rises. ||5||
338. Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra—[15th Praśna], clear. 6.

Because of the fear [of whom] you fled, so [one should act]. If, after fleeing, he does not return, one should perform a second [sacrifice], having offered another animal that is of the same form, the same color, the same age, the same species, and the same deity, and complete the rite with that. (6) If an animal of that same species is unavailable, goats, sheep, and cows serve as mutual substitutes for one another. (7)

*Apakramaṇaṃ* means fleeing. Āpastamba states: "If [the victim] does not come, one should sacrifice after having consecrated another animal of similar form, color, and age. When it is impossible to bring that very one, one should consecrate another of the same species (*tajjātīya*) that is similar in its configuration, color, and age. Regarding the non-availability of one of that species, the author of the Sūtra has stated the substitute (*pratinidhi*): "Goats, sheep, and cows serve as mutual substitutes. (Sūtras 6 and 7)
If those [materials] are not available, one should conclude the remainder of the rite with clarified butter. ||8||
The meaning is clear. || 8 ||
"Because [they] stand in fear," thus [is the rule for] the second [animal] when it is not intended to be slaughtered. 9.
Death by one's own hand through disease and so forth is the unintentional act of causing death. || 9 ||
"To him who has done this, svāhā!"—with these words he offers the most excellent oblation. || 15.8.10 ||
"Uttamā" means the third [night]. Āpastamba and Vaikhānasa state that it is always the third [night]. || 1 ||

"Or indeed, you do not die here; [I offer] you to all the quarters, from all the quarters. With these four verses, beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss," he should consecrate a sacrificial animal that has become incapacitated, cause it to be carried into the waters, and then, having offered another animal of the same form, color, age, species, and deity, he should complete the rite with that one. This applies when an animal of the same species is unavailable. (Section 29) The case of a [sacrificial animal] that has fled has already been explained. 11.
Having carried the dead animal into the water, one should perform the sacrifice again with another animal as before. || 11 ||

If the cauldron (*ukhā*) should leak and become useless, one should recite over it while it is leaking: "Agni the Hotṛ, who performs no work—earth, atmosphere, and heaven; whatever has fallen from there, that reaches Agni alone; [drive] Nirṛti away. Thus he should consecrate the leaking cauldron, which is the womb of cattle.
Having consecrated another vessel with its opening facing downward, one should place it over the broken one that is leaking. || 12 ||
As many times as there would be portions to be cut from the animal, one should instead take that many portions of clarified butter. || 13 ||

8th Paṭala: Accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 339. The meaning is that whatever was previously stated in the Brāhmaṇa, beginning with "When they lead the animal" and ending with "those who would disfigure the animal," should be understood in that very context. For there, concerning the place and the animal, it is said: "When they lead the consecrated animal toward the north, then one should carry away its *paśuśrapaṇa* (the fire for cooking the animal)."

At whatever time they lead the animal northward for the purpose of immolation after the *prayāja* offerings have been completed, at that time one should take the *paśuśrapaṇa* fire—that is, the *śāmitra* fire—from that *prājahita* fire; this is the meaning. Furthermore, having criticized the extraction from the *āhavanīya* by stating, "They indeed tear the sacrificer asunder when they carry the *paśuśrapaṇa* from the *āhavanīya*," it is said: "That [fire] itself may be used, or one should produce it by friction."

The meaning is that the *prājahita* fire itself, or the fire produced by friction (*nirmanthya*), should serve as the source (*yoni*). In both the preceding and the present context, the reference to the *prājahita* by means of those two pronouns is to be understood precisely through a careful consideration of the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "They carry forward the eastern fire. Baudhāyana also states: "'It may indeed be that,' thus he teaches regarding the ancient *gārhapatya* fire. This same rule applies to the *savanīya* offering as well, because it has that [fire] as its archetype.

However, in the case of an animal sacrifice that has already been commenced (*nirūḍhapaśu*), it must be taken from the Āhavanīya fire itself, because of the specific scriptural injunction. Furthermore, it is stated in the Brāhmaṇa: "If a portion (*avadāna*) of the animal should be lost, one should take a substitute portion from the clarified butter (*ājya*); this is the expiation (*prāyaścitti*) for that. The meaning is that if one or more portions related to the animal should become unfit for offering due to loss, damage, or other defects, one should take [the portion] from the *dhauva* clarified butter in its place. This has been stated by Bharadvāja: "Whatever sacrificial material [is lost], clarified butter is its substitute."

"But if there is total destruction, there must be a fresh taking up [of the animal]. However, some maintain that even upon the destruction of the omentum (*vapā*) or the heart, there should be a fresh taking up, because it is possible for those two to constitute the self (*ātman*) of the animal later on—as in the passages: "The self is the omentum," and "Of the animal that has been taken up, the heart becomes the self. That is incorrect, because no specific distinction is taught [regarding these cases], and because the statement concerning the "self" is merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*).

This has been stated by Kātyāyana: "One should not heed the loss of the portions; however, some say that if the heart is destroyed, one should offer another animal, because of the Vedic text, 'The heart [is the essence] of animals. Or rather, one should sacrifice with clarified butter for all [the organs], since the mention of the animal is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda). If it is thought that this rule does not apply to the omentum (vapā) because it lacks the prescribed portions, that will be refuted in the subsequent sūtra. Even if the omentum and other parts are deficient in measure, as long as a portion remains, one should sacrifice with that very part as a substitute, because the substance is primary. As it has been said: "In the event of a deficiency in measure, one should complete the rite with what remains. (13)

If those who have slaughtered an animal should desire, "May they meet with misfortune," one should offer an oblation in the Āgnīdhra fire—with the verse beginning "kuvidaṅga" containing the word "namovṛkti"—or in the Āhavanīya or Śāmitra fire in the case of the Nirūḍhapaśubandha sacrifice. 14.

If robbers should plunder his cattle, or if they should seize him by force while he is alive or in the state of a corpse, and if the sacrificer should desire, "May they meet with destruction," then he should offer this oblation. But in the absence of that [desire], it serves as a rite for those who have fled. || 14 ||
If they should perceive [the fire] as "the eight-stepped one," he offers two oblations on the Gārhapatya fire with the verses, "Dhātṛ" and "Rātiḥ Sūryo Devaḥ."

240: *Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra*—[In the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), a female animal is to be sacrificed. If one should discover that it is "eight-footed" (*aṣṭāpadī*)—meaning it is pregnant—for it has eight feet including the limbs of the fetus, and because the purpose is to reveal the pregnancy. This same rule applies even in cases of twelve feet and so on, due to the presence of two fetuses or more. Therefore, if this is discovered prior to the immolation (*saṃjñapana*), one should release that animal and bring up another. But if the discovery occurs after that point, one should offer oblations with the verses: "Dhātṛ, Rāti, Sūrya, the God... (etc.). 15.
Having consecrated [the cow] with the mantra, "O you whose embryo is tawny," he causes the embryo to turn clockwise with the words, "Turn around, turn around."

"Then the Adhvaryu addresses her," says Āpastamba. He addresses the pregnant [cow] with the mantra beginning, "She who has... The meaning is that at the time of slaughter, he turns the cow's womb in a manner conducive to the exit [of the fetus]. || 16 ||
"I split open thy womb," with these words he extracts the fetus from between the hips. || 17 ||
Then, one cuts through this very distinction called "the non-existence of that which obscures. || 17 ||

Thinking "let it be outside," he discards the embryo and holds up the vessel for the juice with the verses, "The drop has run forth from the thigh," "The one of all forms," and "Indu. Having struck down the animal-cooking fire with the spit, he cooks the embryo. ||18||

Then, having extracted [the fetus] from the womb through the middle of the earth, having placed it upon a spit, and having fixed it with the tip of the spit, he strikes it and cooks it. The meaning is that, having driven the spit into the ground near the fire in accordance with the requirements for cooking the fetus, he cooks it on the *śāmitra* fire. || 1.8 ||
Having offered the sacrificial cake for Paśu, he does not [offer] the cake for Heaven and Earth; instead, he offers the embryonic sacrificial cake. || 19 ||

If it is known at the very time of the offering of the *paśupuroḍāśa* that [the animal] is pregnant, then immediately after offering that [paśupuroḍāśa], one offers the *garbhapuroḍāśa* as a secondary offering (*anunirvapati*). However, if it is known beforehand, one should offer it at the very moment one becomes aware of it. And that [offering] is offered with two potsherds (*dvikapāla*) dedicated to Heaven and Earth, not to the deity of the embryo. Nor do the ritual rules for the single-potsherd cake (*ekakapāla*) apply here, because the remaining portion is prescribed for disposal later on; otherwise, since the entire substance would have been offered (*sarvahuta*), no remainder would be possible. (19)

Having cut off the portions of the victim, he should cut one portion from the side of the embryo's navel and another from above; having thus cut them, he places them among the portions for the deities. || 15.8.20 ||

When the portions for the deities have been cut from the animal, one cuts a single portion from the thigh of the fetus and places it among the portions for the deities; at that time, one cuts below the navel, meaning for the *sauviṣṭakṛta* (oblation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt). This is because of the indicative mark [in the scripture]: "The out-breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed in front of the navel, and the in-breath (*apāna*) is above. || 20 ||
He divides the *rasa* into three portions: for the deities, for the *Sviṣṭakṛt*, and for the *iḍā*.
[Chapter 8] With the commentary *Yogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.

The particle *ca* (and) is to be construed out of its natural order for the purpose of indicating a conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the broth (*yūṣṇa*). Furthermore, since there is no other element to be conjoined with the deities and so forth already included within the compound, [the meaning is as follows]: having sprinkled it with broth, one distributes the essence of the embryo among the three [parts]. || 21 ||
He offers at the utterance of "vaṣaṭ" with the verses beginning "ekapadī" and "dvipadī. || 22 ||
"Before the Sviṣṭakṛt," says Āpastamba; because of the statement "before Vanaspati," this oblation is indeed offered before that [Vanaspatisava]. || 22 ||
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers a portion of the embryo from the southeast with one of the two verses: "O Viṣṇu, today that name of thine, Śipiviṣṭa... || 23 ||

This is because of the indicative mark [in the scripture]: "He offers to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. Likewise, the authors of other ritual manuals (kalpa) state: "In this manner, he offers to Viṣṇu. Therefore, he offers according to the procedure for a Darvihoma. || 23 ||
At the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), gold weighing eight prūḍhis is the fee. In the third inner sheath, it is enveloped by a turban; he gives that away. He makes the sheaths loose. ||24||

In this rite, he gives eight measures of gold together with its sheaths to the Adhvaryu. Regarding this, Āpastamba says: "Having wrapped the eight-fold gold—which consists of gold with eight spots—with a turban and a long cloth, having placed it in one sheath that has a lid, he places that sheath into another sheath, and having done the same for that as well, he places it into a third sheath. Thus, according to Āpastamba, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consists of the eight-fold gold.
With either of the two verses, "O Maruts, in whose house... or "O Maruts, you who carry the sacrifice with sacrifices," he offers an embryo-oblation upon the animal-cooking fire.
He offers the embryo and the embryo-oblation (garbhapuroḍāśa) into the Āhavanīya fire. || 25 ||
And he does not utter "svāhā" over the embryo-cake. || 26 ||
Because it is prohibited. || 26 ||
Or else, with the verse, "May the great heaven and earth protect us," he places the embryo into the cold ashes of the animal-cooking fire.
The word "api vā" (or rather) is for the purpose of indicating an alternative view. "Upohana" means concealment. || 27 ||
The embryo is the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). || 28 ||
The term "upohati" (he brings near) is to be supplied [from the preceding context]. || 28 ||
"I give this youth over to you"—having consecrated [the water] with these five [verses]. (kha030) || 29 ||
Having consecrated this youth with the mantra "etaṃ yuvānam," he then proceeds with the ritual actions beginning with the Sviṣṭakṛt offering. || 29 ||
349. *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[15th Praśna]:

If the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of one who has not yet performed the rite should sprout, he should perform the ritual of touching the animal for the *savanīya* sacrifice—a male with testicles, hairy, tawny, and multicolored—to the deity Tvaṣṭṛ; and he should offer an oblation with the verse: "The thirty-three threads which have been stretched out... (TS 7.5.24.1).

In the case of multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*), if the sacrificial post should sprout before its purpose is completed, then at that very post, by the principle of incidental application (*prasaṅga-nyāya*), he should perform the ritual of touching the animal for Tvaṣṭṛ using an animal that has reached the appropriate stage for that time. 30.

If a black bird, flying repeatedly over the *havirdhāna* sheds, should alight upon them when fear has arisen—if it is possible to sacrifice—one takes portions from all the *havis* offerings and from all the *soma* juices into the *droṇakalaśa* and offers an oblation with the mantra: "To those gods whose portion this has become, to whom belong the *prayāja*s and the *anuyāja*s; to the gods who have Indra as their chief, Varuṇa as their king, and Agni as their hotṛ—*svāhā*! (31). When there is no longer fear, one should sacrifice again. (32)

The "black bird" is a crow. While fanning the sacrificial offerings (*havis*) that have been set out with the wind from its wings, it should approach them or perch upon them; then one should offer the oblation there with the words, "O gods! One should then cast that defiled offering into the water and produce another. || 31 || 32 ||

If a failure in the sacrifice occurs on account of the *ṛc*, one should offer an oblation in the *gārhapatya* fire with the word "bhūḥ"; if on account of the *yajus*, with the word "bhuvaḥ" in the *dakṣiṇāgni*; if on account of the *sāman*, with the word "suvaḥ" in the *āhavanīya*. If the failure occurs on all accounts, one should offer a single oblation in the *āhavanīya* using all [three words], or the *brahmán* may offer it.
"From the Ṛc" means by way of the Ṛgveda; that is to say, the omission of some ritual act or mantra prescribed in the Ṛgveda. The same applies to "from the Yajus," and so forth. || 33 ||
Or one may meditate with the mind. || 34 ||
"Brahman" is the understood remainder. || 34 ||

"If the Audumbarī pillar should perish or break, one should cut another and raise it with the mantra: 'Bestow strength upon me; stand as prosperity, firmly established; supporting the sky and the atmosphere, be firm upon the earth—supporter, sustainer, and progenitor. Thus he raises it. || 35 ||
The Adhvaryu, the Udgātṛ, and the sacrificer raise [the sacrificial post], according to Āpastamba. "Destruction" (nāśaḥ) means being eaten by worms or stolen, and so forth. || 35 ||
The Adhvaryu, the sacrificer, or the Brahman priest raises it. || 36 ||
This is according to the principle that "rites [performed] with a single mantra [yield a single result]. || 36 ||
He consecrates it with the eternal *yajuṣ* formula. || 37 ||
Having silently dug it in, the Adhvaryu consecrates it with the Yajus formula, "dyutānastvā. (37)

If the two *havirdhāna* carts should fall down, the Adhvaryu should lift up the southern one and the Pratiprasthātṛ should support it; the Pratiprasthātṛ should lift up the northern one and the Adhvaryu should support it. || 38 ||

If both or either one of the two *havirdhāna* carts should fall, the Adhvaryu should lift it up from the south and not drag it; the Pratiprasthātṛ should support it and tie a cord around its middle. For the northern cart, this same procedure is reversed.
They support [the post] with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu; they level it with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu; they touch it together with a verse addressed to the Aśvins. || 39 ||

In that regard, first, the lifting (*udgrahaṇa*) of both [the posts] is performed with the *tuṣpīka* verse. The propping (*upastambhana*), however, is done from the side with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu (*vaiṣṇavī ṛc*). Then, with that same [verse], they touch (*samṛśataḥ*) and fashion (*kalpayataḥ*) the upper part (*upamāya*). In this context, "touching" refers to the firming of the propping after it has been established in its proper place. The verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" is the one addressed to Viṣṇu. When, however, there are two separate verses for each—namely, "divo vā viṣṇo" and "viṣṇor nu kam"—as is seen in the case of their permanent installation (*nityasthāpana*), then the term "with two verses addressed to Viṣṇu" (*vaiṣṇavībhyām*) should be stated. The verse "yā vāṃ kaśā" is addressed to the Aśvins (*āśvinī*). || 39 ||

With the three *uṣṇih* verses beginning "O Agni, [lord] of booty consisting of cattle," the Adhvaryu offers oblations in the Āgnīdhra fire; the Pratiprasthātṛ offers with the *kakubh* verses. "May Agni, when invoked, be auspicious to us; may his gift be auspicious, O fortunate one; may the sacrifice be auspicious; and may our praises be auspicious. May our praises indeed be auspicious; make your mind auspicious for the slaying of Vṛtra, so that you may prevail in battles. With which [mind] you may prevail in battles, with that [mind], O steadfast one, strike down the many hosts of the arrogant. In the forest, [protect] us with your aids"—these are the verses recited. (15.8.40)

The Adhvaryu offers with the first three *uṣṇih* verses, and the Pratiprasthātṛ with the other three *kakubh* verses. Thus the Śruti has cited the formula: "Six *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* verses. Regarding this, Āpastamba explains: "The Adhvaryu [offers] with the former *uṣṇih*s; the Pratiprasthātṛ with the latter *kakubh*s" (ĀpŚS 14.30.7).

Having taken four or five spoonfuls of clarified butter with the formulas, "Let the head of the sacrifice be placed; let the immortal, consisting of the deities, be made by means of the verse addressed to Viṣṇu; let the head be placed by means of the verse addressed to the Aśvins," they both offer two identical oblations. (41)
This offering also belongs to the Āgnīdhra, because of the governing context; the two oblations are identical, and their identity consists in the identity of the mantra. || 11 ||
If the fire-pan belonging to the Āgnīdhra should break while still unbaked, one should scrape it out and make another.

If the *āmā* (the vessel) is destroyed, then one should collect those very potsherds, prepare them anew, and fashion [the vessel] again, either silently or with mantras, according to the principle stated regarding its re-establishment. || 42 ||
If it should break while still uncooked, one should mix another clay with those very potsherds that have been well-ground and fashion [another vessel]. || 43 ||
If it should break while baking, then one should grind the shards, mix them with that same clay, and fashion [the vessel] again. || 43 ||
If the *ukhya* fire should go out, one should lead forward the *āhavanīya* fire; that very fire is then to be circumambulated again.

The *ukhya* fire is that which exists in the *ukhā* (fire-pan). If it should go out before the scattering [of the grains], one should bring another *āhavanīya* fire from the *gārhapatya* into its proper place. Then, that very same *āhavanīya* must again be "encircled" (*paridhi*), meaning it must be produced once more in the *ukhā* by means of the procedure for kindling (*pravṛñjana*), beginning with the formula "not with a tuft of hemp" and ending with the worship of the [fire] that has been born.

But for one who, having given away [the fire], becomes free from his original womb—whether by desire or by some other cause—for him also the *ukhya* fire may be established from its own womb due to its self-sufficiency (*svārhatva*), but it is not to be carried around (*parīdhya*). This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating "again, the *parīdhya*," and also because of the indicative mark stating "he does not generate it from its own womb. || 44 ||
A black garment should be given, as well as a black cow, a black bull, and gold weighing one śatamāna.
A bull with a white mark on its forehead; the word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction. || 45 ||
In that he takes the Vasatīvarī waters on the previous day for the Yajñāyajñiya chant of the following day, by that he fastens the days together; by that he makes the sacrifice continuous. || 46 ||

That which is performed on the previous day for the sake of the subsequent day—such as the fetching of the *imā* grass and the *barhis* for the *savanīya* offering—is what constitutes the connection between the rites of the preceding and following days; that is to say, it links the rituals of those two days. By this means, one indeed extends the sacrifice (*yajña*). Otherwise, it would be severed. Therefore, this "joining" (*abhyāsaṅga*) is necessary; such is the meaning. || 46 ||
[Chapter 1] Accompanied by the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī: 345.

When, on the preceding day, he recites the *stotriya* (the verse for the chant) and the *anurūpa* (the corresponding verse) for the following day, by that he connects the days; by that he continues the sacrifice. When he issues the *atipraiṣa* (the call for the next day), by that he connects the days; by that he continues the sacrifice. Thus it is said. 47.

At the *yajñāyajñiya* [stotra], at the time of the *yajñāyajñiya*, he instructs regarding the milks intended for the *āśira* mixture. He gives various directions. At the time of the *sūktavāka*, [he does so] also with the formula beginning "Tomorrow is the pressing for Indra and Agni," etc. The remainder is as before. || 47 ||

If any one of these [omissions] occurs, one should offer this expiation: "Homage to Brahman, homage be to Agni, homage to the Earth, homage to the Plants; homage to Speech, homage to the Lord of Speech, homage to the Great Viṣṇu, I perform [this], Svāhā! One should offer this expiation; one should offer this expiation. (Khaṇḍa 32) 48.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the fifteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Thus ends the fifteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.

If even for one of these rites it is not performed on the preceding day, one should offer these two oblations; how much more so, then, if two or many are omitted? This repetition is intended to mark the conclusion of the question. || 48 ||

... thus. This concludes the eighth chapter in the fifteenth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. Thus ends the fifteenth book in the commentary on the *Sūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.

16.1 Now begins the first chapter of the sixteenth book. I joyfully salute the Lord of Sages, the ocean of compassion known as Guru Hiraṇyakeśin—the preeminent among all perfected masters attended by disciples, who knows the meaning of the Sūtras, and who possesses the bliss of radiant consciousness and bliss. The expiation has been declared in the fifteenth book; now, in this sixteenth book, he explains the procedure for the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha). Now the ritual of the twelve-day sacrifice is described:
"By means of the twelve-day sacrifice, one is indeed born again. (ŚB 10.2.6.1)
Now begins the first chapter of the sixteenth book:
By means of the twelve-day rite, one is indeed born again. || 1 ||
He attains preeminence, for he indeed experiences this. ||2||
And the Ahīna sacrifice is also a Sattra. ||3||
His [penance] is explained as being like that of fire. || 4 ||
Those whose prosperity has departed should perform sacrifices according to their desire.

Whatever desire one may have when sacrificing with a specific meter, that desire is fulfilled for him. Regarding the injunction "he sacrifices" and "they sacrifice": if he were without austerity (*tapas*), his sacrifice would be unconnected; therefore, he should be austere, for it is known that he thereby connects the sacrifice itself. 6.
One who is fat undergoes initiation; one who is lean performs the sacrifice.
The Kāmyā Vidyā causes one to desire forty-eight things. || 8 ||
Fifteen [priests] should be initiated, for they have the half-month as their abode.
Seventeen [stotras] for those desiring offspring. 16.1.10.

Those desiring cattle [should perform it] twenty-one times; those desiring a firm foundation, twenty-three times; those desiring spiritual luster, twenty-four times; those for whom the months are the foundation, thirty times; those desiring vigor, thirty-three times; those desiring sensory power, forty times; those desiring strength, forty-four times; and those desiring livestock, forty-eight times. ||11||
"They should undergo initiation for an unlimited [period]," they say at the very least. || 12 ||
These [mantras] also belong to the sacrificer (yājamāna) section of the Ahīna sacrifice, as they occupy their respective positions. || 13 ||

The Brahmins who are officiating priests perform the sacrifice for those who have been consecrated, as well as for those who have not been consecrated, provided they are not excluded from the rite; by means of that [rite], they cause them to sacrifice.
Therefore, one should not act as a sacrificer for the twelve-day rite for the sake of warding off evil. || 15 ||
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the twelve-day rite. || 16 ||
The sacrificer prospers. || 17 ||
He who, knowing thus, accepts [gifts] by means of the twelve-day sacrifice. || 18 ||
He speaks with reference to the officiating priests and the sacrificer. || 19 ||
Now, they approach the sacrificial session of seventeen initiated Brāhmaṇas as they sit. 16.1.20.
Or rather, the *codanā* (the injunction) applies to all who have performed their first desired sacrifice, or to the householder. (Section 1, Sūtra 21)
All [the priests] shall perform the duties of the sacrificer through their priestly office, provided it is not prohibited. || 22 ||

Just as in the case of the householder’s anointing of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the *mṛtuyājyā* offering, and other such matters, when there is a conflict of rules, the rule of the majority is upheld—or rather, that of the householder. || 23 ||
They should perform it according to the ritual procedure for the *sāmidhenī* verses of the householder himself.
"O Varuṇa, you... is the concluding *sāmidhenī* verse for the Vasiṣṭhas and the *rājanyas*; "Offer the oblation... is for other *gotras*.
The second fore-offering (prayāja) is the Nārāśaṃsa for the Vasiṣṭhas and Śunakas; it is the Tanūnapāt for other lineages (gotras).
Those who are about to offer the Sāvitra oblations should pour the fires together; having offered them, they should separate them again.

Those who intend to sacrifice with animals should pile [the fires] together before the sacrifice; or they may pile them together after having sacrificed; or the householder alone may pile the two forest fires together.

"The fire that shall be produced from this [wood] shall belong to all of us. Whatever we shall win by this sacrifice, whatever we shall win by this animal sacrifice—that shall be ours together; it shall be for us equally. But as for whoever does evil in this way, let that belong to him alone. Thus it was said. (29)
The householder performs the installation; either he does it himself or another person acts as the householder. 16.1.30.
Of all [of them]. || 31 ||
It is known from tradition: "They undergo initiation in the cool season; they emerge from it in the spring."
The winter solstice is indeed its commencement, and the spring solstice is its conclusion.
"It is known from scripture that those who, knowing this, undergo initiation in the winter season and emerge [from it] in the spring, prosper. (34)
When six nights of the waxing fortnight have dawned, those intending to perform the sacrifice should undergo initiation.

Having made a mutual agreement and performed the ritual scattering [of the fires], they perform the rites beginning with the *dīkṣaṇīyā* (consecration offering), saying: "Whatever fire shall be produced from this, let that be for all of us; whatever we shall conquer by means of this sacrifice, by this sacrificial session (*sattra*). (Section 2). Regarding this agreement:

Having initiated the Gṛhapati, the Adhvaryu should say: "He initiates the middle officiants—the Hotṛ, the Brahman, and the Udgātṛ. Having initiated the Adhvaryu, the Pratiprasthātṛ initiates the half-sharers—the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and the Stotṛ. Having initiated the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Neṣṭṛ initiates the third-sharers—the Acchāvāka, the Āgnīdhra, and the Pratihartṛ.

The Unnetṛ, having initiated the Neṣṭṛ, initiates those who have a share [in the sacrificial fees]: the Grāvastut, the Potṛ, and the Subrahmaṇya. Then the Pratiprasthātṛ initiates him (the Adhvaryu). Or another initiated Brāhmaṇa may do so; thus they should be initiated in this successive order. He does not conclude one by one because of the lack of a common ritual framework (*atantrībhāva*). Because of the intervention of those of a different lineage (*gotra*), the initiation is repeated for those of the same lineage who belong to the same *ṛṣi* line. They initiate the wives in a single place. Their duties are explained by the rules pertaining to the sacrificer. 36.
Some prescribe the initiation (dīkṣā) for each successive day. || 37 ||
He causes [the horse] to step forward for two days, three days, and so on, up to twelve days.

One should undergo initiation on the thirteenth Upasad day. Therefore, one must become a Brāhmaṇa. Those undergoing initiation, having scattered and piled up the fires, should proceed with the purification of the self; there are twelve initiation days. 39.
No instruction regarding the removal of the sacrificial grass exists when the sacrifice has been completed. || 16.1.40 ||
The sixteenth [digit] is the seller of Soma. || 41 ||
On the twelfth day, he purchases the King (Soma).
There are twelve *upasads*. ||43||
He piles the fire-altar with the anūpasada bricks. || 44 ||
