Each layer lasts for two days. || 45 ||
The best [attainment] lasts for four days. || 46 ||
For three nights, there are four-udder vows. || 47 ||
In this way, there are those with three breasts, two breasts, and one breast. ||48||
If one desires to undertake the vow again, one should pour out a single ladleful of curdled milk.
There are twenty-one roof-coverings. || 16.1.50 ||
The two pressing-boards are perforated. (Section 3) ||51||
Thus ends the first chapter in the sixteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Now begins the second chapter of the sixteenth book.
The single sacrificial post has been explained.
If there is a set of eleven sacrificial posts (yūpaikādaśinī), one should erect one post each day, or all of them together.

On the day of the Upavasatha, as the animals are being immolated day after day, the animal for the Upaśaya rite should be brought forward each day. On the Udayanīya day, he should dedicate the animal at the Agniṣṭha post.
On the following day, the Jyotiṣṭoma is extended.
The Vaiśvānara is an Atirātra. At the time of bringing down [the Soma], he brings down as much of the King (Soma) as has been obtained for the one-day sacrifice, having tied it in another cloth.
He places the other one down facing toward it.
In this manner it is performed day after day; [it is performed] every day for the sake of the release from the bonds of yoga.
According to some, he yokes on the first day and unyokes on the last day.

At the Prāyaṇīya and Udayanīya Atirātras and on the tenth day, he takes the Pṛśni-prāṇagrahas; having measured [the Soma] with the first mantra of the original Yajus-measure while it is being pressed, he measures ten Pṛśni-measures with the ten mantras beginning with "Vāyur asi prāṇo nāma."

Having measured with each successive Yajus-formula, he measures out the ten vessels for the Prāṇagraha libations with the ten mantras beginning with "This [world] was in front" (ayaṃ puro bhuv). || 16.2.10 ||
He interlinks them with the Yajus formula one after another. || 11 ||

The Prāyaṇīya and Udayanīya Atirātras have the cups beginning with the Aindravāyava; so too the tenth day. Now, for the other nine days, the first day has the cups beginning with the Aindravāyava, then the next has the Śukra as the first, and then the Āgrayaṇa as the first; thus the threefold series revolve three times in the Samūḍha arrangement of the metres. (Section 4) 12.

Now follows the expanded arrangement (*vyūḍha*) according to the *chandasya* method: the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* days have the cups beginning with the *aindravāyava*; for the other ten days of the *atirātra*, the first day has the cups beginning with the *aindravāyava*; then two days have the cups beginning with the *śukra*; then [one day] has the cups beginning with the *āgrayaṇa*; then two days have the cups beginning with the *aindravāyava*; then [one day] has the cups beginning with the *āgrayaṇa*; and then two days have the cups beginning with the *aindravāyava*. || 13 ||

In that regard, the food-mantras (*bhakṣamantra*s) and the consecrations for the *pavamāna* [soma]—as well as the *nigada*s—should be adapted by means of those respective meters in their place; this has been explained by way of transposition (*vyūha*). || 14 ||

In the same way, during the subsequent *pṛṣṭhya* days, he takes three *atigrāhya* cups: the one for Agni on the twenty-first day, the one for Indra on the twenty-ninth day, and the one for Sūrya on the thirty-third day.
The Vājasaneyins prescribe for the first three days: "Where the Gaurīvita Sāman is chanted, there one should draw all the cups full. (16)

Now follows the preparation of the animal sacrifices: on the day of the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra, they immolate an animal for Agni; on the following day, a ewe for Sarasvatī. Thus they immolate the distributed sets of eleven animals day by day, with one for Agni on the Udayanīya day, for those desiring spiritual luster.
At the time of the sacrificial fee, he gives twelve hundred [cows] every day during the Ahīna sacrifice. || 18 ||

In the sacrificial session (sattra), however, having offered the two dakṣiṇā-oblations with the formula, "This cow I lead as a dakṣiṇā for prosperity, for fame, and for the heavenly world," the sacrificers follow the black antelope skins; others go by the northern path, while [the cows] pass by the southern path.
In this manner, it is performed day after day.
On the following day, they throw away the black antelope horns.
They cast off their friendships. || 22 ||
On the preceding day, he takes up the Vasatīvarī waters for the Yajñāyajñīya chant on the following day.
On the preceding day, having made the *stotrīya* verse correspond to that of the following day, he recites it. (Section 5) 24.
Thus ends the second chapter in the sixteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Now begins the third chapter in the sixteenth book:
While the Atirātra sacrifice is in progress, he causes the milks to be distributed.

When the Maitrāvaruṇa announces, "Proclaim the Soma for Indra and Agni, for the Viśve Devas, and for the Soma-drinking Brāhmaṇas, for the Soma-pressing tomorrow," the Āgnīdhra enters his own chamber and issues the command: "I proclaim the Soma for Indra and Agni, for the Viśve Devas, and for the Soma-drinking Brāhmaṇas, for the Soma-pressing tomorrow; O Brahman, restrain your speech; O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā. || 2 ||
On this day, he should say, "Today is the Soma-pressing," or else, on other days, he should say, "Tomorrow is the Soma-pressing."
The day concludes with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings. || 4 ||
When he has passed away, Brahmā releases his speech. || 5 ||
They pour out water for the wives. || 6 ||
Those who carry the fuel-bundles take them away. ||7||
Having returned, they place fuel-sticks upon the Āhavanīya fire.
In this manner, they should be performed day after day.
On that day, there is the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha.
The Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is threefold and has the Rathantara as its Sāman chant.
With the sound of the chariot, he introduces the hymn for Mahendra. || 12 ||
The sound of the *upākaraṇa* mantra is a modification.
The Ukthya sacrifice with fifteen stomas has the Bṛhat Sāman.
With the sound of a drum, he begins the hymn of praise to Mahendra. || 15 ||
If there is thunder, that very sound shall be the modification of the mantra used for the introductory rite (upākaraṇa). || 16 ||
The Ukthya sacrifice with seventeen stomas has the Vairūpa Sāman.
With the Ādhāva verse, he begins the Māhendra hymn of praise. || 18 ||
The *barhis* grass is a modification [of the *kuśa*]; when that has been brought forward and the *prastāva* has been chanted, the *udgātṛ* shakes it with a blow. || 19 ||
The twenty-first [stotra] is the ṣoḍaśī, having the Vairāja as its sāman. || 16.3.20 ||
There is the insertion of the *nyūṅkha* at the calls of *haviṣkṛt*, *āśruta*, *pratyāśruta*, and in the *pratigara*. || 21 ||
He introduces the hymn to Mahendra with two fire-drills; this is a modification of the sacrificial grass (barhis). || 22 ||
When that has been brought forward and presented. (Khaṇḍa 6) ||23||
The Udgātṛ, having covered the right thigh with Avakā plants and placed the two fire-drills thereon, churns the fire.
When it has been produced, the Udgātṛ, having uttered the *abhihiṅkāra*, hands it over to the Prastotṛ. || 25 ||
The Prastotṛ [gives] to the Adhvaryu. || 26 ||

Having carried it around the hearth-mounds (dhiṣṇiyas) with the front part [of the ladle] and having thrown it into the Āhavanīya fire, he makes an offering over it with the Virāj verse: "O Agni, kindled, shine forth! (RV 10.8.4). || 27 ||
The Ukthya sacrifice has twenty-seven [verses] and the Śākvara Sāman.

With those waters containing avakā plants, he begins the chant for Mahendra; when that [chant] has been introduced and the Prastāva has been chanted, there is a modification of the sacrificial grass (barhis). || 29 ||
Three cows with bulls go ahead by way of the front of the *sadas* and behind the *āgnīdhra*, crossing over toward the north along the path of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇāpatha*).
The Ukthya sacrifice with thirty-three [verses], having the Raivata Sāman as its chant, is [named]. 31.
This day consists of the *nyūṅkha* chant.
The *ṛtuyāja* offering is performed by the sacrificer himself.
When it is said, "O two Adhvaryus, sacrifice," the Adhvaryu enters the two Havirdhāna sheds and sacrifices with the subsequent ṛc, or rather, with the subsequent *praiṣa*.

"O Aśvins, drink the pressed [mixture] (madhu), you who shine with fire and are pure in your vows, who bring the sacrifice according to the season! By the season, drink the Soma—Vauṣaṭ! Thus he sacrifices even if the [verse] is not interwoven; [he says "drink" when it is not interwoven]. ||35||

The explanation is as before regarding the time: it belongs to Indra, for he draws all the portions for Indra. However, in the *vyūḍha* (expanded) arrangement, [the verse is]: "Yoke today this chariot that carries heroes toward us; here is your place of unyoking. Mix the oblations with honey, for you have come; then drink the Soma, O ye who possess great wealth! Drink the Soma according to the season—*vauṣaṭ*! Its performance takes place with the *marutvatīya* offerings (in the *vyūḍha* arrangement, [the word] "drink" is used).
When that [rite] which precedes the Māhendra [cup] has been performed, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having stretched a cord toward the north behind the Āgnīdhra fire-shed, binds the calves to it.
To the south of the Mārjālīya fire, they obstruct the mothers. || 38 ||
In the place of the sacrificial grass (barhis), he begins the chant for Mahendra with water-grass (dūrvā) spread out; this is a modification of the sacrificial grass.

When that [rite] has been initiated and set forth, having released the calves from their mothers and having brought them together with them, they are driven northward along its southern path; thus the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha concludes. (Khaṇḍa 7) 16.3.40.
Thus ends the third chapter in the sixteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Now, the fourth chapter in the sixteenth book.
When the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha has been completed, they consume either clarified butter or honey.
Every day there are three Ukthya sacrifices, and [three] Chandomas. ||2||
The twenty-fourth, the forty-fourth, and the forty-eight [stomas]; the twenty-fourth is the Avivākya day. The tenth day is an Agniṣṭoma Soma sacrifice with the Rathantara Sāman. ||3||
In this, nothing whatsoever is obstructed for anyone. || 4 ||
If those who are outsiders and observers should speak out there, and if they do not find [the truth] within, then it should be declared as being both existent and non-existent.
If they should not find [a guest] there, they should announce it to the householder.
Having recited the Gṛhapati hymn in the Anuṣṭubh meter, he should then recite that [following verse].
At which [verse] he pronounces the invitation, he should also thereby complete the Anuṣṭubh together with those two. On that day, they bring two pieces of fuel-wood.
And the *audumbarī* posts are permanent.
They add [the fuel] constantly. 16.4.10.
To the north of the Āhavanīya fire, they place a post made of Udumbara wood.

With the two verses beginning "The sunless ones near the sun" and "Those with which the sun is together," he offers oblations into the Gārhapatya fire. [He recites: "These [waters] speed our sacrifice; here is delight, here is pleasure; may you take pleasure here, here is pleasure, here is delight; may your delight be here. With these two verses, he makes the offering in the Gārhapatya fire. 12.

"This one of a thousand rays, the vision of the seers, the thought, possessing the nature of light—having established them, he has set the dawns in harmony; they are faultless, dwelling together, sharing the same seed, conscious, and full of voice and fury. With this *aticchandas* verse, they worship the Āhavanīya fire. (Section 8) 13.
They proceed toward the Prājāpatya cup for the seizing of the mind. || 14 ||

While [the Soma] is flowing, meditating in his mind upon the earth with the words, "With this vessel," he takes the *manograha* for Prajāpati with the formula, "I take what is pleasing to Prajāpati Manu. He should extract it from the space according to its form, or from the *tārtīyasavanika* Soma, having set aside as much as is sufficient for one group of *camasa* cups.
Therefore, he should take [the draught] with the Upāṃśu vessel; he pours out the goblets, of which the Hotṛ’s goblet is the chief.
The Stotra and Śastra are performed. ||17||
Everything for him is performed by means of the mind. || 18 ||
He begins the hymn of praise mentally. || 19 ||
He intones the Prastāva mentally. ||16.4.20||
He sings aloud with his mind. || 21 ||
He responds with his mind. ||22||
He receives [the water] six times with the mind, using the three Sārparājñī verses. || 23 ||

If he recites by half-verses, the response for the Daśahotṛ is "O Hotṛ! nine times; for the Caturhotṛ, it is "So be it" (tathā); for the Pañcahotṛ, it is "Om"; for the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ, it is "So be it"; and for the Saptahotṛ, it is "We have succeeded, O Hotṛ" (arātsma hotar). || 24 ||
The mental *āśruta* and *pratyāśruta*, the *yājyā*, the *saṃpraiṣa*, the *vaṣaṭkāra*, and the *bhakṣa-mantra* [are performed mentally]. 25.

Having offered the oblation, they take [the portions] and eat; whatever they look upon becomes subject to the rule of mutual invitation (*samupahava*). Sitting around the householder, they question him. (Section 9) 26.
"When the Daśahotṛs performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*), by what householder did they prosper? By what means did they create progeny?"—thus the Adhvaryu asks. (27)
"By Prajāpati indeed, acting as the householder, they prospered; by him they created offspring," the householder replies. || 28 ||

"When the Caturhotṛs performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*), by what householder did they prosper, and by what did they release the plants?"—thus the Brahman asks. "By Soma as their householder they prospered, and by him they released the plants"—thus the householder replies. (29)

"When the Pañcahotṛs performed a sacrificial session, by what householder did they prosper? By what means did they drive away the Asuras from these worlds? By what means did they win their cattle?"—thus asks the Hotṛ. "By Agni as their householder they indeed prospered; by him they drove away the Asuras from these worlds; by him they won their cattle," thus replies the Gṛhapati. 16.4.30.

When the Hotṛ-priests ask, "When the Ṣaḍḍhotṛs performed the sacrificial session (sattra), by what householder did they prosper, and by whom did they arrange the seasons?", the Householder replies, "By Dhātṛ as their householder they prospered; by him they arranged the seasons. || 31 ||

"Since the seven Hotṛ-priests performed a sacrificial session (sattra), with what householder did they succeed? With what did they win the heavenly world? With what did they extend these worlds?"—thus the Udgātṛ asks. "With Aryaman as their householder they succeeded; with him they won the heavenly world; with him they extended these worlds," the Gṛhapati replies. || 32 ||
They speak ill of Prajāpati. 33.
"This Prajāpati is unskilled, who would create gadflies and mosquitoes, as well as thieves. || 34 ||

Or rather, they recite the mantras concerning the censures of Prajāpati: "That which Prajāpati created—the wildernesses and the mountains—may Agni, the maker, make that auspicious; whatever is auspicious, grant that to me. That which he joined with heat and darkness, and that which scorched your eye during the day, the water and the excessive heat—Prajāpati [ordained] all that for you. That which you have not [created], namely the wolves, the gadflies, the mosquitoes, and the barley-eaters."

"Then that which is crooked for you, that is their poison; by that you [attain] immortality. 'May you partake of Prajāpati on the tenth day; bestowing the thought of the sages and the bull among men, he who possesses a good dwelling and excellent wealth, being free from evil, establishes the seeker of the gods in the world'—with these [verses] they should recite around him. || 35 ||
Then he chooses a boon. || 36 ||
"May there be food for us," with such a desire they perform [the rite]. (Section 10) 37.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the sixteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.

Alternatively, by means of this [formula]: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! May I be rich in offspring through offspring, rich in heroes through heroes, rich in splendor through splendor, and rich in nourishment through nourishments," all their desires become fulfilled.
Having explained the Caturhotṛ formulas and closed the two doors, having seated the wives according to their respective hearths and closed the two doors, he then offers speech to them.

"Here is steadfastness, here is support, here is delight, here is enjoyment"—saying this, they embrace the Udumbara post with their bellies as if touching it, and having taken hold of the Udumbara together, they sit down. "O Indra and Parvata, you two who fight in the van, slay him who attacks us; strike him down, strike him down with the thunderbolt."

And they cast it far away if it has fallen into thick brushwood; "O Hero, if you have not reached our enemies, do you, the best piercer, pierce them from all sides"—with these words, while holding on to one another, they pass by the southern sides of the northern *havirdhāna* cart, standing still, using either mats or splinters of wood. Having walked forward a little, they utter five formulas: "Let speech come! Let speech come! Let speech approach! Let speech meet us! Let speech come near us! Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! Thus they recite.
When the sun has gone behind the trees, they release their speech with the Subrahmaṇyā formula. ||4||
He places fuel-sticks of Udumbara wood upon the fire. || 5 ||
On the following day, the *udayanīya* [offering] takes place; its form has already been explained. ||6||
The Prāyaṇīya and Udayanīya [offerings] exist here; the continuations of the Ahīna [sacrifices] are not found in this case. || 7 ||
On the preceding day, he takes the Vasatīvarī waters for the Yajñāyajñīya chant of the following day. ||8||
These constitute lineages that are not deficient. ||9||
Moreover, having put on those very garments of the consecrated, they should proceed with the ritual.
At the time of shaving, they have their hair shaved along with the top-knots, or they do so when the sacrificial session has commenced.

At the *udavasānīya* offerings, having chosen other officiating priests, they should perform separate sacrifices with them, either by means of a *jyotiṣṭoma-agniṣṭoma* known as the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya*, characterized by a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*sahasradakṣiṇa*), or one in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee (*sarvavedasadakṣiṇa*).
The twelve-day rite is concluded. (kha11) || 13 ||
By means of the Gavāmayana, they go to Prajāpati as abundance; they find firm standing in these worlds. || 14 ||
The ritual procedure for that [twelve-day sacrifice], which has the nature of a sacrificial session (sattra), has been explained by means of the twelve-day [rite]. || 15 ||
They should undergo initiation four days before the full moon.
And on the full moon day of Māgha or Caitra. || 17 ||

The Prāyaṇīya is an Atirātra; the Ārambhaṇīya is a Caturviṃśa Ukthya. Or there are two days consisting of the Trivṛt: the Jyotis Agniṣṭoma with the Rathantara Sāman, the Gauḥ Ukthya with the Bṛhat Sāman, the Āyuḥ Ukthya with the Rathantara Sāman, the Gauḥ Ukthya with the Bṛhat Sāman, the Āyuḥ Ukthya with the Rathantara Sāman, and the Jyotis Agniṣṭoma with the Bṛhat Sāman. || 18 ||
The Abhiplava is a six-day period. || 19 ||
In this manner, four *abhiplava* periods are prescribed. || 16.5.20 ||
The six-day period consisting of the *pṛṣṭhya* is the summary. || 21 ||
He has a second, a third, a fourth, and a fifth; the sixth is to be supported. || 22 ||
There are three *abhiplava* periods. || 23 ||
The Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha. || 24 ||
There are three Abhijits, Svarasāmans, Ukthyas, or Agniṣṭomas. || 25 ||
The other two lie for two days. || 26 ||
Thus [end] the six months. || 27 ||
In the middle is the Viṣūvan, the twenty-first [stoma], an Agniṣṭoma characterized by the Mahādivākīrtya [sāman]. || 28 ||
Or the Ādityavrata (Sāman). || 29 ||
When the sun has risen, he begins the Prātaranuvāka. || 16.5.30 ||
This day is one on which the Divākīrtya hymn is recited. || 31 ||
The northern wing is reversed; there are three Svarasāman days. || 32 ||
The Viśvajit sacrifice. || 33 ||
There are four types of *śaya* sacrifices: the *trayastriṃśārambhaṇa*, and the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) consisting of sixty [stomas]. || 34 ||
Four Abhiplava periods in reverse order constitute one month. || 35 ||
He is accompanied by a second, a third, a fourth, and a fifth. || 36 ||
The two Abhiplava [periods] are the highest when they are combined. || 37 ||
The Gauh and Āyus are two days. || 38 ||

16.1 Now begins the first chapter of the sixteenth book. I joyfully bow to the Lord of Sages, the preceptor known as Hiraṇyakeśin—an ocean of compassion, a knower of the meaning of the Sūtras, the foremost of all perfected beings attended by disciples, and the bliss of radiant consciousness and bliss. The expiation has been declared in the fifteenth book; thereafter, in this sixteenth book, he explains the procedure for the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha). Now the ritual of the twelve-day sacrifice is stated:
"By means of the twelve-day sacrifice, one is indeed born again. (1)

The ritual procedure for the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha-yāga*) is to be inferred from this *sūtra*. Accordingly, the injunction is heard in the *Āraṇyaka* branch of the Veda: "He who desires, 'May I be propagated,' should sacrifice with the twelve-night rite; he is indeed propagated" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 7.2.5; 7.2.9). That twelve-night rite is of two kinds: the *samūḍha* (interwoven) and the *nyūḍha* (separated). Among these, the method of the *samūḍha* has been shown by the author of the *sūtra*: "We shall explain the *tryanīkā* (the threefold sequence). The opening day (*prāyaṇīya*) and the concluding day (*udayanīya*), as well as the tenth day, have the cups for Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyava*) first."

"Now, for the other nine days, the first day has the *Aindravāyava* cup at its head; then the *Śukra* at its head, and then the *Āgrayaṇa* at its head. In this manner, the threefold series (*trikhyanīkā*) proceeds by rotation, provided it is not interwoven (*avyūḍha*). Having thus described the method of the interwoven (*samūḍha*) sacrifice, he also showed the method of the non-interwoven (*vyūḍha*) sacrifice with the same [text]: "In the non-interwoven (*vyūḍha*), the *Prāyaṇīya* and *Udayanīya* days have the *Aindravāyava* at their heads; then for the other twelve days, the first day has the *Aindravāyava* at its head."

Now, there is the sequence beginning with the *śukra*, then two sequences beginning with the *āgrayaṇa*; then the sequence beginning with the *aindravāyava*, then two sequences beginning with the *śukra*; then the sequence beginning with the *āgrayaṇa*, then two sequences beginning with the *aindravāyava*. Thus [it is said]. || 1 ||
Now he praises the twelve-day rite by way of another aspect: "He attains preeminence, for it indeed attends upon him. (2)

The twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) which exists is the sacrifice of the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*). And so it is heard in another recension: "This twelve-day sacrifice is indeed the sacrifice of the eldest; he who performs it first is the most excellent among the gods" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 19.3). || 2 ||
And the Ahīna sacrifice is also a Sattra. ||3||

This twelve-night sacrifice (*dvādaśarātra*) is of two kinds: that which has the form of a *satra* and that which has the form of an *ahīna*. Now, it is indeed the case that the twelve-day sacrifice possesses both the nature of an *ahīna* and the nature of a *satra*. Regarding this very point, it is considered: is there no difference in the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the *ahīna* and the *satra*, or is there? On this matter, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is no difference. Why? Because they are identical in being a repetition of the *jyotiṣṭoma*.

Just as the nature of the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice applies to the repetition of the *ahīna* sacrifices ranging from the two-night (*dvirātra*) up to the eleven-night (*ekādaśarātra*), so too it would apply to the *satra* sacrifices beginning with the thirteen-night (*trayodaśarātra*). To this we reply: the two injunctions—"they should sit" (*āsīran*) and "they should enter" (*upeyuḥ*)—as well as the plurality of sacrificers, constitute the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of a *satra*. The injunction to "sacrifice" (*yajati*) and the absence of an injunction for a plurality of sacrificers constitute the defining characteristic of an *ahīna*. This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), because these two characteristics are never found to deviate from their respective categories in Vedic usage. || 3 ||
His [penance] is explained as being like that of fire. || 4 ||
For that twelve-day sacrifice, the fire-altar is fixed according to either the Kāṭhaka or the [Taittirīya] tradition.
Those whose prosperity has departed should perform sacrifices according to their desire.

One who has lost his fortune (*gataśrī*) is one from whom prosperity has departed; he is a village leader (*grāmaṇī*) or a member of the royal class (*rājanya*). The plural form "those who have lost their fortune" (*gataśriyaḥ*) is used because, according to the rule, a *sattra* sacrifice must have multiple sacrificers; this is the intended meaning. || 5 ||

Whatever desire one may have when he sacrifices with a *chandas*, that desire of his is fulfilled. Regarding the injunction "he sacrifices" and "they sacrifice": it is understood that if one were not an ascetic (*tapasvin*), his sacrifice would be disjointed; therefore, by [the rule] "one should be an ascetic," he brings the sacrifice itself into union. Thus it is known. 6. *Note: The text provided contains a fragmentary reference to Mahādeva Śāstrī’s commentary, *Payogacandrikā*, which is integrated into the translation for context.*

"He sacrifices" is said with reference to the sacrificer, because of the singular number. The plural number [is used] due to the multiplicity of sacrificers according to the rule to be stated hereafter. Thus, only he who is an ascetic is qualified [for this]. || 6 ||
One who is fat undergoes initiation; one who is emaciated performs the sacrifice.

The word *pīva* (fat) is well known in the sense of bestowing physical strength. One who is emaciated performs sacrifice; thus, through the drying up of the bodily constituents such as flesh, there occurs the destruction of sin. And so it has been concluded by Āśvalāyana: "When the initiated one becomes emaciated, then he becomes fit for sacrifice. (7)

In this context, an option regarding the number of initiations (*dīkṣā*) and so forth is obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction), such as "one initiation" or "three initiations," because such an option is heard in the archetype (*prakṛti*). To set aside that option, the author formulates a rule for the fixed number of initiations:
"One who desires knowledge for the sake of a specific result (*kāmyā vidyā*) desires forty-eight [initiations]. (Sūtra 8)

The *kāmyā* sacrifice knows that the accusative case should be used here to denote continuous connection (*atyanta-saṃyoga*) for a period of forty-eight days. In the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), each day—including its *dīkṣā* and *upasad* rites—would be concluded as a separate action, because each of those [days] has the *jyotiṣṭoma* as its archetype (JS 11.4.5). || 8 ||
Fifteen should undergo initiation; they have the half-month as their abode.
The grammatical connection is "he causes to step. The term *āyatanāḥ* means "measured."
