The author of the Bhāṣya explains: "The *yājamāna* duties belong to whichever person has been initiated (*dīkṣita*). Now, a question arises: should those desiring the fruit perform the *satras* individually one by one, or should many do so collectively?

Regarding the plural number [in the injunction] for the sake of favoring the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), it might be argued that since in the world many lovers perform a *sattra* sacrifice even one by one, this statement can be understood as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) with that intention; thus, they should perform it individually. This is not so. For the number of agents residing in the verb is intended here as well, as a constituent part of the performance, just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Indeed, there is no reason for that number not to be intended. And that [number] sublates the singularity obtained through the *codaka*. Therefore, many should perform it. (Jaimini Sūtra 10.6.14) || 14 ||
Furthermore, he censures excessive attachment to the sacrifice due to an intense greed for receiving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*):
"Therefore, one should not officiate at the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) for the sake of warding off evil. (15)

Since the acceptance of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) is prohibited for one who has officiated at a twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), for that reason, having become a priest, one should not act as the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) by means of the twelve-day rite. This non-officiating serves to bring about the removal of evil. However, if one does officiate, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed in the scriptures must be performed. Such is the distinction between the *sannāha* and the *ahīna*: in the case of a sacrificial session (*sattra*), there is no acceptance of fees even for this person himself, who is the sacrificer.

However, since accepting a gift when it is not deficient (ahīna) is defective because the gift exists [in that context], one must perform an expiation after having accepted it. Now, regarding the doubt as to whether the priestly functions (*ārtvijya*) in that case are to be performed by others or by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) himself: based on the favor of the *codaka* (the rule of extension), they should be performed by others. As for the statement, "Those who are the sacrificers are the priests," this is an injunction for the priestly functions intended as a consecratory rite (*saṃskāra*) directed toward the sacrificers denoted by the word "those" (*ye*), and not an injunction for the sacrificers with respect to the priestly functions themselves. Therefore, the priestly functions must be performed by others.

Alternatively, one might argue that by the statement "the Adhvaryu, having initiated the householder," initiation is prescribed for the purpose of purifying the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); therefore, because of that connection, the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) refers to the sacrificial materials themselves, and this is a restatement (*anuvāda*). This is not so, because it would result in the performance of an unprecedented function (*aprākṛta-kāryatva*) and because the injunction would be rendered meaningless. Furthermore, the office of the officiating priest cannot be a purifier of the sacrificer, precisely because that too would result in the performance of an unprecedented function. Therefore, the officiating priests are prescribed as the performers of the very same functions that belong to the sacrificer in the archetypal rite.

Therefore, there is the sublation of other [elements] not obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction). [The text] enjoins the form of the *ahīna* for that twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*):
"He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the twelve-day [sacrifice]... (Jaimini Sūtra 10.5.16).
In this regard, he praises feeling. || 16 ||
The sacrificer prospers. || 17 ||

Any other person among the Ṛtviks also attains prosperity through the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha). In the previous case, because there is a plurality of sacrificers and because it is prescribed by a *codanā* [injunction] as a *sattra*, the twelve-day sacrifice has the character of a *sattra*. Here, however, because there is only one sacrificer and it is prescribed by a *codanā* as a *yajati* [sacrifice], it has the character of an *ahīna*; this is the distinction. Now, regarding the performance of the twelve-day sacrifice in the form of a *sattra*, he states the prohibition of accepting sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*): "He who, knowing thus, accepts [fees] for the twelve-day sacrifice [is not tainted]. (18)

For there is a prohibition: "He who accepts [gifts] at a *sattra* is indeed a corpse-eater" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 7.2.10). Indeed, since those who are the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the designation of "officiating priest" exists alongside the designation of "sacrificer. For this very reason, in another recensional branch (*śākhā*), they are referred to by terms such as "Adhvaryu" and "Brahman" in passages such as: "Having initiated the master of the house (*gṛhapati*), he initiates the Brahman," and so forth.

This being the case, one who accepts a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) with the notion that he is a priest (*ṛtvij*), like one performing a different sacrifice, becomes a receiver who incurs the same transgression as one who eats the flesh of a corpse. Here, "corpse" does not refer to the carcass of a five-toed animal, but rather to the corpse of a human being or similar beings. Furthermore, whatever food is consumed by him becomes as if it were [the flesh] of a cow; the meaning is that his transgression is equal to that of eating beef.

Furthermore, regarding the recipient: if the bronze vessel or container in which they hold the food has not been purified according to the method prescribed in the scriptures, then, due to the absence of purification, excessive impurity arises in the house associated with that vessel; the meaning is that those who deal with such a vessel incur a greater transgression. (18) Having thus strengthened the rule against giving sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) by means of the prohibition, he now strengthens the rule for the *ahīna* sacrifice by identifying it with the status of the sacrificer, speaking with reference to both the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the sacrificer. (19)

Because of the Vedic injunction, "One alone should sacrifice" (TaiSaṃ 7.2.10), it is established that the *ahīna* sacrifice belongs to a single performer, since he alone is the agent and the recipient of the fruit. || 19 ||
Now, they enter upon the sacrificial session of seventeen initiated Brahmins who sit together. 16.1.20.

By nature, the office of the officiating priest (*ātvijya*) is established as being performed by Brāhmaṇas (Jaimini Sūtra 6.6.3). Since such [an office] serves as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the sacrificer, there is the possibility of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas [acting as priests]. Regarding the statement "there are seventeen Sadasyas," the meaning is that because they are mentioned in the Kauṣītaki recension and because it is a different recension, seventeen persons are initiated (*dīkṣita*) in this ritual. || 20 ||
Or rather, everyone who has performed their first desired sacrifice is a *gṛhapati*. (Section 1) 21.

Āpastamba also says the same: "All officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) must have already performed their first sacrifice; therefore they call it the 'Jyeṣṭha-yajña' (the eldest sacrifice)" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.1.1). Thus, because it has been sacrificed to as the eldest and because it has been sacrificed to first, this Agniṣṭoma is the Jyeṣṭha-yajña; the meaning is that it serves as the fundamental archetype (*mūla-prakṛti*) for all [sacrifices] such as the Ukthya and others. By this, it follows that all officiating priests must indeed be *āhitāgnis* (those who have consecrated the sacred fires). —Satyāṣāḍha-viracita Śrautasūtra, [16th Praśna] 350.

"Command" (codanā) means that one should choose them. Alternatively, the Mīmāṃsakas hold that since the sacrificial fires (vihāra)—even those belonging to others—are capable of assisting another, the twelve-day sattra sacrifice could be performed even by those who have not maintained their own sacred fires (anāhitāgni). || 21 ||
All should perform the duties of the sacrificer through the office of the officiating priests, provided it is not prohibited. || 22 ||
All the officiating priests shall perform the ritual acts of the sacrificer without contradiction. || 22 ||

Just as for the householder there are [acts] for the sake of others, such as the anointing of the sacrificial post and the *mṛtuyājyā* offering—in such cases, when there is a conflict of duties, the duty of the majority is to be followed (or rather, that of the householder). || 23 ||

Regarding that as well, some say it is "without modification" because it is for the sake of another. The householder is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). This has been explained. (23) He states the restriction obtained through the *codaka* rule regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses:
"They should perform [the rite] according to the ritual procedure for the *sāmidhenīs* belonging to the householder alone. (24)

Regarding this, there is a specific rule in the *Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra*: "The *Gṛhapati* alone should proceed according to the ritual procedure for the *sāmidhenī* verses and the ritual procedure for the portions (*avadāna*); and whatever other [acts] are of this nature [should be done by him]" (*ĀpaŚS* 21.2.3). The *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* states: "One should recite seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses for him" (*AiB* 19.4). Thus, the ritual procedure for the *sāmidhenīs* belongs to the *Gṛhapati* alone. Some, having performed the sacrifice for their own benefit with the verse beginning "Consciousness is the ladle" (*cittiḥ sruk*), are then touched by the group (*gaṇa*) while they are being led forward.

In the mantra beginning with *patireva samārabhya*, [the formula] for the lords of the sacrifice is *indrāvāntsvāha*. The Hotṛ [is addressed] as *bhārgava-cyāvana-āpnavāna-aurva-jāmadagnya*. One view is that the selection of the ancestral seers (*ārṣeya-varaṇa*) may be performed by those of other lineages (*gotra*) as long as they do not turn back [from the ritual]. This should also be understood as the case in the *Āśvalāyanakalpa*. Because of the identity of Agni in the mantra *agne mahāṃ asi*, at that time there is a collective selection (*tantra*) for those of the same lineage (*samānagotra*); for others, it is distinct. In a common subject matter, the archetype (*prakṛti*) is either by way of a collective procedure (*tantra*) or by modification (*ūha*). 24.
"O Varuṇa, you... is the concluding *sāmidhenī* verse for the Vasiṣṭhas and the *rājanyas*; "Offer the oblation... is for the other *gotras*.
The phrase "he recites the *sāmidhenī* verses and the *paridhānīyā* verse three times each" is connected to both [the morning and evening pressings]. || 25 ||
The second fore-offering (prayāja) is the Nārāśaṃsa for the Vasiṣṭhas and Śunakas; it is the Tanūnapāt for other lineages (gotras).

The same is the case in the *Āpastamba* [Śrautasūtra] as well. Now, an objection is raised: "For the Kṣatriyas, the Vāsiṣṭhas, and others, the second *prayāja* is the *nārāśaṃsa*; for others, it is the *tanūnapāt*," and so forth. Since this rule is not specifically prescribed for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, it becomes applicable in the context of *satras* (sacrificial sessions) involving multiple performers; therein a doubt arises: may those of different ritual manuals (*kalpa*) perform the *satra* collectively, or must they be of identical ritual manuals?

For that purpose, this is investigated: are the Vāsiṣṭhas and others enjoined as performers (*kartṛ*) with respect to the Nārāśaṃsa and other rites as their constituent parts (*aṅga*), or is the Nārāśaṃsa and so forth enjoined for the sake of the Vāsiṣṭhas and others? In that regard, if they were enjoined for the sake of the Vāsiṣṭhas, there would be the necessity of postulating a result (*phala-kalpanā*).

[Paṭala 1] Accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin: 351. Due to the context and because it would otherwise subvert the ritual framework (*prakaraṇa*), only those belonging to the Vasiṣṭha lineage and others are enjoined as subordinate parts (*aṅga*) to the Nārāśaṃsa and other rites. Furthermore, the genitive case denotes a relationship. And it is established that in sacrificial sessions (*satra*), each of the participants (*sattriṇaḥ*) possesses individual agency (*kartṛtva*).

Therefore, since the *nārāśaṃsa* [offering] performed by those who are not Vasiṣṭhas is indeed performed by a Vasiṣṭha as well, it remains unimpaired; likewise, the *tanūnapāt* [offering] is performed by others. Consequently, one might argue that even those belonging to different *kalpas* (ritual traditions) would be entitled to perform the rite by resorting to some particular *kalpa*. To this we reply: the *nārāśaṃsa* and other offerings are enjoined for the sake of the Vasiṣṭhas and others, who are designated as the owners [of the sacrifice]. This "being for the sake of" (*tādarthya*) is established through the mediation of the benefit to the sacrifice (*ṛtupakāra*); thus, there is no occasion for the assumption of a separate result (*phala*).

And thus, because the meaning of the verbal root is enjoined elsewhere [in the primary injunction], there is a proximate injunction. However, if the Vāsiṣṭha and others were enjoined with reference to the *prayāja* offerings, there would be an injunction of something else regarding the meaning of the verbal root, resulting in an injunction of a remote matter. Consequently, in a *sattra*, if one were to resort to a different ritual procedure (*kalpa*), the other participants would not obtain the benefit for the sacrifice through that [procedure], and thus the sacrifice, being deficient, would not accomplish its fruit. Therefore, only those of identical ritual procedures (*tulyakalpa*) have the entitlement. || 26 ||
Those intending to offer the Sāvitra oblations should pour the fires together; having offered them, they should separate them again.
"He offers the Sāvitra oblations" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1)—this is the injunction pertaining to the fire ritual. || 27 ||

Those intending to sacrifice with animals should pile [the fires] together before the sacrifice; or they may pile them together after having sacrificed; or the householder alone may pile the two forest fires (araṇis) together.

"By means of the animals" means for the sake of five animals each. All should perform the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). In rites such as the murmuring of prayers (*japa*), the summoning (*āmantraṇa*), and the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), first comes the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) and then the duty of the sacrificer; however, in the two forest-dwellers (*araṇya*), either the master of the house (*gṛhapati*) or [another] may do so. The meaning is that there should be only one person subject to the rules regarding the consigning of the fires (*samāropaṇa*) and so forth. || 28 ||

"Whatever fire shall be born from this [wood], let that belong to us all; whatever we shall win by this sacrifice, by this animal-binding rite (paśubandha), let that be common to us all. Let it be equal for us all; as for whoever commits evil in this way, let it be his alone"—thus it was said. (29)

The meaning is that for that purpose, the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ-homa and other rites are performed like those of the Nirūḍhapaśubandha sacrifice, whether by means of the Paśubandha or the Vāyavya sacrifice. || 29 ||
The householder performs the installation; either he himself or another person acts as the householder. 16.1.30.

The intention is that the right to kindle the fires belongs only to the householder himself—either from the two fire-sticks or from his own body—while for others, it is merely the act of taking hold [of the fire]. ||30||
Of all [beings]. || 31 ||

[This applies] only to the officiating priests (ṛtvij). Now, in order to prescribe the specific time for initiation (dīkṣā) in the twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha), he sets forth the opinion of another school: "They undergo initiation in the cool season (śiśira); they emerge [from the vow] in the spring (vasanta)," so it is known.

352: ... *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the 16th Praśna, regarding the *Dīkṣā*]: "She departed from the gods; she was yoked with the two months of spring" (*AiB* 1.4), etc., thus the *Bṛhadbrāhmaṇa* introduces [the topic]. It is the same in the *Āpastamba* [Sūtra] as well. || 32 ||
The winter season is indeed its commencement, and the spring is its conclusion.
"The winter is its departure and the spring is its rising," so says the Kāṭhaka Brāhmaṇa (34.9).
It is known from scripture: "Those who, knowing thus, undergo initiation in the winter and rise [from it] in the spring, prosper. (34)
This Vedic scripture has been cited in praise of initiation during the winter season.
When six nights of the waxing fortnight have dawned, those intending to perform the sacrifice should undergo initiation.

Based on this, the ritual application (*prayoga*) following the view of the *Mahāgni* is as follows: At least seventeen men, who have not yet performed their first sacrifice, having offered at the *ekāṣṭakā* of the *śiśira* season, should then—having consigned the fires either into themselves or into two churning-sticks (*araṇī*)—go together to one place. In the presence of their own fires, all of them, accompanied by their wives, make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "We shall perform the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) as a sacrificial session (*sattra*) involving the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*), for the sake of attaining progeny; heaven is also the fruit. [The ritual continues with] the lightning [rite]. There is no selection of a *somapravāka*; there is no selection of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

However, among ourselves, we should address one another through the sequence of initiations (*dīkṣā*), beginning with "You are the householder" and "You are the Brahman," and so forth; there is no *madhuparka* offering. The sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), the worship of the deities (*devatopasthāna*), and the specification of materials are performed with common property. Having performed the *nāndīśrāddha*, the householder churns the fire as before and spreads it out. Regarding those seeking initiation, a certain animal sacrifice is prescribed: "Before the initiation, he immolates an animal dedicated to Prajāpati" (AiB 19.4).

The man who desires initiation (dīkṣā) should, prior to the commencement of the initiation, sacrifice an animal dedicated to Prajāpati. For the Dvādaśāha sacrifice is of two kinds: that involving the piling of the fire-altar (agnicitya) and that without the piling of the fire-altar. In that case, the animal sacrifice is to be understood as occurring in connection with the piling of the fire-altar; however, in our own school (śākhā), the animal dedicated to Vāyu is prescribed. First, having performed the rites from the Sāvitra oblations up to the gathering of the sacrificial materials (sambharaṇa), one should carry away the human head and smear it with clay; then, on the Parvan day, as before.

Having placed [the fires] together and reached the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), thinking, "We shall sacrifice with the animal offering," they move down from there, prepare the sacrificial ground as before, churn the fire, and place it in its proper station.

Having performed the mutual consultation and the mixing of the fires, they perform the rites beginning with the initiation offering (*dīkṣaṇīyā*). Regarding the fire that will be produced from here, they say: "May it belong to us all; what we shall win by this sacrifice, by this session (*sattra*," so they speak). (Section 2) At this consultation, the Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati, initiates those who perform the central duties—the Hotṛ, the Brahman, and the Udgātṛ.

The Pratiprasthātṛ, having initiated the Adhvaryu, initiates the "half-sharers": the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and the Stotṛ. The Neṣṭṛ, having initiated the Pratiprasthātṛ, initiates the "third-sharers": the Acchāvāka, the Āgnīdhra, and the Pratihartṛ. The Unnetṛ [initiates the remaining ones].
[End of] Paṭala 1, accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. 353.

Having initiated the Neṣṭṛ, he initiates the Grāvastut, the Potṛ, and the Subrahmaṇya, who are entitled to a quarter-share. Then the Pratiprasthātṛ initiates him [the Neṣṭṛ]. Or another initiated Brāhmaṇa may do so; thus they should be initiated in this successive order. He does not conclude one by one because of the lack of a continuous ritual sequence (*atantrībhāva*). Because of the intervention of those of a different lineage (*gotra*), the initiation of those of the same lineage who share a common *ṛṣi* ancestor is repeated. They initiate the wives in a single place. Their ritual duties are explained by the rules pertaining to the sacrificer. 36.

In this regard, the procedure for the *davihoma*, the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), and the *iṣṭi* is as follows: all the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) should perform the duties of the sacrificer. Because of the scriptural injunction that "all should perform [the rites] from 'I take Agni' (*agniṃ gṛhṇāmi*) up to the end of the *gomajjapa*, after the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) have performed their priestly functions (*āvijya*), the sacrificer's duties follow. The binding of the girdles (*yoktra-bandhana*) for all the wives (*patnī*) occurs according to the order of initiation (*dīkṣā*). The rest has been explained. || 36 ||
Some prescribe the consecration (dīkṣā) for each successive day. || 37 ||
Every day, immediately. || 37 ||
He causes him to step forward with "On the second day," "On the third day," and so on, until the twelfth day.
There is an option regarding the fire: one may be initiated on the second day or on the third day, thus according to one's desire up to the twelfth day.

One should undergo initiation as the thirteenth during the Upasads. Therefore, those being initiated must become Brahmins; having piled up the fires and performed the ritual scattering, they should proceed with the self-purification for twelve days of initiation. 39.

Regarding the specific details of the initiation (*dīkṣā*), [the text] prescribes the particular features of the *upasad* rites, stating: "One should be initiated for twelve nights" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 7.2.10). It further explains: "These twelve *upasad*s are indeed fourfold; there are three sets of three nights. By those which are the first, one gathers the sacrifice; by those which are the second, one undertakes the sacrifice; by those which are the third, one cleanses the vessels; and by those which are the fourth, one purifies oneself from within" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 7.2.10).

In this context, there are the *upasads* to be performed, which are accomplished over twelve days; these are divided fourfold into groups of three. Among them, by means of the three belonging to the first group, the preparation of the sacrificial implements is carried out. By means of the three belonging to the second group, one commences the sacrifice. By means of the three belonging to the third group, one purifies the sacrificial vessels. By means of the three belonging to the fourth group, one effects internal purification of oneself. || 39 ||
No instruction regarding the removal of the sacrificial grass exists when the sacrifice has already commenced.
At a Sattra sacrifice, they do not send out the Sāṃnāyya offerings.
The sixteenth is Somavikrayaṇī. || 41 ||
The cow for the purchase of Soma is sixteen years old. || 41 ||
On the twelfth day, he purchases the King (Soma).
Having purchased the king (Soma), he places him upon the cart, saying, "I have bound you for twelve days."
354. Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[In the sixteenth praśna: There are twelve upasad days. 43.

The word "twelve-day sacrifice" (*dvādaśāha*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Āpastamba states: "During the *upasads* of the twelve-day sacrifice, he recites the *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas. ||43||
He piles the fire-altar with the anūpasada bricks. || 44 ||
This is to be explained as before. || 44 ||
For two days, there is one layer each. || 45 ||
For two days or three days, each layer is constructed one at a time. || 45 ||
The best [attainment] lasts for four days. || 46 ||
It becomes consciousness. || 46 ||
For three nights, they observe the vow of four teats. || 47 ||
The word *āṭ* denotes a limit. || 47 ||
In this way, there are those with three breasts, those with two breasts, and those with one breast. ||48||
The remaining [vows] consist of drinking from four teats, three teats, two teats, and one teat respectively; that is, these vows are observed for three days each. || 18 ||
If one desires to undertake the vow again, one should pour out a single ladleful of curdled milk.
If one should desire to fulfill their vow, having drawn up one vessel of curd, he should not draw up another. Thus [it is said]. 49.
There are twenty-one roof-coverings. || 16.1.50 ||

"The Ekaviṃśa is the foundation of the stomas" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.2.1). Because the Jyotis-sacrifices, such as the Trivṛt and others, are included therein, it serves the purpose of providing a foundation. Some explain that the genitive case found in the mantra "the seat of Indra" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.3.1) is used here because of the inclusion of the *taddhita* suffix denoting a deity. Others maintain that this indicates a passage from another recensional branch (*śākhā*) of the Brāhmaṇa. "He places the roof-covering" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.30): he places a mat on top for the purpose of covering.
For it is always connected with the deity Indra; therefore, the *sadas* is called the "seat of Indra," because of Indra's preeminence. || 50 ||
The two pressing-boards are perforated. (Section 3) ||51||
Thus ends the first chapter in the sixteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.

Because one strikes (*hana*) for the purpose of heating (*saṃtapaṇa*), therefore one does not join together the two pressing-boards (*adhiṣavaṇa-phalaka*); having pierced them, one does not weave them through. "That he does not join together the two pressing-boards" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.2.11)—so says the Brāhmaṇa. The remainder of the rule is that "the two pressing-boards are to be joined together," as stated in the Sūtra. Thus ends the first Paṭala in the sixteenth Praśna of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.
Chapter Two [of the Second Praśna], accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.
Now begins the second chapter of the sixteenth book.
The single sacrificial post (*ekayūpa*) has been explained.
He has gone. || 1 ||
If there should be a set of eleven sacrificial posts (yūpaikādaśinī), one should erect each post on a successive day, or all of them together.
Every day, immediately [after the sacrifice], he sets up the sacrificial post (yūpa); that is, he raises it. The singular number is used with reference to a single sacrificial post. || 2 ||

On the day of the fast (aupavasathya), as the animals are being immolated day after day, the animal intended for the next day's sacrifice should be brought forward each day. On the day of the concluding rite (udayanīya), he should dedicate the animal at the very spot where the fire was established.

Because he lies down here after approaching—that which is called the *upaśaya* (resting-place) because "the gods, having approached, lay down against the Asuras"—it is derived with the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134. Therefore, the meaning is that by the fact that he rests upon the *upaśaya* to the south, it serves for the removal of his rival (*bhrātṛvya*). || 3 ||
On the following day, the Jyotiṣṭoma is expanded.

At the time of the cleansing of the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), they desire eleven posts for all [the animals], ending with the one standing near the fire (*agniṣṭha*). The anointing of the posts and the placing of the *gṛhapati*’s bed—all these he places once only to the south of all [the posts]. In this view, on the day of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, there is no modification (*anūha*) regarding the formulas of the great fires up to the spreading of the grass (*paristaraṇa*), because they are taught for the purpose of the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*). Some, however, desire modification. But modification applies to those words denoting the sacrificer and even to those denoting Agni in specific formulas; [it applies] to all [of them].
Roha says: Regarding the designation of the sacrificer, [it is said] "on the following day it is extended"; having understood this at the great night, [the sacrifice] is the Jyotiṣṭoma. ||4||

The Vaiśvānara is an Atirātra sacrifice. At the time of bringing down [the Soma], he ties up as much of the King [Soma] as has been obtained for the one-day sacrifice in another vessel and brings it down. He places the other [portion] back in its place.

The *vaiśvānara-prāyaṇīya* is an *atirātra* sacrifice, seen by Vaiśvānara. At the time of setting out the Soma vessels, having placed the *dhruva* vessel, the *ṣoḍaśī* vessel is carried forward by the sacrificer with the formula, "To the abode of the waters, to the light" (*apāṃ kṣayālokaṃ yajamānenābhi vahata*), and so forth. There are two animal-vessels (*pāśuka-pātra*) consisting of the two *yūpa-raśanā* (sacrificial post-ropes) and one animal. In this same manner, there are the *kumbhī* (pot) and other such items.

After the king has been brought down, when the [Soma] has been prepared, he ties as much Soma as he considers sufficient for one day into another garment; having tied it into that other garment and having placed it upon [the cart], he brings it down. || 5 || 6 ||
In this manner it is performed day after day; [it is] for the daily release from the bonds of yoga. || 7 ||

Thus, having performed [the rite] every day with the exception of the *uttama* [offering], everything beginning with "I yoke the fire" (*agnim yunajmi*) is to be done according to the archetype (*prakṛti*). || 7 ||
On the first day he yokes; on the last day he unyokes—so say some.
356. This ritual procedure (kalpa) belongs to another Vedic branch (śākhā). [Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—16th Praśna] 4.

At the Prāyaṇīya and Udayanīya Atirātra sacrifices, and on the tenth day, he draws the Pṛśni-prāṇagraha cups. Having measured out the original Yajus-measure with the first formula while the Soma is being pressed—saying, "Thou art Vāyu, named Prāṇa"—he measures ten Pṛśni-measures with ten formulas. Having measured with each successive subsequent Yajus-measure, he measures ten Prāṇagraha-measures with the ten formulas beginning, "This one is Bhuvas in front. || 16.2.10 ||

In a low voice, at the time of measuring, during the *pṛśni* and *prāṇagraha* [rituals], the measurement is as follows: having recited the original *yajus*-measurement formula and having said "For Indra, thee, the slayer of Vṛtra," he measures ten measurements with the ten *pṛśni-nahas* formulas beginning with "Thou art Vāyu, named Prāṇa" and ending with "Thee for the light of Truth. In every case where there is a new ninth measurement, having recited the subsequent *yajus*-measurement formula and having said "For Indra, thee, the conqueror of Vṛtra," he [measures] with the ten *prāṇagraha* formulas beginning with "This one was in front."

He measures ten measures. The mantras are: "This one here before [is] the world; with thee, taken by Prajāpati, I take the breath," and so forth. Having spoken thus, he interlinks the measures. Having said, "For Indra, thee, the overcomer of enemies," he recites ten [measures] ending with, "Thou art Vāyu, named Breath... from light. [Then] ten [measures] ending with, "For Indra, thee, accompanied by the Ādityas; this one here before [is] the world; I take," and so forth. [Finally] ten names [of measures] beginning with, "For Indra, thee, accompanied by the Viśvedevas; thou art Vāyu," as before.
Then, five times, [he performed] the silent [recitation] (*tūṣṇīm*) for all the measurements (*māna*) and the silent [rites] (*tūṣṇīka*), each consisting of nine and nine parts. || 9 || 10 ||
He interlinks it with the subsequent Yajus-measure. || 11 ||
The subsequent position (uttarapakṣa) is for the purpose of providing an alternative view (vikalpa). || 11 ||
We shall now describe the procedure based on the *samūḍha* (interwoven) arrangement, beginning with the words "for the majority [of days], for the morning pressing," and so forth:

the two *atirātra*s—the *prāyaṇīya* and the *udayanīya*—as well as the tenth day, have the cups beginning with the *aindravāyava*. Now, among the other nine days, the first day has the cups beginning with the *aindravāyava*, then the next has the cups beginning with the *śukra*, and then the next has the cups beginning with the *āgrayaṇa*; thus the threefold series (*tryanīkā*) revolves three times in the *chandasa* (the interwoven order). (Section 4, Sūtra 12)

At the time of the Āgrayaṇa-graha, when the draught for Indra and Vāyu has been taken, [the Adhvaryu recites]: "He purifies himself for Heaven and Earth; he purifies himself for these pressing sacrificers, for me," and so forth; "Speech in the cattle, breath in the cattle, offspring in me and in the sacrificer," and so forth. At the time of the animal sacrifice, the victim for Agni belongs to all. Therein, the modification (*ūha*) is: "Agni is the god of these pressing sacrificers. For all [sacrificers], the portion from "Paribhūr agniḥ" up to "śrutaḥ tvam asi" remains the same.

Some [teachers] hold that the two verses beginning with "The two oceans... and so forth are for all [the priests], as are the formulas from "The welfare of the wooden sword (sphya)... up to "...O fathers, come hither," performed by the Adhvaryu and the Brahman after they have completed their officiating duties (*ārtvijya*). At the touching of the *savanīya* offerings, during the ritual procedure for the two deities, the householder alone recites the triad beginning with "Thou art the earth (*bhūḥ*... for all. Regarding the taking hold of the *śukra* cup, the householder alone [recites] "Those two gods, Śukra and...
[and so on]. [End of] Paṭala 2, accompanied by the commentary *Mayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin. Page 317.

When all the sacrificers are moving toward the *thimau* [the place of the offering], there is the eating of the *iḍā* and the consumption of the remnants of the oblation by everyone. At the time of consuming the Soma, all the sacrificers consume the cups (*camasa*s) after having performed the priestly consumption (*ārtvijya-bhakṣaṇa*) and then the sacrificer’s portion (*yājamāna*). It is the same for those seated together. Regarding the *caturhotṛ* formulas and so forth, the formula beginning with "Agniṃ naro" and ending with "dūredṛśaṃ gṛhapatim" is not repeated for each individual, because it serves the purpose of others (*parārthatvāt*). Thus, at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), the performance of the prayers for blessings (*pratyagāśis*) must be carried out by all the sacrificers.

At the Mādhyandina Jyotiṣṭoma, one should perform the *hiṃ* for all [verses] beginning with the Cāturhotra; then, after performing the *dadhidharma* consumption for all with the formulas "Suparṇo 'si" and "Viṣṇo tvam naḥ," and having offered the two *dakṣiṇā* oblations, one should recite "Ud u tyaṃ" and "Citram" etc., while omitting the portion beginning with "Vaḥ."

The sacrificers, carrying black antelope skins and bows, proceed by the southern path. Having gone northward between the Āgnīdhra fire and the Sadas, he says, "O Agni, accept the gift for the Gṛhapati. Then, having passed between the Tīvrīvat altar and the Utkara, he proceeds southward. This is the southern path. Thence, the gifts for the Sadasyas and the Adhvaryu are from the Gṛhapati alone; however, there is no separate sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the *ṛtvij* priests, because there is no separate selection (*varaṇa*) of them.

"Thus day by day," says Āpastamba. There is no horn-seat (*viṣāṇāsana*) in the Vaiśvakarman sacrifices; the modification (*ūha*) is "the lords of the sacrifice. The remainder is as before. The third pressing begins with the *āditya* cup; may Agni protect the sacrificers as they sit. "O All-Gods, to those dwelling in the dwelling, grant protection"—this is the touching of the *āditya* cups, and the bringing of the *āśira* milk belongs to the householder alone. Some desire the drinking and the murmuring of the prayer for all [the priests]. In such cases, the holding of the Hotṛ’s cup is by means of a stream, and the offerings belong to the householder alone.

—Some say that for all [the priests], there is the *māna* (measuring) and the *sarpaṇa* (creeping). Starting from Brahmā, with the words "for life, *hiṃkuru*," there is the offering of the *sabaiṣika* (the portion for all). For all, there is the recitation of "Homage to you, O Fathers" (*namo vaḥ pitaraḥ*). The *baḍhotā* (the one who says "well-said") belongs to the *gṛhapati* (householder). Among the *agnidevatya* (deities of fire), there are blessings for the sacrificers. In the *yajñāyajñiya* chant, once it has been introduced with the *prastāva*, then [he recites]: "Homage be to thee; do not harm me. In the case of daily performance, there is the bringing of the *paujanī* (water for washing) for all the wives; at the time of drawing the cups, he draws them separately.

At this time, he takes possession of the northern dwelling (uttarāvasati) with the formula, "As you are the Sun," and [recites], "The life and the senses of all. While the *atirātra* sacrifice is still in progress, once the cups (*camasa*) have been washed, he causes the milks to be assigned from the northern dwelling using the formulas beginning with, "The cow that yields the sacrificer’s vow-milk," and so forth. He causes the milking of the cows and the milking for the *maitrāvaruṇī* curd; the Pratiprasthātṛ milks the evening milk for the sake of the milk-oblation. These and other such rites are common to both the *sattra* and the *ahīna* sacrifices.

Is there not a *jyānikā* (shifting sequence) in the twelve-day sacrifice? There are the *aindravāyava* cups at the opening (*prāyaṇīya*) and concluding (*udayanīya*) days, and on the tenth day; then, for the remaining nine days, the first day has the *aindravāyava* cup first, then the *śukra* cup first, then the *āgrayaṇa* cup first; then the *śukra* cup first, then the *āgrayaṇa* cup first, then the *aindravāyava* cup first; then the *śukra* cup first, then the *āgrayaṇa* cup first.

Among the twelve days of the Dvādaśāha sacrifice, on the second, third, and fourth days—these three days—the *aindravāyava*, *āśvina*, and *śukrāmanthya* cups are respectively prescribed as the *prāyaṇīya* (opening) and *udayanīya* (concluding) offerings. Among these, the first is occasioned by the *rathantara* sāman, and the second is occasioned by the *bṛhat* sāman; this is established in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Both of these are extended here [to the Dvādaśāha] by the general rule of transfer (*codaka*). Regarding this, there is a fourfold doubt: is it a restatement (*anuvāda*), an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*), an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), or an injunction (*vidhi*)?
Among these, it cannot be a restatement because it would be redundant (*vaiyarthyāt*), since they are already obtained through the general rule.

34. ...The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha... [If it is argued that there is no fault because the phrase "O Maitrāvaruṇa, prepare the sacrificial seats" applies to all three days, we say no, because that would result in three logical defects. If it is argued that this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is intended as a praise for the quality of being the *Āgrayaṇa* cup—which is not otherwise established on the fourth day—we say no, because that would entail the necessity of figurative interpretation (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, just as there is an injunction regarding the status of the *Āgrayaṇa*, so too should it be understood for the other two. Nor should it be said that it is not an injunction because the matter is already established.

Because that injunction is accepted as being non-contingent (*anaimittika*). For it is only the two [injunctions] contingent upon the *rathantara* and so forth that are obtained through the extended application (*codaka*). The purpose, however, is that in the modifications (*vikṛti*) of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), even where there is an absence of the contingency of the *rathantara* and so forth, the state of having the *āindravāyava* cup at the beginning is established. P ||15||.

Now, regarding the expanded arrangement (*vyūḍha*) of the *chandasya* sacrifice: the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* are *atirātra*s with the *aindravāyava* cup first; for the other ten days, the first day has the *aindravāyava* first; then two days have the *śukra* first; then two days have the *āgrayaṇa* first; then two days have the *śukra* first; then two days have the *āgrayaṇa* first; and then two days have the *aindravāyava* first. || 13 ||

The fruit of the ritual action of the *Bharata-dvādaśāha* is as previously described. Regarding the *Bharata-dvādaśāha*, there is a distinction: when it is performed as a *sattra* (sacrificial session), it is accompanied by the *agnicityā* (piling of the fire-altar) and the *pakṣyas* (side-altars); however, when it is performed as an *ahīna* (non-sattra sacrifice), it is without these. If one intends to sacrifice alone, [the procedure is] for one who desires the *Kāṭhaka* or is devoted to the *Kāṭhaka*: twelve *atirātras*, *agniṣṭomas* with the *rathaṃtara-sāman*, and the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* *atirātras* as *agniṣṭomas*. Even so, the *sadas* has twenty-one roofs (*chadis*). There are no *pṛṣṭha*-dharmas (rules pertaining to the *pṛṣṭha-stotras*).

Everything else is as before. The *pṛśni* [cows], the seizing of the breaths (*prāṇagraha*), and so forth—the taking of the *grāhya* cups, the consumption of ghee and honey, the silence (*avivākya*), the mental [cup] (*mānasa*), and so on—take place. The *samūḍha* arrangement of the *anīkas* is as before. Even the *kāṭhaka* [textual division] is not obtained, nor is there a *vyūḍha* [arrangement]. [Objection: Indeed, the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is of two kinds: the *samūḍha* and the *vyūḍha*. Of these, the *samūḍha* has been illustrated previously. Now, the *vyūḍha* is illustrated: the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* [days] have the cups for Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyava*) first.

Now, regarding the other ten-day [sacrificial session], the first day has the *aindravāyava* cup as its opening; then two days have the *śukra* cup as their opening; then [one day] has the *aindravāyava* cup as its opening; then two days have the *śukra* cup as their opening; then [one day] has the *āgrayaṇa* cup as its opening; then two days have the *aindravāyava* cup as their opening. In that regard, it is undisputed that the *samūḍha* (the combined form) serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*). Similarly, when there arises a doubt as to whether the *anyūḍha* (the non-combined form) is also the archetype or a modification (*vikṛti*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is the archetype. Why? Because of the equality of the injunctions.

Just as the *samūḍha* (compact) arrangement is prescribed for the sake of the sacrifice, so too is the *vyūḍha* (expanded) arrangement. There is no distinction here by which the relationship of original form (*prakṛti*) and modification (*vikṛti*) between the two could be determined. Nor is it unprecedented for both arrangements to be original forms, since that is seen in the case of the *ṛkthaṃtara* and *bṛhat* *pṛṣṭha* arrangements within the *agniṣṭoma*—this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). The *vyūḍha* is a modification of the *samūḍha*. Why? Because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

"It is the location of the Aindravāyava cup that is the fourth day in the *nyūḍha* [arrangement]," so it is heard in the scripture. And this occurs only when [the arrangement] is a modified form (*vikṛti*), not otherwise. For instance—in the *nyūḍha*, among the ten days excluding the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya*, that which is the fourth is the location of the Aindravāyava because it is the *āgrayaṇa* day. But in the *samūḍha*, that day is the Aindravāyava because it is the second of the triad in the middle of the nine days.

And it has been stated that this [arrangement], being obtained by the *codaka* (the rule of extension) as a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *vyūḍha*, is brought forward for the purpose of praising the non-mention of the injunction. Furthermore, he who...

[Paṭala 2] With the commentary *Mayūkhamālikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin: 359 If one should desire, "May I become many, may I procreate," for that desire the *nyūḍha* (the 'lowered' arrangement) is prescribed. This being the case, since there is no injunction for it as being for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*)—unlike the *samūḍha* (the 'raised' arrangement)—there is no status as an optional archetype (*prakṛti*) based on the disparity with the *rathantara-bṛhat-pṛṣṭha*. Therefore, the *samūḍha* twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is the archetype. The purpose of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that in the *ahargaṇa* sacrifices, there is an extended application (*atideśa*) of either one of these two. The final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is an extended application of the *samūḍha* alone. (1-5-24). 13. |||

In that context, the food-mantras (*bhakṣamantra*s) and the consecrations for the *pavamāna* cups, as well as the *nigada*s, should be adapted by those [verses] according to whichever meter they belong to, in place of the original; this has been explained by means of the rearrangement (*vyūha*). || 14 ||

Now, an objection: when the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is performed in its expanded form (*vyūḍha*), the formulas for consumption (*bhakṣamantra*), the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), and the sacrificial potsherds (*kapāla*)—all three of which are obtained through the rules of extension (*codaka*)—are present. Among those, in the consumption formulas pertaining to the three pressings (*savana*), the three words "of the *gāyatrī* metre," "of the *triṣṭubh* metre," and "of the *jagatī* metre" are heard. Likewise, in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the enclosing sticks, it is recited: "The middle enclosing stick is of the *gāyatrī* [metre], the southern is of the *triṣṭubh*, and the northern is of the *jagatī*."

Likewise, a statement concerning the sacrificial potsherds (*kapāla*) is recited: "The morning-pressing cake is on eight potsherds, the midday-pressing cake is on eleven potsherds, and the third-pressing cake is on twelve potsherds. Here, by means of the three numbers—eight and so forth—the *gāyatrī* and other meters are brought to mind through the recollection of the syllables of their respective feet.

This being the case, in the section concerning the *vyūḍha* sacrifice, a transposition of meters (*chanda-vyatikrama*) is recited: "In the Veda, they indeed intend the world of one [meter] for another—the *gāyatrī* for the *triṣṭubh*, the *triṣṭubh* for the *jagatī*, and the *jagatī* for the *gāyatrī*. Regarding this, there is a doubt: should this transposition of meters be applied to both the objects—namely the *bhakṣa*, the *pavamāna*, the *paridhi*, and the *kapāla*—and the words denoting meters found in the mantras associated with them, or only to those words themselves?

In this regard, since no specific distinction is mentioned—namely, that [the displacement] applies only to those who have become dull-witted—the first position is that there is a transposition in all cases. Consequently, the draught designated by the word *gāyatrī* (belonging to the morning pressing) takes the place of the draught designated by the word *triṣṭubh* (belonging to the midday pressing); and that [midday draught] takes the place of the one belonging to the third pressing; and that [third-pressing draught] likewise takes the place of the one belonging to the morning pressing. Similarly, the *bahiṣpavamāna* takes the place of the *mādhyaṃdinapavamāna*, and the *mādhyaṃdinapavamāna* takes the place of the *tṛtīyasavana*.

The Ārbhavapavamāna chant occurs at the morning pressing; likewise, the middle enclosing-stick (paridhi) is the thickest on the south side, the smallest and longest on the north side, and the most minute and shortest in the middle. Similarly, the cake on eight potsherds (aṣṭākapāla) is for the midday pressing, the one on eleven potsherds for the third pressing, and the one on twelve potsherds for the morning pressing. This is a transposition of the purpose.

When it is argued that this same principle should be applied to the words of the two mantras as well, we reply: in the sentence beginning with "the meters" (*chandāṃsi*), no transposition of the objects is mentioned; therefore, the transposition applies only to the words *gāyatrī* and so forth occurring within the mantras. As for the application of the words *gāyatrī* and so forth to the actual objects, that is for the purpose of praise, because substances such as the *bhakṣa* (portions to be consumed) lack the primary status of being meters. This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) [Sūtra 10.9.25]. || 14 ||

In the same way, during the subsequent *pṛṣṭhya* days, he takes three *atigrāhya* cups: one for Agni on the twenty-first day, one for Indra on the twenty-ninth day, and one for Sūrya on the thirty-third day.
10. ... The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—... [In the sixteenth book: Because of the statement "in the subsequent [sections] it is by means of questioning," that is the case there. 15.
The Vājasaneyins prescribe for the first three days: "Where the Gaurīvita Sāman is chanted, there one should draw all the cups full."
They recite [this] in the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa. || 16 ||

Now follows the arrangement of the animal sacrifices: on the day of the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra, they immolate an animal for Agni; on the following day, a ewe for Sarasvatī. In this manner, they immolate the distributed sets of eleven animals day by day, with an animal for Agni at the Udayanīya sacrifice for those desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa), and one for Sūrya.

Now the *pākayajña* is being demonstrated. The phrase "they seize [the victim]" (*ālabhante*) refers to the case of multiple sacrificers. On the following day at the great night (*mahārātre*), they perform the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* offerings. Both [offerings] possess the *ṣoḍaśin* chant, because of the statement in the *Āśvalāyana Kalpasūtra*: "The *ṣoḍaśin* belongs to the twelve-day sacrifice; it is the nature of the night. With the mantra beginning "O Agni, lead us" (*agne naya*), he brings down everything equally with the words "I yoke the fire" (*agniṃ yunajmi*). At the time of the silent pressing (*upāṃśu-abhiṣava*), the drawing of the *pṛṣadājya* and the *prāṇa-grahas* has already been explained previously.

Regarding the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* [sacrifices], three ritual options (*kalpa*) have been stated by the author of the Sūtra: "on the tenth day," "on the three days respectively," and "in all cases there is an option. According to some, [the sequence] applies to the three days respectively; according to others, it is an option in every instance. At the time for the animal sacrifice, the *āgneya* section begins with the cup dedicated to Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyavāgra*). Regarding the eleven [animals], the author of the Bhāṣya says that one dedicates the largest one to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*), while the opinion of the Sūtrakāra is that one dedicates the ewe to Sarasvatī (*sārasvatī meṣīm*).

The instruction regarding the *upaśaya* (the sacrificial post left over) for one desiring splendor (*brahmavarcasa*) is as follows: "O Sun, [I take] thee... and "Thy black antelope skin..."—this is the daily measurement according to the alternative view. Regarding the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma: he measures the first [post]; that measurement is for the *prāyaṇīya* sacrifice; in that very spot he measures it, and having released the animal dedicated to Agni, the instruction for the *upaśaya* is to its south. On the following day, he releases the animal dedicated to Sarasvatī; they measure the second [post] for the sake of the sacrificial post intended for the animal. (Desires such as splendor and cattle are desired. Therefore, the completion is to the south of the principal [post].

The *upaśaya* (the resting post) is placed to the south of the sacrificial post of Sarasvatī, prior to the removal of the other posts. After having dedicated the animal for Sarasvatī, there is the instruction regarding the *upaśaya*. In this manner, each subsequent animal is treated on the following day. In the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), it is as previously described. || 17 ||
At the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he gives twelve hundred [cows] every day until the sacrifice is concluded. || 18 ||
The father gives hundreds [of gifts] to one who is not deficient.

In the sacrificial session (sattra), however, having offered the two Dakṣiṇā oblations with the formula, "This cow I lead as a sacrificial fee for prosperity, fame, and the heavenly world," the sacrificers follow the black antelope skins, while others pass by on the right-hand path.

In the case of a sacrificial session (sattra), however, there is this specific distinction. [361] 3rd Paṭala: Accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 361. In the case of a sacrificial session (sattra), however, there is this specific distinction. 19.
In this manner, it is performed day after day.
In the manner thus described. ||20||

On the preceding day, he takes the Vasatīvarī waters for the sake of the following day’s Yajñāyajñīya chant.
