The *Kausurubinda* is a ten-night sacrifice. He who should desire, "May I become all this," should sacrifice with this. For it, there are three *agniṣṭoma*s consisting of the *trivṛt* stoma, three *ukthya*s consisting of the *pañcadaśa* stoma, three *ukthya*s consisting of the *saptadaśa* stoma, and an *atirātra*. The *Pauṇḍarīka* is an eleven-night sacrifice. Its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is ten thousand [cows]. Some say it is a thousand horses. There are ten sacrificial fees. One attains all prosperity; one goes to the state of the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhitā*).

The five-day period is repeated; there should be a six-day period; the thirty-third day consists of two pressings (*savana*s); the final [day] has thirty-six [stotras]; it is a *catuṣṭoma* *agniṣṭoma*; there are three *chandoma*s; the *viśvajit* is an *atirātra* with all the *pṛṣṭha* chants. One should give ten thousand [coins] every day; on the final day, one thousand horses; on the final day, one thousand horses. (Section 22) || 36 || Thus ends the eighth chapter in the seventeenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra*.
Thus ends the seventeenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra*. Om. That is the True Brahman. Salutations to Brahman.
The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha,
together with the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.
Herein begins the first chapter of the seventeenth book.

With joy, I bow to the Lord of Sages, whose face is the radiant bliss of consciousness, who is intent upon the welfare and liberation of all those to be disciplined; to him who knows the meaning of the Sūtras, the preceptor of the Hiraṇyakeśins, and an ocean of compassion. Having explained the procedure for the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) within the sixteenth book, [the author now] states the procedure for the one-day (*ekāha*) and other sacrifices in the seventeenth book, which concerns the *Tantra*. Now, the performance of the one-day sacrifices is described:
the Agniṣṭoma is the archetype (*prakṛti*) of all sacrifices. (1)

"Whoever, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Agniṣṭoma"—starting from this [the text continues] until "therefore they call it the Jyeṣṭhayajña" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.1.1). Among all the gods, Prajāpati, the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*), first sacrificed with this [rite] as a means of creation; therefore, because it was sacrificed by the eldest and because it was well-sacrificed (*iṣṭa*), this Agniṣṭoma is the Jyeṣṭhayajña, meaning it is the fundamental archetype (*mūlaprakṛti*) for all [sacrifices] such as the Ukthya and others. Regarding the *aśvin* [deities], [the verse is]: "O you, come to our sacrifice after sacrifice... (*yajñā-yajñā vo agnayaḥ*).
Because this sacrifice is completed by means of that twenty-one-fold hymn (ekaviṃśastoma) being accomplished with the aforementioned mantra, it is called the Agniṣṭoma. || 1 ||
But for those belonging to the schools (nikāya), the first [alternative] applies in all cases. || 2 ||

Among those who perform the Nikāya sacrifices, the first thousand and so forth are the Nikāyins: four [sacrifices] lasting four days, four [lasting] one day (sādyaskas), and four [lasting] two nights; such are the Nikāyins. (2)
Or as has been instructed. || 3 ||

"He gives [the gifts] at the one-day sacrifices (ekāha) and the ahīna sacrifices"—this is the restrictive rule. Or rather, these two sūtras are merely explanatory (anuvādaka) regarding those things obtained through the force of the general injunction (codaka); such is the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya. Here, both ways are heard in the sūtra as it was originally composed.

The *Jyotis*, *Gauḥ*, and *Āyus* are the *Trikadruka* sacrifices. (4) In the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, [the seventeenth book]: Some maintain that, regarding the contradiction here, the *Ekāhas*, *Ahīnas*, and *Sattras* are generally handed down in the *Chandoga-brāhmaṇa*. Therefore, having studied that Sūtra of the *Chandoga-brāhmaṇa*, one should incorporate into this [text] those [details] mentioned therein. For example, after stating "Those who sacrifice for the sake of the season advance," it was said by Āpastamba; however, its specific form was not stated. That was stated by the author of the *Chandoga-sūtra*.

Whatever has been prescribed in the *Chandoga-sūtra* concerning the *Ekāha* and other sacrifices has for the most part been stated by the author of the [present] Sūtra; those matters which have not been mentioned, we shall explain thoroughly. In this same manner, the transmission of the *Bahvṛca* branch must also be performed. In the *Chandoga* tradition, there is a sacrifice named the *Upahavya*, which is prescribed for the attainment of various desires.

Regarding this, the venerable Kapardin stated that since the author of the Sūtra—the Blessed One—said "for one desiring long life and heaven," there must be a synthesis of all desires [in the sacrifice]; furthermore, the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the initiations (*dīkṣā*), and the *upasads* must be synthesized specifically from the *Ādhvaryava* branch. Among the *satras*, even that which is not explicitly mentioned should be brought in from the *Chandoga* and *Bahvṛca* traditions. In the *ekāhas*, the altar should optionally be either the *anirukta* or the *vedī*. In cases such as "by means of two birds" and so forth, the *mahāgni* is indeed fixed; in the *sādyaskas*, the *uttaravedī* is fixed; and in the *satras* and *ahīnas*, it is either the *kāṭhaka* *mahāgni* or the [standard] *mahāgni*. || 4 ||
The first is either an Agniṣṭoma or an Ukthya.

The Agniṣṭoma, however, has primacy; this is stated by the sentence, "Therefore they call it the Jyeṣṭhayajña" (the sacrifice of the eldest). That primacy belongs to the Ukthya as well, though only optionally. || 5 ||
All [are present]. ||6||
The meaning is: the Agniṣṭoma and other [sacrifices]. || 6 ||
"He gives a thousand at the Jyotiṣṭoma," so it is said. || 7 ||
The word "is understood" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The same applies to Bharadvāja as well. || 7 ||

By the rule of the Śyaita [Sāman], the Bṛhat-pṛṣṭha [rite] is for one who has rivals; the Āyu [rite] is for one desiring heaven. The Agniṣṭoma is for one who has rivals. The Viśvajit Agniṣṭoma, with all the Stomas and all the Pṛṣṭhas, is for one desiring preeminence. The sacrificial fee is a thousand, or all one's possessions, or as many [cows] as there are Stotriya verses in the sacrifice. 8.

From the scriptural injunction, "Then one should sacrifice with the *sarvastoma*" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 7.1.3), it is to be inferred that there is a rule stating that one should perform the *stomas*. In the *agniṣṭoma*, there are only four *stomas*, beginning with the *trivṛt*; however, in the *atirātra*, the *triṇava* and *trayastriṃśa* *stomas* are also found. Therefore, this is the *sarvastoma*. In the *ekāha* sacrifices associated with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*sahasradakṣiṇā*), the *nāciketa* [is performed].

Now it is said: regarding the *saṃsthā*, *pṛṣṭhya*, *dakṣiṇā*, and *āgūḥ* in the context of the *vākya-anudrutya*, this rule is indicated for those cases where there is an option (*vikalpa*) concerning the *pṛṣṭhya*. Wherever there is a fixed rule (*ekaniyati*) for the *pṛṣṭhya*, [the rule applies]; wherever there is an option regarding the *saṃsthā*, [it applies] to one of the *saṃsthās*; wherever there is an option regarding the *dakṣiṇā*, there is a fixed rule for one of them; wherever there is a fixed rule through the combination of all three, there is an option through the combination of all three. Wherever there is another... [end of fragment]. [This concludes] the first chapter, accompanied by the commentary *Yogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. Page 397.

For him, there is a fixed rule regarding one of these three; where there is an option between two, there is a choice for either of those two. [The sacrifice is] with the *jyotis* [sacrifice], the *trikadruka*, the *agniṣṭoma* accompanied by the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*), for the sake of protection and heaven. Or alternatively: "with the *jyotis*, the *trikadruka*, and the *ukthya*. Some desire the *pṛṣṭhya* arrangement and the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇās*) everywhere among all the one-day sacrifices (*ekāhas*).

Alternatively, he shall sacrifice at that very time with the *Jyotis* sacrifice, which is the *Trikadruka*, accompanied by the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*), an *Agniṣṭoma* characterized by the *Rathantara* Sāman and having a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of one hundred and twelve [cows], for the sake of attaining heaven. Or: "I shall sacrifice with the *Jyotis* sacrifice, the *Trikadruka*, accompanied by the piling of the fire-altar, an *Ukthya* characterized by the *Bṛhat* Sāman and having a sacrificial fee of one thousand [cows]. Some say: "I shall sacrifice with the *Gāyatrī-Trikadruka*. Everything is like the *Ukthya*. When asked, "Is it not an *Ahīna*? [he replies: "The *Trikadruka* is not an *Ahīna*; there are thirty [cows] and the *Tryaiṣvadhātavīyā*."

It is either the *Sāgnika* or the *Nāciketa*. The *Āyur-ukthya* sacrifice is like the *Agniṣṭoma* for one who has rivals. Regarding the term "Āyuḥ," it is for one afflicted by disease; its ritual procedure follows that sequence. He shall sacrifice with the *Āyus-trikadruka-ukthya*, having the *Bṛhat-sāman* and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of twelve hundred, for the sake of heaven; or he shall sacrifice with the *Āyus-trikadruka-Agniṣṭoma*, or with the *Sarvavedasa* (giving away all one's possessions). When asked, "Is it not an *Ahīna*? the reply is: "The *Viśvajit* is not an *Ahīna*; it possesses all the *Pṛṣṭha* stotras. (8)
In the case of a distribution of all one's possessions, having excluded the eldest son from his share, they may divide the remainder among themselves by mutual agreement. || 9 ||

Having made a division for the eldest son in a sacrifice where all one's possessions are given away (*sarvavedasa*), he may give more than a thousand [cows]. Having completed the *sarvavedasa* sacrifice again and again, if he has no son—or if he does not know [another]—other than land and men. || 9 ||
At the time of the sacrificial fee, he gives away his entire possession. ||10||

"When the time for the sacrificial fee has arrived, he gives a thousand [cows], or all his possessions; in both cases, there is the gift of a mule. For it is stated in the text: 'It is appropriate whether there be all one's possessions or a thousand' (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.1.1). Therefore, as many as there are stotriya verses, so great is the sacrificial fee for the Viśvajit sacrifice. (10)
Whatever else belongs to the Brahmins in all directions—other than wealth, land, and armies. || 11 ||
He has gone. || 11 ||

Having brought the excellent sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and having settled [the sacrifice], or having sat down to the south of the Udumbara post facing east, he should say: "Whatever debt I have here, that I give all of it."

If it is an Ukthya sacrifice, then even so, three *atigrāhya* cups are taken, because of the statement in another Śākhā: "All [three] at the Viśvajit" (*tai0 saṃ0* 7.1.1). Having led the final sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and having departed, he should sit down to the south of the *audumbarī* post facing east and offer with the mantra, "That which is mine... (*yan me adaḥ*). || 12 ||

Having moved out to the Rohiṇī fire, they put on a red cow-hide—complete with its ears, tail, hooves, and dewclaws—as a protection against being spoken ill of. They wrap their heads with turbans; he takes up a cup made of Udumbara wood.
(Satyāṣāḍha’s Śrautasūtra, Book 17)

And [they take] a spade made of Udumbara wood—either of Khadira or of bamboo; it should be spotted, hollow or non-hollow, and sharpened at both ends, or sharpened at one end only. Subsisting either on roots or on fruits, they dwell for three nights in the forest by an Udumbara tree. Digging up a root with a digging tool while they are alive, they place it in an Udumbara vessel and eat it, drinking from earthenware vessels while feeding one another. According to some, there are three [nights] among the Niṣādas, three among the Vaiśyas, three among the Rājanyas, and three among the Brāhmaṇas. (Section 1) 13.
Having performed the Udavasānīyā offering, [he should give] a red cow with a calf's skin; this has already been stated previously. || 13 ||
For a year or for twelve days, he should not beg; nor should he refuse what is being given.
There is an option between a year or twelve days. 1.4.

Indra’s sacrifice is an Abhijit Agniṣṭoma for the sake of conquering what has not yet been conquered. Both the Bṛhat and Rathantara Sāmans are employed; or rather, they are used as the Pṛṣṭha-stotras performed out of sight.

The *Abhijit* is an *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice seen by Indra. [The sacrificer declares: "I shall sacrifice with the *Abhijit* of Indra, an *agniṣṭoma* with both *sāmans*, for which the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a thousand [cows], for the sake of conquering the unconquered heaven—that is, for the purpose of attaining the heavenly world. This may be performed by one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) or by one who does not (*anagnika*). Some say, "I shall sacrifice with the *Abhijit* of Indra. When asked, "Is it an *ahīna*? he replies, "It is not an *ahīna*; it is the *Abhijit* of Indra. There are thirty-three [cows] and a mule in both cases, and the *traidhātavīyā* offering as well. || 15 ||
But for the Hotṛ, there are eleven large animals at a single sacrificial post.

At the time of cutting the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), there is only one post: the *agniṣṭha* and the *upaśaya*, but not the *pātnīvata*. At the time of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, the encircling of the post is performed with two ropes; having taken the cup for the Aśvins and having untied [the rope], one encircles it with two threefold ropes. For the sets of eleven animals (*ekādaśinī*), there is a single post. Having set aside the *upaśaya*, the dedication (*upākaraṇa*) of the animals beginning with the one for Agni and ending with the one for Varuṇa is performed with the instruction: "The animal is a black antelope. || 16 ||
Or there may be twelve hundred of the best [cows], each with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 17 ||

At the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he gives a thousand [cows] and a mule. Having completed the Traidhātavīya sacrifice, if he maintains the sacred fires, [he should perform] the Sautrāmaṇī and the Maitrāvaruṇī; or the Nāciketa, according to the commentator. 17.
By means of the Sarvajit Agniṣṭoma with all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras, one obtains everything and conquers everything. ||18||

The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is as follows: "Having performed the morning *agnihotra*, I shall sacrifice with the *sarvajit-agniṣṭoma*, which includes the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*), has the *mahāvrata* as its *pṛṣṭha*-laud, and involves a gift of a thousand [cows], for the sake of attaining everything. Alternatively, it may be said: "With five hundred and sixty cows as the sacrificial fee. Thus, the *sarvajit* results in the attainment of all, the capacity to consume food without fail, the destruction of all evil, and the crossing over of all sin; for the *Chandoga Brāhmaṇa* states: "He crosses over all evil. This is the liberation consisting in the attainment of all. In some places, when it is not called an *ahīna*, it is the *sarvajit* that is the *nāhīna*.
[Paṭala 1] Accompanied by the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī: 399.

In the *sahasra-pakṣa* (the thousand-day sacrifice), three hundred and one fires are fixed—either the *Nāciketa* or [others]. Some maintain that everything up to the *Dīpavimathya* in the great sacrifice is like the *Mahāvrata*. Here, there are not thirty-three *atigrāhya* cups, but rather only the three original ones. There is no animal sacrifice for Prajāpati; rather, it is the goat for Agni alone, and its performance and so forth are all as before, including the *Maitrāvaruṇī* offering regarding the officiation. 18.
And he becomes an eater of food. || 19 ||
The exposition of the fruit is as before. || 19 ||
For him, the Pṛṣṭhya Mahāvrata with the Arkya hymn is prescribed.
For that [sacrifice] which has all the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras], the *mahāvrata-pṛṣṭhya-ahargaṇa* is praised; the meaning is that it is commended. || 20 ||
The sacrificial fee is one thousand, or twenty-eight times twenty.
With a sacrificial fee of one thousand, or five hundred and sixty. || 21 ||
There are four thousand [verses]. || 22 ||
There are four Nikāyas that give a thousand as their sacrificial fee. || 22 ||

The *Jyotis-Agniṣṭoma* with the *Rathantara-sāman* is the first; it is the foremost of thousands. One becomes firmly established in the vital breaths and in the eating of food. The *Gauḥ-ukthya* with the *Bṛhat-sāman* is the second; one becomes firmly established among cattle. The *Sarvajyotis-Agniṣṭoma* with both *Sāmans* is the third; it is for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything. The *Agniṣṭoma* equal to the three-night sacrifice (*Trirātra*), with either the *Rathantara* or the *Bṛhat* *Sāman*, or with both *Sāmans*, is the fourth. One obtains the fruit of the three-night sacrifice. || 23 ||

The *Jyotiḥ* sacrifice is an *Agniṣṭoma* with the *Sāman* chanted on the *Sthantara* [verse]. It means that he stands firm in the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), in food (*anna*), and in the three [worlds], and thus attains everything. The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is: "With the *Jyotiḥ* day, the *Sāman*, and the *Agniṣṭoma* sacrifice accompanied by a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), I shall sacrifice so that I may attain a full lifespan. Some, having resolved, "I shall sacrifice with thousands," perform everything as in the *Agniṣṭoma*. When asked, "Is it not an *Ahīna*? [the reply is]: "It is the *Jyotiḥ* sacrifice with a thousand [fees], not an *Ahīna*."

There are three parts with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and a mule (*aśvatara*) is used in both cases for the *dhātavīyā* offering. The second [part] is the *ukthya* sacrifice characterized by the *bṛhat-sāman*, [performed] with the thought: "May I be established among cattle; may I become possessed of cattle along with my thousand. The rules of the specific group (*nikāya-dharma*) apply without contradicting the characteristics of the cow (*go-dharma*) obtained through the name [of the sacrifice]. Because of the name, this is an *agniṣṭoma* belonging to the group characterized by the *bṛhat-pṛṣṭha*. The remainder is as before. The third is the *sarvajyotis-agniṣṭoma*. [The formula is: "I shall sacrifice with the *sarvajyotis* accompanied by a thousand [cows], for the sake of attaining all worlds."

The rest is as before. By means of the three-night rite performed on both sides, one obtains the fruit of the four-night *agniṣṭoma*; one obtains that which is the fruit of the *gargāvarātra*. [One should worship] Prajāpati, Bhūmā, and so forth, or the Vasus and Rudras with a thousand [offerings] equal to a *nirāva*.

The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[17th Praśna]: "I shall sacrifice. For those among the aforementioned [sacrifices] that have specific desires, everything is like the Agniṣṭoma. In these, there is an option regarding the fire-altar (agni) and the high altar (uttaravedi). According to the Tāṇḍins, there are four [sacrifices] consisting of four thousand [verses]: the Jyotis-Agniṣṭoma is the first; the Sarvajyotis-Agniṣṭoma is the second; the Viśvajyotis-Ukthya is the third; and the Ubhayasāman Atirātra-equivalent is the fourth.
There are four *sādyaskra* sacrifices.
There are four *sādyaska* groups; they are called *sādyaska* because their consecrations (*dīkṣā*) and sacrificial preparations (*anubhūti*) are performed all at once (*sadyas*).
Their distinction is as follows: || 25 ||
The action of the first among them is now stated. || 25 ||

The first [Soma sacrifice] has either the *Rathantara* as its *sāman*, the *Bṛhat* as its *sāman*, or both as its *sāmans*. In that [sacrifice], there are desires: regarding the procurement of Soma, regarding preeminence, regarding rivalry, and for one who has enemies, regarding the desire to cross over [difficulties]. (Section 2) Heaven or cattle [are the results]. 26.

In the spring, on the thirteenth day, having offered the morning *agnihotra*, [the sacrificer] declares: "I shall sacrifice with the *sādyaska* [rite] so that I may attain the heavenly world," or "so that I may become possessed of cattle. He chooses four *somapravākas* with the formula, "Thou art lightning, O fourfold one. For the purpose of choosing the four classes of officiants (*ṛtvij*), priests are stationed in various directions. One *somapravāka*, mounting a chariot yoked with four horses and proceeding with the same speed, likewise travels to the north for three *krośas*.

One, having mounted a chariot yoked with two horses, travels one *krośa* toward the western direction; another, having mounted a chariot yoked with a single horse, likewise proceeds swiftly for one *krośa* toward the southern direction. The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are stationed at each of these points: the *adhvaryu* in the eastern direction, the *brahmā* in the north, the *hotṛ* behind [the central point], and the *udgātṛ* to the south. Having thus proceeded, the *adhvaryu* asks from the eastern direction:

The *āṅgirasa* is the rival of the sacrificer; he addresses the *somapravāka* regarding him, saying: "On the third day, Soma will belong to Yajñaśarman; is it not an *ahīna*? When asked thus, [the *somapravāka*], having muttered, "It is not an *ahīna*, it is a *sādyaska*; it is indeed the Mahāvrata," stations him upon a chariot and proceeds to the sacrificer's house. The *somapravāka*—who is the *adhvaryu*—while still on the chariot, recites: "Thou art the path, O divine one, leading to the gods. Having thus reached the sacrificer's house from the north, he brings the *brahmā* forward with the words: "O fathers, you have become [this]. Thus he brings the *brahmā*.

Afterwards, [he chooses] the Hotṛ to the south and the Udgātṛ. According to the Commentator, there is a question and answer between the Hotṛ and the Udgātṛ as prescribed in their respective Sūtras. He chooses those officiating priests (ṛtvij), beginning with the Hotṛ. Then, having performed the Madhuparka and the Nāndī-śrāddha together with the *sakṣeda* [rite], he proceeds according to the archetype (*prakṛti*) up to the end of the *sakṣeda*.
On the preceding day, there were the sacrificial animals dedicated to Agni, Soma, and Bṛhaspati. || 27 ||

"I shall sacrifice with the animal sacrifice (paśubandha). Having moved away [from the previous site], there is no *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula. At the beginning of the animal sacrifice, from the bringing of the branch up to the measurement of the altar (*vedi*), it is like [the procedure] for the Āditya sacrifice, namely, "I shall not [be] struck by lightning. In that case, as [it is said] that the place for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is in the middle toward the south, so here is the measurement of the altar. Therefore, some say that the *uttaravedi* is ten paces [in extent], with the staff increased by twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Others, however, say it is merely the measure of a *śamyā*. At the time of cutting the sacrificial posts, one cuts three posts and holds the *upaśaya* [post].
[Paṭala 1] Accompanied by the *Prayogacandrikā* commentary compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin: 401.

The rule regarding the carrying of the Āhavanīya fire to the Uttaravedi is a restatement of what has already been established; the principle is that the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) takes two days. It is not of the *sadyaskāla* (one-day) variety. Following this, [the text says] "he maintains the Āhavanīya," and so forth. On the following day, having performed the rites from the maintenance [of the fires] up to the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) on that very day, one concludes. According to the author of the Bhāṣya, it is mandatory for the husband and wife to consume food mixed with clarified butter (*sarpiṣmad-aśana*).

At night, at the time of lying down, the sacrificer, having become a celibate (*brahmacārī*), places gold in his mouth and lies upon the thighs of his beloved wife (*bhāryā*). Making her thigh the place for his pillow, he does not engage in sexual intercourse or similar acts during the night, because of the injunction regarding celibacy. When morning has dawned, after the rites beginning with the bringing forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) and having set out the clarified butter (*ājya*), some say: "We yoke the two horses" (*yunajmi aśvinā*); others perform the raising of the three sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) with the verse "These have sat down" (*etā asadan*), and the formula "Come with the animals" (*paśubhir ehi*), and so forth. Some offer a black-necked animal dedicated to Agni (*āgneya kṛṣṇagrīva*).

One dedicates a white-backed animal to Bṛhaspati according to the procedure for the *ekādaśinī* (the set of eleven animals). [The formulas are: "To Agni, thee, who art dear... "To Soma, thee, who art dear... "To Bṛhaspati, thee, who art dear... There is no specific designation for the animals lying near [the sacrificial post]. Having performed everything according to the *ekādaśinī* up to the offering of the omentum (*vapā*), the remainder is as before. Some say that one offers nine *samiṣṭayajus* oblations with the verses beginning "Dhātā rātiḥ. The author of the Commentary states that this animal sacrifice concludes with the satiating of the Brahmins. || 27 ||
In the absence of those [specified materials], for these deities, there shall be an offering in sequence: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, and two *caru* offerings for the other two.

Alternatively, Bharadvāja and Vaikhānasa have stated: "For these deities, the first sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is on eight potsherds, while the other two are cooked rice offerings (caru); thus, having performed the iṣṭi, one becomes a performer of animal sacrifice. || 28 ||
He maintains the Āhavanīya fire. || 29 ||
In this case as well, it should be understood as being like [the rule regarding] the animal sacrifice (pāśuka). || 29 ||
He sprinkles the northern altar with clarified butter.
The support (ādhāra) occupies the position of the head of the sacrifice, either because of its preeminence or its primacy. The rest has been explained. || 30 ||
Eating food mixed with ghee. || 31 ||
Of the husband and wife. || 31 ||
Having placed gold in his mouth, he lies between [his legs] as one observing celibacy for the sake of his beloved wife. || 32 ||
This has been explained. || 32 ||
"I shall sacrifice with the iṣṭi. The officiating priests have already mounted [the fires]. || 33 ||
In this manner, having completed the ritual for the sacrificial bricks or the ritual for the animal sacrifice, and having consigned the fires into himself, he proceeds to the place of sacrifice.

Having placed those [animals] there, on the following day, horse-chariots with milk-filled leather bags and Soma-proclaimers (somapravāka) run out in all directions. || 34 || From among them, whatever fresh butter (navanīta) may arise, that he should pour into the clarified butter (ājya). || 35 || With a four-yoked chariot in the eastern direction, and with a single-yoked chariot (sthūrin) moving counter-clockwise (prasavya) by the distance of a krośa in the other directions, he should then cause the mule-chariot to circumambulate once clockwise; or alternatively, he should circumambulate the yojanas and krośas clockwise by means of the horse-chariot. || 36 ||
This has been explained. || 34 || 35 || 36 ||
The general rule has been explained. || 37 ||

Having thus gone to the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) and having resolved upon it, he performs the *agnihotra* oblation; then, having awakened at the end of the night, he offers the morning *agnihotra*, according to the statement of the *Chandogas*: "Having offered [the evening oblation], [he recites] 'The clarified butter is cattle,' etc.; the *saṃbhārayajus* [is performed] during the night itself. Then, for the purpose of serving the *soma*, there is the *saptahotṛ* [formula]; when the sun has risen, having again carried forward the fires and having worshipped them with 'In one's own skill,' [he performs] everything from the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering] up to the mention of the [concluding] rites. Herein lies the omission of the vow (*vratalopa*)."

"Observe the vow"—this is the release of speech; "O Agnis, full of splendor"—as in the archetype, there is no keeping watch. Some perform [the rite] with the formula "Do not lie down," ending with "You are the impellers. Having performed up to "You are the impellers," [he recites] "I am that... and so on, beginning with "Being invoked," which has already been explained. || 37 ||
A three-year-old castrated bull is the purchase-price for Soma. || 38 ||

Having performed the *prāyaṇīyā* [offering], there is the purchase of Soma. The Soma-purchasing animal is a three-year-old bull (*trivatsaḥ sāṇḍaḥ*). Regarding this, the Mīmāṃsakas have stated that there is an adaptation (*ūha*) of the mantras that reveal the Soma-purchase. Some say: "Its soul, its form"—in this regard, one should understand that only the ten [verses] are prescribed as referring to the seasons (*ṛtu*). Others, however, say: having thus purchased the Soma, then follows the performance of the *ātithyā*; but the *pravargya* is not performed because of the absence of the proper time. [Then follow] the *tānūnaptra* and so forth; but not the *pravargya* due to the lapse of time. Some desire [the performance of] the rites beginning with "O Agni, that which is yours" up to the end of the cleansing (*mārjana*). || 38 ||
During the *upasads*, he should close his eyes three times.
The Upasads are the ritual acts; as they proceed, he should wipe [the ladle] three times. By not closing [the eyes] during one of the Upasads, there is a threefold division of the night. || 39 ||
Or he may perform [the rite] with his eyes closed.

Alternatively, there are no afternoon *upasad* rites; therefore, there is an option. For those performed in the forenoon, there is simply an omission. Having proceeded with the forenoon rite, he measures the altar while closing his eyes. 40.
The sacrificial altar is made of the best barley soil. || 41 ||

The word "it becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the remainder. When the sacrificial ground (*vedi*) is a field of barley (*yavabhūmi*), meaning it is filled with grain, one measures it by disregarding that field of barley; thus, [the formula] "O men, prepare this [ground]" (*imāṃ narāḥ kṛṇuta*) does not occur. In the case of animals and other [offerings], after having prepared the sacrificial ground for the purpose of digging, the ritual acts such as the *stambayajus* are performed. Having inspected the excavation, the [formula] "O Vasus, you... (*vasavastvā*) and the [verse] "O unobstructed one... (*apārarum*) are omitted. The [formula] "O men, this... (*imāṃ narā*) is also elided. [In its place], the [formula] "Of the god Savitṛ... (*devasya savituḥ*) and "The four-crested one... in her two birds... (*catuḥśikhaṇḍā tasyāṃ suparṇau*) occur. || 41 ||
[First Paṭala: Accompanied by the commentary *Mayūkhacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 4.3:
Barley-grain (*yavānī*) is the threshing-floor (*khala*); the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) is [the same]. 42.

The threshing floor (*yavakhala*) should serve as the site for the *uttaravedi*; the altar (*vedi*) is prepared accordingly. On that threshing floor, the rites beginning with "Thou art my path to wealth" (*vittāyanī me 'si*) are performed. Likewise, the rites beginning with the placing of the fire (*amyādhāna*) at the location of the *catvāla* pit are omitted. However, everything beginning with "Thou art firm" (*dhruvo 'si*) and "Be prepared for the gods" (*devebhyaḥ kalpasva*) takes place. But there is no pouring of the *uttaranābhi* mound. [The verses] "Four-crested one" (*catuḥśikhaṇḍā*) and "Indra’s roar, thee" (*indraghoṣas tvā*) are recited up to the covering of the altar. But here, the giving of the vow-food (*vratapradāna*) does not take place.

In all cases involving the *sādyaska* sacrifice, whether one has performed the afternoon rites immediately or not, and whether one has performed the morning rites immediately or not, there is an omission of the mantra beginning with "ase tvam sujāgṛhi. After having performed the morning rites for "agnim jyotiṣmantam" and so forth, whether one has performed the afternoon rites immediately or not, the leading forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*), the sprinkling (*vyāghāraṇa*), and so on are carried out, as well as the enclosure of the *uttaravedi*. [The rule is: "The subsequent enclosure is performed over the ground already containing the fire. (42)
On the ascent to the Havirdhāna shed. || 43 ||

The term *ārohaṇa* refers to a cart for the purpose of transporting the *havirdhāna* (sacrificial vessels) to their destination; the procedures such as the movement of the *havirdhāna* and the sweeping of the *āgnīdhra* shed should be understood as being according to the archetype (*prakṛti*). || 43 ||
The hall is measured out. ||44||
The term *sada* has already been explained as a *pāramitā*. Bharadvāja maintains that it has already been established as *sada*. 4.4.
The sacrificial post is a wooden sword, or it has the point of a wooden sword, or it is a threshing-post. || 45 ||

The wooden sword (*sphya*) serves as the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). The rest is clear. Some maintain that the cutting of the *audumbarī* post and so forth, the touching of the post with the formula "Thou art for Indra," and the offering pertaining to the *audumbarī* are omitted. Others, however, desire a stump (*sthāṇu*) to take its place. || 45 ||
At the time of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, he offers an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma. He takes the Vasatīvarī waters from the house of the sacrificer.

At the time of the animal sacrifice for Agni and Soma, there is indeed the *agnīṣomīya* offering itself. There is no carrying away of the *prastara* grass-bundle and so forth, nor the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and enclosing stones (*pārī*) belonging to the *ātithyā* rite, nor the ritual acts such as the setting out of the sacrificial vessels (*yajñapātra*). He sets down the sacrificial vessels and so forth; he employs the *pracaraṇī* ladle as the fifth; the eleven potsherds; the wooden sword (*sphya*) in pairs; (the black antelope skin and so forth—the six items beginning with the *kṛṣṇājina*, and all the eight and so forth); the preparation of the *pavitra* strainers; [he says] "O Sacrificer, restrain your speech"; "May they settle"; "Restrained in speech, the vessels..."; "You are made of wood" (*vānaspatya asi*), and so forth; "To Agni and Soma, agreeable... (*agnīṣomābhyām juṣṭam*), and so forth.

Having performed the rites up to the end of "se brahmaṇaḥ pṛcyas tvā," [the Adhvaryu] proceeds with the preparation of the altar and so forth. At the time of taking the clarified butter (*ājya*), he issues the call, "Place the *prokṣaṇī* waters," and so on, beginning with "The *pracaraṇī* ladle first. Having taken [the butter], they lead forward the Brahman's wife with the formula beginning "May the wife of the Brahman go forward," and likewise perform the sprinkling of the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmāvahiṣoḥ prokṣaṇa*) and so forth. Having consecrated the clarified butters with the formula beginning "The supporting beam for the *sāmidhenī* verses," and having performed the sacrifice with the *agnīṣomīya* cake, the Adhvaryu gives the direction for the sake of the "son-giving" rite (*pitāputrīya*).

"From the house of him who knows"—that is, from the house of one who performs many sacrifices. And from that [house], he takes the *vasatīvarī* waters. Having set them down to the west of the *Śālāmukhīya* fire, the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, is completed according to the established rule. When it has been concluded, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters, he issues the call: "That which belongs to the sacrificer," and so forth. For the purpose of the five milkings, two branches are brought; he silently binds the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) used for the *ātithyā* ceremony. Those enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the fuel (*idhma*) for the animal sacrifice are also prepared.

The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha: [Chapter 17]. Thus, up to the end of the *paristaraṇa* (strewing of grass), the ritual procedure is the same as that for the *savana* (Soma-pressing). At the very time of that offering, the *saumika* (Soma-related) rite begins with "To Agni... and so forth. At the time of appeasing the sacrificial animal (*paśu-prasādana*), there are three cords for the animal and two cords for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Likewise, there are the *vapāśrapaṇī* (flesh-roasting spits) and other implements. Having drawn the cup for the Aśvins, at the time of cleansing the sacrificial post, the threshing-floor beam (*khalevālī*) becomes the sacrificial post. The sacrificial post has already been placed in its position beforehand; accordingly—

The conceptualization of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-kalpanā*) and so forth—including the rules regarding the tree, its carving, cutting, making it eight-cornered (*aṣṭāśrī*), piling it up, and sweeping it—are set aside. Another refinement is also set aside: [the post] is either shaped like a wooden sword (*sphya*) or like a plow-shaft (*lāṅgalīṣā*). The *khalevālī* (threshing-post) is indeed well-known in common worldly usage. After the drawing of the cup for the Aśvins, [the procedure begins with] "Bring the *khalevālī* for the sacrifice" and "Recite the invitatory prayer," and so on. The time at which the sacrificer anoints the sacrificial posts—that same time is intended by the term *caṣāla*, meaning "the ring."

"Measured is the portion for the *caṣāla*," according to the statement of the Chandogas. He anoints it with the formula, "Thou art Aindra, the unmeasured," and fastens it with, "O thou of fair fruit. The formula "Of the god... (*devasya tvā*) is omitted. He touches it at the place of the girth-rope. [The call is made: "Recite for the threshing-floor post as it is being encircled," and so forth. The encircling is done with two [rope-strands], but there is no concealment of the *svaru*; rather, it is done with any sacrificial wood, like the *upaveṣa*. 46.
At the time of the *savanīya* offering, he immolates the animals together.
At this point, at the time of the Savanīya offerings, he immolates the animals together; first, according to their respective positions, he dedicates the Savanīya animal for Agni.
The animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, the Savanīya, and the Anūbandhyā. || 48 ||
A substitute for the Agniṣomīya and Anūbandhya sacrifices will be stated; however, it should not be said that this applies to the Savanīya as well.

In place of the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma; in place of the Anūbandhyā cow, one should sacrifice with curdled milk (āmikṣā) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.
He has gone. ||49||
A white horse that is well-trained is the sacrificial fee. || 17.1.50 ||
The meaning is that he should give a horse born in Bāhrīka from Sindh; Āpastamba states that one should give it equipped with gold ornaments. || 50 ||
One should give it to an Aṅgirasa or to a rival.
The gift of that horse to the Adhvaryu of the Aṅgirasa lineage, or to Śatru, is based on the scriptural statement. || 11 ||
Or, having chosen a Brahmin who is an object of hatred, one should give him a white horse adorned with gold ornaments. || 52 ||

Before the commencement of the *kṛta* sacrifice, the rival (*bhrātṛvya*) becomes a friend; to such a rival, the descendant of Aṅgiras, one should give [the sacrificial fee]. Having set aside the horse as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), some [hold] that for the others it is given to the *udgātṛ* alone, according to the statement of the *Chandogas*. When the day of the *sutyā* sacrifice is completed, for the others, one cow is given to each individual, according to the statement of the *Chandogas*.

On the day of the Sutyā, having made some gift to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), one should perform the disposal of the horn (*viṣāṇaprāsana*) entirely like that of the Agniṣoma sacrifice. The purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) takes place before sunset. In place of the *anubandhyā* cow, there is the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) for Mitra and Varuṇa; this concludes with the *udavasānīyā* offering. For this sacrifice, the Adhvaryu priest belongs to the lineage of Aṅgiras. || 52 ||
[Chapter 1] Accompanied by the commentary *Mayūkhacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.

405. For one year he shall not sit upon a high seat; he shall not eat meat; he shall not approach a woman; he shall not wash his feet, nor anoint them, nor rub oil on his body. That is the consecration (*dīkṣā*). If he does not desire [to complete it] for a full year, [it shall last] twelve days. (Section 4) 53.
Thus ends the first chapter in the seventeenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
For one year, or for twelve days, the vow consisting of washing the feet and other observances must be maintained. Regarding this, there is a verse:

"The sūtra *ekoheṣu* (in the case of single-day sacrifices) is a restatement (*anuvādaka*) of what is already established; some, however, claim it is an injunction (*vidhāyaka*), because otherwise it would be purposeless. When the *bṛhat-pṛṣṭha* has been performed, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) therein consists of a thousand [cows]; since the *śyaita* chant is present, one instructs with a thousand alone. *Agni* and the *uttaravedi* (northern altar) are prescribed as alternatives (*vikalpena*). There are the *jyotis*, the *trikadruka*, and so forth—the *gotrikadruka* and the *āyutrikadruka*. Through these sentences, there may be a non-duality of the *āyus* formulas.

In the *ekāha* sacrifices and the *sādyaska*, the *agni-citi* (fire-altar piling) is not performed with the *pakṣya* bricks. ... In the *ekāha* sacrifices involving a thousand [cows], there may indeed be the *nāciketa* fire-piling; some maintain this as a fixed rule, while others hold that the *aśvatara* horse is prescribed for the thousand. At the beginning, it should be performed with the *traidhātavīyā* offering, and likewise at the end thereafter. ... There is no fixed rule regarding the specification of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the back of the altar (*pṛṣṭha*), or the arrangement (*saṃsthāna*). For in these cases, the *traidhātavīyā* is used, and the *viśvajit* sacrifice has all the *pṛṣṭha* chants. It is declared that the *anāvaśyatara* [offering] is performed, and one's entire wealth is given away.

Having thus divided and given the portion for the eldest, one should again run toward the son; having brought the highest sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he should then mutter the *yan me astu* prayer. Having first established Rohiṇī, the remainder is placed to the north. At Indra’s sacrifice with the Abhijit constellation, a thousand [cows] are given there. Indeed, it is prescribed that there is a single sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and no fire, and likewise the eleven [animals] are remembered. The subsequent rite, "the All-Conqueror" (*sarvajit*), is the remover of sins. The piling of the altar (*cayana*) is declared to be mandatory, as is the vow for exactly one year.
13. Thus ends the first chapter in the seventeenth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Śrautasūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin, compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī.
[The *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha—] Now begins the second chapter in the seventeenth book.

Having made the Agniṣṭoma-sāman of the second [stotra] twenty-one-fold, one should cause one afflicted by illness to sacrifice; with this [rite], one should also cause one who desires food, or one who desires offspring, or one who desires cattle, to sacrifice.

By this, the subsequent [rites] are explained: for the second [rite], one who is afflicted by disease, one desiring food and the like, or one desiring cattle, should sacrifice with the *sādyaskra* for the sake of liberation from long-term illness. "One should sacrifice with this. The remainder is as before. Having made the *pañcadaśa* the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*—so says Āpastamba. The *agniṣṭoma-sāman* has the *pañcadaśa-stoma*. For the Chāndogas, the *ekaviṃśa* is the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* of the second rite. 1.
It repeats with three [verses] each. ||2||
The meaning is "by means of the Ṛg-verses. || 2 ||
For the third [stotra], the fourteenth and fifteenth [verses] are the two subsequent Pavamāna [stotras]. Or [alternatively, they are the eighteenth verses].
The imitation [of the model sacrifice] is performed by one who is inferior, younger, or a follower; its last two Pavamāna chants consist of eighteen verses, according to Āpastamba.

Or, there are four *pṛṣṭhas* and eighteen *stomas*. The fifth is the *ājya* of the Hotṛ; the last two *pavamānas* consist of eighteen [verses]. The *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ is the twenty-four-fold (*caturviṃśa*); the *bahiṣpavamāna* is the twenty-four-fold. Those desiring heaven perform this sacrifice. ||4||
According to the opinion of the Chandobrāhmaṇa:
[the rite] for one who is inferior or has fallen behind consists of imitation. Its two subsequent Pavamāna stotras consist of twenty-four verses each.

The one who is inferior (*hīna*) and junior (*anu-jāvara*) is the qualified person. "Junior" has already been explained; he is indeed "inferior" because he is afraid of suffering or afraid of poverty and so forth. "Rite" (*karman*) is a name for the action; and there is the phrase "the Soma-pressing is tomorrow. His rite is performed through the imitation of the *Sādyaska* sacrifice with the resolve: "I shall perform the Soma-pressing tomorrow; may I obtain the Ādityas. This is entirely like the first [rite]. || 5 ||
The horse-tamer is the announcer of the Soma.
There is only one horseman; there is no chariot-rider. 6.
And Dadhīci spoke thus at the end within the three sheaths.
In the place where the flow of milk occurs, there is a flow of curd. "At the end of the three *kośas*" means at the end of a *gavyūti*. || 7 ||
The female cow is the one for purchasing Soma. || 8 ||

Having approached him in the morning, [he says]: Prajāpati is the wheat; the *urvarā* (fertile field) is the altar (*vedi*); the threshing floor of wheat is the *uttaravedi*; the two *ārohaṇa* ladders are the two *havirdhāna* sheds; the measured space is the *sadas*; the wooden sword (*sphya*) is the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), with its tip being the *syāgra*. Or a threshing-post [may be given]. A white mare is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); she is to be given to the Brahman priest. As in the archetype, the distribution to the others is performed; having announced it to his rival with the Caturviṃśastotrīya, he should sacrifice. Having first performed the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, the sequence proceeds as follows: the *agniṣṭoma* *indrastuta*, the *viśvajit* with all *pṛṣṭha* stotras, and the *atirātra* which is a modification (*vikāra*) of the tenth day; the measurements and so forth are as previously described. This is the ritual arrangement (*klpti*) for the Taittirīyas. Because of the sequence of the third *chandas*, those who follow the *chandas* [tradition] declare: "I shall sacrifice with the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*) consisting of *chandomas*," with the specific mention of results being: "May I obtain a man, cattle, vigor, and food. Regarding the specific days: there is an *abhyāsaṅgya* ending with the sixth day. Wherever there is an *atirātra* following the *chandomas*, there too the *mānasa* cup is included.

What is the meaning of *abhyāsaṅgya*? It is the collection of the thirty-six stotras of the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*). Now, for these, the *pañcāha*, four *chandomas*, an *atirātra* with the *pṛṣṭhya* [sāman] day, and an *atirātra* are prescribed. In both cases, there is the fourth *ṣoḍaśin* and the four *chandomas*. Alternatively, since the name of the fourth *chandoma* is extended by designation (*atideśa*) from another *atirātra*, there is the attainment of the *mānasa* [stotra], and its attainment occurs by virtue of the position of the *atirātra*.

This being the case, some perform both [the rites]. In the Atirātra itself, on both sides, the arrangement of the *āgniṣomīya* animal sacrifice is as before. The fourth is the Kausurabinda: "I shall sacrifice with the Kausurabinda Atirātra; may there be much [prosperity]," and so forth, as before. Regarding the specific details of the days: the *agniṣṭoma* is chosen as the modification of the first six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), consisting of three fifteen-fold (*pañcadaśa*) *ukthya* days. The modifications of the latter three days consist of three seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*) *ukthya* days. There is no interruption of the *chandomas*. The Atirātra is twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*).

Here too, as before, [the ritual] ends with the *payaḥ* (milk) offering, including the mental [offering] and the *anākam*. In the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, there is an eleven-night rite with ten thousand cows as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); the ritual procedure here is like that of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*). On the eighth day of the cool season (*śiśira*), one should resolve: "I shall sacrifice with the Pauṇḍarīka so that I may attain all prosperity," or "so that I may attain the state of the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhitā*)," or "for the sake of heaven. The Great Fire-altar (*mahāgni*) according to the Kāṭhaka school follows the procedure up to the day of fasting (*vaupavasathya*) like that of the twelve-day rite.

In the Agniṣomīya [rite], having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters at night and having performed the distribution of the milks, the Abhyāsaṅgya Ṣaḍaha is commenced. The Abhyāsaṅgya Ṣaḍaha consists of four Catuṣṭomas, an Agniṣṭoma, three Chandomas, and an Atirātra; these are the specific ritual properties of the Chandomas. Some [properties] belong to the end of the Ṣaḍaha, such as the eating of honey and so forth. Now, regarding the distinct modifications of the Catuṣṭomas and Chandomas, he gives thousands every day. On the final day, he gives a thousand horses; on each preceding day, cows weighing a hundred [gold pieces].

Now, regarding the sequence of the cups (*graha*): on the first day, the sequence begins with the cup for Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyavāgra*), followed by the cup for Śukra, and then the *āgrayaṇa*; this threefold rotation occurs throughout the ten-day period, beginning again with the cup for Indra and Vāyu on the tenth day, and so forth. Now, according to the Kāpeyas, there is a displacement of one cup each day; the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) remains the same as the original (*prākṛta*). The wooden ring (*caṣāla*) is placed upon the post. The altar (*vedi*) is "strewn with grain" (*vrīhyuttara*), meaning the altar is described as a threshing floor (*khala*) of rice. Bhāradvāja is the Hotṛ priest, according to Āpastamba; the phrase "in this sacrifice" (*asmin kratau*) is to be understood as the remainder of the statement. The rest is as previously described.
—Chapter 2] Accompanied by the commentary titled *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī; page 409.

The *Viśvajit-Śilpa* is the fourth [form]. Its ritual procedure is as follows: "I shall sacrifice with the *Sādyaskra-Viśvajit-Śilpa*; may I attain the production (*prasava*) of all that is unattained. Due to the contradiction with the name, the rules of the *nikāyas* (grouped sacrifices) apply. Everything is like the first [form]. The selection of priests (*ṛtvij-āvāraṇa*) and so forth do not apply; the *Viśvajit-Śilpa* is a *sādyaskra*, and there are five [animals] for the animal sacrifice. Likewise, when the sun has risen, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are performed on two days; it is a *sādyaskra* and the *sutyā* (pressing day) is according to the statement of the *Chandogas*.

Alternatively, [the ritual] consists of two days: the first day begins with the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and ends with the *prāyaṇīya* offering; the second day, beginning with the purchase of the Soma (*kraya*) and ending with the departure (*udavasāna*), includes the *savanīya* offerings up to the spreading of the grass (*paristaraṇa*). On the final day, there are the characteristics of the *viśvajit*, such as being performed with all the *pṛṣṭha-stotras* and all the *stomas*, with the gift of one's entire property (*sarvavedasa-dakṣiṇā*), and the "all-desiring" artistic performance (*viśvanicchilpa*). This means it is joined with artistic skill. Some say it is joined with the *vālakhilyas*, the *vṛṣākapi*, the *kunta* hymns, and so forth. Then, having performed the rites up to the *udavasānīyā* offering, [one performs] "the red cow and calf" (*rohiṇī vatsam*) and so on.
The meaning is that thereafter the rites of the *sāyaskra* sacrifice, beginning with the washing of the feet (*pādāvanejana*), take place. || 18 ||
One who practices sorcery should sacrifice with the Śyena.

There arises a doubt as to whether words such as *śyena* and others are injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*) or names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*). Because they are extremely well-established [in common usage], they are injunctions of accessory qualities; furthermore, due to their being optional, they set aside the *soma*, which—though enjoined as a constituent element of the original rite—is obligatory. Alternatively, rather than assuming an unknown meaning, it is better to accept a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), as in the case of *soma* and other terms, whereby the word enjoin a ritual qualified by that accessory quality.

Nor is it appropriate to consider the word *karma* as denoting the [sacrifice] figuratively, based on the similarity of action shown in the supplementary passage, "Just as a hawk swooping down," and so forth; for figurative usage involves an extreme remoteness from the primary meaning, and as he will state later, "figurative application arises from a connection with qualities that are merely indicated. Therefore, it is better to resort to indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone. Furthermore, if there were figurative usage, there would be a sublation of the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), because it would then have to refer to an entirely different object.

In the case of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), however, even when the word *śyena* refers to that which possesses the hawk (the sacrifice), it is directed solely toward enjoining the hawk as a subordinate element, just like [the injunctions regarding] the red turban and so forth. Yet, syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the sacrifice—which has become the instrument—and that which has become the instrument is not obtained without the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). Thus, secondary indication is resorted to for the sake of syntactic unity. But since the intended meaning (*tātparya*) lies precisely in the literal sense (*śruti*), there is no sublation of the direct statement. It is said in reply: first of all, in the injunction of the group (*gaṇavidhi*), that very [group] is what must be praised.

Furthermore, since it is illogical for that [sacrifice] to be compared with itself, the supplementary portion of the sentence consisting of that designation becomes untenable. Moreover, a qualified injunction (viśiṣṭavidhi) is improper due to the resulting complexity (gaurava). Nor is there, as in the case of *soma* and other terms, a lack of any other possible interpretation for this other word; for, in accordance with the supplementary statement "Just as the hawk (*śyena*)," it is possible for it to be a name used in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*). Indeed, the sole purpose of the supplementary statement is precisely this: to ensure that the word *śyena* is understood as the name of the sacrifice.

Therefore, the name [of the sacrifice is Śyena] (Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.5). Its ritual procedure is as follows: the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is, "I shall sacrifice with the Śyena for the purpose of the death of my enemy. At the time of choosing the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), he chooses priests who are either his own sons or those learned in the Vedas and skilled in the ritual manuals and scriptures. Ghee from a wind-exposed cow (*vātānavanīta*) is the substitute for clarified butter (*ājya*). According to the statement of the Chāndogas, "All limbs that are the functions of ghee are [satisfied] by the milk of a wind-exposed cow," it becomes [equivalent to] that which has been blown upon or cast away. || 19 ||
The two chariots are the two oblation-holders.
The word "bhavataḥ" (of you two) is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 20 ||

At the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), they should pierce it with thorns. || 29 ||

[They should perform] the *lohitoṣṇīṣā* and other [rites]. They should "overcome" (*vitudeyuḥ*), that is, they should afflict [the enemy]; the Udgātṛ should overcome [him] with the *lohitoṣṇīṣā* and others, according to the traditional designation (*samākhyāna*). Here too, there is a specific rule in the *Āpastamba-śrautasūtra*: "If he desires, 'May he be slain,' he should perform the *kaṇvasthatarapavamāna* and the *bṛhatpṛṣṭha* [stotra]. If he desires, 'May he live,' the opposite of this [should be done]. "May he go to the furthest distance and not find a firm footing"—in this case, one should perform the *plava* as the *brahmasāman*, as before. The *ekatrika* Agniṣṭoma of Prajāpati departs after having pointed out all evil.

"He gives twenty-four cows as the sacrificial fee" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 22.4.29). If one should be killed while desiring [victory], then likewise, at the midday pressing, the Rathantara is used for the Pavamāna-stotra and the Bṛhat for the Pṛṣṭha-stotra; for this is the loss of everything for one whose two wings are reversed. If the Śyena sacrifice has been commenced, then the reversal is that the Bṛhat is used for the Pavamāna and the Rathantara for the Pṛṣṭha; thus, in the case of total loss, he would go to the furthest distance, where even there he would find no firm footing. If the Śyena has been commenced, then it is as before.

The procedure is the same: when the *rathaṃtara* is used for the *pavamāna-stotra* and the *bṛhat* for the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, then one should perform the *plava* as the *brahmasāman*. In the other two cases, however, there is the *plava* and the *āhava*; [in these cases] there is the loss of all [merit]. Wherever there is the cessation of stability, that is the fruit of the *śyena*. The remainder has been stated: "Either the *sādyaska* or the *śyena*, the *ekatrika*—these six are the *sādyaskas*," as Śauci will state.

2. Paṭala: [This work] is accompanied by the commentary *Mayūkhacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 411. Thus, from the statement of the Chandogas; and it has been explained by Śabarasvāmin in the third chapter of the Jaiminīya [Mīmāṃsā-sūtra] that "the Sadyaskra belongs to Āpa. At that time, the characteristics of the first Sadyaskra and the Vajapeya also apply. There is an Ekatrika Agniṣṭoma for Prajāpati. Its ritual procedure: the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is, "I shall sacrifice with the Ekatrika of Prajāpati for the sake of the destruction of all sins.
All else is like the Agniṣṭoma. 29.

There are three Vācastomas; two of them are Agniṣṭomas, and the Sarvastoma Atirātra is the last. In that [Atirātra], all the Ṛg-verses, all the Sāman-chants, and all the Yajus-formulas should be employed. 17.2.30.

Whether one maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) or does not maintain them (*anagnika*), this rite removes the sin of killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*) and removes all sins. It consists of the *Vācastoma* sacrifice performed by the *Nikāyins*, preceded by two *Agniṣṭomas* characterized by the *Rathantara* Sāman. The ritual procedure for the first [of these] is as follows: "I shall perform the Vācastoma for the sake of attaining sovereignty over all beings. Its ritual rule (*kalpa*) is like that of the *Agniṣṭoma*. The Vācastoma is not a deficient (*ahīna*) sacrifice; therein lies its distinction—namely, that in it all *ṛc*s, all *sāmans*, and all *yajus* formulas are employed.

In that very context, after stating the enumeration of the hymns—namely, "With one [verse] the *bahiṣpavamāna*, with a thousand the *ājya*s, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, a million, ten million, a hundred million, a billion, a ten-billion, a hundred-billion, a trillion"—it says: "In that [thousand], all *ṛc*s [are contained]. This means all those recitations (*japya*) prescribed in the *Ṛgveda* are included. Furthermore, wherever there are *yajus* formulas—those prescribed in the *Yajurveda*, whether they be *mantras* for ritual acts (*karaṇa*), or those for silent recitation (*japa*), worship (*upasthāna*), or consecration (*anumantraṇa*)—all of these are to be employed in combination.

Some [mantras] are separated according to their respective portions, such as: "May Pūṣan unfasten your opening," "May the god divide you two," "May Aryaman divide you two"—for these and others, one takes up the spade with four [mantras]. There is a combination of those beginning with "He gathers with eight," and so forth. According to the Chāndoga tradition, it is recited thus: with one [verse] for the first [part], the *bahiṣpavamāna* with ten for the second, and with a thousand for the third at the end.

In that context, when the four *vācastomas* are being recited in this manner, one chooses many *adhvaryu*s; likewise for the *gomṛgas*, and likewise for the groups of *udgātṛ*s. Because the *ṛk*, *sāman*, and *yajus* are infinite, there are officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who have studied the infinite Vedas. Thus it was stated by the venerable Kātyāyana: "A *chandoga* [is qualified] by as many groups of *udgātṛ*s as exist. Since there are no students of the infinite Vedas here, those such as ourselves have no entitlement (*adhikāra*) at this time.

Some say: "Because this [Vedic] period pertains to the authority of the ṛṣis, there is no authority for people such as ourselves at this time. Furthermore, since humans exist [only now], there is no authority for them either. Therefore, the performance of a thousand [repetitions] in the explanatory passage (arthavāda) refers to the application of all the *yajus* and all the *sāmans*."

One should insert many *ṛc* verses at the place of insertion (*āvāpasthāna*) during the chanting, just as in the case of the *stoma-atiśaṃsana*. Likewise, there are the *japa*, the worship (*upasthāna*), and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the *sāman*s, there is insertion (*āvāpa*) during the *pavamāna* chants, just as in the *vidṛc-stoma*. Thus, everything should be performed like the *agniṣṭoma*. There is a specific distinction in the second *sāman*: "I shall sacrifice with the third *vācastoma*, which is a *sarvastoma*, for the sake of sovereignty over all beings. Because this is intended to enjoin a specific quality (*guṇavidhi*), it is not a modification (*vikāra*) of the *sarvastoma*; rather, everything is like the *jyotiṣṭoma-atirātra*.
The rules for the Vācastoma have been stated. Regarding the Sāmaveda, the author of the Bhāṣya says that its application is likewise in the fourth [section].
412. The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the 17th Praśna]: The Praghāsa for the Vrātyas; the Vrātyastomas. 31.

The word "we shall explain" is to be understood as the ellipsis. A *brātya* is one devoid of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*). Exile (*pravāsa*) is residence elsewhere, namely in another continent; or, according to the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakṛt*), exile is residence in a place other than one's own. || 31 ||
The Agniṣṭoma is Trivṛt with the Rathantara Sāman; the Ukthyas have the Dviṣatīs as their Ṣoḍaśī-stotras for all [the days]. || 32 ||

The meaning is that those who have performed the Ukthya sacrifice with the Rathantara-sāman, or for whom a second Agniṣṭoma has been performed, should perform the Vrātyastomas upon their return from the wanderings of the Vrātyas. "Sixteenfold" refers to a specific type of Vrātyastoma. There are three Pavamāna chants and three Acchāvāka-sāmans, as prescribed for the Ājya and Pṛṣṭha lauds. According to another Smṛti, one should perform the Vrātyastoma for the eldest of the Vrātyas—whether they possess three sixteenfold Adhvaryu-stomas, or are the eldest among the Kyas, or by means of meritorious deeds.

In that regard, there are the fifteen-fold (*pañcadaśa*), seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*), twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*), twenty-seven-fold (*triṇava*), and thirty-three-fold (*trayastrimśa*) *stomas*. There is a scriptural statement: "They sacrifice when the sun is in Pisces, using all the *nātyās* [verses] with the sixteen-fold (*ṣoḍaśin*) [stoma]. These [who do not perform these rites] are excluded; these are excluded—you who are *vrātyas*, who wander abroad, who do not practice celibacy (*brahmacarya*), who do not engage in agriculture or trade, and who speak the speech of the uninitiated. Indeed, the sixteen-fold *stoma* of these is capable of destroying their impurity.

"By these four sixteen-fold [sets], one is released from evil," so says the *Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa*. Those who were described by the passage beginning with "those who are fallen" (*hīnāḥ*) and so forth, should undergo the *catuḥṣoḍaśin* sacrifice. Even those who, though devoid of purificatory rites such as initiation (*upanayana*), have previously taken a wife from a family of the same lineage (*samānagotra*)—even for them, like those who have broken their vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), only husbands may perform the sacrifice. Having prepared the sacrificial implements and vessels separately for each, they should sacrifice at the first sacrifice and then perform the *vrātyastoma*, according to the opinion of Drāhyāyaṇa.

"One should perform the *pratipad* for the *brātya* with the verse 'vidyutam'"; this is prescribed in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. Therefore, the opinion of the author of the *Nidāna* is that "having sacrificed with the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, one should sacrifice with the *Brātyastomas*. There are many *brātyas*, some being thirty-three; thus, their number is indefinite. The performance involves many sacrificers, like the twelve-day (*dvādaśāha*) *ahīna* sacrifice; [the rule] "they did not perform [it] in the cold season," and so forth, is entirely like the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. ||32||

A turban, a goad, a bowstring, a yoke-halter, a chariot, a side-vehicle, a chariot covered with wooden planks, a horse, a mule, two draft animals, a black garment, a black-and-white antelope skin, and a silver necklace. || 33 ||

Āpastamba also mentions the turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), the goad (*pratoda*), and so forth. The *uṣṇīṣa* is a cloth for wrapping the head. The *pratoda* is a bowstring, a wooden pommel, or a whip. The chariot (*ratha*) is well known. "Covered with planks" (*phalakāstīrṇaḥ*) means covered with planks alone, not with skins; some say it means with additional planks. The horse and the mule are draft animals that pull the chariot. "Black garment" (*kṛṣṇaṃ vāsaḥ*) means one with black fringes (*kṛṣṇadaśam*).

Two skins—one black and one white—from a sheep, both made of wool, are purchased for a single price. These two skins, joined together at their edges, constitute the black-and-white skin. The meaning is that they are worn together. A *niṣka* of silver refers to a specific type of ornament consisting of silver, joined with or accompanied by silver, intended as an adornment for the neck. 33.
That belongs to the householder. || 34 ||

The householder is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). The householder should provide all of this. These materials are to be supplied by the householder; it has been clearly stated by the Chāndoga that "the householder should provide thirty-three cows. || 34 ||
The fringes of the cords for others are made of wool. || 35 ||
The intention is that they will say of the other sacrificers, "These [robes] have fringes at the ends and are made of woven threads. || 35 ||
Two cords and two sandals. || 36 ||
This is clear. || 36 ||
The skins are joined double. || 37 ||
The *saṃhitā* is the junction (*saṃdhi*). || 37 ||
Thirty-three [deities] approach each householder. || 38 ||

There are thirty-three cows for each individual sacrificer; this is the explanation. "Balūkāntāni" means garments with fringes; some say that "lakāntāni" refers to woolen cloths that are mostly red. It means garments like jeweled blankets (*ratnakambala*). There should be two ropes and two [pieces of cloth] for each region; the meaning is that there is one garment joined with fringes on both sides.

For each sacrificer there are two pairs of sandals; for each, two antelope skins joined together. Three [skins] have been explained by the [description of the] first two antelope skins. There are two sheepskins. "One for each of two..."—thus it has been explained. There are thirty-three cows for each [sacrificer], beginning with the *balūka* and ending with this. For the other sacrificers, [the same applies]. (1) "Nine [cows] for the burning"—the fasting is separate for every single one. The cremation: if he should live, then he performs the rites up to the *udavasānīyā* offering. 38.
These are the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās). || 39 ||
He has gone. || 39 ||
Alternatively, sixty-six cows constitute the sacrificial fee.
Alternatively, one should give sixty-six [vessels], according to the Āpastamba-sūtra. || 40 ||
Moreover, they say that one should give whatever has been acquired by them; for it is known: "That indeed is the wealth of the Vrātyas. ||41||

Now, regarding those things which have been observed for the Vrātyas—beginning with the turban (*uṣṇīṣa*) and the whip (*pratoda*), and ending with the *valūka*—these are for those who are unrighteous (*avrata*) toward their Vrātya teacher, or for a mere nominal Brahmin (*brahmabandhu*), or for one from the Paramagadha region; such is the statement of the Chāndogas. Thus ends the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, up to the *Udavasānīyā* offering. [In the sixteenth chapter of the seventeenth book:
The *Ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice is censured for the low-born; the "twice-Ṣoḍaśin" for the youngest; the "half-stoma" for the eldest; and the "four-Ṣoḍaśin" for all. 42.

One should sacrifice with the *vācastoma*. However, the *vrātyastoma* is not performed in the spring. The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is: "We shall sacrifice with the *vrātyastoma* accompanied by four *ṣoḍaśins*. It is for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and not for the sake of a desired result; therefore, there is no mention of a fruit. The *vrātyastoma* with four *ṣoḍaśins* is not a minor sacrifice (*ahīna*); it stands as the staff on the right side of all the householders (*gṛhapati*s). This has been stated by the commentator Kapardin: "For the others, the staff is indeed the original one; the turban is the goad, and the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) [is the whip]."

Just as a goad, together with a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), serves the purpose of tethering an animal—the turban acting in the place of a rope—because the goad alone is incapable of serving as an accessory for the animal, one measures it together with another piece of wood that is capable. Alternatively, if a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) shaped like a goad were made together with a turban for all the sacrificers, they would do so at the very time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), just as in the case of the quarters. "These thirty-three [objects] they should give to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)," so says the statement of the Chandogas.

Those who have been censured by the *ṣaṭṣoḍaśī* sacrifice should enter [the rite] with the *vātyastoma*. "I shall sacrifice with the *vātyastoma* consisting of six *ṣoḍaśins*," as before; the rest is as before. Or, the remainder is for the *stotra*. Those who are the youngest among the twice-sixteeners (*dviṣoḍaśin*) should enter as in the first case. "I shall sacrifice with the *vātyastoma* consisting of two *ṣoḍaśins*," as before; the rest is as before. Those who are the eldest among the *jyeṣṭha-nātyas* should enter the fourth, the *ūrdhvastoma*. Now, regarding this, the *Chandoga-brāhmaṇa* states: "Of the *medhya* (fit for sacrifice) *stomas* that lead to tranquility, these are the eldest."

According to the statement of the author of the *Chandoga-sūtra*: "They are to be purified through procreation," [the eldest son] says, "I shall sacrifice with the Jyeṣṭhanāman, the Vrātyastoma, and the Ūrdhvastoma" because of his capacity for procreation. Having performed the remaining rites as previously prescribed and having completed the penances enjoined by the Smṛtis, they should settle into the threefold mode of livelihood (*traividhavṛtti*). After that, there is the eating together with others and so forth. Then one may officiate at sacrifices for these others. According to the statement of the *Chandogas*, this is done after performing the initiation (*upanayana*) with the Vājapeya and other such sacrifices.

Now, there are five groups of *nākasad* sacrifices; among them, the first consists of the *ātithya* rites, which are unexpressed (*anirukta*), while the others are *agniṣṭoma*s. The second group consists of the *nākasad*s of the Maruts, and the fourth is the *nākasatrayastriṃśat*, a specific [sacrifice] of the Sāmaveda known as *āgamāyatanya*. This does not exist among the *Chandogas*; therefore, the Commentator stated that one must consult another Sāmavedic text and thereby acquire knowledge of the ritual details (*padārtha*). || 42 ||

The *prayati* sacrifice is for the Ādityas; it is worthy of praise (*ukthya*) and is the first of those who sit upon the firmament (*nākasad*). They go forth with a turning away from evil and from the rival (*bhrātṛvya*). The others are *agniṣṭoma*s. The second belongs to the Aṅgirases; the third to the Sādhyas; by the fourth, one obtains vigor and heroism for the Maruts. According to some, the thirty-three-fold (*trayastriṃśa*) is the fifth; according to others, the fifth belongs to Prajāpati. One who desires offspring [performs it]; he overcomes his rival. By means of this rejection, he rejects the rival. (Fascicle 5) 45.

The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the second [offering] is: "I shall worship the Ādityas, the Nākasads, with a sacrificial gift for the purpose of destroying sin. For the third [offering], belonging to the group (*nikāya*), it is: "I shall worship the Sādhyas, the Nākasads, with a sacrificial gift for the sake of heaven and for the destruction of sin.
[End of] the second *paṭala*, together with the commentary titled *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 415.

"I shall sacrifice with the *nākasad* [cup] using the *prayati* [offering]; the fruit is as before. For the fourth [day], "I shall sacrifice with the *nākasad* using the *prayati*; may I become radiant for the sake of vigor," or so it is said. For the fifth, "I shall sacrifice with the *nākasad* using the thirty-three-fold *prayati*, or with that belonging to Prajāpati," for the sake of heaven. Now, "I shall sacrifice with the *abhibhū* [cup] using the *abhibhū*; may I overcome my rival. All [proceedings] are like those of the *agniṣṭoma*. Now, "I shall sacrifice with the *vinud* [cup] using the *ukthya*; for the purpose of driving away the rival. The remainder is as before. 43, 44, 45.
The Citistoma sacrifice is for one who desires offspring. || 46 ||
The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is: "I shall sacrifice with the Citisoma for the sake of procreation. Everything is like the Agniṣṭoma. || 46 ||
A Brāhmaṇa desiring the office of a domestic priest should sacrifice with the Gāyatra Ukthya and the Rathantara Sāman; for a Brāhmaṇa, the first two [stotras] are Gāyatra. 47.

"One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice with the *gāyatra* [sāman], the *rathantara* sāman, and the *agniṣṭoma*," says Āpastamba. In this ritual, the qualification belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone; the specific rule in the text of Āpastamba is that the *gāyatra* and *agniṣṭoma* are the first sacrifices. || 47 ||
The northern [side] is for the Kṣatriya. || 48 ||
The explanation is as before. || 18 ||

Luster is the spiritual splendor (*brahmavarcasa*) of a Brahmin; it is in the east for a Brahmin and in the north for a Kṣatriya. It is fierce yet free from pain, but they do not possess many cattle. ||49||

The *Bṛhaspatisavana* is its ritual procedure; it is performed with the *Trikadruka* chant and the *Agniṣṭoma*. There is an option for both [classes]. For a Brāhmaṇa, the fruit is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). For a Kṣatriya, the fruit is a kingdom and a territory, provided he desires a fierce and unshakeable host of armed men. The same declaration of results applies even to the inhabitants of the kingdom and the few armed men. However, the statement that they do not become like those with many cattle is a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Thus, these two sacrifices are to be performed as the first sacrifices by Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya sacrificers. (49)
One who has not been purified should sacrifice with the Trivṛt Agniṣṭut Agniṣṭoma.

One who is impure due to being defiled by such faults as the killing of a Brahmin should perform the Agniṣṭut-Agniṣṭoma sacrifice for the destruction of all sins. Everything beginning with the appointment of the Soma-pravāka is the same as in the Agniṣṭoma.
The *purorucaḥ* are addressed to Agni; the *subrahmaṇyā* is addressed to Agni. 51.

It is indeed the same as the tenfold purchase (*daśakraya*). Some [use] a modified version: "O divine Soma, may you who are swift and bright swell; for Agni, the finder of the single-wealth; may Agni swell for you; may you swell with food," and so forth. || 11 ||
They chant the hymns for the Āgneyī verses; a goat and gold are the sacrificial fee.
Because fire and water are similar and because of the principle of substitution.

Having performed this very Catuḥṣṭoma sacrifice, one who is a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya) but has been struck by dice, struck by a woman, struck by lust, or struck by his own conduct, should perform it.

1ka. kha. *cittiṣṭho* | 416 ... The Śrauta Sūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha—[in the 17th Praśna]: "This very Catuṣṭoma," etc. Having performed this very Catuṣṭoma among the Agniṣṭuts, a Śrotriya who has been struck down by dice—a Brāhmaṇa who is a gambler; that is to say, a cheat—he should sacrifice with this Catuṣṭoma Agniṣṭut. Everything is as before. With this Catuṣṭoma, one who has been struck down by women should sacrifice—one who is addicted to prostitutes. Everything is as before. One who has been struck down by desire (*kāmahata*) should also sacrifice with this Catuṣṭoma. The rest is clear. || 13 ||
A dark-brown horse is the sacrificial fee. || 54 ||
He has gone. || 54 ||
That is to be given to a Brahmin. || 55 ||
That is the horse. || 55 ||
As in the case of the original nature, so it is with others. || 56 ||
The intention is that the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) for the Adhvaryu and others are as in the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. || 56 ||

Having made the Vāyavyā verses the fifteen-fold Agniṣṭoma-sāman of this very [sacrifice], one should cause one afflicted by illness to sacrifice; or one desiring food, or desiring offspring, or desiring cattle. 57.
