The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is "he should sacrifice" in all cases. The phrase "in the Vāyavyā [verses]" is an instruction for a distinct ritual (*karmāntara*). One who is wise should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut, which consists of the nature of the *dharma* of Agni. [The formula is: "I shall sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut for the sake of liberation from long-term illness; everything else is as before. One desiring food should also sacrifice with this: "I shall sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut so that I may obtain food. One desiring offspring: "May I obtain offspring. One desiring cattle: "May I obtain cattle"—this is the distinction. || 17 ||

Having performed this very sacrifice with the Vāravantīya as the Agniṣṭoma-sāman upon the Revatī verses for one desiring spiritual luster; having performed this very sacrifice with the Vāravantīya as the Agniṣṭoma-sāman upon the Śakvarī verses for one desiring cattle; having performed this very sacrifice as a Catuḥṣṭoma for one desiring a village. (Some say that these [Agniṣṭuts] are without the Pravargya rite. One desiring spiritual luster [should perform] the Agniṣṭut with the Trivṛt-stoma; one desiring vigor [should perform] the Agniṣṭut with the Pañcadaśa-stoma. 58.

Having made the *Vāravantīya* the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* upon these very *revatī* verses, one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice. The ritual procedure for this is as before. [The intention is: "May I obtain spiritual luster. According to Bharadvāja and Āpastamba, one desiring offspring should sacrifice with the thought, "May I obtain offspring. The specification of the fruit is to be understood in all cases. Having performed the *catuḥṣṭoma* with this same [sāman], one desiring a village should sacrifice with the specification of the fruit: "May I obtain a village. Some maintain that there is no *pravargya* rite in these [sacrifices]. One desiring food should sacrifice with the *trivṛt-agniṣṭut*.
"One who desires vigor [should perform] the Pañcadaśa-stoma sacrifice" (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 22.6.13), so says Āpastamba. || 58 ||
One who has failed in a sacrifice, or in whichever sacrificial rite one might fail, should perform the seventeen-fold Agniṣṭut Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Paṭala 2: Together with the commentary *Prayogacandrikā* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrī. 417

One who has failed in a sacrifice (*yajñavibhraṣṭa*) should perform the seventeen-fold *agniṣṭut* sacrifice. This is an occasional rite (*naimittika*). It refers to a case where, once a ritual action has been interrupted, it must be performed again and again; or rather, when one has failed in a particular *kratu*, one should perform that same *kratu* again. "One should perform it like an *agniṣṭoma*"—so says the author of the *Bhāṣya*. That is not correct. The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is this: if one has failed in a sacrifice due to negligence or laziness, one should perform everything again, beginning from the initial resolve (*saṃkalpa*). The *Chandoga-sūtra* also states this. (59)
One who speaks should speak with a threefold [vocalization]. 17.2.60.
Slander and the like directed toward the king are not to be spoken; [this is] the Trivṛd Agniṣṭut. 10.
The fifteenth [day] belongs to one who slays or causes another to slay. || 61 ||
The Agniṣṭut sacrifice, characterized by such [mantras] as "He who does not strike him down in the teaching, may he drive away with a thousand," consists of fifteen [stotras].

The seventeenth [chapter] concerns one who has eaten food from a person whose future is uncertain; having consumed it, the twenty-first [chapter] concerns one from whom he has received food, such as those from Gāndhāra, Kaliṅga, Māgadha, Pāraskara, or Sauvīra.

One who has killed a Brahmin or committed a similar sin should perform expiation by sacrificing with the Saptadaśa-stoma; since [the text] mentions going to regions such as Gāndhāra, one should sacrifice with the Ekaviṃśa Agniṣṭut. By this, the prohibition against traveling to sinful lands is understood. || 6 ||
One desiring vigor [should perform] the Triṇava [stoma]. || 63 ||

The word "yajeta" (should sacrifice) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Furthermore, from the wording of the mantra, "ojo balaṃ indriyaṃ vīryam" (Ojas is strength, sensory power, and vigor). One who desires ojas should perform the Agniṣṭut sacrifice with the Triṇava stoma; a restrictive rule is to be understood here. || 63 ||

With the fifteen-versed [stoma], one who desires vigor; with the seventeen-versed, one who desires progeny; with the twenty-one-versed, one who desires a firm foundation; (with the thirty-three-versed, one who desires heaven). ||64||
It has been explained. The Agniṣṭut sacrifice for one desiring heaven belongs to the Trayastriṃśa [stoma]. 64.
Or rather, it is in the Jyotiṣṭoma itself; in the Agniṣṭoma, one may desire all desires. (Section 6) 65.
Thus ends the second chapter in the seventeenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.

Alternatively, whatever occasional fruit (*naimittika-phala*) is prescribed for the Agniṣṭut should all be desired within the modification (*vikāra*) of the very archetype (*prakṛti*), namely the Jyotiṣṭoma. In that regard, with reference to the passage "Jyotis is procreation" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 7.1.1), this fruit which is recited—"Whatever he desires, he attains through this"—is an unavoidable option for all the Agniṣṭuts, which are modifications of the Jyotis. The declaration of the fruit is: "I shall sacrifice with all the Agniṣṭuts; may I attain all desires. (End of section 418).
[From the *Śrautasūtra* composed by Satyāṣāḍha, Book 17].
[He] should think thus. || 15 || Thus ends the second chapter in the seventeenth book of the *Prayogacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra* compiled by Mahādeva Śāstrin.
Now begins the third chapter in the seventeenth book:
One desiring food should sacrifice with the threefold *agniṣṭoma* characterized by the *anirukta* [stoma]. || 1 ||

"Four Agniṣṭomas with the Trivṛt-stoma, having the Rathantara-sāman as their chant; one desiring a village should sacrifice with the first of these, which is undefined (anirukta)," so says Āpastamba (ĀpaŚrSū 22.7.12). These are a series of sacrifices characterized by the Trivṛt-stoma, having the Agniṣṭoma as their final form (saṃsthā), and the Rathantara-sāman as their chant. [The declaration is: "I shall sacrifice with the Trivṛt for the sake of attaining a village; I shall sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut-upahava," and so forth; the remainder is as before. || 1 ||
Some say that the morning pressing is undefined.
The word "one" means that everything stated in other recensions is to be performed like the Agniṣṭoma. || 2 ||
A white horse is the sacrificial fee; it is to be given to the Brahman priest. || 3 ||
This has been explained in the context of the Sādyaska sacrifice; for the others, some [portion] of the purchase price has been mentioned.
The Bṛhaspatisava is the second. || 4 ||
The second [is] the second sacrifice. The rest has been explained. || 4 ||

A Brāhmaṇa who desires spiritual luster, or one who desires the office of domestic priest, should perform this sacrifice; or he for whom they might consecrate him to the position of a Sthapati (architect/chief).

The sacrifice belongs to the Brāhmaṇa, not to the Rājanya or the Vaiśya. The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is: "I shall sacrifice with the threefold Bṛhaspatisava; may I attain Bṛhaspati," or "for the sake of the office of domestic priest. Everything is like the Agniṣṭoma.
The Hotṛ becomes one who wears a wreath. ||6||
Because of the statement "he becomes one wearing a garland," at the time of the selection of the Hotṛ, the Hotṛ becomes one wearing a garland.
Aruṇa, Mirmira, and Triśukra. || 7 ||

Aruṇa is so by color. He who repeatedly opens his eyes is called *mirmira*. *Triśukra* is preeminent in terms of actions—whether by reason of his mother, his father, or himself in terms of lineage, learning, and conduct. The meaning is that one should choose such a person as the *hotṛ* priest. ||7||
With the verse, "O Bṛhaspati, be pleased with us," he draws the additional draught for Bṛhaspati.

At the time of the *atigrāhya* cups, having first taken the two ordinary ones, he takes the Bārhaspatya *atigrāhya*. This is a modification (*vikāra*) of any one of the Āgneya, Aindra, or Saurya cups; or rather, it is a mere addition (*samuccaya*) and not a modification. Its placement is at the end, because, by displacing the original [cup], it is a modification of the Saurya. Having recited the verse, "O Bṛhaspati, be pleased with us," he says: "Thou art taken with a support; for Bṛhaspati the Radiant. In the case of the Saurya side, it is exactly the same: "This is thy womb. (8)
An animal sacred to Bṛhaspati is to be immolated. ||9||

And because of the scriptural injunction: "Having dedicated the Savanīya animal to Agni, one dedicates [the second] to Bṛhaspati," [one says] "I dedicate you, who are pleasing, to Prajāpati," and so forth. In the verses beginning with "Those who know" (*prajānantaḥ*), there is a modification (*ūha*) in the dual number. In every respect, there is only a single sacrificial post (*yūpa*), as in the case of the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice; though some desire them to be separate. In that case, there are the two animals, the *upaśaya* and the *pātnīvata*. In the view of a single post, there are two ropes (*raśanā*) and so forth, and the duality of the *svaru* is due to its being for all [the animals]. Some hold that because there is no specific injunction, the properties of a group do not apply to individual members. 9.
At the morning pressing, when the Nārāśaṃsa goblets have been set down, he assigns eleven sacrificial gifts.

At the morning pressing, when the Nārāśaṃsa goblets have been set down, eleven cows are given as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Having distributed them with the formula, "May Tutha Viśvavedas distribute you," the giving takes place. He directs the oblation pertaining to the sacrificial fees and the leading forward [of the cows], and so forth. 10.

At the midday pressing, he consecrates him with clarified butter while he is holding onto the fire on the black antelope skin; or as in the case of the piling of the fire-altar, with the residue of the Śukra and Manthin cups.

On the middle day, having performed only the drawing of the vessels for the morning pressing and the oblation pertaining to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā-homa*), the fees are given during the morning pressing; those not being given here are to be given at the third pressing, and at this time they should be led [to their place] by way of the *tīrtha*.
At the midday pressing, he dedicates twelve horses; at both [pressings], he dedicates those [animals]; and at the third pressing, twelve [horses].
He dedicates that barren cow. 13.

At the midday pressing, he gives twelve horses; one is a horse and the others are cows. He dedicates both of these [sets]. This means that for all those [cows] dedicated to Agni at the midday pressing which are intended for the third pressing, there is a separate dedication of both sets. The consecration takes place with clarified butter (ājya) in response to the Māhendra-stotra. Having spread out a black antelope skin, he sprinkles the sacrificer while he is seated upon it. [He does so] with the mixture of the *śukra* and *manthin* cups. "O Bṛhaspati and you, Indra, you two are masters of celestial wealth and also of earthly wealth."

"Bestow wealth upon the one who praises you; protect us always with your blessings"—with this mantra mentioned in another *sūtra*, at the time of the *atigrāhya* cup, there is the consecration (*anumantraṇa*) with the verses beginning "O Bṛhaspati, you are the radiant one... and ending with "you are well-clad. In the solar ritual (*sauryapakṣa*), eleven cows are given when the *nārāśaṃsa* cups have been pressed in the third pressing. || 12 || 13 ||

Alternatively, there may be eight at the morning pressing, eleven at the midday pressing, and twelve at the third pressing. According to some, one should give a horse at each pressing in thirds; according to others, all [the gifts] at the midday pressing.
"Or rather," thus [the rule is] incomplete. ||14|| The Śrautasūtra composed by Satyāṣāḍha:
"In the other two pressings, [one recites] mentally; or not even mentally. ||15||
This ritual procedure is also found in other recensions, as seen in the Āpastamba [Dharmasūtra]. || 15 ||
Having performed the drawing of the arrow from the threefold Agniṣṭoma, one who practices sorcery should sacrifice.

And because of the principle that "all the rest is like the Agniṣṭoma," the *iṣu* sacrifice is the third [form] for the purpose of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). "I shall sacrifice with the threefold *iṣu* for the sake of the destruction of enemies. It is like the *śyena*. In this regard, the specific rule is: "The rest is the same as the *śyena*. (Sūtras 16–17)
Thus it is said. || 17 ||
The Agniṣṭoma consists of threefold [stomas]. || 18 ||
"A dark-brown horse is the sacrificial fee; that is to be given to the Brahman priest" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 22.7.19), and so forth, as before. 18.
The Śunaḥśepa-stoma; the Sarvasvāra. || 19 ||

The fourth [chapter] is on the *Sarvasvāra* sacrifice, according to Āpastamba. Eligibility for the *Sarvasvāra* is in the latter part of life. Having performed the *Sādyaska* and other such rites, one who has a son born is eligible for this rite. [The declaration begins: "I shall sacrifice with the *Trivṛt-agniṣṭoma*, the *Śunaskarṇa-stoma*, the *Sarvasvāra*, etc. The remainder is as before. || 19 ||
It is known from scripture: "He who desires death should sacrifice; he who should desire, 'May I go to the heavenly world free from disease,' [should sacrifice]. (20)

The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is: "I shall sacrifice with the *Trivṛt*, the *Śunaskarṇastoma*, and the *Sarvasvāra* [sacrifice], so that I may attain the heavenly world. Everything is like the *Agniṣṭoma*. From the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*) onwards, effort must be made so that the death of the sacrificer occurs at the time of the *Ārmaka* [offering], according to the statement of the Chandogas. He consumes all the *bhakṣas*, including those that are not breath-related (*aprāṇabhakṣa*). There are no vows (*vrata*) and so forth. The initiations (*dīkṣās*) conclude after a month of fasting (*anaśana*). Whatever *bhakṣas* have been commenced, he should cast them into a pit.
In the *Sūktavāka*, there is an omission of the *āyus* and other [formulas], because the purpose is the desire for death. 20.
A green parrot is the animal to be sacrificed to Yama. || 21 ||

At the time for the animal sacrifice, having brought forward the Savanīya animal dedicated to Agni, he immolates a white-colored animal dedicated to Yama; the liturgical formula is as follows: "I bring thee forward, acceptable to Yama. || 21 ||
Cooked food is the sacrificial fee.
He has gone. || 22 ||
While the Ārbhava Pavamāna is being chanted, [the sacrificer], having covered himself with a large cloth with its fringes pointing toward the feet on the right side of the Udumbara post, says:
"O Brāhmaṇas, complete this sacrifice! (Section 7). The sacrifice concludes according to its established form. 23.

While the Ārbhava Pavamāna is being chanted, he spreads a black antelope skin to the south of the Udumbara post, wraps it with an unwashed garment having its fringes pointing southward with the head toward the south, and issues the command: "O Brāhmaṇas, complete this sacrifice. Having spoken thus, he remains right there until the rite is concluded and finished. || 23 ||

Having consigned the fires into separate kindling woods and having worshipped the sun with the *uttaranārāyaṇa* hymn, he departs for the forest. If he should dwell in a village, he should consign the fires into separate kindling woods, worship the sun with the *uttaranārāyaṇa*, and settle back in his home. Regarding those sacrificial rites which he might not reach: "The *bhūrukthya* sacrifice, having the *rathantara* as its *sāman*, one desiring prosperity should perform; a cow is the sacrificial fee. 24.

The meaning is already explained. The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is: "Desiring prosperity, I shall sacrifice with the *bhūta* [mantra]; may I attain prosperity. This is to be performed in its entirety, as previously described. || 24 ||
The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is indeed inexhaustible. || 25 ||

"It is indeed inexhaustible. The *Cāturmāsyas* are so called because they are performed every four months; the *Vaiśvadeva* and other sacrifices are those prescribed for them. One who has performed these is a *cāturmāsyayājī*. According to the Pāṇinian rule "the suffix *ṇini* is used after the root *yaj* in the sense of the action" (*Pāṇini* 3.2.89), the suffix *ṇini* is applied here in the sense of the past tense. For that performer of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, the *sukṛta*—the *apūrva* (unseen merit), which is another term for the dharma that serves as the means for the fruits produced by the sacrifice—is inexhaustible, meaning it cannot be exhausted; it can never be depleted by enjoyment.

Regarding the rule *kṣayyajayyau śakyārthe* (Pāṇini 6.1.81), this word is derived from the root *kṣi* (to perish, Dhatupāṭha 236) with a specific grammatical designation (*nipātita*). The rest has been explained elsewhere. Having performed twelve *dīkṣā*s (initiation days) and twelve *upasads* (subsidiary offerings) during the *śiśira* season, the commencement of the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing day) should take place on the full moon of the month of Phālguna, or alternatively, on the full moon of Caitra, so that the *vaiśvadeva* and *śunāsīrīya* sacrifices may occur on the first day of the following lunar fortnight (*pratipad*).

And regarding the subsequent Vāruṇapraghāsika [sacrifice], it begins on the first day (*pratipad*) of the second half of the month following the Vāruṇapravāsa; the *Atirātra* of the subsequent Sākamedha sacrifices begins on the fifteenth day, with the initiation (*dīkṣā*) on the twelfth day, according to the commencement [rules] that do not conflict [with the sequence], based on the statement of the Chāndogas. Adopting the view that it begins on the full moon of Phālguna, the performance is as follows: having offered the morning *Agnihotra* on the sixth day of the cold season (*śiśira*), one makes the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the Cāturmāsya sacrifices so that my merit may become inexhaustible."

The venerable Manu has stated that "this ritual is perpetual. Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) with the words, "I shall sacrifice with the Soma and Cāturmāsya [rites]," one should say, "I shall sacrifice with the Trivṛt," and so forth; the Commentator [Śabara] states that everything from the "Vidyud asi" formula down to the selection of the Soma-proclaimer (*somapravāka*) is to be performed just as in the Agnicayana. [The resolve is made] with the words, "The Cāturmāsyas of Yajñadatta Śarman will take place; by your honor... and so on.

Regarding the *Cāturmāsyas*, there is the statement of the Sūtra that they possess the nature of the *Atirātra* and other multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*). However, according to the statement of the Chandogas—"The *Cāturmāsyas* and the *Rājasūya* are [performed] on that very day"—the initiation (*dīkṣā*) takes place on that same day. Some authorities, even though it is like the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), desire the omission of the *Anvārambhaṇīyā* offering. Having performed the twelve *Upasads*, at the time for cutting the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), one does not cut the post, as is done in the case of the twelve-day sacrifice.

At the time of the *uttaravedi*, one does not sow [the seeds]; there is an omission of the *cātvāla*. Having measured out the altar (*vedi*) and sprinkled it with water while reciting "catuḥ śikhaṇḍā," and having formed the *utkara* heap, everything beginning with "vittāyanī" is omitted up to the end of the covering. All that remains is like the twelve-day *ahīna* sacrifice.

Having driven away the calves for the sake of the *payasyā* (curd-mixture), one subsequently separates the *āmikṣā* for the *vaiśvadeva*. At the time of binding the sacrificial animal for the *agnīṣomīya*, one employs the *paridhi*-sticks used in the *ātithyā* sacrifice; that is, one fastens those capable of securing the animal to the stakes. Having performed the rites for the *agnīṣomīya* up to the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya-abhimantraṇa*) at the time of the *ātithyā*, the rites beginning with the taking of the firewood (*abhyādāna*) are omitted.

The sprinkling is performed with the formulas beginning with "yavamatībhiḥ" and "pṛthivyai tvā. Having poured together all the waters being used for the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), the call is given: "Recite for the one being bound! He anoints [the post] with any wooden splinter whatsoever; there is no *caṣāla* (top-ring), and the binding takes place upon the enclosing-stick at the time of binding.

Having performed the ritual with the omentum at the southern enclosing-stick, he offers the Vaiśvānara-Pārjanya oblation following the *puroḍāśa*, as stated by Āśvalāyana; having performed the "cutting" (*viśasana*) of the milk, the milking of the *vaiśvadevī* curd is said to be as before. Then, having driven away the calves, [the procedure] continues in this manner up to the spreading of the grass-bundle (*paristaraṇa*). || 25 ||
The Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma is in the world of the Vaiśvadevas. || 26 ||

When the next day has dawned, having awakened at the dead of night, [the ritual master] says, "O Agni, lead [them]," and so forth. In the world of the Vaiśvadeva—that is, in the place of the Vaiśvadeva—there is the offering of the *savanīya* oblations at the proper time; he prepares all the *vaiśvadeva* items for the sake of the *savanīya* oblations and sets out all the vessels.

(To the west: the Savanīya potsherds, one large potsherd for roasting, the Vaiśvadeva potsherds, two caru-pots, and the wooden sword (sphyá)—these in pairs; (to the east: two vessels, and the remaining items in common (tantra), such as the vessel for the morning milk-offering (prātardoha) and the vessel for the whey (vājina), etc., just like those for the Savanīya offerings.

Alternatively, according to the *tantra* method, having set aside the *savanīya* offerings for the sake of the *veṣa* (the ritual dressing), he subsequently offers the *vaiśvadeva* oblations. The meaning of "having poured out the poured rice (*niruptān vrīhīn*)" is that the pouring into the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) is done together; that is, for the sake of both sets of offerings. Having poured them out for the sake of both, the threshing and other rites follow. At the time of threshing, having threshed the *savanīya* grains and divided the rice into eight portions, he mixes seven of those portions and separates them according to their respective shares with the formula, "Separate yourselves according to your portions," setting aside the portion intended for the parched grain (*lāja*). Thus, there is a designation of the deities for both [sets of offerings] according to their respective divinities.

The smallest grains should be for the sake of the *lāja* (parched grain) offering; the largest ones are for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva*. Having threshed them, one performs the three-fold husking (*triṣphalīkaraṇa*) in succession. The setting aside of those intended for the *savanīya* offerings is done by way of a single performance (*tantra*). Having divided the *peṣya* (grains to be ground) for the *savanīya* offerings, he divides the gods among the *peṣya* portions. Alternatively, even for the *aindra* [portion] of the *savanīya* offerings, or for those belonging to the *vaiśvadeva*, he includes Pūṣan at the end. Having placed all the *kapāla* (potsherds), the milking for the *maitrāvaruṇī* [offering] takes place. Then follows the milking for the *vaiśvadevī*. "He should place the *madantī* (hot water) over the fire," and so forth.

Having ground the flour in a single vessel and having purified the flour, he purifies the *ṛjiṣa*. Having formed a ball of barley-meal in sequence and having divided it as in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices and designated the portions, the removal from the fire (*udvāsana*) is performed in sequence. At the time of removal, having removed the *saknīya* offerings and having completed the pouring of the *vājina*, the removal of the *Cāturmāsya* offerings is performed up to the pouring of the *vājina*; then follows the decoration in sequence, and so forth.
The animal sacrifice is for Viśvedevas; the *anubandhyā* cow is dedicated to Bṛhaspati.

The word "it happens" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Having performed the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites, and having encircled the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) from left to right (*pradakṣiṇam*), he dedicates the animal for the Viśve Devās (*vaiśvadeva*). This follows the procedure of the eleven animals (*aikādaśināvṛtti*). As before, the tethering of the *savanīya* animal takes place at the enclosing-sticks. Having set out the *savanīya* offerings, he sets out the *cāturmāsya* offerings. Having mixed the whey (*vājina*) of the two [animals], he places it on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*). At the time of the performance, having proceeded with the *savanīya* offerings, he proceeds with the oblations of the Viśve Devās. || 27 ||
They do not erect a sacrificial post. || 28 ||
And because of the restriction of the enclosing-sticks.
They do not throw up the northern altar. || 29 ||
And because of the restrictive rule. || 29 ||
They tie the animal to the enclosing stick, or to a firebrand, or to the sacrificial grass. They erect the [other] posts in the northern part; they strew the earth around the northern altar. || 30 ||

He offers the Vaiśvadeva oblations following the *prātaḥsavanīya* offerings. However, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* are common [to all]. They do not erect a sacrificial post (*yūpa*). They do not prepare the northern altar (*uttaravedi*). They tether the animal to a enclosing stick (*paridhi*), or to a firebrand (*ulmuka*), or to the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). For the subsequent [offerings], they erect the sacrificial posts and prepare the northern altar—thus says Āpastamba. "However, the *sviṣṭakṛt* is common" means that it is performed by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*).

Regarding the *vasā-prāśitra* and the two *payasyā*s, in both cases there is only one branch used according to the *tantra* method; thus, in the case of the postponement (*utkarṣa*), it is postponed along with them. At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives fifty as the fee. There is no worship of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-upasthāna*). Since the casting away of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi-praharaṇa*) has not been performed, all the duties pertaining to the *cātvāla* pit, including the worship and so forth, are omitted, just as in the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice. There is the cessation of the optional *atigrāhya* cup; some say it is indeed optional. Therefore, even here, its binding to the enclosing stick (*paridhi*) takes place.

Then, having performed the rites up to the *udavasānīyā* offering and having put on a new garment, they should undertake the vows of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. The Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is thus completed. || 30 ||

Then, during the four months of the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, there is a three-night rite consisting of an Agniṣṭoma, an Ukthya, and an Atirātra; a sacrificial animal for the Maruts; a second one for Varuṇa; and a Maitrāvaruṇī Anūbandhyā cow.

The commencement of the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing) should take place on the full moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha; having performed twelve *dīkṣā*s and twelve *upasad*s as before, the commencement is made by awaiting that specific time. According to the statement of the Chandogas, there are two days in the space allotted for the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings. On the sixth day, one intends to sacrifice with the second [set of offerings], while some say "with the Virātra"; and all [procedures] are like those of the ten-day period (*daśāha*). On that very day, the *dakṣiṇīyā* (consecration offering) takes place.

At the time of cutting the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), he cuts a single post; having strewn the *uttaravedi* altar on the day of the fast (*aupavasathya*), and having performed the second enclosure as for the fire-altar, the *pratiprasthātṛ* brings the branch of the *māruta* cow, and likewise performs the driving away of the calves for that branch. At the time of the post, they erect the post; having performed the dismemberment of the *payasyā* curd-mixture, there is the milking of the *māruta* cow and the bringing of the *barhis* grass for the *savanīya* animal sacrifice. [The ritual proceeds] from "the braid of flowers bound in three parts," etc., up to the end of the strewing of the grass.

On the following day, at the great night, having awakened, [the ritual proceeds] with "O Agni, lead us," and so forth, as in the Agniṣṭoma. At the time of offering the *savanīya* oblations, one offers the *vaiśvadeva* and *vāruṇapraghāsika* oblations either on the previous day or on the subsequent day, having divided all of them; thus states the Āpastamba Sūtra (ĀpŚS 22.8.11). Since this was not even mentioned by the commentator Kapardin, the following deliberation must be made.
There arises a doubt: "Are all the Vāruṇapraghāsika oblations to be performed on this day," thus dividing them between this [first] and the subsequent [day], or rather, "only on the subsequent day"?

Some explain that the offering (nirvāpa) of all should take place on the first day, because of its priority; for there is no reason to perform the offering on the subsequent day by bypassing the first. Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that they are divided, with some on the earlier day and others on the subsequent day. This is because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga), as the venerable Āpastamba has stated the Sākamedha oblations separately.

Furthermore, regarding the indicative mark (*liṅga*): in all the *iṣṭi*-type offerings of the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the deity is *payasyā* (curd-mixture). Here, in the *soma* sacrifices, the deity is the animal (*paśu*). In the *vaiśvadeva* [parvan], the animal belongs to the Viśvedevas. In the *varuṇapraghāsa*, there is a *māruta* (Marut-related) animal; for the second [offering], it belongs to Varuṇa. In the *sākamedha*, there is no *payasyā*; therefore, the animal is different. In the *śunāsīrīya*, there is milk for Vāyu. Because we see that in the *iṣṭi* type there is an animal for Vāyu, the animal here must be *māruta*, since it is already present in the preceding [parvan].

There are seven oblations beginning with those for the Maruts on the first day; on the second day, or rather on the subsequent day, there is the offering to Varuṇa because of the presence of the Vāruṇī curd-mixture, as well as the offering to Ka on the subsequent day. Furthermore, because of the observation of the opening verses (*pratipad*), the offering to Ka is also on the subsequent day. How so? In the three-day *Sākamedha* sacrifice, after the two days of the *Vāruṇapraghāsika*, in the *Sākamedha*, there is a single cake (*ekakapāla*) dedicated to Varuṇa and Prajāpati, and Viśvakarman is also its deity; thus, a pair of opening verses dedicated to that deity is prescribed.

On the first day of the two days of the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice, the Sākamedha is prescribed for the third day; on the first day of the three-day period, the Vaiśvakarmaṇa rites are prescribed, and therefore the Kāya rite must also be performed on that subsequent day. Such is the procedure to be followed. Now, let us return to the subject at hand.

At the time of the preparation of the vessels for the *savanīya* offerings, he prepares the vessels for the *savanīya* oblations as well as those for the *vāruṇapraghāsika* offerings. Having poured out the *savanīya* rice, and having poured out upon that same heap the *vāruṇapraghāsika* grains up to those for Indra-Agni, the *Pratiprasthātṛ* [prepares] those for the Maruts with the formula "May the Maruts accept you. Then, having performed the sprinkling and other rites together for the sake of the *karambha* vessels, up to the end of the pouring [of the grains], [he offers] to Indra-Agni, to Pūṣan, to Soma accompanied by Pūṣan, and to Sarasvatī; [the portions are] "this for Indra," "for Agni."

Because [the mantras] "of Savitṛ," "of Pūṣan," "of Indra and Agni," and "of the Maruts" serve the purpose of grinding, they do not refer to the water in this way; rather, having placed the potsherds in sequence with [mantras] ending in the dative case, there is the milking for Mitra and Varuṇa.

He places the boiling water on the fire; having formed a lump [of flour], he first distributes the rice grains according to their portions: "Separate yourselves! This is for Indra Harivant; this is for Indra accompanied by Pūṣan"—this is one portion; "This is for Soma accompanied by Sarasvatī"—this is the portion already mentioned. Then, regarding the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśas*), he says, "Separate yourselves! and again, "Separate yourselves! Then, regarding the rice grains, he says, "May we separate," "Separate yourselves," "May you two separate," and "This is for Soma accompanied by Sarasvatī"—this is for the cooked rice (*caru*).

The Adhvaryu prepares the ram for Indra and Agni, followed by that for the Maruts. Then, after the placing [on the fire] of the barley, he proceeds with the curds for Indra; then follows the bringing of the curds for Mitra and Varuṇa. [Paṭala 3] In the Mahādevaśāstrī-compiled *Prayogacandrikā* commentary, then he places the ram for the Vāruṇapraghāsa offerings in due order. Thereafter, the bringing of the curds is omitted for all; at the time of taking them down from the fire, all are taken down in their respective order.

It is according to the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* as in the case of the *dvirātra*. Some [hold that] at the time of the animal sacrifice there is a *māruta* animal. After the *viharaṇa*, at the proper time, one protects the *mārjālīya* fire; having performed the *vājajit* for the *savanīya* animal on the *āhavanīya*, the offering of the *karambha-pātras* takes place at the *mārjālīya*. Having muttered "They have done" (*akran*), and having proceeded with the *savanīya* offerings beginning with "Thou art the pressing" (*savanam asi*), he proceeds with the offerings belonging to the *vāruṇapraghāsa* ending with the two rams. However, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* are the same, as are the specific [offerings]. He gives fifty as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The day concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.

The continuities of the *ahīna* sacrifices are like those of the twelve-day (*dvādaśāha*) sacrifice. Having performed the driving away of the calves for the Maitrāvaruṇī cow, the Adhvaryu performs that same act immediately for the Vāruṇī cow. Having performed the milking of the Maitrāvaruṇī cow, the Adhvaryu alone performs the milking of the Vāruṇī cow. Some say that the Pratiprasthātṛ alone [performs it] up to the end of the spreading of the grass for the *savanīya* offering.

Having understood the *mahāsattra*, [one recites] "O Agni, lead us," and so forth. At the time of pouring out the *savanīya* [oblation], there are two potsherds for roasting, eleven potsherds for the ewe (*meṣī*), or eight for the goat (*kāyā*), and one single potsherd; the wooden sword (*sphya*) and [other implements] are in pairs. All the rest is as before. Having poured out the *savanīya* [grain], [one performs the rites] for that very [deity] with the formula "pleasing to Agni," prior to the sifting [of the grain].

"Separate yourselves according to your respective portions: 'This is for Indra accompanied by the Haris; this is for Indra accompanied by Pūṣan; this is for Indra and Varuṇa; this is for Ka; and this is for the [cups] belonging to Indra and Agni. Having performed the pouring out (adhivāpa) in this sequence, having placed the potsherds, and having performed the milking for Mitra and Varuṇa, [he says]: 'Separate yourselves according to your portions; let us separate them: this is for Varuṇa, this is for Ka,' and so forth. First, having placed the cake for Indra over the fire according to the sequence of the *savanīya* offerings, [he proceeds with] the evening milking and the intervening rites, and so on. At the time of taking down from the fire, the removal is done in sequence."

There is no transposition of the ram and the ewe here. At the time for each respective animal sacrifice, one performs the rite with the Vāruṇa animal at the time of its performance; having performed the rites with the *savanīya* offerings, one then proceeds with the offering of the Vāruṇī. The Adhvaryu says, "Recite for the Kāya [offering]," and so forth. The *sviṣṭakṛt*, the *iḍā*, and the *praśitra* are common [to all]. The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of fifty [cows]. At the time of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), having touched a drop [of water], there is the silent disposal of the flour and the scrapings. The *maitrāvaruṇī anūbandhyā* (the cow to be bound after the sacrifice) follows. This concludes with the *udavasānīyā* (final offering); thereafter, the seasonal vows (*cāturmāsya-vratāni*) are observed.

Alternatively, according to the school of Āśvalāyana, the offering (nirvāpa) of all the Vāruṇaprayāsika oblations and the Karambha-pātras takes place on the very next day. The procedure is as follows: on the preceding day, there is the milking of the three Payasyās—namely, that for Mitra-Varuṇa, that for the Maruts, and that for Varuṇa.

On the following day, at the time for the *savanīya* offerings, having set out the vessels used for both purposes and having poured out the *savanīya* grains, he pours out all the materials for the *Vāruṇapraghāsika* rites into those same grains—those intended for the *karambha* vessels and those for both [the *caru*s]. Having recited the formula for both, and having performed the placing [of the grains] after reciting the formula for both, he performs the actions prior to the pouring [of the grains] with the words: "Separate yourselves according to your portions: this is for Indra accompanied by the Haris; this is for Indra accompanied by Pūṣan; this is for Soma; this is for Sarasvatī"; and for the *caru* materials: "this is for Indra and Agni" and "this is for Indra."

The pouring out [of the grains] is performed in order for Savitṛ, Pūṣan, Indra-Agni, the Maruts, and Varuṇa, ending with that for Pūṣan. Having placed the potsherds in order, the milking is done for Mitra-Varuṇa (and then for the Maruts and Varuṇa). Having mixed the boiling water and formed a lump, he separates the rice grains according to their respective portions: "Separate yourselves; this is for Indra accompanied by the Haris; this is for Indra accompanied by Pūṣan"—thus one portion.

"This for Soma, this for Sarasvatī"—with these words, he separates one portion of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Then [he says], "Separate yourselves," referring to the rice grains for Indra's cake; then, "Separate yourselves, separate yourselves" three times. Again: "May she who is the ewe separate herself; may you two, the goats for Varuṇa and Ka, separate yourselves. "This for Soma, this for Sarasvatī"—thus [he designates] the two *caru* offerings.

It has been stated: "This belongs to Varuṇa; this belongs to whom? The ritual rules for placing [the vessels] on the fire follow in order: [one places] the *lājās* with the formula "You are the Law (*dharma*)," then the *aindra* [oblation]; then the bringing of the curd for the *maitrāvaruṇī*; then the *āgneya*; then the *saumya* pap; then, having placed the oblations beginning with the *sāvitra* and ending with the *aindrāgna* on the fire, one places the ewe; then the bringing of the curd for the *mārutī*; then the *kāya*, which is interspersed among all of them.

At the time of the *udāsana* (removal), having removed the *savanīya* offerings and having performed the drawing out (*uddharaṇa*) into two vessels, he removes the *vāruṇaprayāsī* offerings in due order. At the time of the animal sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Varuṇa. Having performed the maintenance of the *mārjālīya* fire during the distribution of the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths for the *savanīya* animal with the mantra "O Agni, bestower of vigor," the offering of the *karambha* vessels takes place at the *mārjālīya*.

Having muttered "akran" and so forth, and having performed the rites with the *savanīya* offerings starting with "bhuvanam asi," the *sviṣṭakṛt*, the *iḍā*, and the specific portions for all the *vāruṇa* and other offerings are the same. At the time of giving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he gives fifty cows; this is the same as the previous procedure. Some say that on the first day, the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) of all [the offerings] takes place. In that case, the performance follows the third method mentioned immediately above. Even then, one emerges from the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) until the conclusion of the *udavasānīyā* offering. Thus the Varuṇapraghāsa rites are completed. 31.

Then, after four months, there is the *Sākamedha* sacrifice, consisting of a three-night rite: an *agniṣṭoma*, an *ukthya*, and an *atirātra*. Now, on the full moon day of Kārttika, having performed twelve *dīkṣā*s and twelve *upasad*s so that the *sutyā* (pressing) occurs on the first day of the three-night rite, the commencement follows. Alternatively, according to the view of the *Chandogas*, the commencement is made so that the final day of that three-night rite falls on the *parvan* (the new or full moon).

Having performed twelve initiations (*dīkṣā*) according to the procedure of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), his ritual action is as follows: "I shall sacrifice with the Atirātra; you are lightning, O All. It is like the twelve-day rite. There is no piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) and no Sāvitra offering, because of the rule regarding the *uttaravedi*. The ritual action, well-established up to the end of the *aupavasathya* day, involves the fetching of the *vasatīvarī* waters and the distribution of the milks. In this ritual, they erect the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). At the time of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, it continues until the strewing around the *savanīya* offerings. Having awakened at the deep of night, [the ritual begins] with "O food, come hither," etc., as in the *agniṣṭoma*.

At the time of the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) of the *puroḍāśa* cakes for the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*), one pours out the portion for the morning libation with the formula: "I pour out what is pleasing to Agni Anīkavat. In the case of barley, this is done over the poured-out barley; in the case of rice, over the poured-out rice. The division takes place before the threshing, with the thought: "May the rice be separated. Otherwise, the division takes place before the pouring onto the grinding stones (*adhivapana*). [The formulas are: "Separate yourselves! This is for Indra accompanied by the Bays (*harivat*), for Indra accompanied by Pūṣan, for Indra who pierces the enemy. The rest is as previously stated. || 32 ||

The animal for Agni is first; the one for Indra-Agni is second; those of the eleven [deities] are third, or else the one for Prajāpati, with the animal for Sūrya as the *anūbandhya*. The animal for Agni is obtained; [then] that for Indra-Vāyu. Because the day for Pūṣan is a modification of the first day, the *atigrāhya* cups for that three-day period are likewise. Having proceeded with the *savanīya* offerings, there is the performance for Agni Anīkavant. At the midday pressing, together with the *savanīya* offerings, there is the offering of the *caru* oblation for the Maruts Sāṃtapana.
"I offer what is pleasing to the Maruts Sāṃtapana"—this portion is joined with syllables that are not thick.
Now, in the eighteenth book, the first chapter:
Sattras beginning with the Dvādaśāha and the Prajādi.
Those which follow after the first year-long session, having the Gavāmayana as their archetype, are sacrificial sessions (satras) with an Atirātra at both ends.
The third day is an Atirātra with the fifteen-fold Ukthya stoma at its conclusion. || 3 ||
Likewise, the Kuṇḍapāyināmayaṇa sacrifice. || 4 ||
For them, the ritual procedure for a twelve-day sacrifice has been explained by [the rules for] the *kalpa*. ||5||
By means of the eleven-night rite of the seasons, they create offspring; they win offspring; they obtain offspring; they become possessed of offspring. ||6||
The Jyotiratirātra [sacrifice]. || 7 ||
The Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha. || 8 ||
There are three Chandomas.
The Atirātra [sacrifice]. ||18.1.10||
Two [sacrifices] of thirteen nights each. || 11 ||
Whatever desire they desire, that they attain. || 12 ||
An Atirātra, a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, an Atirātra consisting of all the Stomas, four Chandomas, and an Atirātra. || 13 ||
A second [set] should undertake it, desiring spiritual luster.
The Atirātra, twelve days of the Dvādaśāha, the Mahāvrata, and the Atirātra. ||15||

There are three [sacrificial sessions] of fourteen nights each. Whatever desire they may desire, that they attain. An *atirātra*, a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, a reversed *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, and an *atirātra*—those who undertake these attain all prosperity. An *atirātra*, a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period beginning with the *trayastriṃśa* [stoma], and an *atirātra*—this second [set] those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should undertake.

An Atirātra, a Jyotis, a Gau, and an Āyu—this is the three-day period; a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha; an Āyu, a Gau, and a Jyotis—an Atirātra. Those desiring stability should perform this as the third [set]. An Atirātra, a Gau, and an Āyu—two days; the ten days of the twelve-day rite; an Atirātra. (Section 1) 16.
There are four fifteen-night sessions. || 17 ||
They go to the state of divinity. || 18 ||

On the new moon day is the *prāyaṇīya* [Atirātra]; on the eighth day is the *mahāvratam*; on the full moon day is the *udayanīya*. Or else, they may proceed in the other way: Atirātra, Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha, Mahāvratam, Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha, and an Atirātra beginning with the Trayastriṃśa stoma. Regarding the second [form], they should deliberate upon it for use in a bedchamber, in water, or at a wedding. [The third form is: Atirātra, Jyotis, Gauḥ, Āyuḥ—this is the three-day period; Pṛṣ�ṭhya-ṣaḍaha, Mahāvratam, Āyuḥ, Gauḥ, Jyotis, and Atirātra. Those desiring stability should perform the third [form].

The Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma, Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyuḥ; the three-day period; the ten days of the twelve-day rite; and the Atirātra. Those desiring heaven should undertake this fourth [set]. The Atirātra, Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyuḥ; the three-day period; the ten days of the twelve-day rite; and the Atirātra. By means of this sixteen-night rite dedicated to Indra, they conquer all victories and attain food in due order. These same [rites] include the Mahāvrata. 18.1.20.

Those desiring food and sustenance should undertake the seventeen-night sacrifice. It consists of an Atirātra, a Jyotis, a Gauḥ, a Jyotis, a Gauḥ, an Āyus, a five-day period, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an Atirātra. || 21 ||

Those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should perform the eighteen-night sacrifice: an *atirātra*, an *abhiplava* six-day period, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), and an *atirātra*. || 22 ||
Within nineteen nights, they attain lordship over all animals. These very [rites] include the Mahāvrata. || 23 ||

Those who undertake these [sacrifices] become endowed with Vedic splendor and eaters of food within twenty nights. [The structure is as follows: an Atirātra, the Gauḥ and Āyus two days, a six-day Abhiplava period, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an Atirātra. (Section 2) 24.

There are two [sacrifices] of twenty-one nights each. Whatever desire they may wish for, that they attain; they achieve all prosperity and become more wealthy. Those who undertake these [sacrifices]—an *atirātra*, a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, three *svarasāman* days, a *divākīrtya* day, three *svarasāman* days, a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, a *trayastrimśa* day, an *araṇya* day, an *atirātra*—undertake them during the summer heat. They sacrifice an animal to Soma and Pūṣan. The *ṛc*s of Manu serve as the *sāmidhenī* verses. 25.
By the second [set], they prosper in both worlds—both in this one and in that one—who undertake these: an Atirātra, an Abhiplava six-day period, an Abhiplava six-day period, and an Atirātra. || 26 ||

Those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should perform the twenty-two-night sacrifice. It consists of an *atirātra*, a *jyotis*, a *go*, an *āyuḥ*—these three days; an *abhiplava* *ṣaḍaha*; ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*); the *mahāvrata*; and an *atirātra*. || 27 ||

"Those desiring stability should undertake the twenty-three-night sacrifice. It consists of an Atirātra, the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, the Āyus, a Pañcāha Abhiplava, a Ṣaḍaha, the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, and an Atirātra. || 28 ||

There are two [sacrifices] of twenty-four nights. Whatever desire they may desire, that they attain; they achieve all prosperity and become more wealthy—those who undertake these [sacrifices]: an *atirātra*, two *abhiplava* periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), and an *atirātra*. (Section 3) || 29 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the eighteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
Now begins the second chapter in the eighteenth book.

By means of the twenty-four-night *sattra* sacrifice, those who perform it sit in the heavenly world. It consists of an *atirātra*, a twenty-four-fold *ukthya* as the introductory day, and a six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) with the *trivṛt* or the *pṛṣṭhya-stoma*.

Now, the Trayastriṃśa day is described: it is established in the ritual procedure (tantra) of the Upahavya sacrifice. At its midday pressing, there is the Kaṇvarathantara chant. The Trayastriṃśa day is explicit (nirukta). There are two Triṇava days, two Ekaviṃśa days, and a Triṇava day; the Trayastriṃśa day is explicit. The six-day period consists of the Pṛṣṭhya Stomas. The Trayastriṃśa day is explicit. The Trivṛt day is explicit. The Jyotirvaiśvānara Atirātra follows. || 1 ||
Those desiring food and drink should undertake the twenty-five-night sacrifice. It consists of an Atirātra, two Abhiplava periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, the Mahāvrata, and an Atirātra.

Those desiring heaven should undertake the twenty-six-night sacrifice: an Atirātra, the Gauḥ and Āyus two days, two Abhiplava periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (Dvādaśāha), and an Atirātra. || 3 ||
In twenty-seven nights they conquer the world of Āditya; these very [nights] include the Mahāvrata.

Those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should perform this for twenty-eight nights. It consists of an *Atirātra*, the *Jyotis*, *Go*, and *Āyu* [Sāmans], a three-day period, two *Abhiplava* periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), the *Mahāvrata*, and an *Atirātra*. (5)

Those desiring prosperity should perform it for twenty-nine nights: an Atirātra, a Jyotis, a Gauḥ, an Āyus, a Gauḥ, an Āyus, a Pañcāha, two Abhiplavas, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (Dvādaśāha), and an Atirātra. || 6 ||
Those desiring food and drink should perform this for thirty nights: an Atirātra, three Abhiplava periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an Atirātra. (Section 4) 7.
In thirty-one nights they obtain food in due order; these same [days] include the Mahāvrata. ||8||

Those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should perform [this sacrifice] for thirty-two nights: an *Atirātra*, the *Gauḥ* and *Āyus* two days, three *Abhiplava* periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), and an *Atirātra*. || 9 ||

Those desiring prosperity should undertake it for thirty-three nights: an *atirātra*, three five-day periods (*pañcāha*), a *viśvajit* *atirātra*, three five-day periods, and an *atirātra*. By means of this second twelve-night sacrificial session (*satra*), they attain prosperity; by that much is its success: an *atirātra*, an *abhiplava* six-day period, an *atirātra*, an *abhiplava* six-day period, an *atirātra*, an *abhiplava* six-day period, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), the *mahāvrata*, and an *atirātra*. Those desiring a firm foundation should undertake the third [twelve-night rite].
An Atirātra, three Pañcāhas, a Viśvajit Atirātra, one Pañcāha, the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, and an Atirātra. || 18.2.10 ||

Those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should perform this for thirty-four nights: an *atirātra*, the *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus* [sacrifices], three *ahargaṇa*s of three days each, the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) consisting of its ten days, the *mahāvrata*, and an *atirātra*. (Section 5) 11.

Those who undertake these [sacrifices] obtain food from this year, from the thirty-five nights, and from yonder sun. [The sequence is]: an Atirātra, Jyotis, Gauḥ, Āyus; Gauḥ, Āyus, Pañcāha; three Abhiplavas; the ten days of the Dvādaśāha; and an Atirātra. || 12 ||
Those desiring heaven should perform the thirty-six-night sacrifice. It consists of an Atirātra, four Abhiplava periods, the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, and an Atirātra. || 13 ||
In thirty-seven nights they conquer the world of Āditya; these very [nights] include the Mahāvrata.

Those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should perform this sacrifice in thirty-eight nights: an *Atirātra*, the *Gauḥ* and *Āyuḥ* two-day periods, four *Abhiplava* six-day periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), and an *Atirātra*. || 15 ||

By means of a thirty-nine-night sacrifice, they attain sovereignty over all cattle. Those desiring offspring should perform this: an Atirātra, the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, the Āyuḥ, a three-day period, four Abhiplava periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an Atirātra. By means of a forty-night sacrifice, they attain a firm foundation in the supreme Virāj. These same [sacrifices] include the Mahāvrata. (Section 6) 17.
Thus ends the second chapter in the eighteenth book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
Now begins the third chapter in the eighteenth book.

The *vidhṛti* [sacrifice] consists of one [day]; they do not return with the sinless rival. Those who perform these: an *atirātra*, three *trivṛt* *agniṣṭomas*, an *atirātra*, ten *pañcadaśa* *ukthyas*, a tenth day with the *ṣoḍaśin*, an *atirātra*, twelve *saptadaśa* *ukthyas*, an *atirātra*, a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), an *atirātra*, twelve *ekaviṃśa* *ukthyas*, and an *atirātra*—this is the *atirātra*.

This is the second [form] of these; it brings them prosperity. Mitra, Varuṇa, Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Aṃśa, Bhaga, Indra, and Vivasvat—they attain the prosperity of these deities and become more wealthy who undertake these [sacrifices], beginning with the Atirātra, two Abhiplavas, the Go and Āyus [days], two Abhiplavas each, the Abhijit and Viśvajit, two Atirātras, one Abhiplava consisting of all the Stomas, nine Saptadaśa [Stoma days], the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, the Mahāvrata, and the Atirātra. (Section 7) 2.

The third [rite] consists of collyrium and ointment; when people do not know them, or when they apply it or smear it on, they place beauty within themselves, for they recognize them. [This is done] with *gulgulu* resin at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), with *saugandhika* at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina savana*), and with *pautudāru* wood at the third pressing. Those who undertake these [rites] perform: an *atirātra*, four *abhiplava* periods, an *atirātra* consisting of all the *stomas*, a nine-night period (*navarātra*) as the core, two more *abhiplavas*, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), an *atirātra* with a nine-night period as the core, and a fourth [period].

Measured by the year, they attain the productive power of the year for those who undertake these [sacrifices]: an Atirātra, a Caturviṃśa Ukthya as the introductory rite, two Trivṛt Abhiplavas, a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, the Abhijit, three Svarasāmans, the Divākīrtya, the Mahāvrata, three Svarasāmans, the Viśvajit, one Abhiplava, the Pratyāṅga and Āyuṣī, the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, the Mahāvrata, and an Atirātra. (Section 8)

The fifth is the preeminent form of Savitṛ; they proceed toward the procreation of all who undertake these [sacrifices]: an Atirātra, three Trivṛt days, a six-day period (ṣaḍaha) with the Agniṣṭoma as its opening, followed by three more Trivṛt days—the Agniṣṭomas on both sides and the Ukthya in the middle—and likewise nine Pañcadaśa days, nine Saptadaśa days, nine Ekaviṃśa days, twelve days of the Dvādaśāha, the Mahāvrata, and the Atirātra. Those desiring a firm foundation should undertake the sixth of the seasons.

An Atirātra, four Abhiplava periods, the Mahāvrata, two Abhiplavas, the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, and an Atirātra; Indra and Agni are the seventh [day], for they surpass other offspring and become most powerful. Those who undertake these [sacrifices] perform an Atirātra, six Abhiplavas, the Mahāvrata, two Abhiplavas, the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, and an Atirātra. (Section 9) 3.

Within sixty-one nights, they attain whatever desire they may wish for; they achieve all prosperity and become more wealthy. Those who undertake these [sacrifices] perform as follows: an Atirātra, a Caturviṃśa Ukthya as the introductory rite, a Trivṛt, three Abhiplava six-day periods, a Pṛṣṭhya six-day period, an Abhijit, three Svarasāmans, a Divākīrtya Mahāvrata, three Svarasāmans, an Abhijit, a Pṛṣṭhya six-day period beginning with the Trayastriṃśa stoma, one Abhiplava, two Pratyāṅgas Āyus, the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, the Mahāvrata, and an Atirātra. 4.

By means of the Śatarātra sacrifice, they attain the state of the gods. Those who undertake this—consisting of an Atirātra, Jyotis, Gauḥ, Āyuḥ, three Ahar-sessions, fourteen Abhiplava periods, the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, the Mahāvrata, and another Atirātra—whether proceeding toward it or staying in one place, they press the Soma. (Section 10) 5.
By means of the Ādityānām Ayana, they become firmly established in these worlds.
It has been explained by [the rules for] the Gavāmayana. || 7 ||
All the months consist of Abhiplava periods; in their midst is the Pṛṣṭhya [period], followed by fifteen Trivṛt Abhiplavas.
In the place of Abhijit, there is the Trivṛt Bṛhaspatisava. ||9||
In the place of the Viśvajit, there is the fifteen-fold Stoma of Indra.

Having reached the *pṛṣṭha* and *abhiplava* [sections], there are the expanded (*vyūḍha*) *agniṣṭoma*s consisting of the *trivṛt* [stomas] by means of the *udbhid* and *balabhid* sacrifices. In the final month, the *sambhārya* [days] are deficient; the *abhiplava* occurs in the middle, and the *go* and *āyus* [sacrifices] follow after the sixth day of the six-day period.
The Chandomas consist of a ten-night rite (daśarātra):

[the stomas] facing westward are the forty-eight-fold, the forty-four-fold, the thirty-six-fold, the thirty-two-fold, the thirty-fold, two twenty-eight-fold, the twenty-five-fold, the twenty-four-fold, the tenth is the Avivākya, the Mahāvrata, and the Udayanīya Atirātra.
Those desiring heaven should undertake the Aṅgirasām Ayana.
This has been explained by the *ādityānām ayana*. 15.

All the *abhiplava* months are preceded by *pṛṣṭhya* periods before the *viṣuvat*, and followed by *pṛṣṭhya* periods after the *viṣuvat*. Above the *viṣuvat* are the *chandomas*, the ten-night period (*daśarātra*), the ascending *stomas*: the twenty-five-fold, two twenty-eight-fold, the thirty-fold, thirty-two-fold, thirty-six-fold, forty-fold, forty-eight-fold, forty-four-fold, forty-eight-fold, the twenty-four-fold, the tenth day which is the *avivākya*, the *mahāvrata*, and the concluding *atirātra*. Thus ends section 16.

By means of the Dṛtivātavaṭu sacrifice, whatever desire they may desire, they attain it; they achieve all prosperity and become more prosperous—those who perform these Atirātra rites. (Section 11) 17.
Thus ends the third paṭala in the eighteenth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the fourth chapter in the eighteenth book.

One month with the Trivṛt, one month with the Pañcadaśa, one month with the Saptadaśa, one month with the Ekaviṃśa, one month with the Triṇava, and one month with the Trayastriṃśa. These same are the subsequent months; it begins with the Trayastriṃśa and ends with the Trivṛt, followed by an Atirātra. ||1||
In the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana, they remain consecrated for one month.
Having purchased and bound the king, and having performed twelve *upasad* rites, they sacrifice with the *haviryajña* oblations for twelve months. For one month, they offer the *agnihotra*.
For one month they sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

One month with the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, one month with the Varuṇapraghāsas, one month with the Sākamedhas, and one month with the Śunāsīrīya. One month with the Trivṛt-stoma, one month with the Pañcadaśa-stoma, one month with the Ekaviṃśa-stoma, and one month with the Triṇava-stoma. There are eighteen days of thirty-three-fold stomas, ten days of the Dvādaśāha, the Mahāvrata, and the Atirātra.
They sacrifice with every kind of sacrifice. || 7 ||
All [of them] become [so]. || 8 ||
They consume [the Soma] from cups provided with handles. ||9||

He who is the Hotṛ is the Adhvaryu; he is the Potṛ. He who is the Udgātṛ is the Neṣṭṛ; he is the Acchāvāka. He who is the Maitrāvaruṇa is the Brahman; he is the Pratihartṛ. He who is the Prastotṛ is the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; he is the Grāvastut. He who is the Pratiprasthātṛ is the Agnīdh; he is the Unnetṛ. The Gṛhapati is the Gṛhapati; the Subrahmaṇya is the Subrahmaṇya. 18.4.10.
In the sacrificial session of the ascetics (tapasvin), there are consecrations for one year, attendant rites for one year, and soma-pressings for one year.
Through Prajāpati for twelve years, they are born with offspring and cattle. || 12 ||
Those who undertake this [sacrifice] perform three years of the Trivṛt, three of the Pañcadaśa, three of the Saptadaśa, and three of the Ekaviṃśa stomas. || 13 ||

This very sacrifice was performed by the residents of Naimiṣa who desired heaven; it consists of nine years of Trivṛt, nine of Pañcadaśa, nine of Saptadaśa, and nine of Ekaviṃśa stomas. For the Śākyas, there is the thirty-six-year sacrifice with the Tarasa cake, for which Agastya is the Gṛhapati.
On each day that concludes, the Gṛhapati goes out on a hunt, accompanied by some Adhvaryu priest. || 15 ||
The sacrificial cakes for those wild animals which he kills are made of *tarasa* (raw meat). || 16 ||
There are nine years of the Trivṛt, nine of the Pañcadaśa, nine of the Saptadaśa, and nine of the Ekaviṃśa stomas. || 17 ||
By this, indeed, Śākya Gauravīti attained all prosperity; they who practice this attain all prosperity and become more prosperous. 18.

There are twenty-five years consisting of the *trivṛt* [stoma], twenty-five consisting of the *pañcadaśa*, twenty-five consisting of the *saptadaśa*, and twenty-five consisting of the *ekaviṃśa*. || 19 ||

Through the thousandfold accomplishment of Agni, they go to the procreation of all. Those who undertake this perform the Atirātra with the thousand names, the Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma, and the Atirātra. 18.4.20 (Section 12)
There are three [verses] addressed to Sarasvatī. || 21 ||
The first belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa; the second to Indra and Agni; the third to Aryaman. || 22 ||
They undergo initiation by immersing themselves in the Sarasvatī. || 23 ||
On the new moon day, on that very day, they drive away the calves for the Prāyaṇīya day.
When the Atirātra sacrifice has been completed, they perform the Sāṃnāyya offering.
When that has been completed, the Adhvaryu throws the wooden pin (śamyā) away. || 26 ||
Wherever that [line] falls, there is the Gārhapatya fire; from there, at thirty-six steps, the Āhavanīya fire is located. || 27 ||
The Sadas, the Havirdhāna sheds, and the Āgnīdhra shed are provided with wheels. || 28 ||
The sacrificial post has its base in a mortar; it is drawn out and leveled right there. || 29 ||
They do not dig so as to make a noise. || 18.4.30 ||
They perform this sacrifice with the New Moon offering during the waxing fortnight.
On the full moon day, there is the Goṣṭoma Ukthya sacrifice, characterized by the Rathantara Sāman.
When that has been completed, they sacrifice with the Full Moon sacrifice. || 33 ||
They perform this latter fortnight with the Full Moon sacrifice. || 34 ||
On the new moon day, they perform the Āyuṣṭoma Ukthya sacrifice with the Bṛhat-sāman; thus they transpose them.
They proceed along the southern bank of the Sarasvatī, calling out aloud. || 36 ||
At the confluence of the Dṛṣadvatī, they offer an oblation to Apām Napāt and proceed further.
Among a thousand cows, they set free a bull. || 38 ||

When they make a thousand, that is one rising; when they make a hundred thousand, that is one rising; when their householder dies, that is one rising; or when they all suffer loss and are ruined, that is one rising; when they reach the Plakṣa Prasravaṇa tree, that is one rising. Having reached the Plakṣa Prasravaṇa, they perform a sacrifice to Agni Kāma.
Having given a mare and a human female as milch-cows to her, they descend into the Yamunā for the ritual bath at Kārapacava.
They become invisible to gods and humans. || 41 ||
In the second Atirātra, the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, the Āyuḥ, the Ayana, the Viśvajit, and the Abhijit vanish from among men. || 42 ||
In the second *atirātra*, there are the *jyotis*, *go*, *āyus*, *ayana*, *viśvajit*, and *abhijit* [sacrifices], which are the bellies of Indra; other offspring surpass them. ||43||
They become most powerful. || 44 ||
In the third [day] there is an Atirātra; the other two days consist of the Trivṛt and Pañcadaśa stomas, and the Go and Āyus are the two Indrakukṣis.
They go upon the path of Aryaman; they travel the path that leads to the gods.
In the case of a Dārṣadvata, he shall guard the cows of a Brāhmaṇa for one year. || 47 ||
For one year, he should kindle the fire on the Naitandhava barren soil.
After a year, having bound the sacrificial cord, he should establish the sacred fires.
On the southern bank of the Dṛṣadvatī, by means of an oblation on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni, [he performs the rite] with the distance of a yoke-pin's throw.
Three times they descend into the Yamunā at the Plakṣa tree for the ritual bath of purification (avabhṛtha).
That very [form] becomes invisible to human beings. || 52 ||
By means of the Turāyaṇa sacrifice, they attain all prosperity. || 53 ||
They attain the state of the Supreme Lord. || 54 ||
A cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and Agni, and a pap for the Viśvedevas. || 55 ||
The initiated one puts on a black antelope skin. || 56 ||
By that means, she attains prosperity just like a human woman. || 57 ||
Whatever austerity is performed, by that one becomes a performer of the *havirucchiṣṭa* vow for the sake of the divine. || 58 ||
For a year, day after day, he sacrifices with the iṣṭi offerings. || 59 ||
The ritual procedure for the *savana* is as follows. || 18.4.60 ||
By means of the Sarvasatra sacrifice, one conquers death once again. || 61 ||
Their radiance becomes like that of the Ādityas.
There are two Atirātras with an Agniṣṭoma in the middle. || 63 ||
Every year consists of ten decades; the twelfth is the Viṣuvat.

The Gavām Ayana sacrifice lasts for three years; it belongs to the Ādityas and the Aṅgirases. They go to Prajāpati, the Infinite, they conquer the heavenly world, and they find firm footing in these worlds. || 65 ||
By means of a thousand-year sacrifice to Prajāpati, they attain the prosperity of Prajāpati. || 66 ||
Those who undertake this [sacrifice] perform a thousand years of *trivṛt* *agniṣṭoma*s, followed by an *atirātra*. || 67 ||

The thousand-year sacrifice of the Viśvasṛjs (the World-Creators) creates the universe after them. Those who undertake this—fifty-five threefold years, fifty-five fifteenfold years, fifty-five seventeenfold years, and fifty-five twenty-one-fold years—[perform] the thousand-year sacrifice of the Viśvasṛjs; it creates the universe after them. Regarding this, there is a verse: "The Viśvasṛjs first performed the sacrificial session (*sattra*), proceeding for a thousand years with the pressed soma."

From that, indeed, was born the guardian of the world, the golden bird named Brahman. Those who approach this [knowledge] attain union with Brahman and residence in the same world as Brahman—those who approach this, those who approach this. 68.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the eighteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Thus ends the eighteenth book in the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Now begins the first chapter of the nineteenth book: We shall now explain the initiation ceremony (upanayana). || 1 ||
One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at seven years of age.
An eleven-year-old Kṣatriya and a twelve-year-old Vaiśya. || 3 ||
In spring, a Brāhmaṇa; in summer, a Rājanya; and in autumn, a Vaiśya. || 4 ||
During the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, and especially one with a masculine name. || 5 ||
Having served food to an even number of Brahmins and having caused them to recite "An auspicious day! and "May there be well-being!", || 6 ||

When the boy has been fed, his hair has been shorn, he has bathed, and has been adorned and dressed in a new garment, [the teacher]—having leveled the ground on a site that slopes toward the east, or toward the north, or toward the northeast, or on level ground; having sprinkled it with water, churned the fire, or brought a common (laukika) fire, and having established it, adds fuel to it. || 7 ||
He strews grass around the fire with its tips pointing eastward. ||8||
Moreover, they have their tips pointing toward the north both behind and in front. || 9 ||
If they have their tips pointing eastward or northward, one makes the southern ones northern and the northern ones southern.
To the south of the fire, having strewn darbha grass in the place of the Brahman priest.
Having taken the fire into himself with the two verses, "I take into myself that Agni who is ours... and "He who is our Agni... (RV 10.87.1–2), [he should proceed].
Having spread darbha grass to the north of the fire, he arranges the ritual materials as required.

An uncut stone, a garment, and a deerskin; for a Brāhmaṇa, a triple-stranded girdle made of Muñja grass; for a Rājanya, a bowstring; for a Vaiśya, a thread of wool. A staff of Bilva or Palāśa wood for a Brāhmaṇa; of Nyagrodha wood for a Rājanya; of Udumbara wood for a Vaiśya. || 14 ||
He prepares a fuel-stick of twenty-one pieces of wood, or [as many as] the number of oblations.
Upon that [altar], he binds together the sacrificial shavings, the enclosing sticks, and the fuel. || 16 ||
The wooden ladle, the grass-broom, the vessel for clarified butter, the vessel for carrying forward the water, the vessel for the sprinkling water, and whatever else is required. || 17 ||
Either all at once, or according to what is available. || 18 ||

At this time, Brahmā, having placed the sacrificial cord over his left shoulder, having sipped water, having stepped around behind the fire toward the south, having cast away a blade of grass from the seat of Brahmā, and having touched water, sits down facing the fire. || 19 ||

Having made two *pavitra* strainers from two *darbha* blades that are equal, with their tips cut off and measuring a span (*prādeśa*) in length, having cut them with another blade rather than with the fingernails, and having wiped them with water; then, having poured water into a vessel over which the *pavitra* strainers are placed, having filled it up to the brim, and having purified it three times by pouring it out with the *pavitra* strainers whose tips point northward; he places it on *darbha* grass to the north of the fire and covers it with *darbha* blades. 19.1.20.

Having prepared the sprinkling waters across the strainer as previously described, having placed the vessels with their bowls upward and having spread the fuel, he sprinkles it three times with all the waters.
Having heated the ladle, wiped it, heated it again, he sets it down. || 22 ||
Having sprinkled the brooms with water, he places them into the fire.

Having melted the clarified butter (*ājya*) and poured it into the *ājya-sthālī* over which a purifier (*pavitra*) has been placed, having drawn out embers toward the north, having set [the vessel] upon them, having illuminated [the butter], having cast two young *darbha* blades into it, having carried fire around it three times, having removed it from the embers toward the north, having pushed the embers back together, having purified the clarified butter three times by moving the purifiers back and forth with their tips pointing north, having sprinkled the purifiers with water, and having placed them back into the fire. (Section 1) 24.
He encloses [the altar] with yoke-pins; to the west of the fire, he places the middle pin with its notch facing north.
To the south, touching the fire, with the middle [line], having its jar facing east. ||26||
To the north of the fire, one should place [the vessel] touching it, with its opening facing east and positioned between the two middle ones.
To the west [of the fire], he sits down facing east. || 28 ||
To the south, having performed the *yajñopavīta* rite and sipped water, the youth sits down and takes hold [of the teacher]. || 29 ||
Then he sprinkles water around [the fire]. 19.1.30.
"O Aditi, give your consent," [he says] to the south, facing eastward. || 31 ||
With the words "O Anumati, give your consent," he [places it] behind, directed toward the north.
"O Sarasvatī, give your consent," [he says] to the north, facing eastward.
"O God Savitṛ, impel [us]," [reciting this] while circumambulating in a clockwise direction on all sides. || 34 ||

Having sprinkled [water] around, he places the fuel on the fire with the mantra: "This fuel is your self, O Jātavedas; with it, kindle yourself and grow; kindle us and make us grow; prosper us with offspring, cattle, spiritual luster, and the enjoyment of food, svāhā! (35)
Then he offers with the ladle. || 36 ||

Having brought the ladle along the northern junction of the enclosing sticks, while meditating mentally on "Svāhā to Prajāpati Manu," he offers the oblation straight, long, and continuous, directed toward the south-east.

Having led [the ladle] along the southern junction of the enclosing sticks, he pours the two straight Āghāra-libations—one directed eastward and one directed northward—with the formula, "Svāhā to Indra! (38).
He offers the two portions of clarified butter.
With "Svāhā to Agni," [he offers] in the eastern part of the northern half; with "Svāhā to Soma," in the eastern part of the southern half. || 19.1.40 ||
In the interval between those two, he offers the other oblations. ||41||

Be attentive, O Jātavedas; carry [the oblation] forward, O Agni. Know the work being performed here as it is done. You are the physician, the maker of the remedy; through you may we win cattle, horses, and men. Svāhā! You who lie across, saying "I am the supporter"—you, the one who brings about success, I worship with a stream of clarified butter in the fire. Svāhā! To the goddess Saṃrādhinī, Svāhā! To the goddess Prasādhinī, Svāhā! (Section 2) 42.
This is the ritual procedure for all *darvihoma* offerings. || 43 ||
The plural number is used for the spreading [of grass] and the sprinkling, as well as for other [acts]. At the end of a mantra, the utterance of "svāhā" is obligatory. || 44 ||
In the case of deities not addressed by name, one should offer with the formula "Svāhā to such-and-such," according to the specific deity.
He offers oblations with the vyāhṛtis—"bhūr," "bhuvaḥ," and "suvar"—both individually and collectively. || 46 ||
"O Agni, giver of life," this is the verse. || 47 ||

Bestowing long life, O Agni, praised as you grow old, with your face anointed with ghee and your back anointed with ghee—drinking the ghee, the lovely nectar of the cow—lead this man to old age like a father his son; *svāhā*! "This [is] for me, O Varuṇa," "To that I go to you," "You, O Agni, are ours," "So you, O Agni, are ours," "O Agni, you are the Unswerving One (*ayāsi*), established by the unswerving mind; as the Unswerving One, carry the oblation; bestow healing upon us, *svāhā*. "O Prajāpati"—this is the [concluding verse]. 48.

"Whatever of this rite I have done in excess, or whatever I have done here deficiently—may the wise Sviṣṭakṛt make all that well-offered and well-sacrificed for me. To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the consumer of well-offered oblations, the consumer of all oblations, the fulfiller of the desires of offerings—svāhā! With these words, he offers [the oblation] in the eastern part of the northern half [of the fire], without letting it touch the other oblations. ||49||
In this regard, some offer the Jaya, Abhyātāna, and Rāṣṭrabhṛt oblations before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
He offers the Jaya oblations with "cittam ca svāhā cittiś ca svāhā," or with "cittāya svāhā cittaye svāhā. || 51 ||
"Agni is the lord of beings; may he protect me"—thus [he recites] the Abhyātāna formulas.
"In this [Brahman], O Brahman; in this Kṣatra," he thus appends [the formula] to the *abhyātāna* offerings. || 53 ||
Saying, "The fathers, the grandfathers," he offers the oblation with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), or he worships [the ancestors]. || 54 ||
Having recited the sequence of the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* formulas beginning with "Ṛtaṣāṭ ṛtadhāmā," he offers the first oblation with "Svāhā to him! and the second with "Svāhā to them! || 55 ||
Having placed a stone at the front of the junction of the northern enclosing-stick, [he steps] with his right foot. (Section 3) 56.

He places the boy upon it [the stone] with the mantra: "May we stand firm upon the stone; like a stone, may you be steadfast. Crush those who seek to harm us; overcome those who attack us in battle. || 57 ||

Then, having set aside the previous one, he causes him to put on an unwoven garment with [the verse]: "Those goddesses who cut, who spun, who wove, and those divine ones who gave the borders all around—may those goddesses clothe you with old age. Long-lived, put on this garment! Clothe him, dress him in this garment; make him live for a hundred years, grant him long life. Bṛhaspati has given this garment to King Soma to bestow."

"You shall reach old age; put on the garment; become the protector against the curses of rival clans. Live for a hundred autumns with great luster, and clothe yourself in the increase of wealth. || 58 ||

Having caused him to put it on, he consecrates it with the mantra: "Put on this garment for well-being; O Earth, protector against curses among the waters! Live for a hundred abundant autumns, and as one worthy of honor, distribute riches while living. (59)

Then he winds the girdle three times around his waist from left to right at the level of the navel; some say twice. With the verse: "This auspicious sister of the gods, the girdle, has come to us, driving away misfortunes, providing protection and a secure refuge, purifying us, and bringing strength through the out-breath and the in-breath.
