(Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.17.60)
Having made a threefold knot to the north of the navel, he draws it around to the south of the navel.

Then he makes an antelope skin his upper garment: "The eye of Mitra, the supporter, the sustainer, resplendent, glorious, firm, kindled; the unsoiled, enduring garment—put on this powerful antelope skin! May Aditi bind it around you as your girdle, for the sake of speaking the Veda, for wisdom, for faith, for not rejecting what has been spoken, and for sacred knowledge and the splendor of sacred knowledge."
The skin of a black antelope for a Brāhmaṇa, that of a Ruru deer for a Rājanya, and the skin of a goat for a Vaiśya. || 63 ||

Then he entrusts him [to the deity]: "O Indra, we entrust this man to the Brahman for great hearing; may he long remain awake for his hearing until old age"—thus for a Brāhmaṇa. "O Indra, we entrust this man to the Brahman for great sovereignty; may he long remain awake for his sovereignty until old age"—thus for a Rājanya. "O Indra, we entrust this man to the Brahman for great prosperity; may he long remain awake for his prosperity until old age"—thus for a Vaiśya. (64)
Having seated him facing north behind the fire, he causes him to eat the remnants of the oblation with these [mantras] recited in a low tone: "In you, wisdom; in you, progeny. (65)
Some cause him to eat speckled butter.
With the two verses, "In every endeavor, O Agni, make him stronger for life and for splendor," he gazes at him as he consumes [the food]. || 67 ||
Some cause [the child] to eat [it]. || 68 ||

Having sipped water and performed the ritual touching of the body, he consecrates it with the mantra: "A hundred autumns are before us, O gods, within which you have ordained the aging of our bodies; wherein sons become fathers—do not harm our life-span in its course. (Section 4) || 69 ||

Thus ends the first chapter of the nineteenth book in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Gṛhyasūtra*. Now begins the second chapter of the nineteenth book. "May we come together; may we attain [long life]; ward off death! May we move about unharmed; may we proceed with well-being here and with well-being from our homes"—with these words, he addresses the student as he circumambulates the fire, keeping it to his right. || 1 ||
Then he makes him recite: "I have come for the life of a student; lead me near; be a student, impelled by the god Savitṛ. He asks him this.
When asked, "Who are you by name?", he declares himself according to his name.
"May there be well-being! O God Savitṛ, may I today through this [name] attain that [name]," thus he pronounces the two names. || 4 ||

"May the divine waters be auspicious for our protection and for our drinking; may they flow toward us for our well-being and prosperity"—with these words, both of them perform the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*).

Then, having taken hold of the boy’s right shoulder with his right hand and his left shoulder with his left hand, he leads him toward himself with the *vyāhṛtis*, the *Sāvitrī* verse, and [the formula]: "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I initiate you, O So-and-so. (6)

Then, with his own right hand, he takes hold of the bride’s right hand, including the thumb, saying: "Agni has taken your hand; Soma has taken your hand; Savitṛ has taken your hand; Sarasvatī has taken your hand; Pūṣan has taken your hand; Bṛhaspati has taken your hand; Mitra has taken your hand; Varuṇa has taken your hand; Tvaṣṭṛ has taken your hand; Dhātṛ has taken your hand; Viṣṇu has taken your hand; Prajāpati has taken your hand. Thus [he says]. 7.

"May Savitṛ protect you; you are Mitra by virtue of the sacred law (dharma); Agni is your teacher. Impelled by the god Savitṛ, become a student of Bṛhaspati, O [Name]! Drink water; place fuel on the fire; perform your duties; do not sleep during the day"—thus he instructs him.

Then, having repeatedly stroked his right shoulder with his right hand, he touches the region of the heart [of the student] with the mantra: "May your heart be in my heart; follow my mind with your mind; enjoy my speech with a one-pointed mind. May Bṛhaspati join you to me; cleave unto me alone. May your thoughts be in me; may your devotion be toward me; restrain your speech for me. (9)
"You are the knot of the vital breaths; do not loosen," [he says] over the region of the navel. (19.2.10)

Having consecrated him with the mantra: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! May I be rich in offspring through offspring; rich in heroes through heroes; rich in splendor through splendor; rich in nourishment through nourishment; rich in wisdom through wisdom; and rich in sacred knowledge through those who practice the student-life (brahmacārins)," he says: "Bhūḥ! I give you, O [Name], among the Ṛg-verses, in Agni, on the earth, in speech, and in the Brahman. Bhuvaḥ! I give you, O [Name], among the Yajus-formulas, in Vāyu, in the intermediate space, in breath, and in the Brahman. Suvaḥ! I give you, O [Name], among the Sāman-chants, in Sūrya, in heaven, in sight, and in the Brahman. You are my beloved; may I be yours, O [Name]! You belong to Anala."
"O Prāṇa, may I be dear to him; we two shall dwell together in this life, O Prāṇa, we shall dwell together in life; may you dwell [here], O [Name]!"—thus [he says]. || 11 ||
Then, with his own right hand, he grasps the boy’s right hand, including the thumb, with the five verses beginning, "Agni is long-lived. (12)
"Bestowing life upon you from every side," thus [he says]. (Section 5) 13.
He mutters "āyurdā agne" over the right ear, and [the same] over the left.

"Be established in fire, in earth, in wind, in the intermediate space, in the sun, in heaven! That well-being which Agni, Vāyu, Āditya, Candramas, and the waters follow—may you follow that well-being, O [Name]! He appends this to both [the teacher and the student], saying: "O [Name], you have become the student of the breath. || 15 ||

"May Indra grant you wisdom; may the goddess Sarasvatī grant you wisdom; may both the Aśvins, garlanded with lotuses, bestow wisdom upon you"—reciting this, he places his mouth close to the student's mouth and murmurs it. 16.

Then he entrusts him [to various deities]: "I entrust you to Kaśaka; I entrust you to Antaka; I entrust you to Aghora; I entrust you to Gada; I entrust you to Yama; I entrust you to Makha; I entrust you to Vaśinī; I entrust you to Pṛthivī together with Vaiśvānara; I entrust you to the Waters; I entrust you to the Plants; I entrust you to the Forest Trees; I entrust you to Heaven and Earth; I entrust you to Subhūta."
"I entrust you for the sake of spiritual luster; I entrust you to all the gods; I entrust you to all beings; I entrust you to all the deities. || 17 ||
Here he causes him to recite the Sāvitrī, if he has already been initiated previously.
If he has not been initiated, after three days have passed. || 19 ||
Immediately [afterward], Pauṣkarasādi [spoke]. 19.2.20.

To the west [of that], having placed a bundle of grass (kūrca) with its tips pointing northward, he sits upon it facing eastward, reciting: "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom, the teacher's seat; may I not suffer harm. (21)

Having made a reverential salutation with joined palms to the Āditya and having clasped the feet of the teacher, the boy sits down to the south and says, "Recite, sir! Then [the teacher] says, "Recite the Sāvitrī, sir!"

With the verse, "We invoke you, the Lord of hosts, the leader of the hosts," he addresses him. Then he recites for him first quarter by quarter, then half-verse by half-verse, and finally continuously: "Bhūḥ! That desirable splendor of Savitṛ, we meditate upon; may that light of the divine one inspire our thoughts. Bhuvaḥ! That desirable splendor of Savitṛ, we meditate upon; may that light of the divine one inspire our thoughts. Suvaḥ! That desirable splendor of Savitṛ, we meditate upon; may that light of the divine one inspire our thoughts. Bhūr-bhuvaḥ! That desirable splendor of Savitṛ, we meditate upon; may that light of the divine one inspire our thoughts."
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our thoughts. (Khaṇḍa 6) 23.
Then he causes him to place seven fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood—moist, with unbroken tips, a span in length, and anointed with clarified butter.

"I have brought a fuel-stick for Agni, the great Jātavedas; as you, O Agni, are kindled by the fuel-stick, so do you kindle me with wisdom, insight, offspring, cattle, and Vedic splendor—svāhā! Thus [he offers] one. 25.
"Two [verses] beginning with 'To Agni, two fuel-sticks'. || 26 ||
"Oblation for Agni with fuel"—these are four [verses]. || 27 ||
Then he sprinkles water around as before. || 28 ||
He joins the ends of the mantras with the words "thou hast approved" (anvamaṃsthāḥ) and "thou hast sent forth" (prāsāvīḥ). || 29 ||
Then he worships the deities. || 19.2.30 ||

"O Agni, lord of vows, I shall perform the vow," [he says] to Agni; "O Vāyu, lord of vows," to Vāyu; "O Āditya, lord of vows," to Āditya; and "O lord of vows, lord of vows," to the Lord of Vows. || 31 ||
In this case, he gives a boon to the teacher. || 32 ||

Having raised him up with the words, "O long-lived one! This is your son, Sūrya; I entrust him to you," he worships the sun with the mantra: "That eye, beneficial to the gods, which shines white in the east—may we see for a hundred autumns, may we live for a hundred autumns, may we rejoice for a hundred autumns, may we delight for a hundred autumns, may we exist for a hundred autumns, may we hear for a hundred autumns, may we speak for a hundred autumns, may we remain unconquered for a hundred autumns, and may we long behold the sun. || 33 ||

"May Agni extend your life further; may Agni bestow prosperity upon you; may Indra with the Maruts bestow it upon you here; may the Āditya with the Vasus establish it for you"—having spoken thus, he gives him the staff and then presents the food.
Then he says: "Go on the alms-round. || 35 ||
He should first beg from his mother. || 36 ||
Therefore, [this applies] to other families of Rati. || 37 ||
Having brought back the alms, he said to the teacher, "This is excellent alms," and the teacher replied, "It is indeed good alms. || 38 ||
"O you whose first garment we take away, may all the gods protect you; may many brothers and friends follow after you as you grow, well-born!"—with these words he takes his first garment. (39)

When food is available, having taken equal portions of boiled rice, cakes, and parched grain, he offers them mixed with clarified butter, saying: "Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to Agni, the eater of food! Svāhā to Agni, the lord of food! Svāhā to Prajāpati! Svāhā to the Viśvedevas! Svāhā to all the deities! Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt! || 19.2.40 ||
In all such cases where no presiding deity has been specifically assigned, [this same rule applies]. || 41 ||
"To such-and-such, svāhā!"—thus [he offers] according to the deity for those whose deities have been specifically assigned.
Having gathered portions of these very foods, he offers a bali-oblation upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward, saying: "Svāhā to Vāstupati! (43)
Having served the Brāhmaṇas with threefold food and having caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity! (Khaṇḍa 7) || 44 ||
He observes the three-day vow. || 45 ||

Eating food that is not pungent, not salty, and free from legumes, sleeping on the ground, drinking from an earthen vessel, avoiding the remnants of a Śūdra's meal, abstaining from honey and meat, and refraining from sleeping during the day, he should perform the practice of begging for alms and fetch a water-pot twice daily; and every day he should carry a bundle of wood, or twice a day—specifically at evening—he should place fuel-sticks upon the fire.

After the sprinkling around [the fire] as before, he wipes around the fire from left to right with the formula, "As the Vasus [did] for Gaurī," and sprinkles around it as before. He places fuel sticks upon the fire one by one with the *vyāhṛtis* and with all of them together: "This is thy fuel, O Agni; through it mayest thou grow and swell; and may we grow and swell, svāhā! May Indra grant me intelligence, may the goddess Sarasvatī grant me intelligence."

"May both Aśvins, wreathed with lotuses, bestow wisdom upon me—svāhā! May the wisdom that is among the Apsarases and the mind that is among the Gandharvas—may that divine wisdom, born of man, the fragrant wisdom, delight in me—svāhā! May the fragrant, omniform, golden-hued wisdom, which moves through the world and is accessible to all, swelling with milk and full of vigor—that wisdom, fair of face, may it delight in me—svāhā! Having wiped [the vessel] in the same manner, he sprinkles water around it as before. 47.
He worships with these mantras, "O Agni, that splendor which is yours... and also with "May progeny [reside] in me. (48)

When three days have passed, having likewise served the Brāhmaṇas with food consisting of three-fold rice-gruel (trivṛt), and having caused them to recite "Auspicious Day," "Welfare," and "Prosperity," he releases the vow with these joined formulas beginning with, "O Agni, Lord of Vows, I have performed the vow. || 49 ||
From this point forward, he shall remain devoted solely to this vow.
One who dwells in the teacher's family. || 51 ||
He eats alkaline substances, salt, and leguminous grains. || 52 ||
He may carry a staff, wear matted hair, wear a girdle, or have his hair tied in a topknot. || 53 ||
He wears either the saffron robe or an antelope skin, and he does not approach a woman. || 54 ||
For forty-eight years, twenty-four, or twelve, up until the time of his seizure [of power]. || 55 ||
But one must certainly not be without vows. 56.

At the commencement of a section (*kāṇḍopākaraṇa*) and at the conclusion of a section (*kāṇḍavisarga*), [he offers] with the formula: "I have sought Sadasaspati, the wonderful, the beloved of Indra, the desirable, the winner, the wisdom; Svāhā! Then follows the second [offering], that of the *kāṇḍarṣi*. [He recites]: "This for me, O Varuṇa," "To thee I go," "Thou, O Agni, for us," "So thou, O Agni, for us," "O Agni, thou art the messenger," "O Prajāpati, whatever of this rite I have done in excess"—here some offer the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations as was done previously. (Section 8) 57.
Thus ends the second chapter of the nineteenth book in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the third chapter of the nineteenth book.
Having studied the Veda, one performs the ceremonial bath (*snāna*); that we shall now explain. (1)
During the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, one should bathe under the asterisms of Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Tiṣya, the two Uttaraphalgunīs, Hasta, Citrā, or the two Viśākhās.

Having gone to where there is water, having kindled the fire and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛtis*, he places a fuel-stick of *pālāśa* wood upon it with the mantra: "This hymn of praise we fashion for the worthy Jātavedas with our wisdom, as one fashions a chariot; for his providence is auspicious in our assembly. In this sacrifice, in this friendship, may we not suffer harm through thee, Svāhā! (3)
Then he offers oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*, as previously described.
The triple life-span of Jamadagni, the triple life-span of Kaśyapa, that which is the triple life-span of the gods—may that triple life-span be mine; svāhā! || 5 ||

"O Agni, you are this truth for us; you are not that for us; you are not he for us, O Agni. "O Prajāpati, whatever of this rite I have overdone," with these words some here offer the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts* as before.

Having served food to the Brahmins and having caused them to recite "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity!", he releases the vow with these [formulas]: "O Agni, lord of vows, I have performed the vow," and so forth.
Having concluded the vow, he worships the Āditya with the two verses beginning "ud u tyam" and "citram". || 8 ||
Having placed the upper garment, which is the student's cloth, aside with the verse "O Varuṇa, loosen the highest bond from us," and having put on another [garment]. || 9 ||
"‘Not low’ refers to the undergarment; ‘not middling’ refers to the girdle. (19.3.10)

Then, having cast the staff, the girdle, the staff, and the black antelope skin into the water with the verse, "Now we enter your service, O Āditya," he sits down to the west of the fire facing east and touches the razor with the formula: "Razor is your name; the axe is your father; homage be to you; do not harm me. (11)
Having offered water for washing the feet, he touches the water with the mantra: "Be auspicious to us when touched. || 12 ||
Then, having poured hot water into cold water, he moistens the hair at the right side of the head with the formula: "May the waters moisten for life. || 13 ||
With the words, "O herb, protect him," he places an herb with its tip pointing upwards between [the boy and the fire].
"O Svadhiti, do not harm him," with these words he applies the razor. || 15 ||
"O divine Śrī, may these grow," he says as he sows them.
"With the razor that shaves well and is well-fashioned, O barber, as you shave the hair and beard, make the face radiant; do not steal away our life"—with these words he looks at the barber. || 17 ||
First he has his beard shaved, then the armpits, then the hair of the head, then the body hair, and then the nails. || 18 ||

Having tied his hair, beard, body hair, and nails into a ball of bull-dung, he buries it in a cow-pen, at the root of an Udumbara tree, or in a clump of Darbha grass, saying: "I bury this sin of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so," for one who is well-disposed toward him. (19)
Having rubbed himself with bathing powder, he cleanses his teeth with a stick of Udumbara wood. (Khaṇḍa 9) 19.3.20.

"Arrange yourselves for the sake of food; arrange yourselves for the sake of long life; arrange yourselves for the sake of spiritual luster. May I become one who eats food, possesses long life, and is endowed with spiritual luster. ||21||

Then he bathes him with water that is both warm and cold, with the three verses beginning "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss," with the four verses beginning "Gold-colored, pure, purifying," and with this section beginning "Pavamāna, [dwelling] in the light."

Or, having covered it in a cow-pen and enclosed it on all sides, he enters before the rising of the sun; here everything is performed, for, according to some, the sun does not shine upon him on this day. Or rather, he who shines yonder shines with the splendor of those who have bathed (snātaka); therefore, the face of one who has bathed seems to radiate light.

They bring him all-fragrant sandalwood paste, which he sprinkles with water and anoints himself with it, saying: "Homage to the Seizer and to the One who Seizes; homage to Śāka and Jañjabha; homage to those deities who are seizers. Having made an añjali toward the east for the gods, he anoints himself with it, saying: "That fragrance which is among the Apsarases, that splendor which is among the Gandharvas, that divine and human fragrance—may it enter me here! (24)

They bring two unwashed garments for him; having sprinkled them with water, [he puts them on with the formulas]: "Thou art the body of Soma; protect my body! Enter me as my own body! Enter me as an auspicious body! || 25 ||

Having put on the lower garment and touched water, he likewise puts on the upper garment and sits down to the west of the fire facing east. They bring him two earrings and a gem from sandalwood or jujube wood encased in gold; having tied both of these together with a blade of *darbha* grass and holding them over the fire, he makes an offering, saying: "Granting long life, bestowing luster, increasing wealth, and breaking forth—may this gold enter me for the sake of longevity, luster, and victory, Svāhā!"

I have won the assembly that overcomes the high host of horses; I have won Dhananjaya. All prosperities in their entirety have been gathered together in this gold—*svāhā*. Like the name of a father, I have grasped the auspiciousness of gold. May it make me radiant with gold, dear among men, and endowed with the luster of sacred knowledge—*svāhā*. Make me dear among the gods; make me dear among the Brahmins; make me dear among the commoners and the Śūdras; make me dear among the kings—*svāhā*.

"O herb, thou art the protector, the overcoming, the powerful one; may she make me golden-hued, dear among men, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*); *svāhā*!"—with these five [mantras] without the utterance of *svāhā*, he should cause [the student] to float around three times from left to right in a vessel of water. (Section 10) ||26||

"O Virāj and Svarāj, and the prosperity that is in our home, and the fortune that is at the head of the kingdom—with that, unite me! With these words, he puts on his earrings, placing the right one in the right ear and the left one in the left.

With the mantra, "By the seasons, by the seasonal periods, for the sake of life and splendor, with the nourishment of the year—with that, being present, do thou favor me," he takes up the two earrings.

"O herb, you are the protector, the overcoming, the powerful one. May she make me golden-hued and dear among men; may she make me possessed of the splendor of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcas). You are a deliverer," with these words he fastens the amulet on his neck. || 29 ||

"O auspicious one, ascend the auspicious [garland], beautifying my face; beautify my face and increase my fortune. With these two verses—"That which Jamadagni brought for Śraddhā and Kāmā for her—this very [garland] I fasten upon myself, together with fortune and splendor"—he fastens the garland. (19.3.30)

"When the Traikakuda collyrium was produced upon the Himalayas, with that I anoint you together with fortune and splendor; [may] the mountain-man be in me. With these words, he anoints [the bride's eyes] with Traikakuda collyrium; if that is unavailable, with whatever [collyrium] is at hand. || 31 ||
With the mantra "yan me manaḥ parāgatam," he looks into a mirror. || 32 ||
Having taken up a bamboo staff with the mantra "devasya tvā," he wipes it upwards three times with the mantra "indrasya vajro 'si, aśvinau mā pātam."

"O you who are victorious through your speed, protect us from our enemies, from thieves, from reptiles, from beasts of prey, from *rakṣas* and *piśācas*, and from fears caused by men; protect us with your staff from all fear; strike down thieves on every side; you are born naked among all trees as the slayer of rivals; strike down all hosts of enemies everywhere like Maghavan"—with these words, he moves three times clockwise, passing over the head each time.
"You two are supports, O divine ones; do not cause me distress," with these words he steps down onto his sandals.
"You are the refuge of Prajāpati, the covering of Brahman," with these words he receives the parasol. || 36 ||

"The staff which has fallen from me from the sky onto the earth—this very one I take up again for long life and for strength. Thus he takes up the staff again if it falls from his hand. (Khanda 11) || 37 ||
Thus ends the third chapter of the nineteenth book in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the fourth chapter of the nineteenth book:
"They bring for him a chariot, a horse, or an elephant. (1)

"You are the Rathantara; you are the Vāmadevya; you are the Bṛhat—Aṅkau and Nyaṅkau are on both sides," thus [he says]. "O Aśvins, may this chariot of yours not be harmed by either pain or pleasure; may it go unhurt and in safety, warding off those who seek to harm us. Here is stability, here is support, here is delight; may it find delight here. With these words he mounts the chariot, if he enters by means of a chariot. || 2 ||
If [the sacrifice] is with a horse, one should [worship] the horse with the eleven names of the horse: "Thou art a steed, thou art a courser, thou art a racer... and so forth.

"I seat you with Indra’s thunderbolt; carry [me] to my time, carry me to prosperity, bring me hither. "Thou art the elephant; thou art the glory of the elephant; thou art the luster of the elephant; may I become possessed of the glory of the elephant, possessed of the luster of the elephant"—with these words he mounts the elephant, if by that means he goes to where they intend to pay him honor.
"May the quarters flow toward me; may pleasant truths gather together in me. May all our desires come to us; may what is dear flow toward us. With these words, he worships the quarters. || 5 ||
"You are glory; may I become glory in you"—with these words, he gazes at one who is coming toward him, intending to pay him honor. || 6 ||
Then, having prepared a dwelling for him, he said, "The guest-offering (argha)," and [the other] replied, "Perform it."

They prepare for him [the mixture] as either threefold or fivefold: curds, honey, and ghee constitute the threefold; curds, honey, ghee, water, and parched grain constitute the fivefold. Having poured the curds into a bronze vessel, he pours the honey into it.

Having brought a smaller vessel and covered it with a larger one, he causes [the guest] to take up the items one after another separately: a seat of grass (kūrca), water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), and the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Following him closely, she walked behind him; with a voice free from any worldly attachment, she spoke to each one, saying, "A tuft! A tuft! (kūrca).
He sits down facing east upon that [seat] with the formula: "This is the teacher’s seat, the sustainer of the kingdom; may I not abandon thee. || 11 ||
Then he said to him, "Water for the feet," thus.
Therefore, a Śūdra or a Śūdrī washes his feet; for a Brāhmaṇa, the left foot first, and for the other two [castes], the right. (Section 12) 13.
"You are the milking of Virāj; may there be milking for me from the footed Virāj"—with these words, he touches the hands of the one who washes his feet.
He touches himself, saying: "In me be splendor, sensory power, vigor, longevity, renown, luster, fame, and strength. (15)
Then he said to him, "The guest-offering (arghya). || 16 ||
He accepts it with the words: "Come to me; unite me with glory, with brilliance, with luster, and with nourishment. Make me beloved by all creatures and the sovereign lord of cattle. (17)

"I send you to the ocean, O imperishable ones; go back to your own source. May I be without flaw regarding my offspring; may I not spill [this] water"—with these words he consecrates the remainder as it is being poured out. || 18 ||
Then he says to him, "Water for sipping. || 19 ||
With the words, "Thou art the underlayer of nectar," he sips water.
Then he says to him, "The honey-mixture. || 21 ||

Having received it with both hands while reciting the Sāvitra formula, and having placed it upon the earth with the words, "I set thee on the navel of the earth, in the place of Iḍā," [he takes] that which is the honeyed essence of honey, the supreme form of food.

Therefore, he says: "By means of this honey, which is sweet and of supreme form, may I become supremely sweet and an eater of food. Having mixed it three times clockwise with his thumb and ring finger, he says: "I eat thee for the sake of splendor, prosperity, fame, strength, and the enjoyment of food," and having eaten it three times, he gives the remainder to one who is dear to him. || 22 ||
Or, having consumed the whole [of it], he sips water with the formula: "Thou art the covering of immortality. || 23 ||
Then he says to him, "A cow. || 24 ||
Or there may be the relinquishment of her ritual duties. || 25 ||

"The cow is the milch-cow, the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, and the navel of immortality. I declare this to the discerning person: do not slay the cow, the sinless Aditi; let her drink water and eat grass. Om! Release her!"—thus he instructs at the time of release. 26.

When [the rite] is being performed, [he recites]: "O Gaurī, you who have struck away evil, strike away the evil of [my enemy]; destroy the evil of both me and that person; my hater is destroyed, my hater is destroyed—make it so! (27)

At the disposal [of the guest], having prepared food with other meat, he then says to him, "It is become" (*bhūtam*). He replies, "It is well-become; it is the Virāj, the food. May it not perish for me; may I eat it; may it bestow strength upon me; it is well-become. Having said this, he then says, "Feed the Brāhmaṇas. || 28 ||
When they have finished eating, he causes him to be served food that is free from impurities. ||29||
He receives it with the formula: "May Heaven give to you; may Earth receive it. May Earth give to you; may Breath receive it. May Breath eat you; may Breath drink you. (19.4.30)
Having eaten as much as he desires with the mantra, "O Indra and Agni, may you bestow splendor upon me," he gives the remains to whomever is his favorite. || 31 ||

With the thought, "May it not be severed," [he says]: "In whom the past and the future, and all worlds are supported—by that I receive you; by the Brahman I receive you for myself, O So-and-so! Having sipped water, [he does so]. (Section 13) 32.
When he has finished eating, one should take hold of his right hand. || 33 ||

If one should desire that a minister of Yama, a pupil, or a servant be firmly established for him and never depart, he should bathe in the forenoon, wear clean clothes, remain pure throughout the day, and converse with Brāhmaṇas. At night, having gone to his dwelling and having urinated upon the horn of a living animal, he should walk three times around the dwelling from left to right while sprinkling water, reciting: "I have passed you from the mountain; I have passed you from your brother, from your sister, and from all your kinsmen. You shall sit apart and suffer distress."
"You have been sprinkled with a stream that is constantly turbulent, continuous, and unbroken; you have been sprinkled with a stream. || 34 ||
In the Anigupta [muhūrta], one should perform the rite of Jīvaśṛṅga. || 35 ||

Since ministers, pupils, or servants might run away, one should call out after them, summoning them repeatedly and inviting them back, saying: "O you who have turned back! May Indra’s summons summon you forever! If you think, 'This is mine,' O gods, do not deceive me further. Indra is the noose; having sprinkled it anew, may he give it back to me. (36)

Then, having entered his own house and placed a fuel-stick of *sairīyaka* wood upon the fire, he offers it with the drawing-in [of the breath], saying: "O turning one, turn back! (Khanda 14, Sutra 37).

Now, therefore, regarding the protection of the wife: having had coarse and firm powders prepared, the paramour should sprinkle them into the vagina of the sleeping woman with [the mantra]: "O Indra, that which is not for the male organ, nor for other men, but for me alone. (38)
Now, therefore, follows the success in trade. 39.

Having taken up merchandise, he offers an oblation with the verse: "O gods, whatever bargaining we may practice, O gods, desiring wealth by means of wealth—may Soma bestow radiance upon it, as well as Agni, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Īśāna, Svāhā! (19.4.40).
Now, therefore, follows the subduing of anger. || 41 ||

"O gods who are wise and practitioners of sacred study, may you subdue that form of *manas* which resides in the forehead and destroys the gentle. Since this thought in your mouth pierces the forehead like a bolt, I stretch out your heart's anger like an archer draws his bow toward the sky. Day, heaven, and earth—by these means we lead away your wrath, as one removes the embryo from a female donkey. With these words, he addresses the angry person with a mantra. (42)
Now, therefore, follows the method for winning a debate. 43.

At night, having kindled a fire within the inner apartments and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛtis*, he offers oblations of parched grain mixed with clarified butter, saying: "O tongue, bend down, bend down! With this oblation I worship thee, so that I may speak as the superior one, while thou speakest as the inferior one. Speak low! Svāhā! (44)

Then he addresses him while standing near: "From your mouth I take your speech, from your heart that which is in your mind; from every limb of yours I take your speech. Wherever your speech was deposited, that I take back from you. O Rudra with the blue crest, performer of heroic deeds, deed by deed, strike down this one who opposes me, as a tree is struck by a thunderbolt! Speak downward, speak lower, speak below the earth! Like a low-lying trap, he has been laid down for himself by me. That which I speak is the truth: 'May he, so-and-so, fall beneath me! (45)
"O golden-armed one, fortunate one, with conquered eyes, adorned, seated in the midst of the gods, speak for my sake: 'Svāhā!'"—having touched the assembly hall, he mutters this. || 46 ||
"Others are mine, others are mine; this great earth is mine; Agni and Indra have accomplished my divine purpose"—thus he looks upon the assembly and mutters these words. (Section 15) 47.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the nineteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the fifth chapter in the nineteenth book.

Having seen the moon on the day of the new moon (*darśa*), and having sipped water while holding water in his hand, he worships [the moon] with these four verses: "Swell up," "May you be renewed again and again as you are born," "O Ādityas, you who cause the ray to swell," and so forth. || 1 ||
While stretching out his arms for the sake of the rite, he murmurs: "May skill and wisdom be in me. ||2||
If he is insulted with a wet garment, he mutters: "O Vajra, you who destroy the wicked, homage be to you; do not harm me. || 3 ||
Having cut its thread, one should destroy it with the breath from one's mouth. || 4 ||
"Those birds that fly about in fear along with the spirits of destruction—may they favor me with auspiciousness, peace, splendor, and luster"—this he mutters when assailed by a bird. (5)

If an unknown drop of water should fall upon him, he should wipe it from his hand with something else and wash it off with water, reciting: "From the great sky, from the intermediate space, a drop of water has fallen upon me for my well-being; protected by the Veda and by the merit of good deeds, I have come back endowed with sensory power and a clear mind. (6)

If an unknown fruit should fall upon him—whether it falls from the top of a tree or from the sky—it is indeed Vāyu; he should mutter: "Where the tree is, or where the garment is, may the waters drive away Destruction (Nirṛti) far away. Thus he should recite if such an unknown fruit should fall upon him.
"Salutation to Rudra who dwells on the paths, whose arrows are the winds; salutation to Rudra who dwells on the paths"—having approached a crossroads, he mutters this.
"Obeisance to Rudra who dwells among cattle, whose arrows are the winds; obeisance to Rudra who dwells among cattle"—this [formula] is used when there is excrement.
"Obeisance to Rudra who moves among serpents, whose arrow is the wind; obeisance to Rudra," thus [he says] to him who moves among serpents. || 19.5.10 ||
"Obeisance to Rudra who dwells in the intermediate space, whose arrow is the wind; obeisance to Rudra who dwells in the intermediate space. || 11 ||
If the wind of destruction should come upon him, [he should recite]: "Homage to Rudra, who dwells in the waters, whose arrow is the wind; homage to Rudra, who dwells in the waters. || 12 ||
Having plunged into the river Udanvatī, he mutters: "Homage to that being, to Rudra with the wind as his arrow; homage to Rudra, to that being. || 13 ||
Having stepped upon a variegated spot, a place for sacrificing to the gods, or a tree, he mutters [the following].
One who has risen with the sun shall not eat during the day; he shall remain standing for the day, restrained in speech.
Likewise at night, when the sun has set. || 16 ||

One should not touch the sacrificial post; if one should touch it, he would incur the failure of the sacrifice. If he touches one, he should say, "This is for thee, O Vāyu"; if two, "These two are for thee, O Vāyus"; if many, "These are for thee, O Vāyus."

"Uninvited, invited, praised around, and that which has been uttered by birds; the hundred eyes of the deer—may we be free from fear on account of those adverse things," he mutters as he sets out upon his journey. (18)

"Like a *udgātṛ* priest, O bird, you sing the *Sāman*; like a son of a Brahmin, you recite at the libations. May there be well-being for us, O bird; may you be auspicious and well-disposed toward us"—with these words he mutters over an inauspicious bird. (19)
"Since you have entered these beings and speak this divine speech, O Death, speak against those who hate us; lead them to death by means of the single-pointed [weapon]. (19.5.20)
Then, having touched water, he throws a firebrand burning at both ends toward that direction, saying: "O Agni, converse with Agni; O Death, converse with Death. (21)
Then he worships him with this Anuvāka: "Vibhū asi pravāhaṇaḥ" (Thou art the pervasive one, the carrier). (Section 16) 22.

Whether incited by others or acting out of his own desire, let the jackal utter these words: "O Indra and Agni, being in harmony with our sacred prayer, make this female jackal auspicious for us in our homes. (23)
Spreading out your legs you fly, and you close your left eye; who indeed would not call you, O bird, "Maditi"?
"The golden-winged bird, who goes to the abode of the gods—O Kauśika, having circumambulated the village from left to right, speak auspiciousness for us," [he said] to Piṅgalā.

"May my power return to me, may my life return, may my fortune return; O Brahman, may it come back to me, may wealth come back to me. Then let these fires of the hearths be established here in their proper places, *svāhā*. "My self has returned, my life has returned; my breath has returned, my intention has returned. May Vaiśvānara, increasing with his rays, abide within me as the banner of immortality, *svāhā*. "The food that is eaten in the evening does not ward off hunger until the morning."
"May all that not harm us; for that was not seen by day, svāhā!"—having seen an undesirable dream, one offers oblations of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter. || 26 ||

Now, these are the expiations for portents: when a pigeon has entered [the house], when honey has settled in the house, when a cow has desired another cow, when a pillar has sprouted, or when an anthill has risen—such are the types [of portents].

Having bathed in the forenoon, wearing clean garments, having fasted for the day, and having conversed with Brāhmaṇas, he kindles the fire in the inner chamber, performs the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, and offers these: "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa," "For that I entreat thee," "Thou, O Agni, for us," "So thou, O Agni, for us," "O Agni, thou art the messenger," "O Prajāpati, whatever in this rite I have done in excess. Here, some also offer the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations as before. Having served food to the Brāhmaṇas and caused them to pronounce "An auspicious day" and "May there be well-being," [the ceremony is concluded].
(Section 17) 28.

"May Indra and Agni send you forth; may the Aśvins protect you; Bṛhaspati is your herdsman; may Pūṣan drive you back again"—with these words he consecrates the cows as they set out, and also with the verse: "May Pūṣan follow after our cows. (29)
"May these cows that have come hither be free from disease and prolific; may they flow like rivers and pour forth like the ocean"—with these words he awaits the approaching cows. || 19.5.30 ||
"You are established; may you be established for me; you are immovable; do not move me; may I not be moved away from you, O Blessed Ones"—thus they are established. (31)
"May I see you with vigor; may you see me with vigor," [he says] regarding those who have entered the cow-pen, and also, "May I prosper in your thousandfold nourishment. || 32 ||

Therefore, having kindled the fire in the midst of the cows and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛtis*, he offers an oblation of milk with the verses: "Shine forth, O Jātavedas; drive away Nirṛti from me. Bring cattle to me and life from every direction, Svāhā! Do not harm us, O Jātavedas—our cow, horse, man, or moving creature. Bringing [these], O Agni, come hither; protect me on all sides with glory, Svāhā! This is the gathering place of the waters; obeisance to your heat and your flame. (33)

"O Varuṇa, I entreat you for this truth of mine; O Agni, do thou [protect] us; O Agni, do thou [protect] us; O Agni, thou art the messenger; O Prajāpati, whatever in this rite I have done in excess"—here some also offer the Jaya, Abhyātāna, and Rāṣṭrabhṛt oblations as previously described. (Section 18) 34.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the nineteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Gṛhyasūtra.

Now begins the sixth chapter of the nineteenth book. One who has returned from the teacher’s family should support his mother and father; authorized by them, he should take a wife—of the same caste, a maiden (*nagnikā*), one who has lived as a religious student (*brahmacāriṇī*), and not of the same *gotra*. At five times of the day—morning, the time when cattle are gathered, midday, afternoon, or evening—whatever he does during these times, he makes it an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*). Having kindled the fire and performed the rites up to the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he gazes at the bride as she is being led forward, [reciting]: "This bride is most auspicious; come together and behold her."

"Having given her good fortune, go away and return at sunset"—saying this, the wife sits down to the south of the husband. When she has sipped water and taken hold of him from behind, he sprinkles [the fire] as before.

Having performed [the rites] up to the *vyāhṛti* offerings, he makes the oblation: "May Agni come first among the deities; may he release her offspring from the noose of death. May King Varuṇa here grant his approval, so that this woman may not suffer the sin of losing a grandson, Svāhā! May Agni Gārhapatya protect her; may he lead her offspring to a long life. May she have a living mother with an unfailing lap; may she awaken to the joy of seeing a grandson, Svāhā!"

May no cry of lamentation arise in your house at night; let other women, weeping, lie down elsewhere. O Mother, may you not be distressed by the hero; as the wife of a living husband, shine forth in the world of your husband, beholding your offspring with a joyful mind—Svāhā! May Heaven protect your back, Vāyu your thighs, and the Aśvins your breasts. May Savitṛ protect your sons while they suckle. From the time of putting on your garment until you are clothed, may Bṛhaspati and the Viśvedevas protect you from behind—Svāhā!

Childlessness, the death of a grandson, evil, or even sin—I cast this away from my head like a garland and transfer the guilt to my enemies, svāhā! The Brahman-form created by the gods, as it is being fashioned, with that I strike down the Piśācas dwelling in the womb. I cast downward the flesh-eating deaths; may your sons live a long life, svāhā! (2)
"O Varuṇa, I entreat you for this truth; O Agni, you are ours; you, O Agni, are ours; O Agni, you are the leader; O Prajāpati! Thus [he says]. || 3 ||

He causes [the bride] to step upon a stone with the mantra: "Step upon this stone; like a stone, be thou firm. Crush those who seek to do harm; overcome those who attack. To the west of the fire, having spread two bundles of *darbha* grass—one behind the other—with their tips pointing north, they both stand upon them, one behind the other. (Section 19) 4.
Facing east, he should take the hand of her facing west, or facing west, he should take the hand of her facing east.
If he should desire, "May I produce males," he should grasp [the bride's] thumb.
If he should desire women, [he should touch] the fingers.

If he should desire, "May I procreate both [sons and daughters]," he should grasp the thumb together with the fingers as if over the hair, saying: "Sarasvatī, O fortunate one, rich in vigor, I take your hand before all living beings for the sake of good offspring, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband. Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Purandhi—the gods have given you to me for the household. (8)

Turning toward her from the front, having turned her westward so that she faces his right shoulder, he addresses her with the mantra: "Be not of evil eye, nor a slayer of your husband; be auspicious to our cattle, well-disposed, and full of luster. May you be a mother of living sons, a mother of heroes, and pleasant; be a source of blessing to us—blessing to our bipeds and blessing to our quadrupeds. O Pūṣan, impel her toward us as most auspicious, she in whom men sow their seed. She who, longing for us, shall part her thighs, and in whom we, longing, shall deposit the member. Soma first obtained her; Gandharva obtained her next."

"Agni is your third husband; I am your fourth, born of man. Soma gave her to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave her to Agni. And now Agni gives her to me—both cattle and sons—and also you. I am this [earth], you are that [heaven]; I am the Sāman, you are the Ṛc. Come, let us two unite; let us together deposit seed for the sake of obtaining a male son, for the increase of wealth, for good progeny, and for great heroic power. O bountiful Indra, make her rich in sons and fortunate. Bestow ten sons upon her, and make the husband the eleventh. (9)

Having seated her in her proper place, he then spreads a base of clarified butter in her joined palms and pours fried grains (lājāḥ) twice over it, saying: "I pour these grains for the sake of my prosperity; may this fire grant you that favor. While she is pouring the grains into the fire, he offers them from her joined palms with the formula: "May my husband live long; may my kinsmen flourish! Svāhā! || 19.6.10 ||
Having raised [the bride] with the words, "O long-lived one! May we, through you, cross over all enemies as if crossing streams of water," he circumambulates her from left to right. || 11 ||
In the same manner, she scatters fried grains after circumambulating for the second time. || 12 ||
In the same manner, having circumambulated for a third time, he pours out the parched grains and offers the oblation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. || 13 ||
In this case, some offer the Jaya, Abhyātāna, and Rāṣṭrabhṛt oblations as they did previously.
To her west of the fire, he makes her take the Viṣṇu-strides, facing either eastward or northward. || 15 ||
Then he instructs her: "Having stepped forward with your right foot, follow with your left; do not let your left foot overstep your right. (Section 20) 16.

"May Viṣṇu follow you for the sake of food; may Viṣṇu follow you for the sake of vigor; may Viṣṇu follow you for the sake of sacred observance; may Viṣṇu follow you for the sake of well-being; may Viṣṇu follow you for the sake of cattle; may Viṣṇu follow you for the sake of the increase of wealth; may Viṣṇu follow you for the sake of the seven priestly offices"—having thus placed the seventh step, he mutters this. || 17 ||

"Friends we have become through the seven steps; may I attain your friendship; may I not be separated from your friendship; may you not be separated from my friendship. Then, having stepped upon his right foot with his own right foot, and having touched each of his shoulders from above with his right hand, he touches the region of the heart as before, saying, "You are the knot of the vital breaths; do not loosen," and then the region of the navel.

Having seated her to the west of the fire facing east, he stands before her facing west and sprinkles her with water, using the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed the source of happiness," the four verses beginning with "The golden-colored, pure, and purifying ones," and this entire section beginning with "Pavamāna, [the one] born of heaven. ||19||
Here they place the seeds. (Section 21) 19.6.20.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the nineteenth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the seventh chapter in the nineteenth book.
Then they cause her to flow away, or they have her carried away. || 1 ||
Having approached, they carry this fire along with them. || 2 ||
It should be worn constantly. || 3 ||
The fire may be taken from a place where it has been maintained by friction, or it may be brought from the house of a Vedic scholar.
And there is fasting for the wife or the husband when [the impurity] has passed. || 5 ||
Having reached the house, he then instructs her: "Step forward with your right foot first; do not step upon the threshold."
Having piled [the fire] in the eastern half of the hall, he adds fuel; then, to the west of the fire, he spreads out a red bull-hide with its neck toward the east and its hair side upward.

In that place, they both sit facing either the east or the north; afterwards, the wife sits behind her husband, [reciting]: "May cows sit here, may horses sit here, may men sit here; may Pūṣan, who bestows a thousandfold dakṣiṇā, also sit here."
The two of them remained silent until the rising of the stars.
When the stars have risen, having gone out toward the eastern or northern direction, he worships the quarters with the verse: "O six goddesses, the wide ones... (RV 1.164.12). 19.7.10.
"May we not be deprived of offspring," [they said] regarding the constellations.
"To Soma, the king, who hates the abode of Māra," thus [he addresses] the Moon. || 12 ||

The Seven Seers led Arundhatī, the first of the Kṛttikās, to steadfastness. Carrying this conjunction with the six chief Kṛttikās, may she shine as our eighth. Having thus worshipped the Seven Seers, he worships Dhruva: "Firmly established, of firm origin, you are firm; you are firmly situated. You are the most pure among the stars; protect me from those who attack."

Homage to Brahman, the fixed and the imperishable; homage be to Prajāpati, the son of Brahman; homage to the thirty-three gods, the sons of Brahman; homage to the Aṅgirases, the grandsons of Brahman. He who knows you, the fixed and the imperishable, together with your sons and grandsons, as Brahman—his sons and grandsons become fixed; so too his servants, pupils, clothing, woolen blankets, bronze vessels, gold, women, kings, food, fearlessness, long life, renown, splendor, and fame.

"May strength, spiritual luster, and food—may all these be firm and unshakable within me. (Section 22) "I know you as the firm Brahman; may I be firm in this world and in this community. I know you as the unshakable Brahman; may I not be shaken from this world and from this community. May my hateful rival be shaken from this world and from this community."

I know you as the motionless Brahman; may I not move from this world and from this region, and may my hateful rival move away from this world and from this region. I know you as the unshakable Brahman; may I not tremble from this world and from this region, and may my hateful rival tremble from this world and from this region. I know you as the nave of all; may I become the nave of this region.

I know you as the center of all; may I become the center of this region. I know you as the cord of all; may I become the cord of this region. I know you as the central pillar of all; may I become the central pillar of this region.

"If you are the navel of all, may I become the navel of this country, just as the navel is the central point of the vital breaths; likewise, may I be the central point. May that one hundred and first evil reach him who hates us and whom we hate. May more than one hundred merits come to me. (13)
Having conversed here with Manojña and having reached the house, he then causes her to sacrifice with an oblation of cooked rice (sthālīpāka) dedicated to Agni.
The wife husks [the grain]. || 15 ||
Having cooked it, sprinkled clarified butter over it, and removed it from the fire, he makes an offering to Agni and then offers to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. || 16 ||
With that, he serves a learned Brāhmaṇa. || 17 ||
To whomever he is respectful, to him he gives a bull. || 18 ||
From this point onward, he constantly performs worship on the festival days with a *sthālīpāka* offering dedicated to Agni.
Every evening and morning, he offers these two oblations with his hand using rice or barley, saying: "To Agni, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! (19.7.20)
Some authorities prescribe that the first [offering] dedicated to Sūrya should be performed in the morning.
For three nights, they live as celibates, eating food that is neither pungent nor salty, sleeping on the ground, and refraining from ornaments.

On the fourth [night], during the latter part of the night, having established the fire and performed the rites up to the expiation, he offers nine expiatory oblations: "O Agni, expiator, you are the expiation; I, a Brāhmaṇa seeking protection, approach you. Whatever terrible form she has, drive that away from here—svāhā! O Vāyu, expiator, you are the expiation; I, a Brāhmaṇa seeking protection, approach you. Whatever blameworthy form she has, drive that away from here—svāhā!"

"O Āditya, O Prāyaścitti! You are the expiation. I, a Brāhmaṇa desiring protection, approach you for refuge. Whatever part of her is husband-slaying, destroy that from here, svāhā! Having offered oblations with the words: "O Āditya, O Prāyaścitti! O Vāyu, O Prāyaścitti! O Agni, O Prāyaścitti! O Agni, O Prāyaścitti! O Vāyu, O Prāyaścitti! O Āditya, O Prāyaścitti! (23)

Then he offers the remnants of the oblation upon her head: "Bhūḥ! I offer fortune into you, svāhā! Bhuvaḥ! I offer glory into you, svāhā! Suvaḥ! I offer splendor into you, svāhā! Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! I offer radiance into you, svāhā! (24)

Having placed a vessel of water right here, having circumambulated the fire keeping it to his right, and having made her lie down behind the fire—either facing east or north—he then touches her womb with the verse: "With your auspicious, five-fingered hand, which wards off enmity and possesses a thousand glories, we touch you for the sake of good offspring. (25)
Then he marries her with the verse: "United be our names, united our hearts, united our navels, united our skins; may I unite you with the bond of desire, never to be released. (26)

Then he embraces her, saying: "Be devoted to me; be my companion. That body of yours which is destructive to husbands—that I make it destructive to paramours. Be auspicious to me; let the razor-edged [body] belong to the paramours. || 27 ||

Then, as he desires her mouth with his own, [he says]: "O honey-sweet one! This is honey; my tongue is a speaker of honey. In my mouth is the honey of the bees; in my teeth, the charm of conciliation has been made. That charm of conciliation belonging to the cakravāka birds which was drawn from the rivers—by that, may we two, joined by the divine Gandharva, be united in our own hearts. (28)
For three nights, she whose clothes are soiled with menstrual blood performs the vows prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa woman.
On the fourth day, having bathed, wearing clean garments and adorned with ornaments, and having conversed with a Brāhmaṇa, he sips water and invites her. (Khaṇḍa 24) 19.7.30.

May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms. May Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you. O Sinīvālī, bestow an embryo; O Sarasvatī, bestow an embryo. May both Aśvins, wreathed with lotuses, place an embryo within you. The two golden fire-drills from which the Aśvins churned [fire]—that embryo we invoke for you, so that you may give birth after ten months. As the earth has Agni as its embryo, and as the sky is pregnant with Indra.

As the wind is the womb of the quarters, so do I place the embryo within you. Take up the seed for that womb; let a male son be born as an embryo within you. Let the mother bear him for ten months; let him be born as the most heroic among his kin. Let your embryo enter the womb, like a male arrow into its quiver. Let a hero be born here as your son after ten months. I perform for you the rite pertaining to Prajāpati: let the embryo enter your womb. Let him be born complete and full—not blind, not lame, free from the affliction of *piśāca*, and wise.

May the bulls generate for us abundant heroic powers; through them, may you become pregnant, and may he be born as the most heroic among his own kin. That embryo which is in the barren cow and that which is in the cow that miscarries—Indra has placed it in the tree. Through that, may you become pregnant; may you be a mother of a milch-cow. [Recite] "The union of names" and "The cakravāka birds. (31)

"O Bhūḥ! With Prajāpati as the supreme bull, I cause you to flow; bestow a hero, O [Name]! "O Bhuvaḥ! With Prajāpati as the supreme bull, I cause you to flow; bestow a hero, O [Name]! "O Suvaḥ! With Prajāpati as the supreme bull, I cause you to flow; bestow a hero, O [Name]! Thus he indeed procreates a hero. || 32 ||
Ātreya maintains that all sexual unions are accompanied by mantras.
Bādarāyaṇa [holds that it is] both what was done at the beginning and what is done during the performance. (Sūtra 34, Khaṇḍa 25)

The fire [kindled] at the time of taking the hand in marriage and so forth is called the *aupāsana*. In that fire, the domestic (*gṛhya*) rites are performed. By means of this *aupāsana* fire, one possesses the status of an *āhitāgni* (one who has established the sacred fires). Just as one is considered a performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices by means of the *pārvaṇa* oblation of cooked rice, so it is here. If [the fire] is interrupted for twelve days, it must be re-established (*punarādheya*). Alternatively, having calculated [the number], one may offer all the omitted oblations. [The new fire is established] on ground that is enclosed, leveled, sprinkled with water, strewn with sand, and covered with branches of the *udumbara* or *plakṣa* tree.

Having silently gathered the necessary materials as they become available, he churns fire from a sacrificial wood or brings ordinary fire and places it in a vessel, kindling it; he then adds fuel with the formula: "Bhūḥ bhuvaḥ suvaḥ oṃ, may you be established. Then, having enkindled this fire and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he offers two *mindā* oblations with the verses: "Whatever deficiency has occurred in my self, Agni has restored my sight" and "Agni has restored my sight."

He offers three *tantumatī* oblations with the verses: "Stretching the thread," "Awake, O Agni," and "The thirty-three threads. He offers four *abhyāvartinī* oblations with the verses: "O Agni, you who turn back," "O Agni Aṅgiras," "Return with strength," and "Together with wealth. Having offered the *vyāhṛtis* both individually and collectively, he offers this [final] one: "And as one who is blameless, O Agni, and free from curses—truly you are *ayās*; held by a mind that is *ayās*, you shall carry the oblation; bestow healing upon us, Svāhā!"

Having offered oblations with the *manasvatī*, the *prājāpatyā*, and the *saptavatī* formulas, and having mentally recited the *daśahotṛ* formula, he offers the *sagraha* oblation. Then, having offered the verses "imaṃ me varuṇa," "tattvā yāmi," "tvaṃ no agne," "sa tvaṃ no agne," "tvamagne ayāsi," and "prajāpate yadasya karmaṇo 'tyarīricam"—some say [he adds] the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*—he makes the subsidiary offerings as previously described. Having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity!", he proceeds with the rite dedicated to Agni in the established manner.

He performs the sacrifice with a *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering). Here he gives a choice gift (*vara*) to the teacher: either two garments, a cow, or a draft-ox. If he should set out on a journey, the procedure for the oblation has been explained; [the fire] should be consigned into himself, or into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), or he should consign it onto a fuel-stick. In this regard, one of the following—made of *khadira*, *palāśa*, *udumbara*, or *aśvattha* wood—is used according to the rule for the kindling woods. Wherever he halts, having brought fire from the house of a learned *śrotriya*, he places onto that [fire] in which [the fire] was consigned, using the two verses beginning with "Being invoked" (*ājuhvāna*) and "Awake! (*udbudhyasva*).

The ritual procedure for the oblation has been explained. If the Pārvaṇa sacrifice should be interrupted, one should have him perform the Pāthikṛta sacrifice. If two [Pārvaṇas] are interrupted, [one should perform] the Vaiśvānara and Pāthikṛta sacrifices. If many [are interrupted], there is a re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya). In case of loss or destruction, or if the fire becomes mixed with other fires, there is a re-establishment of the fires. (Section 26) 35.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the nineteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the eighth chapter in the nineteenth book: "One intending to have a hall built... (1)

During the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under the asterism Rohiṇī or under the three Uttaras, having established the sacred fire and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he offers these: "Hear this my cry, O Varuṇa," "For that I implore thee," "Thou, O Agni, for us," "So thou, O Agni, for us," "O Agni, thou art the messenger," "O Prajāpati, whatever in this rite I have done in excess. At this point, some also offer the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations as previously described. Having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity! [the rite is concluded].
Having put on an unwashed garment and touched water. || 3 ||

Having taken up the spade with the formula "For thee, O god... and having drawn a line three times clockwise with the formula "It has been traced around...", he digs the pits as required and places the earth from within [the pits] aside.

"Right here I erect a firm hall; stand in safety, dripping with ghee. To you, O Hall, may we move about, possessing good heroes, all heroes, and unharmed heroes. With these words, he raises the southern door-post.

"Right here, O house, stand firm—rich in horses, rich in cattle, rich in pleasant speech; swelling with vigor and milk, rise up for great good fortune!"—with these words, he places the northern [post].

"The youth, the child, together with the moving world, has come to you; the golden jar, reaching up to the mouth, has brought you along with the pitchers"—with these words he touches the two [jars] that have been placed together.
In this very manner, he raises the central pillar. || 8 ||
Thus he touches [it]. || 9 ||

"By means of Truth, ascend the beam like a pillar; standing upright and shining forth, drive away the enemies. Then grant us wealth together with heroes"—with these words, he causes him to mount the spinal column. 19.8.10.

"May there be no rival for us; O Agni, you are a pleasant shelter, fashioned by the gods together with the gods. Clothed in grass, you are well-disposed; be auspicious to us, be auspicious to our bipeds and our quadrupeds"—with these words he touches the covered [fire-place]. 11.

Then, under the asterism Anurādhā, he performs the pacification of the site; having kindled a fire in the inner chamber during the night and having performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he makes the offerings. (Khaṇḍa 27) 12.

"O Lord of the Dwelling, O Lord of the Dwelling"—these two [verses]. "O Lord of the Dwelling, be our furtherer; O Indu, increase our household with cattle and horses. May we remain unaging in thy friendship. Like a father his sons, be gracious unto us, Svāhā! May death depart; immortality has come to us. May the Son of Vivasvat grant us fearlessness. Like the leaf of a tree, may wealth fall upon us; may the Lord of Power (Śacīpati) attend us, Svāhā! Go away, O Death, along your own path, which is other than the way of the gods."

O Lord of the Dwelling, I speak to you who hears me: do not harm our offspring, nor our heroes; *svāhā*! We have now come to this which is better than before, which wins cattle, wins wealth, and wins horses.

"Like a leaf from a tree, may wealth fall upon us; may the Lord of Might attend us. Svāhā! This [is] mine. O Varuṇa, that [I implore]; to thee I go. Thou, O Agni, art for us; thou, O Agni, art for us. O Agni, thou art the Unswerving (Ayās). O Prajāpati, whatever of this rite I have done in excess,"—here some offer the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts* as before. Having served the Brahmins with food, he causes them to pronounce: "An auspicious day!", "Welfare!", and "Success! || 13 ||
Thus is the pacification of the site (vāstuśamana) ordained to be performed year after year.
"‘At every season,’ say some. (Khaṇḍa 28) 15.

O houses, do not fear; do not tremble. Bearing strength, we come to you. Bearing strength, a winner of wealth, wise and rejoicing in my mind, I go to the houses. Those houses from which he who departs on a journey returns with increased goodwill—those houses we call upon; may they recognize us as we recognize them. Invoked here are the cows; invoked are the goats and sheep. And the sweet essence of food is invoked in our houses. Invoked are the friends, many in number, who delight in pleasant company.

"May all our men be free from harm; may our houses always be full of vigor, full of milk, full of refreshment, laughter, and joy; may they be free from hunger and thirst; O houses, do not be afraid of us"—with these words he approaches his home. 16.

"For your security and for peace, I enter that which is auspicious, beneficial, and a source of well-being—well-being, well-being," he says as he enters. On the day he has arrived, he does not engage in quarreling. || 17 ||

"I enter the houses, which are well-disposed, not slaying heroes, most heroic, and very gracious; carrying nourishment and being well-intentioned, may I, well-disposed, lie down among them"—with these words he lies down. "And with you, may we cross over all enemies, as if crossing streams of water"—with this he gazes at his wife, he gazes at her. (18)
Thus ends the eighth chapter and the nineteenth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the first chapter of the twentieth book:
"Now, therefore, follows the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*)."

In the fourth month of her first pregnancy, during the waxing fortnight under an auspicious lunar mansion, having established the sacred fire and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he offers four oblations to Dhātṛ with the verse: "May Dhātṛ grant us wealth. (2)

"O Varuṇa, I entreat you for this truth of mine; O Agni, do you [protect] us; O Agni, may you be such for us; O Agni, you are the Unborn; O Prajāpati, whatever I have done in excess in this rite"—with these words, some here offer the *jayas*, *abhyātānas*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛts* oblations as previously described. Having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to recite "An auspicious day!", "Prosperity!", and "Success!", he seats her—who has bathed, put on clean garments, is adorned, and has conversed with Brahmins—facing east on the western side of the fire in a circular chamber, using a three-striped porcupine quill.

Taking hold of a bunch of *śalālu* fruit, standing in front facing west, he raises the parting of her hair upward with the two verses beginning with "I [invoke] Rākā" and "O Rākā, those [gifts] which are yours," and then consecrates it with the mantra: "Soma indeed is our king, so say the Brāhmaṇī women whose wheels have turned back; sitting on your bank, O Gaṅgā, may we, through you, cross over all enemies like flowing streams of water. (Section 1) 3.
Now, therefore, follows the rite for the birth of a male child.

In the third month, during the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious constellation, having established the sacred fire and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛtis*, he offers four oblations to Dhātṛ with the verses: "May Dhātṛ grant us wealth," "This [is my prayer]," "O Varuṇa," "To thee I go," "Thou, O Agni," "So thou, O Agni," "Thou, O Agni, art the messenger," and "O Prajāpati, whatever in this rite has been left incomplete. At this point, some also offer the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts* as previously described. Having served food to the Brahmins, he pronounces the "Auspicious Day" (*puṇyāha*).

Having had her recite "A blessing, prosperity," he causes her—having bathed, wearing clean garments, adorned, and having conversed with Brāhmaṇas—to sit facing east on the western side of the fire in a circular chamber; then, saying "Thou art a bull," he places a barley grain into her right hand.
With the words "Ye two are eggs," he places two mustard seeds or two grains of *dhānyamāṣa* on either side of the barley grain.
Having returned from the dog's feeding place, he gives her a drop of curd; with that, he causes her to eat it. || 7 ||
When she has sipped water, he touches her belly with the mantra: "With ten [fingers] I touch you, that you may give birth after ten months."

One should cause [the patient] to inhale through the right nostril—using a nyagrodha sprout with ghee, or a silk-worm cocoon with a porridge of priyaṅgu, or a splinter from a sacrificial post, or fire produced by friction from wood taken from the northern side of the post that stands nearest the fire, for one who has placed the root of her thigh beneath her chin. || 9 ||

If the fetus should move, he strokes her three times upward from the navel with his moist hand, saying: "May Tvaṣṭṛ bind you in a bond—turning away, not toward us; having entered the seasons, do not abandon the ten months. (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.13.10)

At the time of delivery, for a swift birth, having placed a water-pot at her head, he then touches her belly with a *pattastūryantī* plant, saying: "Just as the wind blows, just as the ocean surges, so let your fetus stir; together with the afterbirth, let it come forth. He strokes downward. (Kaṇḍikā 2) || 11 ||

When the stone has been placed [on the ground] and an axe set upon it, with gold above those upper and lower [stones], he addresses the boy—who is being held facing eastward—over them with the following verses: "Be a stone, be an axe, be unconquerable gold. You are indeed the Veda, named 'Son'; live for a hundred autumns! From limb by limb you are produced; from the heart you are born. You are indeed the Self, named 'Son'; live for a hundred autumns! (12)

If it does not fall away, he should take water in his joined palms and sprinkle it on her head, saying: "O Tiladevī, fall down; you are not flesh, do not fall upon my limb; fall from your own path. || 13 ||
They bring forth the *aupāsana* fire and carry away the *sūtikāgni*.
This very one is indeed to be heated thoroughly. || 15 ||
In this [rite], no ritual action whatsoever is performed other than the fumigation.

Then he fumigates him with grains mixed with mustard seeds: "Śaṇḍa, Marka, Upavīra, Śāṇḍīkera, Ulūkhala—let Cyavana perish from here, Svāhā! Ālikhat, Vilikhat, Animiṣa, Kiṃvadanta, Upaśruti—Svāhā! Aryaman’s Kumbhīśatru, Pātrapāṇi, Nipuṇi—Svāhā! Āntrīmukha, Sarṣapāruṇa—let them perish from here, Svāhā! Keśinī, Śvalominī, Bajā, Bījopakāśinī—depart, perish from here, Svāhā!"

The Kauverakas, the Viśvavāsas, sent by the King of the Rākṣasas, go through the villages with their kinsmen, seeking those made of *parijā* wood—Svāhā! "Kill them! Bind them! thus says this messenger of Brahmā; Agni has pursued them, Indra has pursued them, Bṛhaspati has pursued them, and I, a Brāhmaṇa, know them as they touch [the victims]: those with false teeth, those with disheveled hair, those with pendulous breasts—Svāhā! Those who wander at night, the breast-ornamented, the thick-handed, those who drink from skulls—Svāhā! "Their father was in front," he whose ear is loud enough to hear it from afar.

"The mother goes last, seeking a mole in the village, svāhā! The night-wandering sister gazes upon the family through a crack; she who stays awake while others sleep—when she has given birth, [I offer] her mind, svāhā! O Agni, you whose path is black, burn away their lungs, heart, liver, and internal organs with your fire, svāhā! With each mantra, he throws [the offering] onto the embers. ||17||

Then, having washed his hands, he touches the earth with the mantra: "O Suśīmā, that heart of yours which is established in heaven in the moon—being thus the lord of immortality, may I not weep for the sin of my grandson. I know your heart, O Earth, which is established in heaven in the moon; being thus the lord of immortality, may I not weep for the sin of my grandson. || 18 ||

Now, therefore, follows the rite for generating intelligence: having tied a piece of gold with a blade of *darbha* grass and holding it [near the child's mouth], he makes the boy—who is being held facing eastward—consume clarified butter, saying: "Bhūḥ! I offer the *ṛc*s into you, svāhā! Bhuvaḥ! I offer the *yajus* formulas into you, svāhā! Suvaḥ! I offer the *sāmans* into you, svāhā! Bhūrbhuvaḥsuvaḥ! I offer the *Atharvāṅgirasaḥ* into you, svāhā! (19)

Then he bathes him with warm and cold water, saying: "For the sake of the field-disease, for Nirṛti, for malice, I release you from the noose of Varuṇa. I make you sinless before the Brahman. May both these, Heaven and Earth, be auspicious to you. May Agni together with the waters be propitious to you; may Heaven and Earth together with the plants be propitious to you. May the intermediate space together with the wind be propitious to you; may the four quarters be propitious to you. As the gods released Sūrya, the Truth, from darkness and from the grasp of the Seizer, so they freed him from sin."
"Thus do I release you from this curse of kinship by birth from a Kṣatriya, from the malice of the oppressor, and from the noose of Varuṇa. || 20.1.20 ||

Then he places him upon his mother’s lap with the verse: "The four divine quarters, whose lord is Vāta, which the Sun surveys; of these I place thee within reach of old age; let consumption depart and Nirṛti far away. (Section 3) || 21 ||

Having placed [the child] there, he consecrates it with the mantra: "May no demon harm your son; may the cow not be one that miscarries. May she be dear to wealth, prospering under her own control. (22)

Having washed the right breast, he gives it to the child to suckle, saying: "May this boy suckle old age; may he attain a full lifespan. For him, swell the breast with life, fame, splendor, glory, and strength. (23)
The same applies to the subsequent [cases]. ||24||

"Where we speak, he does not bend; where we touch, he does not cry. Having touched both [the boy and the girl], he then places a covered water-pot upon her head, saying: "O waters, be watchful in the house! As you are watchful among the gods, so be watchful for this mother of a good son!"
On the twelfth day, the mother and son bathed.
They construct a sanctuary for the pure. || 27 ||
They carry out the birth-fire and carry forward the *aupāsana* fire. || 28 ||
Having placed that [fire] and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛtis*, he offers twelve oblations with the mantra "May Dhātṛ give us wealth," or thirteen, according to some.

"O Varuṇa, I entreat you for this truth of mine; O Agni, do thou [protect] us; O Agni, do thou [protect] us; O Agni, you are the unerring one; O Prajāpati, whatever in this rite I have done in excess"—with these words, some here offer the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts* as before. Having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce "An auspicious day!", "Welfare!", and "Prosperity!", he should give a name to his son consisting of two or four syllables, beginning with a sonant, containing a semi-vowel, and ending in a long vowel or a visarga (*abhiniṣṭāna*), or where [such conditions are met].

The prefix *svit* should be used, for it is known that "that is indeed established"; first the father and the mother should utter [the name], and it is known from the text: "O Jātavedas, my name was the first. (20.1.30)
One should give him two names; for it is known from scripture: "Therefore, a Brahmin with two names is prosperous. (31)
The second name should be that of a lunar mansion (nakṣatra). || 32 ||
One [of the two] should remain secret; they should address him by means of the other. || 33 ||
"It is known from tradition that one should give 'Somayājī' as the third name."
When the son has returned from a journey, he touches him with the formula: "I touch you with the splendor of Soma, with the brilliance of Agni, and with the luster of Sūrya. (35)

"By the *huṃ* sound of the animals, I smell you for the sake of long life and splendor; you are offered as an oblation"—having said this, he smells him on the head. Then, with his own right hand, he grasps the boy's right hand, including the thumb, with the five sections beginning "Agni is long-lived. He murmurs into the boy's right ear the verse "Bestowing long life upon you from every side," just as was done previously. (Section 4) 37.
Now, in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food takes place.

During the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, having established the fire and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he offers these: "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa," "For that I entreat thee," "Do thou, O Agni, protect us," "So do thou, O Agni, protect us," "O Agni, thou art the messenger," "O Prajāpati, whatever in this rite I have done in excess. Here, some also offer the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations as before. Having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce, "An auspicious day! Prosperity! Welfare! Success! [the rite is concluded].
Then he makes him eat the threefold mixture of curds, honey, and ghee, saying: "Bhūḥ! I place you in me; bhuvaḥ! I place you in me; suvaḥ! I place you in me."

Then he feeds him food with [the formula]: "I feed thee the essence of waters and plants; may those waters and plants be auspicious for thee; may those waters and plants be free from disease for thee. (Section 5) ||41||
In the third year, the rite of tonsure (cūḍākarma) is performed. || 42 ||

During the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, having established the sacred fire and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he offers these: "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa," "For that I implore thee," "Thou, O Agni, for us," "So thou, O Agni, for us," "O Agni, thou art the messenger," "O Prajāpati, whatever in this rite I have done in excess"—some say [he offers] with these. They offer the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations as before. Having served food to the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce "An auspicious day!", "Prosperity!", and "Success!", he sits down to the west of the fire, facing east.
To the north, the mother or a celibate student holds a ball of bull-dung; with that, he catches his [the boy’s] hair. || 44 ||
Then he mixes warm and cold water together. || 45 ||
"May the cool and warm waters, being brought, moisten [the hair] for the sake of life"—with these words, he moistens the right side of the head near the ear.
