With the words, "O herb, protect him," he places an herb with its tip pointing upward between [the hair and the razor]. With the words, "O axe, do not harm him," he applies the razor. With the words, "O god-hearing one, shave these [hair] away," he shaves it. 47.

"In the same way, O Brahmins, shave this [hair] of his with that razor with which Savitṛ, the knower, shaved the hair of King Soma and Varuṇa; unite him with vigor, with wealth, and with splendor"—thus [he says] toward the west. "With that [razor] with which Pūṣan, Bṛhaspati, Agni, and Indra shaved [the hair] for the sake of long life—with that I shave you, O so-and-so," thus [he says] toward the north, so that he may long remain well-disposed. "And that he may long behold the sun"—thus [he says] toward the east. (48)
Having sown [the seeds], they cause the topknots to be fashioned as prescribed, or according to the [number of] seers.

Having tied up his hair, he buries [the object] in a cow-pen, at an *udumbara* tree, or at a clump of *darbha* grass, saying: "Where Pūṣan, Bṛhaspati, Savitṛ, Soma, and Agni—they sought a manifold place of deposit between heaven and earth, in the waters, and in the light; for him who is his friend. (20.1.50)
He gives to the Brāhmaṇa according to his faith. || 51 ||
He should give rice with clarified butter to the barber. || 52 ||
Thus is prescribed the rite of giving away the cow (godāna) in the sixteenth year.
He has his hair shaved together with the top-knot; according to some, he leaves the top-knot here; or it may be the *agnigodāna* [tonsure] rite.
He gives a cow to the teacher. (Section 6) || 55 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the twentieth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the second chapter in the twentieth inquiry:
hereafter follows the expiation for the dog-seizure (*śvagraha*).

Wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder and having sipped water, he brings water in an unbaked earthen bowl, digs up the ground for gambling in the middle of the assembly hall, sprinkles it with water, scatters the dice, arranges them, gathers them together, spreads them out, and having arranged grass upon the assembly hall, he brings the boy there by means of that [dice], lays him down supine upon the dice, and sprinkles him with curds mixed with salt-water. They strike a bronze vessel to the south: "Kurkura, Sukurkura, Kurkura, Nīlabandhana!"

Aulava Itta invoked Arjimacchabala, as well as Rāma Ulumbara. A dog runs along, gazing like at the ocean; he wears a golden neck-ornament and a breastplate, leading the pack of dogs with great heroism. O you of great heroism, let loose, let loose! O sole Vratya, let loose! Let loose, Śunaka, let loose! Let loose, Chat! Ṭeka and Sasaramaṭaṅka, Tūla and Vitūla, Arjuna and Lohita—let them go! O Śitimna, you are the slayer of Piśaṅkara.

These some water-fowls run about in the third heaven from here. For you cover the *sīsara*; O dog, homage be to you, O *sīsara*. Your mother’s name is Dulā, and Maṇḍākaka is your father. For you cover the *sīsara*; O dog, homage be to you, O *sīsara*. Dulā is indeed your mother’s name, and Maṇḍākaka is your father. For you cover the *sīsara*; O dog, homage be to you, O *sīsara*. Like horses, like stallions, they do not snort at the feet.

I shall ward off the leaden one, O dog; homage be to you, O leaden one! The carpenter strikes down those who possess wheels, not those who are leaden. I shall ward off the leaden one, O dog; homage be to you, O leaden one. || 2 ||
Then [he said], "Choose a boon. ||3||
"I choose the youth himself as my boon," she said. ||4||
In this manner he should offer [the oblation] three times a day—at dawn, at midday, and at evening—if [the guest] has arrived. (Section 7) 5.
Thus ends the second chapter in the twentieth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the third chapter in the twentieth book:
"Now, therefore, [the ritual of] the spit-ox. (1)

During the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, having established the sacred fire and strewn grass around it, he cooks a *sthālīpāka* (morsel-offering) of rice in milk. Having poured clarified butter over it and removed it from the fire, he constructs two huts to the west of the fire. In the southern one, he invokes the *Śūlagava* (the spit-ox sacrifice) with the mantra: "May the well-disposed bay horses carry you; come quickly for my oblation, O Śarva, together with white horses that possess banners, are swift as the wind, powerful, and fleet as thought! || 2 ||
In the north, [he places] Mīḍhuṣī. || 3 ||
In the center, Jayanta. || 4 ||
Having offered water as it was brought, and having prepared three portions of boiled rice with under-layering and sprinkling of clarified butter—thus [it is said].

He causes [the sacrificer] to touch [the water] exactly as it was brought: "May the Bountiful One touch me; svāhā to the Bountiful One! May the Bountiful Female touch me; svāhā to the Bountiful Female! May Jayanta touch me; svāhā to Jayanta! || 6 ||

Having performed [the rites] up to the *vyāhṛtis* and having brought forward portions of cooked rice, he offers them with the words: "To the god Bhava, svāhā! To the god Rudra, svāhā! To the god Śarva, svāhā! To the god Īśāna, svāhā! To the god Paśupati, svāhā! To the god Ugra, svāhā! To the god Bhīma, svāhā! To the great god Mahat, svāhā! (7)

Then he offers the rice-oblation for the wife to the wife [of the gods], saying: "Svāhā to the wife of the god Bhava! Svāhā to the wife of the god Rudra! Svāhā to the wife of the god Śarva! Svāhā to the wife of the god Īśāna! Svāhā to the wife of the god Paśupati! Svāhā to the wife of the god Ugra! Svāhā to the wife of the god Bhīma! Svāhā to the wife of the great god! ||8||
Then he offers of the middle portion of the cooked rice, saying: "To Jayanta, svāhā! To Jayanta, svāhā! (9)
Then, having taken portions from all the cooked rice dishes, he offers the oblation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the formula: "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā! (20.3.10).

They station the cows around this fire so that they may smell the fragrance of the oblation being offered. Saying, "May he with his full face walk auspiciously around us," they circumambulate it from all sides, keeping it to their right, and then worship it with these Anuvākas beginning with "Homage to you, O Rudra, to your wrath," or else with only the first and the last. (Section 8) 11.
Now, therefore, [the ritual] for the dwelling of a Buddhist monk alone. 12.

"O guardian of the house, touch [this]; svāhā to the guardian of the house! O guardian of the wife, touch [this]; svāhā to the guardian of the wife! O guardian of the door, touch [this]; svāhā to the guardian of the door! O guardian of the wife's door, touch [this]; svāhā to the guardian of the wife's door!"—with these words he offers four palāśa leaves. || 13 ||

"O you who shout, touch [the water]; svāhā to the shouting ones! O you who carry quivers, touch [the water]; svāhā to those who carry quivers! O you who follow along, touch [the water]; svāhā to those who follow along! O you who employ [means], touch [the water]; svāhā to those who employ [means]! O you who discern, touch [the water]; svāhā to those who discern! O you who consume together, touch [the water]; svāhā to those who consume together! (14)
Then ten others: "The divine armies, touch! To the divine armies, svāhā! || 15 ||
"Then there are another ten; those which are named Devasenās and those which are unnamed—touch them with the words, 'Svāhā to them! || 16 ||

Then, having made a leaf-cup and having taken from it a ball of cooked rice over which grass has been spread and clarified butter poured, he goes beyond the distance of a *gavyūti* and offers it upon a tree, saying: "To those who carry quivers, to those who touch [the water], to those who carry quivers, svāhā!"
Then he pays homage: "Homage to the one who carries a quiver and a bow, to the lord of thieves; homage! (18)

Then, with sandalwood, liquor, water, unbroken grains, unbroken grains, cow-dung, a bunch of *dūrvā* grass, and pieces of *udumbara*, *palāśa*, *śamī*, *vikaṅkata*, *aśvattha*, and cow-hair, he sprinkles the cows, beginning with the bull, saying, "Be auspicious! And thus he indeed becomes auspicious. || 19 ||

Then, having cooked a sacrificial mess of rice (sthālīpāka) in milk belonging to Kṣetrapati, having poured clarified butter over it and removed it from the fire, he sacrifices to Kṣetrapati in the midst of the cows, not in the fire.

On four or seven Palāśa leaves, he invokes [the deity] in the same manner as for the Śūlagava sacrifice. He sacrifices with the *Nūrti* hymn, "The god Pāka," and then stands near [the offering] with the verses, "By the Lord of the Field" (*kṣetrasya patinā vayam*) and "Of the Lord of the Field" (*kṣetrasya pate*). Then those who are his kinsmen eat of this offering to the Lord of the Field, according to their own family custom. (Section 9) 21.
Thus ends the third chapter in the twentieth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the fourth chapter in the twentieth book:
"The monthly [śrāddha] is performed on the afternoon of the new moon day, or on the odd-numbered days of the waning fortnight. (1)

Having prepared the food for the ancestors and having arranged seats of *darbha* grass with their tips pointing southward, he invites an odd number of pure Brahmins who are learned in the mantras and possessed of all their limbs, provided they are not related by birth (*yoni*), lineage (*gotra*), or mantra. He should feed them without regard for wealth.

Having kindled the fire and strewn darbha grass around it with the tips pointing southward and eastward, he prepares the clarified butter in a butter-pot over which a single purifier has been placed; having sprinkled water around it from right to left and added a fuel-stick of udumbara wood, he offers oblations with a ladle made of udumbara wood.

Having performed the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he invokes the ancestors with the verse: "Come, O Soma-loving ancestors, by your deep, ancient paths; bestowing upon us progeny and wealth, and long life for a hundred autumns. (5)

He pours water toward this very direction with [the verse]: "O divine waters, send forth this Agni; may our fathers enjoy this sacrifice. May they partake of this monthly strength for our protection; may they bestow upon us wealth consisting of all heroic sons. ||6||

Wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), having performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛtis*, he wears it over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and offers oblations: "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, *svadhā*! Homage! To Yama accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors, *svadhā*! Homage! With the waters that flow eastward and those from the north—with these waters, the sustainers of the entire world—I place a barrier between myself and my father; *svadhā*! Homage! I have placed a barrier with the mountains, with the great earth, with the sky, and with the infinite quarters and protections; I place a barrier between myself and my grandfather; *svadhā*! Homage!"

He disappeared through the seasons, the days and nights with their well-defined junctions, and the half-months and months; thus he established a further interval from his great-grandfather, saying, "To the abode of Svadhā."

Then he offers oblations with their names: "To such-and-such, *svadhā*! Homage! To such-and-such, *svadhā*! Homage! With the verse, "What my mother, wandering unfaithful, has caused me to lose—that seed let my father take; let another man come to her, *svadhā*! Homage!"—he thus performs the second offering, and likewise the third, modifying the mantra to "what my grandmother" and "what my great-grandmother. (Section 10) "And those ancestors who are here, and those who are not here, and those whom we know, and those whom we do not know..."

O Agni Jātavedas, you know them; may they rejoice in that *svadhā* which has been offered by you. *Svadhā! Namas!* Whatever limb of yours the flesh-eater (*kravyād*) burnt while Jātavedas was leading you to the worlds, that I cause to enter into you again. O Fathers, be whole with all your limbs! *Svadhā! Namas!* Carry the clarified butter (*ājya*), O Jātavedas, to the Fathers where you know them to be placed in the distance. May streams of clarified butter flow toward them; may their blessings be realized through their desires! *Svadhā! Namas!*
In this manner, he adapts the mantra for the second [offering] and likewise for the third, saying "to the grandfathers" and "to the great-grandfathers. || 8 ||
In this manner, he offers the food, adapting the mantra to "Carry the food. ||9||
Then he offers the oblation for Sviṣṭakṛt with the formula: "To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, Svadhā! Adoration! (20.4.10).

Then he touches the food with the formula: "The earth is your vessel, the sky is your lid; I offer you into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇas; I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; do not fail among the ancestors there in yonder world. The earth is level; Agni is its witness for the non-neglect of what has been given."

The earth is your vessel, the sky is your lid; I offer you into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇas; I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not perish for my grandfathers in yonder world, in that other world. The atmosphere is equal to it; Vāyu is its overseer, so that what has been given shall not be lost.

"The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer you into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇas. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not perish for my great-grandfathers in yonder world. The sky is the equal [measure]; of it, the sun is the witness, so that what is given shall not be lost. With these words, he causes the Brāhmaṇas to touch [the food]. "Entering into the breath, I offer the nectar," [he says]. (Section 11) 11. He looks at those who are eating: "In Brahman is my self for the sake of immortality. 12.

Having followed after him once he has eaten, and having asked for permission regarding the remainder, he takes a water-pot and a handful of *darbha* grass, goes to the intermediate direction between south and east, spreads out *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south, and with his hands turned downwards, pours three handfuls of water ending toward the south, saying: "May the Soma-loving ancestors purify themselves; may the Soma-loving grandfathers purify themselves; may the Soma-loving great-grandfathers purify themselves"; and [he addresses each individual] saying, "N.N., pour water; N.N., pour water. (13)
With his hands turned downwards, he offers three balls of rice among them, ending toward the south.

"O Father, this for you, O [Name]"—with these words he offers the rice ball (*piṇḍa*) to the father; "O Grandfather, this for you, O [Name]"—to the grandfather; "O Great-grandfather, this for you, O [Name]"—to the great-grandfather; the fourth is offered silently. This [fourth] is optional. || 15 ||

Now, if he does not know their names, he gives the rice-ball to the father with the words, "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling on earth"; to the grandfather with the words, "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling in the intermediate space"; and to the great-grandfather with the words, "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling in heaven. || 16 ||
At this point, he gives collyrium, ointment, and a garment along with each rice-ball.
"Look at me! Look at me!"—thus he says three times while applying collyrium.
"Anoint him! Anoint him! Anoint him!"—thus three times for the anointing. || 19 ||

"O fathers, these are your garments; therefore, O fathers, do not take anything else from us," saying this, he cuts off a fringe or a tuft of wool and lays it down, if [the deceased] was in the earlier stage of life.
Having cut off his own hair, [he should do so] on the northern side. ||21||

Then, having washed the vessel, and having sprinkled water around it counter-clockwise with the mantra: "May these honey-sweet waters, satisfying sons and grandsons, yielding *svadhā* to the fathers and immortality, may the divine waters—both those of the rivers and these watery, seed-bearing ones with good fords—flow for you in that world," he turns the vessel upside down, crosses his hands (placing the right over the left and the left over the right), and worships with salutations, saying: "Obeisance to you, O fathers, to the essence (*rasa*). || 23 ||

Then, having gone to the edge of the water, he pours out three handfuls of water [thus]: (Khaṇḍa 12) "This honeyed wave is for you, O father; as great as Sarasvatī is, and as great as Agni and the Earth are, so great is its measure, so great is its majesty. I give this being to you of such extent. Just as Agni is preserved and not destroyed, so may it be preserved and not destroyed for my father. Be a *svadhā* offering for them! Live upon that inexhaustible *svadhā* together with them, O [Name]! The *Ṛgveda* is your majesty."

O Grandfather, this honeyed wave is for you; as great as Sarasvatī, as great as Vāyu and the intermediate space (antarikṣa), so great is its measure, so great is its majesty. I give it to you as such a being. Just as Vāyu is imperishable and undecaying, so may it be imperishable and undecaying for me, for my grandfather. Be a *svadhā* offering for them; may he, [the deceased], live upon that imperishable *svadhā* together with them. The *yajus* verses are your majesty.

"O great-grandfather, this wave of yours is honeyed; as much as Sarasvatī, and as much as Āditya and the sky, so much is its measure, so much is its greatness. I give it to you as such a being. Just as Āditya is inexhaustible and undecaying, so may it be inexhaustible and undecaying for me, for my great-grandfather; may it be *svadhā* for you. Live upon that inexhaustible *svadhā* together with them, O Sāman-chanters—this is your greatness. Having returned thus, he pours out what remains in the water-vessel while [the ancestors] are established, saying: "Depart, O Soma-loving fathers!"
"By the deep, ancient paths, come back again to our houses this month, O you who eat the oblation, possessing good offspring and heroic sons. (24)
By this, the mid-year [observance] is explained. || 25 ||
In that case, meat is obligatory. || 26 ||
In the absence of meat, vegetables. (Section 13) || 27 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the twentieth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the fifth chapter in the twentieth book:
We shall explain the Aṣṭakā sacrifice. || 1 ||
The eighth day of the dark fortnight following the full moon of the month of Māgha is called Ekāṣṭakā.

Then, on the previous day, in the afternoon during the asterism of Anurādhā, having established the fire and strewn it around with *darbha* grass whose tips point south and east, and having placed purifiers (strainers) over them, he pours out four bowls of rice, saying: "I pour out this cake of four bowls, which brings distress to the ancestors in the world beyond; impelled by the divine Savitṛ, [I take] thee, acceptable to the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, in the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, and with the hands of Pūṣan."

With the formula "I offer," having thus prepared the *prokṣaṇī* waters silently by means of the strainer, having sprinkled [the materials] silently, and having pounded [the grain] silently, he bakes it silently on four potsherds in the manner of a *puroḍāśa*. Having poured clarified butter over it, removed it from the fire, and sprinkled water around it counter-clockwise, he places the Udumbara fuel-stick upon the fire. Then, having spread a base of ghee with the Udumbara ladle, he takes portions from the cake—each subsequent portion larger than the preceding one—pouring clarified butter over them, and offers them, each subsequent portion larger than the preceding one, in a continuous stream toward the south-east.

The mortars and the pressing-stones have raised their voice, preparing the oblation for the year-long rite. O Ekāṣṭakā, may we be possessed of good offspring and heroic sons; may we be masters of riches. Svadhā! Homage! O divine Agni, carry this cake rich in ghee, provided with the *svadhā* offering, for the satisfaction of the ancestors. O Agni, son, convey the oblation exactly as it is; I offer this sacrifice to the ancestors. Svadhā! Homage! This cake, prepared in four dishes, is rich in ghee, rich in milk, O Agni, and full of wealth and nourishment.
"May the ancestors rejoice, being in agreement; may this [offering] be well-sacrificed and well-poured for me; Svadhā! Adoration! || 3 ||
Then he offers an oblation of food with [the verse]: "She who first shone forth, the one who was performing penance with fervor—she who first shone forth. (4)
Having taken equal portions of the cake and the food mixed with clarified butter, he offers them with the formula: "To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, Svadhā! Homage! (5).
Having touched that [food], which is rich in ghee, honey, and food, with the *śrāddhābhimarśana* formula, he gives the rice-balls according to the procedure for the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). || 6 ||
With that, he serves a learned Brāhmaṇa. ||7||
To them he gives food and wealth according to his faith. ||8||
As is well known, the offering of handfuls of modakas and so forth is performed at the monthly [śrāddha]. (Khaṇḍa 14) ||9||
On the following day, he immolates a cow for the ancestors.

Having established the fire and strewn *darbha* grass around it with the tips pointing south and east, he performs the introductory oblation with the formula: "I dedicate this cow to the ancestors; may the ancestors, assembled here, accept it. May she, rich in fat, rich in ghee, and rich in *svadhā*, satisfy my ancestors in the world beyond; *svadhā*! Homage! Having offered the introductory oblation, he dedicates the cow with a single blade of sacrificial grass and a single-pronged *vapāśrapaṇī* made of *udumbara* wood, saying:
"I sprinkle you, acceptable to the ancestors. After sprinkling it and carrying fire around it, they immolate it to the west of the fire, with its head toward the west and its feet toward the south.
Having satisfied her with water while remaining silent and having thus restored her vital breaths, he silently extracts the omentum, the heart, and the kidneys. || 12 ||
He cooks the omentum on a splinter from an Udumbara tree used as a fat-roasting fork, and the other organs separately on Udumbara spits.

Having cooked it, sprinkled it with clarified butter, removed it from the fire, and poured water around it in a counter-clockwise direction, he places a fuel-stick of *udumbara* wood upon the fire and offers the omentum—previously spread with a ladle of *udumbara* wood and sprinkled with clarified butter—with the mantra: "Carry the omentum, O Jātavedas, to the fathers where you know them to be placed in the distance; let streams of fat flow toward them; may their blessings be true through their desires! Svadhā! Homage! (14)
He offers the omentum as a complete oblation; having set aside the remainder, he should feed the Brāhmaṇas. || 15 ||

When the food has been set forth, having taken portions of the boiled rice (*odana*) and of the meats, he offers them together with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*). He beholds the Ekāṣṭakā as she yields her milk: "Food accompanied by meat and ghee, accompanied by *svadhā*—may that food, purified by the Brāhmaṇas, be inexhaustible for me; may it be mine, *svadhā*, homage! "The Ekāṣṭakā, performing penance, the full-grown consort of the year, has yielded her milk. O Fathers, living upon that milk in harmony, may this [offering] be well-sacrificed and well-poured for me; *svadhā*, homage! "Of the year, the image... (so on). 16.
Having offered [the oblations] of food and meats, he takes portions from all together and offers [them] mixed with clarified butter, saying: "To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, Svadhā! Homage! (17).
Just as in the monthly rite, there is the offering of a handful of well-known sweetmeats and so forth.
But in this case, the giving of food and wealth is not restricted. || 19 ||

On the following day, having prepared food for the ancestors with the remaining meat, he offers oblations with the verses, "Thou, O Agni" and "O Prajāpati," in the established manner, including the offering of handfuls of water with rice balls (*odana*) as in the monthly rite. (Section 15) 20.5.20.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the twentieth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the sixth chapter in the twentieth book.
Now, therefore, follows the Śravaṇā-rite. 1.

On whichever full moon day the moon is in conjunction with the asterism Śravaṇa, on that day, after the evening Agnihotra, he establishes the Dakṣiṇāgni; for one who has not established the sacred fires, he establishes the Āvasathya fire.
Then he prepares unbroken grains of rice, parched grains of rice without being split, barley meal, *kiṃśuka* flowers, collyrium, ointment, and clarified butter.

Having spread a base of clarified butter in the ladle and having taken portions of these very foods mixed with ghee, he offers them, saying: "Homage to Agni, the terrestrial, the lord of terrestrial beings, svāhā! Homage to Vāyu, the all-pervading, the lord of the intermediate regions, svāhā! Homage to Sūrya, the ruddy, the lord of celestial beings, svāhā! Homage to Viṣṇu, the tawny, the lord of the quarters, svāhā! Having mixed *kiṃśuka* flowers with clarified butter, he offers them.

The mosquito has been devoured; the lack of vision has been devoured; the one who performs improper rites has been devoured. The one who performs improper rites has been devoured; the lack of vision has been devoured; the mosquito has been devoured. The lack of vision has been devoured; the mosquito has been devoured; the one who performs improper rites has been devoured. || 4 ||

Taking a water-pot and a handful of *darbha* grass, he goes out facing the east, spreads *darbha* grass pointing eastward, and upon them offers four oblations: "To those serpents that are terrestrial, to them I bring this offering; to those that are atmospheric, to those that are celestial, to those that belong to the quarters. Having given ointment for the eyes and ointment for the body, he stands in worship with these mantras: "Homage be to the serpents," and so forth. || 5 ||

Taking a water-pot, he should walk three times around the dwelling from left to right, sprinkling it, as far as he desires, thinking: "By this much may the serpents not step upon me. [He recites: "O white-footed one, strike them away with the front and the back! Seven of these human ones and three belonging to the royal kin—by the approach of the white one, the serpent has killed someone through his practice. Homage, homage to the white Vaidarva; homage to the white Vaidarva! (6)
Then he pays homage to each direction with these mantras: "Thou art Samīcī by name, the eastern quarter," and so forth.
From this point forward, he regularly offers the bali-oblation until the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
In this case, there is no oblation of *kiṃśuka* flowers. ||9||
No sprinkling of water is prescribed. || 20.6.10 ||
Thinking, "I shall offer it, I shall offer it," he finally carries away the oblations. (Section 16) ||11||
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the twentieth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the seventh chapter in the twentieth book.
We shall now explain the *Āgrahāyaṇī* [festival]. 1.

On the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, having established the fire and strewn grass around it, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (milk-rice oblation) in milk, having poured clarified butter over it and removed it from the fire, and having performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* offerings, he sacrifices: "O Jātavedas, enjoy this oblation, the creeping of Iḍā, rich in ghee, moving and unmoving. May there be delight here for these seven domestic animals of all forms, and may there be nourishment, Svāhā! The night which people greet with joy as she approaches like a milch-cow..."

She who is the wife of the year, may she be auspicious for us; Svāhā! May she be propitious to our cattle and our wives, propitious by night and propitious by day; she who is the wife of the year, may she be auspicious for us; Svāhā! May the Full Moon, filling and approaching month after month, dividing the months and half-months—may she, being full, protect us; Svāhā! ||2||

Then he offers the oblation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the verse: "O Agni, make that well-sacrificed; O God, overcome all hostile armies. Show us a wide path and shine forth; bestow upon us a radiant and undecaying life. (3)

Then, having washed his hands, he touches the ground with the formula: "I find support in the *kṣattra*, I find support in the kingdom; I find support in the horses, I find support in the cattle; I find support in the limbs, I find support in the self; I find support in the vital breaths, I find support in prosperity; I find support in heaven and earth, I find support in the sacrifice. The thirty-three gods, the thrice eleven, the bounteous ones, who have Bṛhaspati as their domestic priest—may those gods, by means of the gods, protect me at the impulse of the god Savitṛ. (4)
The householder sits to their south, and the others to the north, in order according to the sequence of their birth; those among them who know the mantras mutter the mantras.
"O Earth, be pleasant, thornless, and a place of rest; grant us wide-spreading protection. With these two verses beginning with "baḍ itthā parvatānām," they lie down on their right sides.
"O long-lived one," they say as they rise. || 7 ||
Having risen, they mutter: "We have stood up; we have become immortal. || 8 ||
In this same way, they rise three times during the night. || 9 ||
Having served food to the Brahmins and having caused them to recite, "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity!", they then dwell for that night. (Section 17) 20.7.10.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the twentieth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the eighth chapter in the twentieth book.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) and the conclusion (*utsarjana*). 1.
The commencement of the term (adhyāyopākarma) takes place when the herbs have grown during the fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, under the asterism Hasta, or on the full moon day.

Having kindled the fire and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛtis*, he offers oblations to the five *kāṇḍarṣis*: "To Prajāpati, the *kāṇḍarṣi*, svāhā! To Soma, the *kāṇḍarṣi*, svāhā! To Agni, the *kāṇḍarṣi*, svāhā! To the Viśvedevas, the *kāṇḍarṣis*, svāhā! To the Self-existent (*svayaṃbhū*), the *kāṇḍarṣi*, svāhā! Having offered these, or having offered the names of the *kāṇḍas* themselves, as well as the *Sāvitrī*, the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda, and Sadasaspati, they study the first three *anuvākas*.

Alternatively, having performed all [the rites] beginning with the *kāṇḍa* offerings up to the end of the *sviṣṭakṛt*, one should wait for three days or one day and then study according to the lesson; so they say.
The ritual of release (utsarga) takes place under the asterism Rohiṇī during the month of Taiṣa, or on the full moon day.

Accompanied by his attendants, having gone out toward the eastern or northern direction, and having plunged into water that is pleasant and easy to enter, he performs three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) with the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn. Then, having bathed with his hands holding purifiers (pavitra), using the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ," the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ," and this entire section beginning with "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ," he gives darbha grass to one another, as if wishing to give it to each other.
Then, in a pure place sloping toward the east, they prepare seats with their ends pointing eastward and arranged so that they conclude toward the north, using *darbha* grass. (Section 18) 7.

To Brahmā, Prajāpati, Bṛhaspati, Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, Candramas, the Nakṣatras, Indra the king, Yama the king, Varuṇa the king, Soma the king, Vaiśravaṇa the king, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the Ṛbhus, the Bhṛgus, the Maruts, the Atharvans, and the Aṅgirases—thus for the hosts of gods. (8)

Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Gautama, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Kaśyapa—these seven ṛṣis, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (nivītin), prepare their seats on the north side, on ground sloping toward the north, with darbha grass blades pointing northward, arranged so that they end toward the east.

They prepare [the offerings] for Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Gautama, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Kaśyapa; between Vasiṣṭha and Kaśyapa, they prepare for Arundhatī; and to the south, on ground sloping toward the east, for Agastya.

Then, on a single sacrificial altar (*ekavedī*), [he gave] to them: to Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, Jātūkarṇya, Tarukṣa, Tṛṇabindu, Varmin, Varūthin, Vājin, Vājaśravas, Satyaśravas, Suśravas, Sutaśravas, Somaśuṣmāyaṇa, Sattvavat, Bṛhaduktha, Vāmadeva, Vājiratna, Haryajvāyana, Udaman, Gotama, Ṛṇañjaya, Ṛtañjaya, Kṛtañjaya, Dhanañjaya, Babhru, Tryaruṇa, Trivarṣa, Tridhātu, and Śibintā.

To Parāśara, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Skanda, the Lord of Kāśī, Jvara, Dharma, Artha, Kāma, Krodha, Vasiṣṭha, Indra, Tvaṣṭṛ, the Maker, the Sustainer, Dhātṛ, Mṛtyu, Savitṛ, Sāvitrī, and to the Vedas individually—to the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvaveda, and the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. || 11 ||

To the south, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), they prepare seats upon grass-blades pointing southward on ground sloping toward the south, with their ends directed westward. (Section 19) [They offer to: Vaiśampāyana, Paliṅgu, Tittiri, Ukha, Ātreya, the author of the *Pada-pāṭha*, Kauṇḍinya, the author of the *Vṛtti*, the authors of the *Sūtras*, Satyāṣāḍha, the authors of the *Pravacanas*, the teachers (*ācāryas*), the seers (*ṛṣis*), forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*), those who have drawn up their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*), and women faithful to a single husband (*ekapatnīs*). || 12 ||

Just as they assign [seats] for their respective fathers and maternal grandfathers, saying, "I assign this seat for so-and-so; I assign this seat for so-and-so," so too [they do so] with the seating. 13.
"I satiate this one; I satiate that one," [he says] with water.

Having paid homage with "Homage to such-and-such! Homage to such-and-such! using perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps; with "Svāhā to such-and-such! Svāhā to such-and-such! using food; with "I satisfy such-and-such" using fruit and water; and having performed the ritual salutation (upasthāna) with "Homage to such-and-such! Homage to such-and-such! || 15 ||

Another [teacher says]: Having established the fire on the altar and performed the rites up to the *vyāhṛti* oblations, he offers to the five *kāṇḍa*-seers, or to the names of the *kāṇḍas*, or having offered the *Sāvitrī*, the *Ṛgveda*, the *Yajurveda*, the *Sāmaveda*, the *Atharvaveda*, and *Sadasaspati*, he studies from the first *anuvāka* or from the beginning of all the *kāṇḍas*. Having completed the rites ending with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, and having rested for either three days or one day, they say that he should study according to his lesson. 16.

With the two verses beginning "From joint to joint" and "Who with a hundred," they plant *dūrvā* grass at the edge of the water after making the ocean wavy; then they run toward the east or north as far as they can reach along the racecourse.
Having returned, they satisfy the Brāhmaṇas with cakes, parched grain flour, and boiled rice. || 18 ||

Thus, at the conclusion of the Pārāyaṇa, having always bathed in this manner—omitting only the planting of dūrvā grass and the running with curd—they satisfy the gods, sages, and ancestors with water, reciting the verse beginning "From section to section" (kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt).
Thus ends the eighth chapter and the twentieth book of the *Gṛhyasūtra* of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
Now begins the first chapter of the twenty-first book.

O Waters, whatever greatness belongs to you, and whatever arrows [of malice] are within me—O Waters, carry all that away from me, whatever evil is in me; whatever I have committed as an offense, and whatever I have sworn falsely, and whatever has been done by force. I take refuge in *bhūḥ*, I take refuge in *bhuvaḥ*, I take refuge in *suvaḥ*; I take refuge in *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ*. (Or: I take refuge in Truth, I take refuge in Righteousness, I take refuge in Immortality. I take refuge in the dear, unafflicted body of Prajāpati. I take refuge in the Gāyatrī, I take refuge in the Triṣṭubh, I take refuge in the Jagatī, I take refuge in the Anuṣṭubh.

I take refuge in the *paṅkti* meter; I take refuge in the meters; I cover myself with the meters; covered by the meters, with this fifteenfold thunderbolt, I trample down my hateful rival—him who hates us and whom we hate. The Ten-Hotṛ: *bhūḥ bhuvaḥ suvaḥ*. *Hiṃ! Homage to Mother Earth!* We take hold of Indra, the chosen Hotṛ-priest, the domestic chaplain, by whose [aid] the Aṅgirasas, the gods, went to the highest heaven, the celestial realm.
Sixty and ninety snares are stretched out between the Adhvaryu and Agni; they bind the simple man, while the wise one passes by. As Hotṛ, I follow the path of Truth. 1.

The four-hotṛ, the five-hotṛ, the six-hotṛ, and the seven-hotṛ. May I not fall into the ocean; may I turn according to the turning of the sun. May the six wide ones protect me from harm: heaven and earth, day and night, cultivation and rain, brilliance and honor, the waters and the plants. Parāvasu is cast out. Those who are our rivals—may they be driven away! By means of Indra and Agni, we drive them down. The Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas have made him a high-reaching, fierce, perceiving overlord.

O Heaven and Earth, do not let us fall today into the pit of the downward slope or the upward height on this day. Sit down, O Hotṛ, in your own place, being wise; establish the sacrifice in the womb of good deeds. As one who pleases the gods, worship the gods with the oblation; O Agni, bestow great vital strength upon the sacrificer. The Hotṛ, knowing his place, has sat down in the seat of the Hotṛ—resplendent, shining, and most skillful. Agni, whose wisdom protects the inviolable vows, the most excellent, the bringer of thousands, the pure-tongued one.

O makers of the world, create for me a world; do not cause me to suffer. This is your world. Declare to me my portion, how it is for you, and by which path I shall carry the oblation unto you. May I today utter speech that is pleasing to the gods, pleasing to the sacred formulations (*brahman*), and pleasing to the *Nārāśaṃsa* hymn. Speech, vigor, power—vigor and the out-breath and in-breath are in me. O Speech, O *Vaṣaṭ*-call, homage be to you; do not harm me. 2.
We shall now explain the *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ priest) for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
When the seat of the Hotṛ has been prepared, he sips water with the mantra: "O gods, that greatness which is in the waters. || 2 ||

Wearing the sacrificial cord (yajñopavītin) and having sipped water (ācānta), he approaches the sacrificial hall (vihāra) and enters between the altar (vedi) and the rubbish-heap (utkara), saying: "I resort to Bhūḥ; I resort to Bhuvaḥ. Having stood to the north of the altar, he covers it with the meters (chandobhiḥ) and mutters: "I am covered by the meters. || 3 ||
With his right foot, he steps upon the northern corner of the altar, saying: "Here I [strike] with the fifteenfold thunderbolt. || 4 ||
Standing here, he recites the sāmidhenī verses.
For one who is veiled, these things must be restrained from speech. || 6 ||

From the *saṃpraiṣa* for the *sāmidhenī* verses up to the *paridhānīyā*, from the *saṃpraiṣa* for the *puronuvākyā* up to the *praṇava*, and from the *saṃpraiṣa* for the *yājyā* up to the *vaṣaṭkāra*—beginning with the *nigada* and continuing until the conclusion—he should recite and sacrifice while maintaining the *añjali* (joined palms) at the region of the heart.

Now, when the Adhvaryu gives the command, "Recite for the fire being kindled," he addresses the Brahman priest, saying, "O Brahman, I shall recite the Sāmidhenī verses," or "O Brahman, I shall recite. Having uttered the *prasava* (impulse), having explained the Daśahotṛ formula, and having murmured the *vyāhṛtis*, he utters the sound *him* three times. || 8 ||
He recites fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses beginning with "pra vo vājā abhidyavaḥ" in a medium tone; so it is known.

That which he recites in the krauñca tone belongs to the Asuras; that which is low-pitched belongs to humans; that which is between these two belongs to the gods. Therefore, it should be recited between the two for the sake of having the gods as one's companions.
He recites the first verse three times and the last verse three times without taking breath; thus they amount to fifteen.

Alternatively, at each recitation he breathes out; at the final recitation, he breathes out at the middle hemistich of the verse "O Agni, come for the feast" (agna āyāhi vītaye), and likewise in the others, he joins the latter hemistich of the preceding verse with the former hemistich of the following verse.
He places the Praṇava at the end of all the Ṛg-verses. || 13 ||

The syllable *oṃ* is high-pitched (*udātta*) when joined with a *ṛc*; it is deficient (*ūna*) or full (*pūrṇa*). "Oṃ" is deficient; "o 3m" is full. That which is full is indeed to be used at the conclusion. Having set aside that which is the final metrical measure (*chandomāna*) of the *ṛc*, in its place, one uses the full metrical measure, and its consonant is not elided. || 14 ||
He recites this *sāmidhenī* verse three times with pauses: "O Aṅgiras, thee with fuel-sticks... and "Kindled, O Agni... (VS 3.27–28). || 15 ||

He sets aside the recitation and the like of the word and establishes [the mantra] instead. For example: at the *srugādāpana*, he says "the highest salutation" (*uttamā namasyā*); at the *iḍā*, "invited is the *iḍā*, invited is the *iḍā*" (*upahūteḍopahūteḍā*); and at the *śaṃyuvāka*, "may it be well with our bipeds, may it be well with our quadrupeds" (*śaṃ no astu dvipade śaṃ catuṣpade*). Whatever else of this kind occurs in the archetype (*prakṛti*), that alone should be restricted there. || 16 ||
With the verse beginning "Invite him, honor him," he concludes with the subsequent one. || 17 ||
"Thou art Varuṇa" is for the Vasiṣṭhas and the Rājanyas.
The *jagatī* [meter] belongs to the Vaiśya. ||19||
If he should desire, "May there be spiritual luster," he should conclude with a Gāyatrī verse.
Thus ends the first chapter of the twenty-first book in the Śrautasūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.

Now begins the second chapter. It is traditionally known: "One should recite three triplets for a Brāhmaṇa; one should recite three triplets for a Rājanya; one should recite three triplets for a Vaiśya. || 1 ||
They may be optionally combined with the fifteen-fold [stoma].
For the Vaiśya, [the *dhāyyās*] are by way of the seventeenfold [stoma]. For him, the two *pṛthupājavatī* verses are the *dhāyyās* placed before the *samiddhavatī*.

"One should recite twenty-one [verses]," thus are explained the optional *sāmidhenī* formulas as taught in the Brāhmaṇa; their ritual rules have been explained by those of the fifteen-fold set. || 4 ||

Regarding the term "one who sacrifices much" (*bahuyājin*): it is known from tradition that one who performs Soma sacrifices in every season through the *gāyatrī*, *triṣṭubh*, and *jagatī* meters is a "sacrificer of much. || 5 ||

"One should recite an unlimited number. Beyond forty-eight verses, they may study as many as they desire among those [verses] that have a fixed measure. However, for those which are prescribed in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) by the term *dhāyyā*—such as "the two *pṛthupājavatī* verses are *dhāyyās*," "the two *anumatī* verses are *dhāyyās*," "the two *uṣṇih-kakubh* verses are *dhāyyās*," or "one should make the two *mānavī* verses *dhāyyās*"—one should introduce them before the *samiddhavatī* verse. One should introduce *gāyatrī* verses addressed to Agni; one should introduce them in such a way that the total number is completed by repeating the first and last [verses]. 6.
At the final recitation, at the point "O Agni, you are great, O Brahmana Bharata," he breathes out.

Then he chooses the *pravara*. According to the lineage of the sacrificer, including the one who stands beyond, three immediate ancestors, and those prior to them—by means of this address, it is understood as "Bhārgava-Vāsiṣṭha. 8.

"He chooses one, he chooses two, he chooses three; he does not choose four, nor does he exceed five. According to some, in place of the entire *pravara*, he should simply say "Mānava. Then he places the *nivid* verses. He begins with "Enkindled by the gods, enkindled by the mind," and having recited seven steps, he exhales.
Then four, and then four. || 11 ||

He invokes the deities: "O Agni, bring hither Agni; bring hither Soma; bring hither Agni; bring hither Prajāpati; bring hither Agni and Soma"—thus at the full moon sacrifice when there is a cake for Agni and Soma. (12)
On the new moon day, there exists the upāṃśuyāja sacrifice.

After the invocation of Agni, [he says] "Bring Indra and Agni" for one who does not offer the *saṃnāyya* (curdled milk), "Bring Indra" for one who offers the *saṃnāyya*, and "Bring Mahendra" for one who sacrifices to Mahendra; "Bring the gods who drink the clarified butter" is common to both cases.
He sits facing upward toward the Varaṇa tree. || 15 ||
It is understood that the reason [for this] is stated in the words, "sitting with knees raised, he should choose. || 16 ||
When he recognizes that "this is a human being," he rises up toward him and touches the earth, saying: "Homage to Mother Earth. || 17 ||
Having recited "The four hotṛs, the five hotṛs, the six hotṛs, the seven hotṛs," he takes hold of the adhvaryu with his right hand, saying, "We take hold of Indra. || 18 ||
With the left hand, he [leads] silently to the Āgnīdhra. || 19 ||

Saying, "Sixty and ninety are the snares, O Adhvaryu," he goes westward between the Āhavanīya fire and the Adhvaryu, and turning to the right, he turns around with the words, "May I not fall into the ocean; I turn according to the revolution of the sun."

Having murmured, "May the six earths protect your speed," and having reached the Hotṛ’s seat, he throws away a blade of grass from the Hotṛ’s seat with the words, "The Parāvasu is cast out," and touches water. He presses down upon the Hotṛ’s seat with the words, "May those who are our rivals be far away," and sprinkles the Hotṛ’s seat with the words, "May I go along the heights and the hollows. He sits down with the words, "Sit down, O Hotṛ! and also with, "Sit down, O Hotṛ! (21).
Sitting down at the Hotṛ’s seat, he mutters: "The Hotṛ has sat down. || 22 ||
He gazes at the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires with the formula: "O you two makers of the world, create a world for me. (23)
"Declare my portion," he says, as he approaches the deities. || 5 || 24 ||
Then he causes him to take up the two offering-spoons with the words: "May Agni, the Hotṛ, know [the sacrifice]; may Agni know the office of the Hotṛ. || 25 ||
With a low pitch before the two *ājyabhāga* offerings; with a medium pitch for the principal offerings; and with a high pitch from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards.

When the call "Recite the offering-verse for the *samidh*s" has been issued, he recites: "O Agni, may the *samidh*s partake of the clarified butter. He recites the second [offering-verse]: "May Tanūnapāt know the clarified butter. For the Vasiṣṭhas and Śunakas, Narāśaṃsa is the second *prayāja*; he recites: "May Narāśaṃsa know the clarified butter, O Agni. He recites the third: "May Iḍ know the clarified butter, O Agni. He recites the fourth: "May Barhis know the clarified butter, O Agni. At the final *prayāja*, he indicates the deities as they have been stated: "Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to so-and-so! || 27 ||
Then he proceeds with the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga). || 28 ||
The yājyā and puronuvākyā verses for these two are as follows. || 29 ||
The *yājyā* alone [is used] for the *prayāja*s and *anūyāja*s. || 21.2.30 ||
Having performed the ritual for them in all the *puronuvākyās*, he places the *praṇava*; that has been explained. || 31 ||
Then, joining the final metrical portion of the *ṛc* of the *yājyā* with an udātta accent, he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call as "vauṣaṭ."

In this regard, where the sounds *e* and *ai* occur at the end of a *yājyā*, one should there make them *ai*; and where the sounds *o* and *au* occur, one should there make them *au*. This applies to the *pragrahas*. Furthermore, where the first letters of the *ka*-group (*ka, kha, ga*) occur at the end of a *yājyā*, they become their respective third letters (*ga, gha, ṅa*) when followed by *ma*. There is a modification [to *ṅa*] when followed by *ṅa*, *ṇa*, or *na*. || 33 ||

Now, where the *visarjanīya* is preceded by a vowel other than *a*, it takes a long *ā*; when preceded by *i*, it takes *ī* with a following *repha* (r); when preceded by *u*, it takes *ū*. The *vaṣaṭ*-call, the endings of *yājyā* verses, protracted vowels (*pluta*), and that which precedes a word ending in a vowel or a consonant; the two *oṃ*s in the *brūhi* and *praiṣya* formulas; the *śrauṣaṭ* at the end of a pause; and the *vīhi*, *vaha*, *ā vaha*, *ye yajāmahe*, and what follows [take the *udātta* accent].

Regarding the rule "na svaṃ mahimānamāvaha," there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) for the forms *āśrāvaya* and *āśrāvaya ghora* (or *ghorā*), as well as for *ye*. Grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) consists in the elision (*plāvana*) of both [the preceding and following vowels] when such a *ayaṇa* occurs. According to Kāśakṛtsna, one should not effect this elision everywhere, nor is it heard [in usage]. 34.

Cekitāna, according to the characteristics [of the ritual], the instruction for the *puronuvākyā* is "Recite the remainder of the proclamation," the instruction for the *yājyā* is "Sacrifice," and the response is "ye yajāmahe. || 35 ||
Having identified the deity according to the specific divinity with the words "ye yajāmahe amum," and having murmured the *vyāhṛtis*, he utters the *vaṣaṭ* at the end of the *yājyā*. || 6 || 36 ||
Some recite it as "vaṣat"; some as "vauṣaṭ"; some as "vāṣāṭ"; and some as "vaṣāṭ. || 37 ||
It is known from tradition that one should utter the *vaṣaṭ* with a continuous *ṛc*.
It is known from scripture that one utters the *vaṣaṭ* with a more powerful *ṛc*. || 39 ||
If he should desire of someone, "May he become worse off," he should utter the *vaṣaṭ* call for that person's *yājyā* at a lower pitch.
If one should desire of someone, "May he be neither worse nor better," one should pronounce the *vaṣaṭ* call for him at the same point as the *yājyā*.
If one should desire, "May he become more wealthy and better off," one should pronounce the *vaṣaṭ* for that person's *yājyā* verse at a higher pitch.
Having made a gesture of grasping, he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call; or rather, the word is uttered loudly because of its connection with the act of striking down. 43.

If one should desire of someone, "May he be short-lived," they should perform the *vaṣaṭ* call loudly after having made a high gesture of threatening; it is known from tradition that for one who desires heaven, one should perform the *vaṣaṭ* call loudly, like the cry of a crane.

Having uttered the *vaṣaṭ* at each *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, he should breathe out and in, and blink his eyes. He consecrates the employed *vaṣaṭ*-utterance with the formula: "Speech, vigor, power; speech, vigor, the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance; homage be to you; do not harm me. (45)

"May Agni strike down the Vṛtras"—this is the *puronuvākyā* for the *ājyabhāga* offering to Agni. "O Soma, you are the lord of the virtuous"—this is the *vṛdhanvatī* verse for the offering to Soma. On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), "Agni by his ancient birth" is the [verse] for the offering to Agni; "O Soma, we [serve] you with songs" is that for the offering to Soma. Some recite the same two *yājyās* for the *ājyabhāgas*. Some recite *ṛc*-verses as the *yājyās*. Some recite identical verses. Some recite different verses. It is known from tradition: "With 'That one here' he says the second [verse]. (46)

Now follow the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the principal offerings: "Agni is the head" (*agnirmūrdhā bhava*) is for the offering to Agni; "O Prajāpati, you who know all" (*prajāpate savedasa*) is for the *upāṃśuyāja*.

"O Agni and Soma, you two... for the offering to Agni and Soma; "Indra and Agni, from the luminous realm... for the offering to Indra and Agni; "Indra, the winner of wealth... and "You have overcome... for the offering to Indra; "Great is Indra by his might... and "Great is Indra, like a hero... for the offering to Mahendra. || 48 ||

"O youngest one, satisfy the longing gods"—this is the *puronuvākyā* for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. "We who sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt; he has sacrificed for such-and-such a deity, he has sacrificed for such-and-such a deity," thus identifying the deities as previously mentioned, he recites the *yajyā*: "O Agni, Hotṛ of the people's sacrifice, today... [7] 49.

It is known [from tradition] that one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should employ two *gāyatrī* verses as the *saṃyājyās*; those desiring vigor (*vīrya*), two *triṣṭubh* verses; those desiring cattle (*paśu*), two *jagatī* verses; those desiring stability (*pratiṣṭhā*), two *anuṣṭubh* verses; those desiring the sacrifice (*yajña*), two *paṅkti* verses; and those desiring food (*anna*), two *virāj* verses. (21.2.50)
Having smelled the joints of his fingers, he touches water. || 51 ||

Then the Adhvaryu spreads an under-layer of ghee between the thumb and the forefinger; the Hotṛ himself takes two portions from the middle, or the Adhvaryu takes one of them, and both have them sprinkled with ghee and held together with the fingers.
And it is known [from scripture]: "One should not hold out an extended hand; for if one were to hold out an extended hand, the cattle would be liable to fall away from him. (53)
He remains as if restraining himself; then he invokes the iḍā.
Having whispered "The Rathantara has been invoked," measured by the mouth, he says "Ho! loudly; from that point onward, the other [formula] is pronounced loudly.

If he should desire of someone, "May he be without cattle," he invokes the *iḍā* for him with [the formula] turned away (*parācīm*). If he should desire of someone, "May he possess cattle," he invokes the *iḍā* for him with [the formula] turned toward him (*pratīcīm*). "The *iḍā* is invoked; the *iḍā* is invoked!"—this is when it is being invoked while turned toward him.
He eats the intermediate *iḍā* portion with the formula: "I eat thee, offered to Vācaspati; I eat thee, offered to Sadasaspati."
He eats the portion for the Hotṛ from the four parts of the *karṇikās*, [reciting]: "Thou art the portion of the Earth. || 58 ||
Having received the anvāhārya rice and returned, he proceeds with the after-offerings (anūyāja) and the subsequent rites. || 59 ||
One does not perform the "ye yajāmahe" formula at the after-offerings (anūyāja). || 21.2.60 ||
One proceeds by means of the *vyāhṛtis* alone. || 61 ||

When the command "Sacrifice to the gods" has been given: he sacrifices with the formula, "May the divine *barhis* know the gift of wealth for the sake of obtaining wealth. He sacrifices the second [anuyāja] with, "May the divine *narāśaṃsa* know the gift of wealth for the sake of obtaining wealth. He sacrifices the final after-offering (*anūyāja*) without pausing, with, "May the divine Agni Sviṣṭakṛt... It is known from tradition that [the formula ends with] either "he is satisfied" (*amatsata*) or "he has been satisfied" (*samata*).

Being prompted with "Recite the *sūkta*," he begins the *sūktavāka* with the words, "This has become auspicious for Heaven and Earth. In the *sūktavāka*, he mentions the deities as they have been specified. In the *upāṃśuyāja*, he says "may they enjoy" (*juṣatām*) and "they have increased" (*avīvṛdhanta*) in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), while the rest is spoken aloud (*uccais*).
"This sacrificer, so-and-so, desires [this]," he says, pronouncing two names of the sacrificer; the third [name] belongs to one who has performed the Soma sacrifice.
When the command "Recite the Śaṃyu" has been issued, he begins the Śaṃyu-vāk with the verse: "That we choose as auspiciousness. (65)
Having recited the Śaṃyuvāka, he consumes the remnants of the oblation.

Taking the Veda, he returns westward, sits down behind the Gārhapatya fire, and performs the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings. He does so either in a low voice or with a distinct tone: for Soma, "Āpyāyasva," "Saṃ te"; for Tvaṣṭṛ, "Iha tvaṣṭāram agriyam" and "Tanno turīpam"; for Rākā, "Rākām aham" and "Yāste rāke"; for Sinīvālī, "Sinīvāli yā supāṇiḥ"; and for Kuhū, "Kuhūm aham" and "Kuhūr devānām."

"May the longing wives of the gods protect us; may the divine wives come hither with Agni," [this is] for the wives of the gods; "Agni is the Hotṛ, the lord of the house; we [approach] thee, O lord of the house of men," [this is] for Agni Gṛhapati. || 67 ||
Having smelled his two finger-joints at the end [of the thumb], he touches water. || 68 ||
He invokes the Ājyeḍā as it has been handed down in the traditional recitation.
After the offerings of the flour-smear and the husks, he gives the Veda-grass-bundle to his wife with the formulas, "Thou art the Veda; thou art gain."
"You are the Veda; for the sake of the Veda, I take you; may the Veda be found by me," or so [it says]. || 71 ||
Reciting the verse, "The seat provided with ghee and a nest," the Hotṛ goes from the Gārhapatya fire to the Āhavanīya fire, spreading the sacrificial grass continuously.
He departs by the same way he came. || 73 ||
The office of the Hotṛ priest for the New and Full Moon sacrifices is concluded.
Thus ends the second chapter in the twenty-first book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Now begins the third chapter in the twenty-first book:
We shall explain the *pravara* (ancestral lineages). 1.
"He chooses the lineage of the Ṛṣis; thus he goes from kinship to kinship, and also for the sake of continuity"—so it is known.
"One should not choose a lineage from among gods or humans; one should choose a lineage only from among sages—so it is known. ||3||
He announces the lineage of the seers (ārṣeya), for it is known that "by means of the seer, the gods bind themselves to the man. (4)
Or, it is known from tradition: "If one who is another chooses the ancestral lineage (ārṣeya) of another, that seer (ṛṣi) takes away whatever he has sacrificed or enjoyed. ||5||
"One chooses one, one chooses two, one chooses three; one does not choose four, nor does one choose more than five"—so it is known.

We shall explain the Bhṛgus first. The Vatsas are descendants of Jamadagni; their *pañcārṣeya* (five-lineage) formula is: Bhārgava, Cyāvana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, Jāmadagnya—meaning "like Jamadagni, like Urva, like Āpnavāna, like Cyavana, like Bhṛgu. Some, however, use a three-lineage formula: Bhārgava, Aurva, Jāmadagnya—meaning "like Jamadagni, like Urva, like Bhṛgu. This very same [three-lineage] formula applies without modification for the Jāmāli, Aitiśāyani, Virohita, Māṇḍavya, Āvaṭa, Maṇḍu, Baida, Retavāha, and Prācīnayogya lineages. Now, for the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas, there is a five-lineage formula.

"Bhārgava, Cyāvāna, Āpnavāna, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and Anūpa"—that is, like Anūpa, like Ṛṣiṣeṇa, like Āpnavāna, like Cyavana, and like Bhṛgu. Some, however, prescribe a tri-lineage: "Bhārgava, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and Anūpa"—that is, like Anūpa, like Ṛṣiṣeṇa, and like Bhṛgu. Now, as for the Vītahavyas—Yāska, Vādhūla, Mauna, Maukara, and Jātūvāha—their tri-lineage is "Bhārgava, Vaitahavya, and Sāvedasa"—that is, like Sāvedasa, like Vītahavya, and like Bhṛgu.

Now, the Pārthas of Vainya have a three-lineage (*tryārṣeya*): Bhārgava-Vainya-Pārtha; [they invoke] "like Pṛthu, like Vena, like Bhṛgu. Now, the Śunakas of Gṛtsamada have a one-lineage (*ekārṣeya*): Gārtsamada as the Hotṛ, and "like Gṛtsamada" as the Adhvaryu. Now, the Mitrayus of Vadhryaśva have a one-lineage: Vādhryaśva as the Hotṛ, and "like Vadhryaśva" as the Adhvaryu. || 10 || 7 ||
Thus, these Bhṛgus have been explained. || 8 ||

Now, therefore, [concerning] the Aṅgirases: the Ayāsyas and the Gautamas; their *ṛṣi*-lineage consists of three ancestors: Āṅgirasa, Ayāsya, and Gautama. One invokes them as "like Gautama, like Ayāsya, like Aṅgiras. Then there are the Autathyas, the Gautamas; their *ṛṣi*-lineage consists of three ancestors: Āṅgirasa, Autathya, and Gautama. One invokes them as "like Gautama, like Autathya, like Aṅgiras. Then there are the Auśijas, the Gautamas; their *ṛṣi*-lineage consists of three ancestors: Āṅgirasa, Auśija, and Kākṣīvata. One invokes them as "like Kakṣīvān, like Auśija, like Aṅgiras. Then there are the Vāmadevas, the Gautamas; their *ṛṣi*-lineage consists of three ancestors: Āṅgirasa, Vāmadeva, and Bārhaduktha. One invokes them as "like Bṛhaduktha, like Vāmadeva, like Aṅgiras. || 9 ||

Now, for the Bharadvājas, there is a three-ṛṣi lineage: Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, and Bhāradvāja—meaning "like Aṅgiras, like Bṛhaspati, and like Bharadvāja. This same [lineage] remains unchanged for Tuthya and Agniveśya, for the Jayas, and for all those whose names contain the words *stambha* or *stamba*. Now, for the Ṛkṣas, there is a five-ṛṣi lineage: Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, Bhāradvāja, Vāndana, and Mātavacasa—meaning "like Mātavacas, like Vandana, like Bharadvāja, like Bṛhaspati, and like Aṅgiras."

Some prescribe three *ṛṣis*: *Āṅgirasa*, *Vāndana*, and *Mātavacasa*—that is, like Mātavacas, like Vandanu, and like Aṅgiras. Now, regarding families of *dvaimuṣyāyaṇas* (those belonging to two lineages), such as the Śauṅga-Śaiśirayas, who are Bharadvājas: the Śuṅgas are Katis and the Śaiśirayas are Katis; for them, there is a fivefold *ṛṣi-lineage*: *Āṅgirasa*, *Bārhaspatya*, *Bhāradvāja*, *Kātya*, and *Ākṣila*—that is, like Akṣila, like Kati, like Bharadvāja, like Bṛhaspati, and like Aṅgiras.
Some, however, prescribe three *ṛṣis*: *Āṅgirasa*, *Kātya*, and *Ākṣila*—that is, like Akṣila, like Kati, and like Aṅgiras. || 11 ||

Now, for the Gargas, the three *ṛṣis* are Āṅgirasa, Gārgya, and Śainya; [the invocation is] "As Śini, as Garga, as Aṅgiras. Some, however, place Bhāradvāja in the place of Aṅgiras: Bhāradvāja, Gārgya, and Śainya; [the invocation is] "As Śini, as Garga, as Bharadvāja. Now, for the Kapis, the three *ṛṣis* are Āṅgirasa, Māhayya, and Aurukṣayya; [the invocation is] "As Urukṣayya, as Mahayyu, as Aṅgiras. Tarasvan, Tila, Vidu, Śālu, Patañjali, Bhūyasī, Daṃdvaki, and Jalandva—these are the eight kinds of offspring of Kapi. 21.3.10.

Now, for the Ātris, there is a threefold lineage: Ātreya, Arcanānasa, and Śyāvāśva; [the invocation is] "like Śyāvāśva, like Arcanānasa, like Atri. Now, for the Gaviṣṭhiras, there is a threefold lineage: Ātreya, Arcanānasa, and Gaviṣṭhira; [the invocation is] "like Gaviṣṭhira, like Arcanānasa, like Atri. This same [lineage] remains unchanged for the Vāmarathya, Sumaṅgala, and Bījavāpa [clans]. 12.11.

Now, among the Viśvāmitras, there are the Devarātas, Cikitakas, Ālabavas, Amanantus, Babhrus, Yajñavalkas, Kaulontyas, Maris, Bṛhadagnis, Sāṃśityas, Vārakis, Tārakāyaṇas, and Śālāvatas. Their *tryārṣeya* lineage is Vaiśvāmitra-Devarāta-Udala; [the invocation is] "like Udala, like Devarāta, like Viśvāmitra. Now, there are the Śraumata-Kāmakāyanas. Their *tryārṣeya* lineage is Vaiśvāmitra-Mādhucchandasa-Dhānañjaya; [the invocation is] "like Dhanañjaya, like Madhucchandas, like Viśvāmitra."

Now, the Aṣṭakas are red; their lineage has two ṛṣis: Vaiśvāmitra-Aṣṭaka—meaning "like Aṣṭaka and like Viśvāmitra. Next, the Pūraṇas are those who cause [the sacrificial post] to be clothed; their lineage has two ṛṣis: Vaiśvāmitra-Pauraṇa—meaning "like Pūraṇa and like Viśvāmitra. Next, the Katas have three ṛṣis: Vaiśvāmitra-Kātya-Akṣila—meaning "like Akṣila, like Kata, and like Viśvāmitra. Next, the Kuśikas are the Aghamarṣaṇas; their lineage has three ṛṣis:
Vaiśvāmitra-Aghamarṣaṇa-Kauśika—meaning "like Kuśika, like Aghamarṣaṇa, and like Viśvāmitra. || 12 ||

Now, for the Kaśyapas, the three *ṛṣis* are Kāśyapa, Avatsāra, and Naidhruva; that is, "as Naidhruva, as Avatsāra, as Kaśyapa"—this very [formula], unmodified, applies to the Dhaumyas, Abhiṣeṇyas, and Māṭharas. Now, for the Rebhas, the three *ṛṣis* are Kāśyapa, Avatsāra, and Raibhya; that is, "as Raibhya, as Avatsāra, as Kaśyapa. (13)

Now, for the Śāṇḍilas, there is a two-ṛṣi lineage: Devalāsita; that is, "as Asita" and "as Devala. Some, however, prescribe a three-ṛṣi lineage: Kāśyapa-devalāsita; that is, "as Kaśyapa," "as Devala," and "as Asita. But according to the correct rule, they are indeed two-ṛṣi lineages.

The Vāsiṣṭhas have a single *ṛṣi* ancestor; except for Upamanyus, Parāśaras, and Kuṇḍinas, the Hotṛ says "Vāsiṣṭha" and the Adhvaryu says "like Vasiṣṭha. Now, for the Upamanyus, there is a triad of ancestors: Vāsiṣṭha, Aindrāpramada, and Ābharadvasu; [the formulas are] "like Ābharadvasu," "like Indrapramada," and "like Vasiṣṭha. Then, for the Parāśaras, there is a triad of ancestors: Vāsiṣṭha, Śāktya, and Pārāśarya; [the formulas are] "like Parāśara," "like Śakti," and "like Vasiṣṭha."

Now, for the Kuṇḍinas, the three *ṛṣis* are Vasiṣṭha, Mitrāvaruṇa, and Kauṇḍinya; [the invocation is] "like Kuṇḍina, like Mitrāvaruṇa, like Vasiṣṭha. Now, for the Saṃkṛtis, Pūtimāṣas, and Taṇḍins, the three *ṛṣis* are Śakti, Sāṃkṛti, and Gaurivīta; [the invocation is] "like Gaurivīta, like Saṃkṛti, like Śakti. || 14 ||

Now, for those of the Agasti lineage, the Hotṛ says "Āgastya" as the single *ṛṣi*, and the Adhvaryu says "like Agastya. Some, however, prescribe three *ṛṣis*: Āgastya, Dārḍhacyuta, and Idhmavāha; [the Adhvaryu] saying "like Idhmavāha, like Dṛḍhacyuta, and like Agastya."

Now, for Kṣatriyas, there is a three-Ṛṣi lineage: Mānava, Aiḍa, Paurūravasa; that is, like Purūravas, like Iḍā, like Manu. Now, if they should choose the same ancestral lineages (*sārṣāḥ*), they have only one single *pravara*; but if they should choose separate lineages, then those who have no composers of mantras (*mantrakṛt*) among them must have their *pravara* through the family priest (*sapurohitapravara*). Those who do have composers of mantras among them have their *pravara* without the family priest (*apurohitapravara*). According to this rule, the Vaiśyas have a single-Ṛṣi lineage: "Vātsapra" for the Hotṛ, and "Vatsapravat" for the Adhvaryu.
Now, for one whose lineage is unknown, [the marriage is performed] by means of the lineage of the preeminent domestic priest or the lineage of the preeminent teacher. || 17 ||

Now, the Tāṇḍins prescribe a single ancestral seer for all social classes: "Mānava" as the Hotṛ and "Manuvad" as the Adhvaryu. For it is said in the Brāhmaṇa, "For offspring are descended from Manu"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. || 14 || 18 ||
Thus ends the third paṭala in the twenty-first praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Thus ends the twenty-first book in the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra. 21.
Now begins the first chapter of the twenty-second book.
Having concluded the New Moon or Full Moon sacrifice with animal offerings for specific desires, one should perform the sacrifice. These [offerings] have been explained in the Brāhmaṇa. 1.
Their ritual procedure is explained by that of the Nirūḍhapaśubandha sacrifice. ||2||

In all rites of sorcery, the sacrificial enclosure is made of *śara* grass, the fuel-sticks are of *vibhītaka* wood, and the officiating priests proceed wearing red turbans, red garments, and with their sacred threads suspended around the neck.
"One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal dedicated to Vāyu," as it is handed down in the traditional recension.

In their respective introductory places, he deposits six verses according to the deity: "pīvo'nnāṃ rayivṛdhaḥ sumedhāḥ" and so forth. These have been handed down according to their form and according to their deities. || 5 ||
"Malhā" means "maṇilā" (necklaces). || 6 ||
"One should immolate on uneven ground"—thus he settles upon an uneven sacrificial site, or he may immolate the animal on uneven ground. || 7 ||
"Paryāriṇī" means she becomes one who gives birth after a long interval. || 8 ||
"The sacrificial post is a wooden sword" means that the sacrificial post has the shape of a wooden sword, or it is the Agnīdhra's assistant.
They mount upon him who is a man, calling him "the son of Tvaṣṭṛ" or "the horse. || 22.1.10 ||
"At the junction of the waters and the plants," that is, either during the rainy season or at the onset of autumn; or alternatively, "at the junction of the waters and the plants. (11)

Regarding the statement "the sacrificial post has two forks": that which is above the rope is the forked part; or rather, both branches at the top should be eight-cornered, including the ring for the cord.
When the bull has grown old among the cows, one should whisper into the ear of a young bull [the verse]: "That which is our bright-colored, most potent... (RV 9.82.3).
Then he releases it among the cows with the verse, "This youth... (RV 10.169.1).
He touches the worn-out [garment]. || 1 ||
At the commencement, he recites the verse, "The mind [belongs] to Prajāpati, to Indra, or to Tvaṣṭṛ; by its greatness," as the subsequent formula. || 15 ||
With the third [verse] he offers the omentum; with the fourth, the sacrificial oblation; with the fifth, the offering to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. || 16 ||
Having offered an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni, he immolates a barren goat.
"One desiring prosperity should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Vāyu"—thus have the deities been declared.
While immolating a barren ewe, he performs the introductory rite for the offering to Vāyu with the verse, "O Vāyu, come hither and prepare yourself. || 19 ||
While the fire is being carried around [the victim], he offers the Apāvya oblations with the formula: "For intention thee! For desire thee! (TS 3.5.4.3).
He recites the mantra, "Thou art the fourth, the controller, the mistress," as she is being led toward the north. || 21 ||
"You are a non-born one, O source of wealth," [he says] as she is being struck down.
"Stretching the thread," with these words he offers the omentum;
"Weave it without flaw," with these words [he offers] the oblation.
With the words, "Thou art the oblation of the mind," they consume the remnants of the oblation. || 25 ||
It is known that this very [sacrifice] is the attainment of these three alone. || 26 ||
Of this very [earth], there is indeed one non-sacrificial ground: when, after she has been seized, it becomes cloudless. || 27 ||
If he cannot obtain it, he should either cast it into water or consume it all. || 28 ||
The Jayas, Abhyātānas, and Rāṣṭrabhṛts have been explained in the Brāhmaṇa. || 29 ||
He offers the Jaya oblations with the formulas: "Citta and Svāhā! Citti and Svāhā! or alternatively, "To Citta, Svāhā! To Citti, Svāhā! (22.1.30).

"Agni is the lord of beings; may he protect me"—with these words he attaches the *abhyātāna* formulas to this [formula]: "In this *brahman*, in this *kṣatra*. Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he offers oblations or worships with the words, "The fathers, the grandfathers. He offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* (kingdom-sustaining) oblations with the formula, "Vartaṣāṭ, ṛtadhām. Having recited each successive verse, he offers the first oblation with "To him, svāhā! and the second with "To them, svāhā! || 2 || 31 ||
Thus ends the first chapter of the twenty-second book in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
Now begins the second chapter of the twenty-second book.
Having concluded either the new-moon or the full-moon sacrifice with the optional offerings (*kāmyeṣṭi*), one should perform the sacrifice. These have been explained in the Brāhmaṇa. 1.

Those performed on the same day have the *upāṃśu* as their ritual procedure and, like the archetype, have a single sacrificial fee; however, those involving the *sāṃnāyya* offering have a two-day interval.
Between the *samidhyamānavatī* and the *samiddhavatī*, there are two *dhāyyā* verses containing the word *pṛthupāja*.

The two *ājyabhāga* offerings are performed without modification; they should be designated by the desire for which the sacrifice is performed, because they serve that purpose, and thus they should have those same deities. Alternatively, they may follow the original model (*prakṛti*), for when there is no specific instruction, the original model is to be understood. The two *saṃyājya* verses are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter: "tvāṃ citraśravastama" and [the second]. ||4||
The *puronuvākyā* has its characteristic mark at the beginning, and the *yājyā* has its characteristic mark at the end; or rather, it may be the reverse of this.

"One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni. For these [offerings], there are four *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses beginning with "Both of you, Indra and Agni"; two belong to the first three [verses] and two to the latter ones. In this manner, when there is an excess of ritual acts beyond this point, they should be divided equally, assigning the former to the former and the latter to the latter. When there is an excess of mantras, the remaining ones are either for the purpose of providing options (*vikalpa*) or serve as supplementary offerings (*upahoma*). 6.

One should offer a *caru* oblation to Pūṣan with the verse "O you, the lord of paths" (*vayamu tvā pathaspate*) as the first *puronuvākyā* and the subsequent one as the *yājyā*; from this point onward, the former is the *pūrvā* and the latter is the *pratiṣṭhā*.
One should offer a sacrificial pap (caru) dedicated to Kṣetrapati; [the mantra for] the offering to Kṣetrapati is: "O Lord of the field... (kṣetrasya patiḥ). || 8 ||

"One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt. When there is a delay in the commencement of what has been undertaken, the invitatory and offering verses for the Vaiśvānara [offering] are "O Agni, lead us to the gods" and "That which is most carrying. The two verses for the concluding oblation are "yad vāhiṣṭham. An ox is the sacrificial fee. One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati; the invitatory and offering verses are "Thou, O Agni, art the guardian of vows" and [the second verse]. || 9 ||

One for whom the *rakṣases* (demons) pursue [him] should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Rakṣohan. On the night of the new moon, having enclosed [the sacrificial ground], he should perform the offering. He recites fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses beginning with "Make thy strength a snare" (*kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ prasitim*), and concludes with the regular verse. The invitatory and offering verses are "With this fuel, O Agni, we would worship thee" (*ayā te agne samidhā vidhema*) and the two subsequent *saṃyājyās*. 22.2.10.

"One performing sorcery should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni accompanied by Rudra. The sacrificial grass consists of *śara* reeds, the fuel-stick is made of *bailvatika* wood, and the officiating priests proceed wearing red turbans, red garments, and with their sacred cords suspended around the neck. This applies to all rites involving sorcery. "Thou, O Agni, art Rudra"—these are the invitatory and offering verses.

"One whose cattle or men have died, or who fears that they might die, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Surabhimat. For Agni Surabhimat, the sacrificer himself should perform the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, [reciting]: "Agni is the Hotṛ; he has made the feast for the gods excellent. || 12 ||
"To Agni Kṣāmavat" and so forth are three verses addressed to Kṣāmavat; for these, "Agni has roared" are the invitatory and offering verses.
"O Agni, for desire"—these eight [verses] have their invitatory and offering formulas (*yājyā-anuvākyā*) in successive order, beginning with "To you" and "O best of Angirases. 14.

"O you who possess food, O eater of food, O lord of food"—these are the invitatory and offering verses for these [deities]: "For the bull, for the food; for the cow, for the food; for the eloquent one. || 15 ||
For Agni Pavamāna, the invitatory and offering verses are "O Agni, three times" for the oblation and "O Agni, you purify our lives. || 16 ||
"O Agni, rich in sons," "The oblation which you [accept]," and "With a yearning heart"—these are the invitatory and offering verses for the two oblations. || 17 ||
For the oblation of cooked rice in goat’s milk for Agni Rasavat, the invitatory and offering verses are "O Agni, with thy essence... and so forth. || 18 ||

"The cake for Vaiśvānara on twelve potsherds"—this is the threefold oblation for one who is being accused because of an act that causes loss of caste. There are twelve offerings to Vaiśvānara; for these, there are eight *yājyā* and *anu-vākyā* verses, two for each of the three [oblations], beginning with "vaiśvānaro na ūtyā. For the offering to Varuṇa, [there are two verses] beginning with "ava te heḷo varuṇa. For the offering to Dadhikrāvan, [there is the verse] beginning with "dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam. || 19 ||
In the Udvāsaneṣṭi sacrifice, "agnirmūrdhā" and "bhuvaḥ" are the invitatory and offering verses for the oblation to Agni.
One who desires a village should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara and a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts.
He places the oblation for Vaiśvānara on the Āhavanīya fire; he places the oblation for the Maruts on the Gārhapatya fire.

Having adorned [the oblation], he offers it to Vaiśvānara; while the *sāmidhenī* verses are being recited, the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyānuvākye*) are addressed to the Maruts: "O Maruts, whatever... (RV 8.96.1) and so forth.
For one about to go forth to battle, the *caru* offering is for Āditya; the invitatory and offering verses are "May Aditi protect us" and "The great mother indeed. (24)
"One who has gone to a place where people are about to engage in battle should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. (25)

One desiring to win cattle should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara; he should drive away the best cow with a rope that has not been used before and send it to his rival, or he should fasten it to his enemy's property, or place it in the latter's cow-pen. 4.26.
Thus ends the second chapter in the twenty-second book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
Now begins the third chapter in the twenty-second book.

Regarding the section beginning with "One desiring cattle should offer a *caru* to Indra," the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for those sacrifices are the section beginning with "Indraṃ vo viśvataspari. (1)
With the verse "To Indra, those that are straight," he offers day after day [the oblations representing] the months. || 2 ||

One whose army is as if unsharpened—that is, not firm—should offer a *caru* oblation to Indrāṇī. Having bound *balbaja* grass together with the fuel-wood, he should place it upon the fire along with that fuel-wood; the final *dhāyyā* verse is "Revatī" as the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*) and the "Śakvarī" as the offering verse (*yājyā*), beginning with "proṣvasmai puroratham."
