One who practices sorcery should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu; the portion for Sarasvatī is clarified butter, and the oblation for Bṛhaspati is a pap of cooked rice—thus there are three oblations. For each of these two [deities], he should employ two invitatory verses (*puronuvākyā*). The verses for the offering to Agni and Viṣṇu should be "O Agni and Viṣṇu, being of one mind" and "O Agni and Viṣṇu. For the offering to Sarasvatī, they are "Forward for us," "O Goddess," and "From heaven for us," and "The daughter of Pāvīru. For the offering to Bṛhaspati, it is "O Bṛhaspati, be pleased with us. || 4 ||

One who is being subjected to malevolent magic should sacrifice with this very [offering]. This sacrifice does not come to one who is not connected to Agni and Viṣṇu; therefore, there is a sacrificial pap (caru) in ghee for Agni and Viṣṇu for one desiring sight. "O Agni and Viṣṇu! O Agni and Viṣṇu!"—these indeed are the invitatory and offering verses (yājyā-anuvākyā).
One should offer a cake on one potsherd to Mitra and Varuṇa with the verse "ā no mitrāvaruṇā"; this is for the offering to Mitra and Varuṇa.

On the full moon of the month of Tiṣya, they cause one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) to sacrifice with the *Somāraudra* [offering] within an enclosed space. There is clarified butter (*ājya*) produced from the milk of a white cow that has a white calf, which has been churned. The sprinkling is done with clarified butter, and they perform the purification (*mārjana*) with clarified butter silently. These two acts are the sprinkling and the purification. One should employ two verses of Manu as the *dhāyyā* verses: two from among these beginning with "makṣū devavataḥ. For the *Somāraudra* sacrifice, there are five [verses]; for all of them, the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākyā*) are those addressed to Soma and Rudra. 7.

If one who suffers from skin disease should fear, "I shall become afflicted with a bad skin condition," he should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Pūṣan; the invitatory and offering verses are: "O gods Soma and Pūṣan, these two... (and so forth). || 8 ||

The offering to Soma and Rudra is for one who has been long ill. The Hotṛ priest gives a bull as the sacrificial fee. He who desires, "May I produce a rival for him in his own abode," should offer a caru-oblation to Soma and Rudra; he should perform the sacrifice on the field of his rival. Having enclosed the altar and having dug up the southern half, he should strew that very half with half of the sacrificial grass (barhis) and place half of the fuel-wood (idhma) upon it.
One who desires a village should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts.
He places the oblation for Indra over the Āhavanīya fire; [he places] that for the Maruts over the Gārhapatya fire.
Having adorned it, he places the oblation for Indra; while the *sāmidhenī* verses are being recited, he places the oblation for the Maruts.
"Indra for you from every side," "Indra, O heroes, Maruts, when you have called"—these are the invitatory and offering verses. ||13||

One who desires, "May I cause strife between the Kṣatra and the Viś," should offer this very sacrifice. While cutting a portion for Indra, he should say, "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra"; the invitatory verse (puronuvākyā) is addressed to Indra. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he should say, "Recite the offering verse for the Maruts"; the offering verse (yājyā) is addressed to the Maruts. While cutting a portion for the Maruts, he should say, "Recite the invitatory verse for the Maruts"; the invitatory verse is addressed to the Maruts. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he should say, "Recite the offering verse for Indra"; the offering verse is addressed to Indra. || 14 ||

Having prescribed this very [procedure], if one should desire that they might be fit for ritual application, one should cut off the portions according to the respective deities and sacrifice according to the respective deities. || 15 ||
"One desiring a village should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and a cake on twelve potsherds to the Viśve Devas. || 16 ||

Having taken the first portion of the offering for Indra, he should take the [first] portion of that for the Viśvedevas; subsequently, he takes the second portion of that for Indra. He issues the call: "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra and the Viśvedevas; sacrifice to Indra and the Viśvedevas. The invitatory and offering verses are "Indra in battles" and so forth. (17)
The gift is a dwelling preceded by the appointment of a teacher. || 18 ||

"In *saṃjñānyā* [the rite for reuniting], join together with double portions, reciting: 'The counsel is common, common is your recognition; may there be recognition for us, recognition for me'—these are five oblations. For the *aṣṭīkā* [rites], there are two additional offerings: 'Here you shake the sky, they make the mountains tremble. At the *ṭīkājī*, one should offer a double portion. At the time of departure, according to some, it ends with the *citrānta*; [for the *māruta*], it is: 'I invoke your dear names, O swift ones. (19)

Having combined the portions together, he should proceed with the offerings to Agni accompanied by the Vasus, Soma accompanied by the Rudras, Indra accompanied by the Maruts, and Varuṇa accompanied by the Ādityas. He issues the direction: "Recite for Agni accompanied by the Vasus, Soma accompanied by the Rudras, Indra accompanied by the Maruts, and Varuṇa accompanied by the Ādityas; recite the offering prayer for Agni accompanied by the Vasus, Soma accompanied by the Rudras, Indra accompanied by the Maruts, and Varuṇa accompanied by the Ādityas. The invitatory and offering verses are "Agni is first with the Vasus" and so forth. Or, one may perform the offerings separately; however, the invitatory and offering verses are the same, and the two subsequent *saṃyājyā* verses are the same. ||6||22.3.20||
"An oblation of cooked rice for the Ādityas who are present in the world," and "The sacrifice of the gods returns"—these are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. || 21 ||

Whether he has been confined or is being confined, he offers an oblation to Abhyathāravatī and remains [there] until they no longer confine him; "O Ādityas, you will surely sustain him," are the invitatory and offering verses. || 22 ||
While being excluded, he should say: "O Aditi, grant your permission! || 23 ||
Taking [the property] from the foot of the oppressor, he departs. || 24 ||
Whichever assembly he should enter, whatever the prevailing rumor there may be, [he should investigate it]. || 25 ||
One should fetch rice grains from his house, both white and black; one should separate them, and whatever grains are white, with those one should offer a *caru* oblation to Āditya.

Those which are black, having bound them upon a black antelope skin and set them down in their proper places, he approaches the sacrificer with the verse: "Come hither, O bounteous Maruts, together with this lord of the people, toward that king; may the blessing be true. He scatters a portion of the earth upon the northern garment of the sacrificer with the words "here is my mind," and the remainder upon his chest. "These indeed are the Kṣatriyas" are the invitatory and offering verses.

If he should not find out [the name of the person], he says, "I offer this portion to the Ādityas, so that such-and-such a person from such-and-such a clan may find me"; he thus pronounces the name of the obstructer, and it belongs to that very clan.

If he does not perceive [the rays], he should strike seven shoots from the *aśvattha* tree with the middle *iṣā* (pole), saying, "I bind these Ādityas," three toward the east and four toward the north.
If he should not understand this, he should offer a caru-oblation to this very Āditya; even while the fuel is being bound, he should tie on the rays, for he has not understood.

He offers a *caru* oblation of black rice to Varuṇa. Or, if the sun has not yet risen, having offered [the oblation] to Āditya, he should offer the one to Varuṇa; the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākye*) are "This to me, O Varuṇa" (*imaṃ me varuṇa*) and "That I implore of thee" (*tattvā yāmi*). The two concluding verses (*saṃyājye*) are "Thou, O Agni, for us" (*tvaṃ no agne*). Thus ends the third chapter in the twenty-second book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
Now begins the fourth chapter in the twenty-second book.
One who desires long life should offer an oblation to Prajāpati consisting of one hundred kṛṣṇalas. ||1||

One hundred *kṛṣṇala* grains of gold are equal in weight to either a *kākiṇī* or a *māṣa*. Having performed the preparation of the medicinal herbs (*auṣadhakalpa*) prior to the threshing, he pours the clarified butter (*ājya*) over them while they are covered by a strainer (*pavitra*). The cooking is merely for the sake of softening (*dharma-mātra*). At the time of the ritual performance, he cuts eight portions for the deity, four for the *sviṣṭakṛt*, two for the *prāśitra*, and eight for the *iḍā*. At the time of the fourfold division, having collected all the portions into the *prāśitra*, he offers them to the Brahman priest in a single lump. The Brahman consumes them; he causes the others to bring their portions for consumption. 2.

One should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya; having enclosed it on the bottom and top with two gold plates (*rukmā*), one sets it down. At each *prayāja* offering, he sacrifices a *kṛṣṇala* weight of gold. Having removed the two gold plates, he proceeds with the *caru*. "Ud u tyam" and "Citram" are the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākye*). These very two gold plates constitute the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). ||3||
"One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni"—this is the threefold oblation; "He, as of old" (*sa pratnavat*) are the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyānuvākyā*).

One whose Soma has been vomited up or who has passed it through should offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) of *śyāmāka* grain to Soma-Indra; the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākye*) are "With the stomach" and "Drunk. (5)

"O Agni, for the giver"—thus three times [is the offering]. Among these, the third is the *prājāpatya* mixed offering (*saṃsṛṣṭahavis*). [The mixture consists of] curds, honey, clarified butter, water, and parched grains; [specifically] curds, honey, clarified butter, water, and rice-grains. Among these, the modification of clarified butter (*ājyavikāra*) takes precedence when honey and water are mixed, because of the greater similarity to its own nature (*svādharmyabhūyastvāt*). "O Agni, give wealth to the donor"—this is for the offering to Agni. "Do not neglect us; come quickly to the gift"—this is for the offering to Indra. "Like purified clarified butter, both [worlds]"—this is for the offering to Prajāpati. || 6 ||

Regarding one who has fallen away from the sacrifice, three [offerings] beginning with that for Agni are introduced: "The one fallen from the sacrifice, being unable [to perform the rites], should join together the offering for Agni and the offering for Soma in the offering for Indra"—this means he places the oblations together in close contact. Or, he should join the two residues (lepau) in this [offering]. "Like an enemy" are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. || 7 ||
There are two offerings to Agni and Soma. The invitatory and offering verses are: "Agni and Soma, together with the sacrificial food... and so forth; these constitute separate ritual procedures.
For Soma Vājina [he offers] of Śyāmāka [grain] with the verses: "Svāhā! Be filled! and "May it swell for thee. || 9 ||
"Of Brāhmaṇaspati, we invoke thee as the Lord of hosts (gaṇapati) of hosts," [he says]. 22.4.10.
He who might desire regarding her, "O Brahman, may I destroy the clan," [should perform this]. ||8||
Everything belongs to Brāhmaṇaspati; the invitatory and offering verses are "maruto yad dha vaḥ" and so forth. || 11 ||
One who desires heaven should offer a caru-oblation to Aryaman with the verse: "Aryaman comes hither, those [paths] which are yours. (12)
For a kṣatriya who is inferior in rank, one should offer this cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Indra-Anuṣūka, with the verse: "From the root of the Anuṣūka rice for Indra, [I take] the top. (13)

(If there should be a Brāhmaṇa who is younger than his younger brother, for him one should offer this *ānuṣūka* oblation to Bṛhaspati. The verse for the offering to Bṛhaspati is: "pra yo jajñe" (He who was born...). 14.

For one seized by the evil *yakṣman*, there is an oblation of rice for Āditya on the new moon day; the horse is the muttered prayer (*japa*), and "O Ādityas" is the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*) and the offering verse (*yājyā*).

He should offer the *tridhātu* cake to Indra Rājā; he places it upon eleven potsherds arranged side-by-side. Having performed everything up to the final heating, he places the second, larger portion over it. Once they are cooked, he decorates them and sets them down. At the time of the ritual performance, he sacrifices to the first deity from the center, to the second from the southern half, and to the third from the northern half. He cuts portions from all of them while ensuring they are brought together, so as not to cause a failure in the ritual; indeed, he should utter the *vaṣaṭ* call at such a point that he does not reach [the end of the sequence].

"In the eastern quarter you are Indra, O King"—with these three verses he recites them in alternation. Having recited the first, he should sacrifice with the middle one; having recited the middle one, he should sacrifice with the last one; having recited the last one, he should sacrifice with the first one. In this way, all [the verses] become invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) and all [the verses] become offering verses (*yājyā*). || 16 ||

"One should offer the *sarvapṛṣṭhā* sacrifice for Indra Rāthaṃtara"; thus it is known that he places [the oblation] upon twelve potsherds arranged lengthwise. At the time of the ritual performance, he sacrifices to the first deity from the eastern half. In this manner, he cuts portions from all sides, proceeding clockwise; so it is understood.

He recites the six verses beginning with *abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ* in alternating order; for it is known: "One should not utter the *vaṣaṭ* call on a *bṛhatī* verse. If one were to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call on a *bṛhatī*, he would cause the meters to reach their end. He performs the sacrifice by adding four syllables from the invitatory verse (*anu-vākyā*) to the offering verse (*yājyā*), thereby bringing both the *anuṣṭubh* and the *paṅkti* together; this is what we consider. When it is said, "Recite for Indra associated with the *rathaṃtara*," he recites: *abhi tvā śūra nonumo 'dugdhā iva dhenavaḥ*.

Having recited "Īśānam asya jagataḥ suvardṛśam, īśānam indra tasthuṣas tvām iddhi havāmahe," he performs the *yajya* with "Tvāmid dhi havāmahe sātā vājasya kāravaḥ | tvāṃ vṛtreṣv indra satpatiṃ naraḥ, tvāṃ kāṣṭhā abhi svardvato 'bhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ. When told, "Recite for Indra Bārhatā," having recited "Yad dyāva indra te śatam," he performs the *yajya* with "Pibā somam. When told, "Recite for Indra Vairūpa," having recited "Yad dyāva indra te śatam," he performs the *yajya* with "Pibā somam."

When it is said, "Recite for Indra Vairāja," having recited [the invitatory verse] *piba somam*, he offers with *yady āvaḥ*. When it is said, "Recite for Indra Śākvara," having recited *revatīr naḥ*, he offers with *pro ṣvasmai puroratham*. When it is said, "Recite for Indra Raivata," having recited *pro ṣvasmai puroratham*, he offers with *revatīr naḥ*. A stallion, a bull, and a ram—this is the sacrificial fee. || 17 ||
One who is being falsely accused should sacrifice with this very [offering] for the sake of virility. || 18 ||

For one desiring eyesight, the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākyā*) are the three beginning with *ud agne śucayas tava*, *vi jyotiṣā*, and *ud u tyam citram*. At the time of the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*), having made three lumps (*piṇḍa*) from the solar portion (*saurya*) using the two verses addressed to Agni, he gives the lumps to the sacrificer, one by one with the respective mantras: *ud u tyam jātavedasam*, *sapta tvā harito rathe*, and *citram devānām*. The sacrificer eats them. 19.

"One desiring a village should offer the *sāṃgrahaṇī* sacrifice dedicated to the Viśvedevas. [The procedure is as follows: "He offers a *caru* cooked in the milk of a spotted cow that has a spotted calf; some say it is cooked in ghee. He lays down the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the formula: "Thou art firm; may I be firm among my kinsmen. The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are: "O Viśvedevas... O Viśvedevas... He offers three oblations on the *āmana* with the formula: "O gods, favor me, favor me... Regarding rites not previously established and for which no specific time is prescribed, Ātreya holds that they should follow immediately after the principal rite; Bādarāyaṇa holds that they should be placed at the end. 10 || 22.4.20 || 4 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the twenty-second book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
Now begins the fifth chapter in the twenty-second book.

For one who has been long ill, or for one who desires, "May I attain a full lifespan," he should offer this sacrifice (*iṣṭi*). At the time of arranging the vessels, he sets out five [offerings] beginning with that for Agni, and a four-cornered vessel made of *khadira* wood. He also sets out a golden *pravṛtta* coin, fashioned from a *śatamāna* weight. Furthermore, it is known from tradition: "It should be of such a measure as he thinks he will live. (1)

"Whatever was fresh became butter"—having thus looked at the clarified butter (*ājya*), at the time of taking the butter, he first silently takes four portions in a *khādira* ladle, and then he takes [portions] in the other [ladles]. At the time of setting them down, he sets it down to the north of the *dhruvā*. Into that, he places the *pravṛtta* [portion]. The invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākyā*) are: "May life be yours," "O Agni, giver of life," "Swell up," "May your [oblation] unite," "Avert your wrath," "Up the highest [knot]," "Forward for us," "From the divine heaven," "O Agni and Viṣṇu," and "O Agni and Viṣṇu. ||2||
He offers four additional oblations with the formula, "Thou art the breath of the Aśvins. (3)
Having carried the ghee in a ladle made of khadira wood around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places it to the south of the Āhavanīya within the altar.
Then the sacrificer gazes at it, [reciting]: "The stream of ghee, the path of immortality. ||5||

Then the Brahman priest takes his right hand; the other officiating priests, having taken hold of the hand of the Brahman, lead the sacrificer around him, saying, "With the purifying hymn, we surround thee."

Then the sacrificer drinks the clarified butter from the gold vessel with the mantra, "O Agni, grant this [butter] for life and luster," and he addresses the one who is drinking it with the same mantra.
Having lifted it up, rinsed it, and placed it on the right ear, the sacrificer binds it on from left to right with the formula: "Thou art life; thou art all-encompassing life. (8)
Then the Adhvaryu takes hold of his right hand, including the thumb, with six verses beginning, "Agni is long-lived. (9)
From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the rite is completed when it is finished. 22.5.10.

For the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who accept a horse, there is a sacrifice to Varuṇa. For as many horses as he may accept, so many four-potherd offerings to Varuṇa should he prepare, with one additional; "This to me, O Varuṇa" (*imaṃ me varuṇa*) and "That of thee I implore" (*tattvā yāmi*) are the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyānuvākye*). || 11 ||
If there should be another recipient, one should offer a cake on one potsherd to Sūrya; "udu tyam" and "citram" are the invitatory and offering verses.

He goes down to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with the Sāman omitted, ending with the after-offerings (anūyāja); "imaṃ me varuṇa" and "tattvā yāmi" are the invitatory and offering verses (yājyā-anuvākyā).
Having returned, he should offer a *caru* oblation dedicated to Apāṃnapāt; the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākye*) are "Apāṃnapāt, coming together with others... and so forth.
One who is seized by evil should offer a cake on one potsherd to Indra and Varuṇa.
Having placed the *payasyā* dedicated to Indra and Varuṇa within the *payasyā*, he covers it and sets it down. ||16||

Then he distributes the *payasyā* toward the various directions with the verses beginning, "O Indra and Varuṇa, that body of yours which is to be restrained," and he gathers it back together again with the same [verses], concluding the mantras with the words, "It has not been released."
"O Indra and Varuṇa, you two for the sacrifice... and "O Mitra and Varuṇa, stretch forth your arms toward us... are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. || 18 ||
The offerings with the verse "yo vām indrāvaruṇā" are for the *payasyā* (curd-mixture). 19.
For Agni with the offering "To Agni, the forward-moving," there are three oblations; the invitatory and offering verses are "This Agni has spread forth" and so on.

For Indra with the offering "To Indra, the deliverer from distress," there are three [oblations]; the invitatory and offering verses are "He has entered me who delivers from distress," "That which has entered me," "O Indra, our dominion," "O Indra, the powers," "O Śatakratu," and "It shall be granted to thee. 21.5.20–21.

One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Saṃvarga. When it has been cooked and placed in position, he should touch it with this *yajus*: "Thou art vigor; thou art power. He recites fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses beginning with "Yukṣvā hi devahūtamān," and concludes with the regular verse. "Kuvitsu naḥ" are the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyānuvākye*). The two subsequent verses are the *saṃyājye*.
For one desiring offspring, there is a *gārmuta* caru-oblation dedicated to Prajāpati; "Prajāpati, he knows the son"—these are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. || 23 ||
"O Soma and Pūṣan," [is the verse] for the offering to Soma and Pūṣan. || 24 ||

One desiring cattle should offer [oblations] on the full moon day of Citrā, beginning with those dedicated to Agni; "By means of Agni one attains wealth" are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. "O Agni, come to us with cattle" are the secondary offerings (*upahoma*).
Having settled in a place where the lunar mansions are auspicious. || 12 || 26 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the twenty-second book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
Now begins the sixth chapter in the twenty-second book:
"One desiring rain should sacrifice with the Kārīrī [offering]. (1)

Having added fuel to the fires, the sacrificer, to the south of the Āhavanīya fire, puts on a black garment with a black fringe, saying: "Thou art of the Maruts, the vigor of the Maruts. Then he touches water.

With the mantra, "O Maruts, delight the cunning falcon," he turns against the wind from behind; thus he generates the east wind with the words, "Come, O Wind! A black horse stands in front, facing westward. ||3||
He rubs him with this garment and makes him cry out; if he should cry out, shake himself, or void excrement or urine, one should know: "It will rain."

Having offered oblations with the eight names of the wind beginning with "The east wind rains," he spreads a black antelope skin within the altar, with its neck pointing eastward and the hair side up.

In that [vessel], he places dates and flour and elephant-milk and flour; having mixed them with black honey while reciting "The gentle ones, the longing ones," and having formed three lumps, he wraps them in lotus leaves and binds them with a black horse-hair cord, saying, "Thou art the tethering-rope of the stallion."

On the heap of grass, there is a three-cow cart with its shaft pointing eastward and its three roofs not yet fixed; upon its uppermost roof, he fastens a black antelope skin with the verse, "O gods who possess wealth... (RV 10.65.2).
It remains attached for a day and night. || 8 ||
If it should rain, one should offer only the piṇḍī offerings. || 9 ||

If it does not rain, he ties [the offering] to the middle post with the verse, “O gods, grant us protection. It remains tied for a day and night. If it should rain, he should offer the *piṇḍīs* themselves. If it does not rain, he ties [the offering] to the rear post with the verse, “O gods, together with your drink. It remains tied for a day and night. If it should rain, he should offer the *piṇḍīs* themselves. If it does not rain, on the following day, he offers three oblations of black rice beginning with the *dhāmacchat* verses. 22.6.10.
Having placed those [implements], he places a black antelope skin to the north.
*tvaṃ tyā cid acyuta* and *iti* are the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyānuvākyā*). || 12 ||
He offers the rice-balls with these verses beginning, "They make the day dark. 13.
Then he recites over them as the smoke rises: "The dark-colored ones, the tawny ones... (RV 7.104.1).
On the heap of rubbish, he fills a black, unbaked cooking pot with water, [saying]: "Release the rain! (VS 2.15).
If it should break, one should know that it will rain.
On the prop of the cart or on the peg, a black ewe is tied with the mantra, "Thou art born from the waters"; upon her, he performs the ritual of making the horse recognize [the path].
Having established a clump of *varṣāhva* grass upon the rubbish-heap and having raised the earth, he offers the *varṣāhva* oblation with the verse, "The Earth. (18)
Having thrown it into the Āhavanīya fire, he consecrates the rising smoke with the mantra: "Golden-haired, from the spreading of the dust... (RV 8.7.3). || 19 ||
With the verse, "The gods who have their portion in heaven," he shakes the black antelope skin over the rubbish-heap.
The two *saṃyājyā* verses are "aurvabhṛguvat" and "śuci."
A black garment, a black horse, and a black cow are the sacrificial fee.

Now, for the Sarvakārī sacrifice, there is an offering to Agni on eight potsherds without any prefix; its secondary oblations (upahoma) are the names of the winds (*vātanāmāni*), with which he binds the black antelope skin, with which he offers the rice-balls (*piṇḍī*), and with which he consecrates the rising smoke. || 23 ||
As before, he places it over the three fires. || 24 ||
The middle [oblation] consists of barley; it is an offering to Indra and Viṣṇu. || 25 ||

The two *dhāyyā* verses are *uṣṇih* and *kakubh*: "O Agni, forward... and "O Agni, three are thy powers, three thy stations. He concludes with the *trivatī* verse: "Threefold is thy seat... The invitatory and offering verses are: "Together through your ritual act, both have you conquered," and the two subsequent *saṃyājyā* verses. 26.
Gold, a silken garment, and a cow constitute the sacrificial fee. || 27 ||

One who has a son born as a Kṣatriya should offer a *caru* oblation to Indra and Bṛhaspati; "This offering is for you both in this mouth" are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. Gold and a necklace are the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). || 14 || 28 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the twenty-second book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Thus ends the twenty-second book in the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the first chapter of the twenty-third book.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the Kaukilī [Iṣṭi]. || 1 ||
The ritual procedure for her is as previously described. || 2 ||
At the time of the offering, one should immolate an animal dedicated to Indra. || 3 ||
A bull is the sacrificial fee. ||4||
A pap of rice for Āditya; a calf [is the sacrificial fee]. ||5||

Previously, having purchased black iron, black salt, black sesame, and black hair-tuft (*tasara-pakṣman*), as well as rice, barley, and *śyāmāka* grain, they tie them in a linen cloth and prepare the rice-grains (*tokma*) from the rice; the barley-grains are slightly parched. Having mixed those with curd or whey (*udaśvit*) and having sprinkled them all around with *darbha* grass, he sets them down. That is *māsara*. The coarse flour of those same grains, sprinkled with the dregs (*saṃsrāva*), is *nanāhuḥ*.

Having made groats of *śyāmāka* grain, at the time of preparing the *surā*, he mixes the *surā* with young sprouts (*tokma*), *māsara*, and *nagnahu*; having scattered a third part of the groats around it, he sprinkles it with the milk of one cow while reciting, "Pour out the pressed juice on all sides" (*parīto ṣiñcatā sutam*). Having scattered [the groats] around it with a second third, he sprinkles it with the milk of two cows using that same verse. Having scattered [the groats] around it with a third third, he sprinkles it with the milk of three cows using that same verse. He remains with the mixture for three nights.
Some prescribe a *kārotara* vessel in place of the pit. 23.1.10.
It is bound with a split hide. || 11 ||
In that [vessel], he places a double-mouthed funnel. || 12 ||
Its opening is covered with a hide. || 13 ||
When it flows into that [fire], it becomes the *parisrut*. || 14 ||
At the time of arranging the vessels, he sets out three vessels for the Aśvins, for Sarasvatī, and for Indra Sutrāman.
He places three portions of barley-meal, wheat-meal, and parched grain-meal into either a hawk-feathered vessel or a wooden trough.
The strainer for the Adhvaryu priest is made of the wool of goats and sheep. || 17 ||
The [portion] of the oxen and horses belongs to the Pratiprasthātṛ. || 18 ||
Having poured out the clarified butter, the Adhvaryu pours out an abundance of milk into a wooden trough (droṇa).
"It should be done with a mantra," says Āśmarathya; "silently," says Ālekhana. 23.1.20.
Having purified the clarified butter with the tuft of hair, he purifies the milk with it.
"Eastward Soma has flowed too much," [is the formula] for one who has vomited Soma; "Westward Soma has flowed too much," [is the formula] for one whose Soma has been over-purified. || 22 ||
"Brahman and Kṣatra purify themselves," [with these words] the Pratiprasthātṛ [presents] the *surā*.
Having taken the portions of clarified butter for the animal sacrifices, the Adhvaryu draws the milk-libations.

"kuvidaṅga"—for all [the cups], there is one *puroruc*, one *puronuvākyā*, one *praiṣa*, and one *yājyā*. Having drawn [the cup] with the formula, "I draw thee, acceptable to the Aśvins," and having mixed it with barley-meal, he cleanses it with a filter and deposits it with, "This is thy womb; for splendor thee. Having drawn [the next cup] with, "Thou art taken with a support; I draw thee, acceptable to Sarasvatī," and having mixed it with wheat-meal, he cleanses it with a filter and deposits it with, "This is thy womb; for vigor thee."

Having set it down with the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Indra Sutraman," and having mixed it with the flour of parched grains (upavāka), wiped it around with a strainer, and set it down with the formula, "This is thy womb; for strength, thee," he worships it with the following verses according to their respective characteristics.

When the *surā* is being brought in, the Pratiprasthātṛ draws the *surā*-cups from the stream with the verse: "For a separate seat has been prepared for you two by the gods. For all [the cups], there is one introductory verse (*puroruca*), one invitatory formula (*puronuvākyā*), one direction (*praiṣa*), and one offering verse (*yājyā*). Having drawn [the cup] with the formula, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, the splendor of the Aśvins, acceptable to the Aśvins," and having wiped it around with a filter, he deposits it with the formula, "This is thy womb; for joy, thee!"

"Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, the vigor of Sarasvatī, acceptable to Sarasvatī"—having thus taken it and wiped it with a strainer, he deposits it with: "This is thy womb; for bliss, thee! "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, the strength of Indra, acceptable to Indra Sutrāman"—having thus taken it and wiped it with a strainer, he deposits it with: "This is thy womb; for greatness, thee! The curdling agents are like those used for *surā*.
The Adhvaryu and the sacrificer worship with the remainder of the *sanna* section and with the subsequent section. 2.27.
As before, he dedicates the animals. || 28 ||
Everything is the same up to the rite of carrying fire around [the sacrificial post], with the exception of the offering to Bṛhaspati.
During the middle round of the fire-circumambulation, he places a portion of the firebrand on the mound (khara) and adds fuel to it.
Having performed the carrying of fire around the remainder, he brings forth this very same [fire] for the purpose of cooking the animal victim. || 31 ||
When the omenta have been offered, he gives forty cows as the sacrificial fee, along with a mare with a foal.
Or they may take the cups here. || 33 ||
The instruction has been stated. || 34 ||
"All [the offerings] should be offered in the Āhavanīya fire," says Āśmarathya; "the Sura-cups [should be offered] in the Dakṣiṇa fire," says Ālekhana. || 35 ||
With the verse "surāvantam," he offers the cups of *payas* (milk); with the verse "yaste rasaḥ saṃbhṛtaḥ," he offers the cups of *surā* (liquor). || 36 ||
Having offered the oblation with a silent *anuvaṣaṭ* call, the Adhvaryu consumes the cup for the Aśvins with the mantra: "O Aśvins, [that which you took] from Namuci... (Yamaśvinā namuceḥ). || 37 ||
That which is smeared here, the Pratiprasthātṛ and the Āgnīdhra take for the Sārasvata [oblation].
"This is the oblation," thus [they say] regarding the offering for Indra; both the Brahman priest and the sacrificer [recite this]. (39)
The ritual application of liquor has been explained. 23.1.40.
To the south of the Āhavanīya fire, he gives the remainder of the milk to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, saying: "To the fathers who partake of the svadhā, svadhā! Homage! (41)
He worships [the sun] with the verse: "May the Soma-loving fathers purify me. || 42 ||
Then they offer the oblations: the Adhvaryu with "Those who are equal," and the Pratiprasthātṛ with "Those who are kinsmen. || 43 ||
At the time of the *manotā* hymn, he places the broth of the animals in separate vessels. || 44 ||
Before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, he performs the secondary oblations with the horns and hooves.
Each hoof of a single [ox] has eight hooves. || 46 ||

Having filled the *kuṣṭhikā* and the hoof with the broth of a horse of the Āśvina type, he should offer each pair of *kuṣṭhikā*s and hoofs with two verses at a time from the eight-verse hymn beginning with "sīsena tantram. In the final verse, he attaches [the offering] to the horns. Having offered each portion, he pours the remnants into his own consecration vessels and casts the *kuṣṭhikā*s and hoofs into the Āhavanīya fire. In the same manner, he performs the rite for the Sārasvata horse with the following eight-verse hymn; for the Aindra horse, he uses the entire Anuvāka.

He establishes that Audumbara stool—having a head-rest (śīrṣaṇya) of one cubit (aratni), with its slats (anūcya) reaching down to the knees and its legs (pāda) reaching to the navel, and woven with Muñja grass—with the formulas, "Thou art Mitra; thou art Varuṇa," at the place of the sacrificer. || 48 ||
The acts of approaching, sitting down, and consecrating with mantras are to be performed as in the Rājasūya sacrifice. || 49 ||

While he is seated facing east upon that [seat], [the officiant], standing facing west, sprinkles him with the *āśvina* mixtures, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle you with the healing medicine of the Aśvins for the sake of splendor and Vedic luster. (23.1.50)
In this manner, with the next mantra, [the offering] for Sarasvatī; with the final one, that for Indra. || 51 ||

Saying, "Who are you? Which one are you? the Adhvaryu, having touched the sacrificer’s hands and muttered the *vyāhṛtis*, calls upon him by an auspicious name as in the *Rājasūya*. Having touched his limbs according to their respective characteristics with the formulas, "May glory be my head," and so forth, and having descended with the formula, "With my two shanks and two feet," he mutters, "I am established in the kingdom, O Pratīkṣatra. Then, having offered the oblations with the verse, "The three gods," he touches his limbs according to their respective characteristics with the formula, "My hair is effort," and so forth. || 52 ||
From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the procedure is the same up to the *avabhṛtha*.

Regarding the statement, "With the verse 'yad devā devaheḍanam,' one offers five oblations at the avabhṛtha," Āśmarathya maintains that they should be offered [in the avabhṛtha fire], whereas Ālekhana maintains that they should be offered in the āhavanīya fire.

Having consecrated the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) with the mantra "O Nicaṅkuṇa," the sacrificer, having immersed himself with the mantra "May the waters be friendly to us; like one released from a wooden post," and having worshipped the sun with the mantra "We have risen above the darkness," throws [the grass-bundle] toward the edge of the water with the mantra "The noose of Varuṇa is cast off. || 55 ||
The kindling of the fuel and the ritual attendance are to be performed as in the case of the animal sacrifice. || 56 ||
Having performed the *samāvartana* rite and offered an oblation with "bhūḥ svāhā," the *pitṛyajña* (ancestral sacrifice) is performed as before. || 57 ||
One should sacrifice an animal to Indra Vayodhas; a bull is the sacrificial fee. || 58 ||
A pap of rice for Aditya; a milch-cow [is the sacrificial fee]. And it is known: "He gives the calf with the eastern [oblation], and the mother with the northern. 59.
The Kaukilī sacrifice concludes. || 23.1.60 ||
One desiring heaven should sacrifice with that [offering]. || 4 || 61 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the twenty-third book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Now begins the second chapter of the twenty-third book:
"One who desires heaven should pile the Sāvitra fire-altar."
It is piled up at the animal sacrifice. || 2 ||

When about to perform the rite, he prepares one hundred and eighty-five gold bricks, as many pebbles smeared with ghee as there are joints on the topmost phalanx of the finger, four naturally perforated stones (*svayamātṛṇṇā*), and an unlimited number of *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks.
One commences the ritual pertaining to the animal sacrifice (pāśuka-karman) with the mantra beginning "ṣaḍḍhotāram."
It is known from scripture that one should sacrifice when there is a third person who knows. ||5||

Having measured out the area for the *uttaravedi* from the northeast boundary and having driven a wooden stake (śaṅku) into the center, he should draw a circle all around it the size of a chariot wheel for the *sāvitra* [rite]. Then, having brought a clump of green darbha grass together with its roots and planted it in the middle of the fire-altar, and having taken five portions of clarified butter into the *juhū* ladle, he offers five oblations upon the darbha-clump with the mantra "In harmony with the year and the days" (*sajūr abdo ayāvabhiḥ*). Having leveled the ground and sprinkled it with water, and having completed the *uttaravedi* up to the pouring of the sprinkling water (*vyāghāraṇa*), he draws nine circular lines within the boundary line.
Having drawn the lines, having strewn them with sand, and having covered them with *darbha* grass, he dwells there after filling the outer line with curd mixed with honey and with sugar.

Having offered the Agnihotra, he touches the Uttaravedi with the formula: "May Prajāpati seat you; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras. Having taken the fire into himself with the two verses, "I take [the fire] into myself" and "The fire which is ours," and having touched it with the *svayaṃcit* verse, "Those logs of yours, O Agni," he pours down sand with the formula, "Thou art the ash of Agni," and saline soil with the formula, "Consciousness. || 7 ||
While scattering them, he offers them with the thought: "Whatever black [part] there was in the moon, may that be here. Thus he meditates in his mind. || 8 ||

Having mixed together the saline earth with the words, "Unite our dear bodies," and the sand with the words, "Ye are piled, ye are piled around," he encloses [the altar] with an unlimited number of pebbles; then he spreads out the sand with the verses, "Swell up! Let [the waters] come together unto thee! (VS 12.105).

Having mixed the saline earth (*ūṣa*) and sand together with the mantra beginning with *saṃ yāvaḥ* and ending with *vitaḥ stha sīdata*, he encloses the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) with an indefinite number of pebbles (*śarkarā*). At the end of the plural [mantra], he simultaneously spreads the sand with the mantra *āpyāyasva*. 9.
Writings do not entice him. || 23.2.10 ||
On the inner half of the hip, he places a water-pot with the formula: "Speech, I place thee upon the ocean; bringing good offspring, bringing abundance of wealth, for me, O vigorous one! || 11 ||
On the ninth outer line, he lays down fifteen bricks representing the days of the waxing fortnight, with the formulas: "Consciousness," "Discernment," and so forth.
In the intervals between these days, he lays down fifteen muhūrtas with the verse beginning, "Citraḥ ketuḥ."
Then, in the intermediate space, he lays down fifteen bricks of the first half-month, beginning with "darśā dṛṣṭā."

In the intervals between these nights, he lays down fifteen *muhūrta*s with the formulas, "The giver," "The bestower," and so forth. (15) Then, in the intermediate space, he lays down the fifteen days of the dark fortnight with the formulas, "The commenced," "The praised," and so forth. (16) In the intervals between these days, he lays down fifteen *muhūrta*s with the formulas, "The impeller," "The progenitor," and so forth. (17)
Then, on the fifteenth night of the latter half of the month, he lays down the inner [bricks] with the words, "The pressed one, pressing... (RV 9.107.1).

In the intervals between these nights, he lays down fifteen *muhūrta*-bricks with the formulas beginning, "The accuser," and "The one who permits. Then, in the inner [space], he lays down twelve *pūrvapakṣa*-bricks with the formula, "Purifying the purifier."
Then, within [the altar], he lays down twelve bricks of the dark fortnights with the formula: "Victorious, more victorious... (Sahasvān sahīyān). || 21 ||
Then, within the middle [space], he lays down thirteen bricks named after the months, beginning with "Aruṇa, Aruṇarajas."
Then he lays down the sand-grains with the formula: "Moving ones, living ones. (23)
Then, within the intermediate space, he lays down fifteen muhūrtas, beginning with "idānīm" and "tadānīm. || 24 ||
Then, within the intermediate space, he lays down six sacrificial rites and three names of four syllables: Agniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Agni, and Ṛtu.
Now, at the navel, he lays down four bricks named after the years: "Prajāpati," "Saṃvatsara," "Mahān," and "Ka. (26)
He places four self-perforated bricks in the directions with the formulas: "Bhūḥ! Agni and the earth and me," and so forth. || 27 ||
He lays down the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks with the formula, "Fill the world. || 28 ||
Having brought earth from the *cātvāla* pit, he spreads it over the altar with the verse addressed to Vaiśvānara: "Thou art asked about in heaven... (RV 10.88.1).
That becomes the layer. || 23.2.30 ||
He mutters the *ārohaṇa* [verse]; he mutters the *avarohaṇa* [verse]. || 31 ||
He attends upon him with attendance, saying: "You alone know yourself who you are; you are that. || 32 ||
He performs it as if for a thousand. || 33 ||
Having made [the bricks] into cows, the sacrificer worships them with the withdrawal and the approach, saying: "Thou art the Saṃvatsara; thou art the Parivatsara. || 34 ||
To the north of the highest brick, he offers goat’s milk with an Arka leaf. || 35 ||
With the verse, "O Agni, you are Rudra," he throws out the Arka-leaf used for the Śatarudrīya rite onto a place where there is no traffic, or he deposits it within the hollow of an anthill. || 36 ||
Sitting behind the fire facing east, the Hotṛ recites the *anuśaṃsana* with the *Anuvāka* beginning "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," according to the *Saṃcita-ukthya* ritual.
The ritual pertaining to the animal sacrifice, beginning with the leading forward of the fire (agnipraṇayana), is undertaken; it is the same up to the Atimukti offerings. || 38 ||
Having offered the *atimuktī* oblations, he offers four portions; "O Agni, you are Rudra"—this is the form of the *Śatarudrīya*.

Another fourfold portion is for Agni and Viṣṇu from the Vasordhārā. Another fourfold portion is for the oblation of food with the verse beginning "O Lord of Food. Another fourfold portion is for the Viśvaprī offering with the verse beginning "Seven are thy fire-sticks, O Agni, seven thy tongues. Another fourfold portion [is offered] with: "I offer thee with the study of the Vasus, with the wave of the Rudras, with the splendor of the Ādityas, with the will of the Viśvedevas, with the essence of the Maruts; Svāhā! (23.2.40).
With the outflow of those [waters], the sacrificer wipes his face with the anuvāka beginning, "The queen, the radiant one. (41)
Then he offers twenty-one oblations with each mantra from the section beginning, "To Asu, svāhā! To Vasu, svāhā! 42.
The ritual procedure pertaining to the animal sacrifice begins with the gathering of the sacrificial grass (barhis) and continues identically up to the offering of the omentum (vapā). 43.
When the omentum has been offered, he gives four-year-old female mules as the sacrificial fee for each brick.
If he should not be able to provide such a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he should cause as many Brahmins as he can afford to drink [the remainder], or he should feed them with boiled rice (odana).
By that very means, indeed, that desire of his becomes attained. || 46 ||

Having performed that which precedes the Manotā hymn, he takes a draught of broth for Mṛtyu in a vessel made of Udumbara wood with the formulas, "For the wise Pavamāna," and so forth; these are the formulas for taking and setting down the draught. Some say that this draught for Mṛtyu belongs specifically to the Nāciketa fire-altar.
The after-offering (anuhoma) follows the sviṣṭakṛt offering for that [rite]. || 48 ||
Before offering the oblation, he should touch water, saying: "Thou art lightning; strike away my evil. Then he offers the oblation, saying: "Away with untimely death! Away with hunger! (49)

Then, having offered the oblation, he should touch water with the formula: "Thou art rain; rain away my evil. His consumption of the *iḍā* portion follows. He consumes it with the formula: "Thou art food; thou art the consumption of immortality. Having consumed it, he establishes the vital breaths within himself with the remainder of the section beginning: "The delightful, the overpowering... From this point onward, the ritual procedure regarding the animal sacrifice is the same. The Sāvitra sacrifice is concluded. 7||23.2.50||
Thus ends the second paṭala in the twenty-third praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the third paṭala in the twenty-third praśna.

By this, the Nāciketa [agni] is explained. Here there are no lines (lekhās). Twenty-one gold bricks or pebbles, anointed with ghee, are placed at the time of laying down exactly upon the navel; it may be either square or circular. "Thou art the world... [the mantra continues].
With the section beginning "Thou art heaven," he offers oblations verse by verse.
For some indeed pile it on the *uttaravedi* at the animal sacrifice; these optional variations have been explained in the Brāhmaṇa. 2.
We shall enumerate them in order. || 3 ||
It should be sought at a Paśubandha sacrifice, a Soma sacrifice, a Sattra, a Sahasra sacrifice, or a Sarvavedasa sacrifice, or wherever the greatest number of oblations are offered. || 4 ||

One who desires a firm foundation, progeny, cattle, heaven, or prosperity [should perform] the sacrificial session (sattra) according to the available space and as it is traditionally handed down. || 5 ||
In all cases, the commencement is from the east, the movement is clockwise, and the conclusion is toward the north.
One who desires cattle should pile the altar in the form of the Paṅkti; five bricks in each direction and one in the middle.
One who desires preeminence, fame, or offspring should perform the Trivṛt [stoma] alone: seven in the east, three in the south, seven in the west, three in the north, and one in the middle.
One who desires preeminence should begin from the middle and lay down the line upwards.
One desiring heaven, having stepped back, should establish the line toward the east. || 23.3.10 ||

If he should desire, "May I be radiant, glorious, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge," he should step forward from the southern hearths toward the Hotṛ’s hearth, saying: "She who has gone forth, the glorious one—may she cover me with radiance, glory, and the splendor of sacred knowledge."

Now, if he should desire, "May they have great faith in me; may they bring abundant sacrificial fees," then while the sacrificial fees are being brought, [he should say]: "Come forward! Come forward! || 12 ||
"May the eastern quarter, being pleased, partake of the clarified butter; Svāhā!"—having thus taken [the portion] with the dipping-spoon (sruva), he should offer it into the Āhavanīya fire. || 13 ||
The subsequent [ritual] is the same, beginning with the naturally perforated stone (svayamātṛṇṇā). || 14 ||
The Nāciketa fire-altar is thus completed. || 15 ||
By this, the Cāturhotra [rite] is explained. ||16||
Up to that point, bricks made of gold or gravel should be smeared with oil.

At the time of piling, he places [the bricks] facing north in front of the bunch of Darbha grass, reciting the Daśahotṛ formula with each respective mantra: four [bricks] for the heart, one for the Graha, four for the ritual materials (saṃbhārāḥ), and two for the wives. || 18 ||

In this manner, he places the Caturhotṛ facing east on the south; the Pañcahotṛ facing north on the west; the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ facing east on the north; and the Saptahotṛ facing east above. Here there are five footprints for the ritual materials, and the remaining ones are for the wives. ||19||
The subsequent procedure, beginning with the naturally perforated stone (svayamātṛṇṇā), is the same. ||23.3.20||
The Cāturhotra [offering] is concluded. || 8 || 21 ||
By this, the Vaiśvasṛja [sacrifice] is explained.
As many as there are mantras for the gold bricks, up to the highest joint of the finger—so many pebbles, anointed, or four naturally perforated stones (svayamātṛṇṇā). || 23 ||

At the time of placing the supporting bricks, he encloses the northern altar three times clockwise, starting from the front of the *uttaranābhi*, with these three sections beginning with "That which is immortal and that which is mortal. || 24 ||
Or there are three layers, corresponding to the three sections of the Anuvākas.
With the verse, "The great [path] of the Ṛcs is eastward," the Hotṛ recites the *anuśaṃsana* for the *ukthya* at the *saṃcita*.

The subsequent [procedures] beginning with the *svayamātṛṇṇā* are the same. [This applies] to the *sārasvata* rites within the hundred-night sessions (*śatarātra*), to the night-sessions (*rātrisatra*) ending with the hundred-night [sessions], to the three *mahāvrata* [sessions], to the *sārasvata* sacrificial sessions, to the *kāṭhaka-cāturmāsya* rites, to the six-day periods of the *sādhyas* (excluding those), and to the *viśvasṛjām ayana*, except for the recitation by Prajāpati. || 27 ||
And at the end of the two thousand-year cycles, the Vaiśvasṛja fire is fixed. || 28 ||

If they should perform the *Abhicāra* rite while proceeding toward the site, he should touch the location of the *uttaravedi* with these mantras: "To him who is his most beloved, as if well-investigated, [he should offer] the *vaiśvasṛja* [oblation], either on the third turn. || 29 ||
They construct the Sāvitra, Nāciketa, Cāturhotra, Vaiśvasṛja, and Āruṇaketuka altars together even at the Soma sacrifice.

The first layer belongs to Savitṛ; the second is the *lokaṃpṛṇā*; the third is the *nāciketa*; the fourth is the *lokaṃpṛṇā*; the fifth is the *cāturhotra*; the sixth is the *vaiśvasṛja*; and the seventh is the *āruṇaketuka*. (31) He draws the cup from the broth of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice for Mṛtyu. (32)

One who piles these fires, whether separately or collectively, gives both kinds of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*): the *kratudakṣiṇā*s as prescribed [in the ritual manuals], and the *agnidakṣiṇā*s. Regarding the *kratudakṣiṇā*s for all [fires], whatever has not been stated in the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas is well-known [from other sources]. (In this case, they are not combined, but performed separately. || 33 ||
Having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī, or with curdled milk (āmikṣā) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. || 34 ||
The Āruṇaketuka [fire] has been explained in the Brāhmaṇa. || 35 ||
One desiring heaven should sacrifice every day with the *divaḥśyenī* verses and the *apādya* verses; these have been explained in the Brāhmaṇa. || 9 ||36||
Thus ends the third paṭala in the twenty-third praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the fourth chapter in the twenty-third book.
Now, the Bṛhaspatisava among the Savas has been explained.
A Vaiśya desiring prosperity offers seven oblations beginning with that for Agni.

A spotted heifer is offered to the Maruts; before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he spreads the hide of a bull upon the sacrificer’s seat, with the neck pointing eastward and the hair facing upward. While [the sacrificer] is seated upon it, he sprinkles him with curds.

A Brahmin desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) offers eight oblations, beginning with that for Agni, prior to the Sviṣṭakṛt offering; having purified the clarified butter with gold, he sprinkles it upon him while he is seated on a black antelope skin.
Now follows the Soma-sava sacrifice. Whatever constitutes the Rājasūya, with the exception of the Soma [sacrifice], all that takes place here. || 5 ||
Having completed the Maitrābārhaspatya sacrifice, he immolates a barren cow dedicated to Soma.
Before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering for that [oblation], he sprinkles him with water while reciting the verse addressed to Soma: "aṣāḍhaṃ yutsu pṛtanāsu papriṃ. || 7 ||

Having completed the remainder, he should sacrifice with the oblations of the *saṃsṛps*, the *diśām aveṣṭi*, the animal sacrifice with two victims, the *sātyadūta* oblations, and the *prayuja* offerings.
One who desires cattle should perform the Pṛthisava sacrifice. Whatever belongs to the Rājasūya, excluding that which requires the high altar (uttaravedi), all of that is included here. || 9 ||
Before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering of the Maitrābārhaspatya sacrifice, he sprinkles [the sacrificer] with water while reciting the Nārāśaṃsī verse beginning with "ye me pañcāśatam."
The subsequent portion is the same as the preceding one, excluding the animal sacrifice.
The Gosava has been explained. || 12 ||
One who desires food and drink should sacrifice with the Odanasava on the Rohiṇī day.
He cooks [the sacrificial food] just before dawn. || 14 ||
There is a *darvihoma* offering. || 15 ||
When the sun has risen, having offered four oblations of boiled rice with the mantras "Lion" and "Tiger," [he should proceed]. || 16 ||

With the mantras, "Thou art the ruler (rāṭ), thou art the sovereign (virāṭ)," they prepare the stirred drinks one by one: the Brāhmaṇa prepares a stirred drink of clarified butter, the Rājanya a stirred drink of milk, the Vaiśya a stirred drink of curds, and the Śūdra a stirred drink of water.

"For Indra, the radiant one, I mix you, the radiant one"—having thus mixed the clarified butter with groats, the Brāhmaṇa consecrates it with the formula "Thou art radiance," and saying "I give this to thee," he hands it to the sacrificer. || 18 ||
Having accepted it with the words, "May my mouth be radiant," he eats it. || 19 ||
In this same manner, for the others, there is the taking up of each subsequent one, the consecration, the offering, and the consumption, according to their respective characteristics.
Having consumed all [the portions], the sacrificer gives gold to a Brāhmaṇa; a bow with three arrows to a Rājanya; a goad to a Vaiśya; and a bowl of beans to a Śūdra. || 21 ||
He ties gold to the sacrificer; while it is being tied, he mutters: "Thou art life; thou art all-encompassing life. (22)
The sacrificer eats the remainder of the cooked rice. || 23 ||
He addresses the one who is eating with the mantra: "O Agni, make him [fit] for long life and splendor. (24)
They take the draughts of water with the verses, "Those who prepare the churnings" and "That which is the essence in the flowing of the waters," using one mantra for each.
With these [verses] combined, he sprinkles him with the words: "From whence the wind, swift as thought... (RV 10.183.1).

Having consecrated him with the mantra, "Thou art deep as the ocean," he then purifies him with three bunches of *darbha* grass; it is known that this serves as a substitute for the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
The chariot stands positioned in front of the Āhavanīya fire. || 28 ||
"Go forth!"—thus the sacrificer approaches him. || 29 ||
"Ascend, O increaser of friends," with these words he addresses him as he is ascending. || 23.4.30 ||
He touches the two wheels of the chariot, saying, "The two hooks, the two hooks," or he touches the two side-pieces.
[He addresses] the one who has mounted [the chariot] with the five verses beginning, "Mount, O slayer of Vṛtra. || 32 ||
"He becomes one who is desirable to see and beautiful to behold; he who sacrifices with this [rite]," so it is known. || 33 ||
The Odanasava sacrifice is concluded. 34 || 11 ||
The Pañcaśāradīya has been explained. || 35 ||
Likewise, the Agniṣṭut [is to be performed]. || 36 ||

Its *puroruc* verses are as follows: "O Agni, these thy life-spans are ageless" (*asyājarāso agne āyūṃṣi*) is for the draught for Indra and Vāyu; the second is for Mitra and Varuṇa; the third is for the Aśvins; the fourth and fifth are for the Śukra and Manthin draughts; the sixth is for the Āgrayaṇa. He joins another verse addressed to Agni for the Ukthya draught. The regular verse is for the Dhruva draught. He joins [verses] for the draughts for Indra-Agni and the Viśvedevas. "The glory of Agni" (*agniśriyaḥ*)—these three are for the Marutvatīya draughts. "Hear, O thou of listening ears" (*śrudhi śrutkarṇa*) is the subsequent one for the Māhendra draught. "Of all, Aditi" (*viśveṣāmaditiḥ*)—these three are for the Āditya draught. The last one is for the Sāvitra draught. (37)
He binds [the victim] for the Vaiśvadeva; the binding for the Pātnīvata is constant; he binds [the victim] for the Hāriyojana. || 38 ||

One who desires sensory power or virility should sacrifice with the Ukthya rite called Indra-stuta, which belongs to Indra. The *puroruṅ* for the cup for Indra is "tiṣṭhā harī," and "kasya vṛṣā" is for the cup for Indra-Vāyu. The third [verse] is for the cup for Mitra-Varuṇa; the fourth is for the cup for the Aśvins; the fifth and sixth are for the cups for Śukra and Manthin; the seventh is for the Āgrayaṇa cup; and the [verses] for the permanent Ukthya are used. He joins [the verses] for the Dhruva, Aindrāgna, and Vaiśvadeva cups. The [verses] for the Marutvatīya and Mahendra cups are the permanent ones.
For the cup for the Ādityas, there are three verses beginning with "ā no viśvābhirūtibhiḥ"; the last one is for the Sāvitra cup. (39)
He joins [the verses] for the Vaiśvadeva and Pātnīvata offerings. Those of the Hāriyojana are constant. The Aptoryāma has been explained. 23.4.40. 12.

When the king is about to be consecrated, while the people of the provinces have assembled, he prepares a sacrificial mound on the first of two auspicious days, kindles the fire, strews grass around it, and dwells there.

When the sun has risen, having offered two oblations with the verses, "Those who are long-haired... and "They dance not without the Brahman...", he establishes a throne made of Udumbara wood at the sacrificer's station with the formula, "Thou art Rāṭ; thou art Virāj."
The king mounts it. || 43 ||
He addresses the one who is mounting with the mantra, "Mount the couch. || 44 ||
Here he bestows a boon. || 45 ||
Seated upon it, he has his hair shaved with [the verse]: "With that razor wherewith Savitṛ shaved [the head]... (RV 9.1.1). || 46 ||
With the verse "mā te keśān," he consecrates the hair as it is being scattered. || 47 ||
Having gathered them together, he places them upon a bunch of Darbha grass with the words, "This is the place for you. || 48 ||

Then he anoints him with milk mixed with clarified butter: with the verse "Strength in thy two arms," he anoints the arms; with the verse "When [he reached] the parting of the hair," the head. Having offered seven oblations with the formula "This tiger [is] in the fire," he spreads a tiger skin on the sacrificer’s seat with the formula "Thou art heaven, thou art earth," having its neck to the east and the hair upwards. Upon it, the King sits down. 49.
He addresses the one who is seated with the mantra: "A tiger, indeed, is the tiger-like one. (23.4.50)
Then he sprinkles him with water containing young sprouts of rice or with dūrvā grass, beginning with the verse "The waters that are divine" and continuing up to the end of the *āpāṅkta* section.
Having consecrated it with the mantra, "The ruddy one, thee, the wolf... (RV 10.86.22). || 52 ||
Having extended the two arms with the words "pra bāhū," [he should perform the rite]. || 53 ||
"Thou art Indra's, made by heroic power"—with these words he brings it down. || 54 ||
The chariot stands in front of the fire; the king approaches it, saying, "Go forward! (abhiprehi). || 55 ||
"Mount, O best slayer of Vṛtra!"—with these words he addresses him as he is mounting. || 56 ||
He touches the two wheels of the chariot, saying, "The two hooks, the two hooks," or he touches the two side-pieces.
"Salutation to you, O Seer," with these words he consecrates the domestic priest.
"Stop the chariot! [he said] to the charioteer. || 59 ||
With the words "Hither the reins," he takes hold of the reins. || 23.4.60 ||
With the six verses beginning with "ā tiṣṭha vṛtrahan," he mounts [the chariot]. || 61 ||
Having caused him to recite the two verses beginning with "pari mā senyā," [he should do so]. || 62 ||
Having consecrated it with the three following [verses], || 63 ||
Having caused [the water] to flow out, he makes him look up at the sun with the words, "Ud asāvīḥ. || 64 ||
"Of those possessing food," thus he surveys the districts. ||65||
The royal consecration is concluded. || 66 ||
The "Cloudless" [attainment] has been explained. || 67 ||
The libations are established; the libations are established. 68 || 13 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the twenty-third book of the *Satyāṣāṅha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
Thus ends the twenty-third book of the *Satyāṣāṅha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.

One who is about to collect the materials for the *Pravargya* rite, on the new moon day, the full moon day, or during the waxing fortnight under an auspicious constellation, silently places a fuel-stick of *Kaṇṭakī* wood upon the fire and offers four spoonfuls of clarified butter with the verse: "They harness the mind. (1)

One should not offer an oblation for one who has been initiated; rather, with this [verse], one should place a thorny fuel-stick on the fire, or some say one should simply recite the sacrificial formula (yajus).

With the formula, "Thee for the god," he takes up the spade—made of Khadira, Udumbara, Vēṇu, or Vikaṅkata wood, and of the same dimensions as before—and consecrates it with the mantra, "Thou art the spade; thou art no woman."
"Arise, O Brahmanaspati!"—with these words he addresses the Brahman priest. The Brahman priest rises after him, both of them muttering the latter half-verse.

With the words, "May Brahmanaspati go forth," they proceed eastward with the horse at their head to where they intend to collect the ritual materials; it is known from tradition that these [materials] have already been brought forward and placed within an enclosed space (pariśrita) to the east of this [site]. || 5 ||

To the east of the Āhavanīya fire, the earth-digging pit (mṛtkhana) is placed first, and the other [the black antelope skin] is placed to the north of the earth-digging pit. Having spread out the black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and the hair on the upper side, he addresses Heaven and Earth with the mantra, "O divine Heaven and Earth. He strikes the earth-digging pit with the wooden mallet (abhryā) with the mantra, "May I increase the earth-digging pit. Having taken up the earth with the mantra, "The head of Makha," he carries it away with the mantra, "For Makha, thee. He pours it out upon the black antelope skin with the mantra, "For the head of Makha, thee. || 6 ||
In this way, he carries off the second and the third as well. || 7 ||
He silently [takes] as much clay as he considers sufficient from the Pravargya vessels up to the fourth [time].
The same applies to the others. || 9 ||

With the words, "So much was there at first," he consecrates the earth dug up by a boar; with "O divine ants," the ant-hill; with "Thou art the vigor of Indra," the *pūtīka* plants; and with "Thou art born of Agni, the seed of Prajāpati," the hair of a black antelope skin and the hair of a goat, having gathered them together.
Having caused the horse to sniff them with the formulas beginning, "Bestow life, bestow breath," he milks it over with a female goat using the formula, "May honey make thee sweet. || 24.1.10 ||
Some authorities prescribe the milking as having occurred previously.
Many noble men, having taken hold [of it], carry it to the north of the monastery; once the area has been enclosed, raised, sprinkled with water, and strewn with sand, he places it down.

With the formula, "May Madhu make thee sweet," he pours in the boiling water; then he mixes [the clay] with these very same ingredients used for the restoration of the *ukhā*. Whatever requires water in the *pravargya* rite is performed with boiling water; this is an absolute rule. A woman does not look at it, nor a Śūdra; one who is performing [the rite] does not breathe over it, but having turned away his face, he works with a reed-pipe without breathing upon it. (13) (Section 1)

One should not allow the sun to pass between oneself and the Pravargya vessel; if the sun should set while the Pravargya rite has been commenced, one should cease at that very point and complete the remainder on the following day. || 14 ||

Having kneaded the clay with the formula, "Thou art the head of Makha," he forms a lump. Having pressed it down with his two thumbs with the formula, "Ye are the two feet of the sacrifice," he fashions the Mahāvīra vessel using the three meters, beginning with, "I fashion thee with the Gāyatrī meter"—making it in the shape of a Vāyavya vessel, with three elevations, five elevations, or an unlimited number of elevations.

With the formula, "Rāsnā art thou for the mouth," he makes a ridge in the middle or at the opening; with the formula, "May Aditi grasp thy opening," he makes the opening with a bamboo joint, as much as he considers sufficient for the portion for the deity, for the Sviṣṭakṛt, for the Agnihotra, and for the consumption.

Having established it on the sand to the north with the formula, "Be protected by the heat of the sun," he consecrates it with the mantra, "Thou art Makha. [He does so] for Makha; likewise for the other two. Or alternatively: the first with the Gāyatrī meter, the second with the Triṣṭubh meter, the third with the Jagatī meter, and the others silently.

From this very clay, for the milk-pail: just as the ladle and the handle are [shaped], so are the elephant-lip-shaped vessels; the Adhvaryu’s portion is larger, the Pratiprasthātṛ’s is smaller; [he also prepares] the butter-pot, two round Kapāla-bricks, the Gharmestakā, and the Kulāyinī, if the rite involves the piling of the fire-altar.

Having placed horse-dung on the Gārhapatya fire, he takes hold of the first-made Mahāvīra with his two hooves while reciting, "Thou art the footprint of the stallion," and fumigates it; he does the same for the other two silently. From this point onward, he takes up the Mahāvīras using only the two hooves.

Having dug a pit in front of the Gārhapatya fire and having spread it with red-heating materials, he brings down the first-made Mahāvīra vessel into them with the formula, "O God, you who go before, I have placed you. He does the same for the other two. Having silently placed the remaining vessels over them and covered them with red-heating materials, he sets fire to bundles of Muñja grass at the Gārhapatya fire and burns them around [the vessels] in each direction with the respective formulas, "For the flame, thee! For the radiance, thee! using all the formulas on all sides.

With the two verses beginning "Abhīmaṃ mahinā divam," he attends to the [Mahāvīras] while they are being baked. When they are baked, for the sake of success, he takes up the two stirring-sticks with the formula "Siddhyai tvā" (For success, you). Having lifted out the first-made Mahāvīra with the formula "Devastvā savitodvapatu" (May the god Savitṛ lift you out), while it is not falling upon the earth, he establishes it in the sand to the north with the formula "Āpadyamānaḥ pṛthivyāmāśā diśa āpṛṇa" (Falling upon the earth, may you fill the regions and the quarters). In the same way he treats the other two; the others he lifts out silently.

With the formula, "I gaze upon you with the eye of the Sun," he gazes [at the fire]. With the formula, "Here I enclose so-and-so, the son of such-and-such, with the people, with cattle, and with Vedic splendor," he thrice sprinkles sand around [the fire] from left to right. He uses "with the people" for a Kṣatriya and "with cattle" for a Vaiśya. With the formulas beginning, "I cover you with the Gāyatrī metre," he covers each [layer] with goat's milk; or he covers each one with all three [metres]. Having tied them together on a black antelope skin, he attaches them with the formula, "O God, go forward;
may I attain you. It is known that this mantra is to be used at the subsequent time. 22.
Thus ends the first chapter in the twenty-fourth book, titled the Pravargya, of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
(Now begins the second chapter.)
When they are about to proceed with the Pravargya rite, they close the doors and enclose the wife.
Afterwards, the Hotṛ sits down in the west, the Adhvaryu in the east, the Brahman and the sacrificer in the south, the Prastotṛ in the southwest, and the Āgnīdhra and the Pratiprasthātṛ in the north.

Having touched water with the *madantī* waters and performed the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the first *anuvāka*, he spreads out *muñja* grass-clippings for the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) with the following [mantra]. Then, with the mantra "O God, go before me; may I attain thee," he brings down the first-made *mahāvīra* vessel upon them; the other two in the same manner, and the others silently.
Right here he completes everything that is to be performed according to the ritual rules, including the weaving with threads of *udumbara* wood.

There are four offering-spoons (*sruc*); of these, two are not fixed, which are the *rohiṇa-havanyau*; of the two that are fixed, the larger one is the *upayamanī*, and the other is the vessel for the sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇī-dhānī*). There are two small spoons (*sruva*), two stirring-sticks (*dhṛṣṭī*), two hooves (*śaphau*) equal in size to the *mahāvīra* vessel, two shavings (*avraskau*) equal to the sacrificial post (*methī*), three pegs (*mayūkha*), six splinters (*śakala*), thirteen enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *vaikaṅkata* wood, and a fuel-stick (*samidh*) from the *kāṇṭakī* tree. There are also fuel-sticks for the *gharma* made of bamboo, or of *khadira*, *pālāśa*, *udumbara*, *arka*, or *śamī* wood. ||5||

(Regarding the black antelope skin: There are three fans made of black antelope skin with white and black hair; their handles are made of bamboo or udumbara wood and are a cubit in length. There are two gold and silver ornaments (*rukmāu*), each weighing one hundred *mānas* separately. We shall now explain the items made of muñja grass: two mats, of which one is perfumed; a cord for tying and two loops; four ropes for the forked posts; cuttings of grass whose tips are not shattered; sand for the two *rauhiṇa* cakes; flour of unhusked grains; and two strainers made of muñja or darbha grass.
Or, silently, having consecrated the clarified butter and the sprinkling water. (Section 3)

"O Brahman, we shall proceed with the Pravargya; O Hotṛ, recite for the Gharma; O Agnīdh, place the two Rauhina cakes on the fire; O Pratiprasthātṛ, distribute the fires; O Prastotṛ, chant the Sāmans," thus he issues the command.

Having recited, "The Brahman is joined with the Yajus, anointed with the Sāmans; O Sky! he gives the impulse, saying, "O you who possess Indra, proceed! Being thus impelled, he sprinkles the entire sacrificial vessel three times with the formula, "For Yama thee, for Makha thee! || 8 ||
It is known that at this time the Pratiprasthātṛ extends the sprinkled [cakes]; meanwhile, the Āgnīdhra silently places the two Rauhiṇa cakes upon the fire after they have been prepared.

Having carried the sovereign’s throne-seat (samrāḍāsandī) around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places it to the east of the King’s throne-seat (rājāsandī). Upon it, he spreads a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and the hair side upward, [saying]: "O God, go before me; may I attain thee. Upon that, he places the other two Mahāvīras facing eastward, and the Upaśaya [Mahāvīra] as well. These two [latter] are not to be used in the ritual procedure. Taking the sacrificial post (methī), the pegs (mayūkha), and the forked ropes (viśākhadāmanī), he passes to the south of the Hotṛ, goes out by the southern door, and drives the post into the ground to the south of the Hotṛ's position.

To the south of this very eastern door-post, he fixes a peg for the calf; to the south of this very western door-post, for the goat; and to the north, further inward, for the kid. Upon these he stretches the ropes with their forked ends; they remain stretched in this very manner until the removal of the fires.

At that time, they tie up the calves with those [ropes] on the north side of the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires; at the time of milking, they tie up the calves, kids, and rams with them. He scatters two mounds (khara) within the Prāgvamśa hall itself. He scatters the two mounds in the intermediate space between the north and the east, having the mound for the leavings outside and provided with a drainage channel; to the north of the Āhavanīya, he places pieces of wood and a fuel-stick of Kaṇṭakī wood. || 11 ||
(Section 4)

The Third Chapter. Having taken up the Mahāvīra vessel, O God, proceed forward; with the formula "With thee that art unperfumed," he cleanses it with a fringed cloth (*veda*). With the formulas "To Prāṇa, Svāhā! To Vyāna, Svāhā! he offers seven oblations of breath (*prāṇāhuti*) into the Āhavanīya fire using the *sruva* ladle, or eleven at the end. Having anointed the Mahāvīra with the remainder [of the ghee] while reciting "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey," and having either set it down or handed it over to another, he places a silver disk (*rukma*) on another mound (*khara*) with the formula "Protect the earth from heat. Then, taking two bundles of *muñja* grass, he says, "Thou art light."

He kindles the tips of the southern blades on the Gārhapatya fire with the formula, "Thou art heat"; their tips [he places] upon the roots of the northern blades with the formula, "Thou art light"; their roots [he places] upon the roots of the southern blades with the formula, "Thou art austerity"; and their roots [he places] upon the tips of the northern blades with the formula, "Thou art fervor.
Having thus placed them crosswise, he sets them down upon the gold plate.

With the words "Settle down," he places the Mahāvīra vessel upon them; with the words "Anointing," he anoints it with clarified butter, or rather, he consecrates it with these formulas, "Invincible in the east," etc., reciting each mantra for each direction without touching [the vessel]. The sacrificer holds the Mahāvīra facing east at the distance of a span; with the words "Thou art the horse of Manu, O thou of many sons," he touches the earth from the north.

Saying "For success," the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ take up the two poking-sticks (*dhṛṣṭī*) and, with the formula "O Agni, in thy heats," draw out embers from the Gārhapatya fire towards the north; then, with the formula "Ye are piled, ye are piled around," they encircle the Mahāvīra vessel clockwise with those embers.

Having strewn [the earth] and enclosed it with enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *vaikaṅkata* wood, the Adhvaryu places two [sticks] pointing eastward with the formula, "Thou art the measure" (*pramā asi*), and the Pratiprasthātṛ places two pointing northward with the formula, "Thou art the fore-measure" (*pramā asi*). In this very same manner, the Adhvaryu places them to the east and the Pratiprasthātṛ to the north. Then the Adhvaryu alone places the thirteenth [stick] to the south with the formula, "Thou art the intermediate space of the atmosphere" (*antarikṣasyāntardhiḥ asi*). ||3|| (Section 5)

Having brought clarified butter [with the words], "O Great Hero, protect the heaven from heat," he covers it from above with a golden plate and worships it with the three verses beginning with "With these songs. He takes up the fans with the formula, "Thou art the Gāyatra."

The first [verse] is "thou art traiṣṭubha," the second is "thou art jāgata," and the third is "thou art [anustubha]. With these three, he fans it upward. [He says] "honey, honey" over them. He gives one of them to the Agnīdh and one to the Pratiprasthātṛ. Those [priests], led by the Agnīdh, go around the Mahāvīra pot three times clockwise, fanning it upward while saying "honey, honey," concluding with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om); so it is known in the tradition. 4.
Having sat down according to the light, they remain fanning the fire while it is burning; it is known from scripture that they take up the gold plate when it has been kindled. || 5 ||

When it is said, "By which they did not release the swallowed wick," he causes the sacrificer to recite this section: "Ten eastward, ten thou shinest southward. When it is said, "O Aśvins, may our speech be effective," he says, "The Gharma has shone," as he stands up; then they walk around three times in the same manner as they came, without fanning [the fire].

At that time, the Pratiprasthātṛ returns, takes up the strainers, carries them around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, and places them on the *samrāḍ-āsandi* throne with the formula: "Svāhā! To thee for the rays of the sun," in the morning; "Svāhā! To thee for the stars," in the evening.
