Having risen according to the light and reciting, "I have seen the guardian," all the officiating priests and the sacrificer look at the Mahāvīra vessel while reciting. In the enclosed space (*pariśrita*), the Pratiprasthātṛ makes the wife recite: "O thou who art accompanied by Tvaṣṭṛ, do not burn me. (Khaṇḍa 6)
Thus ends the third chapter in the twenty-fourth book.
Now begins the fourth chapter.

Having given the command, "O Āgnīdhra, place the two *rohiṇa* rice-cakes upon the fires," the Āgnīdhra, while the fires are not yet obstructed, makes an under-layer of butter and pours butter over them; he then places those two *rohiṇa* cakes down, one following the southern joint of the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) and the other following the northern. Right there, he also places the boiled curd.

Having taken up the halter with the formula, "Thee for the God," and having consecrated it with, "Thou art the girth for Aditi," the Adhvaryu goes out by the eastern door and calls the cow that yields the Gharma-milk: "O Iḍā, come! O Aditi, come! O Sarasvatī, come! He says this three times in a low voice; then three times aloud, "Come, so-and-so! using her actual name. Having returned by the same way he went, the Adhvaryu, the Āgnīdhra, and the Pratiprasthātṛ take the head-stall, the two side-ropes, and the two milking-bowls, and lead her out by the southern door.

With the words, "Thou art the turban of Aditi," the Adhvaryu places the Gharma-milch cow; with "Vāyu art thou, the goat," he [places] the calf; with "May Pūṣan let thee loose," he lets the calf loose. With "That breast of thine which is inexhaustible," the Adhvaryu addresses the Gharma-milch cow. Having set down the calf with "O Dawn, leave some of the Gharma," he sits down with "May Bṛhaspati sit near thee. He touches the teats with "Ye are the Dānavas, the Peravas. He milks her who has a calf into a vessel for the Aśvins with "Swell for the Aśvins;
swell for Sarasvatī," and silently into a smaller vessel for the one without a calf; thus does the Pratiprasthātṛ milk.

Having given the two milks to the Āgnīdhra, they return by the way they came. The Adhvaryu takes up the two hoof-plates: the first with "Thou art Gāyatra," the second with "Thou art Traiṣṭubha," and the supporting vessel with "Thou art Jāgata. While the Pratiprasthātṛ is being addressed, "O cowherd, come hither with milk," the Āgnīdhra steps forward first with the words, "Come hither with a share of vigor. He awaits the two milks as they are being brought with the formula, "O Indra and Aśvins, [bring] the essence of honey. || 4 || (Section 7) ||

"O Great Hero, bring the cow's milk, svāhā! May the rays of the sun [bring] thee," with these words he consecrates the rising steam; "Thou art honey, the oblation," [with this] the Pratiprasthātṛ [consecrates] the goat's milk; some prescribe the goat's milk first. || 5 ||

With the formula, "I enclose you with heaven and earth," he encloses the Mahāvīra with his two hooves; having wiped it with the Veda-grass, [the Adhvaryu says] "I support you with the intermediate space," and the Pratiprasthātṛ supports it with the supporting-stand. Having taken it up with the formula, "May I be able to bear you, permitted by the gods and the ancestors," he stands up.

"Thou art brilliance; follow after brilliance," with these words he carries [the fire]; "For the ocean, for Vāta, svāhā!"—while walking, he recites five names of Vāta without taking breath. With "For Agni accompanied by the Vasus, svāhā! he recites five subsequent [names].
The remaining ones are for the purpose of option. || 7 ||

At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the southern Rauhiṇa cake with the formula, "The day is light" in the morning, and "The night is light" in the evening. Having stepped southward past the rear of the Āhavanīya fire, he looks at the Brahman with the formula, "Seated in the south, [protect] all the quarters," and at the Hotṛ with the formula, "He has sacrificed here to all the gods. Having called for the announcement regarding the Gharma with the words, "Of the Gharma consecrated by Svāhā," he issues the direction: "Recite the offering-verse for the Gharma! (8)

He proceeds with the highest speech: "Svāhā to Agni, the worthy of sacrifice! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the oblation: "Svāhā to Indra! Vaṣaṭ! At the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, [he says] "The Aśvins have drunk the Gharma. He stands in worship before the offered Gharma. || 9 ||

With the remainder of the *anuvāka* beginning with "Homage to Heaven! Homage to Earth!", while the [offering] is being held over the fire, the Pratiprasthātṛ fills it with curdled milk; he consecrates it as it drips with the mantra, "O Food, swell! and causes it to fall into the space between the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). || 24.4.10 ||

With "For brilliance thee! he places [it] in the east; with "For splendor thee! in the south; with "For power thee! in the west; with "For prosperity thee! in the north. Having stepped back and brought the remainder to the supporting vessel, and having placed a silver plate upon the eastern mound, he sets down the Mahāvīra pot upon it with the formula, "Thou art the Law," for one who performs malevolent magic, [adding], "Lest the wind should spill thee. (Section 8)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the twenty-fourth book.
Now begins the fifth chapter.

Having anointed the wood-shavings for the purpose of binding, he places them on the Āhavanīya fire with these mantras one by one: "To Pūṣan, the arrow, svāhā! and so forth; having smeared the sixth [shaving] with all the residues, he throws it out through the northern door with the mantra "To Rudra, the Rudra-hotr, svāhā," without looking back, and touches water. At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the second cake-offering as was done previously.

The Adhvaryu places a thorn-apple fuel-stick on the fire with the mantra: "You have carried me across from day; protect me from night" at evening; and "You have carried me across from night; protect me from day" in the morning.

From the remainder, he performs the Agnihotra with the *upayamana* (supporting ladle): "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā! in the evening; "Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā! in the morning. And at both times, having invoked the remainder with the *vyāhṛtis*, they all consume it after being invited. The invitation is made by name, saying, "N.N., please invite me! and the response is, "I am invited. The Hotṛ is the first to consume, and the sacrificer is the last; or rather, the sacrificer alone consumes first, while the others smell the offered oblation, saying, "The oblation is honey, the oblation is honey."

Having consumed [the portion], he hands the support-vessel (*upayamana*) to the Pratiprasthātṛ; having washed it in the pit for the remains (*ucchiṣṭakhara*), he places it within the altar (*antarvedi*). Having placed two gold plates (*rukma*) upon it and brought the boiling water (*madantī*), they purify themselves with the three verses beginning, "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss" (*apo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*). Having poured out the water and having placed all the contents of the *gharma* vessel into the support-vessel, [he sets it down]. (Section 9)

He issues the command, "Recite for the Gharma as it is being removed," or "Recite for it as it is being removed. When [the verse] beginning with "In whom seven seers... is being recited, he carries it around in front of the Āhavanīya fire and places it upon the royal throne (samrāḍ-āsandī).
Just as one lets loose the cow while reciting, "O inviolable one, eat the grass at all times," at this moment they perform the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the final section (*anuvāka*). || 5 ||

In this manner, they proceed with the Pravargya rite three times each morning and evening for three nights: six times if there are three Upasad days, twelve times if there are six Upasad days, and twenty-four times if there are twelve Upasad days.
Having performed that sacrifice for a year, he shall not eat meat, he shall not approach a woman, he shall not drink from an earthen vessel, and his wife shall not drink the remains of his food.

One chooses the Pravargya at the Agniṣṭoma; one should not choose it at the Ukthya. One chooses it at the Viśvajit when it is performed with all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras; one should not choose it at one's first sacrifice. Or rather, one may choose it for a person of bad Brāhmaṇa lineage, or for one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), provided he is a learned reciter (*anūcāna*). For one who is a learned scholar (*śrotriya*), one may choose it according to his desire. (Section 10)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the twenty-fourth book.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Intending to remove the *pravargya* vessel, he gives a goat to the *āgnīdhra*, a four-year-old cow to the *brahmán*, a milch-cow to the *hotṛ*, and two gold ornaments to the *adhvaryu*.

Having placed another sharp post within the previous one, and having taken the central post (methī), the pegs (mayūkha), and the forked poles with their ropes (viśākhadāma), he carries them around behind the Āhavanīya fire and places them upon the royal throne (samrāḍāsandī). Having set down the royal throne in front of the Āhavanīya, and having taken four portions of clarified butter into a ladle made of Udumbara wood, he offers it at the height of the mouth with the formula: "O Gharma, that heat of yours which is in heaven"; at the height of the navel with: "O Gharma, that heat of yours which is in the intermediate space"; and at the height of the knee with: "O Gharma, that heat of yours which is on earth. || 2 ||

At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ leads the wife out while she is enclosed by an unwashed garment. They go out with the words, "Anu no adyānumatiḥ," and they carry out the two *khara* mounds; first the *ucchiṣṭa-khara*, then the *samrāḍ-āsandī* throne-seat, having established it in front of the *prāgvam̐śa* hall. He gives the command: "O Prastotṛ, chant the Sāman! Together with the wife, they reach the *nidhana* of the entire Sāman three times: the second at the middle point, and the third upon reaching the end. At all these points he gives the command.

Having placed the northern altar (uttaravedi) by the other side, he issues the command: "O Prastotṛ, sing the Vārṣāhāra Sāman; sing the iṣṭāhotrīya Sāman. For the iṣṭāhotrīya Sāman, they all join in at the *nidhana* (concluding syllable), but not for the Vārṣāhāra.
If he were to sprinkle water from above, one would have to urge Vārṣāhāra to come here. ||5||
Taking a water-pot, he goes around the northern altar three times from left to right, sprinkling it while reciting: "Thou art beautiful, a bestower of prosperity. || 6 ||

With the formula, "The navel of the Truth, four-cornered," he pours out the two *khara* heaps upon the *uttaravedi*. With the formula, "Away with hatred, away with crookedness," he pours out the *ucchiṣṭakhara* in the region of the *mārjālīya*. Having washed his hands and placed gold upon the *uttaravedi*, he brings down the *pracaraṇīya mahāvīra* vessel upon it with the formula, "O God, go forward; may I attain thee. In this same manner, he brings down the other two—the southern and northern ones—silently. He thus makes them the very form of the Sun.

With the formula, "Thou art the milk of the great ones," he pours clarified butter into the *pracaraṇī* ladle; with the formula, "The essence of trees and herbs," [he pours] honey; and with the formula, "Thee, the vigorous one, we pour down as the vigorous," he pours curds. In the same way for the other two.
Or alternatively, one may offer clarified butter in the first [offering], honey in the second, and curd in the third.

"O Gharma, this is your food, this is your sediment"—with these words, he fills with curds mixed with honey those vessels that have pouring-spouts, while he sprinkles water over the others so that they are not empty; thus it is known. (24.6.10) (Section 11)

Now, if one should wish to fashion it in the form of a human being, the bringing down of these [materials] is the same; that becomes the head. Upon it he places this [blade] with its tip uncut, facing eastward, as the form of the top-knot.

On both sides of the two udders [he places] the two ears; the *prokṣaṇī* vessel on the mouth; the two *sruc* ladles on the two nostrils; the two pieces of gold and the *sruva* and *ājyasthālī* on the two eyes; the two *dhṛṣṭi* stirring-sticks on both sides of the neck; the two *rauhiṇakapāla* cakes on both sides of the two shoulders; the *methī* pin on the two arms; the two fans on both sides of the ribs; a third [fan] in the middle between the two flanks, on the chest; the *abhri* spade on the two hips; the two *mayūkha* pegs on both sides of the thighs; a third [peg] in the middle between the two thighs; and the two *rauhiṇakapāla* pans on the two heels.

He places within that belly, which serves as a support, everything made of rope; he causes the entrails to disappear by smearing them with the flour of the *rauhiṇa* cakes; having loosened the *veda*-grass, he scatters it over the marrow; he covers the sinews with *avakā* plants and smoke-smoke-grass (*dhūpatṛṇa*); he sprinkles the flesh with curds mixed with honey; he covers the blood with a black antelope skin, its neck pointing eastward and the hair side up; he loosens the *samrāḍ-āsandī* throne and places it on top, thereby giving it the form of sovereignty.

One should remove [the fire] onto the *uttaravedi* for one who desires splendor; one should remove it onto the *uttaravedi* for one who desires food. One may remove it either in front or behind; one should remove it into the midst of the waters. They say that this refers to an island in a river; if one removes it onto an island in a river, one should not sprinkle water around it, nor should one prescribe the *vārṣāhāra* offering here.

If he should practice sorcery, thinking, "By means of this [fire], I burn away the life-breath of such-and-one, the son of such-and-one," he should extinguish it upon an Udumbara branch in the direction where the one he hates may be.

Where the Darbha grass is covered with Upadīka, there he should remove it for one desiring rain; they prescribe the regular procedure on the Uttaravedi, and birds should not sit around it once it has been removed until the carrying forward of the fire.

Then they worship him [the sun] with the verses: "Thou art Ranti by name, the divine Gandharva," and "The bull, the bay, has bellowed. The sacrificer, having performed the purification with "May we have good friends," and having worshipped the sun with "Upwards from the darkness," returns without looking back, offering two oblations at the Gārhapatya fire with the two verses, "Up that" and "The bright," and worships either the Āhavanīya fire with "This one, indeed, for us," or the Gārhapatya. 16. (Section 12)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the twenty-fourth book of the Pravargya-sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
If the sacrificial vessel (gharma) should spill, one should offer oblations with the mantra: "May the sky not fall upon the earth. || 1 ||

If lightning should strike while they are performing the *gharma* sacrifice, he offers an oblation with the words, "The lightning that struck in the east"; likewise for the other directions, according to their respective characteristics.
With the two sections beginning with "To Prāṇa, svāhā! To Pūṣan, svāhā! he offers fourteen oblations into the Gharma for an unrecognised transgression; according to some, eighteen.
Having cast it up with the verse "udasya śuṣmāt," he places the gharma-brick; with "yāste agne ārdrā yonayaḥ," the kulāyinī; and with "agnirasi vaiśvānaro 'si," the aiḍakī layer. ||4||

If, while they are performing the rite with the *gharma*, the *mahāvīra* vessel should fall, one should consecrate it with the mantra "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ" and raise it up with the two verses beginning "ūrdhva ū ṣu ṇa ūtaye. If it should break, one should join it together with the verse "vidhuṃ dadrāṇam. One should cause it to adhere with the verse "yadṛte cidabhiśriṣaḥ," provided that [the damage] is other than flesh or beans.

If they do not circumambulate the cauldron, or even if they do circumambulate it, they should circumambulate it with two verses: "With vigor again, together with wealth... (VS 11.50) and the following. || 6 ||
"O Gharma, do not cause us to tremble when you tremble"—with these words, he offers eight oblations when the Gharma has trembled.
Or rather, he worships with these four [verses] the very Gharma that has been disturbed. ||8||

If the sun should set while he is performing the Gharmahoma, he should tie a piece of gold to a blade of darbha grass at the western door with the verse "ud vayaṃ tamasas pari," and having worshipped [the sun] with the two verses "ud u tyam" and "citram," he should proceed with the rite. On the following day, as the sun is rising, he worships it with the verse "vayaḥ suparṇāḥ. ||9||
If he does not arrive at the time for milking the Gharma, he should milk another cow.
If she does not milk the skin-bag, she should make it into a teat and cause it to swell. ||11||
If there were curd, he should recite the Bārhaspatya hymn.
If there is milk, it belongs to the Aśvins and includes the *sodarka* verse.
If he should seize her by the age, he should offer an oblation with a verse addressed to Indra. 14.
If one should offer for a year with a verse addressed to Vāyu. ||15||
If he should sit down, [he should do so] with a verse addressed to Varuṇa.
If it should be lost, [it should be recovered] with two Ṛg verses. || 17 ||
According to some, [the offering] is with the verse addressed to Agni and Varuṇa.
If one should fall from a height, or be struck by lightning, or be killed by a tiger, one should apply drops of goat’s milk mixed with the milk of the Arka plant. 19.
Now, therefore, follows the investigation concerning the heating of the milk at the Soma-pressing. 24.7.20.

When there is darkness in the east, having moved forward toward the light until the break of dawn before sunrise, or at sunrise, or at the *saṃgava* [period], or when the *mādhyaṃdina-pavamāna* has been chanted, one should move forward in the *āgnīdhra* shed. Having moved forward only once, for it is known from tradition:

"The *hiṃ* is indeed the head. Thus, these [ceremonies] should optionally alternate with the *upasad* movements, using the section beginning with "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ. They consume the *dadhidharma*. 21.

"O Agni, those fierce bodies of yours"—with these [verses] he should look upon one whom he hates, [reciting] "the roaring and the darkening. The group beginning with "dhuniśca dhvāntaśca" is to be recited in the forest. Having run through "O Day and Night, may you two drive him away," he utters the cruel words of speech:
"khaṭ phaṭ jahī. 22.

If, while performing the *gharma* sacrifice, a one-eyed dog should bark, he addresses it with the mantra, "O Indra, moving about, bind him! Then, having thrown a firebrand blazing at both ends toward that direction, he says, "O Agni, converse with Agni," touches water, and then worships it with the remainder of the section beginning, "Once to thee, O Agni, be homage."

Thus, the vulture, the female jackal, the fearful sheep, the owl, the long-faced one, the being possessed by a spirit, and the bird with blood on its beak—whatever is desired here, such as "the owl has swooped down" and "O long-faced one," and "having spread out his thighs over the beings"—these have been explained according to their respective forms; [this concludes] the throwing away of the firebrands and the ritual attendance.
Or rather, these [rites] should be universal. || 25 ||

If she should have worms from a cow that yields warm milk, he should kill her worms with this section beginning, "O worm, I kill you with Atri," or rather, this [rite] should be universal for all cases.
If he should practice sorcery, he should offer blood with this Anuvāka beginning with "āhara āvadya. || 27 ||

If one should wish to overcome him, having fasted for twelve nights, he should go to him and address him with this section beginning, "By the Brahman I curse you," and with this section beginning, "O thou born of the Ucchaśimī. Or, having gone to the cow-pen of one whom he hates, he should place there the herb named *svajā*, or he may shake the southern door-post of the cow-pen; these are the ritual procedures not connected with a sacrifice. 28.
If the Udgātṛ priest should not sing the Sāman, the Adhvaryu himself should sing it with the Anuvāka beginning with "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ."
Now, regarding the office of the Brahman priest: he goes along with those [priests] connected by movement; he stands still with those connected by their position. (Khaṇḍa 14) 24.7.30.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the twenty-fourth book of the Pravargya-sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
We shall explain the intermediate initiation (avāntaradīkṣā).

During the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious constellation, in the afternoon, having had his hair and beard shaved, and having gone out toward the east or the north, he establishes the fire on a barren plot where no roof-covering is visible, spreads grass around it, and causes four moist *udumbara* fuel-sticks—unbroken at the tips and a span in length—to be placed upon the fire, anointed with ghee, while reciting the mantras beginning with "The earth is the kindling-stick."
With the formulas, "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall perform the vow," and so forth, he worships the deities according to their respective forms. || 3 ||
Then he causes him to recite the opening invocations of all the sections (anuvākas), or those of the first and the last.
Having performed the propitiatory rite with the final Anuvāka, he then closes his eyes and restrains his speech.
Then, having wrapped his head from left to right with an unwashed garment while facing it, he causes him to enter the village after sunset. || 6 ||
Restraining his speech, he remains standing or sitting through this night.

On the following day, having gone out toward the eastern or northern direction, and having established the fire on a barren spot where no roof is visible, and having strewn grass around it, he wraps his head with the verse, "The birds, the fair-winged ones," and worships the sun with the verse, "That which has risen, that is the eye. Then he causes him to look at six things; some say seven: the fire, the sun, a water-pot, a stone, gold, a calf, and a pregnant cow as the seventh.
Having first demonstrated three [qualities], he demonstrates the subsequent ones. || 9 ||
(Then, having given this garment to the teacher, he worships the sun with the verse beginning "vayaḥ suparṇāḥ. || 24.8.10 ||
Now, concerning his studentship (brahmacarya). || 11 ||
In the case of the eternal. ||12||
One should not eat at night. || 13 ||
If he should eat, it would burn him. || 14 ||
One should not offer it into an earthen vessel. || 15 ||
He should not converse with a woman or a Śūdra. || 16 ||
One should not carry an umbrella nor wear sandals. || 17 ||
One should not mount [a seat] like a wheel. || 18 ||
One should not look at one whose life has departed; one should not bathe. 19.
One should not look at a gathering. 24.8.20.
Not a vessel for what is not food. || 21 ||
Nor palaces. || 22 ||
One should not eat the food of a corpse. || 23 ||
He should neither anoint himself nor have himself anointed. 24. (Section 15)
One should observe a fast on the eighth day and on the full-moon day, remaining restrained in speech.
One should not lie down at all. || 26 ||
One should observe this vow for one year. || 27 ||
In this very year, he should study. || 28 ||
Furthermore, he should observe this vow for as long as his study lasts. || 29 ||

When the year has elapsed, having stepped out toward the eastern or northern direction, having established the fire on a barren spot where no roof is visible, having strewn grass around it (and having performed the dismissal as before, touched the *madantī* water, and performed the peace-rite with the first *anuvāka*), he adds fuel sticks with the mantras beginning with "dyauḥ samit" repeated, and worships the deities with the mantras beginning with "āditya vratapate" repeated. 24.8.30.
( Having performed the rite of pacification with the final Anuvāka, and having given a gift to the teacher,) he has his hair and beard shaved. || 31 ||
Then, he [should perform] his private recitation with regard to the daily [obligation]. || 32 ||
One should not study without having completed the formal recitation of the Veda.
Not at night. || 34 ||

Nor [should he do so] after committing a fault against the navel, nor after engaging in unchaste conduct, nor after washing his teeth, nor after eating meat, nor after arranging his hair, nor after having his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, nor while wearing a garland. 35.

Not facing north, nor facing south, not when it is damp, nor when it is dry, not when it has not rained, not under a cloud, not in the shade, not when the sun has turned away, not while looking at green barley, not near a domestic animal, not near a wild animal, and not near water. 36.
He did not look at raw meat, nor at blood that had been shed; he did not look at palaces, nor at bodies, nor at corpses, nor at broken vessels.

(When about to study,) having gone out toward the eastern or northern direction, having established the fire in a barren spot where no roof is visible, having strewn grass around it, having touched the *madantī* water, and having performed the pacification rite (*śānti*) with the first section (*anuvāka*), he should sit down to the west of the fire upon *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* blades, and recite [the text] continuously. 38.
Or, having granted a boon, [he should perform it] in the domestic fire (aupāsana). || 39 ||
When being requested [to teach], one should not speak other words.

When about to study, having sipped the *madantī* water and performed the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the first section (*anuvāka*), he should study. Having studied, and likewise in all ritual acts wherever he perceives that a propitiatory rite has been omitted, he should perform the propitiatory rite once more and then study. 41.
Having gone out from the Pravargya ceremony, one should not study anything else until having re-entered; one should not study anything else [until then]. 42.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the twenty-fourth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth book of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra.
Now begins the first chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the modes of living. || 1 ||
The measurement is according to its length. ||2||
Having practiced that for half [the duration]. ||3||
On the third [side], at a point six parts from the end, he makes a mark. || 4 ||
Having fixed the two ends at the two ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord.
Having bent the right [hand] according to the characteristic mark, he makes the sign. || 6 ||
In the same way, [one should proceed] toward the north. || 7 ||
The opposite is the reverse. || 8 ||
That is concentration. ||9||
Decrease or increase [of the vowel] is caused by that [consonant]. 25.1.10.
Having practiced the length, the fourth length is the additional [measurement]; the diagonal cord is the cross-measure; the remainder is the side-measure.
The wandering has been explained. || 12 ||
The diagonal cord of a long rectangle produces both that which the side-measuring cord and the cross-measuring cord produce when they are separate. || 13 ||
The manner of wandering has been described by those who possess such knowledge. || 14 ||
The diagonal cord of a square produces an area twice as large; it is the double-maker of that equal [square].
One should increase the measurement by a third. || 16 ||
And that [is established] by the fourth [chapter], which consists of thirty-four sections.
It is with distinction. || 18 ||

One should increase the measurement by half; one should set aside half of that, and half of that [half], internally; and half of the remainder, externally. Having doubled what remains, one makes a mark in the middle. || 19 || (kha.1)
Now, another yoga: || 25.1.20 ||
He makes a rope of the exact measure [of the altar], with loops at both ends. ||21||

Having stretched a cord along the spine from the middle mark to the middle of the two halves, he drives stakes into the ground at the marks on the two loops. Having fastened the two loops onto the two penultimate stakes, he pulls [the cord] southward by means of the middle mark and makes a sign. Having fastened the two loops onto the middle stake, he makes a sign directly above it, pulls [the cord] southward by means of the middle mark, and drives a stake into the ground.

Having fastened the cord on that [mark], and the other [cord] on the eastern [mark], he should draw a line from the middle mark to the southern shoulder; having released it from the eastern [mark] and fastened the other [cord] on the western [mark], he should draw a line from the middle mark to the southern hip; in the same way, [he should do so for] the northern hip and shoulder.

Then, having driven stakes at the two ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and in the middle, and having doubled that difference and made a mark, one should bring the cord to the middle point; having made loops at the two ends and having fastened the cord with the extra length on the middle stake, one should fasten the other end on the front stake and, by means of the mark, draw out the southern shoulder. Having unfastened it from the front stake and fastened it on the rear stake, one should, by means of the mark itself, draw out the southern hip. In the same way, [one should draw out] the northern hip and shoulder. 23. (Section 2)
The measure for its length is two transverse karaṇīs; the diagonal cord for it is three karaṇīs.
The third case-affix is explained by this [same rule]; however, its division is ninefold. || 25 ||
The compound of two equal squares has been explained. || 26 ||
The combination of two squares of different dimensions [results in a rectangle]. || 27 ||
One should mark the greater [number] with the smaller diagonal. || 28 ||
He joins both [ends] of the diagonal cord of the elder [cord]. || 29 ||

Regarding this, it has been said: "One who wishes to reduce a square to another square should, for as much as he wishes to reduce it, mark out an increase by means of its diagonal; he should draw a line across the side-measure of that increased area and contract the other side toward it. Wherever that [line] falls, there he should cut away. (Śulba-sūtra 25.1.30)
By cutting [the connection], it is cast out. || 31 ||
The diagonal cord has been brought together; it serves as the fourfold multiplier.
Whatever those two do when they are separate, both together do that very same thing. || 33 ||
The crosswise-measuring cord [is] one person; the remaining three [are the side-measuring cords]. || 34 ||
Thus it has been said: || 35 ||
One who desires to make a long quadrangle into a square should cut off a portion along the cross-measure, divide the remainder, and lay it down on both sides. (Section 36) (Khanda 3)
One should fill up any missing portion with an adventitious [substance]. || 37 ||
Its decrease has been explained. || 38 ||

One who wishes to make a square into a long rectangle should make its side-measure as large as he desires; then, having divided whatever is in excess according to that measurement, he should lay it down in the appropriate manner. || 39 ||
Desiring to construct a square mandala.
One should cause it to fall from the center onto the tip. ||41||
Having drawn [the line] from the side, one should draw the mandala together with an additional third part. || 42 ||
That mandala is impermanent. || 43 ||
As much as it is diminished, so much does it come from elsewhere. ||44||
Desiring to make a square mandala, one should divide the diameter into fifteen parts; having set aside two, thirteen remain—that is the variable square.
By means of the measuring cord, the square is established.
Anything other than an injunction [is not dharma]. || 47 ||
From two, four [arise]. ||48||
Nine by three. ||49||
As many times as there are measures of the cord, it forms that many squares.
Likewise, there is perception. ||51||
A cord measuring one and a half puruṣas makes two [spaces] of one and a quarter [puruṣas].
The extreme extension is one and a half or two and a quarter puruṣas, plus six and a half padas. || 53 ||
To whatever extent it exceeds [the required size], he places that [excess] on both sides. || 54 ||
That which he makes square with effort is at the corner. || 55 ||
The measurement of the pedestal is prescribed as half the measurement [of the main image]. || 56 ||
Because it serves to complete the meter, even though it measures twice the length of a half-verse. || 57 ||
In the third [day], the ninth digit. (kha0 4)
Thus ends the first chapter in the twenty-fifth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
Now begins the second chapter.
Regarding the sacrificial ground for the establishment of the sacred fires (*āgnyādheya*), it is known that [the measurements] are between the *Gārhapatya* and *Āhavanīya* fires.

A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fire at a distance of eight steps; a Rājanya, at eleven; a Vaiśya, at twelve; or at twenty-four, or at an unlimited distance, or as far as he might think fit with his eye. Therefore, it is heard in the scripture without distinction for all classes that "it should not be established too far away. (2)
To the south-east, at a distance of one-third [of the space] closer to the Gārhapatya fire, the location of the Dakṣiṇāgni is known.
Having divided the space between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires into five or six parts, one adds the sixth or seventh part as an additional portion and divides the whole equally into three parts.

At the third [mark], he makes a mark: having fixed the two ends of the cord between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires, he draws it toward the south along the mark and makes a sign. This is the location for the Dakṣiṇā fire, according to the force of the scriptural injunction.

The altar for the New Moon sacrifice is known from the injunction: "It should be as large as the sacrificer, or of unlimited size; it should be so wide that the sacrificial oblations can be placed upon it; he raises the two shoulders of the altar facing eastward on both sides of the Āhavanīya fire; the two buttocks face westward reaching toward the Gārhapatya fire; it is more deeply depressed in the middle—for such indeed is a woman. Having measured a space of one's own height behind the Āhavanīya fire and marked out a long square, one doubles that cord and makes loops at both ends.

Having fixed the two ends to the marks on the right hip and shoulder in the middle, he draws it southward along the mark and makes a reference-point (nimitta). Having fixed the cord and brought the two ends together, he should draw a line from the right hip to the right shoulder. He should do the same on the north side. Having likewise doubled the cross-measure (tiyaṅmānī), he should draw lines behind and in front as well. Once the structure is measured out, he should shorten the two side-measures (pārśvamānyau) at the front, according to the force of the scriptural injunction.

"Thirty steps or thirty paces [is the length]. It is known from the *Saumikī Vedi* that "the cross-line is thirty-six [units] to the west, twenty-four to the east, and twenty-four to the north. On a cord of thirty-six units, having joined eighteen together, one makes a mark at twelve and a mark at fifteen. Having fixed the two ends on the two ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā*-line, and having drawn it southward by fifteen units, one drives in a peg; likewise on the north side—those are the two hips (*śroṇī*).
Having turned that [line] around, he pulls it taut with that same [cord] and fixes a peg at the twelfth [mark]; in this way, he establishes the two shoulders on the north side as well.
The measurement with a single cord for the three-by-four and four-by-three [sections] is the diagonal cord of the five-by-five. ||9||
With those [fingers] repeated three times, [he touches] the two shoulders.
The hips are formed by the four [muscles] practiced [on both sides]. ||11||
The diagonal cord for the two [sides] consisting of twelve and five [units] is thirteen [units]; by means of these, the two shoulders are formed.
The hips are formed by [the lines] repeated twice. || 13 ||

The diagonal cord between the fifteen- and eight-unit cords is seventeen units long; by means of these, the two hips [are marked]. The diagonal cord between the twelve- and thirty-five-unit cords is thirty-seven units long; by means of these, the two shoulders [are marked].
There are this many altar-sites for the performance of the ritual. || 16 ||
The great altar is one thousand paces minus twenty-eight.

From the right shoulder, one should mark off twelve [units] toward the right hip; having made the cut, one should place the pieces on the other side in reverse order. That is the long quadrangle, the Mahāvedi; one should observe it as thus prepared.
"He sacrifices on the third part of the Soma-altar," so it is known from the Sautrāmaṇī ritual.
The third side of the prakrama becomes equivalent to the position of the prakrama itself. || 25.2.20 ||
Or by means of the three modes of action. || 21 ||
The two transverse measurements are eight and ten [aṅgulas] respectively.
The *pṛṣṭhya* [stoma] consists of twelve [verses]. ||23||
Three hundred and twenty-four padas constitute the altar for the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
And it is known from the Aśvamedha that "the altar is twice as large. || 25 ||
The double-measure (dvikaraṇī) of a pace becomes equivalent to the position of a pace. ||26||
The *prakrama* consists of two or three *padas*.
In the case of a progression, one may act according to one's desire, because the meaning of the word is intended to apply to all the stages.
Of the sacrificer. || 29 ||
Or rather, [it belongs] to the Adhvaryu. 25.2.30.
For he is indeed the agent of all activities. || 31 ||
"It is known that for one who has performed the Nirūḍhapaśubandha sacrifice, the altar (vedi) is the size of a chariot.
Regarding this, they indeed say:
The front crossbar is as long as a chariot pole; the rear crossbar is as long as a chariot axle; the side crossbars at the front are as long as the yoke of a two-wheeled cart.
Or, as far as there is a gap on the outside, one should pull it out by exactly fifteen [units] using a single cord as described. || 35 ||
With a half-glance and with half a yoke-measure, one should mark off the hips and shoulders.
Moreover, they also cite this: || 37 ||
The pole is said to be one hundred and eighty-eight [units] long; the axle four hundred; and the yoke eighty-six. Such a chariot is called "mobile"; this is the measurement of the chariot.

The eastern side is six *aratnis* long; the western cross-side is four [aratnis]; the eastern cross-side is three [aratnis]. Having marked the measurements on a single cord—namely, one and a half, two, and two and a half [units] out of six—he makes the marks. He ties a loop in the ninth [unit] and fixes the two ends at the ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā*. Having pulled it southward by two and a half [units], he drives a peg into two [units]. Likewise on the north; those are the two hips (*śroṇī*). With the cord reversed, he marks the two shoulders (*aṃsa*); having pulled it outward by that same amount, he drives a peg into one and a half [units].
In this way, the two shoulders [of the altar] extend to the north; it is understood from the *Some* that the *uttaravedi* should consist of ten paces.
Having stated that [the side] is one rope, one should then draw out the hips and shoulders by means of exactly fifteen units minus half.
In the case of a square [altar], one should bring together the two side-measures at the front.
On account of the power of the Vedic revelation. || 42 ||

In the case of the words *pada*, *yuga*, *aratni*, *viyati*, *prādeśa*, *prakrama*, and *śamyā*, when used for the purpose of measurement, one may act according to one's desire, because the meaning of these words is subject to variation.
"It is as large as the sacrificer and has four corners"—thus it is known from the Pitṛka Veda.
Then, having subtracted half of that same cord as stated by the *Pañcadaśika*, one should draw out the hips and shoulders from it.
It is known from tradition that the Sadas measures nine aratnis across and twenty-seven [aratnis] extending toward the north.

According to some, there are eighteen [folds]. That which was described as a single cord by the fifteen-fold [method] should be reduced by four and a half [folds] to determine the hips and shoulders. (47)
"It is known from the injunction regarding the *uparavas* that they have openings of one span (*prādeśa*) and intervals between them of one span. (Khaṇḍa 7) || 48 ||

Having measured out a square of one *aratni* and having driven stakes into its corners, one should trace around each [corner] with a radius of half a *prādeśa*, according to the force of the scriptural injunction.
"It is known from the Gārhapatya altar that it should be four-cornered and of the measure of a vyāyāma. (25.2.50)
According to some, it is square; according to others, it is circular. 51.
One should cause the third and seventh spans of the width to be made as the measure for the exertion. || 52 ||
These amount to twenty-one. || 53 ||
In the foundation, the bricks are oriented eastward in the first layer, and northward in the subsequent one.
Having formed a body of earth within the mandala and having fixed a peg (śaṅku) in the center, one should draw the mandala around it with a radius equal to half the span. || 55 ||
And upon that, one should construct a square altar, as far as it may be possible.
Having drawn that ninefold [mandala]. || 57 ||
Each one of these three is divided into three parts, and thus it is laid down.
One should form the corners toward the intermediate directions of the square. || 59 ||
In the other arrangement, it is brought to the middle. ||25.2.60||
One should pile them in reverse order according to as many layers (prastāra) as one intends to construct.
It is known from the tradition regarding the hearths (*dhiṣṇiya*) that they are merely of the size of a *piśīla*; according to some, they are square; according to others, they are circular. 62.
Having fashioned bodies out of clay. || 63 ||

Having scratched the Āgnīdhrīya fire-place in nine divisions, having placed a stone in the place of one [division], and having scratched the others in their respective order, he should lay them down as appropriate. (Section 8)
Thus ends the second chapter in the twenty-fifth book of the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
Now begins the third chapter.
It is known from scripture: "Verily, he who piles the fire-altar becomes as it were [the sun] himself."
"Or rather, this [altar] is built as a likeness of birds, because of the injunction regarding its form. (2)
Or rather, because it is directly prescribed, [the rule applies] only to that which is explicitly mentioned in the sacred tradition.

With the bamboo pole he measures out seven man-lengths: three man-lengths toward the east and four toward the north; the wings and the tail are each one man-length long; the body is four man-lengths. || 4 ||
With a cubit, he extends the right wing from the south. ||5||
The tail at the back should be one span or one palm in length.
The other wing is one cubit longer. || 7 ||
The first fire is of one kind; the second is of two kinds; the third is of three kinds. These indeed emerge in this very manner from the one hundred and one-fold [fire].
Therefore, one should indeed pile it in sevenfold.
Or rather, it is known that there are seven types of ordinary fire, and from that point upward, they increase by one each time.
For those [diagrams] consisting of one type and so forth, there are no wings or tails. || 11 ||
Because there are seven kinds of supplementary statements. || 12 ||
And because of the contradiction with the Vedic revelation. || 13 ||
Of those beginning with the eightfold [empowerment], whatever remains after the seven, one should divide that into seven parts and infuse it into each person.
Because no modification of the form is heard [in the scripture]. || 15 ||
"It is known from scripture: 'He measures with a man's length,' and 'He measures with a bamboo pole. || 16 ||
He makes an opening in the bamboo at a distance equal to the sacrificer's height with his arms raised. ||17||
The third [syllable] is in the middle. ||18||
With another [line], he lays down a bamboo pole, oriented lengthwise along the spine of the altar, pointing eastward, at the location of the sacrificial post-hole. || 19 ||

Having driven stakes into the apertures and unfastening [the cord] from the other two, one should mark out the southern line toward the east. Having unfastened it from the eastern stake and fastened it to the western one, one should mark out the southern line toward the west until the end.

Having unfastened the bamboo at the middle [hole], having fastened it at the last hole without leaving a gap, and having placed the southern bamboo so that its top is level with the line, he drives a peg into the last hole, fastens the middle hole to it, fixes the other two [ends] at the ends of the line, and drives pegs into the two holes. That man [the space occupied by the bamboo] is a square. 21.
Having thus laid out four persons in a clockwise direction, he measures them within himself. || 22 ||
A man on the right wing, a man at the tail, and a man on the left. || 23 ||
It has been stated that [the measurement] is by a cubit to the south for the southern [side]. || 24 ||
Alternatively, having laid a bamboo pole of human length diagonally from the spine, one should mark out the right shoulder from those two [points] on the eastern side.
Having reversed the hips. || 26 ||
The right shoulder is as before. || 27 ||
Or he measures it with a cord according to the method of the *uttaravedi*, or he measures it with a bamboo pole. ||28||

In the case of the wings, tail, and flanks, whether there is an increase or a decrease by one-third, one should determine the seventh part of the side-measure (vidhāsaptamakaraṇī) corresponding to the person (puruṣa), and proceed with the construction using that.
One should have the bricks made with a fifth part of the size of a man.
One and a half [parts] for each of those; that is the second [set].
One part of the person is on one side, a span (prādeśa) on the other; that is one-third of it. || 32 ||
That fourth [part] is one span on all sides; the fifteen-part [bricks] are equal squares, and that is the fifth [part].
The vertical measurement of the bricks [is as follows]: one should have it made with a fifth part of the knee. 34.
With half [of that] for the Nākasads and the Pañcacoḍas. || 35 ||
Whatever of those being cooked should diminish due to the fecal matter, one should replenish that with [fresh] dung. ||36||
Because the quantity of feces is indefinite. || 37 ||
On the *upadhāna* layer, one should place ten bricks measuring one and a half [units] on the east, facing westward, upon the self.
Ten [lines] to the west, facing east. || 39 ||

There are five at each of the tips of the wings and five at the junctions of the wings; these are the objects [of measurement], and those measuring half a brick in size are for the wings. || 25.3.40 ||
Having laid down five [bricks] on each of the two sides of the tail facing south, and five facing north upon the tail, one should place a span (prādeśa) [of space]. || 41 ||
One should cover the entire fire-altar with bricks that have five parts.
One should complete the count with fifteen parts. || 43 ||
In the subsequent arrangement, one should place ten Adhyardha-bricks on the self (the body of the altar), ten extending northward on the south side and ten extending southward on the north side.
As the two wings are in the first layout, so are the tail; as the tail is, so are the wings. In the case of reversal, it is the opposite.
One should cover the entire fire-altar with bricks measuring five parts; one should complete the count with bricks measuring fifteen parts. || 46 ||
One should pile them in reverse order, as many layers as one intends to construct.
"It is known that there are five layers (citayaḥ) and one piles up with five fillings (purīṣas); the layer ends with the filling, because the filling is a distinct entity. (Sūtra 48)
One building the fire-altar for the first time should build it knee-deep and consisting of a thousand bricks. ||49||
The second [enclosure] was two thousand [bow-lengths] deep, reaching up to the navel. || 25.3.50 ||
The third [layer] is three thousand [yojanas] high, reaching up to the mouth. || 51 ||
It is known from scripture: "One who desires heaven should pile [the fire-altar] higher and higher, more excellent, greater, vast, immense, and immeasurable. || 52 ||

In a two-thousand-brick altar, there are layers of two courses; in a three-thousand-brick altar, there are layers of three courses. From the fourth day onwards, the measurement of the bricks is constant for each day's work.
And it is known from scripture: "Having piled a larger altar, one should not pile a smaller one. (Section 11)
Thus ends the third paṭala in the twenty-fifth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi Sūtra.
Now begins the fourth chapter. It is known from scripture: "One should pile the fire-altar with squares. || 1 ||
They are square, because the word lacks any qualifying suffix.
It is known that they are one foot in measure; they are one finger-joint in measure; they are one thigh-bone in measure; they are one cubit in measure; and they are one span in measure. || 3 ||
The atom (aṇūka) consists of four parts; the cubit (aratni) likewise consists of five parts, as does the span (urva).
A brick for the foot is one-quarter of a measure; in this matter, there is freedom of choice, because the meaning of the word is unrestricted.
On the two shoulder-supports (upadhāna), one should place eight quarter-bricks (pādeṣṭakā) each, which are fourth-parts of the [main] bricks, at the tips of the wings.
And likewise at the two twilights, one should withdraw oneself by six finger-breadths.
On the hips and shoulders, eight lines run both eastward and westward.
In the interval between the junctions, there are five parts plus one-quarter. ||9||
Having placed a span-measure upon the tail. || 25.4.10 ||
One should cover the entire fire-altar with bricks measuring four parts.
One should complete the count with brick-pieces for the base.
In the subsequent arrangement, at the junction of the tail, there are five-part bricks extending [towards the center]. 13.
One should place those [bricks] upon oneself with fourteen foot-measures, as appropriate. ||14||
One should cover the entire fire-altar with bricks having five parts, and complete the required number with quarter-bricks (pādeṣṭakās). || 15 ||
One should pile [the bricks] alternately as many times as one intends to perform the layers (*prastāra*).
(Section 12) For those [altars] beginning with the single-variety (*ekavidha*), one should have the bricks made according to the *karaṇī* measuring twelve or thirteen [parts]. (17)
And there are also brick-pads for the feet.
One should pile them in reverse order, as many layers as one intends to construct.

For those beginning with the single-fold [mudrās], the upper measurement for all of them is according to their respective numbers, as prescribed by the scripture, using the first, second, or third finger-breadth. || 25.4.20 ||
The optional rites are modifications of the qualities, because they belong to the category of teachings concerning qualities.
"One who has rivals should pile the *prauga-cit*," so it is known from the tradition.
It has the shape of a cart. || 23 ||
Having made a square plot of ground twice the size of the fire-altar, which measures one *aratni* and one *prādeśa*. ||24||
From the midpoint of the eastern working-line, one should draw [the lines] toward the two hips; that is the standard *prauga* (forepart).
The instruments [of action] and piling are stated to be of one kind. || 26 ||
One should have the *prauga* bricks made.

"One should pile the fire-altar with two *praugas* on both sides if he desires, 'May I push back my kinsmen who are my rivals, and those yet to be born,' so it is known. It has the shape of a cart on both sides. (28)

Just as in the case of a cart with its face turned away, having thus laid out this very same long rectangle, one should, by implication, place [the markers] on the south and north sides at the distance of the front and back cords; that is the eternally double-prauga altar.
As prescribed for the *prauga-citi*, one should have bricks made that are shaped like a *prauga* on both sides.
"One who has rivals should pile a fire-altar in the shape of a chariot wheel," so it is known. It is circular. || 31 ||
Having made a circular area of ground as large as the fire-altar, which measures one *aratni* and one *prādeśa*. || 32 ||
And upon that, one should construct a square altar, as large as it may be possible.
One should have twelve bricks made from its [the altar's] width; having laid down six of them along the front edge, one should divide the remainder into eight parts.

In the layering of the square altar, one should form the corners toward the intermediate directions. In the subsequent layering, one should pile them in an alternating manner for as many layers as one intends to construct. (Kaṇḍikā 13) || 35 ||
"One desiring food should pile the Droṇacit," so it is known from tradition.
The hilt is the tenth part of the entire length of the blade. || 37 ||
By its tail, the subtraction (or removal) has been stated. || 38 ||
One should have twelve bricks made from its [the altar's] side-measure. || 39 ||
And there are also quarter-bricks measuring one and a half [units].

In the *upadhāna* (laying), one should place bricks measuring one and a half [units] on the front part of the body facing west, and on the two hips facing east, with their tips extending over the whole [body]. One should cover the entire fire-altar with square bricks. One should complete the count with quarter-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*). In the subsequent layer (*prastāra*), one places ten bricks measuring one and a half [units] on the south side of the body facing north. On the north side as well, one places them facing south; and on the two sides of the handle (*tsaru*), one places bricks facing south and north. One should cover the entire fire-altar with square bricks. One should complete the count with quarter-bricks. One should pile the layers in an alternating manner for as many layers as one intends to construct.
"It is known from tradition: 'One who desires cattle should pile the Samūhya fire-altar.'"
He lays down the bricks in groups. || 43 ||
According to some teachers, having dug out pits for the *cātvāla* in the various directions, one fills them back up with earth from those [pits].
"One desiring a village should pile the Paricāyya fire-altar," so it is known.
He encloses the central naturally perforated brick with groups of bricks moving clockwise; that is the *paricāyya*.
"One desiring cattle should pile the *upacāyya* altar," so it is known.
It is stated by Paricāyya: "He who desires, 'May I prosper in the world of the ancestors,' should pile the Śmaśānacit; so it is known. (48)

Indeed, the two types of funeral mounds are either square or circular; in this matter, one may act according to one's desire, because the meaning of the word is subject to [the speaker's] intention. || 49 ||
Or he may be square, whose treatise on qualities is also square.
Except for the handle, it is described as a heap in the shape of a *droṇa* measure. ||51||
"One who desires cattle should pile the Chandaścit," so it is known.
"One should pile with all the meters"—this is one view; "with the natural ones"—this is another. (Section 14)
Thus ends the fourth paṭala in the twenty-fifth praśna of the Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra.
Now begins the fifth paṭala.
"One who desires heaven should pile the Śyenacit," so it is known.
With its wings bent and its tail spread out, it takes the form of a hawk. ||2||
Thereafter, he moves it from west to east.
He pushes it from the front toward the west.
For it is understood that among birds, the spreading of the wings occurs in this very manner. || 5 ||
The fire-altar, including the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, amounts to sevenfold. ||6||
The span is one-fourth of the self, and there are eight fourth-parts.
Of those, three are on the head. ||8||
One should divide [the remainder] between the other two sides. || 9 ||
A man is five cubits in height. ||25.5.10||
A vyāyāma consists of four aratnis, and an aratni consists of twenty-four aṅgulas. || 11 ||
Half of that is a span (prādeśa); such is the established rule.
The length of the wings is nine and a half cubits minus one-fourth of a finger-breadth. || 13 ||
He makes a rope two puruṣas long with loops at both ends.
The characteristic is in the middle. || 15 ||

Having fixed the end at the two rear corners of the wing by means of a measuring cord, one should stretch it forward; likewise from the front. By this, the northern wing is explained along with its curvature. || 16 ||
The Ātman measures two puruṣas in length and one and a half puruṣas in width. || 17 ||
At the tail, one should extend a cord one and a half puruṣas wide, directed toward the west. || 18 ||
To its south [he places] another, and to its north as well. || 19 ||
One should draw them obliquely so that even half a man remains at the end.
Having made a square at the head with a side of half a man's length, one should mark off those same [measurements] from the midpoint of the eastern cord toward the south and north.
One should not cut off the hips or the shoulders with respect to the points of convergence. (Section 15)
For it is just like the hawk. || 23 ||
One should cause the fifth measurement of the person to be the length (karaṇa) and the sixth to be the width (vyāsa); that first [measurement] should be bent according to the proper application.
Those two are joined facing east; that is the second [section]. || 25 ||
One should increase the sixth part of the first [measurement] by an eighth part; that which is bent according to the requirement is the third [measurement].
The adhyardha is four parts; one should divide it diagonally by a measure of one-fourth of that [adhyardha], and that is the fourth part.
The fifth is half of a fourth part. || 28 ||
Its sixth [section] is a division across the diagonal.

One should draw a line five parts long and ten parts wide from west to east. To the south and north of that, one should draw two other lines across from the southern and western corners; that is the seventh [mark].
In this way, the other subsequent [lines] are to be known; one should draw the eighth [line] from the northern extremity. || 31 ||
The ninth [layer] consists of a four-part division with a diagonal split on both sides.
In the placement, there are sixty [bricks] in each of the two wings; one should place the first ones facing north.
On each of the two sides of the tail, there are eight times sixty [hair-whorls]. (kha016)
First three, then one, then three, then one. || 35 ||
When there is doubt regarding two questions, the fourth case endings are used for both.
And after those two, the fifth and the sixth [syllables] are joined with the earth (a). || 37 ||
In the remainder, there are ten fourths.
On the hips and shoulders, eight lines are drawn both eastward and westward.
And in the remainder, there are twenty-six, eight, sixty-four, four, and five [syllables]. (25.5.40)
The two [lines] on the head are in the fourth position; in the field, they are transverse, and in front of those two, they are oriented toward the east.
This is the two-hundred-fold arrangement. ||42||
In the subsequent arrangement, there are five second [notes] on each of the two wings and the tail. 43.
And for the Adhvaryu, the third [part]; he himself consists of eight parts. ||44||
In the remainder, he should place forty-five bricks each, with their first lines facing east. || 45 ||
On the two sides of the tail, there are five [fingers] each on the seventh [toes].
And from either the second or the fourth [note], one [syllable] each is combined. 47.
In the remainder, there are thirteen eighth [notes]. || 48 ||
On the hips and shoulders, eight fourths [of the measure] are for the southern and northern [lines]. || 49 ||
And in the remainder, there are twenty, thirty, and sixty [syllables], and one [verse] of five [syllables].
On the head are two [lines] in the fourth case, and before those, four in the ninth case. ||51||
This is the two-hundred-fold arrangement. || 52 ||
One should pile them in reverse order for as many layers as one intends to construct. (Kaṇḍikā 17)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the twenty-fifth book of the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.
Now begins the sixth chapter:
"One who desires heaven should pile the Śyenacit," so it is known.
With its wings curved and its tail spread out, it takes the form of a hawk. ||2||
Thereafter, he pushes it forward from west to east.
He pushes it out from the east towards the west. || 4 ||
For it is understood that among birds, the fanning of the wings occurs in this very manner. || 5 ||

A man of twenty hundred and sixteen finger-breadths becomes sevenfold when provided with the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*. Of those [finger-breadths], forty are in the body, three in the head, fifteen in the tail, and thirty-one in the right wing; likewise in the left.
Having laid out a long square measuring one and a half puruṣas across and two puruṣas in length, one should remove two sixteen-part squares each from the hips and the shoulders.

Forty [units] remain. Having made that self [the altar] square with a side of one and a half puruṣas at the head, he should mark off from the middle of the eastern working-line toward the south and north by that same measure. 8.
Three remain; that is its head. || 9 ||
The male figure is two units wide; its length is sixteen parts, and the right wing is one-sixteenth part [of that]. ||9||

In the same way, on the northern side, at the tip of the wing, one should construct four squares with a side equal to one-fourth of a man's length; having drawn diagonal lines across them, one should remove the half-portions.
Thirty-one remain. || 12 ||
Leaving a space at the tip of the wing, one should draw an eastward line in the middle of the wing.

At the end of the fortnight, having fixed a man [as a measuring unit], one should make a mark at the end of a man; from that mark, one should make another mark toward the east at the end of a man; between these two marks, one should draw the two ends separately—that is the bending together.
By this, the opposing position has been explained. || 15 ||
Two puruṣas at the back, half a puruṣa at the front, and a puruṣa less a quarter in length; eighteen karaṇīs on the two sides—these fifteen [karaṇīs] comprise the tail. 16.
One should take possession of the Ṣoḍaśī with four [verses]. (kha0 18)
By means of the eighth [day], through three eighths, and by means of the fourth, together with a quarter—thus it is without distinction. ||18||
One half-brick with three [verses]. || 19 ||
And by means of two [meditations], it is with a distinction from the fourth [dhyāna]. || 25.5.20 ||
The foot-brick with three [parts]. || 21 ||
By the fourth [dhyāna], one [attainment] is produced; and by the fourth together with its specific qualities (saviśeṣa), [another]. || 22 ||
The wing-brick with four [verses]. || 23 ||
And by means of two, four, and seven [factors]. ||24||
With four [verses] from the middle of each fortnight. ||25||
And by two [of each] of the fourth [categories], and by two of the seventh. ||26||
The tip of the wing [is marked] with three [lines]. || 27 ||

One [type of concentration] arises from the fourth [dhyāna] alone; one arises from both the fourth and the seventh; and one arises from both the fourth and the seventh when the latter is accompanied by specific qualities. || 28 ||
The seventh [measurement] from the side-line is the transverse measure, and the fourth man’s length is the lateral measure; one should extend the construction by means of its diagonal cord.
One should bend the ribs with the seventh [finger] and the planks [of the chest] with the seventh.
On the foundation, there are four foot-bricks in front, at the head.
Another has five at the top of the head. || 32 ||
The two wings extend eleven [units] to the east and eleven to the west.
Eleven [bricks] to the east. || 34 ||
There is also a question; these five [verses] are by another [author]. || 35 ||
Fifteen [units] at the tip of the tail. || 36 ||
There are four on each of the two tips of the wings.
And the objects [of the senses] during the waning and waxing of the fortnights. || 38 ||
One should place [the bricks] around the self-altar with four, four, and sixteen [bricks], as appropriate. || 39 ||
There are four [groups] of four who study in the middle of the fortnight. ||25.5.40||
In the middle of the two wings, one should cover the two wings with wing-bricks (pakṣeṣṭakā) laid facing eastward. || 41 ||
One should cover the remainder with sixteen [bricks]. ||42||
The ultimate external particulars are the [external] particulars. ||43||
Except for the head. ||44||
In the next layer, one should place two *ṣoḍaśī* bricks with their heads toward the east at the outer edge.
These two other objects [are] internal distinctions. (Khaṇḍa 19) || 46 ||
One should place around [the bricks] two half-iṣṭakās as appropriate. ||47||
One should grasp [the object] by means of both external and internal distinctions. || 48 ||
One should place sixteen additional bricks with specific external characteristics at the joints of the self-forming [altar].
On the two tips of the wings, there are four sets of four half-bricks each.
One should cover the two wings with bricks placed on their sides, oriented towards the north.
There are three half-bricks on each of the two sides of the tail.
One should cover the remainder with sixteen [bricks]. || 53 ||
The last [part] is external to the remainder, except for the tail. || 54 ||
Whatever [space] may remain as a square or a triangle, one should cover that with half-bricks or quarter-bricks. || 55 ||
One should complete the count with brick-pieces for the base.
The fifteen-part bricks stand in the place of the minute bricks.
One should pile them in an alternating manner for as many layers (prastāra) as one intends to construct.
The *kaṅkacit* and *alaja-cit* are explained by [the rules for] the *śyenacit*. || 59 ||
In this very manner, the hawk’s wings are broader than its tail and curved; its tail is bent, its body is long, and its head is not circular. || 25.5.60 ||
Therefore, on account of the force of the scriptural statement. || 61 ||
Or it may be without the head. 62.
Because it is not so prescribed. || 63 ||

And it is known from scripture that one should build with the head-piece (kaṅkacita) for one who desires, "May I be born with a head in that world. If [the head-piece] were already present [in the standard altar], why would he say this? || 64 ||
The two wings are curved as in the natural state, and the tail is bent, because of the mention of modification.
Because the Self does not undergo modification according to its own nature. || 66 ||
"It is known from the Aśvamedha that Agni becomes the Tristobha; in that case, there is repetition of all [the verses], because there is no distinction. (Sūtra 68)
The summary of long quadrilaterals with wings and tails has been stated by way of a general rule. || 69 ||
"It is known in the Aśvamedha that the fire becomes twenty-onefold."
In that regard, the practice of the person [is established] from the connection with numbers of cubits and spans; from the connection with numbers of cubits and spans. || 71 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter and the [twenty-fifth] book in the *Satyāṣāḍha-Hiraṇyakeśi-Sūtra*.
Now begins the twenty-sixth book;
therein, the first chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the duties based on conventions and customary conduct. || 1 ||
The convention of those who know the Dharma. || 2 ||
The Vedas are the authority. 3.
The four castes are the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra. || 4 ||

Having scattered their hair and thrown dust [over themselves], clad in a single garment and facing south, they bathe once, emerge, and sitting down with the left knee bent, they wring out their clothes. Day by day, from the eleventh day until the end, they increase the number of handfuls by one; having returned to the village without looking back, they do whatever is pleasing to them.

In the event of deaths among those who have not yet studied the Veda, one shall observe fasting, suspension of study, sleeping on the ground, and ritual bathing in water for two days, three days, six days, or twelve days; in the case of teachers (gurus), one shall observe these except for fasting; and in the case of a mother or father, or according to some, an ācārya, one shall observe them for a year.
Except for fasting and the suspension of Vedic study, he remains like a deceased person (preta) for the rest of his life; according to some, he is touched by water once [after the period]. 74.
Eating once a day, sleeping on the ground, celibacy, and the avoidance of alkaline salts, salt, honey, and meat. (Section 8)

The wife by means of the *nirmanthya* fire. || 26 ||

The twenty-eighth book is completed.
Now begins the twenty-ninth question.
Therein is the first chapter:
On the day of death, on odd days, or during a day and night, a half-month, a month, a season, or a year, he places [the body]. ||1||

If it has not been determined, one may act according to one's desire; [the initiation] should take place on the new moon that follows either the full moon of Māgha, Phālguna, Caitra, Vaiśākha, or Jyeṣṭha. 2.

Taking up the two mallets, either singly or in pairs, they drive out clods of earth from the north side—either those intended for the altar mound or those intended for the bricks—and carry them away toward the south.

Even before [the cremation], they extract medicinal plants from the cemetery grounds: *pāṭhā*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *karṇikāra*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *kaṇṭakī*, *tilvaka*, *vibhītaka*, *arka*, *śara*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *adhyandā*, and other milky-sap trees that have not been uprooted. || 4 ||
In the afternoon, he measures out a cemetery site, five paces on each side. ||5||
Some say there are six in front.
In the case of those [bricks] placed within the altar, the laying down of the bricks involves a connection with the cardinal directions. || 7 ||
In all cases, the commencement is from the front.

Moving counter-clockwise, with the conclusion toward the south; with a triple-stranded cord made of muñja grass or a rope made of balvaja grass, twisted counter-clockwise, having encircled [the body] three times counter-clockwise, he should sprinkle it with odd-numbered water-pots so that it flows away from the vital breath.
One should not offer [the oblation] upon the vital breaths; if one were to offer it upon the vital breaths, one would indeed offer the vital breaths of those who are living. 29.1.10.

Having placed the ritual materials in a large measure-vessel or on a bed, (Section 1, Sūtra 11), on the following day he prepares food for that purpose with a sacrificial animal and sets it aside on the new moon night. (Sūtra 12).
Now, if they are, however, about to perform the oblation, then they erect either a charcoal altar or a bed of embers.
In its eastern half, middle, or western half, they fix a palāśa wooden post with three projections.
Even before this, a person born of a Śūdra or a "brahmin in name only" (brahmabandhu) sits down after being addressed. || 15 ||

"I will not give," the other replied. || 17 ||
In this same way, he performs it in the second [case]. || 18 ||

Or they may continue shaving for as long as the night lasts. || 29.1.20 ||
Upon these words, he places the bodies at the root of the *medhya* tree. || 21 ||
And [one should offer] a jar with a hundred holes at Triviṣūka. || 22 ||

For five, seven, nine, or eleven nights, or for half a month, a month, or a year—so some say—they churn [the fire]; and food should be given according to one's ability, as well as other materials.
Some say that the relinquishing of the ritual materials takes place on the final day.
In this very fire, they silently cook five caru-offerings that have been prepared. || 33 ||

In the latter part of the night they go forth: first the fire, then a water-pot, an ox, the bones, the ritual materials, and whatever else he may require.
They should not bring back anything inferior; kindling this fire, he remains seated between the village and the cremation ground.
When the dawn has broken, having swept the site of the cremation ground with a branch of *palāśa* or a branch of *śamī* that is reddish-brown, he should throw it away, saying: "Go away! (36–37).

Having pulled up a branch from the south, touched water, dug up [the ground], and sprinkled it with water, he yokes the plough with the formula, "O Savitṛ, these are the bodies," using a team of six oxen, twelve oxen, or twenty-four oxen. || 38 ||
It is understood that there are as many hundreds of bricks as there are ox-yokes [of furrows]. || 39 ||
One makes the bricks and the quarter-bricks from a twenty-fourth part of that [measurement]. 40.
The elephant is made of wood. || 41 ||
It is made of muñja grass and consists of cords. || 42 ||
Other than by verbal instruction. || 43 ||
With the two verses beginning "śunaṃ vāhāḥ," he plows six furrows moving from right to left, proceeding away from himself.

"Savitr has fashioned these bodies"—with these words, he places a jar of bones in the middle of the ploughed field. || 46 ||

He spreads the sacrificial grass with its roots intact, pointing toward the south, with the mantra: "I offer this to the ancestors. || 55 ||

Having thoroughly saturated the bones with aged clarified butter, he, sitting to the north and not looking at them, scatters the bones upon the Darbha grass with the formula: "Savitṛ, these are the bodies. || 58 ||
Having brought together the limbs part by part, he then worships it with the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula: "The sun is your eye," and so forth.

Having wiped the jar containing the bones with a cloth that has already been used for wearing, he throws it over and over his head toward the south, saying: "O Death, go along the further path. || 29.1.60 ||
Then he breaks its potsherds completely apart, so that water may not remain within them. || 61 ||

Having covered the bodies with a garment that has already been worn, he sprinkles them with water from a water-pot using a branch of the *udumbara* tree, [reciting] "May the wind be auspicious" (*śaṃ vātaḥ*).

||62||(kha03) He places the bricks in each direction without looking at them, one by one with these respective mantras: "I set thee in the world of the earth," and so forth; the fifth in the middle, and the sixth to the south of it. ||63||
In this manner, he offers the oblations of cooked rice, cakes, and ghee, reciting a separate mantra for each.
With three handfuls of husked grains, he scatters them around [the vessel] from right to left, saying: "I make these yours as *svadhā*, the immortal ones. (65)
He places the stalks of herbs in each direction without looking at them, reciting the mantra "tvāmarjuna" for each.
The restriction of substances for them is determined by the indicative marks of the mantras. || 67 ||
He places the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks with the formula, "Fill the world. || 68 ||

As far as the front, and then immediately after that toward the back. || 72 ||

He sprinkles [the ground] with water from a water-pot or with an udumbara branch, saying: "May the wind be auspicious. || 74 ||
He mutters the *ārohaṇa* [verse]. || 75 ||
