To the west, he places a branch of the *śamī* tree with the words, "O *śamī*, bring peace!"; to the south, barley with the words, "O barley! || 79 ||
Then he worships it, saying: "Go to the earth; go to the intermediate space."
"Draw a line behind this piled altar; everything from here on is the same as the traditional recitation. According to some, he bathes with clay. (Section 4)
Thus ends the first chapter in the twenty-ninth book of the Śrautasūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin (also known as the Pitṛmedhasūtra). 1.1.
Now begins the second chapter.
I shall explain the supreme procedure for the sacrifice to Yama as taught by himself;
indeed, an offering to Antaka (the Ender) should be performed month after month.
Whether desiring intelligence, wealth, or indeed sons,
a twice-born man who performs this on a Saturday with a favorable constellation attains all his desires.
One should diligently perform the Bali offering on the full moon day of Kārtika at the end of the year;
he who does not perform it on the Kārtika day sinks into hell.
Therefore, on the full moon day of Kārttika, a twice-born man who desires all his wishes should indeed prepare an oblation of one prastha of sesame seeds mixed with molasses.
This should not be performed by one alone, but rather together with many others.

Having set out the sacrificial food, consecrated it with a mantra, and taken up the oblation, he says, "Homage to Brahmā, to Prajāpati, to the gods, to the sages, and to the ancestors; to Yama! Having spoken thus, he goes out from the village toward the east or the north, and in a place that is not saline—whether on a riverbank or on level ground—in another pure location, he prepares for him an altar whose corners face those directions. 2.
On that northern [altar], there are five additional altars (uttaravedi), which form the corners of the directions. || 3 ||
Having dug a water-pit to the south and established the fire to the north, he completely covers the high altar with darbha grass. || 4 ||

Having placed a seat (*viṣṭara*) and a cushion (*prastara*) made of *darbha* grass with their tips pointing eastward, he invokes Yama with the mantra: "May the god Yama come here with his gracious aids, for he is indeed attached to these offerings presented here; may he sit upon this well-prepared sacrificial grass for my strength, for my lineage, and for the slaying of my enemies. Then he recites: "When you two came together like twins striving," and "As they brought you both forth. (5)

Having consecrated the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) with the three verses beginning "This, O Yama, is the sacrificial seat" (*imaṃ yama prastaram*), and having offered water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), bathing (*snāna*), foot-washing (*pādya*), and sipping (*ācamanīya*) with pavitras in hand, he presents whatever is available as fragrant substances, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings (*naivedya*). || 6 ||

With black *pratisarā* grass and a black thread, he offers oblations with a middle or a terminal leaf of the *palāśa* tree, saying: "Svāhā to Yama! Svāhā to Antaka! Svāhā to Dharma! Svāhā to Adharma! Svāhā to Anta! Svāhā to Ananta! Svāhā to Vaivasvata! Svāhā to Mṛtyu! Svāhā to Viṣṇu! Svāhā to Bhūḥ! Svāhā to Bhuvaḥ! Svāhā to Suvaḥ! Svāhā to Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ! Thus he offers the sacrificial food up to the end of the *vyāhṛtis*. (Section 7, Part 1)

Then, having placed either Arka leaves or Udumbara leaves upon the middle high-altar (uttaravedī), they present the sacrificial offering to Yama with the verse: "Press the Soma for Yama; offer the oblation to Yama! To Yama goes the sacrifice, well-prepared, with Agni as its messenger. (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 13.8.1.8)

"On the western *uttaravedi*, offer oblations rich in ghee to Yama and step forward; may he grant us long life among the gods so that we may live. On the eastern *uttaravedi*, "offer this most honey-sweet oblation to King Yama; this homage to the seers, the first-born, the makers of the path."

On the southern *uttaravedi*, they offer the oblation to the two dogs with the verse: "O King, entrust this man to those two dogs of yours, the guardians of Yama, the four-eyed ones who watch the path and observe men; grant him well-being and freedom from disease, Om! On the northern *uttaravedi*, they offer the oblation to the two messengers of Yama with the verse: "The two wide-nosed, well-satisfied, swift and powerful messengers of Yama wander among the people; may they give us back our life today so that we may see the sun here, O Blessed One! (9)
With the three Yama-gāthās beginning with "yo 'sya kauṣṭhya," they sing around him three times, keeping him to their right.

Having gone to the Karakūpa well on the south, having arranged his sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), and having bent his left knee, he takes the sacrificial food and pours out three handfuls of water, saying, "May each [portion] be nourishment, svadhā to the fathers! Then, with the seven vyāhṛtis, they go seven steps forward toward the east for him whose vital breaths [are being offered]. 11.
For it is known that they have ascended to the three heavenly worlds. || 12 ||
Having again replenished his vital breaths with the verse, "I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan... (RV 4.39.6). || 13 ||

Then, having returned to him as he came, there is a salutation; there is a salutation to the wells, [a salutation] to the wells. Having approached the *karakūpa* well with the words "Salutation to the wells," they draw up the oblation with the remainder of the section beginning, "To whatever desire Yama [is saluted]. || 14 ||
They cause [the fire] to flow with the verse, "The fair-winged bird in the firmament. || 15 ||
"King Varuṇa has indeed made wide space," with these words they descend into the water. || 16 ||
They purify themselves with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā. || 17 ||
It is known from the scripture that the officiating priests at the *avabhṛtha* bath, having spoken of the impurity of the Kali age, become free from disease in their bodies. || 18 ||
With the four verses beginning "Trita [found him] given by Yama," he worships the Āditya.
One should tie on the protective amulet with the verse, "Up from the darkness we have risen. (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.2.20)

Having offered all the expiatory oblations with the sacrificial butter (havis), they consume the remnants of the offering here with the formula: "This is the consumption; it is the consumption of the nectar. || 21 ||
They pour out the remainder of the food for a beloved son who speaks kindly; [Vaivasvata] said, "One becomes possessed of sons, one becomes possessed of sons. || 22 ||

Yama, having taken the sacrificer who has departed from here onto his lap like a father taking his son, leads him to the state of a friend; he does not turn back from those worlds, nor does he cut off his path—he does not turn back, nor does he cut off his path. || 23 ||
Thus ends the second chapter in the twenty-ninth book of the Śrautasūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin (also known as the Pitṛmedha).
Now begins the third chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the subsequent rites pertaining to the ancestral sacrifice (Paitṛmedhika).
This is what they call the Brahmamedha.

For the sake of the liberation of the twice-born, this [work] was composed by seers who perceive reality, through the power of austerity and yoga, as the most excellent of men. Having combined the *hotṛ* functions and the *pitṛmedha*, the subsequent ritual procedure was ordained; thus, the highest of sacrifices has been briefly prescribed.
The primary nature and its transformations are as previously described. || 3 ||
The oblation for him is performed by the Hotṛ priests together with the Sagrahas.
Supporting [the child] with the Bhartṛsūkta. || 5 ||
Sleeping with one's wives [is permitted]. || 6 ||
He is free from the path of accepting sacrificial fees. || 7 ||
With their hearts, [they offered] pieces of gold.
The construction of the vessels is performed with the *saṃbhāra-yajus* formulas. || 9 ||
The fasting is performed with the *jyotiṣmatī* verses. ||29.3.10||
The attendance upon the two Nārāyaṇas. || 11 ||
And the consecratory formula is: "O Brahmin, you are the one-priest. || 12 ||
The mind, by way of its continuity, is the offering of the oblation. || 13 ||
With "To exertion, svāhā! he offers oblations with the *sruva* ladle. || 14 ||
The recitation of benedictions with the Mṛtyusūkta. ||15||
The Saumya (Saumyā) is the Saṃgāhana. || 16 ||
The worship of the Sun is performed with the Saurya [mantra]. || 17 ||
"Īyuṣṭa" refers to immersion. || 18 ||
From this point onward, the rites pertaining to the funeral sacrifice (paitṛmedhika) continue until the consumption of barley-rice (yavodana).
They call them the Supreme Brahman.
One should employ them in an uncommon cremation ground. || 21 ||
Not to one who is not a teacher, nor to one who is not learned in the Vedas. || 22 ||
Thus the Brahmamedha sacrifice is established for the twice-born. (Section 1)
Thus ends the third chapter in the twenty-ninth book of the Śrautasūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin (also known as the Pitṛmedha).
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Now, one should maintain the perpetual fires for two days, three days, six days, or twelve days, or as long as one considers there to be a risk of death.

It has been stated: "Without doubt, one who has been suffering from a chronic illness for a long time should cease his regular fires and offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Āyuṣmān, or a five-oblation (or six-oblation) sacrifice consisting of one hundred kṛṣṇala-weights.
(2) He should sacrifice either before the Āyuṣmatī offering or with the Pāthikṛtī offering. (3)

Some prescribe the *pāthikṛtī* sacrifice even in the village. One who has become a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) should either stay outside the village or enter the village with the permission of the king and together with Brāhmaṇas; he may also subsist on forest-grown grain, but he should not perform the daily rites. He should complete his ritual practice before departing for the forest. Some prescribe that the ritual practice should continue even after [the teacher] has passed away. || 4 ||

"It is known that the *prayāja* offerings are for that purpose. It is known that those who die during the northern course of the sun go to the world of the gods by the solar path, and those who die during the southern course go to the world of the ancestors by the lunar path. They teach that death during the day in the bright fortnight of the northern course of the sun at the conclusion of a sacrifice is better. || 5 ||
If one should suspect death during the night of the first half of the month, having offered the evening oblation, he should offer the morning oblation at that very time.
If, during the dark fortnight, one were to lead him through the morning and evening oblations to the bright fortnight. || 7 ||
And one should perform the Darśeṣṭi sacrifice. || 8 ||

If there is an absence of the intended oblation, one should offer to each principal deity with four spoonfuls of clarified butter, reciting the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*) for each deity and then making the offering with the offering verse (*yājyā*). (This applies in all such emergencies. || 9 ||

If, in the midst of an *iṣṭi*, one should offer with the *caturgṛhīta* (four-drawn) clarified butter to the principal deities of the remaining *iṣṭis*, reciting the *puronuvākyā* for each individual deity and then offering with the *yājyā*. (29.4.10) (Section 1).

[Now] if, in the midst of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, one should perform the evening and morning oblations as before and the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, and then bring forward and complete the remaining seasonal festivals (*parvan*). (11)
In the absence of an animal, one should offer a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), curd-mixture (āmikṣā), or a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) to that deity.
It is known from scripture that for one who is dying, there is thus no lapse of the sacrifice. || 13 ||
The expiation for one who has been initiated and then dies has been stated. || 14 ||

In ancient times, there were indeed sages known as Jāyāvaras. While traveling on a journey, they grew weary and failed to perform the Agnihotra for half a month at a time. Therefore, one who is afflicted by illness, or distressed, or on a journey between birth and death, or in times of calamity, should perform the Agnihotra every half-month according to the rule of the Jāyāvaras. || 15 ||

On the first day (pratipad), in the evening, he draws fourteen portions of four spoonfuls each; there is one fuel-stick, a single oblation, a single cleansing of the vessels, and a single ritual approach (upasthāna). In the morning, it is the same; this much is the modification. The rest is as in the archetype (prakṛti). || 16 ||
In the case of the three fortnights, however, there is a re-establishment of the fires.
He either consigns the fires into himself or maintains them; then, on the day preceding the Upavasatha, having churned the fire, he commences the ritual beginning with the Upavasatha. ||18||

If he recites while mounted [on a vehicle]—if one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should travel on a journey, they should follow behind him with the *agnihotra* fire; one should not pass between the fires of the one who has established the fires. As many boundary markers as there are for the village and as many rivers as there are, crossing each of them, the two [attendants] should maintain contact [with the fire]; or else, at the beginning and the end. If they do not maintain contact, they would become ordinary [worldly fires]. And it is known from tradition: || 19 ||

It is known from tradition that if one who has maintained the sacred fires—whether he has abandoned them, whose fires have been extinguished, or whose fires have become disordered—should die, they do not cremate him with the three sacred fires by means of another fire. 29.4.20.
Bharadvāja and others have separately declared the rules for the cremation of the deceased.
From the time of the fire-consecration (ādhāna) onwards, the fires themselves become the sacrificer. || 21 ||

Now, indeed, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "He enters from darkness into darkness along with him whom they burn with other fires than the three sacred fires after he has established the sacred fires. || 22 ||

Wearing the sacred cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), having dug up the ground at the place for the Āhavanīya fire and sprinkled it with water, and having placed the deceased in the sacrificer’s station and laid down the kindling wood (araṇī) at the Gārhapatya station, he churns the fire with the mantra: "Those fires of his who, while he was sacrificing, desired flesh—let them know the flesh of the sacrificer; let them lead this deceased one to the heavenly world for the sake of the oblation that has been set down. || 23 ||

Having remained silent for a while, having filled the ladle with twelve portions [of ghee], and having offered it silently, one proceeds with the ritual beginning with the words, "When he has passed away, the kinsmen... (24) (Section 2).

If the sacrificer should die while the fires have been consigned to the self or to the two kindling woods, one should prepare the fire-places as before; having placed the deceased in the place of the sacrificer and having established an ordinary fire in the place of the *gārhapatya*, the son of the deceased, a brother, or a close relative, taking hold of the deceased’s right hand, causes him to descend with the words: "Descend! Or else: "O Jātavedas, descend; knowing [the way], lead this man to the heavenly world."

"Bestow upon us long life, progeny, and wealth; accept his funeral oblations, svāhā!"—with these words, he causes [the fire] to descend into the common fire (*laukikāgni*). Or, having caused it to descend into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), he should churn it. If the fire that has ascended into the two kindling woods goes out while the deceased is being made to take hold of it, he should mutter this mantra; the procedure for spreading the fires (*viharaṇa*) and so forth is the same. || 25 ||

Upon hearing that an Āhitāgni has died in water, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt, or perform a full oblation; some say that he should offer it wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī). 26.
In this very dwelling, he undertakes the funeral rites for his ancestors. || 27 ||
It has been stated that whether they bring the bodies on this day or on another day, the Agnihotra is to be performed with the milk of that cow whose calf is to be exchanged.

When one who has maintained the sacred fires dies during childbirth, they place him in a vat of oil and carry him away by cart, or having cremated him with fire produced by friction, they place his bones upon a black antelope skin, wrap them in an unwashed garment, tie them to a long bamboo pole, and carry them away on vessels made of clay, remaining pure and self-controlled. Having established those [bones] at the boundary of the village, they carry out the fires and the implements for the *Paitṛmedha* sacrifice. It is known from tradition that if the sacrificer is not present, they should not carry the fires beyond the village boundary; for if they were to carry them beyond, they would become merely worldly (profane) fires. 29.4.30.

When the sacrificer departs on a journey, he goes to his house after entrusting it to the fires; if, while within the boundary, his wife should see the sun set or rise, the fires become common (worldly) ones.

If one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should travel on a journey, he should have the three fires follow him at his side along with the *agnihotra* fire; the one who has established the fires must not allow a gap between them. As many village boundaries and rivers as there may be, they should hold onto the fires while crossing them. If they do not hold onto them, the fires would become common (*laukika*). Therefore, they do not cross beyond the village boundary.
Having brought the fires with their bodies and having chosen a place for cremation as if for burning, the ministers undertake this and the subsequent rites once the deceased has passed away. || 33 ||
Whichever of the two dies first—the sacrificer or the wife—for him the Pitṛmedha is performed in the three sacred fires; for whichever dies later, it is performed with the domestic fire (aupāsana).
If they both die at the same time, the funeral rite for the father is performed together with that for the other. || 35 ||

If one is unable to perform the rites for establishing a wife, one may establish the sacred fires for one's own sake; however, in that case, there shall be no performance of the Agnihotra, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, or any other remaining rites. || 36 ||

If one who has maintained the sacred fires should die from among his livestock, he should offer two oblations of four spoonfuls each with the verse, "The cows have come" (*ā gāvo agman*). If one who has maintained the sacred fires should die struck by lightning, the expiation for him is that he should offer an oblation of four spoonfuls with the verse, "The head of heaven, the messenger of earth" (*mūrdhānaṃ divo aratiṃ pṛthivyāḥ*). If one who has maintained the sacred fires should die in water, he should offer two oblations of four spoonfuls each with the verses, "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa" (*imaṃ me varuṇa*) and "To thee I go" (*tattvāyāmi*). || 37 ||

If one who has maintained the sacred fires dies from being bitten by a snake, he should offer four spoonfuls with each of the three verses beginning, "Homage be to the serpents. If one who has maintained the sacred fires dies from the fangs of a beast of prey, he should offer four spoonfuls with the two verses beginning, "With their fangs [the gods struck] the thieves. If one who has maintained the sacred fires dies abroad and his body is not found, they should burn a thicket of dry grass with his fires in the direction toward which he had set out.

Alternatively, it is known that one should fashion a human figure out of three hundred and sixty palāśa stalks on a black antelope skin and burn it with fires of darkness; having wrapped the joints with palāśa bark or kuśa grass, one should form the head with forty [stalks].

With ten [bricks] he prepares the neck; with twenty, the chest; with thirty, the belly; with five hundred, each of the two arms; with five [more] on each of those, he provides the fingers; with seventy-seven, each of the two feet; with five [more] on each of those, he provides the toes; with eight, the penis; and with twelve, the testicles.

(They fashion a human figure on a black antelope skin); having bathed and adorned it, they spread the black antelope skin within the sacrificial altar with its neck toward the south and the hair facing downward; having laid the deceased upon it supine, and having covered him with an unwashed garment with its fringes pointing northward, the kinsmen sit around and touch him. "This is that [name] of whom these fires are [the attendants]," [they say]; once he has passed away, the ritual beginning with "The attendants... is commenced. || 39 ||

If these are not found, [one should use] young shoots of *darbha* grass or [wood from] sacrificial trees; with these, having fashioned a human figure on a black antelope skin, it is prescribed that they should cremate it with fires. If even these are not found, having dug up earth from the ground and mixing it with honey and clarified butter, it is prescribed that they should fashion a human figure on a black antelope skin with these and cremate it with fires; one should cause it to be cremated according to the rule. 29.4.40.

If, after this has been performed, he should return with the fires, he shall perform the vow for twelve nights beginning from his birth-rite (*jātakarma*) upon emerging from the jar of clarified butter; then, having established the fires with that same wife, he shall sacrifice with an animal dedicated to Prajāpati.
Having gone to a mountain, he should perform a sacrifice to Agni Kāma consisting of a hundred *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces for long life; or he should sacrifice with the *Diśām-aveṣṭi*.
"From this point forward, one should sacrifice with the desired sacrificial rites"—thus it is known; thus it is known. 43. (Section 4)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the twenty-ninth book of the Śrautasūtra of Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin (also known as the Pitṛmedha).
Now, the supplement.

Now, regarding the ritual for a pregnant woman who dies after the *tiṣya* [ceremony]: having carried her to the cremation ground, one should cause a space to be cleared as in the case of cremation. ||1||
Having prepared the funeral pyre, he performs [the rite] in an enclosure to the west of that pyre. ||2||

Having placed her on her back and having drawn a lotus on her left side, and having performed the rite of gazing with the verse "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre," and having looked at the boy, he consecrates him with the words: "May my son live, for long life and for splendor. || 3 ||
Then, having placed gold beneath him, one should bathe the child; while he is still living, he returns to the village.

Having offered the breast with the verse, "That breast of thine which is... (RV 10.87.17), he offers oblations of clarified butter into that stomach with these two sections of mantras: "To him who has a hundred weapons, who has a hundred powers... (VS 16.23–29) and "To Prāṇa, svāhā! To Vyāna, svāhā! (VS 34.1–5). || 5 ||
One should make the corpse free of wounds and, having placed it upon the funeral pyre, burn it according to the prescribed rite.
And the twenty-ninth question is completed.
